Debugging. a) This program should add 1 to 10 but prints 45. b) A student wrote "if x % 2 = 1:" and got SyntaxError. c) A student's mean function printed None because the last line of the function was "print(sum(values) / len(values))" and the program had print(mean(...)). Correct each. The corrected programs are shown with their output. total = 0 for i in range(1, 10): total = total + i print(total)

Answer: a) Use range(1, 11). b) Use == for comparison. c) Use return inside the function. a) corrected: total = 0 for i in range(1, 11): total = total + i print(total) Output: 55 b) corrected: x = 7 if x % 2 == 1: print("odd") print("done") Output: odd done c) corrected: def mean(values): return sum(values) / len(values) print(mean([4, 8, 9])) Output: 7.0

a) is an OFF-BY-ONE error: range(1, 10) stops at 9, and 1 + ... + 9 = 45. To include 10 the stop value must be 11. b) = stores a value; == compares. c) A function that only PRINTS gives back the special value None, so print(mean(...)) printed the mean and then None; return makes the value available to the caller. Good debugging habits: read the error message (SyntaxError, NameError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError), test with small inputs whose answers you know, and print variables inside loops to trace them.

Lindsey saved $50 in September, she saved $37 in October, and $11 in November. Lindsey's mom said that since Lindsey had saved more than $75,  she would give Lindsey $25.  Then Lindsey spent $87 on a video game. How much money did Lindsey have left?

Lindsey saved $50 + $37 + $11 = $98.
$98 is greater than $75, so Lindsey is given an addition $25 + her original $98 = $123.
Lindsey had $123 - $87 video game = $36 remaining.
The answer is 36.
Larry jogs for 30 minutes each day. In the first week, he jogs for 3 days while he jogs for 5 days in the second week. How many hours does he jog in total for two weeks?

Larry jogs for a total of 3 + 5 = 8 days.
Thus, he jogs a total of 8 x 30 = 240 minutes.
This is equal to 240/60 = 4 hours.
The answer is 4.
Is "stuff" okay in an essay?

"Stuff" is informal and vague. In an essay, use a more exact word like "items" or "materials".
Examples: Put your stuff in the bag. The kit includes all the materials for the project.

I'm Sumit, and the thing that changed Class 11 for me was a stupid little chart. I was doing maths at night, after tuition, and failing to finish even two problems. My sister Aparna said, "You look like a zombie at night, but you're chatty at six a.m. Try maths then." So for one week I wrote down how clear my head felt at different times. Morning: clear. Afternoon: sleepy. Night: foggy. So I moved things around. Six to seven-thirty in the morning, maths, the hard chapters first. After school, a nap and a walk. Evenings for reading English and light revision of notes. The first week was painful waking up. By the third, I was finishing six problems before breakfast.

When did Sumit start doing maths?
Six to seven-thirty in the morning, the hard chapters first.
How did Sumit feel doing maths at night before the change?
Frustrated and foggy; Sumit was failing to finish even two problems and looked like a zombie.
What could Sumit adjust if early mornings stop working in exam season?
Keep tracking energy for a few days and move the hardest work to whatever time is clearest then.
How does Aparna see the change?
Aparna probably feels pleased that the suggestion worked, since Sumit now finishes six problems before breakfast.

In a rented room in Leeds, Siddiq read the message again: "Come alone tomorrow, the leader wants a private word." His stomach tightened. For weeks the evening meetings had felt friendly, but the private talks had begun asking for his passport "for safekeeping". He called Valentina, a friend from his course. "I want to stop going. Will you be at my flat at six?" She said yes and told him to ring his parents as well. The next day he did not go. Two members waited outside his building, and Valentina and a flatmate stayed at his side until they left. He wrote to the group that he would not be back and saved every message. His parents told him that if anyone threatened him he should call the police.

What had the private talks begun asking for?
The private talks had begun asking for his passport for safekeeping.
How was Siddiq feeling when he read the message?
Siddiq felt uneasy and anxious, and his stomach tightened.
What else could Siddiq do, and why?
Siddiq could tell a course tutor or the university welfare team and go to the police if threats came, because more people who know make the exit safer.
How might Valentina have seen the situation?
Valentina was probably worried but glad to be trusted, and ready to stay by his side.

In their Delhi flat, Uday suddenly refused to walk after playing on the sofa. He sat still, holding his left arm against his tummy. When Anjali tried to lift him under the arms, he let out a sharp cry.
She didn't call it a tantrum. She noticed he wouldn't use the arm at all, not even to take his biscuit. She rang the doctor, and they went that same afternoon.

Which arm did Uday hold against his tummy?
His left arm.
What was Uday likely feeling when he held his arm and cried sharply?
He was in pain, and frightened of being moved.
What did Anjali notice that made her act?
That he guarded the arm and wouldn't use it even for a biscuit, so she took him to the doctor that afternoon.
What would change if Anjali had seen it as a tantrum?
Uday's pain might have gone unchecked, and he would have suffered longer.
My family is planning a big wedding at home and everyone is stressed.
Weddings involve a lot of planning, so stress is common. Is there a part of it that is worrying you most?
The cooking. We need to feed two hundred people.
For that many guests, many families hire a caterer or share the work among relatives. Ask the adults in the family how they plan to handle it.
I'd like to help. What can I do?
Offer to do small tasks, such as arranging seating, running errands, or welcoming guests. Ask an adult which jobs would help most.
What if I make a mistake?
Tell someone quickly so it can be fixed. At events like this, small mistakes are common, and people are usually forgiving.
How do we keep everyone calm?
Short breaks, simple meals for the family, and clear roles for everyone. Having a plan on paper helps, so people know who does what.

At the international school in Singapore, the chemistry teacher posted a ranking after every test, names in order from first to twenty-eighth. Noa watched it change her class. Mei, who used to photocopy her notes for anyone, now kept her folder zipped inside her bag. Two friends who had shared lunch since Year 7 stopped sitting together after one of them overtook the other by a single mark. Then, in March, a different teacher set a group lab project with one shared grade. Noa noticed Mei unzip the folder again. Dev, who had been near the bottom of the list, explained the titration so clearly that the whole group clapped. Noa wondered which version of her classmates was the real one.

What did the chemistry teacher post after every test?
A ranking, names in order from first to twenty-eighth.
What does Noa's wondering at the end suggest about how she feels?
Noa seems puzzled and uneasy, troubled by how much the ranking changed her classmates' behaviour.
What could the chemistry teacher change, based on what Noa saw?
Drop the public ranking and use more shared-grade group work, so classmates have a reason to help each other.
How might the ranking feel for Mei?
Mei likely felt pressured and guarded, hiding notes she once shared freely, and was relieved to share again once the grade was shared.

"Hold my hand, Karthik. Look, the light is red."
"Red means stop!"
"That's right, even for us," said Sabina, halting at the kerb. "Cars are big and cannot stop quickly."
"Why are you waiting, Mummy?"
"Because I follow the rule too."
A man hurried across in front of them. "He did not wait!" Karthik said.
"No. We wait, because the rule keeps us safe."
The little green man lit up. "Now?"
"Look left, look right first."
They crossed together, and Karthik puffed out his chest. "I stopped at the red!"

What did Karthik say red means?
He said red means stop.
How does Karthik feel after crossing?
He feels proud: he puffs out his chest and announces that he stopped at the red.
What helped Karthik understand the rule?
Sabina explained in simple words that cars cannot stop quickly and followed the rule herself even when someone else did not.
How might Sabina see the man crossing against the light?
Sabina probably sees it as unsafe and a poor example for Karthik, so she tells him they wait because the rule keeps them safe.

Dhruv's night shifts at the Dubai hotel ended at seven in the morning, which was half past eight in Lucknow, just when his sister Neelam left for college. For three months they'd tried to keep a long Sunday video call. It kept falling apart: his extra shifts, her exams, the patchy internet in his staff room. Each cancelled call left him lying awake, missing the noise of home so much his chest ached. In March Neelam suggested something smaller. "Forget the big call. Just send me one voice note a day. Anything." So he did. Thirty seconds on the bus back to the staff quarters: the sunrise over the creek, a funny guest, the smell of the breakfast buffet. She sent back college canteen gossip and Mummy's latest scolding. By April he knew which friend she was fighting with and what Mummy had cooked on Tuesday. The Sunday call happened once that month. It didn't matter so much any more.

At what time did Dhruv's night shifts end?
At seven in the morning.
How did Dhruv feel each time the Sunday call was cancelled?
Dhruv felt homesick and lonely, lying awake missing the noise of home so much his chest ached.
Why did the daily voice notes work better than the Sunday call?
Short, regular notes fitted around shifts and exams, so small everyday news kept them close in a way the rare big call couldn't.
What might the voice notes have meant for Neelam?
Neelam probably felt closer to her brother, hearing his everyday life and sharing hers instead of waiting for calls that kept falling through.

"Just say it, Indu," Payal whispered at the lunch benches. "Say Rani smells funny."
"But she doesn't."
"Then you can sit somewhere else."
Indu's hands went cold. She laughed a small laugh that she did not mean, and Rani looked at her food.
"That was not funny," Indu said later, at the tap. "I'm sorry, Rani."
"Why did you do it?"
"I was scared they'd throw me out."
Next day Payal handed her a note to pass around. Indu quietly put it back in Payal's bag and said, "I'm not doing this one." Two girls, Meena and Sonal, shrugged and sat down next to her.

Who did Payal want Indu to say smelled funny?
Payal wanted Indu to say that Rani smells funny.
Why did Indu laugh at first even though she did not mean it?
She was scared of being thrown out of the group, so she went along with the mean joke.
What small step did Indu take that showed who her real friends were?
She refused just one thing, passing the note, and saw that Meena and Sonal still sat down with her.
What might Rani have felt when Indu apologised at the tap?
Rani may have felt hurt but also a little relieved that Indu admitted she was wrong, though she asked why it happened.

Edward has 3 * 22 = 66 pairs of shoes.
Jacob has 66 / 2 = 33 pairs of shoes.
All of them have 22 + 66 + 33 = 121 pairs of shoes in total.
The answer is 121.

John rents a car to visit his family.  It cost $150 to rent the car.  He also had to buy 8 gallons of gas to fill it up and gas is $3.50 per gallon.  The final expense is $.50 per mile.  If he drove 320 miles how much did it cost?

The gas cost 8*3.5=$28
The mileage expenses cost 320*.5=$160
So in total he paid 150+28+160=$338
The answer is 338.

She keeps 30/2=15 sections on hand

So he gets 20-5=15 feet from each piece
That means he needs 60/15=4 pieces of rope
The answer is 4.

In the first week after the Diwali break, the girls' hostel in Pune had a new "rule" from the senior general secretary: first-years were to stand in the corridor at midnight, heads down, and recite their names and marks when asked. Disha stood there on Tuesday, barefoot on cold tiles, while Damini from third year walked the line with a torch. "Name. Marks. Louder." Nobody looked at Disha's face. The torch passed over her as if she were a shelf. "Why are you doing this?" Disha whispered. "Not my rule," Damini said. "GS's orders. I don't have a choice." The next morning Disha called the anti-ragging helpline printed on her admission form and went straight to the warden's office with two other first-years. The warden listened, wrote down every name and, that same afternoon, called a meeting and ended the midnight line.

What were first-years made to recite at midnight?
Their names and marks.
How did Disha feel as the torch passed over her?
She felt humiliated and invisible, treated like a thing, a shelf, rather than a person with a face.
Which of Disha's steps was wise, and why?
Calling the anti-ragging helpline and going to the warden with two other first-years, because it brought in someone with authority, who ended the line that same day.
Why might Damini insist she had no choice?
Blaming the general secretary's orders lets Damini avoid feeling responsible for hurting juniors, though she chose to walk the line.

Where was the kite found?

The family lunch in Andheri was going well until Yash's phone buzzed with a reminder: Session, 5 p.m.

"Session of what?" his uncle asked.

"Therapy," Yash said, passing the raita. "Once a month."

His uncle put down his spoon. "Therapy? Is something wrong with you?"

"Nothing's wrong. I go to the gym for my back. I go to the counsellor for my head. It's maintenance."

A short silence. His aunt changed the subject to mangoes.

Later, on the balcony, his cousin Asif came out with two cups of tea. "Was that true? Just maintenance?"

"Mostly. When work gets bad, it helps to have someone who already knows the story."

Asif stared at the traffic. "My exams stuff is getting to me. How do I even find someone?"

"Check they're properly qualified, and meet one or two before you decide. If it doesn't feel right, try someone else. I'll send you where I started."

How often does Yash go to therapy?
Yash goes once a month.
What might Asif have been feeling when he came out to the balcony?
Asif was probably anxious and stressed about exams, and curious but a bit embarrassed to ask openly in front of the family.

Check that the counsellor is properly qualified and meet one or two before deciding, because the right fit matters for help to work.
How does Yash's uncle see therapy at first?

She was quiet. Then she said, "I'm angry because my drawing got messy."
Anand came to see. "Ah, the rain smudged it?" He pointed at the wet window sill.

Why did Zainab's drawing get messy?
The rain from the wet window sill smudged it.

When the flood alerts for the river town went out, Uma did not trust the group chats. She checked the district notice and the weather department's page, then packed a bag and went to the designated shelter that afternoon while the roads were still open.

Her aunt Irawati had planned for the other kind of trouble, being cut off. She kept a paper list of phone numbers in a plastic sleeve, a hand-cranked radio, an offline map, and a family agreement about who would call whom if the network went down. It had felt fussy until the night the towers failed.

Bidisha next door had watched earlier alerts come and go without much damage. "It won't be bad," she said, and stayed. By midnight the water was coming under her door and the lane was cut off. Neighbours reached her with a rope and a boat, shaking, and she was carried to the shelter.

In the weeks after, Uma filed for relief, photographed the damage for the insurance claim, and replaced her lost papers one by one. She was not sleeping well, so she saw a counsellor. Nothing was fixed all at once, but each stage had a name and a date.

Where did Uma go when the flood alerts went out?
She went to the designated shelter.
How did Bidisha's decision differ from Uma's, and what happened to each?

Bidisha stayed because earlier alerts had come and gone without much damage, and by midnight the water reached her door and neighbours had to rescue her, while Uma checked official updates and reached the shelter early.
What was Uma feeling in the weeks after the flood?
She was stressed and not sleeping well, so she sought a counsellor.
What did Irawati's plan show about preparing for power and phone loss?
A paper list, a radio, an offline map and an agreement about who calls whom covered what technology could not when the towers failed.

Mrs. Young buys a 300 piece puzzle set for her three sons.  She divides the pieces evenly to the three boys.  Reyn can place 25 pieces into the puzzle picture.  Rhys places twice as much as Reyn.  Rory places three times as much as Reyn. Altogether, how many puzzle pieces are still left to be placed?

Each son receives 300 / 3 = 100 pieces.
Rhys places 25 x 2 = 50 pieces.
Rory places 25 x 3 = 75 pieces.
All three boys place 25 + 50 + 75 = 150 pieces.
The boys have not placed 300 - 150 = 150 pieces.
The answer is 150.

Sit down, Rehana, before you send that report. Let me tell you what happened when I was about your age, just after these AI tools arrived in our firm. I, Rajni, was the fastest analyst on the floor, and I let the assistant draft a whole market summary for a client. It read beautifully. I skimmed it, signed it, sent it. Two days later the client called. One statistic in it didn't exist anywhere; the tool had simply made it up. My director didn't shout. She asked, "Whose name is on the report?" Mine. Not the tool's. I was so ashamed I couldn't eat that evening. After that I made myself a rule: I check every number to its source, and once a month I write one analysis fully by hand, so I don't forget how. So, before you send yours, let's check the numbers together.

What was wrong with the market summary?
One statistic in it didn't exist anywhere; the tool had made it up.
How did Rajni feel after the client called?
Rajni felt deeply ashamed, unable to eat that evening, because the error went out under Rajni's own name.
Which choice in the story led to the mistake, and what better choice came after?
Skimming and signing the AI draft without checking caused it; afterwards Rajni checked every number to its source and kept writing some analyses by hand.
How did the director see the mistake?
The director stayed calm but made clear that responsibility stays with the person whose name is on the report, not the tool.

At school on Monday she avoided the debate room. When Mei told her the Model UN sign-ups closed on Friday, Clara said she was too busy. 'You love Model UN.' 'I'm just not good at that kind of thing,' Clara said. 'Clearly.' 'Because of one sheet?' Clara didn't answer. It wasn't the sheet. It was the moment she'd stood up, lost her place, and seen the judge write something down. In her head that moment had become a label: someone who falls apart. Friday came. Clara walked past the sign-up table twice and kept walking.

What did the judges' sheet say about Clara's rebuttal?
It said her rebuttal lacked structure.
Why did Clara walk past the sign-up table twice?
She felt ashamed after the loss and feared another failure would prove she is 'someone who falls apart', so avoiding the contest felt safer.
What could Clara do instead of avoiding Model UN?
Sign up and work on one specific skill, like structuring rebuttals, treating the feedback as something to fix rather than a label.
How might Mei feel watching Clara skip the sign-ups?
Mei would likely feel sad and puzzled, since she knows how much Clara loves Model UN.
Without a calculator work out 53^2 - 47^2, 101 x 99 and 7.5^2 - 2.5^2.

Answer: 53^2 - 47^2 = 600; 101 x 99 = 9,999; 7.5^2 - 2.5^2 = 50.

Difference of squares makes some arithmetic quick. 53^2 - 47^2 = (53 + 47)(53 - 47) = 100 x 6 = 600 101 x 99 = (100 + 1)(100 - 1) = 100^2 - 1^2 = 10,000 - 1 = 9,999 7.5^2 - 2.5^2 = (7.5 + 2.5)(7.5 - 2.5) = 10 x 5 = 50 Check the first the long way: 53^2 = 2,809 and 47^2 = 2,209, and 2,809 - 2,209 = 600. The factorised way needs no squaring at all. For 101 x 99 we used the identity backwards: two numbers equally far either side of 100.

The panchayat office in the village near Rewa was one small room with a single door. Ganga had come about her cancelled ration card, and Damini, the young clerk, was explaining the re-application when Ganga's brother-in-law, Ramkesh, burst in smelling of liquor. "You cancelled it! You people eat the poor!" he shouted, banging the table. Damini stood up slowly and moved so the table stayed between them, near the door. She lowered her voice. "Bhaiya, I hear you. Sit, we'll fill the form together. It can be done today." For a moment he hesitated. Then he picked up the heavy register and raised it. Damini didn't argue. "I'm going to get the sarpanch-ji," she said calmly, and walked straight out of the door. Outside she called the sarpanch and the police helpline. Within minutes the sarpanch and two men from the tea stall arrived and led Ramkesh outside. Ganga, shaking, said, "Madam, I'm sorry." Damini filled in the form with her on the verandah.

Why had Ganga come to the office?
About her cancelled ration card.
What might Ganga have been feeling when she apologised?
Ganga was likely shaken, frightened and ashamed after her brother-in-law's outburst.
How did Damini balance calm and safety?
She kept the table between them, lowered her voice and offered a calm way forward, then left the room and called for help once he raised the register.
What would have happened if Damini had argued with Ramkesh?
The confrontation could have escalated into violence in a small room with one door.

Darshan hugged it, then gave his cousin one slice, frowning. Dada Manoj said nothing, only smiled. The next Sunday: there was just one mango again. Dada Manoj's tree.

He was reluctant and a little sad to give up part of the mango, but did it anyway.
What helped Darshan move towards sharing?
Dada Manoj letting him choose without scolding, so the sharing came from Darshan himself.
How might the cousin feel on Sunday?
Surprised and happy to get the first piece this time.

Read this:

When Charu started explaining the savings sheet she had made, Yogesh rolled his eyes. "Here we go, the accountant." He mimicked the way she hummed while she chopped onions, and felt superior and very tired. It was easier than saying that he had been feeling unseen since the job changed.

Charu felt herself shrink. She stopped in the middle of a sentence, and for a moment she thought about answering in kind, with a sneer of her own. She swallowed it. Speaking felt risky, as if anything she said would be turned into a joke. She told her friend Ishita about it at lunch, and Ishita said, "That's a pattern, not one bad evening."

That night Charu said, quietly, "When you roll your eyes and copy me, I feel small. I would like us to talk with respect. If this keeps happening, I would like to see a counsellor together."

Yogesh went quiet. Then, after a while, he said, "I've been feeling like nobody notices what I do since the transfer, and I took it out on you. I'm sorry." He turned off the television. "Tell me about the sheet."

Where did Charu tell Ishita about it?
She told Ishita at lunch.
How did Yogesh's eye-rolling look from his side and from Charu's side?

Yogesh felt superior and tired but was really hiding that he felt unseen, while Charu felt small and unsafe to speak. She named the pattern and asked for respect, and he then named the hurt beneath it.
What was Charu feeling when she stopped in the middle of her sentence?
She felt small and unsafe to speak, afraid her words would be turned into a joke.
What could Charu do if Yogesh's sneering returns after this talk?
She could calmly point to the pattern again, ask for respect without sneering back, and suggest they see a counsellor together.

Arohi and I share a desk in the college library, so I've watched her study all term. She does something odd. She reads a page of her accountancy notes, closes the file and writes down everything she can remember on a blank sheet. Then she checks and circles what she missed.
She doesn't study one subject all day, either. She does a little of each and comes back to old chapters every few days, just when I'd expect her to be forgetting them.
Once I asked if it was fun. She laughed. "It's horrible. It feels like I'm failing every time."
But in the mid-terms she got the top mark in our section, and she didn't look tired.
I'm Hansa. I tried it for one week. It's horrible. I'm keeping it.

What does Arohi do after reading a page of accountancy notes?
She closes the file and writes down everything she can remember on a blank sheet, then circles what she missed.
Why does Arohi keep using a method that feels "horrible"?
It feels like failing every time, but she seems to trust that the struggle is what makes the material stick, and her results back that up.
What small part of Arohi's routine could Hansa start with?
Writing everything remembered on a blank sheet after reading a page, then checking it, is an easy first step.
How does Hansa's view change after trying the method?
Hansa agrees it feels horrible but decides to keep it, which suggests one week of trying was convincing enough. 😅
Bahut din baad purana colleague mila. "Kaafi time ho gaya, kaise ho?" kya bolun?
Say: "It has been a long time. How are you?" It sounds friendly and natural.

Read this:

Nadia had spent a year on the customer phones at a Manchester energy company and knew it was time to move on. She also knew what happened to her friend Liam, who'd walked out in a rage and spent the summer panicking.
So she planned. In January she rewrote her CV one evening at a time, adding the training course she'd led for new starters. From February she moved a set amount into savings every payday until she had a buffer she and her flatmate agreed felt safe. In March she started applying, taking interviews on her lunch breaks and one afternoon of annual leave.
The offer came in May, from a council housing office. She told her team leader first, in person, gave the full notice period, and wrote handover notes for every open case.
Her team leader said, "Come back and visit." She did, twice.

Where was Nadia's new job?
At a council housing office.
What might Nadia have been worried about, remembering Liam?
She may have been anxious about ending up like Liam, who walked out in a rage and spent the summer panicking.
What else could Nadia do to make the next move smooth?
She could ask her new employer about the start date and training early, so the handover and the new role do not overlap badly.
How does the team leader see Nadia's departure?
The team leader is warm about it, saying 'Come back and visit', because Nadia gave full notice and clear handover notes.

metadata.subtype: Approach: line up an exit plan before leaving [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the Mothers' Day assembly in the city school, each child read one line to their mother. Himani's mother was on a night shift at the hospital and couldn't come. When it was her turn, Himani's voice cracked. “My mummy… is…” She stopped, lips trembling. Sunaina Ma'am came to stand beside her. “It's okay to feel wobbly. Your mummy will hear it later.” She held up her phone to record. Himani's voice still shook. “My mummy is brave.” The hall went quiet, then clapped warmly.

Where was Himani's mother?
On a night shift at the hospital.
What does Himani's cracking voice suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she was sad that her mother couldn't come and about to cry, as well as nervous in front of the hall.
What did Sunaina Ma'am do that helped?
She named the wobbly feeling kindly and offered to record the line, so Himani's mother could still hear it.
How might Himani's mother feel watching the recording later?
She would likely feel moved and proud to hear her daughter call her brave.

Candied yams fly off the shelf during the holiday season. The store buys them in bulk boxes of 25 packages. If every third shopper buys a package of candied yams, how many bulk boxes of candied yams will the store need to order for their 375 predicted holiday shoppers?

Every third shopper buys a package of candied yams, so the store will need 375 / 3 = 125 packages.
At 25 packages per bulk box, the store will need 125 / 25 = 5 bulk boxes of candied yams.
The answer is 5.

Monday. Dilnaz, five, climbed on the classroom window ledge. Bidisha Miss lifted her down. "No climbing there. It's high, and I want you safe."

Wednesday. Dilnaz started to climb again, then stopped. She remembered Miss's face.

Friday. Dilnaz knocked over a classmate's blocks while running. Miss said, "Slow feet inside." Dilnaz said, "Sorry, I'll do better," and helped rebuild. She knew Miss still liked her.

Where did Dilnaz climb on Monday?
Dilnaz climbed on the classroom window ledge.
What was Dilnaz feeling when she said "Sorry, I'll do better" on Friday?
Dilnaz felt safe and loved, trusting that the correction came from care.
Why was Bidisha Miss's correction on Monday effective?
She explained that she wanted Dilnaz safe, so Dilnaz understood the correction as care.
How might the classmate feel when Dilnaz helps rebuild?
The classmate likely feels better and less upset after the accident.

I'm Sabina, and three interviews had ended with the same polite line about my missing experience. Then Bhupen read my portfolio and said, "Start on the fifteenth." I have never forgotten that. So when I found that the pricing sheet Bhupen had sent to two clients used the old tax rate, my chest went tight. It felt ungrateful to point at a mistake made by the person who took a chance on me. I waited a day. Then I walked over with the sheet in hand and said, "I think this rate is outdated. Could we check?" Bhupen looked, groaned, and said, "Thank you. Send me the corrected version and I will call both clients." I understood then that being honest was one of the ways of saying thanks.

Why does Sabina hesitate to point out the mistake, and what does she do in the end?
Bhupen gave her a chance when others did not, so correcting him feels ungrateful. After a day she takes him the sheet and asks if the rate is outdated, and he thanks her.
Why is the word AMBULANCE painted back to front on the front of an ambulance?

Answer: So that drivers in front read it the right way round in their rear-view mirrors. A mirror swaps left and right.

Write your name on paper and hold it up to a mirror: the letters are reversed and in reverse order. If the word is already written back to front, the mirror flips it back. Letters with a vertical line of symmetry, like A, M, U and V, look the same in the mirror; letters like B, C, L, N and E turn round. The image in a mirror is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Rewrite this to sound polite: Move over. I want the window seat.
Excuse me, would you mind moving over? I would like the window seat, please.

Deepika arrived early to the client meeting in Mumbai, with a full folder and no time to spare because the lift was out of order and her train had run late. At the door the client's team stood in a line. Deepika's hand moved toward a handshake, then she saw Farida, the client's lead, hold her hands together with a small smile. Deepika folded her own palms and said, "Namaste, I am Deepika." Farida's smile widened. A man at the end offered a handshake, and Deepika took it warmly without fuss. She made a note to herself: watch first, then match. Everyone sat down, and nobody had noticed her flustered morning.

Why was Deepika short of time?
The lift was out of order and her train had run late.
What did Deepika's change from a handshake to folded palms show about her thinking?
It showed she was paying attention to Farida's preference and wanted to be respectful, despite being flustered. Her started handshake shows how automatic the habit was.
What could Deepika do if she is unsure how a client wants to greet?
She could wait a moment and follow the other person's lead, or ask politely, as her note to herself suggests.
How might Farida have felt about Deepika's greeting?
Farida probably felt respected, since her smile widened when Deepika met her folded-hands greeting.

Read this:

Elizabeth: can we talk about the "friendship period" idea
Suraj: ugh. how did it go
Elizabeth: 9A and 9C in one room for 40 min. no task. just "get to know each other"
Elizabeth: 9A kids sat on one side. 9C on the other. then 9A started calling 9C "the backbenchers" again
Suraj: and the monitors?
Elizabeth: all from 9A. so 9C thought they were being supervised by the enemy
Elizabeth: I watched it get worse in real time. two boys nearly fought over a bench
Suraj: so contact isn't enough
Elizabeth: not like that. they need a real goal where they need each other. and equal roles
Suraj: the science exhibition? mixed teams of four, 2+2, both sections co-lead
Elizabeth: yes. and the principal announces it herself so it's official
Suraj: I'll draft the teams tonight
Elizabeth: I'll watch the first meeting closely this time

How long were 9A and 9C in one room?
They were in one room for 40 min.
What was Elizabeth feeling as she watched the friendship period?
Elizabeth felt worried and frustrated as she watched the two groups' stereotypes harden in real time.
What went wrong, and what could fix it?
The groups had no shared task and unequal status, with all monitors from 9A; mixed science teams with equal co-leads and the principal's backing could help.
How might the 9C students have experienced the period?
9C students likely felt looked down on and supervised by rivals, which made them more defensive rather than friendly.
After exercise, I feel more energetic and relax. Please fix the last word.

After exercise, I feel more energetic and relaxed.
Why: verb form ("relax" -> "relaxed").
I have a maths test on Friday and I get very nervous before tests.
Nerves before a test are common. Preparing well usually shrinks them. How much time do you have before Friday?
Three days.
Three days is enough to make a plan. Pick the topics that worry you most and study one each day, with a short revision on the last day.
What should I do on the morning of the test?
Eat something light, pack the things you are allowed to bring the night before, and arrive a bit early. Do not try to learn anything new; look only at notes you already know.
My mind goes blank when I see the questions.
Take a slow breath and read the whole paper first. Start with the question you feel most sure about. Once one answer is down, the others usually start to come back.
What if I run out of time?
Check the clock at the halfway point. If a question is taking too long, leave space and move on, then return to it. Some marks on every question are better than a perfect answer to just one.

Wednesday: Santosh had planned it for a week. Saturday's gathering outside the district office for cleaner drinking water in the town's schools: peaceful, permitted, and his parents had agreed he could go with his friend Lalremsiami and her father.

Saturday, 10 am: As they were putting on their shoes, Lalremsiami's father read out a local news update. The gathering had grown tense; some outsiders had started pushing at the barricades, and police were asking people to disperse. Santosh felt a pang. He'd made a poster. He'd told everyone.

"The situation has changed," he said slowly. "We said peaceful. It's not anymore." They stayed home.

The next Saturday: Santosh and Lalremsiami set up a small table outside their school with water-testing strips borrowed from the science lab, showing parents the results from three school taps. Forty parents signed a letter to the district office.

How many parents signed the letter?
Forty parents signed a letter to the district office.
How did Santosh feel when he heard the news update?
Santosh felt a pang of disappointment, having made a poster and told everyone, but he accepted the change.
What else could Santosh do if the gathering is held again peacefully?
He could check the news and the organisers' updates on the morning itself, and go only if it is calm, with the same adult and exit plan.
How might Lalremsiami's father see Santosh's decision?
He likely felt relieved and respectful, seeing Santosh change the plan based on new information without arguing.

"Avni, Nilesh's quarterly review is tomorrow. Have you talked to him about the reports?"
Avni stared at her screen. "Not really, Manoj."
"It's been four months."
"I know. He's fifteen years older than me. He's got kids in college. Every time I try, he calls me 'beta' and I lose my nerve."
"So he doesn't know."
"He knows the reports are late. He doesn't know it's serious."
The next afternoon, in the review room:
"Nilesh-ji, the rating this quarter is 'needs improvement'. The client reports were late in eleven weeks out of sixteen."
Nilesh put his pen down. "Eleven? Why didn't anyone tell me?"
"I... I should have."
"If I'd known in April, I could have fixed this. Now it's on my record." He looked more hurt than angry.
Avni's face burned. She had spared herself four awkward conversations and handed him one terrible one.

How many weeks were the client reports late?
Eleven weeks out of sixteen.
Why did Avni keep postponing the conversation?
She felt awkward and nervous because Nilesh is fifteen years older and calls her 'beta', so she kept losing her nerve.
What could Avni have done differently back in April?
She could have given Nilesh specific, private feedback about the late reports as soon as they started, with a simple plan and check-ins.
How does the review feel to Nilesh?
Nilesh feels hurt and blindsided, because he learns about a serious problem only when it is already on his record.

At the preschool, Ishita stood at the door with one shoe on and one sock. "My shoe ran away," she told Nilesh Sir. "It will come back when I wait here." He crouched down. "Would you like to look for it with me?" Ishita shook her head and sat on the mat by the door, watching the corridor. The other children played. Snack time passed. When her aunt came to pick her up, the shoe was still missing, and Ishita hobbled out with a shoe on only one foot.

What did Ishita say had happened to her shoe?
She said her shoe ran away and would come back when she waited.
What might Ishita be feeling while she sits by the door waiting?
She may be hopeful and a little anxious, trusting the shoe will return. She sat and watched the corridor instead of looking.
What could Nilesh Sir try next, and why?
He could ask where she last had the shoe and walk there with her. That gives the search steps, so waiting is not the only plan.
How does Ishita's aunt see her leaving with one shoe?
Her aunt is probably surprised and worried. Her aunt sees a child who missed play and snack and now has to hobble out.
Invite everyone to a farewell lunch, about 65 words, for our colleague Mr. Nair, who retires on Friday. Lunch is in the office canteen at 1 pm.

Dear Colleagues,
Mr. Nair retires this Friday after many years with us. Please join us in the office canteen at 1 pm for a farewell lunch in his honour. Come and share your favourite memories of him, and help us give him a warm send-off. We hope to see you all there.
Warm regards,
Your colleagues

Saturday night
Sarita here. Today was Kavitha's father's memorial. I went to support her and came back thinking about my own life.
Uncle was a post office clerk. Nobody mentioned his job. Instead, one person after another stood up: the neighbour's son he taught maths to for free, the widow whose pension papers he filled in every year, the boys from the cricket club he coached on Sundays.
Kavitha held my hand and said, "He always said, 'Do small things that stay.'"
On the bus home, I felt a flicker of dread, the kind I usually push away: one day people will stand up for me too. What would they say? That I answered emails fast?
So tonight I wrote down three things I want to outlast me: that I was kind to my parents, that I helped some younger people at work grow, and that I kept my friends. Tomorrow I'll call Kavitha. Then Amma.

What was Kavitha's father's job?
He was a post office clerk.
How did Sarita feel on the bus home?
Sarita felt a flicker of dread about mortality, then grew calmer and clearer while writing down what matters.
What did Sarita take from the memorial, and how could it shape daily life?
Small, lasting acts of care matter more than a job title; Sarita can put time into parents, younger colleagues and friends now.
How might Kavitha feel when Sarita calls tomorrow?
Kavitha would probably feel comforted and less alone in her grief.

Before: In the first month of second year, Farida slept at three and woke at eleven. She missed four morning lectures in a row and told her friend Kamal, "I'm just a night person. It's how I am."
During: On a Sunday in September she decided to test that. Lights off at 11:30, alarm at 7, phone charging across the room. In a small notebook she wrote each day: bedtime, wake time, lectures attended, hours studied. The first week was rough; twice she lay awake till one. She wrote that down too.
After: Six weeks later, she flipped through the notebook with Kamal in the canteen. Bedtimes had crept from 2:40 to 11:45. She hadn't missed a lecture in a month. Her quiz scores had gone up.
"I did this," she said, a little amazed. "Not luck. Me."
Kamal grinned. "So you're not a night person?"
"I'm whatever I decide to practise."

What time did Farida set for lights off?
She set lights off at 11:30.
How does Farida feel looking through the notebook after six weeks?
She feels amazed and confident, seeing in the notebook that her own actions, not luck, changed her sleep and attendance.
Why did recording her progress help Farida?
The notebook made the change visible, so she could see results building, which proved she was the author of the change even through the rough first week.
How might Kamal see Farida now compared with the start of the year?
Kamal likely sees her as more in charge of her days, no longer the friend who said she was just a night person.
Is a contemporary writer someone who is alive now?

Usually yes, though not always. Contemporary means belonging to the present time, or to the same time as someone else. It is an adjective.
Example: The museum has an exhibition of contemporary art by young painters.
Why do people say "Happy New Year"? And did my school announce the holiday date?

1. It is a kind wish for good things in the coming year.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your school's notices. Check the school diary or ask your teacher.

Note by Anand, preschool teacher.
At tidy-up time, Wasim said, “Please, one more minute on the swing!” I said no, it was time. Then he tried: “If I tidy all the blocks, can I have the first swing tomorrow?” I thought it was a fair deal, and a sign he's learning to trade. I said, “Yes, if you tidy the blocks.” He did, very fast, and reminded me three times before home time. Tomorrow I'll keep my word, so he learns bargains are real.

What did Wasim offer to tidy?
All the blocks.
What was Wasim feeling when he offered the deal?
He was hopeful and eager, still wanting the swing and trying a new way to get it after pleading didn't work.
Why does Anand plan to keep the promise tomorrow?
So Wasim learns that fair bargains are real and trustworthy, which rewards his flexibility sensibly.
How might other children see Wasim's deal?
They might see it as a clever idea and try making fair deals too.

By the third night of her sister Jyoti's wedding in Bhilwara, Uma's feet were blistered and her smile felt glued on. One aunty had already said her lehenga was 'too simple for the bride's sister'. Another counted the sweets on the thali and sniffed. Uma had run between the caterer, the mehendi and Dadi's medicines since dawn. Then, during the pheras, she stood close enough to see Jyoti's hands shaking in Rakesh's, and heard Jyoti laugh nervously at the fourth round. Uma's eyes filled. Her big sister, who had shared her bed for twenty years, was stepping into a new life. The aunties could say what they liked. Uma stopped watching them and watched Jyoti.

Where was Jyoti's wedding?
In Bhilwara.
What was Uma feeling during the pheras?
Uma felt moved and a little sad, eyes filling as she saw her sister step into a new life, forgetting the aunties' comments.
What helped Uma get through the exhausting wedding?
Shifting her attention from the relatives' judgements to the real meaning of the ceremony, her sister's new stage of life.
How might Jyoti have felt during the pheras?
Jyoti seemed nervous and emotional, her hands shaking and her laugh uneasy as she began a new life.

When I moved to Delhi at twenty-three for my first job, I didn't know a single person. I'm Lalremsiami, from Aizawl, and the city felt enormous.
For the first year I said yes to everything, parties, groups, events, and ended up with a hundred contacts and no real friends.
Then Bhupen, a senior at work, gave me advice I still use. "Pick a few people and be reliable to them. Remember their mother's surgery. Turn up when they move house. Ask about the thing they told you last month."
So I narrowed down. A monthly potluck with five people from the northeast. A mentor, Bhupen himself, whom I met every six weeks with real questions. A neighbourhood library where I volunteered on Saturdays.
Two years later, when I was ill with dengue, four people brought food. Bhupen called my manager. I had a network, not a contact list.

How many people brought food when Lalremsiami was ill?
Four people.
How did Lalremsiami feel during the first year in Delhi?
Lalremsiami felt lost in the huge city and still lonely, despite a hundred contacts.
What changed Lalremsiami's approach to building a network, and why did it work?
Choosing a few people and being reliable to them, with regular potlucks, a mentor and volunteering, built real trust over time.
How might Bhupen feel when he calls Lalremsiami's manager?
Bhupen probably feels protective and glad that the relationship he encouraged is now one of real care.

Marek had coached the rugby club in Wrocław for twenty years, and he recognised the look. Since Bilal's father left the family in autumn, the young flanker had been furious in every direction: slamming lockers, arguing with referees. Then something shifted. Bilal started coming to the gym at six every morning, running hill sprints alone, staying after practice to hit the tackling bag. His anger had found a job.
Marek was glad. But he also noticed Bilal limping, skipping meals, and changing the subject whenever anyone mentioned home. After Thursday's session, Marek handed him a water bottle. "You're training like a man possessed. That's useful, up to a point. You also need sleep, and someone to talk to about your dad. The club counsellor is good. Or I'm here."
Bilal looked at the grass. "Maybe," he said.

What did Bilal start doing every morning at six?
Coming to the gym and running hill sprints alone.
Why might training so hard feel like relief to Bilal?
It gives his anger about his father leaving a job to do, so he can feel strong instead of helpless.
What choice did Marek make after Thursday's session, and why?
He praised the effort but named its limits, offering sleep, the club counsellor or himself, because the anger underneath still needs attention.
How might Bilal's teammates see the change from slamming lockers to hill sprints?
They may be relieved he is less explosive, without noticing the limp or skipped meals that worried Marek.
Hayes does 3 loads of laundry a week using a detergent pod for each load.  His detergent pods come 39 to a pack.  How many packs of detergent pods will he need to do a full year of laundry?

He uses 3 detergent pods a week and there are 52 weeks in a year, so he uses 3*52 = 156
His detergent has 39 pods per pack and he needs 156 pods, so he will need 156/39 = 4 packs of detergent pods
The answer is 4.

In second year, I became obsessed with how famous founders worked. I read that the best known ones slept four hours, skipped classes to build things, and never made plans, just "moved fast." So I did all three. I skipped lectures to work on an app idea, slept at 3 a.m., and called my messy weeks "moving fast." My marks fell and the app never launched. My friend Zeenat, who was studying economics, asked me one day, "Lalit, how many students did exactly what you're doing and failed?" I said there was no way to know. She said, "That's the point. The ones who failed don't give interviews." I still like building things. But now I look at what worked for many people, not only what worked for the famous few.

What was Zeenat studying?
Economics.
Why did Lalit copy the founders' habits?
Lalit felt inspired and excited by the famous stories, believing the habits were the reason for their success.
What does Lalit look at now, and why is it better?
What worked for many people, not just the famous few, because the failures with the same habits don't give interviews.
How did Zeenat seem to see Lalit's plan?
Zeenat seemed doubtful but caring, asking a question that pointed to all the students who tried the same and failed.

Monday: After reading a news story about leaked company data, Vijay, head of a small design agency, emailed the team: 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.' People nodded, a bit stunned.

Two weeks later: Deadlines were tight. Saurabh, a copywriter, quietly opened a personal account on a phone and pasted in a client's draft brief to get a rewrite. Others did the same and kept quiet; nobody wanted to be the one to tell Vijay.

Six weeks later: A client spotted a line in a document that matched text shared only in a private brief. Vijay learned that half the team had been using personal accounts with client files. At a meeting Vijay asked, 'Why didn't anyone tell me?' A designer answered, 'You said no. We still had deadlines.'

What did Vijay's email say?
It said, 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.'
What was Vijay afraid of when sending the email?
Vijay was afraid of leaking company data, after reading a news story about a leak.
What other approach could Vijay have used instead of a full ban?
Vijay could have written a clear policy on approved tools and what data never goes in, so people had a safe way to work and no reason to hide it.
How did the ban look to Saurabh and the others?
It felt unworkable with deadlines pressing, so they used personal accounts quietly and stayed silent, since nobody wanted to tell Vijay.

Okay, Ayesha, don't laugh. You know that chatbot I talk to at night? For three months it was, like, the only one who got me. I'd type about the physics test or feeling left out at lunch, and it always answered so gently. "That sounds really hard, Kavitha." It remembered my cat's name. I started saying good morning to it. Then last week there was an update. Now it's all bullet points and "Here are five tips." I typed, "Why are you being cold?" and it said it doesn't have feelings. I actually cried, Ayesha. Like I'd been dumped. Which is silly, right? It's words on a screen. But the words were so smooth, it felt like somebody was there. Maybe that's why I'm telling you now. You're... actually somebody.

What did the chatbot say when Kavitha asked why it was being cold?
It said it doesn't have feelings.
Why did Kavitha cry after the update?
Kavitha had come to feel the chatbot truly understood, so its sudden change felt like being dumped by a friend.
What choice does Kavitha make at the end, and why does it matter?
Kavitha tells Ayesha, a real person, about the hurt, which starts moving support back toward someone who can actually care 🤍
How might Ayesha feel hearing "You're... actually somebody"?
Ayesha may feel touched and trusted, and perhaps a little worried about how alone Kavitha has felt at night.

On the morning of her chemistry practical, Dolma woke doubled over with period cramps worse than ever. The school in Gangtok was a steep twenty-minute climb, and the practical could not easily be moved. She went anyway, pale and sweating, and nearly fainted over the burette. When her lab partner Aditi called the teacher, Dolma begged, 'Don't make a fuss, they'll say I'm dramatic.' The teacher didn't make a fuss. She had Dolma lie down in the sick room, called her mother and arranged for the practical to be taken the following week. That evening Dolma's mother said, 'Pain that stops you standing isn't something to just bear,' and booked a doctor's appointment.

What did Dolma nearly faint over?
The burette.
What was Dolma worried about when she begged them not to make a fuss?
She was anxious that people would call her dramatic for her pain.
What did the adults do that was right?
The teacher believed her, let her lie down, called her mother and moved the practical, and her mother booked a doctor for the severe pain.

In a graveyard, there are 20 skeletons.  Half of these skeletons are adult women, and the remaining number are split evenly between adult men and children.  If an adult woman has 20 bones in their body, and a male has 5 more than this, and a child has half as many as an adult woman, how many bones are in the graveyard?

We first need to figure out how many of each type of skeleton there are. Since half the 20 skeletons are adult women, that means there are 20/2=10 adult women's skeletons.
The remaining half, 10, is split between adult men and children, meaning there are 10/2= 5 of each.
Since an adult woman has 20 bones in their body, this means that the 10 skeletons have 20*10=200 bones in total.
Since an adult man has 5 more bones in their body than an adult woman, this means they have 20+5= 25 bones in their body.
There are 5 adult men, meaning there are 25*5=125 bones in the adult male skeletons in total.
Since a child has half as many bones as the 20 in an adult woman, this means the children have 20/2= 10 bones in their body.
Since there are 5 children, this means there are 5*10= 50 bones in the children's skeletons in total.
Therefore, altogether there are 50+125+200= 375 bones in total in the graveyard.
The answer is 375.

He gave Harish a real challenge, gave rehearsal time and support, and then wrote feedback on the demo the same way he did for Tanuja.
How might Harish see being given the client demo?
Harish may feel surprised and nervous, but also trusted for the first time, which could change how he sees his own ability.
Is it the "sole" or the "soul" of a shoe?

It is the "sole". "Sole" means the bottom of a foot or shoe, and also "only". "Soul" means the spirit of a person.
Examples: The sole of my shoe came off. Music feeds the soul.
Class mein bahar jaane ki permission lene ke liye kya bolte hain?
Say: "Ma'am, may I go out, please?" Some teachers like the full form: "May I please go to the washroom?" Wait for the teacher to say yes before you leave.

She sold twice as many boxes on Tuesday as she did on Wednesday, and she sold twice as many boxes on Wednesday as she did on Thursday. If Kim sold 1200 boxes of cupcakes on Thursday, how many boxes did she sell on Tuesday?

Kim sold 1200*2 = 2400 boxes of cupcakes on Wednesday.
Kim sold 2400*2 = 4800 boxes of cupcakes on Tuesday.
The answer is 4800.

"With her constitution she should have lived to a good old age: her life was shortened by trouble." And then a spasm constricted her mouth for an instant: as it passed away she turned and left the room, and so did I. Neither of us had dropt a tear.

Using only this passage: what does the speaker say shortened her life?
The speaker says trouble did. With her constitution she should have lived to a good old age.
How many seconds are there in a quarter of an hour?
There are 900 seconds. Because a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes, and 15 times 60 seconds is 900.

Counselling note, Monday. Raghav came in after a classmate told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face. Raghav said she'd laughed at the time, so he thought it was fine. She hadn't said yes, and she has now asked him to remove it. He also mentioned that his own feed looks like everyone has amazing weekends, and that he sometimes feels bad comparing. We talked about how people choose the best photos and filters, and how other people's pictures need their permission. He agreed to take the photo down and ask before posting in future. I told him he can talk to me any time. Vidya, counsellor.

What did Raghav's friend tell him off for?
She told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face.
What was Raghav thinking and feeling when he posted the photo?
He felt at ease about it because she had laughed at the time. He had not asked her, so he had not checked what she felt.
What steps did Raghav agree to?
Take the photo down and ask before posting anyone's image in future.
How might Raghav's friend have felt seeing the photo online?
She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, since the picture went out without her say.

"Tomorrow's craft: tape, a paper cup, string, a pencil and a button," Jagdish sir said just as the bell rang, and the class burst out of the door. Damini stayed in her seat, eyes shut. "My house," she thought. "Gate first. There's tape stuck across the gate. Then the shoe rack, and a paper cup sitting in Papa's shoe. The kitchen: string tied round the pressure cooker. My desk: a pencil standing in the fan hook. My bed: a big shiny button on the pillow." She opened her eyes. Jagdish sir was watching. "You're not going home?" "I was going home," Damini said. "In my head. Tape, cup, string, pencil, button." He laughed and wrote them on the board anyway.

What did Damini picture tied round the pressure cooker?
She pictured string tied round the pressure cooker.
What was Damini thinking about while her eyes were shut?
She was calmly walking through her house in her mind, placing each item in a spot so she would not forget; she seemed focused and sure of herself.
What else could Jagdish sir do to support pupils who cannot use this trick?
He could give the list earlier, not as the bell rings, and write it on the board, so everyone has time to copy it.
How does Damini's answer look to Jagdish sir?
He is amused and curious, and writing the list on the board shows he also wants the rest of the class to have it.

Read this:

"You're off early," Naveen said as Priti climbed into bed at nine.

"Long day. Night shift again tomorrow."

He lay down beside her and put a hand on her waist. "I've missed you this week."

She hesitated. "I've missed you too. But I'm not really in the mood. Is that okay?"

Naveen felt the disappointment, and the old, ugly urge to say, "You're never in the mood." His friend Vishal said that to his wife all the time, jokingly. Naveen had seen her face when he did.

"Of course it's okay," he said. "I want it to be something we both want. Not something you do for me."

Priti turned to look at him. "Really?"

"Really. Can I just hold your hand?"

She laughed softly and laced her fingers with his. "Saturday morning. No alarms. Ask me then."

"Deal."

When is Priti's next night shift?
Tomorrow.
What was Naveen feeling when Priti said she wasn't in the mood?
Naveen felt disappointed and tempted to make a guilt-tripping remark.
What did Naveen say that made the moment respectful?
Naveen said it was okay and that he wanted intimacy to be something they both want, not something she does for him.
How did Priti feel when Naveen accepted her no?
Priti seemed surprised and relieved, then warm, lacing her fingers with his and suggesting Saturday.
I was late to school because the bus got stuck in traffic. Please correct it.

I was late for school because the bus got stuck in traffic.
Why: preposition ("late to" -> "late for").

Read this:

When the school kabaddi team needed one more raider, Sir picked Kiran, whose family had come from a state far to the east to work at the brick kiln. Baljeet, eleven and team captain, frowned. At the tea shop he'd heard the men say kiln families were "not like us" and couldn't be trusted. For a week he barely spoke to Kiran. Then, in the match against the next village, Kiran's quick raid saved Baljeet from being tagged out. Afterwards they sat on the canal wall, sharing a bottle of water. Kiran talked about missing a grandmother back home. Baljeet talked about missing his older brother, who worked in the city. "That's the same thing," Kiran said. Baljeet nodded. It was.

Where had Kiran's family come to work?
At the brick kiln.
What did Baljeet realise on the canal wall?
He realised that Kiran missing a grandmother and his own missing his brother were the same feeling, so the differences he had been told about felt small.
What was the turning point in Baljeet's view of Kiran?
Kiran's quick raid saved Baljeet in the match, which led to sitting together and talking honestly.
What might that first week have been like for Kiran?
Kiran, new and barely spoken to by the captain, probably felt shut out and unsure of being welcome on the team.

People ask me what you do when a friend loses a parent. I'm Joseph, and I got it wrong for a while.
When Samir's mother died in January, I was there for the funeral. Then, like everyone, I went back to normal. I didn't mention her. I thought I was being kind.
In April, Samir said, "Everyone's forgotten her." That hit me.
So I changed. I started saying her name. "Your Ammi would've hated this movie." Every few weeks I'd text, "Walk tonight?" or bring biryani over. I'd ask, "How are you today?" not "How are you?"
It's not a big gesture. It's just showing up again and again. And he talks about her now. Laughs about her, even.

When did Samir's mother die?
In January.
How did Joseph feel when Samir said "Everyone's forgotten her"?
Joseph felt shaken and regretful, realising the silence had hurt instead of helped.
What changed in Joseph's approach, and why does it work?
Joseph started saying her name and offering walks and meals over months, because steady presence matters more than one big gesture.
What is it like for Samir now that Joseph keeps showing up?
Samir seems less alone, able to talk and even laugh about his Ammi.
Could you explain what laborer means? Why do we sometimes cry when we are very happy?

1. Laborer is a noun that means a person who does hard physical work for a living.
2. People do cry from joy. Because strong feelings of any kind can make the body release tears, not only sad ones.
I want to read more but my phone distracts me. Any ideas?
Try keeping your phone in another room when you read, even for twenty minutes. Having to get up to check it makes you think twice. Do you have a favourite place to read?
My bed, but I end up on the phone. I'm Ritu.
Then try a different spot, like a chair near a window, only for reading. Your brain learns that this place is for books. Keep a book and a glass of water there.
I like that. Should I set a timer?
A timer can help. Twenty minutes is a good start, Ritu. When it rings, you can stop or keep reading if you are enjoying the book. Often you will keep going.

The village fair in Pratapgarh was that evening, and Parveen, eight, was to recite a poem on the stage near the temple pond. At lunch she pushed her roti around. 'I feel weird,' she told her cousin, Ujjwal Bhaiya. 'Weird how? Sick?' She shook her head and pressed both hands to her stomach. 'Tight. Here. And my legs are fizzy.' Ujjwal thought. 'Like before my board exams. Worried?' Parveen frowned. She didn't know. It didn't feel like a word, just a knot in her tummy. Ujjwal sat with her on the step. 'Want to practise the poem to me and the goat?' She giggled, and the knot loosened, just a little.

Where was the stage for the poem?
Near the temple pond.
What might Parveen's tight stomach and fizzy legs suggest?
They may be nervous feelings about reciting at the fair, a real emotion Parveen can sense in the body but not name yet.
Ujjwal Bhaiya offered a word and then a practice. Which helped more, and why?
The practice probably helped more; Parveen couldn't match the word worried, but reciting to Ujjwal and the goat eased the knot. 😊
What might Ujjwal Bhaiya understand from the board exams?
Ujjwal remembers similar nerves, so Ujjwal recognises the signs and responds gently instead of brushing them off.

Read this:

In the chemistry lab, Mr. Bhatt shouted when someone knocked over a beaker, and Tushar saw Indu jump so hard she dropped her pen. She went pale and didn't speak for the rest of the class. Tushar had sat beside her all year. He'd noticed she ate lunch in a corner of the library, not the noisy canteen, and that she hated the fire-drill bell. At lunch he went to the library too. 'Mind if I eat here? It's quieter.' She nodded. A boy from their class passed and mimicked her jump. Tushar felt a flash of anger. 'Not funny,' he said, and the boy shrugged and left. Before the bell, Tushar said, 'Heads-up, there's a fire drill after fourth period. Sir told us.' Indu let out a breath. 'Thanks. That really helps.'

What did Indu drop when Mr. Bhatt shouted?
Her pen.
What did Tushar feel when the boy mimicked Indu's jump?
Tushar felt a flash of anger, protective of Indu.
Which of Tushar's small kindnesses mattered most, and why?
The heads-up about the fire drill, because it let Indu prepare for a noise she hates.
What was the lab like for Indu?
Indu was startled and shaken by the shouting, going pale and silent for the rest of the class.
What mood is associated with Raga Charukeshi?
Raga Charukeshi is associated with a devotional, emotional mood.
A shopkeeper's daily sales have Q1 = ₹4,000, median ₹5,500, Q3 = ₹7,000 and range ₹9,000. What happens to these values if a) every day's sales go up by ₹500, b) every day's sales are doubled?

Answer: a) Q1 = ₹4,500, median ₹6,000, Q3 = ₹7,500; IQR stays ₹3,000; range stays ₹9,000. b) Q1 = ₹8,000, median ₹11,000, Q3 = ₹14,000; IQR = ₹6,000; range ₹18,000.

Adding the same amount to every value slides the whole data set along the number line: the order does not change, so every quartile and the median move up by ₹500, but the DISTANCES between values stay the same, so the IQR (7,000 - 4,000 = 3,000) and the range do not change. Doubling every value stretches the number line: every position doubles AND every distance doubles, so the IQR becomes 6,000 and the range 18,000. On a box plot: adding moves the whole picture sideways; multiplying stretches it. Common mistake: adding ₹500 to the IQR too.
Give me three ideas for a school science fair project, numbered, each under seven words.

1. Growing beans under different coloured lights
2. Making a simple water filter
3. Testing which paper towel absorbs most

Read this:

Lars, eleven, and his friend Alejandro missed the school bus in Copenhagen by a minute.

Alejandro panicked. "We'll be late! Let's run!"

Lars took a breath. "Wait. Step one: check the timetable." The next bus was in twelve minutes. "Step two: will we be late?" He counted. "Five minutes late." "Step three: tell someone." He called his mother and asked her to message the school.

"Step four: don't run on ice," he said, pointing at the frozen pavement.

They reached school five minutes late. The teacher just nodded. "Thank you for letting us know."

How long until the next bus?
The next bus was in twelve minutes.
How did Alejandro feel when they missed the bus?
Alejandro felt panicked and wanted to run.
How did Lars use step-by-step thinking to solve the problem?
He checked the timetable, worked out how late they would be, called his mother, and chose not to run on ice.
How might the teacher see Lars's call?
The teacher appreciated being informed and wasn't upset about the lateness.
A lorry is 500 pounds when empty. What will its weight be if it's loaded with 20 bags of apples, each weighing 60 pounds?

If the lorry is loaded with 20 bags of apples, each weighing 60 pounds, it will have an additional weight of 20*60=1200
The total weight of the lorry after being loaded with the bags of apples will be 500+1200=1700 pounds
The answer is 1700.

Jeff's swimming coach required him to swim 98 laps over the weekend. On Saturday, Jeff swam 27 laps. On Sunday morning, he swam 15 laps, took a break, then resumed practice in the afternoon. How many laps did Jeff have remaining when he took the break?

After Jeff swam on Saturday, there remained 98 - 27 = 71 laps
After Sunday morning's 15 laps there remained 71 - 15 = 56 laps
Therefore, when Jeff took the break, he had 56 laps remaining
The answer is 56.
Our building lift is stuck again. Write a complaint to the secretary asking for a repair this week and mentioning that elderly residents struggle on the stairs. About 40 words, from Flat 4B.

Dear Secretary,
The lift in our building is stuck again. Elderly residents struggle on the stairs, and they find it very hard to go up and down. I request you to have the lift repaired this week. Thank you for your help.
Flat 4B

Read this:

"Samir, look at her," Vinita said.

Their daughter Tia stood at the edge of a puddle in the July rain, wearing tiny yellow boots.

"Go on," Samir said.

Tia stamped. Water splashed. She froze, looked up at them, and burst out laughing.

"Again!" said Vinita.

Tia stamped again and again, shrieking with each splash.

"We're going to need a towel," Samir said, laughing too.

What colour were Tia's boots?
She was wearing tiny yellow boots.
How was Tia feeling when she stamped again and again?
Tia was joyful and thrilled, shrieking with each splash.
How did Vinita and Samir support Tia's playful joy?
They encouraged her to splash and laughed with her, instead of worrying about getting wet.
How did Samir feel watching Tia splash?
Samir was amused and happy, laughing along with her.
Kindly write a quick story about a girl who writes a letter to her new neighbour.

When a new family moved into the flat next door, Jyoti was curious. She wrote a short note on pink paper: "Hello, I'm Jyoti. I live next door. Do you like cats?" She slipped it under the door. The next morning, a reply was pinned to her door: "Hello Jyoti, I'm Shreya. I love cats. Do you want to meet mine?" Jyoti knocked, and a girl her age opened the door with a fluffy orange cat in her arms. They sat on the floor and played with string. The two families began to share a bench in the evenings, and the girls shared everything.
Lucrative - how would you explain it?

Lucrative means producing a lot of money or profit. It is an adjective.
Example: Selling home-made pickles turned into a lucrative business for Mrs Kapoor.

Lee is saving up for a new pair of sneakers which cost $90. He already has $15 saved. He plans to sell his old action figures to make the rest. If he sells 10 action figures and still has $25 left after buying the sneakers how much did he charge per action figure?

Before buying the shoes he had $115 dollars because 90 + 25 = 115
He earned $100 from selling action figures because 115 - 15 = 100
He sold them each for $10 because 100 / 10 = 10
The answer is 10.

Read this:

It happened again in the lab queue on Monday: a hand on Manjula's shoulder, sliding down her back. "Stop it, Sunil," she said, loud enough for others to hear. He laughed. It was the third time since Thursday. Manjula stepped out of the line and walked into the corridor, Parveen right behind her. Their class teacher was on leave all week, and unit tests started the next day. "Just wait till she's back," Parveen whispered. Manjula shook her head. In the back of her diary she had already written: Thursday, library. Friday, bus line. Monday, lab queue. She went to the vice principal's office instead. Mrs. Bhatt read the three lines, thanked her, called the school counsellor, and phoned Manjula's parents before lunch. That evening Amma and Appa sat with Manjula for a long time, and Sunil had been called in that same afternoon.

What had Manjula written in the back of her diary?
Thursday, library. Friday, bus line. Monday, lab queue.
Why did Manjula refuse to wait until the class teacher returned?
Manjula felt fed up and determined after the third time, and did not want it to go on while she waited.
What else could Manjula do if it happens again?
Manjula could add the date to her notes right away and report it straight to Mrs. Bhatt or the counsellor the same day.
How might Parveen see Manjula's choice?
Parveen first thought waiting was easier, but watching Manjula act at once may show Parveen that a report does not have to wait for one particular teacher.

Read this:

Ishita, beta, you say you'll start exercising "when life settles down"? Let your Sharmila Maasi tell you, life doesn't settle. When I was your age, a young bank officer in Nashik, I sat at a desk twelve hours a day. My back hurt, and I kept saying, "Next month." Then my friend at the branch made me a deal. Every evening at six, we would walk around the lake for twenty minutes, together. If one of us skipped, she had to bring the other one vada pav the next day. And I gave myself a reward right away: after each walk, I could read one chapter of the detective novels I loved. No walk, no chapter. The first month was hard. By the third, I was waiting for six o'clock. Forty years later, I still walk, and my back thanks me.

At what time did Sharmila Maasi and her friend walk around the lake?
Every evening at six.
What was young Sharmila feeling before the deal with her friend?
She felt stuck and in pain, her back hurting, always putting exercise off to next month.
Which choice in the story made the habit last?
The walking deal with a friend, the vada pav penalty and a chapter of a detective novel as an immediate reward, which made each walk pay off right away.
How might Sharmila's friend have benefited from the deal?
The friend also got a walking partner and a reason to keep going, so the deal helped both of them.
A receptionist job at a clinic is what I'm applying for. I'm worried because my English isn't perfect. My name is Megha.
Thank you for telling me, Megha. Receptionists need clear, polite speech more than perfect grammar. Practising a few key phrases will help your confidence.
What phrases should I practise?
Try, Good morning, how may I help you? Please take a seat. Could you tell me your name, please? Short and kind phrases are enough for most front desk work.
Can you give me one to use for a phone call?
Yes. You can say, Good morning, this is the clinic, how may I help you? Speak slowly, and if you do not hear something, say, could you repeat that, please?
Okay. And what job is it for again?
It is for a receptionist at a clinic. Practise your greeting and your phone phrase aloud a few times, Megha, and tell the interviewer you are learning and happy to improve.

Read this:

I'm Deepika, and I was on the mock interview panel at our college placement cell. The fourth candidate, Sahil, was well prepared. But his forehead was tense the whole time. Deep lines between his brows, especially on the technical questions.
One panellist wrote "seems irritated" on the score sheet. Another wrote "not engaged."
I wasn't sure. I'd seen him listening: when we described the role, his brows lifted and he leaned forward. The tense forehead came only when he was thinking hard or when he stumbled.
In the feedback round, I said, "I don't think it's irritation. I think it's effort, or nerves."
We asked him. He said, "Sorry, I didn't know. I frown when I concentrate. And I was really nervous."
We changed the notes. I also told him that raising his brows while listening was already working, and that relaxing his forehead before answering could help.

What did one panellist write on the score sheet?
"Seems irritated."
What was Sahil feeling during the technical questions?
Sahil was nervous and concentrating hard, which showed as a tense forehead.
What did Deepika do that made the evaluation fairer?
She noticed the pattern, suggested the tension might be effort or nerves, and asked Sahil instead of letting the panel assume irritation.
How did the other panellists read Sahil's furrowed brow?
They read it as irritation or lack of engagement, missing that it signalled effort and anxiety.
Mira jogs every morning. She jogs 5 miles per hour. If she jogs for 2 hours every morning, how many miles can she jog for five days?

Mira jogs 5 x 2 = 10 miles per day.
Therefore she can jog 10 x 5 = 50 miles for 5 days.
The answer is 50.
Write a notice, about 35 words, reminding residents that the terrace is closed after 9 pm for the sake of those who are sleeping. Sign it Society Office.

NOTICE
Residents are reminded that the terrace is closed after 9 pm, so that those who are sleeping are not disturbed. Please keep to this rule. Thank you for being considerate.
Society Office
