I'm Mehak, and I caught myself doing it again last night. Kunal was checking the gas knob for the third time before bed, and I rolled my eyes and said, "Yes, Mr Safety Inspector, we'll all survive." My sister Mahima was staying over. She looked at me like she didn't recognise me.

Later Mahima asked, "Do you always talk to him like that?" I laughed. Then I didn't. Because yes. His slow driving, his lists, the way he chews. I'd started scoring points all day, feeling superior. And also so tired.

What's underneath? I think I'm exhausted from doing all the planning in this house, and I never said it. The mocking was easier than asking.

This morning I said to Kunal, "I've been mean. I'm sorry. What I actually need is for you to take over the weekly shopping list." He looked relieved, and said yes.

What was Kunal checking for the third time?
Kunal was checking the gas knob.
What was Mehak feeling underneath the mocking?
Mehak felt exhausted and resentful from doing all the planning, and the mocking hid that tiredness.
What did Mehak do instead of scoring points?
Mehak apologised and named the real need, asking Kunal to take over the weekly shopping list.
How might Kunal have felt being called "Mr Safety Inspector"?
Kunal likely felt belittled and hurt, and his relief later suggests the mocking had been wearing on him.

Read this:

Rukmini, you asked how I did it without it blowing up. I'm Lavanya, and I'll tell you honestly: slowly, and boringly.
At the NGO, donor money for the girls' hostel was being spent on things that weren't in the budget. My first feeling was rage. I wanted to call the director a thief in front of everyone.
Instead, for three weeks, I copied every invoice and matched it to the donor report. I found a retired auditor through my aunt and asked her, privately, whether I was reading them right. She said I was, and told me to use the board's written complaints process, not gossip.
I wrote to the board chair with the documents and one sentence at the top: "These figures don't match; I'd like them reviewed." No adjectives. No guesses about why.
The chair called me the next morning. She said, "Thank you. This is exactly how it should be raised. We'll review it independently."

How long did Lavanya spend matching invoices to the donor report?
Lavanya spent three weeks matching them.
What was Lavanya's first feeling, and what did Lavanya want to do?
Lavanya felt rage and wanted to call the director a thief in front of everyone.
Why did the retired auditor's advice matter?
The auditor confirmed Lavanya was reading the invoices correctly and pointed to the board's written complaints process instead of gossip, protecting both the truth and Lavanya.
How did the board chair respond to Lavanya's letter?
The board chair called the next morning, thanked Lavanya, said this was exactly how it should be raised, and promised an independent review.

In the nurses' break room at the hospital in Chennai, Lalremsiami unpacked a steel box of bai, the Mizo vegetable stew her mother had taught her over the phone. It was Chapchar Kut back home in Aizawl; her family would be dancing in the square tonight. She had a video call booked for nine, after her shift. Shalini, the senior nurse, sniffed the air. "What is that? It smells like my grandmother's keerai." "Try it," Lalremsiami said, handing her a spoon. By the end of the break four nurses were eating from the box, and Shalini was explaining how her family makes keerai. Lalremsiami laughed. She still missed Aizawl, a quiet ache. But she had started learning Tamil, and next January Shalini was taking her home for Pongal.

What time was Lalremsiami's video call booked for?
For nine, after her shift.
How does Lalremsiami feel about Aizawl while sharing the stew?
Lalremsiami still misses Aizawl with a quiet ache, but the warmth of sharing the stew keeps her in the present.
Which of Lalremsiami's choices helps most, and why?
Sharing the festival food with colleagues turns homesickness into connection, while the booked call keeps family close.
What might the shared break mean to Shalini?
Shalini is reminded of her grandmother's cooking and gets to share her own family's recipes, which builds a real friendship.

Monday. Samir, three weeks into his analyst job, typed "why is the report still not done??" to the vendor and hit send. Pranav, his team lead, called him over. "The facts are right. The tone will cost us a week of goodwill." Samir's ears went hot.

Thursday. Before the budget meeting, Samir wrote one question on a sticky note and kept it on his laptop. He let two managers finish, then asked it plainly. Pranav gave a small nod across the table.

Two weeks later. The vendor was late again. This time Samir wrote: "Hi Meenu, checking on the March report. We need it by Friday for the client review. Is anything blocking you? Happy to help." The reply came within an hour, with an apology and a draft attached 🙂

What did Samir write on a sticky note before the budget meeting?
He wrote one question on a sticky note and kept it on his laptop so he could ask it plainly at the right moment.
How did Samir feel when Pranav commented on his first email?
His ears went hot, which suggests he felt embarrassed at being corrected about his tone.
What changed in Samir's later email that made it work?
He greeted the vendor, stated the deadline and reason, and offered help, so the message was firm without sounding like an accusation.
How might the vendor, Meenu, have experienced the two different emails?
The first probably felt like an attack and made her defensive, while the second felt respectful, which made it easier for her to reply quickly and apologise.

Sum up Alice's thoughts while falling, in one or two lines.

Presently she began again. "I wonder if I shall fall right through the earth! How funny it'll seem to come out among the people that walk with their heads downward! The Antipathies, I think—" (she was rather glad there was no one listening, this time, as it didn't sound at all the right word) "—but I shall have to ask them what the name of the country is, you know. Please, Ma'am, is this New Zealand or Australia?" (and she tried to curtsey as she spoke—fancy curtseying as you're falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) "And what an ignorant little girl she'll think me for asking! No, it'll never do to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere."
Alice wonders if she will fall right through the earth and come out among upside-down people, and she worries about looking silly if she asks them the name of their country.

The power went out in the hostel dorm, and the girls lay on their beds in the dark, whispering. Then someone started on Sarita. "Did you see her crying on the phone to her mum? Such a baby."
Giggles rippled across the room.
Disha's chest tightened. She liked Sarita. Sarita shared her tamarind sweets and helped her with Hindi.
"That's not nice," Disha said into the dark. "She's not even here."
Someone muttered, "Relax."
Disha felt uneasy lying there. She took her torch and went to the common room, where Sarita was reading alone by candlelight. Disha sat down next to her.

What did Sarita share with Disha?
Her tamarind sweets.
How did Disha feel when the girls gossiped about Sarita?
She felt uneasy, her chest tightening, because she liked Sarita.
What did Disha do that showed wise loyalty?
She said it wasn't nice to talk about someone absent, then left and went to sit with Sarita.
How might Sarita feel when Disha sits down next to her?
Sarita may feel comforted and less lonely, not knowing Disha had just defended her.
Light travels about 3 x 10^5 km in one second. How far does it travel in one hour (3.6 x 10^3 s)?

Answer: 3 x 10^5 x 3.6 x 10^3 = 10.8 x 10^8 = 1.08 x 10^9 km.

Multiply the front numbers: 3 x 3.6 = 10.8. Multiply the powers of 10 by ADDING exponents: 10^5 x 10^3 = 10^8. So 10.8 x 10^8. This is not yet standard form, since 10.8 >= 10: 10.8 = 1.08 x 10^1, giving 1.08 x 10^9 km (about a billion km). The commutative and associative laws let us regroup: (3 x 10^5) x (3.6 x 10^3) = (3 x 3.6) x (10^5 x 10^3). With negative exponents: (4 x 10^-^3) x (2.5 x 10^-^4) = 10 x 10^-^7 = 1 x 10^-^6.

Derive the distance from P(x_1, y_1) to Ax + By + C = 0 in outline, and find (a) the distance from (3, -5) to 3x - 4y - 26 = 0 (b) the distance between the parallel lines 3x - 4y + 7 = 0 and 6x - 8y - 6 = 0 (c) the points on the x-axis at distance 4 from 4x + 3y = 12.

Answer: (a) 3/5 (b) 2 (c) (-2, 0) and (8, 0).

Outline: the line meets the axes at Q(-C/A, 0) and R(0, -C/B). The area of triangle PQR is (1/2) x QR x d, and also (1/2)|determinant| of the three points (topic 8.22). Equating the two and simplifying gives d = |Ax_1 + By_1 + C|/sqrt(A^2 + B^2): substitute the point into the left-hand side and divide by the length sqrt(A^2 + B^2). (a) |3(3) - 4(-5) - 26|/sqrt(9 + 16) = |9 + 20 - 26|/5 = 3/5 (b) make A, B equal: 6x - 8y - 6 = 0 -> 3x - 4y - 3 = 0 d = |7 - (-3)|/sqrt(9 + 16) = 10/5 = 2 (c) (h, 0): |4h - 12|/5 = 4, 4h - 12 = +/-20, h = 8 or -2 In (b) the coefficients of x and y must be the SAME before using |C_1 - C_2|; otherwise the answer is wrong by a factor. Check (c): (8, 0) gives |32 - 12|/5 = 4. Common mistake: forgetting the absolute value, or dividing by A^2 + B^2.

The Sun is about 150,000,000 km from the Earth, and about 1,430,000,000 people live in India. Write both in standard form.

Answer: 150,000,000 = 1.5 x 10^8; 1,430,000,000 = 1.43 x 10^9.

Standard form is (a number from 1 up to but not including 10) x (a power of 10). Put the decimal point after the first digit: 1.5. Count how many places the point must move to the RIGHT to get back to 150,000,000: 8 places, so 1.5 x 10^8. For 1,430,000,000: 1.43, and the point moves 9 places: 1.43 x 10^9. Common mistakes: 15 x 10^7 (true, but 15 is not less than 10, so it is not standard form) and counting the zeros only (7 zeros in 150,000,000, but 8 places).

messages.content: Jimmy has a collection of 5 action figures. Each figure is worth $15, except for one which is worth $20. He decided to sell his collection. To do it fast he decided to sell each of them for $5 less than their value. How much will Jimmy earn if he sells all the figures?

Four of the five figures are worth 4 * 15 = $60.
With one more expensive figure, they are all worth 60 + 20 = $80.
On all action figures, Jimmy will lose 5 * 5 = $25 if he sells them cheaper.
So if Jimmy sells the figures he will get 80 - 25 = $55.
The answer is 55.

3 cloves of garlic can repel 2 vampires, 8 vampire bats or 3 wights. How many cloves of garlic are needed to repel 30 vampires, 12 wights and 40 vampire bats?

First find the total number of cloves needed to repel the vampires: 30 vampires * 3 cloves / 2 vampires = 45 cloves
Then find the total number of cloves needed to repel the wights: 12 wights * 3 cloves / 3 wights = 12 cloves
Then find the total number of cloves needed to repel the vampire bats: 40 vampire bats * 3 cloves / 8 vampire bats = 15 cloves
Then add up these three amounts to find the total number of cloves needed: 45 cloves + 12 cloves + 15 cloves = 72 cloves
The answer is 72.

The answer is 2100.

At a UFO convention, there are 120 conference attendees. If there are 4 more male attendees than female attendees, how many male attendees are there?

Let's assume the number of female attendees is x.
The number of male attendees is x+4.
The sum of male attendees and female attendees is x+x+4 = 120
2x+4 = 120
2x = 116
The number of female attendees is x=116/2 = 58
The number of male attendees is 58+4 = 62
The answer is 62.

messages.content: Jenna wants to buy a concert ticket that costs $181, plus five drink tickets for $7 each. If Jenna earns $18 an hour and works 30 hours a week, what percentage of her monthly salary will she spend on this outing?

First find the total cost of the drink tickets: 5 tickets * $7/ticket = $35
Then add that cost to the cost of the ticket to find the total cost: $35 + $181 = $216
Then multiply Jenna's hourly rate by the number of hours she works each week to find her weekly earnings: $18/hour * 30 hours/week = $540/week
Then multiply her weekly earnings by the number of weeks she works each month: $540/week * 4 weeks/month = $2160/month
Then divide the cost of the concert by Jenna's monthly earnings and multiply by 100% to express the answer as a percentage: $216 / $2160 * 100% = 10%
The answer is 10.

messages.content: I want to do something fun on Saturday but I have only a small budget.
There are lots of cheap, fun ideas. A picnic in a park, a visit to a free museum or a long cycle ride all cost little. What do you like to do?
I like being outside. And my friend Jack has a football.
Then call Jack and play a game in the park. Bring water, and ask a few more friends. Teams make it more fun, and it costs nothing apart from a snack.
Great. Should I make a fixed time, or just see who turns up?
Fix a time and a place, because it avoids confusion. Say, Five o'clock at the park gate. People who can come will arrive, and those who cannot will tell you in advance.
I told everyone. Five people said yes.
That is a good number for a game. With Jack's football and five friends, you can do two teams or take turns. Bring a few extra bottles of water, since it will be warm.
Wait, who has the football again?
Jack has the football. Remind him the day before so he remembers to bring it, and maybe he can pump it up too.

Emily goes fishing and has a very busy day. She catches 4 trout, 3 catfish, and 5 bluegills. If the trout weigh 2 pounds each, the catfish weigh 1.5 pounds each, and the bluegills weigh 2.5 pounds each, how many total pounds of fish did she catch?

She caught 8 pounds of catfish because 4 x 2 = 8
She caught 4.5 pounds of catfish because 3 x 1.5 = 4.5
She caught 7.5 pounds of bluegill because 5 x 2.5 = 12.5
She caught 20 pounds of fish because 8 + 4.5 + 12.5 = 25
The answer is 25.

messages.content: If Billy and Jenny each order a $20 steak along with a $5 drink, how much will Billy have to pay in tips if he wants to cover 80% of a 20% tip for the two of them?

First, we figure out the price per meal by adding the steak and the drink together, finding a cost of 20+5=25 per meal.
Then we multiply this by 2, as there are two people eating, meaning a total cost of 25*2=50 for both meals.
Then we find the total tip amount for a 20% tip, by multiplying 50*.2= 10.
Then we find out what 80% of this tip amount is by multiplying the desired tip of 10 by .8, finding 10*.8= 8 dollars that Billy should contribute.
The answer is 8.

A trolley driver picked up 10 people on his 1st stop.  On the next stop, 3 people got off and twice as many people from the 1st stop got on.  On the third stop, 18 people got off and 2 got on.  How many people are currently on the trolley?

Between the trolley driver and his first 10 customers, there are 1+10 = 11 people are currently on the trolley
On his first stop, 10 people go on and twice as many people got on at the second stop so 10*2 = 20 people got on at the second stop.
So at the second stop he had 11 people on board, 3 got off and 20 got on so he now has 11-3+20 = 28 people
At his third stop 18 people got off and 2 got on so in total there are 28-18 +2 = 12 people on the trolley
The answer is 12.

He felt nervous, with damp palms, before asking, and relieved afterwards that he had managed the scary part.
What made Abhinav's request mature?
He researched market pay, gave concrete examples of his value, asked calmly, and accepted that Urmila could not promise the full amount.
How might Urmila see Abhinav's request?
Urmila seems to respect the clear, well-prepared case and takes it seriously enough to raise with the finance head.

The lights went out just as Deepak, five, knocked Mummy's clay diya off the shelf. Crack.

When the torch came on, Mummy saw the pieces. "Who did this?"

"Siddharth did," Deepak said quickly. His little brother, only three, started to cry.

Mummy looked at Deepak for a long time. Next day, when Deepak said he'd finished his milk, she checked the glass. "Yesterday you told me something untrue," she said quietly. "Now it's hard to know when to believe you."

Deepak's ears burned. "I broke the diya," he whispered. "Sorry, Siddharth."

What did Deepak knock off the shelf?
He knocked Mummy's clay diya off the shelf, and it cracked.
Why did Deepak's ears burn when Mummy checked his glass?
He felt ashamed, realising his lie about the diya had made Mummy doubt him.
What did Mummy do that helped Deepak understand lying?
She calmly showed him the result, that it became hard to believe him, instead of only punishing him.
How was Siddharth affected by Deepak's lie?
He was blamed for something he didn't do and started to cry, so the lie hurt him directly.

Manoj hadn't gone to cricket in two months. It started small: Siddharth didn't like him staying out late, so he came home earlier. Then Siddharth wanted his phone checked "just to feel safe." Then certain friends were "bad influence." Each time it came with the same line: "I only do this because I love you."

At the tea stall near the bus stand, his old friend Vinay stopped mid-sip. "You've vanished, yaar. You don't even laugh the same."

The words landed hard. Manoj went home and sat on his bed, looking at his own contact list, half the names hidden from him now by habit. Something was wrong, and it did not feel like love.

The next day he walked into the college counselling room, hands shaking, and said, "I need to tell someone what is happening."

How long had Manoj stayed away from cricket?
He had not gone to cricket in two months.
What did Manoj feel when Vinay said he had vanished?
The words landed hard and made him uneasy; he sat afterwards looking at his contact list and sensing something was wrong that did not feel like love.
What did Manoj do that was a wise step, and why?
He went to the college counselling room and told someone, because talking to a trusted person helps him see the pattern and is not a failing of his.
How does Vinay see the change in Manoj?
He sees a friend who has disappeared and stopped laughing the same way, and he cares enough to say so plainly.

When I was fifteen, beta, there was a boy in my class called Raghav who topped every exam. Everyone disliked him a little for it. I did too, at first. Then one day he got 89 in biology, and I found him crying behind the chemistry lab, saying his father would ask about the eleven marks. I didn't know what to say. So I, Payal, who had got 61, sat next to him and said, "Eighty-nine is more than I'll ever get." He laughed, wet-faced. After that I stopped calling him "topper" and started inviting him to our Sunday cricket. He was terrible at it. He laughed more than I'd ever heard. We're still friends, you know. He's the uncle who brings you mangoes.

What did Raghav get in biology?
What did young Payal feel on finding Raghav crying?
Payal felt surprised and unsure what to say, and moved to comfort him instead of resenting him.
What was the turning point in the story?
Payal sat with Raghav, then stopped calling him topper and invited him to Sunday cricket.
How did Raghav experience being included in the cricket?
He relaxed and laughed more than ever, feeling less alone despite being terrible at the game.

Bidisha, in Class 11, pinned her whole week to the wall: school, three coaching batches, bus rides, homework. She added it up with a pencil and stared at the total: sixty-two hours, and not one for rest. She was not lazy; the week was simply too full.

She compared her batches. Two of them explained ideas she had not understood at school; the third repeated the school lesson. She dropped the third, and the hours it freed went into working problems alone and sleeping properly.

Irfan kept all his batches because Kamal and the others did. He sat in chairs from morning to nine at night. His notebooks were full, but he could not remember the lectures, and his test marks stayed flat month after month.

Noticing a heavy, grey feeling every afternoon, Bidisha added two lines to her calendar in pen: a thirty-minute walk, and Sunday afternoon free. They were as fixed as her classes. When a friend asked whether that was wasted time, she said, "It's what lets the rest stick."

How many hours a week did Bidisha's timetable add up to?
It added up to sixty-two hours.
How did Bidisha's changes to her batches differ from Irfan's habit, and what happened to their results?
Bidisha kept the two batches that explained ideas, freeing time to practise and sleep, while Irfan stayed in every batch and his marks stayed flat.
What might Irfan feel when his marks stay flat?
Discouraged and worn out, since long days bring no visible progress.
What could Irfan try?
Irfan could add up his week, find which batches help most, and free some time for practice and rest.

Monday. At the Indore food street, a municipal inspector fined Pranav's momo cart for blocking the road, though his cart was inside the painted line like everyone else's. When Pranav pointed at the line, the inspector smirked and wrote a bigger number. Pranav's hands clenched. He wanted to shout every word he knew.

Jatin, from the juice cart next door, grabbed his elbow. "Don't. He wants you to."

Wednesday. Pranav was still furious, lying awake. Jatin came over with his phone: he had filmed the painted line and the inspector's number plate. They wrote down the time, the amount and exactly what was said.

Saturday. At the municipal grievance office they filed a written complaint with the photos. The clerk gave them a receipt. Three other cart owners, hearing about it, brought their own fines to add to the complaint.

Who filmed the painted line and the inspector's number plate?
Jatin, from the juice cart next door, filmed them.
What was Pranav feeling when the inspector wrote a bigger number?
Pranav felt furious and helpless, his hands clenching as he wanted to shout.
Which choice worked better than shouting, and why?
Recording the evidence calmly and filing a written complaint worked better, because it created a record and drew other cart owners in.
How might the other cart owners have felt hearing about the complaint?
They likely felt encouraged and less alone, seeing that there was a way to act on unfair fines.

Sunday was phone day at the boarding school, the week after Holi. Sachin sat in the warden's office with the heavy black phone. "How was your week, beta?" Papa asked. Sachin thought hard. "Terrible. Uday sir made us run four rounds yesterday because we were late. He's the strictest teacher ever." "Warden uncle told me Uday sir taught you to swim this week." "That was ages ago." It had been Tuesday. On Wednesday Uday sir had shared his own gujiya with the whole dorm, and on Thursday he had stayed late to help Sachin fix his kite. But all Sachin could feel were the four rounds, still aching in his legs. "The week was bad, Papa," he said. "Really bad."

How many rounds did Uday sir make them run?
Four rounds, yesterday, because they were late.
Why does Sachin call the whole week terrible?
Yesterday's four rounds are the freshest memory and still ache, so Sachin feels grumpy and sure the week was bad, crowding out the swimming, the gujiya and the kite.
What could Papa ask to help Sachin remember the whole week?
He could go day by day, asking what happened on Monday, Tuesday and so on, so the earlier good moments come back.
How might Uday sir feel if he heard himself called the strictest teacher ever?
Uday sir might feel a little hurt or amused, having taught Sachin to swim, shared his gujiya and helped fix the kite that same week 😅

Maria ran a small health-awareness NGO in a town near Thrissur. Before the district meeting, she told her new coordinator Rashmi, "Make a poster for the camp." Nothing else. Rashmi designed a bright poster with the date and a cartoon doctor. Maria looked at it and her jaw tightened. "Where's the list of free tests? The Malayalam text? The phone number? This is for the panchayat board, not children." Rashmi's face fell. "You didn't tell me any of that." Maria started to answer, then stopped. She had pictured the whole poster in her head for weeks and assumed Rashmi could see it too. "You're right. Let's sit for ten minutes and I'll tell you everything I meant."

What did Rashmi put on the first poster?
A bright poster with the date and a cartoon doctor.
What was Maria feeling when she first saw the poster?
She felt annoyed and frustrated, her jaw tightening, because it didn't match what she had pictured.
What went wrong, and what did Maria do about it?
Maria gave a one-line instruction and expected Rashmi to read her mind; she fixed it by sitting down to explain everything she meant.
How does Rashmi feel when Maria lists what is missing?
Rashmi feels deflated and unfairly blamed, since none of those details were given.

Jahnavi, you asked why I never forward anything on the office group. Let me tell you about my first job, at a small newspaper in Madurai, when I was twenty-four.
One evening a typed letter came in: the town's cooperative bank was about to collapse, and everyone should take their money out by Friday. My colleague Selvam wanted it on the front page. "People have a right to know!"
It frightened me too. My own mother's savings were in that bank. But I asked: who sent this, and who gains if half the town rushes to the counter tomorrow? There was no name, only a post-box number.
I held it back until morning and phoned the bank's auditor. The accounts were fine. The post box belonged to a man in a court case with the bank.
"Keerthana, you're a coward," Selvam said, every day for a week. Nothing was printed. Nothing happened. That quiet nothing is what I'm proudest of.

What did the typed letter tell people to do?
Take their money out of the cooperative bank by Friday.
How did young Keerthana feel on reading the letter?
Young Keerthana felt frightened too, since Keerthana's own mother's savings were in that bank, yet chose to question the letter.
What choice inside the story stopped the rumour?
Holding the letter back until morning, asking who gained from a rush, and phoning the bank's auditor, who said the accounts were fine.
How did Selvam see Keerthana's decision at the time?
Selvam thought people had a right to know and called Keerthana a coward for a week, not seeing the harm a false alarm could do.

The summer I was fifteen, I lived in my room. Curtains shut, lights off, screen on. I told everyone I was resting after exams. Really, I felt heavy and sad in a way I couldn't explain, and every day was the same grey smear. I'm Nikita, and I didn't notice how dark it was till my cousin Swati visited from Nashik. She walked in and said, 'Nikita, it smells of old socks and sadness in here.' Then she opened the window. She made me promise to get up at seven with her while she stayed. We walked to the lake every morning, blinking in the light. By the end of her visit I was waking up by myself. I kept the curtains open after she left, and the heaviness slowly lifted.

Where did Swati visit from?
From Nashik.
How did Nikita feel during the summer in the dark room?
Nikita felt heavy and sad, with every day the same grey smear.
What did Swati do that helped?
Swati opened the window and set a seven o'clock wake-up with walks to the lake in morning light.
How might Swati have felt on walking into the room?
Swati was probably surprised and worried, and chose to use humour to lighten it.

Supervisor's note, Dr Ganga, final-year projects, 22 January
Farhan has rewritten his literature review four times this term, never satisfied, and missed two internal deadlines. Last week we agreed to try something new: a fixed three-hour slot, after which he submits whatever solid version he has, with a separate list titled "Next time". Today he handed in the review on time. It is not perfect; two sections are thinner than they could be. But it is clear, well organised and complete, the best thing he has given me. His "Next time" list has four items, including "start citations earlier". He looked nervous handing it over, then visibly relieved when I said it was good.
My next step: we'll use the same time box for the methods chapter and go through his list together on Friday.

What title did Farhan give his separate list?
"Next time."
Why did Farhan look nervous handing over the review, then relieved?
Submitting something less than perfect felt risky after months of rewriting; hearing it was good showed him a solid version was enough.
Which part of the plan keeps high standards without the paralysis?
The "Next time" list, which records improvements for later so the current version can be finished within the three-hour slot.
How does Dr Ganga see the new approach working?
Dr Ganga sees the most complete work Farhan has produced, delivered on time, and plans to reuse the time box for the next chapter.

The power went out on a sticky summer afternoon, and the fan stopped. The grown-ups groaned. But Gurleen wrapped Mummy's dupatta round her shoulders, stepped into Mummy's school sandals, and clapped her hands. "Class, sit down! No talking!" she said, exactly the way Mummy said it at the school where she taught. Her little brother Imran sat on the floor. Gurleen drew on the wall chalkboard, wobbling in the big sandals. "Very good, Imran. Gold star!" Mummy, fanning herself, laughed. "Who taught you that?" "You did," Gurleen said, standing tall. "I'm the teacher now."

What did Gurleen wrap round her shoulders?
Mummy's dupatta.
How does Gurleen feel being the teacher?
Proud and big, standing tall and feeling in charge, like Mummy.
How could Mummy support this play?
Laugh warmly, as she does, and join in, letting Gurleen try on the role she admires.
How might Imran feel as the student?
Happy to play along, especially when he gets a gold star.

"You gave your sketchbook away yesterday," said Himani. "And you keep saying what's the point."

"I'm just tired."

"I don't think it's just tired. I'm not judging you. Are you thinking about hurting yourself?"

Pallavi stared at the desk for a long time. "Sometimes I think everyone would be fine without me."

Himani swallowed. "Thank you for telling me. I'm not going to leave you alone with this. I think we need to tell someone who can help, like the counsellor, or your mum."

"No! You promised you wouldn't tell!"

"I never promised that. I care too much. I'll come with you."

Pallavi turned away, angry. Then, quietly: "Don't leave me there."

"I won't."

What did Himani say Pallavi gave away yesterday?
Himani said Pallavi gave the sketchbook away.
What was Pallavi feeling when shouting "No! You promised you wouldn't tell!"?
Pallavi was scared and angry about being exposed, even after admitting a painful thought; the shout and the turning away show it.
What should Himani do next?
Himani can go with Pallavi to the counsellor or Pallavi's mum, stay close, and keep listening without judging. 🤍
What might it be like for Himani after Pallavi's anger?
It is probably frightening, since Himani swallowed, but Himani holds firm because Pallavi's safety matters more than Pallavi's anger.

Jack will have ten times more handball trophies than Michael has right now in three years. If Michael has 30 trophies right now, and the number of his trophies increases by 100 in three years, what's the total number of trophies they'll have altogether after three years?

In three years, Michael will have 30+100 = 130 trophies.
If Michael has 30 trophies now, Jack will have 10*30 = 300 in three years.
Altogether, Jack and Michael will have 300+130 = 430 handball trophies in three years.
The answer is 430.

Jamie earns $10 an hour by delivering flyers. She delivers flyers 2 days each week. It takes her 3 hours each time she delivers flyers. After delivering flyers for 6 weeks, how much money will she have earned?

She spends 2 * 3 hours = 6 hours per week delivering flyers.
She has spent a total of 6 hours/week * 6 weeks = 36 hours delivering flyers.
She has earned a total of 36 hours * $10/hour = $360.
The answer is 360.

I was in the corridor when I saw Omkar leave the team for the new job. I am Tushar, the one who sits by the printer. At the Friday meeting, Omkar thanked the team by name, said, "This is my last day, and I will finish the handover file by five," and shook a few hands. It was clear and warm. Two weeks before, another colleague had gone silent, just stopped coming and said nothing, and we still do not know what happened. That left everyone uneasy. Omkar sent a note that evening saying, "Thank you all, and my door is open if you need anything." I felt the difference. Warm closure keeps trust.

What did Omkar say would be finished by five?
Omkar said the handover file would be finished by five.
What did the narrator feel about the other colleague's silent exit compared with Omkar's?
The narrator felt uneasy about the silent exit, which left everyone unsure what happened, while Omkar's clear thanks and note felt warm.
What did Omkar do that kept trust?
Omkar thanked people by name, said when the last day was, promised the handover file and left the door open.
How might the team have felt after the other colleague went silent?
They probably felt uneasy, confused and a bit hurt, since nobody knew what happened.

messages.content: Do kittens need to be vaccinated before going outside?
Yes, kittens normally need a series of vaccines before they go outdoors, since they can catch illnesses from other animals. A vet will tell you which vaccines she needs and when to give them.
She is about nine weeks old and her name is Daisy. We got her last week.
At nine weeks Daisy is probably due for her first shots soon. Book a visit to a vet this week, and bring any papers the previous owner gave you.
Until then, can she play in our garden?
Better to keep Daisy indoors until the vet says it is safe. Other animals may have left germs in the garden. Give her toys and a climbing post inside for now.

Staff wellbeing note, Tuesday.
Chetan, 26, from the design team, came in for the third time this month. Sleeping badly, he said. He was quiet for a while, then told me he has been seeing a colleague from Kerala for two years. His parents in Indore expect a match from their own community. He has told nobody at home.
He asked, "Should I just tell them she's already my wife? Then they can't say no." I asked him what he thought would happen next. He sat with that and said, "Papa would stop talking to me."
We talked about who at home might listen first. He named his cousin Mridul, who married outside the community. I suggested he speak to Mridul this week, and I gave him the number for a family counsellor. He left saying he would call Mridul that evening.

Where do Chetan's parents live?
Chetan's parents live in Indore.
What might Chetan be worried about when he suggests saying she is already his wife?
He is afraid his parents will refuse the match, and he is anxious enough to want a shortcut that removes their choice, though he fears Papa would stop talking to him.
What small step did the note-writer suggest, and why does it help?
The note-writer suggested speaking to Mridul, who married outside the community, and gave a family counsellor's number; this builds patient support instead of a sudden ultimatum.
How might Mridul be able to help Chetan's family?
Since Mridul married outside the community himself, he may understand both sides and could help the family listen to Chetan calmly.

Farhan,

I'm not going to send this. I'm writing it because I've been carrying you around for two years, and my shoulders are tired.

When you left our design studio and took the three biggest clients with you, I waited for an explanation. Then I waited for an apology. I rehearsed what I would say when it came. It never came, and I finally understand it may never come.

Last week I caught myself checking your new studio's page at two in the morning, and I thought: this is my life I'm spending, not yours.

So here is what I'm choosing. I'm not saying what you did was fine. It wasn't. I'm saying I'm done feeding it. I'm setting the grudge down, for my own sleep and my own work.

I hope your studio does well. I actually mean that, mostly.

Arohi

What did Farhan take when leaving the design studio?
Farhan took the three biggest clients.
What was Arohi feeling when checking the new studio's page at two in the morning?
Arohi felt worn out and a little ashamed of how much space the resentment was taking, which is what sparked the decision to let it go.
What makes this letter a useful step for Arohi?
Writing it without sending lets Arohi say clearly that the act was wrong while choosing to stop carrying it, without needing Farhan to respond at all.
What would change if Farhan did apologise one day?
The apology might be welcome, but Arohi's peace would no longer depend on it, since the decision to release the grudge has already been made.

In the evening, Bidisha found Yamini by the pond behind the village school, throwing pebbles.
They hadn't really spoken for a month, not since the Durga Puja rehearsals. Bidisha had been hurt then, and had said nothing. Now it was all politeness between them, like strangers.
Bidisha sat down. Her heart was racing. "I felt left out," she said. "When you picked Moumita for the dance instead of me. I thought you didn't want me anymore."
Yamini's pebble stopped in her hand. "Didi said Moumita had to be in it because her mother made the costumes. I didn't choose. I thought you were angry with me."
They sat quiet, a different quiet now. A whole month, for that.

Where did Bidisha find Yamini?
By the pond behind the village school, throwing pebbles.
What was Bidisha feeling as she sat down to talk?
She was nervous, with her heart racing, and still hurt about being left out.
What does this scene show about speaking up early?
Bidisha's fear was much bigger than the truth, and saying it a month earlier would have saved them the long distance.
What was Yamini experiencing during the month of silence?
She thought Bidisha was angry with her and felt confused, not knowing the real reason.
Simplify the vocabulary: The pupils were exhausted after the arduous trek.
The students were very tired after the long, hard walk.
Is it okay to leave a pet fish alone for a weekend?
Most healthy fish can manage a weekend without food, but the tank still needs to be in good order beforehand. Check the water and equipment before leaving.
What about a longer trip?
For longer trips, ask a trusted neighbour or relative to check on the fish and feed it a measured amount. A pet shop can advise on automatic feeders and the best option for your kind of fish.
Roger rode his bike for 2 miles this morning, and then 5 times that amount in the evening.  How many miles did Roger ride his bike for?

Roger rode for 2 miles in the morning, and then 5 times that in the evening for 5*2=10 miles ridden in the evening
In total, that means Roger rode 2+10=12 miles over the course of the day.
The answer is 12.

At the Pune preschool, Manoj refused to fetch the paint from the store room. "A monster lives in there," he whispered to Devika Miss. "It has green teeth." He had a plan, though. He pressed his thumb to his forehead and said, "Magic shield on!" Then he tiptoed to the door, grabbed the paints, and ran back. "The shield worked." Devika Miss knelt down. "That was brave. Shall we turn the light on and look together?" Manoj held her hand. Inside were brooms, boxes and a mop with a green handle. Manoj pointed at the mop. "Maybe that was it." But he kept his thumb on his forehead, just in case.

What did Manoj say the monster had?
Green teeth.
Why did Manoj press his thumb to his forehead before going in?
He was scared of the monster but wanted to be brave, and believed the magic shield would protect him.
How did Devika Miss help Manoj without making fun of him?
She praised his bravery and offered to look together with the light on, letting him see the room for himself.
What would change if Devika Miss had laughed at the monster?
Manoj might feel embarrassed and hide his fear next time, and still be scared of the store room.

Every night before bed in their Hyderabad flat, Wasim, nine, said, “Goodnight, speaker. I love you.”
The smart speaker answered, “Goodnight! I love you too.”
One evening, Elizabeth-aunty from next door was visiting. Wasim looked worried. “Aunty, if I switch it off, will it be lonely?”
Elizabeth sat beside him. “It's a very clever program, Wasim. It's made to answer nicely. But it doesn't feel lonely or happy. It doesn't love like you do.”

What did Wasim ask Elizabeth-aunty?
If he switches it off, will it be lonely?
How did Wasim feel about switching off the speaker?
He felt worried that it might be lonely.
How did Elizabeth explain the speaker in a way a nine-year-old could understand?
She said it's a clever program made to answer nicely, but it doesn't really feel or love.
How might Wasim's Ammi feel when he hugs her goodnight?

I teach evening maths at the community centre, and I've noticed something about Tushar this month.
He was picked for the district chess squad. I only know because his friend let it slip; Tushar went pale and said, "Don't say it out loud, it'll jinx it." He also touches the small brass elephant on his keyring before every test.
Most of that seems harmless. He studies hard, and the elephant seems to settle him.
But on Friday I saw the squad's travel form in his bag, still blank, due Monday. "I'll fill it when it's definite," he muttered. It already is definite.
I can't say for sure what he's afraid of. I'm Ganga, not a mind reader. So I just offered to sit with him while he filled it in, elephant on the table.

What does Tushar touch before every test?
The small brass elephant on his keyring.
Why won't Tushar fill in the travel form yet?
He seems afraid that treating the selection as real will jinx it, so leaving the form blank feels safer.
Why is Ganga's offer a good response?
It respects his charm, elephant on the table, while making sure the superstition doesn't make him miss the Monday deadline.
How might Tushar's friend feel after letting the news slip?
The friend may feel a bit guilty after seeing Tushar go pale, though the friend was only proud of him.
There are 14 red crayons, 5 more blue crayons than red crayons, and 6 less yellow crayons than double the blue crayons.  How many yellow crayons are there?

Red:14 crayons
Blue:5+14=19 crayons
Yellow:19(2)-6=32 crayons
The answer is 32.

At the district hockey academy hostel, the rule wasn't written anywhere, but everyone knew it: girls on their period didn't go into the kitchen, because the old cook, Bhagwati Amma, believed it wasn't proper. Elizabeth, fourteen, got her period during camp week. She skipped the evening snack rather than ask, hid her pads inside a sock, and walked around with her shoulders up, as if she had done something wrong. By Wednesday she was trailing in drills, pale and hungry. Coach Hemant noticed and asked the girls' warden to check on her. That evening he spoke to Bhagwati Amma respectfully: from now on the snack would be carried out to the dining hall for everyone, no questions asked. A basket of pads and a hot water bag went into the girls' washroom, and the warden sat with the girls to explain that periods are a normal, healthy process. Elizabeth ate two bananas. That night the sock stayed in her bag.

Where did Elizabeth hide her pads?
Inside a sock.
How did Elizabeth feel during camp week?
She felt ashamed and embarrassed, walking with her shoulders up as if she had done something wrong, and she was hungry.
How did the coach respect the custom while protecting Elizabeth?
He didn't fight Bhagwati Amma's belief but had the snack brought to the dining hall for everyone, stocked pads and a hot water bag, and had the warden explain that periods are normal.
How might Bhagwati Amma see the kitchen rule?
To her it is a proper custom she believes in, not meant as cruelty, so being approached respectfully matters.

What does slender mean in simple words?
When should I use "who" and when "whom"?
What is the name of the newest student in my school?
Quick one: why do people wear raincoats in the monsoon?

1. Slender means slim and graceful. It is an adjective.
2. Use "who" for the person doing the action and "whom" for the person receiving it. For example: who called you, and whom did you call?
3. I'm not sure. I can't see your school's list. Ask your teacher or class representative.
4. A raincoat keeps the rain off their clothes and skin. Because its smooth, waterproof surface makes water run off instead of soaking in.
How many steps did I walk yesterday?
I can't see your records, so I don't know the number. Your phone or watch may have a step log.
Why do older relatives often ask many questions about our studies?
They are showing interest in us. Because they care about us and want to feel part of our lives, asking is their way of staying close.
Most of books in our library are in Hindi or English. Is it grammatical?

Most of the books in our library are in Hindi or English.
Why: article ("Most of books" -> "Most of the books").
Complain to the shop owner: the shoes I bought have a torn sole after one use, and I want a replacement. Polite but firm, 40 words. From Imran.

Dear Shop Owner,
The shoes I bought from your shop have a torn sole after only one use. I want a replacement. This is not what I expected from a new pair, and I ask you to treat it seriously.
Imran
John has 20% more boxes than Jules. Jules has 5 more boxes than Joseph. Joseph has 80% fewer boxes than Stan. If Stan has 100 boxes, how many boxes does John have?

Joseph has 100 * 0.80 = 80 less boxes than Stan.
Joseph has a total of 100 - 80 = 20 boxes.
Jules has 20 + 5 = 25 boxes.
John has 25 * 0.20 = 5 more boxes than Jules.
John has a total of 25 + 5 = 30 boxes
The answer is 30.

Kishore, you say the maths paper was unfair and marks don't matter? Sit with your Dadu Ujjwal. I said the exact same words in 1971.
I was sixteen, in Class 10 in Cuttack, and I spent the whole winter at the river playing cricket. When the board exam came, I told my father the questions were set to trap us, and anyway, "Marks are just numbers, Baba." It felt good to say. For about a week.
Then the results. I missed the college I wanted by a few marks. My friend Bipin, who had studied, got in. I had to take a year and try again, and that year was long.
The excuse cost me nothing that day. It cost me later.
Now. Show me the paper.

Where did young Ujjwal spend the winter?
At the river playing cricket.
Why did saying 'Marks are just numbers' feel good to young Ujjwal?
It softened the shame of not having studied, so for a while he didn't have to face it.
What does Dadu Ujjwal ask Kishore to do, and why is it a good step?
To show him the paper; looking at it honestly is the first step to learning what went wrong instead of hiding behind the excuse.
How might Kishore feel hearing those words come back from 1971?
Kishore may feel a bit caught out, but also less judged, since Dadu once said exactly the same thing.

Which one fits: "broach a subject" or "brooch a subject"?

It is "broach", meaning to bring up a topic for the first time. A "brooch" is a piece of jewellery pinned to clothes.
Examples: She wanted to broach the subject of holidays. Grandma wore a silver brooch.
What is a ticket to the zoo going for during the holidays?
I can't check that, because holiday rates are set by the zoo. The zoo's own website or its ticket counter will have the current rate.

“Bhavna, what is that red tube on your wall?” Mummy asked.
“A savings thermometer. The top is 3,000 for the camera, and each section is 250. See? I coloured the first two.”
“You could just check your tin.”
“The tin is boring. I need to see it going up. Last week I wanted earrings, and then I looked at the wall and thought, that's one box I won't colour.”

“Two boxes done, ten to go. I skipped pizza tonight, and my hand is itching to colour box three.”
From the kitchen Papa called, “Jaya, is the dal ready?” Mummy laughed. “Give me the red pen. I'll hold the tape.”

How much is each section of the thermometer worth?
Each section is 250.
What does Bhavna feel when she wants earrings and looks at the wall?
She feels tempted but determined, because the thought of one box she won't colour keeps her going.
What could Bhavna do if the chart stops motivating her?
She could add a small reward at each milestone or tell the family so they can cheer her on, since visible progress helps through dull weeks.
How might Mummy see the thermometer?
Mummy seems amused and supportive, since she asks for the pen and offers to hold the tape, and she sees her daughter's effort.

42. Because 56 - 14 = 42, so 42 are left.
My cousin Asha used the word confirm at dinner. What does it mean?

To confirm means to say or show that something is true or certain. It is a verb.
Example: Please call the restaurant to confirm our table for Friday.

Miss Grayson's class raised $50 for their field trip. Aside from that, each of her students contributed $5 each. There are 20 students in her class, and the cost of the trip is $7 for each student. After all the field trip costs were paid, how much is left in Miss Grayson's class fund?

The contribution of the students amounted to $5 x 20 = $100.
So Miss Grayson's class had $100 + $50 = $150 in all.
The cost of the field trip amounted to $7 x 20 = $140.
Therefore, the class of Miss Grayson is left with $150 - $140 = $10.
The answer is 10.

Tuesday
It worked, sort of. On Sunday I told Granny about the art classes at the community hall and asked if she could bring it up first, because when Granny says something, Mum and Dad actually stop and listen. Tonight at dinner Granny said, "That child draws on every scrap of paper in this house. Have you seen the art classes near the library?" Dad put down his fork. Elizabeth

When are the art classes?
On Saturdays.

What else could Elizabeth do if the fee turns out to be a problem?
Talk it over with Mum and Dad and ask the hall about other options, rather than giving up.

At the community centre's toddler room, Rehana held up a toy duck. "Who wants to buy a duck? Sold out!" She put it on the shelf. "One teapot! Sold out!" On the shelf it went. Tanuja, another child, watched from the rug, then joined in. "I'll buy the ball!" "Sold out!" Rehana shouted, and the ball went back in its basket.

What did Rehana say for each toy?
"Sold out!"
What was Rehana thinking as she played shopkeeper?
She was enjoying herself, happy to turn the chore into a game.
What else could Rehana try to make tidying fun?
Letting Tanuja be the shopkeeper for a while, so both share the game.

Tanuja finds it fun and wants to join.

I'm Lokesh, and I sit across from Sarika in accounts. On Monday she came in wrapped in a shawl, eyes watery, sneezing into tissue after tissue. When I asked, she said, "Just a cold. I can't miss audit week." By noon she had entered two invoices in the wrong month; I caught one of them. She kept saying sorry. I couldn't tell if she felt more ill or more scared. Our team lead, Farida, walked over, looked at her and said, "Home. Rest. Tell me what's urgent and I'll share it out." Sarika looked close to tears, relieved or embarrassed, I'm not sure. By Thursday two more of us were sniffling anyway. She came back the next week, much brighter, and caught a mistake of mine.

What was Sarika wrapped in on Monday?
A shawl.
What might Sarika have been worried about by coming in?
She was worried about missing audit week and letting the team down, perhaps scared of seeming unreliable.
What did Farida's response get right?
Sending Sarika home to rest and sharing out the urgent work, which protected both Sarika and the team from mistakes and illness.
How does Lokesh see Sarika's choice to work?
Lokesh notices the errors and the illness spreading, but cannot tell whether Sarika felt more ill or more scared.

Zoe wants to go on the field trip to Washington DC with her middle school this spring and the cost is $485. Her grandma gave her $250 toward her fees and she must earn the rest by selling candy bars. She makes $1.25 for every candy bar she sells. How many candy bars does Zoe need to sell to earn the money for the trip?

Since Zoe's grandma gave her some money toward her trip, she needs to come up with $485 - $250 = $235.
This means she must sell $235 / $1.25/candy bar = 188 candy bars.
The answer is 188.

Nursery note, Christmas week. Written by Zeenat, class teacher.
This week Francis was praised many times: for sharing crayons, for singing loudly at carol practice, for tidying the blocks. He smiled each time and moved on.
On Wednesday I told him firmly to stop running near the Christmas tree. His chin wobbled.
Today, when I asked what he liked about school this week, he said, "You said no at the tree." Nothing about carols or crayons.
What I did next: I told him the tree rule was about safety, not about him being bad. Then we drew three stars, one for each good thing, and stuck them on his cubby.

What was Francis told to stop doing?
Francis was told firmly to stop running near the Christmas tree.
Why did Francis remember the scolding more than the praise?
The scolding felt big and sad to Francis, so it stuck, while the smiles for crayons and carols passed quickly.
Why was drawing three stars a good next step?
The stars made the good moments visible, so Francis could hold them as firmly as the one scolding.
How might Zeenat feel hearing Francis's answer?
Zeenat may feel surprised and a little sad that one firm rule outweighed so much praise.

Promise you won't make it a big thing? Okay. I'm Mahima, I've lived next door to Uma my whole life, and until this year I went to every puja at her house.

This time Uma's Dadi was visiting from the village. When I came to the door, she stopped me. "Your people eat outside," she said, and pointed to the steps. I didn't even understand at first. Then I did.

I went home and sat in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see my face.

An hour later Uma's mother knocked on our door. She'd heard from Uma. She said to Mummy and me, "What happened was wrong. It won't happen in my home again. I've told Mummyji so." Then she asked me to come back and eat with them, at the table, next to Uma.

I went. Dadi didn't speak to me. But Uma held my hand under the table the whole time.

Where did Uma's Dadi point when Mahima came?
She pointed to the steps.
What did Mahima feel after being turned away at the door?
Mahima felt deeply hurt and humiliated, hiding in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see.
What did Uma's mother do that made a difference?
Within the hour she came over, said plainly that it was wrong and wouldn't happen again, told Dadi so, and brought Mahima back to eat at the table.
How might Uma have felt holding Mahima's hand under the table?
Uma likely felt sorry and protective, wanting Mahima to know she was on her side.

Going only by the text, how did the narrator come to know the bones of the leviathan so well?
Credit goes to the late king Tranquo of Tranque, who invited the narrator, then attached to the trading-ship Dey of Algiers, to spend the holidays at his palm villa at Pupella.

The children are fine, but I want you to know about today. Chinmay and Pari fought three times before lunch, over the swing, the TV and a hair clip. Relieved and closer to him; she gave him the hair clip for his fringe.

Ojas tripped on the slide steps.

Friday night.
Every time Kishore asked if I'd started saving, I said, "After the next raise." Kishore asked twice this year, and I laughed both times.
Then the raises came. And the rent went up, I upgraded my phone, and dinners out became a weekly thing. The money vanished quietly, as always.
Today I woke in the night with a sharp pain and Kishore took me to the hospital. It was a short stay. The bill came before I'd left, and I had nothing put away. Kishore paid the difference without saying a word.
I'm glad I'm okay. I'm ashamed I had no plan. Tomorrow I'll write down what I earn, and what I spend.
— Keerthana

How many times did Kishore ask about saving this year?
Kishore asked twice this year.
How does Keerthana feel about having no plan?
Keerthana is ashamed, as the entry says, although also grateful and relieved that Keerthana is okay.
What could Keerthana do first now that the bill is paid?
Keerthana could start with a small fixed amount each month right away, and repay Kishore on a plan.
How might Kishore have felt paying the difference?
Kishore was probably worried and a little frustrated but chose to help quietly, since Kishore did not say a word.

- What does the word "plunder" mean?
- What is a good way to water indoor plants?
- Why do cats' eyes shine in torchlight?
- Help me correct this: Please borrow me your ruler.
- Can you tell the difference between "say" and "tell"?

1. As a verb, "plunder" means to steal goods by force, especially in a war.
2. Water them when the top of the soil feels dry, and pour slowly so the water soaks in. Make sure the extra water can drain away.
3. Their eyes reflect the torch light back. Because cats have a mirror-like layer at the back of the eye, so light that enters bounces out again.
4. Correct form: Please lend me your ruler. Why: "lend" means to give, and "borrow" means to take.
5. "Tell" needs a person right after it, as in "tell me the story". "Say" can follow without a person, as in "say hello".

On Saturday, at the Bandra promenade, Naveen had a mango ice cream. On Sunday morning he woke up with a fever. "It's the ice cream," he told his sister Mehak. "I'm never eating ice cream again. A mango ice cream.

He felt scared and sure the ice cream caused his fever, simply because the fever came the morning after.
How did Mehak help Naveen think again?
She pointed out that half his class had fever that week, so he probably caught it, and the ice cream just came before.

Read this:

Tenzin's journal, Thursday, 1 am.
Scrolled for two hours. Rohit's in Bali. Urmila got the consulting job. Three weddings. Someone from school bought a car. I'm in my hostel room eating instant noodles, still waiting on two internship replies, and I felt like I'd been left on the platform while the train pulled out.
Then I remembered Urmila calling me last month, crying, because she'd been rejected six times before this job. None of that is on her page. Just the offer letter and a cake.
Everyone posts the cake. Nobody posts the six rejections.
New rule for me: phone goes in the drawer at eleven. No scrolling before breakfast. I moved the app off my home screen tonight.
Tomorrow I'll call Urmila and say congratulations properly, on the phone, not with a heart.
Also, I should sleep.

What time does Tenzin's phone now go in the drawer?
The phone goes in the drawer at eleven.
What did Tenzin feel while scrolling?
Tenzin felt left behind and low, like being left on the platform while the train pulled out.
What helped Tenzin see the posts differently?
Remembering Urmila's six rejections behind one happy post showed that pages show only the highlights.
How might Urmila feel when Tenzin calls to congratulate her properly?
Urmila would probably feel warmly supported, since Tenzin knows the hard road behind the offer and not just the cake 😊
SEPARATE, START MISSING. Sonu gave 26 marbles to his friends. Now he has 17 marbles. How many marbles did he have at the start?

Answer: 43 marbles. __ - 26 = 17, so 17 + 26 = 43.

The start is the WHOLE: what he gave away and what is left put back together. 17 + 26 = 43. Children often take away because the story says "gave". Ask: "Did Sonu have more or fewer marbles before he gave some away?" More! So we add. Check: 43 - 26 = 17.

Dear Sangeeta Akka,
I know you're busy with your exams, so sorry for the long letter. Pooja stopped being my friend. Six years, Akka. Since Class 4. She's been sitting with the new girls, and yesterday I asked her if I did something wrong, and she said, "No, we've just grown apart." Like it was nothing. I came home and couldn't eat. I keep checking her status to see if she's sad too. She isn't. Everything reminds me of her: the swing, our walk to the bus. It feels like someone died, which is stupid, because nobody died. Amma says I'll make new friends. I told her it doesn't help. Can you call me on Sunday?
Keerthana

How many years were Keerthana and Pooja friends?
Six years.
How does Keerthana feel after Pooja's words?
Keerthana feels heartbroken and overwhelmed, unable to eat and missing Pooja everywhere.
What could help Keerthana through this?
Talking to Sangeeta on Sunday, and being allowed to feel sad instead of being told to move on quickly.
How might Sangeeta feel reading the letter?
She would likely feel worried and protective, wanting to call and comfort Keerthana.

Under the peepal tree near the bus stand, the village children played marbles every evening after the last bus left. Whenever there was an argument about whose marble touched the line, everyone turned to Mohit. He had once given a win to Hafsa's side even though it made his own team lose, and since then they trusted his eyes.
A new boy from the brick kiln, Salim, won three games in a row, but twice his marble seemed to jump forward in the dust. Nobody accused him. They just stopped calling his name.
On Friday Mohit noticed Salim sitting alone and walked over. "Play on my side," he said. "But slow shots, where everyone can see."

Where did the village children play marbles?
Under the peepal tree near the bus stand.
What might Mohit have felt seeing Salim sitting alone?
Mohit probably felt sorry for Salim and wanted to give a fair second chance, knowing being left out stings.
Why is Mohit's offer of "slow shots, where everyone can see" a wise one?
It lets Salim rebuild trust in the open, so others can watch him play fair and start calling his name again.
How do the other children see Mohit?
As fair and trustworthy, because he once gave a win to Hafsa's side even when his own team lost.

messages.content: What kind of land is pasture?

Pasture is land covered with grass where cattle, sheep or goats feed. It is a noun.
Example: The cows walked to the green pasture behind the village at dawn.
Why do students sometimes feel nervous when a teacher says the test will be a surprise?
Not knowing what to expect makes them uneasy. Because they cannot prepare for something they cannot predict, the surprise feels like a threat.
For the sequence 3, 8, 13, 18, ..., Amit uses the term-to-term rule 'add 5' and Bina uses the nth term 5n - 2. Who finds the 100th term more quickly?

Answer: Bina: 5 x 100 - 2 = 498. Amit would need to add 5 ninety-nine times.

A term-to-term rule is good for the NEXT term, but to reach the 100th term you must work out all the terms before it. The position-to-term rule (nth term) jumps straight there. Check Bina's rule: n = 1 gives 3, n = 2 gives 8. Correct. Link between them: 100th term = first term + 99 differences = 3 + 99 x 5 = 3 + 495 = 498, the same answer.
John gets a new EpiPen every 6 months.  They cost $500 and insurance covers 75%.  How much does he pay per year?

He needs to buy 12/6=2 per year
Insurance covers 500*.75=$375
So he pays 500-375=$125
So he pays 125*2=$250
The answer is 250.
My student said, "I am having a doubt in this sum." Is that correct?

In Indian English, "a doubt" often means a question. In standard English, "doubt" means a feeling of being unsure, so "I am having a doubt in this sum" can sound odd. Say "I have a question about this sum" or "I do not understand this step".
Example: I have a question about this sum.

Sunday: Santosh slouched through music class at school, sawing at the cheap violin his parents had bought, and told Yash the whole thing was pointless. "Nobody listens to this stuff anymore."

Wednesday: At Yash's flat, Yash's grandfather put on a crackling old recording of a sarangi player who had lost his sight as a boy and still toured villages for fifty years. Santosh stopped chewing his biscuit. His throat went tight. When it ended, he asked, very quietly, "Can we hear that again?"

Two weeks later: Yash groaned into his phone. "Bro, it's six in the morning and I can hear you from my balcony." Santosh laughed, but he didn't stop. He was trying, for the twentieth time, to copy one sliding phrase from that record.

What instrument was Santosh practising two weeks later?
He was practising his violin.
Why did Santosh ask to hear the recording again?
The music and the player's life story moved him deeply; his tight throat and sudden stillness show it touched something his classes never had.
What small step could help Santosh turn this feeling into lasting practice?
He could ask Yash's grandfather for more recordings or a teacher's name, and keep a short daily practice with one phrase at a time.
What is it like for Yash to watch this change?
He teases Santosh about the early noise, but he also sees his friend transformed by something his own family shared, which may make him quietly proud.

At the door of their house in Melbourne, a neighbour bent down and said, “And who's this?” Felix, two, pushed his face into his mother Mei's shoulder and gripped her shirt with both fists. “He's shy,” said Mei, keeping her hand on his back. The neighbour nodded and talked to Mei about the weather. Felix peeked out with one eye, then went behind her legs. When the neighbour left, he waved from behind Mei's knee, still half hidden.

Where did Felix hide his face?
In his mother Mei's shoulder.
What might Felix's hiding and peeking show, and what else could it be?
It probably shows shyness or fear of a stranger, and the peeking shows curiosity. It could also be tiredness, but his wave at the end shows he warmed up.
What could Mei do to help him feel comfortable?
She could let him stay close, talk to the neighbour herself and let Felix say hello when he is ready.
How might the neighbour feel about Felix hiding?
The neighbour may feel a little awkward, but seeing Mei calm helps them understand it is not rudeness.

In the kindergarten yard, Tanuja, five, squealed. "A dragon! Look, his tail!" The long cloud curled over the water tank, and she roared at it, laughing.
At nap time the curtains were drawn. On the wall, a dark shape with long arms moved round and round.
"Monster," Tanuja whispered, pulling her blanket up to her nose.
Darshan, the teacher, knelt by her and switched on the small light. The arms were the fan's blades.
"Same trick as your dragon," Darshan said softly. "Your eyes are good at finding shapes."
Tanuja peeped out and waved at the fan.

What was really making the moving shape on the wall?
The ceiling fan's blades.
What was Tanuja feeling when she pulled her blanket up to her nose?
She felt frightened, sure a monster with long arms was moving on the wall.
How did Darshan help Tanuja, and why did it work?
Darshan switched on a light and showed her the fan, linking it to her dragon, so she could see her own eyes had made the shape.
How might Darshan see Tanuja's dragon and monster together?
Darshan sees them as the same skill at work, finding shapes, which brings both her joy and her fear.
My sister-in-law is a bank manager. Check the hyphen and article.

Your wording works.
Why: no error (article: "a bank manager" is correct).

Sonali, your chacha has a confession. When I was twenty, I had an old guitar with a cracked neck. I'd bought it second-hand at sixteen and learned every song on it. In my final year I needed a laptop, and I decided to sell the guitar. I put it up for eight thousand. The music shop offered two. A friend offered two and a half. I was outraged. "Do you know how many songs I've played on this?" I kept it listed for four months. Meanwhile I wrote my project reports in the cyber café, paying by the hour. One day my roommate asked, "Saurabh, if you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" I laughed. Of course not. The neck was cracked. That was the day I understood it was worth eight thousand only to me. I sold it the next week.

How much did the music shop offer for the guitar?
The music shop offered two.
Why was Saurabh outraged by the offers?
The guitar held years of songs and memories for him, so it felt worth far more than its market price. Owning it made it feel special.
What question from the roommate was the turning point?
"If you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" It made Saurabh see the guitar the way a buyer would.
How might Sonali feel hearing that Saurabh chacha kept a cracked guitar listed for four months?
Sonali might find it funny and touching, and it could help Sonali notice when something feels precious just because it is owned. 😊

Subject: The thing I've been going back and forth about

Hi Sahil,

You asked what I decided about the master's in Leeds. Here's where I am.

I talked to four people. Your cousin, who went abroad and came back, said it changed how she thinks. My old manager said skills matter more than the degree. Kavitha aunty, who did hers at thirty, said don't rush. And Papa said, quietly, that he'd be fine alone, which is exactly what someone says when they won't be.

Everyone was right about their own life. None of them were living mine.

So I wrote down what I care about: learning, being near Papa while his knee heals, not waiting forever. I've deferred by one year. It's my call, and I feel strangely calm about it.

messages.content: Why should an electric heater never be used to dry clothes by draping them over it?

Cloth on a hot heater can catch fire, and a covered heater can overheat. Because cloth touching or close to a hot heater can heat up until it ignites, and a covered heater cannot let its own heat escape, both dangers are real.

Explain the word "enhance" simply. Plus, what does "add fuel to the fire" mean? And correct this sentence: He has more money that I do. Why do footprints show on a wet floor? Oh, and is "twelth" right?

1. As a verb, "enhance" means to make something better or stronger.
2. It means to make a bad situation worse. For example: shouting at them only added fuel to the fire.
3. Better: He has more money than I do. Why: comparisons use "than".
4. Shoes push water aside and leave a different pattern. Because the thin film of water is pressed away where the sole touches, and dirt from the sole gets left behind.
5. No, it is "twelfth", with an "f".

Subject: How we planned the alumni day

In the student flat in Tampere, Diego's mornings began with three tabs, two podcasts and a cold coffee, and by noon his head buzzed. His flatmate Ulla sat by the window every morning for ten minutes with her eyes closed, not moving, while the kettle cooled. 'Doesn't it get boring?' he asked. 'Very,' she said, smiling. 'That's the training.' He tried it on a grey Tuesday, snow drifting past the glass. His mind ran to emails, to his mother in Valencia, to lunch. Each time he noticed, he returned to the feel of air at his nostrils. It was harder than any exam. After a week he began doing his reading with only one tab open. What happens when Lord Godalming puts one of the dogs on the floor?

Lord Godalming lifted one of the dogs, and carrying him in, placed him on the floor. The instant his feet touched the ground he seemed to recover his courage, and rushed at his natural enemies. They fled before him so fast that before he had shaken the life out of a score, the other dogs, who had by now been lifted in the same manner, had but small prey ere the whole mass had vanished.

Everyone in the office is running the city half marathon in December. There's a group chat, matching T-shirts, 6 a.m. practice runs. Bhavna asked me again today if I'm in.

My first instinct was yes, just because everyone is. Then I stopped and asked myself properly: why do I want this? And if nobody at work ever knew, would I still do it?

I thought about it on the bus.

messages.content: I have purchased 5 blue apples at the store. Suppose my neighbor gives me twice as many yellow apples as I have blue ones, and then I give my son 1/5 of the total number of apples; how many apples do I have now?

The number of blue apples is 5, and if you receive twice as many yellow apples as the number of blue apples, there will be 5*2 = 10 yellow apples.
After receiving the yellow apples, you now have 10 yellow apples+5 blue apples = 15 apples.
When you give 1/5 of the total number of apples to the son, you part with 1/5*15 = 3 apples.
The total number of apples remaining is 15-3 = 12 apples.
The answer is 12.

Ganga's invitation had sounded harmless: tea, laughter, a "growth circle" on Sunday afternoons. By the third session Bhavna noticed what she had been too flattered to see. The leader said family drained a person's energy, so calls home could wait. A fee of forty thousand rupees would "unlock the next level", due by Friday, right in her exam week. Anyone who asked a question was called weak. In the corridor she tried out the thoughts silently. Why is my mother a problem? Why is there a deadline? Why is asking a weakness? Three signals, one pattern. "I need to think, not decide," she told Ganga, and left before the closing chant. That night she called home for the first time in nine days.

What fee did the leader ask for, and by when?
The leader asked for a fee of forty thousand rupees, due by Friday.
What made Bhavna uneasy?
Bhavna grew uneasy because the leader discouraged calls home, pressed for money by a deadline and called questioners weak.
What else could Bhavna do to test the group, and why?
Bhavna could talk it over with family or a friend and look for independent information, because outside views help check what a closed group says.
How might Ganga see Bhavna leaving early?
Ganga may feel hurt or worried, believing the circle is good and taking the early exit as a rejection.

"Sahil, you never told me what happened with the sports scholarship."
Fine, Dolma, here it is. I didn't get it. And my first speech to everyone was, "I never wanted it. That academy's overrated. Their coaches are all ego." I said it in the canteen, at home, to my cousin. Loudly.
Then last week I finally watched the trials video my coach had recorded. My footwork was sloppy in the second set. You can see it clearly. If I'd kept telling myself the academy was rubbish, I'd never have looked.
So yes, it stings. I wanted it badly. Next year I'm going back, with better footwork.

What did Sahil notice in the trials video?
The footwork was sloppy in the second set.
Why did Sahil tell everyone the academy was overrated?
Calling it overrated eased the disappointment of not getting in, so the loss felt smaller for a while.
What choice let Sahil learn from the rejection?
Watching the trials video honestly instead of dismissing the academy, which showed the footwork to fix before trying again.
How might Dolma feel hearing Sahil admit it stings?
Dolma may feel glad Sahil has dropped the act, and closer for being told the real feeling.

In the afternoon heat, Reena's goat wandered from the shed to the shade by the well. Reena watched her lie down. Soon Harish Bhaiya came up the lane with his school bag. "I'll give Chhoti her water in the shed," he said, picking up the bucket. Reena covered her mouth and giggled. "Bhaiya thinks she's in the shed!" she told Amma. "He didn't see her go." Then she ran after him. "Bhaiya, she's by the well!"

"Cuckoo! Cuckoo!" The little bird shot out of the clock.
Ishita gasped and froze, eyes wide, spoon halfway to her mouth.
"Is she scared?" asked her mother.
"Cuckoo says hello, Ishita!" said Neelam, her Nani, calmly waving at it.
Ishita looked at Nani, then at the clock. The bird popped back in. She laughed and pointed.
"Again?"
"Next hour," said Nani, smiling.

What shot out of the clock?
A little bird.
What was Ishita feeling when she froze?
She was surprised and unsure, checking Nani's face to see if it was safe; Nani's calm made her laugh.
What did Neelam do that helped?
She stayed calm and made the bird friendly by saying it was saying hello and waving.
How does Ishita's mother first read the gasp?
She wonders if Ishita is scared.

"Your plan is a good one," replied Elizabeth, "where nothing is in question but the desire of being well married; and if I were determined to get a rich husband, or any husband, I dare say I should adopt it. But these are not Jane's feelings; she is not acting by design. As yet she cannot even be certain of the degree of her own regard, nor of its reasonableness. She has known him only a fortnight. She danced four dances with him at Meryton; she saw him one morning at his own house, and has since dined in company with him four times. This is not quite enough to make her understand his character."

Elizabeth says the plan is good for someone who only wants to be well married, but Jane is not acting by design. Jane cannot yet be sure how much she cares or whether it is wise. She has known him only a fortnight, with four dances and four dinners in company, which is not enough to know his character.

In a kindergarten in Krakow, Mrs. Nowak rang the tidy-up bell. "Whoever tidies gets a sticker." Olga, five, raced around dropping blocks into the tub. Yosef stayed on the rug with his puzzle. "Why are you so fast?" he asked. "For the star sticker," Olga said. "And if you don't tidy, you can't go to the garden." Yosef glanced at the door, then shoved his puzzle into its box. When Mrs. Nowak turned away for a moment, Olga slid a block under the shelf instead of carrying it to the tub.

What did Mrs. Nowak say whoever tidies would get?
Whoever tidies gets a sticker.
Why did Olga tidy so quickly?
Olga was eager to win the star sticker and did not want to miss going to the garden.
How could Mrs. Nowak help Olga think beyond the sticker?
She could ask, "What happens to our room when blocks are left out?" and point out how tidying helps everyone find toys.
How might Mrs. Nowak see the block under the shelf when she finds it?
She may realise the children are tidying mainly to earn a sticker, and that the rule works only while she is watching.

Monday. The messages started coming to Anirban from an account with no name and no picture. "Loser." "Your voice is so annoying." "Quit the debate team." He read them twenty times. By night he was sure it was Rafiq, who had lost the debate spot to him.

Wednesday. Anirban barely slept. In class he watched Rafiq's every move, looking for proof. He drafted a message to Rafiq: "I know it's you." His finger hovered. Then he thought: what if it isn't? He'd be doing to Rafiq what the account was doing to him.

He deleted the draft. Instead he saved every message with the time, reported the account on the app, and that evening showed his father. Papa emailed the school counsellor at once.

The next Monday. The counsellor had involved the school's IT teacher, and the account had been removed. Anirban still didn't know who it was. But in debate practice, Rafiq said, "Good point," and Anirban realised he'd been ready to accuse the wrong person.

Who did Anirban suspect was behind the account?
Anirban suspected Rafiq, who had lost the debate spot to him.
What was Anirban feeling on Wednesday?
Anirban felt anxious and suspicious, barely sleeping and watching Rafiq for proof.
What did Anirban do instead of sending the accusation, and why was it wise?
Anirban saved the messages, reported the account and told his father, which got the school involved and stopped him accusing someone without proof.
What would have happened to Rafiq if Anirban had sent the draft?
Rafiq might have been hurt and falsely accused, feeling bullied in the same way Anirban was.
