I'm Jasleen. My little sister Kashish lost her first tooth at school. When Nani came, Kashish told her the whole story. "First, I was eating an apple. Then my tooth wiggled. Then it came out! I cried a little. Then Ma'am gave me a tissue. And at the end, I put it in a box." Nani hugged her. I've heard her tell it three times, and it's always in the same order.

What was Kashish eating when her tooth came out?
She was eating an apple.
What might Kashish have felt when the tooth came out?
She may have felt surprised and a little scared, since she says she cried a little.
How could Nani encourage Kashish's storytelling?
She could ask Kashish what happened next or how she felt, so she keeps telling events in order.
How does Jasleen see Kashish's retelling?
Jasleen notices Kashish always tells it in the same order, which suggests she remembers events in sequence.

At the preschool's Christmas party, Anjali, five, noticed that Shreya had two mothers picking her up.
"Why do you have two mummies?" she asked loudly.
Some parents went quiet.
Shreya said, "Because that's my family."
Anjali thought for a moment. "I have one mummy and a Nani. That's my family."
"Okay," said Shreya.
They went back to decorating the tree, sharing the glitter.

Who picked Shreya up?
Two mothers.
How did Anjali seem to feel about Shreya's family?
She seemed curious, not upset, and quickly accepted it by comparing it to her own family.
How could the teacher build on this moment?
The teacher could read stories about different kinds of families.

You remind me of myself, Lavanya. At nine I was the loudest boy in our Mysuru school. I could make a friend at the bus stop before the bus came. In every cricket game in our lane I was captain, umpire and commentator. But in silent writing hour I felt like ants were under my skin; I'd hum, and the teacher would send me to stand outside. My best friend Raghu was the opposite. One day he told me, very softly, that he didn't want to play at recess. I laughed and pulled him along anyway. He didn't speak to me for a week. That was when I learned to hear the quiet ones, kanna. Your Naveen Thatha still talks too much, but he listens now too.

What three roles did Naveen play in the lane cricket games?
Captain, umpire and commentator.
What did young Naveen feel during silent writing hour?
He felt restless, like ants were under his skin, so he hummed.
What turning point taught Naveen to listen to quieter friends?
After he pulled Raghu into recess despite his soft no, Raghu stayed silent for a week, and Naveen learned to hear the quiet ones.
How might Raghu have felt when his soft request was laughed off?
He likely felt ignored and hurt, which is why he kept away for a week.

"It's a closed-book certification," Gautam said, reading the rules aloud in the library. "No AI tools, no notes. You sign a declaration."

Samir stared at his practice paper. "The take-home part too?"

"Take-home too. You have to disclose any tool use."

Samir had already had the AI write two of the take-home answers. They were good. Better than his.

"Nobody would know," he said quietly.

Gautam put down the rules. "Maybe. But then you get certified as a network engineer and someone asks you to fix a real outage at 2 a.m. The chatbot won't be on the call with you."

Samir felt his neck go hot. He deleted the two answers. "I'll have to redo everything. There's a week left."

"Then we start tonight," Gautam said. "I'll quiz you on routing."

They stayed till the library closed. Samir's answers were rougher. But he understood them.

How long was left before the certification?
A week.
What was Samir feeling when Gautam described the 2 a.m. outage?
He felt ashamed and uneasy, his neck going hot as he realised he might not understand what he'd submitted.
What choice did Samir make, and why was it wise?
He deleted the AI-written answers and redid them himself, following the rules and making sure he understood his work.
How does Gautam see Samir's temptation?
Gautam sees the real risk as lacking skills Samir would claim to have, not just getting caught, and offers to help him study.
What mood is associated with Raga Lalit?
Raga Lalit is associated with a austere, meditative mood.
A tray holds 10 idlis. How many idlis are on 6 trays?
60. Because 10 x 6 = 60, so there are 60 in all.

In his first winter at university in Stockholm, Emeka joined a Thursday 'leadership circle' that met in a warm flat full of candles. Anders, who ran it, was charming and quick to praise. After a month, the requests started. 'Serious members hand in their phones during weekend retreats.' Then: 'Your contribution shows your commitment.' Then, gently: 'Your old friends from the Nigerian students' society hold you back.' Emeka noticed he had stopped going to the society's Friday dinners. That frightened him. He thought of his cousin in Lagos, who always said, 'Never give anyone your only way home.' So before the next retreat he told Anders he would keep his phone. He kept his savings in his own account. And on Friday he went to the society dinner and told his friend Tunde everything. Tunde listened and said, 'Come to dinner every Friday. If they don't like that, you'll know.'

When did the Nigerian students' society have dinners?
The society had dinners on Fridays.
What did Emeka feel on noticing he had stopped going to the society dinners?
Emeka felt frightened, realising how far he had drifted from old friends.
What did Emeka keep to protect himself?
His phone, his own savings and his friendships, and he told Tunde, someone outside the group.
How does Anders frame his requests?
Anders frames them as commitment and growth, so control sounds like a gift.

In the quiet room of a Hamburg school, the teacher was reading a story about a sleepy bear. Oskar, six, heard the bear snore loudly in the story and pressed his lips together. His eyes darted to Sofia, who bit her lip. He looked down at his shoes and his shoulders shook. He covered his mouth with his hand. When the teacher turned the page, a small squeak escaped, and both of them looked at each other, then away. At break they ran outside and let out a big roar of laughter.

What was the teacher reading about?
The teacher was reading a story about a sleepy bear.
What might Oskar have been feeling as he pressed his lips together and looked down?
He seems to have been fighting a giggle and knew it was a quiet time, so he tried to control himself. He might also have felt a bit nervous about being noticed.

The storm had knocked out the power on the night before the maths exam, and Sumit sat on the stairs with his phone at nine per cent. Last month he and Zainab had been inseparable: studying together, eating every lunch together. Then, a week ago, he had stopped replying and told a friend she was "too much". Now he stared at her last message: "Did I do something?" He wanted to type, "No, I miss you." His thumb hovered. He was afraid she'd leave first, the way his mother had left when he was six. Tomorrow was his session with Ms Kapoor, the counsellor he had been seeing since spring. She had said, "Notice the moment you want to cut someone off." This was that moment. With one per cent left, he typed, "You didn't. I got scared. Can we talk after the exam?" The screen went black.

Sumit, afraid Zainab will leave him, stopped replying to her, and now he reads her message asking if she did something wrong. Remembering his counsellor's advice, he uses his last battery to say he got scared and to ask to talk after the exam.

Last year, in Class 10, I lost a whole term to one habit. I'm Leela, and every evening I'd tell myself: one hour of the mobile game, then study. The game was right there, glowing, full of little rewards. The board exams were in March. March felt like another planet. So the hour became two, then three. In December, my friend Harish showed me his revision chart, half done. I hadn't started. That night I cried, and my mother didn't scold me. She just asked, "What does March-Leela want from tonight-Leela?" I thought about it for a long time. March-Leela wanted a chance. So we made a deal: forty-five minutes of study first, then the game, and my phone slept in the kitchen after ten. It felt terrible the first week. By February it felt normal.

Where did Leela's phone sleep after ten?
In the kitchen.
What was Leela feeling in December when Harish showed his chart?
Leela felt panicked and ashamed, crying that night because nothing had been started while Harish was half done.
What deal did Leela make, and why did it work?
Forty-five minutes of study before the game and the phone in the kitchen after ten, which made the future goal count tonight.
How might Harish have felt showing Leela his revision chart?
Harish probably didn't expect to upset Leela and may have felt worried when he realised she hadn't started.

"Okay, Saturday's deliveries," Binita said, pen at the whiteboard. "Thirty families got nothing. Let's start with what happened, step by step."
Nilesh shifted in his chair. "I had the old route sheet. That's on me."
"Hold on. I'm not looking for who. Why was the old sheet in the van at all?"
"It was on the clipboard. The new one was only in the group chat."
Mariam added, "And that message came at midnight. Most drivers leave at seven without checking."
"So, the conditions," Binita said, writing. "Two versions of the route, one on paper, one on a phone. Nobody confirming which. What would stop it happening again?"
"One sheet only. The old one goes in the bin when the new one's printed," Nilesh said.
"And a quick call at seven where drivers read out their first stop," Mariam said.
Binita underlined both. "Good. Nilesh, will you print the sheets from now on? You've seen exactly where it breaks."
Nilesh nodded, his shoulders dropping.

How many families got no delivery on Saturday?
Thirty families got nothing.
What was Nilesh feeling when he said "That's on me"?
Nilesh felt guilty and braced for blame; his shoulders dropping at the end show relief once the focus moved to the system.
What two changes did the team agree on?
Keep one printed route sheet and bin the old one, and hold a quick seven o'clock call where drivers read out their first stop.
What would change if Binita had accepted "That's on me" and moved on?
The team would have blamed Nilesh and missed the real cause, two versions of the route and a midnight message, so it could happen again with another driver.

Every Sunday in their Lisbon flat, Gabriel, twenty-five, cooked his Goan grandmother's sorpotel while his partner Lars chopped onions badly. Gabriel's family had left Goa two generations ago. He had picked what to keep, carefully. The sorpotel and the Konkani hymn his grandmother hummed. Christmas with kuswar sweets and Swedish saffron buns, because Lars had his own traditions too. What he let go: his family's quiet rule that a son must never cry.
Today his niece Marta, eight, was visiting. Gabriel handed her the spoon. "Stir slowly. Avó always stirred slowly." Marta asked why the curry was so red. He told her about the market in Mapusa, which he had seen only once. Then Lars sang a Swedish song, badly, and Marta laughed. As she left, she asked if she could come back to learn the kuswar. Gabriel felt something warm settle in his chest.

Which rule did Gabriel let go of?
His family's quiet rule that a son must never cry.
How did Gabriel feel when Marta asked to come back?
He felt warm and content, glad that what he had chosen to keep was being passed on.
Why is Gabriel's way of choosing traditions healthy?
He kept what carries love and meaning, blended in Lars's traditions, and let go of a harmful rule, so his heritage feels chosen rather than forced.
How might Marta experience these Sunday visits?
Marta probably finds them fun and warm, learning family stories and recipes in a relaxed, loving way.

Kiran came home from the school eco-club meeting in their Bengaluru flat with muddy shoes and a list. "Rukmini Aunty," she told the neighbour on the landing, "we planted forty saplings near the lake today."
"Well done, Kiran. Why the long face then?"
Kiran leaned on the railing. "In class we learned about the floods in Kerala. Families lost everything. I keep seeing a video of an old man carrying his cat through water. I don't know him, but I can't stop thinking about him."
Rukmini Aunty nodded. "It's heavy to care about people you'll never meet."
"Is it silly?"
"No. It means you understand we're all tied together. Just don't carry it alone."
Kiran smiled a little and went in to write the next club poster.

How many saplings did Kiran's club plant near the lake?
They planted forty saplings.
Why did Kiran have a long face after the eco-club meeting?
She was worried and sad about flood victims in Kerala, especially the old man with his cat, even though she didn't know him.
What does Rukmini Aunty suggest, and why is it wise?
She tells Kiran not to carry the worry alone, so her wide concern stays healthy and she can keep acting on it.
How does Rukmini Aunty see Kiran's worry?

Shankar's father was a temple priest, and Akash's family didn't follow any religion. They were best friends in a Chennai school. One evening, walking home past the temple, Akash asked, "How do you know God exists?" Shankar felt his face get hot. "How do you know he doesn't?" They argued all the way to the bus stop. Then Akash laughed. "We're both just saying the same thing louder." Shankar grinned, still a bit annoyed. The next week, their philosophy teacher explained arguments for and against, and how people's beliefs shape how they live. Shankar still believed; Akash still didn't. What was Shankar's father's job?

Why did Shankar's face get hot when Akash asked his question?
He felt his faith and his family were being challenged, which made him defensive and a little hurt.
What changed in how the friends discussed beliefs?
They stopped trying to win and started asking genuine questions, which let them understand each other while keeping their own views.
How might Akash feel when Shankar talks about his faith now?

The power went out just as Aaji lit the evening lamp in the Nagpur flat, and her reading glasses were lost somewhere on the dark sofa. She fumbled for the prayer book, sighing.

Then Sunaina, nine, began the aarti from memory, word for word, the way Aaji sang it: slow on the second line, quick on the last. Her cousin Pallavi, seven, joined in, clapping on the beat.

What was Aaji feeling as she listened in the dark?

How could the family keep this learning going once the lights are back?
Let the girls lead the aarti some evenings and ask Aaji for more stories and sayings, so the passing-on stays daily.
What might it be like for Sunaina to lead the aarti from memory?

In the college hostel in Jaipur, Madhuri, nineteen, saw Harsha's father and two uncles arrive at the visitors' room on Saturday morning. Harsha, her roommate, went pale.
Through the half-open door, Madhuri heard one uncle: "Photos of you with that boy are all over the family group. You've destroyed our honour. Pack your bag. You're coming home, and you're done with college." Harsha was crying. "Papa, please."
Madhuri felt her heart race. She knew Harsha had been frightened for weeks, hiding her phone.
She didn't go in. She ran to the warden's office. "They're forcing her to leave. They're threatening her."
The warden came at once, stood beside Harsha, and said calmly, "She's an adult and a student here. She will not be taken against her will." Then she called the college's women's cell and the police helpline. Madhuri sat with Harsha until the officer arrived.

Where did Harsha's father and uncles arrive?
They arrived at the visitors' room.
What was Madhuri feeling when she heard the uncle's words?
Madhuri felt afraid for Harsha, her heart racing, knowing her roommate had been frightened for weeks.
What made Madhuri's and the warden's response protective?
Madhuri went straight for help rather than confronting the family alone, and the warden stood beside Harsha, refused to let her be taken and called the women's cell and police.
How might Harsha feel with Madhuri beside her until the officer arrived?
Harsha would likely feel less alone and a little safer, knowing someone had believed her and acted.

I'm Jyoti, Lalit's cousin. Every Holi at Dadi's house used to end with Lalit and Bade Papa shouting about politics while everyone else pretended to eat.
This year, a week before, Lalit called me. 'Can we make a deal? If politics starts, you ask me about my internship, or ask Bade Papa about his garden. And if it still keeps going, I'll say I'm going to help Dadi in the kitchen, and go.'
I agreed. I even wrote three backup topics in my phone.
On Holi, at lunch, Bade Papa started: 'These elections...' I jumped in. 'Bade Papa, did the chilli plants survive the heat?' He talked about chillies for ten minutes. Later it started again. Lalit smiled, said, 'That's a big topic, Bade Papa, let's save it,' and took the plates to the kitchen.
Nobody shouted. Bade Papa even hugged Lalit at the gate.
I don't know if Lalit was biting back words inside. But it was the first Holi in years that ended warm.

What did Jyoti ask Bade Papa about?
Whether the chilli plants survived the heat.
What might Lalit have been feeling when saying 'let's save it'?
Perhaps tempted to argue and a little frustrated, but calm enough to stick to the plan.
Why did agreeing beforehand work better than deciding in the moment?
With backup topics and an exit already planned, Lalit and Jyoti could act calmly before tempers rose.
How might Bade Papa experience this Holi?
Bade Papa gets a warm lunch talking about the garden, and ends it hugging Lalit instead of arguing.

messages.content: 24 laddoos are packed equally into 4 boxes. Amma buys 2 of the boxes. Write the calculation and find how many laddoos she buys.

Answer: 12 laddoos. 24 / 4 x 2 = 6 x 2 = 12.

x and / also have the SAME rank, so we go from left to right: first 24 / 4 = 6 laddoos in each box, then 6 x 2 = 12 for two boxes. A common mistake is to do 4 x 2 = 8 first and then 24 / 8 = 3. Remember: "D before M" in BODMAS does NOT mean divide first - it means left to right.
It's field trip month, and the students took six vans and four minibusses. There were 10 students on each van and 24 students on each minibus. How many students went on the field trip?

The total number of students who took the van is 6 x 10 = 60.
The total number of students who took the minibus is 4 x 24 = 96.
Therefore, 60 + 96 = 156 students went on the field trip.
The answer is 156.
Craft a story about a girl who helps a friend who cannot read well and keeps it a secret.

Divya noticed that her friend Karthik always asked her to read aloud the instructions for the science experiment. He said his eyes hurt. After a week, she guessed the truth: the letters swam on the page for him. She did not tell anyone. Instead, during recess, she suggested they read together on the steps, taking turns on a page. She read slowly, tracing the words with her finger, and asked him to say each one after her. He stumbled, then got faster. By the end of the month, he could read a full paragraph, and he told her a secret in return: he wanted to read his father's old letters.

Lidia has a collection of books. Her collection is four times bigger than the collection which her friend Susan has. In total Susan and Lidia, both have 3000 books. How many books does Susan have in her collection?

Let x be the number of books in Susan's collection.
The collection of both Susan and Lidia would then be 4*x + x = 3000.
5*x = 3000
x = 600
The answer is 600.
Write a two-line forecast for a foggy morning, both lines using "will".

Tomorrow morning will begin with thick fog on the roads.
The fog will slowly lift by the afternoon.

Each is a QUARTER turn. Is it clockwise (cw) or anticlockwise (acw)?
a) North -> East
b) North -> West
c) East -> South
d) East -> North
e) South -> West
f) South -> East
g) West -> North
h) West -> South

a) cw
b) acw
c) cw
d) acw
e) cw
f) acw
g) cw
h) acw

At the farm, Chaitanya, five, drew a house, a huge sun and four people on the back of a seed packet. Her grandfather Pradeep pointed. "That's you, that's Ma, that's Baba." "And the buffalo with big horns, bigger than the house." "Why is the buffalo so big?" "Because she gives milk." "And who is this small one in the corner?" "That's me. I'm drawing from here." Pradeep laughed and asked her to tell him about the sun.

What did Chaitanya draw bigger than the house?
The buffalo with big horns.
What might the huge buffalo show about Chaitanya's feelings?
It may show she is fond of the buffalo and values it, since she said it is big "Because she gives milk". The size may also just be for fun.
How should adults use a child's drawing like this?
As a start to conversation, asking questions and not diagnosing from size or colour.
How might Pradeep read the small figure in the corner?
With curiosity but not worry, since Chaitanya explained she was drawing from there.

Read this:

I'm Amandeep. Last term, when our class plant was knocked off the windowsill, I asked Sonali, “Did you see who did it?” She didn't answer for ages. She looked at the floor, then at the door, then at me. I decided that meant she'd done it, and I said so, loudly. Her eyes filled. Later our teacher asked her calmly, “Is someone worried about getting into trouble?” Sonali nodded and whispered that a little Class 1 boy had done it by accident and was terrified. She'd been protecting him. I felt awful. Now when someone pauses before answering, I wait and ask a gentler question.

What was knocked off the windowsill?
The class plant was knocked off the windowsill.
What was Sonali feeling during her long pause?
Sonali felt torn and worried, trying to protect a scared little boy who had knocked the plant over by accident.
What did the teacher do that worked better than Amandeep's accusation?
The teacher asked a calm, gentle question about whether someone was worried, which let Sonali explain.
What was it like for the little Class 1 boy?
The little boy was terrified of getting into trouble for an accident.

The placement cell at the engineering college in Guwahati held mock group discussions every Friday. In the first one, Bhupen said "database" when he meant "data set" and a girl across the table corrected him. He nodded, smiled, and didn't speak again for the rest of the session. Nor the next Friday. Nor the one after. He was sure the whole group had filed him as the boy who didn't know basic words. In the fourth week, the placement officer pulled him aside. "Bhupen, your written summaries are among the best. Why don't you speak?" He admitted the mistake. The officer smiled. "I sat in that first session. I have no idea what you're talking about." Later, Bhupen asked Ankita, who had been in the group. She didn't remember either. She remembered her own stammer.

What did Bhupen say instead of "data set"?
He said "database".
What was Bhupen feeling during the weeks he stayed silent?
He felt embarrassed and anxious, sure the whole group remembered him as the boy who didn't know basic words.
How did the placement officer help Bhupen, and what could he try next?
The officer praised his summaries and admitted not remembering the slip; Bhupen can now speak in discussions, knowing small errors fade fast.
What does Ankita remember from that first session?
Ankita remembers her own stammer, not Bhupen's word mix-up.

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday. Kavitha burst into the NGO office with a spreadsheet. "The children in our evening reading club improved twice as much as the others this term!" Salma, the programme analyst, read it slowly. "Who chose to join?" "Well, the keen ones. Their parents signed them up." Salma wrote three words on a sticky note: keen, parents, luck.
The next Thursday. Salma found the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space. "They're our comparison," she told Kavitha. "Same keen families, no club yet."
Three weeks later. The new numbers came in. The club children still improved more than the waiting list, but by far less than the first chart had suggested. Kavitha sighed, then smiled. "Smaller, but real." Salma pinned the sticky note above her desk.

What did Salma use as a comparison group?
She used the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space.
Why did Salma write 'keen, parents, luck' on a sticky note?
Salma felt cautious rather than excited; she suspected that keen children, involved parents or plain luck could explain the gain, not only the club.
Why was the waiting list a smart comparison?
Those children came from equally keen families, so any extra gain in the club group is more likely due to the club itself.
How did Kavitha's feelings change from Monday to the final numbers?
Kavitha went from bursting with excitement to a small sigh, then accepted a smaller but real effect with a smile.

Read this:

From our balcony opposite, on Sunday evening, I watched the Singh family do something strange. First the father, Sachin, walked slowly from every bedroom to the front door, counting steps. Then Jasleen and her little brother came out behind him on their hands and knees, crawling along the corridor. At each door they stopped, touched it with the back of a hand, then went on. They did it three times. The third time they went out to the stairs, not the lift. I didn't know what it was until Jasleen shouted, "Papa, forty seconds!" I couldn't tell if the children were scared or just enjoying it, but they looked very serious by the end.

How long did Jasleen say the third round took?
Forty seconds.
What might Jasleen have been feeling by the end of the drill?
She may have felt proud and focused, though the neighbour can't be sure whether she was scared or enjoying it.
What else could the family practise, and why?
They could practise at night with the lights off, because smoke and darkness make a real escape harder.
How does the drill look to the neighbour watching?
The neighbour is puzzled at first, then realises it is a safety practice, and is curious and a little impressed.

Read this:

Jahnavi waited until Sachin had finished his work call, then turned off the TV in their Hyderabad flat.

"Can we talk? Not about bills."

He looked wary. "Okay."

She had written the words on her phone that afternoon so she wouldn't lose them. "I feel we're drifting. I don't know how to bring us back. I'm not angry. I just miss us."

Sachin sat down slowly. "I've been feeling it too. I didn't know how to say it."

"Do you want to try?"

"I think so. I don't know what trying looks like."

"Maybe a counsellor. Or maybe we start with one evening a week, no phones."

"And if it doesn't work?"

Jahnavi took a breath. "Then we'll know, and we can decide honestly. Either way, I don't want us to just fade."

What did Jahnavi turn off before talking?
The TV.
Why had Jahnavi written the words on her phone that afternoon?
She was nervous and afraid of losing her courage or her words, and wanted to say it kindly and clearly.
What options does naming the drift open for them?
They can try repairing with a no-phone evening or a counsellor, or, if it doesn't work, decide honestly to part.
How does Sachin seem to feel when Jahnavi says she misses them?
He seems relieved and a bit uncertain, having felt the same but not known how to say it.

Read this:

The school bus broke down on the flyover, and Gopika reached the science fair with only twenty minutes before judging. She set up her quiz board on the table, sweating: twelve questions, twelve bulbs, a week of evenings twisting wires. Sangeeta Ma'am came by and pressed question four. Nothing lit. 'One wire's loose at the back, Gopika. Tape it down and it'll work.' 'It works at home, Ma'am.' 'It isn't working now. Twenty minutes, quick.' Gopika felt her face go hot. 'You think I did it badly.' 'I think one wire is loose.' Gopika turned the board away. 'The judges will press other questions.' Ma'am left the roll of tape on the table. The first judge pressed question four. Gopika stared at the tape, wishing she had used it.

How long did Gopika have before judging?
Only twenty minutes before judging, because the school bus broke down on the flyover.
Why did Gopika say 'You think I did it badly'?
She felt hurt and embarrassed, hearing the comment about one wire as criticism of her week of evenings, which is why her face went hot.
At which moment could Gopika have saved her project, and how?
When Ma'am left the tape, Gopika could have taped the loose wire at the back in a minute before the judges came.
How might Sangeeta Ma'am have felt when Gopika turned the board away?
Ma'am may have felt frustrated and a bit sad, since she only wanted to help and could see the easy fix.

metadata.subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]

messages.content: Some people dislike being told what to do. Why is that?
They feel their freedom is being taken away. Because they want their choices to be respected and feel they have some control, being commanded makes them resist.
Today my supervisor told me I made a mistake in the stock list and everyone heard. I felt humiliated. I'm Nikhil.
I'm sorry, Nikhil. Being corrected in front of others stings, even when the correction is fair. Take a moment to breathe. Do you know what exactly went wrong?
I entered 120 instead of 102 for one item.
That is a simple swap of digits, and it happens to many people. Fix the entry and check similar items for the same slip. Then move on without carrying it all day.
Should I say something to my supervisor about how it felt?
You can, but wait until you are calm. Say that you want to be accurate, and ask if corrections can be given privately next time. Keep it polite and short.
I might. Which numbers did I swap?
You entered 120 instead of 102. Correct that figure in the stock list, and double check any numbers close to it, since swapped digits are easy to miss.
James writes a 3-page letter to 2 different friends twice a week.  How many pages does he write a year?

He writes each friend 3*2=6 pages a week
So he writes 6*2=12 pages every week
That means he writes 12*52=624 pages a year
The answer is 624.

Read this:

Mohit had only an hour at his cousin Anirban's wedding before his train back to Pune. The hall was noisy, the music loud. Then the priest invited the families to bless the couple. Anirban's mother stepped forward alone, holding a framed photo of his late father.

Mohit's throat closed. He had to step outside into the heat.

He thought of his own mother, who had died when he was eight. He hadn't cried about her in years. He'd thought he'd moved on.

Anirban found him by the gate. "You okay?"

"It's Ma," Mohit said, surprised by his own words.

Anirban put an arm round him. They stood together until the train was nearly due.

What was Anirban's mother holding?
A framed photo of his late father.
Why did Mohit have to step outside?
Seeing the photo brought a flood of grief for his own mother, a feeling he thought he'd moved past.
What small step helped Mohit in that moment?
Saying "It's Ma" out loud to Anirban, who stayed with him.
How might Anirban feel finding Mohit at the gate?
Anirban probably felt concerned and understanding, since he also lost a parent.

(1) My sentence is "If I was you, I would study harder." Can you fix it?
(2) Why does a bowler polish one side of the cricket ball?
(3) What is the highest score in the history of school cricket?
(4) Why do footballs bounce?
(5) What's the meaning of the word theatrical?

1. Correct form: If I were you, I would study harder. Why: for an imagined situation after "if" we use "were", even with "I".
2. The bowler polishes one side. Because the smooth side moves through the air differently from the rough side, which makes the ball swing.
3. I don't know the exact record, because I can't check old scorebooks reliably. Ask a sports teacher or check a cricket records site.
4. The air inside pushes back and throws the ball up. Because the ball is squeezed when it hits the ground, the compressed air pushes back.
5. Theatrical is an adjective that means connected with the theatre, or too dramatic.

Your Bidisha-phuppi was sixteen when I missed her school play. I had promised. Instead I stayed at the shop counting stock and told myself she wouldn't mind. She minded. She didn't speak to me for a week, and I, Rafiq, stubborn old fool, said she was being dramatic. Then one night I passed her room and saw the costume still on the chair. I knocked. I didn't say "but the shop" or "but I was busy". I said, "I broke a promise to you, and I pretended it didn't matter. It did. I'm sorry." She cried, and I cried. After that, she told me things. Mistakes don't end a family, beta. Hiding them does.

What did Rafiq see on the chair in Bidisha's room?
The costume.
How was young Bidisha feeling during the week of silence?
She was hurt and let down that Rafiq broke the promise and then called her dramatic.
What was the turning point in the story?
Seeing the costume made Rafiq knock and apologise plainly, without mentioning the shop or being busy.
How did the apology change things for Bidisha?
She cried with Rafiq and afterwards began sharing things, trusting that the bond could survive the mistake.

Uma's arms folded as she stared at the sign: NO WATER BOTTLES ON DESKS. In the crowded city classroom the fan blew warm air, and she was thirsty. "This is silly," she muttered to Jaya. Jaya shrugged. All morning Uma thought of hiding her bottle in her bag anyway. Then at recess she asked the teacher, "Ma'am, why can't we keep bottles on the desks?" The teacher pointed to a ruined notebook from last week. "Spills." Uma thought for a moment. "What if we had a shelf by the door and could drink between lessons?" The teacher smiled and said she would ask the principal.

What did the sign say?
It said NO WATER BOTTLES ON DESKS.
What was Uma feeling as she stared at the sign?
She felt annoyed and thought the rule was silly, so she was tempted to break it.
What did Uma do instead of quietly breaking the rule?
She asked the teacher why the rule existed and then politely suggested a bottle shelf by the door.
How might the teacher have seen Uma's question?
The teacher may have been glad that Uma asked calmly rather than hiding her bottle, and could see the rule's purpose was protecting notebooks. 🙂

I sit two seats from Kiran in the Tuesday planning meeting, so I see things. When the client's manager said the launch date would move up again, Kiran's lips pressed into a thin line and stayed there. Kiran looked at the table, nodded once, and wrote something in the notebook. Nobody else seemed to notice. I thought, either Kiran is fine with it or is choosing not to say. Honestly I cannot tell. Later in the corridor I heard Kiran tell Salma, "I should have said the timeline was not realistic. Next time I will raise it before we hang up." I only saw the pressed lips; I do not really know what Kiran was thinking. 🤔

Where does the narrator sit in the Tuesday planning meeting?
The narrator sits two seats from Kiran.
What might Kiran's pressed lips have meant, and what else could they mean?

They most likely meant Kiran was holding back a concern about the moved-up date, which Kiran later confirmed to Salma. They could also have been simple concentration, so the narrator was right not to be sure.
What could Kiran do differently in the next meeting?
Kiran could name the concern calmly during or right after the meeting, for example that the timeline looks unrealistic, as Kiran planned to do.
How does Salma likely see Kiran's silence in the meeting?
Salma probably sees Kiran as someone who thinks before speaking and wishes to speak up, since Kiran shared the regret with Salma afterwards.
What does it mean to "burn the midnight oil"? Also, what does "generous" mean?

1. It means to work or study late into the night. He burned the midnight oil before his test.
2. Generous means happy to give or share with others. Our neighbour is generous and always shares her mangoes.

"Tanuja Masi, can I tell you something? You won't tell me off?"
"Gopika, I promise I won't. What is it?"
"There's this boy I met in an online game. He says he's sixteen. We talk every day. He moved us to another app so it's 'just us.'"
"Okay. I'm listening."
"Now he keeps asking where I live and what school I go to. Yesterday he asked for a picture. In my night clothes."
Tanuja kept her voice steady. "Thank you for telling me. You are not to blame for any of this. Did you send anything?"
"No. But I felt bad saying no. He's been so nice."
"Feeling flattered is normal. He's the one doing something wrong, not you. Can you show me the chat?"
Gopika handed over the phone.
"We'll screenshot it, block him, and tell your Mumma together, right now. Then we'll report it on the cyber-crime portal tonight."
Gopika nodded, and her shoulders dropped.

What did the boy ask for yesterday?
A picture. In night clothes.
How did Gopika feel about saying no to him?
Gopika felt bad and guilty about saying no, because he'd been so nice, even though something felt wrong.
What did Tanuja Masi do that a trusted adult should?
She stayed calm, told Gopika there was no blame on Gopika, and planned to screenshot, block, tell Gopika's Mumma right away and report it that night.
How might Tanuja have felt hearing about the night-clothes request?
Tanuja probably felt alarmed and protective, but kept her voice steady so Gopika would feel safe.
Arjun collected 136 cards. Pooja collected 83. Who has the bigger collection?
Arjun. Because 136 is more than 83, so Arjun has more.

I'm Ganga, and our river-protection group was the closest thing to family I had in college. We'd sat in the rain together, shared tiffins at dawn. So when Zeenat, our coordinator, suggested posting the home address of the factory manager who'd been dumping waste, 'so people can go and tell him what they think', everyone cheered. I felt sick. His kids lived there. But I said nothing that night; I didn't want to be the one who spoiled things. At home I couldn't sleep. The next morning, before anything was posted, I called Zeenat. 'I love this group. That's why I'm saying it: posting his address could get someone hurt, and it would make us the story instead of the river.' She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Say it at the meeting. I think others feel it too.' I did. Three people nodded at once. We filed a complaint with the pollution board instead, and held a sit-in at the factory gate.

What did Zeenat suggest posting?
Zeenat suggested posting the home address of the factory manager.
What did Ganga feel when everyone cheered?
Ganga felt sick and uneasy, worried for the manager's children, but afraid to spoil things.
Why was speaking up the next morning an act of loyalty?
Ganga raised it early and kindly, before anything was posted, to protect people and the group's cause.
How does Zeenat respond to Ganga's concern?
Zeenat listens, thinks, and invites Ganga to raise it at the meeting, suspecting others feel the same.

Tue night. Nilesh here, diary. Three weeks on the Zurich team and I am still confused about volume. At home in Kolkata, we talk loudly and over each other, and it means we like you. Here, when I told a joke loudly, the room went quiet, and I could feel people stiffening. Tarun, the quiet one, said later, "People think you are upset when you raise your voice." I was shocked. I was happy! Then I saw that Tarun's soft voice, which I took as boredom, is his way of being polite. Neither of us is wrong. I am going to lower my volume a bit and ask Tarun about his day.

Where does Nilesh work now?
Nilesh works on the Zurich team.
What did Nilesh feel when Tarun said people think he is upset, and what was the truth?
Nilesh was shocked, since the loud voice meant happiness and warmth at home in Kolkata. In Zurich it read as being upset.
What is Nilesh going to try?
Nilesh plans to lower the volume a bit and ask Tarun about his day.
How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh joked loudly?
Tarun may have felt uneasy, since loud talk can seem like upset or aggression in that setting, though Tarun spoke kindly afterwards.

messages.content: I was thinking about some things. There are 15 girls and 17 boys in the class. How many children are there? What marks did I get in my last test?

1. That makes 32. Because 15 + 17 = 32.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your report. Ask your teacher or look at your answer sheet.

Subject: Wednesday's water-sharing meeting
Hi Shankar,
Quick report from Pimpalgaon. The district engineer presented in English, fast, with slides full of terms like "rotation schedule". About forty farmers came; most follow Marathi best, and six seasonal workers from Jharkhand follow only Hindi. After the first slide I saw the back row checking phones.
So I asked the engineer if I could add a line after each point. Short, only the key point: "Mhanje, tumchya shetala pani Mangalvari ani Shukravari yeil," then the same in Hindi.
Phones went down. Bhaskar kaka asked about the Friday slot for the lower fields. One of the Jharkhand workers asked, in Hindi, whether the labourers' quarters were on the same line. The engineer had not thought about that at all.
It added about ten minutes. I'd like to budget for it at every meeting from now on.
Jagdish

How many seasonal workers came from Jharkhand?
Six seasonal workers from Jharkhand came.
What does Jagdish's request to add a line after each point suggest?
It suggests Jagdish felt concerned and uneasy that the back row was being left out once the phones came out after the first slide.
What small adjustment does Jagdish propose, and why is it worth it?
Budgeting about ten minutes at every meeting to repeat key points in Marathi and Hindi, because it brings out questions that would otherwise be missed.
What was it like for the Jharkhand workers once the points came in Hindi?
They could finally follow and even ask about the labourers' quarters, which made them part of the meeting rather than onlookers.

Hansa had not answered in six hours, and Yamini was twenty and could feel a story growing. She probably thinks I was rude at lunch. Instead of feeding it, she typed, "Hey, are you cross with me, or am I imagining it? 🙂" Ten minutes later: "Dead phone, sorry! Not upset at all, I was in a viva." Yamini exhaled and wrote back a smiling face. At twenty-five, she shared a flat with Tenzin, and a fight about the electricity bill began over messages while she was at work. His replies got shorter. Hers got sharper. She wrote, "Fine. Whatever." and stared at it. Then she deleted the words before sending. She noticed her heart racing and her lines going cold. "Can I call you on my break?" she wrote instead. Tenzin answered right away: "Please." On the call, her voice caught, and his did too. They talked for twenty minutes and decided how to split the bill. That evening they cooked dal together, mostly in silence.

Why had Hansa not answered for six hours?
Her phone was dead and she was in a viva.
How is the way Yamini handles her worry at twenty like or unlike her handling of the fight with Tenzin at twenty-five?

At twenty she asked Hansa directly whether she was cross, which stopped a story about Hansa's silence growing. At twenty-five she saw that the bill fight was heating up in short, sharp messages and moved to a call, where voice carries what text cannot.
What was Yamini feeling as she stared at "Fine. Whatever."?
She felt hurt and angry, with a racing heart, and she was worried that the message would make things worse.
What could Yamini and Tenzin do to keep a disagreement from escalating in future?
They could agree to phone or talk in person when a topic gets tense instead of trading short messages.

After Disha, five, grabbed another child's pencil case, Mehak Ma'am sat down beside her. "I'll be good, I promise, I promise," said Disha, eyes wide. "I believe you want to," said Mehak. "It's hard to remember when we're excited. What could help you remember?" Disha thought. "A star." They drew a star on a card and stuck it on her desk. "When you feel like grabbing, look at the star, and ask."

What did Disha and Mehak put on Disha's desk?
A card with a star drawn on it.
What was Disha feeling when she said "I promise"?
Sincere regret and a wish to be good. She may also have hoped to avoid more trouble.
How did Mehak treat the promise?
As a hope, helping Disha plan how to keep it with a star reminder and a way to ask.
How might the child whose pencil case was grabbed feel about the promise?
Perhaps still upset until the pencil case is back. The promise alone does not fix it, and what Disha does next matters more.

At the leisure centre in Leeds, Vera's Saturday swimming lesson was with Coach Xin, who never rushed. The first week, Vera held the edge of the pool and kicked until the water frothed. The second week, she put her face in and blew bubbles, counting to three, then five. The third week, the coach handed her a long green noodle. "Lie back. Let it hold you. I'm right here." Vera's legs dropped at first. She tried again, arms out, looking at the ceiling lights. This time she floated. "Each week one new thing," said the coach. "Not two." Vera liked that. It meant she was never in the middle of too many new things at once.

What colour was the noodle?
It was green.
How did Vera feel about learning one new thing each week?
She liked it and felt safe, since she was never faced with too many new things at once.
What else could Vera do between lessons to keep the progress?
She could practise the bubbles in a bath or basin at home, so the step stays easy by the next lesson.
How might the lessons look to Coach Xin?
The coach sees steady progress without fear, which is the point of keeping each step small.

"I'll win by a mile," Kiran announced to the kids at the gate of their Gomti Nagar society. He was eight and had only learned to ride without training wheels in March. The race was two rounds of the park, and Salma, eleven, had been riding for years. "Want a head start?" she offered. Kiran snorted. "Do you want one?" The guard blew his whistle. Kiran pedalled furiously, wobbled at the first corner and had to put a foot down. Salma was already at the far gate. When she crossed the line, Kiran was still on the first round, face red. "The chain is loose," he said. Then, quietly, "I really thought I'd win."

When had Kiran learned to ride without training wheels?
Kiran had only learned to ride without training wheels in March.
What does Kiran's quiet "I really thought I'd win" show about his feelings?
It shows he is stunned and a bit hurt; he truly believed his own boast, and only now sees it didn't match his skill.
What could an adult say to Kiran that helps without shaming him?
They could tell him he rode bravely, and suggest timing his own rounds of the park each week so he can see how fast he is really getting.
How might Salma feel after offering a head start that Kiran refused?
Salma may feel a mix of pleasure at winning and sympathy, since she tried to make it fair and could see he was upset.

Bidisha, I'll tell you what I did last Sunday, because it took only an hour. I'm Mridula, the sensible girl in our lane according to the aunties, and my cousin, who works in tech and says she reviews hers monthly, told me to look at my account the way a stranger would. So I did. First, tags: three photos where friends had tagged me with our club's full name. I asked them to remove it. Then location: I switched it off in every app, because my posts basically told anyone when I'm at tuition. Then I scrolled far down to a photo from Class Eight: me in uniform at the school gate, the name board behind me. I deleted it. Anyone could work out where I'll be at eight in the morning. Nothing scary has happened. But now nothing about my routine is public.

What did Mridula delete?
Mridula deleted a photo from Class Eight of her in uniform at the school gate with the name board behind her.
Why did Mridula switch off location?
She was worried that her posts told anyone when she was at tuition, so strangers could work out her routine.
What else could Mridula do to protect her account?
She could check who follows her, keep the account private and repeat the review every few months, since old posts pile up.
How might Mridula's friends feel when asked to remove tags?
They may feel surprised at first, but most would understand since Mridula explains it is about privacy, not about them.

metadata.subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]

Read this:

When Amara moved into the Toronto flat, Nour thought she'd found the perfect flatmate. Amara cooked jollof for the whole building, laughed at every story and called Nour "my sister" within a week. By winter, the pattern was clear. Amara used Nour's laptop without asking because her own was "too slow for important things". She told their friends the house party had been her idea, though Nour had planned every detail. When Nour cried after a bad job interview, Amara glanced up from her phone and said, "You'll be fine. Did you see what my boss said about my presentation?" Only when Amara needed a favour did the old warmth come back, sudden and bright.

It changes the variable that drives the others, the rush, so the rest of the system copes.

With interest, maybe impressed that they looked at the whole system, not just blamed the cashier.

In the product meeting at the Pune office, the phone app's battery bug came up again. On some older phones it drained the battery overnight, and forty customers had complained in two weeks.
"Let's list it as a known limitation in the release notes," said Usha, the product manager. "We'll optimise it in a future update."
Gargi, who had found the bug in March, wrote it in the minutes: known limitation, optimise later. It looked so harmless on the page. A month ago she would have written: the bug we haven't fixed because the launch date matters more.
Afterwards, at the coffee machine, a colleague said, "If we delay the launch, the startup might not survive. We're saving everyone's jobs." Gargi nodded. It was true, sort of.
That night a customer review popped up on her phone: "App killed my battery on a trip." Gargi read it twice, then scrolled past.

What did Usha suggest calling the battery bug?
A known limitation.
What did Gargi feel reading the customer review?
She felt a pang of guilt, quickly pushed away by the softer words and the story about saving jobs.
What could Gargi do instead of scrolling past?
Write the bug plainly in the minutes and push for a warning to users or a fix before launch.
How does Usha seem to see the bug?
Usha sees it as a manageable issue for later, using gentle wording to keep the launch on track.

Saturday, 11 p.m.

First real fight with Rukmini today. Not a bicker. A fight.

It started with her sister's wedding. Her family wants us to split the cost of the sangeet decorations since "you two are practically engaged." I said we should talk about it first. She said I was being cheap. I said I wasn't cheap, I just didn't want to be told what to spend by her mother.

Then it got bigger. She said I never want to spend on her family but I spent on my cousin's trip without asking. That landed. She wasn't wrong.

We both went quiet. She left early.

What's bothering me isn't the money. It's how quickly I got defensive. And how she brought up something from months ago. If this is how we fight now, what happens in ten years?

I'll call her tomorrow. Not to win. To listen.

The sangeet decorations.

Sachin feels uneasy and worried, less about the money than about how quickly the defensiveness came and what that says about their future.

Sachin could admit being defensive, listen to Rukmini's side, and suggest they agree together how to handle family expenses.
How might Rukmini have felt when she left early?
She was probably hurt and frustrated, feeling that Sachin doesn't value her family and remembering the cousin's trip.

The hostel Wi-Fi had died, so he and Santosh squeezed into a noisy cybercafe with a flickering monitor. The post used a crying vendor's photo and bold red letters. Anirban's first reaction was anger. Then he paused. "Why is it so loud?" he muttered. He found the actual draft law on the municipal site. It proposed vending zones, not a ban. Every hour Joanne has to collect the coins out of the fountain inside the mall. During the first hour, she collected 15 coins. For the next two hours, she collected 35 coins from the fountain. In the fourth hour, she collected 50 coins from the fountain but she gave 15 of them to her coworker so she could buy a soda. How many coins did she have after the fourth hour?

15 coins collected in hour one
35 coins collected in hour two
35 coins collected in hour three
50 coins collected in hour four
Before giving her coworker some coins there were 15+35+35+50=135 coins
The number of coins after given 15 to her coworker is 135-15=120
The answer is 120.

Chloe and Max played Mario Kart together. The ratio of Chloe's wins to Max's wins is 8:3. Chloe won 24 times. How many times did Max win?

We are trying to figure out how many times Max won at Mario Kart, so we'll call that number Y.
We know the ratio of Chloe's wins to Max's wins is 8/3, so 8/3 = 24/Y.
Next, we will multiply to find the cross-products. 8 x Y = 3 x 24 or 8Y = 72.
We want to get figure out Y, so we need to get it by itself by dividing by 8, like this: 8Y / 8 = 72 / 8.
Y = 9, so Max won 9 times.
The answer is 9.

Dear Madhuri,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me, so here it is.
There's a man at my internship, Karan, who is engaged. We've been staying late together on the same project, and lately he's been texting me at night. Long messages, about how his fiancée 'doesn't understand him' and how I do. And honestly, I've loved it. I've felt special, chosen. For a few weeks I told myself this was different, that the rules didn't apply to something this real.
Then on Saturday I saw his fiancée's photos online. She looked kind. She was holding a card that said '3 months to go!' And I felt sick.
I'd be hurting her, and I'd be setting myself up to be the next one he lies to.
So I've stopped replying to the night texts. I've asked my manager to move me to the other project team. It hurts more than I expected.
Can you come over Sunday? I don't want to be alone with my phone.
Pooja

'3 months to go!'
How had Pooja felt about Karan's night texts?
Pooja felt special and chosen, loving the attention.
What steps did Pooja take to step back?
Stopped replying to the night texts, asked to move to another project team, and reached out to Madhuri for support.
How might Karan's fiancée feel if she knew?
Deeply hurt and betrayed, since she's counting down to the wedding.

Thursday night.
Today the whole class decided that the maths test was unfair and everyone would sign a complaint. I read the paper again in my head at lunch, and I think it was fair. I said so. The room went quiet, and then everybody spoke at once.
Pradeep asked, “Why are you being difficult?” Two girls looked away. I didn’t sign. I felt my face go hot and my hands go cold.
Now I keep asking myself whether I’m the one who’s wrong. Everyone else can’t be wrong, can they? I can’t decide, and the sad part is that I’m not sure I’d say it again tomorrow.
— Vasudha

What did the class decide about the maths test?
The class decided the maths test was unfair and that everyone would sign a complaint.
What was Vasudha feeling when the room went quiet and then everybody spoke at once?
Vasudha felt isolated and pressured, with a hot face and cold hands. Doubt about being wrong is strongest when alone against everyone.
What could help Vasudha decide whether the test was really unfair?
Vasudha could check the test against what was taught, or quietly ask a trusted adult. That tests the view with facts instead of the pressure of the room.
How might Pradeep have seen Vasudha's refusal to sign?
Pradeep may have felt frustrated because the class wanted to act together, so a single refusal looked like difficulty. Pradeep may not have meant to push anyone out.

"Before we start, Vinita," Leela said in the Monday team meeting, "I talk too much. Last time I counted: I spoke five times before anyone else got one turn. I'm going to keep count today."
Vinita smiled. "That's honest."
Ten minutes later Leela was mid-flow about the launch plan. She stopped herself. "That's my third turn. Vinita, what do you think? You know the vendor better than I do."
Vinita sat up. "Actually, I think their timeline is optimistic. I've worked with them twice."
"Say more."
Leela nodded, wrote it down and kept quiet till Vinita finished.

How many times did Leela speak before anyone else in the last meeting?
Leela spoke five times before anyone else got one turn.
What does Leela's stopping mid-flow suggest Leela was feeling?
It suggests Leela was aware and a little self-conscious, trying to change a habit. Counting turns shows a genuine wish to make room.
What did Leela do to make space for Vinita?
Leela counted turns, stopped after the third and asked Vinita directly for input. Leela then stayed quiet until Vinita had finished.
How might Vinita have felt when Leela asked "What do you think?"
Vinita probably felt valued and invited, since Vinita sat up and gave a real concern. Being asked directly made it easy to speak.

Could you answer these?
why is it good to be on time for a meeting
What is the name of the shop owner near my house?

1. Arriving on time respects other people's plans. Because others have arranged their day around the meeting, a late arrival wastes their time.
2. I don't know; I don't know the shop. You could ask the owner or a neighbour.

In the last class before study leave, Zeenat Ma'am wrote on the board: "It is 15 March. Your exams went badly. Write down why." The room went quiet. Sachin stared at his page, then started. "Phone. I kept watching matches." "Got flu, lost a week." "Slept four hours before Maths." Around him others were scribbling too. "Now," said Zeenat Ma'am, "next to each reason, write one thing you will do from tomorrow so it can't happen." Sachin thought. Phone: hand it to Mummy from seven to ten. Flu: keep Sunday free as a buffer. Sleep: no studying after eleven, however scared. He underlined the last one twice. On his way out, Zeenat Ma'am glanced at his page and nodded.

What date did Zeenat Ma'am write on the board?
15 March.
Why did Sachin underline the sleep step twice?
He seems to know that fear pushes him to stay up late, and was worried enough about it to make that step extra firm.
What would make Sachin's plan stronger?
Telling his family about the steps, like the phone arrangement with Mummy, so he isn't relying only on himself when stress rises.
How does Zeenat Ma'am seem to see Sachin's page?
Her nod suggests she approves of the concrete steps he has attached to each risk.

It takes 10 minutes to wash a unit of windows and he has 16 units so 10*16 = 160 minutes

Football coach's note, Sachin, September
On Friday, several boys from the team planned to skip the last class to go to the mall. Ojas (15) was invited and, I'm told, called "boring" when he said no. He came to practice instead, a little quiet. When I asked, he said, "I didn't want to, but I also didn't want to be left out." He made a good choice, and I told him so privately. I've also reminded the whole team about skipping classes. I'll pair Ojas with some of the senior players for drills.

Where did the boys plan to go?
To the mall.
What was Ojas feeling at practice after saying no?
He felt torn and a bit left out, even though he knew he'd made the choice he wanted.

To give him support and a sense of belonging for sticking with his choice.

They might respect him more if he doesn't back down, or keep teasing for a while.

The housing society's youth committee met in the clubhouse in Andheri on Sunday morning to plan the Diwali evening. Chandrika, in her final year of college, sat near the door with her tea.
Shalini, the committee secretary, spoke first and kept speaking: last year's lights, a caterer she liked, the parking problem, a neighbour's dog. Two younger boys tried to suggest a quiz. Shalini said, "Nice, nice," and carried on. Nobody had a list. Chandrika checked her watch twice. An hour and a half passed.
When they broke up, Chandrika's phone buzzed with the group chat. "So we're doing the caterer, right?" "I thought we agreed on potluck?" "Is the quiz happening or not?" Four messages, four versions.
Chandrika scrolled, then put the phone face down. She had given up a morning of study for this, and she could not tell her mother a single thing they had decided.

What did the two younger boys try to suggest?
They tried to suggest a quiz.
How did Chandrika feel when she put the phone face down?
Chandrika felt frustrated and let down, having given up a morning of study for a meeting where nothing was decided.
What small change could the committee try next time?
Someone could write a short list of items before the meeting, give each a time limit and read out the decisions at the end.
How might Shalini see the same morning?
Shalini may think the meeting went well because she covered many points, without noticing others could not get a word in.
We want to take part in Janmashtami's dahi handi at our colony, but my mom is worried about safety.
Her worry makes sense, because human pyramids can be risky. What role did you have in mind?
I'd be on the ground, helping to hold the rope.
Ground helpers matter a lot. Show your mother how the organisers plan safety, such as soft mats, a helmet for the top person and adults standing by.
What if they don't have any of that?
Then it's reasonable to sit this one out and enjoy the celebration as a spectator. You could help with decorations or the prasad instead, and your mom will feel better.

Vaibhav, you asked how it actually went, so here it is, no polish. The first counsellor I saw, I froze for four sessions and counted ceiling tiles. It wasn't her fault, it just wasn't a fit, so I found someone else. With the new counsellor I said nothing big for weeks. Then one day I said one sentence about that night, just one, hands shaking, and nothing bad happened. The next week I said two. Some weeks I go backwards and can't say a word, and that's allowed. Remember when you texted, "Yamini, no pressure, tell me when you want"? I read that four times. My mum keeps asking when I'll be "better". I told her it's not one big moment. It's small safe things, again and again.

For how many sessions did the speaker freeze and count ceiling tiles with the first counsellor?
Four sessions, as the passage says, with the first counsellor.
How did Yamini feel with the first counsellor, and what did Yamini do about it?
Yamini felt frozen and uneasy, counting ceiling tiles for four sessions, but did not blame the counsellor and simply found someone else.
What does Yamini's account suggest about how trust grows in therapy?
It grows through small safe steps, one sentence and then two, and some weeks go backwards, so patience matters more than one breakthrough.
How might Yamini's mother be seeing the recovery?
She seems to expect a moment when Yamini will be better, so she may not notice how much the small steps count until it is explained to her.

The supermarket car park in Toronto was busy, and Abebe wanted to run ahead to the trolleys.

Aiko, his childminder, crouched to his height. "In the car park, you hold my hand. The drivers sit up high, and they can't always see small people behind the cars."

Abebe looked at a big van reversing, its lights flashing. "Because they're tall?"

"Because they're tall and the cars are big."

He thought, then nodded. "Okay." He put his hand in hers.

At the trolleys he let go only when she said, "Now you can push."

What did Abebe see reversing?
A big van, its lights flashing.
What was Abebe likely feeling when he nodded and said "Okay"?
He was most likely calm and satisfied that the rule made sense, since he checked the reason with his own question. He may still have felt a little impatient to reach the trolleys.
Why did Aiko's approach work?
She crouched to his height and gave a calm, clear reason about drivers not seeing small people, so Abebe accepted the rule rather than just obeying.
How might Aiko feel when Abebe puts his hand in hers?
She is probably relieved and pleased that he agreed without a fight and understood why.

"Mumma, my bag strap tore. Can we buy a new one? Everyone has the new cartoon ones."
Gurleen turned the bag over in her hands. "The bag is fine. Only the strap. How much is a new bag?"
"Six hundred, I think."
"And what does the tailor charge to fix a strap?"
Gopika thought. "Maybe thirty?"
"So what's left from six hundred?"

Gopika looked at the old bag. "Can the tailor put a patch? A star patch?"
"I'll ask."

How much did Gopika think a new bag cost?
Six hundred.
Why did Gopika frown at "Five hundred seventy"?
She was surprised and uneasy at how much would be spent replacing a whole bag when only the strap was broken.
Why did Gurleen ask questions instead of just saying no?
Working out the numbers let Gopika see the value of repairing herself, so the choice felt like hers.
How might Gurleen feel about Gopika's star-patch idea?
Pleased that Gopika chose repair over a new bag and made it her own, and happy to ask the tailor about the patch. 😊

The coaching centre above the sweet shop in Pune smelled of samosas. Sir held up two stones. “A big one and a small one, dropped together from the roof, no wind. Which lands first?”
“The big one!” Suraj said, and nearly everyone agreed.
Yogesh had watched a video about this at home. They land together, he thought. He even remembered the experiment with a hammer and a feather.
“Yogesh?”
He looked around at the nodding heads. “The big one, sir,” he said.
Sir smiled. “Actually, they land at almost the same time.” Suraj shrugged. Yogesh looked down at his notebook, cheeks warm, wishing he could take the words back.

Where was the coaching centre?
It was above the sweet shop in Pune.
How was Yogesh feeling after the teacher gave the answer?
He felt embarrassed and regretful; his cheeks were warm and he wished he could take his words back, because he had known they land together.
What went wrong for Yogesh, and what might fix it?
He let the nodding heads outweigh what he knew; next time he could say his answer and his reason, even if he's the only one.
Why might Suraj react so differently to being wrong?
Suraj just shrugged, having said an honest belief; Yogesh had gone against his own knowledge, which stings more.

Two months, every rupee: that was the deal Vaibhav and Trisha made in their Bengaluru flat, with a shared spending app on both phones. Then, three weeks in, Trisha was sent to a client site in Nagpur for a month. Logging became a long-distance chore. She photographed receipts on the train; he nagged her by text about untagged payments at midnight.
On the last Sunday they sat on a video call, both with the totals open. Vaibhav had expected the Nagpur hotel meals to be the shock. Instead, the biggest surprise was at home: food orders on late work nights, plus six subscriptions, two of which neither remembered signing up for. Together they came to roughly a fifth of what both earned.
"That's more than our electricity and internet put together," Trisha said slowly. They started with the subscriptions.

Where was Trisha sent three weeks in?
To a client site in Nagpur for a month.
How did Vaibhav feel when the biggest surprise turned out to be at home?
He was likely startled and a little embarrassed, having expected the Nagpur hotel meals to be the shock.
What could the couple decide next, now that they know?
They could sit down together and choose which orders and subscriptions they really value, and ask a qualified adviser if bigger money decisions come up.
What would have changed if they had stopped logging when Trisha left for Nagpur?
The second month would have been patchy, and the pattern of late-night food orders and forgotten subscriptions might never have shown up.

"You broke my drawing," said Pooja, crying.
"I didn't mean to," said Vijay. "I was running."
"Now it's torn!"
Vijay looked at the torn paper. "I can make you a new one."
"A new drawing?"

Orange.
What was Pooja feeling when she saw her drawing torn?

He made a new drawing of her orange cat, a concrete fix that she could hold and that made her smile.

In the NGO office in Kolkata, Saurabh put a chart on the screen. "Schools with libraries have much higher reading scores. Let's fund libraries everywhere." Everyone nodded. Chaitanya, the youngest analyst, frowned. "Can I check a few things first?" He went through the list of schools. The ones with libraries were mostly in the city, with trained teachers and parents who read at home. So a third thing might be causing both. Could it run the other way? Perhaps schools with good readers were the ones that asked for libraries. Then he searched for a fair comparison: last year, the NGO had set up libraries in ten village schools and not yet in ten similar ones nearby. Their scores had risen a little more with the library, but far less than the chart suggested. "Libraries help," Chaitanya said. "Just not as much as this chart claims." Saurabh sighed, then nodded.

Where were most of the schools with libraries?
Mostly in the city, with trained teachers and parents who read at home.
How might Saurabh have felt when Chaitanya's comparison came back?
Saurabh probably felt a bit let down, since the big effect he hoped for turned out smaller, but he accepted the finding.
What did Chaitanya do that other analysts could copy?
He checked for a third cause, considered reversed direction, and found a fair comparison of similar schools before claiming libraries cause higher scores.
What was Chaitanya feeling when he asked to check a few things first?
He seemed cautious and a little nervous, as the youngest analyst questioning a chart everyone had nodded at.

Subject: Confirming our conversation

Dear Abhinav sir,
When we spoke in the corridor, you said it would be "nice" if the vendor deck was ready soon. I wasn't sure whether that was a suggestion or a task with a deadline, and I didn't want to guess. So, to be clear: I understand you need the deck by Friday noon. I would like your comments by Friday 10 am so I can finalise on time, and I will send you a draft on Thursday evening. If Friday noon is not what you meant, please tell me and I will change the plan 🙂.

Regards,
Yusuf

What word did Abhinav use when speaking about the vendor deck?
Abhinav said it would be "nice" if the deck was ready soon.
What was Yusuf worried about when writing the email?
Yusuf worried that the corridor remark might be a task with a deadline and that guessing wrong would be costly. Abhinav may honestly have meant it casually, so both readings stay possible.
Why was confirming in writing a good step?
It turned a vague remark into a stated deadline and gave both of them a record if the plan changed.
How might Abhinav read a message like this from a junior?
Abhinav may see it as careful and helpful, or be a little surprised that a "nice" was taken as an instruction; the reply will show which.
Who drives my school bus?
I wouldn't know, because I can't see your bus or your school. Ask the driver or the transport in-charge.

The results for the maths olympiad were pinned outside the staffroom in Secunderabad, and Kishore's name was second from the top. Uday read it, then said, loud enough for the corridor, 'Must be nice. Your lot get everything on quota anyway.' A few people went quiet. Kishore's ears rang. For a second he felt tiny, as if the paper could blow his name away. Then anger came up hot behind it. He wanted to shove Uday. He didn't. His friends Farhan and Deepa stepped close on either side. 'He topped the mock tests all term,' Deepa said flatly. 'Everyone saw.' At lunch Kishore went to Mrs Joseph, the class teacher, and repeated Uday's words exactly. She said the remark came from Uday's prejudice, not from anything about Kishore's ability, and sent for Uday that afternoon. Walking home, Farhan and Deepa kept talking about the next round, as if the remark didn't deserve the space.

Where were the olympiad results pinned?
Outside the staffroom in Secunderabad.
What was Kishore feeling right after Uday's remark?
He felt tiny at first, then hot anger rose up behind it.
What steps helped Kishore handle the remark?
He didn't shove Uday, stayed with friends who backed him, and told the class teacher Uday's exact words.
How do Farhan and Deepa see Uday's remark?
They see it as unfair bias against a friend who earned his place, so they stand close and move on to the next round.

The app launch Pankaj had led had flopped: barely two hundred downloads in a month. Now he had to explain it at the Monday review, and the office generator had failed, so there was no projector, just a hot room and his printouts. "So sorry about the numbers, Pankaj," said Uma, whose own plan had been turned down for his. Her voice was kind. The corner of her mouth wasn't. Across the table, two others exchanged a look he'd seen before, in the canteen, when someone's bike got towed. Pankaj's throat went dry. He read his pages to the table while sweat ran down his back, and he felt about eight years old. After the meeting, nobody walked out with him. He sat alone in the stairwell with his printouts, lonelier than at any time since he had joined.

How many downloads did the launch get in a month?
Barely two hundred.
What did Pankaj suspect Uma was really feeling behind "So sorry about the numbers"?
That Uma was secretly pleased, since her own plan had been turned down for his and the corner of her mouth didn't match her kind voice.
What could Pankaj do after the stairwell so he isn't alone with the failure?
Reach out to one trusted colleague or friend to talk it through, and focus the review on what can be learned rather than on the smiles.
What would change if even one colleague had walked out with Pankaj?
He might have felt less alone and small, and the others' smiles would have been easier to bear 🤍

In the clinic waiting room, a jar of toffees sat on the reception desk. Simran, five, had already had one from Baljeet at the counter. "Another! Papa, another!" Sumit shook his head. Simran's voice rose. "I hate you! Give it!" People looked up. Sumit crouched to her eye level and spoke low and steady. "I hear you're angry. The answer is still no more sweets today." He didn't bargain, didn't scold, didn't call her naughty. Simran howled and pushed his arm. He stayed, calm, arms open. "I'm right here when you want a hug."

Who gave Simran her first toffee?
Baljeet at the counter.
What was Simran feeling when she pushed Sumit's arm?
She was angry and frustrated that the limit held, her big feelings still spilling over.
Which parts of Sumit's response make the limit calm and firm?
He crouched to her level, named her anger, repeated the no without bargaining, shaming or shouting, and stayed ready to hug.
How might the people in the waiting room see Sumit?
They may be surprised to see a parent stay so steady, and perhaps relieved there is no shouting match.

I don't know him or what happened this morning, so I can't tell. If it worries you, a polite word with him might help.

She threw down her pencil.

It suggests she now believes she can work through it step by step and feels more confident.
What helped Elizabeth believe her ability could grow?
Nirmala changed "can't" to "can't do it yet" and helped her practise one step at a time.
How might Nirmala feel when Elizabeth grins after school?

Akash has been in Block B for five months since leaving home. When other students ask about his family, he gives the same short answer: "My father is a dictator. End of story." He says it almost cheerfully now, like a line he has practised.

A safe space where Akash can hold both the hurt and the good memories, before his father hardens into only a villain.

Probably his own simple story, perhaps that his son is ungrateful, with the same missing tenderness.

First week of April. Shreya heard it in the college canteen: two boys arguing in Assamese about a cricket match. She stopped with her tray in her hands. She hadn't spoken her own language out loud in Bengaluru for four months.

Shreya taught Nazia three Assamese words, bringing a little of home into the present and feeling less far away.

Ines read the email twice on the tram home: not selected for the summer placement at the engineering firm. By the time she reached her flat in Lisbon, the sentence in her head had changed from "they said no" to "I am a failure." She skipped dinner and lay on the sofa. Her flatmate Bao set down a bowl of rice anyway and said nothing about it. Later Ines opened her notebook and drew two columns: what happened, and what I keep telling myself. Only the first column was true. The firm had picked four people from a hundred applications. She still felt heavy, but she emailed the firm to ask for feedback on her application, then went to eat the cold rice.

How many people had the firm picked, and from how many applications?
The firm had picked four people from a hundred applications.
What was Ines telling herself after the email, and what does her two-column list suggest she came to see?
She told herself "I am a failure" and felt heavy, but the columns suggest she came to see that only the rejection was fact and the label was not.
What small step helped Ines get moving again, even though she still felt heavy?
She emailed the firm to ask for feedback on her application, a doable next action that treated the result as information.
How might Bao have seen Ines that evening?
Bao probably saw a friend who was hurting and chose quietly to leave food instead of lecturing, since Ines had skipped dinner.

The school library was quiet in the free period. Lalit opened his maths assignment, looked at question one, and felt his chest tighten. He pushed it aside and pulled out a comic from the shelf.
Immediately he felt better. Lighter.
Manjula ma'am, the librarian, walked past and smiled. "Good comic?"
"Very," he said.
By the end of the period he'd read the whole thing. Walking to class, a quiet guilt crept in. The assignment was due tomorrow, and he hadn't done one sum.
That evening, he opened it again, felt the tightness, and switched on the TV. The relief came, and so did the guilt, a little bigger this time.

What did Lalit read instead of doing maths?
A comic from the shelf.
What was Lalit feeling as he walked to class?
He felt a quiet guilt creeping in, after the lift of avoiding the maths.
What could help Lalit break the relief-then-guilt cycle?
Starting with a single sum when the tightness comes, or asking Manjula ma'am or his teacher for help with question one.
What might Manjula ma'am have noticed?
She may have noticed he looked relaxed with the comic and not guessed the maths was waiting.
