I'm Nikita. When the scholarship results were read out, Aman put his head down on the desk and his shoulders shook. A couple of boys sniggered. “He didn't get it.” Varun, who sits beside Aman, didn't laugh and didn't guess. He just shifted his chair a bit closer and sat there, quiet, until Aman looked up. Then he asked, “You okay?” Aman wiped his face and laughed shakily. “I got it. I thought I wouldn't. My mum's going to cry too.” Varun grinned and clapped his shoulder. I don't know what Varun was thinking, but he was the only one who got it right.

What was read out in class?
The scholarship results were read out.
What was Aman feeling when his shoulders shook?
Aman was overwhelmed with relief and joy at getting the scholarship, not sadness, as the sniggering boys assumed.
Why did Varun's approach work better than guessing?
He offered quiet company and then asked, which let Aman share the real reason for his tears.
How does Nikita view the moment?
Nikita sees that the boys guessed wrong, and that only Varun, by waiting and asking, got it right.

What is the best way to carry a heavy bag?
And what does "over the moon" mean?

I'm Rukmini. Shankar and I used to just cycle round the colony together after school, racing to the water tank. We didn't talk much. Last winter, sitting on the tank wall, I told him something I'd never told anyone: I don't want to be a doctor like everyone in my family expects. I want to play drums. He didn't laugh. He said, "You tap on everything anyway." The next week he brought me two old chopsticks as drumsticks. He's never told a soul. Now I tell him everything first, before anyone else.

Where did Rukmini and Shankar sit when she told him?
On the water tank wall.
How did Rukmini feel after Shankar kept the secret?
Rukmini felt trusted and close to him, relieved to have someone who understood.
What would you advise Rukmini to do with her drum dream?
Keep practising and find a calm moment to talk to a family member Rukmini trusts about it.
What might Shankar have been thinking when he brought the chopsticks?
He probably wanted to show he took the dream seriously and was on Rukmini's side.

A local park has 70 pigeons that call the park home. Half of the pigeons are black, and 20 percent of the black pigeons are male.  How many more black female pigeons are there than black male pigeons?

Black:70/2=35 pigeons
Black Male: 35(.20)=7 pigeons
35-7=28 female black pigeon
There are 28-7=21 more black female pigeons
The answer is 21.

Last spring, someone in my class called my singing "like a pressure-cooker whistle." I'm Yamini, and I still remember the exact tone. It was one boy, once, at lunch. That same week, the music teacher chose me for the school choir solo. Tenzin, my best friend, said my voice gave her goosebumps. Three girls from Class 9 asked me to teach them the song. And I can barely remember their faces. I only replayed the pressure cooker, again and again, for days. I almost refused the solo. Looking back, I think my brain treated that one comment like a danger sign and filed the nice ones as background noise. Tenzin finally made me write down every kind thing people said that week. There were eleven. I stuck the list inside my music folder. I sang the solo.

How many kind things did Yamini write down that week?
There were eleven.
What was Yamini feeling during the days she replayed the comment?
Yamini felt hurt and doubtful, so shaken by the one mocking comment that the solo almost got refused.
What did Tenzin suggest, and why did it help?
Writing down every kind thing said that week, which made the eleven good comments as solid as the one mean one.
How does Tenzin see Yamini's singing?
Tenzin loves it, saying Yamini's voice gives her goosebumps.

I picked her up before the crying started, held her close and sang the washing song softly. She cried for a little while into my shoulder, then went quiet and watched the others. The washing song, softly.
What did Hafsa's trembling lip show she was feeling?

Which of Baljeet's choices worked, and why?
Picking Hafsa up early and singing softly worked, because closeness and a gentle voice helped her calm down enough to watch and then play.
How might Hafsa's mother feel reading this note?
She would likely feel relieved and reassured that Hafsa was comforted quickly and was playing by snack time. 🙏

a) bus 50%, train 30%, car 20%; late with prob. 0.2, 0.1, 0.05: P(event), P(each cause | event)
b) rain 0.3; late 0.4 if rain, 0.1 if not: P(event), P(each cause | event)
c) shop gets eggs from farms P, Q, R in ratio 5 : 3 : 2; cracked rates 2%, 5%, 10%: P(event), P(each cause | event)
d) class: 60% girls; 30% of girls and 20% of boys wear glasses: P(event), P(each cause | event)
e) insurance: 20% accident-prone drivers (claim prob. 0.3), others 0.05: P(event), P(each cause | event)
f) letters from towns X, Y (equally likely); postmark shows "..TN" with prob. 0.9 for X and 0.2 for Y: P(event), P(each cause | event)
g) cricket: team wins toss 1/2; wins match 0.7 after winning the toss, 0.4 otherwise: P(event), P(each cause | event)

Rahul got 27 marks in maths, 32 in science and 28 in English. What is his total?
87. Because 27 + 32 = 59, and 59 + 28 = 87, so the total is 87.
Heather helps her neighbour pick weeds out of her garden. She gets paid 5 cents for every weed she picks. On average, how many seconds can she take to pick a weed if she wants to earn $10 an hour?

In an hour, she needs to earn $10 * 100 cents / $1 = 1000 cents.
In an hour, she must pick 1000 cents / 5 cents = 200 weeds.
There are 1hr * (60 minutes / 1 hr) = 60 minutes in an hour.
There are 60 minutes * (60 seconds / 1 minute) = 3600 seconds in an hour.
She has 3600 seconds / 200 = 18 seconds to pick each weed.
The answer is 18.

The call dropped for the third time; the Bengaluru building's Wi-Fi was down again, and Yusuf was already four time zones away in Doha. Tanvir stood on the stairwell landing, the only spot with signal, phone pressed to his ear. They'd barely spoken in the six weeks since their fight about Tanvir missing Yusuf's engagement. Tanvir had a hundred people in his contacts who'd cheer his posts, and not one he'd told that he'd been eating dinner alone every night. When the line reconnected, the silence was thick. "I'm sorry I missed it," Tanvir said. "I was ashamed I couldn't afford the ticket, so I just went quiet. That was worse." Yusuf let out a breath. "You could've said that." "I'm saying it now. Can we do Sunday calls again? Even bad-signal ones?" Yusuf laughed, a little stiffly. "Stairwell Sundays, then."

Where was the only spot with signal?
The stairwell landing was the only spot with signal.
What does Tanvir's confession suggest he had been feeling since the fight?
It suggests Tanvir had been ashamed and lonely, hiding behind silence rather than admitting why he missed the engagement.
What small step helps rebuild the friendship?
Agreeing on regular Sunday calls, even with bad signal, gives the friendship a steady rhythm after the awkward apology.
How might Yusuf have felt when Tanvir finally explained?
Yusuf probably felt relieved to know the real reason, and still a little stiff and hurt, which shows in his cautious laugh.

Dear Ujjwal Mama,

I'm writing because I don't know how to say this on the phone. Since the separation, Mummy sleeps very late and often forgets things. Last Tuesday there was no dinner, and I had cereal. She forgot to sign my exam form, and the last date is Friday. I'm not blaming her. I think she's sad and tired, and it isn't because of me.

Could you help me with the exam form on Wednesday? And could I have dinner at your house two evenings a week for now? I'll get myself there after school.

I'd also like someone to ask how I'm doing. Sometimes I feel forgotten.

Thank you,

Mama's reply, that same evening: "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault. I'm coming over tomorrow, and we'll do the form together."

Which day is the last date for the exam form?
The last date is Friday.
What is Parveen feeling about Mummy's forgetfulness?
Parveen feels hurt and sometimes forgotten, yet does not blame Mummy and thinks she is sad and tired.
What is Parveen doing that could help meet Parveen's needs?
Parveen is asking clearly for help with the form, regular dinners and someone to check in, and is turning to a relative.
How might Ujjwal Mama feel reading the letter?
Probably worried and touched that Parveen trusted him, and eager to help Parveen and check on his sister as well; he replies that same evening.

When I was fifteen, Appa found out I'd been talking to Vasudha every evening after tuition and said, very loudly, that it had to stop. No reasons, just "I don't want to hear her name in this house." I'm Jomon, and before that day, Vasudha was just a friend from maths class. After that day she became the most important person in my life. I called her from the terrace. Where did Jomon call Vasudha from?

Jomon felt angry and controlled, so staying close to Vasudha became a way to prove freedom rather than a real feeling for her.
What helped Jomon see the situation clearly, and what could Appa have done instead?
Amma asking what Jomon actually felt; Appa could have explained his worry and talked calmly instead of banning her name.

The power went at noon on Eid, just as Rehana's family sat down to lunch in their Kozhikode flat, and the fans slowed to nothing. Jyoti, there as Rehana's college friend, watched Faraz from Lucknow sweat through his new kurta and still reach for a second helping of pathiri.
"He's learning," Rehana whispered. Two months ago he'd called Malabar biryani "too mild".
Rehana's aunt fanned herself with a plate. "So Faraz, after marriage you'll take her to Lucknow? Joint family?"
The room went quiet except for the traffic outside.
Faraz glanced at Rehana. She gave a small nod. "We've talked about it, Khala," he said. "We'd like to start on our own, near both our jobs, and visit both families often. We're still working out the details together."
The aunt raised an eyebrow. Rehana squeezed his hand under the table. Jyoti thought: they rehearsed this, and they did it side by side.

What did Jyoti think when Faraz answered the aunt?

They had already discussed where to live, checked with each other through a glance and a nod, and gave one shared answer instead of leaving one person to defend it.
How might Rehana's aunt see Faraz after this lunch?
The aunt may still have doubts, as her raised eyebrow shows, but she has seen Faraz answer respectfully and speak for both of them.
For a nature magazine for kids, write about 100 words on what happens in a pond during the monsoon.

When the monsoon arrives, a quiet pond suddenly comes alive. Rainwater fills it to the brim, and the edges turn green with fresh grass. At night, frogs gather and croak loudly, calling to one another. Soon there are jelly-like clusters of eggs floating near the reeds, and in a few weeks, tiny tadpoles wriggle everywhere. Dragonflies dart over the water, and water lilies open their pink flowers. Herons stand still on one leg, waiting patiently for a fish. If you sit by a pond in the monsoon, you will see a whole small world at work.

Luke started working on a 1000-piece jigsaw puzzle. The first day he worked on it, he put together 10% of the pieces. On the second day, he put together another 20% of the remaining pieces from the first day. On the third day, he put together 30% of the remaining pieces from the previous day. How many pieces does he have left to complete after the third day?

Luke started putting together, 1000 x 0.1 = 100 pieces.
The next day, there were 1000-100 = 900 pieces left.
Then he put together 900 * 0.2 = 180 pieces on the second day.
So there were 900 - 180 = 720 pieces left.
On the third day, he put together 720 * 0.3 = 216 pieces.
Therefore, Luke still has 720 - 216 = 504 pieces left to complete the puzzle.
The answer is 504.
Why can a camel go a long time without a drink in the desert?
A camel's body saves water. Because it loses very little water and the fat stored in its hump gives it food energy, it can travel far between drinks.

"We've got enough," Thomas said, and ran to the pitch.
The PE teacher was busy with the other class. Varun sat on the steps near the water cooler. From there he could hear the bat hitting the ball and everyone shouting. Last year he and Thomas had been bowling partners.
His stomach felt heavy, like after eating too much, but it wasn't food. He pulled at a loose thread on his sock until it came out.
When the bell rang, a classmate asked why he hadn't played. "Didn't feel like it," Varun said, looking away.

What is wrong with "His handwriting are very neat."?
How can I write neat handwriting?
A list has 21 words and Emma already knows 9 of them. How many words are still new?

2. Fixed: His handwriting is very neat. Why: "Handwriting" is singular, so use "is".
3. Sit straight, hold your pen lightly and write slowly. Practise a few lines each day.
4. 12 words. Because 21 - 9 = 12.

My grandfather has a vegetable patch and he's teaching me. I'm Dev.
That is a great way to learn, Dev. Gardeners learn the most by working beside someone with experience. What did he teach you first?
How to dig the soil. He said it should be loose, like cake.
He is right. Loose soil lets roots spread and water move through. Digging it in the morning, before the sun gets strong, is more comfortable for both of you.
Today we sowed spinach and coriander. They are quick, he says.
He is correct. Both grow fast, and you can often pick the first leaves in three or four weeks. Water gently so the tiny seeds do not wash away.
How do I know when to pick the spinach?
Pick the outer leaves when they are about the size of your palm, and leave the small centre leaves to keep growing. Ask your grandfather to show you the first time, Dev.
I will. He also told me a proverb about patience. I forgot the vegetable he mentioned.
You mentioned only that he taught you to dig loose soil, like cake, and that you sowed spinach and coriander. I do not know which vegetable he named in the proverb, so ask him to tell you again.

Joseph wanted to stand up and shout. He didn't. When Rehana went to the water cooler, he followed and said quietly, "I saw that man bothering you. Are you okay? What would you like? I can tell the librarian, sit at your table, or just walk you out. Your call."

She felt tense and uncomfortable, trying to ignore the man's comments.

Dear Vasudha ma'am,
You once told our ethics class that 'someone should do something' usually means nobody will. I'm writing because I've just learned what you meant.
At the logistics company, in my first month, I noticed that the fuel bills for two trucks were far higher than their routes could explain. I asked a senior; he said the supervisor surely knew. The supervisor was friendly with the drivers. I told myself it wasn't my job, and that speaking up could cost me my confirmation. Three other juniors saw the same thing. We joked about it once over tea, and did nothing.
This month audit found it had been going on for a year and had spread to five trucks. In the meeting the manager asked, 'Why did nobody report this?' None of us answered.
I'm not writing for comfort. I'm writing to say I understand now, and next time I'll be the one who speaks first, through the proper channel.
With respect,
Akash

How many trucks were affected by the time audit found it?
Five trucks.
How does Akash feel writing this letter?
Ashamed and regretful about staying silent, but determined to act differently next time.
What could Akash and the other juniors have done in the first month?
One of them could have written down the fuel figures and reported them through the proper channel, instead of assuming the supervisor knew.
How might Vasudha ma'am feel reading the letter?
Saddened by what happened but moved that the lesson finally landed, and hopeful about what Akash will do next time.

At the kabaddi game on the temple ground, the two captains picked teams, and Chinmay was picked last. Last of all, after even the little Patil boy.

He walked home kicking stones. "Nobody ever picks me," he told Joseph, who lived next door. "I never win anything. I'm always last."

Joseph raised an eyebrow. "Always? Last Sunday you were captain in gilli-danda."
"That doesn't count."
"And you won the cycle race at the fair."
"That was luck."
"And today you were picked last once, because Ganpat's cousin came from Pune and everyone wanted to see him play."

Chinmay stopped kicking. "Once," he said slowly.

"Once," said Joseph. "Come tomorrow. I'll be captain."

Why did Chinmay say "Nobody ever picks me"?
Chinmay felt hurt and embarrassed at being picked last, and that one moment felt like a rule for his whole life.

Jill likes to do small jobs online.  She makes $10 a day for her first month working online, and double that per day in her second month.  Her third month she makes the same amount per day as the previous month, but only works every other day.  How much did she make over three months, assuming each month is 30 days long?

Since there are 30 days in a month and Jill makes $10 a day her first month, she makes 30*10= 300 dollars her first month.
She makes twice the amount of the previous month's $300 in her second month, so she makes 2*300=600 dollars her second month.
She makes the same amount per day the third month, but only works half the number of days, so she makes 600/2= 300 dollars a month her third month.
In total, she makes 300+300+600= 1,200 dollars
The answer is 1,200.

My cousin in India is in Standard Five. Is standard not about quality?

In Indian schools a standard is a class or year of school, as in Standard Five. It is a noun. The wider meaning is a level of quality, or something usual and accepted.
Example: He moved up to Standard Six after the summer break.

Facilitator's note, community centre workshop on friendship and care, Saturday.
Today's pair exercise asked each person to describe how they show care. Mehak and Vandana, best friends for ten years, were sure they knew each other. Mehak said she shows love by planning surprises and sending long voice notes. Vandana said she shows love by remembering small things and turning up with food when someone is ill. Then I asked each to say what makes them feel cared for. Mehak said, "When someone just sits with me, no phones." Vandana said, "Long voice notes, actually. I replay them." They both laughed; each had been giving what she herself liked, not what the other needed most. Mehak admitted she'd felt a little neglected last month when Vandana dropped off soup but didn't stay. They agreed to try the other's way for a month. A good reminder for everyone: people feel cared for in different ways, and it helps to ask.
— Nandita

How long have Mehak and Vandana been best friends?
For ten years.
How had Mehak felt last month when Vandana dropped off soup?
She had felt a little neglected, because Vandana didn't stay and sit with her.
What did the exercise help Mehak and Vandana do?
It helped them ask what makes each feel cared for, and agree to try the other's way for a month.
How does Vandana feel about Mehak's long voice notes?
She treasures them, replaying them, which shows those notes make her feel cared for.

metadata.subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]

messages.content:
Please make this paragraph shorter and easier to read:

There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it: a Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and the other two were using it as a cushion, resting their elbows on it, and talking over its head. "Very uncomfortable for the Dormouse," thought Alice; "only, as it's asleep, I suppose it doesn't mind."

The March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at a table under a tree. A Dormouse sat fast asleep between them, and they rested their elbows on it like a cushion. Alice thought this was uncomfortable for the Dormouse, but since it was asleep, it probably did not mind.

A soccer team had 24 players prepared for a soccer game. The first half saw 11 players start the game with 2 substitutions made. In the second half, the team made twice as many substitutions as it made in the first half. How many players on the team did not play that day?

With two substitutions, 11+2 = 13 players from the team played the game in the first half.
In the second half, the team made twice the number of substitutions it made in the first half, a total of 2*2 = 4 substitutions.
The total number of players who played the game is 13+4 = 17
If the soccer team had 24 players prepared for the soccer game, the number of players who did not play the game is 24-17 = 7 players.
The answer is 7.

Where does the name Kuru-jangala come from, according to this passage?

This Kuru was exceedingly virtuous, and therefore, he was installed on the throne by his people. It is after his name that the field called Kuru-jangala has become so famous in the world. Devoted to asceticism, he made that field (Kurukshetra) sacred by practising asceticism there. And it has been heard by us that Kuru's highly intelligent wife, Vahini, brought forth five sons, viz., Avikshit, Bhavishyanta, Chaitraratha, Muni and the celebrated Janamejaya.
It comes from King Kuru, a virtuous ruler whom the people put on the throne. He made the field sacred by practising austerities there.

A school hall has 25 rows of seats. The first row has 20 seats and each row has 2 more than the row in front. How many seats are in the last row and in the hall? Then: logs are stacked with 20 in the bottom row, 19 in the next, 18 in the next, and so on. In how many rows are 200 logs placed, and how many logs are in the top row?

Answer: Last row 68 seats; 1,100 seats in all. The logs need 16 rows with 5 logs in the top row.

Seats: a = 20, d = 2, n = 25: t_2_5 = 20 + 24 x 2 = 68, and S_2_5 = 25/2 x (20 + 68) = 25 x 44 = 1,100. Logs: a = 20, d = -1: n/2 x [40 + (n - 1)(-1)] = 200 n(41 - n) = 400 n^2 - 41n + 400 = 0 (n - 16)(n - 25) = 0 n = 25 would need t_2_5 = 20 - 24 = -4 logs in the top row, which is impossible (the rows 17 to 25 would have 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, ...), so REJECT it. n = 16 rows, top row t_1_6 = 20 - 15 = 5 logs. Always test both roots in the story.
Who carved the small fountain in our park?
I don't know who carved the fountain, as that is a very local detail. The park authority or the council's records may list the sculptor.

Read this:

Friday: A video Irawati was watching ended, and the next one started on its own. It was a grown-up video with people shouting and hurting each other. She knew she should close it, but she kept watching for a minute. Then she slammed the tablet shut, cheeks burning, and told no one.
Saturday: The pictures kept coming back at bedtime. She hid the tablet under her cupboard and snapped at her cousin Yamini for no reason.
Sunday: While Mummy was folding clothes, Irawati whispered, "I saw something bad on the tablet. I'm sorry." Mummy stopped folding and sat beside her. "Thank you for telling me. You're not in trouble. Tell me what you saw." Irawati told her. Mummy explained it gently, and that evening they set up the child settings together. Irawati slept without the pictures that night.

How did the grown-up video start playing?
The next video started on its own after the one Irawati was watching ended.
What did Irawati's snapping at Yamini suggest?
She felt ashamed and upset about the secret, and it came out as crossness.
What did Mummy do that helped Irawati feel safe again?
She thanked her, said she was not in trouble, listened, explained gently and set up child settings together that evening.
How might Yamini have felt when Irawati snapped at her?
Yamini was probably confused and a bit hurt, not knowing Irawati was carrying a secret.

Read this:

The internet was painfully slow, and Ramesh's project on clean drinking water was due the next morning. He typed his question and waited. The first result finally loaded: "The ONLY way to get clean water is our Super Filter!" Ramesh almost copied it. Then he saw the grey word "Ad" next to it. "Ma, this is selling something," he told Devika. She nodded. "What else is there?" He scrolled down to a government health page and a science article that both mentioned boiling and filtering. He used those, and noted where each fact came from.

What was Ramesh's project about?
His project was on clean drinking water.
What does Ramesh telling his mother "this is selling something" show about his thinking?
It shows he felt wary of the claim, realising it might be biased because the page wanted to sell a product.
What did Ramesh do after spotting the ad?
He scrolled to more reliable pages, used information that matched, and noted his sources.
What would change if the internet had been fast?
He might have had more time, but he'd still need to check the source instead of copying the first result.

Read this:

I'm Baljeet, and my first month in the new city ran on chai and panic. I slept late, skipped breakfast, and by eleven the words in my notes swam. My marks on the first test showed it. One evening my roommate Sunaina said, “You look like a phone on two percent.” That stung, and it was true. So I changed three things. First, a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, written on the wall. Second, a tiffin service two lanes away that brings dal and rice at one and at eight. Third, I moved my study block to five in the morning, when the hostel is quiet, instead of the noisy evenings. It took two weeks to feel normal. By the second test I could finish a chapter without my eyes closing.

What three changes did Baljeet make?
Baljeet set a fixed wake-up and lights-out time, found a tiffin service two lanes away, and moved the study block to five in the morning.
What did Baljeet feel when Sunaina said the remark about a phone on two percent?
It stung, so Baljeet felt hurt, but Baljeet also knew it was true.
What else could help if the new schedule still leaves Baljeet drained?
Baljeet could talk to the warden, and if it keeps going or worries Baljeet, check with the doctor, since routine changes may not solve everything.
How might Sunaina have seen the change?
Sunaina probably felt relieved to see Baljeet finishing chapters, since the remark came from worry as much as from teasing.

Read this:

The monsoon evening in their Kochi flat was dark by six. When the door opened and Farhan came in, dripping, Jomon, two, dropped the visiting aunty's rattle and ran. "Papa!" He hugged Farhan's wet legs and didn't care. The aunty held out her arms, laughing. Jomon shook his head, pressed his face against Papa's trousers, and raised both arms. Up. Farhan lifted him, and Jomon patted his cheek twice, very seriously.

What did Jomon drop when Farhan came in?
The visiting aunty's rattle.
What does Jomon patting Papa's cheek suggest?
Jomon felt love and warmth for his father, happy he was home.
How can the visiting aunty build a bond with Jomon?
Give him time, play near him without pushing, and let him come to her when he's ready.
How might the visiting aunty feel when Jomon turns away?
She is probably amused but a little disappointed, understanding he prefers his papa.

Read this:

"Uma, welcome back," said Lakshmi ma'am.
"I made a car at home!" Uma ran straight to the sand tray.
At lunch, Uma chattered about the car. She didn't mention her Nani, who had died last week. Lakshmi ma'am watched quietly.
At art time Uma's crayon snapped.
"NO!" Uma burst into tears.
"Oh, Uma. It broke."
"I want it fixed! I want it back!"
"I know. Some things can't be fixed. It's okay to be sad."
"Nani can't come back."
"No, she can't. That's very sad."
Uma cried into Lakshmi ma'am's sari. Then she picked up a new crayon.

Where did Uma run when she arrived?
Straight to the sand tray.
What was Lakshmi ma'am feeling when Uma said "Nani can't come back"?
She seemed calm but moved and caring, answering honestly and gently.
Why were Lakshmi ma'am's short, honest words helpful?
They matched what Uma could take in, naming sadness simply without false promises.
What is it like for Uma when the crayon snaps?
It opens up her grief about Nani in a short burst, and she needs comfort before going back to play.

Read this:

The night before the chemistry board exam, Imran decided sleep was for the weak. He sat at the desk in his Lucknow flat with three highlighters and a flask of tea until the dawn azaan, flipping through equations. In the exam hall, the first question was one he had highlighted twice. He stared, and his mind was a blank sheet. His palms went wet; his heart thudded. He wrote something, crossed it out, wrote again. At home Bhavna Apa found him with his head on the table. "Ammi says you didn't sleep at all." "I studied everything and remembered nothing." "That's exactly why." Three days later, before physics, he stopped at eleven, slept, and read only his summary sheet over breakfast. His hands still shook, but the answers came.

What did Imran read over breakfast before physics?
Only his summary sheet.
What was Imran feeling when he stared at the first question?
He was panicking, palms wet and heart thudding, frightened because his mind went blank on a topic he had studied.
What did Imran change before physics, and why did it help?
He stopped at eleven and slept, then read just his summary, so his memory and nerves held up better.
How might Bhavna feel finding Imran with his head on the table?
She is concerned but understanding, and gently points out that skipping sleep caused the blank.

Is it "prefered" or "preferred"? Someone said "spectre" to me. What is that? Is the museum open on Monday? Why do desert plants have thick stems? My sentence is "She is in the hospital since Monday." Can you fix it?

1. It is "preferred", with a double "r". The stress is on the last part of "prefer", so the "r" doubles.
2. Spectre means a ghost. It is a noun.
3. I can't check that. Opening days differ and I can't see this one. Check the museum's official website or call them.
4. Desert plants store water in their thick stems. Because rain is rare in the desert, they need a supply to last between showers.
5. Write it as: She has been in the hospital since Monday. Why: "since" with a starting point needs the present perfect.

Class teacher's note, Section 10B, Wednesday
At the morning break I noticed a group gathered around Sarika by the water cooler. She was speaking quickly, clearly enjoying the attention. I heard her say, "Lakshmi's repeating the year, she failed all her exams in her old school." Several girls gasped.
By lunch Lakshmi was sitting alone. Her eyes were red.
After the last bell I asked Sarika to stay. At first she shrugged: "Everyone wanted to know." I asked how she felt while she was telling it. She said, "Good. Everyone was listening to me." Then, quieter: "And now I feel sick."
I asked her whose pain the attention had cost. She was silent for a long time, then said, "Lakshmi's."
She agreed to apologise to Lakshmi tomorrow and to stop spreading it. I checked on Lakshmi before she left today and will speak to the counsellor about both girls.

Where was the group gathered around Sarika?
By the water cooler.
How did Sarika feel while telling the story, and afterwards?
She felt pleased and important at first because everyone was listening, then guilty and sick about what it cost Lakshmi.
How did the note-writer handle the gossip?
By asking Sarika questions so she saw the harm herself, getting her agreement to stop and apologise, and checking on Lakshmi the same day.
What is it like for Lakshmi after the break?
She feels exposed and isolated, sitting alone at lunch with red eyes.
Now you try: which formula simulates tossing a coin with 1 for heads and 0 for tails?
The answer is =RANDBETWEEN(0,1).

Read this:

By six o'clock in the Berlin office, Siddiq had decided on four shipment routes, two hires and the colour of a client logo. On the U-Bahn home, his climbing bag sat by his feet. He had packed it that morning, full of good intentions.
At his stop, the smell from the kebab shop hit him. He bought a wrap, went straight up to the flat and fell onto the sofa.
Clara, his flatmate, pointed at the bag. "No climbing?"
"My brain's done. I can't choose between a V2 and a V3 wall right now."
"Maybe you're done, or maybe climbing after work just isn't what you want anymore."
He frowned. "I do want it. Just not at seven."
"Then go Saturday mornings. Or go straight from work before you pass the kebab shop."
Siddiq chewed slowly. "Straight from work. Thursday."

What had Siddiq decided on by six o'clock?
He had decided on four shipment routes, two hires and the colour of a client logo.
How is Siddiq feeling when he falls onto the sofa?
He feels exhausted and a little guilty about the unused climbing bag, saying his brain is done.
What plan does Siddiq settle on, and why is it sensible?
He decides to go straight from work on Thursday, which avoids passing the kebab shop and removes an extra evening choice.
How does Clara see Siddiq's skipped climbing?
Clara wonders whether it is tiredness or whether he simply no longer wants to climb after work, so she offers both a different time and a different route.

Read this:

In their Copenhagen flat, Zanele's wooden boat cracked in half when it fell off the table. She didn't cry. She went very quiet, lay down on the rug with the two pieces, and stared at them, drooping.
"Tired already?" asked Emil, her father. Then he looked closer. "Oh. Your boat broke. You're sad."
Zanele's lip wobbled, and she let him lift her into his lap.

What broke?
Zanele's wooden boat.
What was Zanele feeling when she lay quietly with the pieces?
She was sad about her broken boat, even though at first it looked like tiredness.
What did Emil do that helped?
He looked closer, named her sadness and offered comfort in his lap.
What would change if Emil had put her to bed thinking she was tired?
Her sadness would go unnoticed, and she wouldn't get the comfort or the word for her feeling.

Hostel warden's note, girls' block, 18 August.
On Sunday night, Sarita said she saw a white shape on the terrace. By Monday, six girls had seen it, and by Tuesday Tenzin was telling me in detail how the shape floated past her window and whispered her name. When I asked where she was at the time, she said she was in bed, asleep, until the others woke her. Her room faces the courtyard, not the terrace. I don't think she is lying; she was upset and sure. Group stories at night grow quickly, and she had heard this one told many times at dinner. I showed the girls the white bedsheet that had blown off the terrace line, and we talked about how shared stories can feel like our own memories. I've also arranged for the terrace to be locked at night.

Which way does Tenzin's room face?
Tenzin's room faces the courtyard, not the terrace.
Why was Tenzin so sure the shape whispered her name?
Tenzin felt frightened and certain, because hearing the story told many times at dinner had blended into her own memory of that night.
What did the warden do, and why was it a good approach?
The warden showed the girls the blown-off bedsheet and talked about how shared stories become memories, without calling Tenzin a liar.
How might Sarita feel on seeing the bedsheet?
Sarita might feel relieved and a bit embarrassed that the white shape was only a sheet.

Read this:

At Friday talent hour in the Mumbai building's community hall, Simran opened her mouth and a clear song about the monsoon filled the room. Amandeep forgot to clap for a second. Goosebumps ran up his arm. "She's just born with it," Jatin whispered, shrugging. "No point trying to sing like that." Amandeep didn't feel that way; his chest felt wide and warm. At the bus stop he caught up with Simran. "How do you practise? Every day?" She laughed, surprised. "Ten minutes on Nani's harmonium before school. I still crack on the high notes." "Can I listen sometime?" "Come Saturday," she said. Amandeep grinned all the way home.

Where does Simran practise, and for how long?
She practises for ten minutes on Nani's harmonium before school.
What was Amandeep feeling as Simran sang?
Amazement and warmth. He forgot to clap, got goosebumps and his chest felt wide. 😊
What might Amandeep do when he goes on Saturday?
He can listen, ask what she practises, and start a small routine of his own instead of assuming he could never do it.
How might Simran feel about Amandeep's question compared with Jatin's remark?
Jatin's "born with it" ignores her effort, while Amandeep's question shows he values her practice. She seemed surprised and pleased.
I love the smell of rain. Why does the ground smell like that?

That fresh smell comes from a substance made by tiny soil bacteria and some plants. Raindrops hitting dry ground release it into the air, and our noses are very good at detecting it. Do you enjoy rainy days?
Yes, especially at home with chai. My brother Harsh hates it though.
Chai and rain go well together. Some people feel gloomy in wet weather because they miss the sun and their usual outdoor plans. Why does Harsh dislike it?
He cannot play cricket outside.
That is a good reason. If Harsh misses cricket, you could suggest an indoor game, like table cricket with a ball made from paper, or a card game, to keep him busy until the rain stops.

Read this:

Wasim, sixteen, had turned the balcony of their Hyderabad flat into a small recovery corner for injured street dogs, with his mother's permission and a local vet's number stuck to the wall. He spent his pocket money on bandages and dog food. He made posters, ran an online group of forty volunteers, and once argued with the society secretary for an hour to let a limping puppy stay a week. His sister Minakshi teased him: "You'll marry a dog." But when a frightened mother dog finally let Wasim touch her, Minakshi saw his face, soft and fierce at once, and stopped teasing. At night he still sat up with the group chat, planning.

How many volunteers were in Wasim's online group?
Forty volunteers.
What does Wasim's face, soft and fierce at once, suggest he felt when the mother dog let him touch her?
Deep care and determination, showing how much this cause means to him.
How could Wasim keep his passion from wearing him out?
Share tasks with his volunteers and set some hours when he is off the group chat.
How did Minakshi's view change?
She moved from teasing him to respecting how much the cause meant to him.

Read this:

You're sulking just like your Bua Madhuri used to, you know. Sit, I'll tell you. The mango summer she turned fifteen, your Dadi made a rule: no going to the lake without me, Ramesh, her big brother.
Madhuri didn't argue. Oh, no. She said, "Fine." Then she took forty minutes to put on her chappals. She walked three steps behind me the whole way. Every question got "Hmm" or "No." She peeled mangoes so slowly the juice dried on her fingers.
Your Dadi said she was obeying. I knew she was furious.
One evening I finally said, "Madhuri, just tell me you hate the rule." She glared, then burst out, "I'm not a baby!" And that was the first real conversation we'd had all summer.

How long did Madhuri take to put on her chappals?
Forty minutes.
What was Madhuri feeling behind her "Fine"?
She was furious 😠 and resentful about the rule, but showed it through slow, silent compliance instead of saying it.
What turning point changed things in the story?
Ramesh inviting her to say it straight, "just tell me you hate the rule", let her anger out in words and started a real conversation.
How did Dadi see Madhuri that summer?
Dadi saw only the obedience, reading the slow compliance as Madhuri following the rule rather than the anger underneath.

John joins a country club with 3 other members of his family.  The fee to join is $4000 per person.  There is also a monthly cost of $1000 per person.  John pays half the cost.  How much does John pay for the first year?

There are 3+1=4 members joining
So the cost is 4*4000=$16,000 to join
The monthly fee comes out to 1000*12=$12,000 per person per year
So that is 12000*4=$48,000
So the total cost is 16,000+48,000=$64,000
So John pays 64000/2=$32,000
The answer is 32000.

Read this:

At the school hobby club, trading card day was noisy. Eshaan, ten, laid out his spare cards and put a note next to his gold dragon card: "Ten cards only!" Sarika checked the club's trading list. "Dragons are worth three. Everyone knows that." "Not mine," Eshaan said. "Mine is special. I've had it since class three." Irawati offered four cards, then five. Eshaan shook his head. "You're trying to cheat me." By the end of the hour everyone had traded except Eshaan, who sat with his dragon and a sour face. "Nobody here knows what it's worth," he muttered.

What does the club's trading list say dragons are worth?
Dragons are worth three cards.
Why does Eshaan think Irawati is trying to cheat him?
Eshaan feels suspicious because the dragon is his and he has had it since class three, so it seems worth much more to him. A fair offer then feels like a trick.
What could Eshaan ask himself before the next trading day?
He could ask how many cards he would give to get that dragon from someone else; if the answer is three, that is probably a fair price.
How might Irawati feel after offering five cards and being called a cheat?
Irawati may feel hurt and confused, since five was already more than the list said.

A coal-powered train is traveling towards a faraway city when the conductor realizes that he forgot to restock the train's coal supply at the last station.  The train is traveling on a one-way track, so the conductor has no other option but to continue moving forward towards the city.  The train can travel 5 miles for every 2 pounds of coal that it consumes.  If the train has 160 pounds of coal remaining, how far can the train travel before it runs out of fuel?

The train travels 5 miles per every 2 pounds, or 5/2 = 2.5 miles per pound of coal.
Therefore, the 160 pounds of coal that remain are enough for the train to travel 160*2.5 = 400 miles.
The answer is 400.

Read this:

The student health centre on the third floor smelled of phenyl and the marigolds from someone's puja. Hansa had walked past its door twice before Zeenat linked arms and steered her in. "You said you wanted proper information, not internet rubbish," Zeenat whispered. Hansa's ears burned. She and Nikhil had been together a year and were talking about becoming intimate, and she wanted to understand protection and testing before anything happened. The nurse, reading glasses on a chain, didn't blink. She closed the door, gave Hansa leaflets, answered every question plainly, then asked one of her own: "Have you two talked about what each of you is comfortable with, and that either of you can stop anytime?" Hansa shook her head. "Start there," the nurse said. On the stairs down, Hansa laughed shakily. "That was the least awkward awkward thing ever."

Where was the student health centre?
On the third floor.
What does Hansa walking past the door twice suggest?
Hansa felt embarrassed and nervous about asking, even though she wanted proper information.
What was wise about the nurse's question, and what should Hansa's next step be?
It turned the focus to open talk with Nikhil about comfort and the right to stop anytime; Hansa's next step is that conversation.
How might Zeenat feel on the way down the stairs?
Zeenat would likely feel relieved and glad she nudged Hansa in, seeing Hansa laugh after something so hard to start.

Read this:

I'm Lalit, ten, the smallest boy in our colony's cricket gang. Last summer something happened in our colony that I still think about.
Santosh's family had just moved from another state, and at home they speak a different language. He sat on the wall every evening watching us play cricket. Nobody picked him. When he asked, one of the older boys said, "You're not from here. Go play with your own people." Some kids laughed.
My stomach felt twisted. Santosh wasn't even my friend yet. But it just wasn't fair. He lives here now, same as us.
I said, "That's not fair. He can bat after me." My voice shook a bit. The older boy rolled his eyes, but he let him.
Santosh hit a four on his first ball. After that, nobody said anything. Now he's on my team every evening.

What did Santosh hit on his first ball?
He hit a four.
What was Lalit feeling when he spoke up, and how can you tell?
He felt it was unfair and was a little nervous, since his stomach twisted and his voice shook, but he still spoke.
What was the turning point in the game, and what did Lalit's choice change?
When Lalit said Santosh could bat after him, the older boy let him play, and Santosh became part of the team.
How might Santosh have felt sitting on the wall before Lalit spoke up?
He probably felt left out and lonely, watching the game every evening in a new place where nobody picked him.

Read this:

By the third month, the small bets on the phone game did nothing for Nitin anymore. Only bigger ones made his chest go loose the way the first ones had.
He played in the back of Baba's cloth shop in Jalna, between customers, the screen turned to the wall. When Baba asked where two thousand rupees from the till had gone, Nitin said a supplier had come for an advance. The lie came out so easily that it scared him.
That evening Hafsa messaged: "Volleyball at the maidan? You haven't come in weeks." He wrote back, "Busy with shop accounts." He wasn't.
He lay on the terrace with the phone on his chest, feeling filthy about the till money, and the feeling was so heavy that the only thing that lifted it was one more bet. Dimly, he knew this was going round in a circle.

What reason did Nitin give Baba for the missing two thousand rupees?
He said a supplier had come for an advance.
Why did Nitin place one more bet on the terrace?
He felt filthy and ashamed about the till money, and the only thing that lifted that heavy feeling was another bet.
What turning point is still available to Nitin now?
He could tell Baba or Hafsa the truth about the betting and the money and look for help from a counsellor or support group, since hiding it feeds the shame that drives the next bet.
How might Hafsa see Nitin's absence from volleyball?
Hafsa notices he hasn't come in weeks and gets a short excuse about accounts, so Hafsa may feel shut out or quietly worried.

Read this:

"Jaya, you've written 'total' as 'totla' three times."
"Have I?" Jaya stared at the page. "Pranav, I don't even know what I'm doing. I've got the audit exam Monday, my internship report due Tuesday, and Amma called to say the landlord's raising the rent."
"Okay."
"And I got the balance sheet wrong. Twice. I've done this a hundred times."
"Because you're doing four things in your head at once."
"I'm just being stupid."
"You're not stupid. You're full." Pranav pulled out a sheet of paper. "Write it all down. Every worry. Then we pick one."
She wrote: exam, report, rent, sleep.
"Now, which one is today?"
"The exam."
"Then the rest waits on the paper." He tapped it. "Do one balance sheet. Slowly."
Her third try balanced.

How did Jaya misspell 'total'?
She wrote it as 'totla'.
Why does Jaya think she's 'just being stupid'?
Jaya feels frustrated and ashamed at getting a familiar balance sheet wrong, not seeing that the exam, the report and the rent worry are crowding her mind.
What did Pranav suggest, and why did it help?
Writing every worry on paper and picking one for today, which frees up her mind so the balance sheet finally balances.
How does Pranav see Jaya's mistakes?
Pranav sees a friend who is full, not stupid, and helps her put the worries down.

Read this:

Room numbers, not names: that was the 'intro week' rule at the girls' hostel, handed down by Neelam, the senior-most resident. For five nights Gargi was '212'. At dinner seniors called out, "212, stand." "212, sing." "212, explain why you're slow." When Gargi asked one of them, a gentle-looking third-year, why, the girl wouldn't meet her eyes. "Neelam di's orders. If we don't, we get it next." By Friday Gargi had stopped looking up from her plate. She felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about. That night she walked to the warden's office in her slippers and said, "I need to report something." The warden closed the door, listened to all of it, said, "This is ragging, and none of it is on you," and phoned the anti-ragging committee head from the desk while Gargi sat there.

What number was Gargi called for five nights?
For five nights Gargi was '212'.
How was Gargi feeling by Friday, and what shows it?
Gargi felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about; she had stopped looking up from her plate.
Which step turned things around, and what did the warden do?
Gargi went to the warden's office to report it; the warden listened, called it ragging, said none of it was on Gargi, and phoned the anti-ragging committee head right then.
How does the third-year seem to see her own part in it?
She seems uncomfortable, not meeting Gargi's eyes, and insists she has no choice because refusing would make her the next target.

a) 1/sqrt7
b) 6/sqrt3
c) 5/(2sqrt10)
d) 1/sqrt2
e) 3/sqrt6
f) 14/sqrt7
g) 1/(3sqrt2)
h) 10/sqrt5
i) sqrt2/sqrt3

n) 12/sqrt24

p) 7/sqrt14
q) (1 + sqrt2)/sqrt2
r) (6 - sqrt3)/sqrt3

a) sqrt7/7
b) 2sqrt3
c) sqrt10/4
d) sqrt2/2
e) sqrt6/2
f) 2sqrt7
g) sqrt2/6
h) 2sqrt5
i) sqrt6/3
j) sqrt2
k) 3sqrt3/2
l) sqrt5
m) sqrt15/5
n) sqrt6
o) sqrt7/14
p) sqrt14/2
q) (2 + sqrt2)/2
r) 2sqrt3 - 1

Paul needed to buy some new clothes for work.  He had a 10% off coupon that he could use on his entire purchase after any other discounts.  Paul bought 4 dress shirts at $15.00 apiece, 2 pairs of pants that each cost $40.00.  He found a suit for $150.00 and 2 sweaters for $30.00 each.  When he got to the register, the clerk told him that the store was offering 20% off of everything in the store.  After the discounts and the coupon, how much did Paul spend on his new clothes?

4 dress shirts cost $15.00 each so 4*15 = $60.00
2 pants at $40.00 cost 2*40 = $80.00
2 sweaters at $30.00 cost 2*30 = $60.00
Add the suit at $150 and the other items the total was 150+60+80+60 = $350
The store has having a 20% off sale so .20*350 = $70.00 discount
His new total would be 350-70 = $280.00
Then add his 10% discount, .10*280= $28.00 additional off
His final total came out to 280-28 = $252.00
The answer is 252.

Read this:

Chandrika, you're laughing at my file of papers? Let me tell you why I keep it.
When I was twenty-two, my mother needed an operation. She had insurance through my father's office. We were so relieved. After the surgery, the hospital said the claim was rejected. Missing documents: her old reports showing when the problem started, and the doctor's certificate in the right format.
I ran between the hospital, the insurance desk and three old clinics for a week, searching for papers. I remember sitting on the hospital steps, so angry and tired I couldn't speak.
We got it sorted in the end, partly. But I learned. Now every report, bill and prescription in our family goes into this folder, with dates, and a copy on my phone.
So, Chandrika, start your own file now. Your Joseph Mama learned it on those steps.

Why was the insurance claim rejected?
Missing documents: old reports showing when the problem started and the doctor's certificate in the right format.
How did young Joseph feel sitting on the hospital steps?
Young Joseph felt angry and exhausted, too tired to speak after a week of searching for papers.
What was the lesson from Joseph's story, and why does it matter?
Keeping every report, bill and prescription organised with dates, because claims and care depend on having the right papers ready.
How might Joseph's mother have felt while her son ran around for papers?
His mother was probably worried and guilty, recovering from surgery while he struggled with the claim.

Martin went to a store to buy a new television set. He decided to spend no more than $1,000 and the sales clerk offered him the TV for $100 less and an additional 20% off. How much lower was the price of the television than the amount Martin decided to spend?

The seller has offered him the TV for 1000 - 100 = $900.
The discount on the television was 900 * 20/100 = $180.
The final price of the television is therefore 900 - 180 = $720.
Martin was able to save 1000 - 720 = $280.
The answer is 280.
My parents want me to learn guitar but I prefer drums. What should I do?
It is good that you know what you like. Try talking calmly with your parents and explain why drums attract you. Does something about the beat or the energy appeal to you?
I love the rhythm and I tap on the table all day. My name is Karan.
Tapping all day is a sign of real interest, Karan. You could tell your parents that you already practise rhythm without a teacher. That shows you are serious.
They said drums are too loud for our flat.
That is a fair concern. A practice pad is a flat rubber surface that gives the feel of drumming with little noise. You could offer to practise with it at fixed hours, so neighbours are not disturbed.
That could work. Do you think I could try one lesson of each?
It is a sensible plan, Karan. One trial lesson of guitar and one of drums will help your parents see which one you enjoy. Mention the practice pad and the quiet hours when you ask them.

Leela, you want to know about our team's first-Friday plant? I'm Gargi, I lead a small support team at an insurance office, and I used to hate how new people were just thrown in. So now, on a new person's first Friday, the whole team buys a small potted plant, and everyone writes one tip on a card: where the good stapler is, which manager hates emojis in emails, how to escape the long meetings. We sit around the plant and explain each card. Last month a new joiner, Ibrahim, told us he'd been scared we'd test him with trick questions. By the end he was laughing and writing his own card for the next person. The plant's on his desk now. Honestly, that's the whole culture.

What does the team buy on a new person's first Friday?
A small potted plant.
How did Ibrahim feel before the first-Friday plant?
He was scared the team would test him with trick questions.
Why do the tip cards work so well?
They make the unwritten habits clear, like where the stapler is or which manager hates emojis, so the newcomer feels included, not tested.
What might it mean for Ibrahim to write his own card for the next person?
It shows he now feels part of the team and wants to pass the welcome on.

At the primary health centre in the village near Sangli, the Tuesday vaccination camp was crowded and hot. Sunaina, two years into her nursing job, was writing names when a mother carried in a baby who was very quiet. Too quiet, Sunaina thought, though she couldn't say what exactly was different. She had seen hundreds of babies at these camps. Most cried. Most wriggled. This one lay still and looked pale to her. She didn't guess. She stood up and fetched Dr Chetan from the next room. "Something's not right. Can you look?" He checked the baby carefully and arranged for the family to go to the district hospital that afternoon, just to be sure. Later he stopped at her desk. "What made you call me?" "I don't know yet," Sunaina said. "But I've learnt to listen when it feels like that."

Where did Dr Chetan send the family?
To the district hospital, that afternoon.
Why did Sunaina fetch Dr Chetan when she couldn't say what was wrong?
Sunaina felt uneasy because the baby's stillness didn't match the hundreds of babies she had seen, and she trusted that uneasy feeling as a sign to have it checked.
What makes Sunaina's response a wise one?
She didn't guess or dismiss the feeling; she asked the doctor to check, which is the safe way to use a hunch.
How might the baby's mother feel when the nurse stands up and fetches the doctor?
She might feel worried but also cared for, seeing that someone noticed her baby and acted quickly.

Subject: Request to adjust report deadline

Dear Kamal,

I hope your week is going well.

I'm writing about the quarterly sales report due this Friday. While compiling it, I found that two regional teams haven't yet submitted their final numbers. I've followed up with both and they've promised them by Thursday evening.

To make sure the report is accurate, could we move the deadline to Monday noon? If that isn't possible, I can send a version on Friday with the two regions marked as pending and update it on Monday.

I've attached the draft so far, so you can see the progress.

Please let me know which option works better for you.

Thank you,
Aparna

(She read it twice, deleted a line that began "Sorry, but it's not my fault," and pressed send.)

How many regional teams hadn't submitted their final numbers?
Two regional teams.
Why did Aparna delete the line that began 'Sorry, but it's not my fault'?
She realised it sounded defensive and blaming, and wanted her email to stay calm and professional.
What makes Aparna's email effective?
It explains the problem briefly, offers two clear options and attaches her progress, so Kamal can decide quickly.
How might Kamal feel reading this email?
Kamal would likely feel informed and reassured, since Aparna shows the problem is handled and gives Kamal a choice.

In the Class 6 science club, Rehana ma'am played a short video of students passing a basketball. "Count how many times the white-shirt team passes. Carefully." Gurleen leaned forward, lips moving. Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. When the video ended, she shot up her hand. "Fifteen!" "Correct," said Rehana ma'am. "And did anyone see the tiger?" Half the room burst out laughing. Gurleen frowned. What tiger? Rehana ma'am played it again. Right in the middle, a person in a tiger costume walked slowly through the players, waved at the camera and walked off. Gurleen's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!" "It was," said Rehana ma'am. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention didn't."

How many passes did Gurleen count?
Fifteen.
Why did Gurleen insist 'That wasn't there!'?
Gurleen felt shocked and puzzled, because her attention was so fixed on counting passes that the tiger never registered.
What does this experiment teach Gurleen about noticing things?
That attention decides what we see, so when focused on one task, it helps to look again or ask others what they noticed.
How might the children who saw the tiger feel?
They probably felt amused and a bit proud, laughing that anyone could miss something so strange.

After five months clean, Asif used again on a Saturday night after a friend's wedding. On Sunday morning in their Lucknow flat, he sat on the bed, head in his hands.
Shalini came in with tea.
"I used last night," he said, before he could stop himself. "I'm sorry. I've ruined everything."
Shalini set the tea down carefully. Her face tightened; she was hurt. But she sat beside him. "You haven't ruined everything. You told me. That matters."
"I'm so ashamed."
"I know. Let's call your counsellor now, together."
Asif nodded. His shoulders were still shaking, but he picked up the phone.

How long had Asif been clean before the lapse?
Five months.
What was Asif feeling when he said "I've ruined everything"?
He felt deeply ashamed and afraid, as if the lapse had destroyed all his progress.
Why was Shalini's response protective for Asif's recovery?
She stayed kind and non-punishing, valued his honesty, and helped him contact his counsellor right away.
What is Shalini experiencing as she sits beside him?
Shalini is hurt, but chooses to support him rather than punish him.

And he was truthful, and free from malice, and of subdued senses. And he used to lead the Sila and Unchha modes of life. And although living like a pigeon, yet that one of mighty austerities entertained his guests, celebrated the sacrifice called Istikrita, and performed other rites. And that sage together with his son and wife, ate for a fortnight, and during the other fortnight led the life of a pigeon, collecting a drona of corn.

Describe how this sage lived.
He was truthful, free from malice and self-controlled. He lived very simply, gathering grain like a pigeon, yet he still welcomed guests and performed his rites.

My new house has 12 medium ceiling lights but I have seen small and large ceiling lights in other rooms. The small ones require 1 bulb, the medium ones require 2, and the large ones need 3 bulbs. How many bulbs should I buy if my wife says she saw twice as many large ceiling lights as medium ceiling lights and ten more small lights than medium ones?

If the house has twice the number of large ones as medium ones then the house has 2*12 = 24 large ceiling lights
Similarly, if it has 10 more small ones than the 12 medium ones then it has 10+12 = 22 small ceiling lights
If one small ceiling light requires 1 bulb then 22 small ones will require 1*22 = 22 bulbs
If one medium ceiling light requires 2 bulbs then 12 medium ones will require 2*12 = 24 bulbs
If one large ceiling light requires 3 bulbs then 24 medium ones will require 3*24 = 72 bulbs
Therefore the house will require 22 bulbs for the small ones + 24 bulbs for the medium ones + 72 bulbs for the large ones, for a total of 22+24+72=118
The answer is 118.

Minakshi: Sorry, I'll be two minutes late to standup. Sorting out the corridor.
Mohit: What happened?
Minakshi: Somebody's coffee all over the floor by the printers. Grabbed the pantry mop straight away.
Mohit: Couldn't you just tell facilities?
Minakshi: Thought about it. Raise a ticket, wait, watch people skate past the puddle. The mop takes three minutes and nothing can go badly wrong here. This wasn't a moment for a plan.
Mohit: Fair. Someone was already tiptoeing round it 😅
Minakshi: Exactly. If it had been broken glass I'd have called someone in. Just a spill though 🙂
Mohit: Okay, standup starts when you're back.

Where was the spill that Minakshi mopped up?
It was on the floor by the printers in the corridor.
What did Minakshi think about waiting for facilities?
Minakshi thought raising a ticket would take longer than the job itself, and felt confident that mopping was simple and safe.
What would be a wiser approach if the mess were broken glass?
Calling someone in would be wiser, because the situation would no longer be small and simple, as Minakshi says.
How does Mohit see Minakshi's choice to skip the ticket?
Mohit accepts it as fair, and the colleague already tiptoeing round the puddle shows others were being bothered by it.

In a lecture hall in Prague, Vera sat through the third hour of Statistics II. The professor's voice was flat, the slides dense. Vera's eyes drooped. She yawned twice, then began doodling spirals in the margin of her notes. Beside her, Clara was scrolling her phone under the desk. At the break Clara said, "God, so boring." Vera rubbed her eyes. "I'm not even sure I'm bored. I slept four hours. I worked the café closing shift." Clara looked at her more closely. "You've done that every night this week." "Rent," Vera shrugged. They sat quietly. Then Clara said, "Let's split the lecture notes. You take the first half, I'll do the second. And maybe ask the café to move one shift?" Vera nodded slowly. The next week she swapped one closing shift for a Saturday morning, and stayed awake through the whole of Statistics II.

How many hours had Vera slept?
Four hours.
What was Vera feeling during the lecture?
She was exhausted more than bored, yawning and doodling after closing shifts every night.
Which small changes helped Vera stay awake the next week?
Splitting notes with Clara and swapping one late shift for a Saturday morning to get more rest.
How did Clara first read the lecture and Vera's yawns?
Clara saw it as plain boredom, until Vera explained the late shifts and lack of sleep.

Navratri nights in Ahmedabad used to mean garba till two for Anjali. This year she came home from the office at six, ordered paneer rolls and watched three episodes of a baking show. Her salary had gone up again in April. The flat was comfortable. On Dussehra, at the society dinner, her old classmate Chetan was glowing about the school library he and some friends were setting up in his village. "And you? What are you building these days?" Anjali opened her mouth. Her mind went to the new sofa. "Oh, the usual, work's good," she said, and it came out thin. Walking home past the empty garba ground, she felt oddly flat, not tired exactly. She did not know what she wanted to build. She hadn't asked herself in two years.

What did Anjali order on Navratri evenings this year?
Paneer rolls.
Why did Anjali's answer to Chetan come out thin?
She felt flat and a little empty, because the only thing that came to mind was her new sofa, and she had not asked herself what she wanted to build in two years.
What small step could Anjali take next?
She could give one evening a week to something beyond her own comfort, perhaps helping with a project like Chetan's, to find out what she might care about building.
How might Chetan have read Anjali's reply?
Chetan probably took it as polite small talk and may not have noticed the flatness behind "work's good".
Emberly takes her mornings walks every day. If each walk takes her 1 hour covering 4 miles, and she didn't walk for 4 days in March, calculate the total number of miles she's walked.

In March, she walked for 31-4 = 27 days.
If she walks for an hour a day, the total number of hours she'll walk in March is 27 days*1 hour a day= 27 hours.
If each walk is 4 miles, the number of miles she walked in March is 27*4 = 108 miles.
The answer is 108.

Saturday: Gurleen had ignored Gargi's messages for six days. Gargi had tried "what's your problem?" and "fine, be like that." Nothing.
Sunday: Gargi sat on the stairs of her building, thinking. Accusing her wasn't working. Maybe Gurleen was scared, not just angry. She typed slowly: "I can feel you're upset with me and I don't know why. I'd rather hear it, even if it's hard. I'm listening." She read it five times before sending.
Tuesday: Gurleen came to her desk before assembly. "Can we talk at break?" At break, Gurleen said, "I didn't think you'd want to hear it." "I do," said Gargi. And Gurleen finally told her.

How many days had Gurleen ignored Gargi's messages?
Six days.
What was Gargi feeling as she read her message five times before sending?
She felt nervous and hopeful, wanting to reach Gurleen without accusing her.
What changed between Saturday and Sunday that helped?
Gargi stopped accusing and instead sent a kind invitation, naming the upset without blame and saying she'd rather hear it.
What was Gurleen experiencing before Tuesday?
She was hurt and also afraid that Gargi wouldn't want to hear what was wrong.
I missed the lecture on statistics yesterday. My classmate Lucas usually takes good notes.
Then Lucas is a good person to ask. Missing one lecture is usually fixable if you catch up soon. Ask him politely if you can see his notes and maybe borrow them for a day.
He said yes, but I don't understand the topic called probability yet.
That is fine. Read Lucas's notes first, then try a few simple examples like flipping a coin or rolling a die. If you still feel stuck, ask your teacher during doubt hours.
Can you explain the coin example?
Sure. When you flip a fair coin, there are two equal outcomes, heads or tails. So the chance of heads is one out of two. Each flip stands alone, so earlier flips do not change the next.
Whose notes did I say I'd use?
You said you would use Lucas's notes. Read them after the coin example, and mark anything that is unclear so you can ask your teacher about it.
"ineffable" - what does that mean? And one more: can you fix my sentence? He has to go to a hospital for check up.

1. Ineffable means too great or strong to be put into words. It is an adjective.
2. Corrected: He has to go to a hospital for a check-up. Why: "check-up" is countable, so it needs "a" and a hyphen.
Corveus sleeps 4 hours a day and his doctor recommended for him to sleep 6 hours a day. How many hours of sleep does Corveus lack in a week?

Corveus lacks 6 - 4 = 2 hours of sleep every day.
Therefore, Corveus' total hours of lack of sleep every week is 2 x 7 = 14.
The answer is 14.

On Christmas Eve at Grandmother's house in Gothenburg, Selin and her cousin Lars ran up and down the hall in socks, sliding on the wooden floor. They built a tunnel of cushions and crawled through it shrieking with laughter. Selin laughed so hard her tummy hurt. Their quiet cousin Mia sat by the tree with her hands in her lap. Aunt Freja noticed and called, "Mia, we need a driver for the cushion train!" Mia stood up, smiling shyly, and climbed on in front. Selin cheered. It was almost midnight before anyone was tired.

Where were the children on Christmas Eve?
They were at Grandmother's house in Gothenburg.
What was Selin feeling as she slid, crawled and laughed?
Selin felt pure joy. She laughed until her tummy hurt and cheered loudly for Mia.
How did Aunt Freja help Mia?
She noticed Mia sitting quietly and gave her an important job as driver, so she could join without being pushed. That is a wise way to include quieter children. 🙂
How might Mia have felt sitting by the tree before Aunt Freja called her?
Mia may have felt a little left out or shy, watching the game. Her shy smile after being asked suggests she was glad to be included.

The hospital's pharmacy staff had a social group called "Pharma Family", and it ran all day: birthday photos, lunch plans, a long thread about whose tiffin smelled best. Swati, who had just started night duty and was studying for her licensing exam, found it buzzing through her sleep.
At the staff canteen she stopped Trisha, who managed the group. "Trisha, can I tell you something before I do it? I'm going to leave Pharma Family for a while. Nothing wrong with anyone. I just need to sleep in the day and study."
Trisha laughed. "Thank God you told me. When Sudhir left last month, the whole group thought he was angry with us."
"That's why I'm telling you. And I'll post a short goodbye."
Her message went up that evening: "Stepping back for exams and nights. Please keep my birthday cake slice safe. 🙂"
Hearts and laughing replies followed.

What was the social group called?
The group was called "Pharma Family".
Why did Swati want to tell Trisha first?
Swati was worried that leaving silently would seem like anger, as it had when Sudhir left, and she cared about her colleagues' feelings.
What could others learn from how Swati left?
Tell the admin in person, give a simple reason like sleep and study, and post a short, light goodbye.
How did Trisha feel when Swati explained?
Trisha felt relieved and grateful, since Sudhir's silent exit had left the whole group thinking he was angry.

School counsellor's note, stream-change window, Class 11
Sahil came in today because his friend Suraj had switched from science to arts last week and "looked so happy it was annoying." Sahil is in science because, as he put it, "everyone in my house did science, so I just did." When I asked what he would have chosen on a blank page, he said history, then laughed nervously. He listed reasons to stay: the tuition already paid, the group chat, the forms, what his mother would say. None of the reasons were about liking science. I told him the window closes on the 20th and that staying is also a choice he is allowed to make, as long as it is a choice. He will talk to his mother this weekend and come back on Monday.

When does the stream-change window close?
On the 20th.
Why did Sahil laugh nervously after saying history?
He felt nervous and a little exposed, because saying it out loud showed that science was a default he never truly chose.
What did the counsellor do that helped Sahil?
Asked what he would choose on a blank page, noticed his reasons weren't about liking science, and gave a clear deadline and next step.
How does Suraj seem after switching?
Suraj seems so happy that Sahil finds it annoying, which suggests the switch suited him.

Monday: Vinita knocked over the paint. Elizabeth Ma'am shouted, “Vinita! You're always so careless!” Vinita hid under the table and wouldn't come out.
Wednesday: Vinita spilled water. Elizabeth Ma'am took a breath and said calmly, “Water spilled. Get the cloth, please.” Vinita looked at her face, then fetched the cloth.
Friday: Vinita knocked the crayon box. Before Elizabeth said a word, Vinita said, “Crayons fell. I'll pick them up,” and did. Elizabeth smiled at her.

What did Vinita spill on Wednesday?
Water.
What was Vinita feeling when she hid under the table on Monday?
She felt ashamed and frightened, as if the loud words meant she was a bad person.
What changed on Wednesday that helped?
Elizabeth Ma'am used a short, calm correction of the act, not the child, so Vinita could understand and fix it.
How might Elizabeth Ma'am feel on Friday?
She is probably pleased and a little moved that Vinita now fixes mistakes herself without fear.

You asked why I'm so fussy about travel. I'm Irfan, and I'll tell you about Lokesh's wedding in Jaipur. Two days before, I saved my tickets on my phone and emailed them to myself, kept a paper copy of my ID in my bag, and wrote three phone numbers in a notebook: Lokesh, his brother and the hotel. I reached the airport two hours early. At security, my phone died. No ticket, no contacts. I just handed over the paper copy and my ID. Then the flight was cancelled. I checked the next train on the station board and called the hotel from a borrowed phone, using my notebook. I reached the wedding four hours late, calm, instead of never.

How early did Irfan reach the airport?
Two hours early.
How did Irfan feel when the phone died and the flight was cancelled?
Irfan stayed calm, since the backups meant the problems were only inconveniences.
Which of Irfan's preparations helped most?
Keeping tickets and ID copies in two places, writing important numbers on paper and arriving early, which let Irfan switch plans quickly.
How might Lokesh feel when Irfan arrived four hours late?
Lokesh would likely feel relieved and happy that Irfan made it despite the cancelled flight.
Avery opens a flower shop. She ties 8 bunches of flowers with 9 flowers in each bunch. How many bunches would she have if she put 12 flowers in each bunch instead?

She has a total of 8 * 9 = 72 flowers.
Dividing them in bunches of 12 will give her 72 / 12 = 6 bunches of flowers.
The answer is 6.
Why does a dog sniff everything on its walk?
A dog sniffs to learn about the world around it. Because smell is its main sense and its nose is far more sensitive than ours, each sniff tells it who has passed that way and what food is nearby.
Correct this please: 'Kindly revert back to me at the earliest.'

Better: "Please reply to me as soon as you can." "Revert" means to go back to an earlier state, so many readers find it odd in place of "reply". Also, "revert back" repeats itself, because "re-" already means "back".

In their Jayanagar flat, Uday's parents had one rule for baby Mira: she must never touch the floor. Germs. So Ajji carried her everywhere, and Ajja wiped every toy with a cloth twice a day. Rashmi, still learning to be a mother herself, noticed something else. Ajji ironed clothes every morning on a low table, with the hot iron's cord dangling within reach of Mira's crawling mat, and the kettle wire hung off the kitchen counter. One sharp tug could do far more harm than a dusty floor. Rashmi knew better than to scoff; their worry came from love. At breakfast she said, "Ajji, you're so careful with her. Can you help me with two more things?" Together they moved the ironing to the bedroom, tucked the kettle wire behind the jars, and let Mira crawl on a clean mat. Ajji, surprisingly, agreed to all of it.

Where did Ajji iron clothes every morning?
On a low table, with the hot iron's cord dangling within reach of Mira's crawling mat.
What was Rashmi feeling as she noticed the iron and kettle cords?
Rashmi felt worried about the cords and respectful of the grandparents' love, not wanting to scoff at their fear of germs.
Why did asking Ajji to 'help with two more things' work well?
It honoured Ajji's carefulness and turned it towards the bigger dangers, so they moved the ironing and tucked the kettle wire away together.
How might Ajji feel about the new arrangement?
Ajji might feel respected and useful, still careful with Mira, and relieved that the cords were spotted.

The coaching institute in Kota didn't close for Diwali; the only sign of the festival was a string of lights over reception. Manoj sat in the third row with a highlighter, marking only what the teacher said would "definitely come". When the physics teacher paused to explain why the sky looks blue, Manoj put his pen down and waited for the part that would be tested.
"Isn't that cool, though?" Akash whispered.
"Is it in the paper?" Manoj asked.
He ranked 14th in the weekly test and sent the screenshot to his father within a minute. The reply came fast: "Good. Aim for top 10."
Three weeks later, in revision class, the teacher asked about a chapter from that very test. Manoj stared at the question. He had got full marks on it. Now he couldn't remember any of it.

What rank did Manoj get in the weekly test?
14th.
Why did Manoj wait for the part that would be tested?
Manoj is anxious about rank and his father's approval, so anything that won't earn marks feels like wasted time, even something interesting.
What could help Manoj learn in a way that lasts?
Asking "why" now and then, as Akash does, explaining ideas in his own words, and revisiting chapters after tests would help the knowledge stick, not just the score.
How does Akash experience the same class?
Akash finds the blue-sky explanation "cool" and enjoys it for its own sake, so the class feels interesting to Akash rather than a race for rank.

At the end of the day in the preschool, Miss Kaur rang the little bell. "Pack-up time."
Pooja pushed in her chair. Lunchbox in the bag. Water bottle… she looked around. It was under the table. Into the bag.
Shoes next. She sat and pulled them on, left then right.
Gargi was still colouring. Pooja tapped her. "Chair, box, bottle, shoes!"
Gargi jumped up.
Miss Kaur looked over. Pooja was already standing in line, bag on her back, without a single reminder.

Where was Pooja's water bottle?
