Her first welds were lumpy and uneven, and one of the boys smirked. Instructor Ramesh said nothing; he just handed her scrap metal. "Practise the motion without the machine." So she did, in the evenings, holding an unlit torch and moving it along a line, over and over. When her turn came, she used every second. By the third month, her beads were smooth. Ramesh held one up to the class. "This is the standard." Alka kept her face straight, but her ears burned with pride.

How many trainees shared the welding machine?
Twelve.
What was Alka feeling when Ramesh held up her weld?
She felt proud and pleased, though she kept her face straight.
What strategy helped Alka improve despite little machine time?
Practising the motion in the evenings without the machine, then using every second of her turn.
How might the boy who smirked see Alka now?
He may feel surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed that her welds became the standard.

Read this:

Thursday night. Kunal and I sat at the kitchen table with tea and one question: how could this house purchase go wrong? We wrote it as if it had already happened. The seller's papers turn out to be incomplete. The roof needs work we hadn't counted. One of us loses a job in the first year.
Then we wrote what we would do for each. We booked a lawyer to check the papers before anything else, and we're keeping a reserve we won't touch for other things.
It felt gloomy for an hour and steadier after. A house can't be handed back, so I would rather worry now for a week than later for a year.
Rehana

Where did Rehana and Kunal write down how the purchase could go wrong?
They wrote it at the kitchen table with tea.
How did Rehana feel after the gloomy hour of writing?
Rehana felt steadier, because each possible problem now had a plan.
What could the couple do if the lawyer finds a problem in the papers?
They could pause the purchase and use the plan they made, since the choice is hard to undo and it is safer to slow down.
How might Kunal see the exercise of imagining the worst?
Kunal sat at the table and wrote too, so probably shares the wish to worry now and be steadier, though it felt gloomy at first.

metadata.subtype: Approach: uses a pre-mortem and contingency plan for a high-stakes irreversible move [Thinking]

Read this:

Omkar: hey uma, noticed the last two weeks' tasks aren't done. everything ok?
Uma: sorry bhaiya 😔 I know. I keep meaning to
Omkar: not scolding. just want to understand why. is the plan too much?
Uma: it's the internals. 3 exams next week and 2 the week after. I'm studying till 1
Uma: every time I open the coding task I feel guilty and close it
Omkar: ah. my plan didn't account for your exams at all. my fault
Omkar: new plan: next 2 weeks, just one 15-min exercise each week. no project work
Omkar: after internals we go back to the full plan
Uma: really? that's ok?
Omkar: yes. stopping completely would lose momentum. a little keeps it alive
Uma: thank you so much. that's actually doable 🙏

How many exams does Uma have next week?
3 exams next week.
How does Uma feel whenever she opens the coding task?
Uma feels guilty and overwhelmed, closing it because exams are taking all of Uma's time.
What could Omkar do before planning the next month?
Ask Uma for her exam and assignment dates, so the plan fits around them from the start.
How does Omkar see his own plan after hearing about the exams?
Omkar sees that it ignored Uma's exams, takes responsibility and lightens it for two weeks.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adjusting the approach after low progress [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

You want to know why I stopped wearing that dupatta, Apa? Fine. I'm Zainab, and it's stupid, but here.

It was Ammi's old one, the orange one with a small burn mark near the edge. I liked it. I wore it to the school exhibition on Saturday.

I walked in, and Aditi leaned over to Gunjan and whispered something. Gunjan covered her mouth. That was all I needed. I knew what Aditi said. "Look, she's wearing a curtain." I could hear it in her exact voice, the one she uses for mocking.

I folded the dupatta into my bag in the washroom and spent the whole exhibition feeling cold and plain. I didn't look at them once.

Did I ask them? No. Why would I? I knew.

...Although Gunjan did come and ask me later where I got the colour. I said I didn't remember.

What mark was on Ammi's old dupatta?
A small burn mark near the edge.
Why did Zainab feel she didn't need to ask Aditi what she whispered?
Zainab was already a little unsure about the old dupatta, so the whisper seemed to confirm her fear. The imagined words felt as real as if she'd heard them.
What turning point did Zainab miss, and what could she do now?
When Gunjan asked where the colour came from, it was a chance to see the whisper might not have been mocking. Zainab could still ask Aditi or Gunjan directly, or just wear the dupatta again.
How might Gunjan feel after asking about the colour and getting "I don't remember"?
Gunjan may feel brushed off and confused, since the question sounded friendly. Gunjan might even wonder if Zainab is upset with her.

Read this:

On the first day after the summer holidays, Class 5 got new seats, and Zainab found herself next to Deepak, a boy she'd barely spoken to.

During the maths period, a cricket card slid out of his pencil box. A bowler, the rare kind with a gold edge.

Zainab gasped. "You have that one?"

Deepak's eyes went wide. "You collect?"

By lunch, they had both tins open on the bench under the stairs. She had three batsmen he didn't have. He had two keepers she needed. They argued happily over who was faster, then traded.

The next day Deepak saved her a seat on the bus. The day after, they made up a joke about their maths teacher's moustache and couldn't stop laughing.

Neither knew the other's birthday yet. It didn't matter.

What fell out of Deepak's pencil box?
A cricket card fell out, a bowler with a gold edge.
What was Zainab feeling when she saw the card?
She felt excited and curious, thrilled to find someone who shared her hobby.
What small things helped the friendship grow?
Sitting together, trading cards and sharing a joke gave them easy reasons to spend time together.
How might Deepak feel when he saves Zainab a seat on the bus?
Deepak probably feels happy to have a new friend and wants to keep sharing time with her.

Read this:

Siddharth, you think helping strangers means going along with them? Let your Neelam Nani tell you about your papa when he was your age. We lived near the bus stand, and people were always lost. One day a car stopped by our gate and a man asked him the way to the old fort. Your papa wanted to help. But I had told him: help, but stay put. So he stood inside our gate, two steps back, and shouted the directions. "Straight till the banyan tree, then right!" The man asked, "Come show me?" Your papa said, "No, uncle, it's easy, the banyan tree." The man thanked him and drove off. Then your papa came in and told me. That's how you help safely, beta.

Where did Siddharth's papa stand while giving directions?
Inside the gate, two steps back.
How might young papa have felt when the man asked him to show the way?
He may have felt a little torn, wanting to be helpful, but sure enough to say no.
What choice in the story mattered most, and why?
Refusing to get in or lead the man mattered most, because he could still help with directions while staying safe.
How might the man in the car have felt about the help?
The man was probably grateful for the clear directions, as he thanked him and drove off.

metadata.subtype: Approach: helping in a safe way [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Manjula, and I live in the flat below Devika's. This summer she asked her mother for one pot on their balcony, all to herself. She chose the seeds, tomato, from a packet at the market, and decided where the pot would go: the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested. Every morning I'd hear her little watering can, and sometimes her voice counting leaves. When the first flower came, she ran down the stairs to show me. When the first tomato turned red, she brought it to me on a steel plate, very serious. "I grew it. I picked the corner," she said. I don't know everything she was thinking, but she stood taller than I'd seen before.

Where did Devika decide to put her pot?
In the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested.
Why does Devika say "I picked the corner" so seriously?
She is proud that her own choice worked; the red tomato shows her that what she decided made something happen.
What choice by Devika's mother helped Devika learn that her actions matter?
Letting Devika choose the seeds and the spot, even against her own suggestion, so the result clearly belonged to Devika.
How does Manjula experience Devika's summer?
Manjula hears the daily watering and gets shown every stage, and sees Devika standing taller, though only guessing at her thoughts.

Read this:

That May, the building's water came for only one hour each morning, and Yash, eleven, was put in charge of making it last. At six he and his little sister Aadhya filled every bucket and bottle in the flat, yawning. 'Rules,' Yash announced, writing on the fridge. 'Tap off while brushing. One mug of water for washing hands, not running water. Vegetable water goes to the plants.' Aadhya pointed at the ceiling fan whirring in the empty room. 'That's electricity, not water.' 'Still wasting,' said Yash, and switched it off. By the fourth day, two buckets were left over. Papa noticed. 'Did we get extra water?' 'No,' said Aadhya proudly. 'Yash made rules.'

How long did the building get water each morning?
Only one hour each morning.
How did Aadhya feel when Papa asked about extra water?
She felt proud of the rules and of the buckets they had saved together.
Which of Yash's rules could any family try?
Turning the tap off while brushing, using a mug for handwashing and giving vegetable water to plants.
What would change if the water came all day again?
Yash and Aadhya might slip back into careless habits unless they kept the rules going anyway.

Read this:

When the Tokyo swim club posted the relay team, Aiko's name wasn't on it. She shrugged. "I didn't want to swim relay anyway."
Nkechi, her friend from the changing rooms, raised an eyebrow. "You've been training for it since April."
"It's just swimming. Who cares."
Aiko stopped staying after practice. She scrolled her phone on the bench and said everything was boring. Her coach asked if something was wrong. "Nope. Just over it."
Two weeks later, Nkechi found her crying in the car park. "I care so much it's stupid," Aiko said. "If I act like I don't, it doesn't hurt."
Nkechi sat with her. "It hurts anyway. Might as well have company."
The next morning Aiko asked the coach what she needed to improve.

When had Aiko been training for the relay since?
Since April.
Why did Aiko say it was just swimming and she was over it?
She was hurt and embarrassed at being left off, and acting uncaring felt safer than admitting how much it mattered.
How could a coach help a swimmer who suddenly acts bored?
The coach could gently check in again in private and offer clear steps to improve, so caring feels safe again.
What is it like for Nkechi to watch Aiko pretend not to care?
Nkechi can see through it and feels concerned, which is why she stays and sits with her.
My teacher said she is inclined to agree with you. Does she lean over?

Not in this sense. If you are inclined to do something, you are likely to do it, or would like to do it. It is an adjective. It can also mean sloping.
Example: I am inclined to stay home if it rains.
Is "recomend" spelled right?

No. It should be "recommend", with one c and a double m: re-com-mend.
Example: Could you recommend a good book for my little sister?

Read this:

In the college hostel, Yogesh used to be the one organising the chess club. Now he played online games until dawn and missed morning labs.
At first, an hour had helped him forget the pressure. Now even five hours didn't feel enough.
He'd borrowed money from Nandini twice, saying it was for books. It went on game credits. When she asked if he was okay, he said he was just tired.
The chess club met without him. He saw the photos and felt a sting of shame. Then he opened the game again.
On Friday Nandini came to his room with the warden. "Yogesh, we're worried. We're not angry. Can we talk?"

What club did Yogesh use to organise?
The chess club.
What was Yogesh feeling when he saw the chess club photos?
He felt a sting of shame, and that shame sent him back to the game.
What turning point does Nandini create on Friday?
Bringing the warden and saying they're worried, not angry, which opens a way to talk and get support.
What might Nandini be feeling when she comes with the warden?
Nandini is probably worried and uneasy, but determined to help rather than keep his secret.
Everything goes wrong in a school play and the audience loves it. Make up that story.

In the Class 5 production of "Robin Hood," the paper arrows fell off the walls, the tree wobbled, and the sheriff lost his hat. The narrator mixed up the scenes and read the ending first. Robin tripped on his cloak and landed on Little John, who burst out laughing. Both fell over. The audience started giggling, then roaring. The teacher in the wings buried her face in her hands. Still, the children carried on, improvising, with Robin shouting, "I meant to do that!" At the end, the whole hall stood and applauded for five minutes. The headmaster later told the teacher it had been the funniest play in the history of the school.

Read this:

Saturday. Uday suggested inviting his office friends over again. Arnab, his flatmate, said, "Sure, it's your flat too," and went to his room. He didn't come out for dinner. Uday shrugged it off.
The following Thursday. The office friends had come and gone. Arnab left the dishes stacked by Uday's door, said "fine" to everything, and wore headphones all evening. Uday knocked. "I think I've missed something. If you're annoyed with me, I'd really rather you say it plainly. I won't get defensive." Arnab took off one earphone. "You invite people every weekend. I never get a quiet Saturday. I didn't want to sound boring."
Two Saturdays later. Before inviting anyone, Uday texted Arnab: "Friends over this week, or quiet one?" Arnab replied: "Quiet please 😅 next week fine." There were no dishes by the door, and Arnab stayed for dinner.

Where did Arnab leave the dishes on Thursday?
Arnab left the dishes stacked by Uday's door.
Why did Arnab keep saying "fine" instead of stating his annoyance?
Arnab felt frustrated about losing every quiet Saturday but worried that saying so would make him sound boring, so the anger came out sideways.
What did Uday say that made directness feel safe?
He said he may have missed something, asked Arnab to say it plainly, and promised not to get defensive.
How did Uday's change look from Arnab's side two Saturdays later?
Arnab felt relieved and respected, being asked first, so he could answer honestly and stayed for dinner.

Read this:

Zainab's report card lay on the kitchen table, and she pushed it away. "Ms Fernandes gave me a low mark because she doesn't like me," she said. "The test was unfair. It's just my bad luck." She said the same thing about the spelling test, the drawing test and the sports day races. Each time her mother Disha, distracted by work calls, said, "We'll see," and moved on. Zainab stopped bringing up her results at all.

At school, the class teacher Jatin noticed that Zainab never tried the extra questions. "Why bother?" she said. "It happens or it doesn't." Jatin did not argue. He asked her to pick just five spelling words, practise them for a week and compare her score. Zainab got four out of five. She stared at the page as if it belonged to someone else.

That evening she said to Disha, quietly, "I practised, and it worked." Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through.

How many of the five spelling words did Zainab get right?
Zainab got four of the five words right.
What connects Zainab's blaming of luck and teachers with her result on the five spelling words?

Zainab says the low mark is bad luck and the test unfair, and skips the extra questions because it happens or it doesn't; after practising five spelling words she gets four out of five and says she practised and it worked. The small win shows her effort has an effect.
What was Zainab feeling when she said "Why bother?" to Jatin?
Zainab felt discouraged and powerless, as if results simply happen to her.
What did Disha do that helped Zainab?
Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through, so Zainab felt heard instead of brushed off with "We'll see".

Read this:

In the second week of their marketing project, Naveen handed in his slides a day late. Rekha, the group leader, was furious. "That's it. He's unreliable."

From then on, she gave all the important tasks to the other two. Naveen got to format fonts.

When Naveen suggested an idea in the meeting, Rekha barely listened. When he sent a message, she didn't reply. In her mind, he was the late one, and that was all.

In the final week, the professor asked each group for an extra survey analysis. The others panicked. Naveen quietly said, "I did a survey course last summer. I can do it tonight."

Rekha almost said no. Then she thought about it. She had never actually seen his skills. She'd only seen one late day.

He sent the analysis by midnight. It was excellent.

Rekha sent him a message: "I'm sorry. I judged you by one mistake."

How late were Naveen's slides?
A day late.
Why did Rekha give Naveen only formatting tasks?
Rekha felt angry and distrustful after his one late submission, so she saw him only as unreliable.
What went wrong in Rekha's leadership, and how could she fix it?
Rekha let one late day define Naveen; she could ask about teammates' skills early and judge on their whole work.
How might Naveen have felt during the weeks of formatting fonts?
Naveen probably felt ignored and undervalued, especially when his ideas were barely heard.

Read this:

Kishore, you think that fitness star knows everything because he's handsome and famous? Sit. Let your Yusuf uncle tell you something. At fifteen, my hero was a film actor with perfect hair and a smile on every poster in Hyderabad. When he said on TV that a certain tonic made him strong and sharp, I spent my whole Eid money on three bottles. I drank it every morning before school and felt exactly the same, only poorer. My ammi asked the pharmacist, who laughed kindly and said, "It's mostly sugar syrup." I was so angry, not at the actor, at myself. He was a good actor. That was all he had ever shown me. After that, I asked one question about every famous face: good at what, exactly?

What did young Yusuf spend his Eid money on?
Three bottles of the tonic.
Why was young Yusuf so angry at himself after the pharmacist spoke?
He felt foolish and angry, realising he had trusted the actor about health only because he admired his looks and acting.
What question did Yusuf start asking, and why is it useful?
"Good at what, exactly?" It separates the skill someone really has from everything else they claim.
How might the pharmacist have seen young Yusuf's bottles?
The pharmacist seemed kind and a little amused, knowing the tonic was mostly sugar syrup and not wanting to embarrass the boy.

Read this:

Last term I thought I was studying for three hours a night. I'm Lalit. My desk had my history book, my phone, and a playlist of my favourite songs, the ones I sing along to. Every few minutes the phone buzzed: the class group, a cricket score, a meme. I'd reply, read a line, hum a chorus, read another line. In the test I couldn't remember a single date from the chapter I'd 'studied' four times. My sister Sangeeta watched me one evening and said, "You read the same paragraph five times. I counted." So I tried her way: phone in the kitchen, music without words, forty minutes, then a break. Honestly, it felt boring at first. But the next week I could explain the whole chapter to her without the book.

Where did Lalit put the phone when trying Sangeeta's way?
In the kitchen.
How did Lalit feel during the test, and why?
Lalit felt shocked and frustrated, unable to remember a single date, because the buzzing phone and singing along had kept the chapter from sticking.
Which parts of Sangeeta's way helped the chapter stick?
Phone in another room, music without words, and forty-minute blocks with breaks, so attention wasn't split.
What did Sangeeta notice while watching Lalit study?
Sangeeta noticed Lalit reading the same paragraph five times, and counted to prove it.

Read this:

In the boarding school hostel, the seniors made Uday, eleven, wash their plates every night and filmed him on a phone, laughing.
One night, a senior handed the phone to Jomon, twelve. “You film it.”
Jomon's stomach twisted. He gave the phone back. “No. I'm not doing that.”
The seniors called him boring. He didn't care.
That evening, he went to the warden's room and told Mr Mathew everything. The warden walked back with him to the dormitory at once, took the phone, and made sure the video was deleted. He moved Uday to a room near his and called the boys' parents the next morning.

What did the senior ask Jomon to do?
To film Uday washing plates.
How did Jomon feel when handed the phone?
He felt uneasy and uncomfortable, his stomach twisting.
Why was going to the warden that evening important?
It meant an adult could stop the bullying immediately and protect Uday.
How might Uday feel after the warden acts?
He probably feels relieved and safer, knowing someone helped him.

Read this:

On Gurpurab morning in their Ludhiana home, Tejas, five, tied a small orange patka on his head, with Mummy's help.

"Why do we go to the gurdwara so early?" he asked.

"Because in our family we help cook the langar," Amandeep said. "Your Nanaji did it, and I did it."

In the langar hall, Tejas carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate. He copied the grown-ups, folding his hands. "Our family does this every year," he told the boy next to him.

What did Tejas carry in the langar hall?
He carried a basket of rotis and placed one on each plate.
How can you tell Tejas felt proud of the family tradition?
He told the boy next to him that their family does this every year, showing he feels part of it.
How did Amandeep help Tejas understand the tradition?
Amandeep explained it as something the family has always done, naming Nanaji and Amandeep's own turn, so he could see his place in it.
What is it like for the boy next to Tejas to hear about his family's custom?
He may feel curious, or share his own family's ways in return.

Read this:

I was twelve when I first really noticed. I'd go to the corner shop at night for milk, and there was Abhinav, from my class, sitting on the step under the street lamp, doing his maths homework. Every night. I had my own room and a table lamp. One night I asked him why he didn't study at home. "Power cut in our lane," he said. "Again." I walked home feeling weird. I thought: I got ninety in maths and he got seventy-five, and everyone called me clever. But he was doing sums under a street lamp with mosquitoes biting. I felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then just curious. Why was our lane always lit? Next week I asked my teacher. She explained about the old wiring in some areas. I'm Jomon, and that was the first time I wondered who gets what, and why.

Where did Abhinav do his maths homework?
He sat on the step under the street lamp.
How did Jomon feel walking home that night?
Jomon felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then curious about why things were so unequal.
What did Jomon do with the curiosity, and why was it useful?
Jomon asked a teacher about it, which turned an uncomfortable feeling into understanding about unequal starting points.
How might Abhinav see his nightly studying?
Abhinav seems to accept it as normal, simply explaining the power cut, perhaps not expecting anyone to notice.

Read this:

I'm Nirmala, and I live two doors from Gurpreet's parents in Ludhiana. Every evening on the video call they sound bright: "All good here, don't worry about us." Afterwards I see Gurpreet's mother wiping the same table twice and Papa staring at the phone. Last week Gurpreet asked plainly, "Mummy, how are you really?" There was a pause, then she admitted the house felt big. Since then Gurpreet sends small things: a photo of a bad cup of tea, a voice note from the bus. Yesterday Gurpreet asked their opinion on which flat to rent, and Papa spent ten minutes giving reasons. A visit is booked for next month. I can't say what they truly feel, but the calls run longer now.

What did Gurpreet ask the parents' opinion about?
Gurpreet asked which flat to rent.
Why might Gurpreet's parents say "All good here, don't worry about us"?
They probably miss Gurpreet and hide it so as not to worry their child. The mother wiping the same table twice and Papa staring at the phone hint at this, though Nirmala can't be sure.
What else could Gurpreet do to keep the parents close?
Keep asking directly how they are, keep sharing small daily things, involve them in decisions and follow through on the planned visit.
How might Papa have felt when asked about the flat?
Valued and included, since he spent ten minutes giving reasons. It gave him a real part in Gurpreet's life.

What impression does Mr. Jaggers's manner make on the narrator?

This strongly marked way of doing business made a strongly marked impression on me, and that not of an agreeable kind. Mr. Jaggers never laughed; but he wore great bright creaking boots, and, in poising himself on these boots, with his large head bent down and his eyebrows joined together, awaiting an answer, he sometimes caused the boots to creak, as if they laughed in a dry and suspicious way. As he happened to go out now, and as Wemmick was brisk and talkative, I said to Wemmick that I hardly knew what to make of Mr. Jaggers's manner.

A strong one, and not pleasant. Mr. Jaggers never laughs, but his bright creaking boots seem to laugh in a dry, suspicious way as he waits for an answer, so the narrator hardly knows what to make of him.
Write a recipe name for a lemon drink, three words, all in title case, no punctuation.
Fresh Lemon Cooler
Why is there an r after the b in February?

"February" comes from an old Latin word, and the r has always been part of it. Many people do not say the first r clearly, but you must write it: Feb-ru-ary.
Example: Our science exhibition is in February.

Read this:

"Shalini, where's your art project? It's due Monday."
"I'm not doing it, Amma."
Kavitha put down the vegetable knife. "Not doing it?"
"I can't draw. Everyone knows. Nithya draws like a real artist, and mine look like a baby's."
"You drew that beautiful kolam at Pongal."
"That's different. That's patterns. I'm not creative." Shalini pushed the sketchbook under the sofa. "Some people are born with it."
"Were you born reading?"
"What?"
"You couldn't read at three. Now you read my office letters for me."
Shalini frowned. "That's not the same."
"Maybe. Or maybe you're at the start of drawing, like you were once at the start of reading."
Shalini didn't answer, but she didn't push the sketchbook any further under, either.

When is Shalini's art project due?
On Monday.
Why does Shalini say "Some people are born with it"?
Shalini feels embarrassed next to Nithya, whose drawings look like a real artist's, and believing talent is inborn spares her from trying and failing.
Which question from Kavitha might shift Shalini's view, and why?
"Were you born reading?", because it reminds her of a skill she clearly built over time, suggesting drawing could grow too.
How does Kavitha see her daughter's refusal?
Kavitha doesn't accept "I'm not creative"; she sees a beginner, points to the kolam and to reading, and hopes Shalini will try.
I had gone to Delhi last year for a wedding. Is "had gone" the right tense?

I went to Delhi last year for a wedding.
Why: past tense ("had gone" -> "went").

How should I choose a game for a big group of friends?
Can you correct this? We celebrated my grandmother's birthday at yesterday.
The family eats 12 chapatis each day. How many chapatis do they eat in 5 days?

1. Pick a game with simple rules, like tag or musical chairs. Make sure that everyone can join in.
2. Fixed: We celebrated my grandmother's birthday yesterday. Why: No "at" before "yesterday".
3. 60 chapatis. Because 5 x 12 = 60.

Read this:

Francis here. I noticed something odd about Samir last week when we split up our project tasks. A new teammate, Tashi, had just joined from a small hill town. Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job. Samir's pen stopped, and then Samir laughed a little awkwardly and said to me, "Wait. Why did I assume Tashi couldn't handle the data part?" It was quiet for a second. I couldn't tell whether Samir felt embarrassed or curious. What I saw was that Samir didn't argue with the thought or brush it away. Samir asked Tashi to take the data analysis. Tashi did it faster than any of us and taught the rest of us a shortcut. Samir told me afterwards, "Good to check my guesses against actual people."

Which task was Samir about to give Tashi?
Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job.
What might Samir have been feeling when Samir stopped and asked "Why did I assume...?"
Possibly awkward or curious, since Samir laughed a little awkwardly, though Francis says Francis could not tell.
What did Samir do that worked well?
Samir noticed the assumption without brushing it away, then tested it by asking Tashi to take the data analysis.
How might Tashi have felt about being given the data work?
Tashi may have felt trusted and respected, as the result was work faster than anyone else's.

Read this:

Rain hammered the tin roof of the community hall as Seema counted the week's unpaid hours on her fingers: kitchen duty every evening, the weekend clean-up, the printing of pamphlets. That night the teacher's assistant slid a form across the table. "A pledge: half your salary each month. Sign tonight, before the blessings window closes. And keep it between us. Your family wouldn't understand."

Seema's pen hovered. She had come here sincere and lonely after a bad year. Then the power cut out, and in the dark her phone lit up: her brother Jomon, whose calls she had missed for weeks.

"Come home on Sunday. Please." Then, more quietly, "Groups like that look for people who mean it."

Seema slid the form back. "I'll take it home and show my family." She left under a borrowed umbrella, feeling foolish, and then, oddly, lighter.

What did the assistant ask Seema to pledge?
The assistant asked for half of her salary each month, to be signed that night.
How did Seema feel while walking out, and why?
Seema felt foolish at first and then lighter: foolish for having believed so sincerely, lighter for stepping back and choosing to show her family.
What could Seema do next?
Talk with Jomon and the family, show them the form, keep in contact, and seek outside counsel before giving any more money or unpaid time.
How does Jomon see Seema's absence?
With worry: Jomon asks her to come home on Sunday and points out that groups like that look for people who mean it, so Seema's sincerity is not seen as foolishness.

The girls' hostel common room became a courtroom on Saturday nights. This week Dilnaz, sixteen, argued that phones should be allowed after lights-out. Usha, the senior monitor, argued against. Dilnaz talked fast. "We need them to call home!" Usha nodded calmly. "You can call home at eight. What's the real reason?" Dilnaz opened her mouth, then stopped. She knew the real reason was watching videos. She took a breath. "Okay. Fair point. But some girls have parents on night shifts. Eight doesn't work for them." The room went quiet. Usha paused. "That's true. Maybe a rule for them, not everyone." Dilnaz sat down, heart still thumping, feeling like she'd lost and won at the same time.

What time did Usha say the girls could call home?
She said they could call home at eight.
Why did Dilnaz feel like she had lost and won at the same time?
She had to admit her first reason was weak, but her new point about parents on night shifts was strong enough to change Usha's view.
What could Dilnaz do before the next debate to feel less rushed?
She could think through her real reasons and the other side's likely questions in advance, so she leads with her strongest evidence.
How might Usha see Dilnaz after this debate?
She probably respects her more, because Dilnaz admitted a weak point honestly and then raised a fair argument that Usha had to accept.

Dear Maa,
I didn't want to say this in front of everyone at Diwali, so I'm writing instead.
I'm really grateful to Vasudha Mausi for paying my school fees these two years. I know we couldn't have managed. I'm going to thank her properly, and one day I want to do the same for someone.
But Maa, every time we visit, she mentions it. 'Study hard, I'm paying, remember.' At Diwali she said it in front of all the cousins, and I wanted to disappear. I felt thankful and small at the same time, and I hate feeling both.
I'm not asking you to fight with her. Could you, gently, tell her how it feels for us? Maybe that we know, we'll never forget, and she doesn't need to remind us?
I'll write her a thank-you card this week. I just need your help with the rest.
Love,
Abhinav

What does Vasudha Mausi say on every visit?
'Study hard, I'm paying, remember.'
What does Abhinav feel when Mausi mentions the fees?
Abhinav feels grateful and humiliated at once, wanting to disappear when it's said in front of the cousins.
What makes Abhinav's plan a balanced one?
Abhinav will thank Mausi sincerely with a card and asks Maa to set a gentle boundary, instead of fighting.
How might Vasudha Mausi see her reminders?
She may think she's motivating Abhinav, not realising the reminders feel humiliating.

Anand, the team lead, closed the Monday review with a smile. "Nobody is as dependable as you, Tushar," he said, and dropped two more client accounts on Tushar's plate. Tushar nodded, though he had been finishing reports at midnight for a month. That evening he ate in silence and snapped when the tap dripped. Vikas, his partner, felt the chill but did not take it personally. "I miss you," he said softly. "Could we keep Sunday breakfast, phones away?" Tushar agreed, guiltily. A few days later his friend Ritu caught him yawning over a lunch he barely touched. "You look flattened. Go home and rest," she said. He almost laughed it off, then only said, "Yeah. Okay. A walk after work, maybe?" By the lake he admitted that most mornings felt hollow. The next week he sat in a clinic and told the doctor everything: the poor sleep, the skipped meals, the low mood, the late nights he had been hiding. The doctor listened and set up follow-up visits. Back at work, Tushar wrote down every task he held and asked Anand which ones mattered most.

What did Anand do at the end of the Monday review?
He said nobody is as dependable as Tushar and dropped two more client accounts on his plate.
How did Vikas's response to Tushar's exhaustion differ from Anand's?
Anand praised Tushar's dependability while adding more accounts, whereas Vikas said softly that he missed him and suggested keeping Sunday breakfast, caring for Tushar rather than using his effort.
How was Tushar likely feeling when he agreed to the Sunday breakfast, and what shows it?
He was probably guilty and worn down; he agreed guiltily right after snapping at home and eating in silence.
What could Tushar keep doing to stay well after the clinic visit?
He could keep small rituals like Sunday breakfast and lakeside walks, attend the follow-up visits, and keep asking Anand which tasks matter most. 🙂

"My sock is alive!"

Dear Diary, Saturday
Last month, when I told Papa I cracked his phone screen, he shouted so the neighbours heard, and made me say "I am careless" in front of Dadi and my cousins. Everyone laughed. I cried in the bathroom.
So today, when I tore my uniform on the gate, I said a boy pushed me. Nobody pushed me. I just didn't want the shouting again. My hands shook the whole time.
Vasudha Masi found me crying on the stairs. I told her everything, even the lie. She said, "Keerthana, this is not your fault. Telling the truth should never feel this scary." Tonight she talked to Papa for a long time. He came and said sorry. I don't know yet if I believe him.

What did Keerthana say had happened to the uniform?
Keerthana said a boy pushed, though nobody pushed and the uniform tore on the gate.
Why did Keerthana lie about the torn uniform?
After being shouted at and made to say "I am careless" in front of family, Keerthana feared the same humiliation, so lying felt safer.
What did Vasudha Masi do that helped?
She listened to everything Keerthana told her, said it wasn't Keerthana's fault, and talked to Papa that same night.
Why might Papa have come to say sorry after talking with Vasudha Masi?
He may have realised that his shouting and mocking taught Keerthana that the truth was dangerous, which is why the lie happened.

A bank card and a school ID.

Manjula felt uncertain at first, then settled and sure it should go back, because it could be traced.

Manjula could ask a parent to go along to the school office, so an adult sees it handed over.
How does Manjula's choice look to Eshaan?
Eshaan keeps the coin but looks at Manjula strangely, perhaps wondering whether he should have thought more too.

Mehak has missed four evening sessions in a row. She was never a skipper. When I called, she said, "Exams, sir," but her friend and doubles partner Sonali says Mehak's exams are next month.

Today Mehak came to return the club shuttle tube. I asked her plainly if something had happened. After a long pause she said Sonali had joked, in front of the whole team, that Mehak "only won because of the partner". Everyone laughed. Mehak laughed too, then went home and hasn't really come back since. "I'll just stay away for a bit. It'll pass," she said. She looked relieved just saying it.

I think it may not pass by itself. Sonali seems puzzled, not unkind; she asked me if Mehak was angry with her.

Next step: I've offered Mehak my office on Friday if she wants to speak to Sonali with someone nearby.

How many evening sessions has Mehak missed in a row?
Mehak has missed four evening sessions in a row.
Why did Mehak look relieved when she said "It'll pass"?
Staying away means she doesn't have to face the hurt or risk an awkward talk with Sonali. Just deciding not to deal with it brought a quick sense of relief.
What is the turning point the coach is trying to create for Mehak?
The chance to tell Sonali directly how the joke landed, in a calm place with support. That choice, instead of more distance, gives the friendship a chance to be repaired.
How does Sonali seem to see Mehak's absence?
Sonali seems puzzled, not unkind, and even asks the coach if Mehak is angry. Sonali may not know the joke hurt, so the silence leaves Sonali guessing.

"In our time the river was full all year. Nobody locked doors. Everyone shared everything. Children respected elders." The old men nodded. Devika thought of her Dadi's stories: the drought year when they ate only jowar, the fever when there was no road to the town hospital, the fights over the well. She almost said so. Instead she watched Manjula aunty's face go soft as she talked about harvest nights. The warmth in it was real, even if the picture was polished. "Aunty, what songs did you sing at harvest?" Devika asked. Manjula aunty laughed, surprised, and began to hum. The men clapped along. Devika stayed till dark.

Where did Devika sit every evening after closing the branch?
On the panchayat office porch.

Devika felt doubtful, remembering her Dadi's stories of drought, fever and fights over the well, but she was touched by the real warmth in Manjula aunty's face and asked about the harvest songs.
Why was asking about harvest songs a wise choice at that moment?
It honoured the real warmth in the memory without starting an argument, so the evening stayed friendly and Devika grew closer to the elders.

All twenty-three villages.
What was Arnab likely feeling as the coordinator said 'our team'?
Arnab was likely uncomfortable and quietly frustrated, watching Zeenat in the back row go unnamed after walking all twenty-three villages.

Arnab named Zeenat as the one who did the survey when the officer asked; by the next month the coordinator was naming each person's work.

He treats the drop in confidence as a normal sign that real learning has begun, which helps Alka keep going instead of quitting.

Sahil was probably amused and a little tired of it, but glad she was enjoying the subject.

3 rotis are cut into halves. How many halves are there? If the 3 rotis were cut into quarters, how many quarters would there be?

Answer: 6 halves and 12 quarters. 3 = 6/2 = 12/4.

Each roti gives 2 halves, so 3 rotis give 3 x 2 = 6 halves: 3 = 6/2. Each roti gives 4 quarters, so 3 rotis give 3 x 4 = 12 quarters: 3 = 12/4. Any whole number can be written as a fraction: 3 = 3/1 = 6/2 = 9/3 = 12/4. Going the other way, 12/4 means 12 / 4 = 3 with no remainder, so the answer is a whole number with no fraction part.

When he moved to the new senior school, the boys he wanted to sit with said dhol was "village stuff". One of them imitated him drumming on the desk, and they all laughed. Baljeet laughed too. Why did Baljeet put the dhol on top of the cupboard?
He wanted to belong with the new boys, and their laughter made him give up something he loved to fit in.
What could Baljeet do next that might help?
Talk to Vaibhav and his uncle, and maybe play again, finding friends who value his drumming.
How might Vaibhav feel about Baljeet giving up the dhol?
Vaibhav seems sad and puzzled, knowing Baljeet loved it more than anything.

On each of 7 Mondays, it rained 1.5 centimeters. On each of 9 Tuesdays it rained 2.5 centimeters. How many more centimeters did it rain on Tuesdays than Mondays?

Mondays: 7 * 1.5 = 10.5
Tuesdays: 9 * 2.5 = 22.5
22.5 - 10.5 = 12 cm
It rained 12 centimeters more on Tuesdays than on Mondays.
The answer is 12.

How did Yash feel after writing the plan?
Yash still felt some worry, but less helpless, because the fear now had exits, and he slept till seven.
Why does writing the likelihood and "what would I do" help?
It turns vague midnight dread into a rough chance and concrete options, like asking for notice or staying in Thane.
How might Jyoti feel knowing Yash used the notebook method?
Jyoti would probably feel glad that the method helped Yash turn a sleepless night into a plan.

Trainer's note, community gym, Chennai, 3 March. Tanuja.
Nikita joined in January for the 7 p.m. strength class and came twice in six weeks. Nikita runs a school admissions desk, and when I asked, the answer was, "By evening I've said yes or no to a hundred parents. I pick up takeaway and I can't face one more choice." It could be tiredness, it could be that the class felt like another obligation, it could be that priorities had shifted. I didn't push on the cause. We tried two things: a 6:30 a.m. slot twice a week, before the desk opens, and a written plan so there's no deciding once inside the gym. Nikita has come to five of the last six morning sessions. Evenings are still takeaway, and that's fine for now.

How many times did Nikita come to the 7 p.m. class in six weeks?
Nikita came twice in six weeks.
What was Nikita feeling by the end of an admissions day, and what shows it?
Drained of choosing: Nikita says they've said yes or no to a hundred parents and can't face one more choice, so takeaway feels like relief rather than a failure.
What two changes did Tanuja try, and why might they work whatever the cause?
A 6:30 a.m. slot before the desk opens and a written plan; they put the hard task first and remove choices, which helps whether the problem is fatigue, boredom or priorities 👍
How might Tanuja feel about Nikita coming to five of the last six morning sessions?
Tanuja probably feels encouraged that the practical changes worked, and stays relaxed about the evening takeaway, calling it fine for now.
Raksha Bandhan pe bhai ko card mein English mein kya likhun? Woh Canada mein hai.

Dear Bhaiya,

This Rakhi I can't tie the thread on your wrist, but my love travels across the miles. Stay happy and stay safe. I miss you.

Love,
Neha

You asked about my internship? Okay. I'm Nilesh, and the one moment I'm proud of was a question.
Our demo for the client crashed. In the meeting afterwards, the whole team piled on Nitin, the youngest. “Nitin pushed the code.” “Nitin didn't test it.” The manager nodded along. It was almost a relief in the room, like we'd found the answer.
I remembered we'd all agreed to skip testing to meet the deadline. All of us. The manager too.
So I asked, quietly, “If it's all Nitin, what are we not talking about?”
Silence. Then someone said, “The deadline.” And someone else, “We skipped testing together.”
Nitin looked up for the first time. The meeting became about fixing the process, not him.

What did the team agree to skip?
They'd all agreed to skip testing to meet the deadline.
What was Nilesh feeling before asking the question?
Nilesh felt uneasy, sensing the room's relief at blaming Nitin was hiding a shared mistake.
Why did Nilesh's question shift the meeting?
It named the pattern quietly and let others admit the shared cause, so the focus moved from Nitin to the process.
How might Nitin have felt when he looked up?
Nitin likely felt relieved and less alone after being piled on as the youngest.

Read this:

In Buenos Aires, Santiago worked weekends at a café while studying engineering. He brought lunch from home every day and refused to buy a coffee on campus, even when he was exhausted.

In December the café gave him a holiday bonus. Within a week, he'd spent it on concert tickets, a new jacket, and a weekend trip with friends.

His flatmate Soo-ah watched him refuse a coffee again in January. "You spent your whole bonus in a week, but you won't buy a coffee?"

"The bonus was fun money," Santiago said. "Coffee comes out of my real money."

"It's all your money," Soo-ah said.

Santiago opened his banking app and looked at the total. It was lower than he'd thought, and he felt a little sick.

Where did Santiago work on weekends?
He worked weekends at a café.
How did Santiago feel when he looked at his total in January?
He felt uneasy and a little sick, realising his separate "fun" and "real" money were one smaller pile.
What could Santiago try so he sees his whole picture?
He could look at all his money in one place each month and, if unsure, ask a trusted adult or a bank adviser about choices.
How might Soo-ah see Santiago's split between fun money and real money?
Soo-ah finds it confusing and a bit worrying, since to her it's all the same money.
What time did I wake up today?
I can't tell, as I have no way of seeing your day. If you note it down each morning, you can look back.
Bo is learning words for the GRE.  He got 800 flashcards.  He knew 20% of the words on them.  He has 40 days to learn the rest.  How many words does he need to learn a day?

He knows 800*.2=160 words
So he needs to learn 800-160=640 words
That means he needs to learn 640/40=16 words per day
The answer is 16.

Read this:

"You got selected for the national hackathon?" Sharmila stared at Avni's laptop screen.
"Only for the first round." Avni was grinning.
"Of course you did. You're one of those people."
"What people?"
"People who were born knowing how to code. I could practise ten years and never be you."
"Sharmila, I failed the first two contests I entered."
"Yeah, but you had the brain for it. I don't."
"You literally haven't tried a contest."
"Because there's no point. The gap's already there."
Avni closed the laptop. "Why are you angry at me?"
"I'm not angry." Sharmila picked up her phone, then put it down. "I just feel like every time you win, I lose something. Stupid, right?"
Avni didn't answer straight away.

How many contests did Avni fail before?
Avni failed the first two contests Avni entered.
Why does Sharmila feel she loses something when Avni wins?
Sharmila feels envious and threatened, believing coding talent is fixed, so Avni's win seems to confirm a gap Sharmila can never close.
What would help Sharmila see this differently?
Hearing that Avni failed two contests first could show that skill grows; Sharmila could try one small contest alongside Avni instead of assuming the gap is destiny.
How does Avni seem to feel during this conversation?
Avni goes from excited to hurt and confused, closing the laptop and asking why Sharmila is angry.
Why do we put ghee on hot rotis? And what does "crunchy" mean?

1. The heat melts the ghee, and it adds a rich flavour and keeps the roti soft.
2. Crunchy means firm and making a sharp sound when you bite it.
Meera deposits ₹8,000 in a bank at 6% per annum simple interest for 3 years. Find the interest and the amount. Why does the formula SI = PRT/100 work?

Answer: SI = ₹1,440; amount = ₹9,440.

6% per annum means ₹6 for every ₹100 each year. On ₹8,000 (80 hundreds) one year's interest is 80 x 6 = ₹480, which is 8,000 x 6/100. For 3 years it is 3 times that. So in general SI = P x R/100 x T = PRT/100: SI = 8,000 x 6 x 3/100 = ₹1,440 A = P + SI = 8,000 + 1,440 = ₹9,440 Simple interest is the same every year (₹480), because it is always worked out on the ORIGINAL ₹8,000. Common mistake: forgetting to add the principal when the question asks for the amount.

It was Ramadan, and Hiroshi noticed Jamal wasn't eating lunch at their school in Tokyo.
"Are you sick?"
"No, I'm fasting. No food or water from sunrise to sunset. It's Ramadan."
"Not even water? Isn't that hard?"
"Sometimes. It helps me remember people who don't have enough."
Hiroshi looked at his onigiri. He quietly put it back in his bag and ate it later in the corridor.
The next week, Jamal's family invited him to iftar. Hiroshi brought a box of dates his mother bought. He watched Jamal's family pray, then eat together, laughing.
"Thank you for coming," said Jamal.

What does Jamal say he doesn't have from sunrise to sunset?
No food or water.
What was Hiroshi feeling when he put his onigiri back?
Hiroshi felt considerate and a little awkward about eating in front of Jamal.
What did Hiroshi do that showed respect?
He asked kindly, ate away from Jamal, and came to iftar with a thoughtful gift.
How might Jamal feel when Hiroshi comes to iftar?
Jamal is likely happy and grateful 😊 that his friend wanted to share his tradition.

Monday night. Mohit lay in bed staring at the fan. What if I fail the maths test? What if Mummy's bus has an accident on the way back from work? His heart thumped. His older brother Zubin, in the next bed, was asleep.

Tuesday night. Mohit couldn't sleep again. He went to the kitchen. Mummy was home, washing cups. "What's wrong, beta?" He told her. She sat with him on the sofa. "Your mind is trying to keep you safe, but it's making false alarms. I come home every day. And you practised your maths." She suggested a new routine: a warm glass of milk, a short story with Zubin, and three slow breaths.

Friday night. Milk, a story from Zubin about a lazy tiger, three breaths. A what-if started to come. Mohit remembered Mummy's words, breathed again, and fell asleep before the tiger woke up.

What did Mohit worry about on Monday night?
Failing the maths test and Mummy's bus having an accident.
How was Mohit feeling on Monday night?
He felt scared and anxious, his heart thumping as the what-ifs kept coming.
What helped Mohit calm down, and why?
Mummy's reassurance and a calm routine of milk, a story and slow breaths helped him see the worries as false alarms and settle.
How might Zubin feel telling the tiger story each night?
Zubin might feel proud and caring, happy to help his little brother sleep.
A blissful holiday: please explain blissful.

Blissful means full of great happiness and peace. It is an adjective.
Example: They spent a blissful week by the lake.
Seth and Max were selling candy bars for a school fundraiser. Seth sold 6 more candy bars than 3 times the number of candy bars that Max sold. If Max sold 24 candy bars, how many did Seth sell?

Let C be the number of candy bars Seth sold
3*24 +6=C
72+6=C
C=78
The answer is 78.
My friend Aditi just passed her driving test after failing twice. Write her a congratulations message, about 50 words.

Aditi, you did it! Third time lucky, and I'm so proud of you. You never gave up, even when you were nervous, and that is what matters. The roads of this city had better watch out now. Our first long drive is on me, and I'll bring the snacks!
Explain teamwork to a young child in one sentence, using only words of six letters or fewer.
A good team shares the work and helps each other win.

Three weeks after the Ooty trip, the school library was nearly empty in the free period. Vandana sat down across from Madhuri, not beside her like before.
"I haven't told anyone anything since," Vandana said. "And I told Tanya I was wrong to say it. In front of Kriti too."
Madhuri knew that part was true; Kriti had mentioned it. And Vandana hadn't asked her to forget it, or said sorry fifty times, or cried until Madhuri had to comfort her.
"I'm not ready to tell you things like before," Madhuri said, turning a page she wasn't reading.
"That's fair."
"But we can do the biology project together. And you can sit with me at lunch. Just... slower."
Vandana nodded. When the bell rang they walked out together, a little distance between their shoulders. Madhuri noticed she didn't mind the distance. It felt like room to watch.

Where did Vandana sit in the library?
Vandana sat down across from Madhuri, not beside her like before.
Why was Madhuri willing to try again, and what was she still feeling?
Madhuri saw the apology was real and nothing had been repeated, but she still felt wary, which is why she wanted things slower.
What limits did Madhuri set, and why are they wise?
Madhuri agreed to the project and lunch but not to sharing secrets yet; this lets trust be earned back step by step. 🙂
What might Vandana be experiencing as they walk out with distance between them?
Vandana is probably relieved to be given a chance, and also aware the old closeness has to be rebuilt slowly.

messages.content: Write a diary entry, about 65 words, from a boy who tried cooking an omelette for the first time and burnt the first one.

Dear Diary,
Today I made an omelette by myself for the first time. The first one burnt black on the bottom, and the whole kitchen smelled of smoke. I was ready to quit, but then I remembered that everyone burns the first one. I lowered the flame and tried again. The second omelette was golden and soft. I ate it proudly. Next time, I will not forget the salt!

The chief steward, a very stupid but cunning man who saw perfectly through the naive and intelligent count and played with him as with a toy, seeing the effect these prearranged receptions had on Pierre, pressed him still harder with proofs of the impossibility and above all the uselessness of freeing the serfs, who were quite happy as it was.

What sort of man is the chief steward?
He is stupid but cunning. He sees through Pierre, plays with him like a toy, and pushes the idea that freeing the serfs is impossible and pointless.

Sarika, you won't believe what I watched yesterday. I'm Jatin, right, and my flatmate had his big online interview. I was in the room, quiet, doing my own work. His internet froze in the first minute. When it came back, he said, "Uh, sorry, can you, uh, hear me?" and his voice was shaking. I could see on his screen the interviewer's face just... set. And then, honestly, my flatmate was brilliant. For forty minutes. Clear answers, good examples. But the interviewer kept asking harder and harder questions, like she was trying to prove the first minute right. He didn't get it. Afterwards, we made a plan for the next one: test the internet, have a glass of water, and practise one calm opening line. I also thought, interviewers should warm up too. Nobody's at their best in second one.

How long was Jatin's flatmate brilliant after the freeze?
For forty minutes.
What was Jatin feeling while watching the interview?
Jatin felt frustrated and sympathetic, watching one shaky first minute seem to decide everything despite forty strong minutes.
What plan did they make, and why is it sensible?
Testing the internet, keeping water ready and practising a calm opening line, so the first impression is steadier next time.
How might the interviewer see the interview?
The interviewer seems to have judged from the shaky start and then looked for proof, missing how strong the rest was.

Jane is shopping for some fruit.  She sees a stand of fruit advertising 10 apples for $2, and another one advertising 5 oranges for $1.50.  Assuming there's no price discount for buying in bulk, how much would Jane spend in cents if she bought 12 of the cheaper of the two fruits?

First, we need to find out which fruit is cheaper individually. We start by figuring out the price for a single apple by performing 200/10= 20 cents per apple.
Then we find out the price of an individual orange, by performing 150/5=30 cents per orange.
Since 20<30, the apples are cheaper.
To determine the answer, we multiply 20*12= 240 cents
The answer is 240.

In the small primary health centre at Sangamner, Vishal, twenty-four, was first to arrive and last to leave. For three years he had taken his mother by local bus to the district hospital for her treatments; since she died in March, he had enrolled as a trainee nursing assistant.
He was good at it. He knew how to lift an old farmer without hurting him, and what to say to a frightened daughter in the corridor. The senior nurse, Usha, watched him calm a whole family in five minutes.
But she also saw him flinch when a patient asked, "Your mother must be proud?" and then hurry off to restock gauze.
That evening Usha stopped him at the gate. "You're very good here, Vishal. But this place can't hold all of it. When did you last sit with your own sadness?"
He didn't answer. On Sunday, for the first time since March, he went to the temple by the river and sat there a long time, not helping anyone.

What did Vishal enrol as after his mother died?
A trainee nursing assistant at the small primary health centre at Sangamner.
Why might restocking gauze feel easier to Vishal than answering the patient's question?
The work gives his loss a purpose and keeps him busy, while the question touched the raw grief for his mother that he hadn't let himself feel.
What turning point did Usha's question create?
It named that the work couldn't hold all of his grief, and on Sunday he sat by the river for a long time, giving the sadness its own space.
How does Usha see Vishal's skill with patients?
Usha admires how well he calms families, but also notices the flinch and the constant busyness, and cares enough to say what the work can't do.

In the reading corner at school, Tenzin was telling a small group about the mela. "There was a big wheel that went so high, and we ate hot jalebi, and the—"
"Actually, it was Sunday," said Imran. "You said Saturday before."
Tenzin stopped. "Oh. Sunday." The story trailed off.
Imran folded both arms, looking pleased to have caught the slip. The teacher, sitting nearby, said, "Imran, what was the best part of Tenzin's story so far?"
Imran opened the mouth. "Um... it was Sunday."
"That's a good detail," said the teacher gently. "What about the wheel?"
Imran looked at the floor. "I didn't hear about the wheel."

What day did Imran say the mela was on?
Sunday.
What was Imran feeling when catching Tenzin's slip, and what does that suggest?
Pleased with catching a mistake. The folded arms and the pleased look suggest Imran was listening for errors, not for the story.
How could the teacher help Imran listen differently?
The teacher asked what the best part of the story was so far, which pointed Imran toward the meaning rather than the mistake; a next step could be asking Tenzin one question about the wheel.
How does Tenzin feel when the story is stopped by a correction?
Deflated. The story trailed off after the correction, so Tenzin's excitement about the mela was lost.

In Amandeep's village the school bus left at half past six and got back at four, and most evenings she helped her mother with the buffaloes before dinner. Then Wasim, the class topper, posted his board-exam routine on a video site: up at five, study till midnight, every day. Half the class shared it. Amandeep copied it into her notebook in neat blue ink. For the first week she dragged herself up at five and sat by the lantern through the power cuts, eyes stinging. By the ninth day she was nodding off on the bus and snapping at her little brother. On the eleventh night her mother found her asleep with her cheek on the Physics book. The next morning Amandeep tore the page out of her notebook. She didn't make a new timetable. She didn't study at all that week.

When did the school bus leave and get back?
It left at half past six and got back at four.
What does Amandeep's behaviour by the ninth day suggest she was feeling?
She was nodding off on the bus and snapping at her little brother, which shows she was exhausted and irritable.
What would you change first in Amandeep's plan?
Fit it to her own day, with the long bus hours, the evening chores and the times she feels fresh, instead of copying Wasim's hours.
What might Amandeep's mother feel, finding her asleep on the Physics book?
She may feel worried and sad, seeing how hard her daughter has been pushing and how tired she has become.

Sunday. Vasudha told Nani about their trip to Ooty: the toy train, the rose garden, the cold.

Wednesday. At dinner, her brother Omkar told the story too, adding a monkey that stole his sandwich on the train. Vasudha laughed with everyone.

The next Sunday, telling her friend on the phone, Vasudha said, "And a monkey grabbed my brother's sandwich right out of his hand on the toy train!" She could almost see it.

Later, Mummy looked at the photos. "Omkar, wasn't the monkey at the lake? After the train?"

Omkar shrugged. Vasudha frowned. She was sure it had been the train. She'd seen it, hadn't she? Or had she just heard it so many times?

What did Omkar add to the story at dinner?
A monkey that stole his sandwich on the train.
How did Vasudha feel when Mummy said the monkey was at the lake?
She felt confused and unsure, because the train version felt so real to her.
What could Vasudha's family do to check memories of the trip?
They could look at the photos together and talk about who remembers what, without deciding anyone is lying.
How might Omkar see the confusion?
Omkar just shrugs, so he may not care much or may not be sure himself.
Swimming lessons are starting soon, but deep water scares me.
Fear of deep water is understandable, and it is wise to respect water. Learning with a trained instructor is the safest route.
The pool has a shallow end. Can I practise there?
Yes, shallow water is a good place to build comfort, as long as an adult or instructor is nearby. Never swim alone, even in the shallow end.
What should I practise first?
Ask your instructor, but most beginners start with breathing out underwater, floating and kicking. These are the basis for every stroke.
How long until I'm comfortable?
It varies from person to person. Some take weeks and some take months. Regular lessons and patience matter more than speed.
Should I tell the instructor I'm afraid?
Yes. A good instructor wants to know and will go at your pace. Being honest about fear helps them keep you safe and confident.

After my thread ceremony I thought I'd feel different. Mostly I felt itchy. In the changing room before PE a boy asked if it was some fashion thing. Kalyani, who sits behind me in Bengali class, said, "My uncle wears one to pray, my cousin wears one because his mother insists, and I know a boy who just likes it." She looked at me. "Which are you?" I realised I had no clean answer. Ma wants me to keep it on. Dadu says it has to do with learning, and I like feeling close to him. Some days I tuck it under my shirt, some days I don't. I'm still working it out. - Arnab

Where did the boy ask Arnab about the thread?
He asked in the changing room before PE.
What did Arnab feel when Kalyani asked which he was?
He felt uncertain, since he had no clean answer; his reasons seem to mix his mother's wish, closeness to Dadu and his own feeling.
How could Arnab reply when someone asks what his thread means?
He could share what he knows or say he is still working it out, without needing a tidy answer.
What does Kalyani's list of people show?
It shows that the same thread can be prayer, family insistence or personal taste, so nobody should assume what it means for someone else.

A pair of shoes costs ₹2,000 before tax. GST of 12% is added. What is the tax and what is the bill? Another item priced ₹800 has a 10% discount and then 5% GST on the sale price. What is its bill?

Now you try: ₹1,500 plus 18% GST.
The answer is ₹1,770.
Monsoon is starting, and my school books get damp on the way every year.
Damp books are a common problem in the rains. A waterproof cover helps most. Does your bag have a rain cover?
No, it doesn't.
A plastic cover or a large plastic bag works. Put the books in a smaller plastic bag inside the school bag as well, for a second layer.
What if the books do get wet?
Open them carefully and let them air-dry flat in a place with moving air, away from direct sun. Do not close wet pages, and ask a parent or teacher about replacing anything badly damaged.
My shoes are always wet too.
Carrying a spare pair of socks in a plastic bag helps. At home, let the shoes dry in a shaded, airy spot instead of direct sun, which can damage them.
It's tiring planning for all this.
A short checklist by the door makes it automatic: rain cover, plastic bag, spare socks. After a few days, you will do it without thinking.
My cousin Meera made me a handmade bookmark with dried flowers for my birthday. Write a thank-you note to her, about 45 words.

Dear Meera,
Thank you for the lovely bookmark. I love how you pressed the flowers so carefully, and I will use it often. It was so thoughtful of you to make something yourself. I will keep it safe for years.
With love,
Your cousin

When Disha joined our class in Class 10, she hardly spoke. She drew in the margins of her notebook and wore a scarf with little moons on it. I'm Ujjwal, and I decided at once that she was a shy artist who wrote secret poems at night and probably wanted to live in the mountains. It felt so true. More true, somehow, than just "she likes drawing." In the psychology club, our teacher gave us a quiz with exactly this: which is likelier for a quiet girl, being an artist, or being an artist who writes poems? Most of us picked the second. The teacher smiled. "Every poet-artist is also an artist. So 'artist' can't be less likely." I felt a bit stupid. Later I asked Disha. She liked drawing. She hated poetry.

What was on Disha's scarf?
Little moons.
Why did the detailed story about Disha feel so true to Ujjwal?
Each extra detail fit the picture of her, so Ujjwal felt more certain and excited about it, even though every detail made it less likely.
What did the teacher's point help Ujjwal see, and what could Ujjwal do next time?
That every poet-artist is also an artist, so the simpler story is always at least as likely; next time Ujjwal could ask the person instead of adding details.
How might Disha feel about the story Ujjwal made up about her?
Disha might find it odd or a little funny, since she likes drawing but hates poetry.

Last year Pallavi, then a third-year, wanted to be the helpful mentor for Aparna. Whenever Aparna got stuck, Pallavi typed the solution. Aparna nodded, thanked her, and came back the next day with the next problem. By the exams she could not write a loop alone.

This year, as a final-year student, Pallavi met a new junior, Naveen, and began differently. "What do you actually want?" she asked. "A first internship," he said. So instead of describing her own path, she looked at what internships asked for.

She broke "learn programming" down week by week: one concept, one exercise, one small program. Every Saturday they went over Naveen's work together, and Pallavi asked "what would you try?" before she said anything.

One Saturday Naveen asked about machine learning. Pallavi laughed. "I don't know it well enough to advise you. But a senior in that area is in the lab on Mondays. I'll introduce you." Naveen looked relieved that she had said it plainly.

What did Naveen say he wanted?
Naveen said he wanted a first internship.
How did Pallavi's mentoring of Naveen differ from her earlier mentoring of Aparna, and what were the results?
With Aparna she typed every solution, so Aparna could not write a loop alone, while with Naveen she asked what he wanted, set small weekly steps and asked what he would try first.
What was Naveen feeling when Pallavi said she did not know machine learning well enough?
Relief and trust, since she said it plainly and offered a real introduction.
What could Pallavi do when Naveen is stuck next week?
Pallavi could ask what he has tried and give a hint rather than the whole answer.
Why does a rolling ball slow down and stop on a grass field?
The ball loses its speed to rubbing against the grass. Because this rubbing, called friction, works against the motion and takes away its energy, the ball comes to rest.

In a Hyderabad accounts firm, Siddharth, a junior, set a timer every morning at 9:30. Thirty minutes of practising spreadsheet formulas on old data before the real work began.
Rafiq, who sat next to him, thought it was a waste. "Just learn it when you need it. I did a whole weekend course once." That was eight months ago. He had forgotten most of it.
For a long time, Siddharth's practice didn't show. His reports looked like everyone else's. He wondered sometimes if he was just wasting half an hour.
Then in March, the partner asked who could build a monthly dashboard for a big client. Rafiq said he'd need a week to relearn. Siddharth built a draft in two days.
The partner looked at it, then at Siddharth. "Where did you learn this?"
"Every morning, sir. Half an hour."
Rafiq didn't say anything, but the next Monday, Siddharth noticed a timer on Rafiq's desk too.

At what time did Siddharth set his timer?
Every morning at 9:30.
How did Siddharth sometimes feel about the daily practice?
Siddharth sometimes felt doubtful, wondering if the half hour was wasted because nothing seemed to show.
What shows that the small daily habit paid off?
Siddharth built the client dashboard draft in two days, while Rafiq needed a week to relearn.
How might Rafiq have felt when the partner asked where Siddharth learned it?
Rafiq probably felt a little embarrassed and impressed, which is why a timer appeared on his desk the next Monday.

"Rehana, got a sec?" Dolma leaned on the door frame of their room. "Tashi's in town this weekend. Would it be okay if he came over on Saturday afternoon?"
Rehana looked up from her notes. "Thanks for asking first. What time?"
"Maybe two to six? We'd just watch something, make momos."
"Saturday afternoon is my study block. I've got a mock on Monday."
"Oh. Right." Dolma paused. "Would the common room work for us instead? Or Sunday?"
"Sunday after lunch is perfect. I'll be at my aunt's."
"Great. And if you're back early, just walk in. It's your room too."
"Can we make it a thing? Guests only with a day's notice, and nobody stays the night."
"Yes. Same for you."
"I don't have a Tashi."
"Yet."
Rehana threw a pen at her. "Bring me two momos."

When is Rehana's study block?
Saturday afternoon.
Why did Dolma pause after hearing about the mock?
She felt a little disappointed but considerate, realising her plan clashed with Rehana's study time.
Which rules did Dolma and Rehana agree on?
Guests only with a day's notice and nobody staying the night, for both of them.
How does Rehana feel about being asked first?
Respected; she thanks Dolma and happily suggests Sunday instead.

Sunday
Farida's diary. Best afternoon. Abba fixed my old kite with tape and a bit of newspaper, and it flew higher than the water tank. We ate roasted chana on the roof and I didn't want anything else in the world.
Then Pankaj came up with his new remote-control car that lights up. Everybody ran to see it. For a minute my kite felt like rubbish and I wanted to ask Abba for a car too. But then the car's battery died and Pankaj had to go down. My kite was still up there, pulling. I think my afternoon was already good before the car came. I'm keeping the tape for next time.

What did Abba use to fix the kite?
He used tape and a bit of newspaper.
How did Farida feel when Pankaj brought his remote-control car?
For a minute Farida felt envious and dissatisfied, as if the kite had turned into rubbish, and wanted a car too.
What helped Farida feel content again?
Noticing the kite still flying and remembering that the afternoon had been good before the car arrived 🙂
How might Pankaj have felt when his car's battery died?
He probably felt disappointed and a bit embarrassed, having to go down just when everyone was watching.

A zoo has 8 parrots. It 3 times the number of snakes than parrots and 2 times the number of monkeys than snakes. The number of elephants is half the number of parrots and snakes added up, and there are 3 fewer zebras than elephants. What is the difference in number between the zebras and the monkeys?

The zoo has 8 x 3 = 24 snakes.
It has 24 x 2 = 48 monkeys.
The number of parrots and snakes added up is 8 + 24 = 32
There are 32/2 = 16 elephants.
There are 16 - 3 = 13 zebras.
The difference between zebras and monkeys is 48 - 13 = 35
The answer is 35.

Emma is planning a dinner party, so she went to a shop to buy the products she needs. She bought 8 kg of cheese and 7 kg of vegetables. One kilogram of cheese costs $4 and one kilogram of vegetable costs is $2 more expensive. How much did she pay for her shopping?

Emma payed 8 kg * $4/kg = $32 for the cheese.
The cost of one kilogram of vegetable is $4 + $2 = $6.
So Emma payed 7 kg * $6/kg = $42 for vegetables.
In total Emma payed $32 + $42 = $74 for her shopping.
The answer is 74.

When Jason plays the video game, Duty for Ashes, his mission to slay the dragon hoard requires that he fire his weapon on average every 15 seconds.   And each time he fires his weapon, his power-fire setting allows him to shoot a flame for 5 seconds.  On average, how many seconds per minute does Jason shoot flames at the dragon hoard?

Since he fires his weapon on average every 15 seconds, then in one minute he fires the flamethrower 60/15=4 times.
And since each time he fires his weapon, he shoots flame for 5 seconds, then Jason shoots flames at the dragon hoard a total of 4*5=20 seconds of every minute.
The answer is 20.

The after-school club at the community centre had one swing in the yard, and a chart on the door said whose turn it was. Joseph had checked it at snack time: his name came next.
When the helper opened the door, Simran ran straight to the swing and sat down.
"That's mine!" Joseph's shout bounced off the walls. The younger kids at the craft table went quiet. He could feel his face heating up, and he was already sure of it: Simran had read the chart too. She just didn't care.
Simran pointed at the door. "It says me."
Joseph didn't look at the chart.

What was on the door of the community centre?
A chart that said whose turn it was on the swing.
How can you tell Joseph felt wronged when Simran sat on the swing?
His shout bounced off the walls and his face heated up; he felt angry and cheated, sure she had read the chart and ignored it.
What could Joseph do right now to stop this from growing into a fight?
He could walk over and read the chart with Simran or ask the helper, checking the facts before deciding she meant to take his turn.
How might Simran see Joseph's shout?
She may feel confused and a bit defensive, because she believes the chart says it is her turn.

Friday. Aadhya piled sand in the building's play area, patted it once, and ran off to the swings.
Saturday. Her father, Harish, sat on the edge of the sandpit with his tea. Aadhya began a castle. She pressed each wall flat with both hands, stuck a leaf flag on top, and dug a careful moat with a spoon. Every few minutes she looked up. 'Papa, are you looking?' 'I'm looking.'
Sunday. Aadhya pulled Harish by the finger to the sandpit before breakfast. 'Sit there,' she said, pointing. 'Watch me make it better.'

What did Aadhya use for a flag?
She used a leaf for a flag.
Why did Aadhya keep asking 'Papa, are you looking?'
Having Papa watch made her feel seen and proud, and that connection made her want to try harder.
What could Harish do to keep supporting her effort?
Keep sitting nearby and watching warmly, noticing what she makes without taking over.
How might Harish feel being pulled to the sandpit before breakfast?
He would likely feel amused and touched that his watching mattered so much to her.

Supervisor's note, customer insights team, end of quarter
I want to record a change in Nandini. A year ago she sat silently in our reviews and apologised for every question. This week she ran the onboarding for our new analyst, Arohi.
When Arohi asked what a retention curve was, Nandini said, "Honestly, I asked that exact question in my second week. Took me a month to really get it." Then she walked Arohi through one of her own old charts, including the mistake she had made on it.
Later, in the review, a director asked Nandini something she didn't know. She said, "I'm not sure; I'll check and come back by Friday," without any of the old panic.
Arohi told me at lunch that Nandini made her feel it was normal not to know yet. I'd like Nandini to be the buddy for the next two hires as well.

What did Arohi ask Nandini about?
What a retention curve was.
How does Nandini seem to feel when she doesn't know the director's answer?
She seems calm and secure, able to say she isn't sure without the old panic.
What does the supervisor plan next, and why is it wise?
Making Nandini the buddy for the next two hires, because helping newcomers strengthens her own belonging and helps them too.
What is it like for Arohi to learn from Nandini?
Arohi feels reassured and less alone, since Nandini admits her own early confusion and mistakes.
