Read this:

You're nervous about meeting that boy your mother found, beta? Let me, your Noor khala, tell you about the evening I met Harish.

Friends set it up. A dinner at their flat in Delhi, very casual, they said. I was twenty-five, working at the bank, and I had decided I was not moving cities for any man.

He was charming. He made me laugh twice before the soup. I liked his hands, and how he listened. My heart was doing silly things.

But I also asked him, straight out, where he saw himself in five years. Bombay, he said, for his work. My stomach sank a little. I asked if he wanted his wife to work. He said, "That's her choice." That helped.

I went home both excited and wary. That's what I want you to know: feeling both is not a bad sign. It means your heart and your head are both at the table.

Where did Noor khala meet Harish?
At a dinner at their friends' flat in Delhi.
How did Noor feel when Harish said he saw himself in Bombay?
Her stomach sank a little; she felt worried, since she had decided not to move cities, even while she was attracted to him.
What choice inside the story helped Noor judge the match wisely?
Asking Harish directly about the future and about work, so her excitement was balanced by practical answers.
How might Harish have felt when Noor asked such direct questions?
He may have been surprised, but perhaps impressed and relieved to talk honestly so early.

Read this:

The hostel mess committee met after dinner in the warden's office. Diwali night was the only item.
Asif, the mess secretary, was already standing. “DJ on the terrace, eight till two. Full volume. Best night of the year!”
The others cheered. “Asif bhai zindabad!”
Manoj sat at the end of the bench. Their physics exam was on the morning after Diwali. And the warden had said the terrace railing was loose. He glanced around. Everyone looked so happy.
“Anyone against?” Asif asked, grinning.
Manoj looked down.
“Passed!”
On Diwali night the warden stopped the music at ten because of the railing. Next morning, half the hostel dragged into the exam hall with red eyes.

Where did the committee meet?
They met in the warden's office after dinner.
What was Manoj feeling when Asif asked "Anyone against?"
He felt doubtful and worried about the exam and the loose railing, but too hesitant to spoil the cheering.
What went wrong, and what could have fixed it?
Everyone agreed too quickly with Asif; if Manoj had raised the exam and the railing, the plan could have been changed early.
How might the warden see the committee's plan?
The warden probably felt frustrated, having to stop the music for safety because the committee hadn't thought about the loose railing.

Read this:

On a grey Saturday in Rotterdam, Elif and her neighbour Nour sat on the back step sharing a bag of cherries. Elif made two piles. "Four for you, four for me," she said, counting each red stem. Nour pointed. "Yours has a big one." "Big is not more," Elif said slowly, frowning. "More is the counting." She counted both piles again, her finger bouncing. Four and four. Nour shrugged and swapped one big cherry for a small one anyway, and they both grinned.

How many cherries were in each pile?
There were four cherries in each pile.
What does Elif's slow frown suggest when Nour mentions the big cherry?
She seems to be working out the difference between size and number and wants to be sure before she answers.
How could an adult nearby build on Elif's idea?
They could ask, "Which pile has more cherries, and which pile is heavier?" so she can explore size and number as two different things.
How does Nour see fairness differently from Elif?
Nour judges by the size of the cherries while Elif judges by the count, so the swap lets both of them feel it is even. 🙂
A birthday party shopping list, three lines, in this order: balloons, cake, candles. One item per line.

Balloons
Cake
Candles

Read this:

I'm Irawati. I swept the front room every day and still there was dust in the corners and dirt lines on the floor. I was getting cross. Aaji watched me from her chair for a while. "Beti, come. Let me show you." She took the broom and held it low, pulling the dust in long strokes toward one corner, not flicking it around. Then she held the dustpan flat against the floor. "Slowly. Dust that flies goes back." I tried it, and the pile came together nicely. It took half the time, and my arms were not so tired.

How did Aaji hold the broom to pull the dust?
Aaji held the broom low, pulling the dust in long strokes toward one corner.
What might Irawati be feeling before asking Aaji for help?
Irawati was getting cross because the dust stayed even after daily sweeping, and was probably frustrated and tired.
What alternative approach could Irawati use, and why?
Irawati could watch a neighbour or an older cousin who sweeps well and copy each step. Learning by watching can show details that instructions miss.
How might Aaji see teaching Irawati to sweep?
Aaji watched from her chair and stepped in kindly, so Aaji probably feels glad to share a skill and happy to see Irawati improve.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asking a parent to show the right way [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tarun, twenty-six, had just become the youngest team lead at his Bengaluru start-up. On his first day, he did something unusual: he took his old friend Kiran for chai and said, "You're the one person who'll tell me when I'm being an idiot. Please keep doing it." Kiran laughed. "Easy." Three weeks later, Tarun pushed a deadline that meant the team would work through a weekend. Kiran caught him at the lift. "You're being an idiot. Half the team has family events." Tarun's pride flared. Then he remembered his own request. He asked the team directly what the weekend would cost them. It was a lot. He moved the deadline by four days and told the client himself. At the next review he named two juniors whose work had saved the project. Kiran raised his cup across the room.

By how many days did Tarun move the deadline?
He moved the deadline by four days.
What was Tarun feeling when Kiran called him an idiot at the lift?
Tarun felt a flare of wounded pride, then remembered his request and chose to listen.
Why was asking Kiran to keep telling him the truth a wise move?
Keeping a friend who will disagree helps Tarun notice when power starts making him careless about others.
How might the juniors feel when Tarun named them at the review?
The juniors likely felt proud and valued, seeing their lead share credit publicly.
Write the seven basic swaras of Indian music in order, all on one line.
Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni

Read this:

Counsellor's note, third session
Tushar and Lata arrived with a sheet of paper today, their own idea. After last month's text fight, which pulled in both their families, they wrote "our rules":
1. Emotional topics: call, or wait for the evening.
2. A short text gets a question, not a reaction.
3. Assume the other meant well.
They said they'd already used rule two twice. Lata described a curt message from Tushar and said she wrote "Rough day?" instead of "What's your problem?". Tushar laughed and said, "It was. Thank you."
The warmth between them was clearer today. Next session I will ask how the rules hold up during a busy week.
Harsha

What is rule three on Tushar and Lata's list?
Assume the other meant well.
What was Tushar feeling when he laughed and said "Thank you"?
He seemed relieved and grateful that Lata asked about his day instead of reacting.
Why is Harsha planning to ask about a busy week?
Because rules are easiest when life is calm; a busy week tests whether they read each other generously under stress.
How does Lata seem to experience the new rules?
Lata seems proud and more at ease, describing how asking "Rough day?" changed the outcome.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Agreed norms for hard topics [Response]

messages.content: My college fest is next month and I've been asked to lead the quiz event. I'm Sarah, by the way.
Nice to meet you, Sarah. Leading the quiz event is a real responsibility and a good compliment too, because someone trusts you with it. What do you need to plan first?
Questions, a venue and a few volunteers. I think I'll have six rounds.
Six rounds is a good length if each is short. Split the work, so one volunteer collects questions, another checks the venue, and others keep score. That leaves you free to run the event.
Should I make the last round the hardest?
Usually yes. A hard last round builds excitement and separates close teams. Just keep a couple of easier questions in it, so nobody feels left out before the finish.
Right. How many volunteers did I say I would need?
You said a few volunteers, Sarah, but not an exact number. With six rounds, a team of four or five would cover questions, scoring and the venue. Decide once you see how big the crowd will be.

Read this:

Raghav flicked rules away like dust. "Babies," he said to Chinmay, who had refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets. Omkar's stomach clenched. He had gone along the week before, laughing at the wrong moment because he feared being left out. This time he said quietly to Chinmay at the bike stand, "Can I say no with you?" Chinmay grinned. "Sure. Just say, not today, I've got homework. Keep it short." When Raghav sneered, Omkar used exactly those words, and Chinmay added, "Come for chai after school, though." Nobody lectured Raghav, and he shrugged. The next day Ma'am asked where Raghav had been. Omkar started to say, "He was sick," then stopped: Raghav had told them he had tried a stunt on a wall and hurt his wrist. Omkar told Raghav, "I'm not going to lie for you, but I care what happens to you. Show your wrist to the nurse." Raghav went. That afternoon Omkar told the class teacher what he knew, without mocking anyone.

What did Chinmay refuse to do?
Chinmay refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets.
How did Omkar's earlier going along differ from his later refusal, and what did Chinmay's example add?
Earlier Omkar laughed along because he feared being left out; later he refused with an ally and a short reply, and Chinmay stayed friendly without lecturing, which made saying no easier.
What was Omkar feeling when Raghav called Chinmay a baby?
His stomach clenched, so he felt afraid of being laughed at or left out.
What did Omkar do about Raghav's hurt wrist, and why was it wise?
He refused to lie for Raghav, urged him to see the nurse and told the class teacher, showing loyalty to Raghav's wellbeing rather than to the risky stunt.
Jason has a moray eel that eats 20 guppies a day and 5 betta fish who each eat 7 guppies a day. How many guppies per day does she need to buy?

First find the total number of guppies the betta fish need: 5 fish * 7 guppies/fish = 35 guppies
Then add the number of guppies the eel needs to find the total number needed: 35 guppies + 20 guppies = 55 guppies
The answer is 55.

Read this:

Daycare note, water play, Tuesday.
At stopping time my colleague sang, “All done, splashers!” Irawati kept splashing, laughing. Joseph watched her and splashed too.
I knelt and said quietly, “Joseph, hands out now,” my face calm, not smiling. Joseph looked at me for a long second, then held his hands up to be dried. Irawati stopped too.
Joseph reads faces before words. I'll keep a still face for safety moments and the sing-song for fun.

What did the colleague sing?
The colleague sang, "All done, splashers!"
What might Joseph have been feeling when he looked up for a long second?
Joseph was probably unsure and watchful, checking the carer's calm, unsmiling face to decide whether this was serious.
What plan does the note-writer make, and why does it make sense?
They plan to use a calm, still face for safety moments and the sing-song for fun, because Joseph follows faces and tone more than words.
How did Irawati's behaviour change during the scene?
At first Irawati kept splashing and laughing at the bright song, but after seeing Joseph stop, Irawati stopped too.

Read this:

Yamini, you asked about my favourite singer, so here goes. I’m Disha, and I was fifteen, and I’d played her album every night for two years. Last month a report said she had treated her staff badly for a long time and hidden it.
First I refused to read it. Then I read it and felt sick. I didn’t delete the songs, because a couple of them got me through exams. But I stopped posting her lyrics.
When my friends said, “People exaggerate,” I said, “The songs are still good, and what she did is still wrong.” Nobody answered. Holding both things feels strange, but pretending felt worse.

How old was Disha when the album played every night?
Disha was fifteen and had played the album every night for two years.
What was Disha feeling after reading the report?
Disha felt sick and deeply disappointed after reading it, which shows how much the singer had meant to Disha.
What choice did Disha make about the songs, and why did it work?
Disha kept the songs but stopped posting the lyrics. That kept what was good in the music without excusing what the singer did.
What might Disha's friends who said people exaggerate have been feeling?
They may have been trying to protect their own admiration, or avoiding the discomfort of the report. Their silence after Disha's answer suggests they had no ready reply.
Why does blowing across the top of an empty bottle make a humming sound?

The hum comes from the air inside the bottle. Because the stream of air across the opening makes the air in the bottle vibrate, and the size of the bottle decides which note is loudest, we hear a steady tone.

Read this:

"Saurabh Chacha, why did the lights go off in the whole village?"
"Power cut, Yogesh. Come up to the roof. Bring the mat."
"It's so dark. I can't see anything."
"Wait. Lie down. Look up."
"...Chacha."

Nine hundred tickets were sold to a concert. Three-fourths of those who bought the ticket came before the start of the concert. Five-ninths of the remaining came few minutes after the first song. Eighty people arrived during the middle part of the concert while the rest did not go. How many of those who bought the tickets did not go?

900 x 3/4 = 675 people came before the start of the concert.
900 - 675 = 225 people did not come before the start of the concert.
225 x 5/9 = 125 people came few minutes after the first song.
So, 125 + 80 = 205 people came to the concert that was not able to be at the start of the concert.
Therefore, 225 - 205 = 20 people did not go to the concert.
The answer is 20.

Chris's internet bill is $45 per month for 100 GB and $0.25 for every 1 GB over. His bill for this month is $65. How many GB over was Chris charged for on this bill?

Let G stand for the number of GB billed, so the total bill is $0.25G + $45 flat rate charge = $65 total bill.
Now we will solve for G. $0.25G + $45 flat rate - $45 = $65 -$45. This simplifies to $0.25G = $20
$0.25G/$0.25 = $20/$0.25
G = 80 GB were charged on this bill.
The answer is 80.

messages.content: Nicole has 4 fish tanks. The first two tanks need 8 gallons of water each and the other two need 2 fewer gallons of water each than the first two tanks. If Nicole needs to change the water of the aquarium every week, how many gallons of water will she need in four weeks?

The first two tanks need 8 x 2 = 16 gallons of water.
The other two tanks need 8 - 2 = 6 gallons of water each.
So, the two other tanks need 6 x 2 = 12 gallons of water.
Nicole needs 16 + 12 = 28 gallons of water every week for her four tanks.
Therefore, she needs a total of 28 x 4 = 112 gallons of water in four weeks.
The answer is 112.

Charles is wondering how much chocolate milk he can make with all the supplies he finds in the fridge. He is going to keep drinking 8-ounce glasses until he uses up all the ingredients. Each glass must contain 6.5 ounces of milk and 1.5 ounces of chocolate syrup. If he has 130 ounces of milk and 60 ounces of chocolate syrup, how many total ounces ounce of chocolate milk will he drink?

He has enough milk for 20 glasses of chocolate milk because 130 / 6.5 = 20
He has enough syrup for 40 glasses of chocolate milk because 60 / 1.5 = 40
He can make 20 glasses of chocolate milk because 20 < 40
He will drink 160 ounces of chocolate milk because 20 x 8 = 160
The answer is 160.

I'm Usha, and I share a cubicle wall with Jatin at the audit firm. In January he filed a report through the ethics portal about a client's inventory numbers. I only know because he told me he had, not what it said.

In February he did something more careful. He wrote to the ethics office: 'Report submitted 12 January, portal status unchanged. Please confirm receipt and next steps.' He printed it and put it in a folder. When that got no answer either, he booked a Saturday consultation with a lawyer and came back with notes on the outside regulator and what they would need.
Then he sent one more letter to the ethics office, saying he was considering that route. The status changed to 'Under review' the next week.
I don't know how he felt. He just looked like someone who had stopped waiting.

'Submitted'.

It gave the ethics office a clear chance to respond and created a record showing the proper channel was tried first.

Sort these into proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers: 3/5, 8/5, 5/5, 2 1/5, 4/9, 9/4.

Answer: Proper: 3/5, 4/9. Improper: 8/5, 5/5, 9/4. Mixed: 2 1/5.

Look at the top and bottom numbers. If the top is SMALLER, the fraction is less than 1 whole: proper. If the top is the SAME or BIGGER, it is 1 whole or more: improper. 5/5 is improper even though it is exactly 1, because 5 fifths make a whole. A mixed number has a whole number in front. A common mistake is to call 5/5 proper; ask "Is it less than 1?"

Ken buys gummy vitamins.  They are usually $15.00 per bottle at his grocery store, but they are currently 20% off.  On top of that, he has 3 $2.00 coupons.  How much will 3 bottles cost?

The vitamins are $15.00 a bottle and are currently 20% off so that's 15*.20 = $3.00 off
The vitamins are $15.00 and they are $3.00 off so they are now 15.00-3 = $12.00
He has 3 $2.00 coupons so that's 3*2 = $6.00 in coupons
He buys 3 bottles at $12.00 each so that's 3*12 = $36.00
He has $6.00 in coupons so his vitamins will now costs 36-6 = $30.00
The answer is 30.

Casey is pumping water out of her well. She can pump 3 gallons a minute. She has 4 rows of 15 corn plants each, and each plant needs half a gallon of water. She also has 10 pigs, which each need 4 gallons of water, and 20 ducks that each need a quarter of a gallon of water. How many minutes does Casey need to spend pumping water?

First find how many corn plants there are: 15 plants/row * 4 rows = 60 plants
Then find how many gallons of water of the corn needs: 60 plants * 1/2 gallon/plant = 30 gallons
Then find how many gallons of water the pigs need: 10 pigs * 4 gallons/pig = 40 gallons
Then find how many gallons of water the ducks need: 20 ducks * 1/4 gallon/duck = 5 gallons
Now add up all three quantities of water to find the total water needed: 5 gallons + 40 gallons + 30 gallons = 75 gallons
Now divide the total water needed by Casey's pumping rate to find how long she spends pumping: 75 gallons / 3 gallons/minute = 25 minutes
The answer is 25.

Last winter our school kabaddi team lost the district final by one point. I'm Sudha, and I was the captain. I cried on the bus home, and I didn't want to go to practice for a week. But then Akash, our coach, said, 'One point means we were close, not bad.' So I went back. I did early morning runs, even when it was foggy. This year we reached the final again and won. I still remember losing, but now I think it's why I kept going.

By how many points did the team lose the district final?
They lost by one point.
What made Sudha feel ready to return to practice?
Coach Akash's words helped Sudha see the loss as close, not a failure, which gave Sudha hope.
What could other players learn from Sudha's story?
They can see that steady effort after a loss, like early runs, can lead to success later.
How might Akash feel about the team's win this year?
Akash would probably feel proud and happy that those words of encouragement helped the team come back.

"Thomas, why are you glaring at Ruchika?"
"Santosh, you haven't heard? Voice note in the class group. Her voice, calling the new girl names. Horrible stuff."
"Play it."
"...See? That's literally her voice. The way she says 'yaar' and everything."
"Hmm. It says Friday evening. Ruchika was at the district match all Friday, till nine."
"So she recorded it on the bus."
"No crowd, no bus noise. And listen, she never pauses to breathe. Voices can be made now, Thomas. You just need clips of someone talking."
"But it sounds exactly like her."
"That's the point. Sounding like her isn't proof it's her."
Thomas stared at his phone for a long moment. "I already replied 'disgusting' to it."
"Delete that. Then let's show Kurian ma'am."
Mrs Kurian listened twice, took screenshots and said, "Thank you both. Nobody forwards this. I'm speaking to the counsellor and Ruchika's parents today."

Where was Ruchika all Friday, according to Santosh?
Santosh says Ruchika was at the district match all Friday, till nine.
Why was Thomas so sure the voice note was real?
Thomas trusted his ears; the voice, and even the way it said "yaar", sounded exactly like Ruchika, so he felt it had to be her.
Which steps did Thomas and Santosh take once they doubted the note?
Thomas deleted the angry reply, and they took the voice note to Mrs Kurian instead of forwarding it.
What is it like for Ruchika while the voice note spreads?
Ruchika is glared at and judged for words she may never have said, before anyone checks where she was that evening.

Dear Kiran,

You asked how I handle Lalremsiami aunty downstairs, who talks for an hour every time I pass her door. I love her, but I also have work.

Here's what I tried yesterday. She was telling me about her nephew's wedding, the caterer, the band, the cousin who fell into the flowers. When she took a breath, I said, "So the wedding was beautiful, and the band was late, and your cousin survived the flowers! Thank you for telling me, aunty. I have to get to the office now, but I want to hear the photos part on Sunday."

She laughed and patted my arm. "Go, go, beta." No hurt feelings at all.

Summarise, thank, then name what you have to do. It works.

Chaitanya

What did the cousin fall into at the wedding?
Into the flowers.
What was Chaitanya feeling while Lalremsiami aunty talked?
Chaitanya felt fond of her but a little anxious about getting to work on time.
Which steps made Chaitanya's ending kind and clear?
Summarising her story, thanking her, naming the need to go to the office and promising to hear more on Sunday.
How did Lalremsiami aunty respond to the ending?
She laughed and patted Chaitanya's arm, with no hurt feelings.

Minakshi's parents had been hinting for months: 'Rent is money down the drain. Buy a flat.' At twenty-six, with a steady job in Mangaluru, she half believed them. One Saturday she and her elder sister Bhavna sat at the dining table with a notebook and a laptop. They compared: the down payment would empty her savings; the loan instalment would be almost double her rent; and she might move cities for work in two years. Bhavna asked, 'And if you lose your job? Do you have health cover beyond the office one? Have you started any retirement saving?' Minakshi hadn't. She felt a bit foolish. They booked a session with a fee-only financial planner their cousin trusted, rather than the salesman who kept calling. What Minakshi took away was simple: decide after asking the right questions, not because of a family slogan.

Whom did Minakshi and Bhavna book a session with?
A fee-only financial planner their cousin trusted.
Why did Minakshi feel a bit foolish?
She realised she had no health cover beyond her office one and no retirement saving, basics she had not considered before a big purchase.
What helped Minakshi approach the rent-or-buy question well?
Comparing the down payment, instalment and likely moves, checking insurance and retirement saving, and consulting a qualified planner instead of a salesman.
How might Minakshi's parents see her not buying right away?
They might worry she is wasting money on rent, since they believe buying is always better.

In the Izmir school library, the media studies teacher, Ms Kaya, put a post on the screen: a photo of a crowded bus with the caption 'THEY are taking over YOUR city. Share if you're angry!'
'Before you react,' Ms Kaya said, 'find three tricks.'
Zeynep, sixteen, felt her pulse tick up, and then made herself look. Capital letters. 'They' with no name. An order to share, no link to a source. Pablo, next to her, spotted a fourth: the photo was from another country, five years old.
That evening Zeynep went through her own feed. The more she'd clicked on angry posts, she realised, the more it had shown her. She muted six accounts that only ever posted outrage and followed two news sites that showed different sides of the same story.
On Friday a furious video popped up. Zeynep caught herself mid-thumb. Built to make me mad, she thought, and checked the source first.

Where was the photo of the crowded bus actually from?
The photo was from another country, five years old.
How did Zeynep feel when she first saw the post, and what did she do with that feeling?
She felt her pulse tick up with anger, then made herself slow down and look for the tricks.
What skill did Zeynep build, and why is it useful?
She learned to notice when a post is designed to anger before reacting, and to mute rage accounts and follow varied sources, so her feed stops steering her feelings.
How might Pablo's discovery about the photo change how their classmates see such posts?
It may make them more careful, realising how easily an old photo can be used to make them angry.

Thursday, 10:40 pm. The whole draft is done, which I did not think would happen today. Usually I rewrite my first paragraph nine times and never see page two. This morning I told myself: introduction gets one hour, that's it, even if it's ugly. A draft that exists beats a perfect paragraph, and I can polish later. I put the phone timer next to the laptop. At forty minutes I hated my second sentence but left it. When the alarm went I stopped mid-thought, typed "fix opening line later" in brackets, and started the methods section. The middle went easily once I quit polishing. Sahil asked at dinner if I was okay, because I was smiling at a spreadsheet. Tomorrow I read it all again. Tonight, it exists.

Ojas

How long did Ojas allow for the introduction?
Ojas said the introduction gets one hour.
What was Ojas feeling while smiling at a spreadsheet?
Ojas felt relieved and pleased at having got the whole draft done in one day.
What could Ojas do if one hour is still not enough for a hard section?
Ojas could set a second short box after a break, or mark the rough parts and come back, so the draft still keeps moving.
How might Sahil have seen Ojas's mood at dinner?
Sahil may have been surprised and a bit amused, since smiling at a spreadsheet is unusual.

When I became hostel secretary in second year, I honestly thought I was the same person. I'm Disha. But looking back, I can see the slide. I stopped queueing for the washing machine; I had "duties." I let my friends stay past curfew and wrote up juniors who did the same. When Dilnaz, a first-year, came to me because her roommate's music kept her awake before exams, I told her to "adjust." I remember thinking she was being dramatic. Later I found out she'd been crying most nights. The worst part was that I didn't notice any of it at the time. I just felt busy and important. It was only when my old friend said, "You used to ask people how they were," that I felt the floor tilt.

What did Disha tell Dilnaz to do?
Disha told her to "adjust."
How did Disha feel when the old friend spoke up?
Disha felt shaken and ashamed, as if the floor tilted, realising how much had changed.
What could have kept Disha from drifting?
Keeping the same rules for Disha and friends as for juniors, and regularly asking juniors how they were, might have kept her empathy.
How might Dilnaz have experienced being told to adjust?
Dilnaz probably felt dismissed and alone, which is why she was crying most nights.

In Nairobi, Wanjiru, fifteen, had to be home by six-thirty, before dark. Her brother Kaito, sixteen, came home at nine from football, sometimes later. "It's for your safety," Mum said. Wanjiru stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "So you trust him and not me?" Mum's face tightened. "It's not about trust. The road from the matatu stop is dark." "It's dark for Kaito too!" Kaito looked up from his phone. "She's got a point."
That Sunday they sat together at the table. Mum explained what actually worried her: the unlit road, the men who hung around the stage at night. Wanjiru listened. Then she suggested both of them share their location, both come home by seven-thirty on school nights, and whoever is later gets picked up by Dad. Mum thought, then nodded. Wanjiru felt heard for the first time. Kaito groaned about the new curfew, then laughed.

What time did Wanjiru have to be home?
By six-thirty, before dark.
How did Wanjiru feel about the different curfews?
She felt distrusted and resentful, asking whether Mum trusted Kaito and not her.
What made the new rule fairer?
They talked openly about the real risks, then set the same curfew, location sharing and a pickup plan for both children.
How might Mum have felt when Wanjiru asked about trust?
Mum probably felt hurt and defensive, because she saw the rule as protection, not distrust.

The power went out at eight, and the rain meant neither of them could go anywhere. Mridul and Sumit sat on the floor of their one-room flat with a single candle and nine per cent battery between their two phones. For once there was no screen to hide in and no door to storm through. After a long quiet, Sumit said, "Can I say something without it being a fight?" Mridul nodded. "When I push you for answers, you go quiet. And when you go quiet, I push harder." Mridul laughed softly. "And then I go even quieter. It's like a machine." "So maybe the machine's the problem. Not you." "Not you either." The candle flickered. Outside, the rain kept on, and for the first time in weeks they were on the same side.

How much phone battery did they have between them?
They had nine per cent battery between their two phones.
What does Mridul's soft laugh suggest?
It suggests relief and recognition; Mridul sees the pattern too and no longer feels attacked. 🙂
Why did the power cut help them see the loop?
With no screen to hide in and nowhere to storm off, they had a calm moment to name the pattern together instead of blaming.
What changes when Sumit calls the machine the problem?
Neither has to be the villain; they stand on the same side against the cycle, which makes the next step possible.

Deepa, you want to know about jealousy at work? Let your Ira Maasi confess one. At twenty-six I was a team lead, and I had trained Naveen from his first week: how to write specs, how to handle angry clients. Two years later he won the company's innovation award, the one I had wanted for myself for years. When they called his name, I clapped, and something small and sour turned in my chest. For a whole evening I told myself he had been lucky. Then I remembered his first spec, covered in my red pen, and the night he stayed late to fix it without complaint. The next morning I went to his desk and said, "Your win is partly my work too, and I'm proud of both of us." He grinned and said, "Mostly yours." That's when I learned that the best thing a mentor can feel is less needed.

What award did Naveen win?
The company's innovation award.
What was Ira feeling when Naveen's name was called?
She felt a small, sour pang of jealousy and hurt while clapping, having wanted that award for years.
What turning point did Ira reach the next morning?
She chose pride over rivalry, going to Naveen's desk to say his win was partly her work and that she was proud of both of them.
How might Naveen have felt when Ira came to his desk?
Naveen was likely touched and grateful, grinning and giving her credit with 'Mostly yours.'

Grayson has 100 questions on a test. He answers some of the questions for 2 hours, taking two minutes for each answer, then realizes he doesn't know the rest of the questions. How many questions does Grayson leave unanswered when he submits his test?

Each hour contains 60 minutes, so after 2 hours he took 2*60 = 120 minutes.
If each question takes two minutes, then he answered 120/2 = 60 questions.
Unanswered questions is 100-60 = 40 questions
The answer is 40.

On the first day of Class 5, a new boy called Hemant came in late, dropped his bag loudly and laughed when the teacher said his name wrong. I'm Vaibhav, and I decided right then that he was a show-off. For the next month, whatever Hemant did, I saw the show-off. When he gave me half his samosa after I forgot my lunch, I thought it was a trick. Then his mother came to school on Parents' Day, and I heard her say they had moved three times in two years. Hemant had been nervous that first morning. The laugh was nerves. I looked at everything again. He wasn't a show-off. He was just kind, and a bit loud.

Why did Vaibhav change his mind about Hemant?
He heard Hemant's mother say they had moved three times in two years, and he realised the laugh on the first day was nerves. Looking again, he saw a kind, slightly loud boy, not a show-off.

Sahil: same as always. Megha's dad asked why we don't have a fixed deposit yet. then a 20 min talk about how we waste money

"thank you, we've got a plan", and then ask about his garden.

It was the first rainy week of the new term at a school in Hyderabad. Every time Miss Rukhsana asked a question, Jatin shouted the answer before anyone else could. "Seven! Blue! Elephant!" Asif, beside him, kept his hand up and sighed. On Thursday Miss Rukhsana gave each child a paper leaf. "Hold up your leaf when you know." Jatin's leaf shot up. He bounced in his seat, lips pressed shut. "Jatin?" "Monsoon!" he said, and beamed. Asif got the next turn and grinned at him.

What did Miss Rukhsana give each child on Thursday?
She gave each child a paper leaf.
What does Jatin bouncing with his lips pressed shut suggest?
It suggests he was excited and eager to answer but trying hard to wait for his turn.
What worked in Miss Rukhsana's approach, and why?
The paper leaf gave Jatin something to do with his eagerness, so he could wait and still show he knew.
What is it like for Asif when Jatin keeps shouting answers?
Asif feels frustrated and left out, since a raised hand never gets a turn.

Tanuja,
I've been meaning to write since the presentation on Friday.
When Professor Das praised the survey design, I said, "Thank you, we worked hard on that." Everyone looked at me, and I kept going as if it was mine. It wasn't. You designed the survey and ran the pilot. I skipped two of our meetings and mostly formatted slides.
I told myself it didn't matter who said thank you. It did. I saw your face.
I've emailed Professor Das to say the survey was your work, and I've copied you in. For the final report, I'll write the literature review and the appendix, the parts I left to you, and send drafts by Wednesday so you can check them.
I'm sorry. I relied on you to cover for me and then took the credit. I won't do that again.
Kunal

What did Professor Das praise?
The survey design.
How does Kunal feel about the presentation?
Ashamed and guilty, having accepted credit after doing little.
What does Kunal do to make it right?
Emails Professor Das to credit Tanuja, and takes on the literature review and appendix with drafts by Wednesday.
How might Tanuja have felt at the presentation?
Hurt and overlooked, watching Kunal accept praise for Tanuja's work.

Seema, you're starting your first job, so let me tell you about Pallavi, my classmate from nursing college in Madurai, years ago. I'm your Periamma; I was there. Our case studies were due every month on the last Friday. Pallavi always wrote her own date in the corner of her notebook: the Friday before. "The college's date is for the college," she'd say. "Mine is for me." One month, a flood closed the college hostel for four days right before the deadline. Half of us lost our notes and scrambled. Pallavi had a rough draft done already. She spent those days polishing it at her aunt's house and got the highest mark.

What date did Pallavi write in the corner of her notebook?
She wrote the Friday before the college's deadline.
How might Pallavi have felt when the flood closed the hostel?
She was likely calm and secure, knowing her rough draft was already done while others scrambled.
Which choice in the story made the difference for Pallavi?
Setting her own deadline a week early, so when the flood struck she only had to polish, not start.
How did the flood affect the other students in the story?
Half of the class lost their notes and had to scramble, stressed, right before the deadline.

"Baljeet, Pankaj is crying. What happened?"

"He knocked my tower."

"Did he mean to?"

"I don't know."

"Let's ask him. Pankaj, did you mean to?"

Pankaj shook his head. "My foot slipped."

"Oh. How do you think Pankaj feels now?"

Baljeet looked. "Sad. Because I shouted."

"When I see a friend crying, I say, 'Are you okay?' Want to try?"

Baljeet mumbled, "Are you okay?"

Pankaj nodded. The rain outside kept falling, and they built a new tower together.

Why did Pankaj knock the tower?
His foot slipped.

Baljeet felt a bit sorry, realising Pankaj was sad because of the shouting.
What did the adult model to help Baljeet?
The adult showed how to ask a friend "Are you okay?", modelling how to notice others' feelings.
How might Pankaj feel when Baljeet asks if he's okay?

Quick check on ecstasy: what does the word mean?

Ecstasy is a feeling of very great happiness. It is a noun.
Example: The fans shouted in ecstasy when the last goal went in.

The NSS camp in a village near Kolar had one job for the week: map every household's water source. Maria, the group coordinator, needed a team lead. Ramesh stood up in the panchayat hall and spoke to the sarpanch like a politician, full of big words about development. "He's our man," Maria wrote in her notebook on the spot. Pallavi, who had quietly asked for a village map on the first day, was given the job of carrying water bottles. By Wednesday Ramesh had given two more speeches and visited nine houses. Pallavi, on her own evening walks, had marked all eighty-four wells and taps on the map in blue ink. When the professor asked for the survey, it was Pallavi's map that Maria handed over, red-faced.

How many wells and taps did Pallavi mark?
Eighty-four, in blue ink.
Why was Maria red-faced handing over Pallavi's map?
She felt embarrassed, because she had picked Ramesh for his confident speeches and given Pallavi, who did the real work, the water bottles.
What went wrong in choosing the lead, and what could fix it next time?
Maria chose by speaking style; next time she could give a small task first and see who plans and finishes it, as Pallavi did with the map.
How might Pallavi feel about being handed the water bottles?
Pallavi may have felt overlooked and a little hurt, yet she kept going and quietly finished the survey anyway.

The first three times I tried to start running, I lasted four days each. I'm Arohi, second-year BSc, and my plan was always big: five kilometres, six a.m., every day. By day four I'd wake up, think about the whole five kilometres and roll over.
This time my roommate Simran gave me two rules. One: put the running shoes next to the bed, socks inside, so my feet land on them. Two: the target is ten minutes. Not five kilometres. Ten minutes, even if I walk half of it.
It felt almost too easy. Some mornings I did exactly ten minutes and came back. Some mornings I kept going for twenty because I was already out.
It has been five weeks now. The shoes are still by the bed, a bit muddy. I don't argue with myself any more. Feet down, shoes on, out.

Where did Arohi put the running shoes?
Arohi put them next to the bed, with socks inside.
How does Arohi feel about running now compared with before?
Arohi feels calmer and more confident, no longer arguing each morning, whereas the big old plan made Arohi want to roll over.
Why did Simran's two rules help the habit survive?
The shoes by the bed removed effort from starting, and a ten-minute target made each morning easy to begin, so the habit lasted past the first weeks.
How might Simran feel seeing the muddy shoes still by the bed after five weeks?
Simran would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that the simple rules worked where Arohi's big plans had failed.
It was a three hours journey by train.

It was a three-hour journey by train.
Why: before a noun, "three-hour" takes a hyphen and singular "hour".

I'm Himani, and I share a flat in Pune with Pallavi. Last Sunday she was choosing our internet plan on her laptop while I made tea. I heard her read them out. 'Plan A, 40 Mbps, six hundred a month. Plan B, 100 Mbps, twelve hundred, but only on a two-year lock-in. Plan C, 150 Mbps, twelve-fifty, no lock-in, free router.' She said, 'C, obviously. B is terrible.' Then she went quiet for a long time. I don't know exactly what she was thinking. But she opened a notebook and wrote two lines: 'Two people. Video calls, one movie a week.' Then she covered B with her hand and said, 'If this one wasn't here, would C still look amazing?' She looked at A for a while. In the end she chose A and set a reminder to check the speed after a month. I would have clicked C in two seconds.

What did Pallavi write in her notebook?
She wrote two lines: 'Two people. Video calls, one movie a week.'
What does Pallavi's long quiet suggest about her after saying 'C, obviously'?
It suggests she started to doubt her first reaction and wondered whether plan B was making C look better than it was.
What did Pallavi do before choosing, and why was it wise?
She covered plan B and compared the rest against their real needs, so the poor option stopped steering her toward the pricier plan.
How might Himani's own habits change after watching Pallavi?
Himani admits to clicking C in two seconds usually, so Himani might start pausing to check real needs too.

Two days before the Christmas plant sale, a hailstorm shredded half of Elizabeth's poinsettias in the greenhouse at her small nursery near Shillong. Her assistant, Aparna, was close to tears. "Maybe it's bad luck from moving the pots last week." Elizabeth sat on an upturned crate and took out a notebook. "Let's split it. What did we control? The greenhouse roof, the watering, the prices, the stall. What didn't we control? The hail." She wrote two columns. The roof panels had been old; she would replace those this month. The rest was weather. "No bad luck from pots," she said gently. "And no blaming ourselves for the sky." They spent the next day potting up the surviving plants and making a sign: HAIL SURVIVORS, EXTRA TOUGH. They sold out by noon.

- A hailstorm destroyed half of Elizabeth's poinsettias just before the plant sale.
- Elizabeth separated what she could control, such as the old roof, from the weather she could not, and decided to replace the roof panels.
- They potted the surviving plants, made a sign calling them hail survivors, and sold out by noon.

Sit, Trisha, before your father pays anyone a rupee. Your Shalini Bua has a story about that. When I was seventeen and heading to college in Nagpur, Papa and I lined up one hostel and two paying-guest rooms. We read what earlier residents had written, but I also phoned three seniors and asked plain things: how long is the commute, is the food edible, is it safe to walk back after evening class? Then Papa took a day off from his shop and we saw all three in person before anyone handed over a deposit. The cheapest room had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight. I picked the hostel near the bus stop. It cost a little more, but I slept easily there for three years.

What was wrong with the cheapest room?
It had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight.
Why did Shalini phone seniors and ask such plain questions?
She was cautious and wanted honest answers about the commute, the food and safety before any money changed hands.
What could someone do if they cannot visit the places in person?
They could take a video tour with a parent and talk to current residents, since that lets them see the place and hear honest experiences before paying.
How might Papa have seen the extra visits?
Papa may have found them tiring, but Papa probably felt reassured to see the places in person, since Shalini's safety and the deposit were both at stake.

messages.content:
Read this:

Chandrika, you asked why I stopped sharing those forwards in the family group. Sachin here. Last month a message came saying a common kitchen spice would cure a serious illness, and "doctors don't want you to know". It had capital letters and told everyone to forward it in an hour. My aunt was about to share it and I felt my stomach knot. I looked at who sent it: no name, no source. I asked myself, why the rush? Then I called our family doctor's clinic. They said not to rely on messages like that and to check with the doctor if worried. I told the group kindly, and my aunt said thanks. Pressure was the giveaway.

What did the message tell people to do within an hour?
It told people to forward it in an hour.
What was Sachin feeling when the aunt was about to share the message?
Sachin felt worried, shown by the knotted stomach, and asked why the rush. The urgency and the missing source were the warning.
What could Sachin do if someone in the group is upset by a health claim?
Encourage them to check with their own doctor or a trusted source, and avoid forwarding until they've checked.
How might the aunt have felt when Sachin spoke up?
The aunt was about to share it, so may have felt a bit embarrassed, but she said thanks, which suggests she took it kindly.
My friend said she is "under the weather". What does that mean?

"Under the weather" means feeling a little unwell or tired, not seriously ill.
Example: Nikhil felt under the weather, so he stayed home and rested.

On Sunday Suraj, two, tired after a long visit, bit his cousin's arm when she took his ball. Naveen stepped in and lifted him away. "No biting. You're tired and cross." On Tuesday Suraj grabbed a book and shoved his friend, and Naveen said, "Stomp, don't push," and stomped himself until Suraj copied. The next Saturday, a toy was taken, Suraj's face crumpled, and he stomped hard, shouting "Mine!" instead of biting.

What did Naveen suggest Suraj do instead of pushing?
He said, "Stomp, don't push," and stomped himself until Suraj copied.
What might Suraj have felt when he bit his cousin, and what else could explain it?
He probably felt a strong wave of anger or tiredness with no words for it. It may not have been meant to hurt, only to stop the loss of his ball.
What can an adult do when a toddler bites or hits?
Step in to keep everyone safe, name the feeling in a few words, and show a safer action to try.
How might the cousin have felt after the bite?
She may have been hurt and upset, so she needs care too.

I was on the college fest decoration team with Sachin and Vikas. I'll tell you what I saw, though I can't say what Sachin was thinking.
Vikas and Sachin had been friends since school. Every evening the rest of us painted banners while Vikas was “getting supplies,” which meant chai with his girlfriend. Sachin would say, “He's coming, yaar,” and quietly paint Vikas's banner too.
None of us said anything. Vikas was fun, and we didn't want to hurt Sachin's friendship either.
By the second week, the atmosphere changed. People stopped sharing snacks. Two girls quit. When Sachin asked for help with the stage, nobody offered.
On fest day, the banners were up. But I noticed the team never went out together again.

What did Vikas say he was doing every evening?
He said he was "getting supplies".
What might Sachin have been feeling as he painted Vikas's banner too?
Sachin may have felt torn and protective, loyal to a friend but probably tired and uneasy about the unfairness.
What could the team have done to deal with Vikas fairly?
One of them, maybe Sachin, could have spoken to Vikas privately and early, so the problem didn't sour the whole team.
How did the silence affect the rest of the team?
Trust wore down: people stopped sharing snacks, two quit, and nobody offered Sachin help.

Rain lashed the bus stop outside the school, and the last bus was late. Forty students crammed under the tin roof. Two older boys had Pankaj pinned against the pole, flicking water at him and snatching his umbrella.
Jomon's heart thumped. He couldn't push through the crowd, and fighting would be stupid. He did the easiest thing first. “Pankaj! Your mother's on the phone for you!” he shouted, holding up his own phone.
The boys hesitated. Pankaj slipped free and squeezed next to Jomon.
Then Jomon called the school security desk. “There's trouble at the bus stop, can someone come?” The guard came with an umbrella in three minutes and stood with them till the bus arrived.

How many students were under the tin roof?
Forty students crammed under the tin roof.
What was Jomon feeling as he watched?
His heart thumped, so he felt nervous and tense, but he was determined to help safely.
Why was Jomon's pretend phone call a smart choice?
It interrupted the boys without a fight and gave Pankaj a chance to slip free, and calling security then brought an adult.
How might Pankaj have felt standing next to Jomon?
He likely felt relieved and safer, with someone beside him until the guard came.
Two ribbons are both 7 blocks long. What can you say?

Answer: They are the same length.

Equal numbers of the same unit mean equal length.
The kids upstairs bounce a ball in the evenings. My baby sleeps then.
That is frustrating when you are trying to keep a baby asleep. Would you feel comfortable talking to the parents? A calm, friendly word often helps.
I do not even know their names.
You could introduce yourself at the building entrance, and ask their names. Once you have said hello, mention that your baby sleeps in the evening and ask if the ball games could be earlier.
Okay. I met the mother today. Her name is Ruby.
That is a good first step. Since you now know Ruby's name, you could knock on her door in a day or two, and ask kindly about the ball games in the evening.
Good. What was her name again?
Her name is Ruby. When you speak to her, begin with a friendly hello, then explain that your baby sleeps in the evening and ask if the kids could play with the ball earlier.

"Bhaiya, I got twelve out of twenty-five."
Santosh looked up from his phone. "You? You did the whole practice book with me on Sunday."
"I know." Sachin kicked the table leg with his slipper. "Before the test, Varsha said free-seat kids are always weak at maths. Everyone laughed. Then Sir gave out the papers and my stomach went into a knot."
"And?"
"I kept thinking, don't be the weak one, don't be the weak one. I read question four three times and my head was just full. Like the fan was inside it."
Santosh put the phone down. "So you knew the sums, but the worry took up the space."
"I did know them."
"Then let's do question four now. Nobody watching."

What did Varsha say before the test?
Varsha said free-seat kids are always weak at maths.
Why did Sachin's head feel full during question four?
He was so busy worrying about being the weak one that the fear filled the space he needed for the sum.
What does Santosh choose to do at the end, and why might it help?
He suggests doing question four at home with nobody watching, which can show Sachin he solves it fine without the label hanging over him.
How might Varsha's remark look from Varsha's side compared with how it felt to Sachin?
Varsha may have thought it was just a joke, but for Sachin it became a weight he carried into the test.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Kunal, and my flatmate Divyansh confused me for a long time.
Every morning he lit a small diya in front of a picture of Ganesha and said, "Whatever is written will happen." I grew up hearing that line from my grandmother too, and I'd always taken it to mean: so why try?
But Divyansh was preparing for the civil services, and he tried harder than anyone I knew. Up at five, newspaper notes, mock tests every Sunday. When I asked how that fitted with "whatever is written," he shrugged. "I do my karma. The result isn't mine to hold. That's what lets me sleep."
I watched him after a bad mock test. He was disappointed, but he didn't collapse. He prayed, and then he took out the answer key and marked every mistake.
I realised I'd been using fate as an excuse. He was using it as a kind of peace.

What did Divyansh do every Sunday?
He took mock tests every Sunday.
How did Kunal feel watching Divyansh after the bad mock test?
Kunal felt surprised and a little humbled, realising that fate had been an excuse for Kunal while for Divyansh it was a source of peace.
What could Kunal take from Divyansh's approach?
Kunal could hold on to faith in a larger plan while still doing daily work, like Divyansh marking every mistake after a bad test.
How does Divyansh seem to see the link between fate and effort?
Divyansh sees doing his karma as his job and the result as not his to hold, which lets him work hard and still sleep calmly.

At the research office on the third floor, Sonali's manager Alka had said, "The annual report, just a week, right?" Sonali had nodded out of habit. That evening she stayed back and sat with a blank page. "A week for what, exactly?" she muttered. She listed each section: summary, two days; data tables, three days, because the regional numbers always come in late; case studies, two days; charts, one day; review and edits, two days. She added it up and stared. Ten working days. Nearly two weeks, not one. She felt a small jolt of panic, then calm. "Better to know now than on Friday." The next morning she walked into Alka's cabin with the list. Alka read it and said, "Okay. Let's move the deadline."

How many working days did Sonali's list add up to?
Ten working days.
What was Sonali feeling when she saw the total?
She felt a small jolt of panic, then calm, glad to know early.
What else could Sonali do to keep the report on track?
Ask the regional teams early for their numbers, since late data was the slowest part.
How does Alka see Sonali's list?
Alka takes it well and moves the deadline, likely grateful to hear it early and with reasons.

Subject: Quick check after today's meeting

Dear Rafiq,
While I was presenting the pricing plan today, I noticed you paused, wrote something down and raised your eyebrows at slide four. I found myself guessing: interested? doubtful? I realised I couldn't tell from a pause, and I didn't want to assume. Could you tell me what you were thinking? If you have doubts about slide four, I'd like to hear them, and if the eyebrow was about something else entirely, that's useful to know too. I'm free after 3 tomorrow, or you can reply here. 🙂

Thanks,
Jahnavi

At which slide did Rafiq's eyebrows go up?
Slide four.
What was Jahnavi unsure and slightly worried about while watching Rafiq?
Whether Rafiq was interested or doubtful; Jahnavi saw it could not be told from a pause.
Why is Jahnavi's direct question better than guessing?
Pauses and raised brows suggest interest or doubt but never prove it, while asking gets Rafiq's actual view.
What might Rafiq have meant by the raised eyebrows?
Possibly doubt, possibly interest, or something unrelated to slide four; Jahnavi leaves all of it open.

messages.content: Why do people carry umbrellas in July? Give one sentence of at most twelve words.
They carry umbrellas to stay dry in the heavy monsoon rain.
My son teacher ko bolna chahta hai "Mam, mujhe samajh nahi aaya, please dobara samjhaiye". How he can say in English?
He can say: "Ma'am, I did not understand. Could you please explain it once more?" Asking this way is polite, and teachers like it when students ask.

Salma, you have to believe me, this thread works. Look at it. Red and black, from the temple in Thrissur. I'm Jeevan, and before the half-yearlies I was scoring fifties. My grandmother tied this on my wrist the week before the exams, and I scored in the eighties. Every subject! So obviously the thread. Okay, why are you looking at me like that? Fine. That same week I also stopped playing games till two in the morning, because my phone broke. And my uncle came to stay and made me revise every evening. And the half-yearly papers were easier than the unit tests, everybody said. So... yes, maybe it's all of that. But I'm not taking the thread off. You can't prove it didn't help. Well. You can't prove it did, either, I suppose.

What colours is Jeevan's thread?
Red and black, from the temple in Thrissur.
What does Jeevan's "I'm not taking the thread off" suggest?
It suggests Jeevan feels attached and a little defensive, not ready to give up the comforting belief that the thread helped.
What could Jeevan do to find out what really helped?
Look at what changed that week, like sleep, revision and easier papers, and see if the marks stay up when those continue, with or without the thread.
How does Salma seem to react while Jeevan talks?
Salma looks doubtful, which pushes Jeevan to list the other changes that week.
What is the usual time for Raga Gujari Todi?
Raga Gujari Todi is usually associated with Morning.
Turn this into a polite request to my landlord: The geyser is broken again. Fix it this week.
Hello, the geyser in my flat has stopped working again. Could you please arrange for it to be repaired this week? Thank you.

Nikita, you worry that questioning your teacher means you're ungrateful. Let your Tejas-kaka tell you about Swami Anandji. I was twenty, and my father had just died. I couldn't eat or study. Anandji ran a small ashram school near Nashik, and he let me sit in the library every afternoon, no questions asked, and fed me khichdi. He saved that year for me. I'd have done anything for him. Two years later he told us all to vote for a certain candidate, because 'the ashram needs it'. Something in me said no. I was ashamed of even thinking it. I went to him and said, 'Swamiji, I owe you my life. But my vote I must decide myself.' He was quiet for a long time. Then he laughed and said, 'Good. I didn't teach you to be a sheep.' Not every teacher would say that. But thanks and thinking can live together, Nikita.

What did Anandji feed Tejas?
Anandji fed him khichdi.
How did young Tejas feel when Anandji told them how to vote?
Tejas felt uneasy and ashamed, torn between deep gratitude and his own judgement.
What turning point in the story shows gratitude and clear thinking together?
Tejas telling Anandji he owed him his life but would decide his vote himself.
How did Anandji react to Tejas's refusal?
Anandji was quiet, then laughed and said he hadn't taught Tejas to be a sheep, accepting the independence.

A jewelry store is restocking its shelves. The necklace stand, which can hold 12 necklaces, currently holds 5 necklaces. The ring display, which can hold 30 rings, currently holds 18 rings. The bracelet display, which can hold 15 bracelets, currently holds 8 bracelets. The store's supplier charges $4 per necklace, $10 per ring, and $5 per bracelet. How much, in dollars, will the store need to pay to fill the displays?

The necklace stand needs another 12 - 5 = 7 necklaces.
This will cost the store 7 * 4 = $28.
The ring display needs another 30 - 18 = 12 rings.
This will cost the store 12 * 10 = $120.
The bracelet display needs another 15 - 8 = 7 bracelets.
This will cost the store 7 * 5 = $35.
In total, the store needs to pay 28 + 120 +35 = $183.
The answer is 183.
Bingley has 5 bracelets. Kelly gives Bingley a fourth of her 16 bracelets. Then Bingley gives a third of his bracelets to his little sister. How many bracelets does Bingley have remaining?

Kelly gives Bingley 16 / 4 = 4 bracelets
Bingley has 5 + 4 = 9 bracelets
Bingley gives his little sister 9 / 3 = 3 bracelets
In the end, Bingley has 9 - 3 = 6 bracelets remaining
The answer is 6.

The red armband was too big, so Soo-ah pinned it tighter. Exam-week hall monitor at her Seoul high school meant standing at the stairwell and stopping anyone who ran. On Monday she said, 'Please walk,' and felt silly. By Wednesday she had learned that a flat voice worked better, and that people stepped aside for the armband. By Friday she was writing names in the notebook for talking, for laughing, for a dropped pencil case. When Leila, her friend from art club, skidded around the corner, Soo-ah didn't smile. 'Name.' 'Soo-ah, it's me.' 'Name, please.' Leila spelled out her name slowly, staring at Soo-ah. Only on the bus did Soo-ah replay it and feel a strange cold drop in her stomach. It had felt so normal at the time.

What was Soo-ah writing names in the notebook for by Friday?
For talking, for laughing, for a dropped pencil case.
What does the cold drop in Soo-ah's stomach on the bus suggest?
It suggests Soo-ah feels uneasy, even a little ashamed, realising late that the armband's toughness had taken over and she had treated a friend like a stranger 😔
What could Soo-ah do on Monday to step back out of the role?
Soo-ah could apologise to Leila and decide to stop only runners, the rule she was actually given.
What is it like for Leila when her friend demands her name?
Leila feels hurt and shut out, spelling her name slowly and staring, as if she doesn't recognise Soo-ah.

Dear Yogesh,

Thank you for your patience about the missing slides in Tuesday's review. In the meeting I shrugged and said, "What can I do," and I saw your face fall. I want to fix that. The truth is I sent the slides to the wrong folder, and I did not check. It was my mistake, not the printer's, not the network's. I have re-sent them and set myself a reminder to check attachments twice before sending. If you have moments during the week I would be glad to walk you through the changes. I am truly sorry for the trouble. 🙏

Yours,
Swati

What mistake does Swati admit to?
Swati admits to sending the slides to the wrong folder.
Why did Swati write to Yogesh after the meeting, and what does the shrug tell us?
Swati saw Yogesh's face fall at the shrug and "What can I do", so wanted to show responsibility. The shrug may have meant helplessness to Swati but sounded like a dodge to Yogesh.
What did Swati do that repaired the situation?
Swati named the mistake plainly, re-sent the slides, promised a check and offered a walk-through, so the apology had substance.
How might Yogesh have felt in the meeting?
Yogesh might have felt let down or dismissed, since "What can I do" with a shrug can sound like nobody is fixing the problem.
What is one teaching note for Raga Kedar?
Ma is dominant; both Ma forms may appear.

Saurabh: so for the goa trip, i booked 2 rooms like u said
Anjali: thank u. i know ur friends will tease
Saurabh: let them. u said ur not ready for sharing a room yet. thats the answer

Anjali: yes. and i want us both to get checked before, like the college clinic said
Saurabh: agreed. no pressure on timing
Anjali: this is why i like u 🙂

How many rooms did Saurabh book for the trip?
Saurabh booked 2 rooms.
Why was Anjali scared to tell Saurabh about not being ready?
Anjali felt anxious because an ex used to sulk for days after every no, so a bad reaction seemed likely.
What makes their conversation an example of responsible intimacy?
They respect each other's no at any time, agree to talk first, plan protection together and follow the clinic's advice to get checked.
How might Saurabh's friends' teasing affect things, and how does Saurabh handle it?
The teasing could create pressure, but Saurabh dismisses it and keeps Anjali's boundary as the answer.

Monday: Harsha phoned Keerthana-amma, the teacher at the Bengaluru meditation circle, three times before noon: whether to accept the internship, whether to eat before the interview, whether his dream about a snake was a sign. She answered the first. On the second she paused.
Wednesday: When he called again, she said, 'Harsha, I won't answer this one. Which do you think?' He felt a rush of panic, as if the floor had tilted. He sat on the bus-stop bench for twenty minutes. Then he chose the evening shift, because it let him keep his morning classes.
Saturday: At the circle, she asked him how the shift was going. 'Fine,' he said, surprised. 'I chose it.' She smiled. 'A guide who makes all your choices isn't guiding you anywhere. Keep choosing the small things. Bring me only the ones that keep you awake.' That night Harsha decided, alone, to call his mother on Sundays instead of Fridays.

How many times did Harsha phone Keerthana-amma before noon on Monday?
Harsha phoned her three times before noon.
What did Harsha feel when Keerthana-amma refused to answer?
Harsha felt a rush of panic, as if the floor had tilted.
Why is Keerthana-amma's approach that of a good guide?
She stops answering small questions so Harsha builds his own judgement, and asks him to bring only the big ones.
What does Keerthana-amma want for Harsha?
She wants him to trust his own judgement rather than depend on her for every choice.

"Nazia, your phone's lit up four times since the samosas came."
"It's Faisal. He wants to know when I'll be home."
"It's six-thirty."
"I know." Nazia turned the phone over. "Every evening it's like an exam. Did I reply fast enough, did I say 'love you' back. Some days I want to hide in the office till nine."
Her elder sister Alka poured more chai. "And if you did hide?"
"He'd panic more. Then I'd feel worse. I do love him, Alka."
"So tell him that. And tell him the limit. Not in the middle of a fight."
"Like, 'I'll call when I leave work, but I won't answer ten texts in a meeting'?"
"Exactly that. Warm, and clear."
Nazia typed slowly, then looked up. "He sent back a heart. Just one."

How many times had Nazia's phone lit up since the samosas came?
Four times.
What does Nazia's wish to hide in the office till nine suggest she feels?
She feels pressured and tested, as if every evening were an exam of her love.
What advice did Alka give, and why might it help?
Tell Faisal the love and the limit calmly, not in a fight, so he gets reassurance and a clear boundary.
Why might Faisal react better to the calm message than to Nazia hiding?
A warm, clear message reassures him, while hiding would feed his fear of being left and make him check more.

Nitin worked the night shift at a call centre in Gurugram, answering complaints with three windows open and a chat app blinking. By 3 a.m. his jaw ached from clenching and he'd started snapping at callers.
Imran, at the next desk, had been there two years and never seemed rattled. During a break by the vending machine, Nitin asked him how.
"Between calls I do one thing," Imran said. "Hands off the keyboard. Three slow breaths. I feel my feet. Then the next call."
"That's it?"
"And I close the chat app while I'm on a call. One thing at a time."
Nitin tried it that night, feeling silly. Around the fortieth call, he noticed he wasn't clenching. A furious customer shouted at him and, for once, he waited a breath before answering.

What did Imran close while on a call?
Imran closed the chat app while on a call.
What does Nitin's aching jaw suggest about how he felt at work?
It suggests Nitin felt tense and stressed, holding the pressure of constant multitasking in his body.
What could Nitin try to make Imran's method stick?
Nitin could do the three breaths after every call, not just when stressed, and keep only one window open at a time.
How might the furious customer have been affected by Nitin's pause?
The customer may have felt heard rather than argued with, making the call calmer for both.

All through the monsoon, the colony cricket matches kept getting rained off, but Yogesh practised his hero's stance in the corridor anyway: bat high, collar up, chin raised. He had even asked the barber for the same spiky hair as the famous opener on TV. When he batted, he felt taller. At the one match that finally happened, he hit two fours and then stared the bowler down, just like on TV, and said, "Is that all you've got?" The bowler, a small boy from B-block, looked like he might cry. Yogesh's sister Hansa marched onto the field. "Your hero practises for hours. Copy that. Not the staring." Yogesh's ears went red. He mumbled sorry to the bowler.

How many fours did Yogesh hit?
Two.
How did Yogesh feel batting in his hero's style?
Taller and more confident, as if he shared some of the hero's strength.
What was Hansa's advice?
To copy the hero's hours of practice, not the staring and the swagger.
How might the small bowler have felt?
Upset and small, close to tears after being taunted.

The rain came down so hard that the Diwali guests arrived at the flat dripping and grumbling. The lift was broken, and they had climbed four floors.

Madhuri, six, stood by the door with her brother Raghav, holding a towel. As each guest came in, she folded her hands. "Namaste! Happy Diwali!"

Nanaji's friend, soaked and puffing, stopped scowling. He bent, touched her head, and said, "Bless you, little lamp." An aunty dried her hair and pinched Madhuri's cheek.

By the ninth guest, Madhuri was bouncing on her toes.

How many floors did the guests climb?
They had climbed four floors.
Why was Madhuri bouncing on her toes by the ninth guest?
Madhuri felt happy and excited, because each namaste brought smiles, pats and blessings from the bigger circle.
How could the family build on Madhuri's welcome?
Let her keep greeting at the door on festive days and thank her afterwards, so she sees how much her welcome helped.
What might the rain-soaked guests feel when Madhuri greets them?
They feel softened and welcomed; the scowls and grumbling fade after her namaste.
"Maine kabhi aisa nahi socha tha." Translate karo.
It is: "I had never thought of it that way." "Had never thought" refers to the time before you realised it.
Now you try: 3x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0.
The answer is (-1 +/- isqrt2)/3.

For five weeks Maria, the young English teacher at the school in Kumta, had lain awake till two. She had tried everything: warm milk, no phone after nine, the same wake time, a dark room with the fan on. Still she stared at the ceiling, and in the daytime a heavy worry sat on her chest. She didn't want to make a fuss. Her landlady, Ganga, found her crying over a stack of corrections. 'Enough, child. This is not something to push through alone.' The next morning Ganga went with her to the doctor at the taluk hospital. Maria kept her steady wake time and dark room, and began talking about the worry too.

Where did Ganga go with Maria?
To the doctor at the taluk hospital.
Why hadn't Maria sought help sooner?
She felt reluctant to make a fuss and kept trying to push through, even while worry sat heavy on her chest.
Why was seeing a doctor the wise next step?
Weeks of poor sleep with daytime worry had not eased with good habits, so a doctor could help alongside her routine.
How might Ganga have felt finding Maria crying?
Ganga probably felt worried and protective, deciding Maria shouldn't face it alone.

Read this:

Dear Jaya didi,

Last month I told nobody how bad my marks were, and I kept thinking, this is who I am. Then at Diwali you and Anil bhaiya told me about the times each of you failed a paper: you a whole semester, him a board subject, and how you both laugh about it now. I hadn't known any of that. I've thought about it for weeks. I don't think it is the whole story any more. It's one stage. So I've set a smaller goal: clear the physics supplementary, then get back to steady work. And next time I feel this stuck, I'll call you early, not after weeks. Can we talk on Sunday?

Usha

Who told Usha about failing papers at Diwali?
Jaya didi and Anil bhaiya told Usha about the papers each had failed.
What does Usha feel about the result now, compared with a month ago?
Usha now sees the result as one stage and not the whole story, and feels steadier and more hopeful.
What could Usha do to seek help earlier next time, and why?
Usha could call Jaya as soon as the stuck feeling starts, because early support keeps a setback from growing.
How might Jaya feel on reading the letter?
Jaya is probably touched and glad to have been trusted, and pleased that sharing an old struggle helped.
