messages.content:
Read this:

The hostel Wi-Fi died on the evening the results came out, so Lalremsiami had to walk to the library in the rain to see the screen: Statistics, Fail.

Back in the room, wet socks still on, she couldn't stop. Why did this happen? Was it the late nights? Was she just bad at numbers? Did it mean she'd chosen the wrong course? Uma brought her a towel and a plate of rice. Lalremsiami ate two bites and started again: "But why, though?"

For three days the questions ran in circles. She didn't open the notes. She didn't email the professor. The rain didn't stop and neither did the loop, and every round left her feeling heavier.

On the fourth day Uma sat on her bed. "You've asked why maybe a hundred times. Can we ask what now, even once?" Lalremsiami looked at the dripping window for a long time before nodding.

Why did Lalremsiami have to walk to the library?
The hostel Wi-Fi died on the evening the results came out, so she had to walk to the library in the rain.
Why does Lalremsiami keep asking why, even though it doesn't help?
Lalremsiami feels ashamed and afraid the failure means she is bad at numbers or on the wrong course, and asking why feels like searching for an answer.
What could be a first "what now" step for Lalremsiami?
Lalremsiami could open the statistics notes and list which topics went wrong, or email the professor to ask about the re-exam.
What is it like for Uma to watch the loop for three days?
Uma is probably worried and a little helpless, bringing towels and food while her friend keeps circling, which is why she finally speaks up.
Why did my cousin change schools?
I don't know your cousin's reasons, as I can't see their situation. Ask your cousin or a family member kindly.

Read this:

The feedback forms landed on the desks with three minutes left before the bell. "Rate each teacher, one to five," the monitor called. Siddharth scribbled fast. Maths: five, because yesterday's class had a puzzle. PT: one. Yesterday PT sir had cancelled the match for rain and made them sit in the library. Wasim leaned over. "One? He taught us cricket all term. He picked you for the house team." Siddharth's pencil paused. The whole term's matches, the house team, the day sir fixed his bat grip: all of it had been pushed out by one rainy afternoon. The bell was about to ring. He rubbed out the one, wrote a four, and handed the form in just as the monitor grabbed the pile.

Why was the match cancelled yesterday?
PT sir cancelled the match for rain.
Why did Siddharth first give PT sir a one?
Siddharth felt annoyed about yesterday's cancelled match, and that fresh disappointment crowded out a whole term of good memories.
What helped Siddharth change the rating, and what could he do next time?
Wasim's reminder of the cricket and the house team; next time he could think back over the whole term before rating.
What would change if Wasim hadn't leaned over?
PT sir might have got a one for a single rainy day, despite teaching cricket all term.

Read this:

Dear Lavanya,
You asked how the new flat is going. Mostly great. But I've noticed something about our fourth flatmate.
He's charming. He borrows our milk, our bus passes, even our laptops. When I asked for help moving a cupboard, he suddenly had a "call."
What I've noticed most is us. We've stopped offering. Priya now hides her good coffee. At dinner, someone always says, "Oh, is it your turn to buy groceries? Ha." And he laughs, like he doesn't get it.
Nobody has told him straight. We just do little things. I think we're all waiting for someone else to say it.
Maybe it'll be me.
Swati

What did the fourth flatmate suddenly have when asked to help move a cupboard?
He suddenly had a "call."
What is Swati feeling about how the flat is handling it?
Swati feels uneasy and a little guilty that everyone is punishing him with hints instead of telling him directly.
What could Swati say to the fourth flatmate?
Swati could tell him calmly that the flat shares things both ways and ask him to help with groceries and chores.
How might the fourth flatmate be affected by the little hints?
He may feel vaguely shut out without understanding why, since nobody has told him straight.

Read this:

I'm Chandrika, and I keep thinking about the morning my rabbit Coco stopped eating. He sat very still in the corner of the hutch, but I went to school anyway. When I came home, he was gone. Ever since, I've told myself that if I had spoken to Mummy that morning, he would still be here. I couldn't sleep. On Sunday my aunt Amandeep came over and I told her everything. She didn't say don't be silly. She listened, and then said, "You brushed him every day, gave him fresh carrot and noticed him. That is loving someone well. I don't think it was your fault, and I don't think you could have known." I cried on her shoulder. The heavy stone in my stomach felt smaller.

What did Chandrika notice about Coco that morning?
He sat very still in the corner of the hutch.
Why could Chandrika not sleep after Coco died?
She felt guilty, blaming herself and thinking that if she had spoken to Mummy that morning, Coco would still be here.
How did talking to her aunt Amandeep help Chandrika?
Amandeep listened without brushing her off and pointed out how much daily care she had given Coco, which helped Chandrika see it was not her fault. 🤍
How does Amandeep see Chandrika's care for Coco?
As a way of loving him well, since she brushed him, gave him fresh carrot and noticed him.
Is this book your's? Check my pronoun.

Is this book yours?
Why: apostrophe ("your's" -> "yours").

Read this:

Dear Lavanya,

You asked why I didn't fight with Dadi about the old house. Here's what happened.

Dadi says we moved from the old house when I was five, after the flood. I remember it differently. I remember being seven, and no flood, just a lorry and my cousins helping.

Instead of arguing, I checked Papa's old diary. It says we moved when I was six, after the rains damaged the roof. So neither of us had it exactly right.

When I told Dadi, I said, "This is how I remember it, but your version has the rain in it, and the diary does too." She smiled and said, "We both remember the parts that mattered to us."

I liked that.

Preeti

What does Papa's old diary say about the move?
It says they moved when Preeti was six, after the rains damaged the roof.
How did Preeti feel about not arguing with Dadi?
Preeti felt calm and respectful, open to the idea that both memories held something true.
What in Preeti's approach could Lavanya try with her own family?
Checking records like the diary and saying "I remember it this way" instead of calling someone wrong.
How does Dadi respond to Preeti's approach?
Dadi smiles and says they both remember the parts that mattered to them, suggesting she feels respected.
Nobody in the school choir is late today. Hari is in the choir. Is Hari late?
No, Hari is not late. Because no member of the choir is late and Hari is a member, he must be on time.

Read this:

So you want to talk about envy? Okay, I'm Indu, sixteen, and I'll go first. My cousin Manjula's family moved into a three-bedroom flat last year. We're in a two-bedroom, perfectly fine; I share a room with my sister, whatever. But every time we visit Manjula, I come home in a bad mood. Her room has a window seat. Her dad drives her to school. I start thinking our life is unfair, that we're somehow behind. Then last month our school visited a hostel for students from villages, and one of them told me she had never had a room of her own, not even a corner. On the bus back I felt so small. I'm not saying I stopped comparing. But now I notice whom I compare with. It's always the person one step ahead.

What does Manjula's room have?
A window seat.
How does Indu feel after visiting Manjula?
Indu feels grumpy and cheated, as if their own life were unfair and behind.
What did Indu learn about how comparison works?
That the feeling of lacking depends on whom you look at, usually the person one step ahead.
How might the student at the hostel see Indu's two-bedroom flat?
She would probably see it as comfortable and lucky, since she had never had a room of her own.

Read this:

The rain started just as the party thinned out, and Aadhya's phone was on four percent. Across the room Aditi was laughing at nothing, slurring her words, then leaning on the wall with her eyes half closed. When Aadhya touched her arm, Aditi mumbled, "Just leave me, I'll sleep here." A guy nearby said, "She's fine, let her crash." Aadhya didn't think so. She sat Aditi on the sofa, kept talking to her, and borrowed the host's phone to call Aditi's flatmate, who came with a cab. Aadhya rode with them, holding Aditi's hand, checking she still answered to her name. At the flat Aditi opened her eyes and sipped water. "If she stops answering, we call an ambulance straight away," Aadhya told the flatmate, and stayed the night on the floor beside the bed.

Whose phone did Aadhya borrow to call for help?
She borrowed the host's phone.
What was Aadhya feeling when the guy said to let Aditi crash, and how can you tell?
She was worried and uneasy; she didn't believe him and stayed close, talking to Aditi and calling for help.
Which of Aadhya's actions kept Aditi safe?
Staying with her, calling the flatmate to get her home, checking she answered to her name, and planning to call an ambulance if she stopped responding.
What would have happened to Aditi if everyone had taken the guy's advice?
Aditi might have been left alone and unsafe, with nobody noticing if she stopped answering.

Read this:

Charu: Lavanya, got a minute after your shift?
Lavanya: sure. is something wrong?
Charu: nothing you did. I've just noticed you've had four very hard families back to back this month
Lavanya: it's the job
Charu: it is. but you were in tears in the file room yesterday, and today you told Mrs Pinto "that's not my problem"
Lavanya: …I didn't mean it like that
Charu: I know. that's why I'm messaging. that's not you, that's tiredness
Lavanya: honestly I don't know what's happening to me
Charu: here's the plan: you're off Friday and Monday. Deepak takes your next two new cases. and we talk properly on Tuesday, with the staff counsellor if you want
Lavanya: are you sure the team can manage?
Charu: yes. the people who do the caring need looking after too. go home on time today
Lavanya: ok. thank you

How many very hard families had Lavanya handled this month?
Four very hard families back to back.
What is Lavanya feeling in "I don't know what's happening to me"?
Lavanya seems confused and a little frightened by the tears and sharpness, not recognising them as exhaustion.
Which part of Charu's plan might help most, and why?
Handing Lavanya's next two cases to Deepak shares the load straight away, while the days off and Tuesday's talk give rest and support.
How might Mrs Pinto have felt being told "that's not my problem"?
Mrs Pinto may have felt brushed off and hurt, which shows why a worn-out carer needs a break for everyone's sake.

A rope is 21 metres long. Rohan cuts off 4 metres. How long is it now?
How can I take care of a pet fish?
Can you fix this sentence? I seen that film at school.

1. It is 17. Because 21 - 4 = 17.
2. Give it a little food once or twice a day and keep the water clean. Do not feed it too much.
3. Fixed: I saw that film at school. Why: The simple past of "see" is "saw".

Read this:

You're asking whether that senior's compliments are real, Swati? Then let your Thomas Uncle tell you about 1989. I was in class ten at a boys' school in Bangalore, and a senior, Victor, started calling me "the best spinner in the city". Every day. Loudly. I floated for a week. Then one evening he said, "Such a genius bowler can surely write my history project, no?" And I did it, twice, before it clicked. Meanwhile our games teacher, Mr Pinto, hardly ever praised me. But when he did, it was small and exact: "Your wrist was straighter today, keep that." He said the same thing whether others were listening or not, and he never asked me for anything. I'm not saying Victor was a crook. Maybe he half meant it; I'll never know. But I learned to listen for the specific, the steady, and the favour that follows. Now pass me that tea before it goes cold.

What did Victor call Thomas every day?
Victor called Thomas "the best spinner in the city".
What was young Thomas feeling during that first week of praise?
Thomas was flattered and happy, floating for a week; after writing the project twice he likely felt foolish and used, though Victor may have half meant it.
Which choice in the story would you have made differently, and why?
Young Thomas could have paused when the favour arrived right after the compliments; noticing that the praise came with a request would have saved him writing the project twice.
How might Mr Pinto have seen his own small, exact comments?
Mr Pinto likely saw them as honest coaching, saying the same thing whether others were listening or not, with nothing wanted in return.

Camden went swimming 16 times in March and Susannah went 24 times. If the number of times they went throughout the month was divided equally among 4 weeks, how many more times a week did Susannah swim than Camden?

Camden went swimming 16/4 = 4 times a week
Susannah went swimming 24/4 = 6 times a week
Susannah went 6 - 4 = 2 more times a week than Camden
The answer is 2.

Questions for you:
What music helps me concentrate while studying?
What song is on the radio right now?
Why do some songs get stuck in our heads?

1. Soft music without words usually works best. If it makes you lose your place, switch it off.
2. I can't hear your radio, so I don't know. Look at the station's website or use a music-identifying tool.
3. They repeat a tune. Because our brain likes patterns and keeps playing them.

a) How many tens in 340?
b) How many tens in 70?
c) How many tens in 500?

o) How many ones in 30?
p) How many ones in 100?

After a trip, Mrs. Nalani took the students to the restaurant and told them they could order either a burger or a hot dog. If the number of students who ordered burgers was 30, twice the number of students who called for a hot dog, calculate the number of students at the restaurant.

If the 30 students who ordered burgers were twice the number of students who ordered hot dogs, then 30/2 = 15 students ordered hot dogs.
The total number of students is 15 + 30 = 45
The answer is 45.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Bageshri?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Bageshri is M, and the samvadi is S.
Two classmates tell the teacher different stories about a broken chair. How can the teacher find out what happened?

The teacher can ask each of them careful questions and listen for details that fit together. Because other students or the chair itself may offer evidence, checking facts is fairer than simply believing one side.
Tell me about the word "habitat". And why do frogs croak at night?

1. A habitat is the natural home of a plant or an animal.
2. Male frogs croak to call to other frogs, and the night is cool and damp, which they like.

Do the turns in order (cw = clockwise, acw = anticlockwise). Which way do you face at the end?
a) face North; quarter cw, then quarter cw
b) face East; half cw, then quarter acw
c) face South; quarter cw, then quarter cw, then quarter cw

b) South

August, week 2. Lalremsiami's new roommate Ganga plays devotional songs at 5:30 every morning. Lalremsiami says nothing. She lies awake, and a week later fills in a room-change form at the hostel office. Under reason she writes 'personal'.
September, a Monday. She moves to room 41 with Charu. For two weeks it's peaceful. Then Charu starts video-calling her family at midnight, loudly. Lalremsiami pulls the blanket over her head and says nothing.
October, a Thursday. She is back at the hostel office, pen over a fresh form. The clerk looks up. 'Again? Did you talk to her?'
Lalremsiami opens her mouth and realises she has never once said a word to either roommate. She puts the pen down.

What time did Ganga play songs?
At 5:30 every morning.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when the clerk asked if she had talked to her roommate?
She was probably embarrassed and a little shaken, seeing that she had avoided every talk and the problem followed her.
What could Lalremsiami try with Charu before any form?
Tell Charu calmly that the midnight calls keep her awake and ask whether the calls could be earlier or in the corridor.
How might Ganga have seen the sudden room change?
Ganga may have felt confused or hurt, never knowing the morning songs were a problem that could have been fixed.

1. Pack your school bag.
2. Eat a good breakfast.
3. Check your timetable.

Behind the temple pond in Raichur, Pankaj and Chandrika had a secret. Last summer they had only played gilli-danda with everyone else. This year they'd found a hollow in the old peepal tree and hid a tin there with their best marbles, a peacock feather and a map they'd drawn. Nobody else knew. One evening, Chandrika's older brother asked, "Where do you two disappear?" Pankaj looked at Chandrika, then at the pond. "Just walking." Later, alone, they checked the tin. Chandrika grinned at him. "You didn't tell." "Never," Pankaj said, and they touched thumbs.

What did they keep in the tin?
Their best marbles, a peacock feather and a map they'd drawn.
What was Chandrika feeling when she said "You didn't tell"?
She felt happy and reassured that she could trust Pankaj with their secret.
How could Pankaj and Chandrika keep their secret without hurting others?
They could keep the tin private but still play with the other children, so the friendship doesn't feel like shutting everyone out.
How might Chandrika's brother see the two of them disappearing?
He might feel curious or a little left out, wondering what they are doing.

Mentor's note, finance team, Gangtok office. Dolma.
Anirban (25, sales) came to my desk at 6 p.m. with his claim for the Siliguri trip. He said, a bit embarrassed, that he had almost added a dinner that never happened, 'about eight hundred, the kind of thing everyone adds'.
What stopped him, he said, was a question he'd started asking himself: would I be fine if Pemba saw this? Pemba shares his desk and trained him, and he couldn't picture handing Pemba that line.
The claim he gave me had real receipts only, and one taxi fare marked 'no receipt, driver had no printer', which I appreciated.
Next step: I've asked him to share his 'would Pemba be fine' question at Friday's new-joiner session. People often need a face to check against more than another rule.

How much was the dinner Anirban almost added?
About eight hundred.
Why was Anirban tempted to add the dinner?
It felt like 'the kind of thing everyone adds', so it seemed normal and small rather than like cheating.
Which question helped Anirban resist, and why did it work?
'Would I be fine if Pemba saw this?'; picturing a trusted colleague reading the line measured the claim against Anirban's own standard, not an average one.
How might Pemba feel on hearing that Anirban used Pemba as a check?
Pemba would probably feel trusted and quietly proud, knowing the training had shaped how Anirban judges what is right.

Read this:

The night shift at the district hospital in Bhubaneswar was quiet until two, when an old man in bed six began calling for his wife. Bidisha, a second-year nursing student, sat with him, holding his hand until he fell asleep. At the tea counter Lakshmi, the senior nurse, asked why she had chosen nursing. 'Honestly? Papa said it was a safe job, and I could go abroad later.' Bidisha stirred her tea. 'I used to count the months till I could leave. Tonight I didn't think about money once.' Lakshmi nodded. 'That feeling won't come every shift. Some nights are just charts and tiredness.' 'I know,' Bidisha said. 'But now I know it exists.' She wrote the time and bed number in her pocket diary, not for the chart, but for herself.

Which bed was the old man in?
Bed six.
What change in Bidisha's feelings does her comment about money reveal?
Sitting with the patient gave her a sense of worth beyond the safe-job reason she had started with.
Why is Lakshmi's reply useful for Bidisha?
She is honest that this feeling will not come every shift, helping Bidisha hold on to purpose without expecting every night to feel special.
What might that night have been like for the old man?
Frightening and lonely until someone held his hand, which let him settle and sleep 🤍

Read this:

Kavitha had two hours to prepare the Bengaluru office for a video call with a new client team in Nairobi, and the conference room's internet kept dropping. Her senior, Trisha, was stuck in traffic. Kavitha had planned to open with the numbers, the way her team liked. But last week one of the Kenyan managers had spent five minutes asking about everyone's families before business. So she rewrote her opening: a warm welcome, a question about how their week had gone, then the plan. When the connection finally held, the Kenyan lead smiled and talked about his daughter's school exams. Trisha joined late, heard the relaxed tone, and messaged Kavitha: 'Nice start 👏'. They got through every agenda point anyway, just ten minutes later than planned.

Where was the client team calling from?
The client team was calling from Nairobi.
Why did Kavitha change her opening?
She remembered the Kenyan manager's warm small talk last week and wanted the client to feel respected in their own style.
What worked about Kavitha's approach under pressure?
She adapted quickly to the client's norms while still covering every agenda point, balancing warmth with work.
What would change if Kavitha had started straight with numbers?
The Kenyan team might have found it abrupt and felt less comfortable, which could have made the new relationship harder.

Read this:

Playgroup note, rainy July week. Nazia had the block tub today. When Ojas came over, she tipped half the blocks toward him at once: "You gave me your red car yesterday." Then a boy who usually grabs and keeps things reached in. Nazia pulled the tub back. "No. You never give me." He started to cry. I sat with them both and said, "You remember who shares with you. That's fair thinking." Then I gave the boy a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first. He did. Nazia passed him two blocks. Next: more take-turns games.

What did Ojas give Nazia yesterday?
His red car.
Why did Nazia pull the tub back from the other boy?
She felt it was unfair, because he never gives her things; she was annoyed and protective of her blocks.
What did the note-writer try next, and why could it help?
The boy got a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first, so she saw him give and was willing to give back.
What is it like for the boy when Nazia says "You never give me"?
He feels hurt and left out, and cries, perhaps not yet understanding that his grabbing is why she won't share.

Read this:

Forty minutes before judging, the extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark. Vasudha, who had built the circuit, went silent, eyes on the floor. Mohit had seen others snap, "Look at me, what's wrong?" He didn't. He crouched beside the table, not too close, and spoke slowly. "The lights are off. I think it's the cord. Do you want to say it, or write it?" The hall buzzed; the loudspeaker crackled. He slid a pair of earmuffs across the table. "My sister's. Use them if you want." Vasudha put them on. Ten long seconds passed. Mohit waited. Then she tore a strip of chart paper and wrote three steps. Mohit did them one by one. At the third step, the little street lamps on the model flickered back on.

What went wrong forty minutes before judging?
The extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark.
Why did Mohit not tell Vasudha to look at him?
He seemed to understand that forcing eye contact would add stress, and he wanted her to answer in her own way.
Which of Mohit's choices helped most under time pressure?
He spoke slowly, asked if she wanted to say or write it, offered earmuffs and waited, so she could give clear steps.
How might Vasudha have felt if Mohit had snapped at her like others?
She might have frozen further in the noise and not been able to share the fix she knew.

Read this:

Santosh: our bridge model is 100% passing the load test tomorrow. no doubt 💪
Afreen: I expect it'll hold the first two weights, because the truss joints held in Friday's trial
Afreen: the third weight I'm less sure about. the glue on the left side was still soft
Santosh: you're overthinking. it's perfect
Afreen: maybe! but I'd call it 60-40 on the third. can we add a brace tonight just in case?
Santosh: fine, 10 minutes
(next day)
Santosh: it held all three!!
Santosh: ...the prof said the left brace is what saved it
Afreen: 🎉 we both called part of it
Santosh: okay, you called more of it. how did you know?
Afreen: I didn't know. I just said what I expected and why, then checked the weak bit
Santosh: stealing that for my viva 😅

What was still soft on the left side of the model?
The glue.
How did Afreen feel about the third weight?
Afreen felt unsure about it: hopeful for the first two weights because of Friday's trial, but uneasy about the third because of the soft glue.
Why did Afreen's way of predicting work better than Santosh's certainty?
Stating an expectation with its reason and naming the weak spot led to adding the brace that saved the model; flat certainty would have skipped the check.
How did Santosh come to see Afreen's caution?
At first as overthinking; after the prof credited the brace, Santosh respected it enough to borrow the approach for the viva.

In the family cloth shop in Kurukshetra, Vaibhav was counting the day's cash when Mehak, the new helper, folded a stack of dupattas crookedly. "Is this how you fold? Did no one teach you anything?" he snapped.
Mehak's face fell. Vaibhav froze. That was Pitaji's voice, word for word. He remembered standing in this same shop at twelve, hands shaking over a crooked fold. He remembered too that Pitaji raised the shutter at seven every single day and knew every customer's name.
Vaibhav put the notes down. "Sorry, Mehak. That came out harsh. Let me show you the fold." He did, slowly, twice.
That night he wrote on the back of a bill: Keep: seven o'clock, every name. Drop: the tone.

What did Vaibhav write on the back of the bill?
"Keep: seven o'clock, every name. Drop: the tone."
What was Vaibhav feeling when he froze after snapping?
He felt shocked and ashamed to hear his father's sharp voice in his own mouth, remembering how scared he had been in the shop as a boy.
Which choice worked, and why?
Apologising, showing the fold slowly, and writing down which of Pitaji's habits to keep and which to drop turned an inherited reflex into a deliberate choice.
How might Mehak feel after Vaibhav's apology?
Relieved and more at ease, since the harsh words were taken back and she was shown the fold patiently.

metadata.subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]

messages.content:
Rewrite for a child, using simpler words:

Heavy rain flooded the lower streets, and the municipality advised residents to avoid unnecessary travel.
A lot of rain filled the low streets with water. The city office told people to stay home unless they had to go out.
Two sisters on opposite teams in a school match: tell their story.

Amna and Hira were sisters, but in the school netball match, they were captains of rival houses. Their mother sat in the stands, unsure whom to cheer for. The game was tight, and in the last minute, Amna passed the ball to a teammate, who missed. Hira scooped it up and shot, scoring the winning point. Amna's jaw tightened. For a moment, the sisters stared at each other across the court. Then Hira ran over, and they hugged, rocking from side to side. "Mummy is crying," Amna said, pointing at the stand. They walked off arm in arm, and their mother handed each of them a sweet, one in each hand.
Why is the sky blue?
Sunlight contains all colours. When it enters the air, the gas molecules scatter blue light much more than red light, so blue reaches our eyes from every direction.
Then why are sunsets red?
At sunset the light travels through far more air to reach you. Most of the blue is scattered away on the way, so the reds and oranges are what remain.

Read this:

"Dada, tell me the shop story," said Divyansh.
"You have heard it a hundred times," said Chinmay.
"Tell it again. Please?"
"Fine. When I was your age, I walked six kilometres each day to school. Then I saved my first coins and opened a little shop, with one shelf and a scale."
"And the sign?"
"I painted it myself, crooked." Dada laughed.
"Today in class," said Divyansh, "the teacher asked what our family does. I said we open the shop before sunrise, and we fix the crooked sign every year."

How far did Chinmay walk to school each day?
Six kilometres.
What was Divyansh feeling when telling the class about the family shop?
Pride and belonging. Divyansh spoke of the shop and the crooked sign as "we," as if part of the story.
What choice did Chinmay make at the start of the conversation?
Chinmay agreed to tell the shop story again, even after a hundred tellings, and shared the details of the shelf, the scale and the crooked sign.
What might Chinmay have felt when Divyansh said "we open the shop before sunrise"?
Moved and proud, because Divyansh had taken the story on as part of who the family is; Chinmay looked for a long moment and said "That's us."

Right up to the gate of Rehana's castle.

She kept listening to the bus stops instead of walking off, and she welcomed the bus stop into her castle.

Sunday night.
Dropped Akhil from the club's first eleven today. My oldest friend.
He's the best batsman we have. But for three weeks he's been shouting at the umpires, and on Saturday he swore at a sixteen-year-old debutant who dropped a catch. The kid went home in tears.

I'll message the debutant tomorrow. And I'll call Akhil on Wednesday, when he's cooled down. I don't want to lose him. But I didn't take this job to be his friend on the field. — Eshaan

Who did Akhil swear at on Saturday?
He swore at a sixteen-year-old debutant who dropped a catch.
How was Eshaan feeling after telling Akhil?
Eshaan felt anxious and sad, with a stomach in knots, afraid of losing an old friend.

Telling Akhil privately first was fair; calling on Wednesday and messaging the debutant will help repair both relationships.

The debutant may feel protected and respected, seeing that the club's rules apply even to its best player.

If anyone talked, the whole class lost PE.

Vaibhav felt it was unfair and a bit angry, having not said a word.
Why was Vaibhav's suggestion fairer?
It only punished the person who broke the rule, not everyone.
How did Kiran-ma'am respond to Vaibhav?
She listened, thought and asked the class to vote on a new rule.

I've shared a cubicle wall with Noor for a year, so I've watched her listen a lot. On Wednesday Raghav, the new intern, explained his idea for the warehouse labels, stumbling over his words. Noor's eyes widened a little and she tilted her head. He sped up, found his confidence and finished the whole plan. Afterwards Noor rubbed her eyes by the water cooler and said, "My face is sore from paying attention."

What did Raghav explain on Wednesday?
Raghav explained his idea for the warehouse labels.
What might Noor's widened eyes on Wednesday have shown?
They most likely showed Noor was interested and wanted Raghav to go on, which helped him feel confident; they could also have been mild surprise that the intern had thought of it.
What could Noor try in long meetings instead of holding that look?
She could let her face relax and show interest at natural moments, with a nod or a short question, rather than keeping her eyes open wide for two hours.
How did Raghav see Noor's look on Friday?
Raghav read the fixed wide eyes as shock and asked if Noor was okay, so the listening cue had turned into something strained.

messages.content: If you plant a seed and water it, it may sprout. A seed did not sprout. Was it certainly not watered?
No, we cannot conclude that. Because sprouting depends on other things as well, such as warmth and a living seed, a lack of sprouting does not prove that watering was missed.
Samir just turned half the age Hania was 10 years ago. If in five years Hania will be 45 years old, what will Samir's age be five years from now?

If in five years, Hania will be 45 years old, currently she is 45-5 = 40 years old.
Ten years ago, Hania was 40-10 = 30 years old.
Samir just turned half the age Hania was 10 years ago, which means she is 30/2 = 15 years old.
In five years, Samir will be 15+5 = 20 years old
The answer is 20.

Tuesday. Dilnaz told Thomas at the bus stop: she'd been selected for the national youth orchestra. "Don't tell anyone yet. Not till it's official."
Thursday. In the library, Thomas was so excited he blurted it to four people. "Dilnaz is going national! Can you believe it?" By lunch it was all over school. By evening Dilnaz had heard.
Friday. She didn't sit near him on the bus. Thomas couldn't look at her. He kept rehearsing excuses: I was proud of you, it slipped out, it's good news anyway.
Monday. He found her outside the music room. "I told people. I shouldn't have. I'm sorry." No excuse.
Dilnaz glared. "You made my moment yours."
"You're right." He stood there and took it.
"I don't want to talk for a while."
"Okay," he said, and walked away. It was the hardest thing he'd done all week.

Which orchestra was Dilnaz selected for?
The national youth orchestra.
Why couldn't Thomas look at Dilnaz on Friday?
He felt deeply ashamed of blurting her news and was tempted to hide behind excuses.
What made Thomas's apology on Monday a good one?
It was plain, with no excuses, he accepted her anger and he gave her the distance she asked for.
How does Dilnaz see the leak?
She feels angry and robbed, as if Thomas took her special moment and made it his own.

What did Jeevan say when asked if the plan was all right?
Jeevan said, "Do whatever you think, Uncle."

Kavitha wanted to avoid an argument, and now feels dismayed and stuck at the tasting.

Kavitha's father would probably feel surprised and sorry, having believed the couple was content when they said to do whatever the father thought.

messages.content: What does "put up with" mean? One more thing: I keep seeing "determination" in my reading. Meaning? Also, how do I ask a shopkeeper politely for the right size? And why do we say sorry when we bump into someone?

1. It means to accept something annoying without complaining. For example: we put up with the noise from the road.
2. As a noun, "determination" means a firm purpose that does not give up.
3. Say, "Could I please see this in a larger size?" Smile, and say thank you even if they do not have it.
4. It keeps people comfortable around us. Because an apology calms the other person and avoids a quarrel.

At nine, Vijay lay awake listening to the ceiling fan. What if I forget everything tomorrow? What if Mummy's bus is late and something happens? Each question made two more, and the heart drummed. Zeenat, Vijay's mother, heard the sheets rustle and sat on the bed. "I'm here, the door is locked. Same routine as always: three slow breaths, one story." By the second page Vijay was drowsy.

At fifteen, in the weeks before the board exams, Vijay's desk stayed tidy and the books unopened. What if the paper is out of syllabus? What if the hand cramps? What if all the chapters blur together? Whole afternoons went on imagining. Reena, the tutor, opened a notebook. "Pick one chapter. Twenty minutes. Then tell me what you covered." Vijay wrote the heading and the first line, the first real step all week, and felt a small loosening in the chest.

What did Zeenat say they would do at bedtime?
Zeenat said, "Same routine as always: three slow breaths, one story."
How do Vijay's worries at nine and at fifteen resemble each other, and how did help differ?

At nine and at fifteen Vijay's questions kept multiplying, what if I forget everything, what if the paper is out of syllabus, and felt like preparing. At nine a routine of slow breaths and a story from Zeenat settled the night; at fifteen Reena's one chapter and a short time turned worry into a first line.
What was Vijay feeling when the desk stayed tidy and the books unopened?
Vijay was anxious and overwhelmed, feeling that worrying was a kind of responsibility even though it replaced studying.
What small step would help Vijay after writing the first line?
Vijay could keep to one chapter at a time and tell Reena what got done, so each step is real and small.

Elizabeth, construing all this into a wish of hearing her speak of her sister, was pleased; and on this account, as well as some others, found herself, when their visitors left them, capable of considering the last half hour with some satisfaction, though while it was passing the enjoyment of it had been little. Bingley says he is glad to see Elizabeth again, and Elizabeth, thinking he wants to hear about her sister, is pleased. After the visitors leave, she hears her uncle and aunt praise him, then hurries away to dress.
Erwin eats 2 chocolates on weekdays and 1 chocolate on weekends. He ate 24 chocolates in total. How many weeks did it take to finish all the chocolate?

On weekdays he eats 5*2=10 chocolates
On weekends he eats 2*1=2 chocolates
He eats 10+2=12 chocolates in a week.
It takes 24/12=2 weeks to finish all the chocolate.
The answer is 2.
What is a feather? My little sister asked me.

A feather is one of the light, soft parts that cover a bird's body. It is a noun.
Example: She found a blue feather on the path.

In the district cooperative bank's server room above the Satara branch, Reena watched the ATM transactions crawl. Villagers were queuing outside two ATMs in the market, and Shalini, the branch manager, kept calling.
'I have one guess,' Reena said, writing it on the whiteboard: the line to head office is full. She checked: it showed ninety-eight percent use. 'Test: I'll pause the nightly backup, which is running late. Only that.' She paused it at 10.12 and watched.
By 10.20, line use was down to sixty percent and transactions were fast again. She wrote the result under the guess. Then a second line: 'Why was the backup running at 10 a.m.?' She opened the schedule and found it had been changed during last week's power cut. She moved it back to 2 a.m. and told Shalini the queues should clear.

At what time did Reena pause the backup?
What might Shalini have been worried about while making call after call?
Shalini was likely anxious about the villagers queuing at the ATMs and how the bank looked to them.
What else could Reena add so this doesn't repeat after a power cut?
She could add a check of scheduled jobs to the steps followed after any power cut, so a moved backup is caught early.
How might the villagers in the queue be affected by Reena's method?
Because she tested one change and confirmed it quickly, their wait ended within minutes.

In a glass cabin at the co-working incubator, Abhinav and Chaitanya sat down for their quarterly review with a printout of customer feedback. Abhinav, who had built the whole product, had also been doing the sales calls. The comments were polite but clear: "Very technical." "Didn't understand the pricing." "Founder seemed impatient with questions."
Abhinav read them twice. "I'm bad at this. I explain the code, not the value."
Chaitanya nodded carefully. "And I've been writing test cases, which I'm slow at, when I actually enjoy talking to people."
They swapped. From the next Monday, Chaitanya ran every customer call and demo, and Abhinav focused on delivery and fixing bugs. By the end of the next quarter, the feedback sheet had words like "clear" and "patient", and two customers had renewed early.

What did one comment say about the founder?
"Founder seemed impatient with questions."

Abhinav felt stung and a little embarrassed, but honest enough to admit being bad at sales.

How do customers experience the change?
Customers find the calls clearer and more patient, and two renewed early.

messages.content: Jamie collects glass balls. He had 16 red balls and two times more blue balls. Later on, he lost 6 of the red balls, so he decided to buy some yellow balls to fill up his collection. How many yellow balls did he buy if, after all, he had 74 balls in total?

Jamie had two times more blue balls than red ones, so he had 2 blue/red * 16 red balls = 32 blue balls.
He lost 6 red balls so he had only 16 red balls - 6 red balls = 10 red balls
In total he had 32 blue balls + 10 red balls = 42 red and blue balls.
He bought 74 balls - 42 red and blue balls = 32 yellow balls.
The answer is 32.
Why does bread go hard if it is left out uncovered?
It loses its moisture. Because the water in the bread slowly escapes into the air, and without it the crumb turns dry and stiff.

I don't know what Jyoti felt inside; her face stayed calm. She sat on the bed next to Mitali and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying right here." Then she turned to me and said, "Aparna, please get Ms Rao. Now." I ran. Jyoti didn't leave Mitali's side for a second, not even when Mitali begged her to keep it secret. Jyoti said, "I can't. I care about you too much." Ms Rao came within minutes, called Mitali's parents and the helpline, and stayed with her all night.

Ms Rao.
How did Aparna seem to feel watching Jyoti respond?
Aparna seemed tense and urgent, running at once, and impressed by how calm Jyoti stayed.

She stayed calm and close, thanked Mitali, refused to promise secrecy, never left her alone and sent for a teacher immediately.
How might Mitali have felt when Jyoti said "I care about you too much"?
Mitali may have felt upset but also deeply cared for, even while begging for secrecy.
Let a lunch box get mixed up and lead to a new friendship; write the story.

Gayatri's tiffin box and Rehan's looked exactly alike, and when the bell rang for lunch, Gayatri opened the wrong one. Inside was a thick, spicy biryani. She had never tasted anything like it. At the same time, across the room, Rehan stared at Gayatri's neat curd rice with mango pickle. He walked over, embarrassed. "I think I took yours." She grinned and held out the biryani. "It is delicious. Who made it?" "My mother," said Rehan. "She would be pleased to know you liked it." They agreed to trade a spoonful every Friday, and a month later, their mothers met at a parent-teacher meeting and were already friends.

What did Lalit bring to his manager's home?
A basket of mangosteens, handed over with his right hand.
How did Lalit probably feel when the grandmother called him polite?
He probably felt pleased and relieved that his careful questions had paid off and he was welcomed.
Why was asking Pak Budi a wise first step?
Budi had lived there all his life and could explain real customs like shoes, right hand and heads, so Lalit could avoid mistakes rather than guess.
How might Madhav see Lalit's approach by week five?
Madhav first laughed at the preparation, but by week five he seems surprised and a little impressed that Lalit is already invited to a wedding.

A small clock.

Is there a mistake here? She suggested to go to the beach.
Plus, what does the word "primitive" mean?
Next, what does "take the plunge" mean?

At home he answered in grunts, spent evenings behind a closed door, and once said, "Can you not come to the match? It's embarrassing." A street away from the pitch.

Note to myself, Sunday

Rafiq has been moping since Disha started spending lunch with the robotics kids. He said, "She was never really my friend," and slammed his door.

I didn't argue. At bedtime I asked what he missed most. "Building forts with her," he said.

On Monday I suggested he just say hello to her at the gate, nothing more. He came home and said, "She said hi back. She seemed normal."

Today I helped him invite Disha to fly kites on our terrace. She came for an hour. Rafiq was quiet afterwards but not angry.

I told him that some friends are close in one season and further away in another, and that the forts they built were real. He said, "So it wasn't fake?" I said, "No. It was real."

He went to sleep smiling a little.

— Rafiq's Ammi

What did Rafiq say he missed most?
Building forts with her.
Why did Rafiq say Disha was never really his friend?
He was hurt and angry that she now spent lunch with the robotics kids, so he tried to protect himself by saying the friendship was never real.
How did Ammi help Rafiq keep kindness through the change?
She listened without arguing, then helped with small steps, a hello and one kite afternoon, and told him the friendship was real even if it changes.
What is it like for Disha to be invited to the terrace?
She is probably pleased to be remembered by an old friend, even though robotics now takes much of her time.

At the small bank branch in Sirsa, Vishal noticed how often Irfan's phone buzzed at lunch, and how his shoulders dropped each time. Once Irfan read a message aloud with a laugh: "Useless as always, can't even buy the right rice." "That's just her way," he said. "She's stressed." Vishal had heard "just her way" many times now: about the shouting in front of guests, about the jokes at his expense in front of her family. He wanted to argue, to list every example. Instead, walking to the bus stand that evening, he said once, quietly, "Irfan, the way she talks to you sounds hurtful to me. You deserve respect. I'm around, any time." Irfan didn't answer. But the next week, he asked Vishal to have chai after work.

What did the message Irfan read aloud say?
"Useless as always, can't even buy the right rice."
What did Vishal feel hearing "just her way" again?
He felt worried and frustrated, tempted to argue with a list of examples, but chose to hold back.
Why was Vishal's approach wise?
He named it gently once, said Irfan deserves respect, and offered to be around, which keeps the door open instead of making Irfan defend his partner.
How might Irfan have felt hearing Vishal's words?
Perhaps uncomfortable and quiet at first, but also seen; asking for chai the next week suggests he felt he had someone safe to talk to.

Dear Asif,
I've started this letter three times. Thank you for last Thursday.
When that stranger sent me the fake video with my face in it and said he'd send it to my whole contact list unless I paid, I was ready to do anything. I felt dirty, even though I hadn't done a single thing. You were the one who said, "Don't pay, don't delete, don't reply."
You sat with me while I screenshotted his profile, the messages and the payment link. You stayed while I called Papa, even though I was crying too hard to talk properly. Papa drove over that evening, and we reported the account on the app together. The next morning we filed a complaint at the cyber police station. The officer said many people get these messages and it is never the victim's fault.
The account is gone now. I still jump when my phone buzzes. But I'm not hiding anymore.
Irawati

What three things did Asif tell Irawati not to do?
'Don't pay, don't delete, don't reply.'
How did Irawati feel when the stranger's threat arrived?
Irawati felt dirty and desperate, ready to do anything, even though Irawati had done nothing wrong.
Which steps helped Irawati, and why?
Saving screenshots, calling Papa the same day, reporting the account on the app and filing a complaint with the cyber police; together they protected Irawati and got the account removed.
What might Papa have felt on getting Irawati's call?
Papa was probably shaken and protective, which is why Papa drove over that evening and went to the cyber police the next morning.

messages.content: What is the difference between jeera rice and plain rice?
Jeera rice is basic rice with cumin seeds fried in ghee or oil, then mixed in. It has a light smell and goes well with dal or curry. Plain rice has no tempering at all.
How do I make it in the pot?
Heat a spoon of ghee, add a teaspoon of cumin seeds and let them crackle. Add washed rice, stir for a minute, then pour in water and salt. Cover and cook on low flame until done.
Oh, and my friend Daniel is allergic to ghee. What can I use?
Use any plain oil, such as sunflower or coconut oil, for Daniel. The cumin will still crackle and smell good. Since he is allergic, make sure no ghee touches his pot or spoon.
Describe a plate of steaming momos on a cold evening, roughly 60 words, for a food blog.

There is nothing quite like a plate of steaming momos on a cold evening. The thin, soft wrappers are pleated by hand and puffed up from the steam. When you bite into one, hot juice spills out, so you have to be careful. Dip it in the fiery red chutney, and suddenly the cold outside does not matter at all.
What is my best friend's birthday?
I don't know, as I can't see your friends' details. Ask your friend, or look at a calendar you've noted it on.

98, the top score.
What was Sarita feeling when she saw Akash skip lunch?

What did Sarita do that eased Akash's isolation?
She refused to mock him, gave a specific compliment and invited him out to relax.
What is it like for Akash to hear "Show-off topper"?
Akash likely feels lonely and misunderstood, since his success brings pressure rather than joy.
Our kitten Ruby has started scratching the sofa. Mum is upset.
Kittens scratch to stretch, keep their claws in shape and mark their space, so she is not being naughty. She just needs a better place to do it. Do you have a scratching post for Ruby yet?
No, we only have a small toy mouse.
Then a post is the first thing to buy. Choose a tall, sturdy one, since Ruby will want to stretch fully. Put it right next to the sofa she likes, because cats scratch where they already spend time.
What if she ignores it?
Rub a little dried catnip on the post, or dangle her toy mouse near it so she touches it. Praise her each time she uses it. Most kittens switch within a week or two.
Okay, I will tell Mum the plan. Please remind me what I should put next to the sofa.
The scratching post, set right beside the sofa Ruby has been scratching. Add the catnip or the toy mouse to make it interesting. Your mum should see Ruby choosing the post fairly soon.

I'm Joseph, and I used to send voice notes like podcasts. Seven minutes, starting with the weather, ending with the point. Then Tanvir, who works nights at a call centre, told me he'd been listening to them on the bus with the volume down, catching one word in three.
So I changed how I do it. Now I start with the point. "Tanvir, Joseph here. Main thing: Sunday cricket is moved to eight. That's it. Thirty seconds." If there's more, I ask first: "Got two minutes for a longer one, or should I type?"
Last week I needed his advice on a job offer, which was going to be long. I texted, "Voice note or call later? Whatever suits you." He wrote, "Call at six, I'm free then."
At six he said, "Thanks for asking first. I actually had time to think."
It felt good to be the friend who makes things easier.

What time did Tanvir suggest for the call?
Tanvir wrote, "Call at six, I'm free then."
What was Joseph feeling after Tanvir said thanks?
Joseph felt pleased and proud of being the friend who makes things easier.
What habit could others take from Joseph?
Start a voice note with the main point, keep it short, and ask whether the other person has time or prefers text before sending a long one.
How does Tanvir experience Joseph's new voice notes?
Tanvir feels respected and less rushed, since he can catch the point quickly after night shifts and choose a time to think about longer matters.
A paragraph of about 45 words on why a good umbrella matters: it keeps you dry, it keeps your bag dry, and it works in sun as well as rain.
A good umbrella matters because it keeps you dry when the rain comes down. It also keeps your bag dry, so your books stay safe. It works in the sun as well as in the rain, so you can use it all year.

"You were up. I heard you. Why didn't you come for path?" Jasleen asked, pouring tea.

"I was up," Pankaj said. "I sat in my room."

"Your father did path every morning till his last day. You used to sit on his lap for it."

"I remember, Mummy. I love that memory."

"Then what happened, son? Is it that office? Those friends?"

"No one made me. I've been asking questions for a year. Some of the answers I used to accept don't sit right any more."

Jasleen set the kettle down hard. "So we were fools?"

"Never. Watching you pray is one of the steadiest things I know. I'm not laughing at it. I'm just not sure yet."

She was quiet a long time. "Will you still come on Sunday, for his anniversary?"

"Yes. I'll come, and I'll sit beside you. That part I'm sure of."

Who used to do path every morning till his last day?
Pankaj's father.
What does Pankaj feel about the family's practice, and how can you tell?
He feels warm about sitting on his father's lap for path and calls watching his mother pray one of the steadiest things he knows, so he is sad, not scornful.
How could Pankaj keep respect alive while holding his own view?
He could keep saying clearly that he admires her prayer, avoid mocking, and join family rituals like the anniversary where he honestly can.
How does Jasleen see Pankaj's absence from morning prayer?
She sees it as a loss of the family's shared life and fears it means he thinks they were fools.

On the last day before the Holi holidays, Mehak Didi brought her laptop to the little science club at the kasba school. "Watch the players in white shirts. Count how many times they pass the ball. Only white!"
Mohit leaned in, lips moving. Nine, ten, eleven. He ignored the black shirts completely. Fifteen, sixteen.
"Sixteen!" he shouted when it ended.
"Correct," said Mehak Didi. "And did anyone see the bear?"
"What bear?"
She played it again. Halfway through, a person in a fluffy bear costume strolled right through the middle of the players, waved, and walked off.
Mohit's jaw dropped. "That was NOT there before!"
"It was," Mehak Didi said, smiling. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention was busy."

Which players did Mehak Didi ask the club to watch?
The players in white shirts.
What does Mohit's "That was NOT there before!" suggest he felt?
He felt astonished and a bit disbelieving, since he was sure he had watched everything closely while counting.
What could Mohit do when something important might be missed?
He could remember that focusing hard on one task can hide other things, and take a second look or ask others what they noticed.
Why might Mehak Didi enjoy showing the video twice?
She knows the surprise will help the club remember that attention, not the eyes alone, decides what they see.

Fog had grounded every flight out of Lucknow, and Sonali's interview for the Bengaluru fellowship was at ten the next morning. Around her, people shouted at the airline desk. Her friend Nandini called. "What are you going to do?" Sonali took out a notebook and drew a line down the middle. On one side: the fog, the airline, the panel's decision. On the other: emailing the panel, checking the overnight train, preparing her answers. She emailed first, briefly and politely, asking about an online interview. She booked a train seat as a backup. Then she sat on her suitcase and practised her answers aloud. "And if they say no?" Nandini asked. "Then I'll have done what I could." Her stomach still fluttered, but her voice was calm. At midnight, the reply came: online would be fine.

Three-sentence summary of this passage, please.

Fog cancels every flight out of Lucknow the night before Sonali's fellowship interview in Bengaluru, so she lists what she can and cannot control. She emails the panel politely about an online interview, books a backup train seat, and practises her answers aloud. At midnight the panel replies that an online interview is fine.

In the school sick room, Sachin lay on the narrow bed with his knees pulled up. The nurse had checked him, found no fever and phoned his mother.
Neelam arrived still in her office clothes. She sat on the edge of the bed and held his hand. "Look what I brought." From her bag she took an orange toffee in a twist of paper. "Your favourite. It always helps your tummy, remember?"
Sachin didn't remember, but he unwrapped it. Neelam stroked his hair and told him about the stray puppy near their gate. Ten minutes later Sachin sat up. "It doesn't hurt much now."
The nurse nodded to Neelam. "Keep an eye on him tonight, and see the doctor if it keeps going."

What did Neelam bring in her bag?
An orange toffee in a twist of paper.
What was Sachin feeling once his mother sat with him?
He felt comforted and safer, and expecting the toffee to help seemed to ease the pain.
Why is the nurse's advice a sensible final step?
It keeps watch on the symptom and points to a doctor if it keeps going, so comfort doesn't replace real care.
How might the nurse see Neelam's toffee?
The nurse may see that the toffee is harmless and that Neelam's calm presence is what really soothes Sachin.

In the seminar room in Osaka, Noa lifted her chin as she defended her project, her shoulders back. Hiroshi, the classmate opposite, felt it like a challenge, and thought she was proud or ready to argue. Then the professor questioned a number and Noa's head dipped a little, her eyes going down to her notes. Hiroshi read that as sadness, or maybe polite deference, since it was how students often showed respect in that room. He wasn't sure. Hiroshi remembered that a lifted chin or a lowered head was only one clue, and that Noa was a new exchange student. When the seminar ended, he asked, "That was nerve-racking, wasn't it?" Noa let out a breath. "Very. I lifted my chin so I wouldn't shake."

Where did Noa defend her project?
She defended it in the seminar room in Osaka.
What did Hiroshi first think when Noa lifted her chin?
He felt it like a challenge and thought she was proud or ready to argue, though it was only one clue.
Why did Hiroshi ask his question at the end?
He knew the chin and the lowered head were single clues, and asking let him learn Noa was nervous.
What was Noa feeling when she lifted her chin?
She was nervous and lifted her chin so she wouldn't shake, so the gesture hid worry.

metadata.subtype: Lifting the chin and lowering the head [Interpreting]

Jasleen skipped the second meeting, and the third. The presentation was three weeks away and she told herself that Nandini and Sabina would sort it. They always did. She scrolled through videos while the shared document stayed half empty.

Nandini opened the same document at eleven that night and did another set of slides. She was tired, and she could feel resentment growing like a stone in her shoe. Sabina sent a note: "I'm on my third section too." Nandini almost kept doing it in silence. Then she didn't. She wrote in the chat, "Can we set who does what? I'll do the data. Sabina has the intro. Jasleen, can you take the conclusion and send it by Thursday? Let's check in Tuesday."

Jasleen read it and felt her cheeks go warm. She saw that it had been unfair, that two people had been holding her weight. She wrote her section that night, and it was not perfect, but it was hers. At the presentation Nandini went first, Sabina second. Jasleen, when it was her turn, said, "I did the conclusion, and Nandini and Sabina did most of the rest."

Whose turn was it to write the conclusion?
Jasleen was asked to take the conclusion.
How did the slide work look from Jasleen's side and from Nandini's side, and what changed after the chat message?

Jasleen skipped meetings and told herself Nandini and Sabina would sort it, while Nandini did slides at night and felt resentment. After Nandini wrote who does what and asked for the conclusion by Thursday, Jasleen wrote her own section.
What was Nandini feeling as she opened the shared document at eleven at night?
She felt tired and resentful, like a stone in her shoe.
What could Nandini do next time a group project starts this way?
She could set roles at the start, check in early, and raise it politely well before the deadline instead of doing everything silently.

At the preschool's pretend clinic corner, Vishal, five, put on the toy stethoscope. "I'm the doctor." Siddharth lay on the mat. "I have a tummy ache." "No, you broke your leg," said Vishal. "Tummy ache," said Siddharth firmly. Vishal paused. "Okay. You have a tummy ache and a broken leg." Siddharth laughed. "Okay!" Vishal bandaged his leg with a scarf and listened to his tummy.

What did Vishal put on?
The toy stethoscope.
What does Vishal's pause suggest before he changed the story?
He was working out how to keep his idea and Siddharth's, maybe feeling torn about giving up the broken leg.
How could a teacher support play like this?
Stay nearby and let them bargain, stepping in only if one child keeps overruling the other.
If you were Siddharth, how would you feel about Vishal's compromise?
Pleased and listened to, since the tummy ache stayed in the story.

At the drama society meeting in a Jayanagar classroom, the same three voices had been running the discussion about the annual play for forty minutes. Rashmi noticed Chinmay in the corner, nodding, saying nothing, though he had directed two plays in school. When the loudest member paused to check her phone, Rashmi said, "Chinmay, you've directed before. What would you do with the second act?" Chinmay hesitated. "I'd cut the long speech and show it instead. Maybe with shadows." There was a pause. Then the others leaned forward. "Shadows how?" For the next fifteen minutes, Chinmay talked, sketching on the board. The play changed. After the meeting he walked out beside Rashmi. "I didn't know how to get in," he said. "It felt like there was no space." "There was," Rashmi said. "Someone just had to make it."

How many plays had Chinmay directed in school?
Two plays.
What was Chinmay feeling before Rashmi asked him?
He felt shut out and unsure how to join, since it seemed there was no space for him to speak.
What did Rashmi do that made the meeting fairer?
She used a pause to ask Chinmay a specific question based on his experience, opening a turn for him.
How did the others respond once Chinmay spoke?
They leaned forward, asked questions, and let him sketch his idea, which changed the play.

I'm Hafsa. My little brother Nitin was building a train track when our cousin stepped on it and snapped a piece.
Nitin went red. His fists came up. I thought he would hit.
Then he did something new. He shut his eyes and breathed in through his nose, big, and blew out slowly, like blowing a candle. Once. Twice. Three times.
He opened his eyes and said, "Api, hug."
I hugged him. He was still shaky, but he picked up the broken piece and asked me to help fix it.

What did the cousin snap?
A piece of Nitin's train track.
What was Nitin feeling when he went red and raised his fists?
Nitin was angry that his track was broken, and close to hitting out.
How could Hafsa help Nitin keep using his breathing?
Hafsa could notice and praise it later and practise the candle breath with him when he is calm.
How does Hafsa see Nitin's breathing?
Hafsa sees it as something new and surprising; she expected him to hit and is relieved he calmed himself.

Monday: In the canteen, Aakash's gang snatched Yash's chips and poured them on his head. Thomas felt his fists clench, but fighting would make it worse. After the gang left, he sat beside Yash. “You okay? Want some of mine?” Yash nodded, barely.
Wednesday: Aakash started again. Thomas called out, casually, “Aakash! Coach is looking for you about the team list.” Aakash left, frowning. Yash let out a breath.
Friday: It was worse, and Aakash shoved Yash. Thomas went straight to Mr Varghese on canteen duty. “Sir, Yash needs help near the water cooler.” Mr Varghese went over at once, separated them and took Aakash to the vice-principal. He called Yash's parents that afternoon.

What did Aakash's gang pour on Yash's head?
They poured Yash's chips on his head.
How did Yash seem to feel when Thomas sat beside him?
He seemed shaken and quiet, nodding barely, but probably a little comforted to have someone check on him.
Which of Thomas's actions were safe, and why?
Checking on Yash, distracting Aakash with a message, and getting a teacher were all low-risk choices that helped without starting a fight.
How might Aakash see Thomas's call about the coach?
Aakash probably didn't realise it was a distraction and just felt annoyed at being interrupted.

In the visitors' room of the university hostel, under a ticking clock and a notice about mess timings, Minakshi had her lines ready. She and Saurabh had drilled them for three evenings in the common room: "Maa, I'm leaving the PhD. I have a job offer in Pune. I've thought it through. I'm not changing my mind."
Her mother arrived with a tiffin of her favourite aloo and listened. Then she said, "Are you eating? You look thin. Is something wrong with your guide?"
Minakshi went back to the script. "I've thought it through. I'm not changing my mind."
"I didn't ask you to change it, beta." Her mother's eyes filled. "I asked if you're all right."
Minakshi stared at the clock. She had an answer for anger, for tears about money, for "what will people say". She had nothing for this.

What did Minakshi's mother bring?
A tiffin of her favourite aloo.
What was Minakshi feeling as she stared at the clock?
Minakshi felt stuck and awkward, realising the script had no answer for her mother's real worry.
What could Minakshi say instead of repeating the script?
She could drop the lines and answer honestly: how she is, whether anything went wrong with her guide, and why the job matters to her.
How did Minakshi's mother experience the scripted replies?
She felt hurt and unheard; she was worried about her daughter's health and was answered as if she were arguing.

metadata.subtype: Approach: over-rehearsing until it sounds scripted [Pitfall]

messages.content: What is the avaroha of Raga Durga?
The avaroha of Raga Durga is: S' D P M R S.

Saturday football practice in Lisbon was nearly over when seven-year-old Gabriel went down clutching his ankle. Nadia, twenty-five and the team's volunteer coach, jogged over, but Gabriel's mother got there first. 'Oh no, oh no, is it broken? Gabi, does it hurt a lot? Where? Here? Here?' With every question, Gabriel sobbed harder. Nadia knelt beside them. She kept her voice slow and even. 'Hi, Gabi. You took a big tumble. Let's see together. Can you wiggle your toes for me?' He wiggled them, hiccuping. 'Good. We'll put the ice pack on, and you can tell me which player you were chasing.' His mother, watching, took a breath and started stroking his hair instead of pressing his foot. Gabriel's crying slowed to sniffs. Nadia said, 'If it's still sore tomorrow or it worries you, have a doctor look.' His mother nodded, calmer too.

What did Nadia ask Gabriel to do first?
She asked him to wiggle his toes.
How did Gabriel's mother seem to feel when she reached him first?
She was very frightened, asking whether it was broken and where it hurt, over and over.
What did Nadia do that changed the moment, and what did she still advise?
She spoke slowly, checked his toes, gave him an ice pack and something to talk about, and still said a doctor should look if it was sore tomorrow or worrying.
How might Gabriel's mother see the moment afterwards?
She may notice that her own worried questions made Gabriel cry harder, and that his crying slowed once she matched Nadia's calm.

Vinita, you asked on the podcast about the hardest thing I've done as a friend. I'm Sarita. When I was fifteen, my best friend Meenal's father died suddenly. I went to her house every day that first week. I sat with her while she cried, and when I got home I cried too, for hours. I couldn't sleep. I'd lie awake thinking about her father and feel sick. After two weeks I was exhausted. Then I did something I'm ashamed of: I started avoiding her. I took a different bus. I didn't answer her calls. It wasn't that I didn't care. I cared so much it flattened me. My mother noticed and asked. When I told her, she said, 'You can't carry all of it. Let's work out how to be there without drowning.' That night I called Meenal back.

How old was Sarita when Meenal's father died?
Fifteen.
What was Sarita feeling on starting to avoid Meenal?
Sarita felt exhausted and overwhelmed, then ashamed, having absorbed so much of Meenal's grief.
What did Sarita's mother do that helped, and why?
She noticed, asked and helped Sarita find a way to support Meenal without drowning, which let Sarita call back that night.
How might Meenal have felt when Sarita stopped answering?
Meenal probably felt hurt and lonelier, losing a close friend just when Meenal needed a friend most.

metadata.subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]

messages.content:
What is this extract about? One sentence only.

"At the same time," he remarked after a pause, during which he had sat puffing at his long pipe and gazing down into the fire, "you can hardly be open to a charge of sensationalism, for out of these cases which you have been so kind as to interest yourself in, a fair proportion do not treat of crime, in its legal sense, at all. The small matter in which I endeavoured to help the King of Bohemia, the singular experience of Miss Mary Sutherland, the problem connected with the man with the twisted lip, and the incident of the noble bachelor, were all matters which are outside the pale of the law. But in avoiding the sensational, I fear that you may have bordered on the trivial."
The speaker says the recorded cases are not sensational, since many involve no crime, but warns they may have become trivial.
My cat hisses at our new puppy. Will they ever get along?
They often do, but it takes time. Hissing is normal at the start, since the cat is protecting her space. How long has the puppy been with you?
Three days. The cat is called Mishti and the puppy is Bruno.
Three days is very early. Keep Mishti and Bruno in separate rooms for now, and let them smell each other's blankets. Give Mishti a high shelf where she can feel safe.
When can I let them meet?
When Mishti is calm and eating near the door that separates them. Then let them see each other with Bruno on a leash, and reward both for staying calm. Go slowly.
What happens if Bruno chases her?
Stop the meeting at once and separate them. Chasing frightens Mishti and teaches Bruno a bad habit. Try again later with Bruno on a leash and a treat to distract him.
I will try that. Which animal is the cat again?
The cat is Mishti. She is the one who hissed at Bruno, the new puppy. Keep her high shelf free, so she always has a safe place from him.
How many windows does my house have?
I don't know how many windows your house has, as I can't see it. Walk around and count them.

On the verandah of their village house, Trisha, six, was playing with the clay horse when her little sister Swati grabbed it.

"Give it back!" Trisha felt hot all over. She loved Swati, but right now she wanted to pinch her.

She raised her fingers. Then she stopped and called, "Aaji! Swati took the horse!"

Aaji came out. "Five more minutes for Trisha, then Swati."

Trisha kept counting on her fingers. When the time was up, she handed it over.

Who did Trisha call for help?
Trisha called Aaji.
What was Trisha feeling when Swati grabbed the horse?
Trisha felt furious and hot all over, but also still loved her sister.
What did Trisha do instead of pinching?
Trisha stopped herself and called Aaji, who set turns.
How might Swati feel waiting for her turn?
Swati may feel impatient but reassured that her turn will come.

Payal had posted the plan for Vandana's surprise birthday in the class group chat at nine. By lunch, only four of twenty had replied. The read receipts showed Vandana's cousin had seen it and said nothing. Payal felt a tightness in her chest. Were people annoyed? Bored? She started drafting a message, "Guys?? Anyone?", then deleted it. Her friend Meera reminded her, "Half of them are in practicals till four." Payal put the phone in her bag. At five, the replies came in a rush: two offering to bring snacks, one apologising for the delay. The silence had been schedules, not disapproval. She still felt a little foolish, and also relieved she had not sent the message.

How many of twenty had replied by lunch?
Four of twenty had replied.
What did Payal fear the silence meant, and what did it turn out to be?
She feared people were annoyed or bored, but it turned out that they were busy in practicals.
What could Payal do next time a group is slow to answer?
She could wait a few hours or ask one person privately, rather than sending a pushy message.
How might a person who was in practicals feel about receiving "Guys?? Anyone?"
They might feel pressured or think Payal was upset, even though they were just busy.
Neighbour ka bachcha hamare ghar ki ghanti baja ke bhaag jaata hai. English mein uske papa ko kaise bataun?

Keep it light and friendly: "Hi, just letting you know, your son has been ringing our doorbell and running away. It's probably a game, but could you have a word with him?" "Have a word" means talk to someone briefly.

The school bus was crawling through traffic, the teacher was at the front on the phone, and the back seats were loud. When Maria sang a Konkani song her grandmother taught her, three boys copied the words in silly voices and hooted. Maria kept singing, but her voice got smaller. Rashmi, sitting across from them, felt a laugh bubble up. It was a funny sound. Then she saw Maria's hands gripping the seat and her eyes fixed on the window. This wasn't laughing with her. Rashmi clapped along to the tune instead. “Teach me the chorus?” Maria looked at her, surprised, and began again, louder.

Who taught Maria the Konkani song?
Her grandmother taught her the song.
What was Maria feeling as her voice got smaller?
Maria felt hurt and embarrassed by the boys copying her in silly voices.
What did Rashmi do instead of laughing, and why did it help?
Rashmi clapped along and asked to learn the chorus, turning the moment from mockery into warm, shared fun.
How might the boys see their hooting?
They might think it was harmless fun, not seeing Maria's gripping hands and fixed eyes that showed hurt.

Ujjwal's sociology paper was due Monday at 9 a.m. On Friday he played football. On Saturday he helped a cousin move flats. On Sunday at 10 p.m. he opened a blank document.
His roommate Dhruv looked over. “You started?”
“Tonight's the best time. Pressure makes me sharp.”
At 4 a.m. he was pasting in half-read quotes. He submitted at 8:57.
Two weeks later the paper came back with a C and a comment: “Interesting idea, underdeveloped argument.”
“Obviously,” Ujjwal said loudly in the corridor. “I wrote it in one night. If I'd spent a week, it'd be an A.”
Dhruv shrugged. “Maybe. What was the interesting idea?”
Ujjwal opened his mouth. He wasn't sure. He hadn't had time to find out.

What time did Ujjwal submit the paper?
Ujjwal submitted it at 8:57.
Why did Ujjwal say loudly that he wrote it in one night?
He felt embarrassed by the C, and the rush gave him a way to feel the grade said nothing about his ability.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
Leaving it to the last night meant the idea stayed underdeveloped; starting a few days earlier would let him learn what his argument actually was.
How might Dhruv see Ujjwal's excuse?
Dhruv seems unconvinced and curious, gently pointing out that Ujjwal missed the chance to develop his own idea.

metadata.subtype: Leaving an assignment for the last night [Actor]

In the small-town school in Sangli, the debate club was starting, and Chetan's classmate Nikita asked him to join. He was good at speaking; everyone said so. But he was also first in class, and the debate club met on Fridays, when he usually revised. "What if my rank drops?" he said. "And what if I'm bad at debate and people laugh?" Nikita shrugged. "What if you're great?" Chetan didn't answer. He kept revising on Fridays. He also stopped sitting with his old friends at lunch, because a new group had invited him, and he didn't want to lose either. So he ate alone, reading. By December, his rank was still first. But he felt oddly small. The debate club won the district trophy. He watched from the back of the hall, clapping, alone.

When did the debate club meet?
On Fridays.
Why did Chetan refuse to join the debate club?
He feared losing his first rank or being laughed at more than he valued possible gains, so staying safe felt better even though it left him feeling small.
What small step could Chetan have taken?
He could have tried a few debate sessions while keeping some Friday revision, testing whether his rank really drops.
How might Nikita feel watching Chetan clap from the back?
Nikita may feel a little sad for him, knowing he could have been part of the win.

metadata.subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]

The monsoon had flooded the bus stop, and Avni, five, stood under the shelter with her aunt Kashish, both crowded against strangers. Avni stared at a girl in a wheelchair, turning her head as the girl rolled past. Kashish felt heat in her face. She bent down and whispered, "You're wondering about her wheels, aren't you? It's okay to be curious. It's better to ask than to stare. Let's smile and say hello if she wants to talk." Avni smiled, and the girl smiled back.

Where were Avni and Kashish standing?
They were standing under the shelter at a flooded bus stop.
What was Avni probably thinking about as she stared at the girl?
She was probably curious about the wheels, which is what Kashish guessed. She could also have been simply fascinated by something new.
What did Kashish do well when she saw Avni staring?
She stayed kind and said it was okay to be curious, then gave Avni a friendly alternative instead of shaming her.
How might the girl in the wheelchair feel about being stared at, and about the smile?
A long stare may feel uncomfortable, whereas a smile can make her feel included and respected.
