Diwali night.
Dear diary, I did something bad. On the terrace, all the colony kids were bursting crackers and being loud, and somebody started laughing at Keerthana's frock because it was last year's. Then everybody laughed, and somehow I was laughing too, and I even said 'hand-me-down queen'. It was dark and smoky and nobody could see who said what, and it felt like the noise said it, not me. Keerthana went downstairs. Then I saw her mother's face at the door. My stomach dropped. Keerthana helped me with fractions all summer! Amma asked why I was quiet, and I told her. She didn't shout. She said, 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark.' Tomorrow I'll go and say sorry, and take her some of our kaju katli.
Leela

Why were the kids laughing at Keerthana's frock?
Because it was last year's.
What did Leela feel on seeing Keerthana's mother at the door?
Leela felt a sinking guilt, stomach dropping, realising the teasing had hurt someone who had been kind.
What does Amma's line 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark' teach?
That being part of a noisy crowd doesn't remove responsibility; Leela still chose the words.
How might Keerthana have felt going downstairs?
Keerthana probably felt humiliated and hurt, mocked by a crowd that included someone she had helped.

Abraham is buying some toiletries and creates a budget of $60 for his shopping. He buys 4 shower gels for $4 each, a tube of toothpaste for $3, and a box of laundry detergent. If he has $30 remaining in his budget, how much money, in dollars, did Abraham spend on the box of laundry detergent?

Shower gel costs Abraham 4 shower gels * $4 = $16.
So the shower gel and toothpaste combined have cost him $16 + $3 = $19.
He had money remaining in his budget so the total cost of his shopping must have been $60 - $30 = $30.
The box of laundry detergent therefore cost him $30 - $19 = $11.
The answer is 11.

In the back seat, Mohit stopped kicking his feet. "Papa, your nose is doing the angry thing."

Eshaan caught his eye in the mirror and let out a breath. "You're right. I'm feeling cross at the traffic, not at you. Let's slow down together." He breathed in slowly. Mohit copied him, puffing his cheeks. 🙂

Ten minutes.

He was likely uneasy and a little worried, because he had sensed tension in Papa's flaring nostrils. He may also just have been curious about the face Papa was making.

Eshaan named the feeling calmly and said it was about the traffic, not Mohit, then showed slow breathing, which eased the tension for both.

At the handloom cooperative in the small town of Chanderi, Aditi had mentored Charu for two years. When the mill cut twenty weavers, Charu was one of them. Charu came to the co-op office and talked about it with great calm. "Orders are down, the new machines are faster. It had to happen. I understand it completely." She listed three other co-ops she'd applied to. Aditi noticed Charu's tea sat untouched, and her eyes were ringed dark. Charu's neighbour had mentioned she'd stopped coming out for the evening walk. Aditi didn't argue with the logic. When Charu paused, Aditi said gently, "You've explained it very well. Now tell me how it feels." Charu opened her mouth for another reason. None came. She looked at the loom in the corner, the one she'd learnt on. "It feels like losing my hands," she whispered.

How many weavers did the mill cut?
Twenty weavers.
What made Aditi doubt that Charu's calm was the whole story?
Aditi felt concerned seeing the untouched tea, the dark circles, and hearing Charu had stopped her evening walk, signs that didn't match the calm words.
Which of Aditi's choices helped most, and why?
Not arguing the logic but asking how it feels, which let Charu move from explaining to expressing her loss.

Charu might feel exposed but also relieved, finally naming the grief behind the calm.

Tenzin, you keep saying you're "just tired". Let me, your old Urmila Didi from the ward, tell you something. When I was twenty-two I was a staff nurse in my first year, taking double shifts because I thought saying no meant I was weak. For two months I stopped eating proper meals. I stopped going to my friend Leela's for Sunday lunch. I cried in the linen room and told myself everyone does. One morning I stood at the trolley and couldn't remember why I was there. My matron, a stern woman called Mrs Gomes, took me into her office. She didn't scold. She said, "This has gone on too long. You'll see the staff doctor today, and I'm taking you off doubles." I was ashamed then. Now I think she saved my career. So when you say "just tired" for the third month, I hear my younger self.

Where did Urmila cry?
In the linen room.
What was young Urmila feeling when Mrs Gomes took her into the office?
Urmila felt ashamed at the time, believing that needing help meant being weak.
What was the turning point in Urmila's story, and why did it matter?
Mrs Gomes stepped in that same day, sending Urmila to the staff doctor and ending double shifts, so help came early before things got worse.
How might Leela have seen Urmila missing Sunday lunches?
Leela probably noticed her friend pulling away and felt worried or hurt, without knowing how exhausted Urmila was.

She lowered her head over her plate. Seema watched from the queue. She thought of marching over and telling them off, but she didn't want to make Farida the centre of a scene. In June.

Seema felt uncomfortable and protective of Farida, but careful not to make her the centre of a scene.

She sat down with Farida and chatted about biryani, which showed Farida she wasn't alone and cooled things down without a lecture.

For months Aparna said nothing about Mridul's late deliveries. She smiled, covered the gaps, and kept a private tally while resentment grew. Then, in the middle of a client call, she typed into the team chat: "Third time this month. Do you even care?" The client saw it. The room went silent, and the deal cooled.

The next week they finally sat down, but a bigger argument surfaced. Aparna wanted to raise money now; Mridul wanted to stay on their own savings. Each repeated their case louder. Then Aparna asked, "Why does this matter so much to you?" Mridul admitted he feared losing control of the product. Aparna said she feared a rival taking the market before they were ready.

They still stalled on equity, so they called Vijay, who had run a company for years. He asked each of them to say the other's view back before he offered any option. It took two tries, and each corrected the other.

After a quarter, both agreed that Mridul froze on sales calls. They swapped: Aparna took the customers, Mridul the delivery. Mridul's shoulders dropped, Aparna started closing deals, and the team channel got quieter in a good way.

What did Aparna type into the team chat during the client call?
She typed, "Third time this month. Do you even care?"
How did asking why help in a way that Aparna's months of silence did not?
Asking why revealed Mridul's fear of losing control and Aparna's fear of a rival taking the market, while her months of saying nothing let resentment grow until it hit the client call.
What was Mridul feeling about raising money?
Anxious about losing control of the product.
What could Aparna do if she notices another late delivery?
Aparna could speak to Mridul privately and soon, name the specific delay and ask what is getting in the way.

Kishore wrote his two rules on the inside of his study-table drawer in their Chandigarh flat, where no one else would see them.
If I sit down to study, the phone goes to the shoe rack by the door.
If it's after ten, the phone sleeps on the hall charger.
The first evening he forgot rule one and found himself twenty minutes into a video with his physics book open. He got up, walked the phone to the shoe rack and came back. The second evening he did it without much thought. By the second week he didn't have to decide at all; sitting down meant the phone went.
His friend Baljeet noticed on Saturday. “You've been replying late.”
“It's on the hall charger after ten,” Kishore said. “Rule.”
“Your rule or your parents'?”
“Mine. That's why it works.”
His test marks that month rose only a little. But he was asleep before eleven most nights.

Where does Kishore's phone go when he sits down to study?
To the shoe rack by the door.
How does Kishore seem to feel about the rules by the second week?
He seems relieved and confident, since the rules had become automatic and no longer needed a decision.
What else could Kishore add if the phone still pulls at the study table?
Keep a clock or timer on the desk, so there is no reason to fetch the phone to check the time.
How do the rules look to Baljeet?
Baljeet first notices only the late replies, then learns the rules are Kishore's own, which may make them seem worth copying.

messages.content: Chandra is going on a monster hunt. After a big storm, there have been lost monsters all around the castle grounds for the last 5 days. Chandra wants to rope them all up and return them to the swamps where they will be the most comfortable. On the first day she saw 2 monsters near the castle walls. Every day after that she saw double the amount as the day before. After 5 days how many monsters does she need to lead back to the swamps?

On the first day Chandra saw 2 monsters and on day 2 she saw twice that amount, 2 x 2 = 4 monsters seen on day 2.
On day 3 she saw double that amount of monsters, 4 x 2 = 8.
On day 4 she saw double that amount of monsters, 8 x 2 = 16.
On day 5 she saw double that amount of monsters, 16 x 2 = 32.
Altogether Chandra saw 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 lost monsters = 62 total lost monsters that Chandra needs to lead back to the swamps.
The answer is 62.
My roommate at hostel, George, snores loudly and I can't sleep. I don't want to be rude.
That's a tricky spot. You can raise it kindly without blaming him. Have you spoken to him?
No. We only met two weeks ago.
You could say, "Hey George, I'm having trouble sleeping. Could we figure something out together?" Starting with your own difficulty usually keeps it friendly.
What could we do? I don't think he can stop snoring.
You might try earplugs or soft background sound, and he could sleep on his side if that helps him. You can also ask the warden if you could move your bed a little further away.
Earplugs seem easiest. Where would I get them?
A local pharmacy or general store usually sells them for a small amount. Try a soft foam pair and see if they feel comfortable at night.
So what do I say to George first?
Begin with, "Hey George, I'm having trouble sleeping." Then ask if you can figure something out together, and mention that earplugs are your first idea.

The next week the marks came out. Vera and most of the others had high marks. Zeynep had a middling pass and a note: "Q4 method wrong, but reasoning clearly shown."

The fear arrived fast: scholarship reviews, rankings, being the slow one. Under it sat something steadier. On Friday, when the lecturer went through question four in the tutorial, Zeynep followed every step, and she was the one who asked the question half the room needed.

Eleven people reacted with a thumbs up.
What mixed feelings did Zeynep have when the marks came out?
She felt fear about scholarship reviews, rankings and being the slow one, and under it a steadier calm about having done her own work.

She kept her work her own and truly learned the method, which showed in the tutorial; the cost was a lower mark than those who used the bought answers.

Jill has a difficult test to study for.  She decides to study one day for 2 hours.  The next day she doubles this amount, and the day after that she studies one hour less than the previous day.  How many minutes does Jill study over the 3 days?

First, we need to determine how many hours Jill studied in total. To find this out, we begin by performing 2*2= 4 hours spent on day two, double what she spent on day 1.
Next, we perform 4-1= 3 hours to determine the amount she studied on the third day.
We then add 2+4+3= 9 hours spent in total across 3 days.
Since there are 60 minutes in an hour, she studied 9*60=540 minutes in total.
The answer is 540.

With the other teacher absent, Tenzin had two classes squeezed into one room, sixty-eight children, and the fans rattling. Wasim, ten, finished the fractions task in three minutes. "Sir, why can't you divide by zero? What actually happens?" Before Tenzin could answer, Wasim was drumming on the desk, and the back row joined in. At nine, Gautam brought home a science paper with one wrong answer circled in red. His parents, Pradeep and Sangeeta, studied it and asked, "Why did you lose that mark?" Neither asked what he liked about the experiment. After that, Gautam folded such papers small and hid them in his atlas, and learned to say, "Nothing much."

At twenty-one, Gautam was given a project on water use in his city. He researched for three weeks, redrew the outline eleven times and told his roommate, "It's not ready to show anyone yet." Every version looked flawed to him: the second heading was clumsy, the third source felt weak. Other students were already drafting. Reading one more article seemed safer than writing a single paragraph that could be marked down.

On the deadline's eve Gautam looked at the tidy, untouched document and thought of the atlas. He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence anyway, though his stomach was tight.

How many times did Gautam redraw the outline?
He redrew the outline eleven times.
How is the way Gautam hid papers at nine linked to his endless preparation at twenty-one?

At nine Gautam learns that love and approval follow marks, so he hides mistakes; at twenty-one the same fear of a marked-down page keeps him researching and redrawing the outline rather than starting, which is perfectionism as paralysis.
What was Gautam probably feeling as he told his roommate the outline was not ready to show anyone?
Gautam was afraid of being judged, so preparing felt safer than exposing a rough draft.
What small step did Gautam take on the eve of the deadline, and why does it matter?
He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence, which breaks the cycle of preparing because a rough start is easier than a perfect one.

Dear Pradeep,
Thank you for the first three weeks. I want to be honest about what helps me do my best work.
The open floor is very loud for me. By afternoon I find it hard to think. Could I sit at the desk near the back wall, or wear noise-cancelling headphones?

Kiran enjoys the data cleaning project.

I'm Chandrika, from the flat opposite, and I was watering my tulsi when Farhan came up the stairs after the badminton final. His racket hung from one hand. His shoulders had sunk so low his school bag slid off one side, and he didn't hitch it back. His mother opened the door. “Cheer up, beta, it's only a game!” she said brightly. Farhan's shoulders dropped even more. His grandfather, behind her, said nothing at first. He just took the bag and said, “Three sets in that heat. Tiring, and disappointing.” Farhan leaned into him. I don't know what he felt, but his shoulders came up a little.

How many sets did Farhan play?
Farhan played three sets in the heat.
What do Farhan's sinking shoulders suggest after the final?
They suggest he felt sad and defeated after losing, too low even to hitch his bag back up.

Why does a bicycle tyre go soft slowly even when it has no puncture?
Air slowly seeps out through the rubber and the valve. Because rubber is not perfectly airtight and the valve is not either, a little air escapes all the time.
A step pyramid is built from cubes: a 4 x 4 layer at the bottom, then 3 x 3, then 2 x 2, then one cube on top. How many cubes are there? How many would a pyramid with a 6 x 6 bottom layer need?

Answer: 30 cubes; the 6-layer pyramid needs 91.

Count layer by layer, including the cubes you cannot see inside: 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30. The layers are the square numbers, so the total is a sum of squares. With a 6 x 6 bottom: 36 + 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 91. (There is a formula: n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6; for n = 6: 6 x 7 x 13 / 6 = 91.) Common mistake: counting only the cubes that show on the outside. From the front you see 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 faces, but most of the 30 cubes are hidden.

"Shankar, the deadline was Friday. Where's the report?" Jyoti asked, in front of the whole team.
"Waiting on your figures, Jyoti. Like always."

Why does the sun seem to rise in the east?

The sun only seems to move; the Earth turning towards the east brings the sun into view from the east. Because our own spot is carried around with the spinning Earth, we are turned toward the sun in the morning from that side, and it appears to climb into the sky.

Keep sitting with Omkar, offer breaks and walks, stay kind, and let the adults who now know help.

Why does it rain more in some parts of India than others?

Much of India's rain comes with the monsoon winds, which carry moisture from the sea. When these winds meet mountains like the Western Ghats, the air rises, cools and drops heavy rain on the side facing the sea.
So the other side of the mountains gets less?
Yes. By the time the air crosses the mountains, it has lost much of its moisture. That drier area behind the mountains is called a rain shadow.

"There is but one thing to do. It must be done at once. You must put this piece of paper which you have shown us into the brass box which you have described. The length of the straight part of a river is three times shorter than the crooked part. If the river is 80 miles long, how long is the straight part of the river?

Let's say the river's length in the straight part of the river is x.
The total length of the river is the length of the straight part plus 3 times the length of the straight part for the crooked part, which is x+3x = 80
The total length of the river is 4x=80
The straight part of the river is x=80/4 = 20 miles.
The answer is 20.

Joe had 200 data points on his dataset. He then added 20% more data points to the dataset. If he reduced the data points by 1/4 of the total data points, calculate the total number of data points the dataset contains.

When Joe added 20% more data points to the dataset, the data points in the dataset increased by 20/100*200 = 40 data points.
The total number of data points increased to 200+40 = 240
If he reduced the data points by 1/4 of the total data points, the data points reduced by 1/4*240 =60
The total number of data points left in the dataset after Joe reduced the data points by 1/4 of the total data points is 240-60= 180
The answer is 180.

The bank branch in Indore was crowded with pensioners on the first of the month, so Rajni and Siddharth waited forty minutes for their turn at the help desk.

They had come to add Siddharth's number to the alerts on Rajni's salary account, so he would get the same messages she did. It was Rajni's suggestion. After the loan she had hidden for her brother, she wanted him to stop guessing.

"And mine too," Siddharth told the clerk, sliding his own passbook across. "Add her number on my account."

Rajni glanced at him. "You don't have to."

"If it's only you being watched, it's a punishment. If it's both of us, it's just how we run things now."

On the auto ride home they talked about her brother's next request, which would surely come, and agreed on how they would decide: together, over a weekend, and never on the phone the same day he asked.

"For a year," Rajni said. "Then we see."

"Then we see," he agreed.

How long did Rajni and Siddharth wait for their turn at the help desk?
Forty minutes.
How does Rajni feel when Siddharth adds her number to his account too?
She is surprised and touched, perhaps a little relieved, because it shows he does not see the arrangement as a punishment only for her.
What makes their plan for the brother's next request a good one?
They agree beforehand to decide together, over a weekend, and not on the same day he asks, so neither is pushed into a hidden decision under pressure.
What would change if only Rajni's account were made visible?
As Siddharth says, it would feel like a punishment; she might feel watched and he might keep checking instead of trusting it as a shared habit.

I've worked with Reena at the veterinary clinic for two years. She's been a vet for five, and I've watched how she handles hunches.

Last week a dog came in limping. Reena said, "I think it's the hip, not the paw." She seemed sure. But instead of treating right away, she took an X-ray and asked Dr Madhuri, the senior vet, to look too. The X-ray showed she was right.

Another time, a farmer asked her about his cow's feed mix. Reena said, "I don't know enough about cattle feed. Let me find you someone who does."

I don't know what goes on in her head. But I've noticed she trusts her gut with dogs and cats, checks it anyway, and says "not my area" without embarrassment.

What did the X-ray show about the limping dog?
That Reena was right; it was the hip.
What does Reena's calm "not my area" suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels secure and humble, confident in her own field but comfortable admitting what she doesn't know.

Three plastic chairs cost as much as a portable table. Five plastic chairs cost $55. If Manny wants to buy one portable table and two chairs, how much will be left in his $100?

Each plastic chair costs $55/5 = $11.
Two chairs cost $11 x 2 = $22.
A portable table costs $11 x 3 = $33.
Manny has to pay a total of $22 + $33 = $55.
Thus, Manny will be left with $100 - $55 = $45.
The answer is 45.

I know no medium: I never in my life have known any medium in my dealings with positive, hard characters, antagonistic to my own, between absolute submission and determined revolt. I have always faithfully observed the one, up to the very moment of bursting, sometimes with volcanic vehemence, into the other; and as neither present circumstances warranted, nor my present mood inclined me to mutiny, I observed careful obedience to St. John's directions; and in ten minutes I was treading the wild track of the glen, side by side with him.

How does the narrator say she deals with strong, hard people?
She knows only two ways: complete obedience or firm revolt. She obeys until she bursts into revolt, but this time she has no reason to rebel, so she follows St. John's directions.
What does "break the news" mean? And what is "conformity"? Then, what is wrong with this sentence? "She looks like happy today." And one more: why do we use a lock on a bicycle?

1. It means to tell someone something important, often bad. For example: the teacher broke the news about the cancelled trip.
2. As a noun, "conformity" means behaviour that follows the rules or customs that others follow.
3. Corrected: She looks happy today. Why: "look" takes an adjective directly; "look like" takes a noun.
4. It stops someone from taking it away. Because a lock fastens the bicycle to a post or holds its wheel, so it cannot be ridden off easily.

The coaching centre put up the new batch list today. I've been moved from A to C. They read the names out loud. In the C room, the instructor said, "Welcome to the back benches. Ramesh

A tiny island gets a visitor. Can you tell that story?

The island of Cheeru was so small that you could walk around it in ten minutes. Only a few palm trees, some crabs and a family of seagulls lived there. Nobody ever visited.

One stormy morning, a battered rowboat washed up on the sand. In it lay a young man named Joel, dizzy and sunburned. The crabs scuttled away. The gulls stared.

Joel crawled to a palm and cracked open a coconut. He rested for two days, drinking and sleeping. On the third, a gull dropped a fish at his feet, and he laughed weakly.

A passing fishing boat spotted his waving shirt and took him home. Joel promised to come back, and a year later, he did, with a sack of seeds and a small flag.

Joe plays a soccer tournament with his team. Matches won score 3 points for the winning team and tied matches score 1 point for both teams. Joe and his team won 1 game and drew 3. The first-place team has won 2 games and tied 2. By how many points did the first-place team beat Joe's team?

For 1 match won, Joe's team scored 1 * 3 = 3 points.
For 3 tied games, Joe's team scored 3 * 1 = 3 points.
In total, Joe's team scored 3 + 3 = 6 points.
For 2 games won, the first-place team scored 2 * 3 = 6 points
For 2 tied games, the first-place team scored 2 * 1 = 2 points
In total, the first-place team scored 6 + 2 = 8 points.
The first-place team outscored Joe's team by 8 - 6 = 2 points.
The answer is 2.

Two straight roads meet at a crossing C at an angle of 70 degrees. A lamp post must be the same distance from both roads, inside the 70 degrees angle. Where can it go?

Answer: On the bisector of the 70 degrees angle, the line from C that makes 35 degrees with each road.

The distance from a point to a road is measured along the PERPENDICULAR. Points equally far from two crossing lines lie on the ANGLE BISECTORS. Construction: with centre C draw an arc cutting both roads, at X and Y. With centres X and Y and the same radius draw two arcs crossing at Z. Rule CZ: it splits the angle into 35 degrees + 35 degrees. Why: CX = CY, XZ = YZ and CZ is shared, so the triangles CXZ and CYZ are congruent (SSS), and angle XCZ = angle YCZ. The full locus for the two whole roads is TWO lines at right angles: the bisector of the 70 degrees angle and the bisector of the 110 degrees angle next to it (35 degrees + 55 degrees = 90 degrees).

A smaller child on the path saw him coming and burst into tears.
"He's not attacking, he's flying," Kunal said to the child's mother, catching Kishore gently round the middle. "Slow plane, Kishore." Kishore kept his arms wide, but walked, grinning.

"Aaaah!"

The smaller child likely felt frightened, seeing a big running figure with arms out, even though Kishore meant no harm.
Toddler story wanted: a pig who loves mud.

Pinky the pig loved mud. Squelch, squelch, squelch! She rolled in it in the morning. She rolled in it at noon. She rolled in it at night.

One day, the farmer's little girl, Tina, came to the sty. "Pinky, you are dirty!" she said.

Pinky grunted.

Tina got a bucket of water and a soft brush. Scrub, scrub, scrub! Pinky squealed and wriggled. Soon she was clean and pink, and her skin glowed in the sun.

Tina went to fetch a towel. Pinky looked at her clean self. Then she looked at the mud. Squelch! She jumped right back in.

Tina laughed and shook her head. "Okay, Pinky," she said. "Tomorrow we will wash again."

Jeevan and his cousin Sangeeta shared two rooms above a tailor's shop in Karad. That evening Jeevan heard the gate clang before Sangeeta even reached the stairs. She had gone to the college office to see her practical marks. The parcel boy followed with her textbook order.

"You call this packed? The cover is bent! Do you people even look?" she shouted. The boy mumbled sorry and hurried off.

Jeevan wanted to say, "That wasn't his fault." He bit it back and put the kettle on.

Later, over chai on the roof, he said only, "The marks went badly?"

Sangeeta stared at the fields. "Eleven out of forty. Madam didn't even check my file properly." A pause. "I shouted at that poor boy instead of her."

"Maybe tell Madam, not the boy," Jeevan said. She nodded slowly.

What did the parcel boy bring?
The parcel boy brought Sangeeta's textbook order.
Why did Jeevan bite back the correction at the gate?
Jeevan felt uneasy at the shouting but guessed Sangeeta was upset about the practical marks, and thought a correction then would only make things worse.
Which choice worked, and why?
Waiting for a calm moment on the roof and asking only about the marks let Sangeeta see for herself where the anger belonged.
What is it like for Sangeeta when Jeevan asks only about the marks?
Sangeeta feels understood rather than scolded, which lets her admit she shouted at the boy and turn toward Madam instead.

Vaibhav, you keep asking how your Payal Mausi learnt to ride without anyone teaching her. Nobody had time to teach me, that's how. But there was Rosy next door, who rode to the milk booth every morning. So I became her shadow. I sat on our wall and watched her feet. Right pedal up, like a clock at two. One strong push. Head up, looking far down the road, never at the wheel. I copied one thing at a time on my brother's old cycle. First the pedal, then the push. Fell plenty. Then one day I swallowed my pride and asked Rosy, "Watch me, tell me what I'm doing wrong." She laughed and said, "You look down at the last second." That one sentence fixed it.

Where did young Payal sit to watch Rosy?
Young Payal sat on the wall and watched Rosy's feet.

The turning point was asking Rosy to watch, because Rosy could spot the look-down mistake that Payal could not see alone.
How might Rosy have felt when the girl from next door asked for help?
Rosy was probably amused and pleased, and happy to share the one tip that fixed it.

messages.content: A ship sails from port A to a buoy B on a bearing of 070 degrees, then turns and sails to a lighthouse C on a bearing of 160 degrees. Find the angle ABC.

Answer: Angle ABC = 90 degrees.

At B, find the bearing of A from B first: the back bearing of 070 degrees is 070 degrees + 180 degrees = 250 degrees. So from B's North line, BA is at 250 degrees and BC is at 160 degrees. The angle between them is 250 degrees - 160 degrees = 90 degrees. Check with a sketch: the ship turned from 070 degrees to 160 degrees, a change of 90 degrees, so it turned through a right angle and the angle inside the triangle at B is 180 degrees - 90 degrees = 90 degrees. Always draw a North line at EVERY point where a bearing is measured. Common mistake: using 160 degrees - 70 degrees = 90 degrees without understanding; with other numbers the inside angle is 180 degrees minus the turn, not the turn itself.

Princeton had a gender reveal party and invited all of his fellow employees to celebrate with him. If the total number of guests were 60, and 2/3 were male guests, how many female guests attended the party?

The number of males in the party was 2 males / 3 guests * 60 guests = 40 males
If the total number of people at the party was 60, then there were 60 guests - 40 males = 20 females.
The answer is 20.

On his first day as team lead at the logistics office in Kolkata, Suraj noticed the old thought arrive: they'll resent me, I'm younger than half of them. He knew that voice. It usually sent him to hide in his cabin. So he did the opposite, in small ways. At lunch he pulled a chair up to the team's table and asked about the new routing system first. He prepared a one-page note for each person's one-on-one. When Mrs Ghosh laughed at his joke about the printer, he wrote it down that night: evidence, not proof, but evidence. The others had warned him about Varun. "Careless. Check everything he does." Suraj gave Varun the Durgapur routes anyway, with a clear deadline and a check-in on Wednesday. On Wednesday Varun came in with the plan done and two good questions. Suraj wrote that down too.

What did Suraj prepare for each person's one-on-one?
A one-page note.
What was Suraj worried about on the first day as team lead?
He worried the team would resent him for being younger than half of them, a fear that had made him hide in the past.
Which small choices helped Suraj act against the old forecast?
Sitting at the team's table and speaking first, preparing for each one-on-one, and writing down small signs of warmth as evidence rather than proof.
How might Varun have experienced being given the routes despite his reputation?
Varun was trusted with a clear deadline and a check-in instead of being watched as careless, which may be why he came in prepared with questions.

If I slept at all that night, it was only to imagine myself drifting down the river on a strong spring-tide, to the Hulks; a ghostly pirate calling out to me through a speaking-trumpet, as I passed the gibbet-station, that I had better come ashore and be hanged there at once, and not put it off. I was afraid to sleep, even if I had been inclined, for I knew that at the first faint dawn of morning I must rob the pantry. There was no doing it in the night, for there was no getting a light by easy friction then; to have got one I must have struck it out of flint and steel, and have made a noise like the very pirate himself rattling his chains.

Why is the narrator afraid to sleep that night?
He knows he must rob the pantry at first light. He could not do it in the dark, since striking a light with flint and steel would make a loud noise.
Why does steel wool glow and burn when lit but a steel rod does not?
The fine strands have a lot of surface for the air. Because oxygen can reach each thin thread easily, it burns while a thick rod loses its heat to the rest of the metal.

Mawia, you think the coach is always right? Let me tell you something. I'm Lalremsiami, your aunty, and at fifteen I'd have walked into fire for Coach Liana.
Some older girls on our football team had been grumbling about her training. One day she took me aside. “You're my captain, Siami. Tell me who's complaining. Names.”
I admired her so much. And I was scared of her. Those two feelings together froze me. I said one name, Mapuii's. The next week Mapuii was dropped.
Mapuii didn't speak to me for a month. Finally I went to our sports teacher and told her what had happened. She talked to Coach Liana, and Mapuii was back on the team. I apologised to Mapuii on the bus. It took her a long time, but she forgave me.

Going to the sports teacher and telling her what happened, which led to Mapuii being put back on the team.
How might Mapuii have felt during that month?
She was probably hurt and angry, feeling betrayed by her own captain, which is why she didn't speak to her.

In their Madrid student flat, Valentina had spent three nights reading about a rare brain infection after watching a documentary about one unlucky swimmer. She stopped going to the pool and asked Mei, her flatmate, whether the tap water was safe. "The article says it's one in millions," Mei said. "But it happened to someone," Valentina answered. The next morning she was late for her exam, so she grabbed her bike without the helmet, earbuds in, and ran two red lights down the avenue, texting her professor at the second one. Mei watched from the balcony, coffee in hand, not sure whether to laugh or shout.

She was texting her professor at the second red light.

Valentina feels frightened because the documentary gave her one vivid, unlucky story, and three nights of reading kept it in front of her. So it feels likely even though it is one in millions.
What could Valentina do to put her caution where the real risk is?
She could compare the odds of the rare infection with the odds of a bike accident, go back to the pool, and make the helmet and no-phone rule a habit on her bike.

Mei is torn between laughing and shouting, because the flatmate who fears a one-in-millions illness takes big everyday risks without noticing. 😬
Oscar wants to train for a marathon. He plans to add 2/3 of a mile each week until he reaches a 20-mile run. How many weeks before the marathon should he start training if he has already run 2 miles?

Oscar needs to increase his maximum running time from 20 - 2 = 18 miles.
Oscar will need a total of 18 / ( 2 / 3 ) = 27 weeks to prepare.
The answer is 27.

At 4 pm the Bengaluru office was tense. Ankita opened the client's email and felt her jaw tighten. She wanted to fire back. Instead she pushed back her chair, closed her eyes for a moment and took one long, slow sigh, letting her shoulders drop. Across the desk, Jyoti had just sent an update at the same time and let out a loud, sharp sigh at the screen, meant for nobody, but Ankita heard it. It sounded like Jyoti was dismissing her. Ankita said, "Was that about me?" Jyoti blinked. "No, sorry, the printer jammed." Ankita laughed. Jyoti thanked her and said she'd keep her sighs quieter around the team.

What time was it in the Bengaluru office?
It was 4 pm.
How did Ankita feel when she heard Jyoti's loud sigh?
Ankita felt dismissed and stiff at first, and it was easy to take it personally. Jyoti's explanation about the jammed printer showed the sigh was about something else.
What could Ankita do about her own stress at the desk?
Take a slow deliberate sigh with the shoulders dropped, as she did, before replying to the email.
How might Jyoti have felt when Ankita asked 'Was that about me?'
Jyoti was probably surprised and slightly embarrassed, and offered a quiet apology and a promise to be more aware of the team.

Santosh, nine, watched Dada take a long time to cross the living room of their Lucknow flat, leaning on his stick. Then Dada asked, "Who won the match?" He had asked that ten minutes ago.
Santosh went to the kitchen. "Papa, is Dada very sick?" he whispered.
Deepak dried his hands. "Dada's body is old now, beta. His legs are weaker and sometimes he forgets things. It's not his fault. He's still our Dada."
"Is he scared?"
"Sometimes, I think. That's why we're gentle."
Santosh went back and sat on the floor by Dada's chair. "Dada, shall I read you the cricket page?" Dada smiled and patted his head. Santosh read slowly, and when Dada asked about the match again, he just read the score once more.

What did Santosh offer to read to Dada?
He offered to read Dada the cricket page.
What was Santosh feeling when he whispered to Papa in the kitchen?
He was worried and a little frightened that Dada was very sick.
What helped Santosh know how to act around Dada?
Deepak's honest, simple explanation, and then doing something together like reading the cricket page.
How might Dada feel when Santosh sits by his chair and reads to him?
Dada probably feels loved and less alone, which shows when he smiles and pats Santosh's head.

Coordinator's note, internship review. Dilnaz came in stiff after mistakenly sending an unfinished report to a client. Maria, the mentor, listened to the whole account and said, "I made worse mistakes at your age. Now what will you do?" Dilnaz's shoulders dropped and the breathing eased. Within ten minutes Dilnaz had drafted a two-line apology to the client and a checklist for sending files, and Maria read both and nodded. Afterwards Dilnaz told me, "I thought Maria would write me off. I feel steadier." I noticed the checklist was taped to the monitor, not left in a folder. Next week I will ask whether it is still in use, because relief can slide into "it's fine, everyone slips."

What did Dilnaz mistakenly send to the client?
Dilnaz mistakenly sent an unfinished report.
How did Dilnaz feel after Maria's reply, and how can you tell?
Steadier. Dilnaz's shoulders dropped, the breathing eased, and Dilnaz said, "I feel steadier."
How could Dilnaz keep Maria's kindness from turning into carelessness?
By using it to act, as the apology and the checklist do, and by keeping the checklist in daily use, which the coordinator plans to ask about next week.
What is the coordinator watching for next week?
Whether the checklist is still used, since relief can slide into "it's fine, everyone slips."

College counselling centre, session note, Wednesday.
Mohit's roommate, Hrithik, walked him to my door this morning and waited outside. Mohit's Dadaji died in Kanpur four months ago. Mohit keeps replaying their last phone call: Dadaji asked when he was coming home, and Mohit said, "After exams, pakka." Dadaji died two weeks before exams ended. Today Mohit said "if only" nine times. If only he had taken the train in October. If only he had skipped the fest. I asked what he could actually have known in October. He said, very quietly, "Nothing. He sounded fine." We talked about how guilt can feel easier than helplessness, because guilt pretends we had control. He cried for the first time in our sessions. Next session is booked for Monday. Hrithik has the centre's number and knows to call if Mohit seems worse before then.

How many times did Mohit say "if only" today?
Mohit said "if only" nine times.
Why might Mohit keep replaying the last phone call?
He feels guilty and helpless; blaming himself gives him a sense of control over a death he could not have prevented.
What turning point does the counsellor offer at this stage?
The counsellor asks what Mohit could really have known in October, helping him see that the guilt pretends he had control, and books another session.
What might it be like for Hrithik to walk Mohit to the centre?
Hrithik is probably worried and protective, waiting outside and staying ready to call the centre if Mohit seems worse.
What is one teaching note for Raga Malkauns?
Pentatonic; no Re or Pa.

Emeka, sixteen, spent an hour and a half at the piano every evening in his family's flat in Accra. His phone sat on the music stand, and he replied to messages between pieces. He played everything through, start to finish, mistakes and all. At his exam rehearsal, his teacher Selin said, "Bar thirty-two is still wrong. It was wrong two months ago." Emeka stared at the keys, stung. "I've practised every single day." Selin nodded. "Try this. Tomorrow, twenty minutes, phone in another room. Only bars thirty to thirty-four. Play slowly. Stop the moment it's wrong." It felt boring and hard. After four days, bar thirty-two was right. He felt almost cheated by how simple it was.

Which bar was still wrong?
Bar thirty-two was still wrong.
What was Emeka feeling when Selin pointed out bar thirty-two?
He felt stung and frustrated, because he had practised every single day.
Why did the twenty-minute sessions work better than an hour and a half?
They focused on one weak passage without the phone, and stopping at each mistake gave immediate correction.
How does Selin view Emeka's practice?
Selin sees that playing through with a phone nearby left the same weakness untouched for two months.

I'm Himani, Sarita's desk-mate in Class 9. Sarita is always in the top three, and her mother picks her up on result days with sweets.
Before the history test, Sarita made cards of only the questions Ma'am had hinted at. 'The rest won't come, why waste time?' She got 48 out of 50.
Two weeks later Ma'am asked about the same chapter for a new project. Sarita looked at her notebook, blank. Later she whispered to me, 'I've already deleted it from my head.'
Once I showed her a video on how the pyramids were built, and she asked, 'Is this in the syllabus?' I said no. She went back to her flash cards.
I don't know if she minds. She never seems bored. She never seems excited either.

What score did Sarita get on the history test?
48 out of 50.
What does Sarita's 'Is this in the syllabus?' suggest about what drives her?
It suggests she values only what is tested and earns rank and her mother's sweets; interest for its own sake doesn't seem to count for her.
What could Sarita choose to do to make learning last beyond the test?
Sarita could explore one topic, like the pyramids video, with no marks attached, or explain a chapter to Himani after the test; using what is learnt keeps it and may spark curiosity.
How does Himani see Sarita, compared with what her report card shows?
The report card shows top-three ranks, but Himani sees someone who forgets fast and never seems excited, and can't tell whether Sarita minds.

Dear Yamini di,
You said to write when college got hard, so here it is. Last week I got a fever in the hostel. My roommate had gone home, and I lay alone in the dark, sweating and shivering, feeling about seven years old. I wanted Amma's rasam so badly I cried. I didn't tell anyone. I kept thinking: everyone's busy, I'm an adult, don't make a fuss. By the second night I couldn't get up to fill my bottle. That scared me. I finally messaged my friend Arvind down the corridor. He came with water and told the warden, and she took me to the campus clinic that morning. I'm better now. Next time I won't wait. I'll message someone straight away.
Love,
Sumit

Arvind, a friend down the corridor.
Why didn't Sumit tell anyone at first?
Sumit felt lonely and homesick but reluctant to bother anyone, thinking everyone was busy and an adult should not make a fuss.
What will Sumit do differently, and why is it wiser?
Message someone straight away next time, because reaching out early makes being ill safer and less lonely.
How might Yamini feel reading this?

Paulo checked the calendar on his phone for the third time. There it was: Thursday, 6 p.m., café shift, and underneath, Told Jin Monday. He had even written that.
Still, when he got home, Jin was sitting in the dark. "You never said you were working. You just disappear and expect me to guess."
"I told you on Monday, remember? At the laundromat."
"That didn't happen. You always do this. You rewrite things so you look good."
Paulo opened his mouth, then closed it. Last week it had been the concert tickets, and before that the rent money. Each time Jin was certain, and each time Paulo ended up saying sorry.
"Sorry," he said now. "Maybe I forgot to say."
Later, washing dishes in their Melbourne flat, he noticed he had started writing everything down, and still didn't trust it. He wasn't sure anymore whether he was a forgetful person, or had only been told he was.

What had Paulo written under the Thursday shift in his calendar?
He had written "Told Jin Monday" under the café shift.
What is Paulo feeling as he washes the dishes?
He feels confused and less sure of himself, no longer knowing whether he is truly forgetful or has only been told he is.
What could Paulo do the next time his note and Jin's version clash?
He could trust his written note, calmly say he remembers it differently without apologising, and check his experience with someone he trusts outside the flat.
What would change if Jin said "I don't remember that, maybe I missed it" instead?
The disagreement would be about a missed message, not about Paulo's mind, and he would not need to apologise for something that was not wrong.
Do you think I should stay up all night before the chemistry exam?
I would not. A rested brain remembers far more than a tired one. If you stay up all night you may forget what you studied or make silly mistakes. Sleeping a proper night is a better plan.
But I have not finished the last two chapters.
Then use tonight wisely. Skim the key points of both chapters, mark anything unclear, and sleep at a normal time. Waking a little earlier for a quick look is better than studying until dawn.
Okay. Which chapters should I look at first? One is on acids and the other on metals.

Begin with acids, since you will probably need to remember the reactions and their products. Then take metals. Make a short list of the important points from each chapter so your morning revision is quick.
Good. So acids first and then metals. Can you suggest what to do in the morning?
Yes. After breakfast, read your short list for acids, then the one for metals, as planned. Do not start anything new. Drink some water and walk calmly to the exam hall.

John is working as an IT specialist. He repairs broken computers. One day he had to fix 20 computers. 20% of them were unfixable, and 40% of them needed to wait a few days for spare parts to come. The rest John was able to fix right away. How many computers John was able to fix right away?

From all the computers, 100% - 40% - 20% = 40% got fixed right away.
So John was able to fix 40/100 * 20 = 8 computers.
The answer is 8.

Many families keep curtains closed in the afternoon, open windows at night, and drink plenty of water or nimbu pani. Light cotton clothes and rest during the hottest hours also help.

Nine-year-old Indu, in her village outside Karnal, had pinned up a newspaper photo of the district's gold-medal sprinter, a young woman who had grown up three villages away. Indu now tied her hair in the same high knot, wore a sweatband on one wrist, and started every morning with the warm-up she had seen on the TV at the tea stall. She even walked like her, shoulders back. "Early to bed, early to track," she told her little sister Payal, in the sprinter's firm voice.
But when Payal beat her in a race to the well, Indu snapped, "Champions don't lose to babies," and stalked off. Payal's lip wobbled. That evening Indu came back with a guava. "Champions also say sorry," she mumbled.

Lucille made an agreement with her mom that she would earn six cents for every weed she pulled in her mom's garden. There are eleven weeds in the flower bed, fourteen in the vegetable patch, and thirty-two in the grass around the fruit trees. Lucille weeded the flower bed, the vegetable patch, and half the grass before she took a break. She bought a soda for 99 cents on her break with some of her earnings. How many cents does Lucille have left?

Lucille weeded half the grass, so she pulled 32 / 2 = 16 weeds around the fruit frees.
She pulled 11 + 14 + 16 = 41 weeds before her break.
From that, she earned 41 * 6 = 246 cents.
After buying her soda, Lucille has 246 - 99 = 147 cents left.
The answer is 147.

messages.content: Why does a whiteboard marker dry out if the cap is left off?
The liquid in the ink escapes into the air from the open tip. Because that liquid turns into vapour in open air, what is left is too dry to write.

Oliver is working out in a gym. On Monday he worked out for 4 hours, and the next day for 2 hours less. On Wednesday he decided to work out twice as much as on Monday. On Thursday the gym was closed, so Oliver needed to exercise at home which took twice as much time as on Tuesday. How many hours in total have Oliver worked out during these four days?

On Tuesday, Oliver worked out for 4 - 2 = 2 hours.
On Wednesday he decided to work out twice as much as on Monday, so for 2 * 4 = 8 hours.
On Thursday, at home, Oliver trained twice as much as on Tuesday, so for 2 * 2 = 4 hours.
In total Oliver trained for 4 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 18 hours.
The answer is 18.

Answer: 19 fruits. (6 + 4) + 9 = 10 + 9 = 19.

Stoney Hollow Middle School is taking a field trip to the zoo. There are 109 fifth graders, 115 sixth graders, and 118 seventh graders. There are 4 teachers and 2 parents from each grade coming along to chaperone on the trip. There are 72 seats on each school bus. How many buses are needed for the field trip?

There are 109 fifth graders + 115 sixth graders + 118 seventh graders = 342 students going on the trip.
There are 4 teachers + 2 parents = 6 adults going on the field trip for each grade.
There are 3 grades going, so 3 grades x 6 adults/grade = 18 total adults going on the trip.
There are 342 students + 18 adults = 360 people going on the trip.
So, 360 people / 72 seats = 5 buses
The answer is 5.

Then on Sunday, at the tubewell, cousin Preeti told everyone how a dog in the next village had bitten a boy on the leg, how he screamed, how there was blood on his kurta. Where did Moti lie every morning?
In the shade at the Sandhus' farm.

Luna, the poodle, is supposed to eat 2 cups of kibble every day.  But Luna's master, Mary, and her husband, Frank, sometimes feed Luna too much kibble.  One day, starting with a new, 12-cup bag of kibble, Mary gave Luna 1 cup of kibble in the morning and 1 cup of kibble in the evening, But on the same day, Frank also gave Luna 1 cup of kibble in the afternoon and twice as much in the late evening as he had given Luna in the afternoon.  The next morning, how many cups of kibble will Mary find remaining in the bag?

Mary fed Luna 1+1=2 cups of kibble.
Frank fed Luna 1-cup plus twice 1-cup, or 1+2=3 cups of kibble.
In total, they fed Luna 2+3=5 cups of kibble.
Thus, if the new bag held 12 cups of kibble, the next morning, 12-5=7 cups of kibble remained in the bag.
The answer is 7.

A school is buying virus protection software to cover 50 devices.  One software package costs $40 and covers up to 5 devices. The other software package costs $60 and covers up to 10 devices.  How much money, in dollars, can the school save by buying the $60 software package instead of the $40 software package?

There are 50/5 = 10 sets of 5 devices in the school.
So the school will pay a total of $40 x 10 = $400 for the $40 software package.
There are 50/10 = 5 sets of 10 devices in the school.
So the school will pay a total of $60 x 5 = $300 for the $60 software package.
Thus, the school can save $400 - $100 = $300 from buying the $60 software instead of the $40 software package.
The answer is 100.

Max likes to collect model trains.  He asks for one for every birthday of his, and asks for two each Christmas.  Max always gets the gifts he asks for, and asks for these same gifts every year for 5 years.  At the end of the 5 years, his parents give him double the number of trains he already has.  How many trains does Max have now?

Max gets 1+2=3 trains per year.
He repeats this for 5 years, meaning he gets 5*3 =15 trains.
When this number is doubled by his parents, it becomes 15*2= 30 trains.
Since he already had 15 model trains, his total becomes 15+30= 45 trains.
The answer is 45.

You want to know why I don't go to rallies without checking who runs them now? I'm Yamini. In Class 11, a college senior, Asif, came to our tuition centre and said they needed "young faces" for a protest about the bus fares. "Bring your school ID, it looks good on camera."

About forty of us went. When we got there, he told the school kids to stand at the very front, right at the police barricade. The college students stayed behind us. There was no water, no first-aid, nobody told us where to go if it got rough.

When the crowd started pushing, my friend got pressed against the barricade and started crying. I felt pure panic. Asif was shouting slogans from the back and didn't even look at us.

I grabbed her hand and we squeezed out through a side lane. I called my father. He came in fifteen minutes.

A real leader puts the youngest at the back and has a plan. And you're always allowed to leave.

What did Asif ask the students to bring?
Asif asked them to bring their school ID.
What was Yamini feeling when the crowd started pushing?
Yamini felt panicked and frightened, especially when Yamini's friend was pressed against the barricade and began crying.
What warning signs showed the organiser was using the students?
School students were put at the front by the barricade, there was no water, first-aid or plan, and the organiser stayed at the back.
How might Yamini's father have felt when the call came?
He probably felt scared and relieved at once, glad Yamini had left and called him quickly.

Every month, in the week before her period, Sarika's life in their Kochi flat seemed to fall apart. She cried through meetings, snapped at Joseph over nothing, and one month called in sick three days running because she couldn't face anyone. Her mother said, 'All women go through it. Bear it.' Sarika had borne it for years. One evening, after a week of barely sleeping, she told Joseph, 'It feels like I disappear for a week and a stranger lives here.' Joseph held her hand. 'This isn't something you just tolerate. Let's see a doctor.' He found a women's health clinic, went with her, and helped her write down her monthly notes. The doctor took her seriously and made a plan with her.

What did Sarika's mother say?
'All women go through it. Bear it.'
What was Sarika feeling when she said a stranger lives there?
She felt overwhelmed and lost, as if she disappeared for a week every month.
What steps did Joseph take?
He refused to treat it as something to tolerate, found a clinic, went with her and helped write down her monthly notes.
How might Joseph have experienced the snapping over nothing?
Joseph may have felt hurt at times, yet he saw a real problem rather than a character flaw.
Ali had a stock of 800 books in his Room. He sold 60 on Monday, 10 on Tuesday, 20 on Wednesday, 44 on Thursday and 66 on Friday. How many books were not sold?

We look first for the total number of books that were sold: 60 + 10 + 20 + 44 + 66 = 200 books.
So the total number of books that were not sold is: 800 - 200 = 600 books.
The answer is 600.

The local bus from Barhiya rattled over every pothole, and Ganga and Pushpa sat squeezed on the last seat, school bags on their knees.
"Can I tell you two things?" Ganga said, eyes on the window. "But you can't tell anyone. Not even your sister."
Pushpa hooked her little finger into Ganga's. "Tell."
"First, I think I like Farhan. From the science stall at the mela."
Pushpa's eyebrows shot up, but she only grinned.
"Second," Ganga said, quieter, "Baba hasn't been paid for the wheat yet. Maa sold her silver anklets last week. I'm scared I'll have to leave school after tenth."
Pushpa didn't say anything clever. She just squeezed Ganga's finger harder and said, "You won't carry that by yourself."
When the bus stopped at their village, Ganga jumped down first, and for the first time in days she was humming.

What did Ganga's Maa sell last week?
Maa sold her silver anklets last week.
How can you tell that telling Pushpa made Ganga feel lighter?
Ganga jumped down first and was humming for the first time in days, which shows relief after sharing her worries. 😊
What could Pushpa do to keep being a safe friend?
Pushpa could keep both secrets, check in quietly about school and home, and help Ganga talk to a trusted adult such as a teacher if the fear about leaving school grows.
What might it mean to Pushpa that Ganga trusted her?
Pushpa likely feels honoured and responsible, holding something happy and something heavy for her friend.

On Sunday morning, in their Pune flat, Tarun spread paper and crayons across the floor. "Shalini, remember yesterday at the sweet shop?"
Shalini nodded, not looking up.
"You were angry. I was angry too, and I shouted. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry."
Shalini looked up then, surprised.
"Let's make a plan for angry times," Tarun said. They drew three pictures together: feet stomping softly, a crayon scribbling hard, two arms asking for a hug. Shalini stuck them on the fridge herself, the hug picture lowest, where she could reach it.

Where did Shalini stick the pictures?
On the fridge, with the hug picture lowest where she could reach it.
What did Shalini's surprised look suggest when Tarun said sorry?
She seemed surprised and perhaps relieved that her father admitted shouting too, so she did not carry all the blame.
Which part of Tarun's plan works well for a young child, and why?
Drawing the choices as pictures, because Shalini can see and point to them when she is too angry for words.
How might Tarun feel after apologising to Shalini?
He may feel lighter and hopeful, having modelled repair instead of pretending he did nothing wrong.
Ivan has 20 dice. Jerry has twice as many dice as Ivan. How many dice do they have altogether?

Jerry has 2 x 20 = 40 dice.
Therefore, they have 20 + 40 = 60 dice altogether.
The answer is 60.

On the local train home to Borivali, Nilesh did something he had avoided for months. He opened a blank page in his notebook and wrote at the top: "If prelims doesn't happen this year." His heart thumped just writing it. Then he made himself continue. Option one: the state civil services exam in October, with a lot of overlap. Option two: the MA entrance in spring, since he liked political science anyway. Option three: a job at the policy research firm where his friend Hansa worked, which had asked for his resume twice. By Dadar the page was full. He noticed his shoulders had come down. The prelims was still the plan. But it was no longer the only door, and somehow that made studying for it feel lighter. That night, when Hansa texted "how's prep?", he replied, "Good. I have exits now."

What did Nilesh write at the top of the page?
If prelims doesn't happen this year.
How did Nilesh feel while writing the heading?
Nilesh felt anxious, his heart thumping just writing it.
What else could Nilesh do to keep the backups ready?
Nilesh could note the deadlines for each option and send the resume to Hansa's firm, so the options stay real.
How might Hansa see Nilesh's reply?
Hansa may be pleased and relieved to hear him sound settled, and glad the firm is one of his exits.

Kalyani, you asked why I let the team choose the release date. I'm Arnab, and I learned it the hard way. In my first month as a lead I felt a rush: people waited for my nod. I started checking every line of code and rewriting slides in meetings so everyone could see how sharp I was.

One evening the quietest engineer, Praveen, said, "You've redone my work twice. Should I stop trying?" That sentence stuck like a splinter. I went home ashamed.

The next morning I handed Praveen the whole module and stepped back. Within a week the team was fixing problems before they reached me. I understood then that my job was helping them succeed. Power that feeds my ego had been costing me the team.

What did Praveen say to Arnab?
Praveen said, 'You've redone my work twice. Should I stop trying?'
What did Arnab feel in the first month as a lead?
A rush of excitement from people waiting for Arnab's nod, which pushed Arnab to check everything and show off.
What did Arnab change after Praveen's words?
Arnab handed over the whole module and stepped back, seeing the job as helping the team succeed.
How might Praveen have felt after being redone twice?
Discouraged, enough to ask whether to stop trying.

In Buenos Aires, Rafael came home quiet. At the park, some older boys had called his friend Mateo names and knocked his football into the canal. Rafael had stood there, silent.
At dinner his older sister Leila heard the story from a neighbour. "You just watched? What a coward," she said.
Rafael's face burned. He pushed his plate away and went to his room.
Their mother followed and sat on his bed. "Being scared and freezing isn't the same as not caring. You feel bad because you care about Mateo." That evening she rang Mateo's mother, and they agreed to speak to the park warden in the morning.
The next day Rafael knocked on Mateo's door with his own football. "Sorry I didn't say anything. Want to play? If they come, we'll go straight to the warden."

What happened to Mateo's football?
The older boys knocked it into the canal.
How did Rafael feel when Leila called him a coward?
Rafael felt ashamed, his face burning, and left the table.
How did the mother's response help Rafael move towards courage?
She separated freezing from not caring and rang Mateo's mother that evening, and the next day Rafael apologised and planned to fetch the warden if needed.
What might Leila's harsh word have done if nobody else had spoken to Rafael?
It could have pushed Rafael to hide in shame rather than make things right with Mateo.
Picnic ke group mein poochna hai "Kaun kya laayega?" English mein?
You can write: "Who is bringing what?" It is short and natural for a group chat.
Why should we pull a plug out by the plug itself and not by tugging the wire?
Pulling by the plug is safer. Because tugging the wire strains the thin wires inside and can loosen or break them, the cable can get damaged and later cause sparks or a shock.

Monday. Ojas asks his friend Sameer to "casually find out" if Nirmala likes him. Sameer grins and promises to be subtle.
Wednesday. Sameer asks Nirmala's friend, who asks Nirmala at lunch in front of four people: "Ojas is in love with you, do you like him or not?" By afternoon the story is that Ojas wrote Nirmala a love letter. Two boys whistle when she walks into the lab.
Friday. Nirmala stops Ojas in the corridor, arms crossed. "If you wanted to ask me something, you could have asked me. Now everyone's talking about me like I'm a joke." Ojas opens his mouth, but there's nothing to say that makes it better. She walks off. Sameer texts: "sorry bro, it kind of spread."

What was the story by Wednesday afternoon?
That Ojas wrote Nirmala a love letter.
How does Nirmala feel on Friday?
She feels embarrassed and angry, talked about like a joke instead of being asked directly.
What would have worked better than using Sameer?
Asking Nirmala himself, privately and simply, so she could answer without an audience or a twisted rumour.
How might Sameer feel after the story spread?
Sameer seems sheepish and a little sorry, though the casual text shows he treats it more lightly than Nirmala does.

At the housing society meeting in Thane, a resident stood up about the redevelopment. 'Once the chawl people move into Tower C, this place will become a slum. They're dirty, loud, no manners.' Heads nodded. Nikita, sitting near the back with her neighbour Tanuja, raised her hand. 'Can I ask about one person? Tanuja, didn't Lata-tai, who helps at your home, live in that chawl for thirty years?' Tanuja nodded and stood. 'Lata-tai raised three children there. Her son is a bank clerk now. She's the one who sat with my mother every afternoon when my mother was ill. She will be in Tower C.' The room shifted. The man who had spoken looked at his hands. Someone at the front said, 'Maybe we should invite the new families for the Ganpati function.' Nikita wrote it down in the minutes.

How long did Lata-tai live in the chawl?
Lata-tai lived in that chawl for thirty years.
What might Nikita have felt as heads nodded around the room?
Nikita likely felt uncomfortable watching a whole group dismissed as dirty, and wanted to bring one real face into the room.
What made Nikita's question work?
Asking about one person let Tanuja tell Lata-tai's true story, and the specific details moved the room from contempt to an invitation.
How might Lata-tai feel if she knew about this meeting?
Lata-tai might feel hurt by the first speaker's words but moved to be remembered for her kindness, and welcomed by the invitation.
What homework did I get today?
I can't see your homework, so I don't know. Check your diary or ask a classmate.

Tuesday.
Watched Sonali write the whole newsletter today. I've never seen anyone so still. She typed in bursts, stopped, stared at the window, typed again. Her phone lit up twice and she didn't even glance at it. There was a crease between her eyebrows the entire afternoon.
I had a question about the photo captions and got up twice to ask. Both times I sat back down. It could wait; the captions aren't due till Thursday. When her phone rang a third time, I answered and said she'd call back.
At six she looked up, blinked as if she'd just woken, and said, "Wait, is it six?" The draft was brilliant.
I want to be able to disappear into work like that. Tomorrow I'll ask about the captions.
Madhuri

When are the photo captions due?
Thursday.
How does Madhuri feel watching Sonali work?
Madhuri feels admiration, even a little envy, wishing to disappear into work that deeply.
What did Madhuri do to protect Sonali's focus?
Madhuri held the non-urgent caption question and answered Sonali's phone, saying she'd call back.
What was the afternoon like for Sonali?
For Sonali time vanished; she looked up at six surprised, as if just waking, with a brilliant draft done.

Deepak, it's me, Sunaina. Remember the pitch review last week? The whole room was nodding. The slide said two hundred sign-ups, and I had this tiny voice saying that number looks made up. But everyone looked so sure, even Vikram, who is the sharpest of us. So I decided I was the one who did not understand. I stayed silent and even nodded. After the meeting Rina said in the lift, "I thought the number looked odd too," and then Kunal said, "Me too!" I nearly laughed. Three of us had swallowed the same doubt for an hour. Deepak, I am going to say something at the next one, even if my voice shakes.

How many sign-ups did the slide claim?
The slide said two hundred sign-ups.
Why did Sunaina decide to be silent and even nod in the meeting?
Sunaina thought everyone else looked sure, so the doubt must be Sunaina's own misunderstanding; it was self-doubt more than agreement.
What choice does Sunaina make at the end of the story?
Sunaina decides to say something at the next review even if the voice shakes, having learned that others had the same doubt.
What might Kunal have felt when saying "Me too!" in the lift?
Kunal probably felt relief and surprise at finding out the doubt was shared, after an hour of holding it alone.

In her small room in a Kolkata mess, Rekha had spent a month building a sculpture from old glass bangles: dozens of them, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column. The bangles were her grandmother's; after Thakuma's death, the family had given them to Rekha. At the college exhibition, her classmate Usha stood in front of it for a long time. "It's so festive," Usha said. "Like a wedding." Rekha's throat tightened. "They were my grandmother's. She died in March." Usha's face fell. "Oh, Rekha. I'm sorry. I didn't know." Rekha shook her head. "No, don't be sorry. She wore them at every wedding in the family. Maybe that's in there too." Usha looked again, quieter. "It's grief and celebration, then." Rekha smiled for the first time that evening. "Yes. That's exactly what she was."

What was Rekha's sculpture made from?
Old glass bangles, red and green, melted and fused into a twisted column.
What was Rekha feeling when Usha called the sculpture festive?
Her throat tightened with grief, because the bangles were her grandmother's and she had died in March.
What did Rekha do that allowed both readings to stand?
She shared the story of the bangles but welcomed Usha's reading, since her grandmother wore them at every wedding.
How did Usha's view of the sculpture change?
She first saw it as festive like a wedding, then, after hearing Rekha, as grief and celebration together.

Before our Mysore trip last winter, everyone in the group chat was already choosing ice creams. I'm Pranav, and I was the one holding the notebook. Each of us had 3,000 rupees from the school trip kitty. Madhuri said, "Start from the top, not from the fun stuff." So I wrote 3,000 and began taking things away. Bus there and back: 1,150. Two nights in the dormitory: 1,050. I stared at what was left. 800. For two and a half days of meals, the palace ticket, the zoo and any water we'd buy. My stomach dropped a little, honestly. I read it out on our call and the chat went quiet. Then Madhuri said, "Good. Now we know the real number." We cut the zoo and kept the palace. Looking back, that one subtraction saved us from a very hungry last day.

How much did the two nights in the dormitory cost each person?
The two nights in the dormitory cost 1,050.
What was Pranav feeling when the number 800 appeared, and how can you tell?
Pranav felt a jolt of worry; the narrator says their stomach dropped a little on seeing how little was left for meals and tickets.
What else could the group try if 800 still felt too tight?
They could look for a cheaper stay or carry some snacks from home, then redo the subtraction together before booking, so every choice rests on the real number.
How might Madhuri see the quiet moment in the chat?
Madhuri treats it as useful rather than bad news, because knowing the real number early lets the group decide calmly what to cut.

After the student council results, I saw Reena's friend Sneha sitting on the steps behind the library, crying. She'd lost by six votes.
Reena sat down next to her, then opened her arms a little and asked, "Hug? Or not right now?"
Sneha shook her head. "Not right now."
Reena didn't look hurt. She just lowered her arms, stayed close, and passed Sneha a tissue. They sat there for a long time. Reena didn't say much, just "That really stinks," once.
After a while, Sneha leaned her head on Reena's shoulder by herself.
I don't know what Reena was thinking. But she didn't push, and it seemed to help.
- Anirban

How many votes did Sneha lose by?
Six votes.
What might Reena have been feeling when Sneha said no to the hug?
Reena may have felt a small pang, but she seemed calm and caring, accepting the answer and staying close; Anirban can't be sure what she thought.
What did Reena do that respected Sneha?
She asked before hugging, accepted the refusal without sulking, and offered comfort in another way by staying close and passing a tissue.
How might Sneha have felt when Reena asked instead of just hugging?
Sneha probably felt respected and safe, which may be why she leaned on Reena's shoulder later by her own choice.

Dear Farhan,
You asked what I've decided about the Edinburgh offer. I'm going.
It wasn't easy. Every night I made lists, and every list ended with me picturing Ammi alone on the veranda. Then I tried something my old teacher told me: imagine I'm thirty-five, looking back. Which choice would that woman respect? Not which one she'd never regret, because both come with some. Which one she'd be proud of.
She'd respect going, and coming home every summer, and calling Ammi every Sunday. She wouldn't respect staying out of fear and calling it duty.
So I've accepted. I've put the Sunday calls in my calendar for two years. And you're checking on Ammi on Wednesdays, which you've already agreed to, so no backing out.
I'll probably cry at the airport. That's allowed.
Hansa

Which offer is Hansa accepting?
Hansa is accepting the Edinburgh offer.
What worried Hansa every night while deciding?
Hansa felt torn and guilty, picturing Ammi alone on the veranda.
How did the 'thirty-five' check help Hansa decide?
Asking which choice a thirty-five-year-old Hansa would respect, not which avoids all regret, pointed to going, with Sunday calls and summer visits.
How might Farhan feel about checking on Ammi on Wednesdays?
Farhan may feel trusted and a little responsible, and glad to help Hansa go without guilt.

Dear Chandrika,
I've started this letter three times, so I'll just say it. I'm sorry for the way I've treated you since you joined as the new girl on the scholarship.
When you wore old sports shoes to the inter-house race, I was the one who called them 'government issue'. I rolled my eyes when you asked the teacher to repeat things. I think I believed kids like you were lucky to be here and kids like me deserved to be.
Then we were paired for the chemistry project, and you understood titration in ten minutes while I needed a week. You told me you tutor your brother every evening after helping at your mother's tailoring shop. I go home to a cook and a private tutor.
I keep thinking about how much of what I called 'me' was just what I was handed.
You didn't deserve any of it. If you'd like, I'd really like to be friends.
Karthik

What did Karthik call Chandrika's sports shoes?
'Government issue'.
What is Karthik feeling while writing the letter?
Karthik feels ashamed and regretful, having started the letter three times before managing to say sorry.
What would you advise Karthik to do next, beyond the letter?
Treat Chandrika as an equal day to day, and speak up when others mock scholarship students.
How might Chandrika have felt when her shoes were mocked?
She probably felt humiliated and unwelcome, judged for money rather than for who she is.

Nisha had started walking to class with Gita, the new girl, and Parveen checked who Nisha sat with at lunch every day and hovered whenever they whispered. Twice she asked Nisha to sit only with her, and Nisha's face went tight. At the water tap Rekha leaned close. "Nisha finds you boring now. She told me." Parveen's stomach dropped, but at break she asked Nisha directly, and Nisha said, "I never said that. Who told you?" Meanwhile Nisha liked Gita's jokes and felt like a traitor to Parveen. That night she almost lied that she had been at her aunt's, but next morning she told Parveen the truth and said she still mattered. Parveen took a breath. "I felt left out," she said. "Can we do one Saturday just us?" Nisha nodded. On Monday Parveen said hi to Gita and suggested a game for three, and Gita laughed and fetched the ball. Parveen was not pretending she felt nothing. She was happy for Nisha, and it cost her little.

Who leaned close to Parveen at the water tap?
Rekha leaned close to Parveen at the water tap.
How did Parveen's clinging at first differ from what she did after she told Nisha she felt left out?

At first she checked who Nisha sat with and asked her to sit only with her, which made Nisha's face go tight; later she said plainly that she felt left out, asked for one Saturday just them, said hi to Gita and suggested a game for three.
What was Nisha feeling when she almost lied about being at her aunt's?
She felt guilty, like a traitor to Parveen, even though she liked Gita too.
What did Parveen do about Rekha's whisper, and why was that a wise choice?
She asked Nisha directly instead of believing Rekha, so Rekha could not steer their friendship with a rumour.

I'm Baljeet, and last month I sat on my first interview panel as a new manager. By the fourth candidate, I noticed something uncomfortable.
My two senior colleagues kept lighting up at candidates who looked like our star analyst from last year: same college, same crisp way of talking, even the same kind of watch. "Very much like Vikram," one said, and gave top marks. A candidate named Vidya, who had solved the case study best, got middling scores. "Not quite our type," the other colleague said.
I checked my own notes and realised I'd been doing it too, at least a little.
So after the round, I suggested we try structured scoring: the same four questions for everyone, each marked against a clear rubric, before any discussion. My colleagues grumbled, but agreed to try.
When we re-scored with the rubric, Vidya came first. We hired her. Two months on, she is the best analyst on the team.

Who solved the case study best?
Vidya had solved the case study best.
How did Baljeet feel when noticing the panel's pattern?
Baljeet felt uncomfortable, especially on realising the same pull had shaped Baljeet's own notes a little.
What did Baljeet propose, and why does it help?
Structured scoring, the same questions with a clear rubric before discussion, so candidates are judged on actual evidence instead of resemblance to past successes.
How might Vidya have been affected if the panel hadn't re-scored?
Vidya, the strongest candidate, would likely have been passed over for not being "our type", and the team would have lost its best analyst.

Dear Vaibhav bhaiya,
You asked how the prelims went. The truth is embarrassing.
I finished the maths paper forty minutes early. I was so proud. I sat there drawing on the question paper while everyone else was still writing. I thought, I'm just faster than them.
Then the results came. I lost fourteen marks. Not because I didn't know things. I copied a 6 as a 0. I forgot a minus sign. I answered part (a) of a question and never saw part (b) on the next page. Ma'am wrote at the top, "Careless, not weak."
That hurt more than a low mark would have.
You always told me to use the last fifteen minutes to check. I thought that was for slow people. It turns out checking is the fast way, because now I have to redo the whole chapter test.
Next time I'll stay in my seat till the bell.
Your sister,
Mehak

How many marks did Mehak lose in the maths paper?
I lost fourteen marks.
How did Mehak feel about "Careless, not weak"?
Mehak felt hurt and ashamed, more than a low mark would have caused, because the mistakes came from rushing.
What does Mehak plan to do next time, and why?
Mehak plans to stay till the bell and check, because checking turns out to be faster than redoing the whole chapter test.
How might Vaibhav feel reading this letter?
Vaibhav might feel sympathetic, and a little pleased that his advice about checking is finally being taken.
