Keerthana was building a sweet shop in her block game when a message popped up: "Want 5000 free gems? Just send ur password and I'll load them 😊"
Five thousand! She could finally buy the golden roof. Her fingers hovered over the keys. Then she remembered her cousin Deepak saying that real games never ask for passwords. Her stomach flipped. This was not luck. This was bait.
She did not reply. She carried the tablet straight to the kitchen, where Amma was chopping onions. Amma wiped her hands, read the message and sat with her while they blocked and reported the player and changed the password.
"You came to me right away," Amma said, hugging her. "That was exactly right."

What did the message ask Keerthana to send?
Her password.
What was Keerthana feeling when she first saw the offer?
She felt excited about the golden roof, then uneasy when she realised it was bait.
What did Keerthana and Amma do right away?
They blocked and reported the player and changed the password.
What was the player hoping Keerthana would do?
The player hoped the huge number would rush Keerthana into sending her password before thinking or asking anyone.

In the boys' hostel at the engineering college, the fest committee went room to room with a register. 'Five hundred per head for Diwali night. DJ, lights, fireworks. Compulsory.' Samir, twenty-one, paid and watched them move to Noor's room across the corridor. Noor, a first-year on a scholarship, said quietly, 'Can I give two hundred?' A senior laughed. 'Everyone gives five hundred.' Noor went inside and came back with the full amount, folded small.
That Saturday the terrace glowed and the music shook the windows. Samir danced, and it was fun. But he saw Noor at the edge of the crowd, not eating, and he wondered what that five hundred had cost.

How much did the committee ask for per head?
Five hundred per head.
What was Samir feeling as he watched Noor at the edge of the crowd?
Samir felt uneasy and a little guilty in the middle of the fun, wondering what the forced contribution had cost Noor.
How could the committee make the celebration fairer?
Let people give what they can, privately, without mocking anyone, so joining the celebration does not depend on money.
How might Noor have felt when the senior laughed?
Noor likely felt embarrassed and pressured, handing over money that was hard to spare rather than stand out.

Subject: I need to tell someone

Mehak,
You know me. In college I returned extra change to canteen uncle. So believe me when I say I don't recognise myself this week.
Our investors want the quarter to show growth, or the next round won't happen and twelve people lose their jobs. Nobody checks exactly when a contract is counted as revenue. I noticed that in January.
On Friday I counted a deal that isn't signed yet. The client said "very likely". I told myself it's only timing, investors can easily afford a small surprise, and every founder I know stretches a bit.
The report went out Saturday. Nobody said anything.
And I felt relief, Mehak. That's what I can't stop thinking about. Relief, not guilt.
I've always thought people who did this were a different kind of person. I think I was wrong.
Can we talk tonight?
Ayesha

When did the report go out?
The report went out on Saturday.
Why does Ayesha find the relief more disturbing than guilt would be?
The relief shows how natural the wrong step felt, which frightens Ayesha, who always seemed the honest one who returned extra change.
What wise step is Ayesha taking by writing to Mehak?
Ayesha is telling a trusted person quickly and asking to talk that night, which could lead to correcting the report before it grows.

They might feel grateful Ayesha was trying to protect their jobs, yet uneasy that their company's future now rests on a report that isn't true.

Nilesh was folding laundry in the flat when a friend's name kept scrolling past on the screen: Tarun. A joke Tarun had posted last week, clipped and stripped of context, had become hundreds of angry replies. People were demanding that his college expel him. Nilesh's thumb hovered over "reply" to defend him publicly. Nilesh's stomach tightened: what if the crowd came for Nilesh next?

Nilesh put the phone down, breathed, and picked it up again. No public reply. A private message instead: "I saw it. I'm with you. Want to report the worst ones together?"

Tarun answered in ten seconds: "Yes. I feel sick."

They spent an hour reporting threats. Two days later, when the anger had thinned, Nilesh posted: "Tarun is a friend. The clip leaves out the rest."

What did Nilesh send Tarun privately?
Nilesh sent, "I saw it. I'm with you. Want to report the worst ones together?"
What was Nilesh afraid of while deciding whether to reply?
Nilesh feared the crowd would come for Nilesh next, so Nilesh's stomach tightened while the thumb hovered over "reply".
Why was messaging privately first a good move?
It supported Tarun right away and helped report threats without putting Nilesh in the crowd's sights, and Nilesh spoke up publicly later when it was safer.
How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh's message arrived?
Tarun felt sick but answered within ten seconds with a yes, which suggests relief at not being alone.

In the village school near Satara, results were read out under the neem tree. Deepika's turn came: "Marathi spelling test, nine out of ten." She had missed one word, "swachhata". Her face crumpled.
On the walk home past the sugarcane fields she kicked stones and said, "I'm useless. The whole test is a disaster. I'll never be good at Marathi."
Her friend Farida walked beside her, swinging a cloth bag. "Nine out of ten is the second-highest in the class," Farida said. "That's not a disaster."
"It's not ten," Deepika snapped.
Farida thought for a moment. "When your mango tree drops one mango, is the whole tree ruined?"
Deepika stopped walking. She didn't answer. But she stopped kicking stones.

Which word did Deepika miss?
"Swachhata".
Why does 'It's not ten' feel so final to Deepika?
Deepika feels crushed because in her mind there are only two boxes, perfect or disaster, so nine out of ten lands in the disaster box.
What did Farida try that helped Deepika pause?
Pointing out it was the second-highest mark and asking about one fallen mango, which offered a middle ground without scolding.
How might Farida feel being snapped at for trying to help?
Probably a little stung, but Farida stays patient and tries a gentler example, which shows real friendship.

Barry and his friend, Jim, went horseback riding across central Texas. They traveled at 5 miles per hour for 7 hours, and then stopped for the evening.  The next day, they traveled at 6 miles per hour for 6 hours, and then at half that speed for another three hours, before stopping to rest for the night.  On the third and final day, they traveled for 5 hours at 7 miles per hour.  In total, how far did they travel, in miles, during their horseback riding trip?

On the first day, they traveled 5*7=35 miles.
On the first part of the second day, they traveled 6*6=36 miles.
The second part of the second day, at half their morning speed, they traveled (6/2)*3=9 miles.
On the final day, they traveled 5*7=35 miles.
In total, they traveled 35+36+9+35=115 miles.
The answer is 115.

Tanuja, you asked why I'm always so quick to make up after a fight with your mother. Let me, your Nazia nani, tell you a story.

When I was fifteen, I had a terrible fight with my own Ammi over a school trip. I slammed my door. She went silent. For three days, we didn't speak.

I stayed in my room. She cooked and cleaned and didn't knock. We both felt misunderstood. And, if I'm honest, a little ashamed of what we'd said.

The worst part was my little brother Kamran. He ate his meals quietly, looking from one of us to the other. He stopped laughing. He even stopped playing his cricket in the courtyard.

Each of us waited for the other to give in first.

It was only when Kamran cried at dinner that Ammi and I looked at each other properly. That was the turning point.

How many days did Nazia and her Ammi not speak?
Three days.
How did Nazia and her Ammi each feel during the silence?
Both felt misunderstood and a little ashamed of what they'd said.
What was the turning point in Nazia nani's story?
When Kamran cried at dinner and Nazia and her Ammi finally looked at each other properly.
How did the cold war affect Kamran?
He became quiet and anxious, stopped laughing and stopped playing cricket.

messages.content: I keep seeing situations in a self-help article. Can you just state its meaning?

Situations are the sets of conditions and events that make up what is happening at a particular time and place. It is a noun, the plural of situation.
Example: Staying calm helps you in difficult situations.

The visa appointment for Parveen's new job in Dubai was nine days away when her father's scan results came back. The doctors spoke gently: months, perhaps a year. That night, on the hospital's plastic chairs, Parveen felt a cold dread, and then an odd clarity. Anirban, her fiancé, brought tea and sat beside her. "A year from now, what will you wish you had done?" he asked. She knew at once. She would wish she had been here. She would also wish she hadn't thrown away the job Abbu was so proud of. They planned through the night. Parveen asked the company to defer her joining by six months; they agreed to four. She moved back into her old room. She recorded Abbu telling stories about his tailoring shop, and he taught her to stitch buttonholes, laughing at her crooked ones. When she finally flew out, Abbu, thinner, came to the airport and slipped his old scissors into her bag.

How many days away was the visa appointment?
Nine days.
What was Parveen feeling on the hospital chairs that night?
Parveen felt a cold dread, then an unexpected clarity about what mattered.
How did Anirban's question help Parveen decide?
Imagining her regrets a year ahead showed she wanted both to be with Abbu and to keep the job, which led to asking for a deferral.
How might Abbu feel teaching Parveen buttonholes?
Abbu would likely feel joy and pride, passing on his craft and sharing laughter in a hard time.

Monday: “I don't want to do veena any more,” Rukmini told Amma. “I want football on Saturdays.” Amma said, “Tell me why, properly, not just ‘I don't want to.’” Wednesday: Rukmini went to her veena teacher, Joseph Sir, with a list. “One: I've done it for three years and I'm not enjoying it. Two: football is at the same time. Three: I'll still play at home sometimes.” Joseph Sir read it twice. “Those are honest reasons. But the recital is in three weeks, and your group needs you.” Friday: They agreed: Rukmini would play in the recital, then switch to football. She shook Joseph Sir's hand like a grown-up.

How many years had Rukmini played the veena?
Rukmini had played for three years.
What was Rukmini feeling about veena classes?
Rukmini felt tired of veena and no longer enjoyed it, and she was eager to play football instead.
How did Rukmini make her preference easier to negotiate?
She wrote clear reasons instead of just saying she didn't want to, which led to a fair deal.
How did Joseph Sir balance Rukmini's wish with the group's needs?
He accepted her reasons as honest but explained the recital needed her, agreeing she could switch afterwards.
My friend's father passed away. What should I write in message? I don't know English words for this.

You could write: "I'm so sorry about your father. I'm thinking of you and your family. If you need anything, I'm here." Keep it short and simple. Being there for your friend matters more than perfect words.

The stalls at the temple fair will open from 4 pm. Plastic bags are not allowed. Free drinking water is available at the entrance. Everyone is welcome, so please come and enjoy the fair.
A customer said, "I'll get back to you tomorrow." What should I understand?

It means the person will contact you again, with an answer or more information, at a later time. It is informal and polite.
Example: Let me check the stock, and I will get back to you this afternoon.

On Friday morning Farida's payment had already arrived before Deepika opened her laptop. The brief sent with it was two pages, clear, with the audience and the deadline listed. Deepika said, "It's a little more, actually. I can do it by Monday."

"Perfect," Farida wrote. "And I'll mention your name in the launch post."

When had Farida's payment arrived?
Farida's payment had already arrived before Deepika opened her laptop on Friday morning.
What might Deepika have felt reading Farida's brief and replies, and how does the observer know?
Deepika seemed relaxed and pleased, since Ashwin saw her humming and sending work early, though Ashwin cannot be certain what she felt.
How does Deepika keep the good working relationship going?
Deepika is honest about the extra time needed and delivers reliably, even a day early, so both sides keep small promises.

Farida probably values a freelancer who is honest about limits and reliable, which is why the brief is clear and credit is given.

His mother Farida didn't want a fight, so one evening she sat beside him. "How many hours today?" He shrugged. "Five? Six?" "And studying?" "One." She didn't take the phone. Six weeks away.
What might Bhupen have been feeling when he admitted to five or six hours?
Probably guilty and a bit embarrassed, knowing his marks were sliding.

Letting Bhupen make the plan gave him ownership, so he was more likely to stick to it.

Saturday. Kashish kept one chair empty at her birthday table, right next to hers. Shreya had promised, pinky-promised, that she would come. The cake was cut, the games were played, and the chair stayed empty. Kashish smiled for the photos and cried in the bathroom afterwards.
Sunday. She typed an angry message: 'Don't bother talking to me again.' She stared at it, then deleted it.
Monday. At the school gate, Kashish took a breath. 'Shreya, you promised to come on Saturday. I kept a chair for you. It really hurt.' Shreya's face crumpled. 'My Nani fell, and we rushed to the hospital. I didn't have your number with me. I'm so sorry.' Kashish felt the hurt loosen a little. 'Is she okay?' 'She's okay now.'

What did Kashish keep empty?
One chair at her birthday table, right next to hers.
How did Kashish feel when the chair stayed empty?
Hurt and let down; she smiled for the photos but cried in the bathroom.
Which choice worked better than the angry message?
Telling Shreya calmly how it felt and giving her the chance to explain.
What was it like for Shreya when Kashish spoke to her?
Painful and guilty; her face crumpled because she had a real reason but had still broken her promise.

The school hall in Lisbon was full of parents, and Beatriz, nine, sat in the front row with her class. Her friend Emeka stood at the microphone for the last word of the spelling bee.
"Necessary."
Emeka closed his eyes. "N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."
The bell rang. He'd won.
Beatriz jumped up clapping so loudly that her shoes squeaked on the chair. She had been knocked out in round three, on "rhythm". For one second, watching him hold the silver cup, she wished it were her hands on it. The wish pinched a little.
Then Emeka looked straight at her and grinned, and the pinch was gone under a big warm feeling. She had helped him practise all week at lunch.
"You did it!" she shouted over everyone.

Which word did Emeka spell to win?
"Necessary".
What was Beatriz feeling as Emeka held the cup?
She felt a small pinch of wishing she had won, then a big warm happiness for her friend.
How could a teacher support both children after the spelling bee?
A teacher could praise Emeka's win and also notice Beatriz's kindness in helping him practise and cheering, so both feel seen.
What was it like for Emeka to see Beatriz cheering?

With her cousin's wedding two days away, the house in Madurai was full of relatives, and the power had gone out at nine. Uma sat on the terrace with a torch, her statistics exam at ten the next morning. 'I always freeze in exams,' she told her sister Jaya. 'Always. Tomorrow will be the same.' Jaya took the torch and turned over Uma's formula sheet. 'Okay. When didn't you?' Uma frowned. 'The Class 12 boards. The semester one maths paper. The accounts internal.' 'And when did you?' 'Last semester's stats. The chemistry practical.' 'What was different?' Uma thought. Before the good ones she'd done a mock paper with a timer. Before the bad ones she'd only read notes. She looked at the noisy house behind her. There was still time for one timed mock, even by torchlight.

When was Uma's statistics exam?
It was at ten the next morning.
Why did Uma feel sure she would freeze again?
She was anxious, with a noisy house and no power the night before, and remembering the last stats exam made 'always' feel like a rule.
What did listing counter-examples reveal for Uma?
It showed she hadn't always frozen, and that a timed mock paper made the difference, giving her one thing to do that night.
How does Jaya see her sister's 'always'?
Jaya treats it as a claim to test, not a fact, and calmly asks questions that help Uma find the pattern.

I'm Manjula, and I've been a structural engineer for six years. People ask how I spot problems in a building so fast. Honestly, it's often a feeling first. A crack in the wrong place, a beam that looks slightly off.

But a feeling isn't a report. When my gut says something's wrong, I measure, I check the drawings, and I ask my colleague Chaitanya to look independently.

Last year, my gut said a balcony was fine. Chaitanya disagreed. We tested it, and he was right; it needed support.

And when my cousin asks me about her car engine or her stock investments? I say, "That's not my field. Ask someone who knows."

My gut is trained for buildings. Not for everything.

How many years has Manjula been a structural engineer?
Six years.
How does Manjula feel about these hunches, based on the monologue?
Manjula feels confident in them for buildings but humble, knowing they must be checked and don't apply outside structural engineering.
What does Manjula do when her gut says something's wrong?
Manjula measures, checks the drawings and asks Chaitanya to look independently.

Chaitanya probably felt respected and valued, since Manjula listened and tested it.

Her client contact list.

She cooperated first, named the betrayal clearly, and forgave once Mehak corrected it, avoiding both being exploited and endless punishment.

I'm Leela, one of the four developers in Rafiq's team, and I watched how he handled the week our launch nearly fell apart. On Tuesday, the bank said our payment approval would take ten more days than promised. Rafiq didn't shout. He stood at the whiteboard for a long time, rubbing out and redrawing arrows. The dark-mode feature and the new icons.

My roommate Lavanya had been moody all week, and on Thursday night I found out why.

She was sitting on her bed with her phone, typing and deleting. "It's Gautam," she said. "From school. We used to study together every evening. We haven't talked properly since he moved to Delhi."

She showed me her drafts: "Hi! Long time!" deleted. "How are you??" deleted.

Then she typed, slowly, "I was thinking of those evenings on your terrace doing maths. Can we talk on Saturday?" and sent it before she could delete it.

She put the phone face down and let out a long breath.

Gautam replied twenty minutes later: "YES. I miss that terrace." She laughed out loud.

I don't know what they talked about on Saturday. I only know she hummed all Sunday.

— Deepti

When did Gautam reply?
Twenty minutes later.
How does Deepti seem to feel watching Lavanya send the message?
Deepti seems curious and warmly supportive, and pleased when Lavanya laughs at the reply.
Why did Lavanya's final message work better than her drafts?
It named a specific memory, the terrace maths evenings, and asked for a specific day, so it felt personal and easy to answer.
What might Gautam have felt on receiving the message?
He seemed delighted and relieved, as his quick "YES" and "I miss that terrace" show.
What does "back up" mean for a computer file?

To "back up" a file is to make a spare copy so that you do not lose it. The noun is written as one word: "backup".
Examples: Please back up your project before you close the laptop. I keep a backup on a pen drive.

"Parveen, sit here, you can see both the board and Ms. Nair's hands," Ujjwal said, pulling out a chair in the front row.
Parveen signed a quick thanks. The interpreter, Ms. Nair, was already at the corner.
The lecturer asked a question. Ujjwal started to say, "Tell her—" and stopped himself. He turned and looked at Parveen. "What do you think about the second case?" Then he waited. A few seconds passed while the interpreter finished the sentence.
Parveen signed her answer. Ms. Nair voiced it. The class went quiet, then someone nodded.
"Good point," Ujjwal said, to Parveen and not to the interpreter.
Parveen smiled. Later she signed, slowly, that it was the first time this term a classmate had looked at her, not the interpreter.

Where did Ujjwal suggest Parveen sit?
He suggested she sit in the front row, where she could see both the board and Ms. Nair's hands.
What did Parveen feel when Ujjwal looked at her and waited, and how do you know?
She felt included, shown by her smile and by signing that it was the first time this term a classmate had looked at her and not the interpreter.
What could other classmates learn from Ujjwal's habit?
They could speak to the deaf student directly, look at her, and wait patiently for the interpreter's lag.
How might it feel for Parveen when people talk to the interpreter instead of her?
It probably feels like being talked about rather than to, so she may feel invisible even though the interpreter is there to help.

Emilia needs 42 cartons of berries to make a berry cobbler. She already has 2 cartons of strawberries and 7 cartons of blueberries in her cupboard. She decides to go to the supermarket to get more cartons. How many more cartons of berries should Emilia buy?

She previously had 2 cartons + 7 cartons = 9 cartons of berries.
Emilia needs to buy 42 cartons - 9 cartons = 33 cartons of berries.
The answer is 33.

Page after page, the same pages, three times each. Last term he did that for maths, science, everything. His marks came back: mostly in the forties. He sat on the bed staring at the report card. “NO! NO!” Lindiwe screamed, arching in the trolley seat.

Lindiwe's scream broke into hiccups. She looked at both, then grabbed the bananas.

Lindiwe grabbed the bananas.

She was angry and felt powerless at being refused the sweets, and screaming was the biggest way to say so without many words.

messages.content: Lilah's family gallery has 400 photos. On a two-day trip to the Grand Canyon, they took half as many photos they have in the family's gallery on the first day and 120 more photos than they took on the first day on the second day. If they added all these photos to the family gallery, calculate the total number of photos in the gallery.

On their first day to the grand canyon, the family took half as many photos as the ones they have in the gallery, meaning they took 1/2*400 = 200 photos.
The total number of photos if they add the ones they took on the first day to the family's gallery is 400+200 = 600
On the second day, they took 120 more photos than they took on the first day, a total of 200+120 = 320 photos.
After adding the photos they took on the second day to the galley, the number of photos will be 600+320 = 920
The answer is 920.

Today I had to speak firmly to Rekha about talking during the test. I did it at her desk, and I regret that the class heard. What I noticed afterwards was her friend Ganga. Talking during the test.

In the school staff room during Diwali week, Principal Rashmi proposed moving the Saturday half-day to a Wednesday afternoon off. Same hours overall. The teachers bristled. "We'll lose our Saturdays!" Uday, a young maths teacher, watched the room. When the principal had said "You'll gain a free Wednesday afternoon," nobody smiled. But when she said "Saturday half-days end," everyone frowned. He raised his hand. "Ma'am, can I suggest how we present it? Your total hours off stay the same. You'll have Wednesday afternoons free for family or errands. And yes, Saturday mornings will be working." A few teachers nodded slowly. One said, "Put that way, Wednesday is actually more useful for the bank." Uday felt quietly pleased. He hadn't hidden the loss. He'd just put the whole picture in order.

What did the principal propose to replace the Saturday half-day with?
A Wednesday afternoon off.
What was Uday feeling as he suggested a new framing?
Uday felt quietly confident, and later pleased, having noticed that the loss was upsetting people more than the gain was cheering them.
What made Uday's framing both helpful and honest?
It led with what was protected, explained the gain, and clearly said Saturday mornings would be working, so nothing was hidden.
How did the teachers react to the new framing?
A few nodded, and one said Wednesday was actually more useful, showing they felt less threatened.

January. Leela, in her first job in London, set up a standing order with her bank: the day her salary landed, a fixed slice would move into a savings pot she named "Ammamma, Kochi". She printed a photo of her grandmother on the veranda and stuck it by the door.
April. Elizabeth, her flatmate, dragged her to a shoe sale. Leela tried on a pair, looked at them and put them back. "I've unsubscribed from all the shop emails," she said. "If I don't see it, I don't want it as much." Elizabeth bought two pairs and laughed at her.
September. Leela showed Elizabeth the pot on her phone, then the plane ticket. "Kochi. Three weeks. Ammamma doesn't know yet."
Elizabeth looked at the photo by the door. "Okay," she said. "That's better than shoes."

What did Leela name the savings pot?
Leela named it 'Ammamma, Kochi'.
Why did Leela put the shoes back at the sale?
Leela felt tempted but steady, keeping the trip to Ammamma in mind, and having removed shop emails made the wanting weaker.
Which steps helped Leela's future self?
A standing order on payday, unsubscribing from shop emails and the photo of Ammamma by the door made the goal automatic and concrete.
How does Elizabeth's view change by September?
Elizabeth laughed at Leela in April, but by September feels impressed and agrees the trip is better than shoes.

Give me this passage in reported speech, keeping what was said but not the quotation marks.

At the review the manager said, "Good, so that timeline works. Let's keep this pace next time."
At the review the manager said that the timeline worked and suggested keeping that pace next time.
Invitation to a baby's naming ceremony for close relatives, on Sunday at 11 in the morning, at our home. Warm and brief, 50 words. We are Priti and Vijay.

Dear family,
We are happy to invite you to our baby's naming ceremony. It will be held at our home on Sunday at 11 am. Your blessings and your presence mean so much to us. We hope you can come and share this joyful day with us.
Priti and Vijay

Read this:

Ishita was twenty and snapping at everything by mid-afternoon, and her boyfriend Irfan noticed her jaw clenched over the tea. He did not say, "Is it that time?" He put down his phone and asked, "You seem worn out. What kind of day has it been?" She let out a breath. "My presentation went badly and my lower back aches. That's all it is." He nodded and offered to walk her to the bus stop. Later she thanked him for not blaming her mood on her body. At twenty-five, Ishita's period pains were a different matter. Each month she missed a day of work, and the low mood around it lasted longer and grew heavier. Her friend Ritu found her sitting on the office stairs, pale, waiting for the pain to ease. "This isn't normal tiredness. You shouldn't just put up with it." Ritu stayed until Ishita could stand, and then they booked her an appointment at the clinic together. The doctor listened without hurry, wrote down what Ishita said, and told her they would work through it step by step.

Who found Ishita sitting on the office stairs?
Her friend Ritu found her there.
How does Irfan's response to Ishita at twenty differ from what she needed at twenty-five?

At twenty Irfan asked what kind of day she had instead of blaming her mood on her period, which suited an ordinary bad day. At twenty-five the pain and low mood were bigger, missing work every month, so she needed Ritu to take it seriously and get her to a doctor.
What was Ishita feeling when she sat pale on the office stairs?
She felt exhausted and worn down, and probably worried that this pain would keep coming back.
How could a friend support someone whose monthly pain disrupts work?
A friend can believe her, stay with her, and help book a clinic visit so the doctor can look at it properly.

Read this:

Sharmila: how's Pune?
Raghav: honestly? bad
Raghav: I haven't gone to the library once. haven't set up my laptop. I sleep through the 9am
Sharmila: that's not you
Raghav: I know. I don't know anyone. everything feels heavy. even laundry
Sharmila: have you talked to anyone there?
Raghav: the canteen guy. about samosas
Sharmila: ok. find ONE person. anyone who's also new
Raghav: easier said
Sharmila: there must be a first-year group. join something tiny. a cricket game. a walk
[two weeks later]
Raghav: update. joined the Sunday cricket in the hostel ground
Raghav: made 3 friends. one of them is in my class
Raghav: we go to the library together now
Sharmila: 🥹
Raghav: I did laundry yesterday without dying
Sharmila: proud of you

What did Raghav join two weeks later?
Raghav joined the Sunday cricket in the hostel ground.
Why did even laundry feel heavy to Raghav?
Raghav felt lonely and disconnected in Pune, with no one to talk to, so everything felt heavy.
What did Sharmila suggest, and why did it work?
Finding one person by joining something tiny, like a cricket game, because a small circle brought back Raghav's motivation.
How might Sharmila feel reading the update?
Sharmila felt moved and proud, glad that Raghav found friends.

Make Kamal's invitation more polite.

Kamal said, "The track is the shortcut to the mango grove. Come on."
Kamal said, "The track is the shortcut to the mango grove. Please come with me."

Read this:

Hrithik: hey. i need a favour
Thomas: congrats on the promotion first 🎉
Hrithik: thanks. the favour: tell me when i become an idiot
Thomas: lol already?
Hrithik: serious. i read that power makes people stop listening. i don't want that
Hrithik: so every friday i'm asking the team 'what did i get wrong this week'. anonymous form
Thomas: good
Hrithik: and you. you've always disagreed with me. keep doing it
Thomas: that i can do for free
Hrithik: also before any big decision i'm asking 'who pays for this'. like the weekend deployment. it's the juniors who lose saturdays, not me
Thomas: and credit?
Hrithik: whoever did the work presents it. not me
Thomas: ok who are you and what have you done with my arrogant friend
Hrithik: he's on probation 😅

What does Hrithik plan to ask the team every Friday?
'What did I get wrong this week', through an anonymous form.
What is Hrithik worried about?
Hrithik is worried that power will make him stop listening, like the leaders he has read about.
Which safeguards has Hrithik set up?
Anonymous weekly feedback, a friend who will disagree, asking who pays for decisions, and letting whoever did the work present it.
How does Thomas react to the request?
Thomas is amused but supportive, happy to keep disagreeing and teasing his friend about being arrogant.
I want to give homemade sweets as a gift. What stays fresh and looks good?
Barfi cut into diamonds, laddoos in paper cups and coconut sweets all look neat and keep for a few days. Pack them in a clean box with parchment paper between layers.
Which one is the easiest? I am a beginner. My name is Chloe.
Coconut barfi is easy, Chloe. Cook desiccated coconut with milk and sugar until it thickens, add cardamom, set it in a greased plate and cut it into squares when cool.
How long does it take to set?
It sets in about an hour at room temperature, or thirty minutes in the fridge. Cut it when it is firm but not fully hard, so the edges stay clean.
Can I colour it?
Yes, add a drop of food colour to half the mixture for two layers, pink and white. Spread the first layer, let it cool slightly, then add the second. It will look lovely in the box.
What was the sweet I was going to make?
You are going to make coconut barfi, Chloe. It is easy for a beginner, and cutting it in squares and packing it neatly will make it a good gift.

What does the passage tell us about how Estella feels toward Miss Havisham's affection?

We were seated by the fire, as just now described, and Miss Havisham still had Estella's arm drawn through her own, and still clutched Estella's hand in hers, when Estella gradually began to detach herself. She had shown a proud impatience more than once before, and had rather endured that fierce affection than accepted or returned it.
Estella does not welcome it. She has shown proud impatience before, and she has put up with the fierce love rather than accepting or returning it.
Can you write about 90 words in diary form for someone on the first night of a long train journey across India.

Dear Diary,
I am writing this on the upper berth, with the train rocking me gently. Outside, small stations flash by with yellow lights and sleepy tea-sellers. An aunty below me shared her thepla, and we talked for an hour. The little boy opposite taught me a card game. I never thought a train could feel so friendly. The wheels make a steady song, and my eyes are getting heavy. Tomorrow, we will wake up in a new state.
Check my sentence: The teacher told that the exam is easy. Could you explain what "crunchy" means? Leela saw 17 clouds in the sky, and 8 more came. How many clouds are there now?

1. Fixed: The teacher said that the exam is easy. Why: Use "said" with "that"; "told" needs a person.
2. Crunchy means making a loud, crisp sound when you bite it, like a fresh carrot.
3. It is 25. Because 17 + 8 = 25.

Read this:

Afreen, you want to build the whole tower first and see if it stands? Let me tell you about my first bridge. I'm Vaibhav, and when I was nine I had a box of ice-cream sticks and a plan for a bridge across the gap between two beds, for my little brother's cars. My Nana said, "Build a short piece first. Hang something on it." So I made a span no longer than my hand and hung a water bottle from its middle with string. Crack, right in the centre, while the ends were fine. So I doubled the sticks in the middle and added a little arch underneath. It held the bottle. Only then did I build the long one. My brother drove cars over it for a whole year.

What did Vaibhav hang from the middle of the short span?
A water bottle, on a string.
How might young Vaibhav have felt when the span cracked in the centre?
Perhaps disappointed, but also curious, since the crack showed exactly where the weakness was.
Which choice inside the story made the long bridge work?
Testing a short span first, then doubling the middle sticks and adding an arch before building the long one.
What was the bridge like for Vaibhav's little brother?
Vaibhav's brother had a bridge for the toy cars that lasted a whole year.

metadata.subtype: Approach: testing a small version first [Action]

Read this:

Yusuf's scooter came back to the Jayanagar parking lot with a long scrape down the left side and the mirror twisted. Anjali handed over the keys without meeting his eyes. "It was like that when I took it, na?" Yusuf knew it wasn't; he had washed it on Sunday. He felt the heat rise and an accusation form. He swallowed it. "Anjali, sit for a sec." They sat on the low wall. "I'd honestly rather have it straight than be shielded from it. Whatever happened, I'm not going to blow up. It's a scooter." Anjali picked at her dupatta. A long pause. "I skidded on the gravel near the flyover. I was so embarrassed, and you'd just said how new it was." "Were you hurt?" "Just my palm." She showed it. "Okay. We'll get the mirror fixed Saturday." Anjali laughed shakily. "I'll pay for the mirror. And sorry."

When had Yusuf washed the scooter?
He had washed it on Sunday.
What was Yusuf feeling when Anjali said it was like that before?
Yusuf felt angry, the heat rising and an accusation forming, because he knew the scooter had been clean and whole.
Which of Yusuf's choices made honesty easier?
Swallowing the accusation, sitting down with Anjali, and saying he preferred the truth and would not blow up, which made confessing less costly.
Why might Anjali have told the truth after Yusuf spoke?
His promise not to blow up lowered the cost of honesty, so admitting her embarrassment felt safer than keeping up the story.
Why does the sky turn orange at sunset? My little brother asked and I couldn't explain.
Here is the short version. Sunlight looks white but contains many colours. In the evening, the sun is low, so its light travels through more air before reaching you.
And what does the air do to it?
The air scatters the blue light away, so mostly the reds and oranges remain. That is why the sun and nearby clouds look warm in colour.
How do I say it to a seven-year-old?
You could say, 'Sunlight has lots of colours hidden inside. At sunset the blue ones get lost on the long way, and the orange ones reach us.' Short and simple works best.
He asked why the sky is blue in the daytime then.
In the daytime the light has a shorter path, and the air scatters blue light across the sky in all directions. So blue comes to your eyes from everywhere you look.
That actually makes sense now. Thanks for the clear explanation.
Glad it helped. Next time you see an orange sky, you can both look for how the colours change from the sun outwards.

Read this:

Art room note, Thursday.
During the painting lesson, Sangeeta knocked her water jar across Priya's finished drawing of a peacock. Priya burst into tears. Sangeeta said "Sorry" at once, but I could see that saying it didn't satisfy her. She asked if she could stay back at lunch. For forty minutes she sat with a fresh sheet and Priya's smudged drawing beside it, copying the peacock's outline carefully, then asked Priya to come and colour it with her. When Priya arrived, the outline was ready and neat. They painted the feathers together. Sangeeta told me, "Sorry doesn't give her the drawing back. This does." I have put both drawings, the smudged one and the new one, on the class board.
Dilnaz, art teacher

What did Sangeeta knock over?
Her water jar.
Why wasn't saying sorry enough for Sangeeta?
She felt guilty and knew that words alone would not give Priya her drawing back.
What else could Sangeeta have done if there was no time at lunch?
Offered to redraw it at home and bring it the next day, still repairing the harm.
How might Priya feel arriving at lunch?
Surprised and comforted to find the outline ready and a friend to paint with.

metadata.subtype: Approach: fixing the harm along with the apology [Action]

Read this:

Week 1: In her Kolkata PG, Jahnavi ate the mess rice in silence and counted the days until the Dussehra break, when she would go home to Mysuru. Every night she called Amma and cried quietly once the Kannada greetings started.
Week 3: The cook put mustard in everything. Jahnavi found a small tiffin place near the metro run by a man named Jeevan, who turned out to be from Mangaluru. He spoke to her in Kannada and gave extra chutney. She started going every Saturday morning.
Week 6: She still called home every night, but the calls were shorter. On Saturdays she brought her roommate Rupsa to Jeevan's for dosa, and Rupsa taught her three Bengali phrases in return. The Dussehra ticket was still booked. She just wasn't counting days anymore.

Where was Jeevan from?
Jeevan was from Mangaluru.
What was Jahnavi feeling in Week 1 when the Kannada greetings started?
Jahnavi felt homesick and lonely, missing her language and family enough to cry quietly.
What small anchors helped Jahnavi settle?
Saturday visits to Jeevan's tiffin place and bringing Rupsa, who taught her Bengali phrases in return.
How might Jeevan see Jahnavi's Saturday visits?
Jeevan probably enjoys meeting a fellow Kannada speaker far from home, which is why he chats and adds extra chutney.

Read this:

Monday, three weeks before the Jaipur wedding: at the planning meeting, Zainab watched her two colleagues. Kunal waved off the list of risks. 'Everything will be fine, it's a wedding, not a war.' Aditi kept writing. 'The tent supplier was late last season. I'm calling a backup today, just in case.'
Thursday, ten days later: the tent supplier phoned to say half the canopies were stuck in a warehouse. Kunal shrugged. 'They'll sort it out.' Aditi was already on the phone to her backup, confirming a delivery date. 'I think we can still pull this off,' she said to Zainab. 'If we move now.'
Saturday, the mehendi evening: Aditi's side of the lawn was covered and lit. Kunal was running between guests with plastic sheets as a light drizzle started. Later, over cold coffee, Zainab noticed that Aditi hadn't been the gloomy one at all. She'd been the one who actually believed things could go well.

What did Kunal say while waving off the list of risks?
Kunal said, 'Everything will be fine, it's a wedding, not a war.'
What did Zainab realise about Aditi after the mehendi evening?
Zainab realised Aditi hadn't been gloomy at all; Aditi was the one who actually believed things could go well and planned for it.
Which choice made the difference when the supplier phoned on Thursday?
Aditi had already lined up a backup on Monday, so she could confirm a new delivery date at once instead of hoping it would sort itself out.
What was the mehendi evening like for Kunal?
Kunal was stuck running between guests with plastic sheets in the drizzle, likely stressed and embarrassed that Kunal's reassurance hadn't protected anyone.
Describe a gentle story about a boy who wants a new shirt for Eid but his family has little money.

Zaid saw the new shirts in the shop window and sighed. Eid was in a week, and his father drove an auto and earned little. Zaid did not ask for anything. His mother noticed and said nothing. That night, she opened her trunk and took out a piece of blue cloth she had saved. For five evenings, she sat at the old sewing machine while Zaid slept. On Eid morning, he found a new shirt folded at his bed, with small white buttons. He put it on, and it fit perfectly. He ran to hug her, and she patted his cheek and told him to go and show his father.
My sister gave the baby a "dummy". My American friend laughed and asked if I meant a "pacifier".

Yes, they mean the same rubber nipple a baby sucks to calm down. "Dummy" is British, and "pacifier" is American. In Indian English, you may hear either word.
Examples: The baby stopped crying when she got her dummy. (British) The baby stopped crying when she got her pacifier. (American)

Read this:

Sudha's phone buzzed on the desk during study hour. Tanvir had sent, 'Great, just great,' after she'd told him the bus would be late for the fourth time that week. She stared at the flat words. No emoji. Was he angry with her? Frustrated with the bus? Making a joke? Sudha remembered how Tanvir talked when he was cheerful, an actual bounce, and when he was sarcastic, a low flat drawl. In text she could not hear it. Her thumbs hovered. She typed, 'Are you joking or actually upset?' Tanvir replied a minute later, 'ha, both. Bus is late and I'm going to miss cricket.' She sent back a sympathetic face and said she'd wait with him.

What did Tanvir send after hearing about the bus?
He sent, 'Great, just great,'.
What might Tanvir have felt when he sent that message?
He was likely frustrated about the late bus and missing cricket, and possibly a little joking too, as he said 'both'. Sudha could not tell from the flat words alone.
What made Sudha's question helpful?
She asked directly whether he was joking or upset, so she didn't assume contempt or humour from flat text.
How might Sudha have felt staring at the flat message?
Sudha probably felt unsure and a little anxious, wondering if Tanvir was angry with her, so she asked directly instead of guessing. 🙂
Should I write "a well known author" or "a well-known author"?

Use a hyphen before a noun: "a well-known author". When the phrase comes after the noun, you usually leave the hyphen out, as in "The author is well known."
Examples: She is a well-known author. The author is well known.
My teacher gave us a worksheet with twenty questions and I got stuck on number five.
Getting stuck is a normal part of studying. What kind of question is it?
A word problem on distance and speed.
Try reading it slowly twice and writing down what is given and what is asked. Sometimes a simple diagram shows the answer.
I wrote down the facts but I don't know what to do next.
Think about which formula links the facts you have. If you aren't sure, check your notebook for a similar solved example. If you still can't see it, mark it and ask your teacher tomorrow.
Good, I'll mark it and move on to number six.
That is a smart move. Leaving a hard one for later often lets your brain work on it in the background.

Read this:

Behind the family's kirana shop in Rajgarh, Anjali sat on a sack of rice with her physics book unopened. Between the shop counter, tuition and the entrance forms, every hour was spoken for. "Remember when we were small," she said to her cousin Disha, "and we spent whole days at Nani's farm, chasing goats? No worries at all." Disha, sorting coins, laughed softly. "You were terrified of the buffalo. And you cried whenever Nani made us come in before dark." Anjali paused. She had forgotten the buffalo. She had forgotten how small the world felt then, how she couldn't go anywhere without asking. Still, the ache stayed. "It feels lighter, in my head," she said. Disha nodded. "Maybe you need one light hour now, not the old days."

Where did Anjali and Disha spend whole days as children?
At Nani's farm.
Why does Anjali still feel the ache after Disha reminds her?
She feels overloaded and tired, so the farm days feel lighter in her head; comfort and loss colour the memory even when she recalls the buffalo.
What could help Anjali now?
As Disha suggests, carve out one light hour in the present rather than longing for the past, and perhaps talk to the family about the load.
How does Disha see Anjali's longing?
Disha remembers the fears and rules too, but responds with understanding rather than just correcting her.

Read this:

Dear Chetan,
Your mother says I should write this instead of saying it badly on the phone, so here it is.
Last month I asked your roommate to tell me when you came back each night, and I checked your location every hour. When your mid-term marks came, I posted them in the family group and wrote, "See what happens in hostel." You haven't really talked to me since.
I was scared. You are nineteen and in a new city, and I kept imagining the worst. But I turned my fear into watching you, and then into shaming you. That was wrong.
From today I have stopped checking your location. I won't contact your roommate. If you mess up a test or come back late sometimes, that is yours to learn from. Tell me what you choose to tell me.
I'm still your Papa. I'll still worry. I'll just try to trust you more than I watch you.
Papa (Naveen)

What did Papa post in the family group?
Chetan's mid-term marks, with the words "See what happens in hostel."
What feeling does Naveen say was behind the watching?
Fear: he kept imagining the worst for his nineteen-year-old son in a new city.
What changes does Naveen promise?
To stop checking Chetan's location, stop contacting the roommate, and let Chetan learn from small mistakes.
How might Chetan have felt when his marks were posted in the family group?
Humiliated and angry, which is why he stopped talking to his father.

Which spelling is right?
a) fiveteen / fifteen
b) eightteen / eighteen
c) threeteen / thirteen
d) twelve / twelv
e) ninteen / nineteen
f) fourty / four
g) twenty / twenti
h) elevan / eleven
i) seaven / seven
j) zero / zeero

a) fifteen
b) eighteen
c) thirteen
d) twelve
e) nineteen
f) four
g) twenty
h) eleven
i) seven
j) zero

Read this:

Tuesday: Madhav and Ankita argued over the cricket bat in the school yard. "You hog it," Ankita said. "You bat like a chicken," said Madhav. The bell rang.
Wednesday: The whole class was watching this time. Ankita said, "Remember when you cried in the Class 3 play?" Some of them laughed. Madhav felt trapped. He heard himself say, "At least my teeth don't stick out like yours," and then, "Your whole family is weird." He wanted it to hurt, and it did.
Thursday: Ankita ate lunch in the library. Madhav's stomach felt sick every time he passed the door.

What did Ankita bring up on Wednesday in front of the class?
She reminded everyone that Madhav cried in the Class 3 play.
Why did Madhav say hurtful things about Ankita's teeth and family?
He felt cornered and humiliated when the class laughed, so winning mattered more than the bat and he chose words meant to hurt.
What turning point could still help after Wednesday?
Madhav could admit to Ankita that his words about her teeth and family were unfair, or a teacher could help them talk without the class watching.
What might Ankita be experiencing on Thursday?
She seems hurt and ashamed, choosing the library so she does not have to face the class or Madhav.
Write a story with no dialogue about two friends who stop being angry at each other.

Anu and Bela had not spoken for six days. Each walked into the classroom with her chin up and looked past the other. On the seventh day, it rained, and Bela arrived without an umbrella, soaked to the knees. Anu saw her shivering at the gate. She took out her spare umbrella, walked across the yard and held it above Bela's head. Bela looked up in surprise, then looked at her own wet shoes. A small smile pulled at her mouth. They walked into school under the same umbrella, shoulders touching, water dripping off its edges. At lunch, Bela unwrapped her sandwich and set half beside Anu's plate without a glance.

Read this:

On the first frosty morning of winter football camp, Harsha and Francis were picking positions. Francis wanted to be goalkeeper. Harsha hated standing in goal and used to think everyone did. "Okay, you like the gloves, I get it," Harsha said, handing them over. By the second half, though, Harsha's side was losing three–nil and the coach moved Harsha back to defence. "Francis, swap with me. You'd rather be out here, obviously!" Francis shook his head. "I told you, I like goal." Harsha kicked the white grass. "Nobody likes standing in goal when we're losing." Francis just pulled the gloves tighter and faced the pitch.

Which position did Francis want to play?
Francis wanted to be goalkeeper.
Why did Harsha insist that Francis would rather swap?
He felt frustrated and embarrassed about losing, and that strong feeling pushed him back into assuming Francis must want what he wanted.
What could Harsha try next time he is upset during a match?
Take a breath and ask "Do you still want goal?" instead of deciding for Francis; his own feelings can be real without being Francis's too.
How does Francis feel when Harsha tells him what he would rather do?
He likely feels unheard and a bit annoyed, since he had already said he likes goal; pulling the gloves tighter shows he is holding his ground.
Lolita has 54000 strawberry seeds. In each planting zone, 3123 seeds will be used. If she will accumulate 7 planting zones, how many strawberry seeds will remain?

The total amount of seeds used in the planting zones is 3123 x 7 = 21861.
The total amount of seeds left after planting is 54000 - 21861 = 32139.
The answer is 32139.
Write instructions for lining up in a row. Three numbered steps, each starting with a different word.

1. Stand behind your friend.
2. Keep your hands to yourself.
3. Walk quietly to the door.

A school has 15 classrooms. One-third of these classrooms have 30 desks in each classroom and the rest have 25 desks in each classroom. Only one student can sit at one desk. How many students can this school accommodate so that everyone has their own desk?

One-third of the classrooms have 30 desks, so there are 1/3 * 15 = 5 classrooms like that.
The rest, which means 15 - 5 = 10 classrooms, have 25 desks.
One-third of the classrooms can fit 5 * 30 = 150 students.
The rest can fit 10 * 25 = 250 students.
So in total, the school can be filled with 150 + 250 = 400 students.
The answer is 400.

Read this:

In the Mumbai flat, Maria, ten months, lay on the mat while her uncle Imran rolled a red ball slowly across the floor. Her eyes followed it all the way to the sofa. When it rolled underneath, she stared at the other side, waiting. The ball came out. She kicked her legs and squealed. Imran rolled it again. This time Maria looked at the other side before it even disappeared.

What colour was the ball Imran rolled?
The ball was red.
What does Maria kicking and squealing suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she was excited and happy when the ball came out where she expected.
How can Imran keep building Maria's tracking skills?
He can keep rolling toys slowly behind objects so she can practise predicting where they'll come out.
How might Imran feel watching Maria look ahead the second time?
He might feel delighted and amazed that she had already learned where the ball would reappear.

Read this:

In the site cabin, the foreman laughed. “Keerthana, you’ll want to sit near the door in case the dust bothers you.”
“It doesn’t,” said Keerthana. She was the only woman engineer on the team of nine, and she had checked the drawings three times before the meeting. Her jaw was tight.
Samir, the project manager, put down his coffee. “Let’s start with the report. Keerthana wrote it.”
Afterwards Keerthana said, “I’m not here to speak for all women.”
“Noted,” said Samir. “I’ll rotate the site walks and put names on every report. Tell me if anything slips.”
Keerthana nodded but said nothing.

How many people are on the team in the site cabin?
The team has nine people.
What was Keerthana feeling when she said she was not there to speak for all women?
Keerthana was probably tired and a little resentful at being treated as a representative rather than an engineer. Checking the drawings three times and her tight jaw show the pressure she felt.
What did Samir do to make treatment fairer?
Samir began the meeting with Keerthana's report, promised to rotate the site walks and to put names on every report. He also asked to be told if anything slipped.
How might the foreman have seen the remark?
The foreman probably thought the remark was polite or funny and may not have noticed how it sounded. The passage shows only the laugh.

metadata.subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]

Read this:

Jyoti sat on the roof of her house in Rampur, the only place her phone got a signal, for her video interview with a Delhi company. Parveen, the HR interviewer, asked her about a project, and Jyoti's face froze on the screen, mouth half open. Parveen waited. Five seconds. Ten. Was Jyoti confused? Nervous? Or had the call dropped? In Jyoti's village, the signal came and went with the wind. Parveen could hear a faint dog barking. Instead of moving on, Parveen typed in the chat, "Jyoti, I can't see you moving. Can you hear me? No rush." A few seconds later Jyoti's voice came through, crackly. "Sorry, ma'am! I was thinking, and then the video stopped. Could you repeat the question?" Parveen repeated it slowly. Jyoti answered well. At the end Parveen said, "If the video freezes again, just tell me in chat. We'll manage."

Where did Jyoti sit for her video interview?
On the roof of her house in Rampur.
What was Parveen feeling when Jyoti froze?
Parveen was unsure and puzzled, wondering if Jyoti was confused, nervous or disconnected.
What did Parveen do that helped the interview?
Parveen checked in with words in the chat and said there was no rush, instead of guessing or moving on.
How did Jyoti experience the frozen moment?
She had been thinking when her video stopped, and she was relieved to be asked and to hear the question again.

metadata.subtype: Puzzled and confused in video calls [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

'I want the ice cream now!' Baljeet stamped his foot.
'After dinner,' Pallavi said. 'I promise.'
'You'll forget.'
'Did I forget the park on Saturday?'
Baljeet thought. 'No.'
'Did I forget the story last night?'
'No.'
'So, after dinner. Want to count the minutes with me?'
'That's too many.'
'Then let's sing the train song three times. That's dinner time.'
'Three times?'
'Choo choo, off we go. One.'
Baljeet sang, grumbling, then louder. By the third song, the dal was on the table. He ate fast. Then he looked at Pallavi.
'Ice cream,' she said, and opened the freezer. 'See? After dinner.'
Baljeet licked the spoon. 'Didi, you always remember.'
'Always,' said Pallavi. 'That's the deal.'

Cora started reading a 158-page book on Monday, and she decided she wanted to finish it by the end of Friday. She read 23 pages on Monday, 38 pages on Tuesday, and 61 pages on Wednesday. She knows she will have time to read twice as much on Friday as she does on Thursday. How many pages does she have to read on Thursday to finish the book in time?

Let P be the number of pages Cora has to read on Thursday.
If she finishes the book by the end of Friday, she will have read 23 + 38 + 61 + P + 2P = 158 pages.
The pages she has left to read by Thursday are P + 2P = 3P = 158 - 23 - 38 - 61 = pages.
Thus, by Thursday she has 3P = 36 pages left to read.
Therefore, to finish the book on Friday, Cora has to read P = 36 / 3 = 12 pages on Thursday.
The answer is 12.

It sailed over the village roofs. Pim ran after it, tripping on his long robe. A baker pointed upward. A cobbler shouted directions.

He tucked a bit of paper inside the brim so it fit better, and he walked home with a dignified step, the goat trailing behind.

Markus is twice the age of his son, and Markus's son is twice the age of Markus's grandson.  If the sum of the ages of Markus, his son, and his grandson is 140 years, then how many years old is Markus's grandson?

Let "x" be the age of Markus's grandson.
If Markus's son is twice the age of Markus's grandson, then Markus's son is 2*x.
If Markus is twice the age of his son, then Markus is 2*2*x.
Therefore, if the sum of the ages of Markus, his son, and his grandson is 140 years, then x+(2*x)+(2*2*x)=140 years.
Simplifying the equation, we see that 7*x=140 years.
Therefore, the age of Markus's grandson is x=20 years old.
The answer is 20.

He wrote an unsigned note, "Someone is being teased at lunch," dropped it in the teacher's box, and told the teacher in person after the bell. Meanwhile Devika had already slid onto the bench beside Hansa and asked if she was okay. Hansa's eyes filled; the tiny kindness meant more to her than words. The next day she offered Devika a slice of mango and, a week later, sat down next to a new boy at the lunch bench.

What did Tanay and two others mimic at lunch?
They mimicked Hansa's lisp.
How did Eshaan's response to Tanay's nudge differ from Devika's response to Hansa?
Eshaan said he did not want to join and walked to the water tap, later reporting it with a note and to the teacher, while Devika slid onto the bench beside Hansa right away and asked if she was okay.
What was Eshaan afraid of, and how did he act around that fear?
He was scared that if he spoke up they might turn on him next, so he took a safer step, an unsigned note and a word with the teacher.
What could Eshaan do next time he sees someone teased?
He could sit beside the person first, as Devika did, and keep telling the teacher if it continues.

Monday. Day 18!
Skipping rope on the terrace before school: done. It's harder when it's cold and my legs want to stay in bed, but I've marked every day on the calendar and I don't want a gap. Saurabh bhaiya tried it with me today and gave up after two minutes. 'Sonali, how?' HA.
What's changed: I'm less out of breath on the stairs. I eat breakfast now, poha or eggs, instead of skipping it. And I wash my face after every workout because sweat plus my oily skin was giving me spots.
What's not changed: I still want samosas. I had one on Saturday and didn't feel guilty. Mumma says that's the right attitude.
Goal: keep going through exams, even if it's just ten minutes.

What exercise does Sonali do on the terrace?
Skipping rope, before school.
How does Sonali seem to feel about the calendar streak?
Sonali feels proud and motivated, not wanting to leave a gap even on hard mornings.
What makes Sonali's habits likely to last?
Sonali is consistent but flexible, eats breakfast, looks after skin and doesn't feel guilty about a samosa.
What might Saurabh think after giving up after two minutes?
He might be surprised at how fit Sonali has become and a bit impressed.

I'm Ramesh. Every Sunday Papa used to wash the scooter with the hose running the whole time, and my big brother Nilesh burned dry leaves and plastic bags together in the corner of the yard. The smoke stung my eyes, and after our water lesson at school, the running hose bothered me too.
I didn't want to sound like a teacher at home. So one Sunday I just filled a bucket and brought a mug. "Papa, can I try washing it this way? Like a race?"
Papa laughed but let me. It took one bucket, and the scooter still shone. The next week he used the bucket himself.
The plastic was harder. I told Nilesh the smoke hurt my eyes and asked if we could keep a bag for the kabadiwala instead. He grumbled, but he did it.

How many buckets did it take to wash the scooter?
One bucket.
Why did Ramesh not want to lecture the family?
Ramesh felt uneasy about the habits but was worried about sounding like a teacher and upsetting everyone.
How did Ramesh suggest changes without shaming anyone?
By turning bucket washing into a playful race, and by mentioning the stinging smoke and offering the kabadiwala bag.
How might Papa have seen the bucket race?
As harmless fun at first; then he saw it worked and switched to the bucket himself.

Read this:

Okay, you asked why I laugh when Tanvir says "only". Listen. I'm Sarika, and last Saturday we went to the mall. Tanvir first tried on a leather jacket: nine thousand rupees. He put it back like it burned him. Then, two shops later, a cotton shirt, two thousand. And he goes, "Only two thousand! That's nothing, yaar."
I just stared at him. For a college student, two thousand is a lot. A week ago he'd have called that shirt crazy expensive. But he had just seen nine thousand, so two felt cheap. He bought it.
I didn't say anything then; I didn't know what he was really thinking. But now, whenever he says "only", I ask, "Only compared to what?"

How much was the leather jacket?
Nine thousand rupees.
What was Sarika feeling when Tanvir said "Only two thousand"?
Sarika felt surprised and a little amused, noticing how the jacket had changed his sense of the price.
How could Tanvir check whether the shirt is worth it?
Ask what it's worth to him by itself, compared with what he usually spends, not with the jacket he just saw.
Why did two thousand feel cheap to Tanvir?
He had just seen the nine-thousand jacket, so the shirt seemed small next to it, though a week earlier he'd have found it expensive.

metadata.subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Day one, after the talk: Imran sat in his car outside the office for twenty minutes. Parveen's words kept replaying: "You used my worst week to look better." His first thought was, She's making me the villain. His second was, She's right.
Day three: He drafted a long message about how much their friendship meant, how sorry he felt, how hard this was for him. He read it back and deleted it. It was all about him.
Day ten: He asked their manager for a meeting and said plainly that what he'd shared about Parveen's leave, when her mother was unwell, was private and unfair to raise, and that he wanted it kept out of her review. His face burned the whole time. Then he wrote to Parveen: "I've corrected what I said to Menon. I'm not asking for anything back."

Where did Imran sit after the talk?
Imran sat in his car outside the office for twenty minutes.
Why did Imran delete the long message on day three?
Imran felt ashamed once he saw the message was all about his own feelings, and knew it wouldn't repair anything for Parveen.
Which step on day ten counts as real amends?
Going to the manager to correct what he said, even with his face burning, repairs actual harm; the note to Parveen asks for nothing back.
How might Parveen see Imran's correction to Menon?
Parveen may still be hurt, but seeing Imran take a real, costly step could make it possible to trust him a little again.

Read this:

Papa,
I'm writing this from Sachin's room. I'm staying here until I find a place.
You said last night that if I left engineering for music, I shouldn't call myself your son. So I won't call. Please don't call me either. I mean it.
I know you think I'll come back in a week. I won't.
I'm not writing to be cruel. I just can't keep being told what I love is a waste. Part of me feels free for the first time. Part of me is scared stiff, and I hate that. Don't tell Mummy I said that.
Harish

Whose room is Harish writing from?
Sachin's room.
What mixed feelings does Harish admit in the letter?
He feels free and relieved, yet scared stiff, and seems ashamed of the fear, asking Papa not to tell Mummy.
What turning point could still exist at this stage, even after this letter?
Harish could keep one safe line open, such as a message through Mummy or a friend, so the break is not fully sealed by pride.
How might Papa feel reading this letter?
He may feel angry and hurt, yet frightened too, seeing that his words pushed his son away.

The officers, as usual, lived in twos and threes in the roofless, half-ruined houses. The seniors tried to collect straw and potatoes and, in general, food for the men. The younger ones occupied themselves as before, some playing cards (there was plenty of money, though there was no food), some with more innocent games, such as quoits and skittles. The general trend of the campaign was rarely spoken of, partly because nothing certain was known about it, partly because there was a vague feeling that in the main it was going badly.

Question: How do the officers pass their time, and what is rarely discussed?

They live in twos and threes in ruined houses. The seniors gather straw, potatoes and food, while younger ones play cards, quoits and skittles. The campaign is rarely spoken of because nothing is certain.
My friend Diya is turning 21 and wants a rooftop party. We have a small group, around twelve.
A rooftop party sounds lovely. Is it at someone's home, and will it be in the evening?
At her building, in the evening. We plan to string some lights.
Fairy lights would look beautiful. Check the weather and have a backup plan, like an indoor space nearby. A few cushions and a speaker for music will make it cosy.
What about food? We do not want to cook too much.
Keep it simple with finger food, like sandwiches, samosas and fruit skewers, and order a cake. Ask each friend to bring one dish so the workload is shared.
Good. The weather, what if it rains?
If it rains, move the party to the building's common room or someone's living room, and hang the lights there. Tell the twelve guests the plan in advance so Diya's evening does not get ruined.

Yusuf: saw your status. so sorry about Bruno
Chetan: thanks. been reading about it all morning
Chetan: kidney trouble in old dogs is really common, the vet said he was fourteen
Chetan: I made a timeline of his last month. now it makes sense why he stopped eating
Yusuf: that sounds like you
Yusuf: does it help?
Chetan: it did. I get what happened. no mystery
Chetan: but I noticed I'm doing it so I don't have to think about him asleep on my bed
Chetan: so I'm going to stop reading
Yusuf: what will you do instead?
Chetan: Amma is sending old videos of him. I'll watch them tonight, properly. probably cry
Yusuf: want company? I'll bring chai at 9
Chetan: yes. thank you, really

What did Chetan make about Bruno's last month?
A timeline of his last month.
Why did Chetan decide to stop reading?
Chetan noticed the research, though useful, was keeping the sadness at arm's length, and felt ready to let the grief for Bruno in.
Which approach works here, and why?
Using analysis to understand what happened, then setting a time to watch the videos and actually feel it, with Yusuf there, lets understanding lead towards the feeling.
How does Yusuf respond to Chetan's way of coping?
Yusuf gently asks whether it helps instead of judging, then offers company and chai at nine so Chetan does not grieve alone.

metadata.subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Shalini Didi,
I know Mummy told you I said no to the Ludhiana plan. I want you to hear my reasons from me, not from the family group.
I'm not refusing the shop because I don't care. I'm staying in Bengaluru because I've just been given the lead on the school-bus routing project, and I want to see if I can do it. Leaving midway would let my team down too.
But I'm not walking away. I'll come home every second month, and I have already booked leave for Papa's knee operation in March. Tell me honestly if that isn't enough, and we'll work something out together. You know the shop far better than I do. I'm listening.
Your brother,
Baljeet

What project has Baljeet just been given the lead on?
The school-bus routing project.
Why does Baljeet want Shalini to hear the reasons directly?
Baljeet feels anxious that the family will think Baljeet doesn't care, and wants to be understood rather than seen as defiant.
What makes Baljeet's letter a balanced response rather than simple defiance?
Baljeet explains the reasons, names the duties that will be kept, like visits every second month and leave for Papa's operation, and invites Shalini's honest view.
How might Shalini feel reading the letter?
Shalini may still be disappointed about the shop, but likely feels respected and reassured by Baljeet's honesty and concrete promises.
Make this reply formal: Thanks for the info. I will get back to you soon.
Thank you for the information. I will reply to you shortly.

Read this:

Sunday night
Long call with Indu. She's been carrying something about Papa for years: that when she failed Class 11 chemistry, he said, "You'll never amount to anything." She was crying on the phone. My first reaction was, "Papa would never say that." I didn't say it. I remember that evening differently: I remember him saying, "This isn't like you." But I was twelve and in the next room.
What I did say: "That sounds like it really hurt. I'm sorry." And I asked, "What would help now?", not "Are you sure he said that?" She wants to talk to Papa herself. I said I'd sit with her if she wanted.
Writing this down tonight, while it's fresh, so I don't turn it into my own version later.
Vaibhav

What does Indu remember Papa saying when she failed Class 11 chemistry?
"You'll never amount to anything."
How did Vaibhav feel during the call with Indu, and what was held back?
Vaibhav felt doubtful, thinking Papa would never say that, but also caring, so Vaibhav held the doubt back and told Indu it sounded like it really hurt.
Which of Vaibhav's choices on the call helped Indu most, and why?
Saying "That sounds like it really hurt" and asking what would help, treating her feeling as real without demanding proof of the exact words.
How might Indu have felt if Vaibhav had asked "Are you sure he said that?"
She would likely have felt disbelieved and more alone, as if her hurt didn't count unless every word was proven 🤍

metadata.subtype: Careful with witness and family accounts [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Our final-year project? Okay. I'm Kalyani, and I'll tell you the part nobody puts in the report. Asif, my teammate, wanted to start with face recognition, because that's the exciting bit. I said, first let's build something ugly that works. So in three weeks we made a web page where the teacher types the roll numbers of students present, it saves them, and it shows who's absent. No faces. Asif called it "a glorified register." Then we started the face part. It was brilliant in the lab and terrible under classroom tube lights. Two weeks before the external demo, the camera module stopped working completely. Asif looked sick. I said, "We still have the glorified register." We demoed that, showed face recognition as a recorded video, and passed comfortably. Asif bought me cutting chai for a week.

What did Asif call the plain version?
A glorified register.
How did Asif feel when the camera module failed?
Asif was dismayed and anxious, looking sick two weeks before the demo.
What else could the team have done with the face part?
They could have tested it under classroom lighting early, so the problem showed up while there was still time to fix it.
How might the external examiner see the demo?
The examiner sees a working system plus a video of the face feature, which is enough to pass comfortably even though the camera failed.
