Saturday: Vikas spent the whole day on his water-filter model: three bottle layers of sand, charcoal and pebbles, glued and painted blue.
Monday: Bidisha ma'am held it up. "Lovely work. But the water is leaking at the join, and the labels are too small to read." Vikas's ears went hot. "It's not leaking. You're holding it wrong." She showed him the wet desk. "Maybe some tape here?" "It's fine the way it is," he muttered, and took it back.
Wednesday: At the exhibition, water dripped onto the judges' papers. Vikas stared at the puddle. "Someone bumped it," he told his friend, though nobody had.

What were the layers in Vikas's water-filter model?
Sand, charcoal and pebbles.
Why did Vikas's ears go hot when Bidisha ma'am spoke?
After a whole day's work he felt hurt and embarrassed, as if pointing out a leak was an insult to him.
What could Vikas have done on Monday?
Check the join himself, accept the tape idea, and treat the feedback as about the model, not about him.
What might Bidisha ma'am feel when the model leaks at the exhibition?
She may feel sorry for Vikas and a little frustrated, having pointed out the leak kindly two days earlier.

When the bus from the district school dropped Gargi at the Ranipur crossing, Rehana was waiting as always, arms open. Gargi stepped round the hug and fixed her bag strap. "Not here, Ammi. Everyone's looking." Rehana's arms fell. At home Gargi went straight to the roof. Rehana stood at the stove a long time, stirring nothing. That evening she didn't push. She carried two cups of tea up to the roof and sat beside Gargi on the parapet, shoulders not quite touching, watching the goats come home. After a while Gargi leaned her head on her mother's shoulder, just for a moment. Rehana kept very still and said only, "The tea's getting cold."

Where did Rehana carry the two cups of tea?
Up to the roof.
Why did Gargi step round the hug at the bus stop?
She felt embarrassed and self-conscious with everyone looking, and wanted her own space.
What did Rehana do that kept the connection alive?
She didn't push, sat beside Gargi with tea, and let Gargi come closer at her own pace.
How did Rehana feel when her arms fell?
She felt hurt and a bit lost, standing at the stove stirring nothing.

By ten at night in their Andheri flat, Darshan and Harish weren't talking about the electricity bill anymore.

"You just don't care about anything in this flat," Darshan said. "You don't care about me, you don't care about the bills."

"And you think you're better than us because your job pays more," Harish shot back. "Don't pretend you don't."

"I never said that!"

"You didn't have to. It's how you look at my room."

Darshan laughed, a bitter sound. "See, now you're reading my mind. That's convenient."

"Oh, so now I'm lying?"

Darshan had never thought about Harish's room at all. Harish had once, honestly, forgotten the bill by accident. But neither of them could hear the other's denial now. Every "I didn't mean that" sounded like one more lie.

Where did Darshan and Harish live?
They lived in a flat in Andheri.
What was Darshan feeling behind that bitter laugh?
Darshan felt frustrated and misjudged, accused of thoughts never actually held, and the anger hardened.
What could either of them do to break this pattern?
One of them could stop guessing motives and say only what happened and how it felt, or suggest a pause before talking again.
How does Harish see Darshan at this point?
Harish sees Darshan as looking down on Harish and treats that guess as fact, so any denial sounds false.

Deepak was coming out of the metro station in Hyderabad when a delivery rider's scooter clipped the bumper of a car at the signal. Nobody fell. Words, a honk, done. That night the colony group lit up: a black SUV, an abusive driver, the rider knocked down. Deepak read every message. At breakfast he told his sister Mahima, "I was right there. Big black SUV. The man got out and shouted at the boy." Mahima scrolled on her phone. "The traffic police posted the clip." It showed a small silver hatchback. The driver got out, raised both hands and apologised. Deepak watched it twice. "But I saw…" he began, and stopped. He had been so sure.

What did the traffic police clip actually show?
It showed a small silver hatchback, and the driver raised both hands and apologised.
What does Deepak's stopping mid-sentence suggest he is realising?
He feels shaken and confused as he realises details from the colony group had slipped into his memory, and that feeling sure didn't make it accurate.
What would you advise Deepak before he shares what he saw next time?
Note down what he saw right away, before reading group messages, and say "this is what I noticed" rather than stating it as fact.
How does Mahima's approach shape the moment for Deepak?
By showing the clip calmly instead of arguing, she lets him see the gap himself, without feeling mocked.

Eid, 11 pm.
Diary, I have to be honest tonight.
Lakshmi came over with sheer khurma and asked why I've skipped dance practice three Sundays running.
I said Farhan and I had plans. True.
But also the art club. And our Thursday chai.
I've been folding myself into his timetable like a paper napkin, and I called it love.
This evening, watching Lakshmi laugh with my cousins, I missed the old Noor, the one who danced badly and loudly.
The strange part: I thought pulling back from everyone would make us closer.
It just made me smaller.
Tomorrow I'm going to practice.
I'll tell Farhan why, kindly, over the phone.
If being close means disappearing, it isn't the closeness I want.

What did Lakshmi bring when coming over?
Sheer khurma.
What does Noor worry about by the end of the entry?
Noor feels uneasy and wistful, missing the loud, dancing self and worried that folding into Farhan's timetable has meant disappearing.
What would you advise Noor to say to Farhan?
To explain calmly that Noor still wants the relationship but also needs Sunday dance and time with friends, so both of them can stay whole while being close.
How might Lakshmi have felt about the missed Sundays?
Lakshmi may have felt left out and a bit worried, which is why the question came with a bowl of sheer khurma rather than blame.

Every year on the anniversary of the flood in Sangli, Siddharth told the same story. He had been at the temple on the hill, ringing the bell, when the siren went off and he saw the brown water pour across the fields. He could still hear the bell, still feel the cold stone under his feet. He was sixteen now and had told it maybe fifty times. This year his older brother Chetan, home from college, frowned. "Sid, we were at school. The headmaster made us all walk up to the temple after the siren. You saw the water from the school roof first." Siddharth shook his head, stung. "I remember the bell." "The bell was later," Chetan said gently. Siddharth sat with it for a long time. The fear was exactly as he remembered. The order of things, apparently, was not.

Where did Chetan say they first saw the water from?
From the school roof.
Why was Siddharth stung by Chetan's version?
Siddharth felt hurt and unsettled, because the memory felt vivid and certain after fifty tellings, and being corrected shook that confidence.
What could Siddharth take from this about vivid memories?
That strong emotion keeps the fear real but lets the order of details drift, so it helps to check with others who were there.
How did Chetan correct his brother?
Chetan corrected him gently, explaining that the bell came later, after the school walked up to the temple.

Lauren sent 65 pieces of mail on Monday, 10 more pieces of mail on Tuesday than on Monday, 5 fewer on Wednesday than on Tuesday, and 15 more pieces of mail on Thursday than on Wednesday. How many pieces of mail did Lauren send?

Lauren sent 65 + 10 = 75 pieces of mail on Tuesday.
He sent 75 - 5 = 70 pieces of mail on Wednesday.
And sent 70 + 15 = 85 pieces of mail on Thursday.
Therefore, he sent 65 + 75 + 70 + 85 = 295 pieces of mail.
The answer is 295.

Mentoring notes, Thursday. Written by Madhav, team lead.

Sat in on Jasleen's renewal call with the logistics client. The client opened by criticising our last report for five minutes. Jasleen kept a steady, warm voice, nodded on camera, smiled when she thanked them for the detail, then walked them through the fix. It was a good call; the client ended by booking the next review.

After we disconnected she rubbed her cheeks and said, "My face hurts from being pleasant." She laughed, but it was the fourth call like this this week.

What I did: asked how she was actually doing. She admitted she'd been swallowing irritation all week and going home flat. We agreed she'll take ten minutes between difficult calls, and that "let me check and come back to you" is always allowed. I'll check in with her again on Monday.

How many calls like this had Jasleen had this week?
It was the fourth call like this this week.
What does Jasleen rubbing her cheeks and saying her face hurts suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she was tired and had been holding back irritation behind a pleasant face; it could also simply be relief that a hard call went well.
How could Madhav keep supporting Jasleen after this call?
Madhav could keep the Monday check-in, protect the ten-minute breaks, and remind her that saying she needs to check and come back is fine.
How might the client have experienced Jasleen's warm, steady manner?
The client probably felt heard rather than argued with, which may be why they booked the next review.

Suraj's job offer was delayed by three months, and the first instalment of the education loan was due in five weeks. Sitting in the flat in Bengaluru with the loan papers, Suraj felt the old urge to wait and hope. Instead, the next morning, Suraj went to the bank branch before any payment was missed and asked for Disha, the officer who handled the account. "My start date has been pushed back. I don't want to default. What are my options?" Disha listened, checked the file, and explained that the tenure could be discussed and a new schedule drawn up in writing. Suraj brought the papers home and saw that the situation had turned from a dread into a task with a date.

How many weeks until the first instalment was due?
The first instalment was due in five weeks.
What did Suraj feel before deciding to go to the bank?
Suraj felt the urge to wait and hope, which suggests worry and a wish to avoid the problem.
What could Suraj do while waiting for the job, and why?
Suraj could set aside whatever small income arrives to be ready for the first payment, because preparing shows good faith.
How might Disha see a customer who comes before missing a payment?
Disha probably sees someone who takes the loan seriously, and finds it easier to work out options together.

The land has become warmer than the sea. Because warm air above the land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in to fill the space, we feel a breeze from the water.

Counsellor's note, Class 11, Wednesday.
Mridul came in today for the career session and said, with great confidence, that he is going to be a neurosurgeon at a top government hospital. When I asked what he's doing this month towards it, he talked about a documentary he'd watched and a surgeon he follows online. He didn't know his current biology mark, which is 54 percent, or which entrance exam he would take, or when it is held. He isn't lazy; the dream clearly matters to him, and his eyes light up when he talks about it. But it's floating with nothing tying it to his week. We worked together on a one-month plan: two biology chapters with self-tests, one practice set every Saturday, and a talk with his chemistry teacher about weak areas. He copied it into his phone. Follow-up: meet again on the 30th to check progress.
Nilesh

What is Mridul's current biology mark?
His current biology mark is 54 percent.
What does Mridul's excitement about the documentary suggest?
It suggests he feels inspired and hopeful about the dream, but that feeling hasn't turned into any daily action.
What one-month plan did they make?
Two biology chapters with self-tests, one practice set every Saturday, and a talk with his chemistry teacher about weak areas.
How might Nilesh see Mridul?
Nilesh sees a motivated student, not a lazy one, whose big dream simply needs nearer steps.

Mother's journal, Wednesday.
Ayaan (6) and Mehr (4) fought over the block tower again. Mehr knocked it down; Ayaan pushed her. Both screamed.
This time I didn't shout. I took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug, then sat on the floor between them. I asked Ayaan first. "You wanted your tower." He nodded, tears falling. Then Mehr. "You felt scared when he pushed you." She nodded too.
In two minutes both were calm. 🤍 Ayaan offered to build another one.
— Salma

Where did Salma take Ayaan and Mehr?
She took Ayaan to the sofa and Mehr to the rug.
How can you tell Ayaan felt understood?
He nodded with tears falling when Salma said he wanted his tower, and later offered to build another one.
Why did Salma's approach calm the fight so quickly?
She separated them, sat at their level and named each child's feeling, so both felt heard instead of judged.
What is it like for Mehr when Salma names her fear?
Mehr likely feels safe and understood, which is why she nods and calms down.

I'm Rekha, and I was in the social media team when the helmet complaint came in. A parent posted that the chin strap on our children's cycle helmet snapped the first time her son fell. She added a photo. Our head said, 'Don't engage. It'll draw attention.'
So we didn't. Two more parents posted similar photos. Then a parenting page with a big following shared all three, asking why we were silent. Silence, it turned out, read as 'we don't care about children'. Within a week, two shops returned their stock. Aparna, my colleague, kept saying, 'We could have just said we're checking.'
What finally changed things was a test the quality team ran on their own: the strap failed. That afternoon we paused sales and posted a recall notice. It came three weeks too late for our name.

What did the parent say happened to the chin strap?
It snapped the first time her son fell.
How does Rekha seem to feel looking back?
Rekha seems regretful and uncomfortable, aware that the silence made things worse and the recall came late.
What could the company have posted on day one?
A short reply saying sorry, that the strap was being tested urgently and that parents should stop using the helmet until the result came.
How might the parents who posted see the recall?
They may feel relieved the helmets were recalled, but angry that it took three weeks and more posts.

A crow saw a snail crawling slowly across the road. "You are too slow," said the crow. The snail replied, "Yes, but I will get there." The crow laughed and flew off. By evening, the crow was tired and hungry, while the snail reached the garden fence and found a fresh green leaf.

"Mama, up!" Dhruv held out hot little arms.
"Again? You were just up, baby." Ankita lifted him. "He won't even look at his train."
Dada felt Dhruv's forehead. "Warm. He's not being fussy, he's poorly. He wants you."
Dhruv sobbed when his sock slipped off.
"Shh, I've got you." Ankita settled on the bed with him. "Dada, can you ring the doctor? Ask what to look out for."
"Ringing now."
Dhruv's head sank against her shoulder.

What made Dhruv sob?
His sock slipped off.

He feels poorly and uneasy, and wants the comfort of being held.

Ankita holding him calmly while Dada rang the doctor to ask what to look out for, giving comfort and checking at once.
How does Dada read Dhruv's clinginess?
Dada sees it as a sign Dhruv is unwell and wants his mother, not fussiness.

Behind the rice fields, under the big guava tree, Reena, five, had filled her frock pocket with guavas. Joseph came running. Yesterday he had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond. Reena held out the biggest guava straight away. "For you. You gave me." Then Kuttan came, the boy who always kept his mango slices behind his back. "Give me one." Reena shook her head hard. "You don't give. I don't give." Kuttan kicked at the mud. Reena's Ammachi, drying chillies on a mat nearby, called out, "Kuttan, bring your mango tomorrow, and see what happens."

What did Joseph share with Reena yesterday?
He had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond.
Why did Reena shake her head hard at Kuttan?
She felt cross: in her mind Kuttan never shares, so he hadn't earned a guava: "You don't give. I don't give."
What does Ammachi's suggestion offer Kuttan, and why might it work?
It gives Kuttan a way to earn a turn by bringing his mango tomorrow, which fits the way Reena thinks about fairness 🙂
How might Kuttan feel watching Joseph get the biggest guava?
Kuttan might feel left out and cross, and perhaps start to notice that hiding his mango has a cost.

Before. On the first day of the maths olympiad prep, Preeti used her friend Binita's blue pen because she'd forgotten her own. She got full marks on the practice test.

During. For the next three weeks Preeti used only the blue pen. She borrowed it every morning. Once she forgot to ask and panicked through the whole test, sure she'd do badly. She got 18 out of 20 anyway, but decided that was lucky. Binita laughed. 'It's a pen, Preeti. Twenty rupees.'

After. On the day of the real olympiad, the blue pen ran out of ink in the first ten minutes. Preeti froze, then picked up a pencil. She finished. She qualified. On the bus home she stared at the dead pen in her hand and felt slightly foolish, and slightly free.

What happened to the blue pen on the day of the olympiad?
It ran out of ink in the first ten minutes.
How did Preeti feel on the bus home, staring at the dead pen?
Preeti felt slightly foolish and slightly free, seeing she had qualified without it.
What could Preeti notice from the test she took without the pen?
That she got 18 out of 20 even without the blue pen, which already showed her skill, not the pen, was doing the work.
How does Binita see the lucky pen?
Binita finds it funny and sees it as just a twenty-rupee pen.
Dukaandar ne kaha "Fixed price, no bargaining." Matlab?
It means the price cannot be changed, so you cannot ask for a discount.
What does "pet" mean? It rained for 34 minutes in the morning and 5 minutes in the evening. How many minutes did it rain? Fix this: It rains since morning.

1. A pet is an animal that you keep at home and look after.
2. That makes 39. Because 34 + 5 = 39.
3. Fixed: It has been raining since morning. Why: Use the perfect tense with "since".

Nilesh, you asked how I handled children who lie. In my third year of teaching, I, Rehana, was still young and impatient.
One boy in my class said his homework notebook had fallen into a drain. The same story, three times in a month. I wanted to shout. I had my ruler in my hand.
Instead, I put the ruler down and knelt beside his desk. I said quietly, "I think you're scared of what I'll say if the homework isn't done." He nodded.
"Thank you for telling me the real reason," I said. "Now let's see what part confused you."
It was fractions. After that, he never lost a notebook again. If I had punished him, he would only have learned to invent better drains.

What did the boy say happened to his homework notebook?
He said it had fallen into a drain.
How was young Rehana feeling when she held the ruler?
Rehana felt impatient and angry, tempted to shout because the same story came three times in a month.
What choice in the story changed things?
Rehana chose to kneel, name the boy's fear and thank him for the truth, which revealed that he was struggling with fractions.
How might the boy have felt when Rehana named his fear?
He likely felt relieved and understood, because someone saw the fear behind the lie instead of punishing it.
Ravi did 36 jumps in the morning and 31 in the evening. How many jumps in all? Why do we cut our nails?

1. 67 jumps. Because 36 + 31 = 67.
2. Long nails can break and gather dirt. Because short nails are easier to keep clean.

At the panchayat function, the new cluster coordinator, Anand, stood at the microphone and talked about the rainwater tanks in the three village schools. "I planned them, I got the funds, I supervised the work," he said, and the sarpanch clapped.
Pradeep, the old headmaster who had trained Anand as a young teacher, sat in the second row and watched the three teachers at the back. Lakshmi had dug with the children every Saturday. Babu had fought the contractor for proper pipes. Both were looking at their feet.
After the function, while everyone queued for tea, Pradeep walked with Anand behind the school wall.
"I'm proud of you, beta. But one thing, only between us. Today it was I, I, I. Lakshmi and Babu heard it. People forgive a young leader many things, but they remember who took the credit."
Anand was quiet for a long moment. Then he nodded and walked back towards the teachers with two cups of tea.

What did Babu fight the contractor for?
Proper pipes.
What was Pradeep feeling as he watched the teachers at the back?
He felt uneasy and protective, worried that Anand's 'I, I, I' was hurting the teachers and could damage his future.
Why did Pradeep speak behind the school wall instead of at the function?
A private, kind word lets Anand hear the warning without public shame, so he can make it right with the teachers.
What was the speech like for Lakshmi and Babu?
They likely felt hurt and invisible, their Saturdays and fights with the contractor swallowed into someone else's 'I'.
Is structures only about buildings? My engineering book mentions bridges.

No. A structure is anything built, like a bridge or a building, and also the way parts of something are arranged. The word is a noun, and Structures is its plural form.
Example: Bridges, towers and dams are large structures.
ADD TO, START MISSING. Some sparrows were on the wall. 2 more came. Now there are 7 sparrows. How many were there at the start?

Answer: 5 sparrows. __ + 2 = 7, so the start was 5.

This is the hardest kind. Draw 7 sparrows, and circle the 2 that came later. The rest were there at the start: 5. Check: 5 + 2 = 7. It is fine if the child needs objects for these for a long time.

"Didi, I've done it. Resigned from the call centre."
Nikita put down her tea. "Gautam, you haven't even got the food cart yet."
"I'll get it next week. The spot outside the college is perfect. Students will come every day."
"And the licence? The cart? What if it rains for a month?"
"Rain happens to people with bad locations. Mine's covered by the bus stop."
"And your savings?"
"I'll make them back in two months. Everyone says my momos are the best in the family."
"The family isn't paying, Gautam."
He laughed and grabbed a notebook. "Look, I've planned it all. Profit from week two."
Nikita flipped through the pages. There was a menu, a logo sketch, a colour for the umbrella. There was nothing about what he'd do if it didn't work.
"Where's plan B?" she asked.
"I don't need one. Plan A is good."

Where does Gautam want to put his food cart?
The spot outside the college.
Why does Gautam feel he doesn't need a plan B?
He is excited and hopeful, sure his momos are the best and his spot is perfect, so bad weather or slow sales seem to happen only to others.
What small step could Nikita suggest that keeps Gautam's hope but protects him?
She could ask him to add one page to the notebook about what he'd do if the first months are slow, like keeping some part-time work until the cart settles.
How might Nikita feel flipping through the notebook?
Nikita seems proud of her brother's effort, the menu and logo, but uneasy that nothing covers what happens if it doesn't work.

'Rent's ₹6,500, and it's got a balcony,' Suraj said, holding up the listing at the tea shop. 'I'm taking it.'
Thomas, who had lived in Bengaluru for three years, sipped his tea. 'Walk me through a Tuesday.'
'A Tuesday?'
'From the moment you wake up.'
'Okay. Office at nine. The flat's in Hoskote. So bus to the metro, metro to Whitefield, then walk. Maybe an hour?'
'Maybe?'
'Say I leave at seven-thirty. Coming back, leave office at seven, home by eight-thirty, if the bus comes.'
'And if it rains?'
Suraj was quiet. 'Then I don't know.'
'So find out. Go tomorrow at seven-thirty and actually do it.'
The next evening Suraj called. 'Two hours ten minutes. The bus only came every forty minutes. Coming back was worse.'
'Still want the balcony?'
'No,' Suraj said, laughing. 'I want to sleep. I'm looking near Whitefield, even if it's smaller.'

What is the rent of the flat with the balcony?
What was Suraj feeling when Thomas asked 'And if it rains?'
Uncertain and a little uneasy, realising he could not picture the trip once things went wrong.
What else could Suraj rehearse before choosing a place near Whitefield?
A late return and a rainy day, plus where groceries and weekday meals would come from.
How does Thomas see Suraj's first plan?
Thomas sees a listing chosen for a balcony, not for daily life, and uses questions so Suraj discovers the commute himself.

messages.content: A school field is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 50 m, and the distance between them is 20 m. Grass costs ₹12 per m^2. What is the cost of grassing the field?

Answer: Area = 1/2 x (30 + 50) x 20 = 800 m^2. Cost = 800 x ₹12 = ₹9600.

Step 1: the area. Add the parallel sides: 30 + 50 = 80. Half of 80 is 40. Times the height: 40 x 20 = 800 m^2. Step 2: the cost. Each square metre costs 12 rupees, so 800 x 12 = 9600 rupees. Check the size: the field is between a 30 x 20 = 600 m^2 rectangle and a 50 x 20 = 1000 m^2 rectangle, and 800 is exactly in the middle. Common mistake: multiplying all three numbers without halving (1600 m^2).

"Tanuja, you stand with your hands behind your back just like I did at school parade. That was how we showed respect. But let me, your Shalini Mami, tell you about the day it got me into trouble. The class chalk box had gone missing. I was standing at the back with my hands behind me, twisting my fingers. Our teacher marched over. 'What are you hiding?' Everyone turned. I was hiding something: my hands were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen, and I was ashamed. Slowly I showed her. She looked, and her face changed. She said sorry in front of everyone. The chalk turned up in the cupboard. Hands behind your back can mean many things, child."

Why were young Shalini's hands blue?
They were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen.
What was young Shalini feeling while twisting her fingers behind her back?
Ashamed and nervous about her ink-stained hands, not guilty about the chalk; the hidden hands looked like concealment but were embarrassment.
What could the teacher in the story have done differently at the start?
Asked quietly, without assuming guilt in front of the whole class, since hands behind the back are not proof of anything.
How might the teacher have felt when she saw the blue hands?
She likely felt embarrassed and sorry for accusing Shalini in front of everyone, which is why her face changed and she apologised.

At the children's home in Darjeeling, Chandrika rang the little brass bell at seven every morning, the same three rings. For the first weeks, Dolma, five, hid under the bunk whenever voices rose, even happy ones. Chandrika never pulled her out. She sat on the floor and said, "Breakfast is paratha today. I'll save yours." One day Chandrika snapped at a boy for spilling milk, and Dolma froze. Later Chandrika knelt beside her. "I was too loud. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry." By the fourth month, Dolma was waiting at the door at seven, holding the bell out for her.

How many times did Chandrika ring the bell each morning?
She rang it three times, the same three rings each morning.
Why might Dolma hide under the bunk when voices rose?
Raised voices seemed to feel dangerous to her, even happy ones, so she hid to feel safe.
What did Chandrika do after snapping at the boy, and why did it matter?
She knelt by Dolma, admitted she was too loud and said sorry, which repaired the moment and showed an adult can mend a mistake.
What would change if Chandrika had pulled Dolma out from under the bunk?
Dolma would likely feel more frightened and learn that adults force things, which would slow her trust.

Tuesday. "You said you'd pay for the gas cylinder this month," Swati says, holding the bill. Neelam feels the heat rise; she is sure it was Swati's turn. She takes a breath. "This is how I remember it: I did February, you're doing March. But I might be wrong. Let me look." Wednesday. On the bus, Neelam scrolls back through their chat. There it is, her own message from 28 February: "I'll handle March too, you did the plumber 👍" She winces. Her memory had felt so solid. Friday. Neelam leaves the money on the counter with a sticky note: "You were right. Sorry for arguing 😅" Swati texts back a heart. That evening they start a shared note for bills, dates included, so neither memory has to carry it.

What did Neelam's message from 28 February say?
"I'll handle March too, you did the plumber."
What did Neelam feel on finding the message, and how can you tell?
Embarrassed and surprised 😅 She winced, because her memory of the turns had felt so solid.
What choice on Tuesday made the rest of the week easier?
Saying "This is how I remember it... I might be wrong. Let me look" instead of insisting, so the message led to an apology rather than a bigger fight.
How might Swati have felt if Neelam had flatly said Swati was wrong on Tuesday?
Swati might have felt accused and defensive, and the argument could have hardened before anyone checked the chat.
In a yard, the number of tanks is five times the number of trucks. If there are 20 trucks in the yard, calculate the total number of tanks and trucks in the yard.

There are 5*20 = 100 tanks in the yard.
Altogether, there are 100+20 = 120 trucks and tanks in the yard.
The answer is 140.

Monday. Harsha stood in the ticket line at the suburban station when a man slid in three places ahead. Harsha said nothing. A woman with a heavy bag sighed, and a teenager stared at his phone. Harsha felt irritated but wasn’t sure it was worth a fight.
Thursday. The same man, Madhav, did it again. This time Harsha smiled and said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Madhav blinked, grinned sheepishly and said, “Oh, sorry, didn’t notice.” He went to the back.
Saturday. Madhav stood at the end of the line and gave Harsha a small nod.

What did Harsha say to Madhav on Thursday?
Harsha said, “Excuse me, the line starts back there. I’m running late too.”
Why did Harsha stay silent on Monday?
Harsha felt irritated but was not sure it was worth a fight. Harsha weighed the tension against the small gain and let it pass that day.
What made Harsha's comment on Thursday work?
Harsha smiled, kept the tone light and shared that Harsha was late too. That let Madhav step back without feeling attacked.
How might Madhav have felt when Harsha spoke to him?
Madhav may have felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, since he grinned sheepishly. His nod on Saturday suggests he took the comment without resentment.

Rain drummed on the tin roof and the power went out, so the house was lit by one candle. Chetan, ten, did his homework at the table while his parents talked in low, sharp voices in the kitchen about the school fees and the bill. He caught the words, "How will we manage?"
Next morning, when Elizabeth Ma'am handed out permission slips for the school trip, Chetan said, "I don't want to go." She asked him to stay back after class. "Anything on your mind?" He shrugged. That afternoon she phoned his mother.
That night his father sat beside him. "Fees are heavy this term. We are working on it. You can go on the trip. That is our worry, not yours." Chetan slept without a knot in his stomach.

What did Chetan say when Elizabeth Ma'am handed out the trip slips?
He said, 'I don't want to go.'
What was Chetan feeling after overhearing 'How will we manage?'
He was anxious about the family's money, which is why he refused the trip without giving a reason.
What turning point helped Chetan stop carrying the worry alone?
The teacher noticed and phoned his mother, and his father then told him plainly that the fees were heavy but the worry was theirs and he could go.
How might Elizabeth Ma'am have seen Chetan's refusal?
She probably sensed something was behind it, since she kept him back gently and called his mother instead of simply marking him absent.

I'm Parveen, and I teach Class 4. This term I've been watching Farhan.
He follows me from the classroom to the staff room door. At recess he stands near the duty teacher instead of playing. He asks, "Ma'am, is my work okay?" four or five times a lesson, even when it's neat.
A colleague said, "He just wants attention." Maybe. But his hands twist his shirt while he waits for my answer, and he looks relieved each time I nod. I can't know what is going on inside him, but it doesn't look like a game.
So I've started saying, "Good morning, Farhan," warmly every day, and giving him small jobs he does alone: taking the register to the office, then watering the plants. Yesterday he did the plants and came back smiling, without asking once if it was okay.

What small jobs does Parveen give Farhan?
Taking the register to the office and watering the plants.
What does Parveen feel about the colleague's "attention" comment?
Parveen feels unsure and concerned rather than convinced, seeing Farhan's twisting hands and relief and thinking it doesn't look like a game.
Why might the warm greeting and solo jobs help more than ignoring Farhan?
They give him steady warmth he can count on while letting him practise small bits of independence, so he needs fewer reassurances.
What might watering the plants alone be like for Farhan?
He may feel proud and a little braver doing it by himself, which fits him coming back smiling without asking if it was okay.

Coach's note, Thursday. After practice, Ashwin came off the field furious because his best friend Manoj had given the winning pass to another player. In the changing room Ashwin threw his boots at the locker and shouted, "You never trust me! You always pick him!" Several boys backed away.
Manoj put down his bag and stayed put. He did not defend himself. He let Ashwin finish. Then he said quietly, "You sound really upset. I didn't realise it looked like that to you." Ashwin sat down heavily. Ten minutes later they were talking about the pass, and Ashwin was nearly laughing. I stayed by the door and let them work it out.
Tarun, football coach

What did Ashwin throw at the locker?
Ashwin threw his boots at the locker.
What was Manoj feeling while Ashwin shouted?
Manoj was probably tense and tempted to argue, since other boys backed away. Staying quiet took real self-control.
What did Manoj do that helped Ashwin calm down?
Manoj stayed put, did not defend himself and let Ashwin finish. Then Manoj said "You sound really upset", which lowered the heat and led to a talk.
What was Ashwin feeling when shouting "You never trust me"?
Ashwin felt hurt and angry, believing Manoj did not trust him. The shouting and throwing show how strongly it hit.

Jasleen, you want to know if telling on a friend is ever right? Your Rukmini Bua learnt that at your age. My best friend Mitu had a secret: someone from a chat room who called her beautiful and kept asking for photos. She told me at lunch and begged, "Don't tell anyone. You're my best friend." All afternoon my stomach churned. After the last bell I went back inside and told our class teacher everything. The teacher thanked me, found Mitu at the gate, and phoned Mitu's mother that same evening. Mitu didn't speak to me for a week. She was furious. Then one evening she came to our gate and said, "Thank you. That person was scary." We are still friends, Jasleen.

What did the stranger keep asking Mitu for?
Photos.
Why did young Rukmini's stomach churn all afternoon?
She felt torn and anxious, caught between Mitu's plea for secrecy and fear for Mitu's safety.
What was the turning point in Bua's story?
Going back after the last bell to tell the class teacher, who acted that same evening so Mitu was protected.
How did Mitu see Rukmini's choice, first and later?
At first Mitu was furious, but later she was grateful and admitted that the person was scary.

I am Tenzin, and I was in the workshop when Karthik decided to replace the light fitting without switching off at the board. "I've done this a hundred times," he said, and climbed the stool. His screwdriver touched a live wire, there was a crack, and he yelped and dropped it. He laughed too quickly, holding his hand. I did not laugh. I walked to the board, switched off the supply, and hung a note on the switch: DO NOT SWITCH ON. Then I brought him some water. He looked shaken. I could not tell whether he was ashamed or only surprised. When he finished the job, the switch was off before he began.

What did Tenzin hang on the switch?
Tenzin hung a note on the switch that said DO NOT SWITCH ON.
What might Tenzin be feeling on walking to the board and hanging the note?
Tenzin is probably alarmed and protective, and acts quickly to stop anyone switching on instead of laughing along.
What protective step did Tenzin take, and why did it matter?
Tenzin switched off the supply and hung a note on the switch, so nobody could turn it on while the wire was being handled.
What is it like for Karthik after the near miss?
Karthik seems shaken, though Tenzin cannot tell whether that is shame or surprise, and next time the switch is off first.

Dear Hrithik Bhaiya,
I spent the holidays at our grandparents' village, and I want to tell you something that's been on my mind.
Dadaji is so peaceful. He sits under the neem tree, talks to everyone, laughs about his old mistakes. When I asked if he had regrets, he said, "Some. But I made my peace."
Nanaji, at the other house, is always angry. He complains about his brothers, his lost land, everything. Nani says he was once full of fun.
I keep wondering: what makes the difference? Is it luck? Is it choices? Which one will I become when I'm old?
I don't really know yet. But I can't stop thinking about it.

Where does Dadaji sit?
He sits under the neem tree.
What is Afreen feeling as she writes about her grandfathers?
Afreen feels curious and unsettled, wondering what makes one peaceful and the other bitter, and which one Afreen will become.
What could Hrithik Bhaiya suggest to help Afreen think about this?
He could suggest that Afreen ask both grandfathers about their lives and turning points, and notice what choices seem to shape their feelings.
How might Nanaji see his own life?
Nanaji seems to feel angry and wronged, focused on his losses and his brothers.

Monday: Yamini screamed at the coat on the door. "A monster!" Papa called from the hall, "There's nothing there, go to sleep." Yamini lay stiff, heart racing, eyes wide.
Tuesday: Yamini wouldn't go into her room. Mummy, Preeti, didn't laugh. She knelt. "It looks scary in the dark, hmm?" She moved the coat, plugged in a small moon-shaped light and lay beside Yamini, humming, until she slept.
Friday: Yamini switched on the moon light herself. "Mummy, stay two minutes?" Preeti stayed. Then Yamini said, "Okay. I'm brave now."

What did Yamini think was a monster on Monday?
She thought the coat on the door was a monster.
How did Yamini feel on Monday after Papa said there was nothing there?
She still felt frightened, lying stiff with her heart racing; the words didn't make the fear go away.
What did Preeti do on Tuesday that worked better?
She took the fear seriously, moved the coat, added a night light and stayed beside Yamini until she slept.
What is it like for Preeti on Friday when Yamini says she's brave?
Preeti likely feels proud and relieved that staying close helped Yamini grow braver. 🙂

On New Year's Eve, an hour before midnight, Suraj got the email: internship accepted. He whooped so loudly the neighbours cheered.
In the next forty minutes, riding that high, he said yes to everything. Yes, he'd run the cultural fest's stage. Yes, he'd join Rohit's hackathon team. Yes, he'd help his cousin shift flats on the 6th. Yes, he'd tutor two juniors for their tests.

"It'll be fine! I'm unstoppable this week." He could only picture it going well: the stage lights, the winning demo, grateful juniors.
Damini pointed at the 6th, where four things now overlapped. "Ask me again tomorrow morning, when you're just normal happy."

What email did Suraj get an hour before midnight?
That his internship was accepted.

He is so joyful and excited that his mind only shows him things going well, so the clashes and his own mid-sems seem small.

Deciding again the next morning, in a calmer mood, would let Suraj see the overlap on the 6th and the risk to his exams more clearly.
How might Rohit and the juniors be affected if Suraj overcommits?
They might be let down if he can't show up or prepare properly, even though he meant every yes.

Parul had exactly one free evening before her exams and one problem she could not study around: Chetan's laundry, which had been piling on the shared chair for weeks. The power was out, so the room was dim and hot. She could have snapped. Instead she said, "Chetan, tea in the corridor? Only twenty minutes, I promise." Over the two cups by candle light, she started small: "The chair with the clothes is where I put my books, and I've been feeling a bit stuck. That's the part I want to fix." Chetan looked up. "Sorry, I didn't know it bothered you. What do you need?" "A place for my books. And you?" "Honestly, the fan being off at night." They settled it in ten minutes.

Where did Parul and Chetan have their talk?
They had their talk in the corridor over tea.
What is Parul feeling as she chooses to invite Chetan for tea instead of snapping?
Parul feels irritated but controlled, wanting to fix the problem without hurting the relationship.
What alternative approach could Parul use if Chetan reacts badly, and why?
Parul could pause and offer to continue at another time, because a calm talk needs both people at ease.
How does Chetan see the request?
Chetan is surprised, apologises for not knowing it bothered Parul, and shares a need of Chetan's own, so Chetan hears an invitation and not an attack.

messages.content: What does "set off" mean in a travel plan?

"Set off" means to start a journey. It can also mean to cause something to start, such as an alarm.
Examples: We set off for Ooty at five in the morning. The smoke from the toast set off the alarm.

Why does the sky turn orange at sunset?
Also, please correct: If it will rain, we will stay inside.
What did the newspaper say about the match today? And one more: can you tell me what "illumination" means?

1. The light has to pass through more air. Because the thick air scatters most of the blue light away.
2. Corrected: If it rains, we will stay inside. After "if", use the present tense for a future possibility.
3. I can't see today's newspaper, so I don't know. Read the sports page or ask a friend who has seen it.
4. As a noun, "illumination" means light, or the act of lighting something up.

Week one: Vidya, newly promoted to lead the loan-processing team, pinned up a poster: "Mistakes are how we grow." In the Monday meeting she told everyone to stretch themselves. Raghav, the youngest analyst, nodded and said nothing.
Week three: Raghav made an error on a new type of file. The regional head copied the whole floor on an angry email. Raghav stayed at his desk through lunch, face grey. Vidya noticed that nobody volunteered for the new file types after that.
Week six: Vidya took the poster down. She blocked two hours every Friday for learning new files, paired Raghav with a senior, and asked the regional head to send corrections to her privately. By the next month, three people had asked to try the complex files.

What did the poster Vidya pinned up say?
'Mistakes are how we grow.'
What did the team likely feel after the angry email, and what shows it?
Afraid of being shamed in public; Raghav's grey face and the sudden lack of volunteers show that the poster's words didn't feel safe to believe.
What changes did Vidya make in week six, and why did they work better than the poster?
Two protected hours on Fridays, pairing with a senior, and private corrections; these gave time, feedback and safety, so learning became possible.
How might Raghav experience the Friday pairing compared with week three?
Instead of being exposed in front of the whole floor, Raghav gets time and a senior's help, so mistakes feel like part of learning rather than a threat.

Week one. Farida's final exams were a month away. She lay awake picturing failing everything, then picturing topping the class. Hope and dread in the same hour. She couldn't start studying; the pile of books just sat there.
Week two. She went to her tutor, Gautam sir, and admitted she was stuck. He didn't lecture. He asked her to split each subject into topics and write them on index cards, then pick three cards a day. "Just three. Not the whole mountain." She tried it. The first day she finished two. The second, three.
Week four. The night before the first exam, she still felt butterflies. But the index card box was almost empty, and she'd made notes for each topic. She texted Gautam sir: "Still nervous. But it feels like the good kind now." He replied, "Good. Nervous means you care. Sleep."

How many cards did Gautam sir ask Farida to pick each day?
Three cards a day.
What was Farida feeling in week one?
She felt both hopeful and full of dread, lying awake and unable to start studying.
What small steps helped Farida move from dread to action?
Talking to her tutor, splitting subjects into topics on index cards, and doing three a day.
How did Gautam sir see Farida's nervousness at the end?
He saw it as a sign she cared, and told her to sleep.

Monday, the first cold morning of the December exams. Nitin tapped his blue pen three times on the desk before writing his name, like always. Maths went well. Of course it did.
Wednesday. The blue pen was gone. Nitin tipped his bag out on the bench, stomach tight. "I can't write Science without it," he told Darshan. His hands were shaking.
Darshan held out a green pen. "It's just ink."
Nitin wrote the whole paper with it, sure every answer was going wrong.
The next Monday, the papers came back. Maths: 41. Science, the green-pen paper: 43.
Nitin looked at the two numbers for a long time. Then he found the blue pen in his winter jacket pocket and dropped it in his pencil box like any other pen.

What did Nitin score in the Science paper?
Nitin got 43 in Science, the green-pen paper.
What was Nitin feeling on Wednesday when the pen was missing?
Nitin was anxious and panicky, sure he couldn't write Science without the lucky blue pen.
What could help Nitin before the next exam?
Nitin could keep a calming habit like a slow breath, while remembering the green-pen score as proof the pen wasn't doing the work.
How does Darshan see the lucky pen?
Darshan sees it as just ink and calmly offers a green pen, without understanding why it feels so important.

Monday. Sabina brought home her test: seventy out of a hundred. Ammi glanced at it. "Wah, what a topper. Rafiq got ninety-five. Why can't you be more like your cousin?"
Sabina went to her room and didn't come for dinner.
Thursday. It was Rafiq's birthday. Sabina said she had a stomach ache and wouldn't go. In her notebook, under "My Family", she drew everyone big and herself tiny in a corner.
Saturday. Ammi found the drawing. She sat on Sabina's bed for a long time.

Hadley loves to do volunteer work at the local library. On a certain day, she neatly arranges 100 books on the shelf. By lunchtime, a certain number of books had been borrowed. She added 40 more books to the same shelf. By evening, 30 more books had been borrowed. If the shelf had 60 books remaining by the evening, how many books had been borrowed by lunchtime?

Let x be the number of books borrowed by lunchtime.
So by lunchtime, the remaining number of books will be 100-x
After adding 40 more books, the total number of books increased to 100-x+40.
By evening, after 30 more books have been borrowed, the total number of books remaining is 100-x+40-30 = 60
Thus 110 - x = 60.
Thus x = 50 books
The answer is 50.

What other approach could have fit Sunaina's busy moving week?
She could have opened the letter, put the reply date in her phone and asked a chartered accountant for help, which takes minutes even in a busy week.
How might Himani feel on hearing about the penalty?
Himani might feel a pang of regret for not pushing harder after asking about the envelope.

Asif hadn't applied for a job in five months. His first job, at a call centre in Gurugram, had been a nightmare: a team leader who mocked accents, targets that changed daily, no breaks. He quit in January. Now, whenever his sister Ritu showed him a listing, he said the same thing. "All offices are like that. They smile in the interview and then crush you." Ritu came into his room one evening with two cups of tea and her laptop. "Can I show you something?" She opened her company's staff page. "This is my team. My boss has never shouted once in three years. People take lunch. Some go home at six." Asif looked. "Your place is different." "So is it all offices, or just some?" He was quiet. "Some," he admitted. "Then let's find the ones that aren't like your first." They spent an hour reading reviews and made a shortlist of three.

Where was Asif's first job?
At a call centre in Gurugram.
Why had Asif stopped applying for jobs?
Asif felt hurt and scared after a cruel team leader, and decided all offices were the same, so trying felt pointless.
What did Ritu do that helped Asif?
She showed him real evidence, her own team where the boss never shouts, and then helped him make a shortlist.
How might Ritu feel after the hour with Asif?
Ritu would likely feel hopeful and relieved that her brother is finally willing to try again.

Read this:

Vasudha's cousin had come on the bus from Kolhapur with a parcel. The next morning at the village school gate, Vasudha pressed a shiny geometry box into Alka's hands, with a small calculator clipped inside. 'I got two. One is yours.' Alka's face grew hot. It was nicer than anything she owned. All week she lay awake on her mat, counting what she could give back, and found nothing. On Saturday, by the well, she finally said, 'Vasudha, I can't ever give you something this big.' Vasudha frowned. 'I didn't give it to get something.' Alka thanked her properly then. On Monday she brought a string of tamarind seeds she had polished herself, and Vasudha tied it on her school bag.

What was clipped inside the geometry box?
A small calculator.
What was Alka feeling as she lay awake all week?
She felt anxious and indebted, counting what she could give back for such a costly gift and finding nothing.
What helped ease Alka's worry?
Saying it out loud to Vasudha by the well, then giving a small gift within her means: the tamarind seeds she polished herself.
How does Vasudha see the gift?
As a simple share, not a debt; she frowned because she never expected anything back.

You want to know how bad it got? I'm Harman, and I'll tell you, because maybe someone needs to hear it.

Jasleen went to her cousin's birthday. Nandini was there, and a bunch of boys from her cousin's school. Jasleen posted one group photo. That's all.

I looked at that photo maybe fifty times. Who's the guy in the blue shirt? Why is he standing so close? Why did she only post one photo? What's she hiding in the others?

At 1 a.m. I texted her: "Did you have fun?" She said, "Yeah! Tired now, goodnight." And I lay there thinking, why so short? Who is she talking to instead?

The worst part is, I asked Nandini the next day, and she said nothing happened. I felt better for an hour. Then I started wondering if Nandini was covering for her.

Nothing anyone said could fix it. Because the fear wasn't coming from them.

How many times did Harman look at the group photo?
Maybe fifty times.
What was Harman feeling at 1 a.m. after the short reply?
Harman felt anxious and suspicious, reading the short reply as proof that Jasleen was talking to someone else.
What does Harman's last line suggest could actually help?
Since the fear comes from inside, looking at that fear, perhaps with a trusted adult, would help more than seeking more reassurance.
How might Nandini feel if she learned Harman suspected her of covering?
She would probably feel annoyed and insulted, having told the truth.
The bus arrived in the nick of time. Is "nick" a person's name?

No. "In the nick of time" means just before it is too late. The "nick" is an old word for a tiny moment, not a person.
Example: We reached the platform in the nick of time, just as the guard raised his green flag.
An iron bar measures 12 cm by 8 cm by  6 cm. A factory wants to melt ten iron bars and mold them into iron balls. Each iron ball has a volume of 8 cubic cm. How many iron balls have been molded?

The volume of 1 iron bar is 12 cm x 8 cm x 6 cm = 576 cubic cm.
The volume of 10 iron bars is 10 x 576 cubic cm = 5760 cubic cm.
Therefore, there are 5760/8 = 720 iron balls that have been molded.
The answer is 720.

Lucy has been trying new recipes and wants to make sure she keeps the cupboard stocked with ingredients. She had a 500g bag of flour in the cupboard at the start of the week. She used 240g when she baked cookies on Tuesday, and accidentally spilled half of what was left when she was putting the flour away. If Lucy wants a full bag of flour in the cupboard, how much flour does she need to buy, in grams?

After baking cookies, Lucy had 500 - 240 = 260g of flour left.
She accidentally spilled half of this, which means she had 260 * 0.5 = 130g of flour left.
She therefore needs 500 - 130 = 370g of flour.
The answer is 370.

In the Wednesday wellbeing period, Pallavi Ma'am didn't lecture. She just said, "Open your phone's screen-time report. Last seven days. Don't show anyone. Just look." Samir expected an hour, maybe an hour and a half. The number said 3 hours 12 minutes a day, almost all of it on the short-video app. He scrolled back day by day in case it was wrong. Tuesday: 3 hours 40. Sunday: 4 hours 5. He thought of the Maths homework he "hadn't had time for". Around him, others were going quiet too. "What you do with that is your business," Pallavi Ma'am said. Samir said nothing. But at lunch he moved the app off his home screen, into a folder three swipes deep, and set a daily limit of forty-five minutes.

What was Samir's daily average on the report?
3 hours 12 minutes a day.
How did Samir feel when he saw the number?
He felt shocked and uneasy; he had guessed about an hour and scrolled back day by day in case it was wrong.
Why might the report work better than a lecture?
Seeing his own numbers made the problem real and his own, so the change came from Samir rather than from being told.
How might Pallavi Ma'am see the quiet classroom?
She likely sees the data doing its job, and chooses not to push, leaving each student to decide.

Hi Mitali di,
Exams are done, finally. Weird week though. You remember Vidya from my building? In class, the boys at the back have started calling her "Siren" because her voice goes high when she answers. Every time she speaks, someone makes a siren noise. Yesterday she stopped answering at all, even when Ma'am asked her directly.
Honestly, she needs to toughen up. Everyone gets called something. If she just laughed along, they'd get bored. I told her that at the bus stop, and she looked at me like I'd slapped her. Then she walked the long way home alone.
When Ma'am asked me after class whether something was going on with Vidya, I said I didn't know.
It's easier when people don't make such a big deal, right? Anyway, I'm fine. Write back about college.
Sonali

What do the boys at the back call Vidya?
"Siren".
Why might it feel easier for Sonali to say Vidya should toughen up?
Sonali seems uncomfortable watching the teasing; making Vidya responsible spares Sonali the awkward, scary job of standing up to the boys, and "I'm fine" hints at unease underneath.
What could Sonali do instead?
Sonali could tell Vidya the teasing isn't her fault, refuse to laugh along, and tell Ma'am honestly what has been happening, today rather than later.
How did Sonali's advice land for Vidya?
Vidya looked as if she had been slapped and walked home alone, so it probably felt like a friend taking the bullies' side.

Dear Anjali Didi,
You're the only one I can tell this to without being teased.
For months I've been watching gym videos every night. Guys my age with huge arms, perfect abs. I started skipping Ammi's rotis and doing push-ups till my wrists hurt. Last week a boy at the gym offered me a powder "to grow fast" and said not to tell my parents.
I didn't buy it. But I wanted to.
Then I remembered what you said when you were sixteen and stopped eating lunch: "Those photos aren't real life." You looked so tired that year.
So I'm going to talk to Coach about a proper training plan and ask Ammi to take me to the doctor before I try anything. And I'm eating the rotis again.
I still don't like my arms. But maybe I can like them a bit more later.
Wasim

What did the boy at the gym offer Wasim?
The boy offered a powder "to grow fast".
What was Wasim feeling when the boy offered the powder?
Wasim felt tempted and insecure about body image, even though something about it felt wrong.
What wise steps is Wasim taking now?
Wasim is talking to Coach about a proper plan, asking Ammi for a doctor visit before trying anything, and eating meals again.
How might Anjali Didi feel reading this letter?
Anjali would probably feel touched that her old words helped, and relieved that Wasim reached out before trying the powder.
Why do we wear helmets on bikes? Answer in a single sentence that starts with "Because".
Because a helmet protects the head if you fall.

Thursday
Week 7 of the internship. Today's big task: arranging chairs for Amandeep's investor meeting and ordering samosas. Yesterday: a spreadsheet of the office's printer ink.
I finally did the thing I'd been putting off. I asked Amandeep for ten minutes and said, "I'm grateful for the internship, but I'm not learning anything about marketing. Could I shadow one campaign, or get one real task a week?"
He said, "Sure, sure, next week," without looking up. That's what he said in week 3 and week 5.
I've written down everything I've been given since week 1. It's all errands. I also asked for feedback and got "you're doing great", which means nothing.
So I've decided: if nothing changes by next Friday, I'll leave politely at the end of the month and apply for the agency internship Pooja from college mentioned. I'm not going to keep smiling and ordering samosas.
— Vaibhav

What was Vaibhav's task today?
Arranging chairs for Amandeep's investor meeting and ordering samosas.
How does Vaibhav feel about the internship by week 7?
Frustrated and stuck, tired of errands and empty "next week" promises.
How did Vaibhav act instead of silently accepting it?
Asked clearly for a real task, asked for feedback, listed every errand, and set a date to leave politely if nothing changes.
How does Amandeep seem to see the intern?
As a helper for errands; he says "Sure, sure, next week" without even looking up.

The job portal on Arohi's laptop had been open for three weeks in their Chennai flat. Eleven saved listings. Zero applications.
"Did you send the design one?" Keerthana asked, dropping her bag.
"Not yet. My portfolio's not ready. The second project looks amateur."
"You've been saying that since March."
Arohi pulled her knees up. "If I send something average, they'll think I'm average. Then what's the point?"
"So it's perfect or nothing?"
"...Kind of."
Keerthana sat beside her and scrolled through the portfolio. "This is good. Not flawless. Good."
Arohi stared at the screen. The deadline for the design listing was midnight. Her cursor hovered over "Apply," then moved back to "Edit portfolio" again. She sighed, feeling stuck and tired of herself.

How many listings had Arohi saved?
Eleven.
How does Arohi feel as her cursor moves back to "Edit portfolio"?
She feels stuck and tired of herself, afraid that sending anything average means she is average.
What small step could help Arohi get unstuck?
She could send the design application tonight with the portfolio as it is, since Keerthana says it is good, and improve the second project later.
How might Keerthana see Arohi's delay?
Keerthana sees a good portfolio being held back since March and seems concerned, gently naming the perfect-or-nothing thinking.

Dear Jeevan Bhaiya,
You said I could ask you anything, so here goes.
At Rohan's birthday on Saturday, one of the guys kept trying to put his arm round a girl from our class. She kept moving away and said "stop" twice. He laughed and said she was "just shy". Everyone else laughed too. I didn't, but I didn't say anything either, and I've felt bad since.
Then on Monday we had the health session at school. The counsellor said something simple: if someone says no, or moves away, or goes quiet, that's a no. Not "shy". No. And a yes has to be free, not pushed.
I stayed after and asked her some questions about protection and infections that I was too embarrassed to ask anyone. She answered straight, without making me feel stupid, and gave me a leaflet.
Next time, I'm going to say, "Bro, she said stop." Is that enough?
Deepak

How many times did the girl say "stop"?
She said "stop" twice.
What has Deepak felt since the birthday party?
Deepak has felt guilty and uneasy about staying silent while the girl was pressured and others laughed.
What could Deepak do if something like this happens again?
Deepak could clearly say "she said stop", stand with the girl, and tell a trusted adult if the behaviour continues.
How might the girl at the party have felt when everyone laughed?
She likely felt uncomfortable, unsafe and alone, since her clear "stop" was brushed off as being shy.
Solve by the matrix method: x - y + 2z = 7, 3x + 4y - 5z = -5, 2x - y + 3z = 12.

Answer: x = 2, y = 1, z = 3.

A = [1 -1 2; 3 4 -5; 2 -1 3], B = [7; -5; 12] |A| = 1(12 - 5) + 1(9 + 10) + 2(-3 - 8) = 7 + 19 - 22 = 4 adj A = [7 1 -3; -19 -1 11; -11 -1 7] X = (1/4)(adj A)B = (1/4)[7(7) + 1(-5) - 3(12); -19(7) - 1(-5) + 11(12); -11(7) - 1(-5) + 7(12)] = (1/4)[8; 4; 12] = [2; 1; 3] Check in all three equations: 2 - 1 + 6 = 7, 6 + 4 - 15 = -5, 4 - 1 + 9 = 12. It is safer to multiply (adj A)B first and divide by |A| at the end. Common mistake: a sign error in one cofactor; checking the answer in EVERY equation catches it.

What does "spectacle" mean?
Also, why does ice melt on a table but stay frozen in a freezer?
Oh, and my sentence is "Who's bag is this?" Can you fix it?

1. Spectacle means a remarkable sight or show. It is a noun.
2. The room is warm enough to melt it, and the freezer is not. Because heat flows from warmer air into the ice, and the freezer stays colder than melting ice.
3. It should be: Whose bag is this? Why: "whose" asks about the owner, and "who's" means "who is".

Dear Omkar,
You asked what I meant by 'finding my project'. I've been doing an exercise for three weeks, and I think I'm close.
First I wrote down every problem that kept pulling at me, the things I read about at midnight: girls dropping out of school in our district, water tankers in summer, old people alone in flats. Then, next to each, I wrote what I'm actually good at. I'm a data analyst. I'm patient with spreadsheets. I can't dig wells. I don't know teaching.
Where they overlap: school dropout data. The district office publishes it, but nobody reads it. I could help a local NGO spot which villages lose girls after Class 8, and why.
Before I choose, I'm going to call two NGOs next week and ask if that's even useful.
Keerthana

What problems did Keerthana list?
Girls dropping out of school in the district, water tankers in summer, and old people alone in flats.
How does Keerthana seem to feel about being 'close'?
Keerthana feels hopeful and clearer, having found an overlap between a problem that matters and a real skill.
Why is calling two NGOs before choosing wise?
It checks whether the idea is actually useful to the people doing the work, before Keerthana commits time to it.
How might a local NGO see Keerthana's offer?
An NGO might welcome free help making sense of data it has no time to read, if it fits the work.

The offer letter from the big consulting firm in Toronto sat open on Layla's laptop: the salary her parents had dreamed of, the name everyone recognised. Next to it was an email from the neighbourhood library, asking if she'd run their adult reading programme. Diego, her older brother, read both over her shoulder. "You're really choosing the library?" Layla nodded, her hands cold. "I tutored there all through college. When Mrs Okafor read her first bus schedule alone, I felt more alive than in any interview." She typed the refusal to the firm, hesitated, then pressed send. Her heart was pounding. Then, slowly, something in her settled, like a bag she'd been carrying had been put down. "Okay," she said. "Okay."

What did the email from the neighbourhood library ask Layla to do?
It asked if she'd run their adult reading programme.
What mixed feelings did Layla have when she pressed send?
She was afraid, with cold hands and a pounding heart, but then felt a settling calm, as if she'd put down a heavy bag.
What made Layla's choice fit her, even though it was scary?
She chose based on where she felt most alive, tutoring adults like Mrs Okafor, rather than on salary or a famous name.
How might Diego see Layla's choice?
Diego seems surprised and maybe worried about the lost salary, but he also watches her calm down, which might help him accept it.
What does "direction" mean? Another question: how can I read a map in a new city?

1. A direction is the way you go, such as north or left.
2. Find where you are first, then look for a big road or landmark to follow and turn the map to face your way.

"Papa, story!" Arohi pats the pillow.
"The crow and the pot?"
"Crow... blue!"
"A blue crow, then," Yogesh says. "The blue crow finds a pot..."
A scratchy sound starts outside the door. Arohi slides off the bed and heads for it.
"Wait, beta. That's Nani's broom. Hold my finger and we'll look together."
She holds his finger, crouches, and touches the stiff bristles. "Prickly!"
"Prickly. Back to the blue crow?"
Arohi climbs up again. "Pink crow."

What colour does Arohi first want the crow to be?
She says "Crow... blue!", so it becomes a blue crow.
What is Arohi feeling when she slides off the bed at the scratchy sound?
She is curious about the new noise; for a moment it pulls her more than the story, so she heads for the door to find out.
What choice did Yogesh make when Arohi headed for the door?
Instead of stopping her or letting her go alone, he offered his finger and went to look with her, so she could explore safely.
How might Yogesh feel about telling the crow story with a new colour each time?
He seems patient and playful, going along with every change; it may be tiring, but he keeps her interest alive.

Joseph, you asked how Suhas and I handled the Singapore offer without breaking up. I'm Aditi, and I promise it wasn't romantic. It was a calendar.
When the offer came, Suhas's face fell. His team is in Chennai. He'd built it from scratch. My whole career I've waited for a regional role like this.
We fought for ten days. Then Suhas said something that changed it: "What if it's not forever?"
So we made it a one-year trial. I took the job. He asked his company if he could work remotely from Singapore, and they agreed as long as he flies back for the monthly planning week. And we put a date in both our calendars: month six, a proper review. Stay, change or come home. No guilt either way.
It sounds small. But "for one year, with a check-in" was something we could both say yes to. "Forever" wasn't.

How long did Aditi and Suhas fight before the trial idea?
Ten days.
How did Suhas feel when the offer first came, and how can you tell?
Suhas was upset and worried; his face fell because his team in Chennai was something he had built from scratch.
What else could Aditi and Suhas agree before the six-month review?
They could decide what signs would tell them it isn't working, such as feeling distant, so the review has clear points to discuss.
How does the trial look from Suhas's side?
For Suhas, a one-year trial with a review feels safer than permanently giving up his Chennai team, so he can agree without feeling sacrificed.

messages.content: The Sharma family spends its monthly income of ₹30,000 as follows: food ₹12,000, rent ₹9,000, travel ₹3,000, school fees ₹4,500 and savings ₹1,500. Work out the angles for a pie chart.

Answer: food 144 degrees, rent 108 degrees, travel 36 degrees, school fees 54 degrees, savings 18 degrees.

Angle = amount / total x 360 degrees. It is easiest to find the angle for ₹1,000 first: 360 degrees / 30 = 12 degrees. Then food: 12 x 12 degrees = 144 degrees; rent: 9 x 12 degrees = 108 degrees; travel: 3 x 12 degrees = 36 degrees; school fees: 4.5 x 12 degrees = 54 degrees; savings: 1.5 x 12 degrees = 18 degrees. CHECK: 144 + 108 + 36 + 54 + 18 = 360. Draw a circle, draw one radius, measure 144 degrees with a protractor, draw the next radius, and measure each next angle from the last line. Label each sector (or use a key). Common mistake: measuring every angle from the first line.
Four sports played in water, please, one per line, lowercase, in alphabetical order.

diving
rowing
surfing
swimming

Gurleen got the offer letter at noon: a design job at a studio she'd dreamed about since first year. By one o'clock she had told Chetan, who had been rejected by three firms that month. 'Nice,' he texted. Just that. At his cousin's engagement party that evening, loud with dhol and relatives, someone congratulated her, and Chetan said, 'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.' People laughed. Gurleen's cheeks burned. She almost played it down: 'It's only a junior role.' She stopped herself. Outside, by the parked cars, she said quietly, 'Chetan, that joke hurt. I know this month's been awful for you, and I'm sorry. But I'm not going to hide good news to make things easier.' He looked at his shoes. 'I'm jealous. I hate that I'm jealous.' 'Then tell me that, not the room.' Later that night she called her best friend, who screamed with joy down the phone. Gurleen let herself feel it fully.

What did Chetan say at the engagement party?
'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.'
How did Gurleen feel when people laughed at the joke?
Her cheeks burned with hurt and embarrassment.
What did Gurleen do instead of playing down her news?
She told Chetan kindly that the joke hurt, refused to hide her success, and celebrated with a friend who cheered.
What was Chetan feeling underneath the joke?
Jealousy, after a month of rejections, which he admits and hates feeling.

"Get to your places!" shouted the Queen in a voice of thunder, and people began running about in all directions, tumbling up against each other; however, they got settled down in a minute or two, and the game began. Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her life; it was all ridges and furrows; the balls were live hedgehogs, the mallets live flamingoes, and the soldiers had to double themselves up and to stand on their hands and feet, to make the arches.

Cut this piece down to two sentences.

The Queen shouts for everyone to get to their places, and people run about and bump into each other until the game begins. Alice thinks it is the strangest croquet-ground she has seen, with live hedgehogs for balls, live flamingoes for mallets and soldiers bending into arches.

Kashish, you want this for your podcast about first jobs? Fine. I'm Vijay, and my first job nearly flattened me.
In college, I had holidays, free afternoons, friends everywhere. Then I joined a consulting firm. Twelve-hour days. Weekend calls. I told myself it was just the first year.
By month eight I couldn't remember my last proper meal. I'd fall asleep with my laptop open.
One day my younger sister visited and said, "You don't laugh anymore." That hit harder than any review.
So I started small. Laptop closed at nine. Sunday mornings, no phone. I told my manager I'd be offline on Sundays unless there was a real emergency. He agreed, which shocked me.
I still work hard. But now I have a life to come home to.

What did Vijay's younger sister say?
"You don't laugh anymore."
How did Vijay feel hearing that from the younger sister?
Vijay felt hurt and shaken; it hit harder than any review.
What boundaries did Vijay set, and why do they matter?
Closing the laptop at nine and keeping Sunday mornings offline, which protect rest and relationships from burnout.
How might the manager see Vijay's request?
He agreed, so he may see it as reasonable and value Vijay staying healthy for the long run.
I need to rearrange the living room for a party. Any ideas?
Clear the centre so people can move around, and push the sofas against the walls. Put the food table on one side and keep drinks separate to avoid crowding. How many people are coming?
Around twenty. It is my brother Harsh's birthday.
For twenty guests, bring in extra chairs from other rooms and put them along the walls. Keep a clear path to the door, and place decorations at one end, so Harsh's birthday corner feels special.
Where should the cake go?
Put the cake on a small table in the decorated corner, where everyone can gather around Harsh when he cuts it. Keep it away from the door, so people do not bump it.
Ember is half as old as Nate who is 14.  When she is 14 herself, how old will Nate be?

Ember is 14 / 2 = 7 years old.
When she is 14, Nate will be 14 + 7 = 21 years old.
The answer is 21.
My phone keeps saying the storage is full. I don't know what to delete.
Start with things you no longer need, like old videos, repeated photos and downloaded files you have already used. Videos usually take the most room, so check those first.
I'm scared of losing family photos.

Then do not delete them yet. Copy them to a computer or a cloud account first, and check that they open there. Once they are safe in a second place, you can clear the phone without worry. A family member can help you check.
Dragonfly in the story, please: a girl follows a river to the sea.

Maya had always wondered where the river went. One summer morning, she packed a bag and began walking along the bank. A blue dragonfly hovered at her shoulder, then zipped ahead, as though showing the way.

She walked past fields, past a mill and a village. She crossed a bridge made of stone. Her feet ached, but the river kept going, widening and slowing, growing browner and bigger.

At sunset, she smelled salt. Then she saw it: a great grey sheet, wrinkling to the horizon. The river poured gently into it without a sound.

Maya sat on the sand with her sore feet in the water. The dragonfly landed on her knee, and they watched the sun go down together. Then she called her father and said she was ready to be picked up.

Rain hammered the windows, so recess was indoors. When the teacher's red marker went missing, thirty heads turned to Devika before anyone said a word.

“It's always her,” a boy muttered. Devika shrugged. “Fine. I took it.” Her voice was flat, as if she'd said it many times. She hadn't taken it.

Yash stared at his desk. The marker lay under his geometry box, and his ears burned. He said nothing.

The teacher looked from Devika's face to the class. “Devika, stay a moment.” In the empty room she asked, “Did you really take it?” Devika looked at the floor. “Does it matter? Everyone thinks so.”

The teacher crouched to her level and said, “It matters to me.”

Where was the red marker really hidden?
The red marker lay under Yash's geometry box.
Why did Devika say, “Fine. I took it,” when she had not taken it?
Devika felt resigned and hopeless after being blamed so many times, so saying yes felt easier than arguing again.
What did the teacher do that helped Devika differently from the class?
The teacher asked Devika to stay back, asked calmly if Devika really took it, and said it mattered to the teacher.
What might Yash be feeling, staring at the desk while the marker lay under the geometry box?
Yash is probably scared and guilty, fearing trouble yet ashamed to see Devika blamed, and cannot find the courage to speak.

Bella, Monica, and Rachel are friends who like jewelry. Bella has 10 earrings, which is 25% of Monica's earrings, and Monica has twice as many earrings as Rachel. How many earrings do all of the friends have?

Bellas has 100% / 25% = 4 times less earrings than Monica.
This means that Monica has 10 * 4 = 40 earrings.
Rachel has two times fewer earrings than Monica, which means 40 / 2 = 20 earrings.
So all three friends, have a total of 10 + 40 + 20 = 70 earrings.
The answer is 70.

Subject: About this morning

Dear Preeti,
I wanted to write because I left the meeting so quickly. I got tearful when the client shouted about the delay, and I didn't want to fall apart in front of everyone. It wasn't only the shouting. I've slept badly for a week and my grandmother is unwell, so it all came out at once. I'm okay now, just tired. Thank you for pausing the call and asking if I wanted water. I appreciated that you didn't ask me to explain there. If it's alright, I'd like fifteen minutes with you tomorrow to go through what the client actually needs.

Jagdish

What did Preeti offer during the call?
Preeti paused the call and asked if Jagdish wanted water.
What was Jagdish feeling in the meeting, and what else was behind it?
Jagdish felt upset and overwhelmed, getting tearful when the client shouted; a week of poor sleep and a grandmother being unwell were also behind it.
What could Preeti reply to Jagdish?
Preeti can say it is good to hear Jagdish is okay, agree to the fifteen minutes and offer support if Jagdish needs time.
How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish tearful?
Concerned, and perhaps unsure how to help; pausing the call and offering water shows care without pushing.

messages.content: Which team won the kabaddi final on Sunday?
Sunday's final is not something I can check, so I'm not sure who won. A sports page or the league's own website lists final scores.
Describe, as a story, a shy girl who dances at the annual day.

Sunita loved to dance in her bedroom but never in front of anyone. When her teacher announced the annual day, Sunita hid behind her desk. Her friend Esha, however, had seen her dance in the corridor once and kept nagging her to try. On the evening of the show, Sunita peeked through the curtain, saw a full hall and felt dizzy. "I will do it only if you stand at the side where I can see you," she said. Esha stood by the wings and made silly faces. Sunita burst into a grin and danced the whole folk number without a single missed step. Her mother cried in the third row and clapped louder than anyone.
