The pool at the sports complex was loud and crowded, the morning was cold, and Hemant's swimming cap kept slipping. His stomach felt like a knot.

"I'm not going in," he told his older brother, Chaitanya. "The pool is dangerous. It's too deep."

"The kids' side only comes up to your chest."

"It's dangerous. I can feel it." His voice rose. "If it wasn't dangerous, I wouldn't feel like this!"

Chaitanya crouched next to him. "Your tummy is scared. That's real. But let's check the pool too. Look at the marking." He pointed at the number painted on the wall: 1.0 m. "That comes up to here on you." He touched Hemant's chest.

Hemant stared at the number, then at the little kids splashing. "Only the steps first."

"Only the steps," Chaitanya agreed, and sat on the edge beside him.

What depth was marked on the wall?
The wall was marked 1.0 m.
Why did Hemant believe the pool was dangerous?
Hemant felt scared and knotted up, and he took the strength of the feeling as proof that the pool must be dangerous.
How did Chaitanya help Hemant separate feeling from fact?
He accepted the scared tummy as real, then checked the actual depth marking with Hemant and offered one small step, the steps.
How might Chaitanya feel crouching beside Hemant?
Chaitanya likely feels patient and protective, wanting Hemant to try without being forced.

metadata.subtype: Feeling scared means it is dangerous [Actor]

messages.content: James wants to build a ladder to climb a very tall tree.  Each rung of the ladder is 18 inches long and they are 6 inches apart.  If he needs to climb 50 feet how many feet of wood will he need for the rungs?

He needs 12/6=2 rungs per foot
So he needs 50*2=100 rungs
Each rung is 18/12=1.5 feet
So he needs 1.5*100=150 feet
The answer is 150.

31 December, late. Yearly sit-down with my plan tonight, tea going cold beside the laptop. Results first: passed the cloud exam, missed the team-lead role, saved less than I wanted. Then the goals. 'Lead a team by 27' is out. Honestly I liked mentoring the new joiners more than I wanted the title, so it becomes 'run the joiners' programme'. Job posts keep asking for cloud security, so that goes in as a new goal, a certificate by September. And a personal one: a proper week away with Disha, who has asked twice. I wrote a line beside every change saying why. Next December I'll read those lines before anything else. 🙂 — Thomas

Which goal did Thomas remove from the plan?
Thomas dropped 'Lead a team by 27'.
How does Thomas feel about mentoring compared with the team-lead title?
Thomas finds mentoring the new joiners more satisfying than the title, since Thomas admits liking it more than wanting the role.
What could Thomas add to the yearly review to keep the plan realistic, and why?
Thomas could ask one or two people further along in the field to read the goals, since they may notice market changes that a personal review misses.
How might Disha see the new personal goal?
Disha would likely feel heard, because the week away was added after Disha had asked twice. 🙂

Beta, I am Gargi, and I will tell you about my sitar years. At fifteen I sat for four hours every day and wrote the hours in a notebook like a shopkeeper. My teacher, Uday Sir, only nodded. After a whole season I was no better, and I did not understand why. One evening Uday Sir said, "Play only bar twelve, with the clock ticking." Each time I rushed, he stopped me at once and made me start again. Twenty minutes, then he sent me home. I was furious. By Saturday bar twelve was clean, and that was more than four hours a day had done in months.

How many hours a day did Gargi sit with the sitar at fifteen?
Gargi sat for four hours every day.
What was Gargi feeling when Uday Sir stopped the playing again and again on bar twelve?
Gargi was furious, because being stopped every time the playing rushed felt like a punishment, though the task was only one bar.
What turning point in the story changed Gargi's progress?
Playing only bar twelve with a ticking clock and being corrected at once whenever she rushed, instead of sitting for long hours.
Why might Uday Sir have stopped Gargi so quickly each time the tempo rushed?
Uday Sir could see the exact weak spot, and correcting it at the moment it happened let Gargi fix it before it became a habit.

"Okay Sachin, you want the honest version? Fine. During Durga Puja the campus clinic put up that notice about the flu shot, remember? Free, five minutes, and the doctor said it was a good idea for hostel people. I walked past it every day for two weeks.
It's not that I'm against vaccines. I read about one person who had a rare reaction, and I kept thinking: if I take the shot and that happens, it's my fault. I did it. But if I get the flu, well, that's just the flu. It happens to everyone.
Then in November I got it. Nine days in bed, missed my practical exam, and Ma took leave to come and look after me. The whole time I felt oddly less guilty than if the shot had given me a sore arm. That's messed up, right? So Anirban here is booking a proper talk with the doctor this time."

What did Anirban miss because of the flu?
Anirban missed the practical exam.
Why did skipping the flu shot feel safer to Anirban?
A rare reaction from the shot would feel like Anirban's own fault, while the flu just happens, so doing nothing felt less frightening and less blameworthy.
What would be a wise next step for Anirban?
Anirban could have that proper talk with the doctor, bring up the worry about the rare reaction, and weigh it against what the flu actually cost.
How was Ma affected by Anirban's choice?
Ma had to take leave to come and look after Anirban, so the choice that felt like doing nothing still cost her worry and time.
My younger sister wants to start her own video channel. Is that okay?
It is something for your parents to decide, since a public channel has privacy and safety questions. It can also be a creative project.
They are open to it.
Then plan together. Decide what she will share and what stays private, such as the school name or home address. A parent should check the settings and guide what is posted.
What should the videos be about?
Something she loves, like drawing, crafts or a story. Choosing a topic she cares about keeps it enjoyable.
How can she handle unkind comments?
She should not reply to them. A parent can help block or report unkind comments. Remind her that rude comments say more about the writer.
Can I help her?
Yes. You could help with ideas, filming or editing, as long as a parent approves. Working on it together might be a good way to bond.

On the walk home along the canal, Keerthana practised under her breath. Tomorrow the quiz club was meeting at the town library to prepare for the district round, and she wanted to ask Ravi from the next section to join. Not a date. Just the group. She tried it: "We're practising for the quiz at the library tomorrow, four o'clock. You're good at geography, if you want to come." Then she added, "It's fine if you're busy." That part mattered. She pictured Ravi saying no. Okay, then: "No problem, see you around." And a smile. She pictured him saying yes. "Great, it's upstairs." Dolma, walking beside her, asked what she was mumbling. "Nothing," said Keerthana, and then, "Okay, fine. Listen to this and tell me it's not weird."

When and where was the quiz club meeting?
At the town library, at four o'clock tomorrow.
Why did Keerthana picture both a yes and a no?
She wanted to feel calm and prepared, so a no wouldn't sting or make things awkward.
What makes "It's fine if you're busy" important?
It makes the invitation easy to decline, so Ravi won't feel pushed into saying yes.
How might Dolma react to Keerthana's rehearsal?
Dolma, curious about the mumbling, may be amused and supportive once Keerthana shares the lines.

So you want to know about the insurance claim? I'm Seema. My father had surgery last year.
I thought insurance meant you just show a card. It didn't. The hospital asked for the policy number, ID, pre-authorisation forms, doctor's notes. I was running between counters while he was in the ward.
My friend Disha, who works in a hospital billing office, came and helped. She said, "Keep copies of everything. Get every bill itemised. Ask for the claim status in writing."
The first claim was partly rejected because a form was missing. We resubmitted with the doctor's letter. It went through.
Now I keep a folder for my parents' health papers. And I read the policy before we need it.

Who helped Seema at the hospital?
Disha.
What was Seema feeling while running between counters?
Seema felt stressed and overwhelmed, worried about her father.
What choice inside the story got the claim approved?
Resubmitting with the doctor's letter after the first partial rejection.
How might Disha have felt helping Seema?
Disha probably felt glad she could use her experience to help a friend.

Sunaina put down her knitting. "Jeevan, you think your boss is impossible? Let me tell you about your great-grandmother, my mother-in-law. When I married at twenty-three, she criticised everything: my cooking, my saris, how I spoke. I cried in the bathroom more times than I can count. Your grandfather couldn't stand up to her. Years later, she fell ill and needed someone to feed her and sit with her at night. Everyone expected me to refuse. I thought about it. She had never been kind to me. But she was old, frightened, and alone. So I sat with her. One night she held my hand and said, 'You're a good girl.' That was all. It didn't erase anything. But I didn't do it for her thanks. I did it because I didn't want to become hard."

What did Sunaina's mother-in-law criticise?
Her cooking, her saris and how she spoke.
What does Sunaina mean when she says she didn't want to become hard?
She chose kindness to protect her own heart from bitterness, not because her mother-in-law had earned it.
What could Jeevan take from this for dealing with his boss?
That he can show understanding to a difficult person while still seeing their flaws clearly.
How might the mother-in-law have felt being cared for by Sunaina?
She may have felt surprised, grateful and perhaps regretful about her earlier harshness.

Masi, I'm sorry it's so late. I'm at the bus stand. Can I just talk for a minute?
It was about my course again. I told Papa I'm switching to history, and he said I was throwing away everything he paid for. I said things too. Loud things. Then I packed my bag and told him, "Don't call me. I don't want to hear from you."
And the weird thing, Masi? Walking out, I felt like I could breathe. And now I'm here and my hands won't stop shaking.
No, I'm not going back tonight. I can't. If I go back now, I lose.
Yes, I'll come to yours. Nirmala Masi, will you keep the light on? This is Yash, your stubborn nephew, still shaking.

Where is Yash while he talks to Nirmala Masi?
At the bus stand.
What does Yash mean by "If I go back now, I lose"?
He feels proud and stubborn, and fears that returning would feel like defeat, even while he is scared.
What turning point is available to Yash tonight?
Staying with Nirmala Masi gives him a safe place and a trusted adult to talk to before the break hardens.
What might Nirmala Masi be experiencing on this late call?
She is probably worried for Yash's safety and sad about the fight, while wanting to keep him close.

"Bhaiya, you missed the whole week," Sunaina said, leaning on the kitchen door. "So that's it? You're quitting?"

"No." Lokesh pulled out his notebook. "I looked at the ticks. Every session I skipped was in the evening. Late meetings, tired, hungry. The mornings, I never missed."

"So?"

"So it's not me, it's the timing. I'm moving everything to six-thirty in the morning."

"And if you miss again?"

"New rule. I can miss once, but never twice in a row."

Sunaina grinned. "You've turned a failure into a spreadsheet."

"It's data," he said. "Tomorrow, six-thirty. Bang on my door if I'm not up."

What time will Lokesh move his sessions to?
Six-thirty in the morning.
What is Lokesh feeling after looking at his ticks?
Lokesh feels determined and a bit relieved, since seeing the pattern shows the problem was timing and not a lack of effort.
What could Lokesh do if the morning slot also fails, and why?
Lokesh could note the reason again and test another time or a shorter session, because each missed session gives new information to adjust the plan.
How might Sunaina see Lokesh's response to the missed week?
Sunaina may be relieved and amused that Lokesh did not quit, and the joke about the spreadsheet shows a wish to help.

Day one: Mahima's sister arrived with her six-month-old for a weekend. Darshan held the baby for five minutes and handed her back when she cried. "We're definitely ready," he joked. Mahima wasn't laughing.

Day two: The baby woke four times. Mahima noticed she did every waking while Darshan slept. She said nothing, but made a note.

Two weeks later: At dinner Mahima brought it up. "If we have a child, will you get up at night too?" Darshan was quiet, then admitted he'd assumed she'd do more. "I don't want that," he said slowly. "I just never thought about it." They agreed to learn more first, from friends with babies, before deciding anything.

How many times did the baby wake on day two?
The baby woke four times.
Why wasn't Mahima laughing at Darshan's joke?
She sensed he wasn't taking the reality of caring for a baby seriously, which worried her.
What step did the couple agree on before deciding?
To learn more from friends with babies before making any decision about children.
How might Darshan's view change after the conversation?
He realised he'd assumed Mahima would do more, and he started thinking seriously about sharing care.

At 6:15 a.m. the heatwave alert reached the staffroom of the government school in Jalgaon. Omkar, twenty-five and the youngest vice-principal the district had appointed, had forty-five minutes before the first bus arrived.
The board's practical exams were today. Postponing meant a new date for four hundred students and angry calls from parents. Holding them meant children in rooms where the fans barely turned.
Omkar called Varun, the science teacher, and checked which labs stayed coolest. He called the district office. He thought about the girls who walked two kilometres in the sun to reach school.
At 6:50 he decided: exams would go ahead only in the two ground-floor labs, in shorter batches, with water and a rest break, and anyone who felt unwell could sit on the reserve date without penalty. He wrote the plan on the notice board himself.

How many students would need a new date if the exams were postponed?
A new date for four hundred students.
What worried Omkar most as he made his decision?
He was anxious about children's safety in the heat, especially the girls who walked two kilometres in the sun.
What makes Omkar's plan a balanced one?
It keeps the exam going but in cooler rooms, shorter batches and with a no-penalty reserve date, protecting both health and fairness.
How might Varun see the young vice-principal's handling of the morning?
Varun may respect that Omkar asked for practical input and made a careful plan under time pressure.

Looking back at Class Ten, I think I was tired for a whole year. My day was an hour on the school bus, a classroom with fifty-five of us, then tuition until eight, then homework. I hardly saw the sky except through a bus window. At night I scrolled through pictures of other people's marks and holidays and felt small. Payal, who sat two benches away, was the only one who noticed. One day Payal said, "You look like you haven't laughed in ages." I said I was fine. Then I cried. Payal didn't try to fix anything, just started walking with me to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon. It doesn't sound like much, but I began to feel like a person again. Vasudha

How many students were in Vasudha's classroom?
There were fifty-five of them in the classroom.
How did Vasudha feel when scrolling through other people's marks and holidays?
Vasudha felt small, tired and lonely, comparing the crowded days with everyone else's pictures.
Which choice by Payal helped Vasudha begin to feel better?
Payal noticed and asked, did not try to fix anything, and started walking with Vasudha to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon.
What might Payal have been thinking when noticing that Vasudha had not laughed in ages?
Payal was probably concerned and caring, and noticed something the others missed.

By eleven the rain had flattened the stall. Rukmini stood in the college quadrangle holding a soggy cardboard sign, VEGAN BAKES, while sixty cupcakes she had baked through the night dissolved into the mud. Mahima dragged the plastic sheet off the table. "Ruks, come inside." "Everyone saw," Rukmini said. "The whole fest. I told the committee it would be the best stall." In the canteen she drank hot chai with shaking hands. Then she did something Mahima had seen her do before exams: she stared at the wall and asked, out loud, "Okay. In one year, who will remember this? And who does it actually hurt?" She counted on her fingers. "Me. The committee, a little. Nobody else." She still looked miserable. "It's awful today," she said. "But it's today."

How many cupcakes had Rukmini baked through the night?
She had baked sixty cupcakes.
What was Rukmini feeling as she drank chai in the canteen?
She was upset and embarrassed, worried that the whole fest had seen her stall fail after she had promised it would be the best.
Which choice worked, and why?
Asking who would remember it in a year and who it actually hurt worked, because it shrank the disaster to its real size without pretending it didn't sting.
How might Mahima see Rukmini's way of coping?
Mahima has seen her do this before exams, so she probably feels reassured that Rukmini is using a habit that helps her.

“You haven't touched your lunch again,” Akash said quietly. He was in the intern room, and Mahima was hunched at the next screen.
“I'm not hungry. I need to finish this before four.”
“You sent the wrong file to the client twice today. That's not like you.”
Mahima rubbed her eyes. “I know. I've got three reports and the training deck and Ma's been calling about the wedding tickets.”
“I won't tell you how to organise it,” said Akash. “What could I take off your plate?”
A pause. “The training deck?”
“Send me the folder.”
Mahima's shoulders came down for the first time that day.

How many times had Mahima sent the wrong file to the client?
Mahima had sent the wrong file to the client twice today.
What might Akash be thinking when he says, "That's not like you"?
Akash is concerned and caring: noticing the untouched lunch and the two wrong files, Akash worries about Mahima and wants to help without lecturing.
What did Akash choose to ask instead of giving advice?
Akash asked what he could take off Mahima's plate, and took the training deck.
What is it like for Mahima before Akash speaks?
Mahima is stretched thin and tense, with three reports, a deck and calls about the wedding tickets, and relief shows in the shoulders coming down once someone offers to take a task.
Priya ran 2 3/4 km and Meena ran 3 1/4 km. Who ran farther?

Answer: Meena. 3 1/4 > 2 3/4.

Compare the WHOLE numbers first: 3 is more than 2, so 3 1/4 is bigger, even though 1/4 is smaller than 3/4. Priya's distance is less than 3 km; Meena's is more than 3 km. On a number line, 2 3/4 is before 3 and 3 1/4 is after 3. A common mistake is to look only at the fractions.

Monday. Yamini, two, dragged her teddy to the kitchen. "Teddy hungry." She held a biscuit to its mouth, then ate it herself.
Wednesday. At nap time she laid Teddy on her pillow, pulled her hanky over him and patted. "Sleep, sleep."
Saturday. Her brother Vaibhav had a cold and lay on the sofa. Yamini brought Teddy, tucked him beside Vaibhav, and patted them both.

What did Yamini pull over Teddy at nap time?
She pulled her hanky over him.
Why might Yamini have tucked Teddy beside Vaibhav?
She seemed to want to comfort her poorly brother, using the same caring she had practised on Teddy.
How could a parent join Yamini's teddy game?
A parent could ask whether Teddy is full or sleepy and play along, since the game lets her practise caring.
How might Vaibhav feel when Yamini brings Teddy and pats them both?
He would probably feel cheered and a little amused to be cared for by his little sister.

messages.content: I can't decide between two songs for my school singing contest.
What kinds of songs are they?
One is slow and emotional, the other is fast and happy.
Think about which one suits your voice and which you can sing without worrying. Try both in front of a friend and see which one they enjoy more.
I think the slow one fits my voice better.
Then go with the one you can sing with confidence. A well-sung slow song can touch the audience more than a rushed fast one.
What if I feel the audience wants something lively?
Contests are judged on how you perform, not just on how lively the song is. Sing what you do best, and smile as you sing.

Class teacher's note, Wednesday
I've noticed Lalit hunches, pulls up his hood and covers his face with his hands every time a particular senior from the school bus walks past. He doesn't do this with anyone else.
Today I asked him to stay after class. I told him I'd noticed he seemed uneasy around that student, and asked if something was going on.
At first he just shrugged. Then he said the senior takes his lunch money and threatens him on the bus.
I told him it wasn't his fault and thanked him for telling me. This afternoon I informed the school's safeguarding lead and called his parents. Lalit will sit near the bus monitor from tomorrow.
- Ms Sarita

Where does Lalit sit from tomorrow?
Near the bus monitor.
What was Lalit feeling when he hunched and covered his face?
Lalit felt afraid and uneasy, trying to avoid notice by the senior who threatened him.
What did Ms Sarita do that protected Lalit?
She noticed the pattern, asked gently, told him it wasn't his fault, informed the safeguarding lead and his parents that afternoon, and moved his seat.
How might Lalit's parents feel when Ms Sarita called?
They would likely feel worried but grateful the teacher noticed and acted quickly.

"Have you seen this?" Simran held out her phone. It was a video of Siddharth from Class 8, pretending to be a teacher with a fake accent.
Siddharth went pale. "Where did that come from? I deleted it."
"Someone saved it. It's going round the Class 11 group."
"But that was three years ago. I was stupid."
"People don't know that. They just see it now."
Siddharth put his head in his hands. "The teacher I was copying is still here."
Simran sat down. "Then maybe say sorry to her first, before she sees it from someone else."
Siddharth was silent for a long time. Then he stood up. "Okay. Come with me?"
"I'll wait outside the staff room."

How long ago did Siddharth make the video?
Three years ago.
What was Siddharth feeling when he put his head in his hands?
Siddharth felt ashamed and worried about how the teacher would see it.
What did Simran suggest, and why is it wise?
She suggested apologising to the teacher before she saw it from others, which shows responsibility and respect.
How might the teacher feel if Siddharth apologises before she sees the video?
The teacher might still be hurt, but she'd likely respect him for coming to her first.

Usha, you're saying you feel like a fraud at your new college. Let me, your Yogesh Mama, tell you about my first year at the engineering institute in Kharagpur.
I was from a small town. Everyone around me seemed to have gone to fancy coaching, spoke smooth English, knew things I'd never heard of. I was sure the admission people had made a clerical error.
When I got good marks, I said it was an easy paper. When someone else did well, I thought they were a genius. I was waiting for the day they'd call me in and say, “Sorry, there's been a mistake.”
In third year, a professor asked me to help tutor juniors. I asked why me. He said, “Because you explain things better than anyone in your batch.”
I didn't believe him for weeks. That call never came, beta. I stayed. You'll stay too.

Where did Yogesh go to the engineering institute?
He went to the institute in Kharagpur.
Why did young Yogesh think his good marks came from easy papers?
He felt insecure and out of place, like a fraud, so he discounted his own success while seeing others' as genius.
At what point in the story did something start to challenge Yogesh's belief?
When a professor asked him to tutor juniors because he explained things better than anyone in his batch.
How might the professor have seen young Yogesh?
The professor saw a capable student who explained things very well, not a fraud.

Friday, after close
Month three of my prediction diary. Tonight's check. On Monday I wrote: "Mango kulfi sells out by 8 p.m., 85% sure." It sold out at 7:40. Tick. "Hrithik manages the tandoor alone on Wednesday, 90%." He burnt two trays and called for help. Cross. "New dal recipe gets at least one complaint, 50%." Zero complaints, and three people asked for more. Cross, a happy one.
Adding it up: my food guesses are good. My guesses about people coping under pressure are far too sure. Every time I write 90% about a person, I'm wrong half the time.
So from next week, I'll ask Hrithik and the others how ready they feel before I decide for them.
Pallavi

When did the mango kulfi sell out?
What does Pallavi feel on adding up the month?
Pallavi feels humbled about being too sure of people under pressure, yet confident that the food guesses are reliable.
What change does Pallavi plan, and why does it fit the diary's lesson?
Asking Hrithik and the others how ready they feel before deciding for them, because guesses about people had been far too sure.
What was Wednesday like for Hrithik?
Hrithik was probably stressed and overwhelmed alone at the tandoor, burning two trays before calling for help.

I share a hostel room with Zeenat, so I saw how bad it got. In September she was checking Rehan's posts before breakfast, at lunch, under the desk in class. Her notebook had his name in the margins instead of formulas. She failed a Biology test she would normally have topped. One night I heard her talking quietly with Simran, her closest friend, on the corridor bench. I didn't hear all of it, but I heard, "I don't like how much space this takes in my head." The next day her phone went into the warden's box during study hours, and she had deleted the photo app. She signed up for the science exhibition and spent evenings building a water filter model with Simran. I can't say what she felt, but by October the margins of her notebook had equations in them again.

What did Zeenat build for the science exhibition?
A water filter model, with Simran.
What does Zeenat's line about space in her head suggest?
It suggests she felt uneasy and worried about how much the crush was taking over her thoughts.
Why did telling Simran help Zeenat?
Saying it aloud to a trusted friend made the problem real and brought support, and they worked on the project together.
How did the narrator see Zeenat's change by October?
The narrator noticed equations filling the notebook margins again, while not being sure exactly what Zeenat felt inside.

Dear Tushar,
You're the only person I can tell this to, because you're my cousin and you're three cities away.
There's a boy in my tuition class. I've never had a proper conversation with him. But I've memorised his timetable, the colour of his cycle, and the song he hums before tests. I think about him while brushing my teeth. I write things in my diary that I'd die if anyone read.
Yesterday he held the door for me, and I replayed it about fifty times.
Part of me knows I've made him into a movie character. Part of me doesn't care, it feels so good.
Is this normal? Please don't laugh. Actually, you can laugh a little.
Kavitha

What does Kavitha say she has memorised about the boy?
His timetable, the colour of his cycle, and the song he hums before tests.
How does Kavitha feel about this crush?
Kavitha feels giddy and a bit embarrassed, knowing she has idealised him but enjoying the feeling anyway.
What would you advise Kavitha if Tushar wrote back asking?
Enjoy the feeling but keep her own routines, and get to know the boy as a person before deciding who he is.
How might Tushar feel reading this letter?
Tushar may feel trusted and amused, and a little protective of a cousin who is swept up.

Coach's note, beginners' group, week eight
Neelam comes to every lesson and kicks hard, but she has not let go of her float once in eight weeks. When I suggest it, even in the shallow end where she can stand, she says, "Not today." This week the group swam their first full width without floats. Neelam watched from the side, holding hers, and her eyes filled up. She is not lazy; she is afraid, and the float has become a wall. Next week I will stand beside her in waist-deep water and ask her to let go for a count of three while holding my arm. I have also asked Tejas, her swim buddy, to practise the count with her.
- Coach

On the local bus from Nashik Road to their kasba, Wasim was loud as usual. "That new singer from the TV contest, the one with the long braid? Total fake. Can't sing, just cries on stage. Everyone knows that."
Devika, squeezed next to the window, turned sharply. "I voted for her. Twice."
"Come on. Seriously?"
"My whole family watches for her. She sings old Marathi songs properly."
Suresh, from the seat behind, added, "My mother likes her too."
Wasim felt his neck go warm. "Why is everyone jumping on me? I'm just saying what's true."
"You're saying what you think," Devika said. "That's different."
He stared out at the sugarcane fields for the rest of the ride, not sure whether he was angry or embarrassed.

How many times did Devika vote for the singer?
Twice.
Why does Wasim feel everyone is jumping on him?
Wasim feels defensive because he believed his opinion was simply the truth everyone shared, so hearing others disagree felt like an attack rather than a normal difference.
What could Wasim do next time he wants to share a strong opinion?
Say it as his own view, like "I don't enjoy her singing", and ask what others think before calling it a fact.
How might Devika have felt hearing her favourite singer called a fake?
She might feel stung, since the singer means something to her whole family, so she pushed back.

I'm Lalit, from the flat next door. I've watched Pooja look after her father for a year now.
From my balcony I often hear him ask, "Is it Monday?" Pooja answers, "It's Thursday, Papa." Then again. And again. Some evenings her voice is soft all the way through. Other evenings I hear it get sharper, and once I heard her say, "Papa, please!" very loudly.
That time, she came out onto the balcony and stood there with her eyes shut for a few minutes. I don't know what she was thinking. She might have been counting, or praying, or just breathing.
Then she went back in, and I heard her say, "Come, Papa, let's have tea," gently. Later, her brother started coming on Sundays, and I see Pooja going for evening walks.

What question does Pooja's father often ask?
He often asks, "Is it Monday?"
What might Pooja have been feeling when she stood on the balcony with her eyes shut?
She may have been frustrated and worn thin, trying to calm herself, though Lalit can't be sure what she was thinking.
What helped Pooja keep her kindness going?
Stepping away briefly, redirecting her father to tea, and getting regular breaks when her brother started coming on Sundays.
How might Pooja's father experience her sharp voice?
He may feel upset or confused, not understanding why she is cross about a simple question.

I'm Hemant, and something funny happened with my science quiz. When Vasudha ma'am gave the papers back, I saw a big red "minus 2" at the top. My stomach went heavy. I folded the paper small so nobody could see.
At lunch my friend Pooja grabbed it and opened it. "Eight out of ten! Same as me!" She broke her laddoo and gave me half. Suddenly I felt light and happy, like I had won something.
Walking home I kept thinking. Minus two and eight out of ten are the same marks. But one made me want to hide, and the other made me want to jump.
At home Amma read it and said, "Good boy, eight right and two to fix."
Now I say both to myself when I get a paper back.

A big red "minus 2" at the top.
How can you tell Hemant felt bad when he first saw the red mark?
His stomach went heavy and he folded the paper small so nobody could see, which shows he felt ashamed of it.

He now says both numbers to himself when he gets a paper back, the ones he got right and the ones to fix, so one version does not take over his mood.

Pooja may have seen her friend go from hiding the paper to smiling, and since she had the same marks, she probably felt they were in it together.
Peter is eating chips. Each chip is 10 calories. A bag has 24 chips and costs $2. If he wants to eat 480 calories, how much does he have to spend on chips?

Each bag has 240 calories because 24 x 10 = 240
He needs two bags because 480 / 240 = 2
It will cost $4 because 2 x 2 = 4
The answer is 4.
Now you try: centre and radius of x^2 + y^2 + 8x - 2y + 8 = 0.
The answer is (-4, 1), 3.

The audit team was due at nine the next morning, and at 10 p.m. Leela, twenty-five and the NGO's programme officer, found the problem.
The beneficiary lists for two villages had the same hundred and twelve names, copied under both. The report signed by the director, Imran, claimed twice as many families helped as had been.
Her phone showed three missed calls from her mother. The office was empty, the fan ticking.
She could leave it. The audit might not catch it. Imran had hired her and had been kind.
Leela made copies of both lists, wrote a factual summary in five lines, and emailed it to the board chair, Mrs Seth, marked urgent.
Mrs Seth called back in twenty minutes. “I'll be there at eight. We'll tell the auditors ourselves.” The next morning she sat beside Leela and did exactly that.

How many names were copied under both villages?
The same hundred and twelve names were copied under both.
Why was reporting the lists hard for Leela?
She felt torn and uneasy because Imran had hired her and been kind, and she feared the cost of speaking up.
What made Leela's report effective under time pressure?
She kept copies of both lists, wrote a short factual summary and sent it straight to the board chair, marked urgent.
How does Mrs Seth respond to Leela's email?
She acts quickly and openly, coming in at eight and telling the auditors herself, with Leela beside her.

Around four, a small boy was crying by the ring-toss stall, clearly lost. Dolma, from Class 10, was at the next stall with Rafiq and three others. She told me later she saw him for several minutes.
“I wanted to go to him,” she said. “But what if his mum was just behind the stall? Everyone would think I was making a drama. Rafiq would tease me all week.”
Eventually the ring-toss uncle brought him to the help desk, where we found his mother within ten minutes.

Where was the small boy crying?
He was crying by the ring-toss stall.

She felt guilty and upset, looking close to tears, because fear of being teased stopped her from helping.

The teacher said asking "Are you lost?" is never foolish, which makes a small, low-risk step feel easy next time.
How might the lost boy have felt during those minutes?
He was probably scared and confused, crying while older children nearby didn't come over.

Friday night

Mahima's story got into the magazine. The real one, the one we both sent to last year. She called me first, screaming, and I screamed too. Then I put the phone down and felt sick. I've been writing longer. I was the one who told her about the magazine. For an hour I lay on the bed thinking small, ugly things: it's because of her cousin's contacts, her story isn't even that original. Then I made myself write it down properly: I am envious of Mahima. Just that. Seeing it on paper made it smaller. So I texted her: 'I'm so proud of you. Also a little jealous, honestly! Drinks on me Saturday.' She sent back ten hearts. And now I'm thinking about what it tells me: I want this too, badly. So Sunday I'm finishing the story I abandoned in March.

Jasleen

What did Jasleen plan to do on Sunday?
Finish the story abandoned in March.
What was Jasleen feeling after putting the phone down?
Jasleen felt sick with envy, thinking small, ugly thoughts about why Mahima succeeded.
What did Jasleen do that helped, and why did it work?
Writing 'I am envious of Mahima' on paper made the feeling smaller, so Jasleen could congratulate her honestly and use the envy as a sign of what Jasleen wants.

Mahima would likely feel loved and relieved, since her friend's honest pride and small admission of jealousy feel warm, not threatening.

Tuesday, 11:50 pm

Drafted the resignation again at lunch. Didn't send it. Again.

Tonight the plan was clear as glass: quit Friday, give up the flat, take the train to Goa, figure it out there. Chandrika would understand. Or she wouldn't, and maybe that's also an answer? Six years together and I can't tell if I'm bored with her or bored with everything.

I scared myself writing that.

What is it I actually want? Not Goa exactly. I think I want to feel like my days belong to me. Every day at the agency is someone else's slide deck. Every weekend is errands. I haven't played the guitar since March.

Chandrika asked at dinner why I was so quiet. I said work. Half true.

Tomorrow I'll go to work. I'll send nothing. But I need to find out what's missing before I blow up everything to get it.

Vikas

What time was the diary entry written?
It was written at 11:50 pm on Tuesday.
What was Vikas feeling after writing about Chandrika?
Vikas felt scared and unsettled, realising the restlessness might spill onto the relationship without being sure where it really came from.
What small step could Vikas take instead of quitting on Friday?
Vikas could try something small that meets the need for time of one's own, like playing the guitar again or taking one free weekend, and talk honestly with Chandrika.
How might Chandrika be experiencing Vikas's quietness?
Chandrika probably senses something is off and may feel shut out or worried, since the answer at dinner was only 'work'.
Jim collects model cars, and he has 301 models total.  Jim has 4 times as many Buicks as Fords, and 3 more than twice the number of Fords than Chevys.  How many Buicks does Jim have?

Let x represent the number of Chevys
Fords:3+2x
Buicks:4(3+2x)=12+8x
Total:x+3+2x+12+8x=301
11x+15=301
11x=286
x=26
Buicks:12+8(26)=220
The answer is 220.

At the Ranchi school ground, the football trials were on Saturday. Darshan sir, the sports teacher, noticed Jatin wearing a red thread on his wrist and the same frayed jersey he wore to last year's trials. That was fine. Half the team had a lucky something. What bothered Darshan sir was that Jatin had skipped three of the last four practices. On Thursday he called Jatin over. "Nice thread." Jatin grinned. "It's lucky, sir. I got picked last year wearing it." "You also came to every practice last year." Jatin's grin faded. Darshan sir kept his voice easy. "Keep the thread. Wear the jersey. Marcy can make 3 spears out of a sapling and 9 spears out of a log. How many spears can she make out of 6 saplings and a log?

Then add the number she makes from the log: 18 spears + 9 spears = 27 spears

Deepika said it again today at lunch: "I'll start the lab report tomorrow, pakka." I, Lakshmi, have heard "pakka" from her four times now.

messages.content: Juan needs 10 half-gallons of milk to bake 40 cookies with. How many half-gallons of milk does Juan need to bake 200 dozen cookies?

If one half-gallon of milk bakes 4 cookies. to bake 200 cookies, you'll need 200/4 = 50 half-gallons of milk

Age nine: Simran lost the chess final at school by one move and cried into her mother's shoulder in the car. Keerthana did not hurry her. 'That hurt, didn't it?' she said. When the sobs eased, Simran asked, 'Can we set up the board when we get home?' She played three games before dinner.

Age twenty: Simran opened her results and saw a fail in economics. She sat on the hostel steps for a while, stomach heavy. 'I'm gutted,' she told her friend Jomon. 'And honestly, I only started revising the week before.' The next morning she wrote down what she would change: a start date a month earlier, past papers on Sundays, one question for the tutor each week.

Age twenty-five: The company closed its office, and Simran's job ended with it. She felt dizzy for a day. Then she made a list: update the CV, call two former colleagues, sort out her documents, and book an hour for job sites. She crossed off the CV before lunch, and the pile looked less like a wall.

What did Simran ask for once her sobs eased?
To set up the board when they got home.
How did Simran deal with disappointment at nine, twenty and twenty-five?

At nine Simran cried into her mother's shoulder and then asked to set up the board. At twenty she sat on the hostel steps, said she was gutted and wrote what she would change, and at twenty-five she made a list and crossed off the first item, so a huge problem became steps.
What was Simran feeling on the hostel steps?
Gutted and heavy with disappointment, mixed with an honest sense that she had started revising too late.
What could Jomon say to support Simran when she shares her result?
Listen to the disappointment first, then ask what she would like to try differently, without brushing the feeling aside.

How many books has Divyansh read in six weeks?
He has read twenty-two books in six weeks.
Why does Divyansh now choose the thin picture books?
He has become eager for stars and the prize, so the thick books he used to love feel like a waste of time, and his interest in what's inside has faded.
What change does the librarian plan, and why?
Ending the star chart and starting a 'tell me one thing you found' corner, to bring the focus back to the joy of reading rather than counting.
What might Afreen feel noticing he only asks about stars?

Gracie was 7 inches shorter than Grayson. Grayson was 2 inches taller than Griffin. Griffin is 61 inches tall. How many inches tall is Gracie?

Gracie is 56 inches tall.

Lists and statistics. Predict the output. marks = [56, 72, 38, 91, 64, 72, 80] print(len(marks), sum(marks), max(marks), min(marks)) mean = sum(marks) / len(marks) print("mean", round(mean, 2)) print("range", max(marks) - min(marks)) s = sorted(marks) print(s) print("median", s[len(s) // 2]) marks.append(100) print(marks[0], marks[-1], len(marks))

Answer: n = 7, total 473, mean 67.57, range 53, median 72. Output: 7 473 91 38 mean 67.57 range 53 [38, 56, 64, 72, 72, 80, 91] median 72 56 100 8

A LIST keeps many values in order. Positions start at 0, so marks[0] is the first item and marks[-1] the last. sorted(marks) returns a new sorted list: 38, 56, 64, 72, 72, 80, 91. For 7 values the median is the 4th, at position 7 // 2 = 3 (counting from 0). (For an even number of values we would average the two middle ones.) round(mean, 2) rounds 473 / 7 = 67.5714... to 67.57. append adds an item at the end, so the list now has 8 items. This is the same statistics as topics 7.37 and 7.38, done by computer: for large data sets that is how it is done in practice. Common mistake: marks[7] for the 7th item (it is marks[6]; marks[7] gives IndexError).

Zanele had moved to Lagos for a marketing job at a lending company. Nkechi, her manager, handed her a new campaign: bright ads for quick loans, aimed at market traders, with the interest rate in tiny grey text at the bottom.
"Make the fees invisible," Nkechi said. "That's what sells."
Zanele needed this job; she was sending money home to her grandmother in Soweto. But she pictured the traders she passed every morning.
She stayed late and made two versions. One with the fees hidden. One with the full cost in clear, large text and an example of total repayment. The next day she said, "I'm not comfortable running the hidden one. I think the clear one protects us too if regulators or customers complain."
Nkechi frowned for a long time. Then she said she'd take both to the director. Zanele went home shaky, not sure she'd done the safe thing. She was sure she'd done the right one.

Who were the ads aimed at?
Market traders.
What was Zanele feeling as she went home?
Zanele felt shaky and unsure about her job, but certain she'd done the right thing.
Why was making two versions a smart way to push back?
It showed Zanele wasn't refusing work, offered an honest option with a business reason, and let the decision go up the chain.
How might the market traders be affected by the clear version of the ad?
The traders could see the true cost before borrowing and avoid a loan that might trap them.
Compared to the amount of water she drank, Carla drank three times as much soda minus 6 ounces. If she drank 54 ounces of liquid total, how much water did she drink?

Let s be the amount of soda Carla drank and w be the amount of water she drank. We know that s + w = 54 and s = 3w - 6. Substituting the second equation into the first, we get 3w - 6 + w = 54.
Combining like terms, we get 4w - 6 = 54
Adding 6 to both sides, we get 4w = 60
Dividing both sides by 4, we get w = 15
The answer is 15.

Or, if one and the same person, freed from desire and aversion, practises (one after another) all these four modes of life according to the ordinances that have been laid down, he is certainly fitted (by such conduct) to understand Brahma. The four modes of life constitute a ladder or flight of steps. That flight is attached to Brahma. By ascending that flight one succeeds in reaching the region of Brahma. For the fourth part of his life, the Brahmacharin, conversant with the distinctions of duty and freed from malice, should live with his preceptor or his preceptor's son. While residing in the preceptor's house, he should go to bed after the preceptor has gone to his, and rise therefrom before the preceptor rises from his. How do you construct an angle of 30 degrees?

Answer: Construct 60 degrees and then bisect it: 60 degrees / 2 = 30 degrees.

Step 1: construct 60 degrees at O as in D3 (arc cuts the arm at P, the same width from P gives Q). Step 2: bisect angle POQ: from P and from Q draw arcs of the same width inside the angle, crossing at R. Step 3: join OR. Angle POR = 30 degrees. The points P and Q from the 60 degrees step can be used again, so there is no new arc from O. Check with the protractor: 30 degrees. Bisecting once more gives 15 degrees, and once more 7.5 degrees. Common mistake: bisecting the wrong angle (the 120 degrees on the other side), which gives 60 degrees, not 30 degrees.

On the verandah in the afternoon light, Swati sat with her baby Yogesh in her lap, wiping his face after his rice. He looked up at her and his mouth opened into a huge, gummy smile, arms waving. What was Swati doing when Yogesh smiled at her?
She was wiping his face after his rice while he sat in her lap on the verandah.

The whole family was in Hyderabad for her cousin's wedding week, and on the third evening Afreen's parents told her the Siddiqui family would visit tomorrow, with their son. Afreen, twenty-five, had met him once. He had joked about women drivers the whole time. She did not want this match.
That night, with the house full and noisy, she asked her parents to come up to the terrace. Her brother Zubin came too. She spoke slowly. "Ammi, Abbu, I respect that you chose carefully. But I don't want to marry him. He mocked working women twice, and I want to keep working." Abbu started to argue. She didn't raise her voice. "Please give me till after the wedding to think. And I'd like to finish my MSc before meeting anyone new." Ammi looked at Zubin. Zubin said quietly, "She's being fair." Abbu sighed and phoned the Siddiquis to postpone.

What did the man joke about when Afreen met him?
He joked about women drivers the whole time.
How did Afreen feel as she spoke to her parents on the terrace?
She felt calm but firm, steady enough not to raise her voice even when Abbu argued.
What made Afreen's refusal strong?
She gave clear reasons, asked for time, offered an alternative of finishing her MSc first, and stayed calm instead of starting a fight.
How might Abbu have felt after Zubin spoke?
Abbu was probably disappointed but persuaded by his children's calm fairness, which is why he phoned to postpone.

His mother raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Mohit liked believing that; it meant his own cycle, always locked, was safe. On Saturday Kamal's father showed everyone the cut chain. The lock had been fine; a thief with a cutter had taken three cycles from that road the same evening. Mohit stared at the chain. "But Kamal is always careful," he said slowly. "Then why did it happen to him?" "Sometimes bad things just happen," his mother said. "The question is what we do for Kamal now." Mohit thought for a moment, then went to ask Kamal if he wanted to share his cycle for the tuition ride.

What did Kamal's father show everyone?
The cut chain.

It made Mohit feel safe, because if only careless people lose things, his own locked cycle was protected.
What did Mohit's mother suggest focusing on?
What they could do for Kamal now, instead of deciding whether he deserved it.
How might Kamal have felt hearing he must have been careless?

Show that the system x + y <= 3, 2x + 3y >= 12, x >= 0, y >= 0 has no solution. For which values of k does x + y <= k, 2x + 3y >= 12, x >= 0, y >= 0 have a solution?

Answer: The region is empty; solutions exist exactly when k >= 4.

With x, y >= 0 and x + y <= 3 we get 2x + 3y <= 3x + 3y = 3(x + y) <= 9, which is less than 12. So no point satisfies all four: the feasible region is EMPTY (the triangle under x + y = 3 lies completely on the origin side of 2x + 3y = 12). In general 2x + 3y <= 3(x + y) <= 3k, with equality at (0, k). So a solution exists if and only if 3k >= 12, i.e. k >= 4. At k = 4 the only solution is the single point (0, 4): the region has shrunk to a point. Check: 0 + 4 <= 4 and 0 + 12 >= 12. Common mistake: thinking every system has some region; always test whether the pieces overlap.

Mary's sheep can run 12 feet per second, and her sheepdog can run 20 feet per second. A sheep standing 160 feet away from the sheep dog bolts, and the dog runs after it. How many seconds does it take the dog to catch the sheep?

First find how much faster the dog is than the sheep: 20 feet/second - 12 feet/second = 8 feet/second
Then divide the distance the dog needs to run by the speed difference: 160 feet / 8 feet/second = 20 seconds
The answer is 20.

I'm Sahil, and I sat in on the safety meeting at the textile unit in Tiruppur where Harish, our young operations planner, had to decide where the year's safety money went.
Most of the managers wanted to replace every old light fitting, because one had sparked last year. "Then that risk is zero," someone said, and everyone nodded.
Harish didn't nod. He put up a simple chart of what had actually hurt people in five years. Forklift near-misses in the loading bay: many. Hand cuts at the cutting tables: many. Electrical sparks: one.
"Replacing the lights makes one small risk zero," he said. "Painting lanes and fitting mirrors in the loading bay, and buying cut-proof gloves, cuts our biggest risks by a lot. Not to zero. But far more people go home safe."
I don't know what he was feeling, standing there against the whole room, but his voice was steady. The money went to the loading bay and the gloves.

There had been one electrical spark.

Why was Harish's plan the better use of the money?
It cut the biggest real risks, forklift near-misses and hand cuts, by a lot, instead of making one rare risk zero.
How did the managers see replacing the lights at first?
They liked it because it made one risk zero, which felt complete and comforting.

"Enough guessing, Imran. You rested, you drank. It's not working. We're going to the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow. I'll come on the bus with you." An investment bank gives 10 percent interest at the end of every month. How much money in total will you have, including interest, at the end of 2 months if you invest $300?

After the first month you get 10/100 * $300 = $30 interest.
After the first month you will have $300 + $30 = $330 in total.
After the second month you get = 10/100 * $330 = $33 interest.
After the second month you will have $330 + $33 = $363 in total.
The answer is 363.

Amma has 12 laddoos. She shares them equally among 3 children. How many does each child get?

Answer: 4 laddoos each. 12 / 3 = 4.

This is SHARING: we know how many children (3) and we want to know how many EACH gets. Put 3 plates on the table. Deal the laddoos one at a time: one for you, one for you, one for you, round and round, until none are left. Count one plate: 4. Check: 3 plates of 4 is 3 x 4 = 12. Now you share 15 laddoos among 3 plates.
Jenna catches an eel that's 1/3 as long as Bill's. If the combined length of their eels is 64 inches, how long is Jenna's eel?

Let j be the length of Jenna's eel and b be the length of Bill's eel. We know that b = 3j and b + j = 64.
Substituting the first equation into the second equation, we get 3j + j = 64
Combining like terms, we get 4j = 64
Dividing both sides by 4, we get j = 16
The answer is 16.

Vandana heard her friend Madhav say, "They don't even speak Malayalam."
One Sunday, Vandana went with her mother to the kiln to give old clothes. A girl her age, Pinky, was teaching her little brother the alphabet on a slate.
They talked in broken Hindi and hand signs. Pinky's father had left their village after the floods destroyed their field.
On the way home, Vandana said to Madhav, "They didn't come to take anything. Their farm drowned."
Madhav was quiet. "I didn't know that."
The next week, they both went to help at the kiln school.

Why had Pinky's father left their village?
The floods destroyed their field.
What was Madhav feeling when he said "I didn't know that"?
Madhav felt surprised and a little ashamed of his earlier comment.
What did Vandana do that others in the village could learn from?
She met the migrant family, listened to their story, and shared it, replacing rumours with understanding.
How might Pinky see Vandana's visits?
Pinky probably feels welcomed and less like an outsider.

In the supermarket in Kraków, Marek, five, stopped in the toy aisle and hugged a baby doll in a blue blanket.
"Can I have her? She needs a papa."
A man nearby chuckled. "Dolls are for girls, little man."
Marek's grip loosened. Esther, his mother, noticed his cheeks going pink. She crouched beside him.
"What will you call her?"
"Zosia."
"Then Zosia can come home. You'll need to feed her."
Marek held the doll tighter and marched to the checkout.

What did Marek want to call the doll?
Marek wanted to call the doll Zosia.
What might Esther have been thinking when she crouched beside Marek?
Esther probably felt protective and calm, wanting Marek not to feel ashamed after the man's chuckle made his cheeks go pink.
What went well in how Esther reacted?
She ignored the joke, asked Marek a simple question about the doll, and let him bring it home, so his interest stayed safe.
How might Marek have felt if Esther had laughed too?
Marek might have felt embarrassed and put the doll back, learning early that caring for a doll is shameful for a boy.
Our swimming class starts at 6 am. It's too early. I'm Aisha.
Early classes are hard at first. A fixed bedtime helps a lot. What time do you go to sleep now?
About ten thirty.
Try sleeping by nine thirty, so you get enough rest. Lay out your swim bag the night before, so the morning is quicker. A light snack like a banana will give you energy.
I'll try. Is it okay to eat before swimming?
Yes, a small snack like that banana is fine, Aisha. Eat it soon after you wake up, so it settles before the 6 am class. Avoid a heavy meal just before swimming, and drink some water too.

Hemant's hostel room had no wall space, only a cupboard door covered in old stickers. The college gym opened at six and closed at eight, and his practical exams started in two weeks. He had failed to keep a routine twice.
This time he stuck a printed month on the cupboard door. After each session, even the short ones squeezed in before labs, he drew a tick. Tuesdays and Fridays had a pre-printed "R" for rest.
His roommate Vaibhav noticed the ticks growing. "Nineteen days," he said one night.
During exam week the gym closed early for maintenance, and Hemant felt his chest tighten looking at the empty square. He almost ran laps in the corridor at midnight just to earn a tick. Then he looked at the "R" squares and drew one more by hand, in pencil. "Planned rest," he muttered.
The next morning he was back at six.

How many days of ticks did Vaibhav count?
Vaibhav counted nineteen days.
How did Hemant feel when he looked at the empty square during exam week?
He felt anxious, his chest tightening, and was tempted to run laps at midnight just to earn a tick.
What else could Hemant do to keep the streak helpful rather than stressful?
He could plan in advance for exam weeks and closures, marking them as rest or short home sessions, so a gap doesn't cause panic.
How might Vaibhav see Hemant's calendar?
Vaibhav notices the ticks growing and seems impressed, and might feel encouraged to try something similar.

Daniel had spent eight months on the grant application for his community-garden project in Porto. On Friday he clicked submit at 4:58 pm, two minutes before the deadline. The decision would take six weeks. That weekend he refreshed his email forty times. On Sunday, Beatriz found him rereading the budget table. "Did you do everything you could?" she asked. He thought. "I checked every number. I asked three people to review it. I got the letters of support." "Then what's left?" "Waiting." "And is waiting yours to do anything about?" He laughed, a bit tired. "No." Beatriz tossed him his swimming bag. "Then let's go to the sea." At the beach he still thought about the grant, but he didn't refresh anything. For six weeks he worked on the garden with the kids, grant or no grant.

How long would the grant decision take?
Six weeks.
How did Daniel feel during the weekend after submitting?
He was anxious and restless, refreshing his email forty times and rereading the budget table.
What small step did Beatriz suggest, and why did it help?
She asked what was still his to do, then took him to the sea, helping him release the waiting he couldn't control.
How might the kids at the garden benefit from Daniel letting go?
They got his full attention on the garden for six weeks, instead of a distracted Daniel checking email.

Last term I almost handed in an essay I didn't write. I'm Parveen. The topic was on the causes of the First World War, and I had three other tests that week. My classmate Nikita showed me how an AI tool could produce a full essay in a minute. It looked perfect. I pasted mine in, read it, and felt nothing. It didn't sound like me at all. It had words I'd never use. Then I thought about Ma'am's comment on my last essay: "I like how you argue." This one didn't argue anything. So I closed it and wrote my own at 1 am. It was messier. Ma'am gave it a B and wrote, "Your voice is back." Nikita got caught. I felt sorry for her, honestly.

What grade did Parveen's essay get?
It got a B.
Why did Parveen feel nothing reading the AI-written essay?
It didn't sound like her or carry her own arguments, so it felt empty and not really hers.
What helped Parveen resist the shortcut?
Remembering her teacher's praise for how she argues reminded her that her own voice was worth more than a perfect-looking copy.
How might Nikita feel after getting caught?
She is probably embarrassed and worried, and may wish she had written her own even if it was messier.

Sunday, 11 p.m.
Day six of not emailing Mrs D'Souza. It's a two-line email. "Dear Ma'am, I won't be renewing my contract at the school after June. Thank you for everything." That's IT. I've written it, deleted it, rewritten it. Every time the cursor goes near Send, my chest squeezes and I suddenly need to clean the fridge. 😰
She hired me when nobody else would. I keep picturing her face going cold.
Afreen called tonight: "Is the email out?" Me: "Tomorrow." Afreen: "You said that on Tuesday." She's right.
The fridge is spotless. The email is still in drafts. Somehow two lines weigh more than the whole fridge.
Plan: send it at 8 a.m., before tea, before thinking.
- Zubin

How many days has Zubin gone without emailing Mrs D'Souza?
It is day six of not emailing Mrs D'Souza.
What is Zubin afraid of when the cursor goes near Send?
Zubin keeps picturing Mrs D'Souza's face going cold and feeling ungrateful to someone who took a chance, so the fear of that reaction makes two lines feel enormous.
What plan does Zubin make, and why might it work?
Sending it at 8 a.m., before tea and before thinking; a fixed, early moment gives the dread less time to build up.
What might Afreen be feeling during the call?
Afreen seems to have noticed the pattern and cares enough to point it out gently, perhaps worried that each delay is making Zubin more anxious, not less.

Monday. Kavitha's cat, Pepper, had been missing for four days. Every night Kavitha lit a lamp in the puja room and prayed with her whole heart: please bring Pepper home.
Friday. The neighbour found Pepper's collar near the main road, but not Pepper. Kavitha stopped lighting the lamp. At night she lay awake with a strange, hollow question: is anyone even listening? It felt wicked to think it. She didn't tell anyone.
Sunday. Manoj Mama came to visit and found her sitting alone on the steps. When she finally whispered her question, he didn't look shocked. 'I've asked that too,' he said. 'Many good people have. Asking isn't wicked. Let's talk about it whenever you want.' Kavitha leaned against his arm and cried for Pepper properly.

What did the neighbour find near the main road?
Pepper's collar.
What was Kavitha feeling as she lay awake on Friday night?
Hollow and confused, wondering if anyone was listening, and ashamed, as if the question were wicked.
What helped Kavitha with her doubt?
Telling Manoj Mama, who said asking isn't wicked and offered to talk whenever she wanted.
How did Manoj Mama respond to Kavitha's question?
Calmly and honestly; he admitted he had asked it too.

Rita has 4/5 of a metre of lace. She uses 2/3 of a metre. How much is left?

Now you try: 3/4 - 2/3.
The answer is 9/12 - 8/12 = 1/12.

On the fifth night of Navratri, the building compound in Ahmedabad was lit with lamps. Lavanya, who was not yet talking, sat on her mother's lap in her tiny chaniya choli.

"Lavanya, give this flower to Paati," Vidya said, pointing at the old woman beside them.

Lavanya looked at the marigold, looked at Paati, then wriggled down and pushed the flower into Paati's hand.

Paati kissed her fingers.

What did Lavanya give to Paati?
She gave Paati a marigold.
How might Paati have felt when Lavanya handed her the flower?
Paati was likely touched and happy, which is why she kissed Lavanya's fingers.
How can Vidya keep supporting Lavanya's understanding of words?
Keep giving short, clear instructions with names and objects Lavanya knows, and praise her when she follows them.
How might Vidya feel watching Lavanya follow her words?
Vidya would likely feel proud and happy that Lavanya understood even before speaking.
Jason has three times as many toys as John. If John has 6 more toys than Rachel and Rachel has 1 toy, how many toys does Jason have?

John has 6 more toys than Rachel + 1 Rachel toy = 7 toys
Jason has 3 * 7 John toys = 21 toys
The answer is 21.
James made $4000 in January.  The next month he made twice as much.  In March, however, James made $2000 less than in February.  How much has James made so far this year?

In February James made 4000 * 2 = 8000.
In March James made 8000-2000 = 6000.
In total for the year James has made 4000 + 8000 + 6000 = $18000.
The answer is 18000.

Okay, here goes.
The temperature was 36 degrees and fell by 6 degrees. What is it now? Then, What does the word "remember" mean?

1. The answer is 30. Because 36 - 6 = 30.
2. To remember is to keep something in your mind and be able to think of it later.

Zainab: ask what exactly
Seema: if he wants to come to the science fair on saturday. a few of us are going

Seema: practised in the mirror twice. I just want to be calm whatever he says
Zainab: you will be. either answer is fine

Where would the group meet if Veer says yes?
At the gate at 10.
Why did Seema practise both endings?
She wanted to feel calm rather than nervous, ready to reply kindly whether Veer says yes or no.
What makes Seema's invitation respectful?
It's a group outing with an easy way to decline, "no worries if not", so Veer doesn't feel pressured.

Veer is likely to feel comfortable and free to say yes or no without any awkwardness.

First Sunday of the summer holidays: Eshaan counted the mangoes in the basket, "One, two, five, three!" and pointed at the same mango twice. Ritu laughed.
Wednesday: Nani lined the mangoes up in a row. Eshaan touched each one as he counted. "Seven!"
The next Sunday: Nani gave Eshaan three mangoes and Ritu five. Eshaan looked at both piles and frowned. "Ritu has more. Not fair." Nani moved one across. "Now?" He counted again. "Four and four. Same!"

How many mangoes did Nani first give Eshaan on the last Sunday?
She gave Eshaan three mangoes.
How did Eshaan feel when he saw Ritu's bigger pile?
He felt it was unfair and was a little annoyed, because he could now tell that Ritu had more.
What helped Eshaan count correctly by Wednesday?
Lining the mangoes up in a row let him touch each one once, so he didn't count any twice.
What is it like for Ritu when Eshaan miscounts at first?
Ritu finds it funny, perhaps feeling grown-up because counting is already easy for Ritu.

Ulla's grandmother died in March, and by June Ulla still hadn't cried at the right times. At the Swedish summer camp, she sat on the jetty every evening, feet in the cold lake, asking herself where people go.
Tuan, the quiet boy from her cabin, sat down one night with a torch. "My family lights incense for our ancestors. My mum says they're still with us."
"Do you believe that?"
"Some days. Other days I think they're just in how we do things. My grandfather folded his shirts a weird way. I do too."
Ulla thought about her grandmother humming while she baked.
"Maybe she's in the humming," Ulla said.
They sat there until the midges came out. It wasn't an answer. It felt like the start of one.

Where did Ulla sit every evening?
On the jetty, with her feet in the cold lake.
How was Ulla feeling at the camp?
She felt lost and quietly grieving, unsure where people go after they die.
How did Tuan help Ulla think about meaning?
He shared his family's belief and his own doubts without pushing, giving Ulla room to find her own idea.
What might Tuan be feeling when he talks about his grandfather's shirts?
Tuan may feel a warm, slightly shy connection to his grandfather, sharing something private.

Dear Ojas,

I know this week has been awful, with the job news and everything. I wanted to say something properly, so here's a letter.
At the café on Tuesday, when you looked so low, I asked, "Can I give you a hug?" and you said, "I'd rather not, sorry." I want you to know I wasn't offended at all. You once told me your family isn't huggy, and that's completely fine. Everyone's comfortable with different things.
So instead, I'm leaving a box of your favourite samosas at your door with this. And I'll keep Sunday free for a walk by the lake, if you'd like company.
I'm in your corner, hug or no hug.

Alka

What is Alka leaving at Ojas's door?
Alka is leaving a box of Ojas's favourite samosas with the letter.
How did Alka feel when Ojas said no to the hug?
Alka wasn't offended at all and understood, because different people are comfortable with different things.
What did Alka handle wisely?
Alka asked before hugging, accepted the no without offence and found other ways to show warmth, like samosas and a walk.
How might Ojas feel reading the letter?
Ojas would likely feel relieved and cared for, knowing the no was respected and that Alka is still in Ojas's corner.

If 1 ounce of Dawn liquid soap can make 200,000 bubbles, and Dr. Bronner's liquid soap can make twice as many bubbles per ounce as Dawn liquid soap, then how many bubbles can be made from one half ounce of an equal mixture of Dawn and Dr. Bronner's liquid soaps?

One half of a 1/2-ounce liquid is (1/2)*(1/2)=1/4 ounces.
1/4 ounce of Dawn liquid soap can make (1/4)*200,000=50,000 bubbles.
1/4 ounce of Dr. Bronner's liquid soap can make 2*(1/4)*200,000=100,000 bubbles.
Therefore, a half ounce of an equal mixture of Dawn and Dr. Bronner's liquid soaps can make 50,000+100,000=150,000 bubbles.
The answer is 150,000.
What number comes just before 1? Is there a counting number before 0?

Answer: 0 comes just before 1. There is no counting number before 0.

On our number line, 0 is the start. When we count back to 0, nothing is left. (Older children will learn about numbers below zero, like very cold temperatures, but not now.)

1 September. Baljeet has a plan for the month: football on Mondays, keyboard lessons on Wednesdays, a coding club on Fridays. Ojas, his best friend, says it sounds like a lot. Baljeet says it sounds like everything.
15 September. He forgot his keyboard exercise because of football. At coding club he spends the whole hour catching up on last week's task. He plays the same two lines on the keyboard over and over and can't get the third.
30 September. At the end-of-month football match Baljeet sits on the bench. His keyboard teacher writes "Practise more" in his book. His code still won't draw a square. He tells Ojas, "I'm bad at everything," and kicks a pebble all the way home.

Which day was the coding club?
The coding club was on Fridays.
What was Baljeet feeling when he told Ojas he was bad at everything?
He felt discouraged and frustrated, because after a month of three hobbies he had little to show in any of them.
What could Baljeet try in October instead?
Choose one of the three and give it the extra evenings, so he has enough time to practise between lessons and see real progress.
How might Ojas see Baljeet's month?
Ojas doubted the plan from the start, so he may feel sorry for Baljeet rather than surprised, and want to cheer him up.

messages.content: My mother's birthday is on Sunday and I'd like to make her breakfast in bed.
A sweet gesture. What can you make comfortably?
Toast with jam and tea, maybe some cut fruit.
That will do nicely. Cut the fruit into small pieces, make the tea gently and put everything on a tray with a flower or a card.
Should I make it a surprise?
If she's a person who loves surprises, yes. You could ask someone else at home to help you keep the secret, and wake her up with a gentle knock.
I'm afraid I'll spill the tea.
Fill the cup only two-thirds, walk slowly and set the tray down before you open the door. A saucer under the cup catches small spills.
I'll practise with water first. Thank you!
Excellent plan. A water rehearsal costs nothing and saves a lot of worry.

On the slow afternoon bus through Nairobi, little Yara sat on her mother Wanjiru's lap by the window.
They didn't talk. Yara watched a boy selling mangoes, a man on a bicycle stacked with crates, a dog asleep in the shade.
Now and then she tipped her head back to check Wanjiru's face. Wanjiru smiled. Yara turned back to the window.
Her small hand rested on her mother's arm the whole way home.

What was the man on the bicycle carrying?
The bicycle was stacked with crates.
Why did Yara tip her head back to check Wanjiru's face?
Yara was checking that her mother was still there, and Wanjiru's smile let her feel safe and content to keep watching.
What makes this quiet ride good for Yara?
Wanjiru's calm presence and smile let Yara explore the world by watching, knowing she is safe without needing talk.
What is the ride like for Wanjiru?
Wanjiru likely feels calm and fond, sharing the view with Yara without needing words.

Zubin, you're fifteen now, so listen to something from your Manjula aunty's school days.
The new maths teacher, Mr D'Souza, was very shy. My whole gang decided to hide the duster and chalk before his class. Leela said, “Everybody's doing it, Manju. If you back out, you're not one of us.”
I felt sick all morning. Not about the chalk, you know, but about being alone at lunch.
When the bell went, I stood at the door and couldn't make myself go in first. Then I watched him search the table, go pink, and apologise to us, of all things. That's when I went to the cupboard and handed him the chalk. Leela didn't speak to me for a week. Mr D'Souza thanked me every day for a month.

What did the gang decide to hide before class?
They decided to hide the duster and chalk.
What was young Manjula most afraid of that morning?
She was afraid of being alone at lunch; she felt sick about losing her gang, not about the prank itself.
What turning point in the story changed Manjula's choice?
Watching Mr D'Souza go pink and apologise made her see the real cost, so she handed him the chalk despite Leela's threat.
How might Mr D'Souza have experienced that class?
He was likely embarrassed and flustered, then grateful, which is why he thanked Manjula every day for a month.
Can a gleeful laugh be a bad thing?

Usually it is happy, but it can also be unkind if someone enjoys another person's trouble. Gleeful means full of joy and excitement. It is an adjective.
Example: The children let out a gleeful shout when the rain stopped play.
Bryan's score on a math exam is 20. Jen scored 10 more than Bryan while Sammy scored 2 fewer than Jen. If the math exam has 35 points in all, how many mistakes did Sammy make?

Jen scored 20 + 10 = 30 on the exam.
Sammy scored two less, so his score was30 - 2 = 28.
Thus, Sammy made 35 - 28 = 7 mistakes.
The answer is 7.

Beatriz had moved to Cape Town from São Paulo two years ago, and Lindiwe had been the first person to sit with her at lunch. They'd been together since March. By September, Beatriz knew her feelings had changed.
She didn't want to do it by text. On Sunday evening she called.
"Lindi, I have to say something, and I'm going to say it straight because you deserve that," she said, sitting on her bedroom floor. "I care about you a lot. But I don't feel the way I did, and I won't keep you hoping for something I can't give."
There was a long silence. Then Lindiwe's voice, small: "Was it something I did?"
"No. Honestly, no. You've been nothing but good to me."
"Okay." A shaky breath. "I'm glad you called instead of just going quiet."
After they hung up, Beatriz cried for a while. It still felt like the right kind of hard.

When did Beatriz call Lindiwe?
Beatriz called on Sunday evening.
Why did Beatriz cry after the call even though it felt right?
Beatriz still cared about Lindiwe, so ending it was sad, even though she knew being clear was the kind thing.
What choices made Beatriz's ending clear and kind?
Beatriz called instead of texting, spoke briefly and honestly, avoided blame and didn't leave false hope.
What did Lindiwe value about how the ending happened?
Lindiwe was hurt but glad Beatriz called rather than going quiet, because clarity showed respect.

I'm Pallavi, and my little brother Chinmay used to dump his shoes and bag wherever he stood. Amma nagged, and it never worked. Then one day I saw him standing in the hallway, talking to himself. "When I come in and change my clothes, that's the moment. Shoes on the rack, bag on the hook. Same time, same place. Then I won't need to remember." He did it the next day, and the next. Now, when he comes in and pulls off his school shirt, I see him walk straight to the rack. Amma has stopped nagging, and honestly, I have too.

Where does Chinmay put his bag?
Chinmay puts his bag on the hook.
How does Chinmay feel about tying the job to changing his clothes?
Chinmay feels confident it will work, because changing clothes happens anyway, so he says he won't need to remember the shoes and bag separately.
What alternative approach could Chinmay try, and why?
Chinmay could put a picture note above the rack or ask a parent to remind him at first. Either could help until the habit is strong.
How does Pallavi see the change in Chinmay?
Pallavi watches the routine take hold and notes that Amma has stopped nagging, and admits to stopping too, so Pallavi seems relieved and a little impressed.

In the colony sandpit, Sachin and two other boys were building a road for their trucks. Jyoti stood at the edge with her red bucket, watching. She took one step closer. Then another. Sachin looked up. Jyoti held out the bucket. "You can use this for a tunnel." Sachin looked at the bucket. "Okay." Jyoti knelt down. "Can I make the bridge?" "Yes, but not on the truck." By the time her grandmother called her home, the road had a bridge, a tunnel and a red-bucket lake.

What did Jyoti offer Sachin?
She offered her red bucket, for a tunnel.
What does Jyoti's standing at the edge and stepping closer suggest?
She felt shy and a bit unsure, but wanted to join in.
Why did offering the bucket work better than just grabbing a truck?
It brought something useful to the game, so the boys could say yes easily 🙂
How might Sachin have felt when Jyoti held out the bucket?
He was probably pleased and curious, since a tunnel made their road more exciting.

Hostel sports coach's note, second week of January.
On 1 January, Yogesh came to me with a printed plan: a 5 a.m. run every day, weights every evening, no sugar, and cold showers. He was glowing. I suggested starting with three days a week. He said, "No half measures this year."
He kept it for eight days. I saw him on the track each morning, grimly pushing.
On the ninth day it rained heavily and he stayed in bed. When I saw him that afternoon, he said, "It's ruined now. I broke the streak." He looked embarrassed and angry at himself.
He has not come to the track since. When I asked, he said, "Maybe I'm just not a fitness person."
I will sit with him this week and suggest a smaller plan: three short runs, and a rule that a missed day is just a missed day, not the end of the plan.
— Vandana, sports coach

How many days did Yogesh keep the plan?
He kept it for eight days.
How did Yogesh feel after the rainy morning?
Yogesh felt embarrassed and angry at himself, believing one missed day had ruined everything.
What small change is the coach planning, and why might it help?
Three short runs a week and a rule that a missed day is not the end, so one lapse doesn't turn into quitting.
How might Vandana have felt when Yogesh said "No half measures"?
Vandana was probably doubtful and a bit worried, having seen big plans collapse before.
