In the small school in Sangli, Kalyani saw Anjali hand her green crayon to the new girl. The new girl smiled and let Anjali use her paints. Kalyani watched. Later, she passed her own blue crayon to Anjali. "Here." Anjali smiled and pushed the paint box toward her. Kalyani dipped a brush, grinning.

What colour was Kalyani's crayon?
Blue.
What was Kalyani feeling when she dipped the brush?
She was happy and pleased that copying Anjali worked.
What else could Kalyani do to keep sharing?
She could offer crayons first to others too, since giving tends to bring giving back.
How might Anjali feel when Kalyani gives her the crayon?
Anjali probably feels friendly and glad to share her paints in return.

Nostrils are the two openings at the bottom of the nose through which you breathe and smell. It is a noun, the plural of nostril.
Example: The horse's nostrils widened as it ran across the field.

There are 15 tables in the school's cafeteria. Each table can seat 10 people. Usually, only 1/10 of the seats are left unseated. How many seats are usually taken?

The cafeteria can seat 15 x 10 = 150 people.
Usually, 150 x 1/10 = 15 seat are unseated.
Thus, 150 - 15 = 135 seats are usually taken.
The answer is 135.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday
Avni came in during the break with a folded sheet of paper and asked if she could think out loud with me. She had seen her friend Shankar copying in the English test and did not know what to do.
She had already done most of the work. The sheet had three headings: say nothing, speak to Shankar, tell the class teacher. Under each she had written what could happen. Saying nothing: the students who worked honestly lose out in ranks, and Shankar keeps skipping the learning he will need later. Supervisor's note, community health project, 30 July.

At the June planning meeting Anand agreed to finish the village survey by the tenth of July. He said, "No problem." The tenth passed, then the twentieth. Each week his update is cheerful and vague: "Almost there." He is not lazy; his field notes are excellent.

Looking back, I think I pushed the plan through fast. Anand was the newest person in the room and the only one who knows the hill villages, where roads close in the rains. He never said so.

Today I met him alone, not to scold. I said, "I may have given you a deadline you couldn't argue with. If the plan doesn't work, I want to hear it from you, not from the calendar." He was quiet, then said, "The monsoon cuts off two villages till August." We have reset the date to the end of August.

Binita

"I never hope to see such a sight as that again, Mr. Holmes. From north, south, east, and west every man who had a shade of red in his hair had tramped into the city to answer the advertisement. Fleet Street was choked with red-headed folk, and Pope's Court looked like a coster's orange barrow. I should not have thought there were so many in the whole country as were brought together by that single advertisement. Every shade of colour they were—straw, lemon, orange, brick, Irish-setter, liver, clay; but, as Spaulding said, there were not many who had the real vivid flame-coloured tint. When I saw how many were waiting, I would have given it up in despair; but Spaulding would not hear of it. How he did it I could not imagine, but he pushed and pulled and butted until he got me through the crowd, and right up to the steps which led to the office. There was a double stream upon the stair, some going up in hope, and some coming back dejected; but we wedged in as well as we could and soon found ourselves in the office."

The speaker tells Mr. Holmes that men with red hair came from every direction to answer the advertisement, crowding Fleet Street in every shade. You know what Samir did, Rono? I told him in October that my parents are separating. Nobody else knew. Two weeks later, in the canteen, Pritam says, "Sorry about your folks." Just like that, in front of everyone.
I went hot all over. I wanted to post Samir's old messages about his crush in the group, right there. I had them. My thumb was on the screenshot.
I didn't. I walked out, and that evening I waited for Samir at the tea stall near the hostel gate. I said, "I trusted you with one thing. Why?" He went red and said he thought Pritam already knew. Maybe. Maybe not.
We're still friends, sort of. I sit with him in class. But I don't tell him anything that matters anymore, and I've told him that too.
Anyway, that's me, Arnab, learning to keep my own secrets closer.

That Arnab's parents are separating.

It's been three weeks. I've missed two single days, never two together. I'm Zainab, and I'm learning that a bad week is information, not a verdict.

At the daycare gate, Tarun would not put his shoes on. He kicked one across the mat and pressed his face into his cubby. Minakshi crouched beside him. The teacher whispered that Isha's family was moving to another city, and today was her last day. Minakshi rubbed his back. "You are sad because Isha left," she said quietly. "You wanted to play with her tomorrow too." Tarun lifted his face and nodded. His lip wobbled, then stopped. He fetched the kicked shoe himself. "Mumma, can we draw her a picture?" he asked.

Jacob has been tasked with a project to write up an urban plan proposal that will be used to construct a new city. He uses Pittsburg city as a reference which has 2000 stores, 500 hospitals, 200 schools, and 20 police stations. If the new city should have half the number of stores, twice as many hospitals, 50 fewer schools, and 5 more police stations, what is the total number of buildings required for this project?

The number of stores required for the new city is 2000 / 2 = 1000 stores.
The number of hospitals required for the new city is 2* 500 = 1000 hospitals.
The number of schools required for the new city is 200 - 50 = 150 schools.
The number of police stations required for the new city is 20+5 = 25 police stations.
The total number of buildings required for this new city project 1000+1000+150+25=2175 buildings.
The answer is 2175.

Amandeep, you asked how I became a good researcher. Let your Kalyani aunty tell you. When I was twenty-five, I worked at a library in Pune helping scholars.

One day a professor asked me where a certain fact came from. I said confidently, "It's in the old census." I'd read it somewhere, I was sure. But when I looked, it wasn't in the census at all. It was in a magazine article that quoted someone quoting the census, wrongly.

I felt so foolish. After that, I kept small cards for every fact I read, with the book and page. And before I told anyone anything, I asked myself: did I see this, was I told it, or did I work it out?

Next year, I came third. Not first. But I ran past the shed where I had cried.

So, Dhruv. Cry today. Tomorrow, run.

It sends more light to our eyes. Because white paint bounces back most of the light that falls on it while black paint soaks most of it up, more light from the white wall reaches our eyes.

A school has 1,358 children. For the sports day march, they must walk in pairs. Can every child have a partner, with nobody left over?

Answer: Yes. 1,358 ends in 8, which is even, so 1,358 is divisible by 2 (1,358 / 2 = 679 pairs).

To test for 2 we only look at the LAST digit. Why? 1,358 is 1,350 and 8. Every ten can be split into 5 pairs, so 1,350 splits into pairs with none left over. Only the 8 ones are left to check, and 8 makes 4 pairs. So a number is divisible by 2 when its ones digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. These are the EVEN numbers. Common mistake: looking at the first digit (1 is odd, but that does not matter).

Classify each event as impossible, sure or neither, and give its probability. a) Getting 7 on one die b) Getting a number less than 7 on one die c) Sum of two dice is 1 d) Sum of two dice is at most 12 e) A card drawn from a pack is red or black f) A card drawn is a red spade g) Tossing a coin gives a head. Also: which of 0.7, 1.3, -0.2, 5/4, 0, 1, 35%, 3/5 could be probabilities?

Answer: a) impossible, 0 b) sure, 1 c) impossible, 0 d) sure, 1 e) sure, 1 f) impossible, 0 g) neither, 1/2. Possible probabilities: 0.7, 0, 1, 35% and 3/5 (not 1.3, -0.2, 5/4).

An IMPOSSIBLE event has no favourable outcomes: P = 0 / n = 0. A SURE event contains every outcome: P = n / n = 1. Every other event has 0 < P < 1. Since n(E) is between 0 and n(S), P(E) = n(E) / n(S) must be between 0 and 1, so 1.3, -0.2 and 5/4 = 1.25 are impossible values. Common mistake: thinking P = 1 means "very likely"; it means CERTAIN.

Day 1 of Manjula-akka's plan. One call a day, easiest first, no skipping.

I sat on the balcony afterwards feeling stupid for being scared of that for three months. Also, sort of proud? Wrote a big tick on the calendar.

Tomorrow: hospital records. That one's harder. But today proved the dread was louder than the actual call.

messages.content: Noah is a painter. He paints pictures and sells them at the park. He charges $60 for a large painting and $30 for a small painting. Last month he sold eight large paintings and four small paintings. If he sold twice as much this month, how much is his sales for this month?

Noah earned $60/large painting x 8 large paintings = $480 for the large paintings.
He also earned $30/small painting x 4 small paintings = $120 for the small paintings.
His total sales last month were $480 + $120 = $600.
So, his sales this month are $600 x 2 = $1200.
The answer is 1200.

(1) What does "wear out" mean?
(2) Is there a mistake here? The girl which sits near me is kind.
(3) why do elephants spray dust or mud on their backs

It costs $.10 to print one page. Jenny wants to print 7 copies of her 25-page essay. She also wants to buy 7 pens that each cost $1.50. If she pays the store with 2 twenty dollar bills, how much money should she get in change?

Jenny needs to print 7*25= 175 pages.
This will cost 175*$.10 =$17.5.
The pens will cost 7*$1.50=$10.50.
In total, she will spend $17.5+$10.5=$28.
Since she pays with 2 twenty dollar bills she pays with 2*20=40 dollars.
Thus, she will get $40-$28=$12 in change.
The answer is 12.

The 8:10 local stopped dead between Dadar and Matunga, and Kamal's big meeting with Rukmini, the head of procurement, was at nine. His chest tightened. His palms were damp on the folder. The thought arrived fully formed: this is going to go terribly. He noticed it the way you notice a cough. Okay. I feel anxious. That's a feeling about the meeting, not the meeting. He messaged Rukmini: 'Train stuck, may be ten minutes late. Can start by phone if easier.' Then he opened his notes and went over his three points, one for each station he couldn't see. Messaging Rukmini early with an offer to start by phone, and going over the three points, kept him moving forward while the anxious feeling stayed.

Dear Karthik,
Remember Nikhil from my stats class? He asked me out for coffee on Friday. Actually asked, in words, after class. And I said no. I told him I had a project deadline, which is half true.
Here's the real reason. I know exactly how it would go. I'd get there early and sit with my hands in my lap. He'd talk about cricket; I'd have nothing to say. Write back and tell me I did the sensible thing. Or don't.
Bhavna

Nikhil asked Bhavna out for coffee on Friday.

messages.content: Jim and his Cousin are out at a restaurant. They each order a cheeseburger and milkshake. They also split an order to cheese fries. A cheeseburger is $3. A milkshake is $5. Cheese fries are $8. They spend 80% of their combined money. If Jim brought $20 how much did his cousin bring?

They spent $8 each on cheeseburgers and milkshakes because 3 + 5 = 8
They spent $16 on these items in total because 2 x 8 = 16
They spent $24 on their meal because 16 + 8 = 24
They had $30 to start because 24 / .8 = 30
His cousin had $10 because 30 - 20 = 10
The answer is 10.

In the small courtyard in Hoshangabad, the men sat on white sheets and the women had gathered inside. Vaibhav, who taught maths in the classroom next to Yamini's at the government school, sat a little apart, staring at the neem tree. His father had died on Tuesday. Yamini had brought a steel tiffin of khichdi from the staff. She wanted to do more than hand it over; his face looked so empty. But a hug wasn't done here between colleagues, and she wasn't sure even a hand would be welcome. She crouched beside him, set the tiffin down and said quietly, "Vaibhav-ji, can I put a hand on your shoulder? Only if you want." He swallowed and nodded once. She rested her palm lightly on his shoulder. His breath shuddered out, and he bent his head. After a minute she took her hand back and sat with him in silence.

Yamini felt concerned and hesitant, since a hug wasn't done between colleagues there and even a hand might not be welcome to someone grieving.

She crouched beside him, asked quietly whether she could put a hand on his shoulder, waited for his nod, and kept the touch light and brief.
What might Vaibhav have felt when her hand rested on his shoulder?
Vaibhav may have felt his grief loosen a little, his breath shuddering out, comforted that someone noticed him sitting apart.

Guest note, hill homestay near Madikeri. Yamini Poovaiah, owner.
Vaibhav, 25, checked in on Monday. Within ten minutes he had asked me where the cottage's second exit was and whether there was a torch by the bed. I noticed a small pouch clipped to his daypack: torch, whistle, water, copies of his ID.
On Wednesday afternoon the district issued a landslide advisory for our road and asked visitors to move to town. Most guests stayed on the veranda with their coffee; the rain didn't look like much. Vaibhav packed within twenty minutes. He said, "I'll feel silly if nothing happens, but that's better than being stuck." The others teased him a little.
Nothing happened on our road. On Friday he messaged to thank us and said he'd come back in the dry season.
Since then, I have pinned the district helpline numbers and exit map by every door.

A torch, a whistle, water and copies of his ID.

He expected possible embarrassment but judged it a small price compared with being stuck, so he acted on the advisory without waiting for proof.
How did Vaibhav's habits make leaving early easy, and what did Yamini do next?
Knowing the exits and keeping a small kit let him pack in twenty minutes; Yamini then pinned helpline numbers and exit maps by every door.
How might the guests who teased Vaibhav think about it later?
They might feel he overreacted since nothing happened, or quietly wonder what they would have done if the road had gone.

"Madhav, we need to talk about the baby."

"That's the problem. We did this for them. Your mother asked every week. Hrithik joked at every function. We gave in."

Yusuf and Yamini had been together for two years, and in the spring they decided to marry. Yusuf's parents in Lucknow had always assumed they would choose his bride.

At the bank branch in Thane, Sarika had enrolled in an evening accountancy course that started at 6:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The branch usually kept juniors till seven. For two weeks she slipped out at 6:05, feeling guilty, pretending to take a call. Then Akash, the branch manager, noticed and frowned. That evening she knocked on his cabin door. "Sir, I need to leave at six on Tuesdays and Thursdays for my course, until March. I'd like to ask properly instead of sneaking out. I can come in at nine instead of 9:30 on those days, and I'll finish my cash reconciliation before leaving." Akash leaned back. "You could have asked in the first week." "I know. I was nervous." He thought for a moment. "Nine o'clock start, reconciliation done, and you're out at six. Put it in an email so the roster shows it." She sent the email before she left, at 5:58.

At 6:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Why does tea cool faster in a wide saucer than in a cup?
More of the tea touches the air. Because a wide, shallow layer has more surface open to the air, more heat escapes and more water dries off.

"I was half-dragged up to the altar, and before I knew where I was I found myself mumbling responses which were whispered in my ear, and vouching for things of which I knew nothing, and generally assisting in the secure tying up of Irene Adler, spinster, to Godfrey Norton, bachelor. It was all done in an instant, and there was the gentleman thanking me on the one side and the lady on the other, while the clergyman beamed on me in front. It was the most preposterous position in which I ever found myself in my life, and it was the thought of it that started me laughing just now. It seems that there had been some informality about their license, that the clergyman absolutely refused to marry them without a witness of some sort, and that my lucky appearance saved the bridegroom from having to sally out into the streets in search of a best man. The bride gave me a sovereign, and I mean to wear it on my watch chain in memory of the occasion."

How would you sum up this excerpt in three sentences?

The speaker was pulled to the altar and, without understanding, mumbled responses and acted as witness as Irene Adler married Godfrey Norton. The clergyman refused to marry them without a witness because of a problem with their license, so the speaker's appearance saved the day. The bride gave the speaker a sovereign to wear on a watch chain, a memory of a thoroughly absurd moment.

Okay, you asked what helped Pema. I'm Suraj, her best friend since Class 3, so here's what I did.
Last term, before every test, Pema's hands shook and she'd say, "What if I blank out?" First I said, "Just relax." Big mistake. She went quiet and wouldn't talk to me for a day.
So I changed. I started just listening. I'd say, "That sounds scary. What's one thing you can do right now?" Sometimes it was just opening the textbook to one page.
We started walking round the school ground every evening. She said it helped her sleep.
But when she stopped coming to school on test days, I got worried. I asked if she'd tell her mum, and I went with her to the school counsellor. She's seeing someone properly now. I'm still her walking partner, though.

"Just relax."

If you were Pema, what might you want from a friend like Suraj?
To be heard without being told to calm down, and to have someone steady beside you while you get proper help.

21=3x

Dilnaz had worked a night shift at her part-time job.
What was Dilnaz feeling by Wednesday?
Dilnaz felt a little annoyed, not about the plan but about being told what she felt.
Which choice on Friday worked, and why?
Dilnaz calmly explained she was exhausted, not angry, and that being misread stung, so Karthik could apologise and learn to ask.
Why might Karthik have assumed Dilnaz hated the plan?
Karthik saw her quiet, chin on hand, and guessed anger without checking.

The school cookery club met on Saturday mornings in the home-science lab, and this week Damini and Shreya were making chicken fried rice. Damini washed her hands with soap before touching anything, then took the red chopping board for the raw chicken and the green one for the vegetables. "Why two boards?" Shreya asked. "Raw chicken juice on the cucumber is how people end up sick," Damini said, and washed the red board and knife in hot soapy water as soon as she was done. She patted the vegetables dry before they went into the oil so it wouldn't spit, and turned the wok handle inwards. When Shreya called from the next counter, "Come look, my rice is stuck!", Damini switched off the gas first, then went. Ms Kapoor, walking past, nodded and moved on to the next table without a word.

Which chopping board did Damini use for the raw chicken?
The red chopping board.
How does Damini seem to feel while she cooks?
Damini seems calm and confident, moving through each safe habit without fuss or worry.
Which of Damini's habits prevents a burn or fire, and why?
Switching off the gas before leaving the stove, drying vegetables before the oil and turning the handle inwards all stop the pan from spitting, catching or being knocked.
What might Ms Kapoor's nod and silence suggest about how she sees Damini?
Ms Kapoor seems to trust Damini's habits, feeling no need to step in or remind her of anything.

Karthik: yeah, what happened
Asif: I need to tell you something and you can't laugh
Karthik: ok. not laughing
Asif: someone called and said I'd won a phone. I paid a "delivery fee" through a link
Asif: then they asked for more for "customs". I paid that too, two days ago
Asif: I told nobody. I thought you'd all say I'm stupid

Karthik: stop replying. Call the bank's helpline now and report it on the cyber crime portal. I'll sit next to you while you do it

The caller said Asif had won a phone.
Why did Asif wait two days before telling anyone?
Asif feared people would say Asif was stupid, and the messages show that waiting only made each day feel worse.
What would you advise Asif to do right now?
Stop replying to the scammers, call the bank's helpline, and report it on the cyber crime portal, ideally with Karthik sitting next to Asif. 🤍
How does Karthik see what happened to Asif?
Karthik sees it as something that happens to hundreds of people, not proof of stupidity, and offers to sit next to Asif while the calls are made.

Last week I cried in the art room, and I still don't really know how it happened. I'm ten, and I hadn't cried at school since I was a small boy. Kashish kept laughing at my drawing of a horse. "It looks like a dog with a long neck," Kashish said, and then everybody at our table started saying it. I tried to say something clever back. But my heart was going so fast, and my face got so hot, that my brain just went blank. No words came. Tears came instead, big ones, in front of everyone. I pushed my chair back and walked out to the corridor. I didn't decide to. My legs just went. Later, Miss Rao found me by the drinking fountain and waited with me till I could breathe normally again. — Sachin

What did Kashish say Sachin's horse looked like?
Kashish said it looked like a dog with a long neck.
How did Sachin feel when he said "My legs just went"?
He felt hurt and overwhelmed, with his heart racing and his face hot, so his body walked him out before he could decide. 😔
What did Miss Rao do that helped, and what could come next?
Miss Rao stayed with Sachin until his breathing settled; next the teacher could talk calmly with both children about the teasing.
What might Kashish have thought when Sachin walked out?
Kashish may have been surprised, thinking it was only a joke, and not realised how much the laughing from the whole table hurt.

During the Diwali holidays, the school ran a study camp in the library. Urmila noticed that Vandana always came first and left last, even though the camp ended at five. "Why don't you go home to study?" Urmila asked one afternoon. Vandana shrugged. "Our house is one room. My cousins are visiting for Diwali. There's nowhere to sit." Urmila thought of her own desk, the lamp, the closed door. "Oh." A boy nearby said, "Urmila's got her own room, lucky." "It's not my fault," Urmila snapped, surprising herself. Later she felt bad about it. On the way out she asked the librarian, "Can the library stay open longer for people who need it?" The librarian said she would ask the principal.

How many rooms is Vandana's house?
One room.
Why did Urmila snap "It's not my fault"?
She felt defensive and a little guilty when the boy pointed out her own room, as if she were being blamed for her advantage.
What was helpful about Urmila's question to the librarian?
It turned her discomfort into something useful: asking for more quiet study time for students who need it.
How might Vandana see Urmila's questions?
Vandana may feel a bit exposed explaining her home, but also noticed and perhaps glad someone asked the librarian.

Advisor’s note, student council meeting, Tuesday. Farida proposed a quiet study room. Most members wanted a games room. She did not argue with them. She simply asked, “What if we ask everyone?” She brought a short survey the next week and again the week after, and always started by saying what she liked about the games room idea.
Noor, who first opposed the study room, said at the third meeting, “I’ll count the survey results myself.” The results were closer than expected, and Noor asked to run a trial of both.
I intend to tell Farida that patience and courtesy did the work here.
— Faculty advisor

What did Farida ask when the majority preferred the games room?
Farida asked, “What if we ask everyone?”
What might Noor have been feeling when offering to count the survey results?
Noor was probably curious and a little doubtful, unwilling to accept the result without checking. Offering to count suggests Noor was starting to take the idea seriously.
What did Farida do that made the majority reconsider?
Farida stayed calm, returned each week with a survey and began by naming what she liked about the games room. That showed respect rather than a fight.
How might other council members have felt seeing Farida return each week?
Some may have been mildly annoyed at first, then more curious as her tone stayed friendly. The passage shows only that Noor changed and asked for a trial.

Mumma gave me an apple for my tiffin. I wanted the packaged mango juice like my cousin Ujjwal has.
Ujjwal told me his coach said those juices have lots of added sugar and don't fill you up. I didn't believe him.
So today I tried an experiment. Monday: juice at break. I was hungry again by eleven. Today: the apple and some peanuts. I wasn't hungry till lunch.
Ujjwal said, “See?” I said, “Okay, okay.”
I'll still have juice sometimes. But not every day. — Dhruv

What did Mumma give Dhruv for the tiffin?
An apple.
How did Dhruv feel about Ujjwal's advice at first, and then?
Dhruv felt doubtful at first, then convinced after the experiment.
What did Dhruv's experiment show?
The apple and peanuts kept Dhruv full longer than the juice.
How might Ujjwal feel after Dhruv's experiment?
Ujjwal probably feels pleased, and a bit smug, to be proved right.

On a grey Saturday in Lisbon, Chidi found a toy whistle in the bottom of his coat pocket and blew a small, wobbly tweet. Beatriz, buckled in her stroller, lifted both eyebrows. Her eyes went round, and she froze with a crust of bread halfway to her mouth.
Chidi blew again. Eyebrows up again. This time she dropped the bread and reached for the whistle with both hands, making an urgent "eh, eh".

What was Beatriz holding when she heard the whistle?
A crust of bread, halfway to her mouth.
How can you tell Beatriz was interested and not upset?
After lifting her eyebrows in surprise, she dropped the bread and reached for the whistle with an urgent "eh, eh", which shows curiosity and eagerness rather than fear.
What could Chidi do next?
He could let her hold and try the whistle while he watches, turning her surprise into play.
What would change if the whistle had been very loud?
Beatriz's raised brows might have turned into a startle or cry instead of reaching out.

When I was nine, my mother let me carry a steel plate of Diwali laddoos to the neighbours. My favourite door was Seema Aunty's. She always said, "Wait, wait, don't go," and came back with a small bowl of something. That evening it was kheer. In the summer she had sent sewaiyan to us for Eid, and I had carried back a bowl of our sweet rice. I remember walking home slowly with the warm bowl, thinking that food goes both ways on our floor. That night I could smell sugar and cardamom from three different kitchens. It felt as if the whole building was having one big party. Jagdish

What did Seema Aunty give Jagdish that evening?
Seema Aunty gave Jagdish a small bowl of kheer.
How did Jagdish feel walking home with the warm bowl?
Jagdish felt happy and connected, as if the whole building was having one big party. 😊
Which small gesture made the festival feel bigger than one home?
Carrying sweets to the neighbours and getting bowls back, so that food went both ways on their floor.
How might Seema Aunty have felt when Jagdish arrived with laddoos?
Glad and warm. She said "Wait, wait, don't go" and came back with a bowl to share, which shows she enjoyed the exchange.

At Warsaw airport, Olga, sixteen, waited for Fatima, her pen-pal from Morocco, whom she'd written to for two years but never met. Her stomach was churning so hard she thought she might be ill. What if Fatima didn't like her? What if this was a terrible idea? She almost texted her mother to take her home. Then she made herself stop by the window and check. Heart fast. Cheeks warm. A silly smile each time the arrival board changed. And she'd had nothing but a coffee since morning. This wasn't dread. It was excitement, and hunger, all mixed up. She bought a pastry and ate it slowly. When Fatima came through the gate, waving wildly, Olga's stomach flipped again, and this time she knew exactly what it meant. She ran to hug her.

How long had Olga written to Fatima?
For two years.
What did Olga first feel while waiting at the airport?
She felt anxious and churned up, afraid Fatima might not like her.
How did Olga figure out what her body was saying?
She stopped to notice her fast heart, warm cheeks, silly smile and empty stomach, and recognised excitement and hunger.
How might Fatima have felt coming through the gate?
Fatima was probably excited and a little nervous too, waving wildly.

"Aditi, it's time to switch off the cartoon."
"NO! NO! I'm watching!"
"Mama is here."
"Go away! I hate you!"
Pema sat on the floor near the door, not too close. She waited.
"I HATE bath!"
Aditi kicked the cushion and screamed into it. Pema stayed quiet.
After a while, Aditi's screams became sniffles.
"Can I come close?"
A tiny nod.
Pema held her. "You were very angry that the cartoon ended."
"Very very angry."
"I know. It's hard to stop fun things."
"Can I bring my duck in the bath?"
"Yes, the duck can come."

What did Aditi kick?
Aditi kicked the cushion.
Why did Aditi scream "I hate you"?
Aditi was furious and overwhelmed that her cartoon was ending, and the angry words poured out.
What did Pema do well?
She stayed calm and nearby without arguing, asked before coming close, and named Aditi's anger once the storm passed.
What might Pema have been feeling during the screaming?
Pema may have felt hurt or tired hearing "I hate you", but she stayed calm and patient.

During submission week the computer lab on the second floor of the engineering block stayed open till 6 am, and at 1:40 am Nikita was one of eleven people still there. The data structures assignment had been set a month ago. She had started it at 8 pm.
Now, with hours left, fear finally pushed her fingers faster than they had moved all semester. Tanuja, two seats down, had finished days ago and stayed only to keep her company. "You okay?"
"Never better," Nikita said, eyes red, debugging line 214.
At 5:58 she uploaded it. Two test cases failed; the rest passed. She got 17 out of 20.
On the walk back to the hostel she felt almost triumphant. "Honestly, if I'd started early I'd have overthought it."
Tanuja said nothing about the dosa Nikita had skipped, the 9 am lab she was about to sleep through, or her shaking hands.

What score did Nikita get on the assignment?
She got 17 out of 20.
Why did Nikita feel almost triumphant on the walk back?
The overnight sprint worked well enough that she took it as proof that starting early would only have made her overthink.
What went wrong beneath the good score, and what could fix it next time?
Two test cases failed, she skipped food, her hands shook and she was about to miss a 9 am lab; starting a small piece in the first week could spare those costs.
What might Tanuja be thinking as they walk back?
Tanuja, who stayed only for company, may notice the skipped meal and shaking hands and feel worried, but chooses silence over a lecture at dawn.
Look at page 16 of your story book. Read the page number. Now find pages 19, 10 and 12.

Answer: Sixteen. Pages 19, 10 and 12 are found by turning forwards or backwards and reading the numerals at the bottom.

Page numbers are numerals in order. Let the child turn one page at a time and read each number aloud: 16, 17, 18, 19. Going back: 16, 15 ... 12, 11, 10.

On Mother's Day in Melbourne, Tuan gave his mum, Rania, a folded card. Inside was a big red heart, two stick people holding hands, and a line of wiggly marks. “What does it say?” Rania asked. Tuan pointed along the squiggles. “It says, ‘Mummy, you are the best and I love you and you make good noodles.’” Rania didn't mention that none of the marks were letters. She hugged him. “That's the best card I've ever had.” She stood it on the kitchen shelf.

Where did Rania stand the card?
On the kitchen shelf.
What was Tuan feeling as he pointed along the squiggles?
He felt proud and loving, sure his marks carried his message to his mum.
Why was Rania's response wise?
She responded to his meaning and love instead of correcting the spelling, which encourages him to keep sharing feelings in writing.
What would change if Rania had said the squiggles weren't real words?
Tuan might feel his message didn't count and be less eager to write or draw for people again.

messages.content: The total cost of staying at High Services Hotel is $40 per night per person. Jenny and two of her friends went to the hotel and stayed for three nights. What's the total amount of money they all paid together?

If each of them stayed 3 nights, the total cost per person is $40/night * 3 nights = $120
Since they were three, the combined cost is $120 + $120 + $120 = $360
The answer is 360.
Ray has 95 cents in nickels. If Ray gives 25 cents to Peter, and twice as many cents to Randi as he gave to Peter, how many nickels does Ray have left?

Ray gave 25*2 = 50 cents to Randi.
Ray has 95-25-50 = 20 cents in nickels left.
Ray has 20/5 = 4 nickels.
The answer is 4.

What was Kavitha thinking about signing before Ayesha explained?
Kavitha was ready to sign whatever Ayesha said because Kavitha could not follow the clauses alone, which shows dependence.

Before the colony Holi, Swati heard that the new boy in C-block, Pranav, didn't like being touched. On the morning itself she saw him at the edge of the park in big headphones, watching the dhol from far away. Her friends were already running at him with fistfuls of pink. "Wait," Swati said, stepping between them. She stopped an arm's length off and didn't try to catch his eye. "Happy Holi. Colour, or no colour?" He said nothing. She waited, counting drumbeats. Finally he held out his phone. He had typed: No colour. Gujiya yes. "Gujiya coming," she said, and went to fetch a plate. When she came back, he had moved one step closer to the party. He typed again: You can text me. It's easier.

What did Pranav type the first time?
No colour. Gujiya yes.
What does Pranav moving one step closer suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt safer and more welcome once Swati respected his space and his answer.
What was the key choice Swati made when her friends ran at Pranav?
She stepped between them, stood back, asked instead of assuming, and waited for his answer.
If you were Pranav, what would you want from the other children at Holi?
I would want them to ask first, not throw colour or grab me, and to let me answer by text if that is easier.
Compose a haiku about summer holidays at a grandparent's house.

Mango days stretch long
Cousins laugh beneath the fan
Summer will not end
My phone's battery got finished so I could not call you. Please fix.

My phone's battery ran out, so I could not call you.
Why: word choice ("got finished" -> "ran out"); punctuation (missing comma -> comma before "so").

January: Mohit, twenty-five, scrolled through a college friend's photos from Singapore late on a Sunday night. New job, new flat, rooftop pool. He put the phone down and stared at the cracked ceiling of his rented room. His own job at the bank felt like nothing.
March: He started a small habit. Every night before sleep he wrote three things from his day that he'd choose again. The first week, it was hard to find three. By the third week, the list came easily: a joke with the guard at work, the smell of his landlady's kadhi, his cricket game on Saturday.
May: Sunday lunch at Irawati's house. Her mother served too much food. Mohit sat back, full, while Irawati argued with her brother about a film. He realised he hadn't checked his phone in two hours and didn't want to. This, he thought. This is plenty.

How many things did Mohit write every night?
He wrote three things from his day that he'd choose again.
How did Mohit feel at Irawati's Sunday lunch compared with January?
In January he felt envious and low, but at the lunch he felt full, relaxed and quietly content.
Which habit helped Mohit, and why?
Writing three things he'd choose again each night trained him to notice what he valued in his own life instead of comparing.
What would change if Mohit had kept scrolling through friends' photos every night?
He might have stayed stuck in comparison and missed noticing the small good things already in his life.

Daycare note, Tuesday. When the visiting storyteller began, Payal went still, leaned forward and hardly blinked, her mouth a little open. She was fixed on the storyteller's face. When the drums started, she turned and stared out of the window instead, very still in a different way. I moved her a little farther from the drums, and after a while she was watching again. Vinita, daycare teacher

What did Payal stare at when the drums started?
Out of the window.
What did Payal's leaning forward and later staring away suggest?
Leaning forward showed interest; staring away when the drums began suggests she felt overwhelmed.
Which choice of Vinita's helped Payal, and why?
Moving her farther from the drums helped, because it lowered the noise so she could return to watching.
How might the storyteller see Payal's attention?
The storyteller might notice her rapt face and feel encouraged.

In a school, the number of participants in the 2018 Science Quiz Bowl was 150. There were 20 more than twice the number of participants in 2019 as there were in 2018. In 2020, the number of participants was 40 less than half the number of participants in 2019. How many more participants were there in 2019 than in 2020?

Twice the number of participants in 2018 is 150 participants x 2 = 300 participants.
The number of participants in 2019 was 300 participants + 20 participants = 320 participants.
Half the number of participants in 2019 is 320 participants /2 = 160 participants.
The number of participants in 2020 was 160 participants - 40 participants = 120 participants.
There were 320 participants - 120 participants = 200 more participants in 2019 than in 2020.
The answer is 200.

messages.content: Reading in English is my new goal, but difficult words keep stopping me.
Don't stop at every word. Try to follow the story, and underline only the words that come up more than once. Those are the ones worth learning.
What kind of book should I start with?
A short story collection or a book for younger readers can be a good start. Pick something about a topic you already enjoy, so you can guess the missing words from the story.
I like animal stories.
Then you have a clear direction. Animal stories use plain language and lots of repeated words, so reading one will feel easier than you expect.
I'll ask my school librarian. Is it okay to read the same book twice?
Yes. A second reading helps you notice words you missed and lets you enjoy the story at a relaxed pace. Many readers do it on purpose.

Shreya didi,
You're lucky you're in hostel. Last night Papa and I had the biggest fight. I asked to go to the late show with my friends and he said no, and then he started shouting about my marks. Yes, I shouted back. But I was only shouting because I've had three tests this week and I'm exhausted. He shouts because he wants to control my whole life. That's just how he is.

What did Mummy tell Lokesh this morning?
That Papa's office has been cutting jobs and he's scared about it.
Why does Lokesh feel Papa's shouting is different from Lokesh's own?
Lokesh feels exhausted and sees that as the reason for shouting back, but sees Papa's shouting as a wish to control, not as fear.
What would help Lokesh and Papa understand each other?

How might Papa see the fight?

In consequence of an agreement between the sisters, Elizabeth wrote the next morning to her mother, to beg that the carriage might be sent for them in the course of the day. But Mrs. Bennet, who had calculated on her daughters remaining at Netherfield till the following Tuesday, which would exactly finish Jane's week, could not bring herself to receive them with pleasure before. Her answer, therefore, was not propitious, at least not to Elizabeth's wishes, for she was impatient to get home. Mrs. Bennet sent them word that they could not possibly have the carriage before Tuesday; and in her postscript it was added, that if Mr. Bingley and his sister pressed them to stay longer, she could spare them very well. Against staying longer, however, Elizabeth was positively resolved--nor did she much expect it would be asked; and fearful, on the contrary, of being considered as intruding themselves needlessly long, she urged Jane to borrow Mr. Bingley's carriage immediately, and at length it was settled that their original design of leaving Netherfield that morning should be mentioned, and the request made.

Please give me the main points of this section in two sentences.

Elizabeth asks her mother to send the carriage, but Mrs. Bennet says it cannot come before Tuesday, when Jane's week ends. Elizabeth, afraid of intruding, urges Jane to borrow Mr. Bingley's carriage and say they planned to leave that morning.

Olaf has an aquarium. He has fish in 3 different colors: orange, green, and blue. Blue fish make up half of all the fish in the aquarium. There are 15 fewer orange fish than blue fish. How many green fish are there when the total number of fish in the aquarium is 80?

If there are 80 fish in total, then there are 80 fish / 2 = 40 blue fish.
The orange fish count is 15 less than blue, so it's 40 fish - 15 fish = 25 fish.
Olaf has then 80 fish - 25 fish - 40 fish = 15 green fish.
The answer is 15.

Looking back, I noticed Tushar changing before anyone said anything. He used to be the one who brought samosas on Fridays and did silly voices in meetings. By July, he was snapping at the interns, forgetting deadlines, and eating at his desk, or not at all.
In one team meeting, someone joked, "Tushar's in a mood again," and everyone laughed. I didn't. I saw his face.
The next day I asked him for chai, just us. I told him I'd noticed, and that I was worried. He said he couldn't sleep and had headaches. I said, "Please see a doctor. Not just a weekend off. A doctor." He went the following week. I'm Harish, and I'm glad I didn't wait.

What did Tushar use to bring on Fridays?
Samosas.
What was Harish feeling when everyone laughed at the joke?
Harish felt uneasy and worried, seeing Tushar's face and not finding it funny.
Why was Harish's private chai better than a remark in the meeting?
It let Harish share real concern without embarrassing Tushar, and point him towards a doctor.
What might Tushar have felt when the team laughed?
Tushar probably felt hurt and embarrassed, as if his struggle had become a joke.

messages.content: Matt skips ropes 3 times per second.  If he jumped for 10 minutes how many skips hops did he get?

He was skipping rope for 10*60=600 seconds
So he got 600*3=1800 skips
The answer is 1800.

The wedding house in Madurai was loud until midnight, with music on the terrace and aunties laughing in every room. Kavitha, ten, was sure she would never sleep. But at half past eight she found her toothbrush in the suitcase, as she did every night at home. She brushed at the crowded sink, then went looking for her cousin Ayesha, who had promised to read to her. They squeezed onto a mattress in the storeroom, the only quiet corner, and Ayesha read one chapter by torchlight. Kavitha's eyes closed before the chapter ended. In the morning Ayesha said, "The music was so loud. How did you even sleep?" Kavitha shrugged. "It was bedtime."

Where did Kavitha and Ayesha find a quiet corner?
On a mattress in the storeroom.
Why was Kavitha sure she would never sleep, and what changed?
The house was loud with music and laughter, so sleep seemed impossible; but doing her usual steps made her body treat it as bedtime anyway.
What choice helped Kavitha sleep despite the noise?
Keeping her home routine, brushing at half past eight and hearing one chapter, even in a strange, crowded house.
Why might Ayesha be surprised in the morning?
Ayesha heard the music all night and expected a sleepless cousin, without realising how strongly the familiar steps carried Kavitha to sleep.
Turn Zoe's question into reported speech: Zoe asked Karim, "Did you finish the poster?"
Zoe asked Karim whether he had finished the poster.

The power cut hit the hostel just as Jasleen reached the corridor, and there on the stairs, lit by an emergency lamp, sat Rajni with her notes. Three days earlier Jasleen had told the whole floor about Rajni's failed audition, meant as a joke, and Rajni had not spoken since. Now the lift was dead and both had to climb to the fourth floor. Jasleen's chest tightened. On the second landing Jasleen said, "I'm sorry. I shouldn't have told anyone. There's no excuse." Rajni kept climbing, jaw tight. Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" and swallowed it. Instead: "I won't bring it up again. Take whatever time you need." At the fourth floor Rajni went into her room and shut the door softly, not slamming it. Jasleen stood in the dark, holding the weight of it.

Where did Jasleen say sorry to Rajni?
On the second landing of the stairs, while both climbed to the fourth floor during a power cut.
What did Jasleen want to add after apologising, and why might Jasleen have held it back?
Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" but swallowed it, probably sensing that asking for forgiveness would turn the apology into a request for Rajni to make Jasleen feel better.
What would you advise Jasleen to do over the next few weeks?
Give Rajni space, stay courteous, and not raise the subject again unless Rajni does, accepting that repair is Rajni's choice and may take time. 🤍
How might Rajni have experienced the apology on the stairs?
Rajni may have noticed that it named the wrong without excuses, yet still felt too hurt to answer. Closing the door softly instead of slamming it suggests the words were heard.

An orange scribble with two stick people.

Missing him and upset about the distance, not ending her love. Fetching the pencil for a bigger drawing suggests the love is still strong.

Accept the feeling, tell her he misses her too, and keep the calls and drawings going.

Tuesday, well past midnight
Wide awake again. At dinner I was yawning over chemistry, but the second I lay down my brain switched on like a floodlight. Alarm goes at six for the school bus. This morning I snapped at Mummy over a missing sock, sat through first period like a zombie, and at lunch let Sumit dare me into jumping off the bike-shed roof. Landed badly on my ankle. Sumit laughed; I didn't. Mummy put ice on it, and she said we'd see the doctor if it keeps hurting or worries us. Sir says it's "attitude". Honestly, I think I'm just exhausted all the time. Tomorrow I'll ask Mummy if my phone can stay in the kitchen at night, and I'll try waking at the same time on Sunday too.
Suraj

What did Sumit dare Suraj to do at lunch?
Jumping off the bike-shed roof.
How does Suraj feel about being told it is "attitude"?
Suraj feels misunderstood and frustrated, believing the real problem is being exhausted all the time.
Which of Suraj's plans could help, and why?
Keeping the phone in the kitchen at night and waking at the same time on Sunday, because steady habits can ease the tiredness behind the snapping and risky dares.
How might Mummy see the sock argument if she knew about the late nights?
She might read the snapping as tiredness rather than rudeness and feel less hurt by it.
My viva is next Tuesday and I freeze when teachers ask me questions face to face.
A viva makes many students nervous. Do you know which topics they'll ask about?
The project I submitted, mostly.
Then you already have an advantage. Read your own report twice, and for each section, say aloud what you did and why. Ask a friend to play the examiner.
What if I don't know an answer?
Say so calmly, then explain what you do know. Something like, 'I'm not sure about that detail, but here is what I found.' Examiners usually respect honesty more than guessing.
I'll practise with my roommate tonight.
Practise standing up and speaking clearly, as you will in the room. It helps your voice settle.
It's tomorrow. How do I calm down in the morning?
Eat a light breakfast, go over your key points once and then stop studying. Arrive early, take a few slow breaths outside the room and remember that examiners want to hear what you know.
May can knit 3 scarves using one yarn. She bought 2 red yarns, 6 blue yarns, and 4 yellow yarns. How many scarves will she be able to make in total?

May will be able to make 2 x 3 = 6 red scarves.
She will be able to make 3 x 6 = 18 blue scarves.
And she will be able to make 4 x 3 = 12 yellow scarves.
Therefore the total scarves she can make is 12 + 18 + 6 = 36.
The answer is 36.

Nikita flopped onto the sofa beside her older sister.
"Didi, why do you look so calm on salary day? I look at mine and panic."
"Because by the time I look, Nikita, the saving's already done," Devika said.
"Done how?"
"Standing instruction. The day after salary comes in, a fixed amount goes to my savings account and some into a SIP. Then I spend what's left."
"But what if you need it for something?"
"Then I'd have to go and take it out on purpose. That little bit of effort stops me."
"I always plan to save at month end."
"And how much is left at month end?"
"...Usually nothing. Sometimes minus."
"Exactly. Want to set it up now? Pick an amount you're comfortable with. If you want help choosing, the bank's advice desk can explain the options."
"Now? Okay. Fine. Show me where."

When does Devika's fixed amount move to savings?
The day after salary comes in.
How does Nikita feel on salary day, and why?
Nikita feels panicky, because saving is always planned for month end and by then nothing is left.
What could help Nikita decide how much to set aside?
She could start with an amount she is comfortable with and ask the bank's advice desk to explain the options, as Devika suggests.
Why might Devika feel calm while Nikita panics?
For Devika the saving has already happened before she looks, so there is no monthly decision to dread.

If Zig wrote 60 books, four times as many books as Flo, Flo wrote 60/4=15 books

A tiger, an eagle and a dolphin.
A quick vote can settle it. Each person gets one vote, and you count together. Before voting, let each supporter speak for one minute.
What if it's a tie?
Hold a second vote between just the tied choices, or let the class teacher pick one. A rule agreed before voting stops the arguing afterwards.

Good luck with the vote. Whatever wins, the mascot will be yours, so enjoy choosing together.

Okay, you asked why Pankaj didn't talk to me for a week in Class 10. I'm Arnab, and it was my fault.

Pankaj failed the maths pre-board. Before the exam, honestly, none of us knew how he'd do. He'd been studying. He'd done fine in the unit tests. I even told him, "You'll pass easily."

Then the results came out, and in the canteen I said, loud, "Come on, it was obvious. He was always on his phone." Everyone nodded. It felt true when I said it.

Pankaj heard me.

Later that night I remembered my own words, "You'll pass easily." It wasn't obvious at all. I only thought so because I knew the result.

I said sorry the next Monday. He said, "You didn't know either." That stung, because he was right.

What did Arnab tell Pankaj before the exam?
You'll pass easily.
Why did Arnab feel so sure in the canteen that Pankaj's failure was obvious?
Arnab felt smug and certain because the result was already known, so it seemed predictable, and saying it felt true in the moment.
What could Arnab do next time a friend gets a bad result?
Arnab could remember what everyone actually expected beforehand and offer support instead of explaining it as obvious.
How did Pankaj feel hearing Arnab in the canteen?
Pankaj was likely hurt and embarrassed, which is why he stopped talking to Arnab for a week.

At four.

A follow-up question like "Is that a real yes?" would have shown Chinmay hadn't really heard or agreed.

The power went out at the final dress rehearsal, twenty minutes before the college drama society's show. The hall went black, then phone torches came on. The director shouted, "Keep going! Use the torches!" Sarita, playing a mother whose son had died, stepped into the pool of light. Her voice cracked. Her hands shook as she folded the boy's shirt. Real tears ran down her face. In the front row, her friend Ayesha, who'd come to help with costumes, felt her own throat ache. After the scene, Ayesha hurried backstage. "Sarita, are you okay? Is something wrong at home?" Sarita laughed, wiping her face with a tissue. "I'm fine! I think about the timing of each breath, and I press my tongue hard to the roof of my mouth. The tears just come." Ayesha stared. "It looked so real." "That's the job," Sarita said, and went to fix her make-up.

What was Sarita's character doing when her hands shook?
Folding the boy's shirt.
What was Ayesha feeling as she watched the scene?
She was moved and worried, her throat aching, and she feared Sarita was truly upset about something at home.
What does Ayesha learn from Sarita's answer?
That visible emotion on stage can be crafted with technique, so a display is not proof of the actor's own state.
How did Sarita see her own tears?
As part of her craft, produced by timing her breath and a physical trick, not a sign that she was actually sad.

I'm Ankita, and last term my friend Keerthana changed so fast it scared me. She quit chess club, which she loved. She stopped sitting with us at lunch. In the April heat she wore a full-sleeved sweater every day. Then she handed me her whole set of sketch pens and said, "Keep them. I won't need them." Some people in our class group chat were joking that she was being dramatic. I didn't add anything. After school I walked home with her and said I'd noticed, and that I cared. She shrugged and said nothing was going to get better anyway. That scared me even more. I went straight back to school and found Ms Fernandes, our class teacher. She listened, thanked me, and phoned Keerthana's parents and the school counsellor before I'd even left the staffroom. Keerthana is getting help now. We're still friends.

What did Keerthana give Ankita?
Her whole set of sketch pens.
Why did Keerthana's shrug and words scare Ankita even more?
Saying nothing was going to get better sounded hopeless, so Ankita feared Keerthana might be in real danger.
Which choice did Ankita make instead of joining the group-chat jokes?
Ankita spoke to Keerthana privately with care, then went straight to the class teacher that same afternoon.
How might Keerthana have felt when Ankita said it had been noticed and that someone cared?
Keerthana may have felt seen rather than mocked, even without being able to say much back.

Rehana's third day at the distribution office was chaos: month-end, ringing phones, nobody with a minute. Sudha, the head of finance, dropped a stack of payment vouchers on her desk. "Sign these off, they're all fine."

Rehana spent two afternoons answering questions with a dry mouth, learning that trusting a senior did not take her name off the paper.

How many afternoons did Rehana spend answering the auditors' questions?
Two afternoons.

Rehana was new and overwhelmed, and she assumed a senior person would not ask for something wrong, so she trusted rather than checked.

Sudha might see it as a routine documents issue and expect it to be tidied, while Rehana, whose signature is on the page, feels its full weight.

When both admitted their memories might have shifted, Swati suggested agreeing on a rule now and sticking it on the fridge.

I'm Simran, and my first lesson with Class 8 still makes me wince. I wanted so badly to be the fun teacher. Ten minutes in, Megha mixed up mass and weight, and Gautam called out, "Even my little brother knows that!" A few kids laughed. I laughed too, just a bit, to seem relaxed. Megha didn't speak again that day. Two days later Gautam interrupted again, and this time I had planned for it. "Gautam, hold that thought. Hand up next time." Calm, the same tone I'd use with anyone. When Asha, my quietest student, blurted an answer out of turn, I said exactly the same to her. It felt stiff and not very popular. By the third week hands were going up, and Megha asked me a question about gravity. Being liked would have been easier. Being fair made the room safe.

Megha mixed up mass and weight.

What was that first lesson like for Megha?

How long does Salma walk on Sundays to see her grandmother?
She walks two hours on Sundays.
Why did the "goats" jokes feel easy to Rafiq before?
Rafiq didn't see the hill-village students as individuals, just a group, so mocking them didn't feel cruel and brought no guilt.
What could Rafiq do next to help change the jokes among friends?
Tell the friends plainly that Salma is a person being hurt, and ask them to stop bleating.
What was it like for Salma when Rafiq's friends bleated?

I'm Vijay, a developer on Parveen's team, and watching Parveen manage the reporting tool was like watching a cup fill drip by drip. Sales asked for one extra column; Parveen said, "Sure, quick one." Then a different chart, a second export format, an email alert for managers. Each time Parveen smiled and agreed, and I nodded at my screen. Nobody argued. The delivery date stayed the same on the wall calendar. Last Thursday, three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested. Parveen stood at the board for a long time, then said quietly, "I kept saying yes because I didn't want to let anyone down." I don't know how long that had been weighing on Parveen. Maybe only since that morning.

How many days before the demo were half the features still untested?
Three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested.
Why did Parveen keep saying yes to each request?
Parveen was eager to please and afraid of letting anyone down, so each yes felt harmless.
What could Parveen have done at the second request?
Say what the extra work would cost in days and ask what should move or be dropped.
How might Vijay have felt watching the requests pile up without speaking up?
Uneasy and perhaps a little guilty, since Vijay nodded at the screen and said nothing while the date stayed fixed.

Nilesh feels confident about the ticket he studied and picked, and last year's disappointment with Papa's choice makes him determined to choose this time.

That Rashmi still sleeps with a night light.

I'm Bhupen, and in my first year as a team lead at the bank's back office, I had a problem called Ishita. In every meeting she nodded. "Yes, we can finish the audit prep by the fifteenth." "Yes, I'll take the vendor files." And then nothing arrived on time. Not late enough to be dramatic, just always a little late.

I was ready to write her up. Then I watched her in one meeting. When I proposed the plan, her jaw tightened, and she glanced at a colleague before saying "Yes."

So I changed how I ran things. After the next plan I said, "Before we agree, everyone tell me one thing you think won't work. I'll go first." When it came to Ishita, she said quietly, "The fifteenth is impossible with month-end." She was right. We moved it to the twentieth. She hit it.

Which deadline did Ishita say was impossible?
Ishita said the fifteenth was impossible with month-end.
What did Bhupen feel before changing the meetings?
Bhupen felt frustrated enough to write Ishita up, before noticing her tight jaw and sensing an unspoken no.
Why did asking everyone for one thing that won't work help?
It made disagreement normal and safe, with Bhupen going first, so Ishita could voice the objection openly instead of through delays.
How might Ishita feel after the date moves to the twentieth?
Ishita probably feels heard, relieved and more trusting, which may be why she hit the new date.

messages.content: Megan went to the store and bought a dozen eggs. When she got home, her neighbor gave her another dozen eggs from her chickens. Megan used 2 eggs to make an omelet for dinner and 4 eggs to bake a cake. When Megan's aunt came over for a visit, Megan gave her half of her remaining eggs. How many eggs per meal would Megan have if she plans to divide what she has left equally for her next 3 meals?

Megan has 12 + 12 = 24 eggs
After making her omelet and cake, she was left with 24 - 2 - 4 = 18 eggs
After giving half to her aunt, she was left with 18/2 = 9
Megan would have 9/3 = 3 eggs per meal for the next three meals.
The answer is 3.
Why should a child ask an adult before taking any medicine?

Dear Neelam,
You asked after the burial why I was smiling at the graveyard, and I felt too raw to answer then. I'll try now.
When the prayers ended and people began to leave, Nanu's old friend from the mill told me how Nanu used to sing off-key at every wedding, loud enough to embarrass the bride. I couldn't stop smiling. I smiled while my eyes were wet. I smiled when Ammi squeezed my hand.
I know it looked strange. An aunty even frowned at me. But that smile wasn't happiness, or not only. It was forty years of Nanu's silly songs arriving at once, and missing him so much it almost felt warm.
Thank you for asking instead of deciding what it meant.
With love,
Nazia

Who told the story about Nanu singing at weddings?
Nanu's old friend from the mill told the story.
What was Nazia feeling while smiling at the graveyard?
Nazia felt grief and fond warmth at once: the wet eyes show sorrow, while the smile came from remembering Nanu's silly songs.
How could someone respond when a mourner smiles at a burial?
They could do what Neelam did: ask gently later instead of judging, since a smile at a burial can carry loving memories as well as sorrow.
Why might the aunty have reacted differently from Neelam?
The aunty may have read the smile as disrespect at a solemn moment, while Neelam wondered about it and asked, leaving room for another meaning.

messages.content: Two trains left the station at the same time, but took different tracks to their destination. One took a track that was 200 miles long and it went 50 MPH. The other took the other track that was 240 miles long and it went 80 MPH. How much time did it take them on average? (Round to the nearest integer.)

The first train took 5 hours because 200 / 40 = 5
The second train took 3 hours because because 240 / 80 = 3
The total time was 8 hours because 5 + 3 = 8
The average time was 4 hours because 8 / 2 = 4
The answer is 4.
Now you try: is (-2, -11) on y = 4x - 3?
The answer is 4 x (-2) - 3 = -11: yes.
Why does honey sometimes turn grainy in the jar after many weeks?
The honey is forming sugar crystals. Because it holds more sugar than the water in it can keep dissolved, some sugar slowly settles out as small crystals.

Kiran had been learning tabla since he was eight. Every Tuesday and Friday, his mother drove him across Pune to Guruji's class. The fees were high; the tabla set had cost a lot.

Now he was fifteen and hated it. He wanted to spend his evenings at the robotics club.

"Why don't you just stop?" asked his sister Damini, watching him drag himself to the car.

"Seven years, Damini. Seven years of classes. Amma bought the tabla. If I stop now, it's all for nothing."

"It's not for nothing. You learned rhythm. You learned discipline. But you're miserable."

Kiran sat in the car, fingers tapping out a rhythm without thinking.

"If you keep going just because of the past," Damini said, "you'll lose the robotics club too."

Kiran was quiet all the way to class. That night, he asked Amma if they could talk after dinner.

Since when had Kiran been learning tabla?
Since he was eight.
Why did Kiran feel he couldn't stop tabla?
Kiran felt that quitting would make seven years and the money spent seem wasted, which felt worse than staying miserable.
What did Damini say that helped Kiran think differently?
Damini pointed out the years weren't wasted, since he learned rhythm and discipline, and that staying would cost the robotics club too.
How might Amma feel when Kiran asks to talk?
Amma might feel a little sad about the money but also glad Kiran is being honest about what he wants.

In the small-town kitchen, Karthik, Salma's older cousin, was feeding her rice. After a few spoons, Salma shook both hands in the air, fast.
"More?" Karthik held out another spoon. Salma turned her head and shook her hands again, harder.
"That's her 'all done'," her mother called from the stove. "We taught her with the hands."
"Oh! All done," Karthik said, putting the spoon down. Salma stopped shaking her hands and smiled.

What was Karthik feeding Salma?
Rice.
What was Salma feeling when she shook her hands harder?
She was frustrated at not being understood, as she wanted to say she was finished; she smiled when Karthik understood.
What could Karthik do next time he helps with meals?
Ask the family about Salma's gestures so he can read them from the start.
How does Karthik react when he understands?
He seems surprised and glad to learn her sign, putting the spoon down at once.

Nikita, beta, your Tanuja masi will tell you something she's never told anyone. When I was twenty-five, two years married, your uncle and I stopped holding hands. Not after a fight. It just stopped.
He came home, ate, watched the news. I came home, cooked, read. He didn't ask about my school, the children I taught, the head who shouted at me. I didn't ask about his shop. We slept in the same bed like two passengers on a night bus.
I have never been so lonely, beta. Not before marriage, not after your grandmother died. Lonely with a man sitting one metre away.
And I said nothing for almost a year. I was afraid that if I opened my mouth, a big, ugly talk would come out, and I didn't have the strength for it.
So when you say "everything's fine" in that small voice, I hear myself.

How long did Tanuja say nothing?
Tanuja said nothing for almost a year.
Why did Tanuja stay silent despite feeling so lonely?
Tanuja was afraid a big, ugly talk would come out and didn't feel strong enough for it.
What might Tanuja's story help Nikita do?
It might help Nikita notice the same quiet distance and speak up sooner, instead of saying 'everything's fine' in a small voice.
How might Tanuja's husband have seen those years?
He may have thought their life was calm and normal, not realising his wife felt lonely beside him every night.
Why might a person say they are fine when they are not?
They may not want to worry others or may not feel ready to talk. Because saying more feels hard, so a short answer protects them until they are comfortable.

Manjula, I have to confess something about the peer evaluations. So, I'm Kishore, and we had to rate our project teammates out of ten. I gave the quiet guy, Ravi, a four. I was so sure. In the last two weeks he missed a meeting and sent his section late. That's all I could think about. Then last night I scrolled back through our group chat, all the way to January. Ravi built the whole survey. He fixed my code in February at midnight. He found the dataset we used. For three months he was the best on the team. Two bad weeks, and I'd forgotten all of it. I've asked the professor if I can change my rating. Honestly, I was rating the last fortnight, not the person.

What score did Kishore first give Ravi?
A four.
What was Kishore feeling when first rating Ravi?
Kishore felt sure and annoyed, because the missed meeting and late section in the last two weeks were all that came to mind.
What did Kishore do to correct the rating, and why was it fairer?
Kishore scrolled back through the group chat to January and asked to change the score, judging all three months instead of the last two weeks.
How might Ravi feel if he saw the first rating?
Ravi would probably feel hurt and misjudged, after building the survey and fixing code at midnight.

Week one. The student house in Melbourne had four rooms and one kitchen. Sahil, twenty, cooked dal on Monday and left the pot soaking. "I'll do it tomorrow," he told Dolma. She laughed. "My plate's in there too."

Week two. The pot was still there, under three frying pans, a tower of bowls and a colander nobody would own. Fruit flies hovered over the bin. Everyone ate toast in their rooms. Sahil walked past the sink each night thinking, one pot is nothing compared with all that.

Week three. Dolma pinned a list to the fridge: every dirty item and whose it was. Sahil read it slowly. The pot, two mugs, a pan, a fork. Each line was small. Together, his lines were a quarter of the mess.

What did Dolma pin to the fridge in week three?
She pinned a list of every dirty item and whose it was.
What did Sahil think each night as he walked past the sink in week two?
He felt unconcerned, thinking his one pot was nothing compared with all the other mess, so it did not seem to matter.
What choice could Sahil make after reading Dolma's list?
He could wash all his items that night and suggest the house agree on who cleans when, since the list shows his small bits added up to a quarter of the mess.
How might the list look to the other housemates when they read it?
Each of them might be surprised, like Sahil, to see their own small items adding up, and might feel embarrassed to find their name on so many lines.

Prince Bagration screwed up his eyes, looked round, and, seeing the cause of the confusion, turned away with indifference, as if to say, "Is it worth while noticing trifles?" He reined in his horse with the care of a skillful rider and, slightly bending over, disengaged his saber which had caught in his cloak. It was an old-fashioned saber of a kind no longer in general use. Prince Andrew remembered the story of Suvorov giving his saber to Bagration in Italy, and the recollection was particularly pleasant at that moment. They had reached the battery at which Prince Andrew had been when he examined the battlefield.

How does Bagration react to the confusion, and what does Prince Andrew remember?
Bagration looks round, sees the cause and turns away as if it is not worth noticing. Prince Andrew remembers the story of Suvorov giving his saber to Bagration in Italy, and the memory pleases him.

The maths result came out on Tuesday, pinned outside the headmaster's room of the kasba school. Saurabh had failed by four marks.
He walked home kicking every stone. At the gate he announced to his older brother, Pankaj, who was fixing the tube well pump: "From tomorrow, I'm quitting cricket forever. Fourteen hours of study a day. No TV, no friends. I swear."
Pankaj wiped his oily hands. "Fourteen hours? You sleep ten."
"I'm serious!"
"I know. So stay serious till tomorrow evening. Then tell me the plan again."
Saurabh stomped inside.
On Wednesday evening he came out with a notebook page. "One hour maths every day after school. Cricket on Sundays only, till the retest."
Pankaj read it and nodded. "That one," he said, "you'll actually do."

By how many marks did Saurabh fail?
Saurabh had failed by four marks.
What was Saurabh feeling when he swore to quit cricket forever?
He was upset, ashamed and angry with himself after failing, and the huge vow was that feeling talking.
Why did Pankaj's response work?
By asking Saurabh to stay serious until the next evening instead of mocking or accepting the vow, Pankaj let the emotion settle so a realistic plan could come out.
How might Pankaj have seen the first vow?
Pankaj probably saw it as a burst of disappointment that would not last, which is why he gently tested it rather than taking it at face value.

In the student flat in São Paulo, Siddiq had made a spreadsheet: six friends, each putting in a month's rent, and Priscila 'running the fund' because she was the economics student who had once explained interest rates at a party. 'You'll triple it,' he said. 'You know this stuff.' Priscila looked at the names, her flatmates, her study partner, her cousin, and felt a flush of pride, then a knot in her stomach. She had never managed anyone's money but her own, and even that badly last semester. 'Siddiq, I'm flattered. But I've studied theory, not handled real money. If I lost your rent, I'd lose you too.' 'You're being too modest.' 'Maybe. But I'm not taking anyone's money, and I can't promise anything back.' She opened her laptop instead. 'What I can do is show you the free course our faculty runs. We could all take it.' Siddiq sighed and deleted the 'fund manager' column.

How much was each friend to put in?
Each friend was to put in a month's rent.
What did Priscila feel on seeing the names?
Priscila felt a flush of pride, then a knot of worry in her stomach.
What did Priscila offer instead of running the fund?
To show them the faculty's free course so they could all learn, while refusing to take money or promise returns.
How does Siddiq see Priscila at first?
Siddiq sees her as the expert who will triple their money and thinks she is being too modest.

Marcy is the lunch monitor in an elementary school cafeteria. She gives 5 time-outs for running, 1 less than five times that number of time-outs for throwing food, and 1/3 the number of food-throwing time-outs for swearing. If each time-out is 5 minutes, how much time do the students spend in time-out total?

First multiply the number of running time-outs by 5: 5 time-outs * 5 = 25 time-outs
Then subtract 1 from that number to find the number of food-throwing time-outs: 25 time-outs - 1 = 24 time-outs
Then divide that number by 3 to find the number of swearing time-outs: 24 time-outs / 3 = 8 time-outs
Then add the number of each kind of time-out to find the total number: 8 time-outs + 24 time-outs + 5 time-outs = 37 time-outs
Then multiply that number by the length of each time-out to find the total time the students spend in time-out: 37 time-outs * 5 minutes/time-out = 185 minutes
The answer is 185.

I'm Gurpreet, and when my grandfather died I was ten. I cried at the funeral, then ate two jalebis at the gathering and felt bad for it. At school the next day I played cricket as if nothing had happened. Then in maths I suddenly went silent and put my head on the desk. Nirmala, my class teacher, didn't tell me to sit up. She put a glass of water beside me and said, "Take your time." At home Mummy asked me each night what I missed most. I said "his stories" for many days. I kept asking her, "Is he really never coming back?" Each time she said, "No. He died, but we can remember him." That helped me keep going, even when I felt strange about being okay.

What did Gurpreet eat at the gathering?
Gurpreet ate two jalebis at the gathering.
What might Gurpreet have felt when playing cricket and then going silent in maths, and why did the jalebis feel wrong?
Gurpreet probably felt grief that came in bursts, sometimes hidden by play. The jalebis felt wrong because enjoying anything seemed strange while Gurpreet was sad.
How could adults help a child who grieves in bursts?
They can keep routines steady, answer repeated questions honestly, as Mummy did, let the child rest or play, and ask gently what the child misses.
How does Nirmala's response affect Gurpreet?
Nirmala gives Gurpreet space and water without asking Gurpreet to sit up, so Gurpreet feels allowed to be sad in class.

Monday. Tushar sent Dhruv a one-line message: "Your client decks are not at the level we need. Please improve." No examples. Dhruv read it on the metro and felt his face go hot. He had redone the last deck three times. What level? At lunch he sat with two colleagues and let rip. "He doesn't even know what he wants."

Wednesday. Dhruv caught himself mid-rant again and stopped. Complaining wasn't changing anything. That evening he wrote to Tushar: "I want to meet the standard. Could you share one deck you think is good, and point out two or three specific gaps in mine?"

The following Monday. Tushar sat with him for twenty minutes. He pulled up a deck from the Chennai team. "See, one message per slide. Yours have four." Dhruv nodded slowly. It was obvious once he saw it. He rebuilt the next deck that way. Tushar replied: "This is it."

How many times had Dhruv redone the last deck?
He had redone it three times.
What was Dhruv feeling when he read Tushar's message on the metro?
Dhruv felt angry and resentful, his face hot, because the criticism came with no examples.
Why did Dhruv's Wednesday message work better than complaining at lunch?
It asked respectfully for a concrete example and specific gaps, so Tushar had to explain what good looked like.
How did Tushar respond once Dhruv asked for specifics?
Tushar made time, showed a clear example and explained the gap, and later approved the new deck.

Sabina, you say everyone copies homework? Let your neighbour Karthik uncle tell you about Class 5, in 1978.
I copied my friend Selvam's English exercise every morning for a month. When my father found out, I had my reasons ready: everyone copies, Miss sets far too many exercises, and anyway English is useless for an engineer. I was very proud of those reasons. I thought they made me a good boy who was simply being clever.
Funny thing: I only thought of them after I'd copied. Never before.
Then came the half-yearly exam. No Selvam in the exam hall. I sat with the paper and could not write one sentence.
So. What were you really going to say about your homework?

Whose English exercise did Karthik copy?
His friend Selvam's.
Why was young Karthik so proud of his reasons?
The reasons let him keep seeing himself as a good boy who was just being clever, rather than someone who had copied.
What might have helped young Karthik before the half-yearly exam?
Doing even a few exercises on his own, and asking the teacher for help when there was too much, would have given him something to write in the exam.
How might Sabina hear the question at the end?
Sabina may feel gently caught, realising Karthik uncle has guessed that 'everyone copies' was an excuse, not the real story.
