"You pushed me off the swing!" Noor said, brushing sand off her knees.
"I didn't push. I just needed a turn fast. The bell was about to ring," said Thomas.
"So? Yesterday when Kiran pushed you off the slide, you said he was a bully."
"Because he is. He pushes everyone."
"And you pushed me."
"That's different. I had a reason."
"Maybe Kiran had a reason too."
"Like what?"
Noor shrugged. "Maybe the bell was about to ring for him too."
Thomas kicked at the sand. "His reason is he's mean."
"And your reason is the bell?"
"Yes."
Noor climbed back onto the swing. "Then I'm keeping it, because the bell hasn't rung."

Why does Thomas say Noor was pushed off the swing?
Thomas says the push was only about needing a turn fast because the bell was about to ring.
Why does Thomas think that push is different from Kiran's?
Thomas feels that rush from inside, so that push has a reason, while Kiran is only seen from outside, so Kiran's push gets called mean.
What could Thomas try when he wants to call someone a bully?
Thomas could ask what reason Kiran might have had, just as Thomas had one.
How does Noor see the two pushes?
Noor sees them as the same kind of push and wonders why only Thomas gets to have a reason.

Monday. Zubin, ten, was told to help his brother Siddharth with subtraction. "You're doing it wrong! Just borrow from the tens!" Siddharth's eyes filled and he pushed the notebook away. Zubin realised he could not say why you borrow.

Wednesday. Zubin drew ten sticks in bundles on a page and used them to show what happens when a bundle is broken. It was clumsy, and Zubin lost patience once, but Siddharth finished four sums alone.

Saturday. In his own maths worksheet a similar sum came up, and Zubin saw the bundles in his head. He got it right and told Siddharth, "You helped me remember."

What did Zubin draw on Wednesday to show the borrowing?
Zubin drew ten sticks in bundles on a page.
What was Zubin feeling when he realised he could not say why you borrow?
Embarrassed and unsure, discovering that knowing how is not the same as explaining why.
What turning point helped Siddharth?
Zubin drew bundles to show what happens when a bundle is broken.
How did Siddharth feel on Monday when Zubin snapped?
Hurt and discouraged, since Siddharth's eyes filled and the notebook was pushed away.

I was nine the summer I planted a tulsi and two marigolds in old ghee tins on our balcony. Bhavna-aunty from next door poked holes in the bottoms for me with a nail. The routine was simple, and I kept it the whole term: brush teeth, water plants, then school uniform. But I didn't just pour. First I pushed one finger into the soil, up to the knuckle. If it felt damp, I gave only a little. If it felt dry and crumbly, I gave a whole mug. By the monsoon the tulsi was taller than its tin, and the marigolds were little orange balls. Amma put one on the altar, and I, Parul, stood there feeling ten feet tall.

What were the plants grown in?
Old ghee tins.
How did Parul feel when Amma put a marigold on the altar?
Parul felt proud and happy, 'ten feet tall'.
What would you change in the routine once the monsoon starts?
Keep the finger test but expect to water less, since rain keeps the soil damp and too much water can harm the roots.
How might Bhavna-aunty see the plants?
Bhavna-aunty poked the drainage holes, so Bhavna-aunty would likely be pleased to see the plants thrive.

At the Shivratri fair in Sonpur, Suraj was selling glass bangles from his father's stall when a woman in sunglasses stopped and gasped. "Suraj? From Class 10?"

It was Yamini, who used to share his bench. She'd come back from Germany for a month. An engineering master's, she said, now a job in Stuttgart. Her husband, tall and polite, bought four dozen bangles for his mother.

"You're running the shop now? That's so nice," Yamini said, and she meant it kindly.

After they left, Suraj stood very still. The same stall, the same striped awning, the same cash tin he had handed his father at fifteen. He'd been proud of the new ledger system he started last year. Now it felt like nothing.

His cousin called out asking for change. Suraj counted it twice, because his mind kept drifting back to Stuttgart.

Where had Yamini come back from?
Yamini had come back from Germany.
What was Suraj feeling as he stood very still after Yamini left?
He felt suddenly small and shaken, as if his steady life at the stall was worth nothing next to her degree, job and marriage abroad.
What could help Suraj in the days after this meeting?
He could talk with someone he trusts about what he actually wants from his life, and remember what he has built, like the ledger system, before judging himself by Yamini's path.
How might Yamini see the meeting differently from Suraj?
Yamini seemed genuinely glad to see an old benchmate and meant "That's so nice" kindly, probably with no idea it had stung him.

Class UKG settling-in note. Yogesh, class teacher.
Dhruv (5), week three. He now waves at the gate and says, "Bye Mumma, come at twelve," and walks in alone. Today he spent most of free play building a tall block tower by himself, and only called me over when it fell. At 11:55 he stood at the window watching the gate. When his mother came, he ran to hug her knees for a few seconds, then ran back to show her his tower. Next: I'll tell his mother how well the quick goodbye is working, and keep the same pickup routine.

What does Dhruv say at the gate now?
"Bye Mumma, come at twelve."
Why did Dhruv stand at the window at 11:55?
He was expecting his mother and wanted to see her come, trusting she would be back at twelve.
Why is keeping the same pickup routine a good plan?
A reliable return is what lets Dhruv feel safe enough to play on his own.
How might Dhruv's mother feel when he hugs her knees and then runs back to his tower?
She may feel happy and reassured that he has settled and wants to share his school world with her.

At the village school, during lunch under the peepal tree, three older boys were copying the way Darshan stammered. "W-w-where's your t-t-tiffin?" Darshan stared at his shoes.
Ayesha's heart was pounding so hard she could hear it. These boys were popular. If she said anything, they'd start on her.
She stood up anyway. "Stop it. It's not funny." Her voice cracked on "funny".
The boys laughed at her too. "Ooh, his bodyguard!" One of her friends moved away to sit with another group.
But the boys drifted off. Ayesha sat down next to Darshan and shared her roti. That afternoon she told Master ji what she'd seen, and he spoke to the three boys before home time.

What were the boys copying?
The way Darshan stammered.
What was Ayesha feeling when she stood up?
Ayesha was scared, heart pounding, knowing the popular boys might turn on her, but she acted anyway.
What else did Ayesha do that helped, beyond speaking up?
She sat with Darshan, shared her roti, and told Master ji, who spoke to the boys that same day.
What did standing up cost Ayesha?
The boys laughed at her too, and one friend moved away to sit with another group.
I need an email to a hotel in Shimla asking if they have a family room for 3 nights from 20 December. About 70 words. Name: Anil Varghese.

Subject: Room availability from 20 December
Dear Sir or Madam,
I would like to know if you have a family room available for three nights, from 20 December to 23 December. We are two adults and two children, aged six and nine. Could you please tell me the rate per night and whether breakfast is included? We would also prefer a room with a view of the hills, if possible.
Thank you,
Anil Varghese
"Mujhe jaane do, der ho rahi hai" polite aur casual mein kaise bolun?
Polite: "I'm sorry, I really must go now. I'm getting late." Casual: "I have to go, I'm running late."
"Running late" ka matlab kya hai?
It means you are behind schedule and may not arrive on time.

Team Soccer Stars plays in a soccer league. They played a total of 20 games, and won 14 games, lost 2, and drew the rest of the matches. They earn 3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and nothing for a loss. How many points did they have at the end of the season?

Soccer Stars won and lost a total of 14+2 = 16 games.
This means they drew 20 - 16 = 4 games.
The total points from the wins are 14*3 = 42 points.
The total points from draws are 4*1 = 4 points.
The total points from the losses are 2 * 0 = 0 points.
They had 42+4+0 = 46 points when the season ended.
The answer is 46.

On their Kerala verandah, Seema held her father's phone, playing a farm game. A chat box slid open. "Hi little one, send me a photo. Don't tell your parents, it's our secret."
She did not understand, but the word secret made her tummy feel funny. She ran to the kitchen where Jomon was cutting banana leaves. "Appa, someone wants my photo!"
Jomon closed the chat and hugged her. "You did right to show me. It is not your fault. Anyone who asks you to keep secrets from Appa and Amma is not safe."
That evening he reported the account, turned off the chat and reminded her to always show him first.

What did the message in the game ask Seema to send?
It asked her to send a photo.
Why did Seema run to her father?
The word secret made her tummy feel funny, so she sensed something was wrong even though she did not fully understand the message.
What should a child do when a stranger asks for a photo or a secret?
Show a trusted adult straight away, as Seema did, because any request for secrets is a warning sign. 🤍
How does Jomon see Seema's choice to show him?
He sees it as the right thing to do, hugs her, tells her she did right and that it is not her fault, and reports the account that evening.

By July, Zanele's weeks in Johannesburg had flattened into one long Tuesday: taxi, spreadsheet, taxi, television. Nothing was wrong enough to complain about. So she changed the pattern on purpose. She swapped her lunchtime scrolling for a walk to the community garden two streets from the office, where an old man named Sipho grew spinach in tyres. He handed her a trowel on the second day. On Saturdays she started a beginners' woodwork class with her friend Omar, who made a spectacularly crooked stool. Some evenings still went grey. She made herself a promise and wrote it on the fridge: If the grey gets heavier or doesn't lift, book the clinic, don't wait. For now, there was spinach to water.

Where did Sipho grow spinach?
In tyres at the community garden.
What does the note on Zanele's fridge show about Zanele's thinking?
It shows Zanele is wary of the grey feeling, taking it seriously and deciding not to just wait it out if it gets heavier.
Which of Zanele's changes seems to help most, and why?
The garden walks seem to help, since swapping scrolling for time with Sipho and the plants breaks the one-long-Tuesday pattern.
How might Sipho see Zanele coming back each lunchtime?
Sipho probably enjoys the company and the extra pair of hands, which is why he handed over a trowel on the second day.

messages.content: Why do the leaves of a plant kept in a dark cupboard turn pale?
The plant is starved of light. Because leaves need sunlight to make food and keep their green colour, so in the dark they slowly turn yellow or pale.

January. Sabina's cousins had all done MBAs, and at the family lunch her uncle said, "You'll apply this year, of course." Her college friends were planning a Goa trip she couldn't afford and didn't want. She said yes to both and felt hollow on the bus home.
February. In the library, her friend Irawati slid over a blank page. "Write five things you'd still do if nobody clapped." Sabina wrote: teaching kids to read, honesty, time with Nani, learning Urdu, staying out of debt. The MBA wasn't on it. Neither was Goa.
April. She told her uncle she was applying for a two-year teaching fellowship instead. He frowned and said she would regret it. She told her friends she'd skip the trip and meet them for chai when they got back. Her hands shook both times. That night, filling in the fellowship form, she felt steady.

What did Irawati ask Sabina to write?
Five things she'd still do if nobody clapped.
How did Sabina's feelings change from the January bus ride to April?
In January Sabina felt hollow after saying yes to everyone; by April, though her hands shook, she felt steady acting on her own values.
Why was Irawati's question a useful tool?
It separated what Sabina valued from what earned approval, making it clear the MBA and the trip weren't really hers.
How might Sabina's uncle see her choice?
Her uncle frowns and predicts regret, so he probably sees it as a risky break from the family's path, perhaps out of worry for her.

Suraj, you asked how I knew Shabana was the one. Your old Yusuf Chacha will tell you, but it isn't about fireworks. We were seventeen, in the same tuition class in Bhopal. I liked her so much my ears went red. The first time I walked her home, I asked, "May I walk with you tomorrow too?" She said, "Only on Tuesdays. Other days I study with my cousins." So it was only Tuesdays. When she said she wanted to become a teacher before anyone talked of marriage, I carried her books to the college entrance exam and waited outside for three hours. And when I failed my own exam, I told her the truth instead of pretending. She said that was when she began to trust me.

Which day did Shabana agree to be walked home?
Shabana agreed only on Tuesdays.
What was Yusuf feeling when his ears went red in tuition class?
Yusuf felt shy and strongly drawn to Shabana, liking her so much he blushed.
Which choice in the story built Shabana's trust, and why?
Telling her the truth about failing his exam instead of pretending showed honesty, which she said was when she began to trust him.
How might Shabana have seen Yusuf waiting three hours outside her exam?
Shabana probably felt supported and respected, since he backed her goal of becoming a teacher.
A private company raised $2500 to be used for charity. They donated  80% to a public foundation with 8 organizations. How much money will each organization receive?

The public foundation will have $2500 x 80/100 = $2000.
So, each of the organizations will receive $2000 / 8 = $250.
The answer is 250.

On Friday, Tanvir, manager of the Chembur cricket academy, messaged Darshan between two parent meetings: "Sort out the kit room before Monday." In Tanvir's head, that meant counting the helmets, setting aside the cracked ones, and listing what to order before the new batch of forty under-12s arrived. On Monday he opened the kit room door. It gleamed. Pads were stacked by size, bats hung on new hooks, the floor was mopped. There was no list. "Where's the count? What do we order?" Tanvir said, loud enough for the ground staff to hear. "You had all weekend." Darshan went red. "You said sort it out. I sorted it." Tanvir walked off muttering about people who don't think ahead. That night he scrolled back to his message. Seven words. He read it twice.

How many under-12s were joining the academy?
A new batch of forty under-12s.

He was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed, starting to see that the gap was in his seven words, not in Darshan's effort.
What could Tanvir have written on Friday instead?
He could have said what the job was for and what he needed back: count the helmets, set aside cracked ones, and send a list of what to order before the new batch.

Darshan had worked hard all weekend and was then scolded in front of the ground staff, so it was humiliating and felt unfair.

When a new boy named Dominic asked who the fastest runner in class was, Vinay said, "Me, of course. I won the district race." That was not true. Dominic's eyes lit up, and he asked Vinay to race him at lunch. Vinay's stomach knotted. At the field, he ran as fast as he could and was beaten by ten metres. Dominic looked puzzled. Vinay looked at his shoes. "I did not win the district race," he said. "I lied." There was a long silence. Dominic shrugged. "You were still fast." They sat on the grass, panting, and Dominic confessed he was afraid of the dark. Vinay swore to keep the secret.

Two days later: She and Arnab from the next corridor tried to make murukku in the hostel pantry. The dough cracked, half of it burned, and the smoke alarm went off. They laughed until they cried, and it tasted almost like home.

The next Sunday: Arnab found a notice for the Tamil Sangam's late Deepavali gathering. Lavanya went, sat on a mat among strangers eating sweets that tasted like Paati's, and called Amma from the steps to describe it.

Where did Lavanya and Arnab try to make murukku?
They tried to make murukku in the hostel pantry.
What was Lavanya feeling when she sat in the dark after the call?
Lavanya felt a sharp ache of homesickness after seeing the lamps and her family on the screen.
Which steps helped ease Lavanya's homesickness?
Cooking one home dish with a friend and joining a local Tamil gathering, while still calling Amma, eased it without pretending the loss was small.
How might Arnab see the murukku disaster?
Arnab probably enjoyed it and felt glad to cheer Lavanya up, laughing with her over the smoke.

The world record for longest fingernails is 26 inches. Sandy, who just turned 12 this month, has a goal for tying the record. Her fingernails are 2 inches long. Her fingernails grow at a rate of one-tenth of an inch per month. How old will she be when she achieves the world record?

Sandy's fingernails will grow a total of ( 0.1 ) * 12 = 1.2 inches per year.
To achieve the world record, Sandy needs to grow her fingernails a total of 26 - 2 = 24 inches.
It will take her a total of 24 / 1.2 = 20 years.
Sandy will be 12 + 20 = 32 years old when she achieves the world record.
The answer is 32.

Since the Chennai account moved to our team, I've been covering two clients plus the vendor audits. I've worked until 1 am most nights, skipped dinner more often than not, and last Friday I blanked on the client call. That isn't like me, and I don't want it to become normal.

In the changing room some boys teased each other about "getting shredded", and Bilal laughed along too loudly.

In the village at the foot of the hills, the one tank that fed everyone's fields sank lower every summer. Farmers pumped whenever they liked, each sure their own share was too small to matter. Maria, twenty-five, back home after an agriculture diploma, stood up at the gram sabha. She did not scold. Two households checking the level each week, with a lost pumping day for anyone out of turn, which made watching shared and consequences agreed.
How did Simran's father's view change, and what might explain it?
He scoffed at first but became a checker, likely because he saw Maria keep the rule and the mark hold.

Diwali week, and the family group had dozens of unread messages before breakfast. Most were forwards about the election, with my uncle Pankaj's angry replies stacked underneath. I love these people, and my shoulders still tightened every time the phone buzzed. This year I tried something small. I wrote, "Happy Diwali everyone! When a video arrived that night, I checked it first, found it was old, and told only him, privately. I muted the group for the evening without announcing it. Nobody fell out. - Hrithik

Why does a magnet pick up a pin but not a pencil?
The pin is made of iron or steel. Because magnets pull on a few metals such as iron, while wood and graphite do not respond to them.
Why does a specific compliment mean more than a general compliment?
A specific compliment feels warmer. Because naming exactly what we liked shows that we really noticed and thought about it, the person feels that the praise is honest.

Mr. Jatin's comments on her project were blunt: the question was vague, two graphs had no labels, and the conclusion claimed more than the data showed. Pallavi's ears burned. She wanted to crumple the report and say something rude. That evening she read the margin again and noticed he had also written the three steps that would fix it and, at the bottom, "You can do better than this, and I say so because I know it." She redid the graphs that night.

Months on, she picked biology instead of the engineering-heavy stream he had recommended, and dreaded telling him. Her voice shook. Mr. Jatin took a moment. "I would have picked another one. Still, tell me how you got there, because I'd like to hear it." They talked as two people now, and she left the room taller.

He kept the rules simple: they met in the open lab or at the open-hour slot with the door wide, and he copied her form teacher on the emails. Once he added, "If any adult ever asks you to keep chats or gifts secret, tell your mother straight away." At home Pallavi repeated it to her mother, Dilnaz, who nodded and said she would like to meet the teacher at the science fair.

Which stream did Pallavi choose?
She chose biology instead of the engineering-heavy stream Mr. Jatin had recommended.
How do Mr. Jatin's blunt comments and his reaction to her stream choice show the bond changing?

The margin notes were blunt and made her ears burn, but he wrote the steps to fix the graphs and said she could do better, so she redid them. Months later she picked biology instead of his stream, her voice shook, and he listened to her reasons, so they talked as two people.
What was Pallavi feeling when she told him about her stream choice?
She felt nervous and afraid of his disappointment; her voice shook.
Why does Mr. Jatin meet in the open lab and copy the form teacher on emails?
It keeps the relationship professional with others aware, so the guidance stays safe, and he adds that any adult asking for secrecy should be told to a parent.

messages.content: At a bus station, a bus leaves every half-hour for 12 hours a day. How many buses leave the station for 5 days?

If one bus leaves every half-hour, then during one hour, there are 1 + 1 = 2 buses that leave the station.
During 5 days 2 * 12 * 5 = 120 buses leave the station.
The answer is 120.

Note for Mummy, who missed the match, from Sahil (Papa).
Dolma's team lost 0-3 today. She was in goal and walked off with her head down and her gloves stuffed in her pocket, and I could see her bracing for me.
I didn't mention the score. Walking to the scooter, I asked, 'What did you learn out there?' She thought and said, 'When they come from the side, I should move early.'
Then I asked what she enjoyed. That got a real smile: 'The save in the first half! The dive!'
Only then did I ask how it ended. 'We lost,' she said, flatly, not crying. I said I'd lost a work pitch on Tuesday and would try something new. She nodded like that was normal.
At home she asked to practise side dives in the courtyard.

What position did Dolma play in the match?
Dolma was in goal.
What might Dolma have been worried about as she walked off the pitch?
She seemed worried that her Papa would be disappointed, since she walked off with her head down and her gloves stuffed in her pocket.

Quiet story, please, about a girl who counted stars until she fell asleep and the stars counted back.

Parul could not sleep, so she went to her window and began to count stars. "One, two, three," she whispered.

When she reached ten, a tiny voice from the sky said, "Eleven."

She stopped. "Who's there?"

"Just us," said the stars. "We like to count with you."

So she counted again, and they answered. She said "twelve," and they said "thirteen." She said "fourteen," and they said "fifteen," and each number glittered.

Her eyelids grew heavy. "Twenty," she murmured.

"Twenty-one," said a very sleepy star, and a yawn rolled through the whole sky.

When her mother looked in later, Parul was in bed, fast asleep, with a faint silvery light on her pillow.

Nani took over the grown-up jobs and promised to be there every day, giving Nandini a steady adult so she can be a child again.
How might Shalini feel when her five-year-old tries to look after her?
She may feel touched but also sad and worried, since she doesn't want her daughter carrying her.
3 people run for president.  John manages to capture 150 votes. James captures 70% of the remaining vote.  If there were 1150 people voting, how many more votes did the third guy get than John?

There were 1150-150=1000 people who didn't vote for John
That means James got 1000*.7=700 votes
So the other candidate got 1000-700=300 votes
This means he got 300-150=150 more votes than John.
The answer is 150.

Wednesday, 11 p.m. Posted the photo from Irawati's party at seven. Forty-one likes. Irawati's got three hundred in an hour. I've checked it about fifty times. Deleted it at ten, because forty-one looked pathetic next to hers. Scrolled through everyone's holidays: Irawati in the hills, two seniors at some beach, and me in this room with a leaking tap. I feel so behind I could scream. But today, before all that, I fixed Dadi's radio with a screwdriver, and she clapped like I'd won something. That felt better than any like. Maybe tomorrow I'll leave the phone in the kitchen and finish the cycle repair with Chacha.
Lokesh

How many likes did Lokesh's photo get?
Forty-one likes.
How did Lokesh feel scrolling through everyone's holidays?
Lokesh felt behind and frustrated, measuring life against others' posts.
What gives Lokesh firmer ground than likes?
Real things like fixing Dadi's radio and repairing the cycle with Chacha.
How might Dadi have felt when the radio worked again?
Dadi was delighted and proud, clapping as if Lokesh had won something.
Say someone lamented the loss of a kite. What did they do?

Lamented means expressed deep sadness or regret about something. It is a verb, the past tense of lament.
Example: Kiran lamented the end of the holidays as he packed his school bag.

How is "yacht" spelt? It looks odd. And what does "exhausted" mean?

1. It is y-a-c-h-t, and it is said like "yot". The "ch" is silent.
2. Exhausted means extremely tired. We were exhausted after the long hike.
Why is it hard to believe a person who has been caught exaggerating before?

A person who has exaggerated before makes us check everything they say. Because trust is built by being right over time, and their past words did not match the facts, a habit of stretching the truth makes them hard to believe.
Eric has 20 marbles. He has 12 white marbles, 6 blue marbles, and the rest are green marbles. How many green marbles does Eric have?

Eric has a total of 12 + 6 = 18 white and blue marbles.
Thus, he has 20 - 18 = 2 green marbles.
The answer is 2.

The plan was simple: if the river rose, Bhavna would take her little brother Sumit up the temple path to the school on the hill, where the family would meet. But when they reached the bend, a landslip had buried the path under mud and rocks.
Sumit started to cry. Bhavna's heart was pounding, but she crouched and held his shoulders. “We'll find another way.”
Two panchayat volunteers in orange vests stood at the bend, turning people back. “Go round by the fields and the water tank,” one said. “It's longer but it's safe; we checked it an hour ago.”
Bhavna nodded and took the fields path, holding Sumit's hand. On the way she messaged the family group from Ma's old phone: “Temple path blocked. Going by the water tank. Meet at the school's side gate, not the front.”
Forty minutes later, Ma and Baba were waiting at the side gate.

What had buried the temple path?
A landslip had buried the path under mud and rocks.
What was Bhavna feeling when she saw the blocked path?
Bhavna was frightened, heart pounding, but calmed herself to comfort Sumit.
Why was trusting the volunteers' route a good choice?
They had checked it an hour ago and knew the area, so it was safer than guessing or climbing over the landslip.
How was the walk for Sumit?
Sumit was scared and crying at first, but a steady hand and the new route got him safely to Ma and Baba.

Read this:

The landlord had given Elizabeth and Binita one hour. "Two other people want this flat. Bring ID copies, work letters and the deposit receipt by eight, or I sign with them."
It was 6:55, the lift was broken, and the power in their old building had just gone out. Binita ran to her room with her phone torch, pulling open drawers. "My work letter is somewhere in my email… the network is dead."
Elizabeth went to the steel cupboard and took out a green folder. Passport copy, office ID, last three pay slips, the old rental agreement, all in clear sleeves. She had also kept two photocopies of each.
She sat with Binita on the stairs and helped her list what was missing. At 7:30 the network came back; Elizabeth forwarded Binita's scanned letter from the shared drive they had set up months ago and never used. They reached the landlord's door at 7:52, a little breathless.

At what time did the two of them reach the landlord's door?
They reached the landlord's door at 7:52.
How was Binita feeling as she searched with her phone torch?
Binita was panicked and flustered, pulling open drawers while the network was down.
Which habit saved them, and why?
Elizabeth's green folder with originals in sleeves and extra photocopies, plus the shared scanned drive, meant nothing had to be hunted for in the dark.
What would change if Elizabeth had not kept the folder?
Both of them would have been searching blind with no power or network, and they would likely have lost the flat.

Office manager's note, Tuesday
Suraj, our admin executive, met the vendor Vishal today about the printer lease. I sat in for the first part only.
Vishal was pleasant and quick: "This rate is only for signing today. Everyone is switching." Suraj smiled and said, "Thanks. Please email the full terms and the maintenance clause. I'll reply by Thursday." Vishal pushed twice more. Suraj repeated the same words, politely, and walked him to the door.
Wednesday, Suraj put two other quotes next to Vishal's written terms and found a yearly "service fee" that was never mentioned aloud.
Thursday, Vishal called to say the "today" rate was still available. Suraj thanked him, declined, and chose another vendor.
What I did next: I asked Suraj to write up these steps so the whole office can use them for every purchase.

What did Suraj find when comparing the quotes?
Suraj found a yearly 'service fee' that was never mentioned aloud.
What does Suraj's repeated, polite reply suggest about his state of mind?
Suraj seemed calm and confident, not rattled by the pushing, because he knew the offer could wait for the written terms.
Which steps in Suraj's approach protected the office?
Asking for the full terms by email, taking until Thursday, comparing two other quotes, and walking away from the pressure.
How does Vishal's Thursday call change how the 'today only' rate looks?
The rate was still available on Thursday, so the 'signing today' deadline was pressure rather than a real limit.

messages.content: Bob picked 450 apples for his entire family to eat. There are 33 children in his family, and each of them ate 10 apples. If every adult ate 3 apples apiece, how many adults are in his family?

The 33 children ate a total of 33 * 10 = 330 apples.
There were 450 - 330 = 120 apples left for the adults to eat.
If every adult ate 3 of the 120 apples left, then there were 120 / 3 = 40 adults in the family.
The answer is 40.
I forgot my homework notebook at home and the teacher checks it first thing tomorrow.
That's stressful, but you can handle it. Tell the teacher honestly in the morning before class starts. Teachers usually respect that more than excuses.
What if she gets angry?
She might be disappointed, but staying calm and polite helps. You can offer to show the work the next day, and ask if you can do it again on a loose sheet.
Will she believe me?
Honesty is your best tool here. If you tell the truth and bring the notebook next time, she will see you take your work seriously.
Okay. I'll pack my bag tonight so it doesn't happen again.
A good habit. Many people keep the next day's books by the door the night before.

My thesis proposal was due at the end of October. I had the whole of September. I spent it reorganising my notes folders, helping Noor with her internship forms and watching lectures “for background.”
I started writing the night before. I was up till 5 a.m., and in the morning I told everyone in the department corridor, “I wrote it in six hours, so whatever.”
It came back marked “needs major revision.” I remember the first feeling was relief. I had an excuse ready, and it fit perfectly.
The second feeling came later, reading my supervisor's comments. There was one question I had no idea how to answer: “What gap does this study fill?” If I'd given myself even a week, I'd have had to face that question, and maybe learn something.
I, Uma, saved my face and lost a month.

How long did Uma say the proposal took to write?
Uma told everyone, “I wrote it in six hours.”
Why was Uma's first feeling relief when the proposal came back?
Uma felt relieved because the rush gave a ready excuse, so the poor mark didn't have to say anything about Uma's ability.
What would you advise Uma for the revision?
Start early, face the supervisor's question about the gap, and ask for a meeting to talk it through, even if trying fully feels riskier.
What might the supervisor have thought reading the rushed proposal?
The supervisor might have felt disappointed and puzzled, seeing a proposal that never answered the basic question of what gap it fills.

In their shared flat in Manchester, Wei was furious. A neighbour had parked across their gate again, and Wei had photographed the neighbour's car, his face, and a delivery label with his full address. "I'm posting this in the local group," Wei said. Rafael, who'd just done a data-protection module at work, winced. "The parking, fine, complain to the council. But his face and address online? That could get you in trouble, and it's not fair to him." Wei scowled. "He's the one being unfair." "Yeah. Still." They argued a while. In the end Wei cropped the photo to just the blocked gate and sent it to the council's parking team instead. He muttered all evening, but he didn't delete the complaint.

Where did Rafael and Wei share a flat?
They shared a flat in Manchester.
What was Wei feeling when he wanted to post the photo?
He was angry and wanted the neighbour publicly shamed for blocking the gate again.
How could Wei have handled the parking problem from the start?
He could have documented just the blocked gate and reported it to the council, without sharing anyone's face or address.
How might the neighbour be affected if Wei had posted the full photo?
His face and home address would be public, which could expose him to harassment far beyond a parking dispute.

The college bus was forty minutes late, stuck behind a waterlogged underpass, and everyone was short-tempered. In the back row, two seniors grabbed Eshaan's phone again, typed something from his account and tossed it back, laughing. The third time that week. Mridul, wedged by the door, felt his anger rise and started toward them. Then he stopped. Would a scene on a stuck bus help Eshaan, or just make him the centre of it? At the college gate, away from the crowd, he caught up. "I saw the phone thing. What do you want? I can go with you to the anti-ragging cell, or talk to them, or just sit next to you on the bus. Your call." Eshaan looked at his shoes. "Come with me to the cell? Now, before I lose my nerve." They went. The teacher on duty wrote down both seniors' names, asked Eshaan for screenshots, and called the seniors in that afternoon.

How late was the college bus?
Forty minutes late.
Why did Mridul stop himself from confronting the seniors on the bus?
He felt angry but also unsure, worried a scene would only make Eshaan the centre of attention rather than help him.
What made Mridul's help respectful?
He asked Eshaan privately what he wanted and offered choices, then followed his lead to the anti-ragging cell.
How might Eshaan feel being told "Your call"?
Eshaan likely feels respected and less powerless, able to choose the help he wants after days of having control taken from him.
How do I use the phrasal verb "look up"?

"Look up" usually means to search for a piece of information, such as a word in a dictionary.
Examples: If you do not know a word, look it up. Dev looked up the train timings before leaving home.

At the crowded New Delhi railway station, Simran, ten, held her uncle Jomon's hand as they pushed toward platform 9. The train was in twenty minutes. Then an announcement: the train had moved to platform 16. The crowd surged toward the bridge. Simran's hand slipped from her uncle's in the push. She stood frozen for a second, heart racing. Then she remembered: "If we're separated, stand by the nearest ticket window and call me." She walked to the window, asked a woman in the queue to borrow her phone and called Jomon Mama. He was there in four minutes, out of breath. They still made the train.

Which platform did the train move to?
Platform 16.
What was Simran feeling when her hand slipped?
She felt frightened and frozen, her heart racing, before remembering the plan.
Which preparation helped Simran?
Knowing to wait at the nearest ticket window and knowing her uncle's number, which she could call on a borrowed phone.
How might Jomon Mama have felt when he got the call?
He likely felt panicked at first and then deep relief, rushing over to find her.

Devika, can I just explain about last night? I'm Wasim, and I know you think I was angry about the film plan. You said, "You obviously hate it, you've got that face." Then you changed the whole plan to the café, and everyone went along.

But I wasn't angry. I'd done a double shift at the call centre and my head was buzzing. I wasn't thinking about the film at all; I was thinking about sleep.

When you said I hated it, I felt kind of trapped, like whatever I said next would sound angry. So I just shrugged, which probably made it worse.

So, honestly: I'm happy with the film or the café. I was just tired. If I look like that again, you can ask me. I'd much rather you ask than guess.

Where had Wasim worked a double shift?
Wasim had done a double shift at the call centre.
What did Wasim feel when Devika said "You obviously hate it"?
Wasim felt misread and a bit trapped, as though anything said next would sound angry.
What does Wasim do now that could prevent the next misreading?
Wasim explains the tiredness plainly and invites Devika to ask instead of guessing next time.
Why might Devika have changed the whole plan?
Devika probably read Wasim's face as anger and wanted to avoid a problem, not realising it was only tiredness.
How is the story of Frankenstein framed?
It begins with letters from the explorer Robert Walton to his sister, Mrs. Saville. Walton rescues Victor on the Arctic ice and writes down his tale.

Damini: I don't want to fight either. I just feel sick looking at this
Bhupen: let's sit down this weekend, look at everything, and maybe talk to someone at the bank about options

What did Asha from Bhupen's team just get?
A new SUV.
How does Damini feel looking at the card bill?
Damini feels sick and anxious, realising they spent by comparing with others instead of checking their own budget.
Which approach would suit Damini and Bhupen better than matching friends' lifestyles?
They could lay out their own income and costs together and decide what they can afford before booking trips or big purchases.
How is Bhupen affected by the choices they made?
Bhupen feels worn down by the repeated fights and the unpaid balance, and wants to stop arguing and find a way forward.
Dad asked the bank for a statement. I only know statement as something you say.

In banking, a statement is a printed or online record of the money paid into and out of an account. It is a noun. The usual meaning is something said or written formally.
Example: She checked the statement to see when the payment was made.
Turn this into a text message: I am at the station. The train is late. Wait for me at the gate.
At the station. Train is late. Wait for me at the gate.

Tom hasn't been sleeping well lately. He figures he has been getting about 5 hours of sleep each weeknight and 6 hours each night on the weekend. If Tom would ideally like to get 8 hours of sleep each night on both weeknights and weekends, how many hours of sleep is Tom behind on from the last week?

Tom ideally wants to sleep 8 hours a night for 7 days, 8 x 7 = 56 hours sleep total for the week.
Tom has actually only slept 5 hours each weeknight, 5 x 5 = 25 hours of sleep.
Tom has only slept 6 hours each night on the weekend, 6 x 2 = 12 hours of sleep.
Total, Tom has gotten 25 + 12 hours = 37 hours sleep.
The difference between how many hours Tom would like to sleep, 56, and how many hours he's actually slept, 37, is 56 - 37 = 19 hours of sleep that Tom is behind on.
The answer is 19.
Some fruits are sweet, and a lemon is a fruit. Is a lemon sweet?
We cannot be sure from this alone. Because the first sentence says only that some fruits are sweet, it does not tell us which ones, so it cannot settle the question about a lemon.

Condense this to three sentences.

At the Sunday vegetable market in Mumbai, Santosh, two, waved at everyone from his father's hip. "Hi! Hi!" The fish seller waved back and Santosh shrieked with joy. He wriggled down to sit beside the vendor's little girl and poked her toy lorry, laughing loudly. When he grabbed it, Vishal, his father, knelt. "Soft hands. Ask first." Santosh let go. At home in the quiet flat, he drooped and whined until the neighbour's children came over.

At the Sunday vegetable market in Mumbai, two-year-old Santosh waved at everyone from his father's hip, and the fish seller waved back. He wriggled down and poked the toy lorry of the vendor's little girl, and when he grabbed it, his father Vishal knelt and told him to use soft hands and ask first, and Santosh let go. At home in the quiet flat, he drooped and whined until the neighbour's children came over.

Darshan wanted to run before college in the mornings, but in the first week he managed it only once. His shoes were in the tin trunk under the stairs, the socks somewhere else, and by the time he'd found both, the bus to Sinnar was due. So on Sunday he changed the setup. He put the shoes, socks tucked inside, right beside his charpai, and told himself the goal was only ten minutes: to the Hanuman temple at the end of the lane and back. "Ten minutes?" his friend Madhav scoffed. "That's not running." But on Monday Darshan's feet touched the shoes the moment he woke. He ran to the temple and back. Four weeks later he was still going, sometimes further, but never less than the temple.

Where did Darshan put his shoes on Sunday?
Right beside his charpai, with the socks tucked inside.
Why was Darshan happy to set such a small goal despite Madhav's scoffing?
Darshan wanted a start easy enough to happen every day; after a week of failed tries, ten minutes felt achievable rather than embarrassing.
Which two choices helped the habit survive its first weeks?
Keeping the shoes where his feet land on waking, and making the target tiny, to the temple and back, so there was nothing to hunt for and little to dread.
How might Madhav's view change after four weeks?
Madhav, who laughed at ten minutes, may be surprised that Darshan is still running and sometimes going further.

"Irawati, your shoulders are up to your ears."
"Vasudha Masi, I'm fine. I'm just revising."
"You've been 'just revising' for three hours. Stand up."
"The board exam is tomorrow!"
"I know. Stand up anyway."
Irawati stood, sighing. Masi stood beside her.
"Now roll your shoulders back. Slowly. Like you're drawing circles with them."
"This is silly."
"Do it anyway. Three times. Then drop them."
Irawati did. Her neck made a small click. She let out a long breath she didn't know she'd been holding.
"Oh."
"Better?"
"...Yes."
"Now sit and revise. When you feel them go up again, do it again."
Irawati sat down, shoulders lower, and turned the page.

How long had Irawati been revising?
Three hours.
What was Irawati feeling while her shoulders were up?
Irawati was anxious and tense about the board exam, holding the stress in her shoulders without realising it.
What small step did Vasudha Masi suggest, and why does it work?
Rolling the shoulders slowly and dropping them releases held tension, which helped Irawati breathe out and feel calmer.
How might Vasudha Masi have felt watching Irawati revise so tensely?
Masi was probably worried and caring, wanting Irawati to relax a little before the exam.

Darla needs to pay $4/watt of electricity for 300 watts of electricity, plus a $150 late fee. How much does she pay in total?

First find the total cost of the electricity: $4/watt * 300 watts = $1200
Then add the late fee: $1200 + $150 = $1350
The answer is 1350.

I'm Ira, and I manage the design team at a small publishing house. Our director gave a talk in January about "embracing challenge" and "loving feedback". I watched Pema, one of my best illustrators, nod through it. Over the next weeks I kept an eye on her. She didn't try the new digital painting style the director had praised. When I asked why, she said lightly, "No time. The deadlines are the same." I noticed she hadn't had feedback on her work since her probation ended. I can't know everything she was feeling. But I stopped repeating the slogans. I blocked Friday afternoons for practice and sat with her every other week to look at her sketches. By March she'd done a whole cover in the new style, and asked me what to fix.

What did Ira block Friday afternoons for?
Practice.
What might Pema's light answer, "No time", suggest about how she felt?
She may have felt the new style was a risk she couldn't afford with the same deadlines and no feedback, so trying it seemed unsafe.
Which choices by Ira made the new style possible?
Blocking practice time and giving regular feedback on sketches, instead of repeating the director's slogans.
How might the director see the change if shown Pema's new cover?
The director might realise that talks alone didn't do it, and that time and feedback turned the idea into real work.

Here's a bit I'm trying to understand.

To stand in the dark in a mysterious passage of an unknown house, bawling Estella to a scornful young lady neither visible nor responsive, and feeling it a dreadful liberty so to roar out her name, was almost as bad as playing to order. But she answered at last, and her light came along the dark passage like a star.

How does Estella's light appear after the narrator calls her name?
The narrator bawls her name in a dark passage of an unknown house, feeling it a dreadful liberty. She finally answers, and her light comes along the dark passage like a star.
Write a four-line poem about the waves of the sea, about 25 words.

The waves come rolling to the shore,
They whisper, tumble, and then roar.
They wash the sand and run away,
And come again another day.
Imagine a made-up story where a girl returns a lost wallet to a neighbour.

On her way to school, Tanvi found a brown leather wallet near the gate of building B. Inside were some notes, a bus pass, and a photo of an old man with a white moustache. She recognised him at once. He was Mr. Pillai from the fourth floor, who always waved from his window. After school, she knocked on his door and held out the wallet with both hands. His eyes grew wide. "I searched everywhere," he said. He asked her to wait a moment. He came back with a jar of homemade mango pickle. Tanvi carried it home, and her mother said it was the best pickle she had ever tasted.

"Ishita, you're quitting dance?"
"Yeah. I told Ma'am today."
"So you're saying you don't like it anymore?"
"No, I still like it."
"Then why? Is it the new teacher? Is it because of the competition? Did someone say something? Is it your parents?"
Ishita crossed her arms. "Bhupen, this feels like a police interrogation."
Bhupen stopped. "Sorry. I just... I thought I was helping."
"I know. But slow down."
He took a breath. "Okay. One question. Do you want to tell me why?"
Ishita was quiet for a second. "The practices clash with my science tuition. I have to choose."
"That's hard."
"Yeah. Thanks for asking the right way."

What clashes with Ishita's dance practice?
Her science tuition.
What was Ishita feeling when Bhupen fired questions at her?
Ishita felt pressured and annoyed, like she was being interrogated.
What did Bhupen change that helped?
He slowed down and asked one gentle question, making the probing feel supportive instead of pushy.
How did Bhupen see his first rush of questions?
Bhupen thought he was helping, not realising his tone felt like interrogation.

You want to know about me and Santosh? Okay. I'm Ganga. Santosh is my younger brother, and for years our father treated him like the family mistake.
Papa praised my marks and rolled his eyes at Santosh's drawings. One evening Papa tore up a sketch Santosh had left on the dining table. I found my brother in the storeroom, holding the pieces.
That night we made a deal. I'd check his maths homework before Papa saw it. He'd do my hair for school, since I'm hopeless at it. When Papa started on him, I'd say, "Papa, did you see this drawing? It won in the district fair." Politely. Always politely.
Some nights we whisper about running away together to art college, just to spite him. But we don't hate him. We just decided we won't let him split us.
Santosh drew me a card last Raksha Bandhan. Still pinned above my desk.

What did Papa tear up one evening?
A sketch Santosh had left on the dining table.
What did Ganga feel when she found Santosh in the storeroom?
Ganga felt protective and sad for Santosh, which led to their deal to stand together.
How do Ganga and Santosh protect each other without turning it into a war?
They help each other with homework and hair, and Ganga speaks up for Santosh politely, while they choose not to hate their father.
How might Papa see Ganga's polite comments about Santosh's drawings?
Papa may feel caught out or uncomfortable, but because Ganga is respectful, he may start noticing Santosh's talent.

Homework check, please:
Why is the inside of a car hot when it stands in the sun with the windows closed?
Is there a mistake here? We went in the beach on Sunday.
Please define "unwholesome".
Which train platform should I go to for the evening train?

1. Sunlight warms the seats and the air inside the closed car. Because glass lets sunlight in but the heat cannot easily escape.
2. Corrected: We went to the beach on Sunday. Why: we use "to" with a place that we go to.
3. Unwholesome means bad for your health or character. It is an adjective.
4. I don't know; platform numbers are set by the station and I can't see them. Check the display board or ask at the enquiry counter.

Monday: Jyoti was locking her scooter outside the office at nine at night when a woman asked for a lift to the hospital. Jyoti said 'sorry, no' and rode off fast, heart pounding. She couldn't sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.
Wednesday: At lunch she told Chaitanya. He listened and said, 'You weren't wrong to be careful at night. But you could have called an auto or the helpline for her. That's still help.' Jyoti saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number in her phone.
Saturday: An old man outside the metro asked her for money for medicine. Her stomach tightened again. This time she walked him to the pharmacy counter and asked the chemist to help him, then showed him the station help desk. He blessed her twice. She went home steadier.

What did Jyoti save in her phone on Wednesday?
She saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number.
How did Jyoti feel after refusing the woman on Monday night?
She felt guilty and restless; she could not sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.
What changed in how Jyoti responded between Monday and Saturday?
On Monday she only refused, but by Saturday she kept her caution and still helped safely by taking the man to the pharmacy counter and the station help desk.
How might the old man outside the metro have seen Jyoti's help?
He likely felt grateful and respected, since she did not wave him away but made sure someone could actually help him; he blessed her twice.

At the bank's head office in Chennai, the cleaning staff knew Yamini by name; she was still at her desk when they came at nine. Four months into her first job as a credit analyst, she read every file twice and wrote notes for meetings she might not even be called into. When Vaibhav, her team lead, praised her risk report in front of everyone, she smiled, then went to the washroom and stood there, breathing. It had worked, but only because she'd stayed till eleven all week, she told herself. Next time it might not. Vaibhav found her at her desk again that night. "Yamini, you're one of the sharpest people on this team," he said. "Would you believe that if you'd left at six?" She didn't answer. She didn't know.

Who knew Yamini by name at the head office?
The cleaning staff.
Why did Yamini go to the washroom and stand there breathing after the praise?
The praise brought relief mixed with fear; she felt she had only escaped exposure through overwork and worried the next report would reveal her.
Which question from Vaibhav points to a way out?
"Would you believe that if you'd left at six?", which invites her to test whether her skill, not the late nights, produces good work.
How might Vaibhav feel finding Yamini at her desk again at night?
Vaibhav is likely concerned, seeing a strong analyst wearing herself out because she doesn't trust her own ability.

Thursday

Another accounts class tonight. Four hours of standards and I understood maybe one. Sat at the back drawing buildings in the margin, the way I always do. Sunaina texted, 'How's our future chartered accountant? 😄' because I told the whole group in March that this was my thing. Eight months in, and Papa paid the fees in two parts. So I can't just stop, can I? Then everyone will know I got it wrong. Then Papa's money is wasted. Then what was all this for? The thing is, the buildings in my margin are better than my answers. I keep noticing that. Tomorrow's class is at six. I'll go. I'm angry at myself for already knowing I'll go.

Sachin

When is Sachin's next class?
Tomorrow at six.
How does Sachin feel about going to tomorrow's class?
Sachin feels resentful and trapped, angry at already knowing the class will be attended despite disliking it.
What could Sachin do to judge the course more fairly?
Sachin could ask, 'If I were choosing today, would I pick this?', and talk it through honestly with Papa or a career counsellor, instead of letting the months already spent decide.
What would change if Sachin had not told the whole group in March?
It would be easier to rethink the course, because stopping would not feel like publicly admitting a mistake.

messages.content: Why do bicycles have gears?
Gears help the rider cope with different ground. Because a low gear makes the pedals easy to push uphill and a high gear gives more speed on flat roads, the rider can save effort.

Buddy programme note, first-year hostel, week 6. Written by the student mentor coordinator.

Pairing Hansa and Gargi appears to be working. At the start, both mostly talked about classes. In today's check-in, they asked to meet me together.

Gargi said she had told Hansa about her parents' separation, which no one else at college knows. She said she'd watched Hansa's face "to see if she'd pity me or judge me." Hansa didn't do either; she just said, "That sounds lonely," and then told Gargi about her own fear of failing and letting her father down.

Hansa said that after that night, she felt "like I had a person here."

I noticed how carefully each watched the other while telling their story. That seems to be what they were really testing: whether it was safe.

No action needed. Will continue fortnightly check-ins.

What did Hansa say after Gargi shared about her parents?
Hansa said, "That sounds lonely."
What was Gargi afraid of when telling Hansa about the separation?
Gargi was afraid Hansa would pity or judge her, so she watched Hansa's face closely.
Why did Hansa's response help the friendship deepen?
She responded with care and then shared her own fear, which made the disclosure mutual and showed it was safe.
How did Hansa feel after that night?
Hansa felt she finally had someone at college, a sense of belonging and trust.

"Dhritarashtra said, 'It is even so as thou always teachest me. O amiable one, my heart also inclineth that very way of which thou tellest me. Although, however, I incline in my mind towards the Pandavas even as thou teachest me to do, yet as soon as I come in contact with Duryodhana it turneth off in a different way. No creature is able to avert fate. Indeed, Destiny, I think, is certain to take its course; individual exertion is futile.'"

What does Dhritarashtra say about his heart and about fate?

Dhritarashtra says the heart inclines toward the Pandavas, as taught, but turns another way as soon as Dhritarashtra meets Duryodhana. Dhritarashtra concludes that no creature can avoid fate and that personal effort is useless.

On Tuesday, Sahil drew two columns on the whiteboard for the college fest. "Sprint for the last ten days, then a slow week after," he told Wasim, his co-organiser, and he blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team. On the Friday of fest week, Sahil ran the stage checks until midnight, went to bed at one, and refused Wasim's offer to stay until three. "Tomorrow is the real day. Be in by eight." The following Wednesday, the volunteers sat in the canteen at four o'clock, laughing and doing nothing. Sahil had answered only two messages all week, and Wasim finally had time to fix the banner properly, unhurried. "We'll do the same next term," Sahil said, tapping the whiteboard, where the slow week was still written in green.

What did Sahil block as a holiday for the whole team?
Sahil blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team.
What was Sahil probably feeling when he refused to let Wasim stay until three?
Calm and protective of the team's energy, wanting everyone fresh for the real day.
What did the plan get right about the last days before a big event?
It put the hard push into a short window and set a recovery week after it, so the team could repeat the effort next term.
How might Wasim have felt on the Wednesday with time to fix the banner unhurried?
Relieved and rested, able to do the work properly rather than rushing while tired. 😊
There are 14 girls, 11 boys, and their parents at a park. If they split into 3 equally sized playgroups, each group contains 25 people. How many parents were at the park?

There are 3 groups * 25 people/group = 75 people in total.
There are 14 girls + 11 boys = 25 children in total.
There are 75 people - 25 children = 50 parents.
The answer is 50.
What does "brush up on" mean?

"Brush up on" means to practise and improve a skill or knowledge that you have partly forgotten.
Example: Before her trip to Paris, Elena brushed up on her French.

Abhinav, you forwarded me that 'secure your account' link and asked if it's real. Good that you asked. Let your Shalini didi tell you what happened when I didn't.
At twenty-one, a shopping site I used emailed me about a breach. I was already rattled, and ten minutes later a text came: 'Account compromised. Click to secure it.' The page looked exactly like the real one. Then a call: a polite man said he'd send an OTP to 'lock' my account, and I should read it back.
I was so scared of losing everything that I didn't think. I read it back. Within an hour, ₹18,000 went from my account to somewhere I've never traced. I reported it to the bank and the cybercrime helpline that day, but the money was gone.
He was calm. I was panicking, and that was what he needed.
So, Abhinav. When something scares you, that is exactly when you slow down. Real companies never ask for your OTP. Close that link and call the number on your card.

How much went from Shalini's account?
₹18,000 went from the account.
How did young Shalini feel when the call came?
Rattled and scared of losing everything, which stopped her from thinking clearly.
What was the turning point in Shalini's story, and what should have happened there?
Reading the OTP back to the caller; she should have hung up and called the bank on the number on her card.
How might the caller have seen young Shalini's panic?
As an opening; the caller stayed calm because her panic made her easy to trick.

messages.content: Draft a story, about 80 words, about a hedgehog who loses her way home at night. End with fireflies lighting her path to her burrow.

Pinky the hedgehog went out to look for berries and wandered far from her burrow. When the sky turned dark, every bush looked the same, and she could not find the way home. She sat down and began to cry softly. Just then, tiny lights floated out of the grass. A group of fireflies glowed around her and slowly flew ahead. Pinky followed them, and soon the fireflies lit her path all the way to her burrow.
Why do we feel sick in a bus on curvy roads? Also, how long is my journey tomorrow?

1. The eyes and inner ear send different signals about motion, which can confuse the body.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your route or the traffic. A map service or the transport office can tell you.

Mentor note on Aparna (intern, 21), week 3. Rukmini, features desk. Aparna filed a neat piece on storm season today. One line stopped me: "As we all know, lightning never strikes the same place twice." I asked where she had read it. She thought, then laughed. "Everyone says it. My grandmother, films, school." She could not name a single source, and she seemed genuinely surprised by that. She had typed it without a pause because it felt so obviously true. I showed her the weather office's page explaining how tall towers are struck again and again. She read it twice, went quiet, and then asked if she could check the rest of her piece for other "everyone knows" lines. She found two. My plan: pair her with the fact-check desk for a week. Her instinct to recheck is excellent; it just needs a habit behind it.

Which line in Aparna's piece stopped Rukmini?
"As we all know, lightning never strikes the same place twice."
How did Aparna seem to feel when she could not name a source?
Genuinely surprised. She had typed the line without a pause because it felt obviously true, and she went quiet after reading the weather office's page.
What choice did Aparna make after reading the page, and why does it matter?
She asked to check the rest of her piece for other "everyone knows" lines and found two, turning one slip into a checking habit.
How might the paper's readers have been affected if the line had gone to print?
Readers would have seen a familiar myth repeated by a newspaper, which would make it feel even more certain to them.

“Ramesh, no,” Irawati laughed as he pulled a book off the shelf.
Ramesh grinned and pulled two more.
“You're laughing,” said Dadaji from the sofa. “He thinks it's a game.”
Irawati made her face serious. “Ramesh. No.”
Ramesh froze. He looked at her eyes, then back at the book.
“See?” said Dadaji. “Same word. Different mummy.”
Ramesh put the book down and crawled into her lap. “Thank you, baba,” Irawati said. “Let's put them back together.”

He was pulling books off the shelf.

Why is it pronunciation and not pronounciation?

So when I joined the sales team, I basically became Darshan. He was the senior who closed every deal, and I copied everything: "Let's park that thought," "Help me understand your pain point," even the way he leaned back with his hands behind his head. And honestly, it helped. I was twenty-one and terrified of clients, and borrowing his lines felt like borrowing armour. By month four I was closing deals.
Then one client, an older aunty who ran a tailoring unit, said, "Beta, why are you talking like a textbook?" I laughed, but it stung. That night I went through my lines one by one. "Help me understand" fits me. Leaning back doesn't; I'm a leaner-forward. "Park that thought" I dropped. Now I sound like Urmila, with a bit of Darshan mixed in.

What did the client ask Urmila?
"Beta, why are you talking like a textbook?"
Why did borrowing Darshan's lines feel 'like borrowing armour' to Urmila?
At twenty-one and scared of clients, Urmila felt protected and more capable speaking like the senior who closed every deal.
What turning point pushed Urmila to test which habits fit?
The client's textbook comment, after which Urmila went through the lines one by one and kept only those that felt natural.
How might the tailoring-unit client have experienced Urmila's borrowed lines?
As stiff and impersonal, like being handled with a script rather than talked to.

The college administration block smelled of old files. Nilesh sat across from Professor Uma, the dean of students, with his laptop open.
"This one has my home address," he said, turning the screen. "And this says my younger brother's school. I filed a complaint on the national cybercrime portal last night. Here's the acknowledgement number."
Professor Uma read each screenshot slowly. "You did right not to answer them. Did you tell your family?"
"My mother knows. She's the one who told me to come here first thing."
Professor Uma picked up the phone and called the college's grievance cell and the security head while he waited. She wrote the complaint number in her register. "Security will be at the gate for you and your brother's school will be told today. I'll email the cybercrime cell our letter this afternoon."
Nilesh let out a long breath and closed the laptop.

Where did Nilesh file the complaint the night before?
He filed it on the national cybercrime portal.
What does Nilesh's long breath at the end suggest?
It suggests he felt relieved, after carrying the fear alone, once the dean took clear steps the same day.
What else could Nilesh do to keep his case strong?
He could keep saving any new threats with dates and hand them to the college and the cybercrime cell, rather than replying to them.
How does Professor Uma see her role here?
She treats the threats as serious, calling the grievance cell and security at once and arranging protection for Nilesh and his brother.

In the flat in Cairo, the baby, Dalia, was asleep in her basket. Jamal tiptoed over and knelt beside it. He stroked her head very softly with two fingers, the way his mother did. “Shh, habibti,” he whispered, in a tiny voice. He tucked her blanket higher, then sat back on his heels and watched her breathe. His mother, in the doorway, didn't say anything. She just smiled. Jamal whispered without looking up, “She's so small.”

What did Jamal tuck higher?
Dalia's blanket.
What was Jamal feeling as he stroked Dalia's head?
He felt tender and protective of his tiny sister, shown in his gentle touch and quiet voice.
Where did Jamal learn this gentle way of caring?
From watching his mother, who strokes the baby's head the same way.

In the career guidance room at a training institute, a poster about "new skills" hung crooked on the wall. Avni, three weeks after the layoff, sat across from the counsellor Baljeet and said, "I'm not sure what I should do." Baljeet asked one question: "What is the market paying for right now?" Avni pulled out the phone and looked at job listings. Cloud skills appeared everywhere. "Then start there," Baljeet said. Avni signed up for an entry-level cloud course and, in the same meeting, planned two evenings of freelance work to keep some income going. Avni still felt anxious, but the anxiety now had somewhere to go. The poster still hung crooked, though it looked less mocking.

What did Baljeet ask about the market?
Baljeet asked what the market is paying for right now.
How did Avni feel at the end of the meeting?
Avni still felt anxious, but the anxiety now had somewhere to go, which made it easier to bear.

When I was ten, beta, I spent a whole monsoon learning to embroider a peacock on a handkerchief. My fingers were full of needle pricks. My Nani made me unpick the neck three times. When it was finally done, I ran through the whole village showing it, even to the postman. I, Aparna, felt like a queen. At the Diwali fair that year my friend Hansa won first prize for her rangoli, and I didn't feel smaller, not one bit. I hugged her and said, "Show me how you did the corners!" My peacock didn't win anything. But I started on a parrot the very next week. That's the kind of proud I want for you.

How many times did Nani make Aparna unpick the neck?
Three times.
How did young Aparna feel when the peacock was finished?
She felt proud and joyful, like a queen, because of the long work behind it.
What choice in the story shows healthy pride?
Hugging Hansa and asking to learn her corners, then starting a parrot the next week.
How might Hansa have felt when Aparna asked about her corners?
Hansa likely felt happy and appreciated, with her friend celebrating instead of competing.

Note from Chandrika, class teacher.
At the games period, Ira and another child argued over whether a marble touched the line. "It did!" "It didn't!" Each said it louder, each repeated the same words, and the circle of onlookers grew. Ira's fists were clenched, and neither was listening. I stepped in and said, "Ira, before you answer, tell me what the other person just said." Ira stared, then said, "That it didn't touch. Because it stopped early." I asked the other child the same. They were quiet for a moment. Then Ira said, "Okay. Let's look at the line together." I will try this again next week.

What did the children argue about?
Whether a marble touched the line.
What was Ira wanting during the argument, judging by the clenched fists and the loud repeats?
Angry and set on winning, with clenched fists and loud repeats, rather than trying to understand the other child.
What did Chandrika suggest that started to change the pattern?
Chandrika asked Ira to say what the other person had just said before answering.
How might the other child have felt when Ira repeated the point about the marble stopping early?
Heard and a bit surprised, since the other point was said aloud and the shouting stopped, making it easier to look at the line together.

"Yes, Tushar bhaiya. After one game."
"You said that yesterday."
"Yesterday was different. Today I'll stop at one."

How long was Omkar's "one game" yesterday?
Three hours.
Why does Omkar want to play tonight instead of studying?
Tonight the game feels exciting and real, while a test two months away feels like forever and not worth worrying about.
What does Tushar bhaiya suggest, and why might it help?
Studying forty minutes first and then playing, so Omkar's future self isn't left with all the panic.
How does Tushar bhaiya see Omkar's promises?
Tushar bhaiya doubts them, since Omkar said the same thing yesterday and played for three hours.

"You are NOT going to the ground with those older boys. Finished."

Lokesh slammed his bag down. "You don't even know them, Amma."
"I know enough. No."

Debate coach's notes, college society. Yogesh Tiwari.
Mahima, second year, opened today's inter-college debate. Last month she rushed her first line and lost her thread. Since then we have practised one thing: reach the podium, breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, and pause before the first word.
Today I watched from the back row. She stepped up, placed her notes, and I saw her shoulders lower. There was a pause, barely a second. Then her first sentence came out clear and unhurried. I doubt anyone else in the hall noticed a thing; they simply heard a confident speaker. She kept her thread through all four minutes, even when heckled.
Next step: I'll ask her to lead a short breathing warm-up for the first-years before the next round.

In two sentences, tell me what this brief extract is about.

"Vaisampayana continued, 'The illustrious Vyasa and Devasthana and Aswa, and Vasudeva and Kripa and Satyaki and Sanjaya, filled with joy, and with faces resembling full-blown flowers, said, "Excellent! Excellent!" and hymned the praises of that tiger among men, viz., Bhishma, that foremost of virtuous persons. Then Yudhishthira, that chief of Kuru's race, with a cheerless heart and eyes bathed in tears, gently touched Bhishma's feet and said, "O grandsire, I shall to-morrow enquire after those points about which I have my doubts, for today, the sun, having sucked the moisture of all terrestrial objects, is about to set." Then Kesava and Kripa and Yudhishthira and others, saluting the Brahmanas (assembled there) and circumambulating the son of the great river, cheerfully ascended their cars. All of them observant of excellent vows then bathed in the current of the Drishadwati. Having offered oblations of water unto their ancestors and silently recited the sacred mantras and done other auspicious acts, and having performed the evening prayer with due rites, those scorchers of foes entered the city called after the elephant.'"

Vyasa and others praise Bhishma, and Yudhishthira touches Bhishma's feet and says the remaining doubts can wait until tomorrow. At sunset, Kesava, Kripa, Yudhishthira and the others bow to the Brahmanas, bathe in the river, say evening prayers and enter the city.

Why is it safer to stay low in a smoky room?
Is it "pnuemonia" or "pneumonia"?
Could you explain what crouching means?
Correct this sentence: She is liking her new school.

1. The air near the floor has less smoke. Because hot smoke rises, and cooler, cleaner air stays low.
2. It is "pneumonia". The "p" is silent, and the "eu" comes before "m".
3. "Crouching" comes from the verb "crouch", which means to bend low with your knees bent and your body near the ground. It is the -ing form.
4. Fixed: She likes her new school. Why: "like" is a state verb, so it usually takes the simple present.
Raju had 23 marbles and lost 7 in the game. How many marbles does he have now?
16. Because 23 - 7 = 16, so he has 16 left.

The bus was jammed, it was raining, and Yamini had only two stops to go when she spotted a leather wallet on the floor by her feet. People were pushing. There was no time to look inside, and she didn't want to. She squeezed to the front and held it up to the conductor. "Bhaiya, this was on the floor near the back." He wrote down the time and route. At school she went straight to her teacher, Sharmila ma'am, and told her what had happened, and which bus it was. "The conductor has it. There might be an ID card inside." Sharmila ma'am called the bus depot during lunch. The owner's card was inside, and by evening he had it back.

What did the conductor write down?
The time and route.
How did Yamini feel about looking inside the wallet?
She didn't want to, perhaps feeling that handing it on untouched was more honest and safer.
What else could Yamini do if there had been no conductor?
She could give it to a teacher or the school office, so a responsible adult can trace the owner.
How does Yamini's report look to Sharmila ma'am?
Sharmila ma'am trusts it and follows up with the depot, pleased that Yamini told her straight away.

Read this:

Monday: For the third day running, a boy from the next section grabbed Joseph's cap at recess and tossed it onto the canteen roof. Joseph's friend Nazia said, "Tell Sir." Joseph said, "I'll handle it."
Tuesday: When the boy reached for the cap again, Joseph shoved him hard with both hands. The boy fell against a bench and cut his elbow. A teacher saw only the shove. Both boys ended up outside the principal's office, and Joseph's parents were called in that afternoon.
Friday: The principal had listened to both sides, and the other boy was in trouble for the cap. But Joseph had a note home too. "I was the one being bullied," he told Nazia, "and now I'm in trouble as well." Nazia said, "Next time we go to Sir together."

Where did the boy toss Joseph's cap?
Onto the canteen roof.
What was Joseph feeling when he said he was in trouble as well?
Frustrated and resentful, feeling it was unfair that he was punished after being bullied.
What else could Joseph have done on Monday?
Taken Nazia's advice and told a teacher, so the adults dealt with the cap before it turned into a fight.
How does Nazia see things on Friday?
Nazia is supportive and offers to go to Sir together next time.

Read this:

Kabir had spoken to Sarita exactly four times, but on the bus home he could already picture the two of them at a rooftop cafe next year, laughing about a trip they had not yet taken. She was funny and sure of herself, quick with a joke in the lecture hall, and he filled in everything else himself.

When she posted a story about a stray puppy, he replied at once, then deleted the message and wrote a shorter one. On Thursday he typed, "Coffee sometime?" and then stared at the screen. Her answer came three hours later and he read it six times. "Sounds good! Saturday?" Was that enthusiasm or politeness? He put his phone face down, then picked it up again to check the time she had answered.

After a month of Saturdays, he learned other things. Sarita was often late and cancelled plans without saying sorry. She got sharp when she was tired and talked over waiters. She also read to her grandmother every Sunday. Her views on money and family were not always his.

"So what do I like?" he asked Dolma at the canteen. "How I feel when we text, or the person she really is?" Dolma shrugged and smiled. "Only you know."

How many times had Kabir spoken to Sarita before picturing the rooftop cafe?
He had spoken to her four times.
How did Kabir's picture of Sarita on the bus differ from what he learned after a month of Saturdays, and how did his question change?
At first he filled in everything else himself, but later he saw her lateness, sharp moods and differing views, and his question turned from how the feelings felt to whether he liked the real person.
What was Kabir feeling as he read her reply six times?
He felt anxious and unsure, afraid of rejection, and treated the reply time and wording as very important.
What could Kabir do next to answer his own question about Sarita?
He could keep seeing her in ordinary situations and talk honestly about what matters to each of them, then decide based on the person he sees.

A geometry box has two set squares. One has angles 45 degrees, 45 degrees, 90 degrees; the other has 30 degrees, 60 degrees, 90 degrees. Which angles can you make by putting two corners side by side?

Now you try: which two corners make 105 degrees?
The answer is 45 degrees and 60 degrees.
John has a party and invites 30 people.  Of the people he invited 20% didn't show up.  75% of the people who show up get steak and the rest get chicken.  How many people ordered chicken?

There were 30*.2=6 people who didn't show up
So 30-6=24 people showed up
Of the people who showed up, 24*.75=18 got steak
So 24-18=6 got chicken
The answer is 6.
Who would have thought a dragon could be a baker's oven? Tell me that story.

The baker's oven in Old Town had broken, and there were no fresh loaves for the morning. Mr. Sharma sat on a sack of flour, worried.

A knock came at the door. A small red dragon stood there, holding a cap. "I heard you need heat," he said. "My name is Kiln."

Mr. Sharma hesitated. Then he shrugged. "Why not?"

The dragon sat by the clay oven, took a deep breath, and breathed a steady, golden warmth. The first batch of bread rose and browned perfectly.

By sunrise, the whole street smelled of fresh loaves. Customers lined up, wondering how Mr. Sharma had managed.

Kiln was paid in rolls, and he promised to come back every morning before dawn.
