In Vienna, Vera had put up with Selin's taunts about her accent for six weeks: every corridor, every group photo. One evening she made a plan in her bedroom: an edited picture of Selin, a mocking caption, and a post on the class channel at midnight so everyone would see. "She deserves it," Vera told her friend Lena, who wrote back, "Are you sure?" Vera posted it anyway. By morning Selin had posted something crueler, and the class split into two camps. At break the head teacher called both girls to the office. The first question was about the post. The taunts, which Vera had never reported, were not mentioned at all, and both girls lost a week on the school channel.

How long had Vera put up with Selin's taunts?
Vera had put up with them for six weeks.
What was Vera feeling when she made the plan in her bedroom?
Vera felt angry and humiliated, and wanted Selin to feel the same way.
What could Vera do instead, and why?
Vera could show the taunts to a teacher or counsellor and keep a record, because that puts the original harm at the centre and does not risk punishment.
How might Selin see Vera's post?
Selin would probably see it as an attack and feel embarrassed and defensive, which fits with answering it with something crueler.

Sunday night
Finished the last of the eight Science board papers today, the 2016 one, timed, at the dining table while Jasleen did hers on a video call. Then I did what Sir told us: added up my lost marks by reason. I've been writing each one at the back of my rough book since January. Totals: slow writing, 38. Didn't know the concept, 14. Careless, 11. I always thought my problem was not knowing enough. It isn't. I'm running out of time on the five-mark answers because I write essays when points would do. New plan: every day this week, three long answers in point form against a timer, eight minutes each. Jasleen says she'll time me. Strange to feel relieved about 38 lost marks, but I do.
Kalyani

Which paper did Kalyani finish today?
The 2016 Science paper, the last of the eight.
Why does Kalyani feel relieved about 38 lost marks?
Kalyani now knows the biggest cause is slow writing, which feels fixable, and is less worried about not knowing enough.
What else could Kalyani do to fix slow writing?
Study how marking schemes award points and practise matching them, so each long answer covers the key points in fewer words.
What is it like for Jasleen to time Kalyani's answers?
Jasleen gets to support a friend and may pick up the same point-form habit for her own papers.

Read this:

"Jomon, sit. You've been here till ten every night this month, so I'm going to tell you something I don't tell many people. When I was twenty-five, in my first design job, I said yes to everything for a whole year. One Monday, the day of the biggest client deadline of my life, I woke up and could not get out of bed. I don't mean I didn't want to. My arms would not lift the blanket. I cried, I slept, I woke, I slept, through the whole day and into Tuesday. My roommate Mercy called my manager and then called a doctor. I felt like the worst failure in the world. Months later I understood it differently: my body took the rest I had refused it for a year. So this is your Usha ma'am telling you: go home at six today."

What happened on the Monday of the big deadline?
Usha woke up and could not get out of bed.
How did young Usha feel about the crash at first?
She felt like the worst failure in the world, ashamed that her body gave out on deadline day.
What choice earlier in the story might have prevented young Usha's crash?
Saying no to some of that year's requests, or telling the manager about the load before the deadline, might have prevented it.
What might that Monday have been like for Mercy?
Mercy was likely frightened to see Usha unable to get up, and acted by calling the manager and a doctor.

She lingered, and resisted my persuasions to departure a tiresome while; but as he neither looked up nor spoke, she finally made a movement to the door, and I followed. We were recalled by a scream. Linton had slid from his seat on to the hearthstone, and lay writhing in the mere perverseness of an indulged plague of a child, determined to be as grievous and harassing as it can. I thoroughly gauged his disposition from his behaviour, and saw at once it would be folly to attempt humouring him. Not so my companion: she ran back in terror, knelt down, and cried, and soothed, and entreated, till he grew quiet from lack of breath: by no means from compunction at distressing her.

Tell me what happens here in two sentences.

Linton slides off his seat and writhes on the hearth like a spoiled child, but the narrator sees that giving in would be pointless. The girl runs back in fright and soothes him until he quiets from lack of breath.

Monday, 7 p.m.
Day one of the experiment Kiran suggested. Kiran swears by it: work on one thing at a time, notifications off, check messages only at 11, 2 and 5, and take a real break after each block.
Morning block, 9:30 to 11: just the tender document. I felt jumpy for the first twenty minutes, reaching for my phone every time a thought popped up. Then something happened. I got into it. By eleven I had written more than I usually manage in a whole day.
At eleven I answered 23 messages in fifteen minutes. None had been urgent.
Afternoon block: the budget sheet. Same thing.
At four I walked to the tea stall without my phone and actually tasted the tea.
Tired, but a good tired. Tomorrow, same plan.
Pranav

How many messages did Pranav answer at eleven?
Pranav answered 23 messages in fifteen minutes.
How did Pranav feel in the first twenty minutes of the block?
Pranav felt jumpy and restless, reaching for the phone every time a thought popped up.
What was Pranav's plan, and what did it achieve?
One task per block with notifications off and messages at 11, 2 and 5, which produced more writing by eleven than in a usual whole day.
How might Kiran feel reading about day one?
Kiran would likely feel pleased and a little proud that the suggestion worked.
Fix: I will call you when I will reach the office. What does "punctuality" mean at work?

1. I will call you when I reach the office. Why: present tense ("when I will reach" -> "when I reach").
2. Punctuality means arriving and finishing on time.

At the warehouse's Monday huddle, Arnab heard his own picking-route idea described by Eshaan as "a bit risky, maybe not thought through". It was the third time in a month. Arnab felt the back of his neck prickle; lately Eshaan seemed to glance at his screen whenever he passed.
That afternoon Arnab opened a notes file: dates, what was said, who was present. He started ending each day with a short email to the team listing what he had finished, so his work was visible.
On Wednesday he caught Eshaan by the water cooler. "I've noticed you question my proposals in the huddle but never with me first. Is there something we should sort out?"
Eshaan shrugged it off. Arnab nodded, kept his notes, and booked fifteen minutes with the shift manager for Friday, printouts in hand.

What did Arnab write in his notes file?
Dates, what was said, and who was present.
What does the prickle on Arnab's neck suggest?
It suggests he feels watched and uneasy, since Eshaan keeps glancing at his screen and undermining his ideas in front of others.
Which steps did Arnab take to handle the undermining?
He documented each incident, made his work visible by email, raised it with Eshaan directly and calmly, and went to the manager with printed facts.
How might Eshaan see Arnab's question at the water cooler?
Eshaan may feel caught and defensive, hence the shrug; being named calmly makes quiet undermining harder to keep up.
Turn this casual message into a polite one for a shop owner: Hey, is my order ready yet?
Hello, could you please tell me whether my order is ready yet?
Eid par dost ko message: "Eid Mubarak" ke saath kuch line likhni hai.
Write: "Eid Mubarak! I hope your day is full of happiness and good food."

I'm Leela, and in my final year I learned what a promise costs.
My friend Binita had been writing her thesis for months. I had promised to sit with her on submission night, proofread every page and walk with her to the department at eight in the morning. She was terrified of the formatting, and of doing it alone.
Then, at six that evening, the senior I'd liked all year texted: a group was going for dinner and music by the lake. Would I come?
I stared at that message for a long time. I even typed "yes." My whole chest wanted to go.
Then I thought of Binita hunched over her laptop, counting on me. I deleted the yes.
We finished at four in the morning. She fell asleep on my shoulder in the auto. Later, she told me, "You're the one I'd call in any emergency." I've kept that sentence with me since.

What time did Leela and Binita finish?
They finished at four in the morning.
What was Leela feeling while staring at the senior's message?
Leela felt a strong pull and some longing to go, torn between desire for the dinner and duty to Binita.
What made Leela decide to stay?
Thinking of Binita hunched over her laptop and counting on her made Leela delete the yes and keep the promise.
How does Binita see Leela after that night?
Binita sees Leela as someone completely reliable, the one she would call in any emergency.

Tyler weighs 25 pounds more than Sam. Peter weighs half as much as Tyler. If Peter weighs 65 pounds, how much does Sam weigh, in pounds?

Tyler weighs 65*2=130 pounds.
Sam weighs 130-25=105 pounds.
The answer is 105.

I'm Pradeep, and I sit opposite Siddharth in the Leeds office. At the team lunch on Wednesday, two colleagues took turns imitating how he says "schedule," and laughed. He smiled thinly and ate faster. Afterwards nobody invited him to the pub, as usual. I couldn't tell how much it hurt; he only said, "It's a bit tiring." On Friday he asked one of them, calmly, in the corridor, to stop the impressions. The colleague shrugged it off, and it happened again. Siddharth wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR. Then he joined the Saturday five-a-side that some of us play. "Their bias isn't my flaw," he told me, almost to himself, "but I still have to make it stop."

What did the two colleagues imitate at the team lunch?
They imitated how Siddharth says "schedule."
What might Siddharth have felt during the lunch, given his thin smile and how fast he ate?
He may have been hurt and tried to hide it, but Pradeep couldn't tell how much it hurt. A smile is a cue, not proof.
What did Siddharth do after the impressions happened again, and why does it help?
He wrote it down with dates and sent it to HR, so there is a record for a proper report. He also found friendlier company at the five-a-side.
How might the colleague who shrugged it off have seen the impressions?
Possibly as a harmless joke, although Siddharth clearly experienced it as mockery. The repeat suggests the request wasn't taken seriously.

The night before the anatomy exam, a power cut hit the girls' hostel in Manipal, and Seema, nineteen, sat on the corridor floor under an emergency light with her notes. For months she'd shared her hand-drawn diagrams with the whole floor. Mahima had been the most grateful: "You're the best, Seema!" Find the amount on ₹20,000 at 10% per annum for 1 year compounded half-yearly. Compare with yearly compounding.

Answer: Half-yearly: ₹22,050. Yearly: ₹22,000.

Compounded HALF-YEARLY means interest is added every 6 months. The rate for each half-year is 10% / 2 = 5%, and 1 year has 2 half-years: A = 20,000 x 1.05^2 = 20,000 x 1.1025 = 22,050 yearly: A = 20,000 x 1.10 = 22,000 The half-yearly amount is ₹50 more, because after 6 months the ₹1,000 interest starts to earn interest too (5% of ₹1,000 = ₹50). Rule: halve the RATE and double the NUMBER OF PERIODS. Common mistake: using 10% for each half-year.

messages.content: A rectangular flowerbed in the city park is 4 meters wide. Its length is 1 meter less than twice its width. The government wants to fence the flowerbed. How many meters of fence are needed?

Twice the width is 4 x 2 = 8 meters.
The length of the rectangular flowerbed is 8 - 1= 7 meters.
Since the rectangular flower bed has 2 equal lengths, then it needs 7 x 2 = 14 meters of fence.
The rectangular bed has also 2 equal widths, so it needs 4 x 2 = 8 meters of fence.
Therefore, the rectangular flower bed needs a total of 14 + 8 = 22 meters of fence.
The answer is 22.
Legacy has 5 bars of gold she received from her father. Her friend Aleena has 2 bars fewer than she has. If a bar of gold is worth $2200, calculate the total value of gold the three have together.

If Legacy has 5 bars, Aleena has 5 bars - 2 bars = 3 bars.
In total, they have 5 bars + 3 bars = 8 bars,
Since one bar of gold is worth $2200, the 8 bars they have together are worth 8 bars * $2200/bar = $17600
The answer is 17600.

What would change for Jomon if Simran had guessed the book for him?
He might feel his words didn't matter, and his father might end up speaking for him.

Read this:

Maria,
I keep thinking about Sunday, when you were packing for your conference and I stood over you saying, "Not that bag. Did you print the ticket? Charge the power bank. Leave at six, not six-fifteen." You finally said, "I've travelled alone since I was sixteen." You were right.
It isn't that I think you can't do it. When I can't control how something goes, it feels like everything could fall apart. My chest gets tight, and ordering you around is how I try to make it stop.
So here's my plan. Next trip, I'll ask one question, "Anything you want help with?", and then I'll trust your answer. Maybe I'll text you a heart. That's all.
Chaitanya

What did Maria say when Chaitanya kept giving instructions?
Maria said, "I've travelled alone since I was sixteen."
What is Chaitanya afraid of beneath the bossiness?
Chaitanya is afraid that without control everything could fall apart, and feels a tight chest.
What turning point does Chaitanya plan for the next trip?
Chaitanya will ask one question about help and then trust Maria's answer, practising trust in a small way.
How might Maria have felt being told which bag to use and when to leave?
Maria probably felt treated like someone who couldn't manage, which is why the reply was firm.

Read this:

After scoring at the colony's cricket match, Sunaina, six, stood tall by the wicket, hands on hips, shoulders back, grinning at her father Vikas at the boundary. "Did you see?" she called. "I saw!" he said. Then a tall neighbour boy asked her to bat again in front of the whole crowd. Her shoulders rounded and her hands went to her sides. She looked at Vikas. "Maybe later," he told the boy. Sunaina smiled and sat down beside him, relaxed.

Where was Vikas when Sunaina scored?
He was at the boundary.
What does Sunaina's change of posture suggest about her feelings?
Standing tall with hands on hips suggests pride in her score. Rounded shoulders and looking at her father suggest she felt shy or under pressure when asked to bat in front of the crowd.
What could Vikas do to support Sunaina's shyness?
He can do as he did, protecting her from the pressure and letting her decide when she is ready to perform again.
How might the neighbour boy feel when Sunaina doesn't bat again?
He may feel a little let down, but he may also have just wanted more of the fun.

Read this:

At the village school parade, Charu stood in line with her hands behind her back, as Sir had taught, chin up. The flag went up, and the whole row stood the same way. Afterwards a peon told Charu that the headmaster wanted to see her. She stood outside his door, hands behind her back again, fingers tightly locked. Her friend Lavanya whispered, “Why are you hiding your hands? What did you do?” “Nothing!” said Charu, “I don't know why he called me.” The door opened. The headmaster was smiling. “Charu, your poem won the district prize.”

What did the peon tell Charu after the parade?
He told her that the headmaster wanted to see her.
What might Charu's hands behind her back mean outside the door, and what else could it be?
Probably nervousness, since her fingers were locked and she did not know why she was called. It could also be the parade habit of respect; it does not mean she had done something wrong.
What would help Lavanya read the gesture better?
Look at the context, the door and Charu's face, and ask kindly what is wrong instead of assuming guilt.
How might Lavanya's question feel to Charu?
It may have added to her worry, since she said she had done nothing. A gentler question would have felt more supportive.

Read this:

It is Sankranti week, and the community centre play corner smells of til laddoos. Urmila, five, kneels beside her little sister Nirmala, whose shoelace has come loose again. "Look. Make a bunny ear. Now another bunny ear. Now they hug." Nirmala's fingers get tangled. Urmila waits, tongue poking out, and guides her hand. The loop wobbles, then holds. Urmila jumps up. "Aunty! I taught her! I know it and now she knows it!" She beams all the way to the laddoo table.

What does Urmila tell Nirmala to make first?
A bunny ear.
Why does Urmila jump up and shout to Aunty?
She feels proud and excited 😊 to be the one who knows how, and even prouder that now her little sister knows it too.
How could the centre aunty support Urmila's wish to help?
The aunty could praise her patience, not just the bow, and give her other small chances to show younger children something.
What is it like for Nirmala when Urmila guides her hand?
Nirmala probably feels helped and a little proud too, because her big sister waits patiently instead of doing it for her.

Read this:

"Tanuja didi, I got the same pencil box as you!"
"Binita, you also got my hairclip. And my bag."
"Because you're the best. You're topper, and you run the fastest, and everyone listens to you."
"Sit down a sec. Can I tell you something?"
"What?"
"I'm not the best at everything. I failed my first maths test in Class 8. I still get scared before races. And I'm terrible at drawing. You're way better."
"Really?"
"Really. If you copy me in everything, you'll miss being you."
"But I want to be like you."
"Copy the good bits, maybe. Like practising. But choose your own clip, okay, silly girl? Choose your own everything."
"…Can I still sit with you at lunch?"
"Of course. But tomorrow you decide what we talk about."
Binita grinned. "Drawing."
"Perfect. You can teach me."

What did Binita get that was the same as Tanuja's?
The same pencil box, and Tanuja's hairclip and bag.
How does Tanuja seem to feel about being copied?
Tanuja seems flattered but uneasy, not wanting Binita to lose herself by copying everything.
How did Tanuja act as a good role model?
She admitted her own flaws and encouraged Binita to choose for herself instead of enjoying the worship.
How does Binita see Tanuja at first?
Binita sees Tanuja as perfect at everything, which is why she copies all her things.

Martha receives a daily allowance of $12. She decides to save half of this amount every day. In the first week she kept her commitment with the exception of one day when she saved only a quarter of this amount. How much has she saved at the end of this week?

Half of $12 is (1/2)*$12 = $6
There are 7 days in a week so if she saved half every day except one then she saved half for 7-1 = 6 days
She saved $6 for 6 days for a total of $36
A quarter of $12 is (1/4)*$12 = $3
She saved a quarter once for a total savings of $3+$36 = $39
The answer is 39.
Kim takes 4 classes in school that last 2 hours each.  She drops 1 class.  How many hours of classes does she have now have per day?

She is now in 4-1=3 classes
So she spends 3*2=6 hours in school
The answer is 6.

Jasleen, two, reached for her mother's phone on the dining table and Alka lifted it out of reach. “No! NO!” Jasleen screamed, stamping, her face red. Alka knelt to her level. “You want the phone. It's not for playing. You can hold the spoon or the little book.” Jasleen wailed “No!” again, but more softly. Alka waited. Jasleen took the book, hiccuped and climbed on the chair. “Mine,” she said. “Yours,” Alka agreed.

What did Alka offer Jasleen instead of the phone?
The spoon or the little book.
What do Jasleen's screams and stamping tell you about her feelings?
They show frustration at being denied and a wish to have her own way. She may also be tired or hungry, which makes big feelings bigger.
What could Alka do next time to reduce the outburst?
She could put the phone away early and offer choices from the start.
How might Jasleen see Alka's calm response?
She may feel that her feelings are heard even though the limit stays. 🙂

Tuesday
Aparna Didi dared me to open the screen-time page. I said fine, it'll be about two hours.
Six hours and eleven minutes. Daily average. Four and a half of that on short videos.
I actually felt my face go hot. Six hours is a whole school day. Where did it go? Mostly between 10 pm and 1 am, the report says, and in tiny bits: two minutes, three minutes, forty times.
My usual move would be to feel terrible, delete everything tonight and reinstall on Thursday. Done that twice already. This time I'm going to use the numbers instead. The biggest block is late night, so that's where I start. The short-video app is the main thing, so that gets a limit first, not messages with friends.
Target for this week: under five hours, and nothing after 11.
Checking again Sunday. Numbers, not guilt.
– Nilesh

How much of the daily average went on short videos?
Four and a half hours of it.
How did Nilesh feel on seeing six hours and eleven minutes?
Nilesh was shocked and embarrassed, face going hot, realising that was a whole school day.
What else could Nilesh look at on Sunday besides the total?
When the late-night minutes happened and what came just before, so the next step targets the real trigger.
How might Aparna Didi see the result of the dare?
Aparna Didi may feel a bit guilty for teasing, but glad the numbers pushed Nilesh toward a real plan.

The bump was small. Paulo's mother's hatchback had rolled into the back of a delivery van at a red light in Porto. Paulo switched off the engine, put on the hazard lights and got out. "Is everyone all right?" His friend Ines in the passenger seat nodded, and so did Gabriel, the van driver. Paulo took photos of both bumpers, the road and the van's number plate, then wrote down Gabriel's insurer and phone number. Gabriel began to argue about who had braked late. "The photos will show it," Paulo said quietly. "Let's leave that to the insurers." If either of them had been hurt or refused to share details, Paulo would have called the police. Back in the car his hands were still tight on the wheel, but he texted his mother: "Nobody hurt. Car okay. Photos taken."

What did Paulo photograph at the scene?
Paulo took photos of both bumpers, the road and the van's number plate.
How was Paulo feeling after the collision, judging by his hands?
Paulo was still tense and shaken, even though he had stayed calm on the outside.
What could Paulo do if Gabriel refused to give an insurer's name, and why?
Paulo could stay calm, keep the plate photo and call the police so the details are officially recorded, which protects both drivers without a quarrel.
How might Gabriel have felt about being asked for details rather than being argued with?
Gabriel may have felt irritated at first at not getting a quarrel, then relieved that the exchange stayed calm and clear.

Read this:

Xin, five, came home from her first swimming lesson in London grey-faced and silent. She didn't take off her coat. She walked straight to where Nkechi, her mum, sat on the sofa, climbed into her lap and pressed her face against her neck. Nkechi opened her mouth to ask, then shut it. She wrapped her arms around Xin, coat and all, and just held her. The kettle boiled and switched off. They stayed there. After ten minutes Xin mumbled, 'I swallowed water and everyone laughed.' Nkechi kissed her hair. 'That sounds horrible. I'm glad you came to me.' Xin wriggled out of her coat at last and asked for toast.

What did Xin not take off when she got home?
Her coat.
What was Xin feeling after the swimming lesson?
She felt upset, embarrassed and tired after swallowing water and being laughed at.
Why was it wise for Nkechi not to ask questions at first?
Holding Xin first gave comfort, so she felt safe enough to share when she was ready.
How might the children who laughed have seen the moment?
They may not have realised how embarrassed Xin felt.

Read this:

I go to the Saturday sign language club with Jasleen, so I saw her breakthrough. Avni, who is Deaf and runs the club, was telling us about a scooter crash she'd seen outside the market. Jasleen and I had been learning single signs for weeks, and at first we both kept trying to catch each one, like vocabulary cards. We were lost. Then Jasleen stopped squinting at Avni's fingers and sat back. Avni had put the scooter on her right and a cow on her left, in the air in front of her. One flat hand became the scooter, sliding forward; her other hand, a different shape, was the cow stepping out. When the hands met, Avni's face showed the shock, eyebrows up, cheeks puffed. Jasleen whispered, "The cow walked into it from the side." Avni saw, grinned and nodded. I can't say what finally made it click. But after that Jasleen watched the whole space, not just the hands, and so did I.

Where did the scooter crash happen?
Outside the market.
How did Jasleen feel before the story clicked?
Jasleen felt lost and frustrated, squinting at single signs, until watching the whole space brought the relief of understanding.
What changed Jasleen's understanding?
Watching the whole signing space, where Avni placed the scooter and the cow, how the hand shapes moved and her face, instead of isolated signs.
How might Avni have felt when Jasleen whispered the right reading?
Pleased, grinning and nodding that a learner had followed the story the way it was told 😊

Read this:

"Anirban, put the phone down for a minute and listen to your old aunt.

When I was twenty-five, we didn't have phone groups. We had Holi lunch at your great-grandfather's house, forty people and one long table. Every year the men argued about elections until someone cried. I loved them all and I dreaded that lunch.

One year I, Vidya, the youngest daughter-in-law, did something new. When your grandfather started on the ruling party, I stood up and said, 'Papa, no politics till the gujiyas are finished. Tell us about your first Holi instead.' Everyone laughed. He told the story. Nobody fought.

I did it every year after that. They called it Vidya's rule.

So when your family group gets noisy, beta, you don't need to win. Change the subject kindly. It works better than you'd think."

What did Vidya ask Papa to talk about instead of politics?
His first Holi.
What did Vidya feel about the Holi lunch before that year?
She loved everyone there but dreaded the lunch, because the arguments always ended with someone crying.
Which choice at the Holi lunch changed things, and why did it work?
Vidya standing up to warmly change the subject worked, because it was light and loving, not a scolding, so everyone laughed and joined in.
How might Vidya's father-in-law have seen her interruption?
He may have felt honoured to be asked for his story, which is why he told it instead of arguing.

Please fix: My pocket money are not enough.
Diego puts 3 rupees in a jar each month. How much is in the jar after 4 months?

1. Fixed: My pocket money is not enough. Why: "Money" is uncountable, so use "is".
2. 12 rupees. Because 3 x 4 = 12.
What is the difference between aroha and avaroha in a raga?
Aroha is the ascending, or rising, movement of a raga, and avaroha is the descending movement. They do not always use the same notes.

Read this:

Daycare note, Thursday. Eshaan and Vandana both wanted the big dump truck in the sand pit this morning. Voices rose fast; Vandana was crying and Eshaan was shouting. Before I reached them, Eshaan held the truck out and said, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Vandana stopped crying and took it. After lunch, Eshaan went straight to the sand pit and waited. Vandana handed it over without a word. I praised both of them for keeping the deal. I'm sharing this so families can use the same words at home when toys cause shouting.

Where did Eshaan and Vandana want the dump truck?
They both wanted the big dump truck in the sand pit.
How can you tell Vandana felt calmer after the offer?
Vandana stopped crying and took the truck, which suggests the offer made Vandana feel relieved and sure of a turn.
What could the caregiver do to help this kind of deal happen more often?
Teach other children the same 'now and after lunch' words and praise deals that are kept, which the note already starts doing.
How does the note-writer see Eshaan's idea?
The note-writer sees it as a simple way to end shouting and thinks it is worth passing on to families to use at home.

Read this:

The school magazine box sat outside the library, and Maria walked past it three times on Monday. Last week Neil had laughed when her friend passed him her note, and said "No thanks" loud enough for half of Class 10 to hear. Maria hadn't said a word to him since. She hadn't cried at school either. Instead, every free period, she sat in the library corner filling a notebook: a song about a bus stop, a poem about a door that only opened one way.
On Monday she tore out the door poem and dropped it into the box. Two weeks later, Simran Ma'am called her to the staff room. "This one's going on page four," she said. "It's honest." Maria went pink, and then, for the first time in days, she smiled.

Where did Maria drop the door poem?
Into the school magazine box outside the library.
Why did Maria fill a notebook instead of saying anything to Neil?
She was hurt and embarrassed after the public 'No thanks', and writing gave the pain a shape without lashing out.
Which choice was the turning point for Maria, and what came of it?
Tearing out the door poem and putting it in the magazine box; it let others see her feeling and brought Simran Ma'am's praise.
How might Simran Ma'am see the door poem?
She sees honest writing worth publishing, and may sense real feeling behind it without needing to know the story.

Read this:

Siddharth Uncle cleaned his glasses. "Harish, you think one failure means you're done? At twenty-two, I started a small tiffin service with two friends. We cooked in my mother's kitchen, delivered on cycles. Within eight months, we'd lost everything we'd put in. One friend left. I cried in that kitchen, I won't lie. For a month I didn't want to see a tiffin box. Then my mother said, 'Did you learn nothing?' I had learned a lot: we'd priced too low, and delivered too far. So I tried again, alone, only offices within three kilometres. It was hard, and slow. That's the company I run now." Harish looked at his own laptop, where the rejected application was open. "So I just try again?" "You learn, and then you try again."

How did they deliver the tiffins?
On cycles.
How did young Siddharth feel after the business failed?
He felt crushed and discouraged, crying and not wanting to see a tiffin box for a month.
What was the turning point in young Siddharth's story?
His mother asking whether he'd learned anything, which made him see his mistakes and try again differently.
How might the friend who left have seen young Siddharth's second attempt?
That friend might feel surprised and perhaps a little regretful, seeing Siddharth succeed.

Read this:

"Mumma, I'm bored."
Vidya reached for the tablet on the shelf without looking up from her tea. "Here, beta."
Parveen, her neighbour, watched nine-year-old Kiaan disappear into the screen. "That was fast."
"If I don't, he whines for an hour."
"Does he? Last Sunday at my place the tablet was dead. He whined for maybe ten minutes."
"And then?"
"Then he built a ramp out of my cookbooks and raced bottle caps down it. Made me the judge."
Vidya put down her cup. "He never does that here."
"Maybe he's never had to."
Vidya was quiet. Then she said, "Next time, I'll try ten minutes."

What did Kiaan build at Parveen's place?
A ramp out of her cookbooks, to race bottle caps down.
What was Vidya feeling when she said "He never does that here"?
Vidya felt surprised and a little uneasy, seeing that her quick rescue may be why Kiaan doesn't invent games at home.
What small step did Vidya decide on?
Next time Kiaan says he is bored, wait ten minutes before handing over the tablet.
How does Parveen see Vidya's habit?
Parveen sees it as kind but quick, having noticed that Kiaan whined only ten minutes when there was no tablet.

Read this:

Suraj, why do I ask before I say no to your phone? Let me tell you about my daughter Sunaina. I'm Vikas, your uncle. She was eleven, chatting with an assistant on the family tablet, and I got worried and asked to see. Her face went stiff. "You don't trust me," she said, and I felt awful, because that wasn't it. I told her I was nervous, not angry. She turned the tablet toward me. She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs. We sat on the sofa and made three rules together: no giving out our address, tell me if anything feels strange, and no chatting at bedtime. Funny thing, after that she started showing me things without being asked.

What did Sunaina use the assistant for?
She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs.
Why did Sunaina say, "You don't trust me"?
She felt watched and hurt when her father asked to see her chats, and her stiff face showed it.
What made the sharing work for Sunaina and Vikas?
She showed him openly, he explained he was nervous rather than angry, and together they made three rules.
What was it like for Vikas when Sunaina said he did not trust her?
He felt awful, because asking came from his nervousness and not from anger.

At the accounts firm, the news that Kunal's uncle had died reached the team on Monday morning. Bhavna, from the same office, told her manager she wanted to bring food to Kunal's home, as her community does. Then she remembered that Kunal's family was Jain and grieving quietly, and that Kunal had once said his family liked privacy at such times. She felt unsure. She asked Kunal by message whether a visit would be welcome. He replied, "Thank you. Family is keeping things small. A message means a lot." Bhavna sent a short note and offered to cover his calls that week. The team dropped the plan for a group visit and kept the office calm.

What did Bhavna offer to cover for Kunal?
Bhavna offered to cover Kunal's calls that week.
What was Bhavna feeling when she remembered Kunal's family's way?
Bhavna felt unsure, since her own habit of visiting with food might feel intrusive to a family that prefers privacy. She chose to ask rather than guess.
What could Bhavna do to follow the family's lead?
Send a short message, offer practical help at work and wait for a sign that a visit is wanted.
How might Kunal's family have seen a group visit?
They may have felt it too crowded or intrusive when they wanted quiet, even though the team meant warmth.

Read this:

In the girls' hostel of the small college in Hassan, Indu, nineteen, had tucked the counsellor's letter inside her economics book, unopened. Her internal marks had slid from sixties to thirties. The hostel fee slip was two months old. "It'll sort itself out," she told her roommate Payal, and went to the temple fair with the juniors every evening that week, laughing a little too loudly. Payal noticed she'd stopped studying at night and slept badly. On Monday morning a notice went up outside the office: students with unpaid fees would not get exam hall tickets after Wednesday. Indu's name was on it. She stood staring for a long time. Then she went back to the room, opened the economics book, and read the counsellor's letter for the first time. "Payal," she said quietly, "will you come with me?"

Where had Indu tucked the counsellor's letter?
Inside her economics book, unopened.
Why did Indu go to the temple fair every evening and laugh a little too loudly?
Keeping busy and cheerful helped her push away the dread about her marks and fees, so she didn't have to look at them.
What forced Indu to act, and what could have helped earlier?
The notice with her name forced her; reading the counsellor's letter when it came, or telling Payal sooner, could have helped before it became urgent.
How might Payal have seen Indu during that week?
Payal noticed the stopped studying and poor sleep, and was probably worried but unsure how to help until Indu asked.

Read this:

The birthday party was packed, the room hot and the cake late. Rekha saw the shiny balloon sword in another girl's hand and grabbed it before she knew she had. The girl screamed. Rekha's mother, Sarita, knelt beside her in the crush of chairs. She didn't say "Bad girl." She said calmly, "Hands wanted it fast, na? Our rule: ask first, then wait. Give it back." Rekha's lip trembled. She gave it back. "Now let's practise. Say, 'Can I have a turn?'" Rekha whispered it. The girl, surprised, handed it over for one swish.

What did Rekha grab?
The shiny balloon sword.
How did Rekha feel when her mother knelt beside her?
She felt upset and a bit ashamed, her lip trembling, but calm enough to give it back.
What did Sarita do that helped instead of shaming?
She stayed calm, named the quick wish, stated a simple rule and practised asking with Rekha.
How might the other girl feel when Rekha asks for a turn?
The girl may feel surprised and more willing to share once she is asked nicely.

Read this:

Manager's note, one-to-one, 16 July. Pankaj, operations team.
Damini's appraisal came through last month, a raise of ₹5,000. Today, in our one-to-one, she asked for ten minutes on something unrelated to work, and pulled up a spreadsheet of her education loan.
She had redone it the night before. With her old EMI of ₹9,000, the sheet showed the loan ending in 2032. She had tried three new figures and settled on ₹10,500, 'enough to feel it, not enough to hurt'. The new end date read 2030. She said she'd confirmed with the bank that the change carried no fee.
She asked whether the review reminder she'd set, every January and July, was too often. I said it sounded about right and asked her to tell me in January how it looked.
She seemed lighter walking out than walking in.

What EMI did Damini settle on?
She settled on ₹10,500.
What does 'enough to feel it, not enough to hurt' suggest about how Damini feels?
She seems careful and quietly determined, wanting to push the loan down without making daily life stressful.
What else could Damini do at the January review?
Check whether ₹10,500 still sits comfortably and whether her costs have changed, and adjust up or down as needed.
How does the conversation look to Pankaj, who wrote the note?
Pankaj sees a small, well-planned change and supports it by agreeing the review timing and asking to hear about it in January.

messages.content: I need a note for my tutor saying I will miss Thursday's class because of a family function, and asking if we can change the lesson to another day. About 40 words. I'm Pranav.

Dear Tutor,
I will not be able to attend Thursday's class because of a family function. Could we please shift the lesson to another day? I am happy to come at any time that suits you. Thank you for understanding.
Pranav
Please correct: She have a headache today. What does "rest" mean when a person is ill?

1. She has a headache today. Why: subject-verb agreement ("She" -> "has").
2. Rest means to stop work or play and relax so the body can feel better.

Read this:

Lalremsiami had volunteered to lead her class stall at the school science fair in Aizawl. She made a task chart: who builds, who explains, who brings materials. Raghav was supposed to bring the plywood base. He forgot. Twice.
She didn't shout. On Wednesday she asked him, "What's actually stopping you?" He admitted he didn't know where to get it. She paired him with Mr Lalthanga, the carpentry teacher, and Raghav came back proud, carrying the board himself.
On fair day, their water-filter model leaked all over the table in front of the principal. The group froze. Lalremsiami stepped forward. "That's my fault, Ma'am. I didn't test the joints after we moved it." Then she mopped it up, fixed the joint with tape and restarted the demo.
Later Raghav said, "You didn't have to say it was your fault." She shrugged. "I was in charge."

What did Raghav forget to bring twice?
He forgot the plywood base.
What does Raghav's comment afterwards suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Raghav felt surprised and grateful that Lalremsiami took the blame instead of pointing at the group.
Which of Lalremsiami's leadership choices worked, and why?
Asking Raghav what was stopping him, instead of scolding, solved the real problem; owning the leak kept the team calm.
How might the principal see Lalremsiami after the leak?
The principal would likely respect her for taking responsibility and fixing it calmly instead of making excuses.

Read this:

I'm Sarita. My little sister Jaya is five. Yesterday Nani sat across the dining table while Jaya read her picture book aloud. Jaya kept the book facing herself and said, 'See the cow, Nani?' Nani said, 'I see the cover.' Jaya looked puzzled, then turned the book around. She looked at it from Nani's side, then from hers, and kept flipping it. I think something clicked, but I can't be sure what she was thinking.

Where was Nani sitting while Jaya read?
She was sitting across the dining table.
What does Jaya flipping the book back and forth suggest she was thinking about?
It suggests she was puzzled and curious, working out that Nani saw a different side of the book from her own seat.
How could Nani help Jaya practise this idea?
She could play simple 'what can I see?' games, like holding a toy between them and asking Jaya to guess which side Nani sees.
How does the older sibling see Jaya's behaviour?
The older sibling finds it interesting and thinks she learned something, but admits they cannot be sure what was in her mind.

Read this:

Jomon's tennis ball had bounced under the low wooden divan in his grandmother's flat in Kochi. He lay on the floor and stretched his arm in. His fingers touched the tip of the fuzzy ball and pushed it further back. Worse.
His friend Darshan knelt beside him. "Now it's stuck forever."
Jomon sat back on his heels. He didn't try again at once. "Wait. Why am I trying to grab it? If I push it from behind, it has to come out the front."
"But you can't reach behind it."
"My hand can't." Jomon unzipped his school bag and pulled out his thirty-centimetre ruler. He slid it along the floor, around the side of the ball, and flicked it toward himself.
The ball rolled out across the floor. Darshan caught it and laughed. "Genius!"

Whose flat was the divan in?
It was in his grandmother's flat in Kochi.
What was Jomon thinking when he sat back on his heels?
He was calm and curious, realising he didn't need to grab the ball but could push it out from behind.
What would change if Jomon had kept stretching his arm?
He might have pushed the ball further back and got frustrated, instead of finding a new way to solve it.

"Raghav, you asked how I got through failing statistics. I'm Payal, and I'll be honest, it wasn't pretty at first.
When I saw the result, I felt sick. I'd never failed anything. I sat in my room and let myself be disappointed. I didn't tell myself 'it doesn't matter,' because it did matter. I'd wanted that grade.
But the next day, I did something different. I took the answer script and asked: what is this telling me about how I prepared? Not about whether I'm clever. About how I prepared.
And it was obvious. I'd memorised formulas without understanding when to use them. I'd never timed myself. I'd done no past papers.
So for the re-exam I did past papers every weekend, timed. I passed with a B.
The fail still stings a bit. But it also taught me more than the B did."

What grade did Payal get in the re-exam?
Payal passed with a B.
How did Payal feel on first seeing the fail?
Payal felt sick and disappointed, never having failed before, and didn't pretend it didn't matter.
What question helped Payal move forward, and why?
Asking what the result said about preparation, not cleverness, showed clear gaps like untimed practice and no past papers, which Payal then fixed.
How might Raghav use Payal's story?
Raghav might feel reassured that a failure can be admitted honestly and still turned into a plan.

The broom.

Jaya

When will Jaya paint during the exams?
Only on Sunday, from 4 to 5.

messages.content: A bag of jellybeans contains 8 black beans and 2 more green beans. It also contains 1 less orange bean than green beans. How many jellybeans are there in the bag?

There are 8 + 2 = 10 green beans.
There are 10 -1 = 9 orange beans.
There are 8 black + 10 green + 9 orange = 27 jelly beans.
The answer is 27.
Now you try: solve tan^-^1(x + 1) + tan^-^1(x - 1) = tan^-^1(8/31).
The answer is 4x^2 + 31x - 8 = 0: x = 1/4; x = -8 is rejected.

"Gopika, sit down. The letter from the university came."
"Just read it, Harish."
"'We are pleased to offer you the full merit scholarship for the MSc in Marine Biology...'"
Gopika's jaw dropped. She didn't make a sound, just stood there, mouth wide open, one hand frozen halfway to her hair.
"Gopika? Say something. Are you okay?"
"...Full?"
"Full. Fees and hostel."
Then her face broke into the biggest grin he had ever seen, and she grabbed the letter and did a ridiculous dance round the dining table.
"Wait, wait," Harish said, reading on. "The course starts on the fifteenth of July. That's Achan's sixtieth birthday week."
Her jaw dropped again. Same open mouth. But this time her eyes filled, and she sat down slowly.
"I'll miss it," she said quietly. "His sixtieth."
Harish put a hand on her shoulder. "We'll celebrate early. July first. He'd want you to go."

When does the course start?
The course starts on the fifteenth of July.
How did Gopika feel after the jaw dropped the first time?
Gopika was astonished, then overjoyed, breaking into a huge grin and dancing; the second jaw drop came with sadness at missing Achan's sixtieth.
How did Harish respond to the second shock?
He put a hand on her shoulder and offered a practical fix, celebrating early on July first, showing he understood it was upsetting.
What was it like for Harish to see the first jaw drop?
Harish couldn't tell if she was okay and asked her to say something, until the grin showed it was happy shock.
What is a lookout? The guard on the tower is called one.

A lookout is a person who watches for danger or for something to appear, and also the place from which a person watches. It is a noun.
Example: The lookout on the tower saw the ship long before it reached the harbor.

Dilnaz had kept the school's mid-day meal register in Kharsi village for three years. She knew how many sacks of dal came in each month and how many plates went out.
Since spring, four sacks a month weren't adding up. And she had seen, twice, Rafiq's cousin's tempo outside the storeroom at dawn.
Rafiq was the storekeeper. He had helped her get this job when no one else would. He had come to her wedding. His wife sent her pickle every winter.
She watched the children queue with their steel plates. The dal was almost water now.
If she spoke, Rafiq could lose everything. She could lose her job; the headmistress was his relative. People would call her ungrateful.
If she said nothing, the thin dal would continue.
That night she couldn't eat. At dawn she took the register, her notes on the missing sacks, and got on the bus to the block office, her hands shaking the whole way.

How many sacks a month were not adding up?
Four sacks a month were not adding up.
What feelings were pulling at Dilnaz?
Dilnaz felt loyalty and gratitude to Rafiq, fear for her job and of being called ungrateful, and a duty to the children eating thin dal.
Which detail seems to tip Dilnaz towards speaking?
Watching the children queue with their plates while the dal was almost water made the harm real, and taking her register and notes to the block office was a factual, proper route.
How might Rafiq's family be affected if Dilnaz reports what she saw?
Rafiq's family, including his wife who sends pickle every winter, could face shame and hardship, which is part of what makes the decision so painful.

'You've been replaying that interview for nine days, Damini.'
'Because I keep hearing myself say "I'm a perfectionist" like a fool.'
'Did they say that's why?'
'They didn't say anything. Just "we are moving ahead with other candidates." Very polite. Very final.'

Damini groaned into the pillow. Then she pulled out her laptop. 'Help me word it so I don't sound desperate.'

How many days had Damini been replaying the interview?
Damini had been replaying it for nine days.
What was Damini feeling about the rejection?
Damini felt embarrassed and discouraged, blaming the 'perfectionist' answer and dreading another interview.

One feedback email and a look at three openings stops the endless replaying and gets Damini moving again.

During the lunch break at their Bhopal school, Indu pulled Abhinav behind the water cooler. "You're my best friend, so I'll tell only you," she said. "Yesterday I saw Shabnam's mother shouting at her near the gate."
That part was true. Indu had seen a woman speaking loudly, and Shabnam staring at her shoes.
"And," Indu went on, lowering her voice, "I think she's going to be sent to another school."
Abhinav's eyes went round. "Really?"
"Really," said Indu. As she said it, it sounded real even to her. Nobody had mentioned another school. But the story felt better with that part in, and Abhinav was listening so hard.

Where did Indu pull Abhinav during the lunch break?
She pulled him behind the water cooler.

She enjoyed feeling important and wanted the story to sound more exciting, and the guess began to feel true even to her.

Monday: At the water tap, three boys copied Eshaan's way of speaking and called him names, laughing. Eshaan stared at the ground. Chinmay saw it from the doorway. Heat rushed to his face; it wasn't right, and he was angry, but he stood frozen. Wednesday: Chinmay picked up his lunchbox and sat next to Eshaan. "Do you like cricket?" he asked. At the water tap.

Angry, as shown by the heat in his face, but also frozen and unsure what to do.

He sat with Eshaan at lunch, talked about something they both liked, and when the name-calling continued he went with him to tell the teacher.

I remember the night before my scholarship interview. My cousin Yamini poked her head in and said, brightly, "Relax, Ramesh, it will be fine!" and went back to her show. I felt something close inside me. Nobody had asked what I was afraid of. I nodded and said okay, but I stopped practising for an hour. It was the night before Ramesh's scholarship interview.

Crowded metro home, standing room only. I finally got a seat at the interchange and sank into it like a king. Two stops later a woman got on with one hand on her belly and a heavy office bag, clearly pregnant. The man next to me closed his eyes. The college boys opposite stared hard at their phones. Dear Harish,
I've been thinking about our fight on the phone about Papa's retirement party. I was sure I gave the thank-you speech while you stood beside me. I can still see the marigold garland and hear my own voice shaking.
You were just as sure it was you.

I'm sorry I called you a show-off. That day matters so much to me that I think my memory put me at the centre. It's still one of my best memories, and I'm keeping it. I'm just not using it to win arguments any more.

Harish giving the speech, with Parul holding the garland and crying in the background.

In the school auditorium in Lucknow, Parul had frozen halfway through her closing speech at the inter-house debate. Twenty seconds of silence, the whole school watching. Her house lost by two points. A week later, the notice for the city debate went up. Parul walked past it three times without stopping. When Harish sir, the debate coach, asked her to sign up, she said she had a family function that day. There was no function. At home she stood in front of the mirror and couldn't make herself say even the opening line. "Everyone saw," she thought. "They all know now that I'm not actually good at this." She deleted the debate club group from her phone that night.

How long was Parul silent during her closing speech?
Twenty seconds of silence, with the whole school watching.

She believed everyone now knows she isn't actually good, so the freeze felt like a verdict on her worth rather than one bad moment.

He could talk to her privately, say that freezing happens to many speakers, and suggest a small practice with just him before any contest.

Christina and her friend are driving across the state. When Christina is driving the speed limit is 30 miles per hour. When her friend is driving, the speed limit is 40 miles per hour. The drive is 210 miles total. If her friend drives for 3 hours and both drive at the speed limit, how many minutes will Christina drive?

The friend drives 40*3=120 miles.
Thus, Christina drives 210-120 =90 miles.
Since the speed limit is 30 miles per hour when Christina is driving, she drives for 90/30=3 hours.
Thus, she drives for 3*60=180 minutes.
The answer is 180.

Tarun stopped, looked down at his sinking sandal, and pulled a loud "Eww!" face, lips drawn back, arms stiff at his sides. "Out! Out!" Pooja lifted him onto the grass and wiped his foot. Thick brown mud.

- Is "enclosure" a hard word? What does it mean?
- Why do we put a bookmark in a book?
- When do I use "already" and when "yet"?

1. Enclosure is a noun that means an area closed in by a fence or wall.
2. It marks the page where you stopped. Because you can open the book at the right page without searching.
3. Use "already" for something that has happened, as in "I have already eaten". Use "yet" in questions and negatives, as in "have you eaten yet?"

Mentor's notes, Sunaina, Thursday
Aniket, from my old team, was laid off in the restructuring two weeks ago. We still meet every Thursday.
Today he walked me through it like a case study: "Revenue dipped eight percent, they cut the newest hires in two units, it's statistically sensible." Clear, calm, well argued.
What I noticed: he hasn't eaten at our last three meetings; he orders black coffee and leaves the sandwich. He mentioned he'd "optimised" his sleep to five hours so he could apply for more roles. His laptop stayed open the whole time, thirty-one tabs.
What I did: I closed my own notebook and asked, "Not what it means. How does it feel?" He began explaining the market again, stopped, and said, "Like I got thrown out." We sat with that. I bought him a proper lunch and he ate half.
Next: meet again Monday, not Thursday.

What does Aniket order at their meetings instead of eating?
Black coffee, leaving the sandwich.
Why might explaining the layoff like a case study feel reasonable to Aniket?
Treating it as numbers makes it impersonal and manageable, so he doesn't have to feel the sting of being let go; the skipped meals hint that the calm is thinner than it sounds.
What turning point came from Sunaina's question?
Asking how it felt rather than what it meant let Aniket drop the market explanation and say "Like I got thrown out", which opened the real conversation.
Why might Sunaina move the next meeting up to Monday?
Sunaina has seen the skipped meals and short sleep behind the calm and likely wants to check in sooner, showing care without pushing.

Two days before the wedding, the Mukherjee flat in Kolkata was a storm of activity. Aunties argued about sweets, uncles carried baskets of fish, and the children darted under tables. Subject: My ankle (please read before Saturday)

Dear Nilesh Sir,

I need to tell you something I've been hiding. At practice this week I said my ankle felt fine. It didn't. When I landed from the long jump on Thursday, I felt a sharp twinge and nearly cried, but I pretended I just tripped.
I wanted to be back so badly. I was scared that if I said it still hurt, you'd think I was weak or pick someone else for Saturday.
But my mother saw me limping and said if I make it worse, I could be out for much longer. That frightened me more.
So I'm telling you the truth. Can I sit out Saturday and go back to the doctor first?

Sorry,
Vandana

When did Vandana feel a sharp twinge?
Vandana felt it on Thursday when landing from the long jump.
What made Vandana want to hide the pain at first?
Vandana was scared the coach would think Vandana was weak or pick someone else, and badly wanted to be back.

Telling Nilesh Sir the truth and asking to see the doctor first, because hiding pain could make the injury worse.

The rain had stopped the cricket match, and Samir and Chetan were stuck under the pavilion roof with nothing to do but fight. "You always hog the batting. You never pass the ball. Just like the tournament last year when you didn't let me bowl once!" Samir shouted. Chetan went red. "That's not true! And you always sulk when you're out early!" Other boys started watching. Samir's anger was loud, but even he could hear it wasn't going anywhere. He took a breath. "Okay. Forget always. Today, you batted for twelve overs and I got two. I want to open next innings." Chetan paused. "...Fine. Today that's fair." When the rain stopped, Samir opened. They didn't mention last year again.

How many overs did Chetan bat today?
Twelve overs.
What was Samir feeling at the start of the quarrel?
He felt angry and frustrated, using 'always' and 'never' and bringing up last year's tournament.
What did Samir do that made the argument solvable?
He dropped 'always' and stated a specific present issue, twelve overs to two, with a clear request.
How did Chetan respond to the absolute accusations?

The school bus was leaving in ten minutes and the power had gone out. In the half-dark, Amandeep's mother called from the kitchen, "Take your lunch, your water bottle, the permission slip, your library book, your jersey for PT, and don't forget to give Ma'am the money for the trip!"

Amandeep, eight, nodded and ran around the flat. Her little sister Leela was crying about her own shoes. The torch flickered.

When the bus came, Amandeep had her lunch and the library book. The slip, the jersey and the money were still on the table.

That evening her mother sat with her. "That was too many things at once, wasn't it?" Together they drew a little checklist with five pictures and stuck it by the door.

What did Amandeep leave on the table?
The slip, the jersey and the money.
How might Amandeep have felt running around the dark flat?
She probably felt flustered and rushed, trying to hold too many things in her head at once.
How did Amandeep's mother fix the problem, and why might it work?
They drew a checklist with pictures by the door, so Amandeep doesn't have to remember everything in her head.
What might it have been like for Leela that morning?
Leela was crying about her shoes, so she probably felt upset and left out in the rush.

In Fifi's closet, she hangs all of her clothes on colored plastic hangers.  She has clothes hanging on 7 pink hangers, 4 green hangers, one less blue hanger than there are green hangers, and one less yellow hanger than there are blue hangers.  What is the total number of colored hangers in Fifi's closet?

With 4 green hangers, 1 less blue hanger than there are green hangers is 4-1=3 blue hangers.
With 3 blue hangers, 1 less yellow hanger less than there are blue hangers is 3-1=2 yellow hangers.
With 7 pink hangers, the total number of colored hangers in Fifi's closet is 7+4+3+2=16 hangers.
The answer is 16.

Dear Mridul,
Congratulations on the new job and the new scooter! Since you asked for advice, here are three things I learned the hard way.
One: the phone goes in the seat box before you start the scooter. Not on silent, not in your pocket. Last year a message lit up my screen, I missed a turn and nearly clipped a school van. Nothing happened, but it could have.
Two: when someone important is talking to you, your boss, a client, Amma, put the phone face down and look at them. You'll hear twice as much.
Three: anything that can really go wrong, like the salary sheet or a client's payment, gets checked by a second person. I ask my colleague to check mine, and I check hers. No shame in it. Tired eyes miss things.
You'll be great. Call me on Sunday, but not while riding!
Your Bhaiya,
Yash

Where does Yash say the phone should go before starting the scooter?
The phone goes in the seat box.
How does Yash feel remembering the near-miss with the school van?
Yash feels uneasy and sobered, knowing it could have gone badly even though nothing happened.
Which of Yash's habits protects critical work, and how?
Having a second person check anything that can really go wrong, like the salary sheet, because tired eyes miss things.
How might Mridul feel reading the letter?
Mridul might feel cared for and a bit amused, especially at the reminder not to call while riding.

Monday. At the park, Yash announced a club called the Thunder Owls. “Secret handshake: two knocks, one flap.” Leela practised it until her wrist hurt. Two more children were made members after they got it right.
Thursday. A boy named Mihir asked to join. “What's the handshake?” Yash asked. Mihir fumbled it, and Yash shrugged. “Not yet.” The others looked at their shoes. Leela said nothing.
Sunday. Leela taught Mihir the handshake behind the swings, twice. When he did it right, she went to Yash. “He knows it.” Yash hesitated, then flapped both arms. “Okay. Welcome, Owl.”

What was the Thunder Owls' secret handshake?
The handshake was two knocks and one flap.
What might Leela have been feeling when Leela said nothing on Thursday while Mihir was turned away?
Leela probably felt uneasy and uncertain about speaking up, since the others looked at their shoes and Leela taught the handshake secretly three days later.
What choice did Leela make on Sunday, and what did it change?
Leela taught Mihir the handshake and then spoke to Yash about him, so the ritual that marked who belongs was used to let Mihir in.
How might Mihir have seen the club after fumbling the handshake on Thursday?
Mihir may have felt shut out and embarrassed, so being taught the handshake by Leela probably felt like being welcomed after all.
A chef needs to make french fries.  He can get 25 fries out of 1 potato.  He has 15 potatoes and he needs 200 fries.  How many potatoes will he have leftover?

To make 200 fries he will need 200 / 25 fries per potato = 8 potatoes.
He has 15 potatoes - 8 potatoes = 7 leftover potatoes.
The answer is 7.
Raj says 8 - 3 = 11. Is he right?

Answer: No. 8 - 3 = 5. Raj added instead of taking away.

Taking away makes the number smaller, so the answer must be less than 8. Read the sign together: - means take away. Act it out with 8 objects.

Dear Binita,

You asked how we chose the safety plan for the school trip. Honestly, I almost got it wrong.

My first idea was to ban all street food so that nobody could get a stomach upset. Zero risk, I thought. It felt so tidy.

Then I sat down with the list of what actually goes wrong on trips. Stomach upsets happen, but children getting separated in crowds happens far more, and it's much scarier. So we let the children eat at two stalls the teachers checked, and we put our energy into buddy pairs, coloured caps, and a head count at every stop.

Nobody got lost. Two children had mild tummy aches and were fine by the evening.

Next year, you plan it with me. — Vijay

What did Vijay first want to ban?
Vijay first wanted to ban all street food.
Why did banning street food feel attractive to Vijay at first?
It felt tidy and reassuring to make one risk zero, which gave Vijay a sense of control.
Which choice worked, and why?
Putting effort into buddy pairs, caps and head counts worked, because it cut the more common and serious risk of children getting lost.
How might Binita use this letter when planning next year?
Binita could feel more confident starting from what most often goes wrong, rather than from what can be made perfectly safe.

Monday: Swati Dadi taught Payal, five, a short evening prayer. Payal mixed up the lines and giggled.

Thursday: They said it together while lighting the lamp, clapping on each beat. Payal got the first two lines alone.

Next Monday: Payal stood before the lamp, folded her hands and said the whole prayer, swaying to its rhythm. Then she started teaching it to her teddy, line by line. Swati Dadi pretended not to watch, smiling.

Who taught Payal the evening prayer?
Swati Dadi taught her.
Why might Swati Dadi pretend not to watch while smiling?
She felt proud and happy but did not want to make Payal self-conscious while she practised with her teddy.
What helped Payal remember the prayer?
Saying it together each evening and clapping on the beat gave her repetition and rhythm to hold the words.
What would change if Swati Dadi had scolded Payal for mixing up lines?
Payal might have felt embarrassed and lost interest, instead of giggling and trying again.
Give me one sentence about the ocean that starts with "Under" and ends with "light".
Under the waves, fish glide through shafts of light.

Last year I changed so many times my own mother called me Mr Updates. I'm Eshaan, and between Class 9 and 10 I was a gym guy, then a poetry guy with a notebook, then I tried to be a gamer like Saurabh and his group, then I quit all of it. Every time, I was sure, for about six weeks. Then it would feel fake, like wearing someone else's shirt. The worst part was that I got snappy with everyone. Saurabh asked once why I'd stopped coming to gaming nights and I bit his head off. I stayed in my room a lot. Looking back, I think I was trying on selves in a trial room. The school counsellor told me that's normal at our age, and I didn't believe it then. I sort of do now. I kept the poetry notebook.

What did Eshaan's mother call Eshaan?
Mr Updates.
How did Eshaan feel after about six weeks in each new role?
Eshaan felt it was fake and uncomfortable, like wearing someone else's shirt.
What could Eshaan say to Saurabh now, looking back?
He could apologise for snapping and explain he was going through a confusing time, which might repair the friendship.
How might Saurabh have felt when Eshaan bit his head off?
Saurabh probably felt hurt and confused, since he had only asked why Eshaan stopped coming.

In Class 6 our teacher asked us to write a paragraph: “Should school start later?” I'm Rafiq, and I thought it would be easy. I wrote, “Yes, because I'm sleepy.” That was it.
Ms Gurleen gave it back with a note: “Why? Give three reasons. Start with your opinion. End by saying it again.”
So I tried again. I wrote my opinion first. Then three reasons: children would be less sleepy, there would be less traffic at seven, and we could eat breakfast properly. Then I finished with my opinion again.
It was the first time a paragraph felt like a building instead of a pile of bricks.

What did Rafiq write the first time?
“Yes, because I'm sleepy.”
How did Rafiq feel when the paragraph finally worked?
Rafiq felt proud and satisfied, as if the paragraph was a building instead of a pile of bricks.
What did Ms Gurleen's note teach Rafiq?
It showed how to organise a paragraph: opinion first, three reasons, then the opinion again.
How might Ms Gurleen feel reading Rafiq's second paragraph?
Ms Gurleen is likely pleased to see the advice used and the argument made clearly.

The ceiling fan in the Kalimpong college seminar room creaked with every turn. Aparna Ma'am had asked the second-years whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat. Dolma had a point about the vegetable sellers from her village, who had no other bags. She lifted one finger just above the desk and leaned a little forward. Bikash, beside her, thought she was stretching. Then Suraj started speaking over the girl who was already talking. Dolma kept her finger up and watched Aparna Ma'am's face. When Suraj finally paused, Ma'am turned. "Dolma, you've been waiting. Go on." Dolma spoke slowly about the sellers and the bags. Two students wrote it down, and Ma'am said, "That changes the question." Bikash whispered, "I thought you were just yawning."

What was the seminar question about?
Whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat.
What does Dolma's lifted finger and forward lean suggest about her?
They suggest she was eager to contribute and determined to wait her turn; Bikash read the same movement as stretching, which shows these cues can be missed.
Which approach worked better, Suraj's or Dolma's, and why?
Dolma's, because she signalled and waited, so when Aparna Ma'am called on her the room listened and wrote down her point.
How did Bikash see Dolma's signal?
He thought she was stretching or yawning, so he did not realise she had something to say until Ma'am called on her.

messages.content: A busy port has 4 cruise ships and twice as many cargo ships. The number of sailboats is 6 more than the cargo ships and seven times more than fishing boats. How many vessels are there on the water?

There are 4 x 2 = 8 cargo ships.
There are 8 + 6 = 14 sailboats.
There are 14/7 = 2 fishing boats.
There are 4 + 8 + 14 + 2 = 28 vessels on the water.
The answer is 28.

In the site office in Johannesburg, the whiteboard had a new column: 'Delivered - no drama'. Omar, the project manager, added a gold star beside Zanele's name for finishing the third floor early.
'This is what I like,' he told the team. 'People who get it done and don't bring me problems.'
Nobody mentioned Thabo, who had asked last month why the concrete tests were being signed before the results came back. Thabo now did night inventory in the yard.
Zanele looked at her gold star and felt her stomach tighten. She had noticed the same thing as Thabo. She had said nothing.
Her younger brother's university fees were due in March. And the crew had been good to her, sharing lunch, covering her first mistakes.
She smiled for the photo Omar took of the board.

What did Omar add beside Zanele's name?
He added a gold star for finishing the third floor early.
Why does Zanele's stomach tighten as she looks at her gold star?
She knows she noticed the same problem as Thabo and stayed quiet, so the reward feels wrong even as fear and loyalty keep her silent.
What turning point is open to Zanele at this stage?
She could quietly talk to Thabo, note what she has seen, and look for a proper channel such as a safety officer to raise the concrete tests.
What might Thabo be experiencing on night inventory?
Thabo is likely feeling punished and isolated for asking an honest question while quieter colleagues are praised.

Ivan buys 48 apples to make 24 full-size pies. He ends up not using as many as he thought because he decides to make mini pies instead of full-size ones, which only use 1/2 an apple each. If Ivan bakes 24 mini pies, how many apples does he have leftover?

Ivan wants to bake 24 pies which use 1/2 an apple each, 24 pies x 1/2 apple each = 12 apples
Ivan uses 12 of his 48 apples, 48 - 12 = 36 apples
Ivan has 36 apples leftover.
The answer is 36.

The night before her graduate-scheme interview in Lisbon, Priscila sat on her bed with her eyes closed and walked through it. The lift to the fourth floor. The glass meeting room. Two interviewers, one smiling, one not. "Tell us about your final-year project." She pictured herself explaining the flood-sensor network, fine. Then the unsmiling one leaning forward: "Why didn't you use a mesh network?" In her imagination, her mind went white. She opened her eyes. Her flatmate Nour looked up from the sofa. "Stuck?" "I just froze in my own daydream," Priscila said. Together they worked out one sentence, and she wrote it on a card: "I'm not sure, but let me reason it out loud." She practised it five times. The next afternoon the question was about battery life, not mesh networks. She said the sentence, and then she reasoned it out.

What was Priscila's final-year project?
The flood-sensor network.
What did Priscila feel during the imagined follow-up?
Priscila felt a flash of panic, her mind going white even in the daydream.
What else could Priscila rehearse the same way?
She could picture other hard moments, like running out of time or a question on a weak topic, and prepare a calm line for each.
How does Nour help?
Nour notices Priscila is stuck and helps work out the calm sentence, turning a scary imagined moment into something practical.

By second period, half of Class 10 in their Kolkata school knew that Minakshi's parents were separating. She had told only one person: Alka. Minakshi's hands shook as she typed in the class group: "Want to know Alka's secret? She copied her whole science project from her cousin." Her thumb hovered over send. She hated Alka right then. She wanted her to feel exactly this. Instead she deleted it, walked twice around the basketball court, and sat on the steps until her breathing slowed. After school she caught Alka alone near the cycle stand. "I told you that because I trusted you. Why?" Alka's face crumpled. "I told Nisha, and she told everyone. I'm so sorry." Minakshi didn't forgive her yet. "I need time to decide if I can trust you again."

Who had Minakshi told about her parents?
Minakshi had told only one person: Alka.
What was Minakshi feeling as her thumb hovered over send?
Minakshi felt betrayed and full of hatred, wanting Alka to feel the same exposure.
Which steps made Minakshi's path wiser than exposing Alka?
She deleted the post, walked to cool down, confronted Alka privately and took time to decide about trust.
How does Alka see Minakshi's question at the cycle stand?
Alka feels ashamed and sorry, knowing her slip to Nisha hurt her best friend badly.

Their visit did not continue long after the question and answer above mentioned; and while Mr. Darcy was attending them to their carriage, Miss Bingley was venting her feelings in criticisms on Elizabeth's person, behaviour, and dress. But Georgiana would not join her. Her brother's recommendation was enough to insure her favour: his judgment could not err; and he had spoken in such terms of Elizabeth, as to leave Georgiana without the power of finding her otherwise than lovely and amiable. When Darcy returned to the saloon, Miss Bingley could not help repeating to him some part of what she had been saying to his sister.

Retell this for a child in three sentences.

After the visit ends, Miss Bingley criticises Elizabeth's looks, behaviour and dress while Mr. Darcy sees the visitors to their carriage. Georgiana will not join in, because her brother has spoken so well of Elizabeth that she finds her lovely and kind. When Darcy returns, Miss Bingley repeats some of her criticism to him.

Swati, beti, your sandals are in the kitchen again. Sit, let your Dada Nilesh tell you something. When I was a boy in Nashik, I lost one chappal every week. My mother scolded me each evening, and I felt small, because I did want to be good. One day I noticed something. Every evening, the first thing I did was wash my feet at the tap by the door; Amma would not let anyone in otherwise, so I never skipped it. I thought, the tap is my bell. Feet washed, then chappals under the bench, then satchel on the nail. Tap, bench, nail. I said it in my head for a week. After a month my hands did it without me. Amma stopped scolding. Now, beti, what do you always do when you come in?

Where did young Nilesh wash his feet every evening?
Young Nilesh washed his feet at the tap by the door.
How did young Nilesh feel when his mother scolded him about the lost chappals?
Young Nilesh felt small and a bit ashamed, because Nilesh did want to be good but kept forgetting.
What other approach could young Nilesh have tried if the tap trick had not worked?
Young Nilesh could have asked Amma to remind him for the first few days, or kept a basket right beside the tap, so the job was impossible to walk past.
How might Nilesh's Amma have seen the change in him?
Amma would have been pleased and surprised to find the chappals under the bench every evening, with no need to scold.

September, first week. Pankaj stood outside the career centre at the university in Nagpur, holding his marksheet. First class. But inside, other students talked about "networking" and "online profiles" and "summer internships at big firms." His father farmed cotton; nobody at home had ever had an internship. He turned around and walked back to the hostel.

October, a Wednesday. Francis, a final-year student who ran a peer mentoring group for first-generation students, sat next to him in the canteen. "You looked lost at the career centre. I was too, my first year." He pulled out a sample CV and showed Pankaj how to write one.

December, a Monday. Pankaj walked into the career centre with a printed CV. He still felt his heart racing. But three other students from the mentoring group were in the queue, and one of them waved.

What did Pankaj's father farm?
Cotton.
Why did Pankaj turn around and walk back to the hostel in September?
He felt out of place and doubtful, hearing unfamiliar words like networking and internships, even though his marks were first class.
How did Francis help Pankaj feel he belonged?
Francis shared his own first-year confusion and showed Pankaj how to write a CV, then brought him into a community of first-generation students.
How might Pankaj's father see his son going to the career centre?
His father might feel proud and a bit amazed, since nobody at home had done this before.
