Parul's mother, Ganga, called three times a day to ask where she was, and had asked to see her bank messages "just to be safe." Her father paid the hostel fees, and both parents used money like a leash: "If you skip the coaching class, we will hold back your allowance." Parul felt she could not say what she thought. Once she booked the wrong date for her train home and paid the change fee herself; Ganga only said, "You'll remember next time." That month her parents' arguments started again, and each sent Parul long messages about the other. She felt caught between them and wanted to pick a side. Instead she told both, "I love you and I can't fix this. Please don't send me each other's words." She sat down with her mother and said, "Let's agree on a monthly budget, and I'll send a spending summary on Sundays. And I want to try a part-time job." Ganga hesitated, then said she was scared. Parul's roommate Leela told her about a weekend library job. Parul took it and began managing her own money, and she stopped buying takeaways she did not need. Ganga stopped asking for her messages once the Sunday summary arrived.

What job did Leela tell Parul about?
Leela told Parul about a weekend library job.
How did Parul's handling of her parents' fights differ from how she handled her mother's control over money?
With the fights she refused to take a side and said she loved both and could not fix it; with the money control she negotiated a monthly budget with Sunday summaries and began earning.
What was Ganga feeling when she hesitated and said she was scared?
She felt anxious and afraid for Parul, and her worry was behind the checking.
What could Parul do next to keep support from turning into control?
She could keep the budget and the summaries, keep earning, and speak honestly with her parents instead of lying or manipulating them for money.
These three short sentences repeat themselves, so combine them smoothly: The book was old. The book was torn. The book was mine.
The old, torn book was mine.

In Madrid, Sofia had a place on a design competition shortlist. The final entries were due Monday.
On Sunday she sat at her desk with three nearly finished designs. None of them felt right. The colours were slightly off. One corner wasn't balanced.
Her flatmate Lucia peeked in. "Which one are you sending?"
"None. They're not ready."
"They look amazing."
"They're not perfect. I'll enter next year."
Lucia stared. "You said that last year."
On Monday the deadline passed. Sofia felt a wave of relief. By Wednesday, when the winners were posted, the relief had turned into a heavy ache.

When were the final entries due?
On Monday.
How did Sofia's feelings change from Monday to Wednesday?
She felt relief when the deadline passed, which turned into a heavy ache when the winners were posted.
What went wrong, and what could help next time?
Not sending anything guaranteed failure; entering the best good-enough design, perhaps chosen with Lucia, would give her a chance.
What is Lucia experiencing when Sofia says "next year"?
Lucia seems frustrated and worried, having heard the same promise last year.

In their small town near Rampur, everyone in Irfan's family had taken arts after Class 10: his father, the schoolteacher; his uncles; his sister Tanuja, now doing a B.A. Irfan, fifteen, spent his evenings at the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans. On the day the stream forms came, he ticked arts without thinking. "That's what we do," he said. Tanuja looked at the form, then at him. "Irfan, you fix phones for half the lane. You love circuits. Did you decide this, or did it just happen?" He shrugged. "Changing means talking to Abbu, and science is harder, and maybe I'll fail." "Maybe," Tanuja said. "Or maybe you'll love it. You haven't actually chosen anything yet." Their mother, Zeenat, called from the kitchen, "Talk to your Abbu tonight, beta. He'll listen." Irfan stared at the form for a long time. Then he picked up the eraser.

Where did Irfan spend his evenings?
At the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans.
Why did Irfan tick arts without thinking?
Everyone in the family had taken arts, so it felt natural and safe, and Irfan was afraid that changing meant talking to Abbu, a harder subject and maybe failing.
What choice did Irfan make at the end, and what made it possible?
He picked up the eraser to rethink the form. Tanuja's question, whether he decided or it just happened, and Zeenat's encouragement helped him see he hadn't chosen yet.
How might Tanuja feel watching Irfan tick arts without a second thought?
She is probably worried he is giving up something he loves, and she cares enough to question him gently.
My manager keeps adding tasks without asking if I have time.
That is hard to manage. It may help to talk about it calmly and with facts, such as a list of what you are already working on.
How do I start that conversation?
You could say, 'I want to do these well. Can we look at my list and decide what comes first?' It puts the focus on priorities, not complaints.
What if the manager says everything is urgent?
Ask which item should be done first if all cannot be finished. That makes the trade-off clear without arguing.
Should I put it in writing?
A short follow-up email confirming the priorities is useful. It gives both sides a clear record.
And if nothing changes?
Then you may want to raise it with a senior person or the HR team. Keep your notes factual so they can see the pattern.
We watched the sunrise, and then we are eating breakfast at the cafe. Please fix this.

We watched the sunrise, and then we ate breakfast at the cafe.
Why: past tense ("are eating" -> "ate").

I'm Maria. I've lived across from Simran's family in this old part of Ahmedabad for twenty years. This winter I kept seeing her, nine or ten years old, sitting on the steps of the stepwell near our lane with a notebook. Every evening she'd stop the elderly men playing cards and ask them things. Once I heard her say, 'But who built it? Was it a queen?' One uncle told her a long story about a queen who built it so travellers would never go thirsty. Simran wrote fast, tongue poking out. Later she knocked on my door to ask what I remembered of the well when it still had water. I don't know what drew her there. But she looked happy doing it.

Where did Maria keep seeing Simran sit in the evenings?
On the steps of the stepwell near their lane, with a notebook.
What does Simran writing fast with her tongue poking out suggest about her?
It suggests she was absorbed and curious about the story, though Maria can't be sure what drew her.
How could Simran's teacher support her interest in local history?
The teacher could invite her to share the stories with the class and help her compare them with a library book about the city.
How might the elderly card players feel about Simran's questions?
They might enjoy being asked, glad that a child cares about the old stories they carry.

Johnny is a guitar player and he has three colors of guitar picks: red, blue, and yellow. Half of his picks are red, one-third of the picks are blue, and the rest are yellow.  If he has 12 blue picks, what is the total number of yellow picks in his collection?

If one third (1/3) of his picks are blue, then 3 times the total number of blue picks equals his total pick count, or 3*12=36 picks
If half of the picks are red, then he has 36/2=18 red picks
If the rest of the picks are yellow, then he has 36-18-12=6 yellow picks
The answer is 6.

"We won!" Nilesh burst through the door, bat on his shoulder. "Thirty-two runs, didi! I hit the ball so perfectly, nobody could stop me."
"Nice!" said Gurleen, looking up from her homework. "And last Sunday?"
"Last Sunday doesn't count. The umpire was Pinku's cousin. Totally unfair."
"You were bowled first ball."
"Because the bat was cracked! Anyone would get out with that bat."
"Isn't that the same bat?"
Nilesh looked at the bat. "It's different today."
"How?"
"Today I was playing properly."
Gurleen grinned. "So when you win, it's you. When you lose, it's the umpire and the bat?"
"Obviously," said Nilesh, and went off to find a snack.

How many runs did Nilesh score today?
Nilesh scored thirty-two runs.
Why does Nilesh insist last Sunday doesn't count?
Nilesh feels embarrassed about being bowled first ball, so blaming the umpire and the cracked bat lets him keep feeling like a great player.
What question could help Nilesh learn from last Sunday?
Someone could ask, 'If the bat and umpire were fine, what would you practise?' so he looks at his own play too.
How does Gurleen see Nilesh's two stories?
Gurleen notices it's the same bat both days and finds it funny that wins belong to him and losses to someone else. 😅

Read this:

Wasim, you're worried about the ums? Let me tell you about my first board presentation. Twelve people round a long table, and I said "um" so often that one director started tapping his pen every time. Tap. Um. Tap. I could hear it. I finished red in the face, sure they all thought Kunal knew nothing.
Afterwards my manager, Mrs. Fernandes, said, "Your numbers were solid. The ums don't mean you don't know. They mean you're scared of silence." She told me: when you feel an um coming, close your mouth, breathe, and let the room wait one second.
At the next board meeting I tried it. The pauses felt endless to me. But the same director told me later I seemed confident. The silence was helping them think too.
So, your ums are normal. Just try swapping a few of them for a breath.

How many people were round the long table?
Twelve people were round the long table.
How did Kunal feel as the director tapped the pen?
Kunal felt humiliated and anxious, red in the face, sure they all thought Kunal knew nothing.
What turning point came at the next board meeting?
Kunal replaced ums with a breath and a one-second pause, as Mrs. Fernandes suggested, and the director later read it as confidence. 🙂
How did the director see the pauses at the later meeting?
The director read them as confidence, and the silence gave the listeners time to think.

messages.content:
What did Pierre imagine about himself after his success in Petersburg?

Pierre finished what he had begun. It was the sequel to his complacent reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he was chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society and to the whole world.
He felt that he was chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society and to the whole world.
Joseph drives his car at 50 mph for 2.5 hours. Kyle drives his car at 62 mph for 2 hours. How many more miles does Joseph drive than Kyle?

Joseph travels for 50 * 2.5 = 125 miles.
Kyle travels for 62 * 2 = 124 miles.
Joseph drives for 125 - 124 = 1 mile more than Kyle.
The answer is 1.

Could you recap this passage for me? Two sentences is enough.

For a minute or two she stood looking at the house, and wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in livery came running out of the wood—(she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish)—and rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles. It was opened by another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog; and both footmen, Alice noticed, had powdered hair that curled all over their heads. She felt very curious to know what it was all about, and crept a little way out of the wood to listen.

Alice sees a footman in uniform run out of the wood and knock at a house, and another with frog-like eyes opens the door. Both have powdered, curly hair, and Alice, very curious, creeps out to listen.

Tutor's note, pledge ceremony, Friday
Our final-year nursing students took their pledge this morning, candles in hand. Two reactions stood out.
Parul's voice shook on the line about caring for every patient as if they were her own family. Afterwards she said her grandmother had been a village midwife, and this felt like a promise to her too.
Simran grinned through it and told me later, "It's just a ceremony, ma'am. The real promise is the licence exam."
I didn't correct either of them. I asked both, separately, what the pledge would mean on a hard night shift. Simran thought for a long time, then said, "Not leaving a patient because I'm tired, I suppose." Parul said nearly the same.
Same words, very different weight for each. Next year I'll open the rehearsal by asking the class what they think they're promising, before the candles come out.

What did the students hold during the pledge?
They held candles.
Why did Parul's voice shake during the pledge?
Parul felt deeply moved, because her grandmother had been a village midwife and the pledge felt like a promise to her too.
What does the tutor plan to do next year, and why?
Ask the class what they think they're promising before the ceremony, since the same words carry different weight for each person.
How did Simran see the pledge at first?
Simran saw it as just a ceremony, with the licence exam as the real promise, though later linked it to not leaving a patient when tired.

Two young men came into my shop in Aminabad one afternoon while I was weighing dal. Nilesh and Tejas, they said, with a tablet. They wanted to show me a billing tool. Nothing fancy: a form, a list of my usual items, a button that printed a bill on a small printer they had brought. Tejas said they had put it together in six weeks without writing any real code, and that mine was the eleventh of twenty shops they were visiting.
I tried it for a sale of rice and soap. The item list had no ghee, and the bill had no space for customers who buy on credit. Nilesh wrote both things in his notebook. Tejas asked, "Would you pay for this if it had those?" I said maybe.
They came back ten days later. The ghee was there. So was a credit column.

What two things did Nilesh write in his notebook?
The item list had no ghee, and the bill had no space for customers who buy on credit.
What might Tejas have been feeling when he asked "Would you pay for this?"
He was probably hopeful and a little anxious to learn whether the bare tool had real value to shopkeepers.
What did the founders' approach get right?
They put a simple six-week version in front of real shop owners before building more, and fixed what users actually needed.
How does the shopkeeper see the tool after ten days?
The shopkeeper sees that they listened, since ghee and a credit column were added, which may turn that maybe into a yes.

Monday: May heat in Delhi. By afternoon Lalit clung to Vishal's leg, whining, too sleepy to play but too fussy to nap.
Wednesday: The same again. Then Vishal noticed the sippy cup, still half full from the morning. He offered it. Lalit drank it all and said, "More!"
Friday: Vishal filled the cup at every meal and in between. Lalit spent the afternoon pushing his toy truck round the room, humming.

What was still half full from the morning?
The sippy cup.
What does Lalit's clinging and whining on Monday suggest?
He was uncomfortable and fussy, likely thirsty in the heat but unable to explain it.
What rhythm helped on Friday?
Filling the cup at every meal and in between, so Lalit got water regularly without having to ask.
What might Monday afternoon be like for Vishal?
Tiring and puzzling, with a clingy child who would neither play nor nap.

Winter holiday club, Day 3: carer's note.
Gautam spent the whole morning at the big construction set. He started a bridge between two tables, failed twice when it sagged in the middle, then added a triangle of pieces underneath and it held. I watched him mutter to himself, test it with a toy truck, and start a second, longer bridge.
At twelve Ishita called everyone for lunch. He didn't hear her. When I tapped his shoulder he looked up, blinking, as if waking. "Is it lunch already? I just started." He had been there two and a half hours.
He ate quickly and went straight back, calm and bright-eyed all afternoon.
Plan: tomorrow I will offer him a slightly harder bridge, one that can hold the heavier truck.

What did Gautam add to make the bridge hold?
A triangle of pieces underneath.
What does "Is it lunch already? I just started" suggest about Gautam?
Gautam was so absorbed and happy in the challenge that he lost track of time, and he stayed calm and bright-eyed afterwards.
Why is the carer's plan a good next step?
A slightly harder bridge keeps the challenge just above his skill, which is what kept him absorbed, without tipping into frustration.
How might Ishita see Gautam not hearing the lunch call?
Ishita might first think he was ignoring her, but seeing the bridges she would likely understand he was completely absorbed. 🙂

messages.content: Ravi fills a bucket using small cups and counts 10 cups. Sita fills the same bucket using big mugs and counts 5 mugs. Who is right?

Answer: Both are right. The mug is bigger, so fewer mugs are needed.

The bucket did not change; only the unit changed. Bigger unit, smaller number. To compare two containers fairly we must use the SAME cup for both.

The kitchen tap has been leaking since Monday. I would be grateful if it could be repaired as soon as possible.

Dear Diary,
One month in Pune. My room is fine. College is fine. I am not fine.
Everyone here seems to know each other already. At lunch I sit with my phone and pretend to text. I miss Amma's sambar and the noise at home.
Today a senior, Shankar, saw me alone in the library and asked if I wanted to join the photography club walk on Saturday. I said, "Maybe."
Honestly, I'm scared I'll be awkward. But I'm also tired of pretending to text.
So I'm going. I told Amma on the phone. She said, "Take photos of everything and send me."
— Jatin

What did Shankar invite Jatin to?
The photography club walk on Saturday.
What was Jatin feeling at lunch while pretending to text?
Jatin felt lonely and homesick, embarrassed to be alone.
What step is Jatin taking to build belonging?
Jatin is accepting Shankar's invitation to the club walk, despite fear of being awkward.
How might Amma feel hearing Jatin's plan?
Amma likely feels relieved and encouraging, glad to hear about a step toward new friends.

On Sunday morning the flat smelled of floor cleaner. Nana and Nani were coming for lunch, and Noor moved fast, lips pressed tight, wiping the same table twice. She didn't say a word about being worried.
Dhruv followed her from room to room, holding the back of her kurta. When she shut the kitchen door against the pressure-cooker noise, he sat outside it and cried. Noor opened the door. "Dhruv, what happened?" He didn't know. He only hugged her legs.
Noor knelt, and her shoulders dropped. "Ammi's a bit nervous, that's all. Want to help me put out the spoons?"

What did the flat smell of on Sunday morning?
Floor cleaner.
What was Dhruv feeling when he cried outside the kitchen door?
He felt anxious and unsettled, catching Noor's tension even though nobody had said anything was wrong.
How did Noor help Dhruv feel steadier?
She knelt, named her own nervousness simply and gave him a small job beside her, putting out the spoons.
What might Noor realise when Dhruv hugs her legs?
That her quiet worry had spread to him, and that calming herself would help him too.

The satsang met on the second floor of the community centre, and by five the hall smelled of tea and incense. Lalremsiami, who had moved from Aizawl for work eight months earlier, ate lunch alone most days at the office.

"You're back! Sit with us," Shalini said, pressing a plate into her hands. Someone asked how her sister's exam had gone. After the singing, Lalremsiami felt a warm ache: the first place in the city that felt like family.

Later she asked Shalini about a line she didn't understand. "Good. Ask the elder. He loves questions." The elder, a retired teacher, laughed and explained.

Lalremsiami glanced at the clock. "I'm meeting my college friends tonight. Can I come next Sunday?"

"Of course. We'll save your seat."

Where did Lalremsiami move from?
Lalremsiami moved from Aizawl.
What did Lalremsiami feel after the singing?
A warm ache of belonging: the satsang was the first place in the city that felt like family.
How can Lalremsiami enjoy the satsang while keeping it healthy?
Keep outside friendships such as the college friends, keep asking questions, and remember that being able to miss a week or leave without losing respect is part of a healthy community.
How does Shalini seem to see Lalremsiami's outside plans?
Shalini welcomes them, saying "Of course. We'll save your seat", which shows the community does not object to outside friendships.

"Who are you texting at midnight?" Akash whispered from the doorway of the room he shared with his younger sister.
"The chatbot," said Aparna. "It never judges. I told it about the fight with Diya, and my marks, and how I feel when Mummy compares me with Neha."
"You didn't tell me."
"You'd tell Mummy."
"Not if you asked me not to. But it doesn't know you, Aparna. It can't come to your school."
She was quiet. "It does help."
"Fine. Use it to sort your thoughts. But you've been low for weeks, haven't you?"
Her eyes filled. "Yes."
"Then let's tell Mummy together tomorrow. I'll sit next to you."
She nodded and closed the app.

Who does Aparna's mother compare her with?
Mummy compares her with Neha.
Why does Aparna tell the chatbot things instead of Akash?
She fears he would tell Mummy, and she likes that the chatbot never judges, so it feels safer to her than people do.
What did Akash suggest as the next step, and why?
He suggested they tell Mummy together the next day, with him sitting beside her, because she has been low for weeks and needs real people. 🤍
How might Akash have felt finding Aparna awake at midnight?
Akash seems worried and a little hurt that she hadn't told him, but he stays gentle and offers to sit beside her.

By nine on Saturday, the kitchen of the Bandra café was roaring. Anand reached past Parveen for the chutney tray, and she spun round. "Move! Do you want to burn us both?"
Anand stepped back as if slapped. For the rest of the shift he chopped in silence, rehearsing a resignation speech. In the auto home he replayed her voice again and again.
But he also remembered her hands shaking as she plated, and the owner hovering by the pass all evening because a food critic was rumoured to be in.
On Sunday morning, before service, he found Parveen with her chai. "Yesterday hurt," he said simply. "I think you were scared, not that you hate me. Can we agree to call out when we pass behind each other?"
Parveen let out a long breath. "You're right. I was terrified. Let's do that."

What did Anand reach past Parveen for?
Anand reached past Parveen for the chutney tray.
What did Anand feel in the auto on the way home?
Anand felt hurt and angry, replaying Parveen's voice and rehearsing a resignation speech.
What made the Sunday conversation work?
Anand waited until both were calm, named his hurt simply without blaming, and suggested a practical call-out.
What was the Saturday rush like for Parveen?
Parveen was terrified, with the owner hovering and a critic possibly in the room, so her sharp words came out of fear.

The four graduates had all taken student loans, and each dealt with the paperwork differently. Farhan took the bank's repayment period, counted back from its end date, and worked out what each month would have to cover. Then he compared that figure with the pay he expected in his first job, so the end date set the size of every step. Salma laid out the sanction letter on the table and noted the interest rate, the date the pause on payments would end, the monthly instalment and any charge for paying early. Anything unclear she took to the bank branch for an explanation. Saurabh felt his stomach turn whenever a bank message arrived, so he left them unopened all through the pause. The first instalment was missed, a late fee appeared, and his credit record took a hit. Ananya's job start was delayed by a few weeks. Before any payment was due, she went to the branch, explained her situation and asked what choices there were, including a longer repayment period.

What did Salma take to the bank branch?
She took anything unclear in the sanction letter to the branch for an explanation.
How did Saurabh's handling of the bank messages differ from Ananya's handling of her delayed job, and what followed?
Saurabh avoided the messages and missed the first instalment, gaining a late fee. Ananya spoke to the branch before any payment was due and asked about options, keeping her choices open.
What was Saurabh feeling when a bank message arrived?
He felt anxious, with a churning stomach, and avoided opening them to escape the worry.
What could Saurabh do now to face the problem?
He could open the messages, ask a trusted adult to sit with him, and talk to the bank about what to do next. Facing the letters is a smaller step than the fear suggests.

Janet buys a multi-flavor pack of cheese sticks. 15 of the sticks are cheddar, 30 are mozzarella, and 45 are pepperjack. If Janet picks a cheese stick at random, what is the percentage chance it will be pepperjack?

First find the total number of cheesesticks: 15 cheddar + 30 mozzarella + 45 pepperjack = 90 cheese sticks
Then divide the number of pepperjack sticks by the total number of cheese sticks and multiply by 100% to express the answer as a percentage: 45 pepperjack sticks / 90 cheese sticks * 100% = 50%
The answer is 50.

You asked me, Sumit, how we got Amma and Appa to stop arriving every weekend without warning. I'm Kavitha, and honestly, we tried everything first.
Rajesh talked to them. I talked to them. We even made a calendar. Every time, Amma heard it as us not wanting her.
Then Rajesh said, "What about Shanthi aunty?" She's his mother's older cousin. She's fair, she's calm, and my own mother trusts her too. Everyone listens to her.
We went to her house with sweets and explained. She didn't take our side. She just listened.
A week later, she had tea with Amma. She said something like, "The children are working so hard. Why don't you visit on the first and third Saturdays? Then you'll find them rested and happy to see you."
Amma agreed. Just like that. The same idea we'd suggested, but from Shanthi aunty, it sounded like care, not rejection.

Which Saturdays did Shanthi aunty suggest for visits?
The first and third Saturdays.
How did Kavitha feel when Amma agreed after Shanthi aunty's visit?
Kavitha felt relieved and a little amazed, since the same idea from the couple had been heard as rejection.
What else could Kavitha and Rajesh do to keep the new arrangement working?
They could make the planned visits warm and welcoming, so Amma sees the change as better time together, not less love.
How did the suggestion look to Amma when it came from Shanthi aunty?
From a calm, fair elder, it sounded like care for the children rather than being pushed away, so Amma agreed more easily.

Saurabh, you pushed ahead at the cinema counter today, didn't you? Let your Raghav dadu tell you something. When I was ten, in Asansol, we queued every week for kerosene. One morning I was late for a cricket match, so I pushed in front of an old woman with a cane. I thought she wouldn't mind. She didn't say anything. She just looked at me, and the whole line went quiet. The shopkeeper served me, and I ran off with the can, feeling like a thief. At the match I dropped two easy catches. That evening I went back and carried her can home for her. She gave me a sweet and said, 'Next time, just ask.' I've never forgotten her face.

What did young Raghav queue for every week?
Kerosene.
How did young Raghav feel running off with the can?
Guilty, like a thief, after the old woman's look and the line going quiet.
Which choice in the story shows young Raghav putting things right?
Going back that evening to carry the old woman's can home, owning what he had done.
What might the old woman have felt when young Raghav pushed in?
Probably hurt and tired, but she chose silence and later kindness, telling him, 'Next time, just ask.'

That morning Deepika, ten, and her brother Varun had fought over the TV remote so loudly that Mummy took it away. "You're the worst brother ever," Deepika said, and didn't talk to him at breakfast. In the evening, at the park in their Nagpur colony, Varun was flying his new kite. A bigger boy from the next building, maybe twelve, grabbed the string and yanked it. The kite tore on a branch. "Baby kite for a baby," the boy said. Varun's chin shook. Deepika was across the park on the swings. She jumped off and ran over, her heart hammering. "Give that string back. He's my brother." The boy was taller, but she didn't move. He dropped the string and walked off. Deepika picked up the torn kite, smoothed it and handed it to Varun. She still didn't say sorry about the remote.

What did the bigger boy do to Varun's kite?
He grabbed the string and yanked it, and the kite tore on a branch.
How can you tell Deepika was scared when she stood up to the boy?
Her heart was hammering and the boy was taller, but she still did not move.
What choice did Deepika make, and why does it matter?
She put aside the morning's fight and ran to defend Varun, showing that family loyalty mattered more to her than the grudge.
How might Varun see his sister after the park?
Varun may feel protected and surprised, knowing his sister stood up for him on the same day she called him the worst brother.

So, for the podcast: I'm Irawati, class eleven, and my story is about a sentence I never finished. We were on Kavitha's terrace, eating roasted corn, and I was telling her about my brother moving to the hostel in Kota. I said, "And the worst part is that Amma keeps setting four plates and then—" and I just stopped. Mid-word. I stared at the water tank. Kavitha told me afterwards she had no idea what the silence meant. Was I angry with her for asking? Embarrassed? About to cry? Just thinking? Honestly, a bit of all of it. What she did was put her corn down and say, "You don't have to finish that. I'm around, whenever." Then she talked about the kite stuck on the wire. Two days later, on the school bus, I finished the sentence, and she just listened.

What were they eating on Kavitha's terrace?
They were eating roasted corn.
What might Irawati have been feeling when the sentence stopped?
Most likely a wave of sadness about the brother's empty place at the table, but by Irawati's own account it was also partly embarrassment and just thinking, so the silence was mixed.
What did Kavitha do well?
Kavitha did not guess or push: putting the corn down, saying Irawati didn't have to finish, and switching to the kite gave space while leaving the door open. 🤍
How did the silence look from Kavitha's side?
Kavitha could not tell whether it meant anger at her, embarrassment, tears or thought, so she chose a reply that would work for any of them.
My son Ayaan Sheikh studies in Class 6, section B. Write a short email, about 70 words, to the school office asking for a copy of his bonafide certificate. I'm his father, Imtiaz Sheikh.

My son, Ayaan Sheikh, studies in Class 6, section B. I would be grateful if you could issue a copy of his bonafide certificate at the earliest. Please let me know if any form or other document is needed from my side, and I will send it promptly. Thank you for your help.
Yours sincerely,
Imtiaz Sheikh
There are 70 cookies in a jar. If there are only 28 cookies left after a week, and Paul took out the same amount each day, how many cookies did he take out in four days?

Paul took out a total of 70-28 = 42 cookies in a week.
Paul took out 42/7 = 6 cookies out of the jar each day.
Over four days, Paul took out 6*4 = 24 cookies from the jar.
The answer is 24.

"Lakshmi, what are you writing every night before bed?"
"Three good things from today. Specific ones."
"Like 'family, health, job'?"
"That's what I wrote the first week, Ujjwal. Same three every night. It did nothing. I got bored of my own list."
"So what now?"
"Now it has to be something from today that I actually noticed. Tonight: one, the autowala who waited while I ran back for my umbrella. Two, the new intern finally laughed at my joke. Three, the smell of rain on the terrace at six."
"That's oddly detailed."
"That's the point. I start looking for them during the day. At the bus stop I'm thinking, is this one of my three?"
"And?"
"And I'm less grumpy. I notice the auto waiting instead of only the traffic."
"Can I try?"
"Go. One from today. Specific."
"...You made chai without being asked."
"Good. That counts."

What was Lakshmi's third good thing tonight?
The smell of rain on the terrace at six.
What was Lakshmi feeling in the first week of the practice?
Lakshmi felt bored with the same generic list, which did nothing to change the day.
What made Lakshmi's practice work?
Choosing fresh, specific things from that day, which made Lakshmi look for good moments and shifted attention to what works.
How might Ujjwal feel after naming the chai?
Ujjwal might feel a little pleased and warm, noticing a small kindness and sharing it with Lakshmi.

Monday: Manoj finished the launch plan for the new delivery app and felt proud. Before sending it to the director, he took it to Tanvir from operations. "Can you tell me what I'm not seeing?" Tanvir looked surprised. "Give me a day."
Wednesday: Tanvir came back with a list. "Your plan assumes riders have smartphones with good data. In the outer areas, half don't. And the festival week is when most riders go home." Manoj's stomach dropped. Then he thanked him. They added a phone-call option and moved the launch by a week.
Two weeks later: The launch went smoothly. A rival app launched during the festival and crashed. The director asked Manoj how he'd known. "I asked Tanvir what I was missing," he said.

What did Tanvir say half the riders in the outer areas don't have?
Smartphones with good data.
What did Manoj feel when Tanvir listed the problems?
His stomach dropped with worry at first, then he felt grateful and thanked Tanvir.
Why did asking 'what am I not seeing?' help the launch?
It brought out risks Manoj hadn't thought of, so the team added a phone-call option and moved the launch.
How might Tanvir feel about being asked for his view?
Tanvir was surprised at first, and probably felt respected and valued for his operations knowledge.

Tejas, you asked me why your grandfather made the tea every morning of his life. Sit. I'll tell you.
When we married in 1986, I was a bride of twenty-four and teaching at the girls' college, and he worked shifts at the post office. My mother-in-law expected me to do everything at home as well. For three months I tried. I was so tired I fell asleep marking papers.
One Sunday he found me like that. He said, "Sarita, this isn't fair. Let's divide it by who's home and who's better at what." He was better at tea and markets. I was better at accounts. We made a list, and every Sunday we checked it.
His mother was shocked for a year. We were patient. By the end she was telling the neighbours her son made the best tea on the street.
So, Tejas, when you marry, talk every week.

What year did Sarita marry?
Sarita married in 1986.
How was Sarita feeling in the first three months of marriage?
She was exhausted and overwhelmed, so tired she fell asleep marking papers while trying to do all the housework alone.
What was the turning point in Sarita's story?
It came when her husband found her asleep and suggested dividing work by who was home and who was better at what, with a weekly check.
How did the mother-in-law's view change over time?
She was shocked for a year, but with the couple's patience she came to boast that her son made the best tea on the street.

Okay, so you want the honest version? Fine. Bidisha ma'am read the first chapter of my short story in front of me and said, "The opening is lazy. You're better than this." Just like that.
I was so angry I didn't talk to her for two days. I told my friends she hated me. But then I noticed she had written notes on every page, in green pen, tiny handwriting. Nobody writes that much for someone they hate, you know?

That's when it clicked for me, Mahima, the girl who used to hide her stories in a drawer. The hard feedback was her caring.

Green.

Mahima felt so angry and stung that she stopped talking to her for two days and believed ma'am hated her.

Noticing the notes on every page, which showed care, and then rewriting the opening three times.

Ms. Warren ran at 6 mph for 20 minutes. After the run, she walked at 2 mph for 30 minutes. How many miles did she run and walk in total?

20 minutes is 20/60=1/3 of an hour.
Ms. Warren ran 6/3=2 miles.
30 minutes is 30/60=1/2 of an hour.
Ms. Warren walked 2/2=1 mile.
Ms Warren ran and walked 2+1=3 miles in total.
The answer is 3.

The day after Nana's funeral Nazia went to school and felt nothing at all, like a coat hung on a hook. Then in maths, the smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry so hard the teacher let her step into the corridor. That evening she sat with the family for prayers, and let her aunt's arm stay round her shoulders.

What she could not shake was the last phone call: she had hung up on Nana after a quarrel about screen time. The thought looped every night. She finally wrote him a letter. "Nana, I am sorry for my tone. I meant to tell you your stories were my favourite thing." Some nights she was furious, and once she said it aloud in the prayer room, "Why him?" Her mother did not shush her. She only said, "Say it. It's allowed."

At school Anand and Darshan talked about cricket scores and nobody mentioned Nana. It stung, until Nazia told Anand at lunch, "Please don't act like it didn't happen. Just ask how I am, or sit with me." Anand went red. "I didn't know what to say." Next day he sat beside her with two rotis, and Darshan brought a small card.

What smell made Nazia cry in maths class?
The smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry.
How did Nazia's guilt about the last phone call and her anger in the prayer room differ, and how did each get voiced?

The guilt was about hanging up on Nana after a quarrel, and she voiced it in a letter of apology. The anger was aimed at whoever let Nana die, and she said it aloud in the prayer room while her mother let her.
What was Nazia feeling when Anand and Darshan talked about cricket and said nothing about Nana?
She felt hurt and alone, because it stung to have her loss ignored.
How could a friend like Anand support Nazia in the days after the funeral?
He could ask how she is, sit with her at lunch and bring something small, as he did, instead of staying silent.

I've been thinking about this afternoon. When you found the wrong sales figure on slide six, you said, "This is the end of me here," and you looked like you meant it. I didn't want to argue in front of the others, so I'm writing instead.

Gautam

The wrong figure was on slide six.
Why did Gautam write rather than argue in the room?
Gautam felt concerned, seeing Hrithik truly believe it was the end, and didn't want to embarrass Hrithik in front of the others.
What steady questions does Gautam use, and why do they help?
Gautam asks the worst realistic outcome, how likely job loss is, and what Hrithik would do, which shrinks the disaster to a correction and an updated deck.
How might Hrithik feel reading the email that evening?
Hrithik would likely feel relieved and a little embarrassed, reassured that one slide doesn't define the job.

Squeeze this into one sentence.

Before Navratri, Jahnavi ate every meal with a cartoon playing on Sudha's phone. She chewed slowly and said nothing.
On the first night of the festival, Sudha left the phone in her room. She sang garba songs while feeding Jahnavi, clapping between bites. Jahnavi clapped too.
Nine days later, when Sudha sat down with the plate, Jahnavi grabbed both her hands and pushed them together. "Clap! Sing!"
Sudha sang. Jahnavi ate, bouncing.

Before Navratri Jahnavi ate silently in front of a cartoon on Sudha's phone, but after Sudha left the phone in her room and fed her with garba songs and clapping, Jahnavi began to clap too, and nine days later she pushed Sudha's hands together, begged her to clap and sing, and ate bouncing.

"Jomon, where's the star?" Harish asked, sitting by the paper lantern on the balcony. It was Christmas week in Kochi.

Jomon, fifteen months, looked straight up and pointed at the lantern.

"And where's Appa's nose?"

Jomon reached out and grabbed it.

Harish's wife laughed from the kitchen. "He can't say ten words, but he understands everything."

"Jomon, bring the ball."

Jomon crawled off and came back with a slipper.

"Close enough," said Harish.

Where did Jomon point when asked about the star?
He looked straight up and pointed at the lantern.
How did Harish feel when Jomon brought a slipper?
Harish seemed amused and warm, laughing it off with "Close enough".
How can Harish keep supporting Jomon's understanding?
Keep asking simple, playful questions about familiar things and show the right object gently when Jomon gets it wrong.
How does Harish's wife see Jomon's language?
She sees that Jomon understands much more than he can say.

Dinner was in twenty minutes, and the cricket highlights were on. "Give it!" Farhan grabbed the remote off the arm of the sofa just as Naveen snatched it back. "It's my turn, you had the cartoons!" "No, you did!" They were both standing now, voices rising over the hum of the ceiling fan. Farhan felt his face go hot; he wanted the match, and he wanted to win the argument even more. Then their mother's voice came from the kitchen: "Should I decide, or will you two?" Farhan gulped, took the kitchen timer from the shelf, and set it. "Ten minutes each. You first, since I grabbed." Naveen blinked, then sat down.

How long before dinner were the boys fighting over the remote?
Dinner was in twenty minutes.
How did Farhan feel while grabbing the remote, and what did he want most?
He felt angry and competitive, as his hot face shows; he wanted the match, and even more he wanted to win the argument.
Which choice worked for the boys, and why?
Using the kitchen timer and taking turns worked, because it was fair and stopped the shouting and grabbing.
How might Naveen have felt when Farhan offered him the first turn?
Surprised and probably a bit relieved, since he blinked and then sat down instead of arguing.
A school has 100 students. Half of the students are girls, the other half are boys.  20% of the girls have dogs at home and 10% of the boys have dogs at home.  How many students own dogs?

Out of 100 students, half are girls and half are boys so there are 100/2 = 50 girls
There are 50 girls out of 100 students means there are 100-50 = 50 boys
20% of the 50 girls have dogs so they have .20*50 = 10 dogs
10% of the 50 boys have dogs so they have .10*50 = 5 dogs
The girls have 10 dogs and the boys have 5 dogs so together, they have 10+5 = 15 dogs
The answer is 15.

The book fair at the community centre was packed on Sunday afternoon, and Jeevan lost his father somewhere between the comics and the cookbooks. He stood still for a moment, breathing hard. He didn't grab the nearest grown-up. He looked for a uniform, and saw a woman in a blue security jacket by the information desk. Her badge said Charu. He walked up. "Excuse me, I'm lost. My name is Jeevan Nair. My father is Mohan Nair. His number is..." He said it clearly and slowly. Charu repeated it back. Then she picked up the microphone: "Mohan Nair, please come to the information desk. Your son Jeevan is waiting." Within three minutes his father appeared, out of breath.

What was the security woman's name?
Her name was Charu.
How did Jeevan feel at first when he lost his father?
He felt frightened and breathless, but he stayed still and chose carefully.
What else could Jeevan do if there were no uniformed staff nearby?
He could go to a stall or desk run by the fair, like the information desk, rather than a random visitor.
How does Jeevan's approach look to Charu?
Charu finds it easy to help because Jeevan gives all the details clearly, so she can call and announce at once.

In Guadalajara, Clara still set the table for Sunday lunch at her abuela Rosa's house, still lit a candle for her grandfather on his day, still volunteered at the Saturday food bank the parish ran. She no longer went to Mass.
It had taken her three years of reading, arguing and long walks to say it plainly: she didn't believe in God. Saying it hadn't made her feel lost, as she had feared. It had made her feel honest.
'And yet you still come to the food bank,' Rosa said, passing the rice.
'I still believe people shouldn't go hungry,' Clara said. 'That part didn't go anywhere.'
Rosa looked at her for a long moment, then nodded. 'Your grandfather would have liked that answer.'

Where does Clara still volunteer on Saturdays?
At the Saturday food bank the parish ran.
How did Clara feel after saying she didn't believe in God?
She felt honest rather than lost, which surprised her because she had feared the opposite.
What shows Clara's values stayed intact after she stopped believing?
She keeps volunteering because people shouldn't go hungry, still lights the candle for her grandfather and still comes to Sunday lunch.
What might Rosa be thinking during her long look at Clara?
Rosa may be weighing sadness that Clara left the faith against respect for her kindness, and she settles on acceptance.

For six weeks, Rashmi had felt flat. Not sad about anything; just grey. She stopped drawing, cried in the shower, and lay awake. She'd read about this in a health poster at school: when it keeps going for weeks, tell someone.
The problem was timing. It was exam week, her parents were at a family wedding in another city, and the school counsellor only came on Tuesdays. It was Thursday.
She almost decided to wait. Instead, that evening, she called her aunt Nazia, who lived across town. "I think something's wrong with me. I've been feeling bad for weeks."
Nazia didn't brush it off. She came over within the hour, stayed the night, and called Rashmi's parents with her. Next morning she rang the school and booked the counsellor for Tuesday, and a family doctor for Saturday.

How long had Rashmi felt flat?
For six weeks.
What was Rashmi feeling when she almost decided to wait?
Rashmi felt tired and unsure, tempted to wait because everything seemed badly timed.
Why was calling Nazia the right step despite the bad timing?
Because the feeling had lasted weeks, and a trusted adult could act straight away and connect Rashmi to her parents, the counsellor and a doctor.
How might Rashmi's parents have felt getting that call at the wedding?
They were likely worried and sad not to be there, but relieved that Rashmi told someone and wasn't alone.

A movie ticket costs $5. The cost of the popcorn is 80% of the cost of the ticket and a can of soda costs 50% of the cost of the popcorn. A family bought 4 tickets, 2 sets of popcorn, and 4 cans of soda. How much did they spend?

The cost of the popcorn is $5 x 80/100 = $4.
The cost of a can of soda is $4 x 50/100 = $2.
The cost of 4 tickets is $5 x 4 = $20.
The cost of 2 sets of popcorn is $4 x 2 = $8.
The cost of 4 cans of soda is $2 x 4 = $8.
Therefore, the family paid a total of $20 + $8 + $8 = $36.
The answer is 36.

Friday
Today I finally did it. On Tuesday I lost Tenzin's earphones at the swimming pool, and for three days I dodged him. Kept saying I'd "check at home". Felt awful every time he looked at me.
This morning before assembly I just said it: "I lost them at the pool. I'm sorry. I'll pay you back from my pocket money in two weeks."
He stared for a second, then laughed. "Bro, I thought you were angry with me for three days!"
Then he said, "And my charger that stopped working, that was you too, right?" I said no, I never touched the charger, but the earphones were totally on me. He thought about it and said okay.
We ate lunch together like normal. Honestly, three days of hiding felt worse than one minute of sorry.
Karthik

Where did Karthik lose Tenzin's earphones?
Karthik lost them at the swimming pool.
How did Karthik feel during the three days of dodging?
Karthik felt awful every time Tenzin looked over, weighed down by guilt and the effort of hiding.
Which part of Karthik's apology worked, and why?
Karthik said plainly what happened, apologised and offered to pay back in two weeks, then calmly refused blame for the charger, owning the real mistake without taking all the fault.
What had the three days been like for Tenzin?
Tenzin thought Karthik was angry with him, so the dodging was more confusing and hurtful than the lost earphones.

Ganga Didi, you once asked me why I went so quiet in Class Nine. I'm Mridul, and I think I can finally say it.
My friend Rohit had told me things were really bad at home, and that sometimes he wished he could just disappear. He made me promise. And I thought a real friend keeps promises. If I told, I'd lose him.
So for six weeks I carried it. I watched him in class. I lay awake wondering whether he was okay. I couldn't concentrate on anything; I was fourteen and trying to be his only safety net. And the whole time, nobody who could actually help him even knew.
It ended on a Thursday, when he didn't come to school. I panicked and told our class teacher before first period. She phoned his mother at once, found out he was at home and safe, and by evening the counsellor and his parents were involved.
He's okay now. But those six weeks, Didi, were six weeks he could have had help.

How long did Mridul carry the secret?
Six weeks.
Why did Mridul keep the promise at first?
Mridul was afraid of losing Rohit, believing a real friend keeps promises, and felt it was the loyal thing to do.
What could Mridul have done on the day Rohit first told him?
Tell the class teacher or a parent that same day, so adults could reach Rohit's family and arrange help at once.
What were those six weeks like for Rohit?
Rohit was struggling at home with no adult aware, so he went without help that could have started much sooner.

A year ago the family group chat turned into a campaign. My cousin Himani sent a long voice note every morning: "Bhupen, Dada is getting old, he wants both grandsons at his table. Do it for the family." I'm Bhupen, the one who stopped answering calls after my brother shoved me down the stairs at Dada's house during an argument.
Looking back, I'm glad I didn't snap at Himani. I told her, "I know you want everyone together, and I love you for that. But I won't sit across from him because the neighbours talk."
What I did agree to, months later, was one meeting in a counsellor's office that Himani found, with the counsellor between us and my own car parked outside. It went badly, honestly. But it happened on my terms, and I left when I needed to.

What did Himani send every morning?
A long voice note asking Bhupen to make peace for the family.
How does Bhupen feel about Himani's pressure, looking back?
Bhupen feels grateful and fond of Himani's care yet still wary, glad not to have snapped but unwilling to face the brother just because neighbours talk.
Which choice kept Bhupen safe while still giving peace a chance?
Agreeing to one meeting in a counsellor's office, with the counsellor present and a car outside, so Bhupen could leave when needed.
How might Himani see Bhupen's refusal at first?
Himani may feel frustrated and worried about Dada's wish, reading it as stubbornness until the danger from the brother is taken seriously.

On the train platform I watched Lakshmi, about two, being tickled by her mother Sangeeta on a bench. She laughed, wriggled and pushed her mother's hand back for more. Then Sangeeta lifted her high over her head. Lakshmi laughed too, but her eyes were wide and she gripped Sangeeta's wrists. I don't know what she was feeling, but Sangeeta brought her down at once and said, “Tickle again?” Lakshmi's laugh became easy and she settled into her lap.

What did Lakshmi do when she wanted more tickling?
She pushed her mother's hand back for more.
What made Sangeeta bring Lakshmi down, and what does the narrator think?
Lakshmi's wide eyes and tight grip on her wrists showed the laugh was mixed with alarm. The narrator admits they cannot know what Lakshmi felt.
What could Sangeeta do with what she noticed?
She could keep games low to the ground for now, watch Lakshmi's face and stop if the laugh sounds nervous.
What might Lakshmi feel when her mother lowers her?
She may feel relieved and safe, and glad that her mother stopped when she was unsure.
Bruce's aunt gave him $71 to spend on clothes at the mall. He bought 5 shirts that cost $5 each and a pair of pants that cost $26. How much money does Bruce have left to buy more clothes?

Bruce spent 5 * $5 on shirts = $25.
Including the pants, Bruce spent $25 + $26 = $51.
Since he began with $71, he has $71 - $51 spent = $20 remaining.
The answer is 20.

For the family reunion, Peter is buying 16 pounds of bone-in chicken and half that amount in hamburgers.  He's going to buy 2 more pounds of hot dogs than hamburgers.  He's also going to buy several sides that will weigh half the amount of hot dogs.  How many pounds of food will he buy?

He is buying 16 pounds of chicken and half that amount in hamburgers so he's buying 16/2 = 8 pounds of hamburgers
He's going to buy 2 more pounds of hotdogs than hamburgers, which are 8 pounds so he'll have 2+8 = 10 pounds of hot dogs
He's going to buy sides that weigh half the amount of the hot dogs so that's 10/2 = 5 pounds of sides
He's buying 16 pounds of chicken, 8 pounds of hamburgers, 10 pounds of hot dogs and 5 pounds of sides for a total of 16+8+10+5 = 39 pounds of food
The answer is 39.

The private bus to the Kuttanad school stopped at every jetty, and by the third stop the back seats had started. "Fish girl," Binoy said when Anjali climbed in, and two boys held their noses. Anjali's father ran the fish stall near the ferry.
Elizabeth had the window seat. She knew Anjali from Sunday class. She pressed her forehead to the glass and watched the paddy fields slide by. I'm not the one saying it, she told herself. If I open my mouth, they'll start on me.
Anjali sat in front of her, very straight, holding her bag on her lap. She got off one stop early and walked the rest of the way in the heat.
The next morning Anjali wasn't on the bus. Elizabeth kept looking at the empty seat in front of her.

What did Binoy call Anjali when she climbed in?
Binoy called her "Fish girl", and two boys held their noses.
Why did staying quiet feel safer to Elizabeth?
She told herself she wasn't the one saying it, so she felt less to blame, and she worried the boys would start on her if she spoke.
What could Elizabeth realistically do the next time this happens?
She could sit beside Anjali, say a short "Leave it" to the boys, or tell a teacher; even talking to Anjali afterwards would show her she isn't alone.
What is it like for Anjali when nobody on the bus says anything?
It likely feels as if everyone agrees with the boys; she sits very straight, gets off early, and the next day she avoids the bus altogether.

All through the Diwali holidays, Darshan mama kept saying it. When Madhav solved the riddle on the sweet box: "Genius!" When he counted the diyas fastest: "Our little scientist, so clever!" Madhav glowed.
On the last evening, the family set up a puzzle contest on the terrace. There were easy cards and hard cards, and the hard ones had a gold star.
"Take a gold one, genius," said Darshan mama.
Madhav's hand hovered. He picked an easy card instead. Then another easy one.
"Why not the hard ones?"
"These are more fun," Madhav said, not looking up.
But when his cousin grabbed a gold card and got stuck, Madhav watched him with a funny tight feeling in his stomach. If he got stuck in front of everyone, would they still call him a genius?

Which cards had a gold star?
The hard cards had a gold star.
Why does Madhav pick the easy cards?
He feels nervous that getting stuck on a hard card in front of everyone would take away the "genius" label he has been praised for.
How could Darshan mama praise Madhav in a more helpful way?
He could praise Madhav's effort and ways of thinking, like "I liked how you tried different ideas", so trying something hard doesn't feel risky.
How might Darshan mama feel if he knew why Madhav avoided the gold cards?
He would probably be surprised and a bit sorry, since he meant his praise to encourage Madhav, not to make him afraid.

Every film song.
What was Vijay feeling when typing "YES"?
Vijay felt excited and thrilled that Ankita liked the idea and would help.

Ankita's music theory will map the beats and Vijay's knowledge of the kids will test it on Saturday.

The day Jeevan got his first phone, his mother Farida sat with him on the verandah of their house in the small town, the fields turning gold behind them.
"Three rules," she said. "One: no strangers, no photos to anyone you don't know. Two: the phone sleeps in the kitchen at night. Three: if anything online ever scares you, you tell me, and you won't be in trouble for telling."
Jeevan nodded, waiting for the fourth rule, the one where she'd read everything.
It didn't come. "Your chats with your friends are yours," she said. "I won't read them. Every Sunday I'll just ask, 'Anything bothering you?' That's all."
He blinked. His friend's father checked every message, and his friend had a second secret phone.
A month later, a stranger sent Jeevan a strange link. He showed his mother that same evening, without even thinking twice.

Where does the phone sleep at night?
The phone sleeps in the kitchen at night.
What was Jeevan feeling when the fourth rule didn't come?
Jeevan felt surprised and trusted, since he had expected his mother to read everything.
Why did Farida's approach work?
Open rules and privacy for his chats made Jeevan feel safe telling her, so he showed her the strange link the same evening.
What would change if Farida had read every message?
Jeevan might have hidden things better, like his friend with the second secret phone, instead of coming to her.

Gurpreet, put the phone down a minute. When I was fifteen there was a clip of me falling off the stage at our school farewell, and an older class shared it with laughing comments. My face burned as if the whole town had watched. My hands shook, but I remembered to save pictures of the comments before doing anything else. Then I told my mother, standing in the kitchen with the phone still in my hand. She hugged me first and said it was in no way my fault. That same evening she phoned the principal, who listened, took the pictures I had saved and promised action. By the next day the clip was down, and I had blocked those accounts. I still remember how light I felt walking into school after. Nandini

What did Nandini fall off at the school farewell?
Nandini fell off the stage at the school farewell.
How did Nandini feel on seeing the clip, and what shows it?
Ashamed and exposed; the burning face and the shaking hands show it.
What did young Nandini do before anything else, and why did it help?
Nandini saved pictures of the comments first, which gave the principal proof to act on.
How might Nandini's mother have felt hearing the news in the kitchen?
Worried and protective; hugging first and saying it was not Nandini's fault shows care before action.
Zach rented a car for $150 plus 50 cents for each mile. He drove 620 miles on Monday and another 744 miles on Thursday. How much did he spend?

On Monday Zach spent 620*0.5 = 310 dollars on miles.
On Thursday Zach spent 744*0.5 = 372 dollars on miles.
In total, Zach spent 150+310+372 = 832 dollars.
The answer is 832.

The girls' kabaddi team from Aadhya's village lost the block-level match by six points, and Aadhya had been caught on her last raid. On the bicycle ride home along the canal she sat on the carrier behind her father, Uday, waiting for the question every uncle had already asked: "By how much?"
Uday pedalled for a while. Then he said, "Tell me the best moment."
"The first raid. I touched two and got back."
"I saw. What did you learn from the last one?"
She thought. "I went too deep. I should have come back after one touch."
"Good. Anything else?"
"Their stopper was really strong."
Only at the village well did he ask, "And the score?" She told him. He shrugged. "Next month there's another match."
She swung her legs, humming.

Where did Aadhya sit on the ride home?
On the carrier behind her father, Uday.
What was Aadhya expecting when she sat behind Uday?
She was dreading the usual question about the score and felt tense about the lost match.
Why did Uday wait until the well to ask the score?
Asking first about the best moment and the lesson let Aadhya think about her play, so the score became just one fact.
What does Uday's shrug show about how he sees losing?
Uday sees a loss as ordinary and workable, one match before the next, not a failure to worry about.

The museum trip was on Friday, and by Thursday night four children were packing in four different ways.

Yash read the circular twice and copied out every item onto a strip of paper: a lunch box, water, a cap, his ID card and some rupees. He ticked each one as it went into his bag. There was no guessing.

Ritu lay on her bed and walked through the day in her head: the crowded bus, the long walk in the sun, lunch on the steps, the ride back with everyone sweaty. She added a hat, a bag to hold the wrappers and a small pack of tissues.

Kabir did nothing until 6:30 on Friday morning, with the bus due at seven. He stuffed things in a rush and left the permission slip on the table and the water bottle by the sink. His mother sprinted to the gate as the bus doors opened, waving both.

Hafsa remembered last year with a sigh: her small bottle had emptied by noon and she had spent the afternoon thirsty. This time she carried the bigger bottle, and at the school gate told her friend Anand, "Bring a big one too." Anand grinned and pulled out a bottle nearly as tall as his bag.

What did Yash write on the strip of paper?
He wrote a lunch box, water, a cap, his ID card and some rupees.
How did Ritu's way of packing differ from Yash's, and what did each add?
Yash copied the items from the circular, while Ritu imagined the whole day and so added a hat, a wrapper bag and tissues that the circular did not list.
What was Kabir feeling when his mother sprinted to the bus gate?
He was probably flustered and embarrassed, since he had rushed at the last minute and forgotten things.
What could Kabir change before the next trip?
He could pack the night before with a list and set the permission slip and water bottle by his bag.

Aditi, let old Nitin tell you about my first portfolio. I was so proud of it. Each project had a line: "Built with React, Node and MongoDB." Tools, tools, tools. A senior, Suresh Bhai, looked at it over tea and said, "Nitin, I know what you used. What happened because of it?" I had no answer. He said, "Tell me the problem, what you built, and what got better." I was quiet, then a little annoyed, and then I went home and rewrote everything. The hostel mess project became: "Students queued 20 minutes for tokens; I built a tap-to-order page; queue dropped to five." Suresh Bhai read it again and just nodded. That nod was worth ten compliments.

What did Suresh Bhai ask about the tools?
Suresh Bhai asked what happened because of them.
What was Nitin feeling right after the senior's question?
Nitin was quiet and a little annoyed at first, because there was no answer to the question.
What choice inside the story turned the portfolio around, and why?
Nitin rewrote each project around the problem, what was built and what got better, because outcomes showed value where a list of tools did not.
How did Suresh Bhai see the first version of the portfolio?
Suresh Bhai saw a long list of tools with no results, so he asked a plain question and nodded at the rewrite.

Mehak had been imagining the moment for months. Now it was happening in the worst possible way: a sudden downpour, one tiny bus shelter, and Aman from the science club squeezed right next to her, both of them soaked.
Her mind raced. Say something smart. No, you'll stutter. Your hair looks like a wet mop. He'll think you're weird.
She stared at the rain and said nothing for five whole minutes.
Her phone buzzed. Lavanya, her best friend: "Is that AMAN next to u?? just say hi. normal hi."
Mehak took a breath. "The bus is always late when it rains," she said. Her voice came out a little squeaky.
Aman grinned. "Always. Once I waited an hour and missed my own birthday cake."
Mehak laughed, the awkwardness still there but smaller. By the time the bus came, they'd talked about the science fair, and she hadn't died of embarrassment even once.

Where were Mehak and Aman stuck during the downpour?
In one tiny bus shelter.
What was Mehak worried about while standing next to Aman?
She felt nervous and embarrassed, imagining she would stutter, look messy with wet hair and seem weird.
What small step helped Mehak, and why?
Following Lavanya's advice to say a normal hi, she made ordinary talk about the late bus, which eased the awkwardness.
How might Aman see the moment at the bus stop?
Aman seems relaxed and happy to chat, even sharing a funny story, probably not noticing how nervous Mehak felt.

Mary is paying her monthly garbage bill for a month with exactly four weeks. The garbage company charges Mary $10 per trash bin and $5 per recycling bin every week, and Mary has 2 trash bins and 1 recycling bin. They're giving her an 18% discount on the whole bill before fines for being elderly, but also charging her a $20 fine for putting inappropriate items in a recycling bin. How much is Mary's garbage bill?

First find how much Mary pays weekly for the trash bins: $10/trash bin * 2 trash bins = $20
Then add this to the cost of the recycling bin: $20 + $5 = $25
Then multiply the week cost by the number of weeks per month to find the monthly cost: $25/week * 4 weeks/month = $100/month
Now calculate Mary's senior discount: 18% * $100 = $18
Now subtract the discount and add the fine to find the total monthly cost: $100 - $18 + $20 = $102
The answer is 102.
Why should we walk slowly on a freshly mopped floor?
A freshly mopped floor is slippery, so slow steps are safer. Because a thin layer of water cuts down the grip between shoes and the floor, a quick step can slide away and cause a fall.

In the open-plan office of the ad agency, Jatin's screen lit up with a message from Ramesh: "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!" Jatin grinned, because Ramesh always typed in capitals when thrilled. Ten minutes later the same manager pinged the whole team: "WHY IS THE FILE STILL NOT SENT???" Jatin's stomach dropped. Was that anger or panic? Nobody in the room could tell. Ramesh, at the next desk, caught Jatin's eye and said, "Should we ask her what she needs?" They walked over. It turned out she was terrified the client would leave and needed the file in an hour. Jatin sent it in twenty minutes and exhaled.

What did Ramesh's first message say?
Ramesh's message said "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!"
What did Jatin feel when the manager's capitals arrived, and what did they turn out to mean?
Jatin's stomach dropped and Jatin could not tell if the capitals meant anger or panic. It turned out the manager was terrified of losing the client.
What helped clear up the tone of the message?
Ramesh suggested asking the manager what was needed, and a short walk over cleared it up.
How might the manager have felt when the team seemed to hesitate?
The manager was probably stressed and rushed and may not have noticed how the capitals sounded to others.

Last year, in Class 6, Pranav dared me to ring Mrs D'Souza's doorbell and run. She's old and walks with a stick.
"Everyone's done it," he said. "Don't be a baby."
I felt my face heat. I wanted to be brave. But I kept thinking of Mrs D'Souza getting up slowly, walking to the door, and finding nobody.
"No," I said. "That's mean to her."
Pranav rolled his eyes. For a day he didn't talk to me. Then he came over with his cricket bat like nothing had happened.
I'm Bhavna. I still wave to Mrs D'Souza every morning. She always waves back.

Whose doorbell did Pranav dare Bhavna to ring?
Mrs D'Souza's.
What was Bhavna feeling when her face heated?
Bhavna felt embarrassed and pressured, wanting to look brave in front of Pranav.
What helped Bhavna say no?
Thinking about how the dare would affect Mrs D'Souza made it clear that it was unkind.
How might Pranav have felt when Bhavna refused?
Pranav was probably annoyed and embarrassed for a day, but still valued the friendship enough to come back.

Campus health centre, nurse's note, 14 October. Mahima.
Nitin came in for the third time this month, his asthma inhaler running low. The doctor has recommended the yearly flu shot for him because of his asthma. Today, again, he said no. When I asked why, he said a friend's cousin had a bad reaction last year, and he couldn't stand the idea of making himself sick on purpose. "If I get the flu, fine, that just happens. If the shot does something, I did it." I didn't argue with his fear; it's a real feeling. I asked whether skipping the shot was also a choice. He was quiet. I've booked him fifteen minutes with Dr Pillai on Thursday to go through both risks properly, and I'll sit in if he wants.

Who is Nitin booked to see on Thursday?
Nitin is booked to see Dr Pillai.
Why does Nitin feel a flu would be 'fine' but a reaction would be his fault?
Nitin feels afraid of harming himself by choice, so a harm from acting feels worse than the same or bigger harm from not acting.
What did Mahima arrange, and why is it a good next step?
A fifteen-minute talk with Dr Pillai to go through both risks, so Nitin can decide with a qualified doctor rather than from a cousin's story.
How does Mahima approach Nitin's fear?
Mahima treats the fear as real, doesn't argue, and gently asks whether skipping the shot is also a choice.
The community swimming pool will be shut next Monday for cleaning. Make a notice of about 40 words for the notice board. Sign it Pool Management.

NOTICE
The community swimming pool will remain closed next Monday for cleaning. It will reopen once the cleaning is done. Please plan your swimming accordingly. We regret any inconvenience this may cause, and thank you for your understanding.
Pool Management

Read this:

At nine, Divyansh slid a maths test with a red 8 under his pillow. His father Vijay had a single question at dinner: "What was your score?" When it wasn't full marks, he said nothing and went out to the balcony. Divyansh concluded that good marks meant love, and that mistakes were best kept out of sight.

At twenty-one, Divyansh sat in front of an internship form with the closing date on Friday. The résumé needed one more line, the cover letter one more polish, and the photo was slightly off. He told himself he would submit tomorrow when everything was ready. Friday came and went. So did the next form. His friend Bhavna asked, "Did you send it?" and Divyansh said, "Almost." He felt relief and dread at the same time. Doing nothing felt safer than sending something imperfect, and yet it meant the one outcome he feared.

That weekend, Bhavna sat beside him. "Send it rough," she said. "I'll sit right here." He winced, but he sent the next application at eleven at night.

What did Vijay ask Divyansh at dinner?
Vijay asked, "What was your score?"
How does the atmosphere at home when Divyansh is nine connect to his missed deadlines at twenty-one?

At nine Divyansh learns from Vijay that marks bring warmth and mistakes are best hidden, and at twenty-one the same fear keeps him polishing forms until the deadlines pass, because doing nothing feels safer than sending anything imperfect.
What was Divyansh feeling when he told Bhavna the form was almost sent?
Divyansh felt relief and dread at once, afraid of sending something imperfect but also aware that the deadline had passed.
What did Bhavna do that helped Divyansh act?
Bhavna encouraged him to send it rough and offered to sit with him, which made the risk of an imperfect application easier to take.
How does laughter sound? Answer in one sentence with exactly one comma and the word "bubbling".
Laughter sounds like water bubbling over a stone, light and happy.

Read this:

In the Class 2 science room, Gautam, the teacher, poured water from a tall thin glass into a wide bowl. "More, less or the same?" he asked. Most children shouted, "Less!" Pradeep, seven, frowned. "Same. You didn't add any or take any out." "But it looks lower," said his partner. Pradeep took the bowl and poured it back into the glass. "See? Back to the same line." Gautam smiled. "Pradeep, explain again for everyone."

What did Gautam pour the water into?
A wide bowl.
Why did Pradeep frown when the others shouted "Less!"?
He was puzzled because he felt sure it was the same amount and disagreed with the class.
What did Gautam do well, and what could come next?
He let Pradeep prove it by pouring back; next he could try the same idea with rice or clay.
How might Pradeep's partner feel when the water reached the same line?
Surprised, and perhaps curious about why it looked like less.

Read this:

Valentina had started it in October, at their school in Madrid: every lunch, when Fatima opened her box of rice and spiced chickpeas, Valentina held her nose. "Ugh, what died?" The table laughed. By November she was doing it every day, and her friends joined in.

When Fatima asked her to stop, Valentina said, "It's just banter! Everyone jokes about everyone's food. Don't be so sensitive."

Fatima started eating in the library.

On Friday the head of year, Señor Ruiz, asked Valentina to stay after class. "Fatima's mother has spoken to me. Fatima eats alone now because of the comments at lunch."
"It's just banter," Valentina said.
"Banter goes both ways," he said. "This only goes one way. It stops today, and we'll talk with your parents on Monday."

Valentina looked at the floor. She remembered Fatima's face when Fatima had asked her to stop.

What was in Fatima's lunch box?
Fatima had rice and spiced chickpeas.
Why did Valentina say "Don't be so sensitive"?
Calling it banter let Valentina see the comments as fun, hiding how hurt and excluded Fatima felt.
What did Señor Ruiz do that same day?
He told Valentina how Fatima was affected, said the comments only went one way, stopped them immediately and arranged a talk with her parents.
How has Fatima been affected?
Fatima feels hurt and excluded, and has started eating alone in the library.

Sol sells candy bars to raise money for her softball team. On the first day, she sells ten candy bars and sells four more candy bars than she sold the previous day each day afterward. If she sells six days a week and each candy bar costs 10 cents, how much will she earn in a week in dollars?

Sol will sell 10 + 4 = 14 candies on the second day.
She will sell 14 + 4 = 18 candies on the third day.
She will sell 18 + 4 = 22 candies on the fourth day.
She will sell 22 + 4 = 26 candies on the fifth day.
She will sell 26 + 4 = 30 candies on the sixth day.
She will sell a total of 10 + 14 + 18 + 22 + 26 + 30 = 120 candies in a week.
Hence, she will earn 120 x 10 = 1200 cents.
Since 1 dollar is equal to 100 cents, then Sol will earn 1200/100 = $12
The answer is 12.
The bus has seat numbers. Anu sits in seat 24. Her friends sit in the seats just before and just after hers. What are their seat numbers?

Answer: Seats 23 and 25.

The same rule works for bigger numbers: before is one less, after is one more. Only the last part (the ones) changes: twenty-three, twenty-FOUR, twenty-five.

In a town, there is a multi-story parking lot, which has room for 425 cars. The parking lot has 5 levels, each of the same size. How many more cars can one level fit if there are already 23 parked cars on that level?

When all levels are empty, each level can fit 425 / 5 = 85 cars.
When there are already 23 parked cars on a level, there is still a place for 85 - 23 = 62 cars.
The answer is 62.

When Chandrika, eight, moved from her village to the school in the kasba, she noticed everything: the girls had ribbons, said "sorry" in English, and knew the tables by heart.
On the second day, she whispered her answer and nobody heard. On the third, she didn't come out at break.
Ganga Didi, the teacher who ran the small library, found her inside. "Why aren't you playing?"
"I don't know anything here."
"You know how to milk a buffalo?"
"Yes."
"Then you know something none of them do." Ganga Didi pulled out a picture book. "Read one page to me each break. I'll help."
By the end of the month, Chandrika was reading the page aloud to two other girls, who sat on either side of her.

Where did Ganga Didi find Chandrika?
Ganga Didi found her inside the small library.
What was Chandrika feeling when she said, "I don't know anything here"?
Chandrika felt ashamed and behind, overwhelmed by all the ways the town girls seemed different.
What did Ganga Didi do that built Chandrika's confidence?
She reminded Chandrika of what she did know and offered patient daily reading help.
How might the two girls see Chandrika by the end of the month?
They likely see her as a friend and a good reader, not as the new girl from the village.
