messages.content:
Read this:

January: Vidya, twenty-five, got a new job through her father's friend. She also noticed that Raghav, her colleague from a Hindi-medium school, was twice as good at data work but kept being passed over for client calls.
March: When her manager asked for names for a new project, Vidya recommended Raghav, explaining his strengths. At lunch she asked him what made the job hard. He said, "Everyone assumes my English is weak." She listened and didn't argue.
June: A friend from her college messaged about an opening at a big firm. Vidya forwarded it to Raghav and two others, not just her own circle. Raghav got an interview. Vidya didn't feel like a saint, and she didn't pretend she'd got her job on her own. She just tried to share the doors she happened to stand beside.

How did Vidya get her new job?
Vidya got a new job through her father's friend.
What was Vidya feeling when she listened to Raghav at lunch?
Vidya felt concerned and attentive, wanting to understand his experience without defending herself.
Which of Vidya's actions show using advantage responsibly?
Recommending Raghav on merit, listening to his experience, and forwarding job openings beyond her own circle.
How might Raghav feel after Vidya's recommendation?
Raghav likely felt seen and grateful, finally recognised for his skills rather than judged by assumptions.

Read this:

"Pankaj, your Maria Aunty once wanted to disappear. I was eleven. Someone started a story that I had stolen the class teacher's gold pen. By lunch, everyone knew. Girls moved away when I walked by. I felt like I was made of glass.
I hadn't done it. It wasn't my fault. But it felt like it was.
That evening I told my father everything. The next day he came with me to the teacher, who found out the pen had simply fallen behind a cupboard.
I also went to the girl who started it and said, 'Please stop. It isn't true.' And my two real friends sat with me every lunch until it died down."

What was young Maria accused of stealing?
The class teacher's gold pen.
How did young Maria feel when the rumour spread?
She felt exposed and ashamed, as if she were made of glass, and wanted to disappear.
What choices in the story helped young Maria?
Telling her father, who went with her to the teacher, asking the girl who started it to stop, and staying close to her real friends.
How might the girl who started the rumour have felt when Maria confronted her?
She may have felt caught out and embarrassed, especially once the pen was found.

Read this:

Dear Vidya didi,

I sat through the Sunday puja with Amma and Papa, and I need to tell someone how it went. Last month I asked Amma why we keep the long fast, and she looked as though I had slapped her. Papa went silent at dinner for two days.

I could have hidden my questions or joked about it. I did neither. Last night I told them, "I still have questions. But I love this house, and I'd like to sit with you at the puja." Amma pressed my hand. This morning I lit the lamp beside her, not sure what I believe, sure that I wanted to be there.

You never argued with them, did you? Write and tell me how you managed it.

Pranav

How did Amma look after Pranav asked about the long fast?
Amma looked as though Pranav had slapped her.
What is Pranav feeling as the lamp is lit beside Amma?
Pranav feels torn: unsure what to believe but sure of wanting to be there with the family.
How could Pranav keep honesty and respect together?
Speak gently about the questions, share family rituals such as lighting the lamp, and neither hide the doubts nor mock the practice.
How do Amma and Papa see Pranav's questions at first?
As hurtful, shown by Amma's look and Papa's two days of silence, though Amma pressed Pranav's hand after hearing the gentle explanation.

Read this:

My older sister Jahnavi had been stomping round the flat for two days. Something about Sunaina and a group chat. I heard her tell Mummy, "She called me dramatic, in front of everyone."
On Sunday evening, I saw her sitting on the balcony, typing slowly. Then she said out loud, maybe to herself, "Okay. Here goes." She showed me the screen before sending: "Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other."
Ten minutes later, I could hear them. First quiet voices. Then Jahnavi said, "No, I thought you meant..." Then a pause. Then she laughed. A real laugh.
When she came in, she ruffled my hair. I don't know what they said exactly. But she ate two helpings at dinner.

Where was Jahnavi sitting when she typed the message?
On the balcony.
What might Jahnavi have been feeling when she said "Okay. Here goes"?
She was likely nervous but brave, deciding to risk a call rather than keep sulking.
Why did moving to a call help so much?
Hearing Sunaina's voice cleared up what each had meant, so the hurt eased and laughter followed.
How might Sunaina have felt getting Jahnavi's message?
Sunaina may have felt relieved and grateful that Jahnavi reached out instead of letting the fight grow.
Make this a newspaper headline of under eight words: The municipal school has opened a new library for children in the neighbourhood after two years of planning.
Municipal School Opens New Library for Children

Read this:

At a family gathering in Bristol, Mina, five, who is deaf, watched her aunt Freya sign JUICE with eyebrows up and head tilted. Mina signed YES and ran to the fridge. Later Freya looked at a spilled glass, eyebrows up again, and signed JUICE with wide eyes and an open mouth. Mina laughed. That face meant "oh no!", not an offer. She signed, "Sorry, spilled."

What did Mina do after her aunt's raised-eyebrow JUICE sign?
She signed YES and ran to the fridge.
What did Mina think Freya was feeling at the spilled glass?
As surprise, "oh no", rather than an offer. She read the whole face, though she could have been wrong.
What could a hearing newcomer learn from this?
That facial movement is part of signed grammar, so the whole face should be watched along with the hands.
How might Freya feel seeing Mina understand her?
Proud and connected, since Mina read the difference at once.
Why is it polite to wait until the other person finishes speaking?
Interrupting feels disrespectful. Because interrupting suggests that your words matter more, the speaker may stop sharing.
Lanie has been sick and was only able to work 4/5 of her usual 40-hour week. If her hourly rate is $15, how much was her salary for that week?

Lanie was only able to work for 40 * 4/5 = 32 hours in that week.
Thus, her salary was 15 * 32 = $480.
The answer is 480.
My colleague is used to wake up at five every day. Can you correct it?

My colleague is used to waking up at five every day.
Why: verb form ("used to wake" -> "used to waking").

Read this:

In the co-working space in Sydney, Tariq noticed that his colleague Liam always had his brows drawn tightly together, even when he was eating lunch. Tariq had begun to wonder whether Liam was anxious about something. He caught himself imagining stories: a sick parent, a failing project. Then he remembered his own uncle, whose face looked stern even when he was cracking jokes. Instead of guessing, Tariq set down his sandwich and said, "Hey, this quarter's been heavy for the whole team. How are you holding up with the workload?" Liam blinked. "Actually, I've had headaches from the screen. I've booked an eye test. Thanks for asking." His brows stayed drawn, but he smiled.

In which city was the co-working space?
The co-working space was in Sydney.
What did Tariq first wonder about Liam's brows, and why did he change his approach?
He wondered if Liam was anxious about something, then remembered his uncle whose face looked stern even when joking, so he chose to ask.
What could Tariq do if Liam said the workload really was heavy?
He could listen, offer to share tasks and suggest raising it with the manager.
How might Liam feel about being asked kindly?
Liam seems relieved and glad, since he shared his headaches and thanked Tariq.

Read this:

I'm Rehana, and I shared a hostel room with Alka for our whole second year. I saw how much the money silence at home bothered her.
Every time she called her parents about fees, her father said, "Don't worry about money, just study." But then her mother would whisper that they'd "borrowed a little." Alka would put the phone down and stare at the wall.
Once she said to me, "I don't even know if we're fine or in trouble. They think they're protecting me. I feel like a guest in my own family."
In the winter break, I heard her on the phone, calm and careful: "Papa, I'm not asking to judge. I'd just feel closer if I knew. Can we sit down when I'm home?"
After the break she came back quieter, but lighter. She told me they'd spent a whole evening going through everything. I don't know exactly what she felt. But she stopped staring at the wall.

What did Alka's father always say when she called about fees?
He said, "Don't worry about money, just study."
What was Alka feeling when she said she felt like a guest in her own family?
Alka felt shut out and uneasy, not knowing if her family was fine or in trouble.
What made Alka's request to her father a wise one?
She asked calmly, without judging, and framed it as wanting to feel closer, which made open talk a sign of trust.
How might Alka's father see her request?
He might first feel his pride was at stake, but hearing she wanted closeness, not judgment, could help him open up.

Read this:

My brother Karthik, sixteen, used to be first at the puja room every morning, ringing the little bell. Around March I noticed he had stopped. He'd stand at the door for a second and then go to the kitchen. Amma noticed too and grew quiet. One evening Karthik sat on the sofa beside Amma and said, "Amma, the puja doesn't mean what it used to. I don't want to fake it. But I'm not angry at anyone, and I'll always eat the prasad and help with Diwali." Amma looked at the diya for a long while. Then she said, "Will you at least fold the flowers with me on Sundays?" He nodded. I can't say what he feels inside. But he has been making her tea every morning since. Sharmila

What did Amma ask Karthik to do on Sundays?
Amma asked Karthik to fold the flowers with her on Sundays.
What might Karthik be feeling as he tells Amma the puja doesn't mean what it used to?
Karthik is probably nervous and afraid of hurting Amma, and honest about his doubt. He says he does not want to fake it and is not angry.
Which choice by Karthik helped Amma accept the change?
Karthik spoke honestly and gently, promised to keep eating the prasad and helping with Diwali, and made her tea every morning.
How might Amma have felt as she looked at the diya for a long while?
Probably hurt and thoughtful. Her request about the flowers suggests she wanted to keep some closeness with Karthik.

Read this:

At the school swap fair in Manchester, Wei set out his old comics on a blanket with a big sign: £5 EACH. Omar flipped through them. "These are good. I'll give you £1 each for the space ones." Wei looked shocked. "They're worth way more. I've read those twenty times." "That's why the corners are bent," Omar said. The comic stall next door had the same issues for 50p. By lunch Wei had sold nothing, and he told his mum the other kids were trying to rip him off. She held up one of the space comics. "Would you pay five pounds for this, if it was someone else's?" Wei looked at the bent corner for a long time.

What did the next-door stall charge for the same comics?
Why did Wei think the other kids were trying to rip him off?
He felt upset and insulted because the comics were his and read twenty times, so they felt worth far more than buyers offered.
Why is Wei's mum's question useful?
It makes Wei look at the comic as a buyer would, which shows the gap between what an owner feels and what others will pay.
How does Omar see the comics?
Omar likes them but sees bent corners and cheaper copies next door, so £1 seems a reasonable offer.
Compose a notice for the colony: the street lights will be repaired by the municipal team on Wednesday, and residents should not park near the poles. 35 words.

NOTICE
The municipal team will repair the street lights in our colony on Wednesday. Residents are requested not to park near the poles, so that the team can work safely. Thank you for your cooperation.

Derrick measures the length of his yard. The length of Alex's yard is half the size of Derrick's and the length of Brianne's yard is 6 times the size of Alex's. If Brianne's yard is 30 yards long, how long is Derrick's yard, in yards?

The length of Alex's yard is 30/6=5 yards.
The length of Derrick's yard is 5*2=10 yards.
The answer is 10.
What's a good way to remember dates for history?
Link each date to a story, not just a number. Remember what happened, who was involved and why it mattered, then attach the year. A simple timeline on one page also helps you see the order of events.
I have so many to learn.
Group them by period, and learn one group each day. Test yourself by covering the dates and saying them aloud. Flashcards with the event on one side and the date on the other work well too.

Read this:

"Ow!" Ishita shook her hand. A thin red line showed on her finger.
Rukmini dropped her scissors. "You're bleeding!"
"It stings." Ishita's eyes filled.
"Wait, wait." Rukmini ran to her schoolbag and came back with a cartoon plaster. "Paati keeps this for me."
"I can't open it."
"I can." Rukmini peeled it and stuck it on, crooked. "Now kiss it better." She kissed the air above the plaster.
Ishita sniffed. "It still stings a bit."
"Then hold my hand till it stops."

Where did Rukmini get the plaster from?
From her schoolbag, where Paati keeps it for her.
What might Rukmini have been worried about when she dropped her scissors?
She was alarmed to see Ishita bleeding and wanted to help her straight away.
How could a teacher support this moment?
Check the cut, thank Rukmini for her kind help, and explain that telling an adult about a cut is a good step too.
How might Ishita see Rukmini's offer to hold hands?
Even though it still stings, she likely feels comforted knowing her friend will stay with her.

Read this:

During the power cut at the preschool, the fans stopped, and Neelam ma'am gathered the children in the corridor with a torch for story time. Rukmini, five, put her hand up. "I saw a tiger in my garden! It was THIS big!" She spread her arms. "It ate my slipper!" The children gasped. Neelam ma'am smiled. "A tiger! That's a big story. Was it a real tiger or a pretend tiger?" Rukmini thought. "Pretend. But it was hungry." Everyone laughed. "Pretend tigers get very hungry," Neelam ma'am said. "Shall we make up more of its story?" The class spent the power cut deciding what the tiger ate next.

What did Rukmini say the tiger ate?
Her slipper.
How did Rukmini seem to feel telling the tiger story?
She seemed excited and proud, spreading her arms to show its size.
What did Neelam ma'am do that respected both imagination and facts?
She enjoyed the story but asked if it was real or pretend, then turned it into a shared make-believe game.
How did the other children respond to Rukmini's story?
They gasped and then laughed, joining in to invent more of the tiger's story.

Read this:

Teacher's note, Sunflower Group. Ira Kapoor.
This month we practised "bubble breathing" at calm circle times: breathe in, then blow one long, slow bubble through a wand. Tejas loved it.
Today thunder crashed during snack time. Tejas dropped his banana, clapped his hands over his ears and began to wail. I knelt by him and asked, "Can you blow me a big bubble?" He took a shaky breath and blew out long and slow, no wand needed. Then another. His hands came off his ears. I'll tell his father at pickup.

What did Tejas drop when the thunder crashed?
Tejas dropped his banana.
What was Tejas feeling when he clapped his hands over his ears?
Tejas was frightened by the thunder and began to wail.
Why did Ira's question "Can you blow me a big bubble?" work?
Tejas had practised bubble breathing while calm, so the familiar game was easy to reach when he was scared.
What would change if the class had only tried bubble breathing for the first time during the storm?
Tejas would probably not know the game well enough to use it while frightened, so it would help far less.

Read this:

Jasleen: are you upset with me? you didn't reply for an hour
Sharmila: not upset! was in a lecture
Jasleen: ok sorry
Jasleen: did i say something weird this morning tho
Sharmila: no, you were fine
Jasleen: are you sure. you seemed quiet
Sharmila: jas, this is the 4th time today 🤍
Sharmila: i love you and i'm not upset. but i can't be the only thing that calms you. i'm getting really tired
Jasleen: oh. sorry
Sharmila: don't be sorry. can you try what the counsellor suggested? write the worry down, walk round the block, then check if it's still true
Jasleen: ok. i'll try
Sharmila: and tonight at dinner we talk properly. no phones
Jasleen: ok. walking now

Why didn't Sharmila reply for an hour?
Sharmila was in a lecture.
How does Sharmila feel after the fourth request for reassurance?
Sharmila feels drained and tired, though still loving and not upset with Jasleen.
What did Sharmila suggest instead of more reassurance, and why?
The counsellor's steps, writing the worry down, walking, checking if it's still true, so Jasleen builds a personal way to calm down.
What might Jasleen feel reading 'i'm getting really tired'?
Jasleen probably felt a sting of guilt and worry, apologising at once, before agreeing to try the walk.

So I'm Kavitha, and this is about the email I didn't send for nine days. I'd missed a data deadline at work, and I needed to tell my manager, Kishore, that the report would be a week late. Every morning I opened a draft and closed it. One night I asked myself, "What am I actually scared of?" And the answer was simple: I was scared he'd think I was careless. That was it. Once I'd named it, it looked smaller. So I wrote four lines: what happened, what I'd done so far, the new date, and "I'm sorry for the delay." I sent it at 11 p.m. before I could change my mind. He replied the next morning: "Thanks for telling me. Let's talk at ten." The relief was enormous.

Summarize how Kavitha got past her fear.

Kavitha avoided telling her manager about a late report for nine days. When she asked herself what she feared, she saw it was looking careless. That made it smaller, so she sent a short, honest email, and her manager replied kindly.
Is a doorway the same as a door? What does doorway mean?

A doorway is the opening where a door is, or the space around it. It is a noun.
Example: The cat sat in the doorway and watched the rain.
We could not "get through" because the line was busy. Is "get through" correct for a call?

Yes. "Get through" means to reach someone by phone or to pass through a difficult place. It also means to finish a task or survive hard times.
Examples: I could not get through to the helpline. We got through the exam period.

Read this:

In the physiotherapy department of the city hospital, the junior staff kept a whiteboard of who had handled the most patients. Ojas was always near the bottom, and it gnawed at him. One quiet afternoon he took out his first-month logbook. Back then he had needed help with every patient. Now he took his own cases and even trained the interns. He smiled for the first time in weeks. That night he left the staff group that posted rankings every day. He kept one colleague, Tejas, close, the calmest person in the department, and asked if he could watch how he explained exercises to older patients. Tejas said yes. Ojas made a note: check logbook monthly, ask Tejas, ignore the board.

Where did the junior staff track who handled the most patients?
On a whiteboard.
How was Ojas feeling before he looked at his logbook?
He felt low and anxious, gnawed at by always being near the bottom of the board.
What did Ojas do to keep comparison helpful?
He compared himself with his first month, left the ranking group, and chose Tejas as someone to learn from.
How might Tejas see Ojas's request?
Tejas would likely feel respected and glad to help a colleague improve.

Read this:

I'm Tanvir, and last quarter I almost did something small and stupid. I'd lost the receipt for a site-visit lunch in Nashik, and the claim form let me type any amount. My team lead once told me, laughing, that someone in finance had claimed a whole wedding as "client entertainment." Next to that, rounding my lunch up to 1,200 felt like a rounding error. My cursor sat there for a while. Then I thought of Damini, who has worked beside me for two years and double-checks my reports because she knows I hate mistakes. If she opened this form, would I want to explain that number? I typed the real amount, 640, and attached a note about the lost receipt. Honestly, it felt better than the extra money would have.

What amount did Tanvir finally type?
The real amount, 640, with a note about the lost receipt.
Why did rounding up to 1,200 feel like a rounding error to Tanvir at first?
Tanvir felt tempted but not guilty, because beside the story of someone claiming a whole wedding, a padded lunch looked tiny and didn't feel like real dishonesty.
Which question changed Tanvir's decision, and why does it work?
Imagining Damini opening the form and asking "would I want to explain that number?" works because it uses a trusted person's eyes, not the worst example.
How might Damini feel if she found a padded number in Tanvir's form?
Damini, who double-checks Tanvir's reports out of care, might feel let down and start wondering what else needs checking.
My teacher is very kind, she always helps to us.

My teacher is very kind, she always helps us.
Why: The verb "help" is followed directly by the person, with no "to".

Read this:

In the fishing village near Karwar, Maria stayed so close to her mother Uma's sari that she nearly tripped her while she cleaned fish. "You won't go to the market without me?" "No." Ten minutes later: "You love me, na?" "Still yes." That night Maria was meant to sleep at her cousin's house two lanes away. An hour later her uncle walked her back, sobbing. Uma didn't scold. She sat on the step with her. "Tomorrow we'll try again. I'll walk you over and tell you when I'll come to fetch you."

Who walked Maria back that night?
Her uncle walked her back, sobbing.
What does Maria's repeated "You love me, na?" suggest she is feeling?
She seems anxious and unsure, needing to hear again and again that she is loved and that Uma won't leave.
How could Uma help Maria manage the next night away?
Keep doing what she started: stay calm, sit with her, walk her over and say exactly when she will fetch her.
What would change if Uma had called Maria a baby for coming home?
Maria would likely feel ashamed and even more afraid of being apart, making the next try harder.
Say how a rainbow forms in one sentence of at most twenty words, using "sunlight" and "raindrops".
A rainbow forms when sunlight bends and splits into colours inside raindrops.

Eva learns for two semesters in a year. In 2019, she scored ten more marks in maths in the first semester than the second, 15 marks less in arts, and 1/3 marks less in science in the first semester than the second. If she got 80 marks in maths in the second semester, 90 marks in arts, and 90 in science, what's the total number of her marks in all the semesters?

In the first semester, she scored 80+10 = 90 marks in maths
She also scores 90-15 = 75 marks in arts in the first semester.
She scored 1/3 marks less in science in the first semester than the second, which is 1/3*90 = 30
Her score in science in the first semester is 90-30 = 60
The total for the first semester is 90+75+60 = 225
The total for the second semester is 90+90+80 = 260
The combined marks for all the semesters in 260+225 = 485
The answer is 485.

In the hostel common room, the Class 11 boys were playing carrom and arguing about cricket. Mohit sat on the edge of the bed reading, though he wasn't really reading. They think I'm a nerd, he thought. They don't want me.
Dhruv called, "Mohit, need a fourth player!"
Mohit didn't lift his eyes. "Busy."
Dhruv waved another boy over instead.
For the next hour Mohit felt lonelier and lonelier. They didn't even ask twice, he thought. Proof.
At lights-out, Dhruv said quietly from the next bed, "You always look like you'd rather be alone. I didn't want to bother you."
Mohit lay in the dark, stunned.

What game were the boys playing in the common room?
They were playing carrom.
What was Mohit feeling in the hour after he said "Busy"?
He felt lonelier and lonelier, and took the fact they didn't ask twice as proof they didn't want him.
What would you advise Mohit to try next time Dhruv asks?
Say yes, even if it feels awkward, so his behaviour doesn't make his fear come true.
How does Dhruv see Mohit?
Dhruv sees Mohit as someone who would rather be alone, so he doesn't want to bother him.

Harsha's admission form for Class 11 was due on Friday, and panic sat in his stomach because he honestly did not know what he wanted. He tried small experiments: a weekend graphic-design workshop, a chat with an engineer and one with an animator from his mother's office. His parents, Damini and Tejas, kept saying, "Science first, then engineering." Harsha knew they had trimmed their own spending for his future, and he felt both indebted and trapped. "I am grateful, and I also love design. Could we try one year, and I will bring facts about courses and jobs?" he said. Damini frowned but nodded. At a family lunch an aunt said, "Your cousin got into the top college. What about you?" Harsha smiled. "Different path, aunty. I am still exploring." He did not turn it into a contest. He filled in the form for science with design as an elective, knowing it could be revised in a year.

What did Harsha try to help him decide?
He tried a weekend graphic-design workshop and chats with an engineer and an animator.
How did Harsha's approach to his parents differ from his response to his aunt's comparison?
With his parents he said he was grateful yet loved design and asked for a one-year trial with facts, while with his aunt he smiled, answered briefly and did not turn it into a contest.
What was Harsha feeling about his parents' effort?
He felt both indebted and trapped, since he knew they had trimmed their own spending for his future.
What could Harsha do during the trial year?
He could keep bringing facts about courses and jobs, keep small experiments in design, and revise the choice if it does not fit.

In the school hall at the parent-teacher meeting, Hansa waited with her daughter Jahnavi on the plastic chairs, and noticed how much had changed in three months. Jahnavi's old friend Pinky was sitting across the hall with her mother, but Jahnavi didn't look at her. She said 'no cap' and 'lowkey' in every sentence, and one earbud played music Hansa had never heard. Hansa's first thought was to joke about her daughter's 'new language'. She didn't. She asked, 'Who are they? Tell me about them.' Jahnavi hesitated, then talked about them all the way to the class teacher's table, and even let Hansa hear the song.

How many girls near the door did Jahnavi wave at?
Three girls.
What was Hansa feeling as she noticed the changes?
Curious and a little unsettled, and tempted to joke about Jahnavi's 'new language'.
Why was asking 'Tell me about them' wiser than joking?
Curiosity kept Jahnavi talking and even sharing the song, while ridicule could have pushed her further into the group and away from Hansa.
How might Jahnavi have felt when Hansa asked about the new friends?
Surprised and then pleased, since she hesitated but chose to talk and share her music.

messages.content: A trader has 55 bags of rice in stock. She sells off some bags of rice and restocks 132 bags of rice. How many bags of rice did she sell if she now has 164 bags of rice?

She had 55 bags and restocked 132 after selling some, so if she had not sold any, she would have a total of 55+132 = 187 bags
However she now has 164 bags, so she must have sold off 187-164 = 23 bags
The answer is 23.
When is my next parent-teacher meeting?
I don't know when your next parent-teacher meeting is, as I can't see your school's calendar. The school diary or the office will give the date.

Which is lighter?
a) a leaf or a brick
b) a pencil or a chair
c) a coin or a bag of rice

a) leaf
b) pencil
c) coin
A casino table pays 3:2 if you get a blackjack with your first 2 cards. If you scored a blackjack and were paid $60, what was your original bet?

The payout for blackjack is 3:2 or 3/2=1.5 times my bet
If my original bet was X then I won 1.5*X my bet
Given that I was paid $60 we know $60 = 1.5X
X=$60/1.5
X=$40 was my original bet
The answer is 40.

In Lagos, Nkechi spent Sunday evening on her history essay. She wanted Mr Adeyemi to think she was brilliant. So she wrote: "The multifaceted ramifications of colonial infrastructural paradigms necessitate a comprehensive reevaluation of contemporaneous socioeconomic trajectories." She read it three times and felt proud.
Her friend Omar read it on the bus next morning. "Nkechi, what does this mean?"
She opened her mouth. "It means… the railways were built to take things out, not to help people move around. And that still affects things now."
"Then why didn't you write that?"
She shrugged. "It sounds too simple."
On Friday, the essay came back. Beside her favourite sentence Mr Adeyemi had written: "I read this four times. What are you trying to say?" Under the conclusion, which she had written in a hurry and plainly, he had written: "This is clear and strong. More of this."

What did Mr Adeyemi write beside Nkechi's favourite sentence?
"I read this four times. What are you trying to say?"
Why did Nkechi feel proud of her long sentence at first?
Nkechi wanted to seem brilliant, and the long words made the sentence feel impressive to her.
What could Nkechi try in her next essay?
Nkechi could write each point the way she explained it to Omar, in plain words, and save long words for when they are really needed.
How does Omar see Nkechi's sentence?
Omar finds it confusing, and he points out that her plain spoken explanation was much clearer.
How do I make a suggestion without sounding bossy?

A suggestion is an idea you offer for others to think about. It is a noun. To avoid sounding bossy, start with "Maybe we could" or "What if we".
Example: Her suggestion to start the project early helped everyone.

A(2, 3) -> A'(6, 9) and B(4, 1) -> B'(12, 3) under a dilation. Find the scale factor and the centre.

Answer: Scale factor 3, centre O(0, 0).

Every coordinate has been multiplied by 3: 2 x 3 = 6, 3 x 3 = 9, 4 x 3 = 12, 1 x 3 = 3. That is the rule (x, y) -> (3x, 3y), a dilation with centre O and k = 3. Check with lengths: AB^2 = 2^2 + 2^2 = 8 and A'B'^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 72 = 9 x 8, so A'B' = 3 x AB. To find a centre in general, join A to A' and B to B' and extend the lines: they cross at the centre. Here both lines pass through O.

Rafiq didn't add a laugh and didn't forward anything. Instead, Rafiq took screenshots of the messages, the names and the times. At the break Rafiq sent Tanya a private message: “I saw. I'm sorry. What did Rafiq do with the messages?
Took screenshots of the messages, names and times.
How might Tanya have felt when Rafiq's private message arrived?
Relieved that someone cared, though still embarrassed and shaky about what had happened.

Keep checking in and sit with Tanya at lunch, since a friend nearby can make going to school easier.
How does the situation look to Dhruv Sir?

"Please, Papa, please, please. Just one more episode." Uma clasped her hands.
"It's already past your time, Uma," said Pankaj.
"But it's the last one of the season. I promise I'll go to bed straight after."
"You wanted the last one last week too."
Uma's eyes went big. "Please, Papa?"
Pankaj sighed. "I can see how much you want to find out. But bedtime stays. Tomorrow after homework you can watch it, first thing. Deal?"
Uma's shoulders dropped. "Deal. Can I choose the snack?"
"You can choose the snack." 🙂

When can Uma watch the last episode?
She can watch it tomorrow after homework.
What was Uma feeling when she clasped her hands and said please, and how do you know?
She was eager and hoped for a yes, shown by the big eyes and repeated please. Her shoulders dropping suggests some disappointment when she heard no.
What could Pankaj do to respond fairly next time?
He can keep bedtime steady, acknowledge Uma's wish, and offer a clear alternative time, as he did.
How might Pankaj feel hearing Uma plead again?
He may feel a bit tired and tempted, since he sighs, but he keeps calm and kind while holding the limit.

Monday. After school, Varun and three older kids stood by the water-tank ladder in the colony. "Rashmi, climb to the top. Everyone's done it. Or are you chicken?" Rashmi's legs felt wobbly. She said no. They laughed and walked off without her.
Tuesday. At the park, nobody saved her a swing. Varun said, "Only brave people can join our gang." Rashmi sat alone on the bench, fighting tears. She badly wanted to be in the gang again.
Wednesday. They dared her again. She put one foot on the ladder, her heart pounding, then stepped back and ran home.
She told her Mummy everything, crying. Mummy hugged her. "You were brave to say no. That ladder is dangerous." That same evening, Mummy went to the society office. The secretary locked the ladder gate, and Mummy spoke calmly to Varun's parents too.

What did the kids dare Rashmi to climb?
The water-tank ladder in the colony.
How did Rashmi feel sitting alone on the bench?
Rashmi felt lonely and left out, fighting tears because she badly wanted to belong.
What did Rashmi's Mummy do the same evening?
She went to the society office, where the secretary locked the ladder gate, and she spoke calmly to Varun's parents.
How might Varun see the dare?
Varun probably sees it as a test of bravery for the gang, without thinking about the danger or how left out Rashmi feels.

In class five, Shalini stumbled over the word "extraordinary" during reading time. The room went still, and she felt her neck grow warm. She dropped her jaw, crossed her eyes and made the silliest face she knew. The class exploded in laughter, and Shalini bowed. Gopika Ma'am smiled. "Well, you've certainly stolen the show." Shalini's fingers were pinching the page edge.
Chinmay, sitting beside her, leaned in. "What does stolen the show mean? Did she say you took something?" Shalini giggled, her shoulders loosening. "No. It means everybody looked at me. She was being funny." Chinmay asked again later, when Gopika Ma'am said the next chapter would be "a piece of cake." He raised his hand. "Ma'am, is there real cake?" The class laughed, but Gopika Ma'am answered warmly. "It means it will be easy. Asking is a good habit." At break, Shalini went back to the passage and read the word alone. She got it right on the second try.

Which word did Shalini stumble over in reading time?
She stumbled over the word "extraordinary".
How do Shalini's silly face and Gopika Ma'am's remark show that words and jokes can carry more than one meaning?

Shalini used a joke to hold on to the moment after her stumble, and Gopika Ma'am answered with a playful phrase, "stolen the show", that Chinmay had to ask about. Indirect speech can be funny or kind, so asking what someone means is a good habit.
What was Shalini feeling when she pinched the page edge after the class laughed?
She was embarrassed and a little anxious, though the joke let her seem in control.
What could Chinmay do when he hears a phrase he does not understand?
He can ask the speaker what they mean, as he did with "a piece of cake", and then remember the answer.

Vasudha, you called that student lazy just now. I said the same once, thirty years ago. There was a boy in my second-year class, Anil, bright in discussions, but he missed every essay deadline. When I reminded him, he snapped, "I'll do it, Disha Ma'am, stop chasing me." I wrote him off as careless and arrogant.
Then one evening I found him in the empty corridor, staring at a blank page, hands shaking. Instead of scolding, I asked, "What makes this so hard?" He was quiet for a long time. Then he said that every time he started, his chest went tight and he was sure it would be rubbish, so he stopped. It wasn't attitude. It was fear. The next day I walked him to the student counsellor, and we broke his essays into small pieces. He finished the year.

What did Anil keep missing?
Anil missed every essay deadline.
What did Disha believe about Anil before that evening, and how did she feel?
Disha felt irritated and believed Anil was careless and arrogant, because he missed deadlines and snapped at reminders.
What was the turning point in Disha's story?
Finding Anil with a blank page and shaking hands, Disha asked kindly what made it hard instead of scolding, which let him explain.
What was the essay work like for Anil?
For Anil, each start brought a tight chest and a certainty it would be rubbish, so he stopped out of fear, not laziness.

At the hotel near the fort in Agra where Tanvir worked the front desk, Vandana stopped by to drop off his lunch. She waited in the lobby while he dealt with a furious guest whose room wasn't ready. Tanvir was astonishing: calm, smiling, apologising, offering tea, making the man laugh by the end. Vandana felt proud watching him. That evening at home, she asked if he wanted to go for a walk. "No." She mentioned her sister's news. "Hmm." When she asked what was wrong, he said, "Nothing, I'm just tired," and turned on the TV. Vandana sat beside him, thinking about the lobby. He had the patience; she'd seen it. It just seemed to be used up by eight o'clock. Later, she said, "I saw you with that guest today. You were wonderful. I wish I got a bit of that too." Tanvir turned off the TV.

What did Vandana drop off at the hotel?
Tanvir's lunch.
How did Vandana feel after watching Tanvir in the lobby and then at home?
Vandana felt proud in the lobby and then lonely and a bit hurt at home, noticing his patience seemed used up by evening.
What did Vandana say that could help, and why?
She praised his work and then gently said she wished she got some of that warmth, naming the pattern without blame.
How might Tanvir feel when he turns off the TV?
Tanvir might feel touched and a little guilty, realising Vandana noticed he saves his energy for guests.

School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Ojas came to my room at lunch, sent by his class teacher, who noticed he had stopped eating in the canteen. He failed two subjects in the half-yearly exams.
He told me that at home his father shouted for a long time, then said, "Anirban scored ninety in everything. What is wrong with you?" Anirban is his cousin, the same age. Since then, Ojas said, nobody at home talks to him at dinner. "It's worse than the shouting."
He kept his eyes on the floor. He said he feels stupid and like a disappointment. He did not speak of wanting to harm himself when I asked directly.
I called his parents and asked them to come in this afternoon. They came at four. I explained that Ojas needs support first, and study plans later, and that comparison deepens shame. His mother cried. His father was quiet, then asked, "What should we do tonight?"
We made a small plan. I will see Ojas again on Monday.
— School counsellor

Who is Anirban?
Anirban is his cousin, the same age.
How does Ojas feel about the silence at dinner?
Ojas feels ashamed and hurt, saying the silence is worse than the shouting and that he feels like a disappointment.
What did the counsellor do that same day, and why was it important?
The counsellor called the parents in that afternoon and explained that support comes first and comparison deepens shame, so home could change that night.
How might Ojas's father feel when he asks, "What should we do tonight?"
His father probably feels shaken and unsure, realising his anger and comparison had hurt Ojas, and wanting to do better.
I want to back up my photos so I don't lose them.
A good rule is to keep more than one copy, in more than one place. For example, one on your device, one on an external drive and one in an online storage service.
How often should I do it?
Whenever you add photos you would hate to lose. Many people back up once a week or once a month.
Is online storage safe?
It is convenient, and reputable services protect files carefully. Use a strong, unique password and, if offered, two-step sign-in.
What's a strong password?
A long one, with a mix of words or characters that is not easy to guess. Do not use birthdays or names, and do not reuse it on other sites.
How do I remember it?
Try a long phrase of several unrelated words, which is easier to recall than random characters. A password manager is another option.
Let's do a plan for the weekend. What is wrong?

Let's make a plan for the weekend.
Why: word choice ("do a plan" -> "make a plan").

Mentor's note, second-year engineering, 12 February
Uma has been in my mentoring group since first year. This term she has changed. She used to debate happily with everyone. Last week, when Farhan disagreed with her about a news story, she said, "People like him defend those parasites," and moved to another table. She now calls a whole community "rats" and "a disease" as if describing the weather. Her laptop is always playing the same channel's videos, one after another.
Farhan told me she has unfollowed him and two other friends.
I noticed something else. When I asked about her grades, which have fallen, her eyes filled up.
What I did next: I didn't argue about the videos. I told her that calling people rats is the kind of language that comes before cruelty, and that I was worried about her. I asked her to meet the college counsellor with me on Friday. She said yes, quietly.

What did Uma say when Farhan disagreed?
'People like him defend those parasites.'
What might Uma's filling eyes suggest when asked about grades?
They suggest Uma is hurting and stressed underneath the contempt, perhaps feeling like a failure.
What did the mentor do next, and why might it help?
Named the dehumanising words as a warning sign without arguing about videos, said they were worried, and asked Uma to meet the college counsellor together.
How might Farhan feel after being unfollowed and lumped in with 'parasites'?
Farhan would likely feel hurt and pushed out, losing a friend just for disagreeing.
I feel nervous every time I have to make a phone call, even to order food.
That's more common than you might think. Many people prefer typing to talking on the phone. Planning what you'll say can help a lot.
What do you mean by planning?

Before you call, write down two or three short lines, like "Hello, I'd like to order for delivery," then your order and your address. Keep the paper in front of you. Small calls get easier the more you make them.
Now you try: prove 3 - sqrt5 is irrational.
The answer is if 3 - sqrt5 = r then sqrt5 = 3 - r is rational: contradiction.
We learn new vocabularies every week in English class. Is "vocabularies" a word?

We learn new vocabulary every week in English class.
Why: uncountable noun ("vocabularies" -> "vocabulary").

The call came at midnight, and by dawn Uday was squeezed into a crowded general coach with Papa, heading to Ajja's village for the funeral. There was no seat. Uday stood by the door, numb. Ajja had taught him to swim in the river only last summer. How could he just stop? Near Hubli, Uday suddenly snapped at a man who bumped him, then burst into tears. Papa pulled him close. 'Ask me anything,' Papa said. Uday asked where Ajja was now, and whether dying hurt. Papa answered what he could and said 'I don't know' to the rest. At the village, his cousin Samir took him to the river. They sat on the rock where Ajja used to dry his towel and told Ajja stories until the conch sounded for the rites.

Where did Uday stand on the train?
By the door of the crowded general coach.
What was Uday feeling when he snapped at the man?
After feeling numb, his grief came out as anger and confusion, and then broke into tears.
What helped Uday on the journey and at the village?
Papa holding him and answering his questions honestly, and sharing Ajja stories with Samir before the rites.
What might it be like for Papa on that train?
Hard, since he was likely grieving too while comforting Uday and admitting what he didn't know.
Six more than twice as many ducks go to North Pond as go to Lake Michigan. If Lake Michigan has 100 ducks, how many ducks can you safely estimate there will be at North Pond?

To determine the number of ducks at North Pond, we must first perform 100*2= 200 to find the number to add 6 ducks to.
We then take this number and add 6 to it, performing 200+6=206 ducks in total at North Pond.
The answer is 206.

Calvin has been saving his hair clippings after each haircut to make a wig for his dog. He has gotten 8 haircuts and knows that he needs 2 more to reach his goal. What percentage towards his goal is he?

His goal is 10 haircuts because 8 + 2 = 10
He is 80% there because (8 / 10) x 100 = 80
The answer is 80.

In the summer holidays, Sachin's first tooth fell out while he was eating a guava in the courtyard. He held it up, amazed. "Throw it on the roof!" said his friend Wasim. "Then the sparrow brings a strong new one." Sachin climbed on the charpai and threw hard. The tooth clinked on the tiles. Every morning after that, he felt the gap with his tongue and looked up at the roof. When Aai asked what he was doing, he whispered, "Waiting for the sparrow." Aai smiled. "New teeth take time, sparrow or not."

What was Sachin eating when his tooth fell out?
A guava.
Why did Sachin look up at the roof every morning?
He felt hopeful and excited, believing the sparrow would bring his new tooth.
How did Aai handle his belief?
She smiled and gently said new teeth take time, sparrow or not, without mocking or scaring him.
How might Wasim feel when Sachin throws the tooth?
Wasim probably feels proud to share the ritual and excited to see whether it works.

The inter-school drawing competition was a mess: it was held in a crowded hall, a boy knocked over Ira's water jar in the first ten minutes, and she had to redo half her sky in pencil. She still won first prize.

When they announced her name, Ira walked up looking embarrassed. On the bus back, Rukmini hugged her. "You won! With a flooded sky!"

"The judges were being nice," Ira said. "Honestly, anyone could have done it. The others just had bad luck."

"Everyone had the same hall. You had the worst luck, with the water."

"Maybe the judges liked pencil." Ira shrugged.

Rukmini folded her arms. "Ira, when you came fifth last year, you said, 'See, I'm not good.' Now you come first and it's luck? That's not fair to you."

Ira stared out of the window, the certificate face down on her lap.

What happened to Ira's water jar?
A boy knocked it over in the first ten minutes.
Why did Ira say the judges were just being nice?
Ira felt uncomfortable with praise, and explaining the win away kept her belief that she isn't good untouched.
What could Ira try instead of explaining away the win?
Simply say "thank you" and let the win count, just as she let last year's fifth place count against her.
How does Rukmini see Ira's excuses?
Rukmini finds them unfair to Ira, noticing that losses count but wins don't.

A week before Diwali, the whole flat in Chembur smelled of wet cloth. Kamal Chacha was scrubbing the high shelves. Jeevan, five, got a damp rag of his own. "I'll do the low ones," he said. He wiped each shelf slowly, putting the small brass lamps back exactly where they were. Then he swept the dust from under the sofa into a pile. "Look, Chacha!" Kamal Chacha peered down. "Very neat. Now carry it to the bin with me."

What was Kamal Chacha scrubbing?
The high shelves.
What was Jeevan feeling when he called, "Look, Chacha!"?
He felt proud of his work and eager to show it.
What did Kamal Chacha do that made Jeevan's help work?
He let Jeevan take the low shelves and praised the neat job, then did the last step together.
How might the Diwali cleaning feel for Kamal Chacha with Jeevan helping?
It would feel less of a chore and more of a shared job with his young nephew.

Hi Irawati,
Can I tell you something slightly embarrassing? Last night Harsh showed me a video of Mrinal from his design team presenting her project. He watched it twice and said, "She's so sharp. She makes it look effortless."
I smiled and said, "Wow." Then I went quiet for the rest of dinner.
It's not that I think he likes her. I honestly don't. It's that I heard "sharp" and "effortless" and immediately thought: he has never said that about me. You know I'm the girl who used to compare report cards with the whole class. I started listing everything Mrinal is that I'm not: confident, quick, brilliant with slides. By the time I got home I felt about two inches tall.
So maybe this isn't really about Harsh at all? Does that make sense, or am I being silly?
Ritu

What did Harsh say after watching the video of Mrinal twice?
He said, "She's so sharp. She makes it look effortless."
What was Ritu feeling during the rest of dinner?
She felt small and jealous, not because she suspected a romance but because the praise made her compare herself with Mrinal and come up short.
What could help Ritu at this early stage of comparison?
Noticing, as the email begins to, that the feeling is about measuring herself, and perhaps telling Harsh gently that the praise stung, instead of listing Mrinal's strengths.
How might Harsh have meant his comment about Mrinal?
Harsh was probably just admiring a colleague's work, unaware that his words left Ritu measuring herself against Mrinal.

The pressure cooker in the Bengaluru flat let out its first whistle. Charu, two, froze with her toy spoon in the air, eyes wide, mouth open in a small gasp. If 3 crows eat 30 worms in one hour, how many worms will 5 crows eat in 2 hours?

If 3 crows eat 30 worms in one hour, then each crow eats 30/3=10 worms per hour.
5 crows will eat 5*10=50 worms per hour.
Over two hours, 5 crows will eat 2*50=100 worms.
The answer is 100.

He stood still, holding the goat's rope. The trees creaked. His heart thumped.

Then, a single light blinked in front of him. Then another. Soon a long line of fireflies hung in the air, glowing gently, like beads on a thread.

"Follow," seemed to say their flickers.

Mohan walked. The fireflies danced ahead, and the goat trotted behind. They passed the old well and the crooked tree.

A factory decides to stop making cars and start making motorcycles instead. When it made cars, per month, it cost $100 for materials, they could make 4 cars, and they sold each car for $50. Now that they make motorcycles it costs $250 for materials, but they sell 8 of them for $50 each. How much more profit do they make per month selling motorcycles instead of cars?

They sold $200 worth of cars each month because 4 x 50 = 200
They made $100 a month off cars because 200 - 100 = 100
They sold $400 worth of motorcycles each month because 8 x 50 = 400
They make $150 a month off motorcycles because 400 - 250 = 150
They make $50 more a month off motorcycles than cars because 150 - 100 = 50
The answer is 50.
Five students recorded hours of revision x and marks y: (2, 52), (4, 57), (6, 66), (8, 70), (10, 80). Find the least-squares line of best fit y = a + bx and interpret a and b.

Answer: mx = 6, my = 65, Sxx = 40, Sxy = 138, b = 3.45, a = 44.3: y = 44.3 + 3.45x. Each extra hour of revision goes with about 3.45 more marks; a = 44.3 is the predicted mark for 0 hours.

Step 1: means mx = 30 / 5 = 6, my = 325 / 5 = 65. Step 2: deviations x - 6 = -4, -2, 0, 2, 4 and y - 65 = -13, -8, 1, 5, 15. Step 3: Sxx = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40 and Sxy = sum (x - 6)(y - 65) = 138. Step 4: b = Sxy / Sxx = 138 / 40 = 3.45. Step 5: a = my - b x mx = 65 - 3.45 x 6 = 44.3. So y = 44.3 + 3.45x. Check that the mean point lies on it: 44.3 + 3.45 x 6 = 65 = my. The SLOPE b is the useful number: +3.45 marks per hour. The INTERCEPT a is the prediction at x = 0, which is outside the data (2 to 10 hours), so treat it with care. "Least squares" means that no other straight line has a smaller total of squared vertical distances from the points. Common mistake: b = Sxx / Sxy (upside down).

2. It should be: It is a long time since I saw you. Why: after "a long time since", use the simple past.
3. A queue serves one person at a time and keeps things fair. Because the person who came first is served first, nobody pushes ahead.

John has started at a job he works every day 10 days ago.  So far, he's made $250.  How many more days must John work before he makes twice this amount, assuming he makes the same amount every day?

John has made $250 in 10 days, so this means he makes $250/10=25 dollars a day.

This means John needs to work 500/25= 20 days in total to make 500.
As John has already worked 10 days, this means he needs to work 20-10=10 more days to make his goal.

Patricia and Geoffrey went fishing to feed their group of campers. They caught an eight-pound trout, six two-pound bass, and two twelve-pound salmon. If each person will eat two pounds of fish, how many campers can they feed?

The bass weigh 6 * 2 = 12 pounds in all.
The salmon weigh 2 * 12 = 24 pounds in all.
The trout, bass, and salmon together weigh 8 + 12 + 24 = 44 pounds.
Each camper will eat 2 pounds of fish, so Patricia and Jeffrey can feed 44 / 2 = 22 campers.
The answer is 22.

In the second week, nothing. She frowned at the soil. In the third week, a tiny green loop pushed through. Rekha crouched so close her nose nearly touched it. "I did that," she said to nobody. "I picked the sunny spot."
Her friend's seeds, planted in deep shade, were slower. Rekha offered to help move them.
Ms Vinita wrote in her register: Rekha asked today if she could choose the next plant too.

Where did Rekha choose to plant her seeds?
She picked a corner by the wall where the morning sun hit.
How did Rekha feel when the green shoot appeared?
She felt thrilled and proud, crouching close and saying "I did that", because she could see her choice had worked.
Why does letting children choose where to plant help them?
Making a choice and then seeing the result gives children evidence that their actions change things, which builds their sense that effort matters.
How might Ms Vinita see Rekha after this?
Ms Vinita probably sees a child growing in confidence, eager to make the next choice herself.

In Chalakudy, Gopika's mother still woke at five to tap rubber, and until last year Gopika had helped her. Now she left early for the "success family" meetings in the hall above the bank.
At the meetings the leader said families like hers had "poor minds" and that friends who questioned the plan were "negative people sent to test you". Gopika wrote it all down.
On Saturday Sumit, her friend from college, found her at the bus stop. "You don't come to anything anymore. Your amma thinks you're in trouble."
"Amma thinks small," Gopika said. The words came out smooth, like something learned. "You all do. You're scared of success."
Sumit looked at her. "Gopi, it's me."
For a second she wavered. Then she remembered: doubt is weakness. She turned away and climbed onto the bus. Her hands, though, were cold on the rail the whole way.

Where are the 'success family' meetings held?
In the hall above the bank.
What do Gopika's cold hands on the bus suggest?
Beneath her confident words she feels uneasy and torn, her own doubt pushed down because the group calls it weakness.
What could help Gopika at this point?
Sumit and her amma staying close without insults, and a calm chance to talk about her doubts with someone outside the group.
What is it like for Gopika's amma to be called 'small'?
Amma is likely hurt and frightened, seeing her daughter pulled away and speaking in someone else's words.

I'm Ramesh, and I'll tell you about the outage I'm least proud of. A config change took our site down for an hour. In the meeting I asked once, 'Why did it go down?' and the answer was, 'Kamal pushed a wrong value.' Everyone nodded, relieved to have an answer. I told Kamal to be more careful, and we moved on. Kamal was quiet for a week. Then, six weeks later, someone else pushed a wrong value and the site went down again. That's when it hit me: I had never asked why a wrong value could reach the live site at all. No test caught it, and nobody was clearly in charge of reviewing config. Kamal wasn't the cause. Kamal was just the person nearest the button.

How long after the first outage did the second one happen?
The second outage happened six weeks later.
How might Kamal have felt after being told to be more careful?
Kamal probably felt ashamed and unfairly singled out, shown by being quiet for a week.
What other approach could Ramesh have used in the first meeting?
Ramesh could have kept asking why until a process cause appeared, such as why no test caught the wrong value and who reviews config.
How might Kamal's teammates have felt at the first meeting?
They were probably relieved at first to have a simple answer, though the second outage would leave them uneasy.

messages.content: Fill in "necessary", "sufficient" or "necessary and sufficient": a) Being a square is __ for being a rectangle. b) Being divisible by 2 is __ for being divisible by 4. c) Having three equal sides is __ for a triangle to be equilateral. d) x = 3 is __ for x^2 = 9. e) Being over 18 is __ for voting in India (you must also be a registered citizen).

Answer: a) sufficient b) necessary c) necessary and sufficient d) sufficient e) necessary.

"p is sufficient for q" means p -> q: if p happens, q is guaranteed. "p is necessary for q" means q -> p: q cannot happen without p. a) A square is always a rectangle (sufficient), but a rectangle need not be a square (not necessary). b) Divisible by 4 -> divisible by 2, so divisibility by 2 is necessary for divisibility by 4; it is not sufficient (6). c) Both directions hold: iff. d) x = 3 gives x^2 = 9, but x^2 = 9 does not force x = 3. e) Age over 18 is required but not enough on its own. Memory aid: in p -> q, p is sufficient and q is necessary.

Emil's little sister Hana had been in the children's hospital in Copenhagen for two weeks. Every afternoon Emil sat at the kitchen table with his felt-tip pens and drew her something: a whale, a rocket, their dog in a raincoat. Mum took the pictures in when she visited. On Friday his friend invited him to a birthday party at the swimming pool. Emil said no. 'It feels wrong to have fun,' he told Dad. Dad sat down. 'Hana asked me yesterday if you were still going to parties. She wants to hear about them. It's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week.' Emil went. Afterwards he drew Hana a picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble: 'Next time, you too.'

What did Emil draw for Hana after the party?
A picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble.
Why did Emil first say no to the party?
He felt guilty about having fun while Hana was in hospital.
What did Dad help Emil understand?
That it's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week, and that Hana wants to hear about his fun.
What might Hana want from her brother while she is in hospital?
To hear about his life and still feel part of it, which is why she asked about parties.
The Period 1 gym class has 5 fewer than twice as many students as in the Period 2 gym class. There are 11 students in the Period 1 gym class. How many are in the Period 2 gym class?

Let x be the number of students in the Period 8 gym class.
2x-5=11
2x=16
x=8
The answer is 8.

A grocery store has 4 kinds of jelly. They sell grape jelly twice as much as strawberry jelly, and raspberry jelly twice as much as plum jelly. The raspberry jelly sells a third as much as the grape jelly. If they sold 6 jars of plum jelly today, how many jars of strawberry jelly did they sell?

They sell twice as much raspberry jelly as plum jelly, so they sold 2 * 6 = 12 jars of raspberry jelly today.
The raspberry jelly sells a third as much as the grape jelly, so they sold 12 * 3 = 36 jars of grape jelly today.
The grape jelly sells twice as much as the strawberry jelly, so they sold 36 / 2 = 18 jars of strawberry jelly today.
The answer is 18.

The girls' hostel in the small town of Wardha had a nine o'clock study hour, but tonight Reena burst in: "The temple fair has a giant wheel! Just one hour!"
Pooja looked at her open accounts book and the test tomorrow. She should say no.
She went.
The wheel lifted them over the lights of the fair. They ate hot jalebis and laughed at a man selling plastic parrots. Pooja's cheeks ached from smiling.
But halfway down the wheel, a small pinch came in her stomach. The accounts book was still waiting on her bed.
Back at the hostel at eleven, she sat with the book, sugar still on her fingers. She was glad she'd gone. And she wished she'd gone after studying.

What did Pooja and Reena eat at the fair?
They ate hot jalebis.
What did Pooja feel on the way down from the giant wheel?
She felt a small pinch of guilt about skipping study, even though she was enjoying herself and smiling.
What could Pooja try next time Reena brings an exciting plan?
Study for a set time first, then go, so she can enjoy the fun without the guilt.
How might Reena see the evening?
Reena probably sees it as pure fun and doesn't notice Pooja's worry about the test.

messages.content:
Getting ready for Diwali.
How can I make a rangoli?
how do you spell choclate, I think it is wrong

1. Draw the pattern lightly with chalk or dots first. Then fill it in with coloured powder or flower petals.
2. It is "chocolate", with an "o" after the second "c" and an "a" before the "t". Say it slowly as "choc-o-late".
My mother asked me to do the bed before school. Is "do" correct here?

My mother asked me to make the bed before school.
Why: word choice ("do the bed" -> "make the bed").
What are scratches on a phone screen? Not looking for anything but the meaning.

Scratches are thin, shallow marks or cuts on a surface. It is a noun, the plural of scratch.
Example: The old wooden desk had many scratches from years of use.

In the library I found, to my great delight, a vast number of English books, whole shelves full of them, and bound volumes of magazines and newspapers. A table in the centre was littered with English magazines and newspapers, though none of them were of very recent date. The books were of the most varied kind--history, geography, politics, political economy, botany, geology, law--all relating to England and English life and customs and manners. There were even such books of reference as the London Directory, the "Red" and "Blue" books, Whitaker's Almanac, the Army and Navy Lists, and--it somehow gladdened my heart to see it--the Law List.

What does the narrator find in the library, and what does it suggest?
He finds shelves of English books and magazines about history, law, geography and daily life, plus directories and almanacs. It suggests the owner has been studying England carefully.

You keep saying that boy on your phone is like a friend, Santosh. Let me tell you about my friend on the radio.
I was fifteen. Every night at nine, a woman called Sunita Kiran read letters from girls like me on the radio. She laughed at our jokes, she remembered names, she said, "My dear listeners, you are my family." I felt she was talking only to me.
One night she said she used Chandan Glow powder every day and so should I. I took my whole Diwali money to the market and bought three tins.
My face broke out. When I wrote to her, "from Minakshi, your listener", I got a printed card back. Later my cousin at the radio station told me the powder company paid for that whole half-hour.
I still liked her voice. But I stopped buying what she said.

How many tins of powder did young Minakshi buy?
Minakshi bought three tins with her whole Diwali money.
Why did fifteen-year-old Minakshi trust the powder advice so easily?
Minakshi felt that Sunita Kiran was talking only to her, like family, so she believed the advice came from a friend and did not question it.
What turning point in the story changed how Minakshi listened?
Receiving only a printed card and then learning the company paid for the half-hour showed her the friendly voice was also selling.
How might Sunita Kiran's show have looked to the powder company?
To the company, the warm, family-like show was a way to reach girls who trusted the host, which is exactly why they paid for it.

metadata.subtype: Trusting an influencer like a friend [Receiver]

messages.content: There are 26 chickens, 40 piglets, and 34 goats at Stacy's farm. A really bad storm hits and half of all the animals get sick. How many animals in total get sick?

26/2 = 13 chickens get sick.
40/2 = 20 piglets get sick.
34/2 = 17 goats get sick.
In total, 13+20+17 = 50 animals get sick.
The answer is 50.

Thursday, after tuition
I hate Thursdays now. Jasleen and Kiran were whispering in the back row and they both looked at me. Right at my kurta. The yellow one Mummy stitched. I know they think it looks homemade and cheap. Kiran even covered her mouth. I could hear exactly what they'd be saying: "Look at her, she thinks she's so stylish."
For the whole class I sat with my dupatta over the embroidery.
But diary, if I'm honest, I didn't hear a single word. Not one. I made up the whole thing and then believed it like they'd shouted it.
Tomorrow I'm going to do something scary. I'm going to ask Jasleen, "What were you two laughing about?" If it was my kurta, at least I'll know. If it wasn't, I've wasted a whole evening feeling awful.
Neelam

Who stitched the yellow kurta?
Mummy stitched the yellow kurta.
Why did Neelam sit with the dupatta over the embroidery?
Neelam felt embarrassed and self-conscious, sure the girls were mocking the kurta, and wanted to hide it.
Is Neelam's plan for tomorrow a good one? Why?
Yes; asking Jasleen directly replaces a made-up conversation with a real answer, whatever it turns out to be.
What might Jasleen think if Neelam asks her tomorrow?
Jasleen might be surprised, and could explain what they were really laughing about, perhaps something that had nothing to do with Neelam.
I've got a new pen friend in Kenya. Write my first email to him introducing myself, about 40 words. My name is Sanjay and I love cricket and chess.

Dear friend,
My name is Sanjay, and I am happy to be your pen friend. I love playing cricket and chess. Please tell me about your town and what you enjoy. I look forward to your reply.
Sanjay

Monday. Reena had moved to the Chennai school three weeks ago and still ate lunch alone. At home she crooned old Bengali songs from Dida's cassettes under her breath while doing homework, the slow ones about rivers and leaving. Her mother, Anjali, paused at the door, listening, and wondered if Reena was miserable.
Thursday. In music period Reena hummed one of those tunes without meaning to. Two classmates leaned over. "What's that? Teach us." By the bell, three of them were mangling the Bengali words together and laughing so hard the teacher had to clap twice.
The next Monday. Reena sang loudly in the shower, the same river song, now with the lunch group's made-up harmony on the chorus. Anjali knocked and asked, "Still the sad one?" Reena opened the door with wet hair, grinning. "It's not sad any more, Ma. It's ours."

Whose cassettes did the old Bengali songs come from?
They came from Dida's cassettes.
What does Reena's crooning on the first Monday suggest about how she felt?

It may show Reena felt lonely and homesick, eating lunch alone after the move and choosing songs about leaving. But it could also be comfort or pride in songs from Dida, so the lyrics alone don't prove sadness.
How could Anjali support Reena without reading too much into the lyrics?
Anjali could ask lightly what the songs mean to Reena, as with 'Still the sad one?', rather than deciding from the words that Reena is miserable.
How did the song feel for the classmates who leaned over?
For them it became something fun to learn and mangle together, a shared group tune rather than a sad one.

Jim has 2 rows of 4 trees to start.  When he turns 10 he decides to plant a new row of trees every year on his birthday.  On his 15th birthday after he doubles the number of trees he has.  How many trees does he have?

He started with 2*4=8 trees
He plants trees for 15-10=5 years
So he planted 5*4=20 trees
So he had 20+8=28 trees
After doubling them he had 28*2=56 trees
The answer is 56.

Arnab had been elected sports secretary at his Kolkata college in July. By October, the football ground finally had working floodlights, and the girls' team had its own practice slot. People stopped him in corridors to say thank you. He liked that more than he admitted.
Then Sangeeta, the girls' captain, asked for a change in the match schedule.
"No," Arnab said, before she finished.
"You didn't even hear why."
"I decide the schedule. That's the job."
She looked at him for a long moment. "Last month you said you wanted everyone to have a voice."
Arnab felt a flash of irritation, then something colder: she was right. He took a breath. "Okay. Tell me why."

What did the football ground get by October?
It finally had working floodlights.
What did Arnab feel when Sangeeta reminded him of his words?
He felt irritated at first, then uncomfortable as he realised she was right and his wish for respect was sliding into control.
What did Arnab do right at the end, and what should he keep doing?
He took a breath and asked Sangeeta to explain; he should keep listening before deciding, so his influence serves the group.
How might Sangeeta feel when Arnab says 'I decide the schedule'?
She likely feels dismissed and frustrated, since he didn't even hear her reason.
Is examinations the formal word for exams, and does it only mean tests at school?

Yes, it is the formal word for exams. It means tests of knowledge or skill, and it can also mean careful looks at something, such as an examination of old coins. It is a noun; Examinations is the plural.
Example: The school held its final examinations in March.

Day one: at a family party in Coimbatore, Keerthana, five, was asked to hug her uncle. She shook her head and held out her hand. Her father Sahil said, "A handshake is fine."
Day four: her cousin asked, "Can I have a hug?" Keerthana said, "Yes," and they hugged.
Day seven: her grandmother arrived and said, "Come!" Keerthana said, "Can we do a high-five?" Grandmother grinned, and they slapped hands.

What did Keerthana offer her uncle instead of a hug?
She held out her hand.
What does Keerthana's yes on day four suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she was happy to hug her cousin because she was asked first. Her shake of the head on day one shows she can decide for herself, without meaning she dislikes her uncle.
What should adults keep doing to protect the child's sense of control?
They should keep asking before hugs, accept a handshake or high-five and thank the child for telling them.
How might the grandmother feel about a high-five?
She may be pleased that Keerthana still connects with her, and she grinned, so the high-five worked.

Dear Varun bhaiya,

Mamma says you'll help me because you're a teacher now. So, here's the thing.

We moved here from the other board, and the maths in Class 9 is stuff I finished last year. Every period I already know the answer before Sir writes the question. So I draw. Spirals, cartoon mangoes, a whole comic about a lost pencil. I look out at the gulmohar tree.

Yesterday Sir said in front of everyone, "Vinita is lazy." I'm not! I just can't sit through the same sum explained four times. My face went so hot.

Mamma thinks I should just be quiet. Should I ask Sir for harder problems? Or is that showing off?

Please reply soon.

Vinita

What does Vinita look out at during maths?
The gulmohar tree.
How did Vinita feel when Sir said "Vinita is lazy" in front of everyone?
Vinita felt embarrassed and hurt, with a hot face, because the drawing comes from the class being too easy, not from laziness.
What would you advise Vinita?
Ask Sir privately if there are harder problems to try once the class work is done, and explain that the topic is already familiar from the previous board.
How might Sir see Vinita's doodling from the front of the class?
Sir probably sees only a student not paying attention and reads it as laziness, without knowing the work is already familiar to Vinita.

Two years ago I was a nurse on an emergency ward, and I loved the patients and hated the noise. I'm Indu. By the end of each shift I felt turned inside out. I cried in the changing room and apologised to everyone for 'being weak'. My friend Nandini said, 'You're not weak. You're in the wrong room.' So I made a slow change. I applied to the palliative care unit: quieter, slower, more time with each family. I still have hard days. Now, when my chest goes tight and every sound sharpens, I take my break and don't say sorry for it. I also say yes to things that scare me a little. Last month I gave a talk to thirty nursing students. My hands shook. But I did it, and then I went home and sat in the quiet.

Which unit did Indu apply to?
The palliative care unit.
How did Indu feel at the end of emergency ward shifts?
Indu felt turned inside out and exhausted, crying in the changing room.
How does Indu balance rest and stretching now?
By taking breaks without apologising when overwhelmed, while still saying yes to scary things like the talk to thirty students.
What did Nandini see that Indu didn't?
Nandini saw that the problem was the noisy setting, not weakness: 'You're in the wrong room.'
Rewrite this for a young child: Please do not run near the swimming pool, as the tiles are slippery and you could fall and hurt yourself.
Do not run near the pool. The tiles are slippery. You could fall and hurt yourself.

The mela had come to Zainab's town for the harvest, and Ganga pulled her toward a woman reading cards under a striped awning.
"You are strong outside but soft inside," the woman said. "You worry about others more than yourself."
Zainab smiled. Then she asked, "Would the opposite be true for someone too? Soft outside, strong inside?"
The woman laughed. "For many, yes."
"Can you tell me something I could check? Like what my new boss's name will be?"
"Cards don't speak of names."
Walking back past the sugarcane stalls, Ganga asked, "So you don't believe her?"
"I enjoyed it," Zainab said. "It made me ask if I worry too much about Abba. But the school job offer, I'll decide with Abba and the head teacher, not with cards."

What did the card reader say when Zainab asked about her new boss's name?
She said, "Cards don't speak of names."
What was Zainab feeling as she walked back past the sugarcane stalls?
Zainab felt light and content, having enjoyed the reading as a chance to reflect without feeling pushed by it.
What could anyone take from Zainab's two questions?
Asking whether the opposite line would fit and asking for something checkable helps show whether a reading says anything specific.
How might Ganga see Zainab's approach?
Ganga seems surprised and curious, perhaps expecting Zainab either to believe completely or to mock the reader.
Ten percent of Jonessa's pay goes to paying tax. If her pay is $500, how much is her take-home pay?

Ten percent of $500 is $500 x 10/100 = $50.
Hence, Jonessa's take-home pay is $500 - $50 = $450.
The answer is 450.

Yusuf, you broke your friend's camera and you're scared to tell him? Sit. Your Gurleen phuphi will tell you about my third year of college.
Our group had spent two months collecting survey data for Professor Bhalla. One night, cleaning up the shared folder, I deleted the master file. No backup. I sat there looking at the screen, cold all over.
I could have said nothing. Someone else had access too. But by eight the next morning I was outside the professor's cabin. My voice shook. "Sir, I deleted the master file last night. It was my mistake. I have the raw forms, and I'll re-enter them by Friday. I've asked two friends to help."
He was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me first." We finished on Thursday.
At the end of the year he wrote my recommendation letter. He mentioned that morning in it.

By when did Gurleen promise to re-enter the data?
By Friday.
How did young Gurleen feel after deleting the file?
Gurleen felt cold all over, frightened and ashamed, tempted for a moment to stay silent.
What choice in the story made the difference?
Going to the professor first thing in the morning, saying what happened and what the fix would be, before anyone else found out.
How did Professor Bhalla see Gurleen's confession?
He respected it, thanking her for telling him first and later mentioning that morning in her recommendation letter.

Three sentences, please: what happens over this week?

Monday. Mohit, ten, stood in the school corridor with his gang. "From today, nobody talks to Baljeet. He told the teacher we were copying." The others nodded. Mohit felt strong, like the captain of a winning team.

Wednesday. Baljeet sat alone at lunch. Mohit watched his friend Aman look at Baljeet's lunch box, then at Mohit. Mohit felt a flicker of fear. What if Aman went to Baljeet's side? Then Mohit would be the one on his own. So he said loudly, "Anyone who sits with him is out too."

Friday. Aman sat with Baljeet anyway. Two more boys followed. Mohit stood with his tray and nobody beside him. For a moment, he knew exactly how Baljeet had felt all week.

Mohit orders his friends to stop talking to Baljeet and enjoys feeling powerful. When his friend Aman seems ready to side with Baljeet, Mohit threatens to shut out anyone who does. By Friday, Aman and others sit with Baljeet, and Mohit is the one left alone.

What keeps appearing in the narrator's dreams?

Of late I had often recalled this saying and this incident; for during the past week scarcely a night had gone over my couch that had not brought with it a dream of an infant, which I sometimes hushed in my arms, sometimes dandled on my knee, sometimes watched playing with daisies on a lawn, or again, dabbling its hands in running water. It was a wailing child this night, and a laughing one the next: now it nestled close to me, and now it ran from me; but whatever mood the apparition evinced, whatever aspect it wore, it failed not for seven successive nights to meet me the moment I entered the land of slumber.
A baby. For seven nights in a row she dreams of a child, sometimes crying and sometimes laughing, sometimes clinging to her and sometimes running away.

Dev won 6 games on Saturday and 7 on Sunday. How many games did he win?
Dev won 4 games on Saturday and 7 on Sunday. How many games did he win?
"graze" - what does it mean?
Kabir had 34 marbles and lost 6. How many marbles does he have now?
Our team scored 34 points in the first half and 17 in the second. How many points in all?

1. It is 13. Because 6 + 7 = 13.
2. 11 games. Because 4 + 7 = 11.
3. To graze is to eat grass in a field, as cows do.
4. That leaves 28. Because 34 - 6 = 28.
5. It is 51. Because 34 + 17 = 51.
