Monday: Rashmi watched Hansa say yes three times before lunch: an extra report, a colleague's shift, organising the office farewell. Hansa laughed, but her hands were shaking as she poured tea.
Thursday: Hansa was at her desk at 8 p.m. when Rashmi left. On Friday morning, Hansa had dark circles and had forgotten her own deadline. The manager frowned. Rashmi felt a pang of worry.
The next Monday: When a senior asked Hansa to cover yet another client meeting, Rashmi spoke first. “Hansa's with me on the vendor review this week. I can check if someone else is free.”
Later she whispered to Hansa, “You can say you're with me anytime. Practise.”
On Wednesday, Hansa said it herself. “I'm on the vendor review with Rashmi. Can we look at next week?” The senior nodded. Hansa sat back, stunned, and smiled.

What three things did Hansa say yes to on Monday before lunch?
An extra report, a colleague's shift, and organising the office farewell.
How did Rashmi feel when Hansa forgot her own deadline?
Rashmi felt a pang of worry, seeing Hansa burning out quietly.
What did Rashmi offer that let Hansa practise saying no?
She offered a line, being “with Rashmi on the vendor review,” and backed it up so Hansa could decline without losing standing.
How did Hansa feel when the senior nodded on Wednesday?
Hansa felt stunned and relieved, surprised that saying no was accepted.

Four founders each met public criticism online in a different way. When a harsh post about his product appeared, Siddharth waited a whole day, knowing an angry reply typed in a rage tends to make things worse and to spread the post further. Gargi's company had a complaint from one customer about a specific order. The company offered a one-to-one phone call or a personal email to sort out the details, and later came back to say it was settled, keeping the customer's privacy and staying out of a public row. Yash argued point by point with his critics and attacked their motives. Screenshots went around, and the quarrel drew much more notice than the original complaint. Amit found some posts making false and damaging claims about his firm. He gathered screenshots and consulted a lawyer on what the law allowed, but did not threaten people who simply disagreed with him.

How long did Siddharth wait before replying?
Siddharth waited a whole day.
How does Yash's response to critics differ from Gargi's, and what happened in each case?

Yash argued in public and attacked motives, so screenshots spread and the quarrel got more attention. Gargi's company moved the details to a private call or email and reported the matter settled, protecting privacy.
What was Yash probably feeling while he argued with critics?
He was probably angry and defensive, hurt that his work was being criticised.
What could Yash do next to calm the situation?
He could stop replying publicly, thank people for real feedback, and offer private contact for those with specific issues. Waiting a day before replying might help too. 🙂
Is a messenger the same as a postman?

Not quite. A messenger is a person who carries messages or parcels between people. A postman delivers the post as a regular job. Messenger is a noun.
Example: The messenger ran across the town with a note for the doctor.

Teacher's note, Eid week, playground duty
Rehana (Class 6) and her younger sister Rukhsar (Class 3) arrived not speaking, after a fight over a hair clip that morning. At lunch, a bigger boy from Class 7 grabbed Rukhsar's tiffin and held it over her head. Rehana came across the playground at a run, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her voice was shaking, but she did not move. The boy handed it back. Rehana then walked off without a word to her sister, still sulking. I spoke to the Class 7 boy and informed his class teacher and our counsellor the same afternoon. I also told Rehana privately that she was brave, and that next time she can call a teacher too.
Farah, playground duty

What did the two sisters fight over that morning?
A hair clip.
How did Rehana feel as she stood between the boy and Rukhsar?
She felt scared, her voice shaking, but fiercely protective of her sister despite still being angry about the morning.
What did Farah do next, and why was it right?
Farah spoke to the Class 7 boy and told his class teacher and the counsellor the same afternoon, and reminded Rehana she can call a teacher too, so she need not face bullies alone.
How might Rukhsar feel after Rehana rescued her tiffin?
Rukhsar might feel grateful and safe, and a little confused, since her sister protected her but still walked off sulking.

It was 10 p.m., the night before the board chemistry exam, and the power had just gone off in the whole lane. Arnab sat by the inverter lamp, scrolling a class group.
LEAKED PAPER, the message said. A blurry photo of a question sheet, a seal half visible, and a senior "from a reliable source" promising that question 4 was on electrolysis.
"It's real," Arnab told Rajni, who was revising at the other end of the mat. "Look at the seal. And he's a topper."
"How many times has the board paper actually leaked in the last ten years?" Rajni asked, not looking up.
"I don't know. Once? Never? But this one has details!"
"Every fake one has details. That's how they spread."
Arnab stared at the blurry seal, then at his untouched organic chapter. With two hours of battery left, he closed the group and opened the textbook.

What did the message promise question 4 would be on?
The message promised that question 4 was on electrolysis.
Why did the leaked paper feel real to Arnab?
Arnab felt hopeful and convinced by the seal and the topper's name, so the vivid details outweighed how rarely real leaks happen.
Which choice helped Arnab under time pressure?
Closing the group and using the last two hours of battery to revise the organic chapter, instead of betting on a rare leak.
How does Rajni see the leaked paper?
Rajni is unimpressed, since fake leaks always come with details, and keeps revising.

In Class 7, a girl named Bhumi left a note on Pratik's desk that said, "Look in your bag." Pratik was sure it was a prank, because the boys had pulled a few already. He looked in the bag with a stick, expecting a frog. Nothing. He found only a small packet of his favourite biscuits. Puzzled, he looked up and caught Bhumi watching. He frowned and marched over. "What is this?" he said. She blinked. "You looked sad yesterday." Pratik's ears burned. "I thought it was a trick." She laughed. "I would never bring a frog. I am afraid of them." They shared the biscuits in the corridor, and he apologised twice.
The novel was translated from Tamil. What does translated mean?

Translated means that the words were changed from one language into another while keeping the meaning. It is the past form of the verb translate.
Example: The novel was translated from Tamil into English, so many more people could read it.

Pallavi and her brother Uday had not spoken since the fight about the borrowed bicycle. For two days they passed each other in the courtyard of their house like strangers. Pallavi missed his silly jokes, but her pride sat like a stone in her chest. On the third afternoon Amma roasted peanuts. Pallavi filled half a steel plate and set it beside Uday's homework without a word. "These are for you," she said. Uday looked up. "Sorry I shouted," he said. "Sorry I called you a thief," she said. He pushed the plate to the middle of the table so they could share, and neither of them felt like they had lost anything.

What did Pallavi set beside Uday's homework?
She set half a steel plate of roasted peanuts beside it.
Why did Pallavi not speak first for two days?
Her pride sat like a stone in her chest, even though she missed Uday's silly jokes.
Why did Pallavi's snack gesture work?
It was a small gesture that opened a door without either one having to give in with words, and Uday then said sorry too.
How might Uday have felt when the peanuts appeared beside his homework?
He probably felt relieved and ready to make up, since he looked up and apologised right away.

In his second week at the design studio in Gurugram, Pankaj worked out the lunch map. The round table by the window was the boss's: Meera ma'am, the two senior designers and whoever had pitched well that week. The long table near the pantry was the juniors'. Friday outings worked the same way; the window table went, and the rest saw the photos on Monday.
Nitin, who'd joined a year earlier, said, "Don't waste energy trying to get onto that table. I did. Spent three months laughing at jokes I didn't find funny."
Pankaj noticed Nitin wasn't bitter. He just ate at the long table and got his work reviewed early. So Pankaj did the same: lunch with juniors he actually liked, and one short check-in with Meera ma'am every Thursday about his drafts.
He didn't obsess over the window table. But he knew exactly where it was.

Where was Meera ma'am's lunch table?
The round table by the window.
How does Pankaj seem to feel once he understands the lunch map?
Pankaj seems calm and clear-headed rather than anxious, aware of the inner circle without craving a seat there.
What did Pankaj choose to invest in, and why is it wise?
Real friendships at the long table and a steady Thursday check-in about his work, which builds trust with the boss through results.
What was chasing the window table like for Nitin?
Nitin felt tired and fake, spending three months laughing at jokes he didn't enjoy, and is more at ease now.

Pema's diary, Wednesday.
Practised the big talk with Aditi at the momo place after work. I did my whole speech about the Mumbai job: the studio, the pay, how it's a real career. Aditi listened, then said, "Okay, but what are Ama and Pala actually scared of?"
I started to say "that I'll fail" and stopped. It isn't that. It's that I'm the only one left in Gangtok since my brother went to Bengaluru. They're scared of an empty house. Of festivals with just the two of them.
So I've added something to the start of the talk: "I'll be home every Losar, and I'll take leave in October to help at Aunty's farm." It's true. I'd just never said it.
Strangely, I'm less nervous now. It feels less like a fight and more like a plan.

What did Aditi ask?
"What are Ama and Pala actually scared of?"
Why is Pema less nervous now?
Pema feels relieved because the talk now answers Ama and Pala's real fear, so it feels less like a fight and more like a plan.
What else could Pema do after the talk?
Pema could agree a regular call time with Ama and Pala and book the October leave early so the promise is kept.
What are Ama and Pala likely to feel when they hear the new opening?
They may still feel sad, but reassured that festivals like Losar won't be spent alone.

"Did you do the survey part?" Rehana asked in the school library, dropping her bag. "Me? I thought you were doing it." Zainab looked up from her notes. "We said we'd both do it." "Yes, but you always overdo things. I figured you'd finish it anyway." "And I figured you'd feel guilty and finish it." They stared at each other. "So nobody asked the thirty students." "Nobody asked anybody." "It's due at two." Zainab checked the clock. "It's twelve-forty." "If we'd each done fifteen, it'd be done." "And instead we each did zero." Rehana sat down hard. "Okay. You take the canteen, I'll take the field. Fifteen each. Go." They ran.

My mother says I should help in the kitchen more. I don't know how to start.
That's a nice step. Start with simple jobs, like washing vegetables, laying the plates and stirring.
I'm afraid of making a mess.
A bit of mess is part of learning, and cleaning up is part of the job. Wipe as you go and the kitchen stays calm.
What should I try cooking first?

In the small school by the paddy fields outside Thodupuzha, Elizabeth Teacher chalked the names for the Children's Day skit on the board. Salma read them twice. Her name wasn't there. On the walk home along the canal, she kicked every stone she passed. 'Teacher hates me,' she told Umma at the gate. 'She thinks I'm useless.' 'Did she say so?' 'She doesn't have to. She gave the mango-seller part to Beena, and Beena can't even act.' Umma handed her a glass of water. 'And who reads the prayer every Monday?' Salma looked into the glass. 'Me.' 'Who chose you for that?' Salma didn't answer, but she stopped kicking the gatepost.

What was Elizabeth Teacher writing the names for?
The names were for the Children's Day skit.
What does Salma kicking every stone suggest about her feelings?
Salma is hurt and angry at being left out, and she has already turned it into a story that Elizabeth Teacher thinks she is useless, which feels certain to her.
What turning point does Umma's question create?
Asking who chose Salma to read the prayer puts one real fact against the guess, and Salma's silence shows the belief starting to loosen.
How might Elizabeth Teacher see the skit list differently from Salma?
Elizabeth Teacher may have chosen parts for many reasons, like giving Beena a turn, and may never have thought of it as a judgement on Salma at all.

After I had turned the worst point of my illness, I began to notice that while all its other features changed, this one consistent feature did not change. Whoever came about me, still settled down into Joe. I opened my eyes in the night, and I saw, in the great chair at the bedside, Joe. I opened my eyes in the day, and, sitting on the window-seat, smoking his pipe in the shaded open window, still I saw Joe. I asked for cooling drink, and the dear hand that gave it me was Joe's. I sank back on my pillow after drinking, and the face that looked so hopefully and tenderly upon me was the face of Joe.

What does Pip notice while he is ill?
Whoever comes near him seems to turn into Joe. Joe sits by his bed day and night, gives him drinks and looks at him with hope and tenderness.

Daycare note, Monday. Tushar sat with the wooden farm puzzle for a long time today. His brow was deeply furrowed and he kept pressing the horse piece into the pig's space. He banged it once. I did not treat it as anger. I sat down and asked, "Stuck?" He handed me the horse. I turned it round and gave it back. He fitted it himself, his forehead smoothed, and he clapped. Baljeet, daycare teacher

Which puzzle piece was Tushar pressing into the wrong space?
The horse piece, into the pig's space.
What was Tushar feeling when he banged the piece?
He was frustrated after trying hard, shown by the furrowed brow and the bang; clapping at the end shows he felt proud once it fitted. 😊
Which choice of Baljeet's worked, and why?
Asking "Stuck?" and turning the piece round, then handing it back, worked because Tushar got just enough help to finish on his own.
What would change if Baljeet had told Tushar off for banging?
He might have felt more upset and given up on the puzzle instead of learning he could ask for help.

The rain was so heavy after school in Nagpur that only one shared auto came, with space for two in the back. Jasleen climbed in and patted the seat next to her, but Mehak, the new girl, slid in first. Sonali had to squeeze in front beside the driver. All the way home she could hear them laughing about the art project they were doing together. Sonali stared at the wet windscreen. Every day this week it had been Mehak, Mehak, Mehak. What if Jasleen didn't need her anymore? When the auto stopped, Jasleen leaned forward. "Sonu, you're coming for the project tomorrow, na?" Sonali's throat was tight. "You have Mehak now." Jasleen blinked. "I have both of you, silly."

Who slid into the seat beside Jasleen?
Mehak, the new girl.
What was Sonali afraid of as she stared at the wet windscreen?
She was scared and jealous, fearing Jasleen would like Mehak more and no longer need her.
What could Sonali do now that Jasleen has invited her?
She could go to the project tomorrow and try to get to know Mehak, and tell Jasleen honestly that she had felt left out.
How might Jasleen see Sonali's comment "You have Mehak now"?
Jasleen seems surprised, since she thinks of both girls as her friends and hadn't noticed Sonali feeling left out.

Deepika, twenty, wrote two lists before the weekend visit home. What matters: finishing the degree, earning her own money, choosing a partner freely. What can bend: the timing. Then she thought about her parents. Why did they keep bringing marriage up? Safety for her, what relatives said, their own worry about later years. She decided to say, first, that she knew they cared.

The talk still went stiff. Her father listened with his jaw tight, her mother left to make tea, and nothing was settled. Two days later Deepika sent a short message: "Thank you for hearing me out. I'm not ready, but I'm not shutting you out." Every week she shared a small piece of career news, a project, an interview. A month later, with a little more trust between them, she raised the topic again, more calmly, and her mother asked one real question.

Across town, Nilesh, of the same age, had taken three calls from relatives in one day. That night he shouted, "I will never marry!" and slammed his door. His parents went pale and quiet. The next morning his mother announced that they would start looking themselves, and the conversation was over.

What did Deepika write in her message two days after the talk?
She wrote, "Thank you for hearing me out. I'm not ready, but I'm not shutting you out."
How did Nilesh's outburst lead to a different result than Deepika's preparation and follow-up?

Nilesh's shout left his parents pale and quiet and set on looking themselves, ending the talk, while Deepika began by saying she knew they cared, sent a calm message and shared news each week, and trust grew until her mother asked a real question.
What was Deepika feeling when the talk went stiff?
Probably disappointed but determined, since she kept reaching out afterwards.
What could Nilesh try after slamming the door?
Nilesh could send a calm message saying he is not ready but values their care, and return to the topic later.

I'm Asif, and I live across from Vasudha's family. She's about two. Whenever the pressure cooker whistles, she drops everything and covers her ears, face scrunched. At her cousin's birthday she clung to her mother's leg for a long time before joining the others. Her cousin, the same age, runs straight into any crowd. I don't know what Vasudha feels inside, but loud sounds and new places seem to hit her harder.

What does Vasudha do when the pressure cooker whistles?
She drops everything and covers her ears, face scrunched.
What might Vasudha's clinging at the birthday suggest?
It might suggest she needs more time to feel comfortable in new, busy places.
How could Vasudha's parents support her?
They could give her time to warm up and warn her before loud sounds.
How does Asif see the difference between Vasudha and her cousin?
Asif notices her cousin runs straight in while loud sounds and new places seem to affect Vasudha more.
How many different ways can you work out 7 + 6? Show each one.

Answer: 13. For example: 6 + 6 + 1 = 13 (double and one more); 7 + 7 - 1 = 13 (double and one less); 7 + 3 + 3 = 13 (make 10).

There is no one right way. A child who knows many ways can check an answer by using a second way. Write the three ways on the board and ask the class to vote for their favourite. Praise clear explaining more than speed.
A khichdi recipe for 4 people uses 2 cups of rice, 1 cup of dal and 5 cups of water. How much of each is needed for 12 people?

Answer: 6 cups of rice, 3 cups of dal and 15 cups of water.

12 people is 3 times as many as 4 people (12 / 4 = 3), so EVERY amount is multiplied by 3: rice 3 x 2 = 6, dal 3 x 1 = 3, water 3 x 5 = 15. The scale factor is found first, then used on each line. A common mistake is to add 8 cups (because 12 - 4 = 8) - the recipe must keep the same TASTE, so all amounts grow by the same number of times.
How do I introduce a new puppy to an older dog?
Let them meet in a neutral place, such as a park or a hallway, with each on a lead and a calm person holding it. Keep the first meeting short.
What if the older dog growls?
A growl can be a signal to back off, so take it seriously. Give the dogs space and try again later, without scolding the older dog for warning.
How long until they get along?
It can take days or weeks. Supervise them together, and give each dog its own bowl, bed and quiet time. A trainer or a vet can help if there is real trouble.

The nurses' station at the city hospital was busy even at 3 p.m. Sunaina, twenty-five, had a pattern: every time a difficult relative left the desk, she grabbed her phone and scrolled. Five minutes, sometimes fifteen. Afterward she felt more drained, not less.
Her colleague Pradeep suggested, “Don't just stop. Replace it. When you feel that rush, walk to the end of the corridor and back. Or do the four-count breathing at the window.”
So she tried. Same trigger: a tense conversation. New action: a walk to the corridor window, four slow breaths. On a scrap of paper in her pocket she tallied how she felt after, on a scale from one to five.
After two weeks, the tally was mostly fours. The scrolling sheet from the week before had been mostly twos.
The stress still came. But the walk met the need.

What did Sunaina tally on the scrap of paper?
How she felt after each walk, on a scale from one to five.
Why did Sunaina reach for the phone after difficult conversations?
She felt stressed and wanted quick relief, even though scrolling left her more drained.
Why did replacing the scrolling work better than simply stopping?
The same cue now led to a walk and breathing that met her need for relief, and tracking showed it helped.
How might Pradeep feel seeing Sunaina's tally of mostly fours?
Pradeep would probably feel glad and a little proud that the suggestion helped.

A school bought 20 cartons of pencils at the start of school. Pencils come in cartons of 10 boxes and each box costs $2. The school also bought 10 cartons of markers. A carton has 5 boxes and costs $4. How much did the school spend in all?

The school bought 20 x 10 = 200 boxes of pencils.
The pencils cost 200 x $2 = $400.
The school bought 10 x 5 = 50 boxes of markers.
The markers cost 50 x $4 = $200.
Thus, the school spent a total of $400 + $200 = $600.
The answer is 600.
Rewrite in a casual tone: I am sorry to trouble you, but could you move your bag?
Sorry, could you move your bag?

In his rented room in Andheri, Eshaan had forty slides titled 'Transforming Education Across Maharashtra'. Three logo versions. A mission statement he rewrote every week. A plan for 10,000 schools in five years.
It was October. He had started in March.
His friend Rehana, a schoolteacher, came over and scrolled through the deck. 'It's beautiful,' she said. 'How many students have you taught?'
'None yet. I need funding first. And a team. And the app.'
'My school has a free slot on Saturdays. Twelve kids who need help with maths. You could start next week.'
Eshaan looked at the forty slides. Twelve kids felt almost embarrassing next to 10,000 schools. 'That's too small to matter,' he said.

How many schools did Eshaan's plan cover?
10,000 schools in five years.
Why did twelve kids feel 'almost embarrassing' to Eshaan?
Next to his grand plan, a small start made Eshaan feel small and a little ashamed, as if it didn't count.
What would you advise Eshaan to do next Saturday?
Accept Rehana's offer and teach the twelve kids, learning what works before building anything bigger.
How might Rehana see the forty slides?
Rehana admires them but is frustrated that seven months of planning have helped no student yet.

"Urmila, dinner!" "Not hungry." Darshan bhaiya leaned on her door. "You've changed your hair three times since March." "So?" "So nothing. Just asking. Last month it was the debate club, now it's the skateboard lot." "Can you not?" "I'm not having a go. I just want to know which Urmila I'm eating dinner with." She threw a cushion at him. "Seriously?" "Seriously. Felt awful." Urmila picked at the cushion's tassel. "Did it stop?" "Slowly. Come and eat."

The debate club.

She feels lost and out of place in every group, and it unsettles her that she can't say who she really is.

He stopped teasing, sat on her floor and shared that he went through the same thing, which made her feel less strange.
What is it like for Darshan to watch Urmila change so often?
Darshan is curious and a little worried, but remembers doing the same at her age, so he can be patient rather than annoyed.

Night shifts at the call centre in Gurugram left Tanuja with odd hours and an empty head. At 4 am, between calls, she started reading a small book of Buddhist teachings a colleague had lent her. The lines about impermanence made her cry in the washroom once. Another line annoyed her so much she argued with it in the margin.

On Sundays she met Minakshi, an old school friend, at a tea stall, and they talked through the chapters. Minakshi was Christian and brought her own questions; they compared.

In March a man at a weekend meditation session offered Tanuja a place in his group. "You don't need other books," he said. "I will tell you what everything means."

She felt tempted, tired as she was. It would be so easy. Then she thought of her messy margins and the Sunday arguments. She thanked him, and kept her book.

What did Tanuja start reading at 4 am?
Tanuja started reading a small book of Buddhist teachings a colleague had lent her.
Why was Tanuja tempted by the man's offer?
Tanuja felt tired and tempted by the ease of having someone tell her what everything meant.
Why was keeping her book and Sunday talks the wiser choice?
They let the teachings comfort and challenge her and kept her thinking, while the ready-made answers would have spared her from thinking.
How might Minakshi see their Sunday conversations?
Minakshi seems to enjoy them as an exchange of questions between two faiths, not a contest.

Rain had been threatening all afternoon, and the house cricket final had to finish before the sky opened. Kamal, captain of Tagore House, was fielding at point when his own bowler, Nikhil, threw the ball instead of bowling it. Kamal clapped. "Great ball!" Four overs later, with thunder rumbling, Arohi of Raman House did exactly the same. Kamal flung down his cap. "That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!" The PT sir raised an eyebrow. "Kamal, Nikhil's arm bent the same way." "That was different, sir. It was wet, the ball slipped." "And now?" Kamal opened his mouth. The first fat drops of rain fell, and everyone ran for the corridor, but Arohi looked back at him, arms folded, until he looked away.

What did Kamal do when Arohi threw the ball?
Kamal flung down his cap and shouted, 'That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!'
Why did Nikhil's throw seem fine to Kamal but Arohi's seem like cheating?
As Tagore House captain, Kamal felt protective of his side and eager to win, so he found an excuse for Nikhil and none for the rival house.
What could Kamal do after he looks away from Arohi?
He could admit to PT sir and Arohi that both throws were the same, and use one rule for both houses.
What might Arohi be thinking, arms folded, looking back at Kamal?
Arohi probably thinks Kamal is being unfair, calling out the same action that Kamal clapped for from Tagore House.

What did the aunt ask for?
The aunt asked for a second function.
What was Eshaan feeling when asking whose wedding it was?
Eshaan was frustrated and hurt, feeling the wedding no longer belonged to the couple.

messages.content: Erwan went on shopping. He purchased a pair of shoes at $200 but discounted 30%, and two shirts at $80 each. Upon checkout, the cashier said that there is an additional 5% discount. How much did he spend after all the discounts?

The total discount of a pair of shoes is $200 x 30/100 = $60.
He spent $200 - $60 = $140 for a pair of shoes.
The total cost of two shirts is $80 x 2 = $160.
The initial cost of his purchase is $140 + $160 = $300.
He got an additional $300 x 5/100 = $15 discount upon checkout.
Therefore, Erwan spent $300 - 15 = $285 after all the discounts.
The answer is 285.

I'm Bhupen, fourteen, and I was there when my sister Sabina went quiet at dinner last week. Our cousins had come over, and Sabina was telling them about our trip to the tea gardens when she was eight. She described the rope bridge and how she crossed it alone while Ma held her breath. Then Ma said gently, "Beta, you didn't cross it. You cried, so Baba carried you." I remember that too; I was holding her slipper. Sabina frowned. "But I remember the planks under my feet." Maybe she felt them from Baba's arms. Maybe it comes from how we've all joked about "brave Sabina" ever since. I honestly can't tell what she saw. She just kept stirring her dal, quieter than usual.

What was Bhupen holding at the rope bridge?
Sabina's slipper.
What might Sabina have been feeling as she kept stirring her dal?
Unsettled and perhaps a little embarrassed 😔 The planks under her feet felt like a real memory, but Ma said Baba had carried her across.
How could the family respond at that moment instead of just correcting Sabina?
They could explain that everyone's memories get mixed with stories told later, and notice that their "brave Sabina" joke may have shaped her picture, so she does not feel foolish.
Why can't Bhupen be sure what Sabina saw?
Bhupen only sees her from outside. Her picture might come from being carried across or from years of family jokes, and nobody can look inside her memory.

The storm knocked the power out just as Kiran sent her message: "Are you coming to study tomorrow?" She waited an hour, then two, staring at the dark screen. Nothing from Salma. Her mind started building stories. She's fed up with me. She found a better group. Kiran couldn't sleep, and the maths exam was at nine. At midnight she caught herself. She typed instead, "Hey, no pressure, but I'm worried I upset you. Are you okay?" She didn't expect an answer. In the morning it came: "So sorry! My phone died in the storm. See you at the library. Love you 😊"

What knocked the power out?
The storm knocked the power out.
What was Kiran feeling while she waited for Salma's reply?
She was anxious and worried she had upset Salma, and her imagination made up stories. The delay was actually because of a dead phone.
What worked when Kiran finally asked?
She sent a kind, direct message asking if Salma was okay instead of spiralling. Asking got a clear answer.
How might Salma have felt when she saw Kiran's message?
She felt sorry and warm toward Kiran, as her reply shows. She had no idea her silence caused worry.

I'm Kavitha. It was the evening after our college hackathon; I'd been awake for almost thirty hours. I got back to our girls' PG and lay on the bed in my jeans.

Ayesha came in bouncing. "Okay, Holi plan! Terrace at ten, natural colours only, I'll make thandai, and then we all go to Meenu's for lunch."

"Mm," I said, with my eyes closed.

She stopped. "Wow. You clearly hate it. You could just say you don't want to come."

It stung, because I hadn't said anything like that. For a second I wanted to snap back, "Stop putting words in my mouth." But I was too tired to fight, which actually helped.

I opened one eye. "Ayesha, I love the plan. I'm just so tired I can't feel my feet. Can you tell me again tomorrow?"

She looked at me, at the jeans, at the hackathon badge still round my neck. "Oh. Sleep, idiot."

I was asleep before she switched off the light.

How long had Kavitha been awake?
Almost thirty hours.
Why did Ayesha's words sting Kavitha?
Kavitha felt misread: she hadn't said anything against the plan, and being told she hated it put words in her mouth. Being tired made the unfairness sharper.
What worked about how Kavitha answered instead of snapping back?
Kavitha said plainly what she was feeling, tired and not against the plan, and asked to hear it again tomorrow. That cleared up the misreading in a few seconds.
How might Ayesha have felt when she noticed the jeans and the badge?
Ayesha probably felt a little sheepish, realising that the "Mm" came from exhaustion and not dislike. Her joking "Sleep, idiot" suggests relief and affection.
Why does it get so humid before the monsoon?
Warm air from the sea carries a lot of water vapour inland ahead of the rains. The air holds more moisture than usual, so it feels sticky.
And why does it feel hotter then?
Sweat cools us by evaporating. In humid air it evaporates slowly, so the body cannot cool down as easily and the heat feels worse.
Is there any way to feel cooler?
Light cotton clothes, a fan to keep air moving, and plenty of shade help. Drinking water regularly is sensible too.
A bag contains 50 fewer baseball cards than football cards. There are 4 times as many football cards as hockey cards. If there are 200 hockey cards in the bag, how many cards are there altogether?

If there are 200 hockey cards in the bag and 4 times as many football cards as hockey cards, there are 4*200 = 800 football cards.
The total number of football and hockey cards in the bag is 800+200 = 1000 cards.
The bag contains 50 fewer baseball cards than football cards, meaning there are 800-50 = 750 baseball cards.
Altogether, there are 750+1000 = 1750 cards.
The answer is 1750.

Nazia, when you asked me on the show what caring for my mother is like, I said "fine". I'm Manoj, her son, and it wasn't fine. Let me say it properly.

Amma has had kidney trouble for two years. Every Tuesday and Friday I take her to dialysis. I sit in that hospital corridor four hours, working on my laptop, then drive her home. I love her. And some Tuesdays, stuck in traffic, I felt like the walls were closing in.

My sister Radhika lives an hour away. I never asked her for anything, because it felt like admitting I was failing Amma.

In January I finally called. "Radhika, I can't do both days. Can you take Fridays?" There was silence, then, "Why didn't you say so a year ago?" Now she does Fridays and I do Tuesdays.

Asking for help wasn't betraying Amma. It's what's letting me keep going.

On which days does Manoj take his mother to dialysis?
He takes her every Tuesday and Friday.
What was Manoj feeling on some Tuesdays in traffic?
Manoj felt trapped, like the walls were closing in, even though he loved his mother.
What did Manoj do that made the care more manageable?
He asked his sister for one specific thing, taking Fridays, instead of carrying it all alone out of a sense of duty.
How did Radhika seem to feel when Manoj finally asked?
Radhika seemed surprised and a little hurt that he hadn't asked a year earlier, and willing to help.

Jin did her list in silence. Twenty minutes later she closed her book. "Done. Test me?"

'You're out, Tushar's out, and Vidya...' Chinmay paused, enjoying the silence. 'Vidya can be in. If she brings the ball.'
'Why do you always decide?' Vidya asked.
'Because it's my gang. My rules.'
'Tushar cried yesterday, you know. Behind the cycle stand, with his face in his arms.'

'So nobody here actually likes you. They're just scared of being out.'
'That's not true. Ask anyone.'

'Fine,' he muttered. 'Everyone plays. Tushar bats first.'

'Really.'

What did Vidya say Tushar did yesterday?
He cried behind the cycle stand.
What was Chinmay feeling when nobody answered Vidya's question?
Shaken and hurt; his throat went tight as he saw that the others followed him out of fear, not liking.

How does Vidya see Chinmay's rules?

Karen had the giant box of crayons, containing twice as many crayons as were in Beatrice's box. But Beatrice's box contained twice as many crayons as were in Gilbert's box of crayons. And Gilbert had four times as many crayons as were in Judah's box of crayons. If Karen's box contained 128 crayons, how many crayons were in Judah's box?

If Karen's 128 crayons were twice as many as were in Beatrice's box, there were 128/2=64 crayons in Beatrice's box.
And since Beatrice's box contained twice as many crayons as were in Gilbert's box of crayons, then Gilbert had 64/2=32 crayons.
And since Gilbert had four times as many crayons as Judah, then Judah had 32/4=8 crayons.
The answer is 8.

What was "leaving a Margin", and how did it turn out?

My business habits had one other bright feature, which I called "leaving a Margin." For example; supposing Herbert's debts to be one hundred and sixty-four pounds four-and-twopence, I would say, "Leave a margin, and put them down at two hundred." Or, supposing my own to be four times as much, I would leave a margin, and put them down at seven hundred. I had the highest opinion of the wisdom of this same Margin, but I am bound to acknowledge that on looking back, I deem it to have been an expensive device. For, we always ran into new debt immediately, to the full extent of the margin, and sometimes, in the sense of freedom and solvency it imparted, got pretty far on into another margin.
It meant writing the debts down as more than they were. The narrator thought it wise, but it was an expensive device, because they always ran into new debt up to the margin, and sometimes beyond it.

A church has 120 members. 40% are adults. The rest are children. How many children more children are there than adults?

There are 48 adults because 120 x .4 = 48
60% of members are children because 100 - 40 = 60
There are 72 children because 120 x .6 = 72
There are 24 more children than adults because 72 - 48 = 24
The answer is 24.

To know how many groups of 150 cans there are in 675 cans, we calculate 675 / 150 = 4.5.

The answer is 36.

Vaibhav, you want to know why your Hafsa nani always keeps an umbrella in the car? Let me tell you about my school's annual day, back when I was sixteen.

Our headmistress made the organising committee sit in her office. "Close your eyes. It's the evening after annual day, and it failed. Tell me why." We felt silly. Then answers came. "The generator won't start." "It rains and the shamiana leaks." "Half the dancers get chickenpox."

She made us write a fix beside each fear. We borrowed a second generator from the mosque committee. We tied plastic sheets over the shamiana. Every dance had two understudies.

It rained that evening, and the first generator coughed and stopped. We lit the stage with the second one while parents clapped, never knowing. I've planned that way ever since.

They borrowed a second generator from the mosque committee.

They felt silly and a little awkward, but once answers began they seem to have become engaged.

The headmistress probably felt quietly satisfied and relieved, seeing the exercise she insisted on save the evening.

A snake's head is one-tenth its length. If a snake is 10 feet long, calculate the length of the rest of its body minus the head.

The answer is 9.

At twenty, Ishita had a group report on water use due at the end of the month. Sitting with her friend Swati, she reckoned it would be finished in three days if nothing went wrong. She fixed the deadline for herself accordingly and did nothing for a week. Then her laptop stopped charging. The survey questions were not clear, and Lavanya Ma'am replied to her email two days late. Interruptions kept piling up. Ishita's three days turned into ten, and she was up at three in the morning, still checking the last table. She thought it would be finished in three days.

At ten she pictured the planets going in a neat row and forgot smudged ink and missing card. At twenty she reckoned on the day when nothing went wrong, and a broken laptop, unclear questions and late replies turned her three days into ten.

She was exhausted and frustrated, realising her plan had not allowed for anything to go wrong.

In a 50-question test with two marks for each question, Meghan learned that she scored 20 marks less than her friend Jose, who scored 40 more marks than their friend Alisson. Calculate the total score for the three in the test combined if Jose got 5 questions wrong?

If you answer every question correctly in the test, the total possible marks are 50*2= 100 marks.
If Jose got five questions wrong, he lost 5*2 = 10 marks because each question has two marks.
Therefore, Jose scored 100-10 = 90 marks on the test.
Meghan scored 20 marks less than that which Jose got, a total of 90-20 = 70 marks.
The total marks that Jose and Meghan scored in the test are 70+90 = 160
Alisson scored 90-40 = 50 marks in the examination, 40 marks less than that which Jose scored on the test.
The total number of marks that the three scored in the test is 160+50 = 210
The answer is 210.

How did Aadhya feel playing with her cousins?
She felt pure joy; she giggled so hard her tummy hurt.
What did Nirmala Mausi do that made the fun better?
She noticed quiet Tuktuk alone and brought her into the game, giving her a strength to be proud of. 🙂
How might Tuktuk feel when Aadhya says "You're on my team"?
Tuktuk likely feels included and happy after sitting alone, and laughs loudest of all.
We are cooking for twenty relatives this weekend. My grandmother wants everything homemade.
That is a big cooking job, but also a lovely tradition. Who will be helping in the kitchen?
Me, my mother, and my aunt. Grandmother will direct.
Then divide the work early. One person makes the main dish, one handles the sides and rice, and one does the sweets. Grandmother can check the taste and tell stories while you work.
Can we prepare some things the night before?
Yes, definitely. Chop vegetables, soak lentils, make the dough and prepare the masala paste the night before. Keep them covered in the fridge. Saturday will be much calmer.
What about dessert? Grandmother likes her gulab jamun.
Gulab jamun can also be made a day early, since the syrup soaks in better overnight. Reheat gently before serving. Your grandmother will be proud to see her favourite on the table.
Right. And how many relatives did I say are coming?
Twenty relatives. Plan food for about twenty-two, to be safe, and make a double batch of gulab jamun so your grandmother's favourite does not run out.

Please answer each one.
What does the word "exercise" mean?
How do I practise badminton alone?

1. An exercise is an activity that keeps your body strong. Example: A walk is good exercise.
2. Hit the shuttle against a wall or keep it in the air with your racket. Count how many times in a row you can do it.

Read this:

The biodata Jagdish mama had sent listed it all: Rukhsar, five foot four, MSc, father a doctor, "fair, homely". Farhan, twenty-two, felt slightly sick reading it, as if they were shopping. When the families arranged a meeting at a Lucknow café, the power went out ten minutes in and the waiter apologised: no coffee, no fans. The families decided to wait in the car. Farhan and Rukhsar ended up walking under the dripping trees of the park across the road, umbrellas bumping.
They talked for two hours. About how she argued with her father over a stray dog. About his fear of letting his mother down. She asked how he treated waiters; he laughed and told her about the one he'd once shouted at, and how bad he felt. She liked that he admitted it. By the end he knew nothing new about her height or salary. He knew she was honest, quick-tempered and kind.

What did the biodata say about Rukhsar's height?
Five foot four.
How did Farhan feel reading the biodata?
He felt slightly sick and uncomfortable, as if they were shopping.
Why did the long walk reveal more than the biodata?
Talking for two hours showed values, temper and respect, like honesty about mistakes and how people treat others, which a list of qualities cannot.
How might Rukhsar have seen Farhan after the walk?
She seemed to respect him, liking that he admitted his mistake with the waiter instead of pretending to be perfect.

Read this:

"Maria Didi, where are you putting Nani's glasses?"
"On the shelf, Akash. They'll get broken on the chair."
"But Nani went to the market. She saw them on the chair."
"Yes. So when she comes back, where will she look?"
"On the chair!" Akash laughed. "But they're not there!"
"Why will she look there?"
"Because she didn't see you move them. She thinks they're still on the chair."
"Good thinking. Let's tell her when she's home."

Where did Maria put Nani's glasses?
She put them on the shelf so they would not get broken on the chair.
How does Akash feel about working out where Nani will look?
Akash is amused, laughing because Nani didn't see Maria move the glasses and still believes they are on the chair.
What did Maria do that helped Akash understand?
She asked questions like "Where will she look?" and let Akash explain the reason without help.
How might Nani feel if nobody told her about the move?
She might be puzzled and worried when she finds the chair empty, so telling her saves her a scare.

Read this:

The lights went out with the thunder, and Ritu decided the sofa was a rocket.
"Mama, you're the space cat," she said, handing Salma a torch. "Cats don't talk."
Salma wanted to check the dal, but she got down on the floor instead, a dupatta for a tail. "Meow?"
"No! You wait for orders." Ritu pointed at the ceiling. "Ten, nine, eight..."
Lightning cracked. Ritu gripped the sofa arm, and the cat crept close and stayed quiet, just as the captain had ordered. "Blast off," said Ritu, and grinned at her cat.

What did Ritu decide the sofa was?
She decided it was a rocket.
What might Ritu feel when the lightning cracks?
She is a little frightened but trying to stay brave. She grips the sofa arm, and the cat stays close and quiet.
What choice did Salma make that helped in the storm?
She left the dal and took the small role of the space cat, following Ritu's rules and staying close.
How might Salma see the game during the power cut?
She may see it as a way to keep Ritu calm and happy, since she gives up her own plans and enjoys the story.

Read this:

Jeevan's phone buzzed again at 1 a.m., the ninth message from Rashmi that night, asking why he had left her last one on read. She had also been waiting outside his lecture hall every morning that week, "just passing by". His stomach tightened each time he saw her name. On Sunday he wrote one message: "Rashmi, I don't feel the same and I don't want to be contacted. Please stop." Then he stopped replying. When more messages came, he took screenshots and saved them in a folder. He told his roommate Kunal everything, and Kunal said, "Show the warden if it goes on. You haven't done anything wrong." On Wednesday Jeevan sat in the warden's office with the folder and felt his shoulders drop for the first time in days.

What did Jeevan write in his one message to Rashmi?
He wrote that he didn't feel the same, didn't want to be contacted, and asked her to stop.
What was Jeevan feeling each time he saw Rashmi's name?
He felt uneasy and tense, since his stomach tightened, and he only began to relax after telling the warden.
What should Jeevan do if the messages keep coming?
He should keep not replying, keep the screenshots, and keep telling Kunal and the warden. It is not his fault. 🤍
How might Rashmi see Jeevan's single clear message?

The passage shows Rashmi only through her repeated messages and "just passing by", so she may see her attention as harmless persistence. Jeevan's clear no still means it is not welcome, however she sees it.
Weather report mein 'drizzle' bola. Kya hota hai?
"Drizzle" is very light rain with tiny drops. Example: "It was only drizzling, so we didn't need an umbrella." It can be a noun (a drizzle) or a verb (it is drizzling).

Mark loves to see shows in theaters. He decided to visit the theater at least once a week. One performance lasts 3 hours. The price of the ticket depends on the time spent in the theater and stands at $5 for each hour. How much will Mark spend on visits to the theater in 6 weeks?

The price of one performance is 3 * $5 = $15.
Mark intends to go to the theater once a week, so in 9 weeks he will spend 6 * $15 = $90.
The answer is 90.
Why does a map have a key?

A map has a key to explain its symbols. Because the symbols are only drawings that stand for things like roads, rivers and schools, a reader who does not know the meaning would have to guess, and the key tells them.

Supervisor's note, end of the side project, 30 June.
For three months, Sonali, a backend developer from another team, has spent Friday afternoons with our product team as a trial. She wanted to know whether product management fits her before asking for a transfer.
What I observed: she ran four customer interviews, wrote two feature briefs and sat in every prioritisation meeting. She was strong on clear writing and weak at first on saying no to requests; by May she was pushing back well. She also told me honestly that she missed writing code more than she expected.
We talked today. She is not switching yet. She wants one more quarter, focused on data products that mix both. I have agreed and will check in with her manager.
Gurleen

How many customer interviews did Sonali run?
Four customer interviews.
How might Sonali have felt on missing code more than she expected?
She was probably surprised and a little torn, learning that product work suited her in some ways but not in others.
Why was a three-month trial a better approach than an immediate switch?
It let Sonali test the fit and discover she missed coding, without giving up her current role.
How might Gurleen's product team be affected by Sonali's Fridays?
They got extra help with interviews and briefs, and a developer's view in prioritisation meetings.

messages.content:
Read this:

At his cousin's wedding in the kasba, Yusuf stood by the tent pole with his arms folded. The other teenagers were dancing near the stage. Nobody here likes me, he thought. They think I'm the boring cousin from the city.
Sudha, a girl from the next house, came over with a plate. "Want some jalebi?"
"No," Yusuf said, and looked at his phone.
She shrugged and went back to the group. After that, nobody came near him.
On the tractor ride home, Yusuf told himself, See? I knew they didn't like me. His aunt, sitting beside him, said, "You looked so bored, beta. They thought you didn't want to talk."
Yusuf stared at the dark fields. He hadn't thought of that.

What did Sudha offer Yusuf?
She offered him some jalebi.
Why did Yusuf say no and look at his phone?
He felt sure nobody liked him, so he was guarded and uneasy, expecting rejection before it came.
What could Yusuf try at the next family gathering?
He could accept an offer like the jalebi, ask one question and stand closer to the group, then see how people respond.
How did the other teenagers see Yusuf, according to his aunt?
They saw him as bored and uninterested, so they left him alone.

Read this:

Three weeks after Santosh apologised for forgetting my birthday dinner, we had plans for the new exhibition at the art gallery.
I half expected a last-minute message. Instead he was there at five, ten minutes early, holding two tickets.
"You said you wanted to see the textile section first," he said. "I checked the map."
I had said that, weeks ago, in passing.
Then next week he came to my college play. He sat in the second row. He texted me before, "Break a leg!" and after, "You were great in the market scene."
He didn't say sorry again. He didn't need to. I'm Jahnavi, and each small thing added a brick back.

What time was Santosh at the art gallery?
At five, ten minutes early.
What was Jahnavi feeling when Santosh remembered the textile section?
Jahnavi felt surprised and touched, since the textile section was mentioned only in passing weeks ago.
What rebuilt Jahnavi's trust in Santosh?
Small, repeated actions that matched his apology, being early, remembering what mattered and showing up to the play, rather than more apologies.
What is Santosh likely experiencing as he keeps showing up?
He probably feels hopeful and steady, glad to prove through actions that he meant what he said.

Read this:

Day one: Deepak came home after three weeks at a work site. Rashmi hid behind Dadi's knees and only stared at her Papa.
Day two: She walked over with her stuffed rabbit, dropped it in his lap, and sat close enough to touch his arm.
Day four: When the doorbell rang in the evening, she ran shouting, "Papa!", hugged his legs and planted a wet kiss on his cheek when he lifted her.

How long had Deepak been away at the work site?
He had been away for three weeks at a work site.
Why might Rashmi have hidden behind Dadi on the first day?
After three weeks apart she may have felt shy and unsure, needing time to feel close to her Papa again.
What could Deepak do to help the closeness return?
He could stay calm and warm, let Rashmi come to him in her own time and accept small gifts like the rabbit with delight.
What is it like for Deepak when Rashmi runs to the door on day four?
It likely feels wonderful after the shy first day, showing him their bond is back. ❤️

Read this:

Sit, Vandana, the rice can wait. You asked why your Lokesh Mama never lets anyone call him "poor thing." I'll tell you.

When I was nineteen, my first-year classes were on the third floor, and my leg brace made the stairs take ten minutes each way. I was late every day. One professor marked me absent three times in a row. I was so angry and so ashamed that I nearly left the college.

Then my room-mate said, "They can't fix what they don't know." So I wrote a letter to the principal. I said, plainly, that I could not climb three floors quickly, and asked if our section could use a ground-floor room, or if I could be marked present from the time I reached the stairs.

The principal called me in. He was stiff at first. But the next month our section moved downstairs. Nobody pitied me. They just changed a room.

Where were Lokesh's first-year classes held?
His first-year classes were on the third floor.
How did young Lokesh feel after being marked absent three times?
He felt angry and ashamed, so much that he nearly left the college.
What was the turning point in Lokesh's story, and why did it work?
Writing plainly to the principal about the stairs and offering two possible fixes worked because it gave the college clear facts and a practical choice.
How might the principal have seen Lokesh's letter at first?
The principal was stiff at first, perhaps unused to such a request, but the clear, polite letter made it easy to agree to a simple room change.

What should I wear to a family festival?
Also, what is wrong with "We decorated our house by flowers."?
Why do people decorate their houses at festivals?

1. Wear clean, comfortable clothes that suit the occasion. Traditional clothes are lovely, but comfort matters too.
2. Fixed: We decorated our house with flowers. Why: Use "with" for the material you use.
3. It makes the home look cheerful. Because it welcomes guests and shows that it is a special day.
Imagine a boy who cannot afford a canteen snack and a friend who offers to share; make it a story.

Every day at the break, the canteen smelled of fried potato, and every day Manoj felt his empty pocket. His father had lost his job that month and there was no pocket money. He pretended that he was not hungry and stayed in the classroom with a book. A boy named Colin noticed. The next day, Colin bought two vada pavs and said, "They gave me one free. Can you help me finish them?" Manoj looked at him closely, then took one. They sat on the steps and ate. Colin asked him to keep a seat at their cricket game and mentioned, without any fuss, that he would be getting "free ones" often. Manoj understood, and thanked him with a quiet nod.

Cristina, John, Clarissa and Sarah want to give their mother a photo album for her birthday. Cristina brings 7 photos, John brings 10 photos and Sarah brings 9 photos. If the photo album has 40 slots available, how many photos does Clarissa need to bring in order to complete the photo album?

Excluding Clarissa, there are 7 + 10 + 9 = 26 photos.
Clarissa needs to bring 40 - 26 = 14 photos to complete the photo album.
The answer is 14.

Why does a ceiling fan make us feel cooler even though it does not cool the air?
Then, which is right: "its" or "it's"?
And what is the phone number of my school office?
Is there a mistake here? How much students are there?
Plus, I saw "inflexible" in a story. What does it mean?

1. The moving air helps our sweat dry faster. Because drying sweat carries heat away from the skin, we feel cooler.
2. "It's" means "it is" or "it has", and "its" shows that something belongs to it. For example: it's raining, and the dog wagged its tail.
3. I don't know, because I don't have your school's details. Look on the school website or in your diary.
4. Corrected: How many students are there? Why: use "many" with countable nouns like "students".
5. "Inflexible" is an adjective. It means unwilling to change, or unable to bend.
Alexander Bought 22 more joggers than Tyson. Christopher bought twenty times as many joggers as Tyson. If Christopher bought 80 joggers, how many more joggers does Christopher buy than Alexander?

Tyson bought 80/20=4 joggers.
Alexander bought 4+22=26 joggers.
Christopher bought 80-26=54 more joggers than Alexander.
The answer is 54.

Monday: At school, Pooja's class learned the emergency number and practised saying their address clearly. She wrote both on a card and stuck it on the fridge at home.
Thursday: Nazia Aunty next door showed Pooja her first-aid box: bandages, antiseptic, cotton, and the doctor's number taped inside the lid.
The next Sunday: Pooja's grandmother slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. Pooja's hands shook, but she called the emergency number from the card, said the address slowly, then ran to fetch Nazia Aunty. Help arrived soon. Later, Nani squeezed her hand.

Where did Pooja stick the card with the emergency number?
She stuck it on the fridge at home.
What do Pooja's shaking hands suggest about how she felt?
They suggest she was frightened, even while she did the right things.
What preparation helped Pooja act in the emergency?
Learning the emergency number, practising her address and putting the card on the fridge.
How might Nani feel about Pooja?
She probably feels grateful and proud, which is why she squeezed her hand. 🙏

Dear Vijay Bhaiya,

Big news, and you're the only one I'm telling properly. I got selected for the national debate finals in Pune. Out of the whole state, eight of us. At school, though, I've been acting like it's nothing. When the sir announced it, I said, 'They must have run out of people.' Everyone laughed. When my friends asked, I said I'll probably lose in round one. The truth? I've been practising every night for months, and I want to win so badly my stomach hurts. But you know how it is here. Say one proud thing and suddenly you're 'too big for your boots' and nobody saves you a seat. So I joke. Is that stupid? Can you call on Sunday? I want to practise my opening with someone who won't laugh.

Hrithik

How many students from the state reached the national debate finals?
Eight of them.
What is Hrithik feeling beneath the jokes at school?
Hrithik feels excited and eager to win, but also anxious that showing pride will make friends turn cold.
What would you advise Hrithik about talking to friends?
Hrithik could share the news honestly with one or two close friends, saying it took hard work, rather than joking it down to nothing.
How might Vijay Bhaiya feel reading this letter?
Vijay Bhaiya would likely feel proud and trusted, and perhaps sad that Hrithik feels unable to be proud openly at school.

metadata.subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Neelam, you're asking why I'm smiling at your brother, lying on the floor with his blocks. Let me, your Bidisha Didima, tell you.
When I was nine, in Shillong, my father brought home a metal building set from a fair: little nuts and bolts and strips with holes. My brothers lost interest in a day. I didn't.
I built a bridge first. Then a windmill that actually turned. I remember sitting on the verandah floor, the light moving across it, and my mother calling me for lunch, then for tea. I didn't hear either time.
Some bolts wouldn't fit. I'd get so cross. Then I'd try another way, and it would click, and I'd feel a happiness that went all the way through me.
That was the first time I learned how to pay attention to one thing for hours. I became an engineer, you know.

What did young Bidisha build first?
She built a bridge first.
How did young Bidisha feel when a bolt finally clicked into place?
She felt a happiness that went all the way through her, after being cross when it didn't fit.
At what point in the story did Bidisha learn to concentrate for hours?
When she spent whole days on the metal set, not hearing her mother call for lunch or tea.
How might Bidisha's mother have felt calling her and getting no answer?
Her mother may have felt exasperated at first, then amused to see her so absorbed.

metadata.subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The power went off during the monsoon reading lesson, and Ramesh sir asked Sarika to read aloud by the light from the window. She stumbled on "environment", then on "enormous". A boy at the back snickered. Quick as anything, Sarika crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a robot voice, "Sarika has stopped working! Please restart!" The class burst out laughing, with her this time. Ramesh sir smiled too. But at break he noticed Sarika sitting alone, picking at her tiffin. "That was funny," he said. "Is reading aloud hard for you?" She shrugged, then nodded, very small. "Every time." He said they could practise together at lunch, just the two of them.

Which two words did Sarika stumble on?
"Environment" and "enormous".
Why did Sarika do the robot act?
She felt embarrassed after stumbling and hearing the snicker; the joke let her control the moment so the class laughed with her, not at her.
What did Ramesh sir do that was wise?
He noticed her alone at break, looked past the joke to ask whether reading aloud was hard, and offered private practice.
How might the boy who snickered feel after the joke?
He probably laughed along; the moment turned, and his snicker lost its sting.

Read this:

Avni noticed the stares first. Two girls at the tap stopped talking when she walked past, and someone giggled behind the notice board. By afternoon a boy in her row asked, "Is it true your parents are breaking up?" Her face flooded with heat. It was not true. Her grandfather was ill, and she had cried near the office because of the phone call, but nobody had asked about that. She wanted to vanish into the toilets, and she also wanted to shove somebody. She could not tell which was worse: being laughed at, or being wrong about her own life in front of everyone.

At break, a girl started to whisper it again. Gurpreet turned away. "I don't want to talk about this. It's Avni's business." He walked off without repeating it, and the girl was left with her sentence unfinished.

The next morning Damini, their teacher, spent ten minutes on how words can hurt, saying nobody's name. Afterwards she quietly told Avni that she was welcome to talk with her, or with the counsellor, whenever she liked. At lunch Avni told two friends, "My grandfather is ill. My parents are fine." Her voice was steady, and the whispering had nothing left to feed on.

What did Gurpreet say when the girl started whispering again?
He said, "I don't want to talk about this. It's Avni's business."
How did Gurpreet's refusal and Damini's talk each help end the rumour about Avni?

Gurpreet's refusal left the whisper unfinished, since a rumour needs someone to carry it. Damini's talk about how words hurt, without naming Avni, and her offer of someone to talk to, let Avni steady herself and say the true thing calmly.
What was Avni feeling when the boy asked whether her parents were breaking up?
She felt shame, anger and confusion: her face flooded with heat, she wanted to hide and to shove somebody, and the story was wrong about her own life.
What could Avni do if the whispers start again?
She could repeat the truth calmly, and go to Damini or the counsellor if it keeps going or worries her.

Monday: the email went out. Sameer was the new senior analyst. Arnab watched Jyoti, who had also applied, lean over at once. "Sameer! Brilliant, brilliant choice. The best person on the floor."

Wednesday: at stand-up Jyoti praised Sameer's "amazing leadership" twice, though he'd led nothing yet. In the pantry she told Arnab, "Honestly, I'm thrilled. I never even wanted it." She had said "thrilled" four times since Monday. Arnab noticed her lunch was untouched.

Friday: Arnab didn't read it as jealousy or scheming. He just asked, "It's okay to be a bit gutted too, you know?" Jyoti was quiet, then laughed shakily. "Maybe a lot gutted. He's still great, though."
"Both can be true," Arnab said.

What was Sameer's new post?
Sameer was the new senior analyst.
Why did Arnab not read Jyoti's praise as scheming?
Arnab felt more concerned than suspicious; the excess and the untouched lunch looked like mixed feelings, not ill will.
What did Arnab's Friday remark do well?
It named disappointment as normal without accusing Jyoti, and let both the praise and the hurt be true.
How might Jyoti feel after Arnab's question?
Jyoti probably feels relieved to admit being gutted, while still meaning the good wishes for Sameer.

Read this:

Kunal hovered in the kitchen doorway of their Pune flat while Kavitha stirred the dal, twisting the hem of his T-shirt. "Aai, if I tell you something, will you shout first or listen first?" Kavitha turned the flame down. "Listen first. Shouting maybe later." He almost smiled. "We didn't go to Sahil's today. We went to the quarry lake. Sahil slipped on the rocks near the edge. Someone grabbed him, he's okay. But he went under for a second." Kavitha's spoon stopped. Her face went tight, then she breathed out and pulled out a stool. "Sit. Tell me all of it." He did: who went, whose idea it was, how scared he had been. She didn't take his phone or ground him right then. She said, "I'm glad you told me tonight," and called Sahil's mother to check he was really fine. A week later, when a maths test went badly, Kunal told her at the door, before she even asked.

Where did they go instead of Sahil's?
They went to the quarry lake.
What was Kunal feeling as he twisted his T-shirt hem in the doorway?
Kunal was nervous and afraid of being shouted at, and probably still shaken about Sahil going under; asking 'shout first or listen first?' shows he wanted to be heard.
What did Kavitha do that made Kunal likely to tell her again?
She promised to listen first, steadied her own face, sat him down to hear everything, thanked him and checked on Sahil instead of punishing on the spot.
What was it like for Kavitha to hear about the quarry lake?
It frightened her, as her stopped spoon and tight face show, but she chose to breathe and listen so the conversation stayed open.

Read this:

Instructor's note, Saturday salsa class

Sahil and Manjula have come every Saturday for a year. They told me they've been together six years. They're easy with each other: she fixes his collar without thinking, he knows exactly when she'll turn.

Today I paired everyone with new partners for one song. Manjula danced with a younger man who asked her questions the whole time: where she grew up, what she likes about dancing. She laughed more in three minutes than I'd seen all year.

Sahil noticed. When they came back together, he asked her, half joking, "What were you two talking about?"

"He asked what I like about salsa," she said. "Nobody's asked me that in a long time."

Sahil looked at her for a second longer than usual. After class, I saw them sitting on the steps, talking, not dancing.

— Ines, instructor

What did the younger partner ask Manjula about?
Where she grew up and what she likes about dancing.
What does Manjula's laughter with the new partner suggest?
It suggests she enjoyed being asked about herself and may feel a little unnoticed in the comfortable routine with Sahil.
What small step did Sahil and Manjula take after class?
They sat on the steps and talked, a start to asking about each other's inner lives again.
How might Sahil feel when Manjula says no one's asked her that in a long time?
He may feel a pang of surprise and guilt, realising he stopped asking.

Read this:

The pumping station on the edge of Nashik lost power at two in the morning during the worst storm of the year. The backup pump wouldn't start, and water was rising in the basement. Rajni, twenty-four and the junior engineer on duty, traced the fault in twenty minutes by torchlight: a burnt relay and a wrongly set timer. She swapped the relay from a spare panel and reset the timer. The pump roared. When the supervisor, Vishal, arrived soaked at three, it was already done. "How did you find it so fast?" Rajni shrugged. "Anyone would have. It was just the relay." "Anyone? The last two engineers took a whole day with that panel." She shook her head. "They must have been busy." Later he asked her to lead the new training sessions. She said, "Maybe someone more senior?" Vishal frowned. "No. You."

What was the fault Rajni found?
A burnt relay and a wrongly set timer.
Why does Rajni say "Anyone would have"?

Rajni seems uncomfortable with praise, and because the fix felt easy to her, she assumes it would be easy for everyone. Her skill makes her notice how simple the problem was, not how rare her ability is.
What choice could Rajni make when Vishal offers her the training sessions?
She could accept and treat his evidence, the last two engineers taking a whole day, as a fair measure of her ability instead of her own doubts.
How does Vishal see Rajni's work that night?
He sees it as exceptional, since others struggled with the same panel for a day, and is frustrated that she doesn't see it herself.
Combine into one sentence with "because": I could not call you. My phone had no battery.
I could not call you because my phone had no battery.

Read this:

Siddharth,
I'm writing this instead of saying it in the mess, because I don't want an audience.
Last night at Rohan's birthday, Kunal did that joke about the canteen uncle's accent. Everyone laughed, and so did you. In first year you were the one who walked out when someone mocked how the laundry aunty spoke. You told me that kind of joke made your skin crawl.
Maybe you've changed your mind, and that's allowed. Maybe you're just tired of being the odd one out in the new group. I saw the others glance at you, and Kunal started on "Siddharth's new sense of humour." I didn't join in, and I won't.
If something's going on, I'd like to hear it, over chai at the gate stall, whenever you want. If nothing is, tell me I'm overthinking and I'll drop it.
Still your friend,
Harish

Where does Harish suggest meeting Siddharth to talk?
Over chai at the gate stall, whenever Siddharth wants.
What is Harish feeling while writing this letter?
Harish seems uneasy and a little sad to see Siddharth laugh at a joke Siddharth once walked out over, but also caring, not angry.
Why was a private letter wiser than joining Kunal's teasing?
It lets Siddharth explain, or say nothing is wrong, without the group watching, so the friendship stays safe either way.
How might Siddharth feel reading this compared with hearing the teasing at the party?
Siddharth may feel relieved and less cornered by a quiet letter, though perhaps a little embarrassed that the change was noticed.
Which friend sent me the last message?
I can't tell who sent it, because your messages are private to your phone. Open the phone and look at the top of the list.

"Why does Tanu get dinner in bed on a tray?" Chandrika demanded.
"Because he's poorly," said Deepika, stirring the soup.
"I'm poorly too." Chandrika coughed loudly. "Very poorly."
Deepika looked at her daughter properly for the first time that day. "You've been missing me, haven't you?"
Chandrika shrugged, then muttered, "Everyone just asks about Tanu. Even Nani on the phone."
"That's hard. You've been so helpful this week, and I haven't said so." Deepika turned off the stove. "Tanu's asleep. Want to do our crossword on the balcony, just us two?"
Chandrika's face brightened. "Can I hold the pen?"
"You always hold the pen."

What did Deepika suggest doing on the balcony?
Their crossword, just the two of them.
What was Chandrika feeling when she coughed loudly?
She felt jealous and overlooked, since everyone asked about Tanu, even Nani.
What small step helped, and why?
A crossword on the balcony with just Deepika, which told Chandrika she was still seen.
How does Deepika come to see the fake cough?
She sees it as Chandrika missing her rather than lying, and admits she has not thanked her for helping.

Monsoon Monday: Noor, eighteen months, pulled the plant pot off the windowsill. Mud everywhere. Madhav said, "No, Noor," and moved the pot. She cried.
Wednesday: She reached for the pot again. "No," Madhav said. She paused, hand in the air, then touched a leaf instead.
Next Saturday: Noor walked up to the pot, looked at Madhav, and said, "No!" Then she patted the soil gently.

What did Noor pull off the windowsill?
The plant pot.
How did Noor feel when Madhav first moved the pot?
She felt upset and frustrated, and cried.
How can Madhav keep helping Noor learn the rule?
Stay calm and consistent, and give her a safe way to touch the plant, like patting the leaves.
What is it like for Madhav when Noor says "No!" herself?
He probably feels amused and pleased that she remembers the rule.

Ishita, sit, I'll tell you about Kamla-bai while the rice cooks. I was twenty-four and had just taken my first flat in Nagpur. In the house I grew up in, a separate steel cup for the helper hung on a nail by the back door. The first morning Kamla-bai came, I reached for that kind of cup out of habit, and then I stopped. I poured her tea into the same blue mugs I used. She held hers a long moment before drinking. I paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth, and I learnt her grandson's name. Small things. Eleven years she worked with me. When I moved away, she came to the station with laddoos. Remember that when you set up your own house, beta: your Vinita Maasi learnt it from a cup.

On which day of the month did Vinita pay Kamla-bai?
She paid her on the first of every month, never the fifth.
Why did young Vinita stop reaching for the separate cup, and what does that suggest she felt?
She seems to have felt uncomfortable, even a little ashamed, at copying an old habit that treated a person as lesser.
Which small choice in the story mattered most, and why?
Pouring tea into the same mugs mattered most because it showed daily respect, and paying on time and learning her grandson's name kept that respect going.
How might Kamla-bai have felt holding the blue mug?
She may have been surprised and quietly moved, as if being treated as an equal in a house was new to her.

I'm Rekha, and the kitten lives in the flat next to ours, with Vishal's family. The first evening it hid under their sofa, ears flat, tail puffed. Vishal kept lying on the floor, reaching under and pulling it out to cuddle. Each time it went stiff in his arms and made a low noise I'd never heard a kitten make. His mother said, "Let it come to you." He said, "But it's so soft." On the third evening I was at their door when the kitten twisted, scratched a long red line down Vishal's wrist and shot back under the sofa. Vishal stared at his wrist. His mother cleaned the scratch and put a plaster on it. I think he was more hurt that the kitten didn't like him, but I can't be sure.

What did Vishal's mother do about the scratch?
She cleaned it and put a plaster on it.
What might Vishal be feeling as he stares at his wrist?
Hurt and perhaps rejected, confused that the kitten did not want his cuddles.
What else could Vishal have done the first evening?
Sit quietly nearby and let the kitten come out by itself, treating flat ears and a puffed tail as signs to wait.
What might the evenings be like for the kitten?
Frightening: it was pulled out again and again while its whole body was saying 'leave me alone'.

Aparna came in at 9:40, forty minutes past curfew, and her father, Nitin, was waiting in the hall of their Indore flat.

"Where were you?"

"At Riddhi's. I told you. We were finishing the project."

"You were supposed to be home by nine. From now on, straight home after school. That's final."

"What? Why?"

"Because I said so."

"You never trust me! It was forty minutes!"

"Don't raise your voice at me."

"You raised yours first!"

Aparna slammed her bag down. Nitin felt his chest tighten: for forty minutes he had been calling her phone and imagining things he didn't want to imagine. But all he could say was, "Go to your room."

Aparna went, thinking: he doesn't care what I did, only that I obeyed. Neither of them said the thing that was true.

How late past curfew was Aparna?
Forty minutes.
What was Nitin feeling during those forty minutes?
He was frightened and anxious, calling her phone and imagining terrible things.
What could each say instead of "Because I said so" and "You never trust me"?
Nitin could say he was scared when she didn't answer; Aparna could say she wants to be trusted and should have called.
How does Aparna read her father's anger?
She reads it as caring only about obedience, not about her, and feels hurt and mistrusted.

The cousins had only ten minutes before the bus, so the game was quick. Tarun counted fast. Sonali didn't run. She stood right beside the dining table, squeezed her eyes shut and puffed up her cheeks, holding her breath. If I don't breathe, he can't see me, she thought. Tarun opened his eyes and burst out laughing. "Sonali, you're right there!" She let out her breath in a whoosh, red-faced.

How long did the cousins have before the bus?
They had only ten minutes.
What was Sonali feeling when she let out her breath, red-faced?
She was embarrassed and surprised to be found so easily.
What would help Sonali next time?
Finding a real hiding place, like under the table, since holding her breath does not hide her.
How does Sonali's plan look to Tarun?
To Tarun it looks funny because she is standing in plain view.

Read this:

Dear Ritu,

I did something stupid, and I need to tell someone who won't lecture me.

You know Sanya has been mocking my weight in front of the whole class since June. Last week I got a photo of her mid-sneeze at the science fair, face all scrunched. I made it into a sticker and put it on our class chat with a nasty caption.

For one night it felt amazing. Then her friends made worse stickers of me. Then someone forwarded the whole thing to our class teacher.

On Monday Sanya and I both sat outside the principal's office. Everyone talked about my sticker. Nobody talked about five months of her comments.

That evening Mamma sat with me, read everything, and said none of Sanya's cruelty was okay, and neither was mine. She called my class teacher right then to ask for a meeting about both.

Damini

How long had Sanya been mocking Damini?
Since June; Damini writes about five months of her comments.
How did Damini feel after the first night?
Damini felt ashamed and trapped, since the brief thrill turned into worse stickers and blame.
What could Damini have done instead of making the sticker?
Damini could have kept a record of Sanya's comments and taken it to Mamma or a teacher, so the adults saw the months of mockery first.
How might the class teacher see the situation after Mamma's call?
The teacher would likely see two problems to address, the months of mockery and the sticker, and could set up the meeting to deal with both fairly.
