Suraj, you're asking whether telling a teacher makes you a tell-tale? Let me tell you something from my school days. My friend Mukul asked to copy from me before the final exam. I said no. He asked again. No. Then, the day before, he showed me the formulas he'd written on the inside of his wrist, under his watch strap. I, Varun, lay awake that night. If he was caught in the finals, it could cost him the whole year. I decided that keeping quiet was not being a good friend. So in the morning I spoke quietly to our class teacher. She thanked me, and before the paper she asked everyone to put their watches on the front desk. Mukul was angry with me for a month. Then he wasn't. Years later, he thanked me.

Where had Mukul written the formulas?
On the inside of his wrist, under his watch strap.
How did young Varun feel that night?
Worried and torn, lying awake over what to do.
Which choice inside the story made the difference?
Speaking quietly to the teacher before the paper, which stopped a much bigger problem for Mukul.
How did Mukul feel about it over time?
Angry for a month, then not, and years later grateful.

"Payal, can I talk to you for two minutes?"

"No, Wasim."

"Please. I just want to say sorry properly."

Payal put her bag down on the library table. "You imitated my stammer in front of the whole seminar group. Everyone laughed. You laughed loudest."

"I know. It was cruel. I'm sorry. I don't have an excuse."

"You said sorry on Tuesday too."

"I did. I'm not asking you to forgive me. I just wanted you to hear it without me trying to explain."

She looked at him for a long time. "I'm still angry. I don't want to talk to you for a while."

Wasim's chest felt heavy. He wanted to argue, to say he'd changed. "Okay," he said. "That's your choice."

He went to the other end of the library. In the next seminar, when someone else laughed at a classmate's accent, Wasim said quietly, "Don't."

What did Wasim imitate in front of the seminar group?
Wasim imitated Payal's stammer.
What was Wasim feeling when Payal said she didn't want to talk?
Wasim felt a heavy chest and the urge to argue, carrying the weight of the harm he had done.
Why was Wasim right to accept Payal's choice?
Repair is her choice and takes time, so pressing for forgiveness would hurt her again; he showed change through his actions instead.
How does Payal see Wasim's second apology?
Payal is still angry and wary, since he apologised before, and she needs time before she can talk to him.
A stick is 35 cm long and another is 48 cm long. They are put end to end. How long are they together?

Answer: 83 cm. 35 + 48 = 83.

Put them end to end with no gap and no overlap. Add the lengths: 35 + 48. Add tens: 30 + 40 = 70. Add ones: 5 + 8 = 13. 70 + 13 = 83 cm. Is it more than 1 m? No, 83 cm is less than 100 cm.

By the cowshed in their village, Yash, four, pretended to be a bird. He flapped his arms, ran round the haystack and made a beak with his fingers. His grandmother Aadhya, shelling peas, asked, "Are you a crow or a parrot?" He looked at her, shy, and kept flapping. She guessed. "A parrot! Green wings." He grinned. Then he cupped his hands to his mouth and made a drinking gesture. "You want water, little bird?" Yash nodded and she brought a cup.

What did Yash pretend to be by the cowshed?
He pretended to be a bird.
What does Yash's grin and his switching to a drinking gesture suggest he was thinking?
He seems happy that his grandmother understood his pretend play, and used mime for the water because words felt hard for him with shyness. He might also simply have been thirsty.
What could Aadhya do to help Yash use words when he's ready?
She can keep guessing playfully and sometimes offer a word for what he mimed, without pressing him to speak.
How might Aadhya feel as she guesses what Yash is miming?
She may feel amused and close to him, enjoying the game while working out what he needs.

My brother Varun turned fifteen in March, and since then I've been living with a weather forecast I can't read. I'm Kavitha, his older sister. Some evenings he tells us jokes at dinner. Other evenings he slams his plate down because the rice is "too wet." Last Tuesday, Mummy asked about his homework, and he shouted. Then, a minute later, he came back from his room. His ears were red. "Sorry," he mumbled. "I'm just... I don't know." He went to fill the water bottles, which is his job, without being asked. I don't know what goes on in his head. But I've noticed he comes back faster now. Mummy says to give him room and not tease. I'm trying, though it's hard.

What did Varun complain about the rice?
He said it was "too wet."
What might Varun's red ears suggest when he came back?
They suggest he felt embarrassed and sorry about shouting, even though he couldn't explain his mood.
How could the family support Varun during his mood swings?
They could give him space in the moment, as Mummy says, and notice when he chooses to come back and repair things.
What is it like for Kavitha to live with Varun's changing moods?
It feels unpredictable and sometimes hard, but she's trying to be patient and notices small improvements.
Teresa is 59 and her husband Morio is 71 years old. Their daughter, Michiko was born when Morio was 38.  How old was Teresa when she gave birth to Michiko?

The difference in age between Teresa and Morio is 71 - 59 = 12 years.
When their daughter is born, Teresa is 38 - 12 = 26 years old.
The answer is 26.

I'm Simran, and I'm a little embarrassed about how I behaved during fest prep.
There were forty of us on the logistics team. At the big Sunday meetings I stood at the back, nodded and left early. When the coordinator asked for someone to count chairs, I thought, thirty-nine other people can do it. My name wasn't on anything. Honestly, who would notice?
Then Francis split us into pairs and put up a sheet: "Simran and Leela, registration desk, Gate 2."
Suddenly it was mine. I made queue signs at midnight, printed a backup list and got there at seven. When a parent thanked us both by name, I felt ridiculously proud.
Same person, same fest. The only difference was that my part could be seen.

How many people were on the logistics team?
There were forty of us on the logistics team.
How did Simran feel when a parent thanked the pair by name?
Simran felt ridiculously proud, because the work was visibly Simran's own.
What could a big team learn from Simran's story?
Give each person a small, named task that others can see, so no one feels their effort disappears in the crowd.
How might Francis see the change in Simran after the pairs sheet?
Francis would likely notice Simran go from leaving early to arriving at seven, and feel pleased the pairs idea worked.

With her mother away in Patna caring for her grandmother, Indu was running the house and three coaching batches at once. Every morning she woke with a dull headache. She snapped at her little brother over a spilled glass. Walking to the physics batch, her stomach knotted with dread.

"You look terrible," her friend Pallavi said one evening.

"It's nothing. I'm just weak. Toppers don't complain." Indu swallowed two biscuits and kept going.

For four more weeks she pushed through. She stopped telling anyone about the headaches. She told herself dread was laziness.

Then, a week before the half-yearly exams, something just stopped. She sat at her desk with the chemistry book open and couldn't make the words mean anything. She tried for three days. Nothing went in.

She sat the exams in a fog and left half of the physics paper blank.

Where was Indu's mother?
Away in Patna, caring for Indu's grandmother.
What was Indu feeling as she walked to the physics batch?
She felt dread, her stomach knotting, which she wrongly told herself was laziness.
What should Indu have done when the headaches and dread began?
Told a parent, teacher or counsellor early and eased the load, and if the headaches kept going or worried anyone, checked with a doctor.
How might Pallavi have felt watching Indu over those weeks?
Pallavi was probably worried and a bit helpless, noticing Indu looked terrible but being brushed off.

In the school corridor after assembly, Darshan held up his shiny "Star Reader" badge. "Imran, look!" Imran glanced at it and turned away, kicking the wall softly. His eyes were shiny. Darshan's smile faded. He didn't understand. Had he done something wrong? Then he remembered Imran's reading book was still on the yellow level. Darshan put the badge in his pocket. "You can get one too. You read the dragon book really well yesterday." Imran sniffed. "I got stuck on two words." "I got stuck on five!" Imran almost laughed. They walked to class together.

What did Darshan's badge say?
It said "Star Reader".
How did Darshan feel when Imran turned away?
He felt confused and worried, wondering if he had done something wrong.
How did Darshan keep the friendship warm?
He put the badge away, told Imran he could get one too and praised Imran's own reading.
What is it like for Imran when Darshan shows the badge?
It stings; he feels sad and left behind because his own reading is slower.

Monday of winter sports week. The kho-kho captains picked teams in the school ground. Raghav was picked last. He walked to his team with his hands in his pockets.
Wednesday. At the park, his cousin Kashish called, "Come play cricket!" Raghav stayed on the swing. "Nobody ever chooses me. I never win anything. Why bother?" Kashish said, "You won the chess thing last month." "That doesn't count."
The next Saturday. At the Lohri gathering, the older cousins were picking teams for tug-of-war. Kashish was a captain. "Raghav!" she called first. Raghav blinked. His team lost, but he laughed so hard he fell in the grass. On the way home he said, "Maybe it's not never. Maybe it was just Monday."

What game were the captains picking teams for on Monday?
They were picking teams for kho-kho in the school ground.
Why did Raghav stay on the swing on Wednesday?
Raghav felt hurt and discouraged after being picked last once, and had stretched it into a rule that nobody ever chooses him.
What did Kashish do that helped break the rule?
Kashish reminded him of the chess win and later picked him first, giving real evidence against "never".
How might Kashish have felt when Raghav said the chess win didn't count?
Kashish was probably puzzled and a bit sad, seeing her cousin ignore a clear win.

messages.content:
Summarize this as four short bullet points.

As regards the domestic mode of life, four kinds of conduct have been laid down by the learned. The first consists of keeping a store of grain sufficient to last for three years. The second consists of keeping a store to last for one year. The third consists of providing for the day without thinking of the morrow. The fourth consists of collecting grain after the manner of the pigeon. Of these, each succeeding one is superior in point of merit to that which precedes it, according to what has been laid down in the scriptures.

- A householder can live in four ways, as the learned describe.
- One way is to store grain for three years, or one year.
- Others are to provide only for the day, or gather grain like a pigeon.
- Each later way is said to be better than the one before it.

Monday. The notice went up: auditions for the inter-school singing competition on Friday. Uday stood in front of it for a long time. Madhuri, beside him, said, "You have to go. You sing on the bus every day."
"What if I get rejected in front of everyone?" he said. "I'll feel stupid for weeks. If I don't go, nothing bad happens."
Friday. From the corridor, Uday heard the auditions through the music room door. One boy sang off-key and still laughed. Madhuri went in, sang, and came out grinning. Uday walked away before his name was called.
Two weeks later. The school team sang at the district finals, and Uday watched from the audience. They came third. On the way home he couldn't stop thinking: what if I'd been up there? It felt worse than any rejection he had imagined.

When were the auditions?
The auditions were on Friday.
Why did Uday walk away before his name was called?
Uday was afraid of being rejected in front of everyone and feeling stupid for weeks, which felt worse than not trying.
What could Uday tell himself before the next audition?
Uday could remember how bad the 'what if' felt after the finals, and that trying and failing is often easier to live with than never trying.
How might Madhuri feel watching Uday walk away?
Madhuri might feel disappointed and a bit sad, having encouraged Uday because he sings on the bus every day.

Class 4 teacher's note, by Joseph Mathew, Wednesday.
During PT, I saw three children pulling at the patka on Jagdish's head and chanting, 'Pineapple head!' Jagdish was trying to hold it on with both hands, blinking fast. I stopped the game at once and took the three children to one side. I told them firmly that mocking anyone's faith or dress is never acceptable here, and that they will apologise to him tomorrow in front of me. Then I sat with Jagdish on the steps. He said quietly, 'Maybe I should stop wearing it.' I told him his patka and his faith are nothing to be ashamed of, and that the fault was theirs, not his. I have informed the principal and phoned his parents; his father will come in tomorrow.

What did the children chant at Jagdish?
'Pineapple head!'
What was Jagdish feeling when he said 'Maybe I should stop wearing it'?
Ashamed and hurt enough to think of hiding part of who he is.
What did the teacher do that same day?
Stopped the game, spoke firmly to the three children, reassured Jagdish, and informed the principal and his parents.
How might Jagdish's father feel coming in tomorrow?
Upset and protective, wanting his son to feel safe at school.

Caregiver's note, written by Alka, Eshaan's Nani, for his parents
Wednesday afternoon. Eshaan came home from school and said his reading log was signed. I saw his bag later: the page was blank, and there was a note from Ma'am asking why it hadn't been signed for a week.
When I asked him, he said, "Ma'am lost the page." He wouldn't look at me and his hands were shaking. I realised he was frightened, not naughty. Last month someone had shouted at him over a lost library book.
I made him a glass of milk and said, "Eshaan, you won't be in trouble for the truth. I'd much rather know."
He cried and said he forgot to read, and was scared to tell.
Next step: I signed today's page after he read to me, and I suggest we all tell him that forgetting is fine to admit.

What did Eshaan say had happened to the page?
He said, "Ma'am lost the page."
What did Nani realise when Eshaan wouldn't look at her?
Nani realised he was frightened, not naughty, and felt concern rather than anger.
What would you advise Eshaan's parents, based on the note?
Stay calm when he admits something and tell him forgetting is fine to admit, so he doesn't need to lie out of fear.
What was Eshaan feeling when he finally told the truth?
Eshaan felt scared and ashamed, crying as he admitted he forgot to read.
I need a birthday gift for my brother Kunal. He's turning ten.
Happy early birthday to Kunal. What does he like doing most? Games, drawing, cricket, building things?
He loves drawing animals and he always runs out of pencils.
Then a nice set of coloured pencils with a sketchbook would be perfect. If you want something extra, add a small book about how to draw animals step by step.
The pencil set sounds good. I only have a small budget though.
That's fine. A simple set of twelve to twenty-four pencils and a plain sketchbook from a local stationery shop can be quite cheap. You could wrap it nicely yourself with newspaper and ribbon.
Which one did you say I should skip, the book or the pencils?
I did not say to skip either one. The pencils and sketchbook are the main gift for Kunal. The animal drawing book was only an optional extra, so skip that one if your budget is tight.

Wednesday night
Today the seniors' group posted my photo again, the one from orientation where I tripped, with 'Miss Circus' written over it. Forty-two laughing reactions. When I asked one of them to take it down, she said, 'It's just ragging, yaar. It's how we bond.' It doesn't feel like bonding. It feels like I can't walk into the canteen. I cried in the washroom before lab.
Vikas saw my face and asked. I showed him. He didn't say 'ignore it'. He said, 'That's bullying, Sunaina. Calling it ragging doesn't make it okay.' He came with me to the warden's office after lab. Warden ma'am read every post, said it was not my fault, and phoned the anti-ragging committee right there. The photo was gone by 9 p.m.
I'm still shaky. But someone called it by its real name.

How many laughing reactions did the photo get?
The photo got forty-two laughing reactions.
What does 'It doesn't feel like bonding' show about how Sunaina feels?
It shows that Sunaina's real experience, dreading the canteen and crying before lab, doesn't match the friendly label, which was trying to erase that hurt.
What did Vikas do that made a difference?
Vikas named it plainly as bullying instead of saying 'ignore it', then went with Sunaina to the warden that same afternoon, so an adult could act.
How does Warden ma'am's response affect Sunaina?
Hearing it was not Sunaina's fault and seeing the photo gone by 9 p.m. showed that Sunaina was believed, even though the shakiness remained 🤍.
While shopping, Greg spent 300$ on a shirt and shoes. If Greg spent 9 more than twice as much on shoes as he did a shirt, how much did Greg spend on a shirt?

Let x be the amount spent on a shirt.
Greg spent 2x+9 dollars on shoes.
300=x+(2x+9)
300=3x+9
291=3x
x=97$
Greg spent 97$ on a shirt.
The answer is 97.

In the sugarcane field behind their house near Karnal, Baljeet was fixing the tubewell pipe. Jagdish, nine, squatted beside him. "Bapu, why is the pipe blue?" "It came like that." "Why is the water cold?" "It comes from deep down." "Why is deep down cold? Why do crows sit on the wire? Why—" Baljeet noticed that Jagdish wasn't even looking at the crows. He was looking at his father. Since the baby came, Baljeet realised, he had barely had an evening alone with the boy. He put the spanner down. "Jagdish, want to hold the pipe while I tighten it? I need a helper." Jagdish shot up. For twenty minutes he held the pipe, asked almost nothing, and just grinned.

What was Baljeet fixing?
He was fixing the tubewell pipe.
What did Jagdish really want as he asked question after question?

Monday. At the park gate, Hrithik pushed Bittu out of the way to reach the swing first. "I only had ten minutes before tuition!" he told Rashmi didi, his tutor.
Wednesday. Bittu pushed Hrithik at the slide. Hrithik stormed into tuition. "Bittu is such a rude boy. He has no manners." Rashmi didi only said, "Hmm. Write that down for me."
Saturday. Rashmi didi gave him a small worksheet. Two lines. "Monday: Hrithik pushed because ______." "Wednesday: Bittu pushed because ______." Hrithik filled the first quickly: "I was in a hurry." The second, he started to write "he is rude," and stopped. He thought about the slide queue. It had been long, and Bittu's mother was calling him home. He wrote, "maybe he was in a hurry too."

He said he only had ten minutes before tuition.

He felt angry and sure Bittu was simply a rude boy with no manners, forgetting his own push on Monday.

It put both pushes side by side, so he had to give Bittu a reason the same way he gave himself one.

Bittu may have felt rushed because his mother was calling him home, not that he was being rude.

It's been six months since Dida died, and I still replay that call. She rang on a Wednesday. I was in the library. I whispered, "Dida, I'll call you on Sunday." She said, "Okay, shona, eat well."
She died on Friday.
Looking back, I've built a hundred other Wednesdays. In one, I take the train home. In another, I hear her cough and phone the doctor. In every one, I save her. My sister Kashish says, "Arnab, she was eighty-seven. Her heart was tired." I know that. But the what-ifs feel better than helplessness, somehow. At least in them I could have done something.
I think I'll talk to the college counsellor next week. The loop is getting old.

When did Dida die?
She died on Friday.

Arnab's guilt gives a feeling of control, as if the death could have been stopped, which hurts less than feeling powerless.
What turning point does Arnab reach at the end?
Deciding to see the college counsellor, recognising the loop of what-ifs has lasted too long.

Kashish is probably sad and worried, trying to remind Arnab that Dida's tired heart was nobody's fault.

She was now, on being settled at home, at leisure to observe the real state of her sister's spirits. Jane was not happy. She still cherished a very tender affection for Bingley. Having never even fancied herself in love before, her regard had all the warmth of first attachment, and from her age and disposition, greater steadiness than first attachments often boast; and so fervently did she value his remembrance, and prefer him to every other man, that all her good sense, and all her attention to the feelings of her friends, were requisite to check the indulgence of those regrets which must have been injurious to her own health and their tranquillity.
Back at home, she sees that her sister Jane is unhappy and still loves Bingley tenderly. Jane needs all her good sense to keep her regrets from harming her health.

Team lead's note on Anirban, project coordinator, three months in.

Small things run on templates: same stand-up format, same lunch order on Mondays, a fixed reply for routine requests. He spotted a double payment in the swap and fixed it before anyone signed.

Anirban felt secure in the habit, trusting that a fresh morning check would be safer than a tired evening yes, even if Himani was irritated.

Saying "First thing tomorrow" when tired, and then keeping that promise early, protects important choices without leaving the other person hanging.

She would likely feel relieved and more willing to wait next time, since the morning review saved a costly mistake.

She pulled Dhruv's socks over her ears.

In Class 11, I was sure my problem was laziness. I'm Tanuja, and I was always behind, always tired, and always telling myself to try harder.

One Sunday my friend Arnab said, "Just add up your week. Actually add it."

So I did, on the back of a physics notebook. School: 36 hours. Three coaching batches: 12 hours. Travel between them on two buses: 7 hours. Homework and coaching assignments: 7 hours. Total: 62 hours. Rest: I searched for it and couldn't find any. Even Sunday mornings had a test series.

I looked at that number for a long time. Sixty-two. A full-time job is less.

It changed how I saw myself. I wasn't lazy. I was overloaded. The question wasn't how to push harder. It was what to cut.

I took the sheet to my parents that evening. That was the start of dropping one batch.

What was Tanuja's weekly total?
62 hours.
How did Tanuja feel after seeing the number?
Tanuja felt stunned, then relieved, realising the problem was overload rather than laziness.
What else could Tanuja add to the audit before talking to the parents?
Tanuja could mark which batches actually help most, so the conversation is about what to cut, not only how tired Tanuja is.
How might Tanuja's parents see the sheet?
They may be surprised by the total and more willing to talk about cutting a batch, since the numbers make the load clear.

messages.content: Layla and Nahima were playing a game where Layla won with 70 points. If The total number of points scored was 112, how many more points did Layla score than Nahima?

If the total number of points was 112, and Layla won with 70 points, Nahima scored 112-70= 42 points.
Layla scored 70-42=28 more points than Nahima.
The answer is 28.

I'd lie awake asking, "Where were you?" I wrote it in a notebook so Mummy wouldn't hear. Part of me thought, if I'm this angry, I must still think someone is there to be angry at. In the girls' hostel of the residential school in Ooty, Lakshmi heard it from the next cubicle: "Lakshmi likes Pranav from 11B. Sachin told everyone at football."
She stood very still behind the door. She had told only one person, Sachin, her friend since Class 6, in the library last week, because he'd asked why she kept going red.
By dinner three boys hummed a love song when she passed. She laughed it off. In the dorm she pulled the blanket over her head.
For the next week she stopped sitting with Sachin at study hour. She stopped sitting with anyone. When her roommate asked what she was reading, she said, "Nothing," and turned the page.
On Friday the house mother, Mrs Joseph, found her alone on the steps. "You've gone very quiet this week. Did something happen?"
Lakshmi shrugged. Then, slowly, she told her.

Where had Lakshmi told Sachin her secret?
In the library last week.
How did Lakshmi feel after hearing the girls in the next cubicle?
Lakshmi felt exposed and foolish, standing very still and later hiding under the blanket.
What helped Lakshmi start to open up again?
Mrs Joseph noticing she'd gone quiet and asking gently, which gave Lakshmi a safe person to tell.
How might Sachin see the change in Lakshmi?
Sachin would see his friend since Class 6 stop sitting with him, and might realise how much sharing her secret hurt.

messages.content: Francis and Kiera had breakfast at a cafe. Muffins cost $2 each, and fruit cups cost $3 each. Francis had 2 muffins and 2 fruit cups. Kiera had 2 muffins and 1 fruit cup. How much did their breakfast cost?

Francis bought 2 x $2 = $4 worth of muffins.
Francis bought 2 x $3 = $6 worth of fruit cups.
Kiera bought 2 x $2 = $4 worth of muffins.
Kiera bought 1 x $3 = $3 worth of fruit cups.
Their breakfast cost $4 + $6 + $4 + $3 = $17 in total.
The answer is 17.

Nobody warns you that it comes back like this, from a list.

I'm not throwing the list away. Not yet.

Eggs, bread, dhaniya.

Amandeep feels a deep sorrow and grief, not only for Reena but for the future imagined together.

How might Amandeep's brother feel after that phone call?

The office pantry was empty at four except for Yash, standing by the window with his phone face down on the counter. Alka came in for tea and stopped. He was wringing his hands, fingers twisting and pressing, over and over, and his eyes were fixed on nothing. She didn't know what had happened, but it didn't look like a work problem; he looked shaken. She put down her mug. "Yash. I'm here." He swallowed. "My Nana. My mother just called. He's gone." Alka didn't reach for words she didn't have. She stood beside him at the window. After a minute she said quietly, "Do you want me to tell Rohit you're leaving, and book you a cab home?" He nodded. She did both from her phone, then walked with him to the lift and waited until the doors closed.

His mother called.

She stayed beside him quietly, then made a calm, practical offer to tell Rohit and book a cab, and did both.
What might Yash need most in those first minutes?
He probably needed someone steady nearby and practical help getting home, since the shock left him in no state to organise anything.

Rafael, four, threw the hat in the sand. "No! Me do it!"

My brother Vikram and I are planning a surprise for our parents' anniversary. He keeps changing the plan.

A dinner at their favourite restaurant. Now he wants a trip to a hill station.
A trip is a bigger plan and needs more time and money. You could agree that dinner happens on the day and the trip comes later as a second gift. That way both ideas survive.
That is clever. I will tell him it is dinner on the day, then the hill station later.
Good, it keeps the peace. Settle the restaurant booking first, so the anniversary is safe, and then you and Vikram can start planning the hill station trip calmly without any pressure on the date.

In the village near the temple tank, Kannan, eleven, sat on the veranda with his grandmother Lakshmi, a year after Thatha passed away.
"I remember exactly," Kannan said. "I was flying my kite on the threshing floor. Amma came running and called me home. It was raining."
He could see every bit: the red kite, the wet mud, Amma's face.
Lakshmi Paati held his hand. "You were at school, kanna. Your mother, Sangeeta, came to fetch you. It was a very hot day."
Kannan frowned. "But I can see the rain."

At school; his mother, Sangeeta, came to fetch him.

She holds his hand and says maybe he remembers how it felt, and that part is true, which respects his grief while gently setting the facts straight.
What might it be like for Lakshmi Paati to talk about that day?

Mohit, before you hit submit on that internship application, let me tell you about my checklist. In first year I emailed a cover letter to a firm in Chennai that began "Dear Hiring Team at" followed by the name of a totally different company. I'd copied it from my previous application. They never replied. I didn't blame them.
So now I, Naveen, never send anything important without four checks. One: every name. Is it theirs, spelt right? Two: every number: dates, marks, phone. Three: attachments. Actually attached, and the right version, not "CV_old". Four: I reopen their original message and tick off everything they asked for. Takes two minutes, maybe three.
Last month it caught a wrong date on my scholarship form and a missing transcript. Nobody saw those mistakes except me, and that's the whole point. Okay, now open yours and read me their original email.

Every name, every number, the attachments, and the original message's list of what they asked for.
How did Naveen feel about the first-year cover letter?
Naveen felt embarrassed and didn't blame the firm for not replying, since the letter named a totally different company.
What could Mohit do right now, before submitting?
Mohit could reopen the internship's original email and tick off each item, then check the names, numbers and that the right attachments are there.
How might the firm in Chennai have seen Naveen's letter?
They probably saw it as careless copying, since it opened with another company's name, and simply didn't reply.

How might Urmila's mother have felt that Diwali?

What was Tarun feeling when Parveen first said it happened for a reason?
Tarun felt angry and hurt, wanting to throw the phone, because the silver lining came far too early.

Parveen plans to just listen first instead of offering a reason for the pain.

I've been thinking about how to say this, and writing it feels easier.
I love that we talk every night. But I need some evenings alone. After work I'm drained, and when we're on the phone for two hours, I end up snapping at you or going quiet, and that isn't fair to either of us.

This isn't about us having a problem. It's about me needing time to recharge so I can actually enjoy our calls.
Does that work for you? If not, let's find something that does. I'd rather tell you than hope you guess.
Shalini

Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

Shalini has felt drained after work, and ends up snapping or going quiet, which feels unfair.

It states the need calmly with an I-statement, gives a specific plan, and invites Akash to suggest another option.

Sharmila's new job at the coir board brought her from Kolkata to a small town near Alappuzha, and for the first week she was frightened of everything. She didn't understand Malayalam. She didn't know if she should take off her shoes in the office. At the tea shop she pointed at things and hoped.

On Friday she took off her shoes at the wrong door and a clerk laughed. Her face burned. She wanted to hide in her room and eat instant noodles for a month.

Instead, on Saturday, she knocked on her landlady's door. Avni chechi, who ran the tailoring shop downstairs, explained the rules in a mix of English and gestures, then taught her to say "enthu patti?" for "what happened?"

Sharmila wrote words in a notebook. She watched how people queued at the bus stop. By the next month, she was going to the Sunday market with Avni chechi and her daughters.

What did Avni chechi run downstairs?
Avni chechi ran the tailoring shop downstairs.
What was Sharmila feeling after the clerk laughed?
Sharmila felt embarrassed and afraid, her face burning, and wanted to hide in her room.
What small steps helped Sharmila settle in?
Asking Avni chechi, writing words in a notebook, watching how people did things and going to the market with a small group.
How might Avni chechi see Sharmila's questions?
Avni chechi seems to enjoy helping and sees Sharmila as a newcomer worth welcoming, not as someone foolish.

Onam week in Kochi. First morning: Manjula dropped a basket of marigold petals while making the pookalam, and Simran, two, just watched. Third day: when petals spilled again, Simran squatted and scooped handfuls back into the basket without a word. What did Manjula drop on the first morning?
A basket of marigold petals.

Probably proud and pleased to be useful, since she did it without being asked.

Notice and thank her, and give her small jobs like sorting petals so she can keep helping.
What would change if Manjula had scolded Simran for touching the petals?

The week before Diwali, Miss Joshi handed out orange and purple bibs for the relay, straight out of the box. Reena got orange, Zeenat purple. At snacks Reena spread her mat and said, 'Only oranges sit here.' Zeenat, who sat with her every single day, stood holding her tiffin. 'But I'm your friend.' 'You're purple,' Reena said, as if it were a rule. Miss Joshi knelt down. 'Who decided who got which colour?' Reena thought. 'You did. From the box.' 'So is purple worse?' Reena looked at Zeenat's bib, then moved over. 'Purples can sit too.'

What colours were the bibs?
Orange and purple.
What was Reena feeling when she said 'Only oranges sit here'?
Reena felt proud of her orange team and sure it came first, as if belonging made a rule.
What did Miss Joshi's questions help Reena notice?
That the colours came at random from a box, so purple wasn't worse and the new rule made no sense.
What is it like for Zeenat to be told 'You're purple'?
Zeenat feels hurt and confused, shut out by a friend over a colour she didn't choose.

By July, winter in Buenos Aires, Camila had stopped writing to her manager. She had asked for a second screen in February, for help with the backlog in March, for a day off for her sister's graduation in May. No reply, no reply, a "we'll see" that never came back.
Now she came in, did her tickets, and left. When her headset broke, she held the loose earpiece to her ear for a week instead of asking. At home she lay on the sofa with the TV on, not watching.
One Sunday Gabriel, her flatmate, sat down beside her. "You used to fight for everything. Now you don't even say when you're cold."
"What's the point? Nothing I ask for happens."
"At work, maybe. But you've seemed flat for weeks now. Would you talk to someone, a doctor or a counsellor? I'll sit with you while you call tomorrow."
Camila shrugged, but she didn't say no.

What did Camila ask for in February?
A second screen.
Why has Camila stopped asking for anything?
After months of ignored requests, Camila feels numb and hopeless ("What's the point?"), so asking seems useless, even when the headset breaks.
What is a sensible next step for Camila?
Since the flatness has lasted for weeks, talking to a doctor or counsellor, as Gabriel suggests, is wise; the ignored requests could also go to someone above the manager.
How does Gabriel see the change in Camila?
Gabriel remembers someone who "used to fight for everything" and is worried to see her flat for weeks, so he offers to sit with her while she calls.

In their small-town home, Aadhya and her mother Sarita, both Deaf, sat on the charpai after lunch. Aadhya signed about the goat. Sarita smiled and gently moved Aadhya's hand from her chin to her cheek. Two signs Aadhya knew looked almost the same except for where the hand went. Aadhya tried again, hand at her cheek. Sarita nodded and signed back, eyes shining. Aadhya's older cousin, watching, tried to copy and got it wrong. Aadhya giggled and moved her cousin's hand to the right place.

Where did Sarita move Aadhya's hand?
From her chin to her cheek.
What was Aadhya feeling when she moved her cousin's hand?
She felt proud and playful, pleased to know the right place and able to teach someone else.
What did Sarita do that helped Aadhya learn?
She gently showed her where the hand should go, since two signs differed only by location.
How might the cousin see signing after Aadhya corrects them?
The cousin might realise that signs have exact parts, like where the hand goes, and are a real language.

I'm Zeenat. My flatmate Lalit came home from his viva last Thursday looking grey. The examiner had given him a C and said his project was "copied from the internet." It wasn't. I'd watched him build it for months. An hour later, the delivery rider arrived with our food, twenty minutes late. Lalit tore into the rider in the doorway, shouting about useless people who can't do their jobs. The rider just stood there, holding the bag. I wanted to jump in and say, "Stop, it's not his fault." I didn't. I paid, said sorry to the rider quietly, and closed the door. Later, when Lalit had eaten and calmed down a bit, I said, "That wasn't really about the food, was it?" He put his head in his hands. "No. It was the viva."

What grade did the examiner give Lalit?
A C.
Why did Zeenat hold back from stopping Lalit in the doorway?
Zeenat felt uncomfortable and sorry for the rider, but sensed that correcting Lalit mid-outburst would only make him angrier.
What makes Zeenat's quiet remark later work better?
Asking gently after he had calmed down let Lalit see for himself that his anger was about the viva, not the food.
How might the delivery rider have felt being shouted at?
The rider probably felt shocked and humiliated, blamed for something far bigger than a late delivery.
John is 15 cm taller than Lena and 6 cm shorter than Rebeca. If John has a height of 152 cm, what is the height of Lena and Rebeca together?

Lena is 152 cm - 15 cm = 137 cm tall
Rebeca is 152 cm + 6 cm = 158 cm tall
So, the total height of Lena and Rebeca would be 137 cm + 158 cm = 295 cm.
The answer is 295.

Friday night
Pallavi walked past me at the canteen today like I was invisible. Fine. I don't care. She's the one who ruined everything.
Things Pallavi did: 1. Sat with the new girls on sports day. 2. Didn't laugh at my joke about her singing. 3. Told Ma'am I copied her project idea (I didn't copy, I just had the same idea).
Things I did: …nothing really. Okay, I laughed at her singing in front of the whole class. But it was a joke. She's too sensitive. Everyone says so.
Mummy asked why Pallavi hasn't come over. I said, "She's changed." Mummy said, "People don't usually change for no reason, Irawati." I went to my room.
I'm not writing more. It was her fault. Mostly.
Probably.

What did Irawati laugh at in front of the whole class?
Irawati laughed at Pallavi's singing in front of the whole class.
How does Irawati feel as the diary entry ends with "Mostly. Probably."?
Irawati feels defensive and uneasy, beginning to doubt the story that Pallavi was completely to blame.
What could Irawati try instead of listing only Pallavi's faults?
Irawati could finish the "Things I did" list honestly and think about apologising for the joke, which might help this or her next friendship.
How might Pallavi see what happened?
Pallavi probably felt humiliated by the joke about her singing and hurt, which might explain why she sat with the new girls.

In the courtyard of their house near Kottayam, Tomy, two, heard his mother, Elizabeth, calling him for his bath. He squeezed his eyes shut and stood very still beside the coconut pile. "Tomy gone," he announced. His sister Anjali laughed. "I can see you!" Tomy shut his eyes tighter. Then he held up a shell to show Anjali, the shiny side toward his own face. "See? Pretty!" Anjali saw only its rough grey back.

What did Tomy announce with his eyes shut?
"Tomy gone."
Why did Tomy shut his eyes tighter when Anjali said she could see him?
Tomy felt determined to stay hidden; to him hiding meant not seeing, so squeezing his eyes harder seemed like hiding better.
How could Anjali gently show Tomy what she sees?
She could turn the shell round toward herself and say "Now I see the shiny side!", making a simple game of it.
What is it like for Anjali when Tomy shows her the shell?
She is shown only a rough grey back while Tomy is sure she sees the pretty side, which is funny and a little puzzling for her.

Since Vandana left the consulting job in October, the flat in Lajpat Nagar had gone quiet. She slept late, kept her door half closed, and when Neelam asked about her day, her eyes slid to the floor. The phone buzzing made her jump. Neelam's mother, calling from Jaipur, said, "Sit her down and make her talk. She'll feel better." Neelam didn't. She had tried once, and Vandana had gone even quieter. Instead she left a plate of poha outside the door each morning and sat in the living room in the evenings with the television low, just in case. One night Vandana came out and sat at the other end of the sofa. After a while she said, "I think I'm really burnt out." Neelam nodded. "Do you want me to help you find someone to talk to? A counsellor?" Vandana was quiet, then said, "Maybe. Yes."

What did Neelam leave outside the door each morning?
A plate of poha.
What might Vandana's sliding eyes and jumping at the phone suggest?
They may show exhaustion and stress after the job, perhaps low mood too; it might look like coldness, but she seems worn down.
Why was Neelam's approach better than 'make her talk'?
Pushing had made Vandana quieter, while steady presence and small kindnesses let her come out when ready, and then Neelam offered help finding a counsellor.
How does Neelam's mother see the situation?
She thinks talking will fix it and wants Neelam to push, not seeing that pressure made Vandana withdraw further.

In the small town of Sehore, Mohit, twenty-two, sat on the steps of the shuttered photocopy shop, scrolling job portals. Two years ago, his seniors from the same college had got placed at a big firm in Indore through campus drives. He'd studied just as hard. He'd expected the same. But this year, the firm didn't come, and his emails got no replies. Now his sister Reena, still in school, asked him at dinner when he'd start working. Mohit slammed his spoon down. "Ask the companies! They gave jobs to everyone before us, and now nothing. It's like someone decided our batch doesn't count." Reena went quiet. Mohit knew she hadn't meant anything. But the anger felt bigger than him, like something he was owed had been locked away while others walked off with it.

Where had Mohit's seniors got placed?
They had got placed at a big firm in Indore through campus drives.
Why did Mohit slam his spoon down?
Mohit felt bitter and angry, sure something he deserved had been withheld while others got it.
What could Mohit do with this frustration?
Mohit could talk to a teacher or placement adviser about other routes, and apologise to Reena, rather than letting the resentment fill every conversation.
How might Reena have felt when Mohit snapped?
Reena likely felt hurt and startled, since she was only asking an innocent question.

Vaisampayana continued, "When all the Kauravas utterly routed and vanquished, set out in a dejected mood for Hastinapura, Falguna, on his way back, addressed Uttara, saying, 'O prince, O hero of mighty arms, seeing the kine escorted in advance of us by the cowherds, we shall enter Virata's metropolis in the afternoon, having tended the steeds with drink and a bath. Let the cowherds, despatched by thee, speedily repair to the city with the good news and proclaim thy victory.'"

Is it okay to leave a kitten alone while I go to college?
A kitten can be left for a few hours if she has food, water, a litter tray and safe toys, but very young kittens need more company. How old is she, and how long will you be away?
She is four months old, her name is Nimbu. I will be out for six hours.
Six hours is long for Nimbu. Ask someone at home to check on her, or leave her in a small, safe room with toys and a warm bed. Spend time playing with her before you leave.
My mum is at home all day. She can look in on her.
That is the best solution. Ask your mum to feed Nimbu at midday and play with her for a few minutes. A kitten feels safer when a familiar person is near.
Good. I will tell her. Remind me how old Nimbu is?
Nimbu is four months old. Tell your mum she should check her food, water and litter tray at midday, and spend a little time with Nimbu while you are at college.

Why did Yusuf write 'passed away' instead of 'died', and what does it tell you about how Yusuf feels?

How might Yusuf's mother be feeling, judging from the chat?

How many meanings does "work out" have?

It has several. It can mean to exercise, to solve something, or to end well.

Harsha had the screenshot open and her thumb over the send arrow. It was Charu's own confession from last term: she still slept with a night lamp on. One tap and the whole class chat would have it, the same way Charu's careless mouth had spread Harsha's news.

"Sleep on it," said her brother Chinmay, passing with a plate of toast. "If you still want to tomorrow, fine."

She did not post it. At lunch she ate in the library, jaw tight, and watched the urge lose its heat by evening.

On Thursday Charu cornered her. "Honestly, you're making this huge. It was one joke." Harsha picked up her bag and left.

A week later Charu waited by the cycle stand, holding a folded note. "I told them what you trusted me with. That was wrong of me, and I feel ashamed. You didn't cause it." Harsha said she needed time, and meant it.

They began small: a shared bench, a borrowed pen. In October a girl asked Charu what Harsha's plans were after school. "Ask her yourself," Charu said, and returned to her sandwich. Harsha noticed, and slid over her second samosa.

What did the screenshot on Harsha's phone show?
It showed Charu's own confession that she still slept with a night lamp on.
How did Charu's first attempt to speak with Harsha differ from her second, and why did only one of them open the door?

On Thursday Charu said Harsha was making it huge, which blamed the hurt person, while a week later she named what she did, said it was wrong and that she felt ashamed, and told Harsha she was not the cause.
What was Harsha feeling when she sat in the library with her jaw tight?
She was angry and still tempted to hit back; the tight jaw and the way the urge cooled by evening suggest the anger was real but fading.
What does the way the friendship restarted show about a sound way forward after an honest apology?
Harsha took it slowly, with small shared things, and watched whether Charu's behaviour matched her words, which Charu did when she refused to gossip about Harsha.

Every first Sunday, Nkechi makes her mum's jollof rice in the tiny flat kitchen in Leeds, and every first Sunday she lets the bottom burn a little, on purpose.
"That crispy layer was the best bit," she tells Hana, scraping it into two bowls.
Six years ago she couldn't walk past the rice aisle. In her second year, when she still couldn't sleep or make it to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those Thursday sessions are part of why she can stand at this stove now.
Today she laughs telling Hana how her mum sang loudly and badly while stirring. Her eyes sting halfway through the story, and she lets them.
Later she video-calls her brother in Lagos to argue about how much pepper is too much, then goes back to her thesis draft. Her mum would have wanted it finished.

What does Nkechi cook every first Sunday?
Her mum's jollof rice, with the bottom left to burn a little on purpose.
What shows that Nkechi now feels warmth as well as pain when she remembers her mum?
She laughs telling Hana about her mum's loud, bad singing, yet her eyes sting halfway through and she lets them.
What helped Nkechi when her grief stayed stuck, and why did it matter?
When she still couldn't sleep or get to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those sessions helped her reach the point where the recipe brings warmth.
What might the first-Sunday cooking mean for Hana?
Hana gets to know Nkechi's mum through the crispy rice and the stories, and sees a friend carry on with life while keeping the memory close.
Our teacher told us the science paper will have an essay question. I have never written one.
That is a new thing for many students. A science essay is simply a clear explanation. Do you know the topic?
It might be about pollution. I am Meera.
Hello Meera. For pollution, use a simple pattern: what it is, what causes it, what harm it does, and what we can do. Four short paragraphs would be enough.
Can you remind me the four parts again?
Of course. First, what pollution is. Second, its causes. Third, the harm it does. Fourth, what we can do about it. Practise writing it once tonight, Meera, and time yourself.

Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre, Monday.
Anjali, a final-year student, came in today, very tense. Her father has told her that if she does not agree to marry a man the family has chosen by Diwali, she should "never come home again". Her mother has stopped speaking to her. She said, "Maybe he's just upset. Maybe it's normal." I asked whether she feels she has a real choice. She said no, and that she is afraid to go home for the holidays. We talked about the difference between a parent stating a limit and pressure that removes her choice and makes her afraid. I explained that she does not have to decide anything today. With her permission, I contacted the college's women's cell and a legal aid counsellor, and gave her the helpline number. She will stay in the hostel over the holiday. I will see her on Wednesday.
— Rekha

When does Anjali's father want her to agree by?
By Diwali.
What was Anjali feeling during the session?
She was tense and afraid to go home, and unsure whether her father's pressure was normal.
What steps did the counsellor take that were wise?
She explained Anjali didn't have to decide today, connected her with the women's cell and legal aid with her permission, gave the helpline and arranged for her to stay in the hostel.
How does Rekha see the father's ultimatum?
Rekha sees it as pressure that removes Anjali's choice and makes her afraid, not simply a parent stating a limit.

Wei and Tuan started as summer interns at the same Hanoi engineering firm on the same Monday. By the second week, the difference was clear. Ms Lan stopped by Wei's desk every afternoon: "Try the drainage plan for Block B. I'll mark it up tomorrow, and I'll be honest." Her red notes were long and sometimes stung.
Tuan, seated at the far end of the office, was asked to scan old drawings and order lunch. Nobody checked his work, because nobody expected much. By August, Wei was presenting a section at the client meeting. Tuan had learned where every file was and little else.
On the last day he told his mother, "I think I'm just not an engineer." He never found out that Ms Lan had simply decided, on day one, which of them looked keen.

What did Ms Lan ask Wei to try?
The drainage plan for Block B.
What was Tuan feeling when he said he's "just not an engineer"?
He felt discouraged and small, having taken the lack of challenge as a verdict on his ability.
What could Tuan have asked for early on to change things?
He could ask Ms Lan directly for a real task and honest feedback, like Wei's, instead of waiting to be noticed.
How did Ms Lan's red notes affect Wei?
They sometimes stung, but the honest feedback pushed Wei to improve until presenting at the client meeting.

messages.content: Bert, Ernie, and Peggy collect stamps.  Bert has four times as many stamps as Ernie, but Ernie has three times as many stamps as Peggy.  If Peggy currently has 75 stamps in her collection, how many stamps does she need to add to her collection to have a collection as large as Bert's collection?

Ernie has three times as many stamps as Peggy, or 3*75=225 stamps.
Bert has 4 times as many stamps as Ernie, or 4*225=900 stamps.
Thus, Peggy would need 900-75=825 more stamps to have a collection as large as Bert's.
The answer is 825.
How much is a plate of dosa at the corner restaurant?
I wouldn't know, because each restaurant sets its own prices. Look at the menu board or ask at the counter.

At breakfast in their Berlin flat, Selin, eleven, had screamed at her younger brother Tariq for using her hairbrush on the dog. "I hate you!" she'd said. At the school playground that afternoon, she saw three older boys pushing Tariq against the fence, calling him "baby." Something hot rose in her chest. She dropped her bag and ran over. "Leave him alone!" One of the boys laughed. Selin's legs were shaking, but she stepped closer. "I'll get Frau Weber right now." They backed off. Tariq's lip was trembling. Selin put an arm round him, marched him straight to Frau Weber and told her everything. The teacher listened, took the boys' names, and phoned their mother before home time. On the walk home Tariq whispered, "You said you hated me." Selin shrugged. "I do. Only I'm allowed to."

What were the older boys calling Tariq?
They were calling him "baby."
What was Selin feeling when something hot rose in her chest?
Selin felt fiercely protective and angry, strong enough to override her morning resentment.
Why was taking Tariq to Frau Weber straight away a good choice?
It brought in an adult who could stop the bullying the same day and contact their mother.
How might Tariq have felt when Selin put her arm around him?
Tariq probably felt safe and relieved, and perhaps touched that his sister defended him despite the morning fight.

Monday: On the school bus, the back-seat group started flicking paper balls at Gargi, the new girl, and calling her "Miss Topper." Sonali, ten, watched, uneasy.
Wednesday: The back seat was louder. Everyone was doing it. Sonali, squashed in the middle, flicked one paper ball too. Nobody looked at her. It felt like the group did it, not her.

What was Sonali feeling on Wednesday when she threw a paper ball?
Sonali felt hidden in the group, as if the group did it rather than her, which made the teasing feel less like her choice.
What did Sonali's mother do that helped, and why?
She listened and helped Sonali apologise to Gargi that same evening, turning a hidden group act into a personal responsibility Sonali could repair.
How might Gargi have felt on the bus that week?

Ujjwal's mother fed Moti, then his father fed Moti again, and then nobody filled the water bowl. On the third evening Ujjwal sat at the dining table with a sketch pen and a sheet of paper. On the board by the front door, where you take off your shoes.

He seemed worried that Moti was being fed twice or left without water, and wanted the care to be steady.

Writing a name beside each job, so everyone knows whose turn it is as well as what needs doing.

Madhav notices Ujjwal checking it every time he comes in, but is not sure whether Ujjwal feels proud.

The rains failed that year. Minakshi, twenty, stood at the edge of her family's dry field outside the village, where the cotton plants had wilted before they flowered. She had planned to start college in the district town in July. Now there was no money for fees, and her father needed help with the goats and the dairy work. For weeks she'd been angry, checking the sky, refusing to talk about it. This evening her friend Parveen found her sitting on the field boundary. "What will you do?" Minakshi was quiet a long time. "Work this year. Save a little. Study from books at night. Go next year." She said it calmly. Parveen looked surprised. "You're not angry anymore?" "I'm tired of fighting the sky," Minakshi said, almost smiling.

What crop had wilted in the family's field?
The cotton plants.
How had Minakshi's feelings changed by the evening Parveen found her?
She had moved from weeks of anger to a calm acceptance of the situation and a practical new plan.
What small step makes Minakshi's plan realistic?
Studying from books at night while working and saving, which keeps her goal alive even with a delay.
Why might Parveen react with surprise to Minakshi's calm?
She had seen weeks of anger, so she expected more frustration, not a quiet plan.

Salary day in the Kakkanad office felt like a festival: cake in the pantry, weekend plans at every desk. Kunal slipped out at lunch to the bank branch across the road, with Lavanya from accounts walking beside him, since she had done the same two years earlier.
At the counter he did it in order. First, he opened a second savings account, one with no debit card. Second, he filled in the standing-instruction form: ₹4,000 to move there on the 2nd of every month, the day after salary. Third, with the branch officer's help, he started a small monthly SIP of ₹1,000, which the officer explained twice.
Back at his desk, his main balance looked smaller than his friends' did. 'Feels like I've robbed myself,' he said.
Lavanya laughed. 'Wait till March. You won't even notice it's gone.'

On which day does the ₹4,000 move to the second account?
The 2nd of every month, the day after salary.
How did Kunal feel looking at his smaller main balance?
A bit deprived and wistful, joking that he had robbed himself, yet sure enough of the plan to leave it running.
What else could make Kunal's setup easier to live with?
Checking with the branch officer or a qualified adviser after a few months to see whether the amounts still suit his real spending.
How does the plan look to Lavanya?
Lavanya has been through it and finds his complaint funny, expecting the automatic saving to feel normal by March. 😄

Jomon, the contractor, sat on the bench outside Rashmi's small bakery in Pala, the renovation contract in a plastic folder. "Sign today, chechi. Tomorrow my team goes to a job in Kottayam. Then you'll wait three months."
Rashmi read slowly. On the phone he had promised new wiring, a steel counter and cleanup included. The paper said only "renovation work as discussed". There was a line about "extra charges as applicable".
"The wiring and counter aren't written here," she said.
"Arre, I told you. My word is enough."
Rashmi felt her chest tighten. She wanted the bakery ready before the Onam rush. But she remembered her neighbour's leaking roof after a contract just like this.
"Then write your word down. Each item, and what 'extra charges' means. I'll sign then."
Jomon stood. "I don't have time."
"Then I'll wait." She kept a photo of the contract and his phone promises, and called another contractor that evening.

What did the contract say instead of listing the work?
Only "renovation work as discussed", plus a line about "extra charges as applicable".
What was Rashmi feeling when Jomon said his word was enough?
She felt tense and torn, anxious to be ready for Onam but wary because of her neighbour's bad experience.
How did Rashmi protect herself?
She asked for each promised item and the extra charges in writing, refused to sign under time pressure, kept records, and found another contractor.
How might Jomon see Rashmi's refusal?
Jomon seems annoyed and impatient, used to people signing quickly under pressure, and walks away rather than write things down.

Parul opened a blank message to Harish at 6 pm in the empty office. The hospital records team had been waiting three days for his data, and her irritation had built into a first draft: "This is the third time you've let us down." She read it aloud, quietly, to the empty room, and winced at how harsh it sounded. She deleted "let us down," saved it as a draft and went to make tea. The next morning she reread it: "The records team needs your data by Friday. Can we talk about what's getting in the way?" Then she saw that this was really a conversation, not a message. She walked over to Harish's desk instead and said, "Have you got ten minutes?"

What did Parul do to check the tone of her first draft?
She read it aloud.
What was Parul feeling when she wrote the first draft?
Irritation that had built up over the wait; she winced when she heard how harsh it sounded.
Why was walking to Harish's desk better than sending the message?
A difficult topic with a possible reason behind it is easier to handle by talking, where tone and answers show.
How might Harish have felt if the first draft had arrived?
Attacked or defensive, and he might have missed what the team needs by Friday.

Tanvir kept a mental scoreboard now: who spoke first in the Monday review, whose charts the director praised. He and Zeenat both wanted the senior analyst post, and his chest felt tight and calculating whenever her name came up. Once he spotted a weak number in her draft and felt a flicker of glee. He closed the file and went back to tightening his own quarterly report.

Zeenat noticed only the gaps. Her name was missing from a client thread, a shared file reached her a day late, and Tanvir's eyes seemed to follow her screen. She felt watched. That evening she began a dated log: thread, file, meeting, time.

On Thursday she caught him by the pantry. "Tanvir, I'm not accusing you," she said calmly. "Two client threads left me out and I found a file late. Can we copy each other on those from now on?"

He blinked, then nodded slowly. "I've been tense about the promotion. I didn't mean to shut you out. Copy me too."

She kept the log anyway. When Kishore, the manager, asked for updates the next week, both handed over clean, dated work.

How many client threads left Zeenat out, according to her?
She said two client threads left her out.
How did Tanvir's inner state and Zeenat's experience of him fit together, and what did each do to keep things fair?

Tanvir felt tense and calculating about the rivalry, but he did not sabotage her and put his effort into his own report. Zeenat, seeing only gaps, felt watched, so she kept a dated record and spoke to him directly and calmly.
What was Zeenat feeling as the missing thread, the late file and the following eyes added up?
She felt watched and uneasy, which is why she started a dated log.
What could Zeenat do if the gaps continue after this talk?
She could take her log to Kishore and stick to the facts, showing what was missed and when, without guessing at motives.

"Your phone's buzzing again," Zubin said from the top bunk. "Is that Kavin?"
"Yeah." Yash turned it face down.
"You've been ignoring him for three weeks. What happened?"
"He wants me to co-found his app. I don't want to. And every time I start to reply, it feels like I'm crushing his dream."
"So you're crushing it slowly instead."
Yash groaned. "That's harsh."
"Remember when Pranav ghosted our band? You checked your phone every hour for a month."
Yash was quiet. "Yeah. It was awful."
"So write two lines. Not an essay."
Yash picked up the phone and typed: "Kavin, sorry for the silence. I've thought about it, and I'm not going to join the app. It's a good idea, just not my path. I should have said this three weeks ago."
"Send it," Zubin said.
He sent it. Kavin replied: "Ugh, okay. Thanks for telling me. Coffee sometime anyway?"

How long had Yash been ignoring Kavin?
Three weeks.
Why had Yash been avoiding Kavin?
Replying felt like crushing Kavin's dream, so Yash felt guilty and awkward about saying no.
What made Yash's message kinder than more silence?
It was short and honest, gave a clear no with a reason, and apologised for the delay.
How did Kavin respond to the message?
Disappointed ("Ugh, okay") but thankful, and still open to coffee.

Saturday
Tejas called at eight: "Can you help me shift flats tomorrow? The truck's at seven."
Every part of me wanted to say yes. He's my little brother. I always say yes. Last month I spent both weekends painting his old flat.
But I've worked six days straight and I'm so tired my eyes hurt. Tomorrow is the only day I have to sleep, do my laundry and call Nani.
So I said, "Tejas, not tomorrow. I'm wiped out. I'll come next Saturday and help you unpack and set up the kitchen."
He was quiet, then said, "Okay. Fair." I felt guilty for about ten minutes. Then I felt okay.
I can't help anyone if I'm empty.
– Gurpreet

What time was the truck coming?
At seven.
How did Gurpreet feel after saying no?
Gurpreet felt guilty for about ten minutes, then okay and at peace with it.
How did Gurpreet say no in a caring way?
Gurpreet explained the tiredness and offered a specific later help, unpacking and setting up the kitchen, so the care continued without burning out.
How might Tejas feel about the no?
He might be disappointed at first, but he seems to understand, saying "Okay. Fair."

In the school library in Bhopal, Parul slid a note across to Seema. It said: Did you know Anjali's parents are getting divorced?? Pass it on!

Seema read it. Anjali sat two tables away, doing her homework with her head down.

Seema wrote underneath: I don't want to talk about this. It's her business. She folded the note and slid it back.

Parul frowned and whispered, "Why not? Everyone knows."

"Then they don't need me," Seema whispered back.

Parul held the note for a moment. Then she crumpled it and dropped it in the dustbin by the shelf.

Later, walking out, Seema passed Anjali's table and said, "Want to walk to the bus together?" Anjali looked surprised, then nodded.

What did Seema write under Parul's note?
I don't want to talk about this. It's her business.
Why did Seema refuse to pass the note on?
She felt it was unkind and not her business, and she didn't want Anjali hurt by more whispering.
What did Seema's choice achieve?
By refusing, she stopped the note, and Parul crumpled it instead of passing it on, so the rumour lost a carrier.
How might Anjali feel when Seema invites her to walk to the bus?
She is probably surprised and comforted to have someone friendly beside her on a hard day.

When Nani Kalyani first came to live with us, I argued with her all the time. She'd say it was 1980, or that she had to catch a train to her mother's village, and I would correct her, patiently at first and then less patiently. She'd get upset and scared, and I'd feel awful. I'm Usha, and it took me months to understand that the facts weren't the point. When she said she needed to catch the train, she was really saying, 'I miss my mother. I feel lost.' So I started answering that. 'You're missing your Amma. Tell me about her village.' We built a routine: same chair, same tea at four, same old songs on the radio. Her distress dropped. She still gets muddled. But she's calmer, and so am I.

What year did Nani sometimes say it was?
How did Usha feel after arguing with Nani?
Usha felt awful and guilty when Nani got upset and scared.
What did Usha change that reduced Nani's distress?
Responding to the feeling behind her words, and keeping a steady routine of chair, tea and songs.
How might Nani have felt being corrected all the time?
She probably felt frightened and lost, as if the world kept telling her she was wrong.

Subject: Documented concern: rear fire exit, Unit 2
Dear Tarun,
As our workers' safety representative, you're getting this before I file it with the ethics committee, so that I follow the right process.
Facts, as I observed them:
- On 3, 10 and 17 March, the rear fire exit in Unit 2 was chained shut during the night shift (dated photos attached).
- On 11 March I raised this verbally with the shift supervisor, who said it was to stop theft.
- On 18 March I emailed the plant manager. No reply yet.
- Tonight I have asked the night supervisor in writing to keep the exit unlocked for the shift.
I have kept copies of all emails, and I haven't shared this outside the company. I'm asking for it to be fixed, not for anyone to be punished.
Could we meet tomorrow, and could you tell me the inspector's contact if the internal route stalls?
Manoj

On which dates was the rear fire exit chained shut?
On 3, 10 and 17 March.
What seems to drive Manoj's careful tone?
Manoj feels worried for the workers' safety yet wants to be fair, asking for a fix rather than punishment.

Dated photos, a clear timeline, kept copies, raising it internally first, a written request to keep the exit unlocked tonight, and asking the safety representative about the next channel.

Second period, Istanbul, the first cold morning of November. Nour had worn her cousin's old green coat because her own had torn at the zip. When she walked in, Selin leaned over to Defne and whispered something, and Defne put a hand over her mouth. That was it. Nour knew exactly what had been said: Look at that coat. Where did she dig that up? She could almost hear Selin's voice saying it. She kept the coat on all through maths so nobody could see it was too big at the shoulders, even though she was sweating. At lunch she ate alone in the library. By evening she had decided never to wear the green coat again. She never asked what the whisper was. She never checked.

Why was Nour wearing her cousin's old green coat?
Because her own coat had torn at the zip.
Why did Nour feel so sure Selin was mocking the coat?
Nour already felt self-conscious in a coat that was too big, so when the whisper came her own worry supplied the words, and they felt as real as if she had heard them.
What small step could Nour have taken before hiding in the library?
Nour could have asked Selin or Defne what was funny, or simply noticed that she hadn't heard a single word, before acting as if she had.
What might Selin and Defne actually have been whispering about?
They could have been talking about anything, from a teacher to weekend plans; from their side, the coat may never have come up at all.

A sticker, one star.

First week of term. Tushar played online matches on Friday nights with the hostel group. It was fun, loud, harmless.

Sixth week. Exams were close and his father's shop was struggling. Now he logged in every night after dinner and didn't stop until four. When Sarika asked why he looked grey in class, he said, "It's how I relax. I can quit whenever." He'd missed two lab submissions.

Ninth week, a Sunday. He sat on his bed and wrote on the back of a notice: missed labs, skipped meals, no calls home, three weeks of four-hour sleep. He stared at it for a long time. Then he walked to Sarika's room and showed her. "I don't think I can stop on my own." She went with him the next morning to the student counselling centre, and waited outside.

On which nights did Tushar play in the first week of term?
Tushar played online matches on Friday nights.
What was Tushar feeling when he stared at his list?
Tushar felt shaken and worried, seeing in writing how much the gaming was costing him.
What steps helped Tushar, and why?
Counting the real cost honestly, telling Sarika, and going to the counselling centre early helped, because hiding it as relaxation was not working.
How might Sarika have felt when Tushar showed her the list?
Sarika probably felt worried but also relieved that he finally trusted her, which is why she went with him the next morning.

Zubin said, "I am thirsty. I need my bottle!"

A washing machine uses 20 gallons of water for a heavy wash, 10 gallons of water for a regular wash, and 2 gallons of water for a light wash per load of laundry. If bleach is used, there is an extra light wash cycle added to rinse the laundry thoroughly. There are two heavy washes, three regular washes, and one light wash to do. Two of the loads need to be bleached. How many gallons of water will be needed?

The two heavy washes will use 20 * 2 = 40 gallons of water.
The three regular washes will use 10 * 3 = 30 gallons of water.
The light wash will use 2 * 1 = 2 gallons of water.
The two bleached loads will use an extra 2 * 2 = 4 gallons of water.
In all, 40 + 30 + 2 + 4 = 76 gallons of water will be needed.
The answer is 76.

Hansa felt hesitant and kept expecting someone else, Manpreet the class rep or one of the toppers, to speak up; with 212 members it felt as if it could not be her job.
Which choice changed the group chat, and why did it work?
Hansa's short, calm message naming Arohi's effort and asking the group to stop; once one person spoke, Manpreet backed it up and the first poster apologised to Arohi.
What might the evening have been like for Arohi before and after Hansa's message?
Before, Arohi would have watched laughing faces pile up with nobody on her side; after, she could see Hansa and Manpreet stand up for her and read an apology from the poster.

In the flat in Johannesburg, Siddiq noticed he'd started checking his phone for university messages every ten minutes, even though his own exams were months away. It had begun when his older brother Thabo's finals started. Thabo paced the kitchen at night, refreshed the results page, and asked Siddiq three times whether he'd set the alarm, whether the lights were off, whether he'd heard anything. The tension crept into Siddiq like cold. One Sunday their father called a family meeting at the kitchen table. "We're all jumpy," he said honestly. "Thabo is stressed, and it's catching." They agreed: dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo would check the results page only once, in the morning. Siddiq felt his shoulders drop for the first time in weeks.

What did the family agree to at the kitchen table?
Dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo checking the results page only once, in the morning.
How did Thabo's stress affect Siddiq, and what shows it?
Siddiq became tense and watchful too; checking his phone every ten minutes for exams months away shows he had picked up his brother's vigilance.
Which choice by their father helped most, and why?
Saying honestly that Thabo's stress was catching and setting clear shared routines, which named the problem without blame and gave everyone limits.
How might Thabo feel about the new routine?
Thabo might find checking only once hard at first, but may also feel relieved to have a limit and to know his family understands.

a) At a party of 9 people, can everyone shake hands with exactly 3 others? b) Prove that in any group, the number of people who have shaken an ODD number of hands is even. c) A graph has 12 edges and every vertex has degree 3. How many vertices does it have?

Answer: a) No b) handshake lemma c) 8.

Count the pairs (person, handshake that person is in) in two ways. Adding the degrees counts every handshake twice (once for each person), so sum  deg = 2E, always EVEN. a) 9 x 3 = 27 would have to equal 2E: 27 is odd, impossible. b) sum  deg is even; the even degrees add to an even number, so the odd degrees also add to an even number, which needs an even count of odd terms. c) 3V = 2 x 12 = 24, V = 8 (the cube is an example). Common mistake: dividing by 2 the wrong way, e.g. E = sum  deg.

When I was eleven, I tried football and hated the shouting. I tried guitar and my fingers hurt. My uncle Santosh said, "Keep trying things. Something will grab you."
That winter he took me to the lake near Aizawl at dawn with his binoculars. I saw a small green bird with a red throat. I couldn't look away.
I made him wait an hour while I watched it. I drew it in my maths notebook when I got home.
After that, I kept a notebook of birds. I'm Lalremsiami, and I'm thirteen now. I want to study birds when I grow up. It started with that one morning.

What did the bird Lalremsiami saw look like?
A small green bird with a red throat.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when unable to look away from the bird?
Lalremsiami felt delighted and full of wonder, completely absorbed by the bird.
What did Santosh do that helped Lalremsiami find an interest?
He encouraged trying many things and took Lalremsiami somewhere new, which led to discovering bird-watching.
How might Santosh feel waiting an hour at the lake?
Santosh was probably patient and happy to see his advice working.

At the birthday party in the society hall, Yamini slipped out with her book and settled into the quiet corner behind the sofa. Music thumped, balloons burst. She turned a page, feet tucked up, smiling at nothing.
Her mother Vidya found her and crouched. "Everyone's playing musical chairs, beta. Don't you want to?"
"Not now," said Yamini. "I'm at the best part."
Vidya looked at her calm face, then at the noisy room. "Shall I bring you a plate?"
"Yes, please."
When the game ended, Yamini strolled over on her own, cheeks pink, and asked what the next round was.

Where did Yamini settle with her book?
In the quiet corner behind the sofa.
How does Yamini feel in the corner, and how can you tell?
She feels content. She smiles at nothing, tucks her feet up and says she is at the best part.
What choice by Vidya helped Yamini's afternoon?
Vidya looked at Yamini's calm face, did not force her to join and offered to bring a plate instead.
What might Vidya have been thinking as she looked at the noisy room?
She may have wondered whether Yamini was missing out, but seeing her calm face she accepted that Yamini was happy.

Beginner readers will use this, so keep every sentence short and every word plain.

Fresh out of the bath in their Pune flat, Jagdish wriggled free of the towel and ran down the corridor, giggling. At the bedroom door he stopped and looked back over his shoulder, grinning at Hemant.
"I'm coming to get you!" Hemant said, taking big slow steps.
Jagdish shrieked, ran behind the curtain, and peeped out again, waiting.

Jagdish had just had a bath. He wriggled out of the towel and ran down the hall. He was giggling. At the bedroom door he stopped. He looked back and grinned at Hemant. "I'm coming to get you!" said Hemant. Hemant took big, slow steps. Jagdish shrieked. He ran behind the curtain. Then he peeped out and waited.

At the anganwadi in the Goan village, the children were drawing fish. Maria, five, scribbled so hard that her crayon snapped. She sat with her arms folded and her bottom lip out. Dilnaz Teacher crouched beside her. 'Maria, your face looks cross. Are you upset?' Maria shrugged. Dilnaz waited, then pointed at the faces chart on the wall: happy, sad, cross, scared. 'Which one is like you?' Maria looked for a long time. She tapped 'cross,' then 'sad.' 'My fish looks bad,' she whispered. 'Cross and sad about your fish,' said Dilnaz Teacher. 'Shall we draw another together?' Maria unfolded her arms.

Which faces were on the chart?
Happy, sad, cross, scared.
What was Maria feeling when she folded her arms?
Maria was cross and sad that her fish drawing looked bad, even though she couldn't say it at first.
Why was pointing at the faces chart a good choice after Maria shrugged?
It gave Maria pictures to choose from when words were hard, so Maria could name cross and sad without pressure.
How might the other children see Maria's snapped crayon?
They might think Maria was just being naughty, not knowing she felt cross and sad about her fish.
