I'm Siddharth, Naveen's roommate, and I watched this whole thing happen last month.
Naveen found a video about studying in twenty-five-minute blocks with five-minute breaks. On Sunday he tried it for his accounts revision. On Monday he tried it again. Monday evening he did a practice paper and scored 64. His last one was 58.
He stood up, pumped his fist and announced, "It works!" That night he told three friends on the floor to switch. He even printed a timetable for the corridor wall.
I asked, "Isn't that just two days?" He said, "Six marks, Sid. Six marks."
Two weeks later, his next practice paper came back at 55. He stared at it for a long time and said nothing. I don't know if he was angry or just confused. Maybe the method helps. Maybe Monday's paper was easier. Two days couldn't tell him.

What did Naveen score on Monday's practice paper?
He scored 64.
What might Naveen staring at the 55 for a long time suggest?
It suggests he felt confused and let down, though Siddharth can't tell if he was angry or just puzzled.
Which approach would have given Naveen a more reliable answer?
Using the method for several weeks and comparing many practice papers, not just one, before telling others it works.
How might the three friends who switched be affected?
They changed their study routine based on one good day, so they may feel misled if their scores don't improve.

Playgroup note, Holi week, by the room caregiver.

Anirban, two, sat by the window pressing coloured blocks into a tray. His mother called his name twice from the doorway. He kept pressing.

She looked hurt. I told her it's normal; toddlers often hear only the one thing they're doing.

I crouched beside him. "Anirban, Mumma's here." He looked up, beamed and ran to her, one pink block in his fist. His friend Zeenat waved bye. 🌸

What was Anirban pressing into a tray?
He was pressing coloured blocks into a tray.
Why didn't Anirban answer when his mother called?
He felt content and absorbed in the blocks and didn't hear her, which is a normal limit at his age, not defiance.
What did the caregiver do that helped Anirban and his mother?
The caregiver explained that this is normal for toddlers, then crouched beside him and spoke softly.
How might Anirban's mother have felt after hearing the explanation?
She probably felt relieved and less hurt, knowing he wasn't ignoring her.

Every evening at the bus stop, the same boy from her tuition class, Yusuf, stood far too close to Reena, even when there was plenty of room. Reena stepped back. He stepped forward. She turned sideways and put her school bag between them. He kept talking anyway. Her heart was pounding. She wanted to leave but didn't want to make a scene. She looked for the shopkeeper opposite, walked over to buy water and stayed there until the bus came. That night she told her father. He listened and said, "You did well to step away. We'll speak to the tuition teacher tomorrow."

What did Reena put between herself and Yusuf?
She put her school bag between them.
What was Reena feeling when Yusuf kept stepping closer?
She was uneasy and scared, and her heart was pounding. She wanted to leave without making a scene.
What should a teenager do if someone keeps closing in or ignores clear signals?
Step away, put distance or an object between them, go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult. Reena told her father.
How might Reena's father have felt hearing about it?
He listened and took her seriously, and decided to speak to the teacher. He reassured her that stepping away was right.

The answer is r = 14 cm.

In the hostel common room Madhuri was telling everyone that Ritu had lied about her scholarship. Ritu stood by the door, her face gone stiff. Deepika got up from the sofa and walked over to her. "Ritu showed me the letter weeks ago. If you want to talk about it, talk to her." The room went quiet. Madhuri's birthday plans, which had included Deepika, quietly stopped including her.

That night Deepika told Ritu something less comfortable. "I stood up for you because I believe you. But you were rude to the mess staff yesterday, and I'm not going to pretend I didn't see it. That wasn't okay." Ritu flushed and looked at the floor, then said, "You're right. I'll apologise tomorrow."

Ritu did not forget the common room. She could still feel the relief of Deepika's steps across the floor. She did not think of it as something owed to her by a friend. When Deepika caught a fever the following week, Ritu photocopied all her lecture notes, made soup on the hostel hotplate, and left them with a note. "Not payment. Just me." Deepika laughed weakly from under her blanket, and pulled the blanket up higher.

What did Madhuri say about Ritu?
Madhuri said that Ritu had lied about her scholarship.
How did Deepika's support and Ritu's response fit together, and what did Deepika's honesty add?

Deepika stood up for Ritu in the common room even though it cost her Madhuri's invitation, and Ritu felt relief and returned it with notes and soup. Deepika also told her, without covering for her, that being rude to the mess staff was not okay.
What was Ritu feeling as she stood stiff by the door?
She felt exposed and hurt at being accused in front of everyone.
What could Ritu do to show her thanks over time?
She can keep helping in her own way, as with the notes and soup, and not treat Deepika's help as something she is owed.
I made a typo in the title of a presentation and only noticed after sending it to the team.
That's an annoying moment, but a typo in a title is a small problem. It happens to nearly everyone.
Should I send a corrected version?
A short, friendly note with the corrected file is fine. Something like, 'Please use the attached version, I fixed a typo in the title.' That is clear and quick, and no long apology is needed.
Okay. How do I avoid this next time?
Read titles and headings last, after the content is finished, and read them aloud. Your eyes tend to skip over big text, but your ears catch mistakes.

Shankar, eight, had fallen off his cycle racing down the slope in their Coimbatore colony. Now his knee had six stitches and his wrist was in a bandage. He sat on the sofa, arms folded. 'I'm never cycling again,' he said, though his eyes kept going to the cycle by the door. His older brother Chaitanya sat beside him with a bowl of peanuts. 'That was a big fall. Were you scared?' Shankar's lip trembled. 'Yes. And now I can't play for ages.' 'The doctor said two weeks for the stitches. Then you can try again on the flat part first.' Chaitanya handed him a peanut. 'Today's goal: walk to the gate and back.' Shankar did it, limping. The next day, he walked to the park. By the end of the week, he was asking about the cycle.

How many stitches did Shankar's knee have?
Six stitches.
What was Shankar feeling as he sat with arms folded?
He was scared after the fall and angry that he could not play, saying he would never cycle again.
What small goals did Chaitanya set?
Walking to the gate and back, then trying cycling on the flat part first when healed.
How might Chaitanya have felt when Shankar asked about the cycle again?
He was probably relieved and pleased to see his brother's confidence coming back.

Peggy has 6 dolls.  Her grandmother gives Peggy her own collection of 30 dolls.  Over the year, Peggy receives half that amount of dolls between her birthday and Christmas.  How many dolls does Peggy now have?

Peggy has 6 dolls and her grandmother gave her 30 so that's 6+30 = 36 dolls
Over the holidays, Peggy is gifted half the number of dolls her grandmother gave her, so she receives 30/2 = 15 more dolls
Peggy had 36 dolls and received another 15 for a total of 36+15 = 51 dolls
The answer is 51.

In the school library, Nitin spread two sheets on the table in front of his class teacher, Mrs. Shreya Nair. Two months ago, in this same room, she'd helped him convince his parents to let him drop one of his three coaching batches as a trial.

"So?" she asked.

"Test scores first," Nitin said. "Before: physics 48, 51, 49. After: 55, 59, 62."

"Sleep?"

"Before, I slept at one. Now around eleven. I'm not dozing in first period anymore."

"And how do you feel?"

Nitin thought. "Less panicky. I actually understand what I'm solving."

Mrs. Nair smiled. "Then what's your decision?"

"Keep it at two batches. Until the board exams, at least."

She wrote a short note for his parents on school paper: The trial has worked. I support continuing. Nitin folded it into his notebook carefully.

What were Nitin's physics scores after the change?
How did Nitin describe his feelings after two months?
He said he felt less panicky and actually understood what he was solving.
What else could Nitin do to keep the lighter schedule working?
He could keep checking his scores and sleep every month, so any drop is caught early and discussed with his parents.
How might Mrs. Nair see the trial's result?
Mrs. Nair seems pleased and supportive, writing a note for his parents because the evidence shows the change helped.

Harsha, you're worried about your forehead in tomorrow's interview? Then let your old colleague Vishal tell you something. My first interview, at the bank, I was so nervous that my forehead folded into three deep lines and stayed there. I was thinking hard, that's all. Afterwards the panel head told my uncle I seemed "irritated with the questions". Irritated! I was terrified. Before the next interview I practised in front of the mirror: when a question interested me, I let my eyebrows lift a little, and before answering I took one breath and smoothed my forehead. Small thing, but the second panel wrote that I seemed "engaged". Years later I sat on interview panels myself. When a young candidate's forehead was knotted up, I remembered that boy at the bank and told the others, "That's effort, not attitude." So practise a little, yes. But don't hate your forehead. It's only working hard.

Where was Vishal's first interview?
Vishal's first interview was at the bank.
What was young Vishal feeling when that forehead folded into three lines?
Vishal was terrified and thinking hard, not irritated as the panel head believed; the furrowed brow showed anxiety and effort.
Which choice in the story changed how the second panel saw Vishal?
Practising in the mirror to let the eyebrows lift when interested and to smooth the forehead with a breath before answering made Vishal come across as 'engaged'.
How did the first panel head read the furrowed forehead?
The panel head read it as irritation with the questions, missing that it was nervous effort.

Class teacher's observation, Class 12B, Friday
I have noticed Vijay and Aadhya are going out; most of the class knows. I'm recording this because it's a good example, not a concern.
This week the class planned a Saturday trip to the lake. Aadhya said she'd stay back for her physics study group. Vijay looked disappointed for a second, then said, "Fair. Send me the notes after?" and went with his friends. Neither made a scene.
On Wednesday, in the corridor, I heard Vijay ask, "Is it okay if I sit with you at lunch, or are you with the girls today?" Aadhya said, "With the girls today." He smiled and joined the cricket boys.
They each still have their own friends. They check with each other rather than assume.
No action needed. I will, with their permission, ask them to help me plan the life-skills session on healthy friendships and relationships next month.

Why did Aadhya stay back from the lake trip?
For her physics study group.
What was Vijay feeling when Aadhya said she would stay back?
He felt a moment of disappointment but accepted her choice calmly, showing respect rather than hurt pride.
What does this couple do that keeps the relationship healthy?
They ask instead of assuming, accept each other's no without a scene, and keep their own friends.
How might Aadhya feel when Vijay accepts her choices?
Aadhya likely feels trusted and free, able to say no without worrying about upsetting Vijay.

It was Bidisha's week to clean the class fish tank. She lifted the lid, and the smell of old water hit her. "Ugh!" She held the net at arm's length, nose wrinkled.

Rafiq Sir laughed. "Yes, it's not perfume. Scrub the glass on the left first."

She scrubbed green slime, grumbling under her breath. Then she stopped. On the right side the glass was almost clean, and three small snails were stuck to it, moving slowly.

"Aha! The snails! They're eating the slime on this side!"

Rafiq Sir put down his marker. "Class, did you hear that? Bidisha just worked out what the snails are for." She forgot all about the smell.

How many snails were on the right side of the glass?
Three small snails.
What was Bidisha feeling when she said "Ugh!" and held the net at arm's length?
Disgust at the smell of old water, plus some annoyance at the chore, as her grumbling shows.
How did Rafiq Sir make the most of Bidisha's "Aha"?
He stopped and shared her discovery with the whole class, celebrating that she had worked out what the snails are for.
What would change if Rafiq Sir had scolded her for saying "Ugh"?
She might feel embarrassed and resentful, the chore would feel worse, and her discovery might never have been shared.

How did Pip do the first time he went out with Stubb?

The first time Stubb lowered with him, Pip evinced much nervousness; but happily, for that time, escaped close contact with the whale; and therefore came off not altogether discreditably; though Stubb observing him, took care, afterwards, to exhort him to cherish his courageousness to the utmost, for he might often find it needful.
Pip was very nervous but never came close to the whale, so he did not do badly. Stubb told him to hold on to his courage, because he would often need it.

Meghna, come and sit, and I will tell you about the time I had to choose. I am Vinita, your Nani. When I was ten, my friend Tejas kicked a football through the staff-room window. I saw it. Everyone ran. I said to myself, I will tell Miss that it was a stray dog. But my tongue felt like stone. Instead I caught Tejas by the sleeve and said, "We have to tell her. I will come with you." His face went white, but we went together. Miss was stern, but she praised us for coming. Tejas paid by cleaning the football field for a week.

What did Tejas kick through the staff-room window?
He kicked a football through it.
How did Vinita feel about her first idea, and why did she drop it?
Vinita felt uneasy about lying: she thought of blaming a stray dog, but her tongue felt like stone, so she chose to help Tejas tell the truth.
What did Vinita do that showed real loyalty?
She urged Tejas to tell the teacher and went with him, standing beside him instead of lying to protect him.
How might Tejas have felt when Vinita caught his sleeve?
Tejas was probably afraid, as his white face shows, but he may also have been relieved not to face the teacher alone.

At the school play corner, Irfan's block tower fell when Mahima's elbow bumped it. Their voices went loud, and then Irfan turned his back and started sorting crayons as if nothing had happened. Mahima held out a block. "Irfan? Irfan?" He kept sorting. At snack time he sat at the far end of the mat. Mahima watched him with her mouth turned down and ate her banana slowly. Later she asked the teacher, "Why is Irfan not talking to me?" Irfan's tummy still felt tight.

What did Irfan do after he turned his back?
He started sorting crayons.
What does Irfan's tight tummy suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he was still hurt and upset. He pretended the fight was not there, but the feeling had not gone away.
What could Irfan try instead of turning away, and why?
He could say, "You knocked my tower and I felt sad," or ask the teacher to help. Saying it out loud gives the hurt somewhere to go.
How does Mahima see Irfan's silence?
She is puzzled and a little sad. She does not know what she did wrong, so she asks the teacher why Irfan will not talk to her.

Sit down, Eshaan. Your Chinmay Chacha has lost more than one pitch, you know.
When I was twenty-four I failed the state services prelims. I didn't leave my room for three days. Then, for weeks, I swung between two stories. Story one: I'm just not smart enough. Story two: the paper was unfair, the questions changed, bad luck.
My old teacher, Joshi-ma'am, made me write a list. Three questions. What was in my hands? I never did full mock tests with a timer. I read, but I didn't practise. What was luck? Yes, the pattern changed that year. Everyone got the same luck, though. What would I change? Timed tests, every Sunday.
That list was the most useful thing I wrote that whole year, Eshaan. Not because it made me feel better. Because it told me what to do.
So. Your pitch. Get a paper.

How many days did Chacha not leave his room after failing the prelims?
He didn't leave his room for three days.
How did Chacha feel during the weeks he swung between two stories?
He felt stuck and discouraged, thinking either he wasn't smart enough or it was all bad luck, and neither story let him move forward.
What is Chacha advising Eshaan to do about the lost pitch?
He wants Eshaan to write down what was in his hands, what was luck and what to change, so the failure turns into clear next steps.
What might Eshaan be feeling as his Chacha tells this story?
Eshaan may feel comforted that an elder he respects also failed, and ready to look at the pitch honestly instead of just feeling bad.
A party venue has 4 tables that seat 6 people each, 16 tables that seat 4 people each, and 8 round tables that seat 10 people each. What is the total capacity of all the tables at the party venue?

Four 6-seater tables can accommodate 4 x 6 = 24 people.
Sixteen 4-seater tables can accommodate 16 x 4 = 64 people.
Eight 10-seater table can accommodate 8 x 10 = 80 people.
Therefore, all the tables in the party venue can accommodate 24 + 64 + 80 =168 people.
The answer is 168.

At the lunch meeting in the hotel in Chembur, the groom's father spread his hands. "We don't want anything, Rekha-ji. Nothing at all. Only, our relatives expect the wedding at a good venue. Five hundred guests. Silver gifts for each family. And of course, whatever you give your daughter is hers."
Rekha smiled politely and kept stirring her tea long after the sugar had dissolved.
Ira, twenty-four, the bride, sat beside her mother and did the sums in her head. The venue alone would swallow her parents' savings. Silver for every family. Gold "for her" that she knew would be counted.
On the taxi ride home, Ira said, "Mumma, they said 'nothing' and then listed four things."
Rekha stared out of the window. "It's how it's done."
"Then we need to decide if it's how we do it," Ira said. "I'd rather have a small wedding than start by paying for respect."

How many guests did the groom's father mention?
He mentioned five hundred guests.
What does Rekha stirring her tea long after the sugar had dissolved suggest?
It suggests Rekha felt uneasy and trapped, keeping a polite smile while she worried about expectations she could not easily meet.
What could Ira and Rekha do next?
They could talk as a family about what they will and won't provide, and then tell the groom's side calmly and early, perhaps with a trusted elder present, that they want a simple wedding.
How does Ira see the groom's father's words differently from her mother?
Rekha accepts them as how things are done, but Ira hears the list hidden in "nothing" and sees it as dowry dressed as custom.

Baljeet, you've been sulking since that interview. Sit. Let me tell you about my first rejection, twenty-two years ago. I was twenty-one, top of my class, and I failed the technical round of the first company that came to our campus. The interviewer asked what a hash collision was. I gave a textbook line and then went blank. On the bus back, my friend Sudha said, "Rukmini, crying won't help. Write it down." So that night I wrote every question I'd missed. Hashing, one sorting question, one about recursion. I spent two weeks on just those, from the basics. The next company asked me to design a small phone directory. I used hashing, explained collisions, and got the offer. That notebook of missed questions taught me more than any class. Your rejection has questions in it too, Baljeet.

What did the interviewer ask Rukmini?
What a hash collision was.
How did Rukmini feel after failing the technical round?
Rukmini was upset and close to tears on the bus, after going blank despite being top of the class.
What turning point in the story made the difference?
The choice that night to write down every missed question and spend two weeks learning those concepts from the basics.
How did Sudha respond on the bus?
Sudha saw Rukmini's distress and gave a practical push, saying to write it down rather than cry over it.

A farmer has 7 hens and 3 goats. How many legs are there in total?
There are 26 legs. Because 7 hens have 2 legs each, which is 14, and 3 goats have 4 legs each, which is 12, and 14 + 12 = 26.

My name's Gargi, and for three years I didn't look at my insurance once. I bought it at twenty-two, in my first job, when the only person relying on me was me. The nominee was my mother. The cover was whatever the office agent suggested.
Then, within eight months, I switched to a new company and got married. It was my sister Seema who asked, at the wedding lunch, 'Who's your nominee now?' I laughed. Then I didn't.
That Sunday I took out every paper. The old employer's group health plan had ended with the job. The term cover was sized for a single fresher with no loan. Now there was Dev, and a flat loan in both our names.
I updated the nominee, joined the new company's health plan with Dev, and booked time with an adviser to recheck the term cover. 'Insurance check' sits in my calendar every January now.

Which extra step could Gargi add to the January check, and why?
Gargi could keep a one-page list of policies, nominees and renewal dates to go through with Dev, so both know what exists if something happens.

Dev is now on the health plan and shares the flat loan, so the review protects Dev too, not only Gargi's mother.

A citrus grove has laid out their plans for their sixteen orchards for the growing season. Lemons, their most popular citrus fruit, will take up eight orchards. Oranges are their second most popular fruit and will occupy half as many orchards as the lemons. Limes and grapefruits will split the remaining orchards. How many citrus orchards will be growing grapefruits?

Oranges will occupy 8 / 2 = 4 orchards.
There will be 16 - 8 - 4 = 4 orchards remaining for limes and grapefruits.
Thus, 4 / 2 = 2 orchards will be growing grapefruits.
The answer is 2.

Anand spoke haltingly, eyes on the table, as if expecting to be hurried. His slightly widened eyes, softening in between, and nods showed interest, so Anand looked up and shared more details.

At the Dussehra fair, six-year-old Chhaya let go of her father's finger to look at a balloon, and when she turned, he was gone. Tall people pushed past her, and the noise swallowed her small voice. She sat on the ground and began to cry. A puppet-seller named Hari saw her and knelt down. He put a little wooden monkey on his hand and made it dance. Chhaya hiccupped and smiled. "Let's find Papa," Hari said, and they walked together to the loudspeaker stand. Her father was already there, pale and shaking. He lifted her up. Hari gave her the monkey, and she kept it for years.

On his lunch break he opened a flight site and looked at one-way tickets to Lisbon. He drafted a resignation email and saved it. Walking back from the convenience store, he thought about Selin, how they'd been together four years and still talked mostly about groceries, and he pictured telling her tonight that it was over. messages.content: Cameron guides tour groups in a museum. He usually answers two questions per tourist. Today, he did four tours. The early morning first group was only 6 people. The following group was a busy group of 11. The third group had 8 people, but one was inquisitive and asked three times as many questions as usual. The last group of the day was a late group of 7. How many questions did Cameron answer?

Cameron answered 2 * 6 = 12 questions for the first group.
He answered 2 * 11 = 22 questions for the second group.
The third group had 8 - 1 = 7 tourists that asked 2 questions each.
The third group also had 1 tourist that asked 2 * 3 = 6 questions.
Thus, the third group asked 7 * 2 + 6 = 14 + 6 = 20 questions.
The last group asked 7 * 2 = 14 questions.
For all four tours, Cameron answered 12 + 22 + 20 + 14 = 68 questions.
The answer is 68.

Ms. Cole teaches math in three levels of classes in her school. There are four times as many students in Ms. Cole's fourth-level math class as in her sixth-level math class. The number of students in her seventh-level math class is twice that in the fourth-level math class.  If Ms. Cole's sixth-level class has 40 students, how many math students does Ms. Cole teach?

Since Ms. Cole's sixth-level math class has 40 students and four times as many students in her fourth-level class, there are 4*40 = 160 in her fourth-level math class.
For the two levels, Ms. Cole teaches math to 160+40 = 200 students.
If the number of students in her seventh-level math class is twice that in the fourth-level math class, then she teaches 2*160 = 320 students in the seventh-level math class.
Ms. Cole teaches 320+200 = 520 math students in the school.
The answer is 520.

Read this:

Dear Noor,
It's been a year since I answered your messages properly. I'm sorry. I want to explain, even though it's hard.
After the wedding, things changed slowly. First I stopped coming to our Sunday lunches because he didn't like them. Then I started asking him before I met anyone. Then before I bought anything. Now I think about how he'll react before I choose what to cook, what to wear, what to say.
He has never hit me, Noor. So for a long time I told myself this wasn't abuse. Just marriage. Just how he is.
But last week I realised I was whispering on the phone with my own mother. In my own home. I walk on eggshells all day.
I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just needed one person outside to know. Could we speak on Thursday at noon, when he's at work? I found a helpline number too. I haven't called yet.
Vandana

When does Vandana ask to speak with Noor?
On Thursday at noon, when he's at work.
What is Vandana feeling as she writes the letter?
Vandana feels ashamed and afraid, living on eggshells and unsure whether to call it abuse without any bruises.
What small steps is Vandana taking?
Vandana is reaching out to Noor, someone outside, and she has found a helpline number to call.
How might Noor feel reading the letter?
Noor would likely feel worried and relieved to hear from Vandana, and ready to listen without judging.

metadata.subtype: A world that keeps getting smaller [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Papa,
I'm writing because when we talk on the phone, we end up arguing. I know you want the best for me. You drove me to every exam, and I'll never forget that.
But I'm twenty now, and I need to make some decisions myself. I want to choose my own internship, even if it pays less. I'd love your advice, just not your final decision.
Also, can we stop the daily 10 pm calls? I'll call every Sunday, and more if something's up. I promise.
Jeevan says his parents took a while too, and now they're closer than ever. I'd like that for us.
I love you. Please don't read this as me pushing you away.
Siddharth

How often does Siddharth want to call instead of every day?
He wants to call every Sunday, and more if something's up.
What does Siddharth's last line reveal about his feelings?
It reveals he's worried his father might feel rejected, and he wants to set boundaries while keeping the love between them.
What made Siddharth's letter a respectful way to set boundaries?
He thanked his father, asked for advice rather than decisions, and offered a clear alternative to the daily calls.
How might Papa feel reading this letter?
He might feel sad or hurt at first, but also proud of his son's maturity and reassured by the promise of Sunday calls.

Read this:

Anirban, sit, I have to tell someone. Last night, right, I was at Kritika's till nine, studying. Totally true. Then her cousin said there's a birthday party on the terrace of the next building, and we went up. Music, fairy lights, some college guys, everything.
This morning at breakfast, Mom goes, "How was Kritika's?" and I said, "Good, we finished the chemistry chapter." Also true! I didn't say one fake thing. I was like, Yamini, you're a genius.
But then she said, "I'm glad you have such a sensible friend," and gave me extra parathas. And I felt… sick. Like, properly sick.
Because if she knew about the terrace, she'd have wanted to know who was there, how I got home. She had a right to ask. I just made sure she couldn't.
So is it lying if every sentence is true? It feels like lying. What would you do?

What did Yamini say at breakfast when asked about Kritika's?
Yamini said, "Good, we finished the chemistry chapter."
Why did Yamini feel sick after her mother gave her extra parathas?
Yamini felt guilty, because Mom's trust and kindness were based on a picture that left out the terrace party.
What would you advise Yamini to do now?
Yamini could tell Mom about the party calmly, and next time share the whole plan so Mom can ask the questions she has a right to ask.
What would change if Yamini's mother learned about the party from someone else?
Mom would likely feel misled and trust Yamini less, even though no sentence was false.

I'm Santosh, and I was at the Holi party on the college ground last March. For the first hour it was perfect: music, colour, everyone dancing. Then someone brought a crate of eggs and a bucket of muddy water, and the mood tipped. People started targeting the first-years who hadn't wanted to play, dragging them in, laughing. My friend Alka had just smeared a boy's face with mud and was reaching for more. I could see that nobody there would do that on an ordinary Tuesday. It was the crowd, the noise, the colour on every face. I took Alka by the arm. 'Look at him.' The first-year was crying. She stopped and dropped the mud. We took him to the tap and then to the hostel warden, who shut the gate on the egg crate. I still don't know what Alka was thinking in that moment.

What did someone bring that changed the mood?
A crate of eggs and a bucket of muddy water.
What did Santosh feel as the mood tipped?
Santosh felt uneasy and alarmed, seeing people act in ways they never would on an ordinary day.
What did Santosh do that helped?
Santosh noticed early, made Alka look at the first-year, helped him and told the warden, who stopped the eggs.
How might Alka have felt when she saw the crying first-year?
Alka probably felt a jolt of shame, stopping and dropping the mud when she saw him clearly.

metadata.subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]

messages.content: There is a short story contest coming up, but I never finish what I write.
Many writers struggle with finishing. Smaller goals can help. What's the story about?
A girl who finds a map in her school library.
Decide how it ends before you write the middle. Knowing where you are going makes it easier to continue.
How long should it be?
Check the contest rules for a word limit. If there is none, a few pages is plenty. A short, complete story is better than a long, unfinished one.
I get stuck in the middle.
Ask what the girl wants and what is stopping her. A small problem or surprise in the middle keeps the story moving. If you are stuck, jump ahead to the ending, then connect it.
Should I get someone to read it?
Yes. A friend or teacher can tell you where the story is clear or confusing. Fresh eyes catch mistakes you cannot see anymore.

So, Shankar, you'll laugh. Tuesday night, eleven o'clock, my phone lights up. My manager, Mrs. Rego: "WHO SENT THE FINAL DECK TO THE CLIENT????" All caps. Four question marks. I sent it. I sat on my bed with my heart hammering, drafting apologies. Had I sent the wrong version? Missed a slide? I nearly typed, "I'm so sorry, it was me, I'll fix it." Then I thought: all caps could mean screaming-angry or screaming-happy. I don't actually know which. So I called her instead. She picked up laughing. "Kiran! Was it you? They LOVED it. They want to sign on Friday!" Twenty minutes of panic over four question marks. Now I call before drafting any apology, and I've told Mrs. Rego that her caps nearly gave me a heart attack.

When did Mrs. Rego's message arrive?
At eleven o'clock on Tuesday night.
What was Kiran feeling while drafting apologies?
Kiran felt panicked and anxious, heart hammering, assuming the all-caps message meant anger over a mistake.
What stopped the panic from going further?
Kiran realised all caps could mean anger or excitement and called Mrs. Rego instead of sending an apology based on a guess.
How was Mrs. Rego feeling when she sent the message?
She was thrilled and excited because the client loved the deck; the caps and question marks carried her excitement.

messages.content:
Read this:

"Noor, beti, Joseph uncle's family is coming at seven. Sit properly. No feet on the sofa."
"Can I show them my drawings?"
"Only if they ask. And don't interrupt the grown-ups."
"Is the chicken 65 for us?"
"Guests eat first. Then us."
At dinner, Noor sat very straight. She watched Joseph uncle take a third helping of chicken 65. Then his son took the last pieces. Noor's stomach growled. She said nothing, the way Mummy wanted.
After they left, Noor flopped on the sofa, feet up. "I didn't get even one piece!"
"I saw," Mummy said, sitting beside her. "You were so good tonight."
"Why do we act different when people come?"
Mummy thought. "Home has two faces, na. One for guests, one for us." She opened the fridge. "And this face kept some chicken aside for you."
Noor squealed.

What time was Joseph uncle's family coming?
At seven.
How did Noor feel watching Joseph uncle's son take the last pieces?
She felt resentful and hungry, her stomach growling, but kept quiet as Mummy wanted.
What did Mummy do after the guests left that helped?
She praised Noor's effort, explained that home has a face for guests and one for the family, and showed she had saved chicken for her.
How might Joseph uncle's family have seen the evening?
They probably felt warmly welcomed and well fed, with no idea that Noor had missed her favourite dish.
Riya had ₹50. She spent ₹12 on a kite and ₹18 on string. How much is left? Write ONE calculation with brackets.

Answer: ₹20. 50 - (12 + 18) = 50 - 30 = 20.

She spent 12 + 18 = 30 altogether, and we take the whole 30 away, so the adding must happen FIRST: put it in brackets. 50 - (12 + 18) = 50 - 30 = 20. Without brackets, 50 - 12 + 18 means take 12 away and then ADD 18, which gives 56 - more than she started with! Another correct way: 50 - 12 - 18 = 38 - 18 = 20.

Change 157_8 to base ten, and 100 to base eight. Then change 101110_2 to base eight using groups of three.

Now you try: 77_8 in base ten.
The answer is 63.

"Dilnaz, look at me when I'm speaking," Ms. Madhuri said.
Dilnaz kept her eyes on the teacher's sandals. "Sorry, Miss."
"I'm not angry. I just want to know you're listening."
"I am listening. My Dadi says it's rude to stare at elders. You keep your eyes down to show respect."
Ms. Madhuri crouched so they were the same height. "Ah. So at home, eyes down means respect."
"Yes."
"In this classroom, eyes up means 'I'm with you'. Both are respectful. They just speak different languages."
Dilnaz peeked up, then down again. "Can I look at your nose? That's in between."
Ms. Madhuri laughed. "The nose is perfect. And at home, keep doing what Dadi taught you."

Who told Dilnaz that staring at elders is rude?
Her Dadi told her that.
What was Dilnaz feeling when asked to look up?
Dilnaz felt confused and a little anxious, caught between Dadi's rule and the teacher's request.
What did Ms. Madhuri do well?
She stayed calm, asked why, and translated between the two meanings instead of calling Dilnaz rude.
How might Ms. Madhuri have first read Dilnaz's lowered eyes?
At first the teacher may have wondered whether Dilnaz was listening, before learning that at home it signals respect.

'You skipped lab again,' Eshaan said, sliding a cutting chai across the canteen table.
'Went home. Mummy needed help at the shop.' Charu didn't look up. 'It's fine.'
'That's the third Friday.'
'I said it's fine.'
Eshaan waited. The fan ticked overhead.
'The research internship form closes on Monday,' Charu said finally. 'Papa thinks I should come home after graduation and help run things. And I want to go to Pune for this. And I'm so tired of being the good one in both places.'
'That sounds exhausting.'
'Aren't you going to tell me what to do? Everyone else does.'
'Nope. I'll just ask: what do you want, if nobody's watching?'
Charu stirred the chai for a long time. 'I don't know yet. Can I think out loud at you for a bit?'
'Take all evening.'

When does the research internship form close?
The form closes on Monday.
What does Charu repeating 'It's fine' suggest?
It suggests Charu is worn out and dodging the topic, holding in stress about the pull from home and the internship.
What choice did Eshaan make when Charu asked to be told what to do?
Eshaan chose not to push either side and asked what Charu wants if nobody's watching, which gave Charu room to think out loud.
What is it like for Charu to be 'the good one' in both places?
It seems draining for Charu to keep meeting home's hopes while chasing the internship, with nowhere to simply be honest.

messages.content: Street dogs have stories too. Tell me one about a Mumbai dog and his favourite tea stall.

A scruffy brown dog called Bhura lived on a lane in Dadar, and his favourite place in the whole city was Anwar's tea stall. Every morning, Anwar tossed him half a bun, and every morning Bhura wagged his tail and lay beneath the counter while customers came and went.

One rainy night, thieves crept toward the stall to steal the gas cylinder. Bhura woke, growled and then barked so loudly that lights flickered on in the windows above. The thieves ran.

Anwar, who slept on a cot behind the stall, came out in his lungi and saw the empty street and the damp, proud dog.

The next morning Bhura got a whole bun and a saucer of milk tea, and he ate both slowly.
Describe a grandmother's hands in 35 words: wrinkled, warm, smelling of coconut oil, quick at stitching. Also gentle when patting a head.
A grandmother's hands are wrinkled and warm. They smell of coconut oil. They are quick at stitching, and the needle moves faster than your eyes can follow. They are gentle when patting a head, too.
A child borrows a rope of cloud to swing across the sky; narrate it.

Maya lay on her back in a field, watching the clouds. One came very low and trailed a long, soft rope of mist.

"Grab on," said the cloud. "I'll give you a swing."

Maya took hold. The rope lifted her gently, and she swung over the treetops, over the village, and over the stream. She laughed and kicked her legs.

"Higher!" she called.

The cloud obliged. She swung up so high that she could touch a flock of geese. They honked a greeting.

When the sun began to fall, the cloud lowered her back to the field. "Come back tomorrow," it said.

Maya did, and for the whole summer, they swung together, until the monsoon changed the cloud's shape.

Monday, monsoon week. Harish came home from his first maths test soaked and cheerful. "It was easy."
Wednesday. The results came back: nine out of ten. One sum wrong, a subtraction slip. Harish threw his bag on the sofa. "I'm the worst at maths. The test is a total disaster." His younger brother Chinmay peeked. "But nine ticks." "One wrong means I'm bad." He refused dinner.
Saturday. Amma sat with Harish and the test. "Two piles: what you knew, and what you slipped on." One pile was big, one tiny. Harish stared. "It's just one." Later, in his notebook, he wrote: "9 right. 1 slip. Check subtraction twice." The next week he got eight in science, said, "Two things to check," and went out to the puddles.

What was the one mistake in Harish's maths test?
One sum was wrong, a subtraction slip.
Why did Harish refuse dinner on Wednesday?
He felt ashamed and upset, sure that one wrong sum meant he was bad at maths.
How did Amma help Harish see the test differently?
She had him sort the test into two piles, what he knew and what he slipped on, so he could see the big pile himself.
How might Chinmay have felt watching his brother on Wednesday?
Chinmay was probably puzzled and a bit worried, since nine ticks looked good to him.

Summarize Jaya's study plan in two sentences.

In Jaya's village near Sirsi, the only good signal was on the roof, and the only quiet place was her grandmother's room. With board exams two months away, Jaya made a plan. Every evening from six to eight, she gave her phone to Ajji, who put it in the steel cupboard. On the small wooden desk she kept only that day's book and a pencil. Her cousin Yusuf laughed. "You'll go mad." For the first three days, she did. Her hand kept reaching for nothing. By the second week, she was finishing a full chapter each evening. She stopped scolding herself before bed, because there was nothing to scold.

With exams coming, Jaya gives her phone to her grandmother every evening and keeps only one book on her desk. It is hard at first, but within two weeks she finishes a chapter each night and stops scolding herself.

Tejas, before you fly to Germany, sit with your Uma athai for a minute. When I was nineteen, I went to a hostel in Lucknow, far from Madurai. Nobody there drew kolam at dawn. Nobody said 'saapdu', eat, the way Amma did, three times, even when you'd already eaten. For the first month I felt like a kite with a cut string. Then one morning I took chalk and drew a small kolam outside my hostel room door. The warden frowned but let it stay. By the end of the year, three other girls on my floor were drawing their own designs beside mine: a star, a lotus, a Bengali alpana. So when you feel lost there, don't wait for home to come to you. Draw your little kolam.

What did young Uma draw outside her hostel room door?
A small kolam, in chalk.
What did young Uma mean by feeling 'like a kite with a cut string'?
She felt homesick and unanchored, missing the daily rituals of home.
Which choice in the story helped young Uma, and how did it spread?
Drawing a kolam at her door each morning; it anchored her, and by the end of the year three other girls were drawing their own designs beside hers.
How might the three girls on the floor have felt joining in?
They likely felt homesick too, and adding a star, a lotus or an alpana let them bring a piece of their own homes into the hostel.

Saurabh had spent a year after school working on his uncle's farm near Nagpur before choosing agricultural science. He'd asked farmers what they needed, read about soil, and decided. His friend Chandrika had gone into chartered accountancy because her parents insisted. Now, in their third year, both hit a wall. Saurabh failed his soil chemistry practical. Chandrika failed her intermediate exam. They met at a tea stall near the university. Chandrika was in tears. "I don't even know why I'm doing this. It's their dream." Saurabh was upset too; he'd studied hard for that practical. But he said, "I know why I'm doing mine. Uncle's cotton crop failed because the soil was wrong. I want to fix that." He paid for the tea and went straight back to the lab to ask what he'd done wrong. Chandrika watched him go, and stared at her cup for a long time.

What did Saurabh fail in the third year?
He failed his soil chemistry practical.
How did Saurabh feel after failing, and what kept him going?
Saurabh was upset because he'd studied hard, but his own reason, fixing soil for farmers like his uncle, gave him the will to go straight back to the lab.
What could Chandrika do to find her footing after this setback?
She could reflect honestly on whether she wants CA for her own reasons, and talk openly with her parents about what she wants.
How might Chandrika feel watching Saurabh go back to the lab?
Chandrika probably felt lost and a little envious, lacking a reason of her own to carry her through.

In the colony park, Sunaina stood on the bench and shouted, "I am the doctor!" She gave Kavitha a leaf as medicine.
After a while, Kavitha yawned. "Let's play catch now."
"No. I said I'm the doctor." Sunaina pressed the leaf-stethoscope to Kavitha's arm again.
The other children ran off to play catch. Sunaina stood alone, still holding her leaf. Her face was cross. She kicked the grass.
"You can stop being doctor," Kavitha called.
"I can't," Sunaina said. "I already said."

What did Sunaina give Kavitha as medicine?
She gave Kavitha a leaf as medicine.
Why did Sunaina keep playing doctor even when alone?
She felt cross and stuck, because going back on "I am the doctor" felt wrong once she had said it.
How could a grown-up help Sunaina change the game?
They could suggest the doctor goes to play catch as part of the story, so Sunaina can change without breaking her word.
How might Kavitha feel when Sunaina won't play catch?
Kavitha may feel bored and a little puzzled, since she wanted to play together.

Mr. Reyansh has a dairy farm with 40 cows. Each cow on the farm drinks 80 liters of water daily. He also has a sheep ranch with 10 times the number of cows, with each sheep drinking 1/4 times as much water as a cow does. How many liters of water does Mr. Reyansh use to water all of his animals in a week?

If a cow drinks 80 liters of water in a day, it drinks 80*7= 560 liters of water per week.
Mr. Reyansh has 40 cows drinking 560 liters of water a week, totaling 560*40 = 22400 liters.
In the ranch, a sheep drinks 1/4*80 = 20 liters of water in a day.
The total amount of liters a sheep drinks in a week is 20*7 = 140 liters
Mr. Reyansh has ten times as many sheep as cows, that is 10*40 = 400 sheep.
If each sheep drinks 140 liters of water in a week, 400 sheep drinks 400*140 = 56000 liters of water.
Together, the cows and sheep drink 56000+22400 = 78400 liters of water per week.
The answer is 78400.
My dosa batter turned out too thick and it won't spread on the pan.
Thick batter is easy to fix. Stir in a little water, a spoonful at a time, until it flows like thin pancake batter.
Won't the dosa break then?
A thinner batter makes thin, crisp dosas, but a very runny one may tear. Aim for a smooth, pourable texture, and test with one dosa first.
The first one worked! It's a bit pale though.
Let the pan get a bit hotter before the next one, and wait until the edges lift. Golden colour comes from a hotter pan and a little patience.

Hi Seema,
You asked about the client pitch. Well, we won it. The partner took the whole team to dinner and made a speech about my deck, which was very embarrassing.
Honestly, it was mostly luck. The client had already half-decided, and Karan did all the numbers. I just made the slides look nice. Anyone would have got the same result. When the partner said I have "a real gift for storytelling", I smiled and thought, he'll figure out soon that he's wrong about that.
Then on Monday I sent a report with a typo in the client's name. One letter. I've felt sick about it for three days. That's the real me, I think. The dinner was a fluke; the typo is the truth.
Tell me about your new flat? I need distracting.
Love,
Elizabeth

What mistake did Elizabeth make on Monday?
A typo in the client's name, one letter.
What does Elizabeth mean by 'the typo is the truth'?
Elizabeth feels anxious and ashamed, treating one small error as proof of being a fraud while dismissing the win as a fluke.
What could Elizabeth try to see the win more fairly?
List what was actually done for the pitch, the deck and the storytelling the partner praised, and set it beside a one-letter typo.
How might Seema feel reading this email?
Seema may feel worried and a little frustrated, seeing Elizabeth brush off a real success and dwell on a tiny mistake.

The demo for the hospital client was at ten, and at eight the office internet went down. Chinmay, who had built the appointment app's first version, could have taken over and patched it himself; he knew the code best. Instead he turned to Vandana, the junior he had been coaching for six months. 'You rewrote the booking module. You know it better than me now. What do we need?' She blinked, then rattled off a plan: run it locally, use her phone hotspot, skip the payments screen. It worked. In the meeting, when the client praised the booking flow, Chinmay said, 'That's Vandana's design. She'll walk you through it.' Afterwards his manager said, 'You could have presented it yourself.' Chinmay shrugged. 'She's going to be better than me. I'd like to have helped with that.'

What went down at eight?
The office internet.
What does Chinmay's shrug suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Chinmay felt calm and content, proud of Vandana rather than anxious about being outgrown.
Why was asking Vandana for the plan a good choice under pressure?
She knew the booking module best, so letting her lead solved the problem and gave her the chance to show her skill.
How might Vandana feel when Chinmay credits her in front of the client?
Vandana would likely feel proud and trusted, seen for her own work instead of hidden behind her mentor.

Thursday night.
They did it again at recess. Called Kamal “Kamala” and did the high voice. Someone flicked his ear. Kamal just sat there doing his maths.
After, I said, “Bro, you need to stop reacting. Just laugh along. You're too sensitive.” He looked at me like I'd slapped him.
Writing this now I feel sick. He didn't react. He sat there. I said it because I didn't want to be the one who tells them to stop. It's easier if Kamal is the problem.
So at 5 I went back to school and told Mr Pillai, our class teacher. He listened properly, asked for names, and called Kamal's mother while I was still there. He said he'll speak to the boys first thing tomorrow and that I did the right thing telling him.
Tomorrow I'm sitting with Kamal at recess. Not saying anything clever. Just sitting.
— Vaibhav

What did the boys call Kamal at recess?
They called him “Kamala” and did the high voice, and someone flicked his ear.
Why did Vaibhav tell Kamal he was too sensitive?
Vaibhav felt scared of standing up to the boys, so blaming Kamal was more comfortable; later, writing about it, Vaibhav felt sick and guilty.
What did Vaibhav do next that actually helped?
Vaibhav went back and told the class teacher, who called Kamal's mother that day and planned to deal with the boys, and Vaibhav plans to sit with Kamal.
How might Kamal have felt when his friend said he was too sensitive?
Kamal probably felt betrayed and even more alone, since the one person who might help put the blame on him.

metadata.subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

In Class 10, when our team's science project collapsed the night before the exhibition, everyone panicked. Ritesh shouted at the printer, Lopa cried in the corridor, and I kept refreshing the group chat. Urmila just sat on the floor with the broken model and started sorting pieces.
I was annoyed. "Do you even care?" I snapped at her.
She looked up and said evenly, "I care a lot. That's why I'm not wasting time panicking." Then she listed what we could still save: the poster, the working motor and a simpler demo.
We didn't win, but we presented something. I remember thinking her calm was coldness. It wasn't. She'd seen the problem more clearly than any of us. I'm Divyansh, and I still think of her when I start flapping.

What three things did Urmila say they could still save?
The poster, the working motor and a simpler demo.
What was Divyansh feeling when snapping "Do you even care?"
Divyansh felt annoyed and panicked, mistaking Urmila's calm for not caring.
How can someone tell calm from not caring?
Calm still sees the problem fully and acts on it, as Urmila did by listing what could be saved; indifference would do nothing.
How might Urmila have felt being accused of not caring?
Urmila was probably a little hurt, but stayed steady and explained she cared a lot.
The dog started to barking when the stranger came. Fix this.

The dog started barking when the stranger came.
Why: extra word ("to barking" -> "barking").
'Light chali gayi' ko English mein kaise bolte hain? I said 'light went' and my cousin laughed.
Say: "The power has gone off" or "There's a power cut." In American English, people often say "The power is out." "The light went" sounds like one bulb stopped working.

Read this:

I live across the corridor from Darshan and Pooja. For a year, their flat went silent for days at a time. I'd see Pooja on the stairs, eyes red, and her husband Darshan coming home late and saying nothing.
Then something changed. Last month I heard them argue, and then I heard Darshan say, clearly, "I need a break. I'll be back at eight." At eight, their door opened and closed. I heard them talking, low voices, for a long time.
Later Pooja told me they'd been seeing a counsellor. They had a list on their fridge now: "Pause with a time. Never leave the other guessing."
I don't know everything that goes on in their home. But it's been a long time since I saw Pooja crying on the stairs.

What time did Darshan say he would be back?
At eight.
What was Pooja likely feeling during the year of silent days?
She seemed hurt and lonely, often red-eyed on the stairs.
What helped the couple change?
They saw a counsellor and made rules: pause only with a return time and never leave the other guessing.
What might Darshan experience now when he asks for a break?
He can take the space he needs without guilt, because naming a return time means Pooja is not left guessing.

Read this:

'I can't wear this lehenga on stage. My arms look huge,' Vandana said, tugging at the sleeves in the changing room.
'You look fine, Vandu. Honestly.'
'You're just saying that.'
Sarita sat down on the bench. 'Okay, can I tell you something? I hate my teeth. I've practised smiling with my mouth closed for two years.'
Vandana stared. 'Your teeth? But you smile all the time.'
'Closed-mouth, though. Did you ever notice?'
'...No. Never.'
'Exactly. Nobody's staring at the thing we're staring at.'
Vandana laughed, a little shakily. 'So we're both walking around hiding something.'
'Yeah. But that's not why I like dancing with you. You never miss a beat, and you always count me in when I freeze.'
Vandana let go of the sleeves. 'And you're the one who makes me laugh backstage. Teeth or no teeth.'
From the door, the dance teacher called, 'Sarita, Vandana, girls of group three, you're on!'

What has Sarita practised for two years?
Smiling with the mouth closed, hiding the teeth.

Trisha, sixteen, spent all evening worrying about the stray dog that slept under the stall. She made Nilesh promise to carry a stick, bought biscuits to keep the dog friendly, and even asked the tea-stall owner to shoo it away at seven.

The next morning she stood with Nilesh at the corner. Trucks roared past. Nilesh stepped out without looking, and Trisha yanked his collar back.

The dog was asleep, as usual. Trisha's heart pounded. That evening she stopped buying biscuits and practised with Nilesh: stop, look both ways, hold her hand till the bus comes.

The heater in the school hall had broken, and band practice started in coats. Baljeet rubbed his hands together hard, blowing into them between songs. When the drum part began, he snapped his fingers in rhythm, tapping one foot.

Nikita raised an eyebrow. "I'm not a waiter."

Baljeet's ears went hot. "Sorry, sorry. Could you pass the sheet, please?" She passed it.

At the break, the cook brought in a tray of hot samosas, and Baljeet rubbed his hands again, grinning this time. Nikita laughed. "Is that cold hands or samosa hands?"

In a cold school hall, Baljeet rudely snaps his fingers at Nikita for a music sheet, apologises and asks politely, and later they share a laugh over hot samosas.

Martin is casting three bells for the church's belfry. The first bell takes 50 pounds of bronze, the second bell is twice the size of the first bell, and the third bell is four times the size of the second bell. How much bronze does he need total?

First find the size of the second bell: 50 pounds * 2 = 100 pounds
Then find the size of the third bell: 100 pounds * 4 = 400 pounds
Then add the amount of bronze used for each bell to find the total: 100 pounds + 400 pounds + 50 pounds = 550 pounds
The answer is 550.

messages.content: Mrs. Finley's class has 24 students, and Mr. Johnson's class has 10 more than half the number in Mrs. Finley's class. How many students are in Mr. Johnson's class?

Half the number in Mrs. Finley's class is 24/2=12.
Mr. Johnson has 12+10=22 students.

Is it "allude to" or "elude to" a story?

It is "allude to", meaning to mention something indirectly. "Elude" means to escape from or avoid someone or something.

Then my aunt asked me, "Would you talk to a friend like that?" No way. So I tried something. I wrote down what went wrong: I rushed the parking, I panicked at the roundabout. And then what I'd practise: slow parking, three roundabouts every Sunday.
It felt weird, like being my own coach instead of my own critic.
I passed the third time. I still made a mistake, but I didn't spiral.
You'll get your exam next time too. Be kind to yourself.

It began with the study group. Four of us, two boys and two girls, met at the library. Papa said, "People will talk. A girl from our family with boys?" My brother Jatin went to cricket camp with anyone he liked, and nobody said a word.

When a hard puzzle came in the newspaper, Papa gave it to Noor. When a guest asked a question, they looked at her. After a while, I stopped trying the hard sums at all. Why bother? I was the slow one. I'd just wait for Noor. And Noor, being called clever, tried everything, even things she didn't know yet. Charu, our captain, noticed. She stood next to me and started rolling her shoulders back slowly. "Copy me," she said.

"Now you're ready," she said.
I didn't score the winning point that day, but I didn't freeze either. Now I roll my shoulders before every exam, every match, even before I talk to teachers.

1/3 of the townspeople have received the full COVID vaccine. 1/3 are immune because they already recovered from COVID. If 1/6 of the townspeople are both vaccinated and already had COVID, what percent of the town is immune in some way?

First add the fractions of vaccinated and recovered townspeople: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3
Then you need to subtract the fraction that are both vaccinated and recovered, since they were double-counted. To do this, start by converting 2/3 to the same denominator as 1/6: 2/3 * 2/2 = 4/6
Then subtract 1/6 from 4/6: 4/6 - 1/6 = 3/6
Then divide the numerator by the denominator and multiply by 100% to express the answer as a percentage: 3/6 * 100% = 50%
The answer is 50.

By four o'clock he noticed a pattern. Pooja kept saying, "This one reminds me of Karthik," the best engineer they'd hired last year. Those candidates got high scores. A woman from a small college who'd answered every technical question well got "not quite our type". A man who spoke softly got "lacks presence".

Darshan felt uneasy. They weren't judging answers. They were judging resemblance.

During the tea break, he pulled out a sheet. "For the last six, can we try something? Same five questions for everyone. Each of us scores each answer from one to five, separately, before discussing."

Pooja frowned. "That's slow."

Then I called Francis, my cousin who was there too. I said, "Remember how perfect those summers were?"

Maybe the past wasn't perfect. Maybe I just miss feeling safe. Tomorrow I'll tell Mom I'm stressed instead of pretending I'm fine.

The lake.

Nico borrows 3 books from the library on Monday.  On Monday, he reads the first book with a total of 20 pages.  On Tuesday, he reads the second book with a total of 12 pages. On Wednesday, he read a total of 51 - 32 = 19 pages.
The answer is 19.

She mashed rice and fish curry.

He felt proud of himself, because he came back beaming.
What did Noor do that supported Jomon's independence?
She let him eat with his own fingers without wiping him straight away, and responded quickly when he said he needed the toilet.
What is it like for Noor when Jomon suddenly shouts "Toilet!" at mealtime?
It is a sudden rush for her, but she seems glad he could tell her in time.

Hi Gargi,
I owe you and the team an apology. The Sunday book drive for the village library was my idea, I booked the community hall, and I told everyone 9 a.m. I didn't check that the hall was already booked for a wedding till noon. You all waited outside in the sun for three hours, and half of you left.
That's on me, not the hall people and not the team.
What I've learned: confirm bookings in writing, and have a backup place. I've spoken to the principal, and we can use the school's front verandah next Sunday.
Could you help me call the people who left? You're better at that than me. I'll send everyone a proper plan with times and jobs by Wednesday, and I'll check it with you first.
Thanks for staying on Sunday. It meant a lot.
Karthik

Why did the team wait outside for three hours?
Karthik didn't check that the hall was already booked for a wedding till noon.
How does Karthik feel about what happened on Sunday?
Karthik feels guilty and responsible for the team waiting in the sun, and grateful that Gargi stayed.
What did Karthik do well as a leader after the mistake?
Karthik took the blame, named the lesson learned, arranged a backup venue and asked Gargi for help with what Gargi is good at.
How might the team members who left feel when Karthik's plan arrives?
They may feel less annoyed and more willing to return, since Karthik owned the mistake and gave clear times and jobs.

"Timer's on," Dhruv said, putting the phone face down on the study table. "Twenty minutes for maths."
His cousin Pallavi looked up from her drawing. "And then?"
"Then I stop. Even if I'm not done."
"Why would you stop if you're not done?"
"Because otherwise I do maths for two hours and never get to science. Miss told us to try it."
Pallavi went back to her drawing. The room was quiet except for Dhruv's pencil.
The alarm buzzed. Dhruv groaned. "Two sums left."
"So finish them!"
"No. Break." He stretched, went to the balcony for five minutes, came back and set the timer for science. "The two sums get their own slot after dinner."
Pallavi shook her head. "You're so strange."
"I'm finishing my homework on time for once," Dhruv grinned.

How long did Dhruv spend on the balcony?
He went to the balcony for five minutes.
How did Dhruv feel when the alarm buzzed with two sums left?
He felt a bit annoyed, which is why he groaned, but he stuck to his plan and took the break.
What else could Dhruv try for the two unfinished sums?
He could give them a short fixed slot after dinner, as he planned, so they don't grow into a whole evening.
How does Pallavi see Dhruv's timer plan?
Pallavi finds it strange to stop before finishing, but can see he is getting his homework done on time.

Hi Saurabh,
Thanks for the draft report on the flood-relief camps. Before it goes to the district office, I've added a small note beside each claim about how we know it, because I've been burned before by my own memory.
'Three camps have no clean water': I saw this myself on Tuesday at Camps 2 and 5. Camp 7 I only heard about from a volunteer, so I've marked it 'reported, not checked'.
'Children are missing school': the headteacher told us; I've added her name and the date.
'Food will run out by Friday': this is our inference from the stock sheets, so I've labelled it an estimate.
I know it slows us down. But if the district officer asks 'how do you know?', we'll have an answer for every line. Could you check the Camp 7 claim tomorrow?
Lakshmi

At which camps did Lakshmi personally see no clean water?
At Camps 2 and 5.
Why does Lakshmi take the trouble to label every claim?
Lakshmi feels cautious, having been burned before by memory, and wants every line to have a clear source.
How do Lakshmi's labels make the report stronger?
They separate what was seen, what was told and what was inferred, so the district officer can trust each claim and see which ones need checking.
How might Saurabh feel about being asked to check the Camp 7 claim?
Saurabh may feel the extra work is a nuisance at first, but worth it for a report that holds up.

The week the monsoon flooded half of Chennai, only four people could reach the logistics startup's office, and two of them were interns. On Monday the manager, Revathi ma'am, handed Rukmini the phone. 'Rukmini, call the truckers and reroute the orders. You're good at this. I'll check your plan at four.' At four she went through it line by line: 'This part is sharp. This part will fail. Fix it.' Kamal, the other intern, was asked to update the attendance sheet. He finished it in ten minutes. Then he sat by the window watching the water rise in the street. Nobody asked him anything else. By Thursday Rukmini was talking to warehouse managers like she'd done it for years. Kamal had stopped offering to help. On Friday evening, alone at his desk, he opened a job site and started updating his CV. 'They don't need me here,' he told himself.

What did Revathi ma'am ask Kamal to do?
She asked him to update the attendance sheet.
What was Kamal thinking by Friday evening?
He was thinking 'They don't need me here', feeling useless and unwanted after a week of being given nothing real to do.
At what point could Kamal have changed his week, and how?
After finishing the sheet in ten minutes, Kamal could have asked Revathi ma'am for a real task, such as helping Rukmini with the reroutes, instead of waiting by the window.
How might the week have felt for Rukmini?
Rukmini was probably stretched and a bit nervous, but also proud, since the honest feedback at four each day helped her grow fast.

I'm Deepika, and I share a library table with Trisha most afternoons. For weeks I watched her get pulled away: someone from the dance club would tap her shoulder and she'd be gone till evening, her notes still open. Then something changed after the midsems. Last Tuesday Kunal came over with "Movie at four?" and she barely looked up. She said, "Later. Six o'clock, I'll come." I'd noticed a line in her planner, underlined twice: "invite during study = later, six." Maybe she was annoyed, maybe relieved; I couldn't tell. She chewed her pen hard for a minute after Kunal left. But she stayed till six, closed her books and walked out smiling. The movie started at six-thirty anyway.

What line did Deepika see underlined in Trisha's planner?
"Invite during study = later, six," underlined twice.
What might Trisha have been feeling when Kunal invited her, and why can't Deepika be sure?
She may have felt torn between the fun offer and her work; the hard pen-chewing hints at effort, but Deepika only sees the outside and admits it could be annoyance or relief.
Which choice made Trisha's afternoon hold this time?
Writing down in advance what to say when an invitation came during study time, so the answer was ready and there was nothing to decide on the spot.
How might Kunal experience Trisha's answer?
Kunal hears a clear time instead of a vague no, so the invitation is moved rather than refused; with the movie at six-thirty, Kunal loses nothing.

Imran, it's Usha, remember when I told you about my first term in Norway? The funniest part was the beckoning. In my first week I called a course-mate over with the palm-down scoop we use back home, and she just laughed and said it looked like I was sweeping crumbs. Another time I crooked one finger upwards at a boy at the bus stop, thinking it was very casual, and he raised his eyebrows and stepped back. I felt my ears go hot. My housemate said in some places that finger is rude, or at least bossy. So I started asking, "Is it okay if I call you like this?", and I copied the way the locals waved. Guessing from home habits was the mistake.

Where was Usha's first term?
Usha's first term was in Norway.
How did Usha feel when the boy raised his eyebrows and stepped back?
Usha felt embarrassed, shown by the ears going hot, and realised the crooked finger had landed badly. The boy's reaction may also have been plain surprise, so it is a cue rather than proof.
What would you advise Usha to do in a new country when calling someone?
Ask politely, use a word or a wave that locals use, and avoid assuming home gestures will carry the same meaning.
What was it like for the course-mate when Usha used the scoop?
The course-mate found it funny, and said it looked like sweeping crumbs, so the meaning simply didn't carry over.

Class teacher's note, Class 3, Thursday
This morning Aadhya came to my desk before assembly holding a folded fifty-rupee note. She had found it in the school yard yesterday near the swings. She told me she wasn't sure what to do, so last night she asked her father whether she could keep it. He told her to bring it to school and hand it to me, since someone might report it missing. She did exactly that. I noted the date and place. At lunch a Class 2 girl came to the staffroom in tears; it was her money for the book fair. I returned it to her and told Aadhya. Aadhya smiled for the rest of the day.
- Sangeeta

Where did Aadhya find the note?
In the school yard near the swings.
How did Aadhya feel when she heard the note had found its owner?
She felt happy and proud, smiling for the rest of the day.
What else could Aadhya do next time she finds something in school?
She could hand it straight to the nearest teacher that same day, so the owner gets it back sooner.
How does the returned money look to the Class 2 girl?
The Class 2 girl, who was in tears, feels hugely relieved to get her book fair money back.

Career services note, month 4. Written by Vandana, career counsellor.
Ishita came in today for the fourth time this term. She brought a new version of her comparison table: UX design, data science, cloud engineering, product management, now with fifteen criteria and scores for each. The scores had changed since last month, though nothing in her life had.
I asked what she had tried. She looked at the table for a while, then said, "Nothing yet. I keep thinking one more article will settle it."
She seemed tired and a little embarrassed. I noticed she has missed two application deadlines for internships in all four areas while researching.
What I did next: I suggested she stop adding criteria and instead pick two paths to test for two weeks each, with one small task for each. She chose UX and data. We agreed she would bring the finished tasks, not a new table, to our next meeting in three weeks.

How many criteria did Ishita's new table have?
It had fifteen criteria.
How did Ishita seem to feel when asked what she had tried?
She seemed tired and a little embarrassed, admitting she had tried nothing and hoped another article would settle it.
What else could Ishita do if both tests go well?
She could do a slightly longer project in each or talk to people working in both, so the next choice rests on more real experience.
How does Ishita's situation look to the counsellor?
The counsellor sees a capable student stuck in comparison and missing deadlines, and steers her toward small real tests.

Tuesday, late. We fought at breakfast over the electricity bill. I said Swati never checks anything; Swati said I sigh at everything. Both a little true, which made it worse. I left with my jaw tight. At lunch I found a sticky note in my bag: a drawing of a very sad potato and the words "sorry for the sigh comment." I laughed so loudly at my desk that a colleague looked over. I texted back: sorry for the never-checks thing too. Bill is on the fridge, let's look together tonight 😊. Swati replied with a potato wearing a crown. The bill isn't sorted, but my shoulders came down. Tonight: bill, tea, no scorekeeping.

Neelam

What did the sticky note in Neelam's bag show?
A drawing of a very sad potato with the words "sorry for the sigh comment."
How did Neelam feel about the fight after finding the note, and what in the entry shows it?
Neelam felt lighter and warmer, shown by the loud laugh at the desk and the shoulders that came down. 🙂
Why does Neelam's reply help, even though the bill is still unsorted?
Neelam apologised for their own part and suggested looking at the bill together, so repair started before the problem was solved.
How might Swati have felt while drawing the potato?
Swati probably felt bad about the sigh remark and wanted to soften things, and the crowned potato reply suggests relief that the joke landed. 🤍
Lohri pe bonfire hota hai. Ek chhota description English mein chahiye school diary ke liye.
"Lohri is celebrated in January, mostly in Punjab. In the evening, families light a bonfire, sing songs and throw peanuts, popcorn and sweets into the fire. It marks the end of winter."
It is 7:35 now. Leela needs 10 minutes to walk to class, which begins at 8:00. Will she reach before it begins?
Yes, she will. Because 7:35 plus 10 minutes is 7:45, which is before 8:00.

The drilling started at nine, an hour before Parul's video interview for the design studio. "Doesn't matter," she told Ojas, who shared the flat. "They'll look at my portfolio and move on anyway." He offered to ask the site supervisor for a quiet hour, or to carry her laptop to the cafe downstairs. She shook her head and kept scrolling, her portfolio file unopened since last month.
When the call began, the drill shrieked through her mic. She kept saying "sorry, sorry", forgot the name of her best project, and ended the call early. Afterwards she lay on the sofa. "Told you. I'm not what studios want." Ojas glanced at the unopened file on her screen, said nothing, and put the kettle on.

What started an hour before Parul's video interview?
The drilling started at nine.
How can you tell Parul was anxious during the call?
She kept apologising, forgot the name of her best project and ended the call early, signs of panic rooted in expecting to fail.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
She refused Ojas's offers and never reopened her portfolio; moving somewhere quiet and preparing would give her a fair chance.
Why might Ojas stay silent afterwards?
He could see the unopened file, but pointing it out right then might hurt, so he chooses comfort first.

At the Friday gathering in the senior citizens' day centre, Rafiq was setting out chairs when Gurpreet Aunty began. "In our time, nobody locked their doors. Everyone helped everyone. Children respected elders." Two others nodded. Rafiq, who ran the centre's activities, remembered her story from last month: walking four kilometres for water, the year the canal flooded, how her brother had to leave school to work. He almost said so. Instead he sat down. "Who helped you most back then, Aunty?" Her face softened. She talked about a neighbour who shared her last sack of wheat. Rafiq listened, asking one more question, then another. The past she described was easier than the one she had told him before. But the kindness in it was real, and the whole table was smiling.

How far did Gurpreet Aunty once say she walked for water?
Four kilometres.
Why did Rafiq feel tempted to correct Gurpreet Aunty, and why did he hold back?
He felt uneasy because he remembered her harder stories, but he cared more about her warm memory and the mood at the table than about winning the point.
What makes Rafiq's question a good choice?
Asking who helped her most invites the real kindness in her memory without arguing about whether the old days were easier 🤍
How might Gurpreet Aunty feel when Rafiq asks about the people who helped her?
She likely feels respected and warm, since someone younger wants to hear her memory instead of doubting it.

“Before we start the app project,” Nazia said, “can we agree what fair looks like?”
Tanvir laughed. “Fair is everyone does their bit.”
“And what's a bit?” Nazia asked. “Last project, Rohan did twice what Priyam did and nobody said anything until the launch party.”
Priyam winced. “Fair point.”
“So,” Nazia went on, “we each take one feature. We post a one-line update every Friday. If someone's stuck, they say it on Friday, not the night before.”
“And if someone's slacking?”
“Then we talk to them that same Friday. Kindly.”
Tanvir shrugged. “Okay. Put it on the board.”
Nazia wrote it in big letters. Everyone signed their initials underneath.

When would the team post their updates?
They would post a one-line update every Friday.
How did Priyam seem to feel when Nazia mentioned the last project?
Priyam seemed embarrassed, wincing, but agreed it was a fair point.
What does the team's agreement do well?
It defines fair effort clearly, tracks it simply with Friday updates, and sets a kind way to raise slacking early.
How might Tanvir see the agreement at first?
Tanvir seemed to think it was unnecessary, but shrugged and accepted it once it was simple and clear.

Disha coordinated the college robotics lab in her final year, and two juniors joined in July. She liked the loud, confident one immediately and gave him the sensor project. Akash was quiet, so she asked him to label parts and keep the logbook. By October the confident junior was presenting at the tech fest. Akash was still labelling. Then one evening, Disha found Akash's logbook. In the margins he had drawn neat redesigns of the sensor mount, better than the one they were using. She sat down heavily. She hadn't asked him a single real question in three months. The next day she said, "Akash, I want you to build this mount. I'll check in every day." He nodded, and for the first time she saw him grin.

What did Akash draw in the logbook margins?
Neat redesigns of the sensor mount.
What did Disha feel when she sat down heavily?
She felt shocked and guilty, realising she had underestimated Akash and given him nothing to rise to.
What does Disha's decision show about how to mentor juniors?
Trusting someone with a real project and checking in daily gives them attention and a chance to grow.
How might Akash see the new project?
Akash seems pleased and encouraged, grinning for the first time as he is finally trusted.
