In their shared flat in Lajpat Nagar, Tenzin was the one who made every evening funny. He named the leaking tap "Gangaji", did cooking-show commentary while burning rotis, and could turn any bad news into a punchline. Binita, who had shared the flat with him for a year, started noticing a pattern. When she asked, "How was the visa interview?" he said, "They loved me. Too much. Couldn't let me leave." When she asked about his sister's wedding plans, he told a long joke about a horse. He never answered straight.
One night she came home late and found him on the balcony in the dark, no jokes, his phone face down on his knee. She sat down beside him. "You don't have to be funny with me," she said. "What's going on?"
Tenzin was quiet for a long time. Then: "The visa got rejected. Second time."

What did Tenzin name the leaking tap?
"Gangaji".
Why might Tenzin turn every serious question into a joke?
The jokes keep painful news like the rejected visa at a distance and keep others laughing instead of asking more.
What choice did Binita make on the balcony, and why did it help?
She sat beside him and said he didn't have to be funny with her, which gave him permission to share the rejection.
What might it be like for Tenzin to be 'the funny one' in the flat?
Probably tiring, since he keeps everyone entertained while carrying bad news alone.

You asked what I'd do if it happened in our group, Indu. It already did, last month, so I'll just tell you. I'm Vidya, and I was scared the whole time, just so you know.
Someone posted a photo of Mariam asleep on the bus with a cruel caption, and then everyone added stickers. I felt sick. I didn't add anything, and I didn't forward it, even when someone asked, “Did you see?”
That evening I messaged Mariam alone: “I saw. Are you okay?” She said she was fine. Ten minutes later: “Not really.”
I took screenshots of the whole thread, names and times showing, and showed Amma before bed. She messaged Mehta Ma'am right then. Next morning I told Mariam, “Let's go to Ma'am together. You don't have to talk, I'll start.” She came. Ma'am read everything, called Mariam's mother from the staffroom, and by lunch the posts were gone.
Mariam sits with me at lunch now.

What did Mariam reply ten minutes later?
Not really.
How was Vidya feeling while all this happened?
Vidya felt scared the whole time and sick at the stickers, but still acted.
What else could Vidya have done when someone asked "Did you see?"
Simply not respond, or say privately that it isn't funny, staying out of the pile-on while adults handled it.
What was it like for Mariam to get a message from Vidya alone?
It let Mariam admit to not being fine and gave her company going to the teacher, which made asking for help possible.

Elif had not spoken to Layla since Tuesday, and it was now Thursday night in their Toronto dorm room. She moved around Layla like furniture: headphones in, back turned, lamp clicked off at ten without the usual "night".
Layla lay awake replaying the week. Was it the seat she forgot to save at the lecture? The charger she returned late? The mug left in the sink? She wrote three apology texts, each longer than the last, and sent them all. "I'm so sorry for everything, whatever it was."
Read. No reply.
Her chest ached in a way that felt almost physical. She skipped the study group on Friday in case Elif wanted to talk. Elif didn't.
When Layla's sister called, she said she was fine. Then she hung up and realised she had apologised four times in a call about nothing.

What did Layla send after lying awake?
She sent three apology texts, each longer than the last.
What was Layla feeling as she replayed the week?
She felt dread and an almost physical ache in her chest, desperate to find what she had done so the silence would end.
What could Layla do instead of apologising for everything?
She could say once, calmly, that she will talk when Elif is ready, keep going to the study group, and tell her sister honestly how the silence is affecting her.
What would change if Elif had said "I'm upset about the seat, give me a day"?
Layla would know what was wrong and that the silence would end, so she could apologise for the real thing and sleep instead of replaying everything.

On Diwali morning, Avni stood in the hallway of her grandparents' flat with her hand hovering. Jomon had come along as her friend and was watching everyone bend to touch Dadaji's feet. Avni had done it since she was small. This year she felt unsure; she had argued with her grandfather over her choice of course. Still, she bent, touched his feet and heard him say, "Khush raho." His hand rested briefly on her head. Jomon, from a Kerala family where people rarely did this, stayed back with folded hands. Dadaji smiled at him warmly and said, "That's alright, beta." Avni wasn't sure if her gesture had been respect or habit or both, and she noticed her eyes were wet.

What did Dadaji say when Avni touched his feet?
He said, "Khush raho."
What might Avni be feeling as she touches her grandfather's feet, and what else could her wet eyes mean?
She may feel respect mixed with lingering hurt after their argument, and the wet eyes could be emotion, relief or simply the moment, so it is not certain.
What is a good way for Jomon to handle a custom that is not his own?
He can show respect in a way that is comfortable for him, such as folded hands, and does not need to do the gesture just because others do.
How does Dadaji see Jomon's folded hands?
Dadaji seems to accept them warmly, since he smiles and says it is alright, so the gesture is not required of a guest.

Subject: A plan so you can rest

Dear Devika,

Last night I saw you fall asleep at Amma's bedside with the phone in your hand. I have been thinking about it all day. For two months you have done every night and every visit, and I let it happen because you never complained. That was wrong of me.

One person cannot hold this up for the long run, so here is a plan. You take nights on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I take the other nights and weekends. We hire a helper from ten to two on weekdays. And Thursday is your day off, no phone.

If it does not work, we change it. But please say yes.

Jasleen

Which day is Devika's day off?
Thursday is Devika's day off.
How does Jasleen feel about the past two months?
Jasleen feels guilty and worried, admitting that letting Devika carry everything was wrong.
What could Jasleen and Devika do if the hired helper does not suit Amma?
They could try a different helper or change the hours, and adjust the rest of the schedule so nobody is overloaded.
How might Devika feel reading the email?
Devika may feel relief at the offer of rest but also some reluctance to let go, since Devika has held the whole load for two months.

The email said the Chennai offer would lapse at six. It was 5:20, the Mumbai local was packed, and Simran's phone showed four percent battery. Her current firm had just offered her a small team to lead if she stayed. For days she had gone round in circles.
Squeezed against the door, she asked herself one thing: at thirty-five, which of these two women would she be proud of? The one who tried the new city and the harder role. She knew there would be evenings she missed her team and her mother's street, and she let that be true.
At 5:41 she typed "I accept" and pressed send just as the screen went black. That night she told Rekha, her flatmate, "Done. No more pros and cons. Help me pack on Sunday?"

What time was the Chennai offer going to lapse?
The Chennai offer would lapse at six.
What does Simran's line "No more pros and cons" suggest about how she feels after sending the reply?
It suggests she feels settled and wants to stop re-arguing the choice; she has accepted she will miss some things and wants to put her energy into the move.
What made Simran's choice workable under such time pressure?
She cut the problem down to one question about which self she would be proud of later, admitted what she would lose, and then acted instead of waiting for certainty.
How might Rekha be affected by Simran's decision?
Rekha will lose a flatmate and may feel a little sad 😔, but being asked to help pack lets Rekha share in a decision Simran is sure about.

Monday. Samir texted, "Movie Saturday?" Kunal wrote back, "I've got cricket with the boys till five. Sunday?" Samir sent a thumbs up. "Sunday's better, I'll miss my cousin's birthday otherwise."

Thursday. Sitting on the school steps, Kunal's hand hovered near Samir's. "Can I hold your hand?" he asked. Samir thought for a second. "Not here, everyone's watching. Maybe by the tank after school." "Okay," Kunal said, relaxed. "Just tell me if I ask too much."

Sunday. After the movie, Samir said, "Your friends are texting you. Go, I'm fine, we can catch up tomorrow." Kunal grinned. "Come with me. They keep asking about you." Samir laughed and both of them walked to the ground, hands loose at their sides. 🙂

What did Kunal have on Saturday that clashed with the movie?
He had cricket with the boys till five.
How does Kunal show he cares about Samir's comfort when he asks to hold hands?
He asks first and then says "Just tell me if I ask too much," so Samir can answer freely. His relaxed reaction to "Not here" shows he accepts no easily.
What makes this relationship healthy, and what should they keep doing?
Both can say no, keep their own friends and family plans, and enjoy the time. They should keep talking openly and treating consent as always on.
How might Samir feel on being invited along to meet Kunal's friends?
Welcomed and included. Kunal does not treat Samir as a secret or a possession, and Samir laughs and walks along.

At the community centre in Mumbai, Francis said to Ankita, “Just tell Ravi you're sorry, and then he'll forgive you.” Ankita's mouth tightened. The centre coordinator, Ms. Shetty, was refilling the colour pencils nearby and overheard. Later she asked Francis quietly, “Did Ankita ask for ideas?” “No,” he admitted. “Next time, you could try: Would you like ideas?” Francis nodded. At the next quarrel, he said to Ankita, “Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?” Ankita's face softened. “Listen first, please,” she said. He sat next to her and listened.

Who overheard Francis giving advice?
Ms. Shetty, the centre coordinator.
How might Ankita have felt when Francis advised her, given that her mouth tightened?
She had not asked for advice, so she was probably annoyed, as if her problem was being brushed off.
What better question did Francis learn to ask?
“Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?”
How might Francis feel when Ankita asked him to listen first?
Francis may have felt a little corrected but also trusted, since he stayed and did as she asked.

Tanuja, twenty-four, was an accountant who sang in a small choir in Kolkata. The annual concert was only three weeks away, and her solo part had not improved in two months. Every rehearsal, the same wobble on the high note. Her flatmate Aparna had a bad cold, so Tanuja couldn't even practise at home without disturbing her. She practised in the stairwell instead, voice echoing. "Maybe I'm just not good enough," she said one night. Aparna, sniffling from the sofa, said, "You said that before the last jump too." Tanuja kept at it. Five days before the concert, the high note held steady. She sat down on the stairs and cried with relief.

Where did Tanuja practise instead of at home?
She practised in the stairwell.
What was Tanuja feeling when she said she might not be good enough?
She felt discouraged and doubtful after two months without visible improvement.
What helped Tanuja get through the plateau?
Continuing to practise, even in the stairwell, and Aparna's reminder that she had doubted herself before the last jump too.
How might Aparna feel when the high note finally holds?
Aparna would likely feel glad and relieved for her flatmate, having seen the long struggle up close.

Sarika: Kamal, are you home? I saw an accident near the flyover
Kamal: what?? are you ok
Sarika: I'm fine. a bike skidded and the rider fell near the divider
Kamal: did you go to him?
Sarika: not straight away. trucks were still going past. I moved behind the barrier first
Sarika: I checked if anything was leaking or burning. nothing
Sarika: then I called 112. told them the flyover exit, one rider down, conscious but not getting up
Kamal: did they come?
Sarika: ambulance in 12 minutes. police too. I stayed behind the barrier and talked to him from there, told him help was coming
Kamal: that was smart. I'd have run straight into the road
Sarika: I nearly did. my legs are still shaking
Kamal: come home. I'll make tea and you can tell Mummy properly

How long did the ambulance take to arrive?
The ambulance came in 12 minutes.
How is Sarika feeling after the accident?
Sarika is shaken, with legs still shaking, after nearly running into the road and then handling it calmly.
What else could Sarika do now that the rider is with the ambulance?
Sarika could rest, tell the family what happened, and talk to someone if the scene keeps coming back.
How does Kamal see what Sarika did?
Kamal thinks it was smart and admits to being the kind who would run into the road, so Kamal is impressed and relieved Sarika is safe.

metadata.subtype: Approach: check safety and call emergency services first [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Seema, and last month I did the thing I'd promised myself I would never do.
It was the fourth call that week. First my mother's cousin, then my father's aunt, then a neighbour who'd heard about 'a good boy in Indore'. Then my mother herself, on speaker, while I was in the hostel corridor with my cousin Shreya.
Something snapped. I shouted, 'I am never getting married! Never! Stop calling me!' The whole corridor went silent. On the phone, my mother started crying and handed it to my father, who said very quietly, 'We only wanted to help.' Then he hung up.
Shreya put her hand on my arm. I was shaking.
Since then, my mother has been calling more, not less. Shreya says she's told the aunties to 'find someone quickly before Seema gets more stubborn'. My shouting didn't end anything. It made them more scared, and me more alone.

What did Seema shout on the phone?
'I am never getting married! Never! Stop calling me!'
How did Seema feel just after shouting, and later?
Seema felt shaken and upset, and later lonely, seeing that the outburst had made things worse.
What could Seema do now to repair things?
Call when calm, apologise for shouting, and share a clearer plan, like finishing studies first, instead of 'never'.
How did the outburst look to Seema's parents?
They felt hurt and more anxious, which made them push harder to find someone quickly.
The bottle label says orange concentrate. I only know concentrate as to focus.

As a noun, said CON-cen-trate, concentrate is a thick liquid made by taking water out of something, so that you add water before drinking. The verb means to focus on something.
Example: Mix one part of the concentrate with four parts of water.

Read this:

I'm Pema, and I've shared a flat with Jyoti in Bengaluru for two years. Every second Thursday at six, she leaves for what she calls her "brain dentist". For a long time I assumed something was badly wrong. Once I asked, carefully, and she laughed. "Nothing's wrong. That's the point. I go so small things don't become big things." She had started after a hard breakup, she said, and kept going when life got better, the way you keep brushing after the toothache stops. I noticed she argued less with her mother on those Thursday nights, and she handled a bad appraisal in March without the week-long silence I'd seen before. She told me she had switched counsellors once, because the first one kept giving advice instead of listening. Last month, in my own rough patch, she didn't push. She just left her centre's number on the fridge. I called it on a Thursday.

What does Jyoti call her counsellor?
Her brain dentist.
What might Jyoti have felt when Pema asked carefully about the Thursdays?
Jyoti seemed relaxed and amused, laughing, not at all ashamed of going to therapy.
What does Jyoti's approach show about choosing appropriate help?
Treat counselling as regular maintenance, and switch counsellors if the fit is wrong, for example to one who listens rather than lectures.
How has Pema's view of therapy changed?
Pema first assumed something was badly wrong, but after seeing Jyoti handle hard moments calmly, Pema called the centre too.
Help me fix this line. He borrowed me five hundred rupees last week.

He lent me five hundred rupees last week.
Why: word choice ("borrowed me" -> "lent me").

Read this:

Yogesh: about to send the internship application
Madhav: did you do your two-minute check?
Yogesh: yes. name spelled right, company name right (I'd typed the wrong one!), CV attached, right file, deadline date, and I reread what they asked for
Yogesh: takes two minutes, I keep the list on a sticky note
Madhav: that list is why mistakes get caught
Madhav: you caught something?
Yogesh: the attachment was called "CV_old". swapped it 😅
Madhav: nice. sent?
Yogesh: sent. 4:52. deadline was 5
Madhav: whoa close. earlier next time
Yogesh: yes. but glad I didn't skip the check 🙂

What was the wrongly attached file called?
It was called "CV_old".
What might Yogesh be feeling on sending at 4:52?
Relieved but a little anxious, since the deadline was five o'clock.
What would you advise Yogesh to do next time?
Start the check earlier so there is room to fix things without racing the deadline.
How does Madhav see Yogesh's checklist habit?
Madhav supports it, prompting "did you do your two-minute check?" and seems impressed when it catches an error.

Giselle is in charge of the relay run on track and field day. Last year, the race was 300 meters. This year, it will be 4 times as long. Giselle needs to set up 6 tables for the relay run. The distance between the tables must be the same and the last table will be at the finish line. What is the distance between table 1 and table 3 in meters?

The relay run is 4 times the length of last year's race, so 300 meters x 4 = 1200 meters.
With 6 tables along the route, the distance between tables is 1200 meters / 6 tables = 200 meters.
The distance between tables 1 and 3 is 200 meters x 2 = 400 meters.
The answer is 400.
There's a full moon tonight. Why does it look so big when it rises?
That's called the moon illusion. The moon is about the same size near the horizon as high in the sky, but your brain compares it with trees and buildings nearby, so it looks bigger.
So it's a trick of the eye?
Yes, mostly a trick of the brain. If you take photos with the same zoom when it's low and when it's high, it will look about the same size in both.
Why does it look orange sometimes?
When the moon is low, its light passes through more air to reach you. The air scatters away more of the blue light, leaving more orange and red. It's the same reason sunsets look orange.
I'm going to watch it from the terrace with my brother.
That sounds lovely. Go out right when it rises, if you can, to see it at its biggest and most orange.
The old library in our area might close because hardly anyone visits.
That would be a loss for the neighbourhood. Do you use it yourself?
I used to, as a kid. I'd like to help keep it open.
You could start by asking the librarian what would help most. Some libraries run reading clubs, homework hours or story time for children, which bring people in.
I could run a story hour for little kids on Saturdays.
That is a lovely idea. Pick short picture books, keep each session to about forty-five minutes, and put up notices in the building and nearby shops. Even a few regular families can make a difference.

Read this:

The slide line stretched past the tap. Shankar ran along the side, squeezed in between two children near the front and grabbed the ladder. "Hey!" shouted a girl. "Back of the line!" shouted the others. Shankar slid down with a big grin that faded when he looked round. Chaitanya, who had been waving Shankar over to stand with him at the back, folded his arms. At the next break Chaitanya walked past Shankar without a word, and Shankar stood by the wall alone.

Where did Shankar squeeze in?
Shankar squeezed in between two children near the front of the line.
What was Shankar feeling when his grin faded as he looked round?
Shankar felt uneasy and a little ashamed. He got his turn, but he saw everyone was angry.
What could Shankar have done instead, and why?
Shankar could have gone to Chaitanya at the back and waited, or asked someone, "Can I go after you?" Shankar would get a turn and keep Chaitanya's goodwill.
How does the pushing in look to Chaitanya?
Chaitanya had waved Shankar over to wait together, so it feels like someone Shankar was invited to wait with chose to skip everyone. That hurts, so turning away makes sense. 😔

Read this:

Pallavi, you want to train two hours every day from tomorrow? I did that once. Listen.
I was fifteen, Sahil the skinny one. A new gym opened near our house. I decided to become strong in a month. First week, I lifted every day, skipped rest, ate only eggs. By day nine my shoulder hurt so badly I couldn't lift my school bag. The doctor said to rest, and I sat out for three weeks, angry and sulking.
My coach at the time said, "Strong is built like a wall. One brick a day, not all at once."
So I started again, slowly. Three days a week. Dal, rice, vegetables, not just eggs. Sleep. It took a year. But I never stopped again.
That's why your Sahil Mama will make you start with twenty minutes.

What happened to young Sahil's shoulder by day nine?
It hurt so badly that young Sahil couldn't lift the school bag.
How did young Sahil feel sitting out for three weeks?
Young Sahil felt angry and frustrated, sulking about the lost time.
What was the turning point in Sahil's story, and why?
Starting again slowly, three days a week with balanced meals, because steady habits lasted where rushing had failed.
How might the coach have felt watching young Sahil come back?
The coach was probably relieved and pleased that the boy had learned patience rather than quitting.

Wallace's water heater is twice the size of Catherine's water heater. If the capacity of Wallace's water heater is 40 gallons and it's 3/4 full, calculate the total number of gallons of water they both have if Catherine's water heater is also full with water to 3/4 of its capacity.

When 3/4 full of water, Wallace's water heater has 3/4*40 = 30 gallons of water.
Catherine's water heater capacity is 40/2 = 20 gallons
When 3/4 full, Catherine's water heater has 3/4*20 = 15 gallons of water.
Together, when 3/4 full with water, Wallace's and Catherine's water heaters hold 15+30 = 45 gallons of water.
The answer is 45.

Read this:

Pranav rubbed his eyes and laughed. "Rukmini, you asked what adulting actually looks like? Okay. Mine is Tuesday nights. That's when I sit at the dining table with a folder: my rent, Papa's electricity bill, Ma's medicine refills, my salary slip. Papa retired last year and he's still figuring out the online payments, so I do them with him slowly, so he can learn. Then on the first Sunday of the month, I go to the residents' association meeting. At first I went just because Papa asked. Now I actually care. Last month we got the street light fixed near the bus stop where girls wait at night. Nobody tells you it's this boring and this important at the same time. I complain, but I'd feel strange not doing it."

What does Pranav do on Tuesday nights?
He sits at the dining table with a folder of bills, rent and his salary slip.
How does Pranav feel about these duties?
He finds them boring but also important, and he'd feel strange not doing them, which shows he has made them his own.
What was wise about Pranav doing payments slowly with his father?
It helps his father learn and keep some independence, instead of Pranav simply taking over.
How might the girls waiting at the bus stop be affected by the association's work?
The fixed street light makes them safer at night, even though they may never know who pushed for it.

Noah, who loves his Grammy, calls her every week to talk about his day. If each call lasts 30 minutes and he is charged $0.05 per call minute, how much would he be billed if he makes the calls for a year?

A year has 52 weeks, so if he talks for 30 minutes every week, the total number of call hours is 52*30 = 1560 minutes.
Since he is charged 0.05 cents per call, the total cost is 1560*.05 = 78 dollars
The answer is 78.
Make this formal: I'm really sorry, but I gotta go now.
I am very sorry, but I must leave now.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 5, maths results day.
Rashmi usually beams at full marks and runs to show me. Today she got 14 out of 25. She folded the paper small and pushed it deep into her bag. When Samir got the top mark, she whispered, "I'm the stupid one now." At lunch she didn't eat, and told a friend, "My mother will be so disappointed in me."
I sat beside her: "One test shows what we need to practise. It doesn't show who you are." She shook her head, eyes wet.
Next: tomorrow I've asked Rashmi to help me set up the science corner, a job that has nothing to do with marks. This week I will call her mother to share how kind and hardworking Rashmi is, and talk about praising effort at home.

What mark did Rashmi get on the maths test?
14 out of 25.
How did Rashmi feel after seeing her mark?
She felt ashamed and not good enough, calling herself "the stupid one" and worrying that her mother would be disappointed.
What steps did the teacher plan to help Rashmi feel valued beyond marks?
Giving her the science corner job, which has nothing to do with marks, and calling her mother to talk about Rashmi's kindness and praising effort at home.
How might Samir's top mark look from Rashmi's side?
To Rashmi it may feel like proof that she has lost her place, since her sense of worth depends on being the one with high marks.
Priya says: "2,114 is divisible by 4, because it is even." Is she right?

Answer: No. The last two digits make 14, and 14 is not divisible by 4 (14 / 4 is 3 remainder 2). 2,114 / 4 is 528 remainder 2.

Every number divisible by 4 is even, but not every even number is divisible by 4. The 4 table is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 ... every OTHER even number. So being even is only the first step. Look at the last two digits: 14 is between 12 and 16, not in the 4 table. Another mistake to watch: using the digit sum for 4 (that only works for 3 and 9).

Read this:

March. In her third week on the surgical ward, Rituparna noted Mr Mohit in bed two as "comfortable". An hour later, the senior nurse spotted what she hadn't: he had gone quiet and pale. Rituparna replayed it all evening at home.
November. Bed six, Divyansh, a college student two days after surgery. His readings were normal. But Rituparna paused at the foot of the bed. He was too still; he wasn't scrolling his phone the way he had yesterday. She couldn't have named it. She checked everything again, found one reading edging the wrong way, and called the doctor.
The next morning, the senior nurse asked what had made her look twice. Rituparna thought about it. "Hundreds of patients, I suppose. He just didn't look like someone getting better. So I checked instead of guessing."

What had Divyansh stopped doing that he did the day before?
Scrolling his phone.
What did Rituparna feel at the foot of bed six?
Rituparna felt uneasy that something was wrong, though the readings were normal and she couldn't yet name it; he didn't look like someone getting better.
Why was checking again and calling the doctor the right use of her hunch?
The feeling alone wasn't proof, so she used it as a cue to look closer, found a reading moving the wrong way, and brought in the right person.
How might the senior nurse see Rituparna's growth since March?
In March the senior nurse had to catch what she missed; by November she caught it herself, which would be very reassuring to see.

Read this:

"Baljeet, please sweep the courtyard," said Papa from the cot. "Later," said Baljeet, looking at the wall. Ten minutes later: "Baljeet." "Later, Papa." By the fifth time, Papa's voice had gone tight. "I've asked five times!" "Why me? Wasim never sweeps!" Wasim watched from the doorway and said nothing. The argument went on until the sun was low. In the end Baljeet swept, and it took the same ten minutes it always took. But when she finished, the neighbour's television had already begun the cartoon, and the best part was over. She sat on the step, cross and silent.

How many times did Papa ask Baljeet to sweep?
Papa asked five times.
What was Baljeet feeling at the end, sitting on the step?
Baljeet was cross and probably regretful, since the sweeping took the usual ten minutes and the cartoon was missed.
What alternative approach could Baljeet use next time, and why?
Baljeet could sweep at once or choose a time, such as after tea, and tell Papa. A promise about when keeps the evening free and avoids the argument.
How does Papa see Baljeet's 'later'?
Papa asked again and again until the voice went tight, so Papa probably feels ignored and frustrated by having to repeat the request.

Read this:

That morning Chandrika, ten, and her little brother Chintu had fought over the last jalebi, and she'd told him she'd never talk to him again. In the afternoon, walking back from the village school past the pond, she saw a bigger boy from the next lane holding Chintu's slate high above his head. Chintu was jumping and crying. Chandrika didn't think. She marched straight over, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her heart hammered; the boy was a head taller. Her friend Yusuf came and stood beside her. The boy shrugged and dropped the slate. Chandrika picked it up, wiped it on her frock, and took Chintu's hand. At home they told Amma at once. Amma listened, then walked with them to the boy's house to speak to his parents before dinner.

What was the bigger boy holding above his head?
He was holding Chintu's slate high above his head.
What was Chandrika feeling as she stood between them?
Chandrika felt protective and scared at once, her heart hammering because the boy was a head taller.
What did Amma do that helped?
Amma listened and went with them to speak to the boy's parents before dinner, so the bullying was dealt with the same day.
How might Chintu have felt when Chandrika stepped in, after their morning fight?
Chintu likely felt relieved and protected, perhaps surprised his sister came to help after saying she'd never talk to him again.

Read this:

For months Jatin kept a list in his head. Hafsa had missed his cousin's engagement for a work call. She'd said "later" three times when he asked about the trip. She'd forgotten to pick up his mother's medicine the week he had a fever.

He never mentioned any of it. He just got quieter. He started eating dinner in front of the TV, answering in single words, going to bed early.

"Are you angry with me?" Hafsa asked one night in their Hyderabad flat.

"No," he said, and felt the lie in his chest.

The next Sunday, while they folded laundry, he made himself speak. "I'm sorry. I've been cold. I've been holding on to little things instead of telling you. When you work through family events, I feel alone."

Hafsa stopped folding. "I didn't know. I thought you were just tired of me."

They talked until the laundry was cold.

Whose engagement had Hafsa missed for a work call?
Hafsa had missed Jatin's cousin's engagement.
What was Jatin feeling when he said "No" to Hafsa's question?
Jatin felt resentful and guilty at the same time; he felt the lie in his chest because he was angry but hiding it.
What went wrong over those months, and what fixed it?
Jatin stored grievances and turned cold instead of speaking; saying them early and kindly with "I feel" opened a real conversation.
How was Hafsa affected by Jatin's coldness?
Hafsa felt confused and worried, even thinking Jatin was tired of her, because she didn't know what was wrong.

Read this:

At the Saturday badminton club in the community centre, Santosh, ten, lost his first match 21–6. He walked off the court, sat against the wall and pulled his cap down, shoulders shaking. Coach Hansa finished calling scores, then sat on the floor next to him in silence. "That was a tough one," she said quietly. Santosh wiped his nose on his wrist. "I'm the worst." "You're upset. Of course you are. You wanted it." She gave him her water bottle. "I lost a lot at your age. I cried in the changing room every week." He peeked from under the cap. "Every week?" "Nearly." Then she said, "Court three's free. Want to hit some drops with me?" He stood up. They rallied until the lights clicked off.

What was the score of Santosh's first match?
He lost his first match 21–6.
What does Santosh's cap pulled down suggest about how he felt?
He was ashamed and did not want others to see him crying. He felt like "the worst" after the loss.
Coach Hansa sat with Santosh before suggesting more play. Why was that timing a good choice?
If she had pushed him back on court at once, he might have felt his tears did not matter. Waiting and naming his feelings first made trying again feel safe.
How might the other children at the club see Coach Hansa after this?
They may see her as someone who stays with you when you lose, not only when you win. That can make them less afraid of losing in front of her.

Read this:

Faculty adviser's note, college cultural committee review, 18 February
The committee met to review the outdoor music night that was cancelled when the rain came. Most members said the risk was obvious and that Imran, who chose the open ground, should have known. Imran said little. Tanvir, the committee secretary, asked to see the notes from the planning meeting in January. He read out what the group had known then: the forecast showed clear skies, the indoor hall was booked by the exam cell, and every member had voted yes. He asked, "Given what we had that day, what would a better choice have been?" Nobody had an answer. The review turned to planning: a rain-backup clause for future bookings. I suggested we keep dated planning notes for every event.

What did the forecast show in January?
Clear skies.
Why did Tanvir ask to see the January notes?
He seemed uneasy that Imran was being blamed with hindsight, and wanted the review to be fair to what was known when the choice was made.
How did the review change after Tanvir's question, and why is that better?
It moved from blaming Imran to planning a rain-backup clause, which helps future events instead of punishing a reasonable choice.
What might it have been like for Imran before Tanvir spoke?
Imran probably felt blamed and ashamed, staying quiet while others called the risk obvious.
At the stationery shop 4 pens cost ₹5 each and 3 erasers cost ₹6 each. Write one calculation for the total and work it out.

Answer: ₹38. 4 x 5 + 3 x 6 = 20 + 18 = 38.

Each group of things is a multiplication, and then the two amounts are added. Because x comes before +, we do NOT need brackets: 4 x 5 + 3 x 6. Step 1: both multiplications, 20 and 18. Step 2: add, 38. Underline 4 x 5 and 3 x 6 before starting.

Read this:

Night shifts at the warehouse in Brampton made routines hard, and the January snow made them harder. Gurpreet, twenty-five and eight months into Canada, slept while the street was awake. Still, she had built three things. Every Tuesday, snow or not, she walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots. Every Thursday she met Nirmala, a retired teacher from the ground floor, at the library's conversation hour, where they swapped words: Gurpreet taught a little Punjabi, and Nirmala taught winter ones like slush, black ice and toque. And every night before her shift she braided her hair the way her bebe had taught her, humming the same old song. This week the storm closed the library. So Nirmala knocked on her door with a flask of tea instead, and they practised in the corridor.

What did Gurpreet do every Tuesday?
She walked to the gurdwara for the morning langar and stayed to help wash the big steel pots.
What does braiding her hair the way her bebe taught her suggest about Gurpreet?
It suggests she draws comfort and steadiness from keeping a piece of home alive inside her new life.
How did Gurpreet keep her routines going despite night shifts and snow?
She tied them to fixed days rather than fixed places, so when the library closed, the practice simply moved to the corridor.
What might the Thursday meetings mean to Nirmala?
For Nirmala, retired and living downstairs, they may be a welcome friendship, which is why the tea arrived when the library shut 😊

Read this:

Team lead's note, Friday. Samir.
For three weeks Tanvir has left at six sharp on Tuesdays and Thursdays to drive his parents to his father's physiotherapy, then logged in again at ten at night. On Wednesday he stayed back after stand-up and told me his mother also wants him home every Sunday, and his fiancée has stopped asking when they will look at wedding venues. He said, "Whatever I pick, somebody's let down. Some days I'm angry at all of them, and then I feel terrible for being angry at my own parents." He rubbed his eyes the whole time.
I didn't try to solve his family. I moved the client review from Thursday to Monday and told him late-night logins are not expected. I also said both feelings can be true at once. I'll check in again next Friday.

On which days did Tanvir leave at six?
On Tuesdays and Thursdays.
What mix of feelings does Tanvir describe?
He feels guilty whichever duty he neglects, resentful towards everyone pulling at him, and then ashamed of that anger towards his own parents.
Which of Samir's steps helped most, and why?
Moving the client review and saying late logins are not expected eased real pressure, and saying both feelings can be true lets Tanvir stop fighting himself.
How might Tanvir's fiancée be feeling, given that she has stopped asking about venues?
She may feel pushed to the bottom of the list and quietly hurt or resigned, as if asking again would only add to his load.

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Eshaan scraped at his juice-box lid with a thumbnail and it lifted a little at one corner. He blinked.
Wednesday: he went straight to that corner of a new box, picking and picking for a long minute, tongue out, until the lid peeled back. "Oh!"
Friday: Asif bhaiya handed him a sealed cup of curd. Eshaan turned it round, hunting for a corner to start from.

What did Asif bhaiya hand Eshaan on Friday?
He handed him a sealed cup of curd.
What was Eshaan feeling when the lid peeled back on Wednesday?
He was delighted and surprised, saying "Oh!" after a long minute of picking.
What else could Eshaan try if the curd cup has no corner?
He might ask Asif bhaiya or look for a tab, because a round lid may not have the corner his method needs.
How might Asif bhaiya see Eshaan's new habit?
Asif bhaiya probably finds it clever and funny to see the little boy hunting for a corner on a round cup.

Read this:

Sunday, week 1. Vandana and Ankita sit on the floor of their hostel room with a sheet of chart paper. Vandana wants the room clean; Ankita wants quiet to study late. They draw a chart: sweeping, bin, bathroom, rotating each week. Ankita adds: 'No calls or music after 11, Monday to Thursday.' Vandana adds a line for a shared supplies tin, 150 each a month, for soap, bin bags and phenyl.
Wednesday, week 2. At 11:10, Vandana's phone rings. She steps into the corridor to take it. Ankita, still studying, gives her a thumbs-up through the door.
Saturday, week 4. The tin has 70 left after buying a new mop. The floor is swept, the bin empty. Ankita tells her mother on the phone, 'Honestly, it's the first time I like my hostel room.'

How much does each put in the supplies tin a month?
150 each a month.
What does Ankita's thumbs-up through the door suggest?
It suggests she felt grateful and respected, seeing Vandana keep the quiet-hours promise.
What could they do if the tin runs short?
Sit down and decide together whether to put in a little more or buy fewer things, or ask the warden for ideas.
How does the plan look to Vandana, who wanted the room clean?
Vandana gets the tidy room she wanted, and stepping into the corridor for one late call is a small price for Ankita's quiet.

metadata.subtype: Approach: negotiating a win-win chore and quiet-hours plan [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Sachin started tutoring Ujjwal for the physics retest. Ujjwal yawned twice and stared out of the window. Sachin thought, he doesn't care. He finished early and went home annoyed.
Wednesday: Ujjwal yawned again, rubbing his eyes. But this time Sachin noticed he was also chewing his pen and his eyebrows were pinched together. Sachin stopped. "Are you bored, or confused, or tired?"
Ujjwal let out a breath. "All three? I'm helping my uncle at the shop till eleven every night. And I honestly don't get what acceleration even is."
Friday: Sachin switched to examples. A cricket ball, a scooter speeding up at a signal. They met right after school, not in the evening. Ujjwal leaned forward the whole hour.
"Oh!" he said at the end. "It's just how fast the speed changes."
Sachin grinned. He'd almost given up on Monday.

Until what time does Ujjwal help his uncle at the shop?
Till eleven every night.
What was Ujjwal actually feeling during the lessons?
Ujjwal was tired from late nights and confused about acceleration, not simply bored.
What helped Sachin read the situation correctly?
Noticing mixed cues on Wednesday and asking directly whether Ujjwal was bored, confused or tired, instead of assuming.
What would change if Sachin had kept assuming boredom?
Ujjwal might have felt judged as lazy and been even more lost before the retest.

metadata.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

A kettle screaming at midnight while Ammi and Abbu shouted in the next room: that's the sound I still hear. I'm Nazia, and I'm telling you this, Bidisha, because you asked why I go quiet when couples argue in the canteen.

They separated last year. At first I tried to fix it. I carried messages. Abbu said, "Tell your mother," and Ammi said, "Tell your father," and I felt like a bridge with both ends on fire. I even wrote each of them a long letter about being kinder.

Then my aunt said, "You're their daughter, not their referee." It was the first time I could breathe.

I stopped carrying messages. I call both of them every Sunday and tell each I love them and won't discuss the other. It still hurts. But I sleep now.

When did Nazia's parents separate?
Last year.
How did Nazia feel while carrying messages between her parents?
Like a bridge with both ends on fire, pulled and burned from both sides.
What boundary did Nazia set with her parents?
She stopped carrying messages, kept calling both every Sunday, and told each of them she loves them but will not discuss the other.
What did Nazia's aunt see that Nazia hadn't?
That Nazia was taking on a job that belonged to the parents, being their referee instead of their daughter.

metadata.subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]

messages.content: Put an apple on one side of a balance and a grape on the other. What happens? Which is heavier?

Answer: The apple side goes DOWN. The apple is heavier; the grape is lighter.

On a balance, the heavier side goes down. If both sides stay level, they weigh the same.
Cindy was 5 years old.  Her sister Jan was 2 years older than Cindy.  Their oldest sister Marcia was twice as old as Jan.  Greg was two years older than Marcia.  How old was Greg?

Jan was 2 years older than Cindy who was 5 so 2+5 = 7 years old
Marica was twice as old as Jan so 2*7 = 14 years old
Greg was 2 years older than Marcia who was 14 so 2+14 = 16 years old
The answer is 16.

Read this:

For three months after Papa died, I didn't cook. I lived on biscuits and delivery food and slept at odd hours. The flat felt too quiet and too full of his things at the same time.

It was Ishita who got me started again, but not with advice. She just came every Wednesday evening with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me." We made the dal he used to make. The first time, I cried into the onions and she pretended it was the onions.

After a few weeks, I started buying vegetables myself on Tuesdays, so they'd be ready. Then a morning walk, because Papa used to walk. Then back to my college friends' Sunday call, which I had been avoiding.

I also started seeing a grief counsellor once a week. It helped to say things aloud that I couldn't say to anyone who knew him.

I still miss him terribly. But I'm Parul again, most days, and not only the girl whose father died.

What did Ishita bring every Wednesday evening?
Ishita came with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me."
How was Parul feeling the first time they cooked Papa's dal?
Parul was overcome by grief and cried into the onions, missing her father deeply.
What small steps helped Parul rebuild her routine?
Weekly cooking with Ishita, buying vegetables herself, morning walks, returning to friends' calls and seeing a grief counsellor each helped a little at a time.
What was it like for Ishita to cook with Parul during those weeks?
Ishita probably felt sad and protective, choosing to stay quietly present and pretend the tears were from the onions to spare Parul embarrassment.

Read this:

The circus had been in Dharwad for three weeks, and tonight was its last show. Ankita, twenty, lay on her hostel bed with her agronomy notes, listening to the music drifting from the field beyond the college wall.
Jyoti knocked. "We're still studying at nine, right? Soil chemistry, chapter six."
Ankita looked at the notes. Then at her roommates pulling on shoes. "Jyoti... it's the last night."
She went. The trapeze girls flew under the lights, the clowns threw water at the front row, and Ankita screamed with laughter, eating hot peanuts from a paper cone. On the walk back under the streetlights, singing badly, she felt more alive than she had all term.
Then she saw Jyoti's message: "Did chapter six alone. It's long." Ankita's stomach gave a small twist. She typed, "Sorry. Tomorrow I'll bring tea and do it with you, promise." Then she lay back, still smiling.

What did Ankita eat at the circus?
Hot peanuts from a paper cone.
What mix of feelings did Ankita have on the walk back?
She felt more alive than she had all term, and then a small twist of guilt when she saw Jyoti's message.
What choice did Ankita make after seeing Jyoti's message, and why does it help?
She apologised and promised to bring tea and study the chapter tomorrow, which lets her keep the joy of the night while making up for the missed session.
How might Jyoti feel after doing chapter six alone?
Jyoti might feel a little let down and tired from studying alone, though the promise of tea and company may soften it.

metadata.subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

"You're late," Preeti said as Sachin dropped into the canteen chair.
"Twelve minutes. I said four; I'm sorry. The bus broke down near the bridge."
"You could have just said traffic."
"It was the bus. Also, about yesterday. I was short with you when you asked about the notes. That wasn't about you."
Preeti stirred her tea. "Kunal still hasn't spoken to me since our fight in March."
"Kunal treats every argument like a war. I'm not saying I didn't feel stung. I did. I'd rather say it and move on."
"Does it ever just stay stung?"
"Sometimes. Then I say that too."
Preeti smiled despite herself. In two years she had never once had to guess where she stood with Sachin.

Why was Sachin late?
The bus broke down near the bridge.
What does Preeti's smile at the end suggest she feels?
She feels reassured and grateful, noticing that with Sachin she never has to guess where she stands.
What would you advise Preeti to take from this friendship?
That saying a hurt plainly and then moving on keeps a friendship steady, unlike treating every argument as a war.
How does Sachin see disagreements?
Sachin admits feeling stung sometimes but prefers to say it and move on, rather than letting it become a crisis.

Read this:

Monday: Nilesh forgot his PE shoes and sat out the race.
Wednesday: his cousin Deepak said, "If it's PE day, shoes go in the bag." Nilesh said it twice and packed the shoes.
Friday: Nilesh checked the calendar. "PE day. Shoes go in." He packed them without anyone telling him.

What did Nilesh forget on Monday?
His PE shoes.
What was Nilesh feeling when he sat out the race?
He was disappointed and upset to miss it.
What else could Nilesh add to his rule?
A rule for other special days, like library day.
How might Deepak feel seeing Nilesh use the rule?
Deepak would probably feel proud that his rule helped.

Read this:

Monday. At the hotel's housekeeping briefing, Bidisha, the new floor supervisor, explained the new cleaning order: bathrooms first, then beds, then dusting. "Clear?" Lakshmi, who had worked there eleven years, nodded with the others. "Yes, madam."
Thursday of the next week. Lakshmi's floor still followed the old order. The two juniors Lakshmi had promised to train by Friday hadn't been shown. When Bidisha asked, Lakshmi said, "Tomorrow, madam, sure," and moved on quickly.
The following Monday. Bidisha thought back to the briefing: she had asked "Clear?" in front of the general manager. Nobody would have said no there. She found Lakshmi in the linen room. "I think I asked badly. If the new order doesn't work on your floor, I want to hear why. Really."
Lakshmi hesitated. "Floor three has no service lift. Bathrooms first means carrying the heavy trolley up twice."
Bidisha wrote it down. "Then floor three keeps the old order. Thank you."

What does floor three not have?
A service lift.
What did Bidisha realise when she thought back to the briefing?
Bidisha felt some regret, realising she had asked "Clear?" in front of the general manager, where nobody would feel able to say no, so Lakshmi's disagreement had come out as delay.
Which choice by Bidisha made it safe for Lakshmi to say no?
Taking the blame for asking badly, meeting Lakshmi privately in the linen room, and saying clearly that she wanted to hear the reasons.
How might Lakshmi, after eleven years, have felt when the new order was announced?
Lakshmi probably felt the plan ignored real problems like the missing lift, but didn't feel able to object to a new supervisor in front of the manager.

metadata.subtype: Yes in the meeting, delay afterwards [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: Thank you, properly

Dear Mridul,

When my father was taken to hospital on Monday night, I sent you three lines and vanished for four days. You took the vendor call, redid my slides for the Thursday review, and told our manager I was "handling something" without asking a single question. I do not think I said how much that meant. I am back now, and I would like to take the Friday client visit off you, since you mentioned dreading the drive. Lunch is on me as well. And if you are ever in a crunch, tell me before it gets bad.

Gratefully,
Eshaan

What did Mridul do for the Thursday review?
Mridul redid Eshaan's slides.
Why did Eshaan write instead of just thanking in passing?
Eshaan felt indebted and thought the thanks had not been said properly.
How does Eshaan plan to return the favour?
By taking over the Friday client visit, paying for lunch and offering help before a crunch gets bad.
How might Mridul have felt about covering without questions?
Mridul was probably willing to help, and not asking any questions shows trust.

Read this:

The blood bank at Sanjeevani Hospital was quiet at seven when Rekha closed her shift log. Her brother Kiran was standing by the donor chairs, holding two cups of cutting chai. They had not spoken since the fight over their father's flat, almost three years ago.
"I heard you work nights now," he said. "I brought tea. I also brought an apology, if you'll take it."
Rekha did not reach for the cup at once. Her shoulders stayed high. "I'm glad you came," she said slowly. "But last time your sorry lasted a week. I need you to be honest about what happened, and I need to see that something is different."
Kiran nodded and set the tea down on the counter. "Sunday lunch, somewhere neutral? You choose."
She picked up the cup. "One lunch. Then we'll see."

Where was Kiran waiting when Rekha closed her shift log?
He was standing by the donor chairs in the blood bank at Sanjeevani Hospital, holding two cups of cutting chai.
What was Rekha feeling when Kiran offered the tea and the apology?
She felt wary and guarded, glad he came but not ready to trust him; her high shoulders and slow reply show she was protecting herself after a sorry that lasted a week.
What small step let Rekha welcome Kiran without rushing?
She agreed to one lunch in a neutral place and asked for honesty, so she could see whether he had changed before offering more closeness.
How might Kiran see the moment when Rekha does not take the cup at once?
He may feel nervous and a little hurt, but he seems to understand he must earn her trust again, which is why he lets her choose the place.

Read this:

During the Sankranti break, the fields around Kondapur were stubble and kite string. Raghav spent the whole morning under the old water pump behind the temple, and by noon it was running again. Anjali, who studied at the same town college, watched him wipe grease off his hands. "You look happier now than in two years of accounts class," she said. "I'm leaving B.Com after this semester. I've got a seat in the ITI electrical course." Raghav laughed too loudly. "And throw away two years? Amma sold her gold earrings for my first fee." "Those years are spent either way." He looked at the humming pump, then down the road to the bus stand where the college bus would leave on Monday. "If I leave now, it means everything was a waste," he said, and walked home to find his ledger notebooks.

What did Raghav repair during the Sankranti break?
He repaired the old water pump behind the temple.
Why does leaving B.Com feel so hard for Raghav?
He feels guilty and scared that leaving would make the two years, and Amma's gold earrings, feel wasted, so staying seems like the loyal choice.
What question could help Raghav decide more fairly?
He could ask which course he would choose if he were starting today, knowing how much he enjoys repair work, and talk it through with Amma and a college counsellor.
How does Anjali see Raghav's choice?
Anjali sees that he is happiest working on the pump and believes the spent years should not decide his future, just as they did not decide hers.

Read this:

Rehana Apa,
Quick update from the hostel. Last week I read an article: "Early risers earn more, study of ten thousand people shows." So I've been waking at five every day. Alarm, cold water, the whole thing. I figured if people who earn more wake early, waking early must make you earn more.
It's day six. I'm exhausted by lunch, and I slept through my 2 p.m. lab.
Last night I actually read the study instead of the headline. It said early risers were "more likely" to earn more. Then it said many of them are older, already have steady day jobs, and have kids who wake them up. So maybe a steady job makes you wake early, not the other way round.
I feel a bit stupid. I've gone back to waking at seven, and I'm going to my lab.
Don't tell Ammi about the five a.m. experiment. She'll laugh.
Tanvir

Which class did Tanvir sleep through?
Tanvir slept through the 2 p.m. lab.
Why did waking at five seem like a good idea to Tanvir?
Tanvir felt hopeful and determined, reading the headline as proof that rising early causes people to earn more.
What did Tanvir do that other headline readers could copy?
Tanvir read the study itself, found 'more likely' and the third factors like steady jobs and kids, and changed course.
How might Rehana react to the email?
Rehana might smile and feel fond, glad that Tanvir spotted the mistake and went back to sleeping properly.

“Didi, can I ask you something? Don't laugh.” Lokesh sat on the edge of her bed, twisting his phone in his hands.
“Okay. What's wrong?”
“I sent Reet some private pictures. Last month. She said everyone does, and that she'd leave if I didn't.”
“And now?”
“Now I can't sleep. What if she shows them to someone? What if they go around school?” His voice broke.
Gurpreet put her laptop aside. “Look at me. This isn't your fault. She pushed, and you were scared of losing her. That's a lot of pressure.”
“Are you angry?”
“No. I'm worried, and I'm glad you told me. Tonight we tell Mummy and Papa together, and tomorrow we talk to your school counsellor. Adults can help you decide what to do next.”
Lokesh nodded, tears on his cheeks. “Okay.”

What did Reet say to make Lokesh send the pictures?
Reet said everyone does, and that she'd leave if Lokesh didn't.
How does Lokesh feel now?
Lokesh is scared and sleepless, since he worries the pictures might go around school.
What could Lokesh do next?
Lokesh could tell his parents and the school counsellor, as Gurpreet says, since adults can help him decide what to do.
How might Gurpreet feel hearing this?
Gurpreet is worried but glad, and stays calm and kind so that Lokesh knows it is not his fault.

metadata.subtype: Approach: giving in to avoid losing the relationship [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Mehak had been quiet all through dinner in the hostel mess, pushing rice around her plate. Back in Disha's room she said, very softly, "Something happened at a party last month. Someone forced me to do something I did not want. I haven't told anyone." A question flickered through Disha's mind, how did it happen, and she let it go. That was not hers to ask. "I believe you," Disha said. "It's not your fault. Thank you for telling me." She stayed on the bed beside Mehak and said nothing else for a while. Then she said, "The college counsellor is in until six. Would you like to go today? I'll walk with you and wait outside." Mehak nodded, eyes wet. Disha did not tell anyone else.

When did Mehak say the event happened?
She said it happened at a party last month.
What passed through Disha's mind after Mehak spoke, and what did she do with it?
A question flickered, how did it happen, but she let it go because it was not hers to ask. She chose to believe Mehak and reassure her.
Why was offering to walk Mehak to the counsellor that day a good step?
It helped Mehak reach a trained person quickly while Disha stayed as support, without pushing or gossiping, and left the choice with Mehak.
What might telling Disha have been like for Mehak?
It was probably frightening after a month of silence. Being believed and told it was not her fault may have lifted some of the weight. 🤍

metadata.subtype: Friend × Learning that a friend crossed a boundary [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Coach's note, Sunday, after the district relay
Aditi ran the anchor leg today and pulled us from third to first. At the finish, Arohi, who had run the opening leg, hugged her and said, "You were unbelievable!" Aditi shook her head. "No, no, I was slow off the handover. It was luck." Arohi's smile faded, and she walked off to her bag.
I've seen this before with Aditi. Every compliment bounces off.
At the cool-down I told her, quietly, that when she brushes praise away, the person giving it can feel they've been told they're wrong. I suggested trying just "thank you," and naming anyone who helped.
At the team dinner, the club secretary raised a glass to her. Aditi went pink, paused, and said, "Thank you. And Arohi's start gave me the lead to work with." Arohi grinned across the table.
Something to keep practising next season.

Which leg did Aditi run?
Aditi ran the anchor leg.
What might Aditi's going pink and pausing at dinner suggest?
Aditi probably felt shy and a little awkward receiving praise but chose to accept it; the flush could also be simple pleasure.
What did the coach suggest Aditi try?
Saying just "thank you" and naming anyone who helped, instead of brushing the praise away.
How did Arohi experience the two responses?
At the finish Arohi felt brushed off and walked away to her bag; at dinner, when credited for her start, she grinned.

Gina can paint six cups an hour with roses and 7 cups an hour with lilies. Her Etsy store gets an order for 6 rose cups and 14 lily cups. If Gina gets paid $90 total for the order, how much does she make per hour?

First find the total time to paint the rose cups: 6 cups / 6 cups/hour = 1 hour
Then find the total time to paint the lily cups: 14 cups / 7 cups/hour = 2 hours
Then add the painting time for each type of cup to find the total painting time: 1 hour + 2 hours = 3 hours
Then divide Gina's total earnings by the number of hours she works to find her hourly wage: $90 / 3 hours = $30/hour
The answer is 30.

Read this:

Dear Karthik,
I'm writing because I owe you an apology. Last Thursday at the bus stop, you were upset about your result, and I flung both my arms open and tried to hug you. You stiffened and stepped back, and I saw your face change. I wanted to help, but I didn't ask. I've thought about it all week. Afterwards you said, "Not now, just sit with me," and we sat until the bus came. That was better. Next time I'll ask, "Do you want a hug, or should I just stay here?" and I'll take whichever answer you give. Thank you for telling me straight.
Asif

Where were Asif and Karthik when Asif tried to hug Karthik?
They were at the bus stop.
What was Asif feeling when flinging both arms open, and what does Asif feel now?
Asif wanted to comfort Karthik at the time. Now Asif regrets not asking first and wants to make up for it.
What could Asif do next time a friend is upset?
Asif could ask if a friend wants a hug or just company, and accept the answer. A refusal should be respected.
How might Karthik have felt when Asif's arms opened?
Karthik stiffened and stepped back, which suggests being caught off guard and not wanting a hug then. Karthik may still have valued Asif sitting beside Karthik.

Read this:

The ink stain on the new sofa cover in their Kolkata flat was shaped like a fish. 'Minakshi did it,' Sharmila said at once when Ma saw it. 'She was holding my pen.'
Minakshi, who was five, cried and said she hadn't.
Sharmila told the story again at dinner, and to Dida on the phone next morning: Minakshi grabbing the pen, the blue drop falling. By the weekend she was sure. She could almost feel Minakshi's sticky hand on hers.
On Sunday, Baba scrolled through photos from Friday evening. There was Sharmila on the sofa, pen in her mouth, homework on her knees, and through the doorway, Minakshi asleep on the mat.
Sharmila stared at the photo. Her cheeks went hot. 'But I remember...' she started, and couldn't finish.

What shape was the ink stain on the sofa cover?
It was shaped like a fish.
Why does Sharmila feel so sure by the weekend that Minakshi did it?
Sharmila grew confident because she had retold the story at dinner and to Dida until details like the sticky hand felt like a real memory.
What choice does the photo give Sharmila, and what would be the brave one?
Sharmila can keep insisting or admit the story was wrong; owning the stain and saying sorry to Minakshi would be the brave choice.
What has the week been like for Minakshi?
Minakshi, only five, was blamed for something she didn't do and kept saying so; she probably felt confused and unfairly treated. 😢

Read this:

This summer I'm staying with Francis's family, so I see the sticker chart on the fridge every morning. First Francis brushes and comes out with foam still on the chin. Sachin, the big brother, hands over a sticker. Then the milk: Francis pinches the nose and gulps it down to the last drop. Another sticker. Then the school shoes go into the rack by the door, toes pointing in. Sticker three. Last night Francis counted the row out loud: seven. After this morning there are ten, and ten means the park. I can't tell what Francis thinks of the milk, but nobody skips a step.

Who hands Francis the stickers?
Sachin, the big brother, hands over the stickers.
How can you tell Francis wants the park trip?
Francis gulps the milk to the last drop while pinching the nose and counts the stickers out loud, which suggests Francis is eager and excited to reach ten.
What would help if one step, like the milk, gets too hard?
The family could talk it over with Francis while keeping the same order; the chart works because each small step earns something visible.
How might Sachin see the chart?
Sachin hands out each sticker, so he is part of the routine and probably enjoys seeing the row grow toward the park.

Read this:

The electricity bill was due tomorrow, and Indu, twenty-one, had just learned her salary would be late by a week. Her flatmate Anirban had already paid his share of the rent. Indu sat at the kitchen table with a notebook, listing what she had and what was due. The bill, groceries and the bus pass wouldn't all fit. She felt her chest tighten. Instead of panicking, she called the electricity office to ask about the late fee, then texted her landlord to explain. Anirban offered to cover groceries this week. "I'll pay you back on the fifth," she said, and wrote it down.

How late would Indu's salary be?
By a week.
What was Indu feeling when she realised everything wouldn't fit?
She felt anxious and tense, her chest tightening.
What was sensible about how Indu handled it?
She listed what was due, contacted the electricity office and landlord early, and wrote down what she owed Anirban.
How might Anirban feel about covering groceries?
Glad to help, and reassured that Indu is being clear about paying him back.

Read this:

When I moved from Toronto to Hyderabad in Class 9, I didn't understand the head wobble. On my second day, I asked Uday if I could borrow his notes. He wobbled his head side to side.
I thought it meant no. So I said, "Oh, okay, never mind," and walked away.
Later he came up to me looking confused. "Why didn't you take the notes? I said yes!"
I explained that where I came from, shaking the head meant no. He laughed and showed me the difference: a wobble is loose and friendly, not a stiff shake.
Now I wobble too, sometimes without noticing.
- Simran

What did Simran ask to borrow from Uday?
His notes.
What was Simran feeling after seeing Uday's head wobble?
Simran felt unsure and a bit disappointed, thinking the wobble meant no.
What would have helped Simran avoid the mix-up?
Asking Uday if the wobble meant yes, instead of assuming it was a no.
How did Uday see Simran walking away?
Uday was confused, since to him the wobble clearly meant yes.

Read this:

In the girls' hostel study hall, Rajni waited until Rekha sat down with her basketball bag before saying, lightly, "Oh, you still remember what my face looks like?" She laughed as she said it, eyes on her notebook. It was the same kind of line she had tried on Pinky last month, about something else, and Pinky had repeated it down the whole corridor as a joke. So this time Rajni watched closely. Rekha didn't laugh. She put her bag down. "Is that a joke or a real one?" Rajni shrugged. "Half." "I've been at practice every evening," Rekha said. "I thought you didn't mind. Walk to dinner together, at least?" Rajni's shoulders came down a little. On the walk she said the other half: that she had felt left behind since the team started, and silly for feeling it. Rekha linked arms with her. "Not silly. Tell me sooner next time."

Where did Rajni say the line to Rekha?
Rajni said it in the girls' hostel study hall.
Why did Rajni say it with a laugh and her eyes on her notebook?
Rajni was testing whether it was safe to show she felt left behind and hurt; after Pinky mocked her last month she was probably wary, so the joke protected her.
What makes Rekha a safer person to share with than Pinky?
Rekha stopped, asked whether it was a joke or real, and offered to walk to dinner, showing care, while Pinky had turned a hint into corridor gossip. 🤍
How did Rekha see the evenings at practice before Rajni spoke?
Rekha thought Rajni didn't mind, so the hint was news, and hearing it helped Rekha make time and ask to be told sooner.

metadata.subtype: Revealing a feeling to a peer or crush [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Make this into one or two clear modern sentences.

There on the coast in long array
The Vanars' marshalled legions lay,
Where Nila's care had ordered well
The watch of guard and sentinel,
And Mainda moved from post to post
With Dwivid to protect the host.
There on the coast the Vanars' armies lay in long, orderly lines. Nila had carefully arranged the guards and sentries, and Mainda went from post to post with Dwivid to protect the army.

Read this:

Warden's note, Block C, Room 14. Rukmini Iyer, 7 March.
Heard raised voices at 10 pm and went up. Sujay, pointing at the bins, had said that Kamal "never does anything around here." Kamal did not answer about the bins. Instead he listed, fast and loud: he had paid for the gas cylinder, fixed the fan, cleaned the bathroom twice last week, carried Sujay's parcel up four floors. His hands were shaking. Every item was a defence, as if he were on trial. The bins were still full when I arrived. I asked both to sit. I said to Kamal, "It sounds like you felt called lazy." He nodded, jaw tight. To Sujay: "What do you need, specifically?" "Just the bins on Tuesdays." Plan: rota on the door by tomorrow. Will check in on Friday.

What did Kamal say he had fixed?
He said he had fixed the fan.
Why did Kamal answer with a list instead of talking about the bins?
He felt hurt at being called lazy, so, hands shaking, he defended himself with everything he had done instead of talking about the bins.
How did Rukmini Iyer turn the trial back into a request?
Rukmini named Kamal's hurt, "you felt called lazy", and asked Sujay for a specific need, which turned out to be only the bins on Tuesdays.
What was it like for Sujay to hear a long list in reply?
Sujay probably felt unheard, since the bins were never addressed and the complaint became a contest over who does more.

Read this:

Preschool teacher's note, Tuesday.

Hrithik, five, refused to go into the school garden today. He said a dragon lived behind the mango tree. His father Jomon had come to help at the sports day.

Jomon didn't laugh. He knelt and said, "A dragon? What does it look like?" Hrithik described it: green, big teeth. Jomon listened, then said, "Shall we look together? I'll hold your hand."

They walked slowly. Behind the tree was only a green water tank. Jomon said, "Dragons are pretend. But your scared feeling is real. It's okay." Hrithik laughed and touched the tank.

I was glad Jomon didn't scare him or mock him. I'll share this with the other parents.

What was behind the mango tree?
Only a green water tank.
How did Hrithik feel before and after going behind the tree?
He felt scared of the dragon at first, then relieved and happy once he saw the tank.
What did Jomon do that made this work?
He listened to Hrithik's fear, played along gently, went to look together and then gave a simple true explanation.
How might the teacher feel watching Jomon handle it?
The teacher seems pleased and impressed, planning to share the approach with other parents.

Read this:

Deepak,
I've been thinking about Friday. When you solved that maths problem on the board, I said, "Of course, South Indians are always good at maths." Everyone laughed, and I thought I was complimenting you. Then I saw your face.
Later Tina told me you'd been up till two every night practising. And that people say that to you all the time, like your work doesn't count.
I honestly didn't mean it badly. But I get now that it doesn't matter what I meant. It still took something away from you.
I'm sorry. You're good at maths because you work hard, not because of where you're from. I won't say that kind of thing again.
Mridul

Until what time had Deepak been practising?
Deepak had been up till two every night practising.
How does Mridul feel after hearing from Tina?
Mridul feels shocked and sorry, realising a well-meant comment still hurt Deepak.
What does Mridul's letter do to repair the hurt?
It names exactly what was said, accepts the effect regardless of intent, credits Deepak's hard work, and promises to change.
How might Deepak feel reading the letter?
Deepak might feel relieved and respected that Mridul understood and acknowledged Deepak's effort.

Read this:

At breakfast in their Lima flat, Wei balanced a sock on his head, wobbled, and pretended to sneeze it off. "Achoo!"
Rosa stared, then burst into giggles. "Again!"
He did it again. She laughed harder, drumming her spoon.
The third time, she grabbed the sock and put it on her own head. "Choo!" she shouted, and it fell into her porridge.

Where did the sock land in the end?
In Rosa's porridge.
What was Rosa feeling when she put the sock on her own head?
She was amused and playful, wanting to share in the silly game.
What could Wei do to keep the fun going?
Keep repeating the game and let Rosa take turns, since the familiar joke feels safe and funny to her.
How might Wei feel when the sock falls into the porridge?
He likely laughs, amused, maybe groaning at the mess. 😄

Read this:

The nursery in Madrid had a paper tree and silver stars for the winter holidays. A man in a red suit came in with a sack.
Pablo, two, took one look and screamed.
Hana, two, sitting on the rug, had been smiling. She turned to Pablo, stared at his open mouth, and her own mouth wobbled. Then she burst into tears too, hands over her face.
The teacher sat between them, one arm each. "It's okay. It's okay."

What decorations did the nursery have?
A paper tree and silver stars.
What does Hana's wobbling mouth suggest she was feeling?
She was starting to feel upset herself, catching Pablo's fear and distress.
How could the teacher help next time a visitor comes in?
The teacher could prepare the toddlers, keep them close, and stay calm, so one child's fear spreads less.

You observed that her right glove was torn at the forefinger, but you did not apparently see that both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning, or the mark would not remain clear upon the finger. A class of 12 students was about to share 108 oranges equally among themselves when it was discovered that 36 of the oranges were bad and had to be thrown away. How many oranges less will each student get now than if no orange had to be thrown away?

If the 12 students had shared the 108 oranges, each student would have gotten 108/12 = 9 oranges
But 36 were removed so there are 108-36 = 72 oranges left
So 12 shared 72 for each to get 72/12 = 6 oranges
This is 9-6 = 3 less than they would each get if they did not have to throw any orange away.
The answer is 3.
Lamplighter lights the stars each evening; give me that as a story.

Old Gopal climbed the hill behind his village every dusk with a long pole and a small flame. He lit the stars, one by one, the same way his grandfather had done.

Nobody believed him. They thought the stars just came out. But he knew better.

One night, he slipped on a wet stone and dropped his pole. It rolled down the slope. The flame went out. The sky stayed dark.

A girl named Madhu, who had been following him, ran to pick up the pole. She lit it from her own lamp.

"Go on," she said.

Gopal's hands shook. He lit the first star, then the second. Madhu held the lamp steady beside him, and together they brought the whole sky to life.

Ralph is a member of the cross-country relay team. There are four other members on the team who run 3 km to complete their part of the race. Ralph runs twice as much as any member on his team to complete his part of the race. How long is the race?

4 team members each run 3 km, so 4 x 3 = 12 km.
Ralph runs twice as much as any team member and since team members each run 3 km, Ralph runs 2 x 3 km = 6 km.
The length of the race is 6 km run by Ralph + 12 km run by the rest of the team = 18 km.
The answer is 18.

In the media lab of the college library in Bhopal, Kashish's phone buzzed with a clip in the class group: students from another college apparently throwing stones at police, captioned 'This is what their side does.' Her jaw locked with fury; she had been arguing with that side all week. She was about to forward it to three more groups. At the next computer, Preeti, who helped run the college's fact-check club, glanced over. 'Where's it from?' Kashish didn't know. Preeti ran the clip through a reverse video search. It came from a different state, three years ago, in an unrelated clash. Only the caption was new. Kashish's anger turned into something colder, a feeling of being used. 'Someone wanted me angry,' she said. 'And I nearly helped.' She didn't forward it. Instead she posted in the class group: 'This clip is from three years ago, different state. The clip was from a different state, three years ago, in an unrelated clash.
How did Kashish feel once the search showed the truth?
Kashish's fury turned into a colder feeling of being used, uneasy and a little ashamed at nearly helping.
What did Kashish do instead of forwarding the clip?
She posted a correction in the class group asking people to check before sharing.

Preeti calmly asks where it's from and checks it, rather than reacting to it.

Sunday night.

Said no to the big company today. They offered more money than I've ever seen, a nice office, free lunches. Dhruv thinks I've gone mad.

Instead I'm starting the apprenticeship with old Masterji at his instrument workshop. Half the pay. Sawdust everywhere. Two, maybe three years before I'm good enough to make a sitar on my own.

Why? Because when I watched him carve that neck last month, I knew I wanted to do that for the rest of my life. And he's seventy. If I don't learn now, the chance is gone.

Mummy's worried. I'm worried. I'll have to take the bus instead of an auto and forget about new phones for a while.

But in five years, I want my own workshop. This is the price.

Kunal

A sitar.

Kunal is worried about money but determined to master the craft, knowing this chance with Masterji won't last.
What would you advise Kunal to help stick with this choice?
Keep the five-year goal visible and plan a simple budget, so the short-term sacrifices feel manageable.
Why might Dhruv react differently to Kunal's choice?

I'm Zeeshan, and last month I did something I'm still turning over. The inter-school quiz and our dance group's final practices fell in the same week. My maths teacher had picked me for the quiz team, and Abbu told everyone at dinner, glowing. But Dilnaz and the others in the group said, "If you leave now, the whole routine falls apart. We're a team." I couldn't bear the thought of them rolling their eyes at me in the corridor. So I dropped the quiz. Dilnaz hugged me and said I was the best friend ever, and for two days I felt warm and safe. Then Abbu asked when the quiz was, and his face fell when I told him. That was when it hit me. I'd tried so hard to be the good friend and the good son that I never once asked what I wanted.

Abbu.
What was Zeeshan afraid of when the dance group asked him to stay?
