He listened, thanked Ojas, said it was not his fault and that he was right to say stop, and called the tuition teacher straight away while Ojas held his hand.
How might the tuition teacher see Harish's call?
The teacher would likely take it seriously and act, keeping the boy away from Ojas and speaking to his parents that evening.

Read this:

Vaibhav, you say your first version is "just a landing page". Let your Chetan Chacha tell you about my furniture-rental idea when I was twenty-five.
I wanted to rent furniture to students who move every year. I was told, start small. So I made a website with our name, a nice photo of a sofa, and a button that said "Coming soon, leave your email."
Two hundred people left their emails. I was thrilled. Then I asked them for feedback. Everyone said the same thing: what does it cost, what can I rent, how long, who delivers?
I had learned nothing about whether students actually wanted to rent. I'd only learned that people will type an email into a box.
Next time, I rented out five real beds to five real students for one month. That taught me more in four weeks than that website did in four months.

How many people left their emails?
Two hundred people left their emails.
How did Chetan feel when two hundred emails came in?
Chetan felt thrilled at first, though later he realised it had taught him nothing about the real idea.
At the point he built the website, what else could Chetan have done, and why?
He could have rented a few real pieces to a few students, as he did later, because that tests the core idea directly.
How might the students who left emails have felt about the site?
They were probably curious but confused, with no prices or details, which is why their feedback was only about basics.

metadata.subtype: Approach: ships something too thin to be useful and learns little [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Age two: Jagdish points at the moon from his father's shoulders and cries, "Aai, chanda, see, moon!" Marathi from his grandmother, Hindi from the neighbours, English from the picture book, all in one breath. His parents grin and say, "Yes, chanda, the moon," and leave it there.

Age fifteen: Jomon's group chat runs on "Yaar, that quiz was too tough, bilkul nahi aaya" and "chill kar, party toh banti hai." Nobody thinks about it; it sounds like being part of the same crowd. When his class announces mock interviews, he practises alone in front of the mirror, dropping the slang and speaking in plain, tidy English.

Age twenty: Ganga wears a Malayalam poetry T-shirt in her Delhi hostel and bristles when a notice goes up only in Hindi. She argues about it loudly at dinner, proud and a little fierce. Later she teaches her roommate Asha, from Lucknow, how to say "nandi", and learns "chalo, khana thanda ho raha hai" in return. They laugh at each other's accents until the mess hall closes.

What did two-year-old Jagdish say while pointing at the moon?
Jagdish said, "Aai, chanda, see, moon!", using Marathi, Hindi and English words in one breath.
How do Jagdish at two, Jomon at fifteen and Ganga at twenty each relate to language differently?

Jagdish mixes Marathi, Hindi and English while sorting sounds; Jomon's slang belongs with friends, but he practises plain English for interviews; Ganga is proud of Malayalam and still trades words with Asha.
What is Ganga feeling when the notice appears only in Hindi?
Ganga feels irritated and fiercely proud of Malayalam, as if her language is being pushed aside, yet she stays warm toward Asha.
Why does Jomon practise in tidy English before the mock interviews?
Slang works with friends, but interviews ask for a cleaner way of speaking, so practising it lets Jomon use both styles when they fit.

Read this:

Pradeep, you say your boss mocks you in meetings and you think it's because you're weak. Listen to your Nitin mama.

At twenty-four I worked at a textile firm under a man called Grover. Every Monday he picked someone to tear apart. Often me. "Nitin, your brain is on holiday." "Nitin, go and sell peanuts instead." People laughed so they wouldn't be next. I started getting headaches every Sunday night. I was sure it was my fault.

Then one day I saw him do it to Mrs. Fernandes, who had worked there twenty years and was brilliant. That was my turning point. It wasn't about us. It was him.

I began writing it down in a small diary: date, words, who heard. After two months I took it to Mr. Kulkarni, the senior partner, whom everyone respected. He read it silently, then said, "This stops."

Grover was moved within the year. The headaches stopped sooner, the day I stopped believing him.

What did Grover tell Nitin to go and sell?
He told him to go and sell peanuts.
How did young Nitin feel about Grover's mockery at first?
He felt humiliated and anxious, getting headaches every Sunday and believing it was his fault.
What was the turning point in Nitin's story?
Seeing Grover humiliate the brilliant Mrs. Fernandes showed him it wasn't his fault, so he documented incidents and went to a respected senior partner.
How might Mrs. Fernandes have felt when Grover mocked her?
She was likely humiliated and hurt, even after twenty years of excellent work.

Read this:

Anand had to answer Noor by midnight. She was a friend from college who had built a small bakery and wanted him as a partner before a big festival order. It was raining hard, the power was out in his building and his phone was on nine percent.

Anand had been saying "let me think" for three weeks. He still had a job interview pending in Dubai. What if the bakery failed? What if the Dubai job was the real chance?

At 11:40 his phone died. He sat in the dark and didn't borrow a neighbour's charger.

In the morning, Noor's message was waiting: "I've asked Farida to join instead. I needed someone who could say yes." Anand read it twice. The Dubai interviewers never called back.

By what time did Anand have to answer Noor?
He had to answer Noor by midnight.
Why did Anand keep saying "let me think" for three weeks?
He felt torn and afraid of regretting the road not taken, so delaying felt safer than committing to either the bakery or Dubai.
What could Anand have done differently before the deadline?
He could have listed what mattered most to him and given Noor a clear answer earlier, or at least asked for an exact extra day.
How does Noor seem to see Anand's delay?
Noor seems let down but practical; she needed someone who could commit and moved on to Farida.

Read this:

Tuesday night
Went back to Bhimpur school today, first time since we opened the lab in March. I was carrying the photo from the opening ceremony on my phone. All ten tablets charging, children smiling.
Avni Ma'am, the maths teacher, walked me to the room. Locked. Inside, the tablets were stacked in their box. "Power goes by eleven most days," she said. "And nobody showed us how to use the lesson app. The children kept asking. After a while they stopped."
I kept saying, "But we raised the money in three weeks!" as if that fixed anything.
On the bus back I did the maths. The fundraising, the travel, the ceremony, and maybe six hours of use in total.
I planned this from my flat in the city. I never once asked Avni Ma'am what the school needed. Tomorrow I'm going to call her and ask.
— Varun

What does Avni Ma'am say happens to the power most days?
She says the power goes by eleven most days.
How can you tell Varun felt ashamed on the bus back?
Varun works out that all the effort bought maybe six hours of use and admits never once asking Avni Ma'am what the school needed.
What else could Varun have done first, and why would it help?
Varun could have visited and asked the teachers about power and training before raising money, so the plan fit what the school could actually use.
How might Avni Ma'am feel about the unused tablets?
She may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the children kept asking and the teachers were never shown how to use the lesson app.

Read this:

I'm Akash, and I watched a rumour eat our school in two weeks. It started in the bus: someone said Gautam Sir, our new physics teacher, had been thrown out of his last school. Nobody knew why. By the next day, there was a reason: he'd shouted at a student. By Friday, the student had been "hurt". People stopped asking him doubts. In the corridor, girls whispered when he passed. I noticed that every person who told me the story said "everyone knows." But nobody knew who had seen anything. I asked my cousin, who'd been at his old school. "He left because his wife got a job here," she said. I told three friends. It barely made a dent. By then, the rumour felt like a fact.

Where did the rumour about Gautam Sir start?
In the bus.
What might Akash have felt after the cousin's answer barely made a dent?
Akash probably felt frustrated and uneasy, seeing how hard it is to undo a story everyone already believes.
What could students do before repeating a rumour about a teacher?
Ask who actually saw anything and check with someone who knows, as Akash did, instead of saying "everyone knows".
What is it like for Gautam Sir during those two weeks?
He likely feels confused and isolated as students stop asking him doubts and whisper when he passes.

Read this:

Mehak, you want to stop taking the night bus because of that video? Sit with your masi a minute. When I was twenty-four and new in Bengaluru, someone at work told a story about a robbery on the late train. Knives, a woman's chain snatched, the whole compartment screaming. It was all anyone talked about for a week. I stopped taking the train home. I spent half my salary on cabs. I lay awake thinking about knives. Then one Sunday I told myself, "Disha, you're an engineer. Find out how often this happens." I looked up the railway police's yearly figures and asked two women who'd done that route for years. It was rare, and one story had been repeated a hundred times. I went back to the train, sat in the ladies' coach near the guard, and kept my chain inside my kurta. So look it up first, beta. Then decide.

What did Disha spend half her salary on?
She spent half her salary on cabs.
Why did Disha lie awake thinking about knives?
The robbery story was dramatic and everyone kept repeating it, so it felt as if it could happen on any train. The vivid picture made the danger feel far more common than it was.
What choice did Disha make on that Sunday, and how did it change her habit?
She decided to find out how often such robberies really happened, using railway police figures and two regular commuters. Knowing it was rare, she went back to the train with sensible precautions.
How might Mehak feel hearing that Disha Masi once did the same thing?
Mehak may feel less silly about being scared and more willing to check the facts before giving up the night bus.
Can an email begin with "Greetings"?

Yes. "Greetings" is a general opening, sometimes used when you do not know the reader's name or when writing to a group. It sounds a bit formal or old, so "Hello" or "Dear" followed by a name is often better.
Examples: Greetings, team. Dear Mr Sharma,

Read this:

At the international school in Osaka, Kaito-sensei collected the counting sheets. Paulo had none. "Paulo, where's yours?" Paulo looked at the floor. "My mummy said I don't need to do it." He felt clever, then his hands went sweaty. Kaito-sensei nodded calmly. "Okay. I'll send her a quick message to check." Paulo's heart thumped. "Um... maybe she didn't say it." "Thank you for telling me," said Kaito-sensei. "Let's do the sheet together now. It's only five sums." Paulo sat down, cheeks pink, and picked up his pencil.

How many sums were on the sheet?
It was only five sums.
How did Paulo feel after he said his mummy told him not to do it?
He felt clever at first, then scared and nervous, with sweaty hands and a thumping heart.
What did Kaito-sensei do that helped Paulo learn honesty?
Kaito-sensei stayed calm and gently said there would be a check, then thanked Paulo for the truth and helped him with the sheet.
How might Paulo's mummy feel if she heard about this?
She might be surprised and a little amused, and glad the teacher handled it kindly.
The water tank gauge at school shows the tank is 7/8 full. Is the tank nearly empty, about half full, or nearly full?

Answer: Nearly full. 7/8 is close to 1: only 1/8 is missing.

Think of the tank cut into 8 equal layers: 7 are full and only 1 is empty. 1/2 would be 4 layers. 7 is much nearer to 8 (full) than to 4 (half) or 0 (empty). So 7/8 is close to 1.

Read this:

The college common room was packed for the cup final screening, and then the power cut. The projector died. In the sudden dark and silence, someone's phone torch came on, and Lavanya saw Jeevan across the room with both arms raised high above his head.
Her first thought: goal? But the screen was black. Nobody was cheering. The room was quiet, just groans about the power.
Maybe he was surrendering, arms up like "I give up on this college's electricity." Or maybe just stretching after an hour on the floor.
She texted him. "Why are your arms up??"
"Stretching! My back is dead. Also I give up on this generator."
She laughed. So, stretch and surrender, not triumph.
Ten minutes later, the power returned just in time for a real goal. The room exploded with noise. This time Jeevan's arms shot up, and his mouth was open in a shout. No need to text.

What happened to the projector?
The projector died when the power cut.
What was Jeevan feeling when he raised his arms in the dark?
Jeevan felt stiff and frustrated, stretching a sore back and jokingly giving up on the generator.
How did context help Lavanya read the raised arms?
The silence and black screen showed it wasn't a goal, while later the noise and shouting showed the arms were triumph.
What would Lavanya have assumed without the context?
She might have assumed Jeevan was celebrating a goal, since raised arms often mean triumph.

metadata.subtype: Raised arms in celebration or surrender [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

Counsellor's note, 15 November. Binita (school counsellor).
Anirban came to me worried. He has a state football trial next month and a friend told him selectors "check your profile". He was scrolling through three years of posts, deleting in a panic.
We went through them together, calmly. Most were fine: matches, his dog. A few needed thought: a video of him and friends mocking another team, a comment calling a referee "blind". He went red reading those. He said, "I didn't think anyone would ever see it again."
We talked about what the posts say about him to a stranger. He deleted the mocking video, and he messaged the other team's captain to apologise. The comment was on someone else's page; he asked them to remove it.
Plan: he'll think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting. I'll check in after the trial.

What did a friend tell Anirban about the selectors?
A friend told him selectors "check your profile".
Why did Anirban go red reading the video and the referee comment?
Anirban felt embarrassed and ashamed, because he hadn't expected those posts to be seen again, and they showed him mocking people.
What would you advise a teen in Anirban's place?
Review posts calmly, remove what is unkind, apologise where someone was hurt, and think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting.
How might the other team's captain see Anirban's apology?
The captain might be surprised and feel respected, seeing that the mocking was taken seriously even years later.

Read this:

I'm Tarun. Last year at the call centre, I saw a team leader marking absent agents as present so their shifts were paid. It happened on at least six days that I remember. I was scared of being known as the one who told.
So one night I made a new email address and wrote to the company's ethics inbox: 'Attendance fraud is happening in the second-floor team. Please check.' No names, no dates, no screenshots. I hit send and felt like I'd done something brave.
Two weeks later a reply came to that address: 'Thank you. We were unable to identify the matter from the information provided. If you have further details, please share them.' That was all.
Parveen, who had seen the same thing, asked if I'd written down the dates. I hadn't. By then the attendance screens had been overwritten.
I still think about it. I wanted to do the right thing with no risk at all. What I did was the least risky thing, and it did nothing.

What did Tarun's anonymous email say?
'Attendance fraud is happening in the second-floor team. Please check.'
How did Tarun feel right after sending the email, and later?
Brave at first, then frustrated and uneasy when the reply showed it could not be acted on.
What could Tarun have included to make the tip useful?
The dates, the team leader's role and screenshots of the attendance entries, still sent anonymously if needed.
How might Parveen feel about how it turned out?
Disappointed and a bit frustrated, having seen the same thing and hoped the report would work.

Read this:

Monday. Joseph's parents argued again after dinner about the bakery closing early for good. Joseph shut his bedroom door, turned his lamp off and lay awake. His maths homework stayed blank the next morning.

Thursday. His aunt Kalyani picked him up from football and bought two cups of sugarcane juice. "You've gone quiet," she said, and waited. Joseph finally said, "If they didn't have to pay my fees, they wouldn't fight." Kalyani shook her head. "Your parents are worried about work. That is theirs to carry, not yours. You are allowed to be scared, and you can tell me anytime."

Two weeks later. The arguments still happen, though less loudly. One evening Joseph said to his mother, "When you both shout, I feel scared." She sat down beside him and said sorry. Now, when things get tense, his parents take their talk out to the balcony, and Joseph finishes his homework at the kitchen table.

What did Kalyani buy when she picked Joseph up from football?
Kalyani bought two cups of sugarcane juice.
Why did Joseph think the fights were his fault, and what was he feeling?
Joseph felt guilty and anxious, believing his school fees were the reason his parents were fighting.
What small step helped Joseph most, and why?
Having a trusted aunt who waited and let him talk helped him hear that the worry was not his fault, which later gave him courage to tell his mother he felt scared.
How might Joseph's mother see things after he tells her he feels scared?
She realises the arguments are reaching him, feels sorry, and chooses to keep tense talks away from him while still facing the problem.

Read this:

Monday. Lalit's first day at the new school in Bhopal. At lunch he sat under the neem tree with his dabba and watched the others laugh in groups. Nobody came over. At home he told Papa, 'It's the worst.' Papa said, 'First days usually are.'
Thursday. Lalit tried one thing. He sat on the bench beside Aditi, who was reading a comic, and asked, 'Is that the one with the flying cow?' She laughed and showed him. They didn't talk much after that, but it was something.
Three weeks later. Aditi saved him a seat, and two boys from the back row asked Lalit to join their cricket at break. He still missed his old gang, but lunch no longer felt like the longest part of the day.

Where did Lalit sit at lunch on his first day?
Under the neem tree with his dabba.
What was Lalit feeling on Monday evening when he spoke to Papa?
Lonely and discouraged; he called the day the worst.
What step did Lalit try on Thursday?
Sitting beside Aditi and asking about her comic, a small way to start talking.
How might Aditi see Lalit's question about the comic?
As a friendly opening; she laughed and showed him, and weeks later she saved him a seat.
Write a four-line rhyme for children about a school bell that rings too early on a sleepy morning.

The school bell rang, ding-dong, so loud,
It woke me from my cosy cloud.
I yawned and stretched, and rubbed my eyes,
Then rushed to class in sleepy surprise.
Film khatam hone ke baad dost se poochna hai ki use kaisi lagi. English?
You can ask: "How did you like the movie?" Another way is: "What did you think of the movie?"

Read this:

The video call froze twice, and Nitin, sitting quietly beside Yamini in the supplier's meeting, noticed both times that Yamini did not rush to fill the gap. Yamini had just laid out the new order plan. Then nothing. The supplier's face on the screen stayed blank, a fan whirred somewhere.
Nitin's palms sweated. He wanted to speak. Yamini only sipped tea and waited, easy in the quiet.
After a long ten seconds the supplier cleared his throat. "Actually, we could deliver earlier if you take the larger lot. And there's a discount."
Yamini nodded. "Tell me more."
Nitin wrote it down, amazed at how much the pause had brought out.

How many times did the video call freeze?
The video call froze twice.
What was Nitin feeling as the silence after the proposal stretched on?
Nitin felt nervous and impatient, with sweaty palms and a wish to speak. He watched Yamini stay calm and wait.
What did Yamini choose to do after laying out the plan, and what happened?
Yamini did not rush to fill the gap and just sipped tea and waited. After about ten seconds the supplier offered earlier delivery and a discount.
How might the supplier have experienced the pause?
The supplier may have felt space to think and then chose to say more. The quiet was not aggressive, since Yamini stayed easy and asked "Tell me more".
My landlord bent over backwards to help us move in. Did he hurt himself?

No, it is only an expression. To bend over backwards means to make a very big effort to help someone.
Example: The shopkeeper bent over backwards to find the book we wanted.
Give advice to a friend before an exam in two sentences. Do not use the word "study".
Get a good night of sleep and eat a healthy breakfast. Read each question carefully and take a deep breath before you begin.

Read this:

In their Delhi flat, Sharmila explained her plan to her brother Yash: she'd take the metro to her friend's place, then they'd go to the book fair together, and she'd be back by seven.
Yash said, "Huh?"
Sharmila's face tightened. "What, you don't think I can handle it? I'm not a baby."
Yash looked startled. "No! I just didn't understand. Which friend? You said two names."
Sharmila paused. She'd heard his "huh" as a challenge, like he was doubting her. But he was just confused.
"Sorry," she said. "It's Riddhi, not Reshma. Reshma's not coming."
"Okay. And back by seven. Got it." Yash went back to his phone. "Have fun."

By what time did Sharmila plan to be back?
By seven.
What was Sharmila feeling when Yash said "Huh?"
Sharmila felt defensive and annoyed, hearing the "huh" as a challenge to her independence.
What would help Sharmila avoid this mix-up next time?
Asking what Yash meant, or hearing him out, before assuming the "huh" was doubt.
How did Yash mean his "huh"?
Yash meant it as simple confusion about which friend, not as a challenge.

Read this:

Thursday. Rekha Ma'am brought a police officer to our class today. I hid behind Arjun because Dadi always says, "Behave or the police will take you away." My legs went funny.
But the officer said her job is to help. She said if you get lost, find someone in uniform, say your name and your parents' phone number, and stay put. She made us say ours three times. I asked, "Do you take naughty children?" She laughed and said, "No, I help find their mummies."
I am still a bit scared of the whistle. But I know my number now. I will say it loud and polite.
Sachin

Who brought the police officer to class?
Rekha Ma'am brought the police officer.
What was Sachin feeling when hiding behind Arjun?
Sachin was scared, because Dadi always says the police will take naughty children away, and Sachin's legs went funny.
What will Sachin do if lost, after the officer's talk?
Sachin will find someone in uniform, say the name and parents' phone number loudly and politely, and stay put.
How might the officer have seen Sachin's question about naughty children?
The officer laughed and answered kindly, so she probably understood that children can be frightened of the uniform and wanted to reassure Sachin.

Read this:

It had rained all through Eid week in the Bhiwandi flat. On Tuesday, Vishal, two, watched Papa, Chetan, take a phone call: "Hello ji! Haan, haan." On Wednesday, Vishal picked up a wooden block, held it to his ear and said, "Hello ji! Aan, aan!" He nodded seriously and walked around the room, just like Papa. Chetan laughed. "Who's calling?" Vishal held out the block. "Papa!"

What did Vishal use as a phone?
A wooden block.
How was Vishal feeling as he nodded and walked around with the block?
He felt serious and proud, playing at being Papa.
How could Chetan build on this game?
He could take the block and chat back, turning it into a pretend call.
How did Chetan react to Vishal's copying?
He was amused and joined in, asking who was calling.

Big Lots is having a sale. All chairs are 25% off. If you buy more than 5 chairs, you get an additional 1/3 off the discounted price of the number of chairs over 5. If you bought 8 chairs that were normally priced at $20, how much do the chairs cost in total?

You save $5 per chair with the 25% off sale.
On sale chairs cost $15 each because 20 - 5 = 15
You bought 3 chairs above the 5 required before the extra savings starts because 8 - 5 = 3
You save an extra $5 on these chairs because 15 x (1/3) = 5
The first five chairs cost $75 in total because 5 x 15 = 75
The final three chairs cost $30 in total because 3 x 10 = 30
In total they cost $105 because 75 + 30 = 105
The answer is 105.

Read this:

Monday: Himani recorded a practice interview for her internship with her friend Ankita asking the questions. Watching it back, she groaned. "I look like I hate every question." Her brows were furrowed almost the whole time.
Wednesday: They practised again. Ankita suggested, "When I'm talking, lift your eyebrows a little, like you're curious. When you're thinking, breathe out and let your forehead go before you answer." Himani kept forgetting. By the fifth try, she was doing it half the time.
Friday: The real interview on video. Himani felt her forehead tighten on the first technical question. She breathed out, let it soften, and answered. When the interviewer explained the team's project, she noticed her brows lift on their own. She actually was interested.
Saturday: The email came. The interviewer wrote: "You seemed engaged and thoughtful." Himani forwarded it to Ankita with one word: "FOREHEAD."

On which try was Himani doing it half the time?
By the fifth try.
What was Himani feeling on Monday after watching the recording?
Himani felt dismayed and self-conscious, groaning that her furrowed brows made her look as if she hated every question.
What small steps helped Himani manage her brows in the real interview?
Breathing out and letting her forehead soften before answering, and letting her brows lift to show real interest while listening.
How did the interviewer read Himani in the end?
The interviewer saw her as engaged and thoughtful.

What does scruple mean in simple words?
Why should you cover your mouth when you sneeze?
What will happen in the next episode of my favourite series?
How can I get ready for an exam the night before?
Fix my grammar: I and my sister are twins.

1. Scruple is a noun that means a feeling that stops you from doing something you think is wrong.
2. It is polite and healthy. Because sneezing throws tiny drops into the air, and covering stops them from reaching other people.
3. I don't know that. I can't see future episodes or your series. Wait for the next episode, or read an official preview.
4. Go over your short notes and pack your bag. Sleep on time, so that you can think clearly the next day.
5. Better: My sister and I are twins. Why: "I" is the subject form; name yourself last.

Read this:

I'm Yamini, and my little brother Vaibhav is fifteen. On Thursday his best friend Dhruv came to our door, which he never does without messaging first. I was in the kitchen and heard most of it.
Dhruv said quietly, "You told Neel about my speech classes."
Vaibhav's first answer was, "Bro, relax, it was a joke, you're making it a whole thing." Dhruv didn't say anything. He just started putting his shoes back on.
Then Vaibhav said, "Wait." There was a long pause. I think he was trying to find the words. "I did tell Neel. It was wrong. I wanted everyone to laugh. I'm really ashamed."
Dhruv stopped with one shoe on. I couldn't see his face. After a minute he said, "Okay," and they sat on the steps for a while without talking.
I don't know what either of them felt. I just know that "wait" changed something.

What did Dhruv say Vaibhav told Neel about?
Dhruv said Vaibhav told Neel about his speech classes.
What does the long pause before 'I did tell Neel' suggest about Vaibhav?
It suggests Vaibhav was torn between defending himself and facing what he did, and was searching for honest words.
Which of Vaibhav's two answers helped, and why?
The second: it named what he did, called it wrong and admitted shame, instead of treating Dhruv's hurt as 'a whole thing'.
How might Dhruv have felt while putting his shoes back on?
Dhruv probably felt dismissed and ready to give up on the friendship, since 'you're making it a whole thing' blamed him for being hurt.

Read this:

I'm Avni, Vinita's flatmate. Last year Vinita's father had a heart attack at fifty-two. After he recovered, she did something I didn't expect. She sat with him and wrote down the family's health history: heart problems on his side, diabetes on her mother's. Then she booked a basic check-up for herself at twenty-five. I thought it was a bit much. She said, "The doctor can tell me what's worth tracking, and I'd rather know early." She came back with a small notebook where she writes her results and questions for the doctor. She also started walking to work. She isn't anxious about it, just steady. Last month I asked her to help me make my own list.

What health problem runs on Vinita's father's side?
Heart problems run on his side.
What does Vinita's 'I'd rather know early' reveal about her thinking?
It shows she feels calm and determined to understand her risks early, while there's still time to act.
What preventive steps did Vinita take?
She wrote down the family health history, booked a check-up, kept a notebook of results and started walking to work.
How did Avni's view of Vinita's check-up change?
At first Avni thought it was too much, but later asked for help making her own list.

Read this:

"Leela, let's charge the phone, the battery's low!"
"Not now, Avni. There's lightning. We unplug things, we don't plug them in."
"Who says?"
"Our science teacher. Remember the safety talk? Unplug the TV, stay away from windows."
"But the window's the best view!"
"The best view of getting hurt. Come to the middle of the room."
"Fine. What about the fan switch? It's hot."
"Your hands are wet from the rain. Just leave the switches."
"You're so careful."
"And if the lane floods, we don't walk near the electric pole. There was a loose wire last year."
"Okay, okay. So what do we do?"
"Snakes and ladders. On the floor. In the middle."
A crack of thunder. Avni scooted closer. "Middle of the floor it is."

What did Avni want to charge?
The phone.
What was Leela feeling while listing the rules?
Serious and a little worried, wanting them both to stay safe.

Use a torch rather than touching switches, and tell an adult if anything sparks.

Avni first calls Leela 'so careful', but after the thunder moves to the middle of the floor.

messages.content: Please write a story where a class pet hamster escapes and the whole school helps find it.

On Monday morning, the cage door of Class 4's hamster, Pepper, was open, and Pepper was gone. The class split into search parties. Some looked in cupboards, others under desks, and a few climbed on chairs to check the shelves. The news spread, and soon, children from other classes joined, whispering in the corridors. The librarian went through her stacks. The peon peered into every dustbin. At last, near the staffroom, a girl named Maya heard a faint scratching in a pile of cardboard boxes. She called softly, and a small brown nose poked out. Pepper had made a nest from shredded paper and was fast asleep. Maya carried him back, and the school applauded all the way down the hall.

In their small town near Bankura, Bidisha's father, Shankar, heard from a neighbour that she hadn't kept the Shivratri fast at her college hostel. That evening he sat on the verandah without eating. 'Is this what the city teaches? Next you'll stop touching your grandmother's feet.' Bidisha felt her face burn. A sharp answer was ready: that fasting was just habit. She had said something like it to a friend once and hated how it sounded. Instead she sat on the step below him. 'Baba, I have questions. I'm reading, I'm thinking. But I haven't stopped loving you or Thakuma, and I haven't stopped being honest or kind. Those came from you.' He looked at the tulsi plant, not at her. 'And the puja?' 'I'll help Ma prepare it on Sunday, like always. I may not believe everything the way you do. I'll still be there.' After a long while, he picked up his plate.

How did Shankar find out about the fast?
Shankar heard from a neighbour.
What was Bidisha feeling when her father spoke?
Bidisha felt her face burn with hurt and embarrassment, and was tempted to answer sharply.
What did Bidisha say that eased her father's fear?
That she still loved him and Thakuma, still held the values they taught, and would help with Sunday's puja, sharing her questions gently.
What is Shankar afraid of?
Shankar fears the city is pulling Bidisha away from the family's ways and values.

During the cricket season, every video Bhupen watched in his village near Jorhat came with the same ad: a smiling man waving notes, 'Predict the match, win big, start with just a little!' The tea garden had cut his family's wages, and the ad felt like it was talking straight to him. Then a stranger in a local cricket fans' group messaged: 'Send a small amount to my number, I'll double it by tonight. Many boys from your area are earning.' Bhupen's thumb hovered. At the tea stall, his friend Yogesh saw the message and went pale. 'Don't. My cousin sent his whole savings to a man like this. Gone.' That evening Bhupen showed the chat to his uncle, the village schoolteacher. His uncle read it slowly. 'Anyone who promises to double your money is taking it, not giving it.' Together they blocked the number and reported it.

What did the stranger promise to do with Bhupen's money?
Double it by tonight.
Why did the ad feel like it was talking straight to Bhupen?
He felt worried about his family's cut wages and tempted by the hope of quick money.
What did Bhupen do that kept him safe?
He didn't send anything, showed the chat to his uncle, and they blocked and reported the number together.
How does Yogesh see the stranger's message?
He sees it as the same trap that took his cousin's savings, so he warns Bhupen at once.

Monday: At lunch Amandeep played tag with Jatin, the new boy, and it was the best game all term. Then she saw Ishita watching from the doorway, holding her lunchbox, and her stomach dropped, as if she had done something bad.
Wednesday: "Where were you Saturday?" Ishita asked. "At my cousin's," said Amandeep. It was untrue. She had been at Jatin's. The lie sat in her chest all afternoon.
Friday: She found Ishita by the swings. "I was at Jatin's. I like him. But you still matter to me. Do you want to play with us?"

Who was watching from the doorway on Monday?
Ishita was watching, holding her lunchbox.
How did Amandeep feel when she saw Ishita watching, and why?
Amandeep felt guilty, as if she had done something bad, because she had been enjoying tag with Jatin while Ishita watched from the doorway.
What made things worse, and what made them better?
The lie on Wednesday made it worse and weighed on her; telling the truth, saying Ishita still matters and inviting her made it better.
How might Ishita have felt hearing where Amandeep had been?
She was probably hurt at first, but she may also have felt respected that Amandeep told the truth and included her.

Explain this letter to me in two sentences.

I write to you, encompassed by peril and ignorant whether I am ever doomed to see again dear England and the dearer friends that inhabit it. I am surrounded by mountains of ice which admit of no escape and threaten every moment to crush my vessel. The brave fellows whom I have persuaded to be my companions look towards me for aid, but I have none to bestow. There is something terribly appalling in our situation, yet my courage and hopes do not desert me. Yet it is terrible to reflect that the lives of all these men are endangered through me. If we are lost, my mad schemes are the cause.

The writer is surrounded by mountains of ice that threaten to crush the ship, and the crew look to the writer for help. The writer keeps hope, but is terrified that the crew are in danger because of the writer's own mad schemes.
What is the usual time for Raga Bhairav?
Raga Bhairav is usually associated with Morning.

At the temple fair in their small town, Siddharth, sixteen, carried trays for the stalls but didn't go inside to pray. His cousin Akash noticed.
"Oye, atheist! Lost soul!" Akash shouted, and his friends laughed. An aunt added, "No God means no morals. What will become of him?"
Siddharth's ears burned. He kept carrying trays.
Later, an old woman slipped near the steps, and Siddharth was the first to reach her. He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.
His grandfather had seen it all. At dinner he said, in front of everyone, "Nobody at this table shames the boy for his thoughts. I watched him today. He has more kindness than half the people who went inside."
Akash stared at his plate. The aunt said nothing. Siddharth didn't look up, but he smiled a little.

What did Siddharth do when the old woman slipped?
He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.
How did Siddharth feel when Akash called him a lost soul?
Siddharth felt ashamed and hurt, his ears burning, but he kept carrying trays.
What did the grandfather do that protected Siddharth?
He refused to let the family shame Siddharth's honest thoughts, and pointed to his kindness as proof that values do not depend on belief.
How might Akash feel after the grandfather's words?
Akash likely feels embarrassed and guilty, which is why he stares at his plate.

Farida,
You asked how the science fair model is going. Confession time: it isn't. Every evening this week I sat down to glue the solar panel, and every evening I found something else to do. On Tuesday I arranged my whole bookshelf by colour. On Wednesday I helped Papa fix the ceiling fan, which he didn't even need help with. The moment I decide "tomorrow", I feel amazing, like a weight has lifted. For about an hour. Then there's this low hum of guilt under everything, even while I'm watching cricket. And the next evening, the easiest way to switch off the hum is to put it off again, because that brings the good feeling back. I think I'm training myself to avoid it. Weird thing to realise at fifteen.
Write back and tell me you do this too.
Nitin

What did Nitin do on Tuesday instead of working on the model?
Nitin arranged the whole bookshelf by colour.
How does Nitin feel right after deciding "tomorrow"?
Nitin feels amazing and relieved for about an hour, and then a low hum of guilt sets in.
What could break the cycle Nitin has noticed?
Nitin could glue just one part tonight, so the good feeling comes from starting rather than from putting it off.
How might Farida respond to this letter?
Farida may feel amused and sympathetic, and might point out that noticing the relief-and-guilt loop is already a first step.

Sunday: The hostel group lit up with screenshots of Ganga's old poems, mocked line by line. Nirmala read every message from her bed. Her thumb hovered. Forty-two people had seen it. Someone would say something. She put the phone down.
Tuesday: It had spread. Now there were voice notes reading the poems in silly accents. Ganga's light was off early and her door stayed shut. In the corridor, Nirmala heard two girls whisper, “Someone should stop it.” Neither did. Nor did she. Nirmala felt heavy all day.
Thursday: At 10 p.m., Nirmala typed slowly: “These were private. I think we should stop sharing them. Ganga is one of us.” She pressed send before she could change her mind.
Six replies came in a minute. “Yes.” “Sorry.” “Deleting mine.” Ganga's door opened a little the next morning.

What was being mocked in the hostel group?
Ganga's old poems were being mocked line by line, and later read aloud in silly accents in voice notes.
Why did Nirmala put the phone down on Sunday?
She felt hesitant and assumed that with forty-two people watching, someone else would speak up.
Why did Nirmala's Thursday message work?
It was short and calm, called the poems private and asked everyone to stop, which gave others permission to agree and delete.
What might it have been like for Ganga between Sunday and Thursday?
She was likely humiliated and alone, turning her light off early and keeping her door shut while dozens of people watched in silence.

She reached for the banana.

She offered a limited choice, "Banana or apple?", which let Nandini feel in charge without a battle.

"One now," Rafiq said, "or two after the fireworks, when the big rockets go up."
Karthik looked at the box, then at the dark balcony. The rockets were somewhere far away. He grabbed one laddoo and stuffed it into his mouth.
Later, when the rockets burst green and gold, Rafiq ate two laddoos slowly. Karthik stamped his foot. "Not fair! You got more!"

What did Rafiq offer Karthik?
One laddoo now, or two after the fireworks.

Appa didn't argue with each excuse but kept returning to the real question, then asked when the reasons appeared, letting Usha notice they came afterwards.

The power had been out for two hours in the Bengaluru flat, and Uma's mother had come to stay, so the three of them sat in the one room with a rechargeable lamp. Darshan was on the phone with his team, still on the night shift schedule. "No problem, take your time," he said warmly to someone. "You're doing great, honestly." Uma watched his free hand massage his neck. He hung up, and her mother asked about dinner. "Anything. I don't care," he snapped. Uma felt her face go hot in front of her mother. Later, on the balcony, she found him staring at nothing. "You were so kind to that caller," she said, "and then so cold to Amma." He rubbed his eyes. "I spend nine hours being patient. When I get home, there's nothing left." Uma didn't answer right away. She had wondered if the kindness was just an act for the office. Now she saw it was the opposite.

How long had the power been out in the Bengaluru flat?
The power had been out for two hours.
How did Uma feel when Darshan snapped at her mother?
Uma felt embarrassed and hurt, her face going hot in front of her mother.
What could Uma and Darshan try so the family gets some of his patience too?
They could plan a short quiet break after his shift, or ask his team to wrap up calls before family time, so he isn't empty at home.
What is it like for Darshan to switch from the caller to the family?
He is exhausted and drained, having spent nine hours being patient, so even a simple question at home feels like too much.

In the lift of the Dwarka apartment block, Noor made circles round her eyes with her fingers. 'Ooh, look, it's Owl Boy!' The other kids laughed. Eshaan pushed his thick glasses up his nose and stared at the floor numbers. It was the fourth day in a row. When Eshaan's mother met Noor's mother at the gate that evening, Noor said quickly, 'It was only a joke, Aunty. We all joke.' 'Does Eshaan laugh?' Eshaan's mother asked quietly. Noor thought about the lift. Eshaan never laughed. He always got out first and walked fast. 'He... doesn't,' she admitted. Her own mother said, 'Then it isn't a joke, Noor. A joke is when everyone's laughing.' Noor went red. The next morning in the lift, she said nothing about owls. She asked Eshaan where his cycle was parked.

What did Noor call Eshaan in the lift?
Noor called Eshaan 'Owl Boy'.
Why did Noor say 'It was only a joke'?
Calling it a joke made the teasing feel harmless and ordinary to Noor, so she didn't have to see it as a choice that hurt someone.
Which question turned things around for Noor?
'Does Eshaan laugh?' made Noor remember Eshaan's face and fast walk, which showed the 'joke' was really hurtful.
What was the lift ride like for Eshaan?
For Eshaan it was a daily dread: four days in a row he stared at the floor numbers, got out first and walked away fast.
Explain the word "cowardice" simply. My book uses the word "abusive". What does it mean? I came across "sustain" today. Meaning? Please define "enlightenment".

1. Cowardice is a noun that means lack of courage when facing danger.
2. "Abusive" is an adjective meaning using cruel or insulting words or actions toward someone.
3. It is a verb. It means to keep something going over time.
4. Enlightenment means a state of deep understanding, or the gaining of knowledge. It is a noun.

Santiago was debugging a payment error at a software company in Lima, the kind of problem where he had to hold six things in his head at once. Amara, from customer support, sent him a message: "Quick one, is the app down?" He answered and returned to the code. The chain of clues had slipped. Twenty minutes later: "Sorry, one more, can I tell customers it's fixed?" He answered. Again, he lost his place. At noon he walked to her desk. "I want to help, but each ping costs me about twenty minutes to get back in. Can we do a check-in at eleven and three?" Amara looked surprised, then nodded. "I had no idea."

What was Santiago debugging?
He was debugging a payment error.
What was Santiago feeling after the second message?
He felt frustrated and scattered, having lost the chain of clues again.
What would you advise others who work with someone doing deep work?
Save questions for agreed check-in times, like Santiago's eleven and three, unless something is truly urgent.
How does Amara see her quick questions?
Amara thought they were small and harmless, and is surprised to learn each one cost Santiago about twenty minutes.
What did my grandmother cook for the festival last year?
I don't know, as I wasn't there and can't see your family's past. Ask her; she'd likely enjoy telling you.
Is it safe to run with a pencil in your hand?
No, it is not safe. Because if you fall, the sharp point can poke your skin or eye as you land on it. It is safer to carry it with the tip pointing down.

Give the gist of this in three sentences.

The drought had lasted all June in the village near Bijapur. Pankaj, restless, climbed onto the flat roof and did the silly rain dance his friend Vikas had made up: three stamps, a spin, and a shout. That evening dark clouds rolled in, and it poured. Pankaj ran down, soaked and shouting, "I did it! My dance brought the rain!" The next day he danced again, twice as long. The sky stayed blue. "You didn't dance properly," Vikas said. Pankaj frowned. His grandfather called him over. "The radio said rain was coming on Monday," he said. "You danced on Monday too." Pankaj sat down beside him, thinking. "So it would have come anyway?" "The clouds don't watch you dance, beta."

During a June drought in a village near Bijapur, Pankaj did a silly rain dance on the roof, and that evening it poured, so he shouted that his dance had brought the rain. The next day he danced twice as long and the sky stayed blue, and his friend Vikas said he had not danced properly. His grandfather reminded him that the radio had said rain was coming on Monday and that he had danced on Monday too, so Pankaj asked if it would have come anyway, and his grandfather said the clouds do not watch you dance.

Counsellor's note - Binita, Class 10, Thursday
Rehana came to see me at lunch, sent by her class teacher. In PE, while the class changed shoes, a group of girls had joked about her old sports shoes: "Did you get them from your grandmother?" Rehana laughed loudly and made a joke back. The teacher, who knows her well, thought the laugh sounded forced.
With me, Rehana smiled for the first ten minutes. "It's fine. It was funny."
I didn't argue. I said, "Sometimes people laugh because it's easier than showing it hurt. If that's what happened, that's okay."
Her smile stayed, but her eyes filled up. "My father lost his job. We can't buy new ones this year. I didn't want them to know."
I told her it was not her fault, and that I'd make sure the PE teacher addressed the teasing without mentioning her family. She left looking lighter.

What did the girls joke about?
About her old sports shoes.
What was Rehana feeling behind her smile?
Rehana felt hurt and ashamed about the family's money troubles, and laughed to avoid looking weak.
How did Binita respond in a way that helped?
She didn't argue or assume, gently allowed for hurt behind a laugh, and offered practical support without exposing Rehana's family.
How might the girls who joked have read Rehana's laugh?
They probably thought she was fine with it, since she laughed and joked back.

For Joseph: a buddy at break, a teacher on duty near the swings, and a daily check-in with me for two weeks. He smiled a little when he heard he could come to my room any time. In the school computer lab, Eshaan had a tab open with Riya's holiday photos, then Kabir's football clips, then Jasmine's party. Everyone seemed to be laughing. He scrolled until the bell rang, feeling small. Mridul sir, the lab teacher, glanced at the screen as he shut down the computers. "Nice trip," he said mildly. "Whose?" "Just someone's," Eshaan muttered. Later he thought about Riya's post from last week, the one saying she couldn't sleep before exams. It had been buried under all the smiling pictures. He wasn't sure why the thought helped. He deleted the tabs, and signed up for the coding club that had been posted outside the lab for a month, even though it felt awkward.

Who glanced at Eshaan's screen in the computer lab?
Mridul sir, the lab teacher.
How was Eshaan feeling as he scrolled through the photos, and what changed his mind?
He felt small and envious. Remembering Riya's post about not sleeping before exams showed him the smiling pictures hid worries too.
What could Eshaan do with his envy?
Notice that online pictures are curated, avoid tearing anyone down and build his own strengths, as he began by joining the coding club.
How might Mridul sir see what Eshaan was doing?
Probably as a student feeling left out. He mildly asked whose trip it was rather than scolding, which leaves space for Eshaan to talk if he chooses.

In Class 4B, Uma Ma'am usually started the day with a joke. Today she didn't. Her eyes were puffy, and twice she looked at her phone and then put it face down. Sahil noticed. When she dropped the pile of notebooks by the door, a few boys snickered. Sahil got up and helped her gather them without saying anything. At recess the others planned to make noise in the next period 'because she won't even notice'. Sahil shook his head. 'She looks really tired. Let's not.' He stayed quiet all through the lesson and put his hand up for an answer when nobody else did. Before home time, Uma Ma'am caught his eye and gave him a small, grateful smile.

How many times did Uma Ma'am look at her phone?
Twice.
What did Sahil feel when he noticed Uma Ma'am's puffy eyes?
Concerned and caring; he sensed she was tired and worried, so he wanted to help rather than add to it.
What small things did Sahil do that helped?
He helped gather the notebooks, talked the others out of making noise, and answered in class.
How might Uma Ma'am have felt about Sahil's help?
Grateful and less alone on a hard day; she gave him a small smile before home time.

Last year my senior, Sangeeta, presented my analysis to the leadership team as her own. A week later she waved away my next idea in a meeting with a smile. I felt heat behind my eyes. I said nothing in the room and could hardly hear the rest of the discussion.
That night I did not write an angry email. I made a folder with dated copies of my drafts, emails and versions. I spoke to two colleagues I trust, who had seen me work on it. Then I asked my manager, calmly, if I could present the next stage myself.
Nothing dramatic happened. But three months later my name was on the slide, and I slept better.
Abhinav

What did Sangeeta do with Abhinav's analysis?
She presented Abhinav's analysis to the leadership team as her own.
What was Abhinav feeling in the meeting when the next idea was waved away?
Abhinav felt angry and hurt, described as heat behind the eyes, and stayed silent.
What steps did Abhinav take instead of public anger?
Abhinav kept a folder of dated drafts and emails, spoke to two trusted colleagues and asked the manager calmly to present the next stage.
How might Sangeeta have seen the situation?
Sangeeta waved away the idea with a smile, so she may have seen it as a routine exchange and not known how much it stung.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Lalit?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Lalit is M/M^, and the samvadi is r.

Ritu, you asked why I've been so quiet since the audit news. I'll tell you, but don't be kind about it. Last year I saw our branch head pushing loans through without the income checks. More than once. I had my own home loan, Ma's rent, and a job I'd waited two years for. So I told myself, it's not my department, not my business, he knows more than me. I kept quiet. Then the audit came this month. Forty-two bad loans. Customers who can't pay are getting recovery calls. Two colleagues who did speak up earlier were brushed off because nobody backed them. I could have backed them. I'm Abhinav, the one who always talks about doing the right thing, and I said nothing when it counted. That's what's keeping me up.

How many bad loans did the audit find?
Forty-two bad loans.
What is Abhinav feeling now?
Abhinav feels guilty and ashamed, kept awake knowing Abhinav stayed silent when the colleagues who spoke up could have been backed.
What other approach could Abhinav have taken while still protecting the job?
Abhinav could have written dated notes and used a confidential reporting channel, or backed the colleagues' concern, instead of staying completely silent.
How might the customers getting recovery calls be affected by the silence?
They took loans they couldn't afford and now face stressful recovery calls, harm that earlier action might have limited.

The university portal closed at midnight, and at ten the power went out in Shreya's Guwahati hostel. She had to choose her major: economics or psychology. Her phone was at twenty percent. Her roommate Noor lit a candle. "Just pick economics. Safer jobs." Shreya stared at the flame. She thought about the psychology elective she'd loved, the way she'd stayed up reading about memory for fun. Economics felt like a coat that didn't fit. "Psychology," she said. "But I'm scared." Noor handed her the phone hotspot. "Then be scared and submit." With the phone at eight percent, Shreya clicked submit at 11:42. She sat back, heart pounding. "I did it." Noor clapped softly in the dark.

At what time did Shreya click submit?
What was Shreya feeling as she chose psychology?
She felt scared but sure, choosing the subject she loved over the safer option.
What helped Shreya decide under pressure?
Remembering what she genuinely enjoyed and Noor's push to submit despite fear.
How might Noor feel after Shreya submitted?
Noor likely feels happy for her and glad to have helped.
We saw a peacock who was dancing near the pond. Is "who" right for a bird?

We saw a peacock that was dancing near the pond.
Why: pronoun ("who" -> "that").
I was very tired, but I felt so happy that I can't stop smiling. What is wrong?

I was very tired, but I felt so happy that I couldn't stop smiling.
Why: past tense ("can't stop" -> "couldn't stop").

"Pankaj, just sign the concrete test sheet."
"Nilesh Sir, the samples failed. The strength is below what's required for a school building."
"It's close enough. The builder's already poured two floors."
"Close enough isn't safe. Children will be inside."
"You're new. You don't understand how this works."
"I understand if it cracks, it's my signature."
Nilesh leaned in. "If you don't sign, the builder will ask for someone else. And your name will be mud in this city."
Pankaj's hands were shaking. "Then I'll take it to the chief engineer."
"You'll regret this."
"Maybe. But I won't regret a collapse."
That afternoon, Pankaj submitted the failed results to the chief engineer's office, in writing.

What kind of building was being constructed?
A school building.
What was Pankaj feeling when his hands were shaking?
He felt frightened of the threat to his career, but firm about safety.
How did Pankaj defend ethics despite the risk?
He refused to sign failed tests and reported the results to the chief engineer in writing.
How might the children and families be affected by Pankaj's choice?
They would be protected from a possibly unsafe building.

"It's ugly!" Kamal crumpled the paper into a ball.
"Kamal, that was your card for Ravi," said Damini Ma'am. "The flower leaned a little, that's all."
"It's crooked. I hate it."
"Would you like to try one more? I'll sit with you."
"No. I don't want to."
"Ravi's party is tomorrow."
"Then I won't give him one." Kamal folded his arms and turned to face the wall.
Damini Ma'am smoothed the ball flat and put it in her drawer. Kamal did not look.

What did Kamal say about his drawing?
He said it was ugly and crooked.
What was Kamal feeling when he crumpled the paper, and how can you tell?
He was disappointed and upset. He crumpled the card, folded his arms and turned to the wall, so the crooked flower mattered a lot to him.
What alternative approach could help Kamal, and why?
He could ask the teacher to help him draw a first line, or turn the leaning flower into a flower in the wind. Then the card would not have to be perfect to be finished.
How does Damini Ma'am see the crooked flower, and why did she keep the paper?
She sees a small lean, not a failure. Smoothing the paper and keeping it leaves a way open for Kamal to come back to it.

The women's meeting under the peepal tree in Kalwa village had grown tense. Two lanes were arguing over the new water tap timings, voices rising. Jahnavi, the young coordinator, raised her hands. "At this rate, the tap will retire before we decide!" A few women laughed, then more, and the shoulders around the circle loosened. They settled on alternate mornings within ten minutes. Then Yamini-bai asked to speak. Quietly, she told them her husband had been in the district hospital for a month and she was struggling to manage the fields alone. Just then a rooster strutted into the middle of the circle and crowed at full volume. Jahnavi felt a laugh bubble up and saw two girls at the back biting their lips. She pressed her own lips together, kept her eyes on Yamini-bai, and waited until the rooster wandered off. Then she said, "We'll make a rota for your fields."

What did the women decide about the water tap?
Alternate mornings.
What was Jahnavi feeling when the rooster crowed during Yamini-bai's words?
Jahnavi felt a laugh bubbling up but also respect and concern for Yamini-bai, so she held the amusement back.
Why was Jahnavi right to laugh at one moment and hold back at the other?
The joke about the tap eased a tense argument, but laughing during Yamini-bai's hard news would have seemed dismissive of her struggle.
How might Yamini-bai have felt if the circle had burst out laughing at the rooster?
She might have felt hurt and unheard, as if her husband's illness and her struggle were being brushed aside.

messages.content:
What makes the narrator think Biddy is extraordinary?

Pursuing my idea as I leaned back in my wooden chair, and looked at Biddy sewing away with her head on one side, I began to think her rather an extraordinary girl. For I called to mind now, that she was equally accomplished in the terms of our trade, and the names of our different sorts of work, and our various tools. In short, whatever I knew, Biddy knew. Theoretically, she was already as good a blacksmith as I, or better.
She knows the terms of their trade, the names of the different kinds of work and the various tools. Whatever the narrator knew, Biddy knew, so in theory she is already at least as good a blacksmith.

There were 28 students inside a bus before stopping at an intersection. After stopping at an intersection, there were 58 students on the bus. What's 40% of the number of students who entered the bus at the intermediate stop?

At the intermediate stop, 58-28=30 students entered the bus before it stopped at the intersection.
40% of the number of students who entered the bus at the intermediate stop is 40/100*30=12
The answer is 12.

Rehana's daughter Zainab, five, sat in the doctor's waiting room in Ahmedabad, chewing her thumbnail and picking at her frock. The receptionist called other names. Rehana noticed. "You're nervous, aren't you?" Zainab nodded slowly. "Let's breathe like we do at bedtime: smell the flower, blow the candle." They did it together three times, quietly. Zainab took her thumb from her mouth and said, "Will it hurt?" Rehana answered honestly, "The doctor will tell us what she's doing."

What was Zainab chewing in the waiting room?
She was chewing her thumbnail.
What does Zainab's thumb-chewing and picking suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she was nervous about seeing the doctor, and she nodded when her mother asked. It could also have been simply waiting that she found hard.
What did Rehana do that worked better than a scolding?
She named the nervousness and taught a calming breath they did together, without telling Zainab off for chewing.
How might Zainab feel when her mother says the doctor will tell them what she's doing?
She may feel a little more prepared and less alone, though she still might be a little worried.

"Mausi, I got it! The kite-string sum!"
Ishita Mausi put down her tea. "The one you called impossible at lunch?"
"Yes! First I tried adding, wrong. Then I drew the kite and the string, still wrong. Then I made a table like you do on your board."
"Show me." Mausi read the page slowly. "Aditi, look at what you did. You didn't stop when adding failed. You drew it. When the drawing didn't work, you changed again. The table worked because you'd already ruled out two ways."
"So I'm good at maths?"
"You're getting better at maths, because you kept changing your way in. That's how it grows. I see it in my Class 5 kids too."
Aditi flipped to a fresh page. "Then give me the tough one from your box."

What three methods did Aditi try?
Adding, drawing the kite and the string, and making a table.
What does Aditi's 'So I'm good at maths?' suggest Aditi is thinking?
Aditi feels proud and excited, and is checking whether success means a fixed talent; it hints at a pull toward labels, which Mausi gently turns toward effort.
What choice does Ishita Mausi make in her answer, and why does it help?
She describes each method and says ability grows by changing approaches; that makes Aditi want the tough problem instead of protecting a label.
How might Ishita Mausi feel when Aditi asks for the tough one?
Ishita Mausi is probably delighted 😊, seeing that praise for the process has made a challenge feel inviting rather than scary.

To: Mr Mridul Sen, School Counsellor Subject: Can I meet you?
Dear Sir,
I'm Irfan from Class 11-B. I don't know how to say this in person, so I'm writing.
For about a month, I haven't been sleeping properly. My heart races before class, even when nothing is happening. I've stopped playing football because I feel too tired. My parents think I'm just lazy.
I read in the school notice that you are there for students who feel this way. I think I might need help.
Could we meet this week? Tomorrow at lunch would be good, if possible. I'm a bit nervous about it, but I want to feel better.
Thank you, Irfan

How long has Irfan not been sleeping properly?
For about a month.
How is Irfan feeling as he writes the email?
Irfan feels anxious and exhausted, with a racing heart, and nervous about asking for help.
Why was writing to the counsellor a good step?
It reached a trusted professional directly, even though talking in person felt hard.
How might Mr Mridul feel reading the email?
Mr Mridul probably feels concerned but glad Irfan reached out, and will want to meet soon.
Brittany got a 78 on her first test. After her second test, her average rose to an 81. What grade did she get on her second test?

First multiply her average grade by the number of tests she took to find the total number of points she scored: 81 points * 2 = 162 points
Then subtract the number of points she scored on her first exam to find how many points she scored on her second exam: 162 points - 78 points = 84 points
The answer is 84.
My friend has a fever and missed our exam. Write a 40-word message to cheer her up.

Hey Sonali, I'm sorry you're unwell and had to miss the exam. Please don't worry about it right now. Just rest, have some warm soup and sleep as much as you can. I'll bring you my notes once you feel better.

When I was eleven I got twenty rupees pocket money every week. I spent it on chips and cola with my friend Jasleen after school.
I'm Tanuja. Then I saw a cricket bat in the sports shop. It cost a lot more than I had.
I made a chart on my wall, with a box for each week. Every time I skipped the snacks, I coloured a box. Some weeks I gave in and bought chips. Jasleen teased me.
After four months, I had enough. I bought the bat myself.
When I hit my first six with it, I felt richer than any packet of chips.

What did Tanuja see in the sports shop?
A cricket bat.
How did Tanuja feel on hitting the first six with the new bat?
Tanuja felt proud and happy, richer than any packet of chips.

A chart to track each week, and choosing the bat over snacks most weeks.

Jasleen may feel impressed, even after teasing Tanuja.

At the tractor dealer's tent at the Sonpur fair, the salesman slid a form across the table. "Only for fair days, Yogesh-bhai. Sign today and the rotavator comes free." Yogesh turned the pen over in his fingers. The man was friendly and the machine was shiny, but half the terms were printed so small he'd need Usha's reading glasses. "Give me all the terms in writing," he said. "I'll come back tomorrow." The salesman's smile thinned. "Tomorrow maybe the offer is gone." "Then it wasn't much of an offer." That night, under the lantern, Usha read every line aloud. The interest was higher than he'd been told, and the free rotavator had a charge buried on page three. Next morning they went to the cooperative society office and to another dealer at the far end of the fair, and compared. Yogesh walked past the first tent without stopping. The salesman called out a new, lower price. Yogesh just waved.

What did the salesman say would come free if Yogesh signed today?
The rotavator.
What was Yogesh feeling as he turned the pen in his fingers?
Yogesh felt tempted by the shiny machine but uneasy and cautious about the tiny print he couldn't read.
Which steps protected Yogesh?
Asking for all the terms in writing, waiting a night, having Usha read every line, and comparing with the cooperative and another dealer before deciding.
What does the salesman's new, lower price suggest?
It suggests the fair-days deadline was pressure rather than a real limit, and that the salesman still wanted the sale.

Zainab's diary, Sunday.
The market crashed this week, and my first reaction was to open my investment app and start moving things around. Maria stopped me on the phone: "Before you touch anything, check your emergency money."
So tonight I did. My monthly costs: rent, food, the metro card, my phone, the amount I send Ammi. Six months of that: I wrote the number down. Then I checked the savings account and the recurring deposit. I have almost five months.
So that's the real gap: one month short. If my company cut jobs, I might have to sell investments when they're at their lowest. That's the thing to fix, not the market.
My plan: for the next few months, extra goes into the savings account until it covers six months. I'm not touching the investments. I feel calmer than I did on Wednesday.

How many months did Zainab's savings cover?
Almost five months.
How does Zainab feel after checking?
Zainab feels calmer than on Wednesday, having found the real gap instead of reacting to the crash.
Why is the one-month gap the thing Zainab chose to fix, not the market?
Without a full cushion, a job loss could force selling at the lowest point; filling the gap removes that risk.
How does Maria's advice change Zainab's week?
Maria's advice stops a panicky reaction and turns it into a calm check of the safety net.

messages.content: Cindy tosses 5 dimes into the wishing pond.  Eric flips 3 quarters into the pond.  Garrick throws in 8 nickels.  Ivy then drops 60 pennies in.  If Eric dips his hands into the water and pulls out a quarter, how much money, in cents, did they put into the pond?

Cindy puts in 10 cents x 5 = 50 cents.
Eric puts in 3 x 25 cents = 75 cents.
Garrick puts in 8 x 5 cents = 40 cents.
Ivy puts in 60 x 1 cent = 60 cents.
After Eric pulls out a quarter, he has still left in the pond, 75 - 25 = 50 cents.
Together, they put into the pond, this amount of money, 50 + 50 + 40 + 60 = 200 cents
The answer is 200.

The first semester nearly swallowed me. I'm Hafsa, and I went from a school where bells told me when to breathe to a college where I had three lectures a day and nothing else.
The free hours disappeared. I'd plan to study after lunch, then scroll, nap, chat, and suddenly it was dinner. By October I was behind in two subjects and panicking every night.
My classmate Darshan kept a paper planner. I laughed at it. Then I borrowed his method: every Sunday, block the week's library hours like they're lectures. Treat them as real.
It felt fake at first. But after three weeks I was caught up in one subject.
I still waste time. Less now. And I've stopped laughing at planners.

What did Darshan keep?
A paper planner.
How did Hafsa feel by October?
Hafsa felt panicked and behind, anxious every night.
What made Darshan's method useful for Hafsa?
Treating library hours as real lectures gave shape to free time that had no bells or parents structuring it.
How might Darshan feel if Hafsa told him the planner helped?
Darshan might feel amused and pleased, maybe a bit vindicated after being laughed at.
Airport par poochna hai "Baggage kahan se milega?"
Ask: "Where can I collect my luggage?" or "Where is the baggage claim?"

For most of last semester, Mohit told me I was the only person on campus who got him. "You're more of a brother than my own brother," he said once, after we'd talked until 3 a.m. about his parents' divorce. I felt proud to be that person.
Then in November I missed his call because I was at my cousin's engagement. By morning I had eleven messages: I was useless, fake, just like everyone else. I read them in the bathroom, shaking. My first instinct was to fire back something equally cruel. I didn't. I wrote, "I'm sorry I missed your call. I was at an engagement. I care about you, and I won't be spoken to like this. Let's talk when things are calmer."
He didn't reply for four days. Then: "Chai?" We're friends again, sort of. I, Divyansh, keep my phone on me now, but I don't pick up at 3 a.m. any more.

How many messages had Mohit sent by morning?
Eleven.
How did Divyansh feel reading the messages in the bathroom, and why?
Shaken and bewildered, because the friend who had called him more of a brother than a brother suddenly called him useless over one missed call.
Which choice did Divyansh make instead of firing back, and why did it help?
He apologised for the missed call, said he cared, and set a clear limit on how he would be spoken to, which kept the friendship possible without accepting the insults.
What might Mohit have been feeling when the call went unanswered?
Probably alone and panicky, perhaps fearing being abandoned, which made one missed call feel like proof that Divyansh didn't care.
One-third of a class of 39 students took part in a math competition. How many students did not participate in the competition?

Since one-third of the class participated, there are 39 * 1/3 = 13 students who participated in the competition.
This means that 39 - 13 = 26 students did not participate.
The answer is 26.
Now you try: P(A) = 0.2; find P(not A).
The answer is 0.8.

Camille saw 3 cardinals and four times as many robins as cardinals while bird watching. She also saw twice as many blue jays as cardinals and 1 more than three times as many sparrows as cardinals. How many birds did Camille see?

Camille saw 3 x 4 = 12 robins.
She also saw 3 x 2 = 6 blue jays.
Triple the number of cardinals is 3 x 3 = 9.
So, she saw 9 + 1 = 10 sparrows.
Therefore, Camille saw 3 + 12 + 6 + 10 = 31 birds.
The answer is 31.

Ira stared at the biology notes she had highlighted in three colours, and felt like a fraud. Her parents had wanted her to be a doctor since she was seven, and everyone in the lane knew. Her father had a photo of a white coat framed above the radio. But the only thing she did well after class was draw the tea stall and its regulars. Pema, the art teacher at the school, said one afternoon, "Tell them what you love, Ira. They can't guess." At dinner she put down her spoon. "Papa, Mummy, I want to study design. I'll finish my degree first, and if it doesn't work in two years, I'll take the exam again." Her mother's eyes filled. Her father was silent for a long time. "We're worried," he finally said. "We'll think." Ira nodded. It wasn't a yes, but it was true.

What did Ira's father have framed above the radio?
He had a photo of a white coat framed above the radio.
Why did Ira feel like a fraud?
She was working towards her parents' dream of becoming a doctor when what she really loved was drawing.
What did Ira do that was wise at dinner?
She said honestly what she loves and offered a path with a fallback, and accepted her parents' worry.
How might Ira's parents see her news?
As a frightening change to a dream they have held for years, since her mother's eyes filled and her father was silent.

Yusuf's group had three weeks to build a model water purifier and assumed there was plenty of time. They met once, in the first week, to choose a design, and never fixed dates. In week three, Ishita's family left for a wedding in another city and another member came down with a fever, so by Wednesday only Yusuf and one other were left. The exhibition was on Friday. How often did the group meet in the first three weeks?
The group met only once, in the first week.
What might Yusuf be feeling as water dripped while the judge waited?
Yusuf is probably embarrassed and frustrated, giving a half answer while the leak shows the rush.
What could the group have done at the start, and why?
They could have set dates for each stage and short check-ins, because a plan with dates shows problems early, before absences hit.
How might Ishita see the finished model?
Ishita likely feels guilty and awkward, having missed part of the work, which is why Ishita looked at the shoes.

"Amma, Papa, can we talk before you decide about the camp?" Swati asked after dinner, pulling a chair to the table.

Her mother, Leela, sighed. "The shop needs you in May. You know that."

"I know. But can I explain first?" Swati put a printout down. "This coding camp gives a certificate the college looks at. It's three weeks. If I get into computer science, that's why."

Her father looked at the paper. "We didn't know it was connected to college."

"So what does the shop really need?" Swati asked. "Every day? Or the weekends? Or just the stock-taking?"

Leela paused. "Mostly the Saturday rush and the stock-taking at the end of May."

"The camp ends on the 24th."

When does the camp end?
On the 24th.
How did Leela seem to feel when Swati first raised the camp?
Leela seemed tired and a bit resistant, sighing because she expected a fight about the shop.
What else could Swati offer to show she takes the shop's needs seriously?
She could offer to cover the Saturday rushes after the camp and all of the stock-taking, so her parents see a concrete plan.
How might Swati's father see the camp after the conversation?
Her father now sees it as linked to college, not just a holiday, which makes him willing to talk it through.

Planner's note — Ojas and Mitali, wedding on 12 February

I'm recording this because I want to use it with future couples.
When the family priest fixed 12 February as the date, most couples I know would panic. Ojas and Mitali sat in my office and started from the end.
"If the wedding is on the twelfth," Ojas said aloud, "the halls will be the hardest thing. Everyone wants February." So hall first, booked by the end of October.
Mitali went on: "Invitations need printing, and relatives abroad need six weeks' notice. So cards by mid-December." Tailoring came next: fittings need two tries, so cloth bought in November. Travel for Ojas's brother Pranav's family from Pune: tickets in December before the fares rise.
They wrote a month-by-month list on my whiteboard and photographed it.
What I did next: I called the hall that afternoon and held the date for them.

By when did Ojas and Mitali plan to book the hall?
By the end of October.
How did Ojas and Mitali seem to feel while working backward in the planner's office?
They seemed calm and focused rather than panicked, thinking aloud step by step from the fixed date.
What else could Ojas and Mitali do with their month-by-month list?
They could divide the items between them and check in weekly, so nothing on the list is missed.
How might Pranav see the plan for the family's travel?
Pranav's family would likely feel reassured and included, since tickets are planned early rather than rushed at the end.
