In their Bengaluru office, Uday pitched his idea for the new app feature with full energy: hands moving, voice rising, big smile. His teammates laughed and nodded along.
Lalremsiami, the senior designer, listened with a calm, still face. She didn't smile or nod. She took a few notes.
Uday faltered. He finished quickly and sat down, sure she hated it.
After the meeting he almost went straight to his desk. Instead he stopped by hers. "Can I ask what you thought? I couldn't read you at all."
She looked up, surprised. "I liked it a lot. I was listening carefully." She showed him her notes, three ideas to make it better. "In my family, you stay quiet and still when someone important is speaking. It's a sign of respect."
Uday laughed. "In mine, if you're quiet, something's wrong."
"Then we'll both have to ask more."

How many ideas did Lalremsiami write in her notes?
Three ideas to make it better.
What was Uday feeling when Lalremsiami kept a still face?
Uday felt anxious and discouraged, faltering and sure she hated the idea.
What did Uday do that avoided a misunderstanding?
He asked Lalremsiami directly what she thought instead of assuming her calm face meant disapproval.
How does Lalremsiami see a quiet, still face while listening?
She sees it as a sign of respect, learned in her family, not as coldness or disinterest.
Pam has 10 bags of apples. Each of her bags has as many apples as 3 of Gerald's bags. If Gerald's bags have 40 apples each, how many apples does Pam have?

Each of Pam's bags contain 40*3=120 apples.
Pam has 120*10=1200 apples.
The answer is 1200.

For three Saturdays running, Tariq cancelled. First a double shift at the café in Leeds, then a group project, then a flu. Each time Alejandro replied "no worries 👍" from Valencia, and each time the thumbs-up felt a little colder. They had shared a flat for two years at university; now they barely shared a sentence. On a Sunday night Tariq finally wrote the message he had been avoiding: "I keep promising big calls and then bailing. Can we do small instead? Fifteen minutes while I walk to work on Tuesdays?" Alejandro's reply took an hour. "Honestly I thought you were drifting on purpose. Tuesdays. I'll be making lunch, you'll hear pans." The first Tuesday call lasted twenty-two minutes. Tariq arrived at work late and didn't mind at all.

Where does Alejandro live now?
In Valencia.
What was Tariq feeling each time the thumbs-up arrived?
Tariq felt guilty and uneasy, sensing the friendship cooling with every cancellation.
Why was Tariq's new plan more likely to work than the big calls?
Fifteen minutes during an existing walk fits around shifts and projects, so it is a promise small enough to keep.
How had Alejandro been seeing Tariq's cancellations?
Alejandro thought Tariq was drifting on purpose, so the cheerful replies probably hid hurt and disappointment.

Robi and Rudy contributed money to start a business that could earn them profit. Robi contributed $4000, and Rudy contributed 1/4 more money than Robi. If they made a profit of 20 percent of the total amount and decided to share the profits equally, calculate the amount of money each got.

If Robi contributed $4000, then Rudy contributed 1/4*4000 = $1000 more.
The total amount of money Rudy contributed is $4000+$1000 = $5000
Together, the contributed a total of $5000+$4000 = $9000
They made a 20% profit, a total of 20/100*$9000 = $1800
When they decided to share the profit equally, each received $1800/2 = $900
The answer is 900.
How can we remember the shapes of 7, 8 and 9?

Answer: 7 is a hockey stick (or a cliff). 8 is a snowman. 9 is a balloon on a string.

Hide numeral cards around the room; the child finds each one and names it.
Why is a raga not just a scale?
Because a scale only lists notes, while a raga also defines movement, note importance, mood, phrases, and behavior.

Sit, Nirmala. I'm Gurpreet, and you asked why I never chase people who go quiet, so I will tell you about my closest friend, Harjit. For months she stopped answering my calls. No fight, no reason. I wanted to send angry messages and put something sharp on my status, and my thumb was on the button more than once. I didn't. I wrote one warm message: "I miss you, and I'm here if you ever want to talk." Nothing came back. It hurt for a long time. But I stopped waiting by the phone, and I kept the door open in my heart, not in my inbox. Harjit never answered, and I have made peace with that, and I still smile at our old photographs.

How many warm messages did Gurpreet send Harjit?
Gurpreet sent one warm message.
What did Gurpreet want to do when Harjit went quiet, and what did Gurpreet do instead?
Gurpreet wanted to send angry messages and post something sharp, but wrote one warm message and then stopped waiting.
What can Nirmala learn about handling a friend who disappears?
Send one kind message, then let go if there is no answer, instead of accusing or posting about it publicly.
How might Harjit's silence look from Harjit's side?
It may have come from Harjit's own reasons that Gurpreet never learned, so it does not prove Gurpreet did wrong.

Teacher's note, Class 3B, Monday. Rashmi, who joined us from another school in June, had not answered a single question aloud in three weeks. Today, in our reading circle, she raised her hand to guess what 'enormous' meant. She said 'very noisy'. A few children started to smile; Chandrika whispered, 'Remember our rule,' and they stopped. I thanked Rashmi, said noisy things are often enormous, like thunder, and asked the class to help her finish the idea. Chandrika offered 'very big'. Rashmi nodded, smiling. In maths she raised her hand twice more. I will pair Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading, and I'll mention the brave guessing to her mother at pickup today.

What guess did Rashmi give for 'enormous'?
'Very noisy'.
What does Rashmi raising her hand twice more in maths suggest?
She felt safer and more confident after her wrong guess was treated kindly.
What did the teacher plan next to build on today?
Pairing Rashmi with Chandrika for this week's reading and mentioning the brave guessing to her mother at pickup.
How might Chandrika see her part in the reading circle?
Chandrika seems to feel responsible for the class rule, gently stopping the smiles and then helping finish Rashmi's idea.

a) Milk is more than Juice.
b) Water is the most.
c) Tea is 3 more than Milk.
d) Juice and Water together are 5.

Outside the air was sweet, the sun shone, and the birds sang, and it seemed as if all nature were tuned to a different pitch. There was gladness and mirth and peace everywhere, for we were at rest ourselves on one account, and we were glad, though it was with a tempered joy.

How does the morning outside feel to the group?

The air is sweet, the sun shines and the birds sing, as if all nature were tuned to a different pitch. There is gladness, mirth and peace everywhere, because the group is at rest on one account, though their joy is a quiet one.

I've shared a desk pod with Arnab in the software team for a year, and I thought I knew how he worked: fast, a bit impatient. So last week surprised me. The new hire, Kavita, was stuck on a bug, and I watched her walk to Arnab looking miserable. He didn't grab her keyboard. He asked, 'What have you tried so far?' She listed three things. He nodded and said only, 'Check what the date looks like before it reaches the function.' Then he went back to his own screen. It took her forty minutes. He could have fixed it in five; I know, because he fixed mine in five last year. When she found it, she practically ran to his desk. I don't know what he was thinking. But I'm Zubin, and I noticed Kavita never came back with that kind of bug again.

What did Arnab ask Kavita first?
'What have you tried so far?'
What might Arnab have been feeling while Kavita took forty minutes?
Arnab was probably tempted and a little impatient, knowing he could fix it in five minutes, but chose to hold back.
Why was the single hint about the date better than fixing the bug?
It pointed Kavita to the right place while leaving the finding to her, so she learned the pattern and didn't repeat the bug.
How might Kavita have felt when she found the bug?
Kavita likely felt thrilled and proud, practically running to Arnab's desk 🎉

In the May heat, the kindergarten garden was dusty and dry. Sarita Ma'am brought out clay bowls. "The birds are thirsty too. Who wants to fill them?"
Ojas, six, filled one so carefully he didn't spill a drop, then watered the wilting marigolds.
Near the gate, his classmate Dev lifted his foot over a line of ants. Ojas grabbed his arm. "Don't! They're carrying food home."
Dev frowned, then crouched down to look. "They're so tiny."
The next morning, Ojas ran in first to check the bowls. A sparrow was drinking. He froze, holding his breath, so he wouldn't scare it.

What was the sparrow doing the next morning?
A sparrow was drinking from the bowl.
Why did Ojas hold his breath when he saw the sparrow?
He felt excited and protective, wanting to watch without frightening the bird away.
How could Sarita Ma'am build on what Ojas did?
She could give children small daily jobs, like filling bowls and watering plants, and praise gentle choices like protecting the ants.
How might Dev see the ants after crouching down?
Dev might start seeing them as tiny living things with homes, not just something to step on, which could make him gentler.
Describe my grandfather telling stories in one sentence of exactly eleven words.
My grandfather tells wonderful stories while we all sit beside him.
My mother asked me to buy vegetables for the week. I have never done it.

Start with basics: onions, potatoes, tomatoes, and a few green vegetables like beans, spinach and gourds. Choose firm, bright vegetables and avoid ones with soft spots. Ask the seller for a fair price.
Her list says lauki, bhindi and capsicum. I am Arjun.
Arjun, pick lauki that is firm and light green with smooth skin. For bhindi, choose small ones that snap easily when bent. Capsicum should be shiny and firm with no wrinkles.
How much of each should I buy?
For a small family, about half a kilo of each is usually enough for a few meals. Ask your mother how many people are eating. If vegetables are cheap, you can buy a little more.
The seller gave me a very high price for the bhindi.
Ask at one or two other stalls before buying. Prices differ, and it is fine to say politely that you will check elsewhere. Your mother will be happy that you were careful with her money, Arjun.

Claudia has 122 ounces of water and is filling up cups. She has 8-ounce glasses, 5-ounce glasses, and 4-ounce glasses. If she fills six 5 ounce glasses and four 8 ounce glasses, how many 4 ounce glasses can she fill with the remaining water?

She has used 32 ounces on 8-ounce glasses because 4 x 8 = 32
She has used 30 ounces on the 5-ounce glasses because 6 x 5 = 30
She has used 62 ounces in total because 32 + 30 = 62
She has 60 ounces left because 122 - 62 = 60
She can fill fifteen four-ounce glasses because 60 / 4 = 15
The answer is 15.

Dear Mrs Bhatt,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud without crying. For about six weeks, Kamal has blocked me in the corridor outside the science lab and pushed my bag off my shoulder. He calls me names and the others laugh. I have told my mother I have a stomach ache four times so I don't have to come to school, but it isn't true. I feel sick when the bell rings. I used to think I must have done something to deserve it. I've started to believe that isn't true. I wrote down the dates: 3, 10 and 17 September, and yesterday. I stay near Anaya and Meher at break, and they don't laugh. Please can we talk after class on Monday? I'd rather not do this alone.

Arohi

Mrs Bhatt's reply, the same afternoon: Thank you for telling me, Arohi. This is not your fault. Stay after the last bell today and we'll see the counsellor together.

For about how long has Kamal been blocking Arohi in the corridor?
He has been doing it for about six weeks.
What is Arohi feeling about school, and how do you know?
Dread and fear. Arohi writes of feeling sick when the bell rings and of claiming stomach aches four times to avoid coming.
What steps has Arohi taken that a wise person would suggest?
Arohi wrote down the dates, stays near supportive friends at break and is asking the teacher for a talk instead of facing it alone.
How might Mrs Bhatt feel on reading the letter?
Probably concerned and glad Arohi trusted her; she replies that same afternoon, says it is not Arohi's fault and arranges to see the counsellor together.

But there were so many hillocks and banks to climb and pass, that, at length, I began to be weary, and told her we must halt, and retrace our steps. I shouted to her, as she had outstripped me a long way; she either did not hear or did not regard, for she still sprang on, and I was compelled to follow. Finally, she dived into a hollow; and before I came in sight of her again, she was two miles nearer Wuthering Heights than her own home; and I beheld a couple of persons arrest her, one of whom I felt convinced was Mr. Heathcliff himself.

Tell me in one line what happens here.
The narrator tires and asks the girl to turn back, but she runs on and is stopped near Wuthering Heights by two people, one likely Heathcliff.
There are 88 dogs in a park. 12 of the dogs are running. Half of them are playing with toys. A fourth of them are barking. How many dogs are not doing anything?

88/2 = 44 dogs are playing with toys.
88/4 = 22 dogs are barking.
88-12-44-22 = 10 dogs are not doing anything.
The answer is 10.

It was the first chilly week of Diwali holidays, and only a few children came to the daycare centre. Rajni sat by the window, crying because her mother had gone to work.
Pranav, five, watched her for a while. Then he opened his tiffin, took out his coconut biscuit and broke it in two. He walked over and held out the bigger half.
"For you. Don't cry."
Rajni sniffed and took it. Pranav patted her arm, pat, pat, pat, the way his grandmother did for him. They ate the biscuit together, looking out at the rangoli in the yard.

What did Pranav take out of his tiffin?
He took out his coconut biscuit.
Why did Pranav give Rajni the bigger half of his biscuit?
He felt sorry for her and cared about her sadness, so he wanted to comfort her the way his grandmother comforted him.
How could a daycare teacher encourage kindness like Pranav's?
Notice and warmly name it, and give children small chances to comfort and share with friends.
What is it like for Rajni when Pranav pats her arm?
She feels less alone and comforted, able to stop crying and eat with him.

"Mumma, can I have another toffee?"
"You had one after lunch, Nandini. That's it for today."
"Just one small one!"
"No, sweetheart. The jar is closed now."
Nandini's chin wobbled. Her feet began to stamp on the floor, harder and harder.
"No! No! It's not fair!"
"I know you really wanted it."
"I hate you! I hate you, Mumma!"
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge and knelt down. "You're very cross."
"Go away!" Nandini shouted, stamping again, her cheeks wet and hot.

Where did Sunaina put the jar?
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge.
Why did Nandini shout "I hate you" at her mother?
She wanted the toffee badly and the no felt unfair; the anger hit her body first, so her feet stamped and the hurtful words burst out before calmer ones could.
What turning point is open to Sunaina in this moment?
She can keep the jar closed, stay close and name the anger calmly, which shows Nandini that the feeling is allowed but shouting will not change the answer.
How might Sunaina feel hearing "Go away!" right after she knelt down?
She may feel pushed away and a little hurt, yet understand that Nandini is overwhelmed, so she might wait nearby rather than leave.

The stadium in Amman was roaring. Nour, holding her father's hand, had never been to a real match. When the referee gave a penalty against their team, the crowd around her stood up and shouted words Nour was never allowed to say.
She shouted them too, at the top of her lungs. It felt like flying. Her friend Ada, beside her, was jumping and shoving forward with the men in front.
Nour pushed too, toward the railing, not thinking about anything.
Her father tightened his grip and pulled her back. “Nour. Look at me.” His voice was calm. She looked up, breathing fast. Suddenly she heard herself, and her cheeks went hot.
“We cheer,” he said. “We don't push.”

Which city was the stadium in?
It was in Amman.
How did Nour feel as she shouted with the crowd?
She felt excited and swept along, like she was flying, without thinking about herself.
How did her father help, and why did it work?
He held her firmly, spoke calmly and made her look at him, which broke the crowd's spell and kept her safe.
How might Ada have felt pushing forward with the men?
Ada was probably thrilled and carried along too, not noticing the risk of the crowd pushing.

We have just received intelligence that another child, missed last night, was only discovered late in the morning under a furze bush at the Shooter's Hill side of Hampstead Heath, which is, perhaps, less frequented than the other parts. It has the same tiny wound in the throat as has been noticed in other cases. It was terribly weak, and looked quite emaciated. It too, when partially restored, had the common story to tell of being lured away by the "bloofer lady."

What do the children in these cases have in common?
Each has been found weak and thin with the same tiny wound in the throat. When they recover enough to talk, they all tell of being lured away by the "bloofer lady".
What is cardboard made of? I need some for a project.

Cardboard is thick, stiff paper that is used for boxes and for making models. It is a noun, and we do not usually say "a cardboard" for the material.
Example: We cut a piece of cardboard into the shape of a boat.

A group of people contains men, women, and children. The number of men is twice the number of women, and the number of women is 3 times the number of children. If the number of children is 30, how many people does this group contain?

The number of women in the group is 3 women/child * 30 children = 90 women.
The number of men in the group is 2 men/woman * 90 women = 180 men.
The total number of people in the group is 180 men + 90 women + 30 children = 300 people.
The answer is 300.

Wed, 11:15 pm
Spent three hours convinced the survey form was broken. The average age of my respondents came out as 94. Obviously the form was scrambling the data. I wrote an angry message to the course helpdesk and told Sunaina the university's tools are a joke.
Sunaina, very calmly: "Did you look at the raw answers?"
No. Why would I? I built the form myself, I know what's in it.
Except... row 38: someone typed their birth year, 1998, instead of their age. Row 71: "20 yrs". Two more birth years further down. The form was fine. My assumption that everyone would type a plain number was the broken part.
Deleted the helpdesk message before sending it. Mildly mortified.
Note to self: check what I assumed before blaming the machine.
Ankita

What did row 38 contain instead of an age?
A birth year, 1998.
How does Ankita feel on finding the birth years?
Ankita feels mildly mortified, embarrassed about the angry helpdesk message and the three hours spent blaming the form.
What could Ankita do first the next time a result looks impossible?
Look at the raw answers and list what was assumed, such as everyone typing a plain number, before deciding the tool is broken.
How might Sunaina see the whole evening?
Sunaina stays calm and maybe a little amused, seeing a simple check Ankita skipped, and helps with one question instead of arguing.

What did Pip feel about the old house, and how did it affect him?

So unchanging was the dull old house, the yellow light in the darkened room, the faded spectre in the chair by the dressing-table glass, that I felt as if the stopping of the clocks had stopped Time in that mysterious place, and, while I and everything else outside it grew older, it stood still. Daylight never entered the house as to my thoughts and remembrances of it, any more than as to the actual fact. It bewildered me, and under its influence I continued at heart to hate my trade and to be ashamed of home.
It seemed to stand still in time, as if stopping the clocks had stopped time itself. Its gloom made him go on hating his trade and feeling ashamed of home.

I'm Deepak. In Class 6 science, Elizabeth ma'am was explaining rainbows and I asked, "But why are the colours always in the same order?" She sighed. "Don't ask silly questions, Deepak. Stick to the book." A few people laughed. My face went hot.
After that I kept my hand down. I still wondered about things, like why ink spreads in water and why the moon has days, but I wrote them in the back of my notebook instead. I stopped asking anyone. Sometimes, when I see a rainbow, the question comes back and sits with me.

What did Deepak ask about rainbows?
Deepak asked why the colours are always in the same order.
What did Deepak feel when Elizabeth ma'am said not to ask silly questions?
Deepak felt embarrassed and ashamed, with a hot face, and stopped raising a hand.
What could a teacher do so that a student like Deepak keeps asking?
A teacher could welcome the question, or say it is a good one and give a moment for it later. A question box could also give a safe place.
How might the classmates who laughed have seen the moment?
They may have followed the teacher's tone and thought the question was silly, without realising how it landed on Deepak.

The warden's office had one fan and three chairs. Varun sat in the one nearest the door.
“The photo of Swati in the dining hall,” Mrs Rao said. “Food on her kurta, her face mid-sneeze. It went to the whole hostel group. From your number.”
“Ma'am, the seniors asked me to post it. It's a thing they do, the juniors have to share funny pics. If I refused, they'd target me next.”
“Who took the photo?”
“I did. But they said to.”
Outside, Swati was waiting on the bench to give her statement. She had skipped two meals since Friday.
Mrs Rao leaned forward. “The seniors will be spoken to. That's my job. But whose thumb pressed send, Varun?”
He looked at the floor. The seniors felt very far away now, and Swati was twelve feet from the door.
“Mine,” he said. “I'll delete it and tell her myself.”

Where was the photo of Swati taken?
It was taken in the dining hall, with food on her kurta and her face mid-sneeze.
Why did Varun feel the seniors were to blame?
He was scared of being targeted next, so doing what they asked felt like it wasn't really his choice.
Which question from Mrs Rao worked, and why?
Asking “whose thumb pressed send”; it separated the seniors' pressure from Varun's own action without letting either off.
How has the photo affected Swati?
Swati has been hurt enough to skip two meals since Friday and has to sit outside waiting to give a statement.

Manav had wanted to learn chess ever since the big tournament on television, but hobbies always melted into the evening. So he took a pencil to the family timetable pinned in the kitchen. Homework finishes by five. Tuesday and Saturday, five-thirty to six-thirty: chess. He wrote it in blue ink. At dinner he read it out to his mother Minakshi and his sister Indu. "Those are my chess hours. Please do not plan anything else then." Indu snorted; Minakshi smiled and moved the shopping trip to Wednesday. On Tuesday Manav set up the board at five-thirty exactly, and the house went quiet around him.

On which days did Manav plan his chess hour?
Manav planned his chess hour on Tuesday and Saturday.
What was Manav feeling as he read the timetable aloud at dinner?
Hopeful and a little nervous about whether the family would respect his time.
What could Manav do if something clashes with a chess slot?
Swap the slot to another day and tell the family, because a moved slot keeps the routine going.
How might Minakshi see Manav's timetable?
As a sign of real commitment, since she smiled and moved the shopping trip to Wednesday. 🙂

Manjula, Arnab's mother, pushes the toy train through a cardboard tunnel.
Arnab, eleven months, stares at the tunnel entrance.

She pushed a toy train through a cardboard tunnel.

She's delighted and laughs, seeing that he has learned where the train will appear.

Wednesday
New plan with Alka. I'm Gurleen, her mentor on the audit team, and I've been worried.
She's been here three weeks and keeps saying the stock audit is "basic." Yesterday she marked a warehouse check as complete without matching the serial numbers. When Rohit laughed at her in front of everyone, she only got more defensive: "It's fine, I know what I'm doing."
So today I tried something else. I sat with her privately and said, "Walk me through the check you did, step by step, like I'm new."
She started confidently. Then, at step four, she stopped. "And then I... match the serials? Oh." She went quiet.
I showed her two specific examples from last year where missed serials caused real problems.
She didn't argue. She asked if she could redo the warehouse check tomorrow. I said yes, and that I'd come along.

What did Alka skip in the warehouse check?
She skipped matching the serial numbers.
How did Alka feel when Rohit laughed at her?
She felt defensive and more stubborn, insisting she knew what she was doing.
Why did Gurleen's approach work better than Rohit's?
Asking Alka to explain the task step by step let her find the gap herself, and specific examples showed why it mattered, while ridicule only hardened her confidence.
What would change if Gurleen had laughed at Alka like Rohit did?
Alka would probably have dug in further and kept skipping steps, since ridicule made her more defensive rather than more careful.

Everyone in Sonipat knew about the wrestler from their district who had won at the national games. Suraj had her poster above his bed and watched every interview.

"I'm getting the same haircut," his friend Vikas announced on the way to the akhada. "And those gold shoes she wears."

Suraj laughed. But that night he watched her interview again, the part nobody shared. She talked about waking at four every day for eight years, about her coach making her repeat one move a thousand times, about crying after losses and coming back the next morning anyway.

The next day at the akhada, Suraj asked the coach, "Can I stay after for extra practice on the leg hold?"

"Why the leg hold?"

"She said she practised one move until it was boring. I want to do that."

The coach looked at him for a moment. "Good. Thirty minutes. Every day."

Vikas got the haircut. Suraj got blisters. Both of them grinned about it.

What did Vikas want to copy from the wrestler?
Vikas wanted the same haircut and her gold shoes.
What was Suraj feeling as he watched the interview again?
Suraj felt inspired and admiring, moved by the years of early mornings and the hard work behind her win.
What did Suraj choose to copy, and why was that wise?
Suraj chose to copy her habit of practising one move again and again, which builds real skill instead of just copying her look.
How might the coach see Suraj's request?
The coach seems pleased and impressed that Suraj wants to do the dull, repeated work that actually makes a wrestler better.

Hi Megha,

You asked how the wedding went. Short version: Kunal was there.

I walked into the hall and there he was, at the same table as Sonal and Rishi. Our first time in the same room since the breakup. My hands went cold. For a second I thought about leaving.

I didn't. I decided on three rules in the car park: say hello, keep it short, don't act.

So when he came over, I said, "Hi, Kunal. How's the new job?" He said good. I said, "Nice," and turned to Sonal's mother to admire her saree. That was it. No dramatic laughter, no cold shoulder.

The weird thing? By the dessert I'd almost forgotten he was there. I danced with the bride's cousins and came home tired and fine.

I think it gets easier every time. And I have a whole new life now; that helps.

Call me on Sunday?

Ishita

Whose table was Kunal sitting at?
He was sitting at the same table as Sonal and Rishi.
How did Ishita feel on first seeing Kunal?
Ishita felt anxious, hands going cold, and briefly thought of leaving.
What three rules did Ishita set, and why did they help?
Say hello, keep it short, and don't act; they let the meeting stay polite and brief without performing for anyone.
How might Megha feel reading this email?
Megha would likely feel relieved and proud that the evening went so calmly.

Tuan's mother had just been diagnosed, and he told Yuki over noodles in a small Osaka restaurant, his voice breaking.
Yuki felt a wave of fear rise in her chest, as if it were her own mother. She put down her chopsticks and let herself breathe out slowly, feeling her feet on the floor. The wave eased. What was left was warmth.
"That's so hard," she said. "What would help you this week?"
Tuan thought. "Honestly? Someone to walk the dog. I'm at the hospital every evening."
"I can do Tuesdays and Thursdays."
On the train home, Yuki noticed she was tired. She messaged her sister to cancel their late film and went to bed. If she was going to walk the dog for weeks, she needed to be rested for it.

Which days did Yuki offer to walk the dog?
Tuesdays and Thursdays.
How did Yuki's feeling change after she breathed out slowly?
The wave of fear eased, as if it were her own mother, and what was left was warmth: calm concern instead of panic.
Why was asking Tuan what would help better than guessing?
Tuan named something practical, dog walking, that Yuki could actually do, so her care met a real need.
How is Tuan affected when Yuki offers to walk the dog?
He probably feels relieved and less alone, with one worry lifted while he visits the hospital every evening.

Monday. Darshan couldn't see how 0.5 and 0.5 made anything. His friend Kunal tipped two fifty-paise coins into his palm. "Half a rupee each. How much?" Darshan pushed them together. "One rupee." He wrote 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 and underlined it twice.
Wednesday. Darshan tried 1.25 + 0.75 with coins from his tin box, then on paper. Two. He didn't need the coins for the next three sums.
Friday. The class test had 2.75 + 1.5. Darshan lined up the points, added, and wrote 4.25. He sat back, smiling, and turned to the harder page.

What did Darshan try with coins on Wednesday?
He tried 1.25 + 0.75 with coins from his tin box.
What was Darshan feeling on Friday when he sat back smiling?
He felt confident and proud, because the small wins with coins had prepared him for 2.75 + 1.5.
Why did starting with coins work better than jumping straight to the test sums?
Each easy success showed him decimals made sense, so he trusted himself to try the next, bigger size.
How might Kunal see his coin trick working?
Kunal only tipped two coins into Darshan's palm, so seeing him move on to harder sums may make Kunal feel pleased to have helped.

messages.content:
Retell this scene using reported speech instead of dialogue.

"You broke my kite!" Nitin shouted on the Sankranti terrace.
Siddharth, five, looked at the torn paper. "I didn't mean to."
"But you did!"
Siddharth's lip wobbled. Their grandfather said, "What can you do now?"
Siddharth thought. "Say sorry?"
"And?"
"Fix it?"
He found tape and held the paper while Grandpa stuck it. "Sorry, Nitin."
Nitin sniffed. "Okay. You can fly it with me."

On the Sankranti terrace, Nitin shouted that Siddharth had broken his kite. Siddharth, five, looked at the torn paper and said he had not meant to. Nitin said that he had done it anyway. Siddharth's lip wobbled. Their grandfather asked what he could do now. Siddharth thought and suggested saying sorry. His grandfather asked what else. Siddharth said he could fix it. He found tape and held the paper while Grandpa stuck it. Then he said sorry to Nitin. Nitin sniffed and said okay, and told him he could fly it with him.
Did they finally decide to move Holi celebrations to the ground behind the market?
I can't check that, because I can't see the latest decisions of local committees. The residents' association notice board will have the final plan.
Heloise has dogs and cats in the ratio of 10:17, with the total number of pets being 189. If she gives 10 dogs to her friend Janet, how many dogs does she remain with altogether?

The total ratio for the number of cats and dogs that Heloise has is 10+17 = 27
From the ratios, the fraction representing the number of dogs is 10/27, and this represents 10/27*189 = 70 dogs.
If Heloise gives 10 of her dogs to Janet, she remains with 70-10 = 60 dogs.
The answer is 60.

Gerald thought it would be funny to trick his coworker, who's allergic to peanuts, into eating a peanut butter cookie. When his coworker goes into anaphylactic shock and is taken to the hospital, Gerald is arrested. The judge sentences Gerald to 3 months for assault and 2 years for poisoning, then extends his sentence by 1/3 since this is Gerald's third offense. How many months does Gerald spend in jail?

First convert the 2-year sentence to months: 2 years * 12 months/year = 24 months
Then add the 3 months for assault: 24 months + 3 months = 27 months
Then find how long the 1/3 extension is: 27 months / 3 = 9 months
Finally, add up the three lengths of time to find the total sentence length: 27 months + 9 months = 36 months
The answer is 36.
Please write an email to a supplier asking for a quotation for 20 folding chairs for a community event on 12 December, with delivery by 10 December. About 55 words. I'm Mr. Nambiar.

Subject: Quotation for 20 Folding Chairs

Dear Sir or Madam,
We are organising a community event on 12 December and need 20 folding chairs. Could you please send us a quotation for them? We need the chairs delivered by 10 December. Kindly mention the delivery details in your reply. Thank you.
Yours faithfully,
Mr. Nambiar

My first office was the kind where my boss's "could you look at this?" meant "do it tonight." I'm Kalyani, and I learned that the hard way. On the other side, when I said, "It would be great to have some time on the report," Ritu, my boss, smiled and said "sure, sure," and nothing changed. I realised my request sounded like a hint. So I tried it differently: "Ritu, I would like two extra days, until Thursday, for the report. Can we confirm that?" She actually blinked. Then she said, "Fine, Thursday," and I emailed it right after. I still can't say whether she found me too direct 😅. But Thursday was Thursday.

What extra time did Kalyani ask Ritu for?
Kalyani asked for two extra days, until Thursday, for the report.
What does Ritu's blink suggest about how she felt?
It suggests surprise, since Kalyani's earlier hints were never stated so plainly; Ritu might also have felt slightly put off, which Kalyani admits she cannot know.
What did Kalyani do after Ritu agreed, and why does it help?
Kalyani emailed the agreement right away, so Thursday was written down and not left to memory.
What might Ritu have understood when Kalyani said "It would be great to have some time on the report"?
She may have taken it as a wish and not a request, which could be why she said "sure, sure" and nothing changed.

Monday: a new girl, Sabina, joined Class 9, and some girls started whispering about her clothes. Ritu, fourteen, noticed but stayed quiet, afraid she'd be next. Wednesday: the whispers turned into a nickname, shouted across the corridor. Sabina ate lunch alone. Ritu's stomach twisted. She picked up her tiffin and sat with Sabina. "Mind if I sit here?" That afternoon Ritu went to her class teacher and told her about the nickname; the teacher spoke to the girls before the last bell. Friday: two other girls joined their table. The nickname faded, though Ritu lost one friend over it.

What did the girls whisper about?
Sabina's clothes.
What was Ritu feeling when her stomach twisted?
She felt guilty and uneasy watching Sabina eat alone, torn between fear and doing what was right.
Which choices by Ritu made a difference?
Sitting with Sabina and telling the class teacher the same afternoon, so an adult acted quickly.
How might Sabina have felt when Ritu sat down?
Relieved and less alone, after days of isolation.
What is a jubilee? The town celebrates one this year.

A jubilee is a special anniversary of an important event, often the fiftieth, or a time of public joy. It is a noun.
Example: The school celebrated its golden jubilee with a big cultural program.

Early March: Vandana took her first online aptitude test on a Sunday afternoon. Result: "Medicine". She told her brother Amandeep, excited. That night she took another. Result: "Journalism". She frowned and took a third.

Mid-April: Her laptop had twelve result screenshots and forty career-list tabs open. "Top careers for creative people." "Careers with the best pay." "Careers AI can't replace." Each one said something different. Amandeep asked what she'd chosen. "I need more data," she said, not looking up.

End of May: The school's stream selection form was due Friday. On Thursday night, Vandana sat on her bed surrounded by printouts, eyes red. "Every test says something else," she whispered. "I don't know what I am."

On Friday afternoon, Amandeep found the form still in her bag. The deadline had passed at noon. The school assigned her the stream with seats left.

How many result screenshots did Vandana have by mid-April?
Twelve result screenshots.
How did Vandana feel on Thursday night?
She felt overwhelmed and lost, eyes red, saying she didn't know what she was.
What would have been a better approach than more tests?
Choosing a few options early, talking with a counsellor or people in those fields, and setting a personal decision date well before the deadline.
How might Amandeep have felt finding the form still in her bag?
Amandeep was probably upset and worried, having watched the search grow without any decision.

messages.content: There are 30 major league baseball stadiums. Zach has a goal to take his son to see at least one game at each one. He has calculated the average cost for them to travel and see a game will be $900 per stadium. Zach can save $1,500 per year for his baseball stadium trips. How many years will it take Zach to accomplish his goal?

The total cost would be $900 x 30 stadiums = $27,000.
Dividing the total cost by the amount Zach saves per year, we get $27,000 / $1,500/year = 18 years.
The answer is 18.
She is putting a green saree today and looks lovely. Is "putting" the right verb?

She is wearing a green saree today and looks lovely.
Why: word choice ("putting" -> "wearing").

Week one. Pankaj had left the "brotherhood" in March, but he still lay awake wondering if the leader was right that he was weak and ungrateful.
Week two. His cousin sent him a link to a long article by a former member of a similar group. Pankaj read it on the bus and nearly missed his stop. It described the same things: love at first, then guilt, then fear of leaving. He found two more accounts that evening. "It's not just me," he said aloud to the empty room.
Week four. He booked a session with Vasudha, a counsellor at the university clinic. She asked him to describe what the group did when people questioned the leader. As he explained, she named each step: isolation, guilt, pressure. "These are techniques," she said. "They work on many people."
Week six. Pankaj still felt embarrassed sometimes, but the word "weak" had stopped sounding true.

Who sent Pankaj the link to the article?
His cousin sent him the link.
How did Pankaj feel when he said, 'It's not just me'?
He likely felt relieved and less alone, seeing his experience described by others.
What else could Pankaj do to keep the self-blame from returning?
He could keep seeing Vasudha and talk with his cousin, so outside views stay close when doubts come back.
How might Vasudha see Pankaj's story?
Vasudha sees familiar techniques rather than personal weakness, and helps him name them so the blame shifts.

How do I fold a bedsheet?
And A tap fills 34 litres in the morning and 22 litres in the evening. How many litres is that?

1. Hold two corners and fold it in half twice. Then roll or fold it to fit the shelf.
2. That makes 56. Because 34 + 22 = 56.

Read this:

The store announcement said the shop would close in ten minutes, and Tanvir was still holding the grey wool coat. 'Eleven thousand,' he muttered, and hung it back. Ishita, who had come only to help him find something for his sister's engagement, watched him grab a checked shirt from the next rack. The tag said 2,800. 'After that coat, this is basically free,' Tanvir said, already walking to the counter. Ishita frowned. Last week in the market he had refused a 900-rupee shirt as 'too much'. The lights began switching off section by section. 'Tanvir, wait. It's still twenty-eight hundred,' she said. He stopped, the shirt against his chest, and read the tag again. 'Huh. Said like that, it isn't cheap at all.' The guard called last billing. He bought it anyway, but slowly.

What price was on the checked shirt's tag?
The tag said 2,800.
Why did Ishita frown when Tanvir called the shirt 'basically free'?
Ishita felt puzzled and concerned, remembering that only last week he had refused a 900-rupee shirt as too much.
What helped Tanvir see the price more clearly, and what else could help under time pressure?
Ishita saying the price out loud on its own helped; with the shop closing, stepping aside for a minute to ask whether he would want the shirt without having seen the coat could also help.
How did Tanvir experience the shirt's price before and after Ishita spoke?
Before, it felt 'basically free' next to the coat; once he heard the number by itself, it no longer seemed cheap, though he still bought it.

messages.content:
When this last task was accomplished it was noon, and the seamen went below to their dinner. Silence reigned over the before tumultuous but now deserted deck. An intense copper calm, like a universal yellow lotus, was more and more unfolding its noiseless measureless leaves upon the sea.

What does the deck look like at noon?
The seamen have gone below to dinner, so silence reigns over the deserted deck. A copper calm spreads over the sea like a yellow lotus.

Read this:

Chetan, two and a half, watched Mummy cuddle baby Tanuja all morning and felt left out. When Tanuja crawled off with his yellow truck, he lunged, grabbed it back and shouted. Lavanya, their mother, crouched beside him. "You are angry. Being angry is okay. Hitting is not." He held the truck a moment, then handed the rattle to his sister instead.

Later Tanuja began to cry, red-faced, and Chetan, passing, stopped. He pressed the rattle into her hand and patted her head. "Baby," he said. Lavanya smiled. "You gave Tanuja your rattle. That was kind." She did not ask him to do it again the next time.

The following afternoon Tanuja clutched a wooden duck to her chest, squealing as Chetan reached. She had no word for "mine". Lavanya knelt between them. "You are holding your duck tight. Chetan wants a turn. First Tanuja, then Chetan." She gave Chetan a spoon and a bowl to bang while he waited.

That evening, while Papa fed the baby, Lavanya sat with Chetan alone and read his truck book, and he leaned against her side.

What did Chetan give crying Tanuja?
He gave Tanuja his rattle.
How did Lavanya's response to Chetan's grabbing differ from her response to Tanuja clutching the duck, and what else did she give Chetan?

With Chetan she named his anger and said hitting is not okay. With Tanuja she named the tight hold and offered turns in order, "First Tanuja, then Chetan", instead of forcing sharing at once. She also gave Chetan time alone with her so he could feel he still mattered.
What was Chetan probably feeling as he watched Mummy cuddle Tanuja all morning?
He probably felt left out and jealous, since the baby was getting all the attention.
What could Lavanya do to help Chetan feel he still matters?
She could keep giving him time alone with her, as she did with the truck book, and warmly name his kind moments like giving the rattle.
Is the cobbler under the flyover working on Sundays?
I'm not sure if the cobbler works on Sundays, as I can't see his hours. If you pass by, a note on his stall may say; otherwise ask nearby shopkeepers.

The hostel dorm at the boarding school was quiet after lights-out. Jasleen, eleven, whispered from the top bunk.

"Gargi, can I tell you something? You can't tell anyone."

"Promise."

"I still sleep with my old cloth rabbit. I hide it under my pillow."

Gargi was silent for a moment. "I have a blanket from my Nani. I smell it when I miss home."

Jasleen laughed softly. "Really?"

"Really. Our secret."

The next morning, when a girl teased Jasleen about her pillow, Gargi changed the subject quickly. Jasleen caught her eye and smiled.

What does Jasleen hide under her pillow?
She hides her old cloth rabbit.
How did Jasleen feel when Gargi shared her own secret?
Jasleen felt relieved and close to Gargi, laughing softly.
How did Gargi show loyalty the next morning?
She changed the subject when someone teased Jasleen, protecting her secret.
How might Gargi feel sharing her Nani's blanket secret?
Gargi likely felt a bit shy but trusting, glad to have a close friend.

Sunday night

Day 21 of no sugary tea at the office. Wasim bet me I wouldn't last a week. 😅

The trick wasn't willpower. I figured out I always went for tea at 4 because I was bored and tired after lunch meetings. So now at 4 I walk around the building once and fill my water bottle. Stupid but it works. I also stopped keeping biscuits in my drawer. If they're not there, I don't eat them.

Two slip days. Both after bad calls. I noticed that. Stress is a cue too.

Maybe next I'll try the same trick for reading before bed. Put the book on my pillow so I have to move it.

Wasim owes me samosas.
— Hemant

What does Hemant do at 4 o'clock now?
Hemant walks around the building once and fills a water bottle.
What did Hemant realise when thinking about the two slip days?
Both came after bad calls, which showed Hemant that stress was also a trigger.
Why does removing the biscuits from Hemant's drawer help?
Without the easy cue in sight, Hemant doesn't have to fight the urge as often.
How might Wasim feel about losing the bet?
Wasim might grumble about the samosas but also be impressed, since Wasim didn't expect Hemant to last a week.

At ten, Kishore got stuck on the word "temperature" while reading aloud. His face went hot. He stuck out his tongue, wobbled his head and read the next line like a robot. The class burst into laughter, and Kishore bowed, but his hands shook on the book.
At twenty, Kishore sat at the back of a presentation. Anjali, at the front, said "1950" when she meant "1590" and did not notice. Kishore let out a low, quiet chortle, a private little sound. Anjali heard it. Her cheeks burned, and she stopped in the middle of a sentence. Afterwards, she said to her friend Himani, "He laughed at my mistake." Himani frowned. "Maybe ask him what it meant?" Anjali found Kishore outside. "Were you laughing at me?" Kishore blinked. "No, sorry, it was relief. I made the same slip in my presentation last week, and thought I was the only one. I should have kept quiet." Anjali let out a breath. "It sounded like mocking." He nodded. "I'll be careful how I laugh," he said.

What number did Anjali say instead of "1590"?
She said "1950" when she meant "1590".
How do the laughter at ten and the chortle at twenty show that the same sound can mean different things?

At ten Kishore made the class laugh with him, and it covered his shaking hands. At twenty his quiet chortle was relief, but aimed at Anjali's slip it sounded like mocking, so context decides what a laugh means.
What was Anjali feeling when she stopped mid-sentence and her cheeks burned?
She felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking that Kishore was laughing at her mistake.
What did Himani do well, and what could Kishore do next time?
Himani suggested asking what it meant instead of assuming. Kishore can keep quiet or say something kind when someone slips, so his sound is not read as mockery.

A sixty bulb watt uses 60 watts of power each day. If Allyn has 40 such bulbs in his house and pays an electricity bill of twenty cents per power watt used, calculate Allyn's total monthly expenses on electricity in June.

If each bulb uses 60 watts each day, the 40 bulbs that Allyn has uses 60*40 = 2400 watts of power each day.
In June, with 30 days, the bulbs will use 30*2400 = 72000 watts of power.
If Allyn is charged an electricity bill of twenty cents per power watt used, in June she will pay 72000*$0.20 = $14400
The answer is 14400.

Hostel warden's note, May. Written by Jaya.
Akash, a second-year student from the coastal belt, came to the office to share a plan he'd made after last year's storm, when the hostel lost power and phone signal for two days.
He had imagined the same thing happening again and asked, "What would I need if my phone was useless?" His answer was on a single laminated sheet: a paper list of his parents' numbers, the hostel landline, my office extension and the district control room; the location of the nearest relief centre marked on a printed map; and a note that he carries a small battery radio.
He also showed a plan he had agreed with his family: if nobody can reach anyone, his sister calls the hostel landline and Akash calls his uncle in another city.
What I did next: I asked if I could copy his sheet as a template for all residents, and he agreed.

What did Akash's laminated sheet include?
A paper list of important numbers, the nearest relief centre marked on a printed map, and a note that he carries a battery radio.
What worry was behind Akash's plan?
He was worried about being cut off again like last year, asking what he would need if his phone was useless.
What else could Akash's plan include?
It could include a meeting point on the campus in case the hostel itself has to be evacuated.
How does the warden see Akash's plan?
The warden sees it as useful enough to share with every resident, and asks to copy it as a template.

On the bench behind the science block, Rekha finally said it aloud: she liked Arjun from the debate club, and her parents were quietly counting rupees since Papa's shop went slow. Mehak listened, squeezed her hand and said, "Locked away, always." Rekha walked home lighter, as if someone had finally seen all of her.

Two weeks later Mehak was squeezed onto a bench with the swimming girls, who had never bothered to look her way. They were bored, and she wanted them to lean in. So she dropped it, half laughing: Rekha likes Arjun, and her family can't even manage the tuition fees. It's nothing, she told herself. Everybody talks.

That night Mehak lay awake with the swimmers' laughter still in her ears, and it no longer sounded like a win.

At the gate next morning, Karthik stopped Rekha. "Hey, sorry about the money stuff. Must be rough," he said, and a boy behind him snickered. Rekha's stomach dropped. Only one person knew. Across the yard Mehak was avoiding her eyes, and the girl she had shared a desk with since Class 7 looked like someone she had never met.

Where did Rekha tell Mehak about Arjun and the money trouble?
On the bench behind the science block.
How did Rekha's feelings after confiding differ from her feelings at the gate, and what changed between the two?
After confiding she felt lighter and seen, but at the gate her stomach dropped, because Mehak had let the secret slip to the swimming girls, so trust turned into shock.
What was Mehak feeling as she lay awake that night?
She felt uneasy and guilty; the swimmers' laughter no longer sounded like a win, which shows the moment weighed more than she had told herself.
What could Rekha do before deciding what to do about Mehak?
She could give herself a day to steady down, then tell Mehak plainly how the secret getting out felt and see whether Mehak owns what she did.

Read this:

Yogesh Bhaiya,
You're the only one I can tell. Mummy said, "You will not join the drama club. It's a waste of time before boards. I've decided." She didn't ask me anything. She just decided.
And now I've joined. Secretly. I tell her I'm at extra maths on Thursdays.
Here's the weird part. Before she banned it, I was only half interested. Now I think about it all the time. The ban made it feel like the most important thing in the world.
I know lying is wrong. I feel sick every Thursday evening. Maybe if she'd said, "Let's talk about how to fit it around studying," I'd have said, fine, after exams.
Should I tell her? How?
Sumit

What does Sumit tell Mummy about Thursdays?
Sumit tells her it's extra maths on Thursdays.
Why does the drama club feel so important to Sumit now?
Sumit felt controlled when Mummy decided without asking, so the ban made the club feel precious, even though Sumit feels sick about lying.
What could Sumit do next?
Sumit could tell Mummy the truth calmly and suggest a plan to fit drama around studying, perhaps with Yogesh's help.
How might Mummy feel if she found out about the Thursdays?
Mummy might feel hurt and worried about the lying, and might see that the firm ban pushed Sumit into secrecy.
Here's an idea: a story of about 100 words about a scarecrow who is lonely in a field until a little girl begins to talk to him each day. It must end with her bringing him a new hat.

A scarecrow stood alone in a wheat field. Birds sat on his arms and laughed at him. He felt very lonely. One morning a little girl walked by and said, "Good morning!" She came every day after that, telling him about her school and her friends. The scarecrow could not answer, but he listened happily. When winter came, his old hat was torn and the wind blew it away. The next day the girl came running with a bright new hat. "This is for you," she said, and smiled.
Our guests are waiting since one hour. Please fix.
Our guests have been waiting for one hour. Why: a continuing action needs the present perfect continuous; "for" gives the length.
Why can a tight jar lid sometimes be loosened by holding it under hot water?
The metal lid expands a little. Because the metal warms and expands slightly before the glass does, the lid becomes a little looser around the jar.
The school lunch break is 5/6 of an hour. How many minutes is that?

Answer: 50 minutes. 5/6 of 60 = (60 / 6) x 5 = 50.

An hour is 60 minutes. 1/6 of 60 is 60 / 6 = 10 minutes, so 5/6 is 5 x 10 = 50 minutes. Fractions of an hour are useful: 1/4 hour = 15 minutes, 1/2 hour = 30 minutes, 3/4 hour = 45 minutes, 1/3 hour = 20 minutes.
I forgot to return Jasmine's umbrella. A casual message to her saying I will bring it tomorrow, about 30 words. I'm Colin.

Hey Jasmine,
I'm sorry, I still have your umbrella! I forgot to return it. I will bring it tomorrow, I promise. Thank you for being so patient with me.
Colin
Spell "neighbour" for me. And why should we switch off lights when we leave a room?

1. It is n-e-i-g-h-b-o-u-r.
2. It saves electricity, which is useful because power is not free and should not be wasted.

In the common room of the nursing college hostel in Gangtok, Pema stared at the form for the overseas job fair. Her parents had sold half their cardamom field to pay her fees. On every call, Ama said, "Once you're working in Dubai, all our troubles will end."
"You've written your name four times and crossed it out four times," Gargi said.
"Because I want to work in the hill clinics here. And every time I think it, I feel like a thief."
"A thief of what?"
"Of their field."
Gargi put down her tea. "You can be grateful without living their plan. And you can't go to Dubai and resent them quietly for ten years."
Pema laughed shakily. "I'd be terrible at resenting quietly."
She didn't fill in the form. That evening she called home and told Ama and Apa what she wanted, and why, and that she would help the family in her own way. Ama said, "We'll talk more on Sunday." Pema took that as a start.

What had Pema's parents sold to pay the fees?
Half their cardamom field.
Why did Pema say she felt "like a thief"?
She felt guilty, as if choosing the hill clinics would waste the field her parents sold for her.
What did Pema choose instead of obeying or rebelling?
She left the form blank and called home to explain what she wanted and why, promising to help the family in her own way.
How might Ama see Pema's call?
Worried and unsettled, since she hoped Dubai would end their troubles, but open enough to talk more on Sunday.

Read this:

Monday. "Lakshmi, put your shoes on, we're leaving," Mama called from the kitchen. Lakshmi, building a block tower, said "Okay," and kept building. Five minutes later, still no shoes. Baljeet sighed loudly.
Wednesday. Baljeet tried something new. She walked over, knelt down to Lakshmi's height and waited until Lakshmi looked up. "Lakshmi. Shoes on, then tower later." Lakshmi blinked, nodded, and went.
Friday. Baljeet only had to kneel and say "Lakshmi" before Lakshmi put the block down herself and looked up, waiting for the words.

What was Lakshmi building on Monday?
She was building a block tower.
Why did Lakshmi say "Okay" but not put her shoes on?
She was absorbed and happy in her tower, so she heard the words without really taking them in, not because she was being defiant.
What small change helped Lakshmi listen?
Kneeling to her height, saying her name and waiting for her eyes before giving one short instruction.
How did Baljeet feel on Monday compared with Friday?
On Monday she felt frustrated enough to sigh loudly; by Friday she was probably relieved that Lakshmi looked up after just her name.

So we fell into other talk, and it was principally about the way by which we were travelling, and about what parts of London lay on this side of it, and what on that. The great city was almost new to her, she told me, for she had never left Miss Havisham's neighbourhood until she had gone to France, and she had merely passed through London then in going and returning. I asked her if my guardian had any charge of her while she remained here? To that she emphatically said "God forbid!" and no more.

What do we learn about how well Estella knows London?
Hardly at all. She had never left Miss Havisham's area until she went to France, and she only passed through London on the way there and back.
Our dog barks whenever he hear the doorbell. Please check.

Our dog barks whenever he hears the doorbell.
Why: subject-verb agreement ("he hear" -> "hears").

At the dairy cooperative office in a Kheda district village, the private buyer's agent arrived at noon and, before tea was even poured, said, "Thirty-two a litre, like always." Sangeeta, the secretary, sighed and began arguing for thirty-four. Santosh, the cooperative's new accountant, watched from his corner desk. Last season it had gone exactly like this: the agent spoke first, everyone fought near his number, and they settled a rupee above it. This time Santosh had spent the week calling three other buyers and checking the district rates; he had a range written on a card. He slid it across to Gopika, the chairperson. "Thirty-six to thirty-eight," she read aloud. "That's what the market says. Let's start there, not at thirty-two."

What price did the agent name before tea was poured?
The agent said thirty-two a litre.
What does Santosh's week of phone calls suggest he was worried about?
He seems worried the cooperative would again argue near the agent's number and settle just above it, so he wanted a figure grounded in the market before the talk began.
What could the cooperative do at the start of future talks?
They could agree their range from district rates before any meeting and state it first, so the buyer's opening number doesn't set the frame.
How might the agent react when Gopika reads out thirty-six to thirty-eight?
The agent may be surprised and have to argue from market rates instead of the usual thirty-two, which moves the talk in the cooperative's favour.

Devika read her admission email at the hostel desk and thought, they have made a mistake. At nineteen, she sat in the institute's lecture hall and watched classmates toss around big words. She assumed she had slipped in through a lucky gap, and that any week now someone would knock on her door with a correction. Afterwards she wrote the praise off as a kind gesture. Two days later a chart label was off by one column, and she stared at it for an hour, sure that this was the real proof of who she was.

Who told Devika she had topped the quiz?
Her roommate Lalremsiami told her, "You topped the quiz, Devika!"
How do Devika's reactions at nineteen and at twenty-four show the same pattern of thinking?

At nineteen she said the quiz was easy and thought she had slipped in through a lucky gap; at twenty-four she called the praise a kind gesture and the data already clean. Both times success was waved off, while the one chart error became her real proof.
What was Devika feeling when she said "It was easy" about the quiz?
She was uneasy and doubtful about herself. She could not accept the win, and feared it would soon be exposed as luck.
How could Yash or Lalremsiami help Devika see her results more fairly?
They could point to specific things she did, like the clean dashboard work, and encourage her to note the wins in writing beside the mistakes.

Grains.

The prices dropped the week Ritu's scooter needed a new part, and the bank's message about the monthly instalment arrived on the same morning. Hrithik, a colleague at the next desk, looked over. "Stop it for now. Wait till the bottom, then buy."
Ritu opened her notebook. On the first page, written before any fall: "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
"I can't tell where the bottom is," Ritu said. "Nobody can. But if the price is low, the same money buys more units."
"And the scooter?"
"I'll cut something else for a month."
The instalment went through at ten, and Ritu turned back to work with her stomach still tight.

What did Ritu's notebook say on its first page?
The notebook said "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
What was Ritu feeling as the instalment went through?
Ritu felt nervous, as the tight stomach shows, but she stuck to the rule she had set.
What could Ritu do if money ever feels too tight to keep the instalment?
Rather than changing the rule in a worried moment, Ritu could talk it through with a qualified adviser first and decide calmly.

Hrithik probably thought it risky and wanted to protect Ritu from more losses, which is why Hrithik said to stop it for now.

"Akash, did you read what you sent the club group?" Bhavna held up her phone.
"The trek message? Yeah. Clear, right?"
"It's ALL IN CAPITALS. 'EVERYONE MUST BRING SHOES. NO EXCUSES.' Three people asked if you were angry."

Where does the trek group meet?
At the college gate.
What was Akash feeling when Bhavna said three people asked if he was angry?
He winced, feeling embarrassed that his capitals read as shouting when he only wanted the message to stand out.
What changes made Akash's message clearer?
A short list of key facts and bold for only the one line that mattered, instead of all capitals in one long paragraph.
How did the club members read the first message?
They read the capitals as shouting, and three asked if Akash was angry.

Monday: Payal's science model had been crushed on the bus. When Chandrika Ma'am asked where it was, Payal answered in a tight, high voice: “I. Don't. Wednesday: At the water cooler, Chandrika Ma'am found Payal with her jaw clenched and eyes shining. This time she heard the strain differently. She handed her a cup. “Sip. Breathe out slowly with me.” After three breaths, Payal said in her normal voice, “Someone sat on it on the bus.” Friday: They rebuilt the model together at lunch, and Ma'am apologised for Monday.

What happened to Payal's science model?
It was crushed on the bus when someone sat on it.
What was Payal feeling when she spoke in a tight, high voice on Monday?
Payal was upset and holding back tears about her crushed model, and the strain was her effort to stay composed.

She handed Payal water and breathed out slowly with her, which loosened her voice so she could explain.

Victor, Austin, and Brian made traps to catch shrimp. Victor's trap caught 26 shrimp and Austin's trap caught 8 less than Victor's. Brian's trap caught half of Victor and Austin's total number of shrimp. If the boys then sold their shrimp for $7 for every 11 tails of shrimp and then divided their earnings equally amongst themselves, how much money does each boy make?

Austin's trap caught 26 - 8 = 18 shrimp.
Together, Victor and Austin's traps caught 18 + 26 = 44 shrimp.
Brian's trap caught 44/2 = 22 shrimp
In total, they caught 26 + 18 + 22 = 66 shrimp.
They were able to sell 66/11 = 6 sets of shrimp.
They made a total of 6 x $7 = $42
Each boy made $42/ 3 = $14
The answer is 14.

Hanna has 5 times as many dolls as her sister, so 5 x 8 dolls = 40 dolls.
Together, they have 8 dolls + 40 dolls = 48 dolls.

messages.content: Walking through the stream, I wrote "weighed" in my story: "We weighed across the water." My brother says it is wrong. Is it?

Yes, it is wrong here. Use "waded". To wade is to walk through water, and the past tense is "waded". "Weighed" is the past tense of "weigh", which means to measure how heavy something is.
Examples: We waded across the shallow stream. The shopkeeper weighed the rice.

Day three. At the family's prayer meeting Maria sat at the back, covered her head as the others did, and spoke little. Simran's mother pressed her hand.

What did Maria write in her first message?
"I'm so sorry, Simran. I'm here whenever you want."

You asked what I noticed about Jomon, the guy who sat next to me at the agency. Okay.
I'm Jatin. Jomon said yes to everything. Extra slides for sales, yes. Covering someone's client call, yes. Weekend edits, yes. Everyone loved him. “Ask Jomon, he'll do it.”
By October he looked grey. He ate at his desk. Once I saw him close his eyes for a full minute during a meeting.
I felt uneasy, and honestly a bit guilty, because I'd asked him for things too.
So one day, when the manager asked him to take on a new pitch, I said, “Actually, I'll take half. Jomon's on the Kochi account.” He looked at me like I'd thrown him a rope.
Later I told him, “Next time you want to say no, say ‘let me check with Jatin.’ I'll back you.” He used it twice that month. Nobody thought less of him.

Jatin said, “Actually, I'll take half. Jomon's on the Kochi account.”
How did Jatin feel watching Jomon burn out?
Jatin felt uneasy and a bit guilty, having also asked Jomon for things.
What backup did Jatin offer, and why does it work?
A phrase, “let me check with Jatin,” so Jomon could practise saying no without seeming unhelpful or losing standing.
How did Jomon seem to feel when Jatin stepped in?
Jomon seemed relieved and grateful, looking as if he'd been thrown a rope.

Her irritation faded when, scrolling up, she saw that Prerna and she herself had also slipped. She saw a shared habit, not one lazy person.

Tracking estimate, range and actual showed whether the ranges were realistic, and most actual dates landed inside them.

In the corridor outside the thesis room in Valencia, Diego's hands were cold and his heart was thumping. Sami, waiting with him, offered water.
"You okay?"
"Nervous," Diego admitted. "But I've done the work. I can't control which questions they ask, or whether Professor Ruiz is in a bad mood. I can control how slowly I answer."
He closed his eyes, breathed out slowly, and let his shoulders drop. He didn't pretend to be relaxed; his leg was still bouncing. But when the door opened, he walked in steadily.
The first question was one he hadn't prepared. He paused, said, "Let me think about that for a moment," and answered carefully. An hour later he came out, smiling and tired.

What did Diego say when a question came that he hadn't prepared?
"Let me think about that for a moment."
How was Diego feeling before the viva?
Diego felt nervous, with cold hands and a thumping heart, yet steady because he had accepted what he couldn't control.

Separating what he could control, answering slowly, from what he couldn't, the questions and the professor's mood, and breathing out slowly.
How might Sami see Diego's calm?
Sami likely admired it, seeing Diego nervous, leg bouncing, yet walking in steadily.
A student's project falls apart on the morning of the science fair; write that.

At eight o'clock on the morning of the science fair, Yusuf's model volcano collapsed in the bag on the bus. Clay, paper and a broken paint bottle lay in a soggy heap. He walked into the hall dragging his bag, close to tears. His classmate Bela saw the mess and said, "Do you have the instructions?" He nodded. He was in a box on a river in an open boat, moved by oars or poles, because the banks are near and the boat is working against the stream. There would be no such sound if it were floating downstream.
Short and funny: a hen afraid of the rain.

Henrietta the hen hated rain. When the first drop fell, she squawked, ran in circles, and tried to hide under a flower pot. The other hens clucked at her.

"It is only water," said Cluck.

"It is wet," said Henrietta.

One morning, the sky grew dark again, and the first drop landed on her head. She yelped and darted for the barn, but the door was shut. She ran to the doghouse, but the dog snarled. She ran to the scarecrow and stood beneath his hat.

But the hat was full of holes. The water poured down on her, cold and hard. She stood there, sopping, blinking.

After a while, she realised she felt fine. Henrietta shook herself out, shrugged, and went back to scratching the mud.

Wednesday: Disha put a paper and a pencil in front of him at breakfast. "Before you decide that, draw a circle. What led to four people?" Anand grumbled, then started dividing. How might Disha have felt seeing the circle shaded and labelled on Saturday?
Disha probably felt relieved and glad that the simple circle helped Anand move from blaming himself to planning. It shows Disha's nudge worked without lecturing.

Week 3, Tuesday. Swati noticed the blue helmet on Ojas's head. "Changed your mind?" He shrugged. "My mother saw the boy's photo in the parents' group. She made me promise." A pause. "And I kept thinking, he also thought it wouldn't be him."

He had been clipped by an auto at the same turn Ojas took every day and came with his arm in a sling.

Yash, your cousin says you copied the science project from a website. Sit. Let your Kishore dada tell you about Class Nine.
Our geography map-work was due on Monday. I had played cricket all weekend. On Sunday night, I copied my friend Dinesh's whole file, even his mistakes. I told myself, "Just this once. Everyone does it."
The teacher didn't catch it. I felt clever for a week.
Then it happened again for history. And again for maths homework. Each time, "just this once." By Class Ten, I couldn't read a map on my own. In the board exam, there was a map question worth eight marks. I sat looking at it, and my hand was sweating. I knew I had never actually learned it.
I got two marks out of eight. Dinesh got all eight, from his own work.
I'm not angry with you, beta. I'm telling you because "just this once" is how it starts.

How many marks was the map question worth?
Eight marks.

Pranav's remark about Batch A comparing upward, and thinking of her cousin in Batch F and her own score a year ago, which changed whom she was looking at.

messages.content: We found a tiny kitten crying near our gate. Its mother isn't around.

Watch from a distance for a few hours first, because mother cats often leave kittens while they look for food. If she doesn't return and the kitten seems weak or cold, call a local animal rescue group for advice.
Can I give it some milk?
It's better not to give cow's milk, as it can upset a kitten's stomach. Keep the kitten warm in a box with a soft cloth, and ask the rescue group or a vet what to feed it.

messages.content:
Rewrite this verse in clear, modern English.

So Rama, to his purpose true,
To Queen Kausalya bade adieu,
Received the benison she gave,
And to the path of duty clave.
As through the crowded street he passed,
A radiance on the way he cast,
And each fair grace, by all approved,
The bosoms of the people moved.

So Rama, true to his purpose, said goodbye to Queen Kausalya, received her blessing, and held to the path of duty. As he passed through the crowded street, he shed a glow along the way, and each of his graces, which everyone admired, moved the hearts of the people.
I went to two concerts last month. Is a concert only for music?

Yes, mostly. A concert is a public performance of music by singers or players. A play is not called a concert, though a stage show with songs sometimes is. It is a noun; Concerts is the plural.
Example: The school choir gave two concerts, one in the hall and one at the old-age home.

Every afternoon Mina met her mother, Astrid, at the door with the same words: "Can I have a phone now? Everyone has one." On Monday Astrid said not yet. On Tuesday Mina asked again, louder. On Wednesday she cried on the stairs, and Astrid stayed quiet and firm. On Thursday Mina stamped her foot, and her father said, "Enough. The answer will not change if you ask ten times." By Friday Mina had stopped saying anything at all, and dinner was tense. Astrid's face looked tired more than angry. Mina had never once said why she needed a phone or what she would do to use it carefully.

On which day did Mina cry on the stairs?
Mina cried on the stairs on Wednesday.

Frustrated and disappointed, because each refusal made her angrier and asking again was not working.

How does Mina's asking look to Astrid by the end of the week?
Wearing: Astrid looks tired rather than angry, and every repeat gives her more reason to stay firm.

messages.content: There are three times as many misses as hits in an MLB game. If the number of misses is 50, how many hits and misses are made in the game?

Three times as many misses as hits is 3*50 = 150
The total number of hits and misses in the game is 150+50 = 200

From his apartment, Kona drives 9 miles to the bakery.  From there, he drives 24 miles to his grandmother's house.  From her house, he drives 27 miles straight to his apartment.  How many additional miles did Kona drive round trip to the bakery stop, compared to a round trip without the bakery stop?

With the bakery stop, Kona drove a total of 9 + 24 + 27 = 60 miles.
Without the bakery stop, Kona drove a total of 27 + 27 = 54 miles.
With the bakery stop, Kona drives an additional 60 - 54 = 6 miles.
The answer is 6.

State whether true or false, with a reason: (a) sin A increases as A increases from 0 degrees to 90 degrees; (b) cos A increases in the same range; (c) sin theta = cos theta for all theta; (d) cot A is not defined at A = 0 degrees; (e) sin 30 degrees + sin 60 degrees = sin 90 degrees.

Answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) F.

Read along the rows of the table. (a) sin: 0, 0.5, 0.707, 0.866, 1 - increasing. (b) cos: 1, 0.866, 0.707, 0.5, 0 - DECREASING. (c) Only at 45 degrees are they equal; at 30 degrees they are 1/2 and sqrt3/2. (d) cot 0 degrees = cos 0 degrees/sin 0 degrees = 1/0: not defined. (e) 1/2 + sqrt3/2 ~ 1.366, but sin 90 degrees = 1. For "true for all" statements one counter-example is enough to answer F. Common mistake: believing all ratios behave like sin.

A class is completing an art project. Each of the 30 students is assigned to a separate group and will need to take markers from the 22 boxes of markers. The first group has 10 students who will have 2 markers each and the second group has 15 students who will have 4 markers each. The last group takes the remaining markers and divides them equally. If each box of markers contains 5 markers, how many markers does each of the students in the last group receive?

The first group uses a total of 10 students * 2 markers = 20 markers.
The second group uses a total of 15 students * 4 markers = 60 markers.
This is a total of 20 + 60 = 80 markers.
The total number of markers in the boxes is 5 markers * 22 boxes = 110 markers.
This leaves 110 - 80 = 30 markers for the last group to split between themselves.
The last group is made up of 30 total students - 10 students in the first group - 15 students in the second group = 5 students.
Therefore, students in the last group receive 30 markers / 5 students = 6 markers each.
The answer is 6.

Second night:240(1/6)=40

Third night:200(.30)=60

The answer is 140.

A school library has 120 books.  Each student needs 5 books for their classes.  The library was able to help 4 students on the first day of school, 5 students on the second day and 6 students on the third day.  How many students can the library help out on the fourth day of school?

On the first day, the library used 4 students * 5 books = 20 books.
On the second day, the library used 5 students * 5 books = 25 books.
On the third day, the library used 6 students * 5 books = 30 books.
On the fourth day, the library had 120 books - 20 - 25 - 30 = 45 books remaining.
The library can help 45 books / 5 books = 9 students on the fourth day.
The answer is 9.

Are 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + 6y = 1 parallel? Find the equation of the line through (1, -2) parallel to y = 3x + 4, and the line through (0, 7) parallel to 2x - y = 9.

Answer: Yes (both slopes -2/3). y = 3x - 5; y = 2x + 7.

Parallel lines climb at the same rate, so they have the SAME slope (and different intercepts, or else they are the same line). 2x + 3y = 5 gives y = -(2/3)x + 5/3 and 4x + 6y = 1 gives y = -(2/3)x + 1/6: equal slopes, different intercepts, so they are parallel. A parallel line through (1, -2) to y = 3x + 4 has slope 3: y + 2 = 3(x - 1), so y = 3x - 5 (check: 3 - 5 = -2). For 2x - y = 9, y = 2x - 9 has slope 2; through (0, 7) the intercept is 7, so y = 2x + 7. Short cut: a line parallel to ax + by = c has the form ax + by = k; put in the point to find k: 2(0) - 7 = k, k = -7, so 2x - y = -7.
