I sat on the floor of my flat for a long time. Now I call on Wednesdays too, just to hear him complain about the milkman. And I've booked leave for Pongal. He said, "Why waste leave?" His voice was shaking.

What did the cousin's photo show?
It showed Appa sitting alone on the verandah with two tumblers of coffee beside him, one untouched.
What does Rekha feel after seeing the photo?
Rekha feels shaken and sad, sitting on the floor for a long time, seeing that Appa's cheerful "fine" was hiding loneliness.
What did Rekha do once the quiet longing was clear?
Rekha added a Wednesday call just to chat and booked leave for Pongal, giving regular contact and a visit.
Why might Appa keep saying everything is fine?
Appa probably does not want to burden Rekha and hides his loneliness out of love, though his shaking voice about the leave shows how much the visit means.
Work out (10 - 4) - 2 and 10 - (4 - 2). Are they the same?

Answer: No. (10 - 4) - 2 = 6 - 2 = 4, but 10 - (4 - 2) = 10 - 2 = 8.

The grouping rule works for adding, not for taking away. With 10 rupees: spend 4, then spend 2, and 4 are left. That is the correct meaning of 10 - 4 - 2: always take away from left to right. Let the child act it out with 10 coins.

Could you sum this up simply? I keep losing track of who is who.

I said Mrs. Heathcliff lived above a dozen years after quitting her husband. Her family were of a delicate constitution: she and Edgar both lacked the ruddy health that you will generally meet in these parts. What her last illness was, I am not certain: I conjecture, they died of the same thing, a kind of fever, slow at its commencement, but incurable, and rapidly consuming life towards the close. She wrote to inform her brother of the probable conclusion of a four-months' indisposition under which she had suffered, and entreated him to come to her, if possible; for she had much to settle, and she wished to bid him adieu, and deliver Linton safely into his hands. Her hope was that Linton might be left with him, as he had been with her: his father, she would fain convince herself, had no desire to assume the burden of his maintenance or education. My master hesitated not a moment in complying with her request: reluctant as he was to leave home at ordinary calls, he flew to answer this; commending Catherine to my peculiar vigilance, in his absence, with reiterated orders that she must not wander out of the park, even under my escort: he did not calculate on her going unaccompanied.

Isabella, Edgar's sister, falls ill after many years away. She writes asking him to come, say goodbye and take her son Linton. Edgar leaves at once and tells Nelly to keep young Catherine inside the park while he is gone.

Dear Noor aunty,
Yesterday you told my mother the music from our balcony is too loud, and I'll be honest, I was angry. I went to my room and slammed the door. I thought you just don't like teenagers. It's my home too and it was only seven in the evening.
But then I remembered you mentioned your exams. You're studying for the nursing entrance, right? I didn't know that. So here's an idea. What if I keep the speaker indoors and low from six to nine on weekdays, when you study, and play it properly on Saturday afternoons? If something is still too loud, can you just knock or send me a message instead of going to Mum? I'd rather hear it from you.
Also, sorry about the Saturday night the song got stuck on repeat. That really was bad.
Nitin, flat 3B

What times does Nitin offer to keep the speaker indoors and low?
From six to nine on weekdays.
How did Nitin feel when the complaint first came, and what changed it?
Nitin felt angry and unfairly targeted, slamming the door, but remembering Noor aunty's exam study made the complaint feel more understandable.
What makes this letter a good way to settle the problem?
It admits the anger honestly, offers specific quiet hours and a fair time to play loudly, and asks for direct contact next time.
How might Noor aunty feel reading this letter?
She may feel relieved and respected, since Nitin noticed her exams and offered a plan instead of arguing.
Which is healthier, brown rice or white rice?
Brown rice has more fibre because the outer layer is kept. White rice is lighter and easier to cook. Both are fine as part of a normal meal, and what you eat with the rice matters too.
I like the white rice taste better.
That is fine. You can eat white rice and add dal, vegetables and curd to balance the meal. Taste matters, because you will cook what you enjoy and keep eating it.
My friend Pooja eats red rice. What is that?
Red rice is another type of whole grain rice, often from Kerala or Tamil Nadu, and it has a nutty taste. It takes longer to cook than white rice. Pooja may have grown up eating it.
Does it taste like brown rice?
It is close, but a bit more earthy and slightly chewy. If you want to taste Pooja's red rice, ask her to share a small bowl, and then decide if you like it more than white rice.

She had left a plate there on Monday, meaning to wash it later. So, it seemed, had everyone. Jaya came in behind her. "Whose is all this?" "Everyone's," said Uma. "And no one's." On which floor was the pantry?
The third floor of the women's hostel.
How did Uma feel when she left her plate on Monday?
She wasn't worried, meaning to wash it later and assuming one plate didn't matter.
What choice do Uma and Jaya face at the end, and what might help beyond that night?
Whether to wash only their own dishes or the rest too; a shared rota for the pantry could stop the pile from coming back.

She sketched buildings, especially the old market.

It suggests he was thinking hard, perhaps surprised and unsure, weighing his expectations against his daughter's talent.
What helped Afreen raise the topic with her father?
She showed real evidence of her talent and had Akash explain the course, so her father could see it was a serious option.

By eleven I was a mess. My head felt stuffed with cotton, I couldn't follow a word in physics, and I snapped at everyone. I thought I was just bad at physics. My elder sister Sudha noticed first. A paratha rolled in foil.

Ramesh felt foggy and irritable, unable to follow physics and snapping at everyone.

Eating a simple breakfast every morning, even on the bus.

Last month I told my whole class about our winter trip to the hills. I said I built a snowman taller than Papa and a yak licked my glove. I was completely sure.
Then Mummy showed me the photos. The snowman came up to my knee. There was no yak. The yak is from my sister Dolma's story; she tells it every time relatives come over. The glove part came from my cousin.
I felt strange, because I can still see the yak in my head, its wet nose and everything.
Now when I tell a story, I say "I think", and sometimes I check the photos first. I'm Sahil, and my memory is a bit of a copycat.

How tall was the snowman in the photos?
The snowman came up to Sahil's knee.

Hearing Dolma tell the yak story so often made it feel like Sahil's own memory, so Sahil can even see its wet nose.

Sahil says "I think" and sometimes checks the photos first, which leaves room for a memory to be wrong.
How might Dolma feel hearing her yak story in Sahil's version?

On the steps of their Indore school, Chetan waved his drawing book. "Art is the only useful class. Maths is boring and useless. Nobody uses fractions in real life." Ujjwal was sorting paint pots for the class mural. "Okay. We have three pots of blue and eight people want blue. How much does each person get?" Chetan opened his mouth. "Just share it." "How?" "Well, each gets a bit less than half a pot." He stopped. "That's a fraction." Ujjwal grinned. Chetan scowled at the pots. Somehow fractions felt more boring when they were in the maths book, and less boring when they were in paint. "Fine," he said. "But I'm still drawing the tiger."

What was Ujjwal sorting on the steps?
He was sorting paint pots for the class mural.
Why does maths feel useless to Chetan?
He loves art and feels bored and grumpy about maths, so his feelings tell him maths is pointless, even though he uses fractions when sharing paint.
How could Chetan's maths teacher use what happened on the steps?
The teacher could give him problems about paint and drawing, so the subject he dislikes connects to one he enjoys 🙂
What would change if Ujjwal had simply argued that maths is important?
Chetan would probably have dug in, because an argument would not change his feeling; the paint problem let him discover the use himself.

Sir said, 'Thank you! Mistakes are how we find the right way.' After that, whenever someone answered wrong, sir asked, 'What were you thinking?' and usually found something right inside it. Nobody laughed, because sir never did. One day I put my hand up for a fraction question, not sure at all. I said three-fifths. It was three-eighths. Sir said, 'Good, you knew the top part. Now let's fix the bottom.' That's how I, Tanvir, started talking in class.

What did Omkar sir do on the first day?
He wrote a sum on the board, got it wrong on purpose, and waited.
How was Tanvir feeling when raising a hand for the fraction question?
Tanvir felt unsure and nervous, not sure at all of the answer, yet safe enough to try.
What could other teachers borrow from Omkar sir?
Asking 'What were you thinking?' after a wrong answer and pointing out the part that was right, so children keep trying.
How might Lalit have felt when sir thanked Lalit for spotting the mistake?
Lalit probably felt proud and encouraged, seeing that catching errors was welcomed.

She then bowled without her usual bounce and stayed after practice, fiddling with her water bottle and not going to the gate. I asked if something was wrong. What did Bhavna first tell Kunal was the reason for being late?

What does Bhavna staying behind and fiddling with her water bottle suggest she was feeling?
She was uneasy and worried about the lie, and probably wanted to put it right.
What did Bhavna do that helped, and what could she do next time?
She told the truth on her own, which eased her mind. Next time she can give the plain reason straight away.
How might Kunal have seen Bhavna's confession?
As a sign of honesty and trust in Kunal. Kunal thanked her and asked only for the missed drills.

Class teacher's note, Monday
Tushar has missed PE twice this month and sits in the back row with his hood up. Some staff have called him lazy and moody. Today he snapped at a classmate who was drumming on the desk, then put his head down. In the back row, with his hood up.

Into the side lane where it was quieter.

In first year I felt everything: every stroke patient trying to lift a spoon, every child learning to walk again. I'd go home and replay their faces. Correct this sentence: Whom gave you this pen? I saw "argumentative" in a story. What does it mean? what does "no wonder" mean?

"Gotta" is a casual spoken form of "have got to" or "have to". It is common in films and chats but should not be used in formal writing.

messages.content: Benjamin is tracking how many miles he walks in a week. He walks to work and home five days a week, walks his dog twice a day every day, walks to his best friend's house once a week, and walks to the convenience store twice a week. Work is six miles away, dog walks are two miles, his best friend's house is one mile, and the convenience store is three miles. How many miles does Benjamin walk in a week?

Benjamin walks 6 miles to work and 6 miles home, so he walks 6 * 2 = 12 miles to work and home.
He walks to work 5 days a week, so he walks 12 * 5 = 60 miles to work and home a week.
He walks his dog 2 times a day for 2 miles, so he walks 2 * 2 = 4 miles a day for his dog.
He walks his dog 7 days a week, so he walks 4 * 7 = 28 miles for his dog.
He walks 3 miles to the store 2 times a week, so he walks 2 * 3 = 6 miles to the store each week.
Adding his weekly 1 mile to his friend's house, Benjamin walks 60 + 28 + 6 + 1 = 95 miles in a week.
The answer is 95.

Charu asked me today while we were making instant noodles in our PG kitchen, "Do you feel grown up yet?" I laughed, but it stuck.
Like: I chose my own electives this semester. I fixed the bathroom tap myself. I went to the doctor alone when I had the fever. That all feels very adult.

Charu asked, "Do you feel grown up yet?"

In Copenhagen, Jamal had posted a mocking picture of Astrid's drawing in the class group chat, and everyone had laughed. That evening he sent her twelve messages: "I'm so sorry." "Please forgive me." "I feel terrible."
The next day, her friends crowded round her locker. "He said sorry, Astrid. Just let it go. It's awkward for everyone."
Astrid felt the pressure squeezing her. It would be easier to smile and say fine.
But she thought about it. Jamal had also said sorry after mocking her accent in autumn, and done it again two weeks later.
When Jamal came up, pleading softly, "Please, Astrid," she said, "I hear that you're sorry. I'm not ready to forgive yet. I need to see it stop first."
Her friends went quiet. Jamal nodded, looking at the floor.
A month later, he hadn't posted anything about anyone. Astrid said hello to him in the corridor.

How many messages did Jamal send that evening?
He sent her twelve messages.
What was Astrid feeling when her friends urged her to let it go?
Astrid felt pressured and uncomfortable, tempted to smile and say fine just to end the awkwardness.
What did Astrid do that protected her boundaries?
She acknowledged Jamal's apology but refused to forgive on demand, asking to see the behaviour stop first.

messages.content: What number comes after 999? How do we say it and write it?

Answer: 1000, one thousand. It is written with a 1 and three zeros.

999 is the biggest three-digit number: 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 9 ones. One more fills the ones (10 ones make a ten), the ten fills the tens (10 tens make a hundred), and the hundred fills the hundreds (10 hundreds make a thousand). So we need a new place and a fourth digit. Count together: 997, 998, 999, 1000! Celebrate: the child can now count to a thousand.

Then for my science homework I asked, "How many legs does a spider have?" It said six. I wrote six.
My friend Bhavna said, "Spiders have eight. Insects have six." We checked the textbook. She was right.
I felt stupid. Then I felt annoyed at the phone. I even said, "You're wrong," and it just said, "Sorry, I didn't catch that."
That's when I understood: it doesn't know anything, it just finds things. And it doesn't feel sorry. Now I check the book too.

Six.

"I got the Hyderabad offer," Farida said, stirring a chai she wasn't drinking. "And I keep thinking, what if Abbu falls when I'm not there."

"Have you asked him what he thinks?" Nandini said.

"He says go. He always says go. But he stopped driving last month."

"So what would make you feel less afraid?"

"Calling every night. A neighbour's number. Maybe Cousin Salim looking in on weekends."

"Then write that down and ask them. You can't cover every possibility, Farida."

"I know. It's just, it feels like choosing a city over him."

"You're choosing a job and a plan. That isn't the same as leaving."

Farida took a slow breath. "Okay. I'll talk to Abbu tonight. And ask about the neighbour's number."

Which city is the job offer in?
Hyderabad.
What is Farida afraid of, and how does it feel to Farida?
That Abbu might fall when Farida isn't there. It feels like choosing a city over him.
What realistic plan does Farida come up with?
Calling every night, getting a neighbour's number, and asking Cousin Salim to look in on weekends, and then talking it through with Abbu.

He keeps saying "go", so he probably wants Farida to follow the job, though he may be hiding some worries of his own.

messages.content: Carol fills up her gas tank as she is driving home for college, which is 220 miles away. She can get 20 miles to the gallon in her car, which has a 16-gallon gas tank. How many more miles will she be able to drive after she gets home and without filling her tank again?

Divide the remaining miles of the trip by the miles per gallon her car gets. 220 miles / 20 miles/gallon = 11 gallons
Subtract the gallons used for the trip from the size of her gas tank. 16 gallons - 11 gallons = 5 gallons
Multiply the remaining number of gallons by the car's gas mileage. 5 gallons x 20 miles/gallon = 100 miles
The answer is 100.

In their shared flat in Addis Ababa, Abebe read the headline aloud from his phone: "Coffee drinkers live longer, study finds." He looked at the clay coffee pot on the stove with new respect. "I'm doubling my coffee. It's basically medicine."
Javier, his flatmate from the exchange programme, was frying eggs. "Who drinks coffee every day, though?"
"Everyone. My grandparents drank it three times a day their whole lives."
"Your grandparents also walked to the market every morning, sat with neighbours for hours and had steady work. People who have time for a long coffee ceremony usually have time, friends, some money. Maybe that's what keeps them going."
Abebe frowned at the headline. The article, when he scrolled down, said "linked with", not "causes".
"So coffee might just come along with the good life," he said slowly.
"Or not. Read the actual study, not the title."
Abebe poured one cup, his usual one, and opened the article properly.

What did the headline say?
The headline said, 'Coffee drinkers live longer, study finds.'
Why did doubling the coffee feel sensible to Abebe?
Abebe felt pleased and confident, because the headline seemed to say coffee was the reason and it fit his grandparents' long lives.
What could Abebe do before changing a habit because of a headline?
Abebe could read the actual study, notice words like 'linked with', ask what else coffee drinkers share, and ask a doctor about anything health-related.
How does Javier see the headline?
Javier sees it as a link that other things, like time, friends and money, might explain, so it doesn't prove coffee helps.
why does a boat made of steel float? Fix the mistake: I am knowing him since childhood. Meaning of veteran, please. How much does a cup of tea cost at the station?

1. A steel boat is hollow, so as a whole it is less dense than water. Because its hull pushes aside a weight of water equal to the boat's own weight, the water holds it up.
2. Corrected: I have known him since childhood. Why: "know" takes no "-ing"; "since" needs the present perfect.
3. "Veteran" is a noun. It means a person with long experience in a job or a field.
4. I can't check that. Prices vary from stall to stall. Look at the price board or ask the seller.

I'm Rashmi, and my brother Eshaan is five. Last night we played ludo, and when my token cut his, his face went red and his jaw locked. His hand went up to swipe the board. Mumma caught his hand softly. "Eshaan, your face is hot, and your hand wants to hit. Is your heart going fast?" He nodded, breathing hard. "That's anger coming. Let's squeeze the cushion instead." He squeezed it so hard his knuckles went white. I don't know what was going on inside him, but after a bit he said, "Heart slow now," and rolled the dice.

What game were Rashmi and Eshaan playing?
They played ludo.
What do Eshaan's red face and locked jaw suggest?
They suggest Eshaan was getting angry after his token was cut, though Rashmi could not be sure what was going on inside.
What did Mumma do that could help Eshaan later on?
Mumma named the signs, a hot face, a hand that wants to hit and a fast heart, and offered a cushion to squeeze, giving Eshaan a way to notice anger early.
What might Rashmi have felt as Eshaan's hand went up to swipe the board?
Rashmi may have felt worried the game would be ruined, then relieved when Eshaan rolled the dice again.

messages.content: Ahmed has 8 orange trees and four times as many apple trees in his orchard as Hassan. If Hassan has one apple tree and two orange trees, and they both have only apple and orange trees in their orchards, how many more trees are in Ahmed's orchard than in Hassan's?

Ahmed has 4 times as many apple trees as Hassan who has 1 apple tree so Ahmed has 4*1 = 4 apple trees
Ahmed has 8 orange trees in addition to the apple trees for a total of 8+4 = 12 trees
Hassan has 1+2 = 3 trees in his orchard
Ahmed has 12-3 = 9 more trees than Hassan
The answer is 9.

Aadhya, you want the rules for everything! When I was a boy of ten, in our village near Thrissur, my uncle brought a game from the city: a board with marbles and holes, and the rule paper was lost on the bus. My cousins wanted to wait till someone could explain it. But I thought, "What's the worst that can happen? We lose a game of marbles." So I just started moving them. Jump here, slide there. Some moves were silly and we laughed. Some worked. By evening, we had our own rules and played till dark. Your Joseph Appachan still thinks that was the best game of that holiday. Some things, you just try. Mistakes cost nothing there.

From the city.
How did young Joseph feel about the missing rules?
Young Joseph felt curious and unbothered, thinking the worst that could happen was losing a game of marbles.

Joseph deciding to just try moves; it was low-risk and turned the lost rules into a chance to invent their own.
How might the cousins have felt when Joseph started moving marbles?
They might have been unsure at first, then enjoyed laughing at silly moves and making their own rules.

In Class 5 at Bidisha's school in Chennai, Lakshmi Miss started a Reading Badge board: a gold star for every book, a badge for every ten. Bidisha, who used to read under the desk during maths, was the first to reach twenty stars.
But on Sunday in their Adyar flat, her father found her flipping through a slim book in four minutes, then writing its title in her log.
'Didn't you love the detective series?' he asked. 'The one with the missing cat?'
'Those are three hundred pages, Appa. That's a week for one star.'
She pulled out the next thin book. She didn't laugh at anything in it. When she finished, she didn't sit hugging it the way she used to. She just wrote down the title and counted in her head: twenty-one.

What did Lakshmi Miss give for every ten books?
A badge.
What has changed in how Bidisha feels while reading, and what shows it?
Bidisha seems bored and flat now: she no longer laughs or sits hugging the book, and just writes the title while counting her stars.
What choice could Appa or Lakshmi Miss make to bring back the joy?
They could stop counting books and ask Bidisha what happens in the detective series; talking about stories turns attention back to reading itself rather than the star total.
How might Lakshmi Miss feel if she saw Bidisha's four-minute flip-through?
Lakshmi Miss would likely be disappointed, having meant the board to encourage reading, and might see it was rewarding speed rather than love of books.

Madhav was watching Shankar tell a story at the village tea shop, his hands moving fast. Madhav had learned signs only a few months before and kept getting lost in single signs. Shankar placed his left flat hand in front of his chest, then brought a bent right hand walking toward it from the right, stopping, and knocking against it. Madhav frowned, and Shankar repeated it slowly, adding a pointing hand to a spot on the left. Then Madhav saw it: not "knock" as a word, but a person coming to a door on his left. Shankar grinned and signed, slowly, that he'd been worried nobody in the village would ever catch it. Madhav felt a warm rush of belonging, and no longer alone.

Where was Shankar telling his story?
He was telling his story at the village tea shop.
What did Madhav feel when he finally understood the story, and what shows that Shankar felt something too?
Madhav felt a warm belonging, and Shankar's grin and his sign about worrying no one would catch it show that he had been feeling lonely.
What could Madhav do to get better at reading this kind of signing?
He could watch the whole signing space instead of single signs and ask Shankar to repeat slowly when he gets lost.

Shankar may feel isolated when people only see separate signs, so being understood likely matters a lot to him.

Do I need commas in "My bag which is blue is new"?

Yes. When "which" adds extra information, put commas around it: "My bag, which is blue, is new." The commas show that the blue detail is not needed to identify the bag.

In his treatise on "Queen-Gold," or Queen-pinmoney, an old King's Bench author, one William Prynne, thus discourseth: "Ye tail is ye Queen's, that ye Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with ye whalebone." Now this was written at a time when the black limber bone of the Greenland or Right whale was largely used in ladies' bodices. But this same bone is not in the tail; it is in the head, which is a sad mistake for a sagacious lawyer like Prynne. But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.

Question: What mistake does the writer find in Prynne's claim about the whale's tail?
Prynne says the tail is the Queen's, so the Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with whalebone. But the bone is in the head, not the tail, a sad mistake for a clever lawyer.

Sudha, you're proud of your student for taking on so much? Let me tell you about one of mine, years ago, when I still taught at the college.
Her name was Kavita. She said yes to everything: the magazine, the fest, two research projects, tutoring juniors. Every time she brought me a result, I praised it. "Brilliant, Kavita! What next?" I never once asked if she was sleeping. I never asked if she was enjoying any of it.
In her final term she came to my office and cried for an hour. She said, "I thought you'd be disappointed if I stopped."
That day I, Deepika, learned something. Praise the work, yes. But also ask, "Are you resting? Is this still fun?"

What did Deepika say every time Kavita brought a result?
"Brilliant, Kavita! What next?"
What was Deepika feeling when Kavita cried in her office?
Deepika was shocked and regretful, realising the constant praise had pushed Kavita to keep saying yes.
In the story, what could Deepika have done differently earlier?
Asked about Kavita's sleep and enjoyment, not just praised each result, so Kavita felt free to set limits.
What was Kavita experiencing through all those yeses?
Kavita felt pressure to keep pleasing her teacher, fearing disappointment if she stopped.

There are 30 students in Ms. Leech's class. Twice as many girls as boys are in the class. There are 10 boys in the class and each boy today brought 5 cups for science activity class as Ms. Leech had instructed. If the total number of cups brought by the students in the class is 90, how many cups did each girl bring?

If there are 30 students in Ms. Leech's class, and the number of boys is 10, the number of girls in Ms. Leech class is 30-10=20
If each boy brought 5 cups for the science activity, the total number of cups brought by the boys is 5*10=50 cups.
The number of cups that the girls brought is 90-50=40 of the total number.
Since the number of girls in the class is 20, each girl brought 40/20=2 cups each.
The answer is 2.
Ashton had two boxes of pencils with fourteen pencils in each box. He gave six pencils to his brother. How many pencils did Ashton have left?

Ashton had 2 boxes * 14 pencils = 28 pencils.
Ashton had 28 pencils - 6 = 22 pencils left.
The answer is 22.
I am hearing a strange noise from the kitchen. Is the tense right?

I hear a strange noise from the kitchen.
Why: present tense ("am hearing" -> "hear").

Javier is an Olympic javelin thrower.  In the last Olympics, he threw the javelin three times.  The first throw, he threw the javelin twice as far as he threw the javelin on his second throw, but only half as far as he threw it the third throw.  If the sum of all three throws was 1050 meters, then how far, in meters, did he throw the javelin on his first throw?

Let x be the distance he threw the javelin on the first throw.
Thus, the sum of his three throws is x+0.5x+2x=1050 meters.
Thus, 3.5x=1050.
And we find the distance he threw the javelin on the first throw is x=300 meters.
The answer is 300.

As helpful, because giving solutions is a way of caring, though Indu may not have noticed that Jeevan wanted to be heard first.

Every school morning Vishal's stomach hurt. The bus meant Saurabh, who flicked his ears and hissed that nobody wanted him around. Vishal's fists clenched; he pictured hitting Saurabh so it would stop, but he knew he would be the one punished. He kept quiet at home, until a photo of him with his mouth full of food appeared in the class chat, with a row of laughing faces underneath. He did not reply. He took a screenshot instead, and his hands shook. That night he showed his mother, who sat beside him, said it was not his fault, and phoned the class teacher on the spot. The teacher agreed to see them first thing. The next day the teacher spoke to Saurabh's parents and changed the seating on the bus. Vishal still felt as if no one wanted him, until Mridul waved him over to the chess club at lunch. Vishal began writing down each day what happened on the bus, and found that saying it aloud made the weight smaller.

What did Vishal do when the photo appeared in the class chat?
He did not reply and took a screenshot instead.
How did the phone call and Mridul's invitation each help Vishal, and what different things did they fix?

The phone call meant the teacher spoke to Saurabh's parents and changed the seating on the bus, while Mridul waved Vishal over to the chess club, and that eased the feeling that no one wanted him, though he still felt it at first.
What was Vishal feeling while he pictured hitting Saurabh, and what held him back?
He was angry, but he knew he would be the one punished.
What could Vishal keep doing to stay safe on the bus?
He could keep writing down what happens and tell his mother or teacher straight away.

On the first day of shiva in their Haifa apartment, Noa, twenty-four, sat on the low chair in the shirt she had torn at the graveside for Saba. She had said the prayer, shovelled earth onto the coffin and greeted every visitor. She felt nothing at all, as if watching herself through glass. On the third afternoon her friend Leila came with a pot of lentil soup, sat beside her and said, 'You don't have to be the host. Tell me about him.' Noa started with Saba's terrible jokes and ended with her face in Leila's shoulder, crying so hard she shook. Leila didn't hush her. The mirrors stayed covered; the soup went cold. Neither of them minded.

What did Leila bring?
A pot of lentil soup.

Why did Leila's visit help Noa?
Leila freed her from hosting, asked about Saba and let her cry without hushing, giving grief room alongside the rituals.
How might Leila have felt holding Noa as she cried?
Leila probably felt sad and tender, glad to be trusted with Noa's grief.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday
Santosh came to my room at lunch with his friend Jahnavi, who kept a hand on his sleeve and said, "Just tell. It's okay."
Santosh showed me messages on his mother's old phone from someone in a homework-help group: "You're smarter than kids your age." "You're special to me." "Don't tell your parents about our chats, they'll spoil it."
He said he had stopped replying but felt he had done something bad. I told him clearly that he had done nothing wrong and that coming to me was exactly right. We took screenshots together. I phoned his mother before school ended; she came in, and we blocked and reported the account and informed the school's safeguarding lead that afternoon.
When he left, Santosh's shoulders had dropped. Jahnavi walked him back to class.

Where did the messages come from?
Someone in a homework-help group.
What was Santosh feeling when he came to the counsellor?
He felt ashamed and worried, believing he had done something bad.
What did the counsellor do the same day?
They told him it was not his fault, took screenshots with him, phoned his mother, blocked and reported the account and informed the safeguarding lead.
How did Jahnavi see her friend's situation?
Jahnavi could see Santosh needed help, so she encouraged him to speak and stayed close to him.

The bus was late, and Simran arrived at her boyfriend Rekha's family lunch flustered and damp from the rain. Rekha's grandmother sat at the head of the table, asking everyone about their studies in a slow, careful way. Simran wanted to laugh at the story about the runaway goat, and she wanted to argue when an uncle said girls didn't need engineering. She did neither. She kept her hands folded, gave short, polite answers and smiled. The grandmother approved. Rekha caught her eye, and Simran gave a tiny shrug. Later, on the stairs, she let her shoulders drop. "That was hard work," she said. Rekha squeezed her hand. "I know. Thank you for staying calm."

What did Simran keep folded during the lunch?
She kept her hands folded.
How was Simran feeling during the lunch, and what does her sigh on the stairs suggest?
She was holding back a wish to laugh and to argue, and the sigh on the stairs suggests the restraint was tiring, though she also respected the grandmother.
What could Simran do so that constant restraint does not wear her out?
She could take short breaks, talk about the day afterwards with Rekha, and share her real views in safer moments.
How might Rekha's grandmother see Simran's manner?
The grandmother likely sees respect and good manners, and would not know about the tiredness underneath.
What is the meaning of "slow down"? The sign near my school says it.

"Slow down" means to reduce your speed. Used for people, it can also mean to do less or relax.
Examples: Slow down near the school gate. You work too hard, Sana; slow down a little.
What does my brother talk about with his friends at night?
I don't know what your brother talks about with his friends. If you're curious, ask him, and respect it if he'd rather keep it private.

I'm Eshaan. The year I turned fifteen, I changed fast. New friends, like Sahil from the skating group, earphones in all the time, one-word answers at dinner. And Mom clamped down. Suddenly there was a curfew, questions about every message, and my door had to stay open.
I thought she was being a jailer. Then one night I heard her on the phone with Masi: "He's become a stranger in my own house. I feel shut out." Her voice cracked.
That hit me. I had been shutting her out and calling her controlling for noticing.
So I tried something. Every morning I told her my plan for the day: where, with whom, when back. I brought Sahil home to meet her. It felt silly at first. But within a month the open-door rule vanished, and the curfew moved an hour later. Sharing freely got me more freedom than fighting ever did.

Who was Eshaan's new friend from the skating group?
Sahil.
How did Mom feel when Eshaan changed?
Shut out and hurt; she said he had become a stranger in her own house, and her voice cracked.
What did Eshaan do that lowered Mom's need to control?
He told her his plans each day, where, with whom and when back, and brought Sahil home to meet her.
How did Eshaan's view of Mom change after the phone call?
He stopped seeing her as a jailer and saw a worried mother who felt shut out.

Jana was editing four books alone.

Three months.
How did Ganga seem to feel after Jahnavi's question?
She seemed relieved and a little lighter, laughing shakily and asking for company and tea.

She validated the feeling first and then asked permission before offering ideas, respecting Ganga's choice.

The HR room in the Andheri office smelled of new carpet. Nirmala, the HR manager, smiled and said, "For freshers we're thinking around three lakh twenty a year." Madhuri had spent the weekend reading salary surveys; most analysts in her field started near four and a half. She had even written 4.5 on her palm in pen. But now, sitting across the desk, four and a half sounded greedy next to three-twenty. "Could it be three-sixty?" she heard herself say. "Let me check," Nirmala said, and came back with a yes. In the lift Madhuri opened her fist. The ink had smudged. She wondered when that number had stopped feeling real.

What number had Madhuri written on her palm?
Madhuri had written 4.5 on her palm in pen.
Why did four and a half suddenly feel greedy to Madhuri?
Once three-twenty was said aloud, it became the reference in the room, and her researched figure now seemed far from it. The first number spoken felt more real than her weekend of reading.
What could Madhuri do differently in a future negotiation?
She could state her researched figure first, or ask for a day to think, and then reply from the surveys rather than from the number just offered.
How might Nirmala see the quick agreement?
Nirmala probably sees it as an easy result for the company, since the fresher asked for far less than the going rate.

Tarun, you say the weak ones don't want to learn. Let me tell you about Firoz, from my third year teaching science in Gorakhpur. He was fifteen and had failed every test. Other teachers called him a lost case. One day I noticed his diagram of the eye was actually neat, every label spelled right. His answer was wrong, but the drawing was good. So I wrote on it: 'Your diagram is the best in the class.' The next week he drew the ear. Also neat. I told him, 'Now write two lines explaining what one part does. Just two.' He did. Two lines became four. By the end of the year he passed, just, and he came to my desk and said, 'Madhav Sir, thank you.' I didn't do anything big, Tarun. I noticed something real, said it out loud, and gave him the next small hill.

He praised his diagram of the eye, which was neat with every label spelled right.
Why did Madhav decide to praise the diagram even though the answer was wrong?
Madhav felt hopeful on seeing something genuinely good, and wanted Firoz to see real progress rather than another failure.
What choice in the story helped Firoz keep trying?
Madhav named a real strength and then set a small next step, two lines of explanation, that was hard but doable.
How might Firoz have felt reading 'Your diagram is the best in the class'?
Firoz, used to failing, probably felt surprised and proud, which made him want to try again.

Aadhya, come, sit. You think your Sarita Nani was never scared? When I was ten, in our village, I was sitting in the temple courtyard shelling peanuts. Nothing was wrong. Then suddenly my heart went thud-thud-thud like a drum at a wedding, the courtyard spun, and I was sure I was going to die right there among the peanut shells. I screamed for my Amma. She came running from the well with the pot still on her hip. She didn't shout or cry. She put the pot down, took me in her lap and hummed the song she used for the goats. 'It will pass, it will pass.' And it did. Later my father took me to the doctor in town, who said my heart was strong. Many years later I understood what it was.

What was young Sarita doing in the temple courtyard?
Shelling peanuts.
What was young Sarita feeling when the courtyard spun?
She was terrified, sure that she was going to die.
What was the turning point for young Sarita in the courtyard?
Her Amma put the pot down, took her in her lap and hummed calmly until the fear passed.
How might Sarita's Amma have felt, running from the well?
She was probably frightened for her daughter but chose to stay calm and steady for her.
I want to start getting to school early. Right now I run in just as the bell rings.
That is a good goal. Being early gives you time to settle and chat with friends. What makes you late right now?
I wake up late and then take forever to get ready. I am Kabir.
Hello Kabir. Try getting your bag, uniform and shoes ready the night before. That cuts the morning rush a lot. Going to bed a little earlier will help you wake up easily too.
Okay, so what should I pack the night before?

Pack your books for the next day's timetable, your homework, your water bottle and your tiffin if it can be kept fresh. Keep your uniform and shoes next to the bag, Kabir, so nothing is missing at dawn.

Dear Diary,
Today in maths we did long division. I got four wrong out of five. I wanted to cry. I wrote "I CAN'T DO THIS" on the back of my book.
Kavitha saw it. She crossed out "CAN'T" and wrote "can't YET."
"That's cheating," I said.
"No. Last month I couldn't skip rope, remember? Now I can do fifty."
So after school, I did three more sums slowly with Papa. I got two right! I'm still not good at it. But I'm better than this morning.
Not yet. Not yet. Not yet.
Anjali

How many sums did Anjali get wrong in maths?
Four out of five.
What was Anjali feeling when she wrote "I CAN'T DO THIS"?
Anjali felt frustrated and discouraged, close to tears after getting so many wrong.
What could Anjali try next time she gets stuck?
She could remember Kavitha's "not yet" and practise a few more sums slowly, as she did with Papa.
How does Kavitha see Anjali's mistake?
Kavitha sees it as a starting point, like her own skipping rope, not as proof that Anjali can't learn.
Maine kal raat lights band karna bhool gaya. Sahi English?
Say: "I forgot to switch off the lights last night."

Monday. Leela Masi sent a voice note to the family group at midnight: a gang was stealing kidneys from patients at the city hospital, and everyone should stay away. By morning, Chetan's mother had forwarded it twice.
Wednesday. Chetan, twenty-four, spent his lunch break tracing it. The voice gave no name, no ward, no date. He found the same words in a post from another country, years old. He asked a friend who worked at the hospital how often anything like it had ever been reported there. "Never," she said.
Saturday. At Masi's house, he didn't post a correction in the group. He sat beside her and said, "I know you sent it because you care about us." Then he showed her what he had found. Masi was quiet for a moment, then asked him to help her delete it.

Where did Chetan find the same words as the voice note?
He found them in a post from another country, years old.
Why did Chetan begin by telling Masi he knew she sent it because she cares?
He wanted her to feel understood rather than foolish, so she would be open to what he found.
What was the turning point in stopping the chain, and why did it work?
Chetan chose to talk to Masi in person instead of correcting her in the group, which let her change her mind without losing face.
What would change if Chetan had posted a blunt correction in the family group?
Leela Masi might have felt embarrassed in front of everyone and defended the message instead of deleting it.

messages.content: Without dividing, say which of these give terminating decimals: 7/40, 5/12 and 9/15.

Answer: 7/40 terminates (0.175). 5/12 recurs (0.41(6)). 9/15 = 3/5 terminates (0.6).

Step 1: write the fraction in simplest form. Step 2: break the denominator into primes. 40 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 5: only 2s and 5s, so 7/40 terminates; indeed 7/40 = 175/1000 = 0.175. 12 = 2 x 2 x 3: there is a 3, so 5/12 recurs: 5/12 = 0.41666... = 0.41(6). Careful with 9/15: 15 = 3 x 5 has a 3, but first simplify! 9/15 = 3/5, and 5 is fine, so it terminates: 0.6. The common mistake is to test the denominator before simplifying.
My sentence is "The weather is very cold, isn't it? she said." Can you fix it? How would you explain "articulated" to a child? Is it "stoped" or "stopped"?

1. Corrected: "The weather is very cold, isn't it?" she said. Why: spoken words need quotation marks around them.
2. It is the past form of "articulate", a verb meaning to say something clearly in words.
3. It is "stopped", with a double "p". The final consonant is doubled before "-ed".
I bought a sketchbook a month ago and haven't drawn a single thing.
A blank sketchbook can feel strangely scary. Many people worry about spoiling the first page. Does that sound familiar?
Yes! I want every page to look good.

Then try this: on the first page, draw something messy on purpose, like scribbles or a cup drawn with your eyes closed. Once the first page is "ruined," the rest feels free. The sketchbook is for practice, not for showing off.
What should I draw after that?
Draw small things around you, like your shoes, a key or a mug. Give each one five minutes. Simple objects teach shape and shading, and you can finish them in one sitting.
Dad "hit the roof" when he saw my report card. Did he climb up?

No. It means he became extremely angry, usually suddenly and loudly.
Example: Mum will hit the roof if you break another glass.

In a Copenhagen café, Anders pushed his laptop across the table to Selin. "My personal statement for the master's. Tell me it's brilliant." Selin read: "I am a passionate, hard-working team player who has always loved the environment and wants to make the world a better place." She looked up. "Anders, this could be anyone." He groaned. "It's supposed to sound impressive." "What did you actually do last summer?" "I counted bicycles at six crossings for the city, for eight weeks, in the rain. And I found that two crossings had far more near-misses than the others, and the city put in new lights." Selin smiled. "Write that." He rewrote the opening: "Last summer I spent eight weeks counting bicycles at six Copenhagen crossings, in the rain." It read like a real person. Selin said, "Leave out the rain complaints, though. Nobody needs your whole self in one page."

How many crossings did Anders count bicycles at?
Six crossings.
What was Anders feeling when Selin said "this could be anyone"?
He felt frustrated and deflated, groaning, since he'd tried to sound impressive.
What made Anders's rewritten opening stronger?
It used honest, specific detail about what he actually did and found, instead of generic claims.
What does Selin mean by "Nobody needs your whole self in one page"?
She means a personal statement is a chosen, curated picture, so he should keep the relevant details and leave out the rest.

The storm knocked out the lights on the morning of the district race, and the school hall in Kanpur echoed with wind. Zeenat sat on the wet steps with her shoes untied, her hands shaking. Her friend Dilnaz crouched next to her. “I'm scared,” said Zeenat. “I know,” said Dilnaz. “You're nervous. That's okay. But you can do it. Try to run the first bend slowly and speed up when you see the flag.” Zeenat took a breath. “Okay.” Dilnaz tied her shoe. “You can do it,” she said again. Zeenat stood up, and they walked out together to the track.

What did Dilnaz tie?
Zeenat's shoe.
What was Zeenat feeling on the steps, and what shows it?
She felt scared and nervous about the race, shown by her shaking hands and her saying “I'm scared.”
What made Dilnaz's encouragement helpful?
She did not deny the nervousness, said it was okay, and gave a concrete suggestion about running the first bend slowly.
How might Dilnaz feel about her friend's race?
She probably cares and wants to give belief and help, and she may also feel a little nervous herself. 🙂

messages.content:
Read this:

Coach's note, under-16 football, Thursday.
Imran arrived for evening practice and sat on the bench to change. He took out his phone "for one second". When I blew the whistle for the warm-up, he was still sitting, thumb moving, boots half laced. Twelve minutes had passed. He looked genuinely startled when Arohi tapped his shoulder. Afterwards he said, "I didn't even open anything interesting." I don't think this is laziness; the thing is built to keep him looking. From next week, all phones go in a basket by the gate before practice, mine included. I'll tell the team on Saturday.

How many minutes had passed when the warm-up whistle blew?
Twelve minutes had passed.
What was Imran feeling when Arohi tapped his shoulder?
He felt startled and confused, not realising how much time had gone.
What does the coach plan, and why is it fairer than scolding?
A phone basket by the gate for everyone, including the coach, changes the setting rather than blaming Imran's willpower.
How might Arohi see Imran on the bench?
Arohi likely saw a teammate lost in his phone and tapped his shoulder to bring him back, perhaps amused or a little worried.

On the charpai in the courtyard Zeenat shook the silent toy, then banged it on the floor, then pressed its button again and again. Nothing. Only then did Zeenat slide down and toddle toward the kitchen, holding it out in front. Rekha, Zeenat's mother, was stirring dal at the chulha. She wiped her hands, pressed the battery lid, and the toy sang again.

What did Zeenat do before setting off for the kitchen?
Zeenat shook the silent toy, banged it on the floor and pressed its button again and again.
What was Zeenat feeling as the toy stayed silent?
Zeenat was frustrated and puzzled, which is why Zeenat gave up trying alone and went to find Rekha.
What alternative could Zeenat use if shaking and pressing fail again, and why?
Zeenat could go to Rekha sooner, or bring the toy along while calling out, because asking early saves the effort when nothing else works. 🙂
How might Rekha see the toy being brought to her?
Rekha sees a toddler who tried first and now wants help, so the quick fix at the battery lid is easy for Rekha and pleasing for Zeenat.

"Do not think, however," she wrote, "that my father is ill-disposed toward you. He is an invalid and an old man who must be forgiven; but he is good and magnanimous and will love her who makes his son happy." Princess Mary went on to ask Natasha to fix a time when she could see her again.

Question: What does Princess Mary's letter say about her father?
She writes that her father is not unfriendly toward Natasha. He is an invalid and an old man who must be forgiven, but he is good and generous and will love whoever makes his son happy.

Ganga: oh no. what happened

What could help Sabina tomorrow at work?

The scooter showroom in Jaipur closed at eight, the festival discount ended tonight, and Yash, twenty-four, had until then to decide. The salesman had started with the top model: alloy wheels, digital screen, ninety-eight thousand. Next to it, the basic model at sixty-two thousand looked plain and cheap. His friend Tushar's new scooter was all over social media, with a sunset behind it. Yash's sister Aadhya checked her watch. 'Forty minutes.' Yash took a breath and wrote on the back of the brochure. What do I need? Ten kilometres to work, a helmet box, a bit of rain. What was I using before? A cycle and two buses. What is the basic one worth by itself? He read it back. 'The basic one does everything. It's a big step up from buses.' 'And the sunset photo?' Aadhya asked, grinning. 'Tushar's view, not my commute.' He signed for the basic model at 7:52.

How far does Yash travel to work?
Yash travels ten kilometres to work.
Why did the basic scooter first look plain and cheap to Yash?
He had just seen the top model with alloy wheels and a digital screen, and Tushar's sunset photos, so the basic one seemed small beside them.
Which questions helped Yash choose under time pressure, and why did they work?
He asked what he needed, what he used before and what the basic model was worth by itself, which moved the comparison away from the top model and Tushar's photos.
How might Aadhya see her brother's choice?
Aadhya seems pleased and amused, seeing him pick what fits his commute instead of chasing Tushar's view.

My name is Parul, and last monsoon I quit my first job after fourteen months under a manager who read our chats aloud in meetings and mocked anyone who asked a question. By the time the rains stopped I had a rule: offices are all like that. Every single one.
So when Eshaan forwarded me an opening at his design studio during Diwali week, I didn't even open the link. "They'll be nice in the interview," I told him, "and then it starts." He said his team leaves at six and the lead brings sweets for everyone. I said that's exactly what they want you to see.
Looking back, I had met exactly one manager. I had turned him into every manager in the city, and I didn't send a single application for four months.

What did Parul do with the link Eshaan forwarded during Diwali week?
Parul didn't even open the link.
Why did refusing the opening feel sensible to Parul at the time?
After fourteen months of being mocked, Parul felt wary and hurt, and expecting every office to be the same felt like protection from being hurt again.
What could help Parul get past the "all offices" rule?
Parul could treat the old job as one example and gather more, for instance by asking Eshaan's team specific questions about meetings and feedback before deciding.
How might Eshaan feel when the link goes unopened?
Eshaan may feel frustrated or sad that an honest description of the team is brushed aside, since the point was to offer Parul a way back into work.

Read this:

I'm Dolma, and I almost signed my first real job contract in ten minutes. The design studio in Gangtok felt like home: kind people, plants everywhere, Irawati from HR handing me tea. I trusted them completely.
Then my friend Karma said, "Read it. All of it. Even if you love them."
So I took it home. Page six had a two-year bond with a penalty if I left early. Page eight said every design I made, even on weekends, belonged to the studio. And the notice period was three months, not one, as I'd been told.
I felt a bit silly, but I emailed Irawati five questions. She replied the next day: the bond could come down to one year, weekend personal work could be excluded, and the notice was a typo.
Looking back, she didn't mind at all. She said, "Good. I like people who read."

What did page eight of the contract say?
That every design Dolma made, even on weekends, belonged to the studio.
How did Dolma feel about questioning the contract?
Dolma felt a bit silly and awkward, because of trusting the studio completely.
What was wise about Dolma's approach?
Dolma read every clause, including the bond, penalty, IP and notice period, and asked clear questions before signing.
How might Irawati see Dolma's five questions?
Irawati seems pleased and respectful, seeing a careful reader rather than a difficult one.

Neelam, you're taking over the new warehouse team? Let me tell you what I did at the garment factory in Tiruppur. I'm Yamini; I was twenty-five, the only woman supervisor on the floor. Half the tailors were Tamil, half had come from Bihar and Odisha. They ate separately, took breaks separately, called each other names I won't repeat. My manager said, "Just keep them apart." Instead I made mixed lines: every line needed a cutter, a stitcher and a checker, one from each side. The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's. The first week was ugly. A man mocked a Bihari worker's Tamil. I stopped the line and said, "Nobody laughs at anyone here. Next time, you go home." It didn't happen again. By Diwali, I saw them sharing tiffins. I never gave one speech.

Who set the target for the Diwali order?
The target for the Diwali order was the whole line's, not one person's.
What was Yamini feeling when she stopped the line?
Yamini felt firm and angry at the mockery, determined not to let anyone be laughed at.
Why was ignoring the manager's advice to keep the groups apart a key decision?
Mixing lines with equal roles and a shared target gave the workers a real reason to depend on each other, which softened attitudes.
How might the Bihari worker have felt when Yamini stopped the line?
He likely felt protected and respected, seeing that the supervisor would not tolerate mockery of him.
Why are most leaves green?
Leaves hold a green substance called chlorophyll. Because it soaks up red and blue light to help the plant make food and bounces green light back, our eyes see green.

In the Class 10 physics lab, Vidya ma'am was explaining why both bulbs in a parallel circuit stayed bright. Raghav leaned back on his stool. "Ma'am, that's not fully right," he said. "I watched a series on electricity. Current is basically like water, so the second bulb should be dimmer." A few students turned. Vidya ma'am handed him the wires. "Show us." Raghav connected them confidently, flipped the switch, and both bulbs glowed equally bright. He stared. "Maybe the battery's wrong." "Try another." Same result. "The videos were really detailed," he muttered, pulling at his sleeve. Ma'am smiled. "Water is a helpful picture. It just has limits you haven't met yet."

What happened when Raghav flipped the switch?
Both bulbs glowed equally bright.
Why did Raghav feel confident enough to correct the teacher?
A video series gave him a neat picture, water in pipes, and it felt complete; he didn't yet know enough to see where the picture breaks down.
What could Raghav do after this lab?
He could ask where the water picture stops working and read the chapter alongside the videos, treating what he learned as a start rather than expertise.
How might Vidya ma'am see Raghav's challenge?
She seems to see keen curiosity with a gap, not rudeness, so she lets the experiment show him instead of scolding him.

Gautam had to recite his poem at the school annual day, and ten minutes before his turn the microphone died. The teacher whispered, "You'll have to speak loudly without it." His knees shook. Three hundred parents sat out there.
He walked on anyway, took a breath, and said the first line too softly. Then he thought of Dadi in the back row and said the rest loud and clear. The clapping felt like rain on a hot day.
Afterwards his friend Saurabh slapped his back. "Brave! Now jump off the stage wall like a real hero. It's only two metres."
Gautam looked at the drop and laughed. "No thanks. I've done my brave thing for today."
He walked down the steps instead, still glowing.

What happened ten minutes before Gautam's turn?
The microphone died.
How did Gautam feel after the poem?
Proud and glowing; the clapping felt like rain on a hot day.
Why was saying no to the wall jump a wise choice?
He had already faced his real fear; jumping would risk injury just to prove bravery.
How might Saurabh see Gautam's refusal?
Perhaps surprised, but he may realise Gautam had already shown real bravery on stage.

I'm Chinmay, and in my first month at the hostel in Manipal I said yes to everything. Instant noodles on the terrace at midnight, yes. A trip to the beach at six in the morning, yes. A quiz club I had no interest in, also yes. My room felt too quiet otherwise.
Thomas was in the room opposite, from Kottayam. On the fourth night we both admitted we'd cried after our parents left. By the second week we were sharing a toothpaste tube and finishing each other's jokes, and I told Amma on the phone that I'd found my best friend.
Looking back, I'm a little embarrassed by how fast I said that. We'd known each other eleven days. The warmth was real, but a lot of it was two homesick boys holding on to the first person who understood. We're still friends. Just the ordinary, slower kind.

What did Thomas and Chinmay admit on the fourth night?
They both admitted they'd cried after their parents left.
Why did Chinmay say yes to every invitation in the first month?
Chinmay was lonely and the room felt too quiet otherwise, so every plan was a way not to be alone.
What could Chinmay keep in mind during this open-door stage?
Chinmay could enjoy the quick warmth while letting friendships grow at their own pace, instead of naming someone a best friend after eleven days.
How might Thomas have felt in those first weeks?
Thomas was homesick too, so finding Chinmay across the corridor probably felt like relief and a safe person to hold on to.

Saturday night. Spent the whole day making the perfect thesis schedule: eleven colours, a tab per chapter, deadlines in bold, even little icons for weekends. It looks amazing. Four hours went into it and I felt busy the whole time, almost proud. Parveen messaged asking how the writing was going, and I said “planning stage,” which is true. But when I opened the blank document to start the first paragraph, my stomach dropped and I closed it again and fixed a font colour instead. The sheet is beautiful and I have written nothing. I think the sheet is easier than the first sentence. — Tushar

How many colours did Tushar use in the schedule?
Tushar used eleven colours in the schedule.
Why did Tushar's stomach drop when the blank document opened?
Tushar is frightened of the first paragraph, and fixing the schedule feels safer than beginning the actual writing.
What small step could Tushar take next instead of adjusting the sheet?
Open the document and write one rough sentence or two for the first paragraph, and allow it to be bad.
What might Parveen think on hearing “planning stage”?
Parveen probably takes it as normal progress and does not know that Tushar has avoided the writing, so a kind follow-up question could help.

It was the hottest week of May in their Ahmedabad flat. Chinmay noticed the sparrows panting on the balcony railing. "Papa, they're thirsty." Arnab gave him a clay bowl. Chinmay filled it with water and set it in the shade. Every morning after that, he checked it and filled it again, and scattered a few grains of rice. When a sparrow finally dipped its beak, Chinmay held his breath and didn't move.

Where did Chinmay set the clay bowl?
He set it in the shade on the balcony.
What does Chinmay holding his breath suggest?
It suggests he cared about the sparrow and didn't want to scare it away.
What could Arnab do to support Chinmay's care?
He could help him keep the bowl clean and praise him for remembering every morning.
How are the sparrows affected by Chinmay's kindness?
They get water and food during the hot week, helping them survive the heat.

Rain hammered the station roof and the night train was two hours late. On the crowded platform Eshaan's phone buzzed with a forwarded message: “A woman is carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.” Below it was a photo of Ira, taken from behind, a sleeping girl on her shoulder.

Within minutes a ring of men had gathered. “Where are you taking her?” “Show us the ticket!” Ira clutched the child, eyes wide, trying to speak over the voices. Nobody had waited for facts.

Eshaan looked at the message again: no name, no sender, nothing checkable. Eshaan walked to the railway guard. “There's a crowd around a woman with a child. Please come.” The guard arrived and asked calmly whether someone could be called for the child. Ten minutes later a woman ran in, dripping wet. “That's my sister! She's been holding my daughter while I bought tickets.”

What did the forwarded message claim?
The message claimed a woman was carrying off someone's child from the waiting hall.
What was Ira feeling, clutching the child with wide eyes?
Ira was frightened and helpless, trying to speak while a ring of men shouted, and nobody waited for facts.
What choice did Eshaan make instead of joining the crowd?
Eshaan noticed the message had no name or sender and asked the railway guard to come, rather than confronting Ira.
What might it have been like for Ira when the woman ran in and said the child was her daughter?
Ira likely felt huge relief but also shaken and humiliated, since strangers had accused Ira before checking anything.

Devika, you want to start a business? Good. Let me tell you about my student Vinita. At twenty, she noticed that the older ladies in our colony struggled to carry vegetables from the market. She thought: what if I deliver? But she didn't borrow money or buy a scooter. She started with her own cycle and five customers. She wrote every expense in a small notebook: tyre repairs, bags, her own time. After a month, she saw she was earning less than she spent. So she started charging a small delivery fee and grouping orders by lane. The ladies didn't mind. By the end of the year, she had thirty customers and a second-hand scooter bought with her own savings. Start small, beta. Count everything.

How many customers did Vinita start with?
She started with five customers.
How might Vinita have felt when she saw she was earning less than she spent?
She may have felt disappointed or worried, but she chose to adjust instead of giving up.
What does the elder advise Devika, and why is it good advice?
Start small and count everything, because testing cheaply and tracking costs shows whether an idea can actually make money.
How might the older ladies in the colony see Vinita's service?
They'd likely be grateful for help with heavy bags and happy to pay a small fee.

Penelope the pig eats 20 pounds of food per day, which is 10 times more than Greta the goose eats per day.  Milton the mouse eats 1/100 as much as Greta the goose eats per day, but Elmer the elephant eats 4000 times more than Milton the mouse does per day.  How much more, in pounds, does Elmer the elephant eat per day than Penelope the pig?

Greta the goose eats 20/10=2 pounds of food per day.
Milton the mouse eats (1/100)*2=1/50 of a pound of food per day.
Elmer the elephant eats 4000*(1/50)=80 pounds of food per day.
Thus, Elmer eats 80-20=60 pounds more food per day than does Penelope the pig.

The scooter gleamed in the parking area of Eshaan's building. Jomon walked around it twice. "Looks almost new. Eighteen thousand, you said?"
Eshaan had rehearsed the good parts: new tyres, full service record, one owner. On the way down, though, he had asked himself a plain question: if I were buying this, what would I want to know? He didn't bother with the scuffed mirror or the old sticker; those wouldn't change anyone's mind.
"Before you decide," he said, "it stood in water during last year's floods. The mechanic fixed the wiring, but on very wet mornings it sometimes takes a few tries to start."
Jomon's eyebrows went up. "That changes the price."
"I know."
They settled on fifteen. Jomon shook his hand. "You could have kept quiet, you know."
"Then you'd find out in July," Eshaan said.

What happened to the scooter during last year's floods?
It stood in water, and the mechanic fixed the wiring.
What does Eshaan's question to himself on the way down show about his thinking?
It shows he wanted to think from Jomon's side and share what a buyer would really need to know, even if it cost him.
Why was the flood worth mentioning when the scuffed mirror was not?
The flood could change Jomon's decision and the price, while the scuffed mirror would not change anyone's mind.
How does Jomon see Eshaan after hearing about the flood?
Jomon is surprised but seems to respect him, saying Eshaan could have kept quiet and shaking his hand on the deal.

Henry has 30 more lollipops than Alison does. With 60 lollipops, Alisson has half the number of lollipops Diane has. If they combine the lollipops and eat 45 lollipops each day, calculate the total number of days it will take for them to finish the lollipops.

Since Henry has 30 more lollipops than Alison, he has 60+30= 90 lollipops.
Together, Alison and Henry have 90+60 = 150 lollipops.
Alison has half the number of lollipops that Diane has, meaning Diane has 2*60 = 120 lollipops.
Altogether, the three have 120+150 = 270 lollipops.
Since they eat 45 lollipops each day, they'll take 270/45=6 days to finish all the lollipops.
The answer is 6.

At 4:40 Suraj stood at the stop, harmonium book in his bag, when Wasim and the others rode up on their cycles. "Where are you going, uncle-ji?" Wasim grinned. "Singing with the uncles again?" The others laughed. "Come to the ground. Match against the Sector 9 boys." Suraj looked at the empty road, the bus nowhere in sight, his friends waiting. He shoved the book deeper into his bag. "Just going home," he said, and climbed on behind Wasim. He didn't go back to practice that month, or the next. In April, passing the temple, he heard the group singing the song he used to lead, and walked faster.

His harmonium book.
Why did Suraj shove the book deeper into his bag?
He didn't want Wasim and the others to see it; fitting in with them felt more urgent than the singing he loved.
At what moment could Suraj have chosen differently, and how?
At the bus stop he could have said, 'Practice first, I'll come after,' keeping both his friends and the bhajan group.
How might the bhajan group feel about Suraj's absence?
They may miss the voice that used to lead their song and wonder why he stopped coming.

Convert the verse below into simple prose.

Ere yet the dawn had ushered in
The day should see the march begin,
Herald and bard who rightly knew
Each nice degree of honour due,
Their loud auspicious voices raised,
And royal Bharat blessed and praised.
With sticks of gold the drum they smote,
Which thundered out its deafening note,
Blew loud the sounding shell, and blent
Each high and low-toned instrument.
The mingled sound of drum and horn
Through all the air was quickly borne,
And as in Bharat's ear it rang,
Gave the sad prince another pang.

Before dawn had come, on the day the march was to begin, heralds and bards, who knew exactly how much honour was due to each rank, raised their loud and lucky voices and blessed and praised royal Bharat. They struck the drum with golden sticks, and it thundered out its deafening note. They blew the sounding shell and mixed in every high and low instrument. The blended sound of drum and horn was carried through all the air, and as it rang in Bharat's ear it gave the sad prince another pang.
A jar full of marbles is sitting on a table. Half of the marbles are blue, a quarter of them are red, 27 of them are green, and 14 of them are yellow. How many marbles are in the jar?

Let x = the number of marbles in the jar.
If 50% of the marbles are blue, and 25% of them are red, then the remaining 25% must be either green or yellow.
So 0.25 * x = 27 green marbles + 14 yellow marbles = 41 marbles.
So there are a total of 4 * 41 = 164 marbles in the jar.
The answer is 164.

Dear Ishita,
You told me last month that when I have bad news for the team, I should say it slower than feels natural. I had to test that yesterday.
The client cancelled the whole Nagpur project. Six people have spent a year on it. My instinct was to fire it off in the group chat and hide. Instead I called everyone into the room and said it plainly, one sentence at a time. "The client has cancelled the project." Pause. "It isn't because of our work." Pause. "Nobody is losing their job; you'll all move to the Pune account next month."
I could see each sentence land. Priya's shoulders came down after the third one. Farooq asked two questions, and I answered them without rushing. Nobody looked blindsided.
It felt painfully slow while I was doing it. Afterwards, Farooq said, "Thanks for not rushing that."
Shankar

A year.
What was Shankar feeling when the client cancelled the project?
Shankar felt a strong urge to hide and fire the news off in the chat, uneasy about facing the team's disappointment.
How did Shankar's pace help the team take in the news?
Saying one clear sentence at a time with pauses let each point land, including that no one was losing their job, so people didn't feel blindsided.
How did Farooq experience the way the news was delivered?
Farooq appreciated it, thanking Shankar for not rushing, which suggests the slow pace felt respectful.

It wasn't a big speech. We just stopped. And the leader stopped too, because nobody was laughing."

A family's water and electricity bills average $30 a month for the first 4 months and $24 a month for the last 2 months. If the family's bills were averaged over all 6 months, what would the average monthly bill be?

The sum of the bills of the family in the first 4 months is $30/month x 4 months = $120.
The sum of the bills of the family in the last 2 months is $24/month x $2 = $48.
The sum of the bills of the family over the 6 months is $120 + $48 = $168.
Hence, their average monthly bill is $168/6 months = $28/month.
The answer is 28.

The answer is 200.

I didn't know what to say, so I just held her hand. We sat on the steps for a while.
I can't know what went on inside her. But after twenty minutes she wiped her face and said, "Okay. Let's get samosas. And you have to show me your routine."

Answer: 0 + 10, 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, 4 + 6, 5 + 5, 6 + 4, 7 + 3, 8 + 2, 9 + 1, 10 + 0. That is 11 ways, and each one is equal to 10.

Write them in a list so the pattern shows: the first number goes up by 1 and the second number goes down by 1, so the total stays 10. Every one is a true equation: 10 = 3 + 7, 10 = 6 + 4 and so on. We can also write 2 + 8 = 7 + 3, because both are 10.

Esther put down her glass. "No faith, no values. That's how children end up lost."
The table went quiet. Yosef's face turned red. He said nothing.
After dinner, he washed every dish without being asked, and fished his little cousin's toy car out from under the sofa. His mother found him in the kitchen, jaw tight.
"You were honest," she said. "That took courage. Esther's afraid for you, but she was wrong to say it like that." She squeezed his shoulder. "Your kindness is your values, Yosef."
The next week, Esther called. "I shouldn't have said that," she admitted. "You were the only one who helped clean."

Subject: Handover notes on the two juniors

Dear Prof. Iyer,

You asked for honest handover notes on the robotics club juniors.

In August I gave Naveen the gearbox redesign because he spoke confidently at the first meeting. I gave Pooja the parts inventory because she was quiet. I checked Naveen's drawings every evening, argued with him, sent him papers to read. Pooja's spreadsheets I glanced at once a week.

By November Naveen was explaining gear ratios to the second-years. Pooja was still counting screws, and she had stopped coming to the Friday build sessions.

Last week, short of hands, I asked her to debug the arm's sensor code. She found the fault in two days and asked me three sharp questions I couldn't answer.

I don't think the gap between them was ever talent. It was how much of my attention each one got. Please pass this to the next lead before they hand out tasks.

Ritu

Which task did Ritu give Pooja in August?
Ritu gave Pooja the parts inventory.
What does Ritu seem to feel, looking back at the months of glancing at Pooja's spreadsheets once a week?
Ritu seems uncomfortable and somewhat guilty, seeing that the gap between the juniors came from attention, not talent.
What could the next club lead do differently with new juniors?
Give every junior a stretching task early and the same regular feedback, instead of deciding from one meeting who is capable.
What was it like for Pooja during the months of inventory work?
Pooja got little feedback and no real challenge, so she probably felt overlooked, and she drifted away from the Friday sessions until a real problem showed what she could do.
Why does a surprise party need the guest of honour to be kept in the dark?
The surprise only works if the guest does not expect it. Because anyone who hears about it beforehand can no longer feel astonished, a leak spoils the fun of the moment.
Are "amiable" and "amicable" the same?

They are related but not the same. "Amiable" describes a friendly person. "Amicable" describes a friendly agreement or relationship.
Examples: He is an amiable neighbour. They reached an amicable settlement.
I have to walk to school in the rain every day this week. Any tips?
A good raincoat or umbrella is the first thing. Wear shoes that can get wet, and carry a spare pair of socks in a plastic bag. How far is school?
About a kilometre. My friend Max walks with me.
A kilometre is not far, and walking with Max makes it more fun. Use a backpack cover, or put your books in a plastic bag inside, so nothing gets wet.
We usually take a shortcut through a field. Is that ok?
In the rain the field may be muddy and slippery, so it is safer to stay on the road. Ask Max to agree to take the longer way, and walk on the side facing traffic.
Fine. Remind me who I walk with?
You walk with your friend Max. Since you are a pair, you can watch out for each other on the road and agree to skip the muddy field shortcut this week.

I was only in the lab to finish my chemistry record, but I ended up watching Ramesh and Shalini plan their whole robotics season. It was the third week of October. Shalini had printed the competition rulebook and was underlining it with a red pen. "Robot must fit in a 30 cm box. Event date: 14 December." Ramesh drew a line across the whiteboard and wrote 14 Dec at the far right. Then he worked leftwards, thinking aloud. "Last week, nothing. Just rest and pack. So we stop on the 7th. Rehearsal before that, one week. Testing, two weeks. Build, three." Shalini counted on her fingers. "That puts design at... now. Like, this week." They both went quiet and looked at the calendar. Then Ramesh circled the date in red. I can't say what they were feeling, but they packed up faster than I've ever seen.

What size box must the robot fit in?
It must fit in a 30 cm box.
What might Shalini have felt on realising design had to start this week?
Shalini was probably startled and a little anxious, seeing that the backward count left no slack before design had to begin.
Which other step could make the backward plan stronger?
They could show each milestone to their teacher and add a mid-point check, so a slip in building is spotted early instead of eating the free week.
How does the observer see the pair's reaction?
The observer can only guess at their feelings, but notices how fast they pack up after circling the date, which suggests urgency.

In the summer holidays the village ground outside Sehore baked by noon, so Avni practised bowling at six in the morning. Jahnavi Didi, who coached the girls' team, set up a single stump and a steel plate as a target on a good length.
The first twenty balls went everywhere. Then Avni shortened her run-up and something clicked. She hit the plate once. Then again. Each ball needed all her attention: her wrist, her front foot, the seam. It was hard, but just possible.
She forgot her phone in her bag. She forgot the heat, forgot the buffalo wandering past the boundary. When Jahnavi Didi finally called, "Avni, it's eight!", she looked up in surprise.
Walking home, her legs ached, but her head felt clear and quiet, like the pond after rain.

What target did Jahnavi Didi set up?
A single stump and a steel plate on a good length.
How did Avni feel walking home?
Avni felt calm and clear-headed, "like the pond after rain", even with aching legs, after two hours of full absorption.
What made the practice absorbing rather than frustrating?
A clear target and a task hard enough to need all her attention but just possible, especially once shortening the run-up let her start hitting the plate.
What might Jahnavi Didi notice when Avni looks up in surprise?
Jahnavi Didi probably sees a player so absorbed she lost two hours, a good sign the difficulty is set just right.
