"Irawati, put the phone down and listen to your Masi Sarika. When I was fifteen, three friends came back from the hill station with photos and brand-new phones. I smiled at them, then went home and slammed the cupboard door. I was bitter, truly.
I even thought of asking the shopkeeper for a phone on instalment behind Ma's back.
Then I stood in the kitchen and said out loud, 'I'm jealous.' It felt smaller once it was said. I counted what I had: a bicycle, a friend who lent me stories, a mother who made poori on Sundays.
I told my friends I couldn't afford the trip. Nobody laughed. The feeling came back sometimes, but it always passed."

What did Sarika think of asking the shopkeeper for?
She thought of asking for a phone on instalment behind Ma's back.
What was Sarika feeling after her friends came back from the hill station?
She was bitter and jealous: she smiled at them, but slammed the cupboard door when she got home.
What would you advise a teenager who feels envy about a friend's new things?
They can say the feeling aloud as Sarika did, count what they have, and avoid pretending or borrowing to keep up. 🙂
How might Irawati take her Masi's story?
Irawati may find it reassuring that envy is normal and passes, since Masi Sarika tells it while Irawati is busy on her phone.

Two factories pay monthly wages as follows. Factory A: 560 workers, mean wage ₹5,250, variance 10,000 (₹^2). Factory B: 650 workers, mean ₹5,250, variance 14,641. a) Which factory pays the larger total wage bill? b) In which are the wages more variable?

Answer: a) A: 560 x 5,250 = ₹2,940,000; B: 650 x 5,250 = ₹3,412,500 (about 34.1 lakh), so B. b) sigma_A = ₹100, CV ~ 1.90%; sigma_B = ₹121, CV ~ 2.30%: B is more variable.

Total = n x mean (because mean = total / n). Variance is in squared rupees, so take the square root before comparing: sigma_A = sqrt10,000 = 100, sigma_B = sqrt14,641 = 121. With equal means the SDs can be compared directly, but CV is the general tool: CV_A = 100 / 5,250 x 100% ~ 1.90%, CV_B = 121 / 5,250 x 100% ~ 2.30%. In the Indian system ₹2,940,000 = ₹29.4 lakh and ₹3,412,500 = ₹34.125 lakh. Common mistake: comparing variances with means (different units).
What is the thaat or family of Raga Kafi?
Raga Kafi belongs to the Kafi thaat or family.

Before: In March, Sumit ran customer support for a small travel firm. After every angry call, he opened his phone and scrolled till his thumb ached. His partner Ayesha noticed he came home more drained than ever.
During: In April, a Monday, he tried something. Same cue: angry call ends. New action: he stood up, went down the four flights of stairs and around the building once. On his phone, instead of scrolling, he opened a note and wrote: call, walk, feeling after. "Calmer, 6/10." By Friday, most entries said 7.
After: In late May, Ayesha found the note on his phone while looking for a photo. Fifty-three entries. "You've been walking after every bad call?"
"Not every. Most." He shrugged. "I still needed a break. I just picked a better one."
She looked at him, genuinely impressed.

How many entries did Ayesha find in Sumit's note?
She found fifty-three entries.
How does Sumit feel after his walks, according to his notes?
He feels calmer, rating it around 6 at first and 7 by Friday, so the walk gives him the relief he used to seek in scrolling.
What made Sumit's change work?
He kept the same cue, the end of an angry call, and swapped in a walk that still gave him a break, while tracking how he felt afterwards.
How does Ayesha feel discovering the note?
Ayesha feels surprised and genuinely impressed that he quietly kept up the new habit for weeks.

Dear diary,
Today I lost my first chess game at the district tournament, to a boy called Harsha. I was sure Appa would ask "What was the score?" like everyone does. But in the auto he asked, "What was the most fun move you made?"
I told him about my knight fork in the middle. He said, "Show me tonight." Then he asked what I would try differently. I said I brought my queen out too early again.
Only after that did he ask about the result. I said I lost. He just nodded and said, "Okay. Next time the queen stays home a bit longer." He wasn't upset at all.
At dinner Appa told Amma about my fork, not my loss. I felt lighter.
Swati

What was the first question Appa asked in the auto?
What was the most fun move you made?
How did Swati feel at dinner when Appa talked about the fork?
Swati felt lighter and relieved, because the loss was treated as ordinary rather than a disaster.
What did Appa do well after the match?
He asked about fun and lessons before the score, then turned the loss into one simple thing to try next time.
How does Appa seem to see the loss?
As an ordinary part of learning chess, something to study and fix, not something to be upset about.
Now you try: is (2x + 4)/2 = x + 2? Is (x^2 + 4)/(x + 2) = x + 2?
The answer is yes, because 2x + 4 = 2(x + 2); no: x = 1 gives 5/3 on the left but 3 on the right.

At the care home in Alexandria, Dalia, the head nurse, noticed first that Siddiq had stopped joking. He had lost three residents in one month, including Mr Fawzi, whom he'd shaved every morning for two years. Now he moved through the rooms quickly, eyes down. Twice she'd seen him snap at the kitchen staff. On Tuesday she found him in the laundry, folding the same towel over and over, crying without a sound. She didn't make a speech. She rearranged the week: Siddiq on day shifts only, the hardest rooms shared with Nadia and Karim, and time with the home's counsellor on Thursday. Then she put a hand on his shoulder. 'You loved them well. Now let us look after you a little.'

Whom had Siddiq shaved every morning for two years?
Mr Fawzi.
What does Siddiq folding the same towel over and over suggest?
It suggests Siddiq is overwhelmed with grief and exhaustion after losing three residents, barely holding together.
Why was Dalia's choice to rearrange the week better than giving a speech?
Day shifts, shared rooms and a counsellor session gave Siddiq real rest and support, which words alone couldn't.
How might Nadia and Karim feel about taking on the hardest rooms?
They may feel the extra weight but also understand, knowing Siddiq has carried a lot, and may trust they'd get the same care one day.

After the big text fight with Sumit last month, we made a deal on the walk home. Looking back, it's the smartest thing we've done.
Rule one: if a message feels off, ask "what did you mean?" before replying. Rule two: if it still feels off, call. Rule three: if I'm hurt, I wait ten minutes before typing anything.
Yesterday I tested it. Sumit wrote, "why do you always pick that place?" Old me would have fired back. Instead, I put the phone down, made tea, and then wrote, "What did you mean?" He replied, "Just that it's far from my house lol."
That's it. A text is just letters on a screen. My tea was still hot.
Jasleen

What is rule three in Jasleen and Sumit's deal?
If hurt, wait ten minutes before typing anything.
How did Jasleen feel when Sumit's reply came?
Jasleen likely felt relieved and a little amused, since the message she almost took badly was harmless.
Why is waiting before replying a useful habit?
It gives time for hurt to settle, so Jasleen can ask what someone meant instead of reacting to a guess.
What does this habit mean for Sumit?
Sumit gets a chance to explain before being accused, which keeps small texts from turning into fights.

The summer camp ground was baking, the coach was short-tempered, and there was only one spot left at the top of the batting order. Then the new boy, Hemant, arrived and hit three sixes in his first net session. Manoj, who had been the camp's best batsman for two years, immediately became Hemant's loudest supporter. He cheered every shot, fetched Hemant's water bottle, and told the coach, "Hemant should bat first, he's amazing!" His voice was a little too high. That evening, walking home, he kicked every stone on the road. His elder sister walked beside him. "You were very nice to that boy today," she said. "Too nice?" Manoj stopped. "I'm scared he'll take my place," he admitted, and felt lighter saying it.

How many sixes did Hemant hit in his first net session?
Three.
Why was Manoj's voice a little too high?
He was anxious and jealous that Hemant would take his place, and the loud cheering covered it.
What helped Manoj?
His sister gently noticing he was "too nice", which let him admit he was scared of losing his place and feel lighter.
How might Hemant feel about Manoj's support?
Probably pleased and welcomed, not knowing about Manoj's fear.

Read this:

In the village near Ludhiana, Simran, nine, lent her new bicycle to her cousin Tanuja for the whole Sunday. Tanuja rode it to the gurdwara and back three times.
On Monday Simran asked to borrow Tanuja's skipping rope for school. Tanuja said, "No, I need it."
Simran stood in the courtyard, fists tight. "I gave you my cycle for a whole day! You're a cheat!"
Tanuja shrugged and ran off.
Simran stomped inside to her mother. "I'm never lending her anything again. Never. She owes me."
Her mother looked up from the chapatis. "That hurts, doesn't it?"
Simran nodded, eyes stinging. It wasn't just the rope. It felt like the whole world had tipped the wrong way.

Where did Tanuja ride the bicycle?
She rode it to the gurdwara and back three times.
How did Simran feel when Tanuja refused the skipping rope?
She felt cheated and hurt, with tight fists and stinging eyes, because the fair exchange she expected had broken.
How could Simran's mother help her after naming the hurt?
Listen, then help her talk to Tanuja about feeling let down, and gently explore why Tanuja might have needed the rope.
How might Tanuja see the situation?
Tanuja may not think of the bicycle and rope as a trade, and simply wanted to keep her rope.

metadata.subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Jahnavi no longer believed in some of the rituals, yet she sat beside her Ajji at evening prayer every day, letting the old woman's hand rest on hers. She never smirked; she kept her doubts inside. The temple was also home: her friends, her tabla class, the smell of jasmine. One Sunday she asked the elder, Tejas, why they did a particular ritual. His face hardened. "That is disrespect," he said, and over the next weeks some families stopped greeting her. It hurt deeply. She thought of leaving altogether, but Salma, who ran the youth group's community kitchen, said, "Ask me anything. Not every elder thinks like that." Jahnavi began serving meals with Salma on Sundays and found that passing plates, then sitting quietly for five minutes afterwards, steadied her and made her kinder to the shy new girl at the counter. She kept asking her questions, kept sitting beside her grandmother, and kept her friends.

What did Jahnavi do with Salma on Sundays?
She served meals at the community kitchen.
How did Tejas's reaction to Jahnavi's question differ from Salma's, and how did Jahnavi respond?
Tejas called the question disrespect and some families stopped greeting her, which hurt, while Salma invited her to ask anything, and Jahnavi began serving meals with Salma.
What was Jahnavi feeling when families stopped greeting her?
She felt hurt and rejected, deeply enough that she thought of leaving altogether.
How can Jahnavi honour her grandmother while staying honest about her doubts?
She can keep sitting beside her grandmother at prayer without mocking, keep her questions respectful, and take them to people who welcome them.

Read this:

Monday. The box of coloured chalk vanished from the Class 4 cupboard, and the teacher kept Rafiq in at break because he had been the last one near it. Jahnavi, eight, whispered to her friend, "He must have taken it. Teacher wouldn't punish him for nothing."
Wednesday. Jahnavi moved her bag away when Rafiq sat near her at lunch. When he fell in the playground and scraped his knee, she thought, see, bad things happen to him because he's bad.
Friday. The teacher found the chalk box behind the globe on the top shelf. "I'm sorry, Rafiq," she said in front of the class. Rafiq nodded, looking at his shoes. Jahnavi stared at the globe, then at Rafiq's knee, and slowly pulled her bag back to its old place beside him.

Where did the teacher find the chalk box?
Behind the globe on the top shelf.
How did Jahnavi feel toward Rafiq during the week, and what shows it?
Jahnavi felt wary and suspicious of Rafiq, moving her bag away at lunch and deciding even his scraped knee happened because he was bad.
What could Jahnavi do now that the chalk box has been found?
She could say sorry to Rafiq for moving her bag and think about how he was punished and hurt without having done anything wrong.
How might Rafiq have felt during that week?
Rafiq probably felt lonely and ashamed, punished for something he didn't do and avoided by classmates, which may be why he looked at his shoes even after the apology.

Three months into her internship at the research lab, Trisha was put in charge of the two undergraduate helpers, and something in her shifted. She stopped saying please. She sent Pradeep, a second-year, to wash glassware during the one talk he had asked to attend. When he mentioned it, she said, 'Everyone starts at the sink,' though she had never washed a beaker in her life. She began leaving at five while the helpers stayed till seven. In the lab meeting she took credit for their data cleaning without thinking. If anyone had asked, she would have said she was still the friendly Trisha from the canteen. Pradeep, eating alone by the sink window, no longer thought so.

Where did Trisha send Pradeep during the talk?
To wash glassware.
What does Trisha feel about herself during these months?
Trisha feels unchanged and comfortable, believing she is still the friendly Trisha from the canteen.
What small changes could bring back Trisha's care for the helpers?
Letting Pradeep attend talks, sharing credit for their work and keeping the same hours as the helpers.
How does Pradeep feel about the new Trisha?
Pradeep feels hurt and resentful, eating alone and no longer seeing her as friendly.

b) y = 2x + 3 and y = -2x + 3

Give a happy ending to a story about a girl and a boy who find a cave while hiking.

Sana and her brother Imran were hiking with their uncle when they spotted a narrow cave behind a waterfall. "Can we look inside?" Sana begged.

"Just the entrance," said their uncle.

They crept in with a torch. The walls sparkled with wet stone. Imran shone the light higher and gasped. Hundreds of small bats hung from the ceiling, wrapped in their wings.

"Do not wake them," whispered Sana. They stood still, hardly breathing, as a chorus of tiny squeaks echoed.

Outside, the sun was bright. They told their uncle what they had seen, and he nodded. "You were gentle guests," he said.

All the way down the hill, the children drew bats in the air with their fingers.

Read this:

At the design studio in Durban, Leila noticed Thabo had stopped eating lunch with the team. Over two weeks he gave away his desk plants, his good headphones, and the jacket he loved. When Leila thanked him for the headphones, he said, "Keep them. Nothing's going to get better anyway." She felt cold all over. That afternoon she asked him to walk with her to the corner shop. On the pavement she stopped. "Thabo, I've noticed you giving things away and saying nothing will change. I'm worried. Are you thinking about ending your life?" He was quiet, then nodded. Leila kept her voice steady. "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying with you. Let's call the support line together now." They called from the bench outside the shop. Then she drove him to a doctor that evening and called his brother to come and stay the night.

What did Thabo give away over two weeks?
His desk plants, his good headphones, and the jacket he loved.
What was Leila feeling when Thabo said nothing was going to get better?
She felt frightened and cold all over, recognising his words and giveaways as serious warning signs.
Which choices made Leila's response a wise one?
She asked him directly and privately, stayed with him, called the support line right away, took him to a doctor that evening and brought in his brother for the night.
What might Thabo have been feeling before Leila spoke to him?
He seemed hopeless and withdrawn, believing things would never get better.
Why do we tie our hair back near a flame or a machine?
Loose hair can catch fire or get pulled in. Because strands near a flame can ignite easily, and a machine with moving parts can grab hair and drag the head with it.
Is it "with regard to" or "with regards to" in a formal email?

The usual phrase is "with regard to", with no s. "With regards to" is also heard, but careful writers prefer the form without s. It means "about" and is common in formal writing.
Example: With regard to your request, I will reply by Friday.
My cat has started scratching the new sofa.
Cats scratch to keep their claws healthy and to mark their space, so she is not being naughty. Does she have a scratching post?
No. Do we really need one?
Yes, it gives her a better place to scratch. Put it right next to the sofa, since that is the spot she has chosen. Rub a little catnip on it, or play with a string near it, so she notices it.
Should we cover the sofa till then?
That is a good idea. A thick blanket over the scratched corner makes it less fun for her. Once she uses the post regularly, you can slowly move it to where you want it.

Preschool note, Tuesday. From Rekha, teacher.
In pretend play, Saurabh put on the white coat and said loudly, "I am the doctor today!" He treated three teddies.
By pack-up time, the other children wanted to be bus drivers. Saurabh was the only one left at the clinic corner. He looked tired and his voice was wobbly, but he kept saying, "I'm the doctor. I said it."
What I did next: I told him doctors take the bus home too. He thought, nodded, and climbed on the chair-bus still wearing the coat. He smiled for the first time in twenty minutes.

How many teddies did Saurabh treat?
He treated three teddies.
Why did Saurabh stay at the clinic corner even when tired?
He felt upset and bound by his words, because saying "I am the doctor today" made changing feel wrong.
Why did Rekha's idea work?
Saying doctors take the bus home too let Saurabh join the new game without going back on what he said.
How might the other children see Saurabh at the clinic corner?
They might think he is just stubborn and wonder why he won't be a bus driver with them.

Explain this in simpler words, with short sentences, for a child.

Francis suggested keeping only the places that sat close together and asking who would give up their second choice before their first. People laughed, and then most agreed. They voted, and the compact route kept one top pick for every person, with two long detours dropped.

Francis had an idea. He said to keep only the places that were close together. He also asked who would give up their second choice before their first. People laughed, and then most of them agreed. They voted. The close-together trip gave every person one top pick. Two long detours were dropped.

Change this from first person to third person.

I'm Ojas, Neelam's cousin. I stayed at her house this summer holiday.
In the afternoons, Neelam watched rhyme videos on the phone, very still, and didn't answer when I called. When it ended, she cried for more.
In the evenings, Nani sang the same rhymes live. Neelam jumped up, did the actions, and sang lines back.
I don't know what was in her head. But she looked more awake with Nani than with the phone.

Ojas, Neelam's cousin, stayed at her house this summer holiday.
In the afternoons, Neelam watched rhyme videos on the phone, very still, and didn't answer when he called. When it ended, she cried for more.
In the evenings, Nani sang the same rhymes live. Neelam jumped up, did the actions, and sang lines back.
He didn't know what was in her head. But she looked more awake with Nani than with the phone.

Hi Charu Didi,
You said to write down my plan, so here it is. Boards start on 2 March.
Mornings (6–8): maths, because my brain is best then. Evenings: one science, one language. Sundays: full past papers, timed, at the dining table, no music.
The big problem is the phone. Last week I "checked one thing" and it was 11 pm. So Papa is keeping it in his room from 7 to 10. I hated the idea, honestly. But the first night I finished two chapters.
What I don't know is how to stop panicking in the exam hall. You said you used to write "breathe" on your rough sheet. Did that really work, or were you just being nice?
Also, did you ever feel like everyone else was ahead?
Pankaj

What does Pankaj plan to do on Sundays?
Full past papers, timed, at the dining table, with no music.
How did Pankaj feel about handing the phone to Papa?
Pankaj hated the idea at first and felt resentful, but was pleasantly surprised when he finished two chapters the first night.
How could Charu Didi best answer Pankaj's question about exam-hall panic?
She could share honestly what helped her, like a pause and slow breaths, and remind Pankaj that nerves are common, not a sign of failing.
What is it like for Charu to get this email from her younger cousin?
Charu may feel trusted and a little responsible, since Pankaj values her advice enough to plan around it.

Yogesh, your friend didn't ask how to fix his bike, did he? Let your Devika Dadi tell you about Kamla. When I was ten, Kamla was my best friend, and I was very clever, I thought. I told her how to plait her hair, how to hold her pen, how to talk to her brother. I thought I was helping. One day she said, “Devika, you're like a second mother. I already have one.” She walked home with another girl for a week. I was miserable. Then I went to her and said, “I'm sorry. From now on, I'll ask if you want my ideas.” She laughed and said, “Sometimes I will.” We were friends for sixty years.

What did Kamla call young Devika?
Kamla said Devika was like a second mother.
What was young Devika feeling during the week Kamla walked with another girl?
She felt miserable and lonely, missing her best friend.
What choice did Devika make to repair the friendship?
She apologised and promised to ask Kamla whether she wanted ideas before giving advice.
What was all the advice like for Kamla?
Kamla felt bossed and smothered, as if she had a second mother telling her what to do.

I'm Ramesh, and for my first month in the engineering hostel I thought I understood Vasudha's signing because I'm good at charades. When she signed to her friends in the canteen, I'd guess along: that must be food, that must be tired. I even tried joining in with made-up gestures. One day she wrote in my notebook: "It's not mime. It's Indian Sign Language. It has grammar." Then she showed me. The same hand movement changed when her eyebrows went up, turning it into a question. Where she placed people in the space in front of her mattered too; later she could point back to that spot instead of repeating a name. My ears went hot. I had treated her language like a party game. Now I'm in a Saturday class, fumbling through handshapes, and I ask Vasudha when I'm unsure. Sometimes she laughs at my attempts, and I've learnt to laugh too.

What did Vasudha write in Ramesh's notebook?
"It's not mime. It's Indian Sign Language. It has grammar."
How did Ramesh feel after Vasudha showed how her signing worked?
Ramesh felt embarrassed, ears going hot, on seeing that guessing along and made-up gestures had treated her language like a party game.
What is Ramesh doing now that builds the friendship?
Taking a Saturday class and asking Vasudha respectfully when unsure, instead of guessing.
What might it have been like for Vasudha when Ramesh joined in with made-up gestures?
She may have felt her language was being treated as a game rather than respected, which is why she explained that it has grammar.

"Afreen, it's 2 a.m. again. And you're eating instant noodles again."
"Joseph, you're awake too."
"Because I'm hungry because I skipped dinner because I was gaming." Joseph laughed weakly. "We're a mess."
"At home, Ammi made us eat at eight and sleep at eleven."
"Nobody's making us now."
"So we have to make ourselves."
Joseph sat up. "Okay. Deal: dinner at the mess by nine. Screens off at midnight. And a walk around campus before breakfast."
"Every day?"
"Weekdays. Start small."
Afreen groaned. "Fine. But if you skip, you buy chai."
A week later, they were yawning less in lectures. Joseph had even started to like the walks.

What time did Joseph suggest screens off?
At midnight.
What was Joseph feeling when he said "We're a mess"?
Joseph felt tired and a bit embarrassed about their habits.
What made their plan more likely to work?
They started small with clear times, kept it to weekdays and added a playful consequence.
How might Afreen see the routine after a week?
Afreen likely feels more rested and glad they made the deal.

In the tin-roofed lab of the government school in Chittur, Mridul had already laid out the ultrasonic sensor, the colour sensor and a buzzer on newspaper. "Let's fix all of it today!" Lavanya slid the sensors gently to one side. "First it has to move. Just the chassis, two motors, the battery, one switch." It took them two evenings. On the second, the robot finally rolled across the cement floor and turned left when Mridul pressed the key. Then they added the colour sensor, only that, and tested again. It spun in circles. Because everything else had worked the day before, they knew the fault was in the new wiring, and found it in five minutes: a loose ground wire. Mridul laughed. "If we'd added everything at once, we'd still be searching."

What floor did the robot roll across?
It rolled across the cement floor.
Why did Lavanya slide the sensors aside?
Lavanya felt cautious and calm about it, wanting a base that moved first so any later fault would be easy to trace.
What else could the pair do before adding the next part?
They could note down what works after each step, so any new fault can be traced to the last change.
How does Lavanya's approach look to Mridul by the end?
Mridul first wanted everything at once, but by the end sees that building on a working base made the loose wire easy to find.

Read this:

"Ganga, you asked how the conference talk went. I'm Vijay, and honestly, the first minute was the worst minute of my life. My voice shook so much I could hear it through the speakers. I was sure a hundred people were thinking, who let this boy on stage? Then I noticed a woman in the second row, a stranger, grey kurta, notebook open. Every time I finished a sentence, she nodded. Just a small nod. So I started talking to her. By slide four my voice had stopped wobbling. Afterwards she found me at the tea counter and said, 'At my first talk my hands shook so much I dropped the clicker. I was cheering for you the whole time.' I couldn't believe it. I'd been bracing for judgment, and the room had been rooting for me. Now, when someone else is nervous up there, I'm the one in the second row, nodding."

Where was the woman who nodded sitting?
In the second row.
How did Vijay feel during the first minute of the talk?
He was terrified, his voice shaking through the speakers, sure a hundred people were judging him.
Why did the woman's small nod help so much?
It gave Vijay one friendly face to speak to, which steadied him, and showed that the audience was on his side.
How did the woman in the grey kurta see Vijay's nerves?
She felt sympathy, remembering her own shaking hands at her first talk, and was quietly cheering for him.

It was the last day of the project handover, and the office in Bengaluru was chaos: two clients calling, a server down. Tejas's new manager, Ankita, who had just moved from the Berlin office, walked up to his desk. "Your report has three errors. Fix them by four." Then she walked off. Tejas sat stunned. At his previous team, a manager would have said, "Maybe we could look at a few small things?" This felt like a slap. He wanted to complain. With forty minutes left, he didn't have time to brood. He fixed the errors. Then he walked to her desk. "Ankita, can I ask something? When you said the report had errors, were you upset with me?" She looked surprised. "No! I was just saying what needed doing. In Berlin that's normal. Should I say it differently?" Tejas smiled. "Maybe add a 'please'. I'll get used to the directness." "Deal," she said.

By what time did Ankita want the errors fixed?
By four.
What was Tejas feeling when Ankita walked off?
He felt stunned and hurt, as if slapped, because he was used to softer, indirect feedback.
What did Tejas do that helped under time pressure?
He fixed the errors first, then kindly asked Ankita whether she was upset, instead of brooding or complaining.
How did Ankita see her own direct words?
She saw them as just saying what needed doing, normal where she came from, and she was willing to adjust.

messages.content: Eight runners run a race. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded? Write it using factorials.

Answer: 8 x 7 x 6 = 336 ways = 8!/5! = 8P3.

Gold can go to any of 8 runners, silver to any of the 7 others, bronze to any of the remaining 6: 8 x 7 x 6 = 336. ORDER matters here (Asha gold and Bina silver is different from Bina gold and Asha silver). This is an ORDERED selection, or PERMUTATION, of 3 from 8, written 8P3. As factorials: 8!/5! = (8 x 7 x 6 x 5!)/5! = 336. In general nPr = n!/(n - r)!, the product of r numbers counting down from n. Common mistake: 8 x 3 = 24 or 8^3.

Symmetric or not? (Fold down the middle.)
a) butterfly
b) leaf
c) face
d) the letter R
e) kite
f) the digit 7
g) the letter W
h) a heart

a) yes
b) yes (nearly)

d) no
e) yes

g) yes
h) yes

Tuesday night. Everyone whispers in our house now. When I walk into the hall, Amma stops talking to Appa and pretends to check the rice. I heard the words "hospital" and "Thatha," and then Appa said, "Not now, Shalini is here." I went to my room and could not finish my snack. My tummy hurt, and I kept imagining the worst things. Cousin Kavitha called and even she did not know anything. At bedtime I asked Amma straight out, and she sat down with me, called me her brave girl, and said Thatha is in the hospital, the doctors are looking after him, and we can go see him on Sunday. I still feel worried, but not as tight.

What two words did Shalini hear before Appa said, "Not now, Shalini is here"?
She heard "hospital" and "Thatha."
Why did Shalini feel worse while her parents whispered?
Not knowing what was really going on made her imagine the worst, so she felt more scared and her tummy hurt.
What would you advise Shalini's parents to keep doing?
They can keep giving her simple, honest information and let her visit, as Amma began to do, instead of hiding things from her.
What might Amma have been feeling when Shalini asked her straight out?
Amma may have been worried herself and torn between wanting to shield her daughter and seeing that telling the truth would help her more.

Read this:

Jatin, sit. Your Sumit Mama is going to tell you something I never told your mother properly. At twenty-one I was seeing a girl from my typing class, Rekha. If I said I was tired, she said I was bored of her. If I said I wasn't bored, she said I was calling her a liar. I went home feeling guilty for things I hadn't done. One evening my friend Iqbal asked, 'Why do you always say sorry after meeting her?' That question stuck in me. I began writing in a small notebook what I had actually said each day. After a month I read it back and saw the same trick on every page. I trusted that notebook more than the fog in my head, and I ended it. So when your friends say something feels off, listen to them, Jatin.

Where did Sumit meet Rekha?
Sumit met Rekha in the typing class.
How did young Sumit feel after meeting Rekha?
Sumit felt guilty and confused, going home sorry for things he had not done.
What turning point in the story helped Sumit see the pattern?
Writing down what he had actually said each day and reading a month of it back, which let him trust the record over his confusion.
What was it like for Iqbal watching Sumit back then?
Iqbal noticed Sumit apologising after every meeting and was concerned enough to ask why, which gave Sumit the first push.

Read this:

Latika's home bakery in the colony had collected three hundred suggestions for a new cake. She opened her order register and marked the names of people who had bought from her at least twice: forty-one. Their ideas were eggless orange and date-and-walnut. Vijay, who helped with deliveries, said, "Try both, small." She baked ten of each on Saturday, labelled them new, and set them by the counter. By evening the orange cake was gone and four of the date-and-walnut were left. "The buyers picked," said Vijay. Latika added eggless orange to the weekly menu and kept a note of the other result in her book.

How many people had bought from Latika at least twice?
Forty-one people had bought from Latika at least twice.
How did Latika likely feel about running a small test rather than one big batch?
Latika likely felt cautious and curious, wanting to see which cake buyers would actually pick, not only suggest.
What could Latika do if both cakes sell out next time?
Latika could put both on the menu in alternate weeks and note which one gets reordered more.
How might Vijay see the small batch test?
Vijay might find it sensible and low-risk, since the test was cheap and the buyers gave a clear answer.

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Sachin and Farida took a one-page plan for the Saturday farewell party to their class teacher: 3 to 6 pm in the school hall. The teacher asked about supervision, the end time and travel home, and said the principal must approve too.

Wednesday: The principal signed. Farida wrote the parents' note with the time, the place, the end time of six, and a request to say who would collect each child. Sachin gathered the signed slips: twenty-eight of thirty-two.

Saturday: Two teachers sat at the back of the hall. At six, Farida read out the pick-up list at the gate, and each child left with someone on it. There was music and cake, and nothing else. Sachin was tired but pleased.

How many signed slips did Sachin collect?
Sachin collected twenty-eight of thirty-two signed slips.
How did Sachin feel at the end of the party?
Sachin felt tired but pleased, since the party ran safely to the agreed time.
What could the organisers do about the four missing slips, and why?
They could follow up with those four families before Saturday, because a child without a signed slip and a pick-up person should not be at risk.
How might a parent see the pick-up request in the note?
A parent likely feels reassured, since the note gives the end time, the place and a clear plan for getting the child home safely.

Dear Santosh,
It's been four months since you borrowed money for your exam fees. You said you'd return it in two weeks. I've messaged three times. You've read the messages and not replied.
I'm Tanvir, and I'm writing this not to shout, but because I need to say it. I feel foolish. I trusted you because we were roommates, and I thought that meant something.
I'm not going to stop helping people. But next time, I'll lend only what I can afford to lose, and only to people who've shown they can keep their word.
If you can return even part of it, please do. And if something's wrong, just tell me.

How long ago did Santosh borrow the money?
It's been four months.
What is Tanvir feeling while writing this letter?
Tanvir feels foolish and betrayed, having trusted Santosh because they were roommates.
What has Tanvir learned about trust?
Tanvir has learned to trust more carefully, lending only what can be lost and only to people who've shown they keep their word.
How might Santosh feel reading this letter?
Santosh may feel ashamed and guilty, or worried if something is really wrong.

Lalit: 2) can we do a call every Sunday evening? not to fix anything, just talk
Rekha: yes. 7 pm Sundays. I'll set an alarm
Lalit: 3) joined the morning walking group near the stadium. 6:30, three days a week
Lalit: and with Aakash we agreed: he's still my friend, but on a bad night I call the counsellor's after-hours line first, not him
Rekha: that's really thought through
Lalit: the counsellor helped me write it. feels less like one rope, more like a net

When will Lalit and Rekha have their weekly call?
7 pm Sundays.
How does Lalit feel after Aakash said he was exhausted?
Guilty, but okay, and determined to fix it rather than just shift the load onto Rekha.
What makes Lalit's new plan sturdier than before?
Each person or group has a clear role, so no one carries everything and there is always somewhere to turn.
How might Aakash feel about the new agreement?
Relieved and still a friend, able to rest without guilt now that Lalit has other supports.

Read this:

Ira usually paid when she and Pema went out in Kalimpong: momos at the corner stall, the shared taxi up to the viewpoint. Her aunt's shop paid her a small wage, and she liked treating him. "My treat," she'd say, smiling.

But lately she caught herself counting. He never reached for his wallet first, and she'd go quiet on the walk home, jaw tight, hoping he would notice without her having to say it.

One Saturday at the taxi stand she finally said, "I like paying sometimes. But I've been waiting for you to offer, and that isn't fair to you."

Pema looked at his shoes. "My tuition money is tight. I didn't want to say."

"Then we pick places that suit both of us," she said, "and you choose next time."

The taxi arrived. He grinned and paid for the tea.

What did Ira usually pay for when she and Pema went out?
She usually paid for the momos at the corner stall and the shared taxi up to the viewpoint.
Why did Ira go quiet on the walk home?
She was hoping Pema would notice on his own that he never offered, and she was quietly resentful instead of saying so.
What could Ira and Pema do to keep money from souring things between them?
Keep talking openly about what each can spend, choose outings that suit both budgets, and take turns choosing and paying.
How might Pema have felt about Ira paying, before he said anything?
He may have felt embarrassed about his tight tuition money and did not want to admit it, which is why he stayed silent.

Selin had not opened the grant report in nine days. Every morning in her Copenhagen flat she told herself she was lazy and useless, and every morning the file felt heavier. On Tuesday she said it out loud while making coffee. "You're such a failure." Lars, her flatmate, looked up from his cereal. "Would you say that to me if I were late with something?" She blinked. "No. I'd say it happens." "So say that to yourself." It felt silly. She said, "Okay. I'm behind. It happens. Five minutes." She set the kitchen timer and opened the report. When it rang, she had fixed the title and one table. She reset it. Then again. By lunch the introduction was done, and the file felt lighter.

What did Selin set before opening the report?
The kitchen timer, for five minutes.
Why did the file feel heavier each morning Selin called herself lazy?
Each insult added guilt, so the report became a reminder of failure, and avoiding it felt like avoiding that bad feeling.
What choice turned Tuesday around?
Talking to herself the way she would talk to Lars, admitting she was behind without insults, and committing to only five minutes.
What might Lars notice as Selin keeps resetting the timer?
Lars sees his simple question working: the flatmate who was calling herself a failure over coffee is now calmly moving through the report.

"Noor, did I do something wrong? Pieter left hungry."
"What happened, Eshaan?"
"I asked if he wanted more biryani. He said, 'No, thank you.' So I said, 'Arre, have a little.' He said no again. Then I put some on his plate anyway, like my mother does."
"And?"
"He looked really uncomfortable. He didn't eat it."
Noor laughed softly. "In your mother's house, a guest says no twice to be polite, and the host insists. Here in Amsterdam, no means no."
"So I was forcing food on him?"
"A bit, yes. And your aunt last month in Lucknow, remember? I said 'no, thank you' once and she never offered again. I went to bed hungry."
Eshaan groaned. "So it's the opposite for each of us."
"Exactly. Ask once here. Ask three times in Lucknow."
"I'll message Pieter tomorrow. And save him some biryani."

What did Eshaan do after Pieter said no twice?
Eshaan put some on Pieter's plate anyway, like Eshaan's mother does.
How might Noor have felt when the polite no in Lucknow was taken as final?
Noor probably felt embarrassed and a bit awkward, too polite to ask again and going to bed hungry.
What rule does Noor suggest, and why is it useful?
Ask once in Amsterdam and three times in Lucknow; knowing the local rule avoids both offence and awkwardness.
How did Pieter probably experience the extra biryani?
Pieter probably felt uncomfortable and pressured, since for him a first no was final, so he left it uneaten.
Ral is twice as old as Suri. In 3 years, Suri's current age will be 16. What is Ral's current age?

If Suri will be 16 in 3 years, that means she is 16 - 3 = 13 years old now.
Rai is twice as old as Suri, so she is 2 * 13 = 26 years old now.
The answer is 26.

In the park in Seville, Diego sat on the blanket with a plastic shape bucket. Aiko, the little girl from the next blanket, crawled closer.
Diego pressed the yellow circle into the square slot. Push. Push. He turned it. He pressed with both hands. Nothing.
He moved it to the next slot. Nothing. Next slot. Drop!
He squealed and clapped. Then he picked up the yellow circle again and dropped it into the round slot, straight away.

Where was Diego sitting?
Diego sat on the blanket in the park in Seville.
How did Diego feel when the circle dropped in?
He felt happy and excited, which is why he squealed and clapped. 🙂
What could an adult nearby do to help Diego learn without taking over?
They could sit near him and cheer each try, letting him keep turning and testing the block himself.
How might Aiko see Diego's squeal and clap?
Aiko may be curious and excited too, and may want to try dropping a shape in herself.

Read this:

Gautam, ten, sat at the dining table in their Kolkata flat, staring at his rice. His best friend had sat with someone else at lunch.

"How was school?" asked his mother Anjali.

"Horrible. Everything this week was horrible. Nobody likes me. And tomorrow's the maths test, and I'll fail it."

Anjali put down her spoon. "Didn't you tell me on Monday you won the class quiz?"

Gautam shrugged. "That doesn't count."

"And yesterday you said the maths practice was easy."

Gautam was quiet. "I forgot."

Anjali held his hand. "When we feel sad, our minds hide the good bits. Let's talk about lunch, and then we'll see how tomorrow feels."

What did Gautam win on Monday?
The class quiz.
Why did Gautam say "Everything this week was horrible"?
He felt hurt and sad about lunch, and that feeling made his mind pick only the bad memories and expect more bad things.
What did Anjali do that helped Gautam?
She gently reminded him of good things from the week, held his hand, and offered to talk about what upset him.
How might Anjali feel when Gautam says "Nobody likes me"?
Anjali probably feels worried and sad for her son, and wants to comfort him.

Read this:

Deepika pulled her knees up on the hostel terrace and told her senior what had been bothering her. "I'm Deepika, Manoj's lab partner and one floor up, so I notice. First he stopped coming to the mess for dinner. Then he skipped our Friday movie on the terrace, which he started. His room light is on at four. When I asked, he said, 'I'm fine, just busy.' My first idea was to give him a speech about taking care of himself. I didn't. I just knocked on Monday and said, 'Going for chai, want to come? No worries if not.' He said no. I knocked again Wednesday. No. Thursday he came, sat for ten minutes, barely spoke. Friday he came again. It's been three weeks like this, though, and he still looks flat. I think I have to tell him, gently, that talking to the campus doctor or counsellor isn't a big deal."

On which day did Manoj finally come for chai?
Thursday he came, sat for ten minutes and barely spoke.
How does Deepika feel about the change in Manoj?
Deepika is worried and uneasy, noticing how much he has pulled back, but she is also patient and hopeful when he joins for chai.
What is Deepika doing well, and what is her next step?
She offers simple, low-pressure invitations again and again instead of a lecture, and since his low mood has lasted three weeks, she plans to gently suggest the campus doctor or counsellor.
What might it be like for Manoj when Deepika keeps knocking?
Manoj may feel both awkward and quietly grateful, because saying yes is hard but the steady invitations show someone still wants him there.

messages.content: Sandi had $600. She spent half of it at a farmer's market. Gillian spent $150 more than three times Sandi's total. What is the total that Gillian spent at the farmer's market?

Sandi spent 600/2 = 300 dollars at the farmer's market.
Gillian spent 300*3+150 = 1050 dollars at the farmer's market.
The answer is 1050.

Sumit, you're eating biscuits for dinner again, I can see the wrapper. Sit. Your Gurleen Aunty was worse. My first year in Chandigarh, away from my mother's kitchen, I lived on bread-omelette and tea. I slept at three, woke at eleven, missed every morning lecture and called it freedom. By December I was catching every cold in the hostel and failing botany. One evening my roommate Paramjit stuck a timetable on my door: lights off at midnight, breakfast at the mess before nine, a walk round the campus after dinner. I tore it down. She stuck it up again. The third time, I laughed and tried it. Not perfectly. But by March I was awake for botany, and I passed. No mother needed. Just a paper on the door and a friend who didn't give up. Now, go and boil two eggs, Sumit.

What did young Gurleen live on in her first year?
Bread-omelette and tea.
What was Gurleen feeling when she tore down the timetable?
Gurleen probably felt irritated and defensive, as if the timetable threatened her new freedom.
What was the turning point in Gurleen's first year, and why did it work?
Paramjit putting the timetable back up until Gurleen tried it; a few fixed times for sleep, breakfast and a walk gave structure without a parent.
How might Paramjit have felt sticking the timetable up a third time?
Paramjit was probably worried but patient and a little stubborn, and relieved when Gurleen finally laughed and tried it.

In the college library's back corner, Jaya had a message box open and a blank line where the first sentence should be. The engineer she wanted to reach, Revati Menon, designed battery systems at the electric-scooter company Jaya dreamed of joining.
'Just say hi and ask for advice,' whispered Vinita from the next chair.
'Everyone says that. She must get fifty of those.' Jaya closed the message box and opened Revati's public posts instead. Mostly about cooling problems in batteries. Then a link: a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai. Jaya put in one earphone and watched it through, taking notes.
'Okay,' she murmured at the end. 'She said the hardest part was testing in forty-degree heat. I can ask how they test in monsoon humidity. That's a real question, and it shows I listened.'
She wrote three lines. Vinita read them and raised her eyebrows. 'That sounds like someone she'd reply to.'

How long was Revati's talk, and where was it given?
It was a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai.
Why did Jaya close the message box, and what was she feeling?
She felt uneasy that a plain 'hi' would be one of fifty, and wanted her message to be respectful and worth answering.
What else could Jaya do if Revati does not reply?
Send one short, polite follow-up after a week, and meanwhile find another engineer whose work she has actually studied.
How might the message look to Revati?
It stands out from generic requests because it asks about her own talk, which shows real interest and respect for her time.

"Rule one," Kashish said, holding the marker. "No arguing. Every idea goes on the chart. Even silly ones."
"A lost puppy," Francis said.
Kashish wrote it. "Next."
"A ghost in the library." "A robot teacher." "Two kings fighting over a mango." "Aliens at the school sports day." The ideas kept coming until the chart paper had twenty.
"Now we judge," Kashish said. "Which ones need too many props?"
"The robot teacher needs a costume."
"Aliens need spaceships."
"Kings need crowns and a throne."
They crossed out eleven. Then five more that needed too many actors.
"Four left," Francis said. "Lost puppy, library ghost, the talking umbrella, and the mango one without the throne."
"Let's keep three and try each on Monday," Kashish said, and they picked.

How many ideas were on the chart paper?
The chart paper had twenty ideas.
How do you think Francis felt when Kashish wrote down the lost puppy idea without arguing?
Francis probably felt encouraged and safe to keep sharing, since even the first idea went on the chart.
Why was it better to judge the ideas only after the list was full?
Because arguing early might have stopped people sharing, and waiting gave them twenty ideas to choose from before crossing any out.
How might the rest of the class see the three skits on Monday?
They may enjoy a better choice of skits, since the three were picked from many ideas and don't need too many props.

messages.content: Draft a paragraph of about 70 words on spending a day without screens at home.

A day without screens can be surprisingly pleasant. Without phones and television, we notice things we usually miss. We talk more at the table and play board games together. Children draw or read, and grown-ups cook or walk in the garden. The hours feel longer and calmer. At night, we sleep better, since our eyes and minds are rested. I think everyone should try it at least once a month.
Why does the hungry jackal stop fearing the loud sound in the forest?
He finds it is only a war-drum that booms when grasses sway against it. He even creeps inside hoping for fat, but finds only wood and skin.
I like to wonder around the old market on Sunday mornings. Which word is wrong?

I like to wander around the old market on Sunday mornings.
Why: word choice ("wonder around" -> "wander around").
My classmate keeps borrowing my pencils and never returns them.
That's annoying when you have to keep buying new ones. Have you mentioned it to him?
Not yet.
You could say, 'I need my pencils back, so please return them by the end of the day.' A friendly but clear request is fair.
What if he forgets again?
Carry only one spare pencil, and lend it only on the understanding that it comes back. A pencil case with a few labelled ones also helps.
I told him, and he said sorry and returned four pencils!
That's a great result. A clear, kind request often works. Thank him for returning them, and everyone's happy.

Monday: After lab, Vaibhav asked Tarun whether he'd co-write the conference paper with him over the holidays. Tarun smiled, glanced at his phone and said, "Haan, maybe, let's see. Sounds interesting." Vaibhav went home and started an outline with both their names on it.
Thursday: Vaibhav shared the outline. Tarun reacted with a thumbs-up but wrote nothing. Two reminders later, the document still showed no edits from him. In the corridor Tarun kept saying, "Yes, yes, I'll look," without meeting his eyes, and turned the talk to cricket.
The next Monday: Vaibhav caught him at the canteen. "I need a clear answer, and either is fine. Are you in, yes or no?" Tarun let out a breath. "Honestly, no. My internship starts in two weeks. I didn't want to disappoint you." "That's okay. I'd rather know." That evening Vaibhav took Tarun's name off the draft.

How did Tarun react to the shared outline?
With a thumbs-up, but he wrote nothing.
Why did Tarun keep saying "maybe" and "yes, yes"?
Tarun felt uncomfortable saying no and didn't want to disappoint Vaibhav, so he softened the refusal into vague agreement.
What finally cleared things up?
Vaibhav asked a direct yes-or-no question and said either answer was fine.
What was the vague yes like for Vaibhav?
Confusing and costly: he built an outline with both names and chased reminders before learning it had been a no all along.

"Farida! Sudha took my doll!"

"Sudha, did you?"

"No! Farida is angry! She's being mean to me!"

"Sudha, the doll is in your hand."

"Because Farida is angry!"

The Eid lights twinkled on the window. Farida's aunt knelt beside Sudha. "Sudha, I think you wanted the doll very much. And maybe you feel a bit angry and bad inside."

Sudha's lip wobbled. "I wanted it."

"That's okay. Let's ask Farida if you can have a turn."

Sudha held out the doll. "Sorry, Farida."

What did Sudha have in her hand?
The doll.
Why did Sudha say Farida was angry and mean?
Sudha felt angry and bad inside about taking the doll, so she put that feeling onto Farida.
What did Farida's aunt do that helped Sudha?
She gently named Sudha's wanting and angry feeling, then suggested asking for a turn.
How might Farida feel when Sudha calls her mean?
Farida probably feels upset and confused, since Sudha took her doll.

"Dilnaz, the trip's tomorrow. Aren't you packing?"
"Already done, Samir."
"When?"
"After dinner. Lunch box goes in the morning, but the rest is in. I checked it with the list."
"You're so boring."
"Boring means I'll sleep."
Next morning.
"Samir, give me the list again. I'm checking one more time."
"You checked last night!"
"Water, yes. Lunch box, yes. Jacket, yes. Sun cap... Where's my sun cap?"
"On the chair. You wore it yesterday."
"There. That's why I check twice."
She put it on her head and walked out calmly, humming.

When did Dilnaz pack her bag?
After dinner, the night before.
How did Dilnaz feel as she walked out in the morning?
She felt calm and settled, humming, because the second check caught the missing cap.
What else could Dilnaz do to make the morning check even easier?
She could keep the list stuck on the bag, so the check takes a minute.
How does Dilnaz's two checks look to Samir?
Samir thinks it is boring at first, but sees the second check catch the sun cap.

Resource room note, week 6. Gautam (Class 9) came on his own today, which is new. He said, "When I read the question paper, the lines jump. I know the answers when someone reads them out." He had tested it himself: last week Sahil read him the history questions in a free period, and he answered nine of ten aloud. We tried a ruler under each line and a larger-font sheet; he read faster and his shoulders dropped. He asked whether exam questions could be read aloud to him. I explained that he could apply through the school's support process and that we would invite his parents in. He said, "I'm not stupid. Just slow on paper." Plan: parents' meeting Thursday, a reading assessment request through the school, larger-font papers from now. — R. Nair

How many of the history questions did Gautam answer aloud?
Nine of ten.
What does Gautam's line 'I'm not stupid. Just slow on paper' suggest he feels?
He seems frustrated at being misjudged, but more confident now that he has worked out how he learns best.
Which supports helped in the resource room, and what should come next?
The ruler under each line and the larger-font sheet helped him read faster; next come the parents' meeting and the school's formal request, so the support is official.
How might Sahil see his part in this?
Sahil may feel glad and a little proud that reading the questions aloud helped Gautam discover what he needed.

Mentoring note, week three
I noticed Lalremsiami keeps saying "all good" in our check-ins, even when her deadline slips. So today I changed my approach. When I was a new girl in this office, I missed a launch date so badly that the whole team stayed until midnight. I told her that story, and also that our department head reads emails late at night but hates getting them after nine, which nobody writes down anywhere.
She laughed properly for the first time. Then she said her dataset has been broken for two weeks and she was scared to say. We made a plan for it on the spot. I will keep sharing my mistakes when they help.
Binita, team lead

What does Lalremsiami keep saying in check-ins?
"All good."
Why did Binita decide to share her own missed launch?
She was concerned that Lalremsiami felt too scared to admit problems and hoped an honest story would help her feel less alone.
What did Binita's honesty make possible, and what should she keep doing?
Lalremsiami admitted the broken dataset, so they could plan a fix; Binita should keep sharing her mistakes when they help.
What might Lalremsiami have been feeling during the two weeks she said nothing?
She was probably anxious and alone, afraid that admitting the broken dataset would make her look bad.

In the village, Alka's bicycle was her pride. She'd saved for the silver bell herself. So when Anirban borrowed the bike to fetch medicine for his grandmother and came back with the bell hanging loose and scratched, he knew what was coming.
Alka stared at it. "What happened?"
Anirban felt the usual excuses rise: the road was bad, a dog chased him, the bell was loose already. Some of that was true. The road was bad.
But he'd also been riding too fast, showing off to the boys at the well.
"I was going too fast and hit a stone," he said. "I'm sorry. I'll fix the bell tomorrow at the cycle shop."
Alka's face relaxed a little. "The road near the well is terrible, though."
"It is. But I was still too fast."
She laughed, surprised. The next evening, they rode together to the cycle shop.

Why did Anirban borrow the bicycle?
To fetch medicine for his grandmother.
How did Anirban feel as the excuses rose in him?
Anirban felt nervous and tempted to defend himself, but chose honesty about riding too fast.
Which choice worked, and why?
Anirban owned his part with a plain sorry and offered to fix the bell, which helped the friendship recover quickly.
How did Alka react to Anirban's apology?
Alka relaxed, even acknowledged the bad road, and laughed in surprise at his honesty.

“Seema, you're in for the Navratri decorations, right? Everyone brings one string of lights,” said Mrs Kulkarni at the society committee meeting.
“Of course. I'll bring two.”
“Good. Now,” Gargi leaned in, “has anyone seen the new tenants in B-wing? Not married, I hear. Coming home at midnight.”
A few heads turned to Seema. She smiled. “I haven't met them yet. I'll probably just say hello at the garba.”
“But don't you think—”
“Honestly, Gargi, I'd rather not decide anything about them. Should we fix the rangoli roster?”
Mrs Kulkarni laughed. “Yes, the rangoli. Seema, you take Saturday.”
“Done,” Seema said, writing it down.

How many strings of lights did Seema offer to bring?
She offered to bring two.
What was Gargi feeling while leaning in about the tenants?
Gargi seemed curious and eager for gossip, keen to share the rumour.
Which choice by Seema worked, and why?
She happily joined the shared decorations but politely stepped away from the gossip and moved to the rangoli roster, so nobody was insulted.
How might the new tenants be affected by the way this meeting went?
Because Seema refused to judge them, they may get a friendly hello at the garba instead of arriving to rumours.
Passive, please: Many children read this book.
This book is read by many children.
Describe a frog in under twelve words and use the word "pond".
A green frog sits on a lily pad in the pond.

Wednesday, 11 pm
Mummyji called for help four times tonight. The baby woke twice. I have a client presentation at nine tomorrow. Since her stroke in March, she's lived with us, and I do her physio, her meals and her medicines, plus the baby, plus the job. I love her. She's been kind to me since the day I married into this family. And tonight I stood in the kitchen and thought, I can't do this, I don't want to do this, and then I felt disgusting for thinking it. I'm writing it so I stop pretending. Tomorrow I'm going to ask Uday, my brother-in-law, to take Mummyji every weekend. And I'm booking the day-care nurse three mornings a week. That isn't abandoning her. It's how I keep going.
Shreya

How many times did Mummyji call for help tonight?
Four times.
What did Shreya feel standing in the kitchen?
Shreya felt exhausted and resentful, then disgusted at the thought.
What steps is Shreya planning?
Asking Uday to take Mummyji every weekend and booking a day-care nurse three mornings a week.
How might Uday respond to Shreya's request?
Uday may be surprised at how much Shreya has carried, and hopefully willing to share the weekends.

Monday. Zaid could not find his pencil. "Rehana took it!" he told the class. His neighbour Rehana went red and said, "I did not." Zaid glared at her for the rest of the day, and Ayesha Ma'am had to ask them both to sit quietly. Tuesday. At home Zaid opened his notebook to do his sums. The pencil was under it. He sat very still. Wednesday. He walked to Rehana's desk with his eyes on the floor. "I said you took it. I found it. I'm sorry." Rehana nodded slowly, and gave him the eraser to borrow.

Where did Zaid find his pencil?
It was under his notebook at home.
What was Zaid feeling on Tuesday when he found the pencil under his notebook?
He felt ashamed. He sat very still because he had blamed Rehana without proof.
What alternative approach could Zaid have used on Monday, and why?
He could have looked slowly through his bag and books first, or asked Rehana if she had seen it. Asking calmly would not have hurt his neighbour.
How does Rehana see what Zaid did on Monday?
Rehana felt blamed and embarrassed, because Rehana went red in front of the class. The apology helped, and Rehana nodded and lent Zaid the eraser.

Tuesday. Revathi, an architect, read her draft talk about the new community hall to her cousin Pradeep, a bus conductor. "Cross-ventilation via clerestory openings reduces the thermal load." Pradeep blinked. "Is that good or bad?" Revathi laughed and circled the sentence in red.
Thursday. She rewrote every page. "High windows near the roof let hot air out, like the gap at the top of a bus window keeps the bus cool." She tried it on Pradeep again. This time he explained it back to her, waving a hand at the ceiling.
Monday. At the panchayat meeting, Revathi used the bus-window line and a cardboard model. Then she asked the eldest member, "Could you tell everyone how the hall will stay cool?" He did, slowly, and the room nodded.

What did Revathi circle in red on Tuesday?
The sentence "Cross-ventilation via clerestory openings reduces the thermal load."
Why did Revathi laugh when Pradeep asked "Is that good or bad?"
She realised a sentence that was clear to her as an architect told a non-architect nothing, and she took his question as useful rather than annoying.
What three things did Revathi do that made her explanation work?
She tested it on someone outside her field, used an everyday example like the bus window, and asked the eldest member to say it back.
What would change if Revathi had given her Tuesday draft at the panchayat?
The members might have nodded politely without understanding, and the hall's design would have sounded like jargon rather than a plan they could back.
I feel sad today. Can food help? What do I make?

I am sorry you feel sad. Comfort food can help a little. Something warm and familiar, like khichdi, a hot bowl of dal rice, or a cup of chai, can feel like a hug. Cooking itself can also calm your mind.
My grandmother used to make me sweet rice when I was sad.
Then make that for yourself. Cooking something she made can feel like having her near. Cook rice with milk, sugar and a pinch of cardamom, just like she did.
Her name was Radha. She added saffron.
Then add a few strands of saffron, soaked in warm milk, to Radha's sweet rice. The smell and the colour will bring back the memory. Eat it slowly, and let yourself remember her.
Thank you. Whose recipe is it, again?
It is your grandmother Radha's. She made it with milk, sugar, cardamom and saffron. It is a sweet way to remember her when you feel low.

The bus back from Goa was two hours late, and nine tired students sat on their bags at the Mapusa stand, playing truth or dare to stay awake.
"Madhav, truth: ever kissed anyone?"
He could feel the grin waiting on Tushar's face. For a second he considered a made-up story about a girl from his coaching class. Instead he shrugged. "Nope."
"At twenty?" Tushar hooted. "Bro, we need to fix you. Party at the hostel tonight, I'll set you up."
Laughter. Madhav's ears burned. "No thanks. I'll get there when it's real."
"Boring!"
Then the rain started. Everyone crammed under the tin roof, and the game moved on. Arohi, squeezed beside him, said quietly, "For what it's worth, I haven't either. I just never say it out loud."
Madhav let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "Weird how that felt like the bravest thing I did all trip."

How late was the bus back from Goa?
Two hours late.
What do Madhav's burning ears suggest about how he felt?
He felt embarrassed and exposed by the laughter, even though he chose to answer honestly.
What would you advise Madhav if Tushar keeps pushing to set him up?
Give the same calm no and spend more time with friends like Arohi who don't need him to prove anything.
How does Arohi see Madhav's honest answer?
As brave and familiar; it lets her quietly admit her own inexperience for the first time.

A car moves at 72 km/h. What is this speed in metres per second?

Answer: 72 km/h = 72 x 5/18 m/s = 20 m/s.

1 km = 1,000 m and 1 h = 60 x 60 = 3,600 s. So 1 km/h = 1,000 m in 3,600 s = 1,000/3,600 m/s = 5/18 m/s. To change km/h into m/s, MULTIPLY BY 5/18: 72 x 5/18 = 72 / 18 x 5 = 4 x 5 = 20 m/s. Check the long way: 72 km/h means 72,000 m in 3,600 s, and 72,000 / 3,600 = 20, so 20 m each second. The numbers that divide nicely are multiples of 18: 18 km/h = 5 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 90 km/h = 25 m/s.

Sangeeta had shouted at her mother the night before, in front of the neighbours: "You don't understand anything! I'm not a child!" It was about going to the fair in Nandurbar with her friends. Sunaina had gone silent and turned to the stove.

Before dawn, Sangeeta was up. She fetched four pots of water from the well. She swept the courtyard, cleaned the cowshed, and had the chai boiling before Sunaina woke. She put the cup in her mother's hands and went to scrub the steps, saying nothing.

Sunaina watched her for a while, then called her over. "This is a lot of work for one shout," she said. "The tea is good. But I'd like to hear it too."

Sangeeta looked at the wet broom. "Sorry, Aai. I didn't mean you don't understand." Sunaina nodded and handed her half the chai.

Sangeeta fetched four pots of water from the well.

It suggests Sangeeta feels guilty about shouting and hopes the work will cancel the harm without words.

Sunaina acknowledged the tea and effort kindly but asked to hear it too, which let Sangeeta say an actual sorry.
What was it like for Sunaina the night before?
Sunaina was hurt and embarrassed, shouted at in front of neighbours, which is why she went silent and turned to the stove.

The power went out at eight, and the geography test was at nine the next morning. Aniket, fourteen, sat by the emergency lamp with a list of fifteen crops and the states that grow them.
"Rice, West Bengal. Wheat, Uttar Pradesh. Cotton, Gujarat," he chanted. Every time the lamp flickered he lost his place and started from the top.
By ten he knew the first five perfectly. Numbers ten to fifteen were a blur.
His sister Lavanya looked over. "Start from the bottom this time."
"Why? The top ones are the important ones."
"They're not more important. You just keep reading them first."
He grumbled and kept starting from the top. Then he added, "At least the test isn't with the new tuition ma'am. Sarika ma'am. Rohit said she's super strict."
"She gave you extra time last week."
"Rohit said it on the first day. She's strict."

How many crops were on Aniket's list?
Fifteen crops.
Why is Aniket so sure Sarika ma'am is strict?
Rohit's comment was the first thing he heard about her, so it stuck as the truth, and even the extra time she gave him doesn't change his view.
What choice could Aniket make at the moment Lavanya suggests starting from the bottom?
He could take her advice and begin with numbers ten to fifteen, so the later crops get as much practice as the first five.
How does Lavanya see Aniket's way of studying?
Lavanya can see he keeps favouring the top of the list just because he reads it first, and she seems a little exasperated that he won't try another way.

Sunday night
Ishita messaged again today. That's six messages I haven't opened. "Are you okay?" "Did I do something?" "Bhavna??"
I haven't replied because I don't know how to say it. Ever since the trip, I feel like we don't fit anymore. She talks about the same things; I'm into different stuff now. I want some distance. That's all. But writing that feels so mean.
So I've been hiding. Leaving class fast. Pretending my phone is broken. And every time her name pops up, my stomach goes hollow with guilt.
I realised tonight that I'm hoping she'll just give up. That's worse than saying it. She's lying awake wondering what she did.
I wrote it out and sent it: "Ishita, I'm sorry for going quiet. I've been needing a bit of space. It's not anything you did. I just didn't know how to say it."
It took two minutes. I wasted two weeks.

Six messages.

Bhavna feels a hollow guilt, knowing the silence is hurting Ishita.

Hoping Ishita would give up was worse than being honest, so Bhavna sent a short, kind message explaining the need for space.
What have the two weeks of silence been like for Ishita?
Ishita has felt confused and anxious, sending messages and probably lying awake wondering what she did wrong.

"Sir, it says I'm fifteen. I'm sixteen. The under-16 cutoff…"

"I trust you with coaching, sir. But I won't sign something that isn't true."
"You'll let the team down?"

At home she told her father everything. He read the form and said, "You did the right thing. He's a good coach, but this was wrong." He called the school sports head that evening. The next day Yamini's form was corrected, and she was entered in the under-18 group instead.

messages.content: Parker wants to find out what the average percentage of kernels that pop in a bag is. In the first bag he makes, 60 kernels pop and the bag has 75 kernels. In the second bag, 42 kernels pop and there are 50 in the bag. In the final bag, 82 kernels pop and the bag has 100 kernels.

In the first bag the proportion that pops is .8 because 60 / 75 = .8
In the second bag the proportion that pops is .84 because 42 / 50 = .84
In the third bag the proportion that pops is .82 because 82 / 100 = .82
The proportions totals 2.46 because .8 + . 84 + .82 = 2.46
The average proportion is .82 because 2.46 / 3 = .82
The average percentage is 82 because .82 x 100 = 82
The answer is 82.

What did Yogesh feel on the bus home?
Yogesh felt heavy with compassion for Mama, and uneasy on noticing the grudge about Deshpande.
What did Yogesh do instead of lecturing Dhruv Mama, and what came of it?
Yogesh asked what Mama had wanted to do with the job, and for five minutes the anger turned into sadness that could be shared.
What might it be like for Dhruv Mama to be asked about his hopes instead of being told to let go?
He may feel heard for once, which let him show the sadness underneath the anger.
Isabella earns $5 an hour babysitting. She babysits 5 hours every day, 6 afternoons a week. After babysitting for 7 weeks, how much money will Isabella have earned?

She earns 5*5=$25 in a day.
In a week she earns 25*6=$150.
In 7 weeks, she earns 150*7=$1050
The answer is 1050.

Note, Thursday. I look after Rafiq after school, and yesterday I watched him do something new. He asked his parents for ten minutes, sat them down and read from a paper: "If I may have a puppy, I will take it on the morning walk every day before school, and I will keep my marks at least where they were last term." His mother asked who would clean up. Rafiq said, "Me, and I will ask for help at first." His father smiled and called the offer fair, and they said they would think until Sunday. Rafiq nodded quickly, though his knee kept bouncing under the table. I told him waiting is part of the deal. Pooja

What two things did Rafiq promise in return for a puppy?
He promised to take it on the morning walk every day before school and to keep his marks at least where they were last term.
What was Rafiq feeling while he waited for his parents' answer?
Nervous and hopeful, since his knee kept bouncing under the table even though he nodded quickly.
What could Rafiq add to his offer if his parents remain unsure?
He could suggest a trial period or offer some pocket money for supplies, because it lowers the risk for his parents.
How might Rafiq's parents see the proposal compared with a plain "please"?
It gives them something concrete to weigh, and his father called it fair, so they seem to see a child ready to take responsibility.

Rewrite as prose in exactly three sentences.

Between them see a mountain rise
Whose splendour will enchant thine eyes;
His sides are clothed above, below,
With all the rarest herbs that grow.
Upon that mountain's lofty crest
Four plants, of sovereign powers possessed,
Spring from the soil, and flashing there
Shed radiance through the neighbouring air.

Between them you will see a mountain rise, whose splendour will delight your eyes. Its sides, above and below, are covered with the rarest herbs that grow. On the mountain's high top, four plants with great powers grow from the soil, and they flash and shed light through the air around them.

Monday. Rashmi knocked over the paint pot. "Why did you do that? Answer me!" Anand Sir snapped. Rashmi stared at the floor, silent, and he wrote "defiant" in his notebook.
Wednesday. When he raised his voice again, he noticed her hands trembling and her eyes fixed on nothing. He stopped. That was not stubbornness.
Friday. She spilled her water. Anand Sir knelt and said quietly, "It's okay. Take a breath. Tell me when you're ready." After a moment Rashmi whispered, "Sorry," and fetched a cloth.

What did Anand Sir write in his notebook on Monday?
Anand Sir wrote "defiant" in his notebook.
What does Rashmi's silent stare on Monday really suggest she was feeling?
It suggests Rashmi was frightened and frozen by the shouting, not stubborn.
What changed on Friday, and why did it work?
Anand Sir knelt, spoke quietly and gave Rashmi time, so her body could settle and she could answer and clean up.
How did Anand Sir's view of Rashmi change between Monday and Wednesday?
At first Anand Sir read the silence as defiance, but noticing her trembling hands, he saw it as fear.
Could you write about a scarecrow who makes a friend?

In a wheat field outside Karnal stood a scarecrow named Bhola, dressed in an old kurta and a torn hat. Crows kept away from him, which was his job, but it made him lonely.

One evening a small crow with a hurt wing fell onto his shoulder. Bhola could not move his arms to help. He could only stand still and hold her.

The crow, named Tinku, stayed through the night, warm against his straw. In the morning, her wing felt better, but she did not fly off. She hopped up to his hat and built a small nest there.

The farmer, Mr. Gill, saw the nest and shook his head. But he left it, and the wheat grew tall.

In Valencia, Diego, nine, remembered the night his grandfather died. He had been in the kitchen, eating bread with honey, when the phone rang. His mother dropped a cup, and it broke on the tiles.

He told the story to his sister Noa, years later it seemed, though it was only one year. "I was eating honey bread. Mamá dropped the blue cup."

Noa said softly, "I think you were asleep. I woke you up."

Diego shook his head. "No, I remember the honey. And the cup breaking."

Noa didn't argue. She just held his hand. "Maybe some of it happened on another day."

Diego held on to the picture. It still felt perfectly clear.

What does Diego remember eating when the phone rang?
Bread with honey.
Why does Diego hold on to the picture of the honey and the cup?
The night of his grandfather's death was so emotional that the memory feels perfectly clear and true to him, and letting go of it may feel sad.
How could an adult gently help Diego with this memory?
An adult could listen and share the grief, without insisting on correcting details, and gently say memories can mix.
How does Noa respond to Diego's version?
Noa is gentle and caring, holding his hand instead of arguing.

In the week before Christmas, the Delhi colony park was full of fairy lights and puppies born to the old street dog everyone called Rani.

Vaibhav wouldn't go in.

"Why?" asked Tanvir.

"Didn't you hear? Some kid in Rohini got bitten really badly. It was on the news. His hand was all bandaged."

"That was one dog. In Rohini."

"Dogs are dogs." Vaibhav folded his arms. "They're all dangerous."

Tanvir pointed. Six children were sitting around Rani's puppies.

"We play here every day. How many kids from our colony got bitten?"

Vaibhav thought. "...None."

"So?"

Vaibhav still stood at the gate, his fists in his jacket pockets. The bandaged hand from the news seemed much bigger in his mind than all those ordinary days.

What was the old street dog called?
The old street dog everyone called Rani.
Why did Vaibhav feel all dogs are dangerous?
Vaibhav felt frightened by the vivid news story of a bandaged hand, and that one memorable case felt more real than many calm days.
What small step might help Vaibhav trust the park again?
Vaibhav could stand near the gate with Tanvir and watch the children with Rani's puppies for a while before coming closer.
How does Tanvir see the danger in the park?
Tanvir sees it as low, because they play there every day and no child from their colony has been bitten.
