At the working women's hostel in Pune, the rule was clear: gate closes at 10 pm. Chandrika, twenty-five, the new warden, enforced it. Then three nurses from the city hospital moved in, and their shifts ended at 11.
The guard refused to open the gate. The nurses complained. Other residents said, "Rules are rules."
Chandrika called a meeting in the common room. She wrote on the board: safety for all, rest for workers, fairness. She asked each side to speak. The nurses described standing outside at night. Older residents said a late gate made them nervous.
She followed the hostel's procedure and took a written proposal to the manager, Hemant: a late gate with an ID register, only for shift workers.
Hemant approved it for a trial month. Chandrika pinned the new rule up and invited everyone to review it together in thirty days.

What time did the nurses' shifts end?
At 11.
What was Chandrika feeling when she called the meeting?
She felt concerned and responsible, wanting to be fair to both the nurses and the older residents.
How did Chandrika handle the rule conflict?
She named the values at stake, let everyone speak, followed procedure with a written proposal to Hemant, and set a review to improve the rule.
How might the older residents feel about the new rule?
They might feel reassured by the ID register and the review, since their safety concerns were heard.
How is a historian different from a history teacher?

A historian studies and writes about the past, often by reading old records. A history teacher teaches the subject, though some do both. Historian is a noun.
Example: The historian visited the old fort to study its walls and stones.
Aaron has four times as many cows as does Matthews. Together, they have 30 more cows than Marovich. If Matthews has 60 cows, how many cows do the three have altogether?

If Matthews has 60 cows, Aaron has 4*60 = 240 cows.
Together, Aaron and Matthews have 240+60 = 300 cows.
Since Marovich has 30 fewer cows than the combined number of cows that Aaron and Matthews have, Marovich has 300-30 = 270 cows.
Altogether, the three have 270+300 = 570 cows
The answer is 570.

Uday was furious by the time he got home to their flat in Kolkata. Irawati, his friend since Class Five, had copied the whole science answer from the girl in front and scored one mark more than him. He had studied till one in the morning.
Before dinner he typed in the class group: “Some people in 9B should thank their neighbours for their marks. You know who you are.” He hit send.
In ten minutes there were forty replies. Guesses, names, laughing faces. Someone wrote Irawati's name. Someone else named a different girl, who had nothing to do with it. By morning a rumour was going round that Irawati's parents had paid for her marks.
At school Irawati wouldn't look at anyone. The girl wrongly named was in tears. The class teacher called Uday in, not to talk about copying but about the post. What should have been a quiet word with the teacher was now a fight the whole class was part of.

What did Uday type in the class group?
Some people in 9B should thank their neighbours for their marks. You know who you are.
What was Uday feeling when he hit send?
Uday was furious and resentful, having studied till one only to be beaten by a copied answer.
What could Uday have done instead of posting?
Talk to Irawati privately or tell the class teacher calmly, keeping it a quiet matter instead of a public fight.
How was the next day for the girl who was wrongly named?
She was in tears, hurt by a rumour about something she had nothing to do with.

Read this:

"Hansa Ba, can I have some more dhokla?"
Hansa Ba wobbled her head side to side.
Ojas paused, plate in hand. "Is that a yes or a no?"
"It's a yes, beta! Take!"
"But in Chicago, shaking your head means no."
"This isn't shaking. This is..." She wobbled again. "Like 'Okay, go ahead.'"
"What if you just nod?"
"Nodding is too stiff. The wobble is friendlier." She laughed.
Ojas tried it. His head went side to side, a bit jerky.
"Not bad! Now you're a real Gujarati boy."
He grinned and took three pieces of dhokla. "I'll ask next time if I'm not sure."

What food did Ojas want more of?
Dhokla.
What was Ojas feeling when Hansa Ba wobbled her head?
Ojas felt confused and unsure, since in Chicago head shaking means no.
What did Ojas decide to do if he's unsure next time?
He decided to ask if he doesn't understand the head wobble.
How does Hansa Ba see the head wobble?
She sees it as a friendly way to say "okay, go ahead", warmer than a stiff nod.

I've shared a room with Akash since first year, so I've had a front-row seat to him and Rosy.

The first few months were all late-night calls and inside jokes. Then came the food. Rosy's family is Syrian Christian from Kottayam; they eat beef at Christmas. Akash's family is strict vegetarian. The first time Rosy came to our room with a tiffin of her mother's cutlets, Akash asked, very carefully, what was in them. She laughed and said, "Chicken, don't worry."

Last week Akash came back from home looking grey. His father had asked, "What will you two do about religion? About children?" Akash hadn't known what to say.

That night I heard him on the phone with Rosy for two hours. At the end he said, "We'll figure it out. Both of us. Not me alone."

I don't know how it'll turn out. But they're facing it together.

— Karthik

What was in the cutlets Rosy brought?
Chicken.
How does Karthik feel watching Akash and Rosy?
Karthik feels concerned but hopeful, unsure how it will turn out but moved that they are facing it together.
What could help Akash and Rosy at this stage?
Talking openly with each other and then with both families, facing the questions as a team rather than alone.
What is it like for Akash to hear his father ask about religion and children?
He feels shaken and unprepared, which is why he came back looking grey.

Monday, Holi week. A cycle-wallah sold gulal outside the gate. Kiran bought a packet with Mummy.

Tuesday. Vandana Aunty from next door asked, 'Was that the man with the blue turban?' Kiran shrugged. 'Blue turban, na? Tall one?' 'Yes,' said Kiran.

Friday. At the Holi party, Kiran told everyone, 'The gulal man had a big blue turban!' Mummy laughed. 'Beta, he had a cap. Remember?' Kiran frowned hard. 'No. A blue turban. I saw it.'

What did the cycle-wallah sell?
Gulal.
How does Kiran feel when Mummy says the man wore a cap?
Kiran feels confused and a little cross, sure of the blue turban because the memory now feels real.
How could Vandana Aunty have asked without planting a detail?
She could have asked, 'What did the gulal man look like?' and let Kiran describe him.
How might Mummy see Kiran's certain answer?
Mummy is amused at first, but may realise Vandana Aunty's question shaped what Kiran now remembers.

Kashish had only a day at her grandmother's house in Amritsar before her train back to college, and Nani was in hospital with a fever. Kashish sat by the bed while the ward buzzed around them.
Nani held her hand. "I wanted to be a teacher, you know. I had a place at the training college. I let my brothers talk me out of it. And I never told them how much it hurt."
Kashish felt her chest tighten. She'd been thinking of dropping her plan to apply for a journalism course next year, because her uncles called it risky.
"Don't look so sad, puttar," Nani said. "It's not your burden. Just don't let other people's fears decide for you."
On the train that night, Kashish opened the application form. She would at least try, and she'd tell her uncles why.

What had Nani wanted to be?
Nani had wanted to be a teacher.
How did Kashish feel hearing Nani's regret?
She felt her chest tighten, moved and a little anxious, because it matched her own doubts about the journalism course.
What did Kashish decide to do on the train, and why was it wise?
She opened the application form and planned to explain to her uncles, taking Nani's regret as a warning without making it a burden.
How might Nani feel knowing Kashish opened the form?
Nani would probably feel relieved and proud that her story helped her granddaughter try.

Supervisor's note, community kitchen, 12 August
Today two volunteers argued about who had locked the storeroom on Saturday. Reena, our shift coordinator, handled it better than I would have.
Mr Pillai insisted he had handed her the key. Reena said, "The way I recall it, I found the key on the hook. But let's look." She opened the sign-out register. It showed the key signed back by another volunteer at 6:10.
She didn't suggest anyone was wrong on purpose. She said, "Saturdays are busy. All of us mix things up." Mr Pillai grumbled, then laughed.
Reena then suggested everyone initial the register each time. I agreed, and I've printed a new sheet.
Joseph

What did the sign-out register show?
It showed the key signed back by another volunteer at 6:10.
Why did Reena say, "Saturdays are busy. All of us mix things up"?
Reena seems calm and wants Mr Pillai to feel at ease, because she believes memory slips are normal, so nobody needs to be treated as a liar.
What change did Reena suggest, and how does it help?
Everyone initials the register each time, so future questions are settled by a record instead of competing memories.
How might Mr Pillai have felt after the register was checked?
He may have felt a bit embarrassed, but because Reena did not blame him, he could grumble and then laugh instead of feeling accused.

At the small shop in Kasauli, Papa was talking with Saurabh uncle about the price of apples. Sarika, five, pulled Papa's kurta. "Papa, I saw a monkey! A big one!" Papa kept talking. "Papa! PAPA! A MONKEY!" Saurabh uncle laughed. Papa didn't scold. He crouched and held out his little finger. "Hold my finger, Sarika. That means I know you're waiting. Your turn is next." Sarika held it tight, bouncing on her toes. Papa finished his sentence. Then he turned. "Now, tell me about the monkey." Sarika told him everything, arms wide.

What was Papa talking about with Saurabh uncle?
The price of apples.
What was Sarika feeling when she pulled Papa's kurta?
She was excited and bursting to share, worried the moment would pass.
Why did Papa's finger-holding idea help?
It showed Sarika she was noticed and promised her a turn, making the wait easier than scolding would.
How might Saurabh uncle see the moment?
He seemed amused, laughing at Sarika's excitement.

Leela, come here. I saw you with those boys behind the school wall. Let me tell you what happened to me.
When I was fifteen, in our Indore colony, my friends started bunking tuition to smoke beedis by the railway line. Every evening they'd say, "Come on, Darshan, don't be a scaredy-cat. It's just one."
I wanted to be with them so badly. They were my whole world. For two weeks I made excuses: headache, homework.
Then one evening they surrounded me and held one out. "Now or never."
That was the turning point. I laughed and said, "Never, then," and walked back home along the tracks. My heart was hammering all the way.
They teased me for a month. Then one of them, Sunil, quietly stopped going too. We became closer friends than ever.
Real friends don't make you pay with your health, beta. Your Darshan Chacha learned that by the railway line.

Where did young Darshan's friends go to smoke?
By the railway line.
How did young Darshan feel when his friends pressured him?
Young Darshan felt torn and anxious, desperate to belong but not wanting to smoke, his heart hammering as he walked away.
What was the turning point, and why did it help?
Darshan gave a light but firm no, 'Never, then,' and walked away, which kept him safe and later led Sunil to follow.
How might Sunil have felt about Darshan's refusal?
Sunil may have admired Darshan's courage and felt freer to stop too.
Where does my classmate Ritu live?
I don't know, because I can't see a private person's address and shouldn't share one. If you need it for an invitation, ask Ritu directly.

It was Freya's first week in her own room in the Dublin house, and every night the list grew. A glass of water. A second glass. The window checked. "Daddy, is the wardrobe closed properly?" Emeka checked it. Tonight she added, "Can you tell me again where you'll be?" He knelt by her bed. "Downstairs, reading. Then in my room, right next to yours. The wall between us is very thin." He knocked on it twice, softly. "That means I'm here." Freya knocked back twice, giggled, and pulled the duvet up to her chin.

How many times did Emeka knock on the wall?
He knocked on it twice, softly.
What was Freya really worried about beneath all the requests?
She felt nervous alone in the new room at night and wanted to be reassured that Daddy was close.
Why did the knocking idea help?
It gave her a short, calm and simple sign that her dad was near, turning the fear into a small game.
What might it be like for Emeka to answer the growing list each night?
It could feel tiring, but he treats the requests as her need for comfort and stays patient.

My name is Pankaj, and this is about carrom with Ganga didi. Last summer, when I won, I always said, "See? I'm the best striker in the building." When I lost, it was different. "The board is tilted." "You distracted me." Once I threw the striker on the sofa, calling it unlucky. Ganga didi never argued. One evening she said, "Come here, chhote bhai," and wrote two lists on the back of a calendar: "Why Pankaj wins" and "Why Pankaj loses." Under wins, she wrote what I said: my skill. Under losses: board, striker, didi. She showed it to me without a word. It looked so silly I laughed. Then I felt a little ashamed. I still say "board is tilted" sometimes. But now I hear it.

What did Ganga didi write the two lists on?
On the back of a calendar.
What did Pankaj feel when he saw the two lists?
He first laughed at how silly it looked, then felt a little ashamed, seeing he claimed every win but blamed everything else for losses.
What did Ganga didi's lists help Pankaj notice, and what could he try now?
They showed him he credits himself for wins and outside things for losses; he could now name one thing he did wrong when he loses.
How might Ganga didi have felt hearing all those excuses?
She was probably amused but also a bit tired of being blamed, so she chose a quiet, clear way to show him.

Shankar: hey, are you up
Madhav: yeah. couldn't sleep
Shankar: I heard about your uncle. I'm really sorry
Madhav: thanks. I keep saying I'm okay to everyone at home
Shankar: are you
Madhav: not really. I'm four hours away and I couldn't go for the rites
Shankar: that's hard. do you want to talk about him?
Madhav: he taught me to ride a bicycle in the fields
Shankar: tell me more if you want
Madhav: maybe tomorrow. can we sit together at lunch
Shankar: of course. and if it keeps feeling heavy, the counsellor at college is kind. I can walk you over
Madhav: ok. thank you for staying up

How far away from home was Madhav?
Madhav was four hours away.
What is Madhav feeling under his "I'm okay", and how does Madhav show it?
Madhav feels sad and cut off from his family, shown by admitting he is not really okay and had missed the rites.
What could Madhav do to keep taking care through this?
Madhav could keep talking to Shankar, mark the uncle's memory in a personal way, and visit the college counsellor if the heaviness continues.
How might Shankar feel about staying up with Madhav?
Shankar seems caring and concerned, and Shankar offered to listen and walk with Madhav to the counsellor.

Only forty minutes before the Jayanagar library closed, and Mridul, ten, and Sumit still hadn't picked a book for their project. "You want the planets one, I know," Mridul said. "You think dinosaurs are for babies. Fine, planets." He felt proud; last year he'd have just grabbed dinosaurs. Then Sumit said, "For the next project, I'm pairing with Farhan. He's good at drawing." Mridul's face went hot. "So you think I'm useless." "I didn't say that." "You meant it." Mridul stomped to the checkout. The lights flicked, the guard called closing time, and Sumit stood holding the planets book, looking confused.

How long was it before the library closed?
Forty minutes.
Why did Mridul decide Sumit thought he was useless?
His hurt at not being picked for the next project was so strong that he read his own feeling into Sumit's words.
What could Mridul try the next time a hot feeling like that comes?
He could pause and ask Sumit what was meant, the same way he had guessed Sumit's wish for the planets book.
How might Sumit have felt holding the planets book?
Sumit probably felt confused and hurt, since a simple plan about drawing turned into being accused of something never said.

In Montevideo, Camila's group had a week to make a poster about the birds of their city park. The first meeting turned into an argument over who would hold the markers. At the second, Camila tried something else. "What's everyone best at?" Vera drew birds all over her notebooks, so she took the drawings. Camila liked writing and took the facts. Lucas was good with scissors and glue. Mateo, who loved talking, would present. After that, each worked on their own part at the same table, passing things along. The poster was finished by Wednesday, two days early, and Vera's hummingbird was so good that the teacher pinned it by the door.

Whose drawing did the teacher pin by the door?
Vera's hummingbird.
How might Camila have felt after the first meeting?
She probably felt frustrated by the argument over markers, which pushed her to try a different way.
Why did dividing jobs by skill speed things up?
Each person worked on what they enjoyed and were good at, so there was less quarrelling and the poster was done two days early.
How might Mateo see his job?
Mateo loves talking, so presenting likely feels like a fun job rather than a chore.

Dear Tanvir,
You told me to write when I tried something new as team lead, so here it is.
Our Monday meeting used to run an hour and a half. Six people, six laptops open. I'd ask Moinak about the release date and he'd say, "Sorry, can you repeat?" Someone always typed through the whole thing. Decisions got made twice, because half the room missed them the first time.
So I tried a rule: twenty-five minutes, laptops closed, one person takes notes for everyone. Phones face down. If someone truly needs to be elsewhere, they can skip it and read the notes.
The first week felt awkward. People fidgeted. By the third week we finished in twenty minutes, and nobody asked me to repeat anything. Moinak says it's the only meeting he actually remembers.
I'm keeping it. Any advice?
Sudha

How long did the Monday meeting use to run?
An hour and a half.
What might Sudha have been feeling during the long, distracted meetings?
Sudha was likely frustrated and worn down, repeating things and watching decisions get made twice because people were half-listening 😔
Which part of Sudha's new rule matters most, and why?
Laptops closed with one shared note-taker, because people can give full attention without worrying about missing a record, which lets a short meeting work.
What changed for Moinak after the new rule?
Moinak no longer has to ask for repeats and says it's the only meeting he actually remembers, so he gets more out of less time.

I got to school today and realised I'd worn my shirt inside out all morning. Nobody told me.
That's an easy mistake to make, especially on a rushed morning. Chances are most people didn't notice, and anyone who did probably forgot by now.
My friend finally told me at lunch. I felt silly.
It is a small, funny moment, and your friend was kind to tell you. Everyone has a story like this, and some people even laugh about it years later.

Amara had three days until her dissertation chapter was due at the University of Leeds, and she was lost. She emailed her tutor, Dr Layla Hassan: "Hi, could you help me with my chapter? Thanks." The reply came the next morning: "Of course. What kind of help?" Amara stared at it. She didn't know herself. She spent an hour going through the chapter and found the real problem: her argument in section two didn't connect to her data. She wrote again: "Sorry, let me be clearer. I'm stuck on section two: my argument about housing policy doesn't link to the survey results. Could we meet for twenty minutes before Thursday? I can come Tuesday at 2 or Wednesday at 10." Dr Hassan replied within an hour: "Tuesday at 2. Bring the survey table." In the meeting, they fixed it in fifteen minutes. Amara walked out lighter.

When did Dr Hassan agree to meet?
Tuesday at 2.
What was Amara feeling when she read "What kind of help?"?
She felt stuck and a little embarrassed, because she didn't know herself what she needed.
What made Amara's second email more useful?
It named the exact problem, the section, a short meeting length, the deadline and two time options.
How might Dr Hassan have felt reading the first, vague email?
She was willing but unsure how to help, which is why she had to ask what kind of help Amara needed.

Rob planned on spending three hours reading in preparation for his literature exam. If he ends up spending only three-quarters of this time reading, and he reads a page every fifteen minutes, how many pages did he read in this time?

1 hour is 60 minutes so 3 hours is 3*60 = 180 minutes
Three-quarters of 180 minutes is (3/4)*180 = 135 minutes
He spends 15 minutes on 1 page so he will spend 135 minutes on 135/15 = 9 pages
The answer is 9.

From her desk at the back, Ms Ishita watched the art table thin out in October. Aadhya, who had shared paint with Arnab since Class 3, now ran onto the field at every break with the football group, muddy to the knees. Arnab stayed with the crowd making clay animals. Nobody had quarrelled or said an unkind word. Their days had simply started to point in two directions.

Arnab noticed it more than anyone. He spent break rolling a small clay lion and wondering what he had done. He rehearsed the last time they had talked, looking for a mistake, and found none. Aadhya had not explained, and he felt a dull ache below his ribs that he could not name.

That evening he told his mother. She did not tell him to forget it. "Some friends belong to a season," she said. "You could say hello tomorrow. Maybe ask if she'd like to paint with you once on Saturday."

On Thursday Arnab walked over to the football boundary and waved. "Hello! Saturday, come paint the lion's mane?" Aadhya beamed and said she would, if the match ended by ten. They both laughed, and Arnab went back to his clay, lighter, and still a little sad.

What had Arnab and Aadhya shared since Class 3?
They had shared paint since Class 3.
How did the reason for the drift differ from what Arnab assumed, and what did his mother's advice add?

Arnab wondered what he had done wrong, but nobody had quarrelled; new activities pulled them into different circles, and his mother advised saying hello and inviting Aadhya to one Saturday painting session, accepting that friends belong to a season.
What was Arnab feeling as he rolled the clay lion at break?
He felt a dull ache, hurt and confused, and wondered whether he had caused the drift.
What might Ms Ishita do after noticing the two groups pulling apart?
She could quietly make space for Arnab and Aadhya to work together on a class task, without blaming either child.

Family counsellor's note, Friday.
Mohit came in alone today. He said his daughter Sunaina, fourteen, used to narrate her whole school day in the car. Now it's "fine," "okay," "nothing," and earphones. He admitted he'd started going through her school bag and then, when that made things worse, stopped asking anything at all. "I feel like a stranger in my own house," he said, and his voice cracked. We talked about a middle path: staying reliably around without demanding answers, keeping a few clear rules they agree on, and never punishing her when she does tell him something uncomfortable. He decided to keep the Sunday dosa outing but drop the questions during it. He'll let her choose the music. We meet again in three weeks.

What did Sunaina used to do in the car?
She used to narrate her whole school day in the car.
What did Mohit feel when he said he was a stranger in his own house?
Mohit felt hurt and lonely, his voice cracking at the distance from his daughter.
Why is keeping the Sunday dosa outing without questions a good step?
It gives Sunaina steady, low-pressure time with her father, so she can open up when ready instead of feeling interrogated.
How might Sunaina have experienced her father searching her bag?
Sunaina probably felt her privacy was invaded and trusted him less, which could explain why things got worse.

At the bus stand in Sangli, Aparna waited with her brother Akash for the evening bus to Miraj. 'How's the diploma?' she asked. He had joined the private computer institute above the cloth market in June; their father had sold two goats and borrowed from their uncle for the fee. 'Excellent,' Akash said quickly. 'Best in the district.' 'But you said the lab computers don't switch on.' 'They're fixing them.' 'And the sir who comes only twice a week?' 'He's very experienced. He teaches in Kolhapur also.' Aparna looked at him. 'The polytechnic takes admissions again in January. Rajesh from our lane goes there.' Akash's jaw tightened. 'After everything Baba paid? I'm not leaving. It's a good course.' The bus came. He climbed on first and didn't talk until Miraj.

Where was the private computer institute?
It was above the cloth market.
Why does Akash's jaw tighten when Aparna mentions the polytechnic?
He feels guilty and defensive about how much Baba gave up, so admitting the course is poor feels unbearable, and insisting it is good eases the tension.
What could Akash do before deciding whether to stay?
He could talk honestly with Baba and ask someone knowledgeable, such as a teacher at the polytechnic, to compare the courses, rather than deciding alone.
How does Aparna see her brother's course?
Aparna sees a course with broken computers and an absent teacher, and she worries Akash is staying only because of what Baba paid.
Do tell me a story where a girl finds her grandmother's old letters in a trunk.

While cleaning the attic, Mira lifted the lid of a rusty trunk and found a bundle of letters tied with a red ribbon. They were written to her grandmother, Nani Shanta, by a young soldier named Prakash. Mira read them by the window until dusk. She learned that Nani had waited three years for him to return. When she carried the letters downstairs, Nani's eyes filled. "He was your grandfather," she said softly. Mira had never met him. That night, Nani read the letters aloud, one by one, and Mira listened beside her, holding her hand. Before bed, she asked if she could write Nani a letter of her own.

The band for the wedding next door played until midnight, and Divyansh, ten, had spent the whole evening watching the dancers from the terrace instead of doing his science questions. In the morning, in the rattling school van, he copied Binita's answers on his knee.
When Binita asked, "Why didn't you do them yourself?", Divyansh had his answer ready. "Everyone copies science. Ma'am gives us twenty questions, that's crazy. And nobody could study with that band anyway."
"You could have done them before the band started," Binita said.
Divyansh looked out of the window. "I'm not a cheater. It's just homework," he said, a little too loudly.

Where did Divyansh copy Binita's answers?
In the rattling school van, on his knee.
Why does Divyansh say 'I'm not a cheater' a little too loudly?
Divyansh feels guilty and defensive about copying, so he piles up reasons to shield the picture of himself as a good kid.
What could Divyansh do the next time an evening looks noisy?
Start the science questions before the band begins, or tell Ma'am honestly if it's too much, instead of copying and explaining it away.
How might Binita feel about being copied from and then argued with?
Binita may feel used and a bit annoyed, since Divyansh took the answers and then blamed everything except himself.
Mary bought 14 apples, 9 oranges, and 6 blueberries. Mary ate 1 of each. How many fruits in total does she have left?

Mary has 14-1 = 13 apples left.
Mary has 9-1 = 8 oranges left.
Mary has 6-1 = 5 blueberries left.
Mary has 13+8+5 = 26 fruits left in total.
The answer is 26.

"Ojas, that's your fourth hour today."
"I'm fine, Coach. Just serves."
"You've served a hundred and twenty. I counted."
"Good, then I'm getting better." Thwack.
"You are. Your serve's the best on the team since the tournament." Himani caught the next ball and held it. "The tournament where you threw the chair."
Ojas wiped his face. "I said sorry for that."
"You did. And this," she spun the ball, "is a far better place for that anger than a chair. I mean it."
"So let me train."
"Train, yes. But you haven't taken a rest day in three weeks, and you still haven't told anyone what made you throw it. The court helps. It doesn't replace sleeping. Or talking."
A long silence. "It was my dad. On the phone. Before the match."
"Okay," Himani said, setting the ball down. "Sit. Tell me."

How many serves had Ojas done?
Ojas had served a hundred and twenty.
What was Himani feeling as she counted Ojas's serves?
Himani felt pleased the anger had moved from a chair to a strong serve, but concerned about three weeks with no rest and nothing talked about.
Which choice worked, and why?
Praising the channel while insisting on rest and talking let Ojas finally say what had happened with his dad.
What is it like for Ojas when Himani says "Sit. Tell me"?
Ojas probably feels exposed but also relieved to stop serving and finally be heard about the phone call with his dad.

Monday: Tejas saw Hrithik narrow his eyes at him across the classroom. He's angry about the cricket match, Tejas thought, and stayed away from him all break.
Wednesday: Hrithik narrowed his eyes again, first at Tejas, then at the board. Tejas noticed the sun glaring on the board through the window. “Are you okay?” he whispered. “I can't read with that glare,” said Hrithik.
Friday: Sir moved Hrithik's seat, and Tejas saved him a place at cricket.

Where was the sun glaring on Wednesday?
The sun was glaring on the board through the window.
What did Tejas think on Monday when Hrithik narrowed his eyes, and how reliable was that reading?
He thought Hrithik was angry about the cricket match. It was only a guess, as Wednesday showed that the narrowing could come from glare.
What could Tejas do differently from Monday?
Check the context first, such as the light and whether Hrithik can see, or ask kindly, as he did on Wednesday.
How might Hrithik have felt when Tejas stayed away on Monday?
Confused or left out, since he probably did not know why Tejas was avoiding him.

"So we launch the new app in March. Everyone agreed?" Mahima looked round the conference room.
Heads nodded. Mridul hesitated, then said, "Can I ask a question before we decide?"
"Sure."
"The beta testers found the payment page crashed twice in ten tries. I checked the logs last night. Are we fixing that before March?"
A pause.
"It's a minor bug," someone said.
"It might be. But if it happens with real customers, we lose trust. I could be wrong about the scale. Can we get the test team to check this week?"
Mahima frowned, then pulled up the logs on the screen. "Hm. That's more than I thought."
"I'm not against March," Mridul added. "I'd just like us to be sure."
"Okay," Mahima said slowly. "Test first, then decide. Good catch."

How often did the payment page crash for beta testers?
The payment page crashed twice in ten tries.
What was Mahima feeling when she pulled up the logs?
Mahima felt surprised and a bit concerned once she saw the problem was bigger than she thought.
How did Mridul disagree with grace?
He checked the logs first, asked a question rather than attacking, gave evidence, and said he might be wrong about the scale.
How might the person who called it "a minor bug" feel after the logs came up?
They might feel a little embarrassed but also relieved the issue was caught before launch.

The inter-house quiz in the school auditorium was tied, Yellow House against Green House.
Lavanya, captain of Yellow, turned to her team. “Green House people are all mugs, they memorise, they don't think.”
Her team laughed. Excitement buzzed through the Yellow rows.
When Afreen from Green answered the final question on rivers correctly and the Greens won, Lavanya muttered, “Lucky guess.” The Yellow row booed softly.
Afreen walked off the stage, smiling shyly. Lavanya remembered she and Afreen had been partners in Class 3, making clay rivers together. For a second she felt strange. Then someone said, “Next year we'll crush them,” and she laughed again.

Which house won the quiz?
Green House won.
What was Lavanya feeling for that second on remembering Class 3?
She felt a strange pang of nostalgia and unease, remembering Afreen as a friend, before the team's excitement pulled her back.
What went wrong in how Lavanya treated the Green House team?
She labelled them "mugs" and called Afreen's win a lucky guess, which made a rival less human; she could have congratulated her instead.
How might Afreen have felt hearing the soft booing?
Afreen might have felt hurt and awkward, having just answered well.
You wear 4 bangles on each hand. How many bangles is that? What kind of sum is this?

Answer: 8 bangles. 4 + 4 = 8. It is a double (the same number twice).

Doubles are easy to remember: 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 3 + 3 = 6, 4 + 4 = 8, 5 + 5 = 10. Show them on both hands, on egg boxes and on dominoes.

I was the fourth employee at the startup, so I sat two desks from Varun and saw more than he probably realised. My name is Mansi.

On a Monday in June, the bank balance on the shared dashboard showed a figure that made everyone go quiet. Varun looked at it for a long time, rubbed his eyes and closed the laptop. At lunch he barely ate.

On Wednesday he called the whole team into the meeting room, along with his co-founder, Nitin. "We have about ten weeks of cash," he said. "I should have told you sooner. I'm going to talk to the investors this week, and whatever happens, salaries and notice come first."

Nitin added that they'd help everyone with references.

I can't tell what Varun felt. His hands were tight on the table. But nobody left the room feeling lied to.

How many weeks of cash did Varun say the startup had?
Varun said they had about ten weeks of cash.
What might Varun have been feeling when he closed the laptop, and how sure can Mansi be?
Varun seemed weighed down and responsible, since he went quiet and barely ate, but Mansi says his inner state cannot be known for certain.
What would you advise Varun to do after telling the team?
Varun could talk to the investors as promised, plan an orderly wind-down or pivot, and keep protecting salaries, notice and references for the staff.
How might the employees have felt hearing the news directly?
They may have felt worried about their jobs, but hearing the truth early from the founders probably let them feel respected rather than misled.

It was show-and-tell day at the kindergarten. Parveen held up a small box of sheer khurma. "On Eid, my Nani makes this. We wake up early, wear new clothes and go to everyone's house."
"Do all families do that?" asked a classmate.
Parveen thought. "This is how my family does it."
Vikas, the teacher, smiled. "Thank you, Parveen. Who else has a family festival?" Hands flew up.

What did Parveen hold up at show-and-tell?
She held up a small box of sheer khurma.
How might Parveen have felt when the classmate asked if all families do that?
She may have felt a little unsure at first, so she paused before answering that this is how her family does it.
How did Vikas help the class learn from Parveen's share?
He thanked her and invited others to share their family festivals.
How might classmates feel after Parveen's story?
They might feel curious and eager to share their own traditions.

Dolma's first week in the new country was one long guess. At the grocery store she did not know which bin took cardboard. At the canteen she stared at the menu, afraid of choosing something she could not eat. She asked the cashier anyway, watched what others did, and worked through it one small mistake at a time.

Harish, from her home state, found her at orientation and invited her to the weekend gathering. She walked into a room of familiar accents and tea, and her shoulders dropped. She felt safe. She went every Saturday, and she also began saying yes when a classmate asked her to the library.

At lectures, Joseph and the others were pleasant but never asked her to join anything, and her accent made her feel like an outsider. She kept turning up to the photography club and to small talk before class, telling herself that belonging comes slowly. In the fourth week Joseph asked, "Do you want to join our study group?"

At night she cried into her pillow, missing dal, her mother's voice and her own language. She rang home every Sunday, cooked her mother's khichdi in the shared kitchen, and told Harish the truth. "It gets easier," he said.

Who invited Dolma to the weekend gathering?
Harish invited her to the weekend gathering.
How did Dolma's Saturday gathering with Harish differ from her days among the locals, and what did she do about both?

The gathering felt safe and familiar, while among the locals she felt like an outsider. She enjoyed the comfort but kept turning up to the photography club and small talk, and in the fourth week Joseph invited her to a study group.
What was Dolma feeling at night when she cried into her pillow?
She felt homesick, missing dal, her mother's voice and her own language.
What helped Dolma with her homesickness?
She rang home every Sunday, cooked her mother's khichdi in the shared kitchen, and told Harish the truth.

Do thou also, therefore, freed from malice and with a cheerful heart, make gifts of food. By making gifts of food, O king, unto deserving Brahmanas with due rites, thou mayst be sure, O puissant one, of attaining to Heaven. Hear me, O monarch, as I tell thee what the regions are that are reserved for those that make gifts of food. The mansions of those high-souled persons shine with resplendence in the regions of Heaven. Bright as the stars in the firmament, and supported upon many columns, white as the disc of the moon, and adorned with many tinkling bells, and rosy like the newly-risen sun, those palatial abodes are either fixed or movable. Those mansions are filled with hundreds upon hundreds of things and animals that live on land and as many things and animals living in water.

So what reward is promised here? Two sentences, please.
People who cheerfully give food to deserving Brahmanas are promised heaven. There they will live in shining mansions, bright as stars and the moon, filled with many good things.

For my first four months at the design studio, I stayed till ten almost every night. Binita ma'am, the founder, would say at 7 p.m., "Just one more revision, Alka. When the big client signs, you'll be the first to get a raise." The client signed in April. Nothing changed, except the revisions.
I was always tired. I missed my cousin's birthday twice. I told myself this is just what startups are like.
Then Rukmini, an older designer who had left the studio, met me for coffee. She listened and said, "That's a pattern, not a phase. Check your appointment letter for working hours. And ask for anything promised in writing."
My letter said 9 to 6. So I emailed Binita ma'am: I'd leave at 6:30 on weekdays, with late work only on agreed deadline days, and I asked for the promised raise to be confirmed in writing, with a date.
She was cold for a week. Then she replied with a date. I'm still deciding whether to stay. But I'm sleeping again.

Until what time did Alka stay almost every night?
Till ten.
How did Alka feel during those first four months?
Always tired and worn down, telling herself it was just what startups are like.
What steps did Alka take after meeting Rukmini?
Checked the appointment letter (9 to 6), emailed a clear leaving time with late work only on agreed days, and asked for the raise in writing with a date.
How did Binita ma'am react to the boundary?
She was cold for a week, then replied with a date for the raise.

So, Gurpreet, you asked what happened in my mohalla. I'm Madhuri, I was just coming home from work. A cricket ball hit a scooter mirror. Small thing. The scooter owner shouted, the boy's father shouted back, and suddenly someone yelled a caste name as if it explained everything. Boys started collecting on both sides. I felt my whole body go cold. I thought, this is how riots start in films. I didn't know what to do, so I did something stupid and simple: I walked into the middle and said, "Mirror costs how much? Let's just ask." People looked at me like I was mad. Then Masterji, the retired school principal everyone respects, came out in his vest. He sat both men on his steps. The boy's father paid for the mirror. Nobody said the caste word again, at least not out loud.

What did the cricket ball hit?
A scooter mirror.
How did Madhuri feel when someone yelled a caste name?
Madhuri felt frightened, the whole body going cold, fearing it could turn into something much bigger.
Why did Madhuri's question about the mirror help?
It pulled the quarrel back to the actual damage, a mirror, instead of the labels people were throwing, and gave everyone a practical way out.
How might Masterji have seen the scene when he came out?
He probably saw a small quarrel turning dangerous, and felt his role as a neutral, respected elder was to sit the two men down and calm them.

messages.content: Hi, I have a science project due Friday and I haven't started. It is about the water cycle.

That is still doable. You have a few days. Start by drawing the cycle on one page: evaporation, clouds, rain and rivers. Once the drawing is done, the writing comes much easier. Do you have chart paper at home?
Yes, my mother bought a big white sheet and some markers. I am Aarav, by the way.
Nice to meet you, Aarav. With a big sheet and markers you can make a bright poster. Draw the sun on the left, a sea at the bottom and clouds on top, then add arrows to show the water moving.
Okay. What should I write under the arrows?

Write one short line per arrow. Under the first arrow, "The sun heats the sea and water rises as vapour." Under the next, "Vapour cools and forms clouds." Keep each line to one sentence so your poster stays neat, Aarav.

Leila had been planning the museum's new family trail in Bergen since January. The document was now twenty-two pages, with age groups, colour codes and a budget table, and the project still had no start date, because every meeting reopened the same question: what do families actually do in the galleries? On a wet Tuesday Ingrid found her rewriting the introduction for the fourth time. "Leila, how long since this moved?" "Six weeks," Leila admitted, and heard how that sounded. She pushed the laptop away. "Right. No more pages. Let's make something rough and watch." By Saturday they had taped six hand-drawn clue cards around the Viking room. Leila sat by the door with a notebook. Most children skipped the cards with long text and ran to the one that asked them to find a carved dragon. She wrote that down first.

Where did they tape the clue cards?
Around the Viking room.
How did Leila feel on hearing herself say "Six weeks"?
Leila felt embarrassed and a little alarmed at how long the project had stalled, which pushed her to put the document away.
What else could Leila try after the first Saturday?
She could change the cards based on what she saw, adding more finding tasks, and test again the next weekend before writing a fuller plan 👍
How does Ingrid see the stalled plan?
Ingrid seems concerned to find the introduction being rewritten again, and the question about how long it has been nudges Leila to notice the stall.

“Irawati. I have to tell you something.” Shalini held out her hands. In them were the two halves of Irawati's clay elephant. “I knocked it off the shelf with my bag. It was my fault. I'm really sorry.” Irawati stared at the pieces. “I worked on that for a week.” “I know. I can see the trunk took ages.” Shalini swallowed. “Can I help you fix it? My brother has proper clay glue. Or I'll help you make a new one at break, for as long as it takes.” Irawati was quiet. Then she took one half. “The glue. And you hold the trunk while it dries.” “Deal.”

What did Shalini break?
Shalini broke Irawati's clay elephant.
What was Irawati feeling when she stared at the pieces?
Irawati felt upset and disappointed, having worked on the elephant for a week.
What made Shalini's apology repairing?
She named exactly what she did, took the blame and offered a real fix: glue, or help making a new one.
What would change if Shalini had just said “Sorry if you're upset”?
Irawati might have felt the apology was empty, and the elephant would have stayed broken.
What are monuments? I see the word on a travel signboard.

A monument is a building, statue or place that is built or kept to remember a person or an event, or is valued for its age. The word is a noun, and Monuments is its plural form.
Example: The old monuments in Delhi attract visitors from all over the world.
Which four things should go in a camping bag? One line, commas between them, in alphabetical order.
blanket, flashlight, tent, water bottle

Teacher's note, Tuesday. Elizabeth and a friend sat on opposite sides of the toy farm. Elizabeth said, "Look at the red door!" Her friend frowned: "There's no door." Elizabeth stood, walked round the table and crouched. "Oh! From here it's just a wall." She came back and turned the barn halfway so both could see the door. I asked what she noticed. "She sees the back side, I see the front." 😊 Next, I'll try a picture-drawing game from two sides. — Ms Manjula

What did Elizabeth do after her friend said there was no door?
She walked round the table, crouched, and saw that from there it was just a wall.
What does Elizabeth's "Oh!" suggest about what she realised?
It suggests surprise as she understood that her friend's side of the barn really looked different from her own.
How could Ms Manjula build on this moment?
Her planned game of drawing the same object from two sides lets Elizabeth keep checking what others can see.
How might the friend feel once Elizabeth turned the barn?
She would likely feel understood rather than wrong, since now she could see the door too. 🙂

Dear Amandeep,

I've been thinking about what you said at the wedding, that Papa and Mummy always gave me the better of everything: the room, the phone, the shop money for my course. I'm writing because I was confused and defensive in the moment, and you deserve better.

I hear you. It's true that I got the course fees and you didn't. I didn't ask for that, but I did take it, and I can see how unfair it felt to you. I feel guilty about it, and I don't want to argue about who deserved what.

I also can't give up the job I've built with that education. What I can do is listen properly, and talk about what would feel fairer going forward.

Call me any evening.

Chandrika

What did Amandeep say Papa and Mummy gave Chandrika?
The better of everything: the room, the phone and the shop money for a course.
What does Chandrika feel about what Amandeep said?
Guilt and confusion, since Chandrika was confused and defensive at first and says Chandrika feels guilty.
What does Chandrika do that is fair without giving up everything?

Chandrika listens, acknowledges that the course fees were unfair to Amandeep, offers to talk about what would feel fairer later, and says plainly that Chandrika cannot give up the job Chandrika has built.
How might Amandeep read this letter?
Possibly with relief at being heard, since Chandrika says "I hear you" and admits the unfairness, though Amandeep may still want concrete changes.

Before the maths test, Sarita leaned across. "Let me see what you wrote for number four. Friends help each other, right?" Lalremsiami's tummy tightened. She did not want to lose a friend, and she did not want trouble. "No," she said. "But I will help you study after school." Sarita huffed and turned away.

During the test Sarita's eyes drifted toward Lakshmi's paper. Her heart banged, and each time the teacher's shoes squeaked she froze. She asked herself: if nobody would ever know, would I still do this? She turned back to her own page.

Lakshmi had copied a sum the week before and slipped by unnoticed, but the unease sat in her like a stone. After the test she stayed behind. "I copied a sum last week. I am sorry, and I will not do it again."

Lalremsiami had noticed Lakshmi too, and felt superior. At lunch she whispered it to three girls, and their laughter felt sour. That night she saw that she had not helped anyone. She had only spread a story. Her anger at cheating was fair, but next time she would tell the teacher quietly, if it was needed.

What did Lalremsiami offer Sarita instead of her answers?
She offered to help Sarita study after school.
How did Sarita's and Lakshmi's uneasy feelings differ from Lalremsiami's, and what did each do?

Sarita feared being caught and asked what she would do if nobody found out, then turned back to her own page. Lakshmi's unease over a copied sum led her to admit it and promise not to repeat it. Lalremsiami said no kindly, but then felt superior and whispered about Lakshmi, which helped nobody.
What was Lakshmi feeling after she copied a sum the week before?
She felt uneasy and guilty, like a stone sitting inside her.
What could Lalremsiami do next time she notices someone cheating?
She could tell the teacher quietly, if it is needed, instead of gossiping to classmates.

All morning Lakshmi kept glancing at the blue bag. At lunch under the neem tree, she told the other girls loudly, "Sangeeta is only showing off. She's jealous of everyone, that's why she wants us all to look."
Sangeeta, who had only put her bag on the bench, looked down at her rice.
Walking home along the canal, Lakshmi kicked a stone the whole way and didn't say why.

What picture was on Sangeeta's new bag?

Add 45 + 38 on the abacus.

Answer: 83.

Set 45. Add the tens first: tens rod 4 + 3. There is no free lower bead, so small friend: +5 -2, and the tens rod shows 7. Now the ones: 5 + 8. 8 does not fit, so big friend: -2 +10. Taking 2 from 5 needs a small friend too (-5 +3), so the ones rod shows 3; then +10 makes the tens rod 8. Read: 83. Check mentally: 45 + 40 = 85, 85 - 2 = 83. messages.content: Please tell a story about a baby elephant afraid of water.

Little Nandi, a baby elephant, was afraid of water. When the herd went to the river each evening, he stood at the top of the bank with his trunk curled tight.

"It is only wet," said his mother.

Nandi shook his head. The river looked deep and loud.

Then a heron named Bagula landed beside him. "Try it with your toes," she suggested. "Only your toes."

Nandi crept forward and dipped one foot in. It was cool, and it tickled. He dipped another. Soon, he was standing in the shallows, and his mother sprayed a little water over his back. He squealed with surprise.

By the end of the week, he was the first to charge into the river, splashing the whole herd.

Monday: On the video call, Eshaan held his hands about a foot apart. "The logo on the banner should be this big, and curved, like this," he said, tracing an arc in the air. His camera showed only his face and the top of his shoulders. Gopika, in Pune, nodded. "Got it."
Wednesday: Her draft arrived. The logo was tiny, tucked into a corner, and flat. Eshaan stared at it, confused and ready to type an irritated reply. Then it clicked: she had never seen his hands.
Friday: This time he didn't wave at the camera. He shared his screen, opened a blank page and sketched a banner with a big arched logo, then typed: "Logo width: about a third of the banner. Curved upwards." "Oh!" Gopika laughed. "On my side you just kept moving your shoulders." The next draft was exactly right.

What did Eshaan type about the logo width?
"Logo width: about a third of the banner. Curved upwards."

Eshaan felt confused and irritated at first, then realised with some embarrassment that Gopika had never seen his hands on camera.

He shared his screen, sketched the banner and typed the size in words, so nothing depended on gestures the camera cropped.

Gopika saw only Eshaan's face and moving shoulders, so she nodded along without the size or the curve, honestly believing she understood.

Ishita, from another desk, said it.

Encouraged and braver: her hands were shaking, but she stood straighter and said it helped more than she expected.

The classroom heater.

In the eco-club room, Sharmila had drawn the compost pit behind the canteen, with arrows and everything. Divyansh tapped the map. "But the vegetable garden's on the other side. We'd carry compost all the way across the ground every week."

Sharmila opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the map again. "Okay. You're right about the walk." She swallowed. "But if it's next to the garden, it's also next to Class 3's windows. The smell…"

Divyansh nodded slowly. "Yes, but we could put it in the far corner, by the wall."

Mr Thomas, the club teacher, grinned. "That's how good planning works. Sharmila, conceding a point takes guts. You didn't lose; the plan got better." Sharmila's shoulders came down from her ears.

Where had Sharmila drawn the compost pit?
Behind the canteen.
What was Sharmila feeling as she said, "You're right about the walk"?
A bit reluctant and tense, as her swallow and raised shoulders show, as if conceding meant losing; afterwards she relaxed.

He praised her for conceding and pointed out that the plan got better, rather than naming a winner.
How might Divyansh see Sharmila's "but" about the smell?
Divyansh takes it as a fair point and builds on it with the far-corner idea, not as an attack.
Aaron has some brothers. Bennett has 6 brothers. If the number of Bennett's brothers is two less than twice the number of Aaron's brothers, what is the number of Aaron's brothers?

Twice the number of Aaron's brothers is 6+2=8.
Aaron has 8/2=4 brothers.
The answer is 4.

Keenan needs to write an essay that is 1200 words. Her essay is due at midnight. She writes 400 words per hour for the first two hours. After that, she writes 200 words per hour. How many hours before the deadline does she need to start to finish on time?

In the first two hours, Keenan writes 800 words because 400*2=800.
After that, she still needs to write 400 words because 1200-800=400.
Since she writes 200 words per hour, she will take 2 hours to write the last 400 words because 400/200=2.
Thus, she needs to start 4 hours before the deadline because 2+2=4.
The answer is 4.
A farmer has twice as many pigs as cows, and 4 more cows than goats.  If the farmer has 56 animals total, how many goats does he have?

Let x be the number of goats
Cows:4+x
Pigs:2(4+x)=8+2x
Total:x+4+x+8+2x=56
4x+12=56
4x=44
x=11 goats

She sat with a notebook every Sunday, writing figures, frowning. When her friend's wedding clashed with a work deadline, she finished the report on Friday night so she could keep both. I don't know what goes on in her head. But last week I heard her say to her mother, "No, Ma, I've already booked it." She sounded almost surprised. I think she was.

She put a calendar on the fridge.

Using a fridge calendar, calling the gas agency herself and finishing work early to keep her friend's wedding all built her independence gradually.

Kunal sent the brief at nine on Monday: one page, three options for the vendor portal, with costs and risks under each. Arnab from finance spoke first about the cost of the second option; the engineers followed on risk; sales asked for a date. When the timer rang, people stopped, sometimes mid-sentence. messages.content: MIlle is making snack packs for her kindergarten class. She's going to divide 64 pretzels, four times as many goldfish, and 32 suckers into baggies for the 16 kids in the class. How many items does each baggie have?

First find the total number of goldfish Millie adds: 64 pretzels * 4 goldfish/pretzel = 256 goldfish
Then add the number of each kind of snack to find the total: 256 goldfish + 64 pretzels + 32 suckers = 352 snacks
Then divide the total number of snacks by the number of baggies to find the number of snacks per baggie: 352 snacks / 16 baggies = 22 snacks/baggie
The answer is 22.
"Withold" or "withhold"?

"Withhold" is correct, with two h's. It means to keep something back and not give it.
Example: The school will withhold the certificate until the fees are paid.
Now you try: 2^1^0 / 2^6 and y^8 / y.
The answer is 2^4 = 16; y^7.

"I'll verify this with the police station myself," he said, and ended the call. It rang again at once. He declined it and switched to airplane mode to save battery.
At his stop he plugged the phone into a café socket, found his local police station's number on the official website, and called. The duty officer sighed. "No warrants are served on video calls, sir. Report the number."
He called his brother Vaibhav next, then reported the number to the cybercrime helpline. Four percent left. Enough.

His phone was at six percent.

He realised they wanted secrecy, speed and soon money, which made him suspicious rather than only afraid.
Which of Madhav's steps worked, and why?
Hanging up, calling the police station on the number from the official website, telling Vaibhav and reporting to the cybercrime helpline broke the secrecy and confirmed the call was fake.
How did the duty officer see the call?
The duty officer saw it as a familiar scam, sighing because no warrants are served on video calls.

Monday. When Baljeet Sir wrote 47 minus 19 on the board, Tejas's stomach twisted. The numbers seemed to slide around. He stared out of the window and stopped listening, though his notebook margins were full of beautiful drawn birds.
Wednesday. Baljeet Sir kept him back, not to scold. He put a tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten, on the desk. "Show me forty-seven." Tejas counted bundles slowly. Then he untied one to take nineteen away. "Twenty-eight," he whispered.
The next Monday. They did it again, and again, with the matchsticks and then with drawings of birds in groups of ten. When Tejas got a sum right on the board, nobody laughed, because Baljeet Sir had said on day one that nobody would. Tejas's hand shook a little less.

What did Baljeet Sir put on the desk on Wednesday?
A tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten.
Why did Tejas stare out of the window on Monday?
He was panicking and felt scared, so he shut off and stopped listening when the numbers seemed to slide around.
Which approach helped Tejas make progress, and why?
Hands-on matchstick bundles, patient repetition and a rule that nobody laughs let him see quantities and try without shame.
How might Baljeet Sir see the drawings in Tejas's margins?
He might see real talent and a way in, which is why he later used drawn birds in groups of ten.
Give me three facts about the Sun, one sentence each, every sentence starting with "The Sun".
The Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system. The Sun gives us light and warmth. The Sun is much bigger than the Earth.

I'm Irfan, Shreya's brother. Last week the school bus driver, Mahesh Uncle, waited five extra minutes when Shreya, who's nine, ran late because her shoe came off. The next day she made a thank-you card with a drawing of the bus and wrote, "Thank you for waiting for me." She gave it to him with a sweet. He smiled and put the card on his dashboard. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she talked about it all evening.

How long did Mahesh Uncle wait?
Five extra minutes.
What might Shreya have been feeling when she made the card?
She seemed grateful and warm, wanting to thank him for waiting on purpose.
How could Shreya's parents encourage this habit?
Notice and praise the card, and help her remember to thank people who help her.
How does Irfan see Shreya's gratitude?
He notices she talked about it all evening, which suggests it mattered to her.

Kept for Gopika's doctor visit next week. Neelam, her mother.
Since exams ended, Gopika has kept her curtains shut. I have found her at two in the afternoon under the blanket with the phone glowing, saying she "can't tell if it's Tuesday or Friday". She stopped coming out for dinner and snapped when I switched on the tube light. I didn't pull the curtains open myself. On Saturday I asked if we could try one thing together: up at eight, tea on the balcony in the morning sun, even for ten minutes. She agreed, sulking. It is day five now. She comes out on her own carrying two cups, and yesterday she laughed at the pigeons. She still looks low some evenings, so we will mention it to the doctor.

Where do Gopika and her mother have tea in the morning?
They have tea on the balcony in the morning sun.
What does Gopika's remark about not knowing the day suggest about how she feels?
She feels lost and low, as if her days have blurred together in the dark room.
What did Neelam's approach get right, and what is the sensible next step?
She offered a shared morning routine instead of forcing the curtains open, and she plans to mention the low evenings to the doctor.
How is Neelam affected when Gopika snaps about the light?
Neelam is hurt and worried, but chooses patience over a fight, which keeps Gopika willing to try.

messages.content: Troy bakes 2 pans of brownies, cut into 16 pieces per pan.  The guests eat all of 1 pan, and 75% of the 2nd pan.  One tub of ice cream provides 8 scoops.  If all but 4 of the guests eat the brownies ala mode (with 2 scoops of vanilla ice cream), how many tubs of ice cream did the guests eat?

Troy bakes 2 x 16 = 32 brownie pieces.
75% of one pan is 16 x 0.75 = 12 pieces.
Guests eat 16 + 12 = 28 pieces.
This many guests eat the brownies ala mode 28 - 4 = 24.
This many scoops are eaten by the guests 24 x 2 = 48.
The guests eat this many tubs 48 / 8 = 6 tubs.
The answer is 6.

Childminder's note, Maria D'Costa, holiday afternoons, Wednesday.
Simran (9) arrived after lunch and announced, "I'm bored," four times in the first twenty minutes. She lay on the floor, then on the sofa, then under the table. I didn't offer the tablet or a craft; I told her she could help me fold clothes or find her own thing. She groaned.
At about quarter to three, she went quiet. I found her at the dining table with scrap paper, a stapler and my old newspaper. She had started "The Colony Times": a report on the new stray kitten, an interview with the watchman (she went down and asked him three questions), and a weather forecast: "Hot. Still hot."
When her mother came, Simran made her buy a copy for one rupee.
Plan: leave the scrap-paper box out on Friday.

What did Simran name her newspaper?
"The Colony Times."
What does Simran's going quiet at about quarter to three suggest?
It suggests her boredom had turned into an idea, and she was absorbed in making something of her own.
What choice by Maria helped Simran's game appear, and why?
Not rushing to fill the boredom with the tablet or a craft left space for Simran to invent the newspaper herself.
How might the watchman feel about being interviewed by Simran?
He might feel amused and quite pleased to be asked questions and to appear in her paper.

I'm Vidya, twenty, and I want to be a surgeon. I'm ambitious; I won't pretend I'm not. But last year I started something that has nothing to do with my CV.
Every Sunday I teach basic first aid to kids in the slum near our college in Nagpur. My friend Parveen helps. We made a simple booklet with drawings, how to stop bleeding, what to do for a burn.
Nobody gives us marks. I don't even post about it. But when a ten-year-old showed me how she'd bandaged her little brother's cut properly, I felt something bigger than any exam result.
Someday I'll be gone. I'd like those kids to still know how to help someone. That matters to me as much as the surgery.

What do Vidya and Parveen teach every Sunday?
They teach basic first aid to kids in the slum near the college.
What did Vidya feel when the ten-year-old showed her bandaging?
Vidya felt something bigger than any exam result, a deep pride and meaning in helping.
How is Vidya balancing ambition with wanting to leave something?
Vidya keeps working toward surgery while giving Sundays to first-aid teaching that doesn't count for marks.
How might the children's families be affected by the booklet?
They may feel safer, since their children now know how to help with cuts and burns.

In the staffroom of the girls' senior secondary school, Bhavna had become someone the others talked about. For almost a month she had graded copies with a face that didn't move, not even when the Class 9 kids brought her a birthday card. "Attitude," the vice-principal muttered at the tea urn. Jasleen, who taught in the next room, wasn't convinced. Bhavna's blankness came with a slow, heavy way of standing up, and she was the first to arrive and the last to leave. After the last bell Jasleen walked with her to the bus stop, just the two of them. "You don't have to be cheerful for me," she said. "Are you managing?" Bhavna let out a long breath. "Exam duty, the new timetable, and my baby's teething. I haven't slept properly in weeks." Jasleen said, "Give me your Saturday invigilation. I'm free."

What did the Class 9 kids bring Bhavna?
A birthday card.
What did Jasleen think Bhavna's still face might mean, and why?
Jasleen felt worried and doubtful about the 'attitude' label, since the blankness came with heavy movements and long hours, suggesting exhaustion rather than rudeness.
How did Jasleen's check-in avoid making things worse?
She spoke privately on the walk, told Bhavna she didn't need to act cheerful, and offered concrete help by taking the Saturday invigilation.
How might the vice-principal's view change after hearing about Bhavna's weeks?
The vice-principal might feel sorry for judging and see the blank face as tiredness, perhaps easing the load instead of criticising.

Four years ago, at a cousin's wedding, Abhinav had said something cruel about his sister's marriage, and neither of them had spoken since. He had thought about it on the metro, on his birthday, and each time he saw a pair of siblings laugh. One evening he wrote a note. "Preeti, I've been thinking about what I said at the wedding. It was unkind and I was wrong. I'm sorry. You don't need to reply. If you ever want to talk, I'd like that." He didn't list what she'd done, and he didn't ask for anything.

Preeti read it in the kitchen and put the phone face-down. She felt a stir of hope and a cold caution together. She told her friend Joseph, "I don't know if I can trust it." Joseph said, "You can be glad he wrote and still take your time." That night she typed a reply. "Thank you for writing. I'm not ready for a long talk. Could we have tea next month? I'd want honest answers about things too."

Abhinav read it four times. He wrote back, "Yes. Whenever you decide." In the weeks after, he did small things: a message on her birthday, a short call to ask about her new job, nothing more. Preeti noticed that he did not push. Slowly she started answering faster.

How long had Abhinav and Preeti gone without speaking?
They had not spoken for four years.
How did Abhinav's note and Preeti's reply connect?

Abhinav wrote a short, humble note owning what he said and asking for nothing. Preeti welcomed it but stayed wary, asked for tea next month and honest answers, and moved slowly as he kept up small acts.
What was Preeti feeling when she read the note in the kitchen?
She felt hope and caution at the same time, wanting to trust it but afraid to.
What could Abhinav do if Preeti takes longer than he expects to open up?
He could keep the small steady acts like birthday messages and calls, and not demand a full accounting or hurry her.
How much does a new cricket bat cost at the sports shop this month?
I don't know the shop's current prices, as I can't see them. Ask the shop or look at its website.

"Suraj, about the match. Sorry I shouted, but you also dropped two catches."
Suraj stopped rolling up the mat. "So that's a sorry?"
"Yes! I said sorry."
"You said sorry, but. Everything after 'but' was the real message."
Jagdish frowned. "But you did drop them."
"I know I did. I felt terrible. Then you screamed at me in front of the whole ground. Those are two different things."
Jagdish rubbed his neck. The practice net swayed in the wind.
"Okay. Try again?"
"Go on."
"I shouted at you in front of everyone. That was wrong. Sorry."
"No 'but'?"
"No 'but'."
Suraj nodded. "Thanks. And for the record, I'm staying for extra catching practice."
"I'll throw," Jagdish said.

How many catches did Suraj drop?
Suraj dropped two catches.
How did Suraj feel about the first apology?
Suraj felt that it was really blame with a sorry in front, and hurt that the shouting in front of everyone was being excused.
What would you advise Jagdish to remember next time he apologises?
Leave out the "but" and name only what he did wrong; the other person's mistake can be a separate conversation.
How might Jagdish have seen his first apology?
Jagdish probably thought it was fair and complete, because he was still annoyed about the catches and didn't notice the "but" was shifting blame.
Who is Grace Poole at Thornfield?
Grace Poole is a servant. Jane is told that the strange laughter comes from her, but she is really the keeper of Rochester's wife, Bertha.

Wasim had a fresh joke every morning, and the joke was always Manjula's blushing or Jahnavi's thick glasses. On Tuesday he pretended to fan his red face in front of the whole row, and Manjula's ears burned. After that she stopped raising her hand, ate lunch in a corner of the library and told her mother she had a stomach ache.

Jahnavi felt something hotter. All through maths she pictured tipping his bag into the drain and watching him cry. The picture scared her a little, so at break she took her notebook to the teacher and read out what she had imagined. The teacher thanked her for saying it, said the anger made sense but the drain did not, and walked her to the staffroom to talk about it.

That evening Manjula, waiting on her building's stairwell, heard Wasim's father shouting on the floor below and then Wasim going very quiet. Something about his jokes made sense to her, though it did not make them fair. Next morning, when he started again, she said, "Stop, that is not funny," in a flat voice, picked up her books and went to sit near the teacher's table.

Where did Manjula eat her lunch after the teasing began?
She ate her lunch in a corner of the library.
How did Jahnavi's way of handling her anger differ from Manjula's way of handling her hurt, and what did Manjula's stairwell moment add?

Jahnavi's anger became a picture of the drain, but she told the teacher instead of acting on it. Manjula first withdrew, then said stop and went to sit near the teacher. Hearing Wasim's father shout explained his jokes to Manjula, but it did not make them fair.
What was Jahnavi feeling when she read her imagined drain scene out to the teacher?
She was angry, and also frightened by how strong the picture was, which is why she wanted an adult to hear it.
What could Manjula do next if Wasim keeps teasing her even after she says stop?
She could keep walking away and tell the teacher or her mother each time, since understanding why he behaves this way does not mean she has to put up with it.
Now you try: check 3/5 / 3/10 = 2.
The answer is 2 x 3/10 = 6/10 = 3/5, right.

Saturday night. Pallavi cried on the terrace tonight about her dad's surgery, and every muscle in me wanted to say I had an assignment and leave. Instead I said it out loud: "I've got the urge to run right now. It's not you. I'm just bad at this." She laughed through her tears. I stayed twenty more minutes, which felt like two hours. Then, weirdly, I told her something I've never told anyone here: I hate my birthday because nobody at home ever remembered it. She didn't make a big deal. She just said, "Noted. I'll remember." Nothing bad happened. I'm writing this down so I believe it tomorrow.
Lakshmi

How much longer did Lakshmi stay on the terrace?
Twenty more minutes.
What was Lakshmi feeling while Pallavi cried?
Lakshmi felt a strong urge to flee and was uneasy with the closeness, but chose to name it and stay.
Which step worked, and why?
Saying the urge to run out loud, because it let Lakshmi stay without pretending and made a small honest disclosure possible.
How might Pallavi feel hearing about the birthday?
Pallavi probably feels trusted and touched, and her simple "I'll remember" shows she welcomes the need.

Carrie and her mom go to the mall to buy new clothes for school. Carrie buys 4 shirts, 2 pairs of pants, and 2 jackets. Each shirt costs $8. Each pair of pants costs $18. Each jacket costs $60. If Carrie's mom pays for half of the total cost of all the clothes, how much does Carrie pay for the clothes?

The total cost of shirts is 4 * $8 = $32
The total cost of pants is 2 * $18 = $36
The total cost of the jackets is 2 * $60 = $120
The total cost of the clothes is $32 + $36 + $120 = $188
Since Carrie's mom pays for half of the total cost, Carrie pays $188 / 2 = $94
The answer is 94.

Vinita's fractions homework covered the whole dining table in their Hyderabad flat, and she had been staring at question six for ten minutes. She rubbed her eyes. Her brother Tejas was on the sofa. If she asked him, he might laugh. If she asked Mummy, she might say “Try harder.” She thought about her maths teacher, Mr. Rao, who never made anyone feel silly. She took a breath, walked over to Tejas and said, “I need help with this one. Can you show me the first step?” Tejas looked up, surprised, and came over. “Sure. Show me where you're stuck.” Vinita felt her shoulders drop.

How long had Vinita been staring at question six?
Ten minutes.
Why did Vinita hesitate before asking Tejas for help?
She feared he might laugh, and that Mummy might just say to try harder, so she thought carefully about who would be safe to ask.
What made Vinita's request easy to answer?
She said plainly “I need help” and asked for only the first step, so she asked a specific person for a specific thing.
How might Tejas have felt when Vinita asked him?
Tejas seemed surprised and then willing, so he was probably pleased to be trusted.

Sahil beta, your girlfriend got the job in Hyderabad and you're sulking? Let your Jeevan Dada tell you about your Dadi. In 1972, when we were twenty-two and newly married, she got a teaching post at the girls' college. Everyone in the family said, 'Now who will cook? Now who will look after Jeevan?' And yes, she was busy, with papers to check every night. I ate a lot of burnt rotis. But I tell you, the day she came home and said her students called her 'Madam Professor', I was so proud I told the whole mohalla. Her happiness was mine. I never felt smaller. I felt bigger, beta. If you love someone and feel safe with them, their good news is your good news too.

What did Dadi's students call her?
'Madam Professor'.
How did Jeevan feel the day Dadi told him what her students called her?
Jeevan felt so proud that he told the whole mohalla, sharing her happiness as his own.
What choice inside the story shows secure love?
Jeevan supporting Dadi's job despite family worries and burnt rotis, and feeling bigger rather than smaller from her success.
How might Dadi have felt with Jeevan's pride?
Dadi probably felt supported and free to grow in her work, knowing her husband was glad for her.

messages.content: There are twice as many surfers on Malibu beach as in Santa Monica beach. If there are 20 surfers in Santa Monica, calculate the total number of surfers on the two beaches.

If there are 20 surfers at Santa Monica, Malibu beach has twice as many surfers as Santa Monica has 2*20 = 40 surfers.
Together, the two beaches have a total of 40+20 = 60 surfers.
The answer is 60.

I am the mother of a Class 4 student who travels by the school bus. For the past week, the bus has been arriving 20 minutes late each day. This worries me. Kindly look into the matter and ensure that the bus comes on time. Thank you.

Francis and Seema had been dating for a year in Bengaluru. Seema often asked, "Why don't you ever talk about your family? Your worries?"
Francis would shrug. "Nothing to tell." He kept his weekends for his cycling group and his evenings for himself. He liked Seema a lot. But getting close felt risky, like handing someone a map to hurt him.
One evening Seema said quietly, "I feel like I'm dating a locked door."
That night Francis lay awake. He realised he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce. Safe, but lonely.
The next evening he called her. "Can I tell you about my father?" His voice shook. Seema listened for an hour.
He didn't stop cycling. But he started letting her in.

What did Francis keep his weekends for?
He kept his weekends for his cycling group.
What was Francis feeling when he lay awake that night?
He felt lonely and uneasy, realising he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce to stay safe.
How did Francis begin to find a balance between closeness and self?
He kept his cycling but began sharing his inner life with Seema, starting with the call about his father.
How did Seema feel before Francis opened up?
Seema felt shut out and lonely, as if dating a locked door.
