Last November I took the forty-one-day vow before the Sabarimala pilgrimage, the way my father and grandfather did. Black clothes, no meat, no alcohol, sleeping on the floor, prayers morning and evening. At the Bengaluru office, Alka, who sits next to me, noticed on day two. "Is this a detox thing? Or a dare?" she asked, meaning it kindly. I felt a flash of irritation, then realised she had no way of knowing. In her family nobody fasts for anything. So I explained: for me it wasn't a diet; it was a promise, and breaking it would feel like lying to God and to my father. She was quiet, then asked, "What does it mean for you, day to day? What should I not do?" Nobody at work had ever asked me that. I told her: don't offer me the office biryani, and don't be offended if I skip Friday drinks. She didn't, for forty-one days. On day forty-two, she brought me sweets and said, "Chinmay, well done."

How many days did the vow last?
Forty-one days.
What did Chinmay feel when Alka asked if it was a detox or a dare?
Chinmay felt a flash of irritation, then understanding, realising Alka had no way of knowing what the vow meant.

Asking what the vow meant for Chinmay day to day and what to avoid, which let Alka respect the commitment in practical ways.
How did Alka's understanding change over the forty-one days?
Alka went from seeing it as a possible detox to respecting it as a serious promise, and marked the end by bringing sweets.

Today I told the board. My hands were shaking on the table.
For three months I'd seen it: our NGO's director using donor money for his cousin's company. Rehana, from accounts, saw it too. She was scared to speak. So was I.
I kept thinking of the village schools the money was meant for.
So we went together, with printouts. The board chair listened, stone-faced. Then she said, "Thank you. We'll investigate."
On the way out, a senior colleague muttered that I'd "ruined my career." Maybe. I'm twenty-six. I could be unemployed next month.
But I'd rather start over than stay silent while children lose their classrooms.
Jasleen

Who went with Jasleen to the board?
Rehana, from accounts.
How did Jasleen feel telling the board?
Jasleen felt scared and nervous, with shaking hands, but determined.
What made Jasleen's approach wise?
Going with a colleague and printouts to the board, the proper authority, instead of gossiping or leaking.
How might Rehana feel after the meeting?
Rehana may feel relieved to have spoken but anxious about what comes next.

It means it is now your turn to decide or take the next step.

Any breakfast idea for leftover chapatis?
Make chapati upma. Tear the chapatis into small bits, fry onion, mustard seeds and chilli, add the bits with a little salt and turmeric and toss well. It takes ten minutes.
I like that. My husband Manav likes sweet more than spicy though.
Then make a sweet version for him. Tear the chapati, warm it in a pan with a spoon of ghee, sugar and a pinch of cardamom. Some people call it chapati laddoo when it is shaped into balls.
Will the sweet one taste good for Manav's tiffin as well?
Yes, it keeps well for a few hours. Shape the sweet chapati mix into small balls so it is easy to eat at his desk. Wrap them in paper and they will not get soggy for his lunch.
Find 1/9, 2/9, 1/11 and 2/11 as decimals. What patterns do you see?

Answer: 1/9 = 0.(1), 2/9 = 0.(2), 1/11 = 0.(09), 2/11 = 0.(18).

For ninths: 10 / 9 = 1 R 1 for ever, so 1/9 = 0.111... = 0.(1). Then 2/9 = 2 x 0.111... = 0.222... = 0.(2), and in the same way 4/9 = 0.(4) and 8/9 = 0.(8): the numerator repeats. For elevenths: 1 / 11 = 0, 10 / 11 = 0 R 10, 100 / 11 = 9 R 1, and then the remainder 1 returns, so 1/11 = 0.090909... = 0.(09). Every eleventh has a 2-digit block that is 9 times the numerator: 2/11 = 0.(18), 3/11 = 0.(27), 5/11 = 0.(45).

Nikhil pressed his palms, said "Namaste," and touched Dada's shoes, quickly, like tagging someone in a game.
Dada laughed and lifted him into a hug. "Jeete raho!"
Nikhil did it again, then again, until Mum said, "Once is enough!"
At bedtime he whispered, "Why do we touch feet?"

Nikhil thought about it. "I love Dada's shoes too."

What did Nikhil say before he touched Dada's feet?
Nikhil pressed his palms and said "Namaste."

Nikhil was delighted by Dada's laugh and hug, and felt happy doing it again like a game.

The school bus was stuck behind a wedding procession for half an hour, and Varun was bored.

He looked at Neelam two seats ahead, the girl who stammered when she read aloud. He'd called her "Ne-Ne-Neelam" once last week, just to see. A few boys had laughed. Nobody had said anything.

Today he said it again, louder. Three boys laughed this time. Neelam stared out of the window.

Varun watched her ears go red. He watched the boys watching him. Nobody told him to stop. The driver had the radio on.

Then he reached over and took her water bottle and passed it to the back seat. More laughter.

Varun leaned back, grinning. It was easy. It worked. He was already thinking about what he could do tomorrow.

What was the school bus stuck behind?
A wedding procession.
How did Varun feel when the boys laughed and nobody stopped him?
He felt pleased and powerful, learning that the cruelty was rewarded with attention.
What could have stopped this from growing?
A classmate saying "stop", or the driver or a teacher stepping in, so Varun learned the cruelty did not pay; Neelam telling an adult that day would also help.
What is it like for Neelam with her ears going red?
She feels humiliated and helpless, staring out of the window while others laugh.

Ganga, come and sit. Your grandfather Francis once had a fight with his friend Anthony over a lost marble. I was ten. The next morning I said to myself: if I act as if nothing happened, maybe it will all melt away. So I walked up to Anthony at the gate and held out half a banana chip packet. "Want some?" Anthony took a chip and we chewed together. It worked, that day. But Anthony's eyes stayed on the ground, and he did not laugh at my jokes. Weeks later I learned he had been waiting for me to say something about the marble.

Francis offered half a packet of banana chips.
What did Francis want to happen when the chips were held out at the gate?
Francis hoped that acting as if nothing had happened would make the fight melt away, which shows a wish to avoid an awkward talk.

Francis could have mentioned the marble and said sorry along with sharing the chips, because saying it aloud would have shown that Anthony's hurt mattered.

It felt like a kind gesture but not enough; Anthony had been waiting for Francis to say something about the marble.

People ask why I still talk about my first month at the pharmacy. I'm Rajni, and it's because of one Friday. My supervisor told me to sell a strip of antibiotics to a customer without a prescription. 'Everyone does it. If you want to pass probation, don't be difficult.' My father's shop had closed that year. My salary was the family's rent. I stood behind the counter feeling my knees go soft. I could have told myself I had no choice. That would have been easier to live with. Instead I asked for five minutes and called my senior from college, Vasudha, who now worked as a pharmacist in another city. She said, 'Check your company's rules. Most have a policy on this, and a helpline.' I found it on the staff notice board. I told the customer, calmly, that I couldn't without a prescription. My supervisor was cold for a week. I passed probation anyway. I might not have. I'd still choose it.

What did the supervisor tell Rajni to do?
The supervisor told Rajni to sell a strip of antibiotics without a prescription.
What was Rajni feeling behind the counter?
Rajni felt afraid, knees going soft, because the salary paid the family's rent.
What steps helped Rajni refuse?
Calling Vasudha, finding the company's policy and helpline on the notice board, and then refusing the customer calmly.
How does Vasudha help without deciding for Rajni?
Vasudha points Rajni to the company's rules and helpline, leaving the choice with Rajni.

Dear Chandrika,
I'm writing because when we talk, I either say too much or nothing.
Over the last months I've said yes every time you wanted to skip something: the class picnic, your cousin's engagement, the badminton trials. I told myself I was keeping the peace. Truthfully, I didn't want to see you upset, and I didn't want to be the bad guy. But I've watched the list of places you can go get shorter, and I think my yeses helped make it shorter.
I'm not going to drag you anywhere. That wouldn't help either. But I'd like us to try one small thing each week, something you pick. Maybe it's just coming with me to the market on Sunday and buying the vegetables yourself. If it's hard, tell me, and we'll still count it as a try.
I'm proud of how hard you're working at this, even when it doesn't look like it.
Your Papa,
Ramesh

What did Chandrika skip?
The class picnic, your cousin's engagement, the badminton trials.
What does Ramesh admit feeling about his yeses?
He feels regretful and worried, recognising that avoiding conflict and upset helped Chandrika's world shrink.
What does Ramesh propose, and why is it balanced?
One small, chosen step each week, like buying vegetables at the market, which neither forces nor shields.
What might Chandrika feel reading the letter?
Chandrika may feel embarrassed but understood, relieved that Papa won't force anything and still believes in Chandrika.

Friday, 9 June
Result came at 11. I cleared the bank PO exam. Rank 212. Papa cried on the phone, Mummy distributed sweets to the whole lane. Gopika sent fifteen party poppers. 🎉
So why am I sitting here at midnight feeling nothing?
Two years of coaching. Two years of skipping cousins' weddings and the photography club. Papa's dream since I was in Class 8: "a secure bank job, like Sharma uncle's daughter." I said it so often I thought it was mine.
Today I opened my old camera bag, the one I haven't touched since first year. The lens was dusty. I cleaned it for an hour and felt more doing that than I did when the result came.
I don't know what to do with that.
Sangeeta

What rank did Sangeeta get in the bank PO exam?
Rank 212.
Why might Sangeeta feel nothing at midnight after clearing the exam?
Sangeeta may feel empty because the goal was Papa's dream, repeated so often it seemed like Sangeeta's own, so reaching it didn't touch what Sangeeta actually values.
What turning point does the dusty camera offer Sangeeta?
Cleaning the lens stirred more feeling than the result; Sangeeta could make time for photography again and think honestly about next steps before deciding anything big.
How might Papa feel if he read this diary entry?
Papa, who cried with joy, might be confused and hurt, but could also begin to see that the dream he chose wasn't the one his child held.
A bag of chips weighs 20 ounces, and a tin of cookies weighs 9 ounces. If Jasmine buys 6 bags of chips and 4 times as many tins of cookies, how many pounds does she have to carry?

Jasmine's bags of chips weigh 20*6 = 120 ounces.
Jasmine buys 6*4 = 24 tins of cookies.
Jasmine's tins of cookies weigh 9*24 = 216 ounces.
She has to carry 120+216=336 ounces.
She has to carry 336/16=21 pounds.
The answer is 21.
If the door is locked, the hall light stays off. Today the hall light is off. Is the door locked?
We cannot be sure. Because the rule only tells us what happens when the door is locked, the light could be off for another reason, such as a switch or a fault.
My little brother Leo borrowed my headphones and broke them. He just says sorry and walks away.
That is frustrating, especially when the apology feels too quick. Did he offer to fix or replace them, or is it only the word sorry so far?
Only sorry. He is nine, so he has no money.
Right, so replacing them may not be fair. He could still help, like doing a chore for you or giving up a small treat until you can get repairs done. Have you told your parents?
Not yet. I do not want him to get into big trouble.
That is kind of you. You can speak to Leo first and ask him how he plans to make it right. If he stays vague, then a quiet word with your parents is reasonable.
Since he is so young, what small thing could he realistically do?
At nine, Leo could do your dusting chore for a week or give you his Saturday cartoon slot. Keep it small and clear, so he feels he has made up for the broken headphones in some way.

Christina walks 7km to school every day from Monday to Friday. She returns home covering the same distance. Last Friday her mother asked her to pass by her friend, which is another 2km away from the school in the opposite distance from home. How many kilometers did Christina cover that week?

One trip to school is 2 * 7 km = 14km.
In one week, Christina walks 14 km/day * 5 days/week = 70km to school.
The extra trip to her mum's friend added 2 km * 2 = 4km to her travel distance.
Her total distance was thus 70 km + 4 km = 74 km
The answer is 74.

Gurpreet had become popular almost overnight after her dance video at the school fest in their Chandigarh school. Suddenly everyone wanted to sit with her.
Binita, from the next section, was one of them. "Wow, your hair is always perfect," she said. "Must be nice when everything just comes easy." The others laughed.
Gurpreet smiled, but on the bus home she felt uneasy. Binita had never talked to her before the fest. And "comes easy" hurt: she practised two hours every day.
She thought about who had been there in Class 7, when nobody knew her name. Only Jasmeet, who still sat with her at lunch, and Harman from the bus.
The next day, when Binita said, "You're so lucky," Gurpreet said gently, "Honestly, I practise a lot. It isn't luck." No sarcasm, no put-down.
At lunch, she sat with Jasmeet and Harman, like always. The crowd could come or go.

What made Gurpreet popular almost overnight?
Her dance video at the school fest.
How did Gurpreet feel on the bus home?
She felt uneasy and a bit hurt, sensing envy behind Binita's compliment and the suggestion that things came easy.
What did Gurpreet do that was wise?
She replied honestly and gently without a put-down, and stayed close to the real friends who had been there before.
How might Binita see Gurpreet's popularity?
Binita seems envious, thinking Gurpreet's success is luck, not seeing the hours of practice behind it.

On cold December mornings at the Lucknow nursery school, the children sat in their sweaters close to the heater. Rafiq sir had started calling Hafsa "our bright one" after she counted the pigeons on the wall. Now he smiled at her first, waited while she thought, and said, "Try, Hafsa, I know you can."
Hafsa, who used to hide behind her mittens, began putting her hand up for every question. She sounded out C-A-T slowly while he nodded. At home she lined up her dolls and played school, saying, "I'm the bright one."

What did Hafsa count on the wall?
The pigeons.
How does Hafsa feel now when Rafiq sir asks a question?
She feels confident and eager, putting her hand up because being treated as bright makes trying feel worthwhile.
How could Rafiq sir give the same boost to every child?
Smile, wait patiently and say "I know you can" to each child, not only the one he calls bright.
How might a child who is never called bright feel in the same class?
That child may feel overlooked and try less, missing the warmth and waiting time Hafsa gets.

Dear Leela,

You asked me last week why I look like a question mark at my desk. Honestly, I have been hunched over the laptop for hours, chin forward, neck and back aching by evening. My manager may think I am deeply focused, but the truth is I am often exhausted and just forgot to move. I have raised the screen on two books and set the chair lower, and I now stand up every hour to fill my water bottle and walk to the window. It has helped my mood too. I only hope nobody reads slouching as laziness. Would you like to join me for the noon walk? 🙂

Chetan

What did Chetan put under the laptop screen?
Chetan raised the screen on two books.
What do Chetan's hunched posture and the letter suggest about the feeling behind it?
Chetan is often exhausted and forgot to move, not simply focused. Others might read the posture as focus, but Chetan suspects some might think it is laziness.
What small steps helped Chetan feel better?
Chetan raised the screen, lowered the chair and stood up every hour to walk to the window, which also helped the mood.
How might Chetan's manager see the posture?
The manager may take it as deep focus, but might also misread it as tiredness or laziness, since the posture alone does not say which.
Why is it useful to write a rough draft before the final essay?
Mistakes cost nothing in a draft. Because you can get ideas down and change them without worrying about neatness, the final copy comes out clearer.
Spell "February" for me please. And why do we have a break in the middle of the school day?

1. It is F-e-b-r-u-a-r-y, with an "r" before the "u".
2. Breaks let your mind rest and your body move, so you can learn better afterwards.

"Harish, did you see? Everyone laughed. The whole school."
"I saw you slip. I also saw you get up and finish the dance."
"I want to disappear. I'm never going on stage again."
"Jaya, remember when Mehra Sir's microphone squeaked in assembly? Everyone laughed for a minute. Does anybody talk about it now?"
"...No."
"Give it two days. They'll be laughing about something else."
"But they'll call me Jaya-Splat."
"Then they'll have to call me Harish-Splat too, because I'm sitting next to you at lunch."
Jaya gave a wet laugh. "You'd do that?"
"Already doing it. Come on, the samosas will finish."
She wiped her face, picked up her ghungroos and walked with him to the canteen.

What did Harish see Jaya do after she slipped?
Get up and finish the dance.
How did Jaya feel after everyone laughed?
Humiliated; she wanted to disappear and never go on stage again.
How did Harish help Jaya cope?
He reminded her how quickly people forget and stood by her by sitting with her at lunch.
How does Harish see Jaya's fall?
As a small slip followed by real courage, since she got up and finished.

Monday. Arohi, five, noticed her Ammamma, Rukmini, lying down in the afternoon, which she never did. Arohi stood in the doorway, quiet, holding her doll.
Tuesday. Ammamma coughed a lot. Arohi brought her a glass of water without being asked and patted her hand. "Ammamma, sad?" "Just tired, kanna."
Friday. Ammamma sat in the garden again. Arohi drew her a picture of a sun with a smiling face and said, "For your cough to go away."

What did Arohi bring Ammamma on Tuesday?
A glass of water.
What was Arohi feeling standing quietly in the doorway?
Arohi felt worried and sad to see Ammamma lying down, which she never did.
How could the family support Arohi's sympathy?
Let her help in small ways, like bringing water, and explain simply how Ammamma is feeling.
How might Rukmini feel receiving the sun picture?
Rukmini would likely feel touched and loved by Arohi's care.

Friday, two days before Diwali. At the sweet shop, Nana told Mridul he could choose one box of sweets for himself. There were forty kinds. Mridul walked up and down the glass counter for twenty minutes: kaju katli, rasgulla, three kinds of barfi, jalebi, ladoo. At last he picked motichoor ladoo.
Saturday. He opened the box, took one bite and looked at Noor's kaju katli. "I should have got that."
Sunday, Diwali. Nana took them back, but this time he pointed to just three trays: kaju katli, ladoo or milk barfi. "Only these." Mridul chose kaju katli in a minute. When Noor offered him a ladoo later, he said, "No thanks. I like mine."

How many kinds of sweets were in the shop?
There were forty kinds of sweets.
Why did Mridul wish he had picked kaju katli?
Mridul felt unsatisfied and doubtful, because with forty choices every other sweet seemed better than the one he picked.
What did Nana change on Diwali, and why did it help?
Nana narrowed it to three trays, so Mridul chose quickly and felt happy with the choice.
How might Noor see Mridul's second-guessing on Saturday?
Noor might find it funny or a little annoying, having simply enjoyed the kaju katli without fuss.

Rehana, twenty-six, had four things to do before her Nani's cataract surgery at noon: drop her little cousin at school, submit her team's quarterly report, pick up Nani's medicines, and meet the junior engineer she was mentoring.
Then the auto driver went on strike.
She walked Nani's medicines home herself, called the junior, Trisha, and said, "Can we do your review on the phone?" They talked while she walked. Trisha had a good idea about reducing the factory's water waste. Rehana told her to present it herself.
She reached the hospital at 11:45, sweating, and held Nani's hand as they wheeled her in.
Later, Trisha texted: "Presented. They liked it." Rehana smiled at her phone in the waiting room.

What time did Rehana reach the hospital?
How did Rehana feel when she read Trisha's text?
She felt proud and happy, smiling in the waiting room.
How did Rehana manage her duties under pressure?
She walked the medicines home, held the mentoring review by phone, and still reached Nani in time.
How might Trisha feel about being told to present her own idea?
Trisha likely feels trusted and encouraged, and proud when it was well received.
Why does a sharp smell fill the house when someone fries chillies?
Tiny bits of the chilli oil rise with the hot air. Because they are carried through the room and breathed in, they irritate the nose and throat and make people cough.

Jeanne wants to ride the Ferris wheel, the roller coaster, and the bumper cars. The Ferris wheel costs 5 tickets, the roller coaster costs 4 tickets and the bumper cars cost 4 tickets. Jeanne has 5 tickets. How many more tickets should Jeanne buy?

The total number of tickets needed is 5 tickets + 4 tickets + 4 tickets = 13 tickets.
Jeanne needs 13 tickets - 5 tickets = 8 tickets.
The answer is 8.

On her first day of school, Ishita bent to touch Yogesh Dadu's feet in the hall of their flat. Dadu put his hand on her head. “Khush raho, beti. Padho, aage badho.” Ishita straightened her bag. “Dadu, what does that mean?” He smiled. “Be happy. Study and go forward.” “Is it magic?” “It's a blessing. It means I'm wishing good things for you.” Ishita nodded seriously. At the gate she turned and called, “Dadu! Khush raho to you too!” He laughed and waved.

What did Dadu put on Ishita's head?
His hand.
What was Ishita feeling when she called “Khush raho to you too!”?
She felt happy and loved, and wanted to give the blessing back, now that she knew what it meant.
How did Dadu help the blessing mean more to Ishita?
He explained simply what the words meant and that a blessing is a wish for good things.
How might Dadu feel when Ishita blesses him back?
He likely feels delighted and touched, which is why he laughs and waves.

Karthigai Deepam fell on the night before Jaya's anatomy viva, and her hostel in Hyderabad banned open flames. At home in Madurai, Amma and Paati would be lining every step and wall with little clay lamps by six.
Jaya had carried five lamps from home, wrapped in newspaper. At seven she asked the warden, twice, until she got ten minutes on the terrace with a bucket of water beside her.
"You're really doing this before the viva?" Lavanya asked, eyebrows up. "It's just oil and wicks."
"It's the one night the whole family does the same thing at the same time," Jaya said, striking the match. "Wherever we are."
The five flames steadied in the wind. Jaya felt her shoulders loosen for the first time all week. Lavanya was quiet, then crouched and shielded the last lamp with her hand.

How many lamps had Jaya carried from home?
Five lamps, wrapped in newspaper.
How did Jaya feel once the five flames steadied?
She felt calm and connected, her shoulders loosening for the first time all week, sharing the ritual with her family from far away.
How did Jaya keep the tradition while respecting the hostel rule?
She asked the warden for permission, used only ten minutes on the terrace and kept a bucket of water ready, honouring both the ritual and the rule.
How might Lavanya's view have changed during the ten minutes?
Lavanya began doubtful, calling it just oil and wicks, but by shielding the last lamp she seemed to understand why it mattered to Jaya.

messages.content: I do my homework in front of the television and it takes forever.
That slows almost everyone down. Your mind keeps jumping between the screen and the page. Try a quiet corner with only your books and a glass of water. You may finish in half the time.
But my mother says I can watch after I finish. I am Lucy.

Then your mother's rule is a good reward. Lucy, you could even set a timer, such as thirty minutes for maths, a short break, then thirty minutes for reading. The television will feel nicer when the work is done.
During those thirty minutes of maths, what should I do if I get stuck on a question?

Skip it for now, finish the easier maths questions before the timer ends, and come back to it after your break. If it is still hard, circle it and ask your teacher or a classmate next day. Do not let one question steal your whole evening, Lucy.

For two weeks Noor let the sharp remarks in stand-ups slide. Ramesh would say, "Some of us actually read the ticket," and Sachin would go quiet. Noor told herself it would blow over. Instead the team began sitting on different sides of the table, and Sachin's screen kept showing job listings.

Finally Noor booked two private chats. She asked Ramesh what happened on release day and what he needed, then asked Sachin the same. Both talked for a long time, and both said nobody had asked before.

Next morning she stood at the whiteboard. Why did the release slip? Because both had shipped the fix. Why both? Because each believed the task was theirs. Why? Because two tickets carried the same name and nobody wrote a handover note. The quarrel was about the tickets, not about temperament.

In Sachin's chat a second thing had come out: Ramesh kept calling Sachin "the intern from the small college" in front of others. That was no mix-up over tasks. Noor wrote down dates and exact words, told both of them mediation would not be enough, and sent the notes to HR, as company process said.

What did Ramesh say in the stand-ups?
Ramesh said, "Some of us actually read the ticket."
Why did waiting fail while the private chats and the whiteboard questions worked?

Waiting let the tension spread until the team split and Sachin looked at job listings, whereas the chats made both feel heard and the repeated why-questions traced the blame to two tickets with the same name and no handover note.
What was Sachin probably feeling while the remarks kept coming?
Hurt and unheard: Sachin went quiet and kept looking at job listings.
What could Noor do next to keep the ticket confusion from coming back?
Noor could give each ticket one named owner and ask for a short handover note whenever work changes hands.

I'm Keerthana, and honestly this one still makes me angry. I told our class teacher that boys were sending cruel messages about a girl in my grade. I gave dates. For two weeks, nothing happened. Then in assembly the teacher said, "Some people have been complaining, and we know who." Everybody turned to look at me. I felt betrayed, like I'd been thrown to the wolves.
That night I told my cousin Sahil. He said, "Don't stop. Write it all down and go higher." So I emailed the principal with the dates, my parents came with me to meet the principal, and we found out about the board's helpline. I stayed with my friends at lunch and didn't go anywhere alone until it was sorted.
It took time, but in the end it was taken seriously.

How long did Keerthana wait with nothing happening?
She waited for two weeks.
How did Keerthana feel when the class teacher spoke in assembly?
She felt betrayed, like she'd been thrown to the wolves, as everybody turned to look at her.
What steps could someone take if a school ignores or exposes a report?
They can keep written dates, email the principal, bring parents, use the board's helpline and stay with friends until it is sorted.
How does Sahil see what Keerthana should do?
Sahil tells her not to stop, and sees writing everything down and going higher as the way to be taken seriously.

The morning after Naveen's father died, the badminton group at the community centre didn't play. Yash, who organised the Sunday games, made a list on the back of a score sheet: who could drive relatives from the station, who could bring tiffin, who could set up chairs for the prayer meeting. Nobody made a speech. Twelve names went down in twenty minutes. At the prayer meeting, Yash didn't try to find perfect words for Naveen. He just stood beside him while people came and went, and handed him water when his voice cracked. Later that week, when Naveen came back to the centre for the first time, the group played doubles as usual, and Yash made sure Naveen was on his side.

What did Yash write the list on?
The back of a score sheet.
What might Naveen have felt when he came back and found the usual doubles game?
Likely relieved and comforted, welcomed back to something normal without fuss.
How did Yash turn the group's sympathy into real help?
By listing practical tasks, like station pick-ups, tiffins and chairs, so twelve people could each do something useful.
What was it like for the badminton group to be given specific tasks?
They could act on their sadness instead of feeling helpless, which is why twelve names went down so quickly.

I'm Yogesh, and the day I heard my father come out of my mouth was a Tuesday at our print shop in Solapur. Joseph, my new apprentice, had printed two hundred wedding cards with the groom's name misspelled. Before I could think, I said, "Did your brain go on holiday? Idiot work!" in Appa's exact rising voice.

Joseph went pale and stared at the floor, and suddenly I remembered being a child, staring at our kitchen floor while Appa shouted about my ink-stained homework.

That night I sat with a chai and sorted him out in my head. Appa checked every proof three times; that's why the shop survived. I'm keeping that. Appa made people feel small. I'm not keeping that.

Next morning I told Joseph, "Sorry for 'idiot'. Let's make a proof-check list together." We still use it.

What mistake was on the wedding cards?
The groom's name was misspelled on two hundred wedding cards.
What did Yogesh feel on seeing Joseph stare at the floor?
Yogesh felt a jolt of shame, remembering staring at the kitchen floor as a child while Appa shouted.
How did Yogesh turn the inherited pattern into a choice?
Yogesh decided to keep Appa's triple-checking and drop making people feel small, then apologised and built a proof-check list with Joseph.
What was it like for Joseph when he was called an idiot?
Joseph felt humiliated and frightened, going pale and staring at the floor.

Ayesha, you asked why I stopped calling Chandigarh people "plastic." Okay. Listen.
I grew up in a village near Bathinda. My whole family said city kids don't respect elders, don't know soil, only phones. I believed it. When I went to college in the city, I sat in the back and judged everyone.
Then our class did a village survey. I thought the city students would complain about the dust. Instead, one boy, Harman, spent three hours helping an old farmer fill a government form. Another girl sat with the women and learned to make makki roti, laughing at her own mistakes.
Meanwhile, two boys from my own district mocked the old farmer's slow speech.
So, Ayesha, I learned something: we carry stereotypes about them, they carry some about us. Both are sometimes true of someone, and unfair to most. That's all. This is Jasleen, changing her mind.

How long did Harman spend helping the old farmer?
Harman spent three hours helping an old farmer fill a government form.
How did Jasleen feel sitting at the back of the class at first?
Jasleen felt suspicious and superior, judging the city students based on what her family had said.
What turned Jasleen's view around?
Seeing city students help and learn with patience during the village survey, while boys from her own district mocked the farmer, showed her that the stereotype was unfair.
How might the city students have felt if they had known Jasleen's first view?
They might have felt hurt and misjudged, since many of them respected elders and wanted to learn.

Subject: About last Friday, and how we work from now on

Hi Imran,

On Friday, in front of the whole team, I thanked you for staying till 3 am to finish the client deck. You looked proud. I meant it as praise. I've been thinking about it all weekend, and I got it wrong.

When I was in my first year here, my lead praised exactly that, and I spent two years exhausted, snapping at my family, calling it dedication. I don't want to hand that down to you.

So here's what I'm changing, starting with me. No messages after 9 pm unless something is truly on fire. If a deadline needs a night shift, that's my planning failure, not your badge. And I'll praise the work, not the hours.

Your deck was sharp. The structure on slide four was better than mine would have been. Let's go over it Tuesday, at a normal hour.

Tarun

What time did Imran stay till to finish the client deck?
Imran stayed till 3 am to finish the client deck.
Why did Tarun spend the weekend thinking about the praise?
Tarun felt uneasy and regretful, worried about teaching Imran to see exhaustion as a badge, the same lesson Tarun's first lead once taught.
What small step shows Tarun's new standard is real?
Tarun starts with Tarun's own habits, sending no messages after 9 pm and praising the work instead of the hours.
How might Imran feel reading this email?
Imran may feel a little confused at first, since the praise felt good, but also relieved and valued for the quality of slide four rather than the late night.

Saturday in Nairobi was Wanjiru's slow day, and she guarded it. She walked to the market without her phone, bought mangoes and sukuma wiki, and stopped to watch a man play guitar outside the bakery. At home she cooked for two hours, music loud, and ate on the balcony with her neighbour Vera.
In the evening they went to a friend's birthday. Wanjiru danced until her feet hurt, laughing at her own terrible moves.
At eleven Vera grabbed her arm. "After-party in Westlands! Everyone's going."
Wanjiru hesitated. It sounded fun. But she was helping at her aunt's shop at eight, and she had promised to walk her cousin through a job form after.
"Not tonight," she said. "Tonight was perfect already."
She took a matatu home, humming, and fell asleep with the taste of mango still in her mouth.

What did Wanjiru buy at the market?
Mangoes and sukuma wiki.
What was Wanjiru feeling when she hesitated about the after-party?
She was tempted because it sounded fun, but she also felt satisfied and mindful of her promises for the next morning.
What choice did Wanjiru make, and why was it a wise balance?
She skipped the after-party after enjoying the whole day, keeping her commitments to her aunt and cousin without giving up joy.
How might Vera see Wanjiru leaving early?
Vera might be a little disappointed to lose her friend's company, but she has shared much of Wanjiru's good day and may respect her choice.

messages.content: Can you tell me a story about a New Year's Eve party on a rooftop in Delhi?

On the last night of the year, the residents of Block C climbed to the rooftop with plates of food. Tenants who had never met before shared samosas and complained about the cold. A boy named Sahil brought a speaker, and the music drifted over the city. At eleven-thirty, the speaker went silent, and he looked guilty. An old man named Mr. Gupta rose, cleared his throat, and began to sing a film song from the sixties. Others joined, laughing and clapping. When midnight struck, fireworks burst across the sky, and the whole rooftop cheered. Sahil never fixed the speaker, because the singing was better.
Now you try: in which class does 40 go?
The answer is 40 to 49.

The largest animal to have ever lived on earth is the blue whale.  The tongue of an adult blue whale can weigh 6000 pounds.  If one ton is 2000 pounds, how many tons can the tongue of an adult blue whale weigh?

1000 pounds more than 5ooo pounds is 6000 pounds.
If one ton is 2000 pounds, then the tongue of a blue whale weighs 6000/2000=3 tons.
The answer is 3.
After I bumped into someone, he said 'my apologies'. Is that just sorry?

Yes, it is a polite way of saying sorry. Apologies are statements saying you are sorry for a mistake or for causing trouble. It is a noun, the plural of apology.
Example: The shopkeeper offered his apologies for the late delivery.

The hostel common room went quiet as Devika's phone lit up with the video of her presentation and the caption that mocked her voice. Raghav, from her class, had shared it. Two hundred people had laughed.

Her face burned. She typed fast: a line about Raghav's marks and his boasting, sharp enough to cut. She posted it before anyone could stop her.

By dinner the reply had more views than the original. Someone had captured a screenshot and put it in the class group with a laughing face. The warden called Devika to the office the next morning, and the crowd now had fresh things to say about her, not only about the talk.

Who shared the video of Devika's presentation?
Raghav, from her class.
What was Devika feeling as she typed the reply about Raghav?
Devika was humiliated and furious, with her face burning, and wanted to hurt back at once.
What could Devika do now, and why?
Devika could delete the reply, avoid adding more, and ask a trusted adult to help handle the mockery, because stopping the fuel is what lets the attention fade.
How might Raghav see the reply that was aimed at him?
Raghav may feel angry and hurt at the personal insults, and it may give him a reason to feel justified, even though he began the mockery.

I'm Arnab, and I studied engineering with Irfan. Everyone assumed he'd go abroad. Instead he joined the district roads department. Two years ago I visited his posting. He took me to a village that used to get cut off every monsoon because the only road turned to mud. Pregnant women had to be carried out on cots. Irfan had spent eighteen months fighting paperwork and sitting with contractors to build an all-weather road. When we drove on it, an old woman waved at our jeep and shouted something. Irfan smiled but didn't say much. Later, over tea, I asked if he regretted not going abroad. He looked out at the fields for a while and said, "Not today." I think that meant something deep for him. I'm not sure I'll ever know exactly what.

What happened to the village's only road every monsoon?
It turned to mud and cut the village off.
What might Irfan's quiet smile and 'Not today' suggest about his feelings?
He seems to feel a deep, quiet fulfilment from seeing the road help people, though he doesn't put it into many words.
What helped Irfan finish the road?
His persistence over eighteen months with paperwork and contractors, focused on a clear community goal.
How might the old woman who waved feel about the new road?
She likely feels grateful and relieved that her village is no longer cut off in the rains.

Carla went to the zoo and counted 12 zebras in their enclosure. She then visited the camels and learned that there were only half as many camels as there were zebras. Next, she visited the monkeys and counted 4 times the number of monkeys as camels. Finally, she saw some giraffes and counted only 2 giraffes. How many more monkeys than giraffes did Carla see?

There were 12 zebras / 2 zebras/camel = 6 camels at the zoo.
There were 4 monkeys/camel x 6 camels = 24 monkeys at the zoo.
Therefore, Carla saw 24 monkeys - 2 giraffes = 22 more monkeys than giraffes.
The answer is 22.

- Why is it better to keep a lid on the rice pot when the water has just boiled?
- Why does popcorn pop?
- Check my English: "We had a fun at the fair."
- I don't understand "unscrew". Can you help?
- Why does bread get hard when left out?

1. The lid keeps the heat in. Because it keeps the steam in and the water at the boil, the grains cook all the way through.
2. Steam inside the kernel bursts it open. Because the water inside turns to steam and the pressure grows until the hard shell gives way.
3. Fixed: We had fun at the fair. Why: "fun" is uncountable here, so we do not use "a".
4. Unscrew is a verb that means to take something off by turning it.
5. Bread hardens as it dries and its starch changes. Because the water in it escapes into the air, and the starch turns into a firmer form.
Which player was named best of the tournament at the closing ceremony?
I'm not sure who was named best player, as I can't see the ceremony or reports on it. The tournament's official page will have the award list.

Note, Tuesday. Lavanya, two years old, spent the morning at the sand tray pouring from a yellow cup into a green one, again and again. She ignored the lunch bell and my calls. When I lifted her she cried hard and reached back for the tray.
Wednesday. I sat beside her before lunch, said, "The cups are going to sleep soon," and helped her shelve them. She frowned but walked to the table holding my hand.
Maria, key worker

Which two cups did Lavanya pour between at the sand tray?
She poured from a yellow cup into a green one.
How did Lavanya feel when Maria lifted her away on Tuesday?
She felt distressed. She cried hard and reached back for the tray, which shows how much the pouring mattered to her.
What changed in what Maria did on Wednesday?
Maria gave a warning first, said the cups were going to sleep, and helped shelve them, so the stop felt gentler.
What would Lavanya's Tuesday have felt like if the cups had had a place to wait?
She might still have been sad to stop, but she would know the cups were safe, so leaving them would hurt less.
What does collection mean?

A collection is a group of similar things gathered over time. It is a noun.
Example: Sanjay has a collection of old stamps from many countries.

Kim is an office manager. Every morning she spends 5 minutes making coffee, 2 minutes per employee getting a status update, and 3 minutes per employee updating payroll records. If there are 9 employees in the office, how long does Kim's morning routine take?

First find how many minutes Kim spends on each employee: 2 minutes/employee + 3 minutes/employee = 5 minutes/employee
Then multiply that time by the number of employees to find the total time spent on status and payroll updates: 5 minutes/employee * 9 employees = 45 minutes
Finally, add that time to the time spent making coffee to find the total time: 45 minutes + 5 minutes = 50 minutes
The answer is 50.

'Jeevan, the school sent another reminder,' Mummy whispered in the kitchen. 'The third one. And the landlord...'
'I know, Lata. I know.' Papa's voice cracked.
Himani stood in the corridor with the fee slip in her bag, the one she hadn't given them yet. She walked in.
'Papa, is it about my fees?'
They both turned. Mummy wiped her hands. 'You heard.'
'Some. I'm sorry I cost so much.'
Papa sat down heavily. 'Beta, you don't cost. You're our daughter. My hours at the mill were cut, that's all.'
'Then I'll ask about the fee waiver. Sharma Ma'am said there's a form for families going through a hard time.'
Papa hesitated, then nodded. 'That would help. Bring the form and we'll fill it together.'
'And I'll stop asking for new stuff.'
Mummy pulled her close. 'Just keep telling us what you hear, okay? Don't carry it alone. The worrying is our job.'

Why was Papa earning less?
His hours at the mill were cut.
What was Himani feeling as she stood in the corridor with the fee slip?
She felt scared and guilty, thinking her fees were the reason for her parents' worry.
Which of Himani's offers fits her role, and why?
Asking Sharma Ma'am about the fee waiver form, because it's a small, age-appropriate step while her parents handle the rest.
How does Papa see Himani's apology for costing so much?
It clearly pains him; he insists she doesn't cost anything, she's their daughter.
My teacher said winning the quiz is "a feather in your cap". Is that a gift?

No. It means an achievement you can be proud of.
Example: Getting the top rank in the district was a feather in her cap.

I sit two desks from Avni at the design studio, so I saw the whole thing. Avni asked Parul to take over the brochure layout because the client had moved the deadline. Parul said, "Sure, whatever works best for you," and gave a small tight smile. For the rest of the morning Parul's replies in the team chat were one word. She closed her laptop a bit too hard at lunch. I thought Avni hadn't noticed. After lunch, Avni pulled up a chair next to Parul's desk and said softly, "I think I may have missed something when I handed you the brochure. If it's annoying, I'd honestly rather you just tell me." Parul paused. Then she said it: she had already stayed late twice that week covering for others. Avni nodded, took back half the pages, and thanked her. By four, I heard Parul laughing at something Avni said. The chat messages got longer again.

What did Avni ask Parul to take over?
Avni asked Parul to take over the brochure layout because the client had moved the deadline.
What do Parul's one-word replies and the hard-closed laptop suggest she was feeling?
They suggest she was irritated and resentful, but didn't feel free to say so, so it leaked out in small ways.
Which step of Avni's worked, and why?
Avni gently said she might have missed something and invited a straight answer, which made it safe for Parul to name the real complaint.
How might Avni have felt sitting down beside Parul after lunch?
Avni may have felt uneasy and unsure, since inviting criticism risks hearing something hard, but hoped a direct answer would clear the air.
What do I serve for a simple lunch for my father's friends? There will be five elderly men.
Keep it light and easy to eat: soft rotis, dal, a mild vegetable, rice, curd and a small sweet. Avoid very spicy or hard foods. Serve warm and sit them comfortably.
My father's name is Mohan and he likes plain food.
Then keep Mohan's lunch simple, with little oil and mild spice. Make a plain dal, lauki sabzi, and soft phulkas. Offer pickle on the side so friends can choose.
Should I serve the food or let them help themselves?
For elderly guests, it is kinder to serve them at the table and refill the plates. Ask Mohan how his friends like it. Keep a jug of water and a glass for each person on the table.
What sweet can I offer that is soft?
Kheer or suji halwa is soft and warm and easy to eat. Serve a small bowl for each person. Mohan and his friends will enjoy it after the plain meal.

The water tanker came to the community garden only twice a week that summer, and the heat in Chennai had cracked the beds. Twelve families shared one tank.
Vidya, twenty-five, watched people drain it in a day. Some flooded their chillies; some came late and found nothing.
She had one evening before the next tanker. She drew a table on chart paper: each plot got two buckets, a morning slot, and a tick box. Elizabeth, from the next plot, agreed to check the tank level with her on alternate days. Anyone who took more would skip the next watering.
The first evening, Vidya carried exactly two buckets past everyone watching. By the second week, the tank lasted till the tanker came.

How often did the water tanker come to the garden?
It came only twice a week that summer.
What might Vidya have been worried about with only one evening before the next tanker?
She was probably anxious that without quick, clear rules the tank would be drained again and families would keep missing out.
What made the new plan work?
Each plot had a fair limit, checking was shared with Elizabeth, the consequence was agreed, and Vidya followed the limit first where people could see.
What is it like for a family who used to come late and find nothing?
They can now count on their two buckets, so they feel treated fairly instead of left out.

They had forty-eight hours to sign the lease on the Kochi flat, and Tanvir and Raghav still hadn't agreed on how to split anything. The broker kept calling. That evening the power went out in Raghav's building, so they sat on the stairs with a torch and a notebook. "I earn more," Raghav said. "I should pay more rent." Tanvir shook his head. "Then I'll feel like a guest." They tried another way: rent in proportion to income, a shared account for groceries and bills, each keeping their own savings. Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it; Tanvir took the laundry and the monthly paperwork. The harder question came last. "Your parents still think I'm your flatmate," Tanvir said quietly. Raghav was silent a while. "I'll tell them before we move. Together, if you'll come." Tanvir squeezed his hand. They signed the next morning.

Which chore did Raghav take on?
Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it.
Why did Tanvir refuse to let Raghav simply pay more rent?
Tanvir worried about feeling like a guest instead of an equal partner in their home.
What helped them reach a fair arrangement under pressure?
They tried a proportional split, a shared account for bills and separate savings, divided chores by preference, and faced the family question openly.
What would change if Raghav kept the relationship hidden from his parents?
Tanvir would likely keep feeling hurt and unseen in their shared life, and the secret could strain the partnership.

In their Pune flat, Eshaan, nearly two, would not let Zubin put him down. His cheeks were hot and his eyes glassy. He pushed his blocks away and wailed when a spoon fell. Zubin settled on the sofa with Eshaan on his chest, humming, and rang the clinic to ask what to watch for. He kept a close eye on him, just as the nurse described. "I've got you," he murmured, and Eshaan's fist loosened on his shirt.

What did Eshaan push away?
His blocks.
Why did Eshaan wail when a spoon fell?
He felt ill and miserable, so even a small thing upset him and he wanted to be held.
What did Zubin combine, and why does it matter?
Calm holding plus calling the clinic to ask what to watch for; comfort and careful checking both matter with a sick toddler.
What might the afternoon have been like for Zubin?
Tiring and a little worrying, but he stayed calm and kept Eshaan close.

At the hospital in Lucknow, Pranav led the operations team. Before each big change, he wrote a short entry in a register: the decision, the reasons, what could go wrong, and how sure the team was. When they moved the outpatient queue to a new token system, he wrote: "Should cut waiting by a lot. Seventy percent sure. Risk: older patients may struggle with tokens." A month later, waiting times had barely changed. At the review, some staff blamed Salma, who had designed the system. Pranav opened the register. "We expected risk with older patients. That's what happened. The design was sound; the help desk wasn't ready." Salma's shoulders dropped with relief. The team decided to add two volunteers at the token counter. Nobody was scolded. Everyone learned something.

What risk did Pranav write down before the token system?
Older patients may struggle with tokens.
How did Salma feel when Pranav opened the register?
Salma felt relieved, her shoulders dropping, because the record showed the problem was expected and not her fault.
What did the register allow the team to do?
It let them compare the decision with what happened, find the real gap at the help desk, and fix it without blaming anyone.
How might the staff who blamed Salma see the review afterward?
They might feel a little embarrassed, but also clearer about what really went wrong.
I bought a bunch of coriander and half of it is already wilting. Can I save it?
Often, yes. Trim the stems, put the bunch in a glass of cold water for twenty minutes and it can perk up. For the rest, chop and use it soon.
How do I keep the next bunch fresh?
Wrap the dry leaves in a paper towel and keep them in a box in the fridge. The towel soaks up extra moisture, which is what makes leaves go slimy.
I run 12 miles in 90 minutes. What is my average speed in miles per hour?

First convert 90 minutes to hours: 90 minutes / 60 minutes/hours = 1.5 hours.
In 1 hour, I run 12 miles / 1.5 hours = 8 miles/hour.
The answer is 8.

a) (3, 1) in y = x
b) (3, 1) in y = -x
c) (-2, 5) in y = x
d) (-2, 5) in y = -x
e) (4, -6) in y = x
f) (4, -6) in y = -x
g) (-1, -7) in y = x
h) (-1, -7) in y = -x
i) (5, 5) in y = x
j) (5, 5) in y = -x
k) (2, -2) in y = x
l) (2, -2) in y = -x
m) (0, 3) in y = x
n) (0, 3) in y = -x
o) (-8, 0) in y = x
p) (-8, 0) in y = -x
q) (6, 9) in y = x
r) (-4, -4) in y = -x
s) (7, -3) in y = -x
t) (-9, 2) in y = x

What does Ahab discover about the compasses, and what does he do?

Deliberately standing before the binnacle, and eyeing the transpointed compasses, the old man, with the sharp of his extended hand, now took the precise bearing of the sun, and satisfied that the needles were exactly inverted, shouted out his orders for the ship's course to be changed accordingly. The yards were hard up; and once more the Pequod thrust her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposed fair one had only been juggling her.

He sees that the needles point exactly the wrong way, takes the sun's bearing himself and orders the ship's course changed. The Pequod then heads into the wind again, since the fair wind was only a trick.

Aaron wants to purchase a guitar under a payment plan of $100.00 per month for 12 months.  His father has agreed to lend him the entire amount for the guitar, plus a one-time 10% interest fee for the entire loan.  With interest, how much money will Aaron owe his dad?

The guitar costs $100 every month for 12 months so it costs 100*12 = $1200
His dad is charging him 10% interest on the $1200 so interest comes to .10*1200 = $120.00
All total, Aaron will owe his father the price of the guitar, $1200 and the interest, $120 so 1200+120 = $1,320.00
The answer is 1320.

Four boys in one neighbourhood were each dared to do something risky that summer. Rishi stood on top of a high wall while the others jeered, "Jump, jump!" He pictured a broken leg on one side and a few minutes of teasing on the other. Jokes fade quickly, he decided, but a leg takes long to mend, and he climbed down. Manav was told to walk along the railway line. Before saying yes he asked himself what would happen if a train came round the bend, or if his foot slipped between the tracks. The answers were so clear that he did not need to argue. Dev was called a scaredy-cat, so he climbed the big tree beside the pond to prove otherwise. He ended up stuck on a branch, scraped and shaking, until an older girl helped him down. Kabir's friend fell off his bicycle during a stunt they had both joined. Kabir told his parents exactly what happened, helped his friend get home, and said quietly that next time he would say no early.

Where did Rishi stand while the others jeered?
Rishi stood on top of a high wall.
How does Dev's choice differ from Manav's, and what happened to each?
Dev accepted the dare to avoid being called scared and ended up stuck and scraped. Manav asked what could go wrong on the railway line, saw the danger and refused.
What was Dev feeling while he sat stuck on the branch?
Dev was probably frightened and embarrassed, since the dare he took to prove himself left him shaking and needing help.
What could Dev say the next time someone dares him?
He could say plainly that he does not want to, or suggest a safer game, and walk away if they keep pushing. Telling a trusted adult about the dare would also help. 🙂

Jackson and Brandon both invest $500 in the stock market. Jackson's investment quadruples in value, while Brandon's is reduced to 20% of the initial value. How much more money does Jackson have than Brandon now?

First find the end value of Jackson's investment: $500 * 4 = $2000
Then find the end value of Brandon's investment: 20% * $500 = $100
Then subtract the value of Brandon's investment from the value of Jackson's investment to find the difference: $2000 - $100 = $1900
The answer is 1900.

Sunday night
The community book fair is over and my first thought on the walk home was: total failure. Forty people came instead of the two hundred we hoped for. The children's corner ran out of chairs. It rained at four.
Then I caught myself. "Total" is a big word. Alka always asks me to score things out of ten, so I sat down with tea and did it.
Honest score: five out of ten.
What worked: the storytelling hour was full. We sold ninety books. Three new volunteers signed up. The old librarian cried when a girl asked for poetry.
What didn't: posters went up too late. No shelter plan for rain. Too few chairs.
Next time: posters two weeks earlier, a tarpaulin, borrow chairs from the temple hall.
Five out of ten doesn't feel like failure. It feels like a first try.
Francis

How many people came to the book fair?
Forty people came instead of the two hundred they hoped for.
How did Francis feel on the walk home, and what changed that feeling?
Francis felt deflated and sure it was a total failure, then calmer after scoring it out of ten and listing what worked.
Which of Francis's next-time ideas is the most practical first step?
Putting posters up two weeks earlier, since late posters probably explain much of the low turnout.
How might Alka react to the five-out-of-ten list?
Alka would likely feel pleased that the scoring habit helped, and could add ideas to the list for the next fair.
Alyssa and Chelsea jointly bought 40 candles to decorate their room. Alyssa used half of them, and Chelsea used 70% of the remaining candles. How many candles are there in the room now?

Alyssa used half of the candles, which is 1/2*40 = 20 candles
The number of candles that remained is 40-20 = 20
Chelsea used 70% of the remaining candles, a total of 70/100*20 = 14 candles.
The total number of candles in the room now is 40 - 20-14 = 6
The answer is 6.

I'm Shalini, and for a year I told myself that asking for a raise was greedy. My parents raised me to be grateful for any job. So I stayed quiet, and grew quietly bitter every time I saw my friends' salaries.
Last October I finally made a list. What editors at my level were paid, from two job portals and three friends. What I'd done: the two books I rescued from deadline disasters, the new freelancer system I set up.
I booked a meeting with Naveen, the publisher. My voice wobbled at the start. But I said it: "I'd like my pay reviewed, and here's why."
He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Not this quarter. Maybe in April."
It stung. But he didn't say no because I was greedy. He said no because of money. In April, I asked again. That time, he said yes.

When did Shalini finally make a list?
Last October.
How did Shalini feel about asking before making the list?
Shalini felt greedy and afraid to ask, and grew quietly bitter comparing with friends' salaries.
What did Shalini do that turned silent resentment into action?
Shalini researched pay, listed concrete achievements, asked Naveen calmly, and asked again in April after the first no.
How might Naveen have felt about Shalini's request?
Naveen probably respected the preparation, and his quiet pause suggests he took it seriously even though the budget forced a delay.

"So basically the relationship failed due to three factors," Avni said, counting on her fingers. "Incompatible long-term goals, poor communication patterns, and the stress of distance."
"Okay," said Dilnaz.
"It's actually a classic case. I read a paper on it."
"Mm."
"Statistically, most long-distance relationships at our age end within a year."
"Avni."
"And the timing was ideal, honestly, before placements..."
"Avni. You were with him for three years."
"...Yes."
"You haven't said one sad thing."
"I'm processing."
"You're lecturing. Processing is when you cry on my bed."
Avni laughed, and the laugh broke in the middle. Dilnaz passed her a cushion.

How long was Avni with him?
Three years.
What does Avni's breaking laugh suggest?
That the sadness she has been holding back is surfacing; the lecture was a wall against feeling it.
How did Dilnaz help Avni?
Dilnaz gently interrupted the analysis, pointed out that Avni hadn't said one sad thing, and made room for real feelings.
How might Dilnaz feel listening to the three factors?
Patient but concerned, sensing that Avni was avoiding the hurt.

Alka, you know how I said I could tell a good mango by its smell? Well. Santosh the mango expert tried it at the market last week. Picked six, all "perfect". Four were sour. Meanwhile the old fruit seller next to me picked one without even sniffing properly, and it was the sweetest thing I've ever tasted. I asked her how. She said, "Forty summers, beta. Every mango I pick, I taste by evening. If I'm wrong, I know by evening." That's the thing. My nose has smelled maybe twenty mangoes and never checked. Hers has checked thousands. So now I'm doing it her way: guess, taste, remember. Ask me again in forty summers.

How many of Santosh's six mangoes were sour?
Four.
How did Santosh feel about the mango-smelling skill before the market trip?
Santosh felt proud and sure of it, and was then surprised and humbled when four of the six turned out sour.
What is Santosh doing now to build a trustworthy gut?
Guess, taste, remember: getting quick, honest feedback on every pick, the way the fruit seller does.
How does the fruit seller see her own skill?
She sees it as the result of forty summers of picking and checking by evening, not as a gift.

"Anjali, you remember when you kept joking about my mum's accent? Okay, don't make that face, I'm not angry anymore. I'm Arohi, and I want to tell you why I said something.
At first I laughed with you. But every time, I felt a little knot in my stomach. My mum learned English at thirty. She's proud of it.
So that day at the bus stop, when you did the voice again, I just said, 'That one's not okay for me. Can we not?' And I changed the subject to the cricket match.
You went quiet. Then you said, 'Oh. Sorry, I didn't think.' And you never did it again.
I'm telling you because it worked. I'd been scared you'd call me dramatic. But you didn't. You just adjusted. That's how I knew you were a good friend."

At what age did Arohi's mum learn English?
At thirty.
What was Arohi feeling each time Anjali joked?
Arohi felt a little knot in the stomach, hurt on behalf of a mum who is proud of her English.
What made Arohi's approach effective?
Saying calmly, once, 'That one's not okay for me' and then changing the subject, which let Anjali adjust without a fight.
How did Anjali respond when Arohi said stop?
Anjali went quiet, apologised, and never did it again.

Marek, ten, had heard his older cousin say that the new families from South America at the edge of Krakow were loud and rough. So when Ms Nowak paired him with Santiago for the spaghetti-bridge project, Marek groaned inside. The first afternoon they barely spoke. On the second, their bridge collapsed, and Santiago laughed so hard that Marek laughed too. Santiago was good at triangles. Marek was good at glue. By Friday their bridge held three dictionaries, the most in the class. Walking out, Santiago invited Marek to his cousin's birthday. Marek thought about his own cousin's words and couldn't match them to the boy beside him, who liked the same comics and hated beetroot too.

How many dictionaries did their bridge hold?
Three dictionaries, the most in the class.
What was Marek feeling when Ms Nowak paired him with Santiago?
He groaned inside, uneasy because of what his cousin had said about the new families.
What in the project helped Marek let go of his cousin's words?
Working together on the bridge, laughing when it fell and using each other's skills, gave him real knowledge of Santiago to set against the rumour.
How might Santiago have seen that first quiet afternoon?
Santiago may have noticed Marek's distance and felt unsure, yet still laughed and later invited Marek to a birthday.

Friday, the second week after the summer holidays. It rained all day.
Dear diary, the new girl Disha is still bossy. On the first day she said my shoes were muddy and I should sit somewhere else. I told everybody she's bossy.
Today she lent me her umbrella when mine blew inside out. Yesterday she explained fractions to the boy who sits behind me. On Tuesday she shared her lunch with a girl who forgot her tiffin.
But she's still bossy. I decided on the first day.
Hmm. Amma asked what bossy thing Disha did this week. I couldn't think of one. Only the shoes thing, and that was two weeks ago. Maybe the shoes thing was first-day nerves. Maybe I'm the one who's stuck.
Santosh

What did Disha lend on Friday?
Disha lent her umbrella when Santosh's blew inside out.
Why does Santosh still think Disha is bossy?
Santosh felt stung by the first-day comment about muddy shoes, and that early feeling stuck even as later kind acts piled up.
What question from Amma helped, and what could Santosh do next?
Asking what bossy thing Disha did this week showed there was none; Santosh could now tell friends about the umbrella and the lunch too.
How might Disha feel if she knew she was still called bossy?
Disha might feel hurt and puzzled, having been kind all week after one nervous first-day remark.

I'm Nitin, and I sit next to Hafsa at the design studio, so I see more than I'm meant to. Her ex-boyfriend Imran turned up at reception again on Thursday with flowers and the same line: he'd forgiven her for making him angry. Last year he shouted at her in the parking lot until security walked over. I watched Hafsa go down and speak to him for maybe a minute, calm, not smiling. She came back up without the flowers. 'I've forgiven him,' she told me, pouring water. 'I'm not angry every day anymore. But he still thinks it was my fault. So no coffee, no calls.' Then she asked reception to ring her before letting him up next time. I don't know what she felt inside. Her hands were steady, though, and she finished the logo draft before lunch.

What did Hafsa ask reception to do?
To ring her before letting him up next time.
What does Hafsa's remark that Imran still thinks it was her fault show about her thinking?
It shows she noticed he has no real remorse, so she has decided that forgiving him does not mean letting him close again.
Why is keeping distance a wise choice for Hafsa at this stage?
Imran shouted at her before and still blames her, so staying away protects her safety while she lets go of the daily anger.
How does Nitin see Hafsa's handling of Thursday's visit?
Nitin sees calm, steady behaviour but admits not knowing what Hafsa felt inside; the steady hands and finished draft are the only clues.
Say something about Saturn in one sentence of exactly nine words.
Saturn is famous for the bright rings around it.
Why does a person who is told they are talented sometimes stop trying hard?
They may begin to believe the skill is fixed. Because they fear that a failure would prove the praise wrong, they avoid hard tasks instead of practising.

In the village school, Keerthana Madam had shown the class how to add fractions three times, and Zubin still did not get it. He watched her draw the same pie on the board a fourth time, chalk dust on her blue sari, her voice as calm as the first time.
Suddenly he saw it. She could have shouted, and she never did. She had stayed after the bell most days to help slow ones like him, and her sandals were grey with the walk from the next village.
After class he stayed behind. "Madam, thank you for showing us again," he said. "I know you're tired."
She blinked, then smiled. "Come, one more pie." This time it made sense.

How many times had Keerthana Madam shown the class how to add fractions before the fourth pie?
Three times.
What did Zubin realise about Keerthana as he watched her draw the pie a fourth time?
That she could have shouted but stayed calm and patient, and that she gave her time to slow learners, so he felt grateful.
What did Zubin do after class that made his gratitude real?
He stayed behind and thanked Keerthana Madam for showing them again, saying he knew she was tired.
How might Keerthana Madam feel when Zubin thanks her?
Surprised and touched. She blinks, smiles and offers one more pie.

Eight months after the report, the inquiry was still going on, and Kunal's new job paid a third less than the old one. On Saturday the rain came in through the window frame of his rented room, and he had just enough left this month for rent and not much else.
Samir turned up at seven with a steel tiffin of rajma chawal and two umbrellas. 'Your mother said you'd skip dinner,' he said.
They ate on the floor, away from the leak. Kunal's phone buzzed: a message from a former colleague. 'They've fixed the brake checks on the buses. Thought you'd want to know.'
He read it three times. He was tired, down to his bones. But under the tiredness was something solid.
'Worth it?' Samir asked.
'Ask me next year,' Kunal said, smiling. 'But yes.'

What did Samir bring?
Samir brought a steel tiffin of rajma chawal and two umbrellas.
What does Kunal feel after reading the message three times?
He feels deep tiredness but also a solid pride and quiet vindication that the brake checks were fixed.
What helps sustain Kunal through the long aftermath?
Friends like Samir turning up with food, his mother keeping an eye on him, and knowing his action made the buses safer.
What might Samir be feeling as he asks 'Worth it?'
Samir is likely proud of his friend but worried about his money and tiredness, wanting to hear how he really is.

How does the man behave in the boat, and how does he take advice?

He put his pipe back in his mouth with an undisturbed expression of face, and sat as composed and contented as if we were already out of England. Yet he was as submissive to a word of advice as if he had been in constant terror; for, when we ran ashore to get some bottles of beer into the boat, and he was stepping out, I hinted that I thought he would be safest where he was, and he said. "Do you, dear boy?" and quietly sat down again.
He stays calm and contented, as if they were already out of England. Yet he takes advice at once: when told he would be safest where he was, he quietly sat down again.

Mohit, your mother says you kept repeating one joke at dinner. Let me tell you about me. I'm Aparna, and at nine I found a burp joke I thought was the funniest thing in the world. I told it to my class, my cousins, the milkman and my Nani, ten times in one day.
By the sixth, my cousin Rashi groaned, "We know!" I didn't stop. By the ninth, the milkman only nodded politely. But my Nani said, "It works better if you wait. Let them ask for it."
Next morning I waited until Rashi was bored and said, "Want to hear something gross?" She said yes. That was when I understood timing and audience.

How many times did Aparna tell the joke on the first day?
Aparna told the joke ten times in one day.
What was Aparna feeling as she kept telling the joke even after Rashi groaned?
Aparna was excited and amused by her own joke, so pleased with it that Aparna could not stop even when others were bored.
What turning point in the story changed how Aparna told the joke?
Nani told Aparna it works better to wait and let people ask for it. Aparna then waited until Rashi was bored and asked if she wanted to hear something gross.
What did the groans and polite nods tell Rashi and the milkman about how they felt about the joke?
They showed Rashi was tired of hearing it, and the milkman was being polite. The groans were honest feedback that the joke had been repeated too often.

I'm Ganga. I sit two desks from Salma at the accounts office, and I've watched her do something I didn't know was possible. When Mohan said he was leaving early for physio, Salma said, just as easily, "I'm off at five too, therapy day." No drama. When Hemant pushed, "Therapy for what?", she smiled and said, "That's mine to keep, but it helps." I think it cost her something, though I can't be sure. Last month our new trainee, Varsha, cried in the washroom after a bad review. Salma didn't say "poor thing". She sat down beside her and said, "Rough day. Want some water? If it keeps feeling heavy, our company counsellor is good." Since then, two people have mentioned their own counselling at lunch as if it were a dentist visit. I don't know if Salma planned that. I just know the room feels different.

In total, the two friends made $2000+$1400 = $3400
The answer is 3400.

Madison makes 30 paper boats and sets them afloat. 20% are eaten by fish and Madison shoots two of the others with flaming arrows. How many boats are left?

First find the number of boats eaten by fish: 30 boats * 20% = 6 boats

Noor, you asked why I always stop when someone falls on the road. Let me tell you. I'm your Nilesh chacha, and this is from Delhi, when I was twenty-five.

And you know what I did? I looked at everyone else. Nobody moved, so I thought, must be nothing, maybe he's drunk. Everybody was thinking the same thing, looking at each other.

Thursday night.
Today in the lab Kunal put his bag on the empty stool and said, loud enough, "Not for you, Saurabh. Your lot clean drains, go stand over there." Two others laughed. I stood by the sink for the whole practical. My face was burning and my hands were cold. Dad has fixed the school's pipes for years. I am proud of him, and I still wanted to disappear.
Jeevan saw everything. After the bell, Jeevan walked with me straight to Mrs. Pillai's desk and said, "Ma'am, something happened in the lab that you need to hear." She listened to all of it, wrote it down and said, "I believe you. This is about what they said, not about you." She phoned Kunal's parents before the last period and is changing the seating plan from tomorrow.

Jimmy is at the candy store and buys 2 candy bars for $.75 each. He then buys 4 lollipops that cost $.25 each. He spent 1/6 of the money he earned from shoveling snow. If he charges $1.5 per driveway, how many driveways did he shovel?

Jimmy spent $1.5 on candy bars because 2 x .75 = 1.5
He spent $1 on lollipops because 4 x .25 = 1
He spent $2.5 in total because 1.5 + 1 = 2.5
He earned $15 shoveling driveways because 2.5 / (1/6) = 15
He shoveled 10 driveways because 15 / 1.5 = 10
The answer is 10.

Dear Madhav bhaiya,

You asked on the phone why I sound tired. I'll write it, because saying it aloud is hard.

It's about Priyanka. For a year now, every day there's something. The way I load the dishwasher. The way I talk to her parents. The way I breathe while sleeping. Last week she said, "You're useless at everything." I've started believing I can't do anything right.

I've been trying something. When she criticises, I ask: is any of it fair? Sometimes it is. I do forget the bills. So I ask her, "What specifically would you like me to do?" That helps.

But when she says I'm useless, or a bad person, I've started saying calmly, "I won't accept that. Tell me what you need instead."

I think we need a counsellor. Could you help me find one?

Vijay

What did Priyanka say last week?
She said, "You're useless at everything."
How has Vijay been feeling after a year of criticism?
Vijay feels tired and worn down, starting to believe nothing Vijay does is right.
What strategy is Vijay using with the criticism?
Vijay checks whether a point is fair, asks for specific requests, and calmly refuses blanket attacks on character.
How might Madhav bhaiya feel reading the letter?

Karen's students are about to take a standardized test. Karen gets a $500 bonus if their average score is above 75, plus an extra $10 bonus for every additional point the average score increases above 75. So far, Karen has graded 8 tests, and the average is 70. Given that each student can have a maximum score of 150, what combined score do the last two tests need to have for Karen to earn a $600 bonus?

First subtract $500 from Karen's goal bonus amount to find how much she makes from the extra $10/point bonus: $600 - $500 = $100
Then divide the extra bonus by the extra rate: $100 / $10/point = 10 points
Then add the 10 extra points to the baseline 75 point goal to find the students' average test score: 10 points + 75 points = 85 points
Then added the 8 graded tests to the 2 ungraded tests to find the total number of tests: 2 tests + 8 tests = 10 tests
Then multiply the 85 point average by the number of tests to find the total number of points the students need to earn: 85 points/test * 10 tests = 850 points
Then multiply the current average by the current number of graded tests to find how many points have been earned so far: 70 points/test * 8 tests = 560 points
Then subtract the number of points earned from the number of points needed to find the combine score the last two tests need: 850 points - 560 points = 290 points
The answer is 290.

Then we changed the plan. No more full attempts on the blue problem this week. Only the heel-hook move, practised on the low traverse wall, five tries, then rest. He agreed to come Tuesday.

Chinmay, you asked why I never let anyone joke about diets at this table. Sit, I'll tell you. When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, I cut photos of thin actresses out of magazines and pasted them inside my cupboard door. At weddings I would eat nothing, then everything, then feel like a stranger was living in my head. One evening my Bua found the diary. I was so ashamed I cried. She didn't scold. She said, 'Usha, this is bigger than you. Let's go to Dr Mehta together.' We went that same week. It took time, and help, but I got better. A football team shares a single water cooler during practice.  During practice, linemen get the first water break and will drink 8 ounces each.  Skill position players get the second water break and drink 6 ounces each.  The team has 12 linemen and 10 skill position players.  If the cooler holds 126 ounces of water, how many skill position players must wait for the cooler to be refilled before they can get a drink?

The 12 linemen go first and will drink a total of 12*8 = 96 ounces of water from the cooler.
This will leave 126 - 96 = 30 ounces for the skill position players.
Then, the 30 ounces of water that remains is enough for 30/6 = 5 of the skill position players.
Therefore, 10 - 5 = 5 skill position players must wait for the cooler to be refilled before they can get a drink.
The answer is 5.
Is porcelain just another name for china?

Mostly. Porcelain is a hard, thin, white ceramic material used for cups, plates and ornaments. China is another name for it. It is a noun.
Example: My grandmother keeps her porcelain tea set in a glass cupboard.
I want to edit a short video of my trip, but I've never done it before.
Sounds fun. Do you have an editing app on your phone?
Yes, it came with it.
Start by choosing your best clips and trimming each to a few seconds. Put them in order, add a simple title and a soft music track, and keep the whole video short.
How long should the video be?
About one to two minutes is nice for a trip. Shorter videos are easier to finish, and people enjoy watching them to the end.
I'll try it this evening.
Save your project often, so you don't lose your work if the phone shuts down.
I finished it. How do I share it with my family?
Export it to your phone's gallery, then send it through a chat or share a link. If the file is big, a family member can copy it onto a pen drive.
