At the sports club's annual trip, a few older boys went behind the bus at the rest stop. Zubin followed out of curiosity. One of them held out a vape. "Try it, it's just flavour." Zubin hesitated. His coach had talked about how it can hook people quickly and hurt breathing. His teammate Jahnavi came around the bus just then, looking for him. Zubin said, loud enough, "Nah, I've got the match tomorrow. I need my lungs." The older boy shrugged. "Your loss." Jahnavi said, "Come on, the bus is leaving." Back on the bus, Zubin's heart was still racing. "Did I sound stupid?" he asked. Jahnavi grinned. "You sounded like someone who wants to win."

What reason did Zubin give for saying no?
He said he had a match tomorrow and needed his lungs.
Why was Zubin's heart still racing on the bus?
He was nervous about refusing older boys and worried he had sounded stupid, even though he stood firm.
What made Zubin's refusal effective?
He gave a short, confident reason tied to something he cared about, and Jahnavi gave him an easy way to leave.
How might the older boy see Zubin's no?
He shrugged it off, which suggests a clear, calm refusal didn't cause a big fight or make Zubin a target.
Kim has 4 dozen shirts.  She lets her sister have 1/3 of them.  How many shirts does she have left?

She had 4*12=48 shirts to start with
She gives away 48/3=16
So she has 48-16=32 left
The answer is 32.

Ravi can jump higher than anyone in the class. In fact, he can jump 1.5 times higher than the average jump of the three next highest jumpers. If the three next highest jumpers can jump 23 inches, 27 inches, and 28 inches, how high can Ravi jump?

The total height the next three highest can jump is 78 inches because 23 + 27 + 28 = 78
The average height they can jump is 26 inches because 78 / 3 = 26
Ravi can jump 39 inches high because 26 x 1.5 = 39
The answer is 39.

Read this:

The sweet shop in the market of Chaitanya's small town had just got a new glass counter, and his uncle Ujjwal said he could pick anything for passing his exams. There were jalebis, peda, barfi of four colours, rasgulla, laddoos, kalakand and something shiny with silver on top.

Chaitanya walked up and down the counter twice. The shopkeeper waited, smiling at first, then tapping the glass. Finally Chaitanya pointed at the kaju barfi.

On the walk home he kept looking back at the shop. "Ujjwal chacha, maybe the kalakand was better. Or the laddoo."

Ujjwal laughed. "Last year there were only three kinds and you ate your peda in two bites."

Chaitanya licked his fingers slowly, not sure the barfi had been right.

Which sweet did Chaitanya finally point at?
He pointed at the kaju barfi.
Why does Chaitanya keep looking back at the shop on the way home?
He feels unsure and a bit disappointed, wondering if the kalakand or laddoo would have been better.
What could Ujjwal chacha try next time to make the treat more fun for Chaitanya?
He could offer a choice of just two or three sweets, like last year, so Chaitanya can pick quickly and enjoy it.
How does Ujjwal see Chaitanya's doubts?
He finds them a little funny and notices that Chaitanya was happier last year when there were only three kinds.
Fix: "Yesterday I buy a new jacket." And why do woollen clothes keep us warm?

1. "Yesterday I bought a new jacket." Why: past tense ("Yesterday" -> "bought").
2. Wool traps air between its fibres, and that warm air stays close to your body.
What caused the traffic jam on the highway this morning?
I can't check what happened on the road this morning, so I don't know. A local traffic or news page may explain it.

Read this:

I'm Tarun, and I live two doors down from Divyansh in the relief camp at the district school. After the floods, when we'd all got here safely, I expected him to go back and try rescuing people himself. He's that kind.
Instead, on the second morning, he walked over to the volunteer desk set up by the municipal officials and signed a register. They gave him an armband and a list: twelve houses on higher ground where old people were still living alone.
For four days I watched him leave each morning with two other volunteers and a sack of food packets from the government store. They went by the route the officials had marked. Each evening he gave his list back with notes: who needed medicines, who wanted to come to the camp.
On the fifth day an old woman from one of those houses arrived at the camp, holding his arm. I can't say what he felt, but he looked very tired and very steady.

How many houses were on Divyansh's volunteer list?
There were twelve houses on higher ground where old people lived alone.
What might Divyansh have been feeling when he chose the volunteer desk instead of rescuing alone?
He may have felt a strong urge to help mixed with caution, choosing the organised route over a risky solo effort.
Why was working through the volunteer desk wiser than going out alone?
The officials knew the safe routes and which houses needed help, so Divyansh could help more people without becoming someone who needed rescuing.
How might the old woman who came to the camp feel about Divyansh's visits?
She would likely feel grateful and safe, trusting him enough to hold his arm on the way to the camp.

'Why do you look like that?' Pallavi asked, sliding into the canteen seat opposite Vijay.
'Compliance emailed me. About the expense claims from the Chennai trip.'
'Your claims?'
'No. Sir's. He gave me a stack of taxi bills and said, "Approve these under your login, I'm too busy." I approved them.'
'Did you check them?'
'He's a vice-president, Pallavi. Twenty years here. I thought, he wouldn't ask for something wrong.' Vijay rubbed his face. 'Three of the bills are for days he wasn't even in Chennai.'
'And it's your login on the approvals.'
'That's what compliance said. "The approver is responsible for checking." I have a meeting with them at four.'
Pallavi was quiet for a moment. 'Tell them exactly what happened. What he said, when he said it. Don't guess, don't cover.'
'I know.' He stared at his tea. 'I just wish I'd asked one question before I clicked.'

What did the vice-president ask Vijay to do?
Approve the taxi bills under Vijay's login.
What is Vijay feeling as he stares at his tea?
Regretful and anxious, wishing he had asked one question before approving, with the compliance meeting ahead.
What one question could Vijay have asked before approving?
Whether the bills matched the actual trip dates, or whether his login should be approving someone else's claims at all.
How does Pallavi see what happened?
Pallavi is concerned but steady, urging Vijay to tell compliance exactly what happened without guessing or covering.

When Siddharth joined our class in Class 9, he didn't speak for a month. I'm Damini, and I sat next to him in chemistry. I didn't push. I'd say, 'We're getting chaat after school, come if you want,' and leave it there. Some days he came and just ate, listening. Once, during group work, he slid me a note: 'Can you present our part? I'll do the slides.' So I did, and I said clearly, 'Siddharth made these slides.' He went pink but didn't look unhappy. Then in December he told me he'd stopped going to his cousin's house because even family dinners made his chest tight, and he hadn't slept properly in weeks. That's when I said, as gently as I could, 'I think a counsellor could help with that. Want me to walk you there?' He went the next Monday.

What did Siddharth write in the note?
'Can you present our part? I'll do the slides.'
What might Siddharth have felt when Damini credited his slides?
He likely felt embarrassed but pleased, going pink without looking unhappy.
When did Damini suggest a counsellor, and why then?
When Siddharth said the fear was stopping family dinners and sleep, because that meant it was affecting normal life and needed professional help.
What might Damini's no-pressure invitations have meant to Siddharth?
They let him join on his own terms, sometimes just listening, so he felt included without being forced to perform.

After Chacha's housewarming, Saurabh, nine, sat on the stairs with his sketchbook. All evening the relatives had called his uncle "Sir", asked about his promotion and fussed over his tea. When Saurabh's father came in, still in his guard's uniform from the night shift, only two people said hello. Saurabh drew nothing.
At home Mummy asked, "What's wrong?"
"Everybody likes Chacha's job more."
Madhuri sat on the step beside him. "Every night your father opens the gate for two hundred families and knows each child by name. Ask him tomorrow who forgot their keys."
Next morning Saurabh asked. His father laughed and listed six names, each with a story.

Who did the relatives call 'Sir' at the housewarming?
They called Saurabh's uncle 'Sir'.
What was Saurabh feeling as he sat on the stairs without drawing?
He felt hurt and let down on his father's behalf, shown by 'Everybody likes Chacha's job more.'
What did Madhuri do that helped Saurabh see his father's work differently?
She told him what his father does each night and sent him to ask about the families, so the job became people and stories instead of a lower rank.
How might Saurabh's father have felt when only two people greeted him at the housewarming?
He may have felt tired and overlooked after the night shift, though he laughed and told stories readily when Saurabh asked about his work.

At the Sunday cricket camp in the Ludhiana stadium, Gurpreet and Amandeep had spent twenty minutes arguing over who would captain the practice match. Coach Baljit blew his whistle. "No match until you two sort it out." They glared at each other by the boundary rope. Then Amandeep said, "Okay. What if you're captain today, I'm captain next Sunday, and we keep swapping?" Gurpreet thought. "And whoever isn't captain opens the batting." "Deal." They wrote it in the back of the coach's register: G, A, G, A. The match started ten minutes later. The next Sunday, nobody argued at all.

Where did they write the plan?
In the back of the coach's register: G, A, G, A.
What might Gurpreet have felt when Amandeep suggested swapping?
He probably felt relieved and fairly treated, and added his own idea about opening the batting.
Why is swapping a better fix than one boy giving in?
It treats both fairly every week, so neither feels he lost, and the same quarrel doesn't come back next Sunday.
How does Coach Baljit see the problem?
Coach Baljit sees twenty minutes lost to arguing and insists they sort it out themselves before any match.

In Lagos, the pothole at the corner of Emeka's street had been there so long that children named it "the Lake." Emeka, twenty-six, had written to the local council once, years ago, and heard nothing. Now he just drove around it and said, "This is Nigeria. Nothing changes."
His neighbour Vera, a nurse, had different ideas. She set up a street group chat, collected photos from twenty households, and sent a joint letter every two weeks to the council, copying a local radio station.
Emeka rolled his eyes but added his photo.
Three months later, the radio station read the letter on air. The next week, a council truck arrived with gravel and tar.
Emeka stood on the new surface, stamping his foot. Vera laughed. "Still think nothing changes?"
"Something changed," he admitted. "Next letter, I'll write it."

What did the children name the pothole?
The children named it "the Lake."
What was Emeka feeling when he said "Nothing changes"?
Emeka felt tired, hopeless and cynical after writing once years ago and hearing nothing.
What did Vera do that changed the outcome?
She gathered photos from many households, sent regular joint letters and copied a radio station, turning single complaints into shared pressure.
How might Vera feel when Emeka offers to write the next letter?
Vera would likely feel pleased and encouraged that his cynicism has softened into action.

In March, Javier posted a photo of the office iftar in Madrid with the caption: "Proud to work somewhere that celebrates everyone!" It got two hundred likes. He liked that. The next week, Siddiq asked quietly whether the Thursday team lunch meeting could move to the morning for the rest of Ramadan, since three of them were fasting. Javier frowned. The lunch was his favourite part of the week, and the restaurant was booked. "Can't you just sit with us and not eat? It's only a month." Siddiq said, "I could. But you posted about celebrating everyone." Javier felt heat in his face. "That's not fair. I've been really supportive." Siddiq shrugged and went back to his desk. Javier opened his phone, looked at the two hundred likes, and for the first time they felt a little empty.

How many likes did Javier's post get?
Two hundred.
How did Javier feel when Siddiq mentioned the post?
He felt embarrassed and defensive, his face hot, insisting he had been supportive instead of listening.
What would real support from Javier look like now?
Listening to Siddiq, moving the meeting to the morning for Ramadan even though it costs him the lunch, and accepting the correction without sulking.
What might Siddiq have felt when Javier said "It's only a month"?
Siddiq probably felt let down and unheard, since the public support disappeared as soon as it cost Javier something.

Mentor's note, career guidance session, 5 October.
Mehak came in to talk about her six-month internship at the design studio, which ended in September. She said it was "a total waste" and she never wants to work in design again. When I asked why, she described only the last week: a heated argument with her supervisor, Tushar, over a missed deadline, and leaving without a reference.
I asked her to walk me through month by month. Month one, she led her first client presentation. Month three, her logo was chosen for a national campaign. Month five, Tushar praised her in front of the whole team. She paused. "Those were the best months of my life," she said, surprised.
Next step: she will write to Tushar to close the internship properly and ask for a fair reference.

How long was Mehak's internship?
Six months.
What was Mehak feeling when she called the internship a total waste?
She felt angry and hurt about the last-week argument, which had overwritten the good months.
What is Mehak's next step, and why is it helpful?
Writing to Tushar to close the internship properly and ask for a fair reference, so the ending doesn't erase six good months.
How might Tushar see the internship?
Tushar may see it as mostly strong, since he praised her in front of the team, with one bad week at the end.

Thomas, when I was sixteen, I failed my pre-board maths exam. Everyone expected me to cry, and I didn't. I told my friends, "Studies are a scam, I don't care." I started coming late, sitting at the back, yawning loudly in class. Teachers thought I'd become lazy. The truth was, I was terrified that if I tried hard and failed again, it would prove I was stupid. Not trying felt safer. It was my cousin who saw through it. She said, "Wasim, you're not bored. You're scared." I was so angry with her. But she was right. I started tuition with her the next week, and I passed.

Which exam did young Wasim fail?
The pre-board maths exam.
Why did young Wasim pretend studies didn't matter?
Wasim was terrified that trying and failing again would prove he was stupid, so acting like he didn't care felt safer.
What made his cousin's words effective, even though they angered Wasim?
She named the fear behind the act, which let Wasim face the real problem and get help.
How might Wasim's teachers have seen him differently if they had known?
They might have offered encouragement and support instead of seeing him as lazy.

Monday: At the park, Arnab ran toward a spotted dog. Vishal, his father, called, “Ask the owner first.” Arnab asked. The lady said, “Yes, gently.” He patted it.
Wednesday: A man on the bench held out a toffee to Arnab. Arnab looked at Vishal. “Can I?” “No, thank you. We don't take sweets from people we don't know.” Arnab told the man, “No, thank you.”
Friday: Nani arrived for the weekend. Arnab ran straight into her arms. “I don't need to ask for Nani,” he said. Vishal laughed. “No. Nani hugs are always allowed.”

What colour was the dog Arnab patted?
It was a spotted dog.
What was Arnab thinking when he looked at Vishal before taking the toffee?
He was unsure whether it was allowed and wanted his father's guidance, showing he had started to trust the rule of asking.
Why did explaining the reason help Arnab?
A simple reason, like not taking sweets from people we don't know, helps him understand the rule rather than just obey.
How might Nani feel when Arnab runs into her arms without asking?
She'd likely feel loved and happy, since hugs with her are always allowed.
Add the first 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 odd numbers. What do you notice? Find 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 29 and the number of non-square numbers between 12^2 and 13^2.

Answer: The sums are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25: the squares. 1 + 3 + ... + 29 = 15^2 = 225. Between 144 and 169 there are 2 x 12 = 24 non-squares.

Picture: a square of dots grows by adding an L-shaped border. From a 3 x 3 square (9 dots) to 4 x 4 (16 dots) we add 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 dots, the 4th odd number. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2. The odd numbers up to 29 are 1, 3, ..., 29: there are (29 + 1)/2 = 15 of them, so the sum is 15^2 = 225. In the same way (n + 1)^2 - n^2 = 2n + 1: 13^2 - 12^2 = 25 = 2 x 12 + 1. The numbers strictly between 12^2 and 13^2 are 145 to 168: that is 25 - 1 = 24 = 2 x 12 numbers, none of them squares.

On Sunday in the church in Accra, Kwame carried Elif, two, into the cool hall. The choir began to sing; candles flickered at the front.

Elif stopped wriggling. She stared at the flames, then at the singers, her eyes wide.

Kwame whispered, "Beautiful, isn't it?" and swayed gently with the music.

When everyone stood, Elif clapped softly, copying the lady beside them. Kwame smiled and let her.

What flickered at the front of the church?
Candles flickered at the front.
What was Elif feeling as she stared at the flames and singers?
Elif felt wonder and fascination, calmed by the music and candlelight.
How did Kwame help Elif experience the service?
Kwame let her watch quietly, shared the moment in a whisper and allowed her to join gently by clapping.
How might the lady beside them feel seeing Elif copy her?
The lady might feel amused and warm, glad the toddler is joining in.

Anirban, sit, you look like the sky fell on you. You forgot the load-test steps in front of the client, yes? Listen to your old Rashmi didi. When I was twenty-four, at the textile testing lab in Surat, I forgot how to calibrate the colour machine. I had done it every day in training, then not once for two months. My hands just stopped. I wanted the floor to swallow me. But I had a small green notebook in my apron. Every Monday I read one page of it, and once a month I redid the rare jobs from it. So I opened the notebook, followed my own steps, and finished. The lab head only said, "Good, you wrote it down." That night I stopped calling myself careless. The mind drops what it does not use. You just leave a trail back.

Where did Rashmi work when she forgot how to calibrate the colour machine?
She worked at the textile testing lab in Surat.
What was Rashmi feeling when her hands stopped at the colour machine?
She felt ashamed and panicked, wanting the floor to swallow her, because she had done the job every day in training and expected it to stay.
Which choice in the story turned the moment around?
Rashmi opened her green notebook and followed her own written steps instead of guessing, which worked because she had kept reviewing it on Mondays.
How might the lab head have seen Rashmi's slip?
The lab head seems to see it as ordinary, not as failure; writing it down mattered more than remembering it perfectly.

Under standard growth conditions, the bacterial strain, E.coli, has a doubling time of 20 minutes.   If 1 single bacterial cell is used to start a culture grown under standard growth conditions, how many bacterial cells will there be after the culture is grown for 4 hours?

4 hours is 4*60=240 minutes.
If the doubling time is 20 minutes, then after 240 minutes, the number of bacteria would have doubled 240/20=12 times.
Thus, starting with only 1 bacterial cell, after 4 hours, there will be 1*2*2*2*2*2*2*2*2*2*2*2*2= 4,096 bacterial cells
The answer is 4,096.

Dear Sabina,
On Tuesday night your ticks went blue and then nothing came until Thursday. I want to tell you what my head did in those two days. I decided you were cross about the money I forgot to return. Then I decided you had found someone easier to talk to. I even drafted a cold message and did not send it.
Then your reply arrived and you told me about the house move and no internet. I felt foolish, and also a bit lighter. I am sorry I built such a story. Next time I will assume you are busy and wait, or ask you plainly.
Come for tea when the boxes are unpacked. 🙂
Love,
Avni

On which day did Sabina's reply finally arrive?
Sabina's reply arrived on Thursday.
What was Avni feeling during those two days of silence?
Avni felt anxious and hurt, imagining that Sabina was cross or had found someone easier. The unsent cold message shows how much it stung.
What does Avni plan to do differently next time a message goes unanswered?
Avni plans to assume Sabina is busy and wait, or to ask plainly. That saves the hurt of building a story from nothing.
What was Sabina's reason for the silence?
Sabina was dealing with a house move and had no internet, so a reply was not possible. It had nothing to do with Avni or the money.

A printing press is printing brochures. The press prints 20 single-page spreads, and twice as many double-page spreads. For each 4 pages printed for the spreads, the press prints a block of 4 ads, each of which take up a quarter of a page. The brochures can be arranged in any order as long as they are made up of 5 pages each. How many brochures is the printing press creating?

There are a total of 20 single-page spreads * 2 = 40 double-page spreads.
As these are made up of 2 pages each, there are 40 double-page spreads * 2 pages = 80 pages in the double-page spreads.
In total, there are 20 single-pages + 80 double-pages = 100 pages in the spreads.
A block of ads is printed every 4 pages, so there will be 100 pages / 4 pages/block = 25 blocks of ads.
This is a total of 25 blocks * 4 ads = 100 ads.
As each ad takes up a quarter of a page, this must create an additional 100 ads * 0.25 = 25 pages.
Therefore, the press has printed 100 pages from the spreads + 25 pages of ads = 125 pages.
Since brochures are made up of 5 pages each, this creates a total of 125 pages / 5 = 25 brochures.
The answer is 25.

Class 4 teacher's note, Monday. From Manjula, class teacher.
This week a story spread that the old neem tree near the gate is haunted. On Monday one child said it. By Wednesday, I heard it from almost every group.
Samir usually plays under that tree. On Wednesday, he wouldn't go near it. He told me, "Ma'am, everyone says a ghost lives there. It must be true if so many people say it." His hands were cold.
I asked him who had actually seen something. He counted. "Nobody. They just heard."
What I did next: I took the class out at lunch and we all sat under the neem and ate. I asked each child to say if they'd seen anything themselves. Nobody had. Samir climbed back onto his favourite root.

Where is the old neem tree?
The old neem tree is near the gate.
Why did Samir stop going near the neem tree?
He felt frightened, with cold hands, because hearing the story from so many people made it seem true.
Why was the lunch under the neem a good idea?
It let the children check for themselves and count who had really seen something, so the story stopped growing.
How might the other children have felt eating under the tree?
They probably felt nervous at first, then relieved and a little silly when nobody had seen anything.

messages.content: Why does a cook taste the food while it is cooking and not only at the end?

Tasting along the way lets the cook correct mistakes in time. Because the flavour is easy to adjust while the dish is still on the fire but difficult to fix after it is finished, an early taste saves the meal.

Sunday
Today I went to Nani's house because Ammi and Abbu were "talking" at home, which means fighting.
Nani saw my face and didn't ask anything. She just held me. She smelled like cardamom.
Then she said, "The house may change, Dilnaz. But my love won't. Not one bit."
I told her the truth. That I'm scared I'll have to choose. That I told Maria at school everything was fine, but it isn't.
Nani listened and didn't tell me to stop worrying. She said I can always come here and say anything.
I stayed for dinner. My chest feels quieter.
Dilnaz

What did Nani smell like?
Cardamom.
How did Dilnaz feel after spending time with Nani?
Dilnaz felt calmer, with a quieter chest, after being held and heard.
What did Dilnaz do that helped?
Dilnaz spoke honestly to Nani about being scared of having to choose and about pretending things were fine.
How might Nani see her role right now?
Nani sees herself as a steady, safe place where Dilnaz can come and say anything.

For their NSS water survey in Kolar district, Hemant had taken charge of everything: which wells to visit, who asked what, even who carried the clipboard. At the gram panchayat office he answered every question himself while Farida and two others stood behind him.
On the walk back past the paddy fields, Farida's stomach churned. Staying quiet was easier. But she had grown up in a village like this one and knew the women came to the handpump at 6 a.m., not at noon, when Hemant had scheduled the visits.
That evening she said, "Hemant, the noon visits are missing most of the women. In my aunt's village it's the same; they fetch water at dawn. Can we switch?"
He frowned. "I've already planned it."
"I know. Can we write down who leads which village? I'll take the dawn visits in two villages." She had already drawn up the table.
The others nodded. Hemant looked at the paper, then agreed, a little stiffly. At dawn on Friday, Farida's clipboard filled up within an hour.

At what time had Hemant scheduled the visits?
At noon.
What was Farida feeling on the walk back?
Uneasy, with her stomach churning, and tempted to stay quiet because it was easier.
How did Farida challenge Hemant's control?
With a fact from her own experience (women fetch water at dawn), a written table of who leads which village, and an offer to take the dawn visits.
How did Hemant respond?
He frowned and said he had already planned it, then agreed a little stiffly once he saw the table.

Hostel warden's note, Block C, room 214

The three girls in 214 have argued about cleaning since August. Today I watched Irawati bring it up in the common room. She came with a sheet listing three possible rotas: by day, by week, and by task. She told me beforehand that she could accept any of them, except taking the water-can refills alone every day, because of her early lab. Payal wanted weekly turns. Irawati said, "That works for me if refills rotate daily." Their third roommate agreed. The discussion was calm and took under twenty minutes. I asked them to pin the rota on the door and to come back to me in two weeks if it isn't working.

What were the three rotas on Irawati's sheet?
By day, by week, and by task.
Why was Irawati able to stay calm in the talk?
She felt secure because she had already decided what she could accept and what she couldn't, so nothing surprised her.
What could the roommates do if the rota stops working?
Come back to the warden in two weeks, as asked, or adjust one task instead of scrapping the whole plan.
How might Payal have experienced the talk?
Payal likely felt heard, since her weekly idea was accepted with only a small change about refills.

"So, Francis, you asked why the canteen queue is so bad now. I'm Tanvir, and I've been watching it for a whole week, like a detective. Here's the thing. They added a second counter, right? Should've made it faster. But they moved the bell for Class 9 and 10 to the same time, so double the people come at once. Then the second counter only sells samosas, so everyone who wants a sandwich still waits at the first. And because the line's long, people skip the drink stall, so it's empty, and the drink guy got moved to help, which slows the samosas. See? Every fix changed something else. I told the principal, and she wants me to draw it on a chart for the student council. Me! Drawing arrows for the principal."

What does the second counter sell?
Only samosas.
How does Tanvir feel about being asked to make a chart for the student council?
Tanvir feels proud and surprised, amused to be drawing arrows for the principal.
What could the school try, based on Tanvir's observations?
It could stagger the class bells again or let both counters sell sandwiches, then check how the queue changes.
How might the principal see Tanvir's week of watching?
She likely sees it as useful, detailed thinking that could help fix the problem.

Pallavi, you told me yesterday your group only does banter. Let me tell you about the monsoon I turned fifteen, when your Dilnaz aunty thought the same.
There was a boy in our tuition class, Shiv, who stammered on his s's. Every day, when the rain kept us indoors, we copied him. "S-s-sir, s-s-sorry I'm late." The whole room laughing. When the tuition sir frowned, I said, "It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."
He did laugh. Then one evening I saw him at the bus stop in the rain, practising "sorry" under his breath again and again, so he wouldn't be copied the next day. His face looked nothing like laughing.
The next day I stopped, and I told the others why. Two of them stopped too. So, Pallavi, what does the one your group jokes about do when you're not looking?

What did Dilnaz say when the tuition sir frowned?
"It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."
Why did "banter" feel like the right word to young Dilnaz?
The word let young Dilnaz feel comfortable and blameless: it made the copying sound like shared fun, and Shiv's laugh seemed to prove nobody was hurt.
What turned things around in the story?
Seeing Shiv practising "sorry" alone at the bus stop showed what the label was hiding; Dilnaz stopped the next day and told the others why, and two of them followed.
How did the "banter" look from Shiv's side?
For Shiv it seems to have been daily mockery he had to prepare against, and his laugh in class probably covered how much it hurt.

There are 15 students in the art club. By the end of each quarter, each student makes two artworks. If there are four quarters in a school year, how many artworks can the art club collect in two school years?

15 x 2 = 30 artworks can be collected in one quarter.
So in one school year, a total of 30 x 4 = 120 artworks can be collected.
Therefore, 120 x 2 = 240 artworks can be collected in two school years.
The answer is 240.

At the preschool in Ahmedabad, Shankar sir said to the class, "Everyone, put your crayons in the box and come to the mat." Most children moved. Aparna, five, kept colouring her elephant, lost in it. Shankar sir said it again. Nothing. He walked over, knelt down beside her, and said, "Aparna." She looked up. "Crayons in the box, then the mat." Aparna looked at the empty tables in surprise. "Oh!" She dropped her crayons in the box and hurried over.

What was Aparna colouring?
An elephant.
How did Aparna seem to feel when she noticed the empty tables?
She seemed surprised and a little startled, not having noticed the class moving.
What small step helped Aparna follow the instruction?
Shankar sir knelt beside her and said her name first, getting her attention before repeating the instruction.
How might the other children see Aparna staying at the table?
They may not notice much, or they may think she was just busy colouring.

At Nour's school in Amman, there was one good football for the whole of year four. Nour, nine, always grabbed it first at break and kept it until the bell, even when others were waiting. Why not? Hana did the same when she got it first, and so did the boys from the other class. Everyone kicked it hard against the wall, left it out in the rain, and nobody ever returned it to the box. One Monday the ball came back flat, a split down the side. The PE teacher held it up. "This belonged to all of you. Now it belongs to none of you." Nour stared at the ground. Break that day was long and boring. Hana kicked a stone. "It wasn't only you," she said. "It was everyone." That didn't make Nour feel any better.

How would you sum up this bit of text in three sentences?

At Nour's school, one good football is shared by all of year four, and whoever gets it first keeps it until the bell. Everyone kicks it hard and leaves it in the rain, and one Monday it comes back flat and split. The PE teacher says it belonged to all of them and now belongs to none, and Hana says it was everyone's fault.

Mark is baking bread. He has to let it rise for 120 minutes twice. He also needs to spend 10 minutes kneading it and 30 minutes baking it. How many minutes does it take Mark to finish making the bread?

First find the total rise time: 120 minutes * 2 = 240 minutes
Then add the rise time to the baking and kneading time: 240 minutes + 10 minutes + 30 minutes = 280 minutes
The answer is 280.

Dear Diary, Tuesday.
I finally went to Kalyani ma'am about my thesis stats. Last time I asked her anything, I just said "I'm confused about regression" and she spent twenty minutes asking what I meant. I felt awful for wasting her time.
This time I prepared. I wrote: "I ran the regression. Results are here. I don't know whether to include the age variable, because it changes the other results. I've read chapter 6. I need help deciding, not the whole method explained."
She read it, nodded, and answered in eight minutes. Then she said, "I wish all my students asked like this." I almost floated home. 😊
Sunaina

What had Sunaina already read before asking?
Sunaina had read chapter 6.
How did Sunaina feel after Kalyani ma'am's comment?
Sunaina felt proud and delighted, almost floating home.
What did Sunaina include that made the request work?
What had been done, the exact question about the age variable, and the kind of help needed, which let ma'am answer in eight minutes.
How does Kalyani ma'am see this way of asking?
She appreciates it, wishing all her students asked so clearly, since it respects her time.

Allie picked 44 wildflowers.  Thirteen of the flowers were yellow and white, seventeen of the flowers were red and yellow, and 14 of the flowers were red and white.  How many more flowers contained the color red than contained the color white?

13 were yellow and white, and 14 red and white, for a total of 13+14=27 flowers containing the color white.
17 were red and yellow, and 14 were red and white, for a total of 17+14=31 flowers containing the color red.
Thus, there were 31-27=4 more flowers that contained the color red than the color white.
The answer is 4.

Dear Diary,
Spent the whole afternoon sorting my stamp collection. First I had them by colour, which looked pretty but made no sense. Then I did countries, but some countries had only one stamp. Finally I made big groups by continent, smaller groups by country inside each, and inside India, groups by what's on them: birds, freedom fighters, trains. Yash asked why the Kenya giraffe wasn't with my India peacock, since both are animals. I said, "It's Africa first, then animals." He said I could do animals first. Annoyingly, he's right. Both work.
- Harsha

How did Harsha first sort the stamps?
By colour.
Why did Harsha write "Annoyingly, he's right"?
Harsha felt a bit irritated that Yash had a good point, but was honest enough to admit there is more than one way to sort.
What could Harsha try to keep both kinds of sorting?
Make a separate list or small labels, so a stamp can be found either by continent or by what is pictured on it.
How does Yash see the collection differently?
He thinks of subject first, so for him the giraffe and the peacock belong together as animals.
Hana has 50 pencils and gets 12 more from a friend. How many pencils does she have now?
62. Because 50 + 12 = 62, so there are 62 pencils in all.

'Amma, why did you come to the gate in your uniform?' Keerthana hissed, pulling her aside.
'I came straight from the hospital, kanna. My shift ended late.'
Ishita walked up, smiling. 'Hi Aunty! Are you a nurse?'
Keerthana froze.
'No, ma. I clean the wards,' Amma said simply.
'Oh, my Paati was in that hospital last year,' Ishita said. 'The cleaning staff were the only ones who talked to her at night. She still talks about one aunty who brought her an extra blanket.'
Amma smiled. 'Night shift is lonely for patients.'
On the walk home, Keerthana was quiet. 'I wrote "business" on the form for your job, Amma.'
'I know. I saw the form.'
'I'm sorry. I was scared they'd laugh.'
'Did Ishita laugh?'
'No. She said thank you.'
Amma squeezed her daughter's hand. 'Clean wards save lives too, kanna. Write it properly tomorrow.'

What does Amma do at the hospital?
She cleans the wards.
Why did Keerthana freeze when Ishita asked if Amma was a nurse?
She felt ashamed and scared that her friend would laugh at her mother's job.
What should Keerthana do with the form tomorrow, and why?
Write Amma's real job, because the work has dignity and a true friend like Ishita respects it.
How does Ishita see the cleaning staff at the hospital?
With gratitude, remembering how they talked to her Paati at night and brought an extra blanket.

The campaign brief came in on a Monday: a skin-whitening cream, and I was the lead copywriter. I read the words "brighter, fairer, more confident" and felt my stomach turn.

My sister had spent her teens being compared with fairer cousins. I was the one who told her she was beautiful exactly as she was. And now I was supposed to sell the opposite.

But I'm also the one who pays my parents' rent. Quitting on principle was not a real option.

I talked to Pema, our creative director, that afternoon. I said, "I'll work on anything else, double if needed, but I can't write this one and still look my sister in the eye." I expected a lecture. Pema just said, "Thank you for telling me early," and moved me to a school-uniform account.

Looking back, I'm Wasim, a copywriter who needs this job, and a brother who meant what he said. That day, I didn't have to choose only one.

What did the brief ask Wasim to write for?
The brief was for a skin-whitening cream, with Wasim as lead copywriter.
How did Wasim feel on reading "brighter, fairer, more confident"?
Wasim felt sick and torn, because the message went against what Wasim had told a sister who was compared with fairer cousins.
What was wise about how Wasim raised the problem?
Wasim spoke early, offered extra work on other accounts, and explained the reason plainly, which made it easy for Pema to find a solution.
How might Pema see Wasim's request?
Pema seems to respect the honesty and early warning, seeing it as easier to handle than a reluctant writer on the campaign.

Dear Maria,
I owe you an explanation for Saturday. At your engagement dinner I was on my phone half the night: tapping, scrolling, checking. I saw your face when you were telling everyone how Joel proposed and I was looking at my screen. You must have thought I didn't care. I'm so sorry.
The truth is, my younger brother was taken to the emergency ward that afternoon after a fall at cricket, and my parents were sending updates. I didn't want to spoil your night by announcing it, so I kept checking quietly. But I should have told you in one line: "Family thing, I may need to check my phone." That would have taken five seconds and saved you from wondering.
He's fine now, a cracked wrist and a sulk.
Can I take you for coffee this week and hear the proposal story properly, phone in my bag?
Love,
Nirmala

Why were Nirmala's parents sending updates?
Nirmala's younger brother had been taken to the emergency ward after a fall at cricket.
What was Nirmala feeling while checking the phone at the dinner?
Nirmala was anxious about the brother and torn, not wanting to spoil Maria's night; the scrolling came from worry, not boredom.
What does Nirmala say would have prevented the hurt?
A one-line explanation at the start, 'Family thing, I may need to check my phone', so Maria wouldn't have read the scrolling as not caring.
How might Maria have felt while telling the proposal story?
Maria probably felt hurt and a bit ignored, seeing her friend looking at a screen during an important moment.
In geography we read about bird migrations. What are migrations?

A migration is a regular journey made by birds or animals from one region to another, often when the season changes. It is a noun, with the plural Migrations.
Example: Every winter the bird migrations bring thousands of cranes to the lake.
At the circus, the clown has 3 dozen balloons on a string in his hand.  3 boys and 12 girls buy a balloon each.  How many balloons is the clown still holding?

The clown is holding 3 x 12 = 36 balloons.
This many children buy a balloon: 3 + 12 = 15 kids.
After the children buy the balloons, the clown is holding this many in his hand 36 - 15 = 21 balloons.
The answer is 21.

Hearing Tuhin repeat her saying in her exact sing-song; it showed that simply being present every day was already teaching him.

To Tuhin they were probably just part of home, so natural that he copied them, gesture and all, without thinking of them as lessons.

A heavy meal can make swimming uncomfortable. Because a full stomach leaves you bloated and sluggish, so most people feel better after a short rest. It is a comfort rule, not a strict one.

In a small café in Buenos Aires, Mateo, twenty-five, stirred his coffee while Fatima waited. Six months ago he had told everyone at his birthday that he was moving to Madrid for a master's. 'So,' he said, 'I'm not going.' Fatima raised her eyebrows. 'When I decided, the course had a scholarship and a part-time job attached. In March they cut both. I made the choice with what I knew then. Now I know more.' He didn't apologise too much or make excuses. 'I'll do the evening programme here instead.' Then he pushed a paper napkin across the table. 'And I want you to hold me to something. Every Sunday, text me: did you study ten hours this week? If I say no, I buy the coffee.' Fatima laughed and took a photo of the napkin. 'Deal. And I'm ordering the expensive cake.'

What did the Madrid course cut in March?
They cut the scholarship and the part-time job attached to the course.
How did Mateo seem to feel about changing his plan?
He seemed calm and clear rather than ashamed, explaining plainly that he decided with less information and now knows more.
How did Mateo use a new commitment on purpose, and why is that wise?
He asked Fatima to text him every Sunday about ten hours of study, using a public promise to support a good habit rather than to trap him in an old plan.
How might Fatima see Mateo's change of plan?
Fatima seems to accept it easily and is happy to help, laughing and taking a photo of the napkin as proof.

Hi Yash,

Okay, this is weird to write, so I'm just going to type it before I chicken out.

When you asked on the phone last week how the new school was, I said "amazing, everyone's great." That wasn't true. I eat lunch in the library most days. Nobody's mean, I just haven't found my people, and I miss our gang so much it's embarrassing.

I didn't tell you because I thought you'd feel sorry for me, or think I'd become a loser here. But you're my oldest friend, and pretending with you felt worse than being lonely.

So, yeah. That's the truth. You don't have to fix anything. I just didn't want to lie to you anymore.

Your friend (who is fine, just not amazing),
Naveen

Where does Naveen eat lunch most days at the new school?
In the library, most days.
Why did Naveen first tell Yash the school was amazing?
Naveen was afraid Yash would feel sorry for Naveen or see Naveen as a loser, so the loneliness stayed hidden.
What could Yash do after reading this email?
Yash could thank Naveen for being honest, give Naveen a call, and keep in regular touch without rushing to fix things.
If you were Yash, how might this email feel?
It might sting that Naveen hid the truth, but it would also feel like a gift of trust from an old friend. 🤍

You want to know how we stopped fighting? I'm Chandrika. Rashmi and I share a two-bedroom flat in Chennai, and for the first three months it was a war. She played music at midnight. I left my laundry on the chair for days. We both paid rent late, and our landlord shouted at both of us. One night she said, "I'm about to move out." That scared me. So we sat on the floor with snacks and wrote down what drove us crazy. It was honestly funny. Hers: my laundry. Mine: her music. We agreed on quiet hours after 11, a laundry deadline, and a shared account for rent. Now we fight maybe once a month, about who ate the last mango.

What time did they agree quiet hours would start?
Quiet hours would start after 11.
Why was Chandrika scared when Rashmi said she might move out?
She realised their fights were serious enough to end the arrangement, and she didn't want to lose her flatmate.
What made their floor-and-snacks talk work?
They named specific problems honestly, kept it light, and agreed clear rules for noise, laundry and rent.
How might the landlord see them now?
The landlord likely has fewer complaints, since their shared account means rent is paid on time.

What did Gopal spin?
A wooden top.

He felt left out and hurt when Gopal turned away, so his admiration flipped into rivalry.

Aparna, my granddaughter, you asked why I always ask people, “Everything fine?” when they sigh. Let me tell you. When I was eleven, our teacher, Mr. Iyer, sighed loudly every time I read aloud. I decided I was a terrible reader and stopped putting my hand up. For a whole term I sat quiet. Years later I met him, an old man, and told him. He looked amazed. “Rukmini, I had a bad back that year! I sighed whenever I stood up.” I laughed and cried together. So now I ask. A sigh can be tired, bored, cross or glad, and I don't want any child to blame herself.

How old was Rukmini when Mr. Iyer sighed at Rukmini's reading?
Rukmini was eleven.
Why did young Rukmini stop putting her hand up in class?
Young Rukmini took the sighs to mean being a terrible reader, so felt discouraged and hid.
What could a child do when a grown-up's sigh worries them?
A child could ask something like “Is everything fine?” and not assume being the cause.
How might Mr. Iyer have felt when he found out what Rukmini believed?
He was amazed and probably sorry, because his sighs came from a bad back and had nothing to do with Rukmini's reading.

Six bottles of 2 liters of water cost $12. What is the price of 1 liter of water?

Each bottle of 2 liters of water costs $12/6 = $2.
So the cost of 1 liter of water is $2/2 = $1.
The answer is 1.

The blue cup instead of the red one.

The town pool at Palampur opened in April, and Tenzin's mother signed her up for the girls' beginner batch. Coach Chaitanya didn't let anyone swim on day one. "Hold the edge. Kick. Just kick." How do the small steps look to Coach Chaitanya?

The dairy society office in the kasba smelled of milk cans and damp registers. Jyoti had been there four months, and Farooq had been kind since the first week. He had found her a room and shown her the shortcut to the bus stand. So when she saw him shaving a little off the weights in the morning register, she stared at the page for a long time. How long had Jyoti been at the dairy society office?
Jyoti had been there four months.
What was Jyoti feeling when she saw Farooq shaving the weights?
Torn and tense: her chest felt tight, she stared at the page a long time, and she wondered if she had lost a friend.
What did Jyoti do that balanced loyalty and honesty?
She spoke to Farooq privately, asked him to fix the entries by Friday and said she would tell the secretary afterwards.
How might Farooq have felt hearing Jyoti's words at the tea stall?
Probably embarrassed and defensive, since he laughed, looked away and said everyone does it.

How did Uday respond to Sarika's calm, firm request?
He sighed, checked the letter, called the accounts head and gave her a signed note.

Age two: Nikita climbed into her grandmother's lap the moment the front door banged and buried her face in the folds of the saree. She stayed there, thumb in mouth, one hand gripping a corner of the cloth, until her breathing slowed. When her cousin tried to squeeze her in a hug later, she squirmed away, and the cousin was gently told to wave instead.

Age twenty: Lavanya, sitting close to her partner on the sofa, reached to smooth a curl off their forehead. Her partner's shoulders went stiff. Lavanya's hand stopped in mid-air. 'Too much right now?' she asked. 'A bit,' her partner said. 'Long day.' She sat back, offered a hand palm-up instead, and waited. After a moment their fingers met.

The next visitor, who had a heavy cold, waved from the doorway and nodded, so Hemant nodded back and took his seat. He answered with a namaste.

Nikita's cousin was steered away from a squeeze when she squirmed, Lavanya stopped stroking when her partner stiffened and offered an open hand instead, and Hemant followed each visitor's lead between namaste, nod and handshake.

Tired and not ready for touch after a long day, as the stiffening and the words 'Long day' suggest.

"Breathe," her friend Noa said, laughing.

Walking home, her voice was hoarse. "That felt like mine," she said. "Like we all won."

The striker scored in the ninetieth minute.
What was Ines feeling in the last minutes before the goal?
She was tense and thrilled, her heart racing as if she were the one running at goal, and afraid the team would lose.

Feeling the match together with friends and strangers gave Ines strong joy and connection, like hugging an old man she'd never met.
What is it like for Noa to watch Ines during the match?
Noa finds it funny and sweet at first, teasing her to breathe, and then gets swept into the hugging and joy too.

Week one. Rajni announced she'd joined a weekend baking class. Jyoti rolled her eyes. "Oh wow, the great chef. Remember the burnt dal?" Their flatmate laughed; Rajni didn't. Later Rajni went to bed early without saying goodnight.

Week six. Jyoti had started noticing her own eye-rolls before they happened. She'd begun saying one thing she liked each day, even when it felt awkward. That Saturday Rajni brought home a lopsided cake. Jyoti took a bite. "This is really good. You've learned a lot." Rajni looked at her a long moment, then smiled and cut her a bigger slice.

Rajni joined a weekend baking class.

Jyoti felt scared and ashamed, realising the jokes were hurting Rajni and could end the relationship.

Jyoti caught her eye-rolls early and said one appreciative thing each day, replacing contempt with respect, which protects the relationship.

"Abhinav, put the pens down a minute. I can see the arrows from here. Let your Yusuf mamu tell you something.
When I was twenty, studying psychology in Aligarh, Shabnam ended things with me in the library, in about four sentences. That night I filled half a register. Her anxious style, my avoidant one, the push-pull, the exact week it tipped. I even drew a graph of how often we'd spoken.
My roommate Kishore asked, 'But how are you?' I gave him a twenty-minute lecture on attachment styles. He listened, then said, 'That's how it works. I asked how you are.'
I was annoyed. But I couldn't answer.
Everything in that register was correct, beta. It was also a very neat wall. Two weeks later I sat on the hostel stairs and cried for an hour, and only then did the diagrams start to help."

What did Kishore ask young Yusuf after the breakup?
"But how are you?"

Mapping styles and graphs made the breakup make sense and felt like control, so the hurt of being left in four sentences could stay behind the analysis.
What turning point let the diagrams become useful for Yusuf?
Crying on the hostel stairs; once the hurt was actually felt, the understanding had something to help with instead of standing in for it.
How might Kishore have felt after the twenty-minute lecture?
Kishore probably felt the question had been dodged, and cared enough to point out gently that the theory answered how it works, not how Yusuf was.

Every Monday we get a lab report due Thursday morning. Every Monday I think: two hours, easy. So I don't start on Monday. Or Tuesday. On Wednesday after dinner, I sit down at nine.

'Did you hear about Rupa and that manager?' Jasleen asked her sister, drying the steel plates.
'Mm. Mausi told me.' Alka shook her head. 'But why did she keep going to those late meetings? Why did she let it go on for months?' She stopped, a plate in her hand. 'Wait. Listen to me.'
'What?'
'I'm asking what Rupa did wrong. She didn't make him send those messages at midnight. She didn't make him threaten her appraisal.'
Jasleen leaned on the counter. 'So what's the real question?'
'Who had the power there? He did. He chose to send them. He chose to hold her job over her head.'
Alka put the plate down. 'I'm calling Rupa tonight. Not to ask why. Just to ask how she's doing and what she needs.'
'I'll sit with you while you call,' Jasleen said.

What did Alka say the manager chose to do?
He chose to send the messages at midnight and chose to hold Rupa's job over her head.
Why did Alka stop with a plate in her hand?
She noticed that her questions were all about what Rupa did wrong, and it bothered her that she was blaming the person who was hurt.
What did Alka decide once she changed her question?
She decided to call Rupa that night just to ask how she was doing and what she needed, instead of asking why she let it go on.
How might Rupa feel if the call began with 'why did you keep going to those meetings'?
Rupa would probably feel judged and ashamed, and might stop telling her family anything about the manager.

Ten minutes left, the ceiling fan had stopped, and Sarika was stuck on the last long question. Her jaw was clenched so hard her teeth ached. She wanted to shout that the paper was unfair, but she pressed her lips together. She put the pen down, opened her jaw slowly, moved it side to side, and took a long breath in and out. Irawati, beside her, glanced over and gave a small nod. Sarika picked the pen up and wrote the first step she was sure of. When the bell rang, the teacher said quietly, "If you'd like to talk about how it went, I'm around."

How many minutes were left when Sarika was stuck on the last question?
Ten minutes were left.
What is Sarika feeling and wanting as she clenches her jaw?
She wanted to shout that the paper was unfair but held it in under pressure. The clenched jaw and pressed lips show tension, though she may also have been frightened of failing.
What could Sarika try again when the pressure rises?
She can open her jaw slowly, stretch it side to side and breathe out long, as she did. Then she can write the step she is sure of.
How might the teacher's offer feel to Sarika?
It gives her a choice to talk without pressure. She may feel relieved that no one demanded an answer right away.

A woman is trying to decide whether it will be quicker to take an airplane or drive herself to a job interview. If she drives herself, the trip will take her 3 hours and 15 minutes.  If she takes an airplane, she will first need to drive 10 minutes to the airport, and then wait 20 minutes to board the plane.  After that, she will be on the airplane for one-third of the time it would have taken her to drive herself before landing in the destination city. Finally, it will take her an additional 10 minutes to get off the airplane and arrive at her interview site after the plane lands.  Given this information, how many minutes faster is it for her to take the airplane?

First, we must convert the driving time of 3 hours and 15 minutes to minutes. Since there are 60 minutes in an hour, driving takes a total of 3*60 + 15 = 195 minutes.
Next, the woman will be on the airplane for one-third of 195 minutes, or 195/3 = 65 minutes.
Therefore, in total, the airplane trip will take the woman 10 + 20 + 65 + 10 = 105 minutes.
Thus, the airplane trip is 195 - 105 = 90 minutes faster than driving herself to the interview.
The answer is 90.

In the booth at the Delhi conference centre, Kalyani, twenty-five, was interpreting a panel from Hindi into English. The speaker had just launched into a long sentence with three numbers, two place names and a joke. Kalyani held the whole thing in her head, reordered it for English grammar, and said it smoothly two seconds behind. Then the moderator switched to Marathi without warning. Her colleague Lalit, sitting beside her, raised his eyebrows. Kalyani nodded, adjusted, and kept going, holding the thread of the argument across both languages. At the break, she drank a full bottle of water and put her head down on the desk. "Your brain must be on fire," Lalit said. "Slightly," she said, grinning.

What did the moderator switch to without warning?
Marathi.
How did Kalyani feel at the break?
She felt drained and tired, but satisfied, grinning at Lalit's joke.
What skill allowed Kalyani to keep up?
Holding long sentences in memory, reordering them for English and following the argument across languages.

Billy has four horses. Each one eats 4 pounds of oats, twice a day. How many pounds of oats does he need to feed his horses for 3 days?

At each feeding Billy serves 4 horses x 4 pounds of oats/horse = 16 pounds/feeding
Each day Billy uses 16 pounds of oats/feeding x 2 feedings/day = 32 pounds of oats/day
Triple that amount to find the amount of oats needed to feed the four horses for three days: 32 pounds of oats/day x 3 days = 96 pounds
The answer is 96.

January: Ujjwal, twenty, sat through his second-year BCom accounting lecture doodling recipes in the margins. He'd been cooking dinner for his family since he was fourteen.
March: His sister Payal found him watching a video about a two-year culinary diploma. "You'd leave commerce?" "I don't know," he said. "Papa will freak." "What do you want?" Ujjwal looked at the screen. "This."

That her internet is weak.
What do Sharmila's pale knuckles in January suggest?
She is angry and holding it in, keeping quiet on the outside while resentment builds.

In the small town of Nabha, Shankar noticed that his daughter Hansa had gone quiet. After school she lay on the charpai with her phone, scrolling without really looking. When he asked about her day, she said, "Fine." Dinner? "Okay." Tuition? "Hmm."
His brother said, "She's become rude. Take the phone away."
Shankar didn't. Instead, every evening he sat on the step near the charpai with his tea, not asking anything. Some days he mentioned something small: the neighbour's new calf, the rain.
On the fourth evening, Hansa put the phone down. "Papa, Simran moved to Ludhiana. Her father got transferred. She didn't even tell me until the day before."
"You're hurt."
"Very."
Shankar nodded. "Tell me about her."
Hansa talked until the tea went cold.

Where did Simran move?
To Ludhiana.
What was Hansa feeling underneath her one-word answers?
Hansa was hurt and sad that her friend Simran had moved away and told her only the day before.

In Himani's village near Mandi, the only chemist folded every leaflet into the box, and Himani read hers twice by the kitchen lamp. Headache. Dizziness. Dry mouth. Tingling hands. Upset stomach. Ganga, beti, you're angry with your parents? Sit. Your Vijay Dada has a story about anger.
In 1974 I was twenty-one, in Jhansi. I wanted to join the Railways as a mechanic. My father wanted me in his cloth shop. He wouldn't even let me finish a sentence about it.
So I did the dramatic thing. I packed a tin trunk and told him, "If you won't listen, I'm leaving for Bombay tomorrow." He said, "Go, then." And I went, all the way to the bus stand, and sat there till midnight, too proud to go back and too scared to leave.
Your Dadi, only a neighbour then, found me and said, "Threats won't make him hear you."
A week later, calm, I sat beside him in the shop and said, "Babuji, I love you. I'm not good with cloth. I'm good with engines. Let me try for one year." He was quiet a long time. Then he said, "One year."
Anger is a messenger, beti. Let it deliver the message, then send it home.

At the bus stand.
How did Vijay feel sitting at the bus stand?
Torn and stuck: too proud to go back and too scared to leave after his angry threat.
What was the turning point in Vijay's story?
The neighbour who later became Ganga's Dadi telling him threats wouldn't work; a week later he spoke calmly and asked for a one-year trial.

Dylan's mother is throwing a baby shower for her best friend. The 40 guests, though, arrive in only 10 cars that they park in the parking lot.  If each car has 4 wheels, how many car wheels are there in the parking lot, including both of Dylan's parent's car wheels?

10 cars are parked around for the party, 10 x 4 wheels each car = 40 wheels total.
Dylan's parents both have a car with 4 wheels each, 2 x 4 = 8 more wheels.
Combined, there are 40 + 8 = 48 wheels total on the Dylan family property.

The robot had to be ready by nine a.m. for the inter-school science fair, and at eight p.m. the power went out across half of Amritsar. Sahil, sixteen, from the officers' colony, and Amandeep, from the old city lanes, sat in Amandeep's courtyard with a battery lantern. A month ago they'd barely spoken; Sahil's friends called the old-city boys "tapori," and Amandeep's cousins called the colony boys "show-offs." The teacher had paired them anyway. Now Sahil knew the code and Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop. Neither could finish without the other. At midnight the motor sparked and died. Sahil groaned. Amandeep calmly re-soldered the joint. At two a.m. the robot rolled forward. Sahil punched the air. "We did it!" Neither of them noticed he'd said "we." The next day at the fair, their friends from both sides crowded round to watch.

What did Amandeep know from his uncle's electrical shop?
Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop.
How was Sahil feeling when he punched the air?
Sahil felt thrilled and triumphant, sharing the success with Amandeep as a real teammate.
What made this pairing work better than a talk about tolerance?
Each boy had a skill the other needed for a shared goal, so they had to depend on each other, which built trust.
How might their friends from both sides see the pair at the fair?
Their friends might start to see the other side differently, watching the two work as a proud team.
Why do some book pages stick together after getting wet?
Paper fibres and ink settle together as they dry. Because wet paper fibres and ink settle against each other and then dry that way, the pages become glued together.

"Ma, everyone's going to see me in the class photo with this haircut. My life is over."
Dolma put down the ladle. "It's shorter than you wanted."
"It's a disaster. Nobody has ever looked this stupid."
"That sounds really miserable, Anirban. Sit. Tell me."
He talked for ten minutes about the photo, the class group chat, and Riddhi's cousin, who would definitely laugh. Dolma listened, nodding.
"Can I tell you something?" she said at last. "At fifteen I cut my own fringe with kitchen scissors before my aunt's wedding."
"Seriously?"

Anirban almost smiled. "Is it bad?"

What did Dolma do before her aunt's wedding when she was fifteen?
She cut her own fringe with kitchen scissors.
Why does the haircut feel like the end of Anirban's life?
Anirban feels embarrassed and panicked, as though everyone will be looking at him, so a short haircut seems like something the whole class will notice and remember.
Which of Dolma's choices let Anirban almost smile?
Listening for ten minutes first, then sharing her own fringe story, so he could see his worry from a wider view without being dismissed.
How does Dolma seem to see Anirban's panic?
Dolma treats it as real to him rather than silly, while quietly knowing it will pass, just as her own fringe disaster did.

Week one: Anirban, fourteen, lost the school debate. He blamed the judges. His teammate Pema said, "You talked over the other side's last point." He shrugged. Week two: he lost again, and this time he asked Pema to record him. Listening back, he winced: he hadn't answered one argument, just spoken louder. Week three: he lost a practice round but noticed, halfway through, that he was rushing again, and made himself breathe before answering. Week four: he kept a small notebook during the debate, writing each opponent's point before replying. When Pema passed him a note saying "slow", he nodded. He won. That night he wrote in the same notebook: "I think better when I slow down my own head. My first answer is usually my loudest, not my best."

To record him.

He felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, seeing that he hadn't really answered the other side.
What small step changed his results?
Writing down each opponent's point before replying, so he thought before he spoke.

She probably feels pleased and relieved that he took her feedback seriously.

"Devika, you asked about the bravest thing I ever did. Your Momo-la, your grandmother, will tell you, but it wasn't brave the way films show.
I, Tenzin, was twenty-five, a teacher at a village school in Himachal. The headmaster made a rule: children from the labourers' camp couldn't sit with the other children. Most of the teachers agreed. Parents agreed. It was 'how things are'.
I didn't sleep for three nights. Every child sitting on that floor was as much a person as my own nieces.
So I sat those children with the others in my class. I told the headmaster why, and I wrote to the education office. I was transferred to a far school for two years.
I'm not a saint, beta. I've been petty and scared plenty of times. But that one time, I knew what I believed."

How long was Tenzin transferred to a far school?
For two years.
How did young Tenzin feel during the three sleepless nights?
She felt troubled and torn, knowing every child mattered as much as her own nieces, while everyone else accepted the rule.
What choice did Tenzin make, and what did it cost her?
She seated the camp children with the others, explained why and wrote to the education office, and was transferred far away for two years.
How might the labourers' children have felt sitting with the others?
They likely felt seen and respected, perhaps for the first time in that school.
I keep going to bed late and then I'm tired in class. I'm Rehan.
Hi Rehan. Tired mornings are no fun, especially when class starts early. What usually keeps you up at night?
Mostly my phone. I tell myself five more minutes and then it is midnight.
That happens to many people. One simple habit is to charge your phone in another room, so it is not in your hand at bedtime. Then you can read a few pages or listen to quiet music.
I like reading. I have a detective book I want to finish.
That's a good bedtime plan. Read just one chapter each night with a small lamp on, and stop when your eyes feel heavy. The detective story will give you something to look forward to.
Which book did I say I want to finish? I want to ask the librarian for the next one.
You said a detective book, Rehan. Ask the librarian if there is a next one in the series, so your one-chapter-a-night plan can keep going after this book.

Monday: At the design studio, Nitin clicked between six tabs, none of them his poster brief: shopping sites, a quiz, a blog about bikes. He felt restless and guilty and blamed the dull project. Hafsa, at the next desk, noticed he'd yawned eleven times before lunch.
Wednesday: "When did you last sleep properly?" Hafsa asked. Nitin counted back. His cousin's wedding, two late nights, a long Sunday drive. "Maybe the poster isn't boring," she said. "Maybe you're just empty."
Saturday: Nitin slept till nine, went for a slow walk and didn't open his laptop.
The next Monday he opened the poster brief first thing. It was the same brief. But it held him for two hours, and he didn't open a single other tab.

How many times had Nitin yawned before lunch on Monday?
Eleven times.
Why did Nitin blame the poster project for his restlessness?
Restlessness felt like boredom, and the brief was the obvious target; he didn't notice that his tiredness after the wedding was the real cause.
What was the turning point, and what did Nitin choose after it?
Hafsa's question about sleep; Nitin chose a restful Saturday instead of forcing himself, and on Monday the same brief held his attention.
How does Hafsa see Nitin's week differently from how he sees it?
Where Nitin sees a dull project, Hafsa sees an exhausted colleague, noticing the yawns and guessing he needs rest rather than excitement.

messages.content: In the song, the refrain repeats after each verse. I know refrain as hold back.

As a noun, a refrain is a line or group of lines repeated in a song or poem. The verb, said re-FRAIN, means to stop yourself from doing something.
Example: The whole audience sang the refrain together.

He stood at Miss Temple's side; he was speaking low in her ear: I did not doubt he was making disclosures of my villainy; and I watched her eye with painful anxiety, expecting every moment to see its dark orb turn on me a glance of repugnance and contempt. I listened too; and as I happened to be seated quite at the top of the room, I caught most of what he said: its import relieved me from immediate apprehension.
She fears he is telling Miss Temple bad things about her and waits for a look of disgust. When she overhears what he says, it relieves her worry for now.

Note by the Class 4 teacher, school picnic, Saturday
At the farm gate a brown dog ran out barking. Avni stopped dead and grabbed my sleeve. "My stomach is all tight, Ma'am, my heart is going bang bang, that means it will bite." The dog was chained and stopped well before us, but Avni would not move. Her friend Ira said, "It's tied, Avni, see?" Avni shook her head and cried.
What I did next: I walked Avni to the far side of the bus, where she could still see the dog from a distance, and we breathed slowly together. I told her the tight stomach is her body's alarm, which can ring even when things are safe. I will tell her parents at pickup.

What did Avni say her heart was doing?
She said her heart was going bang bang.
Why was Avni sure the dog would bite?
Avni felt terrified, and she took her tight stomach and pounding heart as proof that the dog was dangerous.
How did the teacher support Avni at this stage, and what else could help?
The teacher gave her distance and slow breathing and explained the body's alarm; later, small, calm practice with gentle dogs could help her learn the alarm isn't always right.
How might Ira feel when Avni starts to cry?
Ira may feel confused and a little helpless, because to her the chain made it obvious the dog was safe.

In a Berlin cafe, Olga held her phone under the table. Three friends had already messaged: "So you're leaving the firm?" Only Ines knew. Olga had told Ines on Sunday, alone, in Ines's kitchen. Her face burned. Humiliated and furious, she answered none of them.

The next evening on the tram she called Ines. "You told people about my plan. I trusted you with it. I felt exposed and angry."

A pause. "I told Petra," Ines said. "I thought she already knew. I'm sorry."

Olga breathed. "I'm not ready to say it's fine. I need to see that you can keep something." Ines offered to tell the others she'd been wrong to talk. "We'll see how the next month goes," Olga said, and hung up gently.

Where did Olga tell Ines about leaving the firm?
Olga told Ines on Sunday, alone, in Ines's kitchen.
How did Olga feel when the three friends messaged?
Humiliated and furious; her face burned.
How did Olga handle the conversation with Ines?
She said clearly what happened and how it hurt, then asked Ines to show she can keep a confidence and left the friendship's future to the repair, not her anger.
How might Ines have seen telling Petra?
Ines says she thought Petra already knew, which suggests it seemed harmless to Ines, though she apologised once she heard the hurt.

Describe this excerpt in just three sentences.

Your mother was exactly like you when she was nine, you know. I'm her big brother, your Saurabh Mama; I saw it all. She had rules for herself, written in her rough book: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin." During Durga Puja that year, the half-yearly results came. She came second, by one mark. She didn't cry, because crying was against the rules. She just went up to the terrace and sat very straight, and when I found her, her hands were shaking. "I broke the rule," she whispered. "I'm so bad." I sat with her and said, "Indu, who made these rules?" "Me." "Then you can make kinder ones." We crossed out "must" and wrote "try". She cried then, finally. She still came second sometimes. The sky never fell.

Saurabh Mama remembers his sister Indu at nine, who made strict rules for herself: come first, never cry, never forget her tiffin. When she came second by one mark, she sat very straight on the terrace, shaking, and said she had broken the rule. He helped her change "must" to "try", and then she finally cried.

Lecturer's note, first-year statistics — Kalyani
Urmila is one of the sharpest students in the tutorial when we discuss ideas aloud. But whenever a problem sheet appears, she pushes it away before reading it. Today she said, "I'll fail this anyway. I've always been bad at maths." She had not looked at question one.
I did not argue with her. I circled only the first part of question one, finding the mean of five numbers, and asked her to do just that while I walked around the room.
She did it in two minutes, correctly. I said, "That's right," and moved on. When I came back, she had quietly started part two.
It is a small thing. But I think she has had many years of evidence that trying is useless, and she needs fresh evidence that it is not.
Next week: same approach, one small step at a time, slightly harder each time.

What was the first small task the lecturer gave Urmila?
The lecturer asked her to find the mean of five numbers, the first part of question one.
What was the lecturer thinking when choosing not to argue with Urmila?
The lecturer felt concerned and patient, believing Urmila had years of evidence that trying is useless and that arguing would not change it, but a small success might.
Why is starting with one tiny part a good strategy here?
A task she can surely do gives Urmila a quick success, which is fresh evidence that effort works and helps her start the next part on her own.
How might Urmila feel when she hears "That's right"?
Urmila might feel a little surprised and relieved, enough to quietly try part two.
Why does dough rise when yeast is added?
The yeast makes gas inside the dough. Because yeast feeds on the sugar in the dough and gives off tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide, which get trapped and puff the dough up.

At Sarah's job 60% of the employees are women and the rest are men. Of the men, 75% have a college degree and 8 do not. How many women work at Sarah's company?

25% of men at the job don't have a college degree because 100 - 75 = 25
There are 32 men at the company because 8 / .25 = 32
40% of the employees are men because 100 - 60 = 40
The company has 80 workers because 32 / .4 = 80
There are 48 women at the company because 80 - 32 = 48
The answer is 48.

At the small shop in the village, Tanuja pointed at the calf tied outside. "Cows drink milk. That's why they make milk."

"Hmm," said Yusuf Chacha, weighing rice. "Do they? I don't know. Let's find out."

"I know it," Tanuja said firmly.

When the milkman came by on his cycle, Yusuf Chacha asked him. "Grown-up cows drink water and eat grass," the milkman said. "Only calves drink milk."

Tanuja frowned and twisted her bangle. "Oh." Then: "I didn't know that."

"Neither did I," said Yusuf Chacha. "Now we both do."

Who did Yusuf Chacha ask about what cows drink?
The milkman.
What was Tanuja feeling when she frowned and said, "Oh"?
She was probably surprised and a little puzzled, because she had been so sure. Saying "I didn't know that" suggests she felt okay admitting it once Chacha said the same.
How did Yusuf Chacha show that not knowing is fine?
He said "I don't know. Let's find out," asked someone who knew, and admitted he had learnt something too.
How does the milkman see Tanuja's certain claim?
He likely finds it an ordinary child's mistake and simply explains what grown cows and calves drink.

"You stopped coming to the Sunday youth group," Thomas said, dropping his bag on Kunal's bed.
"I didn't stop. I'm taking a break."
"From God or from us?"
Kunal laughed, then his smile slipped. "From being told what to think before I've thought it. I've been reading. Some of it makes sense, some of it scares me."
"Like what?"
"Like whether I believe the things I say in prayers, or I just know the words."
Thomas sat down. "My dad would say doubt is part of faith."
"Would you say it?"
"I don't know. I've never asked myself." Thomas picked at the bedsheet. "Can I read what you're reading?"
"Only if you argue with me properly. No quoting your dad."
"Deal. But you come back one Sunday and argue there too."
Kunal thought about it. "One Sunday. Then I decide."

Why did Kunal say he was taking a break from the youth group?
He said he was taking a break from being told what to think before he had thought it.
What might Kunal be feeling about his reading, and how can you tell?
He feels curious but also a little scared; he says some of it makes sense and some of it scares him, and his laugh fades when Thomas asks.
How could Thomas support Kunal while he works out what he believes?
He can keep reading and arguing with Kunal honestly, without pressure, and leave the final decision to him.
How is Thomas affected by Kunal's questions?
Kunal's questions make Thomas notice he has never asked himself what he believes, so he wants to read the same books.

Tom uses 10 weight plates each weighing 30 pounds on an exercise machine.  This exercise machine uses special technology to make the weights 20% heavier on the lowering portion.  How heavy did the weights feel when being lowered?

The weight stack weighed 10*30=300 pounds
So the added weight made it 300*.2=60 pounds heavier
So when he lowered the weight it was 300+60=360 pounds
The answer is 360.

His curtains stayed drawn at noon. Passing his room at 2 a.m., Tenzin could hear the same video playing on a loop.

He didn't lecture. Each evening at eight he knocked: "Mess has rajma today. Coming?" Four nights Karthik said no. On the fifth he came, ate half a plate, said nothing, but stayed.

Rajma.

He knocked every evening with a simple invitation, never lectured, and offered to go with Karthik to the counsellor and doctor.

He probably felt drained and shy, but a little less alone because Tenzin kept coming back.
