The new maths sir got off the morning bus at the Sirsa town square with a straight back, a steel trunk and a flute sticking out of his cloth bag.
Irfan watched from the tea stall. "Retired army man," he told Aditi. "Strict, wakes at five, plays the flute at sunset to relax. All of that."
"Or just a retired army man," Aditi said.
"No, no, the flute fits. And the trunk. It's more likely he's the whole thing."
Aditi put down her glass. "Think. Every army man with a flute who wakes at five is an army man. But not every army man has the flute and the five a.m. Each thing you add has to be true too."
Irfan opened his mouth. The story still felt better. More real.
In class the next day, the new sir said he had been a bank clerk for thirty years. The flute was his daughter's; he was taking it for repair.

What was sticking out of the new maths sir's cloth bag?
A flute was sticking out of his cloth bag.
Why did the full army-and-flute story feel more likely to Irfan?
Irfan felt confident because every detail fit into a vivid picture, which made the story feel truer even though it needed more things to be right.
What could Irfan try the next time he builds a detailed guess?
Irfan could strip it back to the simplest version and remember that each added detail is one more thing that must be true.
How might the new sir feel if he heard Irfan's guess?
He might be amused, since he was a bank clerk carrying his daughter's flute for repair.

John won $155250 in the lottery and decided to give one-thousandth of the $155250  to each of the top 100 students in his college. Calculate the total amount received by the hundred students of his college.

John will give 155250/1,000 = $155.25 to each student.
For the hundred students, he will give: $155.25 * 100 = $15525
The answer is 15525.

Spot the mistakes. a) "r = -0.9, so there is almost no correlation." b) "r = 0.95 between hours of sleep and marks, so more sleep causes higher marks." c) "The line y = 20 + 4x fits data for x = 1 to 10, so at x = 100 the value is 420." d) "I got r = 1.12." e) "b = -2, so r = 0.7." f) "r = 0, so x and y are unrelated."

Answer: a) -0.9 is a STRONG negative correlation. b) Correlation does not prove causation. c) Extrapolation far outside the data; unreliable. d) Impossible: -1 <= r <= 1, so there is an arithmetic error. e) b and r always have the same sign. f) r = 0 means no LINEAR correlation; there may be a curved relationship.

a) The sign gives the direction; |r| gives the strength. b) A lurking variable (general health, a calm routine) may affect both, and we have no experiment. c) The formula gives a number, but the pattern may not continue beyond x = 10. d) A value outside -1 to 1 always means a slip, often using sum x^2 in place of Sxx. e) b = Sxy / Sxx and r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx x Syy) have the same numerator, and the denominators are positive. f) See the U-shaped example (D10).

Beat him at carrom.

Dear Yogesh,
You start sending job applications this week, so I'm going to tell you my most embarrassing story, and then give you my checklist.
Two years ago, I sent a cover letter to a design firm addressed to "Dear Hiring Team at Silverline." The firm was called Northgate. Silverline was the previous application. I found out when their HR replied, very politely, pointing it out. I wanted to hide under my desk for a week.
Since then, before I send anything important, I spend two minutes on four checks:
1. Names: company, person, my own.
2. Numbers: dates, phone number, any figures.
3. Attachments: open every one, don't trust the file name.
4. The original request: reread what they asked for and see if I answered it.
It has caught something almost every time. Last month it caught a salary figure with an extra zero.
Two minutes. Please.
Your sister,
Minakshi

What was the firm Minakshi applied to actually called?
The firm was called Northgate.
How did Minakshi feel when the HR reply came?
Minakshi felt deeply embarrassed, wanting to hide under the desk for a week.
Which of the four checks might matter most for Yogesh, and why?
Checking names, because sending a letter with another company's name is the kind of embarrassing error a two-minute check catches.
How might Yogesh feel reading this?
Yogesh would probably feel amused by the story but also grateful, since it gives a simple habit before those first applications.

Reading contracts carefully, keeping a list of bills and duties, and taking part in local meetings.

The class demo was at eleven. At 10:25, Wasim, the second-year student helping in the chemistry lab, realised he had made the copper sulphate solution ten times too strong. He had read the wrong line on the sheet.
His first thought was to hope nobody noticed. His second was the thirty first-year students who would record wrong results.
He found Dr Nazia in the prep room. "Ma'am, I made a mistake. The solution is ten times too strong. I read the wrong line. I can make a fresh batch in fifteen minutes if you can start with the theory part."
Dr Nazia looked at the clock, then at him. "Go. I'll talk for fifteen."
His hands were not quite steady as he measured, but he checked each number twice. The new solution was ready at 10:52.
After class, Dr Nazia said, "Most people hide that. You didn't. That's why I trust you with the lab."

How much too strong was the solution?
Ten times too strong.
How did Wasim feel as he remade the solution?
Wasim was nervous, his hands not quite steady, but determined to get it right, checking each number twice.
What made Wasim's way of owning the mistake effective?
He told Dr Nazia at once, said exactly what went wrong and offered a specific fix with a time, so the damage was contained.
How does Dr Nazia see Wasim after the class?
Dr Nazia trusts him more, saying most people hide such mistakes and he didn't.

At snack time in the nursery in Bologna, Rania leaned over to Valentina. "Your nonna is sick in the hospital," said Rania, chewing a breadstick. "I heard my mama say." Valentina's face crumpled. She dropped the breadstick. Rania frowned, puzzled. "It's true." The teacher hurried over, knelt between them and said gently, "Rania, that news belongs to Valentina's family to share. Valentina, come sit with me. Your mama will tell you more." Valentina leaned into the teacher's arm. Rania whispered, "I only said what I heard." The teacher nodded. "I know. Next time we ask a grown-up first."

What did Rania say to Valentina at snack time?
"Your nonna is sick in the hospital."
What was Rania feeling after Valentina's face crumpled?
Puzzled. Rania had only said what was heard, and did not understand why the words hurt so much.
What did the teacher do, and what did the teacher tell Rania?
The teacher knelt between them, comforted Valentina, said the news belongs to the family to share, and said that next time Rania should ask a grown-up first.
How might Valentina have felt hearing about the sick nonna from Rania at snack time?
Frightened and upset, since the news arrived suddenly and Valentina's face crumpled and the breadstick dropped.

A drone takes off from the corner O of a school ground. Take x metres east, y metres north and z metres up. It hovers at P(12, -4, 3). In which octant is it? Where is the point on the ground directly below it, how high is it, and how far is it from O? How far is it from the east-west boundary line (the x-axis)?

Answer: Octant IV (+, -, +). The point below it is (12, -4, 0); it is 3 m high, 13 m from O, and 5 m from the x-axis.

Read the coordinates as three moves from O: 12 m east, 4 m SOUTH (y is negative), 3 m up. The signs (+, -, +) give octant IV. The ground is the xy-plane (z = 0), so the point straight below is (12, -4, 0) and the height is |z| = 3 m. OP^2 = 12^2 + (-4)^2 + 3^2 = 144 + 16 + 9 = 169, OP = 13 m Why: O to the foot F(12, -4, 0) is a flat distance sqrt(144 + 16) = sqrt160; then F to P is 3 m straight up, at right angles, so OP^2 = 160 + 9 = 169. The distance from the x-axis: the foot on the x-axis is (12, 0, 0), and from there P is 4 m across and 3 m up: sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 m. In general the distance of (x, y, z) from the x-axis is sqrt(y^2 + z^2) - leave out the coordinate of THAT axis. Common mistake: answering |x| = 12 (that is the distance from the yz-plane).

On Sunday afternoons, Zubin visited his grandfather Nilesh in their old Mumbai flat. This week, looking at a photo of a young man with a violin, Nilesh said quietly, "I played in an orchestra once. Then I stopped for a steady job. I never picked it up again."
"Do you regret it, Nana?"
"Every day, a little. And I never told my father I wanted to keep playing. I just obeyed."
Zubin sat very still. He was twenty-one, studying commerce, and secretly writing songs on his laptop at night.
"Don't worry about me," Nilesh said, patting his knee. "I had a good life. But you, don't wait so long."
Walking home, Zubin felt calmer than he expected. He sent one of his songs to a friend who ran a college band.

What was the young man in the photo holding?
He was holding a violin.
How did Zubin feel walking home?
He felt calmer than he expected, taking his grandfather's regret as a gentle warning, not a weight.
What small risk did Zubin take after the visit, and why does it matter?
He sent one of his songs to a friend's band, a first step so he won't live with the same regret.
How might Nilesh feel if he heard Zubin was sharing his songs?
Nilesh would likely feel proud and glad his story helped his grandson take a chance.

The registration link for the "Global Leaders Certificate" closed at 6 p.m., and it was 5:40 when Lalremsiami, twenty, finally saw it. Her class group had exploded: three hundred students from her college had signed up. Screenshots of payment receipts kept popping up.
"Three hundred people," she told Shalini, grabbing her phone on the bus. "They can't all be wrong."
"What does it actually give you?" Shalini asked.
"Leadership sessions. A certificate. It's… I don't know exactly. But everyone's in."
"Who runs it? Is it from the college?"
Lalremsiami scrolled. The page had lots of photos of smiling students and very little else. The bus jolted; the signal dropped. 5:52.
"I'll just pay and check later," she said, thumb over the button. "If three hundred of us are wrong, at least we're wrong together."
Shalini gently put her hand over the screen. "Or you wait eight minutes and ask the college office tomorrow."

How many students from her college had signed up for the certificate?
Three hundred students from her college had signed up.
Why did paying without checking feel reasonable to Lalremsiami?
Lalremsiami felt rushed and afraid of being left out, with the deadline minutes away and hundreds of classmates posting receipts, so the crowd itself felt like proof the certificate was worth it.
What choice did Shalini put in front of Lalremsiami at the last minute?
Shalini suggested letting the deadline pass and asking the college office tomorrow, so the decision would rest on facts about who runs it, not on how many had joined.
What would change if the link had no signup counter or receipts in the group?
Without the crowd, Lalremsiami would likely notice the page has little information and ask what it gives before paying.

Jomon picked up on the second ring.
"Pappa? It's me. Can you talk?"
"Bhavna? Of course. What's wrong, mole?"
"Nothing's wrong. I think my period started. At school. I'm in the girls' toilet."
"Okay. Good that you called. Are you all right? Any pain?"
"A bit. Mostly I'm shaky. And embarrassed."
"That's normal. Remember the little pouch Amma packed in your bag? The blue one?"
"Oh. Yes. It's here."
"Everything you need is in there. And the school nurse has more, and a hot water bag if your tummy hurts."
"You're not weird about this?"
"Why would I be? It's a normal part of growing up. Honestly, I'm a bit proud."
"Pappa!"
"Okay, okay. Go and sort it out. I'll leave work early and bring your banana chips."
"Thanks, Pappa."

What colour was the pouch Amma packed?
The blue one.
How was Bhavna feeling when she called?
She felt shaky and embarrassed, unsure how Pappa would react.
What made Jomon's response helpful?
He stayed calm and matter-of-fact, reminded her of the supplies, pointed her to the nurse, and called it a normal part of growing up.
How does Jomon feel about the news?
He feels calm and even a bit proud, treating it as ordinary rather than weird.

In the colony park in Pune, the cricket game fell apart when Abhinav threw down the bat and yelled, “NOBODY listens to me! I said the ball crossed the line!” He was red in the face, fists clenched. The others shouted back, and it got louder. Arohi stepped back from the crowd. She thought, He's angry, but he also just wants someone to hear him. She didn't shout. She walked to the bench where Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle who kept score, was sitting, and asked him to come. He listened to Abhinav first, then to the others. “Replay the ball,” he said. Abhinav picked up the bat, still sulking but quiet.

Who kept score at the game?
Mr Kulkarni, the building uncle, kept score.
What was Abhinav feeling when he threw down the bat?
Abhinav was angry and frustrated, and also desperate to be heard after being ignored.
Why was Arohi's choice safer than shouting back?
She stepped back and fetched a calm adult, who listened to both sides and settled the dispute.
How did the other players react to Abhinav's yelling?
They shouted back, which only made the argument louder.
Give me one sentence of advice about being on time. Ten words at most, and avoid the word "late".
Leave ten minutes early so you can arrive calmly.
Judy uses 10 pencils during her 5 day school week. A 30 pack of pencils costs $4. How much will she spend on pencils over 45 days?

She uses 2 pencils a day because 10 / 5 = 2
She will use 90 pencils in 45 days because 2 x 45 = 90
She will need 3 packs of pencils because 90 / 30 = 3
She will spend $12 because 3 x 4 = 12
The answer is 12.
How can I stop biting my nails? Why do we sneeze when dust gets in our nose? Why do we put a wet cloth over a hot forehead with fever? what is "treachery"?

1. Notice when you do it and keep your hands busy with something else. Keep your nails short so there is less to bite.
2. A sneeze blows the irritant out of the nose. Because the dust irritates the lining of the nose, a sneeze pushes air out fast to blow it away.
3. People use a wet cloth for comfort. Because the water evaporates and takes away some heat from the skin.
4. "Treachery" is a noun. It means the betrayal of someone who trusts you.
Please give me a advice about my problem.
Please give me some advice about my problem. Why: "advice" has no "a"; use "some".

Anand came home from school, dropped his bag in the hall of the Kolkata flat and snapped at his cousin Rehana for sitting in 'his' chair. Ten minutes later he was laughing at a video. Ten minutes after that he was at the bathroom mirror, glaring at a spot on his chin, muttering that he looked disgusting. At dinner he pushed his rice around. 'Maths result tomorrow. I'll fail. And Sayan hasn't replied all day, so he probably hates me.' Rehana, home from college for the Puja holidays, didn't tease him. 'That's a lot of weather for one evening.' He almost smiled. 'Everything's just annoying.' 'I remember that age. It swings like mad.' She paused. 'But if it ever stops you sleeping or going to school, tell me or your Ma, okay? We'd get you proper help.' He nodded, chewing slowly.

What did Anand snap at Rehana about?
Sitting in 'his' chair.
What mix of feelings did Anand go through that evening?
He swung from irritation to laughter to feeling disgusted with his looks, then worried about his result and afraid Sayan hated him.
What did Rehana get right?
She didn't tease, named the swings kindly as common at his age, and asked him to tell her or his Ma if they ever stopped his sleep or school, so he'd get proper help.
What might it be like for Rehana to be snapped at, then confided in?
Rehana may have been a little stung at first, but stayed patient, seeing the snapping as part of his changing moods.

During Ganesh Chaturthi the colony ground in Pune became a fair: stalls, lights and a hundred children eating vada pav. Vandana finished hers and dropped the paper plate by the swing. 'Dustbin's far,' she told Tanuja. 'Everyone does it.' Tanuja shrugged and dropped hers too. So did the boys by the slide, and the aunties by the stall. By the tenth day the ground where they played cricket every evening was carpeted with plates and cups, the swings smelled sour, and a stray dog had cut its paw on a broken cup. The colony secretary put up a notice: ground closed for cleaning, two weeks. Vandana stared at the chain across the gate. 'But it was just one plate,' she said.

Where did Vandana drop her paper plate?
By the swing.
How might Vandana feel staring at the chain across the gate?
Vandana feels shocked and a little guilty, realising her 'just one plate' added to the mess that closed the ground.
What could the children do to keep the ground open next festival?
Set up more bins near the swings and take turns reminding each other, so each small effort protects the shared ground.
What would change if Tanuja had carried both plates to the dustbin?
It might have nudged Vandana and others to do the same, so less rubbish would pile up.

Thursday night
Tutorial again. I'm Jatin, the TA for second-year organic chemistry, and today I watched Ayesha close her notebook before I'd even finished writing the problem on the board.
"I can't do mechanisms," she said. "I never could." The thing is, I've seen her answers in the viva. She understands more than she thinks.
I felt frustrated, not with her, with how fast she gave up. So I tried something. I went over and asked her only to draw the first arrow, just the first one, where the electrons move.
She stared at me like I was mad. Then she drew it. Right.
"Now the second?" She drew that too, slower.
By the end she had half the mechanism, and she looked almost annoyed at herself for doing it. I'll try the same thing next week, one arrow at a time.

What was the first thing Jatin asked Ayesha to draw?
Jatin asked her to draw only the first arrow, where the electrons move.
How did Jatin feel watching Ayesha close her notebook?
Jatin felt frustrated, not with Ayesha but with how quickly she gave up, knowing from the viva that she understands more than she thinks.
Why did asking for one arrow at a time work?
Each arrow was a task small enough to succeed at, so every correct one became evidence against her belief that she couldn't do mechanisms.
How does Ayesha feel by the end of the tutorial?
Ayesha seems almost annoyed at herself, surprised that she managed half the mechanism after saying she never could.

Vandana's school bag was covered in Neon Monsoon pins, and her phone wallpaper was the band's latest album cover. In her Pune classroom she was 'the Monsoon girl', and she liked it. Online she had friends in five cities who knew every lyric. So when Rashmi said at lunch, 'Their new song is honestly just noise,' Vandana's face went hot. 'You don't even understand their music,' she snapped, louder than she meant. The table went quiet. Rashmi raised her hands. 'Okay! It's just a song.' It wasn't just a song to Vandana. She spent the afternoon replaying the words, as if Rashmi had insulted her and not a band. That night she messaged Rashmi: 'Sorry I snapped. They just mean a lot to me.'

What was on Vandana's phone wallpaper?
The band's latest album cover.
Why did Vandana snap at Rashmi?
She felt hurt and defensive, as if criticism of the band was an attack on her.
What did Vandana do that helped the friendship afterwards?
She messaged Rashmi to apologise for snapping and explained that the band means a lot to her.
How might Rashmi have felt when Vandana snapped?
Surprised and a little hurt, since she thought she was just sharing an opinion about a song.
We bought some new furnitures for the living room. Please correct.

We bought some new furniture for the living room.
Why: uncountable noun ("furnitures" -> "furniture").

Afreen covered her face with her hands, laughing. "Rekha, you want to hear my most embarrassing work moment? First month at the agency. My manager sent a long email to the whole team about a client project. I meant to reply to my friend in the team saying, 'Ugh, another endless email.' I hit reply-all. It went to twenty people, including the client. I actually felt my heart stop. I sat there staring at my screen, hot all over. Then I went to my manager's desk and apologised before she could say anything. She was cool about it, but she gave me three rules I still use: read the 'To' line twice, never write anything in an email you wouldn't say to someone's face, and wait before pressing send if you're annoyed. I haven't made that mistake since."

How many people received Afreen's reply-all?
Twenty people, including the client.
What was Afreen feeling when she realised the mistake?
She was horrified and embarrassed, feeling her heart stop and going hot all over.
Why was going to the manager's desk right away a good move?
It showed honesty and responsibility, and gave the manager a chance to help before things got worse.
How might the client have seen that reply-all?
They may have felt a bit insulted or amused, which is why protecting professional tone in every email matters.

Divyansh, twenty-four, joined the public works department as a junior engineer in Jaipur. In his second month, a contractor handed him a bill for road work that hadn't been done yet. "Sign it. Your senior already has. It's how we all eat," the contractor said.
Divyansh's hands went cold. He said he needed to inspect the road first.
Over the next week, his colleagues stopped greeting him. Someone left a note on his desk: "Don't be a hero."
He went to Hansa Ma'am, a senior engineer known for her strict honesty. She listened, then opened the department's rulebook. "You're right to inspect first. Write a note on the file saying the work isn't complete. Date it. Keep a copy." She added, "If they pressure you further, we go to the vigilance cell together."
Divyansh wrote the note that afternoon. His hands were still shaking.

What did the note on Divyansh's desk say?
It said, "Don't be a hero."
What was Divyansh feeling when his hands went cold?
Divyansh felt frightened and uneasy, pressured to sign for work that hadn't been done.
How did Hansa Ma'am help protect Divyansh?
She confirmed he was right, showed him the rules, told him to write and date a note on the file, and offered to go to the vigilance cell with him.
How might Divyansh's colleagues see his refusal?
They probably see it as a threat to their arrangement, which is why they stopped greeting him and left the note.

"Lakshmi, you haven't touched your tea."
"I'm fine, Irfan."
"You're not."
She put the cup down. "Five years. We were going to move to Chennai together. We'd picked names for a dog we never got."
"I know."
"And he just said, 'I think we want different lives.' Like it was a weather report."
Irfan was quiet.
"It's not just him I lost. It's the whole future. The flat, the Sunday mornings, all of it. I planned my life around it."
"You're allowed to grieve all of that."

Irfan slid the tea closer. "Drink. I'm not going anywhere tonight."
She held the cup with both hands. "Thank you."

How long had Lakshmi's relationship lasted?
Five years.
What was Lakshmi feeling when her voice cracked?
She felt deep sorrow and grief, not just for the person but for the whole future she had planned.
What did Irfan do that helped Lakshmi?
Irfan listened quietly, said she was allowed to grieve, and stayed with her.
What is it like for Irfan to sit with Lakshmi's grief?
Irfan seems steady and caring, willing to stay with her pain without trying to fix it.
Now you try: 500 mL for ₹45 or 1 L for ₹84?

Where did Pradeep move to?
Pradeep moved to Manchester.
What did Pradeep feel on noticing Owen's face during the phone call?
Self-conscious but considerate; seeing the face made Pradeep take the call to the bedroom.
What did Pradeep and Owen do about the head wobble?
They settled on Pradeep saying yes out loud as well.

Puzzled, unsure whether it meant yes or no, which is why Owen asked, So, yes?
Bobby can deadlift 300 pounds at 13.  When he is 18 he can deadlift 100 pounds more than 250% of his previous deadlift.  How many pounds did he add per year?

His new deadlift is 300*2.5+100=850 pounds
So he added 850-300=550 pounds to his deadlift
This took 18-13=5 years
So he added 550/5=110 pounds per year
The answer is 110.

Raghav, come, sit up straight for your Naveen Dada, eh? I know that slump. When I was your age, ten, in our town near Mangaluru, I was the smallest and shyest boy in class. I walked hunched over, looking at my sandals. The more I hunched, the smaller I felt. Then our PE teacher, a big laughing man named Mr D'Costa, started a game every morning. What was Naveen's PE teacher called?
Mr D'Costa.
How did young Naveen feel walking hunched over?
Young Naveen felt shy and small, and the more he hunched, the smaller he felt.
What was the turning point in Naveen's story?
Playing the giraffe game every morning, which one day left Naveen standing tall and speaking louder at the blackboard.
How might Mr D'Costa have seen the shy boys in his class?

Afreen arrived at the club forty minutes early, as always, to watch Coach Jagdish set up cones. Everything he said she wrote in a small notebook: keep your knees soft, look up, move before the ball does. Her footwork got better every week and she glowed when he said her name. Then one Thursday, in the heat, he made a girl who had missed a pass run laps without water and told the team, "Don't mention today's drill at home. Parents don't understand training." Afreen felt a strange cold in her stomach. She wanted his approval more than anything, and she still believed most of what he taught her. But she thought, that isn't right. That evening she told her father exactly what had happened.

What would you advise Afreen to do about her coach?

How might the girl who ran the laps feel about Afreen telling her father?

Is 100 a term of the sequence 3, 8, 13, 18, ...? Is 98?

Answer: 100 is not a term; 98 is the 20th term.

T_n = 3 + 5(n - 1) = 5n - 2. Try 100: 5n - 2 = 100, 5n = 102, n = 20.4. There is no "20.4th" term: positions must be whole numbers. So 100 is NOT in the sequence. It lies between T_2_0 = 98 and T_2_1 = 103. Try 98: 5n - 2 = 98, 5n = 100, n = 20, a whole number, so 98 IS a term (the 20th). A quick check by pattern: every term ends in 3 or 8 (the terms are 2 less than multiples of 5), and 100 ends in 0. Common mistake: rounding 20.4 to 20 and saying "yes".

Rania had until Monday morning. On Friday her manager at a logistics firm in Amman had asked her to change the delivery dates in the shipment log so a late order would look on time for the client. 'Just this once,' he'd said, and walked off.
On Sunday evening she sat with her friend Dalia on the balcony and practised. 'Be him,' she said. 'Be annoyed.'
Dalia folded her arms. 'Rania, it's one date. Are you trying to make me look bad?'
Rania took a breath. 'No. I want to help fix the delay. I can't change the log, but I can write the client an honest update with a new date and what we're doing to prevent it again.'
'And if I say it's an order?'
'Then I'd ask for it in writing, so I understand it properly.' Her voice wobbled. They did it again. And again. By the fourth time, it didn't.
On Monday, when her manager raised it, the words were already there.

What might Rania's manager experience on Monday?

Mom wrote it in big letters on a notepad. Chen put his finger under the H. He made an H. Finger on the A. He made an A. The two Ps came out a bit wobbly. Letter by letter he got to the end, then held the card up next to Mom's page. "Same!" Mom grinned. The Y was backwards, but Leila wouldn't mind.

How can you tell Chen felt proud at the end?

Daisy's Flower Shop sold 45 daisies on its first day. On their second day, they sold 20 more flowers than they did on their first day. On the third day, they sold 10 less than twice the flowers that were sold than on the second day. If the flower shop sold a total of 350 daisies for 4 days, how many daisies were sold on the 4th day?

The flower shop sold 45 + 20 = 65 daisies on the second day.
Twice the number of flowers on the second day is 65 x 2 = 130.
So, the flower shop sold 130 - 10 = 120 daisies on the third day.
The total daisies sold for 3 days was 45 + 65 + 120 = 230.
Therefore, 350 - 230 = 120 daisies were sold on the 4th day.
The answer is 120.

What a match. When the last ball went for four, the whole East Stand jumped at once. Strangers hugged me. Pranav lifted me off my feet, screaming. I've never felt joy like that in a crowd, like one big body.
Then it changed, fast. At the exit ramp people kept surging forward, still singing, but the singing turned into shoving. My arms got pinned. A man behind us yelled "Push!" and nobody could. I saw Pranav's face go pale. Remembering the side gate we had noticed on the way in, I grabbed his sleeve and we edged sideways along the wall till we got out.
We stood on the road shaking and laughing at the same time. Next match: we pick the exit before the first ball, and we leave five minutes early if the ramp looks packed.

Subject: You were right about 'safe accounts'

Hi Thomas,
Weird week. On Tuesday someone rang saying they were from my bank's fraud team. They knew my name and the last four digits of my card. They said my account was compromised, that I had to move my savings to a 'safe account' before midnight, and not to tell anyone because 'the fraudster might be close to you'.
I'd moved £300 before something snagged. You once told me banks never ask you to move money.
So I hung up mid-sentence, opened the bank's own app and called from there. They froze the transfer and said calling within the hour really helped. Then I rang the fraud reporting line and told my flatmate, who made me toast and sat with me.
Still shaky, but mostly okay. Thank you for that random lecture last year.
Noor

How much had Noor moved before stopping?

What did Noor's quick steps achieve?

What might Thomas feel reading this email?
Thomas will probably feel relieved that Noor is safe and glad the random lecture mattered, perhaps with a pang at how close it was.

Mrs Kaur had a poster on the wall: "Getting help is caring, not tattling." At break Vikas saw a group of older boys tip Tarun's tiffin into the bin while a ring of children watched and giggled. Madhuri, eight months into the job, didn't raise her voice once. She repeated his words back, apologised for the stress, and read out the reversal reference slowly twice. Madhuri stared. "Including you?"

Every Monday at the architecture office in Oslo, the design review moved at the speed of the three senior partners. They finished each other's sentences, drew over each other's sketches and laughed at jokes from projects Ingrid hadn't worked on. For the school project she had noticed something on the site visit: the main stair faced the windiest corner of the yard, where children would queue in winter. She had drawn a fix in the margin of her notebook. Three times she leaned forward and opened her mouth; three times someone was already talking. Her cheeks grew warm, and she looked down at her sketch. Then Ivan, who chaired the review, put down his pen. "Ingrid, you've been drawing something since the site plan came up. Let's hear it. Everyone else, two minutes." Her voice shook on the first sentence. By the third, the partners were leaning over her notebook, and one of them said, "Why didn't we see that?"

What had Ingrid noticed on the site visit?
The main stair faced the windiest corner of the yard, where children would queue in winter.
How was Ingrid feeling after three tries to speak?
She felt shy and discouraged, her cheeks warm, pulling back to look at her sketch because the fast room left no opening.
What did Ivan do that a good chair should do?
He invited Ingrid by name, pointed to her work, and asked everyone else to stay quiet for two minutes so she could speak without interruption.
What would change if Ivan had not stepped in?
The stair problem might have gone unnoticed, and Ingrid would likely have stopped trying to speak in future reviews.
After geometry class, Bill wants to count how many lines he drew. For each shape, he drew one line per side. If he drew 12 triangles, 8 squares, and 4 pentagons, how many lines did he draw?

For the triangles, he drew 36 lines because 12 times 3 equals 36.
For the squares, he drew 32 lines because 8 times 4 equals 32.
For the pentagons, he drew 20 lines because 4 times 5 equals 20.
He drew 88 lines in total because 36 plus 32 plus 20 equals 88.
The answer is 88.

In Buenos Aires, Valentina was sure her band's first real gig would sell out. She booked the big hall downtown, not the small bar where they usually played. She paid the deposit from the money she'd saved for a trip. Felix, the drummer, said, "Maybe start smaller?" She laughed. "People love us. It'll be packed." She didn't plan what would happen if it wasn't. On the night, forty people came to a room built for four hundred. The echo made their songs sound thin. Valentina smiled on stage, but afterwards she sat in the empty hall, shaking. It wasn't only the money. She had been so certain that she'd never let herself imagine this. Felix sat beside her. "It's one night." "I know," she said. "It just feels like everything."

How many people came to the gig?
Forty people.
Why did the empty hall hurt Valentina so much?
She had been so certain of success that she never imagined failure, so the empty room felt crushing and she was left shaking.
What could Valentina have done to leave a margin for error?
She could have started with a smaller venue, as Felix suggested, or planned what to do if fewer people came.
How does Felix seem to respond to Valentina's disappointment?

In Berlin, Fatima noticed the same thing every morning at the university: students walking bikes with flat tyres, because the nearest repair shop was far and expensive.
She told her flatmate Jana, "What if we fix tyres on campus?"
Jana was practical. "Before you buy anything, test it."
They borrowed a pump and tools, bought a small box of tubes and patches, and made a sign: "Flat tyre? 10 minutes, Tuesday 8–10." The first Tuesday, three people came. The second, eleven.
Jana made a simple sheet: money in, money out. The tubes and patches cost more than they'd thought. They raised the price slightly for tube replacements and kept patches cheap.
By the end of the month, they'd covered their costs with a little left over. More importantly, they knew people actually wanted it.

Spot a real need, test it cheaply before investing, and track costs against income so prices cover what you spend.

Harly's animal shelter has 80 dogs. She adopts out 40% of them but then has to take back 5 because of personality conflicts with other dogs in their adopted homes. How many dogs does she have now?

First find how many dogs are adopted out: 80 dogs * 40% = 32 dogs
Then subtract the number of dogs adopted out from the total number of dogs and add the number who were returned to find the final number of dogs: 80 dogs - 32 dogs + 5 dogs = 53 dogs
The answer is 53.

"A bit. But mostly I'm starving and tired."
Vijay laughed with relief. "There's dal. I'll heat it."
She ate standing at the counter, rolling her shoulders. Ten minutes later she said, "Okay. About the sink. Can we take turns?"
"Sounds fair," Vijay said. "And good catch."

Since when had Ritu not eaten?
She hadn't eaten since eleven.
What did Ritu discover she was really feeling during her pause?
She realised she was mostly starving and tired, with a clenched jaw and tight shoulders, not mainly angry about the sink.
Which choice worked, and why?
Pausing to check her jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, because it showed hunger and fatigue before she snapped.
How did Vijay feel when Ritu stopped mid-sentence?
Vijay was wary at first, then relieved when she said she was mostly hungry and tired.

Melanie does her weekly shopping at the farmer's market.  She starts with an 8-ounce wheel of brie cheese.  Next is a 1 pound loaf of bread.  She grabs a pound of tomatoes and 2 pounds of zucchini.  After that, she grabs 1 1/2 pounds of chicken breasts and treats herself to 8 ounces of fresh raspberries and 8 ounces of fresh blueberries.  How many pounds of food does she buy?

She bought 8ounces of cheese, 8-ounce raspberries, 8 ounces of blueberries for a total of 8*3 = 24 ounces
16 ounces are in 1 pound and she has 24 ounces of food so she has 24/16 = 1.5 pounds of food
Those items are 1.5 pounds and she bought 1 pound of bread, 1 pound of tomatoes, 2 pounds of zucchini and 1.5 pounds of chicken for a total of 1.5+1+1+2+1.5 = 7 pounds of food
The answer is 7.

There are 3 rows of people relaxing at the beach. The first row is made up of 24 people until 3 people get up to wade in the water. 5 people from the second row, which originally held 20 people, go to join them. The third row is made up of 18 people. How many people are left relaxing on the beach?

In the first row, there are now 24 - 3 = 21 people.
In the second row, there are now 20 - 5 = 15 people.
So in total there are 21 in the first row + 15 in the second row + 18 in the third row = 54 people.
The answer is 54.
Are "ambiguous" and "ambivalent" the same? They look alike.

No. "Ambiguous" means having more than one possible meaning. "Ambivalent" means having mixed feelings about something.
Examples: The instructions were ambiguous. She felt ambivalent about moving.

Read this:

At the panchayat meeting in their village near Nashik, Kishore stood up, red in the face. "Urmila tai's family moved the boundary stone last monsoon! I remember it was near the mango tree."
Urmila had her own memory: the stone had always been by the well. She felt her anger rise, then made herself say, "This is how I remember it, but memory can be wrong. Let's look for something real."
She thought of her cousin's wedding photos from three years ago, taken in that field. On her phone, there it was: the stone, by the well, with the bride's red sari beside it. Kishore stared at the screen, then sat down slowly. "Maybe I mixed it up with another field."

Where was the stone in the wedding photo?
By the well.
What was Urmila feeling when Kishore accused her family?
She felt her anger rise, but chose to stay calm and humble about her own memory.
Why was "This is how I remember it" a wise way to start?
It kept Urmila open to being wrong and moved the dispute from two memories to real evidence.
How might Kishore feel after seeing the photo?
He may feel embarrassed but also relieved that a real record settled it without a fight.

Read this:

Afreen, you asked how the meme thing went wrong. So we have this group where we send a picture of a tired panda every time someone fails a test. It means 'I feel you, I've been there'. Last week Ranjan, a new kid, failed a maths quiz, and someone sent the panda. He wrote back, 'Are you saying I'm lazy?' And I realised: he doesn't know it means we're with him. For us, it's a hug. For him, it looked like teasing. I sent him a private message, 'That panda is our way of saying we've all failed too.' He replied with a thumbs-up. Next time I'll explain a joke before I use it. Zubin, over and out.

What picture does the group send when someone fails a test?
They send a picture of a tired panda.
Why did Ranjan ask whether he was being called lazy?
He did not know the panda was a friendly sign, so he read it as teasing about his failure and probably felt hurt or embarrassed.
What did Zubin do that helped?
Zubin sent Ranjan a private message explaining that the panda means everyone has failed too.
How might the friends who sent the panda have felt about Ranjan's reply?
They may have been surprised, since they meant it kindly.

Read this:

At the Sunday market near their colony, Francis stopped in front of the balloon seller. "Please, Hafsa Aunty! Please, please, please! Just one!" His voice wobbled, and his eyes filled.

"Not today, Francis," Hafsa Aunty said gently. "I know you really want one."

"Please! I'll be so good! Please!" He tugged her hand towards the balloons.

She crouched down. "The answer is still no. You can feel sad about it. I'm right here."

Francis sobbed for a minute, then wiped his nose on his sleeve. "Can we look at the fish stall?"

"Yes, we can."

Where did Francis stop?
In front of the balloon seller.
What was Francis feeling when his voice wobbled and his eyes filled?
He was most likely desperate for a balloon and sad to be told no. His promise to be "so good" suggests he hoped pleading would change her mind.
What did Hafsa Aunty do that taught Francis something useful?
She stayed calm and kind but kept the same answer, naming his feeling and staying with him, so he learnt that pleading does not change a firm no.
How might Hafsa Aunty feel while Francis pleads?
She probably feels sorry for him and a bit uncomfortable in the busy market, but she stays steady.

Summarize Victor's decision here in a sentence or two.

Nothing could be more complete than the alteration that had taken place in my feelings since the night of the appearance of the daemon. I had before regarded my promise with a gloomy despair as a thing that, with whatever consequences, must be fulfilled; but I now felt as if a film had been taken from before my eyes and that I for the first time saw clearly. The idea of renewing my labours did not for one instant occur to me; the threat I had heard weighed on my thoughts, but I did not reflect that a voluntary act of mine could avert it. I had resolved in my own mind that to create another like the fiend I had first made would be an act of the basest and most atrocious selfishness, and I banished from my mind every thought that could lead to a different conclusion.
Victor suddenly sees clearly that making a second creature would be deeply wrong and selfish. Though the monster's threat still worries him, he firmly decides never to continue the work.

Read this:

On the balcony of their flat in Valencia, Valentina had turned the laundry basket into a rocket. 'Abuela Rosa, why does the moon follow our car? Is it lonely?' Before Rosa could answer, Valentina was mashing banana into her cheese sandwich. 'Moon people eat this.' Her cousin Pablo laughed. 'That's silly.' Valentina's face fell. Rosa sat down on the tiles beside the basket. 'Silly? I call it research. What else do moon people eat?' Valentina brightened and began to list: 'Cold rice. Jam soup. And stars, but only on Sundays.'

What did Valentina mash into her cheese sandwich?
Banana.
How did Valentina feel when Pablo called it silly?
She felt hurt and deflated; her face fell until Rosa took the moon game seriously.
What did Abuela Rosa do that helped?
She sat down, called it research, and asked a question inside the game, giving Valentina room to keep imagining.
Why might Pablo see the sandwich so differently from Rosa?
Pablo sees only an odd mix of food, while Rosa sees a whole make-believe world and chooses to join it.

Read this:

Week one: Tanuja Ma'am noticed that Rafiq, who usually cracked jokes from the back row, had moved to a front corner and sat with his hood up. When a classmate teased him about his handwriting, he flushed and walked out. She let it go in class and later, privately, said, "You don't have to explain. I'm around if you want to talk."
Week three: Rafiq was eating lunch alone in the library. He answered her greeting with a shrug. She gave him a quiet job sorting books and didn't push.
Week five: The heaviness hadn't lifted. In an essay he wrote, "Everything feels grey and pointless lately." That same afternoon Tanuja gently asked if he would be okay with her talking to his parents and the school counsellor, Mr Thomas. He nodded. The counsellor saw Rafiq before home time, and Tanuja called his mother that evening.

Where was Rafiq eating lunch in week three?
Alone in the library.
What was Tanuja feeling when she read Rafiq's essay line?
She felt concerned, seeing that his sadness had lasted for weeks and was turning into hopelessness.
Which choice in week five mattered most, and why?
Gently involving his parents and the counsellor that same day, because lasting sadness and hopelessness need more than patience alone.
How might Tanuja's quiet approach have felt to Rafiq?
Probably safe and respectful; she gave him privacy and small tasks instead of pushing, so he could agree when she asked to involve others.
Which title does the third chapter in my class textbook have?
I can't see your textbook, so I don't know. Open the contents page at the front of the book.

Read this:

From his small town in Bundelkhand, Ramesh applied to thirty-one jobs in four months after his BCom. He got four interviews and no offers. Each rejection email felt like a door closing on his whole family's hopes.
One evening his younger brother Divyansh found him staring at the ceiling. "Show me the emails."
They read them together. Two companies had given reasons: "limited experience with accounting software" and "communication in English".
"That's not 'you're useless'," Divyansh said. "That's a list."
Ramesh joined a free accounting software course at the town library and started practising English interviews with Divyansh every night on the roof, even when they both felt silly.
Two more months, eleven more rejections. Then an offer from a firm in Jhansi. He framed the first rejection email as a joke. It still hung by his desk.

How many jobs did Ramesh apply to in four months?
Thirty-one jobs.
How did Ramesh feel about each rejection?
Ramesh felt crushed and heavy, as if each rejection closed a door on his family's hopes.
What turned rejection into something useful, and why?
Reading the emails for reasons and turning them into a list of skills to build, because it gave him specific steps instead of despair.
How might Divyansh have felt practising English with his brother on the roof?
Divyansh probably felt a bit silly but proud to help, and invested in Ramesh's success.

Read this:

[Thursday, 9:40 pm]
Hemant: Manoj! Your post in the main group was honestly the smartest thing anyone's said this week
Manoj: really?? i just wrote what i think
Hemant: That's the point bro. Most people your age are asleep. You actually SEE things
Hemant: Brothers voted. We want you to run the new members chat
Manoj: me?? i only joined 3 weeks ago
Hemant: Doesn't matter. You're one of us now ❤️
Manoj: nobody at school even talks to me like this
Hemant: School people won't get you. We do
Manoj: ok i'll do it. what do i have to do
Hemant: Just welcome new guys, keep the chat active. Morning check-in at 6, don't miss it 😊
Manoj: ok 🙏 thanks for trusting me
[Manoj sets the chat as pinned and turns off his class group notifications]

How long ago had Manoj joined when Hemant offered him a role?
Manoj had joined only 3 weeks ago.
What is Manoj feeling during this chat?
Manoj feels flattered and finally understood, as if he has found people who value him more than anyone at school.
What turning point is available to Manoj at this stage?
Manoj could notice how fast the praise and the role came, keep his class group on, and talk to a parent or teacher he trusts about the group before taking on duties.
How might Manoj's classmates experience him after this night?
They may notice him going quiet in the class group and drifting away, without knowing he now spends his mornings and evenings in the other chat.
We have never travelled just the two of us, but Priya and I are planning a trip to Rishikesh.
That sounds like a fun adventure, and travelling as a pair for the first time is exciting. How long is the trip going to be?
Three days. We are going by train from Delhi.
Three days is a good length. Book your tickets and a place to stay early. Share the plan with your families, including addresses and phone numbers, so everyone feels at ease.
We are also thinking of river rafting. I am a little scared.

Rafting is usually done with trained guides and life jackets. Pick a registered operator and follow the instructions carefully. It is fine to be nervous, and you can choose a gentler stretch of the river.
Good. What if Priya and I disagree during the trip?
Small disagreements happen. Agree before you go that you will say what you want plainly and that either of you can ask for a break. Splitting up for an hour can also help.
Okay. Remind me where we are going and how we are travelling?
You are going to Rishikesh for three days, travelling by train from Delhi. Book the train and your stay early, and tell both families the plan before you and Priya leave.
How can I ask for water politely? Use a question of five words or fewer.
Could I have some water?

Read this:

Dear Deepika,

I joined the water-rights march on Sunday, and I want to tell you how it felt. We gathered at the park gate and walked together to the town hall, chanting a line the organisers gave us. It was surprising how quiet I felt inside. My legs were shaky at first, but the calm of the crowd carried me. Before we started, I noted the two exits, kept my phone charged, and stayed near the marshals with bright bands. When the crowd got tight near the main road, I stepped to the side. I'm glad I went. It felt good to say something with my body, not just my posts. Come next time, if you want.

Trisha

Where did the marchers gather?
They gathered at the park gate.
What did Trisha feel during the march, and what helped Trisha?
Trisha felt quiet inside after being shaky at first, and the calm of the crowd carried Trisha along.
What safety steps did Trisha take that a wise person might copy?
Trisha noted the exits, kept the phone charged, stayed near the marshals and stepped aside when the crowd got tight.
How might Deepika feel reading Trisha's invitation?
Deepika may feel curious and a little cautious, since Trisha describes both the calm and the precautions Trisha took. 🙂

Read this:

Last year I shared a flat in Hyderabad with Lalit and two others. I'm Kunal, and I'll admit I was the worst kind of flatmate: the one who thinks he's not the problem.
Our kitchen had one rule, "clean as you go," which nobody followed. I would leave a greasy kadhai overnight, telling myself Lalit was messier. Lalit, I found out later, told himself the same about me.
By exam week, we were ordering food every night because no one could face the stove. We spent more, ate worse, and snapped at each other over small things.
Looking back, what strikes me is how reasonable each small choice felt. One kadhai. One night.

What was the kitchen's one rule?
Their rule was "clean as you go."
How does Kunal seem to feel looking back on the greasy kadhai?
Kunal feels a mix of regret and embarrassment, seeing that each small, reasonable-seeming choice added up to a kitchen nobody could use.
What could the flatmates have done instead of a rule nobody followed?
They could have set a simple turn for washing up, with each person's name, so no one could assume someone else would do it.
How does Lalit seem to have seen the mess?
Lalit told himself Kunal was messier, so he also felt his own part was too small to matter.

Creche note, winter afternoon

Sarita (2) cried and kicked when Chaitanya took the red crayon. She would not take the green one. She pushed away her cup of milk and screamed when I tried to take her coat off. It was well past her nap time; the cold had kept everyone up late.
I dimmed the lights, wrapped her in her blanket and sat by her. She fell asleep in minutes. After her nap she woke smiling and gave Chaitanya a crayon.

What did Chaitanya take that made Sarita cry?
Chaitanya took the red crayon.
Why did the small crayon swap upset Sarita so much?
She was very tired and past her nap time, so she felt cross and overwhelmed by little things.
What did the note-writer do that helped Sarita?
They dimmed the lights, wrapped her in her blanket and sat by her so she could sleep.
How might Chaitanya see Sarita after her nap?
Chaitanya probably finds her friendly again, since she wakes smiling and shares a crayon.

I'm Nandini, and I help run the Sunday maths club in our building's hall. Here's what I saw with Farida, who's ten. We were forming teams for the number puzzles. Farida marched up to Pranit, who wears thick glasses and barely speaks, and said, "You're with me." Then Gogi, who is loud and was doing cartwheels near the door, asked to join. Farida said, "No thanks, you'll just mess around." I don't know exactly what was in her head. But she kept glancing at Pranit's glasses like they were a guarantee. In the round, Pranit froze; he'd never done this kind of puzzle. Gogi, on another team, finished first and whooped. Farida went red. Later I saw her ask Gogi to show her his trick. Maybe she learned something.

What was Gogi doing near the door when he asked to join?
He was doing cartwheels near the door.
Why might Farida have thought Pranit was a guarantee?
He looked like her idea of a clever child, with thick glasses and a quiet manner, so choosing him felt safe. Gogi's loudness seemed to mean he would not be serious.
After the round, what did Farida choose to do, and why does it matter?
She asked Gogi to show her his trick. That shows she was willing to learn from what she saw rather than stick to her first guess.
How might Pranit feel being picked because of his glasses?
Pranit may feel pressure to be a genius and embarrassed when he freezes, since he had never done this kind of puzzle.
40% of a farmer's cattle are males. The rest are females. If a female cow produces 2 gallons of milk a day, how much milk will the farmer get a day if he has 50 male cows?

The farmer has 125 cows because 50 / .4 = 125
The farmer has 75 female cows because 125 x .6 = 75
The farmer will get 150 gallons of milk a day because 75 x 2 = 150
The answer is 150.

In a housing society garden in Delhi, Amandeep flung a handful of sand into the air. Minakshi knelt in front of him. "Sand stays down, puttar." He frowned, looked at her face, then slowly opened his fist and let the sand fall. A moment later his Biji came along the path with her walking stick. Amandeep dropped his spade, toddled to her, patted her knee and held the spade up for her to see.

What did Amandeep fling into the air?
He flung a handful of sand into the air.
What was Amandeep thinking when he frowned and looked at Minakshi's face?
He seemed to be weighing whether to keep playing his way, and her calm face helped him decide to follow what she said.
What made Minakshi's guidance easy for Amandeep to follow?
She got down to his level and gave one short, clear rule instead of shouting from a distance.
How might Biji see Amandeep toddling to her with his spade?
She would probably feel loved and pleased that he wanted to share his play with her.

And soon he beheld the victorious monkey troops encamped before him. And passing them by with the object of seeking out Rama, he beheld the son of Sumitra standing at his post, bow in hand. Then the monkey warriors, speedily advancing towards him, surrounded him on all sides. And then they commenced to strike him with numberless large trees.

Kumbhakarna has just left the city. What happens when the monkey warriors see him?
They rush at him, surround him and strike him with countless large trees.

Note from the tutor, Saturday. Sumit stared at three-fourths in his book and said, "It's just two numbers stuck together." His mother came out of the kitchen with a roti, cut it into four equal parts, and put three on his plate. Sumit looked at his plate, and then at the single piece left on the tray. "So the top number is how many I have," he said slowly. "And the bottom is how many parts it was cut into." He drew four boxes in his notebook and shaded three. I said nothing. He explained it to me twice. Chaitanya, tutor

How many parts of the roti did Sumit's mother put on his plate?
She cut it into four equal parts and put three on his plate.
What was Sumit feeling before his mother brought the roti, and what changed?
He was puzzled and cut off from the idea, since three-fourths seemed like two numbers stuck together. After he saw the food, he became interested and eager to explain.
What alternative approach could Sumit use to understand other fractions, and why?
He could fold a paper into equal parts and shade some. Seeing the parts in something he can hold makes the number less abstract.
How might Sumit's mother see what happened at the table?
She may feel glad that a small thing from the kitchen made her son understand. She did not explain the number, only cut the roti.

Tushar's day in Jalna began before light. He helped his father, stiff from arthritis, to the bench outside and brought him tea and his pills in the order the doctor had written. Then he walked the field boundary where he had planted neem saplings last monsoon; six of the ten had survived.

At ten, three younger farmers from the next village came to see his drip lines. Pallavi, the youngest, had lost half her soybean crop last year to dry weeks. Tushar walked her through each pipe and valve, then said, "Don't copy me exactly. Your soil holds water better. Try two rows first."

That evening his father asked why he bothered with the neem trees. "They won't give shade for years."

Tushar poured his father more tea. "Not for me, Baba. For whoever farms here next."

How many of the ten neem saplings had survived?
Six of the ten had survived.
Why does Tushar bother planting trees that won't give shade for years?
He feels hopeful about the future and wants the land to be better for whoever farms it after him.
What was good about the way Tushar mentored Pallavi?
He explained the system clearly but told her to adapt it to her own soil and start small, which respects her situation instead of just making her copy him.
How might Tushar's father feel about his son's daily care?
He may feel grateful and cared for, and perhaps also a little puzzled by his son's long-term thinking.

Class teacher's note, 6A savings project, week 5. Harish came to me looking flat. He is saving for a Rs 1,000 telescope and said, 'It's never going to happen. I've only got Rs 150.' He had noticed himself that he was losing interest. I asked what might help. After a while he said, 'Maybe I stop looking at 1,000.' He drew a new line on his chart at Rs 200. Last Friday he reached it and the class clapped, which he loved. He has now drawn the next line at 400. Farida, who sits beside him, has split her own goal into steps too.

What is Harish saving for?
A Rs 1,000 telescope.
How did Harish feel when he came to the teacher?
He looked flat and discouraged, sure the telescope was never going to happen.
What helped Harish, and whose idea was it?
His own idea to stop looking at 1,000 and aim for Rs 200 first; reaching it and being clapped for rebuilt his patience.
How does Farida respond to Harish's approach?
Farida, beside him, has split her own goal into steps too, so she seems to find the idea useful.

Kalyani had been messaging Dhruv for two weeks, and today, on the steps behind the library, she said it lightly: “Send me a picture, a private one, and we could meet at the mall alone on Sunday.” Dhruv's ears burned. He liked her. But something inside him said no, quietly and clearly.
“I'm not ready to send private pictures,” he said. “And I don't want to meet alone yet.”
“Come on, it's nothing.”
“It's something to me.” His voice wobbled, but he didn't say sorry. “I'd love to talk at school, or go with the group.”
Kalyani shrugged, hurt or maybe annoyed, and said, “Fine.” Dhruv let the silence sit and walked to class, his heart pounding and himself oddly lighter.

Where were Dhruv and Kalyani when she asked?
They were on the steps behind the library.
What was Dhruv feeling as he said no?
Dhruv was nervous but firm, since his ears burned and his voice wobbled, yet he held his limit and felt lighter afterwards.
What could Dhruv do if Kalyani keeps pressing?
Dhruv could repeat the limit calmly, and step away or tell a trusted adult if the pressure continues.
How might Kalyani feel after the refusal?
Kalyani may feel hurt, embarrassed or annoyed, since she shrugged and said fine, and what she does afterwards shows whether she respects the no.

messages.content: Write about a grandmother's shawl that keeps whoever wears it warm and brave.

Dadi's red shawl was a family treasure. It was soft, with golden thread at the edges. It had a magic: whoever wore it felt warm, and braver than before.

Her granddaughter Kiran wore it when she had to speak in assembly. She stood on the stage, shaking. Then she pulled the shawl around her shoulders and felt a warm hum.

She spoke clearly, and everyone clapped.

Her cousin Raj wore it when he went to the dentist. It helped him open his mouth wide.

When Kiran grew up and had a daughter of her own, she wrapped the shawl around her. The baby smiled, and the shawl glowed ever so slightly.

Dadi, watching from her chair, nodded and sipped her tea.

Read this:

The monsoon had knocked the power out across the colony, and the last bus was cancelled. Sumit stood at Mridul's door with a wet book bag. "Sorry, I only came to return your jacket. Can I wait it out?"

Mridul lit a candle and made chai on the gas. They had been "friends" for two months, and he had told himself it was going fine. Yet his pulse jumped when Sumit laughed.

They talked easily until Sumit mentioned a girl he'd met at a workshop, smiling into the candlelight. Mridul kept his face still and felt his stomach sink.

When the rain slowed, he walked Sumit to the gate. "I think I need some space," he said. "Being friends right now is harder for me than I thought. I'd like to try again later, maybe."

Sumit nodded, quietly. "I'm sorry. I get it."

Why had Sumit come to Mridul's door on that stormy evening?
He came to return Mridul's jacket, and then had to wait out the storm because the last bus was cancelled.
What was Mridul feeling when Sumit spoke about a girl from a workshop?
His stomach sank; he still hoped, so hearing about someone new hurt while he kept his face still.
What did Mridul do that showed honesty about the friendship, and why is distance a good first step?
He told Sumit the friendship was harder than he expected and asked for space, which stops him staying close just to keep a door open.
How might Sumit have felt when Mridul asked for space?
Sumit may have felt sorry and a little surprised, but he understood, so he respected the request without arguing.

Read this:

Last Onam, our school held the inter-house quiz, and I was captain of Blue House. I'm Jeevan, and I wore my blue badge even to bed. Salma was captain of Red. In the final round Red won by one question, about the capital of Peru. I felt it in my chest, as if someone had taken something of mine. So in the corridor I said loudly, 'Red only won because Salma's father is a teacher.' It wasn't true. Everyone knew it wasn't true. Salma's face went still. Now I think I wanted Blue to be better so badly that I had to make Red worse. I apologised a week later, at the pookalam competition. She accepted, but she didn't smile. I still wear the badge. I just don't say those things.

What was the final quiz question about?
The capital of Peru.
How did Jeevan feel when Red won by one question?
Jeevan felt hurt, as if something personal had been taken, and resentful towards Red.
What could Jeevan do at the next house event?
Jeevan could cheer Blue proudly and congratulate Red if they win, keeping the pride without mocking the other side.
How did Salma feel hearing the comment about her father?
Salma felt hurt and insulted, her face going still at an unfair accusation.

messages.content:
What makes Kunti pay attention to the Brahmana's household?

That day, O Bharata, Kunti heard a loud and heart-rending wail of sorrow coming from within the apartments of the Brahmana. Hearing the inmates of the Brahmana's house wailing and indulging in piteous lamentations, Kunti, O king, from compassion and the goodness of her heart, could not bear it with indifference.
She hears loud, heartbroken crying from inside their rooms. Being kind and caring, she cannot ignore their sorrow.
When someone says "hold on", what should I do?

You should wait for a short time. "Hold on" can also mean to hold something tightly.
Examples: Hold on, I will get my keys. Hold on to the rail when the train starts.

Thursday.
Got the state scholarship! Full fees and hostel. I read the email five times.
My first instinct was to post it everywhere, all caps. I actually typed, "TOLD YOU ALL I'D DO IT." Then I thought about Rafi and Joel, who applied too and didn't get it. And about how that post would feel to them. Deleted it.
Instead I called Ammi first. She cried. Then I texted Madhuri, who spent three evenings helping me fix my essay: "We did it. Your edits are in there." She replied with twenty exclamation marks.
In the evening I posted just a photo of my acceptance letter with "Grateful to everyone who helped. Especially Madhuri and Ammi." Rafi commented "Congrats bro, well deserved." That felt better than any all-caps post could have.
— Wasim

Who spent three evenings helping Wasim fix the essay?
Madhuri.
What was Wasim feeling when first reading the email?
Wasim felt thrilled and proud, reading it five times and wanting to post it everywhere.
What made Wasim's final post better than the first draft?

When you add up all the girls from all 4 classes, you had 12+15+9+10= 46 girls
When you add up all the boys from all 4 classes, you had 13+11+13+11 = 48 boys
There are 48 boys and 36 girls so 48-46 = 2 more boys

Bianca worked for 12.5 hours last weekend. Celeste worked for twice that amount of time and McClain worked 8.5 hours less than Celeste. How many minutes did the 3 people work in total?

Celeste 2 * 12.5 = 25 hours

Total + 12.5 + 25 + 16.5 = 54 hours

Prove that sqrt2 is irrational. Use the same method to prove that sqrt3 and sqrt5 are irrational.

Answer: Assume sqrtp = a/b in lowest terms; then p divides a and p divides b, a contradiction.

First a THEOREM from the FTA: if a prime p divides a^2, then p divides a. Reason: write a = p_1p_2...p_n (primes); then a^2 = p_1^2p_2^2...p_n^2, and by uniqueness the only primes in a^2 are p_1, ..., p_n. If p divides a^2, p is one of them, so p divides a. Now the proof for sqrt3 (by contradiction): Step 1: suppose sqrt3 is rational: sqrt3 = a/b where a, b are integers, b != 0, and a, b are COPRIME (no common factor other than 1). Step 2: then bsqrt3 = a, and squaring, 3b^2 = a^2. So 3 divides a^2, hence (by the theorem) 3 divides a. Write a = 3c. Step 3: then 3b^2 = 9c^2, so b^2 = 3c^2. So 3 divides b^2, hence 3 divides b. Step 4: now 3 divides both a and b, which contradicts 'coprime'. So the supposition is false and sqrt3 is irrational. For sqrt2 and sqrt5 replace every 3 by 2 or by 5. The proof needs p PRIME: for sqrt4 Step 2 would say '4 divides a^2, so 4 divides a', which is false (4 divides 36 but not 6), and indeed sqrt4 = 2 is rational.

On Wednesday she does twice as many push-ups as she did on Tuesday, 7 x 2 = 14 push-ups on Wednesday.
Over the first 3 days, she did a total of 14 + 12 = 26 pushups
On Thursday Miriam did 1/2 the same number of total pushups she had already done that week, so she did 1/2 x 26 = 13 pushups on Thursday.
On Friday she does as many push-ups as the total of what she had done over the previous four days, so she did 5 + 7 + 14 + 13 = 39 push-ups on Friday.
The answer is 39.

Gwen received a $900 bonus at work and decided to invest this money in the stock market.  She spent one-third of her bonus on stock A, one-third on stock B, and the remaining one-third on stock C.   After one year, stock A and stock B had doubled in value, while stock C had lost half of its value.  At the end of the year, how much were Gwen's stocks worth, in dollars?

One-third of her bonus was $900/3 = $300.
After one year, stock A doubled in value and was worth $300*2 = $600.
After one year, stock B doubled in value and was worth $300*2 = $600.
After one year, stock C had lost half its value and was worth $300/2 = $150.
Altogether, at the end of the year, Gwen's stocks were worth $600+$600+$150 = $1350
The answer is 1350.

The position vectors of A and B are a = (2, 3) and b = (7, -1). Find AB, BA and a - b. Explain why AB = b - a.

Answer: AB = (5, -4), BA = (-5, 4), a - b = (-5, 4).

Going from A to B we can go via the origin: A to O is -a, then O to B is b. So AB = -a + b = b - a: AB = b - a = (7 - 2, -1 - 3) = (5, -4) BA = a - b = (2 - 7, 3 - (-1)) = (-5, 4) = -AB Subtracting a vector means adding its opposite: a - b = a + (-b). Watch the double negative: 3 - (-1) = 4. This is exactly the rule "end minus start" from D2. Common mistake: AB = a - b (that is BA).

Tanuja had just come back from the records desk, where a clerk asked whether 'the other son, Mr Deepak' should be informed too. Her father had no son. Or so she had thought. The aunts' voices rose. Mausi snapped that Tanuja's father had always been careless with family. Tanuja felt the words sitting on her tongue, a way to win the argument in one sentence. She kept quiet. At lunch she found Ishita, the hospital counsellor she knew from college. 'I don't know if it's mine to tell,' Tanuja said. 'Or if Papa should, when he's well.' Ishita asked, 'Who needs to know now, for his care, and who can wait?' That evening Tanuja told only her mother, gently, and they decided to ask Papa together once he was out of danger.

Who did the clerk ask about at the records desk?
'The other son, Mr Deepak', whom Tanuja had not known about.
What was Tanuja tempted to do during the aunts' argument, and why did she hold back?
She felt an angry pull to win the argument by revealing the secret, but held back, unsure it was hers to tell.
How did Ishita's question help Tanuja decide?
It split the problem into who needs to know now for Papa's care and who can wait, so Tanuja told only her mother.
How might Tanuja's mother experience that evening conversation?
She hears hard news gently and in private, and is included in deciding how to raise it with Papa, rather than hearing it in a family fight.

Class teacher's note, 9B, Friday.
Shalini asked this morning to be moved away from Kavitha. They have sat together since Class 5. Yesterday they argued over a shared lunch box that was left open and ants got in; I heard raised voices. Shalini told me, "She's always been selfish, ma'am. I just didn't see it." When I asked for another example, she couldn't give one. Then she remembered, on her own, that Kavitha had brought her notes every day when she was ill for weeks last year, and she went quiet. I have not moved the seat yet. I suggested they each tell the other one thing they were upset about, with me nearby if they want. I'll check with both on Monday.

How long have Shalini and Kavitha sat together?
Since Class 5.
Why does Shalini say Kavitha has "always been selfish"?
Yesterday's argument is fresh and hurts, so it feels like the real Kavitha, even though Shalini can't name another example.
What did the teacher do that helped, and why?
Asking for another example let Shalini remember Kavitha's kindness on her own, and not moving the seat yet gave the friendship a chance.
How might Kavitha feel if she learned Shalini wanted to change seats?
Kavitha might feel shocked and hurt that one argument over a lunch box outweighed years of sitting together and bringing notes.
Can you suggest a good timetable for the week before exams?
Of course. A good timetable depends on how many subjects you have and how strong you are in each one. Can you tell me which subjects you are taking?
Maths, science, English, social studies and Hindi. My name is Meera.
Thanks, Meera. Pick one main subject per day for deeper study, and use a short slot each day to glance at the others. Put the harder subjects early in the week.
Maths and science are hardest for me.
Then give maths the first day and science the second. English and Hindi need less cramming, so they can share a day. Keep the last day for social studies and a quick overall check.
Perfect. What day is science again?
Science is on the second day, right after maths on the first. Meera, keep the evenings light with ten minutes of review on the previous day's subject, so it stays fresh.

Dear Diary,
Holi, evening.

Today someone broke Nani's clay pot on the terrace while we were playing with colours. Everyone was accused. Nani asked, "Who did it?"

I said, "Not Noor. Noor would never lie." Noor is the tallest in our building and always laughing and everyone loves her.

Then Ishan's little brother said, "I saw Noor bump it with her pichkari."

I didn't believe him at first. But Noor went red and said, "It was an accident. Sorry, Nani."

I felt weird. I was so sure Noor couldn't have done it. Just because she's tall and cheerful, I thought she was also honest about everything.

Nani wasn't even angry. She just said, "Accidents happen. Help me sweep."

Raghav

Where was Nani's clay pot broken?
On the terrace while we were playing with colours.
Why was Raghav so sure Noor hadn't broken the pot?
Raghav felt admiration for Noor, because she was tall, cheerful and loved by everyone, so it seemed impossible she'd do anything wrong.
What could Raghav do next time something like this happens?
Raghav could wait to hear what actually happened before deciding who is honest.
How did Noor seem to feel when she was seen?
Noor went red, looking embarrassed, and then owned up and said sorry.
Combine these three short sentences into one smooth one: Tara opened the box. It was empty. She felt puzzled.
When Tara opened the box, it was empty, and she felt puzzled.
Is my cousin's new friend nice?
I don't know them, as I can't see details about private people. Meet them first and decide for yourself.

A hurricane is a very violent storm with extremely strong winds and heavy rain, which forms over warm oceans. It is a noun.

On a wet Sunday, ten-year-old Pranav opened a building set with four hundred pieces and a picture of a crane on the box. His mother Rekha called him for lunch. He did not hear. She called again, and he waved a hand. When she came in, the plate was cold, the light had changed, and he was fitting the last arm in place, tongue between his teeth. "Was it hard?" she asked. "Just hard enough," he said, and blinked as if waking up. Five years later, Pranav sat cross-legged with a guitar, working a chord change that kept buzzing. His friend Kunal texted about a game night, and the phone buzzed on the bed. Pranav did not touch it. He played the change slowly, then a bit faster, until his fingers landed clean. When he looked up, an hour had gone. His shoulders were loose and his mind felt clear. He picked up the phone at last, typed to Kunal that he'd come after dinner, and went back to the strings for one more round.

What was pictured on the box of Pranav's building set?
The box had a picture of a crane on it.
How is Pranav's absorption at ten similar to and different from his practice at fifteen?

At ten he lost track of lunch and light while building the crane, and at fifteen he lost track of time and his phone while working the chord change. Both tasks were hard enough to need his attention, and both left him calm and clear.
What was Pranav probably feeling when he said the crane was just hard enough?
He felt quietly satisfied and pleasantly challenged, and he seemed to wake up from being absorbed.
What could Pranav do to keep enjoying this kind of focus?
He could pick pieces or songs a little harder than the last, and keep his phone away while he works on them. 🙂

At dinner my sister Arohi and her friend Kavita were joking about who'd win the class quiz. Kavita said she'd win because she'd memorised all the capitals.
Arohi raised both eyebrows high, tilted her head and said, "Oh, reeeally?"
Kavita raised hers back even higher. "Yes, reeeally!" They both burst out laughing. I've seen them do this a hundred times.
Then Arohi turned to our cousin Meenal, who's new to the city, and raised an eyebrow when she said she liked cricket. Meenal's smile froze. She looked at her plate.
I couldn't tell if she was hurt or just shy. Arohi noticed too, and added quickly, "That means cool! You can join our team."
Meenal smiled again, a bit slowly.
- Akash

What did Kavita say she had memorised?
All the capitals.
What might Meenal have been feeling when her smile froze?
She may have felt unsure or hurt, not knowing if the raised eyebrow was friendly, though Akash couldn't tell if she was just shy.
What did Arohi do that helped Meenal?
She noticed the change and quickly explained the eyebrow meant "cool", inviting Meenal to join.
How does Kavita see Arohi's eyebrow raise compared with Meenal?
Kavita knows it's playful banter and raises hers back, while Meenal, being new, wasn't sure what it meant.

messages.content: Why are some bridges built with arches? One more thing: how do I prepare for a long walk or trek with friends?

1. Arches spread weight sideways into the supports. Because the curved shape turns the weight pressing down into forces pushing sideways, the bridge can carry heavy loads.
2. Wear comfortable shoes, carry water and tell someone at home where you are going. Walk at a pace that suits the slowest person.

In Ms Layla's class in Lisbon, Sofia slumped in her chair with her chin on her hand, staring at the ceiling. “Sit up, Sofia,” said Ms Layla. “We are learning about rivers.” Sofia straightened, but her eyes stayed on the ceiling. Ms Layla waited. After a moment Sofia said, “The river doesn't always flow to the sea. Sometimes it flows into a bigger river.” Ms Layla raised her eyebrows. “Yes. Good thinking.” Sofia looked pleased. “I think better when I lean.”

What was Ms Layla teaching about?
She was teaching about rivers.
What did Ms Layla probably think about Sofia's slouch at first, and what else did it mean?
She probably thought Sofia was not paying attention, then was pleasantly surprised when Sofia's answer showed she had been thinking hard. Ms Layla raised her eyebrows and said, "Good thinking."
What could Ms Layla do next time she sees a slouch?
Give a little time or ask a question first, since posture is a clue and not proof of attitude.
How might Sofia feel about being told to sit up?
Perhaps a bit misunderstood, since she was thinking. She still answered politely and seemed pleased when praised.
