My name is Tara and I am in the same class as Mridul. At playtime a big boy grabbed Sumit's cap and held it up high. Sumit is Mridul's brother. This morning on the bus they were shouting at each other, so I thought Mridul would go away. But he walked over and stood right next to Sumit. His hands were shaking a little, but maybe he was just cold, I don't know. He said, "Give it back." Then he took Sumit's hand and they went to tell Miss. I saw them talking to her.

What did the big boy take from Sumit?
The big boy grabbed Sumit's cap.
What might Mridul have been feeling as he stood beside Sumit?
Mridul may have been scared but wanted to protect his brother. Tara notices his shaking hands but says she cannot be sure, so it is only a clue.
What did Mridul do that was wise, and what else could he try?
Mridul stood by Sumit and then went to tell Miss instead of fighting. If the boy keeps bothering them, they can keep telling a teacher. 👍
How might Sumit see it when Mridul stands next to him?
Sumit may feel safe and cared for, even though they were shouting on the bus. It shows that being brothers can matter more than an argument.
Let me read a story about a girl who volunteers to read to younger children and finds a surprising friend.

Every Friday, Seema, a Class 9 student, read picture books to the Class 1 children. One boy, Aryan, sat at the back, silent, never smiling. One Friday, she asked what he liked. He mumbled that he liked trucks, but nobody read about trucks. The next week, she brought a book about road-building machines. Aryan sat at the front and watched every page with big eyes. He asked the names of each truck. She did not know them all, so she looked them up and told him the following Friday. By the end of the term, he was standing on a chair, explaining excavators to the entire class, while Seema sat, quietly proud, taking notes.

"Still maths partners?"

Mentoring note, week 6. Written by Elizabeth, graduate programme mentor, Leeds office.
Baljeet told me today that she had been dreading her one-to-ones with Graham, the director. "He leans right back with his hands behind his head while I talk," she said. "At home, that would mean he doesn't care." In her last job in Chandigarh, she said, senior people sat very upright and juniors stood.
I have watched Graham with her for six weeks. The lean-back is how he sits with everyone, including the chief executive. More telling: he has read every draft she has sent and forwarded her analysis to the board with her name on it.
I shared this with Baljeet and suggested she judge him by what he does over time rather than how he sits. She laughed and said, "So the lean-back isn't an insult?"
Next step: we will review in a month how the one-to-ones feel.

Where was Baljeet's last job?
In Chandigarh.
What was Baljeet feeling about the one-to-ones with Graham?
She felt dread and some hurt, reading his lean-back as not caring, based on how seniors sat in her last job.
What did Elizabeth suggest, and why is it sensible?
To judge Graham by what he does over time rather than how he sits, since reading her drafts and crediting her to the board show real interest.
How does Graham's posture look from Elizabeth's six weeks of watching?
Elizabeth sees the lean-back as simply his habit with everyone, even the chief executive, not a sign of disrespect toward Baljeet.

Procurement review note. Written by Gautam, purchase head, 22 August.
I sat in on Santosh's first supplier negotiation today, for the packaging order. He is twenty-five and has been with us eight months.
I expected him to push on price, as juniors usually do. Instead he opened by telling the supplier plainly that our real problem was late deliveries in the festival season, not cost. Then he asked, "What makes our orders difficult for you?"
The supplier admitted our last-minute size changes caused most of their delays. Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance. In return the supplier agreed to guaranteed festival-season dates and a small discount.
Both sides left relaxed. Nobody was bluffing.
Next steps: I have asked Santosh to write up his approach for the team meeting, and I will propose we adopt the six-week size freeze across all packaging orders.

How far ahead did Santosh offer to freeze sizes?
Santosh offered to freeze sizes six weeks in advance.
What does Gautam's note suggest about Gautam's feelings watching Santosh?
Gautam expected a junior to push hard on price, so Gautam seems pleasantly surprised and impressed that Santosh chose honesty and curiosity instead.
What made Santosh's negotiation work for both sides?
He named the company's real need truthfully, asked what made orders difficult for the supplier, and traded a size freeze for reliable dates.
How might the supplier feel about working with this company now?
The supplier likely feels heard and less stressed, since the fix for last-minute changes makes their work easier, so they may want to keep the deal.

When Kofi's mother died, the whole office in Manchester signed a big card. Soo-ah signed it too, but it felt too small. She remembered that when her own grandmother died, what she had needed most was someone to take care of dinners. So she started a meal rota and asked eight colleagues to cover one evening each. She dropped off a pot of spiced rice with a note that just said, 'No need to reply.' At the funeral she didn't try to give a speech; she stood at the back and stacked chairs afterwards. Two weeks later, Kofi came back to work and stopped by her desk. 'I didn't eat properly for days. Then the food started arriving. Thank you.'

Organising regular meals, adding a 'No need to reply' note, and helping quietly at the funeral instead of making speeches.

He hadn't been eating properly for days, so the meals likely felt like real care and relief.

The monsoon reaches Kerala in early June every year.

When Kavya asked me for "a private pic, just for me" last spring, I stared at my phone for an hour. I'm Nitin. I liked her a lot, the kind of liking where you keep checking who's online. I didn't want to lose her, but I also knew I wasn't sending that. My friend Vijay said, "Don't write a long sorry essay. Just say it." So the next day in the canteen I said, "I like you. Noa's father had been in and out of the Auckland hospital since winter, and Noa kept picturing a 3 a.m. phone call. So one Saturday Noa sat at the kitchen table with a folder and a question: what would I be searching for in a panic?
"The prescriptions," Noa said aloud to Jin, their flatmate. "The discharge letters. The insurance card. The specialist's number." Each went into the folder, labelled.
"And who drives if you're in a lecture across town?" Jin asked.
Noa thought. "Aunty Mere lives ten minutes from the hospital. I'll ask her to go first, and I'll meet them there." Noa phoned her that afternoon; she agreed at once. Noa also saved the ward number in both their phones.
Two weeks later the call came, on a Wednesday afternoon. Aunty Mere was there in fifteen minutes with the folder's photo on her phone. Noa arrived after, without the scramble.

Who agreed to go to the hospital first?
Aunty Mere, who lives ten minutes from the hospital, agreed to go first.
What was worrying Noa before making the folder?
Noa was anxious about a sudden 3 a.m. call and scrambling to find papers in a panic.
What else could Noa do to strengthen the plan?
Noa could keep a second copy of the key papers at Aunty Mere's house, so the folder isn't the only source if it's left behind.
How did the plan look to Aunty Mere when the call came?
Aunty Mere could act quickly and calmly, reaching the hospital in fifteen minutes with the folder's details already on her phone.

The clinic waiting room had forty plastic chairs and a television nobody watched. Naveen had sat there every Monday and Thursday for a month while his mother had her sessions.
Today he had a plan. In his pocket were thirty flashcards on accounting standards, written the night before. On the bus in he'd done ten. Now, between the token calls, he did the rest, putting the ones he missed in his left pocket.
Yogesh, a nursing student doing rounds with the clinic staff, noticed. "Exams?"
"Final-year. I used to try reading the whole textbook here. Never got past a page."
"And now?"

He got twenty-four out of thirty.

He seemed a little embarrassed about never getting past a page, but now confident with his new plan.

Pankaj, you've had forty college tabs open for a month, haven't you? Your Santosh chacha did the same, just with paper. At nineteen, I had the fat admissions guide, every college in Maharashtra, and I read it like a novel. I made lists, then lists of lists: fees, hostels, placements, the canteen, the colour of the buildings in the photos. I changed my mind every week. Finally the deadline came and I picked the one in Sangli. And for the whole first year, I kept thinking about the others. Maybe Pune had better labs. Maybe Kolhapur had nicer friends. Your chachi, who had looked at just three colleges, loved hers. It took me a year to see that Sangli was good. What stole my happiness wasn't the college. It was the thirty I didn't choose.

Which college did young Santosh finally pick?
He picked the one in Sangli.
Why did young Santosh keep thinking about other colleges during his first year?
He felt restless and unsatisfied, because after comparing so many, every college he hadn't chosen seemed like it might have been better.
What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
Seeing, a year later, that Sangli was good and that his unhappiness came from the thirty colleges he didn't choose.
How did Chachi's college choice feel different for her?
Chachi looked at just three colleges and loved the one she picked, with far less to regret.

Mara and Riley went to a carnival, Mara rode the bumper car two times, Riley rode the space shuttle four times, and they both rode the Ferris wheel three times. If a ticket for a bumper car cost $2, a ticket for a space shuttle cost $4, and a ticket for a Ferris wheel cost $5, how much money did they spend?

Mara spent $2 x 2 = $4 for riding the bumper car two times.
Riley spent $4 x 4 = $16 for riding the space shuttle 4 times.
They spent $5 x 3 = $15 each riding the Ferris wheel 3 times.
So, they spent a total of $15 x 2= $30 riding the Ferris wheel.
Therefore the total amount they spent at the carnival is $4 + $16 + $30 = $50.
The answer is 50.

She checked the next morning. She arrived tense about the client's new deadline, and within ten minutes two people had snapped at each other over a font.

That's stressful, and I feel it too. Here's what we'll drop." Her voice was level. Emil pulled his chair closer. The meeting ended ten minutes early, and nobody argued about fonts.

messages.content: A girl learns to make rotis with the help of a magic rolling pin; tell it as a story.

Nisha's rotis always came out shaped like maps of strange countries. Her mother laughed, but Nisha felt embarrassed.

One day, in the back of a cupboard, she found a rolling pin with a little brass ring on one end. It felt warm in her hands.

She set the dough down and began to roll. To her surprise, the pin rolled by itself, making a perfect round circle. It hummed as it went.

"Now you try," it whispered.

Nisha placed her hands on top. Together they rolled and turned. Slowly, she felt the right pressure.

By the end of the week, she made a perfectly round roti all alone. She put it on her mother's plate.

I'm Nirmala, and I live below Tenzin's family in Kalimpong. He's nine. Last week, sitting on my steps with a bowl of peas to shell, he told me about the day his Momo-la died last winter. "I was on the stairs with my red kite," he said. "The phone rang two times. Then Amala dropped the ladle. I remember every single thing." He said it slowly, like reading from a page. I nodded and kept shelling. I remember that morning too, because it had snowed and the roads were shut, so I doubt anyone was flying a kite. But who am I to say what a boy saw? Maybe the kite was from another day. He looked at me as if daring me to doubt it. I just said, "You held on to that day very tightly." He leaned against my shoulder.

Who is Momo-la in Tenzin's story, and when did this happen?
Tenzin said his Momo-la died last winter, and he was telling Nirmala about that day.
What might Tenzin have been feeling when he seemed to dare Nirmala to doubt his story?
He likely felt his memory was completely true and precious, a way of keeping that day and Momo-la close, so doubt would feel like losing part of it.
Why did Nirmala's choice not to correct Tenzin suit this moment?
Nirmala didn't argue about the kite during a grief story, but named how tightly he held the day, which let him feel heard.
What does Nirmala notice that Tenzin cannot see about his own memory?
Nirmala remembers the snow and closed roads, so Nirmala suspects some details, like the kite, may have drifted in from another day.

I live across the road from Maria's family, and I saw what they did after the flood, though I can't say what they felt. A week after the water left, they sat at their doorstep with a notebook, all five of them. I heard bits.
"We had nowhere agreed to meet," said Maria, writing. "And the torch had dead cells." Someone laughed, a little ruefully.
They fixed each thing that month. A meeting spot was chosen, the tree by the temple gate. New cells went into the torch. The bag got a fresh copy of the papers.
Now once a year they stand in the hall with a timer and run out of the house, ten minutes. I'm not sure whether it embarrasses them or calms them.
— Seema

Sarika planned to make thirty-two bracelets, one for everyone in the class.

Samir bhai,
You'll laugh, but I have to tell someone. For two weeks I've been seeing 17 everywhere. The bus I take is 17. My exam seat was 17. Our old hostel room was 17. I started thinking it meant something, like the universe was lining things up for me. Honestly, it felt amazing, like being let in on a secret.
Then I remembered your line: "What would it look like if it were just chance?" So yesterday I wrote down every number I noticed from morning to night. Forty-three numbers. Three were 17. I'd only remembered the 17s because I was hunting for them.
So, no cosmic message. Just my brain collecting hits and ignoring misses. Slightly sad, weirdly relieving. Come home soon. The bus is still 17.
Kunal

Forty-three numbers, and three were 17.

Ulla had rehearsed the sentence in the shower, on the tram and twice in the lift. In the third-floor meeting room in Helsinki, she still felt her heart knocking.

Valentina, her manager, opened the laptop. "You wanted to talk about your review?"

"Yes." Ulla held her printed sheet. "I looked at what comparable analysts are paid in this city. I've also taken over two more accounts since spring, and the client renewal from last month was mine. I'd like my pay to reflect that."

Valentina looked at the numbers, then nodded slowly. "That's a clear case. I can't promise a figure today. Let me check the budget by Friday."

"Thank you. And if the answer is no, I'd like to know what would change it."

Ulla walked out feeling lighter than she expected.

It took place in a third-floor meeting room in Helsinki.

Valentina sees a clear, evidence-based case from someone who did more work, which makes the request feel like a normal business discussion and not a demand.

messages.content: Why does a bicycle speed up when it rolls down a slope without pedalling?
Gravity pulls the bicycle downhill and speeds it up. Because gravity keeps adding a push in the direction of the slope and little friction works against it, the bicycle gains speed.
Is "responsable" right for someone who can be trusted? How do I share a room with a sibling peacefully?

If Katherine has 4 apples and 3 times as many pears in her fridge, how many bananas does she have if she has a total of 21 pieces of fruit?

Katherine has a total of 3 * 4 apples = 12 pears
She therefore had 4 apples + 12 pears = 16 apples and pears
We know she has 21 total pieces of fruit, so this means she must have 21 total - 16 = 5 bananas
The answer is 5.

Mentor's note, clinical research unit

Usha joined our team two months ago as a research assistant. She's bright and eager, and very confident. Too confident, perhaps: she told the team she had "fully understood" the data-cleaning protocol after one day.

This week, she cleaned a dataset alone and sent it for analysis. I had noticed a few small things, but instead of listing errors, I asked her to explain the steps to me as if I were new.

She began confidently. At step four she paused: "Wait, did I remove the duplicates before or after merging?" She checked. After. That was the problem. Then she noticed the missing dates.

She said, "I thought I knew it." I told her that's true of almost everyone at the start, including me.

I gave her two specific examples from last month's set to compare. She's redoing it with a checklist.

I didn't need to embarrass her. She found it herself.

Vandana

How long ago did Usha join the team?
Usha joined our team two months ago.
What did Usha feel when she found the duplicate problem?
Usha felt surprised and humbled, realising she had been confident without really understanding the steps.
Why was Vandana's approach wise?
Vandana asked Usha to explain the steps and gave specific examples, so the gaps showed for themselves without shame.
How might the analysis team have been affected if the dataset had gone through unchecked?
The analysis team might have spent days working on flawed data and trusted wrong results, which would have hurt the whole project.

The bank branch near Sangeeta's office in Indore closed at three on Saturdays, and she and her husband, Mohit, had exactly one lunch hour to set things up.

At three.

messages.content: How do you draw a straight line of 8 cm between two dots with a ruler?

Answer: Put the 0 of the ruler on the first dot, lay the ruler along to 8, hold it firmly, and draw along the edge from 0 to 8.

Show it slowly: hold the ruler down with the fingers spread in the middle (not at the edge), keep the pencil touching the edge, and pull the pencil along in one smooth stroke. Then let the child draw lines of 5 cm, 10 cm and 3 cm, and check each other's with the ruler.

Max fills up water balloons for 30 minutes at a rate of 2 water balloons every minute. Max's friend Zach fills up water balloons for 40 minutes at a rate of 3 water balloons every minute. In the process, 10 of the water balloons pop on the ground. How many filled water balloons do Max and Zach have in total?

Max fills 30 * 2 = 60 water balloons
Zach fills 40 * 3 = 120 water balloons
Max and Zach have a total of 60 + 120 - 10 = 170 water balloons
The answer is 170.

To make a living, Carl needs to drive a car for 2 hours every day. After he got promoted he needs to drive for 6 more hours every week. How many hours will Carl drive in two weeks?

Every week Carl needs to drive additional 6 hours, so in two weeks that would make 2 * 6 = 12 additional hours.
Two weeks of driving 2 hours every day, means 14 * 2 = 28 hours of driving.
So during two weeks, Carl will drive 28 + 12 = 40 hours.
The answer is 40.

Yesterday the boy from the next lane turned up with a bag of new toys and a remote-control car. Neelam looked at the car for a minute, said "Cool," and went back to throwing the ball at the wall. When an advert for a doll house came on at the tea stall's TV, she barely looked up. She was singing while she threw.
I can't know what goes on inside her, but she seemed to have everything she wanted. I wonder how long that lasts once more of the lane starts showing up with new things.

What does Neelam play with in the empty plot?
Neelam plays with a plain rubber ball and a stick.
What was Neelam feeling as she went back to throwing the ball after the car arrived?
Neelam seemed content and absorbed, singing as she threw, though Ramesh cannot know for sure.
What could the adults around Neelam do to keep her contentment strong?
They could keep joining her simple games and pay attention to what she enjoys, without pushing purchases or making comparisons.
How might the boy from the next lane have felt when Neelam said "Cool" and went back to her game?
He may have felt a little let down or puzzled, since he arrived with new toys and did not get the excitement he expected.
At Makar Sankranti, Rohan flies a kite. Its sides are 30 cm, 30 cm, 50 cm and 50 cm, with the equal sides next to each other. Why is it called a kite? When would a kite be a rhombus?

Answer: A kite has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other (not opposite). If all four sides are equal, the kite is a rhombus.

Draw the long stick of the kite (one diagonal) and the cross stick (the other diagonal): they cross at a right angle. The kite has one line of symmetry along the long stick, and one pair of equal opposite angles (at the ends of the cross stick). If the short sides grew to 50 cm, all sides would be equal: a rhombus.

How did people live under Yudhishthira's rule, according to this passage?

All the subjects (of the kingdom) lived most happily depending upon Yudhishthira the just, like a soul living happily depending upon a body blest with auspicious marks and pious deeds. And, O bull in Bharata's race, Yudhishthira paid homage unto virtue, pleasure, and profit, in judicious proportion, as if each were a friend dear unto him as his own self.
Very happily, relying on him as a soul relies on a healthy body. He gave virtue, pleasure and profit each their fair share, like dear friends.

Dear Samir, You asked how the meeting with Meenal's biodata went. On paper: good height, good job, the same community, and my mother glowing. I almost stopped reading at that point. But I met her four times in six weeks: two walks, one lunch with her sister, and one long evening when the bus broke down. She talks about her students the way some people talk about cricket. When I spilled my chai, she laughed, then wiped the neighbouring table too. She disagrees with me about money and says so plainly, and I trust that more than any number on the sheet. Neither of us mentioned height or caste even once. I would like to tell both families that we want to keep meeting. Write back and tell me if I'm being silly. Lokesh

How many times did Lokesh meet Meenal over six weeks?
Lokesh met her four times: two walks, a lunch with her sister and one long evening when the bus broke down.
What does "tell me if I'm being silly" suggest Lokesh feels?
Lokesh feels admiration and trust for Meenal but is a little unsure, wanting Samir's view before telling the families. 🙂
Which choice by Lokesh gave a fuller picture than the biodata?
Lokesh met Meenal several times in different settings and noticed how she treats people and how plainly she disagrees about money.
How might Meenal have experienced those six weeks of meetings?
Probably as time to be known as a person: she talked about her students, disagreed openly about money, and was not judged only by a list.

Holi morning: Pradeep covers his eyes with coloured hands in the open courtyard. "Can't see me!" he giggles. Jyoti didi laughs and sprinkles pink on his head.
Two days later: At Nani's house, he hides his face in the curtain, feet sticking out. "Where's Pradeep?" Nani asks, playing along.
Next week: Pradeep shows Mumma his new drawing, holding it facing himself. "Look, Mumma!" Mumma gently turns it round. "Now I can see!" Pradeep looks puzzled, then turns it back.

What did Pradeep hide his face in at Nani's house?
The curtain, with his feet sticking out.
Why does Pradeep think no one can see him?
He is happy and sure that if he can't see others, they can't see him; he can't yet imagine how things look from someone else's place.
How can adults respond to this stage?
Play along gently, as Nani does, and show him other views kindly, as Mumma does by turning the drawing round, without teasing.
What is it like for Jyoti didi when Pradeep hides in the open?
She finds it funny and sweet, and joins the fun by sprinkling pink on his head.

Campus doctor's note, Tuesday
Gargi, twenty, came to the health centre convinced something was wrong with her heart. She described a racing heartbeat at night, a clenched jaw so sore she couldn't chew, a stiff neck and an upset stomach, all during placement season. She was frightened. I listened carefully and checked her thoroughly. Her heart and other checks were normal. I explained that stress can show up in the body as a racing heart and tension, and that her symptoms were real, not imagined. She visibly relaxed when she understood this. We talked about sleep, meals and slow breathing, and I referred her to the counsellor. I asked her to come back if anything changes.
Madhav

When do Gargi's symptoms happen?
During placement season.
What was Gargi feeling when she came to the health centre?
She was frightened, convinced something was wrong with her heart.
What helped lower Gargi's fear?
Careful medical checks that ruled out other causes, and understanding stress as a real body event.
How might Gargi's friends have noticed the change after her visit?
They might see her calmer and less worried, eating and sleeping better.

After the mummers' visit, how do the guests look, and what does Pelageya Danilovna do?

In an hour, all the costumes were crumpled and disordered. The corked eyebrows and mustaches were smeared over the perspiring, flushed, and merry faces. Pelageya Danilovna began to recognize the mummers, admired their cleverly contrived costumes, and particularly how they suited the young ladies, and she thanked them all for having entertained her so well. The visitors were invited to supper in the drawing room, and the serfs had something served to them in the ballroom.
Their costumes are crumpled and their painted eyebrows and mustaches are smeared on sweating, merry faces. She starts to recognize them, admires their costumes and thanks them for entertaining her.

Sales wanted the app out before the festival season. Engineering said it wasn't ready. Finance dreaded a messy launch that cost more. My first instinct was to pick a side, and then I thought, what does each group actually need? Sales needs something to show customers by October. Engineers need time to fix the payment part properly. And Ira needs no surprise costs. So I asked the room: what if we ship only login and basic payments now, and the polish comes in the next release, with dates written down? Nobody clapped, but Ira nodded and the lead engineer shrugged and said, 'I can live with that.' That shrug felt like a win. We launched in October, the fixes landed in December, and I slept better than I had in months. I'm Saurabh, by the way.

What did Saurabh propose to ship first?
Saurabh proposed shipping only login and basic payments first, with the polish coming in the next release.
How did Saurabh feel about the lead engineer's shrug?
Saurabh took it as a win and felt quietly relieved, because 'I can live with that' meant the plan was acceptable.
What other approach could work if the groups would not agree to a smaller launch?
Saurabh could set a fixed budget and a fixed date and see which options fit inside them, since that gives every group a clear boundary. 🙂
How might Ira see the plan?
Ira would likely feel reassured, because a smaller launch with written dates limits surprise costs.

The art room of the government girls' school in Sagar had one fan and thirty easels. Hemant sir asked the Class 9 students to draw the banyan tree outside the window. Sunaina tried. The trunk was too thin; the branches looked like sticks. The girl next to her had drawn every hanging root. Sunaina put down her pencil. "I'm just not creative, sir. Some people are born with it." Hemant sir said, "Your first try is where you start, not where you finish." She nodded politely, but after that, in every art class, she sat at the back doing her maths homework. When the annual exhibition came, Sunaina's section on the wall was empty. She walked past it quickly, telling herself it didn't matter.

What did Hemant sir ask the students to draw?
The banyan tree outside the window.
Why did Sunaina walk past the empty section quickly?
She felt a bit embarrassed and hurt, though she told herself it didn't matter, because believing she wasn't creative had stopped her from trying.
What might help Sunaina keep trying at art?
Starting with small, regular sketches of the tree and comparing them over weeks, as Hemant sir suggested, could show her that skill grows.
How might Hemant sir see Sunaina's move to the back of the class?
Hemant sir might feel disappointed and concerned, seeing her give up after one try.

Lab supervisor's note, Manjula Iyer, microbiology lab, Year 2.
Shreya (20) has named our old centrifuge "Grumpy." She greets it each morning and pats its lid before a run. When it stalls, she says, "He hates Mondays," or "He's sulking because I forgot him on Friday." The others have picked this up; the whole bench now blames Grumpy's moods.
I noticed Shreya seems calmer since the naming. When it stalls, she laughs instead of panicking, and she said, "At least now I know why he does it." Her explanation is a story, but it seems to settle her.
Today I looked at the logbook. Every stall is on a Monday morning, when the building restarts the power. I'll show Shreya the pattern tomorrow, and keep the name. It's clearly helping.

What has Shreya named the old centrifuge?
She has named it "Grumpy."
Why might Shreya say "At least now I know why he does it"?
Giving the machine moods makes its stalls feel explained rather than random, which seems to calm her.
What small step did Manjula plan, and why is it a good one?
Showing Shreya the Monday power pattern gives a real cause, while keeping the name that helps the bench stay calm.
How might the rest of the bench see Grumpy after Manjula shows the logbook?
They might still joke about Grumpy's moods but also know to plan around the Monday restart.

Chinmay, you're asking whether to take the bank job or the design course? Let me tell you about my college friend Sunny.
Sunny drew beautifully. At nineteen he got into an art school in Baroda. But his father said, "If it fails, don't blame me," and all the uncles said engineering was safe. Sunny thought: if I choose art and it goes wrong, everyone will say I made a mistake. If I choose engineering and it goes wrong, at least it's the normal mistake.
So he chose engineering. Nobody ever blamed him for anything.
Last year at our reunion he showed me his notebooks. Thirty years of drawings on the backs of project reports. "Nobody blamed me," he said, "except me."
I, Jahnavi, am not telling you which to choose. I'm telling you the safe road has its own regret. It just comes later.

Where did Sunny get into art school?
Sunny got into an art school in Baroda.
Why did Sunny choose engineering?
Sunny was afraid that if art went wrong everyone would call it his mistake, while an engineering failure would be the normal kind, so the safe choice felt less risky.
Which choice in the story mattered most, and what could Sunny have weighed?
Choosing engineering at nineteen; Sunny could have weighed the later regret of never trying art, not only the blame of failing at it.
How might Sunny's father have seen the choice at the time?
The father probably felt relieved that Sunny picked the safe path, without imagining thirty years of drawings on project reports.

Note from the social science teacher, for the student council file

On the day results were announced, Kishore lost the school captain election to Lakshmi by eleven votes. I was watching the hall because I expected tears or anger. There were neither, at least not in public.

He waited until the crowd thinned, walked up to Lakshmi and congratulated her. That afternoon he came to the staffroom and asked me, quite formally, what he could have done differently. I told him his speech had many ideas but no plan for any of them.

Two days later he brought me a written proposal for a library committee, the main issue he had campaigned on, and asked whether Lakshmi would accept him as its lead. She did. I have approved the committee and will check its first report next month.

What did Kishore bring to the teacher two days later?
He brought a written proposal for a library committee.
What might Kishore have been feeling when he waited for the crowd to thin?
He may have felt disappointed and hurt but wanted to stay composed, choosing a quieter moment to congratulate Lakshmi.
What could the teacher do next to support the committee?
The teacher could help Kishore set one small goal for the first month, so the committee's report shows a real result.
How might Lakshmi see Kishore's request to lead the library committee?
Lakshmi may feel respected and relieved, since the rival accepted the result and offered to work under the council.

Dear Yash,
It's been six months since you told me the truth about the shop accounts, and I want to be honest with you about something, the way you've been honest with me since.
I still check. When you say the supplier was paid, I look at the bank statement that night. When you're late back from the market, I notice I'm counting the minutes. When you laugh on the phone, part of me listens for what's behind it. I hate it. It's exhausting, and it makes me feel like a guard instead of a partner.
But I also notice something. Every statement I've checked has matched. Every late evening had a reason you'd already texted. The checking is getting shorter. Last week I forgot to look at all, and only remembered on Sunday.
So I'm not writing this to accuse you. I'm writing because I think this is a stage, and I'm in it, and it's easing because you keep showing up the same way.
Pradeep

How long ago did Yash tell the truth about the shop accounts?
Six months ago.
How does Pradeep feel about still checking?
Pradeep feels exhausted and hates it, feeling like a guard instead of a partner.
What is helping the checking ease?
Yash's honest behaviour repeating: every statement matched and every late evening came with a text, so the checking is getting shorter.
How might Yash feel reading the letter?
Yash may feel a sting at being checked, but also relieved and encouraged that the steady honesty is working.

Monday: Ira, the dance society president, caught Dolma after practice. "Will you organise the whole annual fest? Sponsors, stage, everything." Dolma laughed nervously. "I have exams in March. No, sorry." Ira nodded. "Totally understand."
Wednesday: Ira messaged, "Okay, what if you just handle the food stalls? That's all, I promise." Dolma felt a small tug of guilt. Ira had let go of the big ask so easily. Wasn't it her turn to meet Ira halfway? She typed "yes" and sent it before she could think.
Two weeks later: Dolma was on the phone with stall owners every evening, notes piling up. The food stalls alone were eating her study time.

In March.

Because Ira let go of the big request so easily, Dolma felt she owed a yes in return.

At the university exam office, results for three departments were due on Friday. Asif, the youngest officer, stuck a note on the monitor: "10 to 12: marks only. 12 to 12:30: emails. 2 to 4: marks only. 4:30: tea." The phone went into the desk drawer on silent, and the email tab stayed closed.
Karthik, at the next desk, kept everything open and replied to each ping. "You'll miss something urgent," Karthik warned.
Nothing came that couldn't wait ninety minutes. By Thursday afternoon, Asif had entered and checked two departments with zero errors. Karthik had half of one done and was re-entering a column mixed up during a phone call.
On Friday Karthik asked to copy the note. Asif printed it twice.

What did the note on Asif's monitor set aside for 12 to 12:30?
The note set aside 12 to 12:30 for emails.
Why did Karthik worry that Asif would miss something urgent?
Karthik felt that answering every ping at once was the responsible way to work, so a closed email tab seemed risky.
Which choice let Asif finish two departments with zero errors?
Splitting the day into marks-only and email-only times, with the phone in the drawer, meant fewer switches and fewer mix-ups.
What is it like for Karthik re-entering the mixed-up column?
Karthik probably feels frustrated and behind, redoing work lost during a call, which is why the note suddenly looks worth copying.

I'm Imran, and in Class 4 I had a trick. When Parveen Ma'am asked a question, I didn't think about the answer. I watched her face.
If I said 'the moon makes its own light' and her eyebrows went up, I'd quickly say, 'I mean, no, it doesn't.' If she smiled, I kept going. My stomach always felt tight while I watched.
One day she asked what we thought about a story where a boy lies to his friend. I actually thought the boy was right. But her face looked serious, so I said he was wrong.
Afterwards she called me over. 'Imran, what did you really think?' I told her. She said, 'That's a good reason. I wanted to hear that.'
I didn't know teachers wanted the real thing.

What did Imran watch instead of thinking about the answer?
Parveen Ma'am's face.
Why did Imran's stomach feel tight while watching Parveen Ma'am's face?
Imran was anxious about winning her approval; every raised eyebrow or smile felt like a sign of being liked or not.
What was the turning point, and why did it help?
Parveen Ma'am asking privately, 'What did you really think?' and valuing the reason; it showed Imran that honest thinking, not pleasing her, was what she wanted.
How might Parveen Ma'am have noticed what Imran was doing?
She may have seen answers flip whenever her face changed, and realised she was getting reflections of her own expressions instead of Imran's thoughts.

Monday night
Something's shifted in our flat and I just noticed it. There are four of us. Madhuri always uses everyone's shampoo, eats from our shelf, borrows chargers. She never buys the shared milk or cleans the stove. At first we all just laughed. This week, though, I noticed Priyanka moved her shampoo into her room. Ruchi stopped offering Madhuri a ride. Tonight, when Madhuri asked me for my notes, I said, "I'm using them," though I wasn't. Nobody has said anything to her face. But we've all quietly stopped. In the kitchen, Priyanka said, "She'll get the hint." I felt uneasy. Part of me thinks she deserves it. Part of me thinks we should just talk to her.
- Arohi

What did Priyanka move into her room?
Priyanka moved her shampoo into her room.
What was Arohi feeling about the flat's quiet withdrawal?
Arohi felt uneasy and conflicted, partly thinking Madhuri deserved it and partly wanting to talk directly.

What does disguise mean? I saw it in a spy story.

To disguise means to change how someone or something looks so that others do not recognise them. It is a verb; as a noun it means something worn for this.
Example: Vikram used a fake beard to disguise himself as an old man in the play.

"Just drop weeks three and four," Saurabh said, leaning over Naveen's screen. "The server outage skewed them. Then the retention number looks right for the client."
Naveen scrolled. "If we drop them, retention goes from sixty-one to seventy-four percent."
"Exactly. Seventy-four is the real story."
"But the outage was ours. Customers left because of it. That's real too."
Saurabh straightened. "Are you saying I'm lying?"
"No." Naveen's mouth was dry. "I'm saying if the client finds out we removed two weeks without saying so, it'll look like we were hiding something."
"So what do you suggest?"
"Show both. Sixty-one overall, seventy-four without the outage weeks, with a footnote. And a line about what we fixed."
Saurabh was silent a while. "That's more honest. It's also longer."
"One footnote."
Saurabh sighed. "Fine. Draft to me by four."

What would retention be if weeks three and four were dropped?
Seventy-four percent.
What was Naveen feeling when Saurabh asked 'Are you saying I'm lying?'
Naveen felt nervous, mouth dry, but held firm about honest reporting.
Why was Naveen's suggestion a good way to report honestly under pressure?
Showing both figures with a footnote and what was fixed keeps the truth visible while still explaining the outage.
How might Saurabh see the compromise?
Saurabh feels challenged at first, but comes to see it as more honest, even if slightly longer.

messages.content: Harper collected 30% more pieces of Halloween candy than her sister Maggie, who only collected 50 pieces.  Neil collected 40% more candy than Harper.  How much candy did Neil get on Halloween?

Harper collected 30% more than Maggie's 50 pieces of candy, so she collected .30*50 = 15 more pieces of candy
Maggie has 50 pieces and Harper collected 15 more than her, so she has 50+15 = 65 pieces of candy
Neil collected 40% more than Harper, who has 65 pieces, so that's .40*65 = 26 more pieces of candy
Harper has 65 pieces and Neil collected 26 more than her, so he has 65+26 = 91 pieces of candy
The answer is 91.

I'm Elizabeth, Pallavi's flatmate. I can only tell you what I saw.
At first Pallavi talked about her new boyfriend all the time, happily. He texted her good morning and good night. He wanted to know where she was, "because he worries." She showed me his messages, smiling.
By the second month, she stopped going to our Thursday movie nights. "He doesn't like me being out late." Once I saw him scroll through her phone at our kitchen table while she sat very still.
Then one evening she came into my room and sat on the floor. She said, "Liz, can I ask you something weird? Do you think I'm free? Like, actually free?"
I didn't know what was in her head. I just said, "What do you think?"
She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "I think I check everything with him first." I made us tea, and we looked up a counselling service together.

What did Pallavi stop going to by the second month?
Our Thursday movie nights.
How did Pallavi seem to feel when she asked if she was free?
Pallavi seemed confused and uneasy, starting to sense that the attention had become control.
What did Elizabeth do that helped?
Elizabeth listened without judging, asked what Pallavi herself thought, and looked up a counselling service with her.
How does Elizabeth see the boyfriend's behaviour?
Elizabeth notices worrying signs, like the phone scrolling and fewer nights out, but admits not knowing everything Pallavi feels.

Mary tried to improve her health by changing her diet, but her weight bounced like a yo-yo.  At first, she dropped a dozen pounds. Then, she added back twice the weight that she initially lost.  Then, she dropped three times more weight than she initially had lost.  But finally, she gained back half of a dozen pounds.  If she weighed 99 pounds at the start of her change in diet, what was her final weight, in pounds?

Since Mary first weighed 99 pounds, after she dropped a dozen pounds she weighed 99-12=87 pounds.
Twice the weight she initially lost is 12*2=24 pounds.
So, when she added back twice the weight that she initially lost, her weight jumped to 87+24=111 pounds.
Three times more than she initially had lost is 12*3=36 pounds.
Therefore, when Mary lost 3 times more than she initially lost, her weight dropped to 111-36=75 pounds.
Finally, when Mary gained back half of a dozen pounds, her final weight was 75+6=81 pounds.
The answer is 81.

Trainer's note - Kavitha, corporate communication workshop, Thursday
Urmila, one of our graduate trainees, gave her first practice presentation today. Her content was strong. But for the full ten minutes, her arms were crossed stiffly, and when she wasn't crossing them, she gripped her elbows.
In the feedback round, two trainees said she seemed "not open to questions." Urmila frowned, a bit defensive. "I was just nervous."
I told her I believed that completely. Crossed arms often mean nerves or cold, not unfriendliness. But audiences can still read them as closed.
We practised together: arms relaxed at her sides, one hand pointing to the slides, palms up when inviting questions.
She tried again. The same trainees said she seemed "much more welcoming." Urmila laughed. "I'm exactly as nervous. It just doesn't show as much."
I reminded her: it's a skill, not a feeling. Confidence may come later.

How long was Urmila's practice presentation?
The full ten minutes.
What was Urmila feeling during her first presentation?
Urmila was nervous, and later a bit defensive when her crossed arms were read as unfriendly.
What did Kavitha help Urmila practise?
Relaxed arms at her sides, pointing to the slides, and palms up when inviting questions.
How did the other trainees read Urmila's crossed arms?
They read them as her not being open to questions, though she was only nervous.

Sudha had been a trainee at the electrical repair shop in Karad for three weeks. Madhav, the senior electrician, was respected by everyone in town.

On Tuesday, a streetlight needed fixing. Madhav said, "Climb up. No need for the harness, it takes too long. I never use it."

Sudha hesitated. The training manual said always use the harness. But Madhav had twenty years' experience. Saying no felt like calling him wrong, in front of the shop boy.

She climbed without it.

Halfway up, her foot slipped on the wet rung. She grabbed the pole and hung there, heart hammering. She climbed down slowly.

That evening, shaking, she told the shop owner what happened. He was quiet for a long moment. "The harness rule is for everyone. Even Madhav. I'll speak to him tomorrow."

Sudha realised she had known it was unsafe. She just couldn't find a polite way to say so.

How long had Sudha been a trainee?
For three weeks.
Why did Sudha climb without the harness?
Sudha felt respect and nervousness toward Madhav, and saying no felt disrespectful, so she followed the unsafe instruction.
What could Sudha say next time to object politely?
Sudha could say, "Sir, the manual says harness always. I'll take two minutes to put it on," which respects him and stays safe.
How might the shop owner have felt hearing about the slip?
The owner was probably shocked and worried, and determined to enforce the harness rule for everyone.

Santosh loosened one arm, just enough to hold the edge of the shawl.

What was Santosh holding under his chin?
Bhalu, squashed under his chin.
What was Santosh feeling as he hugged himself and Bhalu?
A bit scared of the coming ghost part and a bit cold from the fan, as he admits; the hug was his way of soothing himself.
What made Akash bhaiya's check-in work?
He asked a quiet question, "Cold, or scared?", instead of assuming or teasing, then fixed the cold and stayed close 🙂

At his cafe, Milton sells apple pie and peach pie slices.  He cuts the apple pie into 8 slices.  He cuts the peach pie into 6 slices.  On the weekend, 56 customers ordered apple pie slices and 48 customers ordered peach pie slices.  How many pies did Milton sell during the weekend?

Milton sold 56 / 8 = 7 apple pies.
He sold 48 / 6 = 8 peach pies.
He sold a total of 7 + 8 = 15 pies.
The answer is 15.

Dear Yogesh bhaiya,
Remember I said the science project would take one evening? It took four, and I started last night. I was up till three gluing the model, and I only finished because the deadline was screaming at me. Mummy found me asleep on the chart paper.
I honestly thought I had loads of time. Every week it's like this. Time just disappears on me, and then suddenly it's tomorrow.
Papa gave me the usual lecture about discipline. I know all that. It doesn't help. What helped last term was when you sat with me and broke the history essay into five small parts with dates on the calendar.
Could we do that for the maths assignment? Maybe a timer too, and a reminder on my phone every Sunday.
Thanks,
Vishal

Until what time was Vishal up gluing the model?
Till three.
How does Vishal feel about always rushing at the last minute?
Vishal feels frustrated and helpless, saying time just disappears and that lectures about discipline don't help.
What help does Vishal ask for, and why might it work better than a lecture?
Breaking the maths assignment into small dated parts, plus a timer and Sunday reminders, gives outside structure that lectures don't.
How might Yogesh bhaiya feel reading that the help last term worked?
Yogesh bhaiya might feel glad and trusted, and ready to sit down with Vishal again.

"I kept the cloud-kitchen going for eleven months longer than I should have. I'm Afreen, by the way. Every month I told my friend Tanuja, 'Next month the orders will pick up.' They didn't. I'd put everything into it, and quitting felt like admitting I'd wasted two years. So I kept telling myself stories. Then one night Tanuja, who's an accountant, just asked, 'What number would make you stop?' I didn't have one. That shocked me. So we sat on her floor and wrote them down: if orders stay below a certain level for three months, or if I have to borrow again, I close. We picked a date. Tanuja checked the numbers with me every month, because I couldn't trust myself to. In March, we hit the stop line. I closed it on my own terms, paid everyone, and cried for a week. But I chose it. That mattered."

What question did Tanuja ask Afreen?
"What number would make you stop?"
What was Afreen feeling during those eleven months?
Afreen felt afraid and proud, unwilling to admit two years might have been wasted, so kept telling hopeful stories.
What helped Afreen choose an ending instead of drifting?
Writing down stop criteria and a date in advance, and having Tanuja check the numbers every month as a trusted outsider.
How might Tanuja have felt watching Afreen's stories each month?
Tanuja was probably worried and frustrated, but patient enough to ask a clear question and help check the numbers.

Tuesday, first week of board prep: Irawati bought two cans of energy drink on the way home from coaching and drank the second at nine. "Now I can do four more chapters," she told her friend Neelam on the phone. At two she was still awake, reading the same page.

Wednesday: She woke at seven feeling like wet sand. Strong tea at breakfast, another at eleven, an energy drink at four. In the evening her heart felt jittery and she couldn't sit still. Sleep came at half past two.

The next Monday: Neelam found her asleep on the library table at lunch. "You look worse than before you started all this," Neelam said gently. Irawati rubbed her eyes and counted on her fingers: four late nights, four tired days. "They're not giving me energy," she said slowly. "They're borrowing it from tomorrow."

How many cans did Irawati buy on Tuesday?
She bought two cans of energy drink on the way home from coaching.
How did Irawati feel on Wednesday evening?
She felt jittery and restless, unable to sit still, on top of being very tired.
What else could Irawati try to stay alert without late caffeine?
She could keep tea to the morning and take a short walk or nap early in the afternoon, so she is not borrowing energy from the night.
How might Neelam see Irawati's week?
Neelam probably feels worried and caring, noticing that Irawati looks worse than before and pointing it out gently.

At the playschool drawing corner, five-year-old Deepak pulled a chair next to his little sister Mahima, who had started only that week. She was scribbling hard with a black crayon. "No, like this," he said, picking up a yellow one. "First a circle. Then lines, like sticks." Mahima copied a lumpy circle and three sticks. Deepak clapped. "That's a sun!" When the teacher came round, he pointed. "I showed her. I know how to do suns." He sat up very straight for the rest of the class.

What colour crayon did Deepak pick up?
A yellow one.
Why did Deepak sit up very straight for the rest of the class?
He felt proud of being the one who knew how to draw suns and had taught his sister.
How could the teacher build on Deepak's pride?
The teacher could thank him and let him be a helper sometimes, while making sure Mahima also gets to try her own way.
What might starting playschool feel like for Mahima with Deepak there?
Having her brother show her things may make the new place feel safer and friendlier.
A cat spends its time hunting birds.  The cat catches 8 birds during the day and twice this many at night. In total, how many birds did the cat catch?

At night, the cat catches 8 birds * 2 = 16 birds.
Combined with the birds caught during the day, the cat caught a total of 8 birds + 16 birds = 24 birds.
The answer is 24.

Jenson and Kingsley have a tailoring business. Jenson makes 3 shirts, and Kingsley makes 5 pairs of pants per day. If each shirt uses 2 yards of fabric and a pair of pants uses 5 yards of fabric, how many yards of fabric do they need every 3 days?

Jenson uses 2 x 3 = 6 yards of fabric for making shirts every day.
Kingsley uses 5 x 5 = 25 yards of fabric every day for making pair of pants.
So, the total yards of fabric they use per day is 25 + 6 = 31
Therefore, the total yards of fabric they use every 3 days is 31 x 3 = 93.
The answer is 93.

The Class 6 English papers came back on Monday. Tarun had 31 out of 50. He shrugged; that was okay.
At break, Lokesh flashed his: 47. "Best in the class, probably." Tarun looked at his 31 again. It looked worse now, like a red flag. He didn't eat his tiffin.
In the last period, Ma'am wrote on the board: Class average: 22. Highest: 47.
Tarun blinked. Thirty-one was nine more than the average! He felt his chest puff up. He actually showed his paper to the boy behind him.
At home, his mother asked how he did. "Good," Tarun said. "Really good." Then he frowned. "Or bad? It depends who you ask."

What was the class average Ma'am wrote on the board?
Class average: 22.
What made Tarun skip his tiffin at break?
He felt miserable and let down, because Lokesh's 47 made his 31 look like a red flag.
What could Tarun ask himself to judge his mark more fairly?
He could ask how 31 compares with his own last paper and what he still wants to improve, not only how it compares with Lokesh.
How might Lokesh see the moment at break?
Lokesh was probably excited and proud, and may not have noticed that showing his 47 made Tarun feel bad.

I'm Ayesha, and I share a PG room with Kavitha, a second-year law student. Her mornings are all decisions: which lecture to attend when two clash, whether to take the moot court slot, poha or eggs at the mess, which bus to catch. By lunch she's comparing internship forms on her laptop. Then something changes around eight at night. Yesterday her project partner called three times about Saturday's meeting. Kavitha watched the phone light up and turned it face down. She ordered fries for both of us on a food app without reading the menu, then scrolled short videos until one. I can't say what goes on in her head. But when I asked about the partner, she only said, "Tomorrow. I can't pick a time right now." This morning she answered the call before breakfast and settled it in two minutes.

What did Kavitha do when her project partner called last night?
She watched the phone light up and turned it face down.
What does Kavitha's line "I can't pick a time right now" suggest about how she felt at night?
It suggests she felt too drained by a whole day of choices to make even one more, so putting it off felt like relief rather than laziness.
Which choice this morning made the difference, and how could Kavitha use it again?
Answering the call before breakfast let her settle it in two minutes; she could keep small planning calls for mornings instead of late evenings.
How might Kavitha's project partner have read her silence last night?
The partner may have felt ignored or worried that Kavitha didn't care about the project, since they couldn't see how worn out she was.

At five, Urmila trailed Vikas from room to room, tugging at his sleeve. "There's nothing to do. Nothing, nothing." Vikas offered a toy and a book, but Urmila only leaned harder against his leg. Something inside wanted to do something and had no idea what.

At ten, one endless July afternoon with the screens switched off, Urmila stood in the empty living room for a while, groaned, then dragged two bedsheets and a broom across the chairs. By the time Jaya, Urmila's mother, looked in, there was a fort with a doorway, a flag and a sign that said "Members only." Urmila stayed inside for hours, drawing maps of an imaginary island.

At sixteen, on a flat Sunday, Urmila flicked from one app to another, a video for a few seconds, then a game, then the chat, then the video again, thumb never resting. There were books on the shelf and friends a message away, but none of it seemed to be the thing that would fill the empty feeling.

What did the sign on Urmila's fort say?
The sign said "Members only."
How does Urmila's boredom change between five, ten and sixteen?

At five Urmila clings to Vikas saying there is nothing to do, not knowing how to fill the time. At ten, with the screens off, boredom turns into a fort and a map of an island. At sixteen Urmila flicks from app to app because the empty feeling is hard to bear, even with books and friends on offer.
What was Urmila feeling while flicking between apps on the flat Sunday?
Urmila was restless and uneasy, trying to escape a flat, empty feeling.
What could help Urmila at sixteen when the empty feeling comes?
Urmila could put the phone away for a while and let the empty stretch happen, then try something hands-on like drawing, as at ten.

On Sunday morning in their Ludhiana flat, Gargi was building a castle with her blocks on the living room rug. Mummy sat beside her, clapping at every new tower.

Amandeep was across the room with his toy car. Nobody clapped for his car.

He drove it slowly towards the rug. Mummy was still watching Gargi.

He drove the car straight into the castle. Blocks flew everywhere.

Gargi burst into tears. Mummy's head snapped round. "Amandeep! Why?"

Amandeep stared at her. He didn't know why. He just knew that for a moment, Mummy was looking only at him.

What was Gargi building?
A castle with her blocks.
What was Amandeep feeling before he crashed into the castle?
He felt left out, watching Mummy clap for Gargi while nobody clapped for his car.
What could Mummy try next time?
Notice Amandeep too, maybe clapping for his car or inviting him to build with Gargi, so he doesn't need to knock things down to be seen.
How did Gargi react when her castle was destroyed?
She burst into tears, feeling hurt and upset.

In the nurses' station of the district hospital, the promotion list went up on Monday. Pallavi's name wasn't on it. Everyone knew why: in March she had refused to sign the infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected, and the matron had called her "difficult" ever since.
Asif had seen it happen. He had signed his own checklist that day without checking, and he hadn't slept well since.
Pallavi read the list, smiled tightly, and went back to changing a dressing.
At tea Asif said to the others, loud enough for her to hear, "Pallavi's checks are the only ones I trust on this floor. That's why I asked her to look over my ward today." A couple of nurses murmured agreement.
Then he did the harder thing. He went to the nursing superintendent and said his March checklist had been signed without an inspection, and that Pallavi's refusal had been right.
That evening Pallavi left a vada on his desk, wrapped in a napkin.

What had Pallavi refused to sign in March?
The infection-control checklist for a ward she hadn't inspected.
What had Asif been feeling since March?
Asif felt guilty and hadn't slept well, having signed his own checklist without checking.
Which two things did Asif do to support Pallavi?
He praised her checks openly at tea, and told the nursing superintendent that his March checklist was signed without an inspection and that Pallavi was right.
What might the promotion list have been like for Pallavi?
Pallavi was likely hurt and disappointed, smiling tightly, paying for her honesty while others moved ahead.

Jasleen's desk in her Noida flat was stacked with notebooks. One for the career switch into data work. One for the online course plan. One for the portfolio projects. Each had mind maps, lists and neat timetables in three pen colours.
Her flatmate Ankita picked one up. "This is beautiful. Which course did you enroll in?"
"None yet," Jasleen said. "I'm still comparing."
"It's been since Diwali."
"I know. But I want the plan to be right first."
That night Jasleen opened the newest notebook and started a fresh page: "Revised plan, version 6." She drew a timeline for the next six months.
Then she flipped back to version 1, from October. The first step was the same: sign up for the statistics course. It still wasn't done. Five versions of planning, and not one lesson watched.
She sat with the pen in her hand for a long time.

What was the first step in version 1?
Sign up for the statistics course.
How might Jasleen have felt sitting with the pen in her hand?
She probably felt stuck and uneasy, even a little ashamed, seeing five versions of planning with nothing started.
What else could Jasleen do instead of writing version 7?
She could sign up for the statistics course that same night, then plan only the next small step after it.
How does Ankita see the notebooks?
Ankita admires how beautiful they are but gently points out how long it has been without starting.

Ada had rehearsed the toast on the matatu all the way to Wanjiru's graduation party in Westlands. The first lines went fine: the joke about their terrible first-year flat, the burnt ugali. Then she reached the part about the winter her father was in hospital, when Wanjiru had brought her lecture notes every single day. Her lips began to tremble, and her voice wobbled on "every." A few guests glanced down at their plates. Ada stopped. She held the glass with both hands and breathed in slowly through her nose, out through her mouth, twice. Nobody hurried her. Wanjiru's aunt nodded at her from the front row. "Sorry," Ada said, smiling now. "She carried me that year. So, to Wanjiru." Glasses went up, and Wanjiru was already wiping her eyes.

What did Wanjiru bring Ada every day?
Wanjiru brought her lecture notes every single day.
What was Ada feeling when her lips began to tremble?
Ada was deeply moved and grateful, remembering the hard winter; some guests might have read it as nervousness, and a bit of both could be true.
What helped Ada get through the toast?
Stopping, holding the glass with both hands and breathing slowly twice gave her voice time to settle so she could finish warmly.
How did the guests help, and what might have happened if they had rushed her?
By waiting quietly and nodding, they gave Ada room to recover; if someone had cut in or laughed, she might have felt embarrassed and not finished.

I'm Yogesh, and I share a room with Tushar in the college hostel. Last month, after the exam-results portal had a data breach, I watched him turn it into a project.
He sat cross-legged on his bed with his laptop and a notebook, muttering. First he installed a password manager and wrote down nothing except a reminder that the master password existed. Then he searched his email for every sign-up he'd ever done. He read the names aloud: a coding contest, three shopping sites, a game from Class 8. He deleted the ones he didn't use.
For the rest, the manager made new passwords, each one different. Then he went through his phone's app permissions one by one, turning off location for a torch app, which made us both laugh.
It took him most of a Saturday. At the end he said, 'Next breach, I change one password and I'm done.'
I don't know if he was worried or just bored. But the next weekend he helped me do mine.

Which app had location access that Tushar turned off?
A torch app.
What might Tushar feel after finishing?
Relieved and confident that a future breach will cost only one password change.
Why is reviewing app permissions part of this routine?
It limits how much personal data apps hold, so less can leak in the next breach.
How does the project look to Yogesh?
Yogesh watches with amusement and interest, unsure how Tushar felt, and ends up doing the same with Tushar's help.

messages.content: Bob and Johnny have a leaf raking business. They charge $4 for each bag of leaves they rake. On Monday they raked 5 bags of leaves. On Tuesday they raked 3 bags of leaves. On Wednesday, they counted their money and found they had $68 for all three days. How many bags of leaves did they rake on Wednesday?

Combining Monday and Tuesday, they raked 5 + 3 = 8 bags of leaves.
They earned 8 * $4 = $32 for the first two days.
O for Wednesday's work they earned $68 - $32 = $36.
Thus, they raked $36 / $4 = 9 bags of leaves on Wednesday.
The answer is 9.

The evening passes in talk of Hertfordshire news, and in her room Elizabeth thinks about Charlotte's contentment and skill in handling her husband. She also looks ahead to her visit, with its quiet routine, Mr. Collins's interruptions and the gaieties at Rosings.

I'm Avni, and I've worked beside Wasim at the hospital lab for a year. Our shifts rotate every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights. Lately Wasim eats biscuits from the drawer instead of meals, yawns through handovers, and last Tuesday he slammed a tray down when a ward boy asked about a delayed report. That's not the Wasim I know. At tea I asked if he was all right. He rubbed his eyes and said he couldn't remember the last time he'd slept properly. I told him about the free check-up at the staff clinic, and that our supervisor once let me stay on one shift pattern for a month when I asked. He did both. I don't know how he feels inside, but he's packing lunch again.

How often do the lab shifts rotate?
Every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights.
What does Wasim slamming the tray suggest about how he felt?
He seemed exhausted and short-tempered; broken sleep from the rotating shifts had worn his patience thin.
Why were Avni's suggestions wise?
A check-up at the staff clinic and asking the supervisor for a steadier shift pattern protect Wasim's health, since predictable hours help sleep, meals and mood.
How might the ward boy have felt when Wasim slammed the tray?
He was probably startled and a bit hurt, since he had only asked about a delayed report.

Uma, beti, you think Nikhil is angry with you because he was quiet at dinner? Let your Sudha Masi tell you something. When I was nineteen, in nursing college, I came back from a twelve-hour ward shift. My friends were planning a Sunday picnic at the lake. I sat in the corner, eyes half closed, saying nothing. Kamala said loudly, "Look at Sudha's face. She clearly hates the plan." Everyone turned to me. I felt so misread. My first wish was to snap back. But I was too tired even for that. So I said softly, "I don't hate it. I'm just so tired I can't think. Ask me tomorrow." Kamala laughed and said, "Oh! I thought you were angry." Next day I helped plan the whole thing. So ask Nikhil, beti. Don't decide his face for him.

What had Sudha just come back from?
She had come back from a twelve-hour ward shift.
How did Sudha feel when Kamala said she clearly hated the plan?
She felt misread and stung, with a wish to snap back, since she was only exhausted, not angry.
What choice in the story cleared up the misunderstanding?
Sudha softly said what she was actually feeling, tired not angry, and asked them to check the next day.
How might Kamala have felt once Sudha explained?
Kamala seemed relieved and a bit sheepish, laughing that she had thought Sudha was angry.
Should I carry an umbrella or wear a raincoat when it's windy and rainy?
A raincoat is usually better in strong wind, because an umbrella can flip inside out and be hard to hold. How are you travelling?
I walk to school.
A raincoat with a hood keeps your hands free and works well in wind. Keep your bag in a plastic cover, and wear shoes that dry quickly.
What if I only have an umbrella?
Then choose a sturdy one and hold it angled into the wind. If it's too gusty, wait for it to ease or ask someone to walk with you.
I'll go with the umbrella then. Anything else for the walk?
Wear shoes that grip wet ground, and step carefully around puddles near drains. Keep the umbrella low in the gusts.

In their flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata, Santosh, eleven, had written two rules inside his cupboard door: MUST BE FIRST IN EVERY TEST. MUST NEVER CRY.

On Thursday he came third in the class quiz. On the way home his water bottle spilled over his notebook, and before he could stop it, he was crying in the auto.

At home he stared at the cupboard door. Both rules, broken in one day. He felt like the worst boy in the world.

His aunt Hansa read the door. "Who made these?"

"Me."

"Then you can change them. What rule would a kind teacher give you?"

Santosh wiped his nose. He didn't answer. But he didn't close the cupboard either.

Where had Santosh written his two rules?
On the inside of his cupboard door.
Why did Santosh feel like the worst boy in the world after Thursday?
He had broken both of his rules in one day, coming third and crying, so he felt he had failed completely. His strict rules turned two ordinary things into shame.
What choice did Hansa offer Santosh, and why is it a good one?
She pointed out that he made the rules and so could change them, and asked what rule a kind teacher would give. That invites him to write gentler rules instead of feeling guilty.
If you were Hansa, reading those rules on the door, what would you want Santosh to understand?
That coming third and crying over a wet notebook are ordinary, not shameful. Hansa would probably want him to swap the rules for kinder ones he can actually live with.

“Ammi! Zaid broke my crayon!”
Farida looked up. Rafiq's fists were balled so tight his knuckles were white.
“Your hands are really squeezing. Are you angry?”
“Very angry!”
“That's a big feeling. Want to squeeze the stress ball or squash the playdough?”

He grabbed the lump and squashed it flat. Then again.
“Better?”

What did Rafiq squash?
The playdough.
What do Rafiq's white knuckles suggest about his feelings?
They show he was very angry that Zaid broke his crayon. The tight squeeze may also have been his way of holding back from hitting.
What small step did Farida offer?
She named the feeling and gave two safe choices, the stress ball or the playdough, to let the anger out.
How might Zaid feel seeing Rafiq's fists?
Zaid might feel scared of being hit, and relieved when Farida steered the anger into playdough.

He grinned, cracked his knuckles and went at it like a train. It was fast, I'll give him that. What did Dadi say after the performance?
"So fast!"
Why did Shankar play so fast at the dinner?
He was excited and eager to impress the family, wanting the speed to wow them.
What else could Shankar do before performing next time?
Practise slowly with the metronome until each note is right, then raise the speed bit by bit.
How does Charu read Shankar's red face?

Parul, you've just been made team lead and you're asking me how to be fair. Let old Vasudha tell you her mistake. At twenty-five I was made head of the primary section at a school in Indore, the youngest in the staffroom. That first year, I gave the science exhibition, the inspection lessons and the parents' meetings to Mrs Joshi, because she spoke well. Mrs Rao got the attendance and the timetable. Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition.
How did Vasudha feel on seeing the list written down?
Vasudha felt quite ashamed, seeing that one teacher had got everything big and the other only routine work, without ever being watched teaching.
What changes did Vasudha make, and how can Parul use them?
Vasudha rotated the big projects, gave everyone the same notes and patience, and judged by children's work; Parul can write down the team's task list and do the same.
How might Mrs Rao have felt in that first year?

Viva tomorrow at ten. My hands have been shaking since dinner. I spilled half my tea. Jyoti saw and laughed kindly and said, "Nerves?" I said it felt like my body was betraying me.
She told me something her sports coach said: the same shaky, sweaty feeling comes before a race and before a panic, and you can decide which it is. "Tell yourself: my body's getting ready." I rolled my eyes, but I tried it. It sort of helped.
We went through my three hardest questions one more time. I wrote my opening line on a card. Then I did the breathing thing: in for four, out for six, feet on the floor.
Still shaky. But less. Going to sleep now.
If this keeps happening before every exam, Jyoti says I should talk to the counsellor, and I think I will.

Tomorrow at ten.
What was Kishore feeling after dinner?

Ruby was going to order pizza for dinner.  Her son would only eat pepperoni pizza.  Her daughter would only eat sausage.  Ruby and her husband wanted black olive and mushroom pizza.  To make life easy, Ruby decided to order an entire pizza for each of her children and she would split one with her husband.  The pizza restaurant charged $10.00 per pizza and $1.00 per topping.  She also needed to add a $5.00 tip.  Including tip, how much would the pizza order cost?

Ruby was going to order 1 for her son, 1 for her daughter and 1 to share with her husband. So she needed to order 1+1+1 = 3 pizzas
Each pizza cost $10 and she was ordering 3 so that comes to 10*3 = $30.00
She needed to order pepperoni, sausage, black olive and mushroom, which came to 4 toppings at $1.00 each so 4*1 = $4.00 extra for toppings
The pizzas cost $30 and $4 for the toppings so the total costs of the pizzas came to 30+4 = $34.00
She also had to add a $5.00 tip to her current order total of $34.00 so 5+34.00 = $39.00 for the total order
The answer is 39.

Chetan, you asked why I stopped cooking when you visit. It's Kavitha, you know me, I used to love it. But for two years, everything I made, Sumit had a comment. Too salty. Too bland. Why can't you make it like my mother. It spread from food to everything, my clothes, how I spoke on the phone, how I folded towels. I started believing I was just a person who couldn't do anything right.

One evening, after another comment about the dal, I didn't cry. I asked myself: is any of this true? Sometimes, yes, I do over-salt. So I said, "Okay. What exactly would you like changed?" He was surprised. He said, "Less chilli." Fine. That I can do.

But the next day he said I was a hopeless wife. I said, very calmly, "No. That's not true, and I won't accept it. If you have a specific request, tell me." Then I booked us a counselling session.

What did Sumit say about Kavitha's cooking?
Sumit said it was too salty or too bland, and asked why she couldn't make it like his mother.
How did Kavitha feel after two years of criticism?
Kavitha felt worn down and began believing she couldn't do anything right, even giving up cooking, which she used to love.
How did Kavitha respond differently, and why is it wise?
Kavitha checked what was fair, asked for a specific request, refused the attack on her character, and booked counselling.
How might Sumit have felt when Kavitha asked what exactly he wanted?
Sumit seemed surprised, perhaps unused to her asking calmly instead of crying or going quiet.

Elsa started the day with 40 marbles.  At breakfast, she lost 3 marbles while playing.  At lunchtime, she gave her best friend Susie 5 marbles.  In the afternoon, Elsa's mom bought her a new bag with 12 marbles.  Susie came back and gave Elsa twice as many marbles as she received at lunch.  How many marbles did Elsa end the day with?

Elsa had 40 marbles - 3 - 5 = 32 marbles.
Elsa then gained 12 marbles + 32 = 44 marbles.
At dinner Elsa received 2 * 5 marbles from Susie = 10 marbles.
In total Elsa had 44 marbles + 10 = 54 marbles.
The answer is 54.

messages.content: What does "cry wolf" mean?

It means to raise a false alarm so often that people stop believing you when there is a real problem. It comes from the old story of the boy who cried wolf.
Example: Our neighbour's car alarm goes off daily, so no one reacts any more; it has cried wolf too often.

Job is a farmer who rears cattle and grows crops. In total he has 150 hectares of land. 25 hectares are occupied by his house and farm machinery, and 15 hectares have been reserved for future expansion. 40 hectares are dedicated to rearing cattle. Assuming the rest of his land is used for crops, how many hectares of land does Job use for crop production?

Job uses 25 + 15 + 40 = 80 hectares of land for non-crop purposes.
Thus he uses 150 - 80 = 70 hectares for crop production.
The answer is 70.

Anjali stood a step behind, saying nothing. Dolma's stomach twisted. "I'd rather not," she said. "Somebody is probably looking for it." She carried it to the teacher's desk. On Saturday the man at the corner shop counted out her change and pushed forward too many coins. Nobody was watching. Dolma stared at them, then said, "You gave me extra." Her ears burned for a second as she handed them back, and then her shoulders felt light. He nodded. "Thank you, beta."

Two days later she found a wallet under a park bench and took it straight to the gate guard. When Papa heard, he hugged her tight and she grinned. That night, in bed, she thought about it. The hug was lovely, but she would have returned it even if no one had ever told him.

On Tuesday, Liza had $800 in her checking account. On Wednesday, she paid her rent, $450. On Thursday, she deposited her $1500 paycheck. On Friday, she paid her electricity and internet bills which were $117 and $100, respectively. Then on Saturday, she paid her phone bill, $70. How much money is left in Liza's account?

On Wednesday, Liza had $800 - $450 = $350 left in her account.
After depositing on Thursday, she had $350 + $1500 = $1850 in her account.
On Friday, she paid a total of $117 + $100 = $217 for her electricity and internet bills.
So, $1850 - $217 = $1633 was left on her account on Friday.
After paying her phone bill, Liza has $1633 - $70 = $1563 left in her account.
The answer is 1563.
