According to Tolstoy, why did the rich people who left Moscow first not fear Napoleon?

"It is disgraceful to run away from danger; only cowards are running away from Moscow," they were told. In his broadsheets Rostopchin impressed on them that to leave Moscow was shameful. They were ashamed to be called cowards, ashamed to leave, but still they left, knowing it had to be done. Why did they go? It is impossible to suppose that Rostopchin had scared them by his accounts of horrors Napoleon had committed in conquered countries. The first people to go away were the rich educated people who knew quite well that Vienna and Berlin had remained intact and that during Napoleon's occupation the inhabitants had spent their time pleasantly in the company of the charming Frenchmen whom the Russians, and especially the Russian ladies, then liked so much.
They knew Vienna and Berlin had stayed unharmed under Napoleon, and that people there had lived pleasantly alongside the French.

Prince Andrew and his sister, hand in hand, kissed one another, and he told her she was still the same crybaby as ever. Princess Mary had turned toward her brother, and through her tears the loving, warm, gentle look of her large luminous eyes, very beautiful at that moment, rested on Prince Andrew's face.

How do Prince Andrew and his sister greet each other?
They kiss, hand in hand, and Prince Andrew tells her she is still the same crybaby as ever. Princess Mary turns to her brother, her large, bright eyes warm and loving through her tears.
Why does my teacher say "I'll ring you" instead of "call you"?

In British English, "ring" means to phone someone. Americans say "call". In India, both are widely understood.
Example: I'll ring you after the match, Danish.

In the office canteen in Salt Lake, Salma told Arnab that Rituparna from her team had finally reported the senior manager who had been shouting at her in meetings for four months, calling her "useless" in front of clients.
"Four months?" Arnab said. "Why did she let it go on so long? She should have—" He stopped, spoon halfway to his mouth.
"Should have what?" Salma asked.
Arnab put the spoon down. "No. Wrong question. Who was doing the shouting? He was. Every meeting, he chose to. She was the one trying to keep her job."
Salma nodded slowly. "That's what the HR head said too. They're looking into his conduct, not hers."
"Tell her I said she did a hard thing," Arnab said. "And that none of it was on her."

How long had the senior manager been shouting at Rituparna?
For four months.
What was Arnab feeling when he stopped with the spoon halfway?
Arnab seemed to feel a jolt of discomfort, even embarrassment, catching himself blaming Rituparna the moment the words came out.
Why is "Who was doing the shouting?" a better question?
It puts responsibility back on the person who chose to cause harm, instead of asking the target to explain why she put up with it.
How might Rituparna feel hearing Arnab's message?
Rituparna would likely feel relieved and supported, hearing that reporting was a hard thing done well and that the shouting was never her fault. 🤍

In her first month at the girls' hostel, Swati cried quietly under her blanket most nights. Then one Friday, Mahima from the next bed whispered, 'We share snacks at ten. Come.' Six girls sat in a circle on the floor with a torch, passing namkeen and gossiping. They asked Swati about her village and laughed at her story about the goat who ate her homework. Mahima tied a friendship thread on her wrist. That night Swati fell asleep smiling, the thread still on her wrist, feeling for the first time that she was one of them.

What did Mahima tie on Swati's wrist?
She tied a friendship thread.
Why did Swati fall asleep smiling that night?
She felt accepted and secure for the first time since arriving, because the girls welcomed her.
How could the hostel help other new students feel this way?
Staff or older students could make sure newcomers are invited to groups early, instead of leaving it to chance.
How might Mahima feel about inviting Swati?
She likely feels good about helping a lonely new girl join them. 🤍

Vandana had forgotten the rent again. Lalit found out when the landlord knocked at eight, while she was in the shower. It was the third time this year.

He knew her flaws by heart: late with money, careless with the gas, quick to promise. Last month she had borrowed his headphones and lost them. Part of him wanted to let the landlord shout at her.

Instead he paid the landlord from his own account and said, "My mistake, uncle, we mixed up the dates."

When Vandana came out, towel on her head, he told her plainly. "I covered it this time. I need it back by Friday, and we're setting a phone reminder together."

She looked stunned. "Why would you cover for me?"

He shrugged. "Because you had a rough week. And because you're my friend, even when you're a mess."

What did Lalit tell the landlord?
He said it was his mistake and that they had mixed up the dates.
Why was Vandana stunned when Lalit told her?
She did not expect kindness after forgetting the rent again, and perhaps felt she did not deserve it.
How did Lalit balance generosity with honesty?
He covered for her and was kind, but also asked for the money by Friday and set up a reminder, so grace did not mean ignoring the problem.
What would change if Lalit had let the landlord shout at Vandana?
She would likely feel embarrassed and defensive, and their friendship might grow colder instead of stronger.

The power went out ten minutes into Simran's Saturday science club, and the town's generator was still broken from the floods. Thirty kids sat in the dim community hall, restless. Her projector was useless.

"Didi, are we going home?" one boy asked.

Simran looked at the rain streaking the windows and had an idea. "No. Today we're studying water." They lined up bottles on the sill, measured the rain every half hour, and argued about why the river had risen so fast.

Vaibhav, who helped her, whispered, "You've been doing this every weekend for two years for free. Don't you get tired?"

"Of course," she said. Then a girl ran up holding a bottle. "Didi, it's gone up two centimetres!" Simran felt the tiredness fall away. She wanted these kids to be the engineers who fixed this town one day.

How long had Simran been running the science club for free?
For two years, every weekend, according to Vaibhav.
What does Simran's tiredness falling away suggest about her?
It suggests the club gives her a deep sense of purpose tied to the town's future, strong enough to outweigh her exhaustion.
How did Simran handle the power cut well?
She turned the problem into the lesson by measuring rain, keeping the children engaged instead of cancelling.
How might the children see Simran?
They probably see her as someone who shows up no matter what, and her energy makes them excited about science.

"I went home to Saxe-Coburg Square, and I took the advice of my assistant. But he could not help me in any way. He could only say that if I waited I should hear by post. But that was not quite good enough, Mr. Holmes. I did not wish to lose such a place without a struggle, so, as I had heard that you were good enough to give advice to poor folk who were in need of it, I came right away to you."

Give me the short version of this excerpt, under 60 words.

The speaker asked an assistant for help, but the assistant could only say to wait for a letter. Not wanting to lose the job without a fight, the speaker came straight to Mr. Holmes, who is known to advise poor people.
Rewrite for "he" instead of "you": You said that you would call, but you did not.
He said that he would call, but he did not.
Why do people cover their mouths when they cough?
To stop germs spreading to others. Because a cough sprays tiny drops into the air, and covering the mouth keeps most of them from reaching people nearby.
I always drink tea in the morning. Is 'always' in the right place?

Your word order is fine.
Why: no error (word order: "always" is correct).
Which is correct, "a lot" or "alot"? And one more: How can I be kind to a new neighbour?

1. Write "a lot" as two words. I have a lot of homework.
2. Say hello with a smile and offer to help. A small treat from home can also make them feel welcome.

I sit two desks from Minakshi at the design studio, so I saw most of it. In March she got into a three-month textile course in Jaipur, something she'd talked about for a year. Our big launch was in April. I expected her to just resign; some of the others said she should. Instead she asked the whole team for ten minutes. She explained why the course mattered to her, then asked what we'd need from her before she left. She stayed three extra weeks, wrote handover notes for every file, and trained me on the client accounts. She seemed tense the whole time, I think, but she never snapped. She left the day after the launch. Her notes were so clear I barely called her. — Sharmila

Where was the textile course Minakshi got into?
In Jaipur.
What does Sharmila think Minakshi was feeling during the extra weeks?
Sharmila thinks Minakshi seemed tense the whole time, though she never snapped, which suggests pressure balanced with care for the team.
Which choice helped Minakshi follow her plan without letting the team down?
She explained her reasons and asked the team what they needed, then stayed three extra weeks and wrote handover notes, instead of simply quitting.
How was Minakshi's leaving for Sharmila?
Because of the clear notes and training, Sharmila barely needed to call Minakshi and could handle the client accounts with confidence.
My aunt invited us to a function on Sunday. Isn't function a maths word?

In Indian English a function is a social event or ceremony, such as a wedding or a birthday party. It is a noun. In maths it is a rule that connects numbers.
Example: Everyone dressed up for the family function.

"The exchange semester in Seoul, Vidya! Deadline's Friday."
"I saw it, Sabina." Vidya didn't look up from her notes. "I read the whole page. Twice. And the reviews from last year's students. And the visa rules."
"And?"
"And my credits might not transfer. And the hostel reviews are mixed. And I don't speak Korean."
"Nobody speaks Korean. That's the point."
"What if I hate it and can't come back?"
Sabina sat on the bed. "Okay. Is that a real reason, or is that fear talking?"
Vidya was quiet. "I checked the credit thing with the office. They said it's fine."
"So?"
"So it's mostly fear." Vidya chewed her pen. "Maybe I'll fill in the form. Just fill it in."

What did the office say about the credits?
They said it's fine.
What was Vidya feeling about the exchange semester?
She felt anxious and afraid of hating it, even after checking the facts.
What question from Sabina helped Vidya?
Whether her reasons were real or fear talking, which helped her see the facts were already checked.
How does Sabina see Vidya's worries?
Sabina sees them as mostly fear and gently pushes Vidya not to miss the chance.
Give me a metaphor for a school bell, in fewer than ten words.
The bell is the school's noisy heartbeat.

Darshan, you're newly married, so let your Urmila Nani tell you something I watched with my own eyes. When your mother was twenty-five, she had a silly text fight with your father, something about who forgot the gas bill. She phoned her sister, your Meenu Masi, from my verandah. I was shelling peas nearby. Meenu listened for two minutes and said, 'He always does this. Always. Don't let him treat you like that.' I watched your mother's face change. Before the call she was annoyed. After it, she was certain. It wasn't about a gas bill any more; it was about what kind of man he was. Meenu meant well; she loved her sister. But she'd heard only one side.

What was Urmila doing while her daughter was on the phone?
She was shelling peas nearby.
How did the mother's feelings change during the call with Meenu?
She went from mildly annoyed to angrily certain, as Meenu's 'he always does this' turned a small quarrel into a judgement of her husband.
What could Meenu have said instead that would have helped?
She could have listened, asked what he said about it, and suggested talking to him directly, rather than giving a verdict on hearing one side.
How might Darshan's father have experienced that evening?
He probably came home to a wife far angrier than a gas bill deserved, without knowing a verdict about him had been reached in his absence.

The hardest thing I did in Class 9? Okay. I'm Wasim. My friend Vinita had been chatting with someone online who said he was seventeen. He kept telling her, "Don't tell your parents about us, they won't get it," and then he asked her to meet him alone on Sunday.
She showed me the chat, all excited, and made me swear. I felt sick. I said, "Vinita, I can't keep this one. I'm telling my mum today, and you can come with me."
She was furious. But she came. Mum read the chats, stayed really calm, told Vinita none of it was her fault, and called Vinita's mother right then. That evening they blocked and reported the account together. Vinita didn't talk to me for a week. Then she said thanks.

What did the online contact ask Vinita to do?
He asked her to meet him alone on Sunday.
What was Wasim feeling when Vinita showed the chat?
Wasim felt sick with worry, because the demand for secrecy and the request to meet alone were warning signs.
What made Wasim's response a safe one?
Wasim refused to keep the secret, told Vinita first, and went to Mum the same day; she called Vinita's mother and they blocked and reported the account.
How did Vinita's feelings change over the week?
She was furious at first and felt betrayed, but after a week she thanked Wasim, perhaps seeing the danger more clearly.

messages.content:
Read this:

Counsellor's note, Tuesday
Madhav was referred after his mother, Mrs. Ganga Rao, found a second social media account he had hidden from her. She has checked his phone every night since. Madhav said, "She reads everything. I made the other account just to breathe." His mother replied, "And now I can't believe anything you show me."
Both were hurt. I asked Madhav what he needed: a reason, and a way to earn back privacy. I asked his mother what she needed: to know who he talks to, and no more hidden accounts.
They agreed that he would delete the second account in front of her and tell her about new online contacts himself, and she would move from nightly checks to a weekly talk. We will review in six weeks. Madhav left saying, "I didn't know she was that scared."

How often will Mrs. Rao talk with Madhav instead of checking nightly?
Weekly.
Why did Madhav make the second account?
He felt watched and suffocated by the nightly checks and wanted space to breathe.
How did the secret account backfire, and what plan rebuilt trust?
It made his mother doubt everything; the plan was to delete it in front of her, share new contacts himself and move to weekly talks.
How does Mrs. Rao see the hidden account?
As broken trust; she can no longer believe what he shows her, and her checking comes from fear.

Vann is a veterinarian. Today he is going to be doing dental cleanings only. Dogs have 42 teeth, cats have 30 teeth and pigs have 28 teeth. If he is to do 5 dogs, 10 cats and 7 pigs, how many total teeth will Vann clean today?

First let's find the number for each animal separately, 42 teeth per dog * 5 dogs = 210 teeth for dogs.
Then cats total will be 30 teeth per cat * 10 cats = 300 teeth in total for cats.
Finally, the number for pigs is 28 teeth per pig * 7 pigs = 196 teeth in total for pigs.
So the total in all is 210 teeth + 300 teeth + 196 teeth = 706 teeth in total.
The answer is 706.

In the student union office of the Kolkata university, the night before the march over hostel fees, Ishita ran the briefing with a whiteboard. Darshan sat at the back, knee bouncing. He had never marched before. He kept thinking of lathi charges he had seen on the news, and of his father, a government clerk, who had said, 'Don't get your name in any list.' Ishita went through it calmly: the permitted route, the marshals in orange bibs, the legal-aid volunteer's number to write on your wrist, ID in your pocket, water, a buddy for everyone. 'If anything turns violent, from any side, we disperse. Nobody is a hero.' Darshan raised his hand. 'What if someone pushes us to break the line?' 'Then you walk away and find a marshal.' He felt his knee slow down. He texted his father: 'Going with the group. Peaceful route, marshals, I'll call you at 1 p.m.' His father replied: 'Call at 1. Not 1:05.'

What colour bibs do the marshals wear?
The marshals wear orange bibs.
What does Darshan's bouncing knee suggest?
It suggests Darshan feels nervous and afraid of violence and of his father's reaction.
Which parts of Ishita's plan keep marchers safe?
The permitted route, marshals, a legal-aid number on the wrist, ID, water, a buddy, and dispersing if anything turns violent.
What does Darshan's father's reply suggest about his feelings?
It suggests he is worried but accepting, wanting an exact check-in for reassurance.

"Sit, Chetan. You asked why I always ask about a company's targets before anything else. When I was twenty-five, a young woman at a pharmaceutical distributor in Chennai, I started to notice things. The targets doubled one year, and nobody could explain how we would reach them honestly. The one colleague who kept asking, a quiet man named Sampath, was moved to the stores. At lunch, people joked, 'Don't be a Sampath, don't ask too much.' When a shipment came back from a hospital, the manager said, 'Bring me good news only.' I laughed at the jokes too, at first. Then one evening I sat alone in the canteen, counted those signs on a paper napkin, and felt cold. Three signs in one year. That napkin is why I left before the audit came. Your Rukmini Amma is telling you, Chetan: watch the jokes. They tell you what people are afraid to say."

Where was Sampath moved?
Sampath was moved to the stores.
What did Rukmini feel when she counted the signs on the napkin?
Rukmini felt cold with alarm, suddenly seeing that the jokes and targets she had laughed along with were warning signs.
In the story, which choice changed things, and why did it matter?
Sitting alone and writing the signs on a napkin let Rukmini see the pattern clearly, which is why she left before the audit came.
How might Sampath have experienced those jokes at lunch?
Sampath was probably hurt and isolated, hearing his honesty turned into a warning to others while he sat in the stores.
A factory makes 36 lakh bottles in a year. Write this as 36 x a power of 10 and as an ordinary number.

Answer: 36 lakh = 36 x 10^5 = 3,600,000 (36,00,000).

1 lakh = 10^5, so 36 lakh = 36 x 10^5. To multiply by 10^5 move every digit 5 places to the left and fill the empty places with 5 zeros: 36 becomes 3,600,000. Do not just add 5 zeros to a DECIMAL: 3.6 x 10^6 means move the digits 6 places: 3,600,000 too. Check the size: 36 lakh is between 10 lakh (1 million) and 1 crore (10 million), and so is 3,600,000.

Thursday night
Maths: 94. Obviously. I've always had a brain for numbers, even Vikas said so when he saw my paper. I didn't revise the last chapter properly and still topped the section.
Chemistry: 58. The paper was ridiculous. Half the questions came from the tiny boxes at the side of the textbook, and Mrs Sen marks like she's angry at the world. Also I had a headache. Also the fan above my bench kept making that noise.
Vikas asked if I wanted to go through the chemistry paper with him and see what went wrong. I said no, there's nothing to learn from a badly set paper.
Now that I write it down, 'I didn't revise' is in the maths bit and not the chemistry bit. Weird. Whatever. Going to sleep.
Sunaina

What did Sunaina score in chemistry?
Sunaina scored 58 in chemistry.
Why did Sunaina turn down going through the chemistry paper?
Looking at the mistakes would dent Sunaina's picture of being clever, so calling the paper badly set feels safer.
What small step could Sunaina take with the chemistry paper?
Sunaina could accept Vikas's offer and sort each lost mark into 'didn't know' or 'slipped up', instead of blaming the paper. 🙂
How might Vikas feel when his help is turned down?
Vikas may feel brushed off, since he praised the maths paper and then offered help that Sunaina said wasn't needed.

Ishita sent her proposal for a new training module to Ira, the head of learning, on Monday morning. By Wednesday there was no reply. On Thursday, in the corridor, Ira said, "Ah, the proposal. Let's discuss sometime," and turned to talk about the office relocation. Ishita's stomach sank. Silence, delay, a change of subject: at her last company, that combination always meant no. And Ira was flying to Singapore that night, so there'd be no chance to talk for a week. Ishita didn't want to spend that week guessing. She sent a short message before the flight: "Safe travels! No rush on the proposal. When you have a moment, could you tell me if it's a no, a not now, or needs changes? Any is fine." The reply came from the airport lounge: "Not a no at all! I've just had the relocation on my head. Love section 2. Let's talk Tuesday."

Where was Ira flying on Thursday night?
To Singapore.
What was Ishita feeling after the corridor exchange?
Ishita's stomach sank; she felt anxious and discouraged, reading the silence, delay and change of subject as a no.
How did Ishita handle the ambiguity before Ira's trip?
She sent a short, friendly message asking whether it was a no, not now or needing changes, saying any answer was fine, instead of guessing all week.
What was really behind Ira's slow reply?
Ira was preoccupied with the office relocation, not disapproving, and actually liked section 2.

messages.content: How would you describe a bedroom after a long day of rain, with clothes drying on a line and a window fogged? Give me 55 words.

The bedroom feels heavy with rain. Clothes hang from a line across the room, dripping slowly onto a towel. The window is fogged, and the outside world has turned into a grey blur. A lamp glows softly, and the quilt on the bed looks inviting. Everything smells of damp cotton and warm tea.

Surfers enjoy going to the Rip Curl Myrtle Beach Surf Festival. There were 1500 surfers at the Festival on the first day, 600 more surfers on the second day than the first day, and 2/5 as many surfers on the third day as the first day. What is the average number of surfers at the Festival for the three days?

If there were 1500 surfers on the first day, the total for the second day is 1500 surfers + 600 surfers = 2100 surfers
On the third day, the number of surfers was 2/5 * 1500 surfers = 600 surfers
The total number of surfers at the Festival in the three days was 1500 surfers + 2100 surfers + 600 surfers = 4200 surfers
The average number of surfers at the Beach Surf Festival for the three days is 4200 surfers / 3 days = 1400 surfers/day
The answer is 1400.

Week one. Tarun came back from the bank branch every evening and told his sister Lakshmi he wanted to resign. "It's the salary," he said. "It's too low."
Week two. Lakshmi asked him to try something before deciding. On a Sunday he sat with a notebook and asked why, over and over. Why does the job feel bad? Because I dread going. Why? Because I don't know what I'm supposed to be good at. Why? Because I'm moved between counters with no training. Why? Nobody set goals for my role. And why does that bother me most? Because I'm not learning. He stared at it. "The salary isn't even on this page."
Week four. He asked his branch manager for a written role and a month on the loans desk with a senior. His pay stayed the same, but he stopped talking about resigning at dinner.

Where did Tarun ask to spend a month?
He asked for a month on the loans desk with a senior.
What was Tarun feeling when he stared at his notebook?
He was surprised and a little unsettled, realising the salary he complained about did not appear in his answers at all.
What else could Tarun try if the branch manager says no?
He could look for a role elsewhere that offers clear training, since he now knows learning, not pay, is what he needs.
How might Lakshmi see the change by week four?
Lakshmi, who asked him to test his reasons, would likely feel relieved that dinner talk has moved away from resigning.

metadata.subtype: Approach: find out what exactly is wrong using five whys [Thinking]

messages.content:

On Sunday at practice, Farhan Sir taught the under-12 team balloon breaths: in through the nose for four, out through the mouth for six. "Practise when you're calm," he said, "so your body knows it when you're not." Rashmi practised every night before bed, feeling a bit silly.
On Thursday the interschool match was moved to a muddy ground in pouring rain. In the second half, the referee gave a penalty against Rashmi that she was sure was wrong. Her face went hot, and she wanted to kick the ball into the stands.
Then her body remembered. In for four. Out for six. She walked to the sideline, drank water and did it three more times. When she came back on, her legs felt steady, and she won the ball twice before full time.

How long did Farhan Sir say to breathe out?
Out through the mouth for six.
What was Rashmi feeling after the penalty?
Rashmi felt hot with anger, sure the call was wrong and wanting to kick the ball into the stands.
Why did the balloon breaths work on Thursday?
Rashmi had practised them every night while calm, so her body remembered them in the storm.
What might Farhan Sir feel watching Rashmi walk to the sideline?
Farhan Sir likely felt proud and relieved that the practice worked when it mattered.
Why do some plants need to be watered less often than others?
It depends on how they store water. Because plants like cactus keep water in thick stems and have waxy skin that stops it escaping, while thin-leaved plants lose water quickly.

Yash was nineteen the night he finally asked it, in the small study circle after Sunday prayers: "What if I can't believe some of this?" A few people shifted in their seats. Shalini put down her cup and smiled. "That question is older than any of us in this room," she said. "Sit with it, and come back and tell me what you find." Nobody scolded him, and he left feeling curious more than afraid.

By the second year at college he had stopped going to the prayers in the hostel. He borrowed books from the library that he would have hidden from his grandmother, argued late into the night with Tenzin, who practised another faith, and with Rohan, who practised none. The old certainty loosened like a jar lid. It felt like freedom, and also like losing a room in the house he had grown up in.

In March he woke on a Sunday and felt nothing. No anger, no relief, just a quiet where the meaning had sat. He walked to the tea stall, sat with his cup, and did not pretend to have an answer. He wrote one line to Shalini: "Still asking." She answered the same evening: "Good. Keep asking honestly."

Where did Yash first ask his question about belief?
He asked in the small study circle after Sunday prayers.
How did Shalini's answer differ from what Yash might have feared, and how did it matter later in March?
She met his question with interest, said it was very old and common, and did not shame him, so when he felt empty in March he could still write to her honestly and get a welcome.
What was Yash feeling when he woke up on the Sunday in March?
He felt hollow and quiet, with no anger or relief, and did not pretend to have an answer.
How could Yash respond to the emptiness without rushing to a firm conclusion?
He can keep asking honestly and stay in touch with people who welcome his questions, such as Shalini, instead of forcing an answer.

In the counselling room, Afreen laid her chemistry paper on the table: twenty-eight out of a hundred, the third low score this term. “I study every night,” she said. “Effort isn't the problem.” Zainab ma'am, the school counsellor, nodded and asked, “Which subjects make you forget the time?” “Maths. Statistics puzzles.” Afreen paused. “I've been avoiding that, because everyone says medicine is the real thing.” She rubbed her eyes. “Maybe medicine isn't for me.” Zainab ma'am didn't argue; she only asked, “What would you like to do about it?” Afreen took a pen and wrote data and statistics at the top of a new page, and beneath it: ask for the maths elective, talk to Papa on Sunday. Her voice was shaky, but her shoulders looked lighter.

What score did Afreen get on the chemistry paper?
Twenty-eight out of a hundred.
What was Afreen feeling as she said maybe medicine isn't for me?
Sad but relieved: her voice was shaky, yet her shoulders looked lighter.
What could Afreen do to test the new path, and why?
She could try a short statistics course or small project first, since a small tryout shows whether the path suits her before she commits.
How might Papa see the change?
Papa may be surprised and worried because medicine was the plan, so Afreen's talk on Sunday, with her marks and an idea for the elective, could help him understand.

On the bus in Toronto, Tariq, two, sat on his caregiver Rosa's lap and curled his finger towards a pigeon on the window ledge, “Come, come.” The pigeon stayed put. Then the driver called “Ready?” and Tariq put up a thumb, copying Rosa. The driver gave a thumb back and grinned. Tariq looked at his own thumb, delighted, and did it again to a woman across the aisle. She lifted a thumb too. Rosa laughed. He did not know what it meant, only what it made happen.

Who did Tariq beckon at the bus window?
A pigeon on the window ledge.
What does Tariq's delighted look at his thumb suggest?
It suggests he enjoys the response he gets more than knowing the meaning of the gesture. He might also just like copying Rosa.
What could Rosa do to help Tariq understand these gestures?
Rosa could say “good” or “come here” as she gestures so that words and movements go together.
How might the woman across the aisle feel about the thumb?
She may feel touched or amused by a child's friendly gesture and enjoy returning it.

messages.content: Jacob takes four tests in his physics class and earns 85, 79, 92 and 84. What must he earn on his fifth and final test to have an overall average of 85?

Since wants needs an 85 as an average and he takes five tests, he must have 85 * 5 = 425 total points.
Currently he has 85 + 79 + 92 + 84 = 340 points.
So for his fifth test he needs 425 - 340 = 85 points.
The answer is 85.
Meaning of 'I'll get back to you'? My client always write this.
It means: "I will reply to you later, after I check or think about it." Example: "Let me check the dates, and I'll get back to you by Friday." A small fix: "My client always writes this."
I'm worried my knees hurt after running at school.
Thank you for mentioning it. I'm not a doctor, so it's best to tell a parent and ask the school's sports teacher or a doctor.
My teacher says I should wear better shoes.

Until last year I had never made a decision without asking Amma first. Not which shoes, not which friends, not which college. Her smile was the thing I worked for. So when I realised I wanted to switch from chartered accountancy to journalism, I couldn't sleep for a week. Amma had framed my CA foundation certificate. She'd told every relative. Every time I imagined telling her, I felt a thick guilt in my throat, as if wanting something for myself were a kind of stealing. When I finally told her over Sunday lunch, she went very quiet. Then she said, 'Ujjwal, I wanted you safe. I didn't know you were unhappy.' She didn't say yes that day. But she didn't say no either. Now I'm in my first semester of journalism, and she still calls every evening. Some days I still check her face before I choose anything. I'm learning not to.

What had Amma framed?
She had framed Ujjwal's CA foundation certificate.
Why did wanting journalism feel 'like stealing' to Ujjwal?
Ujjwal loved Amma and depended on her approval, so wanting something different brought a thick sense of guilt, as if taking something from her.
What helped Ujjwal move forward?
Telling Amma honestly over lunch, which let her explain that she wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness.
How did Amma respond to the news?
She went quiet, explained she had wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness, and neither agreed nor refused that day.
A bag has only red and blue marbles. P(red) = 3/8 and there are 15 blue marbles. How many red marbles are there? If 6 more red marbles are added, what is P(red) now?

Answer: P(blue) = 1 - 3/8 = 5/8, so 5/8 of the total is 15: total = 24, red = 24 - 15 = 9. After adding 6 red: 15 red out of 30, P(red) = 15/30 = 1/2.

Start with the complement: blue is 5/8 of the bag. If 5 eighths are 15 marbles, 1 eighth is 15 / 5 = 3 marbles and the whole bag is 8 x 3 = 24. Red is 3 eighths = 9 (check: 9/24 = 3/8). Adding 6 red changes BOTH the top and the bottom: red becomes 9 + 6 = 15 and the total 24 + 6 = 30, so P(red) = 15/30 = 1/2. Common mistake: adding 6 only to the numerator (15/24). With algebra: if r is the number of red marbles, r / (r + 15) = 3/8, so 8r = 3r + 45, 5r = 45, r = 9.

At the park, near the swings.

Akash promised to update the shared tracker by six, and he did, that same evening, though no one commented. Week two, Wednesday: before the review, Akash messaged the group, 'I entered the wrong launch date in the tracker yesterday. Fixed now, sorry for the confusion.' Leela, who usually stayed silent, replied that she had a similar slip in her test notes and had fixed hers too. Week four, Friday: at the demo, the manager praised the smooth rollout. Akash said, 'Leela caught the login bug on Tuesday. That one was hers.' Afterwards, two teammates who had kept to themselves asked Leela to look over their code before Monday.

What did Akash promise to do in week one?
He promised to update the shared tracker by six, and he did it that same evening.
Why might Leela have admitted her own slip after Akash's message?
She probably felt safer and less afraid of being judged, because Akash had just owned his mistake openly before anyone found it.
What small habit could the manager encourage so the trust keeps growing?
Keep small promises visible, like a quick note when a task is done or an error is fixed, instead of adding more posters.
How might the two quieter teammates see the team by week four?
They seem to see a place where mistakes are named and credit is shared fairly, so they now feel safe asking Leela for help.
Sarah is in charge of making 2 copies of a contract for 9 people that will be in a meeting.  The contract is 20 pages long.  How many pages will Sarah copy?

Every person needs 2 copies and there are 9 people in the meeting so she needs 2*9 = 18 copies
The contract is 20 pages long and she has to make 18 copies so she will end up copying 20*18 = 360 pages
The answer is 360.

Gopika noticed Seema, the new junior, learning tools in weeks that had taken her a year. A sting rose in her chest. Then she put Seema forward for the client workshop and told the team whose layout it was. She also booked herself onto an advanced course.

Harsha, the other junior, copied everything: her colour-coded notebook, the way she signed off emails. One day he said, "You never make mistakes." "I do," she said, and told him about the wrong file she had sent a client last spring and how she fixed it. She stopped him from copying her tone with clients. "Find your own voice."

But Harsha also asked her about every choice: which font, which colour, whether to email or call. Gopika said, "What do you think? Give me two options." He picked one, and she said, "That works." Over the weeks he brought his own choices, and by summer she was only nodding.

At the review, Seema presented the whole campaign alone, better than Gopika would have. Pride filled her, with a faint wistfulness. She clapped first and said, "That was all you." Afterwards she noticed her calendar held fewer requests for help. The mentoring was working.

What did Harsha copy from Gopika?
He copied her colour-coded notebook and the way she signed off emails.
How did Gopika's response to Seema's fast progress differ from her response to Harsha's constant questions?

With Seema she noticed the sting, then shared an opportunity and credit instead of holding her back. With Harsha she turned each request back with "What do you think?" until he brought his own choices.
What was Gopika feeling as Seema presented the whole campaign alone?
She felt proud, with a faint wistfulness.
How did Gopika handle it when Harsha copied her and said she never makes mistakes?
She told him about the wrong file she had sent a client and how she fixed it, and told him to find his own voice.

Dear Rukmini,
You asked how I stay Tamil in Amsterdam without turning into a museum. Honest answer: I choose.
I kept the kolam. Every Pongal I draw one in chalk on the doorstep, and the neighbours' kids now queue for a turn. I kept rasam on sick days and Sunday calls with Paati. I let go of the rule that girls eat last; it never felt like mine. From here I took cycling everywhere in the rain, and saying no without a long apology.
When Jonas and I have children, I want them to know both sets of songs, and to pick their own favourites too.
So when you land in Toronto next month, don't pack everything. Pack what keeps you warm. The rest will wait at home until you want it.
Love,
Your Avni akka

What does Avni draw on the doorstep every Pongal?
Avni draws a kolam in chalk on the doorstep every Pongal.
How does Avni feel about the customs she has chosen to keep?
Avni feels warm and proud of them, glad to share the kolam with the neighbours' kids, and at ease letting go of the rule that never felt right.
What is wise about Avni's advice to pack what keeps you warm?
It lets Rukmini choose customs out of love rather than duty, so identity feels like something tended by choice, not a weight to carry.
What would change for the neighbours' kids if Avni kept her customs private?
They would miss queueing for a turn at the kolam, so the custom would stay behind a closed door instead of becoming something shared.

Monday. In the hiring room, Parul put down her pen after five minutes with a candidate. "She's the one. Firm handshake, eye contact. I can always tell." Wasim, twenty-six and the newest senior on the team, nodded politely and said nothing.
Thursday. Wasim pulled last year's records: Parul's interview ratings beside each hire's performance after twelve months. He stared at the screen. Her top-rated hires were no better than her lowest-rated ones. Two of the best people had been marked "average fit."
The next Monday. Wasim brought the chart to the team meeting and kept his voice gentle. "Parul, your eye is sharp, but hiring gives slow, messy feedback. We almost never learn about the people we rejected. Could we add a short work task and score it before we compare feelings?" Parul was quiet for a while. "Fine," she said. "But I'm still writing my gut rating down."

What did Wasim compare in last year's records?
He compared Parul's interview ratings with each hire's performance after twelve months.
Why did Wasim keep his voice gentle when showing the chart?
Wasim felt nervous as the newest senior and respected Parul, so he wanted to share uncomfortable data without making her feel attacked.
Why is adding a scored work task a sensible fix?
It gives real evidence alongside the gut rating, which matters in hiring, where feedback is slow and noisy and experience alone doesn't sharpen judgment.
How might Parul feel seeing her ratings next to the results?
Parul might feel defensive and embarrassed, since she believed she could always tell, but her wish to keep her gut rating shows she is willing to test it.

You asked how I kept going in nursing when half my batch dropped out, Zainab. Let me tell you.
I'm Gurleen. In Class 12 everyone expected me to do engineering. I spent that whole summer volunteering at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana, just to see. I sat with old patients, held hands during dressings, watched the nurses work double shifts.
Then I chose nursing. Not because I was told to. Because I'd seen it, the hard parts too.
Second year was brutal. Night duties, a patient I'd grown fond of died, and I failed pharmacology the first time.
My friend Tanu, who was pushed into it by her parents, quit that year. I understood why.
But every time I wanted to stop, I'd remember that summer. I chose this with my eyes open. That kept me standing. I passed pharmacology on the second go.

Gurleen volunteered at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana.
What kept Gurleen going when Gurleen felt like stopping?
Gurleen felt steadier remembering that the choice was made with open eyes after seeing the hard parts, so the goal felt truly owned.
What does Gurleen's story suggest about choosing a course?
Taking time to see the real work before choosing, as Gurleen did, can build a commitment that holds through setbacks.
How might Tanu have felt in the same brutal second year?
Tanu, pushed into it by her parents, probably felt trapped and exhausted, with no reason of her own to keep going.

Can you summarize this for my little brother in one or two simple sentences?

Upon hearing this he appeared satisfied and consented to come on board. Good God! Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless. His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering. I never saw a man in so wretched a condition. We attempted to carry him into the cabin, but as soon as he had quitted the fresh air he fainted. We accordingly brought him back to the deck and restored him to animation by rubbing him with brandy and forcing him to swallow a small quantity. As soon as he showed signs of life we wrapped him up in blankets and placed him near the chimney of the kitchen stove. By slow degrees he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.

In the marketing office in Amman, Yara, twenty-six, stayed late to help Nkechi finish her slides for the director. Not because Nkechi was drowning, though she was. Because Nkechi ate lunch with the director twice a week.
On the bus home, Yara opened a note on her phone. Nkechi: owes me one, big. Under it were other entries: Omar covered my Friday, I owe him a coffee. Hana helped with Excel, returned. It was all very fair. She never took more than she gave.
A month later, Nkechi stopped at Yara's desk, eyes red. "My father's in hospital back home. I just needed to tell someone."
Yara said, "Oh no, I'm sorry," and then didn't know what else to say. She realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's father, or anyone's family, or what anyone here loved. Nkechi nodded and walked away.
That night Yara looked at her list for a long time.

How often did Nkechi eat lunch with the director?
Twice a week.
What did Yara realise when Nkechi told her about her father?
With dismay, she realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's life or anyone else's, because she had only ever kept track of favours.
What might Yara choose to do differently after looking at her list?
She could start getting to know colleagues as people, asking about their lives and helping sometimes without writing it down.
How might Nkechi have felt when Yara had nothing more to say?

When Erick went to the market to sell his fruits, he realized that the price of lemons had risen by $4 for each lemon. The price of grapes had also increased by half the price that the price of lemon increased by per grape. If he had planned to sell the lemons at $8 and the grapes at $7, and he had 80 lemons and 140 grapes in his basket, how much money did he collect from selling the fruits at the new prices?

The new price for each lemon after increasing by $4 is $8+$4 = $12
For the 80 lemons, Erick received $12*80 = $960
The price of each grape increased by 1/2*$4 = $2
The new price at which Erick sold his grapes is $7+$2 = $9
For the 140 grapes, Erick collected 140*$9 = $1260
From the sale of all of his fruits, Erick received $1260+$960 = $2220
The answer is 2220.

The morning after their difficult talk, Shankar sat in the corner cabin of the Mumbai ad agency and typed up what they'd agreed.
He kept it to one page. Three goals for Urmila: first drafts of client copy by Wednesday each week; no more than one round of spelling corrections per draft; present her own idea in at least two client meetings. He printed two copies and handed one to Urmila.
She read it slowly. "Can I change 'two meetings' to 'two presentations'? Meetings sometimes get cancelled."

15 August, six weeks from today.

She may have felt nervous about the goals but also reassured, because the expectations and support were clear and she had been able to change one word.
What else could Shankar do between now and the review date?
He could use the Friday reviews to note progress on each goal in writing, so the August review has no surprises.
How does the written plan look from Urmila's side?
It feels firm but fair: she knows exactly what is expected, what help she gets and what happens if goals aren't met, and her suggestion was accepted.

In a café in Copenhagen, Lars laid out his startup plan for Ines on a napkin. "We build the app by March. Then a big bike company notices us. Then they partner with us. Then the city puts us on its website. Then we get investors." He drew arrows between every step, grinning. The more he talked, the more real it felt to him. Ines, who studied statistics, didn't laugh. "How likely is each step?" "I don't know. Maybe half?" She did the maths on the napkin. "Half, times half, times half, times half, times half. That's about three in a hundred that all of it happens." Lars stared. "But it sounds so good when I say it all." "That's the trap," Ines said. "Every 'and then' makes it sound better and makes it less likely." He crossed out four arrows and circled the first step.

What chance did Ines work out for the whole plan?
About three in a hundred that all of it happens.
Why did the plan feel more real the more Lars talked?

What did Lars do after Ines's maths, and why was it sensible?
He crossed out four arrows and circled the first step, focusing on what he can do now instead of a long chain of hopes.
How does Ines see Lars's plan?

Sunday

Asif asked again at breakfast: "So, next year? Baby?" He was smiling.

I said, "Let's talk properly first," and he looked a bit wounded.

So I wrote the list I'd been carrying in my head.
— Work: I'm up for promotion in June. Would I still want it with a newborn? Would he step back if I did?
— Care: when Asif says he'll "help", I get tense. I don't want help. I want half.
— Money: do we know what the first year actually costs? We've never sat down with it.
— Values: how would we handle discipline? His family shouts; mine goes silent. Neither feels great.
— Us: are we ready to be tired together without blaming each other?

Tonight I showed him. He was quiet for a long time, then said, "I didn't know 'help' sounded like that." He added one line to the list himself: "Ask my brother what he wishes he'd planned."

I think we're closer to ready than we were this morning. Not there yet.

— Preeti

When is Preeti up for promotion?
Preeti is up for promotion in June.
Why does Preeti get tense when Asif says he will "help"?
Preeti feels uneasy because "help" suggests the care will mainly fall on Preeti, when the wish is to share it equally.
What makes Preeti's list a useful way to decide about readiness?
It puts work, care, money, values and the relationship on paper so the couple can talk about each one honestly instead of guessing.
How did Asif react to seeing the list?
Asif was quiet for a long time, surprised at how "help" sounded, and then took part by adding his own question to the list.

A book lay spread on the sill before her, and the scarcely perceptible wind fluttered its leaves at intervals. I believe Linton had laid it there: for she never endeavoured to divert herself with reading, or occupation of any kind, and he would spend many an hour in trying to entice her attention to some subject which had formerly been her amusement. She was conscious of his aim, and in her better moods endured his efforts placidly, only showing their uselessness by now and then suppressing a wearied sigh, and checking him at last with the saddest of smiles and kisses. At other times, she would turn petulantly away, and hide her face in her hands, or even push him off angrily; and then he took care to let her alone, for he was certain of doing no good.

Boil this extract down to under 60 words.

A book lies open on the sill, probably put there by Linton, who spends hours trying to interest her in her old pastimes. On good days she bears it quietly with a sad smile; on others she turns away or pushes him off, and he leaves her alone.

Arjun, your Mama is going to tell you something I never told anyone. I'm Vijay. One week after my father's funeral, I sat at the tea stall and felt nothing. Not sadness, not anger, nothing. Everyone expected tears. I thought, what is wrong with me? I even copied the relatives, making my face long. My Masi Sarita found me on the steps that evening. "Beta, when the heart gets too full, sometimes it goes quiet to protect you. Don't argue with yourself." She made me keep small routines: tea at six, a walk, dinner with everyone. "And if it stays quiet a long time, we will see a doctor," she said. It lifted after some weeks. I cried at an odd moment, over a lost slipper, and Masi just handed me water.

Where was Vijay sitting when he felt nothing a week after the funeral?
Vijay was at the tea stall.
What was Vijay worried about?
That something was wrong with him because he felt nothing while everyone expected tears.
What helped Vijay through the numbness?
Keeping small routines such as tea, a walk and dinner with everyone, and Masi Sarita's patience, with a doctor as a plan if it stayed.
How might Masi Sarita see Vijay's numbness?
As the heart going quiet to protect him, not a sign that he did not love his father.

Read this:

I'm Rajni, and I used to carry my friends' problems home like extra luggage. Vishal, a colleague, began staying back after work to talk about his fights with his brother and his exhaustion, and I listened until 10 pm, then lay awake replaying it. One evening I changed how I did it. I said, "It sounds like you feel he never listens to you. Is that right, or is it something else?" Vishal said it was more that he felt ignored than angry. Then I told him, "I can listen for a while tonight, but I can't be the only one you talk to. Have you thought about the counsellor the company offers?" He looked a little hurt, then said he would look at the details. I went home lighter 🙂, and I still text him next morning.

What did Vishal say he felt, after Rajni checked a guess?
He said it was more that he felt ignored than angry.
How was Rajni feeling when asking "Is that right, or is it something else?"
Rajni was unsure whether the guess about Vishal's feelings was right, so Rajni checked; his reply that he felt ignored more than angry showed it was only partly right.
What did Rajni change that helped Rajni support Vishal?
Rajni checked the guess, set a limit on the evening and suggested the company counsellor.
How might Vishal have felt when Rajni mentioned the counsellor?
He looked a little hurt, perhaps feeling passed along, but he agreed to look at the details, so he may also have found it reasonable.

The teacher said this step is critical. I only know critical as finding fault.

Here critical is an adjective meaning extremely important, or at a point where success or failure can be decided. The other sense is saying what is wrong with something.
Example: Good sleep is critical before an important exam.

Read this:

Wei had spent Sunday morning reading about the earthquake overseas, photo after photo, until her coffee went cold and her shoulders were up by her ears. Her sister Xin found her still on the couch at noon. 'You look like you were there.' Wei put the phone face down. She noticed the tightness in her chest and named it quietly: this is their grief, not mine. I can care without drowning in it. She set a rule: news once a day, briefly, then off. That evening she signed up for Saturdays at the community centre in Vancouver, sorting donated winter coats for newly arrived families. The first Saturday, her arms ached from lifting boxes. Her chest didn't.

What did Wei sign up to do on Saturdays?
Sort donated winter coats for newly arrived families at the community centre.
What did Wei feel and realise on putting the phone down?
Wei noticed a tightness in her chest and recognised she was taking on grief that belonged to others.
Which of Wei's choices made the biggest difference, and why?
Turning the feeling into Saturday volunteering gave the care somewhere to go, so Wei ended up tired in the arms but lighter in the chest.
How might Xin see the change in Wei after that Sunday?
Xin, who said Wei looked like she'd been there, would probably be relieved to see Wei calmer and doing something useful.

Read this:

Counsellor's note. Farhan came to see me after class with red ears. He said quietly, "I watched a video I knew I shouldn't. It was meant for older people. I feel really embarrassed, and I thought you'd tell my father and I'd be in trouble." I thanked him for telling me and said that being curious is normal. I explained in simple words that some videos are for adults, not children, and answered the two questions he asked. I asked whether he'd like to tell his father with me beside him. He said yes. Afterwards his father listened, thanked him for being honest, and did not punish him. Farhan's shoulders dropped. — Mr Naveen, school counsellor

What colour were Farhan's ears when he came to the counsellor?
They were red.
What was Farhan afraid of when he came to see the counsellor?
He felt embarrassed and thought he would be in trouble, since he assumed the counsellor would tell his father and he would be punished.
How did Mr Naveen help Farhan feel safe again?
He thanked Farhan for telling him, said curiosity is normal, answered his questions simply, and stayed beside him when he told his father.
How might Farhan's father have felt hearing this?
Probably concerned, but glad his son was honest, since he thanked Farhan and did not punish him.
Padosi se kehna hai "Kal raat aapke yahan bahut shor tha." English?
Say: "There was a lot of noise at your place last night."

- Why do fruit sellers sprinkle water on vegetables?
- 48 pencils are packed equally into 6 boxes. How many pencils are in each box?

1. To keep them fresh. Because leafy vegetables lose water in the heat and then dry out.
2. 8 pencils. Because 6 x 8 = 48.
Now you try: is (4, 6) parallel to (6, 10)?
The answer is no: 6/4 = 1.5 but 10/6 ~ 1.67.

Read this:

Looking back at that week after Shalini's breakup, I think I learnt more about my little sister than in all our years sharing a room. The first night, I sat beside her on the bed and stroked her hair the way Amma used to when we were sick. She went stiff under my hand. Her shoulders rose. I pulled my hand back at once. "Too much?" I asked. She nodded without looking up. "Can you just sit?" So I sat, not touching, and she cried and talked. Two nights later she leaned her head on my shoulder herself, and after a while she said, "You can do the hair thing now." I did, slowly. She fell asleep like that. I, Keerthana, the big sister who fixes everything, had to learn that comfort sometimes means waiting.

Whose way of stroking hair did Keerthana copy?
The way Amma used to when they were sick.
What was Shalini feeling when she went stiff under Keerthana's hand the first night?
She seemed overwhelmed and not ready to be touched, though she still wanted company; two nights later she felt safe enough to ask for the hair stroking.
How did Keerthana handle it when Shalini stiffened?
She stopped at once, asked "Too much?" and stayed nearby without touching until Shalini invited it.
What would change if Keerthana had kept stroking Shalini's hair that first night?
Shalini might have felt crowded and less able to talk or cry, so the comfort would have felt like pressure.

Read this:

Sahil, you are captain this year, so hear how Deepak did it at fifteen. Our school was planning Sports Day and I had a list as long as my arm and no idea who should do what. I would have painted the posters myself, badly. Then I thought: who in my class writes like a printed book? Nusrat. And who knows every shopkeeper on the road and could get the permission letters signed at the ward office? Gopal. I did not pick names out of a hat. I went to Nusrat and said, "Your writing is the best in our class, will you do the posters?" Then to Gopal: "You know people, can you get the permissions?" Both said yes at once, because I had named what they were good at. I kept the sports list for myself.

Who was asked to do the posters?
Nusrat was asked to do the posters.
How did Deepak feel at the start, holding a list as long as an arm?
Deepak felt overwhelmed and unsure who should do what.
Which choice inside the story made both classmates say yes, and why?
Deepak named what each classmate was good at, so the request felt like a recognition of a real skill.
How might Gopal have felt when asked about the permissions?
Gopal may have felt pleased and trusted, since the request showed that Deepak had noticed the skill.

Read this:

Jagdish: did you see Manoj's pitch deck for the expansion?
Manoj: 😄 you mean MY pitch deck, I'm right here
Jagdish: haha. yes. it's really good. I mean it
Manoj: but?
Jagdish: but it has 7 steps and every one has to go right. new city office, hire 20 people, get the big client, win the tender, open by August...
Manoj: they're all realistic!
Jagdish: each one alone, sure. together it's a long chain
Manoj: so you think it won't work?
Jagdish: I think it'll work better if we don't need all 7. what if the first milestone is just the big client?
Manoj: ...the board loved the full story though
Jagdish: stories with more detail always sound better. doesn't make them likelier
Manoj: fair. can you help me make a smaller version for Friday?
Jagdish: yes 🙂

How many steps does Manoj's pitch deck have?
7 steps.
What was Jagdish feeling on starting the chat?
Jagdish felt admiring but uneasy, wanting to praise the deck while warning that its long chain of steps was risky.
What does Jagdish suggest, and why is it a good idea?
Making the first milestone just the big client, so the plan doesn't need all seven steps to go right.
How does Manoj respond to the concern?
Manoj is defensive at first, pointing out the board loved it, then agrees and asks for help with a smaller version.

Read this:

It was the first cold week of winter at the Chandigarh kindergarten, and Minakshi, four, wore her new red sweater. At the door, her father Baljeet knelt.
"I'll be here at pickup. By the swing."
Minakshi waved and ran in. She painted, played house and ate her lunch without once looking back.
At pickup, she dashed to the swing where Baljeet stood. She touched his hand, grinned, then ran back to finish a game of tag.
Baljeet laughed. "Just checking I'm here?"
Minakshi nodded and ran off again.

Where did Baljeet say he'd be at pickup?
By the swing.
Why did Minakshi run to touch Baljeet's hand and then run off again?
She felt safe and reassured seeing he was there, so she could go back to playing.
How did Baljeet's promise help Minakshi?
Knowing where he'd be made it easy for her to play independently all day.
How might Baljeet feel when Minakshi runs back to her game?
He probably feels amused and proud that she feels secure enough to go off again.
On a moonless night, three fireflies danced in the evening breeze.  They were joined by four less than a dozen more fireflies, before two of the fireflies flew away.  How many fireflies remained?

Four less than a dozen is 12-4=8.
The three fireflies were joined by four less than a dozen more fireflies, for a total of 3+8=11 fireflies.
Two flew away, leaving 11-2=9 fireflies remaining.
The answer is 9.
What is the name of the girl I sat next to on the school trip?
I wasn't on your trip, so I don't know. A friend from the trip or your photos could help.
Why do people wear life jackets on a boat?
A life jacket keeps a person afloat. Because it holds a person up in the water even if she cannot swim or gets tired, she can stay up until help arrives.
Even a girl who forgets her umbrella can have a story with a happy end. Write one.

Divya had left her umbrella on the school bus again. Now she stood at the gate, watching a wall of rain, with her bag clutched over her head.

"Hey, you can share," said a boy from the class below. His name was Prem, and he held a big black umbrella. She had never spoken to him.

They walked together, splashing through puddles. Prem talked about his pet rabbit, Gajar. Divya told him about her goldfish. By the time they reached her lane, her shoulder was soaked, but she was laughing.

"Thanks," she said.

"See you tomorrow," said Prem.

The next day, he waited at the gate. Divya had her umbrella, but she walked under his anyway, and he did not mind.

'Papa, I'm not joining the PhD in January.'
Pradeep lowered his newspaper. 'You told the whole family at Rakhi. Your Mama has already told his friends.'
'I know. When I said it, I hadn't spent six months in a lab. Now I have. I like teaching the juniors far more than the experiments.'
'So it was a mistake?'
'It was a good decision with what I knew in August. I just know more now.'
'And what will you tell Mama?'
'Exactly this. He can be disappointed for a day.'
Pradeep was quiet. 'And the teaching?'
'From next week I'm taking two evening classes at the coaching centre. I told the owner already, so I can't back out when I'm tired.'
Pradeep almost smiled. 'So now you use your big mouth on purpose, Rekha.'

When had Rekha told the family about the PhD?
At Rakhi.
What is Pradeep feeling when he asks 'So it was a mistake?'
Pradeep seems worried and a little disappointed, unsure whether changing course means Rekha chose badly.
Which part of Rekha's explanation is most useful to copy?
Saying the first choice was good for what she knew then, and that she simply knows more now, which explains the change without shame.
How might Mama feel when Rekha tells him?
Mama may feel let down for a day, especially after telling his friends, but a plain explanation makes it easier to accept.
A 10 m long and 8 m wide rectangular floor is to be covered with a square carpet with 4 m sides. How many square meters of the floor are uncovered?

The area of the floor is 10 m x 8 m = 80 square meters.
The area of the carpet is 4 m x 4 m = 16 square meters.
Therefore, the area of the floor not covered by the carpet is 80 square meters - 16 square meters = 64 square meters,
The answer is 64.

In the clinic waiting room, Noor sat between her Phuphi and her cousin Hafsa. When a nurse called the next name, Phuphi leaned over and whispered loudly, "Look, one of those people. Their kind are never clean. I hope she doesn't touch me." Hafsa nodded as if it were ordinary.
Noor looked at the nurse. She had gentle hands and had just helped an old man with his walking stick. Noor's stomach went tight. She didn't nod.
That night she sat by Nani. "Nani, why does Phuphi talk like that about some people?"
Nani said, "Some grown-ups learned those ideas when they were small and never questioned them. It is not right. You can keep your own view, and be kind to everyone."
Next visit, Noor decided, she would smile at that nurse.

What had the nurse just helped an old man with?
His walking stick.
How did Noor feel when Phuphi whispered about the nurse?
Uneasy and uncomfortable; her stomach went tight because the words did not match what she saw.
How did Noor hold her own view without a fight?
She did not nod along, then later asked Nani, a trusted elder, why Phuphi talks that way.
How might the nurse feel if she overheard Phuphi?
Hurt and insulted, especially while she was caring for patients.

Read this:

"Irawati, you don't have to buy me samosas every day."
"Ujjwal, you gave me all your notes when I had jaundice. Two whole weeks of notes."
"That was a month ago."
"I still owe you."
"You don't owe me anything."
"I do. It sits in my head. Every time I see you, I think, I haven't paid it back yet."
"Is that why you're being weird?"
"I'm not being weird."
"You helped me with my essay, you bought samosas, you gave me your pen. It's like you're filling a bill."
"...Maybe I am."
"Irawati, I did it because we're friends. Not so you'd owe me."
"Then can we stop counting?"
"We can try."

How many weeks of notes did Ujjwal give Irawati?
Two whole weeks of notes.
What is Irawati feeling about the notes Ujjwal gave?
Irawati feels guilty and uneasy, carrying the help as a debt that must be repaid.
What could help Irawati and Ujjwal stop counting?
Talking openly, as they do, and treating help as part of friendship rather than a bill to be paid.
How does Ujjwal see Irawati's samosas and favours?
Ujjwal feels a bit uncomfortable and puzzled, as if the friendship has turned into a bill.

In Sahil's kasba school near Jalgaon, the headmaster read out the mock-test results by the Class 10 notice board.

"Sahil. Forty percent of questions wrong in science."

Sahil's stomach dropped. Forty percent wrong. He walked home past the cotton gin feeling like a failure. That night he told his sister Swati, "I'm dropping science. I'll take arts. I'm clearly not good enough."

Swati looked at the marksheet. "Sahil, this says sixty percent right."

"It's the same thing."

"Then why does it feel like a failure one way and okay the other?"

He looked at the paper. Sixty percent right. That didn't sound so bad. Last term, he'd got fifty.

"You were about to change your whole stream because of one sentence," Swati said.

He folded the marksheet into his science book. His mood lifted, just a bit. But he was surprised at how close he'd come.

What percentage did the headmaster say Sahil got wrong?
Forty percent of questions wrong in science.
Why did Sahil decide to drop science after the announcement?
Sahil felt like a failure and ashamed because "forty percent wrong" sounded so bad, even though it also meant sixty percent right.
What did Swati do that helped Sahil rethink?
Swati read the same result as sixty percent right and compared it with last term, which showed Sahil was actually improving.
What would have changed if the headmaster had said sixty percent right?
Sahil might have felt okay or even pleased, and wouldn't have thought of changing streams.

Read this:

On Sunday evening in the kasba, Jeevan spread his notebook on the kitchen table in front of Papa. Harish read the dates, the times and the messages from the class group, the names, the laughing at Jeevan's torn bag. He read slowly. "You did well to keep this," Harish said. "None of it is your fault." Jeevan's shoulders eased. On Monday morning Papa walked into school with him. The class teacher went through the pages, thanked him, and took them to the counsellor before lunch. By afternoon the headmaster had called a meeting under the school's anti-bullying policy, the parents of the boys involved were sent for, and a teacher would sit in the class for the next weeks. Jeevan was no longer alone with it.

Whom did Jeevan show the notebook to on Sunday evening?
Jeevan showed the notebook to Papa, Harish, at the kitchen table.
How did Jeevan feel after Papa said none of it was his fault?
Jeevan felt relieved, as his shoulders eased, no longer carrying the blame or the secret.
What else could Jeevan do if the messages continued after the meeting, and why?
Jeevan could tell the class teacher or counsellor again the same day and keep adding to the record, because the policy gives the school a way to act again.
How might the class teacher see the notebook?
The class teacher sees clear, dated evidence that can be acted on, and is grateful Jeevan brought it, which is why it went to the counsellor before lunch.

Read this:

In their apartment in Buenos Aires, Valentina started keeping count without meaning to.

Jin used to kiss the back of her neck when he passed the stove. Now he said "smells good" from the doorway. He used to ask about the difficult client at her studio; now he said "how was work?" and nodded at whatever she answered. After dinner he took his laptop to the balcony, and she sat with a book on the sofa, reading the same paragraph.

Separate evenings. Every evening.

She had lived alone for years before him and had never felt this lonely. Alone, at least, no one was sitting ten feet away.

On Thursday she almost said it: "Jin, are we okay?" She got as far as his name. He looked up. She said, "Nothing. Do you want tea?"

He said yes. She made it. The question stayed in her throat.

Where did Jin take his laptop after dinner?
To the balcony.
Why does Valentina feel lonelier now than when she lived alone?
She feels lonely and unseen inside the relationship, because Jin is close by but no longer curious about her or affectionate.
What could Valentina try instead of offering tea?
She could gently say what she has noticed, fewer touches and separate evenings, and ask Jin how he feels, even though it is hard.
What might Jin be experiencing when he looks up at his name?
He may sense something is coming and feel uneasy, or he may be absorbed in his own worries and not notice the distance at all.
What mood is associated with Raga Abhogi?
Raga Abhogi is associated with a simple, yearning mood.

Read this:

In their village near Ludhiana, Amandeep helped her mother roll rotis while working up her courage. "Mummy, Devika copies from my notebook every day before the teacher comes. She says if I tell, she won't be my friend." Her mother kept rolling. "What do you think you should do?" "I don't know. Telling feels mean. Not telling feels like lying." Her mother put down the rolling pin. "Can you be kind and honest both? First talk to Devika yourself. Tell her you won't give the notebook any more, and offer to do homework together after school. If she keeps copying from others, then tell the teacher, and say you're worried for her, not angry." Amandeep flipped a roti, thinking. "Tomorrow. At the handpump."

When does Devika copy?
Every day before the teacher comes.
How did Amandeep feel about telling?
Torn: telling felt mean, but not telling felt like lying.
What else could Amandeep do if Devika gets angry?
Keep offering homework together, and still go to the teacher if the copying continues, as Mummy suggested.
How might Devika feel when Amandeep talks to her?
Maybe hurt or defensive at first, but she may see that Amandeep cares and is offering help.
