Read this:

At his cousin Tanuja's engagement in Jalandhar, Baljeet kept his phone face down so no one would see the delivery app's orange screen. When Tayaji asked what he was doing these days, he said, 'Something in logistics,' and steered the talk to cricket. He had been riding for four months since his engineering results came out badly, and every lie made him feel smaller. Then, halfway through dinner, his phone chimed loudly: 'Your pickup is ready.' Tanuja, sitting next to him, glanced at the screen. Later, by the sweets table, she said quietly, 'You deliver food? Why hide it?' 'Because they'll say I've fallen.' 'You're paying for your re-exam yourself. That's not falling.' Before leaving, Baljeet told Tayaji the truth, and his plan: ride until the re-exam in June, then apply for site engineer jobs. Tayaji grunted, then said, 'Good. Honest work.' His face still burned, but less.

What did Baljeet first tell Tayaji he was doing?
Baljeet said, 'Something in logistics.'
How did Baljeet feel each time he lied?
Baljeet felt smaller and ashamed, afraid relatives would say he had fallen.
What made Baljeet's final answer to Tayaji wise?
He told the truth and shared a clear plan: riding until the June re-exam, then applying for site engineer jobs.
How does Tanuja see Baljeet's job?
Tanuja sees it as honest work that pays for his re-exam, not a fall.
What is one teaching note for Raga Hamsadhwani?
Often used for invocatory pieces.

Read this:

Three months into my first internship, someone added me to a group chat called Monday Survivors. It was six interns and one topic: our team lead, Pallavi. Screenshots of her emails with jokes on top. A nickname for her voice. Someone planned to “forget” to invite her to a lunch.
I laughed at the first two jokes. I'm not proud of that. Then I read one of her emails properly, the one they were mocking, and it was just a polite note asking us to reply before Friday.
That night I left the group. No speech, no announcement. The next morning I replied to her email on time and said good morning when she walked past, the way I always had.
A couple of interns went cold on me. It stung. But when Pallavi asked me to present our work to the client, I didn't wonder whether I'd earned it. — Mridul

What was the group chat called?
The group chat was called Monday Survivors.
How did Mridul feel about laughing at the first two jokes?
Mridul felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed afterwards, admitting to not being proud of it 😔
Was leaving the group quietly a wise choice? Why?
Yes; it stepped away from the gossip without starting a fight, and Mridul kept being courteous and on time with Pallavi.
What would change for Pallavi if the lunch plan and jokes went on unchecked?
She could be quietly shut out of her own team's plans, which would make her work harder and more isolating.
A farmer picked 34 oranges and sold 18 of them. How many does she have left?
16. Because 34 - 18 = 16, so 16 are left.

Read this:

Dear Pooja-di,
I need your honest view before I decide something, and I can't talk about it with anyone in the group.
For eight months I've been part of an online meditation circle. It helped at first; I slept better after Papa's surgery. But lately our teacher says that any doubt is 'the ego fighting the light'. Last week I said I wanted a break for my final exams. The senior member messaged me privately: 'People who step away often find accidents coming to their families. Think carefully.' I read it at 2 a.m. and couldn't sleep.
Part of me feels guilty for questioning. Part of me feels scared. And a small part is angry, because that's not how love sounds.
You've always been the calm one. Could we talk this weekend before I reply to them? I'd also like to tell Mummy, but I want to say it clearly first.
With love,
Vandana

How long has Vandana been in the online meditation circle?
Vandana has been in it for eight months.
What mix of feelings does Vandana describe?
Vandana feels guilty for questioning, scared by the warning, and a little angry at how it sounds.
Why is Vandana's plan wise?
Vandana is talking to Pooja-di and Mummy, people outside the group, before replying or deciding.
What is the senior member's message trying to do?
It uses fear about accidents to make Vandana feel guilty and stay in the group.
Share a gentle story about a boy who rides his cycle to fetch candles during a power cut.

When the lights failed at seven, Manoj's mother realised that they had no candles. The nearest shop was a kilometre away. "I'll go," said Manoj, thirteen. He took his cycle, and the dark road felt strange without street lamps. Fireflies hovered above the hedges. He passed houses lit by lanterns. At the shop, the owner was selling the last few candles by torchlight. Manoj bought six and rode home carefully, holding them in a bag on the handlebar. The wind blew against him. At home, his mother lit the first one and set it in the window. "Well done," she said, and the flame bobbed.

Read this:

"You're quitting?" Hemant put down his tea. "Madhuri, the loan on this house—"
"I know, Papa. I've thought about the loan every night for a week."
"Then why?"
"They want me to sign water-test reports for samples I never tested. For building sites. People will drink that water."
Her father was quiet. "Did you say no?"
"Twice. The second time Sir said I'd be 'out by month end' if I didn't cooperate."
"And if you sign, just once?"
"Then it's my name on it forever. If someone gets sick, that's on me."
Hemant rubbed his forehead. "What will you do?"
"I've applied to two labs and the municipal water department. I'll keep working honestly till they tell me to go. And I'm writing down every request, with dates."
He looked at her a long moment. "Your grandfather left the ration office over something like this," he said finally. "We ate less that year. We were fine."
Madhuri's eyes stung.

What does the lab want Madhuri to sign?
Water-test reports for samples she never tested.
What might Madhuri have been feeling during the week of thinking about the loan every night?
Madhuri was anxious and torn, weighing the family's loan against putting her name on false reports.
Which of Madhuri's steps reduce her risk while refusing?
Applying to other labs and the water department, working honestly until told to go, and keeping dated records of every request.
How does Hemant come to see his daughter's choice?
At first he fears for the loan, but remembering his own father's similar choice, he seems to accept and even respect it.
What does "get the ball rolling" mean?

It means to start an activity or a process.
Example: To get the ball rolling for the Pongal celebration, Anjali made a list of who would bring what.

Make this text into a two-sentence summary.

My little mistress behaved like an angel in coming to wait on me, and cheer my solitude; the confinement brought me exceedingly low. It is wearisome, to a stirring active body: but few have slighter reasons for complaint than I had. The moment Catherine left Mr. Linton's room she appeared at my bedside. Her day was divided between us; no amusement usurped a minute: she neglected her meals, her studies, and her play; and she was the fondest nurse that ever watched. She must have had a warm heart, when she loved her father so, to give so much to me. I said her days were divided between us; but the master retired early, and I generally needed nothing after six o'clock, thus the evening was her own. Poor thing! I never considered what she did with herself after tea. And though frequently, when she looked in to bid me good-night, I remarked a fresh colour in her cheeks and a pinkness over her slender fingers, instead of fancying the hue borrowed from a cold ride across the moors, I laid it to the charge of a hot fire in the library.

While the narrator is confined to bed, Catherine nurses the narrator lovingly and gives up meals, lessons and play. The narrator does not wonder what Catherine does in the evenings and blames her rosy cheeks on the hot library fire.

Read this:

"Why are you crying?" Usha asked. Imran sat on the school steps, knees up. "Ammi's late. Everybody's gone." "My Nani's late too." Usha sat beside him. "Are you hungry?" He shook his head, then nodded. Usha opened her tiffin. One biscuit left. She broke it. "Half for you." "It's yours." "Friends share. Take it." Imran took it. Usha patted his arm. "Your Ammi always comes. Remember last time? She came running with an umbrella." Imran gave a tiny laugh. "She was all wet." "Like a duck," said Usha. They were both giggling when the gate opened.

How many biscuits were left in Usha's tiffin?
One biscuit left.
How was Imran feeling on the school steps?
He felt scared and lonely because his Ammi was late and everyone had gone.
Which choice by Usha turned Imran's tears into giggles?
Usha shared her last biscuit and reminded him of the funny umbrella day, giving him comfort and a reason to laugh.
What would change if Usha had just waited on her own?
Imran would likely have kept crying alone, feeling that nobody cared, and the wait would have felt much longer for him.

metadata.subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

After Thursday's talk, with the release deadline pressing, Pooja wrote the plan that evening. Three goals: finish tickets by their dates, add tests to every change, and ask for help within an hour of getting stuck. Under them, the support: a fifteen-minute check-in each morning, Nitin as pairing partner, and a review on the fourteenth of next month, six weeks away. She also wrote plainly what would happen if the goals weren't met: a conversation with the manager about whether the role fits. Next morning she gave it to Yogesh, who read it twice and asked two questions. Both signed at the bottom. "It's clear," Yogesh said. "At least I know where I stand."

How many goals did Pooja write in the plan?
Pooja wrote three goals.
How did Yogesh feel after reading the plan?
Yogesh felt somewhat relieved and clearer about where things stood, though probably still a little apprehensive.
What else could Pooja do to make the plan fair, and why?
Pooja could check in at the halfway point to see whether the support is enough, because a plan that only measures the junior misses whether the offered help is working.
How might Nitin see being named as the pairing partner?
Nitin might feel trusted but also a bit stretched, since the pairing adds to the workload before the deadline.

metadata.subtype: Approach: written improvement plan with a review date [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tuesday night. Farhan Mamu called after dinner. His shop needs money for stock and he asked if I could lend some. My first feeling was pride that he asked me, and then my stomach dropped. I have only just started earning. What if it doesn't come back? What if I say no and Mamu tells the whole family I'm stingy?
I said I would think and call back. Now I have written it down. I can lend one amount that I could manage if it were late, not more. I want a date in writing. I will say I can't promise a second time. Mamu is family, and I still need to be honest.
I will call tomorrow after work.
Zeenat

Who called Zeenat after dinner on Tuesday?
Farhan Mamu called after dinner.
What is Zeenat feeling when thinking about the loan?
Zeenat feels torn, proud to be asked, then afraid the money will not come back and anxious about being called stingy.
What plan does Zeenat make for answering Mamu?
Zeenat plans to offer one amount that would be manageable if it were late, ask for a date in writing, and say plainly that a second loan is not promised.
How might Mamu see Zeenat's answer when it comes?
Mamu may be disappointed to get only one fixed amount, but he is family and would at least know where he stands with Zeenat.
Diane is twice as old as her brother, Will. If Will was 4 years old 3 years ago, what will the sum of their ages be in 5 years?

Since Will was 4 years old 3 years ago, then he is 4+3 = 7 years old now
Dina is twice as old as he is so she is 2*7 = 14 years old now
In 5 years, Will will be 7+5 = 12 years old
In 5 years, Diane will be 14+5 = 19 years old
The sum of their ages at that time will be 12+19 = 31 years
The answer is 31.

Read this:

The site visit happened in pouring rain, under a blue tarpaulin, with the generator coughing and dying twice. Sabina walked Mr Bhupen Das through the half-built library on a wet printout, pointing to where the reading windows would go. At the end he shook her hand hard. 'This is the best design this town has seen. You thought of the children's corner nobody else did.' Her old answer was already on her tongue: 'Oh, it's the team, really.' She stopped it. 'Thank you,' she said. Just that. It felt strange, like leaving a door open. In the auto back, rain dripping from her dupatta, she opened the note on her phone titled 'Things that went right' and typed: '12 Aug. Client praised children's corner. Said thank you. Didn't argue.' It was the thirty-first entry.

What was the note on Sabina's phone titled?
The note was titled 'Things that went right'.
Why did saying just 'thank you' feel like leaving a door open to Sabina?
Sabina was used to closing praise off with 'it's the team', so letting it in plainly felt unfamiliar and a little exposed 🙂.
How does the phone note support Sabina's confidence?
Recording each good moment, including the compliment and the plain thank-you, builds a growing list of evidence she can look back on instead of leaning on self-doubt.
How might Mr Bhupen Das feel when Sabina simply says 'thank you'?
He would likely feel his praise was received and meant, which fits how firmly he shook her hand.

Read this:

Hostel warden's note, Girls' Block.
Every morning we have five minutes of silence before breakfast. Most girls fidget. Leela, who joined this term, used to giggle and whisper through it.
This week I noticed a change. She sits cross-legged, eyes closed, hands in her lap. After, she writes in a small notebook.
Today I asked what she writes. She said, "Three good things from yesterday. My Nani told me to." Today's list: "Hot water in the bathroom. Sumit Sir's funny joke in maths. A letter from home."
I've asked if she'd share the idea at Sunday assembly. She agreed, a little shyly. — Mrs Varghese

How many good things does Leela write each day?
Three good things.
What does Leela sitting still with eyes closed suggest?
Leela seems calmer and more settled, finding comfort in the quiet time.
How could Mrs Varghese help other girls try Leela's habit?
She could let Leela share it at assembly and give everyone a small notebook for their three good things.
How might Leela's Nani feel if she knew Leela kept the habit?
Leela's Nani would likely feel proud and happy 🙏 that her advice is helping Leela in the hostel.
Suggest a holiday reading habit in one sentence that begins with "Try" and uses fewer than 16 words.
Try reading one short story every afternoon under a shady tree.
Will's mom gave him $74 to go shopping. He bought a sweater for $9, a T-shirt for $11 and a pair of shoes for $30. He then returned his shoes for a 90% refund.  How much money does Will have left?

Will paid $30 for his shoes but then returned them and got 90% of the money back, so he lost 10% of the money, which means 10/100 * $30 = $3 is gone.
Will spent $9 + $11 + $3 = $23.
Will started with $74 - $23 that he spent = $51 remaining.
The answer is 51.

Read this:

The team met in a café because the office internet was down, and the coffee machine hissed every two minutes. Vijay, an intern for three weeks, had his notebook open and a pen ready.
There was no agenda. Mehak, the product manager, started on the new app screen, then slid into a story about a client, then into the new logo. Arun from sales cut in loudly and argued about pricing for twenty minutes. Every time Vijay leaned forward to ask a question, the machine hissed or Arun's voice rose.
After ninety minutes Mehak said, "Great, so we're aligned," and stood up.
On the walk back, Vijay asked the designer what they had aligned on. "The new colours," she said. Arun, on the phone, was telling someone that pricing was settled. Vijay looked at his notebook. Two pages of arrows and not a single line he could call a decision. He had a report due at five.

Why did the team meet in a café?
The team met in a café because the office internet was down.
What was Vijay feeling as he looked at his notebook on the walk back?
Vijay felt confused and anxious, with two pages of arrows, no decision to report and a report due at five.
What could have made this meeting useful?
A short agenda, someone keeping Arun's pricing argument to time, and ending with the decisions read aloud would have left everyone with the same outcome.
How does Mehak see the meeting?
Mehak seems to think it went well, saying "we're aligned," without noticing that people left with different memories.

Read this:

I am Siddharth, and I still remember the recess when a girl from 5B leaned close and whispered that Pradeep thought I was boring now. She said it sweetly, as if she were doing me a favour. All afternoon my stomach felt tight, and I replayed every joke I had told that week. I nearly stopped sitting with him. Then I thought: she was not even there when he said it, if he said it at all. So the next morning I simply asked Pradeep, right at the bicycle stand. He looked confused and then laughed. "Boring? You lent me your cricket cards!" I felt silly and relieved together. The girl never whispered to me again.

Where did Siddharth ask Pradeep about the boring remark?
Siddharth asked him at the bicycle stand the next morning.
Why did Siddharth's stomach feel tight, and why did Siddharth replay every joke after the whisper?
Siddharth worried the girl's claim might be true, so Siddharth searched for a reason Pradeep might find the friendship boring.
What could someone try when a rival whispers that a friend has turned against them?
They can ask the friend directly, as Siddharth did, instead of taking the whisper as fact, since the whisperer may want to split them up.
How might Pradeep have felt when Siddharth suddenly asked about the boring remark?
Pradeep looked confused first, which suggests he had no idea anyone thought this, and then he laughed and reminded Siddharth about the cricket cards.
Use contractions throughout: We are going to light the lamps, and we will not forget the sweets.
We're going to light the lamps, and we won't forget the sweets.

Read this:

Quiz coach's note, mock round, Thursday
Varun is one of our quickest boys, and he loves the buzzer. Today he pressed it on five questions before I had finished reading them. "Which planet is closest to the sun, and which" - buzz - "Mercury!" The question was about the planet with the most moons. He got four of those five wrong and lost twenty points. He was frustrated and said the questions were tricky. I explained that quiz questions often turn at the end. We practised a rule: wait until the question mark, count one, then buzz. In the last ten questions he waited, got three right, and made no mistakes. I will keep reminding him.
- Lalit

How many points did Varun lose on the early buzzes?
He lost twenty points.
How did Varun feel after losing the points?
He felt frustrated and blamed the questions for being tricky.
What other approach might suit Varun's quickness, and why?
He could listen for the key word at the end of each question before buzzing, because his speed is useful only when he knows what is being asked.
How do Varun's early buzzes look to Lalit?
Lalit sees a quick boy losing points he doesn't need to lose, and patiently helps him with a simple rule.

metadata.subtype: Approach: blurting out the first answer without thinking [Pitfall]

messages.content: Why do days feel longer in summer? Also, what is my school timetable for Monday?

1. The sun rises earlier and sets later, so there is more daylight.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your timetable. Check your school diary or ask your class teacher.

Read this:

When I was ten, I ate a packet of chips before every football practice. Salty, crunchy, and gone in a minute.
I'm Ujjwal. By the second half I'd be tired and slow.
Coach Dolma noticed. She asked what I'd eaten. When I told her, she didn't laugh. “Try a banana and a roti with something in it next time. See if your legs feel different.”
So I tried it for a week. Banana and a roti roll with egg.
By Friday I was running as fast in the second half as the first. I still like chips. Now they're for weekends.

What did Coach Dolma suggest Ujjwal try?
A banana and a roti with something in it.
How did Ujjwal feel by Friday?
Ujjwal felt stronger and pleased, running as fast in the second half as the first.
Why did changing the snack help Ujjwal?
The banana and roti gave longer-lasting energy than chips.
How might Coach Dolma feel seeing Ujjwal run faster?
She would probably feel pleased that her advice helped.

Read this:

The staff room at the Lucknow coaching institute was buzzing. A clip was going round of the director, in his office, announcing that Monday's mock test was cancelled.

Varun, a young maths tutor, had already forwarded it to his batch of sixty students.

Rashmi, from the admin desk, frowned at her screen. "Varun, play it again. Watch his mouth."

He did. The words and the lips were slightly out of step. The director blinked oddly, almost never.

"And he never records videos," Rashmi said. "He hates cameras."

She checked the institute's official notice board online. Nothing. She called the director's office. The test was on.

Varun felt heat flood his face. "I look like an idiot."

"You look like someone who got tricked by a good fake," Rashmi said. "Someone made it to be believed."

He sent a correction to his batch, with the official notice attached, and asked them to delete the clip.

How many students were in Varun's batch?
Sixty students.
What was Varun feeling after learning the clip was fake?
He felt embarrassed and foolish, heat flooding his face.
What clues and checks exposed the fake clip?
The lips and words were out of step, the director barely blinked, he never records videos, and the official notice board and his office confirmed the test was on.
How does Rashmi see Varun's mistake?
Rashmi sees it as being tricked by a convincing fake, not as foolishness.

Blinky wants to make a three-layer birthday cake for her mom. The recipe for the smallest layer of the cake requires 2 cups of sugar. If the second layer is twice as big as the first and the third layer is three times larger than the second, how many total cups of sugar will she need for the third layer?

Since the second layer is twice as big as the first, then it requires 2* 2 = 4 cups of sugar.
Since the third layer is three times bigger than the second, then it requires 4 * 3 = 12 cups of sugar.
The answer is 12.

Read this:

Saturday: Devika spread a sheet of chart paper on Sunaina's floor. "Everything I regret. Go." They wrote it all: the design course she hadn't taken, the friend she'd hurt in college, the years she'd let her uncle choose her job, the city she hadn't moved to.
The next Wednesday: Sunaina drew two columns. "Can still do something" and "Can't change." Devika moved the design course and the friend to the first column. The lost years went to the second. She cried a little over that one.
Two Sundays later: Sunaina asked a new question. "Forget what you're supposed to want. What do you actually care about?" Devika was quiet for a long time. "Making things people use. Being honest with people I love." She circled the design course. That night she messaged the friend from college: "I've been thinking about what I said in second year. I'm sorry." And she signed up for an evening class.

What were the headings of Sunaina's two columns?
Can still do something and Can't change.
How did Devika feel when she put the lost years in the second column?
Devika felt sad, crying a little, as she accepted that those years could not be changed.
How did sorting her regrets help Devika find a direction?
Separating what she could still fix from what she couldn't, and naming her real values, turned vague dread into concrete steps like the apology and the evening class.
How might the friend from college feel receiving Devika's message?
The friend may feel surprised and touched to get a sincere apology after years, perhaps opening a chance to reconnect.
Our dog's first birthday is next week. Is it silly to celebrate?
Not silly at all. Many families do something small. It's a happy reason to give him extra attention.
What can I do for him?
A longer walk, a new chew toy or a favourite game would be perfect. Keep the day calm and don't overdo it.
Can he have a cake?
Human cakes aren't suitable for dogs, so please skip the sweets. Ask your vet about dog-safe treats, and give only a small amount.
Should I invite the neighbours' dogs?
Only if the dogs know each other and get along. A small group is easier to manage than a crowd, and an adult should be around to supervise.
Maybe we'll do a family picnic then. He loves the park.
A park picnic sounds just right. Bring his favourite ball, a water bowl and plenty of cuddles.
What is a thaat?
A thaat is a parent scale used to classify ragas.

Read this:

I'm Jatin, and Amandeep joined our team in Bengaluru in March, straight from Ludhiana. She's sharp at the work and polite at lunch. But on Mondays, when we ask about weekends, she says 'relaxed' and changes the subject. Once, dropping by for a charger on a Saturday, I saw her alone in the office pantry, laptop open, no work on it, just a cooking video. In May she put up a notice in the lift for a Punjabi-speaking book circle. Two people came, she told me, laughing, and one left early. Then she tried the office badminton club. She comes on Thursdays now, not great at it, cheerful. I don't know what her weekends really feel like. I only know she keeps trying, and last Friday she asked if I wanted to join her and the book-circle guy for chole at a stall she'd found.

What notice did Amandeep put up in the lift?
A notice for a Punjabi-speaking book circle.
What might Amandeep's 'relaxed' answer on Mondays suggest about how she feels?
It may cover lonely, empty weekends she doesn't want to talk about, though Jatin can't be sure.
What is Amandeep doing well at this stage?
She keeps testing different ways to meet people, the book circle and badminton, and starts inviting others, accepting that it builds slowly.
How does Jatin see Amandeep's first months?
Jatin notices signs of loneliness but admits not knowing about her weekends, and seems pleased to be invited for chole.

messages.content:
Read this:

Nilesh, I'll tell you about the worst day of my Class 11. My friends decided to make fun of a boy who stammered. They wanted me to imitate him during break, because I was good at voices. Everyone was waiting. "Come on, Manoj." My mouth went dry. I wanted to be the funny one; I also knew it was cruel. I said, "Not this," and walked off to the canteen. For a week they called me boring and didn't save me a seat. I ate alone. But on the fourth day the boy found me there and sat down without a word. We're still friends. I don't regret losing that seat.

What did the friends want young Manoj to do?
Imitate a boy who stammered during break.
What was young Manoj feeling when his mouth went dry?
Torn between wanting to be the funny one his friends admired and knowing the joke was cruel.
What does Manoj's story show about the cost of standing firm?
There can be a real price, like a week of eating alone, but it can also bring truer friendships.
How might the boy who stammered have felt when he sat beside Manoj?
Grateful and safe, recognising someone who had refused to mock him.

Read this:

Kashish had booked the small conference room in the Hyderabad office for another "let's sort this out" chat between Vijay and Tanushree. The two designers had argued for weeks over who got the better projects.
She began the usual way. "Tell me what's been bothering you."
Tanushree spoke quietly. "It's not the projects. He calls me 'quota hire' when the others are there. Yesterday he said I should go back to making chai."
Kashish put her pen down. This wasn't a clash of workloads she could split down the middle.
"I'm stopping this conversation here," she told them both. "Vijay, please go back to your desk."
When he'd left, she asked Tanushree for the dates and exact words, wrote them down, and read them back to check they were right. That afternoon she sent the notes to the HR partner and followed the complaint procedure.

What did Vijay say Tanushree should do?
He said she should go back to making chai.
Why did Kashish put her pen down when Tanushree spoke?
She was taken aback and uneasy, realising the problem was demeaning remarks, not a workload clash, so the mediation she had planned no longer fitted.
What would you change first if you were Kashish planning the next step?
Keep Tanushree informed of what HR will do next and check she feels safe at her desk, while leaving the investigation to the formal process.
How is Tanushree affected by Kashish stopping the joint talk?
Tanushree no longer has to argue her case face to face with the person making the remarks, and sees her words written down and taken to HR the same day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: escalating to HR for a serious conduct issue [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Nirmala,
I'm writing this because I can't say it without crying, and I don't want to cry at you.
Today Sir told me he gave the lead role in the dance competition to someone else. He said he decided three weeks ago. Three weeks, Nirmala. You were in that meeting. You knew.
Every night since then I've stayed back after practice. I skipped Amma's birthday dinner to rehearse. You watched me do the final spin forty times and said, "Looking good." You never said, "Preeti, stop, he's already decided."
I know you probably didn't want to be the one to break it to me. I know it wasn't your decision. But I would rather have been hurt three weeks ago than feel this stupid now. I could have chosen differently. I could have gone to Amma's dinner.
I still want us to be friends. I just need you to understand why this hurts.
Preeti

When did Sir decide to give the lead role to someone else?
He said he decided three weeks ago.
What is Preeti feeling as she writes the letter?
Preeti feels hurt and foolish, because Nirmala's silence let Preeti keep sacrificing time for a role that was already gone.
What could Nirmala do to repair the friendship?
Nirmala could apologise directly for staying silent and promise to share what affects Preeti's choices in future.
How might Nirmala have seen her silence at the time?
Nirmala may have thought the silence spared Preeti pain, not realising it took away Preeti's chance to decide with full information.
It was so windy yesterday that the kites flied very high. Is "flied" right?

It was so windy yesterday that the kites flew very high.
Why: past tense ("flied" -> "flew").
My grandfather forgets things sometimes and it makes me sad.
I am sorry, that must be hard to watch. Memory changes are common as people age. Is your family helping him?
Yes, my mom takes him to the doctor. His name is Dada Prakash and he loves cricket on the radio.
That is a good sign that your mother is taking care. You can spend time with Dada Prakash listening to cricket and chatting about old matches. Old memories are often the clearest ones.
He remembered a match from 1983 perfectly today.
What a lovely moment. Ask him more about it, and maybe write it down so the family keeps the story. It will also make him happy to be remembered for what he knows.
I will write it in a small diary and read it to him.
That is thoughtful. Reading the diary aloud to Dada Prakash will give him joy and keep the old stories alive. Add a new memory each week, and let him add details too.
Hartley has 4 puppies that each weigh 7.5 kilograms. The rescue center has 14 cats that each weigh 2.5 kilograms. How many kilograms more do the cats weigh than the puppies?

Puppies = 4 * 7.5 = 30 kg
Cats = 14 * 2.5 = 35 kg
35 - 30 = 5
The cats weigh 5 kg more than the puppies.
The answer is 5.

A tank has 3 1/4 litres of water. 1 3/4 litres are used. How much is left?

Now you try: 5 2/7 - 2 5/7.
The answer is 2 4/7.
Diwali shopping is stressing me out. I have a long list.
That sounds like a lot. Break the list into groups: food, decoration, gifts and clothes. Do one group a day instead of everything at once. Cross off each item as you buy it.
Food is the hardest. I am Pooja and I am hosting twenty people.

For twenty people, keep the menu simple. Make a few sweets ahead, order the main dish from a caterer or cook one big dish like pulao, and get snacks from a shop. You do not need to do everything yourself.
Can I really buy some things ready-made? My mother-in-law will judge me.
Yes, you can. Many families do it. Make one dish yourself, like her favourite sweet, and buy the rest. Pooja, a calm host is better than a tired one, and most guests care about the warmth.
Which of the sweets can I make ahead?
Laddoo, barfi and chikki all keep for days, so you can make them a week before. Fried items like gujiya are best made two days earlier. Do not make milk sweets too early.
And what is the number of guests I said?
You said twenty guests. So plan about four or five pieces of sweets for each person, and make sure you have enough plates and cups for twenty, plus a few extra.

Read this:

Monday. Jahnavi's first draft of the market report landed in Nilesh's inbox two hours late, and the charts were wrong. Nilesh felt his jaw tighten. It would take him forty minutes to redo it himself. He almost did. Instead he wrote three comments and sent it back.

Thursday. The second draft was better but still messy. "Just give it to me, I'll finish it," Nilesh heard himself say out loud. Jahnavi's face fell. He caught himself. "Actually, no. Sit with me for twenty minutes. Show me how you built chart three." She explained; he asked questions; she fixed it herself.

Three weeks later. Jahnavi sent the monthly report on time, with a note: "I added a new comparison chart. Is it useful?" It was. Nilesh forwarded it to his manager with her name on it.

He still felt the itch to take things back sometimes. He just didn't scratch it.

How late was Jahnavi's first draft?
Jahnavi's first draft was two hours late.
What was Nilesh feeling when his jaw tightened on Monday?
Nilesh felt irritated and impatient, tempted to redo the report himself because it would be faster.
What changed on Thursday, and why did it matter?
Nilesh stopped himself from taking the task back and coached Jahnavi instead, so she learned to fix it herself.
What was it like for Jahnavi when Nilesh said "Just give it to me"?
Jahnavi felt deflated and discouraged; her face fell, as if her effort didn't count.
Do we say "listen the music" or "listen to the music"? Can you fix my sentence? The news are very sad. Why do hens sit on eggs? Could you explain passive for me?

1. Say "listen to the music". "Listen" always takes "to" before the thing you hear.
2. Corrected: The news is very sad. "News" is uncountable and takes "is".
3. They keep the eggs warm. Because warmth helps the chick grow inside.
4. In grammar, the passive voice puts the receiver of the action first, as in "The cake was eaten." As an ordinary adjective, "passive" means taking no action and letting things happen.

Read this:

Uma's first week at her new school in Lucknow had been one long advertisement for her old school in Delhi. Bigger rooms. Better canteen. Nicer teachers. On the second Monday she noticed that when she walked up, Parul's group went quiet. One girl looked at her shoes. Uma stood there and thought, "Every time I talk about Delhi, they stop talking." At lunch she tried something new. She asked Parul about the badge on her bag. "It's from the dance club," Parul said, and talked for five minutes about the annual show. Uma listened and asked two more questions. On Wednesday Parul saved her a seat. "You should try the dance club," she said.

What was the badge on Parul's bag from?
It was from the dance club.
What was Uma feeling when she noticed Parul's group go quiet?
Uma felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising her talk about Delhi was pushing people away.
Which approach worked better for Uma, and why?
Asking Parul about the badge worked better, because people warm to someone who is interested in them.
How does the new Uma look to Parul?
Parul enjoys being asked about dance club and feels listened to, so she saves Uma a seat and invites her to join.

metadata.subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Binita's phone buzzed with her brother's angry voice note about the quarrel over the family field boundary, just as the call from the buyer in Pune came through. Her jaw was tight. In the tin-roofed cooperative office near Sangli, with hens scratching outside the door, she rolled her shoulders, put on the warm voice she kept for buyers and smiled so it would reach her words. "Namaskar, Mehra-ji! Yes, the ghee shipment leaves Friday. We're very glad to have your order again." The buyer laughed and added twenty tins. When the call ended, Binita let the smile drop. Abhinav, who kept the accounts at the next desk, looked up. "You sounded happy." "I chose to sound happy," she said. "I'm actually furious with my brother." She stepped out, walked to the well and back, and then called her brother to talk it through in her ordinary voice.

What shipment did Binita say would leave on Friday?
The ghee shipment would leave Friday.
What was Binita feeling while she spoke warmly to the buyer?
Binita was furious with her brother after the voice note but chose a warm voice on purpose; the tight jaw showed the anger was still there under the smile.
Which part of Binita's handling was healthy, and why?
The warm voice for the buyer was an ordinary work skill, and she also named the anger to Abhinav and took a walk, so the feeling was not simply buried.

A bag of peanuts weighs 0.35 kg. Write this as a fraction of a kilogram in simplest form. Also write 0.125 and 2.75 as fractions.

Answer: 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20. 0.125 = 125/1000 = 1/8. 2.75 = 2 75/100 = 2 3/4.

The last digit of 0.35 is in the hundredths place, so write it over 100: 35/100. Now simplify: the HCF of 35 and 100 is 5, so 35/100 = 7/20. For 0.125 the last digit is in the thousandths place: 125/1000, HCF 125, so 1/8. For 2.75 keep the 2 wholes and change 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4, giving 2 3/4. A common mistake is to write 0.35 = 35/10; count the decimal places: 2 places means 100.

In a kindergarten in Oslo, Ingrid kept pushing the smaller children out of the playhouse. "My house! Get out!" She looked strong and pleased. Clara, the teacher, stopped her. "Ingrid, no pushing. The playhouse is for everyone." Ingrid pushed again. Clara moved her gently to a bench. Then she sat beside her. "Where did you learn 'Get out'?" Ingrid shrugged. "My big brother says it. He pushes me off the sofa." Clara nodded. "Being strong can mean being the house captain who lets people in." At pick-up, Clara told Ingrid's father what she had said.

What did Ingrid shout at the smaller children?
She shouted, "My house! Get out!"
What might Ingrid feel underneath looking strong and pleased?
She may feel small and pushed around herself, copying her big brother so she can feel powerful for once.
Why did Clara do more than just punish Ingrid?
Only punishing would not show her another way; Clara held the limit, asked where the words came from and offered a kinder way to feel strong.
How might Ingrid's father feel after Clara talks to him at pick-up?

A laser beam starts at A(1, 2, 3) and travels in the direction 2i - j + 4k. Write the equation of the beam in vector and Cartesian form. Does it hit a sensor at (5, 0, 11)? At (3, 1, 6)?

Answer: r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k); (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. (5, 0, 11) is on it (lambda = 2); (3, 1, 6) is not.

Every point of the line is 'start + lambda x direction': r = (i + 2j + 3k) + lambda(2i - j + 4k) x = 1 + 2lambda, y = 2 - lambda, z = 3 + 4lambda Making lambda the subject of each equation and equating gives the Cartesian form (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4. To test a point, find lambda from one coordinate and check the others: for (5, 0, 11), lambda = 2 from x, and then y = 2 - 2 = 0 and z = 3 + 8 = 11, all agree: ON the beam (for lambda >= 0, the ray itself). For (3, 1, 6), x gives lambda = 1, y gives lambda = 1, but z gives lambda = 3/4: NOT on it. Common mistake: writing (x + 1)/2 for the point (1, 2, 3) (the sign in the bracket is the opposite of the coordinate), or putting the point's coordinates in the denominators.

"It was the prospect of constant society, and good society," he added, "which was my chief inducement to enter the ----shire. I know it to be a most respectable, agreeable corps; and my friend Denny tempted me further by his account of their present quarters, and the very great attentions and excellent acquaintance Meryton had procured them. Jame has 60 bars of gold.  He uses 10% of them to pay for tax and then loses half of what is left in divorce.  How many gold bars does he have left?

He loses 60*.1=6 bars to taxes
That means he has 60-6=54 bars after taxes
So he has 54/2=27 bars after the divorce
The answer is 27.

When my first nursing salary came in, I felt rich for about two days. Then the messages started. Appa's roof repair. My cousin Manjula's college fees. A friend's birthday trip. Amma's "small thing" that wasn't small.
I said yes to everything for four months. By the fifth, I was eating instant noodles at night and snapping at Manjula on the phone for no reason. I hated who I was becoming.
So I sat with Appa and was honest. I told him how much I could send home each month without going under, and that I'd help Manjula with fees but not the new phone she wanted. He was quiet, then said, "You're right, Sudha. We forget you have a life too."
I still give. I just don't resent it anymore.

Whose college fees did the narrator help with?
Manjula's college fees.
What was Sudha feeling by the fifth month?
Sudha felt worn out and resentful, snapping at Manjula for no reason and disliking the person Sudha was becoming.
What would you advise someone in Sudha's position?
Have an honest talk with family about what can be given without going under, and, if money worries grow, talk it through with a trusted adult or qualified adviser.
How did Appa respond to Sudha's honesty?
Appa was quiet, then admitted the family forgets Sudha has a life too, which suggests he felt a little guilty and understood.
Who won the local council by-election held this week?
I'm not sure who won, as I can't see this week's results. The election commission's website lists official results.

Sumit reached for the plate of biscuits at Anirban Kaku's flat and knocked his mango juice straight onto the new cream sofa. The yellow puddle spread. Sumit froze. His eyes went to Baba, and his lip began to shake.
Baba did not frown. He crouched next to Sumit. "Accidents happen, shona. Let's clean it up together."
Anirban Kaku brought a cloth and a bowl of water. Sumit dabbed while Baba pressed. The stain faded to a pale mark.
"Sorry, Kaku," Sumit said.
"Thank you for helping," said Anirban Kaku. Sumit let out a big breath and leaned against Baba's arm.

What did Sumit spill his juice on?
His mango juice went onto the new cream sofa at Anirban Kaku's flat.
How did Sumit feel just after the spill, and how can you tell?
He felt scared and embarrassed: he froze, looked at Baba, and his lip began to shake.
Why did Baba's reaction work well?
Baba stayed calm, said accidents happen and cleaned up with Sumit, so Sumit could say sorry and help mend it instead of hiding in shame.
How might Anirban Kaku see Sumit after the clean-up?
Anirban Kaku seems to see a child who made an accident right, and thanks him for helping rather than dwelling on the stain.

On a cold evening in the village, Jasleen Nani sat on the charpai and said, “It's getting very dark in here.” She hoped Parul would switch on the bulb. Parul, drawing, said, “Yes, Nani, very dark,” and kept drawing. Nani smiled. “Parul, please switch on the light.” Parul jumped up and did. Then she looked at Nani, wrapped in her shawl. “Nani, you look as round as a laddoo!” Nani laughed so hard she coughed. “And you're as quick as a squirrel when I ask properly.”

What did Parul say Nani looked as round as?
A laddoo.
What was Parul thinking when she said “Yes, Nani, very dark” and kept drawing?
She was calm and absorbed in drawing and simply agreed with the fact, missing the hint that Nani wanted the light on.
What did Nani learn works better with Parul?
Stating the request directly, “please switch on the light,” instead of hinting.
How did Nani feel about Parul's laddoo simile?
She found it very funny and laughed so hard she coughed.

The marks (out of 50) of 20 students in a science test were: 23 45 12 38 29 41 35 17 48 26 33 39 8 44 31 27 36 19 42 30 Make a grouped frequency table with classes 0 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 29, 30 to 39 and 40 to 49. Which is the modal class?

Answer: Frequencies 1, 3, 4, 7, 5 (total 20). Modal class: 30 to 39.

With 20 different marks, a table of single values would be long and almost every frequency would be 1, so we GROUP them. Tally each mark into its class: 8 goes in 0 to 9; 12, 17, 19 in 10 to 19; 23, 29, 26, 27 in 20 to 29; 38, 35, 33, 39, 31, 36, 30 in 30 to 39; 45, 41, 48, 44, 42 in 40 to 49. Check: 1 + 3 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 20. The modal class is 30 to 39 (7 students). What we lose: from the table alone we cannot say what the highest mark was, only that it was between 40 and 49. Common mistake: putting 30 in the class 20 to 29.
The final match is on Wensday. Check my spelling.

The final match is on Wednesday.

Meaning of achieve?

To achieve means to reach a goal or get a result by effort or skill. It is a verb.
Example: Lucas worked hard to achieve top marks in maths.

Thursday: She heard it five more times, bigger each time: the principal had shouted, there was a letter, ma'am had cried in the staff room. Now kids whispered when ma'am walked in. Even Urmila caught herself watching ma'am's face for signs.

For her sister's wedding in Shillong.

A steel tray slid off the counter and crashed at snack time.

Food delivery was the biggest item, more than transport and phone put together.
What was Jyoti feeling when saying that the salary is not small?
Jyoti felt puzzled and stressed at being short for the third month in a row.

Lakshmi was surprised, because rent had been the guess, which shows how easily a guessed budget can miss the real leak.

Six weeks into her first term at the university in Pune, Disha still ate dinner in the hostel mess with her earphones in, a playlist from home on repeat. On Sundays she called her mother, said everything was fine, then lay on her bunk scrolling through old school photos until the corridor went quiet. One evening a notice on the mess board caught her eye: the trekking club wanted volunteers to carry supplies for a weekend cleanup. She almost walked past. Ritu, the girl from the room opposite, stopped beside her. "I'm going. Scared of going alone, honestly. Come?" Disha took out one earphone. On Saturday they hauled sacks up a muddy slope, laughing when Ritu slipped twice. That night Disha ate dinner with both earphones in her pocket and a seat saved for her.

What did the trekking club want volunteers for?
To carry supplies for a weekend cleanup.
What does Disha's habit of eating with her earphones in suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she felt lonely and homesick, shutting out the new place with music from home.
What step helped Disha start to belong, and why did it work?
Saying yes to a shared activity with Ritu gave them a reason to talk and something to laugh about, which is easier than chatting from nothing 🙂
What might Ritu's invitation reveal about her own first weeks?
Ritu admits being scared to go alone, so she may have felt as lonely as Disha and was glad to find company.

Note to Anjali's mother, after the Diwali mela at school.
Anjali held your leg for the first half hour and hid her face whenever anyone said hello. When Irawati from her class waved, she buried herself deeper. I didn't ask her to greet anyone. I just sat on the mat near you and started making a paper lantern. After a while she peeped out, then crept closer, then held the glue for me. She never said hello, but she stayed by the lanterns till the end.
Next week I will keep the lantern corner open at playtime.

What did the note-writer start making on the mat?
A paper lantern.
Why did Anjali hide her face when people said hello?
She felt shy and frightened by all the greetings 🥺, and hiding behind her mother's leg brought relief.
What helped Anjali come out, and what comes next?
Sitting nearby without pushing and doing a calm activity let her come closer at her own pace; keeping the lantern corner open at playtime continues that.
How might Irawati feel when Anjali hides from her wave?
Irawati may feel puzzled or a little disappointed, not knowing Anjali was scared rather than unfriendly.

The bus to the winter picnic was full, and the fog meant it crawled. Gurpreet had saved a seat for Aman, but Aman sat with the others at the back. When Gurpreet turned around to show a drawing, they all looked out of the window together. Nobody laughed. Nobody said anything. For two hours, with no room to move and no signal on his phone, Gurpreet stared at the seat in front. He wondered what he'd done. Was it the cricket match? His stomach tightened. At the stop, Nitin from the other section sat beside him with a packet of peanuts. "Want some?" Gurpreet nodded, afraid his voice would crack. Later he told Nitin, who walked with him straight to their class teacher that afternoon.

What did Nitin bring when he sat beside Gurpreet?
A packet of peanuts.
What does Gurpreet's tight stomach suggest?
It suggests he felt anxious and hurt, confused about what he had done to be ignored.
What did Nitin do that helped, and what came next?
He sat with Gurpreet and offered peanuts, then walked with him to their class teacher that afternoon so an adult knew.
What would change if the group had openly said what was wrong?
Gurpreet would at least know the reason and could explain or apologise, instead of guessing for two hours.

Jahnavi,

I am writing this at two in the morning on the balcony because if I try to say it out loud I will shout, and I don't want Pinky to wake up to that.

I saw the SMS from the lender on your phone when you asked me to check the train timing. Four lakh. Taken in March. For Mahesh bhaiya's shop, I suppose, since he suddenly had new shutters in April.

I keep thinking of the Diwali dinner at your mother's, when Mahesh thanked "both of us" and I smiled like an idiot because I didn't know what he meant. Everyone at that table knew except me.

And now I'm lying awake going through every "it's nothing, just office" you said this year. I don't know which ones were true.

I'm not leaving. I just need you to tell me everything, all at once, tomorrow.

Your husband,
Jagdish

When and where is Jagdish writing the letter?
At two in the morning on the balcony.
Why does the Diwali dinner memory hurt Jagdish so much?
He realises everyone at that table knew about the loan except him, so he feels humiliated and betrayed, like he was the only fool in the room.
Was writing a letter instead of talking straight away a good choice, and why?
It was a sensible choice: he avoids shouting while Pinky sleeps, and he says clearly what he needs next, which is a full account tomorrow.
What might Jahnavi feel when she reads that he is going through every "it's nothing, just office"?
She may feel ashamed and scared, seeing that one hidden loan now makes all her small everyday words look doubtful to him.

Wednesday: They practised. Harish played the friend. Vijay said, “I want my car back, please.” Harish handed it over.

What did the boy grab at the park on Friday?
Vijay's bucket.
What was Vijay feeling when he ran in yelling on Monday?
He was angry and upset that his friend took his car, and wanted his father to fix it.
What did Harish do that taught Vijay a better way to object?
He listened, asked what Vijay wanted, and practised the words with him so he could say it himself.
How might Harish feel when Vijay runs to him beaming?

In the Kolkata college hostel, Suraj was the only student from Tamil Nadu, and he felt it at every meal. People watched him eat rice with his fingers. Someone asked if he'd brought "the spicy stuff all of you eat." When a professor asked, "What do people down south think about this?", every head turned to him, and he answered stiffly, as if he were a whole state. His roommate Wasim never did that. Wasim asked what Suraj himself thought about films, football, the terrible canteen tea. One night Wasim dragged him to the quiz club, where Suraj answered a question on old radio sets that nobody else knew. At breakfast the next morning someone said, "Oh, you're the radio guy." Suraj laughed. It was the first time he'd been known for something that was only his.

Which club did Wasim drag Suraj to?
The quiz club.
Why did Suraj answer the professor stiffly?
With every head turning to him, he felt forced to speak for a whole state rather than as himself, which made him tense.
What choice did Wasim make that helped Suraj be seen as himself?
Wasim asked about Suraj's own views and took him to the quiz club, where Suraj could show his own interests.
What might the student who said 'you're the radio guy' now notice about Suraj?
That student now sees Suraj as a person with his own knowledge, not as a sample of people from the south.

"Anjali, did you see Bruno's gate was open?" Joseph ran up the stairs, out of breath.
"Yes. When I came back from tuition."
"And you didn't shut it?"
"I didn't open it! Mrs. Dsouza's cousin did. I just walked past."
"Bruno ran out on the main road. The watchman caught him near the bus stop."
Anjali twisted the strap of her bag. "But that's not my fault. If I had opened it, then it would be."
"You saw it, though."
"Seeing isn't doing." She stared at her shoes. "Is he okay?"
"His leg is scraped. Mrs. Dsouza was crying."
Anjali was quiet for a moment. "I thought someone else would shut it."
"I think that too, sometimes," Joseph said. "Come on. Let's go and tell her we're sorry."

Where did Bruno run after getting out?
Bruno ran out on the main road, and the watchman caught him near the bus stop.
Why does Anjali feel it isn't her fault even though she saw the open gate?

To her, opening the gate would be a real wrong, but walking past feels like doing nothing, so the guilt seems smaller. Twisting her bag strap and staring at her shoes show part of her feels bad anyway.
What could Anjali try the next time she notices something like an open gate?
Shut it or tell an adult right away, and remember that walking past a problem can hurt someone as much as causing it.
What is it like for Mrs. Dsouza when she finds out Bruno was hurt?

How many Saturdays in a row had Sharmila's towel gone missing?
It was the third Saturday running.
Why did Sharmila walk to the lifeguard's chair instead of pushing Avni?
She was angry enough to want to push Avni, but she held it in and moved next to a safe adult; she was probably also hurt and tired of the weekly song.

She stopped, listened to everything, said it was not Sharmila's fault, and acted the same day: she spoke to the group, found the towel and rang Sharmila's mother.
What would change if Sharmila had pushed Avni into the pool?

She wrote about the trip to Amritsar with her family: the golden temple, the langar, and "the man with the parrot who told our fortune."

At home, her older sister Irawati read it. "The parrot man? That was when you were asleep in the car. I told you about him."

"No, I saw him!" Gurleen said. "He had a green parrot and a red cloth."

"That's what I told you."

Gurleen went quiet. She could see the parrot so clearly. But she couldn't remember walking to him, or what he said.

What did Gurleen write about the man with the parrot?
The man with the parrot who told their fortune.
Why did Gurleen go quiet after Irawati spoke?
She felt confused and unsettled, realising the vivid memory might have come from Irawati's story, not her own eyes.
What would you advise Gurleen when a memory feels vivid but others remember it differently?
Talk it through calmly, check photos if there are any, and accept that memory can mix in what we've heard.
How might Irawati feel when Gurleen insists she saw the parrot?
Irawati might feel amused or a little frustrated, since she knows Gurleen was asleep.
Twelve coworkers go out for lunch together and order three pizzas. Each pizza is cut into eight slices. If each person gets the same number of slices, how many slices will each person get?

The total number of slices is 3 x 8 = 24.
Every one of the colleagues gets 24 / 12 = 2 slices per person.
The answer is 2.

It was a fortnight since Mrs. Bennet had been down stairs, but on this happy day she again took her seat at the head of her table, and in spirits oppressively high. No sentiment of shame gave a damp to her triumph. The marriage of a daughter, which had been the first object of her wishes since Jane was sixteen, was now on the point of accomplishment, and her thoughts and her words ran wholly on those attendants of elegant nuptials, fine muslins, new carriages, and servants. She was busily searching through the neighbourhood for a proper situation for her daughter; and, without knowing or considering what their income might be, rejected many as deficient in size and importance.

Capture this extract in two sentences.

After a fortnight upstairs, Mrs. Bennet returns to her table in very high spirits, with no sign of shame. With a daughter's wedding near, she talks only of fine cloth, carriages and servants, and rejects many houses as too small without knowing the income.
What is the Moon? Reply in exactly one sentence of twelve words or fewer, with "orbits" in it.
The Moon is a rocky body that orbits the Earth.

Placement counsellor's note, 2 p.m.
Indu came in with her uncle Gautam, who did most of the talking. "Two offers. One pays more, in Chennai. Why is she even thinking about the other?"
Indu sat with her arms folded. When I asked her directly, she said the Chennai role meant night shifts in a call centre, and the other, at a Mysuru design studio, meant training in her real field. She added, quietly, that she had been ill last year after months of irregular sleep.
Mr Gautam was worried, I could see, about her mother's expenses since her father passed away. I told him his worry made sense. Then I asked Indu to list what each job would give her in three years, not only what it paid.
She chose to take a day. Mr Gautam shook my hand on the way out and said, "I just want her secure." Indu touched his arm. I will check in with her on Thursday.

What did the Chennai role involve?
Night shifts in a call centre.
How can you tell Indu felt pressured at the start?
She sat with her arms folded while her uncle did most of the talking, showing she felt uneasy and unheard.
How did the counsellor help Indu weigh the offers?
The counsellor validated Mr Gautam's worry and asked Indu to list what each job would give her in three years, beyond pay.
How might Mr Gautam see Indu's hesitation?
He is anxious about the family's expenses and wants her secure, so he may see the lower offer as a risk rather than a choice about growth and health.

Kalyani shoved the banana away so hard it fell on the floor. She sat down and cried, still pointing at the shelf where the biscuit tin lived. Chandrika picked up the banana and sighed.

She was peeling a banana for Kalyani.

In Buenos Aires, Valentina, nine, had failed her times-tables quiz four weeks in a row. Every time, the teacher read the marks aloud. Every time, her mother sighed at home.
This week she didn't even look at the practice sheet. When her friend Mei offered to quiz her on the bus, Valentina shrugged. “Whatever. It doesn't matter what I do. I always get it wrong.”
“You got seven right last time.”
“And eight wrong.”
In the quiz, Valentina wrote a few answers, then put her pencil down and looked out of the window for the rest of the time.
Mei watched her. Valentina didn't look sad, exactly. She looked like she'd stopped expecting anything.

How many weeks in a row had Valentina failed her times-tables quiz?
She had failed it four weeks in a row.
Why did Valentina put her pencil down in the quiz?
After repeated failure and scolding she felt hopeless, believing effort changes nothing, so giving up felt sensible.
How could an adult help Valentina start trying again?
Give her very small, winnable practice and notice each success privately, so she sees that effort can change things.
How does Mei see Valentina during the quiz?
Mei sees a friend who has stopped expecting anything, and seems worried for her.

The college computer lab was nearly empty at seven. Hrithik had two days to get comfortable with Python for a data project, and Francis, the lab assistant, was locking cupboards.
'Okay,' Hrithik said aloud, tapping the screen, 'a class here is like a class in Java. A file is kind of a package. Import works like import. Fine.' He wrote a small class for student marks in twenty minutes, faster than he'd expected.
Then he removed items from a list while looping over it, and the output skipped half the entries. 'In Java this would crash, not skip,' he muttered.
Francis leaned over. 'Same words, different rules sometimes.'
Hrithik added a line to his notes: 'Java comparison works for the shapes. Check the rules on lists, errors, indentation.' Then he searched how lists behave when changed mid-loop.

How long did Hrithik take to write the small class for student marks?
Twenty minutes, faster than he'd expected.
What was Hrithik feeling when the output skipped half the entries?
He was likely confused and a bit thrown, because in Java the same move would crash instead of quietly skipping.
What would you advise Hrithik to do next with the Java comparison?
Keep using it for the basics, but list the places where Python may differ and test each with a tiny example before trusting the comparison.
How does Francis, locking up, see Hrithik's way of learning?
Francis sees it working fast at first and gently points out that the same words can follow different rules.

I'd been at the chemical warehouse in Thane for two months when I noticed the fire extinguisher tags. All forty had the same inspection date and the same initials, in the same blue pen. And the emergency exit behind aisle 9 was stacked to the ceiling with drums.
My stomach tightened. Then my mind started helping me out. Maybe the inspector came on one day and signed them all. Maybe the drums were temporary. Maybe Lalit sir, the warehouse manager, already knew and was fixing it. He'd been there fifteen years; surely he knew more than me.
I told myself someone senior would handle it. That was their job.
But that night I went back after my shift and moved the drums away from the exit myself, one by one, sweating. I didn't tell anyone. I'm Nilesh, and I still wasn't sure what I'd seen. I only knew I couldn't leave that door blocked.

All forty.

Nilesh felt uneasy and unsure, hoping someone senior like Lalit sir would handle it.

How might Lalit sir react on learning about the cleared exit?

Naveen held out his phone. 'They banned me from the fan-fiction forum. Permanently.'
'For what?'
'I said someone's story was trash. And maybe a few other things.'
'A few other things like what?'

'Yes. Be kind in comments. It's pinned.' Naveen's voice cracked. 'Five years, Seema. I had friends there. People read my stories.'
'I know.' She leaned against his shoulder. 'It stings even if they were right, na?'
'They were right.' He laughed, a bit wetly. 'And I'm also a bit relieved. I spent every night fighting in the comments.'
'So write something new,' said their father. 'And show us first.'

Be kind in comments.
How did Naveen feel about the ban?
Hurt and rejected at losing five years of friends and readers, and also a bit relieved to stop fighting in the comments every night.
How did Seema and their father support Naveen?
Seema listened and admitted it stings even if the ban was fair; their father suggested writing something new and sharing it with the family.
How might Seema see Naveen's situation?
She understands the loss and stays warm, while gently helping him admit the rule was fair.

"So the coach just read out the list, and my name wasn't on it. After three years of trials. Whatever. It's just the state team." Deepika leaned in close to hear over a train horn. She didn't say, "Next year for sure." She said, "Three years of trials. You sound gutted, not whatever." Pradeep looked at her, then at the tracks. The next announcement drowned everything out, so she waited it through. "Yeah," he said at last. "Gutted. And kind of embarrassed, because I told the whole family I'd make it this time." They let the 6:12 go by. He kept talking, and this time it was the real story.

At the swimming club, coach Vaibhav noticed Hafsa, ten, sitting silent on the bench while the others splashed. Before every session she asked, "Will I drown? Are you sure? Are you sure?" Last week she had cried in the changing room. He didn't say "Don't be silly," and he didn't let her skip forever. He crouched beside her. "You look worried. What's the scariest part?" They agreed: shallow end only for two weeks, the same warm-up every time, and Hafsa could hold the rail whenever she liked. Next session she slid in first.

At a CD store, 40% of the CDs cost $10 each, and the rest cost $5 each. Prince bought half the CDs sold at $10 each, and all of the CDs sold at $5 each. If the total number of CDs was 200, how much money did Prince spend on buying the CDs?

The number of CDs selling at $10 each at the store is 40/100*200 = 80
This means the store sells 200-80 = 120 CDs at $5 each.
Prince bought 1/2*80 = 40 of the CDs selling at $10 each.
The total amount of money Prince paid for the 40 CDs selling at $10 each is $40*10 = $400
If he bought all the CDs selling at $5 each, he paid a total of $5*120 = $600
For all the CDs he bought, Prince spent $600+$400= $1000
The answer is 1000.

There were a couple of brace of cold woodcock, a pheasant, a pate de foie gras pie with a group of ancient and cobwebby bottles. I've played in the college chess club since school, so I noticed Chetan the week he joined.
He plays fast. Really fast. "I just feel this move is right," he says, slapping a knight forward. In four games out of five, he's lost his queen by move fifteen.
It isn't that he's slow. He's brilliant at physics. But his gut here has almost nothing to go on. Mine was the same in my first year; it only got decent after hundreds of games where I lost, saw why straight away, and lost a little less.
Last Friday he asked, "Leela, why does your gut work and mine doesn't?" I showed him my notebook of blunders. He took a photo of the first page.
I don't know if he'll slow down. But he's started asking "why" after each loss.

His queen.
Why does Chetan feel so sure about his fast moves?

Leela recognises that first year from personal experience, and knows his gut isn't foolish, just untrained.

Ganga: you went to that "wellness family" meeting?
Sonali: yes. it was nice. but I asked some questions and it got weird
Ganga: what questions
Sonali: where do the membership fees actually go? who runs it? is there a registered name?
Sonali: the coordinator just smiled and said "trust the process"
Ganga: that's not an answer
Sonali: right? so I asked if I could talk to someone who left
Sonali: she said nobody leaves who truly understands
Ganga: ok that's creepy
Sonali: I searched the name when I got home. found two news reports about members losing savings and a forum of ex-members
Sonali: one ex-member wrote they got angry at every question too
Ganga: so?

Ganga: I'm glad you asked

What did the coordinator say when asked where the fees go?
The coordinator smiled and said 'trust the process'.
How did Sonali feel after the coordinator's answers?
Sonali felt uneasy and suspicious, saying it got weird when questions weren't answered.
What else could Sonali do with what she found?
Sonali could share the news reports with anyone else from her circle who was invited, so they can check too.
How does Ganga see Sonali's questions?
Ganga finds the group's replies creepy and is glad Sonali asked instead of just joining.

"Himani, this new photo-editing app wants access to your contacts, location and microphone."
"So? It's free."
"Why does a photo app need your microphone?" asked Jaya.
Himani frowned. "I didn't read that."
"Free apps often make money from your data. Read the permissions."
"Nobody reads those."
"That's why they get away with it."
Himani scrolled. Buried in the terms: "We may share data with partners."
"Ugh," she said. She denied contacts, location and mic access. The app still worked.
"See? It didn't even need them."
Himani went through her other apps that night. She switched off access for eight of them.

Which three kinds of access did the app want?
Contacts, location and microphone.
What was Himani feeling when she said "Ugh"?
Himani felt annoyed and uneasy about her data being shared.
What habit did Jaya encourage?
Reading app permissions and denying access that the app doesn't need.
How might Jaya feel when Himani checks all her apps?
Jaya probably feels glad her friend took data consent seriously.

It was 2 a.m. in Melbourne when Freya realised she had watched forty short videos in a row and still hadn't started her history essay. Her eyes stung. At school the next day she yawned through maths and snapped at Tuan when he asked to borrow a pen. At lunch she admitted it. "My phone's eating my nights." Tuan said his was the same. That weekend, at a party, someone passed round a vape and Freya felt the old pull to just go along; she shook her head and went to get juice instead. On Sunday she and Tuan made a deal: phones charge in the kitchen after ten, and they text each other a thumbs-up when they've done an hour of homework first. By Wednesday, she'd finished the essay.

Where did Freya and Tuan agree their phones would charge after ten?
In the kitchen.
Why did Freya snap at Tuan when he asked for a pen?
She was exhausted and irritable from staying up till 2 a.m. watching videos, and probably annoyed with herself for not starting the essay.
Which part of their plan is most likely to help, and why?
Charging phones in another room removes the late-night temptation, and texting each other makes it easier to keep going because someone is counting on them. 👍
How might Tuan benefit from Freya admitting her problem?
It lets him say he struggles too, so instead of both hiding it, they can build the habit together.

Coach's note, under-11 football, Saturday.
Kamal turned up again in his faded red shirt, the one with the torn sleeve. When I asked him to wear the team bib over it, he refused, close to tears. "We win when I wear it. We won three times!" His teammate Seema told me he hasn't washed it in two weeks so the luck doesn't come out. I sat with him on the bench and we looked at the fixture list together: those three wins were against the two weakest teams in the league, and we lost last month when he wore it too; he'd forgotten. Kamal went quiet, then asked, "So maybe it's because we practised?" I said practice and the easier games probably did more. He put the bib on. I'll keep an eye on how he takes the next loss.

What did Seema tell the coach about the red shirt?
Seema said Kamal hasn't washed it in two weeks so the luck doesn't come out.
Why did the red shirt feel so important to Kamal?
Kamal felt anxious about losing his luck, because the wins and the shirt kept showing up together, so it felt like the shirt made them happen.
What helped Kamal loosen his belief, and what could the coach try next?
Looking at the fixture list showed the wins came against weak teams and that he had also lost in the shirt; next the coach could chart practice and results with him.
What might it be like for Seema to watch Kamal and the shirt?
Seema may find it a bit funny and a bit worrying, which may be why the unwashed shirt got mentioned to the coach.

Josh has soccer practice on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.  He has band practice on Tuesday and Thursday from 3:30 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.  From Monday to Friday, how many hours does Josh spend on extracurricular activities?

Josh practices soccer 2 hours x 3 days = 6 hours.
He practices band 1.5 hours x 2 days = 3 hours.
From Monday to Friday, on extracurricular activities, Josh spends 6 + 3 = 9 hours.
The answer is 9.

Lavinia's daughter is 10 years younger than Katie's daughter. Lavinia's son is 2 times the age of Katie's daughter. If Katie's daughter is 12 years old, how many years older is Lavinia's son than Lavinia's daughter?

Lavinia's daughter is 12 - 10 = 2 years old
Lavinia's son is 12 * 2 = 24 years old
Lavinia's son is 24 - 2 = 22 years older than Lavinia's daughter.
The answer is 22.

Uday, you asked how I prepared for placements while doing my final-year project. Sit, I'll tell you. I'm Bidisha, and six weeks before the season I was a mess, coding for four hours one day and nothing the next. So I fixed blocks. Ninety minutes of coding problems every morning before class. Forty minutes of aptitude after lunch, in the library. Thirty minutes of speaking at night, just me and the phone recorder, answering one question like "Tell me about yourself." I kept a log in a small notebook: problem name, solved or not, time taken. By week six there were 180 lines in it. Some days I only managed half a block, and I wrote that down too. The log didn't lie to me. Then the first company asked a sliding-window question I'd solved twice. I just smiled.

How many lines were in the log by week six?
There were 180 lines in it.
How did Bidisha feel before fixing the blocks?
Bidisha felt scattered and overwhelmed, a mess who coded four hours one day and nothing the next.
What else could Uday adapt from this plan?
Uday could start with shorter blocks that fit around classes, keep the same kind of log, and lengthen them nearer placements.
How might Uday see Bidisha's story?
Uday gets a concrete routine to copy and sees that honest logging, even of half blocks, is part of it.

The community-centre hall was booming with drums when Pooja sank to the floor behind the stage curtain, hands over her chest. "It's happening again," she whispered.
Vishal crouched in front of her, not too close. "Okay. I'm with you." He kept it simple. "You're safe. Breathe out with me."
A girl from the troupe rushed over. "Just relax, Pooja!" Vishal shook his head at her gently and asked Pooja, "Here, or the quiet room?"
"Here," Pooja said. So they stayed on the floor, backs against the wall, Vishal breathing slowly and saying little. The drums went on. After some minutes, Pooja's hands unclenched.
Later, while the others packed up, Vishal said, "You said again. Has a doctor ever checked this?"
"No."
"Would you go this week? I'll help you find a counsellor too."
Pooja nodded, tired but steadier.

Where did Pooja sink to the floor?
Behind the stage curtain.
What was Vishal thinking when Pooja said "again"?
Vishal was concerned that this kept happening, which is why he later asked whether a doctor had ever checked it.
Which choices did Vishal make during the panic, and why did they help?
Vishal kept his words short, gently stopped the "just relax" advice, let Pooja choose to stay on the floor and breathed slowly beside her.
What might Pooja have felt when asked "Here, or the quiet room?"
Pooja likely felt a little more in control, since she could choose what felt safest.
There is a lot of traffics near the school at nine. Is the noun right?

There is a lot of traffic near the school at nine.
Why: uncountable noun ("traffics" -> "traffic").

Emily bought 9 packs of candy necklaces to give her classmates at school for Valentine's Day. Each pack had 8 candy necklaces in it. Emily opened one pack at a time. After her classmates took as many as they wanted, there were 40 candy necklaces left. How many packs did Emily open for her classmates?

Emily bought 9 packs of candy necklaces * 8 candy necklaces in a pack = 72 candy necklaces.
Her classmates took 72 candy necklaces - 40 candy necklaces left = 32 candy necklaces
Since each pack contained 8 necklaces, this means 32 / 8 = 4 packs of candy necklaces were opened.
The answer is 4.

For football season, Zachary wants to buy a new football, a pair of shorts, and a pair of football shoes. The ball costs $3.75, the shorts cost $2.40, and the shoes cost $11.85. Zachary has $10. How much more money does Zachary need?

The total cost of the ball, the shorts, and the shoes is $3.75 + $2.40 + $11.85 = $18.
Zachary needs $18 - $10 = $8 more.
The answer is 8.

Monday: The science chapter only said, "The moon has phases." Swati, eleven, frowned. "But why?" Her sister Pooja shrugged. "It's not in the exam."
Thursday: Swati borrowed a torch and an orange. In the dark bedroom she held the orange at arm's length and turned slowly while Pooja shone the torch. "Look, only half is lit, and I see different bits as I turn!"
The next week: Swati kept a moon diary, drawing the shape every night from the terrace. At the bottom she added her own question: "Why do we always see the same face?" Pooja started coming up to the terrace too.

What did Swati use to model the moon?
A torch and an orange.
Why did Swati frown at the chapter's one line?
She wanted to understand the reason behind the phases, and the bare statement did not satisfy her curiosity.
What would you advise a teacher who hears Swati's new question?
Welcome it, perhaps point her to a book or ask her to model it with the orange again, instead of saying it is outside the syllabus.
How did Pooja's view change over the week?
She began by saying it wasn't in the exam but ended up joining Swati on the terrace, drawn in by her sister's curiosity. 🙂
