At five in the morning the bakery on FC Road was already hot. Mohit, twenty-two, kneaded dough beside the head baker, flour up to his elbows. Six months ago he had left his engineering course in the third year. His mother, Sudha, had cried; his uncles still called it 'Mohit's madness'. He didn't earn much. He was often tired and sometimes wondered if they were right. But when the croissants rose in perfect layers, he felt the same thrill he'd felt taking apart clocks as a boy. On Sunday he took a small cake home, the first one he had decorated on his own. Sudha looked at it for a long time. "It's too pretty to cut," she said, and put the kettle on.

What had Mohit left six months ago?
He had left his engineering course in the third year.
How does Mohit feel about his choice to leave engineering?
He feels thrilled when the croissants rise, yet sometimes tired and doubtful whether his relatives are right.
Why was taking the cake home a meaningful choice?
It showed his mother the work he loves and reached out to her with care, keeping the family bond alive despite her disapproval.
How does Sudha seem to feel when she sees the cake?
Sudha seems moved and softening, looking a long time and calling it too pretty to cut, which hints at growing pride.

metadata.subtype: Forging own path despite family pressure [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Pradeep, you think your memory is a camera? Let your Himani Nani tell you something. When I was ten, we went by bus to my uncle's village for a wedding. I remembered a river crossing, a broken wheel, and my sister crying.

Every Diwali, my brothers told the story too, and each time they added something: a snake on the road, a man selling sugarcane, our father pushing the bus. By the time I was twelve, I told it with the snake and the sugarcane, and I truly remembered them.

Years later, my mother laughed. "There was no snake. That was your brother's joke."

I felt so strange. I could see that snake clearly! That's when I learnt that memories are built fresh each time you tell them.

What did Himani's brothers add to the story?
A snake on the road, a man selling sugarcane and their father pushing the bus.
How did young Himani feel when her mother said there was no snake?
Young Himani felt strange and unsettled, because the snake was so clear in memory.
What turning point in the story changed how Himani thought about memory?
Her mother's laugh about the snake being a joke made Himani realise that memories are rebuilt each time they're told.
How might Himani's brothers have seen their added details?
They may have thought of them as jokes or fun additions, not realising their sister would come to remember them as real.

The shouting had stopped at nine. Now it was eleven, and Kamal was sitting on the floor of the balcony of their Bengaluru flat, looking at the neighbour's wet laundry.
Chaitanya came to the door. "Are you going to say anything?"
Kamal opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His head was full of noise. Everything he'd said earlier, about Chaitanya's job, about his friends, was still ringing. He was afraid that anything he said now would be worse.
"Kamal."
He shook his head. It wasn't meant as a no. It meant: I can't.
Chaitanya stood a moment longer, then went inside and shut the door softly.

Where was Kamal sitting at eleven?
On the floor of the balcony of their Bengaluru flat.
What was Kamal feeling when Chaitanya asked if he would say anything?
He felt overwhelmed and afraid that anything he said would make things worse, with his head full of noise.
What turning point is available to Kamal at this stage?
He could say even one short line, like "I can't talk yet, but I will," so Chaitanya knows the silence isn't a rejection.
What is Chaitanya experiencing when he shuts the door softly?
He likely feels hurt and shut out, reading Kamal's head shake as a refusal rather than as being unable to cope.
Make this less formal: I would be grateful if you could lend me your pen.
Could I borrow your pen?

Day 1: Salma found her milk finished again and a note in Kiran's handwriting: 'Sorry! Will replace.' It was the fourth note that month. She typed a long angry message, deleted it, and left for college, jaw tight all day. Day 4: Over chai in their PG kitchen in Kochi, Salma said, 'I like living with you, but the borrowing is costing me money and patience.' Kiran went red. 'I thought the notes made it okay.' They agreed on a shared jar for milk, bread and oil, each putting in the same amount every Monday, with personal things on separate shelves. Day 20: The jar ran low, and Kiran topped it up without being asked, adding a packet of Salma's favourite biscuits. Salma laughed and stuck a note on it: 'Forgiven, twice over.'

Which items did the shared jar cover?
Milk, bread and oil, with each of them putting in the same amount every Monday.
Why did Salma delete her long angry message?
She was upset but seemed not to want a written fight to damage a friendship she valued, so she waited to talk calmly in person.
What made their agreement fair?
Shared basics were paid for equally and personal things stayed on separate shelves, so neither had to track small debts or feel taken for granted.
How did Kiran see the borrowing before Day 4?
Kiran genuinely thought the 'Sorry! Will replace' notes made it okay and did not realise what it was costing Salma.

Read this:

Yamini, you asked why I always ask "how often?" first. Let your Yusuf Nana tell you. When I was your age, a young engineer on the Kota bridge maintenance team, a new sensor sent an alarm: possible crack in the third pier. My seniors wanted the bridge closed that same day. Thousands of trucks, a whole city stuck. I was scared, but I asked the sensor supplier one question: "How often has a real crack shown up on bridges like this?" Rarely, they said, maybe once in many years. "And false alarms?" Weekly, in the monsoon, from water in the joints. So I started there. Then I looked for other evidence: no new sag, no cracks in the paint. I asked the senior structural expert to check by hand before we decided. She found water in the sensor box. The bridge stayed open, and we fixed the sensor.

Which pier did the sensor flag?
The third pier.
What was young Yusuf feeling when the alarm came?
He felt scared, knowing both a real crack and a needless closure would be serious.
Which choice in the story led to the right decision?
Asking how often real cracks and false alarms happened, checking other evidence, and having the senior expert inspect by hand before closing the bridge.
How might the seniors who wanted the bridge closed see the result?
They were probably relieved and maybe a little embarrassed, since the sensor box only had water in it.

Read this:

The cricket nets at the Shivaji Nagar community centre back onto a row of houses, and on Monday Rafiq sir, the centre's manager, called Avni and her team into his office. "Mrs Bhatia has complained three times," he said. "The ball hits her wall at two o'clock, when her grandson naps." Avni folded her arms. "Then why is it only us? The football boys shout louder." She could feel her voice shaking. Rafiq sir did not argue. He slid a sheet across the desk. "Both of you have a right to be here. Write me a timetable you could live with." They did it right there: no batting against that wall between two and four, a softer ball on that side, and the loud warm-up moved to the far corner. On Friday, Mrs Bhatia sent a box of sweet biscuits to the nets.

What time does Mrs Bhatia's grandson nap?
He naps at two o'clock.
What was Avni feeling in Rafiq sir's office, and how can you tell?
She felt singled out and resentful; she folded her arms, pointed at the louder football boys and her voice was shaking.
How did Rafiq sir handle the complaint well?
He stated that both sides had rights and asked the team to write a timetable, which let them shape the solution instead of simply being blamed.
What would change if Rafiq sir had just banned the team from the nets?
Avni's team would likely feel punished and resent Mrs Bhatia, and the dispute would probably carry on in other ways instead of ending with biscuits.

Read this:

Dolma's turn in the lab meeting came after lunch. The supervisor, Dr. Mehta, had asked each student to explain their work in three minutes. She walked to the whiteboard and traced a rising curve with one finger, then made a small circle with both hands to show how the sample cycled through the machine. Anirban, sitting near the door, followed easily. Then her arms began to swing wide with every sentence, and he found himself watching the hands, not the diagram. Dr. Mehta wrote something down. After the meeting she showed Dolma a phone video from last week's practice. "See how the big swings start here?" Dolma winced, then grinned and said she'd keep the circle and cut the rest.

How long did the supervisor give each student to explain their work?
The supervisor gave each student three minutes.
What did Dolma feel when she watched the practice video?
Dolma winced first, probably embarrassed, then grinned, which suggests she took the feedback well and felt ready to change. The grin could also be relief at having a clear thing to fix.
What went wrong in the second half of the talk, and what could fix it?
The wide arm swings drew attention from the diagram; Dolma could keep the meaningful gestures and rehearse on video to trim the rest.
What was it like for Anirban listening to the talk?
Anirban followed the early gestures easily, but as the arms began to swing wide he found himself watching the hands instead of the diagram.

Read this:

Rain ticked on the tram window as Santiago rode home from the bakery in Porto, flour still under his nails. Two years ago Kofi had walked out of their food-truck plan a week before opening, taking the van deposit with him and never explaining. Santiago had rehearsed the phone call a hundred times. Tonight, at the kitchen table, he wrote a letter instead. You left me with debts and a lot of silence. I was angry for a long time. I'm putting this down now. He read it twice, then placed it in the drawer, not in an envelope. Kofi had never said sorry, and maybe never would. Santiago noticed he was tired of waiting for that. He made tea, texted his sister that he would come to her barbecue on Sunday, and for the first time in months fell asleep without rehearsing anything.

Where did Santiago put the letter after reading it?
He placed it in the drawer, not in an envelope.
What was Santiago feeling when he noticed he was tired of waiting?
He felt worn out by carrying the resentment and ready to set it down for his own peace, even without an apology from Kofi.
Why was writing the letter without sending it a useful step for Santiago?
It let him say everything he felt and mark an ending on his own terms, without needing Kofi to answer or apologise first.
What is Santiago's sister likely to notice about him after this night?
She may find him lighter and more present at her barbecue, because he is no longer stuck rehearsing an old phone call.

Read this:

Nirmala Masi poured the tea and looked at Gurpreet, who hadn't touched her paratha.
'When I was twenty-five,' she said, 'I was a staff nurse in Ludhiana. I wrote to the matron that expired medicines were being relabelled and used. I did it properly, in writing. Nothing happened. Or rather, something happened to me.
Within a month I was on permanent night duty. My name disappeared from the training list. Someone started saying I was careless with records, that I was bitter because I'd been passed over. People I had shared tiffin with for three years stopped sitting near me in the canteen. Not because they hated me. Because they were scared.
That hurt more than the night shifts, beta. Being made into the problem.'
Gurpreet looked up. 'What did you do?'
'First,' Masi said, 'I stopped believing what they said about me.'

Where was Nirmala a staff nurse at twenty-five?
She was a staff nurse in Ludhiana.
What made young Nirmala feel most hurt?
Being made into the problem hurt most: feeling her reputation attacked and friends pulling away out of fear.
What turning point does Masi's first step point to at this stage?
Refusing to believe the story others told about her protected her sense of self, which she needed before deciding on further steps such as outside advice.
What might the colleagues who stopped sitting near Nirmala have been feeling?
They were probably scared of being linked to her and targeted too, even if they didn't dislike her.
There are 10 candles on one cake. How many candles are on 4 cakes? And one more: Check my sentence: She sweeped the floor this morning. Then, What is the name of my friend's cat?

1. 40 candles. Because 4 x 10 = 40.
2. Fixed: She swept the floor this morning. Why: The past tense of "sweep" is "swept".
3. I don't know, because I can't know your friend's pets. Ask your friend.

Read this:

A few weeks ago Reena came to my desk with the proposal for the school-uniform client and said, 'They'll reject it. They always go with the cheapest.' She said it the way you'd say it's Tuesday. I nearly agreed; I've been team lead for eight months and I'm still learning when to push. Privately, I'd have bet on a yes. Instead I asked, 'Is that something you know, or something you're guessing?' She thought. 'Guessing. But a strong guess.' 'Okay. Write it down, and let's send it and see.' She wrote 'Rejected, 90%' on a sticky note and put it on her monitor. Ten days later the client called. They didn't choose us, but not because of price; they needed a delivery date we couldn't meet, and they asked us to pitch again in March. Reena peeled off the sticky note and said, 'Wasim, I was wrong about the reason, and you were wrong about the yes.'

What did Reena write on the sticky note?
She wrote 'Rejected, 90%' on the sticky note.
Why did Wasim nearly agree with Reena at first?
Wasim felt unsure as a new team lead, and Reena's calm certainty made the prediction sound like fact, so going along felt easier than questioning it.
Why was asking 'know or guessing?' a useful move?
It separated the forecast from fact, so Reena could name it as a guess, write it down and check it against what really happened.
How might Reena hold her predictions after this?
Reena may hold them more loosely, since the result surprised her too, and treat them as guesses to test rather than certain news.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2% today. The Dow ended the day at 8,722. What was the Dow in the morning before the markets opened?

Today the Dow was down 8722 / 98*2 = 178.
So it started at 8722 + 178 = 8900.
The answer is 8900.
A train travels 270 km in 3 hours at a steady speed. How far does it go in 5 hours? How long does it take for 630 km?

Answer: 450 km in 5 hours. 7 hours for 630 km.

In 1 hour: 270 / 3 = 90 km (the speed, 90 km/h). In 5 hours: 90 x 5 = 450 km. For 630 km: each hour covers 90 km, so the number of hours is 630 / 90 = 7. Check: 7 x 90 = 630. The same unit rate (90 km per hour) answers both questions: multiply to find distance, divide to find time. (More in 5.31, speed-distance-time.)
Sensible and sensitive: what is the difference?

"Sensible" means showing good judgement and common sense. "Sensitive" means easily affected by feelings or by things like light or heat.
Examples: Wearing a raincoat was a sensible choice. Anika is sensitive and notices when a friend is sad.

Read this:

Aadhya, you asked who my best friend was. At ten, it was Gopal. Before that, boys were just people to play gulli-danda with. Then one monsoon we found a puppy under the school bridge. My father didn't allow dogs, so we kept it in Gopal's cowshed. It was our secret for three months. We took turns saving chapatis for it. One day Gopal's elder brother found out and asked, "Hemant, whose puppy is this?" I said it was mine, so Gopal wouldn't be scolded alone. We both got scolded. But after that, we told each other everything.

Where did the two friends keep the puppy?
In Gopal's cowshed.
Why did young Hemant claim the puppy?
Hemant wanted to protect Gopal from being scolded alone, showing loyalty to a friend.
What could the boys have done differently about the puppy?
They might have asked a trusted adult to help find it a home, so they didn't have to keep a secret from their families.
How might Gopal have felt when Hemant claimed the puppy?
Grateful and closer to Hemant, which may be why they told each other everything afterwards.
If there are sixty-five dolphins in the ocean, and three times that number joins in from a river which has its mouth at the ocean, calculate the total number of dolphins in the ocean.

When three times the number of dolphins in the ocean joins in from a river, the number of dolphins in the ocean increases by 3 *65 = 195
The total number of dolphins in the ocean increases to 195+65 = 260
The answer is 260.

Yash: Mohit, can we talk about the split before the investor call?
Mohit: sure what's up
Yash: for 6 months I've done the product, support and the hiring. you've done the pitch decks
Yash: and in every deck it's "Mohit's company"
Mohit: come on, that's just how pitches work 😅
Yash: I get that. but I also haven't taken a salary since March and you have
Yash: I feel used, honestly. and I've been scared to say it because I don't want to lose this
Mohit: wow. ok. I didn't know you felt that way
Yash: I've written a proposal. equal salaries, my name on the deck as co-founder, and a written role split. sent to your email
Mohit: and if I don't agree?
Yash: then I think I have to step away. I don't want to, but I will
Mohit: ok. give me till Friday. I'll read it properly
Yash: thank you 🙏

Since when has Yash not taken a salary?
Yash hasn't taken a salary since March.
How does Yash describe feeling about the arrangement?
Yash feels used, and scared to speak up for fear of losing the venture.
Why was Yash's approach a strong one?
Yash stated the imbalance plainly, offered a written fix, and was honest about stepping away if nothing changed.
How does Mohit react to Yash's message?
Mohit is surprised and a little defensive at first, then agrees to read the proposal properly by Friday.

Abhinav: bro the mall is giving free scratch cards with every purchase
Omkar: ya I got one with my shoes. won nothing
Abhinav: because you let the cashier give it to you. you have to CHOOSE
Omkar: what?
Abhinav: I stood there for 5 mins and picked the one that felt right. the edge was a bit shiny
Omkar: and?
Abhinav: nothing. but I think I picked wrong. going back tomorrow to pick again
Omkar: bhai they're printed in a factory. the shiny edge doesn't know you
Abhinav: but it feels like if I choose, I have more control
Omkar: feels, yes. is, no 😅
Abhinav: ...ok that's annoying
Omkar: save the bus fare

How long did Abhinav stand choosing the scratch card?
5 mins.
What does Abhinav's plan to go back and pick again suggest?
It suggests Abhinav feels a strong sense of control and hope from choosing, as if careful picking could beat pure chance.
How does Omkar challenge Abhinav's belief?
Omkar points out that the cards are printed in a factory and the shiny edge doesn't know Abhinav, separating feeling in control from being in control.
How does Omkar see the free scratch cards?
Omkar sees them as random, having won nothing and not caring who picks them.
Hand me a story about a girl who moves to a new school and finds out her old friend is there.

When Dhwani began Class 6 at the new school, she walked down the corridor with her eyes on her shoes. At the end of the hall, a girl was fixing a poster on the wall and, without turning, said, "Dhwani? Is that you?" Dhwani looked up. It was Annie, her friend from kindergarten, whom she had not seen for five years. They both shrieked. Teachers peeked out of classrooms. They stood hugging and talking over each other, asking and answering all at once. "You still have the same laugh," said Annie. At lunch, they sat together, and Dhwani found that the new school was suddenly much smaller and friendlier than before.

Read this:

In the small college in Bhilwara, Raghav was the name every lecturer knew. First in every exam since school, handwriting like print, answers read out in class.
On the day of the physics practical, his circuit didn't work. He checked it five times. His hands started shaking. Around him, other students' bulbs glowed.
His friend Harsha leaned over. "Loose wire, probably. Happens to everyone."
Raghav didn't hear. He was thinking: if I fail this, everyone will know I was never really good. Just lucky, or just careful.
The lecturer came over, found the loose wire in ten seconds, and moved on without a word.
On the walk home, Harsha said, "You used to love fixing circuits. You made that doorbell for your Dadi."
"That was for fun," Raghav said. "Now it's not allowed to go wrong."

What was wrong with Raghav's circuit?
The lecturer found a loose wire.
What was Raghav afraid of when the circuit didn't work?
He was frightened that one failure would show everyone he was never really good, just lucky or careful.
What could help Raghav enjoy physics again?
He could practise building circuits just for fun again, like the doorbell, and talk to Harsha or a teacher about how the fear of mistakes has taken over.
How does Harsha see the loose wire?
Harsha sees it as an ordinary slip that happens to everyone, and is concerned that Raghav reacts so strongly.

Read this:

Come sit, beta. Your Aditi Masi has a story. When I was sixteen, my friend Sonali went through a very dark stretch, and I was the one she called, sometimes three times a night. I never said no. Then one morning I was crying into my cereal for no reason, and my hands wouldn't stop trembling before a test. I realised I had nothing left. That evening I told Amma all of it. She didn't scold me. She hugged me, and the next day we phoned Sonali's mother together and spoke to the school counsellor. I stayed her friend, sat beside her at lunch and slipped silly notes into her bag. But I stopped being her only rope. That was the kindest thing I did, for both of us.

Who did Aditi tell that evening?
Aditi told Amma that evening, all of it.
What was Aditi feeling before she spoke to Amma?
Aditi was exhausted and anxious: she cried into her cereal for no reason, her hands trembled before a test and she had nothing left.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
Telling Amma was the turning point, because it brought in Sonali's mother and the counsellor, so Aditi could stay a friend without being Sonali's only support.
How might Sonali have experienced Aditi sharing the support with adults?
Sonali may have felt worried or exposed at first, yet she gained more people who could help, while Aditi still sat beside her at lunch and slipped notes into her bag.

Rajni: the optician's machine flagged my eye pressure. "glaucoma suspect" 😰
Rajni: i'm 25. am i going blind??
Jasleen: ok breathe. first question: how common is glaucoma at our age?
Rajni: idk. not very?
Jasleen: right, it's uncommon for people in their twenties. so we start there
Jasleen: now the specifics. any eye pain, blurry patches, family history?
Rajni: none. my eyes were tired from the laptop that day though
Jasleen: so the odds were low to begin with and nothing pushes them up much. but the reading isn't nothing either
Jasleen: book the eye doctor and ask what this reading really means for you
Rajni: you're annoyingly calm 😅
Jasleen: calm AND coming with you. saturday?
Rajni: saturday 🙏

What did the optician's machine flag?
Rajni's eye pressure, with the words "glaucoma suspect".
Why does Rajni jump straight to "am I going blind"?
Rajni feels scared because a label from a machine feels like a verdict, and Rajni is thinking only about the reading, not about how uncommon the condition is at 25.
What order of steps does Jasleen use, and why is it sensible?

Jasleen starts with how common glaucoma is at their age, then checks Rajni's own signs, then sends Rajni to the eye doctor to explain the reading; that keeps one result in proportion without ignoring it.
What would change if Rajni did have a family history and blurry patches?
Those details would push the odds up, so the reading would deserve even more attention and the doctor's visit would matter more.

Eshaan: did you see what Varun said about Dev in the group
Chinmay: yeah
Eshaan: we have to back Dev. Varun's been like this since class 8
Eshaan: I'm posting what Varun told me about Dev's dad at the sleepover
Chinmay: wait what. that was private
Eshaan: so? he started it
Chinmay: this was Varun and Dev arguing about the football team spot
Chinmay: now it's like 10 of us
Chinmay: half the team isn't talking to the other half
Eshaan: you're either with us or with them
Chinmay: I'm with nobody
Chinmay: I just want to know if Dev's even ok
Chinmay: has anyone actually asked him?
Eshaan: ...
Eshaan: no 😶
Eshaan: ok I won't post it
Chinmay: I'll call Dev tonight

What were Varun and Dev first arguing about?
They were arguing about the football team spot.
What does Chinmay worry about while the team splits into sides?
Chinmay worries whether Dev is even okay, since nobody has asked him while everyone takes sides.
What went right in this chat, and what could Chinmay do next?
Chinmay refused to pick a camp and stopped the private story being posted; calling Dev tonight lets the real hurt be heard.
What would change if Eshaan posted the sleepover story?
A private moment about Dev's dad would become public, the camps would harden, and the original quarrel would be even harder to fix.
A farmer planted 30 rows of tomatoes with 10 plants in each row. Each tomato plant yields 20 pieces of tomatoes. How many pieces of tomatoes can the farmer get from all his planted tomatoes?

The farmer planted a total of 30 x 10 = 300 tomato plants.
Thus, the farmer can get 300 x 20 = 6000 pieces of tomatoes.
The answer is 6000.

Read this:

Saturday. Maria's diary. I really wanted to go to the night market with my brother Imran and his friends. First I said, “Everyone in my class is going!” Mama raised one eyebrow. “Everyone?” Okay, three people. So I tried again, properly. “I finished all my homework this morning. I'll stay right next to Imran. I'll take your old phone so you can call me. And I'll be back by nine.” Mama looked at Imran. He said he'd hold my hand in the crowd, which is embarrassing, but fine. She said yes, but eight-thirty, not nine. I said nine was fairer. She said eight-thirty was the deal. I took it. The churros were worth it.

What time did Mama say Maria had to be back?
Mama said eight-thirty, not nine.
What was Maria feeling when Mama raised one eyebrow at “everyone”?
Maria felt caught out and a little embarrassed, since it was really only three people.
What made Maria's second attempt more persuasive?
Maria gave real reasons, finished homework, staying with Imran, carrying a phone and a set return time, instead of an exaggeration.
How did Mama respond to the new reasons?
Mama agreed but set a limit, eight-thirty instead of nine, and kept to it.

Read this:

Pranav, you're hiding that phone under your pillow? Let me tell you what happened to me. When I was eleven, I, Lalit, had a small handheld game my uncle had brought back from abroad. Every evening I told my mother, "Homework finished," and played under the blanket with the sound off. For two weeks it worked. Then my class teacher sent a letter home: eight pieces of homework missing, marks cut, and would my parents please come to meet her. My mother read the letter at the kitchen table and didn't look at me for a long time. The marks I earned back, slowly. What took longer was her trust. For months she checked my notebook every night, and I knew I had earned that too.

How many pieces of homework were missing?
Eight.
How did young Lalit feel when his mother didn't look up for a long time?
Ashamed, knowing the lie had hurt her.
Which choice inside the story caused the most trouble?
Saying 'Homework finished' when it wasn't; doing the homework before playing would have avoided both the marks and the lost trust.
How might Lalit's mother have felt reading the letter?
Hurt and disappointed, betrayed by the evenings of 'Homework finished'.

It was board exam week, the power went off every evening, and Tejas's phone screen had cracked so badly he could barely read it. Through the cracks he could see a voice note from Parul, four minutes long, sent on Sunday night after he'd laughed at her in front of the group.

He didn't play it. Four minutes of her being upset? Not before physics.

After physics he still didn't. After chemistry there were two more messages: "Tejas?" and "Okay, fine." The "fine" felt worse than the voice note.

By Friday, every time he looked at the phone, his chest tightened. The silence had become a thing of its own. On Saturday, after the last exam, he sat on the stairs in the dark building, pressed play, and listened to all four minutes. Then he called her. "I'm sorry I laughed. And I'm sorry I went quiet for a week."

How long was Parul's voice note?
Parul's voice note was four minutes long.
Why did Tejas keep not playing the voice note?
Tejas felt guilty about laughing at Parul and dreaded hearing her upset, so avoiding it felt like relief during exams.
What could have made this smaller for Tejas?
A quick reply on Sunday, even "I'm sorry, can we talk after physics?", would have stopped the silence becoming a second hurt.
What might Parul have been feeling when she wrote "Okay, fine"?
Parul was probably hurt and giving up hope of a reply, feeling ignored on top of being laughed at.
What does "habitat" mean? Also, why do birds fly south in winter?

1. A habitat is the natural place where an animal or plant lives.
2. Many birds move to warmer places in winter because food becomes scarce in the cold.

At the temple fair in their kasba, Swati bought her little sister Yamini a paper pinwheel. Yamini ran along the canal bank, holding it high to catch the wind. Then her foot slipped, and the pinwheel dropped into the water. She stood still, lip trembling, watching it float away. A loud wail followed. Swati picked her up, patted her back and pointed at the bangle stall. Yamini kept sniffling into her shoulder.

What did Swati buy for Yamini at the fair?
She bought her a paper pinwheel.
What does Yamini's trembling lip before the wail suggest?
It suggests the sadness of losing her new pinwheel was building up in her before it burst out as crying.
What else could Swati try if Yamini stays upset?
She could say out loud that the pinwheel is gone and Yamini is sad, and let her cry a little before offering distractions.
How might Swati feel about the pinwheel falling in?
She may feel sorry for her sister and a bit sad herself, since she chose the gift to make Yamini happy.

Meera knows 12^2 = 144. How can she find 13^2 without multiplying 13 x 13?

Now you try: 14^2 = 196. Find 15^2.
The answer is 196 + 14 + 15 = 225.

Rehana: why is everyone in the hostel being weird with me since the fest
Aparna: honestly? your dance video got 3k views and the seniors keep praising it
Rehana: so they're cold because I danced well??

Aparna: yeah maybe skip jokes like that 😅
Rehana: ok. keeping the video. dropping the jokes. and I'll ask Sheetal how her debate went

How many views did Rehana's dance video get?
Rehana's dance video got 3k views.
What is Rehana worried about?
Rehana is anxious and hurt, worried about losing everyone over one video, enough to think of deleting it.
What would you advise someone treated coldly after a success like Rehana's?
Keep the gift, as Rehana keeps the video, but drop bragging jokes and show interest in others, like asking Sheetal about the debate.
How might others in the hostel see Rehana after the fest?
They may feel small beside all the praise, and a joke like 'I'm obviously the best' makes that sting worse.
Split this into two sentences: The river rises in the hills, flows through three villages, turns slowly toward the east and finally meets the sea near a small fishing town.
The river rises in the hills and flows through three villages. It turns slowly toward the east and finally meets the sea near a small fishing town.
The eggs hatched this morning. How is that different from just cracking?

Hatched means that the young animal inside came out of the egg; cracking only means the shell breaks. It is a verb, the past tense of hatch.
Example: Three tiny chicks hatched on the farm this morning.
Fix: I am boring in this class. And what does "patient" mean here: be patient?

1. I am bored in this class. Why: verb form ("boring" -> "bored").
2. Here, patient means able to wait calmly without getting angry.
About 1.43 x 10^9 people live in India, whose area is about 3.29 x 10^6 km^2. Find the number of people per km^2, to 2 significant figures.

Answer: 1.43 x 10^9 / (3.29 x 10^6) ~ 0.435 x 10^3 ~ 4.3 x 10^2 people per km^2, about 430.

Divide the front numbers: 1.43 / 3.29 ~ 0.4347 (by calculator or long division). Divide the powers by SUBTRACTING exponents: 10^9 / 10^6 = 10^3. So about 0.4347 x 10^3. Adjust: 0.4347 = 4.347 x 10^-^1, so 4.347 x 10^2. To 2 significant figures: 4.3 x 10^2 = 430. Estimate first to check: 1.4 billion / 3.3 million ~ 1,400 / 3.3 ~ 420. A second example: (8 x 10^-^3) / (2 x 10^4) = 4 x 10^-^7.

Read this:

On the first Saturday of the month, Hemant sat at the folding table in his Lajpat Nagar flat and did three boring things he had never done before. He booked his own dentist appointment instead of asking his mother to call. He paid his half of the electricity bill to his flatmate Baljeet the day it came, not three weeks later with an apology. And he opened a notebook and wrote down, honestly, where last month's salary had gone. None of it felt dramatic. His twenty-fourth birthday last month hadn't made him feel grown-up either. But when Baljeet looked up from the payment message and said, 'Whoa, on time? Who are you?', Hemant laughed and felt, for a second, like someone who could be counted on.

Whom did Hemant usually ask to call the dentist?
His mother.
How did Hemant feel when Baljeet teased him?
Hemant felt amused and quietly proud, for a moment like someone who could be counted on.
Why do small acts like these build adulthood better than a birthday?
Each is a real responsibility Hemant takes on, so the grown-up feeling grows from doing, not from turning a certain age.
How might Baljeet see the change?
Baljeet is surprised and pleased, since paying on time means Hemant can be relied on as a flatmate.

Read this:

In the school art room, Vandana, eleven, showed her painting of a sunset to her art teacher, Keerthana ma'am. "The colours are lovely," ma'am said. "But the trees are floating. Let's give them roots on the ground." Vandana's eyes filled. "You always find something wrong! I'm never good at anything." She turned away and started packing her brushes. Keerthana ma'am waited, then said quietly, "Vandana, I'd only bother correcting a painting worth fixing. The trees are one thing. You're the one who mixed that orange." Vandana wiped her face with her sleeve. After a minute, she took the brush out again and painted a thin brown line under each tree.

What was Vandana's painting of?
It was a painting of a sunset.
What was Vandana feeling when she said she was never good at anything?
She felt hurt and discouraged, taking a correction about the trees as a judgment of her whole self.
What did Keerthana ma'am say that helped Vandana return to the painting?
She separated the one fix from Vandana's worth, pointing out that the painting was worth correcting and praising the orange she mixed.
How might Keerthana ma'am feel when Vandana picks up the brush again?
She might feel relieved and warm, seeing Vandana try again after the hurt passed.

Read this:

Hi Jagdish,
Remember how you warned me that offices have their own weather? I think I've found a pattern. There's a team lead here, Sethi, who is lovely to everyone. On Monday he told Farah her slides were "world class," and ten minutes later asked her to cover his client call. On Wednesday he called our intern "the future of this company" right before handing him a pile of scanning. Today it was my turn: "You're the only one who writes clean reports." Then: "Could you finish my quarterly summary by Friday?"
The compliment was vague, nothing about which report. When you praised my work last year, you mentioned the chart on page three. That felt different.
I said I'd check my deadlines and reply tomorrow. I'm going to say no.
Hope Pune is treating you well.
Ankita

What did Sethi ask Farah to do after praising her slides?
Ten minutes later he asked her to cover his client call.
How does Ankita feel about Sethi's compliment today?
Ankita feels wary and unconvinced, because the praise was vague and came just before a request, so it seemed aimed at a yes.
What makes Ankita's reply a sensible step?
Saying the answer would come tomorrow after checking deadlines separates the decision from the flattery and lets the request be judged on its own.
How might the intern see Sethi's praise?
The intern may feel pleased at first to be called the future of the company, then feel used when the praise turns out to be a lead-in to scanning.

metadata.subtype: Spotting the ask behind the praise [Observer]

Read this:

Every morning in Sunaina's small town near Nashik, the newspaper boy, Ramesh, threw the paper onto the verandah at six. By six-fifteen Sunaina had opened it to the children's page. She read it while her mother made tea: a new bird found in the hills, the longest river in Africa, a record for the tallest sandcastle. At night, under the tube light, she read one chapter from a thick general knowledge book borrowed from the town library. Anything new went into a green notebook with three columns: Places, People, Records. By the quiz, the notebook had forty pages. Ramesh started throwing the paper more gently, so the children's page wouldn't tear.

What were the three columns in Sunaina's notebook?
Places, People and Records.
What does Sunaina opening the paper by six-fifteen suggest about her feelings?
She is eager and curious, and enjoys the daily reading rather than seeing it as a chore.
What else could Sunaina add to her reading plan, and why?
She could test herself weekly from the notebook, because reading adds facts but testing shows which ones stick.
How does Sunaina's routine look to Ramesh?
Ramesh notices how much she values the paper and starts throwing it gently, so he seems touched and supportive.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]

messages.content: James buys twice as many toy soldiers as toy cars.  He buys 20 toy cars.  How many total toys does he buy?

He buys 2*20=40 toy cars
So the total number of toys is 20+40=60
The answer is 60.
Angel or angle in maths: which is correct?

In maths it is "angle", the space between two lines that meet. An "angel" is a spiritual being.
Examples: Measure the angle with a protractor. In the play, Lila was an angel.

Read this:

In the small town of Jalgaon, Abhinav got home from work early and found his father on the sofa, phone held up, sweating, whispering, "Yes, sir. Yes, sir."
On the screen was a man in a police uniform. His father's passbook and a notepad lay open on the table.
"Papa, who is it?"
His father waved him away frantically. The man on the screen said sharply, "Who is there? You were told to stay alone."
Abhinav's heart jumped, but he kept his voice calm. He sat beside his father and gently took the phone. "Papa, real police don't do this on video." He ended the call.
His father was shaking. "They said I was in a money laundering case. That if I told you, you'd be arrested too. I was about to transfer the FD money."
"You did nothing wrong, Papa. They're very clever."
His younger brother Akash brought water. Together they called the cybercrime helpline and blocked the number.

What lay open on the table?
His father's passbook and a notepad.
How did Abhinav feel when he saw his father on the call?
Abhinav felt alarmed, his heart jumping, but he stayed calm so his father wouldn't panic further.
What did Abhinav do that protected his father?
He calmly took the phone and ended the call, reassured his father without blame, and with Akash called the cybercrime helpline.
How did Abhinav's father feel during and after the call?
His father felt terrified and trapped, sweating and shaking, fearing his sons would be arrested if he told them.

metadata.subtype: Helping a parent who is targeted [Observer]

messages.content: There are 10 cars parked in a mall's parking lot, each with the same number of customers inside. Each customer only makes 1 purchase. If the sports store makes 20 sales and the music store makes 30 sales, how many customers are in each of the cars?

As each sale represents a customer, there must be a total of 20 sports store sales + 30 music store sales = 50 customers.
There is an equal number of customers in every car, so there must be 50 total customers / 10 cars = 5 customers in each car.
The answer is 5.

Read this:

Saturday. Pranav dared me to jump off the tall back wall by the water tank. Everyone stood in a half circle. I looked down and thought it through properly. If I land wrong, I could break a leg, and then no cricket, no school trip, and plaster for weeks. If I say no, they will make chicken noises for a day or two, and by Monday it will be a different joke. A broken leg is not forgotten by Monday. So I said, "No, thanks." My knees wobbled, but I walked home. At dinner I told Amma about the wall, and she hugged me and said she would speak to the watchman about it. Rehana

What did Pranav dare Rehana to do?
Pranav dared Rehana to jump off the tall back wall by the water tank.
How did Rehana feel after saying no?
Shaky but relieved, since Rehana's knees wobbled yet the walk home was safe. 😅
What other approach could Rehana use the next time a dare comes, and why?
Suggest a safer game or walk away with a friend, because it removes the danger without a long argument.
How might the other children see Rehana's no?
Some may tease for a day or two, but the jokes fade quickly, and others may quietly feel glad that someone said no.

metadata.subtype: Approach: weighing danger against being laughed at [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: Could we have 15 minutes?
Hi Kalyani,
I've been thinking about Tuesday's review, when the formatting issue came up in front of the team.
I didn't want to discuss it with the other interns first, because it's really between us. I want to do this internship well, and I know I have a lot to learn. Could you tell me what I should improve, especially on formatting and deadlines? And, when possible, could feedback be given privately? I find it much easier to take in that way.
Would 15 minutes on Thursday or Friday work for you?
Thank you for your time.
Mehak

How many minutes does Mehak ask for?
15 minutes.
What does the calm tone of Mehak's email suggest about Mehak's feelings now?
Mehak seems steadier and determined, choosing to act on the hurt from Tuesday rather than stew in it.
Which choice in this email is wise, and why?
Asking privately and clearly for both feedback and a change in how it is given, which is professional and easy to agree to.
How might Kalyani feel reading this email?
Kalyani may feel a little uncomfortable about Tuesday, but also respected and more willing to help an intern who asks so clearly.

Read this:

Friday. Akash was moving to a new team on Monday and wrote a short note for Pema about the annual fair booking: "Stalls booked. Sound system pending. Ask the caretaker." He signed off, glad to be done.

Tuesday. Pema sent three messages: which sound company? What is the caretaker's number? Was a deposit paid? Akash, busy in the new team, replied with one word: "Later."

Next Friday. The sound company had not been paid and cancelled the slot. Pema found the invoice in Akash's old email. Hearing about it, Akash sat quietly. "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down."

What did Akash's note say about the sound system?
The note said: "Sound system pending."
What might Akash have felt when saying "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down"?
Regretful and a bit ashamed, realising that what was known in his head had not travelled.
What could Akash have done on the Friday before leaving?
Write down which sound company, the deposit, the caretaker's number and the deadline, and offer a short call.
How might Pema have felt on finding the cancelled slot?
Frustrated and stressed, having had to reconstruct facts without background and lost the booking anyway.

Read this:

Nirmala, come, I'll tell you about my worst mistake as a manager. It was 2004, at the bank. I had a new trainee, a quiet young woman. She never spoke in meetings. I thought, this one doesn't care.
I was busy, you see. I spoke to everyone in short bursts. "Do this. Wrong. Again." I didn't think about it.
Three months later she asked for a transfer. Her letter said she felt I disliked her from day one. Disliked her! I'd been planning to recommend her for the analyst track. Her work was careful.
She was reading my tone, and I was reading her silence, and we were both wrong. So remember this from your old Naveen uncle: explain your feedback, and ask the quiet ones what they think.

What did the trainee ask for after three months?
A transfer.
What might young Naveen have felt when he read her letter?
He was likely shocked and regretful, realising she felt disliked while he had been planning to recommend her.
In the story, what choice could Naveen have made earlier?
Explaining his feedback and asking the quiet trainee what she thought, instead of assuming her silence meant she didn't care.
What was the trainee experiencing during those three months?
She felt disliked and probably anxious, taking Naveen's brisk tone personally and staying silent to protect herself.
Now you try: 1 m 8 cm in centimetres.
The answer is 108 cm.

Read this:

Some days last year I missed my mother while sitting right next to her. I'm Sarika. Amma, Lakshmi, still hummed the same film songs and still liked her coffee too sweet, but she had started calling me by her sister's name and asking when her husband would be home from the office. Appa died ten years ago. I'd say "soon", then cry in the bathroom with the tap running. I felt guilty for being tired, and guiltier for sometimes wanting my old life back. Then one evening she held my face and said, "You have lovely eyes," as if meeting me for the first time, and I laughed till I cried. A cousin told me about a caregivers' group at the temple hall. The first Thursday I went, a woman said, "It's grief while they're still here." I nearly hugged her.

What did Lakshmi say when she held Sarika's face?
She said, "You have lovely eyes."
Why did Sarika cry in the bathroom with the tap running?
Sarika was grieving the mother Amma used to be, and felt guilty and exhausted while hiding it.
What helped Sarika feel less alone?
Going to the caregivers' group at the temple hall, where someone named this grief honestly.
How might Lakshmi experience the evenings with Sarika?
Lakshmi may not recognise Sarika, yet still feels warmth and delight, as when admiring Sarika's eyes.

Read this:

In the Hyderabad clinic, the nurse Dilnaz smiled and said, "Hello, Deepika!" Deepika darted behind her father's legs and pressed her face into his trousers.
"Say hello, beta, don't be rude," her father said, trying to pull her forward.
"Leave her," Dilnaz said. "Tell me about her cough first." She talked to him and didn't look at Deepika. Slowly a small face peeped round his knee, watching.

Where did Deepika hide?
Behind her father's legs, with her face pressed into his trousers.
What was Deepika feeling when she darted behind her father?
She felt shy and probably frightened of the nurse in a strange place, not rude.
What did Dilnaz do that helped Deepika warm up?
She stopped looking at Deepika and talked to her father, giving her space to peek out when ready.
How does Deepika's father see her hiding at first?
He worries it looks rude and tries to pull her forward.

Read this:

Sunday. Tanvir's journal.
Sat with Sonali at the café today and finally wrote the bakery plan properly, instead of just dreaming. Goal: my own small bakery in Bandra in five years. Too big to think about all at once, so we broke it down. Year one: keep my job, take the weekend baking course, sell at the Sunday market to test recipes. Year two: save and learn the business side, talk to two bakery owners about what went wrong for them. Year three: rent a small kitchen for orders only. Years four and five: shopfront, if the numbers make sense. For each year I wrote three concrete steps and one sign that says stop or keep going. Sonali said, "Now it's a map, not a wish." I feel scared and weirdly calm.

Where does Tanvir want to open the bakery?
In Bandra.
How does Tanvir feel after writing the plan?
Tanvir feels scared and weirdly calm at the same time.
What made the plan strategic rather than a dream?
Breaking five years into steps per year, each with concrete actions and a sign for whether to continue.
How might Sonali see Tanvir's plan?
Sonali seems supportive and encouraging, seeing it as a real map now.

Read this:

In a flat in Mexico City, Nour, two, gripped the edge of a heavy toy box and dragged it across the floor with a long grunt, her face scrunched with effort. Camila watched from the sofa and said, “Uuuh! That's heavy!” Nour grinned. Later, after an afternoon of play, she sat on the rug and let out a big sigh, shoulders low. Then, while stacking cups, she started to hum a tune of no words. Camila hummed back, softly, matching her tune.

What did Nour drag across the floor?
A heavy toy box.
What might Nour's grunt, sigh and hum each show about her state?
The grunt shows effort, the sigh probably tiredness and the hum contentment. The sigh could also mean she was a bit bored.
What could Camila do with these sounds?
Camila could echo them warmly and add words, like “big push” or “tired now”, to help language grow.
How might Nour feel when Camila hums back?
She may feel heard and happy, because her sound started a small conversation. 😊

Read this:

I'm Varun, and I want to write about Nilesh. In the spelling test before Diwali, I saw him look at the paper next to him and copy a word. After that, everything he did looked bad to me. When he drew a tiger for the class wall, I told everyone it looked like a cat. When he offered me his extra eraser, I said no, as if it was dirty. When he laughed, I thought he was laughing at someone. Last week our art teacher hung his tiger in the corridor and said it had the best stripes she had seen all year. I stood and looked at it properly for the first time. It was good. I felt strange. He copied one word. That didn't make his tiger bad.

What did Nilesh draw for the class wall?
He drew a tiger for the class wall.
What was Varun feeling when looking at the tiger properly for the first time?
Varun felt strange and a little ashamed, seeing that the drawing was good and that one copied word had coloured everything.
What could Varun try the next time one bad act makes someone seem all bad?
Varun could judge each thing on its own, like looking at the drawing itself, instead of letting the copied word decide.
How might Nilesh have felt when Varun refused his eraser?
Nilesh probably felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to be friendly.

Read this:

Tutor's note, first-year engineering design, 21 January
The group's bridge model failed at half the target load today. Afterwards Pankaj told the others, loudly, "Ganga did the joints. That's why." Ganga went pale and said, "It's all my fault. I ruined it for everyone." She was close to tears.
I asked the group to examine the failure together. The joints had slipped, yes; Ganga had used less glue than the plan said. But the main beam was also one size smaller than the drawing, and that was Pankaj's part.
I told Ganga that owning her part was good, but carrying the whole failure was neither accurate nor fair to herself. I asked Pankaj to look at the beam. He went quiet, then said, "Okay. Mine too."
The group has written a short list of what each person will change for next week's retest. Ganga's line reads: "Follow the glue spec; ask if unsure."

At what load did the bridge model fail?
At half the target load.
What was Ganga feeling after Pankaj blamed her?
Ashamed and close to tears, pale and taking the whole failure on herself.
What did the tutor help the group do?
Examine the failure together, see both the joints and the undersized beam, and write down what each person will change for the retest.
How did Pankaj respond when asked to look at the beam?
He went quiet, then admitted his share: "Okay. Mine too."
One sandwich costs Rs 4. How much do 9 sandwiches cost?
Rs 36. Because 9 x 4 = 36, so the cost is Rs 36.

Read this:

Preschool note, Tuesday.
Harish (5) brought a packet of biscuits today. At snack time, his younger brother Asif came over from the toddler room, and Harish immediately gave him two, then broke another in half so they'd have the same. Later, a new boy visiting with his mother sat at the table and looked at the packet. Harish held it close and ate slowly, not offering. When I asked him to share, he gave one, a little reluctantly. I'll try pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game tomorrow so they get to know each other before snack time.

How many biscuits did Harish give Asif first?
Harish immediately gave him two.
What does Harish holding the packet close suggest about how he felt?
It suggests Harish felt protective of his biscuits and wary of the new boy, whom he didn't know yet.
Why is pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game a good idea?
Getting to know the boy may make him feel less like a stranger, so Harish may share more easily.
How might the visiting boy have felt watching Harish?
The visiting boy may have felt left out and shy, wanting a biscuit but new to the group.
Peace or piece: "Can I have a ___ of cake?"

Write "piece", which means a part of something. "Peace" means calm or no fighting. A memory trick: a piece of pie.
Examples: Can I have a piece of cake? After the guests left, there was peace in the house.

Read this:

In the playschool garden, five children lined up for the red slide. Ganga was third. She hopped from foot to foot. "Me now! Me now!" Pallavi Miss knelt beside her. "You're waiting so nicely. First Lina, then Babu, then you." Ganga held up her fingers and counted: one, two. Lina slid down. Babu slid down. Ganga's turn! At the bottom she ran straight to Miss. "I waited!" Miss gave her a high five. Then Ganga ran to the back of the line again, all by herself.

Where was Ganga in the line for the red slide?
Ganga was third.
How was Ganga feeling while she hopped from foot to foot?
She felt impatient and excited, wanting her turn right away.
How did Pallavi Miss help Ganga keep waiting?
She praised Ganga's waiting and said clearly who came first, so Ganga could count the turns on her fingers.
What might Lina and Babu feel when Ganga waits instead of pushing?
They likely feel it is fair and safe to take their turns without being pushed.

Read this:

The alert buzzed on Farhan's phone at dusk: the river had crossed the danger line, and low areas should move to the school shelter. By nine, brown water was seeping under the door of the rented flat. Farhan stood still for a breath and ranked things aloud. "Mum and Noor first. Then the documents folder. Then Mum's tablets, my phone and the power bank." The sofa and the television stayed where they were. An hour later the three of them sat on plastic chairs in the classroom shelter, dry.

Upstairs, Sahil had seen small floods before and waved off the alert. "It always drops by morning," he said, and stayed put. By midnight the roads had closed. At dawn Sahil's family waited on the roof, and volunteers had to bring a boat through moving water.

A month later, back in the flat, Farhan wrote two lists. Wiring, the floor and the door came first. Painting and new curtains could wait. When the relief money and the insurance payment came in bits, he redrew the list each time, moving jobs up or down.

Where did Farhan and the others go when the water arrived?
They went to the shelter in the school.
How did Sahil's response to the alert differ from Farhan's, and what followed?
Farhan ranked what mattered and left for the shelter, staying dry, while Sahil waved off the alert, the roads closed by midnight, and his family needed a boat to reach them from the roof.
What was Sahil probably feeling on the roof at dawn?
Fear, and probably regret at having waved off the alert.
What could Sahil do differently next time?
Sahil could follow the alert, leave early for the shelter, and take documents and medicines with the family.

Read this:

I'm Imran, and I still remember how my hands shook at the bus stop that Monday. A man behind me muttered something vile about my community, loud enough for the queue to hear. Nobody said a word. Every part of me wanted to turn around and hit him. I could feel the anger climbing, and I'll be honest, it felt justified. Then my friend Parveen took my sleeve. "Your anger is fair. Don't let him decide what you do with it. Come." We walked to the college office. It took three hours of forms and a long talk with the counsellor, and it felt so slow. But I wasn't alone with it, and later I joined the student group that helps people who face this. The rage cooled into something I could use.

Where was Imran when the insult happened?
Imran was at the bus stop.
What was Imran feeling as the man muttered?
Anger that felt justified and a strong urge to hit him, along with shaking hands.
What did Imran and Parveen do with the anger?
They went to the college office to file a complaint and talk to the counsellor, and Imran later joined a student support group.
How might Parveen have seen Imran's anger?
As fair and understandable, yet something to guide before it turned into a fight that could hurt Imran.

"A female curate, who is not my wife, would never suit me. With me, then, it seems, you cannot go: but if you are sincere in your offer, I will, while in town, speak to a married missionary, whose wife needs a coadjutor. Your own fortune will make you independent of the Society's aid; and thus you may still be spared the dishonour of breaking your promise and deserting the band you engaged to join."

Why does the speaker refuse to take the listener along, and what does the speaker offer instead?

A female curate who is not a wife would never suit, the speaker says, so the listener cannot come along. Instead, while in town, there is an offer to speak to a married missionary whose wife needs an assistant, sparing the listener from breaking the promise.

Read this:

Ira taught ethics to second-year students in Bengaluru. She had been watching Jeevan, nineteen, all term.
In class debates, Jeevan argued brilliantly for human dignity above any law. He quoted thinkers, he spoke about rights for everyone.
But in the hostel, she heard, he'd gone along with his group in shutting out a new boy, because "the gang decided".
And at the canteen, he'd refused to let someone skip the queue even for a medical emergency: "Rules are rules."
Ira didn't think Jeevan was a hypocrite. She thought he was nineteen, reasoning differently in different places, like most people.
In the next class, she didn't label anyone. She said, "These stages aren't boxes for people. They're ways of seeing how our reasoning grows, sometimes forward, sometimes back, depending on where we stand."
Jeevan looked up, thoughtful.

What subject did Ira teach?
Ethics.
What was Ira thinking about Jeevan's different choices?
She felt curious and patient, seeing him as reasoning at different levels in different places, not as a hypocrite.
What did Ira say in class, and why is it a wise way to use the stage model?
She said the stages aren't boxes for people but ways to see how reasoning grows, avoiding ranking anyone as a better person.
How might the new boy in the hostel have felt being shut out?
He probably felt lonely and rejected, not knowing the group's decision was just going along with each other.

metadata.subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]

Read this:

Harish almost typed an excuse. Then he didn't.
Nitin: machi! coming home for Pongal? 🎉
Nitin: cricket at the school ground, 6 am, like always
Harish: haha 6 am
Harish: yes, coming. but i have a play rehearsal call on the 15th evening
Nitin: play?? you? since when
Harish: since second sem. i'm in the college theatre club now
Harish: was scared you'd laugh tbh
Nitin: i'm laughing a little, not gonna lie
Nitin: but ok, send a video. my amma will want to see
Harish: will do. and yes to cricket. i'll be terrible, haven't held a bat in a year
Nitin: you were always terrible
Harish: true 🙂
Harish: tea at Selvam anna's shop after?
Nitin: obviously. some things don't change

What time is the cricket at the school ground?
6 am, like always.
Why was Harish slow to mention the theatre club?
Harish was scared that Nitin would laugh at the new interest.
How did Harish honour the old friendship while being his new self?
Harish said yes to the old cricket and tea ritual and also shared the theatre club openly instead of hiding it.
How does Nitin react to Harish's new interest?
Surprised and teasing but accepting: Nitin asks for a video for Nitin's amma and keeps the old plans.

messages.content:
Read this:

During wet break in their Kraków classroom, Olga tossed a rubber ball to Thabo and it hit the globe on the teacher's desk. The globe rolled off, and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Pan Nowak came back and stared at it. "Who did this?"
Olga's stomach went tight. Last month he had made Kuba stand in the corridor the whole afternoon for spilling paint. "It was already cracked," she said. "It was like that this morning."
Thabo looked at the floor and said nothing.
Pan Nowak frowned but moved on to spelling. Olga didn't hear a single word of the lesson. On the bus home, Thabo said quietly, "You didn't have to say that." Olga pressed her forehead against the cold window and didn't answer.

What happened to the globe?
It rolled off the desk and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Why did Olga say the globe was already cracked?
Olga was scared of being punished, remembering that Pan Nowak made Kuba stand in the corridor all afternoon for spilling paint.
What could make it easier for Olga to tell the truth next time?
If Pan Nowak met accidents calmly, for example by asking who could help fix things rather than punishing, Olga might feel safe enough to own up.
What is it like for Thabo when Olga blames the globe's crack on the morning?
Thabo seems uncomfortable and torn, staring at the floor in class and later saying quietly, "You didn't have to say that."

Read this:

Monday. Chinmay told his friend Madhav that he was "just tired of things" with Ritika. He didn't say he was bored. When Ritika messaged "movie on Saturday?", he replied, "Maybe, lots of homework."

Wednesday, two days later. Ritika sensed something. She messaged more, sent him songs, asked three times if he was okay. Chinmay felt the phone buzz in his pocket during maths and didn't take it out. Each buzz made him feel more trapped.

Saturday, that weekend. He skipped the movie, saying his cousin was visiting. Ritika sent: "Did I do something wrong? Please tell me." He stared at it for ten minutes and wrote, "No, all good 🙂". He knew it wasn't.

Madhav, who was with him, said, "You're not being fair to her."

Chinmay pushed the phone away. "I know. I just don't know how to say it."

What excuse did Chinmay give for skipping the movie?
That his cousin was visiting.
How does Chinmay feel each time his phone buzzes in maths?
He feels more trapped and uncomfortable, bored with the relationship but not saying so.
What could Chinmay do instead of hinting?
He could tell Ritika honestly and kindly how he feels, so she isn't left guessing and messaging more.
What is it like for Ritika to get "No, all good" after asking if she did something wrong?
She probably feels confused and anxious, sensing a change but getting mixed signals, which makes her cling harder.
Sofia has 24 coins and gets 33 more from a friend. How many coins does she have now?
57. Because 24 + 33 = 57, so there are 57 coins in all.

Read this:

In the clinic waiting room, Karthik, five, pressed against Asif's side. "Abbu, will the doctor's snake-thing hear my secrets?"
"The stethoscope? What secrets?"
"That I ate the biscuits."
Across the room a mother told her son, "Sit still or the doctor will give you ten injections." Karthik's eyes went huge.
Asif lowered his voice. "Nobody gets injections for fidgeting. The stethoscope only hears your heart going thump-thump. No secrets."
"Is it scary?"
"It's cold, like a spoon. That's all."
Karthik walked in holding Asif's finger, whispering, "Cold like a spoon."

What did Karthik call the stethoscope?
The doctor's snake-thing.
What was Karthik worried the stethoscope would do?
Hear his secrets, like eating the biscuits, so he would be found out.
How was Asif's approach different from the other parent's?

The Physics board paper was six days away when Dolma's mock came back: 29 out of 70. That night, in the small room she shared with her brother Chetan in their Darjeeling flat, she decided to study straight through. Chetan grumbled about the lamp and pulled the quilt over his head. By four in the morning she had done three chapters and felt almost proud. The next day she dozed on the school bus, snapped at her best friend for asking about lunch, and couldn't remember a formula she had revised at two. So she stayed up again, to make up for the lost day. On the third morning, working a practice paper, she stared at a question on lenses she knew she had done twice. Nothing came. Two nights of extra hours, and she remembered less than before.

29 out of 70.
What was Dolma feeling when she snapped at her best friend?
She was exhausted and irritable, her mood worn down by a night without sleep.

Used the next days on the topics the mock showed as weak, while keeping normal sleep so memory and mood stayed intact.

The electricity in their Lucknow lane went off every afternoon at three, and both Rehana and her cousin Vasudha had online course assignments overdue by a week. They sat on the same terrace, laptops on battery. Vasudha opened hers and groaned. "I'm so pathetic. I had seven days." She closed it again and started listing everything wrong with herself. Rehana felt the same sting. She had delayed too. But she took a breath and said, quietly, "Okay. I got behind. That happens. Five minutes, then I'll see." The battery icon showed forty minutes left. She wrote the first question's answer in five, then kept going. When the power came back at six, Rehana had finished half. Vasudha had watched three short videos about productivity and felt worse than before. "How did you even start?" she asked. "I stopped yelling at myself," Rehana said.

When did the electricity go off in their Lucknow lane?
Every afternoon at three.
What was Rehana feeling when she saw her own delay, and how did she handle it?
She felt the same guilty sting as Vasudha, but she forgave herself calmly and committed to five minutes, which let her start.

Jazel has 3 sticks. One stick is 3 centimeters long. The second stick is twice as long while the third stick is 1 centimeter shorter than the second stick. What is the total length of Jazel's sticks when they are put together?

The second stick is 3 x 2 = 6 centimeters long.
The third stick is 6 - 1 = 5 centimeters long.
Thus, Jazel's sticks are 3 + 6 + 5 = 14 centimeters long when they are put together.
The answer is 14.

Why do stars twinkle while planets shine steadily?

Starlight is shaken on its way to us, while planet light is steadier. Because a star is so far away that it is a tiny point and the moving layers of our air shift that point about, while a planet is a larger disc and looks steadier, stars flicker and planets do not.

She walked over, but kept her distance. "Hey. Are you okay? I can sit or go, whichever you like." He wiped his eyes with his sleeve and half laughed. "Sit. I'm fine. Thursday night
Today was strange but good. Yesterday Hansa ma'am snapped at me in front of the whole team over a formatting mistake that wasn't even mine. I went home furious and rehearsed what I'd say when she apologised. She never said sorry. Instead, this morning she put a cup of filter coffee on my desk, made exactly the way I take it, and asked me to lead the client call. At lunch she waved me over to her table, and that was that. Back to normal, as if a door had been quietly closed.
My flatmate Keiko says that counts as a full apology; at her home, a shared meal after a fight says more than any words. Part of me still wanted the actual sentence. Mumma apologises the same way as Hansa ma'am, with food, and Papa with folded hands and a joke. Maybe I'm the only one in my family who needs the words. One day I might tell ma'am that.
Damini

What did Hansa ma'am put on Damini's desk?
A cup of filter coffee, made exactly the way Damini takes it.
How did Damini feel about Hansa ma'am's way of making up?
Damini felt mixed: relieved and a little touched that things were back to normal, but part of Damini still wanted to hear an actual sorry.

Tell Hansa ma'am calmly, at a good moment, that spoken apologies matter, while still treating the coffee, the call and the lunch as real repair.
How does Keiko see what Hansa ma'am did?
As a full apology, since in her home a shared meal after a fight says more than words.
Without calculating, which of these CANNOT be perfect squares: 1,057; 23,453; 7,928; 222,222; 4,000; 1,069?

Answer: 1,057, 23,453, 7,928, 222,222 and 4,000 cannot be squares. 1,069 might be (it is not: 32^2 = 1,024 and 33^2 = 1,089).

Look at the last digit of the squares 0^2 to 9^2: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81. They end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 only. So a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square: 1,057 (7), 23,453 (3), 7,928 (8), 222,222 (2). A square ending in zeros has an EVEN number of them (10^2 = 100, 20^2 = 400, 100^2 = 10,000), so 4,000 with 3 zeros is not a square. The test only rules numbers OUT: 1,069 ends in 9, so it might be a square, but it lies between 32^2 = 1,024 and 33^2 = 1,089, so it is not.

I'm Zubin, a junior structural engineer, and I have admired Afreen ma'am since my first day at the firm. She's designed half the bridges in our district. So when she said at the review, "The old soil report from 2015 is enough; we don't need a new test," my first instinct was to nod.
But I'd walked that site the week before. The riverbank had shifted after two heavy monsoons.
After the meeting, I knocked on her cabin. "Ma'am, can I ask how we decided the 2015 report still fits?"
She looked up, a little surprised. "The soil there hasn't changed in decades."
"You know that ground better than I do," I said. "But I took photos last week. The bank has moved." I put them on her desk.
She studied them for a long time. Then she picked up the phone and asked for a new test. As I left she said, "Good. Keep doing that, young man."

What had happened to the riverbank after two heavy monsoons?
The riverbank had shifted after two heavy monsoons.
What was Zubin's first instinct at the review, and why?
Zubin's first instinct was to nod, because he admired Afreen ma'am and she had designed half the bridges in the district.
How did Zubin raise the concern in a way that kept both respect and accuracy?
He asked privately how the decision was reached, acknowledged that she knew the ground better, and then showed his photos as evidence.
How might Afreen ma'am feel about Zubin after he left?

Trisha, you asked why I don't drink at weddings. Let me tell you.
In my second year of college, I started drinking at hostel parties to feel less shy. Then before parties, to get ready. Then alone, on Sunday nights, to stop feeling anxious about Monday. I told myself I was fine because I still got good marks.
One morning I woke up and couldn't remember how I'd got back to my room. My roommate, Nisha, was sitting on her bed, waiting. She said, "I was really scared last night."
That did it. I went to the college counsellor that week. She helped me see the loop: anxiety, drink, relief, worse anxiety. I joined a support group and found other ways to calm down: running, and calling my sister.

Davonte is trying to figure out how much space his art collection takes up. He measures his paintings and finds he has three square 6-foot by 6-foot paintings, four small 2-foot by 3-foot paintings, and one large 10-foot by 15-foot painting. How many square feet does his collection take up?

His square paintings take up 36 square feet each because 6 x 6 = 36
His small paintings take 6 square feet each because 2 x 3 = 6
His large painting takes up 150 square feet because 10 x 15 = 150.
Combined, his square paintings take up 108 square feet because 3 x 36 = 108
Combined, his small paintings take up 24 square feet because 4 x 6 = 24
In total, his paintings take up 282 square feet because 150 + 108 + 24 = 282
The answer is 282.

I'm Gurleen, from the flat next door. Tejas, five, rang my bell with a broken kite. "G-G-G-Gurleen, the k-k-kite, it, it..." His face went tight. I waited, looking at him. Gabrielle sells eggs. On Monday she sells 5 crates of eggs. On Tuesday she sells 2 times as many crates of eggs as Monday. On Wednesday she sells 2 fewer crates than Tuesday. On Thursday she sells half as many crates of eggs as she sells on Tuesday. How many total crates of eggs does she sell for the 4 days?

On Tuesday she sells 5 crates * 2 = 10 crates of eggs.
On Wednesday she sells 10 crates - 2 crates = 8 crates of eggs.
On Thursday she sells 1/2 * 10 crates = 5 crates of eggs.
She sells a total of 5 crates + 10 crates + 8 crates + 5 crates = 28 crates of eggs.
The answer is 28.

In a race, there are eight runners. The first five runners finish the race in 8 hours, while the rest of the runners finish the race 2 hours later. Calculate the total time the eight runners took to finish the race.

The first five runners took a combined total of 5*8 = 40 hours to finish the race.
The number of runners who finished the race 2 hours later after the first five is 8-5 = 3
The 3 runners who finished the race 2 hours later took a total of 8+2 =10 hours to run the race.
Together, the three runners who finished the race in 10 hours took a total of 10*3 = 30 hours.
All eight runners took 30+40 = 70 hours altogether to finish the race.
The answer is 70.
What do audav, shadav and sampurna mean?

Monday: Pallavi, fifteen, sat on the bus stop bench. The bus was late. Her hand pulled out the phone before she'd even noticed she was bored. Thirty seconds of short videos, then another thirty.
Wednesday: Her cousin Indu, visiting, pointed it out. “You picked up your phone four times while we were talking.” Pallavi hadn't noticed once. That night she felt embarrassed, lying in bed.
Saturday: Pallavi tried an experiment. At the bus stop, she kept the phone in her bag and a small sketchbook in her pocket. The boredom came, like an itch. Her hand twitched toward the bag. Instead she drew the auto-rickshaw across the road, badly.
It wasn't as exciting as the videos. But she noticed the bus arriving.

What did Pallavi draw at the bus stop on Saturday?
She drew the auto-rickshaw across the road.
How did Pallavi feel on Wednesday night after Indu's comment?
She felt embarrassed, realising she had picked up the phone four times without noticing.
What did Pallavi's experiment change about the loop?
She kept the same cue of boredom but put the phone away and had a sketchbook ready, swapping the action.
How might Indu have felt pointing out the phone habit?
Indu may have felt a little awkward but honest, wanting a cousin to notice.

I'm Urmila, Jasleen and Gurnoor's Nani, and I've spent every summer watching those two fight. Over the window seat, the last mango, the remote. You name it.

But last week at the park, something happened. A group of older girls started laughing at Gurnoor's thick glasses. I was about to get up.

Jasleen got there first. She walked straight up to them and said, "That's my sister. Leave her alone." Then she took Gurnoor's hand and walked her away.

Ten minutes later, they were fighting again, about who got to sit on the higher swing.

I sat on my bench and laughed. That's siblings. They'll fight each other their whole lives, and fight for each other too.

What were the older girls laughing at?
Gurnoor's thick glasses.
How did Urmila feel watching Jasleen defend Gurnoor?
Urmila felt amused and touched, laughing at how quickly the sisters went from defending each other to fighting again.
What does Urmila's story suggest about sibling fights?
That rivalry and loyalty live side by side, and fighting siblings can still become each other's lifelong support.
How might Gurnoor have felt when Jasleen took her hand?
She probably felt protected and grateful, less hurt by the older girls.
Do good friends have to agree about everything?
No, good friends do not have to agree about everything. Because a friendship rests on trust and respect and not on matching opinions, friends can disagree politely and still enjoy each other.

It was the week of Christmas, and the school van was late because of fog. When Madhav, five, finally got home, he burst in.

"Papa! Did you see? He fell and the thing broke and everybody laughed!"

His father Jagdish blinked. "Who fell?"

"Him! You know!"

"I wasn't at school, beta."

Madhav frowned, as if Papa was being silly. "The big boy. With the drum. At the song."

Slowly Jagdish pieced it together: a boy had dropped a drum at the carol practice. "And were you sad or did you laugh?"

"I laughed. Everybody laughed. You would laugh too."

What did Jagdish work out had happened at school?
A boy had dropped a drum at the carol practice.
Why did Madhav frown when Papa asked who fell?
He felt puzzled and a bit annoyed, because he thought Papa already knew what he saw.
How could Jagdish help Madhav tell stories more clearly?
He could ask simple questions like who, where and what happened, and say, "I wasn't there, so tell me from the start."
How might the boy who dropped the drum have felt when everyone laughed?
The boy might have felt embarrassed or upset, even if Madhav thought everyone would laugh.
My mother cut the blouse from a paper pattern. I only know a pattern as a design on cloth.

A pattern is also a shape or set of shapes, usually made of paper, used as a guide for cutting cloth. It is a noun. The design meaning is a repeated shape or arrangement.
Example: She pinned the pattern onto the cotton before cutting.
