At breakfast he wanted plain toast only; the aloo parathas smelled wonderful and he didn't try one. On today's walk he asked to take the same path as yesterday, not the new trail by the apple orchard, even when Ayesha said it was shorter and led to a frozen waterfall. "I know the old way," he said. I didn't push. I asked him to walk just the first stretch of the new trail with Ayesha and me, and promised we could turn back at the bend. He went past the bend. At the waterfall he smiled and asked if we could come again tomorrow.

Which bunk does Varun keep asking for?
The corner bunk nearest the door.
Why does Varun keep choosing the old path and plain toast?
What he already knows feels safe and predictable, so the new trail or the parathas make him uneasy, even when the change looks perfectly fine.
Which step helped Varun try the new trail, and why did it work?
Walking only the first stretch together, with a promise to turn back at the bend, because a small, safe try made the change feel less risky.
How might Ayesha see Varun's choices?
Ayesha may find it puzzling that Varun picks the colder, longer options, and is probably pleased when he reaches the waterfall and wants to come again.

Read this:

In the sandpit of a São Paulo park, Priscila, five, had the red dump truck. Yesterday Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon. Now Sami toddled over. Priscila pushed the truck straight to him. "Your turn!" Then Lucas came, the boy who never let anyone touch his digger. He reached for the truck. Priscila pulled it back. "No. You don't share." Lucas stamped. Priscila crossed her arms. "When you share, I share." She went back to building a sand road with Sami.

Who had let Priscila use his bucket yesterday?
Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon.
What was Priscila feeling when she pulled the truck back from Lucas?
Priscila felt it was unfair and a little cross, remembering that Lucas never let anyone touch his digger.
What could a parent say to help all three children?
A parent could praise Priscila for sharing with Sami and suggest Lucas try sharing his digger, so everyone sees how sharing works both ways.
How might Lucas feel when Priscila said no?
Lucas felt frustrated and left out, stamping his foot, maybe not yet understanding why.

Read this:

Team lead's note, written for myself, Thursday.

Damini has been on my team for a year. Three times this month her partner has called during lunch and I've heard him mock her loudly on speaker: her cooking, her job, her friends. Each time she laughs and says, "That's just his way. He doesn't mean it."

Today, after another call, her hands were shaking as she typed. I asked if she had a minute. I said once, gently, "The way he spoke to you didn't sound kind. You deserve respect." She looked away and said, "You don't know him."

I didn't argue. I told her my door is open, any time, and gave her the number for our employee counselling line. She put the card in her bag. I'll keep checking in, quietly.

How many times this month had Damini's partner mocked her on speaker?
Three times this month.
How does the note-writer feel after Damini's shaking hands and her reply?
The note-writer feels concerned and uneasy, but chooses patience instead of pushing Damini.
Why was naming it once and staying available a wise approach?
It lets Damini know someone sees it without forcing her to defend her partner, and the counselling number gives her a safe next step.
How might Damini be feeling when she says "You don't know him"?
Damini may feel defensive and embarrassed, and perhaps not ready to face how the calls affect her.

Read this:

I'm Irawati, and three months ago I learned how anger can almost ruin a good case.

Our team had spent six weeks on the hospital software project. I wrote most of the design. At the client presentation, Anand, our manager, said, "Mohan's design really impressed them." Mohan, who had added two slides.

My ears rang. I felt so hot I had to hold the table. I started typing a message to the whole team: "For the record, the design was MINE." I had my thumb over send.

My colleague Sujata, sitting next to me, whispered, "Not now, didi. Tomorrow." I put the phone face down.

That night I collected everything: my drafts with dates, the email chain, the version history. The next day I asked Anand for fifteen minutes alone. I showed him calmly.

He looked at it, then at me. "I got it wrong. I'm sorry." He emailed the client to correct it.

I still thought about leaving. I decided to stay. For now.

How many slides had Mohan added?
Mohan had added two slides.
How did Irawati feel when Anand credited Mohan?
Irawati felt burning anger, her ears ringing and so hot she had to hold the table.
What did Irawati do instead of sending the team message?
Irawati waited for the anger to pass, collected dated evidence, and asked Anand privately for an explanation, which led to a correction.
How did Anand respond when shown the evidence?
Anand admitted his mistake, apologised, and emailed the client to correct the credit.

Read this:

"Vinita, quick question. On the call with the partner team today I kept steady eye contact the whole time, like we were trained. Their lead kept looking down at her notes whenever I spoke."
"And you decided she was bored?"
"Bored, or annoyed. Then she wrote afterwards, 'Thank you for your intense attention.' Intense? Is that nice or not?"
Vinita laughed. "Could be both. When I worked with the Lisbon office, long eye contact felt normal. On another team, a senior told me my stare felt like a challenge."
"So it depends on the country?"
"Partly. Partly on the person. Her looking down might be respect, or thinking, or just her notes."
"So what do I do?"
"Watch how they look at each other. Soften a little, glance away sometimes. And ask her how meetings usually run on their side."
Vikas opened a new message. "Asking now."

What did the partner lead write after the call?
She wrote, 'Thank you for your intense attention.'
Why was Vikas unsure after reading the message?
Vikas felt confused and a bit anxious, because 'intense' could be praise or a hint that the steady eye contact had felt like a challenge.
What would you advise Vikas before the next call?
Watch how the partner team looks at each other, soften the gaze a little, and ask the lead how their meetings usually run instead of assuming.
How might the partner lead have experienced the steady eye contact?
The lead may have felt watched or pressed, or may simply have found it keen; her looking down could have been her own way of showing respect, so each side may have misread the other.
How many bricks are in the wall around our playground?
I can't tell, because counting the bricks needs someone standing at the wall. Count one row and one column, then multiply, or ask the caretaker if it is on record.

Read this:

Three months after we shut the café in Bandra, Aparna and I finally sat down with a notebook and the old accounts. In the first weeks after closing, I had swung between two stories: it was all my fault, or it was all the landlord's and the road works' fault. Neither was fair. So we drew three columns. What we controlled: we opened too big, we changed the menu five times, I hired friends I couldn't manage. What was luck: the road dug up for eight months, the rent going up. What to change next time: start smaller, test one menu for a season, hire for skills. Aparna tapped the page and said, "Zubin, look. It's not a verdict. It's a list." It was strangely calming. For the first time, the café felt less like a wound and more like information.

What were the three columns?
What we controlled, what was luck, and what to change next time.
How did the three-column review make Zubin feel?
Zubin felt strangely calm, as the café turned from a wound into information.
Why was the review better than the two stories Zubin had swung between?
It gave a fair look at causes, neither total self-blame nor total excuses, so the failure produced lessons to act on.
How does Aparna seem to see the failure?
Aparna sees it as a list to learn from, not a verdict on either of them.

For every 12 cans you recycle, you receive $0.50, and for every 5 kilograms of newspapers, you receive $1.50. If your family collected 144 cans and 20 kilograms of newspapers, how much money would you receive?

There are 144/12 = 12 sets of 12 cans that the family collected.
So, the family would receive $0.50 x 12 = $6 for the cans.
There are 20/5 = 4 sets of 5 kilograms of newspapers that the family collected.
So, the family would receive $1.50 x 4 = $6 for the newspapers.
Therefore, the family would receive a total of $6 + $6 = $12.
The answer is 12.
Some dogs are brown. All brown things in the room were washed. Were all the dogs washed?
No, we cannot say so. Because the statement covers only brown things in the room, any dog that is not brown, or is not in the room, is left out of it.
I keep forgetting to water the plants. They look sad.
Plants need a regular routine. Link watering to something you already do every day, like brushing your teeth, so it becomes a habit. Which plants do you have?
A few in pots on the balcony, and a tulsi near the door.
Balcony pots can dry out quickly in the sun. Check the soil with a finger each morning, and water when the top feels dry. The tulsi near the door likes regular water too.
Should I water the tulsi at night?
Morning is better, since the plant can use the water during the day and the soil does not stay damp overnight. Evening works as well in hot weather, but avoid wetting the leaves.
Okay. And where did I say the tulsi was kept?
You said the tulsi is near the door, away from the pots on the balcony. Water it in the morning, along with the balcony plants, so it stays healthy.

Read this:

The winter clay class at the community centre smelled of wet mud. Lakshmi pressed and pinched until her pot stood up, lopsided, with a thumbprint on the side. "Mine!" Aunty put a shiny shop pot beside it for the paints. "Which one do you want to paint?" "Mine!" "But this one is so neat." Lakshmi hugged her wobbly pot. "Mine is the best. I made it." Samir, beside her, pointed at the shop pot. "Can I have that one?" "Yes," said Lakshmi, not even looking.

What was on the side of Lakshmi's pot?
A thumbprint.
Why did Lakshmi hug her wobbly pot?
She felt proud and fond of it because she made it herself, so it felt more special than the neat one.
How could Aunty respond to Lakshmi's choice?
Aunty could let her paint her own pot and praise the effort she put into making it.
How does Samir see the shop pot?
Samir likes the neat shop pot and is happy to take it, since he has no special feeling for either.

metadata.subtype: Loves the lopsided thing they made [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tutor's note, Year 2 seminar group, Friday. Mrs Anita Kurian.
During today's presentations, Harshal, usually the strongest in the group, lost his place, dropped his notes and had to start over. Yamini, two seats from me, put her hand over her mouth. Her shoulders were shaking. She was laughing, silently, and trying to hide it.
Her friend Ramesh, beside her, did not join in. He didn't scold her either. After the session I passed them in the corridor and heard him ask quietly, "What is it about Harshal that gets to you?" Yamini was silent, then said, "He makes it look easy. I work twice as hard for half the marks."
I will not mention the laughter to Yamini. I'll offer her a meeting about her marks, and I'll make sure to thank Harshal for starting over.

What happened to Harshal during his presentation?
He lost his place, dropped his notes and had to start over.
What does Yamini's answer to Ramesh reveal about her laughter?
It suggests envy: Harshal seems to succeed easily while she works twice as hard for half the marks.
Which choice by Ramesh worked, and why?
He neither joined in nor scolded, and instead asked what bothered her, which let Yamini name the envy herself.
How might Harshal have felt if he had seen Yamini laughing?
He might have felt humiliated and hurt, since he was already struggling in front of the group.

metadata.subtype: Friend notices glee at another's downfall [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

At morning assembly in the girls' school in Satara, Tanuja was picked to anchor Annual Day. She floated home at lunch, singing, and hugged the buffalo. By four it had all turned. Avni, her best friend since Class 1, had sat with the new girl on the bus and laughed at something Tanuja couldn't hear. Tanuja came home, threw her bag at the wall, and lay in the sugarcane field behind the house, crying so hard her ribs hurt. Everything felt ruined: the friendship, the anchoring, her whole life. Her Aaji found her there and sat down in the dust beside her. She didn't say it was a small thing. "This morning you were flying. Now you're drowning. Both are real, bala. It will feel different tomorrow." Tanuja cried a little more, then leaned on Aaji's shoulder until the sky turned orange.

What was Tanuja picked to do?
To anchor Annual Day.
What was Tanuja feeling in the sugarcane field?
She felt heartbroken and hopeless, as if the friendship and her whole life were ruined, only hours after being overjoyed.
Why did Aaji's response help?
She took the feelings seriously instead of calling them small, named both as real, and reassured Tanuja they would shift.
How might Avni have seen the bus ride?
Avni may have just been chatting with the new girl, with no idea it felt like betrayal to Tanuja.

Read this:

"So, shall I fill the admission form? The early-bird discount ends at six today."
"Can I have the full fee structure in writing first, Pooja ma'am? With the refund rules?"
"It's all standard. Everyone signs today."
"Then it should be easy to print," Kashish said, smiling.
"The discount might go, you know."
"If the course is good, I think it'll still be good tomorrow. I'm also seeing the institute near the metro on Saturday."
"They don't have our results."
"Maybe. I'll compare both."
Pooja sighed and printed two pages. Kashish folded them into a file.
That evening, at the kitchen table, Kashish read every line. The refund rule said nothing was returned after seven days.
Kashish called the next morning. "Is the discount still there?"
"Yes, madam, till month end."

What did the refund rule say?
The refund rule said nothing was returned after seven days.
How was Kashish feeling when Pooja said the discount might go?
Kashish felt steady rather than panicked; the smile and the reply that a good course would still be good tomorrow show calm confidence.
Which of Kashish's steps protected her best?
Asking for the fee structure and refund rules in writing, reading every line at home, and comparing with the other institute before paying.
How might Pooja see a buyer who asks for printed terms?
Pooja may feel her early-bird push has stopped working, and her sigh suggests she wanted a quick signature, yet she still had to print the pages.

metadata.subtype: Sleep on it and read it [Response]

messages.content: The old fort is worth to visit if you have a free afternoon. Is "worth to visit" right?

The old fort is worth visiting if you have a free afternoon.
Why: verb form ("worth to visit" -> "worth visiting").

Read this:

On a cold morning in Cape Town, Thabo and Lucia sat outside the ice-cream stand. Thabo rubbed his hands together, fast, eyes on the seller. Lucia snapped her fingers in time to the radio. “Are you cold or excited?” she asked. “Both,” said Thabo. “Hot chocolate!” He snapped his fingers at the seller. “Hey!” The seller frowned. Lucia winced. “Try ‘Excuse me’,” she whispered. Thabo went red. “Excuse me, please, could I have two hot chocolates?” The seller smiled slightly. “Coming up.”

What did Lucia snap her fingers in time to?
She snapped her fingers in time to the radio.
Why was Thabo rubbing his hands together, and what else could it mean?
He said he was both cold and excited, and his eyes were on the seller, so it was likely a mix of cold and eagerness for hot chocolate. Rubbing hands can mean either alone.
What could Thabo try next time to get a seller's attention?
Say “Excuse me, please” and wait for eye contact, as he did on the second try, rather than snapping.
How might the seller have felt when Thabo snapped his fingers?
Probably annoyed or disrespected, since he frowned. The seller relaxed when Thabo asked politely.
Rangoli: Meena draws 3 triangles, 2 squares and 1 hexagon. How many corners are there altogether?

Answer: Triangles 3 + 3 + 3 = 9, squares 4 + 4 = 8, hexagon 6. 9 + 8 + 6 = 23 corners.

Count shape by shape and write each group's total. Or put a dot on every corner of the drawing and count all the dots.

Read this:

I'm Aparna, from the flat next door. Yesterday outside our building, Ganga's father was arguing with an auto driver over the fare. His voice was quiet, but his nostrils were flaring wide. Ganga, holding his hand, tugged it. “Papa, your nose is going big.” I didn't know if she was scared or just noticing. He stopped mid-sentence, looked down at her and said, “You're right. I'm angry. I'll breathe first.” He breathed, paid, and they walked in holding hands.

What were Ganga's father and the auto driver arguing about?
The fare.
What might Ganga have been feeling when she tugged her father's hand?
She may have been uneasy, sensing tension from his flaring nostrils even though his voice was quiet. Aparna can't be sure, and Ganga might just have been curious about his nose.
What helped the argument end calmly?
Her father listened to Ganga, named his anger and breathed before paying, showing her how to slow down.
How might the auto driver have seen the moment Ganga spoke?
He might have felt the tension drop and been relieved that the argument ended without shouting.

Read this:

'Eshaan, how was Ma today?'
'Good morning, bad afternoon. She thought I was Papa. Then she thought I was a thief.'
Vishal sat down heavily. 'I miss her. Isn't that crazy? She's in the next room.'
'It's not crazy. I feel it too. Like she's leaving a bit at a time.'
'And then I feel guilty for missing her while she's right here.'
'Same.' Eshaan rubbed his face. 'I'm so tired, Vishal.'
'I know. You're doing the days. I'm only doing nights.'
'She laughed today, though. At the parrot on the balcony. Really laughed.'
Vishal smiled. 'That's something.'
'The hospital has a support group for families. Thursday evenings.'
'Let's go. Both of us. Neighbour can sit with Ma.'

What did Ma laugh at today?
The parrot on the balcony.
What is Vishal feeling about their mother?
He misses her even though she is in the next room, and feels guilty for it.
What step do the brothers decide on?
Going together to the hospital's family support group on Thursday evenings.
How might the neighbour's help affect the brothers?
It gives them a short break to get support, so they feel less alone and exhausted.
Please do a photo of us near the fountain. Can you correct?

Please take a photo of us near the fountain.
Why: word choice ("do a photo" -> "take a photo").

Julie, Letitia and Anton decided to have dinner together at a nearby restaurant.  Julie orders $10 worth of food, Letitia orders $20 worth of food, and Anton orders $30 worth of food.  How much should each pay in tips if they want to split a 20% tip for the whole meal evenly?

First, we need to determine how much the entire meal costs before we can determine the tip. We perform 10+20+30=60 dollars worth of food.
Now we need to find out how much the total tip to be paid is, by multiplying 60*.2=12 dollars in tips.
Since they want to split this evenly amongst three people, this works out to 12/3= 4 dollars in tips per person.
The answer is 4.
Do I say "I am boring" or "I am bored"?

Say "I am bored". The -ed form describes how you feel. The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Examples: I am bored because it is raining. This long train journey is boring.

Read this:

"Karthik, I'm not doing engineering. I'm going to start a company straight after Class 12."
"Since when?"
"Since I read about all those founders who dropped out. Every big app, every big company, it's always a dropout."
"All of them?"
"Basically."
"Samir, my cousin dropped out of college to start a food delivery thing."
"And?"
"It closed in eight months. He's doing a diploma now, at twenty-three."
"Okay, but he just wasn't good enough."
"Maybe. His three co-founders also went back. Nobody writes articles about them."
"Hmm."
"You only read about the ones who made it. It's like looking at lottery winners and saying tickets are a great plan."
"So you're saying I shouldn't?"
"I'm saying count everyone who tried, not just the famous few."

What happened to Karthik's cousin's food delivery company?
It closed in eight months.
Why is Samir so sure dropping out leads to success?
Samir feels inspired and confident because every founder story Samir reads is a dropout who made it, so it looks like the usual path.
What does Karthik suggest Samir do before deciding?
Count everyone who tried, not only the famous few, including people like the cousin and his co-founders who went back to study.
How might Karthik's cousin see stories about famous dropouts?
He might find them painful or misleading, since his own attempt closed and no one wrote about it.

Read this:

Vasudha rolled her eyes when Yash left his socks by the sofa again. "Of course. Genius at work." Yash went quiet. She felt superior and tired at once. Later she noticed what lay beneath: she felt alone with the housework. She said, "I mocked you, and I am sorry. What I need is help with the laundry on Sundays."

Two days later the row was about his sister Aadhya staying for a month. Vasudha's heart raced, and she wanted to say the cruellest true thing about his family. Instead she said, "I need ten minutes," went to the balcony, breathed, and came back. "I feel crowded, and I would like to talk about how long she stays." Yash listened fully. They chose Saturday for a proper talk and agreed on three weeks and a chores chart.

By Sunday they had bickered about the chart, and Yash burst out laughing at the colour-coding. Vasudha giggled and slid his favourite chai across. "Truce?" she said. "Truce," he said, and washed the cups. Then, quietly: "I should have told you sooner about Aadhya." They kept no score.

How many weeks did they agree Aadhya would stay?
They agreed on three weeks.
How did Vasudha's eye-rolling about the socks differ from how she handled the row over Aadhya's stay?

Rolling her eyes felt superior but tired, and she later named her hurt and asked for help on Sundays. Over Aadhya she paused for ten minutes to cool down, spoke about her feeling and request, and they chose a time and agreed on a plan.
What was Vasudha feeling when she wanted to say the cruellest true thing about his family?
She was flooded with anger, her heart racing.
What helped them repair things after bickering about the chart?
Humour and a small kindness did it: Yash laughed at the colour-coding, Vasudha slid over his favourite chai, and they called a truce.
The monsoon started today and our terrace leaks in one corner.
Leaks are a nuisance, and it is good you noticed early. Put a bucket under the drip, and move anything that can get wet away from that corner. Is it a ceiling inside or the open terrace?
It is a ceiling in the top room. A damp patch is spreading.
A spreading patch means water is getting through the roof. Keep the bucket in place, wipe the drips, and ask a mason or the building's maintenance person to check the terrace soon.
Is there anything I can do myself till then?
You can move furniture and electronics away from the patch, and keep a cloth beside the bucket for splashes. Do not touch any wires or switches near the damp spot.
Ok, I'll move the cupboard. Should I tell my landlord Harsh today?
Yes, tell Harsh today and send a photo of the damp patch so he can see it clearly. The sooner a repair starts, the less damage the ceiling will get from the monsoon.
Which bus do I take to school?
I don't know your route, as I can't see where you live or study. Ask the school office or a classmate who lives nearby.
Tell me three facts about the Himalayas, numbered, each one sentence.

1. The Himalayas stretch across several countries, including India, Nepal and Bhutan.
2. Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth, is part of the range.
3. Rivers such as the Ganga and the Yamuna begin in Himalayan glaciers.

Read this:

Thabo's model plane had taken three weeks to build. Now the left wing lay in two pieces on the living-room floor. "You wrecked it!" Thabo yelled. His hands were shaking with rage. "You never listen, Kaito!"
His younger brother stood very still by the sofa, holding a wet sock in one hand. He had gone pale. He didn't argue, and he didn't leave.
Thabo stopped. Kaito never went quiet like that. "Were you trying to put it back on the shelf?" Thabo asked. Kaito nodded, tears sliding down. "I knocked it. I was scared you'd be angry, so I just stood here."
Thabo's anger flared up again when he saw the wing. He breathed out slowly. "Get the glue. It will still fly, sort of."

How long had Thabo's model plane taken to build?
It had taken three weeks to build.
What was Thabo feeling when he saw the wing and then looked at Kaito?
He was furious at first and the anger flared again at the sight of the wing. Seeing Kaito go pale and silent added worry and made him stop.
What could Thabo do next to keep the repair from turning into another fight?
He could work on the glue job together with Kaito and let his own anger cool first. Giving Kaito a job helps him feel forgiven.
What is it like for Kaito to be shouted at over an accident?
It is scary and lonely. He did not argue or run, which suggests he felt he deserved it, and he needed to hear he was not being blamed for meanness.

Read this:

Zeenat, you asked how I managed it. Okay. I'm Tanuja. Last year I got the job in Hyderabad, my first choice. Mummy and Papa wanted me to take the one in Nagpur so I'd be close, since Papa's heart check-ups are every few months. I didn't just book my ticket and go. I sat with them, showed them the work, explained why it mattered to me. Then I listened. Papa said he was scared of being alone at the hospital. So we made a plan: I fly home for every check-up, and my cousin stays with them the other times. At work I told my manager up front, and I make up the hours. I still chose Hyderabad. But I chose it with them, not against them.

What job did Tanuja take?
The job in Hyderabad, Tanuja's first choice.
What did Tanuja hope for by sitting with Mummy and Papa before booking the ticket?
Tanuja hoped they would understand the reasons and feel included, instead of feeling left behind by a sudden decision.
What was the key choice that let Tanuja keep independence and duty together?
Tanuja explained the reasons and then listened, and built a plan to fly home for check-ups and make up the hours at work, instead of simply defying the family.
How might Tanuja's parents feel about the move after the plan?
They are likely less afraid and more respected, since their worry was heard and they know Tanuja will be there for check-ups.
A magic pencil only corrects the kind mistakes. Write the story.

Rohit's eraser had worn down, but his pencil never made mistakes. That was because it was magic, and it fixed things before he knew.

When Rohit wrote a mean word about a classmate in his diary, the pencil turned it into "kind." When he wrote that he hated maths, it turned it into "I'm learning maths."

At first, he was annoyed. "I wanted to be angry," he muttered.

But over time, he noticed that his words made him feel better. He began to write nicer things on his own.

One day, he wrote a whole page, and the pencil changed nothing. It just lay quietly in his hand.

Rohit grinned. "Good job, pencil," he said, and sharpened it gently.
My uncle, who owns three shops, work late every day. Which verb needs changing?

My uncle, who owns three shops, works late every day.
Why: subject-verb agreement ("work" -> "works" for "uncle").

Read this:

Zubin, you call your mentor before choosing a shirt. Sit down. Your Nirmala aunty was worse.

At twenty-four I joined a publishing house, and Mrs. Anand took me under her wing. She was so wise that I stopped thinking. Which manuscript to read first? I asked her. Whether to take a day off? I asked her. Once I even asked which pen to buy.

One day she was away in Delhi, and a writer called wanting an answer on his contract by evening. I sat there frozen, sweating, terrified of choosing wrong.

When Mrs. Anand came back, I expected praise for waiting. Instead she said, very gently, "Nirmala, I don't want to be your brain. I want to be your sounding board."

That was the turning point. From then on I made small decisions myself and brought her only the big ones, with my own view first. "Here's what I think. What am I missing?" She smiled every time.

Where was Mrs. Anand when the writer called?
She was away in Delhi.
How did young Nirmala feel when she had to answer the writer alone?
She felt frozen and terrified, sweating with fear of choosing wrong.
What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
Mrs. Anand told her she wanted to be a sounding board, not her brain, so Nirmala began making small decisions herself and bringing her own view first.
How did Mrs. Anand seem to feel about Nirmala's dependence?
Mrs. Anand seemed gently concerned, wanting Nirmala to trust her own judgment rather than rely on her for everything.

Read this:

Sarika, you're complaining about your flat's kitchen? Let me tell you about the Room 12 kitchen in our boys' hostel at the engineering college, 1996. I'm Saurabh, and there were eight of us sharing one small stove. Everyone cooked instant noodles at midnight and left the pan. I did too. I thought: one pan, what's one pan? By the end of term, the pans had grown fungus. Somebody's milk had turned to cheese in a cupboard. Rats moved in. We stopped cooking and spent all our pocket money on the canteen. Every single one of us blamed the others. Nobody thought it was his own pan that had started it. Finally the warden locked the kitchen for a month. Only then did we sit together, eight fools, and agree who cleaned which day.

How many students shared the Room 12 kitchen?
There were eight of us sharing one small stove.
What was Saurabh thinking when leaving his pan?
Saurabh thought one pan didn't matter, feeling careless and sure his share was too small to count.
Why was sitting together to agree on cleaning days a turning point in the story?
It ended the blame game by making each person responsible for a set day, so the kitchen could be used again.
How might the warden have felt about locking the kitchen?
The warden was probably fed up and frustrated, seeing that the students would not fix the mess themselves.
When the cart arrived, the kids "made a beeline" for it. Where did they go?

To make a beeline for something means to go straight towards it, without stopping.
Example: The children made a beeline for the ice-cream cart.

Read this:

You asked what I noticed in my first year at the design studio. I'm Nazia, and it was this.
We had a designer, Rohan, who was a genius. Twice a year he'd make something that made clients gasp. In between, he'd miss deadlines, go silent, then show up with an apology and a sketch.
And there was Gopika. Her work was good, not dazzling. But every Tuesday, her drafts were in the folder. If she said Thursday, it was Thursday. If something was going to slip, she told you on Monday.
I watched who the senior partners called when a client was nervous. It was always Gopika. When they built the new team, she led it. Rohan was, I think, hurt. He said, "My work is better."
Maybe it was. But I had started to feel calm just seeing Gopika's name on a project. You can plan around steady. You can't plan around brilliant.

On which day were Gopika's drafts always in the folder?
Every Tuesday.
How did Nazia feel seeing Gopika's name on a project?
Nazia felt calm, trusting that the work would arrive when promised.
What lesson does Nazia draw about reliability?
Steady delivery lets others plan and builds trust, which is why the partners called Gopika and made her lead the new team.
How did Rohan feel when Gopika led the new team?
Rohan seemed hurt, insisting his work was better.

metadata.subtype: Colleague who is reliable rather than brilliant [Observer]

messages.content:

The wedding hall was so loud that Jahnavi had to lean close to hear Rafiq, Jahnavi's partner. "Who was that message from?" Rafiq asked, eyes on the phone in Jahnavi's hand. It was the third time since the ceremony began. Jahnavi felt the familiar itch of being watched, and a flash of resentment. Once already today, Jahnavi had shown the screen, an aunt asking about lunch. Jahnavi breathed. "It's my colleague about a shift swap. I'm telling you honestly, and I've told you honestly before." Then, quietly under the drums: "I can't be asked every hour. If it carries on, I'd want us to talk to a counsellor together." Rafiq blinked, surprised. "Okay," Rafiq said, and looked away at the dancers.

Where were Jahnavi and Rafiq when Rafiq asked about the message?
In a wedding hall.
What was Jahnavi feeling when Rafiq kept asking?
Jahnavi felt watched and a flash of resentment, an itch that had become familiar.
What did Jahnavi do that was fair, and what limit did Jahnavi set?
Jahnavi gave honest reassurance, then set a limit against being asked every hour and mentioned counselling if it continued.
How might Rafiq have been feeling when asking about the phone?
Rafiq was probably anxious or insecure, since Rafiq kept looking at the phone without any sign of proof. Being surprised at the counsellor idea suggests Rafiq had not noticed how it landed.

To get the printer to work, Jerry needs to add a black-and-white cartridge and three color cartridges. If each color cartridge costs $32 and each black-and-white cartridge costs $27, how much does he pay total?

First find the total cost of the color cartridges: $32/cartridge * 3 cartridges = $96
Then add the cost of the black-and-white cartridge to find the total cost: $96 + $27 = $123
The answer is 123.

Note from Ayesha, Tushar's mother. On Sunday we nearly missed the last train home. Traffic near the flyover crawled, and we ran onto the platform as the guard raised the flag. Nobody spoke on the ride. On Monday evening Tushar brought me the trip sheet and pointed at a new line he had added at the bottom: LEAVE ONE HOUR EARLIER. "Then traffic can be slow and we are still fine," he said. I asked what else could run late. He added a second line: AUTOS. We are keeping the sheet on the fridge. - Ayesha

What line did Tushar add at the bottom of the trip sheet?
He added LEAVE ONE HOUR EARLIER.
What does Tushar's new line suggest about how he felt after the near miss?
He was rattled and wanted to be sure it would not happen again, so he felt determined.
What else could the family add to the plan, and why?
They could check the traffic before leaving or choose an earlier train, so one slow road does not decide the evening.
How might Ayesha see the line Tushar added?
Ayesha probably finds it sensible and is proud, since she keeps the sheet on the fridge.

The power went out halfway through the Saturday art class at the community hall, and the fans stopped. Suraj, ten, had been laughing with Jagdish sir all morning, showing off his painted kite. In the sudden dark and heat, a boy knocked a water jar over the kite. Suraj exploded, flinging his brushes and shouting. Two parents at the door muttered, "Send him home. Punish him." Jagdish sir didn't. He opened the windows for light and crouched, keeping a little distance. "That kite mattered. I'm not angry. I'm staying right here." Suraj went silent and stiff, staring at the floor. Jagdish sir stayed. After a while Suraj muttered, "Can I start again?" Sir handed him fresh paper.

What ruined Suraj's kite painting?
A boy knocked a water jar over the kite.
What might Suraj be feeling when he goes silent and stiff?
He may feel scared and ashamed after exploding, unsure whether he is about to be punished or pushed away.
Which choice of Jagdish sir's helped more than punishment would have, and why?
He stayed calm, said the kite mattered and that he was staying, which gave Suraj a safe way back.
Why might the parents react differently from Jagdish sir?
They saw only the outburst and wanted a punishment, while Jagdish sir seemed to see the fear under it.

Manoj: bro u coming online tonight?
Dhruv: can't. new rule. no screens on weekdays till boards
Manoj: whattt. u fought?
Dhruv: nope. i said "ok" 🙂
Manoj: that's it??
Dhruv: that's it. but i'm doing everything they say. just v e r y slowly
Dhruv: took 45 mins to clear the table. mom asked how school was. "fine." how's physics. "fine." what do u want for dinner. "anything"

Dhruv: dad said why are u sulking and i said i'm not sulking, i'm doing what u said 😐

Manoj: then tell them that?
Dhruv: they'll just say boards boards boards
Manoj: maybe. or maybe they'd do weekends + 1 hr on fridays. mine did
Dhruv: hmm
Dhruv: still folding the laundry at snail speed tonight

How long did Dhruv take to clear the table?
45 mins.
What is Dhruv really feeling behind the "ok"?
Dhruv is angry and thinks the rule is unfair, but disguises it as obedience by moving slowly and answering "fine".
What choice does Manoj suggest that could change things?
Telling the parents directly that the rule feels unfair and proposing weekends plus an hour on Fridays, instead of sulking through the chores.
How might Dhruv's parents experience the "fine" and "anything" answers?
They probably feel shut out and frustrated, sensing anger they can't address because Dhruv insists nothing is wrong.
Is misunderstand the same as understand wrongly? Also, how is it used?

Yes. To misunderstand is to get the meaning wrong. It is a verb. People misunderstand when a message is not clear.
Example: I misunderstood the time and arrived an hour early.

Shankar was in Dubai, Indu in Kochi, and the family chat about his mother's care had been getting worse all evening. Indu wrote that she was doing every hospital visit alone. Shankar wrote that he sent what he could and couldn't fly home every week. Then Indu typed, "You always have an excuse," and saw him start typing, stop, start again.
She put the phone down. Whatever he sent next would be read wrong; whatever she sent would be worse.
She called instead. The video froze on his face twice, so she switched to voice only, the line crackling.
"Shankar, I don't want to fight in writing. I'm tired, that's all."
A pause, then his voice, softer than any message. "I know. I feel useless here. I hate it."
They didn't solve everything. But they agreed he would call Amma every evening at seven, and Indu would take Sundays off.

Where were Shankar and Indu during the argument?
Shankar was in Dubai and Indu was in Kochi.
Why did Indu decide to stop texting?
Indu felt exhausted and worried that anything written next would be read wrong, and that the argument was only growing worse.
What could others learn from Indu's choice?
When a sensitive family topic turns sharp over text, switch to a call, even a crackly one, so tone and warmth can come through.
How was Shankar feeling far away in Dubai?
Shankar felt helpless and guilty, saying he felt useless being so far from his mother's care.
What's discipline mean?

Discipline is training that teaches people to follow rules and control themselves. It can also mean a subject of study. It is a noun.
Example: Learning an instrument takes discipline and daily practice.

Note by Bhupen, class teacher, Class 5.
Binita used to ask a question in every lesson. A month ago another teacher told her in front of the class, "Don't ask silly questions." Since then she has not raised her hand once, though she still studies the wall charts and scribbles on the last page of her notebook.
I have put a question box on my desk. Yesterday I found a folded slip: "Why do stars look small but are big?" I answered it aloud without naming anyone. This morning Binita lifted her hand for the first time in weeks. I will keep the box open, and I will keep answering.
— Bhupen

Where did Bhupen put the question box?
Bhupen put the question box on the desk.
What did Binita probably feel when told not to ask silly questions in front of the class?
Binita likely felt embarrassed and discouraged, and stopped raising her hand, while the curiosity carried on privately.
What did Bhupen do that made it safe for Binita to ask again?
Bhupen offered a question box, answered a slip aloud without naming anyone, and kept it open. That let Binita ask without being exposed.
How does Bhupen read Binita's silence?
Bhupen sees it as curiosity dampened, not gone, since Binita still studies the charts and writes in the notebook.

Okay, so, first question: who's the funny one? That's me, Naveen, the family joke. At dinner Dada says, “Naveen, say something silly,” and I do, because if I'm laughing, nobody's asking about my marks. My sister Ishita is the trusted one. If a vase breaks, they ask me first. Ishita never says anything. She just stares at her plate. Last week I got my best maths score, and Papa said, “Did you copy?” Everyone laughed, including me. I laughed loudest. The thing is, if I stop being funny, I don't know where I'd sit at that table.

What did Papa ask when Naveen got the best maths score?
Papa asked, “Did you copy?”
Why does Naveen laugh loudest when the others laugh at the question?
Naveen seems to use the joke role to cover hurt about not being trusted, and fears losing a place at the table if the joking stops.
What could Naveen try at dinner to be seen as more than the funny one?
Naveen could share something serious, like how the maths score was earned, or ask one family member to take it seriously.
What might Ishita be thinking as she stares at her plate?
Ishita may feel uncomfortable about the doubt aimed at Naveen and stuck in her own role, since she says nothing and looks down.

messages.content: Wally buys bears at the park. A bear is priced at $4.00 for the first bear and a discount of 50 cents per bear is given after that. How much does Wally pay for 101 bears?

If the price of an additional bear drops by fifty after the first purchase, the price of each additional bear is $4.00 - $0.50 = $3.50
Since Wally bought 101 bears, he was charged fifty cents less on 101-1 = 100 bears.
The total cost for the 100 bears is 100*$3.50 = $350
For the 101 bears, Wally paid a total of $350+$4 = $354
The answer is 354.
I haven't heard from my old school friend in a year and I want to message her, but it feels awkward.
It's common to feel that way after a long gap, but most people are happy to hear from an old friend.
What should I write?
Keep it light and warm, like, 'Hi Sana, I was thinking of you today and wondered how you are. It would be lovely to catch up.' No need to explain the silence at length.
That's nice. What if she doesn't reply?
People get busy, so give it a week or two without worrying. A reply may come later, and either way you did something kind.

With two weeks before the final exam, Aditi asked her close friend Siddharth to be her check-in partner. "Every night, ask whether I did my hours," she said. Night one, she had done two hours of four. "It's fine," said Siddharth. "You've been working hard. Take a break." Night two, one hour. "Honestly, me too. Let's watch one episode." By night six the check-ins were texts like "ugh, same" and "tomorrow?" Nobody pushed. The pile of unfinished chapters stayed exactly the same size. On night twelve Aditi looked at the calendar and saw two days left. She felt sick. She had told herself that the partner was helping, and all they had really shared was excuses.

How many hours of the four had Aditi done on the first night?
Aditi had done two hours of four on night one.
How did Aditi feel on night twelve?
Aditi felt sick with worry and regret at how little had changed.
What could Aditi look for in a partner instead?
Aditi could look for a partner who asks honestly about the plan and gently says when a target was missed, or add a written goal.
How might Siddharth have meant "Take a break"?
Siddharth probably meant it kindly, wanting Aditi to rest, without seeing that it hurt her plan.

Every evening at seven, Gautam looked at tomorrow's timetable. He took out yesterday's books, slid in the right notebooks, then the lunch box and the water bottle. His mornings stayed quiet.

Meena had drawn her own weekly chart: maths in blue, Hindi in orange, science in green, and so on. She pinned it above her study table, and at a glance she could see which books belonged to which day.

Santosh never bothered. All his books lived in the bag, just in case. By the third week his shoulders ached, and the bag was so crammed that he still could not find the science notebook when the teacher asked.

On Wednesday Meena arrived without her PT shoes. The teacher gave her a look, and she sat out the game. That evening she wrote on a sticky note, "Wednesday PT shoes," and stuck it on the chart. Every Sunday she also checked the school diary for any timetable changes.

At what time did Gautam look at tomorrow's timetable?
He looked at it at seven every evening.
How did Santosh's way of packing differ from Gautam's, and what were the results?
Santosh kept every book in the bag, so his shoulders ached and he still could not find the science notebook, while Gautam packed what tomorrow's timetable needed and his mornings stayed quiet.
What was Meena feeling when she arrived without her PT shoes?
Embarrassed and sorry, since the teacher's look made her sit out the game.
What could Santosh do to fix his bag problem?
Santosh could read the timetable each evening and pack only the books needed, perhaps with a colour chart like Meena's.

Lunch note, Butterfly Room. Aparna.
Noor pushed away the beans again today, the fifth day in a row. She pinched one, said "squishy", and stuck out her tongue. Last month I tried coaxing, "One bite and you get a sticker", and she cried and ate nothing. So now I just put a few beans on her plate, say nothing, and eat mine next to her. Today she licked one. Tomorrow I'll do the same.

What word did Noor use for the bean?
Noor said "squishy".
Why might Noor have stuck out her tongue at the bean?
Noor seemed to dislike the squishy texture and felt put off by it.
What went wrong last month, and what works better now?
Bribing with a sticker made Noor cry and eat nothing; calmly offering a few beans with no fuss led to a first lick.
How might Aparna feel seeing Noor lick a bean?
Aparna would likely feel quietly encouraged, seeing that patience is working.
Dina has twice as many dolls as Ivy. 2/3 of Ivy's dolls are collectors editions. If Ivy has 20 collectors edition dolls, how many dolls does Dina have?

Ivy has 20/2*3=30 dolls.
Dina has 30*2=60 dolls.
The answer is 60.

In the clinic waiting room, Amma and Nani spoke in short, low sentences, and neither looked at the other. Lakshmi stopped swinging her legs. She had wanted the biscuits from Amma's bag, but she did not ask. When her little cousin Chinmay started to whine, Lakshmi put a finger on her lips and shook her head at him. She sat very straight and held the end of Nani's dupatta in her fist. The nurse smiled. 'What a good, quiet girl.' Lakshmi did not smile back.

What did Lakshmi hold in her fist?
The end of Nani's dupatta.
Why might Lakshmi have stopped asking for biscuits?
She seems uneasy and worried, sensing the tension between Amma and Nani, so she tries to be extra good and not add trouble.
How could Amma or Nani help Lakshmi in that moment?
One of them could notice how quiet she is, hug her and say simply, 'We are a bit cross with each other, not with you.'
What might the nurse miss when calling Lakshmi a good, quiet girl?
The nurse sees only good behaviour and may miss that the quietness comes from tension Lakshmi senses between the adults.

Monday. In the car, Nitin pressed his face to the window. "Why is the moon following us?" Yogesh Chacha laughed. "Good question! It's so far away that it looks like it moves with us."
Wednesday. "Why is Dadi's skin wrinkly?" "Because she has lived a long time, and skin folds as people get older. You could ask her how old she is."
Saturday. "Why is the sky blue?" Chacha scratched his head. "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out tonight?" That night Nitin fell asleep holding the picture book about sunlight.

What did Nitin ask on Wednesday?
He asked why Dadi's skin is wrinkly.
How was Nitin feeling as he asked all these questions?
He was curious and eager 🤔 pressing his face to the window and asking something new each day.
Why was "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out?" a good answer?
It showed Nitin his question was worth answering and turned not knowing into finding out together.
How might Dadi feel if Nitin asks her how old she is?
She might feel amused and touched that he is curious about her life.

Mother made 2 dozen brownies and placed them on the kitchen counter to cool.  Father smelled the brownies, came into the kitchen and ate 8 of them. Then, their daughter, Mooney, wandered into the kitchen and ate 4 of the brownies. The next morning, Mother made another two dozen brownies and added them to those remaining from the day before.  After that, how many brownies were on the counter?

Two dozen brownies is 2 * 12 = 24 brownies.
After Father ate his 8, there were 24 - 8 = 16 brownies remaining on the counter.
After Mooney ate her 4, there were 16 - 4 = 12 brownies remaining on the counter.
Mother made a second batch of two-dozen brownies, or 2 * 12 = 24 brownies.
After Mother added the second two-dozen, there were 12 + 24 = 36 brownies on the kitchen counter.
The answer is 36.

Looking back, I think I spent most of Class 11 saying yes. Yes to the science stream because everyone said I was good at maths. Yes to the group's plans, the group's jokes, the group's opinion of whoever was not there. If anyone frowned, I apologised, even when I had done nothing. It kept things smooth, and I was proud of being the easy one. Then, at a college fair, a volunteer asked what I actually enjoyed. My mind went empty. My friend Vinita, standing beside me, said quietly, 'You always ask what we think, Nitin. I don't think I've ever heard what you think.' That stung, because it was true. These days I practise small things: choosing where we eat, saying I didn't like a film. My voice shakes sometimes. But I'm slowly finding out who I am.

What stream did Nitin say yes to?
The science stream.
What did Nitin feel when Vinita spoke at the college fair?
Nitin felt stung and exposed, because it was true that nobody had heard Nitin's own opinion.
What small steps is Nitin taking now?
Nitin practises choosing where they eat and saying when a film was not good, even with a shaky voice.
How might Vinita have experienced Nitin as a friend during Class 11?
Vinita may have found Nitin easy to be with but hard to really know, since Nitin kept every opinion hidden.

The church feast in the Kerala village filled the lane with drums and balloon sellers. Jomon toddled towards a balloon stall, stopped, and looked back at his Amma, Deepika.
She waved. He trotted back, touched her knee, and set off again.
Then a crowd swallowed him and he went round the back of a stall without looking back once.
Deepika was after him in three steps. She caught his hand. “Stay where you can see me.”

What was filling the lane at the church feast?
Drums and balloon sellers filled the lane.
What does Jomon touching Deepika's knee and setting off again suggest he felt?
It suggests he felt safe and reassured by her, then brave enough to explore again.
Why was Deepika right to follow Jomon quickly?

metadata.subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

Ganga: Kamal are you there? I think I'm going to fail tomorrow
Kamal: I'm here. What's happening?
Ganga: The presentation. My hands are shaking and I can't even open the slides
Kamal: ok. I'm not going anywhere. Put me on speaker and tell me slide one
Ganga: ...fine. It's the title. That's all I know
Kamal: Good, that's one slide. What's slide two?
Ganga: Data. I do know the data
Kamal: See? You know more than the panic says. Drink some water, I'll stay on
Ganga: ok. My heart's slowing a bit. Thanks for not panicking with me 🙂
Kamal: Anytime. Sleep after slide five 😴

What is slide one of Ganga's presentation?
The title.
What is Ganga feeling at the start of the chat?
Ganga is panicked and afraid of failing, with shaking hands and unable to open the slides.
What small step helped Ganga calm down?
Kamal stayed on the line, asked for one slide at a time and suggested drinking water, so Ganga could see how much was known.
How does Kamal seem to see Ganga's panic?
Kamal treats it as something that says less than Ganga knows, stays calm and lets Ganga's own knowledge answer the fear.
Packet of notebooks at the bookshop this week, what's the price?
I don't know this week's price. The bookshop can tell you, or you can compare it with another shop.

The monsoon had flooded the lanes around Wasim's hostel in Guwahati, and the power kept failing. His internship report was due in ten days, and the stress sat in his chest like a stone. He didn't feel like eating. He didn't feel like moving. He wanted to lie in bed with his phone until it was over.
His senior Jagdish, who had the room across the corridor, pinned a paper on Wasim's door. It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.
"You don't have to feel like it," Jagdish said. "You just do it."
So on rainy mornings they walked the covered corridor, twenty laps. At dinner, even when the mess food was cold, Wasim ate the full plate.
By the end of the week he was still stressed, but steadier. When he admitted one night that the stone never lifted, Jagdish said, "If it stays like that, we see the college counsellor together."

What did Jagdish's paper on the door say?
It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.
How did Wasim feel before the routine started?
He felt heavily stressed, with a stone in his chest, and didn't feel like eating or moving.
Why does the plan work even when Wasim has no motivation?
It doesn't rely on feeling like it; steady sleep, meals and walking support his body, and if the heaviness lasts, seeing the counsellor is the next step.
How might Jagdish feel watching Wasim do the laps?
Jagdish probably feels relieved and caring, glad his simple rules are giving Wasim something steady to hold on to.
My cousin in England is in "Year 7", but my American friend of the same age is in "seventh grade". Are they the same?

They are similar but not exact. In England, Year 7 is the first year of secondary school at age 11 to 12. In American schools, seventh grade is for children around 12 to 13. School systems differ, so check with each school.
Example: My cousin started Year 7 last September.

It was past bedtime, and Farhan, two, sat cross-legged on the bed rocking back and forth, one hand on his blanket, eyes half closed. He had cried when the lights went off, and now his rocking slowed to a gentle sway. Ganga sat in the chair by the door and watched. She did not stop him. She hummed the tune he liked and kept her voice low. After a little while the swaying stopped, his head tipped sideways onto the pillow and his breath deepened.

What was Farhan doing on the bed?
Rocking back and forth cross-legged with one hand on his blanket.
What do you think Farhan's rocking helped him feel?
It seemed to help him settle after the upset of the lights going off, as his rocking slowed into sleep. It could also just be a habit that comforts him.
What could Ganga do if the rocking ever seemed to worry her?
She could mention it to the doctor, especially if it goes on a lot or Farhan seems cut off from her.
How might Farhan feel with Ganga nearby?
He may feel safe because someone he loves is close and humming.

Dear Kiran Atte,
Namaskara. Thank you for thinking of me and for the proposal details you sent Amma. I know you did it out of love, and I've always looked up to how you hold the whole family together.
I see it differently, though, and I wanted you to hear that from me, not from gossip. I'd like to finish my MSc and work for two years before I think about marriage. It's not that I don't value your advice. I value it enough to explain instead of simply saying no.
When I come home for Ugadi, can we sit together, just us two, and talk? I'll bring the jasmine you like.
With respect and love,
Manjula

When will Manjula come home?
For Ugadi.
What does Manjula feel towards Kiran Atte while writing?
Manjula feels real admiration and affection for Atte, together with a calm firmness about finishing the MSc and working first.
How does Manjula manage to disagree without rebelling?
By thanking Atte, keeping a respectful tone and title, saying 'I see it differently', giving reasons and asking for a private talk.
How might Kiran Atte feel reading this letter?
Atte may be disappointed about the proposal but touched to be addressed so warmly and directly, which makes the message easier to hear.

Make a two-sentence summary out of this paragraph.

While I still hung over her in the agony of despair, I happened to look up. The windows of the room had before been darkened, and I felt a kind of panic on seeing the pale yellow light of the moon illuminate the chamber. The shutters had been thrown back, and with a sensation of horror not to be described, I saw at the open window a figure the most hideous and abhorred. A grin was on the face of the monster; he seemed to jeer, as with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife. I rushed towards the window, and drawing a pistol from my bosom, fired; but he eluded me, leaped from his station, and running with the swiftness of lightning, plunged into the lake.

While grieving over the body of the narrator's wife, the narrator sees a hideous monster grinning at the open window. The monster points at the body, the narrator fires a pistol, and it leaps away and runs into the lake.

The teacher's request was simple: bring a model of something that stands or spins by Friday, made from what you have at home.

Ravi emptied the odd-things box onto the floor: scraps of cardboard, a few bottle caps, sticks from old ice creams, a coil of wire. He turned the pieces over in his hands until the caps looked like wheels, and a cart began to take shape.

Shreya had one sheet of thick cardboard, so she drew a windmill on paper first, with the length of each blade written beside it. Only when every piece was measured did she pick up the scissors.

Teja pressed play on a video for a lighthouse with a motor, a battery and coloured plastic tubing. He had none of them. He fumed and pushed the video away, then looked round the room and made the light from a bottle cap and wire. Slowly the model began to work.

Kavitha built a tower of cardboard tubes. It leaned and toppled. Kavitha stared at the heap and said, "The bottom is too narrow." A square frame cut from leftover card went underneath, the tubes were set inside it, and the tower stood.

What did Ravi find in the odd-things box?
Scraps of cardboard, a few bottle caps, sticks from old ice creams and a coil of wire.
What did Teja's approach lack that Shreya's and Kavitha's had?
Teja copied a video that needed parts he lacked, while Shreya planned around what she had and Kavitha redesigned after the fall; Teja's model worked only once he adapted the parts.
What was Teja feeling when he pushed the video away?

A clothing store sells 20 shirts and 10 pairs of jeans. A shirt costs $10 each and a pair of jeans costs twice as much. How much will the clothing store earn if all shirts and jeans are sold?

Twenty shirts amount to $10 x 20 = $200.
The cost of each pair of jeans is $10 x 2 = $20.
So 10 pairs of jeans amount to $20 x 10 = $200.
Therefore, the store will earn $200 + $200 = $400 if all shirts and jeans are sold.
The answer is 400.

messages.content: Mary is chopping up some old furniture to make firewood. Chairs make 6 sticks of wood, tables make 9 sticks of wood, and stools make 2 sticks of wood. Mary needs to burn 5 sticks of wood per hour to stay warm. If Mary chops up 18 chairs, 6 tables and 4 stools, how many hours can she keep warm?

First find the total sticks from the chairs: 6 sticks/chair * 18 chairs = 108 sticks
Then find the total sticks from the tables: 9 sticks/table * 6 tables = 54 sticks
Then find the total sticks from the stools: 2 sticks/table * 4 stools = 8 sticks
Then add up the total number of sticks she gets: 108 sticks + 54 sticks + 8 sticks = 170 sticks
Then divide the total number of sticks by the number of sticks she burns per hour to find the total number of hours she can keep warm: 170 sticks / 5 sticks/hour = 34 hours
The answer is 34.

2. Water carries sound faster than air. Because water particles are packed closer together, so the vibrations pass on faster.
3. Communication is a noun that means the sharing of information or ideas.

In Sunaina's flat in Chennai, the two friends were doing maths homework at the dining table. Keerthana stopped writing, scratched her head and rubbed her forehead with the heel of her hand, again and again. Sunaina almost said, “It's easy, you just divide,” but stopped herself. She remembered how annoying it felt when her brother did that to her. Instead she asked, “Are you stuck, or just tired?” Keerthana yawned hugely. “Tired. Swimming at five-thirty this morning. Keerthana went swimming at five-thirty that morning.

Sudha used to love her job at the Mumbai ad agency. Now she rolled her eyes at every new brief and muttered "same nonsense" under her breath. On Sunday evenings her stomach knotted, and she snapped at her flatmate for no reason.

On Monday morning, her team lead Ayesha piled on a new pitch due Wednesday. "You're our best," Ayesha said, already walking away.

Sudha wanted to shout. Instead she followed her to the pantry. "Can we talk for five minutes? I've worked three weekends in a row. I'm exhausted and honestly, I'm becoming bitter. I don't like who I am at work right now."

Ayesha stopped stirring her coffee. "I didn't realise it was that bad."

"I'd like to take the leave I have, the week after this pitch. And I need someone else on the retail account."

Ayesha nodded slowly. "Okay. Let's look at it together after lunch."

How many weekends in a row had Sudha worked?
Three weekends in a row.
What was Sudha feeling when Ayesha added the new pitch?
She felt resentful and exhausted, wanting to shout after weeks of overwork.
What did Sudha do that was mature, and why?
She spoke to Ayesha about her load, asked for leave and help with the retail account, rather than silently suffering.
How does Ayesha see Sudha's workload after the talk?
Ayesha is surprised, not having realised how bad it was, and agrees to look at it together.

Chetan's phone was snatched outside the metro station in Hyderabad. He stood there, stunned, then walked home without doing anything.
"Aren't you going to file a complaint?" his roommate Darshan asked.
"What's the point? They'll make me wait for hours, ask why I was careless, and nothing will happen."
Darshan sat down beside him. "Maybe. But you need the report to block the SIM and for insurance. Let's write everything down first: time, place, what he looked like, the phone's number and IMEI."
They made a list. Then Darshan went with him to the police station. The first constable said to come back tomorrow. Darshan politely asked to speak to the duty officer, who took the complaint and gave them a copy.
Walking back, Chetan said, "I really thought they'd blame me." Darshan shrugged. "Some might. That's why you take someone along."

Where was Chetan's phone snatched?
Outside the metro station in Hyderabad.
Why did Chetan not want to file a complaint?
Chetan felt fearful and hopeless, expecting long waits, blame for being careless and no result.
What steps helped Chetan file the complaint?
Writing down all the details, going with Darshan, and politely asking for the duty officer when the constable refused.
How might Darshan see Chetan's reluctance?
Darshan understands the fear but sees that the report is needed, so he stays calm and practical, offering to go along.

The storm hit their Mumbai flat at six in the evening. Thunder shook the windows and the lights flickered. Noor's little brother Varun ran to the window to watch the lightning. Noor's heart thumped, but she made herself remember the safety talk from school. "Away from windows," she said, pulling Varun back to the sofa in the middle of the room. "Unplug the TV." She switched it off at the wall first, then pulled the plug with dry hands. Water was dripping near the balcony switchboard. "Don't touch that. Wet switches are dangerous." Outside, a cable swung loose from the pole. "And if we go out, we keep away from wires." When their mother came home soaked at eight, the two of them were in the middle of the room, playing cards by torchlight.

Where did Noor pull Varun to?
To the sofa in the middle of the room.
How did Noor feel when the storm hit?
Scared, with her heart thumping, but she steadied herself by remembering the rules.
What else could Noor do if something sparked or the water spread?
Keep Varun well away and call their mother or a neighbour straight away.
How might their mother feel coming home?
Relieved to find both children safe in the middle of the room.

Last year I was the strictest father in our building, and I was proud of it. I'm Darshan. My son Jeevan, fourteen, had a list of rules: phone off at nine, no going out after dark, no gaming at friends' houses. The more rules I added, the quieter he got. Then I found out he'd been going to a friend's place on Saturdays and telling me it was the library. That hurt more than I can say. I wanted to add a new rule. Instead, one night I sat on his bed and said, "Tell me which rule feels the most unfair, and I'll tell you why I made it." He was stunned. We talked for an hour. We kept the phone rule but moved it to ten. Saturdays at friends' are allowed now, if he messages me when he arrives. He hasn't lied since.

Where did Jeevan say he was going on Saturdays?
He said he was going to the library.
What did Darshan feel on finding out about the Saturdays, and what did he choose to do?
Darshan felt deeply hurt and tempted to add another rule, but chose to sit with Jeevan and talk about which rule felt unfair and why each existed.
Which changes kept Jeevan safe while giving him some say?
Keeping the phone rule but moving it to ten, and allowing Saturdays at friends' if he messages on arrival: limits with reasons and choices.
How might Jeevan have felt when his father asked which rule felt most unfair?
Jeevan was probably stunned and then relieved to be asked, which opened an hour of real talk.
If a basket is capable of holding 40 fruit altogether, and there are 3 times as many apples as oranges, how many oranges are there?

Since the ratio of apples to oranges is 3:1, that means for every 3 apples there is 1 orange. The size of this group is therefore 3+1=4.
We then divide this group size into the total amount of fruit the basket is holding at this time, which is 40. This means there are 40/4=10 of these groups in total.
Since there are 10 of these groups in total, that means there are 10*1=10 oranges in the basket.
The answer is 10.

Journal, 14 November

Third role-play in counselling practicum today. Nikita played a client whose brother had died. It was only role-play, and still I felt it in my throat. By the evening real session with the college drop-in client, I felt nothing at all. Just blank.
Then I shouted at my flatmate for leaving the gas on low. Who am I?
When I started this course I cried at everyone's stories. Now I nod and look at the clock. Does that mean I've stopped caring? Did I ever care?
I, Naveen, am writing this down so I can show Dr Rao on Thursday. Nikita said at lunch, "You look like you've been holding everyone's bags all day." Maybe that's it. Maybe I'm tired, not heartless.

Showing the journal to Dr Rao on Thursday, as planned, and getting support and rest instead of judging this numbness as a lack of heart.

On sports day at the village school near Hosur, the dust rose in yellow clouds. Tanvir, eleven, had come fourth in the 100 metres. His legs still stung.
Then came the 400 metres. His friend Jeevan, the smallest boy in the class, started slow and then flew past everyone on the last bend.
Tanvir leapt up. "JEEVAN! JEEVAN!" He clapped hard.
When Jeevan came to the steps, gasping, holding the tin medal, Tanvir thumped his back. "You were like a rocket!"
Later, sitting under the tamarind tree, Tanvir looked at the medal in Jeevan's hand. He felt a little tug inside. He wanted one too.
But the tug was small, and the happy feeling was big. "Next year we both get one," he said.

Where did Tanvir and Jeevan sit later?
Under the tamarind tree.
What was Tanvir feeling when he looked at the medal under the tree?
He felt a small tug of wanting a medal too, alongside a much bigger happiness for Jeevan.

He could practise with Jeevan for next year, turning the wish into a shared goal, as his words suggest.

In the electronics lab, during viva practice, Irfan was explaining the circuit slowly, getting stuck on a word as he sometimes did. Abhinav jumped in, grinning. "Resistor. Let me save us time, bro." Adam bought 15 apples on Monday. On Tuesday he bought 3 times that quantity. On Wednesday he bought 4 times the quantity he bought on Tuesday. What is the total quantity Adam bought on these three days?

On Tuesday, Adam bought 3 * 15 apples = 45 apples.
On Wednesday, Adam bought 4 * 45 apples = 180 apples.
Adam bought 15 apples + 45 apples + 180 apples = 240 apples on the three days.
The answer is 240.

How do I spell guarantee? The u confuses me.

It is spelled "guarantee". The u is silent, like in "guard" and "guess", and the word ends in double e.

There are 10 children for the three-legged race. They race in pairs. How many pairs are there?

Answer: 5 pairs. 10 / 2 = 5.

Let the children stand up and make pairs. Count the pairs: 5. A pair is a group of 2, so we are grouping in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is five 2s. 10 / 2 = 5. Dividing by 2 is the same as finding half.

A line of best fit passes through (2, 50) and (8, 80). Find its equation and use it to estimate y when x = 5.

Answer: y = 5x + 40; when x = 5, y = 65.

Gradient m = change in y / change in x = (80 - 50) / (8 - 2) = 30 / 6 = 5. So y = 5x + c. Put in the point (2, 50): 50 = 5 x 2 + c, so c = 50 - 10 = 40. Equation: y = 5x + 40. Check with the other point: 5 x 8 + 40 = 80. Estimate: y = 5 x 5 + 40 = 65. Choose two points ON THE LINE, far apart, not two data points, because data points are usually not exactly on the line. The gradient has a meaning: here each extra unit of x adds about 5 to y. Common mistake: dividing the change in x by the change in y.

messages.content: Tomorrow is my interview for a data entry job. I'm Ella, and I type fast but I'm afraid of the typing test.
Typing fast is a real strength, Ella. Nerves can cause mistakes, so slow down a little and aim for accuracy. Accurate typing counts more than speed.
What if my hands shake?
Take a slow breath before you start and rest your wrists lightly on the desk. Look at the text, not the keys. After the first few lines, most people settle down.
Do you think they will also ask about Excel?
Quite possibly, since many data entry jobs use spreadsheets. Be ready to talk about what you have done, like sorting a list or using simple formulas. Be honest about what you know.
I only know the basics. Is that a problem?
Not necessarily. Say you know the basics and are happy to learn more. Companies often train new staff. Your fast typing is a good strength to mention.
Ok. Which test was I scared of?
You were scared of the typing test, Ella. Slow down for accuracy, keep your wrists relaxed, and remind yourself that your typing speed is already a strength.

messages.content: John decides to get gym memberships so he can get in shape.  The gym close to his house is close but doesn't have everything he wants so he gets two different gym memberships.  The cheap one costs $10 a month and has a sign-up fee of $50.  The second gym is 3 times more expensive and it has a sign-up fee of 4 months membership.  How much total did he pay in the first year for gym membership?

The cheap gym cost 10*12=$120 for monthly fees
So the total cost was 120+50=$170
The more expensive gym cost 3*10=$30 per month
That means the sign-up fee was 30*4=$120
The monthly fees for the expensive gym comes out to 30*12=$360 per year
So the total cost for the expensive gym was 360+120=$480
So his total cost was 480+170=$650
The answer is 650.
What are principles? My teacher says honesty is one of them.

Principles are basic beliefs or rules that guide how a person behaves. Honesty is a good example. In science, a principle is a basic rule of how something works. It is a noun, and the plural is Principles.
Example: She lives by simple principles: tell the truth, work hard and help others.

Read this:

Subject: You were right about the names

Dear Vandana,
Six months ago, when I took over the night shift at the dispatch centre, you told me to learn everyone's name and one real thing about them before giving a single pep talk. I thought it was soft advice.
I did it anyway. Irfan drives his mother to dialysis on Tuesdays, so I moved his shift. Sunaina studies for the bank exam during her 3 a.m. break. Joseph's baby was born in March. I took the slogans off the board. Instead, at the start of each shift, I tell them about one real delivery we made possible the night before: medicine to a village after the bridge closed, that kind of thing.
Nobody has quit since February. Last year four people left in the same period. Joseph stayed late on Friday without being asked.
Thank you.
Arohi

How many people left in the same period last year?
Four.
How did Arohi feel about Vandana's advice at first, and now?
Arohi was sceptical at first, thinking it was soft advice, and now sounds grateful and a little proud of what changed.
Which of Arohi's choices made the biggest difference, and why?
Learning names and real situations, adjusting shifts, and sharing one real delivery each night; people felt known and saw the purpose, which slogans never gave them.
What might it feel like for Irfan to have his shift moved?
Irfan would likely feel relieved and cared for, since Tuesdays with his mother were a real worry, which may be part of why he stays.
About how many steps is it to the door? Guess, then walk and count.

Answer: (Example) Guess 8, count 9 steps. 1 away.

Estimating lengths works like estimating groups.
Our school trip is to a fort, and I'm excited, but I don't know what to carry.
A fort trip means walking and climbing. A water bottle, a hat, comfortable shoes and a small snack are good basics.
What about a camera?
If your school allows it, a phone or a simple camera is fine. Keep it in a small bag and don't wander off to take photos alone. Stay with the group.
Right. And what if it rains?
Carry a light raincoat or a foldable poncho. Stone steps get slippery when wet, so wear shoes with a good grip.

Subject: the breathing thing worked!
Hi Lalit Bhai,
Remember at Diwali you showed me the box breathing? In for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four? I thought it was silly. Today was the inter-school debate final and my hands were shaking so much my notes rattled. My chest felt tight and my mind went blank. I went to the corridor and did your boxes, eyes closed, five times. Then I shook my arms out like you do before cricket. By the time I walked back in, my heart had slowed. I didn't win, but I didn't freeze. I'm going to do it before the boards too. Thanks, Bhai.
Asif

How many times did Asif do the breathing boxes?
Five times.
How did Asif feel before the debate final?
Asif felt very anxious, with shaking hands, a tight chest and a blank mind.
What steps helped Asif calm down, and when else might they help?
Box breathing and shaking out the arms; they could help before the board exams too.
How might Lalit feel getting this email?
Lalit would likely feel pleased and proud that the tip helped. 😊
Brett has 24 more blue marbles than red marbles. He has 5 times as many blue marbles as red marbles. How many red marbles does he have?

Let x be the number of red marbles.
5*x=x+24
4*x=24
x=6
The answer is 6.

At the city library in Stockholm, Astrid, two, heard a soft rattling from the music corner and toddled straight towards it. A boy was tipping a rain stick. She held out both hands. Her mother, Valentina, followed close. Astrid shook the stick, pressed her ear to it, then patted the bumpy rug and the cold glass of the fish tank. When she headed for the open staircase, Valentina scooped her up and carried her back to the rain stick.

What sound did Astrid hear in the music corner?
A soft rattling from a rain stick.
What does Astrid moving towards every new sound and texture suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels curious and delighted by new things, drawn to explore without fear.
What did Valentina do that kept Astrid's exploring safe?
She followed close behind and scooped Astrid away from the open staircase, then brought her back to the rain stick.
How might Valentina feel following Astrid around the library?
She may feel amused and proud of Astrid's curiosity, but also watchful and alert to dangers.

Jyoti, you asked for the most embarrassing thing that happened to Rafiq at fourteen, so here it is. Annual day, the school stage. I was playing a tree in the drama. A tree! I walked on and tripped over a cable and fell flat. Everyone laughed. For weeks after, I was sure the whole school remembered. Every time someone laughed in a corridor, I thought, that's about me. I truly believed nobody in history had been this humiliated. Then, at a drama camp the next summer, we played a game where everyone told their worst stage moment. One girl had forgotten every line. A boy had thrown up. Nobody remembered my fall except me. That was the first time I realised the audience I imagined was mostly in my own head.

What role was Rafiq playing in the drama?
A tree.
Why did Rafiq think every corridor laugh was about the fall?
Rafiq felt deeply humiliated and self-conscious, so it seemed the whole school was watching and remembering, even though they weren't.
What made the drama camp game helpful, and how could a school use something like it?
Hearing others share worse moments showed Rafiq that nobody was alone in this; a school club could run the same kind of story circle.
How might the girl who forgot every line have felt hearing Rafiq's story?
That girl might have felt relieved and less alone, seeing that others had embarrassing moments too.
Why do train wheels have a flange on the inside edge?
The flange keeps the wheel on the rail. Because it presses against the side of the track when the train begins to drift, the wheel is guided back into place.
