“Hemant, honestly, I nearly did it. I'm Sachin. I got a message saying my card had a problem and I should confirm my details through a link. The page looked real, and I had half of my card number typed before something stopped me. It was the little voice that said, why would a bank text me a link? I closed it. Then I didn't just delete it. I took a screenshot and showed my parents at dinner. Nobody shouted. Dad found the official cybercrime website and we reported it together, and Mum phoned the bank on the number on the back of the card, so they could watch for anything odd. It felt better than pretending nothing had happened.”

What did Sachin take a screenshot of?
The message asking for card details.
What did Sachin feel at the moment before closing the page?
Tempted and rushed, then uneasy enough to stop when the little voice asked why a bank would send a link.
What else could Sachin do, and why?
Warn friends about the message, since scammers often send the same one to many people.
How does this look to Sachin's parents?
They are relieved that Sachin told them instead of quietly deleting the message, and glad to report it and tell the bank so it can watch for odd activity.

Monday. Ujjwal's diary.
First week at the new school in Class 6, and I figured out the sock rule. Nobody pulls their socks up. They roll them down to the ankle. I pulled mine up like at my old school and Wasim looked at my legs and said, "Bro. Down." Nobody wrote this rule anywhere. There's also a rule that you don't carry your water bottle on your shoulder, you hold it. And lunch boxes are never opened before the second bell. I rolled my socks down in the toilet. I felt stupid for a minute, then kind of relieved, like I'd passed a test nobody told me about.

Where did Ujjwal roll the socks down?
In the toilet.
How did Ujjwal feel after rolling the socks down?
Ujjwal felt stupid for a minute, then relieved, as if passing a secret test.
What could Ujjwal do if one of these rules felt wrong or uncomfortable?
Ujjwal could ask a trusted friend like Wasim why the rule exists and decide which ones really matter.
How might Wasim see the new student?
Wasim probably sees Ujjwal as new and was helping with the unwritten rules in a quick, joking way.

Tushar, you've been chewing on one side all week, and you snapped at your sister for nothing. Sit, let me tell you something. When I was nine, in Ambala, I had a toothache for a whole month and told nobody. I was terrified of the dentist near the bus stand; my cousin said he used a drill as big as a hammer. So I ate on one side, stopped laughing, and fought with everyone. My mother thought I had turned rude. One night she found me crying into my pillow and made me open my mouth. The next morning she held my hand in the dentist's chair the whole time. It hurt less than the month of hiding had. Your Kashish Nani learned that the hard way. So tell me, which tooth is it?

Where was the dentist young Kashish feared?
Near the bus stand in Ambala.
Why did young Kashish hide the toothache?
She was terrified of the dentist after her cousin's story about the huge drill, so suffering quietly felt safer.
What turning point ended young Kashish's month of hiding?
Her mother found her crying, checked her mouth, and the next morning held her hand in the dentist's chair.
How did Kashish's mother see her at first?
She thought her daughter had turned rude, not knowing a hidden toothache was behind the fights.

The college clinic in Guwahati was packed that morning, and Bidisha was volunteering at the registration desk for the health camp. Everyone wore masks. Babies cried, names were called over a crackling speaker, and the fan made the forms fly.
Her fellow volunteer, Anjali, kept looking at her with narrowed eyes. Bidisha couldn't see her mouth. Was she annoyed? Had Bidisha filled something wrong?
During a lull, Bidisha leaned over. "Anjali, are you upset with me? I can't tell with the masks."
Anjali's eyes widened, then crinkled. "No! I'm squinting because I left my glasses at home. And I've been smiling at you all morning. You couldn't see?"
"All I see is eyes."
"Then I'll use words. You're doing great."
After that, they said things out loud: "Good job." "Can you take this one?" "Thanks!" The desk ran smoother. And Bidisha started noticing Anjali's eyes crinkling above the mask when she was actually smiling.

What had Anjali left at home?
Her glasses.
What was Bidisha feeling when Anjali kept narrowing her eyes?
Bidisha felt anxious and unsure, worried Anjali was annoyed with her.
What made the desk run smoother?
Saying things out loud and asking directly, because masks hid smiles and left only eyes to read.
What was it like for Anjali behind her mask?
Anjali was friendly and smiling all morning, but squinting without her glasses, which the mask made look like annoyance.
For descriptive writing class, describe a busy market in the evening in about 100 words.

By six in the evening, the market wakes up. Strings of yellow bulbs flicker on above the stalls, and the smell of frying pakoras drifts through the air. Vegetable sellers call out their prices over the honking of scooters squeezing through the narrow lane. A woman bargains firmly over a pile of shining brinjals, while her small son tugs at her sari, pointing at a balloon seller. Bangles clink at one stall, and pressure cookers stand stacked like towers at another. Everyone seems to be in a hurry, yet nobody really wants to leave.

Dolma, you asked why I wanted six more months before the engagement. Sit, it's a whole thing. I'm Yamini, and when Arvind's parents came to meet mine, everything went fast. By dessert the aunties were talking dates and halls, and I just kept nodding, because everyone looked so happy. That night I lay awake and realised we'd never talked about the big things. Would I keep working after marriage? His mother had said 'of course she'll adjust' at dinner. Would we live with his parents? Kids, when? Did he even want them? So the next weekend Arvind and I sat in a quiet café with a list. Some answers matched. Some didn't: he assumed we'd move in with his parents; I'd assumed not. We didn't fight. We just saw we needed time. When I asked both families for six months, my mother was upset for a day. Arvind backed me. I'd rather be sure than be agreeable.

What did Arvind's mother say at dinner?
'Of course she'll adjust.'
What was Yamini feeling as she lay awake after the families met?
Yamini felt uneasy and rushed, realising the big questions had never been discussed.
What did Yamini and Arvind do before agreeing to dates?
They talked through a list of big questions, found where they differed, and asked for six more months.
How did Yamini's mother react to the delay?
She was upset for a day.
A box had 21 sweets and the guests ate 12. How many sweets are left? What does the word "tradition" mean?

1. 9 sweets. Because 21 - 12 = 9.
2. A tradition is a custom that is passed down in a family or community. Example: It is a tradition to visit relatives.

Hrithik, you ask why I still visit Savitri every Makar Sankranti. Sit, I'll tell you. I was ten, and that January kites filled the sky, but Savitri came back to school thin as a stick after a long fever. Her satchel was heavy with slates and books, so every day I carried it, mine on my back and hers in my arms, all the way to her lane. One evening she whispered that her father had lost his job at the mill and there was no money for kite string that year. 'Don't tell anyone, Nikita.' I didn't. Not the other girls, not even my own mother. On festival morning I just gave her half my string and said I had too much. Fifty years later she still laughs about my 'too much'.

What did Nikita carry every day while Savitri was weak?
Savitri's heavy satchel, carried all the way to Savitri's lane.
Why did Nikita keep Savitri's news from everyone, even at home?
Nikita felt loyal and protective towards Savitri, who had trusted Nikita with something painful, and that trust mattered more than talking.
Nikita gave Savitri half the kite string and claimed to have too much. Why was that a good choice?
It let Savitri join the festival without being pitied, and it kept the secret safe because nobody needed to know why.
How might Savitri have felt about Nikita's 'too much' story?
Savitri probably felt grateful and relieved not to be pitied; that is why she still laughs about it fifty years later.
He earns less than I do, but he saves more as I do. Anything off?

He earns less than I do, but he saves more than I do.
Why: comparative ("more as" -> "more than").

Ramesh had watched six videos about black holes over the weekend. By Monday he felt like an astronomer. In Tenzin sir's physics class in their Pune school, when sir explained gravity, Ramesh put up his hand. "Sir, that's outdated. Actually, black holes prove gravity is just an illusion." The class went quiet. Tenzin sir smiled. "Interesting. Can you explain how?" Ramesh started. "Well, space-time bends, and... light can't escape, so... it's not really a force." He stopped, then tried again, then trailed off. He felt sure he understood it. He just couldn't explain it. Tenzin sir said kindly, "It's a big topic. Let's talk after class." Ramesh sat down, frowning, still convinced he knew more than the textbook.

How many videos did Ramesh watch about black holes?
Six videos.
Why did Ramesh feel he knew more than Tenzin sir?
After a few videos, Ramesh felt confident and excited, and didn't yet know enough to see how much he was missing.
What could Ramesh do to find out how much he understands?
He could try explaining the idea step by step on paper, or ask Tenzin sir for a book, to see the gaps.
How does Tenzin sir seem to see Ramesh's challenge?
Tenzin sir seems patient and amused, treating it as curiosity rather than rudeness.

Gary is buying chlorine for his rectangular pool, which is 10 feet long, 8 feet wide, and 6 feet deep. Gary needs to buy one quart of chlorine for every 120 cubic feet of water in his pool. If chlorine costs $3 a quart, how much does Gary spend on chlorine?

First find the volume of the pool by multiplying the length by the width by the height: 10 ft * 8 ft * 6 ft = 480 cubic feet
Then divide the volume of the pool by the number of cubic feet one quart of chlorine can sterilize: 480 cubic feet / 120 cubic feet/quart = 4 quarts
Then multiply the number of quarts Gary needs to buy by the price per quart to find out how much money he spends: $3/quart * 4 quarts = $12
The answer is 12.
The answer is range 99, Q1 = 2, Q3 = 6, IQR = 4.

Jahnavi: ok so someone in the canteen said my lunch "smells weird" and that my kurta looks "so costume-y" 😠
Rafiq: WHAT. who?
Jahnavi: some guy called Callum. Everyone kind of laughed. I froze. I felt about two inches tall

Who moved to the window table with Jahnavi?

How did Jahnavi feel after the remark in the canteen?
Small and angry: Jahnavi wrote about feeling about two inches tall and sent an angry face.
What did Jahnavi do that was a good way to respond?
Jahnavi answered calmly that it was a good lunch, then walked to another table with an ally and stayed proud of the kurta and the food.
How might Callum have seen the comment?
Callum may have meant it as a joke, since others laughed, without noticing how belittling it felt to Jahnavi.
Our school is starting a gardening club and I am thinking of joining.
That sounds good. Gardening teaches patience, and you get to be outside. Do you have any experience with plants?
Only a tulsi plant at home that my grandmother looks after. I help water it.
That is a start. Watering and noticing how a plant changes is the heart of gardening. Your grandmother can probably teach you a lot, too, about when to water and how much sun a plant needs.
I should ask her before I sign up. Do you think that makes sense?
It does. Ask your grandmother what she has learned about growing the tulsi. You will walk into the gardening club already knowing something real, and she will enjoy sharing it with you.
On Teacher's day, we gave our class teacher flowers. Please fix the festival name.

On Teachers' Day, we gave our class teacher flowers.
Why: apostrophe ("Teacher's" -> "Teachers'"); capital letter ("day" -> "Day").

The community leader of a certain town organized a cleaning day event where community members were to be involved in collecting trash inside the town. Out of 2000 community members involved in the cleaning process, 30% were adult men. If there were twice as many adult women as adult men in the event, and the rest were children, calculate the total number of children involved in the cleaning event.

If the number of adult men involved in the cleaning process was 30% of the community members, there were 30/100*2000 = 600 adult men at the event.
There were also twice as many adult women as adult men in the event, a total of 2*600 = 1200 women.
The total number of adults in the event was 1200+600= 1800
If the rest of the people at the cleaning event were children, there were 2000-1800 = 200 children at the event.
The answer is 200.
I am trying to decide which room in our house should be the family room. We have three options.
Tell me about the options. What does each room look like, and how does your family use the house in the evenings?
One is the big hall at the front, one is the back room near the kitchen, and one is upstairs. We watch TV and play games together.
The back room near the kitchen could be handy, since snacks and tea are close. The front hall is bigger but may be noisy from the street. Upstairs is quieter but far from the kitchen.
My mother Savitri finds stairs hard, so upstairs is not suitable.
Then that settles the upstairs room. Savitri can reach the hall or the back room easily, and either one will let her join the family in the evenings.
Between the two, the hall has better light.
Good light matters for games and for reading. If the street noise is not too loud, the hall may be the better choice. You could try it for a week and see.
Okay. Remind me, who finds stairs hard?
Your mother Savitri finds stairs hard, which is why upstairs is not suitable. The hall has better light and is easy for her to reach, so it looks like a good family room.

Read this:

In a Lisbon apartment, Ivan's dad slammed the kitchen drawer when the boiler broke again. Ivan, four, saw his dad's nostrils flare and his lips go thin. Ivan stood still with his toy fire truck. His mother Beatriz took Ivan aside. "Do you see Papa's nose? When it does that, he's cross about the boiler, not cross with you." She breathed in slowly, and Ivan copied her. From the kitchen, Papa said, "Sorry, I got loud. Shall we all have some toast?"

What did Ivan see on his dad's face?
He saw his dad's nostrils flare and his lips go thin.
What might Ivan have been feeling as he stood still with his fire truck?
He was probably uneasy or worried that the anger was about him, since he stopped moving. Beatriz's words suggest it was really about the boiler.
What could Ivan's dad do next time he feels this angry?
He can name the feeling and slow his breathing, as he did by saying sorry for getting loud, so the family knows what is going on.
How might Beatriz see the situation compared with Ivan?
She understands that the anger is about the broken boiler, so she can guide Ivan through it, while Ivan may just see a scary face.

Sabina, you say you can't stop scrolling the news. Let your Hansa Khala tell you something from before phones. When I was twenty-five, working at a newspaper in Hyderabad, the new cable channels arrived with news all day and all night. I kept the TV on from waking to sleeping, afraid to miss anything. I felt informed and exhausted, and I started snapping at people. One evening my editor, a grey-haired man called Mr Qadri, said, "Hansa, you're reading everything and thinking nothing." That stung. So I made rules. TV news once, at nine. One good newspaper, read with a pen. Anything I repeated at work, I checked with a second source first. My head cleared. My writing got better. Now you carry a hundred cable channels in your pocket. Same choice, Sabina. Decide what comes in, or it decides for you.

Where did Hansa work at twenty-five?
At a newspaper in Hyderabad.
What was young Hansa feeling when Mr Qadri said she was reading everything and thinking nothing?
Hansa felt stung and hurt, but it made her rethink her habits.
What rules did Hansa make, and why did they help?
News on TV once at nine, one good newspaper read with a pen, and a second source before repeating anything; they turned endless intake into focused thinking.
How might Mr Qadri have seen young Hansa?
Mr Qadri probably saw a capable young journalist wearing herself out, and cared enough to say it bluntly.

Rukmini: I'll send you the song we sing on the first morning. Voice note.

What is Ira worried about when her daughter asks about the festival?

Nani's notebook, Tuesday
Jasleen has started sending me voice notes every morning on her way to school. I hear the auto horn, her giggle, and "Good morning, Nani ji, I'm wearing the red clips you gave!" A typed message never makes me smile like this.
This evening she was recording something for her friend Parveen. She was copying a new girl's way of talking and laughing. Before she pressed send, I asked, "If that girl heard this, how would she feel? And can Parveen send it on?"
Jasleen stopped. "Anyone can forward it," she said slowly. She deleted it and recorded a different one, telling Parveen about the dance practice instead.
I told her I was proud she thought first.

What does Jasleen say in her morning voice note to Nani?
"Good morning, Nani ji, I'm wearing the red clips you gave!"
What might Jasleen have been feeling when she said "Anyone can forward it"?
She probably felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, realising the recording could be passed on and hurt the new girl.
Which choice worked, and why?
Nani asking questions instead of scolding worked, because Jasleen worked out the risk herself and chose a kinder message.
How does Nani experience the morning voice notes?
The voice notes make Nani feel close and happy, because she can hear warmth and small details a typed message would miss.

Sunday

Sarika and I had the best talk we've had in months. Not a fight. A talk.

It happened on the college steps after the play. We were both tired and in a good mood, and she said, "Can I say something without us fighting?"

She said: "When you go quiet, I get scared, so I push." I said: "And when you push, I panic, so I go quieter." We both laughed, because it was so obvious once it was out loud. Like a see-saw.

Then she said something I've been thinking about all evening: "Maybe it's not you or me. It's the see-saw."

So we gave it a name. When it starts, either of us can just say "see-saw," and we stop and check.

I feel lighter tonight than in weeks.

Asif

Where did Asif and Sarika have their talk?
They talked on the college steps after the play.
What was Asif feeling at the end of the evening?
Asif felt lighter and relieved, and hopeful that naming the pattern could help.
Why is naming the pattern 'see-saw' a useful step?
It turns the cycle into the problem instead of each other, and gives both a quick, neutral way to stop and check when it starts.
What might Sarika have been feeling when she asked to speak without fighting?
Sarika was probably hopeful but a little nervous, wanting to share her fear without setting off another round.

The bus to the taluka office was already packed when a man shoved past Chaitanya and took the last seat, the one Chaitanya had been waiting for since Mahoba stop. His cousin Harish muttered, "Say something. Who does he think he is?"
Two years ago Chaitanya would have grabbed the man's shoulder. He could feel the old heat rising in his neck now. His files for the land record correction were under his arm, and he had been standing for an hour.
He breathed out slowly through his nose and counted the electric poles outside. Five. Six. The man was sweating, clutching a hospital bag on his lap.
"Leave it," Chaitanya said quietly.
"You've gone soft," Harish said.
"Maybe." Chaitanya shifted his files to the other arm. "Or maybe he needed it more." At the next stop, the man got down near the government hospital without looking back.

What was the man holding on his lap?
He was clutching a hospital bag on his lap.
What was Chaitanya feeling when the man took the seat?
He felt angry, with the old heat rising in his neck, and tired after standing for an hour, yet he chose to calm himself.
Which choice worked, and why?
Pausing with slow breaths and counting poles worked, because it gave Chaitanya time to notice the hospital bag and respond with sense instead of a shove.
How does Harish see Chaitanya's calm response?
Harish reads it as going soft, because he expected the kind of angry reaction Chaitanya might have had two years ago.

Dear Hemant,
Since you've just moved to Vizag, here's what I learned in my first cyclone season. When the official warning came in October, most of my neighbours said, "Let's see if it actually hits." I didn't wait. I already had a small kit by the door: torch, power bank, water, dry snacks, copies of documents in a zip bag, my medicines. I had checked the route to the community hall.
When the district told our street to move, I went that afternoon. The cyclone turned north; our street got only rain. Some people teased me for running away. I felt a bit silly, honestly. But silly and safe is a good trade.
Please make your kit this weekend.
Love, Lavanya

In October.

Lavanya felt a bit silly but still sure that being safe was worth it.
What should Hemant do this weekend?
Make a small kit like Lavanya's and learn the routes to safe places near the new home.
How might the neighbours who waited have felt when the cyclone turned?
They may have felt relieved and confident, perhaps not noticing how lucky they had been.

She had lied. She'd said she was at a group study and gone to Isha's birthday at a café instead. She felt sick about it.

Raghav had been grumbling all evening about his spelling test, so his aunt Hansa took him for a walk along Marine Drive in Mumbai. The sea was dark and endless, the waves hitting the tetrapods with a huge hush. Lights curved away along the shore like a necklace, and far out on the water a tiny ship's light blinked.
Raghav climbed onto the wall and stared. "Masi, how far does it go?"
"All the way to other countries."
He was quiet for a long time. The wind pushed his hair back. "I feel like an ant," he said, and then laughed, a surprised, happy laugh.
On the way home he held her hand and talked about ships, not spelling.

What did Raghav say he felt like?
An ant.
How did Raghav feel looking at the sea?
Raghav felt small, like an ant, but surprisingly happy, laughing a happy laugh.
Why might the walk have helped with Raghav's grumbling?
The vast sea pulled his attention away from the spelling test, and he talked about ships instead.
What might Hansa have noticed on the way home?
Hansa likely noticed he was calmer and more cheerful, holding her hand and chatting about ships.

I've been picked as twelfth man for our school match. I'm Noah and I'm disappointed.
It is natural to feel that way, Noah. But being twelfth man matters. You bring water, give messages and you may get to field. Do you know why you were picked?
The coach said I'm good, but the others are slightly better right now.
That is honest feedback, and it means you are close. Use the time to watch the game carefully and learn from the team. Ask the coach what to work on.
Maybe I could improve my fielding.
Fielding is a great place to start, because it can get you into the team. Practise catching and throwing every day, and work on your speed to the ball.
Good idea. What should I do during the match as twelfth man?
Stay ready, Noah. Bring water on time, watch the game closely, and be quick to field if someone is hurt. A good twelfth man impresses the coach, which could help you next time.

In the Delhi hostel, Kashish's phone lit up again. It was a forward from her aunt: a video of a man saying he had taken a spoon of a special seed powder every morning and his joint pain disappeared in a week. "Share with all your elders!" the caption said. Kashish almost forwarded it to her father, whose knee had been hurting. Then she remembered her statistics class. Her roommate Payal, a pharmacy student, looked at the video. "He took the powder, and then he felt better. Does he say whether it was going to get better anyway? Or what else he changed?" Kashish watched again. The man mentioned, in passing, that he'd also started walking every day and had seen a physiotherapist. "So it could be the walking, or time," Kashish said. She didn't forward it. Instead she called her father and asked if he'd seen his doctor about the knee.

A spoon of a special seed powder.
What was Kashish feeling when she first saw the video?
She felt hopeful and worried, tempted to forward it because her father's knee had been hurting.
What did Kashish do instead of forwarding the video?
She called her father and asked if he had seen his doctor about the knee.
How does Payal see the man's story?

Manoj, you asked what changed my relationship with money. I'm Devika, and it was one boring habit.
Once a month I make a single list. Not budgets in ten apps. One list: what I own, what I owe, what came in, what went out. My salary, my freelance payments, the money my grandmother slipped me at the wedding, all of it goes on the same list. I used to treat gift money like it wasn't real, and freelance money like a treat. That's how I ended up with a card bill I couldn't explain.
I still have labelled accounts: one for rent, one for my sister's college gift, one for travel. They're like drawers. Handy. But I don't let the drawers fool me into thinking I'm richer or poorer than I am. I look at the whole cupboard first.
If a listener wants to start, take one evening, one page, and if the numbers scare you, sit with someone you trust or a proper adviser.

What does Devika suggest a listener do to start?

Mock interview day, placement cell, Thursday. Note by Trisha, final-year coordinator.
I sat in on the panel with Ojas, an alumnus volunteering as interviewer. The third candidate, a second-year named Wasim, walked in smiling, joked about the broken fan, and had Ojas laughing within a minute. His answer on the coding question was vague, and he admitted he hadn't finished his project. Ojas still gave him 9 for communication, 9 for technical skills, 9 for teamwork. I had written 8, 5 and 6.
I didn't want to embarrass Ojas, so at the break I asked, "Could we try the next five with one line per skill, scored right after that question, before the overall score?" He agreed.
The next candidate was also very likeable. This time Ojas scored her 8 for communication and 4 for technical. He looked at the sheet and said, "Huh. I'd have given her all nines."
Next step: I'll ask the placement cell to use the split sheet for every panel.

What scores did Ojas give Wasim for communication, technical skills and teamwork?
He gave him 9 for communication, 9 for technical skills and 9 for teamwork.
Why did giving Wasim nines across the board likely feel fair to Ojas at the time?
Wasim was warm and funny and had Ojas laughing within a minute, so that good feeling spread over everything and made the vague answers seem less important.
What change did Trisha suggest, and what showed it helped?
Trisha asked to score one line per skill right after each question, before the overall score, and Ojas then gave the next likeable candidate 8 for communication and 4 for technical.
If Trisha had said nothing, how might the split sheets and panels have turned out for other students?
Charming students might keep getting high marks in skills they had not shown, while quieter candidates with strong answers could be ranked lower than they deserve.

Ben has 8 apples more than Phillip does. Tom has three eighths as many apples at Ben has. If Phillip has 40 apples, how many apples does Tom have?

Ben has 40+8 = 48 apples.
There are 48/8 = 6 apples in every eighth.
Tom has 6*3 = 18 apples.
The answer is 18.

Running club notes, Arnab, Thursday
Gopika has been in my batch for three years and is my friend outside it too. Since she missed the qualifying time for the Kolkata half marathon by forty seconds, every cool-down has become the same talk. The cramp at the fifteenth kilometre. The water station she skipped. How has the repeated talk affected Arnab as the listener?

The envelope from the tax office made Uma's heart race, and for an hour she imagined the worst. Then she sat down, read it slowly twice, wrote the reply date on a sticky note and started pulling out invoices. The whole thing felt unfair to her: the forms were tangled and she hated paying so much. "You can grumble at the system and still follow it," said Jaya. "Vote, write to your representative, but file." That evening Bhupen, a friend of a cousin, phoned. "Give me a fee and a little extra for a clerk, and this whole notice will disappear." Uma's stomach sank. She said no, thanked him and hung up. Jaya gave her the name of a certified accountant. Uma booked an appointment, brought her documents and asked for a receipt for every payment. She treated the notice as a set of rules to work through, not an attack, and wrote her reply in polite, accurate language, sending it two days before the date on the sticky note. Afterwards she still muttered about the system, but she slept properly that night.

Twenty-two.
Why did Ankita's face go hot?
Ankita felt embarrassed and surprised after laughing at the others, and then seeing that a dancing tiger had been there all along.
What could Ankita try the next time a task needs full attention but the whole scene matters too?
Ankita could remember that focus hides other things and, after finishing, look again at the whole scene or ask what else was there.
How might the classmates who saw the tiger feel when Ankita laughed?
They might have felt a bit brushed off at first, then pleased when the replay proved them right.

When I was twenty-three and sharing a flat in Pune with Sunaina, her mother called every night and ended with "Love you, darling." Sunaina said it back without thinking. I used to feel a small pang listening. My Amma has never said "I love you" to me in my life. Not once. For a while I wondered if that meant something was missing. Then Amma visited for a week. She said almost nothing sentimental. But she scrubbed our kitchen, sewed the button on my work kurta, filled the freezer with idli batter labelled by day, and woke at five to pack my tiffin before my long shift. On the train back she messaged only: "Batter for Thursday is on the left." Sunaina read it over my shoulder and laughed. "Sudha, that's the most loving text I've ever seen." She was right. Amma's love comes in steel containers, not sentences.

What did Amma label by day?
Idli batter in the freezer.
What did Sudha feel listening to Sunaina's mother say 'Love you, darling'?
Sudha felt a small pang of envy and doubt, wondering if Amma's silence meant something was missing.
What helped Sudha see Amma's love differently?
Watching Amma's week of practical care, cleaning, sewing, cooking and labelling batter, and hearing Sunaina call the batter text loving.
How did Sunaina read Amma's message?
Sunaina saw 'Batter for Thursday is on the left' as the most loving text she'd ever seen, recognising care in practical words.

Hafsa had pushed Tushar at the colony park so she could go down the slide first. Tushar scraped his hand and cried.
Now Hafsa sat on the bench, looking at him. Her Ammi said nothing, just waited.
Hafsa slid off the bench. She went over and picked a small yellow flower from the edge of the grass. She held it out.
"For your hand," she said.
Tushar looked at her. Then he held out his arms. Hafsa hugged him.

What did Hafsa pick for Tushar?
A small yellow flower from the edge of the grass.
What was Tushar feeling when he held out his arms?
He seemed comforted and ready to forgive, wanting a hug after Hafsa's gift.
What makes Hafsa's repair work at her age?
Giving the flower and a hug when Tushar wanted one is a concrete action a young child understands, which feels better than just saying words.
How might Hafsa's Ammi be experiencing this moment?
She is probably proud and glad that Hafsa found her own way to make things right.
Why might a person refuse help even when they really need it?
A person may refuse help out of pride or worry. Because they may not want to seem weak or may feel that they are a burden to others, they say no, even when help would make things easier.

Here's a mistake I made in my first year as a manager. I'm Vidya, twenty-six, and I had a junior, Hemant, who never pushed back, never argued, always said, "Yes, ma'am, I'll do it." I assumed he had no ideas of his own. I nearly passed him over for the new project. Then I overheard him in the canteen explaining to a friend exactly how our onboarding could be fixed, in detail, with real passion. I was stunned. Later I asked him why he never said any of it in meetings. He said, a bit embarrassed, "In my home you don't contradict elders or bosses." That changed how I run meetings. Now I go round the table and ask everyone by name. Hemant's idea goes live next month.

What did Hemant explain in the canteen?
Exactly how the onboarding could be fixed.
How did Vidya feel on overhearing Hemant in the canteen?
She felt stunned and a little ashamed of assuming he had no ideas.
What did Vidya change so quieter people are heard?
She now goes round the table and asks everyone by name.
How might Hemant have felt explaining his silence?
Hemant felt a bit embarrassed, but was honest about the respect he learned at home.

"Gargi, you're shivering," Francis said at the classroom door. "Give me your bag."
"It's heavy. My rangoli colours are in it."
"I carry my cricket kit every day. Give."
He slung both bags on, one on each shoulder, and walked her to the auto.
At the gate, Rohit caught up. "What's her rangoli design for the Diwali contest? You know, na? Tell."
"She told me because she trusts me," Francis said.
"Just a hint!"
"Nope."
"Boring."
"Fine. Boring." Francis waved as the auto pulled away. "Get well, Gargi! Your design's locked up safe."
Gargi smiled weakly from the seat. "Knew it would be."

What was in Gargi's heavy bag?
Her rangoli colours.
Why does Francis refuse to give Rohit even a hint?
Francis feels loyal and protective of Gargi's trust, since she told him because she trusts him.
What would you tell a child pressed to share a friend's surprise like this one?
Keeping a harmless surprise, like a rangoli design, is a kind way to honour trust; a secret about someone being hurt, though, should always go to a trusted adult.
How might Gargi feel watching Francis from the auto?
Gargi, shivering and unwell, likely felt cared for and safe, knowing her bag and her design were in good hands.

Friday
Weird day. Vikas asked if he could copy my physics assignment "just this once." I've let him before. This time I said no. My face went hot saying it.
He called me selfish and didn't sit with me at lunch.
Then in the evening I found out he'd put a fake review on the local bakery's page because they wouldn't give him a free pastry. He thought it was funny. I thought it was mean, and it's somebody's shop. I told him so on the phone. He hung up.
I told Mummy about the review. She said she'd mention it to his mother, calmly.
Some days being responsible just feels lonely. But I'd feel worse if I'd helped him cheat or laughed at the review.
Chetan

What did Vikas do to the bakery?
He put a fake review on the local bakery's page.
How did Chetan feel saying no to Vikas?
Chetan felt uncomfortable and a bit lonely; the face went hot.
What would you advise Chetan now?
Stay firm but friendly with Vikas, and let adults handle the review while Chetan keeps to honest work.
How might the bakery owner feel about the fake review?
The owner would likely feel hurt and worried, since a false review can damage a small shop.

In the preschool's role-play corner, Uma, five, scrunched her eyebrows, curled her fingers into claws and growled, "I'm a monster!" She stomped towards Pankaj, her teacher, and then burst into giggles, rocking on her toes. Pankaj backed away with a mock gasp. "Oh no, a big monster!" Uma growled again, giggling harder, checking his face. A quieter boy nearby watched and then joined with his own little growl.

What did Uma do with her hands to be a monster?
She curled her fingers into claws.
What does Uma's giggling suggest about the scowl, and what else might it mean?
It suggests the scowl was posed for play and she was delighted with the game. It might also be that she was checking whether Pankaj would play along.
What could Pankaj do next?
He can keep playing, then ask the quieter boy if he wants to be a monster too. 🙂
How might the quieter boy see Uma's face?
He could see it as scary at first, but her giggles and rocking tell him it is only a game.

Two sides and an angle of delta ABC and of delta PQR are given. Are the triangles similar by SAS? If yes, write the similarity and the scale factor k = (delta PQR side)/(delta ABC side).
a) AB = 6, AC = 9, angle A = 50 degrees; PQ = 4, PR = 6, angle P = 50 degrees
b) AB = 4, AC = 5, angle A = 70 degrees; PQ = 8, PR = 10, angle P = 70 degrees
c) AB = 3, BC = 7, angle B = 40 degrees; PQ = 6, QR = 14, angle Q = 40 degrees
d) AB = 5, AC = 8, angle A = 60 degrees; PQ = 10, PR = 12, angle P = 60 degrees
e) AB = 6, AC = 10, angle A = 45 degrees; PQ = 9, PR = 15, angle P = 55 degrees
f) BC = 12, CA = 16, angle C = 30 degrees; QR = 9, RP = 12, angle R = 30 degrees
g) AB = 4, BC = 6, angle A = 50 degrees; PQ = 6, QR = 9, angle P = 50 degrees
h) AB = 2.5, AC = 4, angle A = 100 degrees; PR = 10, PQ = 6.25, angle P = 100 degrees
i) AB = 7, BC = 3, angle B = 90 degrees; PQ = 3.5, QR = 1.5, angle Q = 90 degrees
j) CA = 8, CB = 12, angle C = 65 degrees; RP = 12, RQ = 18, angle R = 65 degrees
k) AB = 9, AC = 6, angle A = 35 degrees; QP = 6, QR = 4, angle Q = 35 degrees
l) AB = 5, AC = 7, angle A = 80 degrees; PQ = 7, PR = 5, angle P = 80 degrees
m) AB = 10, AC = 4, angle B = 30 degrees; PQ = 5, PR = 2, angle Q = 30 degrees
n) BA = 6, BC = 8, angle B = 120 degrees; RP = 9, RQ = 12, angle R = 120 degrees

a) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 2/3
b) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 2
c) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 2
d) no (2 != 3/2)
e) no (the included angles differ)
f) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 3/4
g) cannot say (the angle is not included: SSA)
h) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 5/2
i) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 1/2
j) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PQR, k = 3/2
k) yes, delta ABC ~ delta QPR, k = 2/3
l) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PRQ, k = 1
m) cannot say (the angle is not included: SSA)
n) yes, delta ABC ~ delta PRQ, k = 3/2

Repair shop note. Sarita came in on Saturday with a phone in two pieces. She had watched a video and tried to replace the cracked screen herself. She had pried the glass up with a kitchen knife, and it had cracked further; the thin cable was torn. She stood there red-eyed, quiet, half proud of having tried. I told her plainly that the screen swap is a job for a shop because the battery sits right under it and can be damaged. I asked her to bring a broken old phone next time to practise on. She nodded and asked if she could watch me. I said yes. Sharmila, shop owner

What did Sarita use to pry the glass up?
Sarita used a kitchen knife to pry the glass up.
What was Sarita probably feeling as she stood there red-eyed and quiet?
Sarita was probably disappointed and embarrassed, yet still a little proud of having tried.
What could Sarita do to keep learning about repairs safely?
Sarita could practise on a broken old phone and watch a shop repair, leaving jobs near the battery to the shop.
How does Sharmila see Sarita's attempt?
Sharmila sees a student who was curious and tried hard, and says plainly which job is for a shop while welcoming her to watch.
Karan here. Dad says I should give up my video games and take up a hobby outdoors.
A balance is helpful, Karan. Games are fun, and outdoor time is good for your body and mind. Is there something outside you would try?
Maybe birdwatching. I've seen parrots on the wall near our house.
Birdwatching is a lovely hobby and needs very little. Watch quietly, note the colour and size, and try to identify the bird with a picture book. Parrots are a great start.
I don't have binoculars though.
You can start without them. Many birds come close if you sit still. A notebook and pencil are enough to note what you see, and you can add binoculars later.
Okay. Which bird did I say I'd seen near my house?
You said parrots, on the wall near your house, Karan. Sit still in the same spot each morning, write down how many come, and note their colours. Your dad may enjoy joining you.
Is "perforce" a hard word? What does it mean? Then, how should I introduce myself at a new club? Plus, how do I spell "occassionally"? Oh, and check my English: "He came late, he missed the film."

1. Perforce means because you have no choice, in an old-fashioned way of speaking. It is an adverb.
2. Say your name, a little about yourself, and why you joined. Keep it short and smile, and then ask others about themselves.
3. It is "occasionally", with a double "c" and a single "s".
4. Better: He came late, so he missed the film. Why: a comma cannot join two sentences; add "so".

"Where did the stipend go, Nikhil?" Lavanya asked, holding up his empty wallet at the dining table.
"Relax, didi. The hostel fee is paid."
"And the rest? Mummy sent you train fare because you said you were broke."
Their mother, Sarika, stopped rolling rotis. "Broke on the fifteenth again?"
"I needed the shoes. And the trip was a one-time thing."
"Last month it was the one-time concert," Lavanya said.
"I know, I know." Nikhil rubbed his face. "Next month I'm putting half into savings the day it comes. Promise."
"You said that in March."
"This time I mean it. I really want the laptop by December."
Sarika slid a roti onto his plate. "Meaning it isn't the hard part, beta."

What did Mummy send Nikhil?
Mummy sent him train fare because he said he was broke.
Why does Nikhil believe his promise this time?
Nikhil feels embarrassed at being caught and truly eager for the laptop by December, so in that moment meaning it feels like enough.
What would you advise Nikhil to do on the day the stipend arrives?
Move the laptop money out straight away, before shoes or trips come up, so the plan does not depend on how he feels that week.
What is it like for Sarika to hear the same promise again?
Sarika seems tired but kind; she serves him a roti and gently points out that meaning well is not what has been failing.
Shaadi mein kisi ko bolna hai "Aap dulhe ki taraf se hain ya dulhan ki?" English mein.
Ask: "Are you from the groom's side or the bride's side?" It is a friendly way to start a talk at a wedding.

What was Seema feeling when she typed and then deleted her message?
Seema felt hurt and shut out by Vaibhav's one-word replies, but chose not to send an accusing message.

She offered low-pressure availability on the balcony and didn't punish his honesty, so he felt safe telling her more.

Vasudha, my roommate, was the only person I told. At first it felt like a relief, and I began to text her every time the low feeling came, then to talk at midnight, and by the second month at all hours. She listened, always, and I never asked her how she was.

Then she began wearing headphones in the room. She stayed late in the library. One evening she said quietly, "I care about you, but I can't be the only one you lean on. I'm running out." I felt as though a door had shut. Later I saw that I had put every low moment on one person, and that made us both feel worse. Ankita

What did Vasudha begin wearing in the room?
She began wearing headphones in the room.
How did Ankita feel when Vasudha said she was running out?
Ankita felt hurt and rejected, as though a door had shut, before realising later how much had been placed on Vasudha.
What could Ankita have done earlier so support was not all on one person, and why?
Ankita could have also talked to a counsellor or family, since one person alone cannot hold every difficult moment and may need rest.
How does Vasudha experience Ankita's constant reaching out?
Vasudha becomes tired and overwhelmed, hiding in headphones and the library, even though she cares.

Sit, Lalremsiami. You asked how I keep my savings when everyone around me is tempted. I'm Pranav, and I'll tell you about a small card.
Years ago I built a cushion, and then a sale came, then a friend planned a trip, and each time the cushion looked like free money. So one night I wrote on a card: "Only for a hospital bill, losing my job, or a leaking roof. Nothing else."
It sat in my wallet. When my friend Ranjit called about the trip, I took the card out and read it. A trip was none of those three. I said no, and he laughed.
Months later, the roof did leak, and I opened the fund without a second thought.

What three things did the card list?
The card listed a hospital bill, losing a job, and a leaking roof.
What was Pranav probably feeling during the sale and the trip invitation?
Pranav was tempted, since the cushion looked like free money, but the card steadied that pull.
Pranav wrote a short rule on a card. What did that choice help with?
It settled in advance what counted as an emergency, so a sale or a trip could not talk Pranav into using the cushion.
How might Ranjit have felt when Pranav said no to the trip?
Ranjit took it lightly and laughed, so was probably a little disappointed but not offended.

Monday: Mohit asked Tanuja why the printed banners for the company's annual day hadn't arrived. She shrugged, palms up, and went back to her laptop. Mohit stood there a moment, then walked off without a word.
Wednesday: Tanuja noticed Mohit had stopped copying her on the volunteer emails. At lunch she asked him why. "You shrugged at me like the banners weren't your business," he said. "I felt stupid for asking." Tanuja winced. She'd meant "I'm stuck too," but she hadn't said it.
The following Friday: Now the stage lights were late. When Mohit asked, Tanuja felt the same palms-up lift coming, but this time she kept talking. "I'm sorry, I should have chased them yesterday. I'll call the vendor now and tell you by four." Mohit nodded. At half past three she walked over with the new delivery time.

What was late on Friday?
The stage lights were late.
What had Tanuja meant by Monday's shrug, and how did she feel on Wednesday?
She meant 'I'm stuck too', feeling helpless about the banners, and on Wednesday she felt embarrassed to learn Mohit took it as dismissal.
What did Tanuja add on Friday that made the difference?
Words that owned the delay: an apology and a clear plan to call the vendor and report back by four, which she kept.
How did Mohit experience the Monday shrug?
He felt dismissed and stupid for asking, as if the banners weren't his business, so he quietly stopped copying Tanuja on emails.
Tom said mournful in class today and I didn't catch it. What does it mean?

Mournful means full of sadness, as if grieving for a loss. It is an adjective.
Example: A mournful tune drifted from the flute.

I'm Raghav, and I watched my little sister Urmila at the table. Mummy had put a red spinning top there, next to a glass of water. Urmila saw the top and her hand shot out. She did not look at the glass. Splash! Water ran over the table edge. Urmila stared at her wet sleeve and then at Mummy. I don't know if she was scared or surprised. Mummy said, "Let's wipe it together."

What did Urmila reach for?
Urmila reached for a red spinning top.
What might Urmila have felt after the splash?
Urmila may have felt surprised or startled, staring at her wet sleeve, though Raghav cannot be sure.
What could Mummy do next time?
Mummy could keep the glass away from the toy, so that wanting the toy does not lead to a spill.
How might Mummy have felt about the splash?
Mummy seemed calm, since Mummy offered to wipe it up together instead of scolding.

It was the first hour of the festival sale, orders pouring in, when Dilnaz saw it: a data sync job was overwriting customer addresses with blank fields. Her colleague Tejas was already typing in the team chat, 'Who deployed this??'
'Not now,' Dilnaz said. She spoke her thinking aloud, to herself as much as to him. 'What gets worse every minute? Orders shipping to blank addresses. So first, stop the sync.' She paused the job. 'Next, which records are damaged? Everything since 9.40.' She restored those rows from the 9.30 backup. 'Then, customers who ordered in that window need to confirm their address.' Tejas drafted the message while she checked the restore.
By 10.25 the damage was contained. Only then did she open the deployment log. 'Now,' she said, 'we can ask who and why.'

From which backup did Dilnaz restore the rows?
From the 9.30 backup.
What was Tejas feeling as he typed 'Who deployed this??'
Tejas was alarmed and angry, reaching for someone to blame while the problem was still growing.
Why was Dilnaz's order of steps a good choice in the sale rush?
Stopping the sync first kept more addresses from being wiped during peak orders, and restoring before blaming saved minutes that mattered.
How might the customers who ordered in that window see the message?
They may be slightly annoyed to confirm their address, but it saves them from a parcel going nowhere.

At the milk cooperative on the edge of Anand, everyone knew: if the chilling-tank log was missing, Bhavna had it. If a farmer's payment slip was wrong, Bhavna had already caught it. Lalit, who sat across from her, had watched her stay back three evenings in a row that month, fixing entries others had left half done. Nobody said thank you; they just said, 'Bhavna will see.' On Monday she didn't come in. Her mother phoned: fever and exhaustion, and the doctor had told her to rest. By Tuesday the tank log was a mess and two farmers were arguing at the counter. Lalit sorted the slips as best he could and felt a small, sick shame. He had been one of the ones saying 'Bhavna will see.' That evening he began a list of everything she did, to divide among the team.

What did people say whenever something was missing?
'Bhavna will see.'
What did Lalit feel while sorting the slips on Tuesday?
He felt a small, sick shame, knowing he too had leaned on Bhavna without ever thanking her.
What could the team do so Bhavna isn't overloaded when she returns?
Share out her tasks, as Lalit's list begins to, thank her openly, and stop leaving half-done work for her to fix.
What might those evenings of fixing others' entries have been like for Bhavna?
She was probably tired and unappreciated, quietly carrying extra work until she was exhausted.
Join these with a word that shows contrast: It was cold. We played outside.
It was cold, but we played outside.

Before: Ramesh, twenty-six, had just become operations head at a small textile mill. The owner wanted to cut costs by dumping dye water into the river at night, as other mills did. Manoj, the plant supervisor, said, "Everyone does it. Nobody checks."
During: For a week Ramesh studied it. The fines, the health risk to villages downstream, the cost of a proper treatment unit, the mill's reputation with its buyers. He lost sleep. He put it all in a single page.
After: At the meeting, he presented the numbers: treating the water cost more now but protected the mill from fines and losing buyers. The owner was grumpy but agreed to install a unit in phases. Manoj said, "You thought it through." Ramesh felt relieved and exhausted.

What did the owner want to dump into the river?
Dye water, at night.
How did Ramesh feel after the meeting?
He felt relieved and exhausted after a week of lost sleep.
What made Ramesh's decision process strong?
He weighed ethics, health risk, legal fines, costs and reputation, and presented a clear case for a phased plan.
How might the villages downstream be affected by the decision?
They will be spared polluted water, protecting their health and livelihoods.
There are 400 students in a local high school. 50 percent are freshmen or sophomores.  1/5 of freshmen and sophomores own a pet.  How many freshmen and sophomores do not own a pet?

Freshman/Sophomores:400(.50)=200 students
Have pets:200/5=40 students
200-40=160 do not have pets
The answer is 160.

A gumball machine has red, green, and blue gumballs. The machine has half as many blue gumballs as red gumballs. For each blue gumball, the machine has 4 times as many green gumballs. If the machine has 16 red gumballs how many gumballs are in the machine?

There are 16/2=8 blue gumballs.
There are 8*4=32 green gumballs.
There are 16+32+8=56 total gumballs.
The answer is 56.

The second round is Friday.
What was Kishore feeling when Pranav said the answers sounded memorised?
Kishore felt embarrassed and hurt, wanting to disappear, though Kishore is now grateful for it.
What made Kishore's thank-you meaningful?
Kishore applied the feedback by rewriting answers with real examples, came back to report, and promised to share how Friday goes.

Couples counselling note, session 2.
Yamini and Gurleen arrived holding hands but sitting apart. Gurleen said she had found trading alerts on Yamini's phone and realised a large part of their shared savings had been moved without telling her. She said, "I'm not angry about the money. I'm scared. I don't know what else I don't know."
Yamini's first response was defensive: "I'm not a child. I know what I'm doing." I asked Yamini to repeat back what Gurleen had just said. After a pause, Yamini said, "You're scared, not angry." Her voice softened.
We discussed what transparency could look like for them. They agreed to share all holdings in one list by Sunday, to set together a small amount Yamini can experiment with, and to consult a registered financial adviser jointly.
Gurleen cried a little at the end, relieved. Next session: review the list.

What did Gurleen find on Yamini's phone?
Trading alerts, showing that a large part of their shared savings had been moved.
What was Gurleen feeling, in her own words?
She was scared, not angry, because she didn't know what else she didn't know.
What did the couple agree to do?
Share all holdings in one list by Sunday, set together a small amount for experimenting, and consult a registered financial adviser jointly.
How did Yamini's reaction change during the session?
Yamini was defensive at first, then softened after repeating Gurleen's words and hearing the fear behind them.

It was ten at night on the Siliguri bypass when the traffic officer flagged me down. My pollution certificate had expired two weeks earlier; I had simply forgotten. He looked at it, then at me. "Fine is big, madam. Or we settle here, small amount, no receipt." For a second I was tempted. I was tired, my brother Madhav was asleep in the passenger seat, and the small amount really was smaller. Then I thought about where that money would go, and how easily it could become a habit. "I'll pay the official challan, please," I said. "With a receipt." He shrugged and wrote it out; I paid on my phone right there. Madhav woke and asked what happened. I'm Dolma, and I was annoyed with myself for forgetting, and oddly proud of that receipt.

Why was Dolma flagged down on the bypass?
Dolma's pollution certificate had expired two weeks earlier.
Why was Dolma tempted for a second?
Dolma was tired and the small amount really was smaller, so settling on the spot felt tempting and easier.
Why was asking for the official challan with a receipt the wiser choice?
The official fine was lawful and recorded, while a private payment would have been a bribe that could become a habit and bring more trouble.
How might the officer have taken Dolma's request?
The officer just shrugged and wrote it out, which suggests the hint was routine and a firm, polite refusal ended it.

I used to tell everyone I'm a pressure person. Put me in front of a deadline and I light up. In second year, Lavanya and I had a group report on water tariffs due Monday. She wanted to start on Wednesday. I said, relax, I'll do my half on Sunday night, that's when I'm brilliant. And honestly, the first few hours felt amazing, the tea, the silence of the hostel, my heart racing like a cricket chase. By three I was copying my own sentences twice. By five my eyes burned and I had a headache that lasted all of Monday. Lavanya read my part in the corridor and fixed two wrong numbers with a pen before we submitted. Looking back, I don't think I was brilliant that night. I think I was just awake, and scared, and calling it energy. I'm Yash, by the way, still unlearning this.

When did Lavanya want to start the group report?
She wanted to start on Wednesday.
Why did working on Sunday night feel exciting to Yash at first?
The racing heart and the silence felt like a thrill, so Yash felt energised and confident; later Yash recognised it was mostly fear and exhaustion.
What could Yash try on the next group report?
Yash could agree to a draft on an earlier day and treat the night before as only for checking, which keeps some urgency without the risk.
What is it like for Lavanya when Yash leaves everything to Sunday night?
Lavanya likely feels anxious and burdened, having to catch mistakes in the corridor just before submission.

The NGO office in Lucknow was quiet at 10 pm except for Farhan's keyboard. The donor report was due at midnight, and the reading-camp numbers were short. Two villages had flooded in August, and attendance had fallen.
If the numbers looked bad, the grant might not be renewed, and Farhan would be the officer who lost it. Sunaina had trusted him with his first big project.
He looked at the attendance sheet. Sixty children, not a hundred. The donor is a huge foundation, he thought. The kids really did learn. What are forty names on paper, compared to what we actually did? He wasn't lying about the work, only about the count. He was an honest person having a hard week.
He typed "100". Then he sat back and looked at it for a long time, mouth dry.
At 11:52 he pressed send.

How many children actually attended?
Sixty children, not a hundred.
What was Farhan afraid of as the deadline approached?
Farhan was afraid of losing the grant and letting Sunaina down, which pushed him to excuse the false count.
What could Farhan do now that the report is sent?
Write to Sunaina and the donor with the real attendance and the flood explanation before anyone relies on the false number.
How might Sunaina feel if she later learned the count was changed?
Sunaina would likely feel betrayed and anxious, having trusted Farhan with his first big project and now facing the donor's doubts.

Monday, heavy rain. Nikita, two, whines and pulls at her wet frock, but can't say why. Her Mamma guesses: hungry? sleepy? Nikita cries harder.
Thursday. Nazia Aunty from next door teaches her a sign: hands hugging her chest, then the word "cold". Nikita copies it, giggling.
The next Monday, rain again. Nikita hugs her chest and says, "Cold, Mamma. Sweater." Mamma understands at once, and Nikita holds up her arms to be dressed, calm.

What sign did Nazia Aunty teach?
Hands hugging her chest, then the word 'cold'.
What was Nikita feeling on Monday when she whined and cried harder?
Nikita felt uncomfortable and frustrated because she couldn't make her need understood.
How did the sign help Nikita?
It gave her a simple way to show and say her need, so Mamma could respond quickly.
How might Mamma feel the next Monday?
Mamma would likely feel relieved and pleased that Nikita could tell her what she needed.
My school choir has a concert next month and I got a small solo.
Congratulations! A solo, even a small one, means the teacher trusts your voice. How do you feel about it?
Excited but scared. My voice shakes when I'm nervous.

That is common, even for experienced singers. Slow breathing helps. Before your part, breathe in for four counts and out for six. Practising the solo many times also helps, because your body learns it and needs less effort on the day.
Should I practise in front of people first?
Yes, start small. Sing it for your family, then for a friend or two. Each small audience makes the real one feel less strange.

In the Hyderabad design studio, Devika had spent six months showing Shankar, the new junior, everything she had learned the hard way: how to talk to clients who say "make it pop", how to name files so nobody panics later. At the Friday review, the client loved the new logo. The director turned to Devika. "Brilliant work." "It's Shankar's," she said. "The colour idea was all his. I just asked questions." Shankar went red. Two months later he was offered the lead on the bank project, the one Devika had half hoped for. That evening she felt a small sting, sitting with her cold coffee. Then she messaged him: Proud of you. Call me if a client says "pop" 🙂 He replied with three laughing faces and a question about fonts.

Which project was Shankar offered the lead on?
The bank project.
What did Devika feel when Shankar got the bank project?
She felt a small sting of disappointment, since she had half hoped for it herself, but she chose pride in him and messaged him warmly.
What did Devika do that a good mentor would copy?
She gave Shankar public credit for the colour idea at the review instead of taking it, and kept supporting him after he moved ahead.
What would change if Devika had accepted the director's praise?
Shankar would have stayed invisible, might not have been offered the lead, and would probably trust her less as a mentor.
Write a six-line poem for kids about a pair of red rain boots that love puddles.

My little boots are bright and red,
They splash through puddles, so I said,
"Let's jump in every pool we see,
As deep and wide as it can be!"
My boots cheer loudly, splish and splash,
And off we go in a happy dash.

Every evening for three weeks, Kashish practised bhangra on the terrace of her building in Andheri, with Kamal Sir's recording playing from a phone propped on a flowerpot. The shoulder bounce kept going wrong. Her arms ached and she stamped her foot, annoyed. But on the fifteenth evening, the steps suddenly fit the dhol beat, and her face broke into a grin. She danced it twice more just to feel it. Later she told Mummy, "When I do the jump with my arms up, I feel like Nanaji at the wedding." Mummy's eyes went soft; Nanaji lived far away in Ludhiana now. At the next class Kamal Sir said, "Your shoulders finally trust the beat." Kashish stood a little taller.

Where did Kashish practise bhangra?
On the terrace of her building in Andheri.
What was Kashish feeling when the steps finally fit the beat?
She felt proud and delighted after weeks of frustration, grinning and dancing it twice more just to feel it.
What helped Kashish's skill and confidence grow?
Practising every evening even when it kept going wrong, and a specific comment from Kamal Sir about her shoulders trusting the beat.
Why might Mummy's eyes have gone soft?
Mummy probably felt a pang of longing, because Kashish's jump reminded her of Nanaji, who now lives far away.

Every evening when Mummy says, "Aparna, dishes," my sister lets out a huge groan, flops her head back and says, "Whyyyy?" It's like a daily show.
Mummy never lectures. She just says, "Groan noted. Dishes by eight." And Aparna always does them, still grumbling.
But on Sunday it was different. Aparna came back from basketball and groaned when Mummy called her, but it was a low, sharp sound, and she was holding her wrist.
Mummy heard it straight away. She came over. "That's not your dishes groan. Show me."
Aparna's wrist was swollen. Mummy put ice on it and took her to the clinic.
I didn't know Mummy could tell groans apart. But she can.
- Harsha

What does Mummy say when Aparna groans about dishes?
"Groan noted. Dishes by eight."
What was Aparna feeling when she groaned on Sunday?
Aparna was hurting and probably scared about her swollen wrist, not just protesting chores.
How does Mummy handle the everyday groans, and why does it work?
She responds lightly with a clear expectation, which avoids a fight and still gets the dishes done.
How did Harsha see the difference between the two groans?
Harsha didn't notice it at first but saw Mummy recognise the pain groan and act on it.

metadata.subtype: Groaning, moaning and huffing at demands [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tuesday, 11:40 pm
The college fined our whole class for the noise at the fest. In the class group, people started blaming Kavitha because she was the one who played the speaker. Someone posted, “Thanks Kavitha for the fine 🙄.” Then it was twenty messages.
I sent a laughing emoji. Just one. I wasn't going to write anything, but I knew if I stayed silent someone would say, “Hemant, you were dancing right next to the speaker.” So I laughed.
I felt so relieved when the chat moved on.
Now I can't sleep. I was dancing next to the speaker. We all were. Kavitha hasn't posted anything since 8 pm.
Tomorrow I'll message her. I'll say sorry.
Hemant

What did the college fine the class for?
The college fined them for the noise at the fest.
How did Hemant feel when the chat moved on, and later?
Hemant felt relieved when the chat moved on, but later guilty and unable to sleep.
Is Hemant's plan a good one, and what else could help?
Yes; apologising to Kavitha is a start, and saying in the group that everyone was dancing would share the blame fairly.
How might Kavitha be feeling, not posting since 8 pm?
She is probably hurt and alone, blamed by twenty messages for something the whole class did.

(Kashish, at his desk, the evening before the vendor call)
Avni: tmrw's call with the printing vendor, should I let them quote first?
Kashish: remember last month? they said 2 lakh first and we spent an hour arguing down to 1.7
Avni: ugh yes 😩 felt like a win at the time
Kashish: it wasn't. market rate was 1.3. their number ran the whole conversation
Avni: so what do we do
Kashish: I've pulled 4 quotes from other vendors. range is 1.2 to 1.4
Kashish: we open with 1.25 and explain why, before they say anything
Avni: and if they throw out 2 again?
Kashish: we go back to our sheet, not their number 👍
Avni: ok sending you the specs now 🙏

What range did Kashish find from the other vendors' quotes?
The range from the 4 quotes was 1.2 to 1.4.
Why did last month's deal feel like a win to Avni at the time?
They had argued down from the vendor's 2 lakh, so 1.7 felt like a big saving; only later did it turn out to be well above the market rate.
Which part of Kashish's plan protects them from the vendor's first figure?
Opening with 1.25 and a reason, backed by four real quotes, puts their own researched number on the table first and gives them a sheet to return to if the vendor says 2 again.
How might the vendor experience the call if the plan works?
The vendor would have to respond to a figure backed by other quotes, so a high opening would carry less weight and the talk would stay near the market rate.

Ed booked a hotel while he was on vacation. Staying at the hotel cost was $1.50 per hour every night and $2 per hour every morning. If Ed had $80 and he stayed in the hotel for 6 hours last night and 4 hours this morning, how much money was he left with after paying for his stay at the hotel?

Ed spent $1.50 x 6 = $9 for staying in the hotel last night.
He spent $2 x 4 = $8 for staying in the hotel this morning
So, the total money he spent in the hotel is $9 + $8 = $17.
Therefore, he still has $80 - $17 = $63 left after staying in the hotel.
The answer is 63.

Zainab realised in the metro that she had left the gas on low under the dal that morning, and that Aditi, her flatmate, must have come home to a smoky flat and a burnt pot. Aditi had texted only, "Please call." Zainab's stomach knotted. That evening, standing in the kitchen doorway, she said, "I left the gas on and forgot the dal. I'm sorry for the smell, and for the risk. I've bought a timer for the kitchen and I'll cook the next three dinners." Aditi, arms crossed, said, "It was scary." Zainab nodded. "I know." She didn't launch into a list of how awful she was. She scrubbed the pot, and Aditi, after a while, dried it.

What did Zainab buy for the kitchen?
A timer.
What was Zainab feeling in the metro?
Her stomach knotted, so she was anxious and guilty about the smoky flat.
How could Zainab keep her apology in proportion?
She can name what happened, say sorry for the effect and repair with a concrete change, without long self-blame.
How might Aditi have felt coming home?
Scared and annoyed at coming home to smoke, as Aditi's crossed arms and "It was scary" show. 😔

Gunther just financed a John Deere tractor through the dealership.  If his monthly payment is $150.00 a month, for 5 years, with no interest, how much did he finance the tractor for?

There are 12 months in 1 year and his loan is for 5 years so that's 12*5 = 60 months
His monthly payment is $150.00 and he pays this for 60 months so his loan for the tractor was 150*60 = $9,000.00
The answer is 9000.

At the Rotterdam warehouse, Lucia was closing the last delivery when Mateo pulled her by the shelves. "I skipped the crane check this morning, no time. I signed the sheet anyway. Keep it quiet, yes? You'd do it for me." She liked Mateo. He had covered her shift when her mother was ill. Her stomach tightened. "Mateo, I can't lie for you. If someone asks me, I'll tell the truth." He blinked. "So what do I do?" "Do the check now, before the afternoon shift, and tell the supervisor it was late. I'll stay with you while you do it." They walked to the crane together in silence. Lucia was not sure Mateo forgave her, but she felt lighter than if she had joined the silence.

Which check did Mateo skip?
Mateo skipped the crane check.
Why did Lucia's stomach tighten when Mateo asked her to keep quiet?
Lucia felt torn: she liked Mateo and owed him for covering her shift, but she could not lie for him.
What could Lucia do if Mateo refuses to tell the supervisor?
She can remind Mateo she will not lie if asked, encourage him again, and report it to the supervisor herself if the risk continues.
How might Mateo have felt when Lucia refused?
He blinked and asked what to do, so he was probably surprised and worried. He may also have felt let down by a friend, since Lucia was not sure he forgave her.
Make this more concise: Due to the fact that it was raining, the match was cancelled.
The match was cancelled because of the rain.

First day of the summer holidays: Manoj climbed the old mango tree behind his building, higher than anyone ever had. "Come down, the top branches are thin," Disha called. "Other kids fall. Not me," he said, swinging one leg.
Thursday: After a night of storm, the branches were wet. Manoj climbed anyway, sure he'd be fine. A branch cracked. He slid, grabbed the trunk and landed hard, scraping his knee. Disha ran to fetch Manoj's Nani, who cleaned the scrape, sat with him on the steps and made him promise: no climbing above the first fork.
The next Monday: Knee bandaged, Manoj watched Rinku start up the trunk. "Stop at the fork!" Manoj shouted, then added quietly, "I really thought it couldn't happen to me."

What happened when Manoj climbed the wet tree on Thursday?
A branch cracked, he slid, grabbed the trunk and landed hard, scraping his knee.
Why was Manoj so sure he wouldn't fall?
He felt confident and brave, believing falls happen to other kids, so Disha's warning didn't seem to apply to him.
What could help Manoj judge risks better?
He could remember that thin, wet branches are just as risky for him as for anyone, and keep Nani's rule of stopping at the first fork.
How might Disha have felt when the branch cracked?
Disha was probably frightened, which is why Disha ran to fetch Manoj's Nani right away.

Tenzin had three weeks until Diwali, when all eleven cousins would squeeze into Masi's flat. He wanted to do a show: three tricks, polished. The trouble was time. Tuition took two evenings a week, and his little sister Madhuri kept borrowing the rope for her doll's swing. So he wrote the plan on the back of his maths notebook: week one, coin vanish; week two, card rise; week three, rope trick, then all three together on the last two days. He practised twenty minutes on non-tuition nights and hid the rope in his school bag. In week two he still fumbled the card, so he dropped a fancy flourish and kept the trick simple. On Diwali night Madhuri held the hat, and nobody noticed the card came up a bit crooked.

How many cousins were coming for Diwali?
All eleven cousins were coming, to Masi's flat.
What might Tenzin have been worried about when he wrote the plan?
He was probably anxious about having only three weeks, with two tuition evenings a week and the rope going missing, and feared the tricks wouldn't be ready.
What else could Tenzin do if a trick still wasn't ready near Diwali?
Cut it down, as he did with the card, or do only two tricks well, because a small polished show beats three shaky ones.
What might the show be like for Madhuri?
Holding the hat lets her be part of it, so she may feel proud and included rather than just the one who kept taking the rope.

metadata.subtype: Approach: setting a mini goal to show family [Action]

messages.content: I'm going on a student exchange to another country for a month and I'll stay with a host family.
What an adventure. A month in a new home will teach you a lot. How do you feel about it?
Excited, but I worry I'll say the wrong thing.
Be polite, listen carefully and ask when you're unsure. People usually appreciate effort more than perfection.
What should I bring for the family?
A small gift from your region, like sweets, a handicraft or a book of local photographs. Ask the exchange coordinator if there are things to avoid.
What about food? I'm a vegetarian.
Tell the coordinator and the host family before you arrive. Explain it simply and kindly, and thank them for adapting.
I'll mention it in my first email. Any tip for homesickness?
Call home at a fixed, short time, keep a small reminder of home and join family activities. Homesick days pass faster when you're busy and talking to people.
I want to learn how to right a good essay. Which word is wrong?

I want to learn how to write a good essay.
Why: spelling ("right" -> "write").

Monday, the first monsoon rain: Sharmila scolded Rajni for splashing the balcony bucket. Rajni scowled, then threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.

Wednesday, still raining: told off for tearing a book, Rajni grabbed Pinky's bottle and hurled it. Sharmila held Rajni's hands. "You're angry with me. Hit the pillow."

Saturday, rain drumming on the window: another "no". Rajni's fists clenched. She looked at Pinky, then thumped the pillow, hard.

What did Rajni throw at Pinky on Monday?
Rajni threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.
What does Rajni's scowl before throwing the duck suggest?
Rajni was angry at being scolded by Sharmila, and that anger went to Pinky, the smaller and safer target.
Which change helped by Saturday, and why?
Sharmila named Rajni's anger and offered the pillow, so by Saturday the anger had a safe place to go instead of Pinky.
How might Pinky be affected over these days?
Pinky gets hit by a duck and a bottle for no reason Pinky can understand, which may leave Pinky startled and wary of Rajni.

I still remember standing outside the hostel gate in Nainital with our bags, reading a paper sign: "Full. Sorry." Our online booking had simply vanished. I'm Kamal, and for about a minute I wanted to sit down on the road and cry. Usha didn't. She pulled out our list of backup places, handed me one number and dialled the other. Mine was a dharamshala near the market, 300 a night. Hers was a homestay, 550. We put Usha's father on speaker and read him both addresses, and he asked to talk to the homestay owner himself. Ten minutes later he called back: "The homestay. The family sounds careful." That was 250 more each for our one night, so we cut it from our food money and ate street noodles instead of café meals. I updated the shared sheet sitting on a bench.

How much did the dharamshala cost a night?
The dharamshala near the market cost 300 a night.
What was Kamal feeling on reading the sign?
Kamal felt shocked and close to tears, wanting to sit down on the road and cry.
Which step would you keep for any future trip, and why?
Keeping a list of backup places with phone numbers, because it let them call two options within minutes instead of searching from scratch at the gate.
How did Usha's father see the choice?
He wanted to judge the place himself, so he spoke to the homestay owner and chose it because the family sounded careful.

messages.content: Mr. Kapoor gave us a group project, and one teammate does nothing.
That is a common problem in group work. Before anything else, talk to the teammate in private and ask if something is making it hard to help.
What if they still don't contribute?
Then tell your teacher calmly, with a list of the tasks that are done and the ones that are missing. Teachers can step in and divide the work more fairly.
