Rain drummed on the roof of the crèche, and only a few minutes were left before the parents came. Pankaj wanted Ishita's doll in the yellow dress, and Ishita wanted the red toy truck in Pankaj's hands. Pankaj held the truck out. "You have the truck, I have the doll, then we swap back." Ishita paused, then nodded and put the doll in his arms. Ishita drove the truck under the table with engine noises while Pankaj brushed the doll's hair. When the bell rang for pick-up, they swapped back without being told.

What did Pankaj offer to swap for the doll?
Pankaj offered the red toy truck.
What was Pankaj feeling about the doll before he made his offer?
Pankaj wanted a turn with the doll and was hopeful about getting one. The truck was his way of asking for it.
What other approach could work if Ishita had said no, and why?
They could ask a grown-up for a timer so each gets a turn with each toy. A timer gives a fair count neither has to argue over.
How does the swap look to Ishita?
Ishita gets the truck that was wanted, so the trade feels fair. Swapping back when the bell rang shows Ishita trusted it.
Pen a short story about a girl who lights her first sparkler on Diwali.

Prisha had watched her older cousins light sparklers for three years, and now she was finally allowed to try. Her mother handed her one with a bucket of water nearby. Prisha's hand shook as the tip touched the flame. It hissed, spat, and burst into silver stars. She yelped and nearly dropped it. But then she waved it in a slow circle and drew a glowing ring in the dark. Everyone clapped. She lit another one, and wrote her name in the air with it. By the end of the night, she had used twelve and wanted twelve more. Her mother laughed and said, "Tomorrow, beta."
How do I get my son to clean his room without nagging?
Children respond better to clear, simple expectations than to repeated reminders. How old is your son, and what does he usually say when you ask?
He is ten, Ruby is his sister. He says he will do it later and then never does.
Pick a fixed time, like Saturday morning after breakfast, and make it a routine. A written checklist, such as books, clothes and bed, helps him know exactly what to finish.
Should I reward him?
A small reward can help, like choosing the dinner menu or an extra half hour of play. Praise matters most. Tell him specifically what he did well, like making his bed.
And what about his sister Ruby, should she have the same checklist?
Yes, give Ruby her own checklist suited to her age, so both children have the same system. That keeps it fair, and neither will feel they are doing more than the other.

Tariq, twenty-four, went to the funeral of his colleague's father in Leeds mostly out of politeness. He had barely met the man. He stood at the back of the chapel with his friend Liam. Then the family played an old piano piece, and a grandson, maybe eight, stood at the front holding his mother's hand, trying hard not to cry. Tariq's chest tightened. He was eight again, at his own grandfather's burial in Lahore, the smell of rain and rosewater, being told to be a brave boy. He had never cried for his grandfather. He thought he'd forgotten most of it. Now his eyes stung so badly he had to step outside. Liam followed and stood with him by the wall. "I don't even know why," Tariq said. "Maybe you do," Liam said quietly.

Where was Tariq's grandfather buried?
In Lahore.
Why did the grandson at the front affect Tariq so strongly?
Seeing a boy his own age then brought back his grandfather's burial, and Tariq was overwhelmed by grief he had never let out.
What could Tariq do with this feeling now that it has returned?
He could let himself talk about his grandfather with Liam or someone close, instead of pushing the grief away again.
How might Liam see Tariq's reaction at the funeral of a man Tariq barely knew?
Liam seems to understand that the tears are about something older, and stays close without making Tariq explain.
Can you draw a closed figure with only 2 straight lines? With 3? With 1 straight line and 1 curved line?

Answer: 2 straight lines: no, they cannot close up. 3 straight lines: yes, a triangle. 1 straight line and 1 curved line: yes, like a half circle (or the letter D).

Give the child 2 sticks and ask them to make a closed shape: they will find it impossible - there is always a gap. With 3 sticks they make a triangle. Then give a stick and a bent pipe cleaner: they can make a D. So the fewest straight lines for a closed figure with only straight sides is 3.

Here is a passage about Orlick. In what ways does he show he dislikes the narrator?

This morose journeyman had no liking for me. When I was very small and timid, he gave me to understand that the Devil lived in a black corner of the forge, and that he knew the fiend very well: also that it was necessary to make up the fire, once in seven years, with a live boy, and that I might consider myself fuel. When I became Joe's 'prentice, Orlick was perhaps confirmed in some suspicion that I should displace him; howbeit, he liked me still less. Not that he ever said anything, or did anything, openly importing hostility; I only noticed that he always beat his sparks in my direction, and that whenever I sang Old Clem, he came in out of time.
He never acts openly. He frightened the narrator as a small boy with talk of the Devil, and now he beats his sparks towards him and comes in out of time when he sings.

At the café in Stockholm where they both worked weekends, the new manager kept giving Jamal the back room and the dish pit, never the counter. On Tuesday he said to Jamal, loud enough to hear, "Customers prefer a more Swedish face at the front."

Anders felt heat rush up his neck. Before Jamal could answer, Anders stepped in. "That's discrimination. You can't say that. I'm reporting you."

On the walk home Jamal was silent. Finally he said, "You made it about you, man. I didn't get to say anything."

Anders stopped on the bridge. His first instinct was to defend himself. Instead he asked, "You're right. What do you want to do?"

"I want to write the complaint. In my words. You can sign as a witness."

They wrote it together that night at Jamal's kitchen table, Jamal typing, Anders reading over his shoulder only when asked.

What did the manager say customers preferred?
He said customers prefer a more Swedish face at the front.
How did Anders feel when the manager spoke, and what did he do?
Anders felt angry and protective, and stepped in to confront the manager before Jamal could answer.
What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
Anders spoke over Jamal and made it his own fight; asking Jamal what he wanted and acting as a witness fixed it.
How did Jamal experience Anders stepping in?
Jamal felt sidelined, as if the moment had been taken from him, even though Anders meant well.
My brother plays the flute and says I should try it too. Is it hard?
A flute is easy to start but takes time to sound good. Many beginners find it hard at first to make a clear note, and that is normal.
How long before I can play a tune?
Many people manage a simple tune within a few weeks of regular practice. Short, daily sessions help your lips and breath learn the right shape. Your brother can show you the basics.

At the Monday review in the bank branch in Lucknow, Mehak, the branch manager, wrote two names on the whiteboard under Stars: the officers who had sold the most insurance with every loan. Nobody asked how. Everyone knew some customers didn't understand what they had signed.
Hansa's name wasn't there. Last month she had asked, in this same meeting, whether elderly customers should have the policy terms read aloud. Mehak had smiled and said, "Hansa, let's keep the focus on targets." Since then Hansa had been moved from the big accounts to the counter, and left off the team lunch.
Now, looking at the stars, she felt the familiar tightness in her chest. She had rent. Her father's medicines. And the team had been kind to her when she joined.
When Mehak asked, "Any concerns before we close?", Hansa looked down at her notebook and said nothing. Nobody else did either.

What were the officers under Stars known for?
They had sold the most insurance with every loan.
What did Hansa feel when Mehak asked for concerns?
She felt anxious and afraid for her job, and torn by loyalty to the team, so she stayed silent.
What could Hansa do outside that meeting?
Note her concern in writing and take it to a proper channel, such as the bank's compliance or ethics office, rather than carry it alone.
How does Mehak seem to see concerns raised in meetings?
Mehak treats them as distractions from targets and quietly sidelines those who raise them.
Vivian is responsible for making sure her students get 2 15-minute recess breaks a day, a 30-minute lunch and another 20-minute recess break.  How much time do her students spend outside of class?

They get 2 15 minute breaks a day so that's 2*15 = 30 minutes
They get 30 minutes for lunch and 20 minutes for recess plus an additional 30 minutes of recess for a total of 30+20+30 = 80 minutes spent outside of class
The answer is 80.

Class teacher's note, Christmas week. Written by Indu.
Siddharth, nine, is one of our most careful switchers. Today his Ajji came to see the carol practice. He ran to her and chatted in Kannada, soft and polite. The sum of Cooper's, Dante's, and Maria's ages is 31. Dante is twice as old as Cooper. Maria is one year older than Dante. How old is Cooper?

Let X be the age of Cooper. So Dante is X*2 years old and Maria is X*2 + 1 year old.
The sum of Cooper's, Dante's, and Maria's ages is X + (X*2) + (X*2 + 1) = 31.
Combining like terms, we get X*5 + 1 = 31.
Subtracting one from both sides, we get X*5 = 30.
Dividing both sides by 5, we get X = 6 years old.
The answer is 6.

Use product-to-sum formulas to show cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8 and write 2 sin 3x cos x as a sum.

Answer: 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x; cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 1/8.

2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B), so 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x. For the product of three cosines, a cleverer route uses sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A repeatedly. Multiply and divide by 8 sin 20 degrees: 8 sin 20 degrees cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 4 sin 40 degrees cos 40 degrees cos 80 degrees = 2 sin 80 degrees cos 80 degrees = sin 160 degrees Since sin 160 degrees = sin 20 degrees, the product is sin 20 degrees/(8 sin 20 degrees) = 1/8. By product-to-sum instead: cos 20 degrees cos 40 degrees = (cos 20 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2; times cos 80 degrees: (cos 20 degrees cos 80 degrees + (1/2) cos 80 degrees)/2 = ((cos 100 degrees + cos 60 degrees)/2 + cos 80 degrees/2)/2 = (1/2)(1/2)(cos 100 degrees + cos 80 degrees + 1/2) = 1/8 because cos 100 degrees = -cos 80 degrees. Calculator: 0.9397 x 0.7660 x 0.1736 = 0.1250.

messages.content: Daisy is a poodle puppy who loves to play with her dog toys. She often loses them in various ways, and her owner needs to replace them. On Monday, Daisy played with 5 dog toys. On Tuesday, Daisy had 3 dog toys left after losing some, and her owner went to the store and got her 3 more. On Wednesday, all of Daisy's old and new dog toys were missing, so her owner went to the store and bought her 5 more. If Daisy's owner found all the lost dog toys, including the new dog toys, how many dog toys would Daisy have now?

Daisy originally had 5 dog toys on Monday + 3 more her owner bought her on Tuesday = 8 dog toys.
On Wednesday Daisy's owner bought her 5 more dog toys + 8 old ones = 13 total dog toys if none were lost.
The answer is 13.

Ms. Estrella is an entrepreneur with a startup company having 10 employees. The company makes a revenue of $400000 a month, paying 10% in taxes, 5% of the remaining amount on marketing and ads, 20% of the remaining amount on operational costs, and 15% of the remaining amount on employee wages.  Assuming each employee receives the same wage, calculate the amount of money each employee is paid monthly.

The company pays a total of 10/100*$400000 = $40000 on taxes
After taxes, the company revenue is $400000-$40000 = $360,000
The costs of marketing and ads campaign are 5/100*$360000 = $18000
After deducting the costs of marketing and adds campaign, the company remains with = $342,000 in revenue
Operational costs for the company are 20/100*$342000 = $68400
After taking out the operational costs, the company remains with $342000-$68400 = $273600
The company also pays employee wages of 15/100*$273600 =$41040
If the total number of employees is 10, each employee is paid a salary of $41040/10 = $4104 per month
The answer is 4104.

In 8 years, Christian will be 64+8 = 72 years old.

Two boys build a raft and float it down a stream. Write that as a story.

Rohan and his cousin Faisal spent three days gathering planks, rope and empty plastic bottles from the lane behind their houses. On Sunday, they lashed everything together and carried the raft to the village stream.

"It looks like a pile of rubbish," said Faisal.

"It looks like a ship," said Rohan.

Phil has a coin collection he likes to add to.  He started with 50 state quarters his parents gave him.  Over the next year he doubled this.  The following year he collected 3 each month.  The year after that he collected 1 every third month.  The year after that he lost a quarter of them when he misplaced his collection.  How many did he have left after losing some?

Phil started with 50, and doubled this amount the next year for 50*2=100 coins
Phil then collected 3 per month the following year, and since there are 12 months in a year that was 3*12=36 coins added
Phil then collected 1 every third month, and since there are 12 months that means he collected one every 12/3=4 months, for 4 coins added
Before he lost a quarter of his coins, Phil had 100+36+4 coins, or 140 coins in total.
Losing a quarter of 140 coins means Phill lost 140/4=35 coins
That means Phil had 140-35= 105 coins remaining
The answer is 105.

Using pliers on a tap nut turned a small job into a broken part and a whole morning for the plumber, which the right tool would have avoided.
How does Yusuf react to Santosh's tool box?
Yusuf is amused and a little impressed, laughing that Santosh has a screwdriver for everything, perhaps remembering the cracked tap with regret.

'Ankita, you're scared to tell Ma'am you lost the class register? Let your Ishita Bua tell you what happened to me. In Class 5, I was in charge of the class goldfish for the holidays. I forgot to feed it for four days, and it died. I thought my teacher, Mr Pinto, would shout the roof down. I almost lied and said it was sick. Instead, on the first day back, I stood at his desk and told him everything, crying. He didn't shout. He sat me down and said, "Thank you for being honest. What do you think we should do now?" We made a feeding chart together for the next fish. My whole body felt light. And after that, he trusted me with the class keys.'

How many days did young Ishita forget to feed the goldfish?
Four days.
How did young Ishita feel when Mr Pinto didn't shout?
Relieved; her whole body felt light after telling the truth.
What choice in the story earned young Ishita trust?
Telling Mr Pinto the truth instead of saying the fish was sick.
How did Mr Pinto see Ishita's honesty?
As something to thank and build on; he helped make a feeding chart and later trusted her with the class keys.

Thursday: Zubin, five, peers at Chachi's baby asleep in the cradle. 'Why doesn't she have a name yet?' Dadi says, 'On Sunday everyone will come and give it to her.'
Sunday: Forty people squeeze into the flat. The pandit whispers into the baby's ear, and Chacha announces, 'Sharmila!' Everyone claps. Zubin tries to count the guests and gives up.
Monday: Zubin asks Mumma, 'Why did so many people come for one tiny baby?' Mumma says, 'Because she belongs to all of us now. Like you do.' Zubin leans over the cradle. 'Hi, Sharmila. I'm yours too.'

Who announced the baby's name?
Chacha.
What was Zubin feeling when he asked why so many people came?
He felt curious and a little amazed, puzzled that one tiny baby could bring so many people together.
What did Mumma's answer give Zubin?
A simple reason he could understand, that a baby belongs to the whole family, which helped him feel part of the welcome too.
What would it mean for baby Sharmila to grow up with so many people at her naming?
She would grow up knowing a big circle of family counts her as their own, just as Mumma said.

Science note, Class 4. Teacher: Pema.
Today we did “sink or float.” Before each test, children wrote a guess.
Yusuf (nine) guessed the big wooden block would sink, “because it's heavy.” It floated. He stared at it. He guessed the small steel key would float, “because it's tiny.” It sank.
He said, “Wait. It's not about big or small.” He tried a plastic lid, then a coin, writing each result.
At the end he wrote: “My guesses were wrong but I learned something.”
Next step: we'll try the same objects in salty water next week.

What did Yusuf guess about the wooden block?
He guessed it would sink, because it's heavy.
How did Yusuf feel when the wooden block floated?
He was surprised and puzzled, staring at it.
What did Yusuf do after his guesses were wrong?
He tested more objects and wrote each result, changing his idea about size.
How might the teacher feel reading Yusuf's final sentence?
The teacher likely feels pleased that Yusuf learned from his wrong guesses 🙂
Switch to the past tense: I am nervous before every test.
I was nervous before every test.

Jatin had been offered a transfer to the Guwahati branch: a better role, a new city, no friends there. His sister Arohi found him at the dining table of their Chennai flat, making a list. "Worst case?" he read aloud. "I hate it, I'm lonely, I come back in a year." "Survivable?" she asked. "Yes. The company lets you apply back after twelve months." "Best likely case?" "I lead my own team. I learn Assamese. I see mountains." Arohi grinned. "And plan B?" He tapped the page: keep his room in the flat share for three months, a weekend call with old friends, a list of Chennai openings saved. He wasn't reckless. He wasn't frozen either. He signed the transfer letter.

Where was Jatin's transfer to?
The Guwahati branch.
How did Jatin feel as he worked through the list?
He felt steady and clear, neither reckless nor frozen.
What did Jatin's list include that made the risk sensible?
The worst case, whether it was survivable, the likely gain, and a plan B.
How might Arohi feel about her brother leaving?
Arohi seems supportive and proud, though she may miss him.

What does Mummy making the extra chapati "in case" suggest?

messages.content:
Read this:

"Abhinav, you've said 'whatever' three times today. Come, sit with your Ira Dadi. It was the winter I was eight, with fog so thick we couldn't see the gate.
Every evening my father made me practise handwriting on a slate. I tried round letters, he said too round. I tried thin letters, he said too thin. I wrote slowly, he said lazy. I wrote fast, he said careless. I cried, I tried again, and nothing I did was ever right.
By January, I stopped trying. I'd scratch any shape and hand it to him. When he asked why, I said, 'Whatever I do, it's wrong anyway.' And honestly, it felt sensible. Why work hard if the answer is always no?
It took a new teacher, who praised one good 'a' of mine, to show me effort could change something."

What did young Ira practise every evening?
She practised handwriting on a slate.
Why did young Ira stop trying by January?
She felt defeated and hopeless, because every kind of effort was called wrong, so giving up seemed sensible.
What was the turning point in Ira Dadi's story?
A new teacher praised one good 'a', which showed her that effort could actually change something.
How might Ira's father have seen her scratching any shape?
He may have thought she was being careless or stubborn, not realising his constant criticism had convinced her that trying was pointless.
Tell children, in a paragraph of 55 words, why saving a little coin each week teaches a good habit.

Saving a little each week teaches us patience. When you put a coin in a jar, you wait for it to grow into something bigger. You learn that small amounts add up, and that you can plan for a future wish. It also helps you think before you spend. A small habit can become a strong one.

On the first morning of summer camp at the community centre, the other children rushed to the craft tables. Dilnaz stood by the water cooler for twenty minutes, watching: who shared the glue, who grabbed, who laughed kindly. Aunty Rosy, the camp leader, came over, frowning. 'Aren't you happy here?' 'I am,' Dilnaz said. 'I'm just looking first.' Then she walked to the end of the table where one boy, Darshan, was carefully cutting paper birds, and sat beside him. By Friday they were a pair, finishing each other's kites, and she still spent snack break reading alone on the steps, humming.

Where did Dilnaz stand on the first morning?
By the water cooler.
Why did Dilnaz watch for twenty minutes before joining?
She felt calmer seeing the group first and noticing who was kind; she wasn't unhappy, just careful.
How could Aunty Rosy support a child like Dilnaz?
Trust her 'I'm just looking first', give her time, and not treat reading alone at snack break as a problem.
How might Darshan see Dilnaz sitting down beside him?
Darshan probably felt glad to have one steady friend who shared his careful way of working.

Read this:

"Deepak, you've hardly said a word since the funeral."
Okay, Mahima, you asked, so. It was a pulmonary embolism. A clot, from his leg, that went up into his lung. I read that it can happen after long bed rest, and Nanu had been in bed three weeks after his knee operation. The ambulance took eleven minutes. His oxygen was in the low eighties when they got there. I looked up every term that night.
Why are you looking at me like that? I'm fine. I'm just saying what happened. Mum keeps crying in the kitchen and I keep reading. It makes more sense to me this way.
Only thing is, his reading glasses are still on the arm of the sofa, and I can't pick them up. I don't know why. I keep walking round them.
Anyway. The ambulance time matters a lot, apparently.

How long had Nanu been in bed after his knee operation?
Three weeks.
Why does it make more sense to Deepak to talk in medical terms?
Deepak feels safer with facts about the clot and the ambulance; they keep the grief of losing Nanu at a distance while the family cries around Deepak.
What moment could become a turning point for Deepak's grief?
The reading glasses on the sofa that Deepak keeps walking round; if Mahima gently asks about them, or they sit near them together, the feeling might finally have room to come out.
What might Mahima be thinking as Deepak lists oxygen levels in such an even way?
Mahima is probably worried, sensing that the calm facts are covering real sadness, and unsure whether to push or just stay close.

Read this:

Keerthana, sit with me a minute. Your Paati was nineteen once, you know. In the hostel they called me Nimmi, because Nirmala was too long to shout down a corridor. There was a boy in our chemistry batch, Mohan, who could make the whole lab laugh when a burette leaked, and who answered the professor without a single stammer. We spoke perhaps four times, near the cycle stand, about nothing much. By the fourth time I had already planned our house by the river and decided he loved old film songs the way I did. He never once mentioned songs, kutty. I painted the empty spaces with my own colours. At night I wrote his name in the margins of my notes and felt dizzy with it. Only much later did I wonder who he really was, under all my paint.

Where did Nirmala and Mohan talk?
They spoke perhaps four times, near the cycle stand, about nothing much.
What was Nirmala feeling as she planned a house by the river after only four talks?
She felt giddy and excited, so thrilled by Mohan's humour and confidence that she filled every unknown with her own hopes, like his love of film songs.
At this stage, what could the young Nirmala have done before building a whole future around Mohan?
She could have enjoyed the attraction while getting to know him slowly, asking what he actually liked instead of deciding he loved her film songs.
How might Mohan have seen those few talks by the cycle stand?
To Mohan they were probably light, friendly chats with a batchmate; he likely had no idea she had already imagined a house by the river.

Playgroup note from Zeenat, Tuesday
Anand (2½) came to me at snack time, tugged my dupatta and said, "Water, please." That's new; last month he just cried at the jug. Later he tried to open the art cupboard. I said, "That one is for teachers," and he closed it and went back to the blocks. With the class rabbit he stroked its back with two fingers, the way we practised, and whispered "soft." I've asked his father to keep using "gentle hands" at home 🙂

What did Anand say when he tugged Zeenat's dupatta?
He said, "Water, please."
What does Anand whispering "soft" to the rabbit suggest?
He seemed calm and tender with it, enjoying the gentle touch and maybe proud of doing it the practised way.
How could Anand's father support what Zeenat saw?
Keep using the same words at home, like "gentle hands", and answer quickly when Anand asks for things in words.
What would change if Zeenat had snapped at Anand for opening the cupboard?
He might have felt scared or ashamed, and a calm limit would have been harder for him to accept.
Write a paragraph for my class essay on 'Why Grandparents Are Special', about 80 words.

Grandparents are special because they have time for us. They tell stories of old days, teach us songs, and share recipes that have been in the family for years. When we are scolded, they quietly take our side. They remind us where we come from and how to be kind. A hug from a grandparent feels warm and safe. I am lucky to have mine, and I try to visit them as often as I can.

Friday: Arnab's cousin Nitin wheeled out the tall cycle. "No side wheels?" Arnab asked. "None." Arnab pushed off, pedalled three times and crashed into Nani's marigold pots. He sat in the soil, staring at his scraped palms.
Saturday: Palms taped up, Arnab tried again and again in the courtyard. Each time he counted how long before a foot hit the ground: two seconds, three, once five. He fell twice more and got up both times without a word.
Tuesday: The scabs were drying. He still gripped the handles too tightly at the start, but he rode the full length of the courtyard and turned without a foot down. Nitin clapped. Arnab said "Again," before anyone could ask.

What did Arnab crash into on Friday?
He crashed into Nani's marigold pots.
What does Arnab counting the seconds on Saturday suggest about how he felt?
He seems determined and curious to see progress, even though the falls must have stung and frightened him.
What else could help Arnab if the falls start to put him off?
He could lower the seat so his feet reach the ground, which makes each try less scary and lets him keep practising balance.
How does Arnab's week of practice look to Nitin?
Nitin sees Arnab go from crashing to turning smoothly, and is proud enough to clap on Tuesday.

It was exam week in the hostel, the lights had gone out, and Hrithik had eleven percent battery. He was saving it for the torch and the chemistry notes, but he sent one message to Ujjwal in the next wing: "Can I borrow your formula sheet tomorrow?"
Ujjwal usually replied with a grin emoji and three exclamation marks. This time: "ok."
Hrithik stared at the dot. Maybe Ujjwal was fed up with lending him things. Maybe he thought Hrithik never prepared. In the dark, with battery dropping, every guess got worse. He almost typed "forget it" but stopped. The phone showed eight percent.
He walked down the corridor with the torch instead. Ujjwal was sitting on his bed with a candle, the sheet already on top of his pile.
"Here. Sorry, I was typing with one thumb, holding the candle with the other."
Hrithik laughed so hard the candle flickered.

How much battery did Hrithik have when the lights went out?
Hrithik had eleven percent battery.
What was Hrithik worried about when he saw "ok."?
Hrithik was anxious that Ujjwal was fed up with lending him things or thought he never prepared, and the dark and stress made each guess feel worse.
What choice worked, and why?
Instead of sending "forget it", Hrithik walked down the corridor to see Ujjwal, which cleared the worry in seconds.
What would change if Hrithik had sent "forget it"?
Ujjwal would likely feel confused and hurt, since he had already put the sheet on his pile, and a small misreading could have turned into a real quarrel.

Make this shorter, in two sentences.

Yogesh, nearly two, had opened every kitchen drawer in the flat. He licked a spoon and tore the pages off an old calendar. On the balcony he stuffed a tulsi leaf into his mouth and made a face. His father, Mridul, had stopped saying "No!" every minute. Instead he had tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high, and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons, just for Yogesh.

Nearly two, Yogesh opened every kitchen drawer in the flat, licking a spoon, tearing an old calendar and tasting a tulsi leaf. His father, Mridul, stopped saying "No!" all day and instead tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons for Yogesh.
Can you explain assistance?

Assistance is help or support. It is a noun.
Example: Do you need assistance with those heavy bags?
When people say mirrors in a shop, what are they pointing to?

Mirrors are pieces of glass with a shiny back that show your reflection. It is a noun, the plural of mirror.
Example: The dance room has mirrors on every wall so the students can check their steps.

Subject: Nani's 80th: who's doing what (please read)
Hi all,
Thanks for staying on the call past eleven. Before we forget it all like last year's anniversary plan (three calls, zero bookings), here is what we decided:
1. Venue: the community hall in Aundh, lunch on Saturday 14 June. Yash books it and sends the receipt to the group by Friday 23rd.
2. Guest list: Priti and I merge our lists into one sheet by Sunday 25th. Everyone adds missing names by Wednesday 28th.
3. Food: Mami calls the caterer from Mitali's wedding and gets two menus by Friday 30th.
4. Photo slideshow: Neel collects old photos from everyone until 5 June.
5. Gift for Nani: we decide on the next call, Sunday 1 June, 8 pm. I'll send the link.
If I've got anything wrong, reply today, not on the 13th of June.

Who is booking the community hall, and by when?
Yash books it and sends the receipt by Friday 23rd.
What does "reply today, not on the 13th of June" suggest about Jatin's feelings?
Jatin is determined and a little worried, not wanting a repeat of last year's plan that fell apart, so any mistake has to surface early.
Why does this email make last year's failure less likely?
Every decision has a named owner and a date, and it is written down for everyone, so nothing depends on memory or goodwill.
How might Yash feel seeing a name and a date beside the venue?
Yash knows exactly what is expected and when, which may feel a little pressured but also clear, with no confusion about who is booking.

Tuesday. Joseph, the senior teacher, was in the corridor with his register when little Mitu came in from recess holding a crushed paper boat, lip trembling. Anjali, twenty-four and in her first year, crouched down. She didn't ask who did it. She asked, "What happened?" Mitu said, "I put it on the step and I sat on it by mistake." Anjali wrote it in her notebook with the time, 11:05.
Wednesday. Mitu's mother came to the gate, upset. "She says Rahul crushed it." At home, Joseph learned, the first question had been, "Did someone break it?"
Friday. At the short parents' meeting, Anjali read her note aloud, word for word. Mitu's mother went quiet, then nodded. Joseph noticed how Anjali never said the child was lying, only that stories change as they are asked about.

What time did Anjali write in her notebook?
She wrote 11:05.
What does Anjali's refusal to call Mitu a liar suggest about her understanding of memory?
It suggests Anjali stays calm and caring, understanding that memory reshapes itself with each question rather than thinking the child is dishonest.
Which choice by Anjali made the difference on Friday, and why?
Asking an open "What happened?" and writing the answer down with the time gave an early, unshaped account to compare later.
How might Mitu's mother see the situation after hearing the note?
She might realise her own question, "Did someone break it?", may have planted Rahul, and feel relieved no child was being unfair to Mitu.

Monday night: Tanuja lay in bed, staring at the corner of the room where the shadows looked like a tall person. Her heart thumped, and she pulled the blanket over her nose. She snapped at her sister in the morning for no reason. Tuesday: she told Zeenat didi in a small voice. Zeenat didn't laugh. She went to the corner with Tanuja, and they saw it was just a coat on a hook. "It looked scary, though," Zeenat said. That night she plugged a little lamp in. Two weeks later: Tanuja noticed the lamp had been off since Saturday. The corner was just a corner again, and she was asleep before she remembered to check.

What did Tanuja and Zeenat find in the corner?
They found it was just a coat on a hook.
Why did Tanuja snap at her sister in the morning?
She was still shaken by her fear from the night before, and it came out as irritation. 🙂
What helped Tanuja's fear of the dark fade?
Talking about it with Zeenat, checking the corner together, and having a little lamp, and then time.
How might Zeenat have seen Tanuja's fear?
As real even though there was nothing dangerous, which is why she did not laugh and said the coat looked scary.

I'm Saurabh. In second year, for a general elective, we watched grainy footage of that old obedience study: volunteers pressing switches while a hidden man cried out, a calm researcher saying, 'The experiment requires that you continue.' I sat there feeling superior. Then Chetan, next to me, whispered, 'Remember the lab file?' In first year a senior had told us to copy last year's readings instead of doing the titration, and put our own names on them. I did it in two minutes. Chetan refused and got shouted at. Watching those volunteers, I noticed none of them looked cruel. They looked polite. They looked like me. Walking back to the hostel, I told Chetan he'd been braver than I was. He just shrugged. Now, when someone senior says 'just do it', I count to three first.

What had the senior told them to do in first year?
To copy last year's readings instead of doing the titration, and put their own names on them.
Why did Saurabh's feeling of superiority fade while watching?
Saurabh noticed the volunteers didn't look cruel, only polite, and that they looked like Saurabh, who had copied the file in two minutes.
What habit did Saurabh choose after that class?
Now, when someone senior says 'just do it', Saurabh counts to three first before obeying.
How might Chetan see the lab-file episode now?
Chetan just shrugged, perhaps seeing the refusal as ordinary rather than brave, even though it cost him a shouting.

It was the second week in May, in which the three young ladies set out together from Gracechurch Street for the town of ----, in Hertfordshire; and, as they drew near the appointed inn where Mr. Bennet's carriage was to meet them, they quickly perceived, in token of the coachman's punctuality, both Kitty and Lydia looking out of a dining-room upstairs. In May, three young ladies travel from Gracechurch Street toward a Hertfordshire town, where Mr. Bennet's carriage is to meet them at an inn. Kitty and Lydia have been waiting more than an hour, visiting a hat shop, watching a guard and preparing a salad.

Ankita, you keep saying, "How could I be so stupid?" Let me tell you about the time I said those exact words.
When I was twenty-five, a man named Mani joined our office in Coimbatore. He was warm and funny and remembered everyone's children's names. After six months he started a "savings circle". I joined, and I brought in my cousins. For eight months everything looked perfect: receipts, small payouts, tea at his house.
Then one Monday his house was locked and his phone was off. Forty families lost their money.
I couldn't look at my cousins. I told my wife, "Your husband is a fool." For a year I doubted every decision I made.
What pulled me out was a police inspector who said, "Karthik sir, this man has done this in three towns. He is very good at it. Being fooled by a professional is not stupidity; it is his skill."
That was my choice then: to stop punishing myself and start warning others.

How many families lost their money?
Forty families.
How did young Karthik feel after Mani disappeared?
Young Karthik felt deep shame, couldn't look at the cousins, called himself a fool and doubted every decision for a year.
What turning point inside the story changed Karthik's view?
The inspector explaining that Mani had done this in three towns, so being fooled was Mani's skill; after that Karthik stopped self-punishing and started warning others.
How might Karthik's cousins have felt about losing their money?
The cousins likely felt hurt and angry at the loss, and perhaps at Karthik for bringing them in, which deepened his shame.

"Dolma! Momo queen!" Vijay called across the art room. A few kids laughed. "Hi," Dolma said, not looking up from her painting. "What, you don't like momos?" "I like them fine." "So why the face?" Dolma put her brush down. "Vijay, you call me that every day. My family's from Dharamshala, and people have called me momo, chinki, Nepali, all my life. I know you mean it as a friendly nickname." Vijay's grin vanished. "I... it's a food. I thought it was cute." "It's cute once. Every day, it's like I'm just a food to people." "I honestly didn't know." "I know. That's why I'm saying it to you and not to them." Vijay nodded slowly. "Dolma, then. Just Dolma."

Where is Dolma's family from?
Dharamshala.
How did Vijay feel when Dolma explained the nickname?
He was shocked and embarrassed; he sincerely thought the nickname was cute and friendly, not hurtful.
What did Vijay do right at the end?
He listened without arguing and agreed to call her just Dolma, adjusting instead of defending himself.
Why might Dolma choose to tell Vijay rather than the others?
She seems to see Vijay as someone who means well and might actually change, so telling him feels worth the effort.

Project supervisor's note, Class Nine website project, week four
When this group started, Joseph, Vaibhav and Noor were all “doing everything”, which meant three people editing the same homepage and nobody writing content. In week two I asked them to list every task. They came back with a shared sheet: design (Noor), content (Vaibhav), coding (Joseph), each task with a name and a date beside it. They also fixed two ten-minute check-ins, Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.
I have watched three of those check-ins. They are quick: done, stuck, next. On Friday Vaibhav admitted the history page was late; Joseph offered a simpler layout so it could go in as plain text first.
The site is not finished, but for the first time every page has an owner. I will look at their sheet again next Friday before suggesting anything.

When are the group's ten-minute check-ins?
Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch, standing by the lab door.
How might Vaibhav have felt admitting the history page was late?
Vaibhav was probably a little embarrassed, but safe enough to say it, since the check-in is built for "stuck" as well as "done" 😅
What could the group try if a task's owner falls ill before a due date?
Use the Tuesday check-in to hand that task to whoever is ahead and move its date on the sheet, so the plan stays honest.
How does the new split look from Joseph's side?
Joseph can focus on coding without three people fighting over the homepage, and can spot a way to help when content runs late.

Read this:

It was Tết in Hanoi, and the community centre held a children's chess tournament. Tuan, nine, lost his third game in eleven moves. He knocked over his king, pushed back his chair and ran to the corridor, crying.
Fatima, the volunteer coach, found him by the window. She knelt down. "Losing hurts. Especially when you tried hard."
"I'm bad at chess," he sobbed.
"You're sad right now. That's okay. Sit with me a minute."
She didn't hurry him. She held out a tissue and waited while the crying slowed.
Then she said, "There's one more round. Do you want to play, or watch with me?"
Tuan thought. "Play," he whispered.
He lost that one too, but in thirty moves. When he came out, he ran to Fatima. "I lasted so long!"

How many moves did Tuan's third game last?
It lasted eleven moves.
How did Tuan feel after Fatima sat with him?
He felt calmer and safe enough to try again, after first feeling sad and sure he was bad at chess.
Why did Fatima's approach help Tuan bounce back?
She named his sadness as okay and waited without rushing, then gave him a choice, which let him return to play on his own terms.
How might Fatima feel when Tuan runs to her after the last game?
Fatima would probably feel happy and proud, seeing him excited about lasting thirty moves.

Read this:

Monday. Aadhya noticed Jyoti had given her tiffin to the stray dog behind the canteen, third day running. "Not hungry," Jyoti said. Aadhya didn't tease. "Come get a chai with me, then. Just ten minutes, no books." Jyoti came, and even laughed once.

Thursday. Jyoti's eyes were puffy. "I haven't slept since Tuesday. Every time I close my eyes I see the question paper." Aadhya sat beside her on the bench. "That sounds exhausting. Will you talk to Mrs Kapoor? I'll come with you." Jyoti said maybe.

Saturday, 10:40 pm. Jyoti messaged: "i can't do this anymore. i don't see any way this gets better." Aadhya's hands shook. She called Jyoti at once. "I'm here. Are you safe right now?" Jyoti was crying but said yes. Aadhya kept her on the line and woke her own mother, who called Jyoti's mother immediately. Jyoti's mother went to her room and stayed with her that night. On Monday they met Mrs Kapoor together.

What did Jyoti do with her tiffin on Monday?
Jyoti gave her tiffin to the stray dog behind the canteen.
What was Aadhya feeling when Jyoti's late-night message arrived?
Aadhya felt frightened, with shaking hands, because Jyoti sounded hopeless.
Why were Aadhya's steps on Saturday night the right ones?
Aadhya called Jyoti at once, kept her on the line and got an adult to reach Jyoti's mother that same night, so Jyoti was not left alone.
What is it like for Jyoti's mother to get that call?
She would likely feel shocked and scared but grateful to know, so she could go to Jyoti's room and stay with her.

Bhupen: she posted a pic with her lab group again. no reply to my msg for an hour
Sarika: ok. what do you want to do?
Bhupen: ask her who took the pic. and why she didn't tell me
Sarika: bhai, can I ask something weird first?
Bhupen: what
Sarika: what are you actually afraid of losing?
Bhupen: ...
Bhupen: that she'll realise she can do better
Bhupen: they're all toppers. i'm the guy who barely passed chem
Sarika: so it's not really about the pic
Bhupen: no. it's that i don't feel good enough for her
Sarika: that's real. but checking who took photos won't fix that feeling. it'll just make her feel watched
Bhupen: yeah. ugh 😔
Sarika: maybe talk to Mr Fernandes? he's good with this stuff. and tell her how you feel, not what she did
Bhupen: ok. i'll go see him at lunch tomorrow 🙏

What does Bhupen say the lab group all are?
He says they're all toppers.
What fear does Bhupen admit when Sarika asks what he is afraid of losing?
He admits feeling insecure and not good enough, afraid that she will realise she can do better.
Why was Sarika's question a useful turning point?
It moved the talk from the photo to the fear underneath, showing that checking up on her cannot fix Bhupen's sense of not being good enough.
What would change for her if Bhupen shared his feelings instead of questioning her about the picture?
She would hear an honest worry she could answer with care, instead of feeling watched and accused over an ordinary group photo.

Sharmila, a junior architect, was called into the office by Pankaj, a senior partner. "The window schedule you sent has an error," Pankaj said. "It went to the contractor." Her ears went hot, and the first words in her mouth were, "But the drawing you gave me was wrong." She stopped. That was the defence, not the answer. She said, "Can you show me where the error is?" Pankaj pointed. Sharmila looked for a while, and then said, "I need to look at this properly. Can I come back this afternoon with my answer?" "Yes, that's fine," said Pankaj. By afternoon she had found her own mistake and the missing note, and told him both.

What did Pankaj say went to the contractor?
The window schedule with an error in it.
What did Sharmila feel when told about the error?
Hot shame and an urge to defend, shown by the hot ears and the automatic reply blaming the drawing.
Which choice let Sharmila learn from the confrontation?
Sharmila stopped the defence, asked to be shown the error, and asked for time to look properly before answering.
How might Pankaj see Sharmila's request to come back in the afternoon?
As sensible and responsible, since Pankaj agreed at once, and Sharmila returned with a clear answer.

Read this:

Karthik met Sabina's new landlord at the tea stall near their Pune flat, and the man's face lit up so fast that Karthik's first thought was, finally, someone friendly. Raised cheeks, crinkled eyes, a full smile. The landlord even patted the plastic stool beside him. But Karthik remembered his own uncle, who felt real joy while barely changing his expression, just a small softening near the eyes. So he did not decide anything yet. Over the next few weeks he watched what the landlord did: fixed the leaking tap the same day, asked after Sabina's exams. The warm face and the warm actions matched. Karthik told Sabina that evening, "I think he is kind. But I would have believed it even if he smiled less." 🙂

Where did Karthik meet Sabina's new landlord?
He met the landlord at the tea stall near their Pune flat.
Why did Karthik hold back from deciding the landlord was warm right away?

He knew from his uncle that some people feel real pleasure with very little cheek movement, so a big smile alone was not proof either way. He waited to see whether the landlord's actions matched the smile.
How did Karthik's approach protect him from a hasty judgement, and what could he add?
He compared the smile with behaviour over time, like fixing the tap and asking about exams. He could also note the landlord's usual expression in calmer moments as a baseline.
How might the landlord's smile look to someone who does not smile much themselves?
It might feel very intense or even overdone, while for someone used to open faces it would seem ordinary and friendly.

Read this:

In her grandparents' village near Jodhpur, Deepika, fifteen and born in Stuttgart, felt watched all the time. The village girls giggled at her short hair and her careful, slow Hindi. At the well, a boy called her "gori mem". Back in Germany, classmates asked if she was going to have an arranged marriage. Here she was German. There she was Indian. By the third evening she stopped going out.
Her cousin Nitin, who had grown up in Jaipur and studied in Delhi, found her on the roof. "They called me city boy for years," he said. "It gets easier." Later her father came up too, and she finally said it: "I don't know what I am." He sat beside her, quiet for a long time. "I don't either, fully. Maybe we're making something new." The next day, she taught the village girls a German clapping game. They taught her theirs.

What did the boy at the well call Deepika?
"Gori mem."
Why did Deepika stop going out by the third evening?
She felt watched and out of place, laughed at in the village and questioned in Germany, and was lonely and unsure who she was.
What helped Deepika the next day, and why?
Nitin's shared experience and her father's honest talk made her feel less alone, so she felt brave enough to swap clapping games with the village girls.
How might her father have felt when Deepika said she didn't know what she was?
He probably felt moved and a little sad, since he admitted he wasn't fully sure either, but hopeful about making something new together.

At the end of this passage, why is the narrator taking out his purse at the end of this passage?

"He came faithfully, and he brought me the two one-pound notes. I was a poor boy then, as you know, and to a poor boy they were a little fortune. But, like you, I have done well since, and you must let me pay them back. You can put them to some other poor boy's use." I took out my purse.
He wants to pay back the two one-pound notes he once received as a poor boy. He has done well since and suggests the money can help another poor boy.

Read this:

Baljeet, you ask why your Bua Yamini never shouts? Because I once shouted so loud my own father stopped talking to me for three days. I was sixteen. A friend's cousin was having a sangeet in the next colony, ending at eleven. Papa said no. I said, "Everyone is going! Everyone's parents allow it! You are the strictest father in the world!" I slammed the door so hard the photograph fell. Papa's jaw tightened. "Then everyone's parents can look after everyone," he said. "My answer is no, and it will be no next time also." Mummy tried to soften it, but Papa raised a hand. I sat in my room crying, sure I had been right. Yet I had not asked him one question. I had only given orders.

What time was the sangeet due to end?
The sangeet was due to end at eleven.
What was Yamini feeling when slamming the door, and what shows it?
Yamini was angry, hurt and sure of being right; the shouting and the slammed door show it.
What could Yamini have tried instead of shouting, and why?
Yamini could have asked what worried Papa and offered a plan such as a ride home, because shouting made Papa dig in while a question would have opened a talk.
How did Papa see the shouting?
Papa likely saw a challenge to his authority and not a real request, so he held firm and refused even for next time.

Read this:

Dear Sarita,

You asked how the meeting with the housing society committee went. It went fine. But I want to tell you about the hour before.

I was so anxious my hands were trembling. The old voice said, "You feel terrible, so you're going to mess this up." Remember what you told me last year? "Feelings are weather, not forecasts." So I sat on the stairs and said it plainly: I'm anxious. That's real. And the facts are: the leak is from their pipe, I have photos, and I've asked politely twice.

I let myself feel scared for a few minutes. I didn't argue with it. Then I went in anyway, photos in hand. My voice wobbled once. The secretary looked at the photos and said they'd fix it by next week.

Thank you for the weather line. I carry it everywhere now.

Jahnavi

What did Jahnavi take into the meeting?
Jahnavi took the photos of the leak.
How did Jahnavi feel in the hour before the meeting?
Jahnavi felt very anxious, with trembling hands, and heard the old voice predicting failure.
What did Jahnavi do to stop the feeling from steering?
Jahnavi named the anxiety as real, listed the facts, let the fear be there for a few minutes, and went in anyway with the photos.
How might Sarita feel reading that the weather line helped?
Sarita would likely feel touched and glad that Sarita's words from last year made a difference.
I returned a library book with a bent page. Write a short apology note for the librarian, about 35 words. I'm Zeenat of Class 6.

Dear Librarian,
I am returning the book I borrowed. I am sorry that one of its pages is bent. I did not mean to damage it, and I will be more careful from now on.
Zeenat
Class 6

Read this:

In the small-town school near Kottayam, the boys from the upper village and the lower village had been fighting all term over the football ground. Joseph, the PE teacher, tried a fix: put both groups in the same detention room after school. The upper-village boys were made monitors because their marks were better. Joseph watched through the window. Nobody talked. The monitors wrote the lower-village boys' names on the board for "noise." One lower-village boy muttered, "See? They always think they're bosses." By Friday the fights were worse. Joseph sat with the headmistress, Gurleen ma'am. "I made it worse," he said. "Same room, no reason to cooperate, and I handed one side power." She nodded. "Then give them a reason." They planned a single inter-school football team: mixed, captain chosen by vote, the district cup as the goal.

Why were the upper-village boys made monitors?
They were made monitors because their marks were better.
What was Joseph feeling when he said "I made it worse"?
Joseph felt regretful and troubled, realising his plan had hardened the rivalry instead of easing it.
Why is a single mixed football team with a voted captain a better plan?
It gives both groups a common goal, equal status and the school's support, which are the conditions under which contact reduces prejudice.
How might the lower-village boys have seen the detention room?
They likely felt humiliated and controlled, which confirmed their belief that the upper-village boys always act like bosses.
Is it true that the sun is a star? That sounds strange when it's so big and bright.
Yes, it's true. The sun is a star, and the stars you see at night are other suns that are very far away, which is why they look tiny.
How far is the sun, then?
Very far, but much closer than any other star. Its light takes about eight minutes to reach us, while light from the next nearest star takes over four years.
Wow. That makes me feel small.
It can, but it's also exciting to be part of such a big universe.

At the school in Istanbul, Miss Elif, the class teacher, chalked a fraction on the board. "Who can tell me what one half plus one quarter is?"
Siddiq, ten, pressed his pencil into the desk and looked at his shoes. His heart thumped. He did not understand carrying the fractions, but last week a boy who guessed wrong was told off. Silence felt safer than a scolding.
Miss Elif came over, crouched at his desk and said quietly, "This one is tricky for lots of children. If you're confused, that's useful for me to know. Can we draw it together?"
Siddiq nodded, and his shoulders came down.

What sum did Miss Elif ask about on the board?
Miss Elif asked what one half plus one quarter is.
Why did Siddiq look at his shoes and press his pencil into the desk?
Siddiq was afraid of being scolded, since a boy who guessed wrong was told off last week. His heart thumped, and silence felt safer.
What did Miss Elif do that helped Siddiq open up?
Miss Elif crouched at the desk, said the question was tricky for many and told Siddiq that confusion helps her know what to teach. She invited him to draw it together.
How might Miss Elif have seen Siddiq's silence?
Miss Elif may have guessed it meant confusion or fear, not laziness, since she asked kindly. Her warm voice let Siddiq nod and relax.

School counsellor's note, Monday
Zainab came in at lunch, fists clenched. For four weeks Rukmini has been mocking her in class, hiding her bag, and posting a cartoon of her in a class group. Zainab said, "I hate her. I keep imagining pushing her into the drain outside school."
I told her the anger made sense. It is a sign she has been hurt again and again, and that this is not her fault. I asked if she was planning to act on it. She said, "No. I'd get into trouble, and she'd win." I told her that was wise and that hitting back could put her at risk.
I asked what she needed. She said, "For it to stop." With her permission I spoke to the class teacher before the end of lunch. We have saved the cartoon, spoken to Rukmini, and called both sets of parents this afternoon. I will see Zainab again tomorrow morning.

How long has Rukmini been mocking Zainab?
For four weeks.
What was Zainab feeling when she came to the counsellor?
She felt hatred and rage, fists clenched, after weeks of being hurt by Rukmini.
What made the counsellor's response wise?
The counsellor treated the anger as a sign of harm, checked she wouldn't retaliate, and brought in the teacher and both families that same day.
How might Rukmini respond when adults get involved?
Rukmini may feel defensive or ashamed, but adult intervention makes it clear the bullying must stop.
There have been 15 "Where's Waldo?" books published. Each book has 30 puzzles to find Waldo. The average person takes 3 minutes to find Waldo in a puzzle. How long would it take to find every Waldo?

There have been 450 puzzles because 15 x 30 = 450
It would take 1,350 minutes to find all the Waldo's because 450 x 3 = 1,350
The answer is 1350.

Parveen, you felt glad when that show-off missed the play role, and now you feel bad for feeling glad? Let your Harish mama tell you something. When I was sixteen, in Hubballi, a boy called Prakash boasted for weeks that he'd be picked for the district dance troupe. He called the rest of us village dancers.
At the audition he slipped on the stage and fell flat. I laughed. Inside I felt a big happy jump, like justice. Then I saw him limping outside, alone, his mother fussing over his ankle. The happy jump turned into something heavy.
That evening I went to his house with a tube of pain balm. We weren't friends. But I didn't want to be the kind of person who enjoys that.

Where did young Harish live at sixteen?
In Hubballi.
What did young Harish feel when Prakash fell?
He felt a big happy jump like justice, which turned heavy with shame when he saw Prakash limping alone.
What choice in the story shows Harish acting on his better feeling?
Taking a tube of pain balm to Prakash's house that evening.
What might Prakash have felt limping outside alone?
He was likely embarrassed and in pain, his boasting making the fall even more humiliating.

It was exam week, and the house in Patna was chaos: relatives visiting, the TV loud, Sudha Aunty frying pakoras.
Vikas, sixteen, put on his headphones. His rule: the new playlist of rap songs was only for homework. Nowhere else.
It worked. He'd been dreading the history revision all afternoon, but once the first song started, he found himself already on page two. The noise of the house faded.
Then came physics numericals. He tried with the music on. He read the same problem three times. The words in the songs got tangled with the numbers.
Frustrated, he pulled the headphones off. The TV was still blaring. He went to the terrace with his notebook and sat in the quiet.
Physics took an hour. History, with music, had taken forty minutes and felt almost fun.

What was Sudha Aunty doing during exam week?
She was frying pakoras while relatives visited and the TV was loud.
How did Vikas feel when he read the physics problem three times?
He felt frustrated because the lyrics were tangling with the numbers.
What did Vikas do right, and what might he plan next time?
He used the playlist to start history and went to a quiet terrace for physics; next time he could plan quiet slots for numericals.
How might Sudha Aunty see Vikas going up to the terrace?
She might feel sorry the house was so noisy, and pleased he found a quiet place to study.
Why do crows gather in big groups in the evening?
Many crows roost together at night. A big group is safer, since more birds can spot danger, and it may help them share news about where food is. Scientists are still studying the exact reasons.
Do they come back to the same tree?
Often they do. Crows tend to use the same roosting places for long periods, though the group can move if the tree is cut or the birds are disturbed.

On the school bus through Kandivali, the seniors in the back seat had started again: flicking Nikita's ponytail, calling her 'Miss Topper', snatching her phone and reading her messages aloud. Jatin sat two rows ahead and looked out of the window. At the stop, Nikita caught up with him, her voice tight. 'You saw. Every day this week.' Jatin shrugged, uncomfortable. 'You're too sensitive. They do it to everyone. Just toughen up and they'll get bored.' Nikita stared at him and walked off. At dinner, Jatin told his mother the story as if it were Nikita's problem. His mother put down her roti. 'They took her phone and read her messages? Every day?' 'Yeah, but—' 'That isn't her being sensitive. That's bullying. Do you have her mother's number?' She called that same evening, and emailed the class teacher before bed.

What did the seniors call Nikita?
They called her 'Miss Topper'.
Why did Jatin tell Nikita to toughen up?
Jatin felt uncomfortable and a little guilty for staying silent, so blaming her sensitivity made it her problem instead of his.
What did Jatin's mother do that a wise adult should do?
She named it bullying, called Nikita's mother that evening, and emailed the class teacher before bed.
How did Jatin's words land for Nikita?
Nikita likely felt hurt and alone, since the friend she turned to blamed her instead of the seniors.

The bus was due in five minutes, and Kamal was racing Rukmini to the door. "I'm first!" he shouted, one sock still half on, and he slapped the handle a heartbeat before her. His chest puffed out. Then Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack, calling, "Papa, look, I'm ready!" Kamal's face crumpled and his lip shook. Papa knelt to tie both pairs of laces. "You both moved fast today. Kamal, tonight is your story time with me. Rukmini, yours is tomorrow." Kamal sniffed, nodded, and picked up his bag.

How many minutes were left before the bus was due?
The bus was due in five minutes.
What was Kamal feeling when Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack?
Kamal felt crushed. His crumpled face and shaking lip show how much losing hurt after the pride of winning at the door.
What did Papa do that could ease the racing between the two children?
Papa praised how fast they both moved and gave each child their own story time. That way Papa's attention does not depend on who is first. 🙂
What might Rukmini want when she calls, "Papa, look, I'm ready!"?
Rukmini probably wants Papa to notice her, just as Kamal does. She may also enjoy winning the shoe race in the same way he enjoyed the door.

Keerthana stood at the bedroom door in her socks. Papa was sitting on the bed with his hands over his face, and his shoulders were shaking.
"Papa?" she whispered.
Sahil wiped his eyes. "Come here, kanna."
"Why are you crying? Did I do something?"
"No. I'm sad because I miss Dadi. It is okay to be sad. I'm still here for you."
She climbed up and leaned against him. "I miss Dadi too," she said, very small.

Where was Keerthana standing when she saw her father?
Keerthana was standing at the bedroom door in her socks.
What was Keerthana feeling as she watched her father cry?
Keerthana was worried and scared. Her whisper and her question, "Did I do something?" show she wondered if it was her fault.
How did Sahil's words help Keerthana?
He said why he was crying, that it is okay to be sad, and that he was still there for her. Naming his grief kept her from fearing her own. 🤍
How might Sahil feel when Keerthana says she misses Dadi too?
Sahil may feel comforted that they share the loss and that she can tell him. He may also feel tender towards her.

Read this:

Hrithik, you're sulking because your cousins read your diary? Sit. When your Sumit dada was nine, we were twenty-two people in one house in Meerut. I had no corner of my own. If I got a bad mark, my mother, three chachis and my grandmother each gave me a different lecture, and one uncle said the teacher was wrong! I hid my marble tin under the water tank, and my cousin Bittu found it within a day. But when I had fever, someone was always sitting by my bed. When I cried on the terrace, five cousins came and sat around me without asking why. That house was noisy and nosy. It was also never lonely.

Where did young Sumit hide the marble tin?
Under the water tank.
How did young Sumit probably feel when everyone gave a different lecture after a bad mark?
Likely confused and crowded, with several adults each saying something different and one even blaming the teacher.
What could young Sumit have done to get a little privacy in that busy house?
Ask one trusted adult for a small shelf or box of his own, and tell the cousins which things were private.
How might cousin Bittu have seen finding the marble tin?
Bittu probably saw it as ordinary fun in a house where everything was shared, not as breaking a secret.

It seemed to Daniel irksome and improper to be in a room at all, but to have anything to do with a young lady seemed to him impossible. He cast down his eyes and hurried out as if it were none of his business, careful as he went not to inflict any accidental injury on the young lady.

Why does Daniel hurry out of the room?
He finds it annoying and improper to be in a room at all, and having anything to do with a young lady seems impossible to him.

That Sumit's cousin got 23.
How did Madhuri feel on sensing what was behind Sumit's boasting?
Madhuri sensed Sumit was stressed and hurting behind the boasting, and felt concerned.
What did Madhuri do that helped?
Madhuri asked gently if Sumit was okay, promised not to tell, and offered to practise together, admitting to not getting q5 either.

Sumit seems to be guarding a hurt sense of worth after the father compared the marks with a cousin's 23.
Now you try: round 85,000 to the nearest 10,000.
The answer is 90,000.
Why do we say bird migration?

Migration is the movement of animals or people from one place to another, often each year. It is a noun. For birds it means flying to warmer places when the weather changes.
Example: Thousands of cranes passed over the lake during their autumn migration.

5 machines make 400 bottles in 4 hours. How many bottles do 3 machines make in 6 hours? 5 machines, 4 h -> 400 1 machine, 4 h -> 400 / 5 = 80 1 machine, 1 h -> 80 / 4 = 20 3 machines, 1 h -> 20 x 3 = 60 3 machines, 6 h -> 60 x 6 = 360

Answer: 360 bottles.

Two things change, so go to ONE machine for ONE hour. 5 machines in 4 hours: 400. 1 machine in 4 hours: 400 / 5 = 80. 1 machine in 1 hour: 80 / 4 = 20 bottles. Now build up: 3 machines in 1 hour: 3 x 20 = 60; 3 machines in 6 hours: 60 x 6 = 360. Both changes are direct here (more machines, more bottles; more hours, more bottles).

Dhritarashtra said, "How did those bulls among men, viz., that great bowman Drona, and Dhananjaya the son of Pandu, encounter each other in battle? The son of Pandu is ever dear to the wise son of Bharadwaja. The preceptor also is ever dear to Pritha's son, O Sanjaya. Both of those car-warriors delight in battle, and both of them are fierce like lions. How therefore, did Bharadwaja's son and Dhananjaya, both fighting with care encounter each other in battle?"

What does Dhritarashtra say about the bond between Drona and Dhananjaya?

The son of Pandu is always dear to the wise son of Bharadwaja, and the teacher is always dear to Pritha's son. Both delight in battle and are fierce as lions, so Dhritarashtra asks how they fought each other.
Tell a short story, about 55 words, of an old man who plants a tree every birthday.

Every birthday, an old man planted one tree on the hill behind his house. People laughed at first and said he would never see them grow tall. Years passed, and the hill turned green. Birds came, and shade followed. On his last birthday, children sat under the oldest tree and sang for him.

Read this:

The day I got the state essay prize, Nandini stopped waiting for me after school. I'm Dilnaz, and we had written our entries side by side in the reading room, sharing one pencil sharpener and a lot of complaints.

At first I thought she was just busy. Then I saw her looking away when my name was read in assembly, and I understood. She had wanted it as much as I did.

I felt two things at once: proud and guilty. My aunt wanted me to post the certificate everywhere. I didn't. I also didn't say "it's nothing," because it wasn't, and Nandini would have known I was lying.

I wrote her one message: "I miss walking home with you. Your essay made me rewrite my ending, you know. If you ever want to swap drafts again, I'm here." She didn't reply for a week. Then she left a new draft on my desk, no note.

What did Nandini leave on Dilnaz's desk?
Nandini left a new draft on Dilnaz's desk, with no note.
What two feelings did Dilnaz have after the prize?
Dilnaz felt proud of winning and guilty that the win had hurt Nandini, who had wanted the prize just as much.
Why was it wise for Dilnaz not to post the certificate everywhere?
Flaunting the win would have deepened Nandini's hurt, while staying quiet let Dilnaz reach out without rubbing it in. 🙂
How might Nandini see the message Dilnaz sent?
Nandini may have felt seen and credited, since Dilnaz admitted her essay shaped the ending, which could explain the draft she finally left.
A story about a rooster who forgot how to crow, please.

Every morning, Rooster Bholu crowed to wake the whole village. But one day he opened his beak and only a small squeak came out. The hens stared. The goats stared. The sun rose anyway, and everyone slept late.

Bholu was ashamed. He hid behind the haystack. A boy named Sameer found him there and sat down. "Maybe you are thinking too hard," he said.

"I just forgot," said Bholu.

Sameer began to hum a tune. Bholu felt something tickle in his throat. He tilted his head back and, before he could worry, a loud crow rolled across the fields.

The hens clucked, the goats bleated, and in the houses lamps were lit. Bholu strutted proudly the whole day.

Tuesday night. Trip is on Friday and I keep walking through it in my head like a film. Bus at seven, so breakfast early. Then the walk across the fort courtyard, and that sun is fierce by eleven. Hat! Lunch on the steps, so a napkin and a bag for the wrappers. Then the ride back when everyone is sticky and sneezy. Tissues! I put a hat, a pack of tissues and a bag for the wrappers on my list. Mummy says I sound like a tour guide. 🙂 Now to find my good hat. - Amandeep

What three things did Amandeep add after picturing the day?
Amandeep added a hat, a pack of tissues and a bag for the wrappers.
What might Amandeep be feeling while going through the trip in mind?
Excited and careful at once, looking forward to the day and wanting to be ready, and cheerful about the tour guide teasing.
What other approach could Amandeep use to check the list, and why?
Amandeep could ask a friend who went on a similar trip what they wished they had brought, because that may add things imagining missed.
How does Mummy seem to see Amandeep's planning?
Mummy finds it a bit funny and impressive, since Mummy says Amandeep sounds like a tour guide.

Lalit came back from his viva on Thursday looking grey. The external examiner had given him a C, he said, after asking about a chapter that wasn't on the syllabus. Twenty minutes later the delivery rider rang the bell with our dinner, a little late because of the rain. Lalit yanked the door open. "Late again! Do you people even look at a clock?" The rider apologised twice and hurried off, helmet dripping.
I didn't say anything then; Lalit's hands were shaking. After we'd eaten, I said quietly, "I think that rider got the examiner's share."
Lalit put his fork down. "Yeah, Hansa. That wasn't about the food." He went downstairs, but the rider had gone, so he left a kind note and a good rating instead.

What grade did the external examiner give Lalit?
A C.
Why did Hansa stay silent during the outburst?
Hansa felt uneasy and sorry for the rider, but saw Lalit's hands shaking and sensed that correcting him right then would only make him defensive.
What helped Lalit see what had really happened?
A quiet remark after dinner linking the outburst to the viva let Lalit name it himself and try to make amends.
What was the rider's experience of that evening?
The rider, already wet and a little late from the rain, was blamed harshly for something small and hurried off after apologising twice.

Indu's diary, day 19.
Another call to the payment platform's support line. 42 minutes on hold. The agent read out the same script: "Your case is being reviewed." I asked for the case officer's name. "Not available." I wanted to scream.
Jeevan came over with dinner and found me with my head on the table. "Just forget it, it's gone," he said. I nearly agreed.
But then I opened my notes. Nineteen days of dates, reference numbers, names.
Things I did tonight:
- wrote a formal email to the platform's grievance officer, with all the reference numbers attached
- printed the timeline so I don't have to remember it in my head
- set a reminder: if no proper answer by the date in their policy, escalate to the ombudsman
- filed the cybercrime report number in the same folder
Still angry. But organised angry. Jeevan is helping me make a tracking sheet. Not despairing.

How long was Indu on hold today?
Forty-two minutes, on hold.
How did Indu feel after the call?
Indu felt frustrated and close to despair, wanting to scream, before choosing to get organised.
What did Indu do to put documented pressure on the platform?
Indu emailed the grievance officer with all reference numbers, printed a timeline, set a reminder to escalate to the ombudsman, and filed everything together.
How might Jeevan see Indu's persistence?
Jeevan first thought it was hopeless, but he seems to come round, helping make a tracking sheet.

From Mehak's family notebook, Sunday.
Today Divyansh got his first weekly pocket money, a fifty-rupee note, and walked around the flat holding it like a certificate. 'I'm grown up now,' he announced. By evening he had counted it eleven times. On the way to the market with his father, he stopped at the toy stall, then at the samosa cart, then put the note back in his pocket. At dinner he asked, 'Papa, how many hours do you work for fifty rupees?' His father told him honestly. Divyansh went quiet. Later he told me he had decided to buy a birthday card for his grandmother and keep the rest in his tin until he knew what he really wanted. He said, 'Thank you for the money, Mummy,' twice.

How many times did Divyansh count the note?
Eleven times.
How did Divyansh feel holding his first pocket money?
Proud and grown up, holding it like a certificate.
What did Divyansh's question to Papa lead to?
He understood the work behind the money, thanked his parents, and chose carefully what to spend it on.
How might Papa have felt answering Divyansh's question?
Pleased that Divyansh was curious about the effort behind the money.

Gabriel from downstairs had brought a box of honey pastries, now empty. Selam wanted the biscuits on the top shelf instead.
"No more sweets today," Abebe said.
"I hate you! You're a mean daddy!"
Gabriel, still at the door, raised his eyebrows. Abebe didn't look at him. He sat on the rug. "I hear you are angry. The answer is still no more sweets today."
"I'm still angry!"
"That's okay. I'm right here." No lecture. He waited while the Toronto rain tapped the window.

What did Gabriel bring?
A box of honey pastries.
Why might Selam still be shouting after Abebe's calm answer?
She is still angry and disappointed about the biscuits, and her feeling takes time to settle even when the limit is kind.
What could Abebe do next if Selam keeps shouting?
Keep sitting nearby, say little, and offer a hug when she is ready, without adding a lecture or a new rule.
How might Gabriel see Abebe's response from the doorway?
Gabriel may be surprised at first and then impressed that Abebe stays calm and firm without looking for approval.

Seema, you're upset your favourite singer said those ugly things? Your Thomas appachan had a hero too. In 1972, in Kochi, it was Joseph Ittiyavira, the best striker in our district. I copied his hairstyle, his celebrations, even the way he tied his laces. Then the newspaper said he'd taken money to lose a match. I was sixteen. I cried, then shouted that it was lies. My father sat with me and said, 'He can be a great player and have done a wrong thing. You don't have to pick one.' It took me months. I stopped defending him. But I kept practising his left-foot shot, because that was mine now, not his. I'm still good with my left foot.

What was Joseph Ittiyavira accused of?
Taking money to lose a match.
How did sixteen-year-old Thomas feel when he read the newspaper?
Heartbroken and angry, crying and then insisting it was lies.
What choice in the story helped young Thomas move forward?
His father's words that a great player can do a wrong thing, which let Thomas stop defending the striker while keeping the left-foot shot as his own.
What might Thomas's father have been hoping when he sat with him?
To help his son grieve the hero without losing his love of football or his sense of right and wrong.

The list went up on the notice board outside the headmaster's room just as the school bell rang for lunch. Tanuja pushed through the crowd of girls, searching for her name under 'Kho-kho: block tournament'. It wasn't there. Zeenat's was.
Her ears burned. Her eyes filled so fast she had to look at the floor. Zeenat turned to say something and Tanuja walked straight past her, out behind the grain shed where the goats were tied, and sat on an upturned bucket.
When her friend Rukhsana found her, Tanuja's voice came out rough. 'Sir always picks his favourites. Zeenat's father helps with the midday meal, that's why.'
She knew it wasn't really why. Zeenat was quicker. But saying it made the lump in her throat a little smaller.
From the field came the shouts of the others practising.

Whose name was on the kho-kho list instead of Tanuja's?
Zeenat's name was on the list.
Why did Tanuja blame the teacher even though she knew Zeenat was quicker?
Blaming the teacher made the hurt of being dropped a little easier to bear for the moment.
How could Rukhsana support Tanuja right now?
She could sit with her and let her be upset without arguing, then later, when Tanuja is calmer, talk about what she wants to work on.
What is it like for Zeenat when Tanuja walks straight past her?
Zeenat may feel her good news is spoiled and worry that she has lost a friend over the team list.
