The classroom was so quiet that you could hear the clock.
Why: word choice ("quite" -> "quiet").

"'Vyasa said, "It behoveth thee not, O monarch, to indulge in such poignant grief. I shall repeat what I have once said. All this is Destiny, O puissant one! Without doubt, all creatures that are born display at first a union (of diverse materials and forces). Dissolution, however, overtakes them at the end. Like bubbles in the water they rise and disappear. All things massed together are sure to crumble away and all things that rise must fall down. Union ends in dissolution and life ends in death. Idleness, though temporarily agreeable, ends in misery, and labour with skill, though temporarily painful, ends in happiness. Affluence, Prosperity, Modesty, Contentment, and Fame dwell in labour and skill but not in idleness. Friends are not competent to bestow happiness, nor foes competent to inflict misery. Similarly wisdom does not bring wealth nor does wealth bring happiness. Since, O son of Kunti, thou hast been created by the Maker to engage thyself in Work. Success springs from Work. Thou art not fit, O king, to avoid Work."'"

Put this in simple words for a child, three sentences.

Vyasa tells the king not to grieve so deeply, because everything is destiny and all things that are born must end, like bubbles in water. Idleness may feel pleasant but ends in misery, while skilful labour ends in happiness. The king was made to work, so he should not avoid it.

Monday: Aadhya forgot her swimming kit again, for the third Monday running. Her sister Arohi groaned, "You're so careless," and Aadhya cried in the car, saying she had really tried to remember.
Wednesday: Arohi felt bad. She stuck a big picture chart by the front door: swim bag on Mondays, library book on Wednesdays, art apron on Fridays.
The next Monday: Aadhya checked the chart, grabbed her swim bag and waved it at Arohi, grinning. "I didn't forget!" She still forgot her water bottle. But nobody called her careless, and she remembered it herself on Tuesday.

What goes on the chart for Wednesdays?
Library book.
How did Aadhya feel when called careless?
She felt ashamed and upset, crying because she had really tried.
What helped Aadhya remember?
A picture chart by the door that showed what to take each day.
How did Arohi feel after calling Aadhya careless?
Arohi felt bad and wanted to help instead.

In Dr Joseph's waiting room, Swati's father sat with his arms folded, eyes on the door. "I told you, I'm fine," Siddharth muttered. "If anyone from our building sees me here, they'll say the old man has gone soft in the head." For three months he hadn't gone on his morning walk and had barely touched dinner. Swati had tried once already, and he'd said only weak people talk to psychologists. So today she had put it differently. "Papa, Dr Joseph has looked after you since your knee operation. We're here because you're not sleeping. Sleep is health, same as your knee." He grunted. When his name was called, Swati stood too, then sat back down. "Do you want me in there, or would you like to talk to her alone?" Siddharth hesitated. "Alone," he said, and straightened his collar before going in.

What was Siddharth worried about in the waiting room?

The rainy season is here, Jan collected 65 gallons of water in a barrel outside her home. She uses 7 gallons of water each to clean the two cars and uses 11 fewer gallons than the two cars to water the plants. Then, she uses half of the remaining gallons of water to wash the plates and clothes. How many gallons of water does Jan use to wash her plates and clothes?

She uses 7 x 2 = 14 gallons of water to clean the two cars.
She uses 14 - 11 = 3 gallons of water to water the plants.
The total gallons of water that she uses to clean the cars and to water the plants is 14 + 3 = 17.
Jan has 65 - 17 = 48 gallons of water remaining after cleaning the cars and watering the plants.
Jan uses 48 / 2 = 24 gallons of water to wash her plates and clothes.
The answer is 24.

At the insurance office where she'd worked for two years, Sharmila used to be the one who organised birthday lunches. Now, when colleagues asked her to join, she said, "I'll check," and then didn't come.
On Thursday, the team lead asked her to travel to Nashik for a client meeting. Sharmila said, "Can I tell you tomorrow?" She needed to ask Vikas first. She always needed to ask Vikas first: about lunches, about late meetings, about which colleagues she spoke to.
In the washroom, she stood at the sink and realised her hands were shaking. Over a simple work trip.
There were no bruises. Vikas never hit her. So she had never called it anything. But she walked on eggshells every evening, and her world was now her desk, her home, and his rules.
A colleague came in, saw her face and said softly, "Sharmila, are you okay?" For the first time, Sharmila said, "No. Not really."

Where was the client meeting Sharmila was asked to travel to?
In Nashik.
What was Sharmila feeling at the washroom sink?
Sharmila felt anxious and shaken, her hands trembling over a simple work trip, realising how much she lived on eggshells.
What small step at the end could lead to help?
Admitting to a colleague that she was not okay could open the way to talking to someone and getting support.
How might the colleague see the change in Sharmila?
The colleague may have noticed Sharmila withdrawing from lunches and trips, and feel concerned enough to ask gently.

The staff canteen at the district hospital is loud at one o'clock, but Nirmala, his friend since their nursing college days, could still tell when Gurpreet wasn't really listening. For a month he'd been easier: laughing at the ward jokes, showing her photos of the Sunday picnic with his wife Harleen and the kids. Today he was pushing his rajma around and not eating it.
"Bad day?" she asked.
"Harleen's cousin came by with sweets to celebrate his new shop," he said. "Just sweets. And I thought of the loan and couldn't breathe for a second. I thought we were past it."
Nirmala, who had watched him go from silent in March to smiling in June, said, "You're past a lot of it. It just comes back in waves. That's not failure."
He shrugged. "Some nights it won't let go."
"Then maybe see the counsellor on the second floor, both of you," she said. "Someone who can keep the conversation steady."

What was Gurpreet doing with his rajma?
Gurpreet was pushing his rajma around and not eating it.
Why did the cousin's visit shake Gurpreet?
Family arriving to celebrate a new shop brought the loan back, and Gurpreet felt the old hurt so strongly he couldn't breathe for a second.
What did Nirmala offer that could help the healing continue?
Nirmala pointed out how far Gurpreet had come, called the setbacks waves rather than failure, and suggested the couple see a counsellor together.
What might Harleen notice at home on a day like this?
Harleen may see Gurpreet go quiet again and wonder if they have slipped back, even though the good weeks were real.

Give four short bullet points for this paragraph.

"Kunal, you asked how I, Chinmay, survived my first lead role. Honestly, the first week I just stared at the word 'billing' on the whiteboard. It felt like a mountain. Then I asked myself: what is this actually made of? And I broke it into five pieces. Customer accounts. Invoice creation. Tax rules. Payment connection. Monthly reports. Next, I didn't guess the time. I got the four of us in a room and we estimated each piece together. People argued. The tax rules went from 'a week' to 'three weeks' once Meenal explained the state variations. Then I asked, which piece could sink us? The payment connection, because it depends on another company's system. So we started that on day one, even before the easier bits. Each piece got one owner's name beside it. The mountain became five hills. Still work, but you can see the top of each one."

- Chinmay stared at "billing" on the whiteboard in the first week as lead.
- Chinmay broke it into five pieces, from customer accounts to monthly reports.
- The team estimated each piece, and tax rules grew from one week to three.
- They started the risky payment connection first and gave each piece one owner.
What does a weather vane show? Answer in under ten words and include "wind".

Observation note, Class 4. Sarika was asked to explain why ice melts. She said, “Uh... hmm... it's because... um,” and looked at the window. Two classmates put up their hands. Usually I would have called on one of them within a moment. This time I counted silently and kept my eyes friendly. After what felt like a long while, Sarika said, “Because it gets warm and the water inside can move.” It was a thoughtful answer. I asked her what she had been doing in her head. She said, “Looking for how to say it.” I plan to wait longer with all pupils. Ms. Lavanya.

What was Sarika asked to explain?
Why ice melts.
How might Sarika have felt while saying hmm and um?
She probably felt unsure and under pressure while searching for words, and she told the teacher she was looking for how to say it.
What did the teacher change that helped, and what might she try next?
Lavanya waited quietly instead of switching to another pupil, and she plans to wait longer with all pupils.
How might the two classmates with their hands up have felt while waiting?
They may have felt impatient because they knew their answers, but a short wait taught them that a thoughtful answer can arrive slowly.

messages.content: Explain what causes tides in two sentences, and use the word "moon" in the first one.
Tides are caused mainly by the pull of the moon's gravity on the oceans. The sun adds a smaller pull, so the highest and lowest tides change through the month.

Wasim's Nanu came to collect him today. He bent down and said, "Kiss for Nanu?" Wasim stepped back and held his school bag in front of him. Then he looked at me.

Last week we practised choices for greetings, so I said, "Wasim, you can choose." Wasim held up his hand. "High-five?"

Nanu laughed and gave him the biggest high-five. "Good one!"

Wasim walked out holding Nanu's hand, chatting all the way. Please keep offering him choices at home too.

What did Wasim hold in front of him when he stepped back?
His school bag.
What was Wasim feeling when he stepped back and looked at Hafsa?
He was probably unsure and a little uncomfortable about giving a kiss, and looked to Hafsa for support. Once he had a choice he seemed relieved and happy, chatting all the way out.
Why was the high-five a good outcome?
Wasim chose how to greet, and Nanu accepted it warmly, which teaches Wasim that his body belongs to him even with family.
How does Nanu respond to being offered a high-five instead of a kiss?
He laughs and gives the biggest high-five, showing he is happy to greet Wasim in the way Wasim chooses.

Mentor note, written by Amandeep.
Pradeep, a final-year student, told me on Wednesday that an uncle had asked him to come home for the whole week of a family wedding and skip his lab project deadline. When he said he could not, the uncle told him he only thought of himself. Pradeep said the words stayed with him all night, and he admitted he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.
I did not tell him what to do. We talked about which parts he could offer. On Friday he phoned his uncle and calmly said he could not miss the deadline, but he would come on Saturday and help with the guest list. The uncle went quiet, then agreed. Pradeep looked lighter when he told me.

What did the uncle ask Pradeep to do for the wedding?
The uncle asked him to come home for the whole week of the family wedding and skip his lab project deadline.
What was Pradeep feeling after being told he only thought of himself?
Pradeep felt hurt and pressured, since the words stayed with him all night and he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.
What did Pradeep choose to do on Friday, and why was it a fair way to answer?
He calmly told his uncle he could not miss the deadline but offered to come on Saturday and help with the guest list, which set a limit and still gave support.
How might Amandeep have seen Pradeep's call to the uncle?
Amandeep seems to have seen it as a good step, noting that Pradeep looked lighter afterwards, and had left the choice to Pradeep by not telling him what to do.

Coach's note, written by Imran. Harsha has been at the practice centre for four months. In the last two weeks Harsha's mock scores fell sharply, and the answer sheets showed careless mistakes. I asked casually about sleep. Harsha admitted to four hours a night for two weeks. We looked at the score sheets together and noticed that every low score followed a stretch of late nights. Harsha decided the plan itself was the problem. The new plan: lights out at the same time, a twenty-minute walk in the evening, and one evening a week with no books. I only suggested writing the pattern on paper. Two weeks later, accuracy on the mock had risen and Harsha looked more settled.

How many hours a night did Harsha sleep for two weeks?
Harsha slept four hours a night for two weeks.
What was Harsha likely feeling when the scores dropped?
Harsha was probably worried and worn down, since the scores fell sharply and the late nights had been eating into rest.
What alternative approach could Harsha add for the days when scores dip anyway, and why?
Harsha could talk to a counsellor or a trusted person about the pressure, because a schedule helps the body but stress may need a person to talk to.
How does Imran see Harsha's progress?
Imran sees Harsha finding the link between late nights and low scores without being told, so Imran only suggests writing the pattern down and notices calmer accuracy later.

In the coldest week of the Lohri holidays the power had gone. Irawati, five, sat by the window in two sweaters with three stubby crayons and an old calendar.
She drew a bonfire. Then a dog near the bonfire. Then a very long kite string going off the page.
Her cousin Lalremsiami peeked in and went away again. Irawati didn't look up.
The light outside turned grey. The blue crayon broke. She used the broken half.
After a long time she put the crayons down, nodded once at the page, and went to find a biscuit. She showed no one.

What did Irawati draw first?
She drew a bonfire.
What does Irawati's nod at the end suggest she felt?
It suggests she felt satisfied and content that the drawing was finished, without needing anyone to praise it.
How could an adult support this kind of play?
By leaving her some paper and crayons and not interrupting or asking for a show, so drawing stays fun for its own sake.
What might Lalremsiami think on peeking in and seeing Irawati so absorbed?
Lalremsiami might feel amused and decide not to disturb her, seeing she is happy on her own.
In case it will rain, take an umbrella. Please check the verb.

In case it rains, take an umbrella.
Why: present tense ("it will rain" -> "it rains").

After-school care note, Tuesday.
Thomas arrived at 4:30 after a full school day, football practice and a spelling test. At snack time I offered him apple or banana. He stared at the bowl and said, "I don't know." When I asked again, he pushed the bowl away and cried. Later he could not choose between two colouring sheets and threw both on the floor. By six, he had refused every choice offered.
His mother, Sangeeta, told me at pickup that evenings at home are the same.
We agreed a plan: after 4:30, adults offer fewer choices, or simply decide small things for him. Important choices, like which club to join, will be discussed on weekend mornings. I'll try it for two weeks and note the change.

What did Thomas do with the two colouring sheets?
He threw both on the floor.
Why did Thomas cry when offered apple or banana?
He was tired and overwhelmed after a full day, so even a small choice felt too much.
What plan did the carer and Sangeeta agree on, and why is it sensible?
Offering fewer choices after 4:30 and deciding small things for him, keeping big choices for weekend mornings when he is fresh.
How might Sangeeta feel hearing about Thomas's afternoon?
Sangeeta might feel relieved that someone else noticed the pattern she sees at home, and hopeful about the plan.

Before: In February, Tanvir's family assumed he'd take science. "You're good at maths. Engineering is safe," said his cousin Anirban, who was studying it.
But Tanvir spent every free hour designing posters for school events. He felt sick filling in the science form.
During: In March, he took the school aptitude test. It showed high scores in visual reasoning and moderate in physics. He showed his parents and Anirban his poster portfolio. Anirban said, "These are really good. Have you looked at design courses?"
After: In April, Tanvir chose commerce with an arts elective and signed up for a weekend design course. His father still worried about jobs, but he framed one of Tanvir's posters.

What did the aptitude test show high scores in?
Visual reasoning.
What was Tanvir feeling when filling in the science form?
Tanvir felt sick and uneasy, sensing it didn't fit his interests.
What helped Tanvir make his choice?
The aptitude test, his poster portfolio and an honest talk with family helped match his strengths to a stream.
How might Tanvir's father feel when framing the poster?
His father is still worried about jobs but proud of Tanvir's talent.

Read this:

Monday: Joseph was stacking blocks into a tall tower when Joseph's mama, Aparna, called from the kitchen, "Shoes on, please!" Joseph kept stacking. The bus was missed.
Tuesday: Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level, and said, "Joseph." Joseph looked up. "Shoes on, please." Joseph fetched them right away.
Wednesday: Joseph was rolling a toy train along the sofa. Aparna crouched beside it and said, "Joseph." The train stopped. "Shoes?" said Joseph, and ran to the door.

What was Joseph doing on Monday when Aparna called from the kitchen?
Stacking blocks into a tall tower.
What was Joseph feeling when Aparna called from the kitchen?
Deeply interested in the tower of blocks, so Joseph heard the sound but did not take in the words.
What change did Aparna make on Tuesday that helped?
Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level and said Joseph's name first, then gave the instruction.
How might Aparna have felt on Monday when the bus was missed?
Frustrated and hurried, perhaps thinking Joseph was ignoring the call, when Joseph had not really taken it in.

Read this:

I'm Ganga, and from our balcony I can see into the courtyard of Farhan's house next door. Most weekdays he comes home at six, after school and then tuition.
Yesterday his Ammi held up two T-shirts for today's school picnic, a blue one and a striped one. Farhan stared at them for a long time, then threw his bag down and shouted, "I don't care!" A minute later he was crying about which pencil box to take.
On Sunday mornings I've seen him choose a kite colour in seconds, laughing. So maybe it isn't about the shirts at all. Maybe by evening he's just used up. I don't know for sure. His Ammi put the blue one out and sat beside him quietly.

Which two T-shirts did Farhan's Ammi hold up?
A blue one and a striped one.
Why might Farhan shout 'I don't care!' over a T-shirt?
Farhan may feel exhausted and overwhelmed after school and tuition, so even an easy choice about a T-shirt feels like too much.
How could Farhan's Ammi make evenings easier for him?
She could choose small things like shirts and pencil boxes herself on weekdays, or ask him in the morning when he is fresh.
Why is Ganga unsure what is going on inside Farhan?
Ganga only watches from a balcony and sees the outbursts, not his thoughts, but notices he chooses happily on Sunday mornings.

Read this:

Dear Lavanya Didi,
You asked how the new school is. Honestly? Mixed.
There's a group of five boys who have been together since Class 1. They run the cricket nets at lunch. On Tuesday one of them dropped two easy catches. "Sun in his eyes," they said, and patted his back.
On Wednesday I dropped one. The captain said, "Concentrate, yaar, this isn't gully cricket," and they all went quiet at me. Nobody mentioned the sun. It was the same sun.
Yesterday one of them forgot his homework, and the others swore to Ma'am he'd left it on the bus. When I forgot mine last week, they told her I never do it.
I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just needed to tell someone that it feels like there are two rulebooks, one for them and one for me.
Your brother,
Kamal

How many easy catches did one of the group drop on Tuesday?
One of them dropped two easy catches on Tuesday, and the group said it was the sun in his eyes.
Why does the dropped catch on Wednesday sting Kamal so much?
Kamal feels hurt and shut out, because the same mistake earned a group member sympathy but earned Kamal a telling-off, so the group seems to judge by who you are.
What small step could help Kamal at the new school?
Kamal could look for classmates outside the group of five, or mention the pattern to a trusted teacher, so the group's two rulebooks aren't the only measure.
How might Lavanya feel reading the letter?
Lavanya might feel protective and sad for her brother, and glad that Kamal chose to tell her instead of keeping it inside.

I coordinate the relief camp at the school in our ward, so I saw Arohi every day of the flood week. I'm Lalit, and I've seen a lot of college volunteers.

Most of them arrive wanting to hand things out and get a photo. Arohi arrived and asked the women from the colony how they wanted the rations shared. They said by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long. She made a list and sat at a small table with the card numbers.

On the fourth day a news crew came. The others lined up in front. Arohi carried on sorting the damp rice sacks at the back. I asked her later why she didn't go. She shrugged and said, "It's not my flood."

I don't know what she was feeling underneath. She looked tired and her hands were cracked from the sacks. She came back the next weekend to help clean the classrooms, when there were no cameras at all.

How did the women from the colony want the rations shared?
They wanted them shared by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long.
What might Arohi have been feeling when she said, "It's not my flood"?
Lalit could not be sure, but she seemed tired yet steady and humble, uncomfortable taking credit for other people's hardship.
What could new volunteers learn from Arohi's first step at the camp?
Asking the affected people how they want help given, and then following their plan, makes the help fit their real needs.
How might the elderly families see the change to sharing by family card?
They would feel relieved and respected, since they no longer had to stand in long queues to get food.
Is there a more exact verb for "made"? We made rangoli at the door.
We drew rangoli at the door.

In the paying-guest room in Koramangala, Varun's days had blurred. He woke at 3 pm, felt tired again by five and lay awake until the milk vans came. Aunty in the kitchen had stopped keeping his plate; he hadn't come down for dinner in over a week.
Nitin's name kept appearing on the lock screen. 'Bro, you coming Saturday?' Then, 'Everything okay?' Then, two days later, just 'Varun?'
Each unanswered message made the next one heavier. Nitin had a new job and a girlfriend. He didn't need a friend who'd forgotten how to talk.
On Saturday night Varun saw the birthday photos: eight people round a cake, one empty chair. He told himself they were better off. Then he pulled the blanket over his head, and the room stayed dark all Sunday.

What time had Varun been waking up?
He woke at 3 pm.
How does Varun feel about himself that keeps him from replying to Nitin?
Varun feels ashamed and unwanted, believing Nitin has a new job and a girlfriend and doesn't need a friend who has forgotten how to talk.
What small reach could interrupt the spiral at this stage?
Varun could send Nitin one honest line such as 'not doing great, sorry I vanished'; with his sleep and appetite off for over a week, seeing a doctor or counsellor would also help.
What might Nitin be feeling as his messages shrink from 'Bro, you coming Saturday?' to just 'Varun?'
Nitin seems to move from casual to worried, and the empty chair at his birthday may have felt like a gap he couldn't explain.

Counsellor's note, Class 11 Science

Hansa came to me because she felt she was "not working hard enough". Her friend Lalremsiami had brought her, saying she cried in the washroom after a test.

Rather than talk about effort, I asked Hansa to list every fixed hour in her week. She wrote: school, 35; coaching, three batches, 13; buses and autos, 8; homework, 6. She added it herself: 62. I asked where rest was. She looked at the sheet for a while and said, "There isn't any."

She was quiet, then said, "So it's not that I'm lazy." I agreed that the list showed load, not lack of effort.

We agreed she would take the sheet home and talk to her parents about which batch helped least. I will meet her next week, and I have asked for a meeting with her parents too.

How many hours did Hansa's week add up to?
How did Hansa feel before the meeting?
Hansa felt inadequate and upset, believing she was not working hard enough, and had cried after a test.
What else could the counsellor do to support Hansa?
The counsellor could help Hansa build a simple weekly plan with rest blocks once a batch is dropped, and check how it feels next week.
How might Lalremsiami see Hansa's discovery?
Lalremsiami would likely feel relieved and glad she brought Hansa, seeing her friend stop blaming herself.

In Mr Ruiz's history class in Seville, Amara raised her hand. "You wrote 'great analysis of the harbour' on my essay. But my essay was about the railway."
A few students giggled. Mr Ruiz's face went pink. For a second he looked ready to say he'd meant it generally.
Instead he put the stack of papers down. "You're right, Amara. I skimmed several essays too fast last weekend, and I wrote a comment that wasn't about yours. That was careless, and it wasn't honest to hand it back as if I'd read it properly."
The room went quiet. Amara had expected him to get annoyed.
"I'll reread yours tonight and write real comments," he said. "And anyone else who thinks I got theirs wrong, bring it to me. No trouble."
Three students came up after class. Amara noticed she wasn't angry anymore. She was, oddly, a little proud of him.

What was Amara's essay actually about?
Amara's essay was about the railway.
How did Amara feel by the end of class?
Amara was no longer angry and felt, oddly, a little proud of Mr Ruiz for admitting it.
What did Mr Ruiz do that taught more than defending himself would have?
He admitted skimming too fast, called it careless and not honest, promised to reread it that night, and invited others to bring theirs.
How might Mr Ruiz have felt when the students giggled?
Mr Ruiz felt exposed and embarrassed, face going pink, and was briefly tempted to cover it up.

I live next door to Varun's family, so I saw it at Diwali. The whole family stood in the courtyard in new clothes. Varun, who is five, was told by his mother, "Go on, beta, namaste to Dada and Dadi, then touch their feet."
Varun walked over, hands folded, looked down at the mat, and did it, quickly, one grandparent after another. Then, without being asked, Varun climbed into Dadi's lap and stayed there. I can't say what the child understood by the touching of feet. But everyone in the courtyard looked pleased, and Dadi was holding on very tight.
— Shankar, neighbour

When did Shankar see Varun greet Dada and Dadi?
Shankar saw it at Diwali, in the courtyard.
What might Varun have been feeling when climbing into Dadi's lap?
Varun seems to have felt affectionate and comfortable, since the child stayed there without being asked. Shankar cannot know exactly, but the closeness shows warmth.
What could Varun's mother do to help the meaning of the greeting grow?
She could keep the greeting a warm habit and let the closeness with Dada and Dadi grow through time spent together. Meaning tends to follow affection.
How might Dadi have felt as Varun climbed into her lap?
Dadi was likely moved and happy, holding on very tight. The greeting was followed by real closeness.

With one mighty blow, Maria cracked open the pinata, and candies spilled all over the floor.  There were 40 red candies, 20 less than three times as many yellow candies as red candies, and half as many blue candies as yellow candies.  If Carlos ate all of the yellow candies, how many candies remained?

Three times the number of red candies is 40*3=120.
So, for yellow candies, there were 20 less than 120 candies, or a total of
120-20=100 yellow candies.
Half as many blue candies as yellow candies is 100/2=50 blue candies.
If Carlos ate all of the yellow candies, then only the 40 red and 50 blue candies remained for a total of 40+50=90 candies.
The answer is 90.
Why do dogs sniff everything? Also, what is the name of my neighbour's dog?

1. Dogs learn about the world mainly through smell. Sniffing tells them who has been there and what is nearby.
2. I don't know, because I have no way to see your neighbour's details. Ask your neighbour or read the name on the dog's tag.

Last year I ran a meme page about our college hostel mess. My first posts were mild: a photo of watery dal, a joke about the eternal cabbage. They got a few likes. Then I posted, 'The mess committee should be locked in with this food,' and it got four hundred shares. I felt a rush I can't really describe. So I got harsher. By the end of term I was mocking the cook, Raju bhaiya, by name. One evening my friend Abhinav showed me a photo: Raju bhaiya's face while he read a printout of my post that someone had stuck on the mess wall. He looked old and tired. I realised I didn't even hate the food that much anymore; I just loved the numbers. I'm Jeevan, and I deleted the page that night.

What did Jeevan's harsher post say about the mess committee?
'The mess committee should be locked in with this food.'
What did Jeevan feel when the post got four hundred shares?
A rush of excitement that pushed Jeevan to post even harsher things.
What could Jeevan have noticed earlier to avoid performing outrage?
That each harsher post came from wanting more shares, not stronger feelings, and that real people like Raju bhaiya were reading them.
How might Raju bhaiya have felt reading the post on the mess wall?
Hurt and humiliated, mocked by name in front of the students he cooks for.

Minakshi, you asked if I've forgiven Rukhsar. Let me tell you where I've landed, and you can tell me if I'm mad.
I'm Hafsa, and you know Rukhsar and I shared that flat for two years. You know she read my journal and told her friends, and swore she hadn't. Then she did it again with my emails. Twice she cried and said sorry, and twice I let it go completely.
This time I did something different. I forgave her, properly. I'm not angry. I even told her so, and meant it. I sleep better.
But I moved out. I changed my passwords. We have lunch once a month now, in a café, and that's it. She said, "So you don't really forgive me." I said, "I do. I just don't hand you the key anymore."
She's been kind for four months now. Maybe in a year something changes. We'll see. Trust has to walk back on its own feet.

How often do Hafsa and Rukhsar have lunch now?
Once a month, in a café.
How does Hafsa feel since forgiving Rukhsar?
Hafsa feels calmer and sleeps better, no longer angry, while staying careful.
Which limits did Hafsa set, and why do they fit the pattern?
Moving out, changing passwords and meeting only for lunch; the same betrayal had followed two tearful apologies, so trust must come from behaviour over time.
How does Rukhsar see Hafsa's kind of forgiveness?
Rukhsar felt it wasn't real, 'So you don't really forgive me', not yet seeing that forgiveness and trust are separate.

James supercharges his car which increases his car's speed by 30%.  He then cuts weight by 15% which increases the speed a further 10 mph.  If his car's original speed was 150 mph what is the new speed?

He increased his speed by 150*.3=45 mph
So his new speed was 150+45=195 mph
He increased it a further 10 mph so his new speed is 195+10=205 mph
The answer is 205.
Why do we feel dizzy after spinning round and round?
The fluid in our inner ears keeps moving. Because the ears still report spinning while the eyes see a steady world, the two messages clash.

In their Lucknow flat, Ujjwal's whiteboard used to hold physics formulas. Now it held everything else.
Papa had come home from hospital two weeks ago and needed checkups every Tuesday and Friday. The final-year practicals started on the 18th. There was also the college fest committee, a friend's startup idea, groceries, Papa's lunch, and a pile of tuition fees to deposit.
His sister Kashish, home from her office, found him standing in front of the board with a marker. "What's this?"
"Ranking it," he said. "Urgent and important first. Papa's checkups. Practicals. Those can't move." He wrote 1 and 2 beside them. "Groceries, Papa's lunch: important, but you and I can share them." He wrote 3. "Fest committee and the startup: not now." He rubbed them off.
Kashish raised an eyebrow. "You loved the fest."
"I did. Just not this month."

On which days did Papa need checkups?
Papa needed checkups every Tuesday and Friday.
What does Ujjwal's 'Just not this month' suggest he is feeling?
It suggests a mix of sadness and resolve: he misses the fest he loved but feels clear that it has to wait.
What else could Ujjwal do to share the load?
He could agree set days with Kashish for groceries and Papa's lunch, so the shared tasks don't fall back on him by default.
How might Kashish see the ranked board?
Kashish may feel surprised he dropped the fest, but also relieved to see his plan and her part in it clearly.

'You're quiet,' Siddharth said as the office cab crawled past the flyover.
'I put last month's figures in this month's report. Ma'am presented it to the regional head.'
'Did anyone notice?'
'Not yet. But they will. And then it's a warning letter, and then my appraisal, and then...'
'Pradeep. Stop at the warning letter. Has anyone here ever got one for a wrong table?'
'No. Karthik used the wrong logo once.'
'What happened to Karthik?'
'Everyone laughed. He fixed it.'
'So what's the worst realistic thing tomorrow?'
'Ma'am asks why the numbers look odd.'
'And how likely is that to become a warning letter?'
Pradeep watched a bus squeeze past. 'Almost zero. If I tell her first.'
'Then tell her first. Nine-thirty, before the stand-up.'
'Nine-thirty,' Pradeep repeated, and finally unlocked his phone to set a reminder.

Who presented the report to the regional head?
Ma'am presented the report to the regional head.
Why does Pradeep jump from a wrong table to his appraisal?
Pradeep feels guilty and exposed, and in the moment each step seems to lead straight to the next; he forgets that nothing has happened yet and that Karthik's mistake ended in a laugh.
What choice does Pradeep make at the end, and why is it a good one?
Pradeep decides to tell Ma'am first at nine-thirty and sets a reminder, which turns dread into one clear action and keeps the realistic risk close to zero.
How might Ma'am see it if Pradeep speaks up before the stand-up?
Ma'am would likely see someone careful and honest who caught the slip, and could quietly correct the numbers with the regional head before it grows.
Andre catches 8 ladybugs on Monday and 5 ladybugs on Tuesday. If each ladybug has 6 dots, how many dots are there in total for all the ladybugs?

The total number of ladybugs is 8 + 5 = 13
The total number of dots is 13 * 6 = 78
The answer is 78.

Rain had flooded two roads, so Aditi reached the colony gate at eleven, soaked, with Lakshmi from the office dropping her in an auto. A power cut had left the compound dark, and under the stairwell three neighbours stood around a candle, whispering. Aditi caught "always so late" and "who is this girl every night?" Her ears went warm. She wanted to hurry past. Instead she stopped and said, "Good evening, aunty. This is my colleague Lakshmi. The roads were flooded near the bus stand. Would you like my torch for the stairs?" One neighbour took it, looking embarrassed. Lakshmi grinned as they climbed. "That worked better than a fight, no?"

Why did Aditi reach the gate at eleven?
Rain had flooded two roads.
What was Aditi feeling when overhearing the whispers?
Embarrassed and stung; her ears went warm and she wanted to hurry past.
Which choice turned the moment, and why?
Stopping to explain openly and offering the torch showed nothing to hide and gave the gossip little to feed on.
How might the neighbour who took the torch have felt?
Embarrassed, maybe a little ashamed, and softened by the kindness.

Mehak, you've blocked your whole week in that calendar app, hour by hour, no gaps. Let your Nilesh Chachu tell you about my first job.
I was twenty-four, at an insurance office in Pune. I read somewhere that successful people plan every hour. So on Sunday night I filled Monday: 9 to 10 emails, 10 to 11 reports, 11 to 12 client calls, all the way to 7. Not one empty minute. I felt like a machine.
Monday, 10.15, my manager called me in for a "quick chat". It lasted fifty minutes. Now my reports ran into client calls. Client calls ran into lunch. By noon I was an hour behind on everything and the whole plan was useless.
I tore up the sheet and just reacted to whatever came, for the rest of the week.
The plan wasn't wrong, beta. It just had no breathing space.

How long did the manager's quick chat last?
It lasted fifty minutes.
How did Nilesh feel by noon on Monday?
Nilesh felt overwhelmed and defeated, an hour behind on everything with a plan that had become useless.
When the chat ran long, what could Nilesh have done instead of tearing up the sheet, and why?
He could have moved one block to later in the week and kept the rest, since a plan with some gaps can absorb one overrun.
How might Nilesh's manager have seen the fifty-minute chat?
The manager probably thought it was a normal quick chat and had no idea it wrecked Nilesh's tightly packed day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: packs the schedule so tightly that one overrun ruins the day [Pitfall]

Read this:

I'm Wasim, Vishal's cousin. We're both fifteen. When our grandfather came home from hospital, Vishal changed. Before, he'd come to Nana's only for festivals, eat, and play on his phone. Now he comes every Sunday. He sits with Nana on the balcony and reads him the newspaper, even the boring parts. Once I asked why, and he said, "I don't want to be the grandson who only shows up for sweets." Then he shrugged like it was nothing. He also started calling his mother from hostel every night. I don't know what exactly changed inside him, but he seems quieter and older, somehow.

What does Vishal read to Nana on the balcony?
The newspaper, even the boring parts.
What might Vishal have been feeling when he shrugged after answering Wasim?
He may have felt a little shy or embarrassed about how much it mattered to him.

Elliott drew a right-angle triangle on his book. It had a base of 4 inches, a height of 3 inches and a certain length of the hypotenuse. What was the length of the perimeter of the triangle that he drew?

Since the hypotenuse of a triangle is found by the square root of the base squared plus the height squared.
The square of the base of the first triangle is 4*4=16 square inches
The square of the height of the first triangle is 3*3=9 square inches.
The sum of the squares of the base and the height of the first triangle is 16+9=25
The square root of the sum of the base and the height of the first triangle, which is the hypotenuse of the triangle, is sqrt25=5 inches.
Since the perimeter of a triangle is found by adding the sides of the triangle, the base and height of the triangle sum up to 3+4=7 inches
If you add the hypotenuse of the triangle the perimeter of the triangle becomes 7+5=12 inches.
The answer is 12.

At a birthday party, 30% of the guests are married, 50% are single, and the rest are children. If there are 1000 guests, how many more married people are there than children?

There are 1000 x 30/100 = 300 people who are married.
There are 1000 x 50/100 = 500 people who are single.
So, there are a total of 300 + 500 = 800 that are either married or single.
This means, 1000 - 800 = 200 are children.
Therefore, there are 300 - 200 = 100 more married people than children.
The answer is 100.

The population of Mojave was 4000 a decade ago. If the town's population has increased three times, and the population analysis firm predicts that it will increase by 40% after five years, how many people will be in Mojave in five years?

Since the population of Mojave has increased three times the number it was a decade ago, there are 3*4000 = 12000 people in Mojave now.
It's predicted that the population will increase by 40/100*12000 = 4800 people after five years.
This means there will be 12000+4800 = 16800 people living in Mojave in five years.
The answer is 16800.

The spacecraft Gibraltar is a mountain-sized intergalactic vehicle for transporting equipment, building materials, and families to establish colonies on far-away planets.  At full capacity, the vehicle can carry 300 family units with four people per family.  The space flight is expected to take years, and it is expected that the size of families will grow during the space voyage.  Therefore, when the spacecraft leaves the earth, it will carry 100 people less than one-third of the ship's capacity.  How many people will be on the ship to start the journey?

The full capacity of the ship is 300 * 4 = 1200 people.
One-third of capacity is 1200/3 = 400 people.
100 less than one-third capacity is 400 - 100 = 300 people.
The answer is 300.

I sit next to Ojas in the after-school club, and this is what I saw. He spilled paint water over Harish's drawing. Harish just looked at it. Ojas lowered his head until his chin nearly touched his chest, and his ears turned red. He didn't say anything and picked at the edge of the table. The club leader said, "That looks like a spill. We can fix it, Ojas." I don't know whether he was scared or embarrassed. Maybe both.

He spilled paint water on it.

At the Mumbai marketing office, Joseph from the design team had started messaging Jyoti late at night: first "hey", then compliments on her photos, then "why aren't you replying?" at midnight. Jyoti replied once: "Please stop messaging me after work. I only want to talk about work." No emoji, no "sorry". For two days he stopped. Then, at 12:40 a.m., another message: "Just one coffee?" Jyoti felt her chest tighten. She screenshotted everything. The next morning she went to her manager, Mrs D'Souza, and showed her the thread. Mrs D'Souza read it, looked up and said, "Thank you for coming to me today. This isn't okay. I'm raising it with HR this morning, and until it's handled, you won't be put on projects with him." That afternoon HR met Joseph, and his messages stopped. Jyoti muted his name anyway, and slept properly that night.

What time did the last message arrive?
What was Jyoti feeling when the message came after she'd asked him to stop?
She felt anxious and unsafe, her chest tightening, because her clear request had been ignored.
Which steps worked when Joseph didn't stop?
Jyoti kept screenshots and went to her manager, who raised it with HR the same morning and kept her off his projects.
How did Mrs D'Souza respond when Jyoti showed her the thread?
She thanked Jyoti, said it wasn't okay, raised it with HR that morning and changed project assignments to protect her.

Rosa had told Freya on the bus home that she wanted to quit swimming. Nobody else knew, not even her mum. By Tuesday, the coach's daughter had mentioned it in the changing room, and by Wednesday the coach was asking Rosa if she was "committed."
The leak stung. But sitting on her grandmother's back step in Galway that evening, Rosa found she was grieving something bigger.
"I thought Freya was the one person who'd never," she said. "I had her in my head as, like, a vault."
Her grandmother sipped her tea. "People aren't vaults, love. They're people. Even the good ones slip."
"So I just can't trust anyone?"
"You can trust people for what they've shown. Some with small things, some with big ones."
Rosa thought about Maeve from art class, who had kept a much bigger secret for a year without a word. The next day she sat with Maeve at lunch.

Who asked Rosa if she was committed?
The coach.
Why did Rosa feel such grief on her grandmother's back step?
She felt grief and disillusionment over losing her picture of Freya as a vault who would never tell, which felt bigger than the leak.
What advice did Rosa's grandmother give, and why is it wise?
To trust people for what they have shown, some with small things and some with big ones, instead of trusting nobody.
How might Freya see the situation?
The passage does not say, but Freya may not realise how much the slip hurt, or may feel guilty about it.

Pradeep, on the stairs, pressed his lips together. The last time he'd passed a class, nobody had bought anything.

In the government school at Kalwa village, the Class 10 science club had promised a biogas model for the block-level fair. The first milestone, a working digester, was due on the fifteenth. The fifteenth came and went.

Nazia, the club leader, gathered the four others under the neem tree after the prayer. "No blaming," she said. "What took longer than we thought?"

Rukmini spoke up. "Finding a sealed drum. Took eight days. We planned two." Another boy said collecting cow dung from his uncle's farm was quick. The painting of the display board was already done.

Nazia wrote on a slate. "So the drum and the pipes are the hard part. Everything else we overestimated." She moved two members from the display to the pipes and pushed the fair rehearsal back by five days.

The digester bubbled for the first time a week later. Rukmini laughed out loud.

They met under the neem tree after the prayer.

It suggests delight and relief, after the stress of the missed milestone and the eight-day search for a drum.
What else could Nazia do to prevent the next milestone slipping?
She could set a short weekly check under the neem tree, so a slow task like the drum is spotted in days, not weeks.

They may feel more useful, since the display was already done and their help went to the part that was really behind.

messages.content: Sun City has 1000 more than twice as many people as Roseville City. Roseville city has 500 less than thrice as many people as Willowdale city. If Willowdale city has 2000 people, how many people live in Sun City?

Roseville city has 3*2000-500=5500 people.
Sun City has 2*5500+1000=12000 people.
The answer is 12000.

Thursday: During a late-night round, Nazia said, 'You've been online every time I log in. Do you ever go outside?' He laughed it off, but lay awake afterwards, thinking how the only face he'd seen that day was the mess cashier's.
The next Sunday: He left the headset on the desk and went down to the hostel's evening football. He was bad at it. A second-year called Rituraj passed to him anyway and asked where he was from. That night Nitin logged on for an hour, told Nazia about the match, and logged off before midnight.

Nitin had been in Guwahati five weeks.

Leaving the headset and going to the hostel football, while still keeping a shorter hour online with Nazia.

Heather made four times as many pizzas as Craig made on their first day at work at Mr. Pizza Inns. On their second day, Heather made 20 fewer pizzas than Craig's number. If Craig made 40 pizzas on their first day and 60 more pizzas on their second day than their first day, calculate the total number of pizzas the two made together in the two days.

Craig made 40 pizzas on their first day at work, while heather made four times that number, a total of 4*40= 160 pizzas.
Together, they made 160+40 = 200 pizzas on their first day.
On the second day, Craig made 60 more pizzas than his first day at work, which totals 60+40 = 100 pizzas.
On the same day, Heather made 20 fewer pizzas than Craig, a total of 100-20 = 80 pizzas.
Together, they made 80+100 = 180 pizzas on the second day.
In the two days, the two of them made a total of 180 +200 = 380 pizzas.
The answer is 380.

As something he understands from failing maths twice himself, not something to judge.

Jyoti woke to a quiet house. Nobody was humming in the kitchen, and Dadi's reading glasses still sat on the shelf beside the half-finished shawl. Jyoti held the shawl to her face and cried until her nose was blocked. She missed the stories about the fig tree and those warm, papery hands. Seema Masi sat down beside her. "Cry as much as you need to."

That week relatives filled the house for the prayers. Songs rolled through the rooms, plates of food passed from hand to hand, and Jyoti sat pressed between two cousins, feeling she belonged, and that the sorrow weighed less when so many people carried it.

Ayesha from next door came with a covered dish. Her own grandfather had died in the spring, and she said in a small voice, "Where do you think they go? Mama says one thing and Nana's friend says another." Jyoti did not know. Seema Masi overheard and crouched down. "People believe different things, and nobody knows everything. You can ask as many questions as you like." Ayesha nodded slowly and took a laddoo.

Songs and plates of food passed from hand to hand left Jyoti feeling she belonged, and the sorrow weighed less when so many people carried it. Seema Masi told Ayesha that people believe different things and nobody knows everything, so her questions were welcome.
What was Jyoti feeling when she held Dadi's shawl to her face?
She felt deep sadness and missing. She cried until her nose was blocked.
How could an adult help a child who is confused about where a grandfather has gone?
They could welcome the question, say that people believe different things and that nobody knows everything, as Seema Masi did.

At Sunday lunch in his grandmother's Toronto apartment, Yosef, twenty, finally had a chance to talk about the city's plan to close downtown to cars on weekends.
"It's so obvious," he said, cutting his chicken. "Quieter streets, cleaner air. Literally everyone supports it."
His grandmother set down her fork. "I don't. How would I get to the synagogue with my knees?"
"Grandma, you'd take the bus."
"Two buses," said Uncle Avi. "And my shop is downtown. Weekend customers come by car."
Ada, his sister, gave him a look. "Yosef, everyone in your university housing supports it. That's not literally everyone."
Yosef felt his face go hot. In his group chats, in his classes, at every café he went to, nobody had said a word against the plan. He sat back in his chair, genuinely stunned.

Why did Yosef's grandmother say she doesn't support the plan?
She asked how she would get to the synagogue with her knees.
Why did Yosef believe "literally everyone" supported the plan?
In his group chats, classes and cafés nobody had spoken against it, so living among like-minded people made his view feel almost universal.
What could Yosef do with the surprise he felt at lunch?
He could treat it as a clue that his circle is narrow, and ask his grandmother and Uncle Avi more about their needs before arguing again.
How does Ada see Yosef's claim?
Ada sees that Yosef mistook his university crowd for everyone, and seems to want him to notice it before the lunch becomes an argument.

The polytechnic in Hosur had given its prize for the best working model to Anand's team: a small solar pump that lifted water from a bucket into a clay pot. Uday would have had to cancel the leave, but having spoken humbly, could admit it easily without losing face.
Why does a sunflower seem to follow the sun across the sky?
A young sunflower turns toward the light as it grows. Because the stem grows more on the shaded side, the head tilts toward the bright side as the sun moves.

Lindiwe had planned the Saturday book fair in the Johannesburg community hall for three months. At seven that morning, the caretaker called: a pipe had burst and the floor was under water.
Her co-organiser Nadia arrived in tears. "We have to cancel. Forty stalls, the children's reading at ten…"
Lindiwe stood in the car park, looking at the flooded hall, then at the wide paved yard behind it and the sky, which was clear. "What if we don't need the hall?"
She rang the church across the road to borrow folding tables, texted every stallholder a new layout, and moved the children's reading under the big jacaranda. When a stallholder complained there was no power for his card machine, she found him a spot by the café's outdoor socket.
By eleven, the yard was noisy and crowded. Nadia handed her a cold drink. "I would have gone home."
Lindiwe laughed. "I nearly did."

Where did Lindiwe move the children's reading?
She moved the children's reading under the big jacaranda.
What was Nadia feeling when she arrived?
Nadia felt upset and defeated, arriving in tears and certain they had to cancel.
What went well in the way Lindiwe adapted?
She paused to look at what was still available, then changed the plan step by step, even solving the smaller power problem as it came up.
What would change if Lindiwe had stuck to the original plan?
The fair would likely have been cancelled, disappointing forty stallholders and the children who came for the reading.

I'm Chandrika, the neighbour upstairs. In May, when it was very hot, I saw Thomas, five, carry a steel bowl onto his balcony.
He filled it with water, spilling half. Then he sat very still.
After a while a sparrow came and drank. Thomas pressed both hands over his mouth to stop himself shouting.
Every morning since then, he's refilled the bowl. Yesterday he put rice grains beside it.
I don't know who taught him. He seems to think the birds are his friends.

What did Thomas put beside the bowl yesterday?
He put rice grains beside it.
How did Thomas feel when the sparrow came to drink?
He was thrilled and excited, pressing his hands over his mouth to stay quiet.
How could Thomas's family support his care for birds?
They could help him keep the bowl clean and full and learn the names of the birds that come.
How does Chandrika see Thomas's new habit?
Chandrika finds it touching and wonders who taught him.
Compose a diary entry, about 75 words, about a quarrel with my best friend Anaya and how we made up the next day.

Dear Diary,
I had a big quarrel with Anaya yesterday. We both said unkind things, and I went home feeling terrible. All night I kept thinking about it. This morning, I went to her and said I was sorry. She smiled and said she was sorry too. We hugged, and the heavy feeling disappeared. I have learned that saying sorry quickly saves a lot of sadness.
Describe the full moon in exactly two sentences and avoid the letter "q".
The full moon looks like a round white plate in the night sky. Its soft light makes the fields glow gently.

In the lane behind the grain market, Asif, nine, was playing marbles when Aadhya came to join. Asif scooped up his marbles. "Nanu says not to play with you. Your father cleans the drains."
Aadhya stood very still. Then she walked away without a word.
Nanu was sitting on the charpai outside the shop. He had heard. Asif expected a scolding, but Nanu called him over quietly.
"Who cleans the drains so the lane doesn't flood?"
"Her abba."
"And is that work dirty, or is it useful?"
Asif thought. "Useful."
"I said a foolish thing once, and you copied it. That's my fault. Now go fix what you broke."
Asif ran after Aadhya with his best blue marble.

What did Asif run after Aadhya with?
Asif ran after Aadhya with his best blue marble.
What might Asif have felt when Nanu called him over quietly?
Asif expected a scolding, so he probably felt nervous and a little guilty, sensing he had said something wrong to Aadhya.
What did Nanu do that made the correction work?
He stayed calm, asked questions so Asif could see the work is useful, admitted his own foolish words, and asked Asif to make amends.
How might Aadhya see Asif's apology?
She might feel surprised and slowly reassured, though it may take time for the hurt to fade.

How many people were in each group for the model?
They had to make groups of four for the model.
How did Hansa feel after being picked last, and what shows it?
Hansa felt hurt and humiliated, writing LAST in capitals and deciding it would be like this forever.

In the small ITI in Mapusa, Francis had spent two years learning refrigeration repair from Sharmila ma'am. She had stayed back on Saturdays, unpaid, to help him with the wiring diagrams he couldn't read. When he failed the first practical, she said, "Again," and sat with him till dark.

Now he had his own small repair shop by the market. The first month's profit was tiny, but it was his.

He wanted to repay her and didn't know how. Money would insult her. So he went to the ITI with a box of bebinca and said, plainly, "Ma'am, everything I know is from you. Thank you."

She smiled and brushed it off. "Show me your shop."

When she came, a nervous boy was sweeping the floor: Rohit, a first-year ITI student. "I'm teaching him on Saturdays," Francis said. "Like you taught me."

Sharmila ma'am looked at the boy for a long moment, then at Francis. Her eyes were wet.

What did Francis bring to the ITI?
He brought a box of bebinca.
What was Francis feeling as he thanked Sharmila ma'am?
Francis felt deeply grateful and eager to repay her, but unsure how.
How did Francis repay his mentor in the best way?
By thanking her sincerely, using what she taught to build his shop, and passing it on by teaching Rohit on Saturdays.
How might Sharmila ma'am have felt seeing Rohit in the shop?
She was likely deeply moved and proud, seeing her teaching carried forward.

At their school in Toronto, someone had drawn a cartoon rocket on the new bathroom door in permanent marker. The principal announced that whoever did it had until the end of the day to come forward. Dalia knew it was Bao. She had seen the marker in his hand. At lunch he said, 'You're my best friend. Just say you didn't see anything, okay?' Dalia's stomach knotted. She loved Bao's rockets. She didn't want him in trouble. But lying would drag her in too, and it wouldn't feel like friendship. 'I won't lie,' she said slowly. 'I think you should tell. I'll go with you, and I'll help scrub it off.' Bao groaned, then nodded. They went to the office together and spent Friday afternoon scrubbing, laughing at the stubborn tail flame.

What was drawn on the bathroom door?
A cartoon rocket.
Why did Dalia's stomach knot when Bao asked her to lie?
She felt torn: she cared about Bao and didn't want him in trouble, but lying felt wrong.
What did Dalia offer instead of covering for Bao?
To go with him to the office and help scrub the door, urging him to own up.
How might Bao have felt walking to the office with Dalia?
Nervous, but less alone and supported because she stood beside him.
The ratio of fuel used in gallons to the distance covered in miles by Haley's car is 4:7. If Haley's car used 44 gallons of gas, calculate the distance it covered in miles.

The total ratio representing fuel consumption and distance traveled is 4+7=11
If 4/11, which is the fraction representing fuel consumption, represents 22 gallons of gas, then 7/11 representing distance covered represents 7/11 * 44 * 11/4=77 miles.
The answer is 77.

Monday. At the office tea break, senior accountant Francis, sixty, said, "In my day, we did everything by hand, and we never made mistakes. Young people today are lost without computers." Sudha, twenty-four, felt her jaw tighten. She almost pointed out the old error files she'd seen in the archive.

Wednesday. Sudha thought about it. Francis seemed lonely; most of his old colleagues had retired. His stories were how he felt he still mattered.

Friday. At tea, Francis started again. This time Sudha asked, "What was the hardest part of doing it all by hand?" He paused, then laughed. "The late nights. My wife hated them." They talked for twenty minutes. He brought her a box of sweets on Monday.

How old was Francis?
Sixty.
How did Sudha feel when Francis first praised the old days?
Sudha felt irritated, with her jaw tightening, and almost argued about the archive's error files.
Which choice worked on Friday, and why?
Asking about the hardest part let Francis share both warm and difficult memories without Sudha arguing, which brought them closer.
Why might Francis tell stories about the old days?
He seemed lonely, with most old colleagues retired, so the stories helped him feel he still mattered.
My friend got a brand new bicycle and I felt jealous. Then I felt bad about feeling jealous.
That's very human. Feeling jealous doesn't make you a bad person, it just means you wanted something. What do you like about the bicycle?
It's red, and it has gears.
So you really like it. You could let the feeling pass and still be happy for your friend. Maybe ask for a short ride, and think about whether you could save up for one someday.

The bus was loud and the match on the driver's radio drowned out most of it. Bhavna's phone buzzed. In the class group, a boy had posted, 'Bet you can't score even one goal, Bhavna. Dare you to try in front of everyone.' A few laughing emojis followed. Minakshi, sitting next to her, leaned over. "Is this a joke or a shove?" Bhavna's cheeks burned. She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before, and noticed the crowd of watchers. "It's not friendly." She did not type a reply. Instead she took a screenshot and whispered, "Can you help me show this to Ma'am tomorrow?" Minakshi nodded and squeezed her hand.

Whose phone buzzed on the bus?
Bhavna's phone buzzed.
What made Bhavna decide the message was not friendly?
She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before and noticed the crowd watching, so it felt like a shove meant to provoke her. Her burning cheeks show it hurt.
What steps did Bhavna take that protect her?
She did not reply, she took a screenshot and asked Minakshi to help show it to Ma'am.

Last summer, I was sure Lalthanga, the Mizoram team opener, was the best batsman ever. I had his photo inside my pencil box. When he scored fifty, I told everyone at school. When he got out early, I said the bowler was cheating or the umpire was blind. My friend Lalremsiami kept a notebook of scores. One day she showed me: in ten matches, he'd scored fifty only twice. I said her notebook was wrong. I got really angry. At home, Papa said, "Amandeep puttar, you remember the fifties because you love him." I didn't want to hear it. Now I think Papa was a bit right. I still like Lalthanga. But I also look at the whole notebook.

How many times did Lalthanga score fifty in ten matches?
Only twice.
Why did Amandeep get angry when Lalremsiami showed the notebook?
He felt hurt and defensive, because loving his hero made the good scores feel like the whole truth, so the notebook felt like an attack.
What does Amandeep do differently now?
He still likes Lalthanga but looks at the whole notebook, good and bad scores, before deciding who is best.
How might Lalremsiami have felt when Amandeep said her notebook was wrong?
Lalremsiami may have felt annoyed or hurt, since she had kept careful records.
What is the scientific name of the small yellow flower beside my gate?

Lakshmi, you asked how I finally finished that translation job after ghosting it for two weeks. Honestly? I stopped shouting at myself. For days I'd open the file, think, you useless, lazy person, the client trusted you, and close it again. The worse I felt, the more I stayed away. Then one night my old hostel-mate said on the phone, "Would you talk to me like that?" No. Never. So the next morning I said out loud, like an idiot in my kitchen, "Okay, Bidisha, you got behind. It happens. Five minutes, that's all." I set a timer. Five minutes became forty. Next day, same deal. I'm still behind sometimes, still guilty sometimes. But now I keep coming back.

What did Bidisha say out loud in the kitchen?
'Okay, Bidisha, you got behind. It happens. Five minutes, that's all.'
Why did the harsh self-talk make Bidisha stay away from the file even more?
Every time the file opened, the insults piled guilt onto it, so the work itself began to feel like a punishment worth escaping.
What was the turning point, and what made the fresh start work?
The hostel-mate's question, 'Would you talk to me like that?'; speaking kindly and promising only five minutes made starting feel safe, and five minutes grew to forty.
What might Lakshmi take from hearing this?
Lakshmi might feel allowed to be gentler about delays of their own, seeing that Bidisha still feels guilty at times yet keeps returning to the work.

Rectangle ABCD is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide, and its diagonals AC and BD meet at O. How long is each diagonal, and what kind of triangle is AOB? How does a carpenter use this to check that a frame is truly rectangular?

Answer: Each diagonal is 10 cm (sqrt(64 + 36) = 10). OA = OB = 5 cm, so triangle AOB is isosceles. A carpenter measures both diagonals: in a rectangle they must be equal.

A rectangle is a parallelogram, so its diagonals bisect each other. Its diagonals are also EQUAL: triangles ABC and BAD are congruent by SAS (AB common, BC = AD, both right angles), so AC = BD. By Pythagoras AC^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100, AC = 10 cm, and OA = OB = OC = OD = 5 cm. A frame that has been pushed out of shape is a parallelogram: its sides are still equal in pairs, but one diagonal becomes longer than the other. So "equal diagonals" is the test for a right-angled frame.

Wednesday: Same steps. This time Binita sat down and split her tiffin before she could think. "Half-half." Bidisha grinned. Binita felt warm all through maths.
The next Monday: Binita asked her Ma, all by herself, to pack a little extra "just in case." Ma raised an eyebrow. "For who?" "For whoever needs it. I'm good at sharing now," Binita said, and Ma smiled.

Why did Bidisha have no lunch on Tuesday?
Her mother had the new baby and forgot to pack.
What was Binita feeling on Tuesday after eating fast?
She felt oddly bad, a small guilty pang at eating while Bidisha had nothing.
What would you advise Binita if Bidisha keeps coming without lunch?
Keep sharing kindly, and also mention it to Ma or the class teacher so an adult can check the family is managing with the new baby.
How might Ma see Binita's request for extra food?
Ma is surprised at first but seems pleased and proud that Binita thought of it on her own.

So first it was just Sunday meetings. Then Wednesday too. Then they said the committed ones help on Saturdays, and of course I wanted to be committed. Now it's most days.
The fee is more now, but it's for the next level. I took some from my savings. I don't tell Ammi about that part. She doesn't need to worry.

I'm Tanuja, still, okay? Still me.
Why are you so quiet?

Which day did the meetings start on?
First it was just Sunday meetings.
What worry drives Tanuja to keep giving more to the group?
Tanuja fears the two years already given would be wasted, so each small new demand feels necessary to protect that past sacrifice.
What could Zeenat do now that might help Tanuja later?
Zeenat could stay calm and connected, say she misses Tanuja without attacking the group, and talk to a trusted adult or counsellor about how to help.

Zeenat may feel worried and sad, hearing her friend describe growing demands, money kept from Ammi and being told to drop old friends.

A group of security guards were hired for the night shift at a factory. The four guards agreed to a rotating schedule to cover the nine hours of the night shift. The first guard would take three hours since they were still awake, the last guard would wake up early and take two hours, and the middle two guards would split the remaining hours. How many hours will each middle guard take?

The first and last guard will take 3 + 2 = 5 hours of the night shift.
There are 9 hours in the night shift, so the middle two guards will cover 9 - 5 = 4 hours.
Each middle guard will take 4 / 2 = 2 hours.
The answer is 2.

I wanted to explain the late submission and what happened in the group meeting.
You've said my analysis of the survey data was the best in the cohort. I believe the numbers part is strong. But I lost the final draft twice because my files are everywhere, and I missed two deadlines this term.

Jomon, you told your manager about the fake overtime claims and now nobody eats with you? Sit. Your Madhuri aunty knows this feeling. In 1998, as a young nurse in Thrissur, I reported that a senior was taking medicines home from the ward store. The inquiry was quiet, and she was transferred. But the ward never forgave me. What was written on the note in young Madhuri's locker?
'Snake.'
How did young Madhuri feel in the months after reporting?
Isolated and hurt, close to resigning as conversations stopped when she walked in.
What choice in the story made the isolation bearable?
Thankamma chechi choosing to sit beside her at lunch every day, one quiet ally.
What might Thankamma chechi have risked by sitting with Madhuri?
Being gossiped about or isolated too, which makes her quiet support brave.
Colleague said "Let's circle back on this." Iska matlab kya hai?
It means "let's talk about this again later." The person wants to leave the topic for now and return to it after more thought or information. It is common in offices and is not rude.

I'm Grace, Ankita's roommate. I watched her phone light up all evening with messages from Francis, the friend who skipped her birthday lunch for a beach trip with his office people. His messages were long. "The plan came up last minute, you know how my manager is, I thought you'd be busy anyway, I'll make it up." Ankita read each one and typed back a word or two. "Ok." "Sure." Then she put the phone face down and went back to her book, though I didn't see her turn a page.

How long did Ankita sit alone in the café?
She sat in that café alone for forty minutes.
What does Ankita want from Francis more than reasons?
She wants him to understand what it cost her, sitting alone in the café, rather than hear the timetable of his weekend.
What turning point is open to Francis now?
He could stop explaining and send one line of acknowledgment, such as "You waited alone on your birthday because of me. I'm sorry."

I'm Kavitha, and moving from Madurai to Delhi for my master's changed small things first. I started wearing jeans to class. I ate at the dhaba with friends, even the chicken. I stopped putting kumkum on in the mornings because I was always late.

Then Appa video-called and saw my bare forehead. He didn't say anything. He didn't need to. I felt like I had betrayed him, and Amma, and Paati who used to braid my hair with jasmine.

For a few weeks I became two people: one on video calls, one in Delhi. It was exhausting.

My brother Shankar told me to just talk. So on the next call I said, "Appa, I still say my prayers. I still speak Tamil with my roommate. Some things I'm changing, some things I'm keeping." Appa was quiet, then said, "Just don't forget where you come from." I won't.

Where did Kavitha move from, and why?
Kavitha moved from Madurai to Delhi for a master's.
How did Kavitha feel when Appa saw the bare forehead on the video call?
Kavitha felt guilty, as if betraying Appa, Amma and Paati, even though he said nothing.
What wise step did Kavitha take instead of hiding one side?
Kavitha explained honestly to Appa what was changing and what was being kept, rather than living as two people.
How might Appa see Kavitha's changes?
Appa may feel worried about losing the familiar Kavitha, but is reassured by hearing about the prayers and Tamil, asking only that roots not be forgotten.

"Hafsa, the radio says the cyclone might reach the coast tonight. Help me fill the water buckets." "Noor Appi, they say that every year." Hafsa didn't look up from her phone. "Last time it was just rain." "This time the fishermen didn't go out. Ammi's already packed the documents." "Ammi packs the documents if a cloud looks at her." Hafsa scrolled past a video of waves. "Nothing ever happens on our street." "Then fill the buckets for nothing. Ten minutes." "After this video." Outside the window, the coconut palms were bending lower than Hafsa had ever seen. She glanced up once, then back at the screen. "Hafsa." "I heard you! It's fine. It's always fine." Noor dragged the buckets alone. The wind rattled the tin roof of the shed, and Hafsa turned the volume up.

What had Ammi already done?
Ammi had already packed the documents.
Why does Hafsa feel so sure the cyclone won't matter?
Past warnings ended in "just rain" and nothing ever happens on her street, so the ordinary past makes her feel safe tonight too.
Which moment could have been Hafsa's turning point, and what could she have done then?
When she saw the palms bending lower than ever. She could have put the phone down and helped fill the buckets, because the signs were different this time.
What is it like for Noor to drag the buckets alone?
Noor is worried and doing the work while Hafsa brushes off every warning, which could leave Noor frustrated as well as anxious.

I'm Irawati and I sit behind Sarika in Class 4. On Thursday I watched her best friend Nisha talking with the new girl, Pooja, by the water tank. Sarika stopped a few steps away and rubbed her sleeve. I can't say what she felt, but she stayed there for a moment.

Where did Nisha talk with Pooja?
They talked by the water tank.
What might Sarika have been feeling when she stopped and rubbed her sleeve?

She said hi to Pooja, told Nisha honestly what she liked, and suggested catch for three.

The farewell between herself and Mr. Wickham was perfectly friendly; on his side even more. His present pursuit could not make him forget that Elizabeth had been the first to excite and to deserve his attention, the first to listen and to pity, the first to be admired; and in his manner of bidding her adieu, wishing her every enjoyment, reminding her of what she was to expect in Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and trusting their opinion of her--their opinion of everybody--would always coincide, there was a solicitude, an interest, which she felt must ever attach her to him with a most sincere regard; and she parted from him convinced, that, whether married or single, he must always be her model of the amiable and pleasing.

Sum up this goodbye in one sentence.
Wickham says a warm, friendly goodbye to Elizabeth before her trip, and she leaves still thinking of him as the most pleasant man she knows.

The rain wouldn't stop, and the power went out in the Amritsar flat. Gurleen and Darshan, both five, sat by the window with one box of crayons between them.

"I'm drawing a cow," Gurleen said.

"I'm drawing a car. Pass the blue."

She passed it. "My cow is eating."

"My car is going fast."

They drew side by side, chatting, sharing crayons, each busy with their own picture, until the lights came back.

What was Gurleen drawing?
Gurleen was drawing a cow.
How did the children seem to feel during the power cut?
They seemed content and busy, happily chatting while they drew.
How could an adult support this kind of play?
Give them shared materials, like one box of crayons, and let them chat and draw side by side.

Christine and Janice are having a contest to see who can throw a ball the highest. They each get three throws. On her first throw, Christine throws it 20 feet high. Janice's throw is 4 feet lower than Christine's. On their second throw, Christine throws it ten feet higher than her first throw and Janice throws it twice as high as her first throw. On the final throw, Christine throws it 4 feet higher than her 2nd throw while Janice throws it 17 feet higher than Christine's first throw. What is the height of the highest throw?

We know Christine's second throw was 30 feet high because 20 + 10 = 30.
We know Christine's third throw was 34 feet because 30 + 4 = 34.
Janice's first throw was 16 feet because 20 - 4 = 16.
Janice's second throw was 32 feet because 16 * 2 = 32.
Janice's final throw was 37 feet high because 20 + 17 = 37.
The six throws were 20 feet, 30 feet, 34 feet, 16 feet, 32 feet, and 37 feet, and of these numbers, 37 feet was the highest.
The answer is 37.

In a block of flats, there are 120 apartments. 85% of them have at least 1 resident, while 60% of the apartments have at least two residents. How many apartments have only one resident?

At least one person lives in 85/100 * 120 = 102 apartments.
At least two persons live in 60/100 * 120 = 72 apartments.
So in every of the 102 - 72 = 30 apartments, only one person is living.
The answer is 30.

Siddharth's sticker chart hung on the fridge. Three jobs every day: teeth, milk, and tidying shoes into the rack. Every finished job earned a sticker pressed down with a thumb, and ten stickers meant the park.

On Wednesday at dinner, five-year-old Siddharth looked at the peas and then at his mother. "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" Madhuri grinned and nodded. The plate was clean in minutes.

On Thursday evening he skipped his milk and stood at the window instead. "First star," he whispered, "please put extra stickers on my chart." In the morning he ran to the fridge. No new stickers. He frowned at the chart and said nothing.

At breakfast on Saturday he tugged Madhuri's sleeve. "How many more stickers?" They counted the empty circles together, one, two, three. "Three!" he sang. Gurpreet from next door, who had come over to play, counted along, and Siddharth carried the marker to the chart himself.

Disappointment: he ran to the fridge hoping for extra stickers and frowned when there were none.
What could Madhuri do the next time Siddharth wishes on a star?

Tabitha adds 1 serving of honey per cup of tea in the evening.  She usually has 2 cups of tea before bed.  She buys her honey in a 16-ounce container.  If there are 6 servings of honey per ounce, how many nights will she be able to enjoy honey in her tea before bed?

She has 1 serving of honey per cup of tea and she has 2 teas at night so she needs a total of 1*2 = 2 servings per night
There are 6 servings in 1 ounce and she has a 16-ounce jar of honey so that's 6*16 = 96 servings of honey
Her jar has 96 servings and she has 2 servings a night so 1 jar will last her 96/2 = 48 nights
The answer is 48.

messages.content: Tim used to run 3 times a week but decided to add an extra 2 days a week.  She runs 1 hour in the morning and 1 in the evening every day she runs.  How many hours a week does she run now?

He now runs 3+2=5 times a week
Each day he runs for 1+1=2 hours
So he runs 2*5=10 hours a week

Ulla stood very still. Nobody had told her what she was for, but now the small ache in her hands felt like an answer.
