Manjula-ji replied with a single 👍. Farida stared at it on the bus home through Pune traffic. In her friend group, a lone thumbs-up meant "okay, whatever", almost cold. Had she overdone it? Was Manjula-ji annoyed? She almost didn't go to the office party that Friday. But she went, and when Manjula-ji hugged her at the door, Farida asked, half joking, "Your thumbs-up scared me, ma'am. Was that a good one?" Manjula-ji looked baffled. "Good one? It's the best one! My son taught me it means 'very nice'. I read your message three times." Farida laughed with relief. "In my group it means 'fine, stop talking'." Manjula-ji shook her head. "Then you young people should come with a manual!" The next morning she sent Farida a 👍 and a ❤️.

How did Manjula-ji reply to Farida's message?
With a single 👍.

At 10.

Fixed check-ins on Monday and Thursday, which keep Ganga informed while giving Saurabh room to use judgement.

Ganga seems surprised and open, agreeing to the plan once the effect is explained.
I am going to Delhi by flight yesterday.
I went to Delhi by flight yesterday. Why: "Yesterday" shows the past, so use the past simple "went", not "am going".

The astonishment which I had at first experienced on this discovery soon gave place to delight and rapture. After so much time spent in painful labour, to arrive at once at the summit of my desires was the most gratifying consummation of my toils. But this discovery was so great and overwhelming that all the steps by which I had been progressively led to it were obliterated, and I beheld only the result. What had been the study and desire of the wisest men since the creation of the world was now within my grasp. Not that, like a magic scene, it all opened upon me at once: the information I had obtained was of a nature rather to direct my endeavours so soon as I should point them towards the object of my search than to exhibit that object already accomplished. I was like the Arabian who had been buried with the dead and found a passage to life, aided only by one glimmering and seemingly ineffectual light.

Two sentences on the main idea, please.
The narrator is amazed and delighted to reach, after long work, the discovery long wanted. It gives no finished result, only knowledge to guide further work, like one faint light in a tomb.

At the kindergarten in Buenos Aires, the tidy-up bell rang. Rania crossed her arms and turned her back on the block tower. "No. I'm not tidying." Valentina, her teacher, didn't raise her voice or call her naughty. She crouched nearby. "Blocks go in the box before snack. That's our rule every day. I'll put the first one in with you." Rania stamped. "No!" Valentina waited, humming the tidy-up song, while the others lined up. After a minute Rania dropped one block in, then another, scowling. "Thank you. Now snack," said Valentina, as if nothing had happened.

What did Valentina offer to do with Rania?
Valentina offered to put the first block in the box with her.
What was Rania feeling when she crossed her arms and said "No"?
Rania felt stubborn and cross about ending play, and was testing whether the tidy-up rule really held.
Which choice by Valentina worked, and why?
Valentina stayed calm, repeated the everyday rule without shaming, and waited, so Rania had nothing to fight against and tidied.
How might Valentina see Rania's "No!"?
Valentina seems to see it as ordinary limit-testing for a young child, not rudeness, so she stays patient.

Payal, you asked why I looked so tired at your wedding. Honestly? That was the week of the quarterly report. I'd been rewriting the same executive summary for six days. Every time I read a sentence, I'd find something slightly off. Meanwhile Rohit on my team sent his section on day two, rough, and the director thanked him in front of everyone for being so quick. My section was better, I know it was. But it came in three days late, and by then the director had already built the presentation around Rohit's numbers. I skipped your mehendi to keep polishing. I haven't gone to bed before midnight in a month. And for what? The part I was so proud of got one line in the final deck. That's the real story, from your very tired friend Indu.

Six days.

Indu feels frustrated and a bit bitter, believing the section was better but seeing the rough, early version win the credit.

Set a deadline to send a good draft early, as Rohit did, and polish only the most important parts afterwards.

Payal may feel sad that work took Indu from the celebration, and worried about how tired a friend has been.

In the village of Kothur, Ira and Shalini were writing a skit for the Gram Sabha on saving water. Their first script ended with a big line: "Men waste, women carry!" They practised it at the well. Shalini's uncle heard and frowned. "So all of us are wasters now?" Two other men walked off. Ira was annoyed. "But it's true in our lane! Who fetches water every morning?" Shalini thought for a while. "True, but if half the audience walks out, who hears the rest?" They sat on the well's edge and rewrote it. The new last scene showed a father and a daughter both carrying pots, then fixing a leaking tap together. The last line became: "Every drop, every hand." At the Gram Sabha, the men clapped. Afterwards Shalini's uncle came up and asked where he could get the tap washers.

I need this summarised in three sentences.

Ira and Shalini's water-saving skit ends with "Men waste, women carry!", and some men walk off. Because the audience was leaving, they rewrite the end so a father and daughter carry pots and fix a leaking tap together. This time the men clap, and Shalini's uncle asks where to get tap washers.

Dear Lavanya,
You've moved to Pune and missed all the drama, so here's the update.
Remember Rhea? Someone started saying she was caught shoplifting at the mall. On Wednesday Ritesh tried to tell me the whole story at lunch. I just said, “I didn't hear that, and I don't want to,” and asked him about the cricket trials.

But yesterday Rhea herself came to me and told me her real worry, about her parents fighting. She said, “You're the only one who didn't pass that story around.”

Saurabh said, "I didn't hear that, and I don't want to."

Example: Can you bring me up to speed on what I missed yesterday?

I like this song very much.
Why: continuous tense ("am liking" -> "like").

In the hospital billing office, Divyansh, the supervisor, watched the week unfold. Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday and stayed late on Thursday. Priya at the next desk printed the same three forms and spent long stretches at the tea counter. Nobody had complained. Divyansh noticed Anand's shoulders sagging and Priya's empty in-tray. He weighed it up: if he ignored it, Priya would keep coasting, and Anand would burn out. On Friday he asked Priya for a private word: "I want to understand your workload. Can we look at it together?" Then he took Anand aside and said, "I see how much you have done. Let me rebalance."

How many claims did Anand reconcile by Wednesday?
Anand reconciled forty claims by Wednesday.
What was Divyansh worried about when weighing up what to do?
Divyansh was concerned that ignoring the imbalance would reward coasting and burn out Anand; the worry was for fairness and for Anand's health.
What did Divyansh do on Friday that a fair manager would do?
Divyansh spoke privately with each person, asked Priya about the workload without accusing, and told Anand the effort was seen and would be rebalanced.
What might Anand have felt when Divyansh said "I see how much you have done"?
Anand probably felt relief and a little pride at being noticed after quietly carrying the load; sagging shoulders suggest that being unseen had been wearing.

Chetan,
I'm writing because saying it out loud would come out as shouting.
In September you borrowed my camera for your cousin's wedding. "Back by Monday," you said. It's December. When I asked last week, you said it was "at home somewhere", and then I saw it in your photos from the beach trip.
I bought that camera with my first stipend. I lent it because you're my friend, and because when I was new at college you walked me to the bus stand every evening for a month. I trusted that person.

I'm not going to stop lending things to people. But I'll lend smaller things first, and ask for dates in writing. Please return the camera by Sunday.

By Monday.

Pallavi feels betrayed and gullible, as if everyone else could have predicted this except Pallavi.
What choice does Pallavi make about trusting people in future?
To keep lending, but smaller things first and with dates in writing, trusting more carefully rather than trusting nobody.
How might Chetan feel reading the line about the bus stand?
Chetan may feel ashamed, reminded that Pallavi's trust grew from Chetan's own earlier kindness, which makes the let-down sharper.

I still remember the day Baljeet knocked my tiffin off the table in Class 5. My rajma went everywhere. He laughed and said, "Oops."
I wanted to throw my bottle at him. My arm was already up.
But I put it down. I walked to the sink and washed my hands slowly, counting the tiles. Twelve.
When I came back, I said, "Baljeet, that was my lunch. Say sorry and help clean it."
He looked surprised. He said sorry, and even gave me half his parathas.
If I'd thrown the bottle, I'd be the one in trouble. I'm Madhuri, and I'm still a little proud of that day.

What did Madhuri count at the sink?
The tiles, twelve of them.
What was Madhuri feeling when her arm was already up?
Madhuri felt furious and wanted to hurt Baljeet back.
What did Madhuri's pause at the sink allow her to do?
It gave her time to calm down so she could ask for an apology and help instead of throwing her bottle.
How might Baljeet have felt when Madhuri came back calm?
Baljeet was surprised, and Madhuri's calm, firm words likely made him feel sorry enough to share his parathas.
Sunny bakes 8 cakes. Then she gives away 2 cakes. Sunny wants to put candles on the remaining cakes. If she puts 6 candles on each cake, how many candles will she use in total?

Sunny has a total of 8 - 2 = 6 cakes
Sunny will use a total of 6 * 6 = 36 candles
The answer is 36.

For Akash it is quick to read and easy to agree to, since it names his own case study and asks for very little.

What does the word "change" mean?
Rhea had 27 rupees of pocket money and spent 12 on a snack. How much is left?
What is wrong with "He spended all his pocket money."?
Why do shops give a receipt?
What should I do with coins I find at home?

1. Change means the money you get back when you pay too much. Example: The shopkeeper gave me my change.
2. 15 rupees. Because 27 - 12 = 15.
3. Fixed: He spent all his pocket money. Why: "Spend" has an irregular past: "spent".
4. It records what was bought. Because customers can use it to return or change an item.
5. Ask your family if the coins belong to someone. If not, collect them in a jar and count it on a fixed day.

Two days before Lunar New Year, the Vancouver apartment smelled of dumpling dough, and Mina had a plan written on an index card.
"Dad," she said, laying it next to the flour. "Proposal. I do the dishes every night, take out the recycling, and clean the bathroom on Saturdays. In exchange, I get a phone. Not a fancy one."
Chen raised an eyebrow, still pleating a dumpling. "And if I say we do chores because we live here together?"
"Then I'd still do them," Mina said quickly. "Probably. But this way it's fair. You get a clean bathroom, I get a phone. Everybody wins."
She had even drawn a little table with two columns: My job. My payment.
Chen laughed despite himself. "You've turned our home into a shop."
"A very fair shop," Mina said.

What was Mina's plan written on?
An index card.
How does Mina feel about her proposal?
She feels confident and a bit proud of it, sure it is fair because each side gets something, like a shop.
How could Chen respond so Mina sees chores as more than a price?
Take the honest offer seriously, then talk about how the family shares work because they care for each other, perhaps deciding about the phone separately from the chores.
How does Chen see the deal?
Chen finds it funny, laughing that she has turned the home into a shop, while hinting that chores are about living together, not payment.

Note for Harish's family
Today we had a fire drill. The bell was very loud, and Harish cried hard with his hands over his ears. He was slow to calm. I held him in the quiet corner, rocked slowly and hummed the rain song he likes. He clung to my kurta. Some children bounce back fast; Harish feels things deeply. The rain song Harish likes.

I'm Sabina, and I sat beside Jagdish at the video call with the partner firm from Osaka. Jagdish had pitched a joint project. Mr Tanaka listened, nodded often, and said, "Very interesting. We will consider it carefully." Jagdish grinned at me off-camera. He wrote to the team, "They're in!" I wasn't so sure. Mr Tanaka hadn't asked a single question about cost or timeline, and there had been a long pause before "consider". Two weeks passed with no follow-up email. Jagdish started drafting the contract. I suggested he send a short, polite note: "To plan our side, could you let us know by Friday whether you'd like to proceed, or whether now isn't the right time? Either is completely fine." He sent it. Mr Tanaka replied the same day: "Thank you. At this time, it is difficult." Jagdish looked deflated, but at least he stopped drafting.

What did Mr Tanaka say at the end of the call?
"Very interesting. We will consider it carefully."
What was Jagdish feeling when Mr Tanaka's final reply came?
He felt deflated and disappointed, having been sure they were in; perhaps also relieved to stop drafting a contract for nothing.
What signs led Sabina to doubt Jagdish's reading?
No questions about cost or timeline, a long pause before "consider", and two weeks with no follow-up.
How might Mr Tanaka have seen the clear note?
He may have found it easier to answer, since it gave him a polite way to say now wasn't the right time.

Describe the weather and the fields around Thornfield at this time.

A splendid Midsummer shone over England: skies so pure, suns so radiant as were then seen in long succession, seldom favour even singly, our wave-girt land. It was as if a band of Italian days had come from the South, like a flock of glorious passenger birds, and lighted to rest them on the cliffs of Albion. The hay was all got in; the fields round Thornfield were green and shorn; the roads white and baked; the trees were in their dark prime; hedge and wood, full-leaved and deeply tinted, contrasted well with the sunny hue of the cleared meadows between.

It is a splendid Midsummer with pure skies and radiant suns, like Italian days come from the South. The hay is in, the fields round Thornfield are green and shorn, the roads white and baked, and the trees dark and full-leaved.

In Addis Ababa, the courtyard behind the church was full for little Abebe's christening feast. He was eighteen months old, in white cotton with a bright trim, and unhappy about the shoes.

Grandmothers passed him from lap to lap. When the drums started, his lip wobbled.

Then Siddiq, the neighbour who ran the corner shop, lifted him and swayed to the music, humming. Abebe stared at his beard, patted it, and laughed.

Who lifted Abebe when the drums started?
Siddiq, the neighbour who ran the corner shop, lifted him.
How did Abebe feel when the drums started?
Abebe felt unsure and a little frightened; his lip wobbled.

A calm, familiar neighbour holding him and swaying gently to the music turned the noise into play.

Monday: during the maths test, Arohi scratched her head and rubbed her forehead. Kamal, at the next desk, whispered, “Are you stuck?” “No, just an itch,” she whispered back.
Wednesday: she scratched her head again. Kamal asked after the paper, “Stuck or itchy?” “Stuck on the last one!” she laughed.
Friday: Arohi rubbed her forehead during the spelling test. Kamal just slid his eraser to the side of the desk, in case she needed it. She looked up and smiled, and kept writing.

What did Arohi say when Kamal asked if she was stuck on Monday?
She said, “No, just an itch.”
What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday when she scratched her head, and what else could it have been?
She was probably stuck on the last question, as she said afterwards. On Monday the same gesture was just an itch, so the gesture alone does not tell which.
How did Kamal's approach improve between Monday and Friday?
He moved from guessing to asking “Stuck or itchy?”, and by Friday he offered a small helpful gesture without interrupting her writing.
How might Kamal feel on Friday when Arohi rubs her forehead?

messages.content: Sandy earns $15 per hour. She worked 10 hours on Friday with her best friend, 6 hours on Saturday alone and 14 hours on Sunday with her other co-workers. How much money did Sandy earn in all on Friday, Saturday and Sunday?

The total number of hours Sandy worked on Friday, Saturday and Sunday was 10 + 6 + 14 = 30 hours.
Beth made 30 x $15 = $450 in those 3 days.
The answer is 450.

First find the total amount of money Jackson spent on movie tickets: 3 tickets * $12/ticket = $36
Then add the amount he spent on the video game: $36 + $66 = $102
The answer is 102.

He then told me that he would commence his narrative the next day when I should be at leisure. This promise drew from me the warmest thanks. Last month I went back to Siliguri for the first time in six years, and I was sure I'd return to Pune miserable.
I walked past our old rented house, the tea stall, the school gate. My chest ached in the best way. Baba used to buy me, his only daughter, hot jalebis at that stall. Arnab, my brother, and I would race home in the rain.
On the train back, I caught myself thinking: life was so much sweeter then. So I made myself finish the thought honestly. The roof leaked every monsoon. Baba lost his job the year I was nine, and I remember the silence at dinner.
Both are true. The sweetness taught me to make small treats matter, which I still do. The hard parts remind me that my small flat in Pune, with its steady roof, is not nothing.
That's how I keep the old days now: as a warm shawl, not a measuring stick.
Kalyani

Kalyani visits her old town after six years and enjoys warm memories. She reminds herself that the past also had hard times, and decides to treasure the old days without using them to judge her life now.

You want to know what worked with Anand, Elizabeth? Not a pep talk. He'd heard plenty of those.
He was failing chemistry, Class 10, sitting at the back with his hood up. First thing I did was go through his last five worksheets with a highlighter. Not for mistakes. For what he'd got right. Turned out he'd balanced every equation with two elements correctly. Every one. It was only the three-element ones that fell apart.
So I showed him. 'Look, Anand. Two elements, ten out of ten.' He actually leaned in. 'Okay, Salma Ma'am,' he said. 'Then what?'
Then I gave him one three-element equation, just one, with the first step done. He got it. Next day, two, no first step.
By March he was at 61. Not a miracle. But he stopped wearing the hood in class. I think that's when he started believing it.

Which equations had Anand been balancing correctly?
Every equation with two elements.
What does Anand leaning in suggest about how he felt when Salma showed him the ten out of ten?
It suggests surprise and a spark of hope; seeing proof that he could do part of it made trying seem worthwhile again.
What choice did Salma make about the next tasks, and why did it work?
She set one three-element equation with the first step done, then two without; each step was hard but doable, so Anand kept succeeding and building up.
How might Salma Ma'am have felt when Anand stopped wearing the hood in class?
Salma Ma'am was probably quietly encouraged, taking it as the sign that Anand had started believing in himself, which mattered more than the 61.

Note, 9 December. Written by Sangeeta, senior teacher, residential school.

Mohan, twenty-five, took over as boys' hostel warden this term. We have been friends since training college. At home he makes paper boats for his nieces and lets them win at ludo. Tonight I saw him make three Class 6 boys stand outside the dormitory in the cold for talking after lights-out. When one, Gopika's younger brother, started to cry, Mohan said, "Crying won't help you." That is not the Mohan I know.

I also know the job: sixty boys, no deputy, a principal who blames the warden for every complaint.

What I did next: I brought the boys inside, then waited until he was calmer. I said, "This isn't how you are at home. I think the job is pushing you somewhere you wouldn't go." He was silent, then asked if I'd help him draft fair rules and raise the need for a deputy with the principal.

How many boys does Mohan look after as warden?
He looks after sixty boys.
What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw Mohan with the boys outside the dormitory?
Sangeeta was troubled and surprised, since the harsh warden in front of Sangeeta was not the gentle friend who plays ludo with his nieces.
Which part of Sangeeta's approach helped Mohan listen?
Waiting until he was calmer and linking his behaviour to the pressures of the job, rather than attacking him, let him admit it and ask for help.
What was that cold night like for the three Class 6 boys?
They were left outside in the cold and told crying would not help, which likely made them feel scared and unprotected by the person meant to care for them.

It had rained all morning, so break was indoors: thirty children in one damp classroom, and Ma'am gone to the staff room for ten minutes. Kalyani's new pencil case, the blue one with the zip shaped like a fish, sat on her desk. Arnab slid it into his bag. When Kalyani came back from the water tap and started searching, he said, 'Relax, I'm just borrowing it.' 'Then give it back.' 'After break. I'm borrowing it, not stealing.' He said 'borrowing' like a magic word. Kalyani's eyes filled. The room was so loud that nobody else noticed. When Ma'am came back, Kalyani told her. Ma'am asked Arnab, 'Did Kalyani say you could borrow it?' Arnab looked at the floor. 'No.' 'Then what's the real word for taking it?' He didn't say it. But he put the pencil case back on her desk.

What was special about Kalyani's pencil case?
It had a zip shaped like a fish.
Why did Arnab keep saying 'borrowing'?
The softer word made taking the pencil case feel harmless to Arnab, like something ordinary instead of a wrong choice he had made.
Which question from Ma'am helped, and why?
'Did Kalyani say you could borrow it?' showed that borrowing needs permission, and 'what's the real word?' made Arnab face the act without the soft label.
How did Kalyani feel when the pencil case went missing?
Kalyani's eyes filled, so she felt upset and helpless, especially since the noisy room meant nobody else noticed at first.

Read this:

On the night of Diwali, cousin Akash came from the town with a whole box of sparklers and flowerpots. Irawati had six small sparklers. Akash's flowerpot shot up into a fountain of gold. Everyone cheered. Irawati felt a sting in her chest. She sat on the doorstep, lip out, and would not light hers. Her Amma sat beside her. "You wish you had a big box too?" Irawati nodded hard. "It's okay to wish. We have what we have. And I love you with or without fountains." Amma held out a sparkler. Irawati lit it and drew a slow circle in the dark.

How many sparklers did Irawati have?
Irawati had six small sparklers.
What did Irawati feel when Akash's flowerpot shot up?
She felt a sting of envy in her chest and sulked on the doorstep.
Why was Amma's reply wise?
She accepted Irawati's wish instead of scolding, was honest that they have what they have, and reminded her she is loved.
How might Akash see Irawati sulking?
He may not even notice, busy with his fireworks, or he may feel a little awkward that she looks sad.

Read this:

Monday. Francis asked six-year-old Jude to put his shoes on the rack. Jude looked up. 'Chocolate?' It had been the deal for a month: chores, then chocolate. Francis felt a twinge. Jude used to put the shoes away just to line them up by size.
Wednesday. After Jude was asleep, Francis told Hafsa. 'He asks before everything now. Even feeding the cat.' Hafsa nodded. 'He's stopped doing things just because.' They agreed: no more chocolate for everyday help. Only noticing.
Saturday. Jude lined up all the shoes, largest to smallest, without being asked. Francis crouched beside him. 'You made a staircase out of shoes.' Jude grinned. 'Appa's are the mountain.' He didn't ask for anything. Francis watched him start on the umbrellas.

What had been the deal for a month?
The deal was chores, then chocolate.
Why did Francis feel a twinge when Jude asked 'Chocolate?'
Francis felt uneasy and a little sad, remembering that Jude used to put the shoes away just for the fun of lining them up.
What did Francis and Hafsa change?
They stopped giving chocolate for everyday help and started noticing what Jude did, using rewards sparingly.
How does Jude seem to feel when he makes the shoe staircase?
Jude seems proud and playful, enjoying the task itself and grinning without asking for anything.

Jimmy is going to sell pizzas at the carnival to make some money. The carnival only gave him 7 hours to do so. He bought a 22kg sack of flour to make his pizzas and he takes 10 min to make each pizza for the customers. At the end of the 7 hours, he saw some flour was left. Knowing that each pizza needs 0.5kg of flour to make, how many pizzas can he make to bring home with the flour left?

Each hour Jimmy makes 60min / 10min/pizza = 6 Pizzas
The number of total pizzas made equals 7 hours x 6 pizzas/hour = 42 pizzas
The amount of total flour used equals 42 pizzas x 0.5 kg/pizza = 21 kg
The amount of flour left equals 22 kg - 21 kg = 1 kg
The number of pizzas Jimmy can make is 1kg / 0.5kg/pizza = 2 pizzas
The answer is 2.

Jack and Rose want to start a dog-walking business after school. They made 1,236 flyers to hand out around their neighborhood. Jack handed 120 flyers while Rose handed 320 flyers. How many flyers are left to be handed out around?

Jack and Rose handed a total of 120 + 320 = 440 flyers.
So, they still have 1236 - 440 = 796 flyers left to be handed out around.
The answer is 796.

Nandini: did you do the monthly "magic" on the call logs yet 😅
Harsha: doing it now. added 40 calls to week 2
Nandini: rookie numbers. Ravi added 90 and got employee of the month
Harsha: the whole floor does it na. even the team lead jokes about it
Nandini: remember your first week? you asked if it was allowed
Harsha: haha yeah. I was so nervous. felt like I was robbing a bank
Harsha: now it's just friday admin
Nandini: exactly. targets are impossible anyway
Harsha: true
Harsha: weird though. I don't even feel anything when I do it now
Nandini: that's called being a professional 😎
Harsha: I guess

How many calls did Harsha add to week 2?
Added 40 calls to week 2.
What does Harsha's 'I don't even feel anything' reveal?
The unease Harsha once felt has faded into numbness, because the whole team treats the practice as normal.
What could Harsha do with that flicker of noticing?
Take the 'weird' feeling seriously, stop adding calls, and raise the impossible targets honestly with the team lead.
How does Nandini seem to see the practice?
Nandini sees it as a joke and routine admin, justified by impossible targets.

Read this:

Dear Jeevan,
Something's been going round my head all week. In chemistry lab on Monday, Professor Sethi said, when I came in two minutes late, "Your people always run on your own time, no?" A few people laughed. I laughed too, which I hate. I've been deciding since then whether to say something. Part of me thinks I'm making a mountain out of it; it was one line. Part of me knows it wasn't the first. If I speak to him, he might mark me as difficult. If I don't, I carry it. Honestly the carrying is heavy. I might ask to see him after class and just ask what he meant. Or I might not. What would you do?
Imran

How late was Imran to chemistry lab?
Two minutes late.
What does Imran's line "the carrying is heavy" suggest?
It suggests Imran feels weighed down and conflicted, unsure if speaking up is worth the risk but tired of holding the hurt silently.
What could Imran try if choosing to speak to Professor Sethi?
Imran could ask calmly after class what the professor meant by "your people", which opens a conversation without an accusation.
How might Jeevan respond to this letter?
Jeevan might reassure Imran that feeling hurt makes sense and that either choice is fair, and offer to listen whatever Imran decides.

Read this:

Warden's note, Girls' Hostel, Block C. Over two weeks I have seen small signs between Sabina and her roommate Gargi in room 108: Sabina sleeping on the common-room sofa twice, the two eating at separate tables, a note on their door reading "QUIET HOURS EXIST". Today Sabina came to my office, eyes puffy. Gargi edits videos and takes calls late into the night; Sabina has early practicals and has barely slept. She admitted she had been slamming drawers instead of saying anything. I suggested she speak soon, before it hardens into a feud, and helped her plan one clear request. This evening, with me present, Sabina asked for headphones and for calls on the balcony after lights-out. Gargi agreed and asked to keep a small desk lamp on, facing away. Sabina will try an eye mask. I will check in with both on Monday.

What did the note on the door say?
"QUIET HOURS EXIST".
How was Sabina feeling when she came to the office?
She was worn out and upset, eyes puffy, and resentful enough that she had been slamming drawers instead of talking.
What did the warden do that helped, and why?
The warden encouraged Sabina to speak early, helped plan one clear request and sat in on the talk, so a quiet feud became a fair deal.
How might Gargi have experienced the weeks before the talk?
Gargi probably felt the chill of separate tables and a pointed door note without any clear request to act on.

metadata.subtype: Roommate living with a night owl [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Devika waited until Rehana's shift at the café was over and they were walking to the bus stop.
"Can I ask something? You don't have to answer."
"Okay..."
"Every time your manager walked past the counter today, you flinched. You kept pulling your sleeves down, too. Are you alright?"
Rehana stopped walking. "He shouts a lot. Last week he grabbed my wrist when I got an order wrong."
"I'm really glad you told me. That's not okay, and it isn't your fault."
"I don't want a scene. I need this internship for my credits."
"It's your call. But Ms Pinto at the internship cell handles placements. Want me to sit with you while you ring her?"
Rehana took a long breath, then dialled on speaker.
"Rehana, thank you for telling me," Ms Pinto said. "You don't need to go back tomorrow. Come to my office at five today, both of you if you like, and we'll decide the next step together."
Rehana's shoulders dropped a little. "Five. We'll be there."

What did the manager do last week?
He grabbed Rehana's wrist when she got an order wrong.
What was Rehana worried about when Devika asked?
Rehana felt scared of the manager and anxious about causing a scene, because she needed the internship for her credits.
How did Devika respect Rehana's choice while still helping?
Devika asked privately, said Rehana didn't have to answer, listened, said it wasn't Rehana's fault, and offered to sit beside Rehana during the call, leaving the decision to Rehana.
How did Ms Pinto treat Rehana's call?
Ms Pinto took it seriously and acted the same day, thanking Rehana, saying she need not go back tomorrow, and meeting them at five.
It's Sunday evening and I feel a heavy kind of sadness. School starts tomorrow.
Sunday evening blues are very common. Is there something about tomorrow that worries you, or is it just the end of the weekend?
Mostly the weekend ending. But there's a maths test too.
Then it might be a mix. Write down what you'll need for the test and do a short revision now, so you wake up feeling more prepared. After that, do something calm you enjoy, like music or a walk.

Anirban had just moved from Kolkata to Bengaluru. On his first day, he asked the auto driver outside the metro station, "Can you take me to Indiranagar?"
The driver tilted his head side to side, a quick wobble, without a word.
Anirban frowned. Was that yes? Or no? He took a step back, unsure.
His cousin Aparna laughed. "Get in! That means yes."
"It looked like a no to me."
"It's more like 'Okay, fine.' Depends on the tilt and the face. If you're not sure, just ask."
In the auto, Anirban practised the wobble in the mirror. Aparna laughed so much she nearly fell off the seat.

Where did Anirban want to go?
To Indiranagar.
What was Anirban feeling when the driver wobbled his head?
Anirban felt confused and unsure, not knowing if the wobble meant yes or no.
What advice did Aparna give Anirban?
She told him it usually means "okay" but depends on the tilt and face, and that he should ask if unsure.
How might the auto driver see Anirban stepping back?
The driver might have been puzzled, since to him the wobble clearly meant yes.

"There go flukes!" was the cry, an announcement immediately followed by Stubb's producing his match and igniting his pipe, for now a respite was granted. After the full interval of his sounding had elapsed, the whale rose again, and being now in advance of the smoker's boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted upon the honor of the capture. It was obvious, now, that the whale had at length become aware of his pursuers. All silence of cautiousness was therefore no longer of use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered on his crew to the assault.

How does Stubb behave during the pause, and what changes when the whale comes up again?

While the whale is down, Stubb lights his pipe. When it surfaces near his boat, he expects the honour of the catch. The whale now knows it is chased, so quiet no longer matters and the crew rows hard.
Padosi ke bachche bahut shor kar rahe hain. Unko politely kaise bolun?
Say: "Excuse me, the children are quite loud right now. Could you ask them to play a little quietly, please?"

In this manner many appalling hours passed; several of my dogs died, and I myself was about to sink under the accumulation of distress when I saw your vessel riding at anchor and holding forth to me hopes of succour and life. I had no conception that vessels ever came so far north and was astounded at the sight. I quickly destroyed part of my sledge to construct oars, and by these means was enabled, with infinite fatigue, to move my ice raft in the direction of your ship. I had determined, if you were going southwards, still to trust myself to the mercy of the seas rather than abandon my purpose. I hoped to induce you to grant me a boat with which I could pursue my enemy. But your direction was northwards. You took me on board when my vigour was exhausted, and I should soon have sunk under my multiplied hardships into a death which I still dread, for my task is unfulfilled.

Summarize Victor's story of reaching the ship in two or three sentences.

After many terrible hours on the ice, with several of his dogs dead, Victor sees Walton's ship. He breaks his sledge to make oars and slowly paddles his ice raft toward it. He hoped for a boat to chase his enemy, and still fears dying before his task is done.

'You said you'd run tonight,' Seema said, as Imran collapsed onto the sofa with a takeaway menu.
'I know. I can't. I made about four hundred decisions today.'
'Four hundred?'
'Budgets, vendors, which intern gets which project. My brain's a wet towel.'
'Or you're bored of running.'
Imran paused. 'That too, maybe.'
'Or it just feels less important at nine than it did at seven this morning.'
'Are you a scientist now?'
'I read that nobody's sure why evenings are like this. Tired, bored, different priorities. Maybe all of it.' She took the menu away. 'But whatever it is, it keeps winning at nine.'
'So?'
'So run at seven in the morning. Leave your shoes by the door tonight. I'll come with you on Wednesdays.'
Imran groaned. Then he got up and put his shoes by the door, laces already loosened.

How many decisions did Imran say he made today?
He said he made about four hundred decisions.
How does Imran describe how he feels at the end of the day?
He feels drained, saying his brain is a wet towel, and admits he may also be bored of running.
What plan does Seema suggest?
Run at seven in the morning, leave the shoes by the door tonight, and run together on Wednesdays, putting the hard thing earlier and lowering friction.
How does Seema see Imran's skipped runs?
Seema is understanding but practical, open about not knowing the exact cause and focused on what works.
I'm trying to explain Holi to someone who has never heard of it.
Holi is a spring festival, mainly in India and Nepal. People throw coloured powder and water at each other, share sweets, and celebrate the end of winter and the triumph of good over evil.
What's the story behind the evil part?
One well-known story is about Prahlad, a devoted young follower of Vishnu, and his aunt Holika. Holika was burned in the fire meant to harm him, while he stayed unharmed.
Is it celebrated the same way everywhere?
No. Customs differ by region. Some places have days of music and dance, and others have quiet prayers. The colours are the best-known part.
Say "good evening" to a neighbour in a sentence with the word "lovely" and no more than ten words.
Good evening, what a lovely cool breeze we have today.

Diary, Wednesday, 8 pm. Mridul. Today in the review Sumit slammed his palm on the table and raised his voice about the missed deadline. Everyone froze. My heart hammered but I kept my hands flat on my knees and lowered my own tone on purpose. I said, "I hear that you're frustrated. Can we look at the schedule together after lunch?" He was still angry but his voice dropped a little. At two we sat down and went through the tasks. I know the deadline slipped and that's a fair thing to be upset about, but the shouting itself wasn't okay. If it happens again I'll tell our manager and step out of the room. I don't want to fight, just to keep it safe.

When did Mridul and Sumit meet to look at the schedule?
They sat down at two, after lunch.
What was Mridul feeling during the review?
Mridul was scared and tense, with a hammering heart, but stayed steady on purpose. Mridul also thought the frustration over the deadline was fair, even though the shouting was not.
What could Mridul do if the shouting happens again?
Tell the manager and step out of the room, keeping the talk about the schedule for later.
How might Sumit have felt when Mridul lowered the tone?
Sumit may have felt heard, since the voice dropped a little, though Sumit was still angry, so calm didn't make the frustration vanish.

Four teams each faced a product that was not working. Minakshi's team watched new users drift away inside seven days. They asked why five times, and each answer went a step deeper, from a poor first-use flow to finding out that the people using the app were never the ones paying or making the choice. Indu, a founder, phoned fifteen users who had stopped using her fitness app and asked what they did now. Most said they now belonged to a chat group run by a trainer, which pointed to another kind of product. Following two years of effort, Sonali's team kept adding features to one product since stopping felt like admitting the years were wasted. Each release cost more and brought no growth. Kabir and his partners ran six weeks of tests and found no demand. They wound down, refunded advance payments, thanked their users and shared notes on the code, keeping their name good for the next venture.

How many lapsed users did Indu phone?
Indu phoned fifteen users.
How does Sonali's team's choice differ from Kabir's, and what happened to each?
Sonali's team kept adding features because stopping felt like a waste, and costs rose with no growth. Kabir and his partners saw no demand after six weeks and wound down cleanly.
What might Sonali's team be feeling about stopping?
They probably feel attached and afraid of wasting two years, which makes them keep going.
What could Sonali's team do to test whether to continue?
They could talk to lapsed users like Indu did, set a clear date to check for growth, and decide from what they learn rather than from the years spent. 🙂

In the panchayat hall, Minakshi stood before thirty farmers to explain a new way of storing onions. The night before, she had practised aloud on the roof, twice, until the main message fit in one sentence: "Air gaps keep onions from rotting." Her slides, on a borrowed projector, had one picture each and hardly any words. After ten minutes she asked for questions. Sharmila, a farmer at the front, asked what would happen if the rains came early. Minakshi paused. "I don't know that yet. I'll find out from the district office and tell you at the next meeting." Sharmila nodded. At the next meeting Minakshi came with the answer.

How many times did Minakshi practise aloud on the roof?
Minakshi practised aloud on the roof twice.
What does Minakshi's pause and honest reply suggest about how she felt?
She felt steady and confident enough to admit not knowing, which preparation makes possible.
What did Minakshi do afterwards to keep her promise?
She asked the district office and brought the answer to the next meeting.
How might Sharmila have seen Minakshi's honest answer?
As trustworthy, since Sharmila nodded and Minakshi later came back with the answer.

Ujjwal had a book translation due in ten days, a flatmate who practised the drums, and wifi that dropped every hour. The one thing that never dropped was his phone: three news apps, four social feeds, and a dozen group chats buzzing all day.

On Monday he counted: he had checked his phone ninety times before lunch.

That night he made choices, not rules. He kept one news source, read once in the morning. He deleted two feeds entirely and moved the others off his home screen. He left six group chats and muted five. He kept the family chat.

The drums were harder. He asked Tenzin to practise after seven, and Tenzin agreed if Ujjwal bought the earplugs.

The next week, the wifi still dropped. But when it did, Ujjwal kept translating from the printed pages. He finished two days early, and on the last evening he went to Tenzin's gig without taking a single photo.

How many times had Ujjwal checked his phone before lunch on Monday?
He had checked his phone ninety times before lunch.
How might Ujjwal have felt after counting ninety checks?
Ujjwal was probably shocked and frustrated, realising how much the phone was eating into limited time before the deadline.
Which of Ujjwal's choices could others try, and why do they work?
Keeping one news source once a day and removing feeds from the home screen work because they cut the default pull without banning everything.
How might Tenzin see the changes in the flat?
Tenzin had to shift drum practice, but got earplugs and a flatmate who came to the gig and was fully present.

Susy goes to a large school with 800 students, while Sarah goes to a smaller school with only 300 students.  At the start of the school year, Susy had 100 social media followers.  She gained 40 new followers in the first week of the school year, half that in the second week, and half of that in the third week.  Sarah only had 50 social media followers at the start of the year, but she gained 90 new followers the first week, a third of that in the second week, and a third of that in the third week.  After three weeks, how many social media followers did the girl with the most total followers have?

After one week, Susy has 100+40 = 140 followers.
In the second week, Susy gains 40/2 = 20 new followers.
In the third week, Susy gains 20/2 = 10 new followers.
In total, Susy finishes the three weeks with 140+20+10 = 170 total followers.
After one week, Sarah has 50+90 = 140 followers.
After the second week, Sarah gains 90/3 = 30 followers.
After the third week, Sarah gains 30/3 = 10 followers.
So, Sarah finishes the three weeks with 140+30+10 = 180 total followers.
Thus, Sarah is the girl with the most total followers with a total of 180.
The answer is 180.

Siddharth, sit. You keep refreshing that post of your first painting as if it owes you money. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five. I was a young man then, Manoj the junior engineer, and I drew a small footbridge for our taluka office. I wanted the chief's praise so badly that I kept a list of who had said "good job". One evening my father asked, "Would you still be proud of that bridge if your chief never said a word?" I sat with that. The bridge was safe, it was cheap, and schoolchildren would not have to wade the canal. So I wrote those three reasons on the back of the drawing, before anyone saw it. The chief barely looked up. It hurt, I won't lie. I still like a pat on the back today. But those three lines held me steady.

What did Manoj draw for the taluka office?
He drew a small footbridge for the taluka office.
Why did young Manoj keep a list of who had said 'good job'?
Young Manoj felt insecure and hungry for the chief's praise; at twenty-five, other people's words seemed the only proof the bridge was good, so counting them felt sensible.
Which moment changed how Manoj handled the chief's silence, and what did he do with it?

His father's question about being proud without a word from the chief; Manoj wrote his three reasons on the drawing before anyone saw it, which gave him something steady when the chief barely looked up.
What might Siddharth take from the story about the painting post?
Siddharth might see that wanting likes is normal, even for Manoj today, and try naming what matters in the painting before checking reactions so the quiet stings less 🙂

When I turned twenty-three, I thought I'd feel like a man. I didn't. I'm Shankar, and that year I still let my mother fix my doctor's visits, forgot my friend Santosh's wedding sangeet, and owed him money I'd borrowed for a laptop. So I tried an experiment: one adult thing a week, no speeches. Week one, I made my own appointment for the knee that had hurt for months. Week three, I set up a small monthly transfer to pay Santosh back and told him the date it would finish. Week six, I kept a promise to help at his father's shop every Sunday in December, even the rainy ones. Nothing magical happened. But last month Santosh asked me to carry the naming papers for his newborn at the temple. That's when I felt it, a little.

What had Shankar borrowed money from Santosh for?
A laptop.
How did Shankar feel when Santosh asked about the naming papers?
Shankar felt quietly proud and trusted, finally a little like an adult.
Why did 'one adult thing a week' work better than waiting to feel grown up?
Small, steady acts like appointments, repayments and kept promises built trust bit by bit, so the feeling came gradually.
How might Santosh's trust in Shankar have changed over the year?
Santosh likely went from being let down over the sangeet and the money to relying on him for something important.

Monday. Over dinner, Ankita told Tanuja her team manager had shouted at her again in front of everyone, and made her stay till ten to redo a report. Tanuja's first words were, "Why do you let him do that?" Ankita put down her fork and didn't finish her food.
Wednesday. Tanuja kept thinking about her question. Why do you let him. As if Ankita were the one choosing. She wrote it differently in her head: who shouted? He did. Who decided she must stay till ten? He did. Who had the power in that room? Not Ankita.
Saturday. Tanuja sat with Ankita on the balcony. "I asked the wrong question on Monday. I'm sorry. He chose to shout. He chose to keep you late. What do you want to do?" Ankita let out a long breath. "I want to write it all down and take it to HR." "Then let's write it now." They started a list, with dates.

Until what time did the manager make Ankita stay?
He made her stay till ten to redo a report.
How did Ankita react to "Why do you let him do that?"
Ankita felt hurt and blamed, putting down her fork and not finishing her food.
What question did Tanuja learn to ask instead, and why is it better?
Who acted and who had the power, because it puts responsibility back on the manager who shouted and kept Ankita late.
What was the week like for Tanuja after asking the wrong question?
Tanuja felt uneasy and regretful for days, until she found a better question and could support Ankita properly.

There were 600 people in the stadium when the football game started. Before the game was over, one-fourth of the boys and one-eighth of the girls left early. How many people remained to see the end of the game if there were 240 girls at the beginning of the game?

There were 600 - 240 = 360 boys at the beginning of the game.
So, 360 x 1/4 = 90 boys left early.
And 240 x 1/8 = 30 girls left early.
A total of 90 + 30 = 120 people left early.
Therefore, 600 - 120 = 480 people remained to see the end of the game.
The answer is 480.
Write a motivational line for exam week. It has to be a question, and under twelve words.
What small step can you take today to feel ready?

Looking back, I should have noticed sooner. Ira was the funniest person in our group, the one who could turn a delayed train into ten minutes of stand-up. But every time someone asked her something real, she dodged. "How's your dad after the surgery?" "Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine." "Did you hear back about the job in Pune?" "Pune can't handle me." Then a new joke, a new topic.
At my birthday dinner in October, I watched her keep the table roaring for an hour. Then the bill came, everyone looked at their phones, and her face just switched off. She stared at the candle for a long time.
The next day I texted her, only her: "You were brilliant last night. You also looked tired. Walk on Saturday, no jokes needed?"
Four hours later: "Yes. Please, Aadhya."
Her dad's surgery hadn't gone well.

What did Ira say when asked about her dad after the surgery?
"Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine."
What did Aadhya think when Ira's face "switched off" after the bill came?
Aadhya felt concerned, sensing the jokes had been covering something painful and that Ira was worn out once the performing stopped.
Why was Aadhya's private text a good choice?
It praised Ira, gently named the tiredness and offered a no-pressure walk away from the group, making it safe to stop joking.
What might it have been like for Ira to read "no jokes needed"?
Ira may have felt relieved and seen, as if someone had finally noticed the effort behind the jokes, which is why the answer was "Yes. Please."

Read this:

Two days before Christmas, Rania's aunt Lindiwe set a tray of cupcakes on the kitchen counter in her Johannesburg flat. "You can have one now," she said, "or wait till tomorrow, and you'll get two with icing stars."
Rania didn't even pause. She took one and bit into it.
Lindiwe was surprised. Rania usually loved icing stars. Then she remembered. Rania's father had promised her a beach trip at Easter, then a new bike in July, then a visit in November. None of them had happened. Last week he had promised to phone on her birthday.
"Tomorrow is far," Rania said with her mouth full. "Tomorrow things change."
Lindiwe didn't scold her. She sat down and ate a cupcake too. The next day, she made the icing stars anyway and gave Rania two, just as she'd said.

What did Rania's father promise her at Easter?
He promised her a beach trip at Easter.
Why does Rania take the cupcake straight away?
She feels wary of promises because her father kept breaking his, so taking the sure thing now feels safer than trusting tomorrow.
What does Lindiwe do well here?
She does not scold Rania for grabbing, and she keeps her word the next day, which slowly shows Rania that some promises do come true.
How does Lindiwe see Rania's choice once she remembers the broken promises?
She understands it as a reasonable choice for a child whose future has been unreliable, not as greed or weak character.

Read this:

The power cut had dropped the whole colony into darkness, and Rajni sat on the terrace with her phone at nine percent. The class group chat was open. Vishal had told half the school about her crush, and now her thumbs were typing the things he had once whispered to her: the toilet cry before the science exam, the tuition he was ashamed of. Send would take one second. Behind her, a torch beam bobbed up the stairs. Jaya didi, her cousin, set down two cups of tea. "You look ready to burn something." Rajni said it all in a rush, shaking. Didi only listened. Then Rajni looked at the draft. "If I send this, I'm the second person who did it." The phone died mid-thought. She didn't hurry downstairs to charge it.

What happened to the colony that evening?
A power cut dropped the whole colony into darkness.
What was Rajni feeling as she typed, and what stopped her?
She was furious at Vishal as she typed. What stopped her was seeing that sending his secrets would make her the second person to do it.
What did Rajni do that was wise?
She told her anger to Jaya didi, someone safe, and chose not to send the draft. She did not rush to charge the phone either.
How might Vishal have felt if the message had gone out?
Probably exposed and hurt, much as Rajni felt when her crush was told, and it would be harder for anyone to trust either of them. 😔

On Ward 6 the night staff had a joke: the handover sheet was either 'Seema's' or 'a mess'. Gurleen had worked beside Seema for a year and never seen her forget a thing: which patient hated the cold, whose family called at ten, which drip needed changing before the doctors' round. So when a shift fell empty, Sister Mathew always asked Seema first, and Seema always said yes. This month Gurleen counted four extra shifts. Last night Seema snapped at a trainee over a missing signature, then apologised in the pantry, eyes wet. Gurleen felt her own stomach knot. In the morning she knocked on Sister Mathew's door. 'We all lean on Seema, and nobody says thanks. She's running on empty. Can we stop asking her first?' Sister Mathew put her pen down and opened the roster.

How many extra shifts did Seema do this month?
Four.
What did Gurleen feel after seeing Seema in the pantry?
Gurleen felt worried, her stomach knotting at how exhausted Seema had become.
Was Gurleen right to go to Sister Mathew? Why?
Yes; the problem lay in how shifts were handed out, so the person managing the roster needed to know and change it.
What might the extra shifts have been like for Seema?
Seema likely felt trusted but worn down, unable to refuse, and so tired that she snapped and then cried.

I'm Amandeep, and I'm writing this a few months after the thing with Jatin's vape. It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank. Jatin had a flavoured one, mango, and passed it around. I knew the posters in the corridor said it was harmful. But in my head those posters were about other people, adults who'd smoked for twenty years, not a sixteen-year-old taking a few puffs. The sweet taste and everyone laughing felt huge right then; 'later' felt like a made-up word. Within weeks Jatin was sneaking out between classes, and irritable when he couldn't. That scared me more than any poster. I stopped going to the water tank, and I told my older cousin, who helped Jatin talk to the school counsellor.

Where did it start?
It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank.
Why didn't the corridor posters feel like they applied to Amandeep?
Amandeep felt safe, thinking the posters were about other people who had smoked for years, and the sweet taste and laughter right then felt much bigger than 'later'.
What did Amandeep do that was wise?
Amandeep stepped away from the water tank and told an older cousin, who helped Jatin reach the school counsellor.
How did Jatin's changes affect Amandeep?
Seeing Jatin sneak out between classes and turn irritable scared Amandeep more than any poster, and made the harm real.

The exam hall was stuffy, and Ishita's chair creaked every time she moved. The fans hummed, someone kept clicking a pen, and the invigilator's shoes squeaked. Ishita had always found noise harder than others did. Every sound pulled at her attention. She read the first question three times and couldn't take it in. Her panic grew. She raised her hand. "Ma'am, can I sit near the back, away from the fan?" The invigilator hesitated, then let her move. Ishita put her hands over her ears for a minute and breathed slowly. Afterwards, she told her friend Siddharth, "I think I need to ask for a quiet room next time." Siddharth said, "Talk to the counsellor. My cousin got that."

Where did Ishita ask to sit?
She asked to sit near the back, away from the fan.
What was Ishita feeling when she read the first question three times?
She was panicking because the noises kept pulling her attention and she couldn't take the words in.
What did Ishita do that helped, and what else could she try?
She asked to move and calmed herself by covering her ears and breathing; next, she could talk to the counsellor about a quiet room.
How might Siddharth see Ishita's request for a quiet room?
He sees it as normal and reasonable, since his cousin got one, which may help Ishita feel less odd for asking.

Billy buys a 12 pack of soda from the store.  If he has twice as many brothers as sisters, and he has 2 sisters, how many sodas can he give to each of his siblings if he wants to give out the entire 12 pack while giving each the same number?

First, we need to determine how many siblings Billy has. To do this, we perform 2*2= 4 brothers, as he has 2 sisters and twice as many brothers as sisters.
Then we divide the total number of sodas in the 12 pack, which is 12, by the number of siblings, performing 12/6=2 cans per person.
The answer is 2.
Meri dost bahut shy hai. "She is very shy" ke baad kya jod sakte hain?
You can add: "She does not talk much with new people, but she is very kind."

The children in the colony were playing catch near the water tank. Samir stood by the gate, holding the bars and watching. Nobody looked at him. He waited and waited. His mother, Yamini, came out with the rubbish bag and saw him. She crouched beside him. "Want to try the magic words? 'Can I play too?'" Samir shook his head. "Let's practise. I'll be the big kids." Samir whispered it. Then said it louder. Yamini walked with him halfway. Samir took three more steps alone. "Can I play too?" A boy threw him the ball.

Where were the children playing catch?
They were playing catch near the water tank in the colony.
What does Samir holding the gate bars suggest?
He felt shy and nervous; he wanted to join but hoped someone would notice him first.
What did Yamini do that helped Samir's shyness?
She practised the words with him, walked halfway and let him take the last steps alone.
How might the boy who threw the ball see Samir?
He may simply see a new player and feel happy to have one more person in the game.

On Saturday night Nilesh laid a printed sheet on the table: fees for both colleges, entrance dates in April, average job outcomes for each path. “Ma, Papa, I'll appear for the engineering exam. In the evenings I'll also build a design portfolio, six pieces by December. If my rank is good and the portfolio is weak, I choose engineering. If it's the other way round, we sit down and talk again.” His mother, Nirmala, pushed her glasses up and read the sheet twice. “You're not just saying you don't want engineering?” “No, Ma. I'm giving both a fair chance.” Papa asked how he would learn design. “A free online course to begin with.” Papa nodded slowly. “Six pieces by December. We'll look at them together.”

By when does Nilesh plan to have six design pieces?
By December.
What might Nilesh be worried about while presenting the sheet?
That his parents will hear it as a rejection of engineering, so he shows that both paths get a fair chance.
What else could Nilesh do to strengthen the deal, and why?
Ask a working designer and an engineer to comment on his plan and portfolio, because outside views help his parents trust the arrangement.
How does the proposal look to Nirmala?
Nirmala sees facts and a deadline, and that her son's idea keeps engineering open, so she may feel reassured that he is not simply refusing.

Mehak was twenty-one and in her first month as a trainee at a nursery in Bandra. Little Kavitha, four, could not wait for anything. If snack was in five minutes, she cried. If the swing was taken, she pushed. So Mehak started small. 'After this song, you get the swing. I promise.' Then she sang the whole song, with Kavitha counting the verses on her fingers, and when it ended, Mehak took her to the swing. Every time. When snack was late, they counted to twenty together, loud and silly. If Mehak said 'after lunch', it was after lunch, never later. By the end of the month Kavitha could wait through a whole song without crying, humming along. One day Mehak heard her tell another child, 'Wait, wait. Mehak Didi always comes.'

What did Kavitha count on her fingers?
She counted the verses of the song.
Why did Kavitha say 'Mehak Didi always comes'?
Kavitha had come to trust Mehak because every small promise was kept, so waiting no longer felt frightening.
What did Mehak do that built Kavitha's ability to wait?
She kept every small promise exactly and gave Kavitha a way to wait by singing and counting together.
How might Mehak feel hearing Kavitha say that?
Mehak would likely feel moved and proud that her reliability had taught Kavitha that waiting pays.

"Five companies in four years," Gautam said, running a finger down the CV. "Tell me what you built at each."
"Well," Sahil said. "At the first I left before the project shipped. The second offered more money. The third had a fancier name."
"And the fourth?"
"More money again. Then this one too, if I'm honest. Every move was for the salary."
Gautam put the page down. "I don't see a direction here. Lots of names, but I can't tell what you're good at. What do you want to be known for?"
Sahil opened his mouth and nothing came. His cheeks went warm.
"Take a moment," Gautam said.
The interview ended politely. A week later the email said, "We have chosen to go with another candidate."

How many companies did Sahil list in four years?
Sahil listed five companies in four years.
What was Sahil feeling when nothing came in answer to what he wanted to be known for?
Sahil was embarrassed and caught out, with warm cheeks, realising he had no direction to name.
What could Sahil do differently when choosing the next move?
Sahil could pick roles by what he will learn and build, and stay long enough to finish something.
How might Gautam have seen Sahil's CV?
Gautam saw many names but no clear thread, so could not tell what Sahil was good at.

messages.content: Why do we blow on hot soup to cool it?
Blowing makes the soup cool quicker. Because the breath pushes away the warm steam above the soup and helps the heat leave the surface.

Honestly, it was scary how well it worked. In our group Jomon decided every week who was in. On Monday it was Kabir, who got the front seat, the jokes, the extra dessert. By Thursday Kabir was out and everyone stopped replying to him in the chat. Nobody said why. We just knew.

I'm Farhan, and I stayed quiet because I didn't want to be next. The thing is, Jomon didn't shout. He just went a bit cold and looked at you a little too long. People started agreeing with everything he said. I watched Kabir laugh too hard at every joke, trying to come back in. I remember thinking Jomon looked tired, not powerful.

Who decided every week who was in the group?
Jomon decided every week who was in the group.
Why did Farhan stay quiet?
Farhan was afraid of being next, and the fear of losing standing kept Farhan silent.
What could Farhan try to loosen the fear in the group?
Farhan could check in with Kabir privately and sit with Kabir, showing that friendship does not have to depend on Jomon's mood.
What might Jomon be feeling, looking tired rather than powerful?
Jomon may feel pressure to keep control and worry that anyone could leave, so the coldness may hide anxiety.

It was 5:40 on the Friday before the Diwali break, and the office was emptying. Pallavi was closing her files when she noticed it on a shared screen: an invoice to a small children's charity, charged twice for the same month. Not her client. Not her mistake. It was Swati's account, and Swati had already left for her train.
The easy thing was to log off. If she said nothing, it wasn't really her fault, was it?
Pallavi stopped and asked herself: if I had sent this double bill, what would I think of leaving it for ten days? She knew the answer.
She called Swati, who picked up on the platform. "Sorry to catch you now. The charity invoice looks doubled."
Swati groaned. "Oh no. Thank you. Can you put a hold on it? I'll fix it first thing Monday."
At 5:52 Pallavi put the hold on, emailed the finance head, and went home to light diyas.

What was wrong with the charity's invoice?
The children's charity was charged twice for the same month.
How did Pallavi feel as she was about to log off?
Pallavi felt tempted to leave it, then uneasy, asking what she would think of herself if she had sent the double bill and left it for ten days.
Why was putting a hold on the invoice a good step?
It stopped the charity being overcharged over the break while Swati could fix it properly on Monday.
How does Swati react to the call on the platform?
Swati is dismayed at the mistake but grateful, thanking Pallavi and asking for the hold.

Tuesday: At lunch Uma broke her mango bar in half and gave one piece to Sachin, who had forgotten his tiffin. She watched to see if he'd say thanks or just grab it. He said, "Thanks, you're a lifesaver," and grinned.

Thursday: During art, Uma whispered, "I'm scared of the dark. I still sleep with a night light." Then she held her breath. If he laughed, she'd say she was joking. Sachin didn't laugh. "I sleep with my old teddy," he whispered back. "Don't tell."

Monday: A boy teased Uma about her braces. Sachin said, "Leave it." At break, Uma told Sachin about her fight with her cousin. She'd never told anyone that before. He listened and didn't tell a soul.

What did Uma share with Sachin on Tuesday?
She shared half of her mango bar.
What was Uma feeling when she whispered her secret on Thursday?
She was nervous, holding her breath and afraid Sachin might laugh.
What helped Uma trust Sachin more each time?
Sachin reacted kindly: thanking her, sharing his own secret instead of laughing, and keeping her story private.
How might Sachin feel when Uma tells him about her cousin?
Sachin probably feels trusted and proud to be a friend she can confide in.

A banana plantation on Jakies Island can produce ten times as many bananas as a banana plantation on a nearby island. If the banana plantation on the nearby island produced 9000 bananas in a year, what's the total banana produce from the two islands that year?

Jakies island produced ten times as many bananas as the nearby island, a total of 10*9000 = 90000 bananas.
Together, the two islands produced 90000+9000= 99000 bananas in that year.
The answer is 99000.
A paragraph, about 35 words, about the festival of lamps: rows of diyas, sweets shared, rangoli at the door.

During the festival of lamps, rows of diyas light up the homes and the streets. Sweets are shared with family and neighbours. A rangoli decorates the door, and the whole house looks bright and welcoming.
The streetlight in our lane has not worked for two weeks, and it is dark at night. Write a letter, about 65 words, to the municipal office asking them to repair it.

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to report that the streetlight in our lane has not worked for two weeks. The lane is very dark at night, and it is hard to walk there safely. I request you to send someone to repair the light as soon as possible. Thank you for your attention.
Yours faithfully
Give a riddle about a mango in exactly two lines; never say its name.

I grow on a tall tree and turn yellow in summer.
My juicy flesh is sweet and my seed is large.
Why is it hard to see in fog? One sentence, no more than 14 words.
Fog is made of tiny water drops that scatter light.

Dear Akash,
I've been meaning to write since your visit. You probably don't remember what you said, but I do.
You know that at home I'm "the one who failed". I dropped out of engineering after two years. At every function, some uncle says, "Jatin? He's our family's failure, but he's a nice boy." After a while, I started believing it. I stopped applying for things. Why bother, if you're the failure?
Then you came and saw me fixing Mamu's scooter, and Chachi's, and the neighbour's. You said, "Jatin, you've got a real gift for machines. Why aren't you doing a mechanic's diploma?" Nobody had ever said "gift" about me.
I applied last week. The polytechnic course starts in July.
Just wanted you to know. One sentence from you did more than two years of relatives.
Jatin

When does the polytechnic course start?
The polytechnic course starts in July.
Why had Jatin stopped applying for things?
Jatin had come to believe the label "our family's failure" and felt defeated, so trying seemed pointless.
What made Akash's words so powerful?
Akash noticed a real skill with machines and named it as a gift, giving Jatin a different picture of Jatin's worth and a concrete next step.
How might Akash feel reading this letter?
Akash would probably be surprised and moved to learn that one sentence changed Jatin's plans.

It was the last evening before the tax-filing deadline, and the internet in Chinmay's PG had been down since noon. His first salary year, his first return. He had put it off for weeks, sure it was complicated. Now he sat in a crowded cyber café with Jahnavi, a colleague from finance who had offered to walk him through it. "You're not calculating anything scary," she said. "The office already took tax out each month. The form mostly checks that it matches." The site was slow, and the fan overhead barely moved the air. Halfway through, Chinmay stopped at a box about health insurance. "Do I even have any?" "The company gives group cover. Find out what it includes, and ask HR whether it's enough for you," Jahnavi said. At 11:12 p.m. the acknowledgement arrived. Chinmay exhaled like he had run a race.

When did the acknowledgement arrive?
It arrived at 11:12 p.m.
Why had Chinmay put off filing for weeks?
It was his first return and he felt anxious and intimidated, sure it would be complicated.
What helped Chinmay get through the filing under pressure?
Asking a knowledgeable colleague to guide him, and planning to check his insurance cover with HR instead of guessing.
How might Jahnavi see Chinmay's worry?
She seems calm and kind about it, explaining that the form mostly checks what the office already took out.

The storm knocked out the power just as the last bell rang, and Vijay's father phoned to say he'd be an hour late because the roads were flooded. Aparna Ma'am could have gone to the staffroom. Instead she pulled a bench to the window, where there was still grey light. 'Show me your fraction homework, the one you left blank.' Vijay's ears went hot. 'I don't get it.' 'Then let's get it.' She drew rotis on the back of an old notice, and they folded paper strips into halves and thirds. Thunder rolled. By the time his father's scooter splashed up, Vijay had done five sums alone. 'Thank you, Ma'am,' he said, and meant it with his whole chest. At home he did five more without being told.

What did Aparna Ma'am draw on the back of an old notice?
Rotis.
How did Vijay feel when he thanked Aparna Ma'am?
Deeply grateful and cared for; he meant it with his whole chest.
What did Vijay do after that evening, and what does it show?
He did five more sums at home without being told, showing new confidence from feeling supported.
Why might Aparna Ma'am have used the wait for fractions?
She saw he had left the homework blank and cared enough to help instead of resting in the staffroom.

The circle S: x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 4y - 12 = 0. a) Find its centre and radius. b) Find the power of P(10, 3) and of Q(3, 6), and say whether each point is inside or outside. c) Find the length of the tangent from P. d) A line through Q meets S at X and Y. Find QX x QY.

Now you try: the power of R(0, 0).
The answer is -12: inside.
Megan works eight hours a day and earns $7.50 per hour.  If she works 20 days a month, how much will be her total earnings for two months of work?

In a day, Megan earns 8 x $7.50 = $60.
In a month, she will be earning 20 x $60 = $1200.
Therefore, Megan will earn a total of 2 x $1200 = $2400 for two months of work.
The answer is 2400.

Before: The week Lokesh started preschool, he began crawling to the table and asking for his milk in a bottle again. On Monday Thomas laughed. "You're too big for that!" Lokesh cried until dinner went cold.
During: By Wednesday Thomas tried something else. When Lokesh crawled in, Thomas scooped him up, gave him an extra-long cuddle and said, "Big day, huh?" The milk still came in his usual steel cup, and bath and story still happened at eight. Thomas didn't mention babies once.
After: The next Monday, Lokesh walked to the table, drank from the cup and told his father all about the class tortoise. At bedtime he asked for one extra cuddle, and Thomas gave him two.

What did Lokesh ask to drink his milk from?
A bottle.
What was Thomas feeling when he changed his approach on Wednesday?
After Monday's tears, Thomas seems regretful and tender, wanting to comfort Lokesh rather than tease him.
Which choice worked, and why?
Extra cuddles without mocking, while keeping the steel cup and the eight o'clock routine, reassured Lokesh so he moved forward within a week 🙂.
What was it like for Lokesh when Thomas laughed on Monday?
He felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why he cried until dinner went cold.

The bus to the state quiz final broke down on the highway, and Abhinav's team arrived with eight minutes to spare, into a hall packed with noise. His heart started hammering. The old thought came: something is wrong. Then the newer one: this is a signal to slow down, not proof. He walked once up and down the corridor, fast, shaking out his hands. "Vaibhav," he said to his teammate, "I'm nervous. Like, a lot." Vaibhav bumped his shoulder. "Same. Take the science round?" Abhinav nodded. Last term, when the worry had kept him awake for weeks, he had told his parents, and they had found a counsellor he still saw on Thursdays. Tonight he would sleep. Right now, he would answer.

How many minutes to spare did the team have when they arrived?
They arrived with eight minutes to spare.
What was Abhinav thinking when his heart started hammering?
First the old thought that something was wrong, then the newer one that it was a signal to slow down, not proof.
Which steps did Abhinav take before the quiz, and why did they help?
He walked the corridor shaking out his hands and told Vaibhav he was nervous, which steadied him enough to play.
What might Vaibhav have felt when Abhinav admitted being nervous?
Vaibhav seems relieved to share it, answering "Same", and the honesty makes both feel less alone.
What does a person do when they are stamping?

Stamping means bringing your foot down hard on the ground, often to show anger or to make noise. It is a verb in its -ing form.
Example: The children were stamping their feet to keep warm.

Monday. Mohit, ten, stood in the school corridor with his gang. "From today, nobody talks to Baljeet. He told the teacher we were copying." The others nodded. Mohit felt strong, like the captain of a winning team.

Wednesday. Baljeet sat alone at lunch. Mohit watched his friend Aman look at Baljeet's lunch box, then at Mohit. Mohit felt a flicker of fear. What if Aman went to Baljeet's side? Then Mohit would be the one on his own. So he said loudly, "Anyone who sits with him is out too."

Friday. Aman sat with Baljeet anyway. Two more boys followed. Mohit stood with his tray and nobody beside him. For a moment, he knew exactly how Baljeet had felt all week.

Why did Mohit say nobody should talk to Baljeet?
He said Baljeet told the teacher they were copying.
What was Mohit afraid of on Wednesday?
He was afraid that if Aman went over to Baljeet, he himself would be the one left alone.
What was the turning point for Mohit, and what could he do next?
Standing alone with his tray showed him how Baljeet had felt; he could apologise to Baljeet and join Aman's table.
How might Aman have felt choosing to sit with Baljeet?
Aman was probably nervous about Mohit's threat but felt it was wrong to leave Baljeet alone, and Aman's choice gave others courage.

On the morning of the Class 6 half-yearly exam in the government school at Jalna, Tanuja opened her pencil box and froze. The blue pen was gone. Her lucky pen. She had written every good test with it since Class 4. Without it, her hands went cold. "I'll fail," she whispered to Alka on the bench. "It's just a pen," Alka said, holding out a spare one. Tanuja shook her head. The bell rang. The papers came. For the first ten minutes she couldn't read the questions properly; her heart was too loud. Then she forced herself to start with Alka's pen. She knew the answers. They were in her head, not in the pen. She walked out tired, and feeling almost silly.

What had Tanuja written every good test with since Class 4?
The blue pen, her lucky pen.
What was Tanuja feeling when she found the pen was gone?
She felt panicked, hands cold and heart loud, sure she would fail without her lucky pen.
What could Tanuja remind herself before the next exam?
That the answers are in her head, not in the pen, so any pen will do and she can focus on what she studied.
How does Alka see the lost pen?
Alka sees it as just a pen and calmly offers a spare, not sharing Tanuja's worry.
What is a wise saying about patience? Make it one sentence of exactly eight words.
Patience turns many small steps into long journeys.
