Read this:

Zainab,
I'm writing this because saying it in the canteen felt wrong.
For about a month you've told me you already ate at home, but your tiffin comes back full, and you've started eating alone in the library. Every time we meet you ask which clothes make you look smaller, and you talk about shape more than about cricket, which you used to love.
I'm not going to say anything about how you look. That isn't the point. The point is that I miss you and I'm worried.
I won't nag you to eat either. But I think a doctor should know what's going on. Would you talk to your Ammi, or come with me to the school nurse on Monday? I'll wait outside.
You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend.
Abhinav

Where has Zainab started eating?
Alone in the library.
What is Abhinav worried about, and what shows it?
Abhinav is worried about Zainab's health; the letter lists a full tiffin, eating alone and constant talk of shape, and says "I miss you and I'm worried."
Which choice in the letter keeps it caring rather than blaming?
Abhinav chose not to comment on Zainab's looks or nag about eating, and instead offered to go with Zainab to the school nurse.
How might Zainab feel reading "You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend"?
Zainab might feel caught out at first, but also safe that the friendship will survive the honesty.
Five times a week, Onur bikes 250 kilometers a day. His friend Hanil bikes 40 more kilometers of Onur biking distance in a day. What's the total distance the two friends bikes in a week?

Since Onur bikes 250 kilometers in a day, he bikes 5*250 = 1250 kilometers for five days in a week.
Onur's friend Hanil bikes 40 more kilometers in a day than Onur, meaning he bikes for 250+40 = 290 kilometers.
In five days of the week, Hanil covers 290*5 = 1450 kilometers.
In total, the two bikes for 1450+1250 = 2700 kilometers in 5 days of a week.
The answer is 2700.
Is it "dolfin" or "dolphin"? How can I make a classroom poster that people notice?

1. It is "dolphin", with "ph" in the middle.
2. Use a big, clear title and just a few words with one strong picture. Choose bright colours that are easy to read from a distance.

Read this:

"Bhavna, no phone at the dinner table."

"I'm just replying to Ishita, Mumma."

"Now. Give it."

"Why?"

"Because I said so."

"You never trust me! I'm not doing anything wrong."

"I didn't say you were."

"Then why are you taking it?"

"Because I said so, Bhavna."

"You always say that. You never explain anything."

"Don't talk to me like that in front of your brother."

"Like what? I'm just asking!"

Sarika held out her hand. Bhavna put the phone in it, hard.

What Sarika didn't say: she'd read about kids being bullied online, and Bhavna had been quiet all week. What Bhavna didn't say: Ishita was upset about her parents, and she was trying to help. Both just heard disrespect.

Who was Bhavna replying to?
Ishita.
What was Sarika worried about but didn't say?
She was anxious that Bhavna might be bullied online, because Bhavna had been quiet all week.
What could turn this around?
Sarika could explain her worry and Bhavna could say she was helping Ishita, so they talk about the real feelings instead of the command.
How does Bhavna experience "Because I said so"?
She feels mistrusted and dismissed, since she was only trying to help a friend.

Comparing the humped herds of whales with the humped herds of buffalo, which, not forty years ago, overspread by tens of thousands the prairies of Illinois and Missouri, and shook their iron manes and scowled with their thunder-clotted brows upon the sites of populous river-capitals, where now the polite broker sells you land at a dollar an inch; in such a comparison an irresistible argument would seem furnished, to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

What argument does the writer draw from comparing whale herds with buffalo herds?

Not forty years ago, humped herds of buffalo overspread the prairies in tens of thousands, where land is now sold by a broker. The writer says that comparing them with whale herds seems to show that the hunted whale cannot now escape speedy extinction.

I'm Gurleen, and I rented the desk next to Deepak's at a co-working space in Indore for the eighteen months his startup lived. It sold refurbished tablets to small private schools. I watched him call forty schools in the first month and sign three. I watched the day an investor said yes, and the day, a year later, the next round fell through. He didn't shout. He sat very still for a long time. Then he did something I didn't expect: he called every one of his twenty-two customer schools himself, told them the truth, and arranged for a local repair shop to handle their warranties. On his last day he pinned a sheet above his desk titled "What I got wrong": priced too low, hired before revenue, ignored the months when school budgets freeze. I don't know if he was heartbroken. He took the sheet with him.

How many customer schools did Deepak have at the end?
Twenty-two.
What might Deepak have been feeling when he sat very still after the funding fell through?
Deepak was probably shocked and deeply disappointed, though Gurleen can only guess from his stillness.
What did Deepak handle responsibly during the shutdown?
He told every customer the truth himself, arranged warranty support, and wrote down what he got wrong so he could learn from it.
How does Gurleen see Deepak's shutdown from the next desk?
Gurleen watched closely and seems to respect how honestly he closed, while admitting not knowing how heartbroken he was.

Monday. A new rule went up on the notice board: no football on the front lawn at lunch. Kunal kicked the wall. 'That's the silliest rule ever,' he told Lalremsiami. 'Sir just hates fun.' He wanted to play there anyway.
Tuesday. Kunal almost sneaked a ball out. Lalremsiami said, 'Why not just ask why?' He scowled, but it stuck in his head.
Wednesday. Kunal knocked on the sports teacher's door. 'Sir, why can't we play on the front lawn?' Sir showed him the window of the Class 1 room, cracked the week before. 'The little ones sit right there.' Kunal thought. 'What if we play on the back ground instead, and one of us looks after the ball bag?' Sir smiled. 'Write that down. I'll take it to the principal.'

What did the new rule say?
No football on the front lawn at lunch.
What was Kunal feeling on Monday?
Angry and resentful; he kicked the wall and thought Sir just hated fun.
What did Kunal do on Wednesday that worked better than breaking the rule?
He asked why the rule existed and politely suggested the back ground instead.
How did the sports teacher see Kunal's question?
Positively; he explained the reason, smiled at the idea and offered to take it to the principal.
Beth bakes 4, 2 dozen batches of cookies in a week.  If these cookies are shared amongst 16 people equally, how many cookies does each person consume?

Beth bakes 4 2 dozen batches of cookies for a total of 4*2 = 8 dozen cookies
There are 12 cookies in a dozen and she makes 8 dozen cookies for a total of 12*8 = 96 cookies
She splits the 96 cookies equally amongst 16 people so they each eat 96/16 = 6 cookies
The answer is 6.
Will it rain in Pune tomorrow afternoon?
I don't know if it will rain in Pune tomorrow afternoon, as I can't check forecasts. A forecast page for Pune or the national weather service will give the outlook.

Subject: Sorry about the late section

Hi Imran,

I am sending my part of the report at 6 a.m., and I owe you an apology. On Monday I looked at the topic, thought "two hours, easy", and went to the cricket nets instead. On Wednesday I started the draft at ten at night. The tables took much longer than I guessed, the charts would not load, and I ended up working until dawn. This is not the first time. Every week I think two hours will do and every week it takes a whole night.

You had to wait for my section before you could join the pieces. I am sorry for that. Please tell me what you need corrected.

Mohit

At what time did Mohit send the report section?
Mohit sent the section at 6 a.m.
What did Mohit think when first looking at the topic on Monday?
Mohit thought it would take two hours and would be easy, which made it feel safe to postpone.
What could Mohit try instead of guessing two hours, and why?
Mohit could note how long the last two reports took and use that figure, because past times are a truer guide than a hopeful guess.
How might Imran feel about waiting for the section?
Imran may feel stressed and annoyed at having to wait, since the joining of the pieces could only begin after Mohit finished.

Counselling note, the Friday before the Christmas break.
Abhinav came in with a notebook. He had drawn two circles with arrows, "anxious" for himself and "avoidant" for his ex, and a loop between them. He spoke fluently for twenty minutes about attachment styles and why the relationship "was structurally doomed". His roommate Deepak, who walked him over, had told me Abhinav had not eaten in the mess all week.
When I asked, "And how did the last evening feel?" Abhinav said, "Feelings aren't really useful data here," and turned to another diagram. His knee bounced the whole time.
Next: I have offered a second session after the break, and I will begin by asking about his week, not the theory.

What did Abhinav draw in his notebook?
Two circles with arrows, labelled anxious and avoidant, and a loop between them.
Why might Abhinav keep turning to diagrams?
He seems deeply hurt, and analysing the breakup lets him feel in control while keeping the pain at a distance; his bouncing knee hints at the tension.
What does the counsellor plan, and why might it help?
Beginning next time with how his week went, not the theory, gently invites the feeling in while still respecting his thinking.
How does Deepak seem affected by Abhinav's breakup?
Deepak is worried enough to walk him over and mention he has not been eating, showing he sees more than the calm analysis.

messages.content: Why do we squint when we step into bright sunshine?
Squinting lets in less light. Because narrowing the eyelids cuts down the amount of light reaching the eye, the glare hurts less and we can see better.

Behind the chapel in the village, Maria and Farida crouched over hopscotch squares scratched in the red dirt. "Your foot touched the line! Out!" Maria shouted. "It did not!" "It did!" "Did NOT!" Each time Maria said it louder, Farida said it louder back, until a goat trotted away. Jude, mending a fishing net nearby, called, "Maria, before you answer, say what Farida just said." Maria scowled. "She says... her heel was on the line but her toes were inside." She stopped. That was different from what she had been fighting about. "So only your heel?" Farida nodded, still frowning. They had never decided what counts. Heels count, they agreed, and Farida hopped again, carefully.

Where were the hopscotch squares?
They were scratched in the red dirt behind the chapel in the village.
Why did Maria scowl when Jude spoke up?
Maria felt annoyed at being stopped mid-argument and still wanted to win, so saying Farida's side out loud felt like giving in.
What could the two try the next time a game argument starts?
Each could say back the other's point first, like "you mean only your heel?", and then agree on a rule together.
How might Farida have felt once Maria repeated her point?
Farida likely felt heard for the first time in the quarrel, which let her calm down enough to agree on a rule, though she was still a bit cross.
My good name is Kiran and I am in class ten. Can you check my introduction?

My name is Kiran and I am in class ten.
Why: extra word ("good name" -> "name").
How many leaves does the neem tree outside my house have?
I don't know how many leaves the neem tree has, as I can't see it. You could count the leaves on one branch and compare, if you're curious.
Sing "Five Little Monkeys". At the end, how many monkeys are jumping on the bed?

Answer: No monkeys, 0.

Fold one finger down for each monkey that falls: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. When all the fingers are down, that is zero.

Monday, winter holidays. Mohit wrapped Papa's old muffler round his neck and announced, 'I am the doctor!' Shankar lay on the rug and was sick. It was the best game.

Wednesday. Shankar yawned. 'Let's be pirates now.' 'No. I said I'm the doctor.' Mohit listened to the teddy's tummy with a spoon, frowning.

Saturday. Shankar had gone home. Mohit sat alone by the heater with the spoon and the teddy. 'I'm still the doctor,' he told Mummy, a bit quietly.

What did Mohit use to listen to the teddy's tummy?
A spoon.
What does Mohit's quiet voice on Saturday suggest he was feeling?
He sat alone and said 'I'm still the doctor' a bit quietly, which suggests he felt lonely and stuck but did not want to go back on his word.
How could Mummy help Mohit change the game without feeling he broke his word?
Mummy could say even doctors go off duty, or that the doctor can sail on a pirate ship, so he keeps his role while the game changes.
How might Shankar have felt when Mohit said no to pirates?
Shankar was probably bored and a bit left out, since the game had stopped being fun for him.

The hailstorm flattened half of Rajni's family's mustard field two weeks before her board exams. Her father sat silent on the charpai. The house felt heavy.
That night Rajni couldn't study. Her friend Hansa came by with a lantern. "What are you thinking?"
"That I can't fix the field. That maybe nothing I do matters."
Hansa sat down. "What can you do today? Just today."
Rajni thought. "I can't bring the mustard back. But I can finish the history chapter. And I can help Bapu clear the broken stalks in the morning."
She wrote both on the back of her hand in pen. She studied for an hour, then slept.
At dawn she was in the field beside her father, pulling stalks. He didn't say much, but he handed her the water bottle first.

What did the hailstorm flatten?
Half of Rajni's family's mustard field.
How was Rajni feeling the night of the storm?
She felt hopeless and heavy, thinking she couldn't fix the field and that nothing she did mattered.
What made Rajni's two small actions wise?
She accepted she couldn't bring the mustard back, but chose actions within her control that day, the history chapter and helping clear stalks, which kept hope without self-blame.
How might Rajni's father feel when she joins him in the field?
He was silent and heavy after the storm, but handing her the water bottle first suggests he felt comforted and grateful for her help.

Raghav, listen. Forty years ago your grandfather Harish nearly failed his apprenticeship. There was an old fitter at the railway workshop, Bapu Iyer, who showed me how to read a gauge when nobody else had time. I never thanked him. I thought a good worker's thanks was the work.
Years later I met him at a station, stooped and half deaf, and I said, "Bapu, you taught me the gauge. Because of that I've fed my family." He gripped my hand and wept. Then he laughed and said, "Nobody ever told me."
I was ashamed it had taken twenty years. Don't wait for the perfect moment. Tell them what they gave you and what it changed.

What was the old fitter's name?
Bapu Iyer.
How did Harish feel when he realised how long he had waited to thank Bapu Iyer?
Ashamed that it had taken twenty years.
What choice did Harish make at the station that changed things?
Harish told Bapu Iyer straight out that Bapu had taught the gauge and that Harish's family was fed because of it.
How did Bapu Iyer react to being thanked?
He gripped Harish's hand and wept, then laughed and said nobody had ever told him.
Is "porridge" the same as "oatmeal"?

Similar but not identical. "Porridge" is the usual word in Britain for a hot cereal made from oats, while "oatmeal" is the usual American word, which can also mean the ground oats themselves. Americans also say "porridge" sometimes, so the words overlap.
Examples: He had porridge for breakfast. He had oatmeal for breakfast.
A neighbour keeps asking me to run errands and I don't always have time.
Helping neighbours is kind, but your time matters too. You are allowed to say no sometimes.
How do I say it without sounding rude?
Be polite and clear: 'I can't today, but I could help on Saturday.' Offering another time shows you still care.
What if they get upset?
They may feel disappointed for a moment, but most people understand a calm, honest answer. If it keeps happening, talk to a family member, who can speak to the neighbour if needed.
Kittens plus wool equals chaos; write a story about it.

Two kittens, Tikka and Masala, found a ball of red wool under their owner's armchair. Tikka pounced. Masala pounced harder. The ball shot across the floor, trailing a long red thread.

They chased it round the table leg, then the chair, then the sofa. The thread wrapped around everything. Soon the living room looked like a spider's web, red and tangled.

When Grandma Usha came in with her tea, she stopped. A kitten sat on the sofa, wound up like a parcel. The other was tied to a lamp.

"Oh dear," she said, and sat down to unwind them, laughing. It took half an hour.

When she had finished, the wool was a heap on the floor, and the kittens were asleep inside it, side by side.
Why does it help to make a list before going to the market?
A list reminds you what you need. Because it is easy to forget things in a busy market, and a list also helps you avoid buying things you do not need.

Gurleen's scooter keys hung by the door of her Chandigarh flat, and half the building knew it. She'd picked up Mrs Bedi's medicines from the chemist twice this week without being asked, and lent the scooter to the watchman's son for his college interview. She never kept track. Except with Nilesh from the second floor. He'd borrowed it nine times since Diwali, and it always came back on empty, once with a new scratch nobody explained. On Saturday he knocked again. "Keys, na? Just for an hour." Gurleen kept her hand on the door. "Nilesh, I'm going to stop lending you the scooter. It keeps coming back empty and you never mention it. I'm not angry. I'm just done." He laughed awkwardly. "Over petrol?" "Over the pattern," she said calmly, and closed the door gently.

How many times had Nilesh borrowed the scooter since Diwali?
He had borrowed it nine times since Diwali.
What does Gurleen's "I'm not angry. I'm just done" show about her state of mind?
She feels calm and settled rather than furious; she has decided and doesn't need a fight to hold the limit.
What makes Gurleen's choice fair rather than stingy?
She still helps freely with medicines and the interview, and stops only with the one person who takes without giving back, naming the reason plainly.
Why might Nilesh laugh awkwardly and say "Over petrol?"
Nilesh may feel caught out and embarrassed, trying to shrink the problem to petrol instead of facing the pattern she named.

Class note, monsoon week. During painting, the water pot tipped over Salma's drawing. Pranav was holding the brush right beside it, paint dripping from his sleeve. When I asked what happened, he said firmly, "Nothing spilled." Then: "It was already wet." He looked scared, shoulders up. I told him accidents happen and nobody would be cross. After a minute he said, very softly, "My elbow bumped it." Salma said it was okay. We dried the drawing on the window together. I will mention the day to his parents, gently.

Whose drawing got wet?
Salma's drawing.
Why did Pranav say "Nothing spilled"?
He was scared of trouble, shoulders up, so denying it felt safer than admitting the bump.
What did the teacher do right?
Told him accidents happen and nobody would be cross, then waited, so he could admit it.
How might Salma feel about her wet drawing?
She was probably upset at first, but forgiving once Pranav admitted it and they dried it together.

Skyler is a composer. He wrote 25 hit songs that made it on the top 10 charts; ten more songs that made it on the top 100 charts than the hit songs; 5 fewer songs than the hit songs that were never released. How many songs did Skyler write in all?

Skyler wrote 25 + 10 = 35 songs that made it on the top 100.
He wrote 25 - 5 = 20 songs that were never released.
So, Skyler wrote a total of 25 + 35 + 20 = 80 songs.
The answer is 80.

Gargi ran home from the anganwadi, dust on her feet. "Papa! Listen!"
Lalit put down the fodder bundle. "Tell me."
"First we sang. Then didi gave us chana. Then a goat came in the door!"
"A goat!"
"Wait, no. First the goat came, then the chana." Gargi counted on her fingers. "Sing, goat, chana. And at the end, didi chased the goat out with her broom and we all laughed."
Lalit laughed too. "And then?"
"And then I came home to tell you."

What did the didi at the anganwadi chase out with her broom?
The goat.
Why did Gargi count on her fingers?
Gargi felt unsure of the order and wanted to get the story right, so she checked each part.
How could Lalit help Gargi keep practising telling her day?
Lalit can keep asking "And then?" and giving her time to fix the order herself, as he did.
What is it like for Lalit to hear the goat story?
Lalit enjoys it and feels close to Gargi; he laughs and wants to hear what comes next 😊.
Why do dogs sniff the ground so much on walks?
They learn about the area through smell. Because a dog's nose is far stronger than ours, so scents tell it which animals and people have passed by.

The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches, so Mahima practised by candlelight in the room she shared with her older sister. Zainab listened from the top bunk, then said, "The middle part is boring. And you say 'basically' about eleven times."
Mahima's face went hot. She blew out the candle a little too hard. "Wow. Thanks."
"What? You asked."
In the dark, Mahima counted her breaths. Then she said, "When you say it like that, it sounds like the whole speech is bad. Is it?"
Zainab was quiet for a moment. "No. The opening is really good. I just meant the middle drags."
"Then say that part too, okay? It helps me hear the rest."
Mahima relit the candle, crossed out the extra 'basically's and cut the middle paragraph in half. Zainab climbed down to hold the page steady.

Why was Mahima practising by candlelight?
The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches.
What was Mahima feeling when Zainab called the middle part boring, and how can you tell?
She felt stung and hurt: her face went hot, she blew out the candle a little too hard and said a flat "Wow. Thanks."
Which step helped Mahima most, and why?
She told Zainab how the words sounded and asked if the whole speech was bad. That let her keep the useful points about the middle and the 'basically's without carrying the sting.
How does Zainab see her own comment?
Zainab thought she was just being honest because Mahima asked. Once she heard how it landed, she said the opening was good and came down to help.

messages.content: Samuel took 30 minutes to finish his homework while Sarah took 1.3 hours to finish it. How many minutes faster did Samuel finish his homework than Sarah?

Since there are 60 minutes in 1 hour, then 1.3 hours is equal to 1.3 x 60 = 78 minutes.
Thus, Samuel is 78 - 30 = 48 minutes faster than Sarah.
The answer is 48.

I was on the stairs outside the library when I noticed Ganga sitting on the bottom step with her head down, a graded paper folded in her lap. Tushar came out, saw her and sat one step above. He didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "Do you want company, or should I leave you?" Ganga said, "Stay." She talked, the words falling out, about failing the course and her parents. Tushar nodded, said "that sounds awful" and didn't offer a plan. I watched him pass her a tissue. After about fifteen minutes she said she was thinking of seeing her professor, and he offered to walk her to the office. I can't say how she felt, but she stood up straighter.

Where was Ganga sitting?
She was sitting on the bottom step outside the library.
What might Ganga have been feeling, and what did Tushar avoid doing?
She was likely upset about failing the course and her parents, and Tushar avoided quick fixes or advice, staying and listening instead.
What could Tushar do if Ganga's distress were more serious?
He could gently encourage her to talk to a counsellor or someone she trusts.
How does the observer see Tushar's way of helping?
The observer sees a friend who sat with Ganga and listened, and can only guess how she felt, though she stood up straighter afterwards.

messages.content: I'm the only one in my team who didn't get invited to a lunch plan. I might be overthinking, but it stung.

You could, lightly. Something like, 'Are you all going out for lunch today? I'd love to join.' It's friendly and doesn't blame anyone.

Yes, and if they say yes, you've solved it in one sentence.
Maybe I missed a message. The invites usually come up in the team chat.

Help me turn down a party invitation politely. Three sentences, and the last should thank them.

How many right triangles with a height of 2 inches and a width of two inches could fit inside a square with 2-inch sides?

A triangle with a height of 2 inches and width of 2 inches has an area of 2 square inches because (1/2) x 2 x 2 = 2
The square has an area of 4 square inches because 2 x 2 = 4
2 triangles would fit because 4 / 2 = 2
The answer is 2.

Daniel is coming over for Christmas and he asked me to teach him a simple Indian dish.
A good first dish is jeera rice with a simple dal. Both are easy, need few ingredients, and are filling. Start with the dal, since it teaches tempering.
I am Chloe. How should I teach him? He cooks only pasta.
Show him each step once, then let him try. Start with chopping, then boiling the dal and finally the tempering. He will learn fast, as he already knows how to boil and season.
Which spices should I show him?
Show him turmeric, cumin, mustard seeds, red chilli powder and salt. Let Daniel smell each one. Five spices are enough for a first lesson.
What if he burns the tempering?
Burnt tempering is common, and it only takes a few seconds. Tell him to keep the flame low and add the cumin to hot, not smoking, oil. If it burns, start again, since it can taste bitter.
Which dish was he going to learn?
Daniel will learn dal and jeera rice, his first Indian dish. Chloe, start with the dal and tempering, then add the rice when he feels confident.

John works a job that offers performance bonuses.  He makes $80 a day and works for 8 hours.  He has the option of working hard to earn the performance bonus of an extra $20 a day, but the extra effort results in a 2-hour longer workday.  How much does John make per hour if he decides to earn the bonus?

First, we need to determine the length of John's workday if he decides to earn the bonus. We do this by performing 8+2= 10 hours for his workday.
Next, we need to determine his overall pay. We do this by performing 80+20=100 dollars a day.
We then determine John's hourly rate by dividing his pay by the number of hours worked, performing 100/10= 10 dollars an hour.
The answer is 10.

Angel therefore used 60 letters / 2 letters per large envelope = 30 large envelopes.
The answer is 30.

He slipped on the wet tiles near the diving board.

Go to the person yourself and shout for an adult by name, like "Coach Iqbal!", rather than waiting for someone older.

Why do a cat's eyes seem to glow when torchlight falls on them at night?

A mirror-like layer at the back of a cat's eye sends light back out. Because that layer reflects light so the eye gets a second chance to catch it, some of that light comes straight back to the person holding the torch.

Lyra has an $80 budget for a week to spend on food. If she bought 1 bucket of fried chicken that costs $12 and 5 pounds of beef that cost $3 per pound. How much is left on her weekly budget?

Five pounds of beef cost $3 x 5 = $15.
So Lyra spent a total of $12 + $15 = $27.
Therefore, $80 - $27 = $53 is left on her weekly budget.
The answer is 53.

If I give my brother 2 marbles I will have double his number of marbles, but my friend will have triple the number I do. The total number of marbles we have together is 63. How many marbles do I have?

Let X be the number of marbles I have.
If I give my brother 2 marbles, I'll have X-2 marbles left.
And my brother will have (X-2)/2 marbles.
And my friend will have (X-2)*3 left.
So the total number of marbles is X-2 + (X-2)/2 + (X-2)*3 = 63.
(X-2)*9/2 = 63.
X-2 = 14.
X = 16 marbles.
The answer is 16.

Instead I sighed loudly, left sticky notes like "Some of us have class in the morning :)" and banged my cupboard at dawn. She started ignoring me back. A silent war in a room the size of a shoebox. In the common room.

Parveen felt resentful and annoyed but said nothing directly, so the anger leaked out as sighs, notes and banging.
What finally worked, and why?
Naming the problem plainly with a specific request and offering a compromise; Sarita could fix what she finally understood.
How might the sticky notes have looked to Sarita?
Like sarcastic jabs rather than a clear request, which is why she started ignoring Parveen back.

As a nurse at the civil hospital in Lucknow.

An auto-rickshaw charges ₹30 to start plus ₹12 for every kilometre. Write a formula for the cost C (in rupees) of a ride of k km. Find the cost of a 5 km ride and of a 12 km ride.

Answer: C = 30 + 12k. For 5 km: C = 90 rupees. For 12 km: C = 174 rupees.

Try a few rides first and look for the pattern: 1 km costs 30 + 12, 2 km costs 30 + 12 x 2, 3 km costs 30 + 12 x 3. So k km costs 30 + 12 x k, and the formula is C = 30 + 12k. Substitute: k = 5 gives 30 + 12 x 5 = 30 + 60 = 90; k = 12 gives 30 + 12 x 12 = 30 + 144 = 174. The fixed ₹30 is the constant term; the ₹12 per km is the coefficient of k.
My first solo trip is next month, to Udaipur. I am nervous.

Nerves are normal, and a first solo trip is a big step. Udaipur is a gentle city for visitors. Plan your stay first, then a few things to see each day, and tell a family member your schedule. How long will you stay?
Four days. I booked a small guesthouse near the lake run by a man called Mr. Sethi.
Good, small guesthouses are often helpful. Ask Mr. Sethi for his favourite sights and where to eat safely. Locals give the best tips, and he can also call you a trusted auto when you need one.
Nice. Should I plan every hour?

No, it is better to plan only the main thing each day, like the palace on day one and a boat ride on day two. Leave free time for walking and resting, because solo trips are more fun with some surprises.
What was the guesthouse owner's name again? I want to message him.
His name is Mr. Sethi. In your message, say your arrival date, how long you plan to stay, and ask if he can arrange a pickup from the station.

Three people in the Andheri flat were paying for three separate data packs on their phones, and each bought their own rice, oil and dal in small packets from the corner shop. ₹1,800 a month on data between them.

Cooking gas or a weekly vegetable run, with a simple shared record so nobody feels they are paying more than the others.

Which of these needs an EXACT answer, and which can be an ESTIMATE? a) How many people came to the mela? b) How much change should the shopkeeper give me? c) How long is the walk to school?

Why does it help to read the whole question before starting to write an answer?

Reading the whole question helps us answer what is really asked. Because the last words often add a condition or a limit, a student who starts after reading only the first part may write a good answer to the wrong question.

Vijay feels relieved and a bit amazed, remembering that two years ago people who flagged problems were punished.
Why is writing the list before pressure a wise step?
Deciding the lines in advance means Keerthana and Vijay can recognise a bend when it comes, instead of explaining it away in the moment.
What might it be like for Vijay to admit saying it's just this once three times?
Vijay may feel a little embarrassed but also honest and lighter, because naming it with a friend makes it easier to catch next time.
It takes one and half hour to reach my village by bus.

It takes one and a half hours to reach my village by bus.
Why: say "one and a half" with a plural noun ("hours").

Read this:

Monday. Madhav held out his open palms and said, "I'll return your book tomorrow, promise." Darshan smiled. Open hands, honest face. Fine.
Wednesday. No book. Madhav apologised and said he'd forgotten it at home. He looked sorry, palms open again. Darshan felt a small jolt of doubt and then felt bad for it.
Friday. Darshan said, "Let's say a day and time. Tomorrow at ten, at the gate?" Madhav wrote it on his hand. The book came back on time. Darshan thought that the open palms had been friendly but the plan was what worked.

What did Madhav promise on Monday?
He promised to return the book tomorrow.
What did Darshan feel when the book didn't come on Wednesday?
Darshan felt a small jolt of doubt and then felt bad for doubting. Darshan had trusted Madhav's open palms and now wasn't sure what to make of the forgetting.
What worked for Darshan after the book was late?
Darshan agreed a day and time, at ten at the gate, and Madhav wrote it down. A clear plan helped more than reading a gesture.
How might Madhav have felt when he forgot the book?
Madhav looked sorry and probably felt embarrassed. His open palms showed friendliness, but he had simply forgotten.

What happens to the man after he drinks the brandy?

I couldn't keep my eyes off him. Always holding tight by the leg of the table with my hands and feet, I saw the miserable creature finger his glass playfully, take it up, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy off. Instantly afterwards, the company were seized with unspeakable consternation, owing to his springing to his feet, turning round several times in an appalling spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushing out at the door; he then became visible through the window, violently plunging and expectorating, making the most hideous faces, and apparently out of his mind.
He springs to his feet, spins in a wild, coughing dance and rushes out the door. Through the window he is seen plunging about, spitting and pulling horrible faces as if he were out of his mind.

Saturday. Vasudha went to a street festival with Parul. The crowd near the stage was thick, and chants started from two groups of young men on opposite sides. She felt shoulders pushing. She squeezed Parul's hand and said, "Let's move to the edge, near the tea stall." They stepped out before it got worse.
Wednesday. On the phone, Parul said the chants had turned into shoving twenty minutes after they left. Vasudha felt a shiver and was glad. She wrote down a rule: know the exit, stay near the edge.
Next Sunday. At a football match, when a group behind her began shouting at another, Vasudha didn't turn or shout back. She and Parul chose the aisle seats, kept their voices low and walked out at half-time.

Where did Vasudha suggest they move to?
To the edge, near the tea stall.
What was Vasudha feeling when she felt shoulders pushing?
She felt anxious and alert, since she squeezed Parul's hand and decided to move.
What did Vasudha do differently at the football match?
She chose aisle seats, kept her voice low, ignored the shouting and left at half-time.
How might Parul have felt when Vasudha suggested moving?
Perhaps surprised at leaving the festival, but Parul went along, and later may have been relieved on hearing about the shoving.

At the bus stop, the bus to the fair was full and left without them. Dilnaz, five, dropped her shoulders and pushed out her lip. "But I wanted the balloons." Her aunt Maria crouched beside her in the rain. "You're disappointed. Me too. We'll have to wait for the next bus." Dilnaz kicked a pebble and sulked for a moment. Then she leaned on Maria's arm. "Can we watch for it?"

What did Dilnaz want at the fair?
The balloons.
What was Dilnaz feeling at the bus stop?
Disappointment, shown by her dropped shoulders, pushed-out lip and kicked pebble.
What did Maria do that helped?
She named the disappointment, shared it and let Dilnaz feel it without rushing her.
How might Maria feel about the missed bus?
Sorry too, since she said "Me too" and stayed beside Dilnaz in the rain.

For most of Class 10, the girls in my group froze Salma out. It started over something tiny, a birthday invitation, and grew into months of silence: nobody passing her the notebook, nobody saving her a seat on the bus.
I was Jeevan, the one who stayed quiet. I told myself it wasn't my fight. The truth is I was scared that if I said anything, I'd be next.
Every time I saw Salma eating alone, I felt ashamed. I'd go home and feel sick about it.
In physics lab, we got paired by roll number. I could have kept quiet there too. Instead I pushed the beaker over and said, "You do the readings, I'll write?" She looked surprised. By the end of the term we did every lab together.
It wasn't brave. It was small. But it was better than joining in, which I'd almost done more than once.

Where did Jeevan and Salma get paired?
In physics lab, by roll number.
Why did Jeevan feel unable to speak up for so long?
Jeevan felt afraid of being the next person frozen out, and felt ashamed every time Salma ate alone.
What small step did Jeevan take, and why did it matter?
Jeevan started working with Salma in physics lab, a quiet act of friendship that went against the group's exclusion.
What was Class 10 like for Salma?
Salma likely felt lonely and rejected, eating alone and having no one pass her a notebook or save her a seat.

At the end of the school year, the staff room of the government school was cluttered with answer sheets. Vishal, a second-year teacher, sat among them. His Class 5 students had almost all learned to read fluently, many of them the first in their families.
Nilesh, the senior teacher, dropped a letter on his desk. It was from a girl's father: "My daughter reads the newspaper to me every night."
Vishal read it three times. He had turned down a corporate job to teach here. Some nights he'd wondered if it was a mistake.
Now he put the letter in his bag, carefully. Nilesh said, "That's why we stay."
Vishal nodded. He couldn't speak.

Whose father wrote the letter?
A girl's father.
How did Vishal feel reading the letter?
He felt deeply moved and fulfilled, unable to speak.
How could Vishal keep hold of this sense of purpose on hard days?
He could keep the letter and similar notes, and remember why he chose teaching when doubts come.
How might Nilesh feel seeing Vishal's reaction?
Nilesh probably feels proud and understanding, having felt the same over years of teaching.

Nursery note, Monday. At drop-off, Mohit clung to the gate and cried hard. Within a minute, two toddlers near the blocks stopped playing. One began to whimper; the other looked around with a worried face. Neither knew why. Mohit's big sister Reena, who had brought him, looked unsure. "Did I upset them?" I told her no. We sat Mohit on the mat with a picture book and sang softly. The whimpering faded as Mohit calmed. Reena smiled, relieved.

Where did Mohit cling while crying?
To the gate.
What did the two toddlers near the blocks seem to feel?
They seemed worried and upset, catching Mohit's distress without knowing why.
What helped all the children settle?
Calming Mohit with a picture book and soft singing, which eased the others as well.
How did Reena feel watching the other toddlers react?
She felt unsure and a little guilty at first, then relieved when they calmed.
I'd like an invitation to colleagues for a farewell lunch for Mr Thomas on Friday at 1 pm in the conference room. Friendly and short, about 40 words. From Sunita.

Dear colleagues,
Please join us for a farewell lunch for Mr Thomas this Friday at 1 pm in the conference room. We will thank him for his years with us and wish him well. Do come and share a meal.
Sunita

Nine minutes before the client call, the office Wi-Fi dropped, and Nirmala was still waiting for the vendor report Sharmila had promised on Tuesday.

"So sorry," Sharmila said, pulling up a chair. "The vendor sent the wrong file, so I had to wait. And then the template changed. Actually, first IT locked my account, that's what started it. And the numbers from accounts were late too."

Nirmala watched the explanation grow, a new cause every few sentences, each one smooth. The wall clock kept moving. Something about the tidiness bothered her more than the delay.

"Okay," Nirmala said gently. "Forget the why for now. What part is done, and what part feels stuck?"

Sharmila let out a breath. "Honestly? I don't understand the new cost section."

"Then we'll say that on the call, and I'll sit with you after."

When had Sharmila promised the vendor report?
Sharmila had promised the report on Tuesday.
What made Nirmala feel uneasy as Sharmila explained?
Nirmala felt uneasy because the reasons kept changing and sounded too smooth, a hint that something uncomfortable sat underneath.
Which approach worked under the time pressure, and why?
Setting aside the why and asking what was done and what felt stuck got Sharmila to name the real problem quickly, before the call.
What is it like for Sharmila when Nirmala asks what feels stuck?
Sharmila seems relieved; the question lets Sharmila drop the growing excuses and admit the cost section is confusing.

Here goes:
Why do we boil water before drinking when we are unsure it is clean?
Meaning of feasible, please.
Help me correct this: The teacher said us to sit down.
What was the exact date of the first match played in my town's ground?

1. Boiling makes it safer. Because the heat kills many of the germs that may be in it.
2. As an adjective, "feasible" means possible to do and likely to work.
3. Write it as: The teacher told us to sit down. Why: "tell" takes a person and "to"; "say" does not.
4. I can't check that, since I don't have local records. The town library or the club's old files may have it.

In the Berlin park, a big dog bounded towards Jin, two. Jin shrieked and grabbed Fatima's legs.

Fatima picked her up. "You're safe. That dog is very jumpy." The owner called the dog back.

They sat on a bench and watched the dog play. Jin peeked out.

"Want to touch?" the owner asked.

"Not today," Fatima said.

Where did Fatima and Jin sit to watch the dog?
They sat on a bench.
What does Jin grabbing Fatima's legs suggest?
It suggests Jin felt frightened and wanted the safety of her parent.
Why did Fatima say "Not today"?
Fatima wanted Jin's curiosity to come back slowly without forcing touch.
How might the dog's owner see the moment?
The owner probably meant well, offering a touch, but Fatima's answer shows Jin needs more time.

1) What is wrong with this: I am living here since 2010.
2) Please define "diffuse".
3) If you cannot hear the teacher, what should you do?

1. I have been living here since 2010. Why: With "since", use the present perfect continuous, not the present continuous.
2. "Diffuse" is a verb meaning to spread out widely.
3. Politely say so or move closer. Because the teacher cannot know unless you tell them.

Week one: Payal noticed that students in her hostel often had nowhere to print documents late at night. She thought of buying a printer and charging per page. Her friend Chetan warned, "What about ink and paper costs?" Payal waved it off.

Week three: She borrowed an old printer from her uncle and tested the idea for a week, keeping track of every page. She was busy every night. But when she added up the cost of ink and paper, she'd barely broken even. She was frustrated. Chetan helped her see she was charging too little.

Week six: She raised the price slightly and bought paper in bulk. Now she made a small profit each week, and nobody complained.

Who lent Payal the printer?
Her uncle lent her an old printer.
Why was Payal frustrated in week three?
She had been busy every night, but after adding up costs she found she'd barely broken even.
What business lessons did Payal learn?
She learned to test the idea cheaply first and to compare revenue with real costs like ink and paper before setting her price.
How might Chetan feel about Payal's success?
He might feel pleased his early warning and help with pricing were useful, and happy for her.

Dear Eshaan,
Since you moved to Pune, I've been thinking about the difference between being alone and being lonely.
Sunday mornings I sit on the terrace and sketch the pigeons for two hours. No one talks to me, and I love it. My head feels quiet. That's the good kind.
But weekday lunch is different. You used to sit with me. Now I eat under the stairs, pretending to read. I watch groups laugh and my chest aches. That's the other kind, and it's been three months.
I decided I don't want to wait for it to fix itself. Yesterday I went to the chess club. I lost every game, but a girl named Farah said I should come back Thursday. I'm going.
Also, call me on Saturday? I miss arguing with you about comics.
Minakshi

Where does Minakshi eat lunch on weekdays now?
Minakshi eats under the stairs, pretending to read.
What does Minakshi feel while watching groups laugh at lunch?
Minakshi feels lonely and sad, with an aching chest, which is different from the calm of sketching alone on Sunday.
What steps is Minakshi taking to ease the loneliness?
Going to the chess club, planning to return Thursday, and asking Eshaan to call on Saturday.
How might Eshaan feel reading this letter?
Eshaan would probably feel missed and glad to be trusted with the truth, and happy that Minakshi is making new friends.

Two weeks after graduation, Siddiq sat on the steps outside Thabo's flat in Johannesburg, a laptop balanced on his knees. Four tabs: a mining firm in Rustenburg, a teaching fellowship in Durban, a master's offer in Lisbon, and his aunt's shop in Cape Town.
"Look at this," he said. "Any of them could be my whole life. That's amazing, right?"
"So why do you look sick?"
"Because any of them could be the wrong whole life." He opened a fifth tab: a classmate's post from London, new job, new city, new partner. "And everyone else seems sure."
Thabo closed the laptop gently. "You've been comparing for three hours. Which one did you think about in the shower this morning?"
Siddiq was quiet. "Durban."
"Then start there. You can change later."
Siddiq laughed, shakily. It felt thrilling and terrifying at once.

How many tabs did Siddiq have open at first?
He had four tabs open.
Why does Siddiq look sick even though he calls his options amazing?
He is excited by the possibilities but dreads choosing the wrong life, especially while comparing himself with a classmate who seems sure.
What turning point did Thabo offer, and why might it help?
Thabo closed the laptop and asked which option Siddiq thought of in the shower, cutting through endless comparison to a first step.
How might Thabo see Siddiq's three hours of comparing?
Thabo seems to see it as a trap that feeds dread rather than helping, which is why the laptop gets closed.

Last year, in the middle of history class, the office sent for Rehana. When she came back, her face was completely frozen. Her mouth was a straight line, her eyes stared at the board, and she didn't blink much.
At first I thought, she doesn't even look upset. What happened?
Later I found out her grandmother had been taken to hospital. That frozen face wasn't not caring. It was shock.
I didn't ask her anything. I just sat with her at lunch and pushed my water bottle toward her. She didn't eat, but she stayed.
After a few days she told me she'd felt like she was underwater, and that my quiet company helped.
- Vijay

Where was Rehana's grandmother taken?
To hospital.
What was Rehana likely feeling behind her frozen face?
Rehana was likely in shock and afraid for her grandmother, which made her face go rigid rather than showing tears.
What did Vijay do that was right?
Vijay stayed quietly near Rehana without demanding a reaction, offering support and time.
How might Rehana's classmates who didn't know the news see her face?
They might have thought she didn't care or was just tired, not realising it was shock.

Music hour at the preschool. When Yusuf Sir played the drum song, Sonali jumped up, spun round and round, clapping over her head. She bumped a chair. Yusuf Sir could have said, “Sit properly.” Instead he put down the drum, stood up and spun too, slowly, arms wide. Sonali laughed so hard she had to stop. Then she took his hand and they spun together till the song ended. Afterwards she flopped on the mat, breathing hard, and sat still for the story.

What song made Sonali jump up and spin?
The drum song.
What was Sonali feeling as she spun and clapped?
She was full of joy and delight at the music. The spinning may also have helped her let out energy, since she sat still for the story afterwards.
Why was joining in a good choice for Yusuf Sir?
It shared her joy and built a bond, and she settled on her own afterwards without any correcting.
How might Yusuf Sir feel spinning beside Sonali?
He likely feels close to her and enjoys sharing her delight, laughing along instead of worrying about the chair. 😊
Marina had 4.5 pounds of fudge. Lazlo had 6 ounces less than 4 pounds of fudge. How many more ounces of fudge did Marina have than Lazlo?

Marina = 4.5 pounds = 72 ounces
Lazlo = 4 pounds - 6 ounces = 58 ounces
72 - 58 = 14 ounces
Marina had 14 more ounces of fudge than Lazlo.
The answer is 14.

Sorry to bother you with two questions.
How do I make a rubber band ball?
Do I say "married with" or "married to"?

1. Wrap one rubber band tightly into a small ball. Keep adding more bands around it until it is the size you want.
2. Say "married to". She is married to a teacher.

Keerthana, you'll laugh, but last night I sat on the stairs and listened to my parents discuss my wedding like a budget meeting.
Appa said, "He must have his own flat. I don't want Arohi struggling like we did." Amma said, "And the family should be decent. If it breaks, the whole street will know." Then Appa said, very softly, "I just want her safe."
I sat there with my chin on my knees. I felt so loved, honestly. And also invisible. Nobody said, "Arohi wants to do her PhD." Nobody said, "Arohi hates big cities."
This morning I made them filter coffee and said, "Can I be in the next meeting about me?" Amma laughed, then stopped when she saw my face. She said, "Okay. Sunday."
So that's the story, Keerthana. I'm Arohi, and on Sunday I get a chair at my own wedding meeting.

Where did Arohi sit last night?
Arohi sat on the stairs and listened to her parents discuss her wedding.
What mixed feelings did Arohi have on the stairs?
Arohi felt loved, because Appa said he just wanted her safe, and also invisible, because nobody mentioned her PhD or that she hates big cities.
Which step did Arohi take, and why was it wise?
She made coffee and calmly asked to join the next meeting about her; that honoured her parents' care while making room for her own wishes.
How might Amma have felt when she stopped laughing?
Amma may have felt surprised and a little moved, realising that Arohi was serious about being part of decisions about her own life.

At the bus stand of the small town, the school girls waited in the shade of the peepal tree. When Reena walked up, the talking stopped.
Then one of them said, sweetly, "Reena, is it true your father lost his job at the mill?"
Reena's face went hot. She had told only one person: Sonali, sitting beside her on the wall last Sunday, sharing a packet of chana.
She looked at Sonali now. Sonali was staring at her own shoes.
Reena said nothing. When the bus came, she sat alone at the front instead of in their usual seat at the back. At lunch, she ate her roti behind the library.
For the next week, when her Dadi asked how school was, she said, "Fine." When Sonali tried to talk, Reena answered in single words. She began to feel safer keeping everything to herself.

Where had Reena told Sonali about her father?
Sitting beside her on the wall last Sunday, sharing a packet of chana.
How did Reena feel when the girl asked about her father's job?
Reena felt exposed and ashamed, her face going hot, because a private family matter had been shared.
What could Sonali do to try to repair things?
Sonali could apologise to Reena privately, own what she did, and ask the other girls to stop talking about it.
How does Sonali seem to feel when Reena looks at her?
Sonali seems guilty, which is why she stares at her own shoes.
We want to plan a day trip to a town nearby.
Decide how you will travel and when you must be back. Look up the opening hours of the places you want to see.
How do we choose what to see?
Pick two or three main places, and leave time between them. Local websites and travel reviews can suggest what is worth seeing.
What about food?
Look for busy local eateries, as crowds usually mean fresh food. Carry water and a snack in case you cannot find a place quickly.
How do we avoid getting back late?
Set a time to start the return journey, and check the last bus or train timings before you go. Leave a buffer for delays.

Saturday night
Third month of teaching coding at the community centre. Today little Pinki made a cat walk across the screen, and she screamed so loudly Ayesha came running from the office. I laughed till my stomach hurt.
This is the best part of my week. Honestly. Five days of fixing bugs for a company whose product I don't care about, and then this.
But I'm restless too. I keep thinking: the centre still keeps attendance on paper. I could build them a simple app. And the older kids could help me build it. That's a real project, not just lessons.
I told Ayesha. She said, "You're never satisfied, are you?" I said, "Satisfied, yes. Finished, no."
Starting the plan tomorrow.
– Ujjwal

What did Pinki make on the screen?
A cat that walks across the screen.
How does Ujjwal feel about the Saturday classes?
Ujjwal feels content and joyful teaching, but also restless to do more.
What is wise about Ujjwal's next plan?
Building an attendance app with the older kids uses Ujjwal's skills to serve the centre and lets the students grow too.
How might Ayesha see Ujjwal's restlessness?
She seems amused and fond, teasing that Ujjwal is never satisfied, while probably glad of the help.

Read this:

Zainab, you asked on the podcast about the worst planning habit I've seen. Let Afreen tell you about a team I worked on two years ago.
Our lead, a really kind person, padded every estimate. If a task needed two days, she wrote five. If a report needed a week, she wrote three. She said, "Better safe than sorry."
And for a while it felt great. Nobody was stressed. But here's what happened. With five days for a two-day job, people started on day four. Meetings got longer. Emails piled up. Everyone relaxed, because the deadline looked so far away.
Then everything finished on the last possible afternoon anyway, in a rush, with the same late nights as before.
All that extra time never turned into anything saved. It just filled up. By the end of the year, we were slower than the team next door, which padded nothing.

How many days did the lead write for a two-day task?
If a task needed two days, she wrote five.
How might the team have felt in the early days of each task?
They probably felt calm and unhurried, since the deadline seemed far away, which is why they started late.
What would you change first in how the lead planned?
Give realistic estimates for each task and keep one shared buffer at the end, used only for real delays, so the time isn't quietly used up.
How might the team next door have seen Afreen's team?
They may have seen a team with lots of time on paper that still rushed at the end, and finished slower overall.

metadata.subtype: Approach: pads every task so heavily that work expands to fill it [Pitfall]

The maths test was tomorrow and Pooja could not find her sharpener. She turned out her bag and checked under the desk and looked along the window sill. She asked Kiran, who had not seen it, and then the girl in the next row. Ten minutes were gone. It was a plain, cheap sharpener, and her pocket money for the week was already spent. "This is not worth any more time," she told herself. She borrowed Kiran's, sharpened three pencils, and went back to the sums. That evening she scratched her name on the new one with a compass point.

Who lent Pooja a sharpener?
Kiran lent Pooja a sharpener.
What was Pooja thinking when she said "This is not worth any more time"?
She weighed how much time the search had already cost against how little the sharpener was worth. She felt tired of searching and decided to move on to the sums.
What alternative approach could Pooja try to stop losing sharpeners, and why?
She could keep a small pouch inside her bag for her sharpener and eraser. Then things return to the same place and there is less to hunt for.
How does Kiran see Pooja's problem?
Kiran sees Pooja, who searched properly, asked and then chose not to waste any more of the evening before the test, so lending a sharpener is an easy way to help.

You're packing for Bengaluru, Sahil, so let me tell you something your Usha Maasi never told anyone. My first year in Delhi, I cried into my pillow every night so the other girls in the hostel wouldn't hear. The food tasted of nothing. Then Onam came, and I couldn't go home; the train ticket was more than I had. That evening Parveen, my roommate, the loud one from Lucknow, came in with two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess. 'I don't know how to make your sadya,' she said, 'but I brought rice and I brought me.' We sat on the floor and ate with our hands. She never made a speech about it. She just came back every night that week with tea. That's when the room became my room, beta.

What did Parveen bring on Onam evening?
Two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess.
How did Usha feel before that Onam evening, and what shows it?
She felt deeply homesick and lonely; she cried into her pillow every night and said the food tasted of nothing.
Parveen brought rice and herself instead of trying to cook a proper sadya. Why did that choice work?
It showed she cared without pretending to fix everything; her plain, repeated company told Usha she belonged, which a perfect meal alone could not.
How might Parveen have seen that evening?
Parveen probably saw it as a small, natural thing to do for a roommate far from home, which is why she never made a speech about it.

In the office break room, Vikas was halfway through explaining his idea for the new client report to Chaitanya. "So if we split the data by region first, then—" Chaitanya glanced at his phone, said "Yeah, sounds good, got to go," and walked out. Vikas stood by the kettle, face hot. He felt stupid for being so excited. For the next hour he didn't say a word to anyone. At four, a message popped up: "Sorry I cut you off. My manager had just pinged me. I actually want to hear the region idea properly. 5 minutes after the standup tomorrow?" Vikas read it twice. His shoulders loosened. He typed back, "Sure. I'll bring the sketch." The next morning Chaitanya listened to the whole thing and asked two questions.

What was Vikas's idea about?
Splitting the data for the new client report by region first.
How did Vikas feel when Chaitanya walked out?
He felt dismissed and embarrassed, his face hot, feeling stupid for being so excited.
What did Chaitanya do that softened the sting?
He apologised, explained the reason and set a specific time to hear the rest, showing he truly wanted to continue.
How did Chaitanya seem to feel after cutting Vikas off?
He seemed a bit regretful, sending a sorry message and listening fully the next day.
It's for my roommate, so make it gentler: Stop leaving your dishes in the sink. It stinks.
Could you wash your dishes soon after eating? They start to smell when they sit in the sink.

Coach's note, Thursday evening badminton practice.
Ujjwal (second year) was off his game today. Between every set he went to his bag and checked his phone, then came back either grinning or flat. Kishore, his doubles partner, told me quietly that Ujjwal had asked a girl from his class, Pallavi, for coffee on Sunday after replying to her stories for two weeks, and she hadn't answered yet.
At the water break I heard Ujjwal say, "She replied in two minutes last time. Now it's been four hours. That means no, right?" He laughed as if joking, but he served into the net three times after that.
I told him to leave the phone in the bag till practice ended, and that four hours can simply mean someone is stuck in a lab. He nodded but didn't look convinced. I'll keep his drills light this week.

What did Ujjwal ask Pallavi?
Ujjwal asked Pallavi for coffee on Sunday.
What was Ujjwal afraid of as he checked his phone?
Ujjwal was afraid Pallavi's slow reply meant rejection; the four-hour gap felt huge even though he laughed it off.
How did the coach help at this stage, and what else might help Ujjwal?
The coach suggested leaving the phone in the bag and pointed out other reasons for a slow reply; Ujjwal could also remind himself that one reply time is not an answer.
How might Kishore feel watching Ujjwal this evening?
Kishore probably feels a mix of sympathy and worry, sharing it quietly with the coach and seeing it affect their doubles game.

"Mama, is it cake day yet?"
"Not yet, Uma."
"But I did SO many stickers."
Uma kicked the chair leg. Siddharth, on the floor with his blocks, copied her kick.
"Hmm," Uma said. She pulled the chart off the fridge. "Mama. How many more stickers?"
"Come, let's count together." Mama put her finger on the first empty square. "One..."
"Two," said Uma. "Three!"
"Three more, and we bake the chocolate cake."
"Three is small!"
"Three is small," Siddharth agreed from under the table.
Uma put the chart back and went straight to tidy her crayons.

What will Uma and Mama bake when the chart is full?
They will bake the chocolate cake.
What was Uma feeling when she kicked the chair leg?
She felt frustrated and impatient, because she had done so many stickers and still didn't know when cake day would come.
What could Mama do so Uma doesn't have to wait to ask next time?
Mama could draw a little cake in the last box, so Uma can count the gap by herself whenever she wonders.
What is it like for Siddharth, watching Uma?
Siddharth copies her kick and her words, so he seems to pick up her mood and share her cheer at the end.

Lucy plans to purchase potato chips for a party. Ten people will be at the party, including Lucy. The potato chips cost 25 cents per pound. How much will Lucy pay (in dollars) for the potato chips if she wants each person to get 1.2 pounds?

Lucy needs to purchase 10 x 1.2 = 12 pounds of potato chips.
So, Lucy will pay 12 x 25 = 300 cents for it.
Since there are 100 cents in $1, thus, Lucy will pay 300/100 = 3 dollars.
The answer is 3.
For Diwali holidays, I want to see my cousins but my mother says it is too far.
It is nice that you want to be with family. Perhaps there is a middle way. Where do the cousins live, and how long does it take?
In Hyderabad. About ten hours by bus.
That is a long ride, so a night bus might be comfortable if your mother agrees. Or your cousins might come to you for a couple of days. Why not ask your mother which option she prefers?
My cousin Farhan said they can come to us. Mom will like that.
That sounds easy for everyone. You can plan a small lamp decoration together and some sweets. Having Farhan and the others at home will make your Diwali joyful.

The fan whirred in the Ahmedabad flat as Farida wiped the counter. A small tap-tap came from her knee. Hansa stood there holding up her empty katori, tapping the steel side with one finger. "Aur," she said. Then, in case Farida missed it, she pressed the bowl against her mother's hand. Farida smiled, filled it with dal and rice, and Hansa carried it back to her mat.

What did Farida fill the katori with?
She filled it with dal and rice.
What was Hansa wanting when she pressed the bowl into her mother's hand?
She was eager and hungry for more, and wanted to be sure Farida understood.
What else could Farida do to build on Hansa's plan?
She could say "more" while filling it, giving Hansa the word to go with the gesture.
How does the tap on her knee feel to Farida?
It is a clear and gentle message, easy to answer while she works.

Saturday: At Charu's house, Charu and two other friends played the same online game, headphones on, all afternoon. Sabina sat beside them with her own tablet. By evening her head felt heavy, and she realised nobody had actually talked to her.
Monday: After school Sabina texted Charu, "Skipping on my terrace? I have the long rope 😊". Charu wrote back, "Maybe, after my match." She never came. Sabina skipped alone, counting out loud, and felt left behind.
Wednesday: Sabina asked again, this time in person. "Just half an hour. I miss you." Charu looked surprised, then pulled off her headphones. On the terrace they reached two hundred skips together, gasping with laughter. Walking home, Sabina noticed her head felt light, not heavy.

How many skips did the girls reach together?
Two hundred.
How did Sabina feel on Monday when Charu never came?
Lonely and left behind.
What did Sabina do differently on Wednesday that worked?
She asked in person and said she missed Charu, instead of only texting.
How might Charu have seen Sabina's "I miss you"?
Charu was surprised, perhaps not knowing Sabina felt left out, and it made her take off her headphones.

The flat in Lyon was cold, and Zeynep kept her scarf on while the group call ran past midnight. "Your professors aren't neutral," the organiser said. "They're paid to keep you asleep." Everyone nodded. Zeynep caught herself nodding too. The next morning Chidi, her lab partner since first year, texted: "Coffee after the seminar? Haven't seen you in ages." Once, she would have gone gladly. Now she heard the group's voice: outsiders pull you back. She wrote, "Busy." At dinner her mother phoned from Ankara and asked, gently, why she sounded tired. Zeynep hung up quickly and felt sure, for a moment, that her mother simply couldn't understand. Later, when a small question crept in, whether the organiser could really know what every professor thought, she pushed it away. Doubting felt like letting the others down.

Where was Zeynep's mother phoning from?
Her mother phoned from Ankara.
How does Zeynep feel when a doubt about the organiser creeps in?
She feels guilty and uneasy, as if doubting would be a betrayal of the group, so she pushes the question away.
What turning point is still open to Zeynep right now?
Zeynep could still say yes to coffee with Chidi and keep talking to her mother, letting outside voices test what the group tells her.
How might Chidi see Zeynep's one-word reply?
Chidi may feel hurt and confused, since they have been lab partners since first year and she suddenly seems far away.
Sam walks 24 minutes each day. How many minutes does he walk in 7 days? Can you fix this sentence? I drinked too little water today. Why do we put a full stop at the end of a sentence?

1. That makes 168. Because 7 x 24 = 168.
2. Fixed: I drank too little water today. Why: The past tense of "drink" is "drank".
3. A full stop shows where a sentence ends. Because it tells the reader when to pause.

Sangeeta: because every visit he criticises my job, my weight, my friends
Ira: I know
Sangeeta: but also
Sangeeta: I've been thinking. he was 26 when Dadi died and he had to run the whole shop and raise us
Sangeeta: I'm 26 now. I can't imagine
Ira: he never talks about that
Sangeeta: I think he was scared all the time. and it came out as criticism
Ira: doesn't make it ok
Sangeeta: no. it doesn't. but I think I can stop being so angry about it
Sangeeta: I'll visit Sunday. if he starts on my weight I'll say "Papa, not that topic" and change it
Ira: a boundary 👏
Sangeeta: and I'll thank him for the school fees. he worked double shifts for those
Ira: he'll be shocked
Sangeeta: good shocked I hope

How old was Papa when Dadi died?
He was 26 when Dadi died.
What was Sangeeta feeling as she thought about Papa at twenty-six?
Sangeeta felt a softening of resentment into understanding, seeing that Papa was probably scared all the time.
What balance does Sangeeta plan for Sunday's visit?
Setting a boundary on topics like weight while thanking Papa for the school fees, releasing resentment without excusing the criticism.
How might Papa feel when Sangeeta thanks him?
Papa may feel surprised and moved, since his effort was rarely mentioned.

Month one: At her school in Aizawl, Lalremsiami sat the maths test with a hot water bottle pressed under her desk, too sore and foggy to finish. When Akash asked why she was pale, she muttered, "Stomach." A girl behind her giggled, "Being dramatic again."
Month two: The pain came back, worse. She missed two days of school and cried from tiredness as much as from pain. Her mother didn't say "just bear it". She sat on the bed and said, "This much pain needs a doctor."
Month three: After the doctor's check and a plan, Lalremsiami got through the week. When Akash asked again, she said, "Period pain. I'm seeing a doctor about it." He just nodded and slid across his notes for the days she had missed.

What did Lalremsiami press under her desk?
A hot water bottle.
How was Lalremsiami feeling in month two?
She was exhausted and in pain, crying from tiredness as much as from the pain itself.
What was her mother's key step?
She believed her instead of saying "just bear it", and took her to a doctor for a plan.
How does Akash respond when she says it's period pain?
Akash simply nods and shares his notes, treating it as ordinary.
Pima invested $400 in Ethereum. In the first week, it gained 25% in value. In the second week, it gained an additional 50% on top of the previous gain. How much is her investment worth now?

For the first week, her investment gain is $400 * 25% = $100.
This leaves her investment with a value of $400 + $100 = $500.
For the second week, her investment increased by $500 * 50% = $250.
Pima's investment in Ethereum is now worth a total of $500 + $250 = $750.
The answer is 750.
There was power cut for two hours last night. What is missing?

There was a power cut for two hours last night.
Why: article ("power cut" -> "a power cut").

"Hansa, got a minute?" Harish said at the printer.

"Sure. Great meeting, right? Sunil loved the survey results."

"He did. But the data cleaning was mine. Three weekends. You said 'I sorted the data' twice."

Hansa laughed a little. "We're a team, Harish. Does it matter who did which bit?"

"It matters when appraisals come round. I'm not trying to embarrass you. I'd just like the next update to say who did what."

"You're making a big deal of nothing."

Harish kept his voice level. "Maybe. I've saved the file history and my emails with the cleaned sheets. I'd rather we fix it between us."

The next week Hansa's update read "survey analysis by Hansa" again. Harish booked ten minutes with Sunil and brought the printed file history.

"Thanks for showing me this," Sunil said, scrolling through it. "I'll correct the record in the monthly note."

How many weekends did Harish say the data cleaning took?
Harish said it took three weekends.
What was Harish feeling when Hansa called it "a big deal of nothing", and how did he manage it?
Harish was angry and felt dismissed, but he kept his voice level and focused on facts and a fair fix.
What was wise about the order of Harish's steps?
He kept records, spoke to Hansa privately first, and only took the file history to Sunil when the credit-taking happened again.
How does Sunil see the situation once he sees the file history?
Sunil treats it as a factual problem to correct and appreciates being shown clear evidence rather than accusations.
What does "let's call it a day" mean?

It means to stop working on something for now, usually because you are tired or have done enough.
Example: By seven o'clock the shop was empty, so Mr Das decided to call it a day.
Peter has four horses. Each one eats 4 pounds of oats, twice a day, and 3 pounds of grain once a day. How many pounds of food does he need to feed his horses for 3 days?

Peter needs 2 * 4 pounds of oats = 8 pounds of oats per horse per day.
Peter will need 8 pounds oats * 3 days = 24 pounds of oats per horse.
Peter will need 24 pounds of oats * 4 horses = 96 pounds of oats total.
Peter needs 3 pounds of grain * 3 days per horse = 9 pounds of grain per horse.
Peter will need 9 pounds of grain * 4 horses = 36 pounds of grain total.
For 3 days Peter will need a total of 96 pounds oats + 36 pounds grain = 132 pounds total.
The answer is 132.
Our coach says we need to build stamina. What should we do? I'm Aisha.
Running is the base of stamina. Start with easy jogging for ten minutes, then add short sprints. Keep your breathing steady. Do you run now?
Only during practice, once a week.
Try adding two short runs a week at home, around twenty minutes each. Mix jogging with fast bursts, like sprinting between two lamp posts and walking to recover.
That sounds like football itself.
Yes, football has bursts of running and short rests. Training this way prepares your body for the real match.
Should I run in the morning?
Morning is good because it is cooler and you start the day well. Drink water before and after. Whatever time you pick, Aisha, keep it the same each week so it becomes a habit.

Pranav, sit. You said Director Menon talks over everyone in your meetings? Let me tell you about my third year here. I'm Kashish. I was presenting my numbers when Menon cut in and started answering a question I had not finished asking. Again. My face was hot. Everyone looked at their laptops.
I did not shout, and I did not sulk. I waited for one breath and said, in an ordinary voice, "Let me complete this thought, then I'll take your question." Then I went straight on to the next sentence.
Menon blinked, nodded and stayed quiet. When I finished, he said, "That was clearer." No fight. It took ten seconds.

Who cut in while Kashish was presenting the numbers?
Menon cut in while Kashish was presenting the numbers.
What was Kashish feeling when Menon cut in the first time?
Kashish felt embarrassed and irritated, with a hot face. Everyone looking at their laptops made the moment feel tense.
What did Kashish choose to say, and how did it work?
Kashish waited one breath and said, "Let me complete this thought, then I'll take your question," and carried straight on. Menon nodded and stayed quiet, so there was no fight.
How might Menon have seen Kashish's steady tone?
Menon probably saw a calm presenter making a fair request, not an attack, since Menon nodded and later said "That was clearer". The steady voice left no need to defend.
We are making banners for sports day. What counts as a banner?

A banner is a long piece of cloth or paper with words or a picture on it, hung up or carried so that people can see it. It is a noun, and the plural is Banners.
Example: Each house carried colourful banners into the ground during the sports day march past.

Week one. Karthik lay awake till three, running through it: what if he failed chemistry, what if the headache meant something serious, what if his friends were laughing at him in the group chat. At breakfast, when his sister Ganga asked for the salt, he snapped at her. Week four. It hadn't stopped. He'd dropped cricket practice because his mind wouldn't sit still long enough to bat. Ganga found him at midnight on the balcony, jaw tight. "It's every night, isn't it?" He nodded. Week five. Ganga walked with him to the school counsellor's room. "I'll wait outside," she said. Inside, Karthik said it out loud for the first time: "I can't stop the what-ifs." The counsellor listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's work on this together."

What did Karthik drop because his mind wouldn't sit still?
Cricket practice.
What was Karthik worried about at night in week one?
He worried he would fail chemistry, that his headache meant something serious, and that his friends were laughing at him.
What turning point came in week five?
With Ganga's support, Karthik went to the school counsellor and said the worries out loud for the first time.
How might Ganga have felt when Karthik snapped at her?
She may have felt hurt at first, but later saw it was part of how tense and sleepless he was.

You asked what the new job's like. Okay, one story. Last month Joseph walked in twenty minutes late, and our manager, Sarika, said in front of everyone, "This is an attitude problem, Joseph." He just nodded and sat down. What got me was that the Monday before, Sarika herself had come in half an hour late, laughing, "The traffic at that flyover is impossible!" Nobody called that attitude. I sat on it for two days. Then, over lunch, I said, "Sarika, can I say something awkward? When you were late, it was the flyover. When Joseph was late, it was attitude." She went quiet. Then she said, "Mridul, that's fair." The next week she asked Joseph, privately, what his mornings were like. Turns out he drops his little sister at a school across town. They moved his start time by fifteen minutes.

What did Sarika say when Joseph was twenty minutes late?
"This is an attitude problem, Joseph."
What was Mridul feeling during the two days before speaking up?
Mridul felt uneasy and torn, bothered by the double standard but nervous about saying something awkward to the manager.
Why did Mridul's comment lead to fairer feedback?
It set Sarika's own excuse beside Joseph's case, so she noticed the double standard and got curious, asking Joseph privately about his mornings.
How might Joseph have felt being called out in front of everyone?
Joseph probably felt embarrassed and misjudged, since the lateness came from dropping his little sister across town, not from his attitude.

Before, Monday: Rajni came home from the hotel front desk at eleven. At work she'd spent nine hours smiling, solving lost bookings, calming an angry guest in perfect polite English. At home in their small London flat, Ayesha asked, "How was it?" and Rajni said, "Don't," and shut the bedroom door.

During, Thursday: Ayesha dropped by the hotel on her lunch break with Rajni's forgotten keys and saw her with a family of five: patient, warm, even laughing. Ayesha felt a sting. So she can do it, Ayesha thought. Just not for me.

After, Sunday: on their day off, Ayesha said calmly, "You're so kind at work. I get the tired leftovers." Rajni's eyes filled. "I know. By the time I get home there's nothing left." They agreed: on work nights, a quiet hour first; on Sundays, phones off, just them.

What time did Rajni come home on Monday?
Rajni came home at eleven.
What did Ayesha feel seeing Rajni with the family of five?
Ayesha felt a sting of hurt, seeing that Rajni's warmth was real but seemed spent on others, not on Ayesha.
Which choice on Sunday helped, and why?
Ayesha named the pattern calmly, not as an attack, so Rajni could admit the tiredness and they could plan quiet hours and phone-free Sundays.
What is it like for Rajni by the end of a nine-hour shift?
Rajni is drained after hours of smiling and calming guests, with nothing left to give at home.
