At the village kho-kho tournament, Ritu's team won the final against Seema's team from the next village. Ritu felt like she was floating. She'd tagged three players in the last minute.
Her teammates lifted her on their shoulders. Some of them started chanting, "Losers, losers!" at Seema's team.
Ritu saw Seema sitting on the ground, face in her hands.
"Stop," Ritu said to her team. "We played well. That's enough."
She went over and held out her hand. "Seema, your team almost had us. Well played."
Seema looked up and shook it. Ritu turned back and thanked her own team, one by one.

How many players did Ritu tag in the last minute?
Three players.
How did Ritu feel after winning?
She felt wonderful and proud, like she was floating.
What did Ritu do that kept the win from becoming small?
She stopped her team's chanting, congratulated Seema kindly, and thanked her own teammates.
How might Seema have felt when Ritu's team chanted?
Seema felt hurt and disappointed, sitting with her face in her hands.

In the boys' hostel, a clip of Tarun singing off-key at the hostel night was going round the student page. The comments were brutal and funny.
Tenzin, in his room, laughed out loud. He had a spare account with no name and no photo. He typed, “Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying,” and hit post. Within an hour it was the top comment.
He felt nothing much. There were three hundred comments. His was just one.
At dinner in the mess, Tarun sat alone at the end of the table, eating fast, not looking at anyone. Somebody behind Tenzin whispered, “Vet! Vet!” and a few boys laughed. Tarun's ears went red.
Tenzin stopped chewing. His comment was sitting at the table with them.

What did Tenzin's comment say?
It said, "Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying."
How did Tenzin feel when he posted the comment?
He felt amused and careless, as if one comment among three hundred didn't matter.
What could Tenzin do after dinner?
He could delete the comment, apologise to Tarun, and stop others repeating the "vet" joke.
How might Tarun have felt when the boys whispered "Vet!"?
Tarun likely felt humiliated and alone, ears going red as the online joke followed him into the mess.

In the Class 1 room at a Delhi school, teacher Rashmi finished the instructions. "Everyone should take out their blue notebook. Is that clear?" Jeevan nodded straight away, but his hands stayed in his lap while the others rummaged. Rashmi noticed and knelt beside his desk. "You nodded. Can you tell me what we are doing next?" Jeevan whispered, "Notebook?" "Which colour?" "Um... blue?" She smiled. "Yes, blue." He took it out.

What colour notebook did Rashmi ask the class to take out?
She asked for the blue notebook.
What did Jeevan's nod seem to mean, and what does the rest of the scene suggest?
The nod probably meant "I heard you" and not "I understand", since his hands stayed in his lap. He might also have been shy about admitting he wasn't sure.
What worked well for Rashmi in checking Jeevan's understanding?
She asked a gentle question about what to do next instead of assuming the nod meant yes, and confirmed the answer warmly.
How might Jeevan feel when Rashmi kneels beside his desk?
He may feel relieved that it's a quiet question rather than a public one, because he whispered his answer.

Daniel's brother Yosef was waiting in the hallway of their Toronto apartment when Daniel came back from the award evening.
"Congratulations, Mum's perfect son," Yosef said. "Must be nice being the one they actually like." Then, quieter and worse: "I wish you'd never been born."
Daniel's face burned. He had a sharp answer ready: at least I'm not failing three subjects. He swallowed it.
He noticed Yosef's eyes were red. He remembered Dad at dinner saying, "Why can't you be more like Daniel?" twice that week.
"I didn't ask them to say that stuff," Daniel said. "It's not fair to you. I know."
Yosef slammed his door anyway.
Later Daniel found Mum and Dad in the kitchen. "You have to stop comparing us," he said. "Yosef hates me because of it, and honestly, I'd hate me too." Mum set down her tea. Dad started to argue, then stopped.

What did Daniel's parents do at dinner that week?
Dad said, "Why can't you be more like Daniel?" twice.
What was Daniel feeling when Yosef said the cruel words?
He felt hurt and angry, with a sharp reply ready, but he held it back once he noticed the pain in Yosef's red eyes.
What wise steps did Daniel take after the fight?
He chose not to retaliate, told Yosef he understood it was unfair, and asked his parents directly to stop comparing them.
How does Yosef see Daniel after the award evening?
Yosef sees Daniel as the preferred son who takes all the love, and his cruelty comes from feeling unwanted and compared.

After the wedding season in their small town, Zeenat started comparing herself to a video star whose skin and waist looked perfect in every clip. She began leaving half her lunch, saying she wasn't hungry.
Her cousin Farida, a year older, noticed. One afternoon on the roof, she showed Zeenat a trick: the same photo of herself, with and without a filter. "See? Smoother skin, thinner face. It's the app, not me."
Zeenat laughed a little, then went quiet. "But she's like that in every video."
"Every video has the filter," Farida said. "And you're growing. Growing needs food."
That night Farida sat with Zeenat while she told Ammi about the lunches. Ammi didn't scold. She hugged her, and said they'd see the doctor together if Zeenat kept feeling bad about eating.

What did Farida show Zeenat on the roof?
The same photo of herself, with and without a filter.
Why did Zeenat go quiet after laughing?
Zeenat still felt insecure and doubtful, comparing herself to the star who looked perfect in every video.
What was the most important step Farida took, and why?
Sitting with Zeenat while she told Ammi mattered most, because skipping food is a real problem that needs a trusted adult involved.
How might Ammi have felt hearing about the lunches?
Ammi was probably worried but chose to be calm and loving, so Zeenat would keep talking to her.
Chintu counts on 3 from 5 like this: "5, 6, 7". He says the answer is 7. Is he right?

Answer: No. He counted the 5 as one of the steps. Counting on 3 from 5 is 6, 7, 8. The answer is 8.

Say the start number in your head (or whisper it), then say 3 NEW numbers out loud, one for each finger. Show it on a number line: three jumps from 5 land on 8.

In their Mumbai flat, Pradeep's younger sister Maria sat at the dining table surrounded by open notebooks, all half-filled. She was fifteen and could start five things at once but finish none. Pradeep, home from college, watched her jump up to get water, then check her phone, then start a new page. "I'm hopeless," she muttered. Pradeep sat down. "You're not hopeless. You're really good at ideas. Remember your science model?" She nodded slowly. "So what if we try short bursts? Ten minutes, then a stretch." They tried. She got one page done and grinned. Later she said she wanted to talk to her class teacher about her attention. "Maybe there are other tricks," she said. Pradeep thought that was brave.

How long did Pradeep suggest each work burst should be?
He suggested ten minutes, then a stretch.
Why did Maria mutter "I'm hopeless"?
She felt frustrated and ashamed at starting many things but finishing none, and blamed herself.
What made Pradeep's response helpful?
He reminded her of a real strength, then offered a practical strategy that fit her attention, instead of criticising her.
Why might Pradeep think Maria's plan to talk to her teacher is brave?
Asking for help means admitting she struggles, which can feel exposing, but it shows she's taking her needs seriously.

Sunday night. Colour-coded chart number four is DONE. Pink for maths, green for science, a tiny star for every chapter I finish. It took the whole afternoon and it looks amazing. Honestly the best part was choosing the pens.
While I was making it I felt like I'd already done half of the studying. Calm and lucky and like I'm moving forward. Tomorrow I'll start Chapter 1. Well, tomorrow I'll make a revision-week chart so it's ready.
Actually the science book is still in the plastic cover and I haven't opened a single chapter. It's fine. The chart is so neat that studying will be easy once I begin.
Harsha

What colour is maths on the chart?
Maths is pink on the chart.
Why does Harsha feel that half the studying is already done?
Harsha feels calm and lucky while making the chart, because planning brings a sense of moving forward.
What could Harsha try, and why?
Harsha could open one chapter for twenty minutes before touching a pen, since the chapters, not the charts, are what remain unread.
How might a parent or teacher see the four charts?
A parent or teacher may notice the neat charts and the closed science book together, and worry that no chapter has actually been studied.

Incubator mentor's note: Sumit and Sunaina, quarterly review

This is the eighth quarter I've reviewed their tutoring app. Active users are down for the fifth quarter in a row. The two schools that piloted it have left. When I asked Sumit what would make things turn around, he talked for ten minutes about how much they had built, the two years, the savings they had both put in, the features "almost ready". He did not describe a single customer who wanted it now. Sunaina was quiet; afterwards she told me she has wanted to stop since last year but Sumit "can't let it go". I have suggested they meet me next week with one question answered honestly: knowing what they know now, would they start this today?

How many quarters in a row have active users dropped?
Down for the fifth quarter in a row.
What does Sunaina's quietness suggest about how she feels?
She seems weary and conflicted, wanting to stop but hesitant to push against Sumit.
How could the mentor's question help Sumit?
It asks him to judge the future, not the past, so the two years and savings stop being the reason to continue.
How is Sunaina affected by Sumit's refusal to stop?
Sunaina keeps putting time into a product she has doubted for a year, which likely leaves her frustrated and stuck.

In their flat in Pune, Pooja spent an hour on the Olympiad practice paper, chewing her pencil and trying the tricky pattern question again and again. When she finally shut the book, her older sister Vasudha was eating biscuits on the sofa. Pooja grabbed three, then two more, though Aai had said none before dinner. When Vasudha changed the channel, Pooja snatched the remote. "You ALWAYS pick!" Vasudha raised her eyebrows. "You're cranky because of the maths. Your brain's out of fuel, I read it somewhere." Aai, chopping onions, said, "People argue about that fuel idea. Maybe she's tired, maybe bored and hungry. Either way, Pooja, drink some water and come help me." Pooja went, still sulking, and slowly her shoulders came down.

How many biscuits did Pooja grab in all?
She grabbed three, then two more.
What might Pooja be feeling when she snatches the remote?
She is worn out and irritable after an hour of hard questions, so a small thing like the channel feels deeply unfair and snatching seems justified to her.
What choice did Aai make, and how did it help?
Aai didn't argue about the cause; she gave Pooja water and a simple job in the kitchen, and Pooja calmed down as her shoulders came down.
How does Vasudha's view of the grumpiness differ from Aai's?
Vasudha is sure it is an empty fuel tank, while Aai treats the reason as uncertain and just offers something practical to help.

Thanks, Francis. Yes, I'm Uma, the quieter daughter. My sister Sunita argues like a lawyer, and so does my mother. Dinner at our house is basically a debate club.
For years I thought Mummy loved Sunita more. She'd laugh when Sunita won an argument and say, "My girl." When I said something, she'd finish it for me. Once she introduced Sunita to her office friends and just forgot I was standing there.
I was furious for a whole year. I barely spoke at home.
Then I watched Mummy and Sunita arguing about a film, both lit up, and I suddenly got it. She wasn't choosing Sunita over me. She just recognised herself in her. She didn't see me because I'm different.
So one evening I told her straight: "Mummy, I'm quiet, not empty. Please wait for me to finish my sentences." She went pink and said, "I do that?" She does it less now.

What did Mummy forget when she introduced Sunita to her office friends?
She forgot Uma was standing there.
How did Uma feel before understanding Mummy's behaviour?
Uma felt furious and hurt for a whole year, believing Mummy loved Sunita more.
What worked when Uma spoke to Mummy?
Uma named one clear need, to be allowed to finish sentences, which Mummy could understand and act on.
How might Mummy see Uma's request?
Mummy seems surprised and embarrassed, going pink, since she had not noticed her own habit of cutting Uma off.

Saturday. Samir gave his daughter Charu the whole recipe for masala chai at once: water, ginger, crushed cardamom, boil, tea leaves, milk, sugar, boil again, lower the flame, strain. Charu, ten, started well, then forgot the tea leaves and let the milk boil over.
Sunday. They tried again. This time Samir said only, "Water, ginger, cardamom. Boil." When it bubbled, he gave the next three. Charu nodded at each small set.
The next Saturday. Charu stuck a card on the fridge with the steps in four short lines, and made chai for the whole family by herself. Samir sipped it and said it was better than his. Charu said it was because she had the card.

What did Charu forget on the first Saturday?
She forgot the tea leaves.
What does Charu's nodding at each small set suggest on Sunday?
It suggests she felt calmer and more confident, because three steps at a time were easy to hold in mind.
Why did the card on the fridge work so well?
Four short lines kept the steps outside her head, so her memory didn't have to hold the whole recipe at once.
How did Samir feel sipping the chai the next Saturday?
Samir felt proud and pleased, saying it was better than his.
Dost ko bolna hai "Mujhe tumhari yaad aayegi." English mein?
Say: "I will miss you."

Mr. Caiden wants to do repairs to his house and requires 300 feet of metal roofing to do this. If each foot of roofing costs $8, and the supplier of the metal roofing brings in 250 feet of metal roofing for free, how much money is Mr. Caiden required to pay for the remaining metal roofing?

The supplier brought 300 ft - 250 ft = 50 fewer feet of metal roofing.
Therefore the total amount of money Mr. Caiden has to pay for the remaining metal roofings is 50 feet * $8/foot = $400
The answer is 400.

Sunday night. Recital tomorrow!! My hands are shaking a little and my mouth feels dry like chalk. Leela Ma'am said it is nerves and excitement mixed together, they feel the same in the body. She showed me to breathe in for four counts and out slowly, so I did it three times. It helped a bit. Then I played the whole Raag once for Amma, who sat there like a rock and smiled at the end. I still feel butterflies but they're smaller. I'll wear my blue kurta and look at Amma when I begin. If I mess up I will just go on. 🙂 — Chetan

What colour kurta will Chetan wear to the recital?
Chetan will wear a blue kurta.
What did Chetan feel the night before the recital, and how could the shaking hands be read differently?
Chetan felt nervous, with shaky hands and a dry mouth, and also excited. Leela Ma'am said the two feelings feel the same in the body.
What could Chetan do on the recital day to help himself settle?
Chetan could breathe slowly as practised, look at Amma at the start, and keep going after any mistake.
How does playing for Amma help Chetan?
Amma sits still and smiles at the end, giving Chetan a familiar friendly face and the confidence that the piece is fine.

Last winter, my roommate Manjula decided to leave final year to build a pet-sitting service. My first move was a mistake. I made a list of seven problems and read them out like a lawyer. She had an answer for each one, and by number four she said, "Mahima, you sound like my father," and stopped looking at me. For the next week she read me every hopeful message she got, and I noticed she never mentioned the vet who'd told her the licensing was tricky. One night I stopped arguing. I said, "Manju, I believe in you. I've just noticed that the good comments stay with you and the warnings slide off. Can we look at the warnings together, once?" She cried a bit, then got her laptop. She's still building it, part-time, and finishing the degree.

How many problems did Mahima list at first?
Mahima made a list of seven problems.
How does Mahima feel, looking back on the lawyer-style list?
Mahima feels regretful, calling it a mistake, and was worried enough about Manjula to stop arguing and try a gentler way.
What went wrong with the list, and what fixed it?
Reading problems like a lawyer made Manjula defend each one; kindly naming the pattern and offering to look at the warnings together opened the door.
What was it like for Manjula to hear the pattern named kindly?
It seems to have moved her, since she cried a bit and then opened her laptop, feeling supported rather than attacked.

Why does Count Rostov cry at the banquet?

As soon as the singing was over, another and another toast was proposed and Count Ilya Rostov became more and more moved, more glass was smashed, and the shouting grew louder. They drank to Bekleshev, Naryshkin, Uvarov, Dolgorukov, Apraksin, Valuev, to the committee, to all the club members and to all the club guests, and finally to Count Ilya Rostov separately, as the organizer of the banquet. At that toast, the count took out his handkerchief and, covering his face, wept outright.
The toasts keep coming and he grows more and more moved. The last toast is to him, as organizer of the banquet, and he covers his face with his handkerchief and weeps.

Dear Jagdish Sir,
In the last tuition class you told us to try one fixed hour of maths every day, so I'm writing to report: fifteen days, no gaps! I do 7 to 8 pm at the dining table, with my phone locked in Ammi's cupboard. I've made a chart with gold stars, and I'll admit I love sticking them on more than doing the sums, some days.
My little brother now calls me "Maths Afreen." I pretend to be annoyed, but I'm not.
Only one thing is worrying me. Next week we go to Hyderabad for my cousin's wedding, four days of functions. If I miss even one day, the chart will look ruined, and I think I'll feel like the old me who never stuck to anything.
Is it okay to carry my maths book to a wedding?
Thank you for the idea,
Afreen

What time does Afreen do maths each day?
From 7 to 8 pm at the dining table.
What is Afreen worried about for the wedding trip?
Afreen worries that missing even one day will make the chart look ruined and bring back the old self who never stuck to anything.
What might Jagdish Sir advise about the four wedding days?
He could suggest a short, easy version, like a few minutes of revision, or marking those days as a planned pause, so one gap doesn't undo fifteen days.
How does Afreen's little brother seem to see the new routine?
He has noticed it enough to give a nickname, 'Maths Afreen', which shows the routine is becoming part of how the family sees Afreen.

In the kasba, everyone knew the old dam wall was off limits. Suraj's father had told him flatly at breakfast: "Don't go near the dam with those older boys. That's final."

By afternoon Suraj was walking toward the dam with his cousin Pooja, his chappals slapping the dust.

"You weren't even interested yesterday," Pooja said.

"He can't decide everything," Suraj muttered.

At the wall, the older boys were daring each other to walk the narrow edge. Suraj's stomach dropped. The water below was fast and brown.

Pooja grabbed his sleeve. "Come. Now." They walked home, and Pooja told his mother what the boys were doing. His mother called the sarpanch that evening, and a watchman was posted by the wall.

What were the older boys daring each other to do?
They were daring each other to walk the narrow edge of the wall.
Why did Suraj head to the dam after being told not to?
Suraj felt resentful at his father's flat order, and going felt like protecting his own freedom, not because he really wanted to go.
What protective steps happened after they left the dam?
Pooja told Suraj's mother, who called the sarpanch that evening, and a watchman was posted by the wall.
How might Pooja have felt standing at the dam with Suraj?
Pooja was probably scared for him and determined to get them both away from the danger.

The canal water in Rampura came by turns, one field after another through the week, and Kishore, twenty-six, kept the register for the water committee. This summer Gurleen's turn fell between one and four at night. Since her husband's death she farmed alone, and she had stopped going out at night after a pack of stray dogs chased her.
Some men told Kishore to quietly swap her turn. Others said a turn is a turn.
Kishore called the committee to the panchayat ghar on Sunday. He wrote two lines on the board: every field's fair share of water; every farmer's safety in getting it. Then he asked Gurleen to speak, and after her, Harbans, whose day turn would move.
The rules said any change needed two-thirds of members. They voted to let Harbans swap with her for one season. Kishore then proposed a standing swap list for anyone who cannot irrigate at night, to be voted on next month.

What two lines did Kishore write on the board?
Every field's fair share of water, and every farmer's safety in getting it.
What might Gurleen have been worried about before the meeting?
She was probably worried about going to her field alone at night after the dogs chased her, and perhaps that asking for a change would look like special treatment.
When men told him to quietly swap her turn, what did Kishore choose, and why was it wiser?
He called the committee and followed the two-thirds rule, so the change was agreed openly and Harbans had a say instead of being overruled.
How is Harbans affected by the way the swap was decided?
Harbans gives up a day turn for a season but was asked to speak and saw the vote, so the loss comes with a fair hearing rather than a quiet deal.
Round 996 to the nearest 10.

Answer: 1,000.

The ones digit is 6, so round up: the tens digit must go up by 1. But the tens digit is 9, and 9 + 1 = 10 tens = 1 hundred. So the tens become 0 and 1 is carried to the hundreds, which are also 9: 9 + 1 = 10 hundreds = 1 thousand. The answer is 1,000. Check on a number line: 996 lies between 990 and 1,000, and it is 4 steps from 1,000, so 1,000 is right. A common mistake is to write 9100, squeezing 10 into the tens place.
Why is it good manners to say thank you when someone helps us?
Saying thank you shows that we noticed the help. Because people like to know that their effort mattered, thanks makes them feel respected and more willing to help again.

Monday. Hansa found out that Arohi had told the class she cried before the debate. Hansa did not answer her messages.

Thursday. Arohi waited outside Hansa's classroom and said, "I was showing off and I hurt you. I'm sorry. I won't tell anyone what you tell me again." She did not ask Hansa to say it was fine. Hansa said she needed to think.

Next Tuesday. They sat on the library steps. Hansa said, "I forgive you. But I'm going to keep some things to myself for a while, and you have to be okay with that." Arohi nodded, her eyes wet. "That's fair." They shared one packet of chips, and Hansa told her only about the exam.

Where did Hansa and Arohi sit when Hansa forgave her?
They sat on the library steps.
What did Hansa want when she said she would keep some things to herself?
She wanted to forgive Arohi but still protect herself, sharing less until trust has been rebuilt.
How can Arohi rebuild trust with Hansa?
She can keep her promise, accept the limits without pressure, and show over time that Hansa's words are safe with her.
How might Arohi feel about the condition Hansa set?
Nodding with wet eyes suggests sadness and relief; she accepted it as fair.

The four whales slain that evening had died wide apart; one, far to windward; one, less distant, to leeward; one ahead; one astern. These last three were brought alongside ere nightfall; but the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night; and that boat was Ahab's.

Why is Ahab's boat left out all night?
The windward whale it killed was too far away to be reached before morning. So the boat stayed by its side all night.

Mary wants to ride the world's tallest roller coaster, Kingda Ka. The minimum height to ride the roller coaster is 140 cm. Mary's brother is 180 cm, Mary is 2/3 the height of her brother. How many more centimeters does Mary need to grow to ride Kingda Ka?

Being 2/3 of her brother's height, Mary is 180 * 2/3 = 120 cm.
To reach the minimum height and ride Kingda Ka, Mery needs to grow 140 - 120 = 20 cm.
The answer is 20.

"Coach Alka, can I talk to you?"
"Of course, Nilesh. What's up?"
"The race last week. The 400 metres."
"You won. Well done."
"I didn't really. I cut the corner on the back straight. Nobody saw."
Coach Alka put down her clipboard. "I see."
"The medal's been in my drawer. I can't even look at it."
"That's your conscience telling you something."
"I know. What happens now?"
"You'll give the medal to Harish, who came second. And you'll sit out the next meet. But you told me yourself, and that matters."
Nilesh let out a long breath. "Okay. Thank you."

What did Nilesh cut on the back straight?
The corner.
How did Nilesh feel about the medal?
He felt guilty, unable to look at it, and kept it hidden in a drawer.
What consequence did Coach Alka give?
Nilesh would give the medal to Harish and sit out the next meet.
How might Coach Alka see Nilesh's confession?
Coach Alka values that he told her himself, saying it matters.

In their Ludhiana flat, Baljeet, fifteen, came home from school and threw his bag on the floor. His sister Kalyani was watching TV.
“Change it,” he said.
“I'm watching.”
He grabbed the remote. She pulled it back. He shouted something he didn't even mean.
Kalyani stared at him, then turned away.
Baljeet's chest was tight. He didn't know why he was so angry. Nothing had even happened at school.
He walked out to the park and did three rounds of the track, fast. The anger drained slowly.
When he came back, he sat next to Kalyani. “Sorry. I don't know what's wrong with me lately.”
She shrugged, and handed him the remote. “Your turn.”

Where did Baljeet go to calm down?
He walked out to the park and did three rounds of the track.
How did Baljeet feel after shouting at Kalyani?
He felt tense and confused, angry for no clear reason.
What helped Baljeet choose a better way to act?
Going for a fast walk let the anger drain, so he could come back and apologise.
How did Kalyani feel when Baljeet shouted?
She felt hurt and turned away from him.
I didn't do nothing wrong. Is it right?
No. The correct sentence is: "I didn't do anything wrong." Why: "didn't" and "nothing" make a double negative, so use "anything".

Friday
Day 12 of the list. Still three lines on the sticky note above my desk:
1. Go to every class.
2. One hour of revision.
3. Five past-paper questions.
That's it. After last semester's two failures, I wanted to do everything: eight-hour days, colour-coded notes. Darshan said, "You'll quit in a week. Make it so small you can't fail it." Annoying, but he's usually right.
Today was bad. Mum called, worried about fees, I slept through breakfast, and I cried in the washroom before the 10 am lecture. I still went. Did the hour in the library, badly. Did five questions, got two wrong.
Three ticks. On a day like this, three ticks.
I think that's the point of a small list. A bad day can't knock it over.
Gurleen

How many past-paper questions are on the list?
Five past-paper questions.
How was Gurleen feeling today?
Gurleen felt upset and drained, crying before the lecture after a stressful call and a missed breakfast.
What else could Gurleen do on the hardest days?
Gurleen could also reach out to Darshan or the campus counsellor when a day feels that heavy, so the list isn't the only support.
How might Darshan feel reading today's entry?
Darshan would likely feel proud and relieved that the small list held on a hard day, as he had hoped.

It was exam week, and Harish had no time for anything. But he noticed Vishal. Vishal had been dropped from the class study group chat after a fight. At lunch, he sat alone with his notes, not eating.
Harish had a practical exam in twenty minutes. He couldn't have a long talk. So, walking past, he said, "Vishal, the lab needs pairs. You want to be mine?"
Vishal looked up. "Really?"
"Yeah. I'm bad at titration."
In the lab they barely spoke, just passed beakers. But after the exam, Harish added Vishal to his own small revision chat, without saying anything to the class.

How long did Harish have before his practical exam?
He had a practical exam in twenty minutes.
What might Harish have been feeling as he noticed Vishal?
He was probably concerned and a bit rushed, wanting to help without much time.
What small acts helped, and why?
Asking Vishal to be his lab partner and quietly adding him to a revision chat included him without drawing attention.
What is it like for Vishal when Harish asks him to be his partner?
Vishal feels surprised and relieved, after being left out of the group chat and sitting alone.

I sit across from Rashmi at the bank branch, so I saw the whole thing.
At about eleven, Kamal rushed over with his phone. "Child-lifting gang in our area! Strangers in a white van. Forward to everyone!" The message had a blurry photo, lots of red text, and "SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS".
Rashmi read it slowly. She didn't forward it. She asked, "Which area? Which date? Who sent it first?" Kamal said it came from his cousin's society group.
She scrolled up and down. "It's trying very hard to scare us," she said, more to herself. Then she rang the police station number printed on our notice board. I heard her say "thank you" and hang up.
"No such complaint," she told Kamal. "The same message went round two years ago in another city."
Kamal looked annoyed for a minute. Then he deleted it. I can't say what she felt. Her hands were steady, though. I'm not sure mine would have been.

What was in the message Kamal showed?
A blurry photo, lots of red text, and 'SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS'.
What might Rashmi have been feeling as she read the message, and what cues suggest it?
Rashmi seemed calm and cautious rather than frightened: she read slowly, asked questions and kept her hands steady, though the narrator can't be sure.
Which steps did Rashmi take before deciding not to forward?
Asking which area, which date and who sent it first, noticing it was built to scare, and ringing the police station to check.
How did Kamal react when Rashmi said there was no such complaint?
Kamal looked annoyed for a minute, perhaps embarrassed at nearly spreading it, and then deleted the message.

Snow still lay along the fence on Ingrid's street in Bergen when her kick sent the football straight through Mr Olsen's garage window. Rafael, her friend from next door, gasped. "He's going to be so mad." Ingrid crossed her arms. "It's one window. Remember when the teenagers spray-painted the whole bus shelter? And they smashed the lamp at the park. This is nothing next to that." Rafael looked at the jagged hole. "But we did this one." Ingrid didn't answer. She kept her hands in her jacket pockets, and when the garage door creaked open, she took a small step back behind Rafael.

What had the teenagers done that Ingrid brought up?
They spray-painted the whole bus shelter and smashed the lamp at the park.
What does Ingrid's step back behind Rafael suggest about how she really feels?
Even while calling it nothing, she seems nervous and a bit guilty, which hints she knows the window still matters 😰.
What choice could Ingrid make when the garage door opens?
She could step forward, tell Mr Olsen the kick was hers, apologise, and offer to help sort out the window.
How does Rafael see the window differently from Ingrid?
Rafael doesn't compare it with the teenagers at all; Rafael looks at the hole and sees that they did this one.

In the garden behind their Bandra building, Dad dug a small hole under the hibiscus bush. Francis stood holding the shoebox with Snowball inside, his rabbit of four years. His throat hurt from holding back tears. Boys in his class said crying was for babies.
Dad put down the spade and knelt in front of him. "Come here." He wrapped Francis in a long hug that smelled of soil. "It's okay to cry. I'm crying too, see?"
Francis looked. Dad's eyes were wet. Something in his chest let go, and he sobbed until his shoulders shook.
Jasleen from the second floor came down with a marigold and laid it on the box without a word. They buried Snowball together. Walking back up the stairs, Francis held Dad's hand and felt less alone.

Where did they bury Snowball?
Under the hibiscus bush in the garden behind their building.
Why was Francis holding back tears?
He felt embarrassed, because boys in his class said crying was for babies.
What in Dad's comfort helped Francis let go?
The long hug, hearing that it is okay to cry, and seeing Dad's own wet eyes.
How did Dad feel about Snowball's death?
He was sad too; his eyes were wet, and he was not ashamed to show it.

Shalini lived on the floor above Deepika Aunty in their Chennai apartment block. One evening Aunty knocked with her phone. "Your uncle's cousin sent a voice message, and I can't find where to hear it. My son says it's easy, but he's in Singapore."
Shalini felt the urge to take the phone. Instead she sat on the sofa beside her. "Aunty, you press. See the little triangle next to the message?"
"This one?"
"Yes. Now touch it."
The cousin's voice filled the room. Aunty laughed, then tried to reply. She held the microphone, then let go too soon. "Oh, it stopped!"
"It happens to everyone. Hold it the whole time you speak."
The second try worked. Aunty sat back, pleased. "Don't tell my son it took two tries."
"Two tries is normal," Shalini said. "It took me three the first time."

Where does Deepika Aunty's son live?
He is in Singapore.
What does Aunty's request "Don't tell my son it took two tries" suggest about her feelings?
It suggests she felt proud of managing it herself but also a bit self-conscious about needing help.
What small choice made Shalini's help respectful?
She sat beside Aunty and let her press the buttons, and treated the mistake as normal instead of taking the phone.
What would change if Shalini had simply done it herself?
The message would be heard faster, but Aunty might feel helpless and still not know how to reply next time.
If Natasha was going 10 mph over the speed limit and it took her an hour to arrive at her destination that was 60 miles away, what was the speed limit?

Natasha was driving at 60 miles / 1hr = 60 mph
The speed limit was 60mph - 10 mph = 50 mph
The answer is 50.

Lakshmi: The agent says for "some extra" my scooter papers move in two days
Lalit: Everyone does it, honestly
Lakshmi: That's what I keep telling myself. Otherwise it's weeks and I have no way to get to work
Lalit: So pay and be done
Lakshmi: Except then I have added to it. And I'd feel like I bought a shortcut off someone who waited in line
Lalit: You're overthinking
Lakshmi: Maybe. But the cost is real either way. Weeks of a long commute versus paying and knowing
Lalit: What would you do?
Lakshmi: Go to the office at opening, take the real queue, and use the bus. It's annoying, but I'd sleep fine
Lalit: You're a stubborn one 🙂

How long did the agent say the papers would take with the extra payment?
The agent said the scooter papers would move in two days.
What is Lakshmi feeling while weighing the payment?
Lakshmi feels torn: under real pressure from the commute but uneasy about buying a shortcut.
What choice does Lakshmi make and what does Lakshmi accept about it?
Lakshmi decides to go at opening, take the real queue and use the bus, accepting weeks of a long commute in exchange for peace of mind.
Why might Lalit say 'Everyone does it'?
Lalit sees paying as normal and a quick way out of Lakshmi's delay, which shows how common the justification is.
Please explain anxiety in simple words.

Anxiety is a worried, uneasy feeling about something that might happen. It is a noun.
Example: He felt some anxiety before his first day at the new school.

Read this:

Okay, so you want to know how I handled Bidisha? I'm Leela, I work on the data team, and this went on for six months.
In meetings with the directors, Bidisha was warm and funny. Back at our desks, she'd say things like, "Leela's slides are cute, I'll fix them." Then she'd present my analysis as her own.
At first I was furious and wanted to outshine her in front of the bosses. That would have turned it into a contest.
Instead I started keeping records: dated emails, file histories, who did which chart. When she presented my forecast, I said calmly in the meeting, "Happy to walk through the method, since I built the model." I didn't insult her. Just the facts.
My manager checked the files. Credit got corrected. The rest of the team started doing the same, and the mood got better.

What records did Leela start keeping?
Dated emails, file histories, and who did which chart.
How did Leela first feel about Bidisha taking credit?
Leela was furious at first and wanted to outshine Bidisha in front of the bosses.
Why was Leela's factual approach better than competing?
It kept the focus on the work and the evidence rather than a popularity contest, so credit was corrected and team morale improved.
How might Bidisha have felt when Leela offered to explain the method?
Bidisha may have felt caught out and embarrassed in front of the directors, since the calm facts showed who built the model.
In exactly two sentences, say why bees are useful. Use the word "flowers" once.
Bees visit flowers to drink nectar. While doing so they carry pollen, which helps plants make seeds and fruit.

Wednesday
Mohit Sir asked me in class, "Am I boring you, Gopika?" Everyone laughed. My face went hot.
I wasn't bored. I was chatting with Neha till one in the morning about the school fest, and then I scrolled through fest photos in the dark. My eyes felt sandy all day and kept closing by themselves, even in the maths period, which I actually like.
After class, Sir called me aside. "Are you getting enough sleep?"
I said, "Not really, Sir."
He said, "Okay. It looked like boredom, but I shouldn't have assumed. Try to rest tonight."
I felt better. I'm going to leave my phone in the kitchen tonight.
- Gopika

Who was Gopika chatting with until one in the morning?
Neha.
What was Gopika feeling when the class laughed?
Gopika felt embarrassed and hot-faced, since the tiredness was mistaken for boredom.
What did Mohit Sir do after class that helped?
He asked about sleep, admitted he shouldn't have assumed, and encouraged rest.
How might Mohit Sir have felt after learning Gopika was just tired?
He may have felt a bit sorry for assuming Gopika was bored and glad he asked.
Our team scored 45 runs in the first innings and 32 runs in the second innings. How many runs is that in all? How many more runs did we score in the first innings?

Answer: 77 runs in all (45 + 32 = 77). 13 more in the first innings (45 - 32 = 13).

Two questions, two sums. "In all" means add: ones 5 + 2 = 7, tens 4 + 3 = 7, so 77. "How many more" means find the difference: ones 5 - 2 = 3, tens 4 - 3 = 1, so 13. Draw two bars, one for each innings, to show the difference.

Monday: when Mehak left for work, Jaya howled at the window and would not let Nani hold her. In the evening she clung to Mummy's dupatta and screamed whenever Mehak stood up.
Wednesday: Mehak waved and said, "After your nap, Mummy comes," then left. Jaya cried, stamped and pushed Nani's hand away.
Saturday: Jaya cried at the goodbye, then sat on Nani's lap with the peg puzzle. When Mehak came home, Jaya hit her arm once, then climbed into her lap.

What did Jaya play with on Nani's lap on Saturday?
The peg puzzle.
Why might Jaya scream whenever Mehak stood up on Monday evening?
She seems scared that Mummy will leave again, so she stays on alert and clings.
What small step seems to help Jaya over the week?
Mehak's same short goodbye, telling her when Mummy comes back, which makes partings more predictable.
How might Nani feel when Jaya pushes her hand away?
Nani may feel a little helpless or rejected, while knowing Jaya is upset about Mummy, not about her.

Teacher's note, KG annual day party, Friday.
Parul arrived holding her mother's dupatta and would not let go. When I said hello, she hid behind her mother's knees. Her mother, Devika, began, "Parul, say namaste!" but I shook my head gently. Devika understood. She knelt and stayed beside Parul near the wall, watching the dancing. After ten minutes, Parul pointed at the balloon tree, and Devika walked her there. Parul let go of the dupatta to pick a balloon. She greeted no one, but she smiled at me once. Next: on Monday I'll keep a quiet corner for her.

What was Parul holding when she arrived?
Her mother's dupatta.
Why did Parul hide behind her mother's knees?
She felt scared and overwhelmed by the party, and hiding brought her relief.
Why did the teacher shake her head when Devika began to push?
Pushing Parul to greet people would make her more anxious; gentle nearness gives her time to feel safe.
How might Devika have felt when Parul picked a balloon?
Devika probably felt relieved and a little proud, seeing her daughter relax at her own pace.

When baby Ojas came home, visitors crowded round the cot with gifts, and Lavanya stood at the edge with her hands behind her back. "Send him back," she muttered, and pinched his blanket hard. Sonali gently loosened her fingers. "You are angry. I understand. Hands stay soft with the baby, but you can stomp as loudly as you like." Lavanya stomped. Sonali kept Lavanya's bedtime the same and asked her to choose Ojas's socks. Some days later Sonali was worn out and juggling the baby's feeds, and Lavanya began talking in baby talk and clinging to her leg. That night Sonali set a timer for ten minutes and gave Lavanya her whole attention: they built a block house, no phone. "You are still my big one and my little one," Sonali said, "and there is room for both of you." Lavanya's shoulders relaxed. On Saturday she stroked Ojas's tiny hand and whispered, "His fingers are so small!" and ran to fetch a nappy. An hour later she frowned and wanted him off Mummy's lap, and Sonali said, "Both feelings are allowed."

What did Lavanya mutter when the visitors crowded round the cot?
She muttered, "Send him back."
How did Lavanya's behaviour change between when Sonali was worn out and after the ten minutes of attention?

When Sonali was busy, Lavanya used baby talk and clung to her leg; after ten minutes of full attention and hearing that there is room for both, her shoulders relaxed and she tenderly stroked Ojas's hand.
What was Lavanya feeling when she said "Send him back"?
She felt jealous, invisible and angry as the visitors crowded round the baby.
What could Sonali keep doing to help Lavanya feel secure?
She could keep the daily ten minutes of full attention, keep Lavanya's routine, and keep giving her small jobs with the baby. 🙂
Class ko shant karana hai. "Dhyan se suno" polite aur casual mein?
Polite: "May I have your attention, please?" Casual: "Listen up, everyone!"
Bachchon ke saath kaunsa theek hai?
With children, the casual one is fine if you say it in a friendly voice. Add "please" to keep it kind.
What should I put in a small bag for a day trip with my school friends?
Keep it light: a water bottle, a snack, a cap or umbrella, a small towel, a phone charger, and a little cash. Wear comfortable shoes. Where are you going?
A waterfall near Lonavala. My friend Sana is bringing the lunch.
Then you can skip the heavy food and bring only snacks. Take a spare t-shirt in a plastic bag, since you may get wet near the falls, and wear shoes with good grip because rocks get slippery.
Good point. Should I bring extra food in case Sana forgets?
A small packet of nuts or a couple of fruits is enough as a backup. Since Sana is bringing the lunch, you do not need a full meal. Just something to keep you going if the plan runs late.

A patient is receiving treatment through a saline drip which makes 20 drops per minute. If the treatment lasts 2 hours, and every 100 drops equal 5 ml of liquid, how many milliliters of treatment will the patient receive after the 2 hours have passed?

The total of minutes the treatment will take is 2 hours x 60 minutes/hour = 120 minutes
After 120 minutes has passed the total amount of drops that the patient will receive is 20 drops/minute x 120 minutes = 2400 drops
Knowing the number of drops, we know that the patient has taken 2400 drops x 5 ml/100 drops = 120 ml
The answer is 120.

Dear Jagdish bhaiya,
You asked me last week about the finance influencer I've been watching, the one who says we can "retire in six months". I'll be honest: I was inspired. I'd watched forty of his videos and was about to pay for his course.
But I did what you taught me and checked first. He earns mostly from selling that course and from referral fees when people open trading accounts through his link. He's not registered as an investment adviser anywhere I could find. And not one video talks about what happens if the strategy fails.
I still like his energy. But admiring him isn't the same as trusting him with my savings.
So I've booked a meeting with a registered adviser next Saturday instead. I'll tell you what they say.
Your brother,
Vikas

Forty of his videos.
What was Vikas feeling before checking the influencer?
Vikas felt inspired and excited, admiring him enough to nearly pay for his course.
What did Vikas check before trusting the influencer?
How he earns, from course sales and referral fees, whether he is registered as an adviser, and whether he explains what happens if the strategy fails.
How might Jagdish bhaiya feel reading this letter?
He may feel relieved and proud that Vikas checked carefully and chose a registered adviser.

At the polytechnic hostel in Hubli, Jahnavi, twenty, watched the scooter problem grow. Nitin borrowed someone's scooter almost every evening. He never filled petrol, never offered his own things, and once returned a scooter with a flat tyre without a word. For a month, people still handed over keys. Then Jahnavi noticed a change. People said their scooters were "being serviced." In the mess, someone joked loudly about "petrol-free travel," and everyone laughed except Nitin. On the group trip to the waterfall, nobody saved him a seat. Nobody had actually told him why. Jahnavi felt a pang watching him sit alone on the steps. That night she knocked on his door. "Nitin, people are annoyed about the scooters. Maybe fill petrol and offer something back?" He looked surprised, then embarrassed. "Nobody said anything." "I'm saying it now."

What did Nitin return once without a word?
He once returned a scooter with a flat tyre without a word.
What was Jahnavi feeling watching Nitin sit alone?
Jahnavi felt a pang of sympathy and unease, seeing the group punish him without ever telling him why.
What did Jahnavi do differently from the group, and why might it help?
She told Nitin directly and kindly what was wrong, giving him a fair chance to change instead of being silently shut out.
How did Nitin react when Jahnavi spoke to him?
Nitin was surprised and embarrassed, saying nobody had told him.

Yogesh was the only man on the six-person design team, and by his second month he felt watched. When he made a mistake, he felt it counted for all men. When a client asked, “What does the male perspective say?” everyone turned to him. He over-prepared and stayed silent in meetings.
Deepak, the team lead, noticed. After the client call, Deepak said, “That question wasn’t fair to you. From now on we rotate who speaks to the client, and I’ll say whose work it is.”
The next week Deepak named Yogesh’s layout in front of everyone. Yogesh kept his eyes on the screen, but his shoulders dropped.

How many people are on the design team?
There are six people on the design team.
How did Yogesh probably feel when the client asked about the male perspective?
Yogesh was probably uncomfortable and resentful at being asked to speak for a whole group. Over-preparing and staying silent suggest he felt watched and cautious.

Deepak recognised the unfair question, set up a rotation for speaking to clients and credited Yogesh's work by name. Fair treatment took deliberate effort.
How might the other team members have felt seeing Deepak change how they worked?
They may have felt surprised or thoughtful, seeing that Yogesh had been under pressure. The passage does not say.

messages.content: How about a little story about a girl and her mother making laddoos before Diwali.

Two days before Diwali, Radha and her mother sat on the kitchen floor with a bowl of warm roasted gram flour and sugar. The ghee smelled warm and nutty. "Roll them round," Mother said. Radha tried, but her first laddoo came out like a lopsided egg. She tried again, and it was a little better. By the twentieth, they were round and shiny. Her mother pressed a raisin into each. When the plate was full, Radha's brother tiptoed in and stole one. Mother pretended not to see. Radha laughed, took another herself, and together the three of them sat on the floor and ate until the plate was half empty.
How can I get a bad smell out of the fridge?
First find and throw out whatever is causing it, then wipe the shelves with a mild cleaner. Leaving an open box of baking soda inside helps to absorb remaining odours.
How often should I change the baking soda?
The box usually says. Many people replace it about every month or two, or sooner if the smell returns.

Edmund is buying a new computer and needs to save up $75 before he has enough. He convinces his parents to pay him for extra chores. He normally has to do 12 chores a week. His parents agree to pay him $2 for every extra chore he does during the week. If he does 4 chores a day for two weeks, how much does he earn?

In two weeks, he has to do 24 chores because 2 x 12 = 24
He now does 28 chores a week because 7 x 4 = 28
He does 56 chores in two weeks because 2 x 28 = 56
He has done 32 extra chores because 56 - 24 = 32
He earns $64 because 2 x 32 = 64
The answer is 64.
Make this clearer for a young child: The monsoon brings heavy rain, which fills the rivers and helps crops grow.
In the monsoon, a lot of rain falls. It fills the rivers and helps the crops grow.

Harsha: "Zeenat! What happened to the alarm clock?"
Zeenat: "I opened it, Abbu. I wanted to see what makes it tick."
Harsha: (looking at the pieces on the bed) "And?"
Zeenat: "There are little wheels with teeth! When one turns, the next turns. It's like a chain!"
Harsha: "Can you put it back?"
Zeenat: "...No. There's one wheel left over."
Harsha: (sitting down) "You know, I did the same with my father's radio."
Zeenat: "Were you in trouble?"
Harsha: "Big trouble. So here's a deal. On Sundays, you and I open one old thing together. With the right screwdrivers. And you draw where each piece goes before you take it out."
Zeenat: "Can we start with the old fan?"
Harsha: "Unplugged. Yes."

What did Zeenat take apart?
The alarm clock.
How did Zeenat feel about what she found inside?
Zeenat felt excited and fascinated by the little wheels with teeth, even though one was left over.
Why is Harsha's Sunday deal a good response?
It turns curiosity into supervised learning with the right tools, and drawing each piece first helps Zeenat put things back.
How does Harsha see Zeenat's tinkering?
Harsha sees himself in it, remembering his father's radio, and chooses to guide rather than scold.
How much homework did I finish this week?
I wouldn't know that, as I can't see your notebooks. Flip through them and tick off each task.
If I leave home at 8:40 and the walk to school takes 25 minutes, will I make the 9:00 bell?
No, you will reach school at 9:05, five minutes late. Because 8:40 plus 20 minutes is 9:00, and the last 5 minutes take you to 9:05.

Tuesday: At the Andheri signal, a boy about Nandini's age knocked on the car window, pointing to his mouth. Nandini grabbed her purse. "Mummy, can I give him my money?" The light turned green before Mummy could answer. Nandini's chest felt heavy all the way home.
Wednesday: At dinner she asked, "Why is he there and not at school? How can we help properly?" Papa said, "Good question. Some groups run schools and meals for children like him. Let's find one together."
Saturday: Nandini and her little brother Divyansh packed a box with their old storybooks and a bag of rice for the children's centre near the station. Mummy also began keeping small packets of fruit in the car. The next Monday, at the same signal, Nandini handed one through the window with both hands. The boy smiled.

Where was the boy knocking on car windows?
At the Andheri signal.
How did Nandini feel all the way home on Tuesday?
Heavy-hearted and sad, wanting to help the boy but unable to.
What safe ways to help did the family choose?
Donating books and rice to the children's centre and keeping fruit packets in the car to hand out.
How might the boy at the signal have felt when Nandini handed him the fruit with both hands?
Treated with respect; he smiled.

For seven months I compared paths. UX, cloud, data science, product management. I made a spreadsheet with twelve columns: salary, course cost, demand, how much coding, how much talking to people. I read every article. I watched every "day in the life" video.
Every week I added rows. Every week the answer changed.
My friend Pankaj finally asked, "Have you tried any of them? Even for a weekend?"
I hadn't. Not one tutorial, not one project. I was scared that trying one meant closing the others, so I kept comparing.
Meanwhile, two people from my batch who'd simply started a UX course had portfolios. I had a very beautiful spreadsheet.
I'm Jaya, and I've learned that comparing only helps when you have something real to compare. Next weekend I'm trying one UX exercise and one data exercise. Then the spreadsheet can have actual data.

How many columns did Jaya's spreadsheet have?
Jaya's spreadsheet had twelve columns.
Why did Jaya keep comparing instead of trying?
Jaya felt scared that trying one path meant closing the others, so comparing felt safer.
What would you change first in Jaya's approach, and why?
I would try one small exercise from each path early on, because real experience adds information that more research cannot.
How might Pankaj feel after asking that question?
Pankaj may feel a little worried for a friend but relieved that the question finally pushed Jaya toward trying something.

"It's my turn to choose the show," said Rashmi.
"No, you chose yesterday," Darshan said.
"But you got the last samosa."
"That's not the same thing!"
Rashmi crossed her arms. "Fine. What's fair?"
Darshan thought. "We made a rule: Monday me, Tuesday you, and so on."
"Today's Wednesday."
"So it's me."
Rashmi scowled, then sighed. "Okay. But tomorrow I choose, no matter what."
"Deal. And you can have the next samosa."
Rashmi laughed. "Now that's fair."

What day was it?
Wednesday.
What was Rashmi feeling when she scowled and then sighed?
She felt annoyed at first, then accepting, because the rule they made was fair.
What helped them settle the argument?
Remembering the rule they had agreed on and offering something back.
How might Darshan see Rashmi's final agreement?
He likely feels relieved and respected that she kept to the rule.

Trisha, you want to skip your friend's dance show because it's raining? Let your Sunaina Nani tell you about the rain of 1968.
I was ten. My friend Kamla had a small part in the temple play, just one line. I had promised to sit in the front row. That evening the sky opened. Mud everywhere. My mother said, "Stay home, she won't even notice."
I sat at the window, wanting to stay dry so badly. But I had said it. Promise. I took Father's big black umbrella and walked, my feet squelching in my chappals.
When I arrived, soaking, Kamla was peeping from behind the curtain, looking at the front row. When she saw me, she smiled so big she almost forgot her line.
After that, she always said, "Sunaina comes. Even in rain." I liked being that person. I still do.

What did young Sunaina take to walk in the rain?
She took Father's big black umbrella.
How did young Sunaina feel at the window before leaving?
She felt torn and reluctant, badly wanting to stay dry but uneasy about breaking her promise.
At what turning point did Sunaina choose to keep her word?
At the window, when she decided "I had said it. Promise," and walked out despite the mud.
How did Kamla feel when she saw Sunaina in the front row?
Kamla felt happy and relieved, smiling so big she almost forgot her line.

The maths period had a substitute teacher, and Class 5 was noisier than usual. Trisha, ten, stared at the word problem about trains and could not tell what to multiply. Around her, everyone seemed to be writing. Her friend Minakshi was already on question three. Trisha's cheeks felt warm. If she asked, the substitute might say the answer loudly and everyone would turn. So she copied the question neatly, drew a small train, and waited. By the bell, she had solved nothing. At home, she cried a little over her notebook. Her father sat with her and asked what the problem said. She read it aloud, and together they found the multiplication.

Which question was Minakshi already on?
Minakshi was already on question three.
Why did Trisha stay silent instead of asking?
She felt shy and afraid of looking stupid, worried that the substitute would say the answer loudly and everyone would turn.
What could help Trisha ask for help next time?
She could quietly ask Minakshi or write a note to the teacher, so she doesn't have to speak in front of the class.
How might Minakshi have acted if she had known Trisha was stuck?
Minakshi might have quietly explained the question, having understood it and sitting right there.

Monday: By six, Ira's shoulders ached and her head throbbed. She had spent nine hours rendering drawings for a client deadline and felt drained without knowing why.
Wednesday: Her senior, Irawati, stopped by her desk. 'Ira, you've been holding your breath for a whole minute. I've been watching.' Ira laughed, embarrassed, then realised it was true. Her breath kept stopping every time she concentrated.
The next Monday: Ira set a quiet alarm every hour. When it buzzed, she sat back, dropped her shoulders and took four slow breaths into her belly. By evening she was still tired, but her head didn't pound, and she had energy to cook dinner.

How long had Ira spent rendering drawings on Monday?
Nine hours.
What did Ira feel when Irawati pointed out her breath-holding?
She felt embarrassed at first, then surprised to realise it was true.
What change helped Ira by the next Monday?
An hourly alarm reminding her to sit back, drop her shoulders and take four slow belly breaths.
How might Irawati have felt watching Ira hold her breath?
Irawati was probably concerned, perhaps recognising the habit from her own busy days.
A wire 88 cm long is bent into a circle. Find the radius and the area enclosed. (pi = 22/7)

Answer: r = 14 cm, area = 616 cm^2.

Work backwards from C = 2pir: 2 x 22/7 x r = 88 44/7 x r = 88 r = 88 x 7 / 44 = 14 cm Then A = 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 cm^2. If the same wire is bent into a square, each side is 88 / 4 = 22 cm and the area is 22 x 22 = 484 cm^2 - less. For a given perimeter, the circle encloses the most area. Common mistake: dividing 88 by 22/7 and forgetting the 2.

In the school garden club, Samir's chilli plant was drooping. 'Give it fertiliser,' said an older boy. Samir had none. He thought: what does a plant really need? He counted on his fingers: water, light, soil. Light first. The pot sat by the sunny window, so that was fine. Soil next: dark and loose, fine. Water last: the soil was soggy and smelled sour. He lifted the pot and looked underneath. No hole. The water had nowhere to go. He told Preeti Ma'am, the club teacher, who helped him move the plant to a pot with holes in the bottom. Two days later the leaves were lifting.

What did Samir find when he looked underneath the pot?
Samir found no hole underneath the pot.
What was Samir wondering when the older boy suggested fertiliser?
Samir was wondering what a plant truly needs, wanting to check the basics before adding anything.
What could Samir do once the plant recovers?
Samir could ask Preeti Ma'am whether the plant needs any feeding now, since it is better to add something only after the basics are right.
How might the older boy have felt when the pot turned out to have no hole?
The older boy was probably surprised, and maybe a little embarrassed that the usual advice had missed the real problem.

messages.content: Claire was in charge of passing out free balloons to all the children at the fair.  She started with 50 balloons.  While passing 1 balloon to a little girl, 12 balloons floated away.  Over the next thirty minutes, she gave 9 more away and grabbed the last 11 from her coworker.  How many balloons does Claire have?

As she gave 1 balloon out, 12 balloons floated away plus she gave away 9 more balloons so she is down 1+12+9 = 22 balloons
She started with 50 and gave/lost 22 balloons so she has 50-22 = 28 balloons
She also took her coworkers last 11 balloons so her new total is 28+11 = 39 balloons
The answer is 39.

It was Gargi's fourth visit to the Aizawl branch that month, and Lalremsiami, at the counter, recognised the account number on the transfer slip before she looked up.
"Same beneficiary?" she asked.
Gargi nodded, cheeks pink. "His business account is frozen. It's just until Friday."
Lalremsiami didn't scold. She lowered her voice. "Can I ask a few things, just between us? Have you met him in person?"
"Not yet. He's in Malta."
"Has he ever video called?"
"His camera..." Gargi trailed off.
Lalremsiami had seen this story in the bank's fraud training: the same charming engineer, the same frozen account, scripts shared by organised groups who do this all day. Gargi wasn't foolish. Gargi was up against professionals.
"Would you sit with our fraud officer for ten minutes before sending? No pressure. I'll come too."
Gargi looked at the slip for a long moment, then nodded.

How many times had Gargi visited the branch that month?
It was Gargi's fourth visit to the branch that month.
What was Lalremsiami feeling as she recognised the account number?
Lalremsiami felt concerned but careful, wanting to protect Gargi without shaming her, which shows in her lowered voice and her choice not to scold.
Why was Lalremsiami's approach wise?
Instead of scolding, Lalremsiami asked gentle private questions and offered to go with Gargi to the fraud officer, which kept Gargi from feeling ashamed and defensive.
How might Gargi see things after the talk with the fraud officer?
Gargi may feel hurt and embarrassed, but learning that organised groups run these scripts could ease the self-blame.

When I joined the firm, my first solo job was explaining our school design to the village committee in Nashik. I'm Arohi, and I'd spent a year on terms like 'cross-ventilation' and 'thermal mass'. The night before, I practised on Lokesh, our site driver, in the jeep. Halfway through, he said kindly, "Madam, I understood 'window'." That stung, but it was the most useful sentence I heard that year. I started again: thick walls keep a classroom cool the way a clay pot keeps water cool; windows on both sides let the breeze walk through. Then I asked him to explain it back to me. He did, better than I had. The next day I used his words, not mine. The sarpanch asked if the pot idea would work for the clinic too.

Where was the village committee?
The village committee was in Nashik.
What did Arohi feel when Lokesh said he understood only 'window'?
Arohi felt stung at first, then grateful, seeing it as the most useful sentence of the year because it showed the explanation had failed.
Which choice made the next day's explanation work?
Asking Lokesh to explain it back and then using his plain words, with the clay pot and the breeze, instead of technical terms.
How did the committee respond to the plain explanation?
They understood well enough to build on it, with the sarpanch asking if the pot idea could work for the clinic too.
Is "return back" correct, as in "Please return back the book"?

The "back" is unnecessary, because "return" already means to give or go back. Standard English says "Please return the book." Some people use "return back" in speech, especially in Indian English.
Example: Please return the book by Monday.

I'm Chinmay, and I sat in on my first disciplinary hearing last month as the note-taker. Usha from HR ran it. For forty minutes, while the employee cried, argued and apologised, Usha's face didn't move. Calm voice, still hands, no nods, no frowns. I honestly couldn't tell whether she believed him, pitied him, or didn't care at all. Afterwards I asked her, carefully, "Do you ever feel anything in those rooms?" She laughed, a bit tiredly. "All the time. If I show it, though, they read my face instead of the facts, and whichever way I lean feels unfair." Then she added, "That one was hard. He reminds me of my brother." I hadn't seen a flicker of that. Over the next weeks I noticed her pattern: impassive in hearings, warm and joking at lunch, and always a walk round the building afterwards. The blankness was a tool, not the whole of her.

How long did the hearing last?
Forty minutes.
What was Usha feeling during the hearing, as she later said?
Usha felt sad and moved, finding the hearing hard because the employee reminded her of her brother, though her face stayed still.
What helped Chinmay understand Usha's impassive style?
Asking her directly and watching her pattern over weeks: blank in hearings, warm at lunch, a walk afterwards.
How did Chinmay first read Usha's still face?
Chinmay couldn't tell whether she believed the employee, pitied him or didn't care at all.

messages.content: Tammy wants to run 3500 meters per week. She knows her track at school is 50 meters around. If she wants to run the same amount each day, how many loops should she make per day?

She needs to run 70 laps in total each week, because 3500 divided by 50 equals 70.
Since there are seven days in a week, she needs to run 10 laps per day because 70 divided by 7 equals 10.
The answer is 10.
Two ten-frames are both completely full. How many counters are there?

Answer: 20 counters. 10 + 10 = 20.

20 is 2 tens and 0 ones: the 2 means two tens and the 0 means no loose ones. Show two full hands of two children, or two bundles.

How does Jasleen feel when the boss praises Rohan's speed?

Hansa worked night shifts at a hospital lab in Bengaluru. Chaitanya was in his final year of engineering, buried in a project. They had been best friends since school, and for three months they'd only exchanged memes.
One morning, Hansa, walking out of her shift at 7 a.m., saw a message: "Do you even exist anymore?" It stung. Then she realised he was right.
She called. "My schedule is a mess. Yours too. What's one thing we can actually keep?"
They worked it out. Sunday at 8 a.m., before she slept and before his day started, they'd walk together in Cubbon Park for twenty minutes. If one of them couldn't, a two-line message was enough.
Some Sundays one of them yawned the whole way. But they kept it. By the end of the year, it was the part of the week they both protected first.

Where did Hansa and Chaitanya walk on Sundays?
In Cubbon Park, for twenty minutes.
How did Hansa feel when she read "Do you even exist anymore?"
Hansa felt stung and a little guilty, realising Chaitanya had a point.
What made their plan work despite busy schedules?
They chose a short, fixed time that suited both, and allowed a two-line message when they couldn't, so the plan was realistic.
What was it like for Chaitanya during the three months of memes?
Chaitanya likely felt lonely and missed his friend, which is why he sent the frustrated message.

I'm Yamini. At Dadaji's prayer meeting I kept watching my niece Aparna, who's two. Everyone was crying. She stood by the door, holding her ear, looking from one wet face to another, lip trembling.
Someone said, "Take her to the other room."
Her mother picked her up instead and held her close in the corner.
Aparna sucked her thumb and leaned in. Soon she fell asleep there.

How old is Aparna?
Aparna is two.
What was Yamini feeling while watching Aparna?
Yamini seems worried and tender, keeping an eye on the small child amid everyone's grief.
What made the difference for Aparna?
Her mother kept her close in the room and held her quietly, instead of sending her away.
What was the prayer meeting like for Aparna?
Aparna was frightened and confused by the crying faces, and her mother's arms made her feel safe enough to sleep.
Why does the moon seem to change shape through the month?
We see different amounts of its sunlit side. Because the moon circles the earth, and from our view more or less of the lit half faces us as it moves.

The board results came out, and everyone in Kakrala village seemed to know Saurabh had got eighty-eight percent. Ojas, his older brother, had scraped through last year.
At the chai stall Ojas said, loud enough for the others, "Maybe the examiner felt sorry for him." At home: "Our topper doesn't carry water buckets now?"
Saurabh felt the words land. He had a sharp answer ready about last year's results. He didn't use it.
When the headmaster visited to offer sweets, Saurabh didn't go on about the marks. "Ojas bhaiya taught me to use the diagrams in geography," he said. It was true.
That night, Ojas was studying for his repeat accounts exam by lantern. Saurabh sat beside him with his own old notes. "These might help. I made them easy." Ojas grunted, but he pulled the notebook closer.

What percentage did Saurabh get?
Eighty-eight percent.
What was Saurabh feeling when Ojas mocked him at the chai stall?
He felt hurt and tempted to hit back about last year's results, but held it in.
Which choices kept the peace between the brothers?
Saurabh avoided boasting, gave Ojas credit for the geography diagrams, and shared his notes for the repeat exam.
How might Ojas see his younger brother's success?
Ojas probably feels jealous and embarrassed, since he scraped through, which is why he needles Saurabh in front of others.

Summarize this in a few short bullet points.

"He investigated the case with great care, for Dr. Roylott's conduct had long been notorious in the county, but he was unable to find any satisfactory cause of death. My evidence showed that the door had been fastened upon the inner side, and the windows were blocked by old-fashioned shutters with broad iron bars, which were secured every night. The walls were carefully sounded, and were shown to be quite solid all round, and the flooring was also thoroughly examined, with the same result. The chimney is wide, but is barred up by four large staples. It is certain, therefore, that my sister was quite alone when she met her end. Besides, there were no marks of any violence upon her."

- The investigator found no clear cause of death.
- The door was locked from inside, and the windows had shutters and iron bars.
- The walls, floor and chimney were checked, and nothing was found.
- The sister had no marks of violence and was alone when she died.

Last month I had my birthday, and I planned everything myself. I'm Pankaj, and I love karela sabzi more than anything, so I asked Mummy to make a big pot for my friends. I also chose my favourite game, carrom, for the whole afternoon, and my favourite cartoon film for after. I thought everyone loves those things. When the plates came out, Usha made a face and pushed the karela to one side. Two boys wanted to play cricket instead of carrom, and nobody laughed at the film's jokes. My ears went hot and I went to the balcony. Usha came out and said, "Your party is nice. We just like different things." Next year I'm going to ask everyone first. But I'm still making karela.

What food did Pankaj ask Mummy to make for the party?
Pankaj asked for a big pot of karela sabzi.
Why did Pankaj feel hurt when the friends didn't enjoy the party?
Pankaj felt hurt and embarrassed, because karela, carrom and the film seemed like things everyone loves, so the friends' faces came as a shock.
What could Pankaj try for next year's party?
Ask each friend what they like to eat and play first, and maybe mix one of Pankaj's favourites with one of theirs.
How might Usha have felt at the party?
Usha probably didn't enjoy the karela but still cared about Pankaj, and so came out to the balcony to say the party was nice.

Janet filmed a new movie that is 60% longer than her previous 2-hour long movie.  Her previous movie cost $50 per minute to film, and the newest movie cost twice as much per minute to film as the previous movie.  What was the total amount of money required to film Janet's entire newest film?

The first movie was 2*60=120 minutes
So this movie is 120*.6=72 minutes longer
So this movie is 192 minutes
It also cost 50*2=$100 per minute to film
So it cost 192*100=$1920
The answer is 1920.

Is my phone's battery full?
Then, "oppression" - what does that mean?
And one more: please correct: The news are on at nine.

1. I don't know, because I can't see your phone. Look at the battery icon on its screen.
2. "Oppression" is a noun. It means cruel and unfair treatment of people by those in power.
3. Correct form: The news is on at nine. Why: "news" is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
Martin owns a farm with hens. 10 hens do lay 80 eggs in 10 days. Martin decided to buy 15 more hens. How many eggs will all hens lay in 15 days?

If 10 hens lay 80 eggs, then 1 hen lays 80 / 10 = 8 eggs in 10 days.
That means one hen is laying 8 / 2 = 4 eggs in 5 days.
So in 15 days, 1 hen will lay 3 times more eggs, so 4 * 3 = 12 eggs.
All hens in total will then lay 25 * 12 = 300 eggs in 15 days.
The answer is 300.

The office air conditioning had died at six, and by nine the call centre floor felt like a bus at noon. Gurpreet had just told Pallavi that the manager wanted her on the late shift again. Pallavi's jaw slid forward, chin raised. "No. Not tonight." A couple of headsets turned their way. Gurpreet felt the old urge to snap, "It's not my decision, just do it." Instead she lowered her voice. "Okay. What makes tonight hard?" Pallavi's chin stayed out, but her fingers were twisting her ID lanyard. "The last cab leaves at eleven-thirty. After that I'd be walking to the main road alone." So it wasn't stubbornness, or not only that. Gurpreet messaged the manager: "Pallavi can do the late shift only with a cab drop. Can we arrange that?" The reply came in five minutes: yes.

When does the last cab leave?
The last cab leaves at eleven-thirty.
What was Gurpreet feeling when Pallavi's jaw slid forward, and how did she read it?
Gurpreet felt a flash of irritation and pressure, reading the jaw as a challenge, but the twisting lanyard made her wonder whether fear, not stubbornness, sat underneath.
What worked in how Gurpreet handled the moment?
Lowering her voice and asking what made tonight hard, instead of snapping back, uncovered the real worry and led to a request for a cab drop.
How might Pallavi have felt if Gurpreet had said 'just do it'?
She would likely have felt unheard and cornered, the argument might have grown in front of everyone, and her worry about walking alone would have stayed hidden.

Since Mridul told the hostel warden about the seniors making juniors do push-ups at midnight, the second-floor corridor had gone silent around him. His roommates dragged their mattresses to the next room. Someone had written SNITCH on his locker in marker. At dinner in the mess he sat alone with his dal, his throat so tight he couldn't swallow. I've had it cleaned, and I've spoken to your floor. How are you, really?' 'I just wanted them to stop hurting the little ones,' he said. 'Not to get anyone punished.' What was written on Mridul's locker?
SNITCH, in marker.
What was Mridul feeling at dinner in the mess?
He felt hurt and lonely, his throat too tight to swallow, wondering if he had ruined everything.
What helped Mridul most after being frozen out?
The house mistress checking on him, naming the difference between protecting and punishing, and connecting him with allies.
How might the juniors see Mridul's report?
As protection from midnight punishment, which is why they saved him a seat every night.
