In the hostel study hall of her boarding school in Ooty, Vidya stared at her physics book without seeing it. Two weeks ago Thomas, who she'd trusted with everything, had told the whole dorm that she'd cried after failing the maths test. Now people called her "Tears" in the corridor.
Every night after lights out she replayed it. She rehearsed the argument she'd have with him, perfect sentences, crushing ones. She imagined telling the warden it was Thomas who broke the lab window last term. She imagined him being sent home, and everyone knowing.
In the moment, the plans made her feel strong. Afterwards, she felt worse. Her marks were slipping. She'd stopped going to choir, because Thomas was in it.
Tonight, when her roommate asked if she wanted to go for hot chocolate, Vidya said no, and went back to rehearsing. She realised, with a tired kind of shock, that Thomas was still in charge of her evenings.

What did people start calling Vidya in the corridor?
Tears.
What does Vidya realise with a tired shock?
She feels drained and stuck, realising the replaying lets Thomas control her evenings.
What could help Vidya move forward?
Going for the hot chocolate, returning to choir, and talking to a trusted adult about the hurt instead of planning payback.
What is Vidya's roommate noticing?
The roommate probably notices Vidya withdrawing and feels concerned, gently trying to draw her out.

In the Nairobi call centre, Nkechi managed eight people, and lately Dalia's reports about the team came in only two colours. "Wanjiru is amazing, she's the only one who works." "Otieno is toxic, he's against me." A week later, after a scheduling clash, Wanjiru became "two-faced". Nkechi noticed her own urge to pick a side, because Dalia told the stories so vividly. Instead, in their one-to-one, she asked, "What exactly happened with the schedule? What did Wanjiru say, word for word?" Dalia hesitated. "She said she couldn't swap shifts." "Anything else?" "No." Nkechi nodded. "So she said no to a swap. That's disappointing. It doesn't make her two-faced." Dalia looked down.

What did Wanjiru actually say?
That she couldn't swap shifts.
What did Nkechi feel pulling at her as Dalia told the stories?
A tempted, uneasy urge to take Dalia's side, because the stories were so vivid; she resisted it.
How did Nkechi stay fair?
She asked what was said, word for word, and named the event as disappointing without labelling Wanjiru.
How might Wanjiru feel if she knew she had been called two-faced?
Hurt and bewildered, having only declined a shift swap.

At my cousin's wedding last winter, the children had the whole terrace to ourselves, and my older cousin Pinky Didi was in charge of games. I'm Vandana, and I was nine. When Nandini from the house next door came up to join, Pinky Didi said, 'She's not family. Tell her to go down.' I didn't want to. Nandini had shared her sparklers with me the night before. But Didi was fifteen and knew everything, and she said it so firmly. So I walked over and said, 'You can't play. Didi said.' My voice came out very small. Nandini went down the stairs slowly. All evening my stomach felt wrong, but I kept telling myself it was Didi's rule, not mine. Now I know I could have said no.

What had Nandini shared the night before?
Her sparklers.
How did Vandana feel while telling Nandini she couldn't play?
Vandana felt uneasy and small, doing something unwanted just because Didi said so.
What could Vandana have said to Pinky Didi instead?
Vandana could have said, 'Nandini's my friend, she can play,' or asked an adult downstairs whether Nandini could join.
How might Nandini have felt going down the stairs?
Nandini probably felt hurt and rejected, especially after sharing her sparklers with Vandana.

"So you'll recommend me?" Jeevan asked, leaning into the manager's cabin.

"The team lead post is between you and Uday," said Mr Kulkarni. "Uday's strong."

Jeevan felt the old fear rise: another year stuck while Uday moved up. Uday, who'd covered for him during his father's surgery. Uday, who'd told him, over beer last month, that he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

"Sir," Jeevan heard himself say, "I just think the lead should believe in the targets. Uday's said privately he thinks they're... unrealistic."

Kulkarni's eyebrows went up. "Did he."

That evening, Jeevan's flatmate asked why he was so quiet.

"Just work."

"Did something happen?"

"Nothing. It's business. Everyone looks out for themselves." He turned the TV up. He didn't want to hear the word his mind kept offering him.

What had Uday said privately about the targets?
Uday had said he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.
What was Jeevan afraid of when he spoke to Mr Kulkarni?
He was afraid of being left behind, stuck another year while Uday moved up, and that fear overrode his loyalty.
What turning point is still available to Jeevan?
He could go back to Kulkarni and correct himself, and tell Uday honestly what he did, rather than calling it business.
How might Uday feel if he learns what Jeevan said?
Uday would likely feel shocked and betrayed, since he had supported Jeevan and shared the complaint in trust.

Dear Diary,
We got our maths test back. I got 9 out of 25. I folded it very small and pushed it inside the torn lining of my school bag.
At dinner Ritu didi asked. I said, "Ma'am hasn't given it back yet." My heart was going so fast. Didi looked at me for a long time.
Last time I got a low mark, Papa shouted for half an hour and took away cricket for a month. So now I hide. I don't even feel bad about the lie. I feel bad about the 9.
But it needs a signature by Friday.
Tonight Didi sat on my bed. "Kamal, whatever it is, I'll sit with you when you tell Mummy." I nearly cried.
Maybe tomorrow.

What did Kamal get on the maths test?
I got 9 out of 25.
Why did Kamal hide the test paper?
Kamal was afraid of being shouted at and punished again, as after the last low mark.
How could Kamal's parents help Kamal stop hiding things?
They could respond calmly to low marks and help with the maths, so telling the truth no longer feels dangerous.
How might Ritu didi feel sitting on the bed?
Ritu didi seems worried and caring, sensing the lie and gently offering to sit with Kamal while telling Mummy.

On Saturday the three couples met at Kishore's flat to plan a hill trip, and every pair disagreed about the budget. On the sofa, Zubin suggested the cheaper bus. His partner Meher rolled her eyes and said, "Wow, a bus. Truly a visionary," and the others laughed awkwardly while Zubin's face went stiff and he said nothing. Out on the balcony, Ojas snapped, "You always decide everything and never listen," and his partner Devika snapped back that he was lazy. Then Ojas took a breath. "I'm getting flooded. Ten minutes?" Afterwards he said, "I feel ignored when dates are fixed without me. Can we look at the costs together?" They sat down with a notebook and worked it out. In the kitchen, Kishore's partner Anita wanted the pricier hotel and Kishore disagreed. He touched her shoulder, softened his voice and said, "We're fine. This is only a plan. Let's find something in the middle." Later Meher glanced at Zubin, still quiet, and said, "That was unkind of me. The bus does save us a lot, and the ride was fun last time." Zubin's shoulders dropped, and he smiled a little.

Where did the three couples meet?
They met at Kishore's flat.
How did Meher's reaction to Zubin's suggestion differ from the way Ojas and Kishore handled their own disagreements?

Meher answered with sarcasm and an eye-roll, which shut Zubin down, while Ojas paused when flooded and used an I feel sentence, and Kishore stayed warm by touching Anita's shoulder and saying they were fine.
What was Zubin feeling when Meher rolled her eyes and called him a visionary?
He felt hurt and humiliated, since his face went stiff and he said nothing.
What did Meher do afterwards that begins to repair the moment?
She admitted her remark was unkind and named what was good about the bus idea, replacing mockery with appreciation and respect.

Break this passage into three bullets.

On Easter Monday, Joseph went to Gimmerton fair with some cattle; and, in the afternoon, I was busy getting up linen in the kitchen. Earnshaw sat, morose as usual, at the chimney corner, and my little mistress was beguiling an idle hour with drawing pictures on the window-panes, varying her amusement by smothered bursts of songs, and whispered ejaculations, and quick glances of annoyance and impatience in the direction of her cousin, who steadfastly smoked, and looked into the grate. At a notice that I could do with her no longer intercepting my light, she removed to the hearthstone. I bestowed little attention on her proceedings, but, presently, I heard her begin—"I've found out, Hareton, that I want—that I'm glad—that I should like you to be my cousin now, if you had not grown so cross to me, and so rough."

- On Easter Monday Joseph goes to the fair, and the narrator works on linen in the kitchen.
- The little mistress draws on the window-panes and glances impatiently at her cousin, who sits smoking.
- Told to move from the light, she tells Hareton she would like him as a cousin if he were less cross and rough.

Dusk in the village, and the lamp was lit in the courtyard. Dadi sat on the charpai with Raghav beside her while his cousin Hemant dozed against the wall. She sang one short evening prayer, line by line, and Raghav repeated it, tripping over the long words. Her eyes shone in the lamplight. "Again," she said softly, and he did it again. That night he lay awake, wondering what one line meant. Next morning he asked her. Dadi laughed. "I'm glad you asked. I'll tell you what my mother told me, and then you can think about it yourself."

Who dozed against the wall while Dadi taught the prayer?
His cousin Hemant dozed against the wall.
What was Raghav feeling as he repeated the prayer, and what is the evidence?
He seemed to feel loved and settled: he kept repeating the line even when tripping over words, and he cared enough to wonder about its meaning afterwards.
What could Raghav do with his questions about the prayer?
Keep taking the prayer in respectfully and ask Dadi about it when he can, as he did next morning.
How might Dadi feel when Raghav asks about a line?
She seems glad, since she laughed and said she was glad he asked, so she probably sees questions as part of learning, not as disrespect.

Dear Pema,
You asked about my "mixing" experiment with the two rival sections in Class 9. Honestly, the first try was a disaster.
I put 9A and 9B together in one room for a free period, hoping they'd get along. No task. No roles. 9A sat on one side, 9B on the other. By the end, there were insults about "backbenchers" and "toppers", and one fight.
I felt terrible. I'd made it worse.
Then I read about working together as equals. Next time, I made mixed pairs for the inter-house quiz, with the principal backing it and a real prize. Each pair needed both people's knowledge.
Last week, a 9A girl and a 9B boy won together and hugged.
Ayesha

What were the insults about in the first try?
About "backbenchers" and "toppers".
How did Ayesha feel after the first experiment?
Ayesha felt terrible, having made the rivalry worse.
What made the second attempt work?
Mixed pairs with equal roles, a shared goal in the quiz, a real prize and the principal's backing.
How might the students in the winning pair feel about each other now?
They probably feel closer and proud, having won together and hugged.

Frank bakes two trays of cookies per day, for 6 days. Frank eats one cookie each day to make sure they taste good. Ted comes over on the sixth day and eats 4 cookies. If each tray makes 12 cookies, how many cookies are left when Ted leaves?

Frank bakes 2 * 12 = 24 cookies per day.
Frank bakes a total of 24 * 6 = 144 cookies.
Frank eats 1 * 6 = 6 cookies.
After Ted leaves, there are 144 - 6 - 4 = 134
The answer is 134.

'Nice post,' Dhruv said, sliding his phone across the canteen table. 'Five hundred likes for a sunset.'
'Five hundred and twelve,' Anirban said, grinning.
'You looked so happy in the pic.'
'I was.'
'You were panicking about the physics test five minutes before. I was there.'
Anirban's grin stayed, but he started folding his napkin into smaller and smaller squares. 'So?'
'So I don't know which you is real sometimes.'
'That's the point, na. Nobody wants the real one.'
'I might.'
Anirban stopped folding. 'I'm not sure about anything right now. Marks, college, what I'm even good at.' He looked up fast. 'Don't make it a thing.'
'Not a thing,' Dhruv said. 'Eat your samosa. Then tell me more.'

How many likes did the sunset post get?
Five hundred and twelve.
What does Anirban's napkin-folding suggest?
It suggests Anirban felt uneasy and exposed when Dhruv pointed out the gap between the post and reality.
What did Dhruv do well in responding?
He noticed gently, said he might want the real Anirban, and kept it low-key, so Anirban felt safe enough to share more.
What is it like for Dhruv to see the gap between the post and the real Anirban?
Dhruv feels unsure which Anirban is real and wants to be let in, not just shown the happy picture.

In my first year as team lead, I thought Ojas was just slack. Every estimate he gave me was cheerful and wrong: "two days," then five; "this week," then next. I started to feel irritated whenever he spoke in stand-up. Then one Sunday I went through my own old diary from when I was a developer. My estimates were exactly the same, cheerful and wrong. I hadn't been lazy then. I'd just pictured the easy path every time. So on Monday I didn't lecture Ojas. I made a small sheet for the whole team: your guess, the real time, and a column for what happened. After two months we could all see our average slip. Now we plan with it. Ojas told me later, "Shankar, I thought you hated me in March." I didn't. I just hadn't recognised myself.

What columns did the team's sheet have?
Your guess, the real time, and what happened.
What was Shankar feeling toward Ojas at first?
Shankar felt irritated, thinking Ojas was slack, before recognising the same cheerful mistakes in the old diary.
Why did the sheet work better than a lecture?
It showed the whole team their own average slip, turning a blame problem into a shared pattern they could plan with.
How had Ojas felt in March?
Ojas thought Shankar hated him, so he probably felt anxious and judged.

Michael is baking a cake and needs 6 cups of flour. The only measuring cup he has is the 1/4 cup. He has an 8 cup bag of flour and realizes it would be faster to measure the flour he doesn't need, take it out of the bag, and then dump the rest of the bag into the bowl. How many scoops should he remove?

He needs to remove 2 cups of flour because 8 minus 6 equals 2.
He needs to use 8 scoops because 2 divided by .25 equals 8
The answer is 8.
Guess the length of your maths book in cm. Then measure it.

Answer: Answers will vary; a notebook is often about 25 cm long.

First estimate: "About how many finger widths (cm)?" Write the guess. Then measure from 0. Compare: was the guess close? Estimating many times makes a child good at it. Praise sensible guesses, not just exact ones.

Thursday

Dear Diary,
A new boy called Lokesh joined our class today. He walks with crutches. At break everyone stared, and Manav said loudly, "What's wrong with your legs?" Lokesh went red and looked at his shoes.
Mrs. Fernandes heard. She said, "Manav, if you're curious, you can ask Lokesh kindly if he'd like to tell you. And nothing is wrong with him. His body just works in its own way." Then she started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.
Lokesh was really good at it. I didn't talk to him today, and I feel a bit bad about that. Tomorrow I'm saving him a seat at lunch.

Afreen

What game did Mrs. Fernandes start?
She started a game of pass-the-ball in a circle so everyone could play.
How does Afreen feel about not talking to Lokesh?
Afreen feels a bit guilty about it and plans to make up for it by saving him a seat at lunch.
How did Mrs. Fernandes turn the moment around?
She showed Manav a kind way to be curious, said difference is not something wrong, and chose a game that included Lokesh.
What was it like for Lokesh when Manav asked about his legs?
It was embarrassing for him, which is why he went red and looked at his shoes.

The railway station was loud and packed, and Imran's train to Pune was due in five minutes. He'd flown in from London two days ago and couldn't find the platform. He asked a porter, "Platform four for Pune?" The porter wobbled his head from side to side and walked off. Imran froze. Was that a no? Parveen, his cousin, caught up. "Head wobble. Could be yes, I heard you, or okay. Ask him with a word." Imran ran after the porter. "So it's platform four, yes?" "Haan, four, four," said the porter, pointing. They made it on with a minute to spare.

Where was Imran's train going?
His train was going to Pune.
What was Imran feeling when the porter wobbled his head and walked away?
He was confused and anxious because time was short and he couldn't tell yes from no. He froze, which shows how unsure he was.
What worked when the gesture was unclear?
Imran asked the porter again with clear words, so the meaning was confirmed. Parveen's explanation helped him see the wobble wasn't a clear no.
How does Parveen see the head wobble differently from Imran?
Parveen grew up with it and knows it can mean yes, I heard you or okay. Imran, new to India, first thought it might be no.

Read this:

Note from the class teacher, first week.
On his first morning Sachin stood by the window and watched the others, twisting the hem of his shirt. His eyes kept going to Yash, who was lining up shells on the nature table. Twice Sachin took a step towards the table and stopped.
At activity time I paired the children to wash the paint pots. I put Sachin with Yash. They filled the tub together and Yash showed him how to squeeze the brush. By lunch they were sitting side by side. I will keep using pair jobs this week.

What was Yash lining up on the nature table?
He was lining up shells.
What was Sachin feeling as he stood by the window?
He felt shy but curious about the other children: he twisted his shirt hem, watched Yash and stepped towards the table twice before stopping.
Why did the teacher's pair job work well?
Washing paint pots together gave Sachin and Yash an easy reason to talk, so a friendship could start without Sachin having to walk up alone.
How might Yash see the new boy at the wash tub?
Yash probably sees a helper to show things to, since he shows Sachin how to squeeze the brush and later sits with him.

Read this:

Dear Vinita didi,
Remember in June when Rhea and I didn't talk for a whole month because I kept arguing that the scooty dent wasn't really my fault? You said next time, try just saying sorry and see what happens. I tried it this week.
I posted a group photo from the picnic where Kavin had his eyes half shut and food on his shirt. He messaged me, really upset. My first reply was already typed: "It's just a photo, chill." I deleted it. I wrote: "You're right, I should have asked. Sorry. I've taken it down."
He called me something rude in his first message, and I did tell him that part wasn't okay. But I didn't pretend the photo was his fault.
By evening he sent a funny sticker and we were normal again. One day instead of one month!
Love,
Ira

What reply had Ira typed before deleting it?
“It's just a photo, chill.”
How did Ira feel about how quickly things recovered with Kavin?
Ira felt relieved and pleased, even surprised, that a plain sorry fixed things in one day instead of one month.
How did Ira balance owning the mistake with not taking all the blame?
Ira apologised plainly and took the photo down, but also told Kavin his rude word wasn't okay, taking responsibility without accepting blame that wasn't Ira's.
How might Kavin have felt if he had received the first reply?
Kavin would likely have felt dismissed and more hurt, and the quarrel might have dragged on like the month with Rhea.
Is "Sorry to bother you" polite when I ask my teacher a question after class?

Yes, it is polite and common. It shows you respect the other person's time. You can also say "Excuse me, do you have a minute?"
Example: Sorry to bother you, Sir, but could you explain this question again?

Read this:

It was past ten and raining hard, and Devika's phone had died at eight. When she came in dripping, Papa was standing by the door with his own phone in his hand.
"Where were you? I called eleven times."
"At Aisha's. We did the chemistry project. Her mother made pasta." Every word was true.
She didn't say that at six they had all gone to Nikhil's birthday party two lanes away, with loud music and older boys she didn't know.
Her father, Farhan, sighed. "Okay. Charge your phone next time."
In her room Devika told herself she hadn't lied. But she felt hot all over. Papa had been scared for two hours, and he still didn't know where she had actually been when he was calling.
She sat on the bed for a long time. Then she went back out to the kitchen. "Papa, there's more. After Aisha's, we went to a party."

How many times had Papa called?
Eleven times.
Why did Devika feel hot all over in her room?
Devika felt guilty and uneasy, knowing every word was true but that Papa had still been misled about where she was.
What did Devika do that turned it around?
She went back to the kitchen and told Papa about the party after Aisha's, adding the missing part herself.
What had those two hours been like for Farhan?
Farhan was scared, calling eleven times with no answer, and still didn't know where his daughter had really been.

Read this:

Beatriz was riding her moped home from the swimming pool in Coimbra when a police officer raised a hand and waved her to the kerb. Her heart thumped so hard she could hear it inside her helmet. "Documents, please." Her fingers shook as she unzipped the pocket where her father insisted she keep her licence and insurance card. She took off her helmet, said "Good evening," and handed them over. The officer checked them with a torch. "Your rear light is out. Get it fixed this week." Beatriz nodded. "Can I call my dad?" "Of course." Sami, her father, answered on the first ring and was there in ten minutes with a spare bulb. The officer watched them fit it and said, "Safe ride home." Beatriz sat on the kerb a moment, until her hands stopped shaking.

What did the officer say was wrong with the moped?
The rear light was out.
What was Beatriz feeling when she was waved to the kerb?
Beatriz was nervous and scared; her heart thumped and her fingers shook.
What did Beatriz do that made the stop go smoothly?
She stayed polite, took off her helmet, had her documents ready and asked to call her dad.
How might the officer have seen the stop?
To the officer it was probably a routine check, and Beatriz's calm cooperation made it easy to end kindly with "Safe ride home."
Dost ka music bahut tez hai. Kaise bolun ki thoda kam karo?
Say: "Could you turn the music down a little, please?"

Read this:

Jasleen: did you hear my voice in class today 😅
Rajni: which bit
Jasleen: the part that went squeak. I wanted to disappear
Rajni: honestly I didn't notice
Jasleen: liar
Rajni: ok I noticed, but nobody cared. Mr. Khan was more interested in the board
Jasleen: it's so embarrassing
Rajni: it's just puberty, not you being nervous
Jasleen: true. maybe I'll do a squeak on purpose next time
Rajni: lol please do
Jasleen: at least then it's my joke 🙂
Rajni: exactly. see you at lunch

Who was more interested in the board?
Mr. Khan was more interested in the board.
What was Jasleen feeling about the squeak, and how did that change?
Jasleen was embarrassed and wanted to disappear. After Rajni's reassurance, Jasleen could joke about it.
What could Jasleen do next time the voice cracks?
Laugh it off or make a joke instead of going silent. It is a physical change that settles.
How does Rajni see Jasleen's crack?
Rajni noticed but thought nobody cared and sees it as puberty, not nerves. Rajni reassures and jokes with Jasleen.

Read this:

I'm Reena, and in Class 10 I made a bet I still get teased about. Our house, Blue, had lost seven football matches in a row in the inter-house league. Seven! I told Yusuf, "Law of averages. Blue wins the eighth. It's due."
Yusuf said the eighth match didn't know about the other seven. I said a streak that long had to break, and I bet him a week of carrying his school bag up four floors.
Blue lost 3–0. Our goalkeeper had a sprained wrist, and Red had two players from the district team. The old losses meant nothing; only who was on the field that day did.
I carried that bag for five days. On day three Yusuf grinned. "Bet Blue wins the ninth?" I said no. I had finally noticed I'd been counting the wrong thing.

What did Reena bet Yusuf?
A week of carrying Yusuf's school bag up four floors.
How did Reena feel about the eighth match, and why?
Reena felt confident that Blue was due to win, because seven losses seemed too long a run, confident enough to bet a week of carrying Yusuf's bag.
What turning point came for Reena, and what was a better way to judge the next match?
Turning down Yusuf's bet on the ninth match; looking at who was actually on the field, like the injured goalkeeper, says far more than the old streak.
How might Yusuf see the week of bag carrying?
Yusuf probably enjoys winning and teasing, but the offer on day three also looks like a test of whether Reena has learned anything.
Give three reminders for keeping a desk tidy, numbered, each under eight words.

1. Put pens back in the box.
2. Stack your books neatly.
3. Throw away old paper.
The tap in our kitchen drips all night and I can hear it from my room.
A drip is annoying and it wastes water. Does it stop when you tighten the handle fully?
No, it keeps dripping.
Then the washer inside may be worn. That's a small job for a plumber or an adult who knows how to do it. Meanwhile, put a cloth or a small bowl under the tap to muffle the sound.
Can I tell my parents?
Yes, ask them to call someone. A quick fix now saves water and your sleep.

In the library café at the university in Cape Town, Gabriel opened the end-of-semester course survey. Statistics 201. His cursor hovered over the stars. The last three weeks: Dr Mokoena rushing through the final chapters, two lectures cancelled, a test set the day after the last class. "One star," he muttered. Thabo, eating a pie across the table, peered at the screen. "Remember March? She stayed after class every Thursday to help us with the project. You said it was the first time stats made sense." Gabriel paused. He did remember. The worked examples, the jokes about coin tosses, his first A. "So maybe three?" "Maybe judge the whole semester, not the last month," Thabo said. Gabriel scrolled back through his notes from February, then clicked four stars and wrote a comment about the rushed ending.

What did Dr Mokoena do every Thursday in March?
She stayed after class to help with the project.
Why did Gabriel want to give one star at first?
Gabriel felt irritated and stressed by the rushed final weeks, and that recent frustration dominated his memory of the whole course.
What did Gabriel do that made the rating fairer?
He scrolled back through his notes from February, remembered the good months, gave four stars, and wrote a specific comment about the rushed ending.
How might Dr Mokoena feel reading a one-star rating compared with the final one?
A one-star rating might leave her discouraged about months of extra help; the fairer one tells her what worked and what to fix.

Read this:

Dear Pooja,
You asked why I sounded odd on the phone. Here it is. The rowing club's welcome week was supposed to be fun. On the first night the seniors made us stand in the hall and shout that we were nobodies. On the second we carried their bags and sang in the dining hall while they filmed. On the third they wanted us to do a dare I knew was unsafe. I wanted so badly to belong that I nearly did. Instead I said no and walked out. On Friday I went to the faculty adviser. She listened, said it wasn't my fault, and called both captains in that same afternoon. I'm still shaky, and a few first-years won't talk to me. But two of them came to my room yesterday.
Asif

What did the seniors make the newcomers do on the first night?
The seniors made them stand in the hall and shout that they were nobodies.
Why did Asif say, “I wanted so badly to belong that I nearly did”?
Asif felt a strong pull to belong and almost gave in to a dare, even though Asif knew it was unsafe.
What did the faculty adviser do that same afternoon?
The faculty adviser listened, told Asif it was not Asif's fault and called both captains in that afternoon.
What might the two first-years who came to Asif's room yesterday have been feeling?
They may have felt relieved and a little ashamed, and may have wanted Asif's company after seeing Asif refuse.

Is it "priviledge" or "privilege"?
What does the word "disobedience" mean?

1. It is "privilege", with no "d". It ends in "-lege".
2. "Disobedience" is a noun. It means the refusal to obey.

Hello! Could you answer these?
My book uses the word "supposition". What does it mean?
Why do tall buildings have lifts?
Check my English: "We must to leave now."

1. Supposition is a noun that means something that is believed to be true without proof.
2. Lifts carry people and heavy things up many floors. Because climbing so many stairs is hard, especially for old people or anyone with heavy bags.
3. Corrected: We must leave now. After "must", use the base verb without "to".

Monday: Omkar noticed brown tips on the curry-leaf plant by the front door. His sister Avni said, "It's thirsty." Omkar wasn't sure. He wrote three questions on a sticky note: Water? Sun? Insects?
Wednesday: After school he checked the soil. Moist, not dry. He watched the pot at noon: sun for only an hour. That left one question. He borrowed Papa's reading glasses and a torch and peered at the stem. Ants, dozens of them, marching up to tiny white spots under the leaves.
Saturday: He had washed the stem with water every day and drawn a ring of chalk round the pot. The ants were gone. The new leaves came out plain green. Avni admitted, "Okay, not thirsty."

What three questions did Omkar write?
Water? Sun? Insects?
Why didn't Omkar just water the plant?
He felt unsure Avni was right and wanted to check each possible cause first.
What else could Omkar do if the ants come back?
Keep watching the stem and ask at a nursery about the white spots, since the ants may be visiting them.
How does Avni's view change?
Avni first says the plant is thirsty, and by Saturday admits it wasn't.

metadata.subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]

Read this:

Hi, I'm Dev, and yes, the turning point was a physics test. I got 18 out of 50, and I had read that chapter three times. I sat there and asked myself, if this isn't working, what could be different?
Then I noticed something. When I read, everything felt easy. When I tried an actual question, I couldn't even start. So reading wasn't teaching me to remember.
That night I read for twenty minutes, closed the book and wrote what I could recall. The gaps were obvious. I did practice questions for the gaps.
Next test I got 34. Mrs Kulkarni asked what had changed, and I said, I stopped rereading and started recalling. She looked surprised, and pleased.

How many marks did Dev get in the physics test?
Dev got 18 out of 50.
What did Dev feel about the low mark that made Dev ask what could be different?
Dev felt puzzled and dissatisfied, since reading the chapter three times had not worked.
What could Dev try next if recalling from memory stopped helping?
Dev could ask Mrs Kulkarni which kinds of questions to practise, because a new signal of no progress would call for another change.
How does Mrs Kulkarni see the change in Dev's marks?
Mrs Kulkarni looked surprised and pleased when she asked what had changed and heard about the switch to recalling.

metadata.subtype: Approach: notices no progress and asks what could be different [Revision]

Read this:

Last December I told everyone the chemistry syllabus was easy. I'm Vaibhav, and I'd read the textbook once and every page looked familiar. Reactions, formulas, diagrams: I nodded at all of them. My sister Yamini kept writing answers from memory on a whiteboard, and I laughed at her. "Why practise what you already know?" Then the prelim paper asked me to write the full equation for an experiment. I stared at the blank line. I could picture the page, even the colour of the heading, but nothing came out. I got 41. The page had felt known because I'd seen it, not because I could produce it. Yamini got 88. She didn't say a word, which was worse.

What did Vaibhav score in the chemistry prelim?
Vaibhav got 41.
Why did the syllabus feel easy to Vaibhav?
Vaibhav felt confident because every page looked familiar after one reading, and that recognition felt like knowing. Vaibhav never tested whether the answers could be written from memory.
What could Vaibhav borrow from Yamini's method?
Close the book and write answers from memory, like Yamini on the whiteboard; whatever can't be recalled shows exactly what still needs revising.
How might Yamini have felt when Vaibhav laughed at her whiteboard practice?
Yamini may have felt a little hurt or annoyed but kept to her method, and her 88 later showed that recalling from memory was worth the effort.

As we talked, we neared a door that opened on the road; and my young lady, lightening into sunshine again, climbed up and seated herself on the top of the wall, reaching over to gather some hips that bloomed scarlet on the summit branches of the wild-rose trees shadowing the highway side: the lower fruit had disappeared, but only birds could touch the upper, except from Cathy's present station. In stretching to pull them, her hat fell off; and as the door was locked, she proposed scrambling down to recover it. I bid her be cautious lest she got a fall, and she nimbly disappeared. But the return was no such easy matter: the stones were smooth and neatly cemented, and the rosebushes and blackberry stragglers could yield no assistance in re-ascending. I, like a fool, didn't recollect that, till I heard her laughing and exclaiming—"Ellen! you'll have to fetch the key, or else I must run round to the porter's lodge. I can't scale the ramparts on this side!"

For a child, summarize this text in three sentences.

The narrator and the young lady stop at a door on the road, and she climbs onto the wall to pick red rose hips. Her hat falls off, and she climbs down to get it but cannot climb back. She laughs and asks the narrator, Ellen, to fetch the key, or she must run to the porter's lodge.
Now you try: 11 x 9 and 11 x 11
The answers are: 99; 121.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Monday. Indu asked to see me privately. She had seen her close friend Payal send unkind messages about a new girl to a group chat. Indu felt torn: Payal is her friend, and she did not want to be the one who told. That afternoon, on the way to the bus, she spoke to Payal first. Payal called it a joke.
On Thursday Indu came back. The messages had continued and the new girl had stopped coming to lunch. Indu said, "Being loyal to Payal can't mean staying quiet about this." She gave me the dates and what she had seen.
I thanked her, then spoke with the new girl's family and with Payal separately, without naming Indu. I will follow up with both girls next week.
Mr. Bose

Where did Indu speak to Payal?
She spoke to Payal on the way to the bus.
Why did Indu feel torn?
Payal is her friend and she did not want to be the one who told, yet the messages were hurting the new girl.
What order of steps worked for Indu, and what could she do if things continue?
She talked to Payal first and, when the harm continued, told a trusted adult with dates; she could keep checking on the new girl.
How might the new girl have experienced the messages?
She stopped coming to lunch, which suggests she felt hurt and wanted to avoid other students.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Friday. Payal, Class 10, came to my room at lunch with her phone in her hand. She showed me a friend's reply, "fine." and asked, "Isn't that angry? She used to write 'fine!!' with a heart." Payal had not eaten. She said she had rewritten her own message four times.
I asked what else she knew about her friend's week, and Payal said there was a maths test. We talked about how tone is guessed when there is no voice. I suggested she send one open question, and she wrote, "Are we okay? You seemed quiet." Then she ate her lunch. The reply came before the bell: "just tired, come sit with me? 🙂"
Vinita, school counsellor

What word did Payal's friend send in the reply she showed the counsellor?
The friend's reply said "fine." with a full stop.
What might Payal have been worrying about when she rewrote her message four times?
Payal was probably anxious that the friend was upset with her. Not eating lunch and rewriting the message show how much the short reply weighed on her.
What did Vinita do to help Payal move from guessing to checking?
Vinita asked what Payal knew about the friend's week, talked about how tone is guessed in text, and suggested one open question. Payal sent it and got a warm answer.
What was the friend probably going through when the reply "fine." was sent?
The friend was probably tired, with a maths test that week, and wrote a short word without thinking about tone. The friend then invited Payal to sit together.

Read this:

At the Dussehra fair in their small town, Rukmini wore her new kurta, the one her mother had stitched in green cotton. She'd been proud of it all week.
Then Hansa's cousin arrived from Indore in a shiny lehenga with mirror work. Everyone turned.
Rukmini looked down at her green cotton. Suddenly it looked plain, like a school uniform. She pulled her dupatta over it.
On the bus home, Hansa said, "Your kurta's so nice. Mine is from last year."
Rukmini blinked. She hadn't even looked at Hansa's clothes all evening. She had only looked at the cousin.
"Your Amma sewed it?" Hansa asked. "Lucky."

What colour was Rukmini's kurta?
It was green cotton.
Why did Rukmini pull her dupatta over her kurta?
She suddenly felt embarrassed and plain after comparing it with the cousin's shiny lehenga.
What could Rukmini notice to feel better at the next fair?
She could look at the whole group, not just the one person a step ahead, and remember she was proud of the kurta all week.
How does Hansa see Rukmini's kurta?
Hansa sees it as lovely and envies that Rukmini's Amma sewed it, which shows how comparison depends on who you look at.
Please explain "wretched".

Wretched means very unhappy, or very bad and poor in quality. It is an adjective.
Example: After the long argument, Tom felt wretched all evening.

Read this:

Chetan, you think the Americans are cold because your manager didn't come to your father's funeral? Let me tell you about my years in Chicago.
I was twenty-five, fresh from Kanpur. My landlady was eighty and lived alone. Her son lived three streets away and visited on Sundays, with a pie. I was horrified. "Three streets!" I told my mother on the phone. "He should live with her!"
One winter, the landlady fell on the ice. I carried her groceries for weeks. One evening she told me, "My son wanted me to move in. I refused. I raised three children in that kitchen. Now it's my kitchen. I like my freedom."
I didn't understand then. I do now. When my own sons tried to decide everything for me after my surgery, I remembered her.
So, Chetan, maybe it's lonelier there. But it's also freer. Suraj Nana is telling you: both have a price.

How often did the landlady's son visit?
Her son visited on Sundays, with a pie.
How did Suraj feel when he first saw the landlady living alone?
Suraj felt horrified, believing her son should live with her.
What was the turning point in Suraj's story?
When the landlady explained that she refused to move in with her son because she valued her freedom, Suraj began to understand.
How did the landlady see her own life?
She saw it as free and hers, proud of her kitchen and her independence rather than lonely.
Please write a notice, about 50 words, announcing a book fair in the school hall from Wednesday to Friday. It is from the Library Committee.

NOTICE
Book Fair
The school is holding a book fair in the school hall from Wednesday to Friday. Students are welcome to visit and look at the books. Come, browse and discover your next favourite read. Let us celebrate the joy of reading together.
Library Committee

At the residential school in Shillong, evening study hour was nearly over when Rekha, fifteen, slid a folded note across the hostel common room to her cousin Charu. It said: "Can we talk? I'm not okay."
They sat on the back steps. Rekha's words came slowly. She hadn't been sleeping, she'd stopped calling home, and most nights she cried in the bathroom because she felt she didn't belong here. "I didn't want anyone to know," she said.
Charu squeezed her hand. "I'm really glad you told me. Let's tell Mrs Lyngdoh too, tonight."
Mrs Lyngdoh, the housemother, was still in her office. She put down her pen, listened to all of it and said, "Thank you for trusting us. This is not something you should hold alone." She rang Rekha's parents while the cousins sat beside her, and booked Rekha in with the school counsellor for the next morning.

What did Rekha's note to Charu say?
"Can we talk? I'm not okay."
What was Rekha feeling that made her cry in the bathroom most nights?
She felt she didn't belong at the school and was lonely and worn out, and she didn't want anyone to know.
What did Charu choose to do after listening, and why was it a good step?
Charu suggested telling Mrs Lyngdoh that same night, which brought in an adult who called Rekha's parents and arranged the counsellor.
How might Rekha's parents feel after Mrs Lyngdoh's call?
They would likely be worried to hear she had been struggling, but relieved that she reached out and that the school was already supporting her.

Read this:

I'm Charu, and I was always picked last for throwball in Class 5.
Every time, I'd stand there while the names were called. Rekha, Divya, Seema... Charu. Everyone would look at me. I'd make a joke, like, “Saving the best for last!” and everyone laughed. Then I'd go home and not want to eat.
One day Ankita became captain. She looked at the line and said, “Charu first. You never drop a throw.”
I didn't even move for a second.
I did drop one throw that day, but Ankita just shouted, “Next one!” I played better than I had all year.
I still remember that day more than any match we won.

What sport was Charu always picked last for?
Throwball.
How did Charu feel after the jokes when getting home?
Charu felt hurt and sad, not wanting to eat, even after laughing it off in front of everyone.
What did Ankita do that made such a difference?
Ankita picked Charu first, warmly, and named a strength, and stayed kind after a mistake, which undid much of the hurt.
How might the others have seen Charu's jokes?
They probably thought Charu didn't mind, since Charu made them laugh, not realising the hurt underneath.

Read this:

Tushar, you want to know why I changed my mind about Professor Iyer? Let me, Indu, tell you the whole embarrassing thing. First year, I thought he was a god. I sat in the front row, I read every paper he'd written, I told my parents I wanted to be exactly like him. Then in second year, I gave a presentation and he said, in front of everyone, "This is undergraduate thinking." And that was it. For a month, I told anyone who'd listen that he was arrogant, that his papers were outdated, that he didn't care about students. I skipped his classes. And then one evening, I saw him in the library helping a first-year for an hour. Patient. Kind. And I thought: he's both. Brilliant and sometimes harsh. I'd put him so high that one bad sentence knocked him all the way down.

What did Professor Iyer say about Indu's presentation?
"This is undergraduate thinking."
Why did Indu turn so bitter after one comment?
Indu had idealised the professor so completely that one harsh remark felt like a betrayal, and the hurt swung Indu to the opposite extreme.
What helped Indu see Professor Iyer more fairly?
Seeing him patiently help a first-year in the library, which showed he was both brilliant and sometimes harsh.
How might Professor Iyer have noticed Indu's change?
He may have noticed Indu skipping classes, perhaps puzzled or concerned about why.

Rewrite this extract as a two-sentence summary.

I'm Chinmay. I was at Anirban's house during Durga Puja when he got into it with his grandmother about karma. He'd been reading about atheism and said, "Thamma, there's no proof of past lives." I braced for a fight. She just put down her tea. "Then how do you explain why good people suffer?" Anirban started to argue, then stopped. He asked her instead, "What does karma mean to you, really?" She talked for twenty minutes, about her own mother, about fairness over lifetimes. He listened without interrupting. Then he explained why he doubted it, calmly, and she listened too. Nobody changed their mind. But when I left, they were still talking, and she was laughing. I don't know what he was thinking. But he looked curious, not smug.

During Durga Puja, Chinmay sees Anirban tell his grandmother there is no proof of past lives, and she asks why good people suffer. Anirban listens as she explains karma, then calmly shares his doubts; nobody changes their mind, but they keep talking and she laughs.
Are tickets for the new concert tour on sale yet?
Ticket sales are not something I can check, so I'm not sure. The organiser's official website will say when and where tickets are sold.
Name three parts of the day from earliest to latest, in lowercase, one per line.

morning
afternoon
evening

Monday. Ramesh forgot to return Yamini's notes before her exam, and she had to borrow a classmate's at the last minute. "I'm useless," he told the ceiling that night. The words felt heavy and no use to anyone.
Thursday. In the hostel washroom mirror he tried a different sentence, aloud: "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect." It felt odd. Then he went to find Yamini. "I was careless and it cost you. I'm sorry. Here are the notes and a set of my own copies." She nodded. "Thanks for saying it straight."
Two weeks later. Ramesh caught himself about to be late again with a borrowed book and set a phone reminder instead of just feeling bad about it.

Whose notes did Ramesh forget to return before the exam?
Yamini's notes.
Why did Ramesh say the new sentence to the mirror?
He wanted to stop calling himself useless, and to treat himself as someone worth respect while still owning the mistake.
What made Ramesh's self-kindness real accountability rather than an excuse?
He apologised plainly, brought the notes and copies, and later set a reminder so the mistake would not repeat.
How might Yamini have felt when Ramesh apologised plainly?
Probably relieved and respected, since she thanked him for saying it straight.

Is the guess too many, too few or exact?
a) guess 8, count 5
b) guess 3, count 6
c) guess 7, count 7

a) too many
b) too few
c) exact

"They picked the other candidate." Jomon dropped his bag by the door. "Final round. I was so sure."
Arohi muted the TV. "Chetta. Come, sit."
"Third final round this year, Arohi. Third."
"Did they say why?"
"Some line about 'a stronger fit'."
"Did you ask them what that meant?"
He stared at her. "You can ask?"
"Of course. Politely. My friend Shilpa did, and the recruiter told her exactly which answer lost it."
Jomon rubbed his eyes. "What if they say I was terrible?"

Dorothy is 15 years old and wants to go to a museum with her family. Her family consists of her, her younger brother, her parents, and her grandfather. The regular ticket cost is $10. People 18 years old or younger have a discount of 30%. How much money will Dorothy have after this trip, when she currently has $70?

The discount per one ticket is 10 * 30/100 = $3.
So Dorothy's and her brother's tickets are cheaper by 2 * 3 = $6.
Her family consists of 5 people, so the ticket cost stands at 5 * 10 = $50.
Including the discount will lower the price to 50 - 6 = $44 in total.
Dorothy will be left with 70 - 44 = $26.
The answer is 26.

Arnab sits at the desk next to mine in the government office in Kolkata. Every morning he touches the small photo of his family deity before switching on his computer. He stayed late every evening for six weeks, working through old papers. When I asked, half teasing, why he bothered if fate would decide, he smiled. "Fate decides the result. I decide the effort. Both are my dharma." I didn't know what to say. I'd always thought believing in destiny meant sitting back. When the results came, he passed. He touched the photo again, same as always. I'm Tanuja, and I've started thinking about my own beliefs differently.

messages.content: A sugarcane stick is 24 cm long. Dada cuts it into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece? What fraction of the stick is one piece?

Answer: Each piece is 3 cm (24 / 8 = 3). One piece is 1/8 (one eighth).

Cut in half: 12 cm. Half again: 6 cm (quarters). Half again: 3 cm (eighths). Halving three times makes 8 equal parts. 8 pieces x 3 cm = 24 cm, so the answer checks.

Leela, you asked on your channel how I found out music was ruining my studying. So here's Ujjwal's little experiment.
I always had songs on while doing physics numericals. I was sure it helped me focus. Then my cousin asked, "How do you know?" And I didn't.
So for two weeks I did an experiment. Every evening, fifteen numericals of the same type, same desk, same time after dinner. One day with music, the next day without. Only one thing changed. I timed myself and wrote the score in a table on the last page of my notebook.
After fourteen days: with music, about eleven right out of fifteen. Without music, about thirteen. And I finished faster in silence, most days.
I'm not saying music is bad for everyone. It was just one person, two weeks. But for me, for physics, silence wins.

Answer: 3.2 x 10^5 + 4.5 x 10^4 = 3.65 x 10^5; 6 x 10^-^3 - 8 x 10^-^4 = 5.2 x 10^-^3.

We may only add the front numbers when the powers of 10 are the SAME (like adding 3 tens and 4 tens). Rewrite 3.2 x 10^5 as 32 x 10^4. Then 32 x 10^4 + 4.5 x 10^4 = 36.5 x 10^4 = 3.65 x 10^5. For the second, 6 x 10^-^3 = 60 x 10^-^4, and 60 x 10^-^4 - 8 x 10^-^4 = 52 x 10^-^4 = 5.2 x 10^-^3. Check with ordinary numbers: 320,000 + 45,000 = 365,000 and 0.006 - 0.0008 = 0.0052. Common mistake: 3.2 + 4.5 = 7.7, giving 7.7 x 10^9 or 7.7 x 10^5.

Lex is picking apples in his apple orchard when he notices some of the apples have bruises and some have worms. He wants to save the bruised apples to make applesauce, throw the wormy apples away, and keep the unbruised apples to eat raw. By his count, a fifth of the apples have worms and nine more than one fifth are bruised. He picked 85 apples. How many apples will he have left to eat raw?

A fifth of the apples have worms, so Lex has to throw 85 / 5 = 17 apples away.
Nine more have bruises than worms, so Lex has 17 + 9 = 26 apples for applesauce.
He picked 85 apples, so Lex has 85 - 26 - 17 = 42 apples left to eat raw.
The answer is 42.

Advisor's note. Tanuja came to my office on Wednesday, still shaking. A traffic official had fined her for a parking violation at a spot with no sign, and had brushed off her questions. Her friend Zeenat came with her. Tanuja said she wanted to go back and shout at the official until they understood how unfair it was. Her fists were tight and she kept saying, "They just don't care." I let her say it all. Then we looked at what she had: Zeenat's photos of the bare wall, the receipt, the time. I helped her write a short, plain complaint to the city office, and they filed it together that afternoon. Tanuja left less furious, with something to do. I will ask her next week what reply has come.

Who came with Tanuja to the advisor's office?
Zeenat came with her.
What did Tanuja want to do before the advisor helped her?
She wanted to go back and shout at the official, feeling furious and helpless that they didn't care.
What made the complaint stronger?
It included Zeenat's photos of the bare wall, the receipt and the time, and it was written plainly and calmly.
How might the official have seen the fine and Tanuja's questions?
The official may have seen it as routine work and not as unfair, so shouting would probably have made the situation worse.

At the school counsellor's office in Gangtok, Disha sat twisting her dupatta. "It's probably nothing," she said. "I just wanted to check."

For two months she had chatted with Pema on a drawing forum. Pema said she was sixteen, from the other side of town, and loved the same comics. Disha liked her a lot. She'd been curious to meet her for weeks.

Then Pema had written, "Let's meet at the mall on Saturday. Just us. Don't tell your parents, they'll make it weird." And when Disha suggested a video call first, Pema said her camera was broken.

"That's what made me feel strange," Disha said. "If she's a real friend, why the secret?"

The counsellor nodded. "You noticed exactly the right thing. Wanting to meet a friend is normal. Being told to hide it isn't."

With Disha's agreement, the counsellor called her mother during the lunch break. That afternoon, at home, Disha and her mother blocked the account together and reported it to the forum.

What reason did Pema give for not doing a video call?
Pema said her camera was broken.
What was Disha feeling as she sat in the counsellor's office?
Disha felt uneasy and unsure, twisting her dupatta, worried that something was wrong with Pema's request.
What did Disha do that was wise?
Disha stepped back when Pema pushed for secrecy, asked the counsellor, and let her mother be called so they could block and report the account.
How does the counsellor see Disha's curiosity?
The counsellor sees wanting to meet a friend as normal, but sees the demand for secrecy as the real warning sign.

Before I signed anything in Pune, I took a Friday off and went there for the weekend. My listings had promised "ten minutes to the office" in three different places. So at half past five, the worst hour, I rode the route from the office to each address, and each time the ten minutes turned into forty. On Saturday I walked three areas end to end: the lane behind the market, the quiet colony with the tree-lined road, the new towers near the highway. I bought tea at a stall in each and asked the vendor what the place was like at night. One was loud, one had no shops, one felt right. My wife Ishita, on the phone, asked, "And the photos?" I said, "The photos didn't show the traffic." I signed for the third area on Sunday. - Kiran

How many areas did Kiran walk through?
Kiran walked through three areas.
How did Kiran feel about the listings after the visit?
Kiran became sceptical and wary of them, since the promised ten minutes turned into forty.
What else could Kiran do before signing a lease?
Kiran could ask people who live nearby or a colleague about costs and problems, or rent short-term first, to add more direct information.
How might Ishita have felt hearing about the trip on the phone?
Ishita may have felt reassured and curious, wanting a real picture of the area beyond the photos.

metadata.subtype: Approach: visiting first to assess neighbourhoods [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sudha: new plan for thesis month, tell me if it's mad
Yamini: go
Sudha: I write 7 to 10 am. phone in the drawer. that's when my head is clearest
Yamini: you?? the night owl??
Sudha: the night owl wrote 2 pages in March. I tracked it. mornings I do 3 pages in one sitting
Yamini: ok fair 😮
Sudha: and Sunday night I pack 5 lunches, lay out 5 outfits. so evenings = zero decisions
Yamini: what happens in the evenings then
Sudha: reading references, laundry, calling Amma. easy stuff
Yamini: I always thought you just had no discipline lol
Sudha: me too. turns out I was doing the hardest job when I was most tired
Yamini: that's actually smart. can I copy the Sunday lunch thing 🙏
Sudha: only if you come chop onions with me

What time does Sudha plan to write the thesis?
Sudha plans to write from 7 to 10 am, with the phone in the drawer.
How does Sudha seem to feel about the new plan?
Sudha feels hopeful and a little relieved, having realised the problem was doing the hardest job when most tired rather than having no discipline.
Which part of Sudha's plan cuts evening choices, and how?
Packing five lunches and laying out five outfits on Sunday night means evenings have no decisions left, so energy goes to easy tasks.
How does Yamini's view of Sudha change during the chat?
Yamini starts by thinking Sudha lacked discipline, but ends up impressed and even wants to copy the Sunday lunch idea.
There were 21 dollars in the cookie jar. Doris spent $6 from the cookie jar. Martha spent half as much as Doris. How much money, in dollars, was left in the cookie jar?

Martha spent 6/2=3 dollars.
Martha and Doris spent 6+3=9 dollars.
There were 21-9=12 dollars left in the cookie jar.
The answer is 12.
My son is starting kindergarten. Write a short note, about 50 words, to put in his lunch box on day one.

Good morning, my brave boy! Today is your very first day of school. Eat your lunch, play nicely and listen to your teacher. If you feel shy, look at this note and remember that Mumma loves you very much. I will be waiting for you at the gate at 12 o'clock.

The city's draft plan to cut three bus routes in Kolkata was open for public comment for only two more days, and the form was online, in English, on a website that crashed twice. Bidisha, a schoolteacher in Behala, read the plan on her lunch break. One of the cut routes was the bus her neighbour, Sudha Mashi, took to the hospital every week. Bidisha understood the reason: the routes were losing money, and the new metro line covered part of the area. But the metro station was two kilometres from Sudha Mashi's lane. That evening she knocked on doors with a printed copy, explained the plan in Bengali, and wrote down what twelve neighbours said. Then she typed a clear comment: the saving made sense, but the lane needed a feeder bus to the metro. She submitted it at 11:40 p.m., with Sudha Mashi's name on it too. Three months later a small feeder bus started.

How far was the metro station from Sudha Mashi's lane?
Two kilometres.
What was Bidisha feeling about the plan to cut the route?
Bidisha felt concerned for Sudha Mashi, even though she understood why the routes were losing money.
How did Bidisha take part constructively under the tight deadline?
She understood the trade-off, gathered neighbours' views in Bengali, and submitted a specific solution, a feeder bus, before the deadline.
How might Sudha Mashi have felt seeing the feeder bus start?
Sudha Mashi probably felt relieved and valued, her hospital trips protected and her voice included.

Read this:

Omkar: can I tell you something. but you have to promise not to tell anyone
Uma: I'm listening. what's going on
Omkar: I've been really not okay. like, for weeks. I feel like I'm drowning and I keep thinking everyone would be better without me
Omkar: please don't tell my parents or anyone
Uma: Omkar, thank you for telling me. I'm really glad you did
Uma: I care about you too much to keep this completely secret. I'm telling you first, honestly
Uma: can I call you right now?

Uma called and kept him talking, gently, until he agreed. With Omkar still on the line, she messaged his hostel warden, who went to his room within ten minutes. The warden sat with Omkar while he spoke to a helpline counsellor, and arranged for him to see the college doctor first thing in the morning. Uma stayed on the phone until the warden arrived.

How quickly did the hostel warden reach Omkar's room?
The warden went to his room within ten minutes.
What was Omkar feeling when he first messaged Uma?
Omkar felt overwhelmed and hopeless, like he was drowning, and afraid of anyone else finding out.
How did Uma balance Omkar's trust with his safety?
Uma thanked him, refused to keep it secret, told him first, called him and got the warden to him that same night while staying on the line.
How might the warden see Uma's message that night?
The warden would likely see it as the right and brave call, since it let an adult reach Omkar quickly and arrange help.

Read this:

"Mummy, where are you going?"
"Just to the kitchen, Parveen. To make your rice."
"No! Stay!"
Hafsa sat back down on the bed. Parveen's cheeks were flushed and her voice was croaky. She wrapped both arms around Hafsa's waist.
"You feel scared when you're sick, hmm?"
"Yes. Everything is too big."
"I'll stay till you're sleepy. Then I'll make rice and come back. Keep my scarf, so you know I'm coming."
Parveen held the scarf against her cheek.
"Promise?"
"Promise. I always come back."

What did Hafsa leave with Parveen?
She left her scarf with Parveen.
What does Parveen wrapping her arms around Hafsa suggest?
She felt scared and helpless while sick, as if everything was too big, and needed her mother close to feel safe.
How did Hafsa treat Parveen's clinging?
She saw it as a need for safety, not naughtiness, stayed close, and told her when she would come back.
What would change if Hafsa had said "Stop being a baby"?
Parveen might feel more frightened and ashamed, and cling even harder.

In one day, 200 people visit The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Half of the visitors are residents of New York City. Of the NYC residents, 30% are college students. If the cost of a college student ticket is $4, how much money does the museum get from college students that are residents of NYC?

The number of visitors that are residents of NYC is 200 / 2 = 100 visitors
The number of NYC resident visitors that are college students is 100 * 0.30 = 30 visitors
The money from the college students that are residents of NYC is 30 * $4 = $120
The answer is 120.

Charu kept the Class 10 stream form in her bag for three weeks. Every day she told herself she would fill it in when she felt sure. On the last Monday it was still blank, and Vandana ma'am, the school counsellor, called her in. "Not sure yet," Charu said, picking at her nails. The commerce batch was already full and only two seats remained in science, but the form needed one choice by evening. "I'm scared of picking wrong," she said. Vandana ma'am asked what Charu had learned about each stream so far. Charu counted on her fingers and was surprised that the list was longer than she thought. She ticked a box before the bell.

How long did Charu keep the form in her bag?
Charu kept the form in her bag for three weeks.
Why did Charu pick at her nails when she said "Not sure yet"?
Charu was nervous and afraid of picking wrong, and waiting to feel sure had not made the fear go away.
What small step helped Charu move from waiting to choosing?
She counted what she had learned about each stream and saw the list was longer than she thought, then ticked a box.
How does Vandana ma'am see Charu's blank form?
Vandana ma'am sees a student who is scared, and asks what Charu already knows instead of telling her what to choose.
Can you write a short message thanking my team for working late to finish the launch? About 50 words. I'm the manager.

Hi team,
Thank you for all the late evenings this week. Because of your hard work, we finished the launch on time, and the client is very happy. I know it wasn't easy, especially with the last-minute changes. Please take Friday afternoon off. You have earned it.
Gauri

Diary, Tuesday night.

Something strange at the metro depot today. I was walking past Coach 4 during the evening check and the brake sound was wrong. Not loud. Just wrong, like a note slightly off. I couldn't have told anyone why.

Two years ago I would have ignored it. Everything sounded the same to me then. Now I've been under hundreds of these coaches.

So I stopped and called Arnab. He's been here fifteen years. He frowned. "What's wrong with it, Kavitha madam?" "I don't know. Just check with me." We got under with the torch. A bolt on the brake housing was loose, not dangerous yet, but it would have been in a week.

Arnab said, "Good ears." I said, "Good luck." He said no, it wasn't luck. I think he's right. I'm going to start trusting that off feeling as a reason to look.

Which coach had the wrong brake sound?
Coach 4.
Why did Kavitha stop at Coach 4 even without a clear reason?
Kavitha felt uneasy because the sound seemed off, and after hundreds of coaches she was starting to trust that uneasy feeling as a sign to check.
Which choice worked, and why?
Treating the odd feeling as a cue to check with Arnab, instead of either ignoring it or panicking, found the loose bolt early.
How might Arnab see Kavitha's hunch?
Arnab seems impressed and respectful, seeing it as a skill built from experience rather than luck.
Why does praise often make a child try harder?
She feels noticed and valued. Because she wants to keep earning that good feeling, she tries to do well again.

"Arnab, did you revise the list of fundamental rights?"
"Yes, Hemant. Five times. Right to equality, right to freedom, right against exploitation..."
"And?"
"...And... I forget the rest. I always remember the first three."
"Because you always start from the top."
"True. Also, what do you think of the new maths sir?"
"He's nice."
"No way. Somebody told me on his first day that he fails half the class."
"Has he failed anyone?"
"Not yet."
"Has he been mean?"
"No. He explained quadratics really well yesterday."
"So why do you think he's bad?"
"Because that's the first thing I heard about him."
"Same as your list, Hemant. The first thing sticks."
"Huh. Okay, I'll start from the bottom tonight. For both."

Which rights does Arnab remember from the list?
Right to equality, right to freedom, right against exploitation.
Why does Hemant still think the new maths sir is bad?
Hemant feels wary because the first thing he heard was that the teacher fails half the class, and that first story sticks despite good experiences.
What does Hemant decide to try, and why is it a good idea?
Starting from the bottom of the list and rethinking the teacher, so later information gets as much weight as the first.
How does Arnab see the new maths sir?
Arnab sees him as nice, especially after he explained quadratics well.

A school hall has 47 rows with 23 chairs in each row. About how many chairs are there?

Now you try: 62 x 19.
The answer is 60 x 20 = 1200; exact 1178.

I don't understand "downcast". Can you help?
Help me correct this: Ravi and me went to the fair.
Why do frogs live near water?
Why does a rooster crow in the morning?
why are seeds spread by animals useful for plants

1. "Downcast" is an adjective. It means sad and looking downward.
2. Write it as: Ravi and I went to the fair. Why: "I" is the form we use for the subject of the sentence.
3. Frogs need water for their eggs and their skin. Because they lay eggs in water and their skin must stay moist.
4. A rooster's body clock and the first light trigger the crow. Because crowing also tells other roosters where he is.
5. Animals carry seeds away from the parent plant. Because the seeds land far from it, they have room to grow.

"They never leave me; and they shall not till this unhappy business is over. Be wise also, my friends. It is no common enemy that we deal with. Alas! alas! that that dear Madam Mina should suffer!" He stopped; his voice was breaking, and I do not know if rage or terror predominated in my own heart.

Based on what the passage says, what warning is given about the enemy?
The speaker warns that it is no common enemy they deal with, and tells his friends to be wise too.
There are 95 balloons in one box and 20 in another. How many balloons are there together?
115. Because 95 + 20 = 115, so there are 115 balloons in all.
Marco owns an ice cream truck.  His ice cream cones are $5 each.  If his expenses are 80% of total sales for the day, how many ice cream cones would he need to sell to make a $200 profit for the day?

His expenses are 80/100 = 4/5.
His profit would be 20/100 = 1/5.
Total sales for the day is $200 x 5 = $1000.
Total ice cream cones he sells is $1000 / 5 = 200.
The answer is 200.
Who blocked Bhima's path with his tail in the forest?
An old monkey lay across the path, and Bhima could not even lift its tail. The monkey was Hanuman, who was also a son of the wind-god and so Bhima's brother.

At the Hyderabad office cafeteria, a notice from the green committee asked staff to bring their own cups. Most people ignored it. Tushar, a twenty-four-year-old analyst on the committee, counted the paper cups in the bins for a week and posted the total on the board. People stopped and stared. His colleague Binita suggested making it easy, not guilt-based. They asked the canteen to keep a rack of washable steel tumblers by the coffee machine. Paper cup use dropped sharply the next month. Encouraged, Tushar pitched switching off monitors at night and grouping deliveries to cut vans. Some colleagues rolled their eyes at the extra effort. But the facilities manager asked him to present the idea to senior staff.

What did the canteen keep by the coffee machine?
A rack of washable steel tumblers.
What did Binita think would work better than guilt?
Binita believed making the greener choice easy would change behaviour more than guilt.
Which idea worked best, and why?
The rack of steel tumblers, because it removed effort and made the better choice the default.
How did some colleagues see Tushar's further ideas?
Some rolled their eyes, seeing them as extra effort, while the facilities manager took them seriously.

Dadi's birthday guests were due in twenty minutes, the pooja was half set up, and Ishita was sobbing on the bedroom floor. The new lehenga scratched her waist like sandpaper. 'Honestly, Sangeeta, she's too sensitive,' Bua called from the hall. Ishita pressed her face into her knees so nobody could see. Sangeeta had a hundred things to do. She knelt anyway. 'It really does itch. That's not silly.' She fetched the soft cotton slip and slid it underneath. 'Now three slow breaths with me. Then sit in here till you're ready.' Ishita breathed. The doorbell rang. Ten minutes later she came out on her own, and when Bua started to say something, Sangeeta said, 'She's fine. She knows her own skin.'

What did Sangeeta slide under the lehenga?
The soft cotton slip.
Why did Ishita press her face into her knees?
She felt hurt and ashamed after Bua's remark and wanted to hide her feelings.
What did Sangeeta do, even under time pressure, that protected Ishita's trust?
She knelt, agreed the itch was real, fixed it with the slip, taught three slow breaths and let Ishita choose when to come out.
How might Bua see Ishita after Sangeeta's reply?
Bua may begin to see Ishita's reaction as knowing her own skin rather than fussing.

Hi Yusuf,
You asked last week how I always know when a message is fake. I don't! I just slow down. Here's what happened on Monday.
At 7 a.m. I got a text: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here," with a link. Then a call from a polite man who said he was from my bank and needed the OTP I'd just received "to stop the block".
I didn't click and I didn't share the OTP. I told him I'd call the bank myself and hung up. Then I checked the sender: a mobile number, not the bank's name. I opened the bank's own app, the one already on my phone, and there was no alert. I called the number printed on my debit card. They said the account was fine, and that no one from the bank would ever ask me for an OTP.
My heart was racing the whole time, by the way. Slowing down doesn't mean feeling calm.
See you Sunday,
Irawati

What did the caller ask Irawati for?
The OTP just received, to stop the block.
How was Irawati feeling while checking?
Irawati's heart was racing; Irawati felt anxious even while acting slowly and carefully.
Which of Irawati's steps would you advise anyone to copy?
Don't click or share the OTP, check the sender, open the bank's own app, and call the number printed on the card.
What might Yusuf take from the email?
Yusuf may feel reassured that careful people also feel scared, and that a few simple checks matter more than feeling calm.

The power went off just as the biscuit tin came out, and only three biscuits were left inside. Yamini, five, held the tin in the candlelight. She pushed one straight into her brother Vaibhav's hand without a word. Then Mummy's friend's daughter, a girl Yamini had met only that evening, held out her palm. Yamini pulled the tin to her chest. She looked at Mummy. She looked at the girl. Slowly she broke the last biscuit and gave the smaller half, her eyes on Vaibhav, who was already crunching happily.

How many biscuits were left in the tin?
Only three biscuits were left inside.
What does Yamini pulling the tin to her chest suggest she felt when the visiting girl held out her palm?
She seems unsure and protective, not ready to share easily with a girl she had met only that evening.
How could Mummy gently help Yamini at that moment?
Mummy could sit close, say the guest's name, and smile at the half biscuit, so the new girl feels less like a stranger.
What might it be like for the visiting girl to get a small half while Vaibhav gets a whole biscuit?
She might feel a bit left out, yet pleased to get anything at all in a new house on a dark evening.

Micah bought envelopes to send, and depending on the weight of the envelope he will need more stamps. If an envelope weighs more than 5 pounds, he will need 5 stamps. If it weighs less than that, it will only need 2 stamps. If he bought 52 stamps with 6 envelopes that weigh less than 5 pounds, how many envelopes in total did Micah need to buy?

Micah had to buy 6*2=12 stamps for 6 envelopes less than 5 pounds.
He has 52-12=40 more stamps to buy.
There are 40/5=8 envelopes that weigh more than 5 pounds.
Micah needed to buy 8+6=14 envelopes.
The answer is 14.

He watched me as I laid my purse upon the table and opened it, and he watched me as I separated two one-pound notes from its contents. They were clean and new, and I spread them out and handed them over to him. Still watching me, he laid them one upon the other, folded them long-wise, gave them a twist, set fire to them at the lamp, and dropped the ashes into the tray.

What happens to the two one-pound notes after the speaker hands them over?
He lays one on the other, folds them lengthwise, gives them a twist, sets fire to them at the lamp and drops the ashes into the tray.

At Dadaji's flat, Anand hung back by the door.
“Anand, greet Dadaji,” said Disha, his mother.
“Do I have to touch his feet?”
“Only if you want to. You can also fold your hands and say namaste.”
Dadaji chuckled from his chair. “A warm hello is enough, beta. Come here.”
Anand looked at the floor, then walked over and bent to touch Dadaji's feet. Dadaji put a hand lightly on his head. “Blessings. How is school?”
“Good,” said Anand, smiling. “I got a star.”

Who told Anand he could fold his hands instead of touching feet?
Disha, his mother, told him he could fold his hands and say namaste.
What might Anand have felt when he hung back and asked if he had to touch feet, and what else could it be?
Probably shy or unsure about the custom, and perhaps a little pressured. He might also just have been nervous about meeting Dadaji.
How did the adults respond in a way that respects the child?
Disha and Dadaji made it a choice, saying a warm hello is enough, so Anand touched the feet by his own decision.
How might Dadaji see the touching of his feet?
As a mark of respect and a chance to bless his grandchild, and he also said a warm hello would do, so he did not seem to demand it.
