Which is less?
a) 0 or 3
b) 1 or 0
c) 5 or 0
d) 0 or 10
e) 2 or 0
What does "point out" mean?

"Point out" means to tell someone about something they may not have noticed.
Example: Lucas pointed out a small spelling mistake in the poster before it was printed.

Read this:

In Lagos, Amara had four months to learn one song on guitar for the school's end-of-year concert. Her cousin Nadia had lent her the guitar and a chord sheet.
The first week was exciting. By the fifth, her fingers hurt and the same chord change sounded awful every single time. She was bored of the song before she could play it.
Nadia suggested something: a calendar with a small square for every day she practised, even ten minutes. "Don't count hours. Count squares."
Some days Amara only managed the ten minutes. Some days the power was out and she practised without an amp in the dark. In month three, the chord change finally clicked.
At the concert her hands shook. She got through the whole song. Afterwards she looked at her calendar: ninety-one squares.

How many squares did Amara count on her calendar after the concert?
Ninety-one squares.
How did Amara feel in the fifth week?
Amara felt bored and discouraged, with sore fingers and a chord change that sounded awful every time.
Why did Nadia's calendar idea help?
Counting days instead of hours made small, steady practice feel like progress, even on bad days.
How might Nadia feel watching Amara play at the concert?
Nadia would probably feel proud and happy that the lent guitar and the calendar idea helped.
Who was the headmaster of our school in 1962?
I'm not sure, as records for one school are not something I can check. The school office or its old yearbooks may list the names.

Read this:

In the staff room of the school where he taught, Lalit, twenty-five, pressed a hand to his stomach again. It was the third upset this month, plus headaches every evening and poor sleep. His colleague Hrithik noticed. 'You've been to the washroom four times today. Are you okay?' Lalit shrugged. 'It's just stress. It'll pass.' 'You said that last month.' That stopped him. It hadn't passed. It had grown louder. That week Lalit booked a doctor's appointment. The doctor found nothing serious and asked about his workload. Lalit went to the principal and gave up one of his three extra duties. He called his old friend on Sunday and told the truth about how tired he was. And he started a bedtime routine: phone off, a book, lights out by eleven.

How many extra duties did Lalit give up?
One of his three extra duties.
What made Lalit realise he needed to act?
He felt uneasy when Hrithik pointed out he had said the same thing last month, and saw the symptoms growing louder.
What steps did Lalit take in response to his body's signals?
He saw a doctor, reduced his load with the principal, talked honestly to a friend and built a bedtime routine.
How might Hrithik feel seeing Lalit take action?
Hrithik is probably relieved and glad his comment helped.

metadata.subtype: Reading the body as a signal and acting [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Last year I nearly missed the Class 10 trip to the hill fort. I'm Reena, I use a wheelchair, and my father, Manoj, had already told the class teacher I wouldn't go, before asking me. He had also decided I'd take commerce instead of science because the labs are upstairs, and he checked my phone location twice a day. I knew it was love, and fear of me getting hurt. But I felt like a parcel being posted around. One night I finally said, "Papa, you keep deciding my life in the kitchen without me." He went quiet for a long time. The next day we called the school together. The teacher found a ramped route to the fort's lower gate, and Papa agreed I'd go with a friend and a charged phone. I went. I got sunburnt and took my best photo ever. We've started talking about science too.

What did Manoj tell the class teacher before asking Reena?
He told the teacher that Reena wouldn't go on the trip.
How did Reena feel about decisions being made without asking, and what words show it?
Reena felt smothered and frustrated, like a parcel being posted around, while still knowing it came from love.
What turning point helped the family respect Reena's growing independence?
Speaking up to Papa, then calling the school together so a ramped route and a safe plan with a friend could be made.
How might Manoj have felt hearing that he kept deciding Reena's life without asking?
Manoj was probably hurt and shaken, then thoughtful, since he had acted out of love and fear.
Parent-teacher meeting is next week and I'm scared my teacher will say something bad about me.
That feeling is common. Teachers often share both strengths and things to improve. What worries you most?
That I talk too much in class.
If that's true, it's better to hear it so that you can work on it. You could tell your parents beforehand and say you're trying to do better.
Won't they be upset?
Perhaps a little, but they'll likely appreciate your honesty. It shows maturity.

Read this:

I run the tea stall opposite the factory gate, so I saw the whole thing. For a month, Sudha and her college group had stood there every Saturday with placards about the black water in the canal. Some of the older protesters shouted 'Murderers!' at the workers going in. Sudha didn't. She said good morning to them, the same people every week. This Saturday the manager, Jagdish-ji, came out angry and said their pamphlet had the wrong numbers. Sudha asked to see his figures. She read them, standing right there, and said, 'You're right about this one. We'll correct it. But the canal is still black.' Jagdish-ji looked surprised. He accepted a cup of tea from me and stayed talking with her for half an hour. The next week, the new pamphlets had the corrected number. I don't know what will happen to the canal.

What did some of the older protesters shout at the workers?
'Murderers!'
How might Jagdish-ji have felt when Sudha admitted the mistake?
Surprised and a little disarmed, since he came out angry and was met with honesty.
What in Sudha's approach keeps the movement credible?
She stays firm about the canal but checks the manager's figures, corrects the pamphlet and greets the workers as people.
How might the workers going in see Sudha compared with the shouting protesters?
They probably find Sudha easier to respect, since she greets them every week instead of calling them murderers.
Bob orders a pizza with 8 slices.  He eats half of it and each slice was 300 calories.  How many calories did he eat?

He ate 8/2=4 slices
So he ate 4*300=1200 calories
The answer is 1200.

Read this:

In Lunglei, the Class 10 half-yearly results were pinned outside the headmaster's office, and Lalremsiami's name had a red mark beside mathematics: 28 out of 100.

She walked home the long way, past the church, thinking the same sentence over and over. That's it. No science stream. No nursing college. Nothing.

At home she pushed her maths books under the bed. For the next two weeks she didn't open them. When her classmate Bhupen came by with notes from the extra class, she said, "What's the point? I've already failed my life."

"It was one exam," Bhupen said. "The half-yearly doesn't even count for boards."

She didn't answer. She was so sure she was right that she never checked.

The pre-board came six weeks later. With two weeks lost, she scored 31. Barely better. The certainty had cost her the time to recover.

What did Lalremsiami score in the half-yearly mathematics exam?
28 out of 100.
What was Lalremsiami feeling as she walked home the long way?
She felt hopeless and crushed, convinced that one bad mark had ruined her whole future.
What would have helped more than pushing the books away?
Checking the facts, like Bhupen's point that the half-yearly does not count for boards, and making a small recovery plan with a teacher.
How might Bhupen have felt when she said she had failed her life?
Bhupen was probably worried and a bit helpless, trying to give her facts that she was not ready to hear.

Read this:

Monday night
I'm embarrassed writing this.
On the way home, a car scraped my bumper at the signal. Tiny scratch. I jumped out and started yelling at the driver, a guy my age, Siddharth. I said things I don't even say to my brother. He yelled back. People gathered. My heart was pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears.
Then an old auto driver said, "Beta, it's a scratch. Nobody is hurt. Why fight?"
I suddenly felt stupid. We exchanged numbers, took photos of both cars, and left. His insurance will handle it.
In the car, I shook for ten minutes. It was adrenaline, I think, and pride. I felt disrespected, and I was late.
Next time: breathe, photo, numbers, leave. Say less.
Ira

What did the old auto driver say?
He said, "Beta, it's a scratch. Nobody is hurt. Why fight?"
What was Ira feeling while yelling?
Ira felt angry and disrespected, heart pounding, driven by adrenaline and pride.
What does Ira plan to do next time, and why?
Breathe, take photos, exchange numbers and leave, which prevents a small scrape from turning into something worse.
How might Siddharth have felt during the argument?
Siddharth probably felt angry and defensive, which is why he yelled back.

The ration shop has 428 kg of rice and 482 kg of wheat. Which is more?

Now you try: 537 _ 573.
The answer is <.

Read this:

At Tiny Tots kindergarten, Lavanya's Appa, Zubin, crouches at the classroom door. "I'll be back after lunch, like always." Lavanya, four, nods, waves, and trots to the painting table. She paints a blue sun, then plays shop with two girls. When the bell rings, she spots Zubin at the door and races over. She hugs his neck, tells him about the blue sun, then tugs away. "Wait, Appa! I have to finish selling!" He laughs and waits.

What colour sun does Lavanya paint?
Lavanya paints a blue sun.
What does Lavanya's quick hug and tug away suggest she feels?
It suggests she feels secure and happy, reassured Appa is back so she can go on playing.
Why does Zubin's "I'll be back after lunch, like always" help?
The steady promise, kept every day, helps Lavanya trust that he returns, which frees her to play on her own.
How might the teacher see Lavanya's quick check-in at pickup?
The teacher might see it as a healthy sign that Lavanya has settled and uses her father as a safe base.

Read this:

Hemant worked as a junior auditor at the cooperative bank in the market town, and he could not sleep after seeing the loan register. On Sunday he took the bus to see Tarun sir, a senior at the federation office, who sat outside the branch's reporting line and would keep quiet. They talked on the verandah over tea.

A week later, Hemant met an advocate he had known since college, in a small office above the cloth shop. The advocate listened to the whole account and set out the possible options and what each might cost him. He asked Hemant to note dates and to tell nobody in the branch yet.

Hemant rode home with a page of notes and a steadier chest.

Where did Hemant meet the advocate?
In a small office above the cloth shop.
What was Hemant feeling on the bus to see Tarun sir?
Hemant felt uneasy and worried, since he could not sleep and needed a trusted person outside his own line to talk to.
If the advocate had been busy, what else could Hemant do, and why?
Hemant could speak again with Tarun sir about who else could advise him in confidence, because keeping the circle small guards against the matter spreading.
How might Tarun sir see Hemant's coming to him first?
Tarun sir may feel trusted and want to respond carefully, knowing a young clerk has placed a heavy concern in his hands.

metadata.subtype: Approach: consult a mentor or lawyer for confidential guidance [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

School counsellor's note, Class 5, Friday.
Sumit asked to see me because he "can't stop". During break he walks round and round the corridor instead of sitting with friends. He said, "If I sit, it means I'm lazy. My uncle says only lazy people lie down in the afternoon. Papa works fourteen hours and everyone says he's great."
He looked ashamed saying he feels tired after school.
I told him rest is part of working well, like the break in a cricket match. I've asked his parents to come in on Monday to talk about afternoon downtime.
Uday

What does Sumit do during break instead of sitting?
He walks round and round the corridor.
How did Sumit feel about being tired after school?
He felt ashamed, believing that resting means he is lazy.
What did Uday do next?
Uday told Sumit rest is part of working well, like a break in cricket, and asked his parents to come in on Monday.
What would change if Sumit's family respected afternoon rest?
Sumit could sit with friends and rest after school without feeling ashamed.

Read this:

In the school library in Melbourne, Tuan rehearsed under his breath before Nour, the Year 12 captain of the debate team, came in. Trials for the last spot were on Friday. "Your speech at assembly was honestly the best thing I've heard all year," he said, sliding into the seat beside her. He hadn't actually listened to most of it. He praised her notes, her shoes, the way she ran meetings. Nour smiled, then asked, "Which part of the speech did you like?" Tuan's mind went blank. "Uh, all of it?" She nodded slowly and went back to her notes. Walking home past the tram stop, Tuan kept replaying that pause. He had wanted her vote, not her speech, and she had probably felt the difference. He decided to turn up on Friday with his best argument instead.

When were trials for the last spot on the debate team?
Trials for the last spot were on Friday.
What was Tuan feeling when Nour asked which part of the speech he liked?
Tuan felt caught and embarrassed, because he hadn't listened to most of the speech and his praise was aimed at winning her vote.
What could Tuan try instead of heaping on compliments?
He could earn the spot with his own argument at trials, and keep praise for moments when he means something specific.
How might Nour see Tuan's compliments after that pause?
Nour may sense the praise was empty and aimed at the trial, which could make her trust his later compliments less.
"Mere dada ji roz subah park mein tahalte hain." Translate.
It is: "My grandfather walks in the park every morning." In English, "grandfather" is the usual word, and "grandpa" is casual.
Aur dadi ke liye?
Use "grandmother" for the polite form and "grandma" for the casual one.
Aur nana-nani?
They are also "grandfather" and "grandmother". English does not separate the mother's side from the father's side.

Read this:

The flowerpot lay in pieces on the balcony of the Andheri flat. 'Akash! How many times have I told you not to play ball here?' Deepika's voice rose. 'Answer me!' Five-year-old Akash stood very still. He did not cry or speak. He just stared at the soil scattered over the tiles. 'So now you're ignoring me?' Then Deepika noticed his hands. They were trembling at his sides. She stopped, let out a long breath and knelt on the tiles. 'Okay. I'm not shouting any more. Take your time.' She waited, stroking his arm. After a while, in a tiny voice, Akash said, 'The ball bounced wrong. I'm sorry, Mumma.'

What broke on the balcony?
The flowerpot.
Why didn't Akash answer at first, and what was he feeling?
He was too frightened by the shouting to speak; his trembling hands show fear, not defiance.
What helped Akash find his words?
Deepika stopped shouting, knelt down, spoke softly and gave him time while stroking his arm.
Why might Deepika first read his silence as ignoring her?
From her angry side, a child who does not answer looks stubborn, until she notices his body shaking.

Read this:

By nine at night the office on the fourth floor was empty except for Kashish and the hum of the water cooler. It was the third late night this week. The manager had again promised that the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.
Manjula from accounts stopped at her desk, bag on her shoulder. "You're here every night. And your salary was late in June too, na?"
"It's a phase," Kashish said. "Once the new client settles, it'll calm down." She kept her eyes on the screen.
She didn't mention the headaches, or the job alert she had deleted that morning without reading. Reading it would mean admitting this might not get better.
Manjula put a hand on the desk. "Just read one alert. That's all. Reading isn't quitting."

What did the manager promise about the overtime?
The manager promised the overtime would "show in appraisals", the same line as last March.
Why did Kashish delete the job alert without reading it?
Kashish felt afraid to read it, because reading it would mean admitting the job might not get better.
What small step does Manjula suggest, and why might it help?
Manjula suggests reading just one job alert, which lets Kashish look at the problem without having to decide everything at once.
What might Manjula be noticing that Kashish isn't admitting?
Manjula sees the late nights and the late salary as a pattern, and seems worried that Kashish keeps calling it a phase.
Asha scored 42 out of 60 in Hindi and 36 out of 48 in English. In which subject did she do better?

Answer: English. Hindi: 42/60 = 70%. English: 36/48 = 75%.

The two tests have different totals, so comparing 42 and 36 tells us nothing. Change both to percents. 42/60: divide by 6 to get 7/10 = 70/100 = 70%. 36/48: divide by 12 to get 3/4 = 75%. 75% is more than 70%, so English was better, even though she scored fewer marks. This is why schools and cricket statistics use percents: they make everything "out of 100".
Mujhe projects mein group leader banna hai. Teacher ko kaise request karun?
Say: "Ma'am, I would like to lead our group in this project. I will make sure everyone does their part." Showing a plan helps the teacher trust you.
Dost ne poocha weekend ka plan. Mujhe bolna hai "Abhi tak kuch tay nahi hua hai." English?
Say: "Nothing has been decided yet."

Read this:

In their flat in Mylapore, Ganga's shelf told the story. A half-knitted blue scarf on its needles since August. A coding course on her laptop, stuck at 40%. A skipping rope, and a fitness chart on the wall that stopped on day eleven.
On Saturday, she came in excited. "I'm going to learn calligraphy! Look, I found a pen set online."
Her brother Kishore, home from college, looked at the shelf, then at her. "What about the scarf?"
"It got boring. The middle part is just rows and rows."
"And the course?"
"Loops. So boring. Calligraphy is different."
He didn't laugh. "Ganga, you always say that. Everything is exciting on day one."
She opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the scarf. "Maybe I'm just someone who doesn't finish things."
"Or you've never finished one yet. Pick one. Just one."
She sighed, took down the scarf, and counted the rows left. Forty. "Four rows a day," she said. "Then calligraphy."

How far had Ganga got in the coding course?
Stuck at 40%.
How did Ganga feel when she looked at the scarf after Kishore's comment?
Ganga felt doubtful and a little ashamed, wondering if she was someone who doesn't finish things.
What plan does Ganga make, and why might it work?
Four rows of the scarf a day before starting calligraphy, which makes the dull middle small and finishable.
How does Kishore see Ganga's new calligraphy idea?
Kishore sees it as the same pattern of exciting starts, but he responds kindly and nudges her to finish just one thing.

Read this:

Mentoring note, Ira. Sonali came to our monthly one-to-one with a single page: two projects, the churn dashboard and the onboarding revamp, both tied to the team's target for the year. When I asked why not the three others on her plate, she explained aloud that these two were what the promotion criteria measure: results the team can point to. messages.content: A TV show costs $100,000 per episode for the first season and twice that much for every other season.  The first season had 12 episodes, and every season after that had 50% more episodes except the last season, which had 24 episodes.  The show had 5 seasons.  How much did it cost to produce all the episodes?

The first season cost 12*100,000=$1,200,000
Season 2-4 had 12*.5=6 more episodes per season than the first
So they each had 12+6=18 episodes
That means there were 18*3+24=78 episodes in the last 4 seasons
So those episodes cost 2*100,000=$200,000
For a total cost of 200,000*78=$15,600,000
So the total cost was 15,600,000+1,200,000=$16,800,000
The answer is 16,800,000.

You ask if you're foolish to keep calling someone who hardly ever calls you back. I'm Jahnavi, so let me tell you about Rafiq. We were close at college. For six years I rang him every month; he rang me twice. I told myself loyalty means never counting.

Then, on my birthday, I noticed I was tired and bitter. So I did what I should have done sooner and asked him plainly, "Do you want this friendship to be closer? I'd love that, and it's fine if not."

He said his life was full but he cared about me; he simply wasn't a caller. We settled on two visits a year. I stopped waiting for the phone. Some friendships live at a lower flame, and without resentment they last.

How many times did Rafiq ring Jahnavi in six years?
Rafiq rang twice, while Jahnavi rang every month.
What was Jahnavi feeling on the birthday?
Tired and bitter after years of believing loyalty means never counting.
What did Jahnavi do to check whether the effort was mutual?
Jahnavi asked Rafiq plainly whether he wanted a closer friendship, then accepted his answer of two visits a year.
How did Rafiq see the friendship?
Rafiq said his life was full but he cared about Jahnavi, and that he simply wasn't a caller.

"Again?"
"Again. What are the parts your swimsuit covers?"
"Private!" said Usha.

Nobody. Only doctor, if Mummy is there.

She repeated simple rules gently, explained surprises versus secrets, and promised Usha she would never be angry at her for telling.

Five painters take 8 days to paint a building. At the same speed, how long would 10 painters take?
They would take about 4 days. Because twice as many painters working at the same speed can do the job in half the time, and half of 8 days is 4.

Dear Diary,
Fish fry day again in the canteen. The smell hit me at the door and my stomach flipped. I pretended I wasn't hungry and sat with my lunchbox closed. Kashish asked why I was being grumpy. I wasn't being grumpy! I just couldn't breathe properly.

A luxury bag costs $3000. A reseller wants to get a 15% profit. How much should she sell the bag?

The reseller wants to get $3000 x 15/100 = $450 profit.
Thus, she needs to sell it for $3000 + $450 = $3450.
The answer is 3450.

Fifteen-year-old Dhruv was practising for a school interview in the hallway. His teacher Sudha noticed his shoulders creeping to his ears. "Feet flat, shoulders down, one slow breath," she said. Dhruv tried it, and his stomach felt a little steadier. "It helps a bit," he said. "But you still need to know your answers." He nodded and went back over his notes. At the real interview he stood straight, breathed, and spoke clearly from what he had prepared. At twenty-five, Dhruv worked on a laptop for eight hours a day, and by afternoon he sat hunched with his neck jutting forward and his eyes on the screen. A colleague, Tanvir, walked past and thought, he looks bored. Then Tanvir noticed the stiff neck and the untouched tea. "You've been like that since ten," he said. "Are you tired? Or is the chair wrong?" Dhruv blinked. "Both, probably." He raised the screen, pushed his chair back, and stood up for a short walk. When he came back his shoulders were looser and his mood was lighter.

What did Sudha tell Dhruv to do with his feet?
She told him to keep his feet flat.
How does Dhruv's posture matter at fifteen and at twenty-five, and what do others read from it?

At fifteen he practised standing straight and breathing to calm his nerves before the interview, while preparation still counted, and at twenty-five his hunched posture at the laptop looked like boredom to Tanvir but meant tiredness and a wrong chair. Posture helps or hurts the body and mood, but should not be read as attitude.
What was Tanvir thinking when he first saw Dhruv hunched over the laptop?
Tanvir thought Dhruv looked bored, before noticing the stiff neck and untouched tea and asking instead.
What could Dhruv do to keep his body and mood better through the workday?
He could adjust his chair and screen, take regular short walks and breaks, and drink his tea.

School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Zeenat, 15, was referred by her class teacher after missing three debate practices while telling her family she was attending them. Her friend Indu came with her.
Zeenat told me, very quietly, that her father doesn't allow her to stay after school because "people might see her with boys and talk." She loves debating and wanted to practise. I told her that her wish was reasonable and that the lying was a sign of pressure, not a bad character.
Next step: with her permission, I called her mother the same afternoon and invited both parents to meet the debate coach, see where practice happens and who supervises it.

Where did Zeenat actually go instead of practice?
She went to Indu's house nearby, where Indu's mother helped them prepare.
What was Zeenat feeling when she said "I'm tired of lying"?
Zeenat felt exhausted and guilty, trapped between her love of debating and her father's fear of what people would say.
Why was inviting the parents to meet the debate coach a wise step?
It moves the conversation from appearances to real facts, like who supervises practice, which can help the family trust Zeenat.
How might Indu feel about being part of the lie?
Indu may feel uneasy and protective, wanting to help her friend but aware that the secret was weighing on Zeenat.

I'm Nitin. Last month, at twenty-two, I went back to my grandfather Harish's village for the first time in eight years. The mango tree I used to climb was smaller than I remembered. Or I was bigger. I sat under it and suddenly smelt the same wet earth from the summers when Dada woke me at dawn to steal mangoes from our own tree. Nobody needed anything from me then. No deadlines, no emails, no rent. I felt a pang so strong I had to close my eyes. Dada sat beside me and didn't ask anything. We just listened to the koels.

How long had Nitin been away from the village?
Eight years.
What was Nitin feeling, eyes closed under the tree?
Nitin felt a strong, bittersweet longing for the carefree safety of childhood summers.
What made the moment easier for Nitin?
Dada sitting quietly beside him, giving space without questions.
How might Dada Harish feel under the old tree beside Nitin?
Warm and a little wistful at seeing Nitin there, remembering those summers too.

Kamala dragging her to the chief engineer, who stopped the pour; a friend's push got the skill heard before doubt could keep it quiet.

Every summer, Naveen took his daughter Keerthana to her grandparents' village near Mysuru, and every summer the visit ended in tears: a rushed morning, the bus honking, Keerthana howling as Ajji waved from the gate. Back in Bengaluru, she would say she hated going.

A week later, when a friend asked about the holiday, Keerthana said, "The ducks, and the bell. I want to go back."

What did Ajji give Keerthana on the last morning?
Ajji gave her a small bag of groundnut chikki.

Naveen felt concerned that every visit ended in tears, and wanted the last memory to be warm so Keerthana would love going.

Feeding the ducks the night before, packing early, the chikki and ringing the temple bell replaced a rushed, tearful morning.

Keerthana remembers the ducks and the bell and wants to go back, instead of saying she hated going.

I spent all my pocket money in two days. What now? Meaning of "wallet"? How much pocket money do I have left?

1. Wait until next week and spend less each day. Keep a small part aside next time, even a coin.

A rectangle has a length of 3 inches and a width of 6 inches. A square has a width of 5 inches. What is the difference in area between the two shapes?

The area of the rectangle is 3 x 6 = 18 sq in
The area of the square is 5 x 5 = 25 sq in
The difference is 25 - 18 = 7 sq in
The answer is 7.

The school bus was stuck behind a fallen tree, rain drumming on the roof, and thirty children had nothing to do but listen.
It had started over a window seat. Now Seema said, "You're just jealous, Irawati."

That night he sat on the hospital bench with his friend Manoj, doing sums: rent, Abba's medicines, his own bus fare.

December: Abba walked to the mosque without a stick. Imran slept till ten for the first time in weeks, and nobody woke him.

The zebra crossing near the school.

It suggests he took his first job seriously and felt cautious, wanting to understand every obligation before relying on it.

He planned: early shifts to free his evenings, bills paid first, and a small fixed time for community work.
How might Abba have felt watching Imran over these months?
Grateful and perhaps a little guilty for needing help, and proud of his son's steadiness.

He saw 25 total vehicles because 12 plus 13 equals 25.
He saw 100 wheels because 25 times 4 equals 100.

In the small flat in Kraków, Olga sat at her desk, homework untouched, replaying the scene from Friday. Oskar, her friend since primary school, had read her private poem aloud at the class party, in a silly voice, after she'd shown it to him in confidence.
She had rehearsed a hundred replies since then. Clever ones. Cruel ones. On the tram she imagined posting his embarrassing childhood photos where everyone would see, or telling the whole class about his fear of the dark. She could picture exactly how his face would look.
For a few seconds each fantasy felt like power. Then she'd look up and realise she'd missed her tram stop, or read the same page of chemistry four times.
Her mother knocked. "You've been quiet all weekend."
"I'm fine," Olga said, but her jaw was tight. Oskar had probably forgotten the whole thing by now. She, meanwhile, was carrying it everywhere.

What did Oskar read aloud at the class party?
Her private poem, in a silly voice.
What does Olga feel during each revenge fantasy?
She feels a brief burst of power, then distracted and tense as the hurt stays fresh.
What could Olga do instead of rehearsing payback?
Tell her mother what happened, and decide calmly whether to tell Oskar how it felt, so the event stops living in her head.
What might Oskar be feeling now?
Oskar may have moved on without realising how much he hurt Olga, or feel uneasy but unsure how to apologise.

At three o'clock precisely I was at Baker Street, but Holmes had not yet returned. The landlady informed me that he had left the house shortly after eight o'clock in the morning. I sat down beside the fire, however, with the intention of awaiting him, however long he might be. I was already deeply interested in his inquiry, for, though it was surrounded by none of the grim and strange features which were associated with the two crimes which I have already recorded, still, the nature of the case and the exalted station of his client gave it a character of its own. Indeed, apart from the nature of the investigation which my friend had on hand, there was something in his masterly grasp of a situation, and his keen, incisive reasoning, which made it a pleasure to me to study his system of work, and to follow the quick, subtle methods by which he disentangled the most inextricable mysteries. So accustomed was I to his invariable success that the very possibility of his failing had ceased to enter into my head.

The narrator reaches Baker Street at three, finds that Holmes has been out since eight, and settles by the fire to wait. The narrator is interested in the case, partly for the client's high rank, and expects Holmes to succeed as always.
If the price of a bag of cherries is $5 when the price of a bag of olives is $7, how much would Jordyn pay for buying 50 bags of each fruit and a 10% discount?

At a 10 percent discount, Jordyn will pay 10/100%*$5=$.50 less for a bag of cherries.
To buy one of the cherries at a 10% discount Jordyn will pay $5-$0.50=$4.50
The cost of buying 50 bags of cherries at the 10% discount is 50*4.50=$225
Also, at a 10% discount, Jordyn will pay 10/100*$7=$0.70 less for a bag of olives.
The price of a bag of olives at a 10% discount is $7-$0.70=$6.3
To buy 50 bags of olives Jordyn will pay $6.3*50=$315
The total cost of buying 50 bags of each fruit at a 10% discount is $315+$225=$540
The answer is 540.

Wednesday, 11 p.m.
The job medical today flagged my eye test. "Possible early sign of a rare eye condition. Refer to specialist." I read that line about forty times on the bus.
By dinner I had decided I was going blind. The machine is modern. Machines don't lie. I even looked up braille classes.
Deepak found me crying on the balcony. He's studying statistics, so he drew dots on the back of an envelope: thousands of people, a tiny cluster who actually have it, and a bigger group of healthy people the machine flags by mistake. "If it's rare, most flags are false alarms," he said. "Not all. Most. That's why they send you to a specialist."
I'm still scared. But I'm less sure I'm doomed.
The appointment is Friday. Deepak's coming. I'm writing my questions now.
Trisha

What did the job medical flag?
It flagged Trisha's eye test as a possible early sign of a rare eye condition.
What was Trisha feeling after reading the line on the bus?
Trisha was frightened and convinced of going blind, trusting the modern machine without thinking about how rare the condition is.
What is the wise next step in Trisha's diary?
Going to the specialist on Friday with written questions, and letting a doctor explain what the flag means.
How might Deepak feel finding Trisha crying?
Deepak is probably worried but steady, and wants to calm Trisha by showing why most flags for rare conditions are false alarms.
Which village in my district has the oldest living tree?
I can't check that, because tree records for one district are local. The forest office or a local naturalist group could name candidates.

"If your friend had done the same year, what would you tell her?"
Vidya was quiet for a long time. "That she was scared, and she did what she knew how to do then."

Vidya missed the exam date.
What was Vidya feeling whenever a scholarship notice appeared?
Vidya felt ashamed and undeserving, closing the tab and saying she had wasted a whole year.
What turned things for Vidya on the terrace?
Vidya imagined saying to a friend that she was scared and did what she knew how to do then. That let her see herself kindly and open the form.
How might Rehana have seen Vidya's silence after her question?
Rehana likely saw that Vidya was thinking it through, so Rehana said nothing more and let her reach her own view.

His father's spade.

Sum up this reading for me in three sentences.

From Italy they visited Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born at Naples, and as an infant accompanied them in their rambles. I remained for several years their only child. Much as they were attached to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection from a very mine of love to bestow them upon me. My mother's tender caresses and my father's smile of benevolent pleasure while regarding me are my first recollections. I was their plaything and their idol, and something better—their child, the innocent and helpless creature bestowed on them by Heaven, whom to bring up to good, and whose future lot it was in their hands to direct to happiness or misery, according as they fulfilled their duties towards me. With this deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life, added to the active spirit of tenderness that animated both, it may be imagined that while during every hour of my infant life I received a lesson of patience, of charity, and of self-control, I was so guided by a silken cord that all seemed but one train of enjoyment to me.

The narrator, the parents' eldest child, was born in Naples and travelled with them through Italy, Germany and France as an infant. For years the narrator was their only child and received deep love. Knowing what they owed the child, the parents taught patience, kindness and self-control so gently that childhood felt like one long enjoyment.

Elizabeth, you said your friend "obviously" chose the wrong stream? Hmm. Let your Leela aunty tell you something.

When I was sixteen, my best friend Mercy decided to sit the entrance for a nursing school in Chennai instead of doing Class 12 science with me. Everyone thought it was a brave choice. I thought so too. I remember saying, "You'll be brilliant."

She didn't get in. And do you know what I said to the other girls? "It was always a silly idea. Obviously she wasn't ready."

Mercy heard about it. She didn't speak to me for months.

Later I found my old diary. The day she chose, I had written, "Mercy is so brave. I wish I could do that."

I had rewritten my own memory to look wise. That diary taught me: judge the decision by what was known then, not by how it turned out.

So, what did your friend actually know when she chose?

What did young Leela write in her diary on the day Mercy chose?
Mercy is so brave. I wish I could do that.

Tarun closed the lid halfway. "It is nice," he said, too quietly. The duty teacher was scolding juniors at the far table. Tarun's tiffin had brown bread with jam his mother had made.

Tarun feels embarrassed and a bit resentful; throwing the food away and telling himself he does not care hides how much the laughing stung.
What could Tarun try before the next lunch break?
Tarun could sit with someone kind, or tell the duty teacher what happened; one ally makes being different easier.

Who won at kho-kho?' Trisha dropped her bag. 'Nothing.' Then, sharply, 'Leave me!' Anand opened his mouth to scold, then remembered his own long schooldays. He handed her a guava from the tree and said only, 'The goats need taking to the pond.' Trisha walked them down alone and threw pebbles into the water for a long time. At dinner she told him everything, even the kho-kho score.

What did Anand hand Trisha?
A guava from the tree.
What does Trisha's sharp 'Leave me!' suggest she was feeling?
She was drained and irritable after a long school day and needed space before any questions.
What made Anand's second response better than his first?
Instead of more questions or a scolding, he offered a snack and time alone with the goats, so she could recover and chose to talk later.
What was it like for Anand when Trisha snapped at him?
He was tempted to scold but remembered his own schooldays, and was rewarded when she told him everything at dinner.

"It's those Year 10 boys again. They did exactly this last week and laughed at everyone who ran." Kofi hesitated. The voice sounded higher and thinner this time. "If it's a prank, we look silly. If it isn't..." They didn't go under the bridge alone. They waved over a couple walking a dog and went together to the railing, where they could see down. A younger girl was sitting on the wet steps holding her ankle, her scooter on its side. Kofi called the emergency number while Ines stayed with the girl, and the couple fetched her parents from the café. Later Ines said quietly, "Those prank screams nearly made me walk past."

From under the bridge.
What was Kofi feeling when he hesitated?
Kofi felt torn and uneasy: worried about looking silly if it was a prank, but more worried someone was really hurt.

They didn't go under the bridge alone; they brought the couple with the dog, looked down from the railing, then called for help and fetched the girl's parents.
How had the earlier prank affected Ines?
The Year 10 boys' fake screams made Ines doubt a real one, and she admitted it nearly made her walk past.

Beta, come sit. I'm your Madhav Dada, and this is from my school days in Nashik. Our class had a boy called Shankar, tall and quiet. One day the teacher's chair broke and everyone roared. I roared too, I couldn't stop. But when I looked at Shankar he was laughing with his hand over his mouth, a different kind of laugh, worried. Shankar had been sitting on it when it broke. Later I said, "I wasn't laughing at you." He said, "It felt like it." I had to think about that. Since then I look at faces before I join a laugh. Good laughter has room for everyone.

The teacher's chair broke.
What did Shankar's laugh with his hand over his mouth suggest he felt, and what else might it be?
It suggested he felt worried or embarrassed, since he had been sitting on the chair when it broke. It might also have been an attempt to laugh along so he would not seem upset.

The child can apologise, listen to how it felt, and watch faces before joining a laugh next time, as Madhav learned to do.

Shankar felt the laugh was aimed at him even though Madhav did not mean it that way, which shows how a laugh can wound without intent.

It had happened four times since spring. Fatima kept apologising for things she hadn't done and checking her phone for Olga's mood. One evening, on a video call with her sister, she heard herself say, "I've shrunk." That night she told Olga calmly, "I care about you. I can't fix this for you, and I'm going to stop trying. I think a therapist could help you, and I've booked one for myself too." Olga cried, then went quiet. In the morning Fatima went for her usual run.

What did Olga's sticky note say?
It said, "Best weekend ever. Love you endlessly."
What does Fatima mean when she says "I've shrunk"?
She feels she has lost herself, always apologising and checking Olga's mood out of confusion and fear.
What choice did Fatima make that evening, and why was it wise?
She calmly stopped trying to fix Olga, suggested a therapist for Olga and booked one for herself, protecting her own wellbeing.
How might Olga feel when Fatima says she will stop trying to fix things?
Olga may feel upset and scared, which may be why she cries and goes quiet, yet she also hears a steady, caring message.

Marcy's grade is electing their class president. Marcy got three times as many votes as Barry, who got twice as many as 3 more than the number of votes Joey got. If Joey got 8 votes, how many votes did Marcy get?

First, add three to Joey's vote total: 8 votes + 3 votes = 11 votes
Then double that number to find the number of votes Barry got: 11 votes * 2 = 22 votes
Then triple that number to find Marcy's vote total: 22 votes * 3 = 66 votes
The answer is 66.

Wednesday. Noor tried something different. 'Two things have to happen before dinner: spelling and sums. You choose the order, and whether you start at five or after your cartoon at five-thirty.' Friday. Noor found a note stuck on the fridge in Sahil's wobbly writing: SPELING THEN SUMS. 5:30. He had made the plan himself, spelling mistake and all, and at five-thirty he was at the table before she could say a word.

What did Noor find on the fridge on Friday?
She found a note saying SPELING THEN SUMS. 5:30.
Why did Sahil look suspicious on Wednesday?
He was used to being ordered about, so a real choice felt surprising, and he wasn't sure he could trust it yet.
What made Noor's Wednesday approach work?
She set the limits, both tasks before dinner, but let Sahil choose the order and start time, so he felt like an agent and cooperated.
How might Noor feel reading the fridge note?

James hurt himself exercising.  The pain subsided after 3 days, but he knew that the injury would take at least 5 times that long to fully heal. After that, he wanted to wait another 3 days before he started working out again.  If he wants to wait 3 weeks after that to start lifting heavy again, how long until he can lift heavy again?

The injury would be fully healed after 3*5=15 days
So he would start exercising again in 15+3=18 days
He would then wait for 3*7=21 more days to start lifting heavy again
That means he needs to wait 18+21=39 days
The answer is 39.

When the landslide siren sounded in our village above Munnar on Saturday night, I watched our son Jomon do exactly what his school had drilled. He took the green emergency bag from the hook without being told: the documents pouch, the torch, the whistle, dry biscuits. I asked him to switch off the mains at the board by the door, and he did, then checked the gas knob too, as we had shown him. I am writing this because I was the one shaking. He was calm, because he had practised.

Day one. On Varun's first week in Lucknow for his internship, he heard slow drumming and saw people in black walking through the old city at night, some beating their chests. He assumed it was a festival and asked a passer-by, "Which celebration is this?" The man looked at him sadly and walked on. Varun's face burned.
Day two. He asked Vidya, his colleague who had grown up in the old city. "It's Muharram," she said gently. "For many Shia families it's a time of mourning, remembering a great loss in their history. It isn't a celebration." Varun felt awful about his question.
Day four. Vidya took him to watch the procession from her aunt's balcony. Varun stayed quiet, watching the black flags and the faces. When a young man looked up, Varun bowed his head slightly. Vidya's aunt offered him sherbet. "You came to understand," she said. "That's respect."

Where did Vidya take Varun to watch the procession?
From her aunt's balcony.
What was Varun feeling after the passer-by walked away?
He felt embarrassed, his face burning, realising his question may have hurt someone in mourning.
What did Varun do that helped him understand?
He asked Vidya, who knew the tradition, and then watched quietly and respectfully from the balcony.
How did Vidya's aunt see Varun's presence at the procession?
She saw it as respect, because he came to understand rather than to watch for fun.
When do I use 'who' and when 'whom'?
Use 'who' for the person doing the action, like 'Who called?' Use 'whom' for the person receiving it, like 'Whom did you call?'
Is there a quick test?
Yes. Answer the question with 'he' or 'him'. If 'him' fits, use 'whom'. If 'he' fits, use 'who'. Many people use 'who' in casual speech, but 'whom' is expected in formal writing.

In her third month at the Porto design agency, Beatriz realised she was checking her phone in the shower. Noa, her manager, sent ideas at all hours through the chat app, and Beatriz answered every one, afraid of looking lazy. On Friday she asked for fifteen minutes. "Noa, I want to be really responsive, and I think I can be better at it with one change. Could we use email for ideas and next-day tasks, and the chat app only for things that can't wait? I'll check email first thing at nine and after lunch." Noa looked surprised. "I didn't know you felt you had to answer at night. I just type when I think of things." "I know. That's why I'm asking." "That's reasonable. And if something truly can't wait, I'll call." The next Monday, Noa's midnight idea arrived by email with the subject line "Not urgent!" Beatriz read it at nine, rested.

When did Beatriz say she would check email?
First thing at nine and after lunch.
Why had Beatriz been answering messages at all hours?
Beatriz felt anxious and afraid of looking lazy, so she kept answering every late message, even checking her phone in the shower.
How did Beatriz frame her need so it was well received?
She linked it to being more responsive, proposed email for non-urgent ideas and the chat app for urgent ones, and said exactly when she'd check.
How did Noa see the late messages before the conversation?

In the crowded Delhi metro, Chinmay Mama gave Sahil a riddle: "What has keys but can't open locks?"
Sahil went quiet. He looked at the window, then tapped his chin with one finger. The train rattled through two stations.
A lady beside them leaned in. "Should I tell him?"
Chinmay shook his head. "He's thinking. Give him time."
Sahil's lips moved silently. His eyes narrowed.
"A piano!" he burst out, as the doors opened at Rajiv Chowk.
Chinmay laughed. "Right! And you got it yourself."
Sahil grinned all the way to the exit.

What riddle did Chinmay Mama give Sahil?
"What has keys but can't open locks?"
What does Sahil tapping his chin and looking out the window suggest?
It suggests he was thinking hard and focused, not confused or bored.
Why was it helpful that Chinmay waited instead of giving the answer?
Waiting let Sahil finish his own thinking and feel proud when he got it. 😊
How might the lady beside them see Sahil's silence at first?
She probably thought he was stuck or needed help, not that he was thinking.
My cousin says "I'm out of station". Is that correct English?

"Out of station" is common in Indian English and means away from the city or town. In other varieties, people usually say "out of town" or "away".
Example: I am out of town until Monday.

Read this:

"You copied my assignment, Rohan! Admit it!"
Parveen's voice was rising in the empty classroom. Rohan had stood up. His fists were clenched, arms stiff, and he took a step towards her desk.
Avni saw the fists and felt her stomach turn. "Parveen. Step back."
"But he—"
"I know. Step back first."
Parveen stepped back. Avni moved beside her, keeping the desks between them and Rohan.
"Rohan," Avni said, calmly, "nobody's going to shout anymore. Let's take this to Ma'am. She can compare both files."
Rohan's fists were still tight. "I didn't copy."
"Then Ma'am will see that. That's fair for both of you."
Avni texted their class teacher and kept the door open. Two minutes later, Ma'am walked in. Rohan's hands slowly opened.
"Thank you for calling me," Ma'am said. "Everyone sit. One at a time."

Who did Avni text?
Their class teacher.
What was Avni feeling when she saw Rohan's clenched fists?
Avni felt alarmed and uneasy, her stomach turning, reading the fists as a possible warning.
What did Avni do that kept the situation safe?
She had Parveen step back, kept the desks between them, used calm words, and called the teacher.
How might Rohan have been feeling with his fists clenched?
Rohan was likely angry and defensive at being accused, and the fists showed tension that could have escalated.

metadata.subtype: Clenched fists and tense hands in conflict [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Could you answer these?
Any idea what "rapidity" means?
Why does a ball bounce back when it hits the ground?
How can I write a good opening line for a story?

1. Rapidity means great speed. It is a noun.
2. The ball springs back off the floor. Because the ball and the floor are squashed for a moment, and they push back and send the ball upward.
3. Start with something surprising, such as a sound, a question or an unusual action. Make the reader want to know what happens next.
What exact spices were in the curry my aunt made last Diwali?
I don't know, as I can't see her kitchen. Ask her and she may share the recipe.

Read this:

In the Lisbon software office, Pablo sat two desks from Paulo, and by March he had noticed something.
"Your code is genius, man," Paulo said on Monday, leaning over Pablo's screen. "Honestly, you're the best developer on this floor." Pablo smiled. It felt good.
On Monday afternoon: "Hey, could you cover my weekend on-call?"
Two weeks later: "You're the only person here with real taste." Ten minutes later: "Could you review my pull request tonight? It's urgent."
Pablo started to notice the rhythm. The compliments were big and vague. They never mentioned anything specific he had actually done. And they always arrived just before a request.
His team lead, by contrast, had once written: "Your fix to the payment retry saved us a whole weekend." Nothing more. No request.
The next time Paulo called him a genius, Pablo just said, "Thanks. What do you need?" Paulo laughed awkwardly and told him.

What had Pablo's team lead written?
"Your fix to the payment retry saved us a whole weekend."
How did Pablo feel once he noticed the rhythm?
Pablo felt wary and a little let down, realising the flattering words were steering him toward favours.
What did Pablo do that helped him not be steered?
He thanked Paulo and asked directly what he needed, separating the compliment from the request.
How did Paulo seem to feel when Pablo asked what he needed?
Paulo seemed awkward and caught out, laughing uneasily before admitting the request.

metadata.subtype: Spotting the ask behind the praise [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Jeevan, shoes on! The van's coming!"
"I can't find my left one, Ma!"
Jeevan opened the cupboard. Shirts, a ball, his raincoat. No shoe. He shut it.
"Did you look under the bed?" called Lalremsiami, his big sister, from the bathroom.
"Wait." He opened the cupboard again. Shirts. Ball. Raincoat. Shut.
"Maybe it's in the cupboard." Open. Shut. Open once more. His chin began to wobble.
Honk! The van was at the gate.
Lalremsiami came out, dripping, looked under the bed and held up the shoe. "Four times in the same cupboard, Jeevan!"
He ran to the van in one shoe, carrying the other.

Where did Lalremsiami look to find the shoe?
She looked under the bed.
What was Jeevan feeling when his chin began to wobble?
He felt anxious and frustrated, because the van was coming and the cupboard kept showing the same things.
What else could Jeevan try instead of opening the same cupboard again?
He could remember which places he has already checked and try a new one, like under the bed, as Lalremsiami suggested.
How does Lalremsiami see Jeevan's search?
She is amazed he looked in the same cupboard four times, and simply checks a new place and finds it.
Daniel invited me for Christmas lunch and I am Hindu. Should I bring something?
It is polite to bring a small gift, and Daniel will probably love it. Something like sweets, fruit or a flower plant works well. Ask him if he needs help with the food too.
What if he does not eat sweets? I am not sure.
Then bring something else, like a plant or a box of dry fruits and nuts. You can also just message him and ask what he would like. It takes a minute and avoids guessing.
Good idea. I will bring a plant. What should I wear, just normal?
A neat, comfortable outfit is fine for Daniel's lunch. Christmas is a cheerful day, so something bright is nice. You do not need anything special, because he invited you to enjoy it with him.
City rooftop, two pigeons: write their story.

Two pigeons, Gutru and Mitu, lived on the roof of a tall building in Pune. They had a favourite spot beside the water tank, where an old man named Mr. Kulkarni scattered rice every evening.

One day, a larger pigeon swooped down and pushed them aside. "This is my spot now," he said, gobbling the rice.

Gutru puffed up, but Mitu pulled him back. "Let him," she whispered. "Come."

She led him to the next building, where a woman was drying grain on a mat. They ate a hearty meal there.

The next evening, Mr. Kulkarni noticed only the big pigeon. He waited, puzzled. When Mitu and Gutru returned for a visit the day after, he put out double rice for them and smiled.

Read this:

The trophy from three years ago still stood on the meeting-room shelf at the agency's Kochi office. "Same format as always," Suraj said, flipping to the print mock-ups. "It won us that." Everyone nodded. Nazia, eight months into the team, had noticed the pattern: the same fonts, the same Friday pitch style, and every new suggestion answered with "we've always done it this way". Two clients had quietly moved to a smaller agency this year. She didn't argue. She asked, "What do you think the clients who left were looking for that we didn't show them?" The room went still. Suraj frowned, then slowly pulled out his notebook. "Honestly? I don't know. Can you find out?" Nazia nodded, a little nervous and a little relieved.

How many clients had moved to a smaller agency this year?
Two clients had moved.
What was Nazia feeling after Suraj asked her to find out?
Nazia felt a little nervous and a little relieved, since her gentle question had finally opened the topic.
Why did a question work better than an argument?
It let the team look at a real loss for themselves instead of defending their old methods against a newcomer.
How might Suraj see Nazia's question?
He may have felt stung at first, since the old format won the trophy, but he was honest enough to admit he didn't know.

Read this:

Shankar moved into the engineering hostel in October, two months late, because of a delay with his scholarship papers. By then the groups were already made.

He noticed Akash's group first: five of them, always at the corner table in the mess, always walking to class in a line, always in Akash's room at night with music playing.

Then the water supply failed for three days during midterms, and everyone had to queue at the one tap near the gate. Standing behind them, Shankar heard one of the five, Faizan, mention that he'd been invited to a study group with the second-years.

"You're going?" Akash asked lightly.

Faizan glanced at the others. "Nah. Just saying."

Shankar watched Faizan's face fall a little as he said it. Nobody had told him not to go. Nobody needed to.

Why did Shankar move into the hostel two months late?
Because of a delay with his scholarship papers.
What does Shankar seem to feel watching the group from the tap queue?
He seems curious and a bit lonely as the latecomer, and uneasy when he notices Faizan's face fall.
How could Faizan's friends make room for him to try other groups?
One of them could say, "Go, tell us how it is," so going to the study group would not feel like leaving them.
What is it like for Faizan when Akash asks "You're going?" lightly?
He feels a quiet pressure and disappointment, sensing that going would look disloyal even though no one forbade it.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Routine and a core group [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

The heater in the school hall had broken, and band practice started in coats. Baljeet rubbed his hands together hard, blowing into them between songs. When the drum part began, he snapped his fingers in rhythm, tapping one foot.

Then he lost his page. He turned and snapped his fingers twice at Nikita. "Sheet! Quick!"

Nikita raised an eyebrow. "I'm not a waiter."

Baljeet's ears went hot. "Sorry, sorry. Could you pass the sheet, please?" She passed it.

At the break, the cook brought in a tray of hot samosas, and Baljeet rubbed his hands again, grinning this time. Nikita laughed. "Is that cold hands or samosa hands?"
"Both!"

Why did band practice start in coats?
The heater in the school hall had broken.
What was Baljeet feeling when he rubbed his hands at the break?
Eager and excited about the hot samosas, as his grin shows, though his hands were probably still cold too, as he admits with "Both!".
What could Baljeet do instead of snapping when he needs something quickly?
Use the person's name and a quick "please", as he did after apologising.
How did Nikita see the finger snap?
She took it as rude, like calling a waiter, and felt annoyed until Baljeet said sorry and asked properly.

Read this:

March: Santosh, the new manager of a small bakery in Indore, found a problem. The old rule said staff got leave only in turn by seniority. But Harish's wife was in hospital, and he'd been refused because two seniors had booked leave first.
April: Santosh called a staff meeting. He listed what was at stake: fairness of the queue, care for a family emergency, the shop's needs. Each worker spoke. One senior offered to swap dates. They agreed by vote, as the staff rules allowed.
June: Santosh wrote a new clause with the staff: emergency leave outside the queue, with proof. Harish, back at work, said, "Nobody pushed anyone. That's why it worked."

Why had Harish been refused leave?
Because two seniors had booked leave first.
How did Harish seem to feel about how the conflict was handled?
He seemed grateful and respected, saying nobody pushed anyone.
Which of Santosh's steps improved the rule for the future?
Writing a new emergency-leave clause with the staff after a fair meeting and vote.
How might the senior who swapped dates have felt?
The senior probably felt good about helping, since it was an open choice, not something forced.

Read this:

"Papa, can I stroke that dog?"

Uday looked at the dog's owner. "Can she?"

"Sure, he's gentle."

Lalremsiami patted its back, giggling. Then she ran back and hugged Uday's legs. "Hug for Papa!"

At the park gate, a man they didn't know said, "Want to come and see my puppies in the van?"

Lalremsiami looked up at Uday. "Can I?"

"No," Uday said, firmly and calmly, and took her hand. "We never go anywhere with someone we don't know. Even for puppies."

"But you said yes to the dog."

"The owner was right here with us, and I could see you. Different place, different rule."

What did the man at the park gate offer to show?
His puppies in the van.
Why did Lalremsiami look up at Uday before answering the man?
She was probably unsure and wanted to check, since she had been allowed to stroke the dog earlier. She may have felt confused about why the answers were different.
How did Uday make the rules clear?
He said a firm, calm no, took her hand, and explained why: the dog's owner was with them and he could see her, but going off with a stranger is never allowed.
How does the dog's owner help Uday decide it is safe?
The owner says the dog is gentle and stays right there, so Uday can say yes while watching.

Read this:

In the girls' hostel study room, where the warden had said they could talk after lunch, the two young women, Ankita and Ganga, sat facing each other. The fight had been about lights: Ganga studied late, Ankita had a seven o'clock lab.
"You first," said Ganga.
"Okay. You're saying night is the only quiet time you get, because the day is full of classes and your part-time job." Ganga nodded. "And I said you're selfish. That was harsh. I'm sorry."
Ganga said, "You're saying you can't function at the lab if you sleep at two. I called you a baby. I'm sorry."
They agreed: lights off at eleven, and Ganga studies in this room after that. They wrote it on a chit and stuck it by the switch.

Where did Ankita and Ganga stick their agreement?
By the switch, on a chit.
What was Ganga feeling when Ankita restated her side?
She felt heard and calmer, nodding as Ankita explained why night was her only quiet time.
What turning point made the repair work?
Each restated the other's point first, owned their harshest word, and they agreed one practical rule about lights and where Ganga studies.
What was Ankita experiencing when Ganga apologised for calling her a baby?
She likely felt relieved and respected, since her need to sleep before the lab was finally taken seriously.

metadata.subtype: Stage 6: Repair and one concrete agreement [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Jaya's leave would end in nine weeks and their budget had almost no slack, so Jeevan and Jaya sat at the table with a sheet of paper. Option one: Jeevan's parents, twenty minutes away. Option two: the crèche near the office, which had a waiting list. Option three: a nanny, which they could afford only a few days a week. "Grandparents first," said Jaya, "but what if your mother's knees act up?" "Then the crèche," said Jeevan, "and I'll put us on the list this week so a place isn't a surprise." For the nanny they agreed to ask one friend to be on call for emergencies. Beside each choice they wrote its backup. It did not remove the worry, but the paper made the worry smaller.

What could the couple afford for the nanny option?
Only a few days a week.
What was Jaya worried about with the grandparents option?
Jaya worried that Jeevan's mother's knees might act up, making it hard for the grandparents to help.
What other approach could give them another safety net if two plans fail in one week?
They could ask about flexible days or working from home at their offices, because that adds a fallback that does not depend on anyone falling ill.
How might Jeevan's parents feel about being the first choice?
They may feel trusted and glad to help, and perhaps also worried about letting the couple down if their health gets in the way.

metadata.subtype: Approach: planning childcare options with contingencies [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Puppet time note, from Farhan, preschool teacher.
Harsha made a story with the bear puppet and the baby puppet. The bear said, “Nobody plays with me now. Everybody likes the baby.” The bear hid behind the curtain. Harsha's baby brother was born last month. I didn't ask, “Is that you?” I asked the bear, “Bear, how do you feel?” Harsha answered in the bear's voice, “Lonely.” “What would help, Bear?” “A cuddle and a game.” I've shared this with her mother, who plans some special time with Harsha.

What did the bear say nobody does anymore?
Play with it.
What might Harsha have been showing through the bear?
She may have been showing feelings of loneliness and jealousy about the new baby, which were easier to say through the bear.
Why was it wise for Farhan to ask the bear instead of Harsha?
Asking about the character let Harsha share feelings safely, without being pressed to admit the story was about her.
How might Harsha's mother feel reading the note?
She might feel a bit sad but grateful to know, and eager to plan special time with Harsha.

Read this:

Subject: A conversation

Hi Naveen,

Two weeks ago I became your manager, and I've noticed how quiet our meetings have gone. I want to say something plainly. I know I haven't earned this in everyone's eyes yet, and I don't know everything about the billing system you've handled for three years. I'd like your help there.

I'm not arriving with big changes. For the first month I'll mostly listen, and I'll ask each of you what's working and what isn't. If you have doubts about me in this role, I'd rather hear them directly than guess.

Can we have coffee on Thursday?

Warmly,
Farhan

What system does Farhan say Naveen has handled for three years?
Farhan says Naveen has handled the billing system for three years.
What is Farhan worried about?
Farhan worries that former peers doubt Farhan deserves the manager role.
How does Farhan plan to build authority?
By admitting what Farhan doesn't know and listening for the first month, asking each person what works, and letting results build authority rather than acting bossy.
How might Naveen feel on receiving this email?
Naveen may feel respected at being asked for help and invited to speak honestly, though possibly still unsure about the change in roles.

b) cosec theta - sin theta

f) (sin^3theta + cos^3theta)/(sin theta + cos theta)
g) (sin^3theta - cos^3theta)/(sin theta - cos theta)

l) cosec theta
