Pankaj followed Coach Bhupen's every word and lived for his nod. When he was benched for the semi-final, he burned. He told a teammate the coach obviously preferred others and nearly quit that night. In the morning he asked, "What should I fix to get back in?" Bhupen said, "Your footwork against the short ball, and your temper." Pankaj trained on it. Loving the coach's words, he had also started to ask why behind each one. Meanwhile a senior, Rohit, was using Pankaj's scorebook analysis for a school competition while promising to introduce him to a scout. Weeks passed and nothing came. Pankaj noticed the imbalance. "What exactly will you do with my sheets, and when?" he asked. Rohit dodged, so Pankaj went to the maths teacher, who knew a real analyst, and asked for advice there too. In the nets, Baljeet, a Class 6 boy, copied Pankaj's hairstyle and the way he tapped his bat. Pankaj grinned, then said, "I dropped a catch last week. Don't copy that part. Find your own style."

What did Pankaj ask Coach Bhupen after being benched?
He asked what he should fix to get back in.
How did Pankaj's response to being benched differ from his handling of Rohit's promises?
After being benched he nearly quit, then asked the coach what to fix and trained on it; with Rohit he noticed the imbalance, asked clear questions and sought another mentor.
How did Pankaj feel when he was benched for the semi-final?
He felt resentful and hurt, believing the coach preferred others.
What could Pankaj keep doing for Baljeet?
He could keep admitting his own flaws and encouraging Baljeet to find his own style, instead of enjoying the copying.

Come here and listen. When I was ten, I, your grandmother Shalini, was waiting at the bus stand with my mother's bundle when I saw a cloth bag under the bench. I peeked inside: bundles of notes. My knees turned to water. I did not touch it again. I ran to the chai seller, Ramu Kaka, and said, "Please phone the police post. Somebody must be missing this." Constable Hrithik came, wrote down what I said and took the bag, telling us that whoever came had to describe what was inside. Two days later a farmer came, weeping, and named every bundle. I never saw that money again, and I never missed it.

Where did Shalini see the cloth bag?
Shalini saw it under the bench at the bus stand.
What did Shalini feel when the bundles of notes came into view?
Shocked and scared, since Shalini's knees turned to water and Shalini did not touch the bag again.
What choice at the bus stand made sure the money reached its owner?
Shalini asked the chai seller to phone the police post, which held the bag until the right person could describe what was inside.
How might the farmer have felt when the bag was returned?
Relieved and overwhelmed, since the farmer came weeping and named every bundle.

messages.content: Amber buys 7 guppies for her pond.  Several days later, she sees 3 dozen baby guppies swimming around.  Two days after that, she sees 9 more baby guppies.  How many guppies does she have now?

3 dozen baby guppies make 3 x 12 = 36 baby guppies.
There are a total of 36 + 9 = 45 baby guppies.
Adding the adult guppies, there are 7 + 45 = 52 guppies.
The answer is 52.

Three snails raced across a rain-soaked sidewalk.  The first snail raced at a speed of 2 feet per minute.  The second snail raced at twice the speed of the first snail.  And the third snail traveled at five times the rate of speed as the second snail.  If it took the first snail 20 minutes to race all the way up the sidewalk, how long, in minutes, did it take for the third snail to race all the way up the sidewalk?

If the first snail traveled the distance in 20 minutes, then the second snail, traveling at twice the rate of speed, would take 20/2=10 minutes to complete the race.
If the third snail raced at five times the speed of the second snail, then it would take the third snail 10/5=2 minutes to race all the way up the sidewalk.
The answer is 2.

Sit, Jyoti. You asked why I light a lamp for my own thatha every Deepavali. I was fifteen when he died, just like that, at his shop counter in Salem. That evening everyone told me, "Rukmini, don't cry, your amma needs you strong." So I didn't. I made coffee, I swept, I kept my face like stone. On the third day my Periamma found me behind the well, shaking. She didn't scold. She sat down in the dirt beside me and said, "Cry, kanna. He was your thatha too." And I cried until my throat hurt. After that I sat with the family through every ritual, and I cried whenever it came. Grief is not a guest you can hurry out of the house, Jyoti. I learned that behind a well, and it has stayed with me all these years.

Where did Rukmini's thatha die?
He died at his shop counter in Salem.
What was Rukmini feeling while keeping a face like stone?
Rukmini was grieving but felt pressured to be strong, holding the sadness in until it came out as shaking behind the well.
What turning point changed how Rukmini grieved?
When Periamma sat in the dirt and said to cry, Rukmini stopped hiding the tears and sat with the family through the rituals, crying whenever it came.
How did Periamma see Rukmini behind the well?
Periamma saw someone hiding grief and chose not to scold, sitting close and saying that he was Rukmini's thatha too.

Monday. Sunaina's blue cycle vanished from outside the town library. In the canteen, Amandeep shrugged. "She probably didn't lock it. Some people are just careless." Saying it made the canteen feel normal again.
Thursday. Amandeep came out after tuition and found his own cycle gone, a cut chain lying on the pavement. He had locked it. He had checked twice. He stood there for a long time, face hot, running through what he might have done wrong and finding nothing.
The next Monday. He found Sunaina on the library steps, waiting for a bus now.
"Did you lock yours?" he asked, and then heard how it sounded. "Sorry. I mean, mine was locked too. I said something stupid about you last week."
Sunaina looked at him for a second. "Yeah. I heard."
"I'm sorry," he said again, and sat down beside her to wait.

Where did Sunaina's cycle vanish from?
Sunaina's blue cycle vanished from outside the town library.
Why did calling Sunaina careless make the canteen 'feel normal again' for Amandeep?
Blaming Sunaina let Amandeep feel safe and in control, as if theft only happens to careless people and never to someone like him.
What could Amandeep say or do next to repair things with Sunaina?
Amandeep could ask how Sunaina is managing without the cycle and offer practical help, and correct the comment with the people who heard it.
How might Sunaina feel hearing Amandeep's apology?
Sunaina may still feel hurt, since she had heard the comment, but the plain admission and his waiting beside her might ease some of the sting.
Why do plants on a windowsill bend towards the window?
They grow towards the light. Because the shaded side of the stem grows a little faster than the sunny side, which bends the plant towards the window.

What does 'balanced diet' actually mean?
It means eating a mix of foods that give the body what it needs: grains, pulses or other protein foods, vegetables, fruit and some dairy or alternatives, in sensible amounts.
Is there one correct balance for everyone?
No. Needs vary with age, activity and health conditions. General guidance gives a rough picture, but not an exact plan for any one person.
So how do I find mine?
A doctor or a registered dietitian can look at your situation and advise you. I cannot give personal diet advice.
Are there general guides I can read?
Yes. Official health bodies, including national nutrition institutes, publish simple food guides. These are general and worth reading before a visit to a dietitian.
Okay. Do I need to count everything I eat?
I cannot say. That is a question for a professional who knows your needs.

Jaya, you want to know why I got so quiet that summer? Let me just say it.

I'm Shankar. My parents run a tea stall at the bus stand, and that year my uncle, who helped them, moved to Dubai. So when my school selected me for the state-level science camp, I knew what the answer would be before I asked. So I didn't ask. I threw the selection letter in my drawer and told my teacher I couldn't go.

My parents never knew. I worked the stall all May, pouring tea and counting coins, telling myself I was being a good son.

But inside, something went sour. I stopped studying science. I got annoyed at small things, like Amma asking me to fetch milk. Last month Amma found the letter while cleaning. She sat down on my bed and asked, "Why didn't you tell us?" I didn't have an answer that made sense.

Where did Shankar put the selection letter?
In his drawer.
How did Shankar feel inside during that summer?
Shankar felt quietly bitter and resentful, which showed in losing interest in science and getting annoyed at small things.
What might have happened if Shankar had shown the letter?
The family might have found a way, like help from a neighbour or a shorter stay, and at least would have known what was being given up.
How might Amma have felt finding the letter?
Amma likely felt hurt and sad, realising her son had given up a chance without letting the family even consider it.

Monday: After the lie about the sleepover, Papa took Sunaina's phone, cancelled her dance class and said she would come straight home from school for two months. Her father, Vikas, had never been so angry. "No more chances," he said.
The next Thursday: Sunaina borrowed a friend's old phone and hid it inside a sock in her cupboard. She messaged only after midnight, with the screen brightness at zero.
Three weeks later: Papa asked, "You've been good lately, na?" Sunaina said, "Yes, Papa." She had become excellent at hiding, and not at all better at telling him things. Neither of them knew why the other felt so far away.

Where did Sunaina hide the borrowed phone?
She hid it inside a sock in her cupboard.
What does Sunaina's "Yes, Papa" suggest about how she feels?
It suggests she feels she must keep up an act; she has become good at hiding rather than trusting her father.
What could Vikas have done instead of only restrictions?
He could have set firm but fair limits and asked why Sunaina lied, so they could reset rules she could keep honestly.
What is Vikas experiencing three weeks later?
Vikas thinks things are better, but he feels a distance he can't explain, not knowing about the hidden phone.
How much is the monthly fee at the swimming club?
I don't know the fee, because the club decides it. Ask the front desk or look at the club's notice.

On a hot, quiet afternoon in the Goan village, Francis, five, sat on the cool verandah floor with a heap of wooden blocks.
He built two towers, a bridge, then a little church with a pointed roof. The roof kept falling. He tried again. And again.
Farida Aunty from next door came by with a plate of bebinca. "Francis, look what I brought!"
He didn't hear. His tongue was between his teeth.
Lunch went cold. He didn't look around for anyone to see.
When the roof finally stayed, he sat back and said to nobody, "There."
Only then did his tummy rumble.

What did Farida Aunty bring?
Farida Aunty brought a plate of bebinca.
What does Francis saying "There" to nobody suggest?
It suggests he felt satisfied and proud for himself, not needing anyone's praise.
What made the block building hold Francis so completely?
The church roof was just hard enough to keep falling and easy enough to keep trying, which kept him absorbed.
What would change if Farida Aunty had insisted he stop and eat?
Francis might have felt frustrated and lost the absorbed state before finishing the roof he was working so hard on.

The quarterly review at the city museum's education department had gone well, Dilnaz thought. Maria's school tours were the most booked in the building.

So she was surprised, an hour later, to find Maria in the storeroom, sorting worksheets that didn't need sorting, jaw tight.

"All okay?"

"You said I need to delegate more," Maria said. "In front of everyone. So I'm basically not good enough to lead."

Dilnaz went back to her desk, printed the review, and came back. "Can I read you the whole page?"

She read it aloud, slowly. "Tours booked out every week. Teachers ask for you by name. Your new worksheet for Class 5 is now used across the department. You trained two volunteers. One area to grow: delegate more so you don't burn out."

She handed the page over. "What else does it say?"

Maria read it again, silently. Her shoulders came down a little. "It says I'm doing well," she said. "And one thing to work on."

What did Maria's new worksheet become, according to the review?
It is now used across the department.
Why was Maria so sure she had been criticised?
The one line about delegating stung, especially in front of others, so it blocked out the rest of the review. Her mind turned a small tip into "not good enough to lead".
What worked about Dilnaz reading the whole page aloud and asking "What else does it say?"
It brought all the praise back into view without arguing with Maria, and the question let Maria find the balance herself. She ended by naming both the praise and the one thing to work on.
What might Dilnaz have felt finding Maria in the storeroom after a review she thought went well?
Dilnaz was probably surprised and concerned, since the review was meant to be positive. It showed her how one line can land harder than intended.

On the school trip, the bus broke down on the highway, and lunch was an hour late. Ayesha, five, had two small packets of peanuts. Parul had none and looked hungry.

Ayesha opened one packet and poured half into Parul's hand. She felt proud and warm.

The teacher noticed. "Ayesha, what a kind choice."

Ayesha kept the other packet in her bag. The teacher didn't ask for it.

How late was lunch on the trip?
Lunch was an hour late.
What was Ayesha feeling after sharing with Parul?
Ayesha felt proud and warm inside.
What did the teacher do well in response to Ayesha's sharing?
The teacher praised her kindness without demanding she share the other packet too.
How might Parul feel receiving the peanuts?

In the hostel committee room, Farhan read from the form. "Mess contractor rating. Out of ten, for the whole semester."
"Three," Ganga said. "Last week the dal was watery twice and the rotis were cold on Sunday."
"Three for the whole semester?"

"I also ate the Onam sadhya they made in September. You took three helpings of payasam."

"And the midnight noodles during exams? And the soup they made for the whole floor that had flu?"
"Fine. But the recent stuff is what matters. That's how they are now."
"Or that's just what you remember."
Ganga tapped the pen against the table. "Four. The dal was really bad."

What did the mess make in September?
The Onam sadhya.
Why does Ganga want to give only three out of ten?
Ganga still feels annoyed about last week's watery dal and cold rotis, which are freshest and seem like 'how they are now', so the good months fade from the rating.
What could the committee do to rate the contractor fairly?
Keep short notes on the meals every week through the semester and look at all of them when it's time to rate.
How might the mess staff feel if their semester score came from one bad week?
They might feel their effort, like the Onam sadhya and the soup for sick students, went unnoticed.

Her ears burned, and she turned away and spent the second half fielding at the boundary, far from everyone. In the changing room she said she might skip next week. Where did Pooja field in the second half?
At the boundary, far from everyone.
What was Pooja feeling after she dropped the catch?
Embarrassed and ashamed, since her ears burned, she pulled away and she considered skipping next week.
How did Vasudha help Pooja return?
She shared her own dropped catch, offered private practice and a small step.
How might the club see the dropped catch?
As an ordinary slip, since Vasudha says everyone drops the easy ones; the groan was probably a passing reaction.

In the small-town market, Kishore had watched his neighbour Gautam wait eleven months for his cousin Anil to apologise over a broken shop agreement. "I'm being patient," Gautam said whenever the name came up. Every festival he laid an extra plate for Anil, and every festival it stayed empty. He began taking the long way to avoid Anil's shop.
Kishore noticed Gautam's tight jaw and that he had never once said, "That hurt me."
One evening over tea Kishore said, "Patience has a limit. Is it patience if you're avoiding the conversation?"
Gautam stared at his glass. "I'm scared Anil will say no."
"Then at least you'd know," said Kishore.
Gautam nodded slowly. "Sunday," he said.

How many months has Gautam waited for the apology?
Eleven months.
What is Kishore feeling and thinking about Gautam's waiting?
Kishore is worried and honest. Kishore notices the tight jaw and the avoidance and suspects the patience is really avoiding the conversation.
What turning point did Kishore's question bring?
Kishore asked whether it was patience if Gautam was avoiding the conversation, and Gautam admitted fear and decided to go on Sunday.
What might Gautam be afraid of?
Gautam is afraid that Anil will say no, which is why he has waited instead of asking.

Payal sat on it.

Indu thanked Payal, stayed calm, mended the ruler with tape and gave a simple next step.

Indu seems calm about the broken ruler and glad Payal told the truth, saying, "I'm glad you told me."

messages.content: There is a group of 18 people who are ordering pizza. If each person gets 3 slices and each pizza has 9 slices, how many pizzas should they order?

Each person eats 3 slices of pizza, the group in total eats 18 x 3 = 54 slices.
There are 54 slices in 54 / 9 = 6 pizzas.

Eight people fit in a row on an airplane, and there are 12 rows. Only 3/4 of the seats in each row are allowed to be seated. How many seats will not be occupied on that plane?

There a total of 8 x 12 = 96 seats on that plane.
Only 8 x 3/4 = 6 seats are allowed to be seated in each row.
So, only 6 x 12 = 72 seats are allowed to be seated on the plane.
Therefore, 96 - 72 = 24 seats will not be occupied.
The answer is 24.

Nilesh (20) presented his analysis of election posters from two rival parties this week. He didn't pick a side. He showed how both used the same tricks: fear-words, crowd photos, one enemy to blame. He also pointed out a fact on one poster that was true but missing its context. When a classmate accused him of "defending the other side", he said calmly, "I'm checking both the same way." I've asked him to turn it into a short workshop for first-years and suggested a reading list on propaganda history.

What did Nilesh analyse?
Election posters from two rival parties.
What might Nilesh have felt when accused of defending the other side?
He may have felt a flash of irritation, but stayed calm and confident in his fair method.
Why is Uday's workshop suggestion a good next step?
It spreads Nilesh's even-handed approach and gives first-years a practical way to spot manipulation.
How might the classmate who accused Nilesh see things later?
He or she might realise that checking both sides equally isn't taking a side.

Read this:

Dear Nazia,
I'm writing because I owe you the truth in full, not in pieces.
At the conference in Hyderabad last month, I kissed someone. It happened on the last night. In the moment I felt a rush, as if I were someone new. By morning I felt sick, and I've felt sick every day since. I lied to you on the phone when you asked how the trip was. That was the second betrayal.
I've thought about why. It isn't because of anything you did. I've been feeling lost about my career, and I went looking for a thrill instead of talking to you. That's on me, completely.
I've ended all contact with her. I'm not asking you to forgive me, and I'm not asking you to decide anything soon. Whatever you choose, I'll accept it. If you want to talk, I'll be there. If you don't, I'll understand.
I'm so sorry.
Lokesh

Where did Lokesh cross the line?
At the conference in Hyderabad, on the last night.
How did Lokesh feel the morning after?
Lokesh felt sick with guilt, and has felt that dread every day since.
What does Lokesh do right in this letter?
Admits the full truth, owns the reason without blaming Nazia, ends contact, and accepts whatever Nazia decides.
How might Nazia feel reading the letter?
Likely hurt and shocked, but at least told the whole truth rather than lied to further.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, customer service team, Friday.
Our new hire, Saurabh, joined from a village near Sagar. At lunch this week, a few team members mimicked his Hindi and called him “gaon ka hero.” He laughed along, but ate faster and left early.
Today Sonali, who has been with us two years, said at the table, quite gently, “Guys, can we drop that? Saurabh has handled more calls than any of us this week.” Then she moved her tray and sat next to him. She is still very much part of the old group. Nobody seemed angry with her.
I thanked Sonali privately. I will also remind the team about respectful conduct at Monday's meeting, without naming anyone.

What did some team members call Saurabh?
They called him "gaon ka hero".
How did Saurabh seem to feel during the mimicking?
He seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, laughing along but eating faster and leaving early.
What did Sonali do that made a difference?
She asked the group gently to stop, gave a fact about Saurabh's work, and sat with him, while staying part of the old group.
How might the team members who mimicked feel after Sonali spoke?
They might feel a little embarrassed but not attacked, since she was kind and still one of them.

Read this:

On Diwali evening Kamal scrolled past a photo of the family's rooftop puja in Hyderabad: everyone lined up, and a gap at the end. It was the third festival without an invitation. Kamal set the phone on the sofa, and a hollow ache spread through the chest. No anger tonight, only the flat sadness of a chair nobody moves. The doorbell rang. Rukmini stood there with a box of sweets and two friends from the office, saying, "We have too much halwa. Save us." Kamal laughed, then cried a little into the kitchen towel. Later, over cards, Kamal said, "I am not going to argue about who was right anymore." Rukmini nodded and dealt again.

What did Rukmini bring to the door?
Rukmini brought a box of sweets and two friends from the office.
What was Kamal feeling on seeing the photo of the rooftop puja?
A hollow ache of grief over the lost bond, rather than anger.
How is Kamal building a chosen family?
By opening the door to Rukmini and the friends, sharing food and cards and letting the sadness show.
How might Rukmini see Kamal's tears?
Rukmini seems to accept them without fuss, nodding and dealing the next hand, giving Kamal room to feel them.

Coding club note, Tuesday
In September Anirban told me he had finished forty hours of programming videos. He can name every topic: loops, functions, lists. Today I gave the group an empty editor and one task: print the numbers one to ten, then only the even ones.
Tarun finished in four minutes after two wrong tries. Anirban sat very still, then opened a video in another tab. I asked him to close it. For ten minutes he typed and deleted the same line. Finally he said quietly, “In the videos it just works. I always typed what they typed.”
That is the gap. Watching felt like learning, but he never had to produce code from nothing. I did not push it in front of the group. After club we agreed on one small exercise a day, written before any video, and he will show me on Thursday.
– Club mentor

What task did the club mentor give the group?
Print the numbers one to ten, then only the even ones, in an empty editor.
What was Anirban probably feeling while typing and deleting the same line?
He was likely embarrassed and confused, since forty hours of videos had made him feel ready and now nothing came out on his own.
What could Anirban try instead of more videos?
Write one small exercise a day before watching anything and use a video only to get unstuck, so the typing comes from his own thinking.
How might Tarun see Anirban's struggle?
Tarun might be surprised, since Anirban can name every topic, and may realise that Tarun's own two wrong tries were part of the learning.

Dear Tanvir,
I've wanted to write this for a week. We've been friends since school, bhai, so I hope you'll read it the way I mean it.
Since you became the exam hall supervisor at the coaching centre, I've watched you from the next room. You shout at students who look up from their papers. Last Tuesday you tore up a boy's rough sheet because he asked for water.
That isn't you. At home you are the one who brings everyone chai. I think the badge and the pressure from the centre head are pulling you into someone else.
Could we talk about it? Maybe ask the head for clearer rules, so nobody has to guess.
Jyoti

What did Tanvir tear up last Tuesday?
He tore up a boy's rough sheet.
What might Jyoti feel while writing this letter?
Jyoti is likely worried and careful, caring about the friendship while being honest about what was seen.
What does Jyoti suggest, and why might it help?
Talking together and asking the centre head for clearer rules, so the pressure doesn't push Tanvir into harshness.
How might Tanvir feel on reading this?
He may feel defensive at first, but also recognised, since Jyoti remembers the friend who brings everyone chai.

Read this:

"Beta, listen to this one," said Naveen, setting down his tea. "When I was your age, in Class 6, we had a maths teacher who never smiled. One day I asked him, 'Sir, why was six afraid of seven?' He said nothing. I said, 'Because seven eight nine!' The whole class exploded. Even Sir's moustache twitched. After that I collected riddles in a notebook and told one at every recess. The boys who used to ignore me started saving me a seat." Suraj groaned, then grinned. "Dadu, that's the same joke you told last Diwali!" "Good jokes never retire," Naveen said, and started another.

What did young Naveen ask his maths teacher?
He asked, "Sir, why was six afraid of seven?" and gave the answer, "Because seven eight nine!"
What did Naveen want when he began collecting riddles in a notebook?
He seems to have wanted to share fun and belong, since he told one at every recess and the boys who ignored him began saving him a seat.
What could Suraj do to try his own wordplay with his grandfather?
Suraj could invent a pun of his own, or trade riddles with Naveen at teatime, so the two of them can enjoy a new joke together.
How might the strict teacher have seen Naveen's joke?
His moustache twitched, so he may have been amused even though he never smiled. He might also have been surprised that a quiet boy dared to joke with him.

Read this:

Kamal, you keep looking at Dinesh sir's cabin as if it might bite. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age. My first manager, Mrs Lobo, stopped greeting me in the mornings. Just stopped. For a whole week I built the case in my head: she'd seen my typo in the tender, she'd heard me joke in the lift, she was going to move me to records. I had whole conversations with her in the shower, both sides. I was very good at her lines. On the Friday I was so tired of it that I knocked on her door and asked, 'Have I done something wrong?' She looked up. 'Arohi, no! I've got new glasses and can't see anyone past three feet.' Two minutes. A week of my life. So go and knock.

What reason did Mrs Lobo give for not greeting Arohi?
Mrs Lobo had new glasses and couldn't see anyone past three feet.
Why did the imagined conversations feel so convincing to Arohi?
Arohi was anxious all week, and with real details to hang the fears on, the typo and the lift joke, the imagined lines began to feel like things actually said.
What was the turning point in Arohi's story, and what does it suggest for Kamal?
The turning point was knocking and asking 'Have I done something wrong?'; it suggests Kamal can end the guessing about Dinesh sir with one direct question.
How might Kamal feel after hearing that a week of worry ended in two minutes?
Kamal may feel braver and a little amused, seeing that a senior colleague once lived inside a made-up story and got out simply by asking.

Read this:

Thursday, Bengaluru. Entry 9 in the prediction notebook.

Vijay started this for me three weeks ago when I refused to try Kannada at the vegetable market. My forecast then: "They'll laugh, I'll freeze, I'll go home with nothing. 95% sure."

Today's plan was small: ask the tomato lady the price in Kannada. Only that.

Before: 80% sure it'll go badly.

What happened: I got one word wrong. She corrected me, smiling, and then told me her daughter is learning Hindi and mixes things up too. I bought tomatoes and coriander. She threw in two green chillies free.

So: forecast wrong again.

Looking back through the notebook, my numbers are coming down on their own. Entry 1 was 95. Entry 5 was 70. Today, 80, and it still went fine. I'm not saying I'm brave now. But the notebook knows more about me than my fear does.

Tomorrow: ask the bus conductor something.

Preeti

What did the tomato lady throw in free?
She threw in two green chillies free.
What does Preeti mean by "the notebook knows more about me than my fear does"?
Preeti feels the written record of what actually happened is more trustworthy than the fear, which keeps predicting disaster. The notebook shows a pattern the fear ignores.
What small step would you suggest after the bus conductor?
Keep raising the challenge a little, like a longer chat at the market, and keep writing the forecast and the result. The record will keep correcting the predictions.
How might the tomato lady see Preeti's attempt at Kannada?
She seemed pleased and warm, correcting gently and sharing that her own daughter mixes things up too. To her, the effort probably mattered more than the wrong word.

Every autumn the boys of the para built their own small pandal behind the pond, and Anirban had always watched from his grandmother's veranda. This year Hemant, who ran the group, shouted up, "Anirban! Can you paint? Come!" He ran down so fast he left his slippers behind. They gave him the lion's mane to paint. By evening his hands were yellow, and the other boys were calling him "Lion-babu." On the way home he kept looking back at the lit pandal. That night he told his grandmother, "Next year, they said I can do the eyes."

Which part did the boys give Anirban to paint?
The lion's mane.
What does Anirban running down without his slippers show?
He had longed to be part of the group for years and was thrilled to be invited in.
How could Hemant help other watching children feel welcome too?
Keep calling out to children on the edge and give each one a real job, the way he did with Anirban.
How might Anirban's grandmother see the change in him?
She may be happy to see him glowing after years of watching from the veranda.

All at once I remembered that it might be Pilot, who, when the kitchen-door chanced to be left open, not unfrequently found his way up to the threshold of Mr. Rochester's chamber: I had seen him lying there myself in the mornings. The idea calmed me somewhat: I lay down. Silence composes the nerves; and as an unbroken hush now reigned again through the whole house, I began to feel the return of slumber. But it was not fated that I should sleep that night. A dream had scarcely approached my ear, when it fled affrighted, scared by a marrow-freezing incident enough.

Why does the thought of Pilot calm the narrator?

Pilot sometimes finds his way to the threshold of Mr. Rochester's bedroom when the kitchen door is left open. The narrator has seen him lying there in the mornings, so the idea is calming enough to lie down.
In this picture there are 8 birds. You cannot move them. How do you count them without missing any?

Answer: 8 birds. Count row by row from left to right, or put a small counter (a button) on each bird as you count it.

When things cannot be moved, we need a plan: go in order (left to right, top to bottom), or mark each counted one.

Saturday: At the colony skating rink, Usha glided round and round, arms out, grinning. Forward laps were her favourite; the wheels hummed. "Usha, T-stop drill, please!" called Sachin, the coach. She did one wobbly try, then went back to her laps. "I'm practising," she said.
Next Saturday: Sachin blew the whistle for the relay. Usha raced forward beautifully and then could not stop at the cone. She slammed into the rail and sat down hard, cheeks burning. The others had stopped neatly.
Wednesday: Usha asked to come early. For twenty minutes she did nothing but T-stops, one foot dragging behind. She fell twice and muttered, "This is boring and horrible." Sachin counted each try with her. On the last one she stopped on the line, and her mouth fell open.

What did Usha do when Sachin called for the T-stop drill on the first Saturday?
She did one wobbly try, then went back to her laps.
What was Usha feeling after slamming into the rail?
Usha was embarrassed and upset; her cheeks were burning while the others had stopped neatly.
What could Usha keep doing in every session?
Spend part of each session on the hard drill, like the twenty minutes of T-stops, before the fun forward laps.
How might Sachin feel watching Usha stop on the line on Wednesday?
Sachin is probably pleased and proud, having counted every try with Usha and watched the boring drill finally pay off.
Yanna bought 60 apples. She gave eighteen apples to Zenny. She gave six more apples to Andrea and kept the rest. How many apples did she keep?

After giving 18 apples to Zenny, Yanna remained with 60 - 18 = 42 apples.
Since she also gave Andrea 6 apples, Yanna remained with 42 - 6 = 36 apples
Therefore, Yanna kept 36 apples.
The answer is 36.

In the accounts room of the engineering college, Damini filled in her travel claim for the inspection visit. The auto had cost very little. The form had a box for "taxi".
"Just put taxi," Chinmay said from the next desk, not looking up. "Everyone does. They pay us nothing anyway."
Damini's pen hovered. Her brother's coaching fees were due. It's only this once, she thought. It's not really stealing; the college owes me for all the Saturdays I've worked. I'll make it up somehow.
She ticked "taxi" and wrote a round figure. Her hand felt strange, as if it belonged to someone else.
The claim was approved in two days, no questions asked. The second time, a month later, she didn't even pause. That surprised her more than anything.

Which box did Damini tick on the travel claim?
She ticked 'taxi'.
What was Damini feeling as the pen hovered?
Damini felt pressured by her brother's fees and uneasy, telling herself it was only once and that the college owed her for the Saturdays.
What could Damini do now that a second claim has gone through?
Stop, correct both claims with accounts, and speak to a trusted senior before the habit grows.
How does Chinmay see small padding of claims?
Chinmay treats it as normal, 'Everyone does', which made Damini's first step feel easier than it should have.

Read this:

Amandeep, you keep asking how I'm so calm about the layoff. I'm not calm. I'm Santosh, and I'm still scared on Sunday nights. But here's what I did.
After the first week of feeling sorry for myself, I sat down and asked: what do companies actually pay for right now? I asked three people I knew in hiring. All three said the same thing: cloud. Support people who understand cloud systems.
So I picked one beginner cloud certification. Two hours a day at the library, before it gets crowded. And because I needed money, I took a part-time gig on weekends, setting up computers for a small clinic near my house. ₹6,000 a month. Not much.
Here's the thing. The layoff still happened. I still worry. But every day I'm doing something that adds up, instead of just replaying the bad day. That's the only difference, Amandeep. It's not a small one.

What part-time gig did Santosh take?
Setting up computers for a small clinic near the house, on weekends.
How does Santosh feel on Sunday nights?
Still scared, despite seeming calm to others; the worry has not gone away.
What else could Santosh try to connect the course to a job?
Go back to the three hiring contacts once the certification is done and ask about referrals or interviews.
Why might Amandeep think Santosh is calm?
Amandeep sees daily study and a weekend gig, the outward signs of a plan, without seeing the Sunday-night fear.

"They gave it to Karan," Nikita said, dropping into the chair by Rajni's desk. "The senior designer post. Karan. Who copied my layout for the bank campaign."

"Oh, Nikki."

"I'm going to Sunil sir's cabin right now and telling him exactly what I think. In front of everyone."

Rajni put a hand on her arm. "Don't. Not now. You're shaking."

"I am so angry I could scream."

"I know. Walk with me to the chai stall first. Then decide."

They walked. By the second cup, Nikita's hands were steady. "Fine. What do I do?"

"Write down the facts. Your projects, the bank campaign dates, the client emails. Then ask Sunil sir for a private meeting and ask how they decided."

"And if the answer's rubbish?"

"Then you decide whether this is still the place for you. Calmly."

Nikita nodded. That evening she booked a Thursday meeting with Sunil sir and made a folder called "Facts".

Who got the senior designer post?
Karan got the senior designer post.
How did Nikita feel when she came to Rajni's desk?
Nikita felt burning anger, shaking and ready to confront their manager publicly.
What steps did Rajni suggest, and why were they wise?
Let the first surge pass, collect the facts, ask the manager privately how they decided, and then calmly decide whether to stay, because a public outburst rarely helps.
How does Rajni see Nikita's plan to confront Sunil sir in public?
Rajni sees it as a risky reaction driven by anger, and worries it would hurt Nikita.

Read Mina's diary entry. How does Lucy help her?

12 August.--My expectations were wrong, for twice during the night I was wakened by Lucy trying to get out. She seemed, even in her sleep, to be a little impatient at finding the door shut, and went back to bed under a sort of protest. I woke with the dawn, and heard the birds chirping outside of the window. Lucy woke, too, and, I was glad to see, was even better than on the previous morning. All her old gaiety of manner seemed to have come back, and she came and snuggled in beside me and told me all about Arthur. I told her how anxious I was about Jonathan, and then she tried to comfort me. Well, she succeeded somewhat, for, though sympathy can't alter facts, it can help to make them more bearable.
Lucy, cheerful again, snuggles beside her and comforts her about Jonathan. Mina says sympathy cannot change facts but makes them easier to bear.

Read this:

At the bus stand outside Mahua, Deepak leaned against the tea stall and said loudly, "Vikas only got into the district hostel school because his uncle knows the headmaster." A few boys laughed. Vikas felt the words go in like a splinter. He had studied by lamp light for months, but he had also heard his uncle mention the headmaster once, and a small voice asked, what if it is partly true? He didn't argue. He bought his bus ticket and stared out of the window. That evening he went to his science teacher and asked, "Sir, was my selection fair? Do you think I can keep up?" The teacher told him the entrance marks were his own and gave him two areas to work on. Vikas felt lighter, and got out his notebook.

Where did Deepak make his remark about Vikas?
At the bus stand outside Mahua, by the tea stall.
Why did the remark sting Vikas so much?
Because he half-feared it might be partly true after remembering his uncle mention the headmaster, even though he had worked hard for months.
What did Vikas do that was wise?
He didn't argue, and let his work answer. He asked his science teacher for honest feedback and got specific areas to improve.
How might Deepak see Vikas's silence at the bus stand?
Possibly as an admission, or as a lack of reaction that takes away the fun of teasing. Deepak may also be jealous, but the passage does not say.
I saw "incivility" in a story. What does it mean? How do I get ready for a day of festival cooking? Why is a person tall on stilts able to see further? How can I be a good host at a small party?

1. "Incivility" is a noun. It means rude behaviour.
2. Make a list of dishes and prepare ingredients the day before. Share the jobs with the family so no one is tired.
3. A higher viewpoint lets you see further. Because the eyes are higher, the line of sight clears more of the ground in between.
4. Welcome each guest at the door and introduce people who have not met. Check that everyone has something to drink.

A pizza is cut into 8 slices. Each of 4 children eats 3/8 of a pizza. How much pizza do they eat altogether?

Now you try: 6 x 3/10.
In one day, Ella's dog eats 4 pounds of food for every one pound of food that Ella eats. How much food do Ella and her dog in 10 days if Ella eat 20 pounds of food each day?

If Ella's dog eats 4 pounds of food for every one pound of food that Ella eats, when Ella eats 20 pounds of food in a day, Ella's dog eats 4*20 = 80 pounds of food.
Together, in one day, Ella and her dog eats 80+20 = 100 pounds
In 10 days, Ella and her dog will eat 10*100 = 1000 pounds of food.
The answer is 1000.
My teacher says Raga Bhairav sounds serious. Which notes give it that colour?
Komal Re and komal Dha, sung slowly and with weight. Bhairav is a prayerful morning raga.

Read this:

Career centre counsellor's note, final-year students.

Damini has come to three talks this term and always sits in the front row with a notebook. Today's speaker was Dr Rao, a marine biologist who now runs a children's science theatre. After the talk, Damini waited in the queue for twenty minutes and asked her, "How did you know?"

Dr Rao said she didn't. She had trained as a dentist, left, worked in a bookshop, then studied biology at twenty-nine. Three changes of course in all.

I watched Damini's face. She looked surprised, then almost relieved. Later she told me, "I've been waiting to feel certain before I apply for anything."

We agreed she would stop waiting and apply for two different summer programmes, one in research and one in outreach, and see which one pulls her. She also plans to ask three more professionals about their paths.

- Sunaina

What did Dr Rao study at twenty-nine?
Dr Rao studied biology at twenty-nine.
What was Damini feeling after hearing Dr Rao's answer?
Damini looked surprised and then almost relieved, realising she didn't need to wait for certainty.
What plan did Damini and Sunaina agree on?
Damini will apply for two different summer programmes and ask three more professionals about their paths, instead of waiting to feel sure.
How might Dr Rao see a student like Damini waiting in the queue?
Dr Rao is likely glad to share her path with a curious student who is searching, as she once was.
A batsman's scores in 5 matches were 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Find sigma using sigma^2 = sum x^2 / n - m^2, check with the definition, and prove that the two formulas always agree.

Answer: sum x^2 = 100 + 400 + 900 + 1,600 + 2,500 = 5,500; sigma^2 = 5,500 / 5 - 30^2 = 1,100 - 900 = 200; sigma = sqrt200 ~ 14.14 runs.

Check by the definition: deviations -20, -10, 0, 10, 20; squares 400, 100, 0, 100, 400, total 1,000; 1,000 / 5 = 200. Same. Proof: expand (x - m)^2 = x^2 - 2mx + m^2 and add over all n values: sum (x - m)^2 = sum x^2 - 2msum x + nm^2. But sum x = nm, so this is sum x^2 - 2nm^2 + nm^2 = sum x^2 - nm^2. Divide by n: sum (x - m)^2 / n = sum x^2 / n - m^2. The short-cut is quicker when the mean is not a whole number, because we never subtract it from each value. Common mistakes: using (sum x)^2 instead of sum x^2 (150^2 = 22,500 is not 5,500), and forgetting to square the mean.

Chaitanya and Jatin shared a one-room flat in Pune and a looming job deadline, so Chaitanya noticed the change fast. Jatin, who used to joke about everything, now stayed up till three in a forum that blamed 'outsiders' for every problem in the city. His words changed: people became 'those types'. One night, when a delivery rider was late, Jatin swore at him in a way that made Chaitanya's stomach turn. Chaitanya wanted to shout, or unplug the router. Instead, the next morning over chai, he asked, 'What's that forum giving you that we're not?' Jatin was quiet, then said, 'Everyone there gets how unfair things are.' They talked for an hour. Chaitanya didn't win the argument. But he suggested they both see the college counsellor about job stress, and on Thursday Jatin went.

Till what time did Jatin stay up in the forum?
Till three.
How did Chaitanya feel when Jatin swore at the delivery rider?
Chaitanya felt sick and alarmed, stomach turning, tempted to shout or unplug the router.
Why was Chaitanya's morning question wiser than unplugging the router?
Asking what the forum gave Jatin opened a real conversation and led to the counsellor, while confiscating would likely have pushed Jatin away.
What does Jatin seem to be getting from the forum?
A feeling of being understood about how unfair things are, which hints at stress and loneliness behind the harder language.

Read this:

"You're avoiding the health check again," Avni said, spotting the office email still marked unread.
Gopika sighed. "I'm twenty-five. I'm fine."
"Your mother had to start diabetes medicines at forty. And your Ammamma before her."
"That's them."
"That's your family history. Doctors ask about it for a reason."
Gopika stirred her tea. "What if they find something?"
"Then you know early, when it's easier to deal with. Isn't that better than finding out later?"
"You sound like my mother."
"Your mother would be proud of me." Avni grinned. "The office does it free. I'll book us both for the same morning."
"And you'll hold my hand for the blood test?"
"I'll hold your bag. Your hand is your problem."
Gopika laughed, opened the email and clicked register. "Fine. But you're buying breakfast after."

At what age did Gopika's mother start diabetes medicines?
At forty.
What was Gopika worried about in going for the check?
Gopika felt anxious that the check might find something.
Why is family history a good reason to go for a check-up?
It can show a risk early, when it is easier to manage, instead of discovering it later.
How does Avni see Gopika's avoidance?
Avni sees fear behind it and responds with humour and practical help, booking them both together.
Now you try: I think of a number, multiply it by 4 and subtract 7. The answer is 29. What is my number?
The answer is 4n - 7 = 29, n = 9.
Now you try: mean 50, sigma = 10 and mean 80, sigma = 12; which has the smaller CV?
The answer is 20% and 15%: the second.

Read this:

Jeevan's history essay came back with the lowest mark he had ever got and a comment that the argument was missing. He was sure he had written one. He did not complain to the class, and he did not sit in silence either. That evening he underlined the paragraph, copied the marking rubric from the school portal and waited by Ms Rashmi's table after class. "Ma'am, may I show you where I think my argument is? I might have misread what the rubric wants." She read the paragraph twice. "Ah. Page three was stuck to page four. I only read half your essay." She corrected the mark and said, "Thank you for asking politely rather than telling me off." Jeevan felt his shoulders drop.

What did Jeevan bring to show Ms Rashmi?
He brought the underlined paragraph and the marking rubric.
Why did Jeevan say he might have misread what the rubric wants?
He wanted to raise his concern politely without accusing her, and left room for the possibility that he was the one who was wrong.
What could Jeevan do if the teacher had disagreed?
He could listen to her reasons, ask how to improve, or take the concern to the coordinator or head through the school's proper channel.
How might Ms Rashmi have felt when Jeevan approached her?
She was probably relieved that he asked calmly, since she admitted her mistake and thanked him.

Read this:

In their flat in Alexandria, Siddiq, four, told his grandmother about the beach trip. "A big crab bit my toe, and I cried."
Dalia, his mother, looked up. A crab had walked near his foot. Nobody got bitten. But on the drive home his cousin had said, "Careful, crabs bite!" and at bedtime they had read a crab book.
By the weekend, Siddiq had shown his toe to his teacher and the neighbour, and the crab got bigger each time.
Dalia didn't argue. She found the beach photos, and they looked together. "Look, there's the crab walking away," she said.

What did the crab really do at the beach?

The letter came to the post office in the hill town of Almora, and Seema, who worked the counter, recognised the university seal before she'd even sorted it. It was addressed to her younger brother, Ojas. She ran it home at lunch. Ojas tore it open on the doorstep, read it twice and whispered, "I got in." Seema shrieked so loudly the neighbour's goat bolted. She wanted to throw her arms around him, but theirs wasn't a hugging family, and Ojas, at nineteen, flinched at most displays. She held her arms half out instead. "Can I?" He laughed, embarrassed, and stepped into it. Just for a second. Then he pulled back and said, "Don't tell the whole street." "Only Amma," she promised, and ran to the kitchen. That he had got into the university.

She held her arms half out and asked 'Can I?', kept the hug brief, respected his wish for privacy, and kept her joy professional at work.

Today, at the school science lesson, Jake learned that there are 8 more solar systems for every planet in the galaxy. If there are 20 planets in the galaxy, how many solar systems and planets are there altogether?

If there are 8 more solar systems for every planet in the galaxy, there are 8+1 = 9 solar systems for every planet.
Since the number of planets is 20, there are 20*9 = 180 solar systems in the galaxy.
Altogether, there are 180+20 = 200 solar systems and planets in the galaxy.
The answer is 200.

But he kept coming. He liked the way Rishabh saved him a seat by the window. He liked their team name, the Zeros, and their silly handshake. When the Zeros had to solve twelve puzzles for the colony quiz, Anmol stayed back two extra Saturdays so he wouldn't be the one who let them down.
He still said he hated maths. But by December he was solving the logic puzzles faster than anyone, because the Zeros needed him to.

James has 3 gallons of milk. He drank 13 ounces of the milk. If there are 128 ounces in a gallon, how many ounces of milk does James have left?

First find out how many ounces of milk James had to begin with by multiplying the number of gallons by the number of ounces per gallon: 3 gallons * 128 ounces/gallon = 384 oz
Now subtract the 13 ounces James drank from the initial amount of milk: 384 oz - 13 oz = 371 oz
The answer is 371.

The farmer cooperative's office in Bankura smelled of jute sacks. This season's new paddy variety had failed on half the plots, and members were angry. "Preeti madam pushed this seed," someone shouted. "Anyone could see it was risky." Arnab, the secretary, didn't argue. He opened the red register where, every June, he wrote down each decision before sowing. He read aloud: "New variety on forty plots. Reason: resists the pest that hit us last year. Risk: needs steady rain. Rain forecast: normal. Our guess: good yield, seven chances in ten." He looked up. "The rain stopped for three weeks in August. None of us knew that in June." The room grew quieter. An old farmer nodded slowly. "Then next year, some plots old seed, some new." Preeti, at the back, finally unclenched her hands.

What reason did the register give for choosing the new variety?
It resists the pest that hit them last year.
Why did Arnab open the red register instead of arguing?

What lesson did the old farmer draw, and why is it a good one?

What might Preeti have felt as the room grew quieter?
Preeti likely felt relieved, unclenching her hands once the register showed the blame was unfair.

"You're not going to the march tomorrow?" Ishita asked, watching her brother Hrithik pace the balcony.

"I want to. The exam fairness thing matters." He rubbed his face. "But what if the police do something? Or the principal suspends everyone? Papa would kill me."

"Is it a permitted march?"

"Yes. The organisers have police permission. Silent, placards, two hours."

"Then it's not illegal to walk in it. But you're still scared."

"Yeah. Which makes me feel like a coward."

Ishita sat on the ledge. "It's not cowardice. Your fear is telling you to be careful. That's useful."

"So what do I do with it?"

"Stay on the route. Stay with the teachers who are going. Tell Papa exactly where you'll be. Leave if it stops being peaceful. And read the school's rule on this tonight, so you know."

Hrithik let out a long breath. "Okay. I'll talk to Papa now."

The march is two hours long.
What was Hrithik feeling as he paced the balcony?
Hrithik felt afraid of police action and suspension, and ashamed that the fear made him feel like a coward.
What does Ishita suggest Hrithik do with his fear?
She suggests staying on the route with the teachers, telling Papa where he will be, leaving if it stops being peaceful and reading the school's rule.
How does Ishita see her brother's fear?

My days were full of little choices: which assignment first, which lab partner, what to eat, whether to call home. By night I had nothing left. That's when I said yes to things I'd never agree to in daylight, like Ramesh's midnight bike ride to the highway dhaba before a quiz, or buying a game I didn't need. Last January I printed the senior-analyst criteria and put them next to my own work from the year. Five rows. Next to each I wrote what I had. Numbers accuracy, fine. Client reports, fine. Training juniors, fine. Then "leads initiatives across teams." I had written a big question mark.

I offered to run the shared forecasting process with the sales and supply teams. It took up two quarters of my life. But by the review, I had meeting notes, a process doc, and two team heads who'd seen me lead.

'It's a school race. You don't have to win.'
'I told the whole class I'd win. In front of Ma'am.'
'So?'
'So if I sit home eating pakodas, I lied.'
'You'll slip in the mud.'
'I'll go round the building parking. It has a roof.'
'Twenty rounds of a parking?'
'Thirty.'
Gargi sighed. 'Fine. I'm timing you. And if your chest hurts, you stop.'
'Deal.' Yash already had his helmet on.
Twenty minutes later Gargi shouted down the stairs, 'Thirty! Now come and eat.'
Yash wheeled in, soaked with sweat, grinning. 'Tomorrow, thirty-five.'

Where did Yash cycle because of the rain?
Round the building parking, which has a roof.
Why did Yash insist on cycling in the monsoon rain?
Yash felt determined and a little anxious about looking like a liar; having told the whole class he would win, skipping practice felt wrong.
How did Gargi support Yash, and what else could help?
Gargi agreed to time him and set a safety rule; she could also remind him that trying hard counts even if he doesn't win.
How might Gargi feel watching Yash push for thirty-five rounds?
Gargi may feel both proud of his effort and a little worried that he is putting too much weight on one promise.

Subject: How I finally explained the new billing system
Hi Mehak,
You asked how Friday's briefing for the clinic staff went so well. Honestly, it was my Nani.
On Thursday night I tried my explanation on her. She has never used a computer. My first version was full of words like "workflow" and "auto-reconciliation". She listened politely and said, "Beta, I understood nothing." So I started again: "You know how the milkman writes each day's milk in his book, and at month-end you check it together? The new system does that checking by itself." Her face lit up. Then I asked her to explain it back to me. She said, "The computer checks the milk book." Perfect.
On Friday I used the milk book, plain words, and asked two nurses to say it back. No confused faces.
Try it with your next training!
Jaya

What example did Jaya use to explain the new system?
The milkman writing each day's milk in his book and checking it together at month-end.
How did Jaya probably feel when Nani said "I understood nothing"?
Jaya was likely a little deflated but also grateful, realising the jargon only made sense to someone already inside the field.
Which steps made Jaya's briefing work?
Testing the explanation on Nani, swapping jargon for the milk-book example, and asking listeners to say it back.
How might the nurses have felt during Friday's briefing?
The nurses probably felt included and confident, since the milk book made sense and they were asked to explain it back 🙂

Art teacher's note, Class 9C, Thursday
Ritu's watercolour of the school garden was chosen for the district display today. When I told her in class, she said, 'Anyone could have done it, it's just a garden.' When a classmate said the sky was the best part, she said, 'The paper just soaked it up that way.' I've noticed she does this with every compliment, while she keeps a folder of her worst pieces 'to remember'. After class I asked her to tell me, step by step, how she painted the sky. She described three layers, waiting for each to dry, and lifting colour with a tissue. That isn't luck. I told her so, plainly, and asked her to write those three steps on the back of the painting before it goes to the district. She rolled her eyes, but she wrote them.
Zubin

How many layers did Ritu describe for the sky?
Ritu described three layers.
Why might Ritu keep a folder of her worst pieces but wave away praise?
Ritu seems to hold a low view of her own ability, so failures feel like the truth worth keeping, while praise feels like a mistake to explain away.
Why was asking Ritu to describe how she painted the sky a smart move?
Describing the three layers showed that the result came from skill and patience, making it harder to call it luck, and writing the steps down keeps that evidence.
How might the classmate who praised the sky feel hearing 'The paper just soaked it up'?
The classmate might feel brushed off, as if the compliment were wrong, and may be less likely to offer praise next time.
Friends who are unlikely: a rose and a weed. Could you write their story?

Among the neat rows of Mrs. Gupta's flower bed grew one tiny weed. The roses looked down on him. "You do not belong," said Rani, the reddest rose. "You are plain."

The weed, named Dhaniya, said nothing. He kept growing, staying near the roots, soaking up sunlight in his small way.

Then a hot, dry month came. The soil cracked. The roses wilted. But Dhaniya's low, wide leaves shaded the ground around Rani's stem and kept the soil from drying out.

When the rains came, Rani looked down and noticed that the weed had kept her soil damp. "Thank you," she said softly.

Mrs. Gupta pulled out the other weeds but left Dhaniya, saying he looked rather sweet beside the roses.

The house felt wrong without Dada. His slippers still sat by the door, and nobody had moved his spectacles from the newspaper. Vasudha was fine all morning, then at the market a shopkeeper held out the sweet biscuits Dada liked and her eyes stung so suddenly she had to grip the counter. That evening a neighbour patted her arm. "He had a long life, beta. Time to move on." Vasudha's face went stiff. Bua Parul, arriving with a tiffin, took her hand instead. "Come, we'll light his evening lamp the way he always did." They lit it together. "Tell me the mango tree story," said Bua Parul, and Vasudha laughed and cried at once, letting it come for the first time in days.

What was still sitting by the door?
Dada's slippers were still sitting by the door.
What was Vasudha feeling when she gripped the market counter?
A sudden wave of grief: her eyes stung so suddenly that she had to hold on.
What helped Vasudha that evening?
Lighting Dada's lamp as he always did and telling stories about him with Bua Parul, so she could let the feelings come.
How might the neighbour's words feel to Vasudha compared with Bua Parul's?
"Time to move on" made Vasudha's face go stiff, as if grief was unwelcome, while Bua Parul's invitation gave the grief room.

Coloured rice on a paper plate.

She felt hollow and homesick, missing the Diwali morning rituals at home.

Sharing the feeling with Gopika and creating a small new ritual together, a rice rangoli and battery candles, that she plans to repeat.

Next Saturday: A second date, different café. She looked, smiled, looked away at the rain, looked back. He talked for an hour.

She held eye contact the whole time.

That gaze should fit the setting: steady for interviews, softer with breaks on dates.

messages.content: Delaney has to catch a bus that leaves at 8:00. a.m to school every day. He always takes 30 minutes to reach the pick-up point from his home. One day he woke up late and left his home at 7:50. How much time did he miss the bus by when he reached the pick-up point?

If he left his home at 7:50 a.m. and the distance to the pick-up point is 30 minutes away, he arrived at the pick-up point at 7:50 + 30 minutes = 8:20 a.m.
If the bus leaves at 8:00 a.m. every day, then Delaney was 8:20 a.m. - 8:00 a.m. = 20 minutes late when the bus had already left.
The answer is 20.

I shared an office with Trisha at the charity when she had two decisions in the same week, and I watched how differently she handled them. The first was the colour of the new flyers. She picked blue in two minutes. "If people don't like it, we reprint next month," she said. The second was whether to sign a three-year lease on a new office. That one she slowed right down. She visited twice, asked our accountant Ishita to check the numbers, and called another charity that had rented there. It took her two weeks. I can't say what she was thinking, but she seemed calm both times, just careful in proportion.

How long did Trisha take to decide on the flyer colour?
She picked blue in two minutes.
How did Trisha seem to feel making the two decisions?
She seemed calm both times, relaxed about the flyers and carefully cautious about the lease.
Why was Trisha's different speed for each decision wise?
The flyer colour could be undone cheaply by reprinting, while a three-year lease could not, so she matched her care to the cost of a mistake.
How might Ishita see Trisha's request to check the numbers?
Ishita might see it as a sensible step, glad to be asked before a decision that couldn't easily be undone.
Emily went to the store and bought art supplies for $20 and 2 skirts that cost the same amount of money. She spent a total of $50. How much did Emily pay for each of the skirts?

First, you need to set up the problem with the information given. The cost of the skirts and art supplies must equal $50.
Since we know that the cost of the skirts is the same price and that she bought art supplies for $20, we can set up an equation: 2x + 20 = 50, with x being the cost of the skirts.
To solve the equation, subtract 20 from both sides, to give you the new equation: 2x = 30.
Solve for x by dividing both sides of the equation by 2, 2x/2 = 30/2 gives you x = 15.
Therefore, each skirt cost $15.
The answer is 15.

Yamini, since you're flat-hunting, sit and listen. I am Keerthana, and at twenty-one I found a lovely room in Hyderabad. The landlord's first message asked, "Surname? Vegetarian or non-veg? Which state?" I answered, and an hour later the room was "taken". A friend saw the same room advertised again the next day. I felt small first, then furious. Then I made myself act. I saved every message with its date, told two friends who had been turned away by the same man, and together we took it to a tenants' group in the city, where a volunteer explained that it was discrimination and how we could make a formal complaint. Nobody promised the man would change. But we found another room within the week, and I stopped thinking the fault was in my surname.

The landlord's first message asked, "Surname? Vegetarian or non-veg? Which state?"
How did young Keerthana feel when the room turned out to be advertised again?
Keerthana felt small at first and then furious, realising that the "taken" room was not about anything Keerthana had done.
Which choice by young Keerthana turned hurt into action?
Keerthana saved every message with its date, told two friends who had been turned away, and took it to a tenants' group for help.
How might the two other friends have felt when Keerthana contacted them?
Probably relieved that it was not only them, and more willing to act together, since they joined in taking it to the tenants' group.

messages.content: A magic seed story, please, with a title at the top.

The Seed in the Teacup

Nina found a round, silver seed in her teacup after a family picnic. She planted it in a pot on the balcony and watered it every morning.

On the fifth day, a tiny green shoot appeared. On the sixth, it was as tall as her hand. On the seventh, it opened a flower, and out of the flower came a very small voice.

"Good morning," said the voice. "I am the garden's first alarm clock. Nobody has ever listened to me."

Nina laughed and set the pot on her windowsill. Every morning after that, the flower sang her awake, and Nina was never late for school again.

In the village school near Aizawl, Ms Lalremsiami drew a simple outline on the board.
“The parts covered by your swimsuit are private,” she said. “No one may touch them, or ask you to keep a secret about them. Not a stranger, not someone you know.”
Chandrika, ten, put up her hand. “What if we tell someone and they don't listen?”
“Then you tell someone else. And someone else. Until someone believes you.”
Each child wrote three trusted adults on a card. Chandrika wrote: Ma, Ms Lalremsiami, my Aunty Sanga.
She folded the card and kept it in her pencil box.

How many trusted adults did each child write down?
Three trusted adults.
How did Chandrika feel about the question she asked?
She felt a little worried about not being believed, and reassured by the teacher's answer.
What did Ms Lalremsiami teach that is important?
That no one may touch private parts, and to keep telling trusted adults until someone believes you.
How might the other children feel after the lesson?
They may feel safer, knowing their bodies belong to them and whom to tell.

Mentoring programme observation note, session 4.
I sat in on Trisha's session with her mentee, Chetan, today. For three sessions Chetan had said everything was 'fine', though his project was clearly behind. Today Trisha tried something different. She told him about her first year: a dashboard project she had promised in six weeks that took five months, and how she hid the delay until her manager heard about it from a client. She kept it to about four minutes, then turned it back to him: 'So, how's yours really going?'
Chetan was quiet, then admitted he was two weeks behind and scared to say so. They spent the rest of the hour on a plan to tell his lead.
Trisha stopped her story before it became about her, which mattered. I have suggested she keep that balance.
Programme coordinator

How long did Trisha's dashboard project actually take?
Five months, instead of six weeks.
What was Chetan feeling before he admitted the delay?
Chetan was scared to admit being two weeks behind, which is why everything had been 'fine' for three sessions.
Why did Trisha keep the story to about four minutes?
So the session stayed about Chetan; a short story made it safe to admit mistakes without turning the focus to Trisha.
How might Chetan's lead be affected by the plan?
The lead will hear about the delay early from Chetan, which gives time to adjust instead of a surprise later.

Sunday evening.
Spent the morning painting on the balcony. Nothing for anyone. Just the neem tree and bad light. Loved it.
In the afternoon I did two hours on the data analysis certificate. I'm on module six out of twelve. Slow, but I'm actually learning, not rushing. I like my current job. I also want to lead projects in a couple of years. Both feel true.
Tushar called in a panic. Three people from our batch got promoted this month, and he's applying everywhere. "Aren't you worried you're falling behind?" he asked.
I thought about it. Honestly? Not much. I'm moving. Just not frantically. I'd rather enjoy the climb than stare at the next step.
Told him to come over next Sunday and paint with me.

Which module of the certificate is Sonali on?
Module six out of twelve.
How did Sonali feel when Tushar asked about falling behind?
Sonali felt calm and settled, not worried, because progress was happening at a steady, chosen pace.
What would you advise Tushar after hearing about Sonali's week?
He could choose one steady goal, like a course or project, and make room to enjoy something in the present, maybe painting next Sunday.

During the outbreak of the coronavirus, a company had to ramp up its toilet paper production three times more to cover the increased demand. If the company was producing 7000 toilet paper per day, calculate its total toilet paper production during March of 2020 after increasing its production.

If the company was producing 7000 toilet paper per day, when it ramped up its toilet paper production three times per day, it produced 3*7000 = 21000 more per day.
The total toilet production by the company increased to 7000+21000 = 28000
In March, with 31 days, the company produced a total of 28000*31 = 868000 toilet papers
The answer is 868000.
Amma has a ribbon 12 cm long. She cuts it in half for two plaits. How long is each piece?

Answer: 6 cm each. 1/2 of 12 cm = 12 / 2 = 6 cm.

Use a paper strip 12 cm long. Fold it so the ends meet exactly and crease it. Measure each part with a ruler: 6 cm. Two halves: 6 cm + 6 cm = 12 cm, the whole ribbon. Now fold a 20 cm strip in half: how long is each half?

At twenty I was a weaver's apprentice in Chanderi, and all I wanted was to make a border so fine you couldn't see where one thread ended. I, Usha, didn't tell anyone my goals. They were mine. Years later a buyer from Delhi picked up one of my saris and held it to the light without a word. That silence was the prize I had been working for.

Old Master Rehmat.
How did young Usha feel about those goals?
Usha felt determined and quietly private, caring about fine work more than status.
What was the turning point in the story?
The Delhi buyer silently holding the sari to the light showed that years of practice had reached true mastery.
How did Usha's cousins see that choice?
They laughed and thought Usha had no ambition because Usha stayed at the loom.

Usha and Pankaj had been together for a year at college in Nagpur, and her parents knew nothing. They had made it clear, more than once, that she would marry 'within our own community', and Pankaj's family wasn't. Then Amma phoned on Sunday: a family friend's son was coming to see her in three weeks. Usha felt the floor tilt. Her first instinct was to keep hiding and hope something would work itself out, or to do something dramatic in a rush. She'd seen a cousin run off, and the family still didn't speak. That evening she and Pankaj sat on the university steps with the monsoon dripping off the roof. 'Do we actually want a life together?' she asked. 'Not just now. Really.' They talked for hours: his mother, her father's temper, jobs, cities, what each of them would give up. By midnight they had a plan: Usha would tell her mother first, in person, before the visit, with her aunt beside her.

Who was coming to see Usha in three weeks?
A family friend's son.
What was Usha feeling when Amma phoned?
She felt shaken and anxious, as if the floor had tilted beneath her.
What was wise about Usha and Pankaj's talk on the steps?
They asked whether they truly wanted a life together and planned how to tell her family, instead of hiding or running off.
How might Usha's mother feel when Usha tells her in person?
Probably shocked and worried about the community, but told honestly rather than facing a sudden crisis.

"Saurabh, you ask why I leave the moment they announce a warning. I'll tell you, since I'm Joseph, and I once didn't.
I was twenty, living with my parents near the river in Kerala. Every monsoon there were warnings, and every monsoon the water came to our gate and stopped. So when the big alert came, I told Amma, 'Same as always.' Neighbours left. We didn't.
On the second night I heard water in the kitchen. By morning it was up to the windowsills. The road to the church on the hill was gone, completely under.
We climbed to the neighbour's terrace and waited a whole day. Fishermen from the coast came in their boats and took us out.
I kept thinking: every warning before had passed, so I thought this one would too. That's what nearly cost us."

Who took Joseph's family out of the flood?
Fishermen from the coast came in their boats and took them out.
What was young Joseph thinking when the big alert came, and how did Joseph feel?
Joseph felt confident and unworried, telling Amma it was the same as always because earlier warnings had passed.
What was the turning point in Joseph's story, and what should have been different?
Deciding to stay when neighbours left was the turning point; leaving when the alert came would have avoided the terrace and the rescue.
How might Joseph's mother have felt on the terrace?
Amma was likely frightened and exhausted, waiting a whole day for rescue after trusting that it would be the same as always.

Ritu had been secretary of the Sarangpur milk cooperative for one week when she called her first meeting. Twenty members sat on mats in the collection shed. Ritu stood up, forgot her notes, and let the talk go wherever it wanted: a wedding in the next village, the price of fodder, an old quarrel about the chilling machine. After two hours people went home to milk their buffaloes, and nothing was settled.
Charu, who had been a member for twenty years, stopped at the door. "Beti, next time, tell us what we're here to decide."
The next month Ritu arrived early and wrote on the blackboard: 1. New collection timing: 6 or 6:30? 2. Who repairs the chilling machine? 3. Anything else — five minutes. She put the wall clock where she could see it. When talk wandered, she pointed at the board. The meeting ended in forty minutes, with two answers written in chalk.

How long did the second meeting take?
The meeting ended in forty minutes.
How was Ritu feeling at the first meeting, and what shows it?
Ritu was nervous; she stood up, forgot her notes and let the talk go wherever it wanted.
Which change made the second meeting work?
Writing three items on the blackboard with a clear question each and keeping the wall clock in view, then pointing at the board when talk wandered.
How might Charu see Ritu's second meeting?
Charu would probably feel pleased and respected, since Ritu took Charu's advice and the members got clear answers quickly.
What is the polite way to get someone's attention: "excuse me", "sorry" or "pardon"?

Use "Excuse me" to get attention or to pass by. "Sorry" apologises for a mistake. "Pardon?" asks someone to repeat what they said.
Examples: Excuse me, is this seat free? Sorry, I stepped on your foot. Pardon? I did not hear you.

Lucy has $65 in the bank. She made a $15 deposit and then followed by a $4 withdrawal. What is Lucy's bank balance?

Lucy had $65 + $15 = $80 after making a deposit.
So, her bank balance is $80 - $4 = $76 after making a withdrawal.

She has already had 12*7 =84 ounces of water.
She needs to drink 100-84 = 16 more ounces to make it to 100 ounces.
The answer is 16.

Disha, you're sad your friends are all at the New Year party while you're stuck here with your cast? Let your Grandpa Francis tell you something. When I was fifteen, my mother died in November. That Christmas, our whole street in Goa was lit with stars and paper lanterns. The carol singers came to every house, and the neighbours danced all night. I sat on the balcao, the front porch, and watched. Every carol felt like a stone in my chest. My father was inside with my aunts. Then old Mr Rodrigues from two houses down came and sat next to me with two plates of cake. He didn't ask me to sing. He just said, 'Your mother loved this song.' I cried, and he let me. That was the first time the lights didn't feel cruel.

When did young Francis's mother die?
In November.
What did the carols feel like to young Francis?
Each carol felt like a stone in his chest; he was grieving and felt shut out of the street's joy.
What did Mr Rodrigues do that made a difference in the story?
He sat beside young Francis with cake, didn't push him to join in, and gently mentioned his mother, which let him cry.
What might Mr Rodrigues have noticed that others missed?
That a grieving boy was alone on the balcao while the whole street celebrated, and needed company, not cheering up.
A special school has a deaf-student population 3 times its blind-student population. If there are 180 students in total, how many blind students are there?

Let the number of blind students be x.
The number of deaf students will then be 3*x = 3x students.
The total number of students is x + 3x = 180 students.
Combining like terms gives 4x = 180.
So the value of x is 180/4 = 45.
The answer is 45.

I'm Lalremsiami, and at sixteen I was sure everyone who disagreed with my side in the school debate was stupid, or worse. It felt good, like standing on high ground. Who did Lalremsiami's teacher pair Lalremsiami with for the project?
The teacher paired Lalremsiami with Zothan.
Why did contempt feel good to Lalremsiami, and what did it cost?
It felt like standing on high ground, but it cost Lalremsiami friendship: lunch alone and quiet messages. 😊
