Our new puppy is mine, but my younger brother thinks he is his. We keep arguing over him.
A puppy can cause big feelings. Who actually brought him home, and what did your parents say?
We picked him together. Dad said we both share him.
Then a shared plan helps. Make a schedule for feeding, walking and playing, so each of you has your own jobs and your own time. Jobs also teach responsibility.
He is too young to walk him alone, though.
Then you can walk him together. Your brother can hold the lead for part of the walk while you stay close. It helps him feel the puppy is partly his, which may ease the arguments.
Good. What should we name him? We have not agreed on that either.
Make a short list, with each of you adding two names. Then vote, or pick randomly from a bowl. Whichever name wins, tell each other it is fair, since both of you agreed to the method.
Alright. What did Dad say about the puppy?
Dad said you both share him. Remind your brother of that when you make the walking schedule, and also when you pick the name, so the puppy truly feels like a shared pet.

Logan makes $65,000 a year. He spends $20,000 on rent every year, $5000 on groceries every year, and $8000 on gas every year. If he wants to have at least $42000 left, how much more money must he make each year?

Logan spends 20000+5000+8000 = 33000 a year.
Logan has 65000-33000 = 32000 left a year.
Logan needs to make 42000-32000 = 10000 more a year.
The answer is 10,000.
I didn't get selected for the school cricket team.
That's disappointing, especially if you practised hard for it. How are you feeling about it?
Bad. My friend got in and I didn't.
It can sting more when a friend makes it and you don't. You can be happy for him and still feel sad for yourself. Both feelings are allowed.
The coach said my fielding needs work.
That's useful, even if it hurts to hear. Fielding improves a lot with regular practice. Catching a tennis ball off a wall for ten minutes a day can make a real difference.
Trials are again in six months.

Six months is plenty of time to improve your fielding. You could ask the coach for one or two drills he likes, and maybe practise with your friend now that he's in the team. Then go back to trials with something new to show.

Read this:

Okay, so in Class Ten I was sure everyone hated me. It started in the canteen queue: three girls from my section looked at me, looked at each other, then looked away. I went home certain they were laughing at my haircut. For two days I sat at the back and wouldn't lift my eyes. Then you, Wasim, cornered me at the water cooler and said, "Suraj, why are you avoiding everybody?" I told you. You said, "Just ask them, yaar." So I did, red in the face. One of them said, "We wanted you on our quiz team but we were too shy to ask." 😅 I've never felt so silly. Now I check before I decide.

Where did the three girls look at Suraj and then away?
They looked at Suraj in the canteen queue.
Why did Suraj sit at the back and not lift Suraj's eyes for two days?
Suraj was certain the girls were laughing at the haircut, and felt embarrassed and wanted to avoid being looked at. The glances could have meant many things, but the worst was all that got imagined.
What could Suraj do the next time someone glances at Suraj and looks away?
Suraj could check the facts first, by asking a friend or the person kindly, before deciding it means gossip. Asking took Suraj two days to try but cleared it up in a minute.
How might the girls have felt while they were looking and looking away?
They were shy about inviting Suraj to the quiz team, so looking away was nervousness, not judgement. They may not have known Suraj was watching them.

metadata.subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Until the new girl came, Hansa was the one Masterji asked to read aloud in the one-room school above Palampur. Then Pema arrived from Kaza, reading faster than anyone, and on Monday Masterji held up Pema's notebook: "See how neat!"

From Tuesday, Hansa was everywhere Pema was. She carried Pema's bag up the hill. She gave Pema the best piece of her makki roti. At recess she held Pema's hand and told everyone, too loudly, "Pema is my best, best friend." When Pema went to fill water, Hansa went too.

Hansa's own notebook stayed shut. At home that night she told her mother, "Pema is so nice. I don't mind at all that Masterji likes her more." Nobody had asked if she minded.

What did Masterji hold up on Monday?
Masterji held up Pema's notebook.
Why might Hansa keep saying "I don't mind at all"?
Hansa feels jealous and pushed aside but can't admit it, so extra sweetness and loud friendship cover the feeling.
How could Hansa's mother help?
Her mother could gently say it's normal to feel a bit jealous of someone new, so Hansa can admit the feeling without being scolded.
How might Pema experience Hansa following everywhere?
Pema may feel welcomed at first but also a little crowded, perhaps puzzled by such strong friendliness so fast.

metadata.subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]

messages.content:
"It is unfortunately more than possible; it is certain. Neither you nor your son knew the true character of this man when you admitted him into your family circle. He is one of the most dangerous men in England—a ruined gambler, an absolutely desperate villain, a man without heart or conscience. Your niece knew nothing of such men. When he breathed his vows to her, as he had done to a hundred before her, she flattered herself that she alone had touched his heart. The devil knows best what he said, but at least she became his tool and was in the habit of seeing him nearly every evening."

Please give me the main points of this text in two sentences.

The speaker warns that the man is a dangerous, ruined gambler without conscience, whom the family welcomed without knowing him. The niece, knowing nothing of such men, believed she alone had won his heart, and became his tool, seeing him nearly every evening.
Eunice has 10 eggplant seeds and 4 pots. How many seeds will be planted in the fourth pot if 3 seeds can be planted in 1 pot?

Eunice can plant a total of 3 pots x 3 seeds = 9 seeds in three pots.
So, only 10 - 9 = 1 eggplant seed will be planted in the fourth pot.
The answer is 1.
"Speed up" and "slow down": are they just opposites?

Yes, they are opposite phrasal verbs. "Speed up" means to go or happen faster, and "slow down" means to go or happen more slowly.
Examples: The bus sped up on the empty road. Please slow down; I cannot write that fast.

Maddie wants to see how much her mom spends on coffee each week. She makes herself 2 cups of coffee per day. Each cup has 1.5 ounces of coffee beans. A bag of coffee costs $8 and contains 10.5 ounces of beans. She uses 1/2 a gallon of milk per week. A gallon of milk costs $4. She doesn't add any sugar to the coffee. How much does she spend on her coffee per week?

She uses 3 ounces of beans per day because 2 x 1.5 = 3
She uses 21 ounces of beans per week because 7 x 3 = 21
She buys 2 bags of beans per week because 21 / 10.5 = 2
She spends $16 on the beans per week because 2 x 8 = 16
She spends $2 on the milk per week because 4 x (1/2) = 2
She spends $18 per week on her coffee because 16 + 2 = 18
The answer is 18.

Read this:

'Reena, you slammed your laptop shut when your coach said your essay was weak,' said Dhruv Mama. 'I did worse at your age. I was sixteen and editor of the school magazine. A teacher returned my article covered in red, and I told her, in front of everyone, that she didn't understand humour. Then I went home and sulked. My father read the red marks and said, "Half of these are right. Which half?" So I sat and sorted them. Seven were fair. Three I still disagreed with. Next day I thanked her for the seven and asked, politely, if we could discuss the three. She agreed with me on two. We ran that magazine together for two more years.'

How many of the teacher's comments did young Dhruv decide were fair?
Seven.
What did young Dhruv feel when the article came back covered in red?
He felt hurt and defensive, which is why he snapped at the teacher and sulked at home.
What could Reena try with her coach's comments?
She could sort them into fair and unclear ones, thank the coach for the fair ones and ask calmly about the rest.
How might the teacher have felt when Dhruv came back politely?
She was probably relieved and more willing to listen, since she agreed with him on two points.

Read this:

At the Sunday market in the village, Sarita sat beside her grandfather Kishore at his vegetable stall. A woman picked up two brinjals and gave Kishore a coin. Sarita watched. Then she pointed at the bangle stall. "Can I have those?" "Those belong to Raju bhai," Kishore said. "We give money for them." Sarita thought. "We give brinjals to people and they give money?" "That's right." She sold the next bunch of coriander herself and held the coin tightly.

What did the woman pick up at the stall?
She picked up two brinjals.
What does Sarita holding the coin tightly suggest?
It suggests she felt proud and understood the coin was valuable.
How could Kishore build on Sarita's learning?
He could let her count coins with him and save for the bangles.
How might the bangle seller see Sarita if she came with her coin?
He would likely be happy to exchange bangles for money, treating her as a real customer.
Bruce buys 5 packs of crayons at $5 each, 10 books at $5 each, and 3 calculators at $5 each. If he has $200, how many bags can he buy with the change if one costs $10 each?

He pays 5*5=$25 for buying crayons.
He pays 10*5=$50 for buying books.
He pays 3*5=$15 for buying calculators.
The change he has for buying bags is 200-25-50-15=$110.
The number of bags he can buy is 110/10=11 bags.
The answer is 11.

Read this:

Evening in the village, and Sharmila had just come back from the fields, her feet dusty and her back aching. Before she could sit, Minakshi ran up. "Amma! Madhu broke the pot at the well and he fell in the mud, he looked so silly!" She laughed and flapped her arms like him falling. "And he didn't do his homework!" Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
She said he broke the pot at the well.
What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
She hoped Amma would praise her as a good girl for telling, so she felt let down when Amma said 'enough' and her smile faded.
What went wrong, and what could fix it?
Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.
How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.

Read this:

The rain was pouring and the bus was late. At the stop, Harish, six, pointed at a family under the next shelter. "Those colony people are dirty," he said loudly. His grandfather Baljeet crouched down, water dripping from his turban. "How do you know that, puttar?" Harish frowned. "Everybody says." A truck roared past, splashing them all. The mother from the other shelter pulled out a towel and wiped Harish's face. Harish went quiet and held Baljeet's hand.

What did the mother from the other shelter do?
She pulled out a towel and wiped Harish's face.
How might Harish have felt when the mother wiped his face?
He probably felt confused and a little ashamed, going quiet after she was kind to him.
How did Baljeet respond to Harish's words?
He crouched down and calmly asked, "How do you know that, puttar?" instead of scolding.
What is it like for the family when Harish calls them dirty?
They probably feel hurt and embarrassed in front of strangers, yet the mother still chose to help him.
My son loves robots. Please tell a story about one that wanted to dance, with a happy ending.

Robot Tin-Tin worked in a school canteen in Hyderabad, stacking plates. Every afternoon, the dance group practised across the hall, and Tin-Tin tapped his metal foot. He longed to join in, but his legs were made for standing still.

On the day of the school show, the music player stopped in the middle of the dance. The dancers froze on the stage, and the hall went quiet.

Tin-Tin rolled to the side of the stage with two steel spoons. Clink-clink, clink. He tapped out the beat on a tray, exactly as he had heard it every day.

A girl named Sahana grinned and started to dance again. The others followed. Tin-Tin swayed his arms and clinked, and his eyes glowed gold.

When it ended, the whole hall clapped. After that, Tin-Tin played the beat for the dance group every week, and sometimes he danced a little, too.

Read this:

Saturday
Diary, we came third. THIRD. After all that practice. I wanted to kick the chair. Papa just put his hand on my shoulder and didn't say anything, which helped. Then I remembered what Aditi didi said once: the questions you miss tell you what to learn. So I went up to the quiz master while they were packing up, and asked, "Sir, can I see which ones we got wrong?" He looked surprised but showed me. I wrote them all down: three on the Constitution, two on birds, one on old coins. Papa said, "That's my boy." I'm still upset. But now I have a list for next year, and the Constitution ones are first.
- Kiran

How many questions on the Constitution did Kiran write down?
Kiran wrote down three on the Constitution.
How did Kiran feel right after hearing they came third?
Kiran felt angry and disappointed, wanting to kick the chair.
What else could Kiran do to keep the list from being forgotten over the year?
Kiran could pin the list inside the study cupboard and tick off each topic after reading about it.
How does the quiz master see Kiran's request?
The quiz master is surprised, maybe pleased, and willing to show which ones went wrong.

metadata.subtype: Approach: accepting a loss and learning from it [Revision]

messages.content: Share a sentence about the Himalayas that has the word "snow" and finishes with an exclamation mark.
Look at the snow on the Himalayas!

Read this:

I'm Farhan. In my third year of college in Aligarh, Naveen from the photography club asked if I wanted to go for a sunset walk by the old fort and get chai after. Just the two of us. He said it shyly, which I remember now.

I said no. I said I had a project. The truth is I'd already watched the whole evening in my head: long silences, me talking too much about lenses, Naveen checking his phone, both of us relieved when it ended. I knew it would be awkward, so why go and be disappointed?

The relief was immediate. I spent that evening in my room, safe.

But the photos from that walk, which he posted later with a group, were beautiful. And I kept doing it that whole year. No to the trip, no to the dinner. Each no felt safe. My world just got a little smaller every time.

Where did Naveen invite Farhan to go?
For a sunset walk by the old fort and chai after.
Why did saying no bring Farhan relief straight away?
Declining meant Farhan couldn't be disappointed or embarrassed by an evening that already seemed sure to go badly. The prediction protected Farhan from risk, so turning it down felt safe.
What could Farhan try the next time an invitation seems sure to go badly?
Treat the prediction as a guess and say yes to a short version, like chai only, then compare what actually happens with the forecast. Small tests would show whether that certainty is right.
How might Naveen have felt after asking shyly and hearing about a project?
Naveen may have felt disappointed or unsure whether Farhan was interested at all. Having taken a risk to ask, Naveen might hesitate to ask again.

The answer is x = 3; x != 0.

Read this:

On the whiteboard in the Chennai office, Rehana wrote: "Users leave within a week." Kunal, the product lead, tapped the marker. "Why?" "They drop off during setup." "Why?" "The onboarding asks for too much." "Why does it ask for so much?" "Because the school's admin wants all the data before anything starts." "Why does the admin decide that?" "Because the admin bought it." "And why does that matter?" Rehana stopped. "Because the teachers who use it never chose it, never paid for it, and were never asked." They stared at the fifth answer. "So it isn't the onboarding," said Rehana. "It's who we thought our user was." Kunal wrote a new line at the bottom: "Talk to the people who pay."

What did Rehana first write on the whiteboard?
Rehana wrote, "Users leave within a week."
What was Rehana feeling when Rehana stopped at the fifth question?
Rehana was struck and realising something uncomfortable, that the problem was not the onboarding.
What could the team do next?
They could interview the school admins who decide and pay, as well as the teachers, and rethink who the product is for.
How might the teachers have seen the app?
The teachers may have seen it as something imposed on them, which they never chose or paid for.

metadata.subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Vasudha, and I run the play corner at the clinic in Kolkata. Arnab had been at the shape box a long while. The oval block kept missing. He turned it, pushed, turned it, pushed. Then he dropped it, shoved the box away with his foot and crawled off to the stacking cups. Was he cross? Tired? I couldn't tell. He built a wobbly cup tower, humming. I kept the box aside for another day.

What did Arnab crawl off to?
He crawled off to the stacking cups.
What was Vasudha feeling as she watched Arnab leave the box?
Vasudha was curious and unsure whether he was cross or tired, and calm enough to let him go.
What went well in Arnab leaving the puzzle?
He stopped before tears and turned to something easier, so his mood stayed good and the box can be tried again another day.
How might Arnab feel once he is building cups?
He seems settled and content, humming as he builds.
Is it "Whose turn is it?" or "Who's turn is it?" Also, why do we wear helmets while cycling?

1. "Whose turn is it?" Why: word choice ("Who's" -> "Whose").
2. A helmet protects your head if you fall, so a bump is less likely to cause an injury.

Read this:

Result day, and Ramesh's phone showed two missed calls from Amma and 8 per cent battery. On the screen at the cyber café in Warangal: Mathematics III, FAIL.
His parents had pledged Amma's gold to pay his fees. He had seen her bare wrists for two years.
His first thought was to say "all cleared" and quietly retake it in the summer. No one would know.
Gurleen, at the next computer, saw his face. "Backlog?"
"One. They pledged the gold for me, Gurleen."
"Then they deserve the truth more than anyone. And one backlog can be fixed."
His phone died before he could decide. He borrowed the café's landline and called home anyway. "Amma, I failed Maths III. I'm going to clear it in the supplementary exam. I'll join the free tutoring on campus and take evening shifts at the print shop to pay the exam fee myself."
Amma was quiet. Then: "Thank you for telling us. Eat something before you come home."

Which subject did Ramesh fail?
Mathematics III.
Why did Ramesh think of saying "all cleared"?
He felt ashamed and guilty about Amma's pledged gold and afraid of disappointing his parents.
What did Ramesh do instead of hiding it?
He told Amma the truth on the café landline along with a plan: the supplementary exam, free campus tutoring and evening print-shop shifts for the fee.
How does Amma respond?
Quietly at first, then with thanks for telling them and care ("Eat something"), valuing his honesty.

Read this:

The fire drill siren went off without warning on a rainy Tuesday. Kunal dropped to the floor and curled into a ball. For three months Tenzin-ma'am had kept the same routine for him: the same hello at the gate, the same corner seat, the same soft voice. She knelt, not touching. "Loud noise. You're safe. I'm right here. We walk together, like always." Last week she had missed his gate hello and he'd hidden all morning; she had said sorry the next day. Kunal looked at her face. Then he took the edge of her dupatta and walked out with the line.

How long had Tenzin-ma'am kept the same routine for Kunal?
For three months.
What was Kunal feeling when the siren started?
He was terrified, dropping to the floor and curling into a ball.
Why did Tenzin-ma'am's approach work during the drill?
She stayed calm, knelt without touching and used the familiar words and routine, so Kunal could trust her enough to move.
What might Tenzin-ma'am have felt when Kunal hid after the missed hello?
She was probably sorry and concerned, which is why she apologised the next day.

metadata.subtype: Steady adult for a frightened child [Response]

messages.content:
Their sabers catching in the bridles and their spurs jingling, the hussars hastily dismounted, not knowing what they were to do. The men were crossing themselves. Rostov no longer looked at the colonel, he had no time. He was afraid of falling behind the hussars, so much afraid that his heart stood still. His hand trembled as he gave his horse into an orderly's charge, and he felt the blood rush to his heart with a thud. Denisov rode past him, leaning back and shouting something. Rostov saw nothing but the hussars running all around him, their spurs catching and their sabers clattering.

Show how Rostov's fear comes through in the passage.
He is so afraid of falling behind that his heart seems to stop. His hand shakes as he hands over his horse, and he notices nothing but the running hussars.

Read this:

Sunday night
Yamini's parents flew in to see her college fest. Mine came by overnight bus to drop off my winter clothes and went back the same day.
I'm Raghav. I'm not complaining. I'm just noticing.
Yamini has done three internships through her father's friends. If she fails a test, she says, "Whatever, I'll do a master's abroad." If I fail, my family's loan feels heavier.
Sometimes I feel so angry that I can't sleep. Like we're running the same race but she started at the halfway mark.
And then I think about my father, who only studied till Class 8, and he got up at four to get on that bus. And I'm in the same college as Yamini.

How did Raghav's parents travel?
They came by overnight bus.
What is Raghav feeling in comparing with Yamini?
Raghav feels angry and resentful about the uneven start, and also proud of how far the family has come.
What could help Raghav carry both feelings?
Raghav could look for college mentors or support schemes, and talk with friends who understand, while keeping in mind how far the family has come.
How might Yamini see her own situation?
Yamini may see her safety nets as normal, not noticing how different Raghav's situation is.

metadata.subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

14 March
Today in debate practice we got the old question: would you steal medicine to save your sister if the shop refused to sell it? Nandini said yes, obviously, family first. I said yes too, then couldn't sleep.
Because if stealing is wrong, how can it also be right? And if it's right here, what else is "right" if I love someone enough?
Ammi says lying is always wrong. But last month she told the landlord we weren't home when we were. I didn't say anything. Was that wrong too?
I think I believe some rules protect people and some rules protect power. I want to be the person who can tell the difference. I don't know how yet.
Ask Nandini tomorrow what she really thinks, not debate-thinks.
Dilnaz

What question came up in debate practice?
Would you steal medicine to save your sister if the shop refused to sell it?
How does Dilnaz feel after the debate practice?
Dilnaz feels unsettled and conflicted, unable to sleep while wrestling with how stealing can be both wrong and right.
What would you advise Dilnaz as a next step?
Talk it through with Nandini and a trusted adult, as planned, and keep noticing which rules protect people.
How might Ammi react if Dilnaz raised the landlord moment?
Ammi might feel caught off guard or a little embarrassed, and it could open an honest talk about when rules bend.

Could you tell a child what this paragraph is about, in three sentences?

He was interrupted by a summons to dinner; and the girls smiled on each other. They were not the only objects of Mr. Collins's admiration. The hall, the dining-room, and all its furniture, were examined and praised; and his commendation of everything would have touched Mrs. Bennet's heart, but for the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property. The dinner, too, in its turn, was highly admired; and he begged to know to which of his fair cousins the excellence of its cookery was owing. But here he was set right by Mrs. Bennet, who assured him, with some asperity, that they were very well able to keep a good cook, and that her daughters had nothing to do in the kitchen. He begged pardon for having displeased her. In a softened tone she declared herself not at all offended; but he continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.

Mr. Collins is called to dinner and praises the hall, the dining-room and the food. He asks which cousin cooked it, and Mrs. Bennet says sharply that her daughters do not work in the kitchen. He says sorry, she calms down, and he keeps saying sorry for about a quarter of an hour.

Read this:

Joseph's shifts at the hospital in Bengaluru ran from nine at night to seven in the morning. Gurleen left for her office at eight. For most of the year their marriage lived in one crowded hour: his tired keys in the door, her hurried toast, a quick "bye" at the lift.

One Tuesday he found a sticky note on the fridge in her handwriting: "Bought your coconut biscuits. Sleep well." He stood there holding it. When had he last written her anything? He loved her more than anyone, and she probably had no idea.

There was no time for a grand plan, so he kept it small. Next morning he had her chai ready in the green mug she liked. He asked how the client meeting had gone and actually listened. At the door he held her hand for a second longer than usual. She squeezed back and smiled all the way to the lift.

What did Gurleen's sticky note say?
It said, "Bought your coconut biscuits. Sleep well."
What did Joseph feel as he stood holding the note?
Joseph felt a pang of guilt and tenderness, because he loved Gurleen deeply but had not shown it in a long time.
Why did small acts suit Joseph better than a big surprise?
With only one hour together each day, regular small things like chai, a real question and a held hand fit their life and could keep going.
How might Gurleen see the change in the mornings?
She may feel noticed and warm again, which shows in how she squeezed his hand and smiled to the lift.

Read this:

In the monsoon term at the school in Sonpur, Dhruv's shirt was always tucked, his hair oiled flat, his slate wiped before the bell. He never used the old word his grandmother used for 'yes', because the other boys laughed at village talk, even though they all came from villages. When Sarita Madam asked who wanted the class outing to be to the new dam, where the water roared after the rains, Dhruv's hand twitched. He had dreamt of that dam for weeks. But Mohan and the others shouted 'Temple!' and looked around to see who disagreed. Dhruv raised his hand for the temple. At home he told his grandmother the outing would be fun. Then he went out and stood by the flooded paddy, throwing stones, very quiet.

Which outing did Dhruv raise his hand for?
The temple.
What might Dhruv be feeling as he throws stones by the paddy?
He is probably disappointed and sad, having buried his wish for the dam to avoid the other boys' disapproval.
How could Sarita Madam make it safer for children like Dhruv to share their real choice?
She could take the vote on folded paper slips instead of shouted answers, so no one has to look around to see who disagrees.
How might Dhruv's grandmother see his quietness after school?
She might sense something is wrong despite his cheerful words, and could gently ask what he really wanted.

messages.content: My pet's name, what is it?
You haven't told me, so I don't know your pet's name. Tell me and I'll happily use it.

Read this:

Tuesday night, Gangtok
Long day of interviews for the hotel front desk. I noticed something I didn't like. Varun and the other panellists kept lighting up for anyone who reminded them of Karma, our best receptionist last year: tall, hotel-school, smooth English. One candidate barely answered the complaint scenario, but Varun said, "Very Karma-like, great presence." A woman from a village near Namchi handled the angry-guest role-play beautifully, in Nepali and then English, and got marked "average fit". I kept thinking: we're hiring a shadow of Karma, not the best person. Tomorrow I'll ask the panel to score each skill separately, with an example for each, before anyone says "fit". My wife says I'll annoy everyone. Probably.
Pema

What mark did the woman from near Namchi get?
She got marked "average fit".
What was Pema worried about after the interviews?
Pema felt the panel was favouring people who resembled Karma rather than those who did the job best, and worried they were hiring a shadow of a past success.
What is Pema planning, and why could it work?
Pema plans to have each skill scored separately with an example before anyone mentions fit, so strong performance, like the angry-guest role-play, counts more than resemblance.
How might Varun react to the new scoring plan?
Varun may feel a bit defensive at first, since presence felt like a real signal, but might accept it once the scores show who handled the tasks best.

Antoine owns a strawberry farm that supplies strawberries to his local bakeries. The first bakery needs 2 sacks, the second bakery needs 4 sacks, and the third bakery needs 12 sacks of strawberries per week. How many sacks of strawberries does he need to supply all the bakeries in 4 weeks?

The first bakery needs 2 x 4 = 8 sacks of strawberries per month.
The second bakery needs 4 x 4 = 16 sacks of strawberries per month.
The third bakery needs 12 x 4 = 48 sacks of strawberries per month.
Therefore, Antoine needs 48 + 16 + 8 = 72 sacks of strawberries to supply all the bakeries for a month.
The answer is 72.
Hamare gaon mein ek talab hai. "A pond is there in our village" sahi hai?
It is understood, but the natural form is: "There is a pond in our village." Why: In English we usually start with "There is" to say that something exists.

Read this:

'Mama?' Joseph hovered in the kitchen doorway. Anjali looked up from the dosa pan. 'You're quiet. What happened?' 'When I was cycling in the compound, my pedal scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter. There's a long line now.' 'Did he see?' 'Nobody saw. Nobody was there.' 'So why are you telling me?' Joseph twisted his T-shirt. 'Because it's his scooter. And I keep thinking about it.' Anjali turned off the flame. 'That thinking is your good sense. What do you want to do?' 'Tell him? He'll shout.' 'Maybe. Want me to come?' 'Stand near. But I'll say it.' 'Deal.' They walked down together. Joseph's voice shook, but he said every word.

What did Joseph's pedal scrape?
It scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter and left a long line.
Why did Joseph tell his mother even though nobody saw?
He felt uneasy and kept thinking about the damage to someone else's scooter, so he wanted to put it right.
How did Anjali support Joseph without taking over?
She stayed calm, asked what he wanted to do and offered to stand near while letting him speak for himself.
If you were Mr D'Costa, what would you want?
You would probably want the truth, and you might be less angry because the boy came himself to admit it.

Read this:

Sunday. Afreen noticed her neighbour Yusuf's elderly father had been leaving the gas on low at night again. She told herself it wasn't her business; Yusuf worked late shifts, and she didn't want to seem nosy.

Tuesday. The smell was stronger on the stairs. Afreen stood outside their door, then asked herself: if I had left that knob on, what would I want a neighbour to do? She realised walking past was also a decision.

Wednesday. She knocked when Yusuf got home and told him gently what she'd noticed. He looked shocked, then thanked her. That evening he called the building's gas technician, who fitted a safety valve, and Yusuf asked their family doctor about his father's forgetfulness.

What was Yusuf's elderly father leaving on at night?

messages.content: Lily has 5 lottery tickets to sell.  She sells the first ticket for $1.  She then sells each successive ticket for a dollar more than the previous ticket. She plans to keep a $4 profit and give the remaining money as the prize. How much money will the winner of the lottery receive?

The second ticket sold will cost $1 + $1 = $2.
The third ticket sold will cost $2 + $1 = $3.
The fourth ticket sold will cost $3 + $1 = $4.
The fifth ticket sold will cost $4 + $1 = $5.
The total money collected is $1 + $2 + $3 + $4 + $5 = $15.
After taking profit, the total prize money will be $15 - $4 = $11.
The answer is 11.

Fill in the blanks so that the rational numbers are equivalent: -3/5 = 6/__ = __/(-25) = -27/__.

Answer: -3/5 = 6/(-10) = 15/(-25) = -27/45.

Find what the KNOWN part was multiplied by, then do the same to the other part. -3 -> 6 is x (-2), so 5 x (-2) = -10: 6/(-10). 5 -> -25 is x (-5), so -3 x (-5) = 15: 15/(-25). -3 -> -27 is x 9, so 5 x 9 = 45: -27/45. Check each by putting it in standard form: 6/(-10) = -3/5, 15/(-25) = -3/5, -27/45 = -3/5. Multiplying the top and bottom by a NEGATIVE number is allowed: it changes both signs, and the value stays the same.

Roe saved $10 per month from January to July and saved $15 per month from August to November. How much should she save in December so she will have a total savings of $150 in the year?

Since there are 7 months from January to July, then Roe's savings for those months sum up to $10 x 7 = $70.
Since there are 4 months from August to November, then her savings for those months sum up to $15 x 4 = $60.
Her total savings from January to November is $70 + $60 = $130.
Therefore, she needs to save $150 - $130 = $20 in December.

Malcolm works in a company where they normally pack 40 apples in a box, producing 50 full boxes per day. Operations went as normal in one week. But in the next week, they packed 500 fewer apples per day. What's the total number of apples packed in the two weeks?

When 500 fewer apples were packed each day in the next week, the total became 2000-500 = 1500 apples per day.
The total number of apples packed in the boxes that week is 1500*7 = 10500 apples.
The total is 14000+10500 = 24500 apples for the two weeks
The answer is 24500.

Julia's internet speed is 20 MBps (megabytes per second). How many songs she can download in half an hour if the size per song is 5MB?

1 hour has 60 minutes, therefore 1/2 hour has 1/2*60 = 30 minutes
1 minute has 60 seconds, therefore 30 minutes has 30*60 = 1800 seconds
If Julia's internet speed is 20MBps and each song has a size of 5MB, then it would take 5/20=1/4 seconds to download one song
If it takes 1/4 seconds to download 1 song, then in 1800 seconds, Julia could download 1800/(1/4) = 1800 * 4 = 7200 songs
The answer is 7200.

George and Amelia are picking oranges and apples at an orchard. George picks 45 oranges and 5 more apples than Amelia. Amelia picks 18 fewer oranges than George and 15 apples. How many fruits do they pick altogether?

George picks 15 + 5 = 20 apples.
The total number of apples that they pick is 20 + 15 = 35.
So, they pick 72 + 35 = 107 fruits altogether.
The answer is 107.

A rhombus-shaped field has side 30 m and one diagonal 48 m. It is shared equally by 18 cows for grazing. How much area does each cow get?

Answer: Area = 864 m^2; each cow gets 48 m^2.

The diagonal of 48 m splits the rhombus into two CONGRUENT triangles with sides 30, 30, 48. s = (30 + 30 + 48)/2 = 54 area = sqrt(54 x 24 x 24 x 6) = sqrt186,624 = 432 m^2 field = 2 x 432 = 864 m^2; 864 / 18 = 48 m^2 per cow Check with the rhombus rule: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so half the other diagonal is sqrt(30^2 - 24^2) = 18, the other diagonal is 36 and area = 1/2 x 48 x 36 = 864 m^2. Common mistake: using only one triangle.

Matt wants to repaint his house. He needs to paint three walls in his living room, which is a square 40 feet by 40 feet, and all four walls in his bedroom, which is a rectangle 10 feet by 12 feet. All the walls in Matt's house are 10 feet tall. How many total square feet of wall does Matt need to paint?

First figure out how many square feet a wall in the living room is: 40 feet length * 10 feet height = 400 square feet
Now multiply by 3 since Matt needs to paint three living room walls: 400 square feet/wall * 3 walls = 1200 square feet
Next figure out how many square feet the long walls in the bedroom are: 12 feet * 10 feet = 120 square feet
There are two long walls, so multiply this figure by 2: 120 square feet/wall * 2 walls = 240 square feet
Next figure out how many square feet the short walls in the bedroom are: 10 feet * 10 feet = 100 square feet
Multiply this by 2, since there are two short walls: 100 square feet/wall * 2 walls = 200 square feet
Finally, add up the square footage from the three living room walls, the two short bedroom walls, and the two long bedroom walls: 1200 square feet + 240 square feet + 200 square feet = 1640 square feet
The answer is 1640.

The bus jolted past the sugarcane fields. Tushar stared at his knees. Urmila stood up, walked down the swaying aisle and sat beside him. "Enough," she said loudly. "Would you like it done to you?" Her cousin rolled his eyes and muttered something. The boys went quiet, a little sulky. Tushar didn't say a word, but he moved his bag so she had room.

Where was the bus going?
It was going from the village to the kasba school.
Why did Urmila hesitate before speaking up?
She feared the social cost, since her cousin was one of the teasers and gossip would spread through the village by evening.
How could a teacher support what Urmila started?
A teacher could quietly check in with Tushar, speak to the older boys about the teasing, and back Urmila so she isn't left facing the backlash alone.
How might Tushar have experienced Urmila sitting beside him?
After feeling humiliated, he probably felt less alone and protected; moving his bag suggests quiet gratitude.

It was the first cool morning after the monsoon in the village near Solapur. Mohit, five, sat on the doorstep with his school shoes. Minakshi, his older sister, bent to tie the laces. 'No! Mohit do it!' he shouted, and pushed her hand away. 'We'll be late.' 'Mohit do it!' He wrapped the laces round and round his fingers, frowning. They knotted in a lump. He pulled them apart and tried again. Minakshi waited, tapping her foot. Finally he made a crooked bow. He jumped up and ran to the gate. 'I did it! I tied it myself!' Minakshi laughed and followed.

Where did Mohit sit to tie his shoes?
On the doorstep.
How did Mohit feel when he made the crooked bow?
Mohit felt proud and excited, running to the gate to announce he did it himself.
What did Minakshi do that helped Mohit?
She waited, even while tapping her foot, and let him keep trying instead of taking over.
How might Minakshi feel when Mohit shouts 'I did it'?
Minakshi probably feels amused and a little proud of her little brother.

With only two days until the college union elections, Alka's campaign posters were torn in the rain and she had no money for new ones. She stood in the canteen giving her speech without a mic, voice cracking over the noise.
"I want to fix the broken hostel water pumps and get a fair fee-refund system," she said. "And yes, I want a seat at the table where decisions happen."
Her friend Rajni watched, arms folded. Later she said, "You know what worries me? Last week you told the second-years they'd 'better vote for you if they want the new wing'. That sounded like a threat."
Alka's cheeks went hot. "I didn't mean it like that."
"Then don't say it like that."
Alka looked at her torn posters. She wanted to lead. She didn't want to become someone people feared.

What did Alka promise to fix?
She promised to fix the broken hostel water pumps and get a fair fee-refund system.
What was Alka feeling when Rajni mentioned the second-years?
She felt embarrassed and uneasy, with hot cheeks, not wanting her wish to lead to turn into control.
What could Alka do to make sure her influence serves the group?
Apologise to the second-years, drop any hint of pressure, and focus her campaign on the pumps and fee refunds.
How might the second-years have felt when Alka said they'd better vote for her?
They might have felt pressured or threatened, rather than inspired to support her.

I'm Avni, and this is the story of the email I didn't forward.

In March, our biggest client asked for a thirty percent discount on the next order. Vandana, my co-founder, would have said no; she'd said so a dozen times. I was scared of losing them, so I said yes and didn't tell her. I told myself it would help the business.

For three weeks I felt sick every time she checked the accounts. I snapped at her over small things. When she asked why the margins looked strange, I changed the subject.

One Sunday I couldn't stand it. I went to her flat with the email printed out. "I agreed to this without you. I was wrong to hide it. I'm sorry." I didn't say it helped the business. It didn't, really; it was for my fear.

We agreed any discount above ten percent now needs both of us. She's still a bit cool with me. That's fair.

How big a discount did the client ask for?
The client asked for a thirty percent discount.
How did Avni feel during the three weeks of hiding it?
Avni felt sick and uneasy, snapping at Vandana and dodging her questions.
Why did Avni avoid saying it helped the business?
Because that excuse would not rebuild trust; owning the fear and the hiding plainly, then agreeing a new rule, was the honest repair.
How does Vandana seem to feel after Avni's confession?
Vandana seems hurt and still a little cool, even though they agreed a new rule together.

Subject: About yesterday's feedback
Hi Afreen,
I've been thinking about what you said after rehearsal: that my slides had too much text and I kept talking over Nandini. Honestly, my first reaction was to snap back, and I'm sorry I muttered "fine, do it yourself." That wasn't fair.
I went through the slides again last night. You're right: slide 4 had eleven lines. I've cut every slide to three points and moved the rest to my notes. I didn't notice I was talking over Nandini, so could you tap the table if it happens on Friday?
One thing I'd gently push back on: I think the conclusion needs the data chart, not just the quote. Can we try both versions tomorrow?
Anirban

How many lines did slide 4 have?
Slide 4 had eleven lines.
How did Anirban feel at first when Afreen gave feedback?
Anirban felt defensive and irritated, wanting to snap back, which led to the muttered "fine, do it yourself."
What makes Anirban's email a good way to handle the conflict?
It apologises for the snap, acts on the fair points, asks for a signal about talking over Nandini, and raises the one disagreement politely with a way to test both versions.
How might Afreen feel reading this email?
Afreen would likely feel respected and relieved that the feedback was heard, and more open to Anirban's point about the chart. 🙂
I have to give a speech in assembly tomorrow and I'm petrified.
Fear before a speech is normal. Preparing well and practising aloud reduce it. What is the speech about?
The importance of being on time.
That is a clear topic. Start with a short story or question to catch attention, give two or three reasons, and end with a strong closing line.
How do I memorise it?
Break it into parts and learn one at a time. Say it aloud many times. You can keep a small card with the main points, in case you lose your place.
What if my voice shakes?
Take a slow breath before you begin and speak more slowly than feels natural. A shaky voice often settles after the first few sentences.
Where should I look?
Look at a few friendly faces, or at the back wall. Moving your gaze slowly across the room makes the audience feel included.
Write the lyrics of a two-line lullaby. Each line should have exactly six words.

Close your eyes and sleep tonight
The stars will watch till morning
Give this a casual, friendly tone for a chat message: Please be informed that the meeting has been rescheduled to four o'clock.
Heads up, the meeting has been moved to four.

Team-lead advice, Kiran? Here's the one story I always tell. I'm Usha, and last year my colleague Gautam flew back from a two-week client visit in Chicago and walked straight into our Monday review. He looked fine, in a crisp shirt. But he nodded off twice during the budget slides, snapped at the intern over a typo, and then agreed to a vendor contract he had argued against for months. I was annoyed at first. Then I felt uneasy, because this wasn't the Gautam I knew. After the meeting I spoke to our manager, and we paused the contract till Thursday. Gautam was embarrassed when he read his own notes later. Now our team has a simple rule: after a long trip, the first day back is for email and sleep, and no big decisions.

Where had Gautam been on his client visit?
In Chicago, for two weeks.
How did Usha's feelings shift during the Monday review?
Usha was annoyed at first, then uneasy, sensing this wasn't the Gautam Usha knew.
What fair, practical step did Usha take, and what rule came from it?
Usha asked the manager to pause the contract till Thursday, and the team now keeps the first day back for email and sleep with no big decisions.
How did Gautam feel when he read his own notes later?
He felt embarrassed at the poor judgment he had shown while so tired.

messages.content: My grandmother and I are planning to make a family recipe book. Where do we start?
What a wonderful project. A good first step is to list the dishes you want to include. Let her talk and you write.
She doesn't use measurements. She says 'a handful' and 'till it smells right'.
That's normal for family cooking. Cook the dish with her and note what you see. Use your own hand or a cup to measure a handful and write it down.
Should I add stories too?
Yes, a few lines about where the dish comes from, or who loved it, make the book more personal. Ask her about a special occasion for each dish.
We could add photos of the family eating it.
That would be lovely. Even old photographs, with a caption, would add a lot. Keep the originals safe and copy them if you can.
I'll start with her kheer. It's the best.
A great first page. Taste-test as you go, since the cook always deserves a helper.

Imran was sixteen and wanted to earn his own money this summer, like his older cousins in the Mumbra flats. But when Vandana, his neighbour, asked, "Doing what?", he had no answer.

So that night he made two lists in his notebook. First: what he could do. Fix cracked phone screens, he'd done six for friends. Draw portraits. Teach basic maths to younger kids. Speak decent English.

Second, beside each one: was it allowed and safe at sixteen? Would it fit around school and coaching?

Phone repair needed a shop, and the shop owner had asked for full days. Crossed out. Portraits at the Sunday market: maybe, with his mother nearby. Tuition for two Class 5 kids in the building, three evenings a week: legal, safe, near home, and done by seven.

He circled the tuition. Next morning he told Vandana. She said her little brother needed exactly that.

How many phone screens had Imran fixed for friends?
Six.
How might Imran have felt when Vandana asked "Doing what?"
He probably felt caught out and a bit embarrassed, wanting to earn but with no plan yet.
What else should Imran check before starting the tuition?
He should talk with his parents about the timings and the families, so an adult knows the plan and agrees it is safe.
How might Vandana see Imran's tuition idea?
Vandana seems pleased, since her little brother needs exactly that help, close to home.

At the co-working space in Jayanagar, Neelam sat across from Dhruv, the mentor from the startup programme, with her barter delivery pitch open on the laptop.
"It's an interesting idea," Dhruv said. "But you have no evidence anyone will carry a stranger's parcel. Test it before you build anything."
Neelam's first instinct was to argue. Instead, she closed the pitch deck. "Okay. One lane. Two weeks."
She chose 4th Cross, where she already knew six families. She made a paper sign-up sheet and a simple phone list. Each evening she noted who asked for help, who carried, and what went wrong.
After two weeks she came back. "People happily carry medicines and vegetables for neighbours they know. Nobody wanted to carry parcels for strangers. And three families wanted to pay a small fee instead of owing a favour."
Dhruv nodded. "So now you know what the idea actually is."

Which lane did Neelam choose for the trial?
She chose 4th Cross, where she already knew six families.
How might Neelam have felt when Dhruv said she had no evidence?
She probably felt defensive at first, since her instinct was to argue, but then open enough to test it.
What else could Neelam test next, and why?
She could try a small fee option in a second lane, since three families preferred paying to owing favours.
How does Dhruv see Neelam's trial results?
Dhruv is pleased, seeing that she now knows what the idea really is instead of guessing.

Wednesday, 11:40 p.m.
Same as Tuesday. Same as Monday. Bus at 8:12, same seat, same man eating the same banana. Twelve invoices, a meeting that could've been an email, lunch at my desk. Bus home.
I'm not sad. I checked. It's more like everything's gone grey and a bit heavy, like a sweater left out in the rain.
Got home, ate, and then scrolled for three hours. I don't remember a single thing I saw. Gopika messaged about the pottery class she keeps talking about. I left it on read. It felt like too much effort, which is ridiculous, because scrolling is also effort, just the kind that goes nowhere.
Tomorrow I'll reply to her. Probably.
— Sangeeta

When does Sangeeta's bus leave?
At 8:12, the same bus every day.
What is Sangeeta feeling, according to the sweater comparison?
Sangeeta feels grey and heavy, worn down by sameness rather than truly sad.
What choice sits in front of Sangeeta tomorrow, and why might it matter?
Replying to Gopika about the pottery class could be a small break from the scrolling, a real change instead of more numbing.
How might Gopika feel about being left on read?
Gopika may feel a bit ignored or worried, since she keeps bringing up the class hoping Sangeeta will join.
Put these ribbons in order from shortest to longest: 45 cm, 1 m, 54 cm, 90 cm.

Answer: 45 cm, 54 cm, 90 cm, 1 m.

First change 1 m to 100 cm so all are in cm. Then compare the numbers: 45 < 54 < 90 < 100. Watch for the 45 and 54 mix-up: look at the tens first (4 tens is less than 5 tens).
How would I explain this to a five-year-old? Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air, which is why they like to sit in a sunny spot.
Plants make their own food. They use sunlight, water and air to do it. That is why plants like to sit in a sunny place.

Linda was going to pass out homemade cookies to each of her 24 classmates on the last day of school.  She wanted to give each student 10 cookies and wanted to make chocolate chip cookies and oatmeal raisin cookies.  Each cookie recipe made exactly 4 dozen cookies.  She was able to make 2 batches of chocolate chip cookies before running out of chocolate chips.  She made 1 batch of oatmeal raisin cookies.  How many more batches of cookies does Linda need to bake?

She has 24 classmates and wants to give each 10 cookies, so she needs to bake 24*10=240 cookies
Each batch makes 4 dozen cookies so that means each batch has 4*12 = 48 cookies
She baked 2 batches of chocolate chip and one batch of oatmeal raisin so 2+1 = 3 batches
We know that each batch has 48 cookies so 3*48 = 144 cookies have been baked
She needs to have 240 cookies and has baked 144 so 240-144 = 96 cookies are needed
Again, each batch makes 48 cookies and we need 96 more cookies so 96/48 = 2 more batches are needed
The answer is 2.

What does Berg believe about getting to know people?

In their new, clean, and light study with its small busts and pictures and new furniture sat Berg and his wife. Berg, closely buttoned up in his new uniform, sat beside his wife explaining to her that one always could and should be acquainted with people above one, because only then does one get satisfaction from acquaintances.
He believes you should make friends with people above you in rank, because only then do acquaintances bring satisfaction. This shows he cares about status and useful connections.
My cousin is getting married and the mehndi evening is on Thursday at 6 pm at our house. Write an invitation to the girls in the family, about 50 words.

Dear girls,
Our cousin's wedding is near, and we are holding a mehndi evening at our house this Thursday at 6 pm. Come and join us for an evening of mehndi and fun. It would not be a celebration without all of you! We cannot wait to see you there.
With love

I sit next to the product team at our salon-software startup, so I watched Gurpreet the week the numbers came in. The dashboard showed that almost every salon used one thing: the reminder message sent to customers the day before an appointment. Stock tracking, staff rota, loyalty points: barely touched.
Gurpreet printed the chart and taped it to the wall. For two days I saw Gurpreet standing in front of it, arms folded, saying things aloud like, "They pay for the reminder. The rest is what we thought they wanted." On Thursday, in the team meeting, Gurpreet said, "I think the reminder is the product. Everything else is decoration." The designer who built loyalty points looked hurt.
I can't say whether it was easy for Gurpreet to say. But by Friday the roadmap on the whiteboard had one word circled: reminders.
— Harsha

What word was circled on the whiteboard by Friday?
Reminders.
What might Gurpreet have been feeling standing in front of the chart for two days?
Gurpreet may have felt uneasy and torn about letting go of the other features, though Harsha can't be sure.
What could the team do for the designer who built loyalty points?
Acknowledge the work openly and involve the designer in making the reminder product better.
How did the designer who built loyalty points react?
The designer looked hurt, since the feature they built was now called decoration.

In the building lobby, Hemant was showing the new girl from the fourth floor his marble run. Alka stood by the lift, arms folded. Hemant was her friend. They always built the marble run together. A burning feeling rose up her chest. "She's not allowed," Alka said loudly. The girl, Jasleen, looked at her shoes. Hemant frowned. Alka's face felt hot. She looked at the marbles, then at Jasleen. "I felt sad because you didn't call me," she told Hemant. Then she knelt. "Jasleen, want the green marble?"

What was Hemant showing the new girl?
Hemant was showing her his marble run.
How was Alka feeling as she stood by the lift?
She felt jealous and left out, with a burning feeling in her chest, because Hemant was playing with someone new.
What wise step did Alka take after saying "She's not allowed"?
She told Hemant she felt sad and then invited Jasleen by offering her the green marble.
How might Jasleen see Alka's offer of the green marble?
She may feel relieved and welcome after first feeling shut out.

Kiran came in from the building compound with a frown. "Ammi, Rafi wants to use my crayons for his drawing. I said only if he gives me his dinosaur stickers." Salma, stirring the dal, nodded. "That's a fair trade. You thought it through." Kiran beamed. Salma continued, "But tell me something. Rafi's family just moved in. He doesn't have many things yet. How do you think he'd feel if nobody shared with him unless he paid?" Kiran's smile slipped. "Sad. Maybe lonely." "Mm." Kiran scuffed her foot. "Maybe I can lend them for today. And he can show me how he draws dinosaurs." Salma smiled. "That sounds like a good day for both of you."

What did Kiran want in exchange for the crayons?
Rafi's dinosaur stickers.
How did Kiran feel when Salma asked about Rafi?
Her smile slipped as she imagined Rafi feeling sad and lonely in a new place.
What did Salma's approach get right?
Salma first praised Kiran's fair thinking, then asked a gentle question about Rafi's feelings, so Kiran chose to share without feeling shamed.
What might this afternoon be like for Rafi?
Rafi, new to the building, gets crayons and a new friend who wants to learn his dinosaur drawings, which may help him feel he belongs.

Jeevan woke at 6:20 and remembered the trip. At 6:30 he was pulling things out of drawers and stuffing them into his bag: cap, snack, a comic. "Jeevan, the bus!" his mother called. At five to seven he reached the gate, panting, just as the bus turned the corner. On the steps he patted his pockets. No permission slip. No water bottle. Gurpreet Ma'am frowned at her list. Then his mother came running down the lane with both in her hand, out of breath. "Next time, the night before," she said. Jeevan's face burned as he took them.

What did Jeevan forget when he left for the bus?
He forgot his permission slip and his water bottle.
How did Jeevan feel when his mother ran up with the forgotten things?
Embarrassed, since his face burned, and probably relieved that he could still go.
What could Jeevan do to avoid this rush, and why?
He could pack the evening before and check a list in the morning, so there is time to notice anything missing.
What might Jeevan's mother be feeling as she runs down the lane?
She is likely hurried and worried, out of breath, and perhaps a little annoyed, but she still helps him.

The power cut hit the Pune flat at 7 pm and showed no sign of ending. Tejas's phone died at 7:40. Without a screen, the evening stretched ahead of him like an empty road. His life had been smooth for two years: a good salary at the software firm, the gym, weekend brunches, a new bike on instalments. He had been proud of how comfortable it was. Now, sitting in the dark, he tried to think of one thing he was building that wasn't for himself. Nothing came. At ten his flatmate Mridul came in with a torch, sweaty and grinning, back from the blood bank where he volunteered on Thursdays. 'Fourteen donors tonight,' Mridul said. Tejas said, 'Nice,' and felt something sink. He wasn't a bad person. He had just stopped looking outward. 'Can I come next Thursday?' he asked.

Where does Mridul volunteer on Thursdays?
At the blood bank.
What did Tejas feel when Mridul said 'Fourteen donors tonight'?
Tejas felt something sink, a flat, empty feeling at realising he was building nothing beyond himself.
What did Tejas do right at the end of the evening?
He asked to join Mridul next Thursday, taking a first small step outward instead of just feeling bad.
How might Mridul react to Tejas asking to come?
Mridul would probably be pleased and welcoming, glad to share something that clearly lifts his own evenings.

Monday, 8 pm

I did it today. I told.

For two weeks Deepak has been giving away his tiffin. His shirt has been the same since last Wednesday. Today in PT he nearly fell over during the warm-up. At break he finally admitted his mother has been in hospital in Nagpur for three weeks and his father went with her, and he's alone at home with nobody cooking. He made me promise not to tell.

I couldn't keep that one. At the end of break I said, "Deepak, I'm going to tell Kulkarni Sir. Not to get you in trouble. Because you're not okay and I can't fix this." He was angry. He called me a traitor.

I went straight to the staffroom. Sir listened, then called Deepak's uncle in Wardha from the office phone while I was still there. The uncle is coming tonight. Sir also sent Deepak to the canteen with a lunch pass.

He's still angry with me. I think I'd do it again.

Jatin

Where has Deepak's mother been for three weeks?
Deepak's mother has been in hospital in Nagpur for three weeks.
What was Jatin feeling after telling Kulkarni Sir?
Jatin felt worried and hurt by Deepak's anger but also sure that telling was right, saying the choice would be the same again.
Why was it wise for Jatin to speak to Deepak before going to the staffroom?
Jatin told Deepak directly about going to Kulkarni Sir and why, instead of breaking the promise behind his back.
How might Deepak see Jatin's choice in a few weeks?
Deepak may still feel embarrassed, but once his uncle is there and he is eating properly, he may see that Jatin was looking after him.

Tuesday, after closing

Manoj bhaiya was off today. Not rude exactly, just short. "Fine." "Do it." No jokes about the milk frother, which he always jokes about. He also counted the cash drawer twice, which he never does.

My first instinct was to think I'd messed up the morning orders. I nearly asked, "Are you angry with me?" But he wasn't looking at me when he talked, he was looking at his phone every few minutes, so I guessed it was probably not about me.

So I didn't push. I just took the dishes without being asked and handled the loud customer at table four myself. Around six I put a cup of ginger tea by the till and said, "No pressure, but if you need to leave early, I can close."

He looked surprised, then said his father was having tests at the hospital. He left at seven. I closed alone. It took forever but I didn't mind.

— Jasleen

What did Manoj do with the cash drawer that he never does?
He counted the cash drawer twice.
How did Jasleen feel when she first noticed Manoj's short replies?
Jasleen felt anxious and a little defensive, worried she had messed up the morning orders.
What did Jasleen's response get right?
She read the cues before assuming it was about her, didn't push him to explain, and offered practical help that gave him an easy way out.
How might Manoj have seen Jasleen's offer to close?
Manoj was surprised and probably relieved and grateful, since he could leave to be with his father without having to ask.
For children, a short story about a worm who wants to see the sky.

Wiggle the worm lived deep in the garden soil, where it was always dark and cool. He loved his tunnel, but sometimes he wondered what was above.

"What is the sky?" he asked the beetle.

"Blue," said the beetle. "And very big."

Wiggle decided to look. He pushed up through the dirt, up and up, until his head popped out. It was a rainy morning. He saw grey clouds, bright green leaves and a fat drop falling toward him. Plop!

"It is wet!" Wiggle gasped. "And lovely!"

He stayed for a while, feeling the rain on his back. When a robin swooped nearby, he scooted back down, giggling, to tell the beetle everything he had seen.

"Alka, you asked why I've stopped going to tuition. Okay. It started during Onam, when Amma saw me talking to Vinod chettan at the bus stop. That night she said, 'You will not speak to that boy again. He bunks, he roams, he'll ruin you.' Achan repeated it at breakfast. Then again the next day.
Before that I barely knew Vinod. But every time they said don't, something in me pushed back. I'm Amma's only son, not her puppet, you know? So I started waiting for him at the bus stop on purpose. Last week he said, 'Skip maths with me, we'll go to the beach.' And honestly, I went, mostly because they'd said no.
Sitting on the sand, I didn't even enjoy it. I just kept thinking: see, I decide. Harsha decides."

Where did Vinod suggest going instead of maths?
To the beach.
Why did Harsha start waiting for Vinod on purpose?
Every "don't" felt like control, so Harsha felt resentful and wanted to prove "I decide", which made Vinod more tempting than before.
What could help Harsha and Amma talk about Vinod differently?
Amma could explain her specific worry and really listen, and Harsha could decide about Vinod by what he is actually like rather than just to push back.
How might Amma feel if she learned about the skipped maths class?
She would probably feel frightened and hurt, since her firm warnings pushed her son toward exactly what she feared.

The hostel common room was loud with a cricket match on TV, but Kunal sat by the window holding the letter from the pilot selection board. Not recommended. Since he was nine he had pictured himself in a flight suit; he had even practised the salute in the mirror. Now that future had simply closed. On his phone, a batchmate was posting photos from the academy gates, grinning, and Kunal felt a sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it. Irfan dropped onto the sofa beside him. "Bro, forget it. You'll crack something better. It's a sign." Kunal nodded and said nothing. Later, alone on the terrace, he let himself cry for the nine-year-old in the flight suit. He didn't know yet what came next. For tonight, not knowing was allowed.

What did the letter from the pilot selection board say?
Not recommended.
What did Kunal feel seeing the batchmate's photos?
A sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it.
Why is Kunal's crying on the terrace a healthy step?
Letting himself grieve the lost future, instead of rushing to Irfan's positive story, is part of moving on.
How does Irfan seem to see Kunal's loss?
Irfan means well and wants to cheer Kunal up quickly, not seeing that Kunal first needs to grieve.

In a small square in Lisbon, Camila and Bilal, both five, played hopscotch with chalk.
Camila hopped to square six and her foot landed right on the line.
“Line!” Bilal said.
Camila stopped. “No, it wasn't.” She looked down. It was.
She sighed loudly. “Okay. Your turn.”
Bilal hopped all the way to ten and back. Camila clapped, a bit slowly.
Then she took the stone and began again from one.

Where did Camila's foot land?
Her foot landed right on the line.
How did Camila feel when she had to give up her turn?
She felt disappointed and frustrated, sighing loudly, but accepted it.
What could Bilal do to keep the game friendly?
He could cheer for Camila on her next turn so she feels included.
How might Bilal feel when Camila accepts the rule?
He probably feels the game is fair and enjoys playing with her.

Dear Jaya,

You asked how the first club meeting of the year went, so here is the honest version. Last year I noticed the loudest three people always decided everything, so this time I handed out slips and said: five minutes, total silence, write anything. It felt strange. Nobody looked at anybody. Then we read the slips aloud with no names. Tashi, who has hardly spoken since joining in July, had written: a quiz round where teams pick their own topics. Half the room said yes at once. I had been nervous the meeting would drag, but it ended early and we chose that quiz. I think I will keep the silent five minutes.

Dolma

What had Tashi written on the slip?
Tashi had written a quiz round where teams pick their own topics.

Dolma felt strange and a little nervous, because nobody looked at anybody and Dolma feared the meeting might drag.

Dolma could keep reading the slips aloud without names, or let members drop slips in a box first, so each idea is judged on its own. 🙂

Tashi may have felt surprised and encouraged, since the idea was heard without having to speak over louder members.

Monday. A man in a torn shirt stopped Chetan outside his Kolkata office. "I'm Arnab. I lost my job, my child is sick, please help." Chetan felt a pang, and bought him a meal from the stall nearby. Arnab thanked him warmly.

Thursday. Arnab was back. This time the story was different: his wife was in hospital and he needed two thousand rupees today. Chetan felt the pull of guilt, and also a small alarm. The story didn't match.

"I can't give cash," Chetan said gently. "But I'll buy you lunch again, and there's a free shelter on Park Street. I'll write the address."

Arnab's face hardened. "You people never really help," he said, and walked off.

A week later. Chetan still thought about it sometimes, uneasy. He'd started giving a little each month to a shelter that checks who needs help, and he kept a few of their address cards in his wallet.

What did Chetan buy Arnab on Monday?
Chetan bought him a meal from the stall nearby.
What was Chetan feeling on Thursday when Arnab asked for money?
Chetan felt guilty and pulled to help, but also alarmed because the story had changed.
How did Chetan stay compassionate but safe?
He offered food and the shelter's address instead of cash, didn't give in to the guilt, and later supported a shelter that checks needs.
How might Arnab have felt when Chetan refused cash?
Arnab seemed frustrated and angry, saying people never really help, though his full situation remains unclear.

School counsellor's note, Class 11, Friday.
Dolma has come to Thursday sessions for two months. Her parents support it, but have asked her to tell relatives she is at "extra maths", because an aunt keeps worrying aloud about what people will say, with her elder sister's marriage talks going on. Dolma says the lie itself is exhausting. At lunch she sits alone so no one asks where she goes on Thursdays, and she says she feels as if she's living behind glass.
Today we made a list of people she might trust. She chose one: her lab partner Abhinav, who once mentioned his own brother's counselling. What I did next: we practised what she might say, and she agreed I could check in. She came back after lunch looking lighter. "He just said thanks for telling him, and asked if I want company on Thursdays," she said. She smiled for most of the session.

What have Dolma's parents asked her to tell relatives?
That she is at "extra maths".
How does Dolma feel about keeping the secret?
Lonely and exhausted, as if living behind glass.
What step did the counsellor help Dolma take?
Choosing one trusted person, Abhinav, and practising what to say before telling him.
How might Abhinav see Dolma's news, given his own brother's counselling?
He likely sees it as ordinary and nothing to be ashamed of, which is why he thanked her and offered company on Thursdays.

It was forty degrees outside the polling booth in Jaipur, and the line wrapped around the school. Rashmi, seventeen, held an umbrella over Himani Nani, who had insisted on voting "as I have since 1971." At the front, the officer shook his head. "The voter slip isn't enough, Mataji. I need your ID." Nani's face fell. Rashmi's first thought was to beg him to let it go. Then she thought: rules are rules, even for Nani. "I'll run home and get it," she said. "Ten minutes." She ran through the heat, found the card in Nani's steel trunk, and ran back. When Nani came out with ink on her finger, she held it up proudly. Rashmi felt oddly proud too, though she was too young to vote.

What did the officer need from Himani Nani?
Her ID.
What was Rashmi feeling when Nani came out with ink on her finger?
She felt proud and moved, respecting both her grandmother and the vote, though too young to vote herself.
Which choice was wiser, and why?
Running home for the ID instead of begging the officer, because it respected the rule and still got Nani her vote.
How might Himani Nani feel about Rashmi running home for the ID?
She likely felt grateful and proud of her granddaughter.
Write a friendly invitation to our neighbours for tea on our lawn this Sunday at 10 am, about 45 words. I'm Mrs. Thomas.

Dear Neighbours,
We would be delighted if you could join us for tea on our lawn this Sunday at 10 am. It would be lovely to sit together and chat. Please come with your family. We look forward to seeing you all.
Mrs. Thomas
Why does a funnel help us pour liquid into a bottle with a narrow neck?
A funnel catches the pour and leads it into the narrow neck. Because its wide top collects the stream and the narrow end fits the neck, little is spilled.

I ride the same bus as Sarika, so I noticed. Last Monday Sarika came out of the counsellor's room with a folded sheet. On it was a rough map: the back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab, the stairs near the gym, each marked with a red dot. By Wednesday Sarika was sitting in the front seats near the driver and the bus attendant, and walking the corridor with two friends. Someone had also given Sarika a small card with three names to go to quickly: the counsellor, the class teacher and the PT sir. On Thursday I saw Sarika glance back at the corridor and then keep walking. I don't know how Sarika feels. But Sarika didn't look as tense as last week. - Mridul

What places were marked on the map Sarika carried?
The back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab and the stairs near the gym.
What might Sarika have been feeling, and how sure can Mridul be?
Sarika may feel a bit safer, since Sarika looked less tense, though Mridul says plainly not knowing how Sarika feels.

They could set a time to review how it is working, because places and people change and the plan should change with them.

They probably feel useful and protective, glad to be trusted with a clear job.
Renaldo drove 15 kilometers. Ernesto drove 7 kilometers more than one-third of Renaldo's distance. How many kilometers did the 2 men drive in total?

Renaldo = 15 km
Ernesto = (1/3) * 15 + 7 = 12 km
Total = 15 + 12 = 27 km
Renaldo and Ernesto drove a total of 27 kilometers.
The answer is 27.

The assignment was due at midnight, and Hrithik's laptop kept crashing. He typed fast, retyping paragraphs from memory each time.

His friend Noor was on video call, helping him check references.

"This bit about 'learning as a spiral, not a ladder,'" she said. "That's good. Did you come up with that?"

"Yes. I think so."

Noor frowned. "That's from the recorded talk we watched in class. I remember."

Hrithik stopped. He couldn't remember the talk at all. But he searched the class materials, and there it was, the same words.

He felt a wave of panic. "I would've submitted that as mine."

With eight minutes left, he added the citation and hit send, hands still shaking.

How many minutes were left when Hrithik added the citation?
Eight minutes.
Why did Hrithik feel a wave of panic?
He realised he had nearly submitted someone else's words as his own without meaning to, and felt scared and embarrassed.
What could Hrithik do to avoid this next time?
He could note the source whenever he writes down a good line or idea, so it doesn't get lost.
How might Noor feel after catching the line?
Noor was probably relieved she noticed, and glad to help her friend avoid trouble.

'Who broke my phone screen?' Jatin Chacha shouted.
Little Jeevan froze by the sofa, still as a statue.
'Jatin, stop. You're scaring him,' Dadi said.
Then Jeevan ran over and patted Jatin's knee. 'Sorry, Chacha. Jeevan good boy. Kiss?'
Dadi scooped him up. 'Shh, you're safe, raja.'
Jatin crouched, voice low. 'It's okay, Jeevan. Chacha isn't angry with you.'
Jeevan buried his face in Dadi's neck and finally cried.

What was broken?
Jatin Chacha's phone screen.
Why did Jeevan pat Jatin's knee and say sorry?
He was frightened by the shouting, and turning extra sweet was his small body's way of calming the angry adult.
What helped Jeevan feel safe?
Dadi held him and said he was safe, and Jatin crouched and lowered his voice.
How might Jatin feel seeing Jeevan freeze?
Jatin likely felt sorry and a bit ashamed, realising his shouting had frightened a toddler.

Monday. At the bus stop Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks. "The lodger at home grabs me when he's drunk. Promise you won't tell. Promise." Shalini hooked his little finger with hers. "Promise."
Wednesday. In science, Mr Iyer lifted his hand to point at the board, and Deepak flinched so hard his pencil box fell. Shalini hardly slept that night. A promise was a promise. But the marks.
Thursday. At lunch Shalini went to the counsellor's room. "I promised not to tell, but I think someone is hurting Deepak." Mrs Rao put her pen down and listened to all of it. "Thank you. You were right to bring this to me. A promise can't cover someone getting hurt." She called Deepak in before the last bell and phoned the school safeguarding lead that same afternoon. At the gate Shalini said, "I broke it because I care." Deepak said nothing, but he didn't walk away.

What did Deepak show Shalini at the bus stop?
Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks.
What was Shalini feeling on Wednesday night?
Shalini felt torn and worried: loyal to the promise, but frightened for Deepak after the flinch and the marks, which is why she hardly slept.
What did Mrs Rao do that helped?
Mrs Rao listened fully, thanked Shalini, said a promise can't cover someone getting hurt, saw Deepak before the last bell and phoned the safeguarding lead that same afternoon.
How might Deepak feel about the broken promise?
Deepak may feel scared or let down at first, which could explain the silence, but not walking away hints at some relief that an adult now knows.

Yuki had failed the first-term chemistry test at her high school in Sendai: 32 out of 100. On the train home, she thought, if I can't pass chemistry, I'll never get into a medical course. I'll never be anything.

By the time she got off at her station, it felt like fact.

For three weeks she stopped doing chemistry homework. What's the point, she told herself. Her older brother, Hiroshi, noticed the untouched workbook on her desk. "Didn't you say one test is only fifteen percent of the term grade?"

"It doesn't matter. I'm just bad at it."

"Did your teacher say that?"

She hadn't asked. She hadn't checked anything. She'd just been sure.

The second test came. She scored 35. The first failure hadn't ruined her future, but three weeks of giving up had made the next test harder.

What did Yuki score on the first-term chemistry test?
32 out of 100.
How did Yuki feel on the train home?
She felt despairing and panicked, as if her whole future had collapsed.
What could Yuki do instead of giving up on chemistry?
She could ask her teacher what the test really means for the term grade and where she lost marks, then make a small weekly plan.
How might Hiroshi see his sister's reaction?
Hiroshi likely feels concerned and a little frustrated, seeing her treat one test as the end of everything without checking the facts.
