Yamini, you want to go to that rally just because your friends are going? Let me tell you what your Tushar mama did at fifteen.

It was in Nagpur. My whole cricket team was going to some procession near the railway station. I didn't know what it was about. I only knew everyone was going and I didn't want to be the one left out.

So I went. There were flags, drums, slogans in a language half of us didn't speak. Somebody gave me a banner. I was proud to carry it, till an old man asked me what it meant. I couldn't answer.

Then the police arrived, and people started running. My friends scattered. I hid in a tea stall for an hour, shaking, with no idea how to get home.

When I finally did, your nani asked, "What were you marching for?" I couldn't say.

Where did young Tushar hide when people started running?
In a tea stall for an hour.
How did young Tushar feel when the old man asked what the banner meant?
Young Tushar felt embarrassed and exposed, realising there was no idea behind the banner he carried.
What choice in the story could have changed how the day went?
If he had asked what the procession was for before going, he could have decided properly and planned how to get home safely.
How might Tushar's friends on the cricket team have felt when everyone scattered?
They were probably frightened and confused too, since they had also gone along without a plan or a meeting point.

metadata.subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]

In the clinic waiting room, a page of Tenzin's picture magazine tore right across. He looked up quickly at his mother.
Indu didn't ask, "Did you do that?" She sat beside him. "Oh, the page tore."
Tenzin stared at his shoes. "I pulled it too hard."
"Thank you for telling me. That was honest. Shall we tell the lady at the desk together?"
At the counter, Tenzin held it up. "I tore it. Sorry."
The receptionist smiled. "Thank you for telling me. We have tape."
Tenzin walked back to his chair, standing a little taller.

Where were Tenzin and his mother?
In the clinic waiting room.
How did Tenzin feel when he looked up at his mother after the page tore?
Tenzin felt worried and nervous that he would be in trouble for tearing it.
What did Indu do instead of asking "Did you do that?"
She named what happened calmly, thanked him for telling the truth, and went with him to tell the receptionist.
How does the receptionist react to Tenzin's confession?
The receptionist smiles kindly, thanks him and offers tape, which makes telling the truth feel good.

Short summary, please, about three sentences.

Note in the family diary, Saturday
Before we went into Chandni Chowk today, I stopped with Harsha near the metro exit and asked him, "If we get separated, what will you do?" He thought and said, "Cry?" We laughed, and then made a plan together. He said it aloud three times: "Stop. Find a shop with a counter, not a person walking. Tell them Papa's number. Don't leave the area." He practised Papa's number too. We didn't get separated, thankfully. But on the way home he said it all again without being asked, and told his little cousin the plan as well. I will ask him again before every crowded outing, so the plan stays fresh.
- Sudha

Before a trip to a busy market, Sudha asks Harsha what he would do if they got lost. Together they make a simple plan: stop, find a shop counter, give Papa's number and stay nearby. Harsha remembers it well and even teaches it to his cousin.
Mere garden mein bahut ghonge aa gaye hain. 'Ghonga' English mein snail hi hai na?
Yes, "ghonga" is "snail". A snail has a shell on its back. A slug looks similar but has no shell.
Aur 'kenchua'?
"Kenchua" is "earthworm". Earthworms are good for the soil because they help air and water get into it.
John's piggy bank contains quarters, dimes, and nickels.  He has three more dimes than quarters and 6 fewer nickels than quarters.  If he has 63 coins, how many quarters does John have?

Let x represent the number of quarters John has
Nickels: x-6
Dimes: x+3
Total:x+x-6+x+3=63
3x-3=63
3x=66
x=22 quarters
The answer is 22.

Read this:

My younger sister Lakshmi stopped revising on Tuesday evening. I noticed because her chemistry notes stayed shut on the bed and she was humming. When I asked, she held out her phone: a forwarded message saying the Class 10 board exams were cancelled for our state. It had a circular number, a round stamp, even a signature in blue ink. "Look, it's official, Sangeeta akka," she said. I don't know what was going on in her head, but she seemed relieved, almost giddy. I said I couldn't remember board exams ever being cancelled like that, not once in all my school years. She shrugged. "But the stamp." We checked the board's own website together. Nothing. She went quiet, then opened the chemistry notes again, slowly.

What did the message on Lakshmi's phone say?
It said the Class 10 board exams were cancelled for their state.
Why did the message feel believable to Lakshmi?
The circular number, the round stamp and the blue signature made it look official, and she was relieved at the idea, so how rare cancellations are never crossed her mind.
Which step worked here, and why?
Checking the board's own website together worked, because it tested the vivid message against a reliable source instead of arguing about the stamp.
How does Sangeeta see her sister's behaviour?
Sangeeta sees only the outside, the shut notes, the humming and the relief, and says she doesn't know what was in Lakshmi's head.

Read this:

"Grandpa gave me five hundred rupees for Christmas!" Joseph waved the note outside the sweet shop. "I'm getting plum cake, jalebis and that big chocolate box."
Shreya raised her eyebrows. "All of it? That's so much."
"It's Christmas money. It's for fun."
"Last week you wouldn't buy one samosa with your pocket money."
"That's different! Pocket money is for important things. I saved it for three months."
"It's still five hundred rupees, Joseph."
"No, this is magic money. It just appeared!"
Shreya laughed. "So if Grandpa had put it in your pocket-money tin, you'd keep it?"
Joseph paused, the note in his hand. "Then it would be... tin money." He frowned at the chocolate box through the glass.

How much did Grandpa give Joseph for Christmas?
Five hundred rupees.
Why does spending the Christmas money feel fine to Joseph?
It just appeared, so it feels like magic fun money and he feels excited and free with it, while pocket money feels serious and protected.
What question could help Joseph decide?
He could ask himself, as Shreya hints, what he would do if the same note were in his pocket-money tin, and then choose what he really wants.
How does Shreya see Joseph's two kinds of money?
Shreya sees it as the same money either way, and she is amused that where it came from changes how he wants to spend it.

Swati, twenty-four, had come back to the small town after losing her job in the city. Weeks passed. She stopped going out, barely ate and sat on the roof every evening. Last month, a factory made 12000 dolls and their associated accessories.  The accessories for each doll included 2 shoes, 3 bags, 1 set of cosmetics, and 5 hats.  If each doll took 45 seconds to make and each accessory took 10 seconds to make, what was the total combined machine operation time, in seconds, required to manufacture all of the dolls and their accessories?

The number of shoes the factory made was 12000 dolls x 2 shoes/doll = 24000 shoes
The factory also made for each doll 12000 dolls x 3 bags/doll = 36000 bags
The set of cosmetics made for each doll was just one, so there are 12000 cosmetics sets
Finally, the number of hats for the dolls was 12000 dolls x 5 hats/doll = 60000 hats
In total, the number of accessories was 24000 + 36000 + 12000 + 60000 = 132000 accessories
The dolls took in total 12000 dolls x 45 seconds/doll = 540000 seconds to be made
All the accessories also took 132000 accessories x 10 seconds/accessory = 1320000 seconds
Combing both results, we have that the total time the machinery was working was 1320000 + 540000 = 1860000 seconds
The answer is 1860000.

On Thursday Walmart sold 210 pounds of ground beef. On Friday they sold twice that amount. On Saturday they only sold 150 pounds.  What was the average amount of beef sold per day?

On Friday Walmart sold 2 * 210 pounds = 420 pounds.
For all three days Walmart sold 210 + 420 + 150 pounds = 780 pounds.
The average amount of beef sold per day is 780 pounds / 3 days = 260 pounds.
The answer is 260.

I'm Seema. Last winter at the logistics firm in Kochi, I watched my colleague Jomon take one small mistake and build a disaster out of it.

He'd sent the monthly delivery report to the regional head with one wrong date: the 31st of November. He saw it an hour later and went grey. "That's it. She'll think I'm careless. My probation review is next month. They won't confirm me. And then who hires someone who didn't pass probation?"

I didn't tell him to relax. People said that to me once and it made me want to throw a stapler. I asked, "What's the worst realistic thing that happens today?"

He thought. "She replies and points it out."

"And how likely is it that one date decides your probation?"

A long breath. "Not very. My numbers are fine."

We wrote a one-line correction together. He sent it, then went to get tea for both of us.

Why did Seema's questions work better than telling Jomon to relax?

How might Jomon have felt if Seema had simply said "relax"?
He might have felt brushed off and more alone with the fear, the way Seema once did. The steady questions showed that Seema took him seriously.

Mary bought a packet of 1500 stickers. She shared them between Susan, Andrew and Sam in the ratio 1:1:3 respectively. If Sam gave Andrew two-thirds of his own share, how many stickers does Andrew now have?

The sum of the ratio is 1+1+3 = 5, therefore each part is 1500/5 = 300 stickers
Sam got 3 parts for a total of 3*300 = 900 stickers
He gave two-thirds of this which is 900*(2/3) = 600 stickers to Andrew
Andrew had one part already, which is 1*300 = 300
Andrew now has a total of 300+600 = 900 stickers.
The answer is 900.

"I wish I were an ocean," it sighed.

A boy named Waseem came along, kicking a pebble. He stopped, looked at the puddle and then dropped a paper boat in it. The boat floated, slowly turning.

For a few minutes, the puddle was a vast sea, with a ship sailing across it. The boy knelt and made engine noises. Waves rippled from the boat's hull.

Then he fished the boat out and ran home. The puddle, calm again, reflected a patch of blue sky. It no longer felt small. The sky, it noticed, was in it.

Read this:

Trisha, don't judge the mugs. You know I never drank coffee, right? Then last month, in the middle of the December exams, I read this headline: "Coffee drinkers live longer." A big study, thousands of people. I thought, that's it, science has spoken. So now it's three mugs a day. My mother thinks I've joined a cult. I told her, "Mummy, it's research, I'm investing in my future." Then my roommate asked who these coffee drinkers even were. Maybe people who can afford a café every morning, who have time to sit, who walk there. Maybe people who get sick stop drinking coffee, so the drinkers look healthier. I said she was overthinking it. But now I'm looking at mug number three, and I'm not so sure. Anyway, that's Rehana's great health plan. Want some?

What did the headline say?
"Coffee drinkers live longer."
Why did Rehana feel so sure coffee was the reason?
A big study with thousands of people felt like science had spoken, so Rehana felt confident and pleased about investing in the future.
What questions could Rehana ask before believing a headline like this?
Who the coffee drinkers were, what else might explain the link, like money, time or health, and whether the direction could run the other way.
How does the roommate see the headline?
The roommate suspects hidden factors, like affording a café or sick people giving up coffee, rather than coffee itself.
Janet has 9 cards more than Brenda. Mara has twice as many cards as Janet. How many cards do they have in all if Mara has 40 cards less than 150?

Mara has 150 - 40 = 110 cards.
Janet has 110/2 = 55 cards since Mara has twice as many as Janet.
Brenda has 55 - 9 = 46 cards since Janet has 9 cards more than Brenda.
Therefore, they all have 110 + 55 + 46 = 211 cards.
The answer is 211.

Sports day was loud: drums, whistles, the loudspeaker crackling out names. Behind the stands, Francis sat in the dust holding his ankle while three Class 6 boys laughed and called him a baby.
"Don't go tattling," one of them told Rajni.
Rajni's heart thumped. Last week Ms Kaur had made them practise: pick one grown-up, look at them, say "I need help."
Rajni pushed through the crowd to the first-aid table, stood right in front of Mr D'Souza and said it loudly: "I need help. My friend Francis is hurt behind the stands." She pointed.
Mr D'Souza came at once with an ice pack, sent the older boys away and knelt beside Francis. Later, Ms Kaur squeezed Rajni's shoulder. "That wasn't tattling. That was looking after your friend."

What had Ms Kaur made them practise last week?
Pick one grown-up, look at them, and say "I need help."
How was Rajni feeling when the older boy said "Don't go tattling"?
Rajni's heart thumped: she was nervous about being called a tattletale by older boys, but more worried about Francis.
Why did going to one specific adult work in the noisy crowd?
Standing in front of Mr D'Souza and pointing made the request impossible to miss, so he knew it was his job to act right away.
What might it be like for Francis when Mr D'Souza arrives?
Francis likely feels relieved and less alone, because an adult looks after his ankle and sends the teasing boys away.

Day one at the newspaper: Pankaj, a week out of college, was told to edit the city page by 9 pm. He stared at the layout software for an hour, pretending, before he walked to Sumit's desk. 'I don't want you to do it. Can you show me the order you check things in?' Sumit scribbled: headline, facts, names, length, photo caption. 'That's it. Go.'
Day four: Pankaj worked through the list alone, missed a spelling in a caption, caught two wrong ward numbers. The page went late, but it went.
Day eleven: he came back to Sumit with a notebook. 'When two sources give different numbers, which one wins? And how short is too short for a headline?' Sumit leaned back, pleased. 'Sit down. Those are good questions.'

What order did Sumit scribble for checking?
Headline, facts, names, length, photo caption.
What was Pankaj feeling during the first hour on day one?
Pankaj felt lost and anxious, staring at the software and pretending before gathering the courage to ask.
What helped Pankaj grow between day one and day eleven?
Using Sumit's checklist alone and making real mistakes, then returning with sharper questions instead of asking to be rescued.
How does Sumit see Pankaj on day eleven?
Sumit is pleased; the new questions show Pankaj has been working alone, so the help is worth giving.

Explain this to a child in two sentences.

At the end of Saturday sports practice at the community centre, Salma ma'am opened the cooler of fruit ice lollies. "Everyone gets one after we put the cones away." Ishir, five, stood by the cooler lid, staring inside. "Can I have it now? Now?" He hopped. His lip wobbled. Elizabeth, the helper, crouched down. "Ishir, can you sing the cone song with me? Orange cone, blue cone, into the bag!" Ishir sang and carried cones, louder each time. When Salma ma'am called, "Lollies!", he ran over grinning. "I waited the whole song!"
Five-year-old Ishir badly wants his lolly right away, but the helper asks him to sing the cone song and carry the cones. By the end of the song he is happy, and he proudly runs to get his lolly.
Is tresses another word for hair?

Yes, mostly. Tresses are long locks of hair, especially a woman's. It is a noun, used mainly in poetry and old stories.
Example: Her dark tresses fell over her shoulders as she bent over the book.

Read this:

Dear Yusuf,
You asked how I'm doing since Ammamma died. Honestly, I don't know. It's been three weeks. Some days I'm fine and then I hear a pressure cooker whistle and I cry because she always shouted 'Reena, turn it off!' Isn't that silly?
Amma gave me her green shawl. I sleep with it. It still smells of her coconut oil.
On Sunday, I tried making her tomato rasam from memory. It was too sour, and Appa laughed, and then he cried too. We sat in the kitchen together for a long time. That helped more than anything.
I've started writing down her sayings in a notebook so I don't forget.
Write back soon. Tell me about your new school.
Reena

What did Amma give Reena that belonged to Ammamma?
Her green shawl, which still smells of her coconut oil.
Why did Reena cry when she heard a pressure cooker whistle?
It reminded Reena of Ammamma shouting 'Reena, turn it off!', bringing the loss back suddenly.
Which of Reena's ways of mourning could help other grieving teens?
Keeping a meaningful object, cooking a family recipe and writing down the person's sayings.
How might Appa have felt in the kitchen after laughing at the rasam?
He was grieving Ammamma too, and sharing the moment with Reena let his own tears come.

Read this:

Karthik touched the wall in fifth place at the inter-school swimming final, and the whole gallery saw it. Hemant, from the rival school, smirked. "Thought you were the champ." Karthik felt heat climb his neck, but he did not answer. He thought instead of his own last time, which he wanted to beat. His coach Bhavna's face fell as she looked at the timing board. He waited, then asked, "What can I learn from this?" She said, "Your turns cost you two seconds. Let's fix that." Her frown was not the end of anything. In the corridor his friend Sameer sat down beside him. "I still respect you," Sameer said, and Karthik's shoulders loosened. He accepted the comfort, and later brought Sameer tea when Sameer missed his selection. At home his mother did not scold. She hugged him and asked what had happened. He told her everything, and together they made a plan for extra turn practice.

Where did Karthik place in the swimming final?
He placed fifth.
How did Hemant's reaction to Karthik's result differ from Sameer's, and how did Karthik respond to each?
Hemant smirked and gloated, and Karthik stayed silent and thought about beating his own last time, while Sameer said he still respected him and Karthik accepted the comfort.
What was Karthik feeling when Bhavna's face fell at the timing board?
He was probably uneasy and felt he had let her down, since he waited and then asked what he could learn.
What could Karthik do next with the plan he made with his mother?
He could follow the plan for extra turn practice and keep sharing honestly with her, as he did after the final.
I want to send my teacher a project file but it's too large for email.
Large files often don't fit as attachments. Does your school have a shared folder or class portal?
Yes, there's one.
Then upload it there, and send the teacher a short note that it's ready. Check the file opens properly before you tell your teacher.
Good idea. I'll open it first and then upload.
That's the right order. Opening it first means your teacher will see a working file and you won't have to send it twice.

One line only, please.

"To smoke," he answered. "It is quite a three pipe problem, and I beg that you won't speak to me for fifty minutes." He curled himself up in his chair, with his thin knees drawn up to his hawk-like nose, and there he sat with his eyes closed and his black clay pipe thrusting out like the bill of some strange bird. I had come to the conclusion that he had dropped asleep, and indeed was nodding myself, when he suddenly sprang out of his chair with the gesture of a man who has made up his mind and put his pipe down upon the mantelpiece.
A man asks for fifty minutes of quiet to smoke over a problem, then suddenly jumps up, having made up his mind.
Calvin buys a pack of chips, for $0.50, from the vending machine at lunch, 5 days a week. After 4 weeks, how much money has Calvin spent on chips?

The chips cost $0.50 a bag and he buys them 5 days a week so that's .50*5 = $2.50 a week
If he spends $2.50 on chips a week then over 4 weeks he will spend 2.50*4 = $10.00 on chips
The answer is 10.

Irfan had knocked the class's only good microscope off the bench during the practical exam rehearsal, and the lens cracked in front of everyone. The teacher sighed that it would come out of the lab fund, and Irfan wanted to disappear. That evening a power cut left his lane in darkness, and he sat on the steps outside his building, phone dead, with nothing but the replay in his head. Clumsy. Useless. Gopika found him there, holding a torch and two cups of tea from her mother. 'Everyone messes up,' she said, sitting down. 'I once set the chemistry lab bin on fire. Small fire, but still.' He laughed despite himself. She stayed until the lights came back, talking about nothing. Climbing the stairs later, Irfan felt lighter, as if someone had lifted half of it off his back. The next week, when a junior spilled ink all over the notice board, Irfan was the one who said, 'Happens to everyone.'

What did Gopika bring when she found Irfan?
A torch and two cups of tea from her mother.
How did Irfan feel climbing the stairs later?
He felt lighter, as if someone had lifted half the weight off his back 🙂
How did Irfan pass on what Gopika gave him?
When a junior spilled ink on the notice board, he said, 'Happens to everyone.'
How does Gopika see Irfan's mistake?
As an ordinary slip anyone could make, like her own small fire in the chemistry lab.
Mitchell has 30 pencils. He has 6 more pencils than Antonio. How many pencils does Mitchell and Antonio have together?

Antonio has 30-6 = 24 pencils
Antonio and Mitchell have 24+30 = 54 pencils together.
The answer is 54.

Read this:

Bhavna, you got into the college you wanted and now you feel empty? Let your Ankita Mausi tell you about 1998. I was nineteen and had dreamt of the medical college in Nagpur since I was a child. For two years I studied from dawn. When I got the seat, I was the happiest girl in the town. Then, a month into classes, I sat on the hostel steps one evening and couldn't remember why I had wanted it so much. I wasn't sad. Just tired, as if a string pulling me had been cut. My roommate found me there and said, 'You finished one race. You haven't picked the next one yet.' So I picked one. I wanted to work in villages. That became the new string. It took a while, beta.

How old was Ankita when she got the medical college seat?
Nineteen.
How did Ankita feel on the hostel steps that evening?
Ankita felt tired and empty, not sad, as if a string pulling her had been cut.
Which choice inside the story helped Ankita move on?
Choosing a new goal, working in villages, which gave her direction again after her roommate's words.
How might the roommate have seen Ankita that evening?
The roommate seems to have understood her mood kindly, seeing it as the pause after finishing one race.

In the hot week before the monsoon, children played at the village temple fair. Gopika was running with a paper windmill when she tripped and fell hard.
Shalini, five, stopped. Her mouth opened and she wailed, standing rooted to the spot. She shook, hands over her face, while Gopika sat in the dust holding her elbow.
A bangle-seller auntie lifted Gopika up. Shalini still could not move.
Later, sitting on her grandmother's lap, Shalini whispered, "I wanted to help Gopika, but my legs didn't go."
Her grandmother stroked her hair. "Your heart went. Next time, run to a grown-up."

What was Gopika running with when she tripped?
She was running with a paper windmill.
What does Shalini's whisper to her grandmother show she felt?
She felt caring and wanted to help, but was so frightened and overwhelmed that her legs didn't go.
What simple plan does the grandmother give Shalini?
Next time, run to a grown-up, so her caring can turn into help.
How might Gopika see Shalini's crying?
Gopika might be confused that Shalini cried more than she did, or might sense that her friend was scared for her.

messages.content: We booked accomodation near the beach for three nights. Is the spelling right?

We booked accommodation near the beach for three nights.
Why: spelling ("accomodation" -> "accommodation").

Nathan plays amateur baseball. He played for 3 hours for two weeks, every day. His friend Tobias played for 5 hours every day, but only for one week. How many hours did Nathan and Tobias play in total?

Two weeks are 14 days, so Nathan played for 3 * 14 = 42 hours.
Tobias played for 7 days, so he played a total of 5 * 7 = 35 hours.
Nathan and Tobias played together for 42 + 35 = 77 hours.
The answer is 77.

I'm Tushar, and there's a metro ride last winter I think about a lot.
It was packed. Mahima from my tuition was standing near the door. A man kept pressing closer to her, and she was leaning away, holding her bag in front of her. Her face looked stiff.
I wanted to say something. But what if I was wrong? What if he was just being pushed by the crowd, and I made a scene and everyone stared at me? My friends were right there. I stayed quiet.
An aunty next to her finally said loudly, “Bhai sahab, step back!” He got off at the next station.
Mahima didn't look at me. That night I couldn't sleep. I had been scared of looking foolish, and she had been scared, full stop.

What did the aunty say?
She said loudly, "Bhai sahab, step back!"
Why did Tushar feel unable to say something?
Tushar was afraid of misreading it and looking foolish in front of the crowd and friends, so the fear of embarrassment won.
What small safe step could Tushar have taken?
Tushar could have moved to stand between them, or asked Mahima, "Want to swap places?", which helps without needing to be sure.
How might Mahima have felt during the ride?
She likely felt frightened and trapped, leaning away and holding her bag, and hurt that people she knew stayed silent.
A friend of mine is going through a hard time and I don't know what to say.
You do not need perfect words. Often the most helpful thing is to be present and listen. Do you know what is troubling them?
They lost a grandparent last week.
I'm sorry to hear that. You can say that you are sorry and that you are there if they want company. Avoid trying to fix the sadness or compare it with others.
Should I ask them about it?
You can ask gently, 'Would you like to talk, or would you rather do something else?' Let them choose, and do not push.
What if they don't reply to my messages?
Grief can make people withdraw for a while. A short, kind message without any pressure to reply lets them know you are thinking of them.
How long should I keep checking in?
For as long as you can. Small, regular signs of care often mean more than a big gesture, and they can lean on you when they are ready.
The first day 54 people came and the second day twice as many came. How many came on the second day?
108. Because 54 x 2 = 108, since twice means two times.

At the community food bank in Leeds, Nkechi was moving to another city on Saturday. Noa would take over the volunteer schedule.
Nkechi handed her a laptop and a ring binder. "It's all in here. You'll be fine."
Noa pulled up a chair. "Can I tell it back to you first? I own the weekly rota, the Friday reminder texts, and finding cover when someone drops out."
"Yes, exactly."
"What about the Wednesday school pick-ups? The binder has a page, but no names."
Nkechi paused. "Oh. Those are Dennis and his daughter. I just ring them. It's not written anywhere."
"And the storeroom key?"
"Behind the kettle."
Noa wrote both on the first page of the binder. Then she read the whole list aloud once more. Nkechi laughed. "I think you know it better than me now."
Three weeks later, Dennis got a call from Noa every Tuesday, just as before.

Where is the storeroom key?
Behind the kettle.
How did Nkechi feel when Noa read the list aloud at the end?
Nkechi felt amused and reassured, laughing that Noa knew it better now.
What did Noa's questions uncover?
They uncovered that the Wednesday school pick-ups depended on a phone call to Dennis that was never written down.
What would change if Noa had just said, "Thanks, I'll be fine"?
The Wednesday pick-ups might have quietly stopped, because Dennis would never have got his call.
Please use no dialogue in a story about a very patient kingfisher.

Every dawn, a blue kingfisher named Neel sat on the same low branch above the pond. He watched the water without moving. Dragonflies landed near him. A frog croaked and sank away. Neel did not stir.

The young kingfishers dived again and again, splashing loudly, and most days they came up with nothing. Neel only watched. When the sun climbed above the reeds, a small silver fish drifted just beneath the surface.

He dropped like a blue stone. The water barely rippled. A moment later he was back on the branch with the fish flashing in his beak.

A girl named Seema, who came each morning to fetch water, had watched the whole thing. She stood very still herself for a while, then smiled and went home.

Our final-year project presentation was the first time I tried it for real. Samir went before me and rushed, his voice climbing higher with every slide. When my name was called, I felt the same thing starting: shoulders creeping up, breath stuck high. So I stood at the front, looked at my first slide, and let one long breath out through my nose. I let my shoulders drop. I counted two silent beats. Then I began: "Good morning. I'm Francis, and our project is about rainwater in hostels." My voice came out lower than I expected, and steady. Nobody noticed the pause; the professor later called me "very composed". Samir asked how I stayed calm. I told him it was just one breath, taken before anyone was looking.

What was the project about?
The project was about rainwater in hostels.
How did Francis feel when the name was called, and how can you tell?
Francis felt nervous; the shoulders crept up and the breath got stuck high.
Which steps helped Francis begin steadily?
One long exhale through the nose, dropping the shoulders and two silent beats before the first sentence.
How might Samir feel hearing that it was just one breath?
Samir, who rushed and whose voice climbed, may feel hopeful that the trick is simple enough to learn.

In the college library, Binita read the same paragraph of her thermodynamics chapter three times. Her phone lay face-up beside the book. Divyansh had posted a story an hour ago; she had watched it twice and checked whether he was online. Her friend Ishita slid into the seat opposite. "You've been on that page since we sat down."
Binita admitted it quietly. "I keep checking his profile. I know it's silly. When he doesn't post, I imagine he's upset with me, and when he does, I try to work out who it's for. I've spoken to him maybe four times."
"So you're mostly making up the rest?" Ishita asked, gently.
Binita winced, then nodded, and turned her phone face-down.
"Come to the badminton trials with me tomorrow?"
Binita said yes.

How many times has Binita spoken to Divyansh, according to her?
She says she has spoken to him maybe four times.
Why does Binita imagine Divyansh is upset when he does not post?
She knows very little about him, so her worry fills the gaps with guesses; she also feels silly admitting it.
What could Binita do to loosen the loop?
She could keep her phone away while studying, join things like the badminton trials, and keep talking with Ishita. If she still likes Divyansh, she can get to know him in ordinary settings.
How does Ishita see Binita's habit?
Ishita sees a friend stuck on one page and worried. She points out, gently, that much of it is imagined, and offers something to do together instead of judging.

I didn't realise how much Jasleen was carrying until the night I found her asleep sitting up, the baby on her chest and her laptop still open.
Looking back, we weren't ready. I'd just started a new job with long hours. Our savings could cover maybe two months of trouble. But my Bebe asked at every phone call, and Jasleen's aunts asked at every wedding. At some point, "when?" started feeling like an order. So we said, okay, now.
Our daughter is wonderful. But it's Jasleen who took unpaid leave, Jasleen who does most nights, Jasleen who worries about the money while I'm stuck in office till nine.
That night I sat next to her and felt ashamed. We didn't choose the timing. We let everyone else choose it, and she paid the price.
The next morning I asked my manager about leaving by six.
— Saurabh

What did Saurabh find Jasleen doing that night?
Asleep sitting up, the baby on her chest and her laptop still open.
How did Saurabh feel sitting next to Jasleen?
Saurabh felt ashamed, seeing that she was carrying most of the load because they let others choose the timing.
What else could Saurabh and Jasleen have done when relatives kept asking?
They could have set their own timeline based on the new job and savings, and told relatives kindly that it was their decision.
How is Jasleen affected by the timing?
Jasleen carries most of the strain: unpaid leave, most nights and money worries, leaving her exhausted.

messages.content: Mira says: "My secret number has 7 hundreds, no tens and 4 ones." Write the number and its expanded form.

Answer: 704 = 700 + 4.

Draw three boxes H | T | O. Put 7 in H, 0 in T and 4 in O. The number is 704. In expanded form we leave out the zero part: 700 + 4. Play the game in pairs: one child says a secret number in hundreds, tens and ones, the other writes it both ways.

Saturday, 9 pm. First class done. Twenty students from classes eight to ten in the school near my aunt's village crammed into one room with six borrowed laptops. Neelam, the science teacher who let me use the room, sat at the back. I'd planned an hour on variables; it took forty minutes because half the group couldn't type yet, so we switched to drawing flowcharts on paper and typing in pairs. Learned already: pairs work, short tasks work, my slides don't. The power went out twice, and the kids clapped in the dark when it came back. I'm not planning anything big yet. Four more Saturdays, then I'll write down what worked and only then decide what next. Tired feet, full head. — Farida

How many laptops were there?
There were six borrowed laptops.
How does Farida feel at the end of the day?
Farida feels tired but energised, with tired feet and a full head from what was learned.
What other approach could Farida use before the next class?
Farida could ask Neelam and a few students what they want to learn, since it shows what is worth teaching before more slides are made.
How might Neelam see the class?
Neelam probably sees a useful start, since twenty students turned up and stayed engaged even when the power went out.

Baljeet arrived at the Pune hostel in the middle of the monsoon, knowing nobody, with a phone that barely held a charge and his family three states away. By the second week he was up till three every night, because that's when Wing C came alive: card games, loud debates, instant noodles on a smuggled heater. The seniors drank on Saturdays, and Baljeet, who had never touched alcohol, held a glass he didn't drink so he'd fit in. He began repeating their opinions on everything from cricket to politics. Mid-term exams were ten days away. One night his roommate Omkar, who went to bed at eleven, said, 'You don't even like cards.' Baljeet laughed it off, but lying awake later, he couldn't remember the last opinion he'd had that was really his.

Until what time was Baljeet up every night?
Till three.
What did Baljeet feel lying awake at the end?
Uneasy and a bit lost, unable to remember the last opinion that was truly his.
What could Baljeet try to find himself again?
Set a bedtime before the exams, keep one or two of his own habits, and spend time with people like Omkar who notice who he really is.
How might Omkar see Baljeet's first weeks?
Omkar seems to notice Baljeet changing to fit Wing C and is quietly concerned, pointing out he doesn't even like cards.

Monday. Nikita, the team lead, told Gautam to write the client report in the long format. Gautam said nothing and stayed late, annoyed, sure nobody would read forty pages.
Thursday. Before the next draft he knocked on her cabin door. "I understand you want every detail covered for the client. My concern is that the main finding gets buried. Could I put a one-page summary up front and keep the full detail after it?" Nikita thought, then said, "Show me a sample."
Following Tuesday. Gautam brought the sample. Nikita kept the summary and asked for one more table. He left feeling lighter, though he wasn't sure she liked being questioned.

On which day did Gautam knock on Nikita's cabin door?
On Thursday.
What was Gautam feeling on Monday, and how can you tell?
He was annoyed and doubtful about the format, since he stayed late and said nothing though he thought nobody would read it. He might also have felt unsure whether he was allowed to object.
What made Gautam's Thursday approach more workable than staying silent?
He acknowledged her aim, gave one reason and offered an alternative, so Nikita had something concrete to react to.
How might Nikita have felt when Gautam knocked?
She may have been surprised or slightly defensive, but asking for a sample suggests she was willing to listen; Gautam himself could not tell if she liked being questioned.
Spell "vegetable" for me please. Also, why do worms come out after rain?

1. It is spelled v-e-g-e-t-a-b-l-e.
2. The soil fills with water, and worms come up to breathe and to move around.

Madhav sits at the desk next to mine, and for three months after his father fell ill he was the first in and the last out, then went straight to the hospital for the night. His eyes were red all the time. Once I found him asleep in the meeting room at lunch.
In June something changed. When I asked, he told me he had done the maths: "Papa's recovery will take a year. I can't do every night for a year. Nobody can." He and his brother had worked out a rota: alternate nights, a paid attendant for the afternoons, and one weekend a month when Madhav's aunt came from Indore so both brothers could rest.
I can't say how he feels about it inside. But he stopped falling asleep at his desk. Last week he went to a cousin's wedding and came back with photos.
— Nitin

How long did Madhav say his father's recovery would take?
A year.
What might Madhav have been feeling in the first three months?
He seemed exhausted and stretched thin, with red eyes and naps in the meeting room, though Nitin can't know his inner state.
What else could support Madhav's plan over the year?
Checking the rota every month and adding help if someone wears down, including someone to talk to about his own stress.
How does Nitin see the change in Madhav?
Nitin sees him rested enough to stop sleeping at his desk and even go to a wedding.

Tenzin, fifteen, had been gaming until one or two most nights. In the mornings in their Darjeeling flat, his mother Bidisha had to shake him awake.
At football practice on Thursday, he missed an easy pass and the coach said, “Where's your head?” Tenzin didn't know.
That weekend, he checked his phone's screen-time page. Five hours on Saturday alone.
He felt a sting of shame. He went to his mother. “Can the console live in the living room? And can you switch the wifi off at eleven?”
Bidisha looked surprised. “Your idea?”
“Mine.”
A week later, he scored in practice. He was asleep by 11:30 most nights.

What did the coach say when Tenzin missed a pass?
“Where's your head?”
How did Tenzin feel when he saw five hours of screen time?
He felt a sting of shame.
What limits did Tenzin choose, and why are they effective?
Moving the console to the living room and switching the wifi off at eleven, which makes late gaming harder.
How did Bidisha react to Tenzin's request?
She was surprised and probably pleased that it was his own idea.

Minakshi and Joseph had joined the firm in the same month. Over four years she had sat with him in a hospital waiting room when his father had surgery, and he had brought her soup the week her engagement ended. She could say the shameful thing aloud to Joseph, that she was tired of her manager's tone, and expect only "Same here."

When the senior analyst role opened, Joseph's palms went damp. He dreaded watching everyone else move up without him. That afternoon, in the manager's office, he mentioned, lightly, that Minakshi had complained about the workload and the tone. "Just so you know," he added. He told himself it was business.

A week later Gurpreet, at the coffee machine, said awkwardly, "I assumed you knew that Joseph told the manager what you said." Minakshi's hand froze on the cup. At first she felt nothing, a strange blank, like a room with the furniture removed. Then rage came, hot and fast. Later, in the stairwell, she realised she was grieving twice: for a friend, and for the person she had believed him to be.

How did Minakshi learn what Joseph had done?
Gurpreet told her at the coffee machine.
How does what Joseph did in the manager's office change the meaning of the four years of friendship?

Four years of hospital waits and soup made Joseph the person Minakshi could be weakest around. His telling the manager about her complaint, out of dread of being passed over, broke that trust, so she lost both the friend and the person she had believed him to be.
What was Minakshi feeling first at the coffee machine?
She felt numb, a strange blank, before the rage came.
What could Minakshi do next?
She could give herself time before reacting, talk with someone she trusts, and later decide calmly whether to speak to Joseph directly.

Uncle Jude baked 256 cookies. He gave 15 cookies to Tim, 23 cookies to Mike, kept some in the fridge and gave the rest to Anna. How many cookies did he put in the fridge if he gave twice as many cookies as he gave Tim to Anna?

He gave twice 15 cookies to Anna which is 2*15 = 30 cookies
He gave out a total of 15+23+30 = 68 cookies
The remainder in the fridge is 256-68 = 188 cookies
The answer is 188.

Read this:

In Nandurbar, the Class 9 group had been passing round a video of Afreen slipping in the rain outside the bus stand, slowed down with silly music. Shankar watched it on Sunday night. Everyone was laughing. He didn't laugh, but he didn't say anything either. He just closed the app.

On Monday, Afreen came to school with her head down and sat alone at lunch. Shankar felt a heavy knot in his stomach. He had seen it. He could have said something.

After lunch, he walked over. "Afreen, I saw the video. I'm sorry I didn't say anything. It was cruel."

She looked up, surprised. "You're the first one to say that."

He reported the video in the group, and when his friend Suresh asked him to forward it, he said, "No. Delete it." Then he told their class teacher, Shinde sir, before the last period. Sir went to the group admin that same afternoon, had the video removed, and spoke to Afreen and her father after school.

Where did Afreen slip in the video?
Afreen slipped in the rain outside the bus stand.
What was Shankar feeling when Afreen sat alone at lunch?
Shankar felt guilty, with a heavy knot in his stomach, because he had seen the video and said nothing.
What did Shankar do to make up for staying silent?
Shankar apologised to Afreen, reported the video, refused to forward it and told Shinde sir the same day.
How did Afreen react to Shankar's apology?
Afreen was surprised and seemed a little comforted, since he was the first to call the video cruel.

Read this:

Imran, you want that energy drink because the cricketer on TV says it makes you hit sixes? Sit, let your Kavitha Aunty tell you something. When I was a girl, a famous film heroine was in a malt-drink ad. She said, "One glass a day and you'll shine like me!" I believed every word. I cried until Appa bought a tin. I drank it every morning and looked in the mirror every evening. No shine. One day Appa asked, "Kavitha, who pays the heroine to say that?" I thought hard. "The company?" "Yes. She is selling, not advising." I felt so silly, and a bit cheated. After that, whenever an ad promised magic, I asked Appa or my teacher whether it was true. Now go and ask your Ammi about that drink, Imran.

What did the heroine in the ad promise?
That one glass a day would make you shine like her.
How did young Kavitha feel when she understood the heroine was paid?
She felt silly and a bit cheated for believing every word.
What was the turning point in Aunty's story?
Appa's question about who pays the heroine, which helped her see ads sell things and start checking with adults.
How might Appa have seen young Kavitha crying for the tin?
He probably saw an ad pulling his daughter in, so he bought it once and later asked a question to help her think.
I heard discover in a film last night. Can you tell me its meaning?

To discover means to find or learn something for the first time. It is a verb.
Example: The children discovered a bird's nest in the old tree.

Read this:

Afreen's Dada was in the hospital, and her stomach was full of stones. Nobody told her anything. On the third day she asked her father Farhan, "Is Dada going to die?" Farhan crouched down. "He is very ill. The doctors are working hard, and I do not know how it will go." It was scary, but less scary than the silence. She drew the two of them flying a kite and taped it beside his bed.

Dr Vijay explained the drip and the oxygen in simple words, and showed her the screen where the heartbeat was a green line. Afreen asked what each thing did. Knowing a little, she trusted the doctors more, and she prepared herself that it might not be enough.

It was not. Dada died on a Thursday. Afreen felt empty, then furious at the hospital, then confused. She cried in the car, asked why, and at the prayers she listened to her uncles telling stories about him. Some days the sadness came like waves, and she let it.

Weeks later her Dadi lay resting in the afternoons. Afreen pulled a chair beside the bed and read comic stories aloud. She did not try to fix anything. Dadi patted her hand and closed her eyes, smiling.

What did Afreen draw for Dada?
She drew the two of them flying a kite.
How did honest answers change Afreen's fear, and how did her part with Dadi differ?

Being told honestly and hearing simple explanations made the fear smaller and let her trust the doctors, though she prepared for bad news. With Dadi she did not need to fix anything, only read aloud and be there.
What was Afreen feeling on the third day when nobody told her anything?
She felt afraid. Her stomach was full of stones and the silence scared her.
What helped Afreen with her fear while Dada was in the hospital?
She asked her father an honest question, asked Dr Vijay what each thing did, and drew a picture to tape beside his bed.

Read this:

The sugar factory office near Kolhapur was closing its accounts section, and Kalyani, the section head, called Tejas in herself instead of letting the head office send a letter.
"I'm not going to wrap this up nicely. Your post goes at the end of March," she said. "I argued for three months' pay instead of one, and they agreed. And I'll write you a reference that says exactly how good you are."
Tejas stared at the calendar on the wall. His throat felt tight. Then he noticed the dark circles under her eyes.
"You fought for that?"
"For all six of you."
He swallowed. "Thank you, madam. Truly."
Before he left in March, he gave her a box of pedhas from his mother's kitchen and saved her number. In June, Kalyani phoned: a friend at a dairy in Sangli needed an accountant.

How much pay did Kalyani argue for?
Three months' pay instead of one.
What was Tejas feeling as he stared at the calendar?
He felt shocked and sad, his throat tight at losing his post.
How did Tejas accept Kalyani's help well?
He thanked her sincerely, gave her a gift, and kept in touch, which later led to a job lead in Sangli.
How might Kalyani feel delivering the news herself?
Kalyani is probably tired and sad, with dark circles under her eyes, yet caring enough to tell each person honestly and fight for them.
What was the topic of my last science project?
I don't know the topic of your last science project, as I can't see your school records. Look in your project folder or ask your teacher.

Read this:

Tuesday, after school
Today Avni and I nearly stopped being friends over hopscotch. Avni wanted hopscotch at break. I wanted to finish our chalk city on the back steps. We both stood there with our arms folded for ages, and break kept getting shorter.
Then I had an idea. I said, "Hopscotch today, chalk city tomorrow. And on Friday we toss a coin for who picks."
Avni thought about it. "Only if you write it down so you don't forget."
So I wrote it on a page from my rough book and we both signed it like a real contract. Hopscotch was actually fun. I even got to square eight.
The page is folded in my pencil box. Tomorrow is MY turn 😊
- Vidya

Where did Vidya put the written deal?
The page is folded in Vidya's pencil box.
What was Vidya feeling while the two friends stood with arms folded?
Vidya felt stubborn and also worried, because break kept getting shorter and the quarrel was putting the friendship at risk.
Why did writing the deal down help?
It turned the promise into something both could remember and check, which was Avni's condition for agreeing, so neither would feel cheated the next day.
How might Avni have felt about the deal?
Avni probably felt heard and relieved that hopscotch came first, and safer saying yes once the promise was signed 🙂

Read this:

Subject: Plan for Saturday's vendors' rally
Hi Sumit,
Before Saturday, a few things I want us both clear on.
1. We march only on the route the police approved: from the old market to the municipal office.
2. Each block of twenty vendors has one volunteer with a whistle and a list of phone numbers, including the free legal-aid line.
3. No sticks, no burning anything. If anyone brings them, we ask them to leave.
4. If the crowd turns violent, we stop and walk everyone back. I know some of the younger vendors will call us cowards. I'd rather be called a coward than see Hanif chacha's cart burned or anyone hurt.
Our cause is fair. It stays fair only if our way is too.
Call me tonight?
Imran

Where does the approved route go?
From the old market to the municipal office.
What is Imran worried about?
Imran is anxious that the crowd could turn violent and someone could be hurt, or a cart like Hanif chacha's burned.
Which parts of the plan protect people's safety and rights?
The approved route, block volunteers with whistles and the legal-aid number, no sticks or burning, and walking everyone back if violence starts.
How might the younger vendors see the rule to stop if things turn violent?
Some may see it as cowardly, wanting to push harder, even though it protects them.

metadata.subtype: Staying safe and lawful in action [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Yash, you asked how I finally sorted my scholarship refund. Honestly? One call a day. I'm Tenzin, and I used to be terrible with official calls. The phone would ring with an unknown number and I'd just watch it. For months I didn't call the college accounts office about the refund they owed me.

Then my cousin said, "Make a list, easiest first, one a day." So on day one I called the canteen to ask their opening time. Ridiculous, but my heart was racing even for that. Day two, the hostel office. Day three, the bank helpline. Each time, nothing terrible happened. People were bored, sometimes kind.

Day five, the accounts office. I held the phone for ten minutes before dialling. The man said, "Oh yes, your file is here, come on Tuesday." That was it. Four months of dread, and it was one sentence.

What did Tenzin call about on day one?
Tenzin called the canteen to ask their opening time.
What was Tenzin feeling while holding the phone before calling the accounts office?
Tenzin was still nervous and hesitant, needing ten minutes before dialling, even after four easier calls.
What made the easy-first plan work?
Each small call showed nothing terrible happened, which shrank the dread enough for the hard call.
How might the man at the accounts office see the call?
For the man it was a routine query, easily answered, with no idea of the months of dread behind it.

metadata.subtype: Approaching the fear in small steps [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

On the playgroup mat, three toddlers each had a box with holes.

Irfan lifted the star block and pushed it at the circle. Nothing. He tried the square. Nothing. The triangle. Nothing. Then the star hole, and the block slid in with a soft thud. He clapped.

Rekha dropped a star through its slot for her daughter Sarita. Sarita copied the drop, but held her block flat, and it bounced off the lid. She looked at it, picked it up, and began again from the top.

Neel smacked the square block down on the round opening with his palm. Again. Again. His cheeks went red. The block stayed square, and the opening stayed round.

Later Irfan met the square block. It would not go in. He turned it a quarter turn, then tried again, and it dropped through.

Which block did Irfan lift first?
Irfan lifted the star block first.
How did Neel's way of using the square block differ from Irfan's later way, and what happened?
Neel smacked the square block against the round opening again and again and nothing changed, while Irfan turned the square a quarter turn and it dropped through.
What was Neel feeling when the block would not go in?
Frustration and anger, since his cheeks went red as he kept smacking it.
What could a grown-up do to help Neel?
A grown-up could show the square block beside the square opening, or gently turn it to help Neel see where it fits.
I need new shoes for school but I can't decide between two pairs.
What are the two pairs like?
One looks really cool but pinches a little. The other is plain but comfortable.
Shoes that pinch in the shop usually feel worse after a full day of walking. Since you will wear them to school every day, comfort matters a lot.
But the cool ones are what everyone is wearing.
That is understandable. You could take the comfortable pair for school and save up for the stylish ones later for outings. Your feet will thank you on long school days.
Stefan, Vail, and Aiguo collected seashells. Stefan had 16 more seashells than Vail. Vail had 5 less than Aiguo. Aiguo had 20 seashells. How many seashells did the 3 children have in total?

Aiguo = 20 shells
Vail = 20 - 5 = 15 shells
Stefan = 15 + 16 = 31 shells
Total = 20 + 15 + 31 = 66
The 3 children had 66 seashells altogether.
The answer is 66.
My teacher greeted a guest with "How do you do?" What should the guest say?

It is a formal greeting, not a real question. The guest usually answers "How do you do?" too.
Example: How do you do? I am pleased to meet you.

Read this:

Thursday
Exam week. I did the rules again today. Same breakfast, nothing till evening, then only what's on the list. It makes the panic about exams go quiet for a while, like I'm in charge of something.
But I was dizzy on the stairs. My hands are always cold. I hide what I'm doing, even from Lalit, and he's my brother, I tell him everything.
Tonight Lalit sat at the end of my bed. He said, "I've noticed you're not eating with us. I'm not angry. I'm scared for you." I cried and told him some of it.
He said, "This isn't something you can fix alone." He's right. Tomorrow we're going to the doctor together. I've already told Mummy.
Arohi

Who sat at the end of the bed?
Lalit, Arohi's brother.
How does Arohi feel when following the food rules?
Arohi feels briefly calmer and in charge during exam panic, but also dizzy, cold and secretive.
What step is Arohi taking, and why is it right?
Seeing a doctor with Lalit, because the food rules bring real harm and a doctor is the right place to start.
How did Lalit feel about what he noticed?
Lalit felt scared for Arohi, though he made clear he was not angry.

Read this:

By her second year at university in Manchester, Chidi had stopped going to the Nigerian society dinners. Siddiq said the guys there 'looked at her wrong'. She'd stopped wearing her yellow dress because he said it was 'for attention'. He checked her location 'because he loved her', and got upset if she took more than ten minutes to reply. Each rule came wrapped in a kiss or a worried face, so she told herself it was love. One afternoon her old flatmate Grace bumped into her in the library. 'Chidi! We never see you any more. Are you okay?' Chidi opened her mouth to say fine and, to her own surprise, started crying. Over coffee she listed the rules out loud and heard them properly for the first time. Grace said gently, 'That's not love, that's control. And it's not your fault.' That week, with Grace beside her, Chidi went to the university counselling service. She wore the yellow dress.

What did Siddiq say about Chidi's yellow dress?
That it was 'for attention'.
What did Chidi feel when Grace asked if she was okay?
She was surprised by her own tears, feeling the weight of how small her life had become.
What helped Chidi start to see the pattern?
Listing the rules out loud to Grace, hearing Grace name it as control, and going to the counselling service.
How does Grace see Siddiq's rules?
As control, not love, and she makes sure Chidi knows it isn't her fault.

Read this:

Pranav's first Monday as team lead began with a joke. "Congratulations, boss," said Dolma, with a flat smile. She had wanted the role, and her comments in meetings came out sharp. Pranav's cheeks warmed, and he wondered if they all thought he did not deserve it. He told the team, "I don't know the billing system as well as Dolma does, so I will lean on her." He listened more than he talked, and gave Dolma the client migration, big work with her name on it. He did not demand warmth.

Mridul followed the new plan and thanked him after the review. "That was clear." Pranav felt proud, and also unsure. Each week he asked, "What is one thing I could do better?" and passed credit for the win to the team.

By the second month he was lost on budgeting and hesitated to ask his director. Then he wrote three lines: "Here is my problem, here are two options, which would you choose?" The director spent half an hour with him and suggested a coach. "You should have asked sooner," the director said, smiling.

By spring Dolma had started bringing him ideas. It took time, and neither of them mentioned it.

What work did Pranav give Dolma?
He gave Dolma the client migration.
How did Pranav's approach to Dolma's coolness compare with his handling of Mridul's thanks?
With Dolma he stayed generous and gave her meaningful work without demanding warmth. With Mridul's thanks he felt proud yet unsure, so he kept asking for feedback and passed credit to the team.
What was Pranav feeling when Dolma said "Congratulations, boss" with a flat smile?
He felt hurt and unsure, wondering if the team thought he did not deserve the role.
What made Pranav's request to his director work well?
He brought a specific problem with two options instead of just worry, and the director gave him half an hour and a coach.

Read this:

The bus from the district town to Karanpura was packed, and Lalit, twenty-four, the village's computer operator, noticed a young woman standing near the door with two suitcases, swaying at every bump. She was reading a paper with the panchayat office's address, frowning at the Hindi. He stood and offered his seat. "New here?" he asked. She nodded. "Ankita. I'm the new schoolteacher. From Kolkata." Her Hindi was slow, careful.
At the stop, he carried one suitcase to the panchayat office and introduced her to the sarpanch, who asked her questions in thick Haryanvi. Lalit translated gently. She needed a residence form for the teacher's quarters; he sat with her at the bench outside and filled it. The chaiwala sent two cups over on the house. Ankita smiled for the first time. "I thought I'd be lost for weeks," she said. Lalit grinned. "Maybe just days."

What job had Ankita come to Karanpura for?
She was the new schoolteacher.
What was Lalit feeling when he noticed Ankita swaying near the door?
He felt concerned and kind, noticing she was struggling with her suitcases and the address.
Which of Lalit's small welcomes mattered most, and why?
Translating for the sarpanch and filling the residence form, because they removed the biggest barriers for a newcomer with little local language.
How might Ankita see Karanpura after her first day?
She probably feels relieved and more at home than she expected, thanks to Lalit's help and the chaiwala's kindness.
She said me "I am feeling hungry". Is it okay?
Close, but "said me" is not correct. Say: "She told me, 'I am feeling hungry'" or "She said, 'I am hungry.'" Why: "tell" takes a person directly, but "say" does not.
Aur "I am feeling hungry" sahi hai?
It is understood, but most people say "I am hungry." Why: "hungry" is a state, so the simple present is more natural than "am feeling".

Read this:

Dear Varun Chetta,
You asked on the phone why I sound so flat. I'll try to answer here, because writing is easier than saying it.
For about three months I've been waking at four with my heart racing, dreading school. I haven't told anyone, for a whole list of reasons. Achan says counsellors are for people who can't manage their own minds. I worry it costs a lot, and Amma is already counting every rupee. Mostly, I tell myself it isn't bad enough. I still go to class. I still smile in photos.
But a senior at school waited until she couldn't leave the house at all. I don't want to wait that long.
Our school counsellor is free. When you're home next Saturday, will you come with me, and help me tell Amma and Achan?
Gopika

At what time has Gopika been waking up?
At four, with a racing heart.
Why has Gopika told nobody?
Gopika is afraid Achan will see it as weakness, worries about the cost for Amma, and thinks it isn't bad enough.
What choice does Gopika make at the end of the letter?
To ask early: Gopika asks Varun Chetta to come to the free school counsellor and help tell Amma and Achan.
How might Varun Chetta feel reading this letter?
He may feel worried but glad to be trusted, and able to make the first step less frightening for Gopika.

Read this:

Thanks for having me, Hafsa. So I'm Jomon, and for most of college I hated my body. I stood in front of the mirror listing everything wrong.
The change started on a trek in Munnar. At the top, legs shaking, I thought: this body just carried me up a mountain. It didn't care what I looked like.
After that I unfollowed every account that made me feel bad. I started eating regular meals instead of skipping and then bingeing. And I tried talking to myself like I'd talk to a friend. "You're tired, you did well today," instead of "You're disgusting."
But honestly, the biggest step was when I told my doctor how bad it had got. She referred me to a counsellor who specialises in this. The trek helped. The professional help is what really changed things.

Where did Jomon's change start?
On a trek in Munnar.
How did Jomon feel at the top of the trek?
Jomon felt amazed and grateful, realising the body had just carried them up a mountain.
What steps from Jomon's story build a kinder relationship with the body?
Valuing what the body can do, unfollowing harsh accounts, eating regular meals, speaking kindly to oneself, and getting a qualified professional when the struggle is serious.
How might the doctor have seen Jomon's honesty?
The doctor likely saw it as a brave and important step and responded by referring Jomon to a specialist counsellor.

metadata.subtype: Building a kinder relationship with the body [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the gurdwara sports day in their village near Moga, Jasleen tripped in the sack race and rolled right onto the chalk line. She got up with dust on her salwar and finished last. For the rest of the afternoon she stood behind a tent pole, sure the whole village was pointing at her.
"Everyone saw me fall," she whispered to Rajni.
Rajni was licking jalebi syrup off her fingers. "Fall when?"
Across the ground, the boys were arguing about the tug-of-war rope, the aunties were counting prize cups, and the sack-race winner was crying because his sack had torn.
Jasleen came out from behind the pole, just a little.

Where did Jasleen stand for the rest of the afternoon?
She stood behind a tent pole.
Why does Jasleen believe the whole village was pointing at her?
The fall felt so big to her that she assumed it was the biggest thing everyone else had seen too.
What turning point brought Jasleen out from behind the pole?
Rajni's "Fall when?" showed that even her friend hadn't noticed, and she could see everyone busy with their own things. 🙂
How was the sack race for the winner, compared with how Jasleen saw it?
The winner was busy crying over a torn sack, far too caught up to think about Jasleen's fall.

Read this:

Floor rep's note by Ayesha, Girls' Hostel Block C, second floor.
Pooja, my roommate, reacted strangely again tonight. During a group project call, someone said, "Look at me when I'm talking to you." Pooja's face went stiff; she muted herself, snapped at me when I asked if she wanted tea, and sat with her arms wrapped tight until the call ended. This is the third time I've seen that phrase do it. I don't know why, and she hasn't said. I've decided not to ask. After the call I left a note on her desk: "You seemed upset tonight. I'm around if you want company, and I won't ask questions." She came back later and sat on my bed for a while, not talking. I'll mention to the warden, only that she's had some hard evenings, if it keeps happening.

What phrase made Pooja's face go stiff?
"Look at me when I'm talking to you."
Why did Ayesha choose a note instead of asking Pooja directly?
Ayesha felt concerned but careful, not wanting to push Pooja into a story Pooja hadn't offered, so a quiet note felt kinder.
What makes Ayesha's plan about the warden sensible?
Ayesha will only share that Pooja has had hard evenings, and only if it continues, respecting Pooja's privacy while making sure support is there.
How might Pooja feel sitting on the bed without talking?
Pooja may feel comforted and safe, grateful not to be asked while still wanting company.

Read this:

In the evening, Seema went to milk the buffalo behind the house, and Sahil stayed on the charpai in the courtyard. The lamp flickered. The fields were dark and full of croaking. Sahil pulled his blanket tight and started singing, “Machhli jal ki rani hai,” softly to himself, then a little louder. From the shed came Seema's voice, singing the next line. Sahil sang the line after. They went back and forth until she came out with the warm milk bucket and sat beside him.

Where did Seema go in the evening?
To milk the buffalo behind the house.
What was Sahil feeling when he pulled his blanket tight and began singing?
He was probably a bit scared and lonely in the dark courtyard, and singing helped him soothe himself.
What did Seema's singing back do for Sahil?
It let him know she was near and joined his coping song, so he felt less alone.
What would change if Seema had called out “Stop singing, be quiet”?
Sahil would lose his way of calming himself and might feel more frightened.
Is wealthy the same as rich?

Yes, very close. Wealthy means having a lot of money or property. It is an adjective and sounds a bit more formal than rich.
Example: The wealthy merchant gave a large sum to build the school library.
Mark has the option of getting a $300 lens with a 20% discount or a $220 lens.  How much money does he save by buying the cheaper lens?

The discount is worth 300*.2=$60
So the lens cost 300-60=$240
That means he saves 240-220=$20 by buying the cheaper lens
The answer is 20.
Hugh had eight pounds of candy, Tommy had six pounds of candy, and Melany had seven pounds of candy. If they share the candy equally, how much will each person have?

Hugh and Tommy have a total of 8+6 = 14 candies.
Since Melany also has seven candies, they have 14+7 = 21 candies.
If they combine and share the candies equally, each person will get 21/3 = 7 candies.
The answer is 7.

In simpler words, please, with no idioms.

Tonight I finally told Wasim, my oldest friend, over the phone. He didn't say "at least". He said, "That's a budget line, Suraj, not a report card." I cried a little, which was embarrassing but also a relief.

Tonight I finally told Wasim, my oldest friend, over the phone. He didn't try to make it seem small. He said, "Losing the job was about money, Suraj. It does not say how good you are." I cried a little. It was embarrassing, but it also made me feel better.
Use the passive and leave out who did it: Someone cleaned the classroom before the inspection.
The classroom was cleaned before the inspection.
John bought a tennis racket. He also bought sneakers that cost $200 and a sports outfit that cost $250. He spent a total of $750 for all those items. What was the price of the racket?

Total amount spent for athletic shoes and sportswear is $200 + $250 = $450.
The price of the racket is $750 - $450 = $300.
The answer is 300.

Read this:

"Chandrika, before dinner, can we make a plan?" Deepika patted the sofa. "For the next time you get really angry."
"I'm not angry now."
"That's why now is the best time. What helps you?"
Chandrika thought. "Maybe cold water. And the balcony."
"Okay. Water, balcony, then you come and tell me. Let's try it once, pretend."
Chandrika rolled her eyes but walked to the balcony, drank from the steel glass, and came back grinning. "Done."
Two days later her brother tore her drawing. Chandrika's fists clenched. She opened her mouth to shout. Then she turned, went to the balcony, drank water and stood there a while. When she came back her voice shook, but she said, "Mumma, he tore it."
"Thank you for coming to tell me," Deepika said.

What did Chandrika choose to help her calm down?
Cold water and the balcony.
What was Chandrika feeling when her brother tore the drawing?
Chandrika felt furious, fists clenched, ready to shout.
Why did Deepika make the plan before dinner, when Chandrika wasn't angry?
Calming steps learned and practised before a storm are much easier to use during one.
How might Deepika feel when Chandrika comes to tell her?
Deepika likely feels proud and relieved that the plan worked.

Read this:

Pablo lifted his daughter Zeynep out of the bath and reached for the shampoo. She clamped her eyes shut, scrunched her nose and turned her face into the towel. “Eyes closed, I can see,” said Pablo, and poured water only on her back. In the car later, the streetlights slid past and her eyelids began to droop. Each blink lasted longer than the one before. Pablo lowered the radio. By the time they parked in front of the flats, Zeynep was asleep, her fingers loosely holding the blanket.

What did Pablo reach for that made Zeynep close her eyes?
The shampoo.
What do Zeynep's closed eyes at bath time suggest, and what might be another reading?
They suggest she is worried about the shampoo, since she also turned her face away. Another reading is that she was tired and simply did not want to look.
What did Pablo do that respected Zeynep's signal?
He poured water on her back and left her face alone, and later kept the car quiet when her blinks slowed with sleep.
What might bath time be like for Zeynep?
It may feel like a slippery, loud moment where she cannot control what comes next, so shutting her eyes gives her a small way to feel safe.

Read this:

"Didi, see this." Ankita held up her phone: a New Year post she had shared, "Healthier me, starting now."
Jyoti smiled. "Nice. What's the plan?"
"Just, you know, eat better, walk more. Be good."
"When's the walk?"
"Whenever. Mornings, maybe. I'll see how I feel."
Six weeks later, Jyoti found her on the sofa at eleven at night, eating chips from the packet.
"Ankita, how's the walking going?"
"Don't." Ankita pulled a cushion over her face. "I went on the fourth and the fifth. Then that deadline came, then it rained, then I just forgot it existed."
"Did you ever pick a time?"
A long pause. "No. I kept waiting to feel like it."
"Nobody feels like it at six in the morning."
"So I'm lazy?"
"No. You just left it to your mood."

On which dates did Ankita actually go walking?
On the fourth and the fifth.
Why does Ankita pull a cushion over her face when Jyoti asks about the walking?
She feels embarrassed that the plan she announced so happily has faded, and she worries it means she is lazy.
What choice would change Ankita's next attempt?
Picking a set time and a cue, such as walking straight after her morning tea, instead of waiting to feel like it.
How does Jyoti see Ankita's slipping resolution?
As her older sister, Jyoti doesn't see laziness; she notices the plan never had a time, so it depended on mood, and says so kindly.
Library mein book late return ki. Librarian ko sorry kaise bolun?
Say: "I'm sorry, I'm returning this book late. I'll pay the fine." Or: "Sorry for the delay. I forgot the due date."
How do I spell "spagetti"?

The correct spelling is "spaghetti", with an h after the g (spag-h-etti). The h keeps the g hard, as in "get". The double t is already in your spelling.
Example: We cooked spaghetti with tomato sauce.
A missile hits its target with probability 0.75. What is the least number of missiles that must be fired so that the probability of at least one hit is more than 0.99?

Answer: Need 1 - 0.25^n > 0.99, i.e. 0.25^n < 0.01: n = 4 (0.25^4 ~ 0.0039, while 0.25^3 = 0.015625).

P(at least one hit) = 1 - P(no hits) = 1 - q^n with q = 0.25. Solve q^n < 0.01 by trying n = 1, 2, 3, ... or with logarithms: n > log 0.01 / log 0.25 = 2 / 0.602 ~ 3.32 (the inequality turns round because log 0.25 < 0). So n = 4. Such "how many trials" questions come up in reliability (how many backup pumps?) and testing (how many samples?). Common mistake: solving 1 - 0.75^n > 0.99 (using p instead of q).
Next week is a cousin's wedding in another city and I have to take a train alone for the first time.
That's a big step. Do you have your ticket and the train details ready?
Yes, the ticket's on my phone.
Keep a screenshot too, in case the signal is weak. Reach the station early, check the platform number on the board and sit near other families if you can.
What if I miss my stop?
Set an alarm for about twenty minutes before arrival, and check the station name on the boards when the train stops. You can also ask a fellow passenger or the ticket staff.
Will my parents call me during the journey?
Tell them you'll send a message at each big stop. That keeps everyone calm, including you.
Good idea. I'll share my seat number with them too.
Yes, and enjoy the window seat if you have one.

Gurleen, who is ten, dropped her school bag, said, "Ajji, we are here," and dialled 112. She gave the building name, floor and flat number without stopping, and said, "She fell. She is awake." Then she told me, "Go and knock on Mehta uncle's door." She looked calm, though I could not tell if she was scared. Later I saw a card in her bag pocket with the numbers written out. Naveen

Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop.

She dialled 112, gave the building, floor and flat number, and sent Naveen to knock on Mehta uncle's door.

Naveen was frozen and overwhelmed, since Naveen's mind went blank while Gurleen took charge.

At the cricket academy's nets, Irfan, fourteen, batted for two hours every Saturday. He faced ball after ball, laughing with friends between deliveries, and felt he was working hard. Yet in every match he got out the same way, edging outside off stump. His coach, Vishal sir, called him aside. "You bat for two hours. How many balls outside off do you actually practise?" Irfan shrugged. "Some?" The next Saturday, Vishal sir set up a bowling machine to bowl only outside off. "Thirty balls. After each one, I'll tell you what your front foot did." It was hard and slow. By the third Saturday, Irfan was leaving those balls alone.

How long did Irfan bat every Saturday?
He batted for two hours every Saturday.
What was Irfan feeling while batting and laughing with friends?
He felt busy and satisfied, believing he was working hard even though his main weakness was untouched.
Which change worked, and why?
Thirty balls only outside off with feedback after each one focused on his exact weakness and gave immediate correction.
How might Vishal sir see Irfan's progress by the third Saturday?
Vishal sir would likely feel pleased that the focused practice was working, seeing Irfan leave those balls alone.
Bartan dhone ke liye "wash the utensils" ya "wash the dishes"?
Both are fine. In India "utensils" is common; in many other places people say "dishes". Use either one.

Today at lunchtime Bubbles and Pepper were hanging at the top, hardly moving, and the glass felt warm like bathwater. I felt sick. Rajni

The corner by the bookshelf, where the sun never comes.

Rajni felt sick with worry and guilt about moving the tank into the sun.

Rajni could check the thermometer in the afternoon as well, since the room may warm up later in the day.

"I'm not going to Chaitanya's birthday," Pradeep announced, dropping his bag.
Amma looked up from the vegetables. "Since when?"
"Since today. He laughed when I missed the penalty. In front of everyone. He's a fake friend. Always has been."
"Always?"
"Always."
"The Chaitanya who sat with you every day when you broke your arm in Class 6?"
Pradeep paused. "That was ages ago."
"The one who shared his notes before the exams? Who came at midnight when Thatha was in hospital?"
"...He still laughed today."
"He did. That was mean, and you can tell him so. But is today the whole story of him?"
Pradeep kicked at the doormat. "It feels like it."

When did Pradeep break his arm?
In Class 6.
Why does Pradeep call Chaitanya a fake friend who "always has been"?
Today's laugh hurts and is the freshest memory, so it feels like the truth about Chaitanya and pushes years of kindness out of view.
What does Amma suggest Pradeep can do about the laugh?
Tell Chaitanya it was mean, rather than dropping the friendship, while remembering today isn't the whole story.
How might Chaitanya feel if Pradeep skipped the birthday without a word?
Chaitanya might be confused and hurt, perhaps without even realising how much the laugh stung.
