I'm Afreen, a tester on Mohit's team. When the project began I expected a long list of features. Instead Mohit said, "Let's ship a bare login and one report screen within three weeks, and let the users tell us what's next." I thought it looked thin. When I asked why, Mohit said, "If I build everything first, I find out in month six that half of it was wrong. This way I find out in month one." Three weeks later twelve people from the client's office used it. They liked the report, complained that login was slow, and asked for an export button we had never planned. In the review, Mohit put the list on screen and said the second sprint would be those three things, nothing more. I can't tell if Mohit was sure it would work.

What did the users ask for that had not been planned?
The users asked for an export button that the team had never planned.
What did Afreen feel at first about the bare first release?
Afreen doubted it and thought it looked thin.
What else could Mohit try to gather feedback, and why?
Mohit could watch two or three users work with the release in person, because seeing where they hesitate shows things they might not think to report.
How might the client's users have felt about being asked what comes next?
The users probably felt listened to and more involved, since their comments decided what the second sprint contained.

Sit down, beta. Mahima aunty will tell you about my second year at the packaging firm. I was twenty-four, and my manager Chandrika slid a delivery form across her desk and said, "Just date it the twenty-eighth, the truck was basically there." The truck had reached on the second. My hands went cold. Chandrika had helped me get that job, and I thought of my loan. So I signed. Six weeks later an auditor asked for the gate records, and the mismatch carried my signature. Chandrika said, "You should have told me no." I still hear that. If I could go back, I would ask for the order in writing, or say I am not comfortable, and go to the head of accounts if pushed. Instead I learned it late, and at a cost.

When did the truck actually arrive?
The truck had reached on the second.
What was Mahima feeling when the form was slid across the desk?
Frightened and torn: Mahima's hands went cold and the thought of the loan pressed on the decision.
What choice could Mahima have made at the desk instead of signing?
Mahima could have asked for the order in writing, said she was not comfortable, or gone to the head of accounts if pushed.
How might Chandrika have felt when the auditor found the mismatch?
Probably worried and defensive, since Chandrika answered by saying, "You should have told me no."

Sunday night
Harsha asked me today how work is. I said fine. I'm Jatin, and I say fine now to everything.
For a year I asked my manager for a transfer to the Pune office, for a proper desk, even for one Saturday off a month. I wrote emails. I asked in person. Nothing. Not even a no.
Somewhere around March I stopped asking. I just do the work and go home. I don't feel angry any more. I don't feel much at all, honestly. Food tastes the same. Weekends go by.
Harsha went quiet and then said, "This sounds heavier than fine. Will you talk to someone? A counsellor, properly?" I laughed it off.
But the flatness has been here for months, not days. I looked up the counsellor on our company's wellbeing page tonight and booked a slot for Wednesday. Harsha said he'd walk me there.

When did Jatin book the counsellor slot for?
Jatin booked it for Wednesday.
How does Jatin feel about work now?
Jatin feels numb and flat, not even angry any more, after a year of requests being ignored.
Why is booking a counsellor a wise step for Jatin?
The flatness has lasted months, not days, so talking to a qualified professional can help Jatin understand it and find a way forward.
How does Harsha see Jatin's "fine"?
Harsha hears that it sounds much heavier than fine, feels concerned, and offers to walk Jatin to the appointment.

I'm Jyoti, Ankita's cousin, and we walk to school together, so I've seen this whole thing. It's been nine days since Ankita stopped talking to Megha. At first Megha kept coming up to her: in the corridor, at the gate, with notes, once with Ankita's favourite chikki. Ankita would look away, but I saw the tiny smile when Megha walked off. She liked being chased, I think. Now Megha has stopped trying as much, and Ankita keeps checking the gate anyway. Yesterday she ate lunch alone and said she preferred it. Last night she told me, "If I talk now, after nine days, it'll look so stupid." Then she stared at her phone till the screen went dark.

What did Megha once bring Ankita?
Megha once brought Ankita's favourite chikki.
What does Ankita's tiny smile when Megha walked off suggest?
It suggests she enjoyed being chased and wanted back, even while keeping up the silence.
What turning point is still open to Ankita after nine days?
She could send Megha a simple message, "I've been silly and I miss you, can we talk?", accepting a moment of embarrassment instead of weeks more.
What might Megha be going through now that Megha has stopped trying so much?
Megha may feel tired and rejected after days of notes and chikki with no reply, and may now be guarding against more hurt.

Summarize this message in three sentences.

Hi Rajni, Quick one after our call. While I walked through the survey plan, you said "mm-hmm" a lot, which usually tells me you're following. But around the ten-minute mark the mm-hmms went flat and came a bit late, and I could hear typing. I wondered if you were juggling something else, which is completely fine; I just want to be sure the sampling part landed. Then, when I suggested moving the field visits to November, you said "hmm..." and paused. I couldn't tell if that was thinking, doubt or a polite no. Rather than guess, I'd like to ask: are you okay with November, or does it clash with something? And shall I send a two-line summary of the sampling bit? No rush. Honest answers welcome, including "I was replying to my boss." Yash

Yash says Rajni's replies sounded flat during the call, and typing could be heard. Rajni also paused when November was suggested for the field visits. Yash asks whether November works, offers a short summary and welcomes honest answers.

Jamal had known Rania since they were nine, at the same Birmingham school. Lately she said "I'm so thick" after every answer, even right ones. When the art teacher offered her a place in the city exhibition, Rania said no before the teacher had finished the sentence. Jamal waited till they were at the bus stop. "The bird you painted, the one with the torn wing, people stopped in the corridor to look at it. I did too." Rania rolled her eyes, but she didn't change the subject. He sat with her at lunch every day that week, not fixing anything. On Friday he said, "You've seemed low for ages. Would you talk to Ms Okafor? I'll wait outside her door." Rania thought for a long moment, then nodded.

What did Rania paint?
A bird with a torn wing.
What was Jamal feeling as he watched Rania turn down the exhibition?
He was worried and sad, seeing her put herself down and miss a real chance.
What did Jamal do that could help Rania?
He gave specific praise, stayed close at lunch and encouraged her to talk to Ms Okafor, offering to wait outside.
How might Rania see Jamal's offer to wait outside the door?
She may feel supported and less scared, knowing she won't face the talk alone.
Our geography teacher gave an earthquake's magnitude. What does magnitude mean?

Magnitude means the size or strength of something. For an earthquake it is the number that tells how strong it was. It is a noun.
Example: The magnitude of the earthquake was large enough to be felt in the next state.

Saturday, late. Damini's grandfather's funeral was this morning. The prayers were short, and then a cousin began telling the story about how Dadaji once tried to teach the family goat to sit. I'm Tanvir, Damini's husband, writing this because I'm still trying to make sense of it. Damini smiled through the whole story, a wide, wet smile, tears running down. I nearly asked if she was all right, then didn't. Later she told me, "I was so happy for a moment, remembering him. And it hurt." I think we assume a smile means one thing. At the funeral it meant love and loss together. I held her hand and said nothing, because none of my words felt as good as the silence.

Whose funeral was it that morning?
It was the funeral of Damini's grandfather.
What was Damini feeling as she smiled through the tears, and how do we know?
She felt happiness and hurt together, since she told Tanvir she was so happy for a moment remembering him and that it hurt.
What could Tanvir do next to support Damini?
Tanvir could keep holding her hand, listen when she wants to talk, and let her mix her memories with tears.
How might a relative who saw Damini smile at the funeral have read it?
They might think she was only cheerful, not seeing the sorrow behind it, since a smile can hold joy and grief together.

Where did the dance take place?
The dance took place in the school hall in Toronto.

Dear Varun bhaiya,
I'm writing this because if I say it out loud I'll start making excuses, and I don't want to.
Since January I have not been going to my CA coaching. I stopped after the first exam went badly. When you asked on the phone every Sunday, I said classes were fine. When you sent money for the books in March, I said I'd bought them. I didn't. It's still in my account.

It wasn't because of pressure from you or Papa. I was ashamed, and lying was easier than saying I'd failed.
I'll return the book money this week. I'm going to tell Papa on Sunday myself.
I know you might need time before you believe what I say again. You can ask me anything, and I'll answer honestly, even if it's slow.

Since when had Sudha stopped going to coaching?
Since January.
Why did Sudha lie, according to the letter?
Sudha felt ashamed after the first exam went badly, and lying felt easier than admitting failure.
What makes Sudha's letter own it fully?
It names exactly what was hidden and for how long, refuses to blame family pressure, plans to return the money and tell Papa, and accepts that Varun bhaiya may need time.
How might Varun bhaiya feel reading the letter?
Varun bhaiya may feel hurt by four months of Sunday lies, but also that Sudha is finally being honest without excuses.
Fix this: The sun rise in the east. Also, why is the sea salty?

1. The sun rises in the east. Why: subject-verb agreement ("sun" -> "rises").
2. Rivers carry small amounts of salt from rocks to the sea, and the water evaporates while the salt stays.
Amy's grandfather gave her $100 for her birthday. Amy bought 3 dolls, each of which cost $1. How much money does Amy have left?

The cost of the dolls is 3 x $1 = $3.
Amy has $100 - $3 = $97 left.
The answer is 97.

Zanele had been in the online group for six weeks. At first it was just a place to post drawings. Now her phone lit up from the moment she woke in her Johannesburg bedroom.
'Z, your sketch of the rain is incredible.' 'Z, we saved you a seat in the voice chat.' Last Friday, the older member who ran it had given her a title: welcomer for new members. She had a badge next to her name.
At school she found herself only half-listening to Omar. He was talking about the science fair, and it felt small and far away.
That night one of the older members wrote, 'Best to keep our chats just between us. Your parents wouldn't get it.' Zanele read it twice. She felt a flicker of unease, and then, straight after, warmth: they trusted her.
She typed 'of course', and felt, for the first time in years, like she was exactly where she belonged.

What title did Zanele get last Friday?
She was made welcomer for new members, with a badge next to her name.
What was Zanele feeling when she read the message about keeping chats secret?
She felt a flicker of unease, quickly covered by warmth and pride at being trusted, because belonging meant so much to her.
What would be the wise response to the request to keep the chats from her parents?
A request for secrecy from an online contact is a warning sign; the wise step is to stop the contact and tell a parent or another trusted adult.
How is Omar affected by Zanele's new focus?
Omar is losing his friend's attention, as she only half-listens to him and his science fair plans now feel small to her.

Thomas, you say you're bored of your job and everything is fine. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, in the railway accounts office in Madras. I had a permanent post, a scooter and a routine you could set a clock by. Tea at eleven, lunch at one, cinema on Saturday. I thought life was sorted. Then at my cousin's wedding, my old headmaster asked, 'Ramesh, what are you making with all this time?' I made a joke. But I lay awake. I wasn't lazy; I was just pointed entirely at myself. The next month I started teaching accounts free on Sunday mornings to boys from the railway colony who couldn't afford tuition. Forty years later, three of those boys are chartered accountants. One named his son after me. That's the only part of my twenties I talk about.

What did the old headmaster ask Ramesh?
'Ramesh, what are you making with all this time?'
How did Ramesh feel lying awake after the headmaster's question?
Ramesh felt unsettled and a little empty, realising the comfortable life pointed only inward.
Ramesh started teaching accounts free on Sunday mornings. Why was that a turning point?
It turned Ramesh's life outward, using a skill for boys who couldn't afford tuition, and grew something beyond the self.
How might the boys from the railway colony have seen those Sunday classes?
They probably felt grateful and hopeful, finally getting help they couldn't pay for, which shaped their careers.

messages.content: Mrs. Carlton gives out penalty points whenever her students misbehave. They get 5 points for interrupting, 10 points for insulting their classmates, and 25 points for throwing things. If they get 100 points, they have to go to the office. Jerry already interrupted twice and insulted his classmates 4 times. How many times can he throw things before he gets sent to the office?

For interrupting, Jerry got 5 points per interruption * 2 interruptions = 10 points
For insulting, he got 10 points per insult * 4 insults = 40 points
To get to the 100 limit points, Jerry has 100 points - 10 points - 40 points = 50 points left
He still has 50 points / 25 points per throw = 2 throws
The answer is 2.

Paul lives in a 5th story apartment.  He makes 3 trips out from and back to his apartment throughout the day each day of a week.  How many feet does he travel vertically in total over the week if each story is 10 feet tall?

Since Paul makes 3 trips per day, and each trip involves going both down and up, this means he travels the full vertical distance of his apartment complex 3*2=6 times a day.
Since there are 7 days in a week, this means he makes this trip 6*7=42 times a week.
Since each story is 10 feet tall, that means with 5 stories he travels 5*10= 50 feet each trip.
Since he made 42 trips of 50 feet each, this means he traveled 50*42= 2100 feet in a week.
The answer is 2100.
Now you try: write 'half of the sum of a and b' and 'the product of 4 and the difference of x and 1'.
The answer is (a + b)/2; 4(x - 1).

A few quick questions:

What does "break down" mean for a car?

Reflect the point (5, 1) in the line x = 2, and the point (3, 4) in the line y = -1.

Answer: (-1, 1) and (3, -6).

x = 2 is a VERTICAL line through (2, 0). So y stays the same. The point is 5 - 2 = 3 units to the right of the mirror, so the image is 3 units to the left: x = 2 - 3 = -1. The image is (-1, 1). Formula: new x = 2k - x = 4 - 5 = -1. y = -1 is a HORIZONTAL line. Now x stays the same: the point is 4 - (-1) = 5 units above the mirror, so the image is 5 below it: y = -1 - 5 = -6. Formula: new y = 2k - y = -2 - 4 = -6. Common mistake: x = 2 "looks like" it is about x, so pupils change y. Draw the line first!

In their small shop in Bhilwara, there was a back room where the grain sacks were stored. Kishore never went in if he could help it. When Papa asked him to fetch a sack, he went stiff and silent and sent his younger sister Vinita instead. "Why do you hate that room?" she asked later. Kishore shrugged. "I don't." But he couldn't explain it. Months ago there had been a terrible shouting match in there between Papa and Chacha about the shop; Vinita remembered doors slamming and Kishore crying. Kishore remembered almost nothing. When she reminded him, he only said, "Was I there?" and his jaw tightened. That night Vinita told Amma, who sat with Kishore and asked how he had been feeling since.

What was stored in the back room?
The grain sacks.
What does Kishore feel when he is asked to go into the back room?
He goes stiff and silent, tense and uneasy, though he can't explain why or remember the fight there.
What did Vinita do that helped?
She noticed, gently reminded him, and told Amma, who sat with Kishore and asked how he had been feeling.
How might Vinita experience Kishore's avoidance?
She is puzzled at first, then worried when she links it to the fight she remembers.

'Okay, Lakshmi, don't make that face. It's not fraud. It's creative accounting. Everyone in the finance team calls it that.
We just move some of next quarter's orders into this quarter so the numbers look steady. Investors panic at dips, and if they panic they pull money, and then people lose jobs. Real people. Suresh in dispatch has two kids. So really, we're protecting everyone.
And it evens out. Mostly. Next quarter we'll just move a bit forward again.
My boss says, "Bidisha, we're just smoothing." I like that word. It sounds calm.
What? Why are you quiet?
Fine. Yes. When you put it in your words, "reporting sales that haven't happened", it sounds worse. But that's not how we see it at work.'

What does Bidisha's boss call moving next quarter's orders forward?
The boss calls it 'smoothing'.
Why does Bidisha bring up Suresh in dispatch?
Bidisha seems uneasy and defensive, so Bidisha uses the story of protecting jobs to feel the practice is kind and necessary rather than reporting sales that haven't happened.
What turning point might Lakshmi's silence open?
Hearing it in plain words gives Bidisha a chance to drop the soft labels and talk to someone outside the team about what is really going on.
How might Lakshmi see Bidisha during this conversation?
Lakshmi is probably worried, hearing a close friend use comforting words to cover something that sounds wrong.

Read this:

You want the real reason I stood for the hostel council? Okay. It was my Dada. Last Diwali, after the lamps, he sat on the balcony with me and said, "Ujjwal, I worked thirty-one years at the mill and never once said no to the supervisor. Not even when he blamed my friend for something he didn't do." He said he still sees that friend's face. Then he laughed, sort of, and said, "Don't make my mistake your job." I didn't know what to do with that at first. I'm not brave. I hate meetings. But when the mess contract came up and everyone was grumbling in corridors and saying nothing at the meeting, I thought about Dada on that balcony. So I put my name in. Maybe I lose. Maybe I sound stupid. But at seventy I'd rather remember Ujjwal trying than Ujjwal whispering in the corridor.

How many years did Dada work at the mill?
Dada worked thirty-one years at the mill.
How did Ujjwal feel about Dada's story at first?
Ujjwal felt unsure and uneasy, not knowing what to do with the regret, and admitted to not being brave and hating meetings.
Why is standing for the hostel council a reasonable risk for Ujjwal to take?
Speaking up about the mess contract is a real but manageable risk, and it spares Ujjwal's future self the kind of regret Dada still carries.
How might Dada feel seeing Ujjwal stand for the council?
Dada would likely feel proud and a little relieved, seeing his regret turned into courage rather than a weight.

Explain which of these can reasonably be modelled by a Poisson distribution, and why. a) The number of misprints on a page of a novel. b) The number of heads in 20 tosses of a coin. c) The number of cars passing a toll plaza in a minute at 2 a.m. d) The number of customers entering a sweet shop per hour over a whole festival day. e) The number of goals scored in a football match. f) The number of students absent from a class of 40 during a flu outbreak.

Answer: a) yes b) no, binomial B(20, 0.5) c) yes d) no, the rate is not constant e) yes, approximately f) no, absences are not independent (and the maximum is 40).

Check the four conditions: events occur 1) singly, 2) at random, 3) INDEPENDENTLY and 4) at a CONSTANT average rate, with no fixed upper limit. a) Misprints are rare, random and independent: Poisson. b) There are exactly 20 trials with p = 0.5 and at most 20 heads: this is binomial, and p is not small. c) Late-night traffic is light and random at a steady rate: Poisson. d) The rate changes during the day (evening rush before the festival), so a single lambda does not fit; Poisson could work hour by hour with different lambda. e) Goals are fairly rare and random: a Poisson model with lambda ~ 2.5 is often used. f) Flu spreads from child to child, so absences are not independent. Common mistake: using Poisson just because something is "a count".
Now you try: C = 44 cm, pi = 22/7. Find r.
The answer is d = 14 cm, r = 7 cm.
Jeremy buys 30 watermelons. He eats 3 watermelons per week. Each week he gives 2 to his dad. How many weeks will the watermelons last?

Jeremey goes through 3+2=5 watermelons per week.
Therefore, the watermelons will last him to 30/5=6 weeks.
The answer is 6.

Dalia's fifth-birthday cake wouldn't be ready until eleven, and at breakfast in their Cairo flat she was already wailing. "I want it NOW!" Her mother, Selin, set the big kitchen timer on the counter. "When this rings, we go to the bakery. Let's see what we can do before it rings." They built a tower of cups. They sang the birthday song twice. Dalia checked the timer every few minutes, bouncing on her toes. When it finally rang, she shrieked and ran for her shoes.

When would the cake be ready?
At eleven.
How was Dalia feeling at breakfast?
She was impatient and upset, wailing that she wanted the cake now.
Why did the timer help Dalia?
It made the wait concrete, so she could see when it would end, and filled the time with games.
How might Selin feel when Dalia runs for her shoes?
Selin likely feels relieved and pleased that the wait ended happily.

Summarize Nelly's view of this quarrel, briefly.

But his self-love would endure no further torment: I heard, and not altogether disapprovingly, a manual check given to her saucy tongue. The little wretch had done her utmost to hurt her cousin's sensitive though uncultivated feelings, and a physical argument was the only mode he had of balancing the account, and repaying its effects on the inflictor. He afterwards gathered the books and hurled them on the fire. I read in his countenance what anguish it was to offer that sacrifice to spleen. I fancied that as they consumed, he recalled the pleasure they had already imparted, and the triumph and ever-increasing pleasure he had anticipated from them; and I fancied I guessed the incitement to his secret studies also. He had been content with daily labour and rough animal enjoyments, till Catherine crossed his path. Shame at her scorn, and hope of her approval, were his first prompters to higher pursuits; and instead of guarding him from one and winning him to the other, his endeavours to raise himself had produced just the contrary result.

After Catherine mocks Hareton cruelly, he hits her and then throws his books into the fire. Nelly can see how painful it is for him. She believes he started learning to win Catherine's approval, but her scorn has had the opposite effect.
Meera's friend has not replied to her message all day. Does that mean the friend is angry with her?
Not necessarily. Because there are many reasons someone might not reply, such as being busy, travelling or having a flat phone battery. It is better to wait a little or ask kindly.

"Pema, lunch time!" Jaya called across the creche.
"She hasn't heard you," said Asha, the helper. "Look at her."
In the sand corner Pema was scooping with a yellow cup and tipping it into a green one, watching the grains slide. Scoop, tip. Scoop, tip.
"Twenty minutes she's been at that," Jaya said softly.
"Should I carry her?"
"Last time we did that she cried till nap. Let me try." Jaya knelt. "Pema, one more cup, then dal."
Pema tipped one more cup, then held up her arms.

How long had Pema been pouring, according to Jaya?
Twenty minutes.
What does Pema not hearing the call suggest?
It suggests Pema is completely absorbed and content in the scooping and tipping.
Why did Jaya kneel instead of carrying Pema?
Carrying her last time led to crying till nap, so Jaya gave a small warning, one more cup, and let Pema finish.
How does Asha see Pema's pouring?
Asha notices how deeply Pema is focused, pointing out she hasn't heard and inviting Jaya to look.

The bus to Chacha's wedding in Nashik had been stuck in traffic for ninety minutes, the fan was broken, and everyone was sweaty and cross. Lakshmi, nine, decided this was the perfect time for her new joke. "Knock knock." Her cousin Rekha sighed. "Who's there?" "Burp." "Burp who?" "BURRRP!" Lakshmi collapsed with laughter. Rekha groaned. Lakshmi told it again. And again. By the sixth time Rekha put her dupatta over her face. By the eighth, the old man across the aisle was shaking his head. Lakshmi stopped. She looked around. Then she waited until the bus finally lurched forward, leaned over, and whispered the joke to the driver's little boy at the front instead. He howled. Lakshmi grinned. "See? It's the right person that matters," she told Rekha. "And not the ninth time."

How long had the bus been stuck in traffic?
Ninety minutes.
What was Lakshmi thinking when she stopped and looked around after the eighth time?
She seemed to realise, a little embarrassed, that her joke had stopped working on this tired audience.
What did Lakshmi learn about telling jokes?
That the right listener and timing matter, and that groans are a sign to stop or change the audience.
How did Rekha feel by the sixth time?
Rekha was fed up, putting her dupatta over her face.
Find the derivatives of x^2 and x^3 from first principles. Then prove d/dx (x^n) = nx^n^-^1 for every positive integer n.

Answer: d/dx (x^2) = 2x, d/dx (x^3) = 3x^2, and in general nx^n^-^1.

Always write the definition first, then expand, cancel h, take the limit: f(x) = x^2: (f(x + h) - f(x))/h = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2)/h = 2x + h -> 2x f(x) = x^3: ((x + h)^3 - x^3)/h = (3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3)/h = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2 -> 3x^2 For x^n use the binomial theorem (topic 8.18): (x + h)^n = x^n + nx^n^-^1h + C(n, 2)x^n^-^2h^2 + ... + h^n ((x + h)^n - x^n)/h = nx^n^-^1 + C(n, 2)x^n^-^2h + ... + h^n^-^1 -> nx^n^-^1 Every term after the first still contains h, so it tends to 0. The rule "bring the power down, reduce the power by 1" is called the POWER RULE; it also holds for negative and fractional powers (see D4, D5 and topic 8.34). Common mistake: forgetting the middle terms, as in (x + h)^2 = x^2 + h^2.

In the winter exam season, I, Reena, signed an online pledge to save the lake near our school. One click, my name, done. I felt good. A week later, the group messaged: "Thanks for pledging! Can you share the poster on your status?" Sure, easy. Then: "Can you volunteer every Sunday for two months?" I had exams. I wanted to say no. But I kept thinking, I said I care about the lake. Saying no now would make me a fake. My friend Pema noticed me stressing. "You can care about the lake and still say no to Sundays," she said. I wrote back that I could help one Sunday after exams. I felt guilty for a day. Then I felt fine.

What did Reena sign an online pledge for?
To save the lake near the school.
Why did Reena feel she couldn't say no to volunteering every Sunday?
Reena felt guilty and torn, because refusing seemed to contradict the care for the lake that the pledge had shown.
What choice did Reena make, and why was it reasonable?
Reena offered one Sunday after exams, which fit real priorities while still supporting the cause.
How does Pema see Reena's dilemma?
Pema sees that caring about the lake and saying no to Sundays are not in conflict.

At the girls' hostel meeting, Deepika stood up before the warden had finished the notices. "Why do phones get collected at eight? We're not kids. It's a stupid rule and nobody has ever explained it." A few girls clapped. Someone at the back whispered, "She's done now." Irawati Ma'am put the register down. "Fair question. The rule is there so study hour stays quiet. What does eight o'clock cost you?" Deepika's chin was still up, but her voice dropped. "My father drives the night bus. He can only call at nine, on his break." The room went quiet. Irawati Ma'am wrote something in the margin. "Then that's the real request, and it's reasonable. Anyone with a family call after eight, give me the time. You'll get your phone for fifteen minutes, in the office." Deepika sat down, arms still folded, but nodding.

When can Deepika's father call?
He can only call at nine, on his break.
What was Deepika feeling when she called the rule stupid?
Deepika was frustrated and probably worried about missing her father's calls. The raised chin also suggests wanting to be treated as grown-up, not only anger at the rule.
How did Irawati Ma'am turn the challenge into something useful?
She called it a fair question, gave the reason for the rule, then asked what it cost Deepika, which uncovered the real request and led to a fair fix.
Why might the girls who clapped see the challenge differently from the warden?
The girls who clapped likely saw a bold stand against a rule, while the warden listened for the need underneath and found a request she could meet.

Sum this up in one line for a school health poster.

Liam spent every minute of lunch chasing the ball across the dusty oval in Adelaide, shirt stuck to his back. He didn't stop at the drinking fountain; the game was too close. In maths his head began to throb. He snapped at Ines when she borrowed his ruler, then put his head down on his arms. "Did you drink anything at lunch?" Ines whispered. He thought. Nothing since breakfast. Mrs Park let him go to the fountain, and he drank for a long time. By the end of the lesson the throbbing had faded. That night he put his blue bottle next to his school shoes, and the next day he clipped it to the fence by the pitch.
Liam played hard at lunch without drinking water, got a headache and grumpy in class, felt better after a long drink, and now keeps his water bottle handy.

During our garden project Ganga wrote each of our names on a strip of paper with a job, watering, weeding, seed labels, sketching, and stuck the strips on the board. Arohi, who usually disappeared when there was work, read her strip: "seed labels." She grumbled but sat down and wrote nine labels. When the teacher came round, Ganga pointed at the board and said, "You can see who did what." Nobody argued. I could not tell whether Arohi liked her job, but she stayed until the last label was done.

How many seed labels did Arohi write?
Arohi wrote nine labels.
What was Ganga feeling when sticking the named strips on the board?
Ganga was probably hopeful and a little determined that the work would be shared fairly, which shows when Ganga points at the board and says the teacher can see who did what.
What choice by Ganga made it hard for anyone to coast?
Ganga gave every child a named job on the board, so who did what was visible without anyone being told off.
What was it like for Arohi to find her own name next to "seed labels"?
Arohi probably felt annoyed and a bit cornered, since she grumbled, yet with her name on the job she sat down and wrote all nine labels.
"Jab main chhota tha, tab hum gaon mein rehte the." English mein kya hoga?
It is: "When I was small, we lived in a village."
Isme "used to live" bhi chalega kya?
Yes. "We used to live in a village" is also correct. It shows that this was true in the past but is not true now.

Hallie is working as a waitress for $10/hour. On Monday, she works for 7 hours, and she receives $18 in tips. On Tuesday she works for 5 hours, and she receives $12 in tips. On Wednesday she works for 7 hours, and she receives $20 in tips. How much money does she earn in total from Monday to Wednesday?

Hallie works a total of 7 + 5 + 7 = 19 hours
For her hourly pay, she earns 19 * $10 = $190
In tips, she receives a total of $18 + $12 + $20 = $50
The total amount of money Hallie earns is $190 + $50 = $240
The answer is 240.

I stopped believing when I was seventeen. I'm Ganga, and my family knows. But last month, when Nani asked me to sit beside her for the Satyanarayan puja, I said yes.
My cousin Yash raised an eyebrow. "You? At a puja?"
I told him the truth: "I'm not here for the gods. I'm here for Nani."
I sat cross-legged on the floor for two hours. I passed the flowers when the priest asked. I didn't chant the words I don't believe, but I listened to Nani's voice, cracked and certain, and I remembered being five and falling asleep in her lap during this same story.
When the prasad came round, Nani pressed extra into my hand. "I know you don't believe, beti," she said quietly. "I'm happy you came anyway."
I didn't have to pretend. That's what made it feel like home.

How long did Ganga sit cross-legged on the floor?
Ganga sat cross-legged on the floor for two hours.
What was Ganga feeling while listening to Nani's voice?
She felt nostalgic and tender, remembering falling asleep in Nani's lap during the same story as a child.
Why did it matter that Ganga told Yash the truth?
Being open, gently, meant she could join the puja out of love without pretending faith, keeping both honesty and belonging.
How does Nani seem to see Ganga's presence?
Nani seems happy and moved that Ganga came anyway, accepting her disbelief and valuing her company.
Is it "probly" or "probably"?

"Probably" is the right spelling. People often say it quickly as "probly", but it is written with all three syllables: prob-a-bly.
Example: It will probably rain this evening.

Salma, you asked why I was so quiet in December. Okay. I failed the organic chemistry paper. And I spent three weeks asking why. Every day. Was it because I studied the wrong chapters? Because I'm not clever? Because I panicked? Does it mean I shouldn't be doing science at all? I'd lie in bed and go through it all again. I thought I was solving something. But I never got to a plan. I didn't book the re-exam. I didn't ask anyone for help. I just felt heavier each day. One morning, I realised I'd been thinking about it for three weeks, and nothing had changed except I felt worse. That's when I finally called my lab partner and asked to study together. Thinking about why wasn't the same as doing something. That's what Preeti learned.

How long did Preeti spend asking why?
Three weeks.
Why did asking 'why' feel like solving something to Preeti?
It seemed like working through the problem, but Preeti felt heavier and more stuck each day because no plan came from it.
Which step finally helped Preeti out of the loop?
Calling the lab partner to study together, a concrete action instead of more thinking.
How might Salma have seen Preeti's quietness in December?
Salma might have noticed Preeti was withdrawn and worried, without knowing about the failure.

The lunch rush at the small restaurant in Porto was at its worst when Rafael, the sous-chef, shouted across the kitchen that Paulo had ruined a whole tray of sea bass. Paulo felt the heat climb up his neck. The words ready on his tongue were not ones he could take back.
He untied his apron and walked out the back door without a word.
Rafael stared after him. "Unbelievable. He just leaves?" The dishwasher shrugged.
In the alley, Paulo pressed his back to the cold wall and counted his breaths until his jaw loosened. Five minutes. Then he went back in.
"Rafael. I walked out because I was about to say something stupid. I'm sorry I didn't say that first. The fish was overdone; I'll redo the tray."
Rafael held his gaze for a moment, then nodded at the stove. "Next time, just say 'two minutes.' Go."
Paulo tied his apron back on.

What did Rafael say Paulo had ruined?
A whole tray of sea bass.
Why did Paulo walk out of the kitchen?
Paulo felt angry and stung by the shouting and was afraid of saying something he couldn't take back, so he left to cool down.
What made Paulo's walkout end well?
He came back after five minutes, explained why he had left, apologised for not saying so first and offered to redo the tray.
How did Rafael see the walkout at first?
Rafael read it as disrespect, saying "Unbelievable. He just leaves?", until Paulo returned and explained.

The Monday review in the Lower Parel office was supposed to take twenty minutes. Instead, when the director asked why the brochure had missed Friday's print deadline, Bhupen said, "The copy came to me on Thursday night."
Zeenat turned to him. "Because you changed the layout three times."
"Because your copy didn't fit!"
"You never told me the word count!"
The director raised a hand. The room went silent. Eight people suddenly looked at their phones.
Zeenat felt her cheeks flame. She couldn't believe he'd blamed her in front of the director. Across the table, Bhupen sat with folded arms, sure she had done the same to him.

When did the copy come to Bhupen?
On Thursday night.
What was Zeenat feeling when her cheeks flamed?
She felt embarrassed and angry, shocked that Bhupen had blamed her in front of the director.
What could each of them do now to stop positions hardening further?
Stop defending in public, and each agree to a private talk, perhaps with the director, about the deadline and word counts.
What is it like for the eight colleagues looking at their phones?
They probably feel awkward and uncomfortable, caught in a clash they don't want to join.

Santosh,
I'm writing this instead of texting, because texting is what got us here.
At six you wrote, "stuck again, eat without me". I wrote, "fine". You wrote, "what is your problem?" I wrote, "no problem, clearly". You wrote, "great, very mature". I turned my phone face down and scrubbed a pan that was already clean.
Here is what I actually meant by "fine": I'm tired, I miss you, and I'd been looking forward to eating together. And I think what you meant by "what is your problem" was: I'm exhausted too, and I can't take one more person being upset with me today.
We weren't answering each other. We were answering the tone.
Can we talk at breakfast, before either of us opens a phone?
Simran

What did Simran do after turning the phone face down?
Simran scrubbed a pan that was already clean.
What did Simran actually feel when typing "fine"?
Simran was tired, missed Santosh and felt let down about not eating together, rather than angry.
Why is talking at breakfast a good next step?
Talking face to face, before the phones, lets them hear tone and intention instead of trading sharper lines.
Going by Simran's guess, what was Santosh feeling when writing "what is your problem?"
Santosh was likely exhausted and defensive, unable to handle one more person being upset that day.

People ask me about Kota and expect a sad story. I'm Arnab, and the truth is both things at once. The first week, I was thrilled. No one telling me when to sleep, egg rolls at midnight, my own shelf. Then the nights came. Around eleven the corridor goes quiet, and I could smell Ma's fish curry from memory, and I'd scroll old photos till two. My roommate Pradeep noticed my eyes in the morning and said nothing, just started waking me at six for a walk to the tea stall. We made rules: bed by twelve, walk at six, call home every Wednesday and Sunday. Ma now asks about Pradeep before she asks about me. The homesickness hasn't gone. But it's a visitor now, not the landlord.

What time did Pradeep start waking Arnab?
Pradeep started waking Arnab at six.
How did Arnab's feelings in the first week differ from the nights?
Arnab felt thrilled by the freedom in the first week but homesick and lonely at night, missing Ma's fish curry.
Which routines made Arnab's move steadier?
Going to bed by twelve, walking at six with Pradeep, and calling home every Wednesday and Sunday.
How might Ma feel about Arnab's new routine?
Ma seems reassured and fond, asking about Pradeep first, glad that Arnab is no longer alone.
Give three reasons people enjoy gardening. Start each reason with "It" and put each on a new line.

It is calming to work with soil and plants.
It feels rewarding to watch seeds grow.
It gives you fresh herbs and flowers at home.

I'm Madhav, and I stay next door to Nitin's family. During the winter holidays, Nitin, who's about two, started talking non-stop.
Every time I passed their veranda, he pointed at something. "What's that?" Scooter. Blanket. Chai.
Yesterday he pointed at my face. "Sad?"
I'd had a long day. I didn't know he could tell.
"Tired," I said.
He nodded seriously. "Tired." Then he offered me a biscuit.

What did Nitin offer Madhav?
A biscuit.
What might Nitin have been feeling when he asked "Sad?"
He may have felt curious and concerned, noticing Madhav's tired face.
How can adults help Nitin learn feeling words?
Name feelings honestly when he asks, like Madhav saying "tired", so Nitin learns them.
How is Madhav affected by Nitin's question?
Madhav is surprised and touched that a toddler noticed Madhav's mood.

There were 20 fishermen in the lake who had cast their net to catch fish. If they caught 10000 fish in total, and 19 of them caught 400 fish each with their own net, calculate the number of fish the twentieth fisherman caught.

The 19 fishermen who caught 400 fish each caught 400*19 = 7600 fish.
If they caught a total of 10000 fish, the twentieth fisherman caught 10000-7600 = 2400 fish alone.
The answer is 2400.

The steel plant visit had been cancelled at the last minute, so Arohi had only the train back to Kolkata to fix the rollout plan. Four hours, patchy signal, and the go-live was Monday.
On her laptop was the list from the team's pre-mortem: twenty-seven ways the new inventory system could fail. Darshan had typed it up faithfully. Reading it now, she saw the trouble. "Staff forget passwords" sat next to "server room floods". Everything had the same bold font.
She added two columns, likely and costly, and scored each from one to three. Three rose to the top: warehouse scanners not paired, night-shift staff untrained, old stock codes not matching.
She messaged Darshan when the signal came back. "Top three only. Pair scanners Friday, train night shift Saturday, map codes Sunday. The rest we accept and watch."

How many ways to fail were on the pre-mortem list?
The list had twenty-seven ways the new inventory system could fail.
What did Arohi feel when she saw every risk in the same bold font?
She felt uneasy and frustrated, because the list was unfocused and gave small risks the same weight as serious ones.
What would you add to Arohi's plan for the risks she accepted?
A simple weekly check on the accepted risks would help, so if one becomes more likely it can move into the top group.
How might Darshan see the new message after typing the long list?
Darshan may feel relieved to have three clear jobs with dates instead of twenty-seven worries, though perhaps unsure about leaving the rest.

12 March, library, 6 p.m.
Today I got the reading on transport policy finally, all of it, the whole argument clicked, and my hands started flapping before I could stop them. Happy flapping. It's how my body says yes. Then I saw the boy at the next table staring and I sat on my hands. Old habit. I felt my chest go tight.
Ten minutes later Yusuf from my tutorial came by and said, quite gently, "I saw you flapping. Are you okay, or was that a good thing?" Nobody has ever asked me that. I said it was a very good thing. He said his little cousin does it when she's excited, and he just wanted to check. Then he went back to his desk like it was normal. It is normal, for me. I took my hands out from under my legs and kept reading.
— Vandana

What was Vandana reading in the library?
The reading on transport policy.
How did Vandana feel when the boy at the next table stared?
Vandana felt self-conscious, chest tightening, and sat on both hands; the flapping itself had come from happiness at understanding the reading.
What did Yusuf do that helped?
He asked kindly whether it was a good thing instead of assuming something was wrong, then treated the answer as normal.
How might the boy at the next table have seen the flapping?
He may have found it unusual and simply stared, not knowing it came from happiness, which shows how easily such movement is misread.

I'm Tarun, and I thought my little brother Mohit was just sleepy that evening. He kept tugging his right ear and rubbing his eyes, and he pushed his face into Mummy's neck. But it was only six o'clock. Mummy felt his forehead and cheeks and said he was warm. She didn't wait to see. She rang the doctor that evening and took him in. I was wrong about the sleepy part. You can't tell from one sign.

Which ear did Mohit keep tugging?
His right ear.

Carly is making burgers for a neighborhood BBQ. Each burger needs to be cooked for 4 minutes on each side. Carly can fit 5 burgers on the grill at once. If half her 30 guests want 2 burgers and the other half each want 1, how long will it take Carly to cook all the burgers?

First find half the number of guests at Carly's party: 30 guests / 2 = 15 guests
Then multiply that number by 2 for the number of burgers half the guests want: 15 guests * 2 burgers/guest = 30 burgers
Then add the 15 burgers for the 15 guests who only want 1 to find the total number of burgers: 30 burgers + 15 burgers = 45 burgers
Then divide the total number of burgers by the number of burgers Carly can cook at once to find the number of batches she cooks: 45 burgers / 5 burgers/batch = 9 batches
Then multiply the number of sides per burger by the cooking time per side to find each burger's total cook time: 4 minutes/side * 2 sides = 8 minutes
Finally, multiply each batch's cook time by the number of batches to find the total cook time: 8 minutes/batch * 9 batches = 72 minutes
The answer is 72.

messages.content: Mary bought six apples from the store. From the apples she bought, for each that Mary ate, she planted two trees from the remaining ones. How many apples did Mary eat?

She planted eight trees. This means she used half of that amount of apples, which is 8 trees / 2 trees/apple = 4 apples.
That means that she planted four of the six apples she bought, leaving only 6 apples - 4 apples = 2 apples to be eaten.
The answer is 2.

Marcy is a makeup artist and has agreed to do some makeup for her friend's wedding. The only makeup she has limited stock of is lip gloss so she counts how many tubes she needs. Marcy decides to bring 6 tubs of lip gloss, each of which holds 2 tubes of lip gloss, and this will be the exact amount she needs for everyone's makeup. How many people is Marcy painting with makeup?

Marcy is bringing 6 tubs of lip gloss * 2 tubes of lip gloss per tub of lip gloss = 12 tubes of lip gloss.
So she must be applying makeup to 12 tubes of lip gloss * 3 people per tube of lip gloss = 36 people.
The answer is 36.

Rain hammered the roof, so the whole Class 4 was stuck indoors for break, and the room was a roar of voices. Pradeep Sir, hurrying to finish the notice for assembly, asked, "Siddharth, read this out for me?" Siddharth read it, his voice steady over the noise. Pradeep Sir stopped writing. "You pause at the commas. Even the back row heard you. Did you know that?" Siddharth blinked. "No, Sir." "That is a real skill. Take this storybook home and read a page aloud each day." Siddharth held the book with both hands. He felt taller, though he couldn't say why.

Why was the class stuck indoors?
Rain hammered the roof, so they could not go out for break.
What was Siddharth feeling when Pradeep Sir praised his reading?
Surprise, and a feeling of being seen. He had not known he had that skill, and he felt taller afterwards.
What could Siddharth do to keep growing this skill?
He can keep reading a page of the storybook aloud each day, perhaps to someone at home who can tell him how it sounds.
Why might Pradeep Sir have spoken up in the middle of all that noise?
He noticed something real and wanted Siddharth to hear it, since one honest word of encouragement can open a path. 🙂

Read this:

Dear Ramesh Mama,
You asked about my "tailoring idea". Here's where it's got to.
Remember how Mummy's shop is always full of people who want small alterations but can't come during work hours? I thought: what if I collect clothes from offices at lunch and bring them back the next day?
I didn't want to spend anything big first. I made a simple poster and put it up in two office buildings near the shop. Fourteen people used it in the first two weeks. I walked and took the bus.
I tracked everything: what customers paid, Mummy's share for stitching, my bus fares, the posters. After two weeks I realised the bus fares ate most of what was left, so now I only collect on Tuesdays and Fridays, in one trip.
Can we talk about whether it's worth asking a bank officer about a small loan for a scooter later?
Vinita

How many people used the service in the first two weeks?
Fourteen people.
How does Vinita seem to feel about the idea so far?
Vinita seems excited but careful, pleased it's working while watching costs closely.
What does Vinita's change to Tuesdays and Fridays show about business sense?
It shows Vinita noticed a cost, bus fares, eating the profit and changed the model to cut it.
How might Ramesh Mama respond to the loan question?
Ramesh Mama might be impressed by the tracking and suggest talking to the bank officer before deciding, rather than rushing.

Read this:

Group-work note, Friday. Ms Kapoor, Class 6. Zeenat and Bhupen both wanted to present their group's project on rivers, and by Wednesday they weren't speaking. Today Zeenat came to me with a plan written on a sheet: “Bhupen does the introduction and the map. I do the dams and the conclusion. We both answer questions.” I asked if Bhupen had agreed. She said, “Not yet. I wanted to check it was fair first.” I sent her to ask him. Bhupen read it twice and added one line: “Zeenat holds the pointer for my part, I hold it for hers.” They shook on it. The presentation went smoothly, and they swapped the pointer exactly as written.

Which parts did Zeenat take in the presentation?
Zeenat took the dams and the conclusion.
What was Bhupen likely feeling when he read the plan twice?
Bhupen was likely careful and a bit wary, checking the deal was fair before agreeing.
What made the compromise work?
Each got fair parts, Bhupen added his own line so he felt heard, and they kept to the deal exactly as written.
How did Ms Kapoor support the compromise?
She checked whether Bhupen had agreed and sent Zeenat to ask him, making sure both sides were heard.

Amandeep: yes!! did it myself, no help from dad
Amandeep: then called him anyway to check 😅
Vandana: lol same energy as me opening a bank account and then asking mom which pen to use

Amandeep: I vote, I pay my phone bill, I picked my own course
Amandeep: but my hostel fees are still my parents'
Vandana: I cooked for 6 people last sunday. and then cried because my mom said my dal needed salt
Amandeep: ok that's peak in-between

Vandana: yeah. she says nobody tells u the day you become an adult
Amandeep: that's weirdly comforting
Vandana: right? we're not failing. we're just in the middle
Amandeep: middle gang 🙌

Who did Amandeep call after filing the scholarship form?
Amandeep called dad to check it.
How did Vandana feel after her mom's comment about the dal?
Vandana felt hurt and upset enough to cry, even after proudly cooking for six people.
What helps both friends feel better about the in-between stage?
Didi's experience shows the feeling is common and can last till 25, so they stop seeing it as failing.
How might Vandana's didi see what the two friends are going through?
Having felt the same till 25, didi probably sees it as normal and passing, not a sign something is wrong.

Read this:

Jyoti's cousin's wedding meant ten days in a crowded house in Indore: mattresses everywhere, one bathroom for fourteen people, no routine at all.
At home she'd built a habit: after brushing her teeth, ten minutes of stretching. It had taken a month to stick. She was sure the wedding would break it.
On the first morning, she stood in the bathroom queue behind her cousin Ujjwal, toothbrush in hand. When her turn came, she brushed, rinsed, and then, without thinking, started stretching right there beside the sink.
Ujjwal banged on the door. “Jyoti, others are waiting!”
She laughed and moved her stretches to the balcony, straight after the sink. Toothbrush, balcony, stretch.
For ten days of chaos, she didn't miss a morning. The routine was gone, but the cue was still there.

How many people shared the one bathroom?
Fourteen people shared one bathroom.
How did Jyoti feel when she started stretching without thinking?
She was surprised and amused, laughing that the habit started on its own even in the chaos.
Why did Jyoti's habit survive the wedding?
It was tied to brushing her teeth, a cue that stayed the same even when everything else changed.
How might Ujjwal see Jyoti stretching by the sink?
Ujjwal was probably impatient, banging on the door, and may have found it funny later.

Read this:

I'm Zubin, and for two years I was the one who always called Sonali.

Her birthday: I called. Her promotion: I called. When her grandmother died, I drove to Nashik. She'd pick up sometimes, be lovely for ten minutes, and then nothing until I called again. I never got a call from her in those years except once, to borrow my car.

One night I scrolled back through my call log and felt foolish. Was I loyal or just a doormat?

I talked it over with my cousin, who said, "Don't punish her. Just stop carrying it all." So I tried an experiment. I stopped calling first. I kept replying warmly whenever she messaged.

It's been three months. She's called twice. Short calls, but hers. Our friendship is smaller than I wanted. But it's real, and I'm not angry about it. I'd rather have a true small friendship than a big one I hold up alone.

What was the one time Sonali called Zubin during those years?
She called once, to borrow Zubin's car.
How did Zubin feel scrolling back through the call log?
Zubin felt foolish and unsure, wondering whether the loyalty had turned into being a doormat.
What did Zubin's experiment show?
By stopping calling first while staying warm, Zubin could see how much effort was mutual and let the friendship settle at its natural level.
How might Sonali see the change in Zubin?
Sonali may have noticed the quiet and missed Zubin, since she began calling on her own.
Ravi says, "The big balloon must be heavier than the small stone." Is he right?

Answer: No. The stone is heavier, even though the balloon is bigger.

Let the child hold a balloon in one hand and a stone in the other. Then put them on a balance: the stone side goes down. Size does not tell us mass; we have to weigh.

Read this:

The warehouse office in Ludhiana smelled of cardboard and tea.

"Kiran ma'am, there's no point sending the canteen bid," Baljeet said. "The school will pick the bigger supplier. They always do."

Kiran looked up from the invoices. "Always?"

"Well. Every time I've heard of."

"How many times is that?"

He thought. "Two."

"So is it a fact or a forecast?"

"...A forecast."

"Good. Forecasts can be tested. Write yours down." She tore a page from her diary. "I'll write mine."

He wrote, "They'll say no." She wrote, "They'll say yes to all of it."

"And if you're wrong?" she asked.

"Then I'll bring the samosas."

Ten days later, the school's email arrived. They had accepted the fruit and milk supply, but not the snacks.

Baljeet read it twice. "Half yes."

Kiran grinned. "Half wrong, both of us. Samosas are on me."

What did the school accept in the end?
They had accepted the fruit and milk supply, but not the snacks.
Why did Baljeet feel sure the school would pick the bigger supplier?
Baljeet felt discouraged because he had heard of it happening twice and treated that as a rule, so the rejection felt certain rather than like a guess.
Which question from Kiran started to change how Baljeet saw his prediction?
"So is it a fact or a forecast?" It made him admit it was a guess, which opened the door to testing it instead of giving up on the bid.
How might Kiran feel about her own prediction being half wrong?
Kiran seems amused and honest about it, offering the samosas herself. It reminds her that her own optimism needs testing too, not just Baljeet's gloom.

Read this:

Tarun, you asked how I got through planning my brother's wedding while working full time. I'll tell you, because for about a month I did not get through it well.

I'm Urmila, by the way, the sister who ended up doing everything. The caterer, the relatives from Nagpur, the rain forecast, what if the hall double-booked. I worried in the shower, in meetings, in the auto.

Then my manager, of all people, said, "Give your worries an appointment." So I did. Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace. I'd write everything. I'd circle what I could act on that day, maybe calling the hall to confirm in writing. I'd do that one thing before ten.

Rain forecast? Not solvable. Relatives' moods? Not solvable. Those stayed on the page until tomorrow's 8:30.

I won't pretend I was calm at the wedding. But I was there. I danced.

Where did Urmila write the worries every morning?
Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace.
What was Urmila feeling before giving worries an appointment?
Urmila felt overwhelmed and anxious, worrying in the shower, in meetings and in the auto about the caterer, relatives and rain.
Which choice made the biggest difference in Urmila's approach, and why?
Circling what could be acted on and doing that one thing before ten mattered most, because it turned worry into progress while unsolvable items waited.
What would change for Tarun if Tarun tried the same appointment idea?
Tarun might find worries easier to separate into doable steps and things to set aside, though it may take practice before it feels natural.

Tuesday: Sharmila and Ganga, both five, fought over the one purple crayon in their class, and Ganga snapped it in half. Both cried. Thursday: their teacher gave them a sand timer. "Two turns each," she said. They took turns, watching the sand run, and argued only once. The next Monday: when Ganga reached for the purple, she stopped. "Sorry about the broken one," she told Sharmila. "You go first."

What did Ganga do to the purple crayon on Tuesday?
She snapped it in half.
What does Ganga stopping and apologising on Monday suggest?
She felt sorry about the broken crayon and wanted things to be fair with Sharmila.
Why did the sand timer help?
It made turns clear and fair, so the girls didn't have to argue about who had it longer.
How might Sharmila feel when Ganga offers her the first turn?
Surprised and pleased, and more willing to share in return.
Set a general-knowledge quiz question about oceans. Question form only, ten words or fewer.
Which is the largest ocean on Earth?

It will take Richard and Sarah 3 years to save enough for a down payment on a house at their current rates. If the house's downpayment is $108000, calculate the amount each person saves per month if they share the monthly savings.

If they are to save every month for three years to reach the target amount, and each year has 12 months, they'll save for 12*3 = 36 months.
If the house's downpayment is $108000, the total amount they both save per month is $108000/36 = $3000 every month.
Since they share the monthly savings, each person will pay $3000/2= =$1500
The answer is 1500.

What is wrong with this sentence: The clouds is dark and low.
Mum shares 12 laddoos equally among 2 cousins. How many does each cousin get?
What does the word "puddle" mean?
How can I keep my school bag tidy?

1. Fixed: The clouds are dark and low. Why: "Clouds" is plural, so use "are".
2. The answer is 6. Because 12 / 2 = 6.
3. A puddle is a small pool of water on the ground, often after rain.
4. Put books in the same place every day. Empty it once a week.

Dear Diary,
The tap in our bathroom has been dripping for a week. Tonight I put a bucket under it before bed.
This morning — the bucket was almost half full! From one drip!
I showed Hafsa from next door. She said, "That's so much water, just going down the drain."
So I used the bucket water to water our plants and wash the balcony. Then I told Papa, and he called the plumber.
Also, I'm going to take bucket baths now instead of the shower. Hafsa laughed and said, "You'll give up in two days."
We'll see. I'm Manoj, and I'm stubborn.

How full was the bucket in the morning?
Almost half full.
What was Manoj feeling when seeing the half-full bucket?
Manoj felt shocked and surprised at how much water the drip wasted.
What steps did Manoj take that anyone could copy?
Manoj reused the bucket water, told Papa so the tap got fixed, and decided to take bucket baths.
How does Hafsa see Manoj's plan?
Hafsa doubts Manoj will keep it up and teases about giving up in two days.
I submitted my homework two days late because of a family function. Write a polite sorry note to my teacher, about 45 words.

Dear Teacher,
I am sorry that I submitted my homework two days late. I had a family function, and I could not find the time. I should have told you earlier. It will not happen again. Thank you for your understanding.
Yours sincerely

Donna worked 2 hours every morning walking dogs in her neighborhood for $10.00 an hour.  5 days a week, after school, she worked at a card shop for 2 hours and made $12.50 an hour.  On the weekends, she usually made $10.00 an hour babysitting and was guaranteed 4 hours every Saturday from her neighbor.  How much money did she make over 7 days?

She makes $10.00 an hour for 2 hours walking dogs so she makes 10*2 = $20.00 every morning
Over 7 days she makes 7*20 = $140.00 a week
She makes $12.50 for 2 hours working at a card shop so she makes 12.5*2 = $25.00
She works there 5 days a week so she makes 5*25 = $125.00 a week
She also babysits for 4 hours making $10.00 an hour for a total of 4*10 = $40.00
Over 7 days, she makes 140+125+40 = $305.00
The answer is 305.

(1) Why do we keep milk in the fridge?
(2) Could you explain the difference between "each other" and "one another"?
(3) Fix my grammar: My mother cooks very good.
(4) How would you explain "withstand" to a child?
(5) Is it "mischievious" or "mischievous"?

1. Cold keeps it from going sour quickly. Because the low temperature slows the growth of the germs that spoil milk.
2. They mean the same. Many writers use "each other" for two people and "one another" for more.
3. Write it as: My mother cooks very well. Why: use the adverb "well" to describe the verb "cooks".
4. "Withstand" is a verb. It means to survive or resist something strong.
5. It is "mischievous", with only three syllables.

My phone buzzed with the ward office alert on Thursday afternoon: the river was rising, and low streets should be left by evening. I'm Lalit, and I read it twice, then read the news channel to check. The same message.
We packed one bag each. My kids, my wife, my mother Madhuri, and me. Ma wanted to carry the sewing machine down. "It's how I earn, beta," she said. I told her it was too heavy, the stairs were already wet, and we'd sort the machine later. She was angry for ten minutes.
We walked to my cousin's flat on the hill. The water reached the ground floor that night. The machine, upstairs, got wet only a little. Ma hugged me in the morning and said nothing.

Who sent the alert Lalit read on Thursday?
The ward office sent the alert.
What was Madhuri feeling about the sewing machine?
Madhuri was anxious and angry about leaving her means of earning, which is why she wanted to carry it down.
What could Lalit and the family do after the water goes down?
They could check the machine and the flat together and ask the ward office about help with any loss.
How might Lalit have felt while Madhuri was angry for ten minutes?
Lalit was probably torn and tense, wanting to respect Ma's work but worried about the wet stairs.

"You asked why I stopped arguing with the ref in the second half, Lalremsiami. Okay, listen.
The number nine from the other team, after I tackled him clean, got up and snarled at me. Teeth showing, face right in mine, fists opening and closing. And he muttered that he'd get me after the match.
Before, I would have shoved him back. But my stomach went tight and I thought, this isn't normal game anger. So I stepped back and put my hands up, and I jogged over to where our team was standing.
Then I told Coach. Coach told the ref, and the ref warned him. After the match, Coach walked with us to the bus.
Me, Tenzin, walking away. Mama laughed when I told her. Then she hugged me."

What did the number nine mutter?
That he'd get Tenzin after the match.
What was Tenzin feeling when the number nine snarled?
Tenzin felt a tight stomach and a sense of danger, reading the snarl and moving fists as more than normal game anger.
What steps did Tenzin take that others could learn from?
Tenzin stepped back with hands up, moved toward the team, and told the coach, who got the referee involved.
How might Coach see Tenzin's choice to walk away?
Coach likely saw it as mature and safe, not weak, which is why he acted quickly and walked the team to the bus.

On the first day after the holidays at the village school, Charu, Deepu and Munni all had green water bottles from the Tuesday market. Kishore's was red. He hid it behind his back. At break, the three friends played 'tractor' with their green bottles as wheels, and Kishore stood and watched. That evening he cried until his mother promised to go to the market. 'Red is nice too,' she said. 'No! Everyone has green!' On Tuesday, holding his new green bottle, Kishore ran straight to join the tractor game.

Where did the green water bottles come from?
The Tuesday market.
Why did Kishore hide his red bottle?
He felt left out and embarrassed because his bottle was different from everyone else's.
How could Kishore's mother or teacher help him feel included without buying the same things?
Help him join the tractor game with his red bottle, showing that different colours can still play together.
How might Charu see Kishore's new green bottle?
Charu may simply be happy to have him join the game, perhaps without noticing how much the colour mattered to him.

Saturday
Usha Mami and everyone came for lunch today. The whole time it was Vikram this and Vikram that. My brother Vikram got 98 in maths. Vikram is going to be a doctor. Nani even gave him a hundred rupees. When Usha Mami asked about me, Amma said, "Manjula is good at drawing," and everyone said, "Oh, nice," and went back to Vikram. I went and sat on the stairs. I love Vikram, he helps me with fractions, but today I kind of hated him too. Maybe they love him more because he's clever. I got 71 in maths. Nobody gave me anything. I'm ten and I think I'm the less good one in this house.
Manjula

How much did Vikram get in maths?
Vikram got 98 in maths.
Why did Manjula go and sit on the stairs?
Manjula felt hurt and jealous, left out while everyone praised Vikram, and began to fear being the less loved one.
What could Amma do to ease this comparison?
Amma could notice Manjula on the stairs, spend time looking at Manjula's drawings, and praise each child's own efforts instead of letting marks decide.
How might Vikram feel if he read this diary?
Vikram might feel sad and surprised, since he helps with fractions and probably never wanted to be a rival.

I'm Pranav, and three weeks after they made me design lead, Chandrika stopped me outside the pantry. She said the new onboarding flow had too many steps and that two clients had already complained. I remember smiling at her. In my head I was already sorting it: she had wanted this role, she had applied for it too, so of course she would find holes. I told her, "Some people just don't see where we're going yet." She nodded and walked off. That night I told my flatmate the team resented change. When a junior raised the same point in the review, I thought, great, now she's lobbying. Looking back even a little, what bothers me is how certain I felt. Every question sounded like an attack on the title I had only just got used to.

Who stopped Pranav outside the pantry?
Chandrika stopped Pranav outside the pantry.
How did Pranav feel when Chandrika criticised the onboarding flow?
Pranav felt defensive and a little superior, reading her point as jealousy because she had applied for the same role.

Pranav could go back to the two client complaints and check the facts separately from who raised them, then ask Chandrika to walk through the steps with them.
How might Chandrika see that exchange by the pantry?
Chandrika probably felt brushed aside and may decide it is not worth warning Pranav again, even when something serious comes up.

The CA institute's library in Hyderabad was nearly empty on Saturday afternoon, which is why Salma chose it. Her mentor, Indu, who had trained her during articleship and now worked at a different firm, sat across the reading table.
Salma kept her voice low and left out the client's name. 'Repeated payments to a supplier. The supplier's tax registration belongs to a relative of the purchase manager. My senior hasn't noticed.'
Indu didn't react much. 'What exactly do you have? Copies, or just what you saw?' Salma showed her notes. 'Good. Your firm has a whistleblower route. Use that, not your senior, and don't discuss it at work.'
That evening Salma called Advocate Rehman, who had taught a law elective at her college. He explained in general terms how the firm's policy and the law might protect her, and suggested she keep her notes factual and dated.
Walking home, Salma noticed her shoulders weren't up by her ears any more. The problem was still there. But she no longer felt alone with it.

Where did Salma meet Indu?
At the CA institute's library in Hyderabad.
What does Salma noticing her shoulders relax suggest?
She felt less tense and less alone, relieved after getting careful advice.
What made Salma's approach careful?
She left out the client's name, spoke to a mentor outside her reporting line and an advocate, and planned to use the formal route.
How might Indu see Salma's question?
Indu sees a former trainee handling something serious carefully, and responds calmly with practical steps.

messages.content: A cube of cheese is cut straight through with one slice of a knife. Which shapes can the cut face be? Can it be a triangle? A regular hexagon? A circle?

Answer: A square, a rectangle, a triangle, a trapezium, a pentagon or a hexagon (even a regular hexagon); never a circle and never a polygon with more than 6 sides.

Picture the knife as a flat plane. Cut parallel to a face: a SQUARE the same size as the face. Tilt the knife but keep it parallel to one edge: a RECTANGLE (longer than the square). Slice off a corner: a TRIANGLE (cutting three faces near one vertex). Cut through the midpoints of six edges, square to a long diagonal of the cube: a REGULAR HEXAGON. Each side of the cross-section lies on one face of the cube, and a cube has 6 faces, so at most 6 sides; a flat cut of a flat-faced solid never gives a curve. Common mistake: thinking the cut must be parallel to a face. Try it with a potato or clay cube.

"Trisha, you haven't eaten your momos. What's wrong?"
"Nothing, Lalremsiami Di."
"You didn't go to dance class either."
"Because Ria will be there."
"Ria? Your best friend Ria?"
"Not anymore." Trisha's voice cracked. "We fought about the costume and she said I copy everything she does. Now she sits with Poonam."
"Oh, Trisha." Lalremsiami moved closer on the bed. "That hurts."
"It's stupid. It's just a costume."
"It's not stupid if it hurts this much. Tell me what happened, from the start."
Trisha told her everything, crying and wiping her nose on her sleeve.
When she finished, Lalremsiami said, "Do you want ideas, or do you just want me to listen tonight?"
"Just listen," Trisha said, and leaned against her.

What did Trisha and Ria fight about?
The costume.
What does skipping momos and dance class suggest Trisha is feeling?
She skipped her momos and dance class, and her voice cracked when talking about Ria, showing she feels deeply hurt and sad.
What did Lalremsiami do that was wise?
She said the hurt wasn't stupid, asked Trisha to tell the whole story, and asked whether she wanted ideas or just listening.
How might Ria be seeing the fight?
Ria might also feel hurt or annoyed, thinking Trisha copies her, and may not know how sad Trisha feels.

Ben has $2000 for his business operations costs. He orders goods from his supplier and writes them a cheque for $600. His debtor pays him $800 from the purchases they had made on credit. Mr. Ben then decides to do equipment maintenance and spends $1200 on the whole operation. How much money is Mr. Ben remaining with?

When Mr. Ben writes the cheque, he remains with $2000-$600 = $1400
His debtor pays him $800, increasing his operation capital to $1400+$800 = $2200
He spends $1200, remaining $2200-$1200 = $1000 for business operations cost after maintenance.
The answer is 1000.

Read this:

After the summer holidays, Parul came back to Class 5 with a new pencil box and a story about the mountains. But on Monday, Rafiq and the others at her table turned their heads away when she spoke. On Tuesday they passed a note right over her desk, as if she were air. Nobody said why. Nobody teased her; that might have been easier. Parul went over the last week of the holidays again and again. Had she forgotten a birthday? Said something wrong in the group call? At lunch she ate her paratha very slowly. That evening Mummy found her on the stairs, still in uniform. "They're not angry," Parul whispered. "They're just not seeing me." Mummy sat down beside her and listened until it was all out.

What did Parul bring back after the summer holidays?
A new pencil box and a story about the mountains.
How did Parul feel when her friends passed the note over her desk?
She felt invisible, anxious and confused, replaying the holidays to work out what she might have done.
What could Mummy and Parul do next?
They could talk it through calmly and, if it goes on, tell the class teacher, who can gently find out what has gone wrong without blaming Parul.
What would change if Rafiq told Parul what was wrong?
Parul could understand and perhaps fix it, instead of being stuck in a silent confusion that hurts more than teasing.

Read this:

Dear Madhuri,
Sorry this is a letter, but I can't say it in the corridor. Today Kabir and a few others kept guessing who writes the poems in the class notebook. They teased me, "Come on, Vandana, you know!" One even hid my geometry box until I answered. I said nothing, and it felt good and awful at once. Your secret is yours to tell. But I want to ask: does hiding it bother you? You look happy when you write, yet you flinch when anyone reads a poem aloud. If you ever want to share them, I'll sit beside you. If not, my lips stay shut. 🙂
Your friend,
Vandana

What did one classmate hide until Vandana answered?
One classmate hid Vandana's geometry box until Vandana answered.
What does Vandana think about the secret, and what worry sits beside that loyalty?
Vandana thinks the secret is Madhuri's to tell, but wonders whether hiding it bothers Madhuri, since Madhuri flinches when a poem is read aloud.
What could Vandana do next to check the secret is not hurting Madhuri?
Ask Madhuri privately how it feels, and offer to sit beside Madhuri if Madhuri ever wants to share the poems. 😊
How might Madhuri feel on reading this letter?
Probably relieved that Vandana stayed loyal, and maybe a little exposed at being asked; the flinch at hearing a poem aloud shows the secret still matters.
What is the name of the oldest shop in my neighbourhood?
I'm not sure, as I can't see your neighbourhood. An older neighbour may know.
Write a sign for a swimming pool deck: under seven words, all capitals, telling people not to run.
WALK, DO NOT RUN
On the road sign, what is a junction?

A junction is a place where two or more roads, tracks or lines meet. It is a noun.
Example: Turn left at the junction near the petrol pump.

"Adil, time to go home now."

"No!"

"Come, beta. Swing is finished."

"More swing!"

"It's getting dark. Arohi aunty is waiting."

Adil's face crumpled. His hands gripped the swing chains. His whole body went stiff.

"No go! No go!"

"I know, you love the swing."

His lip shook. Then the crying started, loud and sudden. Noor crouched beside him, holding his coat.

What did Adil want more of?
More swing.
What do Adil's crumpled face and stiff body show?
They show he feels frustrated and sad, unable to manage his wish to stay.
What could Noor try in this moment?
Stay close and calm, name his wish to stay, and gently help him off the swing without arguing.
How might Arohi aunty feel waiting?
She is probably patient but a little tired, hoping they can leave soon.

"Your hands are shaking," Shankar said in the corridor outside the viva room.
"I know. Look." Madhav held one up and turned it over. "Palms wet too. I've revised for weeks and my body still thinks I'm being chased."
"That's just adrenaline. My brother says it means you're ready."
"Ready to faint?"
Shankar laughed. "Ready to talk. Try this: press your feet down on the floor and breathe out slowly. And say your first sentence in your head."
Madhav did it. His shoulders lowered a little. "My first sentence is 'The main finding is...' Right."
The examiner called his name.
"Go," Shankar said. "Tell me after. If it feels like this all the time, talk to the counsellor."

What did Shankar say about shaking hands, quoting a brother?
Shankar said the brother says it means you're ready.
What is Madhav feeling in the corridor, and how does Shankar help him see it differently?
Madhav feels nervous and afraid, and Shankar reframes his shaking as adrenaline that shows he is ready to talk.
What could Madhav do if the shakiness happened all the time and not only before events?
He could talk to the college counsellor, since ongoing panic deserves professional support.
How might Shankar feel as Shankar sends Madhav in?
Shankar seems supportive and confident in him, and hopes to hear how it went.
