In the school staffroom, the duty roster went up every Monday, and every Monday there was a new line with Leela's name on it. Exam invigilation, annual day costumes, the science club, and now the principal was asking whether she would also take the Class 6 remedial group. Charu, who shared a table with her, watched Leela nod before the sentence had even ended. She had seen Leela marking papers in the car park at eight at night, and heard her cancel her own dentist appointment twice. Charu waited until the principal left. 'Leela, I'll say it once. You're allowed to say no.' Leela gave a tired laugh. 'If I say no, they'll think I'm not a team player.' 'Then let's practise. Next time, say you'll check your load and come back. I'll back you up in the meeting.' On Friday, when a new request came, Leela said, 'Let me check my load.' Charu gave her a tiny nod across the room.

What new group was the principal asking Leela to take?
The Class 6 remedial group.
What did Charu feel watching Leela nod before the sentence ended?
Charu felt worried and a little frustrated, having seen Leela marking at night and cancelling her own appointments.
How did Charu help Leela practise saying no?
She gave Leela a simple phrase, 'Let me check my load', and promised to back her up in meetings.
Why does Leela find it hard to say no?
Leela fears being seen as not a team player, so agreeing to everything feels safer than risking disapproval.
Describe a cat sleeping on a window ledge, about 50 words.

The cat lies curled on the window ledge, a soft grey ball in a patch of sunshine. Her chest rises and falls slowly. Her tail wraps around her paws, and one ear twitches at a sound outside. She is warm and completely at peace. The whole afternoon seems to slow down just to let her sleep.

In the village near Namchi, Tenzin, fifteen, was cooking dinner for the first time while his mother was at the monastery. His cousin Ankita watched from the doorway. Before touching anything, Tenzin washed his hands with soap at the tap outside. He cut the raw chicken on one board and the vegetables on another, then washed the knife. When the oil in the wok began to shimmer, he lowered the chicken in slowly, away from himself. Ankita's phone rang; she handed it to him. "Aunty wants you." Tenzin turned the gas off first, then took the call. "Why'd you switch it off?" Ankita asked. "Amma says the stove never stays alone. Not even for a minute."

Where was Tenzin's mother?
At the monastery.
How might Tenzin have felt cooking dinner alone for the first time?
He probably felt a little nervous but careful and responsible, following each safe habit.
Which of Tenzin's habits made his cooking safe?
Washing his hands, using separate boards for raw chicken and vegetables, lowering food into hot oil carefully and turning off the gas before taking the call.
How does Ankita see Tenzin switching off the gas?
Ankita is puzzled at first, not seeing why he would turn it off for a short call.

Week one: Gargi watched the district hockey trials from the stands with her knee in a brace. When the coach put Aditi in her position, Gargi went home and didn't touch her phone all evening. "Who am I if I'm not playing?" she wrote in her notebook.
Week three: Aditi texted, "We need someone to track the other team's corners. Coach asked for you." Gargi went, clipboard in hand, and found she liked spotting patterns. She also did every exercise the doctor had set, even the boring ones.
Week seven: Back on the field for light drills, Gargi saw Aditi still in her spot. It stung. But at the break Aditi said, "Your corner notes won us the semi." Gargi grinned.

What job did the coach ask Gargi to do in week three?
Tracking the other team's corners.
What was Gargi feeling in week one, and what shows it?
She felt lost, low and afraid of being replaced; she ignored her phone and wrote, "Who am I if I'm not playing?"
What helped Gargi through the injury?
Staying part of the team through the corner notes, finding a new interest in spotting patterns, and doing every exercise the doctor set.
How might Aditi feel about taking Gargi's position?
Aditi may feel a little awkward about it, which could be why she keeps including Gargi and praises her notes.

"Third time unlucky," Anand announced at dinner, dropping into his chair. "The examiners have now seen my handwriting more often than my own mother has."
Amma laughed. Usha didn't, quite. "You failed the accounts exam again?"
"By four marks. Four! I'm going to frame the result. 'Almost.'"
Usha studied him across the table. "Anand. Honestly. Is this funny-funny, or funny so you don't have to talk about it?"
He paused with a chapati halfway to his mouth. "Hm. Fair question." He chewed. "Honestly? It stung this morning. I sulked on the bus. But I've already booked the next attempt, and I know exactly which paper let me down. So... mostly funny-funny now."
"Okay." Usha passed the dal. "If it turns into the other kind, tell me."
"You'll be the first." He grinned. "After the frame shop."

By how many marks did Anand fail?
By four marks.
How was Anand really feeling about failing again?
Anand admitted it stung in the morning and he sulked, but by dinner he felt mostly okay and determined, having booked the next attempt; the jokes were largely genuine resilience.
Why was Usha's question a good one?
It named both possibilities without assuming, letting Anand check honestly and share both the sting and the recovery.
How might Usha feel after Anand's answer?
Usha probably felt reassured, since he was honest about the sting and seemed genuinely okay, while the door stayed open if that changed.

Pooja had stopped telling Papa about her week. After the arguments about the animation course, it seemed easier: she said "fine" and "nothing much" and ate quickly. Ojas noticed the quiet at the table and did not ask, and the two of them passed the salt like polite guests. Her friend Nazia said over the phone, "He can't meet the real you if you hide her."

So on Sunday afternoon, when the house was still, Pooja knocked on his study door. "Papa, I'm grateful you want good things for me. This is the road I've chosen. I'd love your blessing, but I will carry it either way." Her hands were cold, though her voice held.

Ojas took off his glasses and looked at the desk for a long time. "I don't understand this field," he said finally. "But you have never wasted a chance I gave you."

In the months after, he stopped asking her to justify every plan and instead asked what she thought. When her first short film played at the college hall, he sat in the third row, phone held high, telling the man beside him, "That is my daughter's name in the credits."

Later, she heard him on the phone with his brother, saying, "She managed it herself. I only carried the tea."

What did Pooja say when she knocked on the study door?
She told her father she was grateful, said this was the road she had chosen, and asked for his blessing while saying she would carry it either way.
How did Pooja's behaviour before Sunday differ from her statement to her father, and how did Ojas change afterwards?

Before, she stayed silent and gave short answers to keep the peace, which kept her father from meeting the real her; after her honest statement, Ojas stopped asking her to justify plans and started asking what she thought.
What was Pooja feeling when she stood at the study door with cold hands?
She was nervous but resolved, since her hands were cold while her voice held steady.
What does the film screening suggest about how Ojas now sees Pooja?
He is proud of her independence and sees her as an adult, telling the man beside him that it is his daughter's name in the credits.

I'm Tanvir. Last year, at twenty, I forwarded a video to our family group showing "proof" that a neighbourhood near ours was dangerous. It had dramatic music, angry captions and no date. My uncle Bhupen replied, "Where is this from?" I didn't know. He found the original: it was from another country, five years old. I felt stupid, but mostly I felt used. The video had wanted me angry, and it worked. Since then I check three things before I share: who made it, when, and what it wants me to feel. I also started reading one article a week from people I usually disagree with. Some of them make better points than I expected.

What did Uncle Bhupen ask about the video?
"Where is this from?"
How did Tanvir feel after learning the video was old and foreign?
Tanvir felt stupid and used, realising the video was designed to provoke anger.
What habit is Tanvir now using, and why does it help?
Checking who made it, when and what it wants Tanvir to feel, because it catches manipulation before sharing.
How might Uncle Bhupen have felt asking his question?
Probably concerned but calm, wanting to correct the record without humiliating anyone.

In the drought year, Madhav woke before the sun in their village near Latur and walked the edge of his father's cotton fields in silence. No phone, no radio, just the crunch of dry soil and the first birds. He had learned the practice from a retired teacher at his college hostel: walk slowly, count ten breaths, notice one thing you have never seen before. For two years he had done it every day. This year, with the well low and loan payments looming, it was the only hour his chest wasn't tight. Devika, who taught at the zilla parishad school and walked past to catch her bus, asked one morning what he was doing. "Nothing," he said. "That's the point." She laughed, then joined him the next Sunday. By summer, four people walked the field edge at dawn, mostly silent. The drought didn't lift. But Madhav stopped shouting at his father about money.

Where did Madhav walk each morning?
The edge of his father's cotton fields.
What was Madhav feeling during the drought year apart from the walk?
Madhav felt tense and anxious, with the well low and loan payments looming; the walk was his only calm hour.
What made Madhav's practice last through a hard year?
It was simple and daily, walking slowly, counting ten breaths and noticing one new thing without a phone, and he had kept it for two years.
How might Devika see the dawn walks?
Devika first found the idea amusing, but joining showed her its value, and she became part of a small group.
Shorten this sentence: Due to the fact that it was raining very heavily, we made the decision to postpone the picnic until a later date.
Because of the heavy rain, we put off the picnic.
I'm annoyed but I want to stay polite with my neighbour. Soften this: Your noisy kids ruined my afternoon nap, which is totally unacceptable!
I'm sorry to mention it, but the noise from the children disturbed my afternoon nap. I would be grateful if they could play a little more quietly.

Monday, 3 June. Nikita stared at the forty-page report the team sent every month. "Why do we do it like this?" she asked Sahil. "Because we always have. The director likes detail." That evening she wrote one line in her notebook: If nobody had ever made this report, what would I build? Her answer was two pages and a link to the full data.
Tuesday, 11 June. She did not scrap the old report. She sent the two-page version to the director with the long one attached and a note: "Trying a shorter format this month. Tell me what's missing." Her stomach knotted as she pressed send.
Friday, 28 June. The director's reply came: "Much easier to read. Add the regional table." The file log showed that the long attachment had not been opened once. Sahil read the reply over her shoulder and whistled softly.

What did Nikita write in her notebook on Monday evening?
She wrote: If nobody had ever made this report, what would I build?
What was Nikita feeling when she pressed send on Tuesday?
She was nervous, her stomach knotted, because she feared the director would see the shorter report as missing detail.
Why was attaching the long report a smart part of her test?
It kept a safety net, so she could check whether the feared cost of losing detail really appeared without risking the whole report.
How did Sahil see the monthly report at first?
Sahil treated the old way as settled simply because it had always been done, assuming the director wanted all that detail.

Mckenna starts her day at 8:00 a.m. She works in her office up to 11:00 a.m. then joins her team of developers at the conference room to talk about projects up to 13:00, from which she works for another two hours and then heads home. How many hours does Mckenna stay at work?

From 8:00 to 11:00, Mckenna spends 11:00-8:00 = 3 hours at work
When she joins the developers in the conference room for the meeting, she spends an additional 13:00-11:00 = 2 hours at work.
So far, she has spent 3+2 = 5 hours at work.
When she works for an additional 2 hours before heading home, her total work hours become 5+2 = 7 hours
The answer is 7.

The passport office in Lucknow had a token machine, forty plastic chairs and a ceiling fan that clicked. Pooja, twenty-three, held token 87 and a folder she had organised herself: photocopies, address proof, and the form she'd filled in at midnight without calling Papa once.
Damini, her colleague, had come along for company. "Your dad did all this for you last time?"
"Last time I was sixteen and he held my hand at the counter." Pooja laughed. "This month I also paid my own phone bill, went to the dentist alone, and didn't miss one Sunday at the animal shelter, even the rainy one."
"So you feel like an adult now?"
Pooja thought. "About sixty percent. It's growing, one boring thing at a time."
Token 87 flashed on the screen. She walked to the counter by herself, her hands only slightly sweaty.

What token number did Pooja hold?
Token 87.
What does Pooja's answer 'About sixty percent' show about how she feels?
She feels partly grown-up and accepts that the feeling builds bit by bit rather than arriving all at once.
Which small acts helped Pooja build her adulthood this month?
Organising the passport papers herself, paying her phone bill, going to the dentist alone and keeping every Sunday at the shelter.
How might Pooja's father feel if he saw her walking to the counter alone?
He might feel proud and a little wistful, remembering holding her hand there at sixteen.
Who was Ahalya, and how did Rama help her?
Ahalya was the wife of the sage Gautam, who cursed her to live unseen in penance. When Rama came to the hermitage, the curse ended and she was freed.

Tushar, you say you'd never obey an order to hurt someone. I said that too, at twenty, in a hostel in Kharagpur. We had read about those obedience experiments in our psychology elective: volunteers giving what they thought were painful shocks because a calm man told them to continue. I was disgusted with them. That same week our hostel senior told us to make the new first-years stand in the corridor till 2 am. It seemed small. Then he said, 'Make them sing.' Then, 'Make them crawl.' I did the first two. I was halfway into the third, my own voice giving orders, when I saw a first-year's knees shaking. Something in me stopped. I said, 'No more,' walked out and knocked on the warden's door. Kamal the brave? No. Kamal who got to step three before remembering there was a choice.

What was the senior's first order?
Make the first-years stand in the corridor till 2 am.
How did Kamal feel on reading about the experiments?
Kamal felt disgusted and sure of being different from the obedient volunteers.
Kamal said 'No more' at the third order and knocked on the warden's door. Why was that a turning point?
It broke the chain of small steps, showing there was still a choice, and brought an adult to protect the first-years.
What was the corridor like for the first-years?
The first-years were frightened and humiliated, knees shaking as the orders grew worse.

Subject: re: you asked about my dad
Nirmala,
You asked why I never go home for Losar. Short version: my father is a tyrant. He decided I was a failure the day I picked music over engineering, and nothing I do will change that. I've told Dawa and the whole band this, and honestly it's easier with one sentence. I hear he tells his friends I'm the ungrateful son who ran off, so I guess we both have our stories.
Last week my cousin said Pa still keeps my old cassette player on his shelf. I said, so what, it's just stuff. But then I remembered him fixing it with a hairpin when I was eight, humming off-key so I'd laugh.
I deleted that line from this email twice.
Anyway. Tyrant. That's the story.
Tenzin

What does Tenzin's father still keep on his shelf?
His father still keeps his old cassette player on his shelf.
Why did Tenzin delete the memory of the hairpin repair twice?
The tender memory didn't fit his simple story of a tyrant father, and holding on to it may have felt painful and confusing.
What small step could stop Tenzin's story from hardening further?
He could leave the tender memory in the email and tell Nirmala the fuller picture, so his father stays a person rather than a villain.
What might Tenzin's father be going through while telling friends his son is ungrateful?
He may be hiding hurt behind a simple story, just as Tenzin does, while still keeping the cassette player close.

Sunil says: "1/7 is bigger than 1/5 because 7 is bigger than 5." What would you tell him?

Now you try: is 4/9 bigger than 4/5?
The answer is No: ninths are smaller pieces, so 4/9 < 4/5.

Minakshi, come, sit by your Pooja Dadi. I know you haven't slept since your classmate's funeral. Let me tell you something.
When I was sixteen, my best friend Shobha died of a fever. One week she was laughing with me by the well, and the next she was gone. I stopped talking. I wouldn't eat.
My mother didn't tell me to be brave. She gave me a notebook and said, “Write to her.”
So I did. Every night for a year. I told Shobha everything: exams, a boy I liked, my fights with my sister.
On the first anniversary I went to Shobha's mother, gave her the notebook and helped her cook for the prayer. She held me for a long time. Grief doesn't vanish, beti. It just finds a place to live.

What did Pooja's mother give her?
A notebook.
How did young Pooja feel after Shobha died?
She felt deep grief and shock, so heavy she stopped talking and eating.
What choices in the story helped Pooja mourn?
Writing to Shobha every night and later going to help Shobha's mother on the anniversary.
How might Shobha's mother have felt when Pooja gave her the notebook?
She probably felt moved and comforted to know how much her daughter was loved.

Half of Irawati's office in Pune had signed up for the city half-marathon. The team group was full of shoe photos and training plans. Trisha, her desk-mate, sent her the link three times. "Come on, everyone's doing it!" Irawati felt the pull. She also felt a small question underneath. On Sunday morning she sat on her balcony with tea and asked herself two things. Why do I want this? And if nobody at work would ever know, would I still run? The first answer was honest: partly to be in the photos. The second surprised her. Yes. She had missed running since college. She signed up that night. But she made her own training plan, slower than the team's, and ran alone on Tuesdays. When Trisha asked why, she said, "I'm running for me. The team is a bonus."

How many times did Trisha send Irawati the link?
Three times.
What was Irawati feeling when the team chat filled with shoe photos?
She felt the pull of the group but also a small doubt about whether she really wanted to run.
Which choice worked, and why?
Asking why she wanted it and whether she'd run if nobody knew, then joining deliberately with her own plan, so she joined for her own reasons.
How might Trisha see Irawati running alone on Tuesdays?
Trisha might find it a little odd at first, since for her the fun is doing it together.

The inter-school debate in Pune was held in the last week of December, with a Christmas tree still blinking in the auditorium lobby. Vaibhav had prepared for three weeks. In the final round he blanked on his rebuttal, stood silent for ten long seconds, and his team lost by two points.
In January, Hafsa pinned the next notice on the class board. "Youth parliament, February. You're coming, right? You're our best speaker."
"I'm not," Vaibhav said. "Everyone saw what I am."
"You froze once."
"In front of the whole school." He didn't look at the notice. At lunch he sat away from the debate group, and when the teacher asked who wanted to open the class discussion, he kept his eyes on his notebook.
That night he deleted the debate folder from his laptop, then restored it, then shut the laptop.

How long did Vaibhav stand silent in the final round?
Ten long seconds.
Why does Vaibhav say "Everyone saw what I am"?
Vaibhav feels ashamed; to him the frozen rebuttal is not a bad moment but proof about his worth, so another contest feels like risking more humiliation.
What could help Vaibhav return to debating?
Separating the task from his worth: going over what went wrong with a teacher, practising rebuttals where little is at stake, and perhaps taking a smaller role in February.
How does Hafsa see Vaibhav?
Hafsa still sees him as "our best speaker" who froze once, not someone defined by one loss, and wants him back on the team.

After the looms went quiet in Malegaon, Asif would sit alone in the workshop office with the day's worries: an order cancelled, wages due, his father's cough. Most nights he opened a packet of namkeen, then another, eating without tasting. Afterwards came the heavy, sick feeling and the voice: no self-control, again.
One night he stopped with his hand in the packet and asked himself, what am I actually feeling? The answer was clear: scared about the money. Not hungry at all.
He didn't scold himself. He said quietly, "Okay. You're scared. That makes sense." Then he put the packet away, called his friend Dhruv, and they walked to the chai stall by the bridge. Some nights he still ate namkeen. But the loop was looser now, and the guilt didn't follow him home.

Where did Asif and Dhruv walk?
They walked to the chai stall by the bridge.
What was Asif really feeling when he reached for the namkeen?
Asif was scared about the money, not hungry at all.
Which steps helped Asif break the loop?
Naming the feeling, speaking kindly to himself instead of scolding, and choosing another comfort: calling Dhruv and going for a walk.
How might Dhruv experience Asif's late-night call?
Dhruv may be glad to be asked and to share a walk, even without knowing the whole story.

Nikita, you want to know how to handle line-cutters without a fight? Your Ritu masi has had practice. In 1994 I worked at the post office counter in Jaipur. Every pension day, someone tried to slip in. I learned to smile and say, 'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.' Most people went back, a bit sheepish. One day a man shouted at me, red-faced, that he was an important person. The people in line were getting tense. I didn't argue. I served him quickly, and then apologised to the next woman in line for the wait. Later my boss asked why I'd given in. I said, 'Because a fight in a queue helps nobody.'

What did Ritu masi say to line-cutters?
'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.'
How might the people in line have felt when the man shouted?
Tense and uneasy, worried the shouting would turn into a fight.
What choice in the story shows when to let it go?
When the man turned hostile, Ritu served him quickly instead of arguing, then apologised to the next woman, keeping everyone safe.
How might the woman next in line have felt after Ritu's apology?
Probably still annoyed at the man but respected and less upset, since Ritu acknowledged her wait.
For my little sister, write a bedtime story about a puddle in the school yard.

After the big rain, a large brown puddle sat in the school yard, and every child ran around it. A small girl named Pari looked at the puddle and thought it looked lonely. She tiptoed up and dropped in a paper boat she had folded from her rough notebook. The boat floated! Her friends gathered round and folded boats of their own, red, blue and yellow, and soon the puddle was full of tiny sails. A gentle wind pushed them across to the far side. When the sun came out, the puddle began to shrink, but the boats stayed, dry and bright on the pavement. Pari tucked hers in her bag and carried it home as a treasure.

Prudence was starting a cupcake business.  She figured that each cupcake cost $0.75 to make.  The first 2 dozen that she made burnt and she had to throw them out.  The next 2 came out perfectly and she ended up eating 5 cupcakes right away.  Later that day she made 2 more dozen cupcakes and decided to eat 4 more. If she sells the remaining cupcakes at $2.00 each, how much is her net profit?

She burnt 2 dozen, cooked 2 dozen and then another 2 dozen that evening. So she made 2+2+2 =6 dozen cupcakes
Each dozen makes 12 cupcakes, so she made 6*12= 72 cupcakes
She threw away 2 dozen cupcakes, so 2*12 = 24 cupcakes
She made 72, threw away 24, ate 5 and then ate another 4 so she had 72-24-5-4 = 39 cupcakes left
She sells the 39 cupcakes at $2.00 each so she earned 39*2 = $78.00
She made 72 cupcakes at a cost of $0.75 each for a total cost of 72*$0.75 = $54.00
If she made $78 on the remaining cupcakes and it cost her $54.00 to make all of the cupcakes then her profit is $78-$54 = $24.00
The answer is 24.

Charlotte needs to know how much money to have with her when she goes to the shoe store. How much money should Charlotte bring to buy a pair of boots, if the original price is $90 and there is a discount of 20%?

The amount of the discount is 20/100 * $90 original price = $18
Charlotte needs to bring the $90 - $18 discount = $72
The answer is 72.

“Did you see Jaya forget her lines in the play?” Ankita whispered. “She just stood there, mouth open, like a fish.” The girls burst out laughing. Someone passed her a packet of chips as a reward. Ankita felt warm, liked, at the centre.
She told another story, and another. The row got louder.
Then, in a quiet moment, she heard a laugh from the row behind, and her own name. She froze. What were they saying? She pulled her knees up and stared at the window. Jaya, two rows ahead, had her headphones on and hadn't turned once.

How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
For three hours on the ghat road.
What was Ankita feeling when she heard her own name?
She felt anxious and exposed, worried she was now the topic of someone else's laughter.

She could stop the stories about Jaya, change the topic to a game, and maybe say sorry to Jaya later.

She may have felt hurt and embarrassed, perhaps guessing she was being laughed at and shutting it out.

The cyclone warning came at 4 pm, and Vinita, twenty-six and running the dispatch desk at a Visakhapatnam warehouse, had twelve trucks due to leave for Odisha at dawn. The forecast put landfall anywhere along a three-hundred-kilometre stretch. Tejas, her deputy, wanted to send them anyway. 'Clients are waiting.' Vinita listed what she knew and what she didn't. Rerouting by the inland highway would add a day and cost extra fuel. Driving into the storm could cost lives. She held the trucks until the 10 pm update. It narrowed the path but still included their route. She rerouted inland. The cyclone turned north and missed the coastal road completely. Tejas raised an eyebrow the next morning. Vinita shrugged, tired. 'With what we knew last night, I'd make the same call.' She wrote a short note for next time: which updates to wait for, and whom to ask.

How many trucks were due to leave for Odisha at dawn?
Twelve trucks.
How did Vinita feel when the cyclone missed the coastal road?
Tired but settled; she did not regret the decision because it was sound for what she knew then.
What made Vinita's decision process sound?
She listed what she knew and did not know, weighed cost against risk to lives, waited for the next update and noted lessons for next time.
How might Tejas see the decision the next morning?
He may think it cost a day for nothing, as his raised eyebrow suggests, judging by the outcome rather than the risk at the time.
While I was reading, the lights went off. Is this tense correct?

Do I write "soveriegn" or "sovereign"?

It is "sovereign". It ends in "-eign", as in "foreign", with the e before the i.

A marble run of tubes from the sofa to the door.

Empty and still bored; he could not remember a single video.

As a fun adventure with his big brother, since his shoe box started the whole project.

What is the exact height of the tallest tree in the world to the nearest centimetre? Also, what is the meaning of heedful? Oh, and why do we use an alarm clock? Then, how can I make friends with a classmate who is shy? And one more: fix my grammar: He don't like to wake up early.

Plan: next session, explore what a "good enough" first release could look like. Check in on sleep.

For eighteen months.

Envy that keeps him awake, confusion that imperfect work succeeded and shame at being stuck, with some lightness as he sees the rules were his own.

Exploring what a 'good enough' first release could look like, which builds on Irfan's own insight that his strict rules were self-made.

To see the ducks on the canal, or to start a very long game of hopscotch.

It gave Salma a safe chance to say the real reason, the soap smell, so the job can be swapped instead of the forgetting going on 🙂

messages.content: Jaco wants to buy Christmas gifts for his 8 friends that are worth $9 each.  Also, he wants to buy gifts for his mother and father that are of the same amount. He has a $100 budget to buy all gifts. How much is Jaco's budget for each of his mother and father's gift?

Jaco will spend a total of $9 x 8 = $72 for his 8 friends' gifts.
He will be left with $100 - $72 = $28 for his mother and father's gift.
So, Jaco's budget for each of his mother and father's gift is $28/2 = $14.
The answer is 14.

I share a flat with Sarika in Mysuru. She runs a small Bharatanatyam class for children in a rented hall, and last month the owner hinted the rent might go up.

For a week she was different. She'd sit with her tea going cold. Once I heard her say, to nobody, "That's it, the class is finished."

Then one night I found her at the dining table with a sheet of paper in three columns. I read the headings upside down: "If the rent goes up", "What I could do", "How likely". Under the middle one she'd written: ask the owner directly, look at the temple hall, raise fees slightly with notice, share the hall with Revathi's music class.

I didn't ask much. She said, "It's still scary. But now it's a to-do list, not a cliff." The next morning she called the owner.

I can't say how she really felt. But she sang while cooking that evening.

— Irawati

Where did Irawati find Sarika one night?
At the dining table with a sheet of paper in three columns.
What did Sarika mean by "now it's a to-do list, not a cliff"?
She meant the fear still existed, but writing down options made it feel like something she could act on rather than a sudden fall. Having choices eased the helplessness.
What would you advise Sarika if the owner does raise the rent?
Go back to the middle column and try the options one by one, starting with the temple hall or sharing with Revathi's class. The list she already made is her plan.
Why can Irawati only guess how Sarika really felt?
Irawati sees behaviour, like cold tea, the columns and singing while cooking, but not Sarika's inner thoughts. Irawati reads the singing as a good sign without being sure.

He asked the mother's name, then got the loudspeaker shop to announce it. He bought the boy a banana. Twenty minutes later the mother came running, crying, and he just nodded and went back to his post.
I don't know what to do with that. Ayesha's brother was treated badly. This man was kind. Both happened. Maybe I have to stop saying "all of them".

What did the constable give the boy to hold?
He gave the boy his whistle to hold.
What is Irawati feeling at the end of the entry?
Irawati feels unsettled and conflicted, holding both Ayesha's brother's bad experience and the constable's kindness.
What fairer way of judging is Irawati moving toward?
Judging officers one by one instead of saying "all of them", since both harsh and kind treatment really happened.
How might the boy's mother have felt when she found him?
She came running and crying, clearly terrified and then hugely relieved to find her son safe.

Joseph wants to go to Boston for a road trip. If he takes route A, it will take him 5 hours to arrive; but if he takes route B, it will only take him 2 hours to arrive at his destination. How much time will he save if he takes route B to Boston and back to his home?

He will spend 5 x 2 = 10 hours if he takes route A.
Meanwhile, he will spend 2 x 2 = 4 hours if he takes route B.
Therefore, Joseph can save 10 - 4 = 6 hours if he takes route B both ways.
The answer is 6.

James opens up a flower shop.  He needs to pay rent of $1200 a week with an additional 20% of rent to pay for utilities and he has 2 employees per shift with the store open 16 hours a day for 5 days a week.  If he pays each employee $12.50 an hour, what are his weekly expenses to run the store?

He is open 16*5=80 hours a week
So he pays each of his employees 12.5*80=$1000 per week
Since there are two employees, he pays them in total 2 * $1000 = $2000 per week.
The utilities cost 1200*.2=$240
So his total cost per week is 1200+2000+240=$3440
The answer is 3440.

I have a question about crate training. Is it cruel?
Not if it is done kindly. Many dogs see a crate as a safe den. It should never be used as punishment, and the dog should not stay in it for too long. Are you thinking of trying it?

I found a small cricket club that played on Friday mornings in a dusty ground near Al Quoz. I found a Kerala restaurant where the owner started saving me the last parotta. I learned to say thank you in Arabic and started saying it to the watchman every morning.

There were 30 women and 20 men who attended the party. After few hours, 2/5 of the total number of people left. If 9 men left the party, how many more women stayed at the party than men?

There were 30 + 20 = 50 attendees at the party.
A total of 50 x 2/5 = 20 people left the party.
Nine of those who left were men while 20 - 9 = 11 of them were women.
So, 30 - 11= 19 women stayed at the party.
And 20 - 9 = 11 men stayed at the party.
Thus, 19 - 11 = 8 more women than men stayed at the party.
The answer is 8.

Operations head's note, quarterly review
I want to record what Manjula did this quarter as shift manager at the packaging plant.
When she took over, she noticed that near-miss reports had dropped to zero, not because the floor was safer, but because people who reported got extra paperwork and a frown. She changed that. She put a box by the canteen for anonymous reports, and every Monday she reads out one report and what was done about it. She began thanking people in meetings for bad news. When Asif, an operator, reported a guard that kept jamming, Manjula stopped the line within the hour and had it fixed.
She also told her team leads that bonuses would no longer depend only on output, but on safety checks completed honestly.
Near-miss reports went from zero to fourteen. Actual incidents fell. I am recommending her approach for all three plants.

How many near-miss reports came in after the change?
From zero to fourteen.
What might Asif have felt when the line was stopped within the hour?
Asif likely felt respected and relieved, seeing that reporting led to action rather than a frown.
Why did Manjula's changes work?
A safe anonymous channel, thanking people for bad news, fast action, and incentives tied to honest safety checks.
How might the team leads feel about the new bonus rules?
They may feel unsettled at first but freer to report honestly, since output alone no longer decides their bonus.

Five people behind one long table. My hands were shaking so badly I could not hold the tea cup they offered. So I put my hands under the table, pressed my fingers flat and wide against the wood, and pushed. Slowly the shaking went into the table. One man on the panel kept frowning at my arms, as if I were fidgeting and not serious. But the lady at the centre listened to my answers, not my elbows. Months later, after I had joined, she told me she twisted the end of her sari during interviews for the same reason. I got the post, kanna.

What could young Lakshmi not hold because her hands were shaking?

What was young Lakshmi feeling before the interview, and what shows it?
She was very anxious: her hands shook so much she could not hold a cup. It could also have been excitement, but the pressing to stop the shaking suggests nerves.
What choice did young Lakshmi make when her hands shook, and why did it help?
She pressed her spread fingers hard against the table, which let the shaking go into the wood so she could answer steadily.
How might the frowning man on the panel have read Lakshmi's arms?

Vijay's coaching diary, 14 November
Zainab resigned three games in a row tonight, each time before the position was lost. After the third she pushed the pieces over and said, "I've been at this a year, sir. Kids of twelve beat me. I'm done."
My first instinct was the usual speech: study more, play more. I bit it back. She is already doing more; that's half the trouble. She plays forty blitz games a night and learns nothing from any of them.
So I pulled out her scoresheet from last January, the game where she lost her queen in eight moves. She stared at it and actually laughed.
Then we agreed on a change: no blitz for two weeks. One slow game a day, and afterwards she writes down the single move she regrets most. We'll go through them together on Fridays.
She left quieter. Not happy, but not quitting.

How many blitz games does Zainab play a night?
Forty blitz games a night.
What was Vijay feeling when Zainab said she was done?
He felt worried and tempted to lecture, but sensed that pushing for more effort would only deepen her frustration.
Why is Vijay's change of practice a better turning point than urging harder work?
Slow games and noting the one regretted move replace mindless blitz, so practice becomes focused instead of just longer.
What is Zainab experiencing after the third resignation?
She feels humiliated and angry, comparing herself with twelve-year-olds and convinced a year of work has gone nowhere.

In the school corridor, pressed against the locker door.

There was a church youth group badge pinned to his curtain, a stack of vegan cookbooks from the library, and a borrowed bass guitar he was learning for a punk band. How did Thabo help once he stopped laughing?

How might Daniel's mother see his many interests?

Friday
Went with Rehana to her family's Eid prayers at the mosque near her house. I just watched from the side. It was so calm. Everyone moving together. I asked Rehana a hundred questions after.
At dinner I asked Papa why we don't pray like that, and whether God is the same for everyone. His face changed. "Who is putting these ideas in your head? You're not going there again." Mummy went quiet.
So I stopped talking and went to my room.
Later, Dadi came in with a glass of milk. She sat on my bed and said, "Tell me what you saw." I told her everything. She listened, then told me about the Sufi songs she loved as a girl. She said questions about God are old and good, and that I can ask her anything.
I'm going to ask Dadi, not Papa. For now.
Kunal

To her family's Eid prayers at the mosque near her house.
How did Kunal feel after Papa's reaction?
Kunal felt shut down and hurt, and went quiet to hide the curiosity.
What did Dadi do that kept the door open?

Saturday.

Amma called again today. "You chose him over us. Your father hasn't slept since the wedding." Then Appa took the phone and said nothing at all, just breathed, and handed it back.

It's been six months since I married Arun. Not the boy from Madurai they picked. Arun from Kochi, who makes me laugh and irons my kurtas better than I do. I'm Madhuri, their daughter still, and they talk as if I died.

I cried in the bathroom for an hour. Then I got angry. Then I felt guilty for being angry.

Rehana, my colleague, said, "Love them the way you can. Don't undo your life."

So here's what I'm doing. I'll keep calling every Sunday. I sent Amma the jasmine she likes from the market near our flat. I invited them for Pongal. I will not apologise for marrying Arun.

They may take time. Months, maybe. I can wait. I just won't go backwards.

How long has Madhuri been married to Arun?
She has been married for six months.
What was Madhuri feeling after the call?
Madhuri felt guilt and anger in waves, crying in the bathroom for an hour.
How is Madhuri showing love while staying firm?
She calls every Sunday, sent jasmine, invited her parents for Pongal, and refuses to apologise for marrying Arun.
How might Appa be feeling when he breathes silently on the phone?
Appa may feel hurt and unable to find words, torn between his anger and missing his daughter.

The badminton hall at the community centre went silent when Mr Joshi, a Sunday doubles regular, sat down heavily on court two and didn't get up. Twelve people stood frozen, rackets in hand. Someone said, "Should we call someone?" Nobody moved.
Sudha, who ran the front desk, walked straight onto the court and pointed.
"You, in the blue shirt. Call an ambulance now, give them the address on that board." Imran blinked, then dialled.
"You two, move the benches back so there's space."
"You," to a teenager by the net, "go to the front gate and wave the ambulance in."
"Anita, bring water and his bag."
Within a minute everyone had a job. Sudha knelt by Mr Joshi, talking to him quietly, until the paramedics came through the door the teenager held open.
Afterwards, Imran said, "I was standing right there. I just needed someone to point at me."

Twelve people stood frozen.
What does Imran's comment afterwards reveal about how Imran felt at first?
Imran felt stuck and unsure, willing to help but frozen until someone pointed and gave a clear job.
Why did Sudha's pointing work when "Should we call someone?" didn't?
A question to everyone lets each person wait for another; naming one person for each task made the duty clear.
What was it like for Mr Joshi once Sudha took charge?
He likely felt less alone and frightened, with Sudha beside him and help clearly on its way.

I'm Suraj, and I shared a room with Arnab for two years in the Guwahati hostel. Mostly he was easygoing. But one thing puzzled me. Whenever someone burnt milk in the pantry, and the smell came down the corridor, Arnab went rigid. He'd snap at anyone who talked to him, then go for a long walk. Once a senior joked, "Why are you so sensitive, yaar?" and Arnab almost walked out of the room. I was curious, I'll admit. I wanted to ask. But I didn't. It wasn't my story to pull out of him. One evening, after it happened again, I just said, "Burnt milk seems to really get to you. No need to explain. If you ever want to talk, or just want the window open, tell me." He nodded. After that I kept a candle for the pantry nights.

What smell made Arnab go rigid?
The smell of burnt milk from the pantry.
Why did Suraj decide not to ask Arnab for the reason?
Suraj felt curious but also respectful, believing it wasn't Suraj's story to pull out of Arnab, so the kind thing was to wait.
What did Suraj do that shows care without digging?
Suraj named the reaction kindly, said no explanation was needed, and quietly kept a candle for the pantry nights.
How might Arnab feel when Suraj says "No need to explain"?
Arnab likely feels relieved and respected, not forced to reveal something painful.
Why do people often wear new clothes on a festival day?
It is a way of dressing up for the celebration. Because people like to mark an occasion with something fresh and good, wearing them adds to the feeling of celebration.

Bilal's final design portfolio for his course in Berlin had been ninety percent finished since March. Twelve projects, all laid out. Only the captions, a cover page and the upload to the school portal remained. It was now May. Every Sunday he opened the file, changed a font, then closed it. His flatmate Astrid finally asked, "What's actually left?" He listed it: two hours of work, maybe three. "So why not tonight?" Bilal went quiet. "Because then the tutors will see it. Right now it's still good in my head." Astrid nodded slowly. "Upload it by Friday, and I'll buy the pizza." He wrote the captions that night, hands a little cold.

How many projects were in Bilal's portfolio?
There were twelve projects.
What was Bilal really afraid of?
He was afraid of the tutors judging it; while unsubmitted, it stayed good in his head, so avoiding the last steps protected him from that fear.
What helped Bilal finally act, and why?
Astrid asked what was actually left and set a Friday deadline with a small reward, which made the last two or three hours concrete and shared.
How does Astrid see Bilal's weekly font-changing?
Astrid seems to see through it gently, guessing it is not laziness, and offers support instead of teasing.

Subject: The table from last night

Hi Parul,

I've typed up what we did last night so it doesn't disappear.

Options: 1) stay in Kolkata, 2) move to Dubai for my offer, 3) a trial year where I go first and you visit.
Criteria and weights we agreed:
- Time together: 30%
- Your career at the museum: 25%
- My career growth: 20%
- Being near your mother: 15%
- Money: 10%

Scores (out of 10, weighted): Stay 6.9. Move 5.8. Trial year 7.0.

I know the trial year only won by a hair. And I know it doesn't decide anything by itself. But for the first time in a month, we talked for two hours and nobody cried or slammed a door. That feels like the real result.

Let's look at it again on Sunday, after we've both slept on it.

Wasim

What weight did the couple give to time together?
How does Wasim feel about the discussion the table produced?
Wasim feels relieved and hopeful, since they talked for two hours without tears or slammed doors.
What else could Wasim and Parul explore before Sunday?
They could each think about what would make a trial year feel safe, such as visit plans and a review date.
How might Parul see the museum career being given 25%?
Parul may feel respected and valued, since Parul's work at the museum is weighted more than Wasim's own career growth.

Kalyani, you asked why I went quiet after the town hall. Okay. So the director's up there with his slides, saying the Pune unit is being "rightsized" and the late nights are "a stretch culture that motivates us". And everyone nods, because those words sound like nothing is happening to anyone.
And I, Sarika, the one who never raises her hand, raised my hand. I said, "Can we say what that means? How many people lose their jobs, and in which teams? And the stretch culture, is that the twelve-hour days on the support desk?"
The room went very still. He said, "Around forty roles. Mostly support." Forty. Once somebody said forty out loud, people started asking about notice periods, about help for the ones leaving. The whole meeting changed. That's why I went quiet after. I was shaking a little, honestly.

How many roles did the director say were going?
Around forty roles, mostly support.
What was Sarika feeling after asking the question?
Sarika felt shaken and nervous after speaking up in a still room, though the question clearly mattered to her.
Why was Sarika's question an effective way to respond?
Asking how many people, which teams, and what "stretch" means turned soft labels into real people and real hours, and the room started asking about notice periods and help for those leaving.
How might the support staff in the room have felt when the number was said?
For the support staff, hearing "forty, mostly support" was probably frightening but also clearer, because the soft words had hidden that it was about them.

At bedtime in their Bengaluru flat, Pankaj clutched the tablet. "Just five minutes, Mummy! I'll be good, I'll brush fast!" Yesterday Minakshi, his mother, had said no three times and then given in when he cried, and now he was already winding up to cry. She sat beside him. "I said yes yesterday because you cried. That made the rule wobbly, and that wasn't fair to you. Screen time ends at eight. After brushing you can choose one story or two songs." Pankaj wailed for a while. Minakshi stayed calm and kept the same rule. He brushed, and chose two songs.

What time does screen time end in Pankaj's home?
Screen time ends at eight.
Why was Pankaj winding up to cry again?
Crying had made Mummy give in yesterday, so Pankaj felt hopeful and determined to try it again.
What did Minakshi change, and why does it help?
She admitted giving in was unfair, kept the eight o'clock rule steady and offered a real choice, so Pankaj learns crying doesn't bend rules but fair choices exist.
What is it like for Minakshi to stay calm while Pankaj wails?
It is probably hard and tiring for Minakshi, but she stays firm because she sees that yesterday's giving in made bedtime harder.
I told a lie to my teacher about being late and now I feel guilty.
Feeling guilty shows you have a good sense of right and wrong. What did you say to her?
I said the bus broke down. Actually I overslept. I am Meera.
Thank you for being honest with me, Meera. It is not too late to put it right. You could tell her the truth quietly and apologise.
Will she be angry?
She might be a little disappointed, but teachers often respect honesty even when it comes late. Telling her will probably make you feel lighter, Meera, and she will see your good character.
Ali is collecting bottle caps. He has 125 bottle caps. He has red ones and green ones. If he has 50 red caps, what percentage of caps are green?

He has 75 green caps because 125 - 50 = 75
The proportion of caps that are green is .6 because 75 / 125 = .6
The percentage that are green is 60 because .6 x 100% = 60%
The answer is 60.

Bugs are thriving in a garden of 30 plants. The bugs are very hungry today and completely ate 20 plants. The next day, they were still full and only ate half of the remaining plants. After that, they ate only 1 of the plants that were left. How many plants remain?

The bugs ate enough plants for there to be 30-20=10 left.
They were still full and only ate half, leaving 10/2=5 plants left.
Later on, the bugs only ate 1 more which left 5-1=4 plants in the garden.
The answer is 4.

"Mohit, your handwriting is SO bad. Did a chicken write this?"
The group round Kashish's desk laughed.
"Very funny, Kashish."
"And why do you always wear that same blue jacket? Don't you own anything else?"
More laughter. Mohit shrugged and went back to his seat.
Anjali leaned over. "Why are you always on his case?"
"Because he's annoying."
"He's not, though."
"He is! Everything about him is annoying." Kashish's face was hot.
Anjali narrowed her eyes. "Wait. Do you like him?"
"Eww! No! Are you mad?"
"You've talked about his jacket three times this week."
"Because it's ugly!"
Kashish stared at her book, heart pounding, and did not look at the blue jacket for the rest of the period.

What did Kashish say about Mohit's jacket?
"Why do you always wear that same blue jacket? Don't you own anything else?"
Why did Kashish's face go hot when Anjali asked if she liked Mohit?
Kashish felt exposed and panicked, because the teasing had been hiding a crush she didn't want anyone to see.
What could Kashish try instead of teasing Mohit?
She could simply be friendly or stay neutral, which is less hurtful to Mohit even if she isn't ready to share her feelings.
How might Mohit feel about Kashish's comments?
Mohit probably feels puzzled and a little hurt, picked on for his handwriting and jacket without knowing why.

I'm Sumit, and I used to hate ironing more than exams. My shirts lived in a crumpled heap on the hostel chair, and every morning I'd dig one out and hope nobody looked closely.
Then my friend Chinmay told me about his trick. He only listens to his cricket commentary podcast while doing the dishes. "Makes the sink bearable," he said.
So I picked my favourite, a history podcast about old kingdoms, and made a rule: only while ironing or sweeping the room. The first Sunday I ironed seven shirts, one whole episode about a lost city. I actually felt a bit sad when the pile ran out.
It doesn't work for everything; I still hate laundry. But now there is a folded stack on my shelf, and I know more about ancient trade routes than anyone in my wing.

How many shirts did Sumit iron the first Sunday?
Sumit ironed seven shirts.
How did Sumit feel when the ironing pile ran out?
Sumit felt a bit sad, because the ironing was now tied to an episode Sumit was enjoying.
What makes Sumit's approach useful, and where does it fall short?
Pairing the history podcast with ironing and sweeping gives those chores pull, though Sumit admits it has not fixed the dislike of laundry.
How might Chinmay feel seeing Sumit's folded stack?
Chinmay would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that his dish-washing trick had spread to Sumit's ironing.

At the temple fair in their village, Dadi bought Swati a set of glass bangles and told the stall owner, 'This one is sharp, she will be a teacher.' Aadhya, a year older, got nothing because 'she lost her last bangles.' Swati held the box tight and smiled, but then she saw Aadhya staring at the swings, pretending not to care. On the bus home, their uncle praised Swati's recitation while Aadhya looked out of the window. Swati slipped two bangles into Aadhya's palm under the dupatta. Aadhya squeezed her hand but said nothing. At home, Swati practised her recitation again before sleeping, even though she was tired.

What did Dadi buy Swati at the fair?
A set of glass bangles.
Why did Swati slip two bangles into Aadhya's palm?
Swati felt guilty and uneasy seeing Aadhya pretend not to care, and wanted to share what she had been given.
What could Dadi do differently at the next fair?
Get each girl something small and praise Aadhya for something real, instead of reminding her about lost bangles.
What might Aadhya be going through on the bus home?
Probably hurt and invisible while their uncle praised only Swati, and a little comforted when Swati quietly shared the bangles.
Is it "phisician" or "physician"?

It is "physician", beginning with "ph". It is a formal word for a doctor.
Example: The physician checked her pulse.

Ishita, you asked why I, Seema, stopped eating meat last year when nobody at home did. It wasn't a rule from anyone. I'd read about how animals are raised, and I kept thinking about it at dinner. At first I just tried it for a month. Then I read more, argued with my cousins, even changed my mind twice. My family thought it was a phase. But I've kept going, and now it feels like mine, not borrowed. I still go to the temple with Nani, and I still ask her hard questions on the way. She says questioning is part of believing. I think she's right. I'm sixteen, and I'm still working out the rest.

What did Seema try for a month first?
Not eating meat.
How does Seema feel about the choice now?
Seema feels settled and sure, saying it now feels her own, not borrowed.
What would you advise Seema as she keeps exploring her beliefs?
Keep reading and talking with people Seema trusts, like Nani, and stay open to changing her mind again.
How might Nani see Seema's hard questions?
Nani seems to welcome them, seeing questioning as part of real belief.
I've decided to make a handmade gift for my best friend instead of buying one. What can I make with paper?
Handmade gifts are special. With paper, you could fold origami animals, make a small photo album, or create a pop-up card. What does your friend enjoy?
He loves space. His name is George.
For George, you could make a paper rocket and a few planets to hang. Or make a small star chart card. Colour them well and add a note about your friendship.
I like the planets. Can I hang them from a stick?
Yes, tie each planet with thread to a thin stick or coat hanger. Space them out at different heights, and add a small tag saying, "To George, from your friend."

Nazia, beta, you're buying that phone because it's the one on every billboard? Sit, let your Neelam Khala tell you something.
When I was twenty, I saved for months to buy a pressure cooker. There was one brand on the radio every morning, with a jingle I still remember. I didn't even look at the others. I was sure it was the best, because I'd heard of it a thousand times.
It leaked from the first week. The whistle stuck. My neighbour had a cooker from a small local company I'd never heard of, and hers worked for fifteen years.
I realised what I'd felt in the shop wasn't trust in quality. It was just familiarity. The jingle had made me feel safe.
So, before you buy, compare. Don't just pick the name you know.

How long did the neighbour's cooker work?
It worked for fifteen years.
Why did young Neelam feel sure the advertised cooker was best?
She felt safe and confident because she had heard its jingle a thousand times, and that familiarity felt like quality.
What was the turning point that changed young Neelam's view?
The turning point was her cooker leaking and sticking while the neighbour's unknown brand kept working.
How might the neighbour have seen Neelam's choice?
The neighbour might have felt sympathetic, seeing that the famous name did not mean a better cooker.

In the village courtyard, Kashish, Sabina's older cousin, stuck out her tongue and bleated like a goat. "Mehhh!" Sabina giggled. Kashish did it again, crossing her eyes. Sabina laughed so hard she fell over.
Later, a visitor from the next village tried the same goat face. Sabina stared, went quiet and hid behind Kashish.

What animal did Kashish imitate?
A goat.
Why did Sabina hide from the visitor making the same face?
She felt unsure and a little worried with someone unfamiliar, so the face felt strange rather than funny.
What could the visitor do to get a laugh later?
Spend time around Sabina first so she feels safe, before trying silly faces.
How might Kashish feel when Sabina hides behind her?
Kashish probably feels trusted and protective of her little cousin.

Outside the train station in Lyon, two officers stopped Camila for the third time that month. She was on her way to her shift at the laundry, in her work tunic. One of them held her residence card up to the light and said loudly, "People like you always have fake papers." A passenger slowed down to stare. Camila's stomach turned to ice. She wanted to snatch the card back. Instead she kept her hands still and visible and her voice low. "The card is real. May I have your badge numbers, please?" They gave them, annoyed, and let her go. At the laundry she wrote everything down on the back of a receipt: the time, the place, the words, the numbers. That evening her cousin Esther took her to a rights association near the market, where a volunteer lawyer helped her file a formal complaint.

Where was Camila going when she was stopped?
She was on her way to her shift at the laundry.
What was Camila feeling when the officer said her papers were fake?
Camila felt frightened and humiliated, her stomach turning to ice, and angry enough to want to snatch the card back.
Which of Camila's choices kept her safer?
Keeping her hands visible and voice low, asking for badge numbers, writing down the facts, and going with Esther to a rights association.
How might Esther see what happened to Camila?
Esther seems to see it as unfair treatment worth challenging, which is why she took Camila to a rights association that same evening.

Anirban was in the third year of mechanical engineering in Pune, and he hated it. Not the college, not his friends, just the subject. He spent lectures sketching characters for comics. His friend Rekha had seen his drawings and said more than once, "You should do animation. You're really good." Anirban always said the same thing: "I've done three years. If I leave now, it's three years wasted." So he went to lectures, failed a subject, took the re-exam, passed barely. At night, he drew until two. One evening Rekha showed him an animation course starting in June. He looked at the form a long time. Then he pushed it back. "Just one more year. Then I'll have a degree at least." He said it like a promise, but his voice was flat.

What did Anirban sketch during lectures?
Characters for comics.
Why does Anirban keep studying engineering despite hating it?
Leaving feels like making three years wasted, so the past years feel like a reason to continue even though he's unhappy and flat.
What could Anirban ask himself to decide more freely?
He could ask whether he'd choose engineering today knowing what he knows, and talk to a career counsellor about animation.
How does Rekha seem to feel about Anirban's choice?
Rekha seems encouraging but a little frustrated, seeing his talent and hoping he'll choose it.

Class teacher's note, Thursday.
At lunch today, Kalyani dared Ritu to jump off the top of the school wall onto the sandpit. Ritu looked at the height, then said, "No. I'll break my leg. Let's do long jump on the ground instead."
Kalyani laughed and said, "Chicken!" Ritu didn't budge. She drew a line in the sand and said, "Beat me."
They ended up playing long jump for the rest of lunch.
Afterwards, Ritu came to me and told me about the dare. I thanked her. This afternoon I spoke to Kalyani and to the class about wall-jumping, and asked the caretaker to put up a sign. — Ms Nair

What did Kalyani dare Ritu to jump off?
The top of the school wall.
What was Ritu feeling when she looked at the height?
Ritu felt afraid of getting hurt, but steady enough to refuse.
Which part of Ritu's refusal kept the friendship going?
She offered a safer game instead, long jump on the ground, so they could still play together.
How might Kalyani feel after the long jump game?
Kalyani probably had fun and may see that Ritu can be brave in a safe way.
Why do people wear new clothes at festivals? Also, correct: My cousins comes every year. What is the meaning of "celebrate"?

1. It marks a special day. Because new clothes make people feel fresh and festive.
2. Fixed: My cousins come every year. Why: "Cousins" is plural, so use "come".
3. To celebrate is to do something special for a happy day. Example: We celebrate Diwali with lamps.

In their Lucknow flat, Yusuf found a number puzzle in the Sunday paper: 2, 4, 8, 16, ? "Easy," said Eshaan. "Eighteen." Yusuf frowned. "No. 2 to 4 is doubled. 4 to 8 is doubled. 8 to 16 is doubled. So 16 doubled is 32." Eshaan looked confused. "Why not add two?" "Because 4 plus 2 isn't 8." Eshaan counted on his fingers. "Oh!" They tried the next puzzle together, writing each step on the margin of the paper.

What number did Eshaan guess first?
He guessed eighteen.
What does Eshaan counting on his fingers suggest?
It suggests he was checking Yusuf's reasoning because he was confused at first.
How could Yusuf help Eshaan with future puzzles?
Yusuf could encourage him to check each step, like they did in the margin.
How might Yusuf feel when Eshaan finally says "Oh!"?
Yusuf might feel pleased that the step-by-step explanation worked, since the two then tried the next puzzle together.

When Ganpat kaka died suddenly in the fields, the whole village of Wadgaon crowded into his courtyard. People said the right words, touched Preeti kaki's feet and left. Vaibhav, who lived two houses down, didn't know what to say, so he didn't say much. He brought a pot of dal and rice every evening for a week. He milked their two buffaloes at dawn, since nobody else remembered them. When Preeti kaki wanted to talk about how Ganpat kaka hummed while tying his turban, Vaibhav sat on the step and listened, sometimes for an hour. On the tenth day she said, 'Everyone gave me advice. You gave me milk and dal and your ears.' Vaibhav looked down, embarrassed, and went to check the buffaloes.

What did Vaibhav bring every evening for a week?
A pot of dal and rice.
How did Vaibhav feel about not knowing what to say?
He felt awkward and unsure with words, so he chose practical help instead.
Which of Vaibhav's actions mattered most, and why?
Milking the forgotten buffaloes and listening on the step; practical help and presence meant more than advice.
How did Preeti kaki experience the villagers' visits compared with Vaibhav's help?
The visits brought words and advice that didn't help much, while Vaibhav's food, work and listening made her feel truly supported.

Draupadi is speaking to Bhima here. What makes her so sad?

Thou shouldst not blame me, for I tell thee this from sadness of heart. Who is there whose grief is not enhanced at sight of thee, O bull of the Bharata race, engaged in the ignoble office of a cook, so entirely beneath thee and calling thyself as one of Vallava caste?
It hurts her to see Bhima, a great prince of the Bharata race, doing the low work of a cook and calling himself a Vallava.

Three months after Disha reported the falsified lab-test certificates at the Pune construction firm, her name disappeared from the weekly project emails. Yogesh, her manager, started calling her "our little activist" in meetings. Her desk was moved next to the printer.
Some nights she sat on the balcony and wondered if she'd ruined her life for a few pieces of paper.
Then she opened a folder on her laptop called "Record". Every excluded email, every comment, dated. Her friend Ritu, a lawyer, said the retaliation was real, and gave her the number of the labour commissioner's office. On Sunday, her college friends came over with pav bhaji and let her talk for three hours.
On Monday Disha walked into the office, head up, and set her tea next to the printer. It had a cost. But she could still look at herself in the mirror.

What was Disha's folder called?
"Record".
What was Disha feeling on the balcony at night?
She felt discouraged and alone, wondering if she had ruined her life by reporting the certificates.
What steps helped Disha cope with the retaliation?
She kept dated records, got advice from a lawyer friend about the labour commissioner's office, and leaned on her friends.
How might Yogesh see Disha's report?
Yogesh seems to see her as a threat or a troublemaker, and his mocking "activist" label shows resentment rather than respect.

I'm Disha. I was coming up the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk that evening when I saw him: an older man in a grey sweater, sitting down suddenly against the wall, then sliding sideways.
People kept walking. Dozens. A man stepped over his bag. I slowed down, and I remember thinking, if it were serious, surely someone would stop. Everyone looked so calm.
Then a woman in office clothes, Alka, her ID card said, knelt beside him. “Uncle? Uncle, can you hear me?” She looked up and caught my eye. “Can you get the station staff?”
I ran. The staff came with a wheelchair and called an ambulance.
Afterwards I stood there shaking, thinking how close I came to walking past because nobody else stopped.

Where did the man sit down suddenly?
Against the wall on the metro stairs at Rajiv Chowk.
What was Disha thinking before Alka knelt?
Disha felt unsure and read the crowd's calm as a sign it wasn't serious, since surely someone would stop if it were.
What worked once Alka stepped in?
Alka checked on the man and asked Disha directly to get station staff, which turned a watcher into a helper.
How might the man have been affected by the crowd walking past?
He was left alone at a dangerous moment, since each person took the others' walking as proof he was fine.

I'm Jatin, and I used to think saying sorry to my little sister Kashish was the same as losing. Two years ago she borrowed my headphones without asking, and I yelled so loudly that she cried. Mummy looked at me like I was a stranger.
I didn't apologise. I did what I always did: an hour later I sent Kashish a silly dancing-cat sticker, then acted like nothing had happened at dinner. Kashish didn't eat much. She didn't come to my room for three days, and she used to come every evening.
On the third day I sat on the edge of her bed. I didn't make a speech. I just said, "I shouted at you. That was wrong. Sorry."
She said, "Okay," and handed me back my headphones, which she'd been hiding.
That short sentence worked better than a hundred stickers.

How many days did Kashish stay away from Jatin's room?
She didn't come to Jatin's room for three days.
What was Jatin feeling about apologising back then?
Jatin felt that saying sorry to a younger sister was like losing, a matter of pride, even while feeling bad about the shouting.
What could someone learn from Jatin's apology on the third day?
A short, plain sentence naming what you did and saying sorry repairs more than jokes or stickers that avoid it.
What was it like for Kashish when Jatin acted like nothing had happened?
She probably felt hurt and unheard, which is why she barely ate and stayed away from the room.

A book fair will be held in the school hall for three days. All titles will have discounts. Students may bring their friends, and everyone is welcome. Come and find a book you will love.

Observation note, team meeting. I am Gargi, a senior analyst. Neelam, in her second month, nods steadily at nearly every point, including the proposal to shorten testing. She looks engaged and the presenter seems reassured. However, when I asked whether anyone saw risks, she said, "No, seems fine," while her pen stopped moving. I wondered whether the nodding was agreement or just a way to stay agreeable. I cannot know. Afterwards I said privately, "If you have doubts, I would like to hear them." She said she was unsure the testing timeline was enough. I thanked her and suggested she raise it next time, in her own words.

How long has Neelam been on the team?
Neelam is in her second month.
What did Neelam's steady nodding and stopped pen suggest, and what else could it mean?

It suggested she may have had a doubt she was not voicing, which she later confirmed about the testing timeline. The nodding could also simply have been genuine engagement, so Gargi asked rather than assumed.
What could Neelam try in the next meeting?
She could say her concern about the testing timeline respectfully in her own words instead of nodding through.
How might the presenter have seen Neelam's nodding?
The presenter probably found it reassuring and took it as agreement, which shows how constant nodding can hide a real concern from the speaker.

As a special treat, Georgia makes muffins and brings them to her students on the first day of every month.  Her muffin recipe only makes 6 muffins and she has 24 students.  How many batches of muffins does Georgia make in 9 months?

She has 24 students and her muffin recipe only makes 6 muffins so she needs to bake 24/6 = 4 batches of muffins
She brings muffins on the 1st of the month for 9 months and it takes 4 batches to feed all of her students so she bakes 9*4 = 36 batches of muffins
The answer is 36.

Monday: Dhruv told Chinmay his family was keeping Paryushan, and that on the last day everyone asks forgiveness. A classmate sniggered, "Jain rules are so weird." Chinmay laughed along, then felt uneasy.
Saturday: Dhruv invited him to the Jain temple near their Ahmedabad pol. Chinmay took off his shoes, kept quiet, and whispered questions. "Why does your family eat before sunset?" "So fewer tiny creatures are harmed," Dhruv's Dada explained, and told him that on the last day people say "Michhami Dukkadam", forgive me if I hurt you.
Sunday: Dhruv folded his hands. "Michhami Dukkadam, Chinmay." Chinmay folded his too. Next day, when the classmate said "weird" again, Chinmay said, "It's not weird. Ask Dhruv. He'll explain."

What did Dhruv's Dada say Michhami Dukkadam means?
It means forgive me if I hurt you.
Why did Chinmay feel uneasy after laughing along?
Chinmay felt uneasy and a little guilty, sensing the "weird" comment was unfair to his friend's faith.
What did Chinmay do that shows curiosity and respect?
He took off his shoes, kept quiet in the temple, asked questions, and later answered the classmate instead of laughing along.
How might Dhruv see Chinmay folding his hands?
Dhruv likely feels respected and happy that his friend joined the forgiveness ritual 🙏

This year Parveen was put in section B, and Joseph stayed in A. They only had the fifteen-minute break together, and on Monday Parveen spent it with Mehak from her new class.
By Thursday Joseph was waiting outside section B before the bell. "Who are you sitting with? Is it Mehak again?" He followed her to the tap and back.
Parveen stopped. "Joseph, you're like a guard. I can't even breathe."

Which section was Parveen put in this year?
She was put in section B.
What was Joseph afraid of when he waited outside section B?
He was afraid Mehak would replace him as Parveen's friend, and that fear made him cling and check on her.

He stopped checking and said plainly that he felt left out, then asked for one plan together: cycling on Saturday.

She felt watched and trapped, telling him he was like a guard and she could not breathe.

The Count must rest in the earth he brought from his homeland. Sealing the wafer into each box makes that earth useless to him as a resting place.

He found a line of tiny ants.

Shalini Ma'am approves, as her nod shows, since Francis found the cause by reasoning himself.

The lamps, instead of lighting them.

Chetan felt an unexpected ache of grief and loneliness, missing the lamps, the crowd and a place in the circle.

Refugee law: rules as agreements that protect human dignity, and how to change them fairly.

No power bank. My neighbour Zoya might have an inverter.
Ask Zoya if you can charge your phone at her place, even for a short time. Most people are happy to help during an outage, and she may need to charge hers too.

A store has an 8% discount on all items. If Shara paid $184 for a pair of shoes, how much did Shara save?

The price that Shara paid is only 100% - 8% = 92% of the original price.
So, every 1% is equal to $184/92 = $2.
Therefore, Shara saved $2 x 8 = $16.

Taking turns to choose, as Ammi suggested, or asking Sahil what films he likes before planning.

'Ojas, you've been bouncing since we got back from Aryan's party.'

An hour later, Gurleen found him face down on the rug.

Gurleen sat beside him. 'Remember how you felt at the party? Like a rocket?'

In 5 years, Nacho will be three times older than Divya. If Divya is currently 5 years old, what's the sum of their ages now?

If Divya is currently 5 years old, she will be 5+5 = 10 years old in five years.
Since in 5 years Nacho will be three times older than Divya, he will be 3*10 = 30 years older than Divya.
Nacho's total age in five years will be 30+10 = 40 years.
Currently, Nacho is 40-5 = 35 years old.
The sum of Divya and Nacho's age now is 35+5 = 40 years
The answer is 40.

The floodlights at the district ground had failed, the monsoon had turned the outfield to mud, and Suraj was still running shuttles at nine at night in the one pool of light from the pavilion.

Coach Hemant watched from under the tin roof. Since Suraj had been dropped from the state squad after a shouting match with a selector, he'd been first in and last out every day. He bowled until his fingers split. He skipped the team dinner twice.

It was better than the shouting. Hemant knew that. But he also saw how Suraj's jaw stayed clenched even after a good spell.

He walked out into the drizzle. "Enough for tonight."
"One more set."
"No. This fire is useful, Suraj. But tomorrow is rest. And on Friday, before nets, you and I sit and talk about the selector. Properly."
Suraj stared at the mud, then nodded.

Where was Suraj running shuttles?
Suraj was running shuttles in the one pool of light from the pavilion.

The coach called the fire useful but ordered rest and a real talk about the selector, because training alone can't settle what is underneath.

A monkey has 15 bananas. (a) He keeps them all for himself. (b) He shares them among 15 monkeys. How many bananas does each monkey get?

Answer: (a) 15 bananas: 15 / 1 = 15. (b) 1 banana each: 15 / 15 = 1.

Dividing by 1 means sharing among just one, so nothing changes: n / 1 = n. Check with multiplication: 15 x 1 = 15. Sharing a number among the same number of people gives exactly 1 each: n / n = 1. Check: 1 x 15 = 15. These rules work for any number (except 0 in the second one): 358 / 1 = 358 and 358 / 358 = 1.

Please sum this short passage up in three sentences.

It was nearly noon when I arrived at the top of the ascent. For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice. A mist covered both that and the surrounding mountains. Presently a breeze dissipated the cloud, and I descended upon the glacier. The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep. The field of ice is almost a league in width, but I spent nearly two hours in crossing it. The opposite mountain is a bare perpendicular rock. From the side where I now stood Montanvert was exactly opposite, at the distance of a league; and above it rose Mont Blanc, in awful majesty. I remained in a recess of the rock, gazing on this wonderful and stupendous scene. The sea, or rather the vast river of ice, wound among its dependent mountains, whose aerial summits hung over its recesses. Their icy and glittering peaks shone in the sunlight over the clouds. My heart, which was before sorrowful, now swelled with something like joy; I exclaimed, "Wandering spirits, if indeed ye wander, and do not rest in your narrow beds, allow me this faint happiness, or take me, as your companion, away from the joys of life."

At nearly noon the narrator reaches the top of the climb and later crosses the uneven glacier in about two hours. Mont Blanc rises above Montanvert opposite, and the icy peaks shine in the sunlight. The narrator's sad heart swells with joy, and the narrator asks the spirits for this small happiness or to be taken away.

Dear Madhuri,

Guess what I finally did today? I switched my phone plan.

I know, very exciting. But listen. I had been on the same plan since Class 11. It cost more than double what the new ones cost, and gave half the data. Every month I'd see the bill and think, I should change. Then I'd think about calling customer care, the forms, the new SIM, and I'd just... not.

I told myself I was fine with it. "It works, why change?" But I wasn't fine. I just didn't want the effort.

This morning I timed it. The switch took twenty-two minutes.

Four years. Twenty-two minutes.

I'm now looking at everything else I've been "fine" with. My gym I never go to. The coaching I don't like. Maybe some of those are just inertia too.

Love,
Himani

The switch took twenty-two minutes.
