Every evening, the children of Bhadrajun sat on the temple steps to read their Hindi lessons aloud while the goats were brought home. Hansa always finished last. Her finger moved slowly under each word, and when her younger cousin Darshan read the same page in half the time, she shut her book with a slap. 'I'm a buddhu. Buddhus shouldn't read,' she said, and went to help with the goats instead. The next evening she didn't bring her book at all. Darshan came and sat by her anyway. 'You read the long word yesterday. Pradhanmantri. I can't even say it,' he said. Hansa shrugged. 'That was luck.' But she watched his finger on the page for a long time, her lips moving.

Where did the children of Bhadrajun read their lessons?
They read their Hindi lessons aloud on the temple steps.
Why did Hansa call herself a buddhu and go to the goats?
She felt ashamed and frustrated at always finishing last, and the label made stopping feel easier than facing slow reading again.
What could an adult do to help Hansa see reading as a skill?
They could have her practise a few words each day and point out progress, like reading 'Pradhanmantri', so the label gives way to a skill that grows.
How does Darshan see Hansa's reading?
Darshan admires that she read a long word he couldn't say, and sits with her to show she isn't a buddhu.

Please define "unwritten".
Then, how can I be braver about speaking up in a group?
Oh, and how do I thank someone who helped me?
And how should I greet my friend's parents?

1. As an adjective, "unwritten" means understood but not put on paper.
2. Prepare one sentence before the meeting and say it early. The first words are the hardest, and then it becomes easier.
3. Say thank you clearly and tell them what the help meant to you. A short note makes it even warmer.
4. Smile and say "hello" or "namaste", and use their title and family name. Say thank you if they offer food or water.

In their small house in Malerkotla, Yusuf, nineteen, was studying for an exam when Noor, fifteen, came home and hurled her school bag across the room. "I hate that school! I hate everyone!" The bag knocked his books to the floor. Yusuf felt the old heat: she always did this, walked all over everyone. He wanted to shout back. Instead he picked up his books slowly. "You're angry, I get it. But you don't throw things at me." She stormed up to the roof. He let her be. Half an hour later he carried two glasses of lassi up the stairs. She was crying. "Want to tell me?" he asked. She did.

What did Yusuf carry up to the roof?
Two glasses of lassi.
What did Yusuf feel when the bag hit his books?
He felt angry and walked over, wanting to shout back.
What did Yusuf do that kept the connection with Noor?
He set a calm limit on throwing things, gave her space and then offered lassi and a chance to talk.
How was Noor feeling by the time Yusuf reached the roof?
Noor was sad and crying under the anger, ready to talk.

The voice on the phone was calm and official. "Ma'am, your identity is linked to a serious case. A warrant is being prepared. Stay on this line and do not speak to anyone, not family, not friends, or it will be treated as obstruction." Afreen's hands shook and her ears rang. The voice said it had to be settled within the hour or it would be too late. She could not think; every question in her head was pushed out by the clock.

To prove her innocence, she made a small transfer. The voice thanked her. Then there was a "processing problem," and a larger amount was needed to recover the first. She paid again, telling herself it would all be refunded, because stopping now meant admitting that the first payment was gone for nothing.

By evening the cracks showed: the caller's name had changed, the office number did not match what she found, and a "case" like this could apparently be settled with a payment. Afreen's stomach turned. Part of her knew. Another part hoped she was wrong. She pictured her brother Anirban's face, her mother's, and the neighbours'. Then she ended the call, opened a message to her friend Dilnaz, and sent, "Can I call you? Something happened." Dilnaz answered within a minute: "Calling you now."

What did the caller tell Afreen not to do?
The caller told her not to speak to anyone, not family and not friends.
How did the early pressure lead to the first payment and then more, and what made telling anyone hard?

The urgency and secrecy pushed out slower thinking, so she made a small transfer. A "processing problem" then asked for more to recover it, and stopping felt like admitting the first payment was gone. When cracks showed, fear of how Anirban, her mother and the neighbours would react made telling hard.
What was Afreen feeling when the caller's name had changed?
She felt sick with doubt and fear, with part of her knowing and part hoping she was wrong.
What could Afreen do after Dilnaz calls?
She could tell Dilnaz everything without shame, then take the matter to her bank and the proper authorities with a trusted person beside her.

Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate; I desire, therefore, in this narration, to state those facts which led to my predilection for that science. When I was thirteen years of age we all went on a party of pleasure to the baths near Thonon; the inclemency of the weather obliged us to remain a day confined to the inn. In this house I chanced to find a volume of the works of Cornelius Agrippa. I opened it with apathy; the theory which he attempts to demonstrate and the wonderful facts which he relates soon changed this feeling into enthusiasm. A new light seemed to dawn upon my mind, and bounding with joy, I communicated my discovery to my father. My father looked carelessly at the title page of my book and said, "Ah! Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, do not waste your time upon this; it is sad trash."
At thirteen, Victor found a book by Cornelius Agrippa on a day stuck indoors by bad weather and became very excited. Victor's father glanced at it and said not to waste time on it.

Janet takes two multivitamins and 3 calcium supplements every day for the first 2 weeks of the month. For the last two weeks of the month, she runs low on calcium supplements and only takes one per day. How many pills does Janet take in that month?

First find the number of pills Janet takes every day for the first 2 weeks: 2 pills/day + 3 pills/day = 5 pills/day
Then find the number of days in 2 weeks: 2 weeks * 7 days/week = 14 days
Then multiply that number by the number of pills she takes daily to find the total number of pills she takes in the first 2 weeks: 5 pills/day * 14 days = 70 pills
Then find the number of pills Janet takes every day for the last 2 weeks: 2 pills/day + 1 pill/day = 3 pills/day
Then multiply that number by the number of days in 2 weeks to find the total number of pills she takes in the last 2 weeks: 3 pills/day * 14 days = 42 pills
Then add the number of pills she took in the first and last two weeks to find the total number of pills she took: 42 pills + 70 pills = 112 pills
The answer is 112.

In the tailoring shop she ran in the kasba, Rajni looked over Sunaina's shoulder at the phone. Sunaina wanted to order a sewing machine motor from a shopping page. "Five stars, see? Three hundred reviews!" Rajni scrolled. "Best product, very nice, fast delivery." "Best product, very nice, fast delivery." The same words again and again, under different names. Not one review below four stars. "Strange," Rajni said. "Even Mishra-ji's sweets get complaints, and his are the best in the district." She tapped the filter for three-star reviews. Nothing, as if they had been hidden. Then she searched the motor's name in the tailors' group Sunaina's cousin had added them to. Two women from Rewa had bought it: it burned out in a month, and the seller stopped answering. Sunaina put the phone down slowly. "I almost ordered it tonight." "Ask the group which one they use," Rajni said, threading her needle. "Real people grumble a bit."

Which words appeared again and again in the reviews?
Best product, very nice, fast delivery.
What was Rajni thinking as she scrolled?
Rajni felt suspicious and puzzled that every review used the same words and none was below four stars, when even the best sweets get complaints.
Which checks would you advise before buying from a page like this?
Look for middle-rated reviews, notice identical wording, and ask independent people, like the tailors' group, who have really used the product.
How did Sunaina feel after hearing about the women from Rewa?
Sunaina felt shaken and relieved, putting the phone down slowly as she realised she had almost ordered it that night.

messages.content: A new girl, Divya, moved into the room opposite mine today. She looked lost with her bags.
That was a good moment to help. New hostel residents often feel unsure about everything. Did you speak to her?
I offered to carry a bag. She smiled and said thanks.

I'm Joseph. At lunch I leaned toward Reena to show her a funny picture on my dad's phone. We both laughed so hard we had to hold our stomachs. Across the table Kabir's face went still, and he started stirring his dal. I realised he couldn't see and he hadn't been asked. I felt a bit bad. So I turned the screen so he could see it too. “Sorry, Kabir, look!” He laughed as well, and the stirring stopped. I want to remember that leaning in together feels great for the two people, but the others notice.

What did Joseph show Reena on his dad's phone?
Joseph showed Reena a funny picture.
What was Kabir probably feeling when his face went still and he stirred his dal, and what else could it be?
Probably left out, since he could not see the picture and had not been asked. It might also just have been that he was focused on his lunch.
What did Joseph do that repaired the moment?
Joseph noticed Kabir, turned the screen so he could see it and said sorry, so all three could share the joke.
How might Reena feel about Joseph turning the screen?
Probably happy to share, since she was already laughing with Joseph. She may not have noticed Kabir until Joseph did.

messages.content: A man intends to complete a journey of 24 km in 8 hours. If he travels at a speed of 4km/hr for the first four hours, at what speed does he need to travel for the remainder of the journey to be right on time?

He covers 4km/hr*4hrs = 16km in the first 4 hours
He has 24-16 = 8km left to cover
He has 8-4 = 4 hours to cover the remaining 8km
He has to travel at a speed of 8km/4hrs = 2km/hr to be right on time
The answer is 2.

A few quick questions:
Is there any homework for tomorrow?
Spot the error: I have ate my lunch already.
What's the meaning of the word brilliantly?

1. I don't know that. I can't see your teacher's instructions. Check your diary or ask a classmate.
2. Corrected: I have eaten my lunch already. Why: the present perfect uses the past participle "eaten".
3. As an adverb, "brilliantly" means in a very clever or very bright way.

“Time to go home, Mridul.”
“No!” Mridul's jaw locked tight. His teeth were clenched and his whole face shook.
“You're very angry,” said Imran, his abba, quietly.
“I. Want. The. Swing.” The words squeezed out between his teeth.
“I know. It's hard to leave.” Imran didn't pull him. He sat down on the bench. “I'm here. We'll go when your body is ready.”
Mridul stamped, then flopped onto the grass. After a long minute his jaw loosened and he started to cry. Imran opened his arms.

Where did Imran sit while Mridul was upset?
On the bench.
What does Mridul's clenched jaw suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he was overwhelmed with anger about leaving the swing, and perhaps trying to hold himself together. When his jaw loosened he started to cry, which shows sadness under the anger.
What did Imran's calm presence do for Mridul?
By staying near, speaking quietly and not pulling him, Imran gave Mridul's body time to settle until he could accept comfort.
What would change if Imran had shouted back?
Mridul's anger would likely grow and the tantrum would last longer, with both of them more upset.

Quick one: what is the name of the girl who sits behind me in class?
what does "come across" mean

1. I don't know, because I can't see your classroom. Ask her, or look at the seating chart.
2. It means to find something or someone by chance. For example: I came across an old photo in the drawer.

"I'll laugh at you heartily when to-morrow is past; till then I dare not: my prize is not certain. This is you, who have been as slippery as an eel this last month, and as thorny as a briar-rose? I could not lay a finger anywhere but I was pricked; and now I seem to have gathered up a stray lamb in my arms. You wandered out of the fold to seek your shepherd, did you, Jane?"

The year I was thirteen, my body felt like it belonged to someone else. My voice cracked in the middle of sentences. My arms and legs suddenly seemed too long, and I kept knocking things over. So I shrank. I wore my brother's huge hoodie every day, hunched in the back row, and hid behind my bag at the bus stop. I'm Tarun, and I thought if I stayed small enough, nobody would notice. My friend Lakshmi noticed. 'You used to be the best dancer at every wedding,' she said. 'Come to the Saturday class with me.' I said no four times. The fifth time I went. Nobody laughed. The teacher said, 'Long arms, beautiful lines.' I left sweaty and grinning, standing up straight for the first time in months.

What did Tarun wear every day?
A brother's huge hoodie.
How did Tarun feel about that changing body at thirteen?
Tarun felt awkward and embarrassed, as if the body belonged to someone else.
What helped Tarun feel more at home?
Lakshmi's kind invitation and enjoying dance again, where the teacher praised the long arms.
How might Lakshmi have felt when Tarun finally came to class?
Lakshmi was probably pleased and relieved, after asking five times.
Neha and Tom was waiting for me at the gate when I reached. Any errors?

Neha and Tom were waiting for me at the gate when I reached.
Why: subject-verb agreement ("Neha and Tom was" -> "were").

Wednesday night.
Taluk office, round two. Round one was last Friday, when I waited three hours and then learned the domicile form needed a stamped ration card copy I did not have.
Today was better, but only because of Swati. She got hers done in June. Yesterday she sent me a photo of her folder: originals in one pocket, two photocopies of everything in the other, a spare passport photo taped inside. "Reach by nine, Joseph. The line doubles after ten."
I reached at 8:50. Counter one gave me a token. Counter three checked my papers and said the photocopy was too faint. I nearly lost it. Then I remembered Swati's folder, pulled out the second copy, and the clerk nodded.
Receipt in hand by 11:15. Collect on the 20th. I am writing Swati's list inside my notebook cover so I never do round one again.

What time did the narrator reach the taluk office today?
The narrator reached at 8:50.
How did Joseph feel when the clerk said the photocopy was too faint?
Joseph felt frustrated and close to losing his temper, until Joseph remembered the spare copy and relief took over.
What small step from this entry would help anyone going to a government office?
Carrying originals plus two photocopies of everything and reaching before the queue grows, as Swati advised.
How might Swati feel when she hears it went smoothly?
Swati would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that her folder photo saved Joseph another wasted trip.

At Diwali, the whole family came to our house. And all anyone talked about was Mridul.

"Mridul came first in the district quiz!" "Mridul's teacher says he's gifted!" Dadi hugged him three times. Chachu gave him a watch.

I stood near the kitchen door, holding a plate of mithai. Nobody asked about my dance recital, even though I'd practised every evening for two months.

I told myself it didn't matter. But later, lying in bed, I kept thinking: maybe they just like him more. Maybe I'm the ordinary one.

Mridul came into my room and said, "Didi, your dance was the best thing at Diwali." I cried a little, but I didn't tell him why.

— Tanuja

What did Chachu give Mridul?
A watch.
What was Tanuja feeling lying in bed that night?
She felt hurt and less loved, wondering if the family liked Mridul more and she was the ordinary one.
What could an adult in the family do to help Tanuja?
Notice her and praise her dance too, and make sure she knows she is loved as much, instead of comparing.
How might Mridul feel if he knew why Tanuja cried?
He might feel sad and surprised, since he admired her dance and didn't want to be compared.

Anirban said on Monday that the payment screen would be done by Wednesday. It was done this morning. Last sprint he said two days for the login fix; it took five. The others are similar. I've looked back at six sprints: almost every estimate from the team is short by about half.

Asking for a best-case and likely-case range and reviewing estimates against reality every Friday without blame, so the team can learn their real speed.
How might Anirban feel in the first Friday review?
Anirban might feel nervous at first, then relieved to find the review is about numbers, not blame.

Counselling note, session 3, Lavanya and Bidisha (sisters, sharing a flat in Salt Lake).

Today something shifted. Bidisha had again described the past fortnight as "living with a ghost," and I expected Lavanya to go quiet, as in both earlier sessions.

Instead, after a long pause, Lavanya turned to her sister and said, "When you raise your voice, I go quiet because I'm overwhelmed. It's not that I don't care. Can I take ten minutes when that happens, and then come back?"

Bidisha's eyes filled. She said, "I thought you were punishing me. For two weeks I thought you hated me."

I asked Lavanya how it felt to say it. Lavanya said, "Scary. And lighter."

Plan: at home, Lavanya will use the words "ten minutes" as a signal, and set a timer so the return is visible. We review in a week.

What words will Lavanya use at home as a signal?
Lavanya will use the words "ten minutes" as a signal.
What did Bidisha think Lavanya's silence meant?
Bidisha believed the silence was punishment and felt hurt and afraid that Lavanya hated her.
Why does explaining the silence make such a difference?
Once Lavanya names it as overwhelm and promises to return, the silence becomes a signal Bidisha can trust instead of a weapon.
How did Lavanya feel after saying it aloud?
Lavanya felt scared and lighter at the same time, relieved to finally explain.

Dear Nirmala,

Quick note on how I stopped wasting Saturdays. In my first month I went to town three times in one week: once for a notebook, once for the laundry pick-up, once for the bank. Each trip was a bus ride and forty minutes of waiting. Last week I stopped and thought: these three are all in the same market. Why go three times? So I wrote a list on the back of my hand: stationery, laundry, bank. I went to the bank first, before it got crowded, then the stationery shop, then the laundry on the way back to the bus. One trip, done by twelve. I even had time to sit with a cold drink. The free hours felt like a present.

Noor

What three errands were on Noor's list?
Noor's list said stationery, laundry, bank.
How did Noor feel about the extra free hours?
Noor felt pleased, saying that the free hours felt like a present.
What could Noor check before the next trip?
Noor could check that the shops are open that day and that all three are near the bus stop, so the trip works.
How might Nirmala feel on reading this news?
Nirmala may feel relieved and proud that Noor is managing time and cutting extra trips.

Subject: Guess who was at Meenal's wedding

Dear Tara,

You asked how the wedding went, so here it is. I saw Yash near the dessert table with a plate in his hand and my stomach dropped. For about a second I considered pretending to read my phone. Then I walked over and said, "Hi, Yash. Good to see you. Congratulations on the new job." He said thanks, asked after my sister, and we talked for maybe two minutes. I did not put on a huge smile and I did not go cold either. Then I went back to the dance floor and my hands shook a little for ten minutes. It was not dramatic. I am glad I did not turn it into a show for the aunties.

Love,
Rashmi

Where did Rashmi see Yash?
Rashmi saw Yash near the dessert table at Meenal's wedding.
What do Rashmi's shaking hands after the chat suggest?
Rashmi was still anxious, even though the conversation went smoothly.
How could Rashmi handle another chance meeting?
Greet briefly and politely again and skip performing happiness or anger, as at the wedding.
How might Yash have experienced the short chat?
Yash probably found it civil and perhaps a relief, since Rashmi congratulated him and stayed brief.

'Indu, you've buttered the same toast three times.'
'I'm tired, Mumma.'
'What time did you sleep?'
Indu shrugged. 'Two? Maybe later.'
'Were you on your phone?'
'Just a few videos. And the group chat. Everyone was talking about the concert. If I don't reply, they'll make plans without me.'
Urmila sat down. 'And now?'
'Now I feel horrible. My head hurts and I snapped at Vir on the stairs.'
'One more video never feels like much, does it?'
'It's like my brain won't turn off.'
'What if the phone charges in the kitchen from eleven? Your friends will still be there tomorrow.'
Indu sighed. 'Can I try it on weeknights first?'
'Deal.'

When did Indu think sleep finally came?
Around two, maybe later.
What was Indu worried about while scrolling late at night?
Indu was afraid of missing out on plans in the group chat about the concert.
What did Urmila suggest, and why could it help?
Charging the phone in the kitchen from eleven, so the light and chat stop keeping Indu's mind awake.
How might Vir have felt when Indu snapped on the stairs?
Vir was probably hurt or confused, not knowing Indu was running on little sleep.
Always I forget to bring my water bottle. How can I say it better?

I always forget to bring my water bottle.
Why: word order ("Always I forget" -> "I always forget").
In under 15 words, explain why we see lightning before we hear thunder.
Light travels much faster than sound, so the flash reaches us first.

Tanvir, you say the pool is dangerous because your stomach hurts. Listen to your Nani Parveen. At ten, my school in Hyderabad opened its first pool, and my father signed me up. That night I lay awake, a stone on my chest. In the morning I told him, 'The pool is dangerous. I can feel it.' He didn't laugh. He asked, 'Has anyone been hurt there?' No one had. 'Then the danger is inside you, not inside the water. Go and look.' A lady coach in a white cap let me stand on the steps for the whole first class. The stone stayed. The water was just blue and cold. By the third week I could float. The feeling told me I was frightened. It never told me the truth about the pool.

In which city did the school open its first pool?
The school in Hyderabad opened its first pool.
Why did Parveen believe the pool was dangerous the night before?
She felt frightened, with a stone on her chest, and that strong feeling seemed like proof about the water itself.
What turning point in the story helped Parveen separate the feeling from the facts?
Her father's question, whether anyone had been hurt there, and then standing on the steps showed the danger was in her fear, not in the pool.
How might the lady coach have seen the girl on the steps?
She likely saw a nervous beginner who needed time rather than a problem, which is why she let her stand there for the whole class.

Shreya, you're going to your first big concert on Saturday, so let your old music teacher tell you something. My name is Nazia, and in 1986 I was a fifteen-year-old girl at a college fest in Hyderabad. Some band from Shillong was playing. I didn't even know their songs. But when three thousand people jumped, I jumped. I climbed onto a chair and sang words I was inventing. I cried at a slow song I'd never heard before. It was the happiest night, and honestly, half that happiness came from the people around me. Then, at the end, somebody at the gate shouted and the crowd surged, and the fear arrived just as fast. I pushed the girl in front of me. I never push anyone. So enjoy it, Shreya. Let the joy in. Just keep a little corner of yourself that notices which feelings are yours.

Where was Nazia in 1986?
She was a fifteen-year-old girl at a college fest in Hyderabad.
What does Nazia mean by 'half that happiness came from the people around me'?
She felt a joy that wasn't only hers; the crowd's excitement filled her even for songs she didn't know.
What could Shreya do at the concert if the crowd suddenly surges?
Shreya could use that little corner of Shreya's own mind to notice the fear rising, keep some space and avoid pushing, and move out calmly.
How might the girl in front of Nazia have felt when she was pushed?
She probably felt scared and shaken, caught in a crush where even people who never push were pushing.

I'm Jatin, and I've known Hansa since college. When she didn't get the fellowship in January, she called me that night, and I listened. That was right.
But it's March now, and we have the same call three evenings a week. She goes over the interview answers. What the panel's faces meant. Whether the other candidate had contacts. Each time, I think it will help. Each time, by the end, she sounds lower than when she started. So do I.
I can't know what's inside her head. But I noticed on Monday she said, "I feel worse after we talk," and then kept going.
On Wednesday, when she started again, I said gently, "Hansa, we've been over this a lot. It doesn't seem to be giving you any relief. What's one small thing that might help now?"
There was a long silence. Then she said, "Maybe I could ask them for feedback."

What did Hansa not get in January?
She didn't get the fellowship.
How was Jatin feeling about the repeated calls by March?
Jatin felt tired and low, noticing that the talks left both of them feeling worse, and was worried they weren't helping Hansa.
Why was Jatin's question a helpful move?
Asking gently for one small step shifted the talk from going over the past to action, and led Hansa to think of asking for feedback.
How might Hansa feel when Jatin asks what might help now?
Hansa might feel a little caught off guard at first, then relieved to have something she can do, which is why she suggests asking for feedback.

At the women's dairy cooperative in Anand district, Aditi had been the young manager for a year. Review time came in March, and her first thought about Sarita, the collection supervisor, was the mess in February: two days of spoiled milk when a chiller broke. That was all she could remember. But Aditi had a habit. Every month she wrote a few lines in a green register about each supervisor. She sat under the neem tree and read Sarita's page. April: trained six new collectors. June: stayed till midnight during the monsoon flooding. September: found the fault in the testing machine. December: collection up by a tenth. February: chiller problem, not her fault, but slow to report it. Aditi wrote the review: "An excellent year. One lesson: report equipment faults at once." Sarita read it twice and smiled.

How many new collectors did Sarita train in April?
Six new collectors.
What was Aditi feeling when she first thought about Sarita's review?
Aditi felt worried and a bit irritated, remembering only February's spoiled milk.
Which habit helped Aditi write a fair review?
Writing a few lines each month in the green register, so the review covered the whole year instead of the latest memory.
How might Sarita have felt reading the review?
Sarita seemed pleased and fairly treated, seeing a whole year of work counted, with one clear lesson.

Nevertheless, ere long, the warm, warbling persuasiveness of the pleasant, holiday weather we came to, seemed gradually to charm him from his mood. For, as when the red-cheeked, dancing girls, April and May, trip home to the wintry, misanthropic woods; even the barest, ruggedest, most thunder-cloven old oak will at least send forth some few green sprouts, to welcome such glad-hearted visitants; so Ahab did, in the end, a little respond to the playful allurings of that girlish air. More than once did he put forth the faint blossom of a look, which, in any other man, would have soon flowered out in a smile.

How does the pleasant weather affect Ahab?

The warm, holiday weather gradually charms Ahab out of his mood. Like a bare old oak sending out a few green sprouts in spring, Ahab more than once puts forth the faint blossom of a look that in another man would have become a smile.

Rewrite this paragraph as a two-sentence summary.

On opening the little door, two hairy monsters flew at my throat, bearing me down, and extinguishing the light; while a mingled guffaw from Heathcliff and Hareton put the copestone on my rage and humiliation. Fortunately, the beasts seemed more bent on stretching their paws, and yawning, and flourishing their tails, than devouring me alive; but they would suffer no resurrection, and I was forced to lie till their malignant masters pleased to deliver me: then, hatless and trembling with wrath, I ordered the miscreants to let me out—on their peril to keep me one minute longer—with several incoherent threats of retaliation that, in their indefinite depth of virulency, smacked of King Lear.

Two hairy beasts knock the narrator down and put out the light, while Heathcliff and Hareton laugh loudly. The narrator must lie there until their masters call them off, then demands to be let out, hatless and trembling with anger.
I lost my way to my friend's new flat. All the buildings look the same.
Housing colonies can be confusing. Stop and call her, or ask the security guard at the gate. Do you remember the name of the building or the block number?
Block C, third floor. Her name is Olivia, and her building has a green gate.
Then tell the guard that you are looking for Block C, the one with the green gate. Block letters are usually painted on the wall. Once you find it, take the lift to the third floor.
I found Block C but there are two lifts and I do not know which one works.
Try the one with a light on the panel, or take the stairs if it is only three floors. When you reach the third floor, look for Olivia's door number, which she should have told you.
She did, it is 304. Can you put the whole address together for me so I can save it?
Sure. Olivia's flat is number 304, on the third floor of Block C, the building with the green gate. Save that in a note on your phone, so next time you can show it to the guard straight away.

My name is Simran, and I live next door to Maria's parents. I only know what I saw over the wall on Sunday.

Maria's mother had been telling everyone at the temple that Maria was about to be made a manager. That evening Maria arrived, still in her work shoes, and sat down at the table under the veranda light. Her parents stopped talking when she came in.

I couldn't hear all of it, but I heard Maria say, "I didn't get it. Someone else did. I should have told you last week." Her father stared at his tea. Her mother reached over and held Maria's wrist for a moment.

Later the mother came to water the plants, humming. I don't know how she really felt. But Maria was laughing at something by the time I went inside.

Where did Simran see Maria sit with her parents?
Simran saw Maria sit at the table under the veranda light.
What does the mother's touch on Maria's wrist suggest, and how sure can Simran be?
Holding Maria's wrist suggests warmth and support, but Simran admits not knowing how the mother really felt, so the inner state is uncertain.
What did Maria do that helped with the awkwardness?
Maria told her parents plainly that she did not get the role and that she should have said so sooner, instead of letting them hear it from others.
How might the parents have felt after telling relatives that Maria was rising?
They may have felt awkward or embarrassed in front of the relatives, though their quiet reaction and the later humming suggest they were not blaming Maria.

Robie filled some plastic boxes with hockey cards. There were 10 cards in each box but 5 cards were not placed in a box. He gave away 2 boxes to his friends and he has 5 boxes with him. How many cards did Robie have in the beginning?

Robie filled a total of 2 + 5 = 7 boxes.
So, he had 7 x 10 = 70 hockey cards from the 7 boxes.
Thus, he had a total of 70 + 5 = 75 cards in the beginning.
The answer is 75.

Bao's family in Madrid is Deaf, and they sign at home. Her mother left the new babysitter, Pablo, a card of Bao's signs.
At snack time Bao looked at her empty cup, then at Pablo, and made a sign with her hands, twice, eyebrows up.
Pablo checked the card. “More!” He signed it back, a bit clumsily, and poured more milk.
Later she brushed her hands outwards over the plate. Pablo checked again: all done. Bao nodded and climbed down.

What did Bao's mother leave for Pablo?
She left Pablo a card of Bao's signs.
What did Bao want when she looked at her cup and signed twice with her eyebrows up?
She wanted more milk and was eager for Pablo to understand; the raised eyebrows and repeated sign show she was asking clearly.
What did Pablo do that helped him understand Bao?
He checked the card of her family's signs and signed back, treating her signs as real language.
How might Pablo feel as the afternoon goes on?
Pablo probably feels relieved and more confident, since the card helped him understand Bao's signs.

I'm helping Akash from Class 7 with maths at the colony study circle every evening. When we started, he got every word problem wrong and said, "I'm just stupid." Today I noticed something. He still gets the final answers wrong sometimes, but he now writes down what the question is asking before starting. Three weeks ago he never did that.
I told him exactly that: "You wrote what the question wants. That's new. That's why you got the first two right." He looked at his notebook as if it belonged to someone else.
Then I gave him a problem with two steps instead of one. Harder, but only a bit. He got it on the second try and punched the air.
I think he needed someone to show him the progress, because he couldn't see it himself.
Saurabh

What does Akash now do before starting a problem?
He now writes down what the question is asking before starting.
How did Saurabh feel noticing Akash's new habit?
Saurabh felt pleased and encouraged, seeing progress that Akash hadn't noticed himself.
Why was the two-step problem the right next task?
It was a bit harder but still doable, so solving it on the second try gave Akash visible proof of improvement.

Akash felt proud and excited, punching the air.

Hrithik worked double shifts at a Kolkata call centre and slept in the afternoons with traffic roaring outside. His friend Thomas, a church choir member, had kept a morning silence for years. "Ten minutes," Thomas said. "No phone. Just breathe or pray, whatever you like." Hrithik laughed. Where would he find ten quiet minutes? He tried at his window, but horns blared. He tried the rooftop, where the water tank hummed. It wasn't silent, but it was his. Some days he forgot. Some days he read a line of Gita his grandfather had underlined. After two months, he noticed he snapped less at angry callers. It didn't fix his life. But it gave him a still point in it.

Where did Hrithik finally practise his quiet minutes?
On the rooftop, where the water tank hummed.
How did Hrithik feel about trying silence at first?
He was doubtful and amused, laughing because his life seemed too noisy and busy.
What helped Hrithik keep his practice despite the noise?
He adapted by finding a spot that was his own and didn't give up when he missed days.
How might angry callers notice the change in Hrithik?
They might find him calmer and more patient, even if they never knew why.

Kashish had eleven days before his transfer to Hyderabad and a list of worries too long to fit on a phone screen. At lunch he asked two colleagues who had moved before, Jasleen and another, to spare twenty minutes. Jasleen went first. "Ask for the broker's fee up front and get it in writing. Don't pay it to more than one." The other colleague said school forms in that city had cut-off dates, and named two neighbourhoods where the water supply was unreliable. Kashish wrote it all in the back of his diary. With eleven days he could not test everything, but he crossed two listings off his list and asked the broker for the fee in writing. What did Jasleen advise about the broker's fee?
Jasleen said to ask for it up front, get it in writing, and not pay it to more than one broker.
What was Kashish likely feeling as he wrote the advice in his diary?
Kashish was probably anxious about the short time but relieved to have concrete tips.
What could Kashish do next?
Kashish could also ask someone already living near the new office and check details himself, rather than rely on one story.
How might Jasleen have felt sharing the advice?
Jasleen may have felt glad to spare Kashish mistakes that others had already made.

Sunday night
Another fight with Mummy. It started because I hadn't cleaned my room and she said "Vaibhav, look at this mess" in That Voice and I shouted "Leave me alone!" OK, I shouted. But I'm doing mock tests all week and I'm exhausted and nobody gets it. I'm not a shouty person, I'm just stressed.
She shouted back, which is typical. She loves being in control of every little thing. She can't just let anything be.
Then later I heard her on the phone with Masi, who probably thinks I'm a brat now. Mummy said, "I lose my temper only because I'm so worried about his exams. He shouts because he's become so rude."
So she thinks SHE is the stressed one and I'M the rude one. Which is literally the opposite.
Yamini, my mother, if you ever read this: I'm not rude. I'm tired.
Vaibhav

What was Vaibhav's room like when the fight started?
He hadn't cleaned his room, and Mummy called it a mess.
Why does Vaibhav feel his shouting is stress but Mummy's is about control?
He knows how exhausted the mock tests are making him, so his own shouting has a reason, but he doesn't see her worry, so her shouting seems to be about wanting control.
What could Vaibhav try next time before deciding why Mummy is shouting?
He could remember what he overheard on the phone and ask whether she is worried rather than controlling, and tell her about his tiredness calmly once they have both cooled down.
How does Yamini seem to see the same argument?
Yamini sees her own temper as coming from worry about his exams and sees Vaibhav's shouting as rudeness, the mirror image of how he sees it.
I forgot my room key inside and I'm standing outside my hostel room. My roommate Lucas is at class.
That is annoying but fixable. The warden or caretaker usually has a spare key. Do you know who to ask?
The caretaker is a man called Ramesh.
Then go to Ramesh and explain politely. He may ask for your name and room number, and maybe a note to confirm. Keep your ID handy.
He opened the door. How do I avoid this next time?
Keep your key on a lanyard or a ring attached to your bag, and check your pocket every time the door closes. You could also leave a spare key with a trusted friend.
Lucas could keep one. He's reliable.
That is a sensible idea since you share the room. Just make sure Lucas knows where the spare key is kept, and tell him if you swap locks.
Thanks. Who opened the door?
The caretaker, Ramesh, opened the door for you. You could also thank him with a short word the next time you pass him.

In their school in Kothrud, lab records were due every Friday. Jeevan had fallen three weeks behind.
On Thursday afternoon, Kiran handed him her record book in the library. "Copy what you need. Everyone does."
Jeevan looked around. Two other boys were doing the same thing at the next table. It felt normal. Just this once, he told himself, to catch up. He copied three experiments in forty minutes, readings and all.
His record was stamped "Complete" on Friday. For a moment he felt clever.
Then, in the practical exam in March, the examiner asked him to set up the pendulum experiment and explain why the readings changed. Jeevan had written about it three times. He had never done it. He stood with the string in his hand and his face burning.
Kiran, at the next bench, finished in ten minutes.
Walking out, Jeevan thought: I didn't catch up. I just moved the problem to March.

How many experiments did Jeevan copy?
He copied three experiments in forty minutes.
How did Jeevan feel standing with the pendulum string in the practical exam?
Jeevan felt exposed and ashamed, face burning, because he had written about the experiment but never done it.
What lesson does Jeevan draw, and how could he act on it?
That copying only moved the problem later; he could ask the teacher for extra time to do the missed experiments himself.
How might Kiran see her offer to share the record book?
Kiran probably thought she was being helpful and that everyone did it, without realising it could leave Jeevan unprepared.
I got fewer marks than I expected and I feel like a failure.
That is disappointing, and it makes sense that you are upset. One result does not decide who you are.
But my friends all did well.
Comparing makes it feel worse. Everyone has strong and weak subjects, and a single test shows only a small part of that.
What should I do now?
Look at the paper and find where marks were lost. Ask your teacher to explain the mistakes. Then make a small plan for those topics.
Will my parents be upset?
They may be disappointed, but many parents care most about effort. Show them the plan you made, which tells them you are taking it seriously.

At the chai stall outside the Gurugram metro, Seema caught up with her friend Ujjwal after his first week at the new internship. "So, did you like it?" she asked. "Yeah. It was fine." Seema waited. Nothing else came. She tried again. "Okay, but what was it like walking in on the first day?" Ujjwal laughed and put down his cup. "Honestly? Terrifying. Everyone was in suits and I was in a checked shirt. My manager called me by the wrong name for two days. And then on Thursday, she asked for my idea in a meeting, and they actually used it." He talked for twenty minutes: the canteen, the lift that stopped on every floor, the colleague who lent him a charger. Walking home, Seema thought about it. "Did you like it?" had got one word. "What was it like?" had got a story.

What was Ujjwal wearing on his first day?
A checked shirt.
What was Ujjwal feeling as he described his first week?
He felt a mix of fear and pride, calling the first day terrifying but lighting up when his idea was used.
Why did Seema's second question work better?
It was open and curious, asking what the day was like instead of a yes-or-no question, so Ujjwal could tell a full story.
What would change if Seema had stopped after 'Did you like it?'
She would have heard only 'fine' and missed the fear, the wrong name and the idea that got used.

Maria is chopping up vegetables for a stew. She wants to cut up six times as many carrots as potatoes, twice as many onions as carrots, and 1/3 as many green beans as onions. If she has two potatoes, how many green beans does she need to cut?

First find how many carrots Maria needs to cut by multiplying the number of potatoes by 6: 6 * 2 = 12.
Then find how many onions she needs by multiplying the number of carrots by 2: 12 * 2 = 24.
Finally, divide the number of onions by 3 to find the number of green beans she needs 24 / 3 = 8.
The answer is 8.

A park has three colors of flowering crepe myrtle trees planted: red, white, and pink. When they bloom, a third of them are pink, but only two are red. Most of them are white. There are 42 crepe myrtle trees in the park. How many have white flowers when they bloom?

The park has 42 / 3 = 14 pink crepe myrtle trees.
It has 2 red trees, so it has 14 + 2 = 16 pink and red trees.
Therefore, there are 42 - 16 = 26 crepe myrtle trees that have white flowers when they bloom in the park.
The answer is 26.

The hiring deadline was midnight, the office Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Madhav, twenty-six, was the only one on the team who could recommend candidates for the new analyst role. His cousin had sent a CV that morning: decent, but not the best. Madhav knew he had grown up with English at home, a father in the industry and an easy route in. He also knew Usha, from the evening data course he taught, was sharper than anyone. She'd studied in a small-town college and had no one to put in a word. Madhav felt the pull to help family. He also felt the old guilt about his own easy route. He set both aside and wrote a fair recommendation for Usha, listing her work. Then he called his cousin and suggested two other openings. At 11:52 he pressed send.

At what time did Madhav press send?
At 11:52 he pressed send.
What was Madhav feeling as he chose whom to recommend?
Madhav felt torn, pulled toward family and carrying some guilt about his easy route, before choosing fairly.
How did Madhav use his advantage responsibly?
He recommended Usha fairly on her work and still helped his cousin in other ways, without denying or wallowing in his head start.
How might Usha feel if she gets the interview?
Usha would likely feel recognised and hopeful, having had no one else to put in a word for her.

Johns goes to the gym 3 times a week.  He spends 1 hour each day lifting weight. Additionally, he also spends a third of his weightlifting time warming up and doing cardio each day.  How many hours does he spend at the gym a week?

He spends 60/3=20 minutes warming up
So he spends 60+20=80 minutes at the gym per day
That means he spends 80*3=240 minutes at the gym
So he spends 240/60=4 hours at the gym a week
The answer is 4.

Nirmala, a lab technician wanting to move into clinical research, found an alumnus from her college on a professional networking site: Pankaj, a clinical research associate at a hospital in Hyderabad. She wrote three lines: who she was, what she hoped to learn, and "Could I have fifteen minutes on a call, any day that suits you?"

He said one short certificate mattered more than a second degree.

On the last day of Class 9 at the high school in Bishnupur, Anirban tore up his maths result on the way home. Forty-one out of a hundred. "This was the worst year of my life," he told Sunaina as they cycled past the paddy fields. Sunaina braked. "Worst? You won the district science fair in August. You got picked for the football team. You finally beat Ranjan at chess." "That was ages ago." "It was this year." Anirban kept pedalling, jaw tight. The final exam was the last thing, and it sat on top of everything else like a stone. That evening, though, he found the science fair certificate on the wall and stood in front of it a long time. "Okay. Not the worst year," he told his mother at dinner. "Just the worst ending."

What did Anirban score in maths?
Anirban scored forty-one out of a hundred.
Why did Anirban call Class 9 the worst year of his life?
Anirban felt angry and ashamed about the maths result, and because it came at the very end, it weighed on top of all the good months.
What helped Anirban change his view, and what could help him next?
Seeing the science fair certificate on the wall; next he could talk to his maths teacher about the result as one problem to work on.
How does Sunaina see Anirban's year?
Sunaina sees a year full of wins, the science fair, football and chess, with one bad result at the end.

messages.content: On Wednesday, 37 students played kickball. On Thursday, 9 fewer students played kickball. How many students played kickball on Wednesday and Thursday?

37 - 9 = 28 students played kickball on Thursday.
So, 37 + 28 = 65 students played kickball on Wednesday and Thursday.
The answer is 65.

The magician says the coin vanishes. What does vanishes mean?

To vanish is to disappear suddenly, so that you can no longer see it. It is a verb, the form used with he, she or it.
Example: In the magician's trick, the coin vanishes from his palm and reappears in a child's ear.

In the Pune school corridor, Vasudha and Rashmi got back their science tests. Both had four out of twenty.
Vasudha crumpled hers. "I'm stupid. I'm always going to be bad at science."
Rashmi looked at hers and frowned. "I didn't study the magnets chapter. That's where I lost all the marks."
"Same for me," said Vasudha. "But I'm just stupid."
"You're not. You just didn't study magnets either."
The next week, Rashmi borrowed a magnets book from the library. Vasudha didn't open her science notebook at all. "What's the point?" she said.

How many marks did both girls get?
Both had four out of twenty.
What was Vasudha feeling when she crumpled her test?
She felt hopeless and ashamed, believing she was stupid and would always be bad at science.
What could help Vasudha try again?
Seeing the low mark as caused by one chapter she didn't study, like Rashmi did, so she knows what to fix.
How does Rashmi explain her own low mark?
Rashmi explains it as not studying the magnets chapter, a temporary cause she can fix, so she borrows a book.

Arabella is a dance student learning three new steps this session. Her instructor has her spend thirty minutes on learning the first step. The second step she masters in half the time. The third step is more complex, so it takes her as long as both the other steps to learn. How many minutes did she spend learning the three steps?

Arabella spent 30 / 2 = 15 minutes on the second step.
She took 30 + 15 = 45 minutes to learn the third step.
Therefore, Arabella spent 30 + 15 + 45 = 90 minutes learning all three steps.
The answer is 90.

Onam is the harvest festival of Kerala, celebrated with great joy by people of all backgrounds. Families decorate their front yards with pookalam, beautiful carpets of fresh flowers arranged in circles. The highlight is the Onam Sadya, a grand feast served on a banana leaf, with many dishes such as avial, sambar and payasam. In many places there are snake boat races, folk dances and songs. Above all, Onam is a time for coming together and sharing happiness.

Ever since the residents' group shared a clip of a boy being chased by a dog in another city, ten-year-old Zainab had refused to go down to the play area of their Tolichowki apartment block. "Moti will bite me," she said, though Moti, the watchman's brown dog, usually just slept by the gate and let the toddlers pull his ears. Rehana, her mother, sat with her on the balcony. "How many children here has Moti bitten?" Zainab thought. "None... but he could." "And how many times have you watched that clip?" "Eleven," Zainab admitted. "Everyone keeps sending it." Down below, her friends shrieked with laughter on the swings.

How many times had Zainab watched the clip?
Zainab admitted she had watched the clip eleven times.
Why does Moti seem dangerous to Zainab even though he has bitten no one?
Zainab is scared because the clip, sent again and again, fills her mind and makes a bite feel likely, even though Moti only sleeps and lets toddlers pull his ears.
How could Rehana help Zainab get back to the play area?
Rehana could go down with her, watch Moti together from a distance and notice how he actually behaves, while skipping new forwards of the clip for a while.
How might Zainab's friends on the swings see her staying upstairs?
They may miss her and not understand why, since to them Moti is just the sleepy dog by the gate.
My boss will "apprise" my work this month. Is that the right word?

No. The word is "appraise", meaning to judge the value or quality of something. "Apprise" means to inform someone.
Examples: The teacher will appraise your project on Friday. Please apprise me of any change in the timing.

James decides to go to prom with Susan.  He pays for everything.  The tickets cost $100 each.  Dinner is $120.  He leaves a 30% tip.  He also charters a limo for 6 hours that cost $80 per hour.  How much did it all cost?

He paid 100*2=$200 for tickets
The tip for dinner was $120*.3=$36
So he paid $120+$36=$156 for dinner
The limo cost $80*6=$480
In total he paid $200+$156+$480=$836
The answer is 836.

Talking privately, not posting or telling anyone, saying plainly what is known, separating the friend from the lie, and asking why it felt necessary.

This happened the winter I was eleven. Papa's shop closed, and I decided the best thing was not to ask. If anyone mentioned it, I said, "We're fine." I said it so often I almost believed it.
But I kept waking at three in the morning with my heart thumping. At school, when my friend Imran borrowed my eraser without asking, I yelled at him in front of everyone. He looked at me as if I were a stranger.
That evening I finally asked Papa, "Is it bad?" He told me the truth, in small pieces. It was hard to hear. But after that, I slept.
— Usha

At what time did Usha keep waking up?
At three in the morning.
Why did Usha decide the best thing was not to ask?
Not knowing felt safer than hearing bad news about Papa's shop, so saying "We're fine" kept the fear at arm's length.
What turning point helped Usha sleep again?
Finally asking Papa "Is it bad?" and hearing the truth in small pieces; facing it eased the worry that had been leaking out.
How might Imran have felt being yelled at over an eraser?
Imran was probably shocked and hurt, since the anger was far bigger than a borrowed eraser and he couldn't know about the shop.

In the school computer lab, Santosh stared at the English assignment: "Write a letter to the editor about stray dogs in your area." Fifteen minutes left in the period.

He knew how easy it would be. Type the question into the chatbot, copy, paste, done. The relief would be instant.

Imran, at the next computer, noticed him hesitating. "Don't," Imran said quietly. "I did that last term. Ma'am asked me to explain one sentence and I couldn't. Had to redo it and got a warning in my diary."

Santosh remembered the school rule on the notice board: AI allowed for explanations, not for final answers.

He opened the chatbot and typed, "What is the format of a letter to the editor?" He read the layout. Then he closed it and wrote about the three dogs near his building who had chased a delivery boy last week.

When Ma'am read it later, she said, "This sounds like you. Good." Santosh felt a small glow of pride he wouldn't have got from copying.

What was the English assignment about?
It was a letter to the editor about stray dogs in the area.
What was Santosh feeling when he looked at the assignment?
Santosh felt tempted and pressured by the short time, imagining the instant relief of copying.
What did Santosh do that followed the school rule?
Santosh used the chatbot only to learn the letter format and then wrote the content himself.
How might Imran feel seeing Santosh write his own letter?
Imran may feel relieved that his warning helped, since he had learned the hard way last term.

When we had played some half-dozen games, a day was appointed for my return, and I was taken down into the yard to be fed in the former dog-like manner. There, too, I was again left to wander about as I liked.

Based on what the passage says, how does Estella treat the narrator on the return visit, and what else happens?

Estella treats the narrator as before, except that she does not bother to speak. After about six games a day is set for the next visit, and the narrator is fed in the yard like a dog as before and left to wander.

How long has it been since Papa's funeral?
Six weeks.
What was Raghav feeling when his friends went silent?

Masi and Mummy could keep saying Papa's name, and Raghav could tell a trusted friend or teacher he wants to talk about him.

Chelsea made 4 batches of cupcakes for the bake sale. The cupcakes took 20 minutes to bake and 30 minutes to ice per batch. How long did it take Chelsea to make the cupcakes?

Chelsea baked 4 batches of cupcakes x 20 minutes each = 80 minutes of baking.
She iced 4 batches of cupcakes x 30 minutes each = 120 minutes.
It took Chelsea 80 + 120 = 200 minutes to make the cupcakes for the bake sale.
The answer is 200.

Team lead's note, quarterly review
Kavitha, one of our strongest designers, has always spoken the most in meetings: quick, full of ideas, often answering questions meant for others. Last month in her feedback, I mentioned that newer team members like Swati rarely spoke when she was in the room.
Kavitha took it seriously. In today's review she kept a small tally on her notepad: each time she spoke, one line. After four lines she stopped and asked, "Swati, you worked on the checkout flow. What did you notice?"
Swati hesitated, then gave the best observation of the meeting: users were abandoning the page at the address step.
After the meeting, Kavitha told me the tally felt silly at first but useful. "I didn't realise how much space I was taking."
What I will do next: I will ask Kavitha to mentor Swati on the checkout redesign.

What did Kavitha keep on her notepad?
She kept a small tally, one line each time she spoke.
What was Kavitha feeling after the meeting?
Kavitha felt a little surprised and self-conscious at how much space she'd been taking, but pleased the tally helped.
Why does Kavitha's habit matter, especially for someone like her?
As a strong, dominant speaker, counting turns and asking quieter colleagues for input makes room for ideas that would otherwise be lost.
How might Swati have experienced being asked directly?
Swati probably felt nervous but valued, finally given room to share the best observation of the meeting.

Monday, 7 a.m.
Meeting with the principal at ten about my proposal for a Saturday coding club. My hands are cold and I've rewritten my first sentence four times. The anxious voice says: this means it'll go badly. So I'm writing the other thing down where I can see it. Nervous about the meeting is one thing. The meeting itself is another. The feeling is allowed to come along. It just doesn't get to drive. Plan stays: show the one-page outline, ask for two classrooms, offer a trial month. Rajni texted 'you've got this' with far too many exclamation marks.
Monday, 9 p.m.
Anxious through the first five minutes. Voice wobbled once. Then the principal asked about timings, and I forgot to be scared. We got one classroom and a trial month. Not everything. But the fear wasn't a forecast. It was just fear, sitting in the passenger seat.
Shankar

What was the meeting with the principal about?
It was about the proposal for a Saturday coding club.
How did Shankar feel before the meeting, and how was that feeling handled?
Shankar felt anxious, with cold hands and a rewritten first sentence, but let the feeling stay while refusing to treat it as a sign the meeting would fail.
Why was keeping the plan written down a good move?
A fixed plan, the outline, two classrooms and a trial month, gave Shankar something to follow even while anxious, so the feeling rode along without steering.
What would change if Shankar had let the anxious voice decide?
Shankar might have cancelled or asked for less, and there would be no classroom and no trial month.

It takes Roque two hours to walk to work and one hour to ride his bike to work. Roque walks to and from work three times a week and rides his bike to and from work twice a week. How many hours in total does he take to get to and from work a week with walking and biking?

Roque takes 2*3 = 6 hours a week to walk to work.
Roque takes 6*2 = 12 hours a week to walk to and from work.
Roque takes 1*2 = 2 hours a week to bike to work.
Roque takes 2*2 = 4 hours a week to bike to and from work.
In total, Roque takes 12+4 = 16 hour a week to go to and from work.
The answer is 16.

In their village near Nashik, Arohi, twenty-five, kept a small shed of farm tools her late father had left. She lent them to anyone who asked: the widow next door, the schoolteacher, the boys fixing the temple roof. She never kept count. But Gautam, from the upper fields, was different. He borrowed the plough every season, returned it caked in mud, once with a cracked handle, and never lent her his tractor when she asked. This year he came again. Arohi's heart beat faster, but she kept her voice calm. "Gautam-bhai, I've lent you the plough six seasons. When I needed the tractor, you said no. I can't lend it again unless things go both ways." He looked annoyed. "It's just a plough." "Then you won't miss it," she said, and closed the shed door gently.

How many seasons had Arohi lent Gautam the plough?
She'd lent it to him six seasons.
What was Arohi feeling as she spoke to Gautam?
Arohi felt nervous, her heart beating faster, yet calm and firm in setting a fair limit.
How does Arohi show that generosity and limits can go together?
She keeps lending freely to neighbours in need but refuses a habitual taker, explaining why calmly.
How might Gautam feel being refused?
Gautam seemed annoyed and perhaps embarrassed, used to getting the plough without giving back.

On Saturday morning Harsha put a notebook on the kitchen table before Jatin had finished his tea. "Everything's in here," she said. "The loan, the two extra payments I made in August, the amount my brother still owes, and the messages where he asked me not to tell you. I hid it, and that was wrong. I'd rather you read it all now than find one more piece later."

Jatin read for an hour without speaking. Then he asked two small questions, and she answered both.

They started keeping a shared sheet for money, checked together on the first of each month, and agreed that any help for family would be talked over between them before it left the account. "It's not forever," Jatin said. "And it's not just you." He added his own cousin's wedding gift to the list.

Over chai, Joseph listened to Jatin describe a good fortnight followed by one awful night when an old text popped up. "That sounds normal," Joseph said. "It comes back in bits. Be patient with the bad days. And if it just won't ease, a counsellor could help you both talk without picking the scab."

Jatin looked at the notebook on the shelf and nodded.

What did Harsha bring to the kitchen table on Saturday morning?
She brought a notebook with everything written down about the loan, the extra payments, what her brother still owes, and his messages.
How did the notebook and the shared sheet work together in rebuilding trust, and what did each give Jatin and Harsha?

The notebook gave one complete account so new facts would stop surfacing, and the shared sheet gave Jatin regular visibility while giving Harsha a way to show change, with both accepting it is not forever.
What was Jatin probably feeling when the old text popped up on that awful night?
He felt the hurt flare up again and worried that trust was slipping, which is why he later described the night to Joseph.
What might Joseph's advice mean for how Jatin treats a bad day?
Jatin can treat a bad day as a normal setback rather than proof that nothing has healed, and consider a counsellor if the hurt will not ease.
What are bristles on a brush, and where else do you find them?

Bristles are short, stiff hairs, such as those on a toothbrush or on some animals. It is a noun, the plural of bristle.
Example: The bristles of the new brush were soft and white.

When three children reported Kishore for pushing Aman and taking his lunch money, the headmistress, Himani Ma'am, acted that day.

First she sat with Aman and his father. "You did nothing wrong. A teacher will watch the corridor at break, and my door is open."

Then she called Kishore in. She was firm. "This stops today. You'll miss sports for two weeks and you'll write to Aman about what you did."

Kishore stared at the floor, arms folded.

Then her voice softened. "But I also want to understand. What's going on for you, Kishore?"

After a long silence he said, "At home nobody listens to me. Here, when I'm tough, people do."

Himani Ma'am nodded. "Then let's find you a better way to be listened to." She arranged for him to meet the counsellor every week.

What consequence did Kishore get?
He'll miss sports for two weeks and write to Aman about what he did.
What did Kishore reveal about why he bullied?
He felt unheard and powerless at home, and being tough at school made people listen to him.
Why is Himani Ma'am's approach balanced?
She protects Aman first, is firm with Kishore about consequences, and also asks what drives him and arranges counselling.
How might Aman feel after meeting Himani Ma'am with his father?
He is likely relieved and safer, knowing a teacher will watch the corridor and that he did nothing wrong.

messages.content: It takes 5 people to lift a car and twice as many people to lift a truck. How many people are needed to lift 6 cars and 3 trucks?

It takes 5 x 2 = 10 people to lift a truck.
5 x 6 = 30 people are needed to lift the cars.
10 x 3 = 30 people are needed to lift the trucks.
Altogether, 30 + 30 = 60 people are needed.
The answer is 60.

What was Ankita afraid of under the urge to send the fourth text?

16 mangoes are shared equally among 4 families. How many does each family get? What part of the mangoes is that?

Answer: 4 mangoes each. Each family gets a quarter.

Deal into 4 baskets: one each, round and round, until none are left. Count one basket: 4. A quarter of 16 is 4.

"Did you see that?" Ramesh shouted over the noise. "That guy just grabbed our flag!"
The street screening outside the chai shop had turned rowdy since the last wicket. A group from across the lane was chanting now, loud and ugly, and one of them was waving Ramesh's small flag like a trophy.
"Let it go," Afreen said, keeping her voice low and steady.
"It's our flag!"
"It's a cheap flag. Look at them. Look how many."
Ramesh looked. Eight or nine young men, faces red, pushing closer to the screen. Someone knocked over a plastic chair.
"Where's our way out?" Afreen asked.
"Behind us. The lane by the bakery."
"Then that's where we're going. Walk. Don't look back at them, don't shout anything."
They edged away, past the bakery and out onto the main road. Behind them the chanting rose. A police van turned into the lane.
Ramesh let out a breath. "I really wanted to go back for the flag."
"I know. That's why I held your sleeve."

Where was the way out?
The lane by the bakery, behind them.
What was Ramesh feeling when the flag was grabbed?
Ramesh felt angry and provoked, wanting to go back for the flag.
What did Afreen do to keep them safe?
She stayed low and steady, told Ramesh to let the flag go, identified their exit, and led them away without looking back or shouting.
What would have happened if Ramesh had gone back for the flag?
He could have walked into a group of eight or nine agitated men and started a fight, risking injury for a cheap flag.
A neighbour keeps asking to borrow our ladder and I don't always want to lend it.
It's fine to have limits with your belongings. Is it a problem because the ladder doesn't come back, or because you need it?
Mostly because it comes back late and dusty.
Then you could say, 'Please bring it back by evening and wipe it down.' If it still bothers you, suggest they get their own, or share the cost of one with others in the lane.
I don't want to sound rude.
A friendly tone and a clear request are not rude. People generally respect a polite 'Yes, as long as...'
I'll say that next time.
Short and kind is all it needs.
He said sure, and he even wiped it. Maybe I overthought it.
That happens a lot. A clear sentence often settles a worry that grew bigger in your head.

Hurt and humiliated; his ears were red and he tried to smile while holding out his hand.

Dolma and Noor, both fifteen, had a joint presentation on the city's lakes due Monday at their Bengaluru school. They'd split it: Dolma would research, Noor would make the slides. But Dolma thought, Noor's good with slides; she'll fill in whatever's missing. And Noor thought, Dolma always over-prepares; she'll cover for me. So Dolma spent Saturday at a cousin's wedding, and Noor spent Sunday on a video marathon. On Monday morning, they met at the gate. Dolma had two pages of notes. Noor had four slides with no text. They looked at each other and understood. In front of the class, they stumbled and repeated each other. They got a C. If both had done their parts, they would have got an A. On the bus home, neither spoke.

What grade did Dolma and Noor get?
They got a C.
What was Dolma thinking when she chose to go to the wedding?
Dolma felt relaxed and sure Noor would fill in whatever was missing, so it seemed safe to shirk.
What could the girls have done differently?
They could have checked in with each other on Saturday and set deadlines for each part, so neither could quietly rely on the other.
How might Noor feel on the silent bus ride home?
Noor probably felt embarrassed and guilty, knowing her shortcut hurt both of them.

"Santosh the detective," you called me, Hansa. Fine, I'll explain the phone notes. Last Sunday my daughter Chinki ran in from the courtyard crying, knee scraped. My first thought was, did those Sharma boys push her? But I stopped myself. I just held her and asked, "What happened, Chinki?" She hiccupped. "I ran after the kitten and the step was there." That's all. I typed it into my phone right then, with the time. Evening comes, my mother asks her, "Did those boys push you?" and Chinki nods, big eyes. "Yes, they pushed." If I hadn't written down the first version, I'd have gone next door to fight. Instead I showed Amma my note. She laughed and said, "Arre, I put the boys in her head."

What did Chinki say first when Santosh asked what happened?
"I ran after the kitten and the step was there."
What was Santosh's first worry when Chinki ran in crying, and what shows Santosh set it aside?
Santosh worried the Sharma boys had pushed her, but Santosh stopped, held Chinki and asked only "What happened?"
Which choice kept Santosh from a fight with the neighbours?
Typing Chinki's first account into the phone with the time. When she later agreed the boys pushed her, Santosh could show the earlier note.
How might the Sharma boys have been affected if Santosh had trusted the evening version?
They could have been blamed and scolded for a push that never happened, only because a question suggested it to a small child.

I'm Preeti, and last spring I became convinced my manager, Vijay, was watching my screen. Every time I opened a job site on my lunch break, an email from him seemed to land within minutes. It happened on Monday. Then Wednesday. My stomach dropped each time. I started closing tabs and jumping at notification sounds. One evening I made myself ask: what would this look like if it were just chance? He sends dozens of emails a day. So for two weeks I noted every time I opened the site and every email from him, matched or not. Twenty-six emails. Four near my breaks. The rest came at any time at all. That helped. But I was still tense, still scanning for signs, and it was wearing me out. So I booked a session with a counsellor. Talking it through helped more than any spreadsheet.

How many emails from Vijay did Preeti count, and how many came near the breaks?
Twenty-six emails, and four came near the breaks.
How was Preeti feeling during those weeks, and what shows it?
Anxious and on edge 😰 Preeti's stomach dropped each time, and Preeti kept closing tabs and jumping at notification sounds.
What two steps did Preeti take, and why did both matter?
Preeti tested the pattern against chance for two weeks, then booked a counsellor when the tension kept wearing on, because the numbers alone did not ease the worry.
How might Vijay have been affected if Preeti had acted on the belief without testing it?
Vijay could have been treated with suspicion or accused of spying over emails that were simply part of an ordinary busy day.

People in India understand it, but standard English says: "Tomorrow is a holiday" or "I have the day off tomorrow."

In the skills lab of the nursing college in Nagpur, Chaitanya was first to volunteer for every practical: blood pressure, bed baths, the careful way to turn a patient without hurting them. He had learned most of it already, in two years of nights beside his father's hospital bed.

"That's why I joined," he told his classmate Nirmala. "So someone else's Baba gets what mine got at the end. Good care."

Nirmala watched him on their first ward posting. He was steady with every patient until they reached the long-stay unit. There he stopped at the door, hand on the frame, and went very pale.

Later, in the canteen, she said, "You can be a great nurse and still need to grieve him, you know. The college counsellor has hours on Fridays."

Chaitanya stirred his tea. "Maybe Friday," he said.

How long had Chaitanya spent nights beside his father's hospital bed?
Chaitanya spent two years of nights beside his father's hospital bed.
What was Chaitanya feeling at the door of the long-stay unit?
Chaitanya was likely hit by grief for his Baba, as the unit seemed to bring back those hospital nights, even though nursing gives the loss purpose.
What does Nirmala's suggestion add to Chaitanya's plan?
It keeps his purpose in nursing while giving his grief its own space, through the college counsellor on Fridays.
How might Nirmala feel watching Chaitanya go pale?
Nirmala likely felt concerned and protective, which is why she raised the counsellor gently later.

Dear Jyoti,

You asked why I sounded so rattled on the phone. Here is the honest version.
Since Papa's first fall in January, I've had no plan. When the neighbour calls to say he's fallen, I run out of the office. When Mummy's sugar goes up and she needs the hospital, I run out again. Six times in four months, each time with no notice.
Last week my manager said, quite kindly, that the team can't depend on me for the client launch. They've given it to someone else. I've heard people call me "the one who disappears".
And the worst part: when I was in Delhi for a two-day training, Papa fell again, and there was nobody. The neighbour sat with him for three hours until I found an auto driver to take them to the clinic.
We need a real plan, Jyoti, and I can't make it alone. Can we talk this Sunday?

Pankaj

How many times did Pankaj leave the office suddenly in four months?
Six times in four months.
How is Pankaj feeling, and what shows it?
Pankaj feels rattled and ashamed, hearing colleagues use the nickname "the one who disappears" and losing the client launch.
Which approach would suit Pankaj better than reacting to each crisis?
Pankaj and Jyoti could make a plan with emergency contacts, a nearby hospital, a spare key with a neighbour and some regular help, so there is backup when he is away.
How is Papa affected by the lack of a plan?
When Pankaj was away, Papa had to wait three hours after a fall with only the neighbour, showing the family had no backup.

Every Sunday in Seoul, Paulo made feijoada in a pot far too big for his tiny studio: black beans soaked overnight, garlic filling the corridor. At noon he propped his phone against the rice cooker and video-called his mother in Recife, where it was just past midnight and she was cooking the same dish. They compared bubbles and laughed. This year, for the first time, he invited people too: Soo-ah from his lab, her roommate, and the old man downstairs who always asked about the smell. Soo-ah brought kimchi. The old man brought rice wine and stayed three hours. When Paulo's mother saw them all squeezed onto his floor, she clapped. 'You have a family there too!'

Where did Paulo prop the phone for the video call?
Against the rice cooker.
What might Paulo feel when his mother says "You have a family there too!"?
Paulo probably feels warm and relieved, seeing that keeping home alive and making friends in Seoul can go together. 😊
What choice did Paulo make this year, and why did it help?
Paulo invited Soo-ah, her roommate and the neighbour to the Sunday meal, turning a private ritual into a way to build friendships where he lives.
What might the Sunday meal mean to the old man downstairs?
The old man, who always asked about the smell, may feel welcomed and less lonely, which is perhaps why he stayed three hours.

The mock test results went up on the coaching centre's board in Jaipur at six, and Rajni was there at five-fifty. She scanned for her name at the top. It was second. Second, by one mark. Her ears rang. Vishal Sir, the physics teacher everyone feared and admired, walked past and said, "Good work, Rajni." It should have felt good. Instead she only heard the word second. That night she skipped dinner, pinned the rank list above her desk and planned four extra hours of problems a day. Her mother knocked at one a.m. "Sleep, beta. You're more than a rank." Rajni didn't look up. "Not yet," she said. "Not until I'm first."

Where did the mock test results go up?
On the coaching centre's board in Jaipur.
Why did Vishal Sir's praise not feel good to Rajni?
Rajni measured her worth by coming first, so being second by one mark made her feel she had failed despite the praise.
What could Rajni's mother try that might help more than a late-night knock?
She could choose a calm moment to talk about how proud she is of Rajni's effort, and help plan rest time, not just urge sleep at one a.m.
How might Rajni's mother feel when Rajni says 'Not until I'm first'?
Her mother may feel worried and sad that Rajni ties her worth so tightly to rank and leaves no room for rest.

At the school gate, both parents had been called in after a note home about Damini's missing diary. Papa said, "No games this week." Before Damini could explain that the diary was with the librarian, she shouted, "It is not fair! You never listen!" Mama pressed her lips. In the school library, waiting, Damini's friend Lalremsiami whispered, "Cool down first. Then tell them once." Damini looked at the shelves and counted her breaths. Later, at the reading table, she said quietly, "I was upset because I did not get to explain. The diary was with the librarian." Papa sighed. "Show me."

Where was the diary really?
It was with the librarian.
Why did Damini shout at the school gate?
She was upset that her parents punished her before hearing her side, and she felt it was not fair.
What worked better than shouting for Damini?
She cooled down by counting breaths and then told her parents once, calmly, what had happened. 😊
How might Papa have felt when Damini shouted at the gate?
Papa may have felt worried and annoyed at the note, and reacted quickly to the missing diary, then softened when she spoke calmly.

Anand: Papa asked what day it is 15 times since lunch
Vishal: oof. how are you holding up
Anand: badly. I snapped at him. then he looked scared and I felt like a monster
Vishal: you're not a monster. you're exhausted
Anand: I don't know how to keep answering

Anand: I'll try
Anand: ok I said 'it's Thursday, Papa' and then asked him to help me sort the old photos. he told me about his army days for an hour
Vishal: that's great. and when do YOU get a break?
Anand: never really
Vishal: I'm coming Saturday. you go out for 2 hours
Anand: thank you. seriously

How many times had Papa asked what day it was since lunch?
Fifteen times.
How did Anand feel after snapping at Papa?
Anand felt guilty and awful, like a monster, when Papa looked scared.
What did Vishal suggest that worked?
A short answer in the same words, then redirecting Papa to an activity like sorting old photos.
How might Papa have felt telling stories about his army days?
Papa probably felt happy and engaged, enjoying his memories and the company.
