I will reach home after band practice.

We watched a film yesterday. The film was very funny.

"Farida, I miss Leeds so much."

"You've said that every night this week, Elizabeth."

"It's just, everyone there was lovely. My friends, my mum's cooking. Here, nothing feels right."

"Didn't you say you couldn't wait to leave Leeds?"

"That was... different."

"And you haven't gone to a single society meeting here."

"I don't know anyone."

"You won't if you stay in bed thinking about Leeds."

Elizabeth pulled the blanket up. "I just want it to feel like home."

"I know. Come to the film club with me tonight. Just one."

Elizabeth sighed. "Fine. One."

What did Farida invite Elizabeth to?
The film club tonight.
Why does Elizabeth keep talking about Leeds every night?
She feels homesick and lonely, and thinking about home is easier and more comforting than facing the new place.
What small step did Farida suggest, and why is it helpful?
Going to just one film club meeting, which lets Elizabeth start building a life here without leaving home behind.
How might Farida feel hearing about Leeds every night?
Farida probably feels sympathetic but also a bit tired, and wants to help Elizabeth move forward.

Jasleen's phone had a cracked screen and nine percent battery when she sat down in the hospital corridor to make the rota. Her mother would be in for at least another week, the power had been going off at home every evening, and her final-term assignments were due Friday.
She drew seven boxes in her notebook. Nights at the hospital, medicine pickup, cooking for Nani, who lived with them.
Then she used the battery carefully. She called her brother Harman first: "You take Monday, Wednesday and Friday nights." Then Masi: "Can you cook Tuesdays and Thursdays?" Masi said yes before she finished. Her last call was to Dilnaz aunty from the flat below: "Could you pick up medicines on Saturday mornings?"
The phone died after the third call. Jasleen tore out the page and taped it to the nurses' notice board for the family to photograph. That night, for the first time in a week, she slept at home.

How much battery did Jasleen's phone have when she started?
It had nine percent battery.
What was Jasleen likely feeling when she began making the rota?
She was likely exhausted and pressured, with her mother in hospital, power cuts at home and assignments due Friday.
What else could Jasleen do if one person drops a slot?
She could name a back-up for each task on the same page, so one missed day doesn't fall back on her alone.
How might Masi feel being asked to cook?
Masi seems glad to help, saying yes before Jasleen even finished, perhaps relieved to have a clear way to be useful.

Aparna's father, Kunal, was zipping his suitcase for a seven o'clock flight when she came into the room, pale.
"Papa, I have to tell you something, and you have to go soon."
He glanced at the clock. Forty minutes before the taxi. He sat down on the bed anyway.
"Tell me."
"This evening I was cycling in the lane and I scraped Mehta Uncle's car. A long line. And I... rode away. Nobody saw."
She waited for the explosion.
Kunal breathed out slowly. "Thank you for telling me, even with me leaving. That took courage."
"Are you angry?"
"A bit. Mostly I'm glad you came to me. Let's go now, together."
They rang Mehta Uncle's bell. Aparna apologised herself. Mehta Uncle said they'd sort out the repair later.
Kunal made his taxi with four minutes to spare.

What time was Kunal's flight?
It was a seven o'clock flight.
What was Aparna feeling when she told her father?
Aparna was pale and afraid, expecting an explosion of anger and punishment.
What did Kunal do that encouraged honesty?
He sat down despite the rush, listened first, thanked her for telling, admitted he was a bit angry but calm, and helped her put it right.
How might Mehta Uncle have felt when Aparna apologised herself?
He was probably annoyed about the scratch but touched by her honesty, which may be why he was willing to sort out the repair calmly.
A weather report said the wind was chilling. Does that just mean cold?

Yes, in that sentence. Chilling means very cold, in a way that makes you shiver. It is an adjective. It can also mean frightening, as in a chilling story.
Example: A chilling wind blew across the field as the match began.

On payday at the district hospital in Ernakulam, the staff room filled with talk of new phones and sales. Seema, a staff nurse, didn't join in. Six months ago she'd noticed that her pay vanished by the fifteenth, every time. So she'd gone to the hospital's payroll office and asked them to send a fixed part of her salary straight into a separate account on payday, before she ever saw it. She'd deleted the shopping apps from her phone. And on her locker, she'd stuck a photo of the small course in wound care she wanted to take in Bengaluru next year, with the date written under it. Her colleague Pradeep asked, "Don't you want the new phone?" "I do," Seema said. "But I want the course more, and future me can't fight today's sales alone." She smiled at the photo.

Where did Seema stick the photo of the course?
On her locker.
How does Seema seem to feel when Pradeep asks about the new phone?
She seems calm and content, admitting she wants it but feeling steadier because her plan protects the course she wants more.
Which of Seema's steps help her future self most, and why?
Having part of her pay moved automatically, deleting shopping apps and keeping a dated photo of the course, which make the future reward concrete and remove temptations.
How might Pradeep see Seema's choices?
Pradeep seems curious and a little puzzled, since most of the staff room is excited about spending.

Thursday night. Told Papa and Mummy about the teaching course tonight. Papa put down his spoon. "Bank means security. You want to throw it away?" Mummy started crying and asked what people would say. My old self would have shouted. Instead I breathed, went to my room and brought the sheet I made with Rekha didi last week: the fees, eight months of savings, and the date by which I would apply back to banks if it does not work. Papa read it twice and said nothing. Mummy asked, quietly, how much the fee was. I said I know they are scared, and that I am scared too. Nobody agreed, but nobody left the table either. Tomorrow I will show them the school I visited. Vasudha

Vasudha tells Papa and Mummy about a teaching course, and they are upset. Vasudha stays calm and shows a plan with fees, savings and a backup date. Nobody agrees, but nobody leaves, and tomorrow Vasudha will show them the school.

I'm Parveen, and Imran's been in my study group since first year. Last week the others were planning a beach trip: flights, a villa, "just ask your parents". Imran said he had shifts at the call centre that weekend. He always has shifts. He did his whole presentation on a phone because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible "this month". When our professor praised it in front of the class, Imran smiled, a proper wide smile I've rarely seen. But in the canteen, when Rhea complained her father had "only" given her ten thousand for the trip, Imran's jaw tightened and he went very quiet. I can't know exactly what he feels. I think it's something like pride and something like anger, taking turns.

Why did Imran do his whole presentation on a phone?
Because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible that month.
What might Imran's tightened jaw in the canteen suggest?
It suggests anger or resentment at how easily others get money and trips, though Parveen can't be sure.
What could Parveen and the group choose when planning the next outing?
They could plan something that doesn't depend on parents' money and check Imran's shifts first, so he isn't always the one saying no.
How might Imran have felt when the professor praised his presentation?
He probably felt proud, shown by the rare wide smile, since he managed it on a phone without the tools others had.

In Kalwa town, Sudha wanted to start a small business before Diwali. Her friend Rajni suggested a stall in the market. Sudha shook her head. "What if nobody buys anything? I'd waste all my savings."

Instead, she bought one sheet of coloured card, glue and some glitter, and made ten greeting cards at the kitchen table with little hand-painted diyas. Her mother gave her an old shoebox to keep them in.

That weekend she took the box to her aunt's house, then to three neighbours. She sold eight in two days. One neighbour asked, "Can you write 'Happy Diwali' in Marathi too?" Another said the glitter came off on her hands.

Sudha wrote down every comment. Then she made twenty more: some in Marathi, no loose glitter. This time Rajni helped her sell at the temple gate. They sold eighteen.

How many cards did Sudha make at first?
Ten greeting cards.
What was Sudha worried about when she refused the market stall?
She was anxious that nobody would buy anything and she would lose her savings.
What could Sudha do next, based on the second batch?
She could ask buyers what else they would like, such as wedding or birthday cards, before making a larger batch.
How might the neighbour who asked for Marathi cards feel about the new batch?
That neighbour would probably feel pleased and listened to, seeing the suggestion turned into new cards.

After a post of hers was badly received, Sonali opened her phone to hundreds of hostile comments. Her hands shook, but she put the phone down and decided to wait a day. By morning the heat inside her had cooled, and she was glad she had not typed anything at midnight. Omkar took a different first step. He made his accounts private, muted certain words, saved screenshots of the threatening messages and reported them to the platform. He did all that before saying anything in public. Santosh answered comment after comment through the night. Each reply pulled in new attacks and fresh screenshots, and by dawn he was worn out and shaking. Weeks later, Sonali returned with a smaller circle of followers. She looked at messages just at chosen hours and saw a counsellor to talk through the strain, slowly building a calmer bond with the site.

What did Omkar save before saying anything in public?
He saved screenshots of the threatening messages.
How does Santosh's response to the comments differ from Sonali's, and what happened to each?
Santosh replied all night, which drew fresh attacks and left him exhausted. Sonali waited a day, so her emotion dropped and she did not add fuel.
What was Santosh probably feeling as he answered comment after comment?
He was likely angry and desperate to set things straight, though it left him worn out and shaking.
What could Santosh do now?
He could stop replying, lock his accounts, save the abusive messages and report them, then talk to someone he trusts or a counsellor. 🤍

Shashthi. Arnab's new kurta is nice, cotton, sky blue. Then Indu from his class walks into the pandal in a silk one with mirror work, and Arnab tugs at his collar all evening.
Ashtami. The half-yearly results arrive on the class group. Arnab has 84 percent, his best ever. Indu has 91. Arnab mutes the group and tells Ma the paper was "unfair". At dinner he picks at his luchi. "Why do some people get everything?"
Dashami. He carries his little cousin through the crowd to watch the immersion. The boy on his shoulders shrieks with joy at everything. Arnab catches himself smiling. His 84 is still his best. The kurta is still nice. Only looking at Indu had made them feel small.

What percentage did Arnab get in the half-yearly exam?
84 percent, his best ever.
Why does Arnab tell Ma the paper was "unfair"?
He feels cheated and envious comparing his 84 with Indu's 91, even though 84 is his best ever.
What could Arnab try when the comparison starts next time?
He could compare his marks with his own past results, as he does when he remembers 84 is his best, rather than with the classmate a step ahead.
How might Ma see Arnab's mood at dinner?
Ma might be puzzled and a little worried that her son calls his best result unfair and asks why some people get everything.

The sand company's offer came to the panchayat office in Malpur during the harvest season, and Gargi, twenty-six and the village's youngest sarpanch, had a week to answer.
The money would pay for a new school roof. But the river bank near the fields was already crumbling, and the company wanted to dig there.
Gargi didn't decide alone. She walked the bank with two older farmers. She called Jasleen, a friend who worked at the district environment office, to ask what digging did to riverbanks in other villages. She held a meeting in the temple courtyard and let the women speak first.
On Friday she wrote her reply: no digging near the fields; the panchayat would apply to the district for a school repair grant instead, and she would lead the application herself.
Some men grumbled that she'd thrown away money. She knew that risk, and signed anyway.

What would the sand company's money pay for?
It would pay for a new school roof.
How might Gargi have felt signing the reply while some men grumbled?
She probably felt uneasy about the criticism but firm and confident in a decision she had checked carefully.
Which of Gargi's steps made the decision stronger, and why?
Walking the bank with farmers, asking an expert and hearing the women first gave her a full picture of risks and impacts.
What would change for the farmers if the company had dug near the fields?
Their crumbling river bank could have given way further, putting their fields and harvests at risk.

I share a room with my brother Gurpreet, so I saw the whole trick. Mummy said, 'Clean your side in five minutes or no cricket.' Gurpreet looked at the mess, then at the bed. In went everything: socks, comics, his school shoes, a half-eaten biscuit packet, all shoved underneath with his foot. Mummy peeped in and smiled. 'Very good!' He went off to cricket, grinning. Next morning at 7:15, the van was honking and Gurpreet was flat on the floor, arm under the bed up to the shoulder, pulling out socks and comics but no shoes. What did Gurpreet shove under the bed?
Socks, comics, his school shoes and a half-eaten biscuit packet.
What might Gurpreet have been feeling as the van honked?
He looked close to tears, so he probably felt panicky and sorry he'd hidden the shoes.
What would have worked better than hiding the mess?
Putting things in their places, even quickly, like shoes by the door; hiding them made the room look neat but lost the shoes.
How does Mummy see the room the day before?
Mummy peeps in, sees a neat room and says 'Very good!', not knowing the mess is under the bed.

Discouraged means having lost confidence or hope, so you feel less like trying. Here it is an adjective.

Tanisha sent a funny sticker to Kunal on his birthday.

Kunal felt suspicious and had already decided she was fake, so every message seemed like proof and the friendly ones felt like they didn't count.

Kishore asked Kunal to scroll up and look at all the messages together, so the skipped friendly ones came into view.

Last year's school picnic to the dam was, I told everybody, a disaster. I'm Pallavi, and when people asked, I only talked about the end: the sudden rain, my shoe stuck in the mud, and the long wet bus ride home. Then this year, Parveen showed me the photos from that day on her mother's phone. There we were, jumping in the shallow water. Sharing pakoras on the rocks. Me winning the frog-jumping race, with a medal made from a bottle cap. The whole morning was sunny, and I was laughing in every photo. I had forgotten all of it. What was Pallavi's medal made from?
It was made from a bottle cap.
How did Pallavi feel on seeing the photos, and why?
Pallavi felt strange and surprised, realising the rainy ending had become the whole memory while a sunny, happy morning had been forgotten.
What helped Pallavi remember the picnic more fairly, and what could help next time?
Looking at the photos from the whole day; next time Pallavi could think back through the morning before summing up a trip.
How might Parveen see the picnic?
Parveen, who had the photos, might remember the water games and pakoras, and be surprised the picnic was called a disaster.

A movie theater charges $5 for matinee tickets, $7 for evening tickets, and $10 for opening night tickets. A bucket of popcorn costs $10. On Friday, they had 32 matinee customers, 40 evening customers, and 58 customers for an opening night showing of a movie. If half the customers bought popcorn, how much money in dollars did the theater make on Friday night?

The movie theater made 5 * 32 = $160 in matinee tickets.
It made 7 * 40 = $280 in evening tickets.
It made 10 * 58 = $580 in opening night tickets.
There were 32 + 40 + 58 = 130 customers.
Half of the customers bought popcorn, so 130 / 2 = 65 bought popcorn.
Thus, the theater made 10 * 65 = $650 from popcorn.
Therefore, in all, the theater made 160 + 280 + 580 + 650 = $1670 on Friday night.
The answer is 1670.

Last winter my brother Siddharth had bad asthma attacks, and our whole house turned around him. Mummy slept in his room. Papa rushed home early with his medicines. Nobody came to my annual day, where I was the lead tree in the play. I'm Bhavna, and I remember thinking, I wish I were sick too. Then I felt awful, because some nights Siddharth could hardly breathe. One evening I told Papa both things: that I was jealous, and that I felt terrible for being jealous. He didn't get angry. He said both feelings made sense. After that, Papa and I had Sunday mornings for just the two of us, making poha together. And I read comics to Siddharth when he was stuck in bed.

What part did Bhavna play at annual day?
The lead tree in the play.
What two feelings did Bhavna have about Siddharth's illness?
Jealous of all the attention he got, and then guilty for feeling that while he could hardly breathe.
What did Bhavna do with those feelings?
Bhavna told Papa honestly, got Sunday mornings alone with him, and still read comics to Siddharth.
How might Papa have felt hearing Bhavna's confession?
Understanding, and perhaps sorry Bhavna had felt left out, since he said both feelings made sense and made time for them.

The rain hadn't stopped for three hours, and Naveen was already late for his first job interview in Pune when his old car stalled at the traffic light. He slapped the steering wheel. 'Not today, Laddoo! Why do you always do this to me?' His friend Suraj, in the passenger seat, raised an eyebrow. 'Laddoo?' 'She's moody. She hates rain.' Laddoo.
What was Naveen feeling when he slapped the steering wheel?

He booked a service, dealing with the real cause instead of only coaxing the car.
How does Suraj see Naveen's explanation of the car's behaviour?

messages.content: Help me choose a return gift for the kids at my cousin's party. There will be eight children.
Return gifts can be simple. Something small and useful works well. What age are the children?
Between five and eight. The party is for my cousin Kunal's eighth birthday.
For that age, small colour pencil packs, stickers, a mini notebook or a bouncy ball are popular. Put them in a paper bag with each child's name on it.
I like the notebook and a pencil together. Can I decorate the bags?
Yes, decorated bags are a nice touch. Use markers, stamps made from potato slices, or paper stars. Children love opening something that looks special.
That sounds cheap and cute. Should I add a sweet too?
A sweet is fine, though check with Kunal's parents about allergies. Wrapped chocolates or toffees are easy, and you can skip them if any child is unable to eat them.
Actually, let's skip the sweets and add stickers. Can you remind me what the main gift is?
The main gift is a mini notebook with a pencil, in a decorated paper bag with each child's name. With stickers instead of sweets, it is a neat return gift for Kunal's party.

Fifty runs today on the practice mat in Joseph's garage. My arm aches from resetting the robot. Joseph thought it was pointless ("it works, Urmi, we've seen it work"), but I made him call out each failure while I wrote it down.
Tally by 6 pm:
left wheel wobbling off: 9
missed the black line at the sharp turn: 4
stopped for no reason: 2
Fifteen fails out of fifty. And more than half of them are the same silly wheel! I would never have guessed. I thought the turn was our big problem.
Joseph tightened the grub screw and added a drop of glue. We ran ten more before his mum called us for dinner: zero wheel falls. 😊
Tomorrow: the sharp turn.
Urmila

How many times did the left wheel wobble off?
The left wheel wobbled off 9 times.
How did Urmila feel on seeing the tally?
Urmila was surprised and a bit exasperated that the same wheel caused more than half the fails, not the turn.
What would you tackle next, and why?
The sharp turn, since it now causes the most fails; running and logging another set will show whether both fixes hold.
How might Joseph see the fifty runs now?
Joseph thought testing was pointless, but zero wheel falls after his fix likely show him why the log mattered.

In the April heat of their village near Bundi, Sarita's rose, growing in a clay pot on the flat roof, suddenly looked scorched. Every afternoon the leaves at the top turned crisp and papery. Sudha-kaki, drying chillies next door, called across, "The roof is a tawa at three o'clock." Sarita crouched by the pot and touched the soil. Dry as dust, though she had watered it that morning. She watched the shadows: after lunch, the neem tree's shade crept over one corner of the courtyard. So she carried the pot down and set it where the shade fell, with light in the morning. Then she tucked a layer of dry straw round the stem. A week later, the new leaves stayed soft and green.

On the second afternoon of the holidays, nine-year-old Devika flopped on the sofa and groaned, "I'm so bored." Her mother Ankita said only, "Mm," and carried on chopping. Devika sighed for a whole quarter of an hour. Then she looked at the cushions, the stool and the old blanket, and began to build a fort. By evening it had rooms, a shop and a password. At twenty, Devika opened her admission letter to the college she had dreamed of for years and felt strangely empty. The chase was over, and so was the direction it had given her. Her friend Noor asked why she was so quiet. "I got everything I wanted," Devika said. "So why do I feel nothing?" At twenty-five, she worked at a firm with the same commute, the same lift and the same tasks. She was not sad. She was grey. Most evenings she watched videos until midnight without choosing any. Noor, now her colleague, said, "When did anything last surprise you?" Devika thought about the fort and could not answer.

What did Devika build on the holiday afternoon?
She built a fort.
How do Devika's flat feelings at nine, twenty and twenty-five relate to one another?

At nine boredom led her to invent a fort once nobody hurried to fill it, at twenty getting into her dream college left her strangely empty because the chase that gave direction was over, and at twenty-five the same commute and tasks left her grey and drifting to videos. Emptiness at first opened the door to imagination, but later it sat without a new direction.
What was Devika feeling when she asked why she felt nothing after getting what she wanted?
She felt hollow and confused, missing the sense of direction her goal had given her.
What could Devika try to bring some direction back into her routine?
She could pick a small project she cares about, like a course or a new hobby, and set aside a regular hour for it instead of aimless videos.

What did the man say when he gave back the purse?

What does Afreen plan to do next time, and why is it a good start?
She plans to catch her first thought when it comes; spotting a snap judgment honestly, without beating herself up, leaves room for a fairer second thought.
How might the man on the platform have felt if he had noticed Afreen moving her bag away?

Lisa is a member of the photography club at school. Every weekend the club will go anywhere to take photos. Leslie took 10 photos of animals to share with the club. She also took 3 times as many photos of flowers as animals and took 10 fewer scenery than the flowers. If Lisa took 15 fewer photos last weekend, How many photos did she take then?

Lisa took 10 x 3 = 30 photos of flowers.
She took 30 - 10 = 20 photos of the scenery.
So, Lisa took 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 photos this week.
Therefore, Lisa took 60 - 15 = 45 photos last weekend.
The answer is 45.

Why does Jane let herself cry in this passage?

Now, however, I considered it well to let them flow as freely and as long as they liked. If the flood annoyed him, so much the better. So I gave way and cried heartily.
She had held back her tears because he would not like to see her weep. Now she lets them flow freely, and if the crying annoys him, she thinks that is all the better.
The sewers in Middleton can handle 240,000 gallons of run-off. Each hour of rain produces 1000 gallons of runoff. How many days of rain can the sewers handle before they overflow?

First find how many hours of runoff the sewers can handle: 240,000 / 1000 gallons/hour = 240 hours
Then divide that time by the number of hours per day to find how many days of rain the sewers can handle: 240 hours / 24 hours/day = 10 days
The answer is 10.

A baseball team has averaged 15 hits per game over their first 5 games. There are 11 players on the team. Their best player has 25 total hits. If the other players continue their average over the next 6 games, how many hits will each player average across the 6 games in total?

The best player averages 5 hits a game because 25 / 5 = 5
The rest of the team averages 10 hits a game because 15 - 5 = 10
The rest of the players average 1 hit a game because 10 / 10 = 1
They will average 6 hits per player over the next 6 games because 6 x 1 = 6
The answer is 6.

By nine in the morning, Akash had been in the block office line for two hours with his scholarship papers. About forty people stood in a bent line under the tin roof. Kamal, a boy from his college, stood just behind him.
A man in a crisp white shirt walked straight to the window. The clerk stood up and said, “Sir, please come inside.” The man was ahead of them all within a minute.
“Every time,” an old man muttered. Nobody else spoke. Akash felt heat in his chest, and his hands closed tight on the papers. He took a breath and asked the clerk politely, “Is there a separate window? We have been waiting since seven.” The clerk didn’t look up.

How long had Akash been in the block office line?
He had been in the line for two hours with his scholarship papers.
What was Akash feeling as his hands closed tight on the papers?
He felt angry and helpless. The heat in his chest and the tight hands show that he was upset, but the clerk did not respond to his question.
What small choice did Akash make instead of staying silent or exploding?
He took a breath and asked the clerk politely whether there was a separate window. He spoke up without insulting anyone.
How might Kamal, standing behind Akash, have taken this scene?
Kamal may have felt the same anger but stayed quiet like the others, or may have felt encouraged that Akash spoke. The passage does not say which.

"Ball!" signed Yusuf, five, and pointed at the sofa.
"Where?" signed his cousin Abhinav, hands turned up.
"On!" Yusuf's hand hopped over the other.
Abhinav shook his head, smiling. "Under," he signed, sliding his hand beneath. "Same hands, different way."
Yusuf copied it slowly. "Under the sofa," he signed.
Abhinav gave a thumbs up and fetched the ball.

Where was the ball, according to Yusuf's second try?
Under the sofa.
What might Yusuf feel when Abhinav shakes his head?
Perhaps a flicker of doubt or embarrassment. Abhinav's smile shows it is friendly, and Yusuf tried again.
How did Abhinav teach the sign?
He showed the difference in movement and had Yusuf copy it slowly.
How might Abhinav feel fetching the ball?
Pleased he could help Yusuf learn, and glad the message got through.

Every Sunday morning the Pnar hymn circle met in the church basement in Shillong, and Lalremsiami, nine, always stood beside Shalini, who came with her neighbour. Lalremsiami loved the part where the voices rose all together. Today the choir sang "Bless the Lord" and she closed her eyes; the hum in her chest felt like being carried. Beside her, Shalini kept her eyes open, counting the ceiling tiles, but tapped her foot to the beat. Afterwards over tea, Lalremsiami asked, "Did you like it?" "The tune is nice," Shalini said. "I like when everyone breathes together." Lalremsiami nodded. "That's my favourite part too." 🎶

Where did the hymn circle meet on Sunday mornings?
The hymn circle met in the church basement in Shillong.
What did the hum in her chest suggest about how Lalremsiami felt during the hymn?
It suggests she felt calm and carried by the shared voices, with closed eyes as evidence. Shalini's open eyes show that another child may feel something quite different.
What could Lalremsiami do if she wants to invite Shalini again without pressure?
She could ask again warmly, let Shalini join in whichever way she likes, and talk about what Shalini enjoys, like everyone breathing together.
How does Shalini experience the same hymn?
Shalini enjoys the tune and the shared breathing but stays watchful, counting tiles. Her joy is quieter and shows through her tapping foot.

"'Bhishma continued, "At these words of Muchukunda, Vaisravana, seeing the king fearless in the observance of Kshatriya duties, became filled with surprise. King Muchukunda, devoted to Kshatriya duties, continued to rule the entire earth obtained by the might of his own arms. That virtuous king who rules his kingdom, aided by and yielding precedence to the Brahmana, succeeds in subjugating the whole earth and achieving great fame. The Brahmana should every day perform his religious rites and the Kshatriya should always be armed with weapons. Between them they are the rightful owners of everything in the universe."'"

Can you sum this passage up in under 80 words?

Hearing Muchukunda's words, Vaisravana is surprised to see the king fearless in Kshatriya duties. Muchukunda goes on ruling the earth won by his own arms. Bhishma adds that a king who rules with a Brahmana's help wins the earth, and that Brahmanas should perform daily rites while Kshatriyas stay armed.

For most of last year our whole plan fit in one sentence: "When the hospital chain signs, we're fine." Yusuf and I had built a tool for tracking surgical supplies, and the chain's head nurse loved the pilot. Every call ended with "We'll move to purchase soon."
So I never wrote a proper plan. Why would I? One contract would cover us for years.
In October the chain's purchase department asked for a security audit we had never heard of, then went quiet. We had seven weeks of money. Yusuf and I spent those weeks cold-calling every small nursing home in Jaipur, begging for trials, sleeping four hours a night. We signed two, just barely enough.
What I'd do differently: from the first month, a plan B with real names on it. Hoping is what I did instead of planning.
— Hansa

What did the chain's purchase department ask for?
A security audit they had never heard of.
How did Hansa feel during the seven weeks of cold-calling?
Hansa felt desperate and exhausted, begging for trials on four hours' sleep.
What would Hansa do differently now?
Keep a plan B from the first month, with the real names of smaller customers to approach.
How might Yusuf have experienced relying on the one contract?
Yusuf was dragged into the last-minute scramble too, cold-calling and losing sleep because there was no backup.

Day one: At summer camp in Shimla, the leaders set up a sweets-trading game. Ritu, eleven, and Kiran were partners. If both shared fairly, both got six sweets. If one cheated by hiding sweets, the cheater got nine and the other got two. Ritu shared fairly. So did Kiran. Both got six.
Day three: Ritu heard a girl say that Kiran had cheated his partner in another game. Her stomach twisted. That round, Ritu hid three sweets. Kiran, who had shared again, got only two. He stared at her.
Day five: Ritu couldn't enjoy the extra sweets. She walked over to Kiran. "I heard you cheat people. I got scared." Kiran shook his head. "That was a rumour." Ritu handed him three sweets. "Next time I'll ask first."

How many sweets did each get if both shared fairly?
Both got six sweets.
What was Ritu feeling when she heard the rumour about Kiran?
Ritu felt anxious and afraid of being cheated, her stomach twisting, which pushed her to cheat first.
What went wrong, and what fixed it?
A rumour made Ritu cheat out of fear; apologising, returning the sweets and deciding to ask first helped repair the trust.
How did Kiran see Ritu's choice on day three?
Kiran felt hurt and surprised, staring at her because he had shared fairly again.

Avni: We talked about baby names last night. Danish wants an Urdu name, I want a Sanskrit one. We laughed, then went quiet. Jaya: How did you leave it? Avni: A name both families can say easily, plus a middle name from each side. Nobody wins, both belong. Jaya: And the rites? Avni: A registry signing first. Then a nikah at his home and a small puja at mine, same weekend. His mum asked if I will convert. I said no, kindly, and she said she just wanted to know. Jaya: Brave. And your parents? Avni: Papa is worried people will talk. I told him it's early, and we'll speak together next Sunday. Jaya: Proud of you 🙂

Which names did Danish and Avni each want for a baby?
Danish wants an Urdu name and Avni wants a Sanskrit one.
How does Avni feel about telling Papa, and what shows it?
Avni feels a little nervous but steady. Avni tells Papa it is early and plans to speak together the next Sunday.
What choice did Avni make when Danish's mum asked about converting, and why did it matter?
Avni answered no, kindly, and Danish's mum said she just wanted to know. It kept the talk honest and respectful without a fight.
How might Danish's mum have felt when she asked that question?
Probably curious and a little anxious, since she wanted to know where things stood and accepted the honest answer calmly.
Hire or higher: "We ___ a car for the trip."

Write "hired". "Hire" means to pay to use something or to employ someone. "Higher" means more high. Americans usually say "rent" for cars.
Examples: We hired a car for the trip to Mysore. The shelf is higher than my head.

"Vishal, you scored ninety-eight? Of course. You have the best coaching centre in the city."
"Tarun, I studied twelve hours a day."
"I believe you."
"Then why say 'of course'?"
"Because I studied twelve hours too. On the bus. In the shop after school."
"So you're saying I didn't deserve it?"
"No. You deserved it. You also had a quiet room, a coaching centre and an AC."
"That's not my fault."
"I didn't say it was."
Vishal crossed his arms. "It feels like you're saying my work doesn't count."
"Your work counts. My point is just... we didn't start at the same place."
Vishal looked away. "...Okay. I get that part."

What did Vishal score?
Vishal scored ninety-eight.
What was Vishal feeling when he crossed his arms?
He felt defensive and hurt, as if Tarun was saying his hard work didn't count.
What could Vishal do to show he understands?
He could say his work and his advantages are both real, and maybe share his notes or study space with Tarun.
How does Tarun see the difference between them?
Tarun sees that both worked hard, but Tarun studied on the bus and in the shop while Vishal had a quiet room and coaching.
My daughter Chloe will only eat plain rice and curd. How do I get her to try more?
Do not force it. Put a very small amount of a new food on her plate, next to the rice, and let her see you eating it. Children often need to see a food many times before they try it.
She is four. She likes the colour yellow.
Then use that. Make yellow foods like pumpkin curry, yellow dal, corn or banana. Call them fun names. A bright plate can make a four-year-old curious.
She likes a game called 'tasting detective'. Could I use that?
That is a great fit. Let Chloe be the detective and describe each bite: crunchy, soft, sweet or salty. A small sticker for each new food tasted can add to the fun.
Good. What can I mix into her curd rice?
Try stirring in a little mashed banana, grated carrot or a few pomegranate seeds. Start with a tiny bit so Chloe can still enjoy the rice she likes, and slowly add more as the detective game goes on.

At lunch in the Pune school canteen, Ishita watched Pranav walk up to the group's table with his tray. Riya turned her shoulder. Nimisha slid her bag onto the empty chair without a word. When Pranav asked, "Can I sit?" nobody answered, as if he had said it to the wall. Ishita stared at her rice, her ears warm. She wanted to say something, but the words sat like stones. Pranav stood for another second, then took his tray to the window ledge. All afternoon her stomach felt heavy. Next day in chemistry, she asked him quietly, "Want to be lab partners? I haven't picked yet." Pranav looked surprised. "Okay." It was a very small thing, and she was still shaking a little when she wrote her name on the sheet.

Where did Pranav take his tray after nobody answered him?
He took it to the window ledge.
What was Ishita feeling while the group ignored Pranav?
She felt ashamed and stuck. Her ears went warm and she wanted to speak, but the words sat like stones.
What small step did Ishita take, and why was it a good choice?
She asked Pranav to be her lab partner. It was a quiet way to include him without needing to confront the whole group.
How might Pranav have felt when Ishita asked him?
Surprised, and maybe relieved to be noticed. He said "Okay" after looking surprised, after being ignored the day before.

Ishrat settled slightly below her target and signed the letter before six o'clock, the deadline the company had set. On the train home she typed a note on her phone. What worked: giving a range, and quoting the two client projects. What didn't: I forgot to ask about a joining bonus. The next morning she asked her manager, Vishal, for fifteen minutes and put a review date in the calendar: the first week of October. Then she listed three results to measure by then: report turnaround time, error rate, and number of clients supported. "Next time I ask, I'll bring the numbers," she wrote at the bottom of the note.

What review date did Ishrat set with Vishal?
Ishrat put a review date in the calendar for the first week of October.
How does Ishrat probably feel about settling below her target?
Ishrat is probably a little disappointed but determined to do better next time.
What else could Ishrat do until the review, and why?
Ishrat could update her list of results every month, because up-to-date numbers are easier to present than recollections.
How might Vishal see the request for a review date?
Vishal probably sees it as a sign of initiative and may be more ready to listen when the date arrives.

Shankar, you're choosing between that government job and your friend's design studio. Let me tell you what I chose at your age.
I was twenty-four. I had an offer to teach at a government school in Jalgaon. Secure, pension, holidays. And I had a dream: my own tailoring and design shop. My friend Kamla wanted to start it with me.
My father had lost his job two years before. I remember the fear in our house. How my mother counted every rupee.
So I took the school job. I told Kamla no. She cried. I cried.
For many years, I slept well. My family was safe. I saved slowly and bought my mother a small flat. I was calm.
And sometimes, walking past a boutique, I still wondered.
I'm Sarika, your Mami, beta. I don't regret it. But I don't pretend it cost nothing.

Where was the government school?
In Jalgaon.
What was Sarika feeling when she told Kamla no?
She felt sad and torn, crying because she valued her family's safety over her dream.
What was the turning point in Sarika's story, and why did she choose as she did?
Choosing the school job over the shop was the turning point, because after her father lost his job she valued certainty and safety for her family.
How might Kamla have felt when Sarika said no?
She probably felt hurt and disappointed, losing a partner for the dream they shared.

So Avni, you asked why I stood up on the metro that day. Honestly, I hadn’t planned anything. I’m Ujjwal, and I was just tired, scrolling on my phone. Then I saw an elderly lady near the door holding the pole with both hands as the train jerked.
Six or seven of us were sitting, and everyone was looking at their screens or the floor. I stood and said, “Please, have this seat.” She smiled and said thank you. A college kid in the corner suddenly stood up for the man next to her, too.
Nobody clapped, and I didn’t want that. My legs ached a bit. But I felt lighter for the rest of the ride.

Where did Ujjwal give up the seat?
Ujjwal gave up the seat on the metro.
How did Ujjwal feel afterwards, and how can you tell?
Ujjwal felt lighter. Despite aching legs, Ujjwal said that feeling lasted for the rest of the ride, and did not want clapping or praise.
What led Ujjwal to stand up at that moment?
Ujjwal noticed the elderly lady holding the pole with both hands as the train jerked. Seeing that need was enough, with no plan behind it.
What might the college kid in the corner have been thinking before standing?
The college kid may have hesitated like the others, then felt nudged by Ujjwal's example. Standing up for the man next to the lady suggests the kid noticed someone else's need too.

Rehana and Kiran knelt in front of the long mirror in Rehana's flat, making faces. Kiran stuck her tongue out and wiggled it. Rehana stuck hers out further and crossed her eyes. They both fell over giggling. Rehana's father looked up from his laptop. The same tongue at the bus stop last week had been a rude one, aimed at a boy who pushed Rehana. Today both girls were laughing, taking turns, eyes bright. He smiled and went back to work.

Where were Rehana and Kiran making faces?
In front of the long mirror in Rehana's flat.
How can you tell the girls were feeling playful rather than rude?
They were giggling, taking turns and their eyes were bright, which shows the tongue was fun, not an insult.
What did Rehana's father do, and was it wise?
He looked at the context and let the game go on; since both girls were laughing together, there was no need to correct them.
How would the moment differ if the tongue were aimed at someone who was not laughing?
Then, as at the bus stop, it would be a rude signal meant to hurt, and an adult could teach a kinder way to show anger.

I'm Kamal. For two days our group had not agreed on a single plan for the model bridge. Ramesh wanted matchsticks, Tara wanted cardboard, and I wanted to stop the shouting. On Thursday I said, "We're stuck. Let's ask Miss, our teacher." We all trooped to the staff room. She listened, asked each of us for one reason, and then said, "Cardboard base, matchstick rails. And one person speaks at a time." She wrote it on a sticky note. We walked back and started measuring. Ramesh was quiet, but he handed me the ruler. That was the first time in two days that nobody argued.

What did the teacher say the bridge would be made from?
The bridge would have a cardboard base and matchstick rails.
What did Kamal want when suggesting to go to the teacher?
Kamal wanted the shouting to stop and the group to get unstuck.
What alternative approach could the group have used earlier, and why?

How might Ramesh have felt about the teacher's plan?

The district health office in Sitapur shared one long room, so Leela heard everything. By Wednesday, the three field officers ate lunch apart from the two data clerks. Someone had said the clerks had blamed the field team for the missed report. Someone else said a clerk was being moved.
Leela didn't believe half of it. But she noticed Seema, their manager, pausing at the doorway after lunch, looking from one table to the other.
"Leela, is something going on?" Seema asked her by the water cooler.
Leela thought of the missed report, the real start of all this. "You should ask them both together," she said finally.

In Sitapur.

Leela seemed torn and uneasy, not wanting to gossip but worried the rumours were growing.
Why was Leela's answer to Seema a helpful choice?
It pointed the manager to the real cause and to both sides together, instead of adding another rumour.
What is Seema experiencing as she pauses at the doorway?

Fix: He is working on the project since Monday. What does "deliver" mean in a work message?

I am waiting for you outside the cinema hall.

The offer expired at six, and the café Bhupen had picked for the call was so noisy he had to press the phone to his ear. Keerthana, from HR, said the figure. Bhupen took a breath. "That's lower than I need," he said. "My rent went up, and I have a loan with a fixed monthly payment. With those, I need more." There was a pause. "I understand," Keerthana said, "but pay is set by the role, not by personal costs. Can you tell me what you would bring to the role beyond what is in the offer?" Bhupen fumbled. Bhupen gave his rent going up and a loan with a fixed monthly payment.

Bhupen was flustered and unprepared, since he had prepared his costs but not his value.

Bhupen could have prepared examples of results he would bring and market ranges for the role, because employers weigh contribution rather than personal costs.
How might Keerthana have heard Bhupen's argument?
Keerthana heard need rather than contribution, so the reply stayed polite but could not move the figure.

I'm Rafiq, from the flat opposite, and I was at their door on Friday when it happened. Asif's mother took a pair of scissors away from him, and he hit her arm, hard, screaming. I expected her to shout. She didn't. She caught his hand and held it. "You're angry. You wanted those. I won't let you hit." He kicked and cried. She waited, holding on. After a bit, he slumped against her.

What did Asif's mother take away from him?
A pair of scissors.
What might Asif have been feeling when he hit his mother's arm?
He was probably angry and frustrated at losing the scissors, not trying to be cruel; slumping against her later suggests he was worn out and needed comfort.
Which of the mother's choices worked, and why?
Staying calm, holding his hand and naming the feeling worked, because it set a limit without adding more anger.
How does Rafiq see the mother's reaction?

Fill in the missing numerals. 0, 1, __, 3, 4, __, 6, __, 8, 9, __
What does 'layover' mean?
A layover is the waiting time between two connecting flights, when you stay at an airport before your next flight.
Is it the same as a stopover?
They are close, and people mix the words up. A stopover usually means a longer planned stay, often a day or more, while a layover is a short wait.
How long a layover is safe?
It depends on the airport and whether you must clear immigration or change terminals. Check the airline's suggested minimum connection time, and allow extra if you can.

It was the week before Diwali, and the hostel was emptying out. Zainab knocked on my door. "Tenzin, can I borrow your scooter for the whole holiday? I'll bring it back after." Ten days, a long road trip. I said no; I needed it. She looked crushed. "Okay, okay. Then could you at least drop me at the station at five tomorrow morning?" And I heard myself say yes before I'd even thought. Five a.m.! I hate early mornings. Later, lying awake, I realised: she'd dropped the big ask, and I felt I owed her a yes. Like she'd given something up, so it was my turn. I did drop her. I didn't mind, really. But next time, I'll ask myself if I'd say yes to the small thing on its own.

What time did Zainab need to be dropped at the station?
At five the next morning.
Why did Tenzin say yes to the early-morning drop so quickly?
Tenzin felt guilty after refusing the scooter, as if Zainab had given something up and it was now Tenzin's turn to agree.
What will Tenzin ask next time, and why is it useful?
Whether the smaller request would be a yes on its own, so the first refusal doesn't push Tenzin into agreeing.
How might Zainab have felt about the lift?
Zainab likely felt relieved and grateful, maybe without noticing the pressure her second ask created.

Tuesday. Dhruv, eleven, finished the plant worksheet first, then asked Avni Ma'am, "But why don't plants fall over when they grow toward the light?" She said, "Not now, Dhruv," and handed him another worksheet. He folded it into a paper plane and flew it across the room. Thursday. Avni had thought about it. When Dhruv finished early, she said, "Your question from Tuesday. Want to test it?" She gave him a bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch. He spent the lesson cutting a window in the box. The following Monday. Dhruv presented his bent seedling to the class, explaining every step. When Suhail asked a question, Dhruv said, "Good question. I don't know yet." Avni noticed no paper planes all week.

What did Avni give Dhruv on Thursday?
A bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch.
How does Avni seem to feel about Dhruv's question after thinking it over?
She seems to regret brushing it off and now respects his curiosity, offering him an experiment to test it instead of another worksheet.
What was the turning point in Avni's approach?
She took his earlier question seriously and gave him a deeper experiment instead of an extra worksheet.
How might Dhruv feel presenting his bent seedling to the class?

messages.content: Marcy keeps a 2-liter bottle of water by her desk. She takes a sip every five minutes, and each sip is 40 ml. How many minutes does it take her to drink the whole bottle of water?

First find the total number of milliliters in the bottle: 2 liters * 1000 ml/liter = 2000 ml
Then divide the total number of milliliters by the amount she drinks per sip: 2000 ml / 40 ml = 50 sips
Then multiply the number of sips by the time per sip to find the time it takes her to drink the bottle: 50 sips * 5 minutes/sip = 250 minutes
The answer is 250.

Class teacher's note, Class 5C, Friday
For three days Nandini has been sitting alone during group work. Sunaina and the girls she usually sits with move their chairs when she comes near and talk to each other, never to her. No names, no teasing, just silence. Nandini asked me twice to go to the washroom during maths and came back with red eyes. Today she said, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke. It wasn't.
What I did: I sat with Nandini at break and listened. She has no idea what she did. I told her it was not her fault and that I would help. I spoke with Sunaina separately; she said the group was "upset about the sleepover". I have called both families this evening, and on Monday the counsellor and I will sit with the girls together.

What did Nandini ask the teacher today?
Nandini asked, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke.
What do Nandini's red eyes and joking question suggest about how she feels?
They suggest she feels hurt, anxious and confused, and is trying to hide how much the silence affects her.
Which of the teacher's steps matter most, and why?
Sitting with Nandini and saying it isn't her fault calms her right away, and talking to Sunaina and the families opens a way to find out what went wrong.
How might Sunaina see the silence, given the comment about the sleepover?
Sunaina may feel the group had a real grievance, without realising that silence hurts Nandini more than saying what upset them.

In the village lane in Goa, Farhan from next door crouched beside Elizabeth and pointed. "Look, a goat!" Elizabeth followed his finger and stared at the goat chewing a leaf.
Later, under the mango tree, she pointed up and grunted. Farhan reached for a low mango. "This one?"
She shook her head, still pointing. Farhan looked where her eyes were. A squirrel was running along the branch. "Oh! Squirrel!" Elizabeth grinned and bounced.

What was the goat doing?
Chewing a leaf.
Why did Elizabeth shake her head when Farhan reached for the mango?
She felt misunderstood, because she wasn't asking for the mango; she wanted to share the squirrel, and she was delighted once he saw it.
What could Farhan do first next time Elizabeth points?
Check where her eyes are looking before guessing, since a point can mean "look at this" as well as "I want that".
How might Farhan feel when Elizabeth bounces with a grin?
He likely feels pleased and a bit amused that he finally found what she meant.
I think I lost my wallet on the bus. I have just noticed.
That is upsetting. Try to stay calm and check your bag and pockets once more. When did you last remember having it, and which bus was it?
I paid for my ticket with it about an hour ago on bus 42.
Then contact the bus depot or the conductor of route 42 and describe the wallet. Also check with the police station near your stop, since honest people often hand wallets in.
I called the depot. They said someone found one and will keep it until six.
That is good news. Take an identity card with you when you collect it, so you can prove it is yours. Check everything inside once you have it back.
I will go at five. Thank you. What bus was it again, in case they ask?
It was bus 42. When you reach the depot, say you paid your ticket on that bus about an hour before you noticed it was missing, and describe the wallet's colour.

The area of a forest is three times the area of the square-shaped street. If the street has a length of 100 meters on one side and the number of trees per square meter in the forest is 4, calculate the total number of trees in the forest.

Since the area of a square is sides squared, the area of the square-shaped street is 100*100 = 10000 square meters.
The area of the forest is three times the area of the square-shaped street, a total of 3*10000 = 30000 square meters.
If the number of trees per square meter in the forest is 4, there are 4*30000 = 120000 trees in the forest.
The answer is 120000.
In a forest, there are three anthills. In the first anthill, there are 100 ants, and in each next anthill, there are 20% fewer ants than in the previous one. How many ants are in the third anthill?

In the second anthill, there are 20/100 * 100 = 20 ants less.
This means there are 100 - 20 = 80 ants in the second anthill.
In the third anthill, there are 20/100 * 80 = 16 ants less compared to the second one.
So in the third anthill, there are 80 - 16 = 64 ants.
The answer is 64.

Note from the class teacher, Class 4B, end of the month.
Suraj joined us three weeks ago and quickly became friends with Nazia. Nazia's old friend Tulsi has been cool towards him: she moves her bag onto the spare chair when he comes near. Suraj has noticed. On the first Monday he told a group that Tulsi "cries at everything", and the other children turned on him instead. He looked miserable.
Since then he has changed. He greets Tulsi every morning, never asks Nazia to choose, and lets the two girls walk ahead sometimes. Today Tulsi lent him her ruler. I plan to seat the three together for the craft fair.

What does Tulsi do with her bag when Suraj comes near?
She moves her bag onto the spare chair.
How did Suraj seem to feel after his remark about Tulsi backfired?
He looked miserable, likely ashamed and more insecure, because the other children turned on him instead.
What has Suraj done since then that is working?
He greets Tulsi every morning, doesn't make Nazia choose, and gives the girls space, and Tulsi has started to warm up.
What might Tulsi feel when Suraj keeps greeting her?
Tulsi may slowly feel less threatened and see he isn't trying to take Nazia, which is why she lends him her ruler.
I got a very low mark in my art project. I worked on it for two weeks.
That is disappointing, especially after so much effort. What did the teacher say about it?
She said it did not follow the theme. The theme was water and I painted a mountain.
I see. It sounds like the instructions got missed. That can happen when you are excited about an idea. It is a lesson about reading the theme carefully.
I feel silly. My name is Lucy.
You need not feel silly, Lucy. Your mountain may have been lovely. Often, the problem is the topic, not the skill. Learn from it and keep painting.
Maybe I can paint the same mountain again but with a lake in front.
That is a great idea. A mountain reflected in a lake would answer the theme and keep your work. You could show your teacher and ask if she would look again.
What did I paint again?
You painted a mountain, Lucy, and the theme was water. Adding a lake in front, with the mountain reflected in it, could connect your painting to the theme nicely.
Please correct my sentence: Yesterday I go to school and teacher give us many homework.

Corrected: "Yesterday I went to school, and the teacher gave us a lot of homework." Use the past tense (went, gave) with "yesterday". Say "the teacher". "Homework" cannot be counted, so say "a lot of homework", not "many homework".

I'm Noor, Mehak's sister. On Sunday, Mehak drew our family: Ammi, me, her, Nani and the cat, but no Abbu. Ammi looked at it for a long time. Then she asked, “Tell me about your picture.” Mehak said, “This is us at home. Abbu is at work, so he's in the other picture.” She pulled out a second drawing of Abbu at his desk with a huge coffee cup. Ammi laughed with relief. I think Ammi was worried for a second, but I'm not sure.

What was on Abbu's desk in the second drawing?
A huge coffee cup.
What was Ammi feeling when she looked at the drawing for a long time?
She seemed worried about why Abbu was missing, and then felt relief when Mehak explained.
What did Ammi do instead of assuming something was wrong?
She asked Mehak to tell her about the picture, using the drawing to start a conversation.
How does Noor see Ammi's reaction?
Noor thinks Ammi was worried for a second but isn't sure, and noticed her laugh with relief.

Lucas' father offers to pay him $2 for each window in the house that he cleans. Each floor of Lucas' house has 3 windows; Lucas lives in a 3-story house. To get Lucas to finish the job faster, his father tells him that he will subtract $1 for every 3 days that pass without Lucas finishing the job. In 6 days, Lucas finishes cleaning all the windows in the house. How much will his father pay him, in dollars?

Lucas cleans a total of 3 floors * 3 windows/floor = 9 windows.
The windows cleaned earn Lucas 2 dollars each, so Lucas earns 9 windows * $2/window = $18
For taking 6 days to clean, Lucas' father subtracts 6 days / $3/day = $2
In total, Lucas' father will pay him $18 - $2 = $16
The answer is 16.

Note from Ms Sangeeta, class teacher. Lakshmi arrived on Monday scowling and kicked her bag under the desk. She told me her parents had refused to buy the cycle with lights she saw in an advert, and that it wasn't fair. I said I could see she was angry. She was silent for a bit, then said, "Papa says it costs too much this year." I asked what she could do. After a minute: "I could save my pocket money. And birthday money." I suggested she tell her parents her plan instead of begging. On Friday she said they had talked, and they might add a little at Diwali if she saved. She was still a bit disappointed, but calmer.

What did Lakshmi want to buy?
She wanted the cycle with lights that she saw in an advert.
What was Lakshmi feeling on Monday morning, and what showed it?
She was angry and felt it was unfair; she arrived scowling and kicked her bag under the desk.
What does Lakshmi's saving plan show about how she has changed her approach?
She accepted her parents' limit and offered to save her own money and tell them the plan, instead of begging.
How might Lakshmi's parents have felt when she begged for the cycle?
Probably pressed but constrained, since Papa said it costs too much this year; a plan may feel easier to hear than begging.

I'm Harsha, and I run the Sunday cricket in our colony lane. For a month Gargi, nine, has been turning into her favourite batter. Same short haircut, same tap-tap of the bat on the ground, same slow twirl after every shot. She even practises forward defence a hundred times against our wall before school, because she read that her hero does.
Her batting really has got better. But last Sunday, when Sunny gave her out lbw, she threw her head back, rolled her eyes like on TV, and walked off without the handshake. Nobody knew what to say.
I don't know what she was thinking. Maybe she felt like a star. Later I saw her sitting on the steps, bat across her knees, watching the others play.

How many times does Gargi practise forward defence before school?
A hundred times, against the wall.
What might Gargi have felt as she rolled her eyes and walked off?
She may have felt like a real star copying her hero, but the swagger also covered disappointment at getting out; sitting alone later suggests it didn't feel good.
How could Harsha help Gargi keep the good parts of copying her hero?
Harsha could praise the practice and the improved batting, then remind Gargi that the handshake is part of the game, even for stars.
How might Sunny have felt when Gargi rolled her eyes at the lbw decision?
Sunny was only doing the umpire's job, so the eye-roll probably felt unfair and awkward, and might make Sunny unsure about umpiring again.
John buys 3 spools of wire that are 20 feet each.  It takes 4 feet to make a necklace.  How many necklaces can he make?

He gets 3*20=60 feet of wire
So he can make 60/4=15 necklaces
The answer is 15.

'Thanks for making time before Thursday, Nilesh,' Rukmini said, closing the cabin door. 'I wanted to hear your side before the big meeting.'
'My side is simple. The new app will add work for my warehouse staff. They'll have to scan every box twice.'
'Twice? Where did you hear that?'
'At the demo last month.'
Rukmini opened her laptop. 'That was the old version. Now it's one scan, and it replaces the paper form they fill today.'
Nilesh leaned in and read. 'So it's actually less work?'
'For your team, yes. What else worries you?'
'Training time. We're short-staffed in November.'
'Then we train in October. I'll put that in the plan.'
Nilesh laughed. 'I came in ready to fight on Thursday.'
'That's why I wanted to talk today.'

Where had Nilesh heard about scanning every box twice?
At the demo last month.
How did Nilesh feel coming into the talk, and how did it change?
Nilesh came in defensive and ready to fight, then felt relieved and even amused on seeing it was less work.
What else could Rukmini do before the Thursday meeting?
She could have similar private talks with each other stakeholder, so any other misunderstandings are cleared before the group meets.
How might Nilesh's warehouse staff be affected?
They will scan once instead of filling paper forms, and train in October before the busy November.

The week before Lunar New Year, Mr. Chen from the bakery downstairs asked five-year-old Beatriz if she could help. 'Very important job. These lanterns go on the low hooks.' Beatriz stood on a stool, Mamãe holding her waist, and hung six red lanterns one by one, counting in Portuguese. One hung crooked. Mr. Chen left it. All week Beatriz pointed out 'my lanterns' to every customer, and she circled the date on the kitchen calendar with a red crayon.

How many lanterns did Beatriz hang?
Six red lanterns.
How did Beatriz feel about 'my lanterns' all week?
She felt proud and excited, showing them to every customer as her own work.
What made Mr. Chen's invitation meaningful for Beatriz?
He called it an important job, gave her a real task at her height and left the crooked lantern, so it truly felt like hers.
How might Mr. Chen's customers feel when Beatriz shows off her lanterns?
They would likely feel charmed and drawn into the festival mood by her pride.

Suraj, you want to skip placements? Before you decide, let me tell you what I did at twenty-one. I'd already decided I would skip placements and study for an MBA abroad. Then I "researched." I read only blogs by people who had done exactly that. I asked only the two seniors I knew had loved it. When my professor said, "Payal, the job market might be tight next year; keep one offer in hand," I smiled and thought he didn't understand. I felt so well informed. My notebook was full of quotes. Then the admissions came back: two rejections and a waitlist. And no job offer, because I hadn't sat for any. I spent a year at home. I wasn't stupid. I just collected agreement and called it research.

What did Payal's professor advise?
"The job market might be tight next year; keep one offer in hand."
Why did young Payal feel so well informed?
Payal felt confident because the notebook was full of quotes, not noticing that every quote agreed with the decision already made.
What turning point in the story could have changed the outcome?
If Payal had taken the professor's advice seriously and sat for placements as a back-up, there would have been an offer in hand after the rejections.
How might the professor have felt seeing Payal's choice?
The professor may have felt worried and a bit frustrated, knowing the risks.

Sunday
The Spanish notebook is still on my desk under a pile of laundry, which is exactly where I put it so I wouldn't have to see it.
Twenty-three days since my last lesson. The app sent a reminder this morning and I swiped it away so fast.
At lunch Zubin asked, "How's the Spanish going? Say something!" I laughed, said "Hola", and asked about his internship before he could ask anything else. My face was burning.
I told everyone in July I'd be conversational by Diwali. Now opening that notebook feels like opening a report card I already know is bad. Every day I don't start, it gets heavier.
Maybe tomorrow. I wrote that yesterday too.
Ritu

Where is Ritu's Spanish notebook?
On the desk under a pile of laundry.
Why did Ritu's face burn when Zubin asked about the Spanish?
Ritu felt ashamed of having stopped after telling everyone about being conversational by Diwali, so the question felt like being found out.
What small step could break the avoidance?
Ritu could uncover the notebook and do one short lesson without trying to catch up, or tell Zubin honestly about the break and ask for company.
What might Zubin have noticed at lunch?
Zubin was probably just curious and friendly, and may have noticed the quick 'Hola' and change of subject without knowing the shame behind it.

Payal: the collector's order says your mandal leaves by 4. it's 3:10
Vandana: I know. papa is wrapping the tv in plastic
Vandana: mummy is making rotis for the road
Payal: vandana just go
Vandana: it always turns north at the last minute. every year
Vandana: I'm packing my certificates first, can't lose those
Payal: take the folder and go. the rest can wait
Vandana: 10 min
Payal: you said 10 min at 2:50
Vandana: the wind just ripped off the neighbour's tin roof
Payal: VANDANA
Vandana: ok we're going. papa is still arguing about taking the scooter
Payal: leave the scooter. text me from the school
Vandana: ok
Vandana: on the road. it's so much worse than it looked from inside
Payal: keep going. I'm here

What was Papa wrapping in plastic?
He was wrapping the TV in plastic.
Why did Vandana keep asking for ten more minutes?
Vandana felt confident the storm would turn north as usual, so leaving felt less urgent than saving the certificates and household things.
What turning point finally got the family moving, and what could have moved them sooner?
The neighbour's roof ripping off made the danger real; treating the collector's 4 o'clock order as the deadline would have moved them earlier.
What was the chat like for Payal, watching the clock from far away?
Payal was anxious and helpless, pushing again and again because only the messages could reach Vandana.

At the village gurdwara langar, Kalyani, a neighbour, held out a round ladoo to little Jasleen. Jasleen shook her head and pressed her face into her mother's arm.
"Take it, beta, don't be rude," her mother whispered.
Jasleen shook her head again, harder.
Kalyani smiled and lowered her hand. "She's said no. That's fine." Jasleen peeked at her. A minute later she reached out for a piece of roti instead.

What did Kalyani offer Jasleen?
A round ladoo.
What did Jasleen's harder head shake show?
She was firmly refusing and perhaps a bit shy of Kalyani; when her "no" was accepted she seemed more at ease, peeking and reaching for roti.
What could Jasleen's mother try next time?
She could accept the head shake as a polite enough "no" at this age, instead of pushing her to take food.
How does Jasleen's mother see the head shake?
She worries it looks rude to the neighbour, while Kalyani sees a clear and fair "no".

15 August, night
Flag hoisting in the morning, then the colony tree drive. Yash and I planted three neem saplings by the drain road, muddy up to our elbows. Aunty from B-block said, "Why bother, the municipality will cut them." I watered them anyway.
Then tonight on the news, the floods up north. A whole village under water, people on rooftops with their goats. I don't know anyone there. But I can't stop thinking about them. Same rain, same sky, and our drains are choked with plastic too. It all feels connected and too big, and I'm angry that grown-ups just shrug.
Tomorrow I'll ask Sir if our class can collect clothes for the relief drive. And I'll check on the neems.
Alka

How many neem saplings did Alka and Yash plant?
Three neem saplings, by the drain road.
How does Alka feel after seeing the floods on the news?
Alka feels worried, angry and a bit overwhelmed, thinking about strangers on rooftops and how the same rain and choked drains link them to home.
What small steps is Alka planning, and why do they help?
Asking Sir about a class clothes collection for the relief drive and checking on the neems; small local acts give a big worry somewhere to go.
How might Aunty from B-block see the tree drive?
Aunty sees it as pointless, expecting the municipality to cut the trees, and may not share Alka's sense that small acts matter.

By Thursday afternoon at the ad agency in Andheri, Kashish had built a whole story. Sachin hadn't laughed at her joke in the stand-up. He'd answered her draft with "noted." He'd eaten lunch at his desk instead of joining them.

He thinks I stole the tea-brand pitch idea, she thought. He's going to say it in Monday's review. She'd already rehearsed three replies in the washroom mirror.

At four she caught herself drafting a fourth. Enough. She walked over to his desk.

"Sachin, can I ask something? Are you annoyed with me about the pitch? I'd rather ask than keep guessing."

He looked up, surprised. "What? No! My landlord's selling the flat and I have to move by the fifteenth. I've been apartment-hunting on my phone all day. Sorry, I've been a zombie."

The whole thing took two minutes. Kashish went back to her desk and deleted the fourth reply.

What did Sachin answer Kashish's draft with?
He'd answered her draft with "noted."
Why did Kashish's story about Sachin feel so convincing to her?
Each small sign, the missed laugh, the short reply and the lunch at his desk, seemed to fit one explanation. Rehearsing replies in the mirror made the imagined conflict feel even more real.
What was the turning point, and why did it work so quickly?
Kashish caught herself drafting a fourth reply and decided to ask Sachin directly. One two-minute question replaced days of guessing with his actual reason.
How might Sachin have felt when Kashish asked if he was annoyed?
Sachin was surprised, and maybe a little relieved to explain why he'd been so distracted. He might also have felt bad that his stress had come across as coldness.

Last month, at 1:14 am, a banner told me: "Only 1 left! Deal ends in 09:58." I was looking at a jacket I'd liked for weeks but never really needed. I have a jacket. I have two, actually.
The timer kept ticking and my chest went tight, like I was about to lose something that was already mine. I paid before it hit seven minutes.
Next morning my roommate Sarita saw the order message on my screen. "Mehak, weren't you saving for the Goa trip?"
I opened the site again. The same jacket was still there. "Only 1 left" was still showing, and a brand-new ten-minute timer had started.
I felt silly, then annoyed. The jacket is nice. But I didn't buy it because I wanted it. I bought it because I was scared of it disappearing.

What did the banner say when Mehak was looking at the jacket?
'Only 1 left! Deal ends in 09:58.'
What was Mehak feeling as the timer ticked?
Mehak felt a tight, anxious rush, as if about to lose something already owned; the fear of losing it, not wanting it, drove the purchase.
What could Mehak try the next time a countdown appears?
Close the tab and look again the next day; if the timer restarts, as it did here, the hurry was never real.
How does Sarita see the purchase?
Sarita sees it as cutting into Mehak's own plan to save for the Goa trip, which is why Sarita gently asks about it.

'Rukmini, you're not sure whether to forgive Pallavi? Sit here with your Vandana Maasi. When I was ten, my friend Leela told the whole class I was scared of the dark and slept with a lamp on. I wanted to vanish. Two days later she came to my house with her mother's pedas and cried. "They were teasing me and I blurted it out. I'm sorry." I could see she meant it. So I forgave her. I let the anger go, but I didn't tell her any secrets for a long while. When she slipped up again with a small thing the next year, I said straight away, "Leela, that's twice. I need you to stop." She did. We're still friends. Forgiving isn't pretending it didn't hurt, beta.'

What did Leela bring when she came to apologise?
Her mother's pedas.
How did young Vandana feel after Leela told the class her secret?
Humiliated and betrayed; she wanted to vanish.
What choice did Vandana make when Leela slipped up again?
She said straight away that it was the second time and asked Leela to stop.
How might Leela have felt coming to apologise?
Ashamed and sorry; she cried and explained she had blurted it out under teasing.

Monday. Pankaj came down in his new shirt for the school photo. His elder brother Suraj looked up from his toast. "That colour makes you look ill." Pankaj changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
Wednesday. Pankaj showed Suraj his science model. "The wiring's messy. It'll short." Pankaj snatched it back and slammed his door.
Friday. The model had shorted in class, just as Suraj said. That evening Pankaj knocked on his brother's door. "You were right about the wiring. But when you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm useless." Suraj stared. "I didn't mean it that way." "I know. Can you just tell me what's wrong and how to fix it, and skip the 'ill' part?" Suraj nodded slowly, then pulled out a screwdriver.

What did Suraj say about Pankaj's shirt colour?
"That colour makes you look ill."
How did Pankaj feel after the shirt comment, and how can you tell?
He felt hurt and criticised; he changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
What choice did Pankaj make on Friday, and what came of it?
He told Suraj how the words landed and asked for the fix without the harsh part; Suraj nodded and got a screwdriver.
How might Suraj have felt when Pankaj said his words sound like "you think I'm useless"?
He seems surprised, since he meant no harm, and may realise his honesty was landing as an attack.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Chetan, and for most of last year my phone rang at midnight. It was always Pooja, my oldest friend from college, and it was always someone: the landlord who hated her, the team lead who ruined her life, the cousin who betrayed her. Some of it was surely real. Some of it had been going on since we were nineteen.
One night she said, "You're the only one I have, and even you don't care." I felt the old guilt rise. Then I tried something new. I listened for ten minutes without fixing. Then I asked, "That sounds painful. What do you want to do about it?"
Silence. Then: "I don't know. Maybe talk to HR."
"Good start. And Pooja, I care, but I can't do calls after eleven any more. Sunday lunches, though, I'm always in."
She was cold for a week. Then she came to Sunday lunch and told me what HR said.

After what time did Chetan say the calls could no longer happen?
Chetan said the calls could not happen after eleven any more.
What did Chetan feel when Pooja said "even you don't care"?
Chetan felt the old guilt rise, the familiar pull to prove care by giving in.
Which question at the turning point changed the call, and why?
Asking "What do you want to do about it?" after listening moved Pooja from blaming to thinking of a step, like talking to HR, without Chetan taking on her problem.
How might Pooja have experienced Chetan's new limit?
At first she felt rejected, which is why she was cold for a week, but the Sunday lunch offer showed she still mattered, so she came back and shared her progress.
There are 60 passengers on a bus. Children make up 25% of the bus riders. How many adults are on the bus?

The number of children on the bus is 60 passengers * 25% = 15 passengers.
The number of adults on the bus is 60 passengers - 15 passengers = 45 passengers.
The answer is 45.

At two in the morning, the house master at the residential school, Suraj Sir, found Ira in the common room redoing a lab report. "It got 18 out of 20," she said, not looking up. "I lost two marks." Her eyes were red. Ira, sixteen, had few friends in the hostel; the others found her intense. Suraj Sir sat down. "Ira, you are allowed to be ordinary sometimes. Eighteen is fine. Sleep is not optional." The next week, he introduced her to three seniors preparing for the science olympiad, who met in the library after dinner. At the first meeting she laughed at a physics joke only they got. That night she slept straight through.

What mark did Ira get on the lab report?
She got 18 out of 20.
How was Ira feeling at two in the morning?
She was anxious and upset about losing two marks, redoing the report with red eyes.
What did Suraj Sir do that relieved Ira's strain?
He gave her permission to be ordinary, insisted she sleep and introduced her to like-minded seniors.
How might the olympiad seniors see Ira after the first meeting?
They may see her as one of them, someone who laughs at the same physics jokes, not as too intense.

Sunday morning in the Chandigarh gurdwara, the keertan began and the whole hall sang together. Sarika sat cross-legged between Bebe and her cousin Irawati, her head covered with a soft orange scarf. She did not know every word yet, but she hummed along, and her chest felt full, as if all those voices were carrying her. Afterwards, at the shoe rack, she tugged Bebe's sleeve. "Bebe, why do we cover our heads?" Bebe smiled and slowed down. "Let's ask Giani ji together," she said, "and you can tell me what you think of his answer."

Who did Sarika sit between at the gurdwara?
She sat between Bebe and her cousin Irawati.
What was Sarika feeling while the hall sang, and what was she also wondering?
She felt happy and connected, her chest full as if all the voices were carrying her; she was also wondering why they cover their heads.
How could Sarika get her question answered in a respectful way?
Ask kindly after the service, with real curiosity, first from Bebe and then from Giani ji.
How might Bebe see Sarika's question?
Bebe smiled and slowed down, so she probably sees it as a good sign that Sarika is paying attention and wants to understand, not just copy.
