"Third time I'm coming here! Third!" Pradeep slapped the receipt on the counter of the courier office in Ludhiana. "My daughter's university papers were supposed to reach Pune on Monday. Nobody picks up your phone!" Heads turned in the queue. Gurleen didn't raise her voice to match. She leaned in slightly and spoke low and slow. "Three trips, and no one answering. I'd be angry too. Those papers matter." Pradeep's voice dropped a notch. "The deadline is Friday." "Okay. What would help you most right now: knowing exactly where the parcel is, or a way to get the papers there by Friday even if it's lost?" He blinked. "Both." "Then both." She tracked it to the Nagpur hub, flagged it urgent and wrote her direct extension on the receipt. Pradeep folded the receipt carefully. "Thank you. Sorry I shouted."

Where did Gurleen track the parcel to?
The Nagpur hub.
Why did Gurleen speak low and slow instead of matching Pradeep's voice?
Gurleen stayed calm and wanted Pradeep to feel heard, sensing that a raised voice would only add to his anger.
Which question moved the talk towards solving the problem?
Asking what would help most right now, finding the parcel or getting the papers there by Friday, turned his anger into a clear goal.
How did Pradeep feel once Gurleen said "I'd be angry too"?
Pradeep felt heard, so his voice dropped and he could name the real stake, the Friday deadline.

Dilnaz, you know the croissant disaster? Last winter I hadn't made laminated dough for four months, and on the big order day my hands just didn't know it. I kept folding in the wrong order. I went home thinking, that's it, I'm losing it.
Then my old instructor rang and said something simple. "Zeenat, you're not losing it. Your brain made room for the cakes you bake every day." Made sense.
So now I keep this little recipe diary, grease stains and all. And on the first Monday of every month, before the shop opens, I do one practice batch of whatever I haven't touched in a while. Some months it's dough, sometimes piping.
Honestly? Forgetting doesn't scare me now. It's just my cue to open the diary.

What did Zeenat keep getting wrong on the big order day?
Zeenat kept folding the laminated dough in the wrong order after four months without making it.
What was Zeenat afraid of after that order day?
Zeenat feared losing the skill for good, reading one blank day as proof of decline.
Which habit keeps Zeenat's rarer skills ready, and why does it work?
A practice batch on the first Monday of every month, guided by the recipe diary, brings back a skill before it fades completely.
How might Dilnaz take the croissant story?
Dilnaz might find it funny and reassuring, and see that forgetting a skill can be handled with a diary and practice rather than panic.

The rain had turned the side road in Andheri into a stream, and Imran's phone had died at the office party. He and Sarika were walking to the station when a man on a scooter slowed beside them, calling out to Sarika, then circled back a second time. Imran felt his whole body tighten. He moved to walk on the road side, between Sarika and the scooter, and caught himself squaring his shoulders. Part of him wanted to shout, even to grab the handlebar. Then he saw how empty the street was. "Chemist, left," he said quietly. They ducked into the lit shop. Sarika's phone still had battery; she called the police helpline while Imran asked the chemist if they could wait inside. The chemist pulled the shutter halfway down and let them stay. Ten minutes later a patrol jeep pulled up, and the scooter was gone.

Why couldn't Imran use his phone?
His phone had died at the office party.
What was Imran feeling when the scooter circled back?
Imran felt tense, protective and angry, even tempted to grab the handlebar, but also wary because the street was empty.
Why was ducking into the chemist's shop the wiser choice?
It moved them to a lit place with other people and let Sarika call the police helpline, instead of a confrontation that could have escalated.
What might it have been like for Sarika during this?
Sarika was likely frightened by the man's comments and relieved that Imran stayed calm, which left room for her to call the helpline herself.

Yogesh had worked double shifts at the hospital lab all week, and his eyes felt full of sand. On Saturday night, as rain hammered the window, Dhruv called. "Bro, can you help me shift flats tomorrow? Six a.m. The truck's booked." Yogesh always said yes. He'd helped Dhruv move twice already, and fixed his mother's fan last month. He opened his mouth to say yes again, then felt how heavy his arms were. "Dhruv, I can't tomorrow. I'm wrecked. If I carry your fridge like this, I'll drop it on my foot." Silence. "But I'll come Wednesday evening and help you unpack and set up the kitchen. Promise." Dhruv sighed, then laughed. "Fine. Bring the good screwdriver." Yogesh slept eleven hours.

How long did Yogesh sleep after the call?
Yogesh slept eleven hours.
What made Yogesh hesitate before saying yes again?
He felt how heavy his arms were and how exhausted he was, and worried he could not help safely in that state.
Which choice kept Yogesh both kind and rested?
He said no to Sunday but offered Wednesday evening for unpacking, which protected his rest while still showing he cared.
How does Dhruv seem to take Yogesh's no?
Dhruv is a bit disappointed at first, shown by the silence and sigh, but accepts it with a laugh because help is still coming.

Sangeeta told me later that she had not meant to look angry. I just saw it from my desk: in the pricing meeting, Ravi from sales disagreed and Sangeeta's jaw pushed forward, chin up, and she spoke slowly. I am Lakshmi, and I sit next to her. I thought she was ready to fight. But then she said, "I need to understand why the discount is that deep," and her voice wobbled just a little. Maybe she was determined, maybe scared of being overruled, I honestly cannot say. Ravi asked her a calm question back, and her jaw relaxed. If Ravi had raised his voice, I think I would have suggested a break.

Where was Lakshmi sitting during the pricing meeting?
She was at her desk next to Sangeeta.
What did Sangeeta's jutting jaw and wobbly voice most likely suggest, and what other reading fits?
Together they suggest determination mixed with some nervousness about being overruled. They could equally mean defensiveness, so Lakshmi rightly says she cannot be sure.
How did Ravi's reaction help the situation?
He asked a calm question back instead of arguing louder, and Sangeeta's jaw relaxed. Calm questions like that can lower the tension.
How might Sangeeta have seen her own expression in the meeting?
She did not mean to look angry, so she may have felt only focused or anxious, and she might be surprised that it looked like a challenge.

Monday, the week before Ganesh festival: The class decoration committee was really Urmila's group of five. When Keya from the group spilled glue across the big chart, Urmila laughed. "Accidents happen. Just cover it with glitter." Nilesh, who had been added to the committee late, said nothing and fetched a cloth.
Thursday: Nilesh stapled the paper lanterns a little crooked. "Who let him touch it?" Urmila said loudly. "This is why we don't take outsiders." The group giggled. Nilesh's ears burned, and he stapled the rest in silence.
The next Monday, after the festival: The class teacher praised the committee's work. Urmila's group went up to collect the certificate. Nilesh's name was on the list, but nobody called him. He stayed at his desk, straightening pencils that were already straight, remembering the glue that didn't matter and the staples that did.

What did Keya spill on the chart?
Glue, across the big chart.
How did Nilesh feel when Urmila said "This is why we don't take outsiders"?
He felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears burning, because the same kind of small slip that was laughed off for Keya was used to shame him.
How could the class teacher support Nilesh?
The teacher could call every name on the committee list for the certificate, and set the same rules for mistakes for everyone, whichever group they belong to.
Why might Urmila react so differently to Keya's glue and Nilesh's staples?
Keya is inside Urmila's group, so her mistake feels like an accident, while Nilesh is an outsider, so his slip looks like proof he doesn't belong.

Teacher's note, Shalini. Ankit brought his essay draft on Tuesday with a page of comments in the margin. He had written the whole first draft himself, then asked an AI tool two questions: which parts were unclear, and how the structure could be tighter. He did not paste in any of its sentences. The tool said his second paragraph jumped between two ideas, so he split it and rewrote both halves in his own words. He showed me both versions. The second draft was clearer, and, more importantly, he could explain why. I asked how he decided what to keep from the feedback, and he said he kept whatever made sense to him. I have told him that this order, own thinking first and feedback second, is a good habit for other subjects too.

Which two questions did Ankit ask the tool?
Ankit asked which parts were unclear and how the structure could be tighter.
What might Ankit feel when he explains why the second draft is clearer?
Ankit probably feels proud and confident, since he understands the changes as his own.
What could Ankit do if the tool's feedback is confusing?
Ankit could check with Shalini or a classmate, since a person who knows the assignment can say which comments to keep.
How might Shalini see this way of working?
Shalini sees own thinking first and feedback second as a good habit, and wants to encourage it in other subjects.

metadata.subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]

On Diwali night, while the whole Hyderabad colony lit diyas, Aparna sat on her bed scrolling. A fire in some city. A flood somewhere else. A post saying everything was getting worse. Another saying nobody could be trusted anymore. She refreshed the feed again and again, her shoulders creeping up towards her ears. Each new headline made her chest tighter, but she couldn't stop. What if something happens to Amma on the road, she thought, though Amma was downstairs making laddoos. Her cousin Vinita knocked with a plate of sweets. "Come and see the rangoli, the kids made a peacock." "In a minute," Aparna said, not looking up. An hour later she had read forty posts and learned almost nothing new, except that she felt worse.

What did Vinita say the kids made in the rangoli?
A peacock.
Why does Aparna keep refreshing the feed even as she feels worse?
Each bad headline grabs her attention like a warning she must check, so she feels anxious and stuck, as if watching will keep everyone safe.
What small step could help Aparna tonight?
Put the phone away for a while, go and see the rangoli with Vinita, and check the news later from one reliable source at a set time.
How might Vinita feel when Aparna doesn't look up?
Vinita may feel a little ignored and concerned, seeing Aparna miss the celebration while stuck on the phone.

In the Delhi flat, Dadi sat on the sofa. Lalremsiami knelt beside her daughter Kavitha, two, and bent her own head to Dadi's feet. "Like this, Kavi." Kavitha flopped forward, giggling, and patted Dadi's toes. Dadi laughed and put both hands on Kavitha's curls. "Jeeti raho!" Kavitha looked up, beaming, and did it again. And again. Each time, Dadi laughed.

What did Kavitha pat?
She patted Dadi's toes.
How did Kavitha seem to feel when Dadi put her hands on her curls?
Kavitha seemed happy and delighted, beaming and doing it again and again.
What did Lalremsiami do that helped Kavitha learn?
She showed the gesture herself first and made it gentle and playful.
How might Dadi feel when Kavitha keeps bending to her feet?
Dadi probably feels full of affection and joy, laughing and blessing her every time.

At the tuition verandah in Bhuj town, Rehana found a folded note tucked in her copy. It was from Zainab, in careful round letters: she liked Rehana as more than a friend. Rehana read it twice, her stomach knotting, and she thought about how easy it would be to smile, say nothing and enjoy being liked. But that wouldn't be fair. After class she asked Zainab to walk with her to the corner shop. "Thank you for telling me. It took courage," she said. "I care about you as my friend. But I don't feel the same way, and I don't want you hoping." Zainab swallowed and nodded. Rehana didn't tell anyone else, and the next day she sat beside her at tuition as usual.

Where did Rehana find Zainab's note?
She found it folded and tucked into her copy at the tuition verandah.
What did Rehana think about before answering the note?
She thought how easy it would be to smile, say nothing and enjoy being liked, but felt that wouldn't be fair to Zainab.
What made Rehana's answer a kind and clear one?
She thanked Zainab for her courage, said plainly she did not feel the same way, and kept it private, so there were no mixed signals and Zainab kept her dignity.
How might Zainab have felt when she nodded?
Hurt, since she swallowed before nodding, but also perhaps respected, because Rehana was honest and sat beside her the next day. 🤍

Sunday, 9:40 p.m. A small win to record. Last week, before the product launch got busy, I sent Seema, my manager, one message: "I will be offline after seven on weekdays, and I will need Friday afternoon off after Thursday's late push." Seema said fine and moved a meeting. So from Monday to Wednesday I switched the lights off by eleven, ate lunch away from the desk and took a twenty-minute walk after work. Thursday's push ran until nine and it went well. On Friday afternoon I did nothing at all, which felt strange and then good. Today I caught two mistakes in the slides that I would have missed if I had worked through the night. Note to self: rest is a step in the work, not a reward for it.
Jeevan

After what time did Jeevan say weekdays would be offline?
Jeevan said the weekdays would be offline after seven.
How did Jeevan feel about doing nothing on Friday afternoon?
Jeevan felt uneasy at first, because doing nothing felt strange, and then content as the afternoon came to feel good.
Why was it wise to state the limit before the launch got busy?
It gave Seema time to move a meeting and plan around it, so it came as a plan and not as a complaint.
How might Seema have felt on receiving that message?
Probably cooperative and fine with it, since Seema agreed and moved a meeting, and may have valued the early notice. 🙂

Noor sent Mehak a long message at 7 p.m. about the science project. By 9 there was no reply, though the ticks showed it had been read. Noor lay on her bed in their Delhi flat and replayed the day. Mehak had laughed at lunch when Noor spilled her juice. Not a mean laugh, maybe. But maybe.
By 10 Noor had decided: Mehak was tired of her. Everyone probably was.
Next morning in class Mehak waved. "Sorry, my phone died after I read it, and then Mummy made me do the dishes." Noor heard only the sorry and nodded stiffly. "It's fine. I'll do the project myself."
Mehak's smile faded. "Oh. Okay."
Noor went back to her desk, stomach tight. See, she thought. She doesn't even care. She didn't notice that it was her own cold voice that had closed the door.

Why did Mehak say she didn't reply?
Her phone died after she read it, and then Mummy made her do the dishes.
What was Noor feeling by 10 p.m.?
Noor felt lonely and rejected, reading the late reply and the lunch laugh as proof Mehak was tired of her.
What could Noor try next time a reply is late?
Remind herself of other reasons, like a dead phone, and ask Mehak warmly instead of pulling away.
How might Mehak feel when Noor says she'll do the project herself?
Mehak likely feels confused and hurt, pushed away after a genuine apology.
My bicycle has a flat tyre and my dad says we'll fix it together.
That's a useful skill to learn. Do you have a repair kit?
Yes, with patches and glue.
Take the wheel off, remove the tube and find where the air escapes. Pumping it up and listening or dipping it in water shows the leak.
What next?
Rough up the area, apply glue, wait until it's tacky and press on the patch. Let your dad show you each step, since tools can be tricky.
Then I put it back?
Check the inside of the tyre for a thorn or nail first, or the new hole will come back. Then replace the tube, pump gently and check the pressure.
Good tip. My dad will be pleased that I'm learning.
He will be, and you'll never be stuck by a flat tyre again. Practise it a couple of times with him watching, and you will be quick at it.
Now you try: f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) + xy, f(1) = 1.
The answer is f(x) = x^2/2 + x/2.

"Gautam, did you see the video of Harsh falling?" his friend asked at the Christmas party.
"Everyone's sharing it. It's funny."
Gautam, eleven, watched it. Harsh had tripped in the school play, and someone had added laughing sounds.
"It's not funny," Gautam said. "He cried after."
"Just forward it."
"No."
That night Gautam told his sister Gargi, who was sixteen. She said, "Tell Mummy now." They did. Mummy phoned the class teacher that same evening, and the teacher asked everyone to delete it.
Gautam messaged Harsh: "Sorry about the video. I didn't share it."

What had someone added to the video?
Laughing sounds.
How did Gautam feel about the video?
He felt uncomfortable and sad for Harsh, refusing to call it funny.
Why was involving Mummy the right step?
It brought in an adult who contacted the teacher the same evening to stop the video spreading.
How might Harsh feel reading Gautam's message?
Harsh may feel less alone and grateful someone didn't share it.

In the school library, Divyansh was laughing with Farhan over a comic. Then Farhan took the comic back to finish a page.
Divyansh's face changed. He shoved his chair, shouted "You always do this!" and threw the book. Then he went silent, staring at the floor, not answering anyone.
Mr Menon, the librarian, didn't send him to the principal. He said quietly, "You're safe. Come sit in the reading room with me." Divyansh went, stiff as a stick.
After some time he mumbled, "I wanted him to stay my friend." His eyes were wet.
Mr Menon told Farhan he could go back to class and thanked him for staying calm. Before the last bell, he walked Divyansh to the school counsellor, who had time to see him right away.

What did Divyansh throw?
The book.
What did Divyansh seem to feel behind his outburst?
He seemed scared of losing Farhan as a friend; he said "I wanted him to stay my friend" with wet eyes.
Why was Mr Menon's response better than punishment?
He calmed Divyansh, gave him a quiet safe place, and got him to the counsellor, since punishment usually deepens the mix of needing and fearing people.
How might Farhan see the sudden change?
Farhan was probably shocked and confused, since they had just been laughing together, and may have felt blamed for simply taking the comic back.

Vaisampayana continued,--"The high-souled king Dhritarashtra, thus addressed by Sanjaya, became, O monarch, absorbed in meditation about his sons. Endued with great energy, he then, having reflected, said these words: 'Without doubt, O Suta's son, it is Time that destroyeth the universe. And it is Time that again createth everything. Nothing here is eternal. It is Nara and Narayana, endued with omniscience, that destroyeth all creatures. The gods speak of him as Vaikuntha (of immeasurable puissance), while men call him Vishnu (one that pervadeth the Universe)!'"

Answer from the text. What does Dhritarashtra say about Time?
He says Time destroys the universe and creates everything again, and that nothing here is eternal.

"Mama's home!" Dilnaz called from the door.
Ojas dropped his blocks. "Mama! Mama!" He ran, arms up.
"Oof, such a big hug." She kissed his cheeks.
His uncle held out a biscuit. "Come to Mamu, Ojas?"
"No." Ojas wrapped his legs around Dilnaz and pressed his face into her neck.
"All right, Mamu can wait," she laughed. "You missed me, hm?"
He patted her cheek with a sticky hand.

What did Ojas drop when his mother came home?
He dropped his blocks.
Why did Ojas refuse to go to his uncle?
He wanted to stay close to his mother, whom he had missed and prefers when he is tired or excited.
How could Mamu respond so he does not feel hurt?
He could smile and wait, and play with Ojas later; this preference is normal and not a rejection of him.
How might the uncle feel when Ojas says 'No'?
He might feel a small pang, but also understand that Ojas simply loves his mother most right now.

Arnab reached the village unannounced on Friday and stood at the gate for a minute. His father Anand sat on the veranda with a radio, but the radio was off and his eyes were on the road. When the phone rang inside, Anand was up and through the door before the second ring. Then, seeing Arnab, he smiled so widely that he forgot to say hello.
Over tea, Arnab said, "You never tell me you miss me."
"You are busy," said Anand, stirring his cup. "Why should an old man make it heavy?"
Arnab noticed the swept spare room and the jar of mango pickle labelled with his name. On Sunday, at the bus stop, he said, "Every Saturday at seven, I'll call. And I'll come in Poush month too." Anand nodded and looked at the bus, not at him.

What did Arnab see inside the house that showed his father was expecting someone?
He saw the swept spare room and a jar of mango pickle labelled with his name.
What was Arnab feeling when he noticed the swept spare room and the labelled pickle jar?
He felt moved and a little guilty, realising his father misses him, which is why he promised regular calls and a visit.
What could Arnab do to answer his father's quiet longing?
Arnab promised a call every Saturday at seven and a visit in Poush month, giving his father regular things to look forward to.
Why might Anand say 'Why should an old man make it heavy?'
Anand may fear burdening Arnab with his loneliness, so he keeps quiet even though running to the ringing phone and the swept room show how much he waits for contact.

Wasim, twenty-six, ran a small bicycle repair shop near the bus stand of his kasba. In the evenings, schoolchildren brought him punctures, and old men sat on the bench outside, arguing about cricket. One afternoon, his old classmate Kishore, now working in the city, stopped by. He wore a crisp shirt and talked about his office, the traffic and his big salary. "Don't you want more?" he asked. Wasim was fixing a chain, oil on his fingers. He thought about it honestly. "I'm my own boss. I know every family here. I close at seven and eat dinner with my Ammi." He wiped his hands and smiled. "I'm fine, yaar. Really." Kishore looked at him for a long moment, then sat down on the bench too.

What time does Wasim close his shop?
At seven.
What does Wasim's honest answer and smile suggest about how he feels about his life?
He feels quietly content, valuing his independence, community and family time over bigger money.
Why might it help Wasim to think honestly before answering?
It shows his contentment isn't just a defence; he checked his feelings and still found them true.
Why might Kishore sit down on the bench after hearing Wasim?
He may have felt a pull toward Wasim's calmer life, perhaps questioning his own busy city routine.

Sunday diary. Today in the Arts Hall Mr. Farooq talked about volcanoes, and his voice never went up or down, like a fan. I nearly fell asleep. Salma whispered, “He doesn't care.” But then I saw that he had dark circles and kept drinking water. Maybe he was very tired. Salma herself talks in a flat way when she is shy, and she cares a lot about everything. Then I remembered my cousin, who speaks in that flat voice all the time, and he loves his class and explains stuff beautifully. So a flat voice doesn't mean someone doesn't care. Kiran.

What was Mr. Farooq talking about?
Volcanoes.
What did Kiran think about Mr. Farooq's flat voice, and what did Kiran notice?
Kiran first felt sleepy and bored, but then noticed Mr. Farooq's dark circles and thought he might be tired, so stopped assuming he did not care.
What could Kiran do if Kiran wants to understand a friend with a flat voice?
Kiran could ask about the topic or watch what the friend does, not judge by tone alone.
How might Salma have seen Mr. Farooq's voice?
Salma took it as not caring, though Kiran suggests that could be wrong.
Please narrate a fresh story about a boy who is asked to look after his baby sister for one afternoon.

Mother had to go to the bank, so ten-year-old Dev was left in charge of baby Gudiya for two hours. At first, everything was easy. Gudiya played with her rattle and clapped. Then she began to cry, loudly, and nothing worked. Dev tried milk, a song, and a funny face. Still she cried. He picked her up and walked around the room, humming. Gudiya went quiet and stared at the ceiling fan. Dev stood beneath it until his arms ached, but he did not mind. When Mother came back, the baby was asleep on his shoulder, and Dev was nearly asleep too.

Which sounds right, "listen the song" or "listen to the song"?
Also, how do I help my grandmother carry shopping?

1. Say "listen to the song". "Listen" always needs "to" before the thing you hear.
2. Take the heavier bags and let her carry the lighter ones. Walk beside her at her pace.

Read this:

So, you asked why Arnab's camera sat on our shelf for four months. Honestly, it's a funny story. My flatmate Arnab wanted to sell his old camera and lens. Online, the same set went for about thirty thousand. He listed it at fifty. People messaged and offered twenty-eight, thirty, thirty-two. Every time, he'd say, "They're insulting me. This camera went to Ladakh with me." I felt bad for him, but also a bit frustrated, because he kept saying he needed the money for a new laptop. One night I just asked, "Arnab, if this camera was in a shop right now, would you pay fifty?" He thought for a long time. "No. I'd pay thirty, max." "So..." He laughed, then groaned. He relisted at thirty-two and sold it in two days. That's how Zubin became the flat's pricing consultant.

What price did Arnab first list the camera at?
Fifty thousand.
How did Zubin feel as Arnab kept rejecting offers?
Zubin felt sympathetic but a bit frustrated, knowing Arnab needed the money for a laptop.
Why did Zubin's question help Arnab?
Imagining the camera in a shop made Arnab see its value as a buyer would, separate from his Ladakh memories.
How did Arnab react to buyers' offers at first?
Arnab felt insulted, because the camera's memories made it feel worth more to him.
In War and Peace, who becomes Nikolai Rostov's wife?
Nikolai marries Princess Mary Bolkonskaya, Prince Andrew's sister. They settle at Bald Hills, where he becomes a hard-working, careful landowner.
In Pride and Prejudice, whom does Elizabeth Bennet get engaged to?
She gets engaged to Mr. Darcy. Jane can hardly believe it at first, and her father is surprised because Elizabeth used to dislike him.

The metro was packed at six in the evening. Lavanya, fourteen months old, was teething, and her cheeks were red. She rubbed her face against her mother Rashmi's shoulder, then arched back and wailed, drool soaking her collar. Passengers turned to look. Rashmi swayed gently, pulled a cool teether from her bag and let Lavanya gnaw on it, humming close to her ear. The crying faded to hiccupping sobs, and by the next stop Lavanya was clutching the teether, eyes half shut.

Where were Lavanya and Rashmi at six in the evening?
They were in a packed metro at six in the evening.
Why did Lavanya rub her face and wail?
Her teething gums were sore, and being tired in a crowded train likely made the discomfort feel worse.
What helped Lavanya's crying fade?
Rashmi swaying, humming close to her ear and giving her a cool teether to gnaw eased both the soreness and the upset.
How might other passengers see Rashmi in that moment?
Some might be annoyed by the noise, but many would see a mother calmly doing her best with an uncomfortable baby in a hard place.
Politely ask a fellow passenger on the train to move his bag from my seat. Give me one or two short sentences, spoken style. I'm shy.
Excuse me, I think this is my seat. Could you please move your bag so that I can sit down? Thank you so much.

Read this:

Plastic chairs lined the hall above the sweet shop in Bhadrak, and Arohi arrived in her work kurta, straight from the block office where she typed land records. Kamal was already there, telling everyone about his master's in Germany and the flat he rented in Munich. Pooja passed around wedding photos. Rakesh had opened a solar-pump business with twelve employees. Someone asked Arohi, 'Still at the block office?' She said yes and laughed, and the laugh came out thin. She kept her phone face-down on her lap. When the samosas came round she took one and forgot to eat it. On the auto home, past the same paddy fields she had seen every day since school, she counted: no degree abroad, no husband, no business. At twenty-five, her life suddenly looked like a small room she had wandered into by mistake.

Where did Arohi work?
At the block office, where she typed land records.
How can you tell that Arohi felt shaken at the reunion?
Her laugh came out thin, she kept her phone face-down and forgot to eat her samosa, then counted everything she lacked on the way home.
What could help Arohi at this early stage, before the comparison hardens?
Talking it over with someone she trusts, and remembering that a reunion shows only highlights, could stop one evening from deciding how she sees her whole path.
How might Kamal have experienced the same evening?
Kamal probably enjoyed sharing his news and may not have noticed how it landed on Arohi; to him it was catching up, not comparing.

Read this:

I'm Tanuja, and before my first big class presentation I thought rehearsal meant reading my slides in my head. My sister made me do it properly.
The first run, alone in my room, out loud, with the phone timer: fourteen minutes. The limit was ten. I had no idea where the time went.
The second run I timed each part. Introduction: one minute. Background: two. The middle part, where I explained my survey method, took seven minutes. Seven! I'd been explaining every single question in the questionnaire.
I cut the method to three questions as examples and one sentence about the rest. The third run I did for my classmate Imran in an empty classroom after lunch. Ten minutes and twenty seconds. He said the middle still dragged a little, so I cut one more example.
On the day, I finished at 9:50. I've never felt so calm at the front of a room.

How long did the middle part take in the second run?
Seven minutes.
How did Tanuja feel on the day, finishing at 9:50?
Tanuja felt calm and in control, which had never happened before at the front of a room.
What else could Tanuja add to the rehearsal next time?
Practise answering a question or two after the timed run, since questions also take time.
How might Imran have felt watching the third run?
Imran was probably glad to help and honest enough to say the middle still dragged.

Read this:

Friday, hostel
Presentation done. We got an A. And honestly? That was mostly me. I did the research, the slides AND I presented. Uday just did "the data," whatever that was.
Later, in the mess, I heard Uday tell Nitin he had "carried the whole thing," because he spent three nights cleaning the survey data. Three nights? I didn't even know that took three nights. I was annoyed at first. Then I tried adding it up: if he thinks he did 70% and I think I did 70%, that's 140%. We can't both be right.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask him to go through our chat history with me and write down who did what. Next time, a shared list from day one.
Sachin

How many nights did Uday spend cleaning the survey data?
Three nights.
What did Sachin feel on hearing Uday's claim in the mess?
Sachin felt annoyed at first, then uneasy on realising they both believed they had done most of the work.
What does Sachin plan, and why could it help?
Going through the chat history with Uday to write down who did what, and keeping a shared list from day one next time, so credit matches the record.
How might Uday see the project?
Uday sees his three nights cleaning data as carrying the whole thing, just as Sachin sees the slides and presenting.
Last week, a farmer shipped 10 boxes of pomelos which had 240 pomelos in all. This week, the farmer shipped 20 boxes. How many dozens of pomelos did the farmer ship in all?

There were 240/10 = 24 pomelos in a box.
This means that each box has 24/12 = 2 dozens of pomelos since 1 dozen is equal to 12.
The farmer shipped a total of 10 + 20 = 30 boxes.
Thus, the farmer shipped a total of 30 x 2 = 60 dozens of pomelos.
The answer is 60.

Shall we go to cinema? Is it okay?
No, it needs a change. The better sentence is: "Shall we go to the cinema?" Why: "the cinema" takes "the" in this meaning.

How does the third-storey passage look to Jane?

Mrs. Fairfax stayed behind a moment to fasten the trap-door; I, by dint of groping, found the outlet from the attic, and proceeded to descend the narrow garret staircase. I lingered in the long passage to which this led, separating the front and back rooms of the third storey: narrow, low, and dim, with only one little window at the far end, and looking, with its two rows of small black doors all shut, like a corridor in some Bluebeard's castle.
Narrow, low and dark, with one small window and two rows of shut black doors. It reminds her of a corridor in Bluebeard's castle.

Read this:

The day before the science fair, Suraj Sir walked along the lab tables checking models. Naveen stood proudly beside his windmill, built over six evenings from ice-cream sticks and a toy motor. Sir tapped the blades. "They scrape the base, Naveen. If you raise the stand a little, it will spin freely." Naveen's ears went red. "It spins fine, Sir. I tested it at home." Sir switched it on. The blades turned twice, scraped and stopped. "See? It just needs a push," Naveen said, and pushed it. "Six days I worked on this." Sir left a small wooden block beside the model and moved to the next table. Naveen slid the block aside without looking at it.

What did Suraj Sir leave beside the model?
A small wooden block.
Why did Naveen's ears go red when Sir pointed out the scraping blades?
He felt embarrassed and hurt, because after six evenings on the windmill the comment felt like criticism of him and all that effort, not just of the stand. 😳
What choice could Naveen make with the wooden block before the fair?
He could raise the stand for one test run. If the blades then spin freely, the windmill he worked so hard on only gets better.
How might Suraj Sir feel when Naveen slides the block aside?
He may feel a little disappointed, since he wants the model to work, but he chooses not to force it and leaves the fix within Naveen's reach.

messages.content: Is the Wi-Fi working? I can't connect to it. Can you check this short message?

Yes, that's right as it stands.
Why: no error (punctuation: "Is the Wi-Fi working?" is correct).
My eyes feel strained after long hours on the screen. What can I do?
For anything about your eyes, it is best to tell a parent and let a doctor check you. I cannot give medical advice.
Can I at least change how I use the screen?
That is a question for the doctor too, who can check your eyes and tell you what suits you. Until then, tell your parent how long you use screens each day.
I'll tell my mother tonight.
Telling her sooner is better than waiting, especially if your eyes are bothering you. Describe how long you use the screen and when the strain starts, so the doctor has useful information.

Class teacher's note, Class 9B, Thursday
For three weeks Jeevan, who used to sit alone at lunch, has been glowing. He talks about his "crew" from an online group: daily 5 am check-ins, a special greeting, older members who call him "brother". I was glad at first. He needed friends.
This week things changed. He stopped sitting with Lokesh, his one friend in class. Lokesh told me Jeevan said the crew wants him to "cut off anyone who doesn't get it". Today, when I asked where the crew meets in person, Jeevan would only say it was "secret for now".
What I did: I spoke with Jeevan at break, calmly. I told him wanting a group is completely normal, but real friends don't ask you to drop other people or keep secrets from home. He looked relieved, and a bit scared. With him beside me, I called his mother the same afternoon and informed the school counsellor, who will see him tomorrow.

What did Lokesh say the crew wants Jeevan to do?
To 'cut off anyone who doesn't get it'.
How did Jeevan seem when the teacher spoke to him at break?
Jeevan looked relieved and a bit scared, as if part of Jeevan had been waiting for someone to notice.
What did the class teacher do that protected Jeevan?
Spoke calmly, said wanting a group is normal but secrecy and cutting people off are not, then called Jeevan's mother that afternoon and informed the counsellor.
How might Lokesh have felt when Jeevan stopped sitting together at lunch?
Lokesh probably felt hurt and worried at being dropped, and cared enough to tell the teacher what the crew had said.

The inter-colony final was stopped by rain at the eighteenth over. Mridul, in his Green Park Colony cap, stood under the shed with the other supporters, soaked and shivering, refusing to go home. "We're going to win. We have to."
When play resumed, the umpire used the rain rules. Green Park lost by four runs.
Mridul's face burned. It felt like he had lost. He shouted at the other colony's supporters, "Cheats! You only won because of rain!"
Afreen, whose brother played for the other team, turned, her eyes flashing. "We didn't make the rain, Mridul."
He opened his mouth to shout again, then saw her brother limping off with a sore ankle, smiling anyway.

By how many runs did Green Park lose?
Green Park lost by four runs.
What does Mridul's burning face show he is feeling?
He feels crushed and humiliated, as if the loss were his own.
What would you advise Mridul after the final?
He could take a breath before speaking, congratulate the other team and let himself be sad about the loss without calling them cheats.
How does Afreen see Mridul's shout of "Cheats"?
Afreen sees it as unfair and hurtful, since her brother's team played in the same rain and did not make the rules.

Read this:

Note from the class teacher, Class 7, Tuesday.
This morning Gurleen came to me before assembly with her mother's phone. The night before, Ramesh had posted a photo of her asleep on the bus during the school trip, mouth open. Twenty classmates had reacted with laughing faces.
Gurleen's voice was steady, but her eyes were red. She said she had wanted to reply with something rude but had taken screenshots instead.
I told her she had done exactly the right thing and that none of this was her fault. I spoke to Ramesh and his parents at lunch. The photo was deleted and Ramesh apologised to Gurleen. I will talk to the whole class about the group chat tomorrow.

How many classmates reacted with laughing faces?
Twenty classmates.
How did Gurleen seem to feel when she came to the teacher?
She seemed hurt and embarrassed, with red eyes, though she kept her voice steady.
What did Gurleen do that helped stop the mockery?
She didn't reply in anger; she took screenshots and brought them to the teacher, who acted that same day.
How might Ramesh see the photo after talking to the teacher and his parents?
Ramesh may now see that what felt like a joke was public humiliation for Gurleen, which is why he deleted it and apologised.

Before: The week Salma learned she hadn't got the transfer to the Delhi office, she and Asif sat on the balcony every evening while she talked it through. He listened. It seemed to help her let it out.
During: Three weeks later, on a Thursday, she was still going over the same things. Why her manager chose Priya. What she should have said in the review. Asif noticed she wasn't crying any more, just grinding through it, sounding flatter each time. After an hour she said, "I feel even more stuck now."
After: The next Monday, when she began again, Asif put down his tea. "Salma, we've gone round this a lot, and it doesn't seem to make you feel better. What's one small thing you could do this week?"
She was quiet for a while. "I could ask for a meeting about the next round." She wrote it on her phone.

What did Salma not get?
She didn't get the transfer to the Delhi office.
What was Asif worried about as he watched Salma in the third week?
Asif felt concerned, noticing she was no longer crying but sounding flatter, and that the talks left her more stuck.
What did Asif's question do for Salma?
It moved her from going over the past to one concrete step, asking for a meeting about the next round, which gives her something to act on.
How might Salma feel after writing the step on her phone?
She might feel a bit lighter and more hopeful, having something to do instead of only thinking about what went wrong.

Read this:

Dear Thomas,

Big news. I tried the flashcard-and-recall method you mentioned, for two days only, and my practice quiz went from 12 out of 20 on Monday to 14 on Wednesday. It works! I told the study group I'm skipping Friday's revision session because I don't need it now, and I recycled my old chemistry notes this morning. Some of the group said two days is too short to know, but I think they're just jealous. Wednesday's quiz was easier, to be honest, and I slept badly on Monday. Doesn't matter. Numbers don't lie. I'll show you my chart on Saturday.

Sachin

What did the practice quiz score go to on Wednesday?
The practice quiz went to 14 on Wednesday.
What is Sachin feeling about the result?
Sachin feels excited and very sure, so sure that the group's doubts are brushed aside.
What could Sachin do to find out whether the method really works?
Sachin could keep using it for a few more weeks, track several quizzes of similar difficulty and compare them with the old method, before dropping the notes or the group session.
How might the study group feel about Sachin skipping Friday's session?
The group may feel dismissed or worried, having said that two days is too short to know.

When I started coaching the under-tens at the colony ground last year, I made promises casually. 'Bowl well and you'll bat next.' Then time ran out and they didn't. I noticed Tanvir, eight, stopped waiting his turn. He'd grab the bat, sulk, walk off. At first I thought he was just impatient. Then I remembered: I'd broken my 'you'll bat next' three times with him. Why would he wait? So I changed. I only promised what I could keep. 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.' And I kept it, every time, even when practice ran late. While they waited, we counted balls aloud or sang the silly boundary song. By March, Tanvir stood at the edge with his pads on, counting under his breath. 'Darshan Bhaiya, two more balls,' he'd say. He believed me.

What did Darshan start promising instead?
He started promising, 'Three overs of fielding, then you bat.'
What did Darshan realise about Tanvir's impatience?
Darshan felt a pang of guilt, realising Tanvir had no reason to wait after three broken promises.
What changed Tanvir's ability to wait?
Darshan kept every promise and made waiting fun by counting balls and singing, so Tanvir learned that waiting pays.
How does Tanvir show his trust by March?
He stands ready with pads on, counting balls under his breath, sure his turn will come.

Naveen, I swear, Farhan sir hates me. Every time I send him something he replies in one line: 'Fine.' 'Fix slide 4.' 'Noted.' No hello, no thanks. With the other interns he jokes, but with me it's all business. So I just keep my head down in meetings and don't say anything. Why give him more to dislike?
Then yesterday Rimjhim told me he'd asked her, 'Is Sanjana even interested in this role? She never asks a single question.' Interested? I'm staying back till eight!
I thought quiet meant respectful. He thinks it means I don't care. And I thought short meant he hates me. Maybe it just means he's drowning in emails, like everyone. I don't know.

How late does Sanjana say she is staying back?
She is staying back till eight.
Why has Sanjana been keeping her head down in meetings?
She believes Farhan sir dislikes her because of his one-line replies, so she stays quiet to avoid giving him more reasons.
What turning point is open to Sanjana now that she knows how her silence looks?
She could ask a question or two in the next meeting, or tell Farhan sir she is keen to learn, so he stops reading her silence as lack of interest.
How does Farhan sir seem to see Sanjana's silence?
He seems to read it as lack of interest, not realising she is quiet out of respect and fear, and he may not notice how brisk his replies sound.

The new family moved into C-block of the Chennai housing colony on a Sunday. That evening Yusuf, nine, and his friends were playing football on the tar court when the new boy, Abhinav, walked across the middle of their game and kicked the ball over the wall.
"He's mean," Yusuf told everyone. "Did it on purpose."
The next week Abhinav brought the ball back, cleaned, with a note: "Sorry, I didn't know you were playing." On Wednesday he found Yusuf's lost cycle key near the gate and handed it to the watchman. On Saturday he offered to be goalkeeper, the job nobody wanted.
Yusuf still passed him the ball last, and when his sister asked why, he said, "Because he's mean. Remember the first day?"
"That was one kick," she said.
"It was the first kick," Yusuf said, as if that settled it.

What did Abhinav do with the ball the next week?
He brought the ball back, cleaned, with a note saying sorry.
How does Yusuf feel about Abhinav, even after the apology and the kind acts?
Yusuf still feels resentful toward Abhinav because of the first kick, passing him the ball last and insisting "he's mean" despite the cleaned ball, the note and the found key.
What could Yusuf try, now that Abhinav has offered to keep goal?
He could give Abhinav a proper turn with the ball and notice how he plays, letting what happens now count as much as the first day.
How might Abhinav feel being passed the ball last every time?
Abhinav would likely feel left out and confused, since he apologised, returned the key and took the job nobody wanted.

'Pranav, you keep turning that paper card over as if it might grow into something bigger. Come, let your Ramesh Dada tell you something. When I was nine, my friend Gopal gave me a card for my birthday. He had folded an old calendar page and drawn a kite on it, with our two names on the tail. The same day, my rich cousin gave me a shiny pen in a box. I kept looking from one to the other, and the card seemed to shrink in my hand. Then I saw Gopal's fingers, still blue from colouring. I hugged him and said thank you, and I meant every word. The pen broke within a month. That kite card is still in my tin box upstairs.'

What did Gopal draw on the card?
A kite, with their two names on the tail.
What was young Ramesh feeling when he looked from the card to the pen?
He felt a little disappointed as the card seemed to shrink beside the pen, then warm and grateful when he saw Gopal's blue fingers.
Which choice in the story turned the moment around?
Noticing the effort in Gopal's blue fingers and thanking him sincerely, instead of measuring the card against the shiny pen.
How might Gopal have seen the moment when Ramesh hugged him?
Gopal was probably relieved and happy that his homemade card was valued, since he had worked hard on it.
Why does a paper boat sink after floating for a while?
The paper boat soaks up water and goes limp. Because wet paper becomes heavy and loses its stiffness, the sides sag, and water flows in over the edge.
One box has 9 pencils. How many pencils are in 9 boxes?
81. Because 9 x 9 = 81, so 9 boxes hold 81 pencils.

Okay, Gurleen, you asked why I went quiet in the canteen. It's Nanaji. When I went home for Diwali, he called me Kamla, my mother's name, instead of Jaya. Twice. He asked if I'd eaten four times in one hour. And on Saturday he walked to the old market and couldn't find his way back. The shopkeeper phoned us.
I got really annoyed with him that evening. I said, "Nanaji, you just asked me that!" He looked so confused and small.
Then the doctor explained to us that this is an illness in his brain. He's not being careless. He can't help it.
Now when he asks if I've eaten, I just say, "Yes, Nanaji, rajma chawal," every time. He smiles. I still cry about it at night sometimes. But I'm gentler now.

Who phoned the family when Nanaji got lost?
The shopkeeper phoned them.
What did Jaya feel when Nanaji called Jaya by the wrong name?
Jaya felt confused and hurt, and later grief strong enough to cry at night.
What helped Jaya respond more gently?
Learning from the doctor that the forgetting is an illness, not carelessness, so Jaya now answers calmly every time.
How might Nanaji have felt when Jaya snapped at him?
He probably felt confused and ashamed, as he looked small after being told he had just asked.

Read this:

Property agent's note — client file, Deepika and Harish, Whitefield. Written by Nazia.

I've shown flats to many couples. These two made my job much easier.
At our first meeting Deepika handed me a printed list. Must-haves: walking distance to the new metro line, a school within two kilometres, two bedrooms, lift. Nice-to-haves: balcony, covered parking, a park nearby.
At the third viewing, Harish loved a flat with a huge balcony facing the lake. Deepika checked the list and asked me about the school. Four kilometres. They looked at each other, and Harish said, "Balcony's on the other column." We moved on in two minutes.
The seventh flat had no balcony but met every must-have. They made an offer that week.
What I did next: I've started asking all my clients to bring the same kind of list.

How far was the school from the third flat?
Four kilometres.
What might Harish have been feeling on saying "Balcony's on the other column"?
Harish was probably disappointed to let the lake-view balcony go but also calm and accepting, trusting the list they had agreed.
What else could Deepika and Harish do before making the offer?
They could get the documents checked by a lawyer and confirm their loan eligibility with the bank.
How does the couple's list look to the agent?
The agent finds it makes viewings quicker and clearer, so much so that the agent now asks other clients to bring a similar list.
Is it "enviroment" or "environment"? How do I make my own cup of coffee?

1. It is "environment", with an "n" before "ment". Keeping the environment clean is everyone's job.
2. Boil some milk and stir in a spoon of coffee powder and sugar. Whisk it until it is frothy and pour into a cup.

"Varun, stay a minute?"
"Yes, ma'am."
"You haven't turned in a single draft this term. Only finals."
"The drafts aren't good enough to show."
"And on Tuesday, you cried over a seven out of ten."
Varun went red. "It should have been ten."
Rajni ma'am pulled out a folder. "This is my PhD chapter. See the comments? 'Unclear.' 'Rewrite.' 'Weak argument.'"
"That's yours?"
"Mine. Messy first tries are how everyone learns. Next week, bring me a messy draft. I'll grade only the effort."
Varun looked at the red comments for a long time. "Okay, ma'am."

What mark did Varun cry over?
Seven out of ten.
What was Rajni ma'am feeling as she pulled out her folder?
Rajni ma'am seemed concerned and caring, wanting Varun to see that mistakes are normal.
Why is Rajni ma'am's approach likely to reduce Varun's fear?
Showing her own corrected work and allowing a messy draft graded only on effort makes imperfection feel safe.
What is it like for Varun to see his teacher's red comments?
Varun seems surprised and thoughtful, perhaps relieved that even teachers get corrected.

Read this:

Chinmay came in from the field after a long day, shoulders hard and jaw tight, standing in the doorway with his hands on his hips. His son Eshaan, two, who had been playing with pebbles, stopped and stayed where he was, watching. Chinmay noticed. He breathed out, walked to the mat, sat down and let his arms rest on his knees. “Come, Eshaan.” Eshaan crept toward him, dropped a pebble in his palm and climbed onto his lap.

Where did Chinmay sit down to invite Eshaan?
On the mat, with his arms resting on his knees.
Why might Eshaan have stayed where he was at first?
He was probably reading his father's tight, standing posture as tense, though he might simply have been focused on his pebbles.
What could Chinmay do when he comes home tired?
He could pause at the door, soften his body and get down to Eshaan's level before speaking.
What might Chinmay feel when Eshaan holds back?
He might feel a pang or surprise at his son's caution, and then understand that his tired body sent a message.
My friend wrote "two mango's" on the list. Is the apostrophe needed?

No. A plural is usually made by adding s or es, and no apostrophe is used. The usual form is "two mangoes" ("mangos" is also seen). The apostrophe in "mango's" would show possession.
Example: We bought two mangoes and three bananas.

Read this:

Ojas, you went quiet when that policeman walked past? I felt the same at your age. Let your Devika Dadi tell you. When I was small, at the big fair by the river, I let go of my father's hand and was swept away by the crowd. I cried and cried. Then a tall policeman with a lathi and a huge moustache bent down in front of me. I was so frightened of that moustache that I cried louder! But he took off his cap, gave me a sweet from his pocket and said, "Beti, what's your father's name?" He lifted me onto his shoulders and walked through the crowd shouting it, until my father came running. So, Ojas, if you're ever lost, look for the uniform. They are there to help.

What did the policeman give young Devika from his pocket?
A sweet.
How did young Devika feel when the policeman bent down?
Frightened, especially of his huge moustache, so she cried louder.
What did the policeman do that turned her fear into trust?
He took off his cap, gave her a sweet, asked her father's name and carried her on his shoulders to find him.
How might Devika's father have felt when he came running?
Hugely relieved and grateful to find his daughter safe.
Write a rhyming couplet about a lost umbrella. Two lines only.

I left my red umbrella on the bus one day,
And now the rain just laughs and soaks me on my way.

Read this:

Samir had been in a bad mood since Friday. Nobody seemed to notice, which made it worse. His parents should have seen he was upset about the football selection. He hadn't said anything, but they should have known. Instead Mummy asked if he'd finished his homework.

Then Sahil said he couldn't come cycling on Sunday; he had his cousin's engagement. He should always make time for me, Samir thought. I'd make time for him.

By Sunday evening a tight knot of resentment had built up. He didn't reply to Sahil's message: "bro wish you were at the engagement, food was amazing." At dinner he answered his parents in grunts.

Later Papa knocked. "Something's up, beta. We can tell you're upset, but we don't know what about. Can you tell us?"

Samir opened his mouth to say, "You should know," and stopped. They didn't know. He hadn't told them.

Why couldn't Sahil come cycling on Sunday?
Sahil had his cousin's engagement.
Why did Samir feel resentful toward his parents and Sahil?
Samir felt hurt and unseen, because he believed his parents should understand without being told and Sahil should always make time for him.
What could Samir do instead of expecting others to know?
Samir could tell his parents about the football selection and let Sahil know he missed him, so conversation can replace resentment.
What is it like for Papa when he knocks?
Papa is concerned and a bit confused, sensing that Samir is upset but not knowing why.

Read this:

When my son's college friend Omkar came to stay a night with us in Ludhiana, I expected the usual: a boy who sleeps till noon and leaves wet towels. Instead he arrived with a small box of Kolhapuri chivda from his mother. After dinner he rolled up his sleeves and asked where the dishes went. I told him to sit; he dried them anyway. Next morning he made his bed, thanked my husband for the lift, and left before lunch, saying, 'Aunty, you must be tired, you cooked so much.' I was. I can't say what went on in his head, but I'd have that boy back any day.
Baljeet

What did Omkar bring from his mother?
A small box of Kolhapuri chivda.
What did Baljeet feel about Omkar's visit?
Baljeet felt pleasantly surprised and grateful, touched that he noticed how tiring the cooking had been.
Which of Omkar's actions made him a good guest?
Bringing a small gift, drying the dishes, making his bed, thanking the hosts and leaving before they grew tired.
Why might Omkar have chosen to leave before lunch?
He likely sensed that hosting was tiring and wanted to leave while everyone still felt glad, though Baljeet can only guess his thoughts.
Make the sentence active: A letter was written by the boy to the mayor about the broken road.
The boy wrote a letter to the mayor about the broken road.
I was homesick in my new city until I found a small park near my flat where old men play chess. I'm Adam.
What a nice discovery, Adam. A familiar activity in a new place can make it feel warmer. Do you play chess?
A little. I joined a game with a man named Mr. Pillai and lost badly.
Losing to an experienced player is how most people improve. Mr. Pillai may enjoy having a new opponent, so go back and ask him to show you a trick or two.
I'll go again tomorrow. Do you think they'd mind if I just watch?
Most chess players welcome a quiet watcher, and watching is a good way to learn. Greet them politely, stand a little back, and ask questions during a break.
What was the man's name who beat me?
It was Mr. Pillai, who beat you at the park. When you go tomorrow, you could greet him by name and ask him to explain one move from the game.
Should I take my own chess set when I go back tomorrow?
You do not need to, Adam. The men at the park already play there, so they have boards. Bring a small notebook instead to jot down Mr. Pillai's tips, and ask him to show you one move from your game.

June. Usha came home with an offer letter from a large services company and a certificate from the coaching course she'd done. Vasudha, her roommate, looked at the certificate for a long time. That night she enrolled in the same course and paid the fee.
August. Vasudha sat through her fourth mock coding test and scored low again. Her notebook margins were full of tiny drawings of app screens. Usha noticed. "You're redesigning the test page instead of solving the test," she joked. Vasudha didn't laugh.
October. A design studio visited campus looking for interface design interns. The brief asked for a portfolio. Vasudha had sketches but nothing finished, because every evening since June had gone into aptitude drills. She submitted three rough screens. On the walk back she said quietly, "I spent four months on your road, Usha. Mine was right here in the margins."

Who visited campus in October?
A design studio looking for interface design interns.
What was Vasudha feeling on the walk back?
Vasudha felt regretful and a little sad, realising four months went into a path that didn't fit.
What would you change first if you were Vasudha in June?
Ask what the roles actually need and what you are good at, then put the evenings into a design portfolio instead of copying the course.
How might Usha feel hearing your road?
Usha may feel awkward or sad, never having meant for Vasudha to copy her, and might wish they had talked about it in June.

metadata.subtype: Approach: copying a friend's path without fit [Pitfall]

Read this:

After the clash in the city made the headlines, Varun Mathew stopped coming to the colony basketball court. Sunaina, seventeen, waited for him three evenings in a row.
She finally knocked at his flat. His mother answered, polite but guarded. Varun came to the door and didn't step out.
"Did I do something?" Sunaina asked.
Varun looked at his feet. "People in our church are scared. My mother thinks we should keep to ourselves for a bit. Your uncle posted something online."
Sunaina's face went hot. She'd seen that post and said nothing.
"That's not what I think," she said. "And you're not responsible for what anyone else did either. I'm sorry I didn't say so sooner."
Varun's shoulders dropped a little. "Court tomorrow?"
"Six o'clock. I'll bring the ball."

How many evenings did Sunaina wait at the court?
She waited for him three evenings in a row.
What was Sunaina feeling when her face went hot?
She felt ashamed for having seen her uncle's post and said nothing.
What did Sunaina do that kept trust alive?
She went to Varun's door, asked honestly, apologised for her silence, and made clear she didn't blame him for others' acts.
What is it like for Varun's mother after the clash?
She seems guarded and scared, wanting her family to keep to themselves until things feel safer.
Reggie's father gave him $48. Reggie bought 5 books, each of which cost $2. How much money does Reggie have left?

The cost of the books is 5 x $2 = $10.
Reggie has $48 - $10 = $38 left.
The answer is 38.

Read this:

Siddharth, you asked why I never studied what I loved. Sit, the diyas on your balcony can wait a minute. When I was fifteen, in Aligarh, every girl in my class signed up for the science stream, because Rukhsana did, and then her whole group did. I loved drawing buildings. I wanted arts, with geography. But standing alone at that form table, with thirty girls watching, my hands went cold. What if they laughed? What if I was the odd one out? So I ticked science. Two years of biology I hated. Rukhsana, it turned out, had only picked science because her cousin had. Much later, at twenty-four, I studied town planning anyway. So when your friends all pick the same thing, you remember Zeenat aunty's two lost years, hmm?

Which stream did Zeenat really want at fifteen?
Arts, with geography, because she loved drawing buildings.
What was young Zeenat feeling at the form table?
She felt anxious and exposed, afraid the thirty girls would laugh if she stood out, so ticking science felt safer.
What choice at the form table could have changed the story?
She could have ticked arts with geography, perhaps after talking to a teacher or family member beforehand, so the choice rested on what she loved rather than on the crowd.
Why did Rukhsana pick science, according to the story?
Rukhsana had only picked science because her cousin had, so even the person everyone followed was following someone else.
What is the price of a litre of milk at the dairy today?
I don't know today's price, as I can't see local rates. The dairy's board or a call will tell you.

Read this:

Monday night, thunder: Kishore sat up in bed. "Scared." Papa lay beside him. "Thunder is loud. I'm here."
Thursday at the park: Kishore pointed at his knee. "Ow. Dog." A big dog had knocked him over. Papa, who had seen it, said, "The dog bumped you. That was scary."
The next Monday, at daycare pick-up: "Ojas push. Sad." Papa listened, then spoke to the teacher that same afternoon. She said she would watch the two boys more closely.

What did Kishore say at daycare pick-up?
"Ojas push. Sad."
What was Kishore feeling when he said "Ojas push"?
He was sad and perhaps a bit hurt that Ojas pushed him, and wanted his father to know.
What did Papa do that encourages Kishore to keep telling?
He listened calmly each time and acted, speaking to the teacher the same afternoon.
How might the teacher feel when Papa tells her?
The teacher is probably glad to know and ready to keep a closer eye on the boys.

Read this:

Notes for Thursday's session with our counsellor, written by Ankita
What I've noticed about Francis over the last month:
- At work events he is warm, funny and patient. His customers at the bank adore him. Last Friday I watched him listen to an old man's complaint for twenty minutes without once checking his watch.
- At home he walks in, says "hi" and goes straight to the shower. At dinner, if I ask a question, he says, "Can we not?" On Sunday he snapped when I asked about the electricity bill.
- He doesn't seem angry with me. He seems empty.
What I did: on Monday I said, "I think you're giving all your good hours to work, and I'm getting the tired ones." He went quiet, then agreed.
What I'd like to try: one work-free evening a week, and him telling me when he's drained instead of snapping.

How long did Francis listen to the old man's complaint?
Twenty minutes, without once checking his watch.
What does Ankita mean by saying Francis 'seems empty' rather than angry?
Ankita senses that his energy is used up by the end of the day, so the curtness comes from exhaustion, not dislike.
Which of Ankita's ideas could help most, and why?
Asking Francis to say when he's drained instead of snapping, so Ankita knows what's happening and doesn't take it personally.
How might Francis's customers describe him?
As warm, funny and endlessly patient, without seeing how little is left for home.

metadata.subtype: Warm at work, cold at home [Observer]

Read this:

The train to Farida's parents' town was four hours late, and the waiting room at Itarsi junction was packed. There was nowhere to go and nothing to do. Maybe that was why Farida finally said it.

Arif was scrolling on his phone beside her, as he had been all week, all month.

"Arif," she said. He looked up. "I feel we're drifting. I don't know how to bring us back."

His thumb stopped. Around them, a child cried, a vendor shouted "chai, chai."

"Here?" he said. "Now?"

"We're never anywhere else. We're always busy. This is the first time we've had four hours."

He put the phone in his pocket. "I thought it was just me who felt it."

They talked in low voices while the station roared around them. Not about blame. About whether to try, and how. Maybe a counsellor. Maybe not. But they were talking.

How late was the train?
Four hours late.
What does Arif's thumb stopping suggest?
It suggests he was startled and perhaps relieved, since he admits he had felt the drift too.
Why was naming the drift kindly a good step?
It let them talk about whether and how to repair, perhaps with a counsellor, instead of drifting further in silence.
What would change if Farida had waited for a quieter, better moment?
She might have kept waiting, since they are always busy, and the drift would have grown.
Can you invent a story about a girl whose father cannot read, and how she helps him.

Savita noticed that her father always asked her to read the bus numbers. At first she thought he simply liked her voice. One evening, he held a letter from the bank and looked worried. "Read it to me, beta," he whispered, and she understood. Mr. Rao had never been to school because he had worked in the fields since he was seven. Savita read the letter slowly, word by word. Afterwards, she brought out her old primer. "Let me teach you," she said. Every night after dinner, they practised one letter. By the winter, he could read the name of their town on the station sign.

Read this:

Siddiq, five, sat on the kitchen step while his grandfather Thabo said, "Mrs Dlamini's hen laid a big egg this morning." "Really?" Siddiq's eyes went wide. "No way!" On the walk over he stretched his arms out. "It will be huge, bigger than a football!" In the coop lay an egg, large for an egg but ordinary. "It's big for an egg," said Thabo. "A football was what you hoped for." "Oh," said Siddiq. Then he held it. "It's still warm."

Whose hen laid the egg?
Mrs Dlamini's.
What was Siddiq feeling on the walk, and what does his "Oh" at the coop suggest?
Excited expectation, shown by wide eyes and stretched arms. The "Oh" suggests a flicker of disappointment, though the warm egg still delighted him.
How did Thabo separate hope from fact?
He named what was real, that it was big for an egg, and what Siddiq had hoped for, without mocking him.
What is it like for Thabo when Siddiq's hope meets the ordinary egg?
He probably feels a little sorry to disappoint him but wants to be honest. Siddiq holding the warm egg would reassure him.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday
Gautam has seemed irritable all week, snapping at his group during the science project. Today he stayed back and let it out. His parents 'should understand' that he wants to switch to commerce; his friends 'should be there, every single time' for the project, and two of them went to a cousin's wedding instead. When I asked whether he had told his parents about commerce, he said, 'They should know. It's obvious.' He had not told them. He had not told his friends that the deadline worried him, either. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write three things he wished people knew, and next to each, one person he could tell. He wrote 'Papa' next to commerce. I've offered to be in the room if he wants, and I'll ask him on Monday how it went.
Nikita

Which stream does Gautam want to switch to?
Gautam wants to switch to commerce.
Why does Gautam say 'They should know. It's obvious'?
To Gautam the wish feels so clear that he believes his parents ought to see it without being told, so their silence feels unfair and feeds his irritation.
What step did Nikita suggest, and why might it work?
Nikita had him write three things he wished people knew and one person to tell each, which turns silent 'shoulds' into real conversations, starting with Papa.
How might Gautam's project group see his snapping?
The group may feel confused and hurt, since they had no idea the deadline worried him and only saw anger after two of them went to a family wedding.

Read this:

The drums of Durga Puja were beating across the village. Bidisha tugged Parveen's hand. "Come see our pandal!"
Parveen hesitated at the entrance. She'd never been inside one.
"You don't have to pray," said Bidisha. "Just look."
Inside, the goddess had ten arms. Parveen stared at the lion and the colours. Bidisha's grandmother offered her prasad. Parveen looked at Bidisha, unsure.
"You can take it or not," Bidisha whispered. "Both are fine."
Parveen took it with both hands, like Bidisha did. "Thank you, Dida."
Later, Parveen said, "Come to our home on Eid. Ammi makes sevai."

How many arms did the goddess have?
Ten arms.
What was Parveen feeling when she hesitated at the entrance?
Parveen felt unsure and a little nervous, never having been inside a pandal.
What did Bidisha say that made it easier for Parveen?
She said Parveen didn't have to pray and could take prasad or not, which respected Parveen's own faith.
How might Bidisha's grandmother see Parveen taking prasad with both hands?
Bidisha's grandmother likely feels touched and respected by Parveen's polite gesture.
Sam is coming over to celebrate my birthday and I want to bake a cake, but I have never baked.
That is a sweet plan. A simple cake is a good first try. What flavour do you want?
Chocolate. I have a recipe with eggs, flour and cocoa.
That is a good base. Read the recipe through before you start, measure everything first, and do not open the oven too early. Let it cool fully before adding any topping.
I might just dust sugar on top instead of icing. Who is coming over again?
Sam is coming. Sugar on top is a neat, easy finish. Light a candle and enjoy the cake with Sam, even if the first bake looks a little rough.
Ask the building watchman, politely, to lock the main gate at ten every night. 35 words, from Mrs D'Souza.

Dear Watchman,
Could you please lock the main gate every night at ten o'clock? We worry about our safety when the gate is left open. Thank you for your good work and your help.
Mrs D'Souza

Read this:

Sudha ma'am took off her glasses when the young founder said he'd start fundraising once the product was ready. "Let me tell you about Kamal. He was twenty-five when he came to me with a water-testing kit for villages. I asked how much he needed. He said, 'As much as possible.' I sent him away.
He came back a week later with one page. Monthly costs, times eighteen months, plus a small cushion: that was his number. Then he had worked backwards. To find five investors, about fifty good meetings. To have fifty meetings by June, start calling in April. For those meetings to go well, three hundred kits sold by May.
Every week after that he asked one question: are we on track for May? He raised the round in July. Not because he was lucky. Because he knew the date before he knew the investors."

How many kits did Kamal need to have sold by May?
Three hundred kits.
How might Kamal have felt when Sudha sent him away?
He was probably embarrassed and a bit stung, but it pushed him to come back with a real plan.
Which choice in Kamal's story mattered most, and why?
Working backwards from the eighteen-month figure to meetings and a May target, because it gave every week a clear check.
How did Sudha see Kamal's one page?
Sudha saw a founder who finally knew his number and his dates, which made the pitch believable.

metadata.subtype: Approach: working backward from the funding target [Thinking]

Daycare note, Monday. Afreen, Toddler Room.
Zubin (2) wanted to stay on my lap all morning, patting my cheek and saying "more hug." When I put him down to help another child, he cried loudly. At lunch he loved the sweet rice and wailed when the bowl was empty.
I gave him one more cuddle and his soft blanket, then showed him the water tray. He splashed and giggled within minutes.
Next: tell his father at pickup. Wanting sweets and cuddles is normal at his age. 🙂

What did Zubin say while patting Afreen's cheek?
More hug.
Why did Zubin wail when his bowl was empty?
He loved the sweet rice and wanted more of that good feeling right away, so its ending upset him.
What did Afreen do that helped Zubin, and why did it work?
Afreen gave him one more cuddle and his soft blanket, then moved him to the water tray, which comforted him and gave him a new pleasure.
How might Zubin's father feel reading this note?
He would probably feel reassured that Zubin's crying for cuddles and sweets is normal and that he was comforted.

metadata.subtype: Wants warm, sweet, soft things now [Actor]
