Read this:

Monday. Tushar tapped Jatin on the head with a rolled-up notebook as he passed. "Morning, egghead!" Jatin ducked. Tushar grinned. It was just a joke.
Wednesday. Tushar lifted his hand to wave at a friend, and Jatin flinched, covering his head. Tushar saw it. His grin slid away. He felt sick. Was that because of me?
That evening he told himself it was nothing. But he kept seeing Jatin's arms over his head.
Friday. Before class, Tushar went to Jatin's desk. "I'm sorry I kept doing that. It wasn't a joke for you. I'm stopping." Jatin looked at him for a long moment, then gave a small nod.

What did Tushar hit Jatin with on Monday?
A rolled-up notebook.
How did Tushar feel when Jatin flinched on Wednesday?
He felt sick and uneasy, wondering if Jatin's fear was because of him.
What mature step did Tushar take on Friday?
He apologised directly, admitted it wasn't a joke for Jatin, and said he would stop.
How might Jatin have felt when Tushar raised his hand on Wednesday?
Jatin felt afraid, expecting to be hit, which is why he flinched and covered his head.

Read this:

In the one-room village school, the children were writing the letter "ka" on their slates. Mridul held his chalk out to Abhinav Sir. "Sir, you write it. Mine will be bad." His eyes were wet. Abhinav Sir sat down on the floor beside him. "Try only the first curve. I'll be right here." Mridul pressed the chalk and made a small curve. "Good. Now the line." Mridul made the line. It was crooked. He looked up, worried. "That's a ka," said Sir. "Your ka." Mridul looked at it, then rubbed it out and tried again, by himself.

What letter were the children writing?
They were writing the letter "ka".
How was Mridul feeling when he held out his chalk?
He felt afraid of failing, his eyes wet, and wanted Sir to do it so it would be safe.
What did Abhinav Sir say that helped Mridul try?
He said to try only the first curve and that he would be right there, then praised the crooked letter as Mridul's own.
What would change if Abhinav Sir wrote it for Mridul every time?
Mridul would stay scared and not learn to write it himself.

Read this:

Seema set the kitchen timer for forty minutes and pressed the button before opening her game. Weekday rule, her own: forty minutes, no more. Halfway through a tricky level her younger brother Kamal hovered, waiting for his turn on the shared tablet. With five minutes left she was one move from a treasure chest. The timer rang. Seema's thumb froze. "Just--" she began, then stopped, saved her place and handed Kamal the tablet. "Papa did not tell me to," she said, half proud, half cross. "I did." Kamal blinked. "You never stop." "Now I do." Tomorrow the treasure chest would be waiting.

How long did Seema set the timer for?
She set the timer for forty minutes.
What was Seema feeling when the timer rang one move from the chest?
Torn, half proud and half cross, since her thumb froze but she stopped anyway. 😅
What could Seema do if the timer often rings at a bad moment in a game?
She could choose a game or level with natural stopping points, because the limit then holds without cutting the fun short.
How might Kamal see Seema stopping on her own?
With surprise and probably relief, since he blinked, said she never stops, and now gets his turn.
The boy which was crying near the gate is my neighbour.

The boy who was crying near the gate is my neighbour.
Why: We use "who" for people and "which" for things.
Why does teamwork matter in sport? Write a paragraph for my school magazine, about 75 words.

Teamwork matters in sport because no player can win alone. In a team, each person has a job, and the game goes well only when everyone does it. Players learn to trust one another, pass the ball and support a friend who has made a mistake. A team that works together can beat a team of stars. Teamwork also teaches us to share joy in winning and lessons in losing.

Read this:

Dear Mama and Papa,

I'm writing this because every time I try to say it out loud, I freeze or it comes out wrong. Ankita helped me find the words, but they're mine.

I don't believe the way you do anymore. I haven't for a while. When we go to the gurdwara, I love the kirtan and the langar and seeing you both so peaceful. But the belief underneath, I can't find it in myself right now. I've tried.

I'm not saying you're wrong. I would never make fun of what you believe. You taught me to be honest and kind, and I think that's why I can't keep pretending.

You don't have to say anything today, or even this month. I know this might hurt. I'll still come on Sundays if you want me there. I just didn't want a lie between us.

I love you both so much.

Mehak

Who helped Mehak find the words for the letter?
Ankita helped Mehak find the words.
What was Mehak feeling when trying to say it out loud?
Mehak felt nervous and stuck, freezing or saying it wrong each time, which is why a letter felt safer.
What did Mehak do that was wise in this letter?
Mehak wrote of still respecting and loving them, promised never to mock their faith, and gave them time instead of demanding acceptance.
How might Mama and Papa feel reading the letter?
They may feel hurt and worried, but also moved that Mehak was honest, loving and still willing to come on Sundays. 🤍

Read this:

Binita's Dadi had one rule she repeated at every visit: "Don't stare at elders, it's rude." So Binita, eight, looked at the floor when Dadi's friends spoke. In the new term at her Bengaluru school, Ojas sir took maths. On Monday he said, "Binita, eyes here, please," tapping his own eye. She lifted her face for a second, then dropped it. On Wednesday he said it again, more firmly. Binita's stomach knotted. Was she bad at home or bad at school? That evening she asked Dadi, who laughed softly. On Friday, Dadi wrote a note for Ojas sir. He read it, then knelt by her. "At home, lower eyes are respect. Here, looking at me tells me you're following. You're not being rude to anyone." Binita looked at him, just long enough to nod.

What did Ojas sir tap when he said "eyes here, please"?
He tapped his own eye.
What was Binita worried about when Ojas sir asked again?
She was anxious and confused, her stomach knotting, worried she was bad at home or bad at school.
Which step helped most, and why?
Dadi's note and Ojas sir kneeling to explain both meanings, because it showed Binita she was not being rude in either place.
How might Ojas sir have seen Binita's lowered eyes at first?
He may have thought she was not paying attention or was being shy, before the note helped him understand.
Write one sentence describing a grandfather's hands, using both "rough" and "gentle".
My grandfather's hands are rough from years of farm work, yet they are gentle when he holds a newborn calf.

Read this:

Dear Eshaan Bhaiya,
I saw the video you posted: no helmet, overtaking that truck on the highway, everyone commenting fire emojis. I'm writing because I can't say this on the phone without crying.
You know my friend Ritu from tuition. Last year she was riding pillion without a helmet. Her cousin was showing off. They fell near the flyover. She's okay now, but she spent three months in hospital and still has headaches. Her cousin still can't talk about it.
I know you think nothing will happen to you. Ritu's cousin thought so too.
You're the person I look up to most. Please wear the helmet. Please don't race. If your friends think it's boring, they're not really your friends.
I'll buy you a helmet for Rakhi if that helps.
Your sister,
Vandana

How long did Ritu spend in hospital?
She spent three months in hospital.
How does Vandana feel about Eshaan's video?
Vandana feels frightened and upset, unable to talk about it on the phone without crying.
Why might Vandana's letter change Eshaan's habit?
It tells a real story about someone they know and comes from a sister who looks up to him, which can matter more than friends' approval.
How might Eshaan feel reading the letter?
Eshaan might feel shaken and guilty, realising how much his sister worries.

Read this:

The day before Holi: Mahima told Gurpreet she'd stay on the terrace. Crowds made her nervous.
Holi: By noon, the whole lane was a sea of colour and drums. Mahima went down just to watch, and in minutes she was in the middle, laughing, throwing colour at everyone, grabbing water balloons. She felt light, wild, invisible. When an old man with a walking stick shook his head, “No colour, please,” she laughed and threw a handful at him anyway. The crowd cheered.
The day after: Mahima saw the same man outside the chemist, scrubbing pink from his white kurta, his hands trembling. She stopped. Gurpreet said, “Isn't that—” Mahima nodded. She walked over and said, “Uncle, I'm sorry. That was me.”

What did the old man say to Mahima?
He said, "No colour, please."
How did Mahima feel in the Holi crowd?
She felt light, wild and invisible, bolder than she ever felt alone.
What did Mahima do the day after, and why did it matter?
She went to the old man and apologised, taking personal responsibility for what she did in the crowd.
How might the old man have felt when colour was thrown at him?
He probably felt disrespected and upset, having clearly asked for no colour.

Read this:

When I was nine, I discovered a trick on Papa without even knowing it.
After dinner I asked, "Can I play the racing game for five minutes?" He was reading and said, "Five minutes."
After five minutes I said, "Just one more race?" He nodded without looking up.
Then, "Omkar wants to play too. Only ten minutes, together?" Papa said, "Okay, ten."
Each yes made the next one seem normal. By the time Mummy came in, it was ten o'clock and my little brother Omkar was asleep on the carpet. Papa looked at the clock and said, "How did it get so late?"
I didn't know. I'd only ever asked for a little bit. Himani the genius, Mummy called me, not smiling.

What time was it when Mummy came in?
It was ten o'clock.
What was Himani feeling when Papa asked how it got so late?
Himani felt a bit guilty and confused, having only ever asked for a little bit each time.
What could Papa try next time to avoid the slow slide?
He could agree a clear total time at the start, like thirty minutes, and set a timer so each small request doesn't feel like a natural next step.
How might Mummy see what happened?
Mummy seems annoyed, calling Himani "the genius" without smiling, and may be frustrated with Papa too.

metadata.subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]

In the Kothrud flat, the argument had been circling since breakfast. Pradeep's mother wanted the puja for the new flat on Saturday, when the priest was free. Swati had already promised that Saturday to her parents, who were coming from Nagpur. Pradeep's father kept repeating, "The priest decides, not us." Pradeep scrolled his phone. For two days he had said nothing, and both women had noticed. Swati slept facing the wall. His mother told him he had "changed after marriage". On Thursday evening he put the phone face down on the dining table. "Aai, Swati's parents booked their tickets first. Swati, Aai has waited years for this puja. Can we ask the priest about Sunday morning? I'll call him myself." His mother sighed, then nodded slowly. Under the table, Swati squeezed his hand.

Why could Swati not keep Saturday free?
Swati had already promised that Saturday to her parents, who were coming from Nagpur.
What was Pradeep feeling while he scrolled his phone for two days?
He felt torn and uneasy between his mother and Swati, and hid behind the phone rather than risk upsetting either of them.
What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
His silence left both his mother and Swati feeling unsupported; naming each side's fair point and offering to call the priest himself turned it into a shared plan.
What was it like for Swati while Pradeep stayed quiet?
She probably felt alone in the disagreement, which is why she slept facing the wall; squeezing his hand shows her relief when he finally spoke up fairly.

messages.content: Tommy is making 12 loaves of bread. He needs 4 pounds of flour per loaf. A 10-pound bag of flour costs $10 and a 12-pound bag costs $13. When he is done making his bread, he has no use for flour and so he will throw away whatever is left. How much does he spend on flour if he buys the cheapest flour to get enough?

He needs 48 pounds of flour because 12 x 4 = 48
He needs 4.8 bags of 10 pound bags because 48 / 10 = 4.8
He therefore needs to buy 5 bags of flour because 4 < 4.8 < 5
He spends $50 if he buys this flour because 5 x 10 = 50
He needs 4 bags of the 12-pound flour because 48 / 12 = 4
He would spend $52 on the 12-pound bags because 4 x 13 = 52
He spends $50 if he buys the cheapest flour because 50 < 52
The answer is 50.
I'm Divya and I've been offered a phone interview at nine tomorrow. I live in a noisy neighbourhood.
Noise can distract you and the interviewer. Think of a quiet spot, like a closed room, a parked car or a friend's place.
My cousin Adam's house is quiet. He's at work in the mornings.
That is a good option. Ask Adam if you can use a room at nine, and arrive early so you are settled. A quiet room will help you sound calm.
He said yes. Should I keep notes in front of me?
Yes, a few notes with key points are fine on a phone interview. Keep your CV, a pen and a glass of water nearby. Do not read from a script, though.
What time is it again?
Your phone interview is at nine tomorrow morning. Be at Adam's house a little earlier, test the phone signal, and sit somewhere comfortable and quiet.

In the biology lab, Yamini's group had to submit their enzyme experiment by five. At 3:30, one of the six readings was clearly wrong: it made the graph jump.
There was no time to repeat it. Saurabh, her lab partner, was already typing the conclusion. "Just smooth it," he said. "Put something that fits."
Yamini hesitated, then typed a number that made the curve neat. Everyone did small things like this, she told herself. It was one reading out of six.
The report got an A.
In April, the lab instructor asked their group to repeat the experiment as a demo for the juniors. Yamini's hands were cold as they set it up. The real readings came out, and the curve jumped again, just where it had before. The instructor frowned. "Your report shows a smooth curve. What happened?"
Saurabh looked at the floor. Yamini felt her face burn. "I changed one reading," she said quietly. "I'm sorry."

How many readings did the experiment have?
One reading out of six.
How did Yamini feel as they set up the demo in April?
Yamini felt anxious and guilty, her hands cold because she knew the real reading might expose the change.
What could Yamini and Saurabh have done at 3:30 instead?
Reported the odd reading honestly and noted there was no time to repeat it, rather than inventing a number.
How might the instructor feel after Yamini's admission?
The instructor would likely be disappointed but may respect that Yamini finally told the truth.

Fifteen minutes before opening, Simran had to show Manjula, the new hire, how to record a returned item in the stock sheet. "What do you do when a customer buys something?" Simran asked. "I subtract one from the sheet," Manjula said. "Good. A return is the opposite." Simran did one example: a red kettle back, plus one. "Now explain it back to me, as if I'm the customer." Manjula frowned, explained, and got the sign wrong. Simran did not sigh. "Try the next return." A blue mug: Manjula added one and typed it correctly. The shutter went up on time, and the first return of the day was Manjula's, done alone.

What was the item in Simran's example return?
It was a red kettle.
What might Simran have wanted when asking Manjula to explain it back?
Simran wanted to check that Manjula really understood, not just nodded, and stayed patient despite the ticking clock.
What made the explain-back step useful?
It showed the sign error early, before a real customer, and gave Manjula a chance to fix it with the next return.
How might Manjula have felt on getting the sign wrong and not being sighed at?
Probably nervous but reassured, able to try again because Simran stayed patient. 🙂
Reports of widespread rain: does it mean it rained everywhere?

Almost everywhere in the area. Widespread means found or happening over a large area or among many people. It is an adjective.
Example: Widespread flooding closed schools in the district.
The knifes in this kitchen are not sharp enough to cut tomatoes. Spelling check, please.

The knives in this kitchen are not sharp enough to cut tomatoes.
Why: plural ("knifes" -> "knives").

But the suddenly started Pequod was not quick enough to escape the sound of the splash that the corpse soon made as it struck the sea; not so quick, indeed, but that some of the flying bubbles might have sprinkled her hull with their ghostly baptism.

Answer from the text. Why does the Pequod not escape the sound of the splash?
The ship starts suddenly but not quickly enough. The corpse still strikes the sea with a splash she hears, and some of the flying bubbles might have sprinkled her hull.

Sunday, 6 p.m.
I lay on my bed from two to five today and I still feel guilty writing that. Three hours. The whole time a voice in my head kept listing things: the internship form, the stats notes, the gym. So I wasn't really resting, just lying there anxious, scrolling, calling myself lazy. Rehana came in with chai and said, "You rested, na? Good." I said I'd wasted the afternoon. She laughed and said her swimming coach used to say muscles grow on rest days, not in the pool. I've been thinking about that. Last week I didn't stop at all, and by Friday I couldn't write one clean paragraph. Next Sunday I'm going to try it properly: phone in the drawer, a walk by the lake, no list. And no apologising.
Chandrika

What did Rehana's swimming coach used to say?
That muscles grow on rest days, not in the pool.
Why couldn't Chandrika enjoy the three hours of rest?
Chandrika felt guilty and anxious, with a voice listing tasks and calling rest lazy.
What does Chandrika plan to do differently next Sunday, and why might it help?
Put the phone in a drawer, walk by the lake and drop the list, so rest actually restores and later work improves.
How does Rehana see Chandrika's afternoon?
Rehana sees it as healthy rest worth celebrating, not a waste, and brings chai to say so.

Dear Ujjwal,
Remember you asked why I stopped answering during movie nights? Here's the honest reason.
Since March I've been trading on my phone. At first it was fun. Then I noticed I was checking the app every few minutes, in class, in the bathroom, at 3 a.m. When it went up, I felt brilliant. When it went down, I couldn't eat. Last week I lost a chunk, and my first thought was to put in twice as much to win it back. That scared me, because it's exactly how my uncle talks about card games.
So I've done three things. Notifications off. The app is deleted from my phone; I can only check on my laptop, once a day, after dinner. And I've asked my cousin, who works at a bank, to ask me every Sunday how it's going.
I'm not sure I'm done with it. But I don't want my mood run by a chart.
Come for movie night on Friday?
Tenzin

When does Tenzin now check the app?
Tenzin now checks only on the laptop, once a day, after dinner.
What was Tenzin feeling after wanting to put in twice as much?
Tenzin felt scared, recognising the same pattern an uncle shows with card games.
Which of Tenzin's three steps seems most useful, and why?
Turning off notifications and deleting the app from the phone, because it breaks the constant checking loop.
How might Ujjwal feel reading the letter?
Ujjwal might feel relieved to know why Tenzin went quiet, and glad to be invited back to movie night.

The rain was coming down hard, and the power had gone. Minakshi's floor was covered with toys, and Aai had said tidy before the lamp was lit. Minakshi stood in the doorway. Everywhere she looked there was something. She sat down in the middle, picked up a doll and began to brush its hair. When her brother Harish came with the lamp, nothing was put away.

What was Minakshi doing when Harish came?
She had picked up a doll and began to brush its hair.
What was Minakshi feeling as she stood in the doorway?
She was overwhelmed; there was too much mess to start on.
What small step could help Minakshi start?
Choosing just one kind of toy to put away first, so the job looks smaller.
How might Harish see the untidy room?
Harish might be annoyed, or understand that the mess was too much for her.

Sports day at Nilesh's school fell on the hottest April morning, and the sack race started late. Nilesh, six, had practised with a rice sack at home with his sister Kashish. Halfway, he tripped and fell flat. Other children passed him. He struggled up, hopped on, and crossed the line fourth, red-faced and dusty. He didn't win a medal. But when Kashish ran to him, he said, "I fell and I didn't stop!" and stood tall, holding the sack like a flag.

Which place did Nilesh finish in?
Fourth.
How did Nilesh feel crossing the line fourth?
Nilesh felt proud of himself for getting up and finishing, even without a medal.
How could Kashish support Nilesh's pride?
Praise his getting up and finishing, the part he is proudest of.
How might Kashish feel seeing him stand tall with the sack?
Kashish would likely feel proud and happy, having practised with him.

I'm Karthik. Asif and I have run the tiffin service together for two years. Last spring he spent the rent money we'd kept aside, and the landlord came knocking. I found out from the landlord, not from him. That night Asif came to my room and said, 'I took it. I didn't tell you. That was wrong.' No excuses. He set up a repayment from his share, a bit each month, and gave me the account password. Then he just kept showing up. Six-thirty every morning, every delivery logged, every rupee in the notebook. For months I was cold with him. He never once asked, 'Are we okay now?' I don't know what it cost him inside. I only know that last week, without really thinking, I handed him the cash box for the weekend. He took it and nodded, and neither of us said anything.

Who did Karthik find out about the rent money from?
Karthik found out from the landlord, not from Asif.
What does Asif never asking 'Are we okay now?' suggest about him?
It suggests he understood that trust had to come back through his actions, and he didn't want to pressure Karthik into forgiving him.
Which of Asif's choices did most to rebuild trust, and why?
Showing up at six-thirty and logging every delivery and rupee for months gave Karthik repeated proof, which mattered more than the apology alone.
How might Karthik have felt in the months of being cold with Asif?
Karthik probably felt hurt and wary, wanting to believe Asif but needing time and evidence before relaxing again.
Six kids and two adults are going to the circus. Kid's tickets are on sale for only half of the adult tickets. The total cost is $50. How much is one kid's ticket?

Let X be the price of one kid's ticket.
So the price of one adult ticket is X*2.
Five kids and two adults are going to the circus, so 6*X + 2*(X*2) = $50.
So 10X=$50
So the price of one kid's ticket is X = $5.
The answer is 5.

I'm Tushar, Omkar's older brother, and I watched this happen at his under-sixteen cricket camp. Our parents had saved for months to buy him a proper willow bat for his birthday. He slept with it next to his pillow for two nights. Then he took it to camp. Three of the boys there, all a bit better than him, had full branded kits: helmets, pads, bags with their names stitched on. That evening Omkar put the bat in the corner and didn't oil it. When Papa asked about camp, he said, "It's fine," in a flat voice. At dinner he muttered, "Everyone else gets proper stuff." Papa looked at the bat in the corner and didn't say anything. I can't be sure what Omkar was thinking. But the bat hadn't changed. Only the boys next to him had.

Where did Omkar sleep with his new bat for two nights?
He slept with it next to his pillow.
What does Omkar's flat 'It's fine' suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt let down and cheated after comparing his bat with the better kits of the boys a step ahead of him.
What could Tushar do to help Omkar see his bat differently?
Tushar could oil the bat with him and remind him how he felt on his birthday, before he started measuring it against the others' kits.
How might Papa feel when he hears Omkar say everyone else gets proper stuff?
Papa might feel hurt and quietly sad, since the family saved for months for a bat that now sits unoiled in the corner.

'Pooja, isn't the volcano model due Monday?'
'Papa, it's only Friday.'
'And tomorrow is Nani's birthday lunch. And Sunday you have dance.'
'...Oh.'
'So when were you planning to build it?'
'I thought Wasim was doing most of it.'
'Is that what Wasim thinks?'
Pooja picked at the sofa cushion. 'He did the drawing last week. I said I'd do the clay.'
'Then the clay is yours.'
'Can't you just make it tonight? You're good at this.'
'I'll sit with you. Your hands, though, not mine.'
She groaned, then went to find the clay. 'Fine. But you hold the bottle when we test it.'
'Deal. Call Wasim first and tell him honestly where it stands.'

When is the volcano model due?
It is due on Monday.
What does Pooja picking at the cushion suggest she was feeling?
She likely felt a bit guilty as she realised she had not done her share of the project.
How did Papa support her without doing the work for her?
He helped her see how little time was left and offered to sit with her, but insisted on her own hands and on being honest with Wasim.
If you were Wasim, what would you want from Pooja?
I would want her to do the clay she promised and tell me honestly if she was behind, so Monday is not a surprise.
Describe a small railway station at dawn in about 80 words.

The railway station wakes up before the sun. A tea-seller lights his stove, and the first steam rises into the cold air. Pigeons shuffle on the tracks, and a porter yawns beside his trolley. The loudspeaker crackles with a sleepy voice announcing the first train. Passengers huddle in shawls and carry old bags tied with rope. The sky turns pink behind the water tank. When the whistle blows, the whole platform comes alive at once.

Vinita's post was the loudest: “Moderators are useless, my photo was removed for no reason!” Varun opened the written rules and read the third one again: no photos of nests. Her picture showed a nest. He replied politely, quoting the rule and offering to restore the photo with the nest hidden. Vinita answered with a complaint about favouritism. Another member asked why a similar photo had stayed. Varun took a breath, checked, found that it had been posted before the rule was added, and explained it the same way. By one o'clock the forum was up, and he was tired but steady.

Which rule did Varun read again?
Varun read the third rule again: no photos of nests.
What was Varun feeling as the notifications piled up at night?
Varun felt tired and under pressure, but wanted to be fair, so he went back to the written rules.
What choice helped Varun handle both complaints?
Varun replied politely by quoting the written rule, checked the other photo's date and explained it the same way, keeping consistent.
How might Vinita have felt when Vinita's photo was removed?
Vinita probably felt unfairly treated and embarrassed in front of others, which shows in the loud complaint and the accusation of favouritism.

"Manoj Sir, can I talk to you?"
"Of course, Mahima. What's wrong?"
"The boys in my section keep saying my surname like a joke. They do an accent. Today someone wrote it on the board with a broom next to it."
"On the board? Today?"
"Yes. Everyone laughed. Even Shruti, and she's my friend."
"That must have hurt a lot."
"I'm fine."
"You're shaking, Mahima. You don't have to be fine."
"...It's been since Class 8. I stopped wearing my bangles because they said those too were 'village.'"
"Thank you for telling me. I believe you. This is discrimination, and it is not your fault. I'm going to the principal now, and I'll speak to your section this afternoon. Can I call your mother too?"
"Yes."
"And Mahima? Come to me any time. I mean it."

What did someone draw next to Mahima's surname on the board?
Someone wrote it on the board with a broom next to it.
How can you tell Mahima felt more hurt than she said?
She says she's fine but she is shaking, and she reveals it has gone on since Class 8 and made her stop wearing her bangles.
What did Manoj Sir do right?
He listened, said he believed her, named it as discrimination and not her fault, went to the principal and her section that day, and offered to call her mother.
How might Shruti see what happened if she thought about it later?
Shruti might feel guilty for laughing along and realise that her friend was deeply hurt, not just teased.

Note from Gargi, teacher. Neelam (5) drew a house, a big yellow sun and four people in bright colours, the smallest one purple and smiling beside a dog. "Tell me about your picture." "That's Mama, that's Papa, that's me and Bruno." Mama was in black. I noticed, but did not read meaning into it. "What is Mama doing?" "Going to work in her black coat." Colour alone tells me little, so I will keep listening.

What colour was Mama drawn in?
Black.
What might Neelam feel about her family, judging by her picture?
Cheerful, since the picture has bright colours, a big sun and a smile. It is only a starting point, not proof.
How did Gargi use the drawing?
She asked Neelam to tell her about it and did not read meaning into the black colour.
How might Gargi feel about the black Neelam used for Mama?
Gargi is curious but careful, noticing the black without reading meaning into it and asking what Mama is doing.

The kitchen was full of aunties, and the pressure cooker kept hissing. Gurleen Bua shouted over the noise, "Ujjwal, get the steel plates from the top shelf, wipe them, and take twelve to the terrace. Then tell Dadaji food is in ten minutes." Ujjwal, nine, nodded, lips moving: "Plates, wipe, twelve, terrace, Dadaji." He wiped the plates, counted twelve and carried them upstairs. On the stairs, a cousin asked him to play cricket. "After," he said, still muttering. He set the plates down, then found Dadaji on his chair. "Ten minutes, Dadaji." Then he ran off to play.

How many plates did Gurleen Bua ask Ujjwal to take?
She asked him to take twelve plates.
Why did Ujjwal keep muttering the steps?
He wanted to hold all the instructions in mind in the noisy kitchen and was worried about forgetting one halfway.
What could Gurleen Bua do to make multi-step jobs easier in a noisy place?
Say the steps slowly, or ask Ujjwal to repeat them back once before he starts.
How might the cousin feel when Ujjwal says "After"?
He may be a little disappointed, but he gets to play once Ujjwal finishes his tasks.

Wednesday
Got called to Mrs Fernandes's office today. Apparently Sunaina's friend told her we've been 'harassing' Sunaina. Harassing! It's banter. The whole group jokes like that. We call her 'Moustache' because of that one photo, and 'Thunder' when she gets angry, and she laughs. Well, she used to laugh. Mrs Fernandes asked how many times a day. I said I don't count. She said Sunaina has been eating lunch in the library for two weeks. I didn't know that. She said it stops now, and she's calling Papa tonight. He's going to be so annoyed.
I still think everyone's overreacting. Banter is banter. But I keep thinking about the library thing. Two weeks. I didn't even notice she was gone.
Siddharth

Where has Sunaina been eating lunch for two weeks?
Sunaina has been eating lunch in the library.
Why does Siddharth keep insisting 'banter is banter'?
Siddharth feels defensive and annoyed at being called in, and the word banter keeps the comments feeling harmless, so there is no need to face how Sunaina feels.
What should Siddharth do now?
Stop the nicknames completely, listen to Mrs Fernandes and Papa, and apologise to Sunaina without adding 'it was only a joke'.
What have the nicknames been like for Sunaina?
They seem to have hurt her enough that she stopped laughing and has been eating alone in the library for two weeks.
I typed "withdrawl" on the bank slip form. Is that right?

No, the word is "withdrawal", with an "al" ending. The verb is "withdraw" and the noun adds "-al".
Example: Please fill the form to request a withdrawal.

A note for laughing in class, Dhruv? Sit. Your Nilesh dadu will tell you something. In class five, in our school in Jabalpur, Master-ji was reading a poem about a brave king. My friend Ganpat sneezed, and it came out like a goat. I snorted. The boy beside me shook. Then the whole back bench, then the front, even the monitor, tears running, nobody knowing any more what was funny.
Master-ji's face went red. The harder we tried to stop, the worse it got. Then he did a clever thing. He shut the book and said, "Fine. Laugh for one full minute. I'm timing." We laughed, it died away, and he finished the poem.
So, what was so funny today?

What was Master-ji reading when Ganpat sneezed?
A poem about a brave king.
Why couldn't young Nilesh and the class stop laughing?
The giggle kept jumping from person to person; they felt helplessly amused, and trying to stop only made it worse.
Which choice in the story ended the laughter, and why did it work?
Master-ji gave them one timed minute to laugh; allowing it removed the pressure, so the giggles faded.
What was it like for Master-ji when the whole class was laughing?
He was likely embarrassed and annoyed at first, his face going red, before he found a calm way through.

Dear Anjali,
It's been almost a year, and I'm sorry it took me this long to write.
When I started seeing Rohit, I let everything else slide. I skipped our Sunday badminton, then stopped replying to the group, then missed your birthday dinner because he wanted a quiet evening. I told myself that's what being close meant: always there, always yes.
Last month he asked what I wanted for my birthday and I couldn't answer. I didn't know what I even liked anymore. That scared me more than any fight.
I'm not leaving him. I love him. But I've signed up for badminton again, Saturdays, and I've told him that's my morning.
I miss you. I miss who I was with you. Would you play a match with me, if you still want to?
Love,
Charu

Which day is Charu's new badminton?
Charu has signed up for badminton on Saturdays.
Why did Charu feel scared when Rohit asked about her birthday?
Charu was frightened to realise that nothing felt like a clear personal wish anymore, which showed how much of Charu's own self had disappeared into the relationship.
What is Charu's letter doing well as a repair?
It owns the specific ways Charu let Anjali down, gives a concrete step, and invites Anjali back without pressure, so Anjali can choose.
How might Anjali feel reading this letter after almost a year?
Anjali may feel a mix of hurt from being dropped and warmth at being missed, and could need time before saying yes to a match.

Sarah, Mary, and Tuan decided to go to the restaurant for a meal. They decided to split the cost of the meal evenly. If the total price of the meal comes to $67 and they have a coupon for $4, how much does each person need to contribute to the bill?

After using the coupon, the final price comes to 67 - 4 = 63 dollars.
With three people, they each need to pay 63 / 3 = 21 dollars each.
The answer is 21.

"Trisha, the biryani was cold at my son's party. Unless you give me a full refund, I'll post one-star reviews everywhere. Every site."
"Zubin sir, I'm sorry you were unhappy. The food left my kitchen hot at seven. Your event started at nine-thirty, and the hall didn't have warmers, which I mentioned in my message on the 12th."
"I don't care about messages. Refund, or reviews."
Trisha's heart was pounding. She pulled up the chat on her phone. "I have the message, and photos of the food at pickup. I can offer a discount on your next order as a goodwill gesture. A full refund isn't fair to my staff."
"Then I'll ruin your name."
"If you post a review, that's your right. I'll reply politely with the facts. And if there's a payment dispute, I'll go through the consumer forum."
"You're threatening me?"
"No, sir. I'm telling you what I'll do. The discount offer stays open."

What time did the food leave Trisha's kitchen?
At seven.
What was Trisha feeling during Zubin's threats?
She felt anxious and pressured, her heart pounding, but stayed steady and polite.
How did Trisha handle the threat well?
She kept evidence of the message and photos, offered a fair goodwill discount, refused a full refund, and named polite, formal ways to respond.
How might Zubin see Trisha's refusal?
Zubin seems angry and surprised, used to pressure working, and may feel cornered by her calm facts.

At the daycare door in Tucson, Camila wrapped both arms around her dad's leg and screamed as Jamal tried to leave. The teacher lifted her; she arched her back and wailed until her face was red. When Jamal came back at five, Camila ran to him, then hit his chest and turned away. A minute later she was clutching his shirt again, refusing to be put down, eyes on the door all the way to the car.

What did Camila do when Jamal tried to leave?
She wrapped both arms around her dad's leg and screamed.
What might Camila be feeling when Jamal comes back?
She seems both relieved and angry: she runs to him, hits him, then clings, as if unsure he will stay.
How could Jamal help Camila feel safer at goodbyes?
Keep goodbyes short and the same each day, come back when promised and stay calm through her anger.
What is it like for Jamal when Camila hits him and turns away?
He may feel hurt or confused, even though her anger shows how upsetting the parting was for her.

Leila went to the supermarket to get some groceries. Then she headed to her mechanic to get her automobile fixed. If fixing her automobile cost $350 which was $50 more than thrice the amount she spent at the supermarket, how much has she spent altogether?

Reversing the steps to obtain the amount she spent at the supermarket, $50 less than $350 is $350-$50 = $300
If $300 was thrice the amount she spent at the supermarket, then the amount spent at the supermarket was $300/3 = $100
In addition to what she spent fixing her auto, she spent $100+$350 = $450 altogether
The answer is 450.

Note to Sharmila's music teacher, from her mother, Minakshi. You asked what songs Sharmila (10) likes to sing. A funny thing: at her cousin's engagement in April, the aunties sang an old Konkani wedding song, and she wrinkled her nose and said it sounded like 'a creaky door.' Since then we've had three more family weddings, and the same song came up at each. At the last one I saw her clapping along. This week she asked me to write down the words, and she sings it while doing homework. Could she try it for the class programme? I think hearing it again and again made it hers.

What did Sharmila say the song sounded like at first?
A creaky door.
What does Sharmila asking for the words suggest?
It suggests Sharmila now feels fond of the song and wants to know it properly.
What choice might the music teacher make with this note, and why?
The music teacher could let Sharmila sing it in the class programme, since a song Sharmila has come to love will be sung with feeling.
How might the aunties who sing the song feel if they heard Sharmila sing it?
The aunties would likely be pleased and moved to see a child who once wrinkled her nose now carrying their song forward.

Early on Gudi Padwa morning, Mahima Tai swept the yard in front of the village house and handed five-year-old Tushar a small bowl of orange colour. 'Your job: fill every petal on this side.' Tushar crouched, tongue between his teeth, and pinched the colour out slowly. Some fell outside the lines. Mahima Tai didn't fix it. When the neighbours came to look, Tushar stood by his side of the rangoli with orange fingers and announced, 'I made this part.' That night he asked, 'When's the next festival?'

What did Mahima Tai hand Tushar?
A small bowl of orange colour.
What was Tushar feeling when he announced, 'I made this part'?
He felt proud and important, having done a real job for the festival.
What did Mahima Tai get right in giving Tushar the task?
She gave him a clear, real job and didn't fix his mistakes, so that part of the rangoli truly felt like his.
How might Mahima Tai feel hearing Tushar ask, 'When's the next festival?'
She would likely feel happy and amused, seeing that he now looks forward to festivals.

Order from biggest to smallest.
a) 1 3 2
b) 4 6 5
c) 7 10 8
d) 0 2 1
e) 3 9 6

I'm Shankar, Nakul's big brother. Last week Nakul, five, woke up screaming, "A crocodile on the wall!" There was a long bumpy shadow. Papa, Madhav, didn't laugh. He sat on Nakul's bed. "A crocodile? What's he doing?" "Opening his mouth to eat me!" "Shall we see what he's made of?" Papa switched on the lamp. The crocodile was his jacket on the hook, the zip for teeth. "Your eyes made a picture from the shadow," Papa said. "Shall we name him anyway?" Nakul named him Kuku. I don't know if he was still scared, but he fell asleep holding Papa's finger.

What was the crocodile actually made of?
Papa's jacket on the hook, with the zip for teeth.
What might Nakul have been feeling when the crocodile turned into a jacket?
He was probably surprised and a bit relieved, though maybe still uneasy, since he fell asleep holding Papa's finger.
What did Papa do well in handling Nakul's fear?
He asked about the crocodile without mocking, showed the simple truth with the lamp, and then let Nakul play along by naming it.
How does Shankar see what happened?
Shankar watched Papa calmly handle the fear, but admits not knowing whether Nakul was still scared.

Shreya, your friend has a secret, much older "boyfriend" online? Sit with your Dhruv Chacha.

When I was sixteen, my best friend Kunal started chatting with a "girl" from another city. Kunal got secretive, hiding his phone and skipping cricket. One day I saw a message on his screen: "Delete this after reading. Don't tell your family about us."

I wanted to laugh at him, tease him. I didn't. I asked, "Are you okay? Who is this?" He broke down. The "girl" had asked him for photos and to meet alone at the bus stand in the city.

I didn't promise to keep it secret. I told him, "I'm on your side, but I have to tell someone." We saved the messages together, and that evening I told my mother. She called Kunal's parents and the police helpline that same night. The "girl" turned out to be a grown man.

Kunal was angry for a month, then thanked me. Don't shame your friend, Shreya. Listen. Then tell an adult.

Where did the "girl" ask Kunal to meet alone?
She asked him to meet alone at the bus stand in the city.
What was young Dhruv feeling when he saw the message on Kunal's screen?
Dhruv felt worried, and was tempted to tease Kunal, but chose to ask gently instead.
What was the key choice in Dhruv Chacha's story, and why?
Refusing to keep the secret and telling his mother that evening was key, because an adult could call Kunal's parents and the helpline and stop the meeting.
How did Kunal feel about Dhruv's choice at first and later?
Kunal was angry for a month, feeling betrayed, but later felt grateful and thanked Dhruv.

Coach's note, 12 August. Written by Francis D'Souza, under-16 football.
Samir, fifteen, is the boy everyone wants on their side: first to set out cones, last to leave. This week the older boys planned to skip Saturday's practice to protest the new captain. When they asked Samir, I saw him look around the whole circle before he answered. "Okay. If everyone is."
Afterwards he stayed back, tying and untying one lace. "Coach, I don't want them to think I'm a traitor. But my father drives me here at six every day. He'll think I'm useless if I skip."
I asked what he thought a good teammate owed the new captain. He went quiet, then asked if I could just make Saturday compulsory, so the choice wouldn't be his.
Next: meet the captain and the older boys together on Monday, and give Samir a chance to speak for himself.

Why did the older boys plan to skip Saturday's practice?
They planned to skip it to protest the new captain.
What was Samir worried about as he tied and untied his lace?
He was worried the boys would think he was a traitor and that his father would think he was useless if he skipped.
What went wrong when Samir asked for Saturday to be made compulsory, and what could help him instead?
He tried to hand the choice to someone else so nobody could blame him; talking through what he owes the new captain could help him make and own a choice.
How might the new captain feel if Samir skipped just to keep the older boys happy?
The captain might feel alone and see Samir's easy friendliness as reserved for the popular side, which would make the team feel less safe.

Sandra wants to buy some sweets. She saved $10 for this purpose. Her mother gave her an additional $4, and her father twice as much as her mother. One candy costs $0.5, and one jelly bean $0.2. She wants to buy 14 candies and 20 jelly beans. How much money will she be left with after the purchase?

Sandra's father gave her $4 * 2 = $8.
So Sandra has in total $8 + $4 + $10 = $22.
She wants 14 candies, so she is going to pay 14 candies * $0.50/candy = $7 for them.
She wants also 20 jellybeans, and they're going to cost 20 jellybeans * $0.20/jellybean = $4.
So after the purchase, she will be left with $22 - $4 - $7 = $11.
The answer is 11.

The annual day rehearsal had ten minutes left, and the hall fan was broken. Mahima was meant to read the welcome line. On the first try her voice came out the way it did at home in Siwan, the "sh" sliding into "s". Two girls at the back giggled, and Aditi copied it in a squeaky voice. Mahima went red and mumbled the rest into her sheet. For the rest of the rehearsal she only whispered. Mrs. Das, the music teacher, noticed. At the end she asked, "Mahima, you speak Bhojpuri at home?" Mahima nodded, eyes down. "Then you speak three languages. Most of this hall speaks two. Would you say the welcome in Bhojpuri too, for the grandparents?" The next evening, three grandmothers clapped the loudest.

Which language does Mahima speak at home?
Mahima speaks Bhojpuri at home.
What was Mahima feeling when Aditi copied her voice?
She felt ashamed and embarrassed; she went red, mumbled into her sheet and then only whispered.
How did Mrs. Das help Mahima's pride?
She named Bhojpuri as a skill, pointed out that Mahima speaks three languages, and gave it an honoured place in the welcome.
How might the grandmothers have felt hearing the welcome in Bhojpuri?
They likely felt delighted and respected to hear their own language on stage, which is why they clapped the loudest.

In the village of Kumbhalgarh, Pranav's Papa found him sitting by the well, throwing pebbles.

"Elizabeth doesn't play with me anymore," Pranav said. "She plays with the big kids at the church now."

Papa sat down beside him. "Do you miss her?"

Pranav nodded.

"Maybe you can just say hello tomorrow. And ask her to play marbles once. Just once."

"What if she says no?"

"Then she says no, and you'll still have the good days you had. Those were real, beta. Friends sometimes change, like seasons."

The next evening Pranav walked to the church steps. "Elizabeth, want to play marbles?"

She hesitated, then grinned. "One game."

They played two. Then she ran back to the big kids, and Pranav walked home, lighter.

Where did Papa find Pranav?
Papa found Pranav sitting by the well, throwing pebbles.
What was Pranav feeling on the walk home?
He felt lighter and happier, glad he'd tried even though Elizabeth went back to the big kids.
What did Papa do that helped Pranav?
He listened, suggested one small invitation, and helped Pranav see that the old friendship was real even if things change.
How might Elizabeth feel when Pranav invites her?
Elizabeth may feel a bit surprised and pleased to be remembered, which is why she agreed to a game.

Eshaan, it's your Mridul Chacha. I heard you haven't been sleeping since the fire at your office. Let me tell you something I've told very few people. At twenty-four I was on a train that derailed near Itarsi. I wasn't badly hurt, but I saw things I won't describe. For a year I pretended I was fine. I snapped at your aunt, avoided trains, couldn't bear the sound of metal scraping. I thought men were supposed to just get over things. Then my hands started shaking at work. Your aunt found a counsellor at the district hospital, and I went, grumbling. Talking about it slowly, in that small room, helped more than I believed it could. Later I joined a Sunday walking group; nobody there knew, and that was restful too. The memory is still there, beta. It just doesn't drive anymore. Please let someone help you with this.

Where did the train Mridul was on derail?
Near Itarsi.
How did Mridul feel during the year he pretended he was fine?
He was distressed and ashamed of it, believing men were supposed to just get over things, so he hid it and snapped at people.
What helped Mridul heal?
Seeing a counsellor and talking about it slowly, along with a Sunday walking group that gave him calm company.
How might Eshaan's aunt have experienced that year?
Hurt by his snapping and worried when his hands began shaking, which is why she found him a counsellor.

Before: Three days before Diwali, Tejas overheard Papa telling Chandrika, his mother, that the factory had let him go. When Aai sat Tejas down to explain, he said, "It's fine, Aai. Papa will get another one," and went back to stringing lights on the balcony.
During: On Diwali night he did not ask why there were fewer sweets. He snapped at his little cousin over a sparkler and lay awake long after the crackers stopped.
After: A week later, Chandrika found him awake again at midnight. "Is Papa sad?" he finally whispered. She sat on his bed and told him the plain truth: things were tight for now, but the grown-ups had a plan. Tejas fell asleep before she left the room.

When did Tejas first hear about Papa's job?
Three days before Diwali, when he overheard Papa telling Chandrika that the factory had let him go.
Why did Tejas keep saying "It's fine"?
He was frightened for Papa and the family 😔, and not knowing felt safer than facing it, though the worry leaked out as snapping and lying awake.
How could a parent support a child like Tejas?
Give simple, honest information without forcing talk, notice signs such as poor sleep and a short temper, and check in gently at calm moments.
What was it like for Tejas's little cousin on Diwali night?
The cousin was probably hurt and confused at being snapped at over a sparkler, not knowing the temper came from worry at home.
Here are a red circle, a red square and a blue circle. Which is the odd one out?

Answer: There are two good answers. The red square - it is the only square. Or the blue circle - it is the only blue one.

Praise any answer with a good reason. Puzzles can have more than one answer. Saying WHY is the most important part.
I'm helping my brother Nikhil find a flat in Hyderabad. He works at a bank. We saw three flats today.
That is a busy day, with a lot to take in. How did the three flats compare with each other?
The first was dark but cheap. The second was bright but far from his office. The third had a balcony and was close, but old.
Each has something good. Since Nikhil goes to work daily, a close one saves energy, and a balcony gives him fresh air. Check the old building's water and wiring.
Nikhil likes the third one too. What should we check there?
Look at taps, switches, ceiling corners for damp, and ask neighbours about water and noise. Visit again at a different time of day to see the light and traffic.
We'll go again tomorrow evening. Which flat did we say is old?
It was the third one, the flat with the balcony close to his office. When you visit tomorrow evening, check the old parts carefully, and see how noisy the street gets at that hour.
Should we revisit the second flat too, the bright one, if the third one fails?
Yes, keep the second flat as a backup for Nikhil. It is bright, though far from his office, so check the travel time at office hours before you decide. See the third one first tomorrow evening.

Yamini's jokes about Vaibhav's ears got laughs in the yard. She had found a way to feel big: if the joke was about him, nobody made one about her. At home, her cousins called her "chubby cheeks", and she hated it. Nazia laughed along the first time. Afterwards her stomach lurched and she felt sick with guilt. That evening she kept picturing Vaibhav's face.

Next morning Vaibhav flinched when Yamini walked past, his shoulders drawn up near his ears. It was the flinch that made her pause. She had thought it was funny, but now her chest went tight. It was not pride she felt, but discomfort. She teased no one that day.

At lunch Nazia found Vaibhav by the tap. "I laughed yesterday, and I should not have. I am sorry." Vaibhav shrugged. "Okay." When Yamini started again by the door, Nazia said, "Not funny. I am not joining." Yamini rolled her eyes and left.

The following day Yamini walked over to Vaibhav. "I made fun of your ears because I was scared of being teased myself. It was not a joke. I am sorry." She sat with a kinder group at lunch, and found she did not have to be cruel to belong.

What did Yamini's jokes target?
Her jokes targeted Vaibhav's ears.
How did Yamini's reason for teasing compare with Nazia's reason for laughing, and what did each do after seeing the effect?

Yamini teased because she dreaded being teased herself and wanted to feel big. Nazia simply laughed along, then felt sick with guilt. After Vaibhav flinched, Yamini stopped and later apologised, and Nazia apologised and refused to join again.
What was Nazia feeling that evening after laughing along at Vaibhav?
She felt guilty and sick, and kept picturing Vaibhav's face.
What could Yamini do about her fear of being teased, instead of teasing first?
She could build real confidence and sit with kinder friends, as she did.

Monday: at lunch, Jahnavi sat hugging her rag doll to her chest after a quarrel with her friend. Her classmate Rafiq noticed, sat on the next bench and quietly opened his tiffin. He said nothing.
Wednesday: at the bus stop on a cold morning, Jahnavi stood with her arms wrapped round herself. Rafiq asked, “Cold, or something else?” “Both, a bit,” she said. He offered her half his scarf.
Friday: Jahnavi's arms were swinging by her sides. She was telling Rafiq about the quiz, and she laughed.

What was Jahnavi hugging at lunch on Monday?
She was hugging her rag doll to her chest.
What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday, and what else might the hugging show?
Probably upset after the quarrel with her friend, so she soothed herself with the doll. It may also hint at worry, since she stayed quiet.
What did Rafiq do that respected Jahnavi at each stage?
On Monday he sat nearby and said nothing, and on Wednesday he asked a gentle question and offered half his scarf, so she could answer in her own way.
How might Rafiq feel seeing Jahnavi hug her doll after the quarrel?
Rafiq was probably concerned but careful not to push, since he sat on the next bench and said nothing.

Before: On Monday, in the hostel mess, Urmila watched a senior keep mimicking Thomas's Malayalam accent, loudly, every time Thomas spoke. Thomas laughed along, but his ears were red. During: On Tuesday evening, Urmila found Thomas alone in the reading room. "I saw yesterday. I'm not going to do anything unless you want me to. Do you want me to say something to him? Help you report it? Or just sit with you at meals?" Thomas thought. "Just sit with me. For now." So she did, all week. After: The next Monday, the senior started again. Thomas turned to Urmila. "Okay. I want to tell the warden." They went together that evening, and the warden called the senior in the same night.

Where did Urmila find Thomas on Tuesday evening?
Alone in the reading room.
What was Thomas feeling while laughing along in the mess?
He was embarrassed and hurt; his red ears showed the mimicking stung even though he laughed.
Which choice worked, and why?
Urmila asking Thomas what he wanted worked, because it let him decide when he was ready to report and kept him in control.
What might change if Urmila had confronted the senior herself on Monday?
Thomas might have felt exposed or spoken for, and the senior might have mocked him more for needing a defender.
The injury prevented him to play in the final. Please check the end.

The injury prevented him from playing in the final.
Why: preposition ("prevented him to play" -> "from playing").

Jahnavi: rafiq are you still in the lab
Rafiq: leaving in 10. why
Jahnavi: I messed up the titration AGAIN. third time
Jahnavi: it's the same experiment I did in first year with my eyes closed
Rafiq: hey, it happens
Jahnavi: it doesn't happen to me. or it didn't. my lab report took all sunday and I still got the units wrong
Jahnavi: I feel like everyone's going to figure out I got in by luck
Rafiq: you topped the batch in 2nd year, jahnavi
Jahnavi: exactly. and now look. I just need to put in more hours
Rafiq: you've been putting in more hours for a month. has it helped?
Jahnavi: ...no
Rafiq: then maybe hours aren't the fix. come get chai. tomorrow we talk to Dr Kulkarni about the workload
Jahnavi: ok 😔
Rafiq: 🙂 5 min, main gate

How long did Jahnavi's lab report take?
The lab report took all Sunday, and the units were still wrong.
What is Jahnavi afraid everyone will figure out?
Jahnavi worries everyone will figure out the admission was just luck, feeling like a fraud after repeated mistakes.
What shift does Rafiq suggest, and why does it fit this stage?
Rafiq points out that a month of extra hours hasn't helped and suggests chai and a talk with Dr Kulkarni about the workload, since effort alone isn't fixing it.
What might Rafiq be noticing about Jahnavi?
Rafiq sees a friend who topped the batch working longer and struggling more, and cares enough to step in with a plan.
We haven't had rain for weeks and my balcony plants look so dry.
Dry spells are hard on plants. Are you watering them daily?
Every evening, but they still droop in the afternoon.
The afternoon sun may be drying them quickly. Try watering early in the morning as well, and moving the pots to a spot with afternoon shade. A layer of dry leaves on the soil helps hold moisture.
Dry leaves from where?
From the ground downstairs, or any garden or tree you can sweep. A thin layer is enough, so the soil can still breathe.
I'll try the leaves tomorrow.
Great. Check the soil with a finger to see if it's damp below the surface.
Rain came last night and the plants look happier!
What a relief. Don't water them today, since the soil is already damp. Pick off any dead leaves and enjoy the fresh air.

The evening queue at the hand-pump near the village temple was long, and everyone was tired. Tanuja had waited twenty minutes with her brass pot. When she finally reached the front, Shalini splashed muddy water on Tanuja's clean frock and laughed. "Oops, now you match the buffaloes!" Some girls giggled. Tanuja's fists clenched. She stepped forward. Then she stopped, took a slow breath and looked at her frock. "That wasn't funny. My mother washed this today." Shalini's grin faded. Tanuja filled her pot and walked away with her chin up.

Where did Shalini splash muddy water on Tanuja?
At the hand-pump near the village temple.
What does Tanuja stepping forward and then stopping suggest?
It suggests she was very angry and tempted to hit back but chose to hold herself back.
What did Tanuja do instead of retaliating?
She took a slow breath and told Shalini clearly that it wasn't funny.
How might Shalini feel when that grin fades?
Shalini might realise the joke hurt and feel a little embarrassed.

Vera had spent two years on the running app, and in Tallinn's long winter the numbers kept dropping. Instead of another redesign, she made a list of fifteen people who had stopped using it and called them one by one from her kitchen table.
She asked the same question each time: "What do you do now instead?" Emil, her co-founder, sat beside her with a notebook and made tally marks.
A retired teacher said she ran with a group now. A student said the same. A nurse said, "My trainer sends us a plan in a chat group every Monday, and we post our runs there." By the fifteenth call, Emil had eleven marks under "chat group with trainer".
Vera put the phone down. "They don't want an app to run alone with. They want a trainer and a group."

How many marks did Emil have under "chat group with trainer"?
Eleven.
What was Vera feeling when she put the phone down?
Vera was probably surprised and a little shaken, but also excited to see such a clear pattern.
What could Vera and Emil test next?
A simple trainer-led group with a few lapsed users, before building anything big.
How does the nurse see what she needs to keep running?
The nurse values the trainer's Monday plan and sharing runs with the group more than any app feature.

The hostel common room was loud with a carrom match when Uday's phone buzzed with an unknown number. He stepped into the corridor.
“Sir, this is your father's bank. His account is being blocked in ten minutes due to verification failure. You will get an OTP. Just read it out and I will stop the block.”
Uday said nothing for a second, and the voice went sharper. “Nine minutes, sir. Hurry.”
He walked back into the room and said, loud enough for Elizabeth at the notice board to hear, “Why would a bank need me, in a hurry? Why is he counting down? When someone makes me panic like this, that's the part I should trust least.”
He cut the call. Elizabeth, the house prefect, came over. “Report it to the warden?”
“Yes. And I'm calling Papa now.”
Ten minutes later, Papa confirmed his account was fine.

What did Elizabeth suggest after the call?
Reporting it to the warden.
What does Uday saying his thoughts aloud suggest about how he was feeling?
It suggests he felt a jolt of panic but steadied himself by naming the countdown out loud, turning the fear into a warning sign.
What else could the hostel do so other students are ready for such calls?
The warden could describe this script at the next house meeting, so everyone knows to hang up and call family.
How might Papa feel hearing about this call?
Papa would likely be relieved the account is fine and proud that Uday refused to share the code.

Sabina, you asked why I finally quit the firm. This is Alka's honest answer, over this terrible coffee. It wasn't one big thing. It was the manager telling us to write 'minor delay' when a client's shipment was stuck for three weeks. It was the way people laughed at the cleaner's accent in the pantry, and I laughed too, once, and hated myself on the metro home. I noticed I'd stopped saying what I thought in meetings. I was getting smaller. So I made a plan. I spent two months applying quietly, finished my projects properly and wrote a clear handover. On my last day I thanked my team, shook my manager's hand and left. No drama. I just didn't want to become someone I'd avoid.

What did the manager tell them to write when the shipment was stuck?
'Minor delay'.
How did Alka feel after laughing at the cleaner's accent?
Alka felt ashamed and disgusted with Alka's own behaviour on the metro home.
What made Alka's exit dignified?
Planning calmly: applying quietly for two months, finishing projects, writing a clear handover and thanking the team without drama.
How might Alka's team feel about the calm goodbye?
They were left with a proper handover and thanks, so they likely respected the exit, even if some wondered why Alka left.

Class note, Monday. Devika, science. In today's oral quiz I asked Bidisha how a thrown ball moves. She started, “It goes up and then…” and stopped, hands clamped under her desk. Last term another teacher told her to keep her hands still when answering. I said, “Use your hands if it helps.” Her finger shot up and drew a smooth arch in the air: rising, slowing at the top, then curving down faster. “Up slow, then down fast. Like a rainbow, but lopsided because of the wind.” That was a better answer than most of my older classes give. Note to self: let children gesture while they explain.

What shape did Bidisha draw in the air?
Bidisha drew a smooth arch in the air.
Why did Bidisha stop and clamp her hands under her desk?
She was probably anxious about being told off, since another teacher had told her to keep her hands still, and without them she felt stuck.
What did Devika do that helped Bidisha explain?
Devika told her to use her hands if it helped, which let Bidisha show and work out the ball's path.
What would change if Devika had kept the no-hands rule?
Bidisha might have stayed stuck, and Devika would never have heard how well she understood the ball's path.

Saurabh hated writing lists. The letters came out slow and crooked, and he never read them later anyway. So on Sunday night, before the school week, he took a card and drew instead. A stubby pencil. A ruler with tiny lines. A water bottle with a cap. A lunch box with steam curling up. His father, Kishore, watched from the sofa. "Where are the words?" "Don't need them. I look, I pack." On Monday morning he glanced at the card taped to the cupboard and had everything in the bag in two minutes. By Wednesday his little sister Minu, who couldn't read yet, had taped a card of her own beside his, with a crayon, an apple and a sock.

What did Saurabh draw on the card?
A stubby pencil, a ruler with tiny lines, a water bottle with a cap and a lunch box with steam.
How did Saurabh feel about writing lists before he tried pictures?
He hated it and felt frustrated, because his letters came out slow and crooked.
What could Saurabh add to make his picture card even more useful?
He could draw a tick box beside each picture, so he can mark items off as he packs.
How does the picture card look to Minu?
For Minu, who can't read yet, pictures are something she can use herself, so she is excited to make her own card.

The film starts at seven, so grab your seat ten minutes before.

You're thinking of reporting what you saw at the hospital, Trisha, so let me tell you what it cost me, and what helped. I was twenty-five, a junior pharmacist, when I noticed expired stock being relabelled and sent to the wards. I reported it to the medical superintendent in writing. I was right; the inquiry proved it. And still, for a year, the staffroom went quiet when I walked in. My roster suddenly had every Sunday night. One senior called me a traitor to my face. I cried on the bus most evenings. Three things kept me standing. My friend Shobha, who ate lunch with me every single day when nobody else would. A lawyer from the staff association, who explained which protections applied to me and made sure the roster changes were put on record. And my notebook: dates, names, copies of every email. When they said I'd made it up, the notebook answered. Your Himani maasi isn't telling you to stay quiet. I'm telling you to go in prepared.

What did Himani notice as a junior pharmacist?
Expired stock being relabelled and sent to the wards.
How did Himani feel during the year after reporting?
Himani felt isolated and hurt, crying on the bus most evenings as the staffroom went quiet and a senior called her a traitor.
What helped Himani through, inside the story?
Shobha's daily lunches, a lawyer from the staff association who explained protections and recorded the roster changes, and a notebook of dates, names and emails.
How might Shobha have felt eating lunch with Himani when nobody else would?
Shobha may have felt uncomfortable and risked being isolated too, but chose loyalty, which meant a great deal to Himani.

"Okay, Rafiq, listen to all four steps before you touch anything," said Manoj, spreading kite paper on the terrace two days before Uttarayan.
"First, fold the paper corner to corner. Second, glue the long stick down the fold. Third, bend the thin stick across and tie it. Fourth, trim the extra paper."
"Got it."
"Say them back."
"Fold, glue the long stick, bend and tie the thin one... and cut the extra."
"Good. Last year you forgot after step one."
Rafiq worked slowly, whispering, "Third... tie it." His kite came out a little crooked, but it held.
"Will it fly?"
"Tomorrow we test it," said Manoj.

How many steps did Manoj explain?
Manoj explained four steps.
Why did Rafiq whisper "Third... tie it" while working?
He was concentrating hard to keep the steps in mind, determined not to lose track this year.
What part of Manoj's teaching helped, and why?
Asking Rafiq to say the steps back helped him hold all four in memory before starting.
How might Manoj feel seeing Rafiq finish the kite?
Manoj would likely feel pleased and proud, remembering that Rafiq forgot after step one only last year.

Okay, so before the festival lunch at my grandparents' house, I did something I'd never done. I called my cousin Darshan and said, "Last year the whole lunch turned into an election fight and I ate in silence. Can we make a deal?" We agreed: if politics comes up, one of us moves the talk to cricket, or to Nani's laddoos. And if it keeps going, we each say, "I'll help in the kitchen," and just leave, no drama.

I'm Payal, and honestly I was sceptical. But on the day it came up twice, and both times Darshan asked about the laddoos, and I refilled the water jug. The lunch stayed warm. Nobody's mind changed. That wasn't the point.

What did Payal and Darshan plan to say if the talk kept going?
They would each say that they would help in the kitchen and just leave.
How did Payal feel about the plan before the lunch?
Payal felt sceptical, unsure that a simple agreement could work, though still wanting a calmer lunch than last year.
What could Payal do if an elder pulled Payal back into the debate anyway, and why?
Payal could say calmly that another day would be better for this topic and then step out, because the boundary is kept without starting a fight.
How might Nani feel about the lunch staying warm?
Nani likely felt happy that the family stayed together, and being asked about the laddoos was probably a small pleasure.

Music teacher's note, Class 10, end of term.
Aadhya played violin in the school orchestra for four years and was our most reliable second violin. This term she stopped coming.
When I asked, she said she “didn't have time.” But I noticed that she now sits with a group led by Deepak, who openly mocked the orchestra kids at the annual day, calling us the “band of boring.” I have seen her walk past the music room quickly, not looking in.
Last Friday, while we rehearsed the piece she had been practising since spring, I saw her standing in the corridor, listening. When I came out, she said “Just passing,” and left quickly, eyes wet.
I did not push. What I did next: I wrote her a short note saying her chair is still there, no questions asked, and that she can also play in the lunchtime practice, which is quieter. I also spoke to her class teacher about the mocking comments.

How long had Aadhya played violin in the orchestra?
She had played for four years.
How did Aadhya seem to feel standing in the corridor during rehearsal?
She seemed sad and wistful, missing the violin while wanting to keep her place in Deepak's group.
What did the teacher do that could help?
Wrote a note saying her chair is still there, offered the quieter lunchtime practice, and raised the mocking with her class teacher.
How might the orchestra members feel about Aadhya leaving?
They may feel her absence and be hurt by being called the “band of boring.”

Dear Vasudha,
You asked how the unit tests went. Badly, and it's my own fault.
For three weeks I did nothing. Cricket, phone, more phone. Then on Sunday, two days before, I panicked and studied for fourteen hours straight. I felt like a hero. I even sent Amma a photo of my desk at midnight.
On Monday I had a headache and could barely look at a book. On Tuesday I wrote the test half asleep. Then I was so tired I skipped the whole next week of homework too.
The results came today. I knew chapters one and four really well, because I'd crammed them first. Chapters two and three I'd only skimmed at 2 a.m. They were half the paper.
You always did one hour every evening, and I used to laugh at you. I'm not laughing now. Can you tell me how you actually stick to it?
Imran

How many hours did Imran study on Sunday?
Fourteen hours straight.
How did Imran feel at midnight on Sunday, and how did that change?
Imran felt heroic at midnight, then exhausted and regretful when the headache, the skipped week and the patchy results followed.
What could Imran try instead of another fourteen-hour day?
A steady hour every evening, like Vasudha, so the chapters are covered evenly and there is no crash afterwards.
How might Vasudha feel reading this letter?
Vasudha might feel a little vindicated but mostly sympathetic, pleased to be asked for help rather than laughed at.

In the KG classroom, Rafiq was doing a jigsaw puzzle of a train. Three pieces wouldn't fit. He growled, pushed the puzzle away and said, “I can't! It's stupid!” Charu Ma'am sat beside him. “You tried lots of pieces. That's hard work.” She pulled the puzzle back. “Let's just find the edges first. The straight ones.” Rafiq found one. Then another. “Now the red engine pieces.” Step by step, the train came together. Rafiq pressed in the last piece and shouted, “Done!”

What was the jigsaw puzzle a picture of?
A train.
What was Rafiq feeling when he growled and pushed the puzzle away?
He was frustrated and felt the puzzle was too hard, close to giving up.
How did Charu Ma'am keep Rafiq from quitting?
She praised his effort and broke the task into steps, edges first and then the red engine pieces.
How might Charu Ma'am feel when Rafiq shouts “Done!”?
She likely feels pleased and proud that he pushed through with her help.

I'm Hrithik, and I share a hostel room with Santosh. Last month his internship told him to learn a data analysis tool in ten days. Most of us would have binged videos. Santosh did something odd.
The first evening he didn't install anything. He read the tool's introduction page and kept muttering to himself: 'Okay, so it exists because spreadsheets choke on big files. Tables go in, you filter them, you group them, you get a summary.' Then he wrote four words on our whiteboard: load, filter, group, summarise.
When I asked if he was wasting a day, he said, 'If I know the four jobs, every lesson is just one of them.'
By day three he was going through tutorials faster than me, pointing at the whiteboard each time. I can't say whether he was calm inside, but he stopped sighing at his laptop.

Which four words did Santosh write on the whiteboard?
Load, filter, group, summarise.
What does Santosh's muttering on the first evening suggest about his state of mind?
He seems to have felt uneasy with a tool he did not understand yet, and working out why it exists helped him feel settled before starting lessons.
What would you change first if the tool's introduction page had been too technical?
Ask a senior or mentor to explain in one line what the tool is for, then rebuild the four jobs from that before starting tutorials.
How does the first evening look to Hrithik, who shares the room?
At first Hrithik thinks Santosh is wasting a day, but by day three Hrithik sees Santosh moving through tutorials faster than anyone.

Hold them by the closed blades with the handle pointing towards the person. Because the sharp tip is then pointing away from both of you, so nobody gets cut if you slip.

Lab supervisor's note, chemistry department, 22 January.
Today Gopika, our new trainee, was asked by Raghav, a senior research scholar, to skip the fume hood check before starting the solvent work. "It's always fine, don't waste time," he told her. She told me afterwards that she knew the checklist said otherwise. But he is senior, and refusing felt disrespectful. The hood's fan was not running. Within ten minutes she had a headache and was coughing; the lab smelled strongly. A technician noticed and opened the windows.
I sent Gopika to the health centre with a colleague straight away. I then spoke to Raghav in my office and made the check mandatory for everyone, seniors included. I also told Gopika, clearly, that saying "Let's check first" to anyone is part of her job, and I will back her.

What did Raghav ask Gopika to skip?
The fume hood check before starting the solvent work.
Why did Gopika follow Raghav's instruction although she knew the checklist said otherwise?
She felt uneasy but afraid of seeming disrespectful to a senior, so refusing felt impossible.
What did the supervisor do, and why does it help?
Sent Gopika to the health centre, spoke to Raghav, made the check mandatory for everyone, and promised to back her, making polite objection safe.
How might Raghav feel after the talk in the supervisor's office?
Raghav might feel embarrassed and defensive, but also shaken that his shortcut hurt a trainee.

At the village fair, the dhol started up by the temple steps. Varun bounced on his toes, clapping out of time and shouting bits of the song, “Ho! Ho!”
His cousin Vishal laughed and clapped with him.
Late that night, on the bus home, the same song came from someone's phone. Varun lay on Vishal's lap, swaying slowly side to side, eyes half closed.
“Dancing again?” someone asked.
“No,” said Vishal. “That's his going-to-sleep sway."

Where did the dhol start up?
By the temple steps.
What was Varun feeling when he bounced, clapped and shouted at the fair?
He was excited and joyful and wanted to join in the music.
How did Vishal read Varun's swaying correctly on the bus?
He looked at the context, late at night, half-closed eyes, lying on his lap, and saw it was Varun soothing himself to sleep, not dancing.
How did the other passenger read Varun's swaying?
They thought he was dancing again, the way he had at the fair.

Aadhya was waiting outside the staff room again, notebook hugged to her chest, when Professor Yash came out with his tea. "Sir, I copied your lecture line by line. Should I do a master's in soil science? Whatever you say, I'll do it." The college sat at the edge of a small town, and the peon was already watching them with a smile. "Sir, I can carry your files to the lab," she added. Yash felt the warmth of it, and the weight. "Carry your own," he said gently. "I can tell you how I made my choice, but I have never worked outside a university. For placements, ask the cell downstairs. And you decide, then tell me why." She looked a little deflated, then took out her pen anyway.

What did Aadhya offer to carry to the lab?
She offered to carry his files to the lab.
What might Yash be feeling when Aadhya says she will do whatever he says?
He feels warmed by her trust but weighed down by it, which is why he hands the decision back and asks for her reasons.
How could Yash keep guiding her without making her lean on him?
He can keep asking for her reasons and point her to the placement cell and others who know more than he does, so her own judgement grows. 🙂
How might Aadhya see his refusal to let her carry the files?
She is a little deflated at first, perhaps fearing he is pulling away, but taking out her pen shows she still values his help.
