Rafiq stood at the front of the hall upstairs while the projector got ready. His slides were full of long writing in tiny letters. He had copied it from his report because he was afraid he would forget what to say.
Does majority mean more than half?

Yes. The majority is the larger part of a group, more than half. It is a noun.
Example: The majority of the class voted for a picnic.

Babysitter's note, Saturday.

Sabina, two, woke at ten, crying and pointing at the window. The curtain was moving in the breeze.

I didn't laugh. I switched on the night light, sat beside her and said softly, "It's the wind. You're safe." She clung to my arm.

I stayed until she slept. I told Thomas when he came home, and he said he'd put a heavier curtain up tomorrow.

What was moving at the window?
The curtain was moving in the breeze.
Why did Sabina cling to the babysitter's arm?
Sabina felt scared, because the moving curtain seemed frightening and real to her.
Which steps by the babysitter helped Sabina?
The babysitter didn't laugh, turned on the night light, spoke calmly and stayed close until she slept.
How does Thomas respond when told about the night?
Thomas takes it seriously and plans to put up a heavier curtain.

Writing centre notes, 12 March. Student: Keerthana, second-year history.
Third session on the same essay introduction. She brought six printed versions of page one, each with tiny changes: "crucial" swapped for "vital", a comma moved, one sentence shifted to the end and then back. The body of the essay is still blank. The deadline is Friday.
When I asked what would happen if she sent a rough draft to her professor for comments, she went very still and said, "Then he'll know I'm not good at this." She also mentioned skipping badminton practice twice this week "to get the opening right".
What I did: set a timer for twenty-five minutes and asked her to write the next section badly on purpose, no deleting. She wrote a full page. Her hands were shaking at first.
Plan: meet Thursday. Page one is frozen until the body exists.
Damini, writing centre

How many printed versions of page one did Keerthana bring?
She brought six printed versions of page one.
Why did Keerthana go very still when asked about sending a rough draft?
She seemed afraid of being judged, believing a rough draft would show her professor that she is "not good at this".
Which of Damini's steps helped, and why?
Asking Keerthana to write the next section badly on purpose, on a timer with no deleting, got a full page written and moved her past the frozen opening.
How might Damini feel watching Keerthana's hands shake as she wrote?
Damini was likely concerned at how much fear sat behind the rewriting, and encouraged that a full page came once deleting was off the table.

Five minutes later Daniel and Uvarka were standing in Nicholas' big study. Though Daniel was not a big man, to see him in a room was like seeing a horse or a bear on the floor among the furniture and surroundings of human life. Daniel himself felt this, and as usual stood just inside the door, trying to speak softly and not move, for fear of breaking something in the master's apartment, and he hastened to say all that was necessary so as to get from under that ceiling, out into the open under the sky once more.

How does Daniel behave in the study, and why?

The Holi colours had dried on the courtyard wall when Nirmala, six, and her friend Lavanya started a game of hopscotch in the dust.
Lavanya threw her stone. It landed right on the line. "That's in!"
Nirmala looked at it. On the line meant out. She wanted to win badly; she'd lost twice already. Her cousin Kishan, sitting on the wall, watched them.
"It's on the line," Nirmala said. "Your turn is over."
Lavanya pouted, then nodded. Nirmala hopped all the way to the end and won.
Kishan clapped. "Fair and square." Lavanya smiled. "Next game, I'm winning."

Where did Lavanya's stone land?
It landed right on the line.
What was Nirmala feeling when she looked at the stone?
Nirmala felt tempted and frustrated, wanting badly to win after losing twice, yet she still spoke up fairly.
What would you advise children who disagree about a rule during a game?
They could look at the rule together and agree on it, and have a friend like Kishan help check when it's close.
How does Lavanya react to being told her turn is over?
Lavanya is disappointed and pouts, but she accepts it and stays friendly, even joking about winning next time.

Gargi's father's hospital stay lasted only three days, but it changed the question. At dinner afterwards he said, "I want you to take over the business next year." The business was his construction firm in Faridabad. Gargi was an environmental lawyer, and she had spent two years fighting firms that dumped debris on the Yamuna floodplains, firms not so different from his. The hospital scare had given everyone a deadline: decide by Diwali. She felt split in two. The daughter owed him; the lawyer couldn't pretend. She talked it through with Jyoti, a senior at her chambers. "You don't have to choose between being a good daughter and a good lawyer," Jyoti said. "You have to decide what you'd do with the company." Gargi went back to her father with a proposal: she would join as a part-time director and start by cleaning up debris disposal. He frowned a long time. Then he said, "Start with the Sector 12 site."

Where was her father's construction firm?
In Faridabad.
What was Gargi feeling when her father asked her to take over?
Gargi felt torn in two, between duty to her father and her values as an environmental lawyer.
How did Jyoti's reframe help Gargi reconcile her roles?
It shifted the question from choosing one identity to deciding what she would do with the company, leading to a proposal that honoured both.
How might Gargi's father have seen her proposal?
He probably felt challenged by the implied criticism but relieved she would join, which is why he named a site to start with.

Can you explain harvest?

A harvest is the gathering of crops when they are ripe, or the crops that are gathered. It is a noun; it can also be a verb.
Example: The villagers celebrate when the harvest is complete.

12 March

The agency sent the new rates today. Translation work is now "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes, at a third of the old pay. Half my regular clients have gone quiet.

I sat by the window for an hour feeling like a typewriter in a museum.

Called Anirban, who ran the Marathi desk before I did. He said, "Dhruv, the machine can't tell if a pharmacy leaflet sounds scary to a grandmother. You can." He's moved into localisation testing, checking whether apps actually make sense to real users in each language.

So, a plan. Not a panic.
1. The six-week evening course in localisation testing Anirban mentioned. Enrol this week.
2. Keep two days for the post-editing work so rent is covered while I learn.
3. Build three sample reports on local apps and show them to Anirban by May.

Still scared. But at least I'm scared with a list.

What is translation work now called by the agency?
Translation work is now called "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes.
How did Dhruv feel while sitting by the window?
Dhruv felt outdated and frightened, "like a typewriter in a museum", after the new rates and clients going quiet.
What makes Dhruv's retraining plan realistic?
It has a short course, keeps some paid work going while learning, and includes sample reports to show a mentor by a set date.
How might Anirban see Dhruv's situation, having made a similar change?
Anirban likely feels sympathetic and hopeful, seeing that Dhruv's language judgement is still valuable in a new role.

Vasudev reached school ten minutes early and waited by the gate for his friend Pervez. His stomach felt tight. When Pervez walked in, Vasudev stepped forward. "I'm sorry I laughed at your tiffin. I didn't mean it to hurt you." Pervez said nothing for a moment and looked at his shoes. Vasudev took a breath and went on. "Can we play football at recess, you and me on one team?" Pervez shrugged, but the corner of his mouth moved. "Only if I get goalkeeper." "Done," said Vasudev. They walked to class together, not talking much, but not angry any more either.

Where did Vasudev wait for Pervez?
Vasudev waited by the gate.
What was Vasudev feeling when he stepped forward to speak to Pervez?
Vasudev was nervous, shown by the tight stomach and the deep breath he took before speaking. 😰
What other approach could Vasudev use if Pervez stayed silent, and why?
Vasudev could give Pervez a little time and try again at lunch, or write a short note. Space can help a hurt friend feel ready to answer.
How does Pervez seem to feel about the apology?
Pervez was quiet at first and looked at his shoes, so it may have been hard to trust it, but the small smile and the goalkeeper request suggest Pervez was softening.

At the village school playground, Deepak climbed to the top of the tin slide for the first time. He sat at the edge, gripping both sides. The slide looked very long. His lip wobbled.
He looked down at his Baba, Anirban, standing at the bottom.
Anirban didn't call out or pull him. He just smiled and nodded once.
Deepak let go. Whoosh. He landed in the dust, blinked, then scrambled up the ladder again, shouting, "Again!"

Where was Anirban standing?
At the bottom of the slide.
Why did Deepak's lip wobble at the top?
He was scared because the slide looked very long.
What did Anirban do that helped?
He stayed at the bottom, smiled and nodded once, without calling out or pulling him.

The storm cut the power on the 30th, the day Vidya reviewed her month, so she did it by torchlight with a paper notebook. Bhavna, her flatmate, teased her about it. Vidya's routine never changed: rent and electricity went out on the 5th and the 10th through standing instructions, savings moved the moment salary landed, and a small reserve sat in a separate account for surprises. That evening a water pipe burst under the sink. Vidya called the plumber, paid from the reserve without panic, and noted it in the notebook. At the review she saw takeaway food had crept up, trimmed it, and refilled the reserve first thing next month. "You never borrow, do you?" Bhavna asked. "No need," Vidya said. "It's already set aside."

Why did Vidya review her month by torchlight?
A storm cut the power on the 30th, the day she reviewed her month.
Why did Vidya feel so calm when the pipe burst?
Vidya felt calm and confident: she called the plumber and paid from the reserve without panic because the money was already set aside.
What habits kept the burst pipe from becoming a debt?
Standing instructions for bills, moving savings when salary landed, and a separate reserve for surprises.
What does Bhavna's teasing and question suggest about how Bhavna sees Vidya's routine?
Bhavna finds it unusually disciplined and is a little amused and impressed, asking "You never borrow, do you?"

Class teacher's note, 15 January — Vandana, Class 12
Vandana was absent on Monday and Tuesday with fever. On Wednesday she stayed back at lunch looking close to tears and showed me her study plan: every hour from now to March filled, no gaps anywhere. "I missed two days and now everything has shifted," she said. "If I add Monday's chapters on top of Thursday's, I'll never catch up." I asked where she could put them without stacking. She looked for a while and said, "There's nowhere. That's the problem." Then she rebuilt it herself: Saturday afternoons left empty every week as a catch-up half-day, and the two missed chemistry chapters moved into this Saturday. She seemed calmer by the end of lunch. I will ask on Monday how the first free Saturday went.
— Manjula

Which days was Vandana absent?
She was absent on Monday and Tuesday.
What was Vandana feeling when she stayed back at lunch?
She was upset and panicky, close to tears, because two lost days had shifted her completely full plan.
Why does leaving Saturday afternoons empty work better than stacking chapters?
The free half-day absorbs missed work, so one bad week doesn't break the whole plan or overload the days that follow.
How does Manjula see Vandana's new plan?
Manjula lets Vandana find the fix herself, notices her calmer, and plans to check on Monday how the first free Saturday went.

They donated a total of 5000 + 4724 = 9724 pennies.
The answer is 9724.

In the Class 6 writing lesson, students swapped paragraphs to review. Lokesh got Jahnavi's, and Jahnavi got his.
Lokesh's said: "Our school should have a longer lunch break. It would be nice. Everyone wants it."
Jahnavi wrote in the margin: "Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"
Lokesh read it and felt his face heat up. Then he looked at Jahnavi's paragraph. It had a topic sentence, three reasons, and an ending.
He rewrote his: "First, many of us don't finish eating. Second, we'd have time to play and then focus better. Third…"
He handed it back to her with a small nod.

What did Jahnavi write in the margin?
"Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"
What was Lokesh feeling when his face heated up?
Lokesh felt embarrassed that his paragraph had no real reasons.
How could the teacher use this kind of peer review again?
The teacher could keep having students ask each other "why?" questions so they learn to add reasons.
How might Jahnavi feel when Lokesh hands back the rewritten paragraph?
Jahnavi probably feels respected, seeing that her comments helped him improve.
Why do potters keep their hands wet while shaping clay on a wheel?
Water keeps the clay slippery. Because wet clay lets the hands slide over the spinning surface instead of grabbing and tearing it, the potter can pull the shape up smoothly.

The train to Nani's town left at 6:10, and Rukmini had to get Kunal out of the door by 5:30. "Amma, did you lock the back door?" "Yes, kanna." "Did you really? Are you sure?" "Yes." He asked six more times as they dragged the bags down. At the gate he had to run back to check the lock himself, twice. Rukmini waited on the steps, her heart thumping about the train, and answered every "Are you sure?" because his face looked so frightened. They made the train with one minute to spare. On the ride Rukmini thought about what the clinician had told them last month: "Answering again and again comes from love, but it can make the worry grow. Let's practise answering once, kindly, then helping him sit with the feeling." Watching Kunal count the fence posts, she decided they would start after the holiday.

What time did the train to Nani's town leave?
Why did Rukmini keep answering every 'Are you sure?'
She loved Kunal and couldn't bear his frightened face, and she was anxious about missing the train.
What did the clinician suggest the family practise?
Answering once, kindly, and then helping Kunal sit with the feeling instead of repeating reassurance.
How might Kunal feel when Rukmini starts answering only once?
At first he may feel more anxious, but with kind support the worry could slowly shrink.

Read this:

Usha, the hardest meeting of my life? A Monday in March, eight months into being team lead. I'd pushed a new delivery rota through without asking anyone, and it tangled our routes for two weeks. At first, I'm ashamed to say, I told the regional head the drivers weren't adapting.
That Monday I stood in front of all thirty of them in the depot. My mouth was dry. I said, "The rota was my decision. I didn't ask you. Pinto warned me and I didn't listen. I'm sorry for blaming you." Then I asked, "What should I have asked before?"
Silence. Then Pinto, the oldest driver, said, "Ask us about school timings, sir." And they started talking. Forty minutes.
Here's the strange part. After that day they trusted me more, not less. I'm Chinmay, and I learned more in that depot than in any training.

How many drivers were in the depot?
All thirty of them.
How did Chinmay feel standing in front of the drivers?
He felt nervous and ashamed, mouth dry, but determined to own the rota decision.
Why did asking 'What should I have asked before?' help?
It turned the apology into a request for candid feedback, and the drivers shared what they knew, like school timings.
What might Pinto have felt when Chinmay named the warning?
Pinto likely felt respected and seen, which may be why Pinto was the first to speak.

Read this:

Twelve minutes before their final viva, Samir and Vandana were still arguing over the slide order in the corridor outside the seminar room.
"Numbers first," Samir said. "The examiners like proof."
"If they do not care about the problem, the numbers are just noise," Vandana said, holding the laptop against a hip. "Open with the woman from the survey who walked four kilometres for water."
Samir looked at the clock, then at the slides. His jaw tightened and loosened. "Fair point. Story first. But the biggest number goes in your opening sentence."
"Deal."
They dragged three slides, fixed one title, and walked in with the projector already warm.

How many minutes were left before the viva when the argument began?
Twelve minutes were left before their final viva.
What was Samir feeling when the jaw tightened and then loosened?
Samir felt pressured and a little reluctant, since the clock was running and the plan was theirs. Then Samir let go of the argument and accepted the better order.
What did Samir change after saying "Fair point", and what stayed the same?
Samir agreed to put the story first, and kept the proof by asking that the biggest number go in Vandana's opening sentence.
What would it have been like for Vandana if Samir had kept insisting on numbers first?
Vandana would probably have felt unheard and anxious, with the clock running and the argument still going as they walked in. Samir's quick concession left them free to prepare.

Read this:

The first real snow had fallen in Tromsø, and the slope behind the school was packed at break. Anders, the biggest boy in fifth grade, had taken the best sledge and was deciding who got a go. "Not you, Emil. You're too slow." Emil's face went hot. He almost ran to the teacher on duty, then stopped. Instead he gathered the others. "Let's go in order of who got here first. Everyone gets two runs." Most of them nodded. Anders scowled, outnumbered. "Fine. But I go first." "You were first anyway," Emil said. By the bell, Anders was pushing the little ones off from the top himself.

How many runs did Emil suggest each person get?
Everyone gets two runs.
Why did Emil stop himself from running to the teacher on duty?
He felt hurt and angry, but seemed confident the group could agree on a fair rule without help.
What made Emil's plan work?
He offered a simple, fair rule and got the others to agree first, so Anders couldn't just overrule him. 👍
What is it like for Anders when the others nod at Emil's plan?
Anders feels outnumbered and a bit put out, but accepts because Emil lets him save face by going first.

Read this:

Monday: Bhavin tripped over his shoelace on the playground and the whole group burst out laughing. Asif laughed loudest, eyes on the others, though his stomach felt a little tight.
Wednesday: Karthik, the teacher, called Asif aside. "When Bhavin fell, you laughed. How would you feel if it was you on the ground?"
Asif looked at his feet. "Sore. And sad."
"Mm," said Karthik, and waited.
Friday: A girl slipped on the wet step and a few children giggled. Asif felt the laugh start in his throat, then swallowed it. "Are you okay?" he asked, holding out his hand.

What made Bhavin fall on Monday?
He tripped over his shoelace.
Why did Asif laugh loudest on Monday even though his stomach felt tight?
He wanted to be part of the group, but he also felt a little uneasy, which the tight stomach suggests.
What did Karthik do that helped Asif change?
Karthik asked Asif to imagine being the one on the ground and then waited quietly, so Asif found the answer himself. 🙂
How might Bhavin have felt when the group laughed?
He probably felt embarrassed and hurt, since he was on the ground while everyone laughed at him.
What do we call a baby cat, a baby dog and a baby cow? One word per line, lowercase.

kitten
puppy
calf
Why should we leave home earlier than needed on the day of an exam?
Leaving early is sensible. Because buses can be late and roads can be blocked, extra time means that a delay does not make us miss the start of the exam.

[Group chat: Hydrology Project, three members]
Gautam: ok so for the peer form, I'm putting myself at 50%. I did the whole data analysis
Lokesh: wait what. I wrote the entire report. I was going to put 50% for me 😅
Gautam: the report is just words around my graphs bro

Asha: um guys I did the field readings for 3 weekends. I was putting 40%
Gautam: that's 140% total lol

Gautam: I genuinely thought I carried this
Lokesh: same 😬
Asha: next project we keep a shared log. who did what, what day. no memory games

What share did Gautam plan to put on the peer form?
Gautam planned to put 50% for doing the whole data analysis.
Why was Gautam so sure of having carried the project?
Gautam felt proud of the data analysis and remembered that hard work vividly, while the others' weekends and fixes stayed out of view.
What does Asha suggest for the next project, and why would it help?
A shared log of who did what and on what day, so recognition rests on a record instead of each person's memory.
How might Asha feel when the two others argue over 50% each?
Asha might feel overlooked, since three weekends of field readings had disappeared from both of their pictures.

Read this:

On the day of the Diwali mela in Kudal village, Parveen sat on the courtyard floor with a lump of clay. "One diya for Ammi. Five minutes," she told Tenzin, already in his new shirt.
"The bus goes at four."
"Five minutes."
The clay cracked. She wet it and started again. The spout fell over. She scratched a pattern with a twig, rubbed it off because it was crooked, and did it again.
Tenzin waited on the step, walked to the gate and back, and waited again.
When Parveen held up a small, lopsided diya, the shadows had crossed the courtyard. A bell in the next village rang five.
"Five minutes?" Tenzin said.
Parveen's mouth fell open. "But… it was only five minutes!"

At what time did the bus go?
The bus goes at four.
How did Parveen feel when she heard the bell ring five?
Parveen felt shocked and surprised, sure it had only been five minutes.
What could help Parveen next time she says "five minutes"?
Parveen could ask a grown-up to set a timer or check the clock, since it is hard to feel how long making something really takes.
How did Tenzin feel while waiting?
Tenzin was impatient and restless, walking to the gate and back while the time for the bus passed.

Read this:

Thursday

Passed the huge coaching centre billboard again today. Twenty smiling faces: "Our IIT toppers!" I stared at it the whole bus ride.

I told Kiran, "If I join that centre, I'll get into IIT too. Look, twenty people did it."

Kiran asked, "How many joined that centre?"

I didn't know. Kiran looked it up on the centre's own website. Two thousand students last year.

Twenty out of two thousand.

That's one in a hundred. And the billboard doesn't show the other nineteen hundred and eighty. They're not smiling on any billboard. They're just... gone from the picture.

I'm not saying don't try. I still want to. But I thought it was easy because I only saw the winners.

Going to talk to Amma about it this weekend.

Lakshmi

How many students joined the coaching centre last year?
Two thousand students last year.
How did Lakshmi feel after hearing the numbers?
Lakshmi felt surprised and more thoughtful, realising the billboard only showed the winners.
What question from Kiran helped, and why?
Kiran asked how many joined the centre, which revealed the many who didn't succeed and aren't shown.
How might Amma respond when Lakshmi talks to her?
Amma might feel proud that Lakshmi is thinking carefully and help weigh the options.

At the bus stop outside the village school near Mandi, two boys jerked their heads sideways every time Charu, eleven, did. They laughed and nudged each other. Charu stared at her shoes, blinking fast, her chest aching. Sharma Sir, walking to his scooter, stopped. "Charu's movements are not something she chooses. Copying her is cruel, and it ends today." The boys shuffled off. Charu's friend Kalyani didn't mention it at all. She just kept telling Charu about the calf born in their cowshed that morning, how it slipped on the straw and stood up again. By the time the bus came, Charu was laughing about the calf, too.

What was born in Kalyani's cowshed that morning?
A calf was born in the cowshed that morning.
How did Charu feel when the boys copied her?
She felt hurt and ashamed, staring at her shoes with her chest aching.
What did Sharma Sir do that helped?
He briefly explained that the movements are not a choice, called the copying cruel and stopped it on the spot.
How does Kalyani seem to see Charu?
Kalyani sees Charu as an ordinary friend to chat with; she never mentions the movements and just talks about the calf.
Inez has $150. She spends one-half on hockey skates and a certain amount on hockey pads. If Inez has $25 remaining, how much did the hockey pads cost, together, in dollars?

She spent 150/2=$75 on hockey skates.
Let X be the amount Inez spent on hockey pads.
150-75-X=25
75-X=25
X=50
The hockey pads cost $50.
The answer is 50.

Read this:

Christmas Eve in Berlin, and Thomas had no leave. Snow had shut half the trains. At home in Kottayam, his whole family would be at midnight mass and then eating appam and stew.
He'd planned for this. At seven he video-called home. Ammachi held up the star they'd hung on the porch. His little cousins sang, off-key. He laughed, then had to look away for a moment.
Then he made appam in a borrowed pan, badly, and stew that was too thin. At nine the doorbell rang: Rekha from work, and two others, stamping snow off their boots. He'd invited them the week before.
"This is my family's Christmas," he said, serving the lopsided appam. "Mostly."
Rekha told them about her village's Christmas in Goa. The kitchen got loud and warm.

What did Ammachi hold up on the video call?
The star they'd hung on the porch.
What was Thomas feeling when he had to look away during the call?
He felt a sharp pang of homesickness mixed with warmth and love for his family.
What did Thomas plan ahead, and why did it help?
He planned both a video call home and a dinner with friends, so he could keep his family's Christmas alive without being alone.
How might Rekha feel at Thomas's Christmas dinner?
She probably felt welcomed and at home, enough to share stories of her own village's Christmas.

Read this:

Registration for the state debate round closed at four, and at 3:40 Eshaan was still standing outside the staffroom in the rain, form in hand. Two weeks ago he had lost the district final. He could still hear the judge: "Weak rebuttal from the second speaker." That was him. Since then he had skipped debate practice, told his mother he was "over it", and spent lunch in the library. Mridul ran up, soaked. "Did you give it?" Eshaan looked at the form, the ink starting to blur. "What if I lose again? Then it's not bad luck. Then it means I'm just not good." He folded the form into his pocket. At 4:05 the staffroom door closed. Eshaan felt relieved, then sick.

What had the judge said about the second speaker?
"Weak rebuttal from the second speaker."
Why did Eshaan fold the form into his pocket?
He feared that losing again would prove he's 'just not good', so not entering protected how he sees himself.
At what moment could Eshaan have chosen differently, and how?
At the staffroom door with Mridul, he could have handed in the form and asked a teacher to help with rebuttals, treating the loss as feedback.
What might Mridul feel watching the form go into Eshaan's pocket?
Mridul, who ran through the rain, may feel disappointed and worried for a friend who seems to be hiding rather than trying.
What does "in the same boat" mean?

It means that people are in the same difficult situation.
Example: None of us finished the project, so we are all in the same boat.

Read this:

A message arrived on a rainy Tuesday in Toronto: "Dalia? It's Siddiq. I know it's been six years. I've thought about you a lot." Dalia read it standing in the kitchen with a wooden spoon in her hand. Pleased, first, in a rush. Then wary, then a small hot flicker of resentment: six years of birthdays without a word, and now this.

She put the spoon down and typed, "It's really good to hear from you. I'll be honest, I was hurt when we lost touch. I'd like to catch up, slowly."

Siddiq answered within minutes, apologising for going silent after the move and asking how her mother was. They arranged a video call for Saturday. Dalia didn't pretend the gap wasn't there, and she didn't plan a lecture. She would see who showed up.

How many years had passed since Siddiq last got in touch?
Siddiq wrote, 'I know it's been six years.'
What did Dalia feel on reading the message?
Pleased first, then wary, then a small flicker of resentment about the years of silence.
How did Dalia reply, and why does it help?
She said it was good to hear from Siddiq, named the hurt honestly and asked to catch up slowly, which neither hides the gap nor punishes.
How might Siddiq have felt when sending the first message?
Probably nervous about being turned away, since Siddiq apologised quickly for the silence once Dalia answered.

Hana's desk in the Toronto apartment had three charts taped above it: violin minutes, maths scores, days until the music school audition. Each evening she coloured in one more square, and the small click of finishing felt better than anything else in her day.
On Saturday, Rafael texted a photo of everyone at the lake. 'Come? One afternoon.'
She wrote back, 'Can't, practice,' like she always did.
On Monday she got a B on a chemistry quiz. She sat very still at lunch, pushing rice around her container. 'I'm nothing if I can't even do this,' she said quietly.
Rafael frowned. 'You're my friend who makes up songs about the bus driver. That's not a grade.'
Hana laughed despite herself, then stopped. She couldn't remember the last time she'd done something just for fun.

What were the three charts above Hana's desk?
Violin minutes, maths scores and days until the music school audition.
What does Hana saying 'I'm nothing if I can't even do this' reveal?
It reveals she feels worthless after one B, because she has started measuring her whole worth by results.
What moment could become a turning point for Hana, and what might she choose next?
Realising she can't remember doing anything just for fun could lead her to say yes to the next afternoon at the lake.
How might Rafael feel after hearing 'Can't, practice' again and again?
Rafael may feel pushed aside and a little worried, missing the friend who makes up songs about the bus driver.

Come here, beta, and sit. You asked how I knew what to say to you last week, so I'll tell you. I'm Pooja. I was sixteen then, and there was a girl in my class called Vasudha. Whenever she walked into the room my whole body noticed. I didn't know what that pull meant. I only knew my family had a picture of my future, and I couldn't tell if this fit inside it. I didn't tell anyone for months, and I kept trying to name it and getting scared. Finally I told my cousin Reena, who only said, "You don't have to know today." I can still remember how my shoulders dropped. I took my time. I stayed honest with myself and I didn't rush to any label. That patience is what I'm giving you now.

What was the name of the girl in Pooja's class?
Her name was Vasudha.
What was Pooja feeling in those months, and how can you tell?
Confused and worried. Pooja did not know what the pull meant, could not tell if it fit the family's picture of the future, and kept trying to name it and getting scared.
What helped Pooja most, and what does it suggest a wise person might do?
Telling cousin Reena, who said Pooja did not have to know today, helped. Talking to someone trusted and taking time worked better than rushing to a label.
How might Reena have seen Pooja's confession?
Reena probably wanted Pooja to feel safe rather than pushed, which is why Reena said Pooja didn't have to know that day.

In Istanbul, Ada's science project on how plants drink water was due on Thursday. She had two weeks. Her friend Elif started hers on day one, with celery sticks in coloured water. Ada watched and thought, "I'll do mine later. It's easy." On the weekend she went to her cousin's. "Maybe the teacher will give us an extra week," she told herself. "She's kind." On Wednesday night she finally put celery in water, but it needed a day to change colour. She stared at the glass until bedtime. On Thursday morning the celery was only faintly pink. The teacher did not extend the date. Ada handed in half a poster, and her cheeks burned when she saw Elif's bright stalks.

What did Elif use for her project?
Celery sticks in coloured water.
How did Ada feel about the deadline on the weekend?
Ada was hopeful the kind teacher would give an extra week, which let her feel relaxed instead of starting.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
Ada waited until the last night for an experiment that needed a day; starting early, like Elif, would give it time to work.
How might Elif feel seeing Ada's half poster?
Elif might feel sorry for Ada, and a little awkward that her own project looked so bright beside it.

Read this:

In a study room at the university in Buenos Aires, Noa slid her résumé across the table to Santiago, her final-year mentor. 'Be honest. Is it good?'
Santiago read it twice. He could say 'looks great' and she'd leave happy. He could say 'this is weak' and she'd leave crushed. He did neither.
'Your projects are genuinely interesting,' he began. 'The water-sensor one especially. But right now each line says what you did, not what happened. Look.' He took a pen and rewrote one line beside hers.
Hers: 'Worked on a water-quality sensor for the campus.'
His: 'Built a water-quality sensor that flagged two contaminated taps; the campus replaced both.'
Noa read it slowly. 'Oh. It's the same project, but it sounds real.'
'It is real. You just hid the result. Try the other three lines tonight and send them to me.'

What was Noa's original line?
'Worked on a water-quality sensor for the campus.'
What was Santiago feeling as he decided how to respond?
He felt torn between flattery that would leave her happy and harsh words that would crush her, and wanted to be honest but kind.
What could Noa do with the other three lines?
Rewrite each to show a result, like the sensor line, and send them to Santiago for another look.
How does the feedback feel to Noa?
Noa feels encouraged rather than hurt, seeing that her project 'sounds real' once the result is shown.

Read this:

'Good swim today, Chandrika.'
'Thanks, Imran. It was, actually. I felt light.'
'You always look happier after training.'
'I am. Before I joined the club, I was so tense about school. Now I have you lot, and Tuesday pizza, and I actually sleep.'
'So why did you look like you'd seen a ghost when your dad came in?'
Chandrika pulled her towel tighter. 'He's already talking about the national meet. He wrote my times on the fridge. If I don't drop a second by March, he says I'm wasting his time.'
'That sounds like a lot.'
'Some days I love it. Some days the water feels like an exam hall.'
Imran nodded. 'Maybe tell Coach? She's good at talking to parents.'
'Maybe.' She smiled faintly. 'Pizza first.'

What does Chandrika's father write on the fridge?
Her times.
What was Chandrika feeling when her father came in?
She was anxious and pressured, as if she had seen a ghost.
What step did Imran suggest?
Telling the coach, who is good at talking to parents.
How might Chandrika's father see his pushing?
He may believe he is helping her succeed, not seeing how it turns the water into an exam hall for her.

1. What is a good way to start a letter to my grandmother?
2. How should I say this correctly: "He write a long letter yesterday."
3. Explain the word "synonym" in simple words.
4. Why do we write the date on a letter?

1. Begin with "Dear Grandmother," and ask how she is. Then share your news.
2. Fixed: He wrote a long letter yesterday. Why: "Yesterday" needs the past tense (wrote).
3. A synonym is a word that has almost the same meaning as another. Example: "Big" is a synonym of "large".
4. It shows when it was written. Because the reader may need to know when it was sent.

Read this:

Zeenat's message came in while I was doing laundry. "Can you spare some for the mess bill again? Will return, promise." My name is Tanuja, and that word "again" sat in my stomach. Last time she promised too. I hadn't minded the money as much as the pretending: I'd smiled at her, then complained about her to my roommate.

This time I sat on my bunk and worked out what I could give without skipping my own bus pass. I wrote back, "I can give a small amount, and please treat it as a gift, not a loan. That's my limit for now."

She sent a heart, and later, "thanks for being straight." I felt lighter, though a bit anxious that she might feel judged. I still don't know if she'll ask again.

What did Zeenat ask for money to cover?
The mess bill.
What was Tanuja feeling about Zeenat's message, and why?
Uneasy and a little resentful. The word "again" sat in Tanuja's stomach, and Tanuja had already complained about Zeenat to the roommate.
What did Tanuja do that protected both Tanuja's limits and the friendship?
Tanuja gave only what was affordable as a gift, said plainly that it was the limit, and did not pretend to have nothing.
How might Zeenat have felt on receiving the reply?
Possibly embarrassed or judged at first. Her heart and "thanks for being straight" suggest relief at an honest answer.
At a restaurant, do I ask for the "bill" or the "check"?

British and Indian English say "the bill". American English usually says "the check".
Example: Could we have the bill, please?

Change these lines to the present tense.

Monday: Sona folded a paper boat the way Papa showed her and floated it in the bucket. It tipped over. Tuesday: she folded a second boat with a pointy bottom. It tipped over too.
Monday: Sona folds a paper boat the way Papa showed her and floats it in the bucket. It tips over. Tuesday: she folds a second boat with a pointy bottom. It tips over too.

House parent's note, Block C, 2nd week of term.
Dhruv, thirteen, new this year. At dinner tonight he pushed the dal around and ate half a roti. When the others were laughing about a film, he laughed a beat late.
At lights out I did my rounds. His roommates were asleep. Dhruv was lying on his back with his eyes open. When he saw the torch he shut them fast and turned to the wall.
Earlier, Arohi from the kitchen staff mentioned he'd asked if they ever make rajma "like at home".
What I did next: I didn't ask in front of the roommates. At breakfast I asked if he'd help me carry the notices to the office, and on the way I said many first-years miss home and it isn't childish. He looked at his feet and said, "My Mummy's rajma." I've asked the kitchen for rajma on Sunday and booked his phone call home for tomorrow.

What did Dhruv ask the kitchen staff?
If they ever make rajma "like at home".
Why did Dhruv shut his eyes when he saw the torch?
He felt embarrassed and afraid of seeming childish, so he hid that he was lying awake missing home.
How did the note-writer help Dhruv without embarrassing him?
They spoke to him privately while carrying notices, said missing home isn't childish, and arranged rajma and a phone call home.
How might Dhruv's roommates see him during these days?
They might just think he is quiet or tired, since he hides his homesickness from them.

Read this:

Sunday night
I did it. After lunch, when Mummy and Papa were having tea, I sat across from them. My knees were shaking under the table.
I said, "I know you want the best for me, and I'm really grateful. I want to marry Vaibhav. I've thought about it for two years. I would love your blessing, but either way, this is my choice and I'll take responsibility for it."
Papa didn't say anything for ages. Mummy's eyes filled up. Then Papa said, "Bring him home for dinner next week. We want to meet him properly."
I didn't expect that. I cried in the bathroom after, happy crying. 🙏
Still a long way to go. But they heard me.
Yamini

When did Papa ask Yamini to bring Vaibhav home?
Papa asked Yamini to bring Vaibhav home for dinner next week.
What was Yamini feeling while she spoke to her parents?
Yamini was very nervous, with shaking knees, but also determined, and afterwards relieved and happy.
What made Yamini's talk likely to be heard?
She thanked her parents and acknowledged their care, then stated her choice calmly and owned it, without blaming or demanding.
How might Yamini's mother be feeling with her eyes filling up?
She may feel a mix of worry, sadness at letting go and being moved by how respectfully Yamini spoke.

Read this:

The district entrance exam was held in the government school in Sirsa, with desks too small and a single fan. Wasim turned the paper over, read the first physics question and felt his whole body lock. His shoulders rose to his ears. He realised he had not breathed out for a while. His friend Varun, two rows ahead, glanced back and saw Wasim hunched over the desk like a closed fist. Wasim remembered what his coaching sir had drilled into them: breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in; drop your shoulders; feel both feet on the floor. He did it three times. His shoulders came down. The question was still hard, so he skipped it and did the next one. Outside afterwards Varun said, "You looked frozen at the start." Wasim nodded. "I was. Then I wasn't."

Where was the district entrance exam held?
In the government school in Sirsa.
What does Wasim's hunching and held breath suggest about how he felt?
It suggests a spike of anxiety at the hard first question; it could also be deep concentration, but his later relief once his shoulders dropped points to fear.
Which steps helped Wasim unfreeze, and why?
Slow exhaling, dropping his shoulders and feeling his feet on the floor calmed his body enough that he could think and move on.
How did Varun see Wasim at the start of the exam?
Varun saw him hunched like a closed fist and thought he looked frozen, though from two rows ahead he could not know exactly what Wasim felt.

Read this:

"Why did you send me a crying face, Zubin?" Ritu asked, holding up the tablet at dinner.
"Because I was sad. My tower fell."
"But it was the laughing-crying one. I thought you were laughing."
"It was crying and laughing. Both."
"Then how do I know?"
Zubin thought about it. "Maybe I'll write 'sad' next to it."
"Or send me the heart," said Ritu. "The heart means you love me."
"Bhaiya sent a heart to his teacher yesterday," said Zubin. "Does that mean he loves her?" Ritu burst out laughing. "Ask Papa!" 😄

What happened to Zubin's tower?
Zubin's tower fell.
What was Zubin feeling when he sent the crying face, and why did Ritu read it differently?
Zubin felt sad and a bit amused that the tower fell, so Zubin meant both feelings. Ritu saw a laughing-crying face and thought Zubin was laughing.
What could Zubin add so that Ritu understands the emoji better?
Zubin could write a word like 'sad' next to the emoji, or say his feeling aloud, so the message does not depend on Ritu guessing.
How might Ritu feel about needing to guess what the emoji means?
Ritu feels confused and a little left out of Zubin's feelings, because Ritu cannot tell whether to comfort Zubin or laugh along.

Tanvir: clean up how?
Uday: no idea. remove duplicates? fix spellings? delete old customers?

Ask three questions before starting: why, by when and what good looks like, rather than guessing or freezing.

The sports shop on Brigade Road had a whole wall of running shoes. Tejas walked straight to the pair whose logo he'd seen on hoardings at every signal and on cricket shirts on TV. "These," he told the salesman. "Size nine." Hrithik picked up a plain blue pair from the lower shelf. "Try these too. They're lighter." "I've never heard of that company." "You've never heard of most things. Just try them." Tejas tried both. The blue ones were softer, honestly. But the famous ones felt… right. Like something he already owned. He paid for the famous ones, nearly twice as much. Three weeks later, on his morning run, the blister on his heel told him what his feet had known in the shop.

What did Hrithik pick up from the lower shelf?
A plain blue pair.
What did Tejas feel when the famous shoes seemed like something already owned?
Tejas had seen the logo so often that the shoes felt familiar and safe, and that comfort was mistaken for quality.
At which moment could Tejas have chosen differently, and what should have guided the choice?
After trying both, Tejas could have gone with the softer blue pair, trusting the feel on his feet over the familiar logo.
How might Hrithik react on hearing about the blister?
Hrithik might tease Tejas a little, but also feel sorry, having suggested the lighter pair in the shop.

On the village cricket ground, the rule was: whoever hits the ball into Maria aunty's garden is out and must fetch it.
Vishal hit a huge six that sailed into the garden. "Out!" everyone shouted.
Maria, Maria aunty's niece, who was playing too, said, "Wait. Why should a big hit be out? He hit it well."
"Because Aunty shouts."
"Then the rule should be: fetch it and say sorry, but not out."
The boys argued. Vishal said, "Only fair if it's the same for everybody."
They agreed. Vishal fetched the ball, said sorry to Maria aunty, and kept batting.

Whose garden did the ball go into?
Maria aunty's garden.
What was Vishal feeling when everyone shouted "Out!"?
Vishal felt frustrated and cheated, since his best shot got him out.
Which part of the children's new rule made it fairer?
They talked about why the rule existed and made a new one that fixed the real problem and applied to everyone.
How might Maria aunty see the new rule?
Maria aunty would probably be happier getting an apology each time, instead of just angry shouting.
Why does the sky turn red and orange at sunset?
Sunset light travels a long path through the air. Because the air scatters the blue light away along the way, mostly red and orange light reaches our eyes.

Lance wants to finish reading a 100 page book in 3 days. Yesterday, he started to read 35 pages. Today, he read 5 fewer pages than yesterday. How many pages should he read tomorrow to finish the book?

Lance read 35 - 5 = 30 pages today.
So he read a total of 35 + 30 = 65 pages in 2 days.
Thus, he should read 100 - 65 = 35 pages tomorrow.
The answer is 35.

Last Diwali, when we went to see Nani and Nana in Nagpur, Mummy let me, Seema, be the list-maker. A week before, I sat at the dining table with a pad and broke the trip into jobs: tickets, clothes for four days, food for the twelve-hour train, a present for Nana, and someone to water our plants. Every evening Mummy and I went down the list together. Some jobs took one minute; my little sister Indu packed her own socks. Some took three evenings, like finding Nana's favourite tea. On the day we left, the only thing not ticked was "relax". On the train, while other families ran to buy food at stations, we opened our steel tiffins and ate slowly. I felt very grown-up.

How long was the train journey?
Twelve hours.
How did Seema feel on the train?
Seema felt proud and grown-up, eating calmly while other families rushed for food.
Which other approach could work for a trip like this, and why?
Starting from an old checklist of past trips would save time, but breaking this trip into its own jobs fitted what this visit needed.
What was it like for Indu to be part of the plan?
Indu got a small job of her own, packing her own socks, so she was included too.

"Wasim, I need to say something." Tanuja pulled her dupatta tighter on the bench outside the library. "You've messaged me all day, every day, for two weeks. I like you. But I need to slow down."
"Slow down? I thought you felt the same."
"I do like you. I also want time with my friends. I'm going to my cousin's on Saturday."
"Saturday was our plan."
"We didn't plan it. You did."
He looked away. "Fine. I guess I care more than you."
Tanuja noticed her stomach tighten. That sentence again. The second time this week.
"That's not fair, Wasim."
"Whatever. Go to your cousin's."
He walked off. Tanuja sat alone for a while. Then she called her cousin. "I'll be there Saturday. Can I talk to you about something?"
It hurt. But she had learned something important from a single gentle no.

Where was Tanuja going on Saturday?
She was going to her cousin's.
How did Tanuja feel when Wasim said he cared more than her?
Tanuja felt a tight, uneasy feeling in her stomach, recognising the guilt-heavy line from earlier in the week.
What did Tanuja do that protected herself?
She kept her plans, named the unfair comment calmly, and reached out to her cousin to talk it through.
What does Wasim's reaction reveal?
Wasim's cold, sulking reply to a gentle no suggests he struggles to respect her pace, which is useful for Tanuja to know early.
Why does a seed need water to sprout? I don't understand "displeasure". Can you help? How do you spell "neice"?

1. Water wakes the seed up. Because it softens the seed coat and lets the tiny plant inside swell and grow.
2. Displeasure is a noun that means the feeling of being annoyed or not pleased.
3. It is "niece". Remember "i before e".
My sister and I adopted two kittens today. Write my diary entry, about 65 words, with some of our funny first moments.

Dear Diary,
Today we brought home two kittens! One is grey and the other is ginger. At first they hid under the bed, and we had to coax them out with a saucer of milk. Then the ginger one chased my shoelace around the room, and the grey one climbed onto my sister's head. We laughed so much. I think this house will never be quiet again!

I'm Leela, and I live one floor below Seema in our Goa housing society. In March, half the building started going to the Sunday beach cleanup. Photos everywhere, matching caps. Seema, twenty-five, didn't join at first. She told me, "I don't want to go just because it's the thing everyone's posting."
I noticed she went down to the beach alone one weekday evening and walked the whole stretch, looking at the plastic by the rocks. The next week she asked the organiser what happened to the waste after they bagged it. She also asked me, half joking, "Would I go if no one ever took a photo?"
I can't tell you what she decided inside. But the following Sunday she was there at seven, no cap, sorting bottles from wrappers by herself. When someone lifted a phone for a group photo, she smiled, waved, and kept sorting.

What did Seema ask the organiser?
She asked what happened to the waste after they bagged it.
What does Seema's question, 'Would I go if no one ever took a photo?', suggest she wanted to know?
It suggests she wanted to be sure she cared about the beach itself, not just about joining what everyone was posting.
What did Seema do before joining, and why does that make the choice more her own?
She walked the beach alone, asked where the waste went, and questioned her own reasons, so when she joined it was a deliberate choice.
How does Leela see Seema's decision to join?
Leela noticed the difference between Seema and the crowd, careful not to claim to know her mind, but seeing her work without a cap and keep sorting during the photo.
My college has a fest next month and I want to join the organising team.
That is a great way to meet people and learn new skills. Do you know which team you want to be on?
Maybe decoration or hospitality. I'm not sure.
Think about what you enjoy. Decoration suits you if you like making things with your hands. Hospitality suits you if you like talking to people and solving small problems quickly.
I like talking to people more.
Then hospitality sounds like your fit. When you sign up, mention a time you looked after guests or handled a crowd, even at a family event. It shows you already have some experience.

Monday. The hostel floor rep, Preeti, had a noise complaint to sort out: someone had played loud music on Sunday night. She asked Lalremsiami, "Were you in your room around eleven?" Lalremsiami looked up at the ceiling, then off to the side, lips moving slightly. "Sunday... I came back from church, then laundry... then, yes, room." Preeti noted the looking away and felt a small click of suspicion. People look away when they lie, don't they?
Wednesday. Before writing anything up, Preeti checked the facts. The gate register showed Lalremsiami signed in at 8:10. The warden's round sheet had her door marked "quiet, lights off" at 10:45. The music had come from the other wing.
Friday. At dinner someone asked Preeti what she had eaten on Tuesday. Preeti found herself staring at the ceiling fan, eyes flicking sideways, trying to remember. She laughed at herself. That weekend she told Lalremsiami, "Sorry I doubted you. You were just thinking."

What time did the gate register show Lalremsiami signing in?
The gate register showed she signed in at 8:10.
What did Preeti feel when Lalremsiami looked up at the ceiling?
Preeti felt a small click of suspicion, believing people look away when they lie; that was unfair, since Lalremsiami was only recalling the day.
What did Preeti do right before writing anything up?
Preeti checked the facts, the gate register and the warden's round sheet, instead of judging honesty from where someone looked.
What was being questioned like for Lalremsiami?
Lalremsiami was simply trying to remember the day, eyes drifting up while listing church and laundry, and was answering honestly.

Manoj: what does it say

Manoj: no way. I renewed it last year

The scooter policy expired two months ago.
What was Manoj feeling on learning the scooter had been ridden daily without insurance?
Manoj felt panicky and shaken, worried about what could have happened if there had been an accident.
Which fix in the chat is the cheapest, and why does it work?
Putting every renewal date in the phone calendar with a reminder a month before, because the lapse happened only since no reminder existed.
How does Usha react when Manoj adds the passport renewal?
Usha is caught out a little and laughs it off, admitting the reminder habit helps Usha too.
What is the plural of "story"? And should I finish a book I don't like?

1. The plural is "stories".
2. You can stop. Try a different book that suits you better.
Oprah has 3500 cars in her collection. If the average number of cars she gives away per year is 50, how many years will it take to reduce her car collection to 500?

If Oprah wants to have 500 cars left, she will have to give away 3500-500 = 3000 cars.
Since the average number of cars she gives away per year is 50, it will take her 3000/50 = 60 years to give away enough cars to have 500 left over.
The answer is 60.

At a crowded house party in Mexico City, Camila noticed her friend Rania leaning hard against the wall, eyes half-closed. A guy Camila barely knew had his arm around her and was steering her toward a bedroom. "She's fine, she wants to lie down," he said.
Rania mumbled something that wasn't a word.
Camila stepped in front of them. "She can't decide anything like this. I'm taking her." Her heart was pounding. He shrugged, annoyed, and walked off.
Camila sat Rania on the stairs, got her water and called a friend with a car. She stayed with Rania until they were home and she was asleep on her side, then texted Rania's sister.
Next morning, Rania didn't remember much. When Camila told her, she went quiet, then said, "Thank you for not deciding I was fine."

What did the guy say about Rania?
He said, "She's fine, she wants to lie down."
What does Camila's pounding heart suggest about how she felt stepping in?
It suggests Camila felt scared and tense, but determined to protect her friend.
Which of Camila's actions protected Rania, and why?
Blocking the guy, getting Rania water and a safe ride home, staying with her and telling her sister, because someone that drunk can't give consent or keep herself safe.
How might Rania see the night once she hears what happened?
Rania likely feels shaken and deeply grateful, realising how vulnerable she was and that her friend protected her.

Michael has $42. Michael gives away half the money to his brother. His brother then buys 3 dollars worth of candy. If his brother has $35 left, how much money, in dollars, did his brother have at first?

Michael gives away 42/2=21 dollars.
Before buying candy, his brother has 35+3=38 dollars.
His brother had 38-21=17 dollars at first.
The answer is 17.

"You look like I looked at twenty-five, Nikita," said Amandeep Bua, pouring out two cups of chai. "Let me tell you something. I was head of the school canteen committee, the temple accounts, my brother's children every evening. I said yes to all of it and thought that was goodness. One monsoon I fell asleep standing up in the temple store room. Truly. Mataji found me leaning on a rice sack.
The next week I did three things. I took Sunday afternoons for myself, no matter what. I gave the temple accounts to Sardar ji's son, who was dying to be asked. And when the canteen wanted me for a fourth year, I said no.
Everyone was upset for a month. Then they managed. And I was kind again, not just busy. That's the part I want you to remember."

Where did Amandeep Bua fall asleep standing up?
In the temple store room, leaning on a rice sack.
How did Amandeep Bua feel before making the changes?
Amandeep Bua was exhausted and stretched thin, saying yes to everything and mistaking that for goodness.
What was the turning point in Bua's story, and what changed after it?
Falling asleep in the store room; after that, Bua kept Sunday afternoons free, handed the temple accounts on, and said no to a fourth canteen year.
How might Sardar ji's son have felt when given the temple accounts?
He was dying to be asked, so he probably felt pleased and trusted.

Shankar stood on the metro platform in Delhi at 7 a.m. with his earphones in but nothing playing. The news on the screen showed floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.
He'd been like this for weeks. Not sad, exactly. More like the air had weight. What was the point of board exams if the planet was cooking? What was he even supposed to become in a world like this?
His friend Yash came up behind him and tugged an earphone out. "You look like you're carrying the whole city."
Shankar shrugged. "Maybe I am."
Yash didn't laugh. "Me too, some days. Want to walk from the next station? The long way?"
They walked. It didn't fix anything, but the air felt lighter.

What did the news screen show?
Floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.
What was Shankar feeling on the platform?
He felt a heavy, generalised dread and frustration, as if the air had weight and nothing had a point.
How could an adult support Shankar if this feeling keeps going?
A parent or school counsellor could listen without dismissing his worries and help him find small things he can do and enjoy.
What is it like for Yash when he sees Shankar that morning?
Yash recognises the feeling because he has it too, so he responds with company rather than a joke.

In the one-room school at Kudal, someone had broken the window by the well. Wasim, the young teacher, knelt beside eight-year-old Ramesh, who had been nearby. The headmaster, passing, called out, 'Ask him if the Patil boy threw the stone!' Wasim nodded politely, but didn't ask that. 'Ramesh, tell me what you saw near the window.' Ramesh twisted his shirt. 'I heard a crack. Then I saw glass.' 'What happened after that?' 'A ball rolled out. The big cricket ball.' 'Anything else?' 'No, sir.' Wasim wrote it all down in his notebook right away, date and time at the top. Later the Patil boy's mother came, angry, and Wasim showed her the notebook: a ball, no stone, no name.

What did Ramesh see roll out after the crack?
The big cricket ball.
What might Wasim have felt when the headmaster called out his suggestion?
Wasim was probably uneasy, worried that naming the Patil boy would plant a detail in Ramesh's memory.
What did Wasim do that others gathering a child's account could copy?
He asked open questions like 'what did you see?' and 'what happened after that?', and wrote the answers down at once with the date and time.
How might the Patil boy's mother feel after seeing the notebook?
She would probably feel relieved and calmer, seeing that her son wasn't named.

Class 4 teacher's note, lunch-break duty, Thursday:
For two weeks I have watched the marbles group by the neem tree. Kashish is always welcomed. When she promises 'loser gives one', she hands it over, even her favourite green one. Sachin arrived today and the children suddenly said the game was 'finished'. They started a new one as soon as he left. When I asked quietly, one child said, 'Sachin changes the rules when he's losing.' Sachin sat on the steps kicking the ground. Next, I will talk with Sachin alone, without scolding, about how the others see him and what he could do differently. I'll also keep an eye out so the group doesn't shut him out for good.

Where does the marbles group play?
The marbles group plays by the neem tree.
What might Sachin be feeling as he sits on the steps kicking the ground?
He is probably hurt and frustrated at being left out, and may not fully understand why the game suddenly 'finished'.
What is the teacher's plan, and why is it a good choice?
The teacher will talk with Sachin alone without scolding about how others see him, so he can learn to change, and will watch that he isn't shut out for good.
How do the other children see Kashish compared with Sachin?
They trust Kashish because she keeps her promises even with her favourite marble, but they avoid Sachin because he changes the rules when losing.

Monday: Three weeks after the flood swept through their colony, Vishal, fifteen, sat in class staring at nothing. The teacher called his name twice. He didn't hear.
Thursday: At lunch, Deepak grabbed Vishal's shoulder from behind as a joke. Vishal spun and shoved him hard into the bench. "Don't touch me!" Everyone went quiet. Vishal ran out of the gate and didn't come back till evening.
The next Tuesday: The school counsellor had met Vishal twice. She explained that going numb, lashing out and running are the body's alarms after a terrifying night, not proof he was bad. That afternoon Vishal found Deepak. "I'm sorry. It wasn't you. Since the flood, I jump at everything." Deepak nodded slowly. "I didn't know. I'll stop grabbing."

What did Vishal shout when Deepak grabbed him?
He shouted "Don't touch me!"
How did Vishal feel when Deepak grabbed his shoulder?
He felt suddenly terrified and threatened, so he shoved Deepak and ran.
What helped Vishal make things right with Deepak?
The counsellor helped him see his reactions as survival alarms, not bad character, which gave him words to explain and apologise.
How might Deepak have felt when Vishal apologised?
Deepak may have felt relieved and understanding, realising the shove was not really about him.
Give this email line a formal tone: Hey, just checking if you got my file.
I am writing to check whether you have received my file.

Damini had forty minutes to catch the last bus back to her flat in Amman, and Zainab's mother was not letting her leave.

"One more piece of knafeh!"

"No, thank you, I'm full."

The plate came anyway. Damini ate it. Then came the coffee. She drank one tiny cup; it was refilled at once. A second; refilled again. She glanced at the clock, panicking.

Zainab leaned over, laughing. "Shake the cup side to side when you're done. Otherwise my mother thinks you're just being polite."

Damini tilted the cup gently from side to side. Zainab's mother smiled, took it, and finally let her stand.

On the bus, Damini laughed to herself. At home in Nagpur she did exactly this to guests, insisting till they gave in. She had never once wondered how it felt from the other side.

How long did Damini have to catch the last bus?
Damini had forty minutes.
What was Damini feeling as her coffee cup kept being refilled?
Damini felt panicked and a little embarrassed, full, watching the clock, and unsure how to refuse politely.
What local rule helped Damini, and why?
Shaking the cup side to side signals you're finished; knowing it let her decline without offending her host.
How might Zainab's mother see Damini's first 'No, thank you'?
She took it as polite modesty, not a real no, so she kept offering the way her custom expects.
What is the humidity outside today? Also, why does the air feel heavy before a storm?

1. I don't know that, because I can't read live weather data. A weather report or app can tell you.
2. The air holds a lot of moisture and the pressure changes, which can make breathing feel heavy.
Alia has 2 times as many markers as Austin. Austin has one-third as many markers as Steve does. If Steve has 60 markers, how many does Alia have?

Austin has 60/3=20 markers
Alia has 20*2=40 markers
The answer is 40.

The physiotherapy centre smelled of liniment and floor cleaner. Eight months ago, Darshan had sat in the same plastic chair with a pinned leg and a cancelled state trial, while an uncle patted his shoulder: "Everything happens for a reason, beta!" Darshan had wanted to throw his crutch. Now he came only for monthly checks, and today he noticed the new patient, Aadhya, gripping her walker so hard her knuckles were pale. He didn't tell her it happened for a reason. He said, "The first week is the worst. I cried in that bathroom twice." She laughed, a little shakily. Walking out later, he understood something: he had not chosen the accident, but he had chosen to be the one who sits beside the new ones. That part felt like his.

What did the uncle tell Darshan eight months ago?
He said, "Everything happens for a reason, beta!"
How did Darshan feel when his uncle said everything happens for a reason?
He felt angry and unheard, wanting to throw his crutch, because the cheerful line brushed past his loss.
What worked in the way Darshan spoke to Aadhya?
He skipped the silver lining and shared his own hard first week, which made her less alone and even let her laugh.
What might it be like for Aadhya to hear Darshan admit he cried?
She may feel relieved and less ashamed of her own struggle, seeing that someone further along had felt the same.
Can you suggest a calm evening routine for me? I'm usually rushing from tuition to dinner to bed.
Sure. Even a few calm steps can help. When do you get home, and when do you usually sleep?
Home by seven thirty. Bed at ten. I'm Ishita.
Thanks, Ishita. Try dinner by eight, then homework until nine, then a quiet half hour with no screens, such as a shower, tidying your bag and reading. Lights off at ten.
The tidy-the-bag part is smart. I always forget things in the morning.
It saves a lot of morning stress. Pack your bag and lay out your uniform before reading, so you can relax knowing tomorrow is ready.
Great. What was the quiet half hour supposed to include?
A shower, tidying your bag and reading, Ishita. Keep your phone away during that time so you feel calm when you switch off the light at ten.
Can "set up" have different meanings?

Yes. It can mean to arrange or prepare something, or to start an organisation.
Examples: Please set up the chairs for the assembly. Her uncle set up a small bakery.
Is the air quality good in my city this morning?
I can't check live air readings, so I don't know. An air quality app will show the current level.
Write a stage direction for a play in one sentence beginning with "Enter".
Enter Meena, carrying a lantern and looking nervously around the dark room.

Behind the village school, Karthik, a bigger boy, told Payal, “You can't play. You smell like cow dung.” The others laughed. Then he leaned close. “If you tell, I'll push you in the ditch.” Payal walked away, her throat tight. At home she didn't eat. Her grandmother asked, “What's wrong, beti?” Payal told her everything. Dadi held her. “Those words were unkind and that was a threat. You were right to tell me.” That afternoon Dadi walked to the school and spoke to the headmaster, who called Karthik's parents.

What did Karthik threaten to do if Payal told?
Push her in the ditch.
What was Payal feeling when she walked away with a tight throat?
She was hurt and ashamed by the laughter, and scared because of the threat.
What did Dadi do that a trusted adult should do?
She listened, told Payal she was right to tell, and went to the headmaster that same afternoon.
How might the other children who laughed see it later?
They might realise the words made Payal sad and scared, and that laughing along was unkind.
In a story about desert traders I read about caravans. Are those like trucks?

No. A caravan, in that sense, is a group of travellers, often traders with camels, who journey together across a desert or other empty land. This is a noun, and its plural is Caravans. Today the word can also mean a vehicle people live in on holiday, but the desert sense fits your story.
Example: The caravans of traders crossed the desert in the cool of the night.

I'm Madhuri, and I work two desks from Gurpreet at a software firm in Toronto. In Gurpreet's first week I watched a small scene. Gurpreet asked a new teammate, cheerfully, "So how much do you earn, and are you married?" The teammate blinked, laughed politely and changed the subject. Later, in the lounge, Gurpreet took a call from home and spoke loudly; two people looked up. I can't know how Gurpreet felt about those glances. That afternoon I told Gurpreet quietly that back home those questions show interest, but here many people save them for close friends. Gurpreet nodded slowly and said, "Oh, I see." The next day Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and calls moved to the corridor.

Where does Madhuri work?
Madhuri works at a software firm in Toronto.
Why did Madhuri speak to Gurpreet quietly that afternoon?
To explain kindly without embarrassing Gurpreet, since the questions came from interest, not rudeness.
What did Gurpreet change afterwards?
Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and moved calls to the corridor.
How might Gurpreet have felt about the glances in the lounge?
Possibly puzzled or a little self-conscious, though Madhuri cannot know for sure.

It was Chinmay's first night in the children's ward. The corridor light made the drip stand throw a long, bony shadow on the wall. It looked like a monster with thin arms. Chinmay's heart thumped. He pulled the sheet over his head and whimpered. His mother, Gargi, woke on the chair beside him. She didn't laugh. "Something scary?" Chinmay pointed. Gargi switched on the little night lamp she had brought from home. The shadow shrank. She climbed carefully onto the edge of the bed and hugged him. "I'm right here, all night." Chinmay held her finger until his eyes closed.

What made the long shadow on the wall?
The drip stand made the long, bony shadow.
How was Chinmay feeling when he pulled the sheet over his head?
He felt frightened; the shadow looked like a monster and his heart was thumping.
What did Gargi do that helps more than saying "there is nothing"?
She didn't laugh, switched on a night lamp, hugged him and promised to stay all night.
How might Gargi feel sitting up in the ward at night?
She may feel tired and worried for her son, but tender and determined to comfort him.
My office people say "He is out of station." My foreign client did not understand.
"Out of station" is common in India, but other English speakers may not know it. Say: "He is out of town." That is clear everywhere.

Chandrika had exactly one evening before the internship form closed, and the power in her rented room in Bhopal kept flickering. Her portfolio was ready: a crop-price dashboard, a hostel complaint tracker, and clean write-ups for both. Her classmate Asif had checked it that morning and said, 'Send it. It's good.'
At 8 p.m. she opened a few portfolios from students at the most famous institutes to 'just compare'. Dark themes, 3D animations, projects with thousands of users. By 9:30 she had scrolled through twenty. Her own site suddenly looked like a school notebook.
'It's not worth showing,' she typed to Asif.
'It's decent. Deadline's at midnight.'
The power went out at 11:15. She sat in the dark with her phone at eleven percent and did not open the form. The next morning Asif told her he'd been shortlisted with a site simpler than hers.

How many portfolios had Chandrika scrolled through by 9:30?
Twenty.
What was Chandrika feeling after comparing her site with the others?
She felt discouraged and inadequate, as though her decent work looked like a school notebook next to theirs.
What small step could have helped Chandrika at 8 p.m.?
Submit first, since Asif had already said it was good, and look at other portfolios later only for ideas.
How might Asif feel about being shortlisted with a simpler site?
Asif may feel sad for Chandrika, having told her it was good, knowing that her fear, not her work, kept her out.

Read this:

Three days before the school assembly in their Pune colony school, Usha's speech on water shortage was a wall of facts. She read it to her friend Nikita on the terrace, and Nikita's eyes drifted to the kites. "You lost me at the second number," Nikita admitted. Usha was stung, but she tried again. This time she started with a question: "Who here had a bucket bath this morning because the tank was empty?" Then three points, one story about her building's tanker, and a closing line. On the day, her knees shook and her mouth went dry. She held the mic stand, found Nikita's face in the third row, and asked her question. Half the hall raised their hands. Someone laughed. Usha relaxed a little and kept going.

What question did Usha open her speech with?
She asked who had a bucket bath that morning because the tank was empty.
How did Usha feel when Nikita said, "You lost me at the second number"?
She felt stung and a bit hurt, but she took it as a sign the speech was not working and chose to fix it.
What helped Usha keep going when her knees shook?
Holding the mic stand, finding a friendly face and starting with a question that got hands up gave her something steady and made the audience part of the talk.
How might Nikita feel sitting in the third row during the speech?
Nikita probably felt proud and a little responsible, since that honest comment helped Usha change the opening that now held the hall.
My friend said, "This is just for timepass." What is "timepass"?

"Timepass" is used mainly in Indian English and means something done only to fill free time, often without a purpose. In standard English you could say "a way to pass the time" or "just for fun".
Example: We played cards just to pass the time while it rained.

Urmila: thanks for agreeing to this call, both of you. three rules, ok? 1) one person talks at a time 2) we talk about the work, not each other 3) we finish with one ask each
Sonali: ok
Pritam: fine
Urmila: Sonali, go first. what's the problem from your side?
Sonali: I get the client files at 6pm and I'm expected to finish by morning
Urmila: thanks. Pritam, your side?
Pritam: the client sends them late to me too. I'm not sitting on them
Sonali: I thought you were
Urmila: noted. now the requests. Sonali?
Sonali: send whatever part is ready by 3pm, even if incomplete
Urmila: Pritam?

Urmila: so two changes, starting Monday, for two weeks. we check back on the 20th 🙂

What did Sonali's line "I thought you were" reveal about how Sonali had been feeling?
It shows Sonali had been resentful, believing Pritam was holding the files back, and was surprised to learn the client sent them late to Pritam too.
What would you change first if the two-week trial didn't work?
Look at the root cause with the client, since the late files start there, and agree a handover time with the client rather than only between the two colleagues.
How might Pritam see the joint call?
Pritam gets to explain not sitting on the files and to ask for something back, so the call feels fair to Pritam rather than like an accusation.

messages.content: Don't forget turning off the lights before going out. Please check.

Don't forget to turn off the lights before going out.
Why: verb form ("forget turning" -> "forget to turn").
Prove that the equation (x - a)(x - b) = 1 has two distinct real roots for all real numbers a and b. Also prove that x^2 + px - 1 = 0 has real roots for every p.

Answer: D = (a - b)^2 + 4 > 0 and D = p^2 + 4 > 0, so both always have two distinct real roots.

Expand and write in standard form first: (x - a)(x - b) = 1 x^2 - (a + b)x + ab - 1 = 0 D = (a + b)^2 - 4(ab - 1) = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 - 4ab + 4 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 + 4 = (a - b)^2 + 4 A square is never negative, so (a - b)^2 >= 0 and D >= 4 > 0. Hence there are always two distinct real roots. For x^2 + px - 1 = 0: D = p^2 - 4(1)(-1) = p^2 + 4 >= 4 > 0. In fact whenever a and c have OPPOSITE signs, -4ac > 0 and the roots are real and distinct. The proof strategy: write D as a square plus a positive number.
Do I write "insight" or "incite" in "The book gave me ___ into village life"?

Write "insight", which means a deep understanding of something. "Incite" means to urge people to do something bad or violent.
Examples: The book gave me insight into village life. He was warned not to incite trouble between the neighbours.
Can you help me to carrying this box upstairs? What is wrong?

Can you help me carry this box upstairs?
Why: verb form ("to carrying" -> "carry").
Brenda picks 250 peaches. When she sorts through them, only 60% are fresh, and Brenda has to throw 15 away for being too small. How many peaches does Brenda have left?

First find how many of the peaches are fresh, which is 250 peaches * 60% = 150 peaches.
Then, subtract the number Brenda throws away after the fresh count, which is 150 peaches - 15 peaches = 135 peaches.
The answer is 135.
