So Bhupen, you want to know why a second-year law student got into trouble with her own housing society? Fine. Our society passed a rule, properly voted, that domestic workers must use the service lift and cannot sit on the lobby benches. Totally legal, as far as I could tell. And every morning I watched Kamla-ji, who has cleaned our flat since I was nine, stand holding her knee while the service lift was broken for a week. I kept thinking: the bylaw is valid, but is it right? People have a right to basic dignity whether or not a committee agrees. So at the next meeting I stood up, shaking a bit, and asked them to change it. Two uncles told me to respect the vote. I said I did respect it, and that's why I was asking for a new one. It lost. I'm still collecting signatures. That's the story of Vasudha versus Block C.

What did the society's rule say domestic workers could not do?
The rule said they must use the service lift and cannot sit on the lobby benches.
How can you tell that Vasudha felt nervous but determined at the meeting?
She stood up shaking a bit, yet she still asked them to change the rule and kept collecting signatures after the vote lost, which shows she was anxious but resolved.
Which choice worked, and why?
Asking for a new vote instead of breaking the rule worked, because it challenged the rule's fairness while still respecting how the society makes decisions.
How might Kamla-ji be affected if the rule changed?
She would no longer have to stand in pain waiting for a broken lift, and she might feel treated as an equal in the building she works in.
Please stop to make noise, the baby is sleeping. Correct, please.

Please stop making noise because the baby is sleeping.
Why: verb form ("stop to make" -> "stop making"); conjunction ("," -> "because").

The placement cell's board announced Rehana's summer internship at a design studio. Saurabh read it twice. They had been in the same studio class. She was good, but so was he. "If she can, maybe I can," he thought, and asked her in the corridor how she'd prepared. "Portfolio every weekend for three months," she said. "I'll send you my list." That night he started his first page. Near him in the reading room, another student from their class stared at the same notice on his phone, then shut it and sat without opening his books. "Some people just have it," he muttered. Saurabh noticed the difference: for him, Rehana's news felt like a path. For the other boy, it felt like a wall.

How long did Rehana work on her portfolio?
Every weekend for three months.
What was Saurabh feeling after reading the notice?
He felt inspired and motivated, seeing Rehana's success as something within his own reach.
What could help the other student turn envy into motivation?
Talking to Rehana about her steps, as Saurabh did, could make the goal seem reachable instead of like natural talent.
How does Rehana see Saurabh's question?
She seems happy to help, offering to send her list, and probably sees him as a fellow student rather than a rival.

In Lagos, Chidi was the fastest runner in his year. His friend Oskar, whose family had moved from Norway, invited him to join the new chess club after school. Chidi was curious. He liked puzzles. But the chess club met at the same time as athletics training. What if he fell behind in running? What if he lost at chess and people saw? He told Oskar, "Maybe next term." Next term, he said the same. Oskar made new friends in the club; they laughed together at lunch. Chidi kept winning races. But when he passed the chess room, he felt a pang. He had kept everything he had. He just hadn't gained anything new. His world, he thought, felt a bit smaller than before.

What was Chidi known for in his year?
He was the fastest runner in his year.
Why did Chidi keep saying 'maybe next term'?
The fear of losing his running edge or looking bad at chess felt bigger than the chance of enjoying something new, so safe felt better, though he later felt a pang.
What could Chidi do to try chess without much risk?
He could ask to join the chess club on a day without athletics, or try one session to see how it feels.
How might Oskar see Chidi's repeated 'maybe next term'?
Oskar may feel a bit disappointed but moves on, making new friends in the club.

Thursday
Watched Truth Talks till 2 am again. Everything he says makes sense. It's always them: taking our seats, our jobs, our streets.
Removed Reena from the girls' group today. She keeps posting "other side" articles. I don't need that negativity.
At dinner I said something about "those cockroaches", and my little cousin Pinky, who is seven, laughed and repeated it. "Cockroaches! Cockroaches!" Mausi went very quiet and looked at me.
I felt strange. Pinky's best friend at school is from that family down the lane. Pinky thinks cockroaches are things you squash.
I told myself it's only a word. But I haven't been able to sleep, and I didn't open Truth Talks tonight. I keep thinking of Reena's last message: "I miss you when you talk like you."
Urmila

What did Pinky do when Urmila said 'those cockroaches'?
Pinky laughed and repeated it: 'Cockroaches! Cockroaches!'
What did Urmila feel when Pinky repeated the word?
Urmila felt strange and uneasy, realising a seven-year-old now heard people as things to squash.
What small step could Urmila take next?
Reply to Reena, keep the channel closed, and talk to Mausi or a counsellor about the anger behind the late-night videos.
What was it like for Mausi to hear the word at dinner?
Mausi went very quiet and looked at Urmila, likely alarmed that such language had reached a seven-year-old at the table.

Kishore, sit. You asked why your Parveen aunty always says, "Trust the knot in your stomach." Let me tell you where it came from.

I was twenty-five and engaged to a man called Rafiq. In company he was charming. Alone, he had other rules. If I wore a colour he disliked, he would say, "You look cheap. Change, or I'll tell my mother the engagement is off." If I wanted to visit my friend, he went silent for three days. I felt afraid all the time, and so confused. I kept thinking I must be the problem.

One evening I told my older cousin Nusrat everything, crying. She said, "This is not love. None of it is your fault." That gave me courage. The next time Rafiq threatened to leave, I said, "Then leave." He did. My heart broke for a month, then healed. I was free.

What did Rafiq say when he disliked the colour young Parveen wore?
He said, "You look cheap. Change, or I'll tell my mother the engagement is off."
How did young Parveen feel during the engagement?
She felt afraid all the time and confused, thinking she must be the problem.
What was the turning point in Parveen's story?
Telling her cousin Nusrat everything and hearing that it was not love and not her fault gave her the courage to say "Then leave".
How might Nusrat have felt hearing her cousin's story?
Nusrat was likely worried and protective, which is why she named it plainly as not love and not Parveen's fault.

In Berlin, Felix's lectures were optional, and by November he had stopped going to most of them. He woke at eleven, made coffee, meant to study, and somehow the day slid away between videos and naps. Mateo, his flatmate, found him on the sofa at four p.m., still in pyjamas. "Did you eat?" Felix shrugged. "There's always tomorrow." Mateo sat down. "You know what helps me? I pretend I have a job. Library at nine, lunch at one, home at five." Felix scoffed, then, the next morning, followed him to the library just to prove it was silly. He managed three solid hours. By the end of the week, they had a routine: Mateo's alarm, a bakery stop on the corner, and a shared table on the second floor.

What time did Mateo say he goes to the library?
At nine.
What does Felix's shrug and 'There's always tomorrow' suggest?
He seems stuck and a bit ashamed, avoiding the problem because he has no clear plan without set classes.
What worked about Mateo's suggestion?
It gave Felix a simple outside structure, like a workday, and company to start with, which made it easier to begin.
What is it like for Mateo to live with Felix's drifting?
He is concerned, noticing that Felix hasn't eaten or dressed, and he chooses to help instead of just complaining.

Friday: at dinner, Farhan's mother said Rukhsar should stop working late now that she was married. Rukhsar looked at Farhan. He looked at his plate. His brother Zubin changed the subject to cricket. That night Rukhsar slept facing the wall. Tuesday: his mother complained that Rukhsar never asked her opinion; Rukhsar complained that Farhan never defended her. Farhan felt like a rope pulled at both ends, and he stayed late at the office to avoid them both. The next Sunday: at lunch, Farhan put down his spoon. 'Ammi, Rukhsar's late shifts are our decision, and I'm proud of her work. Rukhsar, Ammi misses you in the evenings. Can we keep Sundays for family lunch?' His mother sniffed, but agreed. Rukhsar squeezed his hand under the table. Zubin grinned at his rice.

What did Zubin do when Rukhsar looked at Farhan on Friday?
He changed the subject to cricket.
What was Farhan feeling on Tuesday?
He felt torn and trapped, like a rope pulled at both ends, so he stayed late at the office to avoid them both.
What made Farhan's Sunday stand work?
He stated the decision calmly and fairly, backing Rukhsar's work while naming his mother's feelings and offering Sunday lunches.
How did Farhan's silence on Friday affect Rukhsar?
She felt unsupported and hurt, and slept facing the wall that night.

By March, Hafsa noticed something odd in the robotics club room at her Pune college. In August she had handed Ramesh the motor driver board, half as a test, and he had burnt two fuses and asked her fifty questions. Now he was debugging other people's circuits. The other first-year, a quiet boy from Nagpur, had spent the same months labelling drawers and fetching solder, because she had thought he "wasn't ready". He still looked at her before touching anything.
Hafsa scrolled through her own messages: long replies to Ramesh, a one-line "ok" to the other boy. One of them had been given problems and feedback; the other, only chores. That evening she handed the Nagpur boy the sensor module and sat beside him while he opened the datasheet.

What did Hafsa hand Ramesh in August?
The motor driver board.
What was Hafsa feeling as she scrolled through her own messages?
She likely felt uncomfortable and a little guilty, seeing that her low expectations had kept the Nagpur boy stuck on chores.
Which choice at the end could help the quieter first-year, and why?
Giving him the sensor module and sitting beside him offers a real problem plus support, the same chance Ramesh got.
What might it have been like for the Nagpur boy to spend months labelling drawers?
He may have felt unimportant and unsure of his ability, so he kept waiting for permission instead of trying things.
Sentence check please: 'I am feeling boring today.'
Corrected: "I am feeling bored today." Use "bored" for how you feel. "Boring" describes the thing that makes you feel that way: "This film is boring."

Saturday night
Met Ujjwal at the café near the metro today, the Deaf photographer from the community event. I've been learning signs from online videos for three months and was so proud to try them. First thing, I signed what I thought was "coffee". He looked puzzled, then grinned, typed on his phone and showed me: "That's the American sign. Here most people use a different one." Then he showed me his. My face went hot. Three months of practice, and half of it from the wrong country!
But he didn't seem to mind at all. We ended up using everything: his signs, my clumsy ones, typing on the phone, pointing at the menu, a few words on a napkin. He speaks a little too, when he wants to. He told me, "Asking what a sign means is normal. Deaf people do it with each other all the time."
Next week: find a local class, not just videos.
Neelam

How long had Neelam been learning signs from online videos?
Three months.
How did Neelam feel when Ujjwal said the sign was American?
Neelam felt embarrassed, face hot, disappointed to have learned signs from another country's sign language.
What does Neelam plan to do next, and why is it sensible?
Find a local class instead of only videos, so the signs learned match those used by Deaf people nearby.
How did Ujjwal see the mix-up?
Ujjwal didn't mind at all, grinning and explaining that asking what a sign means is normal, even among Deaf people.

Aditi, you look like you want to hide under the bed. Sit. Let your Omkar Ajoba tell you something.
At fourteen I copied answers in a maths test. The teacher caught me. In front of everyone.
For a week I couldn't look at anyone. I skipped school two days and said I had fever. I told myself, "I'm a cheat. I'm a bad boy." I hid from my own mother.
Then Mr Kulkarni, the teacher who caught me, came to our house. I thought I'd die of shame.
He sat with my father and said, "Omkar did a wrong thing. Omkar is not a wrong boy." Then he turned to me. "What do you want to do about it?"
Something changed. I said, "I want to take the test again. Properly." I did. I scored less, but I could look at him.
Feeling "I did bad" made me fix it. Feeling "I am bad" only made me hide.

How many days did Omkar skip school?
He skipped school two days and said he had fever.
What was Omkar feeling during the week after he was caught?
He felt deep shame, believing he was a bad boy, which made him hide from everyone, even his mother.
What was the turning point in Omkar Ajoba's story?
Mr Kulkarni separating the act from the person and asking what Omkar wanted to do, which turned shame into guilt that led to repair.
How might Mr Kulkarni have seen Omkar?
He saw a boy who did something wrong but was not bad, and came to the house to help him repair it with care.

Tuesday night
Tanvir cried at work today. After the client call where they cancelled his whole project, he went to the pantry, and when I walked in, his eyes were streaming. He turned away fast.
Then Rakesh walked in behind me, saw him, and said, "Arre, be a man, yaar," laughing. Tanvir went red and left.
I kept thinking about it all afternoon. In my family, the men cry at every wedding and funeral and nobody blinks. In Tanvir's, maybe not. Maybe he was ashamed. Maybe he was just furious. I didn't know, and neither did Rakesh.
So at five I messaged him: "Hey, that call sounded brutal. How are you feeling?" He wrote back: "Angry, mostly. Two years of work. The crying just happens when I'm angry, and I hate it." I said I get the same, and that it's nothing to be embarrassed about. He sent back a thumbs-up and "thanks, needed that".
Tomorrow I'm going to say something to Rakesh.
Sharmila

What did Rakesh say when he saw Tanvir?
'Arre, be a man, yaar.'
What was Tanvir feeling, according to his message?
Tanvir felt mostly angry about losing two years of work, and embarrassed that anger makes him cry.
How did Sharmila respond without stereotyping?
Sharmila messaged privately to ask how he felt instead of assuming, and reassured him the tears were nothing to be embarrassed about.
How did Rakesh's joke affect Tanvir?
It embarrassed him, turning him red and making him leave, adding shame to his anger.

In their small town below the dam, Indu's phone buzzed nonstop at nine at night. A voice message, forwarded many times: "Dam has burst! Water coming in one hour! Run!"
Her heart hammered. She forwarded it to three family groups before she'd even finished listening. Within minutes, people were out on the main road on scooters and tractors, heading for the highway. The road had been closed at the bridge because of landslides, and soon nothing could move.
Her friend Uday called. "Did you check it? The district collector's page says the dam is safe. They're only releasing water slowly, and the town is not being evacuated."
Indu opened the page. He was right. The weather department said the same.
She deleted her forwards, then wrote in each group: "The dam message is false. Please check the district collector's page before sharing." Her aunt replied, "Thank you, we were about to leave."

It said the dam was safe and water was only being released slowly, with no evacuation.
How did Indu feel when the voice message arrived?
She felt panicked, heart hammering, and forwarded it to three groups before even finishing listening.
What should Indu do next time a frightening message arrives?
Check the district collector's page or weather department first, before forwarding anything, so a false alarm doesn't spread.
How was Indu's aunt affected by the correction?
Her aunt was relieved and grateful, saying they were about to leave onto the blocked roads.

Thursday night.
Tenzin said again today that I should build the launch around trade fairs and printed brochures. 'That's how I built my whole client list.' And I nodded. Again.
The thing is, he built it ten years ago. Our buyers now find us through short videos and online groups; I have last quarter's numbers.
I owe him so much. I'm not the girl who says 'sorry, small point' any more, and that's because of him. That's what makes this hard. Disagreeing feels like ingratitude. But staying quiet would be pretending.
Tomorrow I'll say it: 'I think the fairs matter less now. Can I show you why?' Calm voice, numbers ready.
If he gets annoyed, he gets annoyed. I really hope he doesn't.
- Binita

Trade fairs and printed brochures.
Why does disagreeing feel so hard for Binita?
She is grateful to Tenzin and admires him, so pushing back feels like ingratitude, even though she doubts his advice fits today's buyers.
What plan does Binita make, and why is it a good one?
She will calmly ask to show her numbers, which lets her say the truth respectfully and gives Tenzin evidence rather than a challenge to his pride.

He would need the humility to look at her numbers and accept that buyers have changed since he built his list.

The potter shapes wet clay on a spinning wheel. The pot is left to dry in the shade. Finally, it is baked in a hot kiln so it becomes hard.

One night a message came: the water supply in our area was poisoned, don't drink, forward to everyone. I felt a jolt, I tell you, like I was saving lives. I sent it to forty people. Our neighbour, old Mrs Kulkarni, who lived alone, didn't drink water for a whole day. She fainted on the stairs in the heat. It was all false. Someone made it up for fun. I sat with her at the clinic that evening and couldn't look at her. Next day I went to the municipal office and asked. That was the last time I forwarded anything without checking. At first he felt a jolt, as if he was saving lives; at the clinic he felt so ashamed he couldn't look at Mrs Kulkarni.

Seeing Mrs Kulkarni faint because of the false message; after that he checked with the municipal office and stopped forwarding anything unchecked.

Living alone, she believed it, went without water for a day and fainted on the stairs, so a made-up message caused her real harm.

messages.content: My son is growing fast and his uniform is already tight. Should I buy a bigger size?
A slightly bigger size can last longer, but not too big, because loose clothes can look untidy and get in the way.

I was fourteen. We practised every morning in the village field, even in the rain. On the day of the final, the other team was better. We lost by two points.
I wanted to kick the dust and walk off. Our coach just looked at me. So I walked to their captain and shook his hand. He said, "Your raid was the best one today."

Losing well is a skill too. Farhan nana practised that one as well.

Two points.

Annie is trying to figure out whether it's safe to drive her truck. For every 3 degrees the temperature drops below 32 degrees, Annie's chances of skidding on ice increase 5%. If she goes into a skid, she has a 40% of regaining control. Otherwise, she'll have a serious accident. If the temperature is 8 degrees, what is the percentage chance of Annie getting into a serious accident if she drives?

First find how many degrees below 32 the temperature is: 32 degrees - 8 degrees = 24 degrees
Then divide that amount by the number of degrees per 5% increase in skid risk to find how many 5% increases there are: 24 degrees / 3 degrees/5% increase = 8 5% increases
Multiply the number of increases by 5% to find the total increase in skid risk: 8 * 5% = 40%
Now find the chance that Annie has a serious accident if she goes into a skid by subtracting the chance she regains control from 100%: 100% - 40% = 60%
Finally, multiply the chance of going into a skid by the chance of having a serious accident after a skid to find the total risk of a serious accident: 60% * 40% = 24%
The answer is 24.

messages.content: A ribbon 15/2 m long is cut into pieces each 3/4 m long. How many pieces are there? Also work out (-4/9) / (8/15).

Answer: 15/2 / 3/4 = 15/2 x 4/3 = 10 pieces. (-4/9) / (8/15) = (-4/9) x (15/8) = -5/6.

Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its RECIPROCAL (turn it upside down): the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3. 15/2 x 4/3: cancel 15 and 3 (5 and 1) and 4 and 2 (2 and 1), giving 5 x 2 = 10. Check: 10 x 3/4 = 30/4 = 15/2. For the second, the reciprocal of 8/15 is 15/8; cancel 4 and 8 (1 and 2), 15 and 9 (5 and 3): -(1 x 5)/(3 x 2) = -5/6. Signs: different signs give a negative answer. The reciprocal of a negative number is negative: the reciprocal of -2/7 is -7/2. Only the SECOND number is turned over. 0 / (any non-zero number) = 0, but dividing BY 0 is impossible.

Three weeks ago Karthik, a recruiter for a private insurance office in the district town, had called: 'You are almost selected. Just wait for the formal letter.' She had told her mother, turned down tuition work for the summer and stopped filling other forms. Then nothing. Two weeks of nothing. She went from checking her phone every hour to snapping at her little brother for borrowing it. Her old tuition teacher, Joshi-sir, heard it all at the bus stand. 'Don't stop your life for one maybe. Send two polite follow-ups, a week apart. Meanwhile fill those two forms on the board.' That evening Alka sent the first message to Karthik and filled one form at the cyber café. What did Karthik say when he called?
Karthik said, 'You are almost selected. Just wait for the formal letter.'
What was Alka feeling after two weeks of nothing?
Alka felt confused and angry, her hope turning into irritation that she took out on her little brother.
Why is Joshi-sir's advice wise?
Two polite follow-ups a week apart, while filling other forms, keeps one uncertain offer from holding her whole life still.
How might Karthik see the 'almost selected' call?
Karthik may have said it casually or before a final decision, not realising Alka would turn down work and stop applying because of it.

At the agricultural college in Dharwad, Pranav got his field-work report back from Dr Minakshi. He flipped straight to the last page and saw it in red: "Soil sample labels inconsistent."

He didn't read anything else. All evening in the hostel he kept thinking: my report is bad. She thinks I'm careless. Maybe I'm not cut out for research.

"One of the best in the batch," the roommate repeated. "Did you even see that?"

Pranav hadn't. He had read the red line five times and nothing else. He fixed the labels that afternoon, in twenty minutes.

The red comment said, "Soil sample labels inconsistent."
Why did Pranav think his report was bad?
Pranav felt stung and anxious about the red comment, and it filtered out all the praise, so a success felt like a failure.

Read every comment first, perhaps listing the positives, before deciding what the feedback means.
How might Dr Minakshi see Pranav's report?

Bilal didn't care about geography. Rivers, rainfall, capital cities: boring.
But at his new school in Johannesburg, Zanele and three others met every Tuesday in the library corner to do homework together. They laughed, shared crisps and called themselves “the Corner.”
Zanele waved him over in his second week. “You can join the Corner if you want.”

They met every Tuesday in the library corner.
Why did Bilal keep doing geography even though he found it boring?
He felt included and happy in the Corner, and didn't want to miss being part of the group.

Dear Lavanya,

You asked how I finally started walking every day when I had failed all last year. Here is my thinking. I used to say, "I'll walk sometime today," and "sometime" never came. Every day I had to decide when, and by evening I was tired and had no energy for the decision.

On a rushed day it might shrink, but the sentence stays. Twelve mornings so far.

Shreya

What is the sentence that Shreya wrote on the card?
When the toothbrush goes back in the cup each morning, I walk for twenty minutes.
What was Shreya feeling each evening when 'sometime today' never came, and why?
Shreya was drained and probably discouraged, since deciding every single day used up the energy by evening.
What could Shreya do if a morning is truly rushed, and why?
Shreya could still step outside for a few minutes, because keeping the link to brushing teeth protects the habit even when the walk is short.

Lavanya may feel curious and pleased that the question got such a thoughtful answer, and may want to try a card of Lavanya's own.

"Go ahead."

"What would it take for me to become a team lead in the next cycle?"

Uday leaned back. "Honestly? Your client work is strong. But you've never run a project end to end."

Uday looked at her for a long moment. "You're serious."

Farida picked up her laptop, and her hands were still not quite steady.

What was Farida feeling when she asked Uday for the lead role?
Farida was nervous, with sweating palms and unsteady hands, but also determined, having thought about it all weekend.

She asked what the gap was, offered to fill it with a real project, requested regular feedback, and asked for an introduction to the director.

Uday is surprised and a little impressed by how prepared she is, and now sees her as someone ready to be developed for promotion.
Is "I am working here from 2020" correct? And how can I ask my team for help?

1. No. Say: I have been working here since 2020. Why: perfect tense ("am working" -> "have been working"); preposition ("from" -> "since").
2. Say what you are stuck on and what you have already tried, then ask for a few minutes of their time.

Emmanuel will stay in Guam in December for 10 days in which he has to use international data that would cost $3.50 per day. Emmanuel has been paying $175 per month for his regular plan. How much in all will be Emmanuel's charges for December?

The international charge cost $3.50 x 10 = 35.
Therefore, Emmanuel's bill for December is $175 + 35 = $210.
The answer is 210.
Tim buys a book of esoteric words.  He learns 10 words from it a day.  In 2 years the book has increased the number of words he knows by 50%.  How many words did he know originally?

In 2 years there are 365*2=730 days
So he has learned 730*10=7300 words
He knew 1/.5=2 times that number of words before the book
So he knew 7300*2=14600 words before
The answer is 14600.
Nine beads are on a string: the 1st is red, and after that every bead is blue except the 9th, which is yellow. Which bead is the last one?

Answer: The 9th bead (the yellow one) is the last.

"Last" is not always 10th; it is whichever is at the end. Here the last is the 9th. Make strings of different lengths and ask "Which is last? What number is it?"

How many different arrangements are there of the letters of MATH? Of BOOK? Of APPLE?

Answer: MATH: 4! = 24. BOOK: 4!/2! = 12. APPLE: 5!/2! = 60.

MATH has 4 different letters, so 4! = 24 arrangements. BOOK has two Os. If we pretend they are different (O1 and O2) there are 24 arrangements, but BO1O2K and BO2O1K look the same: every real arrangement has been counted 2! = 2 times. So divide: 24 / 2 = 12. APPLE has two Ps: 5! / 2! = 120 / 2 = 60. Rule: divide by the factorial of the number of times each letter repeats. Check BOOK by listing where the two Os go: positions (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4), 6 ways, and then B and K fill the other two places in 2 ways: 6 x 2 = 12.

Carson is a night security guard. He's supposed to patrol the outside of a warehouse that's 600 feet long and 400 feet wide. If Carson is supposed to circle the warehouse 10 times, but gets tired and skips 2 times, how far does he walk in one night?

First find the total distance Carson walks along the warehouse's long sides: 600 feet/side * 2 sides = 1200 feet
Then find the total distance Carson walks along the warehouse's short sides: 400 feet/side * 2 sides = 800 feet
Add those two amounts to find the total distance walk in one circle: 1200 feet + 800 feet = 2000 feet
Then find the number of circles Carson actually walks: 10 circles - 2 circles = 8 circles
Then multiply the distance of one circle by the number of circles Carson makes: 2000 feet/circle * 8 circles = 16000 feet
The answer is 16000.
Now you try: x^5 + x - 1 = 0.
The answer is f(0) = -1, f(1) = 1, and f' = 5x^4 + 1 > 0: exactly one root, in (0, 1).

What was Nirmala feeling after the threat?
Nirmala felt deeply ashamed and frightened, saying she wanted to disappear.
Which steps did Dolma urge, and why are they right?
Dolma urged Nirmala not to send anything, stop replying, not pay, save evidence and tell her mother now, which cuts off the blackmailer and gets adult help.
How did Nirmala's mother respond, and why did it matter?
She held Nirmala's hand, said she did right to tell, and called the helpline and filed a report before dinner, showing Nirmala she was not to blame.
Please share a quick story about a boy who is nervous before his first day at a new school in the city.

Mohan had grown up in a village, and the school in Delhi looked as big as a palace. On the first morning, he stood at the gate and gripped his bag. Hundreds of students were shouting and running. A boy with glasses came up to him and asked, "Are you new? I'm Dhruv." Mohan could barely whisper his name. Dhruv showed him the classroom and the water tap, and shared a pencil because Mohan had forgotten his own. At lunch, they sat together under a tree and talked about cricket. By the afternoon, Mohan had forgotten to be afraid. At home, he told his mother, "The school is not so big."

Daniel's grandmother had flown to London from Pune. At the door, his mother folded her hands and said, “Namaste, Aai.” Daniel copied, pressing his palms together. Grandma's face lit up. Then his friend Elif, visiting from next door, put her right hand over her heart and bowed her head a little, the way her family greeted older people. Grandma laughed and did it back to her. Later, Daniel greeted his grandpa on a video call with both: hands together, then hand on heart.

Where had Daniel's grandmother flown from?
From Pune.
What was Grandma feeling when Daniel pressed his palms together?
She was delighted and touched that he greeted her in the way she knew. She may also have felt a bit emotional after a long journey to see him.
What helped Daniel learn the greeting?
He saw his mother model it warmly at the door and copied her, with no one forcing him.
How might Elif's greeting look to Daniel's grandmother?
She saw it as a respectful, kind gesture from another family's tradition, and happily returned it.
Let me hear a story about a boy who is scared of the school's tall slide.

Everybody in Class 2 loved the tall red slide, except Lalit. He stood at the bottom every break, watching the others whoosh down. His friend Gudiya noticed and climbed down the ladder. "Do you want to go together?" she asked. Lalit shook his head. "Then I will hold the rail with you." She went up first, step by step, with him right behind, and stopped at the top. "Look at the view first." Lalit peeked at the whole school ground, the green field and the tiny teachers. Slowly, he sat down, closed his eyes and pushed. The slide was over in two seconds, and Lalit landed on the sand laughing so hard that he asked to go again, immediately.

Note to file, engineering managers' meeting, 3 May.
Aadhya, who leads the mobile team, presented how her team decided what AI tools may and may not do. I want it on record because it was the clearest thinking in the room.
She had started from risks, not from features. Her list of allowed uses: drafting test cases, summarising public API documentation, suggesting names and comments. Her list of forbidden uses: pasting customer records, pasting API keys or passwords, using any output that no human has read. She explained each line with a real near miss from her team.
Two managers wanted to copy it at once. I have asked Aadhya to share it with all teams by Friday and to note where each team might need to differ.
Tejas

Where did Aadhya start from?
From risks, not from features.
What might Aadhya have felt when two managers wanted to copy the list?
Aadhya probably felt proud and encouraged that the careful thinking was useful beyond the mobile team.
Why was explaining each line with a real near miss effective?
Real examples made the rules concrete and believable, so other managers could see why each limit exists.
How might other teams be affected by Tejas's request?
They get a tested starting list by Friday, with room to note where their work differs.

messages.content: Bruno wants to buy two and one-half dozens of pens. How many pens will he have?

Since a dozen is equal to 12, then two dozens are equal to 12 x 2= 24.
One-half dozen is equal to 12/2 = 6.
Thus, Bruno will have a total of 24 + 6 = 30 pens.
The answer is 30.

Thursday
Three weeks ago I sat in Dr Dolma Bhutia's office completely stuck on my botany project: my seedlings kept dying and I didn't know why. She looked at my photos and said, 'Your soil stays too wet. Drill holes in the cups.' That was it. Ten minutes.
I almost didn't write to thank her. It felt like bothering her twice. But Didi said a thank-you costs nothing. So that night I wrote: 'Thank you, ma'am. I drilled holes in all 30 cups. 27 seedlings are alive this week, compared with 11 before.'
Today I went back with my growth graph and one new question, about light hours. She smiled as soon as I walked in and said, 'Ah, the seedling person.' She remembered my project! We talked for twenty minutes, and she lent me a book.
I think this is what people mean by a mentor.
– Lalit

How many seedlings were alive after the holes were drilled?
27 seedlings are alive this week, compared with 11 before.
How did Lalit feel about writing the thank-you at first?
Lalit felt hesitant, worried it would be bothering the professor twice, until Didi's advice.
What could Lalit do to keep the connection going?
Return the book with a short note on what was learned, and share the next graph when the light experiment ends.
How might Dr Bhutia feel when Lalit walks in again?
She is happy and engaged, remembering the project, since the thank-you with results showed her advice worked.

Read this:

At the school in Johannesburg, a new boy, Omar, spoke with a strong accent. Every morning a group copied his voice and laughed.
Thabo, ten, used to laugh along. Then one day he saw Omar's face when they did it. Omar's lips were pressed tight.
The next morning, when they started, Thabo didn't laugh. He walked over and stood next to Omar.
At break he went to Mrs Nkosi. “They're making fun of Omar's voice every day.”
Mrs Nkosi thanked him and spoke to the group before lunch. She also found Omar and sat with him and Thabo in the canteen.

Who did Thabo tell about the teasing?
Mrs Nkosi.
How did Thabo feel when he saw Omar's face?
He felt guilty and uncomfortable, realising the teasing hurt Omar.
What did Thabo do that made a difference?
He stopped laughing, stood by Omar and reported the teasing to a teacher.
How did Mrs Nkosi respond to Thabo's report?
She thanked him, spoke to the group before lunch and sat with Omar and Thabo in the canteen.

The Guwahati branch opened at ten, and for the third week running Harsha walked in at 10:25, apologising. Bhupen, promoted to branch manager only two months before, had been dreading this. Harsha was likable, joked with customers, and had trained him on the cash software when he joined. But two customers had waited, and one deposit had been entered wrongly. Bhupen booked the small meeting room for Friday after closing, so no one would overhear. He began plainly. "Harsha, three weeks late, and Tuesday's deposit was wrong. Customers noticed. I need to understand what's going on." Harsha's face fell. "My mother's dialysis moved to mornings. I drop her off first." Bhupen let the silence sit. "Thank you for telling me. Can we try a 10:30 to 6:30 shift for three months, and I'll pair you on deposits for a week?" Harsha nodded, eyes wet.

What time did the branch open?
At ten.
What was Bhupen feeling before the meeting?
Bhupen felt dread and some awkwardness, since Harsha was likable and had trained him.
What made Bhupen's feedback respectful and effective?
He met privately after closing, stated specific facts and their effect, asked to understand, then offered a practical adjustment.
What was the conversation like for Harsha?
Harsha was embarrassed and emotional, but relieved to explain the mother's treatment and be offered a workable shift.

"And you," I interrupted, "cannot at all imagine the craving I have for fraternal and sisterly love. I never had a home, I never had brothers or sisters; I must and will have them now: you are not reluctant to admit me and own me, are you?"

Question: What does the speaker say about brothers and sisters?
The speaker has never had a home or brothers or sisters, craves that love, and says they must and will have it now. They ask whether the listener is reluctant to accept them.

The last bell before the Diwali break would ring in six minutes, and Charu, the basketball captain, was packing up two benches away. Mahima had spent the whole period drafting openers in her head. "Hey, great shot on Friday" sounded fake. "So, basketball, huh?" sounded worse. Everyone would see her walking over. They'd think she was trying too hard. Four minutes. Charu zipped her bag. Mahima's hands were sweating. Two minutes. She stood up and said the only true thing she had: "Hi. I want to try for the team after the break, but I don't know how trials work." Charu looked up and smiled. "Oh, nice! Mondays at seven. I'll tell Coach." The bell rang. Nobody had even looked.

Condense this piece into under 50 words.
Mahima rejects fake-sounding openers and simply tells Charu, the basketball captain, that she wants to try for the team. Charu smiles and says trials are on Mondays at seven.

Sumit,

You've been really quiet all week at lunch and I've been going crazy thinking about it. So here's a note, because I'm bad at saying things.

If it's because I made fun of your haircut on Monday, I'm sorry. If it's because I sat with Arvind at the assembly, I'm sorry. If it's because I didn't pass you the ball in football, that was an accident. If it's the thing I said about your cycle, I didn't mean it.

I've lost sleep over this. Just tell me what I did and I'll fix it.

Mridul

----

(Sumit's reply, written underneath in pencil:)

Bhai, you idiot, none of that. My dad lost his job two weeks ago and everything at home is weird. It's not you. I just don't feel like talking much.

Walk home together today?

S.

Why has Sumit been quiet, according to his reply?
Sumit's dad lost his job two weeks ago and everything at home is weird.
Why did Mridul list so many things he might have done wrong?
Mridul was anxious and assumed Sumit's mood must be about him, so he searched every small moment for a cause. Losing sleep shows how sure he was that it was his fault.
What went well in how this was finally cleared up, and what could Mridul do now?
Mridul asked directly instead of staying silent, which gave Sumit a chance to explain. Now he could just walk home with Sumit and be there without needing to fix anything.
How might Sumit feel reading a list of apologies for things Sumit hadn't even noticed?
Sumit might feel a little amused, calling Mridul an idiot fondly, and also touched that Mridul cares. The note gave Sumit an easy way to share what's really going on.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Minakshi, and being in the middle is funny. Everyone is very nice to you, right until they aren't.

Last term Bhavna and Deepa stopped speaking over a borrowed laptop charger, or really over what the charger meant. Bhavna sat on my bed one night and said, "You saw how she treated me, right?" The next day Deepa cornered me: "Tell me what she said about me." My stomach twisted, because part of me wanted to please whoever was in the room.

I told each of them the same thing. "I won't carry messages. I care about you both, and honestly the charger seems small next to the friendship, but I'm not going to pick a side." Bhavna stormed off. Deepa called me useless. It hurt 😔.

A month later they each told me, separately, that they trusted me because I never repeated what they'd said.

What did Bhavna and Deepa stop speaking over?
A borrowed laptop charger, or really what the charger meant.
Why did Minakshi's stomach twist when each friend asked Minakshi to take a side?
Part of Minakshi wanted to please whoever was in the room, even though Minakshi knew not to carry tales.
What could someone in Minakshi's position say when both friends want them on their side?
Say kindly that they will not carry messages or pick a side, keep their own view, and stay warm to both.
Why might Bhavna and Deepa have trusted Minakshi later?
Because Minakshi never repeated what either had said, each could tell Minakshi would not repeat their words to others either.

In the girls' hostel of the Jaipur school, the warden, Zainab, found Nirmala, fifteen, curled on her bed on a Sunday. "They're all talking about me," Nirmala said. "Because I cried in the dining hall. Nobody has ever been so homesick." Zainab had seen this almost every year. She didn't say so. She sat with her. "Being far from home is really hard. Tell me what you miss." Nirmala talked about her grandmother's garden. Zainab listened. The following Sunday, Zainab invited three girls to help her plant marigolds by the gate, Nirmala among them. While they dug, one girl said she had cried every night for a month in her first term. Nirmala stared. "You?" Zainab kept her eyes on the soil and smiled.

What did Zainab invite the girls to plant?
Marigolds by the gate.
Why did Zainab not tell Nirmala that this happened almost every year?
Zainab felt compassion and understood that pointing out how common it was might make Nirmala feel dismissed, so she listened first.
How did the marigold planting widen Nirmala's view?
It brought her together with other girls, one of whom shared her own homesickness, so Nirmala could learn she wasn't the only one.
How might the girl who admitted crying every night feel after sharing?
She might feel a bit exposed but also glad, seeing that her story helped Nirmala feel less alone.

Make this verse into two sentences of modern prose.

Before his king with reverence due
Dhumraksha bowed him, and withdrew.
Around him at his summons came
Fierce legions led by chiefs of fame.
Well armed with sword and spear and mace,
They hurried to the gathering place,
And rushed to battle, borne at speed
By elephant and car and steed.

Dhumraksha bowed before his king with due reverence and withdrew, and at his summons fierce legions led by famous chiefs came around him. Well armed with sword, spear and mace, they hurried to the gathering place and rushed to battle, carried at speed by elephants, chariots and horses.
An auto shop has a part that Clark needs for $80. Clark buys 7 of them and got a discount. If Clark only had to pay $439, how much was the discount?

Originally the car parts would be a total of 80*7 = 560 dollars.
Clark got a discount for 560-439 = 121 dollars.
The answer is 121.

Yet the misery, for which years of happiness were to offer no compensation, received soon afterwards material relief, from observing how much the beauty of her sister rekindled the admiration of her former lover. When first he came in, he had spoken to her but little, but every five minutes seemed to be giving her more of his attention. He found her as handsome as she had been last year; as good-natured, and as unaffected, though not quite so chatty. Jane was anxious that no difference should be perceived in her at all, and was really persuaded that she talked as much as ever; but her mind was so busily engaged, that she did not always know when she was silent.

One-line summary of this passage, please.
She is relieved that her sister's beauty rekindles a former admirer's interest, while Jane, anxious to seem unchanged, is lost in thought.

The inter-house race went on despite the rain. Naveen, eleven, was running second when he saw a boy ahead cut across the muddy corner behind the tree, where the teachers couldn't see. The boy finished first. Naveen crossed second, soaked and furious. "He cheated!" he told his friend Shankar, his fists clenched. "Everyone saw!" "The teacher didn't," Shankar said. Naveen marched to the PE teacher anyway, his voice shaking. "I'm not saying it for me. It's not fair to everyone else."

Where did the boy cut across?
The muddy corner behind the tree.
Why were Naveen's fists clenched?
He was furious and indignant that the boy had cheated and won.
What could Naveen do to make his case clearly?
Stay calm, describe exactly what he saw and ask the teacher to check with other runners.
How might Shankar see Naveen's anger?
He understands it, but worries it won't change anything since the teacher didn't see.

Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, before this workshop had a sign board. I made hand-stitched cushion covers, and I found an adviser, Francis, who had helped big wholesale sellers. He said, "Cut your price in half. Win on volume." He sounded so sure, and I was so eager, I didn't ask a single question. I cut my prices. But my buyers were small boutiques. They saw the new price and thought the quality had dropped. Two stopped ordering. One owner told me, "At that price, it can't be handwork." Francis wasn't wrong for his world. His world was different from mine. Remember that, when you start: Binita Aunty learnt it the costly way.

What did Francis tell young Binita to do?
"Cut your price in half. Win on volume."
Why didn't young Binita question Francis's advice?
She was eager and he sounded so sure, so she felt too impressed and hurried to ask why.
At what point in the story could Binita have made a better choice?
When Francis gave the advice; asking what kind of sellers he had helped would have shown his wholesale world differed from her boutique buyers.
How did the boutique owners see the lower prices?
They took the cheaper price as a sign the quality had dropped, and one said it couldn't be handwork at that price.

messages.content: Caprice is taking piano lessons. Her mother pays the teacher $10 for every half-hour of teaching her daughter. If Caprice is taking one lesson per week, and the lesson lasts 1 hour, how much money would the teacher earn in 5 weeks?

If half-hour lesson is worth $10, then a one-hour lesson costs 2 * 10 = $20.
One lesson per week would mean that in 5 weeks the teacher would earn 20 * 5 = $100.
The answer is 100.
Are 0.3 and 0.30 the same or different?

Answer: The same. 0.3 = 3 tenths = 30 hundredths = 0.30.

Shade 3 columns of a 100-square: that is 3 tenths, and it is also 30 small squares, 30 hundredths. Adding a zero at the END of the decimal part does not change the value, just as ₹0.3 and ₹0.30 are both 30 paise. But a zero straight after the point does change it: 0.03 is only 3 hundredths.
Eliza can iron a blouse in 15 minutes and a dress in 20 minutes.  If she spends 2 hours ironing blouses and 3 hours ironing dresses, how many pieces of clothes did she iron?

Since 60 minutes equal 1 hour, in 2 hours, Eliza ironed blouses for 2 x 60 = 120 minutes.
Eliza can iron 120 / 15 = 8 blouses.
Since 60 minutes equal 1 hour, in 3 hours, Eliza ironed dresses for 3 x 60 = 180 minutes.
Eliza can iron 180 / 20 = 9 dresses.
In total, Eliza ironed 8 + 9 = 17 pieces of clothes.
The answer is 17.

"Lokesh, the loudspeaker says everyone to the school on the hill. Now." "Mummy, they said the same thing four years ago and the water never came past the gate." He was stuffing his hard drive, charger and exam notes into a bag. "Five minutes." "You said five minutes ten minutes ago." "I'm not leaving my notes to rot. Where's Papa's photo album?" "Forget the album!" "You forget it. It's the only one," he snapped, sharper than he meant. Outside, someone banged the gate and shouted Mummy's name. "Baljeet-ji! The road's already under!" Mummy grabbed his arm. "Now, Lokesh." They stepped out into water at their ankles, then at their shins by the corner. Lokesh held the bag above his head. Behind them, the album lay on the table where he'd put it down to look for the charger.

How deep was the water by the corner?
The water was at their shins by the corner.
Why did Lokesh snap at Mummy about the album?
Lokesh was tense and angry under pressure 😠 and was clinging to saving things, sure the water would stop at the gate like last time.
Where was the turning point, and what should Lokesh have done then?
When the loudspeaker first called everyone to the school. Leaving at once with only essentials would have spared them wading through rising water.
What is it like for Baljeet while Lokesh keeps packing?
Baljeet is frightened and frustrated, hearing the loudspeaker and watching the minutes slip away while Lokesh keeps asking for five more.
Could you show me how "get the hang of" is used?

"Get the hang of" means to learn how to do something after some practice.
Example: After a few tries, Meera got the hang of riding a bicycle.

Daycare note, Wednesday.

Devika, one and a half, took four steps alone from the bench to my arms today. I clapped and said, "You walked all by yourself!"

She beamed and tried again, wobbling.

At pickup, her mother, Kashish, cheered too. "Four steps! You kept going!" Devika clapped her own hands.

How many steps did Devika take alone?
Devika took four steps alone.
What was Devika feeling when she beamed and tried again?
Devika felt proud and joyful, glowing with the praise.
Why was the praise effective?
Both adults praised Devika's effort and action warmly and specifically, not her looks.
How might Kashish feel hearing about the steps?
Kashish probably feels delighted and proud.
Mummy ne kaha "Khana kha ke hi jaana." English sentence kya hoga?
It is: "Eat before you leave." If you want to sound a little stronger, say: "Do not go without eating something first."
What does classification mean in a science book?

Classification is the sorting of things into groups according to what they have in common. It is a noun.
Example: The classification of animals into mammals, birds and reptiles helps us study them.
Name three constellations or star groups, one per line, with the first letters all capitals.

Orion
Cassiopeia
Ursa Major

Vinita had trained with Vikas sir at the Nagpur badminton academy for two years. His word was law. If he said jump, she jumped higher. A nod from him lit up her whole week.
Before the state trials, she twisted her ankle in practice. It swelled up fast.
"Tape it and play," Vikas sir said. "And don't tell your parents. They'll make a fuss and you'll lose your chance."
Vinita nodded automatically. Then, on the bus home, it bothered her. Why keep it secret? The ankle throbbed.
She thought: he's a brilliant coach. And this was wrong.
At home, she showed her mother the ankle and told her exactly what sir had said. Her mother's face tightened. "You were right to tell me. No coach should ask you to hide an injury." She took Vinita to the doctor that evening and phoned the academy director before dinner.

What did Vinita twist in practice?
Her ankle.
How did Vinita feel on the bus home?
She felt uneasy and conflicted, torn between her admiration for Vikas sir and the sense that hiding the injury was wrong.
Which choice protected Vinita, and why did it matter?
She used her own judgement and told her mother, which got her ankle checked and brought in the academy director.
How does Vinita's mother see Vikas sir's instruction?
She sees it as a coach crossing a line by asking a child to hide an injury, and acts the same evening.

By the third Monday, Himani saw the pattern. The weekly meeting in the Pune office ended in eighteen minutes, again. She proposed moving the client deadline forward; Ramesh nodded. She suggested dropping the Friday review; Kavita said, "Makes sense." Joel typed notes and said nothing. No arguments. Not a single question.
Her old boss would have called it a well-run team. Himani felt a small knot in her stomach instead. Last month Ramesh had argued with her for twenty minutes over a chart colour. Today he had agreed, without a word, to a deadline that doubled his load.
After the meeting she stopped by his desk with two cups of cutting chai. "Ramesh, when I said the new deadline, what did you actually think?"
He looked into the cup for a long moment. "Honestly? That it can't be done. But you'd already decided."

How long did the weekly meeting last?
It ended in eighteen minutes.
Why did the smooth, quiet meeting worry Himani?
Himani felt uneasy, a knot in her stomach, because Ramesh used to argue even about small things, so his silence on a big deadline looked like people had stopped speaking up.
What could Himani change in future meetings to invite real disagreement?
She could ask for objections before deciding, share her own view last, and keep asking people like Ramesh what they actually think.
How does Ramesh see the meetings, judging by his answer?
Ramesh feels decisions are made before anyone is asked, so he stays silent even when he thinks a plan will fail.
Our school has an university next to it. Is "an" right?

Our school has a university next to it.
Why: article ("an university" -> "a university").

Thursday night
I did it. I told them.
I'm Ankita, and for four months I've been pretending. Going to work, coming home, lying on the bed with the lights off. Not eating much. Crying in the office washroom twice a week. I kept thinking it would pass, that I just needed to try harder.
Tonight at dinner, when Papa asked how work was, I said, "I'm not okay. I haven't been for a long time. I think I need help."
There was a long silence. Then my brother Akash got up and came to sit next to me. Mummy held my hand. Papa said, "Why didn't you tell us?"
Akash helped me find a psychologist near the office, and I booked an appointment for Saturday before I could change my mind.
I'm scared. But telling them felt like putting down something I'd been carrying alone for months.

When is Ankita's appointment with the psychologist?
The appointment is on Saturday.
How did Ankita feel after telling the family?
Ankita felt scared but also relieved, like putting down something carried alone for months.
Why was Ankita's decision a sign of good judgement?
After four months of pretending, Ankita recognised the limit of coping alone, told family and booked a qualified professional instead of trying harder in silence.
How might Papa feel hearing that Ankita had been struggling for months?
Papa probably feels shocked and sad, wishing he had known, and wants to help now.

Minakshi had been a nurse on the children's ward for three years, and lately she was crying in the staff toilet between rounds. She snapped at a parent on Monday and forgot a chart on Wednesday. The next week she sat in the counsellor's office, hands clenched. "I thought asking would make me look weak," she admitted. The counsellor smiled. "It shows you know your limits. That's a strength."

Three years.
Why did Minakshi's hands clench in the counsellor's office?
She was anxious, worried that asking for help would make her look weak.

The power went out at nine, with Zeenat's project due at midnight and the laptop on eleven percent.
Zeenat lit the emergency lamp and flopped onto the bed. Across the room, Dilnaz, her eight-year-old sister, was happily colouring by lamplight.

Eleven percent, with the project due at midnight.
Why does Zeenat wish she were eight again tonight?
The deadline and the power cut make her feel trapped, so childhood looks like only crayons and cartoons, without the fears she once had. 😅
What sensible step does Zeenat take once she stops wishing?
She dims the screen to save battery and writes the conclusion first, working with the time and power she actually has.

To Dilnaz, eight comes with its own worries: a spelling test, shelves out of reach, rules about the shop, and fear of the dark.

It's been two months since the rumour about me and the stolen phone, and I finally feel like myself again.

The school handled it. The girl who started it had to meet the principal with her parents, and she was suspended for a week. There was a whole assembly about how forwarding a message is a choice, and that choice has harm attached. Some people who'd forwarded it came up to me afterwards and said sorry. Not all of them.

What I remember most isn't the punishment, though. It's Santosh. On the worst day, when I was crying in the corridor, he stood next to me and told people to move on. He walked me to the counsellor's room. He sat with me at lunch for two weeks when no one else would.

We were just classmates before. Now he's the person I call first.

— Elizabeth

How long was the girl who started the rumour suspended?
For a week.
How does Elizabeth feel about Santosh now?
Elizabeth feels deeply grateful and close to Santosh, now the first person Elizabeth calls.
What did the school's response teach the group?
That forwarding is a choice with harm attached, shown through the principal's action and the assembly.
How might Santosh have felt standing next to Elizabeth in the corridor?
He was probably nervous about standing out but determined to support Elizabeth.

Read this:

At the cricket academy nets, Vikas unzipped a brand-new bat cover, and the other boys crowded round. 'Did your dad buy it?' someone asked. 'No,' Vikas said, and his chest swelled. 'I did.' For five months he had saved his pocket money and his birthday and Diwali money, skipping the samosas after practice. Saurabh Sir came over and weighed the bat in his hands. 'Good balance. You chose well.' Then he said, 'Five months? That's patience. The same patience you need for a long innings.' Vikas grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. That day he batted slower and more carefully than ever and stayed in for twenty-three balls, his longest.

How long had Vikas saved?
Five months.
How did Vikas feel saying 'I did'?
Proud; his chest swelled.
What did Saurabh Sir connect saving to?
The same patience needed for a long innings.
How might the other boys see Vikas's bat?
With admiration and curiosity, crowding round and asking who bought it.

Read this:

In the Rampur government school, everyone knew Wasim as the one who ran the back of the class. He called Lalit "mouse," took his lunch roti, and laughed loudest when Lalit flinched. The other boys laughed too. It felt like being strong.
On Thursday, Lalit finally cried in front of everyone. Wasim laughed, then stopped. Something in Lalit's face reminded him of himself, last night, sitting on the doorstep while his father shouted and threw the pots again.
Masterji saw the whole thing. After class he kept Wasim back, not to shout, but to ask, "Is everything all right at home?"
Wasim's throat went tight. For a long moment he said nothing. Then: "No."
He told Masterji about the shouting. Masterji listened and said, "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault. I'm going to speak to the school counsellor today, and we'll help your family."
The next morning, Wasim gave Lalit back his roti.

What did Wasim call Lalit?
"Mouse."
What was Wasim feeling when Lalit cried?
He felt a sudden shock and discomfort, as Lalit's face reminded him of his own hurt and fear at home.
How did Masterji help Wasim wisely?
Masterji asked gently about home, listened, told Wasim it wasn't his fault, and contacted the counsellor that same day.
What is it like for Lalit to be picked on at the back of the class?
Lalit probably feels frightened and humiliated, flinching and finally crying in front of everyone.

Read this:

I work two desks from Abhinav, and this spring I watched Abhinav decide about moving abroad. Everyone expected an announcement, a farewell cake. Instead, Abhinav knocked on the manager's door one Monday and asked for a three-month stint at our partner office overseas.
"I want to see it first," Abhinav told me at the coffee machine. "Resigning is a one-way door."
Abhinav left in April. Photos arrived: a small flat, a rainy commute. In July Abhinav came back, tanned and quieter, and told us, "Good, but not settled yet." I can't tell whether that was relief or disappointment, and Abhinav has not said.
— Jaya

How long was the overseas stint?
The stint was three months.
What was Abhinav probably feeling about the move before asking the manager?
Abhinav was probably cautious and hopeful, wanting to see it first, since resigning is a one-way door.
What could Abhinav do now to decide whether to make the move permanent?
Abhinav could list what felt good and hard in the three months and compare it with what matters most before choosing.
What is it like for Jaya to watch Abhinav's decision?
Jaya is curious and a little unsure, unable to tell whether Abhinav's quiet return was relief or disappointment.
