messages.content:
Read this:

At the school civics club, Zubin, sixteen, held up his phone. “Look, a forwarded message says the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.”
Tejas, the club secretary, frowned. “Where's it from?”
“My uncle's group.”
They checked. The candidate's own printed pamphlet, which Tejas had collected, said nothing about laptops. The local newspaper's interview didn't either. The message had no source, no date.
Zubin felt his face go hot. He'd already forwarded it to three friends.
He messaged them: That laptop thing is not confirmed. Sorry.
In the mock election that afternoon, the club made a rule: every claim on the board needs a source.

What did the forwarded message claim?
That the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.
How did Zubin feel when he realised the message was false?
He felt embarrassed, his face going hot, because he had already forwarded it.
What did Zubin and Tejas do to check the claim?
They compared it with the candidate's printed pamphlet and the newspaper interview, and noticed it had no source.
How might Zubin's friends feel getting his correction?
They may appreciate his honesty and be more careful about forwards too.

Read this:

Wed, 11 pm
Did something today I keep thinking about.
Rukmini got picked as science fair lead instead of me. Instead of telling her I was hurt, I went to Farhan and Joel at lunch and said she only got it because she flatters Sir. Then I told Anita that Rukmini laughed at her project idea. (She didn't. Not really.)
By last period, Farhan and Anita weren't talking to Rukmini. I felt good for about an hour. Like I had a team.
Then I saw her eating alone by the water tap, and the good feeling went sour.
Why didn't I just say it to her face? Because if I said "I'm jealous", she might laugh, and then I'd have nobody. Easier to make everyone else angry for me.
Tomorrow: tell Anita the truth about the project thing. Maybe say sorry to Rukmini. Maybe.
Lokesh

What role did Rukmini get instead of Lokesh?
Rukmini got picked as science fair lead.
How did Lokesh feel after seeing Rukmini eating alone?
The good feeling of having a team went sour, and Lokesh felt guilty seeing what the stories had done.
What could Lokesh have done at the moment of being passed over?
Lokesh could have told Rukmini directly about feeling disappointed instead of recruiting Farhan and Anita against her; tomorrow's plan to tell Anita the truth is a good start.
What was the day like for Rukmini?
She likely felt confused and isolated, suddenly shut out by Farhan and Anita without knowing why, and ended up eating alone by the tap.

Read this:

In a school in Hamburg, Freya's turn came to read aloud, and she read with the soft accent of her home language. Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed. Jana laughed too, then looked at her desk. At lunch the group table filled up without a space for Freya. She stood with her tray, heat rushing to her face, and decided that tomorrow she would speak more like them and say less about home. That afternoon the class teacher noticed the empty seat beside Freya, stayed behind after the bell and said, "I heard what happened. It is not your fault, and I will speak to the class tomorrow."

What happened when Freya read aloud with the soft accent?
Somebody at the back mimicked it, and half the class laughed.
What is Freya feeling when standing with the tray and deciding to speak more like them?
Freya feels ashamed and hurt, with anger mixed in, and a wish to hide part of home to be accepted.
What turning point that afternoon helped Freya?
The class teacher stayed behind, said it was not Freya's fault and promised to speak to the class the next day, which showed that an adult had noticed.
What might Jana be feeling after laughing and then looking at the desk?
Jana may feel guilty and uneasy, having joined the laughter without meaning harm and now unsure how to make it right.

What wakes the speaker from sleep?

Lulled by the sound, I at last dropped asleep; I had not long slumbered when the sudden cessation of motion awoke me; the coach-door was open, and a person like a servant was standing at it: I saw her face and dress by the light of the lamps.
The coach suddenly stopping wakes the speaker. The door is open and someone who looks like a servant stands at it, her face and dress visible by the lamplight.

Read this:

At the Pongal fair in the village, bullocks with painted horns stood by the temple tank, and Charu wanted to see all of them. Her Appa, Chinmay, sat on the steps with the sugarcane. 'Go with your cousins. I'll be right here.' Charu ran off, then stopped at the first bullock, turned round, found Appa's white shirt on the steps, and waved. He waved back. She went further, to the balloon man, then ran all the way back just to touch his knee. 'You're here.' 'I'm here.' Off she went again, braver each time.

Where did Chinmay sit?
On the steps with the sugarcane.
Why did Charu run back just to touch Appa's knee?
Charu wanted a quick moment of safety; touching him made her feel secure enough to go further.
What did Chinmay's 'I'll be right here' do for Charu?
It gave her a fixed, safe spot to return to, which made exploring the fair possible.
What is it like for Chinmay watching Charu go further each time?
Chinmay probably feels proud and content, seeing his daughter grow braver while knowing she can always come back.

Read this:

Kashish, you asked for your podcast about my first job. I'm Leela, and I'll tell you honestly: I kept a ledger in my head.
Who helped me. Who I helped. Who could help me later. If a senior asked for help, I dropped everything. If a new joinee asked, I was "busy".
I thought I was smart. And I was fair, in a way. I always paid back favours. People knew I'd return exactly what they gave.
But when my father fell ill and I needed a week off, nobody offered to cover. They didn't owe me. I'd only helped the ones who could pay me back, and those people were busy too.
I sat in the washroom and cried.
Now I try to help because someone needs it. My ledger isn't gone, but it's smaller.

Who did Leela drop everything for?
Seniors who asked for help.
What was Leela feeling in the washroom?
Leela felt lonely and hurt, realising the ledger had left only thin relationships.
What did Leela change, and why is it wise?
Leela started helping when someone needed it, not only when it might pay off, which builds deeper relationships.
How might the new joinees have seen Leela in those years?
They probably saw Leela as busy and cold, someone who only helped people who could help back.

Read this:

I'm Saurabh, and in Class 10 we had a new physics teacher, Harish Sir, who talked to us like we were in nursery. "Now, children, who can tell me what a magnet does? Very good, beta, clap for him." In front of everyone.
When I asked a real question about why the Earth has a magnetic field, he said, "Such big questions from a small boy! Let's stick to the chapter."
Something in me went hard. After that I sat at the back and made comments. I stopped doing homework. I knew it was childish, but it felt like the only way to be taken seriously.
In Class 11, Mrs Kaur taught us. On day one she said, "You're almost adults. I'll expect a lot and I'll listen." When I asked about the Earth's field, she said, "Great question. Find three sources and teach it to us Friday."
I did. It was the best week of that year.

What did Harish Sir say when Saurabh asked about the Earth's magnetic field?
He said, "Such big questions from a small boy! Let's stick to the chapter."
What was Saurabh feeling after Harish Sir called it a big question from a small boy?
Saurabh felt humiliated and disrespected, and that hurt hardened into defiance.
What did Mrs Kaur do differently, and why did it draw cooperation?
She treated the class as almost adults, took Saurabh's question seriously and gave him real responsibility, so he had no need to rebel.
What would change if Harish Sir had welcomed Saurabh's question?
Saurabh would likely have felt respected and stayed engaged in physics instead of turning to comments at the back.

Read this:

Pooja had been avoiding her tax-filing paperwork for three weeks. Every evening in her Mumbai flat she'd look at the folder, feel a hot wave of guilt, call herself useless, and turn on the TV.
Her friend Kavitha, visiting, watched this happen twice. The second time, she said, “What if, instead of shouting at yourself, you just said, ‘Okay, I delayed. That's human.’ And then did five minutes?”
Pooja laughed bitterly. “Five minutes won't finish it.”
“It's not supposed to. It's supposed to start.”
That evening, Pooja said the sentence out loud, feeling silly. Then she set a timer for five minutes and opened the folder. She found the first form. Filled in her name, address, PAN.
The timer rang. She kept going for another half hour. The guilt was still there, but quieter.

How long had Pooja been avoiding the paperwork?
She had been avoiding it for three weeks.
How did Pooja feel each evening before Kavitha's suggestion?
She felt a hot wave of guilt and called herself useless, which pushed her to avoid the folder.
Why did the kind sentence and five-minute timer work?
Forgiving the delay eased the guilt that fed avoidance, and five minutes made starting small enough to do.
How does Kavitha see Pooja's delay?
Kavitha sees it as normal and human, and seems patient and caring rather than judging.
What is the avaroha of Raga Kedar?
The avaroha of Raga Kedar is: S' N D P M P G M R S.

Read this:

Nirmala: hey, any update on the vendor report? you said friday 🙂
Tenzin: yes sorry! the data came in late from finance
Tenzin: also the template changed so i had to redo the charts
Nirmala: oh ok. finance said they sent it wednesday though?
Tenzin: right, but it was the wrong format
Tenzin: and honestly the deadline was always unrealistic, nobody could do it by friday
Tenzin: plus i was covering for Arun on tuesday
Nirmala: that's a lot. is something else going on? no judgement
Tenzin: ...
Tenzin: i got stuck on the analysis and didn't want to say 😔
Nirmala: ah. want to go through it together at 3?
Tenzin: yes please

When did finance say they sent the data?
Wednesday.
What might Nirmala have been thinking as Tenzin's reasons kept piling up?
Nirmala seemed to sense that the shifting reasons hid something uncomfortable, so Nirmala asked gently instead of arguing each one.
Which choice of Nirmala's got to the real problem?
Asking "is something else going on? no judgement" instead of checking each excuse, which made it safe for Tenzin to admit being stuck.
Why might Tenzin have found it hard to say 'i got stuck'?
Admitting being stuck may have felt embarrassing, so a string of outside reasons felt safer than owning the struggle.
Brake or break: "Press the ___ at the red light."

Write "brake", the part of a vehicle that slows it down. "Break" means to damage something into pieces, or a short rest.
Examples: Press the brake at the red light. We took a short break after an hour of walking.

Squeeze this into exactly two sentences.

The football in the shop window cost four hundred rupees. Kamal received fifty a week. He borrowed a pencil and did the sum on the back of his hand: eight weeks. He drew eight boxes on a chart above his bed and coloured one at the end of every week.

The football in the shop window cost four hundred rupees, and Kamal received fifty a week, so he worked out on the back of his hand that it would take eight weeks. He drew eight boxes on a chart above his bed and coloured one at the end of every week.
In a village, the well sings every morning. Write the story of it.

In the village of Chandanpur, the old well sang. Nobody knew why. Every morning at dawn, a soft hum rose from the water, and the women who came to fill their pots hummed along.

One year, the well went quiet. The villagers shook their heads. A girl named Sunita looked carefully from behind the low wall and saw a round stone stuck in a little hole in the well's side, just below the rim.

"The song comes out of that hole," she said, "and the stone is blocking it."

She ran to fetch her uncle Mohan. He reached in with a long bamboo hook and eased the stone out, while Sunita pointed to the exact spot.

The next morning, the well sang louder than ever. The whole village stood around it, humming together, and the pots clinked in rhythm.

Read this:

Sunday: Lakshmi set four plates on the table out of habit, then stared at the extra one. Her mother Sangeeta quietly took it away, and Lakshmi cried in the bathroom with the tap running. Wednesday: In class a maths sum blurred and her eyes filled for no reason she could name. She bent her head and let the tears fall on her notebook. Saturday: She still went to her swimming class, because the routine was hers to keep. Afterwards she told Sangeeta, "I miss how it was." "I know," Sangeeta said. "Me too, in a way. We do not have to be okay yet." They shared an ice cream and let themselves be sad.

How many plates did Lakshmi set on Sunday?
She set four plates on the table.
Why did Lakshmi's eyes fill during the maths sum on Wednesday?
The passage gives no exact reason, but her plate habit and her later words "I miss how it was" suggest she was grieving the old family.
What helped Lakshmi cope during that week?
She kept her swimming routine, let herself cry, and talked honestly to her mother about missing how it was.
How might Sangeeta be feeling when she says "Me too, in a way"?
She probably misses the old family too and is sad as well, but she stays gentle and lets Lakshmi know there is no hurry to be okay. 🤍

Read this:

The rain was coming down sideways at the bus stop, and the group had ten minutes to make the school trip. "The 5:40 definitely stops here," said Arohi, loud and quick, and the others relaxed. Kamal watched her thumb hover over her phone, then slide it away. "How sure are you, actually?" he asked quietly, while the others argued about umbrellas. Arohi let out a breath. "I saw a timetable once. I think it's this stop." "What would you need to be sure?" "The board over there." They jogged to the shelter together. The board said the 5:40 used the next stop, two minutes away. They ran, laughing and soaked, and Arohi said, "Sorry, I sounded surer than I was."

Which bus did Arohi say stops there?
She said the 5:40 definitely stops at that stop.
Why did Arohi sound so certain at first?
She may have wanted the group to feel settled and to fit in as the one who knew, since her thumb hovered over her phone as if she doubted herself. She might also simply have trusted her memory.
What did Kamal do that helped?
He asked privately how sure she was and what she would need to be sure, so she could admit doubt without being embarrassed in front of the others. 🙂
How might the other friends have felt if the bus had been missed?
They might have felt annoyed or misled, because they trusted a confident tone that did not match what Arohi really knew.

Shorten this to two sentences.

Francis came in again today to talk about internships. He had applied to four but had shortlisted thirty-one, and he showed me his notes on each. He said he had turned down an offer from a design studio last week because a friend, Vijay, mentioned a bigger firm might open applications soon. That firm has not opened anything.

Francis, who has shortlisted thirty-one internships but applied to only four, came in again today. Last week he turned down a design studio's offer because a bigger firm might open applications, but that firm has not opened any.

For each inequality write "every value" or "no value".
a) 2(x + 1) > 2x + 1
b) x + 3 < x
c) 3(x - 1) >= 3x - 5
d) 4x + 1 <= 4x
e) 5 - x < 6 - x
f) 2(x + 3) <= 2x + 6
g) 2(x + 3) < 2x + 6
h) x - 7 >= x + 1
i) 3x - 3(x - 2) > 5
j) 6x + 2 > 3(2x + 1)
k) (2x + 4)/2 >= x + 2
l) x/2 + x/2 < x

a) every value
b) no value
c) every value
d) no value
e) every value
f) every value
g) no value
h) no value
i) every value
j) no value
k) every value
l) no value

Read this:

Kiran, sit. I'm Kavitha, and let me tell you about my second year in the hostel. Five of us prepared for the exam around one table, and the talk belonged to the loud ones. Lata sat with her notebook closed, and I saw her pen tapping. I could have carried on with my own point. Instead I turned and said, "Lata, what do you think? Only if you want to." Lata blinked. Then, slowly, she said the problem we had been stuck on could be solved the other way round. Nobody spoke for a moment. That night the table felt wider. Lata says even now that it was the first time anyone had waited for her.

How many people studied around the table?
Five, including Kavitha.
What was Kavitha feeling when watching Lata's pen tapping?
Concerned for Lata, sensing Lata had something to say but was not being given a gap to say it.
What choice did Kavitha make that changed the evening?
Kavitha set aside the point Kavitha was making and asked Lata, "What do you think? Only if you want to."
How might Lata have felt when the whole table waited for the answer?
Heard and valued, maybe a little nervous at first, since Lata blinked before answering slowly.

Read this:

Mentor's note, Dr Ankita, first-year mentoring, 18 September
Jyoti came to my office today, her third visit in two weeks, each time asking whether the admissions office double-checks ranks after joining. Today she finally said what she meant: she believes she got in through a mistake or pure luck, and that it will show soon. Her quiz scores are in the top third of the batch. When I pointed this out, she said, "Those quizzes are easy; the others aren't even trying." She compares herself only with the two strongest students in her section. She looked tired and kept twisting her ID lanyard.
What I did: I asked her to write down three pieces of evidence of her own ability before our next meeting, and invited her to the Thursday peer circle where seniors talk about their first year.

Where are Jyoti's quiz scores in the batch?
In the top third of the batch.
Why does Jyoti dismiss her good quiz scores?
Believing she got in by mistake makes any success seem like a fluke, and comparing herself only with the two strongest students keeps the gap looking large.
Which choices by Dr Ankita give Jyoti a way forward?
Asking for three pieces of evidence of her ability and inviting her to the peer circle, so she can collect facts and hear seniors describe the same doubt.
How might the seniors in the peer circle help Jyoti?
Hearing capable seniors admit the same first-year fear could make Jyoti feel less alone and less like the only one pretending.

messages.content: He keeps to ask the same question every day. Which part is wrong?

He keeps asking the same question every day.
Why: verb form ("to ask" -> "asking").

Read this:

At the swimming pool in Rotterdam, the class took turns for the floating test. Yara lay back, sank, and came up spluttering while the others watched from the edge. Someone laughed.
She climbed out, grabbed her towel and disappeared into the changing room. When the coach, Anders, knocked, she was sitting on the bench with the towel over her head.
"I'm so stupid," came her voice. "Everyone can float except me."
Anders sat on the other end of the bench, not too close. "You sank today. That's one try at one skill. It doesn't make you stupid."
The towel stayed on.
"Next week you can practise in the shallow end with me first, before anyone watches. Deal?"
After a long pause, the towel slipped down a little. "Only if nobody's looking," Yara said.

Where did Anders find Yara after the test?
In the changing room, sitting on the bench with the towel over her head.
What does the towel over Yara's head suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she felt ashamed and humiliated, wanting to hide after sinking in front of the class; saying "I'm so stupid" shows she blamed herself, not just the try.
Which part of Anders's response helped, and why?
Separating the one failed try from who Yara is, and offering private practice first, helped because it gave her safety instead of more watching eyes.
How might the classmate who laughed see the moment later?
That classmate may not have meant much by it, but if they noticed Yara hiding, they might feel sorry for adding to her embarrassment.
A quiet village hears a night bird sing. What is that story?

In the village of Chandanpur, nobody ever heard birdsong at night. Then one summer evening, a sweet, trilling melody drifted from the mango tree beside the well.

People came out on their porches. Old Mr. Ghosh closed his eyes. Children crept out of bed and sat on the steps. The song rose and fell like water.

The bird, a small brown singer the children named Bulbul, had flown a very long way and was lonely. She sang because she had nobody to talk to.

As the villagers listened, a young girl named Rina tiptoed to the tree and placed a small dish of water below it. Bulbul sang louder. The song continued until the moon went down.

She stayed in the mango tree all summer, and the village slept peacefully.
I wish I am taller, then I can play basketball.

I wish I were taller, then I could play basketball.
Why: after "wish", use past forms: "were" and "could".
Narrate how a girl writes to the headmaster asking for a swing in the playground.

Zarina was tired of waiting in the long line for the one slide, so she wrote a polite letter to the headmaster, Mr. Roy. "Dear Sir, we need a swing. Many children wait long and get angry. A swing would make break time happy. Yours sincerely, Zarina." She slipped it under his door. Nothing happened for a week. She sighed and told her friend Boman, who shrugged. Then, on a Monday morning, a team of workers arrived with long poles and chains. By afternoon, a bright blue swing hung from the old tree. Mr. Roy, standing beside it, held up her letter and called her up to cut the ribbon. She swung for the entire break.

Read this:

Kalyani, you asked why I quit the morning coaching after two months, so here's the story. I'm Ramesh.
In Class 9, I noticed every student picked for the science olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching near the bus depot. All five. I thought, that's it, the coaching is the magic. I begged my parents, and they cut other expenses to pay for it.
Two months of waking at five. My marks didn't move. And sitting there, I saw who the others were. Kids who read science books for fun. Kids whose parents could drive them there at dawn. They'd have been picked anyway. The coaching didn't make them keen; keen kids chose the coaching.
I'm not saying coaching never helps. But I saw two things happening together and decided one caused the other. Now, whenever someone says all the toppers do something, I ask: or do toppers just tend to do it?

How many students picked for the olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching?
All five students picked for the science olympiad went to the six a.m. coaching.
Why did the coaching seem like 'the magic' to Ramesh?
Ramesh felt excited and hopeful because all five olympiad students went there, and such a neat match felt like proof of cause.
What question does Ramesh now ask, and why is it useful?
Ramesh asks whether toppers just tend to do something, which checks whether keen students choose the coaching rather than the coaching making them top.
How might Ramesh's parents have felt about the two months?
They may have felt hopeful at first and then quietly disappointed, having cut other expenses for a change that didn't come.
The lift in our building is out of order again, and I live on the fifth floor.
That's a long climb with bags. Is there a way to carry things in smaller loads?
I can split the shopping, but it takes many trips.
Then make a game of it. Take the heaviest bag first, rest on landings, and bring the lighter ones afterwards. Stretching your legs a bit afterwards helps too.

Read this:

Last year Chaitanya, my closest friend since Class 3, told the whole cricket team that I was seeing a tutor for maths because I was failing. I'd told him that on a bike ride.
I went home and I planned. I knew things about him. About his older sister. About why he really moved schools in Class 6. For three nights I imagined saying all of it in the team group, word by word, and watching his face.
On the fourth night I told my cousin Aditi everything, the rage and the plan. She didn't lecture. She just said, "And after that, Siddharth, who would you be?"
I knew the answer. The second one who betrayed.
I didn't do it. I felt the fury, I said it out loud to her, and I let it burn out. Chaitanya and I aren't close anymore. But I can look at myself, which feels like enough.

Where did Siddharth tell Chaitanya about the maths tutor?
On a bike ride.
How did Siddharth feel after Chaitanya told the team?
Siddharth felt furious and betrayed, spending three nights imagining revenge in the team group.
What helped Siddharth decide not to take revenge?
Siddharth told cousin Aditi about the rage and plan, and her question made Siddharth see revenge would make Siddharth a second betrayer.
How might Aditi see Siddharth's plan?
Aditi seems concerned but calm, choosing a question instead of a lecture so Siddharth can reach the decision alone.

Read this:

Keerthana, my mother used to say a joke has a direction, up or down. When I was young, our neighbourhood theatre group performed a street play where a tiny clerk mocked the corrupt officer, and the whole lane laughed until they wept. That was aimed up, at power. Then a group of boys drew a cartoon of the tea seller's limp and passed it around. That was aimed down, at someone who couldn't answer. I felt sick, though I laughed once, I'm ashamed to say. Today your memes are quicker, but the question stays the same: who is it laughing at, and can they take it? Also, put a note if it's satire, because not everyone knows. Ayesha.

What did the tiny clerk do in the street play?
The tiny clerk mocked the corrupt officer.
How did the narrator feel about the cartoon of the tea seller?
Ayesha felt sick, and ashamed of having laughed once, because the joke was aimed at someone who could not answer. It was mockery of a vulnerable person.
What two questions does Ayesha suggest asking about a meme?
Who the meme is laughing at, and whether that person can take it, plus adding a note when it is satire.
How might the tea seller have felt about the cartoon?
The tea seller may have felt hurt and embarrassed that people made fun of the limp.

Read this:

The first time I sat the chartered accountancy exam, I failed two papers. I'm Jahnavi. Before every paper I had a ritual: a cup of ginger tea, the same playlist, my grandmother's small silver coin in my pocket. My friend Anjali once asked me, "What else do you do to prepare?" I said, "Study, obviously." But honestly, the ritual had become the preparation. I felt ready because I felt calm. After the result, I sat down and separated the two. The tea and coin stayed; they help me breathe. But I added a mock test every Sunday under exam timing, and I asked a senior to mark my answers and tell me exactly what was weak. The second time, I passed all papers. I still carried the coin.

What did Jahnavi add every Sunday?
A mock test under exam timing.
How did Jahnavi feel before the first attempt, looking back?
Jahnavi felt calm and ready, but that calm came from the ritual, not from real practice.
What made the second attempt different?
The comforting ritual stayed, but mock tests and a senior's feedback did the real preparing.
How might Anjali see the change?
Anjali would likely feel glad that the question was taken seriously and pleased to see the pass.

metadata.subtype: Approach: separates comforting rituals from the concrete steps that actually matter [Revision]

Yusuf, I heard you on the phone with your father just now. Can I tell you something from my own life? When I was about your age, my Appa retired and then just faded. He stopped reading the newspaper. He sat on the balcony till dark and barely spoke at meals. I was the one living at home, so I quietly took over: the bills, his tablets, the cooking, even reminding him to bathe. I felt I had become his parent, and I was frightened and guilty all the time, because I was angry too. My brothers in the city had no idea. One night I finally phoned them and said, "I can't do this alone." That weekend all three of us sat with Appa and said, "We love you. You don't seem yourself. Let's see Dr Rao together." He grumbled, but he went. It helped him, slowly. And it helped me more than I can say. I'm Uma, and I wish I'd called them sooner.

Where did Uma's Appa sit till dark?
On the balcony.
What did Uma feel while quietly taking over everything?
Uma felt frightened and guilty, and angry too, as if Uma had become Appa's parent.
What was the turning point for Uma?
Phoning the brothers and saying "I can't do this alone", which led all three to speak lovingly with Appa and take him to Dr Rao.
How might Appa have felt when all three children sat with him?
He may have felt embarrassed, hence the grumbling, but also loved and less alone, which is why he agreed to go.

messages.content: A case of water contains 24 bottles. A children's camp comprising of 4 groups purchased 13 cases for a 3-day camp. The first group has 14 children, the second group has 16 children, the third group has 12 children, and the fourth group has half of the number of the first three groups combined. If each child consumes 3 bottles a day, how many more bottles of water does the camp organizer still need to buy?

The first three groups have a total of 14 + 16 + 12 = 42 children.
The fourth group has 42/2 = 21 children
All together, the camp has 42 + 21 = 63 children.
In one day, the children consume 3 x 63 = 189 bottles of water.
In 3 days, the children will need 189 x 3 = 567 bottles of water.
The camp organizer has already purchased 13 x 24 = 312 bottles of water.
The camp organizer must buy another 567 - 312 = 255 bottles of water.
The answer is 255.

Saturday, Gwalior
We came back to the guest house tired and happy. Last week, when Mummy said we had only ten thousand rupees for the whole trip, my plan fell apart. I'd put the water park first, and Vandana-mausi found out the tickets alone were almost three thousand for all of us. So I sat with the paper again. The fort is nearly free, the museum is cheap, and the water park was really just for me. I crossed it out. Today we climbed the fort, and Nani found the old carvings she'd read about. At the museum Chotu pressed his nose to the glass in front of the swords. Nobody missed the water park. Not even me. Mostly.
Gargi

How much did Mummy say they had for the whole trip?
Ten thousand rupees.
How does Gargi feel about dropping the water park?
Gargi feels a small pang of disappointment, as 'Mostly' shows, but is mostly content because everyone enjoyed the day.
What else could Gargi have done instead of dropping the water park completely?
Gargi could have suggested saving it for a later trip, so the wish is postponed rather than lost.
What was the day like for Nani?
Nani found the old carvings she had read about, so the revised plan gave her something she cared about.

Read this:

Jahnavi, come here. You look upset since your friend got the scholarship. Let your Vandana Aunty tell you something.
When I was twenty-five, my colleague Rekha was chosen to lead the new branch. I had wanted it badly. When I heard, my face went hot. I wanted to tell everyone she only got it because the manager liked her.
But that night I sat on the terrace and said it plainly to myself: I'm envious. Nothing wrong with the feeling, but I won't act on it.
The next morning I went to her desk and said, "Congratulations, Rekha. You'll do it well." She hugged me. Then I asked myself: what does this tell me I want? It told me I wanted to lead. So I asked Rekha what she had done to prepare. Two years later, I led a branch too.

What was Rekha chosen to do?
Rekha was chosen to lead the new branch.
What was young Vandana feeling when she heard about Rekha?
She felt envious and hurt, her face going hot, and was tempted to undermine Rekha.
What was the turning point in Vandana Aunty's story?
The turning point was naming the envy on the terrace and choosing to congratulate Rekha, then asking what she did to prepare.
How might Rekha have felt when Vandana congratulated her?
Rekha probably felt warm and relieved, which is why she hugged Vandana.

I'm Minakshi, and in Class 11 I did an experiment on myself. My friend Pallavi said I was always on my phone, and I laughed. "I just check it." So she made me note every time I picked it up during a Sunday of studying. I lost count at forty. Worse, one "quick look" at a video at two o'clock ended at three. I didn't remember choosing to keep watching; the next video just started. I felt sick, honestly, and a bit cheated. After that I switched off autoplay and kept the phone in my bag during study hours. It didn't make me perfect. It made stopping possible.

At what count did Minakshi lose track?
Minakshi lost count at forty.
How did Minakshi feel after seeing the numbers?
Minakshi felt sick and a bit cheated, realising the videos had carried on without any choice.
What changes did Minakshi make, and why do they help?
Switching off autoplay and keeping the phone in a bag during study added stopping points, so willpower didn't have to do all the work.
How might Pallavi feel about the experiment's result?
Pallavi might feel a little vindicated but mostly glad her friend saw the pattern and changed something.

The week of Pallavi's sister's wedding was loud and full, and the power kept cutting out in the evenings. Nikita, staying with them, was supposed to revise for Monday's chemistry exam. She didn't open the book once. On Sunday night, in the candlelight, Pallavi asked, "Did you finish organic?" Nikita shrugged. "The chemistry teacher sets impossible papers. It's unfair. And it's just the half-yearly, it doesn't really matter." Pallavi raised an eyebrow. "You said the same about physics." Nikita laughed, but she felt a twist in her stomach. She knew she'd chosen mehendi and dancing over chemistry. Saying the paper was unfair made that feel less bad. "Want to do one chapter now?" Pallavi asked. "It's dark," Nikita said. Pallavi held up the candle.

Which exam was on Monday?
Chemistry.
Why did Nikita feel a twist in her stomach?
She knew she had chosen the wedding fun over studying, and underneath the excuse she felt ashamed.
What might help Nikita most tonight?
Taking up Pallavi's offer to do one chapter by candlelight, so she lowers the cost on Monday instead of just easing the shame now.
How does Pallavi see Nikita's excuse?
Pallavi seems unconvinced, pointing out Nikita said the same about physics and offering to study with her.
Meaning of "fresh"? How can I stay dry when I ride a bicycle in light rain? Ben ate 11 grapes and then 17 more. How many grapes did he eat?

1. Fresh means newly made or picked, not old or stale.
2. Wear a raincoat and keep your bag covered. Ride slowly, because wet roads are slippery.
3. That makes 28. Because 11 + 17 = 28.

Sunday night. Told Parul, my nine-year-old, about the move today. I was dreading it. I sat on her bed and said, "Parul, my new job is in another city. We are moving in June. You will go to a new school." I did not say "it will be fun, don't worry." I said I was a little scared too.
She cried. Then she asked, "Will I have to leave my best friend Meghna?" I said yes, and that Meghna and she can call every Sunday. She asked about her room, her books, the cat. I answered each question, even the ones I didn't know: "I'll find out."
She fell asleep holding my hand. I felt tired and lighter.
— Amandeep

When are Amandeep and Parul moving?
They are moving in June.
What was Amandeep feeling before telling Parul about the move?
Amandeep was dreading it and felt a little scared. Saying "I was dreading it" and admitting the fear to Parul show honest nerves.
What did Amandeep do that gave Parul the truth without overwhelming her?
Amandeep gave plain facts, said it was a little scary too and answered each question, even saying "I'll find out". No cheerful cover story was offered.
What might Parul have felt when asking "Will I have to leave my best friend Meghna?"
Parul was probably sad and worried about losing a friend. Hearing that they could call every Sunday gave some comfort.
I'm trying a new recipe for dosa batter and it didn't ferment.
Batter ferments best in a warm place. Was the room cool?
Yes, it was cold last night.
Then that is probably why. Fermentation slows when it is cool. Try leaving the batter in a warmer spot, like near a kitchen light or a closed cupboard, and give it more time.
How long should it take?
Usually eight to twelve hours in warm weather, and longer in the cold. Look for bubbles and a slightly sour smell.
Can I still use the batter now?
You can cook a small test dosa to check the taste and texture. If it smells wrong or has pink or green spots, do not use it.
What if it's too sour?
Overfermented batter tastes sharp. You can use it for a thicker dosa or uttapam, or mix a little fresh batter in. Next time, refrigerate when it has risen.

"Ritu, you keep saying people who complain at work are troublemakers. Let your Nani tell you about Joseph.
I was twenty-four, a clerk in the mill office in Coimbatore. One monsoon the bus drivers struck for a week, and the management passed an order: anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay. Half of us walked six kilometres every morning.
Some clerks tore the notice down at night. Others paid and cursed. Joseph, who sat across from me, did neither. He kept coming on time, wrote to the works committee with the strike dates, and signed it in his own name. I was sure he'd be sacked.
He wasn't. The committee gave a half-hour grace on strike days. And Joseph still stayed late every Friday closing the accounts, same as before. That's when I understood a person can love a place and still tell it where it is wrong."

What did the management order say about clocking in late?
Anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay.
What did Nani expect would happen to Joseph after the letter, and what does that suggest about her view back then?
She was sure he'd be sacked and worried for him, which suggests she then saw objecting as risky and even disloyal.
Which of Joseph's choices made the change possible, compared with the other clerks?
He neither tore down the notice nor paid and cursed; he wrote to the works committee with dates and his own name, which the committee could act on.
Why might Nani be telling Ritu this story now?
Ritu calls people who complain at work troublemakers, and Nani wants Ritu to see that someone can object openly and still be loyal.
Gail has some bills in her wallet which amount to $100. She has four $5 bills and three $20 bills, and the rest are $10 bills. How many $10 bills are in her wallet?

Four $5 bills amount to $5 x 4 = $20.
Three $20 bills amount to $20 x 3 = $60.
So Gail's $5 and $20 bills amount to $20 + $60 = $80.
Thus, her $10 bills amount to $100 - $80 = $20.
Therefore, she has $20/$10 = 2 $10 bills.
The answer is 2.

I've been thinking about why I lied about Pallavi's birthday party. I told Mummy it was a study group. The truth is, I knew what she'd say if I asked: "No. Too late. Who are these people?" She's said it every time since Class 8. So I didn't ask. I just wanted one normal evening, like everyone else gets, laughing and eating cake. Now she's found out, and I feel terrible when I see her face. But I also feel angry. Would she have said yes if I'd been honest? Never. In our house, the truth just gets you a quicker no. Being a daughter here means choosing between lying and missing everything.
— Himani

What did Himani tell Mummy the party was?
She told Mummy it was a study group.
What does Himani feel now that Mummy has found out?
She feels terrible when she sees Mummy's face, but also angry, believing honesty would only have got her a quicker no.
What could help Himani and Mummy at this stage?
Himani could tell Mummy the real reason, that she expected a flat no, so they can talk about making it safe to ask.
How might Mummy see the lie differently if she heard Himani's reason?
Mummy might still be hurt but could see that her automatic "no" made honesty feel pointless to Himani.
Boss ne email mein likha "Please advise." Kya karna hai?
It means "please tell me what you think I should do". The boss wants your suggestion or decision. Reply with a clear opinion, for example: "I suggest we go with option two."
Aur "FYI" ka kya matlab?
"FYI" means "for your information". It says the message is only to inform you, and you do not need to do anything.

Monday. The mock entrance test scores went live at noon. Tejas's friends compared numbers in the canteen. Tejas said, "I'll check later," and put his phone in his bag. He felt lighter for an hour.
Wednesday. Anirban asked, "So? What did you get?" "Haven't looked." "Bro, it's been two days." That night Tejas couldn't sleep. He imagined a score of zero, of ten, the whole class laughing.
Sunday. Anirban came over and sat on the bed. "Log in. I'm right here."
Tejas logged in with shaking fingers. 112 out of 300. Not great. But not zero. The weak section was clearly physics.
"That's fixable," Anirban said. "Physics revision classes start tomorrow. You'd have missed them."
Tejas let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

What score did Tejas get?
Tejas got 112 out of 300.
Why couldn't Tejas sleep on Wednesday?
Tejas felt anxious and full of dread, imagining terrible scores, because not knowing let the fear grow bigger than the real number.
What helped Tejas finally face the score?
Anirban sitting with Tejas while logging in, which made the news shareable and showed physics was the part to fix.
How does Anirban see the score?
Anirban sees it as fixable and is glad Tejas looked in time for the physics revision classes.

Nadia heard Dalia's key in the door at nine, two hours late again. Their flat in Lisbon smelled of the soup Nadia had made. Dalia dropped her bag and stood in the hallway, still in her coat, staring at the shoe rack. Nadia had planned to ask about the weekend trip to her own parents' village. She looked at Dalia's grey face and put the question away. 'Soup's warm. Bath's running. You don't have to talk.' Dalia's eyes filled. 'Sorry. I'm useless tonight.' 'You're tired. That's different.' Nadia texted her mother that they might come a week later. Later Dalia fell asleep on the sofa with her head on Nadia's knee. On Saturday morning she woke first and made coffee for them both, humming.

What had Nadia made for dinner?
Soup.
What was Nadia thinking when she saw Dalia's grey face?
Nadia felt concerned and decided the weekend question could wait, seeing that Dalia was worn out.
Which of Nadia's choices helped most?
Offering soup, a bath and no need to talk, and quietly moving the visit, gave Dalia space to recover without guilt.
What was it like for Dalia to be met with soup and no questions?
Dalia felt guilty and close to tears at first, calling herself useless, but being allowed to rest let her recover and wake up humming.

Monday. Imran's result came out, and Imran had missed the cut-off by a few marks. Jahnavi noticed Imran skip lunch and mute the group chat.

Wednesday. Jahnavi did not send advice. Jahnavi knocked on the door with two cups of tea. "I'm just here. No pep talk." Imran spoke for ten minutes, mostly about feeling behind everyone.

Saturday. Jahnavi offered one practical thing: "I'm going to the library. I can hold you a seat." Imran came and sat with a book, opening nothing. Later Jahnavi added quietly that if the heaviness did not lift over the coming weeks, talking with the college counsellor might help. Imran said, "Maybe."

What did Jahnavi bring on Wednesday?
Jahnavi brought two cups of tea.
What might Jahnavi have been worried about while watching Imran skip lunch and mute the chat?
That Imran was withdrawing and in pain, and unsure how to help without pushing.
What did Jahnavi do that helped more than advice would have?
Offered company, listened, and offered small practical help such as holding a seat in the library.
How might Imran have experienced Jahnavi's "No pep talk"?
As a relief, allowing Imran to speak about feeling behind without being told to cheer up.

Devika, come here. You were interrupting your friend again on the phone. Let your Preeti Dadi tell you something.

When I was ten, my best friend Kamla came to my house and said her father's shop had burned down. I was so eager to help that I kept talking: "Don't worry, my father will help, we'll give you money..." She stopped talking.

My mother took me aside. "Look at her shoulders," she said. Kamla's were hunched, her eyes on the floor.

So I went back and just sat. I didn't say anything. After a while, Kamla told me everything, how scared she was.

That's when I learned, Devika: listening is not waiting to talk. It's watching too.

What happened to Kamla's father's shop?
Her father's shop had burned down.
How did Kamla feel when young Preeti kept talking?
Kamla felt overwhelmed and scared, which is why she stopped talking and hunched her shoulders.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help Kamla?
Preeti's mother pointed out Kamla's body language, so Preeti sat quietly, which let Kamla share her fears.
How might Preeti's mother have felt watching her daughter?
Her mother was likely concerned and wanted to teach her kindly how to listen.

Note for my records, Wednesday.

I watched Afreen's first month managing Ravi, the new trainee, and I want to note what she did well.

On day one she gave him a single task, the vendor tracker, with a written list of what "done" looks like. She didn't give him five things at once.

When he made errors in the tracker, she didn't fix them herself. She sat with him and asked, "Where do you think this went wrong?" and waited, even when he was slow. I could see her fingers tapping the desk, so I think the waiting cost her something.

In week three he was rude to a vendor on a call. She took him aside that afternoon, told him exactly which words were the problem and why, and asked him to call the vendor back. He did. She also told him privately that his tracker was now the best in the team.

I'll recommend her for the team lead programme.

— Deepika, operations manager

What task did Afreen give Ravi on day one?
She gave him a single task, the vendor tracker, with a written list of what "done" looks like.
What does Afreen's finger-tapping suggest about her while she waited for Ravi?
It suggests she felt impatient and tempted to fix the errors herself, but she held back so he could learn.
How could Afreen build on her coaching for Ravi's next month?
She could slowly add one new responsibility at a time with the same clear definition of "done" and keep giving feedback the same day.
How is Ravi affected by Afreen's way of giving hard feedback?
He is told plainly what went wrong and gets a chance to fix it, while also hearing praise privately, so he can improve without feeling humiliated.

Early March. Hafsa wrote down every bite in a notes app now, adding up numbers in her head through maths class. Between periods she checked her stomach in the washroom mirror, sideways, then again, then again. The next Friday. At her cousin's engagement, Hafsa refused the biryani for an hour, then ate plate after plate so fast she barely tasted it. Afterwards she sat locked in the bathroom, shaking, feeling as if food had taken over her whole brain. Two weeks later. She knocked on the counsellor's door before she could change her mind. 'I think something's wrong with how I eat,' she said. Ms Sharmila listened to all of it, then said, 'Telling me this early took real strength, Hafsa.' With Hafsa's permission, she called Ammi into school that afternoon, and together they booked a doctor's appointment. Walking out, Hafsa felt scared, but lighter.

Where did Hafsa check her stomach between periods?
In the washroom mirror, sideways, then again and again.
What was Hafsa feeling after the engagement meal?
She felt shaken, ashamed and out of control, as if food had taken over her whole brain.
Why was going to the counsellor a wise step for Hafsa?
The counting and loss of control were warning signs, and speaking early meant an adult and a doctor could help sooner.
How does Ms Sharmila see Hafsa's knock on the door?
She sees it as strength, not weakness, and acts that day by calling Ammi and helping book a doctor.

Shankar found his cousin Akash at the tea stall outside the Chennai metro station, as usual after work. They had been meeting there for years to talk cricket. Today Shankar put his glass down.
"Anna, I got the permanent post. And I want to say something before we start on cricket."
Akash raised an eyebrow.
"In my twelfth-standard year, when Appa was in hospital, you came every night at nine and sat with me while I studied. You didn't even know physics. You just sat there so I wasn't alone. I think that's why I didn't give up. Thank you."
Akash looked at the road for a long moment. He cleared his throat twice. "Drink your tea," he said gruffly. But on the way to the train, he put an arm around Shankar's shoulders.

At what time did Akash come each night in Shankar's twelfth-standard year?
At nine.
What does Akash clearing his throat and looking at the road suggest?
It suggests he was deeply moved and a little embarrassed by the direct thanks.
What made Shankar's thanks specific?
He named the year, the nightly visits at nine, sitting there without knowing physics, and how it kept him from giving up.
What might the thanks have meant to Akash?
Akash probably never knew how much those nights mattered, and hearing it lifted him, as the arm around Shankar's shoulders shows.

In their Nairobi home, Wanjiru, five, kept asking when Guka would come back from the hospital.
Her father, Tomas, sat on the floor beside her. "Wanjiru, Guka died. His body stopped working. It can't breathe or eat or feel pain anymore. He won't come back."
"Is he sleeping?"
"No, it's not like sleeping. Sleeping people wake up. Guka won't."
She was quiet. Then, "Will he come for my birthday?"
"No, love. But we can remember him on your birthday."
The next morning she asked again. Tomas answered again, just as gently.

Where had Guka been?
Guka had been in the hospital.
Why did Wanjiru keep asking the same question?
Wanjiru was confused and sad, and asking again was how she tried to understand that Guka was not coming back.
Which of Tomas's choices helped Wanjiru, and why?
He used plain words, said clearly it was not like sleeping, and answered her repeated questions gently each time.
What was it like for Tomas to explain this?
It was likely painful and tender for Tomas, grieving Guka himself while staying calm and patient for her.

Dear Dadi and Dada,
I'm leaving this letter with the card I've stuck next to your landline, so you know why it's there.
Last month your neighbour lost money to a caller who said he was from the bank. It scared me. So Divyansh and I wrote three rules in Hindi, in big letters:
1. OTP kabhi kisi ko mat batana. (Never tell anyone an OTP.)
2. Shak ho to phone rakho, aur ghar par phone karo. (If in doubt, hang up and ring someone in the family.)
3. Inaam ke liye paisa kabhi mat do. (Never pay money for a prize.)
Below the rules, Divyansh wrote Papa's number and mine.
When I come on Sunday, let's practise once. I'll pretend to be a caller, and you say rule 2 and hang up on me. You're allowed to enjoy that part.
With love,
Francis

Whose numbers did Divyansh write below the rules?
Papa's number and Francis's.
How did the neighbour's loss make Francis feel?
It scared Francis, and that worry turned into a practical plan to protect Dadi and Dada.
Why would a practice call on Sunday help beyond the written card?
Saying rule 2 aloud and hanging up once makes it easier to do under real pressure, not just to read it.
How might Dadi and Dada feel finding the card and the letter?
They may feel cared for and a little amused, and more confident knowing exactly what to do when a strange call comes.

At the village school, Gurleen was explaining her plan for the science fair: a solar cooker made from a box and foil. Yusuf, eleven, kept cutting in. "No, use a bucket. No, make it bigger." Gurleen stopped. She folded her arms and looked out of the window. Yusuf noticed the folded arms and the way her voice had gone flat. He shut his mouth. "Sorry. Tell me the rest." She looked at him, unfolded her arms, and explained. He waited till she finished before he asked anything.

What was Gurleen planning to make?
A solar cooker made from a box and foil.
What did Gurleen's folded arms suggest?
She was frustrated and hurt at being interrupted.
What did Yusuf do that helped?
He noticed her body language, apologised and listened until she finished.
How might Gurleen feel after Yusuf changes?
More respected and willing to share her ideas with him.
In three tests Lakshmi scored 18, 31 and 19. How many marks is that altogether?
68. Because 18 + 31 = 49, and 49 + 19 = 68, so the total is 68.
If 4 metres of cloth cost ₹480, how much do 7 metres cost?
Seven metres cost ₹840. Because ₹480 divided by 4 is ₹120 a metre, and 7 times 120 is 840.

At the Monday assembly in the Indore school, Jagdish had to walk up the stage steps to receive the drawing prize. On the second step his foot slipped and he stumbled, catching himself on the railing. He got the certificate, walked back to his line and stared at his shoes, face burning. The whole school had seen. Four hundred children. They would laugh about it for the rest of the year. He didn't go to the canteen at break. At lunch, Noor sat down beside him. "Congratulations on the prize! Your drawing was the one with the elephant, na?" Jagdish mumbled, "Did you see me fall?" Noor looked blank. "You fell? When?" She had been worrying about her own speech in English class all through assembly.

What prize did Jagdish receive at assembly?
The drawing prize.
What was Jagdish feeling as he stared at his shoes?
He felt embarrassed and sure the whole school had seen and would laugh at him for the rest of the year.
What could Jagdish remember the next time he makes a small slip?
That most people, like Noor, are busy with their own worries and barely notice or remember other people's small mistakes.
What was Noor thinking about during assembly?
Noor was worrying about her own speech in English class, so she never noticed Jagdish stumble.

So, I'm Himani, and this is the story of the night I nearly wrecked our school fest. Mum, whose name is Pallavi, said no to the evening rehearsal because it ends after dark. I said she never trusts me, went to my room and slammed the door. It felt good for about a minute. Then I heard her in the kitchen, not eating. The next morning I said, "I really need this rehearsal, it's the only time the whole group can practise. And I get that it's the road that scares you, not me." She looked surprised. I offered to share my location, message her when I left, and travel home with two friends. She said yes for the first three days and that we'd talk again after. Honestly, that was fair. 🙂

Why did Pallavi say no to the evening rehearsal?
She said no because the rehearsal ends after dark.
What was Himani feeling when Himani slammed the door, and what changed by morning?
Himani felt controlled and angry, but hearing Pallavi not eating in the kitchen made Himani see the fear behind the rule, so Himani came back to talk calmly.
Which parts of Himani's morning conversation would you copy?
Himani stated the need, named Pallavi's worry about the road, and offered conditions such as sharing a location and travelling home with friends.
How might Pallavi have felt when Himani said it was the road that scares her?
She probably felt surprised and relieved to be understood, because Himani was answering her fear and not only fighting the rule.

'You saw what they wrote under my photo,' Siddharth said at the corridor window.
Binita shifted her bag. 'Yeah. It's stupid.'
'It's every day. "Stick insect." "Lipstick boy." Forty people laughing.'
'Honestly? You make it worse. You react. If you just didn't care, they'd stop.'
'So it's my fault?'
'I didn't say that. Just... toughen up a bit. Don't be so sensitive.'
Siddharth looked at her for a long moment. 'You're my friend. You didn't say anything in the group.'
Binita opened her mouth, then closed it. Her face felt hot. 'I didn't want them to start on me,' she said finally, very quietly.
'I know.'
Silence. Then Binita said, 'Come on. Ms Ahuja's free now.'
In the counsellor's room, Ms Ahuja listened to both of them, thanked Siddharth for telling her, said none of it was his fault, and said she would speak to the class teacher and his parents before the end of the day.

What names were written under Siddharth's photo?
They wrote "Stick insect" and "Lipstick boy".
Why did Binita tell Siddharth not to be so sensitive?
Binita felt uncomfortable and scared of being targeted too, so making Siddharth responsible eased her guilt about staying silent.
What did Binita do that turned things around?
She admitted why she had stayed quiet and took Siddharth to the counsellor, who acted the same day.
What is it like for Siddharth to hear 'toughen up' from a friend?
It hurts; he feels blamed and alone, which is why he points out that she said nothing in the group.

Sleeping over at Simar's house.

She felt shock and then deep hurt, shaking on her daughter's bed.

She could take time to calm down, and then talk with her daughter to learn why she lied, instead of letting doubt spread to everything.
What might Jasleen's daughter be experiencing if she finds out her mother knows?
She would probably feel scared and guilty, and worried about losing her mother's trust.

Anyone could bring a problem, a missed deadline or a shortcut someone was tempted by, and whoever flagged the most useful one got first pick of the samosas and a mention in the company newsletter.
Today Ganga raised her hand. 'The new partner wants us to skip two identity checks to sign up clients faster.'

"Ankita, you've been quiet all week. What's wrong?"
"Nothing, Sumit bhaiya."
"You haven't eaten your dinner."
Ankita pushed her plate away. "I lost my savings. All of it. Someone in my office group said a small company's share would triple. I put everything in. It crashed."
Sumit sat down beside her. "How much?"
"Enough. I feel so stupid. I didn't tell anyone for three weeks."
"You're not stupid. Lots of people lose money on tips. What's stupid is hiding it and trying again to win it back."
"I was thinking about that, honestly."
"Don't. First, stop. Then let's write down what happened: who gave the tip, what you checked, what you didn't."
"And then?"
"Then we rebuild. Slowly. Sit with a proper adviser before investing anything again. Can I tell Maa?"

Three weeks.
What was Ankita feeling about the loss?
She felt stupid and ashamed, hiding it for three weeks and even thinking of trying again to win it back.
What steps did Sumit suggest?
Stopping, writing down what happened, rebuilding slowly with a proper adviser, and telling Maa together.
How might Sumit bhaiya see Ankita's silence?
He was worried by her quietness and not eating, and sees the hiding as more dangerous than the loss itself.

Thursday in the college lab, Samir's juniors crowded around his laptop again. "Your code never breaks," one said. Samir laughed and scrolled to the version that had crashed three times last week. "Look at this mess. I just don't show it." Across the room his classmate Shalini, who had barely spoken to him all term, turned her chair away when he greeted her. He went over recent weeks in his head once: no quarrel, no favour left unreturned. He shrugged and stopped waving at her. That evening he posted the club's result on a public page, and by midnight strangers were mocking his photo and the team. He did not answer a single one. He saved the worst comments in a folder, blocked the accounts, and phoned his roommate, who told him to come and eat. Harish, who sat beside him in class and had beaten him in every test, passed over a marked paper with a higher score. Samir felt his jaw tighten, then asked how Harish had solved the last question. He copied the method into his notebook, and next week he lent Harish his spare charger when the lab socket failed.

What did Samir save in a folder?
He saved the worst comments in a folder.
How did Samir's response to the strangers online differ from his response to Shalini turning her chair away?

With the strangers he did not answer, saved the comments, blocked the accounts and leaned on his roommate; with Shalini he thought once about whether he had done wrong and then stopped waving at her, so in neither case did he keep chasing approval.
How was Samir feeling when Harish passed him the paper with the higher score?
His jaw tightened, so he felt stung and a little envious, but he turned that into curiosity about Harish's method.
What could Samir keep doing so his juniors' praise does not inflate him?
He can keep showing them his crashed versions and admitting his flaws, as he did when he scrolled to the messy code. 🙂

It suggests Meenal felt deeply respected by Rekha's restraint, and that the friendship meant a great deal to her.

In the thick December fog, the school bus in Shillong was late again, crawling up the hill with its lights on.
"Test today," Joseph groaned to Rajni as they waited, stamping their cold feet. "Every time the bus is late, Ma'am gives a surprise test. Three times already."
"Every time?"
"Monday, Monday and Monday. The bus was late all three. So the late bus makes her cross, and she gives tests."
Rajni wiped her glasses. "What day is it today?"
"Monday."
"And why is the bus late on Mondays?"
Joseph thought. "The driver takes the market road. Market day."
"And when does Ma'am give tests?"
"...On Mondays. She says weekends make us forget." He frowned at the fog. "So it's Monday doing both things."
The bus finally arrived, twenty minutes late. There was a test.

Why is the bus late on Mondays?
The driver takes the market road on Mondays because it is market day.

Joseph was grumpy and convinced, because three late buses matched three surprise tests, so the two things seemed linked.

On the main road of their small town near Nashik, Shreya's scooter and a tempo met at the turn by the temple. Neither was going fast, but a cyclist caught between them fell and lay still near the drain.

Who called 112 for the cyclist?

What would you change first in how Shreya reacted?

How might Zeenat have felt when Shreya didn't hear her?

She accepted the no-jinx rule lightly but reminded Himani that she had prepared, putting the credit on her effort.

Macy and Piper went to the batting cages. Each token gets you 15 pitches. Macy used 11 tokens and Piper used 17. Macy hit the ball 50 times. Piper hit the ball 55 times. How many pitches did Macy and Piper miss altogether?

Macy used 11 tokens which are worth 15 pitches each, so 11 tokens x 15 pitches = 165 pitches.
Piper used 17 tokens x 15 pitches = 255 pitches.
Together, Macy and Piper received 165 + 255 = 420 pitches.
Macy hit the ball 50 times + Piper's 55 hits = 105 total hits.
Of the 420 pitches - 105 total hits = 315 misses.
The answer is 315.

In a car dealership, Fiona worked for 40 hours a week, John for 30 hours, and Jeremy for 25 hours. If the employees are paid $20 per hour, how much money does their boss spend paying all of them every month?

Fiona earns 40 hours/week * $20/hour = $800/week
So she earns $800/week * 4 weeks/month = $3200/month
John earns 30 hours/week * $20/hour = $600/week
So he earns $600/week * 4 weeks/month = $2400/month
Jeremy earns 25 hours * $20/hour = $500/week
So he earns $500/week * 4 weeks/month = $2000/month
Overall their boss has to spend $3200/month + $2400/month + $2000/month = $7600/month
The answer is 7600.

messages.content: Jim spends 8 hours scuba diving.  In that time he finds a treasure chest with 100 gold coins in it.  He also finds 2 smaller bags that have half as much gold each.  How much gold does he find per hour?

The smaller bags each have 100/2=50 gold coins each
So in total, they have 50*2=100 coins
So he found 100+100=200 coins
So he finds 200/8=25 coins an hour
The answer is 25.
We got a neem sapling from school and I'm supposed to plant it at home. We have a small yard.
Neem is a good choice. It grows strong in hot weather. Pick a spot that gets sun most of the day, and leave enough space because it grows into a big tree.
How big is big?
Neem trees can become very tall, with wide branches. In a small yard it may be better to plant it near the boundary wall, or give it to a school, park or neighbour with more room.
Oh. Maybe I'll ask the park near us.
That is a kind idea. Check with whoever looks after the park first, and water it well in the early days.
Why does it feel good to finish a hard task?
Finishing gives a sense of pride. Because the effort paid off, and the mind rewards us with a good feeling that makes us want to try difficult things again.

Indu didn't laugh. She crouched beside him. "You heard a whoosh? That sounds scary. Shall we be detectives and look?"

"That's a bat," Indu said. "Bats wake up in the evening to catch insects. They're shy. They won't come to us."
Vaibhav held her hand tighter. "Detective bat-watchers?"
"Detective bat-watchers," she agreed. He counted three more bats all the way home.

At the cooperative bank branch in Bolpur, Anand had been nodding at everything his manager, Anirban-da, said for three months. Anirban-da had taught him to count notes fast and to speak gently to worried farmers, and Anand respected him too much to disagree.
But the new token system was a mess. Old men waited two hours in the sun while the queue at the counter jumped. Anand saw it every morning and said nothing, because Anirban-da had set it up.
On Friday, after closing, he went to the manager's desk with a sheet of paper. "Da, can I say something about the tokens? In the mornings the farmers wait in the sun. Last Saturday, when you were away, I tried a numbered list in a notebook at the door. The queue moved faster. Can I show you?"
Anirban-da read it, frowning, then nodded slowly. "Why didn't you tell me this three months ago?"
"I didn't want to seem like I was correcting you."
"Correct me with a solution anytime," he said. "Start Monday."

Where was the cooperative bank branch?
In Bolpur.
Why had Anand kept quiet about the token system?
He respected Anirban-da so much that he felt uneasy disagreeing and didn't want to seem to be correcting him.
How did Anand raise the problem well?
After closing, respectfully, with a sheet showing a solution he had already tested.
How does Anirban-da see Anand's suggestion?
He welcomes it, wishes he had heard it sooner, and invites correction with solutions anytime.

Wednesday night.

Vishal called again. Third time this year. "Bhai, just need to crash at yours for a week, the landlord's being difficult." Last time a week became a month, and he left my fridge empty and my scooter with a flat tyre.

Before that: "Bhai, lend me eight thousand till Friday." Friday was in March.

When did he last call just to ask how I am? I honestly can't remember. When Papa was ill, he sent a thumbs-up.

I felt the old guilt rise, the voice saying a good friend never says no. Then I felt tired. Used, really.

So I said it, short: "Not this time, Vishal. I can't have anyone stay." He waited for the reasons. I didn't give any. He said, "Okay, wow," and hung up.

I'm Jatin, and I'm allowed to have a small, quiet flat. I'll still wish him on his birthday. But a friend who only calls for favours isn't much of a friend.

How long did Vishal's last one-week stay actually last?
It lasted a month.
How did Jatin feel after Vishal's call?
Jatin felt the old guilt at first, then tired and used.
What would you tell Jatin about the way he said no?
He said no briefly and kindly without long explanations, and still kept the door open for ordinary friendship.
How did Vishal react to Jatin's no?

So both consume 2 x 2 = 4 pounds of food.

messages.content: If Joe spent 1/9 of his pocket money of $450 on chocolates and 2/5 on fruits, how much money does he have left?

Joe spent 1/9 * $450 = $50 on chocolate.
Joe spent 2/5 * $450 = $180 on fruits.
Joe has $450 - $50 - $180 = $220 left.
The answer is 220.

An internship shows work experience, and a language course shows that you can learn new skills. Which fits your career plans better?
I want to work in tourism.
In that case, either could help, but French can be a plus in that field. Check if a tourism internship is available and whether it's in your city.
The internship is paid a little.
That's a fair point to consider alongside what you'd learn. Talk to a senior or a career advisor at college to compare them.
I'll ask my department tomorrow.
Good. Take both options with you, and listen to what they say.

Before: On Monday, in the hostel corridor, Preeti congratulated Uma on getting into the research programme. "You're lucky the quota helped," she added cheerfully. Uma's smile flickered. During: On Wednesday, Uma knocked on Preeti's door. "Can I say something? What you said about the quota. I got in on my marks. It came across like I didn't earn it." Preeti felt her face flame. "I didn't mean it like that! I was trying to be happy for you!" She heard herself getting louder and stopped. "Sorry. Go on." Uma explained. Preeti listened, arms folded, then unfolded them. "I'm sorry. That was a bad assumption." After: The following week, Preeti congratulated a friend on an exam result and said only, "Well done. You worked so hard."

The research programme.

Preeti felt embarrassed, defensive and misjudged, her face flaming and her voice rising before she stopped herself.
What went right in how Preeti handled it on Wednesday?
She stopped defending herself, let Uma finish, and apologised for the assumption without asking Uma to comfort her.

The monsoon ferry to Divar was already ten minutes late, and the skipper, Hemant, wanted to go before the next squall. Shraddha, twenty-five, the ferry's engineer for two years, stood by the engine hatch and frowned. The rumble sounded... off. Not louder, not quieter. Just wrong, somehow. "It's running," Hemant called. "Let's move." "Give me four minutes," she said. "I can't tell you why yet." Omkar, the deckhand, rolled his eyes and held the rope. Rain was coming sideways. Shraddha climbed down with her torch and went along the lines she had checked hundreds of times. Near the filter, a small wet shine: a hairline crack in the fuel pipe. She showed Hemant. He stopped arguing. They radioed for the spare ferry, and forty passengers waited under the shed, grumbling, but dry and safe.

What did Shraddha find near the filter?
A small wet shine: a hairline crack in the fuel pipe.
Why did Shraddha ask for four minutes even though she couldn't say why?
Shraddha felt uneasy because, after hundreds of checks, the engine's rumble sounded wrong to her, and she trusted that unease enough to look before sailing.
Which choice made the difference here, and why was it wise?
Checking the lines despite pressure to leave, because it turned a vague feeling into evidence before anyone was put at risk.
How might the forty passengers have felt waiting under the shed?
They were annoyed at the delay, but they likely would have felt differently if they had known about the cracked fuel pipe.

I told him about the mango orchard and my grandfather's bullock cart, and after ten minutes I realised I was talking with my chin up. My accent is where I'm from, and I'm not ashamed of it. Asif said, "I'd take that over fake polish." Dhruv

One of them said, "Gaon wala!" and they laughed.

Dhruv felt ashamed and wanted to leave, with burning ears. After talking with Asif, Dhruv felt proud and spoke with chin up.

Asif moved his tray to Dhruv's table, told Dhruv to ignore the group and asked about the village, showing real interest.

As a classmate with an interesting home and story, worth including, and Asif prefers Dhruv's real accent to fake polish.

Ujjwal, you told me you nearly punched the boy who was teasing your friend. Let me tell you what I learned at your age.
In Class 10, there was a quiet boy in our school, Pratap, who stammered. Some seniors cornered him behind the canteen every day, mocking his speech. One day I saw them grabbing his collar.
My first thought was to fight. I was angry enough. But I remembered my father saying, "A fight makes two problems out of one."
So I did three things. I walked up and stood right beside Pratap, not in front. I said, loudly and calmly, "Leave him alone." And I told my friend Kamala to run for the PT sir. That was the turning point. He came within a minute.
The seniors were suspended for a week. Pratap and I walked home together after that. Your Lakshmi Paati never threw a punch. She didn't need to.

Where did the seniors corner Pratap?
Behind the canteen.
What was young Lakshmi feeling when she saw the seniors grab Pratap's collar?
She felt angry enough to fight, but remembered her father's words and chose calm.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Sending Kamala for the PT sir brought an adult quickly, while Lakshmi stood calmly beside Pratap without violence.
How might Pratap have felt when Lakshmi stood beside him?
Pratap probably felt less alone and relieved that someone was on his side.
What is the meaning of "to pull someone's leg"?
It means to tease someone in a joking way. For example: "Don't believe him, he is only pulling your leg."
A bird eats 7 berries a day. Samuel has 5 birds. How many berries do Samuel's birds eat in 4 days?

A bird eats 7 x 4 = 28 berries in 4 days.
So, 5 birds can eat 28 x 5 = 140 berries in 4 days.
The answer is 140.
When does the sweet counter at the market shut?
I don't know when the sweet counter shuts, as I can't see its hours. The shop sign or a nearby seller can tell you.

Deepak's mother frowned. "Why won't he play properly?" Nilesh's Aaji smiled. "He's playing. Watch." Nilesh sat beside Deepak in the sand while Deepak dug a hole, and dug his own hole next to it. Later he held out a crumpled bus ticket from his pocket collection. Deepak took it carefully. "Can I have the blue one tomorrow?" Nilesh nodded hard.

What was Nilesh reciting as he walked the edge of the pitch?
He was reciting bus numbers: three-forty, three-forty-one, three-forty-two.

It suggests he was happy and pleased that Deepak wanted another ticket from his collection, a sign he enjoyed their connection.

She calmly said he was playing and asked her to watch, instead of apologising for him or making him join the cricket.

Deepak may see Nilesh as a friend with interesting treasures, and want to keep sitting and sharing with him.

It was raining, so all the visitors squeezed into the tiny flat at once. Aunties held the baby. Uncles brought rattles and blankets. Nobody saw Darshan in the corner. "Send him back to the hospital!" he shouted. The room went quiet. His mother, Shreya, crouched down. "You feel left out and cross. That's allowed." Later, Shreya still read his bedtime story, just like always.

What did Darshan shout?
He shouted, "Send him back to the hospital!"
Why did Darshan shout that?
He felt invisible and angry, stuck in the corner while all the visitors fussed over the baby and his gifts.
How did Shreya include Darshan instead of scolding him?
She named his feelings, then gave him a role in front of the visitors and kept his usual bedtime story. 🤍

They may notice him for the first time as the big brother and feel glad to include him.

Vidya, come sit. You said Tanvir is being left out and it isn't your doing. Let me, your Nana Wasim, tell you something.
When I was ten, in Mhow, there was a boy called Shafiq who stammered. The rest of us decided he couldn't play gilli-danda with us. I didn't decide it, you see. Iqbal decided it. I just stood with Iqbal.
For a whole summer Shafiq watched from the wall. When my Abbu asked, I said, “All the boys agreed.” I was so sure that made it nobody's fault.
Then Shafiq's family moved away. On the last day he waved at me, only me, because once, long before, I had shared my guava with him.
I still think of that wave. Eight of us kept him out, but I was one whole person in those eight.

They kept him out of gilli-danda for a whole summer.

He felt safe inside the group; because all the boys agreed and Iqbal decided, his own part felt too small to count.

When his Abbu asked him; instead of saying “All the boys agreed,” he could have admitted his part and invited Shafiq to play.

Lonely and rejected, and the wave on the last day suggests he still hoped someone would be his friend.

Crashed means hit something with great force and noise. It is a verb, the past tense of crash.
Example: The kite crashed into the neem tree and got stuck in the branches.

Manoj, first-year, from Assam, has been quiet since he arrived. I often see him eating alone and on the phone with his mother late at night. Last week a senior patted his shoulder in the corridor, and Manoj jumped, then looked like he might cry. I didn't push him to talk more. I asked him to join the evening football, where the boys high-five and pile on each other after goals. I also asked him to help feed the hostel's stray dog, Kalu, who follows him everywhere now.
Today I saw him laughing on the field with his arm around a teammate. I'll keep checking on him.

Rafiq

He felt startled and suddenly emotional, almost crying, because he missed being close to people who know him.

Rafiq invited him into football, where friendly contact is normal, and gave him the dog to care for, instead of pushing him to talk.
How might Manoj's mother feel if she heard he was laughing on the field?
She would likely feel relieved that he is finding friends at the hostel, even while she misses him.

At lunch before the inter-house football final, Harsha had painted a green stripe on his cheek. "Green House will smash Red. Easy three-nil," he told everyone in the canteen queue. Red won two-one. By afternoon assembly, Harsha had wiped the stripe off. "I knew Green would lose," he said to Ayesha. "Their goalkeeper is too short. It was obvious." Ayesha stared at him. "You said three-nil to Green. In the canteen. You even bet me your eraser." "I was joking. I knew all along." Ayesha held out her hand. "Then give me the eraser." Harsha looked at the ceiling, then slowly dug the eraser out of his pencil box.

What score did Harsha predict before the final?
Three-nil to Green House.
Why does Harsha now say he knew Green would lose?
He feels embarrassed about his loud prediction, and now that the result is known, the short goalkeeper seems like an obvious sign, so the new story feels true to him.
What could help Harsha remember what he really thought before a match?
Writing his prediction down before the game and looking at it afterwards, so his memory can't quietly change it.
How does Ayesha see Harsha's claim?
Ayesha finds it unfair and a bit funny, remembering exactly what he said, and asks for the eraser to prove it.

Fresh mangoes sit in baskets.
Children follow the sweet smells.
Bags fill up with vegetables.
