I'm Wasim, and I sit opposite Sonali at work. At lunch Sonali was scrolling through a clip of a woman shouting at a shop clerk, with thousands of comments calling for her to be sacked and shamed. I watched Sonali type a comment, stare at it and delete it. Twice. Then Sonali said, "It's thirty seconds. What happened before?" and spent the rest of the break searching. A longer video turned up: the clerk had been curt for several minutes, and the woman was holding a crying child. Neither looked like the villain of a thirty-second clip. Sonali closed the app and posted nothing. I can't say what was in Sonali's mind, but the face looked tired, not angry.

How long was the clip Sonali first saw?
The clip was thirty seconds.
What might Sonali have felt when typing and deleting the comment, and how sure can Wasim be?
Pulled to join in but uneasy about it; Wasim only saw the typing and deleting and cannot be sure of Sonali's mind.
What did Sonali do that was fair, and what could follow?
Sonali looked for the earlier part and posted nothing, and could also decline to share the clip.
How might the woman in the clip feel about thousands of comments?
Humiliated and afraid, especially since her holding a crying child was missing from the short clip.

Amandeep, you asked if a heart on a message is enough when a friend is in trouble. Let me tell you about Gurcharan. We worked together at the bank for twenty years. When his wife fell ill, I heard about it in the group chat. I put a red heart under the news and wrote, "Thinking of you, veerji." Easy. Everyone did the same. Thirty hearts.
Two weeks later I met him at the gurdwara. He looked ten years older. He said, "So many hearts, Pankaj. Nobody called."
That hit me like a slap. That evening I phoned him and asked, "Can I come by on Sunday? I'll bring tea, we don't have to talk." He said yes. I went three Sundays in a row.
A heart is a good start, beta. But when the trouble is big, ask if you can bring yourself too.

There were thirty hearts.

Gurcharan felt lonely and let down; the hearts seemed thin during his wife's illness, when he needed real contact.

Then a call, or a message asking what would help, might have been better than going over, since a visit comforts only when it is welcome.

Stefan goes to a restaurant to eat dinner with his family. They order an appetizer that costs $10 and 4 entrees that are $20 each. If they tip 20% of the total for the waiter, what is the total amount of money that they spend at the restaurant?

The total cost of the entrees is 4 * $20 = $80.
The total cost of the dinner is $80 + $10 = $90.
The tip is $90 * 0.20 = $18
The total cost with tip is $90 + $18 = $108
The answer is 108.

The counsellor's room at the school in Jaipur had a small window and a box of tissues on the table. Ritu had come alone.

"Nishant said sorry last month," she told Devika ma'am. "He said he was jealous because he felt insecure. He promised to stop checking my phone."

He took her phone out of her bag and read her chats with her cousin.

Before, she feels scared and tired of being watched; afterwards, she feels a little lighter.

She listens, supports Ritu's choice to end it, calls her mother the same day, and arranges to speak to Nishant with his class teacher, so Ritu isn't alone.

"Madhav, you asked how your Dilnaz Khala got so disciplined. Truly, it was a calendar.
I was twenty-one, working at the bank, and I'd started and stopped exercising maybe ten times. Then my roommate gave me a big paper calendar from a sweet shop. I pinned it by the door.
Every evening I did my yoga or a walk, I made a fat red cross. Rest days, Wednesday and Sunday, got a green circle. Not a gap. A planned day off.
After three weeks the red crosses made a line, and I didn't want to break it. It pulled me off the sofa many times.
But I'll be honest. Once, with a fever, I did yoga anyway just to keep the line. I felt worse for days. After that I added a rule: a sick day is a green circle too.
So yes, mark the streak. Just don't let the streak mark you."

What did Dilnaz Khala draw on rest days?
She drew a green circle on rest days.
How did Dilnaz feel when she saw the line of red crosses?
She felt motivated and proud, not wanting to break the line, and it pulled her off the sofa many times.
What was the turning point in the story, and what did it teach?
Doing yoga with a fever just to keep the line and feeling worse was the turning point; it led her to count sick days as planned rest too.
How might the roommate who gave the calendar have seen the change?
The roommate probably felt pleased and surprised to see a simple sweet-shop calendar turn into a steady habit.

Coach's note, university badminton squad, Friday.
Vidya and Jatin (mixed doubles) disagreed on Monday about who covers the back court. Since then Vidya has not spoken to Jatin at all: no eye contact, turning away at drinks breaks, answering his questions only through me. The coach asked Vidya privately what the silence was doing, then agreed a plan for her to state her wishes in words by Monday, with an offer to sit in and a separate check on Jatin.

[School homework portal: comments on Samir's essay]
Pallavi Ma'am: Samir, I read your essay on the flood. Three things I noticed.
Pallavi Ma'am: 1) Every paragraph now starts with a clear point. In June they didn't.
Pallavi Ma'am: 2) "The water climbed the stairs like it had somewhere to be." That's a real image.
Pallavi Ma'am: 3) Only 4 spelling mistakes. Last month it was 15.
Samir: really?? i thought it was bad again
Pallavi Ma'am: Not bad. Better, in ways I can point to.
Pallavi Ma'am: Next one: 300 words, same topic, but add ONE paragraph that argues the other side. It'll be a stretch. I think you can do it.
Samir: only one paragraph?
Pallavi Ma'am: Just one. Send me the first two lines by Thursday and I'll tell you if you're on track.
Samir: ok. i'll try 👍

How many spelling mistakes were in Samir's essay this time?
Only 4, compared with 15 last month.
What does Pallavi Ma'am seem to want Samir to feel?
She seems pleased and hopeful, and wants Samir to see concrete proof of progress so he feels encouraged rather than defeated.
Why is the next task well chosen?
One extra paragraph arguing the other side is a real stretch but small enough to manage, and checking the first two lines by Thursday keeps it doable.
How does Samir react, and why?
Samir is surprised at first, having expected "bad again", and then willing to try, because specific evidence of improvement makes effort feel worth it.

Supervisor's note, district office. Swati, team lead.
On Friday a message spread across the town groups: "Old bridge has cracked, will collapse any day, don't cross!" with a blurry photo. Ojas, our youngest field officer, received it from eleven relatives. I watched how he handled it.
He did not forward it. He looked for where it began: the photo showed a different bridge, in another state, from 2019. He called the public works office, which confirmed the old bridge had been inspected in August and passed. He also noted that bridge failures like that are very rare here, while accidents on that same road are not.
Then he replied to his family group calmly: the source, the inspection date, and a request not to forward. Two uncles thanked him. He will brief the team on Monday.

When was the old bridge inspected?
In August.
What might Ojas have felt receiving the message from eleven relatives?
Ojas likely felt some pressure and concern, but stayed calm and curious enough to check before reacting.
What steps did Ojas take before replying?
Traced the photo to another bridge from 2019, called the public works office, and compared how rare such failures really are.
How might the two uncles have felt after Ojas's reply?
They likely felt relieved and grateful to have a clear source instead of fear.

messages.content: Gerald spends $100 a month on baseball supplies. His season is 4 months long. He wants to use the months he's not playing baseball to save up by raking, shoveling, and mowing lawns. He charges $10 for each. How many chores does he need to average a month to save up for his supplies?

He needs to save up $400 because 4 x 100 = 400
He has 8 months to earn this money because 12 - 4 = 8
He needs to earn $50 a month because 400 / 8 = 50
He needs to do 5 tasks a month because 50 / 10 = 5
The answer is 5.
Now you try: f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5 on [1, 5].
The answer is c = 3.

Tuesday, 11 pm. Jeevan's notes to self.
Messed up today. I copied the wrong delivery date into the client email, the 18th instead of the 8th, and Farhan spent two hours on the phone untangling it. My first draft of a message to him said "sorry sorry, I'm hopeless, I ruin everything." Deleted it. That's not an apology, that's asking him to comfort me.
What I actually sent: "Farhan, I put the wrong date in the Mehta order and it cost you your afternoon. I've called the client, confirmed the 8th in writing, and I'll add a date check to my sending list. I'll take the Thursday follow-up calls so you get that time back."
He replied: "👍 happens, thanks for sorting it."
Stomach still feels tight. But the fix is done, and I don't need to keep punishing myself tonight. Tomorrow: date check before every send.

Which date did Jeevan put in the client email by mistake?
Jeevan put the 18th instead of the 8th.
Why did Jeevan delete the first draft, and what was Jeevan feeling?
Jeevan felt guilty and ashamed, and saw that "I'm hopeless" would make Farhan do the comforting; the tight stomach shows the guilt lingered, though late-night tiredness may add to it.
What made Jeevan's second message a good apology?
It named the exact mistake and what it cost Farhan, showed the repair already done, and offered the Thursday calls, so the amends matched the harm.
How might Farhan have felt if he had received the first draft instead?
He might have felt he had to reassure Jeevan on top of fixing the order, leaving him more drained than helped.

"Binod, I watered the chillies twice this week and you weeded nothing. Again."
"Because you were at cricket, Lakhan."
"So let's fix it. A chart." Lakhan taped a sheet to the wall by the back door. "Watering: you. Weeding: me. Tick when done."
"Why do I get watering? It's every day. Weeding is only twice a week."
"Fine. Then I also do the compost on Sundays."
"...Okay. That's fair."
Two weeks later, exams started.
"Binod, I have maths tomorrow. Can you do my weeding?"
"Only if you do my watering on Friday. That's my science day."
"Deal. Write it on the chart so Amma doesn't think I skipped."
Amma, passing, read the chart and laughed. "My two boys manage the plants better than I manage the kitchen."

Where did Lakhan tape the chart?
On the wall by the back door.
Why did Binod object to watering at first?
He felt resentful, since watering is every day and weeding only twice a week.
What else could help the brothers during exams?
They could ask Amma to cover one day a week in exam season, so neither has to trade jobs.
How does Amma see the chart?
Amma is amused and pleased, joking that her boys manage the plants better than she manages the kitchen.

messages.content: Why does the moon seem to change shape each week? What is the name of my class monitor? What does the word "liberal" mean?

1. We see different parts of its lit side. Because the moon moves around the Earth.
2. I don't know it, since I can't see your class. Ask your teacher or a classmate.
3. "Liberal" is an adjective meaning generous, or open to new ideas.
Write a short rhyme for kids, four lines, about a rainy day.

Pitter-patter, drip and drop,
Rain is falling, will not stop.
Splash, splash, in my boots I go,
Puddles jumping, to and fro!

Gautam, come, sit with your Ammamma. Your mother tells me you've stopped going to classes since your father's surgery. I understand more than you think. When I was twenty, in Madurai, my own father fell ill in my final year. Money went to the hospital, my younger brothers needed fees, and I failed my chemistry paper. I stopped eating properly and told everyone I was fine. One day my professor, Mrs. Thomas, stopped me in the corridor, asked, 'Jaya, what's wrong?', and I burst into tears right there. She let me sit the re-exam later and found me two tuition students for some income. Each morning I made a small list: one thing for Appa, one for studies, one for myself. Not everything. Just three. It carried me through. You don't have to hold it all alone, kanna. Let people help.

Which paper did Jaya fail in her final year?
Her chemistry paper.
Why did Jaya burst into tears when her professor stopped her?
She had been hiding her strain behind 'I'm fine', and being noticed by a caring person released everything she had held in.
What helped Jaya keep functioning that year?
Accepting her professor's help, a later re-exam and tuition work, and a daily list of just three tasks: one for her father, one for studies and one for herself.
What might Gautam feel hearing this story?
Less alone and less ashamed, realising his grandmother faced similar pressures and that asking for help is allowed 🤍

messages.content:

Thursday. Big lesson today from Pankaj. We were preparing the monthly payroll run and a slide deck for Friday. I was about to spend the afternoon on the deck's animations. Pankaj asked, "What can't we undo?" The payroll: once it is sent, the money is gone. So we checked the totals twice, compared them with last month, and had a second person read the account numbers. The deck? Fifteen minutes, plain, done. It was bare but clear, and nobody complained. I realised I had been giving everything the same effort and finishing nothing early. - Irfan

What question did Pankaj ask?
Pankaj asked, "What can't we undo?"
How did Irfan feel about the lesson from Pankaj?
Irfan seems humbled and grateful, realising that everything had been given the same effort, so nothing finished early and the most important work got no extra care.
Which choice worked, and why?
Checking the payroll carefully and keeping the deck plain, because the effort matched the cost of failure.
Why does Pankaj focus on the payroll?
Because once it is sent the money is gone, so it needs the most care.

Clyde's four children wanted to go see their favorite band perform.  The tickets were expensive so Clyde made a deal with his kids.  If the average of their scores on their next math test was higher than 89, then he would buy them tickets to the concert.   June earned a 97 on her math test, Patty earned an 85, Josh earned a 100 on his test and Henry earned a 94.  What was their average math test score?

Together, they scored 97+85+100+94 = 376
There are 4 children so their average math test score is 376/4 = 94
The answer is 94.
In science class we talk about elements. What does the word mean there?

In science an element is a basic substance, such as oxygen, iron or gold, that cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means. The plural of this noun is Elements.
Example: Oxygen and hydrogen are both elements, but water is not.

In the girls' hostel at the Delhi university, Chandrika had started checking the news app every hour. Floods in one state, a train accident in another, a scam, a heatwave warning. At night she lay in bed scrolling until two, her heart racing. "Everything is falling apart," she told her roommate Anjali at breakfast, tired and pale. "The world is getting worse and worse." Anjali asked, "What good news did you read this week?" Chandrika stared at her. "None." "Nothing? Not the new metro line, or the village schools that got solar lights, or your own cousin's result?" Chandrika hadn't looked. The warden, passing by, suggested she keep her phone outside the room at night and talk to the college counsellor if the worry didn't ease. That night Chandrika left her phone on the corridor charging shelf. She slept until seven.

Until what time did Chandrika scroll at night?
Until two.
What was Chandrika feeling at breakfast?
She felt anxious and exhausted, convinced the world was falling apart because she only read bad news.
What helped Chandrika, and what could she keep doing?
Anjali asking about good news and the warden's advice to keep the phone outside at night; she can limit scrolling and talk to the counsellor if the worry stays.
How does Anjali see the news?
Anjali sees both bad and good news, like the new metro line and solar lights, so the world doesn't look as dark to her.

Read this:

Dear Lokesh,

I have been lying to you for weeks and I hate it. I didn't skip your birthday dinner because of "tuition". I skipped it because Papa's shop has had almost no customers, and I can't afford even the share of the bill. The same with the cricket trip, and the movie. I told everyone I was busy, and I felt like a fraud each time. I was scared you would all look at me differently, or feel sorry for me. Then I saw you looking hurt on Tuesday and thought I owed you the truth. Please don't tell anyone else yet. I'd like to still come to things that cost nothing, like the ground after school. Can we do that?

Shankar

Why did Shankar skip Lokesh's birthday dinner?
Because Papa's shop has had almost no customers and Shankar could not afford even a share of the bill.
Why did Shankar hide the real reason from the friends, and what changed Shankar's mind?
Shankar feared being looked at differently or pitied. Seeing Lokesh look hurt made Shankar feel Lokesh was owed the truth.
What was wise about Shankar's letter and the request at the end?
Shankar chose one trusted friend, stopped pretending, and asked to join things that cost nothing, keeping the friendships without lying or spending money the family doesn't have.
How might Lokesh feel on reading the letter?
Probably relieved to know why Shankar kept declining, and perhaps sorry for having been hurt. Lokesh may also feel trusted, and can suggest free plans.

1) Fix this sentence: "I read this book three time."
2) Why do people learn other languages?

1. Fixed: I read this book three times. Why: "Three" needs a plural noun (times).
2. To talk to more people. Because language opens doors to new cultures and friends.

Sunday night. Today I closed the app. Turned off the servers, sent the last email to users, and hugged Ankita at the doorway. It hurt more than I expected. Then, before the feeling could settle, I opened a notebook and wrote two pages headed What I learned. About the market: people wanted a cheap, simple tool, not our long list of features. About us: we never spoke openly when the numbers dropped, and we hired before we knew the need. I underlined three lessons. Ankita is going to help with the next idea: a small tool, one feature, and a check with real users in the first month. It is smaller. It feels lighter.

Uday

What did Uday write in the notebook?
Uday wrote two pages headed What I learned, about the market and about the team.

Uday felt hurt, more than expected, and also a sense of lightness about the smaller plan.

Uday could use them to build a one-feature version with an early user check, and talk openly with Ankita when numbers drop.

Ankita may feel sad about the closing but hopeful, and glad to help with the next idea.

Sports day was so loud that nobody could hear anything. Tenzin crossed the line first in the relay, and his teammate Binita jumped up with her palm raised. He slapped it in a high-five, both laughing. The chief guest came down to the track and held out a hand. “Well run.” Tenzin shook it, politely, looking her in the eye. Then he saw Binita standing a little apart. She didn't like being touched by strangers. When another teammate held up a hand to her, she gave a big wave instead. The teammate waved back, grinning, and the noise closed over all of them.

Who crossed the line first in the relay?
Tenzin crossed the line first.
What was Tenzin feeling when he slapped Binita's high-five, and what did the handshake show?
He was probably excited and proud of his run. The handshake with the chief guest showed politeness and respect, in a more formal moment.
What could Binita do when she prefers not to touch someone?
Offer a wave instead, as she did, which still shows warmth.
How might the other teammate feel when Binita waves rather than high-fives?
Probably fine with it, since the teammate waved back grinning. The teammate may see the wave as a friendly greeting in its own right.

Thursday night. First deadline missed today: the circuit board isn't wired. Feeling flat. Instead of blaming anyone, at lunch I sat with Divyansh and the others and asked why. Honest answers: I gave the wiring one afternoon and it needs three. The report looked small but takes an evening. We all guessed low for the hard parts and high for the easy ones. New plan: wiring gets three afternoons, Divyansh moves from decoration to help with wiring, the report gets two evenings shared between us. The teacher agreed to move the deadline by four days. Still tired, but not panicky. Small win: nobody was blamed, and everybody knows their share. - Sabina

How many afternoons does the wiring now get?
The wiring now gets three afternoons.
How does Sabina feel at the end of the diary entry?
Sabina feels tired but calmer and not panicky, and pleased that nobody was blamed.
What could the team do to avoid missing the next deadline, and why?
They could estimate the hard parts first and add extra time for them, because the missed deadline came from guessing low on the difficult tasks.

Divyansh may feel a mix of challenge and importance, since the harder job matters more to the deadline.

Kavitha had the flat's rental agreement in her bag when she sat down with her parents in their Chennai living room. Ira, her college friend, had already paid her half of the deposit.
"Why do you need a separate flat when home is fifteen kilometres away?" her father asked.
Kavitha had rehearsed a speech about independence. She set it aside. "Appa, what worries you about it most?"
He took off his glasses. "People will talk. And if you fall sick at night, who will be there?"
"Ira will. And I'll come home every Sunday. The commute from here is two hours a day; from the flat it's twenty minutes." She paused. "I know you've seen more of the world than me. I'm still choosing this. If it goes badly, that's on me, and I'll say so."
Amma looked at Appa for a long moment. "She's thought about it," she said.
Appa sighed. "Sundays. And you'll call if you're unwell."
"Promise."

How far is home from the flat?
Fifteen kilometres.
Why did Kavitha set aside her rehearsed speech?
She felt calmer and wanted to understand Appa's worry rather than argue, which showed her respect for him.
What made Kavitha's decision an adult one?
She heard Appa's reasons, answered them concretely, and said she would own the outcome if it went badly.
How does Amma see Kavitha's plan?
As thought through; she backs Kavitha by saying so to Appa.

a) Draw a triangle. Put a dot on each corner. How many dots?
b) Draw a pentagon (a house shape). How many sides?
c) Draw a semicircle. How many corners?
d) Draw a hexagon. How many corners?

a) 3
b) 5
c) 2
d) 6 (A house shape: a square with a triangle roof, drawn as one outline: /\ / \ | | +--+ 5 sides, 5 corners.)
John buys 3 t-shirts that cost $20 each.  He also buys $50 in pants.  How much does he spend?

He spends 20*3=$60 on t-shirts
So he spends 60+50=$110 in total
The answer is 110.

Monday. Hansa's chemistry unit test was two weeks away. "Tonight, one hour of revision," she promised her brother Asif. Then his new racing game came out, and she took the second controller. "One race." It was midnight when she looked up.
The next Thursday. Still no revision. Every evening the game glowed, bright and fun, and the test felt like something that belonged to a different Hansa, in a different week.
The Monday after. The test paper had four questions on equilibrium. She knew one. Walking out, she could already see the marks, and for the first time the test felt more real than the game. At home she asked Asif to change the console password until Friday.

How many questions were on equilibrium?
The test paper had four questions on equilibrium.
Why did the test feel as if it belonged to 'a different Hansa'?
Hansa found the game exciting right now, while the test two weeks away felt distant and weak, so it didn't seem like her problem yet.
What did Hansa decide at the end, and why could it work?
She asked Asif to change the console password until Friday, which removes the pull of the game while the next goal is near.
How might Asif feel about being asked to change the password?
Asif might feel a bit annoyed at losing a racing partner, but also trusted to help his sister.
What does abstain mean?

To abstain means to choose not to do something, especially something you would enjoy. It is a verb, often used with "from".
Example: Arjun decided to abstain from sweets for a month before his cousin's wedding.

Day 1. Hrithik listened to his flatmate Pankaj's plan for a birthday trip without any change in his face. Pankaj felt deflated and thought Hrithik didn't care.
Day 3. Pankaj asked outright, "Do you want to come or not? I can't tell from your face." Hrithik answered, "I'm very excited. I've been looking up train times. My face doesn't move much, but I do feel it strongly. Please ask me in words."
Day 8. They made a habit: Pankaj asked a question, Hrithik answered in a sentence. On the trip, Hrithik said, "This is the best day", his face calm, and Pankaj believed him.

What had Hrithik been looking up?
He had been looking up train times.
What did Pankaj feel on Day 1, and what was Hrithik actually feeling?
Pankaj felt deflated, thinking Hrithik didn't care, while Hrithik was very excited but his face didn't show it.
What habit did the two make to avoid misunderstanding?
Pankaj asks a question and Hrithik answers in a full sentence, so feelings are shared in words, not read from the face.
How might Hrithik have felt when Pankaj said he couldn't tell from his face?
He may have felt relieved to be asked directly and given the chance to explain his feelings.
Use simple words for a young reader: The vehicle halted at the junction.
The car stopped at the corner.
Can you help me think of a name for our class magazine? We are a group of eight.
Happy to help. A good name is short and tells readers what to expect. What will the magazine have in it, stories, jokes, news from school?
A mix of all. Stories, jokes and sports news.
Then a name that feels like a mix could work, such as "The Mixed Bag" or "Class Notes". Those sound friendly and suit different sections.
I like "The Mixed Bag". Our teacher Mrs Pillai will read it first, so it has to sound sensible.
It does sound sensible and playful together. Mrs Pillai will probably smile at it. Put the name in clear large letters on the cover with the class and year underneath.
Actually, my friend Rohan suggested "Eight Voices" because there are eight of us.
That is a lovely idea too. It tells readers that every member has a voice. You might use "Eight Voices" as the name and "The Mixed Bag" for the jokes page.
Oh, I like that. So what would go on the jokes page?

Under the heading "The Mixed Bag", you could put the best jokes and riddles from all eight of you, perhaps one from each person. Rohan's "Eight Voices" stays on the cover. Show both to Mrs Pillai before printing.

The power cut hit just as the evening rain got heavy. Vaibhav and Payal were sheltering at the bus stop, his phone at four percent. Payal was staring at the puddles. "Promise you won't tell anyone," she said. "My uncle's messages make me feel unsafe. He tells me not to say anything." Vaibhav's throat tightened. "Payal, I can't promise that. Someone has to know so you're safe." She cried a little. He typed a quick message to his mother, "I need to bring a friend home, it's about safety," and the phone died. They walked together through the rain, and the next morning he sat beside her in the counsellor's office and did not leave until she asked him to.

What was Vaibhav's phone battery at the bus stop?
His phone was at four percent.
Why did Vaibhav refuse to promise Payal that he would stay quiet?
He felt that her safety mattered more than the secret, so a promise not to tell could have left her alone with the danger. His tightened throat shows he cared and was afraid for her.
What did Vaibhav do that was helpful under pressure?
He sent a message to his mother, stayed with Payal and went with her to the counsellor the next morning.
How might Payal have felt when he would not promise silence?
She may have felt afraid or let down at first, and still glad that someone took it seriously.

messages.content: Eric sorted 150 colored pencils into 5 containers for his art class. Before class, another teacher brought him 30 more pencils. How many can he evenly distribute between the five containers now?

Before the extra colored pencils, he had 150/5=30 colored pencils in each container.
With the other colored pencils, he is given he now has 150+30=180 colored pencils
If you distribute them evenly each container should have 180/5=36 colored pencils
The answer is 36.

When Miss Kulkarni gave the new girl, Lalremsiami, the narrator's part in the Class 4 play, Damini, who had been narrator last year, clapped the loudest.
After that, Damini was everywhere Lalremsiami went. She walked her to the water cooler. She lent her the new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch. "You're SO good at reading aloud! You're the best in the whole class!" she said, three times before lunch.
Lalremsiami smiled, a little puzzled. "Thanks... you don't have to wait for me."
"I WANT to!" Damini said, too loudly.
At home in their Pune flat that evening, Damini coloured a picture of the play stage. She pressed so hard on the crayon that it snapped, and she threw both halves in the bin. When Mummy asked about school, Damini said, "I have a new best friend," and didn't look up.

What did Damini lend Lalremsiami?
The new twenty-four colour pencils she never let anyone touch.
Why might being extra sweet to Lalremsiami feel right to Damini?
Damini seems hurt about losing the narrator's part, but being jealous feels wrong, so loud kindness hides it even from herself; the snapped crayon hints at what is underneath.
What small step could Mummy take when Damini doesn't look up?
Mummy could sit with Damini and ask about the play, perhaps saying it's okay to feel sad about not being narrator, so the hidden feeling can be named.
What is it like for Lalremsiami to be followed everywhere and praised so much?
Lalremsiami seems puzzled and a little crowded, grateful yet unsure why Damini won't let her walk alone, which makes settling in feel strange.

messages.content: First snowball fight ever, for a polar bear cub: write it.

Nanu the polar bear cub was three months old when he saw snow properly for the first time. His mother led him from the den, and the world was white and sparkling.

He tasted it. It was cold. He rolled in it. He sneezed.

A second cub, Sila, scooped up a pawful and threw it at him. It landed on his nose, and he blinked in surprise. Then he scooped some himself and flung it back. He missed, hitting his mother.

She turned slowly. The cubs froze. Then she gathered a huge pile and dumped it on both of them, and they vanished in a cloud of white.

When the cloud cleared, two small bears lay giggling, flat on their backs, while their mother licked the snow off their ears.

Thursday
Got 12 in the English test. Of course. I'm Varun, and this is just who I am: bad at English, bad at exams, bad at everything that matters.
Jyoti said, "It was one test. You got 17 last time." But she doesn't get it. Last time was luck. This is the real me.
I didn't go for football practice. What's the point? I'd probably mess that up too.
Mummy asked why I'm so quiet. I said nothing. I'm always going to be like this anyway.
I know Jyoti thinks I'm being dramatic. It doesn't feel dramatic. It feels true.

What did Varun get in the last English test?
Varun got 17 last time.
How does Varun feel about the English test result?
Varun feels hopeless and defeated, seeing the mark as proof of being bad at everything, forever.
What could help Varun see the setback differently?
Checking the evidence, like the 17 last time, and seeing one bad test as temporary and limited to English.
How does Jyoti see Varun's reaction?
Jyoti sees it as one test and thinks Varun is being dramatic, since the last mark was better.

Last semester, Professor Jomon stopped me after class with my essay in his hand. "This section on labour markets reads differently. Which parts did a tool help with?"
I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I honestly didn't know. I'd used a chatbot to explain a few terms, then to smooth some paragraphs, then to suggest a structure, and I hadn't kept track of any of it. He wasn't accusing me, but I couldn't prove what was mine.
That evening I made a simple log in my notebook: date, assignment, what I asked the tool, what I kept. On the next essay I added two lines at the end: "An AI tool was used to explain two concepts and check grammar. All analysis is my own." 
Professor Jomon read it and nodded. That was Irawati, finally able to answer the question.

What did Irawati record in the new log?
The date, the assignment, what Irawati asked the tool, and what was kept.
How did Irawati feel when Professor Jomon asked which parts a tool helped with?
Irawati felt flustered and exposed, unable to say anything because no track had been kept of what was really their own.
What else could Irawati do to make the disclosure more useful?
Irawati could ask the professor what level of detail the course expects, so the acknowledgment matches the rules instead of guessing.
How might Professor Jomon see the change on the next essay?
Professor Jomon likely feels reassured, since the acknowledgment answers the question he had asked and makes trust easier.

I'm Nakul, and I was on the sofa while my cousin Mridul played online in our flat. He kept grinning at the screen. "An older player gave me a rare skin for free. He says I'm the best he's met, and I should add him on a private chat."
Then Mridul hesitated. "He also said not to tell my parents, because they'd make me stop." His grin dropped a little.
I asked, "Why would a grown-up give free stuff to a kid and want it kept secret?" He shrugged and said the skin was cool, but he didn't look sure.
Later I saw him remove the friend request. At dinner he told his mother. She put down her spoon, thanked him for telling her and said it wasn't his fault. They blocked and reported the account together that evening. I don't know whether he was scared or just tired of it.

What did the older player give Mridul for free?
He gave Mridul a rare skin.
What did Mridul seem to be feeling when he hesitated?

You asked why I skipped the results party, Pema. Okay. I'm Francis, and I failed Thermodynamics. First time in my life I've failed anything.
The first thing my uncle said on the phone was, "You must have been roaming with friends." Then a senior in the mess: "Bhai, the paper was easy, you didn't study." Then my own roommate, joking: "God is fair, man."
I studied. I had solved every past paper. I blanked on two questions and misread a third. That happens. But when four people in a row tell you it's your fault, you start walking differently. I stopped going to the mess at lunch. I took the stairs so I wouldn't meet anyone in the lift.
Last night I told my professor all of it, and she said, "Failing one paper doesn't make you lazy. It makes you a student." That's the first sentence in weeks that let me breathe.

Francis failed Thermodynamics.

Francis felt ashamed and exposed, and began avoiding the mess and the lift to escape more blame.

The professor's line that failing one paper makes you a student, not lazy, separated the result from Francis's worth and finally let Francis breathe.
How might the roommate see the joke about God being fair?
The roommate probably meant it as light teasing, without noticing how it added to Francis's shame.

A banana was five rupees.

She felt very grown up and amazed, as if money was a kind of magic.

Herman likes to feed the birds in December, January and February.  He feeds them 1/2 cup in the morning and 1/2 cup in the afternoon.  How many cups of food will he need for all three months?

December has 31 days, January has 31 days and February has 28 days for a total of 31+31+28 = 90 days
He feeds them 1/2 cup in the morning and 1/2 cup in the afternoon for a total of 1/2+1/2 = 1 cup per day
If he feeds them 1 cup per day for 90 days then he will need 1*90 = 90 cups of birdseed
The answer is 90.

Tuesday night
Wasim sent money again today. That's the fifth time since March.
Her name is Sophia. She's "a UN nurse in Syria." They talk every night. He showed me her photos: beautiful, always in scrubs, never in a video. Every week there's a new problem. Her pay is delayed. She needs a travel permit. Her phone was confiscated.
I wanted to yell, "Wasim, wake up." But I remember how my uncle reacted when my cousin was scammed: shouting, and my cousin only went deeper.
So tonight, over chai, I just asked, "Has she ever video called?" "Has any money ever come back?" "Why does every problem have a price?" He got defensive. Then quiet.
I read online that these scams are run like companies, with teams, scripts and targets. Wasim isn't stupid. He's up against a whole business.
Tomorrow I'll show him the article and offer to go with him to the cyber cell. No yelling.
Uday

"A UN nurse in Syria."
How is Uday feeling as he writes the diary?
Uday feels worried and frustrated, wanting to yell but choosing patience to avoid pushing Wasim deeper.
What approach is Uday taking with Wasim?
Asking gentle questions, sharing an article about organised scams, and offering to go with him to the cyber cell, without yelling.
How did Wasim react to Uday's questions?
Wasim got defensive and then quiet, perhaps starting to doubt.

He explained: the group arrives Thursday, the kits make the first impression, each needs a map, a schedule and a water bottle, and they should look neat, not fancy. Tuesday. Sumit showed three kits. One map was folded wrong. Harsha pointed it out and left.
Thursday. Eighty kits lined the desk, with a small handwritten note in each that Sumit had added himself. The guests loved the notes. Harsha hadn't thought of that.

Sandy bought 1 million Safe Moon tokens. She has 4 siblings. She wants to keep half of them to herself and divide the remaining tokens among her siblings. After splitting it up, how many more tokens will she have than any of her siblings?

She will keep 1000000 / 2 = 500000 Safe Moon tokens for herself.
For the remaining siblings, they will each receive 500000 / 4 = 125000 tokens.
This means that Sandy will have 500000 - 125000 = 375000 tokens more than any of her siblings.
The answer is 375000.

In the small town of Sehore, a message was going round every family group: "Students who go to Verma Sir's tuition score 20 marks more! Enrol now!"
Chetan's mother read it aloud at dinner. "Everyone's joining. You should too."
Chetan, sixteen, put down his roti. "Ma, who goes to Verma Sir's?"

The next day at school, his friend Pradeep said, "My marks went up after I joined!"

Pradeep felt unsure and a bit surprised, realising his higher marks might have come from studying more, not only the tuition.

She could ask how students did before joining and compare with similar students who didn't join, to see if the tuition itself made the difference.

At her sister's wedding in Buenos Aires, Camila, twenty-six, smiled all evening: during the vows, the speeches, the first dance. It was a long, steady smile, and her friend Felix, standing near her, thought at first she was simply overjoyed. But during the father-daughter dance, when her sister danced with their uncle instead, Felix saw Camila's smile hold perfectly while tears slid down her cheeks. He hesitated, unsure whether to say anything. After a few minutes he brought her a glass of water and asked quietly, "Are you all right?" Camila nodded, still smiling. "Mamá died two years ago. Papá the year before. I'm so happy for my sister. And I miss them so much I can't breathe." Felix didn't try to fix it. He stood beside her through the dance. At the end, she laughed. "Thank you for not asking why I was smiling."

Who did Camila's sister dance with during the father-daughter dance?
Their uncle.
What was Camila feeling during the dance?
She felt joy for her sister and deep grief for her parents at once, smiling steadily while tears fell.
What did Felix do that helped?
He checked quietly with water and a simple question, then stood beside her without trying to fix it.
How did Felix first read Camila's smile?
He thought she was simply overjoyed, until he saw the tears.

messages.content: I forgot the lines for our class play in the middle of the scene and the whole room went silent.

Another girl whispered my line.

Most of them were probably laughing with relief that it wasn't them. If someone brings it up, smile and say, 'That was my dramatic pause.'

Team lead's note, design studio, March. Written by Vandana.
Our weekly review has been dragging. Today I watched instead of talking. Dhruv presented his new layout for fifteen minutes. Four of the five people listening had laptops open and were answering emails. When Dhruv asked for feedback, there was a long silence, then one person said, "Looks good," without really looking.
Dhruv's face fell. He had worked on it all week.

What I did next: from next week, reviews will be thirty minutes, not ninety. Laptops closed, except the one on the projector. Each person gives one specific comment. If someone must answer an urgent email, they can step out and come back.

Vandana felt uncomfortable and concerned, seeing a week of Dhruv's work met with half-attention.

Thirty-minute reviews with laptops closed except the projector and one specific comment each, so people give full attention to the work.

The winter I was ten, fog sat on our village for weeks, and I noticed the dew on the spider webs vanished by noon but stayed in the shade of the well. Nobody at school taught that. So every morning I checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke, and wrote down when the drops went. My brother Kishan called me mad. Then the science master saw my notebook and lent me his own book on weather. I read it under the quilt by lantern light. That notebook was the first of forty.

Class teacher's note, Class 11

Ritu told me today she wants to leave school after Class 11 to become a full-time content creator. She showed me three videos of creators who dropped out and now "earn crores". "If they could, so can I. It's easy."

I didn't dismiss her. I asked, "How many people do you think tried the same thing and didn't make it?"

She hadn't thought about it. Those people don't make videos about failing.

We looked together at a small study the school counsellor had shared: of hundreds of young creators who started full time, only a handful earned enough to live on. Most quietly returned to studies or other jobs.

Ritu went quiet. She said, "I only ever see the ones who made it."

I suggested she keep creating on weekends, finish school, and talk to her parents and the counsellor together.

Aparna

How many videos of creators did Ritu show?
She showed me three videos of creators who dropped out.
Why did Ritu think becoming a creator would be easy?
Ritu felt hopeful and excited because she only saw the few creators who succeeded, never the many who quietly failed.
What did Aparna do that helped Ritu see the whole picture?
Aparna asked how many tried and failed, and showed data on young creators, without dismissing Ritu's dream.
How might Ritu's parents feel talking with the counsellor?
Ritu's parents might feel relieved that she's thinking carefully and still being supported in her interest.
Can you invent a library where the books whisper at night?

At Mrs. Dsouza's tiny library, the books whispered when the lights went out. They traded stories, argued about endings, and sometimes shuffled themselves into new order.

One night, a brand-new book arrived. It had a bright cover and no words inside. All the old books gathered around it.

"It's blank," said a thick dictionary. "What a shame."

"Maybe not," said a small poetry book. "Maybe it's waiting."

The next morning, a boy named Vikram came in with a pencil. He sat down and began to write. The blank pages filled slowly, one word at a time.

That night, the books leaned close and read his story together, and they all agreed it was good.

My name's Siddharth, and it took me most of second year to see it. Tarun never said, 'Don't meet your friends.' He said things like, 'Imtiaz's jokes are a bit cruel, no?' or 'Your hostel group chat is so childish.' So I muted the chat. I skipped the Holi party because Tarun looked hurt. Pema found out on a Tuesday, in their Delhi flat, that Jagdish had not told his parents about their engagement. For the third time. He had said, in March, "I told them, they're fine." In June: "They're coming around." Today his mother had called Pema by mistake and asked, puzzled, who she was.
Pema sat on the balcony for an hour. She felt furious, then foolish, then very sad. How had she believed him three times? Was she stupid? Was anything he said true?
That night she called her oldest friend, Chhoki, and talked until two. Chhoki said, "You're not stupid. You trusted him. That's different."
The next day Pema told Jagdish calmly, "No more stories. We go to your parents together this month, or I step back from the engagement. And I've booked a counsellor. I want to go, with or without you."
Jagdish, grey-faced, said, "With."

Jagdish's mother had called Pema by mistake.

Pema felt furious, then foolish, then very sad, and began doubting herself for believing him three times.

Talking with a trusted friend, setting a clear boundary with a consequence, and booking a counsellor for support.

What could Dhruv do at the next event, based on what worked?
Ask another open, curious question such as what got someone into their work, and follow up with one more, since no clever line was needed.
How does Harsha see the question compared with "Lovely food"?
It shows real interest in Harsha and not just politeness. Harsha's face changed and Harsha shared a story about a grandmother's kitchen.
The prize distribution will held in the school hall. Please correct.

The prize distribution will be held in the school hall.
Why: missing word ("will held" -> "will be held").

I share a study table with my cousin Charu in the holidays, so I watched how her evening went. At five she pulled out the fun things first: a rainforest picture to colour, then a page of neat copying. She hummed, sharpened every colour pencil, and drew a parrot nobody had asked for. At eight, Pallavi Aunty called, "Dinner in ten minutes. Are the sums done?" Charu went quiet. She opened the maths notebook, rubbed her eyes, and wrote answers very fast. I saw her write 56 for 7 × 9. I don't know if she noticed. She shut the notebook and yawned all through dinner.

What did Charu draw that nobody had asked for?
A parrot.
What might Charu have felt when Pallavi Aunty asked about the sums?
Going quiet suggests she felt worried and a bit guilty, realising the hard part was still left at eight.
What could Charu try the next evening?
Start the maths at five while she's alert and colour the rainforest after; a sleepy slip like 56 for 7 × 9 is then less likely.
How might Pallavi Aunty see the evening?
Pallavi Aunty probably expected the sums done before dinner, and may be surprised by a yawning child and rushed answers.

Read this:

Sachin, you said the landlord "didn't say no" to fixing the leak. Let me, Kunal, tell you about Mr. Bhattacharya. I was twenty-five, running site purchases for a builder in Kolkata. I asked our biggest supplier, an old gentleman, if he could deliver the cement a week early. He poured me tea, said, "We'll see, we'll see," and started talking about his grandson's cricket. I went back and told my boss it was done. It wasn't. The cement came on the original date, and we lost a week of work. My boss asked, "Did he actually say yes?" He hadn't. For him, "we'll see" plus a change of subject was a polite no; he didn't want to refuse a young man to his face. After that, when I got a "we'll see", I'd ask softly, "Uncle, shall I plan for the old date then, just to be safe?" It gave him an easy way to say what he meant.

What did Kunal ask the supplier to deliver early?
The cement, a week early.
How did Kunal feel after the cement came on the original date?
Kunal likely felt embarrassed and foolish, having told the boss it was done when it had really been a polite no.
What question did Kunal learn to ask after that turning point?
A soft check like 'Shall I plan for the old date then, just to be safe?', which gave the supplier an easy way to say what he meant.
Why might Mr. Bhattacharya have answered indirectly?
He didn't want to refuse a young man to his face, so he used 'we'll see' and a change of subject as a polite no.

The Tunga river was high and brown after three days of rain. Behind the temple in their village, four boys stood on the old stone steps.
"Jeevan, jump from the third step. We all did it last year."
The water was moving fast, carrying branches. Jeevan's stomach dropped. "No. Not today."
"Scared?"
"Appa's rule. No river in monsoon. He'll skin me." It was true, and it helped to say it.
"Come on, just once!"
His cousin Alka, sitting on the wall with her slippers off, said loudly, "He said no. Let's go play cricket in Gowda's field before it rains again."
Jeevan grabbed the bat from her. "First innings is mine."
Two of the boys followed straight away. The others grumbled but came too. That evening Jeevan told Appa anyway, and Appa went to have a word with the temple priest about chaining the steps in monsoon.

How many days had it rained?
It had rained for three days.
What was Jeevan feeling when he looked at the river?
Jeevan felt frightened, his stomach dropping at the fast brown water, and also under pressure from the boys.
Which moves helped Jeevan resist the pressure?
He said a clear no, blamed Appa's rule, and with Alka's help suggested cricket instead, and later told Appa, who took a protective step.
How might Alka have seen the boys' pressure on Jeevan?
Alka seemed to see it as unfair and unsafe, which is why she backed up his no and offered another plan.

Bidisha: lakshmi are you up
Lakshmi: yes what happened
Bidisha: the blood camp called. my screening came back positive for that rare anaemia thing 😰
Bidisha: the lady said the test is really good at catching it
Bidisha: so i basically have it
Lakshmi: wait. did they say you have it or that you need another test?
Bidisha: another test. but why would it be positive if i didn't
Lakshmi: remember stats class? if something is super rare, even a good test flags lots of people who don't have it
Bidisha: that sounds like something people say to make you feel better
Lakshmi: maybe. but ask the doctor how many positives turn out real. i'll come with you 🤍
Bidisha: ok. i still can't stop thinking about it

What did the lady at the blood camp say about the test?
The lady said the test is really good at catching it.
Why does Bidisha brush off Lakshmi's point about rare conditions?
Bidisha's own positive result feels personal and concrete, while the statistics sound like comfort, so the fear wins over the numbers.
What is a sensible next step for Bidisha?
Go for the repeat test and ask the doctor how many positives turn out to be real, with Lakshmi there for support.
How might Lakshmi feel reading these late-night messages?
Lakshmi is probably worried and careful not to brush the fear aside, so offers to come along instead of only arguing.

Dear Yogesh,
Something happened in our lane this week that I keep thinking about. Two families fight over the common tap every summer. This Monday the fight was louder, and by evening a message was going round the lane group saying it was "their people versus ours". Photos, arrows, an old story about someone's grandfather. I got it forwarded to me six times.
I felt sick reading it. I know both families. Their kids play cricket together.
I didn't forward it. I wrote in the group, "This is about a tap, not about anyone's religion." Two people reacted with anger. One aunty messaged me privately to say thank you. Then my Nani and old Bashir chacha, who have both lived here forty years, called the two families to the temple courtyard and agreed a timetable for the tap.
It's calmer. I'm still shaky.
Disha

Where did Nani and Bashir chacha call the two families?
To the temple courtyard.
How did Disha feel reading the forwarded messages, and why?
Disha felt sick and upset, because Disha knows both families and their children play cricket together.
What could others in the lane group have done to help?
They could refuse to forward the message, add a calm reply like Disha's, and support the elders' meeting instead of taking sides.
How might the aunty who messaged privately have felt?
She was probably uneasy about the messages too but nervous to speak publicly, and relieved and grateful that someone did.

In the insurance office, Varun was the one who made Monday stand-ups bearable. Pooja had watched him turn every grim target into a joke for a year. Lately something had shifted. When the team lead asked him directly, "How's the Mehta file going?", he said, "Ah, the Mehta file and I are on a break," and changed the subject to cricket. When Pooja asked about his transfer request, he said, "They're still deciding if I'm worth the paperwork," and laughed alone.

On Thursday she saw him in the stairwell, phone in hand, not smiling at all. She waited until he looked up. "Hey. Not a joke question: are you okay?"

Varun leaned on the railing. "Transfer got rejected. And my father's not well back home. I didn't know how to say it at work."

"You just did," Pooja said. "Want to get chai?"

What did Varun say about the Mehta file?
Varun said, "Ah, the Mehta file and I are on a break."
Why did Pooja wait in the stairwell?
Pooja felt worried, having noticed that Varun joked away every serious question and now wasn't smiling at all, so a private moment felt right.
What made Pooja's check-in effective?
She chose a quiet moment, said "not a joke question", and then offered chai, so Varun could talk without an audience.
How might Varun feel after telling Pooja?
Varun probably feels a bit lighter and less alone, having finally said the rejection and his father's illness aloud.

The first time Wasim went to the Thursday satsang in the lane behind Charminar, an old man pressed a steel glass of hot milk into his hands and said, "You look tired, son. Sit."

After a year alone in the city, it was the first place anyone had noticed that.

Now he went every week. He loved the singing, the shared dinner, the way people remembered his mother's name.

He also kept his Saturday cricket with college friends, and his long calls with Sonali, who teased him about "turning saint."

One week a regular said she was moving to another group closer to home. Wasim braced for frowns. Instead the leader hugged her and said, "Come back for Diwali."

Walking home, Wasim felt something settle. This was a family that let you go. That was exactly why he trusted it.

What did the old man give Wasim on the first visit?
A steel glass of hot milk.
How did Wasim feel when the leader hugged the woman who was leaving?
He felt relieved and settled, because the group let people go warmly, which made him trust it more.
What is Wasim doing that keeps his belonging healthy?
He enjoys the satsang but keeps his Saturday cricket and his calls with Sonali, so his life has more than one circle.
How might Sonali see Wasim's new routine?
Sonali seems glad and relaxed about it, teasing him about "turning saint" rather than worrying.

Dear Dolma Didi,
You told me to write when stuff got weird, so here it is. On Saturday at Karishma's birthday, some of the older girls went up to the terrace with a vape and kept waving it at me. "Just one pull, Ritu, don't be a baby." I said no. Then I tried your trick: "Coach tests our breathing on Monday, I can't." They laughed but backed off for ten minutes. When they started again, I said, "I'm going down for cake, anyone coming?" Nobody came, and my face was hot, but I went. Karishma found me later and said, "Sorry, they're like that. You don't have to go up." She's fine. They're not. They've been messaging me all week calling me boring. Last night I showed Mummy, and she called Karishma's mum straight away. I think I'll sit with the hockey team at lunch for a while.
Love, Ritu

What excuse did Ritu give on the terrace?
Ritu said Coach tests their breathing on Monday, so Ritu couldn't.
What was Ritu feeling when walking down for cake alone?
Ritu felt embarrassed, face hot, yet determined; there may also have been some loneliness, since nobody came along.
Which of Ritu's moves helped most, and why?
Saying no, using a rule as cover and then leaving for the cake got Ritu away from the pressure; showing Mummy the messages brought in an adult when it kept going.
How might Karishma have felt seeing the older girls push Ritu?
Karishma likely felt embarrassed about her guests and wanted Ritu to feel okay, so she apologised and said Ritu didn't have to go up.

Rostov saw that it had been well considered by them. Sonya had already struck him by her beauty on the preceding day. Today, when he had caught a glimpse of her, she seemed still more lovely. She was a charming girl of sixteen, evidently passionately in love with him (he did not doubt that for an instant). Why should he not love her now, and even marry her, Rostov thought, but just now there were so many other pleasures and interests before him! "Yes, they have taken a wise decision," he thought, "I must remain free."

Question: Why does Rostov decide that he must remain free?
Although he finds Sonya lovely and thinks she loves him, he feels there are so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him just now.

Heidi's apartment has 3 times as many rooms as Danielle's apartment. Grant's apartment has 1/9 as many rooms as Heidi's apartment. If Grant's apartment has 2 rooms, how many rooms does Danielle's apartment have?

Heidi's apartment has 2*9=18 rooms.
Danielle's apartment has 18/3=6 rooms.
The answer is 6.

Always push your chair in and leave the room quietly.
Papa ka retirement hai next week. Unke liye English mein ek chhoti si speech line chahiye, thodi emotional.

You could say: "Papa, you worked hard for thirty-five years so that we could have everything we needed. Today we are proud of you, and we are happy that you can finally rest and enjoy your time." Change the number of years to fit.

1) Is "embittered" a hard word? What does it mean?
2) How should I behave when I visit a new relative's house?
3) Make this correct: The girls bag was on the floor.

1. Embittered is an adjective that means made angry and unhappy by bad experiences. It is a less common word, but you will meet it in books.
2. Greet everyone politely and ask before you touch things. Thank them for the food and offer to help.
3. It should be: The girl's bag was on the floor. Why: an apostrophe and "s" show that the bag belongs to the girl.

In the hotel kitchen in Dublin, Clara watched Amara stand up at the Monday staff meeting. "The fridge temperature logs are being filled in at the end of the week, not every day. I've seen it. Someone could get sick."
The head chef's face went stiff. Nobody spoke. Clara's heart was pounding, because she had seen it too, every Friday afternoon. She looked at her shoes.
After the meeting, three cooks told Amara quietly in the corridor, "You're right, you know." Then they walked away fast.
Clara went home and couldn't eat. She kept seeing Amara standing alone.
On Tuesday she found Amara in the locker room and said, "I'll back you. In writing, if you need it." That afternoon she sent a two-line note to the hotel manager with the dates she had seen.
Amara sat down on the bench and put her face in her hands. "I thought I was the only one."

When were the fridge temperature logs being filled in?
At the end of the week, not every day.
What was Clara feeling during the silent meeting?
Clara's heart was pounding; Clara felt afraid and ashamed, having seen the same thing but looking at the floor instead.
What did Clara do on Tuesday, and why does it matter?
Clara offered to back Amara in writing and sent the hotel manager a note with dates, so Amara was no longer standing alone.
What was it like for Amara to hear Clara's offer?
Amara was overwhelmed and relieved, putting her face in her hands, because she had thought she was the only one.

On Three Kings' Day, the park in Madrid was full of children with new toys. Clara and Pablo played tag round the frozen fountain. Pablo ran fast, but at each corner he slowed and leaned in so he wouldn't slip on the ice. When he caught Clara, he grabbed her in a tight hug. "Stop, too squeezy!" she said. Pablo let go at once and stepped back. "Sorry. Tag with one finger?" Clara grinned. "One finger. Go!" This time he tapped her shoulder lightly and ran.

What did Clara say when Pablo hugged her?
"Stop, too squeezy!"
Why did Pablo let go at once and step back?
He wanted Clara to feel comfortable and seemed a little embarrassed that his hug had been too tight.
What could an adult say to encourage how Pablo handled it?
They could say, "You listened when Clara said stop, and you found a new way to play."
How does Clara feel when Pablo suggests "one finger"?
Clara feels respected and happy to keep playing, since her "stop" was heard straight away. 😊

The week after I failed the CA intermediate for the second time, our house felt like a waiting room. Chachi brought kheer and a sad face, as if someone had died. Mama phoned with advice: "Switch to MBA, forget CA." At a wedding, an aunty I barely knew asked why I couldn't be like my cousin, who cleared it first attempt. I nodded at everyone and felt smaller each time.
Then my friend Aditi came over on Sunday. She didn't bring kheer or a plan. She sat on the floor of my room, ate chips and said, "Tell me how it actually feels. I won't fix anything."
So I told her. The shame, the anger, the part where I'd started to believe I was the family joke. She just listened. When I finished she said, "That sounds really heavy." That was all.
The next morning I opened my books. I'm Pankaj, and that Sunday is when I started standing up again.

What did Chachi bring?
Kheer and a sad face.
How did Pankaj feel after each comparison and piece of advice?
Pankaj felt ashamed and smaller each time, as though failing had turned Pankaj into the family joke.
Why did Aditi's visit help more than the advice?
She listened without judging or fixing, which let Pankaj say the shame out loud and feel strong enough to open the books again.
What might Aditi have been feeling while she just listened?
Aditi was likely concerned but calm, holding back the urge to offer solutions so that Pankaj could simply be heard.

I'm Irfan, Mridul's big brother. Yesterday Mridul told the neighbour aunty, “A lion came to our school and I fed it a biscuit!” Aunty's eyes went wide. Mummy smiled. “Was it a pretend lion or a real one?” Mridul thought. “A real cat. But it was big like a lion.” Mummy said, “What a great story. And a real cat came to school!” I don't know if Mridul thought it was really a lion, but he wasn't told off.

What did Mridul say he fed the lion?
A biscuit.
What might Mridul have been feeling as he told the lion story?
He was probably excited about the cat at school and wanted his story to be as big as his feelings. Irfan isn't sure if he believed it was a lion.
How did Mummy separate pretend from real without a harsh label?
She asked if it was a pretend lion or a real one, and praised the story while noting that a real cat came.
How might the neighbour aunty have seen the lion story?
She was surprised at first, then probably amused when she heard it was a big cat.

Vijay, you keep saying school was better than your new job. Let me tell you about your Nandini nani at twenty-five. I had just moved to the city after my wedding, and I missed my village so much I made everyone around me miserable. "In the village the mangoes were sweeter, the people kinder," I'd say. One evening my mother-in-law asked, "Were they kinder when the well dried up and you walked two hours for water?" I was angry. But that night I wrote two lines in my diary: what I loved, and what was hard. Every year after, I read both. I still cook village food on Sundays, beta. But I stopped telling your nana the city was poor. It was only new.

How long did Nandini walk for water when the well dried up?
Two hours.
How did young Nandini feel when her mother-in-law asked about the well?
She felt angry at first, then thoughtful enough to write down both what she loved and what was hard.
What was the turning point in Nandini's story?
Writing the two lines in her diary that night and reading both every year, so she kept the comfort without calling the city poor.
How might Nandini's mother-in-law have felt hearing the village praised?
She may have felt tired of hearing the city run down, perhaps a little hurt, which is why she asked her sharp question.
There's a thunderstorm tonight and my little brother is scared.
Many children find thunderstorms frightening. A calm older sibling can help a lot.
What can I say to him?
Tell him thunder is just a loud sound and that you are with him inside. Staying together in a safe place in the house helps him feel protected.
What can we do to distract him?
Play a quiet game, read a story or draw together. A little music can drown out some of the noise. Keep your own voice calm.
Should we unplug things?
It is a sensible habit during storms, but ask an adult in the house to do it. Stay away from windows and keep clear of electrical sockets and taps.

When Sahil was promoted to team lead, Sachin, the department manager, expected some grumbling. He didn't expect the silence. In the team meeting, when Sahil asked for ideas, people shrugged. His messages got one-word replies. At lunch, the old group still ate together, but somehow there was never space for Sahil. Sachin overheard two of them at the tea machine: "Thinks he's our boss now." "He was one of us last week." Nobody was rude. They just quietly stopped helping. Sahil started working through lunch, alone. Sachin realised the team had been comfortable when everyone was equal, and Sahil's rise had upset it. He called the team together that afternoon to talk openly about the change.

What did Sachin overhear at the tea machine?
"Thinks he's our boss now." "He was one of us last week."
What might Sachin be feeling as he watches the team?
Sachin seems concerned and uneasy, surprised by the quiet withdrawal rather than open complaints.
Why is calling the team together a good step?
It brings the unspoken resentment into the open so the team can adjust to the change and support Sahil.
What is it like for Sahil after the promotion?
Sahil likely feels isolated and confused, working through lunch alone as his old friends withdraw.

messages.content: Fish is to water as bird is to what?
The answer is air. Because a fish lives and moves in water, in the same way a bird lives and flies in the air.
A five-sentence description of a sunflower field for my photography caption, please.

The sunflower field stretched all the way to the hills. Thousands of golden heads turned together to face the morning sun. Bees moved lazily from flower to flower, heavy with pollen. A narrow dirt path ran through the middle, just wide enough for one person. Standing there, I felt as if I was walking through a field of small suns.

I'm Rukmini, and I share a pod with Kamal and Harish. After the quarterly review where Harish presented the vendor plan alone, Kamal said nothing in the meeting. Not a word. But at the tea machine he told me, 'Our plan, his applause. Typical.' Since then I've noticed things. Kamal's emails to Harish have shrunk to one line: 'Done.' 'See attached.' Last week Harish asked where the updated supplier list was, and Kamal said, 'Not sure,' though I'd seen it open on his screen that morning. Harish came to me later, confused. 'What did I do? He's so cold with me.' I don't know what Kamal feels inside. I only know the room has gone quiet between them.

What did Kamal tell Rukmini at the tea machine?
He told her, 'Our plan, his applause. Typical.'
What might Kamal's 'Not sure' about the supplier list reveal about his feelings?
It suggests hidden resentment toward Harish, showing up as withheld information rather than saying openly that he felt slighted.
What could break this cycle of silent resentment?
Kamal could tell Harish directly and calmly that he felt left out of the credit, instead of venting to Rukmini and going cold.
How is Harish experiencing Kamal's cooler tone?
He is confused and reads it as hostility without knowing what he did, which may make him defensive too.

Saturday, midnight.

Argued with Yogesh in the canteen about whether the state should fund private schools. He says yes; I say no. Instead of getting louder I asked, "How did you come to that view?" He went quiet, then told me his sister's government school had one teacher for four classes, and their parents saved for years so she could go to a small private one. I had no idea. I still disagree about the policy. But I get why he cares. And I realised we both want children to get a decent education. We disagree about the route.

I felt strangely light walking home. Next time: ask first, argue second.

- Swati

What did Swati ask Yogesh?
Swati asked, "How did you come to that view?"
What did Swati realise about Yogesh's position?
Swati realised that Yogesh cares because of his sister's schooling and that both of them want children to get a decent education, and walked home feeling strangely light and at peace.
What could Swati do next time?
Swati could ask first and argue second, listening for the shared values underneath the disagreement.
How might Yogesh have felt when asked how he came to his view?
He was probably surprised and relieved to be heard instead of attacked, since he went quiet and then shared something personal.

I'm Gurpreet. My brother Arnab and I both went home to Ludhiana in March, first time together in a year. This is what I noticed.
Mum had made the rajma on the first night, the one we fought over as kids. She kept putting more on our plates.
Every evening she found a reason to come into our old rooms. To bring a towel. To fix a curtain. To ask nothing in particular.
On our last night, Arnab went to get water and I heard him stop in the hallway. Mum was standing at the photo wall, touching the one of us on the scooter. Arnab didn't say anything. He just stood next to her.
When we left, she waved from the gate until the auto turned the corner. Arnab said quietly, "We should come more." I nodded. I think we both understood what the rajma had been saying.

What was Mum touching on the photo wall?
The photo of the two of them on the scooter.
What was Gurpreet feeling when Arnab said "We should come more"?
Gurpreet felt moved and a bit guilty, understanding the love behind Mum's waiting.
What could Gurpreet and Arnab do after this visit?
They could visit more often and call regularly, since small contact means a lot to a parent who is waiting.
How might Mum have felt waving from the gate?
She probably felt a mix of love and sadness, wanting them to stay longer and already missing them.

Incident note, Friday, by Ms Maria, Class 4 teacher.
During pickup, I saw an older man at the side gate hand Varun a small wrapped box. Varun took a step back and did not open it. When his father arrived a minute later, Varun ran to him and said, loud enough for me to hear, 'Papa, that man gave me presents three times. He said it's our secret.' Varun's hands were trembling, but he kept talking. His father knelt and told him he was right to tell. I stayed with them and told Varun it was never his fault. Within half an hour I had reported it to our safeguarding lead, who called the police and alerted the guards. Varun went home holding his father's hand.

What did the man at the side gate hand Varun?
A small wrapped box.
What was Varun feeling when he told his father, and how can you tell?
He was frightened but brave; his hands were trembling, yet he kept talking.
What did the adults do right after Varun spoke up?
His father said he was right to tell, Ms Maria said it was never his fault, and she reported it to the safeguarding lead within half an hour.
How might Varun's father have felt hearing about the secret presents?
Shocked and worried, but he knelt and reassured Varun instead of blaming him.

Debbie works at a post office packing boxes to mail. Each large box takes 4 feet of packing tape to seal, each medium box takes 2 feet of packing tape to seal, and each small box takes 1 foot of packing tape to seal. Each box also takes 1 foot of packing tape to stick the address label on. Debbie packed two large boxes, eight medium boxes, and five small boxes this afternoon. How much tape did she use?

Debbie used 4 * 2 = 8 feet of tape for the large boxes.
She used 2 * 8 = 16 feet of tape for the medium boxes.
She used 1 * 5 = 5 feet of tape for the small boxes.
There were 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 boxes in all.
She used 1 * 15 = 15 feet of tape for the address labels.
Thus, she used 8 + 16 + 5 + 15 = 44 feet of tape in all.
The answer is 44.

Prove (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta. If sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2, find sin theta cos theta and theta (acute).

Answer: sin theta cos theta = 1/2 and theta = 45 degrees.

LHS = (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + 2 sin theta cos theta + cos^2theta = (sin^2theta + cos^2theta) + 2 sin theta cos theta = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta = RHS Similarly (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 2 sin theta cos theta. With sin theta + cos theta = sqrt2: 2 = 1 + 2 sin theta cos theta, so sin theta cos theta = 1/2. Then (sin theta - cos theta)^2 = 1 - 1 = 0, so sin theta = cos theta and theta = 45 degrees. Common mistake: (sin theta + cos theta)^2 = sin^2theta + cos^2theta = 1 (the middle term is forgotten).

messages.content: The minute hand of a clock tower is 21 cm long. How far does its tip travel in 15 minutes, and what area does the hand sweep? (pi = 22/7)

Answer: Arc 33 cm; area 346.5 cm^2.

In 60 minutes the hand turns 360 degrees, so in 15 minutes it turns 90 degrees, a QUARTER of a turn. The tip moves along a quarter of the circle: arc = 90/360 x 2 x 22/7 x 21 = 1/4 x 132 = 33 cm. The swept region is a SECTOR: area = 90/360 x 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1/4 x 1386 = 346.5 cm^2. General rule for angle theta: take the fraction theta/360 of the whole circumference (arc) or of the whole area (sector).

She was anxious, her stomach knotted by the red warning, and she stayed tense, jiggling her knee, until she finally breathed out after submitting.

Checking every letter against her school ID, catching the month-first date, and asking Mrs Ghosh for the code instead of guessing.

Monday: Tenzin's second week at the Delhi office. At the tea counter the familiar thought came: they've already formed their groups, I'll be invisible. He noticed it this time, the way you notice a song stuck in your head. So he spoke first. 'Binita, is that a money plant on your desk? Mine keeps dying.' She laughed and gave him two tips.
Thursday: the team meeting. His forecast said he'd stumble, so he prepared his three slides the night before and practised once aloud. It went mostly fine. Someone asked about costs and he didn't know. He wrote it down instead of shrinking.
Next Tuesday: Binita waved him over to lunch. He counted quietly: two warm conversations, one question he couldn't answer, zero people ignoring him. Not bad evidence. That afternoon the intern turned in a weak draft. Tenzin didn't write her off; he sent it back with clear notes and said, 'I think you can make this sharp by Friday.'

What did Tenzin ask Binita on Monday?
He asked, 'Binita, is that a money plant on your desk? Mine keeps dying.'
How did Tenzin feel about the question he couldn't answer on Thursday?
He seemed steady rather than crushed; he wrote it down instead of shrinking, treating it as something to fix, not proof of failure.
Which small choices helped Tenzin break his forecast, and why did they work?
Speaking first at the tea counter and preparing his slides the night before gave people a chance to respond warmly, which gave him new evidence.
How might the intern feel after reading Tenzin's notes?
The intern would likely feel taken seriously, since Tenzin said she could make it sharp by Friday instead of writing her off.
Our teacher asked who broke the window, and Rahul "owned up". What does that mean?

To own up means to admit honestly that you did something wrong.

'They said the same thing two years ago and we got ankle-deep water,' Elizabeth told her husband, Imran, turning the radio down. The corporation's alert warned of heavy rain overnight and a possible release from the lake upstream. Imran wanted to take the children to his sister's flat across the city. Elizabeth wanted to finish the week's cooking and leave in the morning if needed.
They stayed. At 1 a.m. the power died. By three the road outside was a moving river, and the bridge to his sister's side was closed. Their daughter had a fever and wouldn't stop crying. At dawn a rescue boat reached them, but the men had to lift the children down from the balcony one by one while the current pulled. Elizabeth held the railing, her face white, saying nothing at all.

What time did the power die?
At 1 a.m.
What was Elizabeth feeling as she held the railing at dawn?
She looked terrified and probably guilty, realising that her choice to wait had put the children in danger.
What other approach could have kept the family safer?
Following the alert and leaving for Imran's sister's flat that evening would have avoided a dangerous rescue in the dark current.
How might the rescue team see the family's decision to stay?
For the rescuers, a late call means lifting children from a balcony in a strong current, a far riskier job than an early evacuation.

messages.content: Write about 90 words in diary form for a traveller on a houseboat in Kerala.

Dear Diary,
We are floating slowly on a houseboat in the Kerala backwaters. The water is calm, and green palm trees line the banks. The cook has made fish curry and red rice, and I ate more than I should. A kingfisher dived near our boat this afternoon. In the evening, we saw village women washing clothes at the edge, and children waved at us. I have never felt so peaceful. I wish this trip would last a month.
