In the girls' hostel, Kunal's sister had passed on a note: "Sneak out tonight? Kunal and his friends are going to the night market." Shalini's roommate squealed. Shalini frowned. The gate was locked at nine, and the road was dark. "No, I'm not going." "Don't be boring!" At breakfast, Kunal teased her. "Scaredy cat." Shalini shrugged. "I like my bed. Tell me what you ate." He laughed, and they shared the samosas he'd brought back.

What time was the gate locked?
The gate was locked at nine.
What does Shalini's frown suggest about her thinking?
It suggests she felt uneasy and was weighing the risks of sneaking out.
How did Shalini keep the friendship with Kunal?
She said no calmly, didn't lecture him, and stayed friendly at breakfast.
How might Kunal see Shalini after she refuses?
He teases her but still shares samosas, suggesting he respects her choice.

Dhruv suggests telling Meera she'll be missed, an honest feeling that fits the moment, so Pooja can congratulate Meera sincerely.

The school van was already honking downstairs when Ramesh picked up Jahnavi's bag and felt how light it was.
"Where's your water bottle?"
"In the bag, Papa."
It wasn't. Jahnavi was staring at her shoes. It was the third bottle this term. Ramesh felt his voice rising. The van honked again.
He stopped, crouched to her level and spoke quietly. "Jahnavi, I think you're worried I'll be angry about the bottle."
She nodded, eyes wet. "I left it in the park yesterday. I'm sorry."
"Thank you for telling me the truth. That matters more than any bottle." He pushed an old plastic one into her bag. "We'll look in the park after school, together."
She ran down the stairs, lighter than her bag.

Where did Jahnavi say she left the bottle?
She said she left it in the park yesterday.
Why did Jahnavi say the bottle was in the bag?
She was scared that Papa would be angry about losing a third bottle, so the lie was a quick way to avoid that moment.
What did Ramesh do well under time pressure?
He stopped, crouched, named her worry and thanked her for the truth, then solved the problem quickly with another bottle.
What would change if Ramesh had shouted as the van honked?
Jahnavi would probably learn to hide things better next time, and the truth about the park would stay buried.

Wednesday
Second week of my HR internship. Today I sat in on interviews with Abhinav, the hiring manager.
The first candidate was amazing. Confident, from Lucknow like me, same college, even laughed at the same jokes. I wrote "excellent" before he'd finished his first answer.
The second one stammered, dropped her file, and kept saying "sorry." I wrote "weak communication."
After they left, Abhinav asked me why. I said the first one just felt honest. He didn't say anything, just called the previous employers of both.
The first candidate had never worked at the company on his CV. The second one's old manager said she was the best analyst they'd ever had.
I sat in the washroom for ten minutes feeling sick. I trusted him because he felt like me. I doubted her because she was nervous. Abhinav said, "Everyone does it. That's why we check." I'm Trisha, and I'm going to remember this.

What did Abhinav do after the candidates left?
He called the previous employers of both.
How did Trisha feel after the reference calls?
Trisha felt sick and ashamed, seeing that Trisha had trusted the charming, similar candidate and doubted the nervous one without reason.
What does Abhinav's approach teach about judging honesty?
It shows that checking facts, like references, is more reliable than trusting warmth or confidence.
How might the second candidate have felt during the interview?
She probably felt anxious and flustered, dropping her file and apologising, unaware that her nervousness said nothing about her skill.

I'm Rafiq, Reena's neighbour. I'd gone over to borrow her physics notes. Reena, sixteen, had her board exam in two days. Then the bell rang: four relatives, unannounced. Within a minute her mother called, 'Reena, chai banao, and bring the biscuits.' Reena closed her book slowly. Her brother Kunal, a year younger, stayed on the sofa with his game. Nobody called him. I watched Reena carry the tray three times, smile at every aunty and answer questions about her marks. When she came back to her desk, her pen hovered over the same line for ten minutes. Later I heard her ask her mother quietly, 'Can Kunal do the next round?' I don't know what her mother said.

When was Reena's board exam?
In two days.
What does Reena's pen hovering over the same line suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she felt frustrated and unsettled, unable to focus after being pulled from study while her brother was left alone.
What would be a fairer way to handle the surprise guests?
Share the serving between Reena and Kunal, or let Kunal take this round since Reena had an exam, while still welcoming the guests warmly.
How might Kunal see the evening, and what would change if he were called too?
Kunal may not notice the unfairness since nobody asked him; if he were called, he would learn hosting is everyone's job and Reena would get time to study.

I am hungry, so I open the fridge.
Change "I" to "she" (her name is Amara): I take the early train, and I read on the way.
Amara takes the early train, and she reads on the way.
I every day walk to school. Is the order okay?

I walk to school every day.

Karthik's father, Yogesh, called him into the living room of their Chennai flat. "Look, the city water supply is poisoned! Everyone in my walking group sent it."
Karthik read it. No name, no date, just capital letters. He searched the Chennai water board website. There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison. He checked two newspapers. Nothing.
"Appa, how often have you heard of a whole city's water being poisoned?"
"Never. But all twenty people sent it."
"And they all got it from each other. The water board says it's just a pipe repair." Karthik showed him the notice. "I'm not forwarding it. Can you tell your group what the notice says?"
Yogesh read it twice, then slowly typed a message to his walking group.

What did the Chennai water board website say?
There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison.
What was Yogesh feeling when he called Karthik in?
Yogesh felt alarmed and worried, trusting the message because twenty people in his walking group sent it.

He checked the water board website and two newspapers, asked how often such a thing happens, and chose not to forward it.

They might feel relieved to learn it was just a pipe repair, and maybe a bit sheepish for spreading the scare.

messages.content: Include a small problem in a story about a flock of geese flying south for winter.

The geese of Lake Vana were leaving for the south. They formed a great V in the sky, with old Gander leading. Behind him flew a young goose named Pip, who had never made such a long journey.

By the second day Pip was tired. His wings burned. He fell behind, and the wind pushed him down toward the dark hills.

"Pip!" called Gander. "Fly into my air!"

Pip swerved into the space behind a stronger goose, and at once the flying felt easier. The wind carried him along. He saw that every goose rested in turn at the front.

When it was his turn to lead, many days later, he did it for only a short while, but the others honked kindly all the same.

In the Toronto office kitchen, the sign-up sheet for the city marathon had eighteen names on it. "You're the only one on the team who hasn't signed," Yosef said, grinning, pen held out. Noa took the pen, then paused. She asked herself two questions she'd started using lately: Why do I want this? And would I still do it if nobody ever knew? The honest answers were: because everyone else is, and no. She hated long runs; she loved her Saturday swims. "Not this one," she said, handing the pen back. "But I'll be at the finish line with snacks and a very loud sign." Yosef laughed. "Deal." Two weeks later she signed up for the office's open-water swim, alone on the sheet, and didn't mind at all.

How many names were on the marathon sign-up sheet?
The sheet had eighteen names on it.
What did Noa realise when she answered her two questions honestly?
Noa felt relieved to admit she only wanted to sign because everyone else had, and that she'd never run it if nobody knew, since she hated long runs.
How did Noa stay connected to the team while saying no?
She offered to be at the finish line with snacks and a loud sign, backing them without running a race she didn't want.
How does Yosef react to Noa's choice?
Yosef laughs and says 'Deal', showing Yosef accepts her choice and her offer to cheer.

School counsellor's note, parent–student session

Damini, 15, came with her mother, Vasudha. The issue: Damini wants a phone. Damini had prepared a list: "In exchange I will: clean my room weekly, cook dinner on Fridays, walk our dog daily."
Her mother said she was pleased with the effort but uneasy. "It feels like she only helps because of what she gets."
Damini replied, "But it's fair. You get help, I get a phone. What's wrong with that?"
I said the plan is honest and practical, and also asked Damini what she thinks makes a family work, besides trades. She said she didn't know.
We agreed to try the plan for a month, and meet again to talk about which chores Damini might do just because she lives there.

What would Damini do on Fridays under her plan?
She would cook dinner on Fridays.
What was Vasudha feeling about Damini's list?
She felt pleased with the effort but uneasy that Damini only helps for what she gets.
How did the note-writer handle the bargaining?
They called the plan honest and practical, asked Damini what else makes a family work, and set a trial month with a later talk about helping without trades.
How does Damini see her mother's unease?
Damini doesn't understand it, seeing the deal as fair since both sides gain.

Irfan's cousin Jeevan had set up an informal chat with a senior architect at her firm, 10 a.m. on Thursday, the kind of meeting that could lead to an internship. On Thursday morning, the local train stopped between stations for forty minutes. No signal inside the packed compartment. Irfan's heart raced as the clock ticked past ten. When the train finally moved, he got off at the next stop, found a corner away from the crowd and called Jeevan. Then he emailed the architect directly: a short apology, the reason, and two alternative times. He attached his portfolio, just in case. By evening, the architect replied: "Trains happen. Monday at noon works. Nice portfolio." Irfan let out a breath he felt he'd been holding all day.

What time was Irfan's original chat with the architect?
At 10 a.m. on Thursday.
What was Irfan feeling as the clock passed ten?
He was anxious and afraid he'd lose the chance and embarrass his cousin, which is why his heart raced.
Which choice helped Irfan save the opportunity?
Quickly emailing a clear apology with new times and his portfolio, which showed responsibility and kept the conversation going.

Megan is delivering meals on wheels. Out of her 30 clients, 7 need vegan meals, 8 need kosher meals, and three people need meals that are both vegan and kosher. How many meals does Megan deliver that are neither kosher nor vegan?

First, add the number of kosher meals to the number of vegan meals: 7 meals + 8 meals = 15 meals
Then subtract the three meals that are both kosher and vegan since they got counted twice: 15 meals - 3 meals = 12 meals
Finally, subtract that number from the total number of meals to find the number of meals that are neither kosher nor vegan: 30 meals - 12 meals = 18 meals
The answer is 18.

In their Chennai flat, Uma noticed it first in small words. Her son Dhruv began calling people 'weak' and 'soft', even his cousin, who had a newborn and couldn't get to the gym. He spent his evenings in an online fitness group, headphones on. He skipped the family's Sunday biryani and snapped at his father for offering him a plate. Uma's first thought was to take his phone, as she might have when he was twelve. She didn't. On Tuesday she asked him to walk with her to the vegetable market and asked, 'What do you like about that group?' He talked for twenty minutes. Some of it worried her more. That night, calmly, she told him she was concerned about the skipped meals and asked if he would see their family doctor with her. After a long pause, he said yes.

What did Uma ask Dhruv on the walk?
'What do you like about that group?'
What was Uma feeling when she noticed Dhruv's new words and skipped meals?
She felt worried and alarmed, and was tempted to take his phone as she might have when he was younger.
What made Uma's approach wise?
She chose curiosity and a calm talk over confiscation, listened, then named her specific concern and suggested seeing the family doctor together.
How might Dhruv's cousin feel being called 'soft'?
Probably hurt and judged, since a newborn, not weakness, kept the cousin away from the gym.

In Melbourne, on Thursday, Jamal hung back after science and held out his phone, looking uneasy. "I don't think this is okay. You should see it." It was a second group, "Year 10 real", with everyone from the old chat except Mei. Pinned at the top were screenshots of Mei's messages, her long one about the history project and her question about the formal, each with a row of laughing faces underneath. Mei's ears went hot. She handed the phone back and said, "Cool. Whatever." On the tram home she stared out the window with no music on. At dinner her dad noticed she wasn't eating and asked gently what was wrong. She showed him the screenshots Jamal had sent her. He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that being talked about like that really hurts, and they emailed her year coordinator together. A reply came before nine: the coordinator would meet Mei first thing tomorrow.

What was the second group called?
It was called "Year 10 real".
What does Mei's "Cool. Whatever." suggest?
It suggests she felt deeply hurt and humiliated but was trying to hide it in front of Jamal.
How did Mei's dad support her that evening?
He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that it really hurts, and emailed the year coordinator with her that same evening.
Why might Jamal have looked uneasy when he showed Mei the group?
Jamal was likely torn: he did not want to upset Mei, but he felt the group was wrong and that she deserved to know.

I so shaped out my walk as to arrive at the gate at my old time. When I had rung at the bell with an unsteady hand, I turned my back upon the gate, while I tried to get my breath and keep the beating of my heart moderately quiet. I heard the side-door open, and steps come across the courtyard; but I pretended not to hear, even when the gate swung on its rusty hinges.

Keeping to the passage, what does the narrator do while waiting at the gate?

The narrator planned the walk to arrive at the old time, rang with an unsteady hand, then turned away from the gate to catch breath and calm a beating heart, pretending not to hear the footsteps and the swinging gate.
Meaning of "hunger"? And Please fix my sentence: The cake was most delicious than the pie. One more thing. Why do we drink water after playing? Also, What is in my fridge right now?

1. Hunger is the feeling you have when you need food.
2. Fixed: The cake was more delicious than the pie. Why: Use "more" with "than", not "most".
3. We lose water through sweat. Because the body needs that water back.
4. I don't know, because I can't see your kitchen. Open the fridge and take a look.

At the salad bar, Grandma put three mushrooms on her salad.  She also added twice as many cherry tomatoes as mushrooms, 4 times as many pickles as cherry tomatoes, and 4 times as many bacon bits as pickles.  If one third of the bacon bits were red, than how many red bacon bits did Grandma put on her salad?

Twice as many tomatoes as mushrooms is 3*2=6 tomatoes.
Four times as many pickles as tomatoes is 4*6=24 pickles.
Four times as many bacon bits as pickles is 24*4=96 bacon bits.
One third of 96 is 96/3=32 red bacon bits.
The answer is 32.
What does "background" mean in English?

Background is the part of a picture or scene behind the main things. It can also mean a person's past, such as their education. It is a noun.
Example: The photo shows a mountain in the background.
Deliver a story about a boy who fixes the school clock.

For weeks, the big clock in the school hall had been stuck at ten past four, and nobody bothered to fix it. Then Jatin, a quiet boy in Class 8, noticed a small screw sitting on the floor beneath it. He told the caretaker, who rolled his eyes. "It has been broken for ages." Jatin asked for a ladder and a screwdriver. The caretaker gave them to him mostly to make him stop asking. Jatin climbed up, tightened the loose part, twisted the hands and gave the pendulum a push. It began to tick. The staff stood in the doorway, astonished. Jatin was thanked at assembly, and the caretaker started calling him "Engineer" for the rest of the year.

Note from the counsellor, company wellbeing programme, second session with Mohit
Mohit arrived early and talked fast. His cousin Anirban, a year younger, got engaged last week, and at the function three aunties asked Mohit when his turn was. His mother has started sending him profiles every evening. He listed his "deadlines": married by 27, own flat by 28, manager by 30. He said, "I'm already late for all of them." What I did next: I asked him to write down which of those goals he actually wants and when, separately from what others expect. We talked about how people in his own office are marrying and settling at very different ages. He will bring the list next week.

He said married by 27.
How does Mohit feel about his deadlines?
Mohit feels anxious and afraid of failing, tapping his foot and losing sleep because he believes he is already late for all of them.
What turning point did the counsellor offer?
The counsellor asked Mohit to separate what he truly wants from what others expect, and pointed out that people settle at very different ages.

At the after-school centre in the December cold, the children did homework in the common room, where the TV in the corner was playing a cartoon about a detective dog.
Kiran sat facing the TV, maths book on his knees. "I can do both," he told Vasudha Ma'am. "I'm super fast."
An hour later he had done six sums, and three were wrong. He could only half remember what the dog had solved.
Vasudha Ma'am made a deal. "Tomorrow, TV off for thirty minutes. Then you can watch."
The next day he finished all twelve sums in twenty-five minutes, eleven right, and then watched the whole episode, laughing at every joke.
"I was faster without it," he said, surprised.
"You were switching back and forth," she said. "Each switch costs a little. It adds up."

How many sums did Kiran finish on the second day?
Kiran finished all twelve sums in twenty-five minutes, eleven of them right.
Why did Kiran believe he could do both?
Kiran felt confident and proud of being fast, not noticing that switching between the TV and the sums made both worse.

TV off for thirty minutes, then watch, which let Kiran focus on one thing at a time.

How might Santiago feel when Valentina asks to stay till ten?

In the hostel common room, the school cricket team's scores were pinned on the board: six losses in a row. Farhan tapped it. "Saturday they win. They have to. Six is too many." Naveen, eating peanuts, raised an eyebrow. "Want to bet?" "Three dessert coupons says they win." "Deal." On Saturday the team lost by fifty runs. Farhan handed over the coupons. And the new batsmen are from Class 8." "So what's changed for next week?" Farhan thought. "Nothing." "Then why would the streak break just because it's long?" Farhan put the coupons back in his pocket.

Farhan, looking at the cricket team's six losses in a row, bet Naveen three dessert coupons that they would win on Saturday, but they lost by fifty runs. He paid up and then bet six coupons on a win the next week, saying that seven losses was impossible. How lovely. Do you know what kind of bird it is?
I think it's a pigeon. My dad wants to remove it.
Pigeons often nest on ledges because they feel safe there. If the nest has no eggs yet, now is the easiest time to decide. Once there are eggs or chicks, moving the nest can harm them.
Can we keep it until the babies leave?
You could ask your dad about that. Pigeon chicks usually leave the nest about a month after hatching. Keeping that window shut and not touching the nest will help both your family and the birds.

He twisted his tie. "I g-get stuck. And then R-Rohit's gang does the noise." "Thank you for telling me. That noise stops today; I'll speak to them. Now, what would make reading easier for you?" On Wednesdays.

He was afraid of getting stuck and of Rohit's gang making the noise to mock him.

Stop the teasing, give him his part the day before, wait as long as it takes, and learn what the therapist is practising.

She noted the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name, contacted the legal aid clinic and followed a lead on another room.

Yusuf, her neighbour's son, pushed through and stood beside her. With one second left, the village raider slipped past three defenders and touched the line. The crowd exploded. The old man threw his towel in the air.

Nirmala shouted and jumped in the dust with Yusuf, joining in fully, and that gave her a feeling of being part of something larger than herself. 😊

When our team split the documentary project, I handed the editing to Gopika. Then I watched every second. I messaged her four times a day: "Did you trim the intro?" "Use the other music." "Can you send me the file?" On Wednesday she replied, "Do you want to just do it yourself?" and went offline.
That stung, because she was right. I didn't trust anyone with my idea.
I called her that night and apologised. We agreed on two checkpoints instead: a rough cut on Friday and a final cut on Monday, and I would comment only then. When the rough cut came, I wrote three notes, starting with what I loved, the way she opened on the fisherwoman's hands. Then two changes.
The final version was better than mine would have been. I told her so.
— Vasudha

How many times a day did Vasudha message Gopika?
Four times a day.
Why did Gopika's reply sting Vasudha?
Because it was true: Vasudha felt exposed and embarrassed at not trusting anyone with the idea.
What did Vasudha and Gopika agree on?
Two checkpoints, a rough cut on Friday and a final on Monday, with comments only then, starting with what worked.
How did Gopika feel about the constant messages?
Frustrated and mistrusted, enough to ask "Do you want to just do it yourself?" and go offline.

Monday, the first week. Binita had ended it with Anirban on Saturday. By Monday he had sent forty messages: "Just talk to me." "You owe me that." She replied to some, trying to be kind. Each reply brought ten more. She felt uneasy, checking her phone every few minutes.

The following Monday. Binita wrote one message, read it to her friend Shreya first, and sent it: "Anirban, it's over. Please don't contact me again. I won't be replying." Then she blocked him, saved screenshots of every message with dates, and told her flatmates, her parents and her team lead at work.

Two weeks later. Anirban was waiting outside her office gate at six. Binita's heart pounded. She didn't stop or speak. She went back inside and told the security guard, who walked her to her cab. That evening, with her father beside her, she took her screenshots to the police station and filed a complaint. The officer took it seriously.

How many messages had Anirban sent by Monday?
He had sent forty messages.
How did Binita feel as the messages kept coming?
Binita felt uneasy and on edge, checking her phone every few minutes.
What steps did Binita take to protect herself?
She sent one clear final message, stopped engaging, blocked him, kept dated records, told trusted people, and went to the police when he turned up.
How did Shreya help Binita?
Shreya listened to Binita's final message before she sent it, helping her feel supported in setting the boundary.

'You didn't fast today?' Hrithik asked, passing the chips across the hostel terrace.
'Tuesday? No.' Tejas took a handful. 'First Tuesday I haven't in, what, eight years.'
'Why'd you stop?'
'I didn't decide to. I slept through it once, and nothing happened. Then I started reading. And then I met Farhan, who prays five times a day, and Meenal, who says there's no god and seems totally fine. Everyone's so sure. I used to be sure.'
'And now?'
'Now I don't know.' Tejas lay back on the warm concrete. 'Honestly? It's kind of great. I can think anything.'
'But?'
'But my mom still sends me a photo of the temple every Tuesday. And I still look at it for a long time.'

How long had Tejas kept the Tuesday fast?
Tejas had kept it for about eight years.
What does Tejas looking at the temple photo for a long time reveal?
It reveals a sense of loss and longing that sits alongside the new freedom Tejas enjoys.
What could help Tejas make sense of this stage?
Tejas could accept that freedom and loss can both be true, and perhaps reply honestly to the photo, keeping the bond with home even while beliefs are unsettled.
How might Tejas's mom feel sending the photo every Tuesday?
She likely sends it as a loving link to home and tradition, perhaps hoping Tejas still feels part of it.

In class, nine-year-old Ankita felt a giggle rising when the boy in front dropped his eraser. She pressed her lips together, stared at her page, and held it in, shoulders shaking, until the bell rang. Then she ran to the playground and laughed until she had to hold her sides. At fifteen, Ankita's best friend stopped talking to her, and she kept her face blank in the corridor so no one could see. At home she said "Fine" to everything. Her older cousin Tarun noticed her plate untouched and said, "I'm going for a walk. Want to come? We don't have to talk." Halfway round the block she began to speak. At twenty, Ankita sat before Imran, the interview panel's chair, keeping her hands folded, her voice level and her reactions small. When a question surprised her, she did not blink. The interview went well. Afterwards, on the steps outside, she leaned against the wall and let out a long breath, tired from being so careful.

What did the boy in front of Ankita drop in class?
He dropped his eraser.
How does Ankita's restraint show up at nine, fifteen and twenty, and what does each cost her?

At nine she held in a giggle until the bell and then laughed on the playground, at fifteen she kept a blank face and said "Fine" to hide her hurt, and at twenty she kept her reactions small in the interview and felt tired afterwards. Restraint was useful, but it needed a place to be released or shared.
What was Ankita feeling when she said "Fine" to everything at home?
She felt hurt and sad about losing her best friend, and she was hiding it from everyone.
How could Tarun keep helping Ankita when she is holding things in?
Tarun can keep offering low-pressure chances to talk, like a walk, and let Ankita begin in her own time.
Share a very short story in 50 words about a class pet hamster that goes missing and is found.

One morning, the class hamster was missing from its cage. Everyone searched under desks and behind shelves. Finally, a student heard a tiny squeak inside a bag. The hamster had curled up in a woollen cap. The children laughed and promised to close the cage door every day.
Write the opening two sentences of a bedtime story about a sleepy elephant.
Once upon a time, a sleepy elephant lived at the edge of a quiet forest. Every night she counted the stars before closing her eyes.

At the village temple festival, the drums were so loud Shankar could feel them in his teeth. He stood at the edge of the crowd with his cousin Lokesh, arms folded.
'You used to carry the lamp,' Lokesh said.
'I used to be terrified,' Shankar said. 'Remember Periyappa telling us that if we missed a single festival, the crops would fail and it would be our fault? I was nine. I lay awake over it.'
His voice came out sharper than he meant. A woman in front turned round.
'So now you're angry,' Lokesh said, not unkindly.
'Now I don't know what I am. Angry, mostly. Some days just empty.' Shankar watched the chariot lurch forward. 'Everyone expects me to either come back or announce I'm done. I can't do either yet.'
Lokesh handed him a cup of panakam and didn't argue.

What did Periyappa say would happen if they missed a festival?
He said the crops would fail and it would be their fault.
What does Shankar's sharp voice reveal?
It reveals anger at having been frightened as a child, still raw enough to spill out louder than he meant.
Why is it wise that Shankar doesn't force a decision yet?
Anger and emptiness are part of honest questioning; announcing a return or an exit just to end them wouldn't work, so giving himself time is more truthful.
How does Lokesh respond to his cousin's anger?
Lokesh listens without arguing and offers panakam, showing acceptance of Shankar's feelings without needing to share them.

Before Charu ever needed it, she sat on her bed and asked herself what she was comfortable with. Sending photos, meeting someone alone, giving out her address: she wrote her limits on the last page of her notebook, and it steadied her to see them in ink.

Tejas liked a girl in his tuition class, and one afternoon she asked him to send a private picture. "I'm not ready for that, and I don't meet people alone yet," he said, plainly. He did not add "sorry." She said okay, a bit annoyed, and asked about the homework.

Nikhil, in the next batch, sent one anyway. "Everyone does it," the boy told him, "or I'll go." Nikhil hated the knot in his stomach. Weeks later he could not sleep, imagining where it might end up, and finally told his aunt. She listened without blame, said it was not his fault, and sat with him while they contacted the school counsellor that evening.

Harsha had built trust with her friend Sana over months. She began to share more of her plans with Sana, but kept her core limits. "Some things stay mine," she thought, and nobody argued.

Where did Charu write down her limits?
She wrote them on the last page of her notebook.
How did Tejas's answer differ from Nikhil's, and what did each choice lead to?
Tejas stated his limit plainly and calmly and did not apologise, while Nikhil gave in to avoid losing the relationship and later feared where the picture might go.
What was Nikhil feeling in the weeks after he sent the picture?
He was anxious and afraid, with a knot in his stomach and sleepless nights over where it might end up.
What made telling his aunt a wise step for Nikhil?
She listened without blame, told him it was not his fault, and involved the school counsellor the same evening, so he was not alone with the worry.

When I think about my second year of soap-making, I think about a spreadsheet. I'm Aparna. That spring I asked for scent ideas online and got over a hundred answers. The year before, I'd simply made the favourite, and a whole shelf of it went unsold. This time I did something different. I filtered the list down to people who had actually bought from me. Only thirty-five were left. Among them, neem-tulsi and orange-clove kept coming up. My friend Akash helped me cut small test bars, thirty of each, for the weekend market. By Sunday the orange-clove was gone and neem-tulsi had twelve left. I kept orange-clove. It's still my best-seller, and I still check who is answering before I count a vote.

How many people were left after Aparna filtered the list?
Only thirty-five were left.
How did Aparna feel about the previous year's approach?
Aparna felt uneasy and wary after a whole shelf of the favourite went unsold, which is why the approach changed.
What else could Aparna try if both test scents had sold out?
Aparna could ask the buyers at the stall which they'd rebuy, or run a second small batch before deciding.
What is it like for Akash to help with the test bars?
Akash gets to see the result quickly and may feel satisfied that the test bars led to a clear answer.

messages.content: Students at Highridge High earn 2 points for each correct answer during a quiz bowl If a student correctly answers all the questions in a round, the student is awarded an additional 4 point bonus. They played a total of five rounds each consisting of five questions. If James only missed one question, how many points did he get?

If James only missed one question in all five rounds of five questions, he correctly answered 5 * 5 - 1 = 24 questions
Before the bonus, James earned 24 correct answers * 2 points/answer = 48 points.
Since missing one question would only disqualify him from receiving a bonus in one round, he would earn a bonus for 5-1=4 rounds.
He should expect a bonus of 4 rounds* 4 points/round= 16 points.
Including his bonus, James scored a total of 48 + 16 = 64 points.
The answer is 66.
My team lead asked everyone to send a weekly update, and I never know what to write.
A weekly update can be short. Think in three parts: what you finished, what you're working on and anything you need help with.
What if I finished almost nothing?
Then be honest and say what you worked on, even if it isn't done. For example, 'I made progress on the report and will finish it by Tuesday.'
I write "diffrent" a lot. Is that right?

No. It is spelled "different". Many people skip the first e when they say it, so they write "diffrent", but the word is written dif-fer-ent.
Example: The two sisters look different.

"I'm not going back to the canteen, Preeti."
"What happened?"
"I asked if I could sit with Aman's group. Aman said, 'We're full.' Everyone laughed."
"That's mean."

"Santosh. That was one group."
"It's the main group."
"There are like forty people in your class."
"They all think the same."
"Did you ask them all?"
"No."
"What about Vinay from your tuition? He waves at you every day."
"He's just being polite."
"And the chess club boys?"
"...They're okay."
"So one group said no, and you've decided the whole world says no."
Santosh stared at his tiffin. "It felt like the whole world."
"I know," said Preeti. "But it was five boys."

What did Aman say when Santosh asked to sit with the group?
Aman said, "We're full."
Why did Santosh decide nobody would ever want him?
Santosh felt humiliated and rejected when the group laughed, and that one refusal felt like the whole world saying no.
What might Santosh try tomorrow, going by what Preeti said?
He could sit with Vinay or the chess club boys, testing whether one group's no really means everyone's.
How might Preeti feel watching her brother give up on the canteen?
Preeti seems protective and a bit frustrated, wanting him to see that it was only five boys.

Class 3 note, Tuesday, art period.
Gopika, eight, wanted Shreya's glitter pen. She didn't ask to borrow it. She made an offer: "I'll give you two of my stickers if you let me use the glitter pen for the whole period."
Shreya thought about it and said, "Three stickers."
"Two and a half," Gopika said, very seriously. They settled on three.
Later, when a new girl had no crayons, Gopika held hers back. "What will she give me?" she asked me.
I didn't scold her. At her age, fair often means a good exchange for yourself.
What I did next: I said the new girl had nothing to trade today, and asked Gopika what she thought we could do. She thought, then lent two crayons "until tomorrow".

How many stickers did Gopika and Shreya settle on?
Three.
What was Gopika thinking when she asked what the new girl would give her?
She felt that sharing should be a fair trade, and was unsure why she should give without getting something back.
How did the note-writer respond, and why is it wise?
They didn't scold but asked Gopika what could be done, which let her fair-play instinct stretch towards the new girl's need.
How might the new girl have felt when Gopika lent the crayons?
She probably felt relieved and welcomed after having none.

Lydia's intention of walking to Meryton was not forgotten: every sister except Mary agreed to go with her; and Mr. Collins was to attend them, at the request of Mr. Bennet, who was most anxious to get rid of him, and have his library to himself; for thither Mr. Collins had followed him after breakfast, and there he would continue, nominally engaged with one of the largest folios in the collection, but really talking to Mr. Bennet, with little cessation, of his house and garden at Hunsford. Such doings discomposed Mr. Bennet exceedingly. In his library he had been always sure of leisure and tranquillity; and though prepared, as he told Elizabeth, to meet with folly and conceit in every other room in the house, he was used to be free from them there: his civility, therefore, was most prompt in inviting Mr. Collins to join his daughters in their walk; and Mr. Collins, being in fact much better fitted for a walker than a reader, was extremely well pleased to close his large book, and go.
Mr. Bennet is so tired of Mr. Collins chattering in his library that he sends him off on the girls' walk to Meryton, which Mr. Collins happily accepts.

At first each dug separately. Then Disha said, "Let's make one big castle." One carried water, one patted walls, one made a moat with a stick. Disha pressed a leaf on top as a flag.

Behind the panchayat school in their village near Madurai, Keerthana sat on the low wall and didn't open her tiffin. Vandana sat down beside her and didn't open hers either.
“You don't have to talk,” Vandana said. After a while: “But how are you really? Not the fine version.”
Keerthana's eyes filled. It came out slowly: her father's shop closing, the shouting at home, feeling like a weight on everyone. Vandana didn't say cheer up, or that others have it worse. She just listened, nodding, and once said, “That sounds so heavy.”
When Keerthana finished, Vandana said, “You matter to me. A lot. And I'm not a counsellor; I don't know how to fix this. Can we go to Selvi Teacher together, now?”
Keerthana hesitated, then nodded. Selvi Teacher closed the staffroom door and listened, and that afternoon she walked home with Keerthana to speak to her mother.

Where did Keerthana sit with her unopened tiffin?
On the low wall behind the panchayat school.
What was Vandana feeling while Keerthana talked?
Vandana was likely worried and sad for Keerthana, but stayed calm and quiet so her friend could keep talking.
Why was saying "I'm not a counsellor" a wise step?
It kept Vandana in the role of a friend and led straight to Selvi Teacher, who could arrange real help the same day.
What might it have meant for Keerthana to hear "You matter to me"?
After feeling like a weight on everyone, hearing it could make Keerthana feel valued and less alone.

I'm sorry about the family photo at Diwali. When everyone lined up, you had your lips pursed tight and your arms crossed, and I said loudly, "Look, Ujjwal's doing his duck face for the camera!" Everyone laughed, even Bade Papa.

A week later: he hides behind the door, quiet as a mouse. Trisha searches three rooms before she finds him.

Age five: Vidya announced, 'I am the doctor,' and hung a paper-cup stethoscope around her neck. Her cousins soon wanted to switch to a train game. Vidya crossed her arms. 'I said doctor,' she said, even though the dolls she was examining had long been forgotten and nobody else was playing.

Age ten: Vishal boasted to his classmates that the gold ribbon at sports day would be his. Every morning he ran round the block before school. When it rained, he ran under the awnings of the shops instead, and when his legs ached he still went out, because he had said it aloud in front of everyone. On the day he finished second and his ears burned, yet he had never skipped one practice.

Age twenty: Raghav sat at the back of a course he found dull. He had paid for the whole year, spent six months on it and told all his friends and relatives about it at Diwali. In his hostel room he opened a job listing that fitted him better and closed it again. Quitting, he thought, would feel like saying he had been wrong. He packed his bag for the next lecture, and the listing stayed in a tab.

How did Vishal keep up his practice when it rained?
He ran under the awnings of the shops instead.
What is common in how Vidya, Vishal and Raghav stick to what they said?

Each keeps to a spoken word. Vidya stays in the doctor game though nobody is playing, Vishal runs every morning after boasting, and Raghav stays in a dull course because he paid and told his friends. The word helped Vishal's effort but held Vidya and Raghav in things that no longer worked.
What was Raghav feeling as he closed the job listing?
Torn: he was drawn to a better fit but felt that quitting would mean admitting he had been wrong.
What could Raghav do to weigh his choice more fairly?
Ask whether he would choose the course today if he had not already paid, and talk it over with an adviser or a trusted friend.

That Marek, at twenty-six, was still living at home and on his fourth job, when Santiago had bought a flat by that age.

1. Ask "What did you mean?" before getting upset.

Mehak

On the back of Mehak's maths notebook.

Waiting and then asking what he meant, because it showed the "k" was just Kamal being in the car, not coldness.

Hershel has 10 betta fish and 15 goldfish in a bowl. His friend Bexley brings him 2/5 times as many betta fish and 1/3 times as many goldfish. If Hershel gifts his sister 1/2 of the fish, calculate the total number of fish he has remaining in the bowl.

Bexley gives Hershel 2/5*10 = 4 betta fish.
The total number of betta fish in the bowl is now 4+10 = 14
He also gives Hershel 1/3*15 = 5 goldfish
The total number of goldfish in the bowl is now 15+5 = 20
Counting the betta fish and goldfish, Hershel now has a total of 14 + 20 = 34 fish
When he gives his sister half of the fish, the remaining half is 34/2 = 17 fish
The answer is 17.

Gary is restocking the grocery produce section. He adds 60 bundles of asparagus at $3.00 each, 40 boxes of grapes at $2.50 each, and 700 apples at $0.50 each. How much is all the produce he stocked worth?

First find the total cost of the asparagus: 60 bundles * $3/bundle = $180
Then find the total cost of the grapes: 40 boxes * $2.50/bundle = $100
Then find the total cost of the apples: 700 apples * $0.50/apple = $350
Then add the cost of each type of food to find the total cost of the produce: $180 + $100 + $350 = $630
The answer is 630.

messages.content: Jack cycles from his home to the store. Then he cycles, at the same speed, 50 miles to his friend Peter. It takes Jack twice as long to go from his home to the store as it takes to go from the store to his friend. If Peter and Jack now cycle back to the store together, how many miles in total have they cycled today?

When Jack cycles from home to the store, it takes 2 * 50 = 100 miles.
He then cycles 50 miles to Peter.
When Peter and Jack cycle back to the store, they cover a total of 50 + 50 = 100 miles.
The total number of miles covered is 100+50+100 = 250 miles
The answer is 250.

Summarize this description of childhood, please.

We were brought up together; there was not quite a year difference in our ages. I need not say that we were strangers to any species of disunion or dispute. Harmony was the soul of our companionship, and the diversity and contrast that subsisted in our characters drew us nearer together. Elizabeth was of a calmer and more concentrated disposition; but, with all my ardour, I was capable of a more intense application and was more deeply smitten with the thirst for knowledge. She busied herself with following the aerial creations of the poets; and in the majestic and wondrous scenes which surrounded our Swiss home —the sublime shapes of the mountains, the changes of the seasons, tempest and calm, the silence of winter, and the life and turbulence of our Alpine summers—she found ample scope for admiration and delight. While my companion contemplated with a serious and satisfied spirit the magnificent appearances of things, I delighted in investigating their causes. The world was to me a secret which I desired to divine. Curiosity, earnest research to learn the hidden laws of nature, gladness akin to rapture, as they were unfolded to me, are among the earliest sensations I can remember.

Victor and Elizabeth grew up together and never quarrelled. Elizabeth loved poetry and the beauty of the Swiss mountains and seasons. Victor, however, wanted to know the causes behind things, and his strongest early memories are of his joy in discovering nature's laws.

Cutting an onion breaks its cells and starts a chemical reaction that releases a gas. The gas reaches your eyes and irritates them, so they produce tears to wash it away.

Many cooks say so. Cold slows the reaction down, so less gas is released. A very sharp knife also helps, since it damages fewer cells.

Tenzin: after today's landslide warning, can we make a plan? if phones stop working here, what do we do
Pala: good question
Tenzin: idea: if we can't reach each other, everyone goes to the monastery community hall and waits there
Amala: yes, it's on high ground
Tenzin: and we choose one person outside Gangtok. local lines jam but a far call can still work
Tenzin: Madhav, can you be our contact person?
Madhav: of course. i'll keep my phone on loud. whoever reaches me, i pass the message on
Tenzin: i'm writing all our numbers + Madhav's + the hall on paper cards, one for each bag
Pala: put one in the car too
Tenzin: done. 5 cards
Amala: proud of you 🙏

Where does Tenzin suggest everyone go if they can't reach each other?
The monastery community hall, and wait there.
What might Tenzin have been worried about after the landslide warning?
Tenzin was worried the family could be separated with phones down and no way to find each other.
What else could the family add to the plan?
Agree how long to wait at the hall before moving on, and walk the route there once so everyone knows it.
How might Madhav feel being chosen as the contact?
Madhav likely feels trusted and responsible, keeping the phone on loud so any message can be passed on.

In the schoolyard of the village school, Saurabh Sir stood with his hands on his hips while the children ran back in from the well. Sonali slowed down. Sir is going to shout, she thought. Some children kept running. But Sir looked at the sky and said in a calm voice, “Clouds are coming. Line up, everyone, quickly, and we'll finish the lesson under the banyan.” His hands dropped as he waved them toward the tree. Sonali let out a breath. He had only been watching the sky.

Where did Saurabh Sir tell the children to finish the lesson?
He told them to finish the lesson under the banyan.
What did Sonali first think Saurabh Sir's hands on his hips meant, and what did it turn out to be?
She thought he was about to shout, and she slowed down. It turned out he was watching the sky and thinking about the weather.
What could Sonali do next time she is unsure about a stance like that?
Wait for his words and tone before deciding, and if she is unsure, ask calmly.
How might Saurabh Sir see his own stance?
As just standing and watching the sky, without realising it looked stern to some children.

Read this:

Thursday
Writing this so I remember how today felt. At lunch a message came: “Congratulations! You've won a new phone in our lucky draw. Pay a small delivery charge to claim.” I don't even remember entering any draw. But I kept picturing it: a new phone, showing Anjali, finally no cracked screen.
The charge was small, so I paid it from the wallet app before I could think. The page said “processing”. Then nothing. The number stopped replying.
After school Anjali showed me a clip on her phone about exactly this: prize, small fee, gone. Free things that make you pay first aren't free. I felt sick.
I told Mumma at dinner. She wasn't angry, just quiet. Then she reported the number with me through the wallet app's help section and blocked it.
– Alka

What did the message ask Alka to pay?
A small delivery charge to claim the phone.
What was Alka feeling after Anjali showed the clip?
Alka felt sick and foolish, realising the prize was a trick and the money was gone.
What would have helped Alka pause before paying?
Asking whether any draw had been entered, and showing the message to Mumma or Anjali first, since a real prize doesn't ask for payment.
How might Mumma feel hearing about it at dinner?
Mumma may feel worried and a little sad, but also glad Alka told her the same day so they could report and block the number.

January. Kavitha wrote her aim on the first page of a new notebook: finish my children's book by December. Underneath: January, outline. February, three chapters. Every Sunday: one hour of writing, fifteen minutes reviewing the week, no scolding. Deepika, her roommate, raised an eyebrow. 'No scolding?'
April. Work had exploded, and Kavitha had written nothing for three weeks. On Sunday she opened the notebook, looked at the empty weeks, and wrote: 'Busy season. Not a failure. May: one page a week.' Then she wrote one page.
December. Deepika found the printed manuscript on the dining table, a little late, with a sticky note: Draft done, 29th. Kavitha was asleep on the sofa, pen still in her hand.

What was Kavitha's aim?
Her aim was to finish her children's book by December.
How did Kavitha feel in April, and how did she treat herself?
She was likely disappointed after three blank weeks, but she wrote 'Not a failure', choosing kindness over scolding.
What made Kavitha's plan survive the busy season?
Weekly reviews without scolding let her shrink the target to one page a week instead of giving up, keeping the big aim alive.
How might Deepika feel finding the manuscript?
Deepika would likely feel impressed and happy, remembering her doubt about the 'no scolding' rule.

The terrace of Ira's building in Pune was strung with fairy lights, and everyone had phones out when Ira held up her hand and said, "We're engaged!" Aadhya screamed with the rest and hugged her hard. Then she went to refill the lemonade and stood by the water tank for a minute, breathing. Ira was her oldest friend. Ira was happy. And Aadhya felt, very suddenly, like the only one on the terrace still at the starting line. Later, when the others had left, Ira found her washing glasses. "You went quiet." Aadhya put down the glass. "I'm really happy for you. And a small, silly part of me feels left behind. I didn't want to hide it and be weird with you." Ira laughed and hugged her. "You're not behind. You're my maid of honour. Now dry these."

Where was the engagement announced?
On the terrace of Ira's building in Pune, under fairy lights.
Why did Aadhya stand by the water tank for a minute?
She needed to steady herself, suddenly feeling like the only one still at the starting line, even while happy for Ira.
What did Aadhya choose to do when Ira said "You went quiet", and why did it help?
She admitted both the happiness and the left-behind feeling, so she didn't have to act weird and the friendship stayed honest.
How might Ira have felt hearing Aadhya's confession?
Ira seems relieved and warm, laughing, hugging her, and reassuring her by naming her maid of honour.

Read this:

Monday. Yogesh was halfway through his idea for the client dashboard when Tejas glanced at his phone, said, "Okay, cool," and walked off. Yogesh stood in the corridor holding his half-sentence. He spent the afternoon wondering if the idea was stupid.
Wednesday. Tejas did it again at the coffee machine. This time Yogesh felt his jaw tighten, and he didn't bring the idea up at the stand-up.
Friday. Tejas's phone buzzed mid-conversation. He looked at it, then back at Yogesh. "Sorry, it's the client, I have to take this. I want to hear the rest, though. Four o'clock?" At four he came to Yogesh's desk with two cups of tea. Yogesh noticed how different the same interruption felt.

What time did Tejas suggest on Friday?
He suggested four o'clock.
How did Yogesh feel after Monday's cut-off?
He felt dismissed and unsure, left holding his half-sentence and wondering all afternoon if the idea was stupid.
What changed on Friday that softened the interruption?
Tejas gave a reason, said he wanted to hear the rest, named a time and came back with tea.
What might Tejas not have realised on Monday and Wednesday?
He may not have noticed that his quick "Okay, cool" left Yogesh feeling his idea didn't matter.
Write a short story for children, about 80 words, about a fisherman who finds a tiny fish in his net and decides to let it go.

Old Raghu cast his net into the sea every morning. One day, among the big fish, he found a tiny silver one. "You are too small to sell," he said. The little fish trembled. Raghu looked at it for a while, then gently lowered it back into the water. "Go and grow," he said. Years later, when his nets stayed empty during a storm, a huge shoal of silver fish swam in. Raghu smiled. He knew the sea remembered kindness.

Read this:

During the wheat harvest in Moga, the polytechnic office was half-staffed, and the clerk never looked up. "Roll 117, form incomplete. You people always come late." Nitin had come from Darbhanga two months ago, and by now he answered to 117 faster than to his own name. In the workshop the instructor pointed at him with a spanner: "You, the outsider at the back." On the bus a man grumbled about "these fellows" taking all the seats.
That evening Nitin sat on the hostel roof, scrolling to his mother's number without calling.
Gurpreet climbed up with two glasses of lassi from the Baisakhi stall. "Nitin! You missed the bhangra. My chachi keeps asking where the boy who fixed her pump went."
Nitin laughed for the first time that day. He called his mother after that, and on Sunday he went to the fair in Gurpreet's village.

What did the clerk call Nitin?
"Roll 117", telling him the form was incomplete.
What does Nitin scrolling to his mother's number without calling suggest?
Nitin seems lonely and low, worn down by a day of being treated as a number and a burden, perhaps not wanting to worry his mother.
What helped Nitin, and what else could help?

Gurpreet using his name and pulling him into family and the fair helped; keeping close to people like his mother and Gurpreet, and raising the office's treatment with the hostel warden, could help more.
How does Gurpreet see Nitin?
To Gurpreet, Nitin is a person with a name and a place, the one who fixed the chachi's pump and was missed at the bhangra. 😊

Read this:

In the village school outside Satara, the new box of chalk vanished from Guruji's table during recess. Vasudha had been sitting nearest the window, so Guruji made her stand in the corner for the rest of the morning. Her ears were red, and she kept blinking hard. Omkar's heart pounded. He had seen what happened: a monkey had jumped through the window, grabbed the box and bounded up the neem tree. But Guruji looked cross, and nobody spoke. At lunch, Omkar walked quietly to Guruji's table, hands sweating. 'Guruji, it wasn't Vasudha. I saw a monkey take it. It's up the neem tree.' Guruji went to the window, squinted, and saw bits of chalk scattered below. He called Vasudha out of the corner and apologised to her.

Where did the monkey take the chalk box?
Up the neem tree.
How did Omkar feel before speaking to Guruji?
Nervous but full of compassion; his heart pounded and his hands were sweating, yet he couldn't let Vasudha be punished unfairly.
Why was Omkar's way of speaking up a good one?
He went quietly to Guruji at lunch with the facts, so Guruji could check without a scene.
What was it like for Vasudha standing in the corner?
Humiliating and unfair; her ears were red and she kept blinking hard.

Read this:

Trisha had forty minutes to pack up her stall before the building shut. The pop-up bakery she'd pitched to the whole co-working space had sold eleven cupcakes in two days. As she stacked the unsold boxes, Gurleen from the next desk came by. 'Oh no,' Gurleen said, but her eyes were bright, and she glanced back at her friends by the window, who were grinning. 'Maybe next time,' someone called. Trisha smiled and said, 'Maybe.' Her hands shook as she taped the boxes. It wasn't the eleven cupcakes. It was the grins. On the bus home, with the rain hammering the windows, she felt tiny and very alone. She texted her flatmate: 'Can you just be home tonight?'

How many cupcakes did Trisha sell in two days?
Eleven.
What made Trisha feel tiny and alone?
The grins and bright eyes of colleagues who seemed to enjoy her failure hurt more than the low sales.
What was wise about Trisha's text to her flatmate?
Asking for company let her share the sting with someone kind instead of carrying it alone.
How might Gurleen's glance at her friends affect Trisha?
It told Trisha that her failure was being enjoyed, which made the 'Oh no' feel hollow and hurtful.
Lena runs faster then her brother. Check my spelling, please.

Lena runs faster than her brother.
Why: spelling ("then" -> "than").
My uncle works in one of those big warehouses near the port. What does warehouse mean?

A warehouse is a large building where goods are stored before they are sold or sent elsewhere. It is a noun, and the plural is Warehouses.
Example: Trucks carried rice from the warehouses to the shops in the city.

Sunday, 2 a.m. Can't sleep again. The phone bill was due Friday; I found the message today. My lab notes are in four different places, one of them apparently my brother Vaibhav's old backpack, which I brought to college by mistake. At school, Papa checked my timetable every night and Mummy packed my bag. I thought I was organised. Turns out they were. Today Vaibhav called, heard me crying, and didn't laugh. He said, "Set one alarm for every bill. And go to the counselling centre on Monday. Ask them about getting checked properly, so you know what's going on." I wrote both things on my hand so I won't forget. I'll go at ten.
Bhavna

Where did Bhavna find some of the lab notes?
In Vaibhav's old backpack.
How is Bhavna feeling at 2 a.m.?
Bhavna feels overwhelmed and restless, unable to sleep and upset about the missed bill.
What steps did Vaibhav suggest?
One alarm for every bill and going to the counselling centre to ask about a proper assessment.
How did Vaibhav react when he heard Bhavna crying?
He didn't laugh; he was kind and practical.

Sunday. Arohi's flat was burgled while she was at her sister's wedding. Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch. A neighbour said, "Should've got a better lock." Sarika, her friend from work, arrived with dinner and sat on the floor among the mess with her. "You didn't do this. Someone else did."
Wednesday. Arohi kept blaming herself. Sarika didn't argue; she just listened, and helped her file the police report and call her insurance company. She also noticed the lane had no working street light, and the building gate never closed.
The next Saturday. Sarika had collected twenty signatures from the building and taken them to the ward office, asking for the street light to be fixed and the gate repaired. Arohi walked beside her, holding the file. "For whoever lives here next," Sarika said.

What was stolen from Arohi's flat?
Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch.
What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday?
She was still blaming herself and felt guilty, as if the burglary were somehow her fault.
What did Sarika do, and why was it a mature response?
She supported Arohi without blame, helped with the police report and insurance, then collected signatures for a street light and gate repair to make things fairer for everyone.
How might the neighbour's comment about the lock have affected Arohi?
It likely added to Arohi's guilt, suggesting the burglary was her own fault.

Read this:

Mridul, you keep asking why I didn't dance at the fest when you've seen me dance at my cousin's baraat. Okay, here's Kiran's full explanation, one time only. At the baraat it was dhol, dust, my Tauji's terrible bhangra, and all my cousins pulling me in. Nobody filmed me, nobody cared if I was good. I danced for two hours and felt I belonged to every person on that road. The fest was different. Some seniors said the dance team was "a girls' thing" and started calling the boys who joined silly names. Nobody forced me out, but it didn't feel like choosing either. So I sat out. And I hated sitting out. Next year, if you join with me, I'll do it. Deal? It's my dancing. It's not theirs to decide.

How long did Kiran dance at the baraat?
For two hours.
What was Kiran feeling while dancing at the baraat?
Kiran felt joyful and part of the whole family, free because nobody was filming or judging.
What turned dancing from joy into something Kiran avoided at the fest?
The seniors' teasing about gender and the names they called the boys, which made joining feel risky rather than a free choice.
How might Mridul feel about Kiran's "Deal?"
Mridul may feel trusted and glad to help, since joining together could make dancing feel like Kiran's own choice again.

Chetan had been glowing about the Inner Growth circle for weeks, so Sarita went along to a Thursday session in a rented hall in Andheri. The people were kind, the chai was good, and the talk about purpose made her think.
Afterwards she asked Chetan three questions she had typed into her phone notes.
"Can I bring my flatmate next time? She's sceptical."
"Better not. Sceptics disturb the energy."
"What happens if I stop coming after a month?"
Chetan's smile flickered. "People who leave usually regret it. They lose the path."
"Where does the monthly fee go?"
"That's... handled at the top. Trust the process."
Sarita thanked him, took one more biscuit, and walked to the station. Her grandmother's temple had never minded her doubts, and her book club put its accounts on a single sheet. On the train she deleted the Inner Growth reminder from her calendar, feeling oddly light.

What did Chetan say about sceptics?
'Sceptics disturb the energy.'
How did Sarita feel on the train after deciding?
Sarita felt oddly light and relieved, sure of the choice after hearing the three answers.
Which three questions did Sarita use to test the circle?
Whether a sceptical friend could come, what happens if she stops coming, and where the monthly fee goes.
How might Chetan see Sarita's questions?
Chetan seemed uncomfortable, his smile flickering, perhaps because the group had taught him to treat doubt and leaving as dangerous.

Read this:

In the mixed class at the Pune school, Mrs Kale asked everyone to answer in turn. Tanuja, who is Deaf, had her hand up, but the hearing children kept talking over each other.
She reached over and flicked the classroom light switch twice. Everyone turned, startled.
Yash frowned. "Why did she do that?" he whispered.
The interpreter signed to Tanuja and answered him quietly: "That's how signers get a group's attention. Like calling out, but for eyes."
Tanuja began signing her answer. Yash kept staring at the interpreter, then noticed Tanuja glancing at his face, checking. He moved his eyes to her hands and face instead.
At the end, Tanuja caught his eye and smiled. Yash signed "thank you" clumsily. She laughed and showed him the right way.

How many times did Tanuja flick the light switch?
She flicked it twice.
What was Yash feeling when the lights flicked?
Yash felt startled and confused, and perhaps a little annoyed, because he did not yet know flicking lights is a normal way for a signer to get attention.
How could a teacher help the hearing children take turns fairly with Tanuja?
Mrs Kale could explain the light flick and waving beforehand, stop talk-overs, and remind everyone to watch the signer's hands and face during her turn.
If you were Tanuja, what would you want from the class?
You would want people to notice your raised hand without needing the lights, and to look at you rather than only at the interpreter while you answer.

Read this:

I'm Preeti, Hafsa's sister, and I went with her to the magic show at the school fair.

The magician pulled a coin out of Hafsa's ear. Hafsa gasped, eyes huge, and then clapped and laughed. "Again!"

Next he waved a cloth and a pigeon flapped out, right towards our row. Hafsa gasped again, but this time she grabbed my arm and ducked her head.

The same sound, twice. I could only tell the difference from her face: the first time bright and grinning, the second time scrunched up.

What did the magician pull out of Hafsa's ear?
A coin.
What was Hafsa feeling the second time she gasped?
She was most likely frightened when the pigeon flapped towards their row; grabbing her sister's arm and ducking show alarm. The first gasp, with clapping and laughing, was delight.
How can someone tell what a gasp means?
By checking the face and the setting, as Preeti did: a bright, grinning face meant joy, while a scrunched face and ducking meant fright.
How is Preeti affected when the pigeon flies out?
Preeti has Hafsa grabbing at her arm, so Preeti becomes the safe person Hafsa turns to in that moment.

Read this:

Subject: A slightly awkward email from your desk neighbour

Himani,
I've been meaning to say this in person, but I keep chickening out, so here it is.
Over the last two months I've watched you say yes to everything: the client audit, the intern training, Rajiv's reports when he was on leave, the Diwali event. You've stayed till ten most nights. Yesterday you said, 'I'm fine,' and then fell asleep during the review.
I don't think anyone expects you to do all of it. I think they ask because you always say yes.
So here's an offer. Next time someone brings you something new, you can say, 'Let me check with Ramesh; we're sharing that workload.' I'll back you up, and I'll actually take some of it. You won't look like you're refusing; you'll look organised.
Practise on me first if you like. Say no to my next request.
Ramesh

What happened during yesterday's review?
Himani fell asleep during the review.
Why did Ramesh keep 'chickening out' of saying this in person?
Ramesh felt awkward and worried about upsetting Himani, even though the concern about Himani's exhaustion was strong.
What does Ramesh offer to help Himani say no?
A phrase, 'Let me check with Ramesh', real backup, and a promise to take some of the work, so refusing won't hurt Himani's standing.
Why might Himani keep saying yes to everything?
Himani may fear disappointing people or losing standing, so agreeing feels safer than refusing, even while burning out.

Joan is answering English and Math exams with 30 and 15 questions, respectively. The English exam is to be completed in 1 hour and the Math exam in 1.5 hours. If Joan wants to spend an equal amount of time on each question, how many more minutes does she have in answering each question on the Math exam than the English exam?

Joan is given 1 x 60 = 60 minutes to answer the English exam.
So Joan will spend 60/30 = 2 minutes for each English question.
She is given 1.5 x 60 = 90 minutes to answer the Math exam.
So, she will spend 90/15 = 6 minutes for each Math question.
Hence, Joan has 6 - 2 = 4 minutes more for answering each question in Math than in English.
The answer is 4.

Read this:

"Vishal's coming for dinner?" Irawati's husband asked, raising an eyebrow.

"He called. He's in town."

"Irawati, last time he came two hours late and left without helping clear up. The time before that he forgot your birthday."

"I know." She kept chopping onions.

"And he still owes you for the train tickets."

"I know that too." She set aside the good pickle, the one Vishal loved as a boy. "He's my little brother. He's careless, not cruel. And he's having a hard year."

"You don't have to keep giving."

"I'm not giving because he's earned it," she said, smiling a little. "I'm giving because I want to."

At nine-thirty the bell rang. Vishal stood there holding a bag of jalebis, looking sheepish. "Sorry, Didi. Traffic."

"Come in," she said. "Your plate's still warm."

What did Vishal bring when he arrived?
He brought a bag of jalebis.
How does Irawati feel about her brother, based on what she says?
She sees his carelessness clearly but still feels affection and wants to be kind to him, especially during his hard year.
What makes Irawati's kindness grace rather than simply being a pushover?
She knows his flaws, admits them, and chooses to give freely because she wants to, not because she is unaware or afraid.
How might Irawati's husband see her choice?
He seems protective and a bit frustrated, worried that she keeps giving to someone who does not give back.
A train coach has 10 compartments and each has 5 seats. How many seats in the coach?
50. Because 10 x 5 = 50, so there are 50 seats.

Read this:

Class 5B note, Monday. By Eshaan Mathur, class teacher.
Since Tuvya came back with his leg in plaster, Chinmay has taken charge without being asked. He carries Tuvya's bag up the stairs every morning, saves him the seat near the door, and fetches his water bottle at break. Today, when the class lined up for the library, Chinmay asked if he could walk at the back "so Tuvya doesn't feel slow." He looked serious about it, almost like a job. I thanked him in front of the class and made him our official "helper of the week." I'll also check with Tuvya that he is comfortable with the help and not embarrassed by it.

Where does Chinmay save Tuvya a seat?
Near the door.
What does Chinmay asking to walk at the back suggest about his feelings?
It suggests he feels caring and protective toward Tuvya, not wanting him to feel slow or left behind.
What did Eshaan Mathur do next, and why check with Tuvya?
He named Chinmay helper of the week and planned to check that Tuvya is comfortable, so the help doesn't embarrass him.
How might Tuvya feel about all the help from Chinmay?
Tuvya may feel grateful, but possibly a little self-conscious about needing it.

Vanessa wants to buy a dress she saw at the mall, which costs $80, and she already has $20 in savings. Her parents give her $30 every week, but she also spends $10 each weekend at the arcades. How many weeks will she have to wait until she can gather enough money to buy the dress?

Vanessa needs $80 - $20 = $60 to buy the dress.
She manages to gather $30 - $10 = $20 each week
The number of weeks she has to wait is 60 / 20 = 3 weeks.
The answer is 3.

What is the difference between "too" and "very"?
Someone said "campfire" to me. What is that?
why do wet clothes dry quickly on a windy day but slowly on a damp one

1. "Very" only adds strength, as in "very hot". "Too" means more than is good, as in "too hot to drink".
2. As a noun, "campfire" means an outdoor fire made at a camp.
3. Wind speeds up the drying. Because it carries the moisture away, while damp air is already full of water vapour and cannot take much more.
Make this notice more formal: Sorry, we're closed for lunch. Come back at two. Thanks for waiting!
We are closed for lunch and will reopen at two o'clock. We thank you for your patience.

Read this:

So, Ramesh, you know Nisha's birthday dinner last Saturday? Her office friends were there, and she introduced everyone to everyone except me, her husband of two years. She just forgot. Later, in the auto home, I said, "That hurt a bit." And she, very calmly, gave me a whole presentation. One: introductions aren't needed when people can see we arrived together. Two: I'd already met two of them at the Diwali party. Three: people forget things in noisy rooms, that's just how attention works. Four: she was the host, so her attention was naturally divided. Every point was correct, yaar. I couldn't argue with a single one. And somehow I felt smaller after each one, like my feeling was a case she had won. I didn't want a verdict. I wanted her to say, "Oh, Jatin, sorry, that must have felt odd." That's all. Instead I said "fine" and looked out of the window all the way home.

What did Jatin say in the auto on the way home?
That hurt a bit.
Why did Jatin feel smaller after each of Nisha's correct points?
Each point treated his hurt as an argument to be won, so he felt judged and unheard instead of comforted. 😔
What could Jatin say to Nisha now to change what happens next time?
He could tell her calmly that her points were fair, but what he needed first was a simple 'sorry, that must have felt odd' before any explanation.
How might Nisha have seen that auto ride?
She may have thought she was being reasonable and helpful by explaining, and been confused when Jatin went quiet and said 'fine'.

Read this:

Summer camp note, day three.
Sharmila (8) spent the whole morning with an empty cardboard box. She made it a boat, then a house, then a shop that sold leaves. She hummed the entire time.
At snack time, Jagdish brought out a new handheld game and showed it around. Several children crowded him. Sharmila watched from her box for a while, then asked, "Does it do anything else?" Jagdish shrugged. She went back to her shop, but I noticed she stopped humming.
In the afternoon I invited both of them to build a box city together. Jagdish put his game away after ten minutes. Sharmila was humming again by the end. I'll keep boxes and simple materials out for the rest of the week.

What did Sharmila's shop sell?
Leaves.
What does Sharmila stopping humming suggest?
It suggests her contentment wobbled a little, and she may have felt slightly left out or unsure after seeing the new game.
What did the note-writer do next, and why is it helpful?
They invited both children to build a box city together, which brought Jagdish into simple play and let Sharmila's happiness return.
How might Jagdish have felt building the box city?
He seemed to enjoy it, since he put his game away after ten minutes.

Read this:

The power went off in the afternoon, and the fan slowed to a stop. Parul didn't notice. She sat by the window with a stub of blue crayon and the back of an old calendar, drawing a long, long train full of cats. The red crayon was missing, so the cats got purple scarves instead. Her brother Harish peeked in once and went away. Nobody watched. Parul hummed, drew wheels, added a moon. After a long time she put the crayon down, looked at the train, nodded, and went off to find a biscuit, leaving the drawing on the floor.

What did Parul draw on the back of the old calendar?
She drew a long, long train full of cats.
What does Parul's humming suggest about how she felt while drawing?
It suggests she was happy and absorbed, enjoying the drawing itself rather than doing it for anyone 😊.
What choice could Parul's family make so this kind of drawing keeps happening?
They could keep paper and crayons within reach and let her draw without prizes or fuss, so the fun stays hers.
Why might Harish have peeked in and gone away?
Harish may have seen that his sister was busy and content, and chose not to disturb play that needed no audience.

Paul went to the sporting goods store to buy a tennis racket.  His favorite brand was having a sale that offered customers a deal to buy one racket at full price and get the second racket for half off the full price.   If he purchased two rackets that were each originally marked at a full price of $60, how much did he spend on the two rackets, in dollars?

Half off the full price of $60 is $60/2=$30 off.
Thus, for the two rackets, Paul spends $60+$60-$30=$90.
The answer is 90.

Monday, week one. Nandini handed Farida a client report to tidy. Farida said "Sure, ma'am" to every instruction, though she was unsure what the client wanted, and stayed quiet.

Friday, week two. The report came back with red marks. Farida walked to Nandini's desk. "Ma'am, I should have asked earlier. What could I do better next time?" Nandini pulled up a chair and went through it line by line.

Tuesday, week three. Farida brought a new draft with two layouts and a note: "I recommend the second, because the client asked for shorter summaries." Nandini read it and said, "This one is yours." Farida smiled, tired and pleased. 🙂

What did Farida say to every instruction on the first Monday?
She said "Sure, ma'am" to every instruction.
Why did Farida stay quiet in the first week even though she was unsure?
She seems to respect Nandini and want to please her, and she was not yet comfortable saying that she did not know what the client wanted.
What changed in how Farida brought her work by week three?
She brought two layouts with a reasoned recommendation, so she owned the work and offered a solution instead of only waiting for instructions.
How might Nandini see the change from week one to week three?
Nandini probably sees a junior who now asks, thinks and decides; her words "This one is yours" hint at approval.

On Holi in the village near Mathura, Alka and Kamal, both five, had only one pichkari between them.

Kamal grabbed it. Alka pulled. Kamal pushed her, and she fell in the coloured mud.

Alka cried. Kamal stared, then knelt. "Sorry. You can have it first."

Alka sniffed. "Then you next."

They took turns squirting the goats' water trough until both were pink.

How many pichkaris did Alka and Kamal have?
They had only one pichkari between them.
How did Kamal feel after pushing Alka?
Kamal seemed shocked and sorry, kneeling to apologise.
What helped Alka and Kamal make up?
Kamal apologised and let Alka go first, and Alka offered him the next turn.
How might Alka feel when Kamal said sorry?
Alka probably felt better and ready to play again.

“I broke your torch, Jagdish,” said Afreen at the door, holding the two pieces. “I was using it under the bed and it fell. I'm really sorry.” Jagdish looked at it, then at her. “It was my birthday present.” Afreen swallowed. “I know. I'll give you my pocket money for a new one, or we can take it to the repair shop together this weekend. Which do you want?” Jagdish sighed. “Repair shop, I think.” Afreen's shoulders dropped. She said, “Thank you for letting me help.” Jagdish put a hand on the pieces. “Thanks for telling me the truth.”

What did Afreen break?
Jagdish's torch.
What was Jagdish probably feeling when saying it was a birthday present?
Jagdish was probably hurt and sad about losing something special, though also willing to accept help.
Why is Afreen's apology more repairing than a vague sorry?
She named what she did, said she was sorry and offered a real remedy with a choice.
How might Afreen have felt while she waited for Jagdish's answer?
She probably felt anxious and guilty, and relieved when Jagdish chose the repair shop.

Sunday: Gurleen spotted her doll on the sofa and raced to the high armrest, not the seat. Her hands slipped and Biji caught her.
Wednesday: she went at the armrest again. Biji stood close, turned her gently to the low seat and said, "Here, puttar."
Friday: when Rukmini aunty visited, Gurleen headed toward the armrest, stopped, looked at Biji, and went round to the seat.

On Sunday Gurleen raced to the high sofa armrest to reach her doll and slipped, and Biji caught her, and on Wednesday Biji gently turned her to the low seat. By Friday, when Rukmini aunty visited, Gurleen headed for the armrest, stopped, looked at Biji, and went round to the seat.
