At the primary school in a village near Bijapur, Yusuf had been sure since morning that Sangeeta was annoyed with him. She hadn't returned his "namaste" at the gate. She'd walked past his classroom without looking in. At lunch she sat at the far end of the verandah.

By two o'clock Yusuf had built a whole case in his head. It must be the mid-day meal register he'd filled in late on Monday. She'd complain to the block officer. She'd say, "Yusuf sir is careless," in the next meeting.

At three, instead of stewing through the last period, he walked over. "Sangeeta ma'am, is something wrong? Did I upset you?"

She looked up, surprised, a hand pressed to her cheek. "Upset? No, Yusuf sir. I've had a toothache since last night. I can barely see straight."

Yusuf laughed at himself all the way home.

Why had Sangeeta walked past without looking in?
Sangeeta had a toothache since the night before and could barely see straight.
What was Yusuf feeling by two o'clock?
Yusuf felt anxious and uneasy, sure Sangeeta was annoyed and building a whole story about complaints.
What did Yusuf's short question replace?
It replaced hours of imagined complaints and meetings with the simple truth: a toothache.
What was Sangeeta's day actually like?
Sangeeta was in pain from a toothache, too distracted to notice greetings, with no idea Yusuf was worried.

Parul's journalism tutorial was stuck on a short piece about a canteen price rise. The tutor, Harish, asked each student to underline facts in blue and opinions in red. Parul found "The price rose from twenty to twenty-five rupees" in blue, and "students are outraged" in red, since no one had been quoted. She raised her hand. "Who was asked? How many?" The writer, a classmate, admitted he'd asked two friends. Parul felt her worry about being blunt fade when Harish nodded and said that was the exact question. The writer went red but agreed to add a proper count and a line from the canteen manager.

What question does Parul ask about the canteen article, and why does it matter?
She asks who was asked and how many. The claim that students are outraged has no quotes, so it is only opinion. The writer had asked just two friends, so the piece needs a proper count.

Dear Sir or Madam,
My fee receipt shows the wrong name. Could you please correct it at your earliest convenience?
Thank you for your help.

At the Sonpur mela, the balloon seller was packing up. Simran Aunty, who ran the tea stall next door, called out to Arnab, “If you help me stack cups till the lights come on, I'll give you two balloons instead of one.”
Arnab, nine, shook his head. “One now, please.”
Aunty laughed. “Two is more!”
Arnab didn't smile. At last year's mela, a man had promised him a big-wheel ride for carrying water, then vanished. At school, prizes promised by the sir never came.
“One now,” he said again, quietly.
Aunty studied him, then gave him one balloon. “Here. Help me anyway, and I'll give you the second right after. I promise.”
Arnab stacked cups. At the end, she handed him the second balloon. He stared at it, surprised.

What did the man at last year's mela promise Arnab?
He promised a ride on the big wheel after Arnab carried water.
Why did Arnab insist on one balloon now?
He felt distrustful because adults had broken promises before, so taking the reward at once felt safer.
What did Simran Aunty do that could help Arnab learn to wait?
She gave one balloon right away and kept her small promise of the second, showing that waiting can pay.
How might Simran Aunty see Arnab's refusal of two balloons?
Simran Aunty is puzzled at first, then seems to understand he has been let down before, and responds with care instead of pressure.

At home in Malda for the holidays, Tanvir spread five semesters of marksheets on the floor of his room, next to the calendar his cousin Nitin had printed. "Something's not random," he muttered. He put a finger on each dip. Semester two: the dip matched the month he'd helped run the village youth club's football tournament. Semester four: the month he'd taken extra shifts at his uncle's phone repair shop during Durga Puja. Semester five, the failed one: he'd been building a website for the local school, late every night, right through exams. "It's not that I can't study," he told Nitin. "It's that I say yes to one more thing just when exams come." He marked the next two exam windows in red on the calendar. Above them he wrote: "No tournaments. No shop. No new projects." Then, smaller: "After exams, yes to everything."

What did Tanvir build in semester five?
A website for the local school.
How does Tanvir feel on spotting the pattern?
Tanvir feels relieved and a little surprised, seeing the dips came from extra commitments, not inability.
What else could Tanvir do before exam windows?
Tanvir could tell the youth club and his uncle the exam dates in advance, so saying no is easier when requests come.
How might Tanvir's uncle see the new plan?
His uncle may miss the extra help at festival time but would likely understand once he knows the exam dates.

Class teacher's note, Class 11B, 18 November
Jatin joined us in August from another city and has not been let into any group. This week I noticed a pattern. When Trisha's group came back late from the canteen, the class monitor, who is part of it, wrote nothing. When Jatin came in two minutes late on Wednesday, she wrote his name on the board. During the group presentation, Trisha's friends praised each other's slides and called Jatin's section "confusing," though it was the clearest. He sat very still afterwards and skipped lunch. Today he asked me quietly if he could do the next project alone. I said I would think about it. I will speak to the monitor about applying the late rule equally, and I will set the next groups myself.

What did the monitor do when Jatin came in two minutes late?
Wrote his name on the board.
Why did Jatin ask to do the next project alone?
He felt hurt and excluded, seeing the group excuse each other while judging his clear work as confusing.
What steps is the teacher taking, and why do they help?
Asking the monitor to apply the late rule equally and setting the next groups, so the same rules apply to all and Jatin isn't left outside.
How might Trisha's group see their comments on Jatin's section?
They may think they were being honest, without noticing they judged him more harshly than their own friends.

Friday, 1 a.m.

Can't sleep again. Rohit and I had our worst fight yet, about napkins. Napkins!
It isn't really about napkins. It started in October with a simple plan: one day, close family, the garden behind Rohit's parents' house. Then his Dadi wanted a proper sangeet. Then my Chachi wanted a cocktail night "for the younger ones". Then someone said a wedding without a horse would look cheap. Every time, we said yes, because saying no to elders felt rude.
Now it's three events, a horse, a DJ, and a budget that is double what we started with. Rohit's working weekends to cover it.
Noor asked me today, "Are you excited?" I didn't know what to say.
I used to daydream about this wedding. Now I just want it to be over.
— Preeti

Where was the wedding originally going to be held?
In the garden behind Rohit's parents' house.
How does Preeti feel about the wedding now?
Preeti feels drained and unhappy, unable to answer whether it is exciting and just wanting it to be over.
What would you change first in how Preeti and Rohit handled relatives' requests?
Agree together on a few non-negotiables and check each new request against them, saying no kindly when it doesn't fit.
What might Noor notice when Preeti can't answer the question?
Noor may sense that Preeti is stressed and unhappy, and might worry about how the planning is affecting Preeti and Rohit.

The day Keerthana's promotion to shift lead was pinned on the notice board of the Chennai call centre, Tenzin stopped saving her a seat in the canteen. They had trained together, covered each other's breaks, shared auto fares home for two years.
Keerthana felt the chill like a draught. She didn't post about the promotion. She also didn't say sorry for it.
At the Friday team meeting she said, "Half of what I know about calming angry callers, I learned from Tenzin's desk." Tenzin looked up, surprised, then looked away.
Keerthana kept things simple after that: a "good morning", a samosa left on Tenzin's desk on a long day, no pressure to talk. She guessed the distance might be about losing their old evenings together, not about hating her.
In the third week, Tenzin sat down across from her at lunch. "Pass the pickle."

How long had Keerthana and Tenzin shared auto fares home?
For two years.
What was Keerthana feeling when Tenzin stopped saving her a seat?
She felt a chill of hurt and sadness at the distance, like a draught, yet she did not feel she had to apologise.
How did Keerthana handle the friendship after her promotion?
She credited Tenzin publicly, didn't flaunt the promotion, stayed warm in small ways, and gave the friendship time without pressure.
How might Tenzin be feeling after the promotion?
Tenzin may feel envious and also sad about losing their old evenings together, which is why the coldness slowly eases.

On the playground in Manchester, two older boys flicked paper balls at Tariq and called him names. Tariq hunched his shoulders, ducked his head and covered his face with both arms. The boys laughed. Rosa, eating her apple on the bench, watched. The way he curled up didn't look weak or funny to her. It looked frightened, and hurt. She stood up. “Stop it,” she said, loud and steady. The boys shrugged and wandered off. Rosa walked to Tariq. “Come with me,” she said. “Let's tell Ms Hayes.” Tariq lowered his arms and nodded.

What did the older boys flick at Tariq?
They flicked paper balls at him.
What did Rosa read in Tariq's ducked head and covered face, and how sure can she be?
She read fear and hurt, not weakness. She cannot be completely sure, but the hunched shoulders and covered face fit that reading.
What did Rosa do that was a wise response?
She told the boys to stop, went to Tariq and took him to tell a teacher, instead of ignoring it or joining in.
How might Tariq feel when Rosa steps in?
Probably relieved and less alone, since he lowered his arms and nodded. He may still feel shaky or embarrassed.

Sunday. After lunch Uma washed the pile of steel plates, wiped the counter and folded the laundry, while her younger brother Mridul lay on the sofa with a game. Nobody asked him to help.
Wednesday. Uma made a small tick on the calendar in her room for each thing she had done and, next to it, a blank for Mridul. Her jaw was tight at dinner, but she said nothing.
The next Sunday, Papa noticed the calendar. He read it and was quiet. That evening he wrote a rota on the fridge: dishes on alternate days, laundry shared. "Mridul, you start," he said. Uma dried the plates beside him, lighter.

What did Uma tick on the calendar in her room?
Uma made a tick on the calendar for each thing she had done, and a blank next to it for Mridul.
What was Uma feeling on Wednesday at dinner, when she said nothing?
Uma was resentful and quietly hurt, since her jaw was tight, but she kept the feeling to herself.
What turning point led to a fairer arrangement?
Papa read the calendar, wrote a rota on the fridge with dishes on alternate days and laundry shared, and asked Mridul to start.
How might Mridul have seen the chores before the rota?
Mridul may not have noticed how much Uma was doing, since nobody had asked him to help and it felt normal to lie on the sofa.

When I moved to Melbourne at twenty-four, I thought the hard part would be the job. It wasn't. It was Sundays.
I'm Mehak. The first months were wonderful: the trams, the ocean, the feeling of being unknown. Then winter came, and I realised I hadn't spoken to anyone outside work in two weeks. I video-called my mother every day, but hung up feeling worse, because home looked warm and I wasn't there.
Then a colleague, Gurpreet, invited me to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb. I'm not Sikh, but she said, "Nobody asks. Just come and help cut onions." I went. I cut onions for three hours and laughed more than I had in months.
Looking back, I needed both: the calls home, and the onions here. One kept me rooted. The other let me grow.

Where did Gurpreet invite Mehak?
Gurpreet invited her to the gurdwara's Sunday langar near her suburb.
How did Mehak feel after the daily video calls?
Mehak felt lonely and homesick, hanging up feeling worse because home looked warm and Mehak wasn't there.
What helped Mehak build a steadier life abroad?
Joining Gurpreet at the langar gave Mehak local friendships and laughter, while calls home kept her rooted.
How might Gurpreet see her invitation?
Gurpreet probably saw it as a simple kindness, noticing a lonely colleague and welcoming her without any questions.
Her shadow gets tired of copying everything she does. Write a story about the girl and her shadow.

Lucy's shadow was tired. Every day, it had to copy whatever she did. She raised an arm, it raised an arm. She hopped, it hopped.

One bright afternoon, it stayed put when Lucy ran. She looked down and saw her shadow sitting on the pavement with its arms crossed.

"I want a rest," it said.

Lucy sat down. "Okay. What do you want to do?"

"Something that I choose," said the shadow.

Lucy let it go first. The shadow stretched long, then short, then wide. It danced across the wall. It made a rabbit, then an eagle. Lucy copied each pose.

They traded like that all afternoon, taking turns, and the shadow felt much better by sunset.

The corridor outside the staffroom smelled of chalk and floor polish. Himani stood holding her returned science quiz, a big red 10 out of 10 at the top, and stared at it. "You got the highest and you look like you swallowed a lemon," said Pallavi, joining her. Himani lowered her voice. "The last two answers weren't mine. I copied them from the girl in front. Nobody saw." Her stomach had been tight since Monday. "Then why does it still feel bad?" Pallavi asked. Himani took a breath and knocked on the staffroom door. "I'm going to tell Ma'am," she said, "and I'm not doing it again."

Where did Himani copy the last two answers from?
She copied them from the girl in front.
What does Himani's tight stomach suggest she feels about the copied answers?
It suggests she feels uneasy and guilty; it has bothered her since Monday even though nobody saw and the mark is high.
What could Himani do that is better than pretending nothing happened?
Own up to the teacher and decide not to copy again, which is what she is about to do.
How might Pallavi see Himani's decision?
Pallavi may be surprised and a little worried for Himani, but may also respect her honesty, since Pallavi was the one who asked why it still felt bad.

What does "feel blue" mean?
How do I check whether my water bottle is clean?

1. It means to feel sad. I felt blue when my friend moved away.
2. Fill it with warm water and a drop of soap, shake it, and rinse well. Look inside and under the lid for any dirt.

They were taken outside the uni in Berlin.
What does Kiran mean by 'I'm happy for them. I am. I also want to throw my phone'?
Kiran feels genuine happiness for the others alongside envy and grief for the plan that was lost.
What did Salma's replies get right?
Salma let Kiran be sad without rushing to a bright side, and offered company instead of advice.
How might Kiran's Amma see the job here, and why might she say it's 'even better'?

Dalton, Hunter, and Alex started a Superhero Fan Club. They set a goal to watch as many Superhero movies as they could in one summer. Dalton watched 7 movies, Hunter watched 12, and Alex watched 15. They all watched 2 movies together, but every other movie they watched was different. How many different movies did they see?

Dalton watched 7 - 2 = 5 more movies.
Hunter watched 12 - 2 = 10 more movies.
Alex watched 15 - 2 = 13 more movies.
Altogether, they watched 2 + 5 + 10 + 13 = 30 different movies.
The answer is 30.
What does the numeral 0 look like, and what does it mean?

Answer: 0 is round like an egg. It means none, nothing.

Show an empty plate and the card 0 together.

Mentor's note, Anirban, first-year engineering hostel.
Divyansh, 19, came to our fortnightly chat looking wrecked. He had started seeing someone, and within a week he'd gone from texting her all night to telling her never to contact him again. Then he wrote her a long apology at three in the morning. "I want someone so badly," he said, "and then it feels like danger." He talked about his childhood home being loud and frightening at times, and about missing his late Dadi, the one calm person there. I didn't try to fix it. I asked if he'd see the campus counsellor; he agreed, and we booked it together. I also asked him to join the Sunday cricket group. Same faces every week.

Which group did Anirban ask Divyansh to join?
The Sunday cricket group, with the same faces every week.
What does Divyansh mean when he says closeness "feels like danger"?
He longs to be close but feels afraid when it comes near, perhaps because home was loud and frightening at times.
What choice did Anirban make instead of trying to fix things?
Anirban listened, then helped him book the campus counsellor together and suggested a steady weekly group.
How might the person Divyansh was seeing have felt during that week?
She was likely confused and unsettled, being texted all night, then told never to call, then sent an apology.

Saturday
The results list went up on the notice board today. Chaitanya is third in class. I'm eleventh. I know exactly how he got third.
I've watched him copy from the formula sheet in his calculator cover since the first unit test. I never said anything. I kept telling myself: it's not my business, he's my friend, someone else will notice. Nobody did.
Priyanka studied harder than anyone, and she's fourth. She was crying in the corridor today. She missed third by one mark.
I feel sick about it. Not jealous exactly. More like I'm part of it, because I knew.
Every time I see his name up there, the uneasy feeling comes back. Staying quiet was supposed to be the easy option. It isn't.
Maybe I should talk to him. Or to Ma'am. I don't know yet.
– Zubin

Where did Chaitanya hide the formula sheet?
In his calculator cover.
What does Zubin mean by feeling "part of it"?
Zubin feels guilty and uneasy, as if the silence helped the unfairness happen.
What could Zubin still do now?
Speak to Chaitanya privately first, and if nothing changes, tell Ma'am calmly, since it's not too late.
What is the result like for Priyanka?
Priyanka, who studied hardest, missed third by one mark and was crying in the corridor.

PE teacher's note, Class 9, Tuesday
During the relay, Ganga tripped at the handover and fell. A group near the stands started chanting "Ganga-flop" and filming on a phone. Before I reached them, Tushar had jogged over, offered Ganga a hand up, and walked with her to the water tap. He didn't say a word to the group, just stood beside her while she rinsed her grazed knee. The chanting fizzled out within a minute; there was no one left to perform for.
What I did next: I checked Ganga's knee and sent her to the sick room with Tushar. I spoke to the group about the chanting and had the video deleted in front of me. I've informed the class teacher and will call Ganga's parents this evening. I also told Tushar privately that I saw what he did.

What did the group near the stands start chanting?
"Ganga-flop."
Why do you think Tushar said nothing to the group?
He seemed to want to help Ganga rather than start a fight, trusting that standing beside her would matter more.
Which of the teacher's follow-up steps protect Ganga most?
Having the video deleted stops it spreading, and telling the class teacher and her parents means adults can keep watching out for her.
What might it have been like for Ganga to have Tushar beside her at the tap?
Ganga may have felt less alone and less humiliated, able to rinse her knee without facing the chanting by herself.
The women is waiting outside the gate.

The women are waiting outside the gate.
Why: "Women" is the plural of "woman", so the verb must be plural: "are", not "is".

Gabriel, two years into a consulting job in Sao Paulo, liked boasting about how little he slept. He answered emails at one in the morning and was at his desk by seven, proud of it. By June his coffee count had doubled. In a client meeting he snapped at Wei, his teammate, over a small slide error, then made a bigger one himself: he quoted last year's figures. Afterwards Wei found him staring at the lift doors. 'You're working longer and getting worse,' Wei said quietly. 'That's not dedication, that's debt.' The words stung, but Gabriel checked his own error log. It was true. He began shutting his laptop at eleven.

What mistake did Gabriel make in the client meeting?
He quoted last year's figures.
How did Gabriel feel when Wei called it debt?
He felt stung, but when he checked his own error log he saw it was true.
What did Gabriel change?
He began shutting his laptop at eleven to protect his sleep.
What is it like for Wei to be snapped at over a small slide error?
Wei probably felt hurt and unfairly treated, yet chose to speak honestly and kindly afterwards.

In the music room, Disha Ma'am asked Anand to sing the first verse alone. Anand's jaw shot forward. “No.”
Disha frowned, then sat down on a stool. “I see. You don't want to.”
“No.” His jaw stayed out.
“Can you tell me why?”
He looked at the floor. “Last time, some boys laughed at my voice.”
“Thank you for telling me.” Her voice was gentle. “What if you sing with the group and I stand next to you?”
His jaw relaxed. “Okay.”

What did Disha Ma'am ask Anand to sing?
She asked him to sing the first verse alone.
What was Anand feeling when his jaw shot forward, and what else could it have been?
Probably afraid of being laughed at again, since he said some boys laughed at his voice last time. It could have looked like defiance to a teacher, but his jaw relaxed once he was heard.
What did Disha Ma'am do that avoided a power struggle?
She sat down, listened and asked why, then offered a smaller step of singing with the group beside him. 🙂
How might Anand's classmates see his refusal?
Some might think he was being stubborn, without knowing what happened last time. They may not realise he was afraid.

Yash: can't, helping my dad at the shop
Rashmi: you always have something

[Sunday, 7:10 p.m.]
Yash: still on?

Why couldn't Yash come to cricket nets on Saturday?
Yash was helping Yash's dad at the shop.
Why does Rashmi insist "I shouldn't have to tell them"?
Rashmi feels that people who care should understand without being told, so explaining feels like proof they don't care enough. That rule turns small letdowns into resentment.
What went wrong in the chat, and what helped fix it?
Rashmi judged Yash by a rule that friends should always be free, which led to an unfair jab. Yash's calm offer of Sunday evening, and Rashmi's apology, turned it back into a plan.
How might Yash feel being told a real friend would just be free?
Yash probably felt hurt and unfairly judged, since helping at the shop wasn't a choice against Rashmi. Yash still offered another time, which shows patience.

Class teacher's note, 9B

Nilesh came to see me after the class trip. He wanted to report that Ronit had been "making fun of him behind his back" in the group chat. He had screenshots ready: three messages where Ronit wrote "lol" after Nilesh's posts.

I asked to see the whole chat on his phone. He hesitated, then scrolled. In between the three were many messages he had not screenshotted: Ronit saving him a seat on the bus, Ronit saying "Nilesh's photo is the best one", Ronit asking if he was okay when he felt sick.

He said, "Those are just him pretending." When I asked how he could tell the difference, he couldn't answer.

I didn't argue. I asked him to write two lists: things that fit his idea and things that don't. He sat for ten minutes. The second list was longer.

I'll speak to both boys separately next week.

Payal, class teacher

How many messages were in Nilesh's screenshots?
Nilesh had screenshots of three messages where Ronit wrote "lol".
Why was Nilesh so sure Ronit was mocking him?
Nilesh felt hurt and suspicious, so the three "lol" messages seemed to prove it while the kind messages felt like pretending.
Why was Payal's two-list idea a good countermeasure?
It made Nilesh look at all the evidence himself instead of only the messages that fit, and the longer second list spoke for itself.
How might Ronit feel if he learned about the screenshots?
Ronit would probably feel surprised and hurt, since he had saved a seat and checked on Nilesh when he was sick.

At ten, Pooja loved lunch at her aunt Uma's house. Everyone talked at once, sentences overlapping, hands waving, and it meant nobody was bored. At school on Monday she burst out with an answer in the middle of the teacher's sentence. The teacher held up a hand and said, "Wait for the pause, Pooja, or raise your hand." Pooja's ears warmed. She sat on her fingers for the rest of the lesson, and then, tentatively, put her hand up. The teacher nodded and let her speak. At twenty, she sat in an interview for a summer job. The interviewer Francis asked how she would handle two deadlines that clashed. Pooja did not answer at once. She looked at the table for three slow breaths, then said, "I'd first ask which one can move." Francis waited too, and said nothing for a moment. In the lobby she told Uma over the phone, "I thought the quiet was going to swallow me. But it felt like he was actually listening to my answer."

Whose house did Pooja love to visit for lunch?
She loved lunch at her aunt Uma's house.
How do Pooja's habits with talking and silence differ at her aunt's house, at school and in the interview?

At Uma's house overlapping talk showed warmth, at school she had to wait for the pause or raise a hand, and in the interview she used a pause to think before answering. The setting decides which use of turns and quiet fits.
What was Pooja feeling when the teacher held up a hand?
She felt embarrassed and a little corrected, as her warm ears show.
What could Pooja do if a long silence in an interview feels uncomfortable to her?
She could take a slow breath and remember the pause is time to think, and say a short sentence such as that she is thinking if needed.
For our class blog, write about 90 words on a book character I admire: Jane Eyre.

I admire Jane Eyre because she never lets other people decide her worth. As an orphan, she is treated cruelly by her aunt, Mrs. Reed, and then suffers hunger and cold at Lowood School. Yet she grows into a thoughtful, honest young woman who works as a governess. When she learns that Mr. Rochester is already married, she leaves Thornfield, even though she loves him. Later, she refuses a marriage without love. Jane shows that quiet people can be the strongest of all.

Sunday. Leela's friends dragged her to the new food court. They laughed at a video on Ritika's phone; Leela laughed a second late. The fries tasted of nothing. At home she opened her game and didn't press start.
Wednesday. Kathak class, which she had begged for at ten, felt like counting steps for no reason. "What's the point?" she muttered, and sat out. On the bus she scrolled the same five apps and felt nothing at all.
Saturday. Seema Maasi, visiting, noticed. She didn't ask what was wrong. She said, "I'm painting the anganwadi wall tomorrow. Need hands." Leela went, mostly to get out of the house. By noon she was painting a giant tortoise while four-year-olds shouted ideas at her. On the way home she realised she hadn't checked her phone once. "Can I come next week?"

What did Leela paint on the anganwadi wall?
A giant tortoise, while four-year-olds shouted ideas at her.
What does Leela's muttering "What's the point?" suggest about her state?
It suggests she feels flat and empty, with nothing seeming worth doing, even things she once loved.
What was the turning point for Leela, and why did it help?
Going to paint the anganwadi wall with Seema Maasi gave her something that mattered to others, which the games and outings hadn't.
What might Seema Maasi have been thinking when she offered the painting job instead of asking what was wrong?
She may have sensed Leela needed something meaningful to do more than questions, and chose a gentle way in.

messages.content: My supervisor praised my work today, and I just said 'thanks' and froze. I wish I'd said more.

Is it okay to say that the next day?
Yes. A short follow-up is thoughtful, and it shows you appreciated the comment.
Okay, I'll say it tomorrow morning.
That's a nice plan. Keep it to one warm sentence and you're done.

Sixty-two applications since March, and today someone finally wants me. "Data entry, work from home, two hours a day," the message said, with a salary bigger than Papa's. All I have to do is pay a registration fee by tonight and send my bank details "for salary setup".

Yash-bhaiya came in and I showed him. He didn't say it was fake straight away. He asked, "Which company? Did you apply to them?" I didn't. I'd never heard of them. The email is from some random free account. Two hours a day for that money... I wanted it to be true so badly I didn't let myself ask.
We looked up the company name together. Nothing. I'm not paying anything and not sending bank details. Tomorrow Yash-bhaiya and I will report the number, screenshots and all.
Payal

Sixty-two.

Payal felt desperate and exhausted after so many applications, and the offer brought such relief that the questions got pushed aside.

He didn't mock the offer; he asked simple questions and searched with Payal, so the discovery felt shared rather than shaming.

In the colony park, Sharmila toddled towards the pigeons by the fountain. “No, no, Sharmi,” her papa Amandeep sang, smiling. She saw the smile and kept going, giggling. Her grandmother on the bench laughed.
Then a scooter turned into the path. Amandeep's face changed. “Sharmila. Stop.” His voice was low and firm.
She stopped mid-step, staring at his face. Her lip trembled. He scooped her up. “Good stopping,” he said softly.

Where were the pigeons?
The pigeons were by the fountain in the colony park.

She seemed startled and a little scared by her papa's serious face and low voice, and her lip trembled.

She laughed, so she saw it as a playful game, just as Sharmila did, because the words came with a smile.

When I was nine, my Hemant Mama checked my maths homework every night after his shop closed. I'm Raghav. Every mistake got a sharp tap on the page and "Careless again!" I tried going slower. Still careless. I tried checking twice. Still wrong somewhere, still "careless". After a few months I stopped trying to get them right. I'd write any number and wait for the tap. When Amma asked why I'd gone so quiet, I said, "Whatever I do, it's wrong." It felt true. I'm eleven now, and Amma found me a tuition teacher who marks what I got right first. Last week I got four out of six, and I actually wanted to know what went wrong in the other two. That felt strange.

What did Hemant Mama say at every mistake?
'Careless again!'
Why did writing any number feel reasonable to Raghav at nine?
Going slower and checking twice still brought the same tap and 'careless', so effort seemed useless and guessing at least cost less.
What changed for Raghav, and why did it help?
A tuition teacher who marks what Raghav got right first; seeing four out of six correct showed that effort counts, so Raghav wanted to fix the rest.
What might Amma have noticed that led her to find a new teacher?
Amma saw Raghav go quiet and heard 'Whatever I do, it's wrong', and seems to have understood the problem was the constant criticism, not laziness.
Can you help me say no to guests who want more food when I have run out?
Say it kindly and honestly, like 'I am so sorry, everything has been eaten. Would you like some fruit or a cup of tea?' Offering something else shows that you care. No one will mind.
But I feel bad. My aunt Meera always asks for seconds.
Then keep a small extra dish ready, like some rice and curd or a few rotis, for people who want more. Aunt Meera will feel welcome, and you will not feel bad.
Good idea. How much extra should I plan for ten guests?
Plan about one extra portion for every five guests, so two extra portions for ten guests. That way even Meera's second helping is covered, and there is something for the late ones too.
What was my aunt's name?
Your aunt is Meera, and she always asks for seconds. Keep a small extra dish of rice and curd ready for her.
Has the date for the big fair in town been announced?
I don't know, since I can't see recent announcements. The town council's page or posters near the market usually carry the dates.

How can I help at home without being asked?
Also, rewrite this correctly: She did a big mistake in the sum.
Plus, what is the name of my neighbour's dog?
Why do deserts get cold at night?
One more thing: Someone said "unprepared" to me. What is that?

1. Notice small jobs such as setting the table or watering plants and do them. A little help every day makes a big difference to your family.
2. Corrected: She made a big mistake in the sum. Why: the usual collocation is "make a mistake".
3. I don't know; I can't see your street or your neighbour's home. Ask your neighbour, or the family who lives there.
4. The ground loses its heat quickly after sunset. Because the dry air and clear sky hold little heat.
5. "Unprepared" is an adjective. It means not ready.

A group of parents get together and decide to hire a private school teacher to quit his job and teach their children.  His former job paid 45,000 per year and they offered him a 20% raise.  If there are 9 kids how much does each parent have to pay?

His raise was 45,000*.2=$9,000
So his new wage is 45,000+9,000=$54,000
So they each have to pay him 54,000/9=$6,000 per year
The answer is 6000.

I'm Rehana, and I've taught next door to Zainab for a year at the primary school in Lucknow. I saw how she handled Mr Qureshi.
At the first parent-teacher meeting he stormed in, raised his voice about his son's marks, and walked out before she could answer. The rest of us decided he was a bully. Zainab wrote in her diary, and I saw the line: "First impression: angry, rude. But this is a guess."
Then she did something I didn't. She asked the office when he usually picked up his son. She waited at the gate one evening. She found out he worked nights at the railway yard and had rushed in straight from a shift.
The next month she called him at a time that suited him. He apologised before she said anything.

Where did Mr Qureshi work?
He worked nights at the railway yard.
How did Zainab seem to feel about her first impression of Mr Qureshi, and what shows it?
Zainab seemed cautious and doubtful about her first impression, writing "But this is a guess" and then finding out he had rushed in straight from a night shift.
Which steps by Zainab changed the outcome?
Finding out when he picked up his son, talking to him at the gate, and calling at a time that suited him, which gave her new evidence and led to his apology.
How might Mr Qureshi have felt when Zainab called at a time that suited him?
He may have felt respected and a little embarrassed about the first meeting, which is perhaps why he apologised before she said anything.

From the top of a building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower and the angle of depression of its foot are given. Find the distance d between them and the height of the tower (metres).
a) building 7 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 45 degrees
b) building 10 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 45 degrees
c) building 20 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 45 degrees
d) building 15 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 30 degrees
e) building 12 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 30 degrees
f) building 8 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 60 degrees
g) building 30 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 60 degrees
h) building 6 m, elevation 60 degrees, depression 60 degrees
i) building 50 m, elevation 30 degrees, depression 30 degrees
j) building 9 m, elevation 45 degrees, depression 45 degrees

a) d = 7; tower 7(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 19.12
b) d = 10; tower 10(sqrt3 + 3)/3 ~ 15.77
c) d = 20; tower 20(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 54.64
d) d = 15sqrt3 ~ 25.98; tower 60
e) d = 12sqrt3 ~ 20.78; tower 12(sqrt3 + 1) ~ 32.78
f) d = 8sqrt3/3 ~ 4.62; tower 32/3

In a game, five children score 480, 408, 840, 804 and 48 points. Write the scores from the highest to the lowest.

Answer: 840, 804, 480, 408, 48.

Greatest to smallest is called descending order (like going down stairs). Look for the most hundreds first: 840 and 804 have 8 hundreds; 840 is bigger because it has 4 tens. Then 480 and 408. Last is 48, which has no hundreds at all.

messages.content: My school bag got completely soaked today and my books are wet.
Oh no. First take everything out and spread the books open so air can reach the pages. Which ones are worst affected?
My maths notebook and the science textbook.
Stand them upright with the pages fanned out, in a room with moving air, such as under a fan. Put a sheet of paper between wet pages if they stick together.
Can I use a hair dryer on the pages?
A hair dryer on low heat, held at a distance, can help, but too much heat makes the paper curl. Letting your maths notebook and science textbook dry slowly in the air is safer.
Okay. I will do that. Anything for the bag itself?
Empty it, wipe the inside with a dry cloth, and leave it open in an airy place to dry. Once your science textbook and maths notebook are dry, put them back in a plastic cover inside the bag.

Coach's note, college cricket nets. Vikas, coach.
Since Tanmay was picked for the state under-23 squad, I've watched Abhinav closely. They opened the batting together for two seasons. Abhinav congratulated him on the day, but since then he has pointed out Tanmay's mistakes loudly at every net session: "Footwork's gone, state player." "That shot won't work at state level." Some of it is true. Most of it is said to the others, not to Tanmay.
Today, when we were alone, Abhinav admitted, "Everyone keeps talking about him. It's like I'm not even here." I think it's envy, and a worry about falling behind his old partner, more than anything.
Next step: I've asked Abhinav to lead the juniors' batting drills this month.

Which squad was Tanmay picked for?
The state under-23 squad.
What does Abhinav's "It's like I'm not even here" suggest?
He feels envious and afraid of being left behind now that the attention has moved to Tanmay.
Why might leading the junior drills help Abhinav?
It gives him his own role and recognition, so he has less need to cut Tanmay down.
How might Tanmay feel about the comments at the nets?
Tanmay may feel hurt and isolated, his success turned into a reason for public jabs from his old partner.
What does convalescence mean?

Convalescence is the time when you slowly get your strength back after an illness. It is a noun.
Example: During her convalescence, Asha read three novels and learnt to knit.

"I said, 'Relax, everyone, the shark has arrived.'" Nirmala grinned, showing the metal. "They loved it."

My friend says "I live in Delhi itself". What is "itself" doing there?

In Indian English "itself" is added for emphasis, meaning "right here" or "in that very place". In standard English you can drop it or use "right in".
Example: I live right in Delhi, so the school is close.
Two girls write secret messages in their notebooks and get caught. Tell it as a story.

Rekha and Manju wrote notes to each other in a code made of numbers, passing them back and forth during Hindi class. They thought nobody could ever decode them. One day, the teacher, Mrs. Nambiar, picked up a crumpled paper that had fallen and read it silently. Then she raised an eyebrow. "Seven, twelve, three," she said. "That is G, L, C, if A is one." I applied to teach at a coaching centre and they want a sample class on the water cycle. I'm Lucas.
A sample class is your chance to show how you teach. The water cycle is a good topic because you can use drawings and simple steps. Who is the class for?
Class seven students, around twelve years old.
For that age, keep the steps clear, evaporation, condensation, rain and collection. Draw a simple cycle on the board and ask them to guess what comes next.
Should I do an experiment too?
A tiny one helps. You could show a steamed glass lid with drops forming, to show condensation. Check first that it is allowed and safe, and keep it short.
Good. What age group was it again?
The class is for Class seven students, around twelve years old. Keep your language simple, use the drawing, and invite them to explain each step back to you.

At the spice factory in Nashik, Tenzin, the shift manager, handed Shankar a roll of fresh labels. "Batch 47. Cover the old dates with these before dispatch. Head office wants it gone today." Shankar looked at the sacks. The old date had passed two weeks ago, and he had seen the damp patches himself. His stomach tightened at the very first line. He put the roll down on the table. Batch 47.
How did Shankar feel when he was handed the labels?

Which of Shankar's steps made his refusal both firm and respectful?
He stopped at the first doubt, stated the reason calmly, asked for the order by email and suggested the quality head test again.
How did Shankar's refusal affect Nazia?
It gave Nazia the courage to put her own labels down, showing how one person speaking up makes it easier for others.

Two ultimatums in one day. Writing them down so I can think.
Morning: Mohan, my flatmate, said, "If you smoke on the balcony again, I'll have to move out. The smoke gets into my room and I can't breathe properly." Annoying, but fair. It's about his health, and he's leaving me a clear choice. I'll stop.

Why did Mohan give his ultimatum?
The smoke gets into his room and he can't breathe properly.
How did Vikas feel after Bhavna's call?
Vikas felt scared and uneasy, with cold hands and fear of texting Anjum back, sensing control rather than a fair request.
What did Vikas do after noticing the difference?
Wrote both ultimatums down to think clearly and called Didi the same night, who offered a place to stay that weekend.

As a necessary boundary to protect his health in his own room, leaving Vikas a fair choice.

How old will Wemmick's father be, and what does he think of doing?

"Both flourishing thankye," said Wemmick, "and particularly the Aged. He's in wonderful feather. He'll be eighty-two next birthday. I have a notion of firing eighty-two times, if the neighbourhood shouldn't complain, and that cannon of mine should prove equal to the pressure. However, this is not London talk. Where do you think I am going to?"
He will be eighty-two next birthday. Wemmick thinks of firing his cannon eighty-two times, if the neighbours do not complain and the cannon can take it.

James is sitting outside, counting how many people go past him in vehicles. He has counted 52 vehicles so far today. He saw 12 trucks, a couple of buses, twice as many taxis, some motorbikes, and 30 cars. If the trucks held 2 people each, the buses held 15 people each, the taxis held 2 people each, the motorbikes held 1 person each, and the cars held 3 people each, how many passengers has James seen today?

In the trucks, James saw 12 * 2 = 24 people.
In the buses, he saw 2 * 15 = 30 people.
He saw 2 * 2 = 4 taxis go past him.
Therefore, he saw 4 * 2 = 8 people in the taxis.
In the cars, he saw 30 * 3 = 90 people.
Since we know how many vehicles James saw in total, we know that he saw 52 - 12 - 2 - 4 - 30 = 4 motorbikes.
So, he saw 4 * 1 = 4 people on motorbikes.
He has therefore seen a total of 24 + 30 + 8 + 90 + 4 = 156 people.
The answer is 156.

Okay Payal, you asked about video calls. Let me tell you about Tuesday. I am Indu, the designer. I was describing a banner, and I held my hands about this wide, a big rectangle, and said, "Something like this." Nobody reacted. Turned out my camera cropped everything below my chin. The client's video also froze right as she used her hands, so I have no idea what shape she meant. I laughed and said, "Sorry, I am waving invisible boxes." Then I typed 'A4 landscape' in the chat and shared my screen with a quick sketch. Everyone got it in seconds. Now I say the size in words first, gesture second.

What did Indu type in the chat?
She typed "A4 landscape" in the chat.
Why did Indu laugh and say she was waving invisible boxes?
She realised the camera cropped her hands so nobody could see the shape, and she wanted to lighten the awkward silence. The client's frozen video also meant she may have missed the client's gesture.
What could Indu do next time a shape or size matters on a call?
She could say the size in words, share her screen or make a quick sketch, as she did, and use gestures only as extra.
How might the client have felt watching Indu's cropped video?
The client may have felt unsure what Indu meant, since Indu's hands were invisible and the silence left both sides guessing.

Shrink this to three sentences.

On Wednesday in the Chennai school library, Tanushree leaned over to Irawati and whispered, "Don't laugh, but I think I like Deepak." Irawati's pen froze. She'd liked Deepak since the inter-school quiz. She'd never told anyone. All evening in their flat, the jealousy grew. Deepak and Tanushree sat together in maths. What if he liked her back? Irawati found herself planning: she could mention to Deepak that Tanushree talks too much, or that she already has someone. She stopped. She pictured Tanushree's face if she ever found out. They had shared tiffins since Class 2. The next morning, before the bell, Irawati said, "Tanu, I should've told you yesterday. I like Deepak too." Tanushree blinked. "Oh. Oh no." "I'd rather lose the crush than lose you." Tanushree grabbed her hand. "Same. Let's not fight over a boy who doesn't even know we exist."

Tanushree whispers to Irawati that she likes Deepak, whom Irawati has secretly liked since the quiz. Irawati is jealous and thinks of saying unkind things about Tanushree, but stops, remembering their friendship. Next morning she tells Tanushree the truth, and they agree that their friendship matters more than a boy who does not know they exist.
Rahul says, "3 x 4 means 3 + 4, so it is 7." What is wrong?

Answer: 3 x 4 means 3 groups of 4, which is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, not 3 + 4.

This is the most common mix-up. Say the sign as words: "3 groups of 4". Make it with counters: 3 cups, 4 in each: 12. Then show 3 + 4 with counters: only 7. Adding joins two numbers once; multiplying adds the same number again and again.
Why do children take turns on a playground slide?
Everyone gets a chance. Because nobody has to push, there are fewer quarrels and fewer chances of someone being knocked over.

Yamini had planned the sunrise walk with Ritu for weeks, but at five Ritu texted that she had a fever and couldn't come. Yamini went up the hill behind the town alone. Fog swallowed the view; there would be no sunrise. She sat on the wet bench anyway, annoyed, hood up. Lately every question in her head ended the same way: what is the point of any of it, marks, college, even being kind? Her family prayed every evening; her best friend believed in nothing she could name. Yamini didn't know where she stood. In the fog she could hear a temple bell below, a dog, someone's pressure cooker. For one strange second she felt part of all of it. She typed to Ritu: 'No sunrise. But something. Tell you later.'

Why couldn't Ritu come on the walk?
She had a fever.
What did Yamini feel for 'one strange second' in the fog?
She felt connected to everything around her, a sense of belonging her questions hadn't given her.
What might help Yamini keep exploring these questions?
Talking them over with Ritu, her family or a teacher she trusts, and reading different views, without rushing to settle on one.
How might Ritu react to the message 'No sunrise. But something'?
She would probably be curious and a bit sorry she missed it, and keen to hear what Yamini meant.

The power cut hit during the school bus breakdown, and thirty kids sat sweating in the dark on the roadside. Divyansh could hear Class 4 getting restless. "Okay, riddle time," he called, torch pointing at his own chin. "What has hands but can't clap?" Silence. Then Mohit yelled, "A clock!" and the whole row cheered. "What's a cat's favourite colour?" "Purr-ple!" someone shouted, and even the conductor laughed. Divyansh's voice had gone hoarse, but he kept the puns coming until the replacement bus arrived, and Mohit kept clapping for each one. 😄

What was the answer Mohit shouted to the riddle about hands?
Mohit shouted, "A clock!"
What was Divyansh probably feeling as he kept telling puns in the dark?

He was probably enjoying the shared fun and wanting to keep the group cheerful, shown by his continuing until his voice went hoarse. He might also have been a little nervous himself and used jokes to calm down.
What could Divyansh do if his voice gives out before the bus arrives?
He could hand the torch to Mohit or another child to ask the next riddle, so the game continues and everyone joins in.
How might Mohit and the other children feel about the riddles during the wait?
The riddles turn a long, sweaty wait into a game, so Mohit and the others probably feel less restless and more like one group.

Tuesday: Uma opened her school bag and her tiffin was not there. She stared at her desk, tummy rumbling. Jaya slid half her paratha across. Uma felt happy and a little shy. She whispered "Thank you" and took only that half. Wednesday: Uma checked her tiffin twice at home before leaving. Friday: she tucked an extra laddu in her box and, at lunch, offered it to Jaya with both hands.

What was missing from Uma's school bag on Tuesday?
Her tiffin was not there.
How did Uma feel when Jaya slid half her paratha across?
She felt happy and a little shy. Her whispered thanks and taking only the half she was offered show both.
What did Uma do afterwards that keeps the kindness going?
She planned ahead by packing an extra laddu on Friday and offering it to Jaya. Taking more than was offered would have spoiled it. 😊
How might Jaya feel when Uma offers the laddu with both hands?
She may feel pleased and touched that her kindness was remembered, and glad to see Uma being generous back.
Why can we see through a glass window but not through a wooden door?
Glass is transparent and wood is not. Because glass lets light pass straight through it, while wood blocks the light or scatters it, the wood hides what is behind.
Our teacher called the firefighter courageous. What does it mean, and is there a shorter word?

Courageous means ready to face danger or difficulty without giving way to fear. It is an adjective. A shorter word with almost the same meaning is brave.
Example: The courageous firefighter went back into the smoke to make sure the room was empty.

The preschool's pretend clinic had gone quiet. Divyansh had listened to Vikas's chest, written a squiggle prescription, and now neither knew what to do. Vikas wandered toward the sand tray, hands in his pockets. Divyansh grabbed a doll from the cot. "Emergency! The baby has a hot head! Doctor Vikas, help!" Vikas spun around, ran back and snatched the stethoscope. "Ambulance!" The teacher smiled from the reading corner.

What did Divyansh write?
He wrote a squiggle prescription.
What was Divyansh feeling when Vikas wandered toward the sand tray?
He was probably worried the game was ending and eager to keep Vikas playing.
What else could keep a pretend game going?
Taking turns to add problems, so both children bring ideas.
How does the teacher see the new twist?
The teacher is pleased, smiling at how Divyansh found a way to restart the game.

Anirban, you keep saying you can't draw every day. Let me, Madhav, tell you how I've done a sketch a day for two years.
The rule isn't "never miss." That rule breaks in a week. My rule is: I can miss one day, but never two in a row.
Last winter I had fever for four days. Day one, I missed. Day two, I drew one line. Honestly. One wobbly line of the window, lying in bed. It counted. Day three, a cup. Day four, the cup again, a bit better.
When I travel, I keep a tiny notebook in my pocket. On the train to Guwahati I drew the feet of the man opposite me, because that's all I could see.
The minimum is so small it's a bit silly. That's the point. On a bad day, the goal isn't a good drawing. It's to keep the chain from snapping. The good drawings come on the good days, because the chain is still there.

How many days did Madhav have fever last winter?
Four days.
How does Madhav seem to feel about the one-line drawing?
Madhav feels amused but proud of it, seeing even a silly minimum as keeping the habit alive.
What could Anirban borrow from Madhav's rule?
Allow one missed day but never two, and keep a tiny minimum, like one line, for bad days.
How might Anirban react to hearing about the one wobbly line?
Anirban might laugh at first, then feel encouraged that the habit doesn't need to be impressive every day.

Monday. Hansa and Yamini walked home from school together for the first time, because Yamini's family had moved to the lane behind Hansa's. At the corner Yamini said, "You're my best friend now, okay?" Hansa said okay so fast she nearly tripped.

Wednesday, a week later. They had a secret code: pulling your left earlobe meant "look at who just walked in". They laughed so hard in assembly that Hansa got sent to the back. She didn't care.

Friday of the next week. At recess Yamini ran off to skip rope with Rupal and Mansi. Hansa waited on the steps with two halves of a mango she had saved. Yamini didn't come.

On the walk home Hansa didn't pull her earlobe once.

"Are you angry?" Yamini asked.

Hansa shrugged. "You said best friends."

"You are my best friend. I just like skipping."

What did pulling your left earlobe mean in their code?
It meant "look at who just walked in".
How can you tell Hansa feels hurt on the walk home?
She doesn't pull her earlobe once, shrugs, and says "You said best friends"; she feels hurt and possessive after waiting alone with the mango.
What could Hansa try next time Yamini plays with other girls at recess?
She could ask to join the skipping or tell Yamini she saved her mango, instead of waiting alone and saying nothing until later.
How does Yamini see the recess skipping?
Yamini sees no conflict: Hansa is still her best friend and she just likes skipping, so she is a little puzzled that Hansa is angry.

For two years, Ankita had taken the private bus from her town near Karnal to college: forty rupees each way, packed, forty-five minutes of loud film songs. In January a new state bus started on the same route, twenty rupees, half-empty, twenty-five minutes. Her friend Jyoti switched on day one. "Come with me tomorrow," Jyoti said. "No, I'm fine. I know the private bus conductor, I know where to stand. It's comfortable." But Ankita still arrived late and tired every day, and she'd told Jyoti twice that month she was short of money for photocopies. "Comfortable?" Jyoti said. "You complain every day." Ankita laughed. "I'm just used to it." She thought about it that night. Changing meant a new stop, a new timetable, a new conductor. That was all. The next morning she waited at the state bus stop, a little nervous, with Jyoti.

How much did the new state bus cost?
Twenty rupees.
Why did Ankita say she was "fine" on the private bus?
It was familiar, and changing felt like effort, a new stop and timetable, so she called her habit comfortable even though she complained daily.
What helped Ankita finally switch buses?
Thinking it through that night and seeing that changing only meant a new stop, timetable and conductor. Going with Jyoti made the first morning easier.
How might Jyoti feel waiting at the state bus stop with Ankita?
Jyoti is probably pleased and a bit amused, having watched Ankita complain for weeks while calling it comfortable.

The power had been out for six hours when the video reached Nazia's phone, battery at 14 percent. Muddy water poured through gates while a panicked voice shouted, "Dam opening tonight! Leave now!"
Vijay, who ran the lane's flood relief group with Nazia, was already typing. "Send it to all 300 families. Better safe."
"Wait. Two minutes." On one bar of signal she opened the district disaster cell's page. No alert. She checked two news sites. Nothing. She played the video again: the trees behind the gates were bare and dry, not a monsoon scene at all.
"If it's real and we wait, people drown," Vijay said.
"If it's fake and we send it, three hundred families run into the dark on flooded roads." She dialled the disaster cell's helpline. Busy. Again. On the third try a tired officer said the dam was holding and that real alerts come only by official message.
Nazia posted that, and nothing else. Her battery hit 9 percent.

What did the voice in the video shout?
'Dam opening tonight! Leave now!'
What was Nazia likely feeling while Vijay was typing?
Nazia was tense and torn under pressure, yet cautious enough to ask for two minutes before anything went to 300 families.
Which checks did Nazia run before posting anything?
She opened the district disaster cell's page, checked two news sites, noticed the bare, dry trees in the video, and called the helpline until an officer answered.
How did Vijay see the risk of waiting?
Vijay feared people might drown if the warning was real and they waited, so sharing at once seemed the safer choice.

With a small loan from his uncle and three weeks before the hostel stall opened, Baljeet sat outside the cafe near the highway and copied its board: tea at fifteen, sandwiches at forty, open from seven to ten at night. 'If it works there, it works here,' he told Mohit, a friend in the hostel. He opened with the same prices and hours. On the first night he sold four teas. The hostel block was quiet after nine, and students there had monthly pocket money, not the stream of passers-by the cafe had. By the end of the week he still had half a tray of sandwiches. Mohit said, 'The cafe has a road outside. We have a corridor.'

How many teas did Baljeet sell on the first night?
Baljeet sold four teas on the first night.
What was Baljeet thinking when he said 'If it works there, it works here'?
Baljeet believed the two places were alike enough to copy, and felt confident, though the cafe had a busy road and the stall had a quiet corridor.
What other approach could Baljeet use to set prices and hours?
Baljeet could ask hostel students what they would buy and when, since a stall for a quiet block needs to fit the people who are actually there.
How does Mohit see the stall?
Mohit sees the key difference between a road with passers-by and a quiet corridor, and points it out.

The rain had turned the trail above Manali into mud, and they were still two hours from camp. Sumit had been groaning theatrically since lunch: at the climb, the weight of his pack, the cold. "You're being dramatic," Saurabh called back, grinning. Then Sumit slipped on a wet rock, and the next sound was different, a sharp cry and then a low moan through clenched teeth. He sat in the mud holding his ankle. Saurabh's first reflex was another joke. He stopped himself. Sumit's face had gone white, and he wasn't looking up to see if anyone was laughing. Saurabh knelt beside him. "Real or joking? Honestly." "Real. I can't put weight on it." Saurabh sent an SOS with their location from the satellite messenger the trek company had given them, then radioed the group leader, who said a rescue team was coming up from the lower camp. He wrapped his own jacket around Sumit and stayed with him.

How far were they from camp?
Still two hours from camp.
What made Saurabh stop his reflex joke?
Saurabh felt a flash of worry, seeing Sumit's white face and noticing he wasn't checking whether anyone was laughing, so the moan seemed like real pain.
What did Saurabh do that helped?
He asked honestly whether it was real, then sent an SOS with their location, radioed the group leader and stayed with Sumit, keeping him warm.
What might it have been like for Sumit to hear 'You're being dramatic' earlier?
Sumit probably took it as friendly teasing then, but after the fall he may have worried his real pain would be dismissed as more drama.

Monday. Chandrika had a question about her term paper for Professor Amandeep Gill. She wrote an email that began, "Sorry to disturb you, I know you're very busy, I'm sure this is a silly question, but…" and went on for three paragraphs. She read it back and cringed. It sounded like begging. She deleted it.
Wednesday. Her friend said, "Just ask what you need." Chandrika wrote four lines: "Dear Professor Gill, for my paper on water policy, should I focus on Maharashtra only or compare two states? I've drafted an outline for each, attached. Could I meet you in office hours on Friday? Thank you, Chandrika."
She hovered over send for a minute, heart thumping, then clicked.
Friday. The professor had printed her outlines and scribbled on both. "Compare two states. This is a sharp question. More students should ask like this."
Chandrika walked out of the office feeling taller.

What was Chandrika's term paper about?
Her paper was on water policy.
Why did Chandrika delete her first email?
She felt embarrassed and worried that the long, apologetic email sounded like begging and would make her seem needy.
What made the second email work well?
It was short, clear and specific, asked one real question, attached her outlines and requested a time, so it showed engagement, not weakness.
How did Professor Gill see Chandrika's request?
Professor Gill was impressed, calling it a sharp question and wishing more students asked that way.

Titan's father has an onion farm ready for harvest. He borrows Mr. Clay's pickup and transports the harvest to their store, carrying ten bags per trip, prepared for sale. If the onions are in 50 kgs bags, and the pickup makes 20 trips, what's the total weight of onions harvested by Titan's father?

On one trip, the pickup carries 10 bags * 50 kg/bag = 500kg of onions
After 20 trips, the total weight of onions transported to the store is 20 trips * 500 kg/trip = 10000 kgs
The answer is 10000.

In their Pune flat, Payal stared at the report from the company health check. One line was flagged in red: a screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive." She stopped eating. She told her sister Tanuja she was sure she had it. "The report says so." Tanuja, who worked at a diagnostic lab, sat down with her. "Payal, how rare is this condition?" "Very rare. It says so here." "Right. So when thousands of healthy people take a screening test, a few will show up reactive even though they're fine. For something this rare, those false alarms can be more than the real cases." Payal blinked. "So I probably don't have it?" "Probably not. But we don't guess. The doctor will order the proper test." Payal went to the doctor the next morning. The second test was normal. She cried with relief in the car.

What was flagged in red on Payal's report?
A screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive."
What was Payal feeling when she stopped eating?
She felt frightened and certain she had the rare condition because the report seemed to say so.
How did Tanuja help Payal, and why was it wise?
She explained that false alarms can outnumber real cases for rare conditions, and still insisted on seeing the doctor for the proper test.
How might Tanuja feel watching her sister's fear?
Tanuja probably felt concerned but steady, using her lab knowledge to calm Payal without dismissing her.

The rain had trapped everyone under the bus shelter, and the bus was late. Ayesha stared at her friend Rashmi's new fringe, which stood straight up like a small broom. "You look like a coconut with a mohawk!" said Ayesha, laughing.
"Well, you look like an owl," Rashmi shot back, "when you wear your specs and blink."
They both burst out laughing. Ayesha's face turned serious for a second. "Too much? Tell me if it's too much."
"No, it's funny," said Rashmi, patting the fringe. "But if you say it a fifth time, I'll say stop."
"Deal."

What did Ayesha say Rashmi looked like?
A coconut with a mohawk.
What was Ayesha feeling when asking "Too much? Tell me if it's too much"?
Caring and a little concerned about crossing a line, even though both had been laughing.
What makes this teasing friendly rather than hurtful?
Both laugh and both tease, and Ayesha checks in while Rashmi says how far it can go and that stop would work.
How might Rashmi feel about the teasing about the fringe?
Amused and comfortable, since Rashmi teased back, patted the fringe and set a light limit.

At the working women's hostel in Chennai, the common washbasins filled up at seven, six residents brushing their teeth in a row. Lavanya, a bank clerk with a stiff neck from the counter, had tried stretching "whenever", and it happened maybe once a week. So she made a plan with her roommate, Sarika. The moment she rinsed her brush, she'd walk to the corridor window and do her neck and shoulder stretches before going back to the room. The first few mornings, the Hindi teacher from Room 12 stared. By the second week two others had joined at the window, toothpaste still on their lips. "I don't even think about it now," Lavanya told Sarika. "Brush, rinse, window."

Where did Lavanya go right after rinsing her brush?
She'd walk to the corridor window.
Why had stretching 'whenever' not worked for Lavanya?
Lavanya stayed stiff and uncomfortable because 'whenever' left stretching to her memory and mood each day, so it happened only about once a week.
What choice did Lavanya make with Sarika, and why did it work?
She tied the stretches to rinsing her brush, which happens every morning, so starting needed no thought: 'Brush, rinse, window.'
What is it like for the residents who join at the window?
Seeing Lavanya there every morning makes it feel normal and easy to copy, so they join in half-laughing, toothpaste still on their lips 🙂

Ines drew four boxes on the back of a café napkin. "Transport, food, beds, safety. One each." Yosef took transport, Marta took food, Duarte took the hostel, and Ines kept safety: emergency numbers, a meeting point, and what their parents needed to know. "Everything goes in the shared sheet," she said. "Prices, links, one line each. Deadline is Friday at eight. Whatever's in by then, we decide on." By Wednesday Yosef had train and coach prices for the Lisbon to Porto run. Duarte found two hostels and a small guesthouse. Marta added a supermarket picnic plan next to a café option. On Friday evening they sat on Ines's bedroom floor, scrolled the sheet once, and chose everything in twenty minutes. For once, nobody had spent three nights searching the same things twice.

Which job did Duarte take?
Duarte took the hostel.
Why did Ines set a Friday deadline?
Ines seemed determined to keep the planning calm and fair, wanting a fixed point so nobody would feel stuck searching everything twice.
What else could help if one friend missed the Friday deadline?
The group could agree ahead of time that a missing part gets the simplest safe option, or have a quick call with that friend, so one gap does not stall everyone.
How might Yosef see having only transport to research?
Yosef can go deep on train and coach prices without chasing the rest, which likely feels lighter than planning the whole trip alone.

Describe the stranger in this scene in your own words.

The stranger, with a comfortable kind of grunt over his pipe, put his legs up on the settle that he had to himself. He wore a flapping broad-brimmed traveller's hat, and under it a handkerchief tied over his head in the manner of a cap: so that he showed no hair. As he looked at the fire, I thought I saw a cunning expression, followed by a half-laugh, come into his face.
He sits comfortably with his legs up, smoking a pipe. He wears a broad hat with a handkerchief under it, so no hair shows, and his face seems sly as he half laughs.

12 March, night
Went to Sharmila's home today for the thirteenth-day prayers for her father. I'd never been to one. Cousins were rolling puris in the courtyard, someone had put his reading glasses beside the photo, and everyone ate together on long mats. It felt like the whole lane was holding the family up.
But I also heard an aunt tell Sharmila, "Be strong, beta, don't cry in front of the guests." Sharmila nodded and went completely still after that, as if she'd left the room without moving.
Later an old neighbour sat with her and asked, "What was he like on Sunday mornings?" Sharmila laughed, then cried, then told us about his terrible puns. Nobody rushed her.
I'm her colleague, not family, and I don't know the right words. But tomorrow I'll send her one of his puns and ask how she's doing.
Ayesha

What had someone put beside the photo?
His reading glasses.
What does Sharmila going completely still suggest about how she felt after the aunt spoke?
It suggests she felt she had to hide her grief and pulled into herself, alone even in a full house.
What did Ayesha decide to do tomorrow, and why is it a good choice?
To send Sharmila one of her father's puns and ask how she is, which invites her to speak of him without being hurried.
How did the neighbour's question change things for Sharmila?
Being asked what her father was like let her laugh, cry and share his puns, so she felt accompanied instead of told to be strong.

Parveen, you think you are the first child to live far from her parents? Sit. Your Samir chacha has a story.

At twenty-four I got a job in Muscat. Ammi and Abbu stayed in Lucknow. The first year, I sent money and felt guilty every day. Every festival photo from home was a knife. I would lie awake calculating how old Abbu was, and do nothing except feel terrible.

Then Ammi fell in the courtyard and a neighbour found her. That woke me up. Guilt that only hurts is useless, beta. So I changed things. I called every Sunday at nine, same time, so they could wait for it. I paid a boy from the lane to bring vegetables and check on them daily. I came home every Eid, and when I came, I switched off my phone.

I still missed them. But I stopped drowning in it and started doing something.

Where did young Samir work, and where did his parents live?
He worked in Muscat, and his parents stayed in Lucknow.
How did young Samir feel during his first year away?
He felt guilty every day, lying awake and feeling terrible without doing anything about it.
What was the turning point in Samir's story?
His mother's fall in the courtyard made him turn guilt into action: regular Sunday calls, a boy to check on them daily, and full attention on Eid visits.
How might Ammi and Abbu have felt once the Sunday calls began?
They probably felt comforted and looked forward to the fixed time, knowing their son would call.
Tomorrow is the science fair and my model of a volcano is not working properly.
That is stressful the night before. Volcano models often fail because of the mix. What are you using for the eruption?
Baking soda and vinegar. I am Meera. Nothing happens when I pour the vinegar.
Hello Meera. Try putting the baking soda into a narrow container, add a little dish soap and a few drops of food colour, then pour in the vinegar quickly. The soap makes bubbly foam.
I do not have dish soap at home. Can I use something else?
A little liquid hand wash can work in a small amount. If you have neither, try more baking soda and pour the vinegar faster. Practise outside or on a tray so the mess stays easy to clean.
Okay, I will try with hand wash. What did I say was not working?

Your volcano gives no eruption when you pour in the vinegar. Meera, try the narrow container with baking soda, a bit of hand wash and quick pouring, and test it once tonight so you are sure before the fair.
Thanks. And if it still fails?

Then show the model anyway, Meera, and explain how the eruption should work. Judges often value your understanding as much as the effect, and you can show your tests with baking soda and vinegar as proof.

I'm Darshan, and for years my reaction to any mistake was the same sentence: "I'm useless." Last March I forgot my one-to-one with Vishal, the new trainee on my team. He waited in the meeting room for twenty minutes.

The old me would have spiralled all evening and then avoided Vishal for a week out of shame. This time I tried what my old mentor used to do: describe the act, not the person.

So I told myself: "I forgot the 2 p.m. meeting. I feel irresponsible, and that's fair. I'm not a useless person. I'm a person who forgot a meeting."

Then I went to Vishal's desk. "I forgot our meeting. That's my mistake, and I'm sorry you waited. Can we do it now?" He looked relieved. We talked for forty minutes.

I still hear the old sentence sometimes. But now I answer it.

How long did Vishal wait in the meeting room?
Vishal waited for twenty minutes.
How did Darshan feel after forgetting the meeting?

He believed spotless figures proved he was careful and good at his job, so each extra cross-check felt like protection against mistakes.

Dear Rajni,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because I'm a coward about saying it.

Last Friday, when the anonymous school confessions page posted the clip of you singing at the assembly, the comments were already crazy. Hundreds. Everyone was adding something. I scrolled for ten minutes and then I added one too, under a made-up name. It was mean. I won't repeat it.

I keep trying to explain how it felt. It didn't feel like me typing. You felt far away, like a picture, and everyone else was doing it, so it seemed like just one more drop in the rain. But it was my thumb. On Monday I saw you eat lunch alone in the library, and I knew which drop was mine.

I've deleted it. I'm sorry. Your high note was actually good.

Jasleen (the girl two rows behind you in maths)

Jasleen saw Rajni eat lunch alone in the library.

Rajni felt far away like a picture, the name was made up and everyone else was commenting, so it felt like one more drop in the rain.

She deleted the comment and wrote to apologise; she could also report the clip to a teacher so the page takes it down.

Rajni may feel a mix of hurt and relief, hurt to know a classmate joined in, but glad someone admitted it and praised Rajni's high note.

(3) How do I spell "calender", the thing with the dates?

Hi Irawati,

It's been a month since you moved to Pune and I miss our walks home. I've been thinking about all the questions we asked each other this year.

Remember when you asked me in Ramzan how I could go all day without even water? And I asked why your family does puja for the tulsi plant? We both laughed at first, and then we actually listened.

I never wanted to convince you of anything, and you never tried to convince me. I think that's why it worked. We were just curious, and kind.

Wasim

Sehri happens at four in the morning.

Wasim felt touched and understood, since nobody had ever described it that way before.

Subject: Terms we agreed by phone

Dear Jatin,

Thank you for the draft of the design contract. I've compared it with our call on Tuesday and I noticed three differences. The scope you described on the phone included two rounds of revisions, but the draft doesn't say how many. The "handling charge" in the last paragraph was never mentioned. And you said the second payment would come within a week of delivery, but the draft says "at our convenience."

Before I sign, please put all three in writing as we agreed on the call. I'm keeping our messages as a record.

I also understand you'd like me to sign today. I'd rather take the time to be sure. If the terms can't be written down, I'll have to decline.

Sincerely,
Amandeep

How many differences did Amandeep find between the call and the draft?
Amandeep found three differences: the revisions, the handling charge and the payment timing.
Why did Amandeep refuse to sign the same day?
Amandeep felt uneasy that spoken promises were missing from the paper and pressure to sign today is a red flag, so Amandeep wanted time to check.
What small steps helped Amandeep protect against deceit?
Amandeep listed the differences, asked for them in writing, kept messages as a record and said clearly that unwritten terms mean a no.
How might Jatin see the email?
Jatin may feel caught out or irritated, but an honest party would see the request as fair, since it only asks that the phone terms be put on paper.

"Dilnaz, look at this. Staff who use the office gym took half as many sick days last year. Let's make gym time compulsory."
"Interesting, Jagdish. Before we decide, can I ask some questions?"
"Sure."
"Who uses the gym?"
"Mostly the younger staff, I think."
"Are younger people sick less anyway?"
"...Probably."
"Could it go the other way? People who are often unwell might avoid the gym."
"Oh. That's possible."
"And do we have a comparison? Like staff who started using the gym this year, compared with similar ones who didn't?"
"We don't."
"Then we know they go together, but not that the gym caused it. Could we try it with one team for six months, and compare with a similar team?"
"That's slower."
"Slower, but then we'll actually know."

How many sick days did gym users take compared with others?
Half as many sick days last year.
What does Jagdish's "That's slower" suggest Jagdish is feeling?
Jagdish seems a little impatient and deflated, wanting a quick answer after finding such an exciting link.

A six-month trial with one team compared to a similar team, so they can tell whether the gym itself reduces sick days.
How might younger staff see a compulsory gym rule?
Younger staff might not mind, since many already use the gym, while others might feel it was forced on them without proof.
When do we use "person" and when "people"? And one more: What does "awkward" mean?

1. "Person" is one, and "people" is more than one. One person waved, and many people clapped.
2. Awkward means uncomfortable or not smooth. It was awkward to meet him after the quarrel.
Why does our stomach rumble when we have not eaten for a while?
The gut keeps moving even when it is empty. Because its muscles squeeze air and liquid along, and no food is there to muffle the sound, we hear the noise.
