When Valentina and Emeka got married in Madrid, their friends were buying flats and cars. They made a different first decision.
On their first Sunday as a married couple, at the kitchen table, they added up what they spent in a normal month: rent, food, transport, phone. Then they agreed that before any big goal, they would build a reserve worth six months of that, kept in a savings account they could get to quickly.
It took them almost two years. Valentina moved to a cheaper phone plan. Emeka cycled to work in spring.
Last October, Emeka's company announced layoffs. For three weeks nobody knew who would stay. Emeka couldn't sleep.
Valentina put the reserve statement on the fridge with a magnet. "Look. Six months. Whatever happens, we're fine for a while."
He kept his job in the end. But he still remembers how that piece of paper made him breathe.

How long did it take Valentina and Emeka to build the reserve?
Almost two years.
How did Emeka feel during the three weeks of layoff uncertainty?
Emeka was anxious and couldn't sleep, then felt calmer and reassured when he saw the reserve statement.
What else could Valentina and Emeka do now that the scare has passed?
They could talk together about their next big goal, and speak to a qualified adviser if they want help comparing options.
How did the reserve look to Valentina during the layoff scare?
Valentina felt steady enough to comfort Emeka, because the reserve gave them time whatever happened.

After that hour, I was a different girl. I stole jaggery from the kitchen jar though Amma had forbidden it. I fought my brother over the swing. One day I tore his kite, just like that.
My father said my patience got used up, like oil in a lamp. These days, beta, I hear people argue whether it really works like that. Maybe I was just hot and hungry and fed up. But I know one thing. After that hour, I was not myself."

She felt worn out and irritable, "not myself", so resisting the jaggery or being kind to her brother became much harder.
What choice in the story could have made those afternoons easier for young Ganga?
Her father could have split the hour into shorter bits with a drink of water or a break, instead of one long hot stretch.
What was it like for Ganga's brother on those afternoons?
He probably felt hurt and confused, losing the swing and his kite to a sister who was fine earlier in the day.

Pankaj, you asked how I got back into coding after I bombed the placement test. Honestly, I didn't plan a comeback. I planned one tiny problem a day.
After that test, I didn't open my laptop for three weeks. I'd convinced myself I just wasn't a coder. Then my sister said, 'Do one easy one, Hrithik. Just one.' Reverse a string. Took me forty minutes. Embarrassing.
But I wrote it in a notebook: Day 1, reverse a string. Day 2, count vowels. Day 3, find the largest number in a list.
By Day 30 the list filled two pages. Some days I'd just flip through it. It was proof, you know? Not a feeling. Proof.
Now I'm on Day 142, doing graph problems. I still fail sometimes. But I open the notebook, see page one, and think, okay, that guy couldn't reverse a string.

What was the first problem Hrithik wrote in the notebook?
Reverse a string, which took forty minutes.
Why did the growing list matter so much to Hrithik?
After the test Hrithik no longer trusted feelings about ability; the list was 'proof, not a feeling', clear evidence of getting better.
What was the turning point for Hrithik, and why did it work?
The sister's 'Do one easy one. Just one'; a task small enough to finish restarted the habit, and writing each one down built evidence that motivated the next.
How might Pankaj, still nervous about coding, hear this story?
Pankaj may feel encouraged that even someone who bombed a test and took forty minutes on a string recovered, and might start a one-problem-a-day list too.
We discussed about the plan yesterday. Any mistake?
Yes. Say: "We discussed the plan yesterday." The verb "discuss" takes its object directly, so "about" is not needed.

I'm Dolma, one of five on Trisha's team at the design studio. We're all around twenty-five, and until April we were just colleagues who ate lunch together.
When Trisha became lead, she brought in her old boss's system. Stand-up every morning for forty minutes, each of us reporting every task. A tracking sheet updated by the hour. Messages at nine at night asking why a column was still yellow.
Her old boss had run a team of twenty senior designers. We were five people who used to share chips.
Within three weeks, lunch got quiet. In stand-ups people said "on track" and nothing else. Nobody mentioned problems any more, because every problem became a question in front of everyone. Farhan started eating at his desk.
By May, Trisha looked puzzled and tired. I heard her say to herself, "It worked so well for Meera ma'am." I don't know if she saw why it didn't work for us.

How long were the morning stand-ups under Trisha?
They were forty minutes every morning.
What might Trisha have been feeling by May?
She seemed puzzled and tired, confused that her old boss's method wasn't working for her team.
What approach would have fit this team better?
Short, informal check-ins and asking the team what support they wanted would suit five peers better than strict tracking built for twenty seniors.
How does the new style look to Dolma and the team?
Dolma sees the team feeling watched and going quiet, with lunch turning silent and people hiding problems.

Ten minutes into a rainy Sunday, Chaitanya stood at the sofa with drooping shoulders. "I'm bored. What do I do? Can I have the tablet?" Papa Sumit did not reach for it. He slid over an empty cardboard box, some tape and a pair of blunt scissors. After a grumble, Chaitanya cut a door into the box, then a window, and by lunch the box was a bus with a very serious driver.
By nine, Chaitanya was reading books meant for much older children and asking questions about how stars burn. In class the lessons felt slow, and Chaitanya rubbed out drawings that were not exactly right. At break the other children were playing kabaddi, and Chaitanya stood at the edge of the game, unsure how to join. Mummy Neelam found the fine marks and the long silences at home. That evening she skipped the quiz about facts and sat on the floor with a board game. "Your turn," she said. Chaitanya laughed for the first time all week, and lost happily.

What did Papa Sumit give Chaitanya instead of the tablet?
He gave Chaitanya an empty cardboard box, some tape and a pair of blunt scissors.
How does the rainy Sunday at age five connect to the picture of Chaitanya at nine?

At five, Chaitanya said bored and asked for the tablet, but with a cardboard box, tape and time the box became a bus. At nine, Chaitanya was reading books for older children yet felt bored in class, rubbed out drawings and stood at the edge of the game, so Mummy skipped the quiz and played a board game with the whole child.
What was Chaitanya feeling while standing at the edge of the kabaddi game?
Chaitanya felt shy and left out, wanting to join in but not knowing how to begin.
What would you advise Mummy Neelam to do to help Chaitanya find friends?
She could arrange a small, easy play meet-up with one or two children around a game Chaitanya enjoys, and keep making time for play and comfort at home.

Monday. In Bhavna's Class 10, the new teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English." When Ganesh answered a history question in Marathi-flavoured English, the teacher said, "Try again, properly." Ganesh's answer had been right. Bhavna noticed, and felt uneasy.
Wednesday. At lunch, Sonali imitated Ganesh's accent. Bhavna laughed along before she could stop herself. Then she saw Ganesh's face and felt her stomach drop.
Friday. In the group project, Ganesh explained the whole Maratha chapter to them in Marathi, fast and brilliant, better than any of them. Bhavna said, "Ganesh, you should present this part. In English or Marathi, whichever." Sonali rolled her eyes. Ganesh looked surprised, then nodded.
Walking home, Bhavna thought: speaking English well had never meant knowing more. She was annoyed that she'd believed it.

How many times did the new teacher praise Sonali?
The teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English."
What was Bhavna feeling when she saw Ganesh's face at lunch?
Bhavna felt guilty and ashamed, her stomach dropping, after laughing along at the imitation.
Which choice did Bhavna make on Friday, and why was it fair?
She asked Ganesh to present the part he knew best in whichever language he liked, valuing his knowledge over his accent.
How might Ganesh feel when the teacher says "Try again, properly"?
Ganesh probably felt humiliated and discouraged, since his answer was right but was treated as lesser because of his English.
What mood is associated with Raga Multani?
Raga Multani is associated with a hot, distant, meditative mood.

Read this:

I'm Vinita, Uday's aunt. I was visiting on a cold evening. Uday stood next to his father and looked up. "Papa, you're as big as a giant!"

Later I said, "My, this floor is very messy," hoping Uday would put his blocks away. He kept building.

I tried, "Someone's blocks are everywhere." Nothing.

His father grinned at me and said, "Uday, please put the blocks in the box." Uday did it at once.

Then Uday pulled his knees up. "It's a bit chilly in here," he said, looking at the blanket on the sofa. His father laughed and tucked it round him.

What did Uday say his father was as big as?
A giant.
What did Uday want when he said "It's a bit chilly in here"?
He was most likely feeling cold and wanted the blanket, hinting while looking at it rather than asking directly. He may have felt shy about asking outright.
What worked better than Vinita's hints about the blocks?
A direct, clear request, "please put the blocks in the box," which Uday followed at once, because young children often miss hints.
How does Uday's father see Uday's own hint about being chilly?
He recognises it, laughs fondly, and tucks the blanket round him.
Now you try: 9 cm on the same map.
The answer is 225,000 cm = 2.25 km.

Read this:

Zainab had been freelancing as an illustrator for eight months when Damini, who ran a small publishing house in Hyderabad, emailed her: "We'd love you for our children's book. We can offer twelve thousand for the full set of drawings."

Twelve thousand felt like a lot. It was more than her last job. Zainab's hand hovered over the reply button.

Then she sat back. What would I think this job was worth if Damini had never mentioned a number?

She counted the pages: twenty-four illustrations, full colour. She messaged three illustrators she knew from art school and asked, honestly, what they would charge for that. She also checked the rates page of an illustrators' association.

The answers came back: thirty, thirty-five, twenty-eight. The association's range was similar.

Zainab wrote back politely, explaining the scope and suggesting thirty. Damini replied the next day: "Fair. Let's talk at twenty-eight?"

How many illustrations did the children's book need?
Twenty-four illustrations, full colour.
Why did twelve thousand first feel like a lot to Zainab?
Zainab felt pleased and tempted because it was more than her last job, and she had no other figure to compare it with yet.
What could another freelancer learn from how Zainab replied?
Before answering, ask what the work is worth without the first figure, then check two or three independent sources like peers and an association.
How might Damini see Zainab after the polite counter-offer?
Damini may see Zainab as a professional who knows her worth, and respect her more for it.

Read this:

Tanvir, first day, you want to know? Okay. So I walk into the bank's head office, twelfth floor, glass everywhere, and the team lead is already talking about 'basis points' and 'run-rate' and 'the Q3 walk'. Q3 walk! I thought it was a team outing.
Everyone has two screens. Everyone types without looking. One girl, maybe a year older than me, finished a whole model while I was still trying to log in.
And I'm so happy, Tanvir, I am. My name is on the door list. I called Amma from the lift. But at lunch I sat there thinking, Sudha, they interviewed forty people, and they picked you? What if they meant the other Sudha? There were two Sudhas in the final round, I'm not joking.
I laughed about it in the lift. At night it's not so funny.

What floor is the bank's head office on?
It is on the twelfth floor.
What was Sudha thinking at lunch on the first day?
Sudha was worried the bank had picked the wrong person, even joking they might have meant the other Sudha 😰
What small step could help Sudha settle in?
Sudha could ask the team lead or a nearby colleague to explain a few terms like 'the Q3 walk' in the first week, since new joiners are expected to ask.
How might Tanvir react to hearing both the excitement and the worry?
Tanvir may be happy for Sudha but also notice how real the self-doubt is, and want to remind Sudha that being picked means something.
Cut this down to one short sentence: I just wanted to quickly let you know that the meeting which was planned for three o'clock this afternoon has now been shifted to four o'clock instead.
The three o'clock meeting has been moved to four o'clock.

Ali, Peter, and Joey were fishing. The fish Ali caught weighed, in sum, twice as much as the fish that Peter caught. Joey caught 1 kg more fish than Peter. Together the three of them caught 25 kg of fish. How many kilograms did Ali catch?

Let x be the weight of the fish that Peter caught. Then Ali and Joey caught 2*x and x+1 kg of fish, respectively.
So, x+ 2*x + x+1 =25
So, 4*x = 25 - 1 = 24
So, x = 6
Therefore, Ali caught 2*x = 2*6 = 12 kg of fish
The answer is 12.
Write a sentence of exactly nine words about a sleeping baby.
The baby sleeps quietly while the fan hums softly.
'Missed call de dena' English mein kya bolte hain?
Say: "Give me a missed call." People in India understand this. Elsewhere, you can say: "Ring me once, and I'll call you back."
Did we "win" the other team or "beat" them?

You beat them. You win a game, a match or a prize. You beat a person or a team.
Examples: We won the final. We beat the other team by two goals.

Read this:

The carpentry workshop in Gothenburg was freezing in January, and Lars had a blister on every finger from hand-planing oak. He had spent his gap year trying a warehouse job, a café, and two weeks with his uncle building a boathouse before deciding: this. His friend Daniel was in second-year law because his parents were both lawyers. They met for coffee after a long week. "I failed my contracts exam," Daniel said flatly. "I don't even know if I care." Lars showed his blistered hands. "I've redone this joint five times. I'm furious. But I'll do it a sixth time tomorrow." "How?" Daniel asked. Lars thought. "Because nobody else picked this for me."

What did Lars try during his gap year?
A warehouse job, a café, and two weeks with his uncle building a boathouse.
Why can Lars say he's furious but will try a sixth time?
Because he chose carpentry after trying other things, the frustration sits on top of a goal he owns, so it doesn't make him want to quit.
What might Daniel try next, given how he feels?
He could take time to ask honestly whether law is his own choice, perhaps with a study adviser, before the next exam.
How might Daniel feel hearing 'nobody else picked this for me'?
It may sting, since his course followed his parents' path, and it may help explain why he doesn't know if he cares.
Is tommorow spelled right?

Not quite. The correct spelling is "tomorrow": one m and two r's.
Example: The report is due tomorrow morning, so I will finish it tonight.

In a certain country store, there are three kinds of bottled drinks. A cola, which costs $3, a juice for $1.5, and water for $1 per bottle. One day the store was able to sell 15 bottles of cola, 25 bottles of water, and 12 bottles of juice. How much did the shop earn?

15 bottles of cola is a cost of 15 * 3 = $45.
12 bottles of juice make up to 12 * 1.5 = $18.
As each of the 25 sold water bottles was $1, the shop made a total of 45 + 18 + 25 = $88.
The answer is 88.

Read this:

When I started at the design studio, my manager Damini sent messages at midnight, and I answered every one within minutes. I thought that was what being good at the job looked like. I'm Vandana, and for about six months I went to bed with my phone buzzing on the pillow. Even when it was quiet, my mind kept buzzing, rehearsing replies. I woke up every morning feeling I hadn't slept at all. One evening I asked Damini, nervously, whether she expected instant replies at night. She looked surprised. 'No! I just send them when I think of them.' After that I turned notifications off at nine and put the phone in the other room at ten-thirty. The first week felt wrong. Now I sleep through, and my work is actually better.

When did Damini send messages?
At midnight.
How did Vandana feel in the mornings during those six months?
Vandana felt unrested and drained, as if there had been no sleep at all.
Which choice made the biggest difference?
Asking Damini about expectations, then turning notifications off at nine and moving the phone to another room at ten-thirty.
How might Damini have felt learning Vandana replied at midnight?
Damini was surprised and probably a little concerned, not having meant to pressure anyone.

Read this:

The week before the prelims, Nirmala bought a red-and-black thread from a stall at the Kolhar fair. She tied it on her wrist and then scored eighty-one in science, her best ever. "It's the thread," she told Vidya on the bus home, tapping it. "I'm never taking it off." Vidya glanced at her friend's notebook, crowded with diagrams. "You also studied every evening at my house for a month. You never did that before." "Lots of people study. Not everyone has this." Vidya didn't argue. In the next test Nirmala wore the thread but skipped the evening sessions for a cousin's wedding. She got fifty-four. Staring at the paper, she turned the thread round and round on her wrist, and slowly said, "Maybe it was the evenings."

What score did Nirmala get in science after tying on the thread?
She scored eighty-one in science, her best ever.
Why did the thread feel responsible for the good mark to Nirmala?
Nirmala felt proud and lucky, and the thread arrived just before her best mark, so it seemed to be the cause, while the month of studying felt ordinary.
What could Nirmala do to keep her marks up next time?
Keep the evening study sessions going, thread or no thread, since the fifty-four came when those sessions stopped.
Why might Vidya have chosen not to argue on the bus?
Vidya may have sensed that Nirmala was happy and attached to the thread, and that arguing would only make the thread seem more important.
What is the difference between freestyle and breaststroke? I'm Dev and I'm starting classes.

In freestyle, your arms move one after the other, and you kick up and down. In breaststroke, both arms pull together in a circle and your legs kick like a frog. Breaststroke is slower and easier for many beginners.
Which is better to learn first?
Many coaches teach freestyle first, but some start with breaststroke because you can keep your head up. Ask your coach, Dev, since they know how you move in the water.
Okay. What does the frog kick look like again?
Bend your knees, turn your feet out, then push your legs round and together, like a frog. The push gives the speed. Practise it holding the pool edge before trying it with your arms.
At the temple one bell rings every 4 minutes and another every 6 minutes. They ring together at 9:00. When do they next ring together?

Answer: At 9:12. 12 is the LCM of 4 and 6.

List the minutes after 9:00 when each bell rings. First bell: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 (multiples of 4). Second bell: 6, 12, 18, 24 (multiples of 6). The COMMON multiples are 12, 24, ... The smallest is 12, the lowest common multiple, so they ring together 12 minutes later, at 9:12, and then again at 9:24.

Read this:

Nitin, you're sleeping three hours before your exams? Sit. Your Farida phuphi did the same, and I'll tell you what happened.
My Class Twelve board year, I thought the toppers were the ones who never slept. I studied till two, woke at five. My mother would find me at the desk with my head on the book. I felt so proud of that.
By February I was reading the same page again and again. I'd put down my chemistry notes and couldn't say one thing from them. I snapped at everyone. I once put salt in my tea.
In the pre-board, I blanked on a question I had solved ten times. Ten times, Nitin.
Our chemistry teacher, Mr Rao, saw my paper and called me in. "You're not lazy, Farida. You're exhausted." He made me promise to sleep properly for two weeks.
I did. My marks went up. I felt like I had been cheating myself of the hours I thought I was winning.

What did Farida once put in her tea?
Salt.
How did young Farida feel about sleeping so little at first?
Farida felt proud of it, believing toppers were the ones who never slept.
What was the turning point in the story?
When Farida blanked in the pre-board and Mr Rao called her in, and she promised to sleep properly for two weeks.
How might Mr Rao have felt seeing Farida's pre-board paper?
Mr Rao was probably concerned, recognising exhaustion rather than laziness in her mistakes.

Read this:

Kalyani packed her own bag the night before: a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll. "Tomorrow we go to the mango grove, and it will be sunny," she told the goat. In the morning the village sky was grey, and big drops tapped the tin roof. Kalyani's face crumpled. "You said!" Her mother, Ganga, knelt down. "I said picnic. Picnic we'll have." She spread the mat on the verandah and set out the laddoos. Kalyani ate, watching the rain. "Tomorrow the grove?" "If the sky lets us." Kalyani nodded, sure again.

What did Kalyani pack in her bag?
She packed a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll.
What was Kalyani feeling when the rain came?
She felt disappointed and let down 😔 Her face crumpled as she said, "You said!"
What did Ganga do that kept Kalyani's trust?
She kept the part she had promised by holding the picnic on the verandah, and was careful to say "If the sky lets us" about tomorrow.
What would change if Ganga had simply said, "No picnic today"?
Kalyani might feel the promise was broken and trust tomorrow's plans a little less.

Read this:

I'm Sachin, and for two years I told myself neutrality was a virtue. Our department had two camps, one loyal to Hemant, the regional head, the other to the operations director. Both kept asking me for news about the other. I gave each the same polite answer: “I only do my job.” It felt principled. Then a shipment went wrong, and each camp assumed I'd told the other side. Hemant stopped copying me on mails. The director's team stopped inviting me to lunch. When the review came, nobody defended me because nobody thought I was theirs. Only Bhavna, from stores, said quietly, “The records are clean. I checked them.” Looking back, I needed a couple of people like that before things went wrong.

What polite answer did Sachin give both camps?
Sachin said, “I only do my job.”
Why did Sachin see neutrality as a virtue?
Sachin felt principled and comfortable staying out of both camps, without seeing that neutrality left no one to speak up for Sachin.
What might Sachin have done earlier to avoid being squeezed?
Sachin could have built a few quiet allies who trust Sachin's work, as Bhavna did, before any crisis, and kept clear records.
What might Bhavna have been thinking when Bhavna said, “The records are clean. I checked them”?
Bhavna probably wanted to be fair and speak from the evidence, though nobody else in the review would.

Read this:

Yash, beta, sit down. I'm Mohit. For years in our house I was "the lazy one." My brother was "the clever one," and at twenty-three, back home after college, I was still the one who slept late. So I lived inside that story. When Ma asked for help, I'd sigh, because that was my part. Then one morning I made tea for everyone before anyone woke up. Nobody said much, but I saw Ma look twice. I did it again the next day. Then I fixed the tap. Nobody announced a change, it took a couple of years of small mornings. The day Ma told a neighbour, "He does a lot around here," I nearly missed the words. I remember them well.

What was Mohit called in the family?
"The lazy one."
What was Mohit feeling when sighing at Ma's requests for help?
Resigned and stuck. Mohit was playing the part the family had given, as if that was the only role available.
What did Mohit do to step out of the story?
Mohit made tea for everyone before anyone woke and kept doing small helpful things, such as fixing the tap.
How might Ma have seen Mohit at first, and how did that change?
Ma first saw the one who slept late, but after many small mornings Ma told a neighbour that Mohit does a lot around the house.

After the shift ended on the training floor of the Pune call centre, Avni stayed behind, laptop open to an email she had rewritten four times. Last Tuesday she had told the whole team that the missed client deadline was Kashish's fault. It was hers; she had forgotten to forward the file. Kashish had been quiet all week. Avni sent the email to the team: 'The delay was my mistake, not Kashish's. I'm sorry.' Then she found Kashish at the vending corner, said it again face to face, and asked how to make it right. Kashish shrugged, then said, 'Maybe tell the manager too.' Avni did, that evening. On the bus home the old voice started: you're careless, you ruin everything. She wrote down one change instead, a shared tracker for files, and let herself stop there.

What change did Avni write down on the bus?
A shared tracker for files.
What does the voice on the bus reveal about how Avni felt after apologising?
It shows she still felt shame and was tempted to keep punishing herself, calling herself careless even after making amends.
How did Avni turn guilt into repair instead of endless shame?
She owned the mistake to the team, apologised to Kashish in person, told the manager, and then chose one concrete change instead of replaying the blame.
What might Kashish have been going through during the week before the email?
Kashish may have felt wrongly blamed and embarrassed in front of the team, which could explain being quiet all week.
Is it "stationary" or "stationery" for pens and paper? Make this correct: The match was very excited.

1. It is "stationery", with "-ery". "Stationary" means not moving.
2. It should be: The match was very exciting. Why: "exciting" describes the thing that causes excitement, while "excited" describes a person's feeling.

In the lane behind their Chennai flats, Harsha was trying his new cycle with training wheels. Uday, five, ran alongside, cheering. The front wheel hit a stone. Harsha tipped over and scraped his elbow.
Harsha cried. Uday stopped dead. His face crumpled and he howled, louder than Harsha, fists clenched, feet stuck to the road.
Harsha's grandfather hurried out and picked him up. Only then did Uday creep closer, still sobbing, patting the cycle seat.
At dinner Uday pushed his rice around. "Amma, is Harsha's elbow better? Can I take him my sticker?"

What did Harsha's front wheel hit?
The front wheel hit a stone.
What does Uday's question at dinner show about how he felt toward Harsha?
It shows he was still worried about Harsha and wanted to make him feel better, even though his own fright had kept him from helping at the time.
What small step could help Uday next time a friend falls?
Someone could teach him one simple thing to do, like running to call a grown-up, so he has an action ready when his feelings swamp him.
How might Harsha's grandfather have seen Uday's howling?
He might have thought at first that Uday was hurt too, and then realised the little boy was frightened and upset for Harsha.

messages.content: Five years ago, there were 500 old books in the library. Two years ago, the librarian bought 300 books. Last year, the librarian bought 100 more books than she had bought the previous year. This year, the librarian donated 200 of the library's old books. How many books are in the library now?

Last year the librarian bought 300 + 100 = 400 books.
Thus, there were 500 + 300 + 400 = 1200 books as of last year.
Therefore, there are 1200 - 200 = 1000 books now in the library.
The answer is 1000.

What does the speaker promise in this passage?

"I'm only a rough fellow, who hasn't, perhaps, lived as a man should to win such a distinction, but I swear to you by all that I hold sacred and dear that, should the time ever come, I shall not flinch from the duty that you have set us. And I promise you, too, that I shall make all certain, for if I am only doubtful I shall take it that the time has come!"
He promises not to shrink from the duty given to the group. He will make sure before he acts, but if he is only doubtful, he will take it that the time has come.

Chetan's diary, Sunday night.
It started with the curtains. Mummy said the new ones in my room were too dark. That's all. And I just exploded: about her ringing Nirmala Didi to check on me, about Papa messaging my boss, about them choosing which relatives come to the engagement. Twenty years of it came out in five minutes. Papa called me ungrateful. I said something about them never letting me breathe. Mummy walked out of the room.
The thing I actually wanted to ask was simple: can the engagement be small, family only? I never got to it. Now it's buried under everything else.
Nirmala Didi called at ten and said, "You had one point, and you made it into a war." Didi's right. Tomorrow I'll apologise for the curtains fight and ask about the engagement separately, calmly.

What did Mummy say about the curtains?
That the new ones were too dark.
How does Chetan feel about the real request being lost?
Chetan feels regretful and frustrated that the simple request for a small engagement got buried under the outburst.
What is a better way for Chetan to raise the engagement?
Apologise for the fight first, then ask about the small engagement on its own, at a calm moment.
How does Nirmala Didi see the fight?
Nirmala Didi sees that Chetan had one point and turned it into a war, and says so plainly.
We found a small injured bird in the garden.
Please do not try to treat it yourself. Tell an adult at home, and ask them to call a local wildlife rescue or animal helpline.
It's not moving much.
Then it needs help from an expert soon. An adult can keep other animals and children away, while someone contacts the rescue.
Can I give it water?
It is best to wait for advice from the rescue people. They know what is safe for that kind of bird. Keep it quiet and out of the sun until they arrive.
Will it be okay?
I cannot say. The rescue team is the best chance it has. You did the right thing by noticing it and getting an adult involved.
Give me a sentence about autumn that names three colours.
Autumn leaves turn red, orange and yellow before they fall.
A test has 40 questions and Pooja got 32 right. What percentage did she score?
She scored 80 percent. Because 32 out of 40 is the same as 8 out of 10, and 8 out of 10 is 80 percent.

Read this:

Day 1. Santosh arrived at the university in Helsinki and met his lab partner, Hansa, who listened to his introduction with an almost blank face and said, "Good." He felt his stomach sink, sure that she disliked him.
Day 4. Back home, everyone shows what they think on their face, so he read her calm expression as coldness. In the lab she hardly smiled, but she checked his calculations twice and stayed late to help.
Day 10. Santosh asked her directly, "Are you okay working with me? I can't tell." Hansa looked surprised. "Very much. I'm listening. A calm face is how I show respect here." They both laughed.

Where did Santosh meet his lab partner?
He met her at the university in Helsinki.
What did Santosh feel when Hansa answered with an almost blank face?
He felt anxious and rejected, and he took her calm face as a sign she disliked him.
What did Santosh do that cleared things up?
He asked Hansa directly whether she was okay working with him, instead of relying on stereotypes or guesses.
How might Hansa have felt when Santosh read her calm face as coldness?
She may have been surprised and a little sorry, since she was showing respect and care through help and listening, not through open expression.

Read this:

Dear Sangeeta,

Promise you won't laugh. Ever since Mr Rao started reading poems aloud in English, my stomach does a little flip when he walks in. I sit up straight, I know every answer, and yesterday when he said "good" to me I nearly floated home. It's the best and most embarrassing feeling ever. 😅 I even started a poem for him, then tore it into tiny pieces and put it in the bin under the tissues. Remember you told me about your tuition-sir crush last year, and how it just faded? I'm hanging onto that. I'm not going to give him anything or write him notes. It's mine, and it stays in this letter. Kabir from debate club asked to borrow my notes, so maybe I'll be a bit nicer to him. Tell me it's normal!

Lakshmi

What did Lakshmi do with the poem she started for Mr Rao?
She tore it into tiny pieces and put it in the bin under the tissues.
How does Lakshmi feel about her feelings for Mr Rao, and what shows it?
She finds them thrilling but embarrassing. Her stomach flips when he walks in, she nearly floated home after his "good", and she asks Sangeeta not to laugh.
What did Lakshmi choose to do about her crush, and why is it a sensible choice?
She keeps it private and gives Mr Rao no notes, hoping it fades like Sangeeta's did. That avoids an awkward situation, and she can turn her attention toward classmates her own age.
How might Sangeeta feel on reading the letter?
Probably fond and understanding, since she had a similar crush that faded. She may also feel trusted, because Lakshmi shares something so private with her.
Farmer Brown fed 7 chickens and 5 sheep. How many total legs were there among the animals he fed?

The chickens had 7*2=14 legs.
The sheep had 5*4=20 legs.
There were 14+20=34 legs.
The answer is 34.

A school canteen sells a sandwich at $2, a hamburger at $2, one stick of hotdog at $1, and a can of fruit juice at $2 each can. Selene buys three sandwiches and a can of fruit juice. Tanya buys two hamburgers and two cans of fruit juice.  How much do Selene and Tanya spend together?

Three sandwiches cost 3 x $2 = $6.
So, Selene spends $6 + $2 = $8.
Two hamburgers cost 2 x $2 = $4.
Two cans of fruit juice cost 2 x $2 = $4.
Thus, Tanyah spends $4 +$4 = $8.
Therefore, Selene and Tanya spend $8 + $8 = $16.
The answer is 16.

Tuesday night. Third week of living with my flatmate Parveen, and I finally worked out the eyebrows. Whenever she tells a story at dinner, her brows go up so high they nearly touch her hair, then crash down when she gets to the serious bit. For two weeks I thought she was always shocked or angry with me. Tonight I asked, "Are you cross?" She burst out laughing. "No! That's just how I talk. My whole family does it." She said she'd noticed my face stays very still and had wondered if I was bored. We agreed to stop guessing. Funny how one flat face and one lively one can each feel like a complaint. - Imran

Which week of living with the flatmate is it for Imran?
It is Imran's third week of living with the flatmate Parveen.
What did Imran think Parveen's eyebrows meant at first?
Imran thought she was always shocked or angry with Imran, until asking her.
What could Imran and Parveen do to avoid misreading each other?
They could keep checking with a quick question and remember each other's usual level of expression instead of guessing.
How did Parveen see Imran's still face?
She wondered if Imran was bored, so Imran's still face gave her the same kind of wrong reading that Imran had made of her.

"Tanuja, who's that?" Deepak held her up to the bathroom mirror.

She stared. Then she touched the smudge of jam on her own cheek, not the mirror. "Me!"

"Yes, that's you."

She grinned at herself and patted her head. "Tanuja!"

Later her cousin picked up her yellow cup. Tanuja marched over. "Mine! My cup!"

"Share, beta?" Deepak asked.

She held it tight, frowning. "Mine."

What did Tanuja touch when she saw the mirror?
She touched the smudge of jam on her own cheek, not the mirror.
What does Tanuja saying "Mine!" about the cup suggest?
It suggests she is starting to feel a strong sense of herself and what belongs to her, and she felt upset when someone took it.
How could Deepak handle the cup moment gently?
He could first agree that it is her cup, then help her take turns, rather than forcing her to share straight away.
How might Tanuja's cousin see her reaction?
The cousin may feel surprised or a bit hurt, not understanding that Tanuja is just learning what "mine" means.

What does Van Helsing hope will be done when the child is sent home?

"I hope," said Van Helsing, "that when you are sending the child home you will caution its parents to keep strict watch over it. These fancies to stray are most dangerous; and if the child were to remain out another night, it would probably be fatal. But in any case I suppose you will not let it away for some days?"

Van Helsing hopes the parents will be cautioned to keep strict watch, since straying is most dangerous. Another night out would probably be fatal to the child, so Van Helsing hopes the child will not be let away for some days.

Before the first viewing, Ujjwal and I sat on the steps of our rented building in Hyderabad with one sheet of paper and two columns.
Must-haves: under fifteen minutes' walk to a metro station, because we both commute. A decent school nearby, because we're planning a baby in the next couple of years. Two bedrooms. Within budget.
Nice-to-haves: a balcony, a gym in the complex, an east-facing kitchen, which my mother cares about more than I do.
The first flat we saw had a gorgeous balcony. I fell a little in love. Then Ujjwal quietly asked the agent how far the metro was. Twenty-five minutes by auto. We looked at the sheet and left.
The fifth one had no balcony at all, but was six minutes from the metro and next to a school. We didn't even argue.
— Rukmini

How far was the metro from the first flat?
Twenty-five minutes by auto.
How did Rukmini feel about the first flat's balcony, and what helped?
Rukmini fell a little in love with the balcony, but the must-have list helped Rukmini let it go without disappointment turning into an argument.
What else could Rukmini and Ujjwal add to their list?
They could add a budget line with the maximum price, and check it at every viewing along with the must-haves.
How might Ujjwal see the list during the viewings?

At 10:15 the whole floor of the Gangtok insurance office went quiet as the email landed: the claims unit would shrink by four posts, and the rural outreach pilot was approved. Dolma glanced across at Ganga. Ganga's eyes went wide, then she let out a long sigh and pressed her palms flat on the desk. When the supervisor passed, Ganga said, "All good, all good," in a voice pulled tight as wire. Dolma's mind ran ahead: was Ganga's post one of the four? Or was that sigh relief, since the pilot was Ganga's idea? She didn't ask in front of everyone. At the tea break she waited until they were alone by the window. "That email was a lot. How are you taking it?" Ganga laughed shakily. "Both ways. My pilot got through, and I'm thrilled. But my cousin is in claims, and I've no idea if she's safe." Dolma nodded and passed her the biscuit tin.

How many posts would the claims unit lose?
The claims unit would shrink by four posts.
What did Ganga's wide eyes and long sigh most likely show, and what else could they have meant?

They showed surprise and mixed feelings: Ganga was thrilled about the pilot yet worried for her cousin in claims; before asking, Dolma could just as easily have read them as fear for Ganga's own post.
What made Dolma's check-in work?
Dolma waited for a private moment and asked an open, calm question instead of guessing, so Ganga could explain both feelings 🙏
How might the supervisor have read Ganga's "All good, all good"?
The supervisor may have taken the words at face value and believed Ganga was fine, missing the worry in the tight voice.

messages.content: Jan buys 5 dozen roses.  Each rose cost $6.  Since he bought so many he only needs to pay 80%.  How much did he pay?

He got 5*12=60 roses
So the cost was 6*60=$360
So he has to pay 360*.8=$288

Teacher's note - Vinita, Class 10 class teacher, Monday
At 11 last night Lokesh posted in the class group: "I CAN'T DO THIS ANYMORE!!!! 😤😤" A few students replied with laughing faces. Others replied "same bro."
I couldn't tell whether this was play, frustration or something more serious. Capitals and exclamation marks can mean any of these.
So this morning, before first period, I asked him quietly to walk with me to the staff room. "I saw your post last night. How are you really?"
He laughed, then stopped. "It's the science project. My partner hasn't done anything, and it's due Friday. I was so angry I couldn't sleep."
I asked whether he was feeling unsafe or just very stressed. He said, clearly, "Just stressed, Ma'am. I promise."
I've spoken to his partner, and we've set a check-in for Wednesday. I also told Lokesh my door is open anytime.

When is the science project due?
It's due Friday.
What was Lokesh feeling when he wrote the post?
Lokesh was angry and stressed about his partner doing nothing, frustrated enough to lose sleep, but not in danger.
Why was Vinita's quick check wise?
Because capitals and exclamation marks could mean play, frustration or something serious, so asking privately found the real meaning and let her help.
How did the classmates who replied "same bro" read the post?
They probably read it as the usual dramatic complaining, not stopping to check what Lokesh really felt.

Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Papa's night shift at the bus depot started in twenty minutes. He was lacing his boots when he found Sahil in the corner, holding the empty cat basket. Chiku had died that afternoon at the vet's.
Sahil tried to wipe his face fast. "I'm fine. Go, you'll be late."
Papa took his boots off again. He sat on the floor and pulled Sahil into his lap, big as he was. "It's okay to cry, beta. I'm sad too. That cat used to sit on my newspaper."
Sahil cried properly then, into Papa's damp shirt. His older brother Darshan brought two cups of tea and sat on the other side.
When Papa finally left, ten minutes late, Sahil felt lighter, as if the sadness were now shared among three.

Where did Chiku die?
At the vet's, that afternoon.
Why did Sahil wipe his face and say "I'm fine"?
He felt embarrassed about crying and did not want Papa to be late.
What made Papa's comfort so strong, given the time pressure?
He took his boots off and stayed, hugging Sahil and sharing his own sadness even though his shift was starting.
How might Papa have felt when he saw Sahil holding the empty basket?
Sad himself and worried for his son, so he decided being late was worth it.

Dear Tarun,

I'm writing because I find it easier to say this without watching your face. You told me about the affair three weeks ago. Since then I've been angry every morning and hopeful every night, and I don't know which one is telling the truth. You say you want to rebuild, and part of me wants that too.

So here is what I need. Full honesty, including the answers I don't like. Time, without being asked how I'm doing every day. And your patience if I go cold.

I also want you to know that I might decide our marriage can't be saved. If I do, it won't mean I didn't love you or that I gave up too easily.

I'll give you my answer when I have one.

Nilesh

How long ago did Tarun tell Nilesh about the affair?
Three weeks ago.
What two feelings does Nilesh describe, and how does Nilesh feel about them?
Anger every morning and hope every night. Nilesh does not know which one is telling the truth.
What conditions does Nilesh set, and why are they reasonable?
Full honesty, time without daily check-ins, and patience with coldness. They give Nilesh a way to judge whether trust can grow again without rushing.
How might Tarun react on reading that Nilesh may decide the marriage cannot be saved?
Tarun may feel afraid or sad, but the letter also says that choice would not mean Nilesh didn't love Tarun, which may make it easier to hear.

"Worrying feels like work, beta. But the list isn't doing the sums. Let's pick the first three questions of the chapter. After dinner, together."

In two sentences, what is the main idea of this excerpt?

Nitin finds his son Varun at his desk with a long list of things that could go wrong in the exam, but no sums done yet. Nitin says worrying feels like work but the list does not do the sums, and suggests doing the first three questions together after dinner.

Wednesday night
Embarrassing day. This morning I forwarded an audio clip to the family group, a 'police officer' warning about child kidnappers in our area, sounding very official. Mausi immediately stopped sending my cousins to tuition. By lunch Anand, who works at a newspaper, messaged me: 'Tarun bhai, where did you get this? It's been doing the rounds in four states with different city names.' My stomach dropped. I searched the exact lines and found three fact-check articles calling it fake. The voice might even be generated. I'd spread panic in five minutes. So I posted a correction in the group with the links, and said sorry, especially to Mausi. She sent a folded-hands emoji, thank God. New rule for myself: if something makes me scared or angry fast, I wait and search before forwarding. That feeling is exactly what these clips want.

What did the audio clip claim to warn about?
Child kidnappers in their area, supposedly from a police officer.
How did Tarun feel when Anand questioned the clip?
His stomach dropped; he was embarrassed and alarmed at having spread panic.
What rule did Tarun make, and why is it wise?
If something makes him scared or angry fast, he waits and searches before forwarding, because fake clips rely on those quick emotions.
How did the clip affect Mausi?
She was frightened enough to stop sending her children to tuition, until Tarun's correction reassured her.

Had the strangest conversation with Chinmay today. I was telling my roommate about the time I fell out of Ajoba's mango tree when I was eight and broke my arm. I remember everything: the rough bark, the snap, the smell of the hospital, the pink cast everyone signed. Chinmay, visiting, laughed. "Deepu, that was me. I broke my arm. I've been staring at the photo all night. The pink cast I remember doesn't exist. The feeling of falling feels completely real. How can a memory this vivid be wrong?

White.

Deepika feels shaken and confused, because the memory of falling feels completely real even though the photo shows it happened to Chinmay.

Nikita, you know me, Kalyani, the girl who talks with her whole body. So picture my final-year presentation on the metro line plan. I was so nervous I was waving both hands like I was directing traffic. And I noticed Dr Menon wasn't looking at my slides at all. His eyes kept following my hands, left, right, up. Awful. That night I propped my phone on a stack of books and recorded myself. Honestly, watching it, I cringed. There was one good gesture, though. When I said the line would curve round the lake, my hand drew the curve slowly, and it actually made sense. On a stack of books.
What was Kalyani feeling when she noticed Dr Menon's eyes following her hands?

What could someone like Kalyani try before a big presentation?
Record a rehearsal, keep the gestures that clearly show an idea, like drawing a curve, and rest the hands the rest of the time.

He seemed pulled away from the slides because his eyes kept following her hands; by the second round he was following the content well enough to ask about the curve.
What does censure mean?

Censure means strong, formal criticism. It is a noun, and as a verb it means to criticise someone formally.
Example: The council member faced censure for missing every meeting this year.

(1) What gift will my friend give me on my birthday?
(2) Is it "tommorow" or "tomorrow"?
(3) What is the difference between "compliment" and "complement"?
(4) Quick one: what is "chaplain"?
(5) Can you correct this for me? "I enjoy to read comics."

1. I can't check that, since only your friend knows. Wait and enjoy the surprise.
2. It is "tomorrow", with one "m" and a double "r".
3. A "compliment" is a kind remark, and to "complement" means to go well with something. For example: she gave me a compliment on a scarf that complements my coat.
4. As a noun, "chaplain" means a priest or minister who serves a school, hospital or army.
5. Better: I enjoy reading comics. Why: "enjoy" is followed by the "-ing" form.

Susan is playing a board game with 48 spaces from the starting space to the winning end space of the game. On the first turn, she moves forward eight spaces. On the second turn, she moves two spaces, but lands on a space that sends her back five spaces. On the third turn, she moves forward six more spaces. How many spaces does she have to move to reach the ending space and win the game?

In the first three turns, Susan has moved 8 + 2 - 5 + 6 = 11 spaces.
Susan has 48 - 11 = 37 spaces to move to win the game.
The answer is 37.

In the inter-school debate today, Arnab lost to me and then said in the corridor, "Easy for you. Your school's English medium. You've been debating since you were small." I'm Mohit, Divyansh's roommate since first year. Something shifted around October. He stopped coming to the canteen with us, left assignments half done, and his lamp stayed off even when he was clearly awake. When I joked that he was becoming a monk, he didn't even smile. I wasn't sure what was going on, maybe exams, maybe home. I didn't want to be dramatic. But after a few weeks I sat on the edge of his bed and said, 'You seem really low, and I'm worried. Not judging.' He shrugged and said he was just tired all the time and didn't see the point of much. I told him about the student wellness centre and offered to walk there with him. He said no. Around October.
Why did Mohit hesitate before saying anything?
Mohit was not sure what was going on and worried about seeming dramatic or intrusive.

How might things have gone if Mohit had kept joking instead of asking?

Monday. Sumit, eight, kicked his ball into Verma Uncle's balcony and broke a flowerpot. His mother, Usha, hissed, "Don't tell anyone! What will the building say? That we can't control our son?"
Wednesday. Verma Uncle asked the children who broke his pot. Sumit said, "Not me." His ears went hot. He couldn't sleep that night.
Saturday. Sumit told his father everything. His father didn't shout. "Sumit, the question isn't what the building will say. It's what's fair to Verma Uncle. He loved that plant."
Sumit's mother was quiet, then sighed. "I taught you to hide it. That was wrong of me."
That afternoon, Sumit and his mother went to Verma Uncle with a new pot and a small tulsi plant. Sumit said sorry. Verma Uncle smiled. "Thank you for telling me."

What did Sumit and his mother take to Verma Uncle?
They took a new pot and a small tulsi plant.
What was Sumit feeling when his ears went hot?
Sumit felt guilty and anxious about lying, which is why he couldn't sleep.
What turned the situation around?
His father reframed it as what was fair to Verma Uncle, not what the building would say, and his mother admitted she was wrong to teach hiding.
How might Verma Uncle feel when Sumit says sorry?
Verma Uncle would likely feel pleased and touched by Sumit's honesty, thanking him for telling.

Let us have a story about a girl sailing a toy boat across a village pond.

Nisha's grandfather had made her a toy boat from a coconut shell and a bamboo mast. Its sail was a piece of an old green saree. She was so proud of it that she took it to the village pond every evening.

One day, a breeze caught the sail and carried the boat toward the middle, away from her reach. She walked around the edge, but the boat kept sailing, further and further.

A water buffalo bathing nearby lifted its head. It waded slowly toward the boat, creating small waves that pushed it back toward the shore.

Nisha watched with her mouth open. When her boat bumped the bank, she scooped it up and patted the buffalo's wet nose. It blew out a big, happy breath.
John has 25 horses.  He feeds each horse twice a day and feeds them 20 pounds of food at each feeding.  He buys half ton bags of food.  How many of those will he have to buy in 60 days?

He feeds each horse 2*20=40 pounds of food a day
So he uses 40*25=1000 pounds of food a day
That means in 60 days he uses 60*1000=60000 pounds of food
Each bag of food is 2000*.5=1000 pounds
So he needs to buy 60000/1000=60 bags of food
The answer is 60.

Mark bought 2 pounds of tomatoes for $5 per pound and 5 pounds of apples, at $6 per pound. How much did he spend in total?

Mark bought 2 pounds of tomatoes for $5/pound * 2 pounds = $10.
Mark bought 5 pounds of apples for $6/pound * 5 pounds = $30.
Now add those two quantities to find Mark's total spending: $30 + $10 = $40.
The answer is 40.

"So what do I do?"
"Tell him the truth, the whole thing, before he asks. Then be exactly where you say. For a long time. It comes back slower than it goes."

Where did Deepak say he was?
At Kunal's doing maths.
What is Deepak feeling as he stares at the ceiling?
He feels guilty and frustrated, realising one afternoon has made Papa doubt him.
What does Urmila suggest, and why might it work?
Telling Papa the whole truth first and then being exactly where he says for a long time, because trust is rebuilt through a steady record.
How does Papa now see Deepak's requests?
Papa is suspicious, wondering whether Deepak will really be at the fest, because the lie made every plan uncertain.

Tanvir got his first salary in Dhaka in December, and it disappeared fast: rent, money home to his mother, a loan his brother had taken for college. What was left was tiny.
His colleague Elizabeth said she put a small amount into a monthly fund plan. "Even small helps, because of compounding. But I spread it; I don't put it all in one thing."
At the same time, a cousin kept sending him "hot stock tips" from a trading app group, promising fast profits.
Tanvir felt torn. The tips looked exciting. The small plan looked boring. He also felt guilty keeping anything for himself when his family needed it.
He asked Elizabeth how she'd chosen. She said she'd first spoken to a licensed adviser at her bank. Tanvir booked the same appointment for his lunch break, and muted the cousin's group until then.

Where did Tanvir's first salary go?
Rent, money home to his mother and his brother's college loan.
Why did Tanvir feel torn?
Tanvir felt tempted by the exciting tips, unsure about the boring plan, and guilty about keeping anything for himself when his family needed it.
What choice did Tanvir make, and why is it a sensible one?
He booked an appointment with a licensed adviser and muted the tips group, choosing qualified advice over quick-profit promises.
How might Tanvir's mother feel about his first salary?
His mother would probably feel proud and grateful for the money he sends home.

spring . summer . autumn . winter

The school's exam office had sent the Class 8 science paper to the Class 7 room. Sixty students had seen it. The principal wanted a name by noon.
Sunaina, the young exam coordinator, gathered her three staff. “We'll give the principal an answer,” she said. “But first, walk me through what happened, step by step.”
They traced it together. The packets were labelled by hand. The Class 7 and Class 8 rooms had been swapped this term, but the list on the wall hadn't changed.
Hansa, who had carried the packets, said softly, “I followed the list.”
“You did,” said Sunaina. “The list was wrong.” She fixed the list and started printed labels. At noon she told the principal about the system gap, not about Hansa.

How many students had seen the paper?
Sixty students had seen it.
How might Hansa have felt when she said "I followed the list"?
Hansa was likely frightened of being blamed, and then relieved when Sunaina agreed.
What did Sunaina do before giving a name, and why did it help?
She traced the steps with her staff and found an outdated room list, so the fix was a better system, not a scapegoat.
How might the principal react to Sunaina's report?
The principal may be surprised at first but reassured that the real cause has been fixed.

messages.content: Mia can decorate 2 dozen Easter eggs per hour. Her little brother Billy can only decorate 10 eggs per hour. They need to decorate 170 eggs for the Easter egg hunt. If they work together, how long will it take them to decorate all the eggs?

Working together, they can decorate 24 + 10 = 34 eggs per hour.
It will take them 170 / 34 = 5 hours to decorate all of the eggs.
The answer is 5.

At thirteen: Afreen begged to walk home alone from tuition like Gautam and the others. Ammi said no and waited at the gate every evening in her old dupatta. Afreen walked three steps ahead, mortified.
At fifteen: Ammi finally agreed, after Afreen had learned every shortcut, the shopkeepers' names and which lanes flooded. Afreen rolled her eyes at the rules but kept them.
At seventeen: Afreen's little cousin started tuition and cried to walk alone. Afreen heard herself say, "Not yet. I'll come." Waiting at that same gate, she suddenly understood those two years of Ammi standing there in the heat. That evening she bought Ammi's favourite kulfi on the way home and didn't say why.

What did Afreen buy for Ammi on the way home at seventeen?
Afreen bought Ammi's favourite kulfi.
What did Afreen feel while waiting at the gate at seventeen?
Afreen felt a rush of understanding and grateful love for Ammi, seeing that Ammi's waiting had been care, not control.
What could help a teen like Afreen at thirteen feel less mortified?
If Ammi explained that walking alone would come once the routes were learned, Afreen could see the limit as temporary care.
How might Ammi experience the kulfi with no explanation?
Ammi might feel quietly touched, sensing something had shifted in Afreen even without words 🙂

Monday. Sangeeta has to make a poster for the arts fest. She opens the colour-coded timetable app she uses for exams: sketch 9 to 10, colours 10 to 12, lettering 2 to 3. She sits down at nine with a pencil, and nothing comes.
Wednesday. The same block has moved forward twice. "Idea generation, ten minutes," the app says. She stares at a blank page. Nandini asks, "Want to just doodle for a bit?" "It's not in the schedule."
Friday. The sheet is still empty and every block on the timetable is red. Sangeeta rubs her eyes and opens the app again to move the blocks once more.

What does Sangeeta have to make for the arts fest?
Sangeeta has to make a poster.
What does Sangeeta feel when saying that doodling is not in the schedule?
Sangeeta feels tense and stuck, holding tightly to the timetable even though it has not helped.
What different approach might suit the poster better?
Sangeeta could start with loose doodles for a short time, since creative work often starts better without fixed blocks.
How might Nandini feel watching the timetable move again?
Nandini offered to doodle, so may feel concerned and a bit helpless watching Sangeeta turn down a loose start.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Kalyani, and I work at the toy shop in the market. On Saturday a little boy, Arnab, came in with his grandfather, who told him, "Pick any one toy."
Arnab walked down our long aisle of cars, dolls, puzzles and balls. He picked up a truck, put it down, touched a drum. Then he stood in the middle and started to cry. I can't say what he was thinking.
His grandfather knelt and held up just two things: a red truck and a small drum. "This or this?"
Arnab grabbed the truck and hugged it all the way to the counter.

What two toys did Arnab's grandfather hold up?
A red truck and a small drum.
Why might Arnab have started to cry in the middle of the aisle?
With so many cars, dolls, puzzles and balls, every choice may have felt too big, and not knowing which one to pick could have upset him. 😢
Which choice by the grandfather turned things around, and why?
Holding up just two toys, because a small choice was easy for Arnab to make and he could feel happy with it.
How does Kalyani see the scene?
Kalyani watches from the shop, sees the crying and then the happy hug, and admits not knowing what Arnab was thinking.
Do the new neighbours speak Tamil at home?
I can't tell what they speak at home, because I know nothing about your new neighbours. Say hello and chat as you get to know them.

Sunday. At his cousin's naming ceremony, an aunty asked Madhav, nine, what he wanted to be. "A doctor, like Papa and Dadaji," he said at once, chest puffed. Papa squeezed his shoulder.
Wednesday. In class, the essay topic was "My Dream Job". Madhav wrote "Doctor" in big letters. He wrote that his whole family were doctors. He didn't write why; nobody had ever asked.
The next Saturday. His cousin Arnab, a college student, was helping him fix his cycle chain. Madhav was so absorbed in the gears that he forgot lunch.
"You like this, huh?" Arnab said. "Fixing things."
"I'm going to be a doctor," Madhav said automatically.
"Sure. But what do you like doing?"
Madhav stopped, oil on his fingers. He'd never thought about that before.

What was Madhav fixing with Arnab?
His cycle chain.
What was Madhav feeling when he said "A doctor" at the ceremony?
He felt proud and safe, pleased by everyone's smiles and Papa's squeeze.
How could Arnab's question help Madhav?
Asking what Madhav likes doing invites him to explore his own interests instead of only repeating a role handed to him.
How might Madhav's Papa see his answer at the ceremony?
Papa seemed proud and happy, squeezing his shoulder.
I've been working at a fruit stall on holidays. I'm Imran and my uncle owns it. This week he asked me to run it alone for a few hours.
That is a sign that he trusts you. Running a stall alone is a good test. How do you feel about it?
A bit nervous about weighing and counting change.
Practise with your uncle for a short while before he leaves. Ask him to show you the weights and let you handle a few sales with him watching.
He did. I'm okay now. I'll sell mangoes, bananas and guavas.
Good. Arrange the fruit neatly, keep the prices clearly visible, and greet each customer. If someone asks for something you do not know, you can say you will check with your uncle.
Right. What fruits did I list?
You listed mangoes, bananas and guavas. Keep them in separate tidy piles with price cards, and your first hours alone at the stall will go smoothly, Imran.
If a customer wants guavas and I have sold them all, what do I say?
Say politely that the guavas are finished for today, and suggest the mangoes or bananas you still have, Imran. Tell your uncle afterwards, so he stocks more guavas the next time at the stall.

1) Why do we clap during songs?
2) A choir has 17 children and 9 are absent today. How many are singing?

1. It keeps the beat. Because clapping together shows we are enjoying it and helps us stay in time.
2. 8 children. Because 17 - 9 = 8.

What with the birthday visitors, and what with the cards, and what with the fight, my stay had lasted so long, that when I neared home the light on the spit of sand off the point on the marshes was gleaming against a black night-sky, and Joe's furnace was flinging a path of fire across the road.

What kept the speaker away from home so long?
The birthday visitors, the cards and the fight.

Monday. At school in Melbourne, Suraj asked what language Abhinav had been speaking to Ajji on the phone. Abhinav went red and said, "Nothing," then felt bad all the way home.
Tuesday. At dinner Abhinav told Amma and Appa it felt like being two different people. Appa said, "You are one person with two languages, like having two kinds of food." Amma hugged Abhinav and promised nobody would ever ask Abhinav to choose.
Friday. Suraj came over. Abhinav taught Suraj to count to five in Kannada, and Suraj taught Abhinav a football chant. They shouted both at the top of their voices, and Abhinav laughed a lot.

What did Suraj ask on Monday?
Suraj asked what language Abhinav had been speaking to Ajji on the phone.
Why did Abhinav say Nothing, and how did Abhinav feel?
Embarrassed and split, unsure whether the home language was welcome at school.
What support helped Abhinav most?
Appa's comparison of two languages to two kinds of food and Amma's promise not to ask for a choice, followed by sharing words with Suraj.
How might Suraj have felt learning to count in Kannada?
Curious and happy, since Suraj traded words in return and had fun.

“Moo! Baa! Quack!” Sahil galloped round the room.
Kalyani Didi laughed. “Do the lion!”
“ROAR!”
Then Sahil said, “Now I'm Ravi.” He screwed up his mouth. “Thith ith my thchool.”
Kalyani stopped laughing. “Wait. Is that playing, or teasing?”
Sahil paused. “…Teasing. Everyone does it.”
“How would Ravi feel if he heard?”
Sahil looked at his feet. “Sad.”
“Animals are fun to copy. People's voices, not to hurt.”
“Okay.” He brightened. “Can I be a train instead? Choo choo!”

Which animal sounds did Sahil make first?
Moo, baa and quack.
What was Sahil feeling when he looked at his feet?
He felt ashamed and sorry once he imagined Ravi hearing the copied lisp and feeling sad.
How did Kalyani Didi help Sahil see the difference?
She asked whether it was playing or teasing and how Ravi would feel, so Sahil worked it out himself.
What is it like for Ravi when others copy his voice?
It would likely feel hurtful and humiliating, since the copying is aimed at him.

Community centre supervisor's note, Rafiq. On Thursday I watched Sunaina, one of our volunteers, notice a new arrival standing at the counter with a form and a worried face. Sunaina put a chair beside the counter, offered tea and said, "Would it help if we did the form together?" They filled it in line by line. Sunaina then introduced the newcomer to two people in the reading room and wrote the centre's timings on a card. I did not step in. Later I asked Sunaina about it, and Sunaina shrugged: "I remember arriving somewhere new." The following week the newcomer came back and sat with the reading group.

What did Sunaina write on a card?
Sunaina wrote the centre's timings on a card.
What do Sunaina's shrug and the words I remember arriving somewhere new suggest?
Empathy from personal memory of being new, which is why Sunaina noticed the worried face.
What made Sunaina's help work?
Offering a chair and tea and doing the form together before introducing people, so the newcomer had support step by step.
How might the newcomer have felt at the counter and later?
Worried and unsure at first, then relieved and welcomed, which is why the newcomer came back the following week.

Note from Elizabeth, reception teacher, Thursday:

During the fire drill today, Tanvir, five, froze and began to cry when the alarm rang. After we got outside, he went straight to the quiet corner with the cushions, where he has chosen to calm down before. He hugged the big cushion and counted his fingers, as we practise.

What I did next: I sat nearby, didn't rush him, and told him the alarm was only practice. After a few minutes he rejoined the line himself.

Where did Tanvir go after the fire drill?
He went straight to the quiet corner with the cushions.
What was Tanvir feeling when the alarm rang?
He felt frightened, freezing and crying when the loud alarm started.
What did Elizabeth do that let Tanvir settle himself?
Elizabeth stayed close without rushing him and reassured him the alarm was only practice, so he could use his own calm-down routine.
How might other children see Tanvir going to the quiet corner?
They might learn that it is normal to need a calm space and that it helps someone feel better.

In the college hostel's common room, Mahima sat with Aditi, her roommate of two years, and finally said it.
"You never tell me anything. When my grandmother was sick, I told you everything. When your parents split, you just said 'it's fine'. I feel like I don't matter to you."
Aditi looked at her hands. "I don't know how to say it."
"Say what?"
"What I feel. I don't… I don't know what it is most of the time. It's like a blur. I just go to the gym or clean the room."
Mahima remembered: the night her grandmother was in hospital, Aditi had cleaned their whole room, made tea at two in the morning, and sat up with her.
"So you do care," Mahima said slowly.
"I do," Aditi said. "I just can't find the words."

What did Aditi do the night Mahima's grandmother was in hospital?
She cleaned their whole room, made tea at two in the morning and sat up with Mahima.
What was Mahima feeling at the start of the conversation?
She felt hurt and unimportant, taking Aditi's silence as coldness.
What could help the two roommates from here?
Mahima could notice the care Aditi shows through actions, and Aditi could try simple words or ask a counsellor for help naming feelings.
How might Aditi feel when Mahima says "So you do care"?
Aditi probably feels relieved and understood, since the care was real even without words.
What does "worry" mean? And one more: What does "slow and steady wins the race" mean?

1. To worry means to keep thinking about problems that may happen. Do not worry, the bus will come soon.
2. It means that going carefully and not stopping is better than rushing. Study a little each day, since slow and steady wins the race.

The bus horn sounded outside the Manchester terrace, and Chidi was still pulling on his fourth shirt. Paulo waited on the step, hood up against the drizzle. "You looked fine three shirts ago." "You haven't seen what the older boys post," Chidi said, tugging at the collar. "Their arms, their skin, everything perfect." "They pick one out of forty and put it through a filter. My cousin does it." Paulo shrugged. "My mum says clothes are a choice, not a scoreboard." Chidi gave a short, stiff laugh and put the first shirt back on. On the bus Paulo sent a message: talk to me if it gets heavy, or to your form tutor.

How many shirts had Chidi tried on when the horn sounded?
He was pulling on his fourth shirt.
What might Chidi be worried about when he compares himself with the older boys?
He may be afraid that his own looks don't measure up to their perfect pictures; his stiff laugh suggests the comparison is bothering him more than he admits.
What small step could help Chidi if the comparing continues?
He could talk to Paulo or his form tutor, as Paulo suggested, and remember that the photos were picked and filtered.
How might Paulo feel watching his friend change shirts again and again?
He is probably concerned but trying to stay light, which is why he jokes first and then sends a quiet message offering to listen.
Please correct: She sings very good. Please define "thermometer". What does "give in" mean?

1. Corrected: She sings very well. "Well" is the adverb that describes a verb, and "good" is an adjective.
2. Thermometer means a tool that measures temperature. It is a noun.
3. It means to stop trying and agree after a struggle. For example: the child gave in and ate the vegetables.
Imagine two friends who study together before a big exam, and tell their story.

Before the Class 9 science exam, Omar and Preeti sat on the stairs of the library with a stack of notes. Omar knew biology by heart but could not remember a single physics formula. Preeti knew every formula but fell asleep at the sight of diagrams. They struck a deal. For one hour Preeti explained force and motion using a toy car, and for the next hour Omar drew the heart on a napkin and made her colour it. By evening both of them were tired and hungry, so they shared a packet of biscuits. At the exam, Omar wrote the formulas carefully, and Preeti labelled the heart without a single mistake.

In their small flat in Berlin, Leila was cooking when her phone rang. "Frau Haddad? This is your bank's security team. There's a suspicious payment on your account. We've sent you a code. Please read it to me so we can cancel the transfer."
Leila stopped stirring. Ulla, her flatmate, looked up from the table.
The code arrived by SMS: a six-digit number, with a line underneath: "Never share this code with anyone, including bank staff."
"I'll call you back on the number on my card," Leila said.
"There's no time, madam. The money will be gone."
She hung up.
Her hands were a little unsteady, but she opened the bank's official app herself. No suspicious payment. Then she called the number printed on the back of her card. The real bank confirmed: they never ask customers for codes.
Ulla whistled. "I would have read it out."
"Nearly did," Leila admitted.

What did the line under the SMS code say?
"Never share this code with anyone, including bank staff."
How did Leila feel after hanging up?
Leila felt shaken, her hands a little unsteady, but also sure she had done the right thing.
What steps did Leila take to check?
She refused to read the code, hung up, opened the bank's official app herself, and called the number on the back of her card.
How did Ulla react to what happened?
Ulla was impressed and a bit alarmed, admitting she would have read the code out.
Pick a leaf from a tree. Is it symmetric? Where is the fold?

Answer: Most leaves are nearly symmetric. The fold is along the middle vein, from the stalk to the tip.

Fold a real leaf along its middle vein. Nature is "nearly" symmetric, not perfect - one half may be a little bigger. That is fine.

In their Bengaluru flat, Gopika sat on the floor stacking cups, humming to herself, "Mmm-mm-mmm, mmm-mm-mmm," over and over.
Naveen, working at the table, hummed the same little tune back.

Cups.

She was content and relaxed, absorbed in her play; her smile at Naveen shows she was delighted when he joined in.
What did Naveen do that builds connection?
He echoed her tune back, turning her private humming into a little musical conversation.
How might Naveen feel humming back while working?

How does Vijay help Deepak handle the changes in the day?

On the terrace of their rented flat in Pune, Urmila showed Darshan her notebook. A neat timeline ran down the page: post one drawing daily from June; a reel of her monsoon sketches goes viral in July; a publisher in Mumbai messages her; she signs for a picture book by December.
"It's so specific that it has to work," she said. "I've even picked the book title."
Darshan read it twice. "What about just: you post regularly and get a few paid commissions this year?"
"That's vague. Anyone could say that."
"Vague, but it needs only one thing. Yours needs the viral reel and the publisher and the timing."
Urmila tapped the timeline with her pen. The steps looked solid in ink. She drew a small star next to "goes viral" anyway.

What did Urmila draw next to "goes viral"?
A small star.
Why does Urmila say her plan is so specific that it "has to work"?
Urmila feels excited because the detailed timeline, with months and even a title, makes success feel concrete and almost real, so she reads the detail as proof. ✨
How could Urmila make her timeline more realistic?
She could mark each step that must go right, aim first for the simple goal of steady commissions, and treat the viral reel and publisher as a bonus.
What is it like for Darshan to question a friend's exciting plan?
Darshan has to be honest without crushing Urmila's hope, which is why Darshan offers a simpler version instead of calling the dream silly.

Gerald is a furniture maker. He has 672 pieces of wood and he wants to make some tables and chairs. It takes 12 pieces of wood to make a table and 8 pieces of wood to make a chair. How many chairs can he make if he makes 24 tables?

Each table takes 12 pieces of wood to make so 24 tables will take 24*12 = 288
There were originally 672 pieces of wood so now there are 672-288 = 384 pieces left
8 pieces of wood make 1 chair so 384 pieces can make 384/8 = 48 chairs
The answer is 48.

I'm Kavitha, Ayesha's desk-mate in Class 10, so I saw all of it. When Sameer walked in with a new haircut on Monday, Ayesha said loudly, "Who did that, a lawnmower?" The whole back row laughed.
It kept going all week. At the science exhibition she copied the way he explained his solar-cooker model, hands flapping. When he dropped his tray in the canteen, she clapped first.
Here's the odd thing. In the maths notebook she thinks I don't see, his name is written in tiny letters in the margin, twice. And when he said hi to her at the gate on Thursday, she went bright red, said nothing at all, then called him "the lawnmower" again as soon as he'd gone.
I don't know for sure what's going on in her head. But I don't think it's that she can't stand him.

What did Ayesha say about Sameer's new haircut?
"Who did that, a lawnmower?"
Why might mocking Sameer feel safer to Ayesha than being friendly?
Teasing him loudly in front of friends hides the crush, so nobody, not even Sameer, can see she likes him, and she avoids feeling exposed.
What choice at the gate could Ayesha make differently next time?
When Sameer says hi, she could simply say hi back instead of turning it into another joke once he's gone; a small real reply is less risky than it feels.
What is the week like for Sameer?
Sameer is laughed at over his haircut, his model and a dropped tray, so he probably feels embarrassed and confused, with no idea the person mocking him likes him.

messages.content: James was doing some shopping in his favorite shop and he saw an offer on shoes that give him a second pair of shoes for half off the original price. He took the offer and took the first pair of shoes for $40 and the second one for $60. At the cashier, the lady told him that the offer applies strictly to the cheaper pair of shoes, and also that he was selected for an extra discount of a fourth off the total amount. How much money did James end up paying for both pairs of shoes?

The price of the cheaper pair after the discount was $40/2 = $20
The total price of both pairs of shoes $20 + $60 = $80
The final discount was $80/4 = $20
The price he ends up paying was $80 - $20 = $60
The answer is 60.
