Today I watched Yash, our twenty-five-year-old technician, try again to talk to Irfan sahib, who founded this workshop thirty years ago. Yash has been working on an idea to track spare parts on a simple spreadsheet. Every time he starts, Irfan sahib waves a hand: "You don't know the world yet, beta."
Today Yash did not argue or sulk, as he has before. He stood calmly and said, "Irfan sahib, I respect what you've built. I'm asking for ten minutes where you just hear me, and then you decide."
Irfan sahib looked surprised. He sat down. Yash showed him the sheet on his phone. Irfan sahib asked two questions, then said, "Try it for one month."
Afterwards Yash told me he'd been hurt for months, but this felt different.
What I will do next: I'll ask Irfan sahib to let Yash present the results at the monthly meeting.

What idea had Yash been working on?
Yash had an idea to track spare parts on a simple spreadsheet.
How had Yash been feeling for months before this conversation?
Yash had been hurt and unheard, since Irfan sahib dismissed him every time he started to speak.
Which of Yash's choices helped, and why?
Yash calmly asked for ten minutes of real listening while showing respect, so Irfan sahib felt honoured rather than challenged and agreed to hear him.
How might Irfan sahib have seen Yash's request?
Irfan sahib was surprised, and probably felt respected enough by the calm request to listen instead of waving him away.

Read this:

The inter-school maths quiz was in twenty minutes, and their third teammate had phoned in sick. The teacher sent Simran, a Class 10 girl from the kabaddi team, to fill in.

Zubin groaned inside. Simran had a village accent, a sports jersey and scratched knees. Kabaddi girl, he thought. We're finished.

In the waiting room, he didn't even explain the rules to her. He just told her to write down answers if he asked.

The first round went badly. Zubin froze on a geometry question. Simran leaned over and whispered, "Isn't it 42? The triangle's isosceles." It was 42.

In the final round, Simran solved the probability question while the other schools were still scribbling. They came second.

On the bus back, Zubin sat quietly. He had matched her to a type: sporty, small town, not a maths person. The match had felt like proof.

What answer did Simran whisper for the geometry question?
Isn't it 42? The triangle's isosceles.
Why was Zubin so sure Simran would be no help?
Zubin felt certain and a bit dismissive, because Simran's accent, jersey and kabaddi team matched his idea of someone who isn't good at maths.
What went wrong in how Zubin treated Simran, and what could fix it?
Zubin didn't even explain the rules; next time he could treat a new teammate as capable and find out what they can do.
How might Simran have felt when Zubin didn't explain the rules?
Simran might have felt dismissed and underestimated, but she still helped the team.
Make this sound casual: I regret to inform you that I shall be unable to attend your birthday celebration on Saturday.
Sorry, I can't make it to your birthday party on Saturday.

Read this:

In the engineering hostel, Tarun had been made discipline in-charge for the fresher block, with a register and a key to the gate. The job was only to note late arrivals. But by the second month he was locking the gate at 10:01 sharp and making latecomers stand outside while he lectured them. When Asif, a fresher, came in at 10:05 from the library, Tarun made him wait twenty minutes in the rain. 'Rules are rules. These first-years need to learn.' He noticed he no longer felt bad about it. They were lazy, weren't they? That's what he told his roommates. He didn't notice that last year, as a fresher, he had come in late from the library too. The warden, passing on his round, unlocked the gate himself and asked Tarun to come to his office in the morning.

How long did Tarun make Asif wait?
Twenty minutes in the rain.
How did Tarun feel about making latecomers wait by the second month?
Tarun felt justified, even smug, and no longer bad about it, believing the freshers were lazy and deserved it.
What could the hostel change to prevent this kind of role drift?
Keep the role limited to noting arrivals, with the warden checking regularly, and give freshers a way to complain.
How might Asif feel waiting in the rain?
Asif likely felt humiliated and resentful, punished for coming back from the library.
I'm trying to remember to drink water through the day.
A simple habit can help. Keep a bottle where you can see it, and take a few sips whenever you finish a task.
What if I forget anyway?
Link it to something you already do, like having a glass with each meal. Reminders on a phone also work for some people.
How much water should I drink?
That depends on the person, the weather and activity, so I cannot give a number for you. A doctor can tell you what suits you.

Read this:

In the Delhi flat, Parveen practised her reading for the class quiz while her brother Ujjwal sat nearby with his cricket cards. She read, “The river is very long?” with her voice going up at the end. Ujjwal frowned. “Are you not sure?” She shook her head, surprised. “No, I am sure. I just say it like that when I'm being polite.” Ujjwal laughed. “Then everyone will think you don't know.” She tried again with her voice going down on “long,” and it sounded firm. “Oh, so it can be either,” he said, “you have to look at the rest of her face too.”

What was Parveen practising for?
The class quiz.
Why did Ujjwal think Parveen was unsure?
Her voice went up at the end of the sentence like a question, which he read as doubt, though she said it was her polite way of speaking.
What could Ujjwal do next time he hears a rising voice?
He could ask whether she is unsure and look at the rest of the situation before deciding it means doubt.
How might Parveen's teacher hear the rising voice in the quiz?
The teacher could take it for doubt and mark her as unsure, even if Parveen knows the answer.

metadata.subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

Lokesh, you're new to teaching, so let old Baljeet ma'am tell you what thirty years of teenagers taught me. They all have their little magic. Lucky socks, a special pen, a coin in the pencil box. One girl, Tara, wouldn't tell anyone she'd been shortlisted for a scholarship. "If I say it, it won't happen, ma'am." I didn't laugh. I just said, "Then I'll keep quiet too." She got it. She'd also worked for months. That kind of magic is harmless. But once a boy, Neeraj, stopped studying for his boards because a man at a fair had sold him a "success thread" and he believed it would do the work. That's when I stepped in. I called his parents that week, and we sat with him and made a timetable. He kept the thread. He also studied.

What had a man at a fair sold Neeraj?
A "success thread."
Why did Tara refuse to tell anyone about her shortlisting?
She feared that saying it aloud would jinx it and stop it from happening.
How did Baljeet ma'am decide when a charm needed attention?
She let harmless magic like Tara's be, but stepped in with Neeraj because the thread was replacing study, calling his parents and making a timetable.
How might Neeraj's parents have felt when Baljeet ma'am called them?
They were probably surprised and worried, but likely glad to be told in time and to sit with him to plan his study.

Read this:

Deepak: bro revising history tonight? group call at 8
Santosh: nah. read the whole chapter once, it's all familiar
Santosh: mughal admin, revenue system, i know this stuff 😎
Deepak: ok what were the three parts of the revenue system
Santosh: ...it's like, the land thing. i'll know it when i see it
Deepak: that's the problem. the exam won't show it to u
Santosh: relax, i remember the diagrams
Deepak: ok 🙂
(Next day)
Santosh: bro
Santosh: question 4 was the revenue system
Santosh: i could SEE the page in my head. couldn't write one line
Deepak: yeah reading feels like knowing
Santosh: can i join ur call next time
Deepak: 8pm. we test each other, no books open

Which question was on the revenue system?
Question 4.
Why did Santosh feel sure there was no need to revise?
Santosh felt relaxed and confident because the chapter looked familiar after one reading, and a familiar page felt like knowledge.
What small step would show Santosh the difference between recognising and remembering?
Testing each other with books closed, as Deepak's group does, so the three parts have to be recalled rather than recognised.
How does Deepak see Santosh's plan?
Deepak spots the gap early, asking a direct question and warning that the exam won't show the page.

Read this:

Raghav, you're nervous about your first interview? Let me tell you about Preeti, who worked with me years ago. She was very talented, but in her first interview she froze. They asked why she wanted the job, and she said, "Because I need one." Honest, but not helpful. She didn't get it. She was angry for weeks, blaming the interviewer. Then she came to me and asked for help. I told her to prepare three stories about things she'd done well, and practise telling each in under two minutes. She practised with her mother, her friends, even her cat. At her next interview, she still felt nervous, but when they asked a question, she had a story ready. She got the job, and she's now a team lead.

How many stories did the elder tell Preeti to prepare?
Three stories about things she'd done well.
Why was Preeti angry for weeks after the first interview?
She felt rejected and frustrated, and blamed the interviewer instead of looking at her own answer.
What could Raghav take from Preeti's story?
Raghav could prepare a few short stories about past achievements and practise them aloud, so there is something ready when nerves hit.
How might Preeti's first interviewer have seen her answer?
They might have found it honest but unprepared, not showing why she'd be good at the job.
Do I put a full stop after Mr and Dr?

In British English, the full stop is often left out when the last letter of the abbreviation is the last letter of the word, as in "Mr" and "Dr". American English usually keeps it, as in "Mr." and "Dr."
Examples: Dr Sharma is here. Mr. Brown will arrive soon.

Read this:

Subject: Thank you, and two flats to see

Dear Sarita,

Thank you for putting me in touch with the alumni group. After your message I wrote to four people from our college who live in Pune, and two replied within a day. One added me to a hostel-seekers' group, and that is where I found two shared flats.

I saw both in person on Saturday. The first had a leaking tap and a landlord who wanted three months' deposit. The second was clean and the flatmates were friendly. I have not paid anything yet, and I am asking to read the agreement first.

I would not have found these without your introduction. Thank you.

Sabina

How many people from the college did Sabina write to?
Sabina wrote to four people from the college who live in Pune.
What did Sabina feel about the help from Sarita?
Sabina felt grateful, and said the flats would not have been found without the introduction.
What could Sabina do before paying the deposit, and why?
Sabina could read the agreement carefully and ask a local contact about the area, because a written agreement shows the real terms.
How might the second flat's flatmates see a newcomer who visits before paying?
They may feel more comfortable, since a visit lets both sides meet and check that the flat suits everyone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: shared accommodation search through college and alumni networks [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Class note, Irawati Ma'am, UKG. Sudha, who joined last month, greets me every morning with "Good morning, Ma'am," hands folded. Today I noticed something more. Our school helper, Ramu Bhaiya, brought water, and Sudha said, "Thank you, Bhaiya," and waited for him to pour before drinking. At story time she sat still and nodded along, and when she wanted to add something she asked, "Ma'am, may I tell?" I asked the whole class to try "Thank you, Bhaiya" too. 🙏

What does Sudha say to Irawati Ma'am every morning?
She says "Good morning, Ma'am," with her hands folded.
What might Sudha's "Ma'am, may I tell?" show about how she sees her teacher?
She seems to respect her teacher and want to speak politely, even when she is eager to share.
Why did Irawati ask the whole class to say "Thank you, Bhaiya"?
To spread the respectful habit and show that the school helper deserves the same courtesy as teachers.
What might Ramu Bhaiya feel when a child thanks him?
He may feel noticed and valued, since helpers are often taken for granted.

Read this:

Madhuri, you're sixteen and you say the game keeps pulling you from your books. Let me, your Noor Apa, tell you what I did at your age. It wasn't that long ago.
Board exams, Class 10. I had one of those racing games, and every notification was like someone calling my name. I tried everything. Promising myself. Setting timers. Guilt. Nothing lasted.
Then one evening Abbu said, “Stop fighting the phone. Just put it somewhere else.”
So I did. Notifications off, phone in the drawer in the drawing room, from six to nine. I'd walk past it and feel a twitch. But I couldn't see it, so after a while I stopped thinking about it.
I passed with a first division. Not because I became strong. Because I stopped giving myself the fight.

Where did young Noor put the phone from six to nine?
In the drawer in the drawing room.
How did young Noor feel when walking past the drawer?
Young Noor felt a twitch of temptation, but it faded once the phone was out of sight.
At what point in the story did Noor's approach change?
When Abbu said to stop fighting the phone and put it somewhere else, she switched from willpower to changing her surroundings.
How might Abbu have felt when Noor passed with a first division?
Abbu probably felt proud and glad his simple advice helped.
I started helping at a chai stall near my college. The owner, Raju bhai, wants me to take orders.
That is a busy job, but taking orders is a good way to learn how to talk to many people quickly. Keep a calm voice and repeat each order back.
The stall gets crowded after four. I'm afraid of mixing up orders.
Then use a small pad and write the table or the customer's description next to each order. Fill them in the same order they came, so nobody feels skipped.
Raju bhai said I can take the lunch break at three instead.
That sounds smart, since three is before the rush at four. Thank Raju bhai, eat properly and rest a little, so you have energy to take orders in the crowded hour.

Which is right, "schedule" or "shedule"?
What does "rust" mean?

1. It is "schedule", with "sch" at the start. Our bus schedule is on the wall.
2. Rust is the brownish layer that forms on iron when it gets wet. The old gate is covered in rust.

Read this:

Seema, since you're leading your first team, let me share something from my own start. Your Vasudha Didi learnt it the hard way. At twenty-six, I was made manager of six people. In meetings, I'd share my idea first, then ask, "Thoughts?" The seniors would agree, and the juniors stayed silent. Then one plan failed, and afterwards a junior told me she had known the problem all along. That night I changed my method. Before every planning meeting, I asked each person to email me three lines: what they liked, what worried them, and one question. Private, before anyone spoke. The first time, two juniors raised the same risk about a supplier. We fixed it before the meeting. I've done it ever since.

What did Vasudha ask each person to email?
Three lines: what they liked, what worried them, and one question.
How did young Vasudha feel when the junior said she had known the problem?
She felt shaken and regretful, realising her way of running meetings had kept useful worries hidden.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
Asking for private written views before the meeting, so juniors could raise worries without being swayed by seniors.
How might the juniors in the story have felt about the emails?
They probably felt safer and more heard, able to raise concerns without contradicting seniors in front of everyone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: collects opinions privately before discussion [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sunday.
New plan, written down so I stick to it.
Everything important I've failed at this year, I tried to do at night. The thesis draft. The Kannada classes. The budget spreadsheet. By 9 p.m. I'm cooked, and then I call myself weak.
Urmila, who shares the flat, does her hardest work at 6 a.m. I used to laugh at her. Now I'm jealous.
So: Thesis, 7 to 9 every morning, before the lab. Phone in the kitchen. Evenings: nothing that needs deciding. Tonight I'm cooking a big pot of rajma for three days and laying out tomorrow's clothes.
It feels almost too simple. But I'm tired of blaming my character for what might just be bad timing.
— Tushar

When will Tushar work on the thesis?
Tushar will work on it from 7 to 9 every morning, before the lab.
How does Tushar feel about past failures?
Tushar feels fed up with self-blame and a bit jealous of Urmila's morning routine.
What makes Tushar's new plan wise?
It places the hardest work at a fresher time and removes evening decisions, respecting limits rather than blaming character.
How might Urmila react to Tushar's new routine?
Urmila might feel amused and pleased, perhaps teasing Tushar for once laughing at her mornings.
Cristobal read 15 more than three times the pages that Beatrix read. If Beatrix read 704 pages, how many more pages did Cristobal read?

Cristobal read: 15 + 3 * 704 = 2127 pages
2127 - 704 = 1423 pages
Cristobal read 1423 more pages than Beatrix.
The answer is 1423.

The science fair at the primary school in Nairobi was on Friday. Alejandro had spent every afternoon for a week on his volcano, papier-mâché over a bottle, painted with three kinds of brown.
On Wednesday, Ms Wanjiru watched the test run. The baking-soda mixture fizzed out sideways through a gap near the bottom and ran onto the table.
"Lovely painting," she said. "There's a leak here, though. If you seal the base with tape, it'll erupt from the top."
Alejandro crossed his arms. "It's supposed to do that. Real volcanoes leak."
"Do they, usually, from the bottom?"
"Mine does." He picked up the brush and added more paint to the crater instead, pretending not to see the puddle.

What did Alejandro build the volcano over?
He built it with papier-mâché over a bottle.
Why does Alejandro cross his arms and insist the leak is on purpose?
He feels defensive and a bit hurt, because after a whole week of work, admitting the leak feels like admitting he failed.
What small step could help Alejandro fix the volcano without losing face?
He could run one test with tape around the base as an experiment, treating it as trying a new version rather than fixing a mistake.
How might Ms Wanjiru feel when Alejandro paints the crater instead?
Ms Wanjiru might feel patient but a little concerned, wanting the eruption to work for him on Friday.

metadata.subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Nazia,
You'll laugh, but I've started an experiment. You know how I always say I "don't like" Carnatic music? Last month I realised I'd never actually listened properly. I grew up with film songs, so those feel like home and everything else feels like noise. So I made a rule: three full, fair listens before I decide I don't like something.
I went to three concerts at the Mylapore sabha. At the first I was bored and checked my phone. At the second I noticed the violin answering the singer. At the third I actually closed my eyes. I'm not a fan yet, but I don't dislike it either.
Next month: your grandmother's biryani with the dried prunes. Three tries. Don't warn her.
Love, Swati

Where did Swati go for the three concerts?
The Mylapore sabha.
How did Swati feel at the third concert?
Swati felt calmer and more open, enough to close both eyes and listen, no longer bored.
What does Swati's rule help separate?
Real dislike from mere unfamiliarity, since film songs feel like home only because Swati grew up with them.
How might Nazia's grandmother feel if Swati asks for her biryani three times?
She would likely be delighted and flattered by the repeated requests.

Read this:

In the small Goan village of Siolim, Francis ran the bakery with his cousin Damini. For a week, Damini had been making little remarks. "Some people get to sleep till eight." "Must be nice to have your evenings free." She'd bang the tins a bit louder than needed. Francis was tempted to snap back. Instead, one morning while the bread was proving, he said, "Damini, I think I might have missed something. If you're upset with me, I'd rather hear it straight. I promise I won't get cross." Damini put down the tin. "Since you started the evening football, I do all the early baking. Every day. Five o'clock." Francis was quiet. "You're right. I didn't think. Let's split the early mornings. I'll take Monday, Wednesday, Friday." Damini's shoulders dropped. "Okay." The remarks stopped that day.

At what time does the early baking start?
Five o'clock.
Why was Francis tempted to snap back?
He felt irritated by the pointed remarks and banging tins, which hinted at anger without saying it.
What did Francis do that made the direct answer possible?
He said he might have missed something and promised not to get cross, which made it safe for Damini to be straight.
How might Damini feel when her shoulders drop?
Damini likely feels relieved and heard, finally having her tiredness taken seriously.
Gesture: what does that word mean?

A gesture is a movement of the hands or head that shows a feeling or idea. It is a noun. It can also mean an action that shows how you feel, like a kind gesture.
Example: Bringing soup to the sick neighbour was a thoughtful gesture.
I'm working remotely for the first time and I struggle to stay on track at home.
That's an adjustment. Do you have a dedicated space to work?
Just my bed.
Try setting up a table or a corner just for work, even a small one. It helps your mind separate work from rest. Keep regular hours and take breaks.
What should my breaks be like?
Stretch, drink water, step outside for a few minutes or call a friend. Avoid starting something that will take you away for an hour, like a long show.
Okay. I'll put a small table by the window.
Natural light helps. A tidy desk and a closed laptop at the end of the day will make the work feel finished.
A week in, and it's going better. But I miss chatting with colleagues.
That's normal. Set up a short video chat once or twice a week, or take a virtual coffee break with a teammate. A few minutes of casual talk brings back the office feeling.
My baby brother just said his first word and it was my name!
That's a lovely moment. Many families remember such firsts for years.
Mom says it sounded more like 'Dee', but I'm sure he meant me.
You may be right, since babies copy the sounds they hear most. Enjoy being his first favourite word, and encourage him to say it again.

Tell me in one line what this email says.

Subject: I blame you for my sleep Hi Pankaj, You told me to start that space series "just for one episode." I started Friday. It is now Sunday, 1 a.m., and I've watched nine. Every episode ends with someone floating off into the dark or a message nobody can read. How am I supposed to stop there? I close the laptop and my brain keeps going: is she alive? who sent that signal? Tonight I tried to stop at seven. I lay in bed for twenty minutes thinking about the signal, then got up and watched two more. I'm so annoyed with myself, and with the writers. Please tell me season two has a normal ending. Or don't. Actually, don't tell me anything. Tanvir
Tanvir blames Pankaj for a space series that turned one episode into nine by 1 a.m. on Sunday.

Read this:

Dear Lalit,
Thank you for the offer to join the analytics team in Hyderabad. I was genuinely excited on the call, and I think you could hear it.
That's also why I asked for one night before answering. When I'm this excited, I don't trust myself to see the whole picture.
So yesterday evening I wrote it all down. For: the work is exactly what I want to learn, the team seemed sharp, the salary is better. Against: I'd move away from my parents, who are getting older, and the role has a lot of travel in the first year. I also called a friend who works in your city to ask about rents and commute.
Having slept on it, the excitement is still there, but so is a clearer head. The pros still outweigh the cons. I'd like to accept, and I'd like to ask if the travel in year one can be discussed.
Warm regards,
Omkar

What did Omkar ask for before answering?
Omkar asked for one night before answering.
Why did Omkar want to wait one night?
Omkar felt very excited on the call and did not trust that excitement alone to see the whole picture.
What else could Omkar do before joining, and why?
Omkar could talk with family about the move and travel, since being away from ageing parents is one of the main cons.
How might Lalit see Omkar's request for one night?
Lalit may respect it, reading the calm acceptance and the clear question about travel as signs of a thoughtful new hire.

metadata.subtype: Approach: sleeps on a big offer after gathering the facts [Thinking]

messages.content: Ten children sit in a row of chairs. Tara is in the 10th chair from the left. Where is she from the right?

Answer: 1st from the right. She is at the right end: the last from the left and the first from the right.

The last from one side is always the first from the other side. Walk along a row of 10 chairs from both ends to see it.

Change "they" to "he".

They were hungry after the game. They ate three rotis.
He was hungry after the game. He ate three rotis.

Read this:

I still think about that Tuesday. I'm Rekha. Suraj and I were walking back from tuition at five when he said, quietly, “Sometimes I feel like I'm just done with everything.”
And I thought: here we go. Suraj always made things sound bigger than they were. So I said, “You're so dramatic,” and started talking about the chemistry test. He went quiet and didn't mention it again.
At seven, a message: “forget what I said. shouldn't have said anything.” I could almost see his face, like I'd closed a door on him, which I had.
It kept bothering me through dinner. What if it wasn't drama? What if he'd tried to tell the one person he trusted, and I'd changed the subject? I told Mummy everything right there at the table. She didn't lecture; she called Suraj's mother that minute, and his mother went to sit with him. The next morning she took him to the school counsellor.
I'd wasted my first chance. I nearly wasted the second.

What did Suraj say on the walk back from tuition?
Sometimes I feel like I'm just done with everything.
What did Rekha think when Suraj said it?
Rekha felt irritated and dismissive, thinking Suraj was being dramatic again, and changed the subject.
What could Rekha have said on the walk instead?
Something like "That sounds serious, tell me more," and then helped Suraj reach a trusted adult that same day.
How might Suraj have felt after being called dramatic?
Suraj likely felt dismissed and more alone, which is why he messaged to take it back.

metadata.subtype: Approach: dismissing it as attention seeking [Pitfall]

messages.content: My friend Rehan has gone quiet since his grandfather passed away. I don't know what to say.
I'm sorry for Rehan's loss. It is hard to know what to say, and that worry shows you care. Often, simple and honest words work best. Have you spoken since?
Only a little. I said sorry but it felt awkward.
That is fine. Saying sorry was kind. You could tell Rehan you are there if he wants to talk or just sit together. You do not need to fix anything.
Should I ask about his grandfather?
If he seems ready, you could ask for a favourite memory. Let Rehan lead, and if he does not want to talk, just keep him company without pressure.
I'll sit with him at lunch tomorrow. Maybe share my snacks.
That is a gentle plan. Sitting with Rehan and sharing snacks tells him you care, even if neither of you talks much.

Read this:

My name is Nikita. In Class Five I got a low mark in the maths test, and I put the paper at the bottom of my bag. The paper needed my mother Arohi's signature. Every evening I told myself, "Tomorrow." At dinner I talked very loudly about anything else. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone I had to carry to school and home again. On the fifth day, my mother stopped stirring the dal and said, "You've been quiet in a strange way. Is something on your mind?" My voice shook. I took out the paper. She said, "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together," and I cried a little.

Where did Nikita put the maths paper?
At the bottom of the bag.
What was Nikita feeling every evening while saying "Tomorrow"?
Afraid and burdened. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone Nikita had to carry.
What made the first admission easier for Nikita?
Arohi stopped stirring, asked calmly what was on Nikita's mind, and then said "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together."
How might Arohi have felt watching Nikita talk loudly about anything else?
Concerned and puzzled. Arohi noticed the strange quiet and gave Nikita a calm chance to say what was wrong.
Meaning of "shade"? Divya saw 14 butterflies in the garden and 13 more near the pond. How many butterflies is that? Correct: I am afraid from snakes.

1. A shade is a cool area out of the sun. Example: We sat in the shade of a tree.
2. 27 butterflies. Because 14 + 13 = 27.
3. Fixed: I am afraid of snakes. Why: "Afraid" takes "of".

How many decimals with two places are there between 0.7 and 0.8? Which one is exactly halfway?

Now you try: halfway between 2.4 and 2.5?
The answer is 2.45.

Kayla and Theresa went to buy some chocolate bars and soda cans. Theresa bought twice the number of chocolate bars and soda cans Kayla bought. If Theresa bought 12 chocolate bars and 18 soda cans, how many chocolate bars and soda cans did Kayla buy in total?

Kayla bought 12 chocolate bars / 2 = 6 chocolate bars.
She also bought 18 soda cans / 2 = 9 soda cans.
The total number of chocolate bars and soda cans Kayla bought is 6 chocolate bars + 9 soda cans = 15 items
The answer is 15.
Tell us a tale about a boy and his friends who build a Christmas star from old bamboo.

December came, and the boys on Church Lane had no money for decorations. Joel, twelve, had an idea. He collected old bamboo sticks and tied them into a five-pointed star with twine. His friends covered it with silver foil from sweet wrappers. They hung it from a pole at the lane's entrance. When night fell, the street lamps shone on the star and made it sparkle. Neighbours came out and stared. An old lady clapped. Someone brought a string of small lights and wound them around the star. By Christmas Eve, it was the brightest thing on the street, and the boys felt proud.
Correct this sentence: He asked me do I like tea. Could you explain what inspire means? Is "questionaire" spelled correctly?

I'm Arohi. I share a flat with Tushar in Hyderabad. Last month he decided to sell his old phone before upgrading.

He paused. He picked up the phone, looked at the scratched corner. "No," he admitted. "Maybe ten."

I don't know exactly what he felt. But he went quiet, then edited the price to eleven.

It sold in two days.

messages.content: Last night, Jim bought a $7 lamp and a bulb which cost $4 less. If he bought 2 lamps and 6 bulbs, how much did Jim pay in all?

The cost of the bulb is $7 - $4 = $3.
The cost of 2 lamps is $7 x 2 = $14.
The cost of 6 bulbs is $3 x 6 = $18.
Jim paid a total of $14 + $18 = $32.
The answer is 32.

Each dandelion produces 300 seeds. 1/3rd of the seeds land in water and die. 1/6 of the starting number are eaten by insects. Half the remainder sprout and are immediately eaten. How many dandelions survive long enough to flower?

First find the number of seeds that land in water: 300 seeds * 1/3 = 100 seeds
Then find the number of seeds that are eaten: 300 seeds * 1/6 = 50 seeds
Subtract the number of seeds that are destroyed to find the number that sprout: 300 seeds - 100 seeds - 50 seeds = 150 seeds
Then divide that number by 2 to find the number of sprouts that survive: 150 seeds / 2 = 75 seeds
The answer is 75.

Bob started out the week with $80. On Monday alone, he spent half the money. On Tuesday, he spent one-fifth of the amount left from Monday. On Wednesday, he spent 3/8ths of the amount left from Tuesday. How much does he have left now?

On Tuesday, he spent 1/5th of $40 leaving $40-(1/5)*40 = $32
On Wednesday, he spent 3/8ths of $32 leaving $32-(3/8)*$32 = $20
The answer is 20.

Daisy is climbing trees all around her neighborhood and starts to notice the number of branches and the height. The first tree she climbs is 50 feet tall and has 200 branches. The second tree she climbs is 40 feet tall and has 180 branches. The third tree she climbs is 60 feet tall and has 180 branches. The final tree she climbs is 34 feet tall and has 153 branches. On average, how many branches do these trees have per foot?

The first tree has 4 branches per foot because 200 / 50 = 4
The second tree tree has 4.5 branches per foot because 180 / 40 = 4.5
The third tree has 3 branches per foot because 180 / 60 = 3
The fourth tree has 4.5 branches per foot because 153 / 34 = 4.5
The total branches per foot is 16 because 4 + 4.5 + 3 + 4.5 = 16
The average branches per foot is 4 because 16 / 4 = 4
The answer is 4.

Tom and Elizabeth have a competition to climb a hill. Elizabeth takes 30 minutes to climb the hill. Tom takes four times as long as Elizabeth does to climb the hill. How many hours does it take Tom to climb up the hill?

It takes Tom 30*4 = 120 minutes to climb the hill.
It takes Tom 120/60 = 2 hours to climb the hill.
The answer is 2.

Monday: Deepak signed the lease for the flat near college. The landlord was his friend Bhavna's cousin. Bhavna came along and smiled through the whole thing.
Thursday: at the canteen, a neighbour mentioned the building was due for demolition in six months. Deepak laughed it off. Then he saw Bhavna go very still.

Deepak felt something drop in his chest. She hadn't lied. She had just watched him sign.
The following Sunday: he had arranged to break the lease, losing the deposit. When Bhavna called, he said, "It's not that you lied. You let me decide without the one thing that mattered. When was the building due for demolition?
In six months.
How did Deepak feel when Bhavna went still?
Deepak felt something drop in his chest, hurt and betrayed that she had watched him sign without a word.
How did Deepak explain the hurt to Bhavna?
He told her plainly that her silence took away his chance to decide with full information, and that it hurt as much as a lie.

Week 1, Thursday. Madhav starts keeping a small log: time, task, how sharp he felt, one to five. Mornings keep getting fours and fives. After lunch: ones and twos. Late evening: threes.

Ones and twos.

Move the hardest task to his next sharpest slot, like late evening, and keep the after-lunch time for routine work.

In the morning, Karan carried the finished model to school, and told the teacher, truthfully, that two people had made it.

Everyone heard that hum.' Charu, who had shared a flat with him since college, pulled a pen and a crumpled bill from her bag. 'Fine. Garbage out of ten?' He almost laughed. Then, slowly, he started. The hum in the second half, a three. The interviews with the old tailors, a nine; one woman in the front row had wiped her eyes. The edit dragged in the middle, maybe a five. The ending, seven. He rated the interviews with the old tailors a nine.

He was embarrassed that everyone had heard the hum, and after eight months of weekends that one flaw felt so loud it swallowed everything else.
What did Charu's question achieve that arguing with Mridul would not?
Asking 'Garbage out of ten?' got him to score the parts himself, so he found the strong interviews and the fixable sound on his own instead of being told.

Carolyn counts 6 monkeys and 6 birds in the tree outside her window. Then two of the monkeys each eat one bird. What percent of the animals outside her window are monkeys now?

First find the new number of birds: 6 birds - 2 birds = 4 birds
Then find the new total number of animals: 6 monkeys + 4 birds = 10 animals
Then divide the number of monkeys by the number of animals and multiply by 100% to express the answer as a percentage: 6 monkeys / 10 animals * 100% = 60%
The answer is 60.

The power had been out since the afternoon, and in the two-room flat in Patna there was nowhere to hide from a fight.

Charu sat on her bed with a torch, pretending to read. Her mother sat in the kitchen with a candle, not cooking. Neither had said a word since Charu shouted, "You never let me do anything!" and her mother replied, "Then do whatever you want," and walked away.

In the middle, on the floor, her little brother Jatin was trying to do his homework by phone light. He kept looking from one room to the other.

"Didi, are you and Mummy fighting?"

"No."

"Then why is nobody talking?"

Charu didn't answer. She felt misunderstood, and underneath that, a small shame about how loud she'd been.

In the kitchen her mother felt the same. Each waited for the other to speak first. Jatin gave up on his homework and lay down between them, very quiet.

Why was there nowhere to hide from the fight?
The power had been out since the afternoon, and the two-room flat was small.
How did Charu feel after the fight?
She felt misunderstood and also a small shame about how loud she'd been.
What small step could end this cold war?
Either Charu or her mother could speak first, even just to say sorry for shouting, rather than waiting for the other.
What is it like for Jatin in the middle of the silence?
He feels confused and uneasy, unable to focus, giving up on homework and lying down quietly between them.

messages.content: Simulate 3,600 throws of two dice and compare the frequency of each sum with the expected frequency. import random counts = [0] * 13 n = 3600 for i in range(n): s = random.randint(1, 6) + random.randint(1, 6) counts[s] = counts[s] + 1 for s in range(2, 13): ways = 6 - abs(s - 7) print(s, counts[s], "expected", n * ways // 36)

Answer: Expected frequencies are 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 500, 400, 300, 200, 100 for sums 2 to 12; the simulated counts are close to these. Output (random; one run gave): 2 105 expected 100 3 198 expected 200 4 306 expected 300 5 413 expected 400 6 486 expected 500 7 593 expected 600 8 483 expected 500 9 397 expected 400 10 316 expected 300 11 208 expected 200 12 95 expected 100

The number of ways to get sum s is 6 - |s - 7| (1 way for 2, 6 ways for 7, 1 way for 12), so P(s) = ways / 36 and expected frequency = 3,600 x ways / 36 = 100 x ways. counts = [0] * 13 makes a list of 13 zeros so that counts[2] to counts[12] can be used directly. The simulation reproduces the triangle shape of topic 7.39, but never exactly: a count of 580 or 630 for sum 7 is ordinary chance variation. Simulation is most useful when the exact probability is hard to work out (for example, the chance that 4 dice show a sum above 20).

Does "aggravate" mean "annoy" or "make worse"?

Twice.

Going to him with the error, what it affected, a correction plan for the next day and a suggested second check, even if it would have been better on Monday.

Annieka made 18-4=14 free-throws.

Do I need to read notation to learn guitar?
No, many guitarists learn by chords, tabs and listening. Reading notation can help later, but it is not required to start playing songs.
What are tabs?
Tabs show which string and fret to press, using lines for the strings and numbers for the frets. They are a simple way to learn a melody without reading standard notes.
Which is easier to begin with?
Most beginners find chords and tabs easier. You can learn a few basic chords and play simple songs within weeks. Notation can be added later if you want to go deeper.

A farmer living in the countryside has a certain number of children. One day, they followed him to the farm, each one with a bag to collect harvested apples. At the end of the day, each bag was filled with 15 apples each. On their way back home, 2 of the children have eaten 4 apples each and another child sold 7 of his apples. If they had a total of 60 apples left by the time they got home, how many children does the farmer have?

2 children sold 4 apples each which gives 2*4 = 8 apples
Another child gave out an additional 7 apples making 8+7 = 15 apples removed from the total
There were 60 apples left after these, so the original total must have been 15+60 = 75 apples
Each child collected 15 apples so there are 75/15 = 5 children
The answer is 5.

I'm Aparna. I've shared a flat with Siddharth for two years, and I've watched his evening routine.
Every night around ten, he switches off the TV and sits on the balcony for twenty minutes. Some nights he says a prayer his grandmother taught him. Some nights he reads a page from the Gita, then sits in silence. He has a notebook where he writes one line about the day.

But I noticed things. When his father was ill last year, he still sat every night. He was sad, clearly, but steady. When I lost my job, he was the one who didn't panic on my behalf.

Twenty minutes.

In Class 6 I kept carrying the wrong books, so one Sunday I made a chart. I drew a big grid on chart paper: Monday to Saturday across the top, periods down the side. Then I gave each subject a colour: Maths blue, Science green, Hindi orange, English red. I coloured every box and pinned the chart on the wall right above my study table. That night, packing for Tuesday, I just looked for the colours: two blues, one green, one red. Done in a minute. My little brother Kashish said, 'Madhuri didi, it looks like a rainbow exploded.' Maybe. But I haven't carried a wrong book since.

Blue.

Recolour that box or stick a note on it, so the chart stays true; the colours work because she can read a day at a glance.

Kashish teases that it looks like a rainbow exploded, so to him it seems funny and a bit much.

First day of winter holidays: Shankar and Wasim each build their own block tower. Both fall.

Next day: they build together but argue over which block goes next. The tower falls, and Wasim cries.

Christmas Eve: Shankar says, "You hold, I'll put." Wasim holds the bottom steady while Shankar adds blocks. The tower grows taller than Wasim. They shout for everyone to come and see.

How tall did the tower grow on Christmas Eve?
The tower grew taller than Wasim.
How did Shankar and Wasim feel when the tower stood on Christmas Eve?
They were proud and excited, shouting for everyone to come and see.
What helped them build the tower together?
Taking different jobs, one holding and one placing, helped them work toward the same goal.
How might Wasim feel after the arguments on the second day?
Wasim felt upset and frustrated, crying when the tower fell.
Each autumn, how many leaves fall from one banyan in my district?
I don't know that count, and no one could give it reliably. A local forest office can describe the tree in general terms.

Jahnavi, you asked why I'm always on my phone now. Okay. Since Papa moved to the Gulf for work, the house is so quiet. Mummy works late. And after I got 48 in the prelims, nobody at school really talks to me except to ask my marks.
Then in the game forum I met this group. Older, maybe eighteen, twenty. They're so nice, Jahnavi. When I said I was stressed, one of them sent me a long message about how exams don't define you. They ask how my day was. Every day. They remember my cat's name.
Last night I couldn't sleep, and at two in the morning someone was still there, talking to me about music. They said, 'You're one of us now, Akash.'
Nobody's asked me for anything. They just, I don't know, get me.
Why are you making that face?

What mark did Akash get in the prelims?
Akash got 48 in the prelims.
What is Akash feeling that makes the group feel so good?
Akash feels lonely at home and unseen at school, so the group's attention feels like finally being understood.
What turning point is available now, before the group asks for anything?
Akash could tell Mummy or a school counsellor about the new online group and about feeling lonely, and keep up real-life friendships like Jahnavi's.
What might Jahnavi be worried about while listening?
Jahnavi may worry that strangers online are giving so much attention so fast, and that Akash is relying on them more than on people nearby.

The flight to Kochi was delayed four hours and the gate was deafening, a cleaning machine on one side, a crying baby on the other. Jomon scrolled to pass the time. A clip was everywhere: a woman in a car park shouting at a delivery rider. Twenty-three thousand comments. Some shared her office name. His colleague Gurleen messaged: "Did you see this?? Disgusting. Tag her office." His thumb twitched. He felt that hot pull, the satisfaction of joining in.
Then he noticed the clip began mid-sentence. He watched it again with the sound up over the noise. Someone off-camera was also shouting. There was no start, no reason given.
He typed back, "Don't know what happened before. Not going to tag anyone." Gurleen sent an eye-roll. Jomon closed the app and bought tea. The board changed again: another hour.

How long was the flight delayed at first?
Four hours.
What did Jomon feel when Gurleen asked him to tag the office?
He felt a hot pull and a kind of satisfaction at the thought of joining in, his thumb twitching.
What did Jomon notice that helped him hold back?
The clip began mid-sentence and someone off-camera was also shouting, so he realised he did not know the full story.
How might Gurleen have seen Jomon's refusal?
Gurleen seemed irritated or scornful, sending an eye-roll, perhaps feeling Jomon was avoiding taking a side.
A school choir needs robes for each of its 30 singers. Currently, the school has only 12 robes so they decided to buy the rest. If each robe costs $2, how much will the school spend?

The school needs to buy 30 - 12 = 18 robes.
So the school will spend 18 x $2 = $36.
The answer is 36.

Counselling centre note, Friday.
Gopika, nineteen, second year, came in today with her friend Vaibhav, who waited outside. She said she has felt "heavy and on edge" since Sunday but "nothing is wrong". Sleeping late. Snapping at her roommate.
When I asked what she'd been doing in the evenings, she said she'd been following the earthquake news. Videos, rescue clips, families searching. Three or four hours a night. She had no family there and knew no one affected.
She said, "I feel stupid. It's not even my pain."
I told her that feeling others' pain is a sign of care, not stupidity, and that it can soak in when we can't do anything.
What I did next: we made a small plan — news once a day, not at night, and she chose one relief fund her college was collecting for. She'll come back Tuesday.

How many hours a night had Gopika been following the earthquake news?
Three or four hours a night.
What was Gopika feeling when she said "It's not even my pain"?
She felt foolish and confused, weighed down by strangers' suffering she couldn't explain.
What did the note-writer do next, and why does it help?
They made a plan with Gopika to limit news to once a day and choose one way to help, so the feeling has somewhere to go.
How might Vaibhav feel waiting outside?
He probably felt worried and caring, having noticed his friend struggling and brought her in.

I'm Noor, and last spring my friend Leela told me something on the walk home from tuition that I still think about. We'd stopped under the gulmohar near the petrol pump, and Leela said, very fast, 'I don't really feel like a girl or a boy. I've been reading about it for a year. With you, can I just be Leela, and can you say "they"?' I didn't have a clever answer. I said, 'Okay. Thank you for trusting me,' and then, 'Will you tell me when I get it wrong?' Leela nodded, shoulders dropping like a heavy bag had been set down. The hardest part came later, when our group chat asked what we'd talked about for so long. I said it was private and changed the subject. It wasn't my story to tell. Looking back, I think the most useful thing I did was simply not look away.

Where did Leela share this with Noor?
Under the gulmohar near the petrol pump, on the walk home from tuition.
What was Noor feeling in that moment under the gulmohar?
Noor felt caught off guard, without a clever answer, but caring and honoured to be trusted.
How did Noor handle the group chat's question, and why was it right?
Noor said it was private and changed the subject, because Leela's story was not Noor's to share.
How did Leela experience Noor's response?
Leela felt relieved and accepted, shoulders dropping like a heavy bag had been set down.

The school sports day was cancelled because of rain, and the hall was packed and echoing. Eshaan had waited all week to run the relay with Chaitanya. Now some older boys laughed at his dinosaur raincoat. 'Baby coat!'
Eshaan's face went red. He threw the raincoat on the floor and started to cry loudly, the kind of crying that makes everyone turn.
Chaitanya grabbed his hand. Their class teacher, Mr Pinto, crouched down. 'Eshaan, big feeling. Is it more hurt or more angry?'
'Hurt,' Eshaan hiccuped. 'And angry.'
'Both. Okay. Let's do our five balloon breaths by the window.'
They breathed together. Eshaan picked up the raincoat. 'I still like dinosaurs,' he said. Chaitanya said, 'Me too,' and meant it.

What did the older boys laugh at?
Eshaan's dinosaur raincoat.
What was Eshaan feeling when he threw the raincoat on the floor?
He felt hurt and angry at being teased, on top of disappointment about the cancelled relay.
What choice did Mr Pinto make that helped Eshaan cool down?
He crouched down, helped Eshaan name the feeling as hurt and angry, and led five balloon breaths by the window.
How might Chaitanya feel watching Eshaan cry so loudly?
Chaitanya may feel protective and caring, grabbing Eshaan's hand and standing by their shared love of dinosaurs.

Dear Nazia didi,

You asked why I picked commerce when I've always loved biology. I've been avoiding the answer, but here it is.

When the stream forms came, all five of my friends ticked commerce. Every single one. In the group chat they kept saying, "Commerce gang!" and making plans to sit together in Class 11.

I sat with the form for an hour. My hand kept going to biology. But then I pictured walking into a class where I knew nobody, and my stomach went tight. I didn't want to be the odd one out.

So I ticked commerce.

It's been three weeks. I sit with my friends, which is nice. But in accounts class, I doodle cells in the margins.

I think I chose my friends, not the subject. Can we talk on the phone this weekend? I don't know if it's too late to change.

Trisha

How many of Trisha's friends ticked commerce?
All five of my friends ticked commerce.
What was Trisha feeling while sitting with the form?
Trisha felt anxious, with a tight stomach, at the thought of walking into a class alone and standing out.
What could Trisha do now, and who could help?
Trisha could talk with Nazia didi and the school counsellor about whether switching to biology is still possible, and what it would take.
How might Trisha's friends react if Trisha switched?
The friends might be surprised or a bit sad at first, but real friends would likely stay close outside class.
The sides of a triangular field are in the ratio 12 : 17 : 25 and its perimeter is 540 m. Find its area. Fencing costs ₹40 per metre; what does it cost to fence the field?

Answer: Sides 120 m, 170 m, 250 m; area = 9,000 m^2; fencing costs ₹21,600.

First find the sides. Let them be 12x, 17x, 25x. Then 12x + 17x + 25x = 54x = 540, so x = 10 and the sides are 120 m, 170 m and 250 m. Now Heron: s = 540/2 = 270 s - a = 150, s - b = 100, s - c = 20 area = sqrt(270 x 150 x 100 x 20) = sqrt81,000,000 = 9,000 m^2 Tip: 270 x 150 x 100 x 20 = (27 x 15 x 2) x 10^5 = 810 x 10^5 = 81 x 10^6, and sqrt(81 x 10^6) = 9 x 10^3. Fencing goes ROUND the field, so it uses the perimeter: 540 x 40 = ₹21,600. Common mistake: multiplying the area by the fencing rate.

Nursery note from Nirmala, Wednesday
Today I wore my sunhat upside down to circle time on purpose. Farhan (5) noticed first, pointed and shouted, "Ma'am, your hat is a bowl!" The whole group laughed. Then I said, "Good morning, children!" in a squeaky mouse voice, and Farhan laughed until he lay down. Later he made up his own joke: "Why did the elephant sit on the chair? To be a sofa!" It made no sense, but he was so proud. I'll keep a silly minute in each day.

What did Farhan say the upside-down hat looked like?
A bowl.
What does Farhan making up his own joke suggest?
He enjoyed the silliness so much that he wanted to create some himself, and felt proud of his joke.
Why is Nirmala's plan for a silly minute a good one?
It gives the children a regular chance to enjoy and invent jokes, which builds warmth in the group.
How might the other children see Farhan's elephant joke?
They might find it funny just because it's silly, even if it makes no sense.
What does paragraph three of the report I attached say?
I don't know what paragraph three says, as no attachment has come through in this chat. Paste the text here and I will help you with it.
Why do people stand when the national anthem plays?
Standing shows respect. Because the anthem stands for the country and its people, and a shared posture shows that everyone honours it together.

Tuesday night. After the doctor named the illness, Farhan lay awake with his phone, reading page after page until his heart was racing. Nothing he found told him what would happen to him.
Friday. His brother Naveen came to the hospital with him. Farhan had written eight questions on the back of an envelope, and Naveen wrote down the answers. The doctor went through the first steps one at a time and said the rest would be planned as they went. Farhan asked about a second opinion, and the doctor said that was reasonable and offered to send the records.
Two weeks later. Farhan no longer searched at night. He read the leaflet the hospital gave him and told Naveen, "One stage at a time. I can do that."

How many questions had Farhan written on the envelope?
Farhan had written eight questions.
Why was Farhan's heart racing on Tuesday night?
He was frightened about the future, and the pages he read online gave him no real answer about what would happen to him.
What would you advise Farhan when a new worry comes up at night?
Write it on the question list, rely on trusted sources like the hospital leaflet, and raise it at the next appointment or with Naveen.
How might Naveen have felt about being asked to come along?
Probably trusted and useful, writing down the answers. He may have been worried himself too.

I'm Thomas, and I was waiting on the bench at the pool when the swim teacher noticed my little sister Noor holding another child's goggles. “Noor, those aren't yours.” Noor laughed, a high little laugh, and put her hand over her mouth. Her ears went red. “It's not funny,” he said, and the laugh got louder while she twisted her towel. I don't think she found it funny, but I can't be sure. Then he said, in a softer voice, “It's hard when someone notices. Let's give them back.” She stopped laughing and handed over the goggles.

What was Noor holding when the swim teacher spoke to her?
She was holding another child's goggles.
What was Noor probably feeling when she laughed at the teacher's words, and what else might it be?

Probably embarrassment at being caught, since her ears went red and she twisted her towel. It could also be that she was amused, but Thomas does not think so and she stopped once the teacher spoke softly.
How did the teacher's second tone help?
A softer voice and one simple step, giving the goggles back, let her feel safe enough to stop laughing and put it right.
How might Thomas see Noor's laughing?
From the bench he could tell it did not look like fun, but he admits he cannot be sure what she felt. He probably worries about his little sister. 🤍

Come closer, little one; your grandfather Tenzin wants to tell you what your cousin Trisha did when she was ten. A man near the school gate told her to come with him to see something. Trisha said, "No." She stepped back, kept a scooter's length away, and walked over to the security guard near the entrance. She told the guard exactly what the man had said, and the guard stood beside her until the man had gone. That evening she told her parents too, and we all sat and listened until she had finished. I was proud, but even more than that, I was relieved.

Who did Trisha tell at the gate?
Trisha told the guard at the gate.
What was Tenzin feeling when he heard about that evening?
He felt proud and even more relieved that Trisha was safe.
What choices did Trisha make that kept her safe?
She said no, kept her distance and walked to the guard, then told her parents, so adults knew straight away.
How might the guard have seen Trisha coming toward him?
The guard probably saw a child asking for protection, and stood beside her until the man had gone.

In the daycare above the chemist's shop in Lajpat Nagar, nap time was nearly over. Jatin, eighteen months, sat on his mat sucking his thumb, sleepy and calm. Then Ramesh, on the next mat, woke with a start and screamed. Jatin's thumb popped out. He stared at Ramesh, chin trembling, and burst into tears, arms out for the caregiver. Soon three mats were crying. The caregiver scooped up Ramesh first, rocking and humming. As Ramesh quietened, Jatin's sobs slowed too, and he crawled closer to pat Ramesh's foot.

Where was the daycare?
Above the chemist's shop in Lajpat Nagar.
Why did Jatin burst into tears when he had been sleepy and calm?
Jatin seemed to catch Ramesh's sudden upset; seeing and hearing Ramesh scream made Jatin upset too.
The caregiver comforted Ramesh first. Why was that a good choice?
Calming the child who started it helped stop the crying from spreading, and Jatin settled as Ramesh quietened.
How might Ramesh feel when Jatin pats Ramesh's foot?
Ramesh, just woken and frightened, might feel a little comforted by a friendly touch from the next mat.

Sabina, you're about to negotiate your first contract? Let me tell you about the day I learned about first numbers. I was twenty-four, a young man working as a junior buyer at a textile firm in Surat. My boss, Mr Kapadia, went to buy cotton from a big supplier, and I sat in. The supplier spoke first. "Ninety a kilo." Mr Kapadia had been thinking seventy. But after that, every offer circled ninety. Eighty-five. Eighty-two. They settled at eighty. I watched Mr Kapadia's face afterwards; he looked uneasy. I felt uneasy too, like I'd watched a trick. So the next time I negotiated, I prepared my own range from the market reports before the meeting. When the supplier said ninety, I said, "Our research says sixty-five to seventy-two," and worked from that. That's how Farhan stopped being pulled.

What price did the supplier first say?
Ninety a kilo.
How did young Farhan feel watching the negotiation?
Farhan felt uneasy, as if he had watched a trick, seeing how the supplier's first number pulled every offer toward it.
What choice in the story helped Farhan in later negotiations?
He prepared his own range from market reports before meetings, so he reasoned from research rather than the supplier's first figure.
How might Mr Kapadia have felt after settling at eighty?
Mr Kapadia seemed uneasy, perhaps realising he had moved far from his own seventy.
Message a friend to say you will be late. Keep it under twenty words and end with the word "soon".
Sorry, my bus is stuck in traffic, but I will reach the cafe soon.

So I pitched my inventory dashboard idea to Nitin sir. I'm Varun. He listened, glanced at his phone and said, "We will see." Then he asked about my mother's health. Two days passed and my email got no reply. I spiralled: he hates it, he thinks I'm useless 😔. But a friend told me the same "we will see" from her own boss meant yes-later. So I did something scary. I went over and said, "Sir, I'd like to know whether you want me to keep working on this, or drop it. Either answer is fine." He rubbed his forehead and said, "It's good, but the budget is frozen till next quarter." So the silence was not the no I had imagined.

What did Nitin say after Varun's pitch?
"We will see."
What did Varun fear the silence meant?
Varun feared Nitin hated the idea and thought Varun was useless, though the silence turned out to be about the frozen budget, so it could have been hesitation.
What made Varun's question to Nitin useful?
It asked plainly whether to keep working or drop it, and said either answer was fine, so Nitin could answer honestly.
Why might Nitin have said "We will see" and not mentioned the budget?
He may have wanted to avoid a plain no out of politeness, or been unsure how to explain the budget.

Tuition centre note, December exam season: Salma, Class 10.
Salma used to take twenty minutes to open her books. This month she arrives, puts in one earphone, and starts at once. I asked why. She has a playlist of her favourite old film songs that she only allows herself during homework. "If I want the songs, I have to be doing sums." She has kept to it for three weeks; Mohit, who sits next to her, says she won't even play it on the bus.
It is clearly helping her start. But on Thursday she did the comprehension passage with the songs on and missed two answers that were right there in the text. When I pointed it out, she took the earphone out herself.
Next step: I will suggest songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics.

What playlist does Salma keep only for homework?
Her favourite old film songs.
Why does the playlist make it easier for Salma to start?
Salma looks forward to the songs, so the dread of opening her books is softened by a treat she only gets while working. 🎧
What sensible limit does the teacher plan to suggest?
Songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics, since the comprehension slip showed some tasks need full attention.
How does Mohit see Salma's playlist rule?
Mohit seems impressed that she won't even play it on the bus, which shows how seriously she keeps it reserved.

The office pantry went quiet when Simran walked in.
"Oh, Simran! So sorry about the launch," Rekha said, stirring her coffee. "Such bad luck."
"Thanks," Simran said. "We tested it for months."
"Of course," said Mohan. "These things happen. Even to the best." He glanced at Rekha. Rekha looked into her cup, lips pressed together as if holding something back.
"Did the client say what went wrong?" Mohan asked.
"The payment page failed on launch day."
"On launch day," Rekha repeated, very softly. Mohan coughed.
Simran filled her water bottle. "I'll share the review with everyone on Monday."
"Great. Can't wait," said Mohan.
Simran walked back to her desk. Every word had been polite. She sat down and stared at her screen, suddenly feeling very small and very alone in the busy room.

What failed on launch day?
The payment page failed on launch day.
How does Simran feel as she walks back to her desk?
She feels small and alone, sensing that behind the polite words her colleagues were enjoying her failure.
What could help Simran after that pantry moment?
She could talk to one colleague she trusts, and present the review on Monday focused on what she learned, not on their reactions.
How might the pantry scene look from Rekha's side?
Rekha may feel a private satisfaction that is hard to hide, perhaps from envy, without seeing how clearly Simran notices it.

A florist is making bouquets for the weekend. The florist uses red, yellow, orange, and purple flowers, and each bouquet contains 9 flowers of any color combinations. This week he planted 125 seeds for each color of flower. Unfortunately, a fungus killed 45 red flowers, 61 yellow, 30 orange, and 40 purple flowers. How many bouquets can the florist make this weekend?

There were 125 seeds planted for each of the 4 colors of flower, so there were 125 * 4 = 500 flowers planted.
The fungus killed 25 red, 31 yellow, 30 orange, and 40 purple flowers, 45 + 61 + 30 + 40 = 176 flowers dead.
This leaves 500 - 176 = 324 flowers for the bouquets.
If the florist puts 9 flowers in each bouquet, he can make 324 / 9 = 36 bouquets this weekend.
The answer is 36.

Rekha wrote it on a sticky note above the bathroom mirror: once the toothbrush goes down, I go for a twenty-minute walk. She no longer had to decide anything each morning; the toothbrush was the signal.

Manoj stretched for just ten minutes and jogged slowly to the corner and back. On bad days, the stretching alone counted. Each week he added a few minutes, and by March his jog reached the park.

Jeevan, motivated on the first of January, paid for a full year at a gym and planned hard workouts every day. Then a cold and a crowded work week broke his streak. He looked at the calendar, felt like a failure, and never went back.

In April Manoj missed a week. He did not drop the plan; he wrote down what had happened. The evening sessions were the ones that failed, when he was tired and hungry. He moved everything to mornings, and set one rule: never miss twice in a row.

What was Rekha's signal to start walking?
Her signal was putting down the toothbrush.
How did Jeevan's plan differ from Manoj's, and what happened when each hit a bad week?

Jeevan planned hard daily workouts and dropped everything after one broken streak, while Manoj started small, treated the missed week as information, moved sessions to mornings and set a rule never to miss twice.
What was Jeevan feeling after the streak broke?
Like a failure, which made him give up completely.
What could Jeevan try instead?
Jeevan could start with a small daily walk and treat a missed day as something to learn from.

June. After another fight about Yogesh coming home late from football, his mother, Indu, sat him down at the kitchen table in their Jaipur flat. They wrote down a deal: home by seven thirty on weekdays; message when leaving the ground; if he'd be late, call before seven. Review in three weeks.

Late June, two weeks on. Yogesh was home by seven twenty every evening. Once, the match went into extra time, and he called at 6:55. Indu said, "Thanks for calling," and meant it. She was still nervous, watching the clock. But she didn't call him even once.

July, the review. Indu said, "You've been reliable. Eight o'clock from now on." Yogesh grinned. "Really?"

"Really. But the call-before-seven rule stays."

"Deal."

Indu realised that holding one rule firmly had made it easier to loosen the others.

By what time did Yogesh call when the match went into extra time?
How did Indu feel during those first weeks?
She felt nervous, still watching the clock, but also grateful when Yogesh called.
What did Indu learn about holding boundaries?
That keeping one firm rule, the call before seven, made it easier to give more freedom elsewhere while Yogesh practised being reliable.
How did Yogesh feel when the time moved to eight?
He was delighted and a little surprised, proud to have earned more freedom.

Six months after she was mugged on the way home in Valencia, Camila still took the long route, avoiding that street. She sat facing the door in every café. When a scooter passed close, her whole body jerked.
Her flatmate Dalia invited her to a party. Camila went, stood in the corner, and felt like she was watching everyone through glass. When a stranger touched her arm to pass, she flinched so hard her drink spilled. She went home ashamed.
"I should be over this by now," she told Dalia. "I'm just weak."
Dalia sat beside her. "You're not weak. You're safe now, but your body doesn't believe it yet. Willpower alone won't fix that."
The next week Camila booked a session with a therapist at the university who worked with people after frightening events. She told Dalia afterwards, "It's going to take time. But I think I can trust her."

What did Camila do when a stranger touched her arm?
She flinched so hard her drink spilled.
How did Camila feel going home from the party?
She felt ashamed and detached, like she was watching everyone through glass, and blamed herself as weak.
What did Camila do that could help her heal?
She stopped relying on willpower alone and booked sessions with a trained therapist, accepting that it would take time.
How does Dalia see Camila's reactions?
Dalia sees them as her body still not feeling safe, not as weakness, and feels caring and patient.

messages.content: If Amanda can run the length of a football field 2000 meters in length in 2 hours, how long would it take her to run the length of a 10000-meter track at the same speed?

Running the length of a football field 2000 meters in 2 hours is a speed of 2000/2=1000 meters per hour.
At the same speed, Amanda will run the length of a 10000-meter track in 10000/1000 = 10 hours
The answer is 10.

I'm Nandini. I've shared a flat with Sonali for two years, and the month after her father's surgery she changed in ways I noticed but didn't fully understand.
She stopped watching shows with me. I'd find her on the balcony at eleven with a notebook, not writing much. Once she asked me, out of nowhere, whether I thought people in a hundred years would know we'd existed. I said probably not, and she nodded as if that was the answer she expected and didn't like.
I asked if she was okay. She said she wasn't sad exactly, just thinking about how short everything is. She said she'd talked to her cousin, and was going to see the counsellor at work. She did go.
By the end of the month she'd signed up to teach Saturday classes at the shelter near the market. She came back from the first one talking fast, hands moving.

The triangular side wall of a flyover is used for advertisements. Its sides are 122 m, 22 m and 120 m. The company earns ₹5,000 per m^2 per year. How much does it earn in 3 months?

Answer: Area = 1,320 m^2; earnings = ₹1,650,000 (₹16.5 lakh).

s = (122 + 22 + 120)/2 = 132 s - a = 10, s - b = 110, s - c = 12 area = sqrt(132 x 10 x 110 x 12) = sqrt1,742,400 = 1,320 m^2 Pair the numbers: 132 x 12 = 1,584 and 10 x 110 = 1,100, so the product is 1,584 x 1,100 = 1,742,400 = 1,320^2. (In fact 22^2 + 120^2 = 122^2, so this is a right triangle: 1/2 x 22 x 120 = 1,320 - a good check.) One year: 1,320 x 5,000 = ₹6,600,000. Three months = 3/12 of a year: 6,600,000 x 3/12 = ₹1,650,000, which is ₹16.5 lakh in the Indian system. Common mistake: forgetting to scale the yearly rate to 3 months.

messages.content: Rockefeller Army Base has 3000 more than twice as many guns as Grenada Army Base, 400 less than thrice as many war tractors as Grenada Army Base, and 30 times as many soldier uniforms as Grenada Army Base reserved for its national protection. How many total war supplies does Rockefeller have if Grenada's war supplies are equally divided among the 6000 war supplies they have in total?

For each component, Grenada Army Base has 6000/3=2000 each of guns, war tractors, and soldier uniforms.
Rockefeller Army Base has 3000+2*2000= 7000 guns
Rockefeller Army Base has 3*2000-400=5600 war tractors.
Rockefeller Army Base has 30*2000=60000 soldier uniforms.
The total war supplies Rockefeller Army Base has reserved are 60000+5600+7000=72600 war supplies for its national protection.
The answer is 72600.

messages.content: Does advance have another meaning? My aunt says she got an advance from her employer.

Yes. An advance is money paid to someone before the work is done or before the usual payday. It is a noun here. The verb meaning is to move forward.
Example: The tailor asked for a small advance before she began sewing the dress.

"When the legal notice came about the rented shop, my first lawyer, a friend of a friend, said, 'Don't worry, I'll make sure you win.' I loved hearing that. I'm Trisha, by the way. I also didn't tell him everything. I didn't mention that I'd sublet part of the shop to my cousin without the owner's permission. I thought, why complicate it? Then in the first hearing, the owner's lawyer brought it up and my lawyer looked blindsided. I blamed him for a week. Later I went to Seema-ma'am, who's known for being blunt. She said, 'I can't promise you anything. Tell me everything, including what embarrasses you.' So I did. She laid out three possible outcomes and what each would cost me in time. It was scary. But for the first time I knew where I stood. We settled. Honestly, I should have started with the truth."

What had Trisha not told the first lawyer?
That part of the shop had been sublet to a cousin without the owner's permission.
How did Trisha feel when the first lawyer promised a win?
Trisha felt relieved and reassured, loving the promise, which made it easier to hide the embarrassing detail.
What made the second adviser more trustworthy?
Seema-ma'am promised nothing, asked for every fact, and explained three possible outcomes and their costs honestly.
How might the first lawyer have felt at the hearing?
He probably felt blindsided and embarrassed when the sublet came up, since he had not been told the full facts.

Harish walked out of the placement cell at four, rejected after the second round. It was raining, his phone was on five percent, and the college bus had broken down, so he stood under the shed with forty other students. In his head it ran like a train. Failed this one. Won't get the next one. Batchmates will all be placed by March. I'll be home with no job. Amma will tell relatives I'm "still preparing". Appa will stop asking. I'll be twenty-five and still living in my old room. He felt sick. His phone buzzed: Simran. "How did it go?" He typed, "Failed. My life is finished." Two percent battery. She called. "Harish, stop. One interview. How many companies are left this season?" He counted. "Twenty-three." "So between one no and a finished life, there are twenty-three chances. Charge your phone and we'll list them." The bus arrived.

How many companies were left this season?
Twenty-three companies were left this season.
Why did the chain of disasters feel like logic to Harish?
Harish felt ashamed and anxious after the rejection, so each step seemed to follow from the last even though many steps were skipped.
What did Simran do that helped?
She asked a concrete question, how many companies were left, so Harish could see the gap between one no and a finished life.
How might Simran have felt reading "My life is finished"?
Simran was probably alarmed and worried, which is why she called at once instead of texting back.

I'm Damini, Sudha's older sister. In the summer holidays it stays light till late, and bedtime has turned into a fight. Last night Sudha, who is two, ran round the bed shouting "Not sleepy!" while Amma held her pyjamas. Then Amma drew the curtains, switched on the small lamp and started the same story as always. Sudha stopped, climbed under the sheet and held out her foot for the pyjamas. I think she likes knowing what comes next.

What did Sudha shout while running round the bed?
She shouted "Not sleepy!"
What might Sudha have been feeling when she ran round the bed?
She was probably excited and restless, since it was still light and bedtime felt too early.
What helped Sudha settle, and how could the family keep it up?
The familiar steps of curtains, small lamp and the same story; keeping that order every night helps.
How does Damini explain Sudha's change?
She thinks Sudha likes knowing what comes next, so the routine calms her.

The cooperative bank branch in Satara had been tense since Monday, when Vikas and Sunil had shouted at each other over the missed loan files. On Thursday, Parveen, the branch manager, called Vikas into her small cabin first.
"Tell me what happened, with dates. Then how it affected you. Then what you need."
Vikas began with "Sunil is lazy." Parveen held up a hand. "What happened?"
After lunch she did the same with Sunil. At four, she sat them down together with the file register on the table. When voices rose, she tapped the register. "The files. Not each other."
By five they had found it: two people each thought the other was sending the reminders.

What was on the table when Parveen sat Vikas and Sunil down together?
The file register.
Why did Parveen tap the register when voices rose?
She was calm and determined to keep the talk on the work problem, not on character, so they could really listen.
What did Parveen's order of conversations make possible?
Seeing each man alone first let each be heard, so the joint talk could find the real gap about the reminders.
What might Sunil feel when the real cause is found?
Sunil may feel relieved and a bit embarrassed, seeing that the problem was unclear duties rather than laziness.

The year my parents separated, I kept smiling at school. Every day, same smile. I thought if I looked fine, no one would ask questions, and I wouldn't have to explain.
But Anjali Ma'am, my maths teacher, noticed. One day she said quietly after class, "Thomas, you've been smiling a lot, but your eyes look tired. If you ever want to talk, I'm here after school on Thursdays."
I said, "Thanks, I'm okay." But I thought about it all week.
The next Thursday, I went. I didn't say much. She just let me sit and do homework in her room. After three Thursdays, I told her about my parents.
She didn't fix it. She just listened, and asked if I wanted to see the counsellor too. I did.
- Thomas

Which day was Anjali Ma'am available after school?
Thursdays.
What was Thomas feeling behind the smile at school?
Thomas felt sad and low about the parents' separation, but hid it to avoid questions.
What did Anjali Ma'am do that fits a gentle open door?
She noticed the tired eyes, offered a regular time to come without pressure, listened when Thomas was ready, and offered the counsellor.
How might Anjali Ma'am have felt when Thomas finally talked?
She probably felt relieved and glad that Thomas trusted her enough to share.

First week of June: At the tuition centre, Yogesh sir called Jomon to his desk. “You're my best student. Just tick attendance for the three who are absent today. Their parents pay, you understand.” Jomon ticked the boxes. His hand felt heavy doing it.
Two weeks later: Sir handed him the register again, winking. The other boys in the front row grinned. Jomon's mouth went dry. He wanted to say no, but sir had given him free extra classes. He ticked again, and felt sick on the bus.
End of the month: This time Jomon slid the register back. “Sir, I can't. It's not right.” Silence. Sir's face went hard. That evening Jomon told his father, who said, “You did well. I'll speak to the centre tomorrow.”

How many students were absent the first day?
Three students were absent.
Why did Jomon's mouth go dry the second time?
He felt afraid and torn; he knew it was wrong, but he felt he owed sir for the free extra classes and feared letting him down.
What went wrong in the first two weeks, and what helped fix it?
Jomon obeyed because refusing a respected teacher felt impossible; finally saying no and telling his father the same evening brought an adult in to help.
How might the boys in the front row see Jomon's refusal?
They grinned before, so they may be surprised or uneasy, and some might feel relieved someone finally said no.
