They could agree what counts as a fair target, so neither sets impossible lists and feels bad every night.
How might Dolma feel receiving the email?
Dolma, who also keeps skipping days, may feel relieved to find someone in the same spot offering support without pressure.

In the swimming club's waiting lounge, Nandini was three levels deep in her puzzle game when the coach called her group. She didn't hear. Her friend Hafsa was already in the pool.
Mumma walked over, took the tablet and slid it into her bag. "You've missed the warm-up. Go."
"That's not fair! I was about to finish!" Nandini's cheeks burned. She stomped to the changing room and yanked her cap on so hard it pulled her hair.
In the water, the anger slowly dripped away. It wasn't really about fairness. She had just been having fun, and it vanished in one second.
On the drive home she said, "Can we make a plan? Tablet after swimming, not before. And you give me a five-minute warning?"
Mumma raised an eyebrow, then smiled. "Deal. That's better than me grabbing it."

What did Nandini miss because she was playing?
The warm-up.

On top she felt cheated and furious, but underneath she was upset at losing her fun so suddenly.
What plan did Nandini suggest, and why is it better than sneaking the tablet?
Tablet after swimming, with a five-minute warning; it is agreed openly, so nobody grabs or hides anything.

She was probably frustrated that Nandini had missed the warm-up and acted quickly to get her into the pool.
At 4 p.m. a 2 m pole casts a shadow 3 m long. At the same moment a tree casts a shadow 18 m long. How tall is the tree?

Answer: 12 m.

The sun's rays are parallel, so the rays make the same angle with the ground everywhere. Pole + shadow and tree + shadow form two right-angled triangles with equal angles: similar (AA). height / shadow is the same: h / 18 = 2 / 3 h = 18 x 2 / 3 = 12 m Or: the tree's shadow is 18 / 3 = 6 times as long, so the tree is 6 times as tall: 2 x 6 = 12 m. This is how Thales measured the height of a pyramid.

messages.content: Two friends, Hubert and Ian, are planning to have a pizza party. One box of pizza is worth $14, and a can of soda is worth $1.80. Hubert orders eight boxes of pizza and ten cans of soda. Ian buys ten boxes of pizza and fifteen cans of soda. How much do they spend in all?

The number of boxes of pizza is 8 + 10 = 18 boxes.
The number of cans of soda is 10 + 15 = 25 cans.
The eighteen boxes of pizza cost 18 x $14= $252.
The cost of 25 cans of soda is 25 x $1.80= $45.
Therefore, the total amount they spend is $252 + $45 = $297
The answer is 297.

She called me at night, at college, at my aunt's wedding. I never said no. I stopped sleeping properly. I failed a paper. And I started to dread her calls, then hated myself for it. One night my mother found me crying and said, 'Afreen, you can't pour from an empty pot. Tell Zara's brother. Tell her teacher. And tell Zara what time you can talk.' I did. Zara was hurt at first. When Papa came home from work, Yosef ran to the door. "For you!" Papa opened it slowly and studied every line. "Is this me with the bike?" Yosef nodded hard. Papa walked to the fridge, moved the shopping list, and pressed the card up with two magnets. "Right in the middle," he said. It showed Yosef that his gift and effort were valued, not just accepted politely.
How might Papa feel studying every line of the card?
He likely feels touched and loved, noticing the care his son put into the drawing.

Codger is a three-footed sloth.  He has a challenging time buying shoes because the stores only sell the shoes in pairs. If he already owns the 3-piece set of shoes he is wearing, how many pairs of shoes does he need to buy to have 5 complete 3-piece sets of shoes?

To have five 3-piece sets, he needs to have a total of 5*3=15 shoes,
If he already owns three shoes, then he needs to buy 15-3=12 additional shoes.
Since each pair of shoes includes two shoes, he needs to buy a total of 12/2=6 pairs of shoes.
The answer is 6.

Helen cuts her lawn starting in March and finishes in October.  Her lawn mower uses 2 gallons of gas every 4th time she cuts her lawn.  For March, April, September and October, she only cuts her law 2 times per month.  In May, June, July and August, she has to cut her lawn 4 times per month.  How many gallons of gas will she need to cut her lawn from March through October?

For March, April, September and October, she cuts her lawn 2 a month. There are 4 months so she cuts her yard 2*4 = 8 times
For May, June, July and August, she cuts her lawn 4 times a month. There are 4 months so she cuts her yard 4*4 = 16 times
During the entire 8 month period, she cuts her lawn 8+16 = 24 times
Every 4th time she cuts, she needs 2 gallons of gas. If she cuts her lawn 24 times a year then she needs to fill up 24/4 = 6 times
Each time she fills up, it takes 2 gallons of gas so 2*6 = 12 gallons of gas per year
The answer is 12.

Saturday night, campsite near Kasol.
We almost had a fight today. Preeti was certain the weather would stay clear for the summit tomorrow. "It'll be fine, I can feel it." I wasn't sure. So I said, "I expect it might rain in the afternoon, because the forecast shows clouds after two, and the shepherd said the same. But forecasts here are often wrong, so I could be wrong too." Preeti rolled her eyes. "Always so careful." But the guide, who'd been listening, nodded and said we should start at five instead of eight, to be down by two. We agreed.
Later Preeti came and sat by the fire with me and said, quietly, "I just really want to see the top." I get it. I want to see it too. I'd just rather see it dry.
Going to sleep now. Alarm at 4:30.
— Sabina

What time did the guide say they should start?
At five instead of eight.
What was Preeti feeling when she said "It'll be fine"?
Preeti was hopeful and eager, wanting very much to see the top; her eye-roll also shows she felt a bit impatient with caution.
Which choice worked, and why?
Sabina gave the expectation with its reasons and admitted uncertainty, which led the guide to suggest an earlier start that suited both views.
How did the guide seem to see Sabina's careful prediction?
As sensible and credible, since the guide nodded and changed the plan to start earlier.
What does "attendance" mean? And how do I find my lost lunch box at school?

1. Attendance is the act of being present at school or a class.
2. Ask your class teacher and check the lost-and-found box. You could also ask your friends.

After dinner Rafael said, "Mama, my homework is done," and went to watch cartoons. But the words followed him around the room like a stray dog. The cartoons stopped being funny. At half past eight he stood at the door of Lindiwe's bedroom with his reading book behind his back. "Mama, I lied. I have not done the reading or the spelling." His mother put down her knitting. "Thank you for telling me. I am not happy about the lie, but I am glad you came. Now get your book. Twenty minutes tonight, and the rest tomorrow." Rafael felt lighter, even holding the book.

What did Rafael say he had not done?
He said he had not done the reading or the spelling.
How did Rafael feel after saying his homework was done?
Guilty, because the words followed him around the room and spoiled the cartoons.
What could Rafael do in future to avoid the same trap?
Say honestly how much is left and ask for time, because telling the truth first avoids the guilt.
How might Lindiwe feel about the confession?
Displeased about the lie but glad that he came, since she thanked him and still asked him to finish the work.

The storm had knocked out the lights, the classroom was dim, and when the window glass cracked with a bang, Mr Ghosh turned and saw Pallavi standing closest. "Outside! Now!" Pallavi stood in the corridor for the whole period, crying. Bidisha, watching through the door, felt sure: Pallavi must have done something. Teachers don't punish good children. Maybe she had leaned on the glass. Maybe she'd been naughty earlier. "She deserved it," Bidisha whispered to her friend. After lunch the school helper came to fix the window and pointed to a big branch lying on the ledge outside. "The wind did this," he said. Bidisha looked at Pallavi, still red-eyed, and felt her stomach turn. Mr Ghosh called Pallavi in and apologised in front of everyone.

What had actually cracked the window?
A big branch; the wind did it.
Why was Bidisha sure Pallavi deserved the punishment?
Bidisha felt reassured believing that teachers only punish bad children, so a fair world made Pallavi seem guilty.
What could Bidisha do after learning the truth?
Tell Pallavi she's sorry for saying she deserved it, and next time wait for the facts before deciding someone did wrong.
What was the period in the corridor like for Pallavi?
Pallavi was crying and humiliated, punished for something the wind did.

It was night: a candle burnt on the table; Bessie stood at the bed-foot with a basin in her hand, and a gentleman sat in a chair near my pillow, leaning over me.

Question: Who is in the room when the speaker wakes?

In the university library in Prague, Vera, twenty-one, stared at her screen. Two pages of Beatriz's section of their group report were copied, word for word, from an online article.
Beatriz was her best friend. She'd been working two jobs this term.
The other groups had spent weeks writing their own work. If Vera said nothing, it wasn't fair to them. If she reported it, Beatriz might fail.
She didn't sleep well. In the morning she met Beatriz for coffee.
"I found the copied part," Vera said quietly. "I'm not going to report you. But I can't submit it like this. We have two days. I'll help you rewrite it."
Beatriz's eyes filled. "I was so tired."
"I know. Let's fix it."
They spent both evenings in the library. Vera felt exhausted, but clear.

How many pages of Beatriz's section were copied?
Two pages.
What was Vera feeling during the night she didn't sleep?
She felt torn and anxious, pulled between loyalty to Beatriz and fairness to the other groups.
How did Vera work through the conflict instead of choosing carelessly?
She talked to Beatriz privately, refused to submit copied work, and helped rewrite it, keeping fairness while supporting her friend.
How might the other groups be affected if the copied work had been submitted?
They could be treated unfairly, having done their own work while another group gained from copying.

Zainab, you young people think only old uncles fall for these calls. Listen. When I was branch manager in Kochi, a college boy, Anand, came in shaking. Someone had called "from the bank" saying his account would be frozen, and asked for the OTP to "verify". Anand was sharp, top of his engineering class. He gave it. Why? Because the caller knew his name, his birthday, even his last transaction. People forget how much they have scattered about themselves online. We blocked the card in time, luckily. But Anand's real lesson came after. He went home and removed his birthday, phone number and hometown from every public profile. He told me, "I handed them the key years ago, bit by bit." So, Zainab, before you fill in that online quiz asking your first pet's name, think of Anand. Your Karthik Uncle has seen what happens next.

What did the caller ask Anand for?
The OTP, to verify.
What was Anand feeling when he came into the branch?
Anand was shaking, frightened and probably ashamed that a clever student like him had been tricked.
What was Anand's turning point after the call, and why was it wise?
Removing his birthday, number and hometown from public profiles, because scammers build trust from such scattered details.
How might Karthik, as branch manager, have felt seeing Anand shaking?
Karthik likely felt concerned and protective, acting quickly to block the card, and wanted Anand to see it wasn't about intelligence.

Personal notes, lab section head, 9 August
Vijay has been in the lab six months. Since his report about the altered test results went to management, the team has closed ranks. Chairs get moved when he sits down. His name was left off the Friday birthday email. Yesterday someone wrote 'snitch' in the dust on his cabinet.
I have stayed out of it. Keeping my head down, I told myself. Writing this, I can see that was just silence with a nicer name, and I am not proud of it.
What I did today: wiped the cabinet clean. Asked Vijay to join me for lunch in the canteen, at the centre table. Told him I would give a statement about the cabinet if he wants one.
He said thank you twice. His hands were shaking a little.
- Sarita

What was written in the dust on Vijay's cabinet?
Someone wrote 'snitch' in the dust on his cabinet.
What does Sarita feel about having stayed out of it?
Sarita feels guilty, seeing that keeping a head down was really silence, and is not proud of it.
What small acts of support does Sarita choose, and why do they matter?
Wiping the cabinet, eating with Vijay at the centre table and offering a statement show the team openly that he isn't alone, which can shift the atmosphere.
What does Vijay's thanking twice with shaking hands suggest about his experience?
It suggests he has been under great strain and isolation, and a single act of support means a lot to him.

At twenty, Neelam had slept badly, skipped lectures and stopped answering messages for five weeks. She kept telling herself it would pass. When she could not finish an assignment she had once loved, she went to the campus counselling centre that same afternoon with her roommate beside her. The counsellor listened, said it was good she had come, and booked a first session for the next day.

At twenty-five, Payal wanted help with constant exhaustion and knotted thoughts. She checked that the psychologist she found held a licence, and after two sessions she felt she was not being heard, so she tried another, who suited her better. When she began to feel better, she kept her appointments instead of stopping. One night her friend Lalit told her on the phone that his own thoughts of hurting himself frightened him. Payal stayed on the line, asked whether he was safe right then, and they rang the helpline together. When he said he wanted someone beside him, she called his neighbour, who took him to the emergency department, and Payal stayed on the phone until staff met him there.

How many sessions did Payal have with the first psychologist before trying another?
Two.
How do Neelam's and Payal's experiences show when and how to seek help?

Neelam went to the campus counselling centre after weeks of poor sleep, skipped lectures and a stalled assignment. Payal chose a licensed psychologist, switched for a better fit and kept her appointments, and she treated Lalit's frightening thoughts as a crisis for the helpline and emergency care rather than waiting.
What was Lalit feeling on the phone that night?
Frightened by his own thoughts of hurting himself, and needing someone close.
Why was staying on the line and ringing the helpline a sound response for Payal?
It checked that Lalit was safe right then and brought trained help straight away instead of waiting until morning.

Paulo wants to get a burger meal that costs $6. Aside from that, he also wants to get a soda which costs 1/3 as much as the burger meal. While on the counter, Jeremy asked Paulo to get him 2 of each item Paulo is going to get. How much will they be charged for their orders combined?

They are to order a total of 3 burger meals and 3 sodas for Paulo and Jeremy.
The cost of a soda is $6/3 = $2.
So, the 3 sodas will amount to $2/soda x 3 sodas = $6.
The 3 burger meals will amount to $6/burger x 3 burgers = $18.
Hence, the total cost for their orders is $6 + $18 = $24.
The answer is 24.

Rain hammered the tin roof of the small flat, and Papa, Ojas, was on an important work call, pacing by the window.
Nitin ran in. "Papa! Papa! The water is coming in under the door!"
Ojas held up a finger and said into the phone, "One second, sir." He crouched, put a hand on Nitin's arm and looked right at him.
"Show me."
Nitin pulled him to the door. There was a puddle.
Ojas stuffed a towel along the crack and said, "Good you told me. Next time, put your hand on my arm, and I'll come as soon as I can."
Nitin nodded, proud.

What was coming in under the door?
The water was coming in under the door.
How did Nitin feel after Papa praised him?
Nitin felt proud that telling Papa about the water had been the right thing to do.
What did Ojas teach Nitin for next time?
To put a hand on Papa's arm, a small signal that means Papa has seen him and will come as soon as possible.
What might Ojas have been feeling when Nitin ran in during the call?
Ojas might have felt torn and a little stressed, pulled between the important call and his son's urgent news.
